Surah al-Baqarah

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim.﴾ These are names whose referents are the letters of the alphabet (huruf al-mu'jam), and for this reason they are pronounced as the letters of the alphabet are pronounced. Their final letter is pausal (mawqufah, i.e. kept in pause). It cannot be said that they are inflected (mu'rabah, subject to i'rab, grammatical case-marking), because no governing agent (amil) has entered upon them so that they would be inflected. Nor can it be said that they are indeclinable (mabniyyah), because there is no cause of indeclinability. Rather, the names of the letters of the alphabet are capable of having governing agents applied to them, so they may be inflected. You say: "Hadhihi alifun hasanah" (This is a beautiful alif). The parallel to the enumeration of these names in pause is the names of numbers: when they count, they say: wahid (one), ithnan (two), thalathah (three), arba'ah (four), khamsah (five). The people have differed concerning what is meant by them, and we will mention their differences, God willing, Exalted is He.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 2 (part 1 of 3):**

﴿Dhalika﴾ *dhā* is a demonstrative noun (*ism al-ishara*). Its form in pronunciation is biliteral, but its original root is triliteral, not uniliteral. Its *alif* is not an added letter, contrary to the Kufans and al-Suhayli. Rather, its *alif* is converted from a *yā'*. Its final letter (*lām*) is also not an addition, contrary to some of the Basrans who claimed it was converted from a *wāw*, from the pattern of *ṭawaytu*. It is indeclinable (*mabnī*). It is also said as *dhā* and *dhā'ihi*, and it indicates nearness. When the *kāf* is added, as in *dhāka*, it indicates an intermediate distance. When the *lām* is added, as in *dhalika*, it indicates remoteness. Some grammarians hold that the referent's rank is near and far: when the demonstrative is bare of the *lām* and *kāf*, it indicates nearness, and when either or both are present, it indicates remoteness. The *kāf* is a particle of address (*ḥarf khiṭāb*) that shows the states of the addressee in terms of singular, dual, plural, masculine and feminine, just as it does when it is a pronoun. They also said *alika* with the meaning of *dhalika*. Demonstrative nouns have rulings that are mentioned in grammar books.

﴿al-Kitab﴾ The word is used for several meanings. It refers to the known contract between a slave and his master for a deferred sum paid in installments in exchange for freedom: ﴿And those who seek a contract [of manumission] from among those whom your right hands possess﴾ [al-Nur: 33]. It also refers to what is obligatory (*al-fard*): ﴿Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers at specified times﴾ [al-Nisa: 103] and ﴿Retribution has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqara: 178] and ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqara: 183]. It refers to a ruling, as al-Jawhari said: "I will surely judge between you both by the Book of Allah," and "the Book of Allah is more deserving." It refers to decree (*qadar*), as in the verse of the poet:

*O daughter of my paternal uncle, the Book of Allah has removed me from you, and would I forbid what Allah has done?*

That is, the decree of Allah. It is also the verbal noun of *katabtu*: you say *katabtu kitaban* and *kutuban*, and from this is ﴿the decree of Allah upon you﴾ [al-Nisa: 24]. It also refers to the written thing, like *al-hisab* meaning *al-mahsub* (the counted thing). The poet said:

*I gave good news to my dependents when I saw a letter that came to you from al-Hajjaj, whose contents are being read.*

﴿La﴾ is a negation particle, and negation is one of its categories, which has already been discussed.

﴿Rayb﴾ *al-Rayb* is doubt accompanied by suspicion. *Raba* means he confirmed the suspicion. The poet said:

*There is no doubt in the truth, O Umayya; doubt is only what the liar says.*

The reality of *rayb* is the restlessness of the soul: "Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt," for doubt is unease and truthfulness is tranquility. From this is the report that he passed by my friend Khafiq and said: "Let no one cause him doubt concerning anything." *Rayb al-dahr* means its vicissitudes and calamities.

﴿Fihi﴾ *Fī* indicates enclosure, literally or figuratively. It may be added (*ziyada*) to indicate accompaniment, causation, comparison, or to match the meaning of *ʿalā* and *bi*. Examples: "Zayd is in the mosque"; ﴿And for you in retribution is life﴾ [al-Baqara: 179]; ﴿Enter among nations﴾ [al-A'raf: 38]; ﴿Surely you would have been touched for what you plunged into﴾ [al-Nur: 14]; ﴿in the life of this world and in the Hereafter﴾ [Yunus: 64]; ﴿on the trunks of palm trees﴾ [Ta-Ha: 71]; ﴿He multiplies you through it﴾ [al-Shura: 11], meaning He multiplies you by means of it. The *hā'* attached to *fī* in *fīhi* is a third-person singular masculine pronoun. It may be joined with a *yā'*, which is the reading of Ibn Kathir. The rulings concerning this *hā'* in regard to its vowel, sukun, *ikhtilas* and *ishbā' * are discussed in grammar books.

﴿Hudan﴾ *Al-Huda* is the verbal noun of *hadā*, and the meaning of guidance (*al-hidaya*) has already been mentioned. *Al-Huda* is masculine, but the tribe of Banu Asad makes it feminine, saying: "This is a good *huda*." This was said by al-Farra' in his book *al-Mudhakkar wa'l-Mu'annath*. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "*al-Huda* is a feminine word." Al-Lihyani said: "It is masculine." That is the end of his statement. Ibn Sidah said: "*al-Huda* is one of the names of the daytime." Ibn Muqbil said:

*Until I had clarified the daylight while the deserts were rushing, they bowed down in the mirage, veiled, or praying for us.*

It is on the pattern *fu'al*, like *al-Sura* and *al-Buka*. Some of our senior grammarians claimed that no verbal noun on the pattern *fu'al* comes except these three, but this is not correct. My teacher, the linguist and imam in this matter, Radi al-Din Abu ʿAbd Allah Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn Yusuf al-Shatibi, told me that the Arabs said *laqītuhu luqan* ("I met him as a meeting"), and he recited to us a verse from one of the Arabs:

*They have claimed that they met you in dream, but I did not increase in praise of the One who gave you forbearance or intellect.*

Other linguists have also mentioned this. The pattern *fu'al* may be a plural that is *ma'dul* (altered) and non-altered, a singular, a proper name that is altered and non-altered, a collective noun for a person or a meaning, and an adjective that is altered and non-altered. Similar examples are: *Jumaʿ*, *Ghuraf*, *ʿUmar*, *Udad*, *Nughar*, *Huda*, *Fusaq*, and *Huṭam*.

﴿lil-Muttaqin﴾ *Al-Muttaqi* is the active participle of *ittaqā*. It is on the pattern *iftaʿala* from *waqā*, meaning to protect and guard. The *iftaʿala* here indicates taking, that is, he took a protection (*wiqāya*). This is one of the twelve meanings that the form *iftaʿala* comes to have: taking (*al-ittikhādh*), causation (*al-tasabbub*), the doer doing something to himself (*fiʿl al-fāʿil bi-nafsihi*), choosing (*al-takhayyur*), snatching (*al-khaṭfa*), being a reflexive of *afʿala* and *faʿʿala*, agreeing with *tafāʿala*, *tafaʿʿala*, and *istafʿala*, the bare form, and dispensing with the bare form. Similar examples are: *iṭṭabakha* (to cook), *iʿtamala* (to work), *iḍṭaraba* (to be agitated), *intakhaba* (to choose), *istalaba* (to plunder), *intaṣafa* (to be just, reflexive of *anṣafa*), *ightamma* (to be grieved, reflexive of *ghammamtuhu*), *ijtawara* (to be neighbors), *ibtasama* (to smile), *iʿtaṣama* (to hold fast), *iqtadara* (to be able), and *istalama al-ḥajar* (to touch the Black Stone). The conversion of the *wāw* in *ittaqā* into *tāʾ*, and the deletion of it together with the *hamzat al-wasl* before it, leaving *taqā*, is mentioned in the science of morphology (*ʿilm al-taṣrif*).

(As for these disjointed letters that are at the beginnings of surahs) the majority of the exegetes hold that they are letters that are both compound and simple. Others maintain that they are names by which the letters of the alphabet are referred to, from which one pronounces the *alif* and *lām* in words like *qāla*, and the *mīm* in words like *malaka*. Some say they are the names of the surahs; this was said by Zayd ibn Aslam. A group said they are openers for attention and for beginning a new statement, so that it is known that the previous speech has ended. Mujahid said: "They are at the beginnings of surahs as people say at the start of recitation of famous poems." Abu ʿUbayda and al-Akhfash followed this approach. Al-Hasan said: "They are the names and openers of surahs." Others said they are names of Allah, oaths that Allah swore by because of their nobility and merit. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and a group: "They are separate letters that indicate different meanings." Those who held this differed about these meanings. One group said: from them is composed the Greatest Name of Allah. This was said by ʿAli and Ibn ʿAbbas, though we do not know how it is composed from them. Or they are the name of an angel among His angels, or of a prophet among His prophets, but we do not know the method of composition. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: "They are the names of Allah, the Exalted, separated; if people composed them well, they would learn the Greatest Name of Allah." Qatada said: "They are names of the Qur'an, like *al-Furqan*." Abu al-ʿAliya said: "There is no letter among them except that it is the key to a name of the names of Allah, the Exalted." It was said: "They are letters that indicate the duration of the community, and they are the abjad reckoning (*ḥisāb abī jād*), as occurred in the hadith of Huyayy ibn Akhtab." This was narrated from Abu al-ʿAliya and others. It was said: "They indicate the duration of the earlier nations," and it was said: "They indicate the duration of this world." Abu al-ʿAliya also said: "There is no letter among them except that it is in the duration of a people and the lifespans of others." It was said: "They are a reference to the letters of the alphabet, as if He said to the Arabs: 'I have only challenged you with a composition from these letters which you know.'" Qutrub and others said: "They are a reference to the letters of the alphabet, as if He says to the Arabs: 'I have only challenged you with a composition from these letters which you know.' So His saying *Alif Lam Mim* is like saying *a b t th*, to indicate by them the twenty-nine letters." Some said: "They are an alert, as in a call." A group said: when the polytheists turned away from hearing the Qur'an in Makkah, these were revealed so that they would be struck by them, open their ears to them, and listen to the Qur'an afterwards, so that the proof would be established against them. It was said: "They are a sign for the People of the Book that a book would be sent down to Muhammad ﷺ, in whose first surahs are disjointed letters." It was said: "They are letters that indicate a praise with which Allah praised Himself." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "*Alif Lam Mim*: I am Allah, the All-Knowing (*a'lam*)," and the intended meaning is "I am Allah, who sees (*ará*)." And *Alif Lam Mim Sad* [al-A'raf: 1]: "I am Allah, who distinguishes (*afṣil*)." This was narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr likewise. It was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that the *alif* is from Allah, the *lām* is from Jibril, and the *mīm* is from Muhammad. Al-Akhfash said: "They are the beginnings of the revealed books of Allah in different tongues, and parts of the Beautiful Names of Allah and His exalted attributes, and the roots of the speech of the nations." Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: "No letter among them is without including many matters around which tongues have turned. There is no letter among them except that it is the key to a name of His names. There is no letter among them except that it is in eternity and for eternity. There is no letter among them except that it is in the duration of a people and their lifespans." Others said: "Their meanings are known to the one who speaks them, and no one knows them except Him." For this reason al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "There is a secret in the Book of Allah, and the secret of Allah in the Qur'an is in the letters at the beginnings of the surahs." This was also the view of al-Shaʿbi. Salama ibn al-Qasim said: "All existence has been sustained only by the hidden and manifest names of Allah, and the hidden lettered names of Allah are the origin of everything of the affairs of this world and the Hereafter. They are the treasury of His secret and the stored knowledge of Him. From them branch out all the names of Allah. They are the ones by which He decreed affairs and deposited them in the Mother of the Book." On this view a group of those who spoke about the sciences of the letters have hovered, among them Abu al-Hakam ibn Burjan, who has a tafsir of the Qur'an; al-Bawni, who interpreted the Qur'an; al-Ta'i ibn al-ʿArabi; al-Jalali; Ibn Hamawayh; and others, and there is disagreement among them about this. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya was asked about *Kaf Ha Ya ʿAyn Sad* [Maryam: 1], and he said to the questioner: "If you were told its interpretation, you would walk on water without it covering your feet." Others said: "Their meanings are known, and the explanation of each letter will come in its place." Others said: "Allah singled out His Prophet ﷺ with knowledge of them." Some of the theologians have denied that there could be in the Qur'an something whose meaning cannot be understood. So look at this widespread disagreement, which almost cannot be contained, about the interpretation of these letters and the discussion of them. What I hold is that these letters at the beginnings of surahs are the *mutashābih* (ambiguous verses) whose knowledge Allah has reserved for Himself, while the rest of His speech is *muḥkam* (clear). This was the view of Abu Muhammad ʿAli ibn Ahmad al-Yazidi, and it is the view of al-Sha'bi, al-Thawri, and a group of later scholars. They said: "They are the secret of Allah in the Qur'an, and they are among the *mutashābih* whose knowledge Allah has alone. It is not required that we speak about them, but we believe in them and they pass as they came." The majority said: "Rather, it is required that they be spoken about, and the benefits beneath them sought, and the meanings that can be derived from them," and they differed about this in the manner we mentioned earlier. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The correct view is that of the majority. We interpret these letters and seek their explanation, because we find that the Arabs have spoken with disjointed letters in verse and in composition in place of the words of which the letters are part, as in the verse of the poet:

*I said to her, 'Stop (qifī),' so she said, 'Qāf' [meaning: I stopped].*

He meant she said *qaftu* ("I stopped"). And like the saying of the speaker:

*With goodness there are goods, even if they are noble; and I do not want evil, except that you (tā') ...*

I would be glad to translate this, but the passage as given is a fairly long and dense Arabic commentary. Here is a faithful English rendering of the full text:

Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 2 (part 2 of 3):

He meant: "and if it is evil, then it is evil," and "except that He wills," and the evidences for this are numerous. Their occurrence in the Qur'an is not something the Arabs deny in their language, so when it is part of the familiar speech of the Arabs, its interpretation should be sought and its aspect investigated. End of his words. He distinguished between what was recited (as poetry) and these letters.

Al-Zamakhshari and others have prolonged the discussion of these letters with what yields little benefit in the science of tafsir, and many of their claims are not supported by proof. The grammarians (al-mu'ribun, those who study i'rab, grammatical inflection) have spoken about these letters, saying: the letters of the alphabet (huruf al-tahajji, the disjointed letters) are not inflected, because they are names of what is pronounced; they are like sounds, so they are not inflected except when you predicate something of them or conjoin them, in which case you inflect them. Their position may be nominative, as the subject, or as the predicate of an implied subject, or accusative by an implied verb, or genitive by an implied oath particle. This is when we take them as names of the surahs. But when they are not names of the surahs, they have no position, because then they are like the letters of the alphabet, presented singly without a governing word, so they are required to be indeclinable, like number-names, presented merely for counting without conjunction.

The grammarians have spoken about these letters as names of the surahs, and discussed which of them can be inflected and which cannot, and what, when inflected, is diptote and what is not, and the detail of that is in the science of grammar (ilm al-nahw).

A disagreement has been reported about whether these letters are a verse. The Kufans said: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾ [al-Baqarah: 1] is a verse, and likewise it is a verse at the beginning of every surah in which it is mentioned; likewise ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim-Sad﴾ [al-A'raf: 1], ﴿Ta-Sin-Mim﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 1] and its counterparts, ﴿Ta-Ha﴾ [Ta-Ha: 1], ﴿Ya-Sin﴾ [Ya-Sin: 1], ﴿Ha-Mim﴾ [Ghafir: 1] and its counterparts, except ﴿Ha-Mim﴾ [al-Shura: 1] ﴿Ayn-Sin-Qaf﴾ [al-Shura: 2], which are two verses; and ﴿Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad﴾ [Maryam: 1] is one verse. As for ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim-Ra﴾ [al-Ra'd: 1] and its counterparts, they are not a verse. Likewise ﴿Ta-Sin﴾ [al-Naml: 1], ﴿Sad﴾ [Sad: 1], ﴿Qaf﴾ [Qaf: 1] and ﴿Nun, by the pen﴾ [al-Qalam: 1]. ﴿Qaf﴾ and ﴿Sad﴾ are letters each of which signifies a word, and they counted the word as a verse, just as they counted ﴿The Most Merciful﴾ [al-Rahman: 1] and ﴿Dark green﴾ [al-Rahman: 64] as two verses. The Basrans and others said: none of that is a verse.

The exegetes mentioned the restriction to these letters at the beginnings of surahs, and that this restriction was for reasons they stated, none of which is supported by proof, so I have left out their mention.

They mentioned that the combination of these letters reaches five, namely ﴿Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad﴾ [Maryam: 1], because that is the most that a bare noun is composed of.

Ibn al-Qa'qa' pronounced (Alif Lam Mim) letter by letter with a pause after each, and likewise all the disjointed letters at the openings of surahs; and between the Nun in Ta-Sin-Mim, Ya-Sin, 'Ayn-Sin-Qaf and Nun he made a clear separation, except in ﴿Ta-Sin﴾ [al-Naml: 1], where he did not make it clear.

That (dhalika) is a demonstrative of distance, and it is possible that in His words ﴿That is the Book﴾ it is on its proper usage, so it is taken as such, and there is no need to make it mean "this" (near), as some have claimed, which would make it refer to the near. If we take it according to its proper meaning, then what is pointed to is: the Qur'an that was sent down in Mecca, said by Ibn Kaysan and others; or the Torah and the Gospel, said by Ikrimah; or what is in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), said by Ibn Habib; or what He promised His Prophet (ﷺ), that He would send down to him a book which water would not erase and which would not wear out through much repetition, said by Ibn 'Abbas; or the Book He promised on the Day of the Covenant, said by 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib; or the Book that you mentioned in the Torah and the Gospel, said by Ibn Ri'ab; or that which has not yet been sent down of the Qur'an; or the distance relative to the interval between the one who sends down and the one to whom it is sent down; or that is a reference to the letters of the alphabet by which I challenged you to compose in their arrangement.

I heard our teacher, the Ustadh Abu Ja'far ibn Ibrahim ibn al-Zubayr, say: "That" refers to the path in His words ﴿Guide us to the path﴾ [al-Fatihah: 6], as if when they asked for guidance to the straight path, it was said to them: that path which you asked to be guided to is the Book. With what the Ustadh mentioned, the connection of Surat al-Baqarah with Surat al-Hamd becomes clear, and this view is better, because it refers to something already mentioned, not to something not previously referred to.

They have constructed several aspects of i'rab in His words ﴿That is the Book, there is no doubt in it﴾. The one we choose among them is that His words ﴿That is the Book﴾ form an independent sentence of subject and predicate, because whenever a statement can be understood without implied elements or dependence, it is better to take it that way, and so is our custom in the i'rab of the Qur'an: we take only the interpretation of the best aspects, the furthest from artificiality, and the most fitting to the language of the Arabs. We are not like one who treats the speech of God, exalted is He, as the poetry of Imru' al-Qays or al-A'sha, loading it with every possible meaning the wording can bear. Just as the speech of God is the most eloquent speech, so its i'rab should be taken according to the most eloquent aspects. This is said while we mention much of what they said so that it may be examined, for perhaps to some reflective people a preference for one of them will become apparent.

They said: it is possible that that is the predicate of an implied subject, its estimated form being "it is that Book," and "the Book" is an adjective, or an appositive, or a conjunctive clarification (ʿatf bayan); and it is possible that it is the subject and what follows is the predicate. In the position of the predicate of ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾ [al-Baqarah: 1] and ﴿there is no doubt﴾ is a clause which may be resumptive, so it has no place in i'rab; or it may be in the position of predicate of "that" (dhalika), and "the Book" is an adjective, or appositive, or conjunction, or a second predicate after a predicate, if "the Book" is a predicate. I say the multiplicity of predicates is not in the sense of one predicate; this is more distant, because one of the two predicates is singular and the second is a sentence. It may also be in the accusative position, meaning free of doubt; the construction of "doubt" with "la" indicates that it is the one acting like "inna," so it is in the accusative position, and "la" is in the nominative position as the subject, so the noun after it by way of predication is a predicate of that subject. The building (binā') of the state only produces accusative in the noun. This is the view of Sibawayh. As for al-Akhfash, that nominative noun is the predicate of "la," so it governs both accusative and nominative in his view. The detail of this is in the books of grammar. When "la" acts like "inna," it conveys totality, so here it negates every doubt. The fath (vowel) is the reading of the majority. Abu al-Sha'tha' read ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾ with raf', and likewise the reading of Zayd ibn 'Ali, where he used raf'; the meaning here is also totality, not from the wording but from the sense, because he does not intend the negation of one doubt alone. It is like the one who reads ﴿so there is no obscenity nor wickedness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197] with building and raf'; but building indicates by its wording the sense of generality, while raf' does not, since it may mean generality or the negation of unity, yet the context of the speech shows that generality is intended. Its raf' could be that "doubt" is the subject and the predicate is implied; this is weak because "la" is not repeated. Or its action may be the action of "laysa" so that it is in the accusative position according to the majority view that "la," when it acts like "laysa," raises the subject and puts the predicate in the accusative, or according to the view of one who attributes to it the action of raising the subject only. As for the predicate, it is nominative, because "la" and what it governs is in the position of nominative by the start, as in its state when it accusates and the noun is built with it; this is the view of Sibawayh. The full discussion of this will come under His words, exalted is He: ﴿so there is no obscenity nor wickedness nor dispute in the Hajj﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197]. Taking "la" in the reading "la rayba" as acting like "laysa" is weak, because "la" rarely acts like "laysa," so this reading is weak.

Al-Zuhri, Ibn Muhaysin, Muslim ibn Jundub and Ubayd ibn Umayr read: fihi (with a dammah on the ha'), and likewise ilayhi, 'alayhi, bihi, nuslihi, nuwallihi and what is similar to them, wherever it occurs, following the original form. Ibn Abi Ishaq read: fahuwa, with a dammah on the ha' and joined with a waw. They allowed in His words that it be the predicate of "la" according to al-Akhfash's view, and the predicate of "la" with its subject according to Sibawayh's view, and that it be an adjective with the predicate omitted, and that it be part of the complement of "rayb" in the sense that an implied verb from the word "rayb" is governing it, so it is attached to it, except that it is attached to "la rayb" itself, since that would then require its i'rab, for it would become the noun of "la" lengthened by its complement, like "la dhariban Zaydan 'indana." What we choose is that the predicate is omitted, because in the predicate of the kind of "la" acting like "inna," when it is known, the Banu Tamim do not pronounce it, and its omission is frequent among the people of the Hijaz; and here it is known, so I take it according to the best aspects of i'rab. The assimilation of the ba' of "la rayba" into the fa' of "fihi" is transmitted from Abu 'Amr, but the well-known practice from him is clear pronunciation, and it is the transmission of al-Yazidi from him. I recited it with both ways to Ustadh Abu Ja'far ibn al-Tabba' in al-Andalus. The negation of doubt indicates the negation of the reality (mahiyya), meaning it is not something doubt may settle in or be found in. This does not indicate negating the act of doubting, because doubt has indeed occurred among many people. So according to what we have said, there is no need to take it as negating suspicion and the possibility of doubt, as al-Zamakhshari did. And the words of God, the Exalted, ﴿and if you are in doubt﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23] do not contradict this, because the situation and the locus differ: there the situation is the addressees, and doubt is the locus, while here the situation is negated and the locus is the Book; so there is no contradiction between their being in doubt about the Qur'an and the doubt being negated from the Qur'an. Some have restricted doubt, saying: "there is no doubt in it" is with respect to the one who speaks it; it was said that it is a generality intended to mean a specific group, meaning with respect to the believers; and some made it an elision of a noun, meaning there is no cause for doubt in it, due to the clarity of its verses, the soundness of its meanings and the truthfulness of its reports.

These estimations are not needed. Al-Zamakhshari's preference is that it has a predicate, and on this basis he raised a question: why was the adverbial phrase not placed before "doubt," as it was placed before "the saying" in His words, ﴿neither in it is intoxication﴾ [al-Saffat: 47]? He answered that fronting suggests what is far from the meaning, namely that another book in which there is doubt exists, just as he intended in ﴿neither in it is intoxication﴾ [al-Saffat: 47] the preference of the wine of Paradise over the wines of this world by saying it does not confuse the intellects as they do, as if it were said: there is not in it that defect and flaw found in others. Al-Zamakhshari moved from the claim of restriction by fronting the object to his claim by fronting the predicate, and we do not know of anyone who distinguishes between "there is not in the house a man" and "there is not a man in the house." As for what was mentioned, that the wine of Paradise does not confuse, the Arabs described the wine of this world with that, as 'Alqamah ibn 'Abadah said:

It cures the headache, and its seeker is not harmed,
and there is no dizziness in the head from it.

And the most remote view is that of those who held that His saying, *la rayba* ("there is no doubt"), is in the form of a statement while its meaning is a prohibition against doubt. They also permitted, regarding His saying ﴿*hudan lil-muttaqin*﴾ ("a guidance for the God-conscious"), that *hudan* be in the place of nominative case as the subject (*mubtada'*), with *fihi* (in it) as the predicate. Or it may be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "it is guidance." Or *fihi* may be a concealed predicate if we take *fihi* as part of *la rayba*. Or it may be a second predicate, so that you have informed about the Book by that, and by His saying *la rayba fihi*, and then this comes as a third predicate. Or the Book is a qualifier (*tabi'*) and *hudan* is a second predicate, as already discussed in the grammatical analysis (*i'rab*). Or it may be in the place of accusative case as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*), and the verbal noun (*masdar*) is made a *hal* with the demonstrative (*ism al-isharah*) or the Book as the one it qualifies. The governing element (*'amil*) of the *hal* in these two cases is the sense of pointing (*ma'na al-isharah*) or the pronoun in *fihi*, and the governing element of the adverbial phrase is the notion of being located (*al-istiqrar*) within it. This is problematic, because a *hal* is a restriction, so the removal of doubt would be restricted by the *hal*, since "there is no doubt in it" would be "settled in it while being a guidance for the God-conscious." However, what removes the difficulty is that the *hal* here is a necessary (*lazimah*) one.

The preferable view is to make each clause independent. *Dhalika al-kitabu* is one clause, *la rayba* is one clause, and *fihi hudan lil-muttaqin* is one clause. No conjunction was needed, because each of them takes hold of the neck of the other. So the first informs that what is pointed to is the complete Book, as you say *Zaydun al-rajulu*, meaning "Zayd is the man," that is, the perfect one in qualities. The second is a qualifying clause (*na't*) stating that no doubt at all attaches to it. The third informs that in it is guidance for the God-conscious. Figurative usage (*majaz*) is either in *fihi hudan*, meaning the continuity of guidance, since the God-conscious are rightly guided, so it becomes like His saying *ihdina al-sirat* ("guide us to the straight path"). Or it is in *al-muttaqin*, meaning those who are approaching the acquisition of God-consciousness, as in His saying:

*"When any dead man from Tamim dies"*

In the Sharia, the *muttaqi* (God-conscious person) is the one who guards himself from engaging in what has been threatened with punishment, whether by an act or an omission. Whether God-consciousness includes avoiding minor sins is a matter of disagreement. Some scholars permitted that the implied meaning is "guidance for the God-conscious and the disbelievers," so it was omitted because one of the two groups indicates it, and the God-conscious were singled out for mention as an honour to them. The content of this clause, according to the grammatical analysis we have chosen, is an informing about the one pointed to, which is the path that leads to God, Exalted is He, that it is the Book, meaning the complete one among books, and it is the one sent down upon the Messenger of God ﷺ, about which He said ﴿*ma farratna fi'l-kitabi min shay'*﴾ ("We have neglected nothing in the Book") [al-An'am: 38]. Since all things are in it, there is no book more complete than it. And He negated that there is any doubt in it, and that in it is guidance.

In the first verse, then, the clause is brought with all its parts complete in reality, with no figurative usage in it. In the second there is figurative usage of omission, since we have chosen to omit the predicate after *la rayba*. And in the third there is the treatment of meanings as physical bodies, since He made the Qur'an a container and guidance something contained, thereby attaching the meaning to the material object. He used the word *fi*, which indicates a vessel, as if it encompasses guidance and contains it, in the way a house contains Zayd in your saying *Zaydun fi'l-bayt* ("Zayd is in the house").

**﴿Those who believe in the unseen﴾.** Al-iman (faith) means al-tasdiq (affirmation). ﴿And you would not believe us﴾ [Yusuf: 17]. Its origin is either from al-amn (security) or from al-amanah (trustworthiness), and the meaning of both is tranquility (al-tuma'ninah). Amanahu means saddaqahu (he confirmed him), and amina bihi means wathiqa bihi (he trusted in him). The hamzah in amina is for becoming (lil-sayrurah), like a'shaba (it became grassy), or for undergoing an action (li-mutawa'at fi'l), like akabba (he overturned it). It was given the sense of acknowledgment (al-i'tiraf) or trust (al-wuthuq), so it takes bi-. It also takes li-, as in ﴿So none believed in Musa except...﴾ [Yunus: 83]. Transitivity with li- includes transitivity with bi-. This is the difference between the two forms of transitivity.

Al-ghayb (the unseen) is the verbal noun (masdar) of ghaba yaghibu, meaning "to be hidden." The raised land is called ghayb for this reason. Alternatively, it is fa'il from ghaba, whose original form was ghayyab, lightened as layyin becomes layin. Al-Farisi does not consider this lightening to be regular (qiyas) in roots with a ya', so he does not allow it in layyin, but he allows it in roots with a waw, such as sayyid and mayyit. Others apply it regularly to both. Ibn Malik agreed with Abu 'Ali in the roots with ya', and disagreed with al-Farisi about the roots with waw, claiming that it is transmitted (mahfuz) and not regular (maqis). The full account of this belongs to the science of morphology (al-tasrif).

**﴿And they establish the prayer﴾.** Al-iqamah (establishment) means al-taqwim (straightening), as in aqama al-'awd, meaning qawwamahu (he straightened the stick). It may also mean al-idamah (continuance), as in aqamat al-ghazalah suq al-dirab, meaning adamat-ha (the sun kept the market of the striking going), from qamat al-suq (the market stood). It may also mean al-tashammur wa'l-nuhud (readiness and rising) to a matter, from qama bi'l-amr. The hamzah in aqama is for transitivity (lil-ta'diyah). Al-salah (the prayer) is of the pattern fa'alah. Its root is waw, since it is derived from al-sala, which is a vein attached to the spine that divides at the base of the tail and extends into two veins, one in each hip. They are called al-salawan. When the one praying bows, he bends and his sala moves, so he is called musalli (one who bends the sala). From this comes al-musalli among racing horses, because it comes alongside the sallawayn (the two flanks) of the leading horse.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The word salah was derived from this, either because it came as the second pillar after faith, so it was likened to the horse that comes second (al-musalli) in a race, or because the one bowing and prostrating bends his sala." Salah is a technical usage (haqiqah shar'iyyah) that consists of specific statements and postures. Salla means fa'ala al-salah (he performed the prayer). As for salla meaning "he supplicated" (da'a), it is a metaphor (majaz), and its link (‘alaqah) is the comparison of the one supplicating, in humility and longing, with the one performing the prayer. Ibn 'Atiyyah took salah to be derived from salla meaning da'a, as in the verse:

*"Upon you is the like of what you have prayed, so sleep, for a man's side has a place to lie down."*

And he said:

*"Her guardian never leaves her house through the ages, and if she is slaughtered he prays over her and over Zamzam."*

He said: "Since salah in the Law is supplication, and statements and postures were added to it, the whole thing was named by the name of supplication. The view that it is derived from supplication is better." That is the end of his words. We have already mentioned that this is a metaphor according to us, and we have mentioned the link between the one supplicating and the one performing the prayer.

**﴿Min﴾** is a preposition (harf jarr). Al-Kisa'i claimed that its original form was mina, citing the words of one of the Qudha'ah:

*"We spent the sharp spear-shaft upon them, and every keen, male, sharp sword, from [mina] when the sun's horn rose until the branch of the shade gave relief to their fugitives."*

Ibn Jinni, may God have mercy on him, interpreted it as a verbal noun on the pattern fi'al, from mana yumna, meaning qadara (to decree). Some people were deceived by this verse and said: "Min may also be written as mina." Min has these uses: to mark the starting point (ibtida' al-ghayah), partitive (tab'id), extra (za'idah, which is added for emphasis), to specify the kind (bayan al-jins), causal (ta'lil), substitutive (badal), passing beyond (mujawazah) and elevation (isti'la'), to mark the endpoint (intiha' al-ghayah), as a separator (fasl), in agreement with ba' (muwafaqat al-ba'), and in agreement with similar meanings. Examples: *sirtu min al-Basrah ila al-Kufah* (I travelled from Basra to Kufa); *akaltu min al-raghif* (I ate from the loaf); *ma qama min rajul* (no man stood up); ﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold﴾ [al-Kahf: 31]; ﴿They put their fingers in their ears because of the thunderbolts﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19]; ﴿Have you been content with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 38]; ﴿You went out early from your family﴾ [Al 'Imran: 121]; *qaraba minhu* (he came near to him); ﴿And We helped him against the people﴾ [al-Anbiya': 77]; ﴿He knows the corrupter from the reformer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 220]; ﴿They look with a furtive glance﴾ [al-Shura: 45]; ﴿What have they created from the earth?﴾ [Fatir: 40].

**Ma** may be relative (mawsulah), interrogative (istifhamiyyah), conditional (shartiyyah), descriptive (mawsufah), an adjective (sifah), or complete (tammah). Examples: ﴿What is with you runs out﴾ [al-Nahl: 96]; ﴿What is this messenger?﴾ [al-Furqan: 7]; ﴿Whatever mercy God opens to the people﴾ [Fatir: 2]; *marartu bi-ma mu'jabin laka* (I passed by something that pleases you); *li-amrin ma jada'a qasir anfahu* (for some matter, Qasir cut off his nose); *ma ahsana Zaydan* (how good Zayd is!).

**﴿We have provided for them﴾.** Al-rizq (provision) means al-'ata' (giving). It is that which is given, like al-tahn (ground grain). Al-rizq may also be the verbal noun (masdar) of razaqtahu, meaning a'taytahu (I gave him). It has been said that al-rizq is also the verbal noun of razaqtahu, meaning a'taytahu. ﴿And whomever We have provided with good provision from Us﴾ [al-Nahl: 75]. And someone said:

*"You were given wealth but you were not given its benefits; indeed the wretched one is the one who is deprived of what he was given."*

It has been said: the root of al-rizq is al-hazz (fortune). The meanings of the verb fa'ala are many, and among them are mentioned: gathering, dispersing, giving, preventing, refraining, harming, overcoming, pushing away, transferring, moving, settling, travelling, covering, stripping bare, throwing, correcting, and making a sound. Examples: *hashara* (to gather), *qasama* (to divide), *manaha* (to bestow), *ghafala* (to be heedless), *shamasa* (to shine), *lasa'a* (to sting), *qahara* (to subdue), *dara'a* (to repel), *sarafa* (to turn away), *za'na* (to journey), *sakana* (to dwell), *ramala* (to run in sand), *hajaba* (to veil), *salakha* (to skin), *qadhafa* (to hurl), *sabaha* (to swim), *sarkha* (to cry out). Here it means giving, like *nahala* (to present as a gift), *wahaba* (to grant), and *manaha* (to bestow).

**﴿They spend﴾.** Al-infaq (spending) means al-infadh (sending forth). *Anfaqtu al-shay'* and *anfadhtu al-shay'* have one meaning, and the hamzah is for transitivity. It is said *nafaqa al-shay'* (the thing was spent), meaning *nafadha* (it went out). The root of this word indicates going out and departing. From it come *nafaqa* (he acted hypocritically), *al-nafiqa'* (the hidden exit of a burrow), and *nafaq* (a tunnel).

[p. 39]

﴿Those who believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you, and in the Hereafter they are certain.﴾

Those who mentioned, in its i'rab (grammatical analysis), the genitive case (khafd) as a qualifier (na't, adjective) of al-muttaqin (the God-conscious), or as an apposition (badal), and the accusative (nasb) for praise (madh) by way of qat' (a shift from the case of the preceding noun, to a separate predication), or by supposing an implied a'ni ("I mean") for explanation (tafsir). They said: or on the place (mawdi') of al-muttaqin. They imagined that it has a place and that it is in the accusative, and they were deceived by the verbal noun (masdar), so they thought it is a mafʿul lahu (object of purpose) governed by the preposition with lam. Here the verbal noun stands in place of the active participle, so it does not govern, even if the active participle does govern. And it remained in its verbal-noun status, so it does not govern, because here it cannot be resolved into a verb-introducing particle and a verb. Nor is it a substitute (badal) for the wording with the verb. Rather, lil-muttaqin is connected to an implied element that qualifies his statement huda (guidance), meaning: guidance existing for the God-conscious. The nominative is by way of qat', meaning: they are those who, or it is as a subject and predicate (mubtada' and khabar).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 5 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful.﴾ "Those" (ūlā'ika) refers back to the previous group, and "those" (ūlā'ika) refers to the later group, and the wāw is superfluous (muqḥama). This last grammatical analysis is objectionable, and the like of it does not befit the Qur'an. The preferred grammatical reading is that the phrase is in the genitive as an adjective (naʿt), while the switch to the nominative or accusative (qaṭʿ) is either for the accusative (naṣb) or the nominative (rafʿ). This descriptive phrase has come for the purpose of praise.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read yu'minūna with a sukūn on the hamza after the yā', the hamza being the root consonant (fā' al-kalima), and they omitted the hamza of af'ala wherever it occurs, as did Warsh and Abu 'Amr when it is recited in continuous speech (idrāj) by dropping the hamza. This is also narrated from 'Asim. Razin read with a vowelled hamza, like yu'akhkhiru-kum. The justification for his reading is that he dropped the hamza which is the root consonant of the word because it was quiescent, and kept the hamza of af'ala because it was vowelled, initial, and weak in the past tense and imperative. The yā' strengthens the connection of the verb to the noun, as in marartu bi-Zaydin, so that it is attached to the verb; or it is for the state (ḥāl), so that it is attached to an omitted element, meaning "those who are engaged with the unseen, away from what is believed in." In this case the verbal noun (maṣdar) is determined. As for when it is attached to the verb, then with the meaning of the absent (al-ghā'ib) the verbal noun is used and the active participle is intended, and they said: and with the meaning of the unseen (al-ghayb) the verbal noun is used and the passive participle is intended, as in: "this is the creation of God" and "a dirham of the minting of the ruler" (dirham ḍarb al-amīr). In this there is scrutiny, because al-ghayb is the verbal noun of the intransitive ghāba, or it is by lightening from ghayyaba, like layyana, and then it would not be a verbal noun. This is according to the view of those who permit the lightening, and az-Zamakhshari permitted that for al-ghayb, but one does not resort to it until it is heard transmitted from the speech of the Arabs.

Al-Ghayb here is the Qur'an, as said by 'Asim ibn Abi al-Najud; or what has not yet been revealed of it, as said by al-Kalbi; or the word of tawhid and what Muhammad ﷺ brought, as said by ad-Dahhak; or the knowledge of revelation, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Zirr ibn Hubaysh, Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Wafid; or the matter of the Hereafter, as said by al-Hasan; or what is hidden of the sciences of the Qur'an, as said by 'Abd Allah ibn Hani'; or God, Mighty and Majestic, as said by 'Ata' and Ibn Jubayr; or what is hidden from the senses but known by inference, as said by Ibn 'Isa; or the divine decree and predestination; or the meaning of "in the unseen" as "in the hearts," as said by al-Hasan; or what God has made manifest to His friends of signs and miracles; or the awaited Mahdi, as said by some of the Shi'a; or it is connected to what the Messenger ﷺ informed about the definition of faith when he was asked about it, namely: God, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the decree, its good and its evil. We choose this, because it describes the state of the pious as those who believe in the unseen. The faith required by the Sharia is that, and this includes inward belief, which is faith in the unseen, and bodily action, which is prayer and giving wealth. These three are the pillars of the actions of the pious, so it is fitting that the unseen be explained by what we have mentioned. What was explained as iqāma earlier is suitable to be explained by his saying: "and they establish the prayer" [al-Baqara: 3]. They said: iqāma is sometimes used to express performance (adā'), which is doing it at its appointed time, they said: because standing (qiyām) is part of its pillars, just as it is expressed by qunūt, and qunūt means standing with bowing and prostration. They said: "sabbaha" means prayed, because of the glorification (tasbīh) present in it: ﴿So had he not been of those who glorify [God]﴾ [al-Saffat: 143], as said by az-Zamakhshari. This is not valid except by assuming a distant metaphor, namely that the original is "qāmat al-ṣalāt" meaning there was standing in it, then the hamza was added for transitivity, so you say "aqamtu al-ṣalāt," i.e., I caused it to stand, i.e., standing occurs in it; standing is truly from the worshipper, not from the prayer, so it is attributed to the prayer metaphorically when it is from its performer. The prayer here is the five daily prayers, as said by Muqatil, or the obligatory and voluntary prayers, as said by the majority. Provision (rizq) has been said to be the lawful, as said by our companions, but what is meant here is the lawful, because it is in the context of describing the pious. The "man" written joined with "mā" with its nūn omitted in the script, when it should have been written separately because it is a relative pronoun meaning "those who," but it was joined because the preposition and its object are like one thing, and because the nūn of man has been concealed in pronunciation, so its omission in writing is fitting. Here min is partitive, since what is required is not the expenditure of all that they have been provided, because extravagance and wastefulness are forbidden. The expenditure in the verse is obligatory zakat, as said by Ibn 'Abbas; or the support of dependants, as said by Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas; or voluntary charity before zakat was made obligatory, as said by ad-Dahhak, meaning; or expenditure in jihad; or the expenditure which was obligatory before zakat became obligatory. They said: the obligation upon a man was to keep from what was in his hand the amount sufficient for his day and night, and to distribute the rest to the poor. It has been preferred that it is obligatory zakat, because it is connected with its sister, the prayer, in many places in the Qur'an and the Sunnah; and because the opening of this surah resembles the beginning of Surat an-Naml and the beginning of Surat Luqman; and because prayer is a purification of the body, and zakat is a purification of wealth and body; and because prayer is thanks for the blessing of the body, and zakat is thanks for the blessing of wealth; and because the greatest of God's rights upon bodies is prayer, and upon wealth is zakat. The best view is that these opinions are an illustration of what is agreed upon, not a point of disagreement. Often God attributes provision to Himself when He commands expenditure or informs about it, and does not attribute it to the servant's earning, so that one knows that what the servant brings out and gives is part of what God has brought out for him and bestowed upon him. He made the relative clauses of those (alladhīna) verbs in the present tense, and did not make the relative pronoun "al" so as to connect it to the active participle, because the present tense in what the rhetoricians mentioned implies renewal and occurrence, unlike the active participle, which they say implies permanence; and the more praiseworthy in describing the pious is the renewal of attributes. He placed the object of expenditure before the verb, showing concern for what God has entrusted to the servant and indicating that what is brought out is part of what He gave the servant; and for harmony of the verse endings, and for the omission of the pronoun referring to the relative, which is understood from the meaning, meaning "and from what We have provided them." The conditions for permissible omission are all met: it is determined for the connection, it is an object of a transitive complete verb. Those who made "mā" an indefinite qualified noun and estimated "and from something We have provided them" are far off the mark, because the meaning is weak after the generality of the provided thing from which expenditure is made, so that the praise that comes from making "mā" a relative for its generality is not present; and because omitting the returning pronoun to the relative or making "mā" verbal would leave no omitted pronoun in "razaqnāhum," but "mā" with the verb would be a verbal noun, requiring that the estimated verbal noun be taken as a passive sense, because the verbal noun itself is not expended from, rather what is expended from is the provided thing. The ordering of the prayer and what follows is according to the degree of obligation. Belief in the unseen is always binding on the responsible person, prayer is binding at most times, and expenditure is binding at some times; and this is of the category of putting the more important first.

Revelation (al-inzāl): conveying and delivering; it need not be from above. "Then when it alighted in their courtyard" [al-Saffat: 177], meaning arrived and settled. "Ila" is a preposition whose meaning is the end of the limit, and it has been said that its usage extends to accompaniment, to specification, to agreeing with "li" and "fi" and "min." Al-Farra' permitted its being superfluous, as in: "I traveled to Kufa" (mithla dhalika); "and do not consume their wealth along with your wealth" [al-Nisa': 2]; "The prison is dearer to me" [Yusuf: 33]; "and the command is yours" [al-Naml: 33].

A line of poetry:
"As if my aim is toward people," i.e., among people.

A line of poetry:
"Does he water and not quench his thirst toward Ibn Ahmar," i.e., when you incline toward them, in the reading of one who reads with a fatha on the waw, meaning "you desire them." Its ruling regarding the retention of the fā' and its change is the ruling of 'ala, which has already been mentioned. The kāf attached to it is the pronoun of the masculine second person, and it takes a kasra for the feminine, and it receives what "anta" receives in the dual and plural as indicating them; and sometimes it takes a fatha for the feminine, or it is restricted to the kasra in its plural, as in:

"And I am not asking the neighbors of my house: are your men absent, or present?"

Qabl and ba'd are adverbs of time, and their origin is the attribute, and they have rulings discussed in grammar. The meaning of qabl is "previous," just as the meaning of ba'd is "subsequent." Al-Akhira is the feminine of al-akhir, the opposite of al-awwal, and its origin as an attribute is "that is the Abode of the Hereafter" [al-Qasas: 83] and "and the abode of the Hereafter" [Yusuf: 109], then it became one of the dominant attributes. The majority read with a sukūn on the lam of the definite article and keep the hamza that follows it as a cut (qaṭʿ), while Warsh deletes it and moves the vowel to the lam. Al-Iqan: attaining certainty of a thing because of its stillness and clarity; it is said: "yaqina al-ma'" meaning the water became still and what was beneath it became visible, and af'ala here has the meaning of istaf'ala, like aballa meaning istaballa.

The majority read "bima unzila ilayka wa ma unzila min qablika" [al-Baqara: 4] in the passive, and an-Nakha'i, Abu Haywa and Yazid ibn Qutayb read both in the active. It was read anomalously as "bima unazzilla ilayka" with a doubled lam, and the justification for this is that he made the lam of anzala quiescent, as Wadah made the final vowel of the past tense quiescent in his saying:

"Indeed my poetry is a fetter, mixed with flaws,"

then he dropped the hamza of ila and moved its kasra to the lam of anzala, so the two identical letters from two words met, and idgham is permitted, so he assimilated them. The majority read yūqinūna with a quiescent waw after the yā', and it is substituted for a yā' because it is from aqana. Abu Hayya al-Numayri read with a quiescent hamza in place of the waw, as the poet said:

"Dear to me are the two lit fires, Musa and Ja'da, when the blaze has lit them up,"

and our companions mentioned that this occurs only in cases of necessity. This reading is justified on the basis that this waw, being adjacent to a damma, is as though it had the damma, and they replace a damma-ed waw with a hamza; they said: in wujūh the waw became "wuqqitat" and "ujūh" and "uqqitat," so they replaced the hamza for this, since they assumed the damma in it. Repeating the relative with a conjunction permits difference in essence, which is the original meaning, so it is possible that what is meant is the believers among the People of the Book, for their belief in every revelation; if you make the relative a conjunction to the first relative, they are included among the pious, provided that by "the pious" in its description the believers among the Arabs are not meant, because the pious are divided into two categories. If you make it a conjunction to "the pious," it is not included, because then it is a counterpart of those who have guidance, not a category of the pious. Difference in attribute is also possible, in which case the waw is for combining attributes, and there is no difference in essence regarding the conjunction. The subject is omitted in the reading of the majority, and both verbs are in the passive because the agent is known, as in "the rain was sent down." Their active form in the reading of an-Nakha'i, Abu Haywa and Yazid ibn Qutayb has a pronoun as subject, said to be God or Gabriel. They said: the strength of the discourse indicates this, and in my view it is an iltifat (shift), because earlier there was "and from what We have provided them" [al-Baqara: 3], so it moved from the first-person pronoun to the third-person pronoun; had it continued in the first, it would have said "what We have sent down to you, and what We sent down before you." The relative clause of the first "ma" was made in the past tense, because most of it had been sent down in Mecca and Medina, so the majority was given the status of the whole, or what existed was given precedence, because belief in the earlier past implies belief in the later, since the requirement of faith is one. As for the relative clause of the second, it is definitely in the past, and the preposition was not repeated with the second "ma," to indicate that it is one faith; for had it been repeated, it would have implied that they are two faiths.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 5 (part 2 of 2):

﴿وبِالآخِرَةِ﴾ ("and in the Hereafter"): It has already been stated that what is meant by it is the Abode of the Hereafter, because this is stated explicitly in some verses. Some commentators understood it as the later creation (al-nash'a al-akhira), since this too is stated explicitly with this description, and both meanings indicate resurrection. He emphasised the matter of the Hereafter by linking it to certainty (iyqan), which is the clearest and strongest level of knowledge and affirmation, although in reality there is no difference in knowledge and affirmation. This was to block the metaphorical use of "knowledge" (ilm) to mean mere opinion (zann). He thus stated that belief and knowledge concerning the Hereafter can only be certainty (iyqan), which is not mixed with any doubt or uncertainty. He varied the wording between belief in what was sent down and belief in the Hereafter in order to avoid the burden of repetition. Certainty was specifically attached to the Hereafter because of the many strange matters related to it: the eternal reward and punishment prepared in it, the detailed kinds of bliss and torment, the creation of its people in a manner different from worldly creation, and the vision of God, may He be exalted. Thus the Hereafter is stranger in matters of belief in the unseen than the revealed Book, and therefore it was specifically linked with the word iyqan. Also, what was sent down to the Messenger is witnessed or is like what is witnessed, whereas the Hereafter is purely unseen, so it was appropriate to link certainty to what is purely unseen.

They said: iyqan is knowledge that is newly acquired, whether it is necessary (daruri) or inferred through reasoning (istidlali). For this reason, the Creator, may He be exalted, is not described with it, because "certain" (muqin) is not among His attributes. The prepositional phrase (bi-l-akhira) was placed first for emphasis and to match the endings of the verse.

The statement of this sentence in nominal form (ism) rather than verbal form, although it is coordinated with a verbal sentence, is more emphatic in reporting that these people have certainty, because your saying "Zayd did it" (zaydun fa'ala) is more emphatic than "did Zayd" (fa'ala zaydun). This is because the noun is repeated in the speech as a pronoun, and because placing it at the beginning as a subject (mubtada') indicates concern with the one about whom the judgement is made, just as placing the verb first indicates concern with what is judged.

He used the word hum in His saying ﴿هم يُوقِنُونَ﴾ ("they are certain") [al-Baqara: 4], but did not use the word hum in His saying ﴿ومِمّا رَزَقْناهم يُنْفِقُونَ﴾ ("and from what We have provided them they spend") [al-Baqara: 3], because describing their certainty concerning the Hereafter is higher than describing them as spending, so the former needed emphasis and the latter did not need it. Also, if He had mentioned hum there, it would have caused a verbal awkwardness, since it would have been: "and from what We provided them, they (hum) spend."

﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ ("those"): It is a demonstrative pronoun (ism isharah) for the plural that is common to the masculine and the feminine. The well-known view among our companions is that it is for the farthest degree of distance, like awla laka. Some said it is for the middle degree, analogising it to dha, since they added to the middle form only the particle of address, unlike awla laka. This view is weakened by the fact that the particle of alerting (ha al-tanbih) does not enter upon it. They wrote it with a waw to distinguish it from ilayka, and it was made indeclinable (mabni) because it requires a present person to whom it points, and it was vowelled with a damma because of the meeting of two unvowelled letters (iltiqa' al-sakinayn), and with a kasra according to the original form of the meeting of the two.

﴿الفَلاحُ﴾ ("success"): It is winning and attaining the desired goal, or survival. It has been said that its original meaning is splitting and cutting. The poet said:

"Indeed, iron is made successful (yuflah) by iron."

In its sharing the meaning of splitting, it shares the first and middle letters with words such as falā, falaqa and faladha, as mentioned in the discussion of the grammatical analysis of ﴿الَّذِينَ يُؤْمِنُونَ بِالغَيْبِ﴾ ("who believe in the unseen") [al-Baqara: 3]. Among the two ways of reading its nominative case is that it is a subject (mubtada'). According to this, ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ together with what follows it is a subject and predicate, in the position of the predicate of alladhina. It is also permissible that it be an apposition (badal) or an explicative apposition (atf bayan). A descriptive adjective (sifa) is ruled out because it is more definite. In that case, the predicate of alladhina is His saying ﴿عَلى هُدًى﴾ ("upon guidance"). If the nominative of alladhina is the predicate of an omitted subject, or if it is in the genitive or accusative, then ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ is a subject whose predicate is ﴿عَلى هُدًى﴾. It has already been stated that we do not prefer the first possibility, because it detaches the phrase from what precedes it and treats it as a new sentence (istīnaf), while its connection to what precedes it and its dependence on it are clear. What is the benefit of forced and strained interpretation for a resumption when the connection with what precedes it is obvious?

Al-Zamakhshari explained the resumptive reading by saying that when He mentioned that the Book was specific to the God-conscious (muttaqun) by being guidance for them, a questioner could ask: "What is the matter with the God-conscious, that they are specified with this?" So it was answered that those who combined these noble attributes of belief in the unseen, establishing the prayer, spending, belief in what was sent down, and certainty concerning the Hereafter, are upon guidance in this world, and are those who attain success in the next. Then he illustrated this resumption that he had established with his saying: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) loved the Ansar, who fought before him and removed distress from his face. Those are worthy of love." He meant that he resumed and began with the description of the God-conscious, just as he resumed with the description of the Ansar.

According to what we have chosen of the connection, He has described the God-conscious with praiseworthy attributes that surpass all aspects of piety. Then He pointed to them and informed that whoever attains these noble attributes is upon guidance, and he is the successful one. The sense of elevation (isti'la') conveyed by His saying ﴿عَلى هُدًى﴾ is a metaphor, in which the meaning is treated as if it were a physical place. Because their firm establishment in guidance is strong, they are treated as if they had mounted it, just as you say "So-and-so is upon the truth." This firm establishment in guidance was achieved for them only through the attributes mentioned, which are contained in the description of the guidance as "from their Lord," meaning existing from their Lord, as an exaltation of the guidance they are upon.

The relevance of mentioning the Lord here is clear: because He is their Lord, in whichever of its interpretations you explain it, it is fitting that He prepare for them the means of both felicities, the worldly and the otherworldly. So He made them upon guidance in this world, and in the Hereafter they are the successful ones. It is possible that there is an omitted adjective, meaning "upon guidance" (of a particular kind), and omitting an adjective when the meaning is understood is permissible. It may also be unnecessary to posit an adjective, because mere guidance attributed to God, may He be exalted, is sufficient. The preposition min is either for the beginning of the limit (ibtida' al-ghaya) or partitive (tab'id), with an omitted noun, meaning "from the guidance of their Lord."

Ibn Hurmuz read ﴿مِن رَبِّهم﴾ with a damma on the ha'. Likewise, all similar plurals such as ﴿آتٍ﴾ (coming), are read in their original form for the masculine and feminine plural, without considering whether a kasra or a ya' precedes them.

When He reported about them two different predicates, He repeated ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ so that each predicate would fall into an independent sentence. This is more emphatic in praise, because the predicate becomes built upon a subject. These two predicates are the outcomes of the preceding attributes, because some of those attributes relate to worldly matters and some relate to the matters of the Hereafter. So He reported about them that they have firm establishment in guidance in this world, and success in the Hereafter.

Since the two predicates differ, as we have mentioned, He used the conjunctive particle with the second subject. If the second predicate had the same meaning as the first, He would not have introduced the conjunction, because a thing is not coordinated with itself. Do you not see His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿أُولَئِكَ هُمُ الغافِلُونَ﴾ ("those are the heedless") [al-A'raf: 179], after His saying ﴿أُولَئِكَ كالأنْعامِ﴾ ("those are like cattle") [al-A'raf: 179]? How did it come without a conjunction, because the two predicates of the two subjects agree in meaning?

It is possible that hum is a separating pronoun (fasl) or an apposition (badal), so that al-muflihun is the predicate of ulā'ika. Or the subject is "hum" and al-muflihun is its predicate, and the sentence ﴿هُمُ المُفْلِحُونَ﴾ ("they are the successful ones") is in the position of the predicate of ulā'ika. The rules of the separating pronoun and the wisdom of its use are mentioned in the books of grammar. The rules of the separating pronoun have been compiled, stripped of evidence, in about six folios, but inserting huwa in such a construction is better, because it is a place of emphasis and it removes the suspicion of one who doubts the predicate of the subject or disputes it, or one who imagines that it is shared. Do you not see His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿وأنَّهُ هو أضْحَكَ وأبْكى﴾ ("and that it is He who makes laugh and makes weep") [al-Najm: 43], ﴿وأنَّهُ هو أماتَ وأحْيا﴾ ("and that it is He who causes death and gives life") [al-Najm: 44], ﴿وأنَّهُ هو أغْنى وأقْنى﴾ ("and that it is He who enriches and grants possessions") [al-Najm: 48], and His saying: ﴿وأنَّهُ خَلَقَ الزَّوْجَيْنِ الذَّكَرَ والأُنْثى﴾ ("and that He created the pairs, the male and the female") [al-Najm: 45], ﴿وأنَّهُ أهْلَكَ عادًا الأُولى﴾ ("and that He destroyed the first 'Ad") [al-Najm: 50]. How He affirmed huwa as an indication of what was mentioned, but did not use it in the attribution of the creation of the pairs and the destruction of 'Ad, because it is not imagined that this is attributed to anyone other than God, may He be exalted, nor that anyone shares in it. As for making laugh, making weep, causing death, giving life, enriching and granting possessions, someone may claim these, or claim a share in them, such as an insolent liar like Numrud (Nimrod).

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿وأنَّهُ هو رَبُّ الشِّعْرى﴾ ("and that it is He who is the Lord of Sirius") [al-Najm: 49], the insertion of huwa is to inform that God is the Lord of this star, even though He is the Lord of everything, because this star was worshipped besides God and taken as a deity. So He brought it to alert that God alone is the Lord of this worshipped object, and no one besides Him shares with Him in that.

The alif and lam in al-muflihun are for definiteness of reference, either external (al-'ahd fi al-kharij) or mental (al-'ahd fi al-dhihn). That is because when you say "Zayd al-muntaliq" (Zayd, the one who departs), the addressee knows the existence of a person from whom departure proceeds, and knows Zayd but does not know the attribution of departure to him, while you know all of that. So you say to him "Zayd al-muntaliq," and this informs him of the attribution he did not know. If you say "Zayd huwa al-muntaliq" (Zayd is the one who departs), you insert huwa to emphasise the attribution. You only emphasise the attribution when you suspect that the addressee doubts it, or disputes it, or imagines that it is shared.

The exegetes mentioned, regarding the occasion of revelation of these verses from His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿الم﴾ ("Alif Lam Mim") [al-Baqara: 1] to His saying ﴿المُفْلِحُونَ﴾ ("the successful ones"), several views. One of them: they were revealed concerning the believers among the People of the Book only, and not others. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and a group. The second: they were revealed concerning all believers. This was said by Mujahid.

They mentioned among the kinds of eloquence in this verse several types. (First): the excellence of the opening, in that He began with something having obscurity and subtlety, to alert the listener to reflection, thought and deduction. (Second): the demonstrative in His saying "dhalika" (that), where the particle of distance (lam) was introduced to indicate the distance of rank. (Third): the transformed mode of address in His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿لا رَيْبَ فِيهِ﴾ ("there is no doubt in it") [al-Baqara: 2]: its form is declarative but its meaning is imperative, and this discussion has already passed. (Fourth): the restriction (ikhtisas) in His saying ﴿هُدًى لِلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾ ("guidance for the God-conscious") [al-Baqara: 2]. (Fifth): repetition in His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿يُؤْمِنُونَ بِالغَيْبِ﴾ ("they believe in the unseen") [al-Baqara: 3], ﴿يُؤْمِنُونَ بِما أُنْزِلَ إلَيْكَ﴾ ("they believe in what has been sent down to you") [al-Baqara: 4], and in His saying "alladhina" (those who). If the described subject is one, it is repetition of word and meaning. If it is different, it is repetition of word without meaning. Among the repetitions is ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ and ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾. (Sixth): emphasis of the explicit by the pronoun, in His saying ﴿وأُولَئِكَ هُمُ المُفْلِحُونَ﴾ ("and those are the successful ones") and in His saying ﴿هم يُوقِنُونَ﴾ ("they are certain") [al-Baqara: 4]. (Seventh): ellipsis (hadhf), which occurs in several places. One of them is these letters, "Alif Lam Mim," according to those who estimate it as such, and it is "guidance," and "they spend" in obedience, and "what has been sent down to you" meaning the Qur'an, and "before you," meaning before your sending or before the sending down, and "in the Hereafter," meaning in the requital of the Hereafter, and "they are certain of the return to it," and "upon guidance," meaning the causes of guidance, or "upon a light of guidance," and "the successful ones," meaning those who remain in the bliss of the Hereafter.
