**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 10 (part 1 of 4):**

﴿In their hearts is a disease, so Allah increased their disease. And for them is a painful punishment because they used to lie.﴾

*Al-maraD* (disease): the verbal noun of *marida*. In the language it is used for weakness and lethargy, and from this it is said: "So-and-so *yumrid al-hadith*," meaning he corrupts it and weakens it. Ibn 'Arafa said: *al-maraD* in the heart is lethargy towards the truth; in the body, lethargy of the limbs; in the eye, lethargy of sight. It is also used to mean darkness, as in the poet's words:

*In a night that was diseased on every side, so that no star or moon could perceive it.*

It is also said that *al-maraD* is corruption. The lexicographers said: *al-maraD*, *al-alam* (pain) and *al-waja'* (ache) are synonyms.

*Al-ziyada* (increase): its verb is transitive to two objects, following the pattern of *a'ta* and *kasa*, though it may be used intransitively, as in *zada al-mal* (the wealth increased).

*Alim* (painful): a *fa'il* form derived from *al-alam*, in the sense of *mufil* (causing pain), like *al-sami'* in the sense of *al-musmi'* (one who causes hearing), or it is for intensification, and its original form is *alam*.

*Kana* (was): a verb that enters upon the subject and predicate under the conditions mentioned in grammar. It indicates the time of the content of the sentence only, or indicates it together with *al-sayyura* (becoming). It is called *naqisa* (defective), and it suffices with a nominative noun. Sometimes it is an intransitive verb and sometimes a transitive one, in the sense of *kafala* (to take charge of) or *gazala* (to spin): *kuntu al-sabiyya kafaltuhu* (I was the child, I took charge of him), and *kuntu al-suf gazaltuhu* (I was the wool, I spun it). This is one of the rare usages. It may also be used as a redundant element with no subject in that case, contrary to the view of Abu Sa'id. Its rulings are fully treated in grammar.

*Al-takdhib* (lying, calling a lie): the verbal noun of *kadhdhaba*, and the doubling in it is for attributing the thing to someone, as in your saying *shajja'tuhu* and *jabbantuhu*, meaning I attributed to him courage and cowardice. This is one of the meanings for which the form *fa''ala* comes, and there are fourteen: attribution (*al-rami*), making transitive (*al-ta'diya*), intensification (*al-takthir*), making into a state (*al-ja'l 'ala sifa*), naming (*al-tasmiya*), supplication for or against something (*al-du'a' lil-shay' aw 'alayhi*), standing over something (*al-qiyam 'ala al-shay'*), removal (*al-izala*), directing towards (*al-tawajjuh*), abbreviation of narration (*ikhtisar al-hikaya*), agreement with *tafa''ala* and *fa''ala* (*muwafaqat tafa''ala wa fa''ala*), and being independent of both. Examples: *jabbantuhu*, *farraHtuhu*, *kaththartuhu*, *fattartuhu*, *fassaqtuhu*, *saqqaytuhu*, *'aqqartuhu*, *marraDtuhu*, *qadhdhaytu 'aynahu*, *shawwaqa*, *amman* (he said "Amin"), *walla* (agreeing with *tawalla*), *qaddara* (agreeing with *qadara*), *hammara* (he spoke the language of Himyar), and *'arrada* in battle. As for lying (*al-kadhib*), its discussion will come.

﴿Because of what was mentioned, the Book is guidance for them﴾: and they are the God-fearing (*al-muttaqun*) who combined the characteristics of faith, from sincere reliance (*al-i'timad*), and the characteristics of Islam, from bodily and financial acts. This was mentioned together with what their affair leads to in this world, namely guidance, and in the Hereafter, namely success (*al-falah*).

Then He followed this with their counterparts among the disbelievers, those upon whose hearts a seal was set by their not believing, and for whom was sealed what they will arrive at of punishment in the Fires.

A third category remained: those who displayed Islam in speech while concealing disbelief in belief. They are the hypocrites (*al-munafiqun*), and He began to mention some of their conditions.

The *min* in His saying ﴿And among the people﴾ is partitive (*li al-tab'id*). Whoever held that it is explanatory of the kind (*li bayan al-jins*) is further from the truth, because nothing ambiguous had preceded it that would require its kind to be specified.

The *alif* and *lam* in *al-nas* (the people) are for the kind (*li al-jins*) or for a previously known reference (*li al-'ahd*). So it is as if He said: "And among the disbelievers previously mentioned, there are those who say," and it is not to be imagined that they are not among those upon whose hearts a seal has been set. This is what al-Zamakhshari held, when he said: "If you ask: how do they make some of those and the hypocrites not sealed upon their hearts?" And he answered: disbelief gathered both groups and made them one kind, and the hypocrites being one of the two types of this kind, different from the other type by an addition they added to disbelief, which gathers them both, namely deception and mockery, does not remove them from being a part of the kind. End of quote. This is because the hypocrites are included in the characteristics mentioned for the disbelievers: the sameness of warning and its absence, their not believing, their having a seal upon their hearts and upon their hearing, a covering upon their sight, and the report that for them is a great punishment. So they are included in the general reference to "those who disbelieved," and they added that they claimed faith, and Allah refuted them in their claim. The explanation of this will come.

**(Continued in the next section)**

Our teacher, the imam Alam al-Din Abu Muhammad Abd al-Karim ibn Ali ibn Umar al-Ansari al-Andalusi by origin, al-Misri by birth and upbringing, known as Ibn Bint al-Iraqi, may God have mercy on him, mentioned that there is one place in the Qur'an where the construction begins with agreement with the meaning (al-haml ʿala al-maʿna) and then is followed by agreement with the wording (al-haml ʿala al-lafẓ). This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say: what is in the wombs of these livestock is exclusively for our males and forbidden to our wives﴾ [al-Anʿam: 139]. The discussion of this will come in its place, God willing.

Some have cited the reading of one who recited, in the irregular reading (shādhdh): wa-inna minkum la-man layubaṭṭiʾanna, with a ḍamma on the hamza, imagining that it is among what begins with agreement with the meaning. The discussion of it will come in its place.

The Kufans (al-Kūfiyyūn, the grammarians of Kufa) do not permit joining the two clauses except with a separator between them, while the Basrans (al-Baṣriyyūn, the grammarians of Basra) did not regard the separator as a requirement. Ibn ʿUṣfūr said: "Transmission has come only with the separator, as the Kufans held." But that is not correct. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say: none will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾ [al-Baqara: 111]? Here agreement with the wording is applied in kāna, since the pronoun is singular, while the predicate comes in agreement with the meaning, since it came in the plural, and there is no separator between the two clauses. Most such cases came with a separator only because it removes the discomfort of dissonance that arises between the two clauses.

The reading of the majority is yukhādiʿūna Allāh, the imperfect of khādaʿa (to deceive). ʿAbd Allāh and Abū Ḥayāt read yakhdaʿūna Allāh, the imperfect of the unaugmented khadaʿa. The words ﴿they deceive God﴾ [al-Baqara: 9] may be an independent new sentence (mustaʾnaf), as if a questioner asks: "Why do they make a show of belief while they are not believers in reality?" So it is said: "They deceive." It may also be a substitute (badal) for the phrase "they say: we believe," and this would be an explanation, because their saying "we believe" while they are not believers in reality is deception. Thus it is a verb substituted for a verb, since it has the same meaning. In both cases the clause has no place in terms of iʿrāb (grammatical analysis). It may also be in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), the subject of which is the concealed pronoun in yaqūlu, meaning: "And among the people is one who says: we believe, while deceiving God and those who believe." Abū al-Baqāʾ permitted it to be a circumstantial clause, with the governing element being the active participle which is bi-muʾminīn, and the subject of the circumstance being the concealed pronoun in the active participle. This is an incorrect analysis, because the negative particle, when it enters upon the clause, negates the attribution of belief to them. When you qualify that attribution with a circumstance, the negation applies to that circumstance, which is the qualifier, and so it negates it. There are two ways of this in the Arabic language. The first, and it is the more common, is that only that qualifier is negated, and in that case the governing element of that qualifier has been established. So when you say: "Zayd did not come laughing," its meaning is the negation of laughter, and he has come without laughing. But the meaning of the verse is not like this, since it does not negate deception from them only while affirming belief for them without deception. Rather, the meaning is: the belief is negated from them absolutely. The second way, which is less common, is that the qualifier is negated and the governing element of it is also negated, as if he said in the previous example: "Zayd did not come and did not laugh," meaning there was no coming from him and no laughing. But the meaning of the verse is not like this, since what is intended is not the negation of belief from them and the negation of deception.

It is strange that Abū al-Baqāʾ, how did he notice something of this and so prohibited that yukhādiʿūna be in the position of a qualifier (ṣifa), saying: "It cannot be in the genitive position as a qualifier of muʾminīn, because that would require the negation of their deception, whereas the meaning is the affirmation of deception." End of his words. Thus he permitted it as a circumstance and did not permit it as a qualifier, though the two are equal, and there is no difference between the circumstance and the qualifier in this matter. Rather, each of them is a qualifier to which negation applies. God, exalted is He, is the All-Knowing, from whom nothing is hidden.

So the hypocrites' deceiving of God is, in terms of its outward form and not its meaning, in respect of their making a show of belief while concealing disbelief; this was said by a group. Or it is in terms of their not knowing God and His attributes, so they thought that He was one who could be deceived. The first interpretation is metaphorical (majāz), and the second is literal (ḥaqīqa). Or it may be by omitting a modifier (muḍāf), meaning: they deceive the Messenger of God ﷺ and those who believe. Sometimes the omitted element is intended and sometimes it is not intended; rather, their deception of the Messenger of God ﷺ is treated as being in the position of deception of God, so it came as: yukhādiʿūna Allāh. This interpretation was stated by al-Ḥasan and al-Zajjāj. When the attribution of their deception to God, exalted is He, is correct by the modes we have mentioned, as we have mentioned, there is no necessity to hold that the word (ism) is superfluous (muqḥam), because the meaning would be: they deceive those who believe, as al-Zamakhsharī held, and he said: "It is of the type: 'Zayd's generosity pleased me' (aʿjabanī Zayd wa-karamuhu), meaning: 'the generosity of Zayd pleased me,' and the mention of Zayd is a preparation for the mention of his generosity, and the attribution of pleasing to his generosity is what is intended." He counted among this: ﴿God and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ [al-Tawba: 62], and ﴿Indeed those who hurt God and His Messenger﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 57]. What he mentioned in this example is not accepted for him. The two noble verses have interpretations that will come in their place, God willing.

As for "aʿjabanī Zayd wa-karamuhu," the pleasing is attributed to Zayd in his entirety, then some of his qualities are conjoined to it to single out the quality of generosity from among the rest of the qualities he possesses, because of the nobility of this quality. Thus it is in meaning like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿His angels, His messengers, Jibrīl and Mīkāl﴾ [al-Baqara: 98]. So it is not claimed, as al-Zamakhsharī claimed, that the noun is superfluous and that it was mentioned as a preparation for the mention of generosity.

The verb khādaʿa, whose imperfect is yukhādiʿu on the pattern fāʿala, and fāʿala comes for five meanings: for sharing the agency (iqtisām al-fāʿiliyya) and the objecthood (al-mafʿūliyya) in the wording; for sharing both of them in meaning; for agreeing with the transitive afʿala; for agreeing with the unaugmented form in the sense of being sufficient without afʿala and without the unaugmented form. Similar to this: ḍārib Zayd-an ʿUmar (the one who strikes Zayd is ʿUmar), and bāʿadtuhu (I distanced him), wārayt al-shayʾ (I concealed the thing), and qāsaytu (I endured). Here khādaʿa is either for agreement with the unaugmented verb, so it has the meaning of khadaʿa, as if he said: yakhdaʿūna Allāh, and the reading of Ibn Masʿūd and Abū Ḥayāt clarifies this, and it has already been mentioned. It may also be that khādaʿa is of the type of mufāʿala (reciprocity), so their deception has already been explained, and God's deceiving them is where He applies to them the rulings of Muslims and is content from them in this world with the outward display of Islam, even if they conceal its opposite. The deception of the believers of them is that they have carried out the rulings of Muslims upon them. In their deceiving the believers there are benefits for them: their being honored among the believers, and their gaining knowledge of their secrets, which they then pass on to their enemies; and the lifting from them of the ruling applied to disbelievers, such as killing and imposing the poll-tax (jizya) and other things; and what they gain of good through guidance and the division of spoils.

[Reading:] The Ḥaramayn (the two Holy Cities, Mecca and Medina) and Abū ʿAmr read: wa-mā yukhādiʿūna. The rest of the seven readers read: wa-mā yakhdaʿūna. Al-Jārūd ibn Abī Sabra and Abū Ṭālūt ʿAbd al-Salām ibn Shaddād read: ﴿wa-mā yakhdaʿūna﴾ [al-Baqara: 9] in the passive. Some read: wa-mā yukhādaʿūna, with a fatḥa on the dāl, in the passive. Qatāda and Muwarriq al-ʿIjlī read: wa-mā yukhaddiʿūna, from khaddaʿa in the intensive form, in the active voice, and some of them read the yāʾ and the khāʾ with a fatḥa and the dāl with a shadda and a kasra. These are six readings.

The explanation of the first: the meaning of deception is only the reaching of the aim from the one deceived, by his being made to comply in what he chooses, and by obtaining from him what is sought while he is heedless and under one's control and being made to act for him. The harm of that does not return to the one deceived; its harm returns to the deceiver. It is as if he did not deceive or plot except against himself, by bringing himself to the places of destruction, while he is unaware of that, through ignorance of the ugliness of his conduct and the badness of his outcome. This meaning has been expressed by "deception" in the form of counter-correspondence (al-muqābala), and by naming the second act with the name of the first act which causes it, as he said:

Let no one among us be ignorant of us,
lest we become more ignorant than the ignorant ones.

He made his vengeance (intiṣār) ignorance. What supports this line of thought here is that the form may come from one party, as in ʿāqabtu al-liṣṣ (I punished the thief) and ṭāraqtu al-naʿl (I made a sandal in pairs). It is possible that the deception is in its original form of two parties: they deceive themselves, in that they make false hopes for themselves, and their own selves deceive them, in that they likewise make those hopes for them. So it is like an interaction between two, and the poet said:

He remembered from where and from which place his drink came;
he consulted his two selves about the joyful, the camel(?).

Ibn al-Aʿrābī recited:

You did not know what, and I am not saying it:
your life, as long as you live, is the last of eternity.
And you did not consult your two selves, doubting
about them and about their sister, and you did not give birth.

And he said:

He consults his two selves, and there is room in life;
does he expect the ruin, or does he not care for it?

Tha'lab recited, from Ibn al-Aʿrābī:

I was like the she-camel of the Ḍayy (a tribe), who did not know when she was struck
whether she consulted her two selves about stealing or about fornication.

In these verses a person is given two selves, in the sense of the two inclinations, and they have two natures. Or fāʿala may be in the sense of faʿala, and then it agrees with the reading: ﴿wa-mā yakhdaʿūna﴾ [al-Baqara: 9]. The Arabs say: khādaʿtu al-rajul, meaning: I employed a trick against him, so I deceived him, that is, the trick was completed against him and the aim was carried out in him, khidaʿan, with a kasra on the kh in the verbal noun, and khadīʿa (deception). Abū Zayd transmitted this. So the meaning is: evil does not take effect except upon their own selves, and by "selves" here is meant their very persons. So the agent is the object. Some claimed that this is an inversion (maqlūb), and that the meaning is: "their own selves deceive them," and he said: because a person does not deceive himself; rather his self is what deceives him, and embellishes for him, and commands him to evil. He cited items which the Arabs have inverted. Among the grammarians there are two positions on inversion: the first is that it is permitted in speech and poetry, as an extension and reliance on understanding the meaning. The second is that it is not permitted in speech, and is permitted in poetry in cases of necessity, and this is the position our companions upheld. The one who claimed inversion, when he saw their saying: "your self made you hope" (mannatka nafsuka), and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Rather your selves embellished for you﴾ [Yūsuf: 18], imagined that the one who makes hopeful and the one who embellishes are other than the one made hopeful and the one for whom it is embellished. But it is not as he imagined; rather the agent here is the object. Do you not see that you say: "Zayd loved himself," and "Zayd magnified himself"? Here no difference between agent and object is imagined except from the viewpoint of the wording; as for what is meant, it is one. And when the meaning is correct without inversion, (p-58) what need is there for it? Moreover, the correct view is that it is not permitted except in poetry, so the Book of God, exalted is He, should be exempt from it.

As for the one who reads: wa-mā yukhādiʿūna or yakhdaʿūna in the passive, the accusative of what follows illā is like the accusative in "Zayd was cheated in his opinion" (ghubina raʾyuhu). It is either an accusative of specification (tamyīz) according to the Kufan position, or an accusative resembling the direct object according to what some claimed, or by dropping the preposition, meaning: "in their selves," or "from their selves," or the verb is taken to include the sense of "they undo and are stripped," so it is accusative as a direct object, just as the verb rafath (to be lewd) was taken to include the sense of ifḍāʾ (to go in to), and so it was transitive with ilā in His saying: ﴿It is made lawful for you on the night of the fast to go in to your women﴾ [al-Baqara: 187], although one does not say rafatha ilā kadhā. And just as ﴿Do you have any desire to purify yourself?﴾ [al-Nāziʿāt: 18] took the sense of "I draw you," although one does not say: "Is there for you in such-and-such?"

As for the reading: ﴿wa-mā yakhdaʿūna﴾ [al-Baqara: 9], the doubling is either for intensification with respect to the two agents, or for emphasis in the act itself, since it is a leading to the punishment of God. Or it is for agreement with faʿala, as in qadara Allāh and qaddara (God decreed), and the meanings of faʿala have already been mentioned.

The reading of the one who reads: ﴿wa-mā yakhdaʿūna﴾ [al-Baqara: 9], its origin is yakhtadiʿūna, then it was assimilated, and iftaʿala here agrees with faʿala, like iqtadara ʿalā Zayd and qadara ʿalayhi (he had power over him). This is one of the meanings for which iftaʿala came, and these are twelve meanings, and their mention has already been given.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 10 (part 3 of 4):

﴿And they do not perceive﴾ [al-Baqarah: 9] is a clause conjoined to ﴿and they deceive none but themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 9], so it has no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis). The object of yash'uruna (they perceive) is omitted, and its estimated meaning is God's informing His Prophet of their deception and their lying. This is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. Or its estimated meaning is the ruin of their own souls and their being cast into everlasting wretchedness through their disbelief and hypocrisy. This is narrated from Zayd.

It is also possible that ﴿and they do not perceive﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah), and its estimated meaning is: ﴿and they deceive none but themselves while not perceiving that﴾, because if they perceived that their deception of God and the believers was in fact deception of themselves, they would not have deceived God and the believers.

The verb is in the present form, yukhadi'una (they deceive) God, rather than the past form, because the past tense indicates termination, unlike the present, which in a context of blame or praise indicates continuity, as in: Zayd pushes away the orphan, and 'Amr entertains the guest.

The readers, apart from al-Asma'i on the authority of Abu 'Amr, read the vowel of the rā' in maraḍ (sickness) as fatḥah in both places. Al-Asma'i read it with sukun in both places. The two forms are dialectal variants, like al-halab and al-halb (milking), but the regular form is fatḥah, and for this reason the majority read it so.

It is possible that maraḍ is meant literally, and that the sickness, which is corruption, darkness, weakness or pain, really exists in their hearts. The cause of its occurrence in their hearts is the manifestation of the Messenger (ﷺ) and his followers, the spread of Islam, and the victory of its people.

It is also possible that it is meant figuratively, so that by it is meant what has settled in the heart of doubt, as Ibn 'Abbas said. Or it refers to envy and rancour, as in the case of 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul. Or it refers to weakness and faintness at seeing the victory of God's religion and its dominance over all other religions. Taking it figuratively is preferable, because if there were a sickness in their hearts, their bodies would be sick by its sickness, or death would have hastened to them.

Some exegetes say that the prophetic hadith and the medical canon support this. As for the hadith, it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, in the body of the son of Adam there is a morsel of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Truly, it is the heart." As for the medical canon, the physicians described the heart according to what the science of anatomy requires, then said: if a thick substance accumulates in it, and it takes possession of it and its covering, or one of the two, then no life remains with that, and death hastens to its owner, though it may be delayed slightly. If the flowing substance does not take hold of it or its covering, life is delayed for a short time. They said: there is no way for life to continue with a sickness of the heart. On the basis of what has been established, their hearts are not literally sick.

In the Qur'an, the causative meanings that occur in the heart total twenty-seven sicknesses, and they are: al-rayn (rust), al-zaygh (deviation), al-ṭab' (sealing), al-ṣarf (turning away), al-ḍayq (constriction), al-haraj (narrowness), al-khatm (sealing), al-iqfal (locking), al-ishrab (saturation), al-ru'b (terror), al-qasawah (hardness), al-iṣrar (persistence), 'adam al-taṭhir (lack of purification), al-nufur (aversion), al-ishmi'zaz (repugnance), al-inkar (denial), al-shukuk (doubts), al-'ama (blindness), al-ib'ad by the form of cursing (distancing), al-ta'abbi (refusal), al-ḥamiyyah (zealotry), al-baghda' (hatred), al-ghaflah (heedlessness), al-ghamzah (winking), al-lahw (diversion), al-irtiyab (suspicion), and al-nifaq (hypocrisy).

The apparent sense of the verses of the Qur'an indicates that these sicknesses are meanings that occur in the heart and overpower it. The heart has sicknesses other than these, such as ghill (rancour), ḥiqd (malice) and ḥasad (envy), which God mentioned attributed to the body of the disbelievers.

Ziyadah (increase) means exceeding a known measure. God's knowledge encompasses what they conceal, and the evil of their belief, hatred and deception. It is known to Him, as God the Exalted said: ﴿And everything with Him is by measure﴾ [al-Ra'd: 8]. At every moment He casts into their hearts from that known measure something of a known quantity in His sight, then He casts after that something else, so the second becomes an increase upon the first. For if the first were not of a known measure, the increase would not be realised. In this sense is understood: ﴿so it added to them uncleanness upon their uncleanness﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125].

The increase of the sickness is either because the darkness of their disbelief settles into their hearts little by little, to which God the Exalted alluded in His saying: ﴿darkness upon darkness﴾ [al-Nur: 40]; or because the sickness came into their hearts through envy or grief at what God the Exalted renews for His religion of the elevation of the Word, and for His Messenger and the believers, of victory and the execution of command; or because of the terror that occurs in their hearts.

Ascribing the increase to God the Exalted is a literal ascription (isnad haqiqi), unlike the ascription in His saying: ﴿so it added to them uncleanness upon their uncleanness﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125] and ﴿Which of you has had this increase it in faith?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 124].

The Mu'tazilah (a theological school) said: it is not permissible for the increase of the sickness to be of the same kind as that to which it is added, since that to which it is added is disbelief. So they interpreted it, taking maraḍ (sickness) to mean grief, because they used to grieve at the elevation of the affair of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Or it means the withholding of increased favours (al-alṭaf). Or it means pain of the heart. Or it means the slackening of intention in fighting, because their hearts were at first strong for that. Or it means that their disbelief increased because of the increase of obligation from God the Exalted.

All these interpretations apply only when His saying ﴿so God increased them in sickness﴾ is a report (khabar). But if it is a supplication (du'a'), then they do not apply. Rather, it is possible that the supplication is literal, so that it is a supplication for the occurrence of an increase in sickness; or figurative, so that by it is not intended the granting of the request, since what is asked for is already occurring. Rather, what is meant is reviling, cursing and disparagement, as in His saying: ﴿God fight them! How are they deluded?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30]; ﴿Then they turned away; God turned their hearts away, because they are a people who do not understand﴾ [al-Tawbah: 127]; and as in his saying (ﷺ): "May God curse Iblis and disgrace him." It is known that this has occurred, and that he has returned with disgrace and a curse to which there is no addition, because it has no end.

The indefiniteness of maraḍ (sickness) in His saying ﴿in their hearts is a sickness﴾ does not indicate that all kinds of sickness are in their hearts, as some exegetes claimed. This is because the indication of an indefinite noun for what it was set for is an indication by way of the individual (badal), since it is an indication that encompasses each and every individual in the manner of generality. There was no need to put maraḍ into the plural, because enumerating the loci indicates enumerating the states by reason. So the singular was sufficient instead of the plural.

The transfer of the increase to them, not to the hearts, since He said ﴿so He increased them﴾ and did not say ﴿so He increased it (the hearts)﴾, admits of two possibilities. One is that it is by elision of a modifier, meaning: God increased their hearts in sickness. The second is that He increased their persons in sickness, because the sickness of the heart is a sickness of the rest of the body. Thus it is correct to ascribe the increase to the persons, and this serves as an indication that there is sickness in their persons. He ascribed it to their hearts only because the heart is the locus of perception and intellect.

Ḥamzah (a Qur'an reader) pronounced ﴿fa-zādahum﴾ with imalah (vocalic inclination) in ten verbs whose alif is converted from yā'. There is one verb whose alif is converted from wāw, and its pattern is fa'ala with fatḥah on the 'ayn, but that verb's pattern is fa'ila with kasrah on the 'ayn. I have gathered them in two lines in my poem entitled 'Iqd al-La'ali fi al-Qira'at al-Sab' al-'Awali, and they are:

Ten verbs are inclined for Ḥamzah: jā', shā', ḍāqa, rāna, and complete (them):
zād, khāba, ṭāba, khāfa together, and ḥāqa, zāgha, except al-Aḥzāb with its ṣād, so do not.

He means that he excepted Ḥamzah's reading of ﴿and when the eyes swerved﴾ [al-Aḥzab: 10] in surah al-Aḥzab, and ﴿have their eyes swerved from them?﴾ [Ṣad: 63] in surah Ṣad, so he did not incline them. Ibn Dhakwan agreed with Ḥamzah on inclining jā' and shā' in the whole Qur'an, and on zād at the beginning of al-Baqarah. There is a difference of report from him regarding this zād in the rest of the Qur'an. I read it for him with both forms. Imalah belongs to Tamim, and tafkhim (non-inclination) belongs to the Hijaz.

Alim (painful) has been explained previously. If we say it is for intensification, then it is transferred from a verb meaning pain, and its ascription to the punishment is figurative, because punishment does not feel pain; rather, its owner feels pain. So it is like the saying "the poetry of a poet", since poetry does not compose poetry; rather, the poet is its composer.

If we say it means mu'lim (causing pain), as 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib said:

Is it because of Rayhanah, the caller who listens?

That is, the one who makes to hear. The pattern fa'il in the sense of mif'il is figurative, because the regular form of af'ala is maf'al. So the first is figurative in the construction, and this is figurative in the single word.

The two punishments combined have befallen the hypocrites: the great punishment mentioned in the verse, and the painful punishment. It was said: this is because they are enrolled among them and included with them. Do you not see that God the Exalted in that verse informed that they do not believe in His saying: ﴿They do not believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6], and informed of that in this verse by His saying: ﴿and they are not believers﴾, and the painful punishment? So the hypocrites became more severely punished than the other disbelievers, by the explicit statement that both mentioned punishments befall them. For this reason God the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed the hypocrites are in the lowest level of the Fire﴾ [al-Nisa': 145].

Then God the Exalted mentioned that the existence of the painful punishment for these people is caused by their lying and their denying. Here, ma is a verbal-masdar particle (ma masdariyyah), meaning: "by their being liars". There is no pronoun returning to it, because it is a particle, contrary to the view of Abu al-Hasan (al-Akhfash). Whoever claims that kana, in its incomplete form (naqisah), has no masdar, his view is rejected. This is the view of Abu 'Ali al-Farisi. Sibawayh's book contains many instances of the masdar of incomplete kana, but the more correct view is that it is not pronounced with it. So one does not say "kana Zayd qa'iman kawnan" (Zayd was standing, a standing).

Whoever permits ma to be a relative pronoun meaning "that which", then the returning pronoun is omitted by their estimate: yukadhdhibunahu (they deny it) or yakdhibunahu (they lie about it).

Abu al-Baqa' claimed that ma being a relative pronoun is more apparent. He said: because the estimated pronoun (ha') refers to "that which", not to the masdar, and it does not follow that there is an estimated pronoun there. Rather, whoever reads yakdhibun with lightness (takhfif), and they are the Kufans, the verb is then intransitive. Whoever reads with doubling (tashdid), and they are the two Meccan and Medinan readers and the two Arabs (Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr), the object is omitted because the meaning is understood, and its estimate is: their lying against God in His reports and against the Messenger in what he brought.

It is possible that the doubled form has the sense of the light form, in the manner of intensification, as they said in: ṣadaqa (he told the truth) and ṣaddaqa (he confirmed); and in: bāna al-shay' (the thing became clear) and bayyana (he made it clear); and in: qalaṣa al-thawb (the garment shrank) and qallaṣa.

Lying (al-kadhib) has several senses in the Arabic language. The first: reporting a thing contrary to what it is. 'Amr ibn Bahr adds to this that the reporter must know of the contradiction, and this is an issue they discussed in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh). The second: reporting something that resembles lying but is intended only as truth. They said: among this is what came in a hadith about Abraham, God's blessings be upon him and upon our Prophet. The third: error, as in the saying of 'Ubadah concerning one who claimed that the witr (night prayer) is obligatory: "Abu Muhammad lied", meaning he erred. The fourth: failure, as in their saying: kudhdhiba al-rajul, meaning his hope and what he expected and planned came to nothing. The fifth: urging the addressee to adhere to the mentioned thing, as in their saying: kadhaba 'alayka al-'asal, meaning: "Eat the honey!" The one urged is in the nominative case with kadhaba, and they said: it is not permissible to put it in the accusative except in a rare word, which al-Qasim ibn Sallam narrated from Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna. The sinful one is the first.

People have differed concerning lying. Some said: all lying is ugly and has no good in it. They said: Malik was asked about a man who lies to his wife and his son to comfort their hearts, and he said: "There is no good in it." Others said: lying is of two kinds, forbidden and permitted. The forbidden is reporting a thing contrary to what it is when there is no legal benefit in keeping to it. The permitted is what has this in it, such as lying for the reconciliation of relations between people.

Scholars of tafsir differed regarding the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of these verses. One group said: they were revealed concerning the hypocrites among the People of the Book, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, Muʿattib ibn Qushayr, and al-Jadd ibn Qays, when they said: "Come, let us find a stratagem by which we may be safe from Muhammad and his companions, and at the same time hold fast to our religion." So they displayed faith with their tongues while believing the opposite. This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Another group said: they were revealed concerning the hypocrites among the People of the Book and others. This was related by al-Suddi from Ibn Masʿud and Ibn ʿAbbas, and Abu al-ʿAliyah, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd also held this view.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 2, verses 11–13:

﴿And when it is said to them, "Do not cause corruption on the earth," they say, "We are only reformers."﴾ ﴿Unquestionably, it is they who are the corrupters, but they do not perceive.﴾

*Idha* (إذا): an adverb of time (*zarf zaman*), and it is most often used as a conditional. It also occurs for sudden occurrence (*lil-mufaja'ah*) as an adverb of time, in agreement with al-Riyashi and al-Zajjaj, not as an adverb of place, which is the view of al-Mubarrad and the apparent position of Sibawayh, and not as a particle (*harf*), against the Kufans. When it is a particle, it is used for something that is certain or considered likely to exist, and it is put in the jussive mood in poetry. Its rulings are fully treated in the science of grammar (*nahw*).

The verb of three root letters whose middle radical has become an *alif* in the past tense, when it is put into the passive voice, has its first letter purely vowelled with *kasrah*, and its middle letter becomes a *ya'* (ي) in the dialect of Quraysh and their neighbours from the Banu Kinanah. In the dialect of most of Qays, 'Uqayl, their neighbours, and the general population of the Banu Asad, the first letter is vowelled with *dammah*. With the first dialect, al-Kisa'i and Hisham recited *qila* (قِيلَ), *ghida* (غِيضَ), *hila* (حِيلَ), *si'a* (سِيءَ), *si'at* (سِيئَتْ), *ji'a* (جِيءَ), and *siqa* (سِيقَ). Nafi' and Ibn Dhakwan agreed with him on *si'a* and *si'at*. Ibn Dhakwan added *hila* and *saqa* (سَاقَ). The rest of the reciters recited in the first dialect. There is a third dialect for this, which is purely vowelling the first letter of the word with *dammah* and making its middle letter a *waw* (و) with sukun. It was not recited with, and it is the dialect of Hudhayl and the Banu Dubayr. The discussion of the justification of these dialects and the completion of their rulings is mentioned in grammar.

*Al-fasad* (الفَسادُ, corruption): change from the state of balance and uprightness. Suhayl said in *al-Fasih*: "fasada" (فَسَدَ, it became corrupt). Its opposite is *al-salah* (الصَّلاحُ, righteousness), which is the balance of a condition and its being firm in a good state.

*Al-ard* (الأرْضُ, the earth) is feminine. It is pluralized as *ardh* (أُرْضٍ) and *aradin* (أراضٍ). With *waw* and *nun* (in the nominative) and with *ya'* and *nun* (in the accusative and genitive), it is an anomalous plural, in which the middle letter takes a fatha. With *alif* and *ta'* it is *aradat* (أرِضاتٍ). *Al-aradi* (الأراضِي) is a plural of a plural, like *awathib*.

*Innama* (إنَّما): *ma* (ما) is a connector to *inna* (إنَّ) that stops it from governing. If a verbal sentence follows it, it is prepared (for the verb). Among the later grammarians and some of the scholars of legal theory (*usul*), it is said to indicate exclusivity (*hasr*). The claim that it is composed of the negating *ma* that entered upon *inna*, which is for affirmation, so that it gives exclusivity, is a weak, corrupt view that comes from someone who does not know grammar. What we hold is that it does not indicate exclusivity by its lexical form, just as exclusivity is not understood from its sisters that were stopped by *ma*. There is no difference between *la'alla Zaydan qa'imun* (لَعَلَّ زَيْدًا قائِمٌ) and *la'alla ma Zaydun qa'imun* (لَعَلَّ ما زَيْدٌ قائِمٌ), and likewise *inna Zaydan qa'imun* (إنَّ زَيْدًا قائِمٌ) and *innama Zaydun qa'imun* (إنَّما زَيْدٌ قائِمٌ). If exclusivity is understood, it is understood from the context of the speech, not because *innama* indicates it. With what we have established, the problem that they raised in verses such as the saying of God Almighty ﴿You are only a warner﴾ [al-Ra'd: 7], ﴿Say: I am only a human being﴾ [al-Kahf: 110], and ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 45] disappears. Some claimed that governing by *innama* (إعْمالُ إنَّما) is heard from the speech of the Arabs, but what our companions hold is that it is not heard.

*Nahnu* (نَحْنُ, we): a detached nominative pronoun for a speaker who is with others, or for the speaker referring to himself in the majestic plural. There are views on the justification for its being indeclinable in the *damm* vowel, which are mentioned in grammar.

*Ala* (ألا, unquestionably): an interjection of alerting (*harf tanbih*). They claimed it is composed of the interrogative hamza and *la* (لا, not), to indicate the certainty of what follows. When the interrogative enters a negation, it gives certainty, as in the saying of God Almighty ﴿Is not He able to do that?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 40]. Because it is among those that are used specifically in this way, a sentence after it hardly occurs except beginning with something like what the oath is introduced with. al-Zamakhshari said the same. What we choose is that the alerting *ala* is a simple particle, because the claim of composition goes against the original form. Also, what they claimed, that the interrogative hamza entered upon the negating *la* to indicate the certainty of what follows, and so on to the end, is an error, because the uses of *ala* do not indicate that *la* is not for negation, so that what they claimed would be complete. Do you not see that you say: *Ala inna Zaydan muntaliqun* (ألا إنَّ زَيْدًا مُنْطَلِقٌ)? Its origin is not *la inna Zaydan muntaliqun*, since this is not among the constructions of the Arabs. This is unlike what they compared it to, the saying of God Almighty ﴿Is not He able to do that?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 40], since the construction *laysa Zaydun bi-qadirin* (لَيْسَ زَيْدٌ بِقادِرٍ) is correct. Also, it occurs before *rubba* (رُبَّ), before *layta* (لَيْتَ), before the vocative, and other things in which it cannot be understood that *la* is a negating particle, so that the interrogative hamza would have entered upon the negating *la* and given certainty. Imru' al-Qays said:

"Unquestionably, many a day is yours from among them, a good one, especially the day at Darat Juljul."

Another said:

"Unquestionably, I wish I knew how the event of her union happens, and how she keeps the union of the absent one."

Another said:

"Unquestionably, O my people, for the phantom that stirs longing, and for the house that moves far away with the beloved, and we meet."

Another said:

"Unquestionably, O Qays and al-Dahhak, go on, for you have passed the wine of the road."

And other examples beyond these where *la* cannot be entered. As for his saying that a sentence after it hardly occurs except beginning with something like what the oath is introduced with, this is not correct. Do you not see that the sentence after it is begun with *rubba*, with *layta*, with the imperative verb, with the vocative, and with *habbadha* (حَبَّذا), in the saying:

"Unquestionably, how wonderful is Hind, and the land in which is Hind."

Nothing of this is introduced with the oath. The sign of *ala* that is alerting and initiating is that the speech is correct without it. It may also be an interjection of offering (*harf 'ard*), in which case a verb follows it. If a noun follows it, it is by implying a verb. ﴿And when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"; and when they go apart to their devils, they say, "Indeed we are with you; we are only mocking."﴾

*Al-liqa'* (meeting) is a person receiving another person near to him. Its verb is *laqiya yalqa* (he met), and it may also be said *laqa* (with the *alif*), which is a verb of the form *fa'ala* with the meaning of the basic verb. Fourteen verbal nouns (*masadir*) have been heard for *laqiya*: *laqiya*, *luqyan*, *luqyatan*, *laqatan*, *liqa'an*, *luqa'an*, *laqan*, *luqan*, *luqya'a*, *liqya'a*, *luqiyyan*, *luqyanan*, *liqyanatan*, and *tilqa'an*.

*Al-khuluww* means solitude, being alone: *khala bihi*, meaning he was alone with him. It may also mean passing on, as in ﴿Indeed, examples have passed before you﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 137].

*Whoever rebels against him, he restrains him, then he is thrown into prison and the shackles.*

Ru'bah said:

*In the furrows of the lashes, the twisted ones, there is a cure for the rebellion of the rebellious dog.*

According to the Kufan grammarians, its pattern is *fa'lan*, and its *nun* is additional, from *shaṭa yashiṭu*, meaning he perished. The poet said:

*The caravan may win in the hidden place of a noon resting place, and the champion may perish upon our spears.*

*Al-shaytan* is every rebellious one among the jinn, humans and animals. This was said by Ibn Abbas. Its feminine is *shaytanah*. The poet said:

*She is the full-grown she-camel, nothing else is like her, and a she-devil whose madness has driven her mad.*

*Shayatin* is the plural of *shaytan*, like *gharathin* being the plural of *gharthan*. Al-Farra' related it. This is on the assumption that its *nun* is additional, so it is like *gharthan*, together with a noun whose meaning is the companionship suitable to the one mentioned.

Its sukun before a vowel is the dialect of Rabi'ah and Ghanm, as related by al-Kisa'i. When it is sukun, the more correct view is that it is a noun. When it meets the *alif-lam* (definite article) or the *alif al-wasl*, the fatha is the dialect of the general Arabs, and the kasra is the dialect of Rabi'ah. The grammatical explanation of the two dialects is given in grammar books.

It is used as a place adverb (*zarf makan*), so it occurs as a predicate (*khabar*) about a physical body and about events. When it is used alone, it is given tanwin with a fatha. Its root is triliteral and it belongs to the category of the *maqsur* (words ending in a weak letter with fixed form), not to the category of *yad*, unlike the view of Yunus.

The most common use of *ma'an* (together) is as a circumstantial state (*hal*), as in *jami'an* (all together). It is more specific than *jami'* (all), because it expresses sharing in time explicitly, whereas *jami'* may include it.

Ahmad ibn Yahya asked Ahmad ibn Qadim about the difference between: "*qama 'Abdullah wa Zayd ma'an*" (Abdullah and Zayd stood together) and "*qama 'Abdullah wa Zayd jami'an*" (Abdullah and Zayd stood all together). He said: "He kept running around with them until night." Ibn Yahya made the distinction that *jami'an* means the standing occurred at two times or at one time, whereas if you say *ma'an*, it occurs at one time.

*Al-istihza'* (mockery) is contempt and ridicule. It is *istaf'ala*, with the meaning of the basic verb *fa'ala*. You say: *hazi'tu bihi* and *istahza'tu bihi* with one meaning, like *ista'jaba* with the meaning of *'ajiba* (he was amazed). This is one of the meanings for which the form *istaf'ala* has come.

(p-63)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 15:

﴿Allah mocks them, and He prolongs them in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾ Al-madd (المَدُّ): extension, prolonging. Madda ash-shay’ (مَدَّ الشَّيْءَ): he lengthened it and spread it out. ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord extended the shadow?﴾ [al-Furqan: 45]. The root meaning of al-madd is increase. Everything that enters into something and multiplies it has, in fact, extended it. This was said by al-Lihyani. Amadda (أمَدَّ) has the same meaning as madda: madda al-jaysh wa-amaddahu means he increased it and added to it something of its own kind that strengthens it. Some scholars said: madda means to increase with something of the same kind, and amadda means to increase with something of a different kind. Yunus said: madda is used for good, and amadda for evil. End of his words. It is also said: the river was extended (madda) and another river extended it (amaddahu). The māddah (مادَّة) of a thing is that which extends it; the ha’ in it is for emphasis (al-mubalagha). Ibn Qutaybah said: madadtu al-dawah and amdadtuha (I supplied the inkwell) have the same meaning. It is also said: madadna al-qawm means we became their helpers, and amdadnahum bi-ghayrina means we supplied them with others besides ourselves. Al-Lihyani said: the commander amadda his army with horses. In the Revelation: ﴿And We supplied you with wealth and sons﴾ [al-Isra’: 6]. At-tughyan (الطُّغْيان): exceeding the known measure. It is said: the water overflowed (taghā al-ma’), and the fire blazed beyond its bounds (taghat an-nar). Al-ʿamah (العَمَه): hesitation and bewilderment. It is similar to blindness, except that blindness is attributed to an eye whose light has gone, and to an opinion from which correctness has departed. It is said: ʿamiha, yaʿmahu, ʿamahan, and ʿamahanan; the doer is ʿamih and ʿamih. It is also said: barriyyah ʿamhāʾ (a desert with no mark) when there is no sign in it by which one can be guided. Ibn Qutaybah said: al-ʿamah is that one charges headlong and does not see what is coming. It was also said: al-ʿamah is blindness to right guidance.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 16 (part 1 of 6):

﴿Those are the ones who have bought misguidance in exchange for guidance, so their trade has not profited, and they were not guided.﴾ The verb *al-ishtira'* (الِاشْتِراءُ) and *al-shira'* (الشِّراءُ) mean the same thing: exchanging one thing for another and taking it in return. However, *al-ishtira'* is used for both buying and selling. It is one of the forms where *if'ta'ala* (افْتَعَلَ) carries the meaning of the bare verb, and this is one of the meanings for which *if'ta'ala* is used. *Al-ribh* (الرِّبْحُ) is the gain that results from an increase over the capital. *Al-tijarah* (التِّجارَةُ) is the work of the merchant (*al-tajir*), who manages wealth in order to seek growth and increase. *Al-muhtadi* (المُهْتَدِي) is the active participle of *ihtada* (اهْتَدى). In it, *if'ta'ala* is used for *al-mutawa'ah* (المُطاوَعَةُ, the sense of the form receiving the action of the bare verb), as in: *hadaytuhu fa-ihtada* (I guided him, so he was guided), like *sawwaytuhu fa-istawa* (I levelled it, so it levelled) and *ghammamtuhu fa-ightamma* (I distressed him, so he was distressed). *Al-mutawa'ah* is one of the meanings for which *if'ta'ala* is used, and the *if'ta'ala* form expressing *mutawa'ah* is only formed from a transitive verb. Whoever claimed that it can come from an intransitive verb, and that this is rare, has erred, relying on the poet's verse:

*Until, when Suhayl rose at dawn, like the flame of the one striking the fire, throwing off sparks.*

In this verse, *ishtala* (اشْتالَ) has the meaning of *fa'ala* (فَعَلَ). One says *shala yashulu* and *ishtala yashtalu* with one meaning, and *al-mutawa'ah* cannot be conceived unless the receiving verb is transitive.

﴿And when it is said to them, "Do not cause corruption"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 11] is a conditional clause. It may be a new independent sentence coordinated with what precedes it, condemning their ugly deeds and words. It may also be a part of the speech, and in the second case it is part of a sentence, since it completes the relative clause. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be coordinated with *yakdhibun* (يَكْذِبُونَ, "they lie"), in which case it would have a place in grammatical analysis, namely the accusative, since it is coordinated with the predicate of *kana* (كانَ), and what is coordinated with the predicate is a predicate. In that case it is part of the cause for which they deserve the painful punishment. On the first two possibilities, it is not part of the speech. This interpretation which the two of them permitted, based on one of the two possibilities for *ma* in His saying ﴿because they used to lie﴾ [al-Baqarah: 10], is an error. It would require *ma* to be a relative pronoun meaning *alladhi* (الَّذِي, "which"), because the coordinated item is a predicate, so *yakdhibun* would have had its returning pronoun to *ma* deleted, and His saying ﴿And when it is said to them…﴾ until the end of the verse has no pronoun in it returning to *ma*. So it is invalid for it to be coordinated with it, since the sense would become: "and for them is a painful punishment because of that which they used to…"

﴿And when it is said to them, "Do not cause corruption in the earth," they say, "We are only reformers"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 11]. This is speech that is not coherent, due to the absence of a returning pronoun.

As for their other possibility, that *ma* is verbal (*masdariyyah*, مَصْدَرِيَّةً), then according to al-Akhfash this parsing is also an error, since in his view the verbal *ma* is a noun to which a pronoun returns from its relative clause, while the coordinated clause is free of it. As for the view of the majority of grammarians (al-Jumhur), this parsing is common. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Baqa' did not mention any parsing of this other than that it be coordinated with *yakdhibun* or with *yaqulu* (يَقُولُ, "they say"). They claimed that the first is a possibility, and we have already mentioned what is problematic about it. What we choose is the first possibility, that the clause is independent, as we have established, since this clause and the two clauses after it are among the details of the lying and the results of their denial.

Do you not see their saying ﴿We are only reformers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 11], and their saying ﴿Shall we believe as the foolish have believed?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 13], and their saying when they met the believers, "We believe" (*amanna*), which is pure lying? It is appropriate to make these into independent sentences, mentioned to reveal their lying and hypocrisy, to attribute foolishness to the believers, and to mock them. The condemnation of them and the refutation of them is multiplied by these sentences and their independence. This is better than making them an extension of a part of the speech, because in that case they would not be intended for their own sake. They are only brought to define the relative pronoun if it is a noun, or to complete its meaning if it is a particle.

The clause after *idha* (إذا) is in the position of a genitive by means of being a complement. The governing element for it, according to the majority, is the response (*al-jawab*). So *idha* in the verse is in the accusative governed by His saying ﴿We are only reformers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 11]. What we choose is that the clause that follows it is the one governing *idha*, because it is conditional, and what follows it is not in the position of a genitive by complement. Its ruling is the ruling of the adverbs through which one is conditioned, even if they fall short of the jussive effect of their operation.

Moreover, some grammarians permitted the jussive effect through them, by analogy with *mata* (مَتى), which is in the accusative governed by the verb of the condition. Thus *idha* is also in the accusative governed by the verb of the condition after it. What invalidates the view of the majority is the permissibility of *idha qumta fa-'amrun qa'im* (if you stand, then Amr is standing), because what follows the *fa'* does not operate on what precedes it. And the permissibility of the occurrence of the sudden *idha* (إذا الفُجائِيَّةِ) as the response to the conditional *idha*, as He the Exalted said: ﴿And when We let people taste mercy after adversity has touched them, behold, they have a scheme against Our signs﴾ [Yunus: 21]. What follows the sudden *idha* does not operate on what precedes it.

The omission of the subject of the verb "said" here is for the sake of vagueness. It may be God the Exalted, or the Messenger (ﷺ), or some of the believers. Each of these has been said. As for the unnamed object (*al-maf'ul alladhi lam yusamma fa'iluhu*, المَفْعُولُ الَّذِي لَمْ يُسَمَّ فاعِلُهُ), the apparent meaning of the speech is that it is the sentence introduced by the prohibitive particle, which is ﴿Do not cause corruption in the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 11]. However, that is not permissible except according to the view of one who permits the subject to be a whole sentence, and this is not the view of the majority of the Basran grammarians.

The positions on this have already been presented when speaking on His saying ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6]. The unnamed object in that case has the same ruling as the subject. Its interpretation according to the view of the majority of the Basran grammarians is that the unnamed object is a pronoun implied as "it," explained by the context of the speech, just as the pronoun was explained in His saying ﴿until it was hidden behind the veil﴾ [Sad: 32], by the context of the speech and its meaning. So when "And when it is said to them a severe saying" is stated, this severe saying is implied and described, and the sentence after it comes explaining it. Thus it has no place in grammatical analysis, because it explains that implied element, which is the severe saying. It is also not permissible for *lahum* (لَهم, "to them") to be in the position of the unnamed object, because a complete meaning cannot be formed from it together with what precedes it. This is because "Do not cause corruption" would remain with no connection, since it would not be an object of the verb "said" explaining it.

Al-Zamakhshari claimed that the unnamed object is the sentence "Do not cause corruption," and he made this part of *al-isnad al-lafzi* (الإسْنادِ اللَّفْظِيِّ, verbal predication), comparing it with your saying, "*alif* (ألِفٌ) is a letter of three letters," and with the saying "they claimed a mount of lying" (*zaA'mu matiyyata al-kadhib*). He said: "It is as if it was said, 'And when this statement and this speech is said to them.'" End of his words.

So he did not make it part of the predication to the meaning of the sentence, because that is not permissible according to the view of the majority of the Basran grammarians. So he turned to verbal predication, which is not restricted to the noun, but is found in the noun, the verb, the particle, and the sentence. When meaningful predication is possible, one does not turn to verbal predication, and it has been possible by the interpretation we mentioned.

The *lam* (اللّامُ) in His saying *lahum* (to them) is for communication (*al-tabligh*, التَّبْلِيغِ). This is one of the seventeen meanings of *lam* which we mentioned when speaking on His saying ﴿All praise is due to Allah﴾ [al-Fatihah: 2].

Their corruption in the earth is by disbelief, said Ibn 'Abbas; or by sins, said Abu al-'Aliyah and Muqatil; or by both, said al-Suddi on the authority of his teachers; or by not carrying out the command and avoiding the prohibition, said Mujahid; or by the hypocrisy by which they made themselves allies of the disbelievers and revealed the secrets of the believers to them, mentioned by 'Ali ibn 'Ubayd Allah; or by their turning away from faith in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Qur'an; (p-٦٥) or by their intent to change the religion, said al-Dahhak; or by their following their desires and abandoning the truth despite its clarity, said some of them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Corruption in the earth is stirring up wars and strife." He said: "Because in that is the corruption of what is in the earth, and the absence of rectitude in the conditions of people, the crops, and the religious and worldly benefits." God the Exalted said: ﴿so that he may cause corruption therein and destroy the crops and the offspring﴾ [al-Baqarah: 205], ﴿Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. From this it was said of a war that took place between Tayy: "the War of Corruption" (*harb al-fasad*). End of his words.

The aspect of corruption according to these statements, all of which have been said, is that they are great major sins and grave disobediences. Their persistence in them increases their severity. Whenever the disobediences of the earth's inhabitants multiply and become frequent, its goodness decreases, its blessings are removed, and the rain, which is the cause of life, is withheld. So their described act is the strongest cause for the corruption and ruin of the earth.

Just as obedience and seeking forgiveness are a cause for the abundance of goods, the descent of blessings, and the descent of rain. Do you not see His saying: ﴿So I said, "Seek forgiveness of your Lord"﴾ [Nuh: 10]; ﴿And if they had remained on the right path﴾ [al-Jinn: 16]; ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and feared Allah﴾ [al-A'raf: 96]; ﴿And if they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 66]; and the verses.

It has been said in its interpretation what is reported in the hadith, that the wicked person is relieved of by the servants, the lands, the trees, and the animals; that God withholds the rain because of his sins, so the lands and the servants perish due to the lack of plants and the cutting off of sustenance.

The prohibition against corruption in the earth is of the type of prohibiting the cause (*al-musabbab*, المُسَبِّبِ) and the intent is prohibiting the means (*al-sabab*, السَّبَبِ). So the true object of the prohibition is befriending the disbelievers and colluding with them against the believers by disclosing secrets to them and empowering them over the believers, because this leads to the stirring up of strife which results in corruption in the earth. So what is ordered as a consequence of the prohibited act, in reality, is itself prohibited in wording.

The prohibition against corruption in the earth here is like the prohibition in His saying ﴿and do not act wickedly in the earth, causing corruption﴾ [al-Baqarah: 60].

The mention of the earth is not merely for emphasis. Rather, in that there is an alert that this place in which your origin and your conduct lie, and from which the substance of your life comes, and which is the covering of your dead, is worthy that corruption not be done in it, since the place of reform should not be made a place of corruption.

Do you not see His saying: ﴿And do not cause corruption in the earth after its reform﴾ [al-A'raf: 56]; and He the Exalted said: ﴿He is the One who made the earth submissive to you, so walk in its broad tracts and eat of His provision﴾ [al-Mulk: 15]; and He the Exalted said: ﴿And the earth after that He spread out; He brought forth from it its water and its pasture; and the mountains He set firm; as provision for you and your livestock﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 30–33]; and His saying: ﴿That We poured down water in torrents﴾ [Abasa: 25], and the verse.

And other verses alerting to the favours bestowed upon us through the earth, and the benefits that Allah placed in it, which cannot be counted.

They answered the prohibition against corruption with their saying ﴿We are only reformers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 11]. So they brought the answer as a nominal sentence to indicate the stability of the attribute for them, and they emphasised it with *innama* (إنَّما, "only") to indicate the strength of their attribution of reform.

Regarding the meaning in which they believed themselves to be reformers, there are several views:

First: the saying of Ibn 'Abbas: "Our alliance with the disbelievers is only intended to reconcile between them and the believers."

Second: the saying of Mujahid, which is: "That alliance is guidance and goodness, and not corruption."

Third: that the alliance with the self and desire is goodness and guidance.

Fourth: that they thought that there was goodness for them in allying with the disbelievers, and this is not so, because if the disbelievers had gained control over them they would not have spared them. For this reason He said: ﴿Behold, they are the corrupters, but they do not perceive﴾ [al-Baqarah: 12].

Fifth: that they denied that they had done what they were forbidden from, namely allying with the disbelievers, and they said: ﴿We are only reformers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 11], by avoiding what we were forbidden.

What we choose is that none of these views is specifically binding. Rather, the prohibition is taken to apply to every kind of corruption. This is because, when they claimed faith, and God refuted them in that and informed that their faith was deception, they were in one of two states. The first is that, while not believing, they were at peace with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers. The second state is that, while not believing, they strove to cause corruption in the earth, to divide the word of Islam and scatter the order of the religion. So they were forbidden from that, and it was as if it were said to them:

(p-66) If you were already committed to affirming faith with your tongues, and your hearts did not believe, then beware of corrupting the earth. They did not respond by refraining from corruption. Instead, they asserted for themselves that they were reformers and that they were not the locus of corruption, so the prohibition against corruption did not apply to them, since they were characterized by its opposite, which is reform.

All of that is slander from them and pure falsehood, in keeping with their habit of lying and their saying with their mouths what is not in their hearts.

Since they had met the prohibition against corruption with the false claim of reform, Allah refuted them with His words:

﴿Indeed, they are the corrupters, but they do not perceive.﴾ [2:12]

So the opposite of what they claimed was affirmed for them, in return for their claim, in a nominal sentence (jumla ismiyya) emphasized by several kinds of emphasis. Among them are opening with inna (the emphatic particle), the use of the pronoun "they" (hum), and the use of the definite article alif-lam, which according to some scholars conveys exclusivity (hasr).

Al-Jurjani said: The alif-lam entered the word "al-mufsidun" (the corrupters) because the word had already been mentioned in His words "do not corrupt" (la tufsidu). It is as though it were a kind of reference to something already known. Had the statement about them come without the word having been mentioned earlier, it would have been "Indeed, they are the corrupters." The end of his words. And it is good.

The sentence opens with alā (a particle of attention), which draws attention to what follows, so that hearts are attentive to this news that was given about them. The word hum may be an emphasis of the pronoun in innahum, even though it is a separating pronoun (damir al-fasl, a pronoun placed between the subject and predicate). On these two views, al-mufsidun is the predicate of inna. Alternatively, hum may be a subject with al-mufsidun as its predicate, and the whole clause is then the predicate of inna. The benefit of the separating pronoun was mentioned earlier, in the discussion of His words "and those are the successful" [2:5].

The point of the contrast (istidrak) here, in His words "but they do not perceive" [2:12], is that the report that they are the corrupters implies that Allah knows this. So the meaning is that Allah knows they are the corrupters, but they do not know this. Thus "but" (lākin) falls between two opposites. The reason for the contrast is that when they were forbidden from producing the kind of corruption they used to engage in, they responded by claiming that they were reformers in this. Allah reported that they are the corruptors, and they were bound to know that this is as Allah the Exalted said, and that they would not claim to be reformers. So the contrast corrected them regarding this meaning, which they missed because they did not perceive it.

You say: "Zayd is ignorant, but he does not know." That is because, insofar as he is characterized by ignorance, and this quality subsists in Zayd, it would be fitting for Zayd to know this quality that subsists in him, since a person should know the qualities that he has. So the contrast was made against him with "but," because this kind of thing is frequent in the Qur'an, and in some places its recognition is obscure.

They said: The object of "they perceive" (yashurūn) is omitted because the meaning is understood. Its implied object is "that they are corruptors," or "that they are punished," or "that death will come upon them, so repentance is cut off." The first is preferable. It is also possible that nothing is intended as omitted, so that perception is denied of them without mention of its object or any intention, and this is more forceful in censure. They made their claim, which was corruption, into reform, from people who lacked perception, and they were as though they were cattle. This is because whoever is able to perceive something but neglects reflection and consideration, until he judges corrupt things to be sound, has joined the ranks of those who have no perception or understanding. Or, [he is like] one who is stubborn and hostile, making the truth false, and he is likewise.

In His words "but they do not perceive" [2:12] there is consolation for the fact that they do not perceive the truth. For whoever is among the ignorant, the knowledgeable should not be troubled by his opposition.

The discussion of His words "And when it is said to them, believe" [2:13] is like the discussion of His words "And when it is said to them, do not corrupt" [2:11], in that this sentence is connected either as a fresh resumption (isti'nāf), or as coordinated with a relative clause from His words "those who say," or as coordinated with "they lie." It is also similar in the governing element of idhā (when), in the rule of the clause after idhā, and in the implied subject (the unnamed agent) of the passive verb.

Scholars differed about who said to them "believe." Ibn ʿAbbās said it was the Companions, without specifying any one of them. Muqātil said it was a particular group from among them, namely Saʿd ibn Muʿādh, Abū Lubāba, and Usayd ibn al-Ḥuḍayr.

When Allah the Exalted forbade them from corruption, He commanded them to believe, because perfection is attained by abandoning what is not fitting and doing what is fitting. The prohibition was mentioned first because it is the more important, and because prohibitions belong to the category of abstentions, and abstentions are easier to comply with than commanded acts.

The kāf in His words "as the people believed" [2:13] is in the accusative position. Most grammarians take it as a qualifier (naʿt, adjective) of an omitted verbal noun (maṣdar), so the sense is: "believe a belief like the belief of the people." They similarly say in "he was driven on it harshly" (sīra ʿalayhi shadīdan) or "I traveled swiftly" (sirtu ḥathīthan) that shadīdan and ḥathīthan are qualifiers of an omitted verbal noun, the meaning being "he was driven on it a harsh driving" and "I traveled a swift traveling."

The view of Sībawayh, may Allah have mercy on him, is that this is not a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun, but is an accusative of circumstance (ḥāl) from the implied verbal noun understood from the preceding verb, after the implicit verb, by way of extension (ittisāʿ). It was not permitted to do so because that would lead to deleting the modified noun and putting the adjective in its place in places other than those they mentioned.

Those places are: where the adjective is specific to the class of the modified noun, as in "I passed by a writer and an engineer"; or where it functions as a predicate, as in "Zayd is standing"; or as a circumstance, as in "I passed by Zayd riding"; or as a qualifier of an adverb of place, as in "I sat near you"; or where it is used as a noun, and this is to be memorized rather than generalized, as in "al-Abṭaḥ" and "al-Abraq" (place names).

When an adjective departs from these places, it can only be a follower of the modified noun, and the noun cannot be dispensed with. Do you not see that Sībawayh prohibited "alā māʾan wa-law bāridan" (ah, water, even if cold), even if something indicating the deletion of the modified noun precedes it, but permitted "wa-law bāridan" (even if cold), because it is a circumstance? The establishment of this is in the books of grammar.

The "mā" in "as the people believed" [2:13] is verbal (maṣdariyya), meaning "like the belief of the people." So from "mā" and the verb following it, a verbal noun (maṣdar) is formed, governed in the genitive by the kāf of comparison, which is a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun or a circumstance on the two views mentioned above. When mā is verbal, its complement (ṣila, the relative clause) is a verbal sentence beginning with a fully conjugated past verb or a present verb. The rare joining of it to laysa (is not) occurs in the verse of the poet:

"By what you two were not, the people of treachery and betrayal."

It is not joined to a nominal sentence, contrary to some people, among them Abū al-Ḥajjāj al-Aʿlam, who used as evidence the words of the poet:

"We found donkeys the worst of mounts, as the Ḥabiṭāt are the worst of the Banū Tamīm."

Al-Zamakhsharī and Abū al-Baqāʾ permitted that in "mā" in His words "as (kamā) he believed," it is the "mā" that prevents the kāf from governing, like it in "rubba qāma Zayd" (perhaps Zayd stood). It should not be made preventive except where it cannot be understood as verbal, because keeping it verbal keeps the kāf in the governing role it has in it, and the kāf in that case would be like the prepositions that enter upon the verbal "mā." This is possible in "as the people believed," so it should not be made preventive.

The alif-lam in "the people" (al-nās) may be generic, so that it is as if He said: "those who are perfect in humanity." Or He expressed "the people" to mean the believers, because they are truly "the people," while whoever else has the form of a person is not among the people, for lack of discernment, as the poet said:

"He is not of the people, but he is such that the people think him to be of the people."

The alif and lam may be for specific reference (al-'ahd, a known, identified group), and the intended people are the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions. This is said by Ibn 'Abbas, or by 'Abdullah ibn Salam, or by someone similar among the Jews whose Islam was sound, as said by Muqatil. Or it refers to Mu'adh ibn Jabal, Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, Usayd ibn al-Hudayr, and a group of the notable Ansar, whom al-Kalbi enumerated. The more preferable reading is that they are for specific reference, meaning those whose faith had preceded this statement made to them. This is a referral to those whose belief came first, because they were known and familiar to the addressees, who had been commanded to believe.

The comparison in ﴿as the people believed﴾ [2:13] indicates sincerity. Otherwise, they uttered the two testimonies of faith without believing in them. *Anu'minu* (أنُؤْمِنُ, "Shall we believe?") is the object of *qalu* (they said). It is an interrogative whose meaning is denial or mockery. Since the thing commanded was comparative, their answer was comparative in their statement: ﴿Shall we believe as the fools believed?﴾ [2:13]. The discussion of the particle *ka* (كَ, "as") and what is related to it is the same as the discussion of it in ﴿as the people believed﴾ [2:13].

The alif and lam in *al-sufaha'* (السُّفَهاءُ, "the fools") are for specific reference, so it refers to the Companions, as said by Ibn 'Abbas. Or it refers to the children and women, as said by al-Hasan. Or it refers to Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions, as said by Muqatil. It is also possible that they are for generic reference (al-jins, the class as a whole), so that it includes all those whom people have interpreted as the specific referents, or those who are absolute in foolishness. Or it is because foolishness is restricted to them, since there is no fool other than them. The weakest view is that the alif and lam are for a descriptive epithet that has become dominant, like *al-'Ayyuq* and *al-Dabaran* (names of particular stars). This is because this description did not become dominant over them, so that when *al-sufaha'* is said, they would be understood as a specific group, just as *al-'Ayyuq* is understood as a specific star.

It is possible that their statement ﴿as the fools believed﴾ [2:13] was an act of obstinacy and self-control, out of fear of being mocked, while they knew they were not fools. It is also possible that it was a firm conviction held by them, so that they attributed foolishness to the believers, believing them to be fools. This is because they neglected rational reflection and sound thinking, which lead to the perception of truth. They were people of leadership and wealth, while most of the believers at that time were poor, and many of them were clients. So they believed that whoever was in this condition was among the fools, because they occupied themselves with what was of no benefit in their view, and they were lax about seeking leadership, wealth, and what brings nobility in this world. That, in their view, is the extreme of foolishness.

In their statement ﴿as the fools believed﴾ [2:13], there is an affirmation from them in their claim of the believers' foolishness that they are described by the opposite of foolishness, which is soundness of judgment and superiority of intellect. So Allah rejected their statement and established that they themselves are the fools. He began the sentence with *ala* (ألا), which is used for alerting, so that the addressees would take note that they are the fools. He emphasized this with *inna* (إنَّ) and with the word *hum* (هم, "they").

When two hamzas meet from two separate words, the first being with a *damma* and the second with a *fatha*, as in *al-sufaha' ala* (السُّفَهاءُ ألا), there are several ways of pronouncing it. The first is to pronounce both hamzas fully, and this is the reading of the Kufans and Ibn 'Amir. The second is to pronounce the first fully and soften the second by changing it into a waw, as happens when it is preceded by a *damma* within a single word, as in *u'ati* (أُؤاتِي), the present tense of *ata* (آتى), an active participle from *ataytu*, and *juʾan* (جُؤَنٍ), where one says *uwati* (أُواتِي) and *juwan* (جُوَنٌ). This is the reading of the two Haramayn (the Meccan and Medinan readers) and Abu 'Amr. The third is to soften the first hamza by making it between a hamza and a waw, and to pronounce the second fully. The fourth is to soften the first hamza by making it between a hamza and a waw, and to change the second into a waw. Some people permitted a fifth way: making the first between a hamza and a waw, and making the second between a hamza and a waw too. Some scholars forbade this, because making the second between a hamza and a waw brings it close to an alif, and an alif does not occur after a *damma*. The three pronunciations that were permitted in *hum* in ﴿they are the mischief-makers﴾ [2:12] are also permitted in *hum* in ﴿they are the fools﴾ [2:13].

The contrast implied by *wa-lakin* (وَلَكِنْ, "but") in ﴿but they do not know﴾ [2:13] is similar to its use in Allah's statement ﴿but they are not aware﴾ [2:12]. He said *la yash'urun* (لا يَشْعُرُونَ, "they are not aware") there and *la ya'lamun* (لا يَعْلَمُونَ, "they do not know") here, because what was affirmed of them there was mischief-making, which is recognized with little reflection, since it is among the perceptible things that do not require much thought. So He negated of them what is perceived by the senses, which are the sensory faculties, as an intensification of their ignorance. The awareness that may be attributed to animals is negated of them. What is affirmed here is foolishness, and what it is introduced by is the command to believe. That requires deep reflection, reasoning, and thorough consideration leading to faith and assent, and they did not carry out what was commanded. So it fits that knowledge is negated of them. Also, foolishness is lightness of intellect and ignorance of what is commanded. Al-Samaw'al said:

> We fear that our judgments will be made foolish,
> so that we become ignorant with the ignorant.
