Knowledge is the opposite of ignorance, so He contrasted it with *la ya'lamun* (they do not know), because not having knowledge of something is ignorance of it.

Ibn al-Sumayfa' al-Yamani and Abu Hanifa read: *wa-idha laqaw alladhina* (وإذا لاقَوُا الَّذِينَ, "and when they meet those who..."). The form *laqa* here is a *fa'ala* form with the meaning of the basic verb, which is one of the five meanings of the *fa'ala* pattern. The *waw* with a *damma* in this reading is the pronoun *waw*, which was moved because the letter after it was unvocalized. The omitted final radical did not return, because the *waw* was moved. Encountering can happen by appointment or without appointment. If it is without appointment, it is called a surprise or a chance meeting. Their statement to those among the believers whom they met, *amanna* (آمَنّا, "we believed"), was in the absolute form of the verb, not emphasized by anything, as an equivocation and deception on their part. It is possible that they meant by it belief in Moses and what he brought alone, and not in anything else, and that was from their wickedness and slander. It is also possible that they meant the qualified belief in their statement ﴿We believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [2:8], and they were not truthful in that. It is also possible that they meant what they showed with their tongues of belief, and of their acknowledgment at the time of meeting, and they called that belief, while their hearts were turned away from it and opposed to it.

* * *

The majority read *khalaw ila* (خَلَوْا إلى, "they went alone to") with the *waw* unvocalized and the hamza pronounced fully. Warsh read it by transferring the vowel of the hamza onto the *waw* and dropping the hamza. *Khala* is transitive with *bi* and with *ila*, and *bi* is more common in usage. *Ila* was chosen because when the verb is used with *bi*, it can have two meanings: one is being alone, and the other is mocking, since in the language one says *khalawtu bihi*, meaning "I mocked him." *Ila* carries only one meaning. Here *ila* keeps its meaning of ending point, with the verb implicitly carrying the sense of directing, that is: they turned their being alone toward their devils. Al-Akhfash said: "*khalawtu ilayhi*" means "I made him the goal of my need." This is an explanation of meaning. Some people, including al-Nadr ibn Shumayl, claimed that *ila* here means *ma'a* (مَعَ, "with"), that is, "and when they were alone with their devils," just as they claimed in Allah's statement ﴿do not consume their wealth along with your wealth﴾ [4:2] and ﴿who are my helpers toward Allah﴾ [3:52], meaning "with your wealth" and "with Allah." From this is the verse of al-Nabigha:

> So do not leave me to threats, as if I were
> with the people, smeared with tar, mangy.

And there is no proof in any of that. It has also been said that "إلى" (ilā) here means "الباء" (bā', "with"), since prepositions (ḥurūf al-jarr) may stand in for one another. This view is weak, because Sibawayh and al-Khalil do not hold that one preposition can substitute for another. The detailed discussion belongs in grammar works.

"Their shayāṭīn" (shayāṭīnuhum) refers to the Jews who used to order them to deny the truth. This is what Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said. Or it refers to their leaders in disbelief, as Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) said. It is also related from Ibn 'Abbas: or it refers to the devils of the jinn, as al-Kalbi said. Or it refers to their soothsayers (kahana, "diviners who claim knowledge of the unseen"), as al-Ḍaḥḥak and a group said.

In the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) there was a group of soothsayers among them: Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf of the Banu Qurayẓa, Abu Burda of the Banu Aslam, 'Abd al-Dar of Juhayna, 'Awf ibn 'Amir of the Banu Asad, and Ibn al-Sawda' in Syria. The Arabs believed that these people had access to knowledge of the unseen, knew secrets, and healed the sick. They were called "shayāṭīn" (devils) because of their rebelliousness and obstinacy, or after their companions among the devils, if they are explained as soothsayers, or because of their resemblance to devils in whispering, deceiving, making immoral acts appear attractive, and making good things appear ugly.

The majority read the vowel of the ʿayn in "maʿakum" with a kasra-type vocalisation as usual. In an irregular reading it was recited "innā maʿakum", which is the dialect of the tribes of Ghanm and Rabi'a. The two statements of these people differ. They said to the believers, "We have believed," but to their devils they said, "Indeed we are with you." Note the difference between the two statements. When they met the believers, they said "āmannā" (we believed) as a bare report, without emphasis, as already mentioned, because their aim was to report that this faith had arisen and come from their side. They did not claim to be unique in it. Or it is because their tongues would not willingly say it, since they had no real motive for faith. Or it is because if they had emphasised it, it would not have been accepted by the believers, so they settled for a plain statement of faith. This differs from what Allah reported of the believers when He said: ﴿Our Lord, indeed we have believed﴾ (Āl ʿImrān 16).

When they met their devils, or were alone with them, they said, "Indeed we are with you." They informed them that they agreed with them. They expressed this report as a nominal sentence (jumla ismiyya) emphasised with "inna", to show by it that they were steadfast in their religion. Then they made clear that what they told the believers was only by way of mockery. They did not stop at reporting agreement, but made clear that the reason for what they said to the believers was only mockery and contempt, not that this came from them out of sincerity and earnestness. They expressed this in a nominal sentence emphasised with "innamā", where the subject is described by an active participle (ism al-fā'il) which indicates permanence. The mockery is a permanent attribute of theirs, not something newly arising in them. Rather, it is part of their character and habit toward the believers.

It seems this sentence was a reply to someone rebuking them for their statement "Indeed we are with you." It is as if he had said: How can you claim you are with us while you make peace with the believers, believe them, increase their numbers, face their qibla, and eat their slaughtered animals? So they answered with their words: ﴿Indeed we are mockers﴾ (al-Baqarah 14), meaning: we make light of them. We placate them with what we show of that, to protect our blood, our wealth and our offspring. So we agree with them outwardly and agree with you inwardly.

The speaker of "Indeed we are with you" is either the hypocrites' leaders, or all the hypocrites in relation to the disbelievers.

"Mustahzi'ūn" (mockers) is also recited with the hamza clearly pronounced, which is the original form. It is also recited with the hamza changed to a ya' with damma, because the letter before it has a kasra. Some drop the ya' and treat it like an original ya' as in "yarmūna", so the ra' is vowelled with damma. Sibawayh (may Allah have mercy on him) held that in pronouncing it the hamza should be made "bayna bayn" (an intermediate sound between hamza and ya'). Abu al-Hasan (al-Akhfash) held that it should be changed to ya' in a sound, regular way. Abu al-Fath said: the status of the damma-ed ya' is unusual, like that of the damma-ed hamza. The Arabs dislike a damma-ed ya' preceded by a kasra. Most reciters follow what Sibawayh held.

Is the "being together" (ijtimā' and ma'iyya) here in religion, or in support and help against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions, or in agreement with the disbelievers in keeping informed about the condition of the believers and informing them of what they plan and hide of schemes, or in agreement with the disbelievers in harming the Muslims, waiting for misfortunes to befall them, rejoicing at what grieves the Muslims, grieving at what pleases them, and intending to extinguish the word of Allah? There are four views. (p-70)

The motives for mockery are: fear of harm, seeking gain, jesting, and play. Allah, exalted is He, is far above all that, so it is not correct to attribute to Allah a mockery whose motives are these. Therefore, it is possible that the mockery attributed to Allah, exalted is He, is a metaphor for requiting them, and the name of mockery is applied to requital so that it may be known that this is the recompense for mockery. Or it is a metaphor for His dealing with them in the same way they dealt with the believers. So He applied to them the rulings of the believers, such as preserving their blood, protecting their property, and giving them a share of the spoils, even though He knew they were disbelievers. The name of a thing may be applied to something resembling it in form but not in meaning. Or it is a metaphor for allowing them room and leaving them ignorant, because they persisted in their disbelief. He called giving them room "mockery" because He did not hasten their punishment, but granted them respite and delayed them until the Hereafter. Or it is a metaphor for opening the gate of Paradise: they hasten toward it, and it is shut, and the believers laugh at them. Or it is a metaphor for the extinguishing of the fire: they walk toward it, and then they are swallowed up by the earth. Or it is a metaphor for the wall erected between them and the believers, the wall mentioned in al-Hadid. Or it is a metaphor for His saying: ﴿Taste, indeed you are the mighty, the noble﴾ (al-Dukhān 49). Or it is a metaphor for Allah bestowing upon them a blessing each time they commit a sin, so they think that this is because Allah loves them. Or it is a metaphor for the barrier between the hypocrites and the light given to the believers, as some have mentioned from a hadith. Or it is a metaphor for their being driven away from Paradise: when some of them are called toward Paradise, they approach it, smell its fragrance, and see what Allah has prepared in it for its people. This is a lengthy hadith related from 'Adi ibn Hatim. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan also took this direction.

Setting Allah's mockery of them against their mockery of the believers indicates the great status of the believers and the high rank they hold. It also lets the hypocrites know that it is Allah who defends the believers and wages war against those who wage war against them. In beginning the sentence with the name of Allah there is great exaltation, since the sentence opens with it. The predicate is a present-tense verb, which according to them indicates renewal and repetition, so it is more emphatic in attribution than the mockery they reported in their words. Furthermore, in this wording there is an explicit mention of those whom Allah mocks, since the verb is transitive to them: "yastahzi'u bihim" (He mocks them). When they attributed mockery to themselves, they did not specify who was the object of their mockery. They did not say: "Indeed we are mockers of them," and this was to avoid conveying that to the believers, lest the believers resent it. So they left the wording open to the possibility that, if they were held to account for it, they could defend themselves by saying they had not mocked the believers. Do you not see their concern to protect themselves in their words: "We believe in Allah and the Last Day," and in their words: "When they meet the believers they say, 'We believe'"? When they meet them, they cannot show the concealment of their true feelings, nor share with them what they dislike. Rather they display obedience and submission.

Ibn Muḥayṣin and Shibl read "yamudduhum" (He extends them). It is also transmitted from Ibn Kathir. Attributing the extension to Allah is literal, since He is the originator of things and the sole creator of them. The meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, prolongs for them their transgression.

Al-Zamakhshari went to the interpretation of the extension attributed to Allah, exalted is He, as meaning that He withholds kindnesses from them and forsakes them because of their disbelief and persistence. Their hearts remain, and the darkness in them increases just as the light increases in the hearts of the believers. So that increase is called extension, and it is attributed to Allah because it is caused by His action toward them because of their disbelief. Or the extension means compulsion and coercion. He said: Or the action of the devil is attributed to Allah because by His enabling and empowering him, and by leaving him free to mislead His servants, it is so. He went for the interpretation of extension only because Allah's extending them in transgression is ugly, and Allah is far above doing what is ugly. The first interpretation that al-Zamakhshari mentioned is the view of al-Ka'bi and Abu Muslim. Al-Jubba'i said: it is extension in life span. In our view, Allah is the creator of good and evil, and He is the guider and the misleader.

The discussion of something similar has already been made when the verse ﴿Allah has set a seal upon their hearts﴾ (al-Baqarah 7) was addressed. "Allah's extending them in their transgression" means enabling them in disobedience. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud. Or it means giving them respite, as Ibn 'Abbas said. Or it means increase in transgression, as Mujahid said. Or it means granting a delay, as al-Zajjaj and Ibn Kaysan said. Or it means multiplying wealth and children, making life pleasant, prolonging life spans, keeping bodies healthy, averting calamities, and increasing provision.

Zayd ibn 'Ali read "fī ṭughyānihim" with a kasra on the ṭā', which is a dialect form. It is said: ṭughyān with damma and with kasra, just as they say luqyān and ghīnān, with damma and with kasra. Al-Kisa'i inclined the vowel in "fī ṭughyānihim" (toward ē), and he attributed the transgression to them because it is their act and their earning. Every act that proceeds from the servant may rightly be attributed to him by direct performance, and to Allah by creation.

What is explained as "ʿamah" (blind wandering) may be understood from His saying: ﴿wandering blindly﴾ (al-Baqarah 15). So the meaning is: they waver and are bewildered, or they go blind to their right guidance, or they ride their heads and do not see. Some exegetes said: this last explanation is closer to the truth, because they were not wavering in their disbelief. Rather, they were persisting in it, believing it to be the truth and everything else to be falsehood.

"Ya'mahūn" (wandering blindly) is a clause in the place of a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), in the accusative as a ḥāl. It may be a ḥāl from the pronoun in "yamuddhum", or from the pronoun in "ṭughyānihim", since it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) attached to its agent. "Fī ṭughyānihim" may be connected to "yamuddhum", or it may be connected to "ya'mahūn".

Abu al-Baqa' prohibited that "fī ṭughyānihim" and "ya'mahūn" both be ḥāls from the pronoun in "yamuddhum", saying: because the governing word does not govern two ḥāls. End of his words.

What he held needs qualification: the two ḥāls must belong to one bearer. If they belong to two different bearers, it is permitted, as in: "I met Zayd going up and coming down." But if they belong to one bearer, as we have stated, then there is disagreement about whether this is allowed. Some held that it is not permitted, just as a governing word cannot govern two verbal nouns, two time adverbs, or two place adverbs; so likewise it cannot govern two ḥāls. Those who held this view limited the rule to cases where the second is not in apposition or conjoined. If they are like that, the matter is allowed. Some of them said: except the elative form (ism al-tafḍīl), since it governs two time adverbs, two place adverbs, and two ḥāls for one bearer, which is allowed. This view was preferred by Abu al-Hasan ibn 'Usfur.

Others held that the governing word may govern two ḥāls for one bearer, and I incline to this view, because an act proceeding from an agent, or befalling an object, cannot occur at two times or in two places. Two ḥāls, however, cannot be impossible for one bearer to have together, unless they are opposites or contradictories. So you may say: "Zayd came laughing, riding," since his coming is not impossible while he is characterised by these two ḥāls. Based on the distinction we have established, two ḥāls may come for one bearer while the governing word for both is one.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 16 (part 5 of 6):

*Ulaʾika* (those) is a demonstrative noun referring to those previously mentioned, who combined the blameworthy attributes of claiming to reform while being corruptors, of attributing foolishness to the believers while they themselves are the foolish ones, and of belittling the believers by showing agreement with them while being with the disbelievers. Al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read *ishtaraw al-dalalah* with a *damma* on the *waw*. Abu al-Simak Qa'nab al-Adawi read it with a *fatha*. The *damma* on the *waw* has four aspects, which are mentioned in grammar (*nahw*). The *kasra* is the original vowel when two unvoweled letters meet (*iltiqa' al-sakinayn*), as in ﴿And that if they had remained upright﴾ (al-Jinn 72:16). The *fatha* follows the *fatha* that precedes it. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i inclined *al-huda* (imalah, pronouncing the *fatha* toward a *kasra*), which is the dialect of Banu Tamim, while the rest read it with a *fatha*, which is the dialect of Quraysh.

*Al-ishtira'* (buying) here is a figurative usage (*majaz*). It is used as a metonym for choosing, because the one who buys something has chosen it and prefers it. It is as if He said: they chose misguidance over guidance. Their being enabled to follow guidance is treated as the price offered for the goods. The reason for taking *al-ishtira'* in a figurative sense is that there is no exchange (*mu'awadah*), which means replacing something in your hand with something in another's hand, and this is absent here. Some people have held that *al-ishtira'* here is literal and not figurative, and that the exchange is realized. They attempted to establish this, but it cannot be established, because in every case the buying is interpreted as figurative. They said: if the verse means the hypocrites, as Mujahid said, then they had an apparent guidance in pronouncing the testimony of faith, performing the prayer, paying the zakat, fasting, joining raids and fighting. When their inner selves did not affirm their outer conduct and they chose disbelief, they exchanged guidance for error, so the exchange was realized, and buying and selling occurred literally. This was one of the kinds of *bay' al-mu'atah* (sale by mutual giving and taking) that do not require a verbal formula. They also said: since they were born upon the *fitrah* (natural disposition) and its ruling continued for them until puberty and the threshold of legal responsibility, they exchanged it for disbelief and hypocrisy, so the exchange was realized. They also said: since they were people of intellect able to reflect correctly, which leads to knowing right from wrong, they exchanged this precious capacity for following desire and blindly imitating their fathers, despite the clear evidence, so the exchange was realized. They said: and if the verse means the People of the Book, as Qatadah said, then they were believers in God and the Last Day, affirming the sending of the Prophet ﷺ, seeking victory through him, invoking his sanctity, and threatening the disbelievers with his coming, so they were truly believers. When the Prophet ﷺ was sent and migrated to Medina, they feared for their leadership, their livelihood, and the turning away of followers from them. So they denied his prophethood, said that what was described was not what they had, and altered his description. They exchanged the faith for the disbelief that had come to them, so the exchange was realized. They said: and if the verse means all the disbelievers, as Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas said, then the exchange is also realized, either through the period in which they were upon the *fitrah* before they disbelieved, or because the disbelievers had the three sources of knowledge: the sensory, the rational, and the reported (*al-hissi*, *al-nazari*, *al-sam'i*), which yield certain knowledge, and they exchanged these for following the ways of their fathers in disbelief. Ibn Kaysan said: He created them for His worship, so they exchanged this pleasing creation for their disbelief. His statement is weak, because if He had created them for His worship, none of them would have disbelieved, since it is impossible for Him to create something for a purpose and for that thing to fail to fulfil it. The discussion of His saying ﴿Except that they may worship Me﴾ (al-Dhariyat 51:56), and of ﴿And for that He created them﴾ (Hud 11:119), will come, God willing.

Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: *al-dalalah* is disbelief and *al-huda* is faith. It has been said: *al-dalalah* is doubt and *al-huda* is certainty. It has been said: ignorance and knowledge. It has been said: division and community. It has been said: this world and the Hereafter. It has been said: the Fire and the Garden.

The conjunction of *fa-ma ribihat* (so their commerce did not profit) with the particle *fa* indicates that the negation of profit follows the act of buying, and that by the very act of buying the absence of profit is established. Some people have claimed that the *fa* in His saying ﴿so their commerce did not profit﴾ entered because the sentence carries the meaning of a condition (*shart*), and the intended sense is "those who bought." The relative pronoun *alladhina* (those who), when it governs a verb in its relative clause, carries the meaning of a condition, like ﴿those who spend their wealth﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:261), where the answer to it is introduced by *fa* in His saying ﴿then they will have their reward﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:262). Likewise, "the one who enters the house, then for him is a dirham." This is an error, because *alladhina* is not a subject (*mubtada'*) that would be compared to a conditional subject, after which *fa* enters the predicate as it enters the answer of the condition. As for *alladhina* being the predicate of *ulaʾika*, and His saying *fa-ma ribihat* not being a predicate, the *fa* does not enter it. Rather, it is a verbal sentence coordinated with the relative clause of *alladhina*, so it is part of the relative clause, because what is coordinated with a relative clause is also a relative clause. Likewise, the claim that the answer is introduced by *fa* in His saying ﴿then they will have their reward﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:62) is an error, because it is not an answer. Rather, the sentence is the predicate of the subject *yunfiquna* (they spend). It is not permissible for *ulaʾika* to be a subject with *alladhina ishtaraw* as a subject and *fa-ma ribihat tijaratuhum* as the predicate about *alladhina*, with *alladhina* and its predicate being the predicate of *ulaʾika*, because this sentence, which is the predicate of *ulaʾika*, has no connecting pronoun. Since the relative clause's past time is established, and when the relative clause has past meaning, the *fa* does not enter the predicate of its relative subject. It is also impermissible for *ulaʾika* to be a subject with *alladhina* in apposition (*badal*) to it and *fa-ma ribihat* as the predicate, because the predicate is only introduced by *fa* when the relative pronoun is general. Since *alladhina* is in apposition to *ulaʾika*, it becomes specific, because it is an apposition to something specific, and the predicate of something specific does not take *fa*. Moreover, the meaning of the verse permits only that *ulaʾika* is the subject and *alladhina* is the predicate about it.

Attributing profit to commerce is figurative, because the one who profits or loses is the merchant, not the commerce. Since he depicted misguidance and guidance as a purchase and a price, he developed this striking metaphor with His saying ﴿so their commerce did not profit﴾. This is from the category of *tarshih al-majaz* (developing a metaphor), which is to present the metaphor in the form of a literal reality and then to judge it by some attributes of the literal reality, so that one figurative usage is added to another. Among this is the poet's saying:

*The fur wept over Rawh, and its skin denied it,*
*and the mantles cried out loudly against Judham.*

He made the fur stand in for a person who came into contact with Rawh and wept at his lack of reproach, then he developed it with "and its skin denied it," then he added to the development of the metaphor with "and cried out," meaning the mantles of fur, from the tribe of Rawh, which is Judham, shouted. The meaning of the verse is that Rawh and his tribe Judham are not fit to wear fur and its mantles, because they have no custom of doing so. So he expressed the incongruity between them by what he expressed in the verse. Among this is al-Shafi'i's saying, may God be pleased with him:

*O owl who has built her nest upon my head,*
*despite me, since her raven has flown away.*

Since he expressed white hair by the owl, he turned to her and addressed her. He developed this metaphor with "has built her nest," because building a nest is one of the actions of a bird. Al-Zamakhshari has cited an example of developing a metaphor in his *Kashshaf*.

Ibn Abi Ablah read *tijaratuhum* in the plural, and its basis is that each one of them has a commerce. The reading of al-Jumhur in the singular is because the singular suffices for the plural, since the meaning is understood. In His saying *fa-ma ribihat tijaratuhum* (so their commerce did not profit) there is an indication that the principal capital was not wholly lost, because He only negated profit, and negation of profit does not indicate a reduction of the principal. This has been answered: He was content to mention the absence of profit instead of mentioning the loss of wealth, because the meaning is indicated in the discourse. Misguidance is the opposite of guidance, and opposites cannot coexist. Their exchange of misguidance for guidance indicates the complete loss of guidance. In my view, this is to be understood in the manner of His poet's saying:

*On a well-worn path whose landmark one cannot be guided by,*

meaning that there is no landmark for it by which one may be guided. He negated guidance while intending to negate the landmark, and the negation of the landmark entails the negation of being guided by it. Similarly in this verse, when He mentioned the purchase of one thing with another, one might suppose that what they did was a form of commerce, since commerce is not merely the act of buying, and they were not merchants. Commerce is rather the disposal of wealth to obtain growth and increase. So He negated profit. The intended meaning is the negation of commerce, that is, it should not be supposed that this purchase they made was commerce, since it is not commerce. And if it is not commerce, profit is negated. It is as if He said: they have neither commerce nor profit.

Al-Zamakhshari said: its meaning is that what merchants seek in their dealings is two things: the safety of the principal and profit. These people have lost both goals together, because their principal capital was guidance. Once only misguidance remained in their hands, they could not be described as attaining profit, even if they obtained some worldly advantages, because misguidance is a loser and destroyed, and one whose principal is not preserved is not said to have profited. That is the end of his words. Nevertheless, this is not a fully satisfactory answer, because the negation of profit from commerce does not indicate the loss of all the wealth, nor a loss within it, since profit is the surplus over the principal. When profit is negated, it does not indicate the loss of the principal entirely, nor its reduction, which is the loss.

It has been said: since His saying ﴿so their commerce did not profit﴾ does not indicate the loss of their principal capitals, He followed it with His saying ﴿and they were not guided﴾, so the meaning is completed by that, and the intended purpose is fulfilled. This type of explanation is called *al-tatmim* (completion), and from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*As if the eyes of wild cattle around our tents and our feet were beads of onyx that has not been pierced.*

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 16 (part 6 of 6):

He completed the meaning with His saying: "who has not been pierced," and completed the description. God, exalted is He, named their exchanging guidance for misguidance a "trade" (tijarah), although trade is the buying and selling from which profit is actually realized, or from which such profit is hoped. This exchange is negated of them, because disbelief nullifies deeds. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We shall turn to what they did of deeds, and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan: 23], and so on. In a hadith, he (ﷺ) was asked about Ibn Ju'dan, whether his maintaining ties of kinship and feeding the poor would benefit him. He said: "No, for he never said, 'My Lord, forgive me my sin on the Day of Judgment.'" This is because they only exchanged that (guidance for misguidance) when they were certain of it and hoped for worldly and otherworldly benefits from it. Do you not see their saying: "We are the sons of God and His beloved," and their saying: ﴿And we will not be punished﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 138]? The Jews used to claim that they would not be punished except for a number of days, some of them saying one day, and some saying ten, and every group of the disbelievers claimed that it was upon the truth and that others were upon falsehood. So, for the sake of attaining worldly comfort and hoping for otherworldly comfort, He named their purchasing of misguidance with guidance a "trade," and God, exalted is He, negated from them that they were guided.

Is the meaning "they were not guided in God's knowledge," or "not guided out of misguidance," or "not for a profitable trade," or "not in buying misguidance," or did He negate from them both guidance and profit? For among merchants there are those who do not profit in their trade yet remain upon guidance and uprightness, whereas these combined the negation of profit and of guidance. What I choose is that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And they were not guided﴾ is an informing that these people had never previously possessed guidance in actuality, lest it be supposed from His saying "with guidance" that they had been upon guidance in the past. So His saying ﴿and they were not guided﴾ clarifies the figurative sense of His saying "with guidance," and it shows that what they exchanged misguidance for is only the capacity to perceive guidance. Thus the affirmed element in the exchange is other than the element negated at the end, because the former is potential and the latter is actual.

The accusative of muhtadin (guided) is as the predicate of kana, so it is governed by kana alone, contrary to one who claimed it is governed by kana and its noun together, and contrary to one who claimed its original status is as a circumstantial accusative (hal), and that is al-Farra', who said: because the noun is occupied by the raising of kana, but when the benefit has been achieved through it, it became a predicate in the sense of a hal, so it came definite, and it is said: "kana akhuka Zaydan," giving priority to the predicate rather than to the hal.

The exegetes mentioned several views regarding the occasion of revelation of these verses. The first: they were revealed concerning the hypocrites. The second: concerning a people whose description God informed of before their existence, and in this is an announcement of unseen matters. The third: concerning Abdullah ibn Ubayy and his companions. It was revealed: ﴿And when they meet those who believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 14], and the preceding verse concerns all the hypocrites. They mentioned something to the effect that he met a group of believers and said to his companions: "See how I turn these fools away from you." He is reported to have praised and extolled Abu Bakr, Umar and Ali, whereupon Ali rebuked him and said to him: "Do not be a hypocrite." He said: "To me you say this? By God, our faith is like your faith." Then they separated, and Abdullah said to his companions: "How did you see me act?" and they praised him greatly. Other opinions than these three have already been mentioned in the course of the discussion before this.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 17:**

﴿Their likeness is like the likeness of one who kindled a fire, and when it illuminated what was around him, Allah took away their light and left them in darkness, unable to see.﴾

The word *al-mathal* (parable, similitude) in the basic usage of the Arabs means *al-mithl* and *al-mathil*, like *shabah*, *shibh* and *shabih*, and it means the equivalent. *Al-mathal* and *al-mithl* are pluralized as *amthal*. Al-Yazidi said: *al-amthal* means *al-ashbah* (the likenesses). The origin of *al-mathal* is description: "this is the likeness of that," meaning its description is equal to the description of the other in some respect. *Al-mathal* is a saying that circulates and has some strangeness in certain respects. It has been said: *al-mathal* is the mention of an apparent description, sensible or non-sensible, by which one is guided to a description similar to it in some respects, in which there is some kind of obscurity, so that it becomes in the mind equal to the first in clarity from one aspect but not from another. The purpose of mentioning a parable is that it affects the hearts in a way that the mere description of a thing in itself does not, because the aim of coining a parable is to liken the hidden to the manifest and the absent to the present, so that the grasp of its reality is confirmed and the senses come into agreement with the intellect.

*Alladhi* (who/that): a relative pronoun for the masculine singular. It has been transmitted from Abu Ali that it is *mubham* (indefinite in reference), functioning like *man* in referring to the singular and the plural. Al-Akhfash said: it is singular, but it may have the meaning of the plural, and this is similar to the statement of Abu Ali. The author of *al-Tashil* (Ibn Malik), when mentioning it, mentioned *alladhina* (those who), and said: *alladhi* substitutes for it frequently without specification, and rarely with it out of necessity. Our companions say: it is permissible to delete the *nun* from *alladhina* so that *alladhi* remains. When *alladhi* refers to a singular, it is heard with a doubled *ya'* either kasra or damma, and with the deletion of the *ya'* while keeping the *dhal* either kasra or sukun. Most of our companions hold that these are dialects of *alladhi*. (p-75)

*Al-istiqad*: with the meaning of *al-iqad* (kindling) and seeking that. *Wuqud al-nar* is the rising of its flame. *Al-nar* (fire) is a subtle, luminous, hot, burning substance.

*Lamma*: a negative particle that operates in jussive mood, and it has the meaning of *illa* (except), and an adverb meaning "when" according to al-Farisi. The answer (the apodosis) governs it, since the clause after it is in a position of genitive. It is a particle of necessity for necessity according to Sibawayh, and this is the correct view, because it precedes what is negated by *ma*, and because its answer comes introduced by *idha* al-fuja'iyya (the sudden *idha*).

*Al-idae'*: *al-ishraq* (shining), which is the excess of illumination.

*Hawlahu*: an adverb of place that does not inflect. It is said *hawalin* with the same meaning, and both are dualized and pluralized as *ahwal*, and all of them do not inflect and necessarily take a genitive construction (idafa).

*Al-dhahab*: *al-intilaq* (departing).

*Al-nur*: the light from every luminous thing, and its opposite is darkness. It is said *nara yanuru* when he fled, and *jariya nawwar*, that is, shy (fleeing); and from it is the name of the wife of al-Farazdaq. It was called *nur* because there is in it agitation and movement.

*Al-tark*: *al-takhliya* (leaving). *Utruk hadha*, that is, leave it, let it be and abandon it. Regarding its implication of the meaning of *al-tasyir* (making) and its transitivity to two objects, there is disagreement; the most correct view is that this is permissible.

*Al-zulma*: the absence of light. It has been said: it is an accident that opposes light, and this is the more correct view, because the act of making in the sense of creating is connected to it, and nonexistences are not described as created. Some have rejected this in favor of the meaning of *al-zulm* (wrongdoing), which is prevention, and he said: because darkness blocks sight and prevents vision.

*Al-ibsar*: seeing (vision).

Deaf, dumb, and blind, so they will not return. *Jumu' kathra* (plural of abundance) on the pattern *fu'ul*, which is the regular pattern for the plural of *fa'la'* and *af'al* when the two descriptive forms are opposed, as in *ahmar* and *hamra'* (red), or when only the physical defect is expressed, as in *'adhal* and *ratq*. If the adjective is shared but the two forms are not used in the pattern of *ahmar* and *hamra'*, as with *rajul aly* (a man with a short, stiff neck) and *imra'a 'ajza'* (a woman with a large rear), then *fa'ala* is not used analogically for it and must be learned by transmission.

*Al-samam* (deafness) is a condition in the ear that blocks the veins and prevents hearing. Its root meaning is hardness, as in they say *qanat samma'* (a hard, solid reed). It is also said that its root meaning is blocking, as in *sammamtu al-qarura* (I stopped up the bottle). *Al-bakam* (muteness) is an affliction in the tongue that prevents speech; this is the view of Abu Hatim. It is also said to be one born mute, and it is also said to be one who does not understand speech and does not find the right way, in which case it is a disease of the heart and not of the tongue. *Al-'ama* (blindness) is darkness in the eye that prevents perception of visible things. Its verb is on the pattern *fa'ila* with the eye vowelled with a kasra, and the active participle is on the pattern *af'al*, which is the analogical pattern for afflictions and defects. *Al-ruju'* (returning), if intransitive, means "return," and if transitive, means "restoring." Some grammarians say it is construed with the meaning of *sara* (to become), so it belongs to the class of *kana* (to be), raising the subject and putting the predicate in the accusative. Al-Zamakhshari said: When He came with the reality of their description, He followed it with the mention of a parable, as an addition to clarification and a completion of the explanation. The Arabs' use of parables, and the scholars' citing of examples and analogues, is a matter that is not hidden in bringing out the hidden meanings and lifting the veils from realities, so that you see the imagined in the form of the established, the supposed in the guise of the certain, and the absent as if present. In it there is a rebuke to the fierce adversary and a suppression of the rebellious, stubborn one. For some reason God has multiplied such parables in His Clear Book and in all His other books, and they spread in the speech of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and in the speech of the prophets and the wise. God the Exalted said: ﴿And these parables We set forth for mankind, but none understands them except the knowers﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 43]. Among the surahs of the Gospel are the surahs of parables. End of his words.

*Mathaluhum* is the subject (*mubtada'*), and the predicate (*khabar*) is the prepositional phrase after it. The estimated sense is "is like," as that is estimated in all the prepositions.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: the predicate is the *ka* (like), and in this case it is a noun, as it is in the verse of al-A'sha:

Will you desist, when the one who exceeds the bounds will not desist? Like a spear-thrust in which oil and wick go away.

End of his words.

What he chose and began with is not the preferred view. It is the view of Abu al-Hasan, that *ka* may be a noun in eloquent speech. We have already stated that we do not permit this except in poetic necessity. Ibn 'Atiyya mentioned the view we began with after mentioning the view he chose. He considered far-fetched the one who claimed that *ka* is redundant, like it in His saying: ﴿So He made them like a stalk eaten up﴾ [al-Fil: 5]. What led him to that, and God knows best, is that once it was settled for him that *mathal* and *mithl* have the same meaning, the sense became one of redundancy, since the meaning is the comparison of a *mathal* to a *mithl*, not to the *mithl* of a *mithl*. Here *mathal* means a story or matter, so He compared their state and described them with the description of one who kindles a fire. On this view, *ka* is not redundant.

As for the aspects of resemblance between them and the one who kindled a fire, there are several aspects that they mentioned. The first: the one who kindles a fire wards off harm with it, and when it goes out, harm reaches him. So too the hypocrite protects his blood by Islam and makes it lawful by unbelief. The second: he is guided by it, and when it goes out he goes astray. So too the hypocrite is guided by Islam, and when he is exposed in his hypocrisy the light of Islam leaves him and he returns to the darkness of his unbelief. The third: if he does not feed it with fuel, its light is gone. So too the hypocrite, if he does not sustain faith, his faith goes. The fourth: the one who is illuminated by it has his light from another source, not from himself. When the fire goes out, he remains in darkness. So too the hypocrite, since he professed with his tongue without belief in his heart, the light of his faith is like a borrowed one. The fifth: God likened their turning to the Muslims to illumination and their turning to the polytheists to departure. This was said by Mujahid. The sixth: He likened the guidance they sold to the light obtained by the one who kindled the fire, and the error they bought to darkness. The seventh: it is a parable God struck for the hypocrite, because he showed Islam, so it protected his blood and he walked in its sanctity and its light, then in the Hereafter He would take it from him when he needed it. This meaning was narrated from al-Hasan. These statements are based on the view that this was revealed concerning the hypocrites, and it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, and Muqatil.

It is narrated from Ibn Jubayr, 'Ata', Muhammad ibn Ka'b, and Yaman ibn Ri'ab that it concerns the Jews. Then the aspects of resemblance are as follows. The first: the one who kindles a fire is illuminated by its light and feels at ease, and the terror of darkness leaves him. The Jews, when they used to announce the Prophet (ﷺ) and seek victory through him over their enemies, and were helped through him, He likened their state to the state of one who kindles a fire. When he was sent and they disbelieved in him, God took that light away from them. The second: He likened the fire of war they kindled against the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to the fire of the one who kindles, and its extinguishing to the going away of the light of the one who kindles. The third: He likened what they used to recite in the Torah concerning the name of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), his description, the description of his community, his religion, and their command to follow him, to the light obtained by the one who kindles a fire. When they altered his name and description, changed the Torah, and denied it, God took away from them the light of that faith.

The discussion of *alladhi* has already been treated. The statement of al-Farisi, that it follows the pattern of *man* in the singular and plural, was mentioned, and the statement of al-Akhfash, that it is singular in meaning and plural, was mentioned. What we choose is that it is singular in form, though in meaning it is a descriptive phrase for what is below it, which includes individuals. The estimate then is "like the group who kindled a fire," as in one of the two interpretations of the saying:

And truly those whose blood was spilled at Falj...

It should not be taken as singular in form and meaning, with the plural pronoun in "God took away their light" and its plural in "their blood." As for the one who claims that *alladhi* here is *alladhina* with the nun dropped because of the length of the relative clause, this is an error, because the pronoun is singular in the reason given, and the singular pronoun is not permitted, since what is omitted is like what is spoken. Do you not see its plural in His saying (p. 77) the Exalted: ﴿And you plunged as those who plunged﴾ [al-Tawba: 69], on one of the two interpretations, and its plural in the poet's saying:

O Lord of 'Abs, do not bless any of them, neither the one who stands nor the one who sits,
except those who stood at the ends of the palm-fiber rope.

As for al-Farisi's statement that it is like *man*, that is not so, because *alladhi* has a form for the singular, dual, and plural, unlike *man*. The word *man* is always singular and masculine, but *alladhi* is not. Al-Zamakhshari made that like His saying: ﴿And you plunged as those who plunged﴾ [al-Tawba: 69], and justified this by two points. He said: One is that *alladhi*, because it is a link to the description of every definite noun, and because its relative clause is extended, deserves to be lightened, and for this reason they reduced it by deletion. They dropped its *ya'*, then its kasra, then they restricted it to the *lam* in the active and passive participles. What he mentioned, that they dropped it until they restricted it to the *lam*, though some grammarians had preceded him to it, is an error, because if the *lam* were the remainder of *alladhi*, it would have a place in inflection, as *alladhi* had, and the governing word would not reach the point of affecting the relative clause itself, raising, putting in the accusative, or putting in the genitive, and its clause would be joined to sentences as the relative *alladhi* is joined when its *ya'* is retained or dropped. He said: The second is that its plural is not like the plural of other nouns with *waw* and *nun*; that is only a sign of added indication. Do you not see that all the relative pronouns have the same form for singular and plural? End of his words. What he mentioned, that its plural is not like the plural of others with *waw* and *nun*, is correct in terms of form. As for meaning, it is not so; rather it is like them in meaning. Do you not see that it is used only of those who combine the conditions of what is pluralized with *waw* and *nun*, namely masculinity and reason? There is no difference between *alladhina yaf'aluna* and *al-fa'iluna* in that it is only the plural of a masculine rational being. But since it is indeclinable, a single pattern was adopted for it in form by most Arabs. The Hudhayl tribe used a plural form for it with *waw* and *nun* in the nominative, and *ya'* and *nun* in the accusative and genitive. All the Arabs adopted plural agreement for the pronoun referring back to it from its relative clause, just as it refers back to the plural masculine rational noun. All this shows that what he mentioned does not justify placing *alladhi* in the position of *alladhina* except under the interpretation we mentioned, namely the intention of plurality or kind. Al-Zamakhshari eventually returned to that.

* *

Ibn al-Sumayfa' recited: *ka-mathali alladhina* (like the parable of those who), in the plural. This reading is problematic, because we have stated that when *alladhi* has *alladhina* as its origin and its nun is dropped for lightness, the pronoun referring back to it is only plural, as with a plural noun. How, then, when it is explicitly plural? If this reading is sound, then in my view its explanation has several aspects. The first: the singular pronoun is used in agreement with the assumption that is customary in Arabic speech, as if he had said *man alladhi* with both form and meaning, just as one who assumes he has said *man* in the conditional form jussives *alladhi*. If that assumption can occur between things that differ in their boundaries, namely treating the relative pronoun in the jussive like the conditional noun, then it is all the more likely to occur between things that agree in their boundaries, namely *alladhina* and *man* as relatives. An example of jussive use with *alladhi* is the poet's saying, which Ibn al-A'rabi recited:

Thus is the one who oppresses people unjustly; the consequences of what he has done will befall him despite himself.

The second: the singular pronoun may be used even though it refers back to a plural, as one uses the singular noun instead of the plural, just as you use the apparent singular in place of the plural. Such usage occurs in the speech of the Arabs. Abu al-Hasan recited:

And among us in the desert is a family that protects us, swift to the summoner, with large ribs.

That is, "their ribs." The third: the agent in *istawqada* is not a reference back to *alladhina*, but refers back to the active-participle notion understood from *istawqada*. The estimate is "he kindled," that is, "the one who kindles," as in His saying: ﴿Then it appeared to them, after they had seen the signs﴾ [Yusuf: 35]; that is, "he," meaning the appearance understood from *bada*, according to one of the interpretations of the agent in the verse. On this interpretation there are two options for the reference back to *alladhina*. One is that it is deleted, and its original form is *lahum* (for them), meaning "like the one who kindled for them a fire," even though the conditions for the permitted deletion are not present. This is like the poet's saying:

If only what I treated of the softness of her heart, with which the hard one would be softened, would soften the rock.

He means "what I treated it with," so he deleted the prepositional particle and the pronoun, even though the conditions for permitted deletion are not present. Those conditions are stated in the detailed books of grammar. Their rule is that the pronoun is in the genitive by a preposition that is not in a nominative position, the relative or the thing modified by the relative, or the noun annexed to the relative, has been put in the genitive by a preposition like that preposition both in form and meaning, and the verb to which the preposition that governs the pronoun is attached is like the verb to which the preceding preposition is attached. The second option is that the first clause, which functions as a relative clause, has no reference back to it, but a clause has been joined to it by *fa*, namely the clause of *lamma* (when) and its answer. In it there is a reference back to *alladhi*, so the link is accomplished through this later reference. It is then like what they permitted for the linking in the topic construction, such as "Zayd, Hind came and I struck her." The reference back to *alladhina* is the pronoun in the answer to *lamma*, which is His saying: ﴿God took away their light﴾ [al-Baqara: 17]. None of those whose statements we have examined mentioned the explanation of Ibn al-Sumayfa's reading.

Al-istawqada (ٱسْتَوْقَدَ) is of the form istaf'ala, which here has the same meaning as af'ala. Abu Zayd reported that awqada and istawqada have the same meaning, as do ajaba and istajaba, and akhlafa li-ahlihi and istakhlafa (both meaning he left a successor for his family). Alternatively, the form may indicate seeking (talab), meaning they sought a fire. The exegetes permitted both of these readings without giving preference to either. That it means awqada is the view of al-Akhfash, and it is the stronger view, because taking it to mean seeking requires omitting a clause for the meaning to be sound, whereas taking it to mean awqada does not require this. Consider that under the seeking reading the meaning would be "they asked for a fire and kindled it," and then ﴿when it lit up what was around it﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:17). Lighting up does not result from seeking; it results from kindling. Therefore reading it as other than seeking is more probable. The comparison is between one story and another story, so such a comparison does not require matching a group against a group. Consider the verse ﴿The likeness of those who were charged with the Torah, then did not carry it, is like the likeness of a donkey carrying books﴾ (Al-Jumu'ah 62:5). And is the phrase in His saying ﴿like the likeness of one who kindled a fire﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:17) also an instance of matching? Consider that the meaning is "like the likeness of the group or company that kindled." It is then singular in wording but plural in meaning. Some exegetes imagined that it is singular and sought to match a plural with a plural, and so claimed that it is an elision of a noun: "like the likeness of the companions of the one who kindled." There is no need for this supposed elision, for if we assume it is singular in both wording and meaning, the elision would not be needed. The comparison occurs between one story and another, and if that is so, matching is not required, as we have already stated. He made nāran (a fire) indefinite and singular because its counterpart in the description of the hypocrite is only a small measure of restriction by Islam, while his inner being is filled with disbelief and hypocrisy. So his condition is compared to the condition of one who kindled some fire, since the indefinite signifies only the unrestricted and does not signify multiplicity or a specific fire. The fa' in fa-lamma is for sequence (ta'qib), and it joins the conditional clause to the relative clause. Whoever claims that it entered because of the conditional sense contained in the relative clause, and supposed the conditional "if he kindled," is mistaken in several respects. A refutation of a claim similar to this was already given in His saying ﴿so their commerce did not profit﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:16), so it is not necessary to repeat it here.

* *

Adā'at (أَضَاءَتْ, "lit up"): It is said to be transitive, and it is said to be both intransitive and transitive. They said: the transitive use is more common and more well known. When it is transitive, the hamza in it is for causation (naql), since one says "the place lit up" (ḍā'a al-makān). This is like the words of al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib concerning the Prophet (ﷺ):

"When you were born, the earth shone, and the horizon lit up with your light."

In this case the subject is the pronoun of the fire, "mā" is a complement, and "ḥawlahu" is a relative clause governed by a deleted verb, not an indefinite qualified noun. "Ḥawlahu" is an adjective because "mā" is rarely used as an indefinite qualified noun. We have already discussed this. The meaning is: when the fire lit up the place that was around him. When it is intransitive, they said: the pronoun in adā'at refers to the fire, "mā" is a superfluous element (zā'ida, i.e., an extra particle without semantic function in the structure), and "ḥawlahu" is an adverbial complement governed by the verb. It is also possible that the subject is not the pronoun of the fire, but rather the relative "mā," and it is feminine according to the meaning, meaning: when the direction that was around him lit up, just as they used the feminine on the basis of meaning in their saying "mā jā'at ḥājatuka" (what came was your need). Al-Zamakhshari touched upon this view, and this is preferable to what they mentioned, because "jalastu mā majlisan ḥasanan" (I sat a good sitting) and "qumtu mā yawma al-jumu'ah" (I stood on Friday) are not preserved in the speech of the Arabs. Agreement on the basis of meaning is preserved, as we have mentioned, and if an addition of "mā" were heard in such expressions, that would not be one of the regular places where the addition of "mā" is used. The better reading of the verse, after that, is that adā'at is transitive, so there is no need to posit an addition or agreement on the basis of meaning.

Ibn al-Sumayfa' and Ibn Abi Abla read: fa-lammā aḍā'at (فَلَمَّا أَضَاءَتْ) in the triliteral form (ḍā'at). This is derived on the basis of the addition of "mā," and with the subject being the fire, either as a relative or as a qualified noun, as already mentioned. The apodosis of lammā is: ﴿Allah took away their light﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:17). The pronoun in bi-nūrihim (with their light) is plural, in agreement with the meaning of "alladhī" (the one who), since we established that the meaning is like the group that kindled; or it is in agreement with that deleted noun some of them posited, namely "like the likeness of the companions of the one who kindled." They also permitted the apodosis of lammā to be deleted, because its meaning is understood, as it was deleted in His saying ﴿So when they took him away and agreed﴾ (Yusuf 12:15), and so on. Al-Zamakhshari said: its deletion is permitted because the speech is lengthy while the intended meaning is clear and the deleted element is indicated. End of quote. His phrase "because the speech is lengthy" is not accepted, because the speech is not lengthy. He posited "they were extinguished" (khumidat), but where is any lengthiness in ﴿when it lit up what was around it﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:17) so that it would be "were extinguished"? Rather, this is lammā and its apodosis, so there is no lengthiness, unlike His saying ﴿So when they took him away﴾ (Yusuf 12:15), where the speech is long because of the mention of the conjunctions joined to the verb and the mention of their complements after the verb that follows lammā. Therefore the deletion there is permissible because the speech is lengthy. His phrase "with clarity of meaning" is also not accepted. Where is any clarity in this, and what indicates the deleted element? Rather, what the arrangement of the speech, its soundness, and its placement in its proper position require is that ﴿Allah took away their light﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:17) be the apodosis. If you make something other than it the apodosis, while the removal of their light by Allah follows strongly from the lighting up, that would be a kind of riddle, since you have left out something that comes to mind immediately and hidden something whose supposition requires a revelation to make it clear, for the deletion of the wording is not indicated when the structure ﴿Allah took away their light﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:17) is present. Al-Zamakhshari did not limit himself to permitting the deletion of this apodosis, but claimed that the deletion is preferable. He said: "The deletion is better than the mention, because of its brevity together with its expression of the attribute the kindler came to have, with a more eloquent wording in conveying the meaning, as if it were said: when it lit up what was around him, it was extinguished, so they remained groping in darkness, bewildered and grieving over the loss of the light, disappointed after the labor of reviving the fire." End of quote. What he mentioned is a kind of rhetoric with no real benefit beneath it, because he could say this only if what follows ﴿when it lit up what was around him﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:17) were not the words ﴿Allah took away their light﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:17). As for what he says after positing "it was extinguished" to the end, it is among those things that burden the wording with what it cannot bear, and posits many suppositions and deleted clauses that the speech does not indicate. This is his habit in most of his exegesis in many passages. The words of God should not be explained by what they do not bear, nor should anything be added to them. Rather, the explanation should correspond exactly to what is explained, without addition to it or reduction from it.

Since they permitted the deletion of the apodosis, they spoke about His saying ﴿Allah took away their light﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:17), and interpreted it in two ways:
One: that it is a new sentence, answering a supposed question, as if it were said: What is the matter with them, that their condition has come to resemble the condition of this kindler? So it was said: Allah took away their light.
Two: that it is a substitute (badal) for the sentence of the likeness, by way of explanation (bayan). Al-Zamakhshari stated both. Both of these views are based on the premise that the apodosis of lammā is deleted, and we have chosen otherwise, namely that the apodosis is His saying ﴿Allah took away their light﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:17). The second of the two interpretations, namely that ﴿Allah took away their light﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:17) is a substitute for the sentence of the likeness by way of explanation, is not evidently correct, because the sentence of the likeness is His saying ﴿Their likeness is like the likeness of the one who kindled a fire﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:17). Making ﴿Allah took away their light﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:17) a substitute for this sentence by way of explanation is not correct, because a substitute among sentences occurs only when a nominal sentence is replaced by a verbal sentence; they have mentioned that this is permitted. But that a verbal sentence be substituted for a nominal sentence is something I know of no one who has permitted. A substitute is by way of repetition of the governing element, and the first sentence has no place in the grammatical structure (i'rab), since it does not occupy the position of a single word. Therefore the second cannot be a substitute on the intention of repeating the governing element, since there is no governing element in the first that could be repeated in the second. So the aspect of substitution is invalid in it.

Whoever makes the apodosis deleted makes the pronoun in bi-nūrihim refer to the hypocrites.

The bā' in bi-nūrihim is for transitivity (ta'diya), and it is one of the fourteen meanings for which bā' is used, which we mentioned earlier. According to the majority of grammarians (nuḥāt), it is synonymous with the hamza of causation. So when you say "kharajtu bi-Zayd" (I went out with Zayd), its meaning is "akhrajtu Zayd" (I took Zayd out), and it does not necessarily follow that you yourself went out. Abu al-Abbas (al-Mubarrad) held that when you say "qumtu bi-Zayd" (I stood with Zayd), it indicates that you stood and made him stand, while if you say "aqamtu Zayd" (I made Zayd stand), it does not necessarily follow that you stood. He thus distinguished between bā' and hamza in transitivity. Al-Suhayli went in a similar direction to Abu al-Abbas's view. He said: the bā' of transitivity enters where the subject has some participation with the object in that act, such as "aq'adtuhu" (I made him sit) and "qa'adtu bihi" (I sat with him), "adkhaltuhu al-dār" (I made him enter the house) and "dakhaltu bihi" (I entered with him). This does not work for something like "amraḍtuhu" (I made him ill) or "asqamtuhu" (I made him sick). So there must be some participation, even if only by the hand, when you say "qa'adtu bihi" and "dakhaltu bihi." This verse and similar ones were used as an objection to Abu al-Abbas. Do you not see that the meaning is "Allah removed their light"? Do you not see that Allah is not described as going away together with light? One of our companions said: this objection does not apply to Abu al-Abbas, since it is possible that Allah described Himself as going away in a sense that befits Him, just as He described Himself, exalted be He, as coming in His saying ﴿and your Lord comes﴾ (Al-Fajr 89:22). What undermines Abu al-Abbas's view of distinguishing between bā' and hamza is the verse of the poet:

"The abodes which were ours, while we were at Mina, they would have been ours, were it not for the departure of the riding camels."

Namely, it makes us lose (*tahullu*), do you not see that the meaning is "it makes us lawful (*halalan*), not in a state of ihram"? It does not enter with them in this, because they were not forbidden, so that they would become lawful afterward? Because the *ba'* (بِ) has the meaning of the *hamzah* (the causative *alif*, هَمْزَة), the two are not combined, so one does not say *adhhabtu bi-Zaydin* ("I made Zayd go with [me]"). And regarding His saying, ﴿تَنْبُتُ بِالدُّهْنِ﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 20], meaning "it grows with oil," in the reading of one who makes it quadriliteral (*rubā'iyyan*), there is an explanation (*takhrij*) that will be mentioned in its place, if God the Exalted wills. The *ba'* of transitivity (*bā' al-ta'diyah*) has rulings other than this, which were mentioned in grammar (*al-nahw*).

Al-Yamani read: *adhhaba Allahu nurahum* ("God took away their light"), and this indicates the synonymy of the *ba'* and the *hamzah*. Attributing the taking away to God the Exalted is literal (*haqiqah*), since He is the doer of all things.

Regarding the meaning of ﴿ذَهَبَ اللَّهُ بِنُورِهِمْ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17], there are three opinions. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is a parable (*mathal*) struck for the hypocrites, who were honored by Islam, so the Muslims married them, inherited from them, and shared the spoils (*fay'*) with them. When they died, God stripped them of honor, just as He stripped the one who kindled the fire of its light. ﴿وَتَرَكَهُمْ فِي ظُلُمَاتٍ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17] means "in punishment."

The second: the going of their light is by God's informing the believers of their disbelief, so the light of Islam went from them because of what they had shown of their unbelief.

The third: He nullified their light in His sight, since their hearts were contrary to what they showed. They are like a man who kindled a fire, then it was extinguished, and he returned to darkness.

These opinions are valid only if the pronoun in *bi-nurihim* refers to the hypocrites. If it refers to those who kindled (*al-mustawqidin*), then the going of the light is the extinguishing of the fire they kindled, and this is by a heavenly matter in which they had no action. Therefore al-Dahhak said: when the fire shone, God sent a violent wind upon it and extinguished it. This interpretation accords with the view of one who says that it is a real fire, kindled by the people of corruption so that they might reach their corruption and their frivolity through it and its light; so God extinguished their fire and made their effort go astray.

But if we say that the mention of fire here is a parable with no real referent, and that what is meant by it is the fire of enmity and rancor, then God's extinguishing it is the repelling of its harm from the believers.

If the fire is metaphorical, then describing it as shining on what is around the one who kindles it is from the metaphor of *tarshih* (the metaphor that is supported by a further term), and the discussion of it has already preceded.

The taking away of the *nur* (light) is more emphatic than the taking away of the *daw'* (brightness), because the more specific is included in the negation of the more general, not the reverse. So if He had said "with their brightness," it would not have entailed the going of the *nur*. The intent is the complete removal of light from them, do you not see how He followed it with His saying, ﴿وَتَرَكَهُمْ فِي ظُلُمَاتٍ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17]?

The attribution of the light to them is attribution with the slightest connection (*bi-adna mulabasah*), since its attribution to the fire is the literal one; but because they benefited from it, its attribution to them is valid.

The majority read *fi zulumatin* with a *damma* on the *lam*. Al-Hasan and Abu al-Sammak read it with a *sukun* on the *lam*, and a group read it with a *fatha* on it. These three forms are permissible in the plural of *fu'lah*.

The noun with a sound middle radical, not doubled and not having a weak final radical, takes the *ta'* (ta' marbutah). If its final radical is weak with *ya'*, as in *kulliyyah*, the *damma* is excluded; or if it is doubled, as in *durrah*; or if its middle radical is weak, as in *surah*; or if it is a descriptive, as in *buhmah*, then both the *fatha* and the *damma* are excluded.

A group read *inna zulamatin* with a *fatha* on the *lam*, as the plural of *zulam*, which is the plural of *zulmah*. So *zulumat* on this reading is a plural of a plural (*jam' al-jam'*). The shift to the *fatha* for lightness is easier than claiming a plural of a plural, because the shift to it has come in words like *kisrat* (plural of *kisrah*) as a permissible option, and to it in words like *jafnah* as obligatory. *Fu'lah* and *fi'lah* are sisters, and the *fatha* has been heard in them under the conditions mentioned earlier, but the plural of a plural is not an analogical (*qiyas*) form, so one should not resort to it except with a decisive proof.

Al-Yamani read *fi zulmatin* in the singular, to match the singularity of *nur* and the plural reading, because each one of them has a darkness peculiar to it, so it was pluralized for that reason. Wherever the *nur* and the *zulmah* are mentioned in the Qur'an, they come in this manner: singular for the *nur* and plural for the *zulumat*. The discussion of that will come, if God wills.

*Zulumat* was made indefinite and not attributed to a pronoun of *hum* as *nur* was attributed, being satisfied with what the meaning indicates of its attribution to them in meaning, and for brevity of expression. Although *taraka* is transitive to one object, it is possible that *fi zulumatin* is in the position of a circumstantial state (*hal*) of the object, so it is attached to an omitted element. And *la yubsirun* is also in the position of a state, either from the pronoun in *tarkihim* or from the concealed pronoun in the genitive phrase, so it is a state that is interlocked (*hal mutadakhilah*); and in both assumptions it is an emphasizing state (*hal mu'akkidah*). Do you not see that whoever is left in darkness necessarily is one who does not see?

If *taraka* is one of the verbs that take two objects, then *fi zulumatin* is in the position of the second object, and *la yubsirun* is a nominal clause in the state position. It is not permissible that *fi zulumatin* be in the position of the state while *la yubsirun* is a clause in the position of the second object. Although it is permissible to say *zanantu Zaydan munfaridan la yakhafu* ("I thought Zayd alone does not fear"), when you intend "I thought Zayd, in a state of being alone, does not fear," because the second object originally is a predicate of a subject (*khabar li-mubtada'*), and when that is so, the predicate does not come in the manner of emphasis; rather that is in the manner of some states, not of predicates. So when you make *fi zulumatin* in the position of a state, it is understood from it that whoever is in darkness does not see, so there is no benefit in His saying *la yubsirun* except emphasis, and that is not permissible in predicates. Do you not see the grammarians' analysis of the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*idha ma baka min khalfiha nhrafat lahu*
*bi-shiqqin wa-shiqqun 'indana lam yuhawwali*

that *wa-shiqqun* is a subject (*mubtada'*), and *'indana* is in the position of the predicate, and *lam yuhawwal* is a state clause that conveys emphasis; and an indefinite noun may begin the sentence because it is the position of the predicate, since that leads to the predicate coming emphasized, because the negation of change is understood from the fact that the side is with him; so when it is established with him, it is established that it was not changed from him.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "darkness" here is punishment. Mujahid said: the darkness of unbelief. Qatadah said: a darkness that God casts upon them after death. Al-Suddi said: the darkness of hypocrisy. The object of *la yubsirun* is not mentioned, and it should not be intended, because the aim is the negation of seeing from them, not in relation to its object.

* *

The majority read ﴿صُمٌّ بُكْمٌ عُمْيٌ﴾ with *raf'* (nominative), and this is by the assumption of an omitted subject whose estimate is "they are deaf." These are predicates that differ in wording and in conventional signification, but they stand in the position of one predicate, since all their meanings return to their not accepting the truth while they have hearing ears, eloquent tongues, and seeing eyes; but they did not incline to the truth, nor did their tongues speak it, nor did they perceive the lights of guidance. They were described by what they were described with: deafness, dumbness, and blindness. Similar examples are heard from the Arabs. Al-Zamakhshari cited some verses of this, and another cited:

*a'ma idha ma jaratī barazat*
*hatta yuwariya jaratī al-khidru*

*wa-asimmu 'amma kana baynahuma*
*udhunī wa-ma fi sam'iha wiqru*

"I am blind when my neighbor appears, until the curtain conceals my neighbor; and I am deaf to what was between us, my ear, and in its hearing is a heaviness."

This, according to the careful scholars, is a eloquent simile (*tashbih baligh*), and it is not from the category of metaphor (*isti'arah*), because the thing borrowed to (*al-musta'ar lahu*) is mentioned, namely the hypocrites. Metaphor is only used where the thing borrowed to is left out and the speech is left empty of it, while being fit for the source and the destination to be intended, were it not for the indication of the situation or the sense of the speech, as in the saying of Zuhayr:

*ladā asadin shākī al-silāḥi muqadhdhafin*
*lahu libadun azfāruhu lam tuqallami*

The subject was omitted there because it was mentioned, so it cannot be said that it is from the category of metaphor, since it is like the saying of Zuhayr:

*asadun 'alayya wa-fi al-hurūbi na'āmatun*
*fat̤ākhā tanfiru min ṣafīri al-ṣāfiri*

The description of them with deafness, dumbness, and blindness is, as we have mentioned, from the category of figurative language (*majaz*), because of their non-acceptance of the truth. It was said: God described them with that because they used to feign deafness, feign dumbness, and feign blindness, without being characterized by any of that, so He warned about the badness of their reliance and the corruption of their belief. When the Arabs hear what they do not like, or see what does not please them, they discard it as if they had neither heard nor seen it. God the Exalted said: ﴿كَأَنْ لَمْ يَسْمَعْهَا كَأَنَّ فِي أُذُنَيْهِ وَقْرًا﴾ [Luqman: 7] ("as if he did not hear it, as if there were a heaviness in his ears"), and they said: ﴿قُلُوبُنَا فِي أَكِنَّةٍ﴾ [Fussilat: 5] ("our hearts are in coverings") and so on.

It was said: it is also possible that what is intended by this is the exaggeration of their blame, and that in their ignorance and dullness they are worse in condition than cattle and more similar in condition to inanimate things that do not hear, do not speak, and do not see. Whoever lacks these three faculties is at the highest rank of blame. For this reason, when Ibrahim, upon our Prophet and upon him be peace, wished to exaggerate the blame of his father's gods, he said: ﴿يَا أَبَتِ لِمَ تَعْبُدُ مَا لَا يَسْمَعُ وَلَا يُبْصِرُ وَلَا يُغْنِي عَنْكَ شَيْئًا﴾ [Maryam: 42] ("O my father, why do you worship what neither hears nor sees nor avails you anything?"). This sentence is declarative, and there is no necessity to believe that it is a declarative statement intended as a supplication, even though some exegetes said it. One said: it is God's supplication against them with deafness, dumbness, and blindness as recompense for their engaging in that, so God made real in them what they engaged in of that. It seems to point to what will happen in the Hereafter from His saying: ﴿وَنَحْشُرُهُمْ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ عَلَى وُجُوهِهِمْ عُمْيًا وَبُكْمًا وَصُمًّا﴾ [al-Isra': 97] ("and We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, dumb, and deaf").

'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Hafsah, the Mother of the Believers, read *ṣumman bukman 'umyan* with *nasb* (accusative). They mentioned several possibilities for its accusative: first, that it is a second object of *taraka* ("left"), with *fi zulumatin* attached to *tarakahum*, or in the position of a state, and *la yubsirun* as a state. Second, that it is accusative as a state from the object in *taraka*, on the basis that *taraka* does not take two objects, or that it did take two objects and had already taken both. Third, that it is accusative by an omitted verb whose estimate is "I mean" (*a'nī*). Fourth, that it is accusative as a state from the pronoun in *yubsirun*, and there is consideration in that. Fifth, that it is accusative as dispraise (*al-dhamm*), "deaf, dumb," so it is like the saying of al-Nabighah:

*uqārī 'awfin lā uḥāwilu ghayrahā*
*wujūhu qurūdin tabtaghī man tujādi'u*

In the four preceding possibilities, it is not necessarily the case that the three descriptions are descriptions of the hypocrites, since they are grammatically connected to what precedes them, and what precedes them is apparently descriptions of those who kindled the fire, unless the speech about the one who kindled is considered complete at His saying: ﴿فَلَمَّا أَضَاءَتْ مَا حَوْلَهُ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17] ("when it lit up what was around it"), and the pronoun in *nurihim* refers to the hypocrites; in that case the three descriptions belong to them. As for the fifth possibility, it appears that they are descriptions of the hypocrites, because the case of the *raf'* is their description. Do you not see that the estimate is "they are deaf," that is, the hypocrites? So likewise in the *nasb*. Some exegetes stated the weakness of the accusative as dispraise, without explaining the aspect of the weakness. Its basis is that the accusative as dispraise occurs where a previously mentioned noun is named and the construction departs from agreement in case to severance (*qat'*), whereas here no previously mentioned noun has preceded with which these descriptions would agree in case so that they would be severed. For this reason, the accusative as dispraise is weak here.

This is a sentence stating a fact, joined to the sentence before it. In meaning it follows from the preceding sentence and comes after it. Whoever has these three attributes, which are a metonymy (*kinaya*) for not accepting the truth, is bound not to return to faith. If the verse refers to specific individuals, this is clear: whoever God has said will not return to faith will never return. If it refers to people in general, the statement is limited to their persisting in the state that God has described them as having.

Qatada and Muqatil said: "They do not return from their misguidance." As-Suddi said: "They do not return to Islam." It was also said: "They do not return from deafness, muteness and blindness." It was said: "They do not return to God's reward." It was said: "They do not return from clinging to hypocrisy." It was said: "They do not return to guidance after they have sold it, or from misguidance after they have purchased it."

The non-return is attributed to them because God gave them intellects for guidance and sent them messengers with conclusive proofs. They turned away from this and followed their own desires and the customs of their forefathers, so the non-return came from their own selves. We have already noted that the act of the servant is attributed to God as its originator and to the servant because he is engaged in it. For this reason He says in this verse: (p-83) ﴿Deaf, dumb, blind, so they do not return﴾, attributing these blameworthy attributes to those who are engaged in them.
