And He says: ﴿Those are the ones whom God has cursed, so He has made them deaf and blinded their eyes﴾ [Muhammad: 23], attributing this to the One who brings things into existence, exalted is He.

All these opinions hold on the assumption that the verb "return" (*yarji'un*) is intransitive. If it is transitive, its object is omitted, and the sense would be: "So they do not return (an answer)" (*fa-hum la yarji'una jawaban*).

Or like a downpour from the sky, in which are darkness, thunder and lightning.

"Aw" (or) has five meanings: doubt (*shakk*), vagueness (*ibham*), choice (*takhyir*), permissibility (*ibahah*), and detail (*tafsil*). The Kufans added two more: that it means "wa" (and), and that it means "bal" (rather). Our teacher Abu al-Hasan ibn al-Sa'igh used to say: "aw" is for one of two things, or one of several things.

Al-Suhayli said: "aw" indicates one of two things without specifying which. For this reason it occurs in a report where doubt is involved, since doubt is hesitation between two matters without preference. But it was not put for doubt itself. It can occur in a report, and there is no doubt when it is left vague to the addressee. As for the "aw" of choice, it keeps its original meaning, since the one given the choice only wants one of two things. As for those they claimed mean permissibility, permissibility is not taken from the word "aw" or from its meaning. It is taken from the imperative form together with contextual indicators. It enters because of the common custom that one occupied with one action does not occupy himself with another. If he combined two permitted things, he would not be sinning. This is known, and it shows that "aw" is not relied upon here.

Al-sayyib: the rain. It is said: *sāba yasūbu*, so it is *sayyib* when it falls. The word is also used for the cloud. The poet said:

*Until its downpour's rain effaced them, reaching all sides, pouring and drenching.*

Al-Shammakh said:

*And a dark cloud, near, with truthful thunder, a downpour.*

According to the Basran grammarians, the pattern of *sayyib* is *fay'il*. This is one of the patterns specific to roots with a weak middle radical, except for what is anomalous in sound roots, such as their saying *sayqil* (with a kasra on the qaf) as a name for a woman. Its pattern is not *fa'il*, contrary to al-Farra'. This view is attributed to the Kufans, and it is a question discussed in *tasrif* (Arabic morphology). The discussion of lightening this kind of word has already passed.

Al-sama': everything that rises above you, such as a roof and the like. The known sky, with its constellations, has as its root a *waw*, since it derives from *sumuw* (elevation). Between it and its singular a *ta' marbuta* may occur, so they say *samawa*, and the *waw* is retained because the word was built upon it. Al-Ajjaj said:

*The folding of nights, stage by stage, the sky of the crescent, until it curved.*

*Sama'* is feminine, and it may also be masculine. The poet said:

*Had the sky raised a people up to Him, we would have reached the sky along with the clouds.*

For a collective noun whose singular is marked with *ta'*, the people of the Hijaz treat it as feminine, while the Tamim and the people of Najd treat it as masculine. Their plurals are *samawat*, *asmiya*, and *sama'at*. He said: "*fawqa sab'i sama'inā*" (above seven of our skies), which is anomalous, because: first, it is a collective noun, so by analogy it should not be pluralized; second, its plural with *alif* and *ta'* does not meet the conditions for what is pluralized that way by analogy; and third, its plural in *af'ila* is not analogous for feminine nouns, and its plural in *fa'a'il* is not analogous for nouns in *fi'al*.

Al-ra'd (thunder): Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Shahr ibn Hawshab and 'Ikrima said: thunder is an angel who drives the clouds with this sound. Some said: whenever a cloud disobeys, he shouts at it, and "ra'd" is his name. 'Ali, 'Ata', Tawus and al-Khalil said: it is the sound of an angel driving the clouds. This was also related from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. Mujahid also said: it is the sound of an angel glorifying God. It was said: it is wind compressed between the sky and the earth. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that it is wind compressed between the clouds, so that it makes that sound. It was said: it is the collision of cloudy bodies, and this is the view of the astronomers (*arbab al-hay'a*). In the language, the known meaning is the name of the audible sound, as 'Ali said. Some said: most scholars hold that it is an angel, and what is heard is his sound as he glorifies God and drives the clouds. It was said: thunder is the sound of the movement of the wings of the angels appointed to drive the clouds.

What is drawn from these reports is two opinions: first, that thunder is an angel; second, that it is a sound. They said: this sound was named *ra'd* because it startles (*yurʿid*) the one who hears it. From this comes *ra'adat al-faraʾid*, meaning the sinews were moved and shaken, as one shakes with trembling. The word was extended, so one says *arʿada*, meaning he threatened and warned, because it arises from distance. *Tahaddud* is the trembling of the one who is threatened.

Al-barq (lightning): a steel whip (*mikhraf*) in the hand of an angel, with which he drives the clouds. This was said by 'Ali. Or it is the trace of a strike with that whip. It is related from 'Ali: or a whip of light in the hand of an angel, with which he drives them. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Or it is the striking of that whip, said by Ibn al-Anbari, who attributed it to Ibn 'Abbas. Something similar is related from Mujahid: or an angel who appears. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: or water. This was said by a group, among them Abu al-Jalad Jilan ibn Farwa al-Basri. Or it is the glitter of water, as related by Ibn Faris. Or it is fire that flashes from the collision of cloudy bodies, said by some. What is understood from the language is that thunder is an expression for this startling sound heard from the direction of the sky, and that lightning is the subtle, luminous body that is seen and does not persist.

﴿They put their fingers in their ears because of the thunderbolts, fearing death. And Allah encompasses the disbelievers.﴾

*Ja'ala* (to make, to place): it can mean *khalaqa* (to create) or *alqā* (to throw), and then it takes one object. It can mean *sayyara* (to make) or *sammā* (to name), and then it takes two objects. It can also indicate the beginning of an action, in which case it is one of the verbs of approximation (*af'al al-muqaraba*), which enter upon the subject and predicate under the conditions mentioned in their chapter.

Al-usbu' (finger): its referent is understood, and it is feminine. They mention nine dialects: the vowel of the *hamza* is fatha, damma, or kasra, and with each of these the *ba'* takes a kasra. They also relate a tenth: *usbūʿ*, with a damma and a *waw* after the *ba'*. All the names of the fingers are feminine except *ibham* (the thumb). Some of Banu Asad say "hādhā ibhām" (masculine), but the feminine is better, and the Arabs follow it, except for those mentioned.

Al-udhun (ear): its referent is understood, and it is feminine. Its diminutive takes the *ta'*: *udhayna*. In counting, it does not take the *ta'*. They say *thalāthu ādhān* (three ears). Abu Thirwan said in a riddle of his:

*What has three ears, outrunning horses in the race?*

He means the arrow, its ears (its sides), and its fletchings.

Al-sa'iqa (thunderbolt): a severe blow from the sound of thunder, with a piece of fire falling along with the sound of the thunder. They said it flashes from the cloud when its bodies collide. It is a subtle, sharp fire that passes over nothing without consuming it, and despite its sharpness it dies out quickly. God destroys with it whom He wills. Labid said, mourning his brother Arbad, who was among those burned by the thunderbolt:

*The lightning and the thunderbolts bereft me of al-Fa-ris (the horseman), on the day of tribulation, the brave.*

One who died quickly is likened to one killed by it. 'Alqama ibn 'Abada said:

*As if a cloud had poured upon them, its thunderbolts a crawling for their birds.*

Al-Khalil related from some Arabs: *al-sā'iqa* with a *sin*. Al-Naqqash said: *sā'iqa*, *sa'qa*, and *sā'iqa* have a single meaning. Abu 'Amr said: *al-sā'iqa* is the dialect of Banu Tamim. The poet said:

*Did you not see that the sinners were struck by thunderbolts? No, they are above the thunderbolts.*

Abu al-Najm said:

*They alight in the walled place of the cutting ones, the splitting of lightning with thunderbolts.*

If that is a dialect, and they have related its conjugation upon it, then it is not of the type of metathesis (*al-maqlub*), contrary to the view of the one who held that. Metathesis is attributed to the majority of the lexicographers.

It is said: *ṣaʿaqathu* and *aṣʿaqathu al-ṣāʿiqa*, if it destroyed him, so he *ṣuʿiqa*, meaning he died. *Al-ṣāʿiqa* also means punishment in any case, said by Ibn 'Arafa. *Al-ṣāʿiqa* and *al-ṣāqiʿa* are either an attribute of the sound of thunder or of thunder itself, so the *ta'* is for emphasis, as in *rāwiya*. Or it is a verbal noun, as they said of *kādhiba*.

Al-hadhar (fear), al-faza' (terror), al-faraq (dread), al-jaza' (distress), and al-khawf (fear) are synonyms of death, which is an accident that follows life. It was said: death is the corruption of the animal's bodily structure. It was said: death is the cessation of life.

Al-ihata (encompassing): confining a thing by preventing it from every direction. The triliteral form is transitive. They say *hāṭahu*, *yaḥūṭuhu*, *ḥawṭan*.

*Aw ka-sayyib*: conjoined to the phrase "like the one who kindled" (2:17). There is an omission of two *mudaf* (nouns in the construct), since the estimate is *aw ka-mathali dhawī sayyib* (or like the example of those in a downpour). This is like God's saying: ﴿like one over whom swooning falls from death﴾ (33:19), meaning like the rolling of the eye of one who swoons over. Here "aw" is for detail. Among those who considered their state, some liken it to the state of the one who kindled, and others liken it to the state of those under the downpour. There is no necessity to make "aw" mean choice, meaning "liken them to whichever of the two you wish", although al-Zajjaj and others took that view. Nor is there a necessity to make it mean permissibility, nor to make it mean "wa" (and), as the Kufans did here. Nor is there a necessity to make it mean doubt regarding the addressees, since that is impossible for God. Nor to make it mean "bal" (rather), nor to make it mean vagueness, because choice and permissibility occur only in an imperative or in what has the sense of one. This is a purely informative sentence.

Also, "aw" meaning "wa" or "bal" was not established according to the Basrans, and what its proponents cite as evidence is interpreted otherwise. And doubt regarding the addressees, or vagueness regarding them, has no sense here. The apparent meaning of "aw" here is detail.

This second simile came to reveal their state after the first one revealed it. By it, God intended detail and elaboration on the state of the hypocrite. In the first simile, He likened him to the kindler of fire: his display of faith is the illumination, and the cessation of his benefit is the going away of the light. In the second, He likened the religion of Islam to the downpour, and what it contains of promise and threat to the thunder and lightning, and what afflicts them of terror and trials from the Muslims to the thunderbolts. Both similes are of the separated type, as we have explained. The better view is that they be of the composite type rather than the separated type, so that one does not strain to match one thing with another. The indication of this was given at the first simile.

So it describes the hypocrites' falling into their misguidance, and the bewilderment and confusion they suffer, with the condition of one who has suffered the extinguishing of his fire after kindling it in the darkness of night, and with the condition of one whom the sky seized on a dark night with thunder, lightning, and fear of thunderbolts. It was estimated as "like the example of those in a downpour" because of the return of the pronoun in "yaj'aluna" (they put).

The second simile is more eloquent, because it indicates more clearly the extreme of bewilderment and the severity of the matter. For this reason it was placed later, making an ascent from the easier to the more severe.

Some exegetes sought to order the states of the hypocrites and balance them against the parable of the downpour, the darknesses, the thunder, the lightning, and the thunderbolts. He said: God likened the Qur'an to the downpour because of what it contains of forms (*ashkāl*); and He likened what they are in of darknesses, threat and warning to thunder, light, and clear proofs, which at times nearly dazzle them like lightning; and He likened their putting their fingers in their ears, the exposure of their hypocrisy, and the legal obligations they dislike, such as jihad and zakat and the like, to the thunderbolts. This is the view of one who holds that it is of the separated type of similitude, in which one thing in the illustration is matched against one thing in the subject illustrated. The rest of the views on this will come, God willing.

It was read: *aw ka-ṣāyib*. It is an active participle from *ṣāba yaṣūbu*, and *sayyib* is more intensive than *ṣāyib*. The *kaf* is in the nominative position, because it is conjoined to what has a nominative position. If we say that the sentence "God took away their light" (2:17) is not a response to something, then it is an interpolated sentence placed between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined. Likewise "deaf, dumb, blind" (2:18), if we say it is an attribute of the hypocrites. On these two views, the two sentences are interpolated sentences between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined. Abu 'Ali prohibited this, and his view was refuted by the verse of the poet:

*By your life, misfortunes are changing, and in prolonged companionship there is estrangement.*

*I have worn out the dwelling of Umm Awfa, but Umm Awfa does not care.*

(p-٨٤)

Then he separated the oath from its answer with the two parenthetical clauses. *Min al-sama'* (from the sky) is attached to *sayyib* and so is in the accusative position. *Min* here indicates the starting point. It is also possible that it is in the position of a qualifier, in which case it is attached to an omitted element, and *min* in that case indicates partitive meaning, with an omitted noun before it. The sense would be: "or like a heavy rain from the rains of the sky." The use of *al-sama'* as a definite noun indicates that this heavy rain descends from the expanse of the sky, so it covers everything. Al-Zamakhshari said: "In it is evidence that the clouds descend from the sky and take their water from it, not as claimed by someone who asserted that they take it from the sea." He supported this with the words of God Most High: ﴿And He sends down from the sky mountains containing hail﴾ [al-Nur: 43]. End of his words.

There is nothing in the two verses to show that the source of the rain cannot be the sea. The two verses only show (p-86) that rain descends from the sky. There is no apparent contradiction between rain descending from the sky and its origin being the sea. The Arabs call clouds "daughters of the sea," meaning that they arise from the seas. Tarafa said:

"Do not blame me, for they are of women
Sleeping through the summer, veiled, few in number,
Like the daughters of the sea, swaying as
The summer has grown the tender green shoots."

They replaced the *ba'* with a *mim* and said *banat al-mahr*, just as they said "I saw him from close (*min kathab*) and from a thicket (*min katham*)."

*Zulumat* (darknesses) is raised by the prepositional phrase acting as its agent, because it has come to rely on the preceding element when it is a qualifier. It is also permissible for the phrase *fihi* to be in the position of a circumstantial qualifier of the indefinite noun specified by ﴿min al-sama'﴾, either by specifying the action or by specifying the qualifier, according to the two options we mentioned earlier in the grammatical analysis (*i'rab*) of *min al-sama'*. They also permitted *zulumat* to be in the nominative as the subject of an inchoative, with *fihi* as its predicate, and the sentence in the position of a qualifier. There is no need for this, because when the qualifier is a single word or a sentence, the better option is to make it a single word and to make *zulumat* plural, since several kinds of darkness have resulted. If *al-sayyib* is the rain, then its darknesses are the darkness of its density, its thickness, and the continuity of its drops, and the darkness of the shadow of its cloud together with the darkness of the night. If *al-sayyib* is the cloud, then its darkness is the darkness of its pouring and the darkness of its covering, together with the darkness of the night.

The pronoun in *fihi* refers to *al-sayyib*. If it is interpreted as rain, then its place is the cloud. However, since thunder and lightning are associated with the rain, they are placed in it by way of figurative extension. *Al-ra'd* and *al-barq* are not made plural, although they may be pluralized in the language of the Arabs, because what is meant by them is the verbal noun, as if it were said: "thundering and flashing." If the two phenomena are meant, then it is because they were originally verbal nouns, as one says: "The sky thundered with thunder and flashed with lightning." The rule of their original form is observed, even though the meaning is plural, just as they say *rajulun khasm* (a man who is a disputant). *Zulumat, ra'd,* and *barq* are indefinite, because the intended meaning is not generality. What is intended is that the heavy rain includes darkness, thunder, and lightning. The pronoun in *yaj'alun* refers to the omitted genitive element, which is known. When it is omitted, it is sometimes attended to, so that it is as if it were actually pronounced, and the pronouns refer to it as if it had been mentioned. Sometimes it is dropped, and the pronoun that took its place refers back. The first type includes this verse and the words of God Most High: ﴿Or like darknesses in a deep sea, covered by a wave, above which is a wave﴾ [al-Nur: 40]. The meaning is: "or like those in darknesses in a deep sea." That is why the object pronoun in His words *yaghsahu* refers to it. Among cases where both attending and dropping occur is the words of God Most High: ﴿How many a town We have destroyed, and Our punishment came upon it by night or while they were napping!﴾ [al-A'raf: 4]. The meaning is "the people of a town." He said *fa-ja'aha* (it came upon it), so he dropped the omitted element, and he said "destroyed" (*ahlaknaha*), and then attended to the omitted element.

The sentence beginning with *yaj'alun* has no place in the grammatical analysis, because it is the answer to an assumed question, as if it were said: "How is their state with such thunder?" It was answered: "They put..." It has also been said that the sentence has a place in the grammatical analysis, namely the genitive, because it is in the position of a qualifier for the owners of the omitted element, as if it were said: "those who put." Some permitted that it be in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in *fihi*, which is the *ha'*. The returning pronoun to the possessor of the circumstance is omitted, and the *alif* and *lam* have taken its place. The meaning is "from its thunderbolts." By "the fingertips" he meant some of them, because all the fingers are not placed in the ears; only the fingertip is placed in them. But this is figurative extension, which is using the whole for a part. Also, because of the extreme terror these people feel from the shaking of thunderbolts, it is as if they are not satisfied with the fingertip; rather, if it were possible for them to block with all the fingers, they would do so. He turned away from the specific name for what is put into the ear to the general name, which is *al-usbu'* (finger), because of the good manners of the Qur'an in leaving the word *al-sababah* (index finger), and because euphemisms in it are expressed with the most becoming word. For this reason they did not turn to *al-misbahah* (the one for glorifying God), *al-muhallilah* (the one for declaring God's oneness), or other beautiful terms. They did not use the terms *al-misbahah* and the like, because these are newly coined words that people had not commonly used in that era; they were introduced later.

Al-Hasan recited *min al-sawaqi'* (from the thunderbolts). It has already been mentioned that this is the dialect of Tamim, and we have reported that it is not one of the transposed forms. *Ja'ala* here means "to place" or "to set," as if he said: "they set their fingers." The *min* is causal, related to *yaj'alun*, meaning "because of the thunderbolts." *Hadhar al-mawt* (fear of death) is an object of purpose. The conditions for an object of purpose are present in it, since it is a verbal noun that shares the same agent and time as the verb. This is how they parsed it. There is something questionable about this, because His words *min al-sawaqi'* are in meaning an object of purpose, and if it were coordinated it would be permissible, as in the words of God Most High: ﴿Seeking the pleasure of God and as a firming of their souls﴾ [al-Baqarah: 265], and the words of the rajaz poet:

"He mounts every barren, massive camel,
Out of fear and the joy of the one who is delighted,
And terror from the frightening of the tempest."

They also said: it is permissible that it be a verbal noun, meaning "they fear with the fear of death," and it is genitive in relation to the object. Qatada, al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, and Ibn Abi Layla recited *hadhar al-mawt*, which is the verbal noun of *hadhara* (to beware). They said its accusative position is as an object of purpose.

Encompassing (*al-ihatah*) here is a metaphor for God's being such that they cannot escape Him, just as the encompassed cannot escape the one who encompasses it. It has been said it means His knowledge, and it has been said it means His power, and it has been said it means His destruction. This sentence is parenthetical, because it came between these two sentences, which are "they put their fingers" and "the lightning almost takes away," and both are part of one story.

It has already been mentioned that this simile is one of the compound similes, in which one of the two sentences is compared to the other in some respect, even if the individual parts of one sentence are not similar to the individual parts of the other. The intended meaning is then to compare the bewilderment of the hypocrites in religion and in worldly life to the bewilderment of someone whose fire has gone out after it was lit, and to the bewilderment of someone seized by the sky on a dark night with thunder and lightning. This is the option that was previously said to be preferred.

They also said: it is one of the dispersed similes (*al-tashbih al-mufarraq*), in which the simile is composed of several elements, the thing being likened is also composed, and each element of the simile resembles each element of the thing being likened. Two opinions regarding taking this simile as a dispersed simile have already been mentioned. The third: the heavy rain is a simile for Islam, the darkness is a simile for the hypocrisy in their hearts, and the thunder and lightning are two similes for what they are threatened with. The fourth: the lightning is a simile for Islam, and the darknesses are a simile for trial and affliction. The fifth: the heavy rain, the life-giving downpour, is a simile for Islam; the darknesses are a simile for the Islam of the hypocrites and the hidden disbelief within it; the thunder is a simile for what Islam contains of protecting lives and mixing with the Muslims in marriage and inheritance; and the lightning, with what it contains of thunderbolts, is a simile for what Islam contains of deterrence through punishment in this world and the next. The meaning of this is transmitted from al-Hasan. The sixth: the heavy rain, the darknesses, the thunder, the lightning, and the thunderbolts were literally something that struck some of the Jews, so God set their story as a parable for the rest of them. A hadith about this is transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas. The seventh: it is a parable God set for the good and evil that befall the hypocrites. It is as if, when their wealth and their boys increased, or when they obtained booty or conquest, they said: "The religion of Muhammad is true," and they remained steadfast in it; but when their wealth and children perished and affliction befell them, they said: "This is because of the religion of Muhammad," and they apostatized as disbelievers. The eighth: He compared the world and what is in it of hardship, ease, blessing, and affliction, to the heavy rain which gathers benefit by giving life to the earth, causing plants to grow, giving life to every creature, and being used for purification and other benefits; and harm by what occurs through drowning and flooding; and what precedes it of darknesses and thunderbolts through thunder and lightning. And the hypocrite gives up the deferred for seeking immediate benefit, so he sells his hereafter and what God has prepared in it of bliss for the worldly life whose purity is turbid, and his final destination is then Saqar (Hell). The ninth: it is a parable for the Resurrection, for what they fear of the threat of the Hereafter because of their doubt in their religion; and what is in it of lightning corresponds to the protection of their lives in outward profession of Islam; and He compared what is in it of thunderbolts to what Islam contains of warnings of punishment in this world and the next. The tenth: striking the heavy rain is a parable for what the hypocrites showed of faith; the darknesses are their misguidance and disbelief which they concealed; what is in it of lightning corresponds to what the good of Islam overshadowed them with and the blessing of it covered them with, and their being guided by it to their worldly benefits, and their safety for their lives and wealth; and what is in it of thunderbolts corresponds to what their hypocrisy required and what they are destined for of worldly and otherworldly destruction.

They have also mentioned other opinions, all of which return to the compound simile. The first: He likened the state of the hypocrites to those who gathered together the darkness of the cloud with these matters, so that this was more bewildering to them, since they see no path, and the one whom the lightning lit and then departed finds the darkness more intense than if there had been no lightning in it. The second: the rain, although beneficial, when it appears in this form, its benefit disappears; likewise the outward display of faith is beneficial to the hypocrite if his inner state agrees with it, but without agreement it is harmful. The third: He likened the state of the hypocrites, in their thinking that what they showed is beneficial to them while it does not benefit them, to someone who has been struck by these matters together with thunderbolts, who thinks that what saves him from them is putting his fingers in his ears, but that does not save him from what God intends for him of death or other things. The fourth: He likened the hypocrite's withdrawal from jihad out of fear of death to someone who wants to ward off these matters by putting his fingers in his ears. The fifth: He likened the hypocrite's failure to escape God's punishment to those who put their fingers in their ears, for although they escape death in that moment, death is behind them.

The Qur'anic verse (in its meaning): "The lightning nearly snatches away their sight. Every time it lights up for them, they walk in it, and when darkness falls upon them, they stand still. And if Allah willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight. Indeed, Allah is over all things competent."

*Yakādu* (يَكادُ): the present tense of *kāda* (كادَ), which is one of the verbs of approximation (af'āl al-muqārabah). Its pattern is *fa'ala yaf'alu*, like *khāfa yakhāfu*; it is derived from a root with a original waw. It has two dialectal forms: *fa'ala*, as we have mentioned, and *fa'ula*. For this reason, when a pronoun of the subject for the first person, second person, or the feminine plural nūn is attached to it, they put a *ḍamma* on the kāf, saying: *kudtu*, *kudta*, *kudna*. The transfer of the kasra of the waw to the kāf has also been heard, even though its attribution is to other than what has been mentioned, in the words of the poet:

*Wa-kīdat ḍibā'u l-qaffi yakalna juththatī / wa-kīda kharāshun 'inda dhālika yuyīmu*

He intends: *wa-kādat*, *wa-kāda*. Of the verbs of approximation, the only ones whose present tense is used are *kāda* and *awshaka*. These verbs belong to the class of *kāna* (كانَ): they raise the subject and put the predicate in the accusative, except that their predicate is always a present-tense verb. They have a full chapter in grammar, and there are about thirty such verbs, which Abū Isḥāq al-Bahārī mentioned in his book (*Sharḥ Jumal al-Zajjājī*). Some exegetes said: *yakādu* is a verb which negates the meaning while affirming it, and affirms it while negating. They have recited poetry in this regard, which riddles with them. What this exegete mentioned is the view of Abū l-Fath and others, but the correct view among our companions is that they are like the rest of the verbs: their negation is negation and their affirmation is affirmation. The arguments for both views are mentioned in the books of grammar.

*Al-khaṭf* (الخَطْفُ): taking a thing quickly. *Kull* (كُلّ): for generality; it is a noun of plurality that necessarily requires an annexed noun, except that what it is annexed to may be omitted and tanwīn is given in its place. It was said that it is the tanwīn of *ṣarf*. If the omitted noun is definite, *kull* remains definite by the annexation, and from it comes the ḥāl. According to most, it is not defined by *al-*; al-Akhfash and al-Fārisī permitted that. It is sometimes put in the accusative as a ḥāl. Its basic function is to follow as a emphasis, like *ajma'*, and it is used as a subject. Its being like this is better than its being an object. This is not restricted to hearing (samā') nor specific to poetry, contrary to what its claimant asserts. When *kull* is annexed to an indefinite noun or to a noun with the generic *al-*, it may well come after the verbal governors. When it begins annexed in wording to an indefinite noun, it agrees with the predicates and others according to what it is annexed to, and with a definite noun; the most eloquent is the singular of the returning pronoun, or in meaning rather than wording, which is the original form, though the plural may be made acceptable. The rulings concerning *kull* are many. We have mentioned most of them in our large book which we named *al-Tadhkirah*, and we set out a portion of them so that people may benefit, for it recurs in the Qur'an many times.

*Al-mashy* (المَشْيُ): the familiar movement. *Law* (لَوْ): Sībawayh's expression is that it is a particle for what would have happened because of the occurrence of something else. This is better than the grammarians' saying that it is a particle of impossibility for impossibility, because Sībawayh's explanation holds consistently wherever *law* occurs, whereas their explanation breaks down in examples like: "If this were a human, it would be an animal." According to the Imam's explanation, the meaning is the affirmation of animality on the assumption of the affirmation of humanness, since the more specific entails the more general. On their explanation this breaks down, for the meaning would be that animality is impossible because humanness is impossible, which is not correct, since the absence of humanness does not entail the absence of animality, for animality can exist without humanness. *Law* may also be a conditional particle for the future, in the sense of *an*, but it does not govern the jussive, contrary to some. The poet said:

*Lā yulfika l-rājūka illā muẓhiran / khuluqa l-kirāmi wa-law takūna 'adīmā*

*Law* may also carry the meaning of wishing (tamannī). The discussion of that will come under His words, exalted is He: "If only we had a return, so that we might disown them" [al-Baqarah: 167], God willing. It is not a relative particle in the sense of *anna*, contrary to the claim of that person.

*Shā'a* (شاءَ): in the sense of *arāda* (wished). Omitting its object is permissible when the meaning is understood, and it is most often omitted with *law*, because the answer indicates it. Al-Zamakhsharī said: this omission is frequent with *shā'a* and *arāda*, meaning the omission of both their objects. He said: they hardly ever bring out this object except with something strange, as in the line:

*Fa-law shi'tu an abkiya daman labakaytuhu*

and His words, exalted is He: "If We had wished to take up a pastime, We would have taken it" [al-Anbiyā': 17], and "If Allah had wished to take a son, He would have chosen" [al-Zumar: 4]. The end of his words. The author of *al-Tibyān* said, after quoting the line:

*Fa-law shi'tu an abkiya daman labakaytuhu / 'alayhi wa-lākinna sāḥata al-ṣabri awsa'u*

Whenever the object of the wish is great or strange, it is better to mention it, as in: "If I wished to meet the caliph every day, I would meet him." The secret of mentioning it is that the listener denies it, or is as one who denies it, so you intend to establish it for him. If he does not deny it, then omission is used, as in: "If I wished, I would stand." In the revelation: "If We willed, We would have said the like of this" [al-Anfāl: 31]. The end of his words, which agrees with al-Zamakhsharī. But in my view it is not as we have said, that when the object of wishing is strange, mentioning it is good; rather the goodness of mentioning it in the verse and the line lies in the return of the pronoun, for if it were not mentioned there would be no antecedent for the pronoun. Both constructions are eloquent, though one is more common. One is omission with the answer indicating the omitted element, for the omitted element may be a verbal noun that the answer indicates; and when they omit one of the two parts of the predication, the predicate, as in "Were it not for Zayd, I would have honoured you," for length by means of the answer; and if the omitted element is of a different kind from the affirmed one, then omitting the object, which is a surplus element, because the answer indicates it, is more fitting, since it is presumed to be of the same kind as the affirmed. The second: the object of wishing is mentioned, and then the answer must contain a pronoun returning to what came before, as in His words, exalted is He: "If We had wished to take up a pastime, We would have taken it" [al-Anbiyā': 17], and the poet's line: "Fa-law shi'tu an abkiya daman labakaytuhu." But when there is no indication of its omission, it is not omitted, as in His words, exalted is He: "For whoever among you wishes to go straight" [al-Takwīr: 28], and "For whoever among you wishes to go forward or fall behind" [al-Muddaththir: 37].

*Al-shay'* (الشَّيْءُ): that which is valid to be known in some respect and to be spoken of. Sībawayh, may God have mercy on him, said: femininity arises from masculinity. Do you not see that *shay'* applies to everything spoken of before it is known whether it is male or female? *Shay'* is masculine, and in our view it is synonymous with *mawjūd* (existent). Its application to the non-existent in the strict sense is disputed. Whoever applies it to the non-existent is the most denying of the denials, since it is applied to the body, the accident, the eternal, the non-existent, and the impossible.

*Al-qudrah* (القُدْرَةُ): power over a thing and the ability to do it. The verb is *qadara*, and its verbal nouns are many: *qadar*, *qudrah*, with the qāf vowelled in three ways; *maqdirah*, with the dāl vowelled in three ways; *qudr*, *qidr*, *qudar*, *qadār*, *qidār*, *qudrānan*, *maqdaran*, *maqdurran*.

The clause "*yakādu al-barqu yakhṭafu abṣārahum*" has no place in the grammatical analysis, for it is a fresh resumption answering one who says: "What then is their state with that lightning?" So it is said: "The lightning nearly snatches away their sight." It is also possible that it is in the genitive position as an adjective of the omitted *dhawī*; the estimate being: "the lightning which nearly snatches away their sight." The *al-* in *al-barq* is for prior reference, since its mention came indefinite in His words: "In it are darkness, thunder and lightning" [al-Baqarah: 19], so it is like: "I met a man, and I struck the man," and His words: "We sent to Pharaoh a messenger" [al-Muzzammil: 15], "But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger" [al-Muzzammil: 16].

Mujāhid, 'Alī ibn al-Ḥusayn and Yaḥyā ibn Zayd recited *yakhiṭfu*, with the kh unvowelled and the ṭ kasra. Ibn Mujāhid said: I think it is an error, and it was argued that no one recited with a fatḥa except one who snatched the snatch. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the fatḥa, meaning in the present tense, is more eloquent. The kasra on the ṭ of the past tense is the dialect of Quraysh, and it is more eloquent; some Arabs say *khaṭafa* with fatḥa on the ṭ in the past and *yakhiṭfu* with kasra in the present. Ibn 'Aṭiyyah said: al-Mahdawī attributed this recitation to al-Ḥasan and Abū Rajā', and that is a mistake. 'Alī and Ibn Mas'ūd recited *yakhtaṭifu*. Ubayy recited *yatakhaṭṭafu*. Al-Ḥasan also recited *yakhaṭṭafu*, with fatḥa on the y, kh and the doubled ṭ. Al-Ḥasan also, and al-Jaḥdarī and Ibn Abī Isḥāq, recited *yakhaṭṭifu*, with fatḥa on the y and kh and doubled ṭ with kasra, and its origin is *yakhtaṭifu*. Al-Ḥasan also, and Abū Rajā', 'Āṣim al-Jaḥdarī and Qatādah recited *yakhiṭṭifu*, with fatḥa on the y, kasra on the kh and the doubled ṭ. Al-Ḥasan and al-A'mash also recited *yikhiṭṭifu*, with kasra on all three and doubled ṭ. Zayd ibn 'Alī recited *yukhaṭṭifu*, with ḍamma on the y, fatḥa on the kh and kasra on the doubled ṭ, from *khaṭafa*, and it is intensive in emphasis, not in transitivity. Some people of Madīnah recited *yakhiṭṭifu*, with fatḥa on the y, sukūn on the kh and doubled kasra ṭ; the verified view is that it is a slight vowelling (ikhtilās) of the fatḥa of the kh, not a true sukūn, for that would lead to the meeting of two sukūns in a way not permitted. Thus this word was read in ten readings: the seven, *yakhṭafu*; the irregular ones, *yakhafu*, *yakhtaṭifu*, *yatakhaṭṭafu*, *yakhaṭṭafu*, whose origin is *yatakhaṭṭafu*, dropping the tā' with the yā' irregularly, as it drops it with the tā' by analogy. *Yikhiṭṭifu*, *yakhiṭṭifu*, *yukhaṭṭifu*, *yakhaṭṭifu*; and the other four whose origin is *yukhtaṭafu*, where assimilation of the tā' into the ṭā' was intended, so the tā' became quiescent for assimilation, which necessitated moving what preceded it; either by the vowel of the tā', which is fatḥa, clearly or slightly, or by the vowel of the meeting of the two quiescents, which is kasra. The kasra on the yā' is following the kasra of the kh. This is an assimilation question which has been disputed, and it is a morphological question in which the active participle, passive participle and verbal noun differ; its clarification is in the science of morphology.

Whoever interprets the lightning as threat and warning says: "That nearly strikes them." Whoever takes it as an image of the Qur'an's proofs and its brilliant demonstrations says: the meaning is "That nearly dazzles them."

*Kullamā* (كُلَّ): in the accusative as an adverb of time, and the adverbial sense has passed to it from its annexation to *mā* (ما) of the verbal (maṣdariyyah) and temporal sort, for when you say: "I will honour you for as long as you kept company with me" the meaning is "for the duration of your companionship with me, I honour you." The usual thing that *mā* of this kind is connected to is the past verb, and the temporal *mā* is meant to convey generality. So when you say: "I will accompany you as long as the sun rises for God," you mean generality. Thus *kull* here emphasises the generality which the temporal *mā* conveys. In the language of the Arabs, the bare act that serves as the relative clause of *mā* is not meant, to be satisfied with a single occurrence; and because it indicates the generality of time, some Arabs make it jussive with it. The repetition which the jurists of legal theory and the jurisprudents mention regarding *kullamā* is only from the generality contained in it; it is not that the word *kullamā* is put for repetition, as their discourse indicates. *Kull* came only as emphasis for the generality derived from the temporal *mā*. So when you say: "Whenever you come to me, I honour you," the meaning is "I honour you in every single instance of your coming to me."

*Mā aḍā'a* (ما أضاءَ): in the genitive position by annexation, for the estimate is "every illumination," and it is also by omitting a noun, meaning "every time of illumination," so the verbal noun stands in place of the adverb, as they say: "I came to you at the setting of the star" (khufūq al-najm). The governing element of *kullamā* is His words "they walked in it." According to al-Mubarrad, *aḍā'a* here is transitive; the estimate is: "whenever the lightning lit the path for them." On this basis the pronoun in *fīhi* may return to the omitted object, and it may return to the lightning, meaning they walked in its light and in the place of its gleam. It is necessary that it returns to the lightning according to the one who makes *aḍā'a* intransitive, meaning: "whenever the lightning flashed, they walked in its light." This is supported by the reading of Ibn Abī 'Ablah: *kullamā ḍā'a*, triliteral, and it has been stated before that this is a dialect. In Ubayy's codex: *marrū fīhi*; in Ibn Mas'ūd's codex: *maḍaw fīhi*. This clause is a third resumption, as if it were said: "Then it illuminates for them in both states, the flash of the lightning and its dimming." It was said: "Whenever it lights up for them," to the end of it.

Yazid ibn Qutayb and al-Dahhak read *wa-idha adhlama* (﴿وإذا أظْلَمَ﴾) in the passive voice (*mabniyyan lil-maf'ul*). The basic use of *adhlama* is intransitive; one says *adhlama al-layl* ("the night grew dark"). The words of al-Zamakhshari apparently indicate that *adhlama* is transitive by itself, taking an object, which is why it can be put into the passive form for the unnamed agent (*ma lam yusamma fa'iluh*). Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Adhlama* is used in the passive form for the unnamed agent," and the following line of Habib ibn Aws al-Ta'i came in his poetry:

*They two darkened my two states, then cleared away*
*their darkness from the face of a beardless, grey-haired one.*

Although he is a later poet and his poetry is not cited as evidence for the language, he is one of the scholars of Arabic, so consider what he says as equivalent to what he transmits. Do you not see that the scholars say, "The evidence for it is a verse of the *Hamasa*," and they are satisfied by it because they trust his transmission and his precision? That is the end of his words. Its apparent meaning, as we have said, is that it is transitive and its passive form is for the unnamed agent, and for this reason one takes comfort in the line of Abu Tammam: *They two darkened my two states.* I have a different interpretation of it from what al-Zamakhshari mentioned: that *adhlama* is not transitive by itself to an object, but is transitive by means of a preposition (*harf jarr*). Do you not see how *adhlama* was made to govern the object with *'ala* ("upon")? On this view, what takes the place of the agent, or what is omitted, is the prepositional phrase (*al-jarr wa-al-majrur*), which is in the place of a nominative. The original would be: *wa-idha adhlama al-layl 'alayhim* ("and when the night darkened upon them"), then it was omitted, and the prepositional phrase took its place, as in the example: *ghadiba Zayd 'ala 'Amr* ("Zayd was angry with 'Amr"), then you omit Zayd and make the verb passive, saying: *ghudiba 'ala 'Amr* ("he was made angry with 'Amr"). The estimate in that case is not: *wa-idha adhlama Allah al-layl*, so that the Name (Allah) is omitted and the pronoun of the night is put in the place of the agent. As for what occurred in the words of Habib, it is not to be cited as evidence. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi was criticized for citing the line of Habib:

*Whoever has as the pasture of his resolve and his cares*
*a meadow of wishes, will always remain emaciated.*

And how can one cite the speech of one who is a *muwallad* (a later, non-classical Arabic speaker), when people have written books about the grammatical errors that occurred in his poetry?

The meaning of *qamu* ("they stood") is: they stopped and halted. The first clause is introduced by *kullama* ("whenever") and the second by *idha* ("when"). Al-Zamakhshari said: "Because they are eager for the existence of what their resolve is tied to, namely the possibility of walking and reaching it, so whenever they find an opportunity from it they seize it; it is not so with stopping and being held back." That is the end of his words. In my view there is no difference in this verse, in terms of meaning, between *kullama* and *idha*; for when repetition is understood from ﴿كُلَّما أضاءَ لَهم مَشَوْا فِيهِ﴾ ("Whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it"), it also necessarily follows that repetition applies to "when it darkens upon them, they stand," because the matter revolves between the lightning's illumination and the darkening; whenever the one exists, the other is absent, so the repeated existence of the one entails the repeated absence of the other. Moreover, some grammarians held that *idha* indicates repetition just as *kullama* does, and they recited:

*Whenever I find the heat of love in my liver,*
*I come toward the water-skins of the people to cool myself.*

He said: "So this has the meaning of *kullama*."

There are several interpretations of this verse. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi said: "Whenever the Qur'an brings them what they love, they follow it." Qatada said: "The lightning's illumination is the attainment of what they hope for of the safety of their souls and their wealth, so they hasten to follow it." Muqatil said: "The lightning is Islam, and their walking in it is their guidance; when they abandon that, they fall into their error." It was also said: its illumination for them is their being left without trial, and their walking in it is their remaining at peace by displaying what they display. It was also said: whenever the hypocrites hear the Qur'an and its proofs, they are at ease and walk with it; but when what troubles them or what they are commanded to do descends, they stand, that is, they remain fixed in their hypocrisy. It was also said: whenever blessings follow upon them, they say, "This is a true religion," and when a calamity befalls them they become angry and remain fixed in their hypocrisy. It was also said: whenever their hypocrisy remains hidden, they walk; but when they are exposed, they stand. It was also said: whenever the truth becomes clear to them, they follow it; but when it is darkened for them by desire, they abandon it. It was also said: they benefit by displaying faith, but when a trial or hardship comes upon the Muslims, they become bewildered, just as those people stood in the darkness, bewildered.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "This is a parable for the severity of the matter upon the hypocrites, by its severity upon the people of the downpour and what they are in of utmost bewilderment and ignorance about what they should do and what they should leave. When they encounter from the lightning a flash, along with fear that it will snatch their sight, they seize that flash as an opportunity and take a few small steps; but when it fades and its gleam weakens, they remain standing, restrained from movement." That is the end of his words.

The object of *shaa* ("if He willed") here is omitted, being indicated by context. The estimate is: "If Allah willed to take away their hearing and their sight." The discussion of the *ba'* in *bi-sam'ihim* ("with their hearing") is like the discussion of it in ﴿ذَهَبَ اللَّهُ بِنُورِهِمْ﴾ ("Allah took away their light," [2:17]). The singular form of "hearing" was discussed earlier, in the commentary on ﴿خَتَمَ اللَّهُ عَلى قُلُوبِهِمْ وعَلى سَمْعِهِمْ﴾ ("Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing," [2:7]). Ibn Abi 'Abla recited: *la-adhhaba bi-asma'ihim wa-absarihim* ("He would indeed take away their hearing and their sight"), in which case the *ba'* is extra (*za'ida*), the estimate being: "He would indeed take away their hearing." This is like what some have said: "I wiped his head" (meaning "I wiped his head with my hand"), "I was rough with his chest" (meaning "I was rough with his chest"). But it is not one of the places where extra *ba'* is analogically permitted. The plural *asma'* ("hearings") corresponds to the plural *absar* ("sights").

The meaning of the sentence is that Allah's taking away their hearing and their sight would occur on the condition of His will to do so. It was also said: the meaning is to destroy them, for in their destruction is the loss of their hearing and sight. It was also said: it is a threat of removing hearing and sight from their bodies, so that they cannot reach by them what is theirs, just as they did not reach by them what is against them. It was also said: He would have made their hypocrisy apparent against them, and the honour of Islam would have departed from them. It was also said: He would have taken away their hearing so that they would not hear the thunderbolts and be wary, and taken away their sight so that they would not see the light to walk. It was also said, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas: He would have taken away their hearing and sight for what they abandoned of the truth after knowing it. It was also said: He would have hastened punishment for them in this world, taking away their hearing and sight, so that they would not benefit by them in this world, because they did not use them in the truth, and so they would not benefit by them in the Hereafter. It was also said: He would have increased the roar of the thunder so as to deafen them, and the brightness of the lightning so as to blind them. It was also said: He would have struck them with what they fear of rebuke and threat. It was also said: He would have exposed them before the believers and given them power over them. Al-Zamakhshari said: "He would have taken away their hearing by the crash of the thunder and their sight by the flash of the lightning."

The apparent sense of the speech is that all of this pertains to the people of the downpour, so to turn its apparent sense to refer to the hypocrites is not evident. Rather, this is an exaggeration of the bewilderment of these travellers and the severity of what befell them from the downpour, which contained darkness, thunder and lightning, to the point that the thunderbolts nearly deafen them and the lightning nearly blinds them. Then He mentioned that if the will had preceded the taking away of their hearing and sight, they would indeed have been taken away. And just as we chose, in His words ﴿ذَهَبَ اللَّهُ بِنُورِهِمْ﴾ ("Allah took away their light") and what follows it, that this is an exaggeration in the state of the one who kindles a fire, so likewise we choose here that this is an exaggeration in the state of the journey and the extreme severity of what befalls the one compared. The extreme exaggeration in the state of the two things compared (the *mushabbah bihi*) entails extreme exaggeration in the state of the thing compared (the *mushabbah*). Although these particulars belonging to the thing used as the comparison are not necessarily found in the thing compared by their counterparts, especially when the figure is one of the single-element figures (*al-tamthilat al-mufrada*). But as for our view that it belongs to the compound figures (*al-tamthilat al-murakkaba*), the exaggeration lies in the comparison with what the state of the thing compared has come to, and this has been discussed before. He specified hearing and sight in His words ﴿لَذَهَبَ بِسَمْعِهِمْ وأبْصارِهِمْ﴾ ("He would have taken away their hearing and their sight") because they were mentioned earlier in His words ﴿فِي آذانِهِمْ﴾ ("in their ears," [2:19]) and in His words ﴿يَخْطَفُ أبْصارَهُمْ﴾ ("it nearly snatches away their sight").

Some have said: the thunder and the thunderbolts were mentioned, and their perceiver is hearing; the darkness and the lightning, and their perceiver is sight. Then He said: if He willed, He would take that away from the hypocrites as a punishment for their hypocrisy. Then Exalted is He follows what He attached to the will with the report about His power, because by these two the completion of actions is achieved, I mean power and will. He used the form of intensity (*sighat al-mubalagha*) because none has a better claim to it than He, Exalted is He. As for *'ala kull shay'* ("over everything"): it is connected to the word *qadir* ("capable"). In the word *qadir* there is something that indicates the specification of the general, since power does not relate to impossibilities.

Some of our discussion has already preceded concerning the harmony (*tanasuq*) of the verses already discussed, and we will summarise that here. Exalted is He began this surah by describing His clear Speech; then He made clear that it is guidance for the believers of this community and praised them; then He praised those who strove alongside them in faith and followed them from the believers among the People of the Book, and mentioned what they are upon of guidance in the present and of success in the outcome. Then He followed them by mentioning their opposites, those whose hearts and hearing are sealed and whose sight is covered, who have despaired of their faith, and the mention of the great punishment prepared for them. Then He followed these with the states of the hypocrites, the deceivers and mockers. He delayed mentioning them, even though they are worse in state than the polytheists, because they displayed in outward appearance the attributes of the believers and in their inner reality the attributes of the disbelievers. So Allah mentioned the believers first, then the disbelievers, the people of wretchedness, in the second place, and then the hypocrites, the apostates, in the third place, and dwelt at length on their disgraceful deeds, sending down about them thirteen verses. All of this is a condemnation of their states and an admonition about the disgrace of their deeds. Then He did not suffice with that, until He displayed their states in the form of parables, and this was more effective in deterring them from the ugly deeds they had committed. Consider the excellence of this arrangement, which has reached the peak of beauty, and has been firmly established in the eloquence of the varieties of rhetorical ornament (*badi'*) and the eloquence of the meanings of expression (*ma'ani al-bayan*).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 21 (part 1 of 4):

﴿O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you, so that you may be mindful (of Him).﴾ ﴿He who made the earth a resting place for you, and the sky a canopy, and sent down water from the sky, and brought forth with it fruits as provision for you. So do not set up rivals to God while you know (better).﴾ [al-Baqarah: 22]

*Ya* (يا): a particle of address (harf al-nida', vocative particle). Some claimed it is an ism fi'l (a verb-like noun) meaning "I call." Despite the frequency of the vocative in the Qur'an, it is never used for the vocative except with this particle, and it is the most general of the vocative particles, since it is used to address the near, the distant, one calling for help, and one being invoked. Some pronounced it with imala (vowel inclination). It may be used purely for alerting (tanbih), in which case it is followed by a subject (mubtada'), a command, a wish (tamanni), or a reason (ta'lil). The more correct view is that no vocative object (munada) is intended after it.

*Ayyu* (أيّ): interrogative, conditional, attributive, and a connective (wasla) to address what contains the definite article *al-*. It is also a relative pronoun (mawsulah), contrary to Ahmad ibn Yahya, who denied its use as a relative pronoun, and it cannot be a descriptive (mawsufah), contrary to al-Akhfash.

*Ha* (ها): a particle of alerting (harf tanbih). It is most often used with a detached nominative pronoun that is the subject (mubtada') and is predicated by a demonstrative, or with a demonstrative not indicating distance. It is used to separate *ayyu* in the vocative from the nominative following it. Its vowelling with a *damma* is the dialect of the Banu Malik of the Banu Asad, who say: *ya ayyuhar-rajulu* and *ya ayyatuha al-mar'ah*.

*Al-khalq* (الخَلْق): creating (ikhtira') without a model. Its original meaning is measuring (taqdir). One says: "He measured (khalaqa) the hide (adim) by its tanning." Zuhayr said:

*"You indeed cut what you measure, and some people measure but do not cut."*

Qutrub said: creation is bringing into existence with measure and arrangement. *Khalq* and *khaliqah* apply to the created thing. The meanings of creation, bringing into existence, originating, innovating, inventing, and producing are close in sense.

*Idha/ba'd* (قبل/بعد) and similar temporal adverbs: it is said that *qabl* is an adverb of time, and no governing word operates upon it to remove it from its adverbial function except *min*. Its origin is a descriptive that replaced its described noun necessarily. When you say "I stood before Zayd," the underlying sense is "I stood for a time before the time of Zayd's standing," and all of that is omitted and *qabla Zaydin* stands in its place.

*La'alla* (لَعَلَّ): a particle expressing hope regarding desirable things and expectation regarding feared things. It is used only with what is possible; one does not say *la'alla al-shabab ya'ud* ("perhaps youth returns"). It does not mean *kay* ("so that"), contrary to Qutrub and Ibn Kaysan, nor is it interrogative, contrary to the Kufans. It has several dialectal forms, of which only the classical one occurs in the Qur'an. After it, the accusative of the two nouns is not attested. Al-Akhfash reported that some Arabs apply the jussive after *la'alla*, and Abu Zayd claimed this is the dialect of the Banu Uqayl.

*Al-firash* (الفِراش): the bedding on which one sits, sleeps, and turns over.

*Al-bina'* (البِناء): a verbal noun, and it may refer to what is built, such as a house, a dome, a tent, or a tent of hair. The tents (abniyah) of the Arabs are their tents (akhbiyatuhum).

*Al-ma'* (الماء): well known. Some said it is a flowing substance by which animal life subsists. Its pattern is *fa'l*; its alif is converted from a waw, and its hamza replaces a ha'. This is shown by *muwayh*, *miyah*, and *amwah*.

*Al-thamarah* (الثَّمَرة): what a tree produces that is edible or fragrant.

*Al-nidd* (النِّدّ): one who opposes and rivals, whether as an equal, an opposite, or a contrary. Abu Ubaydah and al-Mufaddal said *al-nidd* means *al-didd* (opposite). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this restriction is an illustration, not a limitation. Others said: *al-nidd* is the hostile opponent who opposes out of hatred, from *al-nudud* (aversion). Al-Mahdawi said: *al-nidd* is the equal and the like. This is the position of the lexicographers except Abu Ubaydah, who said it means opposite. Al-Zamakhshari said: *al-nidd* is the like, and it is said only of a like who opposes and contends. Jarir said:

*"Do you, Tayyim, make a rival of me, when Tayyim is not one to be opposed by a man of noble lineage?"*

*Nadadtu al-rajul* means "I opposed the man and contended with him," from *nadda, nududan*, meaning "he fled." The meaning of the saying "God has no rival (nidd) and no opposite (didd)" is that it negates what would stand in His place and negates what would contradict Him.

*Ya ayyuha al-nas* (يا أيُّها النّاسُ): an address to all who have understanding, as Ibn 'Abbas said; or to the Jews specifically, as al-Hasan and Mujahid said; or to them and the hypocrites, as Muqatil said; or to the disbelievers and polytheist Arabs and others, as al-Suddi said. The apparent view is Ibn 'Abbas's, since claiming particularity requires proof.

The connection of this verse with what precedes it is this: when God mentioned the responsible believers, disbelievers, and hypocrites, their attributes and conditions, and what each will come to, He shifted from speaking about them to direct address by vocative. This is an iltifat (shift of grammatical person), similar to His words ﴿You alone we worship﴾ [al-Fatihah: 5] following ﴿Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fatihah: 2]. It is one of the kinds of balaghah (eloquence) mentioned earlier, since it jolts and stirs the listener, being a movement from one category to another. This is not a shift from particular address to general address, as some exegetes claimed, since no particular address preceded it, unless this is taken figuratively, meaning that speech is directed at it: it is as if one said that he moved from a particular speech to a general speech. The exegetes said this. It is one of the methods of eloquence, since they specify and then generalize. For this reason, when the verse ﴿And warn your nearest kindred﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 214] was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) summoned them, specifying and generalizing, and said: "O 'Abbas, uncle of Muhammad, I cannot avail you anything against God. O Fatimah, daughter of Muhammad, I cannot avail you anything against God. O children of 'Abd al-Muttalib, I cannot avail you anything against God." A poet said:

*"O my sons, lament, and O people of my house and my tribe, lament for me year after year."*

End of his speech.

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and 'Alqamah that they said: whatever in which "O you who..." (ya ayyuha al-nas) occurs is Meccan, and whatever in which "O you who believe" (ya ayyuha alladhina amanu) occurs is Medinan. As for "O you who believe," this is correct. As for "O mankind," it is taken as the general rule, since this surah is Medinan and "O mankind" occurs in it.

*Ayyu* in *ayyuha* is a singular vocative object (munada mufrad) built on a *damma*. The *damma* is not an inflectional vowel (harakat i'rab), contrary to al-Kisa'i and al-Riyashi. It is a connective to address what contains the definite article *al-*, since what cannot be addressed directly is reached through addressing *ayyu*. It is in the accusative position, and the *ha'* of alerting is as if it were a substitute for what was prevented from being annexed. *Al-nas* is raised as a descriptive (sifah) according to the wording, because the indeclinable form of *ayyu* resembles inflection, and therefore it is permissible to observe the wording. It is not permissible to make it accusative according to its position, contrary to Abu 'Uthman. Abu al-Hasan said, in one of his two views, that *ayyu* in the vocative is a relative pronoun, and that the nominative following it is the predicate of an omitted subject. So when one says *ya ayyuha al-rajul*, the underlying sense is "O he who is the man." The discussion of this view and the view of Abu 'Uthman is fully treated in the grammar books.

﴿Worship your Lord﴾ (اعْبُدُوا رَبَّكُمُ): When God addressed the people with the vocative, He commanded them to worship, and its explanation was given earlier in His words ﴿You alone we worship﴾ [al-Fatihah: 5]. The command to worship includes believers and disbelievers. One might say: believers are already worshippers, so how is it valid to command them to do what they are already engaged in? The answer is that for them it is a command to increase in worship, so it is valid to address all with the command to worship. Note the appropriateness of the word "Lord" (rabb) here, since He is the master and the reformer, and it is fitting that whoever owns or reforms the servant's affairs be singled out for worship and not associated with another in it.

If the address is general, then His words ﴿who created you﴾ are a descriptive of praise. If the address is to the polytheist Arabs, the phrase is explanatory, since the word "lord" for them is shared between God, exalted is He, and their gods. He drew attention, by the attribute of creation, to His deserving worship to the exclusion of others: ﴿Is He who creates like He who creates not?﴾ [al-Nahl: 17]. Or it draws attention to His bounty toward them through creating them in the complete form, distinguishing them from others through intellect, and dealing kindly with them through apparent and hidden blessings. Or it establishes the proof against them by this attribute, which no one can share with Him. The attribute of lordship and creation necessitates worship, since it combines the love of one who does good and the love of one who originates. The lover is at the utmost degree of obedience to the one he loves. The scholars said: love is threefold, and some added natural love, like a father's love for his child.

Abu 'Amr assimilated (idgham) *wa-khalaqakum*, and the lexical meaning of *khalq* was explained earlier. When it means invention and origination, none may be described by it except God, exalted is He.

The Muslims have agreed that there is no creator except God, exalted is He. If *khalq* means measuring, then the linguistic implication is that it may be applied to other than God, exalted is He, as in the verse of Zuhayr. God said: ﴿So blessed is God, the best of creators﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14], and ﴿when you shaped from clay﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 110].

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Basri, teacher of al-Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar, said: applying the name "Creator" to God, exalted is He, is impossible, because measuring and arranging are an expression of thought, conjecture, and calculation, and these are impossible for God, exalted is He. It seems Abu 'Abd Allah did not know that *khalq* in the language applies to origination. The statement of al-Basri contradicts the words of God: ﴿He is God, the Creator, the Originator﴾ [al-Hashr: 24], since he claimed that the name "Creator" is not applied to God. The language, the Qur'an, and consensus refute him.

He coordinated ﴿and those before you﴾ with the pronoun in the accusative in *khalaqakum*. The coordinated element is earlier in time than the element it is coordinated with, yet He began with it, although it is later in time. This is because a person's knowledge of his own state is clearer than his knowledge of others' states, since the nearest thing to him is himself. Also, they are the ones addressed with the command to worship, so alerting them first to the states of their own selves is more emphatic and more important. He began first with the attribute of creation, since the Arabs acknowledged that God is their creator, and they are the ones addressed. Other people follow them, since the Qur'an was revealed in their tongue.

Ibn al-Sumayfa' read *wa-khalaqa man qablakum*, making it a coordination of clauses. Zayd ibn 'Ali read ﴿and those before you﴾ with a *fatha* on the *mim* of *min*. Al-Zamakhshari said: this reading is problematic, and its justification despite its difficulty is that the second relative pronoun is inserted between the first and its relative clause for emphasis, just as Jarir inserted in his verse:

*"O Tayy, Tayy of 'Adiy, may you have no father!"*

where the second *Tayy* is placed between the first and what is annexed to it, and as they insert the particle of annexation (lam) between the annexed and the annexed-to in *la aba laka*. End of his speech. This justification that al-Zamakhshari offered for Zayd's reading is the view of some grammarians, who claimed that if you place after the relative pronoun another relative pronoun with the same meaning as an emphasis for it, the second relative pronoun does not need a relative clause, as in the verse:

*"Of the company of those who, those who harmed them, the niggardly fear the knocker's ring, they clattered."*

فَإذا وجَوابُها صِلَةُ اللّائِي، ولا صِلَةَ لِلَّذِينَ؛ لِأنَّهُ إنَّما أتى بِهِ لِلتَّأْكِيدِ.

[Its] response is the *silah* (relative clause complement) of *allati*, and there is no *silah* for *alladhina*, because it was only brought for emphasis (*tawkid*).

قالَ أصْحابُنا: وهَذا الَّذِي ذَهَبَ إلَيْهِ باطِلٌ؛ لِأنَّ القِياسَ إذا أُكِّدَ المَوْصُولُ أنْ تُكَرِّرَهُ مَعَ صِلَتِهِ لِأنَّها مِن كَمالِهِ، وإذا كانُوا أكَّدُوا حَرْفَ الجَرِّ أعادُوهُ مَعَ ما يَدْخُلُ عَلَيْهِ لِافْتِقارِهِ إلَيْهِ، ولا يُعِيدُونَهُ وحْدَهُ إلّا في ضَرُورَةٍ، فالأحْرى أنْ يَفْعَلَ مِثْلَ ذَلِكَ بِالمَوْصُولِ الَّذِي الصِّلَةُ بِمَنزِلَةِ جُزْءٍ مِنهُ.

Our companions said: this view he adopted is false, because by analogy, when a relative pronoun (*mawsul*) is emphasized, it should be repeated together with its *silah*, since the *silah* is part of its completeness. And when they emphasized a preposition (*harf al-jarr*), they repeated it together with what it governs, because it depends on it; they do not repeat it alone except out of necessity. So it is more fitting to do the same with the relative pronoun, whose *silah* is like a part of it.

وخَرَّجَ أصْحابُنا البَيْتَ عَلى أنَّ الصِّلَةَ لِلْمَوْصُولِ الثّانِي وهو خَبَرُ مُبْتَدَأٍ مَحْذُوفٍ، ذَلِكَ المُبْتَدَأُ والمَوْصُولُ في مَوْضِعِ الصِّلَةِ لِلْأوَّلِ تَقْدِيرُهُ مِنَ النَّفَرِ اللّاتِي هُمُ الَّذِينَ أذاهم، وجازَ حَذْفُ المُبْتَدَأِ وإضْمارِهِ لِطُولِ خَبَرِهِ،

Our companions interpreted the line of poetry so that the *silah* belongs to the second relative pronoun, which is the predicate of an omitted subject. That subject and the relative pronoun stand in the position of the *silah* for the first one. The sense is: "from the group of those [women] who are those who harmed him." The omission and implicit presence of the subject is permitted because its predicate is long.

فَعَلى هَذا يَتَخَرَّجُ قِراءَةُ زَيْدٍ أنْ يَكُونَ قَبْلَكم صِلَةَ مِن، ومِن خَبَرَ مُبْتَدَأٍ مَحْذُوفٍ، وذَلِكَ المُبْتَدَأُ وخَبَرُهُ صِلَةً لِلْمَوْصُولِ الأوَّلِ وهو الَّذِينَ، التَّقْدِيرُ: والَّذِينَ هم مِن قَبْلِكم.

On this basis, the reading of Zayd (ibn Ali) can be explained: *qablakum* is the *silah* of *min*, and *min* is the predicate of an omitted subject. That subject and its predicate form the *silah* of the first relative pronoun, *alladhina*. The estimated meaning is: "and those who are from before you."

وعَلى قِراءَةِ الجُمْهُورِ تَكُونُ صِلَةُ الَّذِينَ قَوْلَهُ: (مِن قَبْلِكم)، وفي ذَلِكَ إشْكالٌ؛ لِأنَّ الَّذِينَ أعْيانٌ، ومِن قَبْلِكم جارٌّ ومَجْرُورٌ ناقِصٌ لَيْسَ في الإخْبارِ بِهِ عَنِ الأعْيانِ فائِدَةٌ، فَكَذَلِكَ الوَصْلُ بِهِ إلّا عَلى تَأْوِيلٍ، وتَأْوِيلُهُ أنَّهُ يَئُولُ إلى أنَّ ظَرْفَ الزَّمانِ إذا وُصِفَ صَحَّ وُقُوعُهُ خَبَرًا نَحْوَ: نَحْنُ في يَوْمٍ طَيِّبٍ، كَذَلِكَ يُقَدَّرُ هَذا والَّذِينَ كانُوا مِن زَمانٍ قَبْلَ زَمانِكم.

According to the majority reading, the *silah* of *alladhina* is the phrase "from before you." This raises a difficulty: *alladhina* refers to persons, while "from before you" is an incomplete prepositional phrase, and predicating it of persons gives no benefit. Likewise, using it as a *silah* requires an interpretation. The interpretation is that a time adverbial (*zarf al-zaman*), once described by an adjective, may validly function as a predicate, as in "we are in a good day." Similarly, this is to be understood as: "and those who existed from a time before your time."

وهَذا نَظِيرُ قَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿كالَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِكُمْ﴾ [التوبة: ٦٩] وإنَّما ذَكَرَ ﴿والَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِكُمْ﴾، وإنْ كانَ خَلْقُهم لا يَقْتَضِي العِبادَةَ عَلَيْنا لِأنَّهم كالأُصُولِ لَهم، فَخَلْقُ أُصُولِهِمْ يَجْرِي مَجْرى الإنْعامِ عَلى فُرُوعِهِمْ، فَذَكَّرَهم عَظِيمَ إنْعامِهِ تَعالى عَلَيْهِمْ وعَلى أُصُولِهِمْ بِالإيجادِ.

This is similar to His saying: ﴿like those before you﴾ [al-Tawba: 69]. He mentioned ﴿and those before you﴾ even though their creation does not in itself impose worship on us, because they are like the roots (*usul*) of these people. The creation of their roots is like a favour upon their offspring. Thus He reminded them of His great favour upon them and upon their roots by bringing them into existence.

ولَيْسَتْ لَعَلَّ هُنا بِمَعْنى كَيْ لِأنَّهُ قَوْلٌ مَرْغُوبٌ عَنْهُ ولَكِنَّها لِلتَّرَجِّي والإطْماعِ، وهو بِالنِّسْبَةِ إلى المُخاطَبِينَ؛ لِأنَّ التَّرَجِّيَ لا يَقَعُ مِنَ اللَّهِ - تَعالى - إذْ ﴿هُوَ عالِمُ الغَيْبِ والشَّهادَةِ﴾ [الحشر: ٢٢]، وهي مُتَعَلِّقَةٌ بِقَوْلِهِ: ﴿اعْبُدُوا رَبَّكُمُ﴾، فَكَأنَّهُ قالَ: إذا عَبَدْتُمْ رَبَّكم رَجَوْتُمُ التَّقْوى، وهي الَّتِي تَحْصُلُ بِها الوِقايَةُ مِنَ النّارِ والفَوْزُ بِالجَنَّةِ.

*La'alla* here does not mean *kay* ("in order that"), because that view is rejected. Rather, it expresses hope and expectation (*tarajji* and *itmaʿ*), and this is with respect to the addressees, since hope cannot be attributed to God, the Exalted, as He ﴿knows the unseen and the seen﴾ [al-Hashr: 22]. It is connected to His saying: ﴿worship your Lord﴾. It is as if He said: if you worship your Lord, you hope for taqwa, which is what brings protection from the Fire and success in Paradise.

قالَ ابْنُ عَطِيَّةَ: ويَتَّجِهُ تَعَلُّقُها بِخَلَقَكم لِأنَّ كُلَّ مَوْلُودٍ يُوجَدُ عَلى الفِطْرَةِ فَهو بِحَيْثُ يُرْجى أنْ يَكُونَ مُتَّقِيًا.

Ibn Atiyya said: it is also valid for it to be connected to *khalaqakum* (who created you), because every child is born upon the natural disposition (*fitra*), so he is such that one may hope he will be God-fearing.

ولَمْ يَذْكُرِ الزَّمَخْشَرِيُّ غَيْرَ تَعَلُّقِها بِخَلَقَكم، قالَ: لَعَلَّ واقِعَةٌ في الآيَةِ مَوْقِعَ المَجازِ لا الحَقِيقَةِ؛ لِأنَّ اللَّهَ - تَعالى - خَلَقَ عِبادَهُ لِيَتَعَبَّدَهم بِالتَّكْلِيفِ، ورَكَّبَ فِيهِمُ العُقُولَ والشَّهَواتِ، وأزاحَ العِلَّةَ في أقْدارِهِمْ وتَمْكِينِهِمْ، وهَداهُمُ النَّجْدَيْنِ، ووَضَعَ في أيْدِيهِمْ زِمامَ الِاخْتِيارِ، وأرادَ مِنهُمُ الخَيْرَ والتَّقْوى، فَهم في صُورَةِ المَرْجُوِّ مِنهم أنْ يَتَّقُوا لِتَرَجُّحِ أمْرِهِمْ، وهم مُخْتارُونَ بَيْنَ الطّاعَةِ والعِصْيانِ، كَما تَرَجَّحَتْ حالُ المُرْتَجِي بَيْنَ أنْ يَفْعَلَ وأنْ لا يَفْعَلَ، انْتَهى كَلامُهُ.

Al-Zamakhshari mentioned only its connection to *khalaqakum*. He said: *la'alla* in the verse is used figuratively (*majaz*), not literally (*haqiqa*), because God created His servants to worship Him through obligation, endowed them with intellects and desires, removed excuses through their capacities and empowerment, guided them to the two paths, placed in their hands the reins of choice, and desired from them good and taqwa. So they are, in the form of one from whom taqwa is hoped, because their situation is balanced, and they choose between obedience and disobedience, just as the state of one who hopes is balanced between doing and not doing. End of his words.

وهو مَبْنِيٌّ عَلى مَذْهَبِهِ الِاعْتِزالِيِّ مِن أنَّ العَبْدَ مُخْتارٌ، وأنَّهُ لا يُرِيدُ اللَّهَ مِنهُ إلّا فِعْلَ الخَيْرِ، وهي مَسْألَةٌ يُبْحَثُ فِيها في أُصُولِ الدِّينِ.

This is based on his Mu'tazili doctrine (*Mu'tazili*: a rationalist school) that the servant is free to choose, and that God wills from him only good. This is a question debated in the principles of religion (*usul al-din*, the theological foundations).

والَّذِي يَظْهَرُ تَرْجِيحُهُ أنْ يَكُونَ: (لَعَلَّكم تَتَّقُونَ) مُتَعَلِّقًا بِقَوْلِهِ: ﴿اعْبُدُوا رَبَّكُمُ﴾ . فالَّذِي نُودُوا لِأجْلِهِ هو الأمْرُ بِالعِبادَةِ، فَناسَبَ أنْ يَتَعَلَّقَ بِها ذَلِكَ، وأتى بِالمَوْصُولِ وصِلَتِهِ عَلى سَبِيلِ التَّوْضِيحِ أوِ المَدْحِ لِلَّذِي تَعَلَّقَتْ بِهِ العِبادَةُ، فَلَمْ يَجِئْ بِالمَوْصُولِ لِيُحَدِّثَ عَنْهُ بَلْ جاءَ في ضِمْنِ المَقْصُودِ بِالعِبادَةِ. وأمّا صِلَتُهُ فَلَمْ يَجِئْ بِها لِإسْنادٍ مَقْصُودٍ لِذاتِهِ، إنَّما جِيءَ بِها لِتَتْمِيمِ ما قَبْلَها. وإذا كانَ كَذَلِكَ فَكَوْنُها لَمْ يَجِئْ بِها (p-٩٦)لِإسْنادٍ يَقْتَضِي أنْ لا يُهْتَمَّ بِها فَيَتَعَلَّقُ بِها تَرَجٍّ أوْ غَيْرُهُ، بِخِلافِ قَوْلِهِ: اعْبُدُوا، فَإنَّها الجُمْلَةُ المُفْتَتَحُ بِها أوَّلًا والمَطْلُوبَةُ مِنَ المُخاطَبِينَ. وإذا تَعَلَّقَ بِقَوْلِهِ: اعْبُدُوا، كانَ ذَلِكَ مُوافِقًا، إذْ قَوْلُهُ: اعْبُدُوا خِطابٌ، ولَعَلَّكم تَتَّقُونَ خِطابٌ.

The view that appears preferable is that "*la'allakum tattaqun*" (so that you may be God-fearing) is connected to the saying ﴿worship your Lord﴾. What they were addressed for is the command to worship, so it is fitting that the hope be connected to it. The relative pronoun and its *silah* came as clarification or praise of the one to whom worship is directed; the relative pronoun was not introduced to be the subject of a predication in its own right, but comes within the intended sense of worship. As for its *silah*, it was not introduced for a predication intended for its own sake, but to complete what precedes it. Given this, since the *silah* was not introduced for a predication that would require it to be unimportant, hope or something else may be attached to it. This differs from "worship," which is the opening clause and the primary demand made of the addressees. When it is connected to "worship," it is consistent, since "worship" is an address and "*la'allakum tattaqun*" is an address.

ولَمّا اخْتارَ الزَّمَخْشَرِيُّ تَعَلُّقَهُ بِالخَلْقِ قالَ: فَإنْ قُلْتَ كَما خَلَقَ المُخاطَبِينَ لَعَلَّهم يَتَّقُونَ، فَكَذَلِكَ خَلَقَ الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ، لِذَلِكَ قَصَرَهُ عَلَيْهِمْ دُونَ مَن قَبْلَهم، قُلْتُ: لَمْ يَقْصُرْهُ عَلَيْهِمْ ولَكِنْ غَلَّبَ المُخاطَبِينَ عَلى الغائِبِينَ في اللَّفْظِ والمَعْنى عَلى إرادَتِهِمْ جَمِيعًا، انْتَهى كَلامُهُ. وقَدْ تَقَدَّمَ تَرْجِيحُ تَعَلُّقِهِ بِقَوْلِهِ: اعْبُدُوا، فَيَسْقُطُ هَذا السُّؤالُ.

When al-Zamakhshari chose to connect it to creation, he said: If you ask, "Just as He created the addressees so that they may be God-fearing, He likewise created those before them, so why did He restrict it to them and not to those before them?" I answer: He did not restrict it to them, but he gave precedence to the addressees over the absent ones in wording and meaning, while intending both together. End of his words. The preference for connecting it to "worship" has already been stated, so this question falls away.

وقالَ المَهْدَوِيُّ: لَعَلَّ مُتَّصِلَةٌ بِاعْبُدُوا لا بِخَلَقَكم؛ لِأنَّ مَن دَرَأهُ اللَّهُ - عَزَّ وجَلَّ - لِجَهَنَّمَ لَمْ يَخْلُقْهُ لِيَتَّقِيَ. والمَعْنى عِنْدَ سِيبَوَيْهِ: افْعَلُوا ذَلِكَ عَلى الرَّجاءِ والطَّمَعِ أنْ تَتَّقُوا، انْتَهى كَلامُهُ.

Al-Mahdawi said: *la'alla* is connected to "worship," not to "created you," because whoever God, the Mighty and Majestic, has created for Hell did not create him in order to be God-fearing. The meaning according to Sibawayh (*Sibawayh*: the founder of Arabic grammar) is: do that in hope and expectation that you may be God-fearing. End of his words.
