The surah of the Qur'an was named so because its reciter, through his recitation, rises above the one who does not have it, like the stages of a building (*kusur al-bina'*). It was also said that it is named for its completeness and perfection, and from this it was said of a complete she-camel that she is a *surah*. Or it is because it is a portion of the Qur'an, from *asARat* (to leave a remnant), and *su'r* (remainder). Its root is with a hamza, and it was lightened. This was stated by Abu 'Ubayda, and the hamza in it is also a dialect form.

*Min mithlihi* (مِن مِثْلِهِ): similarity is achieved by even the slightest resemblance. Sibawayh, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned that *"I passed by a man like you"* (*marartu bi-rajulin mithlika*) can carry three possible meanings. The word *mithl* is necessarily followed by an annexed noun in form. For this reason some later Arabic writers erred in the saying of a poet:

*"And one like you is one who owns all people, yet there is no equal (mathal) among people."*

It cannot be a locative, contrary to the Kufans. In the chapter on the adjective, when it follows a singular, a dual, or a plural, it has a ruling that is mentioned in grammar.

*Al-du'a'* (الدُّعاءُ): calling out someone by his name.

*Al-shuhada'* (الشُّهَداءُ): the plural of *shahid*, in the intensive form, like *'alim* and *'ulama'*. It is not far-fetched that it is the plural of *shahid*, like *sha'ir* and *shu'ara'*. *Fu'ala'* is not a pattern of *fa'il*.

*Dun* (دُونَ): a noun of place, which is necessarily used either in the literal or the figurative sense of location, and it is not used except with *min*. Sibawayh said: *"As for dunaka, it is never in the nominative."* Al-Farra' said: *"He mentioned dunaka and similar adverbs, which are not used as nominative subjects by preference, though they sometimes are."* The apparent view of al-Akhfash permits its free use, and he interpreted the saying of the Exalted ﴿and among us are some below that﴾ (72:11) as a subject, built because it is annexed to a built word. It has also come in the nominative in poetry. A poet said:

*"Do you not see that I defended my pack, and I faced the edge of death, and death is behind it?"*

*Dun* may also function as an adjective meaning "inferior," as in *thawbun dun* ("a shabby garment"). Sibawayh reported this in one of his two positions. In that case it is inflected in all the forms of inflection, and *dun* is a homonym.

*Al-sidq* (الصِّدْقُ): its opposite is *al-kadhib* (lying), and it is the correspondence of the statement to the reality it reports.

*Lan* (لَنْ): a particle of negation of two letters in its original form, simple, not composed of *la* and *in*, contrary to al-Khalil in one of his two positions. Its *nun* is not a substitute for an *alif*, so that its original form would be *la*, contrary to al-Farra'. It does not imply perpetual negation, contrary to al-Zamakhshari in one of his two positions. *Lan* is a shorter negation than *la*, since *lan* negates what is near, and the meaning of negation does not extend in it as it extends in *la*, contrary to the one who claimed otherwise. It is not a supplication, contrary to the one who claimed that. Its function is to put the verb in the subjunctive. They mentioned that its jussive use is a dialect form. Ibn al-Tarawa recited:

*"He will not be disappointed now in your hope, whoever moves the ring at your door."*

It has many rulings, which are mentioned in grammar.

*Al-waqud* (الوَقُودُ): a noun for what is burned with, and it has also been heard as a verbal noun. It is one of the verbal nouns that come in the pattern *fa'ul*, which are few. According to what the teacher Abu al-Hasan Ibn 'Usfur mentioned, nothing has been preserved from this pattern other than this one, along with *al-wudu'* (ablution), *al-tahur*, *al-wulu'*, and *al-qabul*.

*Al-hijara* (الحِجارَةُ): the plural of *hajar* (stone). The *ta'* in it is for emphasizing the feminine of the plural, like *al-fuhula* (masculinity).

*U'iddat* (أُعِدَّتْ): was made ready.

﴿And if you are in doubt﴾: it was revealed concerning all the disbelievers. Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning the Jews. The reason for this is that they said: *"What Muhammad brings to us does not resemble revelation, and we are in doubt about it."* The first view is more apparent.

The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when Allah argued against them with what establishes His oneness and nullifies association with Him, and informed them that whoever sets up a partner for Allah is far removed from knowledge and discernment, He then began to argue against those who doubted prophethood with what removes their doubt, which is the Qur'an being a miracle. He explained to them how they could know that it is from Allah or from himself: by having them and those they rely upon produce a surah like it. They are the eloquent, the articulate, those who excel in weaving speech, in prose and verse, and who turn with ease through the branches of expression, and who are acknowledged for excellence in this.

Since they were truly in doubt, and since the conditional *in* only enters upon what is possible or what is certain but whose time of occurrence is unspecified, some exegetes claimed that *in* here means *idha* ("when"), because *idha* indicates the past of what it is attached to. The position of the verifiers, however, is that *in* is never used with the meaning of *idha*. Al-Mubarrad and those who agreed with him claimed that the past-tense defective verb *kana* has meanings that no other past verbs have, so because of the strength of *kana*, he claimed that *in* does not change its meaning to the future, but remains in its past meaning if *in* enters upon it. The correct view is that of the majority, that *kana* is like the other verbs. Where the apparent wording suggests what al-Mubarrad said, they interpreted it either by supposing an elided *yakun* after *in*, as in the words of the Exalted ﴿if his shirt is torn from the front﴾ (12:26), meaning "if it should be that his shirt was torn," or by taking it to mean clarification, that is, that it becomes clear that his shirt was torn. According to the view of Abu al-'Abbas, their being in doubt is in the past, and it becomes like the case where one says: *"If you have done good to me, then I have done good to you,"* when it is taken in its apparent sense without interpretation.

For this reason some exegetes said about the words ﴿And if you are in doubt﴾: the speech of Allah in this was according to certainty. It is like a man saying to his slave: *"If you are my slave, then obey me,"* because Allah, the Exalted, knows what hearts conceal. He said: this is shown by the fact that the cause of the revelation of this verse was the saying of the Jews: *"And we are truly in doubt about what he has brought."* He took it to mean *idha* and that its past is both in wording and meaning, or like the statement of a speaker: *"If you are my slave, then obey me,"* to escape from making what follows *in* have a future meaning. This is possible. There is no contradiction between *"if they were in doubt"* in the past and its being conditioned on their being in doubt in the future, because what is past may be continued, such that the one holding the doubt in the past is shown the opposite of it, and so the doubt leaves him. So it was said: *"and if you are"*, that is, *"and if you should be,"* by maintaining the past state that had preceded them, *so produce*. This is like one who says to his disobedient son: *"If you are disobeying me, then leave me."* The meaning is: if you are in the future disobeying me, then leave me. He does not intend to make it conditional upon the past, nor does he mean that *in* means *idha*, since there is no contradiction between the occurrence of disobedience in the past and the conditioning of departure upon its occurrence in the future. There is no need to make what is established as a particle mean the temporal *idha*.

It has already been stated for us that there is no contradiction between the words of the Exalted ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾ (2:2) and the words ﴿And if you are in doubt﴾, when we discussed ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾ (2:2). In ﴿in doubt about (fi raybin)﴾, the meanings are treated as if they were physical bodies (*tanzil al-ma'ani manzilat al-ajram*). *Min* (مِن) may indicate the starting point of the action or causation, and it cannot be partitive.

*Ma* (ما) may be a relative pronoun, meaning "from that which We sent down," and the returning pronoun is elided, meaning "We sent it down," and the condition for its elision is present. Some have allowed that *ma* may be an indefinite qualifying noun, and what has been said previously about the indefinite qualifying *ma* has been mentioned. We have taken the doubling of the middle radical here to mean causing to descend, which is equivalent to the hamza of causation. This is confirmed in this verse by the reading of Yazid ibn Qatib: *mimma anzalna* ("from what We caused to descend") with the hamza. The doubling here does not indicate that it was sent down in stages at different times, contrary to al-Zamakhshari, who said: *"If you ask why it was said 'mimma nazzalna' (what We sent down in stages) using the verb tanzil and not inzal, I say: because the intended meaning is descent by gradation and stages, and this is a metaphorical use, due to the challenge."* What al-Zamakhshari went to regarding the doubling of the middle radical here is what is expressed as intensification, that is, doing it again and again. So it indicates this meaning by doubling and is expressed as multiplicity. Al-Zamakhshari overlooked that this usually happens with verbs which, before doubling, are transitive, such as *jaraḥtu Zaydan* ("I wounded Zayd"), *fatahtu al-bab* ("I opened the door"), *qata'tu* ("I cut"), and *dhabahtu* ("I slaughtered"). One does not say *jallasa Zaydun* ("Zayd sat") or *qa''ada 'Umar* ("'Umar sat") or *sawwama Ja'far* ("Ja'far fasted") in that sense. *Nazzalna* was not transitive before doubling; it was intransitive, and its transitivity is conveyed only by the doubling or by the hamza. If it occurs with an intransitive verb, it is rare. They said: *mata al-mal* ("the property died") and *mawwata al-mal* ("he made the property die"), when that happens to it abundantly. Also, the doubling that is meant to indicate multiplicity only indicates the frequency of the act's occurrence, but it does not make the intransitive verb transitive. *Nazzala* before doubling was intransitive and not transitive, so the transitivity derived from doubling is evidence that it is for causation and not for multiplicity, since if it were for multiplicity and had been applied to an intransitive verb, it would remain intransitive, as in *mata al-mal* and *mawwata al-mal*. Also, if doubling in *nazzala* indicated gradual sending down, the words of the Exalted ﴿Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?﴾ (25:32) would require interpretation, since doubling indicates gradation and multiplicity, and His words ﴿all at once﴾ (25:32) contradict that. Also, the readings in both forms for many of the passages show that they have the same meaning. Also, the use of *nazala* where multiplicity and gradation cannot be meant, except by a very far-fetched interpretation, indicates this. The Exalted said: ﴿And they say, "Why was a sign not sent down to him?"﴾ (6:37). He also said: ﴿Say, "If there were angels walking calmly on the earth, We would have sent down to them from heaven an angel as a messenger."﴾ (17:95). The meaning is not that they asked for the repeated sending down of a sign, nor that He made the repeated sending down of an angel-messenger conditional upon the existence of angels on the earth. Rather, the meaning, and Allah knows best, is simply sending down.

In *nazzalna* there is *iltifat* (a shift of grammatical person), because it moves from the third person pronoun to the first person pronoun, since before it is ﴿Worship your Lord﴾ (2:21) and ﴿So do not set up rivals to Allah﴾ (2:22). If the speech had continued in this context, it would have been "what He sent down upon His servant," but in this shift there is a magnification of the one sent down and the one upon whom it was sent down, which a third-person pronoun cannot convey, especially since He used *na* ("We"), which suggests complete exaltation and the magnification of the matter. Its parallel is the words ﴿And it is He who sends down water from the sky, and We bring forth﴾ (6:99). The transitivity of *nazzala* by *'ala* ("upon") indicates the elevation of what is sent down over the one upon whom it is sent down, and its firm establishment upon him, and that it has become as if clinging to him, unlike *ila* ("to"), which indicates reaching and arrival. Because of this meaning which *'ala* conveys, and its repetition in the Qur'an in several verses, the Exalted said: ﴿He has sent down to you the Book in truth﴾ (3:3); ﴿Ta-Ha﴾ (20:1); ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an to you that you should be distressed﴾ (20:2); ﴿It is He who sent down to you the Book﴾ (3:7).

The attribution of the servant to Him, the Exalted, contains an alert to the greatness of his rank and his being singled out for pure servitude, the raising of his station, and his attribution to Himself, the Exalted. The word *'abd* (servant) is general and specific, and this use is specific. A poet said:

*"Do not call me except by 'the Servant of her,' for it is the most noble of my names."*

And whoever reads "upon Our servants" in the plural (ʿalā ʿibādinā bi-l-jamʿ), it is said that it means the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his community. This is said by al-Zamakhshari, and it is parallel to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Lest you should say, "The Book was only sent down to two groups before us"﴾ [al-An'am: 156]. This is because the benefit of what is sent down and the guidance obtained through it, by carrying out the obligations and the promised reward for that, is not restricted but is shared by the followers and those they follow, so it is as if it was sent down to them. This is a type of majaz (metaphor) in which one who did not directly undertake a matter, when he is charged with it, is treated as one who did. It is also possible that it means the Prophets to whom revelation and the Books were sent down, with the Messenger being the first intended by this and the earliest included in the generality, because it is he whom his opponents challenged (tahaddi) to produce a book. This would be an address to those who deny prophethood, as He, exalted is He, said quoting some of them: ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure when they said, "God has not sent down anything upon a human being"﴾ [al-An'am: 91]. It is also possible that the singular is meant as the plural, and this reading clarifies it, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And mention Our servant Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the people of strength and vision﴾ [Sad: 45], according to the reading of the one who uses the singular ('abdinā), in which case it is for the genus.

﴿So produce a sūrah﴾: He demanded of them that they produce any sūrah whatsoever, and a sūrah is a portion of the Qur'an, the shortest of which is three verses. He did not impose on them a long sūrah, which would have caused them difficulty in the matter, but made it easy for them and lightened the burden by demanding a sūrah of any kind, and this is the utmost rebuke and humiliation for them. So if neither you nor your helpers can produce a sūrah like it, how do you claim that it is of the same kind as your speech? And how could doubt about it being from God reach you?

Al-Zamakhshari has touched here on mentioning the benefit of the Qur'an being divided and arranged into sūrahs, but that is not from the science of tafsir; it is rather from the benefits of its detailing and sectioning.

"Min mithlihi" (like it): the pronoun (hā') refers either to "mā" (what) or to "ʿabdinā" (Our servant), and the preferred view is the first, which is the saying of most of the exegetes. Its preference is due to several aspects. The first: the doubt was introduced first as directed at the thing sent down, not at the one to whom it was sent down; and although doubt about what is sent down is, by necessary implication, doubt about the one to whom it is sent down, returning the pronoun to it is more appropriate. The second: it has come in a parallel to this verse and this context, His saying: ﴿So produce a sūrah like it﴾, ﴿So produce ten sūrahs like it, forged﴾ [Hud: 13], ﴿Say: "If mankind and the jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Qur'an, they could not produce its like"﴾ [al-Isra': 88]. The third: this requires that they are incapable of producing it, whether they gathered together or acted individually, and whether they were unlettered or not. Returning the pronoun to what was sent down requires that each individual unlettered person is incapable of it, because its like would be only one unlettered person. As for if they gathered together or were literate, there is no doubt that the miracle in the first way is stronger.

When we make the pronoun refer to what was sent down, then "min" is partitive (li-l-tabʿīḍ), and it is in the position of a qualifier to "sūrah," meaning: a sūrah which is among its like. It appears from al-Zamakhshari's speech that there is a contradiction in this "min." He said: "min mithlihi" is connected to "sūrah" as a qualifier of it, meaning, a sūrah that is from its like. So his saying "connected to sūrah" implies that it is governed by it, and his saying "a qualifier of it, meaning a sūrah that is from its like" implies that it is not governed by it, so his speech is contradictory and its end contradicts its beginning. But it may be understood that he does not mean the technical grammatical connection, like the connection of the "bi" in the phrase "my passing by Zayd is good," but rather the semantic connection, i.e., the connection of the qualifier to the qualified. He avoided the other view, that it connects to his saying "fa-atū" (so produce), in which case "min mithlihi" would not refer back to what was sent down, as will be made clear, God willing.

Al-Mahdawi and Abu Muhammad Ibn ʿAṭiyya permitted that it be for specifying the kind (li-bayān al-jins) on the assumption that the pronoun refers to what was sent down, and that likeness is interpreted as its composition, its arrangement, and the eloquence of its meanings which you know, and that nothing renders them incapable except the composition with which the Qur'an is singled out, or its unseen matters and its truthfulness. They also permitted, on this view, that it be extra (zā'ida). The sayings concerning the interpretation of likeness will come, God willing, when the pronoun refers to what was sent down.

The grammarians differed over establishing this meaning for "min." What our companions (the Shafiʿis) hold is that "min" is not for specifying the kind, and the difference between its being partitive and its being for specifying the kind is mentioned in the books of grammar. As for its being extra in this position, it is not permissible according to the view of the Kufans and the majority of the Basrans.

Regarding likeness, when the pronoun refers to what was sent down, there are several sayings. The first: "min mithlihi" means in the excellence of composition, the wondrous arrangement, the marvelous narration, the strangeness of style, its conciseness, and the perfection of its meanings. The second: like it in its unseen matters, in its informing of what has happened and what will happen. The third: in its containing of command, prohibition, promise, threat, stories, wisdom, admonitions and parables. The fourth: like it in its truthfulness and its freedom from alteration and distortion. The fifth: like it, i.e., the speech of the Arabs which is of its kind. The sixth: in that it does not wear out with repeated recitation, the ears do not tire of it, water does not erase it, its wonders are not exhausted, its strangeness does not end, its freshness does not fade over successive readings, and its sweetness does not depart from the tongues of its reciters. The seventh: like it in the continuance of its verses and the abundance of its miracles. The eighth: like it, i.e., like it in being one of the Books of God sent down to those before him, testifying to you that what has come to you with it is not from God, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: "Produce your proof, if you are truthful"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111].

And if we make the pronoun refer to the one to whom it was sent down, then "min" is connected to the saying "fa-atū" (so produce): "produce from the like of the Messenger a sūrah." The meaning of "min" on this view is the starting point (ibtidāʾ al-ghāya, the origin of the source), and it is permissible that it be in the position of a qualifier, so it is connected to an omitted element. It is also for the starting point, meaning: a sūrah that comes into being from a man like the Messenger, i.e., the starting point of its existence is from one like him.

Regarding likeness when the pronoun refers to the one to whom it was sent down, there are sayings. The first: "min mithlihi" (from one like him) is an unlettered man who does not write well, in his original natural state. The second: like him, one who has not studied with scholars, nor sat with the wise, nor was it transmitted from him before that that he pursued reports, nor did he travel from his land to other cities. The third: like him according to your claim that he is a sorcerer, a poet, a madman. The fourth: like him from among the sons of his kind and people of his region.

The mention of the "like" (mithl) in His saying "min mithlihi" is by way of supposition (ʿalā sabīl al-farḍ) according to most of the sayings by which likeness has been interpreted, when the pronoun refers to what was sent down. And according to some of them it is not by way of supposition. This is the view of one who interprets that by "the like" he meant the speech of the Arabs which is of its kind. As for when the pronoun refers to the one to whom it was sent down, it is not by way of supposition, since there exists an unlettered man who does not write well, and there exists one who did not study with scholars, and there exists one who, according to their claim, is a sorcerer, regarding the one to whom it was sent down.

Al-Zamakhshari chose that there is no like and no equal. After he interpreted the "like" on the assumption that the pronoun refers to what was sent down, he said: "So produce a sūrah of what is of its description in marvelous eloquence and elevated rank in the excellence of composition." And on the assumption that it refers to the one to whom it was sent down, "or produce from one who is in his condition of being a human, Arab, or unlettered, who has not read the books and has not taken from the scholars." Al-Zamakhshari said: "And there is no intention of a like or an equal there, but it is like the saying of al-Qabaʿthari to al-Hajjaj, when he said to him: 'I will surely mount you on the dark horse like the Amir was mounted on the dark and the grey.' He meant one who was in the description of the Amir in authority, strength, and open-handedness, and did not intend anyone to make a like for al-Hajjaj." End of al-Zamakhshari's speech.

On the interpretation of likeness by which it was explained when the pronoun is taken as referring to the one to whom it was sent down, the existence of a like has already been demonstrated, and on the view that it refers to what was sent down, the existence of a like is possible under some interpretations of likeness. Therefore al-Zamakhshari's saying "there is no like and no equal," while interpreting likeness as being a human, Arab, or unlettered who has not read the books, is not correct, because the one who is like him in this particular matter exists.

When He demanded of them a challenge by a sūrah, on the assumption that they were in doubt about it being from God, He did not suffice with their own saying that, until He demanded of them that they call upon their witnesses to gather together on that, to back one another and to help one another and support one another. So He said: ﴿And call your witnesses﴾. Here "call" (idʿū) is interpreted as "seek help" (istaghīthū). Abu al-Haytham said: "Supplication (duʿāʾ) is the seeking of aid. Daʿā: he sought help. And with 'istaḥḍirū' (summon): so-and-so called so-and-so to the judge, meaning he summoned him." Their witnesses are their gods, for they used to believe that they would testify for them before God. This is said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Suddi, Muqatil and al-Farraʾ. Or [witnesses are] those who attend and present themselves to them from among the helpers and supporters, as said by Ibn Qutayba. And it is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, or [it means] those who testify for you that what you produce is like the Qur'an. This was reported from Mujahid. The plural of "shahīd" (witness) as "shuhadāʾ" is fine as the plural of "shāhid" (witness), because it follows the measure of the plural of "faʿīl" like this, and because of the intensity in "faʿīl." It seems he indicated that they should bring witnesses who are mature in testimony, fit for the establishment of proof through them.

﴿Apart from God﴾: it is connected to "call" (udʿū), meaning: and call, apart from God, your witnesses. That is, do not call upon God as witness by saying "God witnesses that what we claim is true," as the one who is unable to establish evidence says. Rather, call upon the witnesses from among people whose testimony validates claims. It is as if he said: call, apart from God, whoever will testify for you. It is also possible that "apart from God" is connected to "your witnesses." The meaning: call those whom you have taken as gods apart from God and whom you claimed would testify for you on the Day of Resurrection that you are upon the truth, or your helpers apart from God, i.e., apart from the friends of God whom they seek help from apart from God. Or the meaning of "apart from God" may be: in the presence of God, as al-Aʿsha said:

*"It shows you the mote in front of it, and it is beneath it."*

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 23–24 (part 3 of 4):

That is, it shows you the speck of dust in front of it (i.e., in front of the speck of dust), because of its thinness and clarity. His command, exalted is He, to them to produce a counterpart and to call upon their helpers and assistants, while He knows that they are not able to do that, is a command of mockery and of rendering them powerless. Exalted is He, has further made clear that this does not occur from them, especially the explanation of "the witnesses" as their gods, because they are inanimate objects that do not speak. So the command that they seek help from what does not speak in opposing the miraculous is the utmost mockery of them. The apparent meaning of His words: ﴿if you are truthful﴾ is: in your being in doubt about what was sent down upon Our servant, that it is from Us. And it has been said: in what you are capable of of opposition.

He related of them in another verse: ﴿Had We willed, we would have said the like of this﴾ [al-Anfal: 31]. However, mention of opposition does not occur in this verse, but their being in doubt requires, in their view, that it is not from God, and whatever is not from God is, in their view, capable of being opposed. So it is possible that the meaning is: if you are truthful in the capability of opposition.

Since His command, exalted is He, to them to bring a surah like it was a command of mockery and of rendering them powerless, because they are not capable of that, He moved on to guiding them, since they are not capable of opposition, and commanded them to beware of the Fire that was prepared for those who denied. He used ﴿in﴾ (in, if), though it is among the places of ﴿idha﴾ (when), in mockery of them, as the speaker says: "If I defeat you, I will not spare you," while he knows that he will prevail; or he used ﴿in﴾ according to their assumption, and that what was incapable among them was before reflection, like what is doubtful in their view, because of their reliance on their eloquence. The meaning of ﴿So if you do not do it﴾ is: so if you do not bring. He expressed bringing by the verb, and the verb functions as a pronoun, so it is used to express every action, and it spares you the length of what it stands for. Al-Zamakhshari said: Had he not turned from the word "bringing" to the word "doing," it would have been lengthy to say: "So if you do not bring a surah like it, and you will never bring a surah like it." The statement of al-Zamakhshari is not binding, because if it were said: "So if you do not bring, and you will never bring," the meaning would be as mentioned, and it would be that the object has been omitted for brevity, just as the object of "you did not do" and "you will never do" is omitted for brevity. Do you not see that the estimate is: "So if you do not do the bringing of a surah like it, and you will never do the bringing of a surah like it"? Thus they are equal in the omission.

In the book of Ibn Atiyyah there is a strange explanation for the action of "lam" in putting the verb in the jussive, he said: "lam" puts the verb in the jussive because it resembles "la" in the sense of negating the category, in that both negate; so just as "la" deletes the tanwin of the noun, similarly "lam" deletes the vowel or the sign from the verb.

In His words: ﴿and you will never do﴾ there is a stirring of their resolve, so that their incapacity afterward is more eloquent and more wondrous. In this there are two proofs of the establishment of prophethood. The first: the soundness of the challenge being a miracle. The second: the report of the unseen, that they will never do it. This is known only to God, exalted is He. What indicates this is that if they had opposed it, the motives to transmit it would have been abundant, especially from its detractors. When it was not transmitted, it indicates that it is a report of the unseen, and that was his miracle.

As for what Musaylimah the Liar produced in his babbling, and Abu al-Tayyib al-Mutanabbi in his maxims and the like, they did not intend by it opposition; they only claimed that a revelation had descended upon them with that. So they brought from it poor wording, foolish meaning, a mixed language, a base style, a paragraph not well-composed, (p-107) an ugly opening, and a weak closing, such that if that were compared with their speech in other than what they claimed to be revelation, there would be between them such a difference in eloquence and such a contrast in rhetoric that it would not be hidden from anyone with slight discernment in that. How then would the expert critics and the eloquent rhetoricians? God deprived them of their eloquence because of their claim and their fabrication of falsehood against God.

His words: ﴿and you will never do﴾ are a parenthetical sentence, so it has no place in the grammatical structure, and in it there is an emphasis of meaning that is not hidden. For when He said: "So if you do not do," and its meaning was a negation in the future, presenting that as a possibility, He informed that it does not occur, and that is a true report; so in that is the emphasis that they will not oppose it. The pairing of the verb with "lan" distinguishes the parenthetical sentence from the circumstantial clause, because the circumstantial clause is not entered by "lan." The negation with "lan" in this sentence rather than "la" was used, though both are sisters in negating the future, because in "lan" there is emphasis and intensification. You say to your companion: "I will not stay tomorrow," and if he disputes it with you, you say: "I will never stay tomorrow," as you do in: "I am staying," and "I am indeed staying." So said al-Zamakhshari. What he mentioned here is contrary to what is reported from him, that "lan" implies negation for ever. As for what Ibn Khatib Zamlakani held, that "lan" negates what is near and that "la" extends the negation, it is almost the reverse of al-Zamakhshari's view. These statements, I mean emphasis, perpetuity, and negation of what is near, are sayings of later scholars; what is referred to regarding the meanings of these particles and their usages are the leading Arabic linguists whose sayings are relied upon. Sibawayh, may God have mercy on him, said: "Lan is a negation of the phrase 'sa-yaf'alu' (he will do)," and he said: "La is a negation of 'taf'alu' (he does) and 'lam taf'al' (he did not do)," end of his words. By "taf'alu" and "lam taf'al" he means the future. This is an explicit text from him that both negate the future, except that "lan" is a negation of what the particle of futurity enters upon, and not a negation of the present tense that is intended to refer to the future. So "lan" is more specific, since it enters upon what has an explicit indicator of the future in its wording. For this reason the disagreement arose regarding "la": does it specialize in negating the future, or may it negate the present? The apparent meaning of Sibawayh's words, may God have mercy on him, here is that it does not negate the present, except that he mentioned among its exceptive particles "la yakunu" and "la yumkinu," whose negation cannot be taken as referring to the future, because it has the meaning of "illa" (except), so it is for the performative, and if it is for the performative then it is the present. So this supports Sibawayh's words: "and la is a negation of 'yaf'alu' and 'lam yaf'al'," and this which was mentioned in the exception. When this which we have mentioned is established, the closest of these sayings is the saying of al-Zamakhshari, first: that in "lan" there is emphasis and intensification because it negates what is future by the particle, unlike "la," which negates what is intended as future from what has no particle to make it clearly future; and because "la" may negate the present rarely, so "lan" is specific to the future and specific to the imperfect; and because "wa-lan taf'alu" is shorter than "wa-la taf'alun." For all this, the preference is for negation with "lan" over negation with "la."

﴿Then guard yourselves against the Fire﴾: is the answer to the condition. He used it as an expression for abandoning obstinacy, because whoever is obstinate after the truth has become clear to him deserves punishment by the Fire. Guarding against the Fire is one of the results of abandoning obstinacy and one of its necessary consequences. He made "the Fire" definite here because it was previously mentioned indefinitely in Surah al-Tahrim, and the one in Surah al-Tahrim was revealed in Makkah, while this one is in Madinah. When an indefinite noun mentioned earlier is repeated, it is mentioned a second time with "al" and becomes definite because of its prior mention, and it is described with "alladhi" and its clause, and the clause is known to the listener because of the earlier mention of His words: ﴿a fire whose fuel is men and stones﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6], or because of hearing that from the People of the Book before the revelation of the verse. The majority read the waw with a fatha. Al-Hasan read with variation, and Mujahid, Talhah, Abu Hayah and Isa ibn Umar al-Hamdani read it with a damma on the waw. Ubayd ibn Umayr read it and vocalized it on the pattern fa'il (waqid, "fuel"). According to the reading of the majority and the reading of Ibn Umayr, it is the firewood; according to the reading with damma, it is the verbal noun with an omitted modifier, i.e., "owner of its fuel," because men and stones are not themselves the fuel, or it is taken that they themselves became the fuel as hyperbole, as one says: "So-and-so is the pride of his town." This Fire is distinguished from others in that it is kindled by men and stones, and these are themselves what is burned. The apparent meaning of this description is that it is one fire, and His words, exalted is He: ﴿Guard yourselves and your families from a fire whose fuel is men and stones﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6], do not indicate that they are many different fires, nor does His words: ﴿So I have warned you of a fire blazing﴾ [al-Layl: 14]; because a description may be of the actual reality and not for distinguishing it from something shared with it. "Men" here refers to the specific ones among those whom God wills to enter it, even though its wording is general. "Stones" means the idols, and they were fuel for the Fire together, just as they were in this world when they carved them and worshipped them as gods besides God. This is clarified by His words: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides God are the fuel of Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya: 98]. Or "stones" means stones of brimstone; this was related from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jurayj. It was singled out for that because of its rapid ignition, foul smell, great smoke, intense adherence to the body, and the strength of its heat when it is heated. It has been said: it is black sulphur, or special stones prepared for Hell, whose fuel never ceases when kindled. It has been said: when the people of the Fire lose patience, they weep and complain, so God produces a black, dark cloud, and they hope for relief and raise their heads toward it, and it rains down upon them great stones like millstones, so the Fire increases in kindling and blazing, since the stones are what they hoarded of gold and silver, which are cast with them into the Fire, and they are branded with them. According to these sayings, the "al" in "the stones" is not for generality but for definition of the genus. Some scholars held that it may be for the comprehensiveness of the genus, and the meaning would be that the Fire promised to them is fit to burn what is cast into it of these two genera; so He expressed its fitness and readiness with the established matter. He said: Men and stones were mentioned only to magnify the matter of Hell and to alert to the intensity of its fuel, so that this would have the greatest effect on souls and produce from it the fear that is not produced by other than it; and the intended meaning is not the literal reality.

What this speaker held, that this description is by fitness and not by actual occurrence, is not apparent; rather the apparent meaning is that this description is inevitably actual, and for that reason the description was repeated. Nor is there in that anything indicating that there is nothing in it other than men and stones, by evidence of what is mentioned in more than one place of the presence of jinn and devils in it. He placed men before stones because they are the rational ones who perceive pain and are tormented, or because they are more kindling for the Fire than inanimate matter, due to their skins, flesh, fat, bones and hair, or because that is greater in causing fear. For when you see a person being burned, your skin creeps and your reason is bewildered, unlike a stone. Ibn Atiyyah said: In His words, exalted is He: ﴿prepared﴾ there is a refutation of those who say that the Fire has not yet been created, and it is the view in which Mundhir ibn Sa'id fell, end of his words. Its meaning is that he claimed that preparation occurs only for what exists, because "i'dad" is the readying and setting aside of a thing. The poet said:

I have prepared for calamities a full coat of mail and a swift, sturdy horse.

Meaning: he prepared it. They said: this is only applicable to something that exists. Some said: or what is in the sense of what exists, such as His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah has prepared for them forgiveness and a great reward﴾ [al-Ahzab: 35]. Munzir, whom Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned, was known as al-Ballut, and he was the Chief Judge (qadi al-qudat) in al-Andalus. He was a Mu'tazili in most of the principles (al-usul) and a Zahiri in the subsidiary rulings (al-furu'), and he has mention and virtues in the histories, and he is one of the distinguished men of perfection in al-Andalus. That view spread to him from the view of many of the Mu'tazila, and it is an issue mentioned in the principles of religion (usul al-din): the position of the People of the Sunnah is that Paradise and Hell are created in actuality. Many of the Mu'tazila, the Jahmiyya and the Najjamiyya held that they have not yet been created and that they will be created. 'Abdullah recited: i'taddat, from al-'attad, meaning al-'uddah (preparation). Ibn Abi 'Abla recited: a'addaha Allah li'l-kafirin. Its being prepared for the disbelievers does not indicate that they are exclusively meant for it, as some interpreters held, that the fire of the sinners is other than the fire of the disbelievers. Rather, it specified the disbelievers only because the addressees are included among them, since their act is disbelief. It is established in the sound hadith that a group of the people of major sins will enter the Fire, but He suffices with mentioning the disbelievers, giving precedence to the majority over the minority, or because "the disbelievers" includes whoever disbelieved in Allah and disbelieved His blessings, or because whoever among the believers is taken out of it, it was not prepared for him permanently, unlike the disbelievers. The clause in His saying, "it has been prepared for the disbelievers," is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) regarding the Fire, and its governing element is "fattaqu" (so beware), as Abu al-Baqa' said. But there is scrutiny in that, because making the clause a circumstantial clause results in the meaning: "beware the Fire while it is being prepared for the disbelievers," and it is prepared for the disbelievers whether they guard against the Fire or not, so it would then be a necessary circumstantial clause. The original for a circumstantial clause that is not for emphasis is that it is transitional, and the better view in my opinion is that the clause has no place in the grammatical structure, and it is as if it were an answer to an assumed question: as if, when the Fire was described as having people and stones as its fuel, it was said: "For whom was it prepared?" So it was said: "It was prepared for the disbelievers."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 25 (part 1 of 4):

﴿And give good tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds, that for them are gardens beneath which rivers flow. Whenever they are provided with a fruit therefrom, they will say, "This is what we were provided with before," and it will be given to them in semblance, and for them therein are purified spouses, and they will abide therein forever.﴾ . Al-bishara (good tidings): the first report that reaches a person of good or of evil, though its most common usage is for good. The apparent statement of al-Zamakhshari is that it is only for good, and for this reason he interpreted ﴿so give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 21] as an exception, but this is refuted by transmission. It is said on the authority of Sibawayh: it is news that affects the skin (bashara) with sorrow or joy. Some of them said: for this reason it is restricted when it concerns sorrow. Al-bushra is beauty, and al-bashir is the beautiful one; this was stated by Ibn Duraid. Tabashir al-fajr (the first signs of dawn) are its beginnings. The verb has two dialects: the doubled form (tashdid), which is the higher dialect, and the single form (takhfif), which is the dialect of the people of Tihama. It has been recited in both dialects in the present tense in various places in the Qur'an, which will come, God willing. Al-salah (righteousness): its opposite is corruption (fasad). Al-jannah: the orchard whose trees cover its ground, and everything that covers something is said to have concealed it (ajannahu), and from this derive al-jinnah, al-jannah, al-jinn, al-mijann (shield), and al-janin (fetus). Al-Mufaddal said: al-jannah is every orchard in which there is shade. It is also said: every land in which there are trees and palms is a jannah, and if there are vines in it, it is firdaws. Taht (beneath): a adverb of place which is not used except with min, as stated by Abu al-Hasan, who said: the Arabs say, "taḥtaka rijlāka (beneath you are your two feet)," and they do not differ on the accusative case of taht. Al-nahr (river): smaller than the sea and larger than the rivulet. Whether it is the very course of water or the water in the wide course is a matter of two opinions. It has two dialects: the vowelling of the ha' (nahr with fatha), which is the higher dialect, and the sukun (nahr with sukun). With the fatha the plural anhar came as a regular analogical form, since af'al is not regular for the form fa'l of a sound-middle noun, although many words have come from it. It was called nahr because of its breadth; anhara means "it widened," and al-nahar (day) is so called because of the breadth of its light. Al-tashabuh: a reciprocal form from al-shabah, and al-shabah is the likeness. The form tafa'ul comes for six meanings: sharing in the agency with respect to the wording, and in it and in the object-hood with respect to meaning; giving the impression; feigning; the meaning of the verb tafa'ala being that of af'ala; corresponding to the unaugmented form; and dispensing with it. Al-zawj: the one that has another with it, and two together are zawjan. It is said of a man, "zawj," and of his wife also, "zawj," and "zawjah" is less common. Al-Farra' mentioned that zawj, when meaning the feminine, has two dialects: zawj, the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and zawjah, the dialect of Tamim and many of Qays and the people of Najd. Everything that is paired with its companion is a zawj for it, and zawj also means kind (sinf), and from it: zawj bahij (a beautiful pair), and ﴿or He weds them males and females﴾ [al-Shura: 50].
Al-taharah: cleanliness. The verb tahara, with fatha on the ha', is the most eloquent, and tahura with damma; the active participle of both is tahir. With fatha it is analogical, and with damma it is anomalous, like hamuda, fa-huwa hamid (it became sour, so it is sour), and khathura, fa-huwa khathir (it became thick, so it is thick). Al-khulud: remaining in life, or in dominion, or in a place for a long period without end. Whether it is applied to a long period that has an end, in the literal or the figurative sense, is a matter of two opinions. Zuhayr said:
"If praise could make people immortal, they would not die, but the praise of people does not make one immortal."
It is said: khalada bi'l-makan (he stayed in the place), and akhlada ila kadha (he inclined to such a thing, he settled into it). Al-mukhallad is the one who has not grown up. For this same meaning, namely settling and tranquillity, this small creature that lives in the earth is called khuld (mole). Its apparent usages and others indicate that khuld is a long stay, and it does not indicate a stay without end except with a contextual indicator. Al-Zamakhshari chose that it is the lasting permanence that does not cease, to strengthen his Mu'tazili doctrine that whoever enters the Fire does not leave it, but remains therein forever.
The authentic and widely transmitted hadiths indicate that some of the believers who entered the Fire will be brought out of it by intercession. The connection of His saying, the Exalted, "And give good tidings" to what precedes it is evident: when He mentioned what included the mention of the disbelievers and what their state would lead to in the Hereafter, and that was among the most eloquent of warnings and admonitions, He followed it with what included the mention of their counterparts, their states, and what God has prepared for them in the Hereafter of everlasting bliss. Thus it is customary in the Qur'an, generally, whenever the mention of the disbelievers and what is theirs occurs, it is followed by the believers and what is theirs, and vice versa, so that the exhortation combines threat and promise, gentleness and severity; for among people there is one whom fear does not draw but gentleness draws, and among them is one who is the opposite. The one commanded to give the tidings is said to be the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is said to be everyone who is fit for giving good tidings, without specification. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is better and more magnificent, because it indicates that the matter, due to its greatness and the grandeur of its status, deserves that every one who is able to give the tidings of it should give them, end of his words. My view is that the first aspect is preferable, because his command with the tidings, given its particularity, is more majestic and magnificent, and it seems that he did not rely upon every hearer giving the believers the tidings, but specified the greatest and most truthful of them, so that this would be more trustworthy for them and more certain in the report of this great tidings, since his giving tidings (ﷺ) is a giving of tidings from God, the Exalted. The clause "and give tidings" is conjoined to what precedes it, and what is relied upon in the conjunction is not the imperative itself, such that a counterpart of command or prohibition would be sought to which it is conjoined; rather, what is relied upon in the conjunction is the clause describing the reward of the believers, which is conjoined to the clause describing the punishment of the disbelievers, as when you say: "Zayd is punished with shackles and execution, and give 'Amr tidings of pardon and release." Al-Zamakhshari said this, and Abu al-Baqa' followed him, saying: the waw in "and give tidings" conjoins the clause of the reward of the believers to the clause of the punishment of the disbelievers, end of his words.

From this it is summarized that conjoining some clauses to others does not require that the meanings of the clauses agree. Accordingly, it is permissible to conjoin a declarative clause to a non-declarative clause. This matter is subject to disagreement. A group of grammarians stipulated the agreement of meanings, but the correct view is that this is not a condition, and it is the doctrine of Sibawayh. According to Sibawayh's doctrine, the parsing of al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Baqa' holds good. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Baqa' also allowed that his saying "wa-bashshir" be conjoined to his saying "fa-ttaqu al-nar," so that it would be the conjunction of a command to a command. Al-Zamakhshari said: as you say, "O Banu Tamim, beware the punishment of what you have committed, and give tidings, O so-and-so, to Banu Asad of kindness to them." What these two went to is an error, because his saying "fa-ttaqu" is the answer to the conditional, and its place is jussive, and the conjoined to the answer is an answer. In his saying "wa-bashshir" it is not possible that it be an answer, because it is a command to give tidings absolutely, not on the condition of "if you do not do," but rather He commanded that those who believe be given tidings in a command not dependent on anything before it. His saying "wa-bashshir" in its parsing is not like what was illustrated by his saying "O Banu Tamim," etc., because his saying "beware" has no place in parsing, unlike his saying "fa-ttaqu." Therefore conjunction was possible in what was illustrated, but not in "wa-bashshir." Zayd ibn 'Ali read "wa-bashshira" as a past verb in the passive voice. Al-Zamakhshari said: conjoined to "u'iddat," end of his words. This parsing is not possible according to the view of one who made "u'iddat" a clause in the place of a circumstantial phrase, because what is conjoined to a circumstantial phrase is a circumstantial phrase, and "wa-bashshir" cannot be in the place of a circumstantial phrase. So the more correct view is that it is a clause conjoined to what precedes it, even if the meanings of the clauses do not agree, as Sibawayh held, and this is the correct view. He cited for this the poet's verse:
"You converse with a gazelle at the gate of Ibn 'Amir, and anoint your fine eyelids with antimony."
And the verse of Imru' al-Qays:
"My cure is a tear if I shed it, and is there at a worn-out trace any relief?"
Sibawayh permitted: "Zayd came to me, and who is your brother, the two reasonable ones?" with "al-'aqilan" being the predicate of an omitted subject. We have previously mentioned that al-Zamakhshari restricts bisharah to the report that shows the joy of the one informed. Ibn 'Atiyya said: its most common usage is for good, and it may be used for evil when restricted and specified with evil for the one given the tidings, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿so give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 21]. Whenever the word bisharah is used without qualification, it is understood as good, end of his words. We have previously mentioned what contradicts their two statements from the statement of Sibawayh and others, and that bisharah is the first report that reaches a person of good or of evil. They said: it was named so because of its effect on the skin (bashrah): if it is good, it produces gladness and expansion; if it is evil, it produces contraction and withdrawal. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Their Lord gives them tidings of mercy from Him and good pleasure﴾ [al-Tawbah: 21], and He, the Exalted, said: ﴿so give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 21]. Al-Zamakhshari made this the reverse in speech intended as mockery, of one who increases the anger of the one mocked and his pain. It is said: its meaning is, place this in the position of the tidings from them. They said: the correct view is that every report other than the skin-affecting kind, whether good or evil, is bisharah. The poet said:
"The crow gives me tidings of the separation of my people, so I said to it: may you be bereaved, what a messenger of tidings!"
Another said:
"You gave me tidings, O Sa'd, that my beloved ones have turned away from me, and that the promise of love is the Gathering."

The doubling in "bashshir" is, as some said, of the intensive kind, and intensity in "bashshir" cannot be realized except in relation to the objects, because bisharah is the first report that gladdens or saddens according to the chosen view; intensity cannot be realized in it in relation to a single object. Therefore, in relation to it, the verb becomes sufficient in place of another verb, since the one who pronounces it doubled is not the Arabs who pronounce it single, as we explained earlier. That the object of "bashshir" is connected to a past verbal clause and not to an active participle indicates that the one deserving the tidings by God's grace is the one who has faith and is established in it, and in the righteous deeds. "Al-salihat" is the plural of salihah, an adjective that has taken the position of nouns in being followed by governing words. Al-Hutay'a said:
"How can there be satire when there persists, a righteous woman, from the house of Lam, coming to me in the absence of the unseen?"

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 25 (part 2 of 4):**

On this reading, *intisabuha* (the accusative of *jannat*, "gardens") is as a direct object (*maf'ul bihi*). The *alif-lam* in *al-salihat* ("the righteous deeds") is *lam al-jins* (the "lam of the genus", which denotes the category as a whole), not *lam al-'umum* (the "lam of comprehensiveness", which denotes every individual). The reason is that a believer can hardly perform all righteous deeds. Rather, he performs a portion of the sound and upright deeds in the religion, according to his condition in the obligations of the religious duties. The difference between *lam al-jins* when it enters a singular noun and when it enters a plural is this: with the singular, it may be intended to mean one member of the genus, whereas with the plural it cannot bear that meaning.

'Uthman ibn 'Affan said: "The righteous (*al-salih*) is that which is sincerely for Allah, exalted is He." Mu'adh ibn Jabal said: "It comprises four things: knowledge, intention, patience, and sincerity." Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah said: "It is that which agrees with the Book and the Sunnah." 'Ali ibn Abi Talib said: "[It is] the prayers at their times, and the balancing of their pillars and their forms." It has also been said: "It is trustworthiness." And it has been said: "It is repentance and free choice." The view of the majority is: "It is every righteous deed performed seeking Allah."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "In the saying of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾, there is a refutation of those who say that the word *iman* (faith), by itself, entails the acts of obedience, for if that were so He would not have repeated it." That is the end of his words.

In this there is also evidence that those whom Allah commanded to be given good tidings are those who combined faith with righteous deeds, and that whoever limits himself to faith alone, without righteous deeds, is not included among those given good tidings by this verse.

*Bashshir* (give good tidings) takes two objects: one directly, and the other by the omission of the preposition. Thus His saying ﴿that for them are gardens﴾ occupies the position of this second object. The omission of the preposition before *anna* is permitted as a regular, consistent rule. The grammarians differed, after the preposition is omitted, as to whether the position of *anna* and its two complements is genitive or accusative. The view of al-Khalil and al-Kisa'i is that its position is genitive; the view of Sibawayh and al-Farra' is that its position is accusative. The arguments are found in the books of grammar.

*Jannat* is the plural of *jannah*, a plural of paucity (*jam' qilla*). It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that they are seven gardens. Some said they are eight gardens. Some of the exegetes claimed that within the texts of the Book and the Sunnah there is what indicates that they are more than the number that Ibn 'Abbas and others pointed to. He said: For Allah says: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and rivers﴾ [al-Qamar 54:54]; ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman 55:46]; ﴿And besides them are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman 55:62]; ﴿near it is the Garden of Refuge﴾ [al-Najm 53:15]; ﴿gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾.

And from the Prophet (ﷺ) it is related that he said: "Two gardens of silver, their vessels and what is in them; and two gardens of gold, their vessels and what is in them; and nothing stands between the people and looking upon their Lord except the cloak of greatness upon His face, in the Garden of Eden." What this exegete cited does not show that they are more than what was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Al-jannah* is the name for the entire abode of reward. It comprises many gardens arranged in ranks according to the merit of those who did the deeds; for each class of them there is a garden from those gardens." That is the end of his words. He has, however, slipped into it his Mu'tazili doctrine (the Mu'tazilah being a theological school) by his saying "according to the merit of those who did the deeds."

The word *jannah* has come in the Qur'an both in the singular and in the plural. When it is singular, the intended meaning is the genus, and the *lam* in *lahum* ("for them") is *lam al-ikhtisas* (the lam of specification, indicating exclusive possession). The placing of the predicate first here is more emphatic than placing the subject first, because the pronoun refers back closely to *alladhina amanu* ("those who believed"); it is therefore more pleasing to the listener. The common rule is that when the subject is indefinite, its placing first is required, as in ﴿Will we indeed have a reward?﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:41].

The verse does not mention remaining steadfast in faith until death, for apostasy nullifies it, and this is understood from other verses. As for al-Zamakhshari, he proceeded according to his Mu'tazili doctrine, that entitlement to reward for faith and deed requires that the one responsible not nullify them by unbelief or by committing grave sins, and that he not regret what he has brought about of obedience and abstention from disobedience. He claimed that stipulating this is like something included within the mention.

It is known from the doctrine of the people of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah, the mainstream Sunni school) that whoever dies upon faith is among the people of Paradise, whether he committed a grave sin or did not, and whether he repented or did not. As for the one who says that *min* ("from/under") is superfluous and that the meaning is "flow beneath them," or that it means *fi* ("in"), i.e., "in beneath them," this does not accord with the established usage of the verifying scholars of Arabic grammar. Rather, it is connected to *tajri* (flows), and it indicates the starting point (*ibtida' al-ghayah*).

If we interpret the gardens as thick trees casting shade, there is no need for any omission. If we interpret them as land with trees, the omission is needed, since the meaning becomes "beneath their trees or their chambers and their dwellings." It has been said: he expressed "beneath them" to mean their lower parts and their roots. It has also been said: the meaning of *tajri min tahtiha* is: "by the command of its inhabitants and by their choice," so "beneath them" expresses their dominion over it and its flowing under their rule, as it has been said regarding the saying of Allah, exalted is He, quoting Pharaoh: ﴿And these rivers flow beneath me﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:51], meaning "by my command and my dominion." This meaning is appropriate only if the recitation were: "for them gardens flow beneath them," which would be parallel to "beneath me" when it is taken with an omitted noun, i.e., "beneath its people." If so, the meaning that was said to be unsuitable becomes sound, since the meaning is not "by the command and choice of the gardens."

It has also been said: the meaning of "from beneath them" is "from their direction." It has been narrated from Masruq that the rivers of Paradise flow without trenches, and that they flow over the surface of the land of Paradise spread out. If this report is sound, it is more eloquent in delight, sweeter to the sight, and more gladdening to the soul. For flowing water spreads over the face of the earth, its substance, so its rushing and breaking is beautiful. The finest gardens are those whose trees are thick, whose shade is abundant, whose water is clear and flows over the face of their ground. This is especially so in Paradise, whose pebbles are pearls, rubies, and pearls, so that the water breaks over those pebbles, and the clarity of the water reveals the radiance of those jewels; one hears from that water, breaking over those rubies and pearls, a murmur.

Our shaykh, the eloquent literary master Abu al-Hakam Malik ibn al-Murahhal al-Malaqi, may Allah have mercy on him, said, in his poem on the letter *mim*:

*"The clear water conversed with the pebbles, so the breeze passed over it, listening to what passed."*

Al-Tirmidhi narrated from the hadith of Hakim ibn Mu'awiyah, from his father, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, in Paradise there is a sea of water, a sea of honey, a sea of milk, and a sea of wine; then the rivers are split off after it." This hadith is supported by the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿therein are rivers of water unaltered﴾ [Muhammad 47:15], and the verse.

Since Paradise does not delight, and the garden is not pleasing, except by water which stands in its place as the spirits stand in the bodies, the mention of Paradise almost always comes accompanied by the mention of rivers, placing this description first among all the other descriptions.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Flowing is attributed to the river, though it is really the water that flows alone, by way of broadening and figurative usage, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf 12:82], and as the poet said:

*"I have been informed that fire was kindled after you, and the assembly quarreled after you, O Kulayb."*"

That is the end of his words. What he said contradicts what he explained of "rivers" just before it, by about five lines, when he said: "*The rivers* are the waters in their extended and wide courses." That is the end of his words.

The *alif-lam* in *al-anhar* ("the rivers") is *lam al-jins*. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Or it is intended to mean *anharuha* ('its rivers'), so the definite article with *lam* is used as a substitute for the definiteness of the genitive construction, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and the head has blazed with grey hair﴾ [Maryam 19:4]." What al-Zamakhshari mentioned, namely that *alif-lam* functions as a substitute for the genitive construction, is not the view of the Basran grammarians. Rather, it is a view taken by the Kufan grammarians. On this basis some people explained His saying, exalted is He: ﴿their doors wide open for them﴾ [Sad 38:50], as meaning "its doors." As for the Basrans, they interpret this otherwise and make the pronoun omitted, meaning "the doors of them." Had *alif-lam* been a substitute for the genitive construction, the pronoun would not have come together with *alif-lam*. The poet said:

*"Frowns of a wide-bosomed one, soft in it, a tender-skinned bare one, with the touch of the boon companions."*

It is also permissible that *alif-lam* be *lam al-'ahd* (the lam of prior reference), the fixed reference in the mind to the four rivers mentioned in Surat Muhammad. This plural came in the form of the plural of paucity, as an indication of the four rivers, if we say that the *alif-lam* in it is for prior reference; or as an indication of rivers of water, which are four or five. It is related in the sound report that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mentioned Paradise and said: "Two rivers are hidden: the Euphrates and the Nile; and two rivers are manifest: Sayhan and Jayhan." In another narration: "Sayhun and Jayhun." And from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about the water of al-Kawthar. He said: 'That is a river which Allah, exalted is He, gave me, meaning in Paradise. Its water is whiter than milk and sweeter than honey.'" The hadith is lengthy.

If they are many rivers, then this is the application of the plural of paucity in the manner of the plural of multiplicity, just as the reverse has come by way of broadening and figurative usage, since both share the quality of being plural.

{Kullamā ruziqū}: the discussion of "kullamā" (whenever) has already occurred at His saying, "Whenever it lights up for them" [2:20], and we explained how its repetition works, contrary to what most people understand. The best view regarding this sentence is that it is a resumptive clause (mustaʾnafah, a new independent sentence) with no place in the i'rab (grammatical analysis). When He mentioned that those who believe and do righteous deeds have gardens whose description is such-and-such, there arose in people's minds, since the Garden had been mentioned, talk of the fruits of the gardens, and they longed to hear a description of their condition. So it was said to them: ﴿Whenever they are provided with a provision of its fruit﴾. It is also permitted that the clause have a place in the i'rab: in the accusative, on the assumption that it is a qualifier of "gardens," and in the nominative, on the assumption that it is the predicate of an omitted subject. This allows two possibilities: either the subject is a pronoun referring back to the gardens, meaning "they are, whenever they are provided with something from them," or it refers back to ﴿those who believe﴾, meaning "they are, whenever they are provided." The first possibility is preferable, because the clause is then self-standing; in the two preceding possibilities it is equivalent to a noun phrase, so it depends on a noun it qualifies or on the omitted subject.

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (hal) from "those who believe," its implied sense being "provided with it continually." This works only if the circumstance is understood as anticipated (hal muqaddarah), since at the time of the good tidings they were not provided with it continually. He also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause from "gardens," since it is indefinite but has been qualified by His saying "flowing," so it has come close to definiteness; this too reverts to the anticipated circumstance. The basic principle regarding the circumstance is that it be concurrent, which is why we have chosen, in analyzing this sentence, a different analysis from what Abu al-Baqa' mentioned.

The "min" in His saying "from it" (minhā) is for the beginning of the extent (ibtidāʾ al-ghāyah). The "min" in "from a fruit" (min thamarah) is likewise, since it is a substitute (badal) for "from it," with a preposition repeated alongside it, as in His saying: ﴿Whenever they wish to get out from it from distress, they are returned to it﴾ [22:22], according to one of the two possibilities. Both are connected to "ruziqū" by way of substitution, as we have explained, because the verb does not govern two prepositions with the same meaning except by coordination or by way of substitution. This substitution is the substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimāl).

Al-Zamakhshari went to great length on the i'rab of "from a fruit," and did not state explicitly that it is a substitution, but his example indicates that this is what he meant. He also permitted that "min thamarah" be an explanatory (bayān) element, following the pattern of your saying: "I saw from you a lion," meaning "you are a lion." He concluded his words. That "min" is explanatory is not the position of the verifying scholars among the grammarians of Arabic; rather, they interpreted what those who affirmed it cited as evidence. Even if we supposed that "min" came for explanation, it would not be valid to assign it that function here, because those who hold that "min" is explanatory assign it a hidden antecedent and make it the head of a relative qualifier if it is preceded by a definite noun, as in: ﴿So avoid the abomination of the idols﴾ [22:30], meaning "the abomination which is the idols." If it is preceded by an indefinite noun, it refers back to that indefinite noun, as in: "Who strikes from a man," meaning "he is a man." This "min" has nothing before it that could serve as its explanandum, neither indefinite nor definite, unless one contrives that it explains what follows, and that the sense is: "whenever they are provided from it with a provision of a fruit," so that "min" explains "provision," meaning "a provision which is a fruit." That would involve inversion and reordering in the sentence. Such a reading ought to be kept far from the Book of God. As for "I saw from you a lion," the "min" there is for the beginning of the extent or for the extent of beginning and end, as in: "I took it from you." "Thamarah" does not mean one single apple, pomegranate, or other item, but rather, God knows best, the type of fruit. Al-Zamakhshari said: "On this view, that is, on the assumption that 'min' is explanatory, 'thamarah' may be taken to mean a kind of fruit, and the gardens as one," concluding his words. We have chosen that "min" is not explanatory, so we do not adopt what he built on it; moreover, his phrase "and the gardens as one" is obscure and its understanding requires reflection. "Rizqan" here means the thing provided, and the verbal noun reading is very remote given His saying: ﴿This is what we were provided with before﴾ and ﴿they were brought it in likeness﴾, since a verbal noun cannot be brought in likeness; this speaks of the thing provided, not of the act of providing.

﴿They said: This is what we were provided with before﴾. They said: this is the governing element of "kullamā." "Hādhā alladhī" is the subject, governed by the verb "said," so the clause occupies the place of a direct object. The meaning is: "this" is like what we were provided with. It belongs to the category where the predicate is treated as the subject. This implied likeness was needed because what is present before them at that time cannot be the very same thing they were previously provided with. Then this implied likeness was omitted because of the strength of the resemblance, so that this very thing seems to be that very thing. The returning pronoun of "alladhī" is omitted, meaning "we were provided with it." "Min" is connected to "ruziqnā" and is for the beginning of the extent. It has also been said that the noun is cut off from its annexation, with a definite genitive noun omitted because the meaning indicates it, and its estimate is "from before it," meaning "before the one provided."

The exegetes differed in explaining this. Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak, and Muqatil said: its meaning is the provision of the morning being like the provision of the evening. Yahya ibn Abi Kathir and Abu ʿUbayd said: the fruit of the Garden, when it is picked, is replaced by its like, so when they see that what has replaced the picked fruit resembles it, they say: "This is what we were provided with before." Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: by His saying "before" they mean in the world, and the meaning is that it is like it in appearance. On the first two views, "before" refers to the Garden; on this view it refers to the world. Some exegetes said: its meaning is "this is what we were promised in the world, that we would be provided it in the Hereafter." On this view the subject is the very predicate, and the estimate is not like... The promise is expressed by its object, which is provision, and this is metaphor. Because the promise was fulfilled, it became as though they were provided it in the world. The predicate being other than the subject is also metaphorical, but this metaphor is more common and more acceptable. On this view "before" also refers to the world, since the promise took place there. However, the fact that "before" refers to the world is made remote by the entry of "min" upon "qabl," since "min" is for the beginning of the extent, so this is the position of "qabl," not the position of "min," because there is a great interval between the two times, and "min" implies the beginning of priority, which contradicts the interval and the beginning. If "before" refers to the Hereafter, there is a difficulty: the first provision they were given could not have a like that they were given before it, since the premise is that it is first; if it is first, nothing was given to them before it. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "This is an indication of the genus, meaning 'this is of the genus of what we were provided with before,'" concluding his words. This is not an indication of the genus; rather, it indicates the provision itself. How could it indicate the genus when he himself explained his words afterward as "of the genus of what we were provided with before"? It is as if he said: "This genus is of the genus which we were provided with before," and you see how this structure is. Perhaps the transmitter miscopied "mithl" as "min," so that the estimate was "this genus is like the genus which we were provided with before." The more apparent view is that it is a miscopy, because the estimate "of the genus" is remote, and it is valid only by a kind of figurative extension, using the whole to mean a part: you say "this is from the Banu Tamim," then extend further and say "this is the Banu Tamim," making it all of the Banu Tamim by figurative extension.

The object of "said" is a declarative sentence by which some of them address one another. This is not in the sense of wonder, as stated by a group. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they say this in the manner of wonder. Al-Hasan and Mujahid said: they are provided with the fruit, and then they are provided after it with its like in form, while the taste differs, so they wonder at that and inform one another. Ibn ʿAbbas said: there is nothing in the Garden of the things of the world except the names; as for the realities, they are different.

The reading of the majority is "wa-utū" in the passive voice, with the agent omitted because it is known, namely the servants and the youths. This is shown by the reading of Harun al-Aʿwar and al-ʿAtaki, "wa-utū bihi" in the plural. The pronoun is implied because the meaning indicates it. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Youths made eternal will go around them﴾ [56:17], ﴿with cups and pitchers﴾ [56:18], down to His saying: ﴿and fruit of what they choose﴾ [56:20]? This shows that the youths are those who bring the fruit. The pronoun in His saying "bihi" refers to the provision, meaning "they were brought the provision which is of the fruits," just as "this" points to it. Al-Zamakhshari said: I said: to what does the pronoun in "wa-utū bihi" return? I said: to the thing provided, in this world and the next, since His saying "this is what we were provided with before" embraces mention of what they were provided in both abodes, concluding his words. That is, since the sense was "this is like what we were provided with," it contained both provisions together. Do you not see that when one says "Zayd is like Hatim," it embraces mention of Zayd and Hatim? What al-Zamakhshari mentioned is not apparent from the verse, because the apparent sense requires that the pronoun return only to their provision in the Hereafter, since that is what is spoken about and what is compared to what they were provided before. Moreover, if "before" is interpreted as what is in the Garden, it is necessary that the pronoun return only to the provision in the Garden, as though he said: "and they were brought the provision in the Garden, resembling," especially if you parse the clause as a circumstantial clause, since the estimate becomes: they said: "this is like what we were provided with before," and they had been brought it in likeness; that is, they said this in this state, and the thing that prompted the aforesaid saying was that they had been brought it in likeness. The coming of a clause introduced by a past verb as a circumstance, with "wa" and an implied "qad," is permissible in eloquent speech.

God the Exalted said: ﴿How do you disbelieve in God, when you were dead and He gave you life?﴾ [2:28], that is, "while you were the ones who said to their brethren and sat," meaning "and they had sat."

﴿وقالَ الَّذِي نَجا مِنهُما وادَّكَرَ بَعْدَ أُمَّةٍ﴾ [Yusuf: 45] That is, [the verb] "had remembered" [is in the perfect with waw, meaning] "and he had remembered," and it is parsed as a circumstantial clause (hal). Likewise, it is not correct for the pronoun to refer back to "what they were provided with" in both the worldly life and the Hereafter, if the sentence is conjoined to the words of God Most High: ﴿قالُوا هَذا الَّذِي رُزِقْنا مِن قَبْلُ﴾ ["They will say, 'This is what we were provided with before.'"] [Al-Baqarah: 25]. This is because the coming (al-ityan) at that point would be impossible to be past in meaning, as a necessary element within the scope of kullama (whenever), and the governing element of it must here be future in meaning, even though it is past in form, since it inevitably carries the sense of a conditional. It is also possible that the sentence is a new resumptive sentence (isti'naf), which contains the report of the coming with this [food] that they were provided, [being] similar.

The saying of al-Zamakhshari regarding the return of the pronoun to what was provided in this world and the Hereafter does not appear [correct] either, because these sentences were only brought as reports about the Garden and its conditions.
