His saying that he [God] informs about what was provided in this world and the Hereafter, that it is similar, is not part of the account of the Garden except with forced interpretation. The apparent meaning is what we mentioned first, namely that the pronoun returns to what was indicated by "this" alone. Mutashabihan (similar) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the pronoun in "bihi" (with it), and it is a necessary circumstance, because the similarity is established for it, whether or not they were brought it. The similarity has been said to refer to quality and choice, since the fruits of the Garden contain nothing inferior. This was stated by Qatadah. This is like His saying: ﴿كِتابًا مُتَشابِهًا﴾ [Az-Zumar: 23] ["a Book, similar in its parts"]. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It seems he means [that it is] harmonious, in that each kind is the best of its genus. This is a similarity in some respect, or in colour, while it differs in taste." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Mujahid. Or [it is similar] in taste, pleasure and desire, even if its colours differ. Or it is similar to the fruit of this world in name, differing in colour, scent and taste. Or it is similar to the fruit of this world in appearance, but not in quantity or taste. This was said by Ikrimah and others.

Ibn al-Mubarak narrated a hadith traced to the Prophet: The Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed God benefits us through the Bedouins and their questions." "A Bedouin came one day and said: 'O Messenger of God, God mentioned in the Garden a harmful tree, and I did not think there was in the Garden a harmful tree that harms its companion.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'What is it?' He said: 'The lote tree (sidrah), for it has harmful thorns.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Does He not say: ﴿فِي سِدْرٍ مَخْضُودٍ﴾ [Al-Waqi'ah: 28] ["among thornless lote trees"]? God has removed the thorns and made in place of every thorn a fruit. Indeed it produces fruit which, from each fruit, splits into seventy-two kinds of food, no two of which resemble one another.'"

Al-Zamakhshari preferred that the fruit of the Garden is similar to the fruit of this world, and he stated this without restriction, that it resembles the fruit of this world and was not of other kinds.

The summary of what has been mentioned is that a person is at ease with the familiar, and when he sees what is unfamiliar, his nature recoils from it. When he obtains something of what he is accustomed to, in which there appears to him a distinction and variation in kind, he is delighted by it and rejoices in its attainment. Then [Ibn Abi Hayyan, i.e., the author] mentioned what was reported concerning the size of the pomegranate, the lote berry, the tree, the manner of the palm trees of the Garden, the cluster [of fruit], and the rivers, which can be found in his book. There is nothing in the verse that indicates what al-Zamakhshari chose. The more evident meaning is that the sense is the establishment of similarity for it, and [God] did not restrict the similarity but left it absolute, so restricting it requires evidence.

Since the foundations of pleasures are a splendid dwelling, a delicious food, and a pure spouse, God Most High mentioned them in what is announced to the believers. He began with the dwelling, because by it there is settled stability in the abode of permanence. He then mentioned the food, because by it the bodies are sustained. Then he mentioned spouses third, because by them is the completion of harmony. So He said, Most High: ﴿ولَهم فِيها أزْواجٌ﴾ ["And for them therein are spouses"]. The better view is that this sentence is a new resumptive sentence, as we chose in His saying: ﴿كُلَّما رُزِقُوا﴾ ["Whenever they are provided"], because making it a resumptive sentence gives attention to the sentence, since it is brought as a complete statement that does not need a grammatical connection (irab-related linking). Whoever makes it a qualifying clause has taken it on a path other than the original basis of sentences. The nominative of azwaj (spouses) is as the subject (mubtada'), and its not sharing the governing element with jannat (gardens) indicates what we have said of its being a resumptive sentence as well. The predicate of azwaj is in the prepositional phrase "lahum" (for them), and "fiha" (therein) is attached to the governing element in "lahum," which is the predicate.

Azwaj is from the plurals of paucity (jam' qillah), because zawj (spouse) is pluralized as zawjah, like 'awd and 'awdah. It is also from the plurals of abundance (jam' kathrah), but it is not used in most of speech, so it was replaced by the plural of paucity as a stylistic expansion and figurative usage. Indeed, the sound hadith has reported what indicates the abundance of spouses among the houris and others. What is meant here by azwaj is the female companions among women who belong exclusively to a man, with no one else sharing them with him.

Muṭahharah (purified) is an attribute of azwaj, formed as the feminine singular of "tahurat." Zayd ibn 'Ali read: muṭahharat, pluralized with the suffix alif and ta' according to "tahurna." Al-Zamakhshari said: "Both are eloquent dialects. It is said: 'The women did (fa'alna),' and 'they are doers (fa'ilat),' and 'the women did (fa'alat),' and 'she is doer (fa'ilah).' From this is the line of the Hamasah:
"And when the virgins are veiled with smoke / and hasten to the pots' [cooking] and grow weary."
The meaning is: a group of purified spouses." End of his words. In this there is an objection: one dialect is better than the other. This is because the plural of non-rational things is either a plural of paucity or a plural of abundance. If it is a plural of abundance, then the pronoun coming in the manner of the feminine singular pronoun is better than its coming in the manner of the feminine plural pronoun. If it is a plural of paucity, then it is the reverse, as in: "al-ajdha' inkasarna" (the trunks broke), and "inkasarat" is also permitted. Likewise, if it is a pronoun referring back to a plural of rational feminine beings, the form with nun is preferred over ta', as in ﴿فَإذا بَلَغْنَ أجَلَهُنَّ﴾ ["When they have reached their term"] [Al-Baqarah: 234] and ﴿والوالِداتُ يُرْضِعْنَ﴾ ["And mothers breastfeed"] [Al-Baqarah: 233]. They did not distinguish in this between the plural of paucity and the plural of abundance, as they distinguished in the plural of non-rational things. Based on what has been established, Zayd's reading is the first, since in its outward form it came in what is better.

The coming of this attribute in the passive form, and not "tahirah" or "tahirat" in the active, is more majestic, because it conveys that it has a purifier, and that is none other than God Most High. The reading of Ubayd ibn 'Umayr is muṭahhirah, and its origin is mutatahhirah, which was assimilated. In the speech of some Arabs: "How much I need the House of God, so that I purify myself with it a purification (aṭṭahharu bihi aṭhurah)", meaning: "so that I purify myself with it a purification (fa-atatahharu bihi tatahhurah)." This reading is compatible with the reading of the majority, because the verb can be understood as intransitive (muta'addi), as in: "tahharTuhu fa-tatahhara" (I purified him, so he became pure), meaning: God Most High purified them, so they became purified.

If these spouses whom God described as purified are of the houris, as has been reported from 'Abd Allah [ibn Mas'ud], then the meaning of purification is that He created them in purity, no inherent or external defilement clinging to them. And if they are from the children of Adam, as was reported from al-Hasan: "[They are] from your old women, the toothless and the bleary-eyed, who will become young women," then it is said: they are purified from inherent and non-inherent defects. It is said: they are purified from evil character and inferior natures, such as anger, hastiness, rancor, deceit, cunning, and what runs in that direction. It is said: they are purified from immorality, obscenity, and looking toward others than their husbands. It is said: they are purified from inherent impurities, such as menstruation, postnatal bleeding, major ritual impurity, urine, feces, and other amounts arising from accidents that turn into corruption, such as bad breath, foul odour, body odour, pus and discharge, or into what is not corruption, such as tears, sweat, saliva, and phlegm. It is said: they are purified from the bad qualities of character, neither proud nor haughty, nor jealous, nor vexing. Al-Nakha'i said: "[They are purified from] offspring." Yaman said: "[They are purified] from sin and harm." All these sayings are not determined by His saying ﴿مُطَهَّرَةٌ﴾ ["purified"]; but the apparent wording requires that they are purified from everything that disfigures, because whoever God Most High has purified and described as purified is in the utmost cleanliness and radiance.

When God Most High mentioned the dwelling of the believers, their food, and their spouses, and these delights do not reach the degree of perfection while there is fear of their ending, for this reason it was said:
"The greatest grief to me, in a joy / whose possessor is certain of its departure."
God then followed this with what removes the disturbance of comfort by mentioning eternity in the abode of bliss, so He said, Most High: ﴿وهم فِيها خالِدُونَ﴾ ["And they therein will abide eternally"]. The dispute concerning khulud (eternity) has already been mentioned, and that the Mu'tazilah hold that it is lasting permanence that never ends, while others hold that it is a long duration, whether or not it ends. And that the everlasting nature of the bliss of the people of the Garden and the punishment of the people of the Fire is not derived from the word khulud, but from verses of the Qur'an and sound hadiths of the Sunnah. God Most High said: ﴿خالِدِينَ فِيها أبَدًا﴾ ["Abiding therein forever"] [An-Nisa': 57], and He said: ﴿وما هم مِنها بِمُخْرَجِينَ﴾ ["And they will never be removed from it"] [Al-Hijr: 48]. And in the hadith: "O people of the Garden, eternal life without death." And in a hadith narrated by Muslim in describing the people of the Garden: "Indeed for you is that you will live and never die forever." And other verses and hadiths besides these.

This is a part of a longer commentary: the translation below covers exactly the text given.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 26 (part 1 of 4):

﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to present an example, [even] of a mosquito or what is above it. As for those who believed, they know that it is the truth from their Lord. But as for those who disbelieved, they say, "What did Allah intend by this as an example?" He misleads thereby many and guides thereby many, and He misleads thereby none except the defiantly disobedient (al-fasiqin)﴾ ﴿[Those] who break the covenant of Allah after its ratification and sever what Allah has ordered to be joined and cause corruption on the earth. Those are the losers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 27] ﴿How can you disbelieve in Allah while you were dead and He gave you life? Then He will cause you to die; then He will bring you to life; then to Him you will be returned﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28] ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth. Then He turned to the heaven and made them seven heavens, and He is Knowing of all things﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29].

Al-hayaʾ (modesty, shame): a change and a breaking that afflicts a person out of fear of being blamed or censured. Its locus is the face, its source is the heart, and its derivation is from life (hayah). Its opposite is al-qahah (shamelessness). Al-hayaʾ, al-istihyaʾ, al-inkhizal, al-inqimaʿ and al-inqilaʿ are close in meaning, so each may take the place of the others.

Anna (أنْ): a particle of dual form (ḥarf thunaʾi al-waḍʿ) which, together with the verb that follows it, forms a verbal noun (maṣdar). Its governance over the present tense is the accusative (naṣb) if the verb is inflected (muʿrab). Its use with the jussive (jazm) is a dialect of the Banu Ṣabaḥ. It may also be attached to the inflected past tense, and they mentioned that it may be attached to the imperative. When it governs the present tense in the accusative, no separation between the two is permitted by anything. Some permitted separation by an adverbial (ẓarf). The Kufans permitted separation between it and its operand by a condition (sharṭ). They also permitted its cancellation (ilghaʾ) and the application of a condition to what would have been its operand had it not been cancelled. Al-Farraʾ permitted placing the operand of its operand before it, and the majority prohibited this. The rulings of anna as a relative particle (al-mawsulah) are numerous. It may also be an explanatory particle (ḥarf tafsir), contrary to the Kufans, who claimed that it never comes as an explanatory particle. The discussion of the explanatory use will come at the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And We charged Abraham and Ishmael: that purify My House﴾ [al-Baqarah: 125], God willing. Anna may also be superfluous (zaʾidah), and its superfluity is regular after lamma, and in that case it conveys nothing but emphasis, contrary to one who added that it conveys the connection of the verb that comes as an answer with the verb before which it was added, and after an oath before law and the answer, contrary to one who claimed that in that case it is a link between the oath clause and what is sworn upon when it is law and the answer. Anna is not for conditioning (al-mujazah), contrary to the Kufans, nor with the meaning of the light, unstressed form of inna, contrary to al-Farisi, nor for negation, nor with the meaning of idh, nor (p-119) with the meaning of li-allaa, contrary to those who claim this. As for anna, the light form of the heavy (muthaqqalah), it is a particle of triliteral form, and its discussion will come at its first mention, God willing.

Al-ḍarb: the contact of one body with another with force. It is used as a metaphor for travelling in the land, and it may mean making or undertaking. It is related that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) struck a ring of gold."

Al-baʿuḍah: the singular of al-baʿuḍ, a very small flying creature well known. Originally it is an adjective on the pattern fuʿul, like quṭuʿ, and it became a noun. Its derivation is from al-baʿḍ in the sense of cutting.

Amma: a particle, containing the sense of a condition. Some call it a particle of detail (ḥarf tafṣil), and some a particle of information (ḥarf ikhbar). Banu Tamim replaced the first mim with a ya', saying ayyama. Sibawayh, explaining amma, said that the meaning is "whatever thing there may be, Zayd is going," and what follows it is a subject and predicate, and the fa' is obligatory in what follows the conditional clause that follows it. Except if the sentence is a supplication, then the fa' is in what follows it, and it is not separated from the fa' by any other sentence. If it is separated by it, there must be a separation between it and the sentence by an operand that follows amma. It is not permitted to separate between amma and the fa' by the operand of the predicate of inna, in agreement with Sibawayh and Abu 'Uthman, and contrary to al-Mubarrad and Ibn Darastawayh, nor by the operand of the predicate of layta and la'alla, contrary to al-Farra'. The issue of amma 'ilman fa'alim (as to knowledge, he is knowing) requires the people of the Hijaz to use the accusative, and Tamim prefers it. The justification of these two issues is mentioned in grammar.

Al-haqq: that which is established and cannot be denied. Haqqa al-amr: it was established and became obligatory. From it: ﴿The word of your Lord has been fulfilled﴾ [Yunus: 33]. Its opposite is al-batil, which is that which vanishes and passes away.

Madha: the original of dha is that it is a demonstrative noun. So when its original meaning is intended, madha is an independent sentence, and ma is interrogative in the position of nominative by inception, with dha as its predicate. The Arabs have used madha in three uses other than the one we mentioned first. One: that ma is interrogative and dha is a relative pronoun, evidenced by the noun coming as an answer to it in the nominative in the eloquent usage, and by the nominative of the substitute (badal). The poet said:

"Do you not ask the man what he is striving for: is it love that is granted, or error and falsehood?"

The second: that madha is all interrogative. This is the view that some grammarians hold, that dha is lagha (superfluous), and they do not mean by this mere addition, but rather that it was compounded with ma and the whole became interrogative. This quality is shown by the noun coming as an answer to it in the accusative in the eloquent usage, and by the Arabs' saying "'amma dha tas'al" with the alif of ma retained, and by the poet's saying:

"O squint-eyed one of Taghlib, what is the matter with your women, that they do not recover their senses toward the two monasteries out of longing?"

Relative use of dha is not valid here. The third: that ma with dha is a relative noun, and this is rare. The poet said:

"Leave what you know; I shall guard against it, but inform me of the unseen."

According to this usage and the first, the verb after it is a relative clause with no place in grammatical analysis, and it does not govern madha. According to the second usage, it governs madha if it is of a kind that can govern it. Al-Farisi permitted that madha be an indefinite qualified noun, and he cited as an example: "Leave what you know."

Al-iradah (will, desire): your seeking a thing by yourself and the inclination of your heart toward it, and it is the opposite of dislike. The discussion of it when attributed to Allah, the Exalted, will come, God willing.

Al-fusuq: going out. Fasaqat al-ratbah: the fresh dates came out. The fasiq in the legal sense is one who goes out of the truth. Its present form comes on the pattern yafʿal and yafʿul.

Al-naqd: undoing the composition of a thing and returning it to what it was originally. So naqḍ al-bina' is demolishing it, and naqḍ al-mubram is untying it.

Al-ʿahd: the covenant, and ʿahida ilayhi fi kadhā: he charged him with it and bound him to it. The word ʿahd in the language of the Arabs has six meanings: the charge (wasiyah), the guarantee (ḍaman), the command (amr), the meeting (iltiqaʾ), the sight (ruʾyah), and the dwelling place (manzil). Al-mithaq: a covenant confirmed by oath. Al-mithaq and al-tawthiqah are like al-mi'ad in the sense of promise, and al-milad in the sense of birth.

Al-khasar: loss or destruction.

Kayfa: a noun. The entry of a preposition on it is anomalous. It is mostly used as an interrogative, and its use as a conditional is rare. Its jussive use is not heard from the Arabs, so we do not permit it by analogy, contrary to the Kufans and Qutrub. There is a difference of opinion about it: is it an adverb or a noun that is not an adverb? The first has been attributed to Sibawayh, and the second to al-Akhfash and al-Sayrafi. Its substitute and its answer, when it is with a verb that is complete, are accusative, and when it is with what is not complete, it is nominative if it is a subject, and accusative if it is an abrogating verb. (p-120)

Amwatan: plural of mayyit, and it is also a plural of mayyitah. The plural of both on the pattern af'al is anomalous, while the analogy for fay'al when broken is fa'ail.

Al-istiwa': evenness and straightness. Istawa al-'ud wa-ghayruhu: when wood or other things became straight and even. Then it was said: istawa ilayhi like an released arrow, when he aimed at it in a straight aim without turning to anything else. Al-taswiyah: straightening and making proper.

* *

﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to present an example...﴾ the verses. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Muqatil and al-Farra' said: it was revealed concerning the Jews, when Allah, the Exalted, struck examples in His Book with the spider, the fly, the dust, the stones and other things that are despised and cast aside. They said: Allah is too exalted and too great to strike examples with such insignificant things, so Allah refuted them with this verse. Al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Suddi and others said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites. They said: when Allah, the Exalted, struck the parable of the one who kindles a fire and of the rain cloud, they said: Allah is higher and greater than to strike examples with such things that have no worth, so Allah refuted them with this verse. It was also said: it was revealed concerning the polytheists. All are possible, since the verse includes breaking the covenant, which is a characteristic of the Jews, since the address concerning fulfilling the covenant is to the Children of Israel, and of the disbelievers, ﴿and those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ [al-Anfal: 49], who are the polytheists and the hypocrites, and all of them were in agreement in harming him. The text from the beginning of the surah until here mentions three groups, and all of them are among those who disbelieved, as al-Qaffal said. He said: it is possible that this was revealed without a specific cause. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: this is a parable that Allah, the Exalted, struck for this world and its people, that the mosquito lives as long as it is hungry, and when it is satisfied and full, it dies. Likewise is the case of the people of this world: when they are filled with it, it becomes a cause of their destruction. It was also said: Allah, the Exalted, struck this as a parable for the deeds of the servants, that it is not impossible that He mention what is small or great among them, in order to reward for them with reward or punishment. The two first statements are more apparent regarding the occasion of revelation. The connection of this verse is clear, since before the mention of the parable of the one who kindles a fire and of the rain cloud, the parable of the spider and the fly had come down, and the ignorant and the obstinate denied that and marvelled at what is not marvellous or objectionable, since the parable reveals the meaning and clarifies the intended matter. The discussion of its benefit has already passed at the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Their likeness is like that of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17]. When the intelligent person hears the parable, the truth becomes clear to him through it. People have continued to strike parables with animals, birds, kinds, insects and vermin, and the tongue of the Arabs is full of that. Do you not see the poet's saying:

"Indeed I encounter from those of rancor among them, and what has become of the sleepless one complaining of passion;
as the she-serpent of al-Safa met from her ally, and the parables have not ceased to circulate among the people."

So he mentioned the story of Dhat al-Safa, a snake that had killed the kinsman of her ally, so they made a covenant by God that she would be a ransom for that slain man and would not harm him, to the end of the story mentioned in that poem. Parables are struck in the Gospel with insignificant things like bran, worms and wasps. Likewise, I have also read parables in the Psalms. So denial of striking parables is extreme ignorance or manifest obstinacy, and the course of this sentence, introduced with inna, is to indicate emphasis. Al-Jumhur read yastahyi with two yas, and the past tense is istahya, which is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. Istaf'ala here came to dispense with the bare triliteral, as in istankafa, istaʾthara, istabadda, istaʿbara, and it is among the meanings for which istaf'ala came. Its mention has already passed at the saying: ﴿And You alone we ask for help﴾ [al-Fatihah: 5], and this here is from hayaʾ. In al-Zamakhshari's speech there is what indicates that istahya does not dispense with the bare form, but rather agrees with the bare form, and this is also one of the meanings for which istaf'ala came. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is said hayiya al-rajul (p-121) just as it is said: nasiya, khashiya, and shadhiya al-faras, when these limbs became afflicted. The one who is hayiyy is made, for what is expressed by breaking and change, one whose strength is broken and whose life is undone, just as they said: so-and-so perished from shame at such a thing, and died of shame, and I saw the crescent in his face from intense shame, and melted from shame, and froze in his place from embarrassment, end of his speech. Its apparent meaning is that one says from hayaʾ: hayiya al-rajul, so istahya upon this is in agreement with the bare form, and upon what we transmitted before, it dispenses with the bare form. Ibn Kathir in the transmission of Shibl, Ibn Muhaysin and Ya'qub read yastahi with one ya', and this is the dialect of the Banu Tamim, who treat it like yastabi, as the poet said:

The first verb form is *istahā*, in the past tense. The poet says:

*"Are you not ashamed before us, O kings, while you guard against our sacred prohibitions? Blood does not pay for blood."*

Another poet says:

*"When they seek water, it presents itself to them; they drink at dawn in a rosy vessel."*

The grammarians disagreed about which radical is elided. One view holds that it is the final radical (*lam al-kalima*), so the pattern is *yastafi'u*, and the vowel of the middle radical was moved to the first radical, leaving the middle radical quiescent, giving *yastfi'u*. Another view holds that the elided radical is the middle one, so the pattern is *yastayfilu*, and then the vowel of the last radical was moved to the first radical and the last radical became quiescent, giving *yastfilu*. Most of the authorities' statements hold that the elided radical is the middle one.

I have discussed this question in my book *al-Takmil li-Sharh al-Tashil*. This elision is not restricted to the past and present tenses; it also occurs in the other derived forms, such as the active participle, the passive participle, and others. This verb is among those that, according to the lexicographers, can be transitive directly, and can be transitive with a prepositional particle. One says *istahyaytuhu* and *istahyaytu minhu*. On this basis, *an yadriba* may be read as the direct object, on the assumption that the verb was transitive to it directly, or that it was transitive to it after the prepositional particle was dropped. This brings us to the disagreement I mentioned regarding the word *anna* in *Allah's* words ﴿*anna lahum jannatin*﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:25], namely whether it is in the accusative position after the dropping of the particle, or in the genitive position.

The exegetes differed about the meaning of "shame" (*al-istihya'*) when it is attributed to God and negated. One view holds that the meaning is "He does not leave off," and that shame is used here to express abandonment. This was said by al-Zamakhshari and others, because abandonment is one of the fruits of shame: when a person is ashamed to do something, he leaves it. This is therefore a case of naming the cause (*sabab*) by the name of its effect (*musabbab*), or the reverse of what is usual. Another view holds that the meaning is "He does not fear," and that fear was called shame because it is one of its fruits. al-Tabari preferred this view. It has been said regarding Allah's words ﴿*wa-takhsha al-nas*﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:37], "and you fear people," that its meaning is "you are ashamed before people." Another view holds that the meaning is "He does not refrain." All these statements are close in meaning, and it is permissible to attribute them to God. These interpretations (*ta'wilat*) are according to the school of those who hold that when a word whose lexical meaning is unsuitable for God is interpreted figuratively, it is correct. Another view holds that such expressions should be left as they came, and we should believe in them without interpreting them, and entrust their knowledge to God, since the essence of His attributes is not known to creation.

What most scholars hold is that God addressed us in the language of the Arabs, which contains both literal usage (*haqiqa*) and figurative usage (*majaz*). Whatever is correct in reason to attribute to Him, we attribute to Him; whatever is impossible, we interpret in a manner befitting Him, just as we interpret what is attributed to others when it is not correct to attribute it to Him. Shame, in its lexical meaning, cannot be correctly attributed to God, so the scholars interpreted it. It has, however, come attributed to God in the affirmative in what was related from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed Allah is Bashful and Generous; He is ashamed when His servant raises his two hands to Him that He should return them empty, until He places good in them." This was interpreted as being in the manner of a figurative image (*tamthil*), like His leaving the servant without His gift, out of His generosity, by abandoning the one who refrains from returning what is needed by the one in need, out of shame before him. It is also permissible to use "shame" for something that cannot be attributed to Him in any way, such as the line of verse we cited earlier:

*"When they seek water, it presents itself to them..."*

Abu Tammam said:

*"He is a lion, the lion of the thicket, in bravery and valor, even if he is more modest in face and more generous."*

It is also possible that Allah's words ﴿*la yastahyi*﴾ ("He is not ashamed") are used by way of contrast (*muqabala*), since it was related that the disbelievers said: "The Lord of Muhammad is not ashamed to coin parables about the fly and the spider." The occurrence of a thing by way of contrast, even if it is not of the same kind as what it is contrasted with, is common in the language of the Arabs. Among examples is Allah's words ﴿*wa-jaza'u sayyi'atin sayyi'atun mithluha*﴾ [al-Shura 42:40], "and the recompense for an evil deed is an evil deed like it." The mention of shame negated of God, even though affirming it by its lexical meaning cannot be correctly attributed to God, is also used: every matter that is impossible for God to affirm may be correctly negated of Him, and the Qur'an was revealed in this manner, and the Sunnah came in this manner. Do you not see Allah's words ﴿*la ta'khudhuhu sinatun wa-la nawmun*﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:255], "Neither drowsiness nor sleep seizes Him"; ﴿*lam yalid wa-lam yulad*﴾ [al-Ikhlas 112:3], "He neither begets nor is begotten"; ﴿*ma ittakhadha Allahu min walad*﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:91], "God has not taken any son"; ﴿*wa-huwa yut'imu wa-la yut'am*﴾ [al-An'am 6:14], "He feeds and is not fed"? We say: God is not a body. The reporting of the negation of these things is pure truth, and the negation of a thing does not indicate that it is permissible for the one from whom it is negated, nor that it is correct to attribute it to him, as Abu Bakr ibn al-Tayyib and others held. He claimed that what is not permissible for God to affirm must not be used in the form of negation. He said: what came of this is in the form of negation, but it is not negation in the literal sense. The occurrence of this, that is, the negation of a thing of what it is not correct to affirm of Him, is frequent in the Qur'an and the language of the Arabs, to the extent that what has come of this cannot be enumerated.

*Yadribu* ("He strikes/sets forth"): it has been said that its meaning is "He makes clear"; it has been said that it means "He mentions"; it has been said that it means "He places," as in *duribat 'alayhimu al-dhilla* ("abasement was struck upon them") and *duriba al-ba'thu 'ala banī fulan* ("the sending was struck upon the sons of so-and-so"). *Yadribu* may be transitive to one object. It has also been said that *yadribu* means *yaj'alu* ("He makes") and *yasiru* ("He becomes"), as you say *daraba al-tina labanan* ("he made clay into a brick") and *daraba al-fidda khataman* ("he made silver into a ring"). On this view, it is transitive to two objects. The more correct view is that *daraba* does not belong to the category of *zanna* and its sisters, which take two objects. The refutation of this view is mentioned in the books of grammar.

*Ma*: when you put *ba'ūḍatan* in the accusative, *ma* is extra, for emphasis, or it is a qualifier of *mathal* that makes the indefinite noun more general, as when you say *i'tini bi-rajulin ma* ("bring me a man, any man"), that is, whichever man it may be. Al-Farra', Tha'lab and al-Zajjaj permitted that *ma* be an indefinite noun, and that *ba'ūḍatan* be in the accusative as a substitute (*badal*) for *mathalan*.

The majority of readers read *ba'ūḍatan* with the accusative. The grammatical analysis (*i'rab*) of the accusative has been disputed in several ways. One is that it is a qualifier of *ma*, if we make *ma* a substitute for *mathalan*, with *mathalan* as the object of *yadribu*. In that case *ma* has been qualified by a general noun that is indefinite, because of the vagueness of *ma*. This is the view of al-Farra'. The second is that *ba'ūḍatan* is an explanatory apposition (*'atf bayan*), and *mathalan* is the object of *yadriba*. The third is that it is a substitute for *mathal*. The fourth is that it is the object of *yadriba*, and *mathalan* is an accusative of state (*hal*) from the indefinite noun, placed before it. The fifth is that it is a second object of *yadriba*, and the first is *mathal*, on the basis that *yadriba* is transitive to two objects. The sixth is that it is a first object of *yadriba*, and *mathalan* is the second object. The seventh is that it is in the accusative by way of supposing the dropping of the prepositional particle, and the meaning is: "that He should strike a parable of what lies between a gnat and whatever is above it." They related: "He has twenty *ma* (camels) of she-camel and then a stallion." Ibn 'Atiyya attributed this to some of the Kufans, al-Mahdawi attributed it to the Kufans, and others attributed it to al-Kisa'i and al-Farra'. On this view *mathalan* is the object of *yadribu*. Abu al-Abbas (al-Mubarrad) rejected this accusative, that is, the accusative of *ba'ūḍatan* in this way.

The precise account of this school of thought is as follows: the Kufans claim that *ma* is originally a conditional particle, and is changed into the form of *alladhi* ("who/that"), so the noun after it takes the accusative, whether it is indefinite or not. It is joined to what precedes it only with *fa* (then), and it cannot be replaced by *wa* (and), *thumma* (then), *aw* (or), or *la* (not). They take the accusative in this noun to be by dropping an annexed noun, which is *bayn* ("between"). When *bayn* was dropped, this noun took its place in the grammatical case. They take *fa* to mean *ila* ("to"), and this has been expressed explicitly in some places. al-Kisa'i related from the Arabs: *mutirna ma zubalata fa-al-Tha'labiyya* ("we were rained upon from Zubala to Tha'labiyya"), where *ma* is accusative with *mutirna*. al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' related from the Arabs: *hiya ahsanu al-nasi ma qarnan* ("she is the most beautiful of people, from horn to ..."), where the accusative of *ma* in this matter is explanatory. You say: *hiya hasanatun ma qarnaha ila qadamiha* ("she is beautiful from her head to her feet"). al-Farra' said: a Bedouin of the Banu Sulaym recited to us:

*"O most beautiful of people, from head to foot, and not the ropes of a lover who connects to a connected one."*

al-Kisa'i said: I heard a Bedouin look at the crescent moon and say: "Praise be to God, from its appearance to its waning," and al-Farra' related from the Arabs: *al-shanq ma khumma fa-'ishrina* ("the sickness is from five to twenty"). The meaning in what preceded is "what is between such and such and such." *Ma* in this sense does not drop out, so it is a mistake to say: "we were rained upon Zubala and then Tha'labiyya." This view that the Kufans held is not known to the Basrans, and refuting it by the principles of the Basrans is mentioned elsewhere.

What we choose among these grammatical analyses is that *daraba* is transitive to two objects, and this is correct, the first being *mathalan*, on the basis of Allah's words ﴿*duriba mathalun*﴾ [al-Hajj 22:73], "a parable has been set forth," and because it is the one brought forward in the construction, and it is suitable to take the accusative by *yadribu*. *Ma* is a qualifier that makes the indefinite noun more general, because its extra use in this position is not a regular pattern. *Ba'ūḍatan* is a substitute, because the Basrans' view is that explanatory apposition does not occur with indefinite nouns; that view is held by al-Farisi alone, and because qualifying by generic nouns is not regular.

al-Dahhak, Ibrahim ibn Abi Ablah, Ru'ba ibn al-'Ajjaj and Qutrub read *ba'ūḍatun* with the nominative. The grammarians agreed that it is a predicate (*khabar*), but they differed about what it is a predicate of. It has been said that it is the predicate of an elided subject, whose assumed form is *huwa ba'ūḍatun* ("it is a gnat"). In this there are two views. The first is that this clause is a relative clause for *ma*, and *ma* is a relative pronoun in the sense of *alladhi*, with the returning pronoun elided. This analysis is valid only according to the Kufan view, since they did not require the relative clause to be long for the elision of this returning pronoun. As for the Basrans, they required that condition for all relative pronouns except *ayy*. According to their view, this reading on this analysis is anomalous, and the grammatical analysis of *ma* on this analysis is a substitute, the meaning being: "a parable, the one which is a gnat." The second view is that *ma* is extra or a qualifier, and *huwa ba'ūḍatun* together with what follows it is a clause, like an explanation of what the preceding speech has enveloped. It has also been said that it is the predicate of a subject that is pronounced, namely *ma*, on the basis that it is interrogative.

Al-Zamakhshari said: When they disdained God's citing of gnats and similar lowly things as a parable for their idols, He said: "Indeed God is not shy to strike a parable of whatever He wills, even something as lowly as a gnat, or what is above it," just as one says, "So-and-so does not care what he gives away, whether it is a dinar or two dinars." The second interpretation is preferred because the first one is not eloquent according to the school of the Basrans (al-Basriyyun, the grammarians of Basra), and the second one has strangeness in it and deviates from the meaning of interrogation. The "ma" in His saying "fa-ma" is coordinated with His saying "ba'udatan" if we put "ba'udatan" in the accusative: then "ma" is either a relative pronoun whose complement is the adverbial phrase, or a qualifying noun whose qualifier is the adverbial phrase, and the qualifying noun is more preferred. If we put "ba'udatan" in the nominative, and "ma" is a relative pronoun, then the second "ma" is coordinated with it, or it is interrogative, and in that case it is coordination of clauses. Or "ba'udatan" is the predicate of an omitted "huwa," and "ma" is redundant; or "ba'udatan" is an attribute, and it is coordinated on "ba'udatan," whether as a relative or a qualifying noun.

"Ma fawqaha" apparently means in size, such as the fly and the spider; this is what Ibn Abbas said. The mention of the gnat is then an indication of smallness, and "what is above it" an indication of largeness. Qatada and Ibn Juraij also said this. It has also been said that the meaning is "what is above it in smallness," i.e., what is smaller than it in size, just as one says, "So-and-so is the lowest of people," and it is said to you, "He is above that," meaning more extreme and deeper in baseness. This was said by Abu Ubayda and al-Kisa'i. Ibn Qutayba said: "Fawq" among the words with opposite meanings (al-adداd) applies to the greater and the lesser. So according to the view that a homonymous word is taken in all its meanings, it indicates what is smaller than the gnat and what is larger. It has also been said: He meant "what is above it and what is below it," and He was satisfied with one of the two for the other, because the meaning indicates it, just as He was satisfied in His saying, "garments that protect you from the heat" [al-Nahl 16:81], without saying "and the cold." The view that "fawq" means greater in smallness was preferred, because the purpose of the parable is to belittle the idols, and the more lowly the thing compared to, the more complete the purpose of this kind of discourse. Also, the point here is that God does not refrain from giving a parable with a lowly thing. Also, the more a thing is small, the harder it is to comprehend its secrets; so when it is at the extreme of smallness, none but God's knowledge encompasses it, and thus a parable with it is stronger in indicating the perfection of wisdom than a parable with something large.

The view we choose is the first one, because "fawq" is used in its well-known linguistic sense. As for the meaning to which God attributes the absence of shyness in striking a parable with these diminutive and weak things, there are several aspects:

First: The gnat was brought into existence by Him to the utmost degree of perfection in craftsmanship, beauty of composition and order, and He displayed in it, despite the smallness of its body, from the wonders of wisdom what He displayed in the elephant, which is at the extreme of largeness and immensity of creation. Since each of the two has achieved the measure of excellence of workmanship and wonders of composition and craftsmanship, striking a parable with the small and with the large is equal to Him when both are equal in fulfilling wisdom.

Second: Since the gnat is among the smallest of God's creations, He singled it out for mention as an example of smallness. So He is not shy to strike a parable with a large thing by a large one, and a lowly thing by a lowly one, and to Him belongs the highest likeness in striking parables.

Third: In the gnat, despite the smallness of its body and the weakness of its structure, there is such fine composition and delicate workmanship, such as the slender waist, the fineness of the proboscis, the subtle formation of its limbs, and the softness of its skin, that its description cannot be encompassed. Yet, despite its softness, it pierces the hide of the buffalo and the elephant with the point of its proboscis, and it finds the spot where the skin is bruised without a guide. So God is not shy to strike a parable with it, since no human being has the capacity to create its like or anything less than it, as He said: "They will never create a fly, even if they gathered together for it" [al-Hajj 22:73].

Fourth: The parable with the fly, the gnat, the spider and what resembles them, which God brought in the extreme of what can be of parable and the best of what can be of comparison. This is because the thing He made a parable for them is at the extreme of lowliness, weakness of strength, and baseness of essence and action. If He had likened them to something other than this, the comparison would not have been fitting, nor would the parable have been sweet in taste, since a thing is only compared to what resembles it and is similar to it. And whoever brings a thing in its proper form is not shy of it.

The opening of the two clauses with "amma," which carries the meaning of a condition, indicates emphasis, since it is more eloquent than "those who believe know" and "those who disbelieve say." It is established that what appears within the scope of "amma" of news is necessarily occurring, and what conveys and evokes this is nothing but the consequence of the ruling upon the meaning of the condition. The pronoun in "annahu" refers to the parable. It has been said that it refers to the verbal noun (masdar) implied by "yadribu," as if He said: "they know that the striking of a parable..." It has also been said that it refers to the verbal noun implied by "la yastahi," i.e., "they know that the absence of shyness regarding mentioning the truth..." The first is more evident, because of the indication of His saying: "What does God intend by this as a parable?" Here God designated what is pointed to by the parable. The division applies to one thing, so it is clear that it refers to the parable. He described the believers with knowledge, because it is the certainty that agrees with evidence, and He described the disbelievers with saying, which is the word that runs on the tongue, and He made its complement the interrogative clause, which includes all-inclusiveness, disparagement, and mockery: His saying "What does God intend...."

The divisions of "madha" have already been discussed, and here it can bear two of those divisions. One: "ma" is interrogative in the nominative position as the subject, and "dha" means "alladhi" (who/what) as the predicate of "ma." "Aradа" is the relative clause of "dha," and the returning pronoun is omitted, since the conditions for its omission are present. The estimate is "ma alladhi aradahu God?" (what is it that God intended?). Two: that "madha" entirely is interrogative, and the combination of "dha" with "ma" is an object of the verb "intend" by estimate, i.e., "what thing did God intend?" Both of these views are eloquent. Ibn Atiyya said: The grammarians differed regarding "madha." It has been said it is like one word meaning "what thing did God intend?" It has been said "ma" is one noun and "dha" another noun meaning "alladhi," so "fa-ma" is in the nominative position as the subject and "dha" is the predicate. End of Ibn Atiyya's words. His statement apparently indicates a disagreement among the grammarians about "madha" here, but this is not so. Rather, they are two permissible and eloquent views in the language of the Arabs, and it is not a matter of disagreement among the grammarians. Rather, everyone who has tasted a part of the science of grammar permits these two views for "madha" here, and likewise every one of the exegetes and grammatical analysts whose words we have seen mentioned both views for "madha" here.

Intention (al-irada), in its linguistic interpretation, is the inclination of the heart toward a thing, and its attribution to God is impossible. Some exegetes said: Intention is an entity that the rational person finds in himself, and he perceives the evident distinction between it and his knowledge, his power, his pleasure, and his pain. The theologians (al-mutakallimun) said: It is an attribute that requires the preponderance of one of the two possibilities over the other in bringing it into existence, not in its occurrence. He excluded this last qualification from power. The People of the Sunna believe that God wills with a single, eternal intention existing in His essence. The Qadariyya, the Mu'tazila, the Najjariyya, the Jahmiyya and some of the Rafida denied the attributes that the People of the Sunna affirmed. The Bahshamiyya and the Basran Mu'tazila say that God's intention comes into being without being in a locus. The Karramiyya say that it comes into being in Him, and that they are many intentions. Most of them claimed, along with the view of origination, that its non-existence is impossible. Among them are those who said that its non-existence is possible. This question is discussed in the principles of religion (usul al-din).

The accusative of "mathalan" is, according to the Basrans, a specifier (tamyiz), i.e., "from a parable." Some permitted its accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the demonstrative pronoun, i.e., "presenting itself as such," and the governing element in it is the demonstrative pronoun. It is like your saying to someone who carries a bad weapon: "What did you intend by this weapon?" So its accusative is from two aspects: the specifier and the circumstantial state of the demonstrative. Some permitted that it be a state from God, the Exalted, i.e., "presenting Himself." The Kufans permitted that it be accusative by severance (qat'). The meaning of this is that it could be inflected in the same case as the preceding noun, but when you do not make it follow in inflection and you sever it from it, it is put in the accusative by severance. They adduced from this:

"And [I] carried clusters of dates from the unripe dates, red."

So "ahmar" (red), in their view, is an attribute of "busr" (unripe dates), except that when you sever it from its inflection, you put it in the accusative by severance, and its original form was "from the red unripe dates." Likewise they said: "What did God intend by this parable?" So when "mathal" was not put in the genitive following the inflection of "hadha" (this), "mathalan" was put in the accusative by severance. And when you say, "So-and-so is in the bath naked," or "Zayd comes riding," then this and similar constructions are accusative by severance according to al-Kisa'i. Al-Farra' made a distinction, claiming that whatever has before it an indication of it is accusative by severance, and whatever does not is accusative as a circumstantial state. All this, according to the Basrans, is accusative as a circumstantial state, and the Basrans did not affirm accusative by severance. The argument against what the Kufans held is mentioned in the extended books of grammar. The preferred view is that "mathalan" is accusative as a specifier. It came in the sense of emphasis, because from the fact that it was pointed to, it is known that it is a parable, so the specifier came after it emphasizing the noun to which it was pointed.

"Yudillu bihi kathiran wa-yahdi bihi kathiran" (He leads many astray thereby, and guides many thereby): these are two resumed clauses, serving as explanation and elaboration of the two preceding clauses introduced by "amma." God described those who know as "the truth," and those who ask about it as asking in mockery with the multitude. Although He said, "And few of My servants are grateful" [Saba' 34:13], and "except those who believe and do righteous deeds, and few are they" [Sad 38:24], there is no contradiction between them, because multitude and fewness are relative matters. So the guided ones are many in themselves, and when they are described as few, it is in relation to the people of misguidance. Or the multitude is in relation to the reality, and the fewness is in relation to individuals, so they are called "many" by way of the reality, as the poet said:

"Indeed the noble are many in the lands, and even if they are few, as others are few, even if they are many."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 26 (part 4 of 4):

Some grammarians (mu'ribun) and exegetes (mufassirun) chose that His saying, ﴿He leads many astray by it, and He guides many by it﴾, is in the position of an attribute (sifah) for (mathalan, "a parable"), and the meaning is: ﴿What did Allah intend by this as a parable?﴾, by which He divides people into going astray and being guided. On this view, it is part of the speech of those who disbelieved. But this opinion is not apparent, because what was mentioned, that Allah is not shy of it, is the striking of a parable of any kind, whatever parable it may be, a gnat or what is above it, whereas those who disbelieved only asked as a mockery, and they did not acknowledge that by this parable Allah leads many astray and guides many, unless the meaning of the statement is understood as: that is according to your belief and your claim, O believers, so it is possible. However, its being a report from Allah the Exalted is the apparent meaning. The attribution of misguidance to Allah the Exalted is a true attribution (isnad haqiqi), just as the attribution of guidance is likewise; He is the Creator of misguidance and guidance. Here, idlal (leading astray) has been interpreted as leading astray from the path of Paradise. Idlal from the religion, in the linguistic sense, is calling to the disparagement of the religion and abandoning it, and this is the idlal attributed to Satan, and idlal in this sense is negated of Allah by consensus. Al-Zamakhshari, in his Mu'tazili method, says: attributing misguidance to Allah the Exalted is an attribution to the cause, because when He struck the parable with it, a people were led astray by it and a people were guided by it, so He is the cause of their misguidance and their guidance. It has been said: (yudillu) means (yu'adhdhibu, "punishes"), as in His saying, ﴿Indeed the criminals are in error and madness﴾ [al-Qamar: 47]. This was said by some of the Mu'tazilah. Al-Qaffal rejected this and said: rather, what is meant in the visible world is: in error from the truth. Ibn 'Atiyyah allowed that His saying, ﴿He leads many astray by it﴾, may be from the speech of the disbelievers, and His saying, ﴿and He guides many by it﴾ up to (p-126) the end of the verse, is from the speech of Allah the Exalted. But what he allowed is not apparent, because it is confusion (ilbas) in the composition, since the speech must either proceed as being from the speech of the disbelievers, or proceed as being from the speech of Allah. As for its proceeding partly as the speech of the disbelievers and partly as the speech of Allah the Exalted without any evidence for that, it would be confusion in the composition, and the Book of Allah is free of it.

Zayd ibn 'Ali read: yuḍalla bihi kathīrun wa-yuhdā bihi kathīrun wa-mā yuḍallu bihi illā al-fāsiqūn, in the three places in the passive voice.

Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Ablah read in the three places in the active voice with an apparent subject, with the imperfect prefix vowelled with a fatha. 'Uthman ibn Sa'id al-Sayrafi said: this is the reading of the Qadariyyah. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he read: (yuḍallu) with a damma on the yā' in the first, (wa-mā yaḍillu) bihi with a fatha on the yā', and al-fāsiqūn with a waw, and likewise also in the two previous readings. These are readings which, in my view, are contrary to the agreed-upon Mushaf.

The apparent view is that the pronoun in (bihi) in the three places refers to (mathalan), and it is with an elided modifier, i.e., he strikes the parable. It has been said: the pronoun in (bihi) in His saying ﴿He leads many astray by it﴾ refers to denial, and in (bihi) in His saying ﴿and He guides many by it﴾ refers to affirmation. The strength of the composition indicates this, in His saying, ﴿As for those who believed, they know﴾, ﴿and as for those who disbelieved, they say﴾.

The meaning of ﴿And He leads none astray by it except the defiantly disobedient (al-fasiqin)﴾ is: and this does not become a cause of misguidance except for those who have departed from the truth. Some scholars said: the meaning of "leads astray" and "guides" is increase in misguidance and guidance, not that the striking of the parable is a cause of misguidance and guidance. On this view, the estimate is: We increase in error the one who did not affirm it and disbelieved, and in faith the one who believed in it and affirmed it, in addition to his faith.

Al-fasiqin is the object of (yuḍillu), because it is an exceptive construction with the anterior element omitted (istithna' mufarragh). Abu al-Baqa' prevented it from being in the accusative as an exception. The object of (yuḍillu) would be elided, its estimate being: and he does not lead anyone astray by it except the defiantly disobedient. This is not impossible. That is because the noun after illa is either left to be governed by the verb (yufarragh lahu al-'amil), in which case it follows the case required by the verb, as in: mā qāma illā Zayd, mā ḍarabtu illā Zaydan, mā marartu illā bi-Zayd, when you make Zayd and bi-Zayd governed by the verb before "not" (lā); or it is not left to be governed. If it is not left to be governed, then either the verb is an agent in the nominative, in which case it is obligatory to mention it before illa, and its pronoun if it is of the kind that is pronominalised; or it is in the accusative or genitive, in which case it may be elided, as it is a complement, and may be stated. If you elide it, the noun after illa is in the accusative as an exception, so you say: mā ḍarabtu illā Zaydan, meaning mā ḍarabtu aḥadan illā Zaydan (I did not strike anyone except Zayd), and mā marartu illā 'Amran, meaning mā marartu aḥadan illā Zaydan ... and mā marartu illā 'Amran. The poet said:

Salim escaped, and the soul of him was by his cheek, ∗∗∗ and he did not escape except with the sheath of a sword and a loincloth.

He means: he did not escape with anything except the sheath of a sword. If you state it and do not elide it, then it has rulings that are mentioned. On this basis, which the grammarians have laid down, al-fasiqin may be governed by (yuḍillu), and it is from the exceptive construction with the anterior element omitted; and it may be in the accusative as an exception, and the object of (yuḍillu) has been elided because the meaning is understood. Al-fasiq is one who has gone out of obedience to Allah the Exalted. Sometimes this is by disbelief, and sometimes by disobedience other than disbelief.

Al-Zamakhshari said: al-fasiq in the Shari'ah is one who goes out of the command of Allah by committing a major sin, and he is the one who is situated between the two positions, i.e., between the position of the believer and that of the disbeliever. It was said that the first to define it thus was Abu Hudhayfah Wasil ibn 'Ata', may Allah be pleased with him and with his followers. Being "between the two" means his ruling is the ruling of the believer in that he is married to, inherits from, is washed, is prayed over, and is buried in the graveyards of the Muslims, while he is like the disbeliever in blame, cursing, disavowal, belief in enmity toward him, and that his testimony is not accepted. The position of Malik ibn Anas and the Zaydiyyah is that prayer behind him is not valid. The term is also applied to the rebellious disbelieving leaders (al-khulafa' al-maradah min al-kuffar al-fasaqah). Both usages have come in the Book of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Wretched is the name of wickedness after faith﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11], meaning defamation and mutual insulting, and ﴿Indeed the hypocrites, they are the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Tawbah: 67]. End of al-Zamakhshari's speech, and it proceeds according to his Mu'tazili school.

What the early community of this Ummah holds is: whoever is a believer and commits disobedience short of disbelief, he is defiantly disobedient by his disobedience and a believer by his faith, and he has not left faith by his disobedience, nor has he reached the level of disbelief. The Khawarij held that whoever disobeys and commits a sin has disbelieved after his faith. Among them are those who said: whoever sins after faith has committed shirk. Among them are those who said: every act of disobedience is hypocrisy, and that the judge's ruling after affirmation is that he is a hypocrite. The Mu'tazilah held what al-Zamakhshari mentioned, and it is mentioned that this question is the reason they were called Mu'tazilah, for they withdrew (i'tazalu) from the community's position on it, since the community had two positions, so they introduced a third position and were named Mu'tazilah for that. This question is established in the foundations of religion (usul al-din).

﴿Those who break the covenant of Allah after its ratification﴾: It may be read in the accusative (naṣb) or the nominative (rafʿ). The accusative has two possibilities: either it is in apposition (ittibāʿ, agreement with the preceding word), or it is in the accusative of detachment (qaṭʿ), meaning "I condemn those who...". The nominative also has two possibilities: either it is in the nominative of detachment (qaṭʿ), meaning "they are the ones who...", or it is the subject (mubtadaʾ), with the predicate (khabar) being the clause ﴿They are the losers﴾. In this case of i'rāb (grammatical case-inflection), the clause would seem to be a separate statement with no connection to what precedes it, except in a remote sense. Therefore the preferable of these grammatical analyses is the ones we have mentioned, and the best of them is ittibāʿ. This attribute is then an attribute of censure, and it is a necessary one, since every sinner breaks the covenant and cuts off what Allah commanded to be joined.

The scholars differed over the interpretation of the covenant ('ahd), giving several views. The first: it is the injunction of Allah to His creation and His command to them to obey Him and His prohibition of disobeying Him, in His revealed books and on the tongues of His sent prophets. Their breaking of it is their abandonment of acting upon it. The second: it is the covenant which Allah took from them when He brought them forth from the loins of their fathers, in His saying ﴿And when your Lord took...﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 172], and their breaking of it is the disbelief of some of them in His lordship and of others in the rights of His blessing. The third: it is what Allah took from them in the revealed books concerning affirming His oneness, acknowledging His blessings, and confirming His prophets and messengers and what they brought, in His saying ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture...﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 187], and their breaking of it is their casting it behind their backs and altering what is in their books concerning his description (ﷺ). The fourth: what Allah the Exalted took from the prophets and their followers, that they should not disbelieve in Allah or in the Prophet (ﷺ), and that they should support him and honour him, in His saying: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets, [saying]: "Whatever I have given you of the Scripture...﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 81], and their breaking of it is their denial of his prophethood and their altering of his description. The fifth: their belief in him (ﷺ) and his message before his mission, and their breaking of it is their denial of his prophethood and his description. The sixth: what He placed in their intellects of proof for His oneness and for confirming His messenger, through reflection upon the miracles which indicate the inimitability of the Qur'an and its truthfulness, and the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). Their breaking of it is their abandonment of reflection on that and their blind imitation (taqlīd) of their fathers. The seventh: the trust (amānah) offered to the heavens and the earth which man bore, and their breaking of it is their abandonment of fulfilling its rights. The eighth: what He took from them, that they should not shed their blood nor expel themselves from their homes, and their breaking of it is their return to what they were forbidden. This view indicates that the addressees of this are the Children of Israel. The ninth: it is faith and the commitment to the sacred laws (sharāʾiʿ), and its breaking is disbelief after faith.

Of these nine views, some indicate generality, applying to every breaker of a covenant, and others indicate that the addressees are a specific people. This difference is founded upon the difference that occurred regarding the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzūl), and generality is the apparent meaning. So whoever breaks the covenant of Allah, whether Muslim or disbeliever, hypocrite or polytheist, or People of the Book, is included in this censure. The particle (min) is connected to the verb ﴿they break﴾, and it denotes the starting point (ibtidāʾ al-ghāya). It indicates that the breaking took place immediately after the covenant was made firm, without any interval between them, and this is a proof of their lack of concern for the covenant. Thus, the effect of what Allah had made firm upon them, they broke.

It has been said that (min) is superfluous (zāʾidah), but this is remote. The word mīthāq is a noun of the form of a passive participle from the root meaning firmness (wathāqah), which is binding in a contract, and we have already mentioned that it is a covenant confirmed by oath. The meaning here is not that, rather it is a metaphor for commitment and acceptance. Abu Muhammad ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "It is a noun standing in the place of a verbal noun (maṣdar), as ʿAmr ibn Shuyaym said:

Is it disbelief, after turning death away from me, and after your giving me the hundred grazing camels?

He meant: after your giving." End of his words. This is not necessarily the only meaning, for al-Zamakhsharī permitted that it be "after the making firm". Just as mīʿād means waʿd (promise) and mīlād means wilādah (birth). The apparent meaning of al-Zamakhsharī's words is that it is a verbal noun. But the basic form of mifʿāl is that it is an adjective, like miṭʿām (food), misqām (sickness), and midhkār (male). I have looked into the words of Abu al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Ḥājj and the words of Abu ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mālik, both of whom are among the most comprehensive scholars on the patterns of verbal nouns, and neither mentioned mifʿāl among the patterns of verbal nouns.

The pronoun in ﴿his covenant﴾ refers back to ʿahd (covenant), since it is what is being spoken of. It is also permitted that it refers back to Allah the Exalted, meaning "after His making it firm over them", or "after He made His covenant firm", according to the two interpretations of mīthāq. Abu al-Baqāʾ said: "If you return the pronoun to the name of Allah, the verbal noun is in the genitive construction with the agent (muḍāf ilā al-fāʿil); and if you return it to the covenant, it is in the genitive construction with the object (muḍāf ilā al-mafʿūl)." This indicates that mīthāq, in his view, is a verbal noun.

﴿And they cut off what Allah commanded to be joined﴾: The word (mā) is a relative pronoun meaning "that which", and in it there are five views. The first: it refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), whom they cut off by denial and disobedience. This was said by al-Ḥasan, and it is weak, for if it were as he said, it would have been (man) in place of (mā). The second: it refers to speech, that Allah commanded it to be joined with action, but they separated the two, and they said but did not act. This points to the view that it was revealed concerning the hypocrites: ﴿They say with their tongues what is not in their hearts﴾ [al-Fatḥ: 11]. The third: it refers to belief in the prophets, that they were commanded to join it, but they cut it off by denying some and affirming others. The fourth: it refers to kinship and blood relations, as said by Qatādah, and this indicates that he meant the disbelievers of Quraysh and those like them. The fifth: that it is general, applying to everything Allah commanded to be joined. This is the most probable view, for in it the wording is taken according to its generality, and there is no clear proof for specificity.

Abu al-Baqāʾ permitted that (mā) be an indefinite qualified noun (nakirah mawṣūfah), and we have shown the weakness of the view that (mā) is qualified, especially here, since the meaning would become: "and they cut off a thing which Allah commanded to be joined", which is unrestricted. Then there would be no severe censure, nor a judgement of defiance and loss, for an unrestricted act of any kind. The command (amr) is the summoning of the superior to the action by the inferior. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "And its impelling to it. And by it the matter (amr) which is one of the affairs was named, because the summons which calls to it from one who does not take charge of it was likened to a commander commanding him with it, so it was called amr, naming the object by the verbal noun, as if it were commanded (maʾmūr bihi), just as it was called shaʾn (affair). And shaʾn means seeking and intending; one says shaʾantu shaʾnahu, meaning I intended his intention." And amr is transitive to two objects, and the first is omitted because the meaning is understood, meaning: that which Allah commanded with it. ﴿That it be joined﴾ is in a genitive position as an apposition (badal) of the pronoun in (bihi), its estimated form being "with it its joining", meaning that Allah commanded them to join it, similar to the saying of the poet:

Is it, because of the remembrance of Salma, that her distance has come upon you, so that she withdraws and you fall short of her for a period and then grow restless?

Meaning: is it because of the remembrance of Salma that her distance (nayʾuhā) has come upon you?

Al-Mahdawī, Ibn ʿAṭiyyah and Abu al-Baqāʾ permitted that ﴿that it be joined﴾ be in an accusative position as an apposition for (mā), meaning its joining, and the estimated form: "and they cut off the joining of what Allah commanded". Al-Mahdawī and Ibn ʿAṭiyyah also permitted that it be in an accusative position as an object of cause (mafʿūl min ajlihi), which al-Mahdawī estimated as: "out of dislike that it be joined", so that the motive for cutting off what Allah commanded is dislike that it be joined. Abu al-Baqāʾ mentioned the object of cause construction and estimated it as "lest" (li-allā). Abu al-Baqāʾ also permitted that ﴿that it be joined﴾ be in a nominative position, meaning "it is that it be joined". All these grammatical analyses are weak, and were it not for the fame of their proposers I would have turned away from mentioning them entirely. The first one we have chosen is the one upon which the words of Allah should be understood, and others among the i'rāb are remote from eloquent speech, let alone the most eloquent speech, which is the speech of Allah.

﴿And they cause corruption in the earth﴾: Regarding it there are four views. The first: their calling people to disbelief and encouraging it, and driving people towards it. The second: their frightening of travellers and their cutting of the road against those who emigrated to the Prophet (ﷺ) and others. The third: breaking the covenant. The fourth: every act of disobedience whose harm extends to someone other than its doer. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "They worship other than Allah, and they make lawful the acts according to their desires, and this is close to the fourth view." The meaning of ﴿in the earth﴾ has already been explained, and attention was drawn to the mention of the earth when speaking of His saying ﴿And when it is said to them, "Do not cause corruption on the earth"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 11], so there is no need to repeat it here.

This great verse contains a type of rhetorical ornament (badīʿ) which the masters of rhetoric call antithesis (ṭibāq). It has already been mentioned in part, and it is that you bring a thing together with its opposite. It occurs here in His saying ﴿a mosquito or what is above it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26], for these two are indications of the small and the great; and in His saying ﴿As for those who believed...﴾ and ﴿As for those who disbelieved...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26]; and in His saying ﴿He leads astray many by it and guides many by it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26]; and in His saying ﴿They break the covenant of Allah...﴾, and in His saying ﴿and cut off what Allah commanded to be joined﴾. In these last three the feature of antithesis is found, namely that each first one of them occurs after its opposite: misguidance comes after guidance, according to His saying: "Every child is born upon the fitrah", and due to the entry of the children of those who disbelieved into Paradise if they die before puberty; breaking comes after making firm; and cutting off comes after joining. So these are three which correspond in antithesis.

The joining of (alladhīna) to the present tense (muḍāriʿ) and the coordination of the two present-tense verbs after it is a proof of the renewal of breaking, cutting off and corruption, and also an indication of their continuance, and this is more forceful in censure. The passive construction of (yūṣal) is more eloquent than its active construction, because it includes what Allah commanded to be joined, whether they join it or someone else joins it.

The arrangement of these connections is in the utmost beauty, for He began first with the breaking of the covenant, which is the most specific of these three, then followed it with the cutting off of what Allah commanded to be joined, which is more general than the breaking of the covenant and other things, then came third with corruption, which is more general than cutting off. All of them are fruits of defiance (fisq). He used the active participle as a relative clause after the definite article (al-) in order to indicate their firm establishment in this attribute, so that the attribute of defiance is established for them, and its consequences are renewed and repeated. Thus the censure for them is more forceful, because it combines the permanence of the root with the renewal of its branches and consequences. When He mentioned the attributes of the defiant ones, He pointed to them with His saying (ulāʾika), meaning: "Those who combine those blameworthy attributes of breaking, cutting off and corruption."

﴿They are the losers﴾: The word (al-khāsirūn, the losers) has been interpreted as those who diminish their own portions and nobility, and as those who are ruined. The cause of their loss is their exchanging breaking for fulfilment, cutting off for joining, and corruption for reform, and their punishment for reward. It was also said: the losers are those cheated by the loss of reward and the incurring of punishment. It was said: they lost the blessings of the Hereafter. It was said: they lost their good deeds which they had done, which they nullified by their disbelief. The verse concerns the Jews, who had acts within their own law. It also concerns the hypocrites, who apparently perform the deeds of the sincere. Al-Qaffāl said: "The loser is a general term applying to everyone who does a deed for which he will be recompensed."

[Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 28 (part 1 of 2):]

﴿كَيْفَ﴾: It has already been mentioned that it is an interrogative particle asking about a state (ḥāl), accompanied by the meaning of affirmation and rebuke, so it has departed from the literal sense of a question. It has been said that it is accompanied by denial and wonder, meaning: whoever is in this position of overwhelming power and complete control, and to whom the final return is, so that He rewards and punishes, it is not fitting that He be disbelieved. Denial with the hamzah (interrogative alif) is a denial of the act itself, while denial with كَيْفَ is a denial of its state, and denying the state entails denying the essence, because the essence is never free of some state in which it exists. So the denial of the state necessarily entails the denial of the essence, and this is more eloquent, since it becomes a case of kināya (metonymy), where the denial of the state is intended while the aim is the denial of the occurrence of disbelief itself. Al-Zamakhshari said: The explanation is that when it is denied that there is for their disbelief a state in which it exists, and it is known that every existing thing does not part from some state and attribute when it exists, and it is impossible for a change of attribute to exist without a state, then this is a denial of its existence by way of demonstrative proof. End of his words.

This address contains an iltifāt (shift from third person to second person), because the speech before it was in the third-person form. Do you not see His saying: ﴿وأمّا الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26] "As for those who disbelieve" and so on to its end? The benefit of this shift is that when denial is directed at the addressee it is more forceful than when it is directed at an absent person, since the denial may not reach the absent person, whereas when one is addressed, denial is more effective in deterring him from falling into what is denied to him. The governing element of كَيْفَ is ﴿تَكْفُرُونَ﴾ "you disbelieve." It was expressed with the form تَكْفُرُونَ in the present tense and not the past, although disbelief had indeed already occurred from them, because what is denied or wondered at is the continuation of that, and the present tense is what indicates it. Also, so that it would not be a rebuke for one who disbelieved and then believed: if it had come as كَيْفَ كَفَرْتُمْ ﴿بِاللَّهِ﴾ "how did you disbelieve in Allah," it would have included those who disbelieved and then believed, such as most of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them.

The waw in His saying: ﴿وكُنْتُمْ أمْواتًا فَأحْياكُمْ﴾ "and you were dead and He gave you life" is the waw of the circumstantial clause (wāw al-ḥāl), like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وقالَ الَّذِي نَجا مِنهُما وادَّكَرَ بَعْدَ أُمَّةٍ﴾ [Yusuf: 45] "And the one of the two who was saved said, and remembered after a period," and ﴿ونادى نُوحٌ ابْنَهُ وكانَ في مَعْزِلٍ﴾ [Hud: 42] "And Noah called out to his son, and he was apart." Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, how is it valid for it to be a circumstantial clause while it is in the past tense? One does not say "I came and the amir stood," but rather "and he had stood," unless qad is implied. I say: The waw did not enter upon "you were dead" alone, but upon the whole sentence of His saying "you were dead" up to "you will be returned," as if it were said: How do you disbelieve in Allah while your situation is that you were dead, as drops in the loins of your fathers, so He made you living? ﴿ثُمَّ يُمِيتُكُمْ﴾ "Then He causes you to die" after this life? ﴿ثُمَّ يُحْيِيكُمْ﴾ "Then He gives you life" after death, then He will call you to account? End of his words. We say: it is with qad implied, as most people hold, meaning: "and indeed you were dead, so He gave you life." The circumstantial clause, in our view, is a verbal sentence. As for trying hard to make that clause nominal so as to avoid implying qad, we do not go that way. What led al-Zamakhshari to that is his belief that all the sentences fall under the circumstantial clause, which is why he said: If you say, part of the story is in the past and part is in the future, and both the past and the future cannot validly be a circumstantial clause unless it is a present act at the time of the thing that is the circumstance, so what is the present that became a circumstance? I say: It is the knowledge of the story, as if it were said: How do you disbelieve while you know this story, and its beginning and its end? End of his words.

It is not necessary that all the sentences fall under the circumstantial clause, since it is possible that the circumstance is His saying "and you were dead, so He gave you life," and the meaning would be: How do you disbelieve in Allah while He has created you? So creation is expressed by His saying: ﴿وكُنْتُمْ أمْواتًا فَأحْياكُمْ﴾. A parallel to this is His saying (ﷺ): "That you set up a rival to Allah while He created you." That is, whoever brought you into existence after pure non-existence deserves that you not disbelieve in Him, because there is no blessing greater than the blessing of origination (ikhtirāʿ), then the blessing of bestowing favour (iṣṭināʿ). Both blessings are included in His saying: ﴿وكُنْتُمْ أمْواتًا فَأحْياكُمْ﴾, because through giving life both were achieved. Do you not see that the sentence includes bringing into existence and kindness to you by nurture and blessings up to the time when the denial of disbelief is directed at you? Since it is fixed in human nature and created in minds that there is no creator except Allah, ﴿ولَئِنْ سَألْتَهم مَن خَلَقَهم لَيَقُولُنَّ اللَّهُ﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 87] "If you asked them who created them, they would surely say, Allah," it became a state that requires that it not be combined with disbelief, and so there is no need to strain to say that the circumstance is the knowledge of this sentence.
