According to what we have explained, His saying, exalted is He: ﴿ثُمَّ يُمِيتُكم ثُمَّ يُحْيِيكم ثُمَّ إلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ﴾ "Then He causes you to die, then He gives you life, then to Him you will be returned" are sentences which Allah, exalted is He, informed of as independent statements, not included under the circumstantial clause. For this reason, He varied from what came before them in the particle of conjunction and in the verbal form. Whoever makes knowledge of the content of these sentences the circumstance makes their awareness of the second giving of life and the return, by means of the proofs set up for it that lead to it, equivalent to the acquisition of knowledge. Their attainment of it is by the two deaths and the first giving of life, and many people knew and then were obstinate. Regarding the arrangement of these two deaths and two lives which Allah mentioned and bestowed upon them, there are opinions:

First: the first death is the prior non-existence before creation, the first giving of life is creation, the second death is the familiar death in the abode of this world, and the second life is resurrection for the Judgment. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, and Mujahid.

Second: the first death is the familiar death in this world, the first giving of life is in the grave for questioning, the second death is in the grave after questioning, and the second giving of life is resurrection. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Abu Salih.

Third: the first death is their being in the loins of their fathers, the first giving of life is their being brought out from the wombs of their mothers, the second death is the familiar death, and the second giving of life is resurrection. This was said by Qatada.

Fourth: the first death is that which followed their being taken out from the loins of Adam as particles like ants, the first giving of life is their being brought out from the wombs of their mothers, the second death is the familiar death, and the giving of life is resurrection. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

Fifth: the first death is the separation of the man's sperm into the womb, where it is dead until the breathing of the spirit, whereupon He gives it life by the breathing, the second death is the familiar death, and the second giving of life is resurrection.

Sixth: the first death is obscurity, and the first giving of life is remembrance and honour through this religion and the Prophet who came to you, the second death is the familiar death, and the second giving of life is resurrection. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

Seventh: the first death is that Adam was of clay, the first giving of life is the breathing of the spirit into him, so you were made alive by his life, the second death is the familiar death, and the second giving of life is resurrection.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya preferred the first opinion and said: It is the best of the opinions, because the disbelievers have no escape from acknowledging it at the start of its order. Moreover, His saying: ﴿وكُنْتُمْ أمْواتًا﴾ "and you were dead," and attributing the causing of death at the end to Him, strengthens that opinion. When the souls of the disbelievers accept that they were dead, non-existent, then that they were given life in this world, then that they were made to die in it, the necessity of the other giving of life becomes strong against them, and their denial of it becomes a claim with no proof. End of his words, and it is excellent speech.

Those ascribed to the science of realities (ʿilm al-ḥaqāʾiq, Sufi esoteric knowledge) have opinions that differ from what preceded: First: dead through polytheism, then He gave them life through monotheism. Second: dead through ignorance, then He gave them life through knowledge. Third: dead through discord, then He gave them life through harmony. Fourth: dead through the life of your souls, and your causing to die is the causing to die of your souls and the giving of life to your hearts. Fifth: dead concerning Him, then He gave you life through Him; this was said by al-Shibli. Sixth: dead in outward appearances, then He gave you life through the unveiling of inner secrets; this was said by Ibn ʿAṭāʾ. Seventh: dead through your witnessing (of created things), then He gave you life through witnessing Him, then He causes you to die to your witnesses, then He gives you life through the subsisting of the Truth in place of them, then to Him you will be returned from all that belongs to you; this was said by Faris.

Al-Zamakhshari preferred that the first death is their being drops in the loins of their fathers, and He made them living, then He causes them to die after this life, then He gives them life after death, then He will call them to account. He also permitted that the intended second giving of life is the giving of life in the grave, and the return is the rising, and that the second giving of life is also the rising, and the return is the going to the recompense. What he permitted, namely that the intended meaning is life in the grave, does not imply that the dead will be living for questioning in the grave, nor for being given bliss or punishment in it, because that is not his school of thought, since the Mu'tazila and their followers denied the punishment of the grave, while Ahl al-Sunna (the People of the Sunna) and the Karramiyya affirmed it with no disagreement between them, except that Ahl al-Sunna say: the dead disbeliever is given life and is punished in his grave, and the wicked may be punished in his grave, while the Karramiyya say: he is punished while dead. The sound hadiths have been widely transmitted about the punishment of the grave, so it is obligatory to affirm it and believe in it.

The author of al-Muntakhab preferred that what is meant by His saying "(dead)" is dust and drops, because the beginning of Adam's creation was from dust, and all the accountable creatures among his descendants, except ʿĪsā (peace be upon our Prophet and upon him), were created from drops. He said: They differed. Most hold that applying the name of "dead" to inanimate matter is metaphorical, because "dead" refers to one upon whom death has come, and it must have the attribute of one who could ordinarily be living. The view that it is literal for inanimate matter is reported from Qatada. End of his words. His interpretation of "dead" as dust and drops does not hold for dust, because what was created from dust never had the attribute that was denied or wondered at at any time, so how could it fall under His saying: ﴿وكُنْتُمْ أمْواتًا﴾? What we choose is that their being dead is from the time they were fixed as drops in the wombs until the completion of the stages after them, and that the first life is the breathing of the spirit after those stages, from the drop, the clot, the lump, and the clothing of the bones with flesh. The second causing of death is the familiar one, and the giving of life is resurrection after death. The first giving of life and the first death, and the second giving of life, are literal. As for their being dead, whoever holds that inanimate matter is literally described as dead, then it is literal in that case; and whoever holds that it is metaphorical, then it is a permissible and near metaphor, because it is in any case existent, so its being described as dead is near. This is unlike the one who claimed that it means their being non-existent and their being in the loins, or when Adam was clay, since the metaphor in that is far, because that is pure non-existence, and non-existence not preceded by existence is far from being called death. Do you not see what the word "death" is applied to in language, of things which life does not inhabit, and how it could be existent and not pure non-existence? ﴿وآيَةٌ لَهُمُ الأرْضُ المَيْتَةُ﴾ [Ya-Sin: 33] "And a sign for them is the dead earth," ﴿فَإذا أنْزَلْنا عَلَيْها الماءَ اهْتَزَّتْ ورَبَتْ﴾ [al-Hajj: 5] "And when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells," ﴿إنَّ الَّذِي أحْياها لَمُحْيِي المَوْتى﴾ [Fussilat: 39] "Indeed He who gave it life is the Giver of life to the dead," ﴿وجَعَلْنا مِنَ الماءِ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ حَيٍّ﴾ [al-Anbiya: 30] "And We made from water every living thing." And the Arabs say: a land that is mawāt (dead, barren). As for the view of those who hold that the first death is obscurity and the first giving of life is fame and remembrance, it is a far metaphor here, because whenever the literal or a near metaphor can be applied, it is the better option.

Thus it is possible by what we have mentioned. Moreover, most of those opinions make the particle of sequence (fa') in His words "then He gave you life" (fa-ahyakum) remote, because between that death and the giving of life there is a long period. But according to what we have chosen, the fa' indicates its meaning of sequence. As for the one who said that the first death is the known death, and the first giving of life is for the questioning (in the grave), then the past tense is in that case used in the place of the future, metaphorically, to indicate that its occurrence is certain, meaning "and you will be dead, and He will give you life," like His words: ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ [an-Nahl: 1]. Some people have used this verse to deny the punishment of the grave, because He, exalted is He, mentioned two deaths and two lives, and did not mention a life between their being given life in this world and their being given life in the Hereafter. They said: It is not permissible to use as evidence His words, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, You caused us to die twice and gave us life twice﴾ [Ghafir: 11], because it is the speech of the disbelievers, and because many people affirmed the life of the atoms (dhar) in the loins of Adam. The answer: The non-mention of this life for the questioning does not necessitate its non-existence before. Also, it is possible that His words "then He will give you life" (thumma yuhyikum) refer to the questioning; therefore He said: "then to Him you will be returned" (thumma ilayhi turja'un), so He conjoined with thumma, which implies delay in time. And the return to Allah, exalted is He, occurs immediately after the life which is for the resurrection, and this indicates that the life mentioned is for the questioning.

Al-Hasan said: The mention of death twice here is for most people, but as for some of them, He has caused them to die three times: ﴿Or like the one who passed by a town﴾ [al-Baqarah: 259], ﴿Have you not seen those who went out of their homes﴾ [al-Baqarah: 243], ﴿Take four of the birds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260], and the verses. In His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then He gave you life, then He causes you to die, then He gives you life again﴾ is evidence of His exclusive power over that, and evidence of the resurrection and the gathering. The apparent meaning of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then to Him you will be returned﴾ is that the pronoun refers to Allah, glorified and exalted is He, because the preceding pronouns refer to Him, exalted is He; and this would be by omitting a modifier, meaning "to His recompense of reward or punishment." It was also said: it refers to the recompense for deeds. And it was said: it refers to the place where Allah will judge between you. And it was said: it refers to the giving of life implied by His words "then He gave you life." The explanation of this is that you will return, after the second life, to the state in which you were at the beginning of the first life, from your not possessing anything for yourselves. The Mujassima (anthropomorphists) used His words ﴿Then to Him you will be returned﴾ as evidence that He, exalted is He, is in a place, but there is no proof for them in that.

The majority (of readers) recited (turja'un) in the passive voice, from raja'a in its transitive form.

Mujahid, Yahya ibn Ya'mar, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Ibn Muhaysin, al-Fayyad ibn Ghazwan, Salam, and Ya'qub recited it in the active voice, wherever it occurs in the Qur'an from raja'a in its intransitive form, since raja'a can be both intransitive and transitive. The recitation of the majority is more eloquent, because the attribution in the preceding verbs is to Allah, exalted is He: ﴿He gave you life, then He causes you to die, then He gives you life again﴾, so the context of this attribution required that the verb of returning be attributed to Him, but that would have disrupted the harmony of the endings and the pauses, since the arrangement would have been: ﴿thumma ilayhi marji'ukum﴾ [al-An'am: 60]. So the agent was omitted, since it is known, and the verb was put in the passive, so that the verbal harmony would not be lost. The semantic harmony has been achieved by omitting the agent, since before being made passive it was active. As for the recitation of Mujahid and those mentioned with him, the semantic harmony is lost, since it does not necessarily follow that when a person returns to something, another has returned him to it, for he may return by himself without anyone bringing him back. The purpose here is to show power and complete control by attributing giving life, causing death, giving life again, and returning to Allah, exalted is He, although we know that Allah, exalted is He, is the doer of all things. And in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then to Him you will be returned﴾ there is an element of warning and encouragement that increases the wrongdoer in fear and turns him back from some of what he commits, and increases the doer of good in desire for goodness, and his hope calls him to increase in good deeds. It also contains a refutation of the Dahriyya (materialists), the Mu'attila (deniers of divine attributes), and the deniers of the Resurrection, since life, death, and resurrection are in His hand, and to Him the whole matter returns.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 29 (part 1 of 2):

﴿He is the One who created for you all that is on the earth﴾: The connection of this verse to what precedes it is clear. He mentioned that the One who brings you into being after non-existence, causes you to perish after existence, and brings you back into being a second time, either to a garden or to a fire, is worthy of being worshipped and not denied, and of being thanked and not disbelieved. Then He began to remind them of His great favour and abundant kindness: the creation of everything on the earth for them, His great power and His governance of the higher world, (p-133) and that the higher world and the lower world are equal in relation to His power, and that He has knowledge of everything. The word (huwa) (هو) is one of the pronouns. It is set for the singular masculine absent, and it is universal in its original setting, like the rest of the pronouns. In its particular usage it came to be used in a specific way, so there is no singular masculine absent that cannot be applied to by (huwa) (هو), but when something is predicated of this word, it becomes specific. The most famous of the Arabic dialects pronounce the waw (و) lightly when it is vowelled with a fatha. Hamdan pronounced it with a shadda, and Asad and Qays pronounced it with a sukun. Omitting the waw is restricted to poetry. Regarding those attributed to the science of realities (haqa'iq) and to Sufism (tasawwuf), there is strange speech in relation to our understanding. I saw fit to mention it here so that the mention of it would occur in this place.

They said: The names of God, exalted is He, are of three kinds: manifest names, pronouns, and hidden names. The manifest names are names of essence and names of attributes, and all of these are derived. The names of essence are derived and numerous, and the non-derived one is one, and it is Allah. It has been said that it is derived, but what should be believed is that it is not derived, rather it is a coined name (murtajal) indicating the essence. As for the pronouns, they are four: (ana) (أنا), as in ﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me﴾ [Ta-Ha: 14]; (anta) (أنت), as in ﴿There is no deity except You; exalted are You﴾ [al-Anbiya: 87]; (huwa) (هو), as in ﴿He is the One who created for you﴾; and (nahnu) (نحن), as in ﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾ [Yusuf: 3]. They said: Given this established, Allah is the greatest of His manifest names indicating the essence, and the word (huwa) (هو) is among the greatest of His manifest and pronominal names for indicating His essence. This is because all of His derived names have a word that includes the permissibility of shared meaning, since both (names) are united in the specific attribute. It is not prevented that one of the two attributes be literal and the other figurative within shared meaning. And it is a name of God, exalted is He, which reveals the reality of His particular essence, which is free from all aspects of plurality, in terms of what He is (min haythu huwa huwa). So the word (huwa) (هو) brings you to the Truth and cuts you off from all else, for you must, along with considering the knowledge of what the derived name indicates, consider the meaning from which it is derived. This name, because of its indication of the essence, makes consideration of anything else cease in it. The eminent among those brought near (al-muqarrabun) have chosen it as the axis of their remembrance and the beacon of their every affair, so they say: O He (ya huwa), because the word (huwa) (هو) is a pointer to the very thing pointed to, on condition that nothing else is present there besides that one. Those brought near do not have any other existent occur to their minds and spirits besides the one its pointing indicates. It is a compound name of two letters, which are the ha' (ه) and the waw (و). The ha' is the root, and the waw is extra, as proven by its dropping in the dual and plural forms (humā and hum). The root is a single letter that indicates the one, the single. The end of what was transmitted from some of our contemporaries regarding (huwa) (هو) in relation to God, exalted is He, affirming what they said and holding to what they related. Regarding the words (ana) (أنا), (anta) (أنت), and (huwa) (هو), they have speech that is very strange and far from what the people of language and Arabic grammar have discussed about them. The discourse of these people who claim affiliation with these sciences has not opened to me any flash of insight, nor have I, until now, perceived any morning or evening visitor from it. We ask God, exalted is He, to illuminate our insights with the lights of guidance, to keep us away from the paths of error, to inspire us to the way of rightness, and to grant us to follow the two radiant lights: the Sunnah and the Book.

(lakum) (لَكم) is related to (khalaqa) (خَلَقَ), and the lam (اللام) in it is said to be for causation, meaning for your sake and for your benefit. Some have estimated it as (for your consideration). It has been said that it is for possession and permission, in which case possession is specific, namely the possession of what creatures benefit from and what necessity calls for. It has been said that it is for specificity, which is more general than possession. The best view is to take it as causation, so it is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), because through what is on the earth the religious and worldly benefit is obtained. The religious benefit is reflection upon it and upon what is in it of the wonders of craftsmanship and the subtleties of creation, which indicate the power and wisdom of the Creator, and from the reminder of the Hereafter and recompense. As for the worldly benefit, it is evident: it is what is in it of food, drink, clothing, marriage, mounts, beautiful sights, and other things. Whoever holds that things before the revelation of the Law are permissible has used the phrase ﴿created for you﴾ as evidence, so anyone may benefit from them. Since it is possible that the lam is for something other than possession and permission, there is no proof in this for what they claimed. Some people held that before the revelation of the Law things are forbidden, so one does not proceed with anything except with permission. Others held that when the proofs of those who say permissibility and the proofs of those who say prohibition conflicted for them, they said suspension (waqf).

Abu Bakr ibn Fawrak related from Ibn al-Sa'igh that he said: The intellect has never been devoid of revelation (al-sam'), so there is no incident except that there is revelation in it, or it has a connection to it, a trace of it, a state that is kept in companionship. When we make the lam for causation, the meaning is not that God did something for a cause; rather, since He did what, if another had done it, he would have done it for a cause, the term "cause" was applied to Him, and under His saying ﴿all that is on the earth﴾ falls everything the earth is a place of rest for, from animals, plants, minerals, and mountains, and everything that exists through an intermediary, from crafts and derived matters. Some used this to prove the prohibition of clay, saying: Because He created for us what is on the earth, not the earth itself.

It has already been mentioned before this favour that He made the earth a bed for us (﴿Who made the earth a bed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 22]), and here He bestowed favour by creating what is in it for us. (jami'an) (جَمِيعًا) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the created object, and it is an emphasizing state, because the phrase (ma fi al-ard) (ما في الأرْضِ) is general, and the meaning of (jami'an) is totality. So it is synonymous in meaning with the word (kull) (كُلّ); as if it were said: what is on the earth, all of it. It does not indicate togetherness in time, and this is the distinction between (ma'an) (مَعًا) and (jami'an) (جَمِيعًا). Some of this has already been mentioned when discussing (ma'a) (مَع). Whoever claims that what is meant by His saying (ma fi al-ard) is the earth and what is in it is far from the indication of the expression, but it is an explanation of a meaning from this expression, and from His saying ﴿Who made the earth a bed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 22]. Thus from these two is put together: the earth and what is in it; God created that for us. Al-Zamakhshari said: If by the earth he means the lower directions rather than the dusty ground, as the sky is mentioned and by it are meant the higher directions, it is permissible, for the dusty ground and what is in it are located in the lower directions.

Some of those attributed to the realities said: He created for you so that He would count His blessings upon you, so that it would require gratitude from you so that you would seek more from Him. Abu 'Uthman said: He gave you the whole, and subjected it to you, so that you would take evidence from it of the vastness of His generosity, and be at rest with what He guaranteed you of abundant reward in the Return, and not consider His great goodness too much for your little deed; for He began you with great blessings before the deed and before monotheism. Ibn 'Ata' said: He created for you so that the whole existence would be yours, and you would be for God; so do not busy yourself with what is yours away from what you are for. Some of the Baghdadis said: He bestowed favour upon you through them, for creatures are slaves of blessings because blessings have taken hold of them; so whoever appears before the Presence, the Benefactor removes from him the sight of blessings. Al-Thawri said: The highest station of the people of realities is detachment from attachments.

The conjunction with (thumma) (ثُمَّ) requires delay in time, but there was no time at that point. It has been said: By (thumma) He indicated the difference between the creation of the heaven and the earth in measure. It has been said: Since between the creation of the earth and the heaven there were acts, such as placing the firm mountains, blessing it, and determining its sustenance, He used (thumma), because between the creation of the earth and the (istiwa') (الاسْتِواء) there is a delay. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in the One who created the earth in two days?﴾ [Fussilat: 9], and the verse.

(istawa) (اسْتَوى): The people of the Hijaz pronounced it with fatha, and the people of Najd with imala, and both were recited in the seven canonical readings. (In the meaning of (istiwa') here there are seven opinions.) The first: He turned toward and purposed the creation of it and aimed at it, without intending during that interval to create anything else. It is a metaphor from the saying: istawa ilayhi like an arrow released, when it aims at something in a straight line without turning toward anything else. This is the view of al-Farra', and al-Zamakhshari chose it and explained what was borrowed from it. The second: He rose and was exalted, without modality or limitation. This was said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas, and the estimate is: His affair and authority were exalted. Al-Tabari chose it. The third: (ila) (إلى) is in the sense of (ala) (عَلى), meaning He istawa over the heaven, that is, He singled out its dominion and did not make it, like the earth, a possession for His creatures. From this meaning is the poet's saying:

"When we rose above them and prevailed over them, we left them fallen prey to the vulture and the hawk."

The meaning of this domination is as the poet said:

"Bishr has taken over Iraq, without sword and without spilled blood."

The fourth: The meaning is that His command turned toward the heaven and settled in it, and istiwa' is settling. So it would be by omitting an annexed word, meaning: then His command turned toward the heaven, that is, settled, because His commands and decrees descend to the earth from the heaven. This was said by al-Hasan al-Basri. The fifth: The meaning is that He turned by His creation and origination toward the heaven. This was said by Ibn Kaysan, and his meaning returns to the first view. The sixth: The meaning is that His work in it was perfected, as you say: the matter became straight (istawa al-amr). This is a meaning the wording does not clearly indicate. The seventh: The pronoun in (istawa) refers to the smoke, and this is very far, being refuted by His saying: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven while it was smoke﴾ [Fussilat: 11], and by the variation of pronouns and their returning to something not previously mentioned, which the context of speech does not support.

These interpretations are all an escape from what is established in the intellects: that God, exalted is He, is impossible to be characterized by the kind of movement that is known in other than Him, and that a created thing (hadith) should inhere in Him, or that He should inhere in a created thing. The discussion of "istiwa'" (settling) with regard to the Throne will come later, God willing.

The meaning of "taswiyah" (making level, equalizing) is: making its creation proportionate and upright, and clearing it of crookedness and flaws. Or it means completing and perfecting their creation, from the expression "dirham sawa'" (a dirham of full weight), i.e., a complete, full, perfect coin. Or it means making them equal, from His saying: ﴿when We made you equal to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 98]. Or it means leveling their surfaces by smoothing them.

The pronoun in (fa-sawwahunna, "so He completed them") refers to the heavens, either on the basis that "al-sama'" is a plural of "sama'ah" (a single heaven), or on the basis that it is a collective noun (ism jins), which can be applied to the singular and the plural, and here the plural is intended. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The pronoun in (fa-sawwahunna) is an ambiguous pronoun (damir mubham), and ﴿seven heavens﴾ is its explanation, like their saying: rubbahu rajulan (a man, how many of him there are)." End of his words. Its implication is that this pronoun refers to what comes after it, and that it is explained by it; so it refers to something not previously mentioned. What it refers to, which is explained by what follows, is of two kinds: one explained by a clause, which is the pronoun of the matter or the story (damir al-sha'n aw al-qissah), whose condition according to the Basran grammarians is that both of its parts be stated explicitly; and one explained by a single word, i.e., not a clause, which is the nominative pronoun with ni'ma and bi'sa and what follows their pattern. Also the genitive pronoun with rubba, the nominative pronoun of the first of the two competing verbs according to the Basran school, the pronoun whose predicate is made to explain it, and the pronoun that is replaced by a substitute which explains it. The existence of this last category is disputed, and an example is: "darabtuhum qawmuka" (I struck them, your people). What al-Zamakhshari mentioned is not one of these pronouns that we have listed, unless one imagines that ﴿seven heavens﴾ is a substitute for it and an explanation of it. This is what al-Zamakhshari's comparison of it to "rubbahu rajulan" requires, and that it is an ambiguous pronoun which does not refer to anything before it. But this is weakened by the fact that this reading makes it not connected to what precedes it in a complete connection, since the statement would then include that He settled toward the heaven, and that He made seven heavens level immediately after His settling toward the heaven, so He would have informed of two matters: one, His settling toward the heaven, and the other, His making seven heavens.

The apparent meaning of the speech is that the one toward which He settled is the very same one that was made into seven heavens. Some have parsed "sab'a samawat" (seven heavens) as a substitute for the pronoun on the basis that the pronoun refers to what is before it, and this is a sound parsing, like: "akhuka marartu bihi Zayd" (your brother, I passed by him, Zayd). They also permitted "sab'a samawat" to be in the accusative as a direct object, the meaning being: "fa-sawwa minhunna sab'a samawat" (so He made seven of them level). But this is not good either in terms of the wording or in terms of the meaning. As for the wording, "sawwa" is not of the pattern of "ikhtara," so it is not permissible to omit the preposition from it in eloquent speech. As for the meaning, it implies that the heavens are many, and He made seven of them level, whereas the matter is not so, since it is known that the heavens are seven. They also permitted it to be a second object of "sawwa," with "sawwa" meaning "sayyara" (made into), but this is not good either, because the transitivity of "sawwa" to one object is the known usage in the language: ﴿so He fashioned you and proportioned you﴾ [al-Infitar: 7], ﴿able to restore even his fingertips﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 4]. As for making it mean "sayyara," this is not known in the language. They also permitted the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). So, what is concluded regarding the accusative of "samawat" is these possibilities: substitution in two respects, the direct object, a second object, and a circumstantial state. The preferred view is the substitution, in respect of the pronoun referring to what precedes it, and the circumstantial state. The substitution is favored by the absence of derivation.

The scholars have differed over which of the two was created first. Some said: the heaven was created before the earth; others said: the earth was created before the heaven. Each one relied in argument on apparent meanings of verses, which will be discussed God willing. What this verse indicates is that the creation of what is in the earth for us precedes the leveling of the heaven into seven, and nothing else. The preferred view is that the body of the earth was created before the heaven, the heaven was created after it, and then the earth was spread out (dahiya) after the creation of the heaven (p-136). By this, the combining of the verses is possible.

Some said: God only created the heavens seven because the number seven and seventy indicates multiplication of strength and intensity, as if it were multiplied seven times. It is characteristic of the Arabs to exaggerate with the numbers seven and seventy, because mentioning them carries an indication of multiplication. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿its length is seventy cubits﴾ [al-Haqqah: 32], ﴿even if you seek forgiveness for them seventy times﴾ [al-Tawbah: 80]. Seven is mentioned in great matters: the days are seven, the heavens are seven, the earths are seven; the stars which are signs by which one is guided are seven: Saturn, Jupiter, Mercury, Mars, Venus, the Sun, and the Moon; the seas are seven; and the gates of Hell.

Dropping the vowel of the "ha'" in "huwa" and "hiya" after the conjunction "wa," "fa," "lam," and "thumma" is permissible. It is rare after the preposition "ka" and the interrogative hamzah, and it is uncommon after "lakinna," in the reading of Abu Hamdun: "lakinna huwa Allahu rabbi" (but He is God, my Lord). This is an assimilation to the dropping of the vowel in "sab'" and "karsh," the two words being treated as one word.

﴿And He is, of everything, Knowing﴾: Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, and Qalun read "wahwa" with a dropped vowel, and the rest read it with a "damma" on the "ha'" according to the original form. Ya'qub paused on "wahwa" with the "ha'" (as in "wahwah").

"Bi-kulli" (of everything) is connected to the word "'alim" (knowing).

The expected construction was that it be transitive with "li" (for) when fronted, or transitive directly. When it is delayed, it is transitive directly, because it is from a transitive verb, and it is one of the five patterns used for intensive emphasis (al-mubalaghah). Because of the intensification, rulings arise in these patterns that do not apply to their verb or to the active participle. This is because this intensive pattern, if its verb is transitive directly, or transitive with a preposition, then if the verb is transitive with a preposition, the pattern is transitive with the preposition, as in: "Zayd sabur 'ala al-adha zahid fi al-dunya" (Zayd is patient in the face of harm, abstemious in worldly life), because "sabara" is transitive with "ala" and "zahada" is transitive with "fi." If the verb is transitive directly, then either it signifies knowledge or ignorance, or it does not. If it signifies knowledge or ignorance, the pattern is transitive with "bi" (with), as in: "Zayd 'alim bi-kadha" (Zayd knows such-and-such), "jahul bi-kadha" (ignorant of such-and-such), "khabir bi-dhalika" (informed of that). If it does not signify knowledge or ignorance, it is transitive with "li" (for), as in the saying of God, exalted is He: ﴿Doer of whatever He intends﴾ [Hud: 107]. The question of whether it governs what follows it without a preposition, taking it in the accusative, is a disputed matter discussed in grammar. The reason these intensive patterns differ from their direct transitive verbs is that, with the intensification they contain, they resemble the elative (af'al al-tafdil), and the elative's ruling is like this. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Your Lord knows best about you﴾ [al-Isra': 25]. The poet said:

*He gave to a splendid mare whose pastures are sweet*

And he said:

*I charge and defend the sanctuary more than they do*

If what follows it appears to be governed by it in the accusative, as in God's saying: ﴿Indeed your Lord, He knows best who strays﴾ [al-An'am: 117], and the poet's saying:

*And more of us strike the helmeted heads with swords*

it is interpreted as governed by a deleted verb indicated by the elative.

"Shay'" (thing): The people have already differed about the signification of "shay'." Whoever applies it to the existent and the non-existent, the connection of knowledge to both is evident from this verse. Whoever restricts it to the existent only, the connection of His knowledge to the non-existent is derived from another proof other than this verse.

"'Alim" (Knowing): We have mentioned that it is among the intensive patterns. God has described Himself as 'alim (knower), 'alim (knowing), and 'allam (all-knowing), and these are for intensification. The Arabs have added the "ha'" to intensify the emphasis in "'allamah" (very learned), and it is not permissible to describe Him with it. Intensification is by one of two matters: either in relation to the repetition of the occurrence of the attribute, whether its object is one or many; or in relation to the multiplicity of the object, not the multiplicity of the attribute. The intensification in God's attributes is of this second kind, because His knowledge, exalted is He, is one with no multiplicity in it. When His knowledge, exalted is He, is connected to all of it, its whole and its parts, its fine and its great, its non-existent and its existent, He described Himself with the attribute which indicates intensification. The ending of this verse suits the description with the intensive form of knowledge, because the mention had preceded of the creation of the earth and the heaven, the disposal of the upper and lower world, and other things including causing death and giving life, and all of this indicates that these things proceed from complete, perfect knowledge encompassing all things. Some people said: "al-'Alim" is one whose knowledge is from his own essence, and "al-'Alim" is one whose knowledge is transmitted from another. This is not good, because God, exalted is He, described Himself as "al-'Alim," and His knowledge was not by learning.

In the generality of God's saying: ﴿of everything, Knowing﴾ there is a refutation of those who claim that God's knowledge, exalted is He, is connected only to universals and not to particulars. God is exalted above that. They said: God's knowledge, exalted is He, is distinguished from the knowledge of His servants by being one, by which He knows all the known things; by not changing with the change of them; by not being acquired through a sense or thought; by being necessary, because its cessation is impossible; by His, exalted is He, not being occupied by one knowledge over another; and by His known things, exalted is He, being unlimited. In their saying "not being occupied by one knowledge over another," they mean "one known over another known," because it has already been established that God's knowledge is one, and the connection of His knowledge to one thing does not occupy it from its connection to another thing.

The saying of God, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed God is not ashamed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26] through to His saying: ﴿and He is, of everything, Knowing﴾ includes that what He struck as parables in His Book, of the one who kindles a fire, the rain cloud, the fly, the spider, and what goes in the same direction, contains wonders of wisdom, hidden and manifest, and marvels of Arabic eloquence, and the agreement of the parable with what it was struck for; and that in its parable, examples are not fitting; and that He, exalted is He, does not abandon that because of the wisdom in it; and the praise of one who knows that this is true, and the blame of one who denies it and finds fault with it; and that in striking it there is guidance for one who believes and misguidance for one who turns away from it; and the blame of one who breaks God's covenant and severs what must be joined, and corrupts on the earth; and His informing that this is the cause of their loss; and the information that the breakers of His covenant, He, exalted is He, is able to bring them back to life after death, as He was able to bring them into existence after non-existence, and that He will gather them, raise them, and recompense them for their deeds; and in that is the utmost frightening and threatening. Then, after the warning, God, exalted is He, reminded them of His blessings which He bestowed upon them: the creation of the earth that bears them, the heaven that shades them, and the numerous created things by which they benefit and take lessons, so that by this He combines warning and encouragement. This is the admonition by which one of sound intellect and upright mind is admonished. Then He concluded that with the greatest favor, which is informing them of the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of all things, from beginning to end.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 30 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I am going to place upon the earth a khalifah (successor/vicegerent)." They said, "Will You place upon it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood, while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You?" He said, "Indeed, I know that which you do not know."﴾ ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them; then He presented them to the angels and said, "Inform Me of the names of these, if you are truthful."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31] ﴿They said, "Exalted are You; we have no knowledge except what You have taught us. Indeed, You are the All-Knowing, the All-Wise."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 32] ﴿He said, "O Adam, inform them of their names." So when he had informed them of their names, He said, "Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you conceal?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 33].

ʾIdh (إذْ): a noun of two-letter origin, built (mabni) because of its resemblance to a particle either in form or in its need (for a complement). It is a temporal adverb referring to the past, and what follows it is a nominal or verbal clause. If it is followed by a verbal clause, it is ugly to place the noun before the verb or to attach it to a clause beginning with the imperfect, and the imperfect's governing of it is among the things that make the imperfect past. It is always adverbial, except that a time noun may be added to it; it does not function as a direct object, nor as a particle of causation or surprise, nor as an adverb of place, nor as a redundant particle, contrary to those who claim this. It has rulings other than these, which are mentioned in grammar works. 

Al-malak (المَلَكُ, "angel"): its mim is original, and it is of the form fa'al from al-mulk, which means power. There is no elision in it, and its plural is formed irregularly as fa'a'ila, as stated by Abu 'Ubayda. It seems they thought it was malak on the pattern fa'al, and they have rarely formed the plural of masculine and feminine fa'al as fa'a'il. It is also said that its original pattern is fa'al'un like shamal'un; then they moved the vowel and elided. Malʾak is also attested, so it may be fa'a'a; in that case the hamza is an extra letter in the first radical and the middle radical. Some said: the first radical is lam and the middle is hamza, from lak, meaning to send; this is an attested dialect form. So malak originally is mal'ak, which was lightened by moving the vowel and eliding, into fa'al. The poet said:

"You are not for a human, but for a malʾak who descended from the air of the sky, bringing rain."

Here he used the original form. This is the view of Abu 'Ubayda, and Abu al-Fath preferred it. In this view, mala'ika is of the pattern mafa'ila. Others said: the first radical is hamza and the middle is lam, from al-alukah, meaning message. In this case its original form is ma'lak, and malak is metathesized, its first radical placed in the position of its middle and its middle in the position of its first. According to this view, its pattern is ma'lan. Others said: the first radical is lam and the middle is waw, from lak al-shay', meaning to turn something in the mouth; the bearer of the message turns it in his mouth, so it is mafal from that, like Mu'adh; then they elided the middle for lightness. According to this view its pattern is ma'lan, and malaika is mafa'ila; the hamza was substituted for a waw, as it was substituted in masa'ib. al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: the Arabs do not derive a verb from malak nor inflect it; it is among what has lost its knowledge. End.

The ta' in al-malaika is for feminine plural; it is said it is for emphasis, and it has come without ta', the poet said:

"I am Khalid; the angels have prayed over you."

Khalifah: fa'ila, and fa'ila comes in the sense of the active participle for emphasis, like 'alim, or in the sense of the passive participle like nati7a, and the ha' is for emphasis. Al-safk: pouring and spilling; it is used only for blood. One says safaka, saffaka and asfaka with the same meaning, and the imperfect of safaka comes as yafil and yaful. Al-dima': plural of dam, whose final radical is a yā' or a elided wāw, as shown by their saying damayan and damawan; its shortened and doubled forms are both attested in the speech of the Arabs. The elided letter is the lam; it is said its original pattern is fa'il, and it is said fa'al. Al-tasbih: declaring God free from evil and clearing Him of it; it is used only for God Most High, and its root is from al-sabh, which is running. The one who glorifies (musabbih) is going in the declaration of God Most High. Al-taqdis: purification, and from it come Bayt al-Maqdis and the sacred land, and from it al-qadas: the basin used for purification, and al-qudas: pearls. The poet said:

"Like the string of pearls whose thread is broken."

Al-Zamakhshari said: from qadasa fi al-ard, when he went into it and went far.

'Allama: transitive from 'alima, which takes one object; they distinguished it from 'alima which takes two objects in transitivity, so they doubled the former and used the hamza for the latter. This was said by the master Abu 'Ali al-Shulubin, and the discussion of it will come at the explanation. Adam: a non-Arabic name like Azar and 'Abir, diptote for definiteness and non-Arabic origin. Whoever claims it is af'al derived from al-udmah, which is like tanning, or from adim al-ard, which is its face, is wrong, because derivation from Arabic words has been stated by morphologists not to occur in non-Arabic names. It is also said he is Hebrew from al-idam, which is dust. Whoever claims it is fa'il from adim al-ard, treating it as a common noun because it is not inflected, is mistaken; al-Tabari went far in claiming it is a quadriliteral verb named after him.

Al-'ard: making a thing appear until its aspect is known. Al-inba': informing; its verb takes one object directly and a second with a preposition, and that preposition may be omitted; it may be used in the sense of a verb taking three objects. Ha'ula': a demonstrative noun for the near, ha for admonition, and the noun ulaa is built on kasra; its hamza may be replaced with ha', so one says hulaa'; it may be built on damma, so one says ulaa'; the damma may be lengthened before the lam, so one says ulaai, as stated by Qutrub. It may also be said hawla' by dropping the alif of ha and the hamza of ulaa while keeping the waw after that hamza, as narrated by the master Abu 'Ali al-Shulubin, who recited the poet's line:

"Be patient; do not say hawla' this... he wept when he wept in sorrow over you."

Al-Farra' mentioned that the lengthened form of ulaa is the dialect of the Hijaz, and the shortened form is the dialect of Tamim; another added that it is the dialect of some of Qays and Asad, and he recited for al-A'sha:

"Hawla' then hawla', all of them; you gave sandals made of sandals."

The hamza, according to Abu 'Ali, is the lam of the verb, so its fa' and lam are hamza; according to Abu al-'Abbas it is a substitute for a yā' that came after an alif and was changed into a hamza. Subhanaka: its meaning is your declaration of purity; subhan is a noun placed in the position of the verbal noun, and it is one of the words that is necessarily in the accusative as a verbal noun, governed by an implied verb from its meaning which may not be pronounced. It is among the nouns that are necessarily accusative as verbal nouns, and it may be made genitive by addition or used alone. When used alone it is nunated, as in the poet's words:

"Subhanahu, then subhanan; we seek refuge in Him, and before us the Judi and the jamad glorified."

It is said he nunated it out of necessity; it is also said because he made it indefinite and not nunated, as in the poet's words:

"I said when his boasting came to me: 'Subhan of 'Alqamah the wicked.'"

He made it a proper name and so withheld it from inflection for definiteness and the addition of alif and nun. Some grammarians claimed that when it is used alone it is detached from the genitive, so nunation returns to it; whoever does not nunate it treats it like qabl and ba'd. This view has been refuted in the grammar books.

Al-Hakim: fa'il in the sense of mufil, from ahkama al-shay': perfected it and prevented it from going out of what he intends. Al-ibda': manifesting; al-katm: concealing.

"And when your Lord said to the angels": no report has come about the occasion of revelation of these verses, and their connection with what precedes is that when He favored them by creating for them what is in the earth, and before that by bringing them out from non-existence into existence, He followed that with the beginning of their creation, and favored them by honoring their father and making him noble, appointing him khalifah, settling him in the abode of His honor, and having the angels prostrate in glorification of his station and as an indication of his rank and his being singled out with knowledge, by which the perfection of the essence and completion of attributes is achieved. There is no doubt that kindness to the root is kindness to the branch, and the nobility of the branch comes from the nobility of the root.

The grammarians differed concerning "idh." Abu 'Ubayda and Ibn Qutaybah went to its being superfluous; this is not correct, and Abu 'Ubayda and Ibn Qutaybah were weak in grammar. Some went to its meaning being qad, the sense being "and indeed your Lord said," and this is not correct. Some went to its being in the accusative as a direct object governed by "udhkur" (remember), meaning "remember when your Lord said" (Sad 71), and this is not correct, because it removes it from its proper category, since it is not used except as an adverb, or with a time noun added to it. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyyah and some before and after them permitted this. Some went to its being an adverb; they differed: some said it is in the nominative position, the sense being "the beginning of your creation." Others said in the accusative position, the sense being "and the beginning of your creation when your Lord said." This estimate suited what preceded: "He created for you all that is in the earth" (al-Baqarah 29). Both of these views are not precise, because the beginning of our creation was not at the time of God's saying to the angels "Indeed I am placing in the earth a khalifah," since the verb governing the adverb must occur within it, and it cannot precede it or follow it, for it would then not be an adverb for it. Some went to its being accusative governed by "qal" after it, which is not correct, because "idh" is added to the clause after it, and the object of an addition does not govern the thing added to. Some went to its being accusative governed by "ahyakum," meaning "and He is the One who gave you life" (al-Hajj 66), "when your Lord said" (Sad 71); this is not correct, because it is an elision without evidence, and because giving life did not occur at the time of God's saying to the angels, and because it elides the relative pronoun and its clause while leaving a complement of the clause. Some went to its being governed by "khalaqakum" in God's words "Worship your Lord who created you" (al-Baqarah 21) and "when your Lord said" (Sad 71), so the waw is superfluous, and the separation between the governor and the governed is by these sentences which almost became surahs of the Qur'an, each verse being independent in what it is brought for and not connected to what precedes it in grammatical connection.

* *

These are eight views, from which the Book of God should be cleared. What Arabic requires is that it is in the accusative governed by His words "They said, 'Will You place'," meaning: at the time of God's saying to the angels "Indeed I am placing in the earth" and "They said, 'Will You place'," just as you say in speech: "When you came to me, I honored you," meaning at the time of your coming I honored you; and "When you told me such-and-such, I told you such-and-such." Look at the excellence of this simple, clear view, and how most people were not guided to it, and they became confused in a bewildering matter and stumbled like a blind camel.

Attributing the saying to the Lord is in the utmost appropriateness and clarity, because when He mentioned that He created for them what is in the earth, that contained the welfare of their conditions and livelihoods, so mention of the Lord was fitting. Its attribution to the Messenger of God, ﷺ, is an alert to his nobility and his being singled out for address, and a stirring to listen to what is mentioned after this of the strange opening of this human species, and the beginning of its affair and its end. This is a variation in address and a movement from general address to special address. In this there is also a subtle indication that the one addressed has the greatest share and the largest portion of the collective matter spoken of, for he is in reality the greatest of His successors. Do you not see the generality of his message and his call, and that the best of His prophets led prayer with them on the night of his Isra', and that He placed Adam and those after him under his banner on the Day of Resurrection? He is the foremost in His earth and His heaven, and in the two abodes of his responsibility and his recompense.

The lam in "li-l-malaika" is for communication (al-tabligh), and it is one of the meanings for which the lam has come. The apparent sense of the word "malaika" is generality, and some held that. Others said: it is general in form but specific in meaning, and they are the inhabitants of the earth among the angels after the jinn; it was also said they are those who fought alongside Iblis. The object of the saying is "Indeed I am placing," and this was introduced with "inna" because the purpose is to emphasize the statement reported, and that this is certainly happening. "Inna" is kasra after a verb of saying, and its opening after it among most Arabs has conditions mentioned in grammar; the Banu Sulaym open it after it without a condition, and their poet said:

"When I say that I am returning to a town, I have pulled from it its kinship by estrangement."

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 30 (part 2 of 3):**

*Jā'il* is an active participle (*ism fā'il*) with the meaning of the future (*al-istiqbāl*). Its genitive construction (*idāfa*) to its object is permissible, unless the two are separated, as here, in which case it is not permitted. When it is permissible to make it operate (*i'māl*) on its object, that is better than the genitive construction. Sibawayh stated this, while al-Kisa'i said that the two are equal. My own preference is that the genitive construction is better, and I have explained the reason for this preference in some of what I have written on Arabic grammar.

Regarding *al-ja'l* (making, appointing) here, there are two views:

The first is that it means *al-khalq* (creating), so it takes one object. Abu Rawq said this. Close to it is what is reported from al-Hasan and Qatada, that it means "one who makes." Ibn 'Atiyya mentioned nothing other than this.

The second is that it means *al-tasyir* (making into something), so it takes two objects. The second object is *fi al-ard* (in the earth), meaning "one who makes a khalifa in the earth." al-Farra' said this, and al-Zamakhshari mentioned nothing other than it.

Both views are acceptable, but in my opinion the first is better, because they said: ﴿Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?﴾. The apparent meaning is that this is set in contrast to ﴿I am placing a khalifa in the earth﴾. If the first *ja'l* were meant in the sense of *tasyir*, He would have mentioned it a second time, and it would have been: "Will You place in it a khalifa who causes corruption therein?" Since it did not come that way, the meaning of creating is more probable. There is no need to supply *khalifatan* (a khalifa) as an object, since what precedes indicates it, because that would be an ellipsis, and a statement without ellipsis is better than one with it. The predicate is in the form of an active participle because it indicates permanence (*al-thubūt*) rather than renewal occurring moment by moment.

Whether *al-ja'l* means creating or making, and whether Adam was the khalifa according to the best understanding, it happened only once. So there is no repetition in it, since He created him, or made him khalifa, only once.

His saying *fi al-ard* (in the earth): its apparent meaning is the whole earth, and this is the view of the majority. It has been said: the earth of Makkah. Ibn Sabit transmitted this interpretation, that it is the earth of Makkah, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ). If that is authentic, it should not be departed from. It has been said that for this reason its middle was named Bakka, because the earth was "bukka" (crushed) beneath it. It was singled out for mention because it is the place where the nations of prophets were destroyed, and Nuh, Hud and Salih are buried there, between the Maqam and the Corner (of the Ka'ba). The *alif* and *lam* here would be for a known reference (*al-'ahd*), like: ﴿So I will not leave the land﴾ [Yusuf: 80], ﴿And thus We established Yusuf in the land﴾ [Yusuf: 21], ﴿They were oppressed in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 5]. The poet said:

*They say to me: "The land of the Hijaz is barren,"*
*So I said: "What do I seek other than the land?"*

The majority read *khalifa* with the *fa'*. It may mean *al-khalif* (one who succeeds), and it may mean *al-makhlūf* (one who is succeeded). If it is in the sense of the active participle, its meaning is: one who stands in the place of another in the matter that has been entrusted to him.

As for *al-khalifa*, it has been said that it is Adam, because he is a khalifa in place of the angels who were in the earth, or in place of the jinn, the sons of al-Jann, or in place of Iblis in ruling the earth, or in place of God Most High. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas. The prophets are the khalifas of God in His earth. Adam was singled out because he is the father of the khalifas, just as Mudar, Tamim and Qays are singled out, where the intended meaning is the tribe. It has been said that it refers to the offspring of Adam, because some of them succeed others: when one nation perishes, another succeeds it. Al-Hasan said this, and then it is singular in form but intended in the plural, as came in: ﴿And it is He who made you khalifas of the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 165], ﴿He will certainly make them khalifas in the earth, as He made those before them khalifas﴾ [al-Nur: 55]. It has also been said that *khalifa* is a name for everyone to whom the management of the people of the earth and the oversight of their interests has been transferred, just as whoever ruled Rome was called Caesar (qaysar), whoever ruled Persia was called Kisra, and whoever ruled Yemen was called Tubba'.

Concerning what the khalifa was appointed to do, Adam's task has two views. The first is ruling with truth and justice. The second is the cultivation of the earth: he plants, harvests, builds, and channels rivers.

Zayd ibn 'Ali and Abu al-Barhtham 'Imran read *khalīqa* with a *qaf*, and its meaning is clear.

As for God's address to the angels with His saying ﴿I am placing a khalifa in the earth﴾: if it was addressed to the angels who fought alongside Iblis against the jinn, then this would be general in the sense that He raised them to heaven, and Adam and his offspring were appointed as khalifas in the earth. Something indicating this is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, and its summary is: God settled the angels in heaven and the jinn in the earth. They worshipped for a long time, then they corrupted and envied, and they fought one another. So God sent to them a force of angels led by Iblis, who was the strongest and most knowledgeable of them. They descended to the earth, drove the jinn to the peaks of mountains, the depths of valleys and the islands of the seas, and settled there. He lightened their worship. God gave Iblis dominion over the earth, the dominion of the lowest heaven, and the treasury of Paradise. He would worship sometimes in the earth and sometimes in Paradise. Then self-admiration entered him, and he said to himself: "God has given me this only because I am the most honoured of the angels in His sight." God Most High said to him and his troops: ﴿I am placing a khalifa in the earth﴾, as a replacement for you, and I will raise you up to Me. They disliked this, because they were the least of the angels in worship, and they said: ﴿Will You place therein...﴾, the verse. If "the angels" means all the angels, then the reason for the statement is God's wish to make the angels aware of what was in Iblis's soul of pride, and to manifest what had preceded in His knowledge.

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, and from al-Suddi, from his shaykhs: or that He might test the obedience of the angels, as al-Hasan said; or that He might show their incapacity to encompass His knowledge; or that He might honour Adam by mentioning the khilafa before his existence, so that they would be reassured about him when they knew; or that He might inform them of his creation so that he would settle the earth, even though his creation began in heaven; or that He might teach us to consult the people of intellect among us and the masters of knowledge, since He consulted the angels out of regard for them, while He had knowledge of the realities of things; or that He might go beyond the address with what was mentioned, so that the angels would acknowledge and retract what they had imagined of perfect knowledge; or that He might show the high rank of Adam in knowledge by His saying to Adam: ﴿Inform them of their names﴾ [al-Baqara: 33]; or that He might teach us good manners with him and obedience to the command, whether we understand its meaning or not, so that pure obedience would be achieved; or that the hearts of the angels might be reassured when God created the Fire: they were afraid and asked: "For whom have You created this?" He said: "For whoever disobeys Me." This was because they did not know of the existence of any creation other than themselves. Ibn Zayd said this.

Some people of allusion (*ahl al-ishāra*) said regarding His saying ﴿I am placing a khalifa in the earth﴾: prior care (*sābiq al-'ināya*) is not affected by the occurrence of transgression, nor does it lower one from the rank of guardianship. That is because God Most High appointed Adam as His khalifa in His earth, although He knew what would occur from him of opposition to His command, which necessitated his removal from the abode of honour and his descent to the earth, the place of troubles. Nevertheless, He did not strip him of the robes of His honour, nor did He lower him from the rank of his khilafa. Rather, He increased His gift to him, and said: ﴿Then his Lord chose him, and turned to him, and guided him﴾ [Ta-Ha: 122]. The poet said:

*When the beloved commits a single sin,*
*His virtues come with a thousand intercessors.*

'Umar used to carry food to the idols while God loved him. The poet said:

*Do you think I reproach you for a slip?*
*My heart is more tender toward you than you suppose.*

It is said that God, glory be to Him, created all that He created and did not say of anything what He said about the story of Adam, when He said: ﴿I am placing a khalifa in the earth﴾. The apparent meaning of this address is an indication of the nobility of the creation of the Gardens (*al-jinān*) and what is in them, and of the Throne with its arrangement of parts and perfection of form. He did not say: "I am creating a throne, or a garden, or a kingdom." He said that only to honour and single out Adam.

They said: it has been established that the preferred construction for the governing verb in *idh* is ("they said"), and its complement is the clause from His saying: ("Will You place..."). Since the angels do not know the unseen and do not precede speech, their saying ﴿Will You place therein...﴾, the verse, could only have come from information and a preliminary. It is said: the hamza, although its original function is interrogation, has been accompanied by the meaning of wonder (*ta'ajjub*). This was said by Makki and others, as if they were amazed that God would appoint as khalifa one who would disobey Him, or one who would disobey the one whom He appointed as khalifa in His earth. It has also been said: it is an interrogation in the manner of magnifying and exalting the khilafa and the disobedience. It has been said: it is an interrogation whose meaning is confirmation (*taqrīr*); Abu 'Ubayda said this. The poet said:

*Are you not the best of those who rode the mounts,*
*And the most generous of all people in the bellies of the wine-cup?*

According to these views, their knowledge of this would have preceded: either by information from God, or by observation on the Preserved Tablet, or there is another creation other than them who are infallible, or they said this by analogy with those who inhabited the earth and corrupted it before the angels dwelt in it, or they inferred it from the word *khalifa*, since a khalifa is one who acts as deputy in judgment, and that happens when there is oppression. It has been said: it is a pure interrogation. Ahmad ibn Yahya said this, and he supposed it as: "Will You make this khalifa on the pattern of those who preceded from the jinn, or not?" Abu al-Fadl al-Bajali interpreted it as: "Or will You make one who does not corrupt?" Others supposed other things, such as: "And we glorify You with Your praise, or shall we change?"

According to the first three views, there is no counterpart (*mu'ādil*) for the interrogative, since it has been taken in the direction of wonder, magnification or confirmation. According to the fourth view, the counterpart is the object of *Will You make*, which is "one who causes corruption." According to the fifth view, the counterpart is from the circumstantial clause, which is His saying ﴿while we glorify You with Your praise﴾.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿and sheds﴾ (*yasfiku*) with a kasra on the *fa'* and a raf' on the *kaf*. Abu Haywa and Ibn Abi 'Abla read it with a damma on the *fa'*. It was also read as *yusfiku* from *asfaka*, and *yusaffiku* from *saffaka* with a shadda on the *fa'*. Ibn Hurmuz read ﴿and sheds﴾ with a nasb on the *kaf*. Whoever read it with raf' made it a conjunction with *yufsidu* (causes corruption). As for whoever read it with nasb, al-Mahdawi said: it is in the nasb as an answer to the interrogative. This is a good analysis, because the accusative after the *wāw* in answer to an interrogative or otherwise is, by the implicit *'an* (that), a conjunction of the meanings together. For this reason the *wāw* is taken to mean *ma'a* (with). So when you say: "Will you come to us and talk to us?" and you put it in the nasb, the meaning is a combination of your coming to us and your talking to us, meaning: there will be from you a coming together with talk. Likewise is the poet's saying:

*Will you spend the night sated with sleep,*
*While I spend the night from you in the night of the one stung by a scorpion?*

Its meaning: will there be from you a sated spending of the night together with my spending the night from you in such-and-such? Likewise here: from You there would be the making of a corrupter together with the shedding of blood.

Abu Muhammad ibn 'Atiyya said: the nasb is by the *wāw al-sarf* (the "wāw of diversion"). He said: it is as if he said: "one who combines causing corruption and shedding blood." That was the end of his words. But the nasb by *wāw al-sarf* is not one of the doctrines of the Basrans. The meaning of *wāw al-sarf* is that the verb deserved a case other than the accusative, but by the entry of the *wāw* it is diverted from that case to the accusative, as in His saying: ﴿and that God may know those who dispute﴾ [al-Shura: 35], in the reading of the one who reads it with nasb, and likewise ﴿and that God may know the patient﴾ [Al 'Imran: 142]. The analogy for the first is raf', and the analogy for the second is jazm (apocope). So the *wāw* diverted the verb to the accusative, and it was called *wāw al-sarf*. According to the Basrans, this is accusative by the implicit *'an* after the *wāw*.

It is strange that Ibn 'Atiyya mentioned this view first, then doubled it with al-Mahdawi's view, and then said: "The first is better." How could it be better, when it is something the Basrans do not hold, and its invalidity is mentioned in the science of grammar?

Since the relative clause ("causes corruption") is a verb in an affirmative context, it does not indicate generality in corruption. They specified the greatest corruption, which is shedding blood, because by it the bodily structures that God created are dissolved. If they had not specified it, it would have been possible that what was meant by their saying "causes corruption" was not this. The repetition of *therein* is because there is an alert that what was a place for worship and obedience to God, how could it become a place for corruption? As a similar case is mentioned in His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Do not cause corruption in the earth"﴾ [al-Baqara: 11]. There was no need to repeat *fīhā* (therein) after His saying "and sheds," being content with what preceded it, and avoiding repeating *fīhā* three times. Do you not see that the critics found fault with Abu al-Tayyib's saying:

*And the plundering of the souls of the plunderers is more fitting*
*For the people of plunder than the plundering of the fine stuffs.*

﴿Wa-nahnu nusabbih﴾ ("while we glorify"): a circumstantial clause (jumlah ḥāliyyah). Tasbīh means declaring God free of imperfection (tanzīh). This is the view of Qatada. Another view is that it means raising the voice in mentioning God, which is reported from al-Mufaddal. A further view is that it means humility and submission (khuḍū' wa-tadhallul), reported from Ibn al-Anbari. Or it means prayer (ṣalāh), i.e., "we pray to You."

﴿Min al-musabbiḥīn﴾ ("of those who glorify"): that is, of those who pray. This is reported from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas. Or it means exalting (ta'ẓīm), i.e., "we exalt You." This is reported from Mujahid. Or it is a specific formula of glorification: "Glory be to the Possessor of dominion and sovereignty; glory be to the Possessor of majesty and might; glory be to the Living who does not die." This formula is known from the glorification of the angels, or from the saying: "Glory be to God and praise be to Him" (subḥāna Allāh wa-biḥamdihi).

It is narrated in a hadith from 'Ubada ibn al-Samit, from Abu Dharr, that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked: "Which speech is the best?" He said: "What God has chosen for His angels, or for His servants: Glory be to God and praise be to Him."

﴿Bi-ḥamdika﴾ ("with Your praise"): this is in the position of a circumstantial (ḥāl), and the bā' here is for accompaniment (lil-ḥāl). The meaning is: "we glorify, accompanied by Your praise," as you say: "Zayd came with his garments." This is an interlocking circumstance (ḥāl mutadākhilah), since it is a circumstance within a circumstance. It has also been said that the bā' indicates cause (lil-sabab), meaning "because of Your praise." Praise (ḥamd) is commendation, and commendation arises from granting success in good and from bestowing favours on the one praised. So what arises from a cause has been placed in the position of the cause, and He said: "we glorify with Your praise," meaning "with Your success and Your favour." Ḥamd is a verbal noun (maṣdar) construed with its object, like His saying: "from the supplication for good" (min duʿā' al-khayr), meaning "from our supplicating for good." The subject (fā'il) is omitted in the case of the verbal noun according to the Basrans, although it is one of their rules that the subject is not omitted; and it is not forbidden in the verbal noun, as some have held, because nouns of kind (asmā' al-ajnās) do not take a pronoun in them. A pronoun is only hidden in what functions as a verb, since concealment is basic in the verb. There is no need to posit that the sentence contains anteposition and postposition, as some have held, that the intended sense is "we glorify and sanctify You with Your praise," so that "with Your praise" is interposed between the conjoined and the conjoined-to. Anteposition and postposition belong to what is specific to poetic necessity (ḍarūrah), so the speech of God is not to be interpreted by it. Rather, "with Your praise" came after "we glorify" because glorification and praise are mixed together. His saying afterward, ﴿wa-nuqaddis laka﴾ ("and we sanctify You"), comes as an emphasis, since taqdīs is purification (taṭhīr), while tasbīh is declaring free of imperfection and clearing of evil. So the two are close in meaning.

The meaning of taqdīs, as we have mentioned, is purification, and its object is: "ourselves for You, from defilements," as al-Ḍaḥḥak and others said. Or "our actions, from sins," as Abu Muslim said. Or the meaning is: "we magnify You and exalt You," as Mujahid and Abu Salih said. Or "we pray to You." Or "we purify ourselves from their deeds," meaning the children of Adam, which is related from Ibn 'Abbas. Or "we purify our hearts from turning toward anyone other than You." The lam in ﴿laka﴾ is superfluous, i.e., "we sanctify You." It has also been said that the lam of purpose (lām al-'illah) is connected with nuqaddis, or with nusabbih. It has also been said that it is the lam that transitivizes the verb, as in "sajadtu lillāh" ("I prostrated to God"). It has also been said that the lam is explanatory, like the lam after "saqyan laka" ("a watering for you"), in which case it is connected to a deleted element indicated by what precedes it, meaning "our sanctification of You." The best view is that it transitivizes the verb, as in His saying: "yusabbiḥu lillāh" ("glorifies God") and "wa-sabbaḥa lillāh" ("and he glorified God").

Whoever held that this sentence, ﴿wa-naḥnu nusabbih﴾, is interrogative has gone far astray. In that view the interrogative particle is deleted, and the intended sense is: "Or are we glorifying with Your praise, or do we not change?" This deletes the hamzah without evidence, and the counterpart of the supposed sentence, which is the entry of the hamzah upon it, is also deleted, namely His saying: "am natagayyar" ("or do we change?"). This is not like the verse:

"By your life, I do not know, though I am knowing,
whether they threw the embers with seven or with eight."

The poet means: "with seven?", because the verb governed before "bi-sab'in" and the counterpart part after it indicate the deletion of the hamzah.

Since the apparent sense of the angels' statement, ﴿Will You place in it one who causes corruption in it and sheds blood, while we glorify You with Your praise and sanctify You?﴾, is not suitable to be answered to God, when He said to them: ﴿I am placing in the earth a khalifah (vicegerent)﴾, and since it is among the legal principles and Islamic beliefs that the angels are protected from sins and from objection, none has dissented on this except a group of the Ḥashwiyyah. This is a question discussed in the principles of religion (uṣūl al-dīn), and its proofs are expounded there. Scholars needed to remove the preceding verse from its apparent meaning, and each speaker among those who came before interpreted his statement according to what he glorified, and what was strong for him of the interpretation that is permissible in the science of the language.

Some of the people of spiritual allusions (ahl al-ishārāt) said: When the angels imagined that God had placed them in the station of consultation, and that they had the benefit of the interest in keeping the caliphate among those who glorify and sanctify, and not transferring it to one who causes corruption and sheds blood, they presented this to God. This was among the sincere counsel in consultation, and sincere counsel is obligatory upon the one consulted. God Exalted is the Judge in what passes of that and what He chooses.

Among the rarest things said in the interpretation of the verse is what was held by the author of the book Fakk al-Azrar (Unbuttoning the Knots), who is Shaykh Ṣafī al-Dīn Abu 'Abd Allah al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Wazir Abi al-Ḥasan 'Ali ibn Abi al-Manṣur al-Khazraji. He said in that book: The apparent speech of the angels indicates a kind of objection, and they are exempt from that. The explanation is that the angels, at the time the address came to them, were in a general state, and Iblis was included among them, so the answer came from them in a general form. When Iblis separated from their collective through his refusal, the manifestation of his Iblis-nature, and his arrogance, the answer divided into two kinds: the kind of objection came from Iblis, and the kinds of obedience, glorification and sanctification came from the angels. The answer was divided into two parts, as the genus divides into two genera, and each answer suited the one from whom it came, and God knows best. End of his words.

This is a good interpretation, and it resembles His saying Exalted: ﴿And they said: Be Jews or Christians, you will be guided﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:135), because the whole statement is spoken, and the speakers are of two kinds, so each statement is returned to the one it suits.

It has also been said regarding His saying: ﴿while we glorify You with Your praise and sanctify You﴾ that it is an indication of the permissibility of self-praise before one who holds the authority of appointment, from one who seeks the office, when one is safe for oneself from injustice and partiality and sees in it a benefit. On this basis it was permissible for Joseph, upon our Prophet and upon him be peace, to ask for the office and to praise himself with what was in him, when he said: ﴿Set me over the treasuries of the land; indeed I am a guardian, knowing﴾ (Yusuf 12:55).

He said: ﴿innī aʿlamu﴾ ("I know") is the present tense of ʿalima, and ﴿mā﴾ in ﴿mā lā taʿlamūn﴾ is a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah) governed by it. It has been said, or it is an indefinite descriptive (nakirah mawṣūfah). It has been previously stated that we do not choose its being an indefinite descriptive. Makki ibn Abi Talib, al-Mahdawi and others permitted that aʿlam here be a noun in the sense of an active participle (ism bi-maʿnā fāʿil). If it is so, then mā may be in the genitive by annexation, and may be in the accusative position, because this noun does not take nunation. Some permitted that it be the elative (afʿal al-tafḍīl). The sense would be "more knowing than you," and mā would be in the accusative governed by a deleted verb indicated by aʿlam, meaning "I have known," and "I know what you do not know."

This view involves departing from the apparent sense and claiming two deletions. One is the deletion of the object of comparison, which is "than you." The other is the verb that governs the relative pronoun. As for what Makki permitted, it rests on two invalid premises. One is the claim that afʿal comes in the sense of fāʿil. This was held by Abu 'Ubayda among the earlier scholars, and the grammarians opposed him and rejected his statement, saying: afʿal is not free of the elative meaning.
