Although it is found in the speech of some later scholars that afʿal may be free of the elative meaning, they built upon that the permissibility of the question "Yusuf is the best of his brothers," to the point that one of them mentioned a disagreement concerning the permissibility of analogical extension of it, conceding that it is heard from the speech of the Arabs. He said: Its use bare, without min, stripped of the elative meaning and interpreted as an active participle or an attributive adjective, is regular according to Abu al-ʿAbbas, but the more correct view is restricting it to what is heard. End of his words. The second premise is that, even if the use of afʿal bare of the elative meaning is granted, it is not granted that it works as an active participle or not. Those who hold the existence of that do not hold that it governs as an active participle, except some of them, who permitted it. The correct view is what the earlier grammarians held, that afʿal is never free of the elative meaning, and there is no regard for the dissent of Abu 'Ubayda, because he was weak in grammar, nor for the dissent of some later scholars, because they are preceded by what is nearly a consensus of the earlier scholars. Even if we grant that this is heard from the Arabs, we do not grant its analogical extension, because the instances cited as evidence for it are extremely few, and even these have been given interpretations. Even if we grant analogical extension, we do not grant that it works as an active participle. How can we establish a universal rule when we have not heard from the Arabs anything of the individual constructions that cannot be memorized, such as: "This is a man afḍaru ʿUmaran," meaning "striking ʿUmar," or "This is a woman aqtalu Khalidan," meaning "killing Khalid," or "I passed by a man akṣā Zaydan jubbatan," meaning "clothing Zayd with a robe"? Is this anything other than the invention of constructions that the Arabs never spoke with any parallel of them? So that is impermissible. And how would one depart in the Book of God from the clear and manifest sense, namely that aʿlam is a present-tense verb, to this which is what you have seen in the science of grammar? I have lengthened in this question only because they follow that path in places of the Qur'an that will come, God willing, so it is fitting to avoid that. Also, the use of afʿal bare of the elative meaning is well known among some later scholars, so I have drawn attention to what is problematic in it, and the question's proofs are fully treated.

We mention in the science of grammar: ﴿mā lā taʿlamūn﴾ ("what you do not know"). That by which God praised Himself, from the knowledge that surpasses them, includes His knowledge of what is in the soul of Iblis together with his rebellion and disobedience. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Suddi, from their shaykhs. Or His knowledge that from that caliph there will be prophets and righteous ones, as Qatada said. Or His knowledge of who will fill Hell from the jinn and mankind, as Ibn Zayd said. Or His knowledge of the ends of matters: He will test one whom you think to be obedient, and the test will lead him to disobedience; and one whom you think to be disobedient, and the test will lead him to obedience, so he will obey. This was said by al-Zajjaj. Or His knowledge of the outward and inward aspects of matters, the manifest and the subtle, the immediate and the distant, the good and the corrupt, according to the differing states and times, with true knowledge, while you do not know that. Or His knowledge without acquisition, without reflection, without contemplation and without thought, while you do not know the known things in this manner. Or His knowledge that Iblis is with them. Or His knowledge of your self-magnification in glorifying and sanctifying.

What the apparent wording indicates is that when they spoke the preceding sentence, "Will You place in it...?", He informed them that He knows what they do not know. He left vague in His information the things He knows and they do not. If that is so, then His information that He will place a khalifah in the earth requires their submission to Him and their returning to Him regarding what He wishes to do, and their contentment with that, because His knowledge encompasses what no knower's knowledge encompasses, may He be exalted and mighty. It is best that this vague element be explained by what He Exalted reported of it in His saying: ﴿Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth?﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:33), and so on.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 31:

﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾: When Exalted God had informed the angels, in summary, of the wisdom behind creating Adam and his descendants, He wanted to make it detailed. So He explained to them the excellence of Adam that had not been known to them, by teaching him the names, in order to show his excellence and their deficiency in knowledge compared with him. Thus the summary answer was confirmed by the demonstration of superiority. It is necessary to assume an omitted sentence before this, because through it the meaning is complete and this conjunction (ʿaṭf) is valid. That sentence is: "So He placed a successor (khalifah) on the earth." Since the word khalifah was omitted along with the assumed sentence, He brought it out in His words "﴿And He taught Adam﴾," explicitly naming it and highlighting it by mentioning it by name. Whoever claimed that "﴿And He taught Adam﴾" is conjoined to His saying "﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, Indeed I am placing﴾" [Al-Baqarah: 30] is far from the truth. Was the teaching by God's speaking to him in the heavens, as He spoke to Musa on the earth, or through an angel, or through inspiration? There are opinions, the most evident of which is that the Creator, Exalted is He, is the Teacher, neither through an intermediary nor through inspiration.

Al-Yamani and Yazid al-Yazidi read ﴿And He taught Adam﴾ in the passive voice (mabni lil-maf'ul), with the agent omitted because it is known, and the doubling (tadʿif) in ʿullima is for transitivity (taʿdiyah), since before doubling it was transitive to one object, and by doubling it became transitive to two. Transitivity by doubling is not analogical; it is restricted to what has been heard. This holds whether the verb before doubling was intransitive or transitive, such as ʿalima, which is transitive to one object. As for a verb that is already transitive to two, nothing is transmitted from the Arabs of making it transitive to three by doubling. Al-Qasim ibn Ali al-Hariri erred in his claim in his commentary on al-Mulhah that ʿalima would be derived from ʿalima, which is transitive to two, so that by doubling it becomes transitive to three; this is not preserved in their speech.

Some grammarians went to the view that transitivity by doubling is analogical. Imam Abu al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Rabi' said in his book (Kitab al-Talkhis), of his composition: The apparent position of Sibawayh is that the transfer by doubling is heard in both transitive and intransitive verbs. As for what He taught him, there are opinions: the names of all created things, as said by Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and Qatadah; or the names of what has been and what will be until the Day of Resurrection, attributed to Ibn Abbas, and this is close to the first; or all languages, then He spoke to each of his sons in a language, and they dispersed into the lands, and each group was specialized in a language or a single word from which all languages branched; or only the names of the stars, said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah; or only the names of the angels, said by al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham; or the names of his descendants, said by al-Rabi' ibn Zayd; or the names of his descendants and the angels, said by al-Tabari, who also preferred it; or the names of the kinds He created, teaching him that this one's name is horse, this one's name is camel, this one's name is so-and-so, and this one's name is so-and-so, and teaching him their states and what relates to them of religious and worldly benefits, which was preferred by al-Zamakhshari; or the names of what He created on the earth, said by Ibn Qutaybah; or the names in one language, then the convention arose among his descendants in other languages; or He taught him everything, even something like Sibawayh, said by Abu Ali al-Farisi; or the names of God, Exalted and Majestic, said by al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi; or names from His stored names, through which he knew all the names, said by al-Jirri; or designations. The meaning of this is that He taught him to name things, and the meaning is not that He taught him the names, because designation is other than the name; this is said by the majority.

As for the manner of God's teaching Adam, did He present the named things to him or describe them to him without presenting them? There are two views. Some of our contemporaries said: The preferred view is the names of his descendants, and He made known to him the obedient and the disobedient, so that he would know the angels by their names and deeds, in response to their saying: "﴿Will You place in it one who causes corruption in it?﴾" [Al-Baqarah: 30]. The names, all of them: this may refer to the names of the named things, so the genitive (muḍāf ilayh) was omitted because the word "names" indicates it. Al-Zamakhshari said: The lam is a substitute for it, like His saying: "﴿and the head glistens with white hair﴾" [Maryam: 4]. End of quote.

It has already been mentioned to us that the lam being a substitute for the annexed noun is not the position of the Basrans. It is possible that the assumed reading is "the designations of the names," so the annexed noun was omitted and the annexed-to noun took its place. The first is preferred, namely that the teaching is connected to the names, just as the informing is connected to them in His saying: "﴿Inform Me of the names of these﴾," and in the verse after it, and He did not say: "Inform Me about these," nor "Inform them about them." The second is preferred by His saying, "then He presented them," if it is taken in its apparent sense, because names are not gathered in this way. This indicates that the pronoun refers to the named things, as in His saying, Exalted is He: "﴿or like darknesses in a deep sea, covered by a wave﴾" [Al-Nur: 40]. The assumed reading is: "or like one with darknesses," so the pronoun in "yaghshāhu" refers to the omitted "dhū," which stands in place of "darknesses" in grammatical function. What the apparent wording indicates is that God taught Adam the names, and did not specify particular names for us; rather, His saying "(all of them)" indicates totality, and the wisdom is achieved by teaching the names even if their named things are not known. It is possible that by "names" He means the named things, so this is the use of a word to mean its referent.

﴿Then He presented them﴾: "Then" (thumma) is a particle of delay and interval. He taught Adam, then gave him respite from that time until He said: "﴿Inform them of their names﴾" [Al-Baqarah: 33], so that this would be firmly established in his heart and the known would be realized. Then He informed him of what he had realized and what he had become certain of. As for the angels, He said to them, in a manner of immediate sequence without any interval, "﴿Inform Me﴾." Since no prior instruction had been given to them, they did not inform. Since teaching had preceded for Adam, he answered, informed and spoke, to show God's earlier care for him, Glorified is He. "Presented them": it means created them, or presented them to Him, said by Ibn Masʿud; or formed them for the hearts of the angels; or presented them while they were like tiny ants; or presented the names, said by Ibn Abbas, and in this the plural is gathered with the word "them." The apparent meaning is that the accusative pronoun in "ʿaradahum" refers to the named things, and its apparent sense is that it is for rational beings, so the intended meaning of the names would then be the names of rational beings; or the group includes non-rational beings and the rational were given precedence. Ubayy read "thumma ʿaradahā" (with the feminine pronoun). Abdullah read "thumma ʿaradahunna," and the pronoun refers to the names, so the names would be what is presented, or the assumed reading is "their named things," so what is presented is the named things and not the names.

﴿to the angels﴾: Its apparent sense is generality. It was said: this is intended; and it was said: the angels meant are those who were with Iblis on the earth. "(Then He said)": the fa' is for sequence, and no interval occurred between the presentation and the command in which a deliberation or thought could take place, and this is most fitting for the absence of an annexed sentence.

﴿Inform Me﴾: this is a command of incapacitation (taʿjiz), not of obligation (taklif). Al-A'mash read "anbūnī" without hamzah. It has been cited, from His saying "Inform Me," as evidence for the permissibility of imposing what cannot be borne; but this is weak evidence, because it is by way of rebuke, and this is indicated by His saying: "﴿if you are truthful﴾" [Al-Baqarah: 23].

﴿of the names of these﴾: its apparent sense is the presence of persons at the time of presentation to the angels. Whoever said that what was presented was only names took the demonstrative to refer to the persons of the names, which are absent, since what is part of them has come present by means of something, and that is their names; and it is as if He said to them, for each name, "for which person is this name?" This has remoteness and artificiality, and departure from the apparent sense without a motivating reason.

﴿if you are truthful﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 23]: the conditional's answer is omitted, its assumed form being "then inform Me," indicated by the earlier "Inform Me," and the earlier "Inform Me" is not itself the answer. This is the position of Sibawayh and the majority of the Basrans. The Kufans, Abu Zayd and Abu al-Abbas disagreed, claiming that the answer of the conditional is the one that precedes it in cases like this; this is the verified transmission. Al-Mahdawi erred, and Ibn Atiyyah followed him, in claiming that the answer of the conditional is omitted according to al-Mubarrad, with the assumed reading "then inform Me," unless they had both seen another transmission from al-Mubarrad, strange and contrary to the well-known report of what people have related; that is possible. Likewise Ibn Atiyyah and others erred, claiming that Sibawayh's position is the placing of the answer before the condition, and that His saying "Inform Me," which precedes, is the answer. Here "truthful" means "correct," i.e., "if you are correct," just as falsehood is applied to error, so truthfulness is also applied to correctness. As for the object of truthfulness here, there are opinions: "if you are truthful" means: "I do not create a creature except that you are better than it"; or "if you are truthful" means: "you are more knowledgeable than it," because it occurred in their souls that they were more knowledgeable than others; or in what you claimed, that My successors will cause corruption on the earth; or in what occurred in your minds, that I do not create a creature except that you would be more excellent than it; or in the matters of those whom I will appoint after you; or "I, if I appoint you as successors upon it, you will glorify Me and sanctify Me, and if I appoint others upon it, they will disobey Me"; or in your saying that there is nothing with which the creation worships except that you are fit for it and perform it; this was said by Ibn Masʿud and Ibn Abbas; or in that there is information, and the answer to the question is with the names. It was narrated that when God created Adam, the angels said: "Our Lord creates whatever He wills; He will not create a creature more knowledgeable than us, nor more honored by Him." So He wanted to show them, from Adam's knowledge and honor, the opposite of what they supposed. They said: because of His saying "if you are truthful," it was not permissible for them to exercise independent judgment (ijtihad); for if He had not restricted it by truthfulness, which is correctness, then independent judgment would have been permitted, just as it was permitted for the one to whom it was said: "How long did you remain?" [Al-Baqarah: 259], and He did not condition correctness upon him, so he was not wrong and was not blamed. Whoever claimed that truthfulness here is the opposite of ordinary falsehood, on account of the angels' infallibility, was far from the truth, just as whoever made "in" (in) mean "when" (idh), removing it from the conditional to the temporal, was far from the truth. When two hamzahs with kasra meet from two words, like "hāʾulāʾ in kuntum" (hā'ulā' in kuntum), Warsh and Qanbul change the second into a long yāʾ; except that Warsh, in "hāʾulāʾ in kuntum" and "ʿalā al-bighāʾ in aradna" [Al-Nur: 33], makes the yāʾ kasra; Qalun and al-Bazzi soften the first and realize the second. Two in "bi-l-suʾ illā" [Yusuf: 53] have several forms: the first, which is the established principle for them both; the second, replacing the first hamzah with a kasra waw and merging the preceding sakin waw into it, and realizing the second; the third, replacing the first hamzah with yāʾ, as in "bi-l-suyy"; the fourth, replacing it with waw without merging, as in "al-suww." Abu Amr read by deleting the first; the Kufans and Ibn Amir read by realizing both hamzahs.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 32:**

﴿They said: "Glory be to You! We have no knowledge except what You have taught us."﴾: That is, [it means] Your exaltation (*tanzih*, declaring God free of imperfection) above claim and above objection. It has been said that its meaning is an exaltation of You after an exaltation. Its wording is in the dual form, but the meaning is as they said in *labbayka* (a response of "here I am" to God), whose meaning is a response after a response. This is a strange view, for it entails that its singular would be *subhan*, that it would not be in the accusative but in the nominative, that the nun was not dropped for the annexation, and that it has committed itself to a fixed vowel (*fath*). The *kaf* in *subhanaka* is a direct object that has been annexed to it. Some have permitted it to be the subject, because the meaning is "You have exalted Yourself." We have already mentioned, when we discussed the individual words, that it is in the accusative on the basis of a verbal sense (*ma'na al-masdar*), with a verb of its own meaning that must be omitted.

Al-Kisa'i (d. 189 AH) claimed that it is an annexed vocative (*munada mudaf*). This is refuted by the fact that it is not attested with the vocative particle preceding it; if it were a vocative, the vocative particle would be permitted before it, and this has not been transmitted to us. When God asked the angels, and they had no knowledge of the answer, and they had already said previously: ﴿Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], they wished to answer with their lack of knowledge, except for what He had taught them. So they put the exaltation of God before the answer, as an apology and as courtesy in the reply, and as an indication that what had proceeded from them before is erased by this exaltation of God the Exalted. So they said: "Glory be to You," and then answered with the negation of knowledge by means of *la*, with which the indefinite noun is built, so that every single kind of knowledge is comprehensively negated. Then they made an exception from this for what He, the Exalted, had taught them, saying: ﴿except what You have taught us﴾. This is the utmost in abandoning claim and in complete submission to the First Teacher, God the Exalted.

Abu Uthman al-Maghribi said: "The trials of creation are only due to claims. Do you not see that when the angels said: ﴿while we glorify You with Your praise﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], how they were returned to ignorance until they said: 'We have no knowledge'?" The meaning of this statement has also been related from Ja'far al-Sadiq. The predicate of *la* ("no") is in the prepositional phrase. The discussion of "(there is no doubt in it)" has already preceded us, and "no knowledge" is similar to it, so we dispense with repeating it. The relative pronoun *ma* may be in the accusative position as an exception, but the better view is that it is in the nominative position as a substitute (*badal*). Ibn Atiyya related from al-Zamakhshari (al-Zahrawi, in the text) that the position of *ma* in their statement "what You have taught us" is accusative, governed by *'allamtana* ("You taught us"). This is not sensible, for *ma* is a relative pronoun, its relative clause is "You taught us," and a relative clause does not govern the relative pronoun. However, a possible reading is strained: that it is a disjunctive exception (*istithna' munqati'*), so that the meaning of *illa* is "but," according to the principle established for disjunctive exceptions. In that case *ma* would be a conditional particle in the accusative governed by *'allamtana*, and the answer would be omitted, as if they had first negated all the sciences and then corrected themselves, saying that in the future whatever He teaches them, they will know. This would be more eloquent in abandoning claim, since they erased themselves from all sciences and negated all of them, and did not make an exception for something earlier and past that they were adorned with; rather they went to pure ignorance and disavowal of every knowledge. This view contradicts what has been related: that He, the Exalted, was the most knowing of them, or that they knew by inspection of the Preserved Tablet that there would be on earth one who would cause corruption and shed blood. If this is established, then they would have gone to extremes in negating every knowledge from themselves, and made this specific knowledge like what does not exist. Whoever believes that the angels are not infallible would consider their statement "we have no knowledge" a repentance. Whoever believes in their infallibility would say: they said that in the manner of acknowledging incapacity and submitting that they know only what they have been taught; or they said ﴿Will You place therein﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30] etc., because He had informed them of that. As for the names, how would they know them, since He had not informed them of that? When they negated knowledge from themselves, they affirmed it for God the Exalted in His most perfect attributes, with the emphasis of the intensive form. Then they followed the attribute of knowledge with the attribute of wisdom, because His saying had preceded: ﴿Indeed I will make upon the earth a vicegerent﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. When there proceeded from this one made a vicegerent what proceeded of the excellence of knowledge, the wisdom in His saying "and He made him a vicegerent" became clear to them.

Look at the excellence of this answer: how they put the exaltation of God before it, then acknowledged ignorance, then attributed to God knowledge and wisdom. The placing of the attribute of knowledge before the attribute of wisdom is appropriate, because it is adjacent to it in His saying: "(and He taught)," ﴿Inform Me﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31], "(we have no knowledge)." The thing by which Adam was distinguished and given excellence is precisely this, so it is appropriate to mention it adjacent to it. Also, wisdom is only effects and things arising from it. For this reason, most of what has come in the Qur'an places the attribute of knowledge before the attribute of wisdom. Also, so that the end of their speech would differ from its beginning, to show their retraction from their statement: ﴿Will You place therein﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. On the view that *al-Hakim* is one who possesses wisdom, *al-Hakim* is an attribute of essence (*sifat dhat*); on the view that it means one who perfects His making, it is an attribute of act (*sifat fi'l*).

As for *anta* ("You"): it may be an emphasis of the pronoun, so it is in the accusative position, or a subject (*mubtada'*), so it is in the nominative position, with *al-'Alim* as its predicate (*khabar*); or it may be a separating pronoun (*fasl*), in which case it has no place in the grammatical structure according to the Basran grammarians, but has a place in the grammatical structure according to the Kufan grammarians. According to al-Farra', its position follows the noun before it; according to al-Kisa'i, it follows the noun after it. The best view is that *al-'Alim al-Hakim* should be taken in a general sense. Some have restricted it, saying: the All-Knowing of what You commanded and forbade, the All-Wise in what You decreed and decided. Another said: the All-Knowing of the secret and the public, and the All-Wise in what He does; and this is close to the first.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) on surah 2, verse 33 (part 1 of 2):

﴿He said, "O Adam, inform them of their names."﴾ He called Adam by his proper name, and this is Allah's practice with His prophets. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿O Noah, descend with peace from Us﴾ (Hud 48); ﴿O Noah, he is not of your family﴾ (Hud 46); ﴿O Abraham﴾ (al-Saffat 104); ﴿You have fulfilled the vision﴾ (al-Saffat 105); ﴿O Moses, indeed I am Allah﴾ (al-Qasas 30); ﴿O Jesus, son of Mary, remember My blessing upon you﴾ (al-Ma'idah 110). He called our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) and the rest of the prophets by their noble attributes of messengership and prophethood, saying: (O Messenger) and (O Prophet). So observe the difference between this call and that call.

The pronoun in ﴿inform them﴾ refers to the angels, and the pronoun in ﴿of their names﴾ refers to those presented (the things named), according to the earlier difference of opinion.

Al-Qushayri said: Among the signs of the special care shown to Adam, peace be upon him, is that when he said to the angels, "Inform me," awe of the address overtook them, and it took them away from themselves, especially when he demanded that they inform him of what their knowledge did not encompass. Since the matter concerned Adam, He returned the informing to them, saying: ﴿inform them of their names﴾. Adam's address to the angels did not require total absorption in awe. When Adam, peace be upon him, informed them of the names of things whose knowledge fell short of them, his superiority over them became manifest, and so He said: ﴿Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens﴾, meaning what the knowledge of creation falls short of, ﴿and I know what you disclose of acts of obedience and what you conceal of the belief in your superiority over Adam﴾. End of al-Qushayri's words.

When a sentence introduced by the verb of saying is arranged in meaning with what precedes it, the more correct usage in the Arabic language is that no particle of sequence is used in it, relying on the meaning-based sequence. Examples include [p. 149] the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They said, "Will You place in it..."﴾ (al-Baqarah 30), after which comes ﴿He said, "Indeed I know..."﴾ (al-Baqarah 30); and like: ﴿They said, "Glory be to You"﴾ (al-Baqarah 32), ﴿He said, "O Adam, inform them"﴾; and like: ﴿He said, "I will surely kill you." He said, "Allah only accepts from the righteous"﴾ (al-Ma'idah 27); ﴿He said, "How will Allah bring this to life?"﴾ (al-Baqarah 259); ﴿He said, "How long have you remained?" He said, "I remained a day or part of a day"﴾ (al-Baqarah 259); ﴿He said, "Rather, you remained a hundred years"﴾ (al-Baqarah 259); ﴿He said, "Have you not believed?" He said, "Yes, but so that my heart may be assured"﴾ (al-Baqarah 260); ﴿He said, "Take four birds"﴾ (al-Baqarah 260). In Surah al-Shu'ara' there are twenty such occurrences in the story of Moses, upon our Prophet and upon him be the best of blessings and peace, concerning his sending to Pharaoh and his dialogue with him, and the dialogue with the magicians, to the end of the story, fewer than three; of them, two are answers and one is like an answer. Similar usage in the Qur'an is abundant.

The majority of reciters read ﴿أَنْبِئْهُمْ﴾ (anbi'hum) with a hamzah and a damma on the ha', and this is the original form, just as you say: akrimhum. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿anbi'him﴾ with a hamzah and a kasra on the ha'. Its basis is that he made the vowel of the ha' follow the vowel of the ba', and did not count the hamzah, because it is quiescent, so it is a barrier that is not solid. It is also read: anbihim, with the hamzah replaced and a kasra on the ha'. Al-Hasan, al-A'raj and Ibn Kathir, through the transmission of al-Qawwas, read: anbihim, on the pattern of a'tihim. Ibn Jinni said: this is by replacing the hamzah with a ya', as if you say anbaytu, like a'taytu. He said: this is weak in the language, because it is a substitution, not a lightening. Substitution, in our view, is not permitted except in poetic necessity. End of Abu al-Fath's words (Ibn Jinni). What he mentioned, that it is not permitted except in poetic necessity, is not correct.

Al-Akhfash related in *al-Awsat*: the Arabs change the hamzah in the position of the lam into a ya', so they say qurayt, ukhtayt and tawaddayt. He said: they sometimes change it into a waw, which is rare, as in rafawtu; the preferred form is rafa'tu, and I have not heard rafaytu. End of al-Akhfash's words. This shows that it is not one of the poetic licences, as Abu al-Fath mentioned, and it is the case in the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿anbi'hum bi-asma'ihim﴾.

As for His saying ﴿فَلَمَّا أَنْبَأَهُمْ بِأَسْمَائِهِمْ﴾ (so when he informed them of their names): it is a deleted sentence; the estimate is: so he informed them of them; when he informed them, the sentence was omitted because the meaning is understood. In His saying ﴿Inform Me﴾ (al-Baqarah 31), then ﴿when he informed them﴾, there is an indication that Allah informed the angels that He had made Adam know about them what He had not made them know about him, because they saw him before the breathing of the spirit as a shaped figure, and so they did not know what he was. It also shows that He raised Adam's rank in their sight, since He taught Adam what He did not teach them, and that He placed him in the position of one who gives benefit and teaches, and placed them in the position of those who benefit from him. For He commanded him to teach them the names of those He presented to them, and He tested them with the lack of courtesy in their saying: ﴿Will You place in it...﴾ (al-Baqarah 30). True obedience is that they should be in a state where they do not know the wisdom of what they were commanded, and do not know the benefit or harm of that command, just as they are when they know and are aware of it. The compliance and submission, without wonder or questioning, was more fitting to their station, because of the purity of their essences and the perfection of their attributes.

In a book by one of our contemporaries, the Mu'tazilites said: a sign (mu'jizah), indicating his prophethood at that time, appeared from Adam, peace be upon him, in his knowledge of the names. The most likely view is that he was sent to Eve. It is not far-fetched that he was also sent to those whom the challenge was directed at, namely the angels, because all of them, although they were messengers, it is permissible for a messenger to be sent to a messenger, like Abraham's being sent to Lot, peace be upon him. They argued by his being a breach of the custom. One may say: the attainment of knowledge of the language by the one whom Allah taught, and its non-attainment by the one who was not taught, is not a breach of the custom. Furthermore, as for the angels: either they knew the assignment of those names to the things named, in which case there is no excellence at first, so how did they know his correctness in that? The answer is in two respects. One: perhaps each kind among them had a language, then all of them gathered and each kind recognised his correctness in that language, except that they, as a whole, were unable to know all of it. Two: Allah made them know the proof of his truthfulness. Why should it not be from the category of *karamat* (wondrous gifts) or from the category of *irhas* (prophetic foreshadowing)?

Those who said he was not a prophet argued with several points. First: the disobedience proceeded from him afterwards, and that is not permissible for a prophet. Second: if he had been sent, he would have been sent to someone, since the purpose of sending is conveying the message; this cannot be the angels, because they are superior; nor Eve, because she is addressed directly by His saying ﴿and do not approach﴾; nor the jinn, because they were not in heaven. Third: His saying ﴿Then He chose him﴾ (Ta-Ha 122), which indicates that the choosing took place after the lapse, while a prophet must be chosen at the time he is a prophet.

﴿He said, "Did I not tell you..."﴾: the answer to (when), and the difference has already been mentioned concerning (lamma) which requires an answer: is it a particle or an adverb? We preferred the first and mentioned that it is the view of Sibawayh. And (did I not say) is a confirmation, since when the interrogative hamzah enters a negation, the speech in many places is a confirmation, as in the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ (al-A'raf 172); ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ (al-Sharh 1); ﴿Did We not raise you among us as a child?﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 18). For this reason it is permissible to conjoin it to an affirmative sentence, as in: ﴿and We lifted﴾ (al-Sharh 2), ﴿and you remained﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 18). And in it is a reminder to them through the address and a stirring of them to hear what is said, as in His saying: ﴿Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?﴾ (al-Kahf 75), where in the second case He alerted him by address. It has already been mentioned that the lam in sayings like "I told you" or "to Zayd" is for conveying (tabligh), and that is one of the meanings we mentioned for it.

(Indeed I know): the ya' of the speaker, when the letter before it is vowelled, and it meets a hamzah of cutting (hamzat al-qat') with a fatha, two possibilities are permitted: vowelling it and making it quiescent. It was read in both ways among the Seven, with some difference among them regarding part of this, and the details are mentioned in the books of readings. The Seven read it as quiescent by consensus in: ﴿tafitni alla﴾ (al-Tawbah 49), ﴿arini anzur﴾ (al-A'raf 143), ﴿fattabi'ni ahdika﴾ (Maryam 43), ﴿wa tarhamni akun﴾ (Hud 47). No reason appears from any of their differences or agreements except following the transmission. The difference mentioned earlier regarding (a'lamu), whether it is in the accusative or the genitive, is permitted here too, and its clarification has already been given there, so we do not repeat it here.

Ibn 'Atiyya related from al-Mahdawi the following text: al-Mahdawi said: It is permissible that his saying (a'lamu) be a noun with the meaning of the superlative in knowledge, so that (ma) is in the position of the genitive by annexation. Ibn 'Atiyya said: If the first is estimated as a noun, then a verb must be assumed to govern the object *ghayb*, its estimate being: "Indeed I know more than everyone knows the unseen," and its being a present-tense verb in both places is more concise and more eloquent. End of quotation. What Ibn 'Atiyya transmitted from al-Mahdawi is an error. Al-Mahdawi, in his exegesis, said the following: ﴿and I know what you disclose﴾: (ma) may be in the accusative governed by (a'lamu) as a verb; it may be with the meaning of (ʿalim) (knowing); or (ma) may be in the genitive by annexation; and the tanwin may be estimated on (a'lamu) if you estimate it with the meaning of (ʿalim) and make (ma) its object, so that it means "pilgrims to the House of Allah" (ḥawājj bayt Allah). End of quotation. You see that he did not hold that af'al is a superlative, nor that (ma) could be in the genitive, and the accusative of (ma) is not permitted when af'al is a noun except where it has the meaning of the active participle (fa'il), not the superlative. It is impossible to say what Ibn 'Atiyya transmitted from al-Mahdawi, that (a'lam) may be a superlative and that (ma) may be governed in the genitive by annexation at all.

﴿the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾: the discussion of these three words has already been given. The meaning of the unseen here is disputed. It has been said: the unseen of the heavens is Adam's and Eve's eating from the tree, because it was the first disobedience to occur in heaven; and the unseen of the earth is Cain's killing of Abel, because it was the first disobedience to occur on earth. It has been said: the unseen of the heavens is what He decreed of the affairs of His creation, and the unseen of the earth is what they did in it after the decree. It has been said: the unseen of the heavens is what was hidden from His closest angels and the bearers of His Throne, of the secrets of the Supreme Kingdom that He reserved for Himself, and the unseen of the earth is what He concealed from His prophets and chosen servants of the secrets of His Lower Kingdom and the matters of the Hereafter and this world.

﴿and I know what you disclose and what you were concealing﴾. Ali, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them all, said: (what you disclose): the pronoun refers to the angels, and (what you were concealing) means Iblis. This is then an address in the plural, while one individual is meant, as in ﴿Indeed those who call out to you﴾ (al-Hujurat 4). It is reported that Iblis passed by the body of Adam between Mecca and al-Ta'if before the spirit was breathed into it, and said: "This was not created for nothing." Then he entered through its mouth and came out through its rear, and said: "It is a creature that cannot hold itself, for it is hollow." Then he said to the angels who were with him: "Tell me, if this one is preferred over you and you are commanded to obey him, what will you do?" They said: "We shall obey Allah." Iblis said to himself: "By Allah, if I am given power over him, I will surely destroy him, and if he is given power over me, I will surely disobey him." So this is His saying: ﴿and I know what you disclose﴾, and so on, meaning: from the saying of the angels and the concealment of Iblis. Al-Hasan and Qatada said: what they disclosed is their saying: ﴿Will You place in it...﴾, and what they concealed is their saying: "Allah will not create anyone more honoured by Him than us." It has also been said: what they disclosed is their saying: ﴿Will You place in it...﴾, and what they concealed is what they hid of obedience to Allah and prostration to Adam. It has also been said: what they disclosed is the acknowledgement of incapacity, and what they concealed is their dislike of Adam, peace be upon him, being made a successor.

And it was said: it is general, covering what they manifested and what they concealed of all their affairs, and this is the apparent meaning. He (Allah) made the verb prominent in His saying "and I know" so that its complement would be a clause intended in itself by the governing verb, and so its object would not be subsumed under the first clause. This indicates emphasis on the announcement, since it was made a separate statement with a governing verb other than the first governing verb. The conjunction of His saying ﴿and what you used to conceal﴾ is from the mode of progression (taraqqi) in the announcement, because the knowledge of God, exalted is He, is one, with no variation in it with respect to any of the things known, whether openly or secretly. The joining of "what" (ma) with "you used to conceal" (kuntum taktumun) indicates that the concealing took place in the past. The meaning is not that they concealed from God, for the angels are more knowing of God and more aware of Him, so they would not conceal anything from God. Rather, the meaning is that something occurred to their souls which some of them did not disclose to others, nor did they make Him aware of it. And if the one referred to is Iblis, then it has already been mentioned that he said within himself what we related, and it was said about him, so he concealed that from the angels. The end of this verse includes, from the science of rhetoric (ilm al-badi'), the antithesis (tibaq), which is His saying: ﴿what you manifest and what you used to conceal﴾.

His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate yourselves to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis. He refused and was arrogant, and he was among the disbelievers.﴾

*Sujud* (prostration) means humbling oneself and submitting. Ibn al-Sikkit said it means inclining. Some said: *sajada* means he placed his forehead on the ground, and *asjada* means he inclined his head and bowed. The poet said:

*You see the sand-hills in it prostrating to the hooves.*

He means that the hooves trample the sand-hills, so he made the sand-hills' being impressed by the hooves a metaphorical prostration. Another said:

*As a Christian woman prostrated, not having been made a hanif.*

Another said:

*The prostration of the Christians to their rabbis.*

He means bowing.

*Iblis* is a non-Arabic proper name, and it is not declined because of foreignness and being a proper noun. Al-Zajjaj said its pattern is *fi'lil*. Abu 'Ubayda and others went too far in claiming that it is derived from *al-iblas*, which means distancing from good, and on this view its pattern would be *if'il*. This is because it is established in the science of morphology (*al-tasrif*) that Arabic derivation does not apply to non-Arabic names. Whoever held that it is derived, and sought to excuse its being undeclined, said that it has no parallel among names. This was refuted with *ighrid*, *izmil*, *ikhrit*, *ijfil*, *i'lit*, *is'lit*, *ihlil*, *iklil* and *ihrid*. It has also been said that it was made similar to non-Arabic names, so it is undeclined because of being a proper noun and a resemblance to foreignness. The resemblance to foreignness is that although it is derived from *al-iblas*, no one among the Arabs was named with it, so it became specific to the one whom God named with it. It is thus like a sign in their language, and it is a proper noun that was coined. It has been related that its derivation from *al-iblas* is from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi, but I do not think this is sound.

*Al-iba'* (refusal) means declining. The poet said:

*As for your saying, "We have refused," the worst of noble qualities is refusal.*

The verb from it is *aba ya'ba*. Since its present tense came in the pattern *yaf'alu* with an open 'ayn, which is not analogical, it was treated as if it were the present of *fa'ila* with a kasra on the 'ayn. So they said *yi'bi*, with a kasra on the present-tense prefix. It has also been heard as *abiya* with a kasra on the 'ayn, so *ya'bi* would be analogical in this dialect, and the form with an open 'ayn matches this dialect. Abu al-Qasim al-Sa'di claimed that *aba ya'ba* with an open 'ayn is undisputed, but this is not correct, for the author of *al-Muhkam* reported *abiya* with a kasra on the 'ayn. The pattern *yaf'alu* occurs in fourteen verbs whose past tense is *fa'ala*, and neither their 'ayn nor their lam is a guttural letter. In some of them, *fa'ila* with a kasra on the 'ayn has also been heard, and in some of their present tenses, *yaf'ilu* and *yaf'ulu* with a kasra and a damma on the 'ayn have also been heard. The morphologists mention these.

*Al-istikbar* and *al-takabbur* (arrogance): this is one of the forms in which *istaf'ala* carries the meaning of *tafa''ala*. It is one of the twelve meanings for which *istaf'ala* is used, which are mentioned in the explanation of (*nasta'in*).

﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate yourselves to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis. He refused and was arrogant, and he was among the disbelievers.﴾ No authentic occasion of revelation (*sabab nuzul*) has been transmitted for this verse. Its connection with what precedes it is that when God honoured Adam with the excellence of knowledge and made him a teacher to the angels, who were learning from him, along with their earlier statement: ﴿Will You place in it one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], God willed to honour this one whom He had appointed as successor by having His angels prostrate to him, in order to show through that the excellence of knowledge over the excellence of worship. Al-Tabari said: the story of Iblis is a reproach to those who resemble him among the children of Adam, namely the Jews, who disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ) while knowing his prophethood, and despite the long-standing blessings of God upon them and upon their forebears.

*Idh* is an adverb of time. As has been said before, it was said to be superfluous. It was also said that the governing element in it is an implied verb, which they indicate as "remember." It was said that it is conjoined to what comes before it, namely his saying: (*And when your Lord said*). The first view is weakened because nouns are not made superfluous. The second is weakened because its adverbial nature is necessary. The third is weakened because the two times differ, so it is impossible for the governing element we chose in the first *idh* to govern this second *idh*. It was said that the governing element in it is *aba*. I think it is also possible that the governing element in *idh* is an omitted one indicated by his saying (*fa-sajadu*), its implied meaning being: they submitted and obeyed, because prostration was a result of submission to the command.

In his saying (*qulna*, "We said") there is an *iltifat*, which is one of the kinds of *badi'* (rhetorical embellishment). This is because the verse before this one had reported about God in the form of the third person absent, then it moved to the first person of the speaker and used *nā*, which indicates glorification and the exaltedness of power. Its treatment as plural is because of the multiplicity of His praiseworthy attributes and His abundant gifts.

The wisdom of this *iltifat*, and that it is in the form of the plural of majesty in which He speaks of Himself, is that the command to the angels to prostrate came from Him, and it was obligatory for them to comply. So it was fitting for the command to be at the greatest degree of exaltedness, because whenever it is so, it is more likely to make the one commanded perform what he is commanded without delay or interpretation, since his mind is occupied with what proceeds from the Exalted. There are parallels to this in the Qur'an, among them: ﴿And We said, "O Adam, dwell﴾ [al-Baqarah: 35], ﴿And We said, "Descend﴾ [al-Baqarah: 36], ﴿We said, "O fire, be cool"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 69], ﴿And We said after him to the Children of Israel, "Dwell in the land"﴾ [al-Isra': 104], ﴿And We said to them, "Enter the gate"﴾ [al-Nisa': 154], ﴿And We said to them, "Do not transgress"﴾ [al-Nisa': 154]. So you see how this command and this prohibition were preceded by the verb ascribed to the speaker who glorifies Himself, because the commander demands superiority over the one commanded, so the one commanded perceives the attribute of greatness, and there is none greater than God, exalted is He.

As for those commanded to prostrate, al-Suddi said: most of the angels. Ibn 'Abbas said: the angels who govern on earth.

The majority read *lil-mala'ikati* with a kasra on the *ta'*. Abu Ja'far Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa' and Sulayman ibn Mihran read it with a damma on the *ta'*, in *ittiba'* (assimilation) to the vowel of the *jim*, and it is reported that this is the dialect of the Azd Shanu'a. Al-Zajjaj said: this is an error on the part of Abu Ja'far. Al-Farisi said: this is a mistake. Ibn Jinni said: because the kasra of the *ta'* is an *i'rab* vowel (a grammatical case vowel). This reading is permissible only when the letter before the hamza is a sound, quiescent consonant, as in ﴿and she said, "Come out"﴾ [Yusuf: 31]. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is not permissible to eliminate the *i'rab* vowel by the vowel of assimilation except in a weak dialect, such as their saying: (*al-hamdu lillah*). End of his words. Since this is in a weak dialect, and it has been reported that it is the dialect of the Azd Shanu'a, the reader who uses it should not be called mistaken or accused of error. The reader of it is Abu Ja'far, one of the famous readers who took the Qur'an by oral transmission from 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas and other Companions, and he was the teacher of Nafi' ibn Abi Nu'aym, one of the Seven Readers. He justified the damma on the *ta'* by its resemblance to the *alif al-wasl* (the connecting alif). The point of resemblance is that the hamza falls away in continuous recitation (*al-darj*) because it is not an original letter, and the *ta'* in *al-mala'ika* also falls away, because it is not original. Do you not see that they said *al-mala'ik*? It was also said: it was given a damma because the Arabs dislike a damma after a kasra because of its heaviness.

*(Uskudu)* is an imperative. This form requires the demand that the act be performed at an unspecified future time, and it does not indicate immediacy by its form. This is the doctrine of al-Shafi'i and al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Tayyib, and al-Ghazali and al-Razi chose it, in contrast to the Malikis of Baghdad, Abu Hanifa and his followers. This is an issue discussed in the principles of jurisprudence (*usul al-fiqh*), and this disagreement applies only where no indicator points to immediacy or delay. Here, however, the conjunction with *fa* (then) indicates that the saying is followed by the act without interval. So the angels must have understood immediacy from something other than the original meaning of the wording, which is why they hastened to the act and did not delay.

The prostration commanded and the object of the prostration is a gesture and submission. This is what the majority said. Or it is placing the forehead on the ground with humility. Or it is their acknowledging his merit and recognising his distinction, and this returns to the linguistic meaning of prostration. He said: whoever acknowledges your excellence has submitted to you.

*(Li-Adam)*: whoever holds that it is the legal prostration (*al-sujud al-shar'i*) says: the prostration was an honour and a greeting to him. This is the view of the majority: 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, like the prostration of the parents of Joseph, not a prostration of worship. Or it was to God, and He made Adam a direction (*qiblah*) for their prostration, like the Ka'bah. So the meaning is "towards Adam," as al-Sha'bi said. Or it was to God, and Adam prostrated, and they prostrated following him as those who follow an imam, and He honoured him by making him an imam whom they follow. The meaning of *li-Adam* is: with Adam.

Some said: God commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam before He created him, so the prostration was obedience to God's command and a prostration to Him. Muqatil said this, but the Qur'an refutes this view.

Some said: the prostration of the angels was twice. It was said: consensus (*al-ijma'*) refutes this view. The apparent meaning is that the prostration was with the forehead, because of His saying: ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, fall down before him in prostration﴾ [al-Hijr: 29]. It was said: there is no proof in this, because one who kneels on both knees is "falling," and the prostration was to Adam as a form of honour. Some of them said: prostration to God is by placing the forehead, and to humans by bowing. End of his words.

It is permissible that prostration at that time to human beings was not forbidden. It is reported that prostration was the greeting in the law of those before us, and that this was abrogated (*nusikha*) in Islam. It was also said that prostration to other than God was permissible until the time of Ya'qub, and then it was abrogated. Most scholars said: it was not abrogated until the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It is related that he (ﷺ) said in a hadith when the Companions offered to prostrate to him: "It is not fitting for anyone to prostrate to anyone except to God, Lord of the worlds." And it is related that Mu'adh prostrated to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he forbade him from doing so.

Ibn 'Ata said: when they regarded their glorification and sanctification of Him as great, He commanded them to prostrate to other than Him, in order to show them by this His independence from them and from their worship.

(fa-sajadū): "then" here is a supposed (mahdhūf, omitted) element, its estimated form being fa-sajadū lahu, i.e., they prostrated to him, that is, to Adam. This is indicated by the statement "Prostrate to Adam" (usjudū li-Ādam). The lām in li-Ādam is for clarification (li-l-tabyīn), and it is one of the seventeen meanings that we mentioned when explaining "Al-ḥamdu lillāh."

(illā Iblīs): He is an exception from the pronoun in fa-sajadū. This is an exception from an affirmative (mūjab) statement in this type of issue, so the accusative (naṣb) is preferred. It is a connected exception (istithnā' muttaṣil) according to the majority: Ibn Mas'ūd, Ibn 'Abbās, Ibn al-Musayyab, Qatādah and Ibn Jurayj. Abu al-Ḥasan (al-Ash'arī) and al-Ṭabarī chose it. Accordingly, he was an angel, then he was made desperate (ublisa), was made angry with, was cursed, and became a devil (shayṭān). Reports on this have come from Ibn 'Abbās, Qatādah and Ibn Jubayr. His name has been disputed: it was said 'Azāzīl, and it was said al-Ḥārith.

It was also said that it is a disconnected exception (istithnā' munqaṭi'), and that he was the father of the jinn, just as Adam was the father of humankind, and that he was never an angel at all. This was said by Ibn Zayd and al-Ḥasan, and it was reported from Ibn 'Abbās. It was reported from Ibn Mas'ūd and Shahr ibn Ḥawshab that he was one of the jinn who were on the earth, whom the angels fought; they took him captive as a child, and he worshipped with the angels and was addressed along with them.

It has been argued that he is not one of the angels by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿the Originator of the heavens and the earth, who made the angels messengers﴾ [Fāṭir: 1], which is general, so disbelief or sinfulness is not permissible for the angels, just as it is not permissible for their messengers among humans. Also by His saying: ﴿They do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded﴾ [al-Taḥrīm: 6]; by His saying: ﴿He was one of the jinn﴾ [al-Kahf: 50]; and because he has offspring, unlike the angels.

The apparent view is that it is a connected exception, since the command was directed at the angels; had he not been among them, the command would not have been directed at him, and blame would not fall on him for leaving what he was not commanded to do. As for ﴿who made the angels messengers﴾ [Fāṭir: 1] and ﴿they do not disobey Allah in what He commands them﴾ [al-Taḥrīm: 6], these are general terms with a specific application, since their infallibility is not from their own essence; it is only by Allah's making it so for them. As for Iblīs, Allah removed from him the angelic attributes and clothed him in the garments of satanic attributes.

As for His saying: ﴿He was one of the jinn﴾ [al-Kahf: 50], Qatādah said: they are a category of angels called al-Jinnah. Ibn Jubayr said: a tribe of angels created from fire, and Iblīs was among them; or he was called "of the jinn" because he is not seen, just as the angels were called jinnah; or because he was named by the name that predominated over him; or by what was done by him; or because the angels are called jinn. Al-A'shā said, describing Sulaymān, upon our Prophet and upon him be peace:

﻿And he subjugated from the jinn of the angels nine,
standing before him, working without wage.

(abā): refused and disdained to prostrate to Adam. (wa-istakbara): he acted proudly and magnified himself within himself. He placed refusal (ibā') before arrogance (istikbār), though arrogance is the first in order, because it is an act of the heart, namely self-magnification, and refusal from prostration arises from it. This is considered in view of what appeared first from him, namely the refusal to prostrate, and because the thing commanded is prostration; when he made an exception of Iblīs, he was judged to have left prostration, or else he is described as one about whom nothing is said and not judged, according to the disagreement that we will mention shortly, if Allah wills. The purpose is to inform about him that his state contradicted the state of the angels. So it was fitting to begin first by affirming what was judged upon him in the exception, or by creating the report of his opposition, and what conveys this meaning is refusal from prostration.

The disagreement that we have pointed to is this: when you say, "The people stood except Zayd," the position of al-Kisā'ī is that the exclusion is from the noun, and that Zayd is not judged to have stood or not stood, so it is possible that he stood and possible that he did not. The position of al-Farrā' is that the exception is from the verb (qawl, i.e., the speech), and the correct view is ours, namely that the noun is excepted from the noun and the verb is excepted from the verb. The proofs of these positions are mentioned in the books of grammar.

The object of abā is omitted, because it transitively takes a single object by itself. The poet said:

He refused injustice while al-Nu'mān burns his tooth
against him, and he resorted to it, and the swords are his refuges.

The estimate is: he refused prostration. Abā is among the verbs that are obligatory (wājiba) whose meaning is negation, and for this reason what follows illā is treated as in the case of a negated verb. The Exalted said: ﴿And Allah refuses except that He perfect His light﴾ [al-Tawbah: 32]. It is not permissible to say "I struck except Zayd" as a restricted exception (istithnā' mufarragh), because illā does not enter into an affirmative statement. The poet said:

Allah refused except His justice and His fidelity,
so neither is the wrong recognized nor is the known lost.

And "Zayd refused injustice" is more eloquent than "he did not do injustice," because negating a thing of a person may be due to incapacity or other causes; but when you say "Zayd refused such-and-such," it indicates negating it from him by way of refusal and disdain. For this reason the Exalted's saying "(abā)" came, because the exception of Iblīs only indicates that he did not prostrate; had it been restricted to that, his failure to prostrate could have been for a reason other than refusal. So He specified the cause of his not prostrating, which is refusal and disdain.

﴿And he was among the disbelievers﴾. It was said: kāna here means "became" (ṣāra). It was also said: it is on its original sense, i.e., he was so in Allah's knowledge, because there is no dispute that he knew Allah before his disbelief. So the meaning is: he was in Allah's knowledge that he would be among the disbelievers. Abū al-'Āliyah said: "among the disobedient." The complement of min (the relative "those who") here apparently refers to the past, so there were disbelievers before Iblīs, namely the jinn who were on the earth; or Iblīs was the first to disbelieve absolutely, if it is not sound that there were disbelievers before him. If it is sound, then it means he was the first to disbelieve after his faith. Or what is intended is disbelief in the sense of covering up the truth.

As for Iblīs's disbelief: it was said he was ignorant, that Allah stripped him of the knowledge He had granted him, so he opposed the command and withdrew his hand from obedience. It was also said it was disbelief through obstinacy, and knowledge was not taken from him; rather pride prevented him from prostrating. Ibn 'Aṭiyyah said: disbelief through obstinacy while knowledge remains is unlikely, but in my view it is permissible and not impossible, when Allah abandons whom He wills. End of his words.

What he mentioned as permissible actually occurs. Pharaoh knew the oneness of Allah and His lordship, to the exclusion of others, yet the love of leadership and self-admiration over the kingdom he had been given moved him, so he claimed divinity despite his knowledge. Abū Jahl was certain of the prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ) and knew that what he brought was true, yet he denied his prophethood and persisted in disbelief. Likewise al-Akhnas, Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt, and others who disbelieved through obstinacy while knowing the truthfulness of the messengers. The scholars have divided disbelievers into one who disbelieves in heart and tongue, such as the materialists and those who deny the prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ); one who disbelieves in heart while believing with the tongue, namely the hypocrites; and one who believes in heart while disbelieving with the tongue, such as Pharaoh and those mentioned with him. So disbelief cannot be denied alongside the existence of knowledge.

The Mu'tazilah have used this verse to argue that disobedience necessitates disbelief. It was answered that he was a hypocritical disbeliever; and if he was a believer, he disbelieved only out of arrogance and belief that he was right in that rebellion, and his proof for that was his saying: ﴿I am better than him﴾.

al-Qushayrī said: When Iblīs for a period was in the favor of his obedience, strutting in pursuit of what pleased Him, they granted him the rank of precedence and believed in him the entitlement to special distinction; so his affair became as is said:

He was the lamp of union, shining brightly among us,
then a wind of separation blew upon him and he was extinguished.

(p-155) Abū al-Futūḥ Aḥmad, brother of Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazālī, was asked about Iblīs and said: That poor wretch did not know that the claws of decree, when they scratch, draw blood, and the bows of destiny, when they shoot, make deaf. Then he recited:

We were, and Layla, in an ascent of love,
but when we met, I stood firm and she slipped.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 35 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And We said, "O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden, and eat from it in abundance wherever you wish, but do not approach this tree, or you will be among the wrongdoers."﴾

*Uskun* (ٱسْكُنْ): *aqim* (remain, dwell). Its verbal noun is *al-uskna*, like *al-rujʿa*. The meaning goes back to *al-sukun* (stillness), which is the absence of movement. The one who dwells in a place stays and settles there without moving, relative to other places.

*Raghadan* (رَغَدًا): meaning wide and abundant, without hardship. Imru' al-Qays said:

*"While a man is seen by you living well, secure from calamities in a comfortable life."*

The Tamim tribe pronounces the ʿayn with a sukun (*tusakkinu al-ghayn*). Some people claimed that every triliteral noun with a guttural ʿayn and a sound lam may have its ʿayn vocalized or unvocalized, such as *bahr/bahar* and *nahr/nahar*, and gave this as a general rule. This is not the case. What has been established on the pattern *faʿal* with a fatha on the ʿayn does not allow sukun, as in *al-saḥar*, which is not said as *al-saḥr*. The real discussion concerns the pattern *faʿl* with a fatha on the fa and a sukun on the ʿayn, and on this there is disagreement. The Basrans held that the fatha found in such forms is limited to what is heard (*al-samaʿ*), and that these words are in two dialects, neither of which is derived from the other. The Kufans held that some of them have two dialects, and that others originally had a sukun and were then given a fatha. Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) preferred the Kufan view, and the evidence for it is mentioned in the books of grammar.

*Ḥaythu* (حَيْثُ): an adverb of place that is indefinite and always functions as an adverb. It is often governed by *min* and by *fi*, and rarely by the construct with *ladā*. Because it is attached to what follows it, it does not form a complete sentence with what comes after it. It is not used as an adverb of time, contrary to al-Akhfash. It does not serve as the subject of two nouns standing for two adverbs, as in *Zayd ḥaythu ʿUmar*, contrary to the Kufans. It is not used as a jussive particle without *mā*, contrary to al-Farrāʾ. It is not added to a singular noun, contrary to al-Kisāʾī. Whatever has come of this kind is judged to be anomalous. It is indeclinable (*mabniyya*), and the three vowels may appear on its final letter. One may also say *ḥawthu*, with a waw, and with the three vowels. Al-Kisāʾī reported that its inflection (*iʿrab*) is the dialect of the Banu Faqʿas.

*Al-qurbān* (القُرْبانُ): known, and it is approaching something.

*Hadhihi* (هَذِهِ): the ha is pronounced with a kasra, either short (*ikhtilas*) or long (*ishbaʿ*), or it is pronounced with a sukun. It is also said *hadhi* with a ya, and the ha in what has been mentioned is a substitute for it. They also said *dhi* with a kasra on the dhal, without ya or ha. It is the feminine of *dha*. Sometimes they added a ta' to mark the feminine of *dha* and said *dhāt*, which is indeclinable on the kasra.

*Al-shajara* (الشَّجَرَةَ): with a fatha on the shin and the jim. Some Arabs use a kasra on the shin, and replacing the jim with a ya with either a kasra or a fatha on the shin is attested. Abu al-Fath disagreed that the ya is a substitute. We have spoken at length about this in our work *Kitab al-Takmil li-Sharh al-Tashil*.

*Al-shajar* is what stands on a trunk. *Al-najm* is what grows low and spreads over the ground without a trunk.

*Al-ẓulm* (الظُّلْمُ): its origin is placing a thing in other than its proper place. It is then applied to polytheism (*al-shirk*), to denial (*al-jahd*), and to deficiency (*al-naqs*). *Al-maẓlūma* is land that has not received rain, and its meaning goes back to deficiency.

﴿And We said, "O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden"...﴾ (the verse). No authentic occasion of revelation (*sabab nuzul*) has been transmitted for it. Its connection to what precedes it is this: when God honored Adam with the rank of knowledge and with the prostration of the angels to him, He granted him the favor of causing him to dwell in the Garden, which is the abode of bliss. He permitted him everything in it except the tree, as will be discussed later, God willing.

*Wa-qulnā* (وقُلْنا) is coordinated (*maʿṭūf*) on the preceding clause, which is God's saying "And when We said" (*wa-idh qulnā*), and not merely on *qulnā*, because the two events happened at different times. The object of the saying is the vocative and what follows it. The benefit of the vocative is to alert the one commanded to what is about to be said to him, and to direct his attention to what he is addressed with, since this is among the matters that deserve careful attention. The command here is to dwell in the Garden.

They said: the meaning of the command here is permission and authorization to dwell, like God's saying, "And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt" (5:2), and "And when the prayer has been concluded, disperse through the land" (62:10), because settling in good places does not fall under worship. Others said it is a command of obligation and of legal responsibility (*takl*īf), because it is a command to dwell in the Garden and to eat from it, and God forbade him from one tree. The more correct view is that the command to dwell and what follows it contains both what is permission, which is benefiting from all the bliss of the Garden, and what is obligation, which is restraining him from taking what he was forbidden.

*Anta* (أنْتَ): an emphatic (*tawkīd*) pronoun for the hidden pronoun in *uskun*. This is one of the places where a pronoun is necessarily hidden. *Zawjuka* (زَوْجُكَ): coordinated on that hidden pronoun. Coordinating on it is made good by the emphasis with *anta*. According to the Basrans, it is not permitted to coordinate on it without emphasis, or without a separating element that takes the place of emphasis, or without a separation between the conjunction and the coordinated word. Anything else is either a poetic necessity or anomalous. It has been transmitted: *qum wa-Zayd* (stand, and Zayd). The Kufans permitted coordination on that pronoun without emphasis or separation. The grammarians and the analysts of i'rab agree on what we have mentioned: that *wa-zawjuka* is coordinated on the hidden pronoun in *uskun*, and in that case it is coordination of single words (*ʿaṭf al-mufradāt*). Some people claimed it is only permitted that it be coordination of clauses, with the estimated meaning *wa-l-tuskin zawjaka* (and let your wife dwell), where *wa-l-tuskin* was omitted because *uskun* indicates it. They cited similar examples of this type, such as *lā nukhlifuhu naḥnu wa-lā anta* (we will not break it, nor will you), *taqūmu anta wa-Zayd* (you stand, and Zayd), and *idkhulū awwalukum wa-ākhirukum* (enter, your first and your last), and the line:

*"We circle what we circle, then there come to rest the wealthy among us and the poor."*

If one analyzes it as an apposition (*badal*) and not as emphasis, it is by supplying a verb. So the estimate in their view is: "and you will not break it," "and Zayd will stand," "and let your first and last enter," "and the wealthy will come to rest." They claimed that they extracted this from the text of Sibawayh, but that is not as they claimed. Rather, Sibawayh explicitly addressed the question of coordination in his book, as the grammarians have gone on to say. Sibawayh, may God have mercy on him, said: "As for what it is ugly for the apparent noun to be joined with, it is the pronoun in the nominative, such as *faʿaltu wa-ʿAbd Allah* (I did, and ʿAbd Allah) and *afʿalu wa-ʿAbd Allah* (I do, and ʿAbd Allah)." Then he mentioned al-Khalil's reasoning for its ugliness. Then he said: "Its attributive (*naʿt*) is good to be joined with the apparent noun, such as your saying *dhahabta anta wa-Zayd* (you went, you and Zayd). And God, the Mighty and Majestic, said: 'So go, you and your Lord, and fight' (5:24), and 'Dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden.'" End of quote.

This is an explicit text from Sibawayh that coordinating the apparent noun on the hidden pronoun is permitted. The grammarians have agreed on the permissibility of *taqūmu ʿĀʾisha wa-Zayd* (ʿĀʾisha stands, and Zayd), and it is not possible for Zayd to directly govern the verb. We know of no disagreement that this is coordination of single words. A fuller discussion of this question belongs elsewhere.

The fact that the command to dwell is addressed to Adam's wife indicates that she existed before him. This is the view of some exegetes, that she was created from the time God taught him the names and informed the angels of them. He slept a sleep, and she was created from his shortest rib before entering the Garden. Most of the leading exegetes hold that she was created after Adam entered the Garden. He felt lonely after Iblis was cursed and expelled from the Garden, so he slept. When he woke up he found her at his head, whom God had created from his left rib. He asked her, "Who are you?" She said, "A woman." He said, "Why were you created?" She said, "So that you may find comfort in me." Then the angels, examining the extent of his knowledge, said to him, "What is her name?" He said, "Hawwa'." They said, "Why was she named Hawwa'?" He said, "Because she was created from a living thing." There are additional details in this story mentioned by the exegetes, which we will not lengthen by mentioning, because they are not among the things on which the meaning or the exegesis of the verse depends.

According to this view, the address is directed to one who did not yet exist, because she exists in God's knowledge. Adam had dwelt in the Garden when she was created, and they were both commanded to dwell together, so that their hearts would be at rest and they would settle in the Garden.

Some people discussed the legal rulings concerning *al-sukna*, *al-ʿumra* and *al-ruqba* (types of life-tenancy grants), and the jurists' statements and their disagreements on them were mentioned when God's saying "Dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden" was explained. But the verse contains nothing that indicates any of what has been mentioned.

*Al-Jannah* (الجَنَّةَ): Abu al-Qasim al-Balkhi and Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said it was on earth, and it was said: in the land of Eden. *Al-hubūṭ* (الهُبُوطُ): moving from one place to another, as in God's saying, "Go down to a city" (2:61). They argued that if it had been the abode of eternity, Adam would not have been deceived by Iblis when he said, "Shall I direct you..." (20:120); that whoever enters this Garden does not leave it, according to God's saying, "And they will never be removed from it" (15:48); that Iblis is accursed, so he would not reach the Garden of eternity; that the abode of reward does not have bliss that ends, according to God's saying, "its fruit is perpetual" (13:35); and that it is not wise for God to begin the creation of humans in a Garden and for their eternal dwelling. Moreover, there is no dispute that God created Adam on earth, and this story does not mention that He transported him to the heavens. If He had transported him to the heavens, that would have been more worthy of mention, since it is among the greatest favors.

Al-Jubba'i said it was in the seventh heaven, based on God's saying, "Go down" (*ihbiṭū*). The first descent was from that heaven to the first heaven, and the second descent was from heaven to earth. The majority said it is in heaven, and it is the abode of reward, because the definite article in *al-jannah* does not indicate generality, since dwelling in all the gardens is impossible. So it must be understood as referring to the previously known one, and the known one is the abode of reward. Also, it is established in the authentic reports in the account of Adam's debate with Moses, where Moses said to him: "O Adam, did you make your descendants wretched and expel them from the Garden?" Adam did not contest that with him.

It was said that it is the heaven, but not the abode of reward; rather it is the Garden of eternity. It was said that in heaven there is a Garden other than the abode of reward and other than the Garden of eternity. The statement of those who said it is a garden in heaven was rejected, because it is not established that there are gardens in heaven other than the gardens of Paradise.

Among what those who said it is on earth cited as evidence is God's saying, "They hear therein no ill speech or sin" (52:23) [sic: 56:25], "except the saying, 'Peace, peace'" (56:26), "No ill speech therein or sin" (52:23), and "And they will never be removed from it" (15:48). Iblis engaged in ill speech there and lied, and expelled Adam and Hawwa' from it. Moreover, if it had been the abode of eternity, Iblis would not have reached it and whispered to them until he expelled them. Also, the Garden of eternity is an abode of bliss and rest, not an abode of legal responsibility, yet Adam was obligated not to eat from the tree. Also, Iblis was among the jinn created from the fire of the scorching wind, and it has been reported that he was among the unbelieving jinn who were driven out onto the earth. If it had been the Garden of eternity, he would not have entered it. Also, it is a place of purification, so how could sin and disobedience occur in it, and those who are not purified settle in it?

The verses were answered by saying that they are to be understood as referring to their state after entering it for settled and permanent dwelling, not to their entering it by way of passage and transit. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) is authentically reported to have entered the Garden on the night of the Ascension and at other times, and it is reported in the hadith of the eclipse that he saw it. As for Iblis's entering it, it was an entry of domination (*taslīt*), not of honor, and that is if it is authentically established. They said: the sound view is that he did not enter the Garden, but stood at its gate and spoke to them, and wanted to enter, but the guardians turned him back. It was also said that he entered inside the serpent, hidden. As for its not being an abode of legal responsibility, that applies after they enter it for continuous residence and reward for righteous deeds. As for an entry that is followed by expulsion because of disobedience, it does not contradict legal responsibility; rather, it is not free from it.

**(وكُلا)**: This is evidence that the address is to both of them after Eve existed, since the command to eat is directed at someone non-existent only with difficulty, unless one assumes her existence. The original form of **(كُلْ)** is **أُؤْكُلْ**. The first hamza is the one added for connection (hamzat al-wasl), and the second is the root consonant of the word. The second was deleted to avoid the juxtaposition of two identical letters, a deletion considered anomalous (shudhudh). So the connecting hamza came to stand before the **كاف**, which carries a vowel. The connecting hamza was introduced only because of the sukun on the letter, so when the cause for introducing it disappeared, it disappeared too. Ibn Atiyya and others said: the nun was deleted from **(كُلا)** for the imperative. Their statement ends here. But what he mentioned is not in accordance with the method of the Basrans. For in their view the imperative verb is built on sukun. When a pronoun attached to it is an explicit (bariz) pronoun, the vowel at its end matches the pronoun, so you say **كُلِي** and **كُلا** and **كُلُوا**. With feminine plurals it remains sukun, as in **كُلْنَ**. Defective (mu'tall) verbs have a different ruling. Given this, his saying **وكُلا** would not have a nun to be deleted for the imperative. What he mentioned would only accord with the doctrine of the Kufans, who claimed that the imperative verb is inflected (mu'rab), and that the original of **كُلْ** is **لِتَأْكُلْ**, which then underwent gradual deletion until it became **كُلْ**. Thus the original of **كُلا** is **لِتَأْكُلا**, and before the imperative particle (lam al-amr) was attached to it, it had a nun, since its original was **تَأْكُلانِ**. On their view, Ibn Atiyya's statement that the nun of **كُلا** was deleted for the imperative holds.

**(مِنها)**: The pronoun refers to the Garden, and the meaning is by way of an elided genitive (hadhf mudaf), i.e., "from its foods," from its fruits and other things. This indicates the permission for them to eat from the Garden as a matter of ease and abundance, since no food was forbidden to them, as He said: **(رَغَدًا)**. The majority read the **غين** with a fatha. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and Yahya ibn Wathhab read it with sukun. It has already been mentioned that the two are dialectal variants. As for the grammatical status of **(رَغَدًا)**, they said it is an adjective of an elided verbal noun, whose implied form is "eating, abundantly." Ibn Kaysan said it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal). Both analyses are open to objection. As for the first: the view of Sibawayh contradicts it, since he does not accept this, and for this type he treats the word as an accusative of circumstance from the pronoun returning to the verbal noun indicated by the verb.
