As for the second: it is restricted to what is attested by usage. Al-Zajjaj said: **al-rag'ad** is abundance that does not burden you. Muqatil said: wide. Mujahid said: that for which one is not called to account. It is also said: free from reproach, pleasant. One says **رَغِدَ عَيْشُ القَوْمِ** and **رَغُدَ**, with kasra or damma on the ghayn, when the people are in wide, abundant provision, and **أرْغَدَ القَوْمُ** means they became prosperous and in ease of life. They also say **عِيشَةٌ رَغْدٌ** with sukun as well.

**(حَيْثُ شِئْتُما)**: He permitted them to eat wherever they wished, so He did not forbid them any place in the Garden, just as He did not forbid them any food except what was explicitly prohibited. There is disagreement about the morphological pattern (wazn) of **(شاءَ)**. It is reported from Sibawayh that its pattern is **فَعِلَ** with a kasra on the ayn, whose vowel was moved to the shin and then the ayn was made quiescent. The lam is quiescent because of the pronoun, so two quiescent letters met, and the first was deleted to avoid meeting of two quiescents. The shin was given a kasra to show that the deleted letter was a yaa, as is done in **بِعْتُ**.

**(ولا تَقْرَبا)**: He forbade them from approaching it. This is more emphatic than prohibiting eating, since if He forbade approaching it, how could eating from it be permitted? The meaning is: do not come near it by eating; it is not that permission was given for eating. Some of our contemporaries related from Ibn al-Arabi, meaning the judge Abu Bakr, who said: I heard al-Shashi in the assembly of al-Nadr ibn Shumayl say: if you say **لا تَقْرَبْ** with a fatha on the ra', its meaning is "do not get involved in the act"; and if it is with a damma on the ra', its meaning is "do not come near." It has already been stated that the meaning of **لا تَقْرَبْ زَيْدًا** is "do not come near him." In this report from Ibn al-Arabi there is a confusion that is surprising in its narrator: he said "I heard al-Shashi in the assembly of al-Nadr ibn Shumayl," yet between al-Nadr and al-Shashi there are hundreds of years, unless there was a place known as the assembly of al-Nadr ibn Shumayl, in which case it is possible.

It was also read **(ولا تِقْرَبا)** with a kasra on the taa'. This is a dialect of the Hijazis for the pattern **فَعَلَ يَفْعَلُ**, in which they vowel the present-tense prefix letters taa', hamza, and nun with kasra; most of them do not do so with the yaa', though some do. If it is of the type **يَوْحِلُ**, there are both kasra and fatha, with the waw retained and also changed into an alif.

**(هَذِهِ)**: A demonstrative for something present and near the addressee. Ibn Muhayşin read **(هَذِيِ)** with a yaa'. The majority read it with the haa'.

**الشَّجَرَةَ**: An adjective of the demonstrative. The demonstrative may refer to a genus of known trees, or it may refer to one tree of the known genus. The latter is more apparent, since the demonstrative indicates a specific thing being pointed to.

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Ja'da ibn Hubayra said: it is the grapevine, and for this reason wine was forbidden to us. Ibn Abbas also said, as did Abu Malik and Qatada: it is the ear of grain, and its grain was like the kidneys of a cow, sweeter than honey and softer than butter. This was reported from Wahb. When God accepted Adam's repentance, He made it nourishment for his descendants. Some of the Companions and Qatada said: it is the fig. Ali said: it is the camphor tree. Al-Kalbi said: it is the tree of knowledge, bearing fruit of every color, and whoever eats from it knows good and evil. Wahb said: it is the tree of eternity, from which the angels eat. Abu al-Aliya said: it is a tree whoever eats from it becomes impure. Some People of the Book said: it is the colocynth tree. Abu Malik said: it is the palm tree. It was said: it is the tree of trial. It was said: it is a tree whose identity God did not inform us of, and this is the most apparent view, since no great matter depends on knowing it; the purpose is only to inform us that doing what was forbidden is a cause of punishment.

It was read **(الشِّجَرَةَ)** with a kasra on the shin, related by Harun al-A'war from some readers. It was also read **(الشِّيَرَةَ)** with a kasra on the shin and a fatha on the yaa' following it. Abu Amr disliked this reading and said: the Berbers and Sudanese of Mecca read it this way. But he should not dislike it, since it is an established dialect. Concerning it al-Riyashi said: I heard Abu Zayd say: we were with al-Mufaddal, and with him were Bedouin Arabs. I said: they say **شِيَرَةٌ**? They said: yes. I said to him: tell them to make its diminutive; they said **شُيَيْرَةٌ**. Al-Asma'i recited:
*"We think him among people a shīra."*

In God's prohibition to Adam and his wife from approaching the tree there is evidence that their dwelling in the Garden was not permanent, since one who is eternal is not commanded, forbidden, or prevented from anything.

**(فَتَكُونا)**: is in the accusative as the answer to the prohibition. According to Sibawayh and the Basrans its accusative is by a hidden **أنْ** after the fa'; according to al-Jarmi it is by the fa' itself; according to the Kufans it is disputed. A full account of these positions is found in the books of grammar. They also permitted **(فَتَكُونا)** to be jussive (majzum) as a conjunction with **(تَقْرَبا)**, as said by al-Zajjaj and others, like the line:
*"I said to him: aim well, and do not exert him, lest he cast you down from the summit of the qata'a and you slip."*

The first analysis is more apparent, because the causal sense is clear, while conjunction does not indicate it.

**﴿مِنَ الظّالِمِينَ﴾** (﴿of the wrongdoers﴾): It was said: wronging yourselves by removing yourselves from the abode of bliss to the abode of misery; or by eating from the tree you were forbidden; or by disgrace before the highest assembly; or by following Iblis; or by committing a major sin, as the Hashawiyya said; or by committing a minor sin, as the Mu'tazila said; or by imposing on themselves what is burdensome, namely repentance and making amends, as Abu Ali said; or by reducing some of the reward that was attained, as Abu Hashim said; or by abandoning what is preferable (tark al-awla). Some said: they were the first of the children of Adam to wrong themselves, and some said: there were wrongdoers before them who were likened to them and attributed to them. In His saying **﴿فَتَكُونا مِنَ الظّالِمِينَ﴾** there is evidence that the prohibition was in the mode of obligation and not of recommendation, since one who abandons it is not called a wrongdoer.

One of the people of allusion (ahl al-isharat) said: what befits created beings is not to incline to creation. Adam was alone, with every good and every well-being. When the companion and the spouse came to him, the coming of trial and the opening of the door of tribulation became evident. When he cohabited with Eve he obeyed her in what she pointed out to him of eating, and so he fell into what he fell into. Indeed it has been said:
*"An ancient disease among the children of Adam is one human's infatuation with another."*

Al-Qushayri said: whatever is forbidden, the motives of the son of Adam to draw near to it are strengthened. Here is Adam, peace be upon him, to whom the Garden was permitted in its entirety, and he was forbidden one tree. Nothing transmitted says that he stretched out his hand to anything of what was permitted to him. It seems his patience was overcome until he tasted what he was forbidden. Such is the nature of created beings. He also said: God alerted to the consequence of Adam's entering the Garden, through his committing what required his exit from it, in His saying: **﴿Indeed I am going to place upon the earth a vicegerent﴾** [2:30]. When He informed of appointing him as vicegerent on earth, how could he remain in the Garden? Adam was one whom no one could match in rank; the calls "O Adam, O Adam" followed one another. Then by evening his garment had been stripped from him and his intimacy taken away. Power is not contested, and God's decree is not opposed. The poet said:
*"By God, how fine are those youths who set out early like kings and returned like the destitute."*

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 36–39 (part 1 of 5):

﴿Then Satan caused them to slip from it, and removed them from that in which they were. And We said: "Go down, some of you enemies to others. On the earth you will have a dwelling place and provision for a time."﴾ ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words, and He turned to him in forgiveness. Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿We said: "Go down from it, all of you. Then when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.﴾ ﴿And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs, those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾

Azalla (to cause to slip): from zalal, which is the stumbling of the foot. It is said: "his foot slipped" and "the sandal slipped with him." Zalal in opinion and reasoning is figurative. Azala (to remove) is from zawal, and its root meaning is removal. The hamza in both verbs is for transitivity (ta'diyah).

Al-hubut (descending): it is nuzul (descent), the verbal noun of habata. Its present tense is yahbitu and yahbutu, with the ba' vowelled either with kasra or damma. Al-habut with a fatha is the place of descent. Al-Mufaddal said: al-hubut is going out from a town, and it is also entering it, and these are antonyms. It is said figuratively of lowering of rank. For this reason al-Farra' said: al-hubut is humiliation. Labid said:

"If they are envied, they will be brought down one day, and if they are commanded..."

Ba'd (some): its origin is the verbal noun of ba'ada, yab'adu, ba'dan, meaning "he cut off." It is applied to a part, and its opposite is kull (all). Both are definite in eloquent speech, since a circumstantial clause (hal) comes from them. They say: "I passed by some standing" and "by all sitting." The idafa (genitive construction) is intended with both, and therefore the alif and lam do not enter upon them. For this reason they erred against Abu al-Qasim al-Zajjaji in his saying: "Ba'd is substituted from kull." The pronoun refers back to ba'd when a group is intended, singular and plural. Likewise the predicate, the circumstantial, and the attribute may be singular or plural in that case.

Al-'aduww (enemy): from 'adawa, which is transgression of the limit. It is said: "so-and-so transgressed his bounds" when he exceeded them. It is also said: al-'adawa is distance in the hearts, from 'udwayy al-jabal, which are its two sides, named so because of the distance between them. It is also said: from 'adā, meaning "he did wrong." All these meanings are close. Al-'aduww applies to the singular, the dual, and the plural, the masculine and the feminine. It has been pluralized as a'da', and it has been feminized, and they said 'aduwwa. From this: ﴿'aduwwat anfusihinna﴾ (the women's self-interest, lit. "their own enemies" in the feminine). Al-Farra' said: the Arabs said to a woman: "'aduwwat Allah," and some of them dropped the ha'.

Al-mustaqarr (dwelling place): mustaf'al from qarar, which is staying and residing. It may be a verbal noun, a time, or a place, because it comes from a verb of more than three letters, so it takes the form of the passive participle for these meanings. For this reason the earth is called qararah. The poet said:

"Every abundant eye poured upon him, so they left every qararah like a dirham."

Istaf'ala here has the meaning of fa'ala: istaqarra and qarra have the same meaning.

Al-mata' (provision): the sustenance sufficient for the moment. It is taken from mata'a al-nahar, meaning "when the day rose high." It applies to what a person acquires of the goods of this world. It is also applied to provision for the journey, to the enjoyment of women, from which: ﴿fa-ma istamta'tum bihi minhunna﴾ (An-Nisa 24), the mut'ah marriage, to clothing (wa-mattiuhunna), and to long life: ﴿yumatti'kum matan hasanan﴾ (Hud 3). They said: from this comes amta'a Allah bika, meaning "may God prolong your companionship with us." All of these return to the meaning of sufficiency.

Al-hin (time): the moment and the period. It is not restricted to a specific duration; rather the unrestricted sense was assigned to it.

Talaqqa (to receive): tafa''ala from liqa' (meeting), like ta'adda from al-'adw. They said: or it means istaqbala (to meet/receive). From this: talaqqa fulan fulanan, meaning he met him. And yatalaqqa al-wahy means he receives it, takes it, and grasps it. We went out to meet (talaqqi) the pilgrims: we went to receive them. Al-Shammakh said:

"When a banner is raised for glory, 'Urabah receives it with the right hand."

Al-Qaffal said: al-talaqqi is putting oneself in the way of meeting, then it is placed in the position of acceptance and taking. From this: ﴿wa-innaka latulaqqa al-Qur'an﴾ (An-Naml 6). I received this word from so-and-so: I took it from him.

Al-kalimah (word): the expression placed for a meaning. Al-kalimah is also speech, and al-kalimah is a poem, named so because it includes a word and speech. It is pluralized by dropping the ta' so that it becomes a noun of genus, like nabqah and nabq (jujube fruit and jujube trees).

Al-tawbah (repentance): return. Taba yatubu tawban and tawbatan and mataban. When it is transitive with 'ala, it is taken to include the meaning of 'atf (turning in compassion).

Tabi'a: with the meaning of laḥiqa (to overtake/follow), with the meaning of talā (to follow/recite), and with the meaning of iqtada (to imitate).

Al-khawf (fear): fright. Khafa yakhafu khawfan, takhawwafa takhawwufan, and afza'a. It is transitive with the hamza and with doubling, and it applies to a future matter.

The root of al-huzn (grief) is the severity of worry. It is taken from al-huzn, which is what is rough of the earth. It is said: hazina yahzanu huznan and hazanan. It is transitive with the hamza and with fatha, like shutirat 'ayn al-rajul (the man's eye was squinted) and shatarahu Allah. There is disagreement about transitivity by fatha. It applies to a past matter.

Al-ayah (sign): the mark. Its plural is aya and ayat. The poet Al-Nabigha said:

"I imagined signs for her, and I recognized them after six years, and this year is the seventh."

Its measure according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh is fa'lah, so the 'ayn was altered and the lam remained sound, which is an anomaly, while analogy would be the reverse. According to al-Kisa'i it is fa'ilah, the 'ayn was dropped so that it would not require the doubling that is required in dabbah, which would be heavy. According to al-Farra' it is fa'lah, and the 'ayn was changed to an alif because doubling is heavy, as in qirat and diwan. According to some Kufans it is fi'lah: doubling was felt heavy, so the first radical was changed to an alif because it was broken and what preceded it was moved. This is an issue whose discussion is completed in the science of morphology (sarf).

Al-suhbah (companionship): association. Sahiba yasahibu. Al-ashab is the plural of sahib, and the plural of fa'il on af'al is anomalous. Al-suhbah and al-sahabah are collective nouns, and likewise sahiba according to the more correct view, in contrast to al-Akhfash. It is for general association at some time.

﴿fa-azallahuma al-Shaytan 'anha﴾: the hamza, as mentioned above in azalla, is for transitivity. The meaning is: he made them slip by his seduction, and he drove them to slip and to fall into the slip. This is the original use of the hamza of transitivity. It may also come with the meaning of making the causes of the action, so the action does not take place. You say: "I made Zayd laugh, but he did not laugh," and "I made him weep, but he did not weep," meaning: I provided him with the causes of laughter and the causes of weeping, but his laughing and his weeping did not follow from that. The original use is the first. The poet said:

"A bay horse whose saddle-blanket slips from the middle of its back, as the saddle of the one who dismounts slips."

Its meaning, as the commentators explain, is that the saddle-blanket slips: it slides from the middle of its back. Likewise his saying:

"The boy's slipper slides off his saddle-pommel."

That is, it slides it off.

It is said that azallahuma means "he removed them far away." You say: "He slipped from his rank," "that slipped from me," and "such-and-such slipped from the month," meaning: it went away and fell. This is close to the first meaning, because the slip is a fall in meaning, since in it the one who slips leaves the path of uprightness and moves far from it. So this comes in accordance with the original use of the hamza of transitivity.

Al-Hasan, Abu Raja' and Hamzah read: fa-azalahuma, and the meaning of izalah is removal (tanhiyah). It is narrated from Hamzah and Abu 'Ubaydah that they used imalah (vowel-inclination) in fa-azalahuma.

Al-Shaytan is Iblis without any disagreement here. They have related that 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) read: fa-waswasa lahuma al-Shaytan 'anha (Satan whispered to them from it). This reading contradicts the consensus text of the Mushaf (sawad al-mushaf), so it should be taken as an explanation (tafsir). Likewise is what has come from him and from others that contradicts the sawad al-mushaf. Most of 'Abd Allah's readings are attributed to the Shi'ah. One of our scholars has said: it is established for us by mass transmission (tawatur) that 'Abd Allah's reading is in agreement with the sawad, not what is transmitted from him that differs. Those are only solitary reports (ahad), and that is on the assumption that they are authentic, so they do not contradict what is established by mass transmission.

Regarding how Iblis reached their seduction until they ate from the tree, there are several sayings. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and the majority said: he spoke to them directly, as evidenced by (wa-qasamahuma) (and he swore to them). It is said: Iblis entered the Garden by way of whispering, as a trial for Adam and Eve. It is said: he entered the belly of the serpent. They mentioned what the form of the serpent was and what became of it, and how Iblis spoke with Adam. Allah has related this story in the best and most truthful narration in Surat al-A'raf and elsewhere. It is said: Iblis did not enter the Garden, but rather he would approach the heaven and speak to them. It is said: he stood at the gate and called out. It is said: he did not enter the Garden, but that was by his authority with which Adam and his descendants were tested, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, Satan flows through the son of Adam like the flow of blood." It is said: he addressed him from the earth and did not ascend to heaven after the expulsion and the curse, and his address was whispering. The commentators have greatly multiplied in relating many stories about the story of Adam, Eve and the serpent, and Allah knows best about that. They discussed the state of Adam when he ate from the tree: was that intentional, or in a state of mental heedlessness from the prohibition through forgetfulness, or through intoxication from the wine of the Garden, as they mention from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib. I do not think this is authentically reported from him, because the wine of the Garden, as Allah mentioned: ﴿neither therein is any intoxication nor are they affected by it﴾ (As-Saffat 47). Unless the Garden is on earth, as some have explained, in which case its wine could cause intoxication. Those who said it was intentional said: the prohibition was a prohibition of discouragement (nahy tanzih). It is said: with him, from the fear at the moment of his action, there was something that made this act a minor sin. It is said: he did it by ijtihad (independent reasoning), and he went against it because it had preceded that the indication is to the individual person, not to the species; so he left that tree and ate from another. Ijtihad in the subsidiary matters (furu') does not require punishment. It is said that the eating was a major sin. It is said: Iblis came to them in a form other than the one they knew, so they did not recognize him, and he swore to them that he was a sincere adviser. It is said: he forgot the enmity of Iblis. It is said: it is possible for Adam to interpret (wa-la taqraba) as a prohibition against approaching together, and that it is permissible for each one individually to approach. What is followed in the case where the apparent meaning suggests some contradiction is: interpreting it in the best possible sense, and declaring the prophets free from deficiencies. The discussion of what comes of that and its interpretation in the proper manner will come, God willing.

In (al-Muntakhab) of the Imam Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Abi al-Fadl al-Mursi, there is the following summary: The Community (ummah) has prevented the occurrence of disbelief (kufr) from the prophets, peace be upon them, except the Fadiliyyah of the Kharijites. They said: sins have occurred from them, and sin in their view is disbelief. The Imamiyyah permitted displaying disbelief from them by way of taqiyyah (precautionary concealment). The Community has agreed on their protection (‘isma) from lying and distortion in what relates to conveying the message, so it is not permissible intentionally or through inadvertence. Some people have permitted that through inadvertence. They agreed on the impossibility of error in giving legal rulings intentionally, and they differed about inadvertence. As for their actions, the Hashawiyyah said: it is permissible for major sins to occur from them intentionally. Most of the Mu'tazilah said: minor sins are permissible intentionally, except in speech, such as lying. Al-Jubba'i said: both are impossible for them except by way of interpretation. It has been said: both are impossible for them, except by way of inadvertence and error, and they are held accountable for that, although it is removed from their community. The Rafidah said: this is impossible in every respect. They differed about the time of protection: the Rafidah said: from the time of their birth; most of the Mu'tazilah said: from the time of prophethood. Our preferred view is that no sin ever proceeded from them during the state of prophethood, neither major nor minor, because if sin had proceeded from them they would have been of lower rank than the disobedient of the Community, given their great nobility, and that is impossible. Also, so that they would not be unacceptable as witnesses, and so that it would not be obligatory to rebuke them and harm them, and so that they would not be imitated in that, and so that they would not deserve punishment, and so that they would not do the opposite of what they were commanded, since they are chosen (mustafawn), and because Iblis excepted them in seduction. End of what we have summarized from al-Muntakhab.

The discussion of the proofs for these positions, and of refuting what should be refuted from them, is mentioned in the books of the principles of religion (usul al-din).

**Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 2, verses 36–39 (part 2 of 5):**

*"Anha"*: The pronoun refers to the tree, which is the apparent reading, since it is the nearest antecedent. The meaning is: Satan caused them to slip by means of it. In this case *"an"* (from) indicates causation, that is, Satan brought about their slip "from the tree," as in the Almighty's words: ﴿And I did not do it out of my own command﴾ [al-Kahf: 82], and ﴿The plea of forgiveness by Ibrahim for his father was only due to a promise he had made to him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 114]. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the Garden, since it is the first thing mentioned. This is supported by the reading of Hamzah and others: *"fa-azalahuma"* (so he caused them to slip away), since it is far-fetched that *"fa-azalahuma al-shaytan 'an al-shajarah"* means "Satan removed them from the tree." It has also been said that the pronoun refers to obedience. They argue for this by the words: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord﴾ [Ta-Ha: 121]. In that case the pronoun refers to something not mentioned, except as it is understood from the meaning of his words "and do not approach," because the meaning is: obey Me by not approaching this tree. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the state they were in of enjoyment, luxury, and dwelling in the Garden, where they could go wherever they wished, whenever they wished, and however they wished, based on the words ﴿And eat from it freely﴾ [al-Baqarah: 35]. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the sky, but this is far-fetched.

﴿So he drove them out of that in which they were﴾: from obedience into disobedience, or from the blessing of the Garden into the misery of this world, or from high rank into the lowest state of sin, or from the good pleasure of God, or from His nearness. All these statements are close in meaning. Al-Mahdawi said: If *"azallahuma"* is taken from *"zalla 'an al-makan"* (to slip away from a place), then his words ﴿So he drove them out of that in which they were﴾ are an emphasis, since it is possible that they slipped away from a place they were in to another place in the Garden. End of quotation. The more preferable view is that it means the earning of their slip, which does not occur through casting. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Here there is an omitted element that is indicated by the apparent text, its estimate being: *"fa-akala minha"* (so they both ate from the tree). He means that the omitted element is assumed before his words ﴿So Satan caused them to slip﴾. He attributed the causing to slip, the causing to depart, and the expulsion to Iblis in a figurative sense (*majaz*), while the true agent of all things is God, exalted is He.

*"Wa-qulna ihbitu"* (And We said: Go down): Al-Jumhur read *"ihbituu"* with a kasrah on the *ba'*. Abu Haywah read *"ihbutu"* with a dammah on the *ba'*. We have already mentioned that both are dialects. The discussion of *"wa-qulna ihbitu"* is like the discussion of ﴿And We said: O Adam, dwell﴾ [al-Baqarah: 35]. Since it was a command to descend from the Garden to the earth, and since this involved a lowering of the commanded one's rank, He did not make him familiar through the call, nor did He turn to him by honouring him with mention of his name and addressing him directly with the call. This is unlike His words ﴿And We said: O Adam, dwell﴾ [al-Baqarah: 35]. The one addressed in the command was Adam, Hawwa', and the serpent, as reported by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. Or they were these and Iblis, as reported by al-Suddi from Ibn 'Abbas. Or Adam and Iblis, as reported by Mujahid. Or they were the two of them and Hawwa', as reported by Muqatil. Or Adam and Hawwa' only, with the address in the plural form even though it falls on the dual, as in the words ﴿And We were witnesses to their judgment﴾ [al-Anbiya': 78]. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari. Or Adam and Hawwa' and the whispering, as reported by al-Hasan. Or Adam and Hawwa' and their offspring, as reported by al-Farra'. Or Adam and Hawwa', with the intended meaning being them and their offspring. al-Zamakhshari preferred this view, saying: Because the two were the origin of mankind and its branches, they were treated as though they were all of mankind. The proof for this is His words ﴿He said: Go down from it, all of you, some of you to others an enemy﴾ [Ta-Ha: 123], and His words ﴿So whoever follows My guidance﴾ (the verse), which is nothing but a ruling that encompasses all people. End of quotation.

In al-Farra's view there is an address to one who has not yet existed, because their offspring did not yet exist at that time. In the view of those who included Iblis together with them in the command there is weakness, because he had already come out before them. However, it is permissible in a certain type of figurative usage. Ka'b and Wahb said: They were sent down all together and landed in different lands. Muqatil said: They were sent down scattered. Iblis descended, it is said, at al-Ubullah, Hawwa' at Jeddah, and Adam in India. It is also said he descended at Sarandib, on a mountain called Wasim. It is said that his food was coconut, and the clouds would wipe his head, which caused his offspring to be bald. This does not hold, because if it were so, all his children would be bald. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the serpent was sent down at Nasibin. al-Tha'labi reported it was at Isfahan, and al-Mas'udi at Sijistan, which has the most serpents of God's lands. It has also been said at Bisan. It is also said that this first descent was from the Garden to the lowest heaven. It is said that when Adam descended at Sarandib in India, with the fragrance of the Garden upon him, it clung to its trees and valleys, so that everything there was filled with fragrance. For this reason perfume is brought from the scent of Adam, peace be upon him. Abu al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzi mentioned, regarding his expulsion, a manner which we have set aside from mentioning. He said: Adam was made to enter the Garden at mid-morning and was expelled from it between the two prayers, so he remained in it for half a day, and the half is five hundred years, by the reckoning of the people of this world.

The more likely view is that His words *"ihbitu"* are a command of obligation, because in it there is great hardship due to what they had been in of the Garden, moving to a place where livelihood is attained only with hardship. This invalidates the view of those who thought that this was a punishment, because intensification in obligation occurs for the sake of reward. How could it be a punishment, when in his descent and his dwelling on the earth there is a manifestation of His eternal wisdom in this, namely the spreading of his progeny in it, so that He may impose obligations upon them, and set upon that their reward and punishment, in a Garden or in a Fire. That eating was the cause of his descent, and God does what He wills. He commanded him to descend to the earth after He had turned to him in forgiveness, as indicated by His words again: ﴿And We said: Go down, some of you to others an enemy﴾. If the addressees are Adam, Hawwa', and their offspring, as Mujahid said, then what is meant is what people have of enmity and the misleading of some by others. The partial relation exists among their offspring, since not all of them are enemies to all of them. Rather, some are enemies to some. And if Iblis or the serpent was with them, as Muqatil said, then not some of their offspring are enemies to the offspring of Adam, but rather they all are enemies to all the children of Adam. Yet this is realised by taking those commanded to descend as one single thing and dividing it into parts, so that each part of it is a part of those who descended, and the part is called "some." Thus the meaning becomes: every kind among you is an enemy to the kind that is distinct from it.

Al-Zajjaj said: Iblis is an enemy to the believers, and they are his enemies. It has also been said that its meaning is the enmity of a man's own soul toward him and of his limbs, but this is far-fetched. This sentence is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), that is, "go down as enemies," and the operator in it is *"ihbitu"*. The subject of the circumstantial clause is the pronoun in *"ihbitu"*. The conjunction *waw* was not needed, since the pronoun suffices as a connective. The combination of *waw* and the pronoun in a nominal sentence that functions as a circumstantial clause is more common than the pronoun alone. In the Book of God, the Exalted: ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection you will see those who lied against God, their faces blackened﴾ [al-Zumar: 60]. Its coming with the pronoun without the *waw* is not anomalous, contrary to al-Farra' and those who agreed with him, such as al-Zamakhshari. Sibawayh reported from the Arabs the expression *"fuhu ila fiyya"* (his mouth to my mouth) and *"raja'a 'uduhu 'ala bad'ihi"* (his stalk returned to its beginning). He explained it in two ways. One is that *"'uduhu"* is the subject (*mubtada'*) and *"'ala bad'ihi"* is the predicate, and the clause is a circumstantial clause. This is common in the language of the Arabs, both in verse and in prose, so it is not anomalous. Makki ibn Abi Talib permitted that the clause be a new independent sentence, a statement from God, the Exalted, that some of them are enemies to others. In that case it would not be in the position of a circumstantial clause. He seems to have fled from the circumstantial reading, because he imagined that a restriction in a command entails that it is itself commanded, or is like something commanded. Do you not see that if you say: "Stand up laughing," the meaning is a command to perform standing accompanied by laughing, so that laughing is commanded or is like what is commanded, since you did not permit him to stand except in the state of laughing? And what leads to the performance of a commanded act is itself commanded. God, the Exalted, does not command enmity, and what is imagined from that does not follow. For when an act is commanded of one to whom it is attributed in a certain state of his, that state is not itself commanded, because the state relation is a restrictive relation (*nisbah taqyidiyyah*), not a predicative relation (*nisbah isnadiyyah*). If the state were itself commanded whenever the operator in it is a command, this would not be permissible here. For when the commanded act cannot come into existence except with that restriction and its opposite is impossible, the restriction is not commanded, because it does not fall within the scope of obligation. This state is of this type, so it does not follow that God commanded it. This state is one of the necessary states.

His words *"li-ba'din"* (to some) are connected with his words *"'aduwwun"* (an enemy). The preposition *lam* strengthens the arrival of *"'aduwwun"* at it. *"'Aduwwun"* is in the singular, following the form of *"ba'd"*, or because it is suitable for the plural, as was previously mentioned when discussing *"ba'd"* and *"'aduwwun"* in the singular.

﴿And for you on the earth is a dwelling place﴾: It is a subject and predicate. *"Lakum"* is the predicate, and *"fi al-ardi"* (on the earth) is connected to the predicate. Its reality is that it is a complement of the operator within the predicate. The predicate here serves to permit beginning with an indefinite noun. It is not permissible for *"fi al-ardi"* to be connected to *"mustaqarr"* (dwelling place), whether it is intended as a place of settling, as stated by Abu al-'Aliyah and Ibn Zayd, or as a verbal noun meaning "settling," as stated by al-Suddi. This is because the noun of place does not govern, and because a verbal noun taken as a relative clause (*masdar mawsul*), some grammarians do not permit fronting its complement before it. Nor is it permissible for *"fi al-ardi"* to be the predicate. *"Lakum"* is connected to *"mustaqarr"* for the reason we have mentioned, or it is in the position of a circumstantial clause from *"mustaqarr,"* because in that case the operator in it would be the predicate, which is a notional operator, and a circumstantial clause cannot precede both parts of the predication. That is not permissible, and it becomes like the example *"qa'iman zaydun fi al-dar"* (standing, Zayd is in the house) or *"qa'iman fi al-dar zaydun"*, and this is not permissible by consensus. *"Mustaqarr"* means the place of your settling in the two states of life and death. It has also been said that it is the grave, or it is settling, as already explained.

*"Wa-mata'un"* (and enjoyment): *al-mata'* is what is enjoyed of benefits, or provision, or a long period of time, or long life. *"Ila hin"* (for a time): until death, or until the Hour, or until a term that God knows, as stated by Ibn 'Abbas. *"Ila"* is connected to an omitted element, meaning: and enjoyment existing for a time. Or it is connected to *"mata'"*, meaning: and enjoyment for a time. This is from the type of *al-i'mal* (the operating of one of two governing words on a shared complement), in which the second is operative and there is no need to supply a pronoun in the first, since its complement is an optional adjunct, so omitting it is preferable. It cannot be from the operating of the first, because it is preferable that nothing be omitted from the second, and the best course is to interpret the Qur'an according to the preferable reading. The most eloquent position is not to say that it is impermissible for it to be an instance of *al-i'mal*, even though each of *"mustaqarr"* and *"mata'"* requires it in meaning, because the first cannot have *"ila hin"* connected to it, since that would entail separating the verbal noun from its complement with a conjunction, and a verbal noun taken as a relative clause cannot be separated from its complement. For the verbal noun here is not a relative clause. The verbal noun is of two kinds: one in which occurrence is considered, and it is then estimated with a verbal particle followed by the verb, and this is the relative clause. It is a relative clause in terms of its being estimated with that particle, which is joined to the verb. Otherwise, the verbal noun as such is not a relative clause. The other kind is one in which occurrence is not considered, such as the example: "For Zayd is knowledge of grammar, and insight into medicine, and for him is intelligence, the intelligence of the wise." Such a verbal noun is not estimated with a verbal particle and a verb. Grammarians have even stated that when this kind of verbal noun is put into a construct, the noun following it is not governed in the nominative or accusative, but is in the genitive. They said: When you say "The standing of Zayd pleases me," Zayd is the subject of standing, its estimate being: "I am pleased that Zayd stands." It is possible that Zayd is devoid of standing, and it is not intended to inform the addressee that he performed the standing in the past or will perform it in the future. Rather, the intention in the statement is like the intention in "The ring of Zayd pleases me," where the ring is known as belonging to its owner and is in the genitive as a verbal noun. In this manner it is not made nominative, nor is it emphasised, nor is it described, nor is it conjoined to, except with what is used with genitive nouns in their proper form. End of quotation.

[p. 165] You see them permitting that it not be a relative pronoun (mawsul) with the verbal noun that can be a relative pronoun, which is their saying: "The standing of Zayd pleases me." So how much more so with what cannot be a relative pronoun, like the example we gave of his saying: "He has the intelligence (dhaka') of the wise," and "a sight (basar) for medicine," and the like. Thus "a dwelling (mustaqarr) and a provision (mata')" is of the kind that is not a relative pronoun.

It is not impossible that it (the verbal noun) governs the prepositional phrase (jar wa-majrur), even if it is not a relative pronoun, as we gave the example of his saying: "He has knowledge of grammar (ma'rifa bi-l-nahw)." This is because the adverbial phrase (zarf), the prepositional phrase, and the genitive phrase are governed in them by the traces of verbs (rawa'ih al-af'al), even proper names, like their saying: "I am Abu l-Minhal at times, and I am the son of Mawiyya when the striking became severe." But as for governing the subject (fa'il) or the direct object (maf'ul bihi), no.

As for if we adopt the view of the Kufans, which is that the verbal noun, when it takes tanwin or when the definite article (al) enters upon it, its nominality is established and its implicit verbal sense is removed from it. So it ceases from producing a case ending (i'rab), and its case becomes like that of Zayd, 'Amr, the man, and the garment. Then it is also possible that the saying of Him, exalted is He, ﴿A dwelling and a provision for a time﴾ be construed accordingly. [p. 165 continues] On this reading it is not far-fetched that the prepositional phrase be attached to each of them, because in them there is latitude that does not exist in other than them, and because the verbal noun in that case is no more remote in governing the adverbial or prepositional phrase than the proper noun is.

The saying ﴿A dwelling and a provision for a time﴾ can be explained by His saying: ﴿He said: In it you shall live, and in it you shall die, and from it you shall be brought forth﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:25). In His saying "for a time" there is evidence of the non-permanence on earth, and evidence of the Return (ma'ad). In this verse there is a warning against opposing the command of God, whether intentionally or by interpretation, and that opposition removes one from the station of guardianship (wilaya).

* *

﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾. Talaqqa: it is the form tafa''ala (the derived form) from liqa' (meeting). Here it carries the meaning of the bare form (tajarrud), i.e., "met (laqiya)," like their saying: "This matter overtook you (ta'addaka)," in the sense of "passed you ('addaka)." This is one of the meanings for which the form tafa''ala has come, and they are seventeen meanings in the sense of being the reflexive of fa''ala, like: "I broke it, so it broke (takassara)"; and the effort (takalluf), like: "he feigned a dream (tahallama)"; and avoidance (tajannub), like: "he avoided (tajannaba)"; and becoming (sayyura), like: "he suffered pain (ta'allama)"; and being characterized by the thing derived from it, like: "he put on a shirt (taqammasa)"; and performing the action with it, like: "he took the suhur meal (tasahhara)"; and taking as, like: "I adopted the boy (tabanaytu al-sabiy)"; and continuity of action over a period, like: "he understood gradually (tafahhama)"; and agreement with istaf'ala, like: "he became proud (takabbara)"; and agreement with the bare form, like: "he overstepped the thing (ta'adda al-shay')," i.e., "overstepped it ('adda-hu)"; and dispensing with it, like: "he spoke (takallama)"; and dispensing with a verb, like: "he cooked (tawbala)"; and agreement with fa''ala, like: "he turned away (tawalla)," i.e., "turned (wallaa)"; and deception (khitl), like: "I deceived him (ta'aqqaltu-hu)"; and expectation, like: "he feared him (takhawwafa-hu)"; and seeking, like: "his needs are fulfilled (tunjazu hawa'ijuhu)"; and multiplicity, like: "you give us much (tu'tina)."

The meaning of receiving the words is: taking them and accepting them; or understanding; or insight; or inspiration; or learning and acting upon them; or seeking forgiveness and asking to be released from sin. As for the view of the one who claims that its origin is talaqqana, so that the nun was changed to alif, it is weak, even though the meaning is sound. This is because that does not occur except in what has its second and third radicals of one kind, like: tazanna, taqadda, tasarra, the origin of which is: tazannana, taqaddada, tasarrara. And one does not say in taqabbala: taqabba.

The majority read "Adam" with a nominative ending (raf') and "the words" with an accusative ending (nasb); Ibn Kathir reversed this. The meaning of the words "received by Adam" is that they reached him, because whoever receives you, you have received him; so it is as if He said: "words came to Adam from his Lord." The apparent sense of His saying "words" is that they are a sentence containing words, or sentences of speech which Adam uttered. Therefore they supposed, after His saying "words," an omitted sentence, which is: "So he said them, and He relented toward him."

They differed about the identification of those words in several views, and they lengthened by mentioning them. God has not informed us of them except in a vague manner. We mention them as the exegetes have mentioned them. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Ibn Ka'b, 'Ata' al-Khurasani, al-Dahhak, 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, and Ibn Zayd said: they are "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us..." (Al-A'raf 7:23), the verse.

It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that the most beloved speech to God is what our father (Adam) said when he committed the sin: "Glory be to You, O God, and praise be to You; blessed is Your name and exalted is Your majesty. There is no god but You. I have wronged myself, so forgive me, for none forgives sins but You." Some of the early generation (salaf) were asked what the sinner should say, and he said: he should say what his two parents said: "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves; my Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me," and what Yunus said: "There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been among the wrongdoers." It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Wahb that they are: "Glory be to You, O God, and praise be to You; I have done evil and wronged myself, so forgive me, for You are the best of forgivers." Muhammad ibn Ka'b said they are: "There is no god but You; glory be to You, O God, and praise be to You; I have done evil and wronged myself, so relent toward me, for You are the Relenting, the Merciful." Al-Suddi related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "My Lord, did You not create me with Your hand?" He said: "Yes." "Did You not breathe into me of Your spirit?" He said: "Yes." "Did Your mercy not precede Your wrath?" He said: "Yes." "Did You not settle me in Your Garden?" He said: "Yes." He said: "My Lord, if I repent and do right, will You return me to the Garden?" He said: "Yes." Qatada added to this: "And Your mercy preceded Your wrath toward me?" It was said to him: "Yes." He said: "My Lord, did You write this against me before You created me?" It was said to him: "Yes." He said: "My Lord, if I repent and do right, will You return me to the Garden?" It was said to him: "Yes." Qatada said they are: "I ask Your forgiveness and turn to You; You are the Relenting, the Merciful." 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: "My Lord, is my sin which I committed something You wrote against me before You created me, or something I originated of my own accord?" He said: "Rather, it is something I wrote against you before I created you." He said: "Then as You wrote it against me, forgive me." It was said that they are: "Glory be to You, O God; there is no god but You. I have wronged myself, so forgive me, for You are the [p. 166] Forgiving." It was said: he saw written on the leg of the Throne "Muhammad is the Messenger of God," so he interceded through it, and that is the words. It was said: it is his saying when he sneezed: "Praise be to God." It was said: they are supplication, shame, and weeping. It was said: seeking forgiveness, regret, and grief. Ibn 'Atiyya said: He called them "words" metaphorically, because what they are in their creation proceeds from words, which are: "Be" (kun) in each of them. This view implies that Adam said nothing except the well-known seeking of forgiveness. End of his speech.

﴿And He relented toward him﴾: that is, He graciously accepted his repentance and singled him out in the report of relenting toward him, even though his wife was a partner with him in the matter of dwelling (in the Garden), the prohibition against approaching the tree, receiving the words, and repentance. This is because he was the one addressed with the command and the prohibition, and she followed him in that. So the story was completed by mentioning him alone, as it came in the story of Moses and al-Khidr, when it says: ﴿Until, when they boarded the ship﴾ (Al-Kahf 18:71), and they (the two) bored a hole in it without a reason. Joshua was with Moses, but he was a follower of Moses, so he was not mentioned and was not joined with them in the pronoun. Or he was content with mentioning one of them, since their action was one, as in His saying: ﴿God and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ (Al-Tawba 9:62), and ﴿So let him not expel you both from the Garden, so that you will be wretched﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:117). Or he omitted her mention, as he omitted it when mentioning the disobedience in His saying: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord and went astray﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:121).

The omission of mention of women has come in most of the Qur'an and the Sunna. He did mention her in His saying: ﴿They both said: Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:23). He did not observe this covering in the case of the wives of Noah and Lot, because they were both disbelievers, and they were given as an example for the disbelievers, because their sins were extreme in ugliness and indecency. The disbeliever does not merit being covered or having his sin overlooked; rather he is called out so that this is more disgraceful to him and lower for his rank. Eve was not like that. Also, their disobedience was repeated, and disbelief and persistence in it continued from them, and repentance was impossible because it had preceded in God's knowledge that they would not repent. Eve was not like that, because what happened from her was light, or because she returned to her Lord. Also, rebuke of the sinner is legislated with the hope of his giving up, and this meaning is bound up in them. Mentioning them with reference to their husbands carries a fame which mentioning their names without reference to them does not carry. The repentance of the servant is his return from disobedience, and God's repentance toward the servant is His turning toward him with acceptance and mercy.

There is disagreement about the repentance required of the servant. Some people said: it is regret, relying on the apparent sense of his saying, may God bless him and grant him peace: "Regret is repentance." Others said: its conditions are three: regret for what has passed, giving it up, and resolving not to return to it. They interpreted regret as repentance, meaning it is the greater part of repentance, like: "The Hajj is Arafat." Some added to the conditions: returning wrongful takings if he is able to return them. Some added: lawful food. Al-Qaffal said: along with those three conditions there must be apprehension (ishfaq) in between, because he is commanded to repent, and he has no way to be certain that he has done it as it was obligatory upon him; so he is fearful. For this reason he came warning of the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that Adam and Eve wept over what they had lost of the bliss of the Garden for two hundred years. They mentioned about the abundance of the tears of Adam and David something that exceeds counting in abundance. Shahr ibn Hawshab said: I have been told that when Adam was sent down to the earth, he remained for three hundred years not raising his head, out of shame before God, exalted is He. It is narrated that God relented toward Adam on the Day of 'Ashura.

The majority read "Indeed He" (innahu) with a kasra on the hamza. Nawfal ibn Abi 'Aqrab read "that He" (annahu) with a fatha on the hamza. Its reasoning is that he made it fatha as an causal clause, the estimate being: "because He." The one with fatha together with what follows it is a complement (fadla), since it is in the sense of a single established noun, a settled occurrence whose establishment is beyond dispute, in which no disputant can contend. As for the kasra, it is a complete established sentence brought forth in the manner of an independent established report, and yet it has a semantic connection to what precedes it, as it came in: ﴿And I do not absolve myself; indeed the soul is much enjoining of evil﴾ (Yusuf 12:53); ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord; indeed the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing﴾ (Al-Hajj 22:1); ﴿And pray for them; indeed your prayer is a comfort for them﴾ (Al-Tawba 9:103). So much so that if the fa' which gives the connection were put in its place, it would suffice in place of it. They said: "inna" is only used to confirm what the addressee doubts about its affirmation or denial. If one of the two matters is decided, it is not among its proper contexts. If it occurs governing what is decided with one of the two matters openly, then that is because the speaker has placed it in the position of one who is doubtful about it for some reason. The discussion of that will come, God willing, in such as: ﴿Indeed you, after that, will surely die﴾ (Al-Mu'minun 23:15). [p. 167]

Thus the emphasis is strengthened by another emphatic device, the pronoun-word (huwa) in ﴿إنَّهُ هو التَّوّابُ الرَّحِيمُ﴾. We have already mentioned its benefit in the discussion of ﴿وأُولَئِكَ هُمُ المُفْلِحُونَ﴾. The two attributes that follow it are also intensified: at-Tawwab is in the form of fa''al, and ar-Rahim is in the form of fa'il. Both are among the patterns coined to express intensity (mubalaghah, intensive emphasis). All of this is an encouragement from God Most High to the servant to repent and return to obedience, and an arousing of hope in His pardon and His beneficence toward whoever turns to Him. At-Tawwab is one of God's names, meaning the One who greatly accepts the repentance of His servant, or the One who greatly helps him to repent. This name occurs in the Book of God both in the definite and the indefinite form, and God has described Himself with it, which shows that it is among the names that He has reserved for Himself. Some scholars held that God is described by it only figuratively. They agreed that God is not described as ta'ib (one who repents), a'ib (one who returns), raqqa' (one who frequently returns), or muneeb (one who turns penitently). A distinction is drawn between applying it to God and applying it to the servant, because their relations differ. Do you not see ﴿فَتابَ عَلَيْهِ﴾ and ﴿وتُوبُوا إلى اللَّهِ﴾? So God's repentance toward the servant is His turning toward him and bestowing favor upon him, while the servant's repentance is his return to obedience of God Most High, seeking reward, or fearing punishment, or seeking elevation of rank. He followed the first attribute with the attribute of mercy, because the acceptance of repentance is caused by God's mercy toward His servant. The placement of at-Tawwab first is for its correspondence with ﴿فَتابَ عَلَيْهِ﴾, and for the good closing of the verse-ending with ﴿الرَّحِيمِ﴾. The discussion of the basmalah concerning the word ar-Rahim and what relates to it has already preceded, so that suffices and need not be repeated.

﴿قُلْنا اهْبِطُوا﴾: He repeated the saying. This is either for pure emphasis, since the cause of the descent was the first act of disobedience, so He repeated it as a reminder of that. Or it is because their objects differ: the first is linked to enmity, and the second is linked to the coming of guidance. Others said these are not for emphasis, but are two actual descents: the first from the Garden to the heavens, and the second from the heavens to the earth. This view is weakened by His saying concerning the first descent: ﴿ولَكم في الأرْضِ مُسْتَقَرٌّ﴾, since settlement on this interpretation would only have been achieved by the second descent. Therefore, settlement should have been mentioned in the second descent, and the second descent should have been stated with the phrase ﴿مِنها﴾. The apparent reference of the pronoun is to the Garden, which requires that the second descent be from both of them.

﴿جَمِيعًا﴾ is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿اهْبِطُوا﴾. The discussion of the word jami'an has already preceded, and that it implies generality in the judgment, not simultaneity in time, in the commentary on the saying of God Most High: ﴿هُوَ الَّذِي خَلَقَ لَكم ما في الأرْضِ جَمِيعًا﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29]. Here it indicates that all of them were addressed with the descent, so the two words together indicate the unity of the time of the descent. Ibn 'Atiyyah went too far when he said: "It is as if he said: a descent altogether (hubutan jami'an), or descending altogether (habitina jami'an)," making it an attribute of an omitted verbal noun or an omitted active participle, each of which is indicated by the verb. He said: "Because jami'an is neither a verbal noun nor an active participle, and his supposition contradicts the judgment he had stated, for he said first that jami'an is a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun in uhbitu. If it is a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun in uhbitu according to what he established first, then how can it be supposed a second time?" It is as if he said: "descent altogether, or descending altogether." So his final statement contradicts his initial judgment, and his position that it is not a verbal noun or an active participant does not prevent its occurring as a circumstantial accusative, so that he would be forced into this supposition. Others also went too far in their claim that the implied meaning is: "And We said: Descend, gathered together, so they descended altogether," making a circumstantial accusative omitted and indicated by jami'an, and an omitted governing word indicated by uhbitu. This supposition does not fit with what follows except by assuming an implied saying, that is: "So We said: If there comes to you..." (fa-qulna: imma ya'tiyannakum).

The discussion of those commanded to descend has already preceded. On the supposition that it is a second descent, it is said that it refers specifically to Adam and Eve, because Iblis does not receive guidance. They were addressed with the plural form to honor them. It is also said that it includes Iblis in the address, because Iblis is by consensus addressed to believe.

﴿إمّا﴾: in is conditional, and ma after it is extra, for emphasis. The nun in ﴿يَأْتِيَنَّكم﴾ is the nun of emphasis. This type of construction occurs frequently in the Qur'an: ﴿فَإمّا تَرَيِنَّ﴾, ﴿وإمّا يَنْزَغَنَّكَ﴾, ﴿فَإمّا نَذْهَبَنَّ﴾. Abu al-'Abbas al-Mahdawi said: "In is the conditional particle to which ma of emphasis has been added, so that the nun of emphasis can attach to the verb. If ma were dropped, that is, if the nun were not attached, the emphasis would fall at the beginning of the sentence and the nun at its end." Ibn 'Atiyyah followed him in this, saying: "If in is conditional, then ma has entered after it emphatically, so that the heavy nun can attach, and it is like the lam of oath that comes with the nun." End of his statement.

What these two have held, that the nun is obligatory with the conditional verb when in is joined to ma, is the view of al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj, who claimed that it is obligatory in imitation of the ma added for emphasis after the lam of oath, as in: "By God, I will surely go out." They claimed that omitting the nun when ma is added after in is a necessity of poetry. Sibawayh, al-Farisi, and a group of earlier scholars held that this is not restricted to poetic necessity, and that it is permissible in speech to include or omit it, although inclusion is better. Likewise it is permissible to omit ma and include the nun. Sibawayh said in this matter: "If you wish, you do not insert the nun, just as if you wish, you do not bring ma." End of his statement.

Omitting the nun after imma has been frequently attested. Ash-Shanfara said:

*"If you see me like the daughter of the sand, going about in the heat, in tender feet, going barefoot without sandals,"*

Another said:

*"O companion, if you find me not one of ready friendship, then abandoning brothers is not my character."*

Another said:

*"Tumadir claimed that if I die, her youngest sons will make my friendship bitter."*

Analogy also permits this, because ma is added where the nun cannot attach, as in the poet's saying:

*"Whether I stay or whether I am traveling, God guards what you leave and what you take."*

Just as ma appears here as extra after in, so also in a construction such as imma taqum ya'tiyannakum, the final vowel is fixed. There is disagreement over whether this fatha is a fixed vowel of the building, or whether it was built on sukun and vowelled with fatha because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. We have clarified this in our book called al-Takmil li-Sharh al-Tashil.

﴿مِنِّي﴾ is related to ﴿يَأْتِيَنَّكم﴾. This resembles iltifat (a shift in grammatical person), because it moves from the pronoun for the plural, or for the self-magnifying speaker, to the pronoun specific to the singular first person. We have mentioned the wisdom of that pronoun in ﴿قُلْنا﴾, in the explanation of His saying: ﴿وقُلْنا ياآدَمُ اسْكُنْ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 35]. The wisdom of this shift here is that guidance comes only from Him alone, so the specific pronoun suits the fact that there is no guide but Him, Most High. He therefore gave the specific one, which no one else shares, the specific pronoun that cannot refer to anyone other than God Most High. In His saying ﴿مِنِّي﴾ there is an indication that all good comes from Him. For this reason it says: ﴿قَدْ جاءَكم بِرِهانٌ مِن رَبِّكم وقَدْ جاءَتْكم مَوْعِظَةٌ مِن رَبِّكم وشِفاءٌ﴾. He used the word min, which indicates origin in things, to draw attention to the fact that this proceeds from Him and originates from the side of God Most High. He used the conditional particle in ﴿فَإمّا يَأْتِيَنَّكم مِنِّي هُدًى﴾, and it is applied to what is uncertain in its occurrence. But the coming of guidance is certain without doubt, since the time of its coming is left unspecified. Or it is because it signals that the affirmation of God Most High's oneness is not conditional upon the sending of messengers from Him, nor upon the sending down of books concerning it. Rather, even if He had not sent messengers or sent down books, belief in Him would still be obligatory, because of the reason He placed within them and the proofs He set before them, and the capacity for inference that He gave them. As someone said:

*"In everything there is a sign for Him, indicating that He is One."*

Az-Zamakhshari stated this meaning, though without reciting the poetry.

﴿هُدًى﴾: the discussion of guidance has already preceded in His saying ﴿هُدًى لِلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾. It is indefinite because the intended meaning is the unrestricted sense, and no prior reference has preceded that would require it to be definite. The guidance mentioned here is: the revealed books, or the messengers, or clarification, or the capacity to obey, or Muhammad (ﷺ) as Messenger of God. These are the views.

﴿فَمَن تَبِعَ﴾: the fa' together with what follows it is the response to His saying ﴿فَإمّا يَأْتِيَنَّكم﴾. As-Sijawandi said: "The response is omitted, and its estimated form is: then follow it." End of his statement. So it seems that in his view it was omitted, indicated by His subsequent saying: ﴿فَمَن تَبِعَ هُدايَ﴾.

The statements of the exegetes and grammarians agree that man in His saying ﴿فَمَن تَبِعَ﴾ is conditional, and that the response to this condition is His saying ﴿فَلا خَوْفٌ﴾. Thus the verse contains two conditions. It is related from al-Kisa'i that His saying ﴿فَلا خَوْفٌ﴾ is the response to both conditions together. We have thoroughly examined the question of the joining of two conditions in the book al-Takmil. In my view, man need not be conditional; it may be relative, and indeed this is preferred, because of His saying in its counterpart: ﴿والَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا وكَذَّبُوا﴾, where He used the relative form. Then ﴿فَلا خَوْفٌ﴾ would be a clause in the position of the predicate. As for the fa' entering a clause that serves as a predicate, the conditions that permit this are present here.

In the phrase ﴿فَمَن تَبِعَ هُدايَ﴾, guidance is treated as an imam (leader) who is followed and taken as a model, so the movements and stillnesses of the follower agree with those of the one he follows, which is guidance. In that case fear and grief depart from him. In attributing guidance to Himself there is an exaltation of guidance that would not exist if it were defined with the article, although the usual manner for such a case is to use the article, as in His saying: ﴿إلى فِرْعَوْنَ رَسُولًا فَعَصى فِرْعَوْنُ الرَّسُولَ﴾. Idafah (the genitive construction) conveys the sense of definiteness that the article conveys, and it adds to that the distinction of exaltation and honor.

Al-A'raj read ﴿هُدايْ﴾ with a quiescent yaʾ, which involves joining two quiescent letters, like the reading of those who read ﴿ومَحْيايْ﴾, and this is treating the connected form as if it were a pause. 'Asim al-Jahdari, 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ishaq, and 'Isa ibn Abi 'Umar read ﴿هُدِيِّي﴾, converting the alif into a yaʾ and assimilating it into the yaʾ of the first person, since it was not possible to vowel with kasra the letter before the yaʾ, because it is a letter that does not accept vowelling. This is the dialect of Hudhayl, who convert the alif of the maqsur (defective noun) into a yaʾ and assimilate it into the yaʾ of the first person. Their poet said:

*"They preceded my passion and hurried after their own desires, so they were cut off, and every people has its place of fall."*

(فَلا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ): The majority of reciters (al-Jumhur) read it with *raf'* (nominative) and *tanwin* (nunation). Al-Zuhri, 'Isa al-Thaqafi and Ya'qub read it with *fath* (accusative) throughout the Qur'an. Ibn Muhaysin, according to a variant reported from him, read it with *raf'* without *tanwin*. The reasoning behind the majority reading is to match the *raf'* in (وَلا هُمْ يَحْزَنُونَ), so they used *raf'* for parallelism. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The *raf'* is based on treating (لا) as operating like (لَيْسَ)." But what he said is not necessarily fixed. The better view is that it is *marfu'* as a subject (*mubtada'*) for two reasons. The first: making (لا) operate like (لَيْسَ) is very rare, its authenticity can be disputed, and even if it is authentic, its analogical extension can be disputed. The second: parallelism is achieved between the two clauses, since (لا) would then have entered both clauses upon a subject without governing either of them. The reasoning behind al-Zuhri's reading and that of those who agree with him is that it is an explicit text on generality, negating every individual instance of the meaning of fear. As for the *raf'*, it permits this but is not an explicit text. So they took what indicates generality by explicit text over what indicates it by apparent meaning. As for the reading of Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn 'Atiyya interpreted it as the operation of (لا) like (لَيْسَ), and that he omitted the *tanwin* for lightness due to frequent usage. We have already mentioned what is involved in making (لا) operate like (لَيْسَ). So the better view is that it is a subject, as we have stated, when it is *marfu'* and *munawwan*, and its *tanwin* is dropped as he said, due to frequent usage. It is also possible that it is without *tanwin* because it is intended with (ال) (the definite article), so the implied meaning would be: "There is no the fear upon them." This would be like what al-Akhfash related from the Arabs: "Salamun 'alaykum" without *tanwin*. They said they intend "as-salamu 'alaykum." This interpretation is better, since parallelism is achieved in that (لا) enters upon a definite noun in both clauses. When (لا) enters upon definites, it is not treated like (لَيْسَ). A verse of this usage has been heard from al-Nabigha al-Ja'di, and the grammarians interpreted it. It is:

*Wa-halat sawada al-qalbi la ana baghiyan*
*siwaha wa-la fi hubbiha mutarakhiyan*

And they [the grammarians] have faulted Abu al-Tayyib for his statement:

*Fa-la al-hamdu maksuban wa-la al-mali baqiyan*

By his statement "*'alayhim*" he metaphorically expressed domination and encompassment, and the meaning was placed in the position of a body. He negated that it was superior and dominating over them. In this there is a subtle indication that fear is not entirely negated. Do you not see that the negation falls upon the state of fear being upon them? And the state of fear dominating does not necessarily entail the negation of fear in every condition. For this reason some exegetes said: "The statement *'fa-la khawfun 'alayhim'* is not evidence for negating the terrors of the Day of Resurrection and its fears from the obedient, in view of what Allah and His Messenger described of the severities of the Resurrection, (p-170) except that they are lightened for the obedient. When they arrive at His mercy, it is as if they had not feared." He placed the negation of fear before the negation of grief, because the negation of fear regarding what is yet to come is more emphatic than the negation of grief over what has passed. For this reason, its clause was presented beginning with the indefinite noun, which is more intensive in the domain of negation, while the second was presented beginning with the definite in his statement "*wa-la hum yahzanun*."

In his statement "*wa-la hum yahzanun*" there is an indication that they are specifically free of grief, and that others do grieve. Had he not intended this meaning, "*wa-la yahzanun*" would have been sufficient. For this reason he mentioned the negation of grief from them and its removal in his statement "*inna alladhina sabaqat lahum...*" up to his statement "*la yahzunuhum al-fazaʿ al-akbar wa-tatalaqqahum al-malaʾika*" [al-Anbiya: 103]. It is known that these two reports and what precedes them of the report are specific to those for whom the best reward from Allah has preceded. And in his statement "*al-hamdu lillahi alladhi adhhaba 'anna al-hazan*" [Fatir: 34], all of this indicates that others are grieved by the terror, and grief does not depart from them. Views have been reported from the exegetes regarding the interpretation of this sentence:

First: There is no fear upon them regarding what they will face of punishment, and they will not grieve at death.
Second: They do not anticipate any harm in the future, nor do they grieve over the loss of what was desired in the past and present.
Third: There is no fear upon them regarding what lies ahead of them, nor do they grieve over what is behind them.
Fourth: There is no fear upon them regarding what lies before them of the Hereafter, nor do they grieve over what has escaped them of the world.
Fifth: There is no fear upon them of punishment, nor do they grieve over the loss of reward.
Sixth: Fear is the sensing of distress over the loss of something sought, and grief is the sensing of distress over the loss of something beloved.
Seventh: There is no fear upon them regarding what lies before them of the world, nor do they grieve over what has escaped them of it.
Eighth: There is no fear upon them on the Day of Resurrection, nor do they grieve therein.
Ninth: He indicated that He will admit them into Paradise, which is the abode of joy and security, where there is no fear upon them nor grief.
Tenth: What Ibn Zayd said: "There is no fear upon them before them. Nothing is greater in the breast of one who dies than what comes after death, so Allah granted them security from it. Then He consoled them about the world, and they will not grieve over what they left behind after their death in the world."
Eleventh: There is no fear when the Fire is closed, and no grief when Death is slaughtered in the form of a ram on the Bridge, and it is said to the people of Paradise and the Fire: "Eternity, with no death."
Twelfth: There is no fear and no grief forever.

All these views are close in meaning. The apparent meaning of the verse is the general negation of fear and grief from them, but it is restricted to what comes after the world, because in the abode of the world the believer may indeed be touched by fear and grief, so it is not possible to take the verse in its general apparent sense in that respect.

(وَالَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا): This is the counterpart (*qasim*) to his statement "*fa-man tabiʿa hudaya*," and it is more eloquent than saying "*wa-man lam yattabiʿ hudaya*," although the verbal division would require it. This is because the negation of a thing can occur in several ways. Among them: lack of receptivity, either by nature or heedlessness; and among them: deliberately abandoning something. So the counterpart was presented with his statement "*wa-alladhina kafaru*" in an affirmative form, so as to remove the possibility that negation would imply. Since *kufr* can mean ingratitude for blessings and disobedience, he clarified that what is intended here is *shirk* (polytheism), with his statement "*wa-kadhdhabu bi-ayatina*." "*Bi-ayatina*" is connected to his statement "*wa-kadhdhabu*," and it is a case of operation of the second (*'amal al-thani*). If we say that "*kafaru*" requires it in meaning, then it is from that operation; if we say it does not require it, then it is not from that operation, and it may bear either possibility. The "*ayat*" here are: the books revealed to all nations; or the miracles of the prophets, upon them be prayers and peace; or the Qur'an; or the signs of Allah in His creations. These are the views.

"*Ula'ika*" is the subject (*mubtada'*), "*ashab*" is its predicate, and the sentence is the predicate of "*alladhina kafaru*." They also permitted that "*ula'ika*" be an apposition (*badal*) and an explanatory appositive (*'atf al-bayan*), in which case "*ashab al-nar*" would be the predicate of "*alladhina kafaru*." In his statement "*ula'ika ashab al-nar*" there is an indication that those who disbelieved and denied are specifically [for] the Fire, and so it is understood that those who followed guidance are the people of Paradise. The counterpart division required that whoever follows guidance has no fear and no grief reaching him, and he is the companion of Paradise; and whoever denies, fear and grief reach him, and he is the companion of the Fire. So it is as if something was omitted from the first clause that is mentioned in its counterpart in the second clause, and from the second clause something was omitted that is mentioned in its counterpart in the first clause. It thus becomes like the statement of the poet:

(p-171)
*Wa-inni la-taʿrunI li-dhikirin fatratun*
*kama intafada al-ʿusfuru ballahu al-qatru*

In his statement "*ula'ika*" there is an indication to the entities characterized by disbelief and denial, and it seems there is a repetition and emphasis of the earlier mentioned subject. *Suhba* (companionship) means being joined to something, and in common usage it generally applies to constant attachment, although its original linguistic sense is applying to mere joining. What is meant here is lasting attachment, which is why he emphasized it with his statement "*hum fiha khalidun*" (they will abide therein). It is possible that this sentence is in a circumstantial position (*hal*), as occurs elsewhere: "*ula'ika ashab al-jannati khalidina fiha*," in which case it would have a place in grammatical analysis (*i'rab*) in the accusative. It is also possible that it is an explanatory sentence clarifying what he warned them of in his statement "*ula'ika ashab al-nar*," so it explains and makes clear that this companionship is not intended as mere joining, but as eternal abiding; in that case it has no place in grammatical analysis. It is also possible that it is a second predicate of the subject "*ula'ika*," so he has predicated two things of it: one singular, and the other a sentence; this is according to the view of one who holds that, in which case it is in the nominative position. The discussion of *khulud* (eternal abiding) has already preceded, namely whether it is remaining for a time without end, or for a time that has an end.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 36–39 (part 1 of 5):

﴿Then Satan caused them to slip from it, and removed them from that in which they were. And We said: "Go down, some of you enemies to others. On the earth you will have a dwelling place and provision for a time."﴾ ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words, and He turned to him in forgiveness. Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿We said: "Go down from it, all of you. Then when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.﴾ ﴿And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs, those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾

Azalla (to cause to slip): from zalal, which is the stumbling of the foot. It is said: "his foot slipped" and "the sandal slipped with him." Zalal in opinion and reasoning is figurative. Azala (to remove) is from zawal, and its root meaning is removal. The hamza in both verbs is for transitivity (ta'diyah).

Al-hubut (descending): it is nuzul (descent), the verbal noun of habata. Its present tense is yahbitu and yahbutu, with the ba' vowelled either with kasra or damma. Al-habut with a fatha is the place of descent. Al-Mufaddal said: al-hubut is going out from a town, and it is also entering it, and these are antonyms. It is said figuratively of lowering of rank. For this reason al-Farra' said: al-hubut is humiliation. Labid said:

"If they are envied, they will be brought down one day, and if they are commanded..."

Ba'd (some): its origin is the verbal noun of ba'ada, yab'adu, ba'dan, meaning "he cut off." It is applied to a part, and its opposite is kull (all). Both are definite in eloquent speech, since a circumstantial clause (hal) comes from them. They say: "I passed by some standing" and "by all sitting." The idafa (genitive construction) is intended with both, and therefore the alif and lam do not enter upon them. For this reason they erred against Abu al-Qasim al-Zajjaji in his saying: "Ba'd is substituted from kull." The pronoun refers back to ba'd when a group is intended, singular and plural. Likewise the predicate, the circumstantial, and the attribute may be singular or plural in that case.

Al-'aduww (enemy): from 'adawa, which is transgression of the limit. It is said: "so-and-so transgressed his bounds" when he exceeded them. It is also said: al-'adawa is distance in the hearts, from 'udwayy al-jabal, which are its two sides, named so because of the distance between them. It is also said: from 'adā, meaning "he did wrong." All these meanings are close. Al-'aduww applies to the singular, the dual, and the plural, the masculine and the feminine. It has been pluralized as a'da', and it has been feminized, and they said 'aduwwa. From this: ﴿'aduwwat anfusihinna﴾ (the women's self-interest, lit. "their own enemies" in the feminine). Al-Farra' said: the Arabs said to a woman: "'aduwwat Allah," and some of them dropped the ha'.

Al-mustaqarr (dwelling place): mustaf'al from qarar, which is staying and residing. It may be a verbal noun, a time, or a place, because it comes from a verb of more than three letters, so it takes the form of the passive participle for these meanings. For this reason the earth is called qararah. The poet said:

"Every abundant eye poured upon him, so they left every qararah like a dirham."

Istaf'ala here has the meaning of fa'ala: istaqarra and qarra have the same meaning.

Al-mata' (provision): the sustenance sufficient for the moment. It is taken from mata'a al-nahar, meaning "when the day rose high." It applies to what a person acquires of the goods of this world. It is also applied to provision for the journey, to the enjoyment of women, from which: ﴿fa-ma istamta'tum bihi minhunna﴾ (An-Nisa 24), the mut'ah marriage, to clothing (wa-mattiuhunna), and to long life: ﴿yumatti'kum matan hasanan﴾ (Hud 3). They said: from this comes amta'a Allah bika, meaning "may God prolong your companionship with us." All of these return to the meaning of sufficiency.

Al-hin (time): the moment and the period. It is not restricted to a specific duration; rather the unrestricted sense was assigned to it.
