It is a relative clause in terms of its being estimated with that particle, which is joined to the verb. Otherwise, the verbal noun as such is not a relative clause. The other kind is one in which occurrence is not considered, such as the example: "For Zayd is knowledge of grammar, and insight into medicine, and for him is intelligence, the intelligence of the wise." Such a verbal noun is not estimated with a verbal particle and a verb. Grammarians have even stated that when this kind of verbal noun is put into a construct, the noun following it is not governed in the nominative or accusative, but is in the genitive. They said: When you say "The standing of Zayd pleases me," Zayd is the subject of standing, its estimate being: "I am pleased that Zayd stands." It is possible that Zayd is devoid of standing, and it is not intended to inform the addressee that he performed the standing in the past or will perform it in the future. Rather, the intention in the statement is like the intention in "The ring of Zayd pleases me," where the ring is known as belonging to its owner and is in the genitive as a verbal noun. In this manner it is not made nominative, nor is it emphasised, nor is it described, nor is it conjoined to, except with what is used with genitive nouns in their proper form. End of quotation.

[p. 165] You see them permitting that it not be a relative pronoun (mawsul) with the verbal noun that can be a relative pronoun, which is their saying: "The standing of Zayd pleases me." So how much more so with what cannot be a relative pronoun, like the example we gave of his saying: "He has the intelligence (dhaka') of the wise," and "a sight (basar) for medicine," and the like. Thus "a dwelling (mustaqarr) and a provision (mata')" is of the kind that is not a relative pronoun.

It is not impossible that it (the verbal noun) governs the prepositional phrase (jar wa-majrur), even if it is not a relative pronoun, as we gave the example of his saying: "He has knowledge of grammar (ma'rifa bi-l-nahw)." This is because the adverbial phrase (zarf), the prepositional phrase, and the genitive phrase are governed in them by the traces of verbs (rawa'ih al-af'al), even proper names, like their saying: "I am Abu l-Minhal at times, and I am the son of Mawiyya when the striking became severe." But as for governing the subject (fa'il) or the direct object (maf'ul bihi), no.

As for if we adopt the view of the Kufans, which is that the verbal noun, when it takes tanwin or when the definite article (al) enters upon it, its nominality is established and its implicit verbal sense is removed from it. So it ceases from producing a case ending (i'rab), and its case becomes like that of Zayd, 'Amr, the man, and the garment. Then it is also possible that the saying of Him, exalted is He, ﴿A dwelling and a provision for a time﴾ be construed accordingly. [p. 165 continues] On this reading it is not far-fetched that the prepositional phrase be attached to each of them, because in them there is latitude that does not exist in other than them, and because the verbal noun in that case is no more remote in governing the adverbial or prepositional phrase than the proper noun is.

The saying ﴿A dwelling and a provision for a time﴾ can be explained by His saying: ﴿He said: In it you shall live, and in it you shall die, and from it you shall be brought forth﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:25). In His saying "for a time" there is evidence of the non-permanence on earth, and evidence of the Return (ma'ad). In this verse there is a warning against opposing the command of God, whether intentionally or by interpretation, and that opposition removes one from the station of guardianship (wilaya).

* *

﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾. Talaqqa: it is the form tafa''ala (the derived form) from liqa' (meeting). Here it carries the meaning of the bare form (tajarrud), i.e., "met (laqiya)," like their saying: "This matter overtook you (ta'addaka)," in the sense of "passed you ('addaka)." This is one of the meanings for which the form tafa''ala has come, and they are seventeen meanings in the sense of being the reflexive of fa''ala, like: "I broke it, so it broke (takassara)"; and the effort (takalluf), like: "he feigned a dream (tahallama)"; and avoidance (tajannub), like: "he avoided (tajannaba)"; and becoming (sayyura), like: "he suffered pain (ta'allama)"; and being characterized by the thing derived from it, like: "he put on a shirt (taqammasa)"; and performing the action with it, like: "he took the suhur meal (tasahhara)"; and taking as, like: "I adopted the boy (tabanaytu al-sabiy)"; and continuity of action over a period, like: "he understood gradually (tafahhama)"; and agreement with istaf'ala, like: "he became proud (takabbara)"; and agreement with the bare form, like: "he overstepped the thing (ta'adda al-shay')," i.e., "overstepped it ('adda-hu)"; and dispensing with it, like: "he spoke (takallama)"; and dispensing with a verb, like: "he cooked (tawbala)"; and agreement with fa''ala, like: "he turned away (tawalla)," i.e., "turned (wallaa)"; and deception (khitl), like: "I deceived him (ta'aqqaltu-hu)"; and expectation, like: "he feared him (takhawwafa-hu)"; and seeking, like: "his needs are fulfilled (tunjazu hawa'ijuhu)"; and multiplicity, like: "you give us much (tu'tina)."

The meaning of receiving the words is: taking them and accepting them; or understanding; or insight; or inspiration; or learning and acting upon them; or seeking forgiveness and asking to be released from sin. As for the view of the one who claims that its origin is talaqqana, so that the nun was changed to alif, it is weak, even though the meaning is sound. This is because that does not occur except in what has its second and third radicals of one kind, like: tazanna, taqadda, tasarra, the origin of which is: tazannana, taqaddada, tasarrara. And one does not say in taqabbala: taqabba.

The majority read "Adam" with a nominative ending (raf') and "the words" with an accusative ending (nasb); Ibn Kathir reversed this. The meaning of the words "received by Adam" is that they reached him, because whoever receives you, you have received him; so it is as if He said: "words came to Adam from his Lord." The apparent sense of His saying "words" is that they are a sentence containing words, or sentences of speech which Adam uttered. Therefore they supposed, after His saying "words," an omitted sentence, which is: "So he said them, and He relented toward him."

They differed about the identification of those words in several views, and they lengthened by mentioning them. God has not informed us of them except in a vague manner. We mention them as the exegetes have mentioned them. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Ibn Ka'b, 'Ata' al-Khurasani, al-Dahhak, 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, and Ibn Zayd said: they are "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us..." (Al-A'raf 7:23), the verse.

It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that the most beloved speech to God is what our father (Adam) said when he committed the sin: "Glory be to You, O God, and praise be to You; blessed is Your name and exalted is Your majesty. There is no god but You. I have wronged myself, so forgive me, for none forgives sins but You." Some of the early generation (salaf) were asked what the sinner should say, and he said: he should say what his two parents said: "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves; my Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me," and what Yunus said: "There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been among the wrongdoers." It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Wahb that they are: "Glory be to You, O God, and praise be to You; I have done evil and wronged myself, so forgive me, for You are the best of forgivers." Muhammad ibn Ka'b said they are: "There is no god but You; glory be to You, O God, and praise be to You; I have done evil and wronged myself, so relent toward me, for You are the Relenting, the Merciful." Al-Suddi related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "My Lord, did You not create me with Your hand?" He said: "Yes." "Did You not breathe into me of Your spirit?" He said: "Yes." "Did Your mercy not precede Your wrath?" He said: "Yes." "Did You not settle me in Your Garden?" He said: "Yes." He said: "My Lord, if I repent and do right, will You return me to the Garden?" He said: "Yes." Qatada added to this: "And Your mercy preceded Your wrath toward me?" It was said to him: "Yes." He said: "My Lord, did You write this against me before You created me?" It was said to him: "Yes." He said: "My Lord, if I repent and do right, will You return me to the Garden?" It was said to him: "Yes." Qatada said they are: "I ask Your forgiveness and turn to You; You are the Relenting, the Merciful." 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: "My Lord, is my sin which I committed something You wrote against me before You created me, or something I originated of my own accord?" He said: "Rather, it is something I wrote against you before I created you." He said: "Then as You wrote it against me, forgive me." It was said that they are: "Glory be to You, O God; there is no god but You. I have wronged myself, so forgive me, for You are the [p. 166] Forgiving." It was said: he saw written on the leg of the Throne "Muhammad is the Messenger of God," so he interceded through it, and that is the words. It was said: it is his saying when he sneezed: "Praise be to God." It was said: they are supplication, shame, and weeping. It was said: seeking forgiveness, regret, and grief. Ibn 'Atiyya said: He called them "words" metaphorically, because what they are in their creation proceeds from words, which are: "Be" (kun) in each of them. This view implies that Adam said nothing except the well-known seeking of forgiveness. End of his speech.

﴿And He relented toward him﴾: that is, He graciously accepted his repentance and singled him out in the report of relenting toward him, even though his wife was a partner with him in the matter of dwelling (in the Garden), the prohibition against approaching the tree, receiving the words, and repentance. This is because he was the one addressed with the command and the prohibition, and she followed him in that. So the story was completed by mentioning him alone, as it came in the story of Moses and al-Khidr, when it says: ﴿Until, when they boarded the ship﴾ (Al-Kahf 18:71), and they (the two) bored a hole in it without a reason. Joshua was with Moses, but he was a follower of Moses, so he was not mentioned and was not joined with them in the pronoun. Or he was content with mentioning one of them, since their action was one, as in His saying: ﴿God and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ (Al-Tawba 9:62), and ﴿So let him not expel you both from the Garden, so that you will be wretched﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:117). Or he omitted her mention, as he omitted it when mentioning the disobedience in His saying: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord and went astray﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:121).

The omission of mention of women has come in most of the Qur'an and the Sunna. He did mention her in His saying: ﴿They both said: Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:23). He did not observe this covering in the case of the wives of Noah and Lot, because they were both disbelievers, and they were given as an example for the disbelievers, because their sins were extreme in ugliness and indecency. The disbeliever does not merit being covered or having his sin overlooked; rather he is called out so that this is more disgraceful to him and lower for his rank. Eve was not like that. Also, their disobedience was repeated, and disbelief and persistence in it continued from them, and repentance was impossible because it had preceded in God's knowledge that they would not repent. Eve was not like that, because what happened from her was light, or because she returned to her Lord. Also, rebuke of the sinner is legislated with the hope of his giving up, and this meaning is bound up in them. Mentioning them with reference to their husbands carries a fame which mentioning their names without reference to them does not carry. The repentance of the servant is his return from disobedience, and God's repentance toward the servant is His turning toward him with acceptance and mercy.

There is disagreement about the repentance required of the servant. Some people said: it is regret, relying on the apparent sense of his saying, may God bless him and grant him peace: "Regret is repentance." Others said: its conditions are three: regret for what has passed, giving it up, and resolving not to return to it. They interpreted regret as repentance, meaning it is the greater part of repentance, like: "The Hajj is Arafat." Some added to the conditions: returning wrongful takings if he is able to return them. Some added: lawful food. Al-Qaffal said: along with those three conditions there must be apprehension (ishfaq) in between, because he is commanded to repent, and he has no way to be certain that he has done it as it was obligatory upon him; so he is fearful. For this reason he came warning of the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that Adam and Eve wept over what they had lost of the bliss of the Garden for two hundred years. They mentioned about the abundance of the tears of Adam and David something that exceeds counting in abundance. Shahr ibn Hawshab said: I have been told that when Adam was sent down to the earth, he remained for three hundred years not raising his head, out of shame before God, exalted is He. It is narrated that God relented toward Adam on the Day of 'Ashura.

The majority read "Indeed He" (innahu) with a kasra on the hamza. Nawfal ibn Abi 'Aqrab read "that He" (annahu) with a fatha on the hamza. Its reasoning is that he made it fatha as an causal clause, the estimate being: "because He." The one with fatha together with what follows it is a complement (fadla), since it is in the sense of a single established noun, a settled occurrence whose establishment is beyond dispute, in which no disputant can contend. As for the kasra, it is a complete established sentence brought forth in the manner of an independent established report, and yet it has a semantic connection to what precedes it, as it came in: ﴿And I do not absolve myself; indeed the soul is much enjoining of evil﴾ (Yusuf 12:53); ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord; indeed the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing﴾ (Al-Hajj 22:1); ﴿And pray for them; indeed your prayer is a comfort for them﴾ (Al-Tawba 9:103). So much so that if the fa' which gives the connection were put in its place, it would suffice in place of it. They said: "inna" is only used to confirm what the addressee doubts about its affirmation or denial. If one of the two matters is decided, it is not among its proper contexts. If it occurs governing what is decided with one of the two matters openly, then that is because the speaker has placed it in the position of one who is doubtful about it for some reason. The discussion of that will come, God willing, in such as: ﴿Indeed you, after that, will surely die﴾ (Al-Mu'minun 23:15). [p. 167]

Thus the emphasis is strengthened by another emphatic device, the pronoun-word (huwa) in ﴿إنَّهُ هو التَّوّابُ الرَّحِيمُ﴾. We have already mentioned its benefit in the discussion of ﴿وأُولَئِكَ هُمُ المُفْلِحُونَ﴾. The two attributes that follow it are also intensified: at-Tawwab is in the form of fa''al, and ar-Rahim is in the form of fa'il. Both are among the patterns coined to express intensity (mubalaghah, intensive emphasis). All of this is an encouragement from God Most High to the servant to repent and return to obedience, and an arousing of hope in His pardon and His beneficence toward whoever turns to Him. At-Tawwab is one of God's names, meaning the One who greatly accepts the repentance of His servant, or the One who greatly helps him to repent. This name occurs in the Book of God both in the definite and the indefinite form, and God has described Himself with it, which shows that it is among the names that He has reserved for Himself. Some scholars held that God is described by it only figuratively. They agreed that God is not described as ta'ib (one who repents), a'ib (one who returns), raqqa' (one who frequently returns), or muneeb (one who turns penitently). A distinction is drawn between applying it to God and applying it to the servant, because their relations differ. Do you not see ﴿فَتابَ عَلَيْهِ﴾ and ﴿وتُوبُوا إلى اللَّهِ﴾? So God's repentance toward the servant is His turning toward him and bestowing favor upon him, while the servant's repentance is his return to obedience of God Most High, seeking reward, or fearing punishment, or seeking elevation of rank. He followed the first attribute with the attribute of mercy, because the acceptance of repentance is caused by God's mercy toward His servant. The placement of at-Tawwab first is for its correspondence with ﴿فَتابَ عَلَيْهِ﴾, and for the good closing of the verse-ending with ﴿الرَّحِيمِ﴾. The discussion of the basmalah concerning the word ar-Rahim and what relates to it has already preceded, so that suffices and need not be repeated.

﴿قُلْنا اهْبِطُوا﴾: He repeated the saying. This is either for pure emphasis, since the cause of the descent was the first act of disobedience, so He repeated it as a reminder of that. Or it is because their objects differ: the first is linked to enmity, and the second is linked to the coming of guidance. Others said these are not for emphasis, but are two actual descents: the first from the Garden to the heavens, and the second from the heavens to the earth. This view is weakened by His saying concerning the first descent: ﴿ولَكم في الأرْضِ مُسْتَقَرٌّ﴾, since settlement on this interpretation would only have been achieved by the second descent. Therefore, settlement should have been mentioned in the second descent, and the second descent should have been stated with the phrase ﴿مِنها﴾. The apparent reference of the pronoun is to the Garden, which requires that the second descent be from both of them.

﴿جَمِيعًا﴾ is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿اهْبِطُوا﴾. The discussion of the word jami'an has already preceded, and that it implies generality in the judgment, not simultaneity in time, in the commentary on the saying of God Most High: ﴿هُوَ الَّذِي خَلَقَ لَكم ما في الأرْضِ جَمِيعًا﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29]. Here it indicates that all of them were addressed with the descent, so the two words together indicate the unity of the time of the descent. Ibn 'Atiyyah went too far when he said: "It is as if he said: a descent altogether (hubutan jami'an), or descending altogether (habitina jami'an)," making it an attribute of an omitted verbal noun or an omitted active participle, each of which is indicated by the verb. He said: "Because jami'an is neither a verbal noun nor an active participle, and his supposition contradicts the judgment he had stated, for he said first that jami'an is a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun in uhbitu. If it is a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun in uhbitu according to what he established first, then how can it be supposed a second time?" It is as if he said: "descent altogether, or descending altogether." So his final statement contradicts his initial judgment, and his position that it is not a verbal noun or an active participant does not prevent its occurring as a circumstantial accusative, so that he would be forced into this supposition. Others also went too far in their claim that the implied meaning is: "And We said: Descend, gathered together, so they descended altogether," making a circumstantial accusative omitted and indicated by jami'an, and an omitted governing word indicated by uhbitu. This supposition does not fit with what follows except by assuming an implied saying, that is: "So We said: If there comes to you..." (fa-qulna: imma ya'tiyannakum).

The discussion of those commanded to descend has already preceded. On the supposition that it is a second descent, it is said that it refers specifically to Adam and Eve, because Iblis does not receive guidance. They were addressed with the plural form to honor them. It is also said that it includes Iblis in the address, because Iblis is by consensus addressed to believe.

﴿إمّا﴾: in is conditional, and ma after it is extra, for emphasis. The nun in ﴿يَأْتِيَنَّكم﴾ is the nun of emphasis. This type of construction occurs frequently in the Qur'an: ﴿فَإمّا تَرَيِنَّ﴾, ﴿وإمّا يَنْزَغَنَّكَ﴾, ﴿فَإمّا نَذْهَبَنَّ﴾. Abu al-'Abbas al-Mahdawi said: "In is the conditional particle to which ma of emphasis has been added, so that the nun of emphasis can attach to the verb. If ma were dropped, that is, if the nun were not attached, the emphasis would fall at the beginning of the sentence and the nun at its end." Ibn 'Atiyyah followed him in this, saying: "If in is conditional, then ma has entered after it emphatically, so that the heavy nun can attach, and it is like the lam of oath that comes with the nun." End of his statement.

What these two have held, that the nun is obligatory with the conditional verb when in is joined to ma, is the view of al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj, who claimed that it is obligatory in imitation of the ma added for emphasis after the lam of oath, as in: "By God, I will surely go out." They claimed that omitting the nun when ma is added after in is a necessity of poetry. Sibawayh, al-Farisi, and a group of earlier scholars held that this is not restricted to poetic necessity, and that it is permissible in speech to include or omit it, although inclusion is better. Likewise it is permissible to omit ma and include the nun. Sibawayh said in this matter: "If you wish, you do not insert the nun, just as if you wish, you do not bring ma." End of his statement.

Omitting the nun after imma has been frequently attested. Ash-Shanfara said:

*"If you see me like the daughter of the sand, going about in the heat, in tender feet, going barefoot without sandals,"*

Another said:

*"O companion, if you find me not one of ready friendship, then abandoning brothers is not my character."*

Another said:

*"Tumadir claimed that if I die, her youngest sons will make my friendship bitter."*

Analogy also permits this, because ma is added where the nun cannot attach, as in the poet's saying:

*"Whether I stay or whether I am traveling, God guards what you leave and what you take."*

Just as ma appears here as extra after in, so also in a construction such as imma taqum ya'tiyannakum, the final vowel is fixed. There is disagreement over whether this fatha is a fixed vowel of the building, or whether it was built on sukun and vowelled with fatha because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. We have clarified this in our book called al-Takmil li-Sharh al-Tashil.

﴿مِنِّي﴾ is related to ﴿يَأْتِيَنَّكم﴾. This resembles iltifat (a shift in grammatical person), because it moves from the pronoun for the plural, or for the self-magnifying speaker, to the pronoun specific to the singular first person. We have mentioned the wisdom of that pronoun in ﴿قُلْنا﴾, in the explanation of His saying: ﴿وقُلْنا ياآدَمُ اسْكُنْ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 35]. The wisdom of this shift here is that guidance comes only from Him alone, so the specific pronoun suits the fact that there is no guide but Him, Most High. He therefore gave the specific one, which no one else shares, the specific pronoun that cannot refer to anyone other than God Most High. In His saying ﴿مِنِّي﴾ there is an indication that all good comes from Him. For this reason it says: ﴿قَدْ جاءَكم بِرِهانٌ مِن رَبِّكم وقَدْ جاءَتْكم مَوْعِظَةٌ مِن رَبِّكم وشِفاءٌ﴾. He used the word min, which indicates origin in things, to draw attention to the fact that this proceeds from Him and originates from the side of God Most High. He used the conditional particle in ﴿فَإمّا يَأْتِيَنَّكم مِنِّي هُدًى﴾, and it is applied to what is uncertain in its occurrence. But the coming of guidance is certain without doubt, since the time of its coming is left unspecified. Or it is because it signals that the affirmation of God Most High's oneness is not conditional upon the sending of messengers from Him, nor upon the sending down of books concerning it. Rather, even if He had not sent messengers or sent down books, belief in Him would still be obligatory, because of the reason He placed within them and the proofs He set before them, and the capacity for inference that He gave them. As someone said:

*"In everything there is a sign for Him, indicating that He is One."*

Az-Zamakhshari stated this meaning, though without reciting the poetry.

﴿هُدًى﴾: the discussion of guidance has already preceded in His saying ﴿هُدًى لِلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾. It is indefinite because the intended meaning is the unrestricted sense, and no prior reference has preceded that would require it to be definite. The guidance mentioned here is: the revealed books, or the messengers, or clarification, or the capacity to obey, or Muhammad (ﷺ) as Messenger of God. These are the views.

﴿فَمَن تَبِعَ﴾: the fa' together with what follows it is the response to His saying ﴿فَإمّا يَأْتِيَنَّكم﴾. As-Sijawandi said: "The response is omitted, and its estimated form is: then follow it." End of his statement. So it seems that in his view it was omitted, indicated by His subsequent saying: ﴿فَمَن تَبِعَ هُدايَ﴾.

The statements of the exegetes and grammarians agree that man in His saying ﴿فَمَن تَبِعَ﴾ is conditional, and that the response to this condition is His saying ﴿فَلا خَوْفٌ﴾. Thus the verse contains two conditions. It is related from al-Kisa'i that His saying ﴿فَلا خَوْفٌ﴾ is the response to both conditions together. We have thoroughly examined the question of the joining of two conditions in the book al-Takmil. In my view, man need not be conditional; it may be relative, and indeed this is preferred, because of His saying in its counterpart: ﴿والَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا وكَذَّبُوا﴾, where He used the relative form. Then ﴿فَلا خَوْفٌ﴾ would be a clause in the position of the predicate. As for the fa' entering a clause that serves as a predicate, the conditions that permit this are present here.

In the phrase ﴿فَمَن تَبِعَ هُدايَ﴾, guidance is treated as an imam (leader) who is followed and taken as a model, so the movements and stillnesses of the follower agree with those of the one he follows, which is guidance. In that case fear and grief depart from him. In attributing guidance to Himself there is an exaltation of guidance that would not exist if it were defined with the article, although the usual manner for such a case is to use the article, as in His saying: ﴿إلى فِرْعَوْنَ رَسُولًا فَعَصى فِرْعَوْنُ الرَّسُولَ﴾. Idafah (the genitive construction) conveys the sense of definiteness that the article conveys, and it adds to that the distinction of exaltation and honor.

Al-A'raj read ﴿هُدايْ﴾ with a quiescent yaʾ, which involves joining two quiescent letters, like the reading of those who read ﴿ومَحْيايْ﴾, and this is treating the connected form as if it were a pause. 'Asim al-Jahdari, 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ishaq, and 'Isa ibn Abi 'Umar read ﴿هُدِيِّي﴾, converting the alif into a yaʾ and assimilating it into the yaʾ of the first person, since it was not possible to vowel with kasra the letter before the yaʾ, because it is a letter that does not accept vowelling. This is the dialect of Hudhayl, who convert the alif of the maqsur (defective noun) into a yaʾ and assimilate it into the yaʾ of the first person. Their poet said:

*"They preceded my passion and hurried after their own desires, so they were cut off, and every people has its place of fall."*

(فَلا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ): The majority of reciters (al-Jumhur) read it with *raf'* (nominative) and *tanwin* (nunation). Al-Zuhri, 'Isa al-Thaqafi and Ya'qub read it with *fath* (accusative) throughout the Qur'an. Ibn Muhaysin, according to a variant reported from him, read it with *raf'* without *tanwin*. The reasoning behind the majority reading is to match the *raf'* in (وَلا هُمْ يَحْزَنُونَ), so they used *raf'* for parallelism. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The *raf'* is based on treating (لا) as operating like (لَيْسَ)." But what he said is not necessarily fixed. The better view is that it is *marfu'* as a subject (*mubtada'*) for two reasons. The first: making (لا) operate like (لَيْسَ) is very rare, its authenticity can be disputed, and even if it is authentic, its analogical extension can be disputed. The second: parallelism is achieved between the two clauses, since (لا) would then have entered both clauses upon a subject without governing either of them. The reasoning behind al-Zuhri's reading and that of those who agree with him is that it is an explicit text on generality, negating every individual instance of the meaning of fear. As for the *raf'*, it permits this but is not an explicit text. So they took what indicates generality by explicit text over what indicates it by apparent meaning. As for the reading of Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn 'Atiyya interpreted it as the operation of (لا) like (لَيْسَ), and that he omitted the *tanwin* for lightness due to frequent usage. We have already mentioned what is involved in making (لا) operate like (لَيْسَ). So the better view is that it is a subject, as we have stated, when it is *marfu'* and *munawwan*, and its *tanwin* is dropped as he said, due to frequent usage. It is also possible that it is without *tanwin* because it is intended with (ال) (the definite article), so the implied meaning would be: "There is no the fear upon them." This would be like what al-Akhfash related from the Arabs: "Salamun 'alaykum" without *tanwin*. They said they intend "as-salamu 'alaykum." This interpretation is better, since parallelism is achieved in that (لا) enters upon a definite noun in both clauses. When (لا) enters upon definites, it is not treated like (لَيْسَ). A verse of this usage has been heard from al-Nabigha al-Ja'di, and the grammarians interpreted it. It is:

*Wa-halat sawada al-qalbi la ana baghiyan*
*siwaha wa-la fi hubbiha mutarakhiyan*

And they [the grammarians] have faulted Abu al-Tayyib for his statement:

*Fa-la al-hamdu maksuban wa-la al-mali baqiyan*

By his statement "*'alayhim*" he metaphorically expressed domination and encompassment, and the meaning was placed in the position of a body. He negated that it was superior and dominating over them. In this there is a subtle indication that fear is not entirely negated. Do you not see that the negation falls upon the state of fear being upon them? And the state of fear dominating does not necessarily entail the negation of fear in every condition. For this reason some exegetes said: "The statement *'fa-la khawfun 'alayhim'* is not evidence for negating the terrors of the Day of Resurrection and its fears from the obedient, in view of what Allah and His Messenger described of the severities of the Resurrection, (p-170) except that they are lightened for the obedient. When they arrive at His mercy, it is as if they had not feared." He placed the negation of fear before the negation of grief, because the negation of fear regarding what is yet to come is more emphatic than the negation of grief over what has passed. For this reason, its clause was presented beginning with the indefinite noun, which is more intensive in the domain of negation, while the second was presented beginning with the definite in his statement "*wa-la hum yahzanun*."

In his statement "*wa-la hum yahzanun*" there is an indication that they are specifically free of grief, and that others do grieve. Had he not intended this meaning, "*wa-la yahzanun*" would have been sufficient. For this reason he mentioned the negation of grief from them and its removal in his statement "*inna alladhina sabaqat lahum...*" up to his statement "*la yahzunuhum al-fazaʿ al-akbar wa-tatalaqqahum al-malaʾika*" [al-Anbiya: 103]. It is known that these two reports and what precedes them of the report are specific to those for whom the best reward from Allah has preceded. And in his statement "*al-hamdu lillahi alladhi adhhaba 'anna al-hazan*" [Fatir: 34], all of this indicates that others are grieved by the terror, and grief does not depart from them. Views have been reported from the exegetes regarding the interpretation of this sentence:

First: There is no fear upon them regarding what they will face of punishment, and they will not grieve at death.
Second: They do not anticipate any harm in the future, nor do they grieve over the loss of what was desired in the past and present.
Third: There is no fear upon them regarding what lies ahead of them, nor do they grieve over what is behind them.
Fourth: There is no fear upon them regarding what lies before them of the Hereafter, nor do they grieve over what has escaped them of the world.
Fifth: There is no fear upon them of punishment, nor do they grieve over the loss of reward.
Sixth: Fear is the sensing of distress over the loss of something sought, and grief is the sensing of distress over the loss of something beloved.
Seventh: There is no fear upon them regarding what lies before them of the world, nor do they grieve over what has escaped them of it.
Eighth: There is no fear upon them on the Day of Resurrection, nor do they grieve therein.
Ninth: He indicated that He will admit them into Paradise, which is the abode of joy and security, where there is no fear upon them nor grief.
Tenth: What Ibn Zayd said: "There is no fear upon them before them. Nothing is greater in the breast of one who dies than what comes after death, so Allah granted them security from it. Then He consoled them about the world, and they will not grieve over what they left behind after their death in the world."
Eleventh: There is no fear when the Fire is closed, and no grief when Death is slaughtered in the form of a ram on the Bridge, and it is said to the people of Paradise and the Fire: "Eternity, with no death."
Twelfth: There is no fear and no grief forever.

All these views are close in meaning. The apparent meaning of the verse is the general negation of fear and grief from them, but it is restricted to what comes after the world, because in the abode of the world the believer may indeed be touched by fear and grief, so it is not possible to take the verse in its general apparent sense in that respect.

(وَالَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا): This is the counterpart (*qasim*) to his statement "*fa-man tabiʿa hudaya*," and it is more eloquent than saying "*wa-man lam yattabiʿ hudaya*," although the verbal division would require it. This is because the negation of a thing can occur in several ways. Among them: lack of receptivity, either by nature or heedlessness; and among them: deliberately abandoning something. So the counterpart was presented with his statement "*wa-alladhina kafaru*" in an affirmative form, so as to remove the possibility that negation would imply. Since *kufr* can mean ingratitude for blessings and disobedience, he clarified that what is intended here is *shirk* (polytheism), with his statement "*wa-kadhdhabu bi-ayatina*." "*Bi-ayatina*" is connected to his statement "*wa-kadhdhabu*," and it is a case of operation of the second (*'amal al-thani*). If we say that "*kafaru*" requires it in meaning, then it is from that operation; if we say it does not require it, then it is not from that operation, and it may bear either possibility. The "*ayat*" here are: the books revealed to all nations; or the miracles of the prophets, upon them be prayers and peace; or the Qur'an; or the signs of Allah in His creations. These are the views.

"*Ula'ika*" is the subject (*mubtada'*), "*ashab*" is its predicate, and the sentence is the predicate of "*alladhina kafaru*." They also permitted that "*ula'ika*" be an apposition (*badal*) and an explanatory appositive (*'atf al-bayan*), in which case "*ashab al-nar*" would be the predicate of "*alladhina kafaru*." In his statement "*ula'ika ashab al-nar*" there is an indication that those who disbelieved and denied are specifically [for] the Fire, and so it is understood that those who followed guidance are the people of Paradise. The counterpart division required that whoever follows guidance has no fear and no grief reaching him, and he is the companion of Paradise; and whoever denies, fear and grief reach him, and he is the companion of the Fire. So it is as if something was omitted from the first clause that is mentioned in its counterpart in the second clause, and from the second clause something was omitted that is mentioned in its counterpart in the first clause. It thus becomes like the statement of the poet:

(p-171)
*Wa-inni la-taʿrunI li-dhikirin fatratun*
*kama intafada al-ʿusfuru ballahu al-qatru*

In his statement "*ula'ika*" there is an indication to the entities characterized by disbelief and denial, and it seems there is a repetition and emphasis of the earlier mentioned subject. *Suhba* (companionship) means being joined to something, and in common usage it generally applies to constant attachment, although its original linguistic sense is applying to mere joining. What is meant here is lasting attachment, which is why he emphasized it with his statement "*hum fiha khalidun*" (they will abide therein). It is possible that this sentence is in a circumstantial position (*hal*), as occurs elsewhere: "*ula'ika ashab al-jannati khalidina fiha*," in which case it would have a place in grammatical analysis (*i'rab*) in the accusative. It is also possible that it is an explanatory sentence clarifying what he warned them of in his statement "*ula'ika ashab al-nar*," so it explains and makes clear that this companionship is not intended as mere joining, but as eternal abiding; in that case it has no place in grammatical analysis. It is also possible that it is a second predicate of the subject "*ula'ika*," so he has predicated two things of it: one singular, and the other a sentence; this is according to the view of one who holds that, in which case it is in the nominative position. The discussion of *khulud* (eternal abiding) has already preceded, namely whether it is remaining for a time without end, or for a time that has an end.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 40 (part 1 of 3):

﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you, and fulfil My covenant, and I will fulfil your covenant, and fear Me alone.﴾ ﴿And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you, and do not be the first to disbelieve in it, and do not exchange My signs for a small price, and be wary of Me alone.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 41] ﴿And do not mix truth with falsehood, nor conceal the truth while you know.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 42] ﴿And establish the prayer, give the zakat, and bow with those who bow.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 43].

Ibn (ابْنُ): its final radical is elided. It is said the elided letter is a yā' (ياء). There is disagreement about its morphological pattern (wazn) on both assumptions. It is said to be fi'l, and it is said to be fa'il. Whoever claims its original root is yā' derives it from the bināʼ (بِناء), which means placing one thing upon another, and the son is a branch of the father, so he is placed upon him. They considered their saying al-bunuwwa (البُنُوَّة, "sonship") an anomaly, like al-futuwwa (الفُتُوَّة, "youthfulness"). Whoever claims its original root is wāw, and al-Akhfash (الأخفش) went this way, took al-bunuwwa as evidence for that, and (took as evidence) that the elided letter being wāw is more common than it being yā'. The broken plural of ibn is abnāʼ (أبناء), and the sound plural is banūn (بَنُون). The latter is an anomalous plural, since the singular's form is not preserved in it, so they did not say *ibnūn (ابْنُون). For this reason, the Arabs in some of their speech treated this plural in the manner of a broken plural, so the taʼ (التاء) was attached to its verb, as it is attached to the verbs of broken plurals. al-Nabigha (النابغة) said:

"The Banu ʻĀmir, the maternal uncles of the Banu Asad, said: 'Woe to ignorance, (which is) harmful to peoples.'"

The sound plural with waw and nun has also been heard in its diminutive form. Yusaddid (يُسَدِّد) said:

"Make the little ones my friends' (kin)..." 

This too is anomalous.

Isrāʼīl (إسْرائِيلَ): a non-Arabic proper noun, diptote (ممنوع الصرف) because of its being a proper name and its foreign origin. They mentioned that it is compounded of isrā, meaning "servant," and īl (إيلَ), a name of God Most High, so it means "the servant of God." This is in the Hebrew tongue, and it is like Jibrāʼīl, Mīkāʼīl, Isrāfīl, and ʻIzrāʼīl. This was said by Ibn ʻAbbas. It is also said that the meaning of isrā is "elect" (صَفْوَة), and īl is God Most High, so its meaning is "the elect of God." This is narrated from Ibn ʻAbbas and others. Some said: isrā is derived from al-asr (الأسر), which means binding, so it is as if Isrāʼīl means "the one whom God bound and perfected in creation." It is also said: he travelled by night (أسرى) migrating to God Most High, so he was named thus. It is also said: he captured a jinn (جِنّي) who used to extinguish the lamps of Bayt al-Maqdis, and the jinn's name was īl, so he was named Isrāʼīl. He used to serve Bayt al-Maqdis, being the first to enter and the last to leave. This was said by Kaʻb. It is also said: he travelled by night fleeing from his brother ʻAysu to his maternal uncle, in a long story they mentioned, and so this was applied to him. These are weak opinions.

In it there are variations by the Arabs in their pronunciation: Isrāʼīl with a hamza after the alif and a yā' after it, which is the reading of the majority (الجمهور). Isrāyīl with two yā's after the alif, which is the reading of Abu Jaʻfar, al-Aʻmash, and ʻĪsā ibn ʻUmar. Isrāʼil with a hamza after the alif and then a lām, which is narrated from Warsh. Isrāʼal with a fatha-vowelled hamza after the rā' and a lām. Isrʼil with a kasra-vowelled hamza after the rā'. Isrāl with a inclined alif (ممالة) followed by a light lām. Isrāl with a non-inclined alif. Umayya said:

"I see no one who will let me live in my life, other than myself and the Banu Isrāl."

This is a narration transmitted from Nafiʻ (خارجة عن نافع). al-Hasan, al-Zuhri, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and others read: wa-Isrāʼinun (وإسْرائِينَ) with nūn in place of the lām. The poet said:

"The people of evil say, when we came: 'This is—by the Lord of the House—Isrāʼīnā.'"

Just as they said: sijjīl and sijjīn, rafl and rafn, and Jibrīl and Jibrīn, the lām being replaced by nūn, as the nūn was replaced by lām in aṣīlān, they said aṣīlāl. When you make its broken plural you say: asārīl (أساريل), and it is reported: asārila and asāril.

Al-dhikr (الذِّكْر): with a kasra or a ḍamma on the dhāl, these are two dialects with one meaning. al-Kisāʼī said: it (with kasra) is by the tongue, and al-dhikr (with ḍamma) by the heart. With kasra its opposite is silence (الصَّمْت), and with ḍamma its opposite is forgetting (النِّسْيان). It means alertness and attentiveness. One says: "Make it be in your mind (ذِكْر)."

Al-niʻma (النِّعْمة): a noun for the thing bestowed. Often a fiʻl pattern comes in the sense of the maf'ūl (object), such as al-dhabḥ (slaughter), al-naqṣ (decrease), al-ruʻy (pasturing), and al-ṭaḥn (grinding). Despite this, it is not systematic (لا ينقاس).

Awfā, wafā, and waffā are three dialect forms with one meaning. Awfā comes in the sense of "rose high" (ارتفع). He said:

"Perhaps I ascended (awfaytu) in knowledge, your garments lifted by the north wind."

Al-mīfāt (الميفات) is a high place. al-Farrāʼ said: the people of the Hijaz say awfaytu, and the people of Najd say wafaytu without an alif. al-Zajjāj said: wafā bi-l-ʻahd and awfā bihi (he fulfilled the covenant). The poet said:

"As for Ibn Tawq, he fulfilled his pledge, just as the one who drove the camels of the star (al-najm) fulfilled (his duty)."

Ibn Qutayba said: one says wafaytu bi-l-ʻahd and awfaytu bihi, and awfaytu al-kayl (I gave full measure), with nothing else. Abu al-Haytham said: wafā al-shayʼ means it was completed (تم), waffā al-kayl and awfaytuhu means you completed it, and wafā rīsh al-ṭāʼir means the bird's feathers reached completion. Dirham wāfin means a complete, whole dirham.

Al-rahab, al-ruhb, al-rahb, and al-rahbah all mean fear (الخوف). It is derived from al-rahāba (الرهابة), which is the breastbone that fear affects. Al-rahab also means a blade (النصل), because one is afraid of it. Al-rahba, al-khashya, and al-makhafa are synonyms.

Al-taṣdīq (التصديق): affirming the reality of a thing and its conformity to what is reported. Its opposite is al-takdhīb (denial).

Awwal (أوّل): according to Sibawayh, it is afʻal, and its first and middle radicals are both wāw. No verb is used from it because of the difficulty of two consecutive wāws. It belongs to the category whose first and middle radicals are of the same kind, of which only the following have been preserved: dudan, quqas, bubun, and bābūs. It is said that bābūs is non-Arabic.

According to the Kufans, awwal is afʻal from wa'ala (وألَ), meaning to take refuge (لجأ). Its original form was awʼal, then it was lightened by replacing the hamza with wāw, then by assimilation (idgham). This lightening is not analogical, since the lightening of such a form is done by deleting the hamza and transferring its vowel to the preceding consonant. Some people said: it is afʻal from āla yaʼūlu, its original form being aʼwal, then it was altered to become awʼal, afʻal, then it was lightened by replacing the hamza with wāw, then by assimilation. These two opinions are weak.

Awwal is used in two ways. The first is that it is treated as a noun, in which case it is declinable (مصروفًا), and it is followed by governing elements, as in afkal. Even if its meaning is that of qadīm (ancient). On this basis is the Arabs' saying: "I left nothing for him, neither first nor last," meaning I left nothing for him, neither ancient nor recent. The second usage is that it is treated as the comparative (أفعل التفضيل), in which case it is used in its three forms: with min pronounced or implied, with al, and with a genitive construction (الإضافة). The Arabs said: "Begin with this first (ابدأ بهذا أوّل)," and here it is built on ḍamma by agreement. The disagreement concerns the reason for its being indeclinable: is it because it is cut off from the genitive (التقدير: أوّل الأشياء, "the first of things"), or because of a resemblance to being cut off from the genitive (التقدير: أوّل مَن كذا, "the first of those who...")? The preferred view is that the reason is being cut off from the genitive. The disagreement, when it is indeclinable, is whether it is an adverb of time (ظرف) or a non-adverbial noun. This disagreement is based on whether what is built due to being cut off must be an adverb or not. All this is fully treated in the science of grammar (nahw).

Al-thaman (الثَّمَن): the compensation given in exchange for the commodity sold. The poet said:

"If you sought worldly gain and attained it, you did not gain anything by abandoning the pilgrimage (ḥajj)."

That is, of compensation (عوض).

Al-qalīl (القليل, "few"): its opposite is al-kathīr (الكثير). They agree in the pattern of the active participle but differ in the pattern of the verb: the past tense of qalīl is faʻala, and the past tense of kathīr is faʻula. The analogy would have been that the active participle of "to be few" be on fāʻil, as in shadda yashidhdhu, fa-huwa shādhdh, but it was modelled on its opposite. Like qalla, fa-huwa qalīl, there is ṣaḥḥa, fa-huwa ṣaḥīḥ.

Al-labs (اللبس): mixing. The Arabs say: labistu al-shayʼa bi-l-shayʼ, "I mixed the thing with the thing," and iltabasa bihi, "it became mixed with it." al-ʻAjjāj said:

"When they mixed truth with false accusation."

Alba also comes in the sense of labbasa. Another poet said:

"And a battalion I mixed with another battalion, until, when they were confused, I shook my hand for them."

Al-katm and al-kitmān: concealment. Its opposite is manifestation. From it is al-katm: a leaf used to dye grey hair.

Al-rukūʻ (الركوع) has two meanings in the language. The first is lowering and bending (التطامن والانحناء). This is the view of al-Khalil and Abu Zayd, and from it is the saying of Labid:

"I tell the reports of the generations that have passed; I bow (adubbu) as if, whenever I stand, I am bowing (rāʻi')."

The second is humiliation and submission (الذلة والخضوع). This is the view of al-Mufaḍḍal and al-Asmaʻi. al-Aḍbaṭ al-Saʻdi said:

"Do not humiliate the weak, lest you bow one day while time has raised him up."

﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you.﴾ This is the opening of the discourse with the Jews and the Christians. The connection of the discourse with them here is evident. This surah began by mentioning the Book, and that in it is guidance for the believers. Then it followed with mention of the disbelievers, those upon whose hearts a seal of wretchedness is set, then with mention of the hypocrites and several aspects of their conditions. Then it commanded all people to worship God Most High, then it mentioned the inimitability of the Qur'an, and other matters it mentioned. Then it alerted them by mentioning their origin Adam, and what befell him of eating from the tree after the prohibition, and that the one who induced him to that was Iblis. These two groups, I mean the Jews and the Christians, were People of the Book, displaying their following of the messengers and their emulation of what came from God Most High. Their mention had been included generally in His saying: ﴿O people, worship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21]. So He singled them out here specifically, since the discourse with the polytheists and the hypocrites had already preceded, and the discourse with the Jews and Christians remained. So He spoke with them here, and mentioned what necessitates their belief in this Book, just as they believed in their earlier scriptures, up to the end of the discourse with them, in a detailed manner that will come. The discourse with them was fitting alongside the story of Adam, upon our Prophet and upon him be prayers and peace, because after they had been given the clear explanation and the manifest proof, mentioned in the Torah and the Gospel, concerning fulfilling the covenant and believing in the Qur'an, there appeared from them the opposite of that by their disbelief in the Qur'an and in the one who brought it. He turned towards them with the address to stir them to hear what was coming upon them of commands and prohibitions, as in His saying: (O people, worship; and O Adam, dwell).

The reference to this has already been made. He attributed them to the name Isrāʼīl, which is Jacob (يعقوب). He did not say "O Children of Jacob," because of what the name Isrāʼīl contains, namely that its meaning is "servant of God" or "elect of God," and that is by the best of its interpretations. So He stirred them by attributing them to it, as if it were said: "O children of the servant of God," or "O children of the elect of God." In this there is an alert that they should be like their father in goodness, as you say: "O son of the righteous man, obey God," attributing him to that which moves him to obey God, because a person loves to follow the footsteps of his forefathers, even if that is not praiseworthy. How much more so when it is praiseworthy? Do you not see: ﴿Indeed we found our fathers upon a community﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 22], ﴿Rather we follow what we found our fathers upon﴾ [al-Baqarah: 170]? In His saying "O Children of Israel" there is evidence that whoever is affiliated to a person, even through many intermediaries, is called his son, and on this basis (O Children of Adam) is said, and that is called "father." God Most High said: ﴿The creed of your father Abraham﴾ [al-Hajj: 78]. In attributing them to Israel there is honour for them by mentioning their lineage to this good origin, which is Jacob son of Isaac son of Abraham, the Friend of the Merciful. It is reported from Abu al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzi that none of the prophets other than our Prophet Muhammad, ﷺ, has two names except Jacob: he is Jacob, and he is Isrāʼīl. al-Jawhari reported in his Sihah that al-Masih is a proper name for ʻIsa, with no derivation. al-Bayhaqi mentioned from al-Khalil ibn Ahmad five prophets who had two names: Muhammad and Ahmad, our Prophet, ﷺ; ʻIsa and al-Masih; Isrāʼīl and Yaʻqub; Yunus and Dhu al-Nun; and Ilyas and Dhu al-Kifl.

The intended audience of "O Children of Israel, remember" is those of the Children of Israel who were in the presence of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in Medina and its environs, or those among the Jews who embraced Islam and believed in the Prophet (ﷺ), or the forefathers and earlier leaders of the Children of Israel. There are three opinions, and the closest is the first. This is because those of their forefathers who had died cannot be addressed with ﴿And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 41], except by a remote interpretation. Likewise, those among them who believed cannot be addressed with ﴿And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you, and do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 41], except by a distant metaphorical usage.

His words "remember" may include remembrance by the tongue and remembrance by the heart. On the first interpretation, the meaning is: keep the blessings running on your tongues and do not neglect them, for keeping them on the tongue and studying them causes them not to be forgotten. On the second, the meaning is: be mindful of the blessings and do not neglect giving thanks for them.

As for the blessing whose thanks or preservation is commanded, there are several opinions:
- What was entrusted to them of the Torah, in which is the description of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).
- What God bestowed upon their forefathers: rescuing them from the family of Pharaoh, destroying their enemy, giving them the Torah, and similar things. This was said by al-Hasan (al-Basri) and al-Zajjaj.
- Their attaining the period of the Prophet (ﷺ).
- The knowledge of the Torah.
- All the blessings upon all of God's creation, and upon their predecessors and successors, at all times and in all changing circumstances.

The most apparent of these opinions is what was specific to the Children of Israel of blessings, due to the apparent wording ﴿which I have bestowed upon you﴾. The blessings of God upon the Children of Israel are many: He rescued them from the trial of Pharaoh and his people, made them prophets and kings, sent down to them the great Books, shaded them with the cloud in the wilderness (al-tih), and sent down upon them manna and quails. Ibn Abbas said: He gave them a pillar of light to illuminate for them at night, their heads did not become disheveled, and their clothes did not wear out.

They were reminded of these blessings because among them is what testified to the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), namely the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms; and so that they would beware of opposing what they were called to: faith in the Messenger of God and the Qur'an. Also, reminding of past blessings incites hope for future blessings, and that hope prevents them from openly opposing. These blessings, although they were upon their forefathers, are also blessings upon them, because through these blessings offspring came about; and because being connected to forefathers who were honored with blessings is a glorification concerning the descendants.

Some of the knowers (al-'arifin) said: The servants of blessings are many, and the servants of the Benefactor are few. So God reminded the Children of Israel of His blessings upon them. When the matter reached the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ), He mentioned the Benefactor, saying: ﴿Remember Me, I will remember you﴾. This indicates the superiority of the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) over all other nations.

In His words "My blessing" (ni'mati) there is a type of iltifat (a shift in grammatical person): it is a departure from the first-person plural pronoun, which magnifies Himself, in His words "Our signs" (ayatina), to a first-person pronoun that does not indicate that. In attributing the blessing to Himself there is an indication of the greatness of its value, the vastness of its goodness, and the excellence of its placement. The "ya'" in (ni'mati) may be pronounced with sukun or with fatha, and the seven canonical readers agree on fatha.

"Anamtu" (I have bestowed) is the relative clause (sila) of "allati" (which), and its returning pronoun (al-'a'id) is omitted; the estimated form is: "I have bestowed it upon you."

﴿And fulfill My covenant, I will fulfill your covenant﴾. The word "al-'ahd" (covenant): its linguistic meaning was already explained in His words ﴿those who break the covenant of God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 27]. The word "al-'ahd" may be construed as being attributed both to the one who makes the covenant and to the one with whom it is made. Concerning the explanation of these two covenants there are several opinions:

1. The pledge He took from them to believe in Him and affirm His messengers; and their covenant is what He promised them of Paradise.
2. What He commanded them; and their covenant is what He promised them. This was said by Ibn Abbas.
3. What was mentioned to them in the Torah concerning the description of the Messenger of God (ﷺ); and their covenant is what He promised them of Paradise. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.
4. Performing the obligations; and their covenant is accepting them and being rewarded for them.
5. Abandoning the major sins; and their covenant is the forgiveness of minor sins.
6. Reforming the religion; and their covenant is the reform of their hereafter.
7. Striving against the self; and their covenant is help in that.
8. Reforming the inner states; and their covenant is reforming the outer states.
9. ﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾ [al-Baqarah: 63]. This was said by al-Hasan.
10. ﴿And when God took the covenant of those who were given the Book: "You shall make it clear to the people and not conceal it"﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 187].
11. Sincerity in acts of worship; and their covenant is bringing them to the stations of the subjects (al-ri'ayat).
12. Faith in Him and obedience to Him; and their covenant is what He promised them in terms of good reward for good deeds.
13. Preserving the outward etiquettes; and their covenant is in the inward states.
14. The covenant of God through the tongue of Moses, peace be upon him, to the Children of Israel: "Indeed, I will raise up from among the Children of Israel a prophet. Whoever follows him and believes in the light that comes with him, I will forgive him, admit him to Paradise, and give him two rewards." This was said by al-Kalbi.
15. The condition of servitude; and their covenant is the condition of lordship.
16. "Fulfill, in the abode of My trial, upon the carpet of My service, by preserving My sanctity, I will fulfill your covenant in the abode of My blessing, upon the carpet of My honor, by My nearness and My vision." This was said by al-Thawri.
17. ﴿Do not flee from the battlefield, I will admit you to Paradise﴾. This was said by Isma'il ibn Ziyad.
18. ﴿And God had certainly taken the covenant of the Children of Israel, and We raised up...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 12], the verse, said by Ibn Jurayj; and their covenant is their admission to Paradise.
19. His commands, His prohibitions and His injunctions; and within that falls the mention of Muhammad (ﷺ) that is in the Torah. This was said by the majority (al-jumhur).
20. "Fulfill My covenant in trust in Me, I will fulfill your covenant in sufficiency for your concerns." This was said by Abu Uthman.
21. "Fulfill My covenant in guarding My limits outwardly and inwardly, I will fulfill your covenant by guarding your secrets from witnessing other than Me."
22. His covenant is the preservation of gnosis, and Our covenant is the conveying of gnosis. This was said by al-Qushayri.
23. "Fulfill My covenant which you accepted on the day of the taking of the pledge, I will fulfill your covenant which I guaranteed to you on the day of meeting."
24. "Fulfill My covenant: be content with Me alone, I will be pleased with you for your sake."

These are the opinions of the early scholars (al-salaf) concerning the explanation of these two covenants.

What appears to be the case, and God knows best, is that the meaning is the demand to fulfill what they undertook for God Most High, and the arrangement of the fulfillment of what He promised them as a covenant by way of reciprocity; or it is a manifestation of what God Most High has graciously bestowed in the form of a condition undertaken, so that the motives to fulfill God's covenant converge. As God Most High said: ﴿And who is more faithful to his covenant than God?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 111]; ﴿except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾ [Maryam: 87]. And the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, he has a covenant with God that He will admit him to Paradise."

Al-Zuhri read "uwaffi bi-'ahdikum" with shadda (intensive form). It may be that it is intended for intensification (al-takthir), and it may be that it agrees with the unaugmented form. If it is intended as intensification, then there is an emphasis in the wording "uwaffi," as if it were said: "Be thorough in your fulfilling," so God Most High guaranteed the giving of much in return for little, as God Most High said: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times the like thereof﴾ [al-An'am: 160].

The apocope (jazm) of the imperfect (mudari') after the imperative, as in "idrib Zaydan yaghdab" (strike Zayd, he will become angry), indicates the meaning of a preceding condition. Otherwise, the imperative itself, which is a demand for the existence of the act, does not necessitate anything else; for this reason it is permissible to stop at it, so you say "idrib Zaydan" (strike Zayd), and nothing is consequently established by a demand that is merely a demand for something at all. But when the meaning of a preceding condition is considered, its consequence is established upon it.

The grammarians differed on this. Some of them held that the imperative clause implies the meaning of the condition: when you say "idrib Zaydan yaghdab," the verb "idrib" is taken to mean "in tadrib" (if you strike). This is the view of the master Abu al-Hasan ibn Kharuf. Others held that the imperative clause takes the place of the condition, and the meaning of "taking the place" is that the original estimate was: "idrib Zaydan, in tadrib Zaydan yaghdab" (strike Zayd, if you strike Zayd he will become angry), then the conditional clause was omitted and the imperative clause was substituted for it. According to the first opinion, there is no omitted clause at all; rather, the first clause performed the apocope because it implies the condition, just as the conditional particle "man" performs the apocope because it implies the meaning of "in" (if). According to the second opinion, it performed the apocope because it substitutes for the conditional sentence; in reality the action is for the estimated condition. This is the choice of al-Farisi and al-Sirafi, and it is what Sibawayh stated on the authority of al-Khalil. The preference between the two opinions is discussed in the science of grammar (nahw).

﴿And Me, fear Me﴾. "Iyyaya" (Me) is in the accusative, governed by a verb omitted and estimated after it, because the pronoun is detached; the estimate is "iyyaya ir-habu" (fear Me). It was omitted because what follows indicates it, and its estimate is before it. Al-Sajawandi is among them, for he estimated it as "wa-rhabu iyyaya" (and fear Me). Its coming as an accusative pronoun is appropriate to what precedes it, because what precedes it is an imperative, and because there is emphasis in it, since the speech is cast in the form of two clauses. Had it been a nominative pronoun it would have been permissible, but these two meanings would be lost. The "ya'" of the accusative pronoun in "farhabuni" was omitted because it is at the end of a verse (fasila). Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with the "ya'" in its original form. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is more emphatic in conveying exclusivity than "iyyaka na'budu" (You alone we worship). The meaning of that is that the speech is two clauses in estimate, and "iyyaka na'budu" is one clause, and the exclusivity is derived in his view from the fronting of the object over the verb. This matter has already been discussed with him, and we do not go with what he went to in that.

The "fa" in His words "farhabuni" entered as the response to an estimated imperative. The estimate is: "tanabbahu, farhabuni" (be attentive, then fear Me). Sibawayh mentioned in his book the following text: "You say: every man who comes to you, then strike (fa-idrib); because 'who comes to you' is a qualifier here, as if you said: every righteous man, then strike." End of quote. Ibn Kharuf said: His saying "kullu rajulin ya'tika fa-idrib" is in the same position as "Zaydan fa-idrib," except that here there is the meaning of the condition because of the indefinite noun described by the verb, so "kulla" was put in the accusative, and this is better than "Zaydan fa-idrib." End of quote. It does not appear to me what the superiority he indicated is; and what shows that this construction, namely "Zaydan fa-idrib," is a correct Arabic construction is His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Rather, worship God﴾ (bali Allaha fa-'bud), and the poet said:

"And do not worship Satan, but worship God."

(p-175)

Some of our companions said: What became clear after investigation is that the original form of "zaydan fa-idrib" (Zayd, so strike him) is "tanabbah fa-idrib zaydan" (Be alert, then strike Zayd). "Tanabbah" was then omitted, giving "fa-idrib zaydan." Since the *fa'* (the conjunctive particle *fa*) came first in the sentence, they moved the noun forward to improve the pronunciation (*islah li-l-lafz*). The *fa'* was introduced here to link these two clauses. The end of what was summarized from his words.

Given this established, the verse admits two interpretations.

The first is that the intended meaning is: "And fear Me (*wa-iyaya arhabu*), be alert, then fear Me (*fa-arhabuni*)." In this case the *fa'* is the answer particle (*jawab al-amr*) that follows the imperative, and it is not a delayed element moved from elsewhere.

The second is that the intended meaning is: "And be alert, then fear Me (*fa-arhabuni*)." The object was then moved forward and separated from its verb, and the *fa'* was delayed when the object was moved forward. The verb of command, which is *tanabbahu* ("be alert"), is elided. After its elision, two particles came together: the conjunctive *wa* and the *fa'* that answers the command. The *fa'* therefore came to the front, so the object was moved forward and the *fa'* was delayed to improve the pronunciation. Then the object was repeated for emphasis and to complete the rhyme (*fasilah*). According to this last interpretation, *iyaya* is not the object of an elided verb. Rather, it is the object of the verb that is actually spoken. It is not far-fetched for a detached pronoun to be emphasized by an attached pronoun, just as an attached pronoun is emphasized by a detached one, as in the phrase *darabtuka iyyaka* ("I struck you, you"). The meaning is: "Fear Me, lest I send down upon you what I sent down upon those who were before you among your forefathers, of the punishments you know of, such as transformation into animals and other things." This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

It was also said that the meaning of "fa-arhabuni" is: do not break My covenant. The command to fear contains a powerful warning. It is not the view of those who claimed that this command means threat, intimidation and terror, like the saying of the Exalted: "Do what you will" [Fussilat: 40]. That is not an intensification, because the first is in reality something demanded, whereas "do what you will" is not something demanded, so the two differ.

It was also said: fear is of two kinds. The first is fear of punishment, which is the share of the people of outward observance and it passes away. The second is fear of majesty, which is the share of the people of the heart and does not pass away.

Al-Sulami said: *al-rahbah* (awe) is the fear of the heart from its base thoughts.

Sahl said: "And fear Me" is the place of certainty through knowing Him, and "And fear Me, so beware of Me" [al-Baqarah: 41] is the place of prior knowledge and the place of cunning and gradual deception (*istidraj*).

Al-Qushayri said: Single Me out with fear, for I am singular in power over bringing things into existence.

"And believe in what I have sent down" [al-Baqarah: 41]: Its apparent meaning is that it is a command to the Children of Israel, because the ones commanded before it are they, and this is coordinated with what precedes it, so its apparent meaning is that the addressee is one. It was also said that it was revealed concerning Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his companions, scholars and leaders of the Jews. The apparent meaning is the first, and Ka'b and those with him are included in it.

The *ma* in "bima anzaltu" ("in what I have sent down") is a relative pronoun (*ma mawsulah*), meaning "in that which I have sent down." Its returning pronoun (*'a'id*) is elided, and its implied form is "anzaltuhu" ("I sent it down"). The conditions permitting this elision are present. What the Exalted sent down is the Qur'an, and what they had is the Torah and the Gospel.

Qatadah said: The intended meaning of "bima anzaltu" is a book and a messenger that you find written with you in the Torah and the Gospel. He considered it far-fetched to take *ma* as a verbal-noun particle (*masdariyyah*), so that the implied meaning becomes: "Believe in My sending down for what is with you of the Torah." In that case the *lam* in "lima" is part of the verbal noun, not part of "musaddiqan" (confirming). According to the first view, "lima maʿakum" ("for what is with you") is part of "musaddiqan," and the *lam* in both implied forms in "lima" strengthens the transitivity (*ta'diyah*), just as in the Exalted's saying: "a doer of what He wills" [al-Buruj: 16].

The grammatical status (*i'rab*) of "musaddiqan" according to the view that takes *ma* as a verbal-noun particle is that it is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) of the *ma* in the phrase "lima maʿakum." We do not say that this is far-fetched because a preposition enters on the one who is the subject of the circumstance (*dhu al-hal*). This is because the preposition, as we have stated, strengthens transitivity, so it is like a superfluous particle. This is similar to the phrase "Zaydun darib mujarradatan li-Hind" (Zayd is a striker, bare-handed toward Hind), whose implied form is "dariba Hindan mujarradatan" (striker of Hind, bare-handed), and then this circumstance was placed first. This is permissible in our view.

It is far-fetched for it to be a circumstance of the implied verbal noun, for two reasons. The first is the separation between the verbal noun and its object by the circumstance that has been placed first. The second is that it is far-fetched to describe the sending down with confirmation, unless this is used figuratively and what is meant is the thing sent down. According to this implied form, "lima maʿakum" is not part of it, because when what is meant is the thing sent down, it cannot be transitive to an object.

The apparent view is that "musaddiqan" is a circumstance of the pronoun that returns to the elided relative pronoun. It is an emphatic circumstance, and the governing element in it is "anzaltu." It was also said that it is a circumstance of *ma* in the phrase "bima anzaltu." This is also an emphatic circumstance.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 41–42:

﴿And do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾: The elative (af'al al-tafdil, the comparative/superlative form) when it is added to an indefinite noun that is not a descriptive, remains singular and masculine, and the indefinite noun agrees with what precedes it. If the preceding noun is singular, it is singular; if it is dual, it is dual; if it is plural, it is plural. So you say: Zayd is the best man (afḍalu rajulin), Hind is the best woman (afḍalu imra'atin), al-Zaydan are the best two men (afḍalu rajulayni), and al-Zaydun are the best men (afḍalu rijalin). That indefinite noun to which the elative is added is either a descriptive or not a descriptive. If it is not a descriptive, then agreement is as we have mentioned. Abu al-'Abbas permitted "your brothers are the best man" (ikhwatuka afḍalu rajulin) in the singular, but the majority (al-Jumhur) prohibited this. If it is a descriptive, and the elative is preceded by a plural, then agreement is permitted and singular is also permitted. The poet, whose verse was recited by al-Farra', said:

*And when they eat, the most base of eaters [ṭā'imin, singular]; and when they are hungry, the worst of the hungry [jiyā'in, plural].*

He used the singular in "ṭā'imin" and the plural in "jiyā'in."

When a descriptive indefinite noun is singular, and the elative is preceded by a plural, then according to the grammarians it is interpreted (muta'awwal). Al-Farra' said: its estimate is "man ṭa'ima" (whoever ate). Others said: it is estimated as a descriptive of a singular that carries the meaning of a plural, as if he said: "the most base eater" (fa'lamu ṭā'imin), and the qualified noun is omitted and the descriptive takes its place, so what is added to it is, in the estimate, in accordance with what precedes it. Some people said: the figurative usage (al-tajawwuz) occurs in the plural. So when it is said, for example, "al-Zaydun are the best scholar" (al-Zaydūna afḍalu 'ālimin), the meaning is: each one of the Zaydis is the best scholar. This indefinite noun, according to Sibawayh, originally has the definite article and the plural form, but they abbreviated the alif-lam and the plural formation. According to the Kufans, the elative is itself indefinite in meaning. So when you say "your father is the best scholar" (abūka afḍalu 'ālimin), its estimate for them is: "your father is the most excellent, the scholar" (abūka al-afḍalu al-'ālimu), and "afḍal" is added to what is, in meaning, the same as it. All the rulings of the elative are thoroughly set out in the books of grammar (kutub al-naḥw).

On the basis of what we have established, they interpreted (ta'awwalū) "the first disbeliever" (awwala kāfirin) as "one who disbelieved" (man kafara), or "the first party to disbelieve" (awwala ḥizbin kafara), or "let none of you be the first disbeliever." The prohibition against being the first to disbelieve in it does not indicate that disbelief is permitted for them as second or last; so the implied meaning of the descriptive (mafhūm al-ṣifa) is not intended here. Since the sense of "firstness" here was problematic, some claimed that "first" (awwal) is ṣilah, meaning superfluous, and the estimate is: "do not be disbelievers in it." This is very weak. Some claimed that there is an omitted coordinated element (ma'ṭūf maḥdhūf) whose estimate is: "do not be the first disbeliever in it, nor the last disbeliever," and they considered this to be among cases where the coordinated element is omitted because the meaning indicates it. They singled out firstness for mention because it is more shameful, due to the initiation involved in it. This resembles the words of the poet:

*Among people in whose character there is no immediate indecency nor bad impatience.*

He does not mean that among them there is a delayed indecency; rather, he means there is no indecency among them, neither immediate nor delayed. Some interpreted it by omitting a noun in the genitive construction (muḍāf maḥdhūf), meaning: "do not be like the first disbeliever in it," that is, "do not be, while you know it is mentioned in the Torah and described, like one who does not know it and is a polytheist with no scripture." Some interpreted it by an omitted descriptive: "the first disbeliever in it among the People of the Book," since they are the ones looked at in this matter and are presumed to have knowledge. Some interpreted it by omitting a relative clause (ṣilah) through which the meaning is sound. The estimate: "do not be the first disbeliever in it while having knowledge," because the disbelief of the Quraysh was with ignorance. This view resembles the one before it. Some estimated another relative clause: "do not be the first disbeliever in it upon hearing its mention; rather, be steadfast regarding it and reflect upon it with your intellects." It was said: the mention of firstness is an allusion that they should have been the first to believe in it, because of their knowledge of it and its description, and because they were the ones who gave good news of its time and who sought victory over those who disbelieved in it. When he came, their situation was the reverse. God the Exalted said: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89]. Al-Qushayri said: Do not establish disbelief as a practice (sunnah), for the burden of those who initiate what they establish is greater than the burden of those who follow what they adopt.

The pronoun in "bihi" (in it) refers to the relative pronoun in "bi-mā anzaltu" (in what I have sent down), which is the Qur'an, as Ibn Jurayj said; or it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), the meaning indicating him, since mention of what was sent down indicates mention of the one to whom it was sent down, as Abu al-'Aliyah said; or it refers to the blessing (al-ni'mah) in the sense of kindness, and for this reason the pronoun is masculine, as al-Zajjaj said; or it refers to the relative pronoun in "limā ma'akum" (what is with you), because when they disbelieve in what confirms it, they have disbelieved in it. The strongest is the first, because it is closest, it is explicitly stated, and it is the intended subject of the discourse, unlike the other three views.

﴿And do not exchange My signs for a small price﴾: The word "purchase" (ishtirā') here is metaphorical, meaning exchange (istibdāl), as the poet said:

*As the Muslim purchased when he became Christian.*

Another said:

*Indeed I have purchased dreams after you with ignorance.*

Since the meaning is exchange, it is permissible for the preposition "bi" (with) to enter upon the signs, although the analogy would be for it to enter upon what is the price; because the price in a sale is, in its real meaning, that with which something is bought. But since the discourse has come to have the meaning of exchange, that is permitted; because in exchange the object of the verb is what is obtained, and what the "bi" enters upon is what is lost. This is unlike what some people suppose: that your saying "I replaced or I substituted a dirham with a dinar" means "I took the dinar as a replacement for the dirham." The meaning, and God knows best, is: do not exchange My great signs for base, worthless things. If the "bi" were attached to the price instead of the signs, this meaning would be reversed, for the meaning would become: they themselves offered a small price and took the signs. Al-Mahdawi said: the entry of "bi" upon the signs is like its entry upon the price, and likewise for everything that has no physical substance. And if there are dinars or dirhams in the speech, "bi" enters upon the price, as al-Farra' said.
