The words of al-Mahdawi end; their meaning is that when there are no dinars or dirhams in the sale, it is correct for each of the things given to be both price and priced item; but the entry of "bi" varies according to the one among the contracting parties who attributes the purchase to himself: if he makes what he obtained the priced item, "bi" does not enter upon it; and if he makes what he gave out the price, he makes "bi" enter upon it. The signs themselves are not what is purchased, so an omitted genitive noun is needed. It was said that the estimate is: "by teaching My signs," as Abu al-'Aliyah said; it was said: "by altering My signs," as al-Hasan said; it was said: "by concealing My signs," as al-Suddi said. It was said: no omitted genitive is needed; rather, the signs are a metonym for commands and prohibitions.

According to the three views before this view, the signs are what was sent down of the scriptures, or the Qur'an, or what clarified the proofs and evidences, or the signs sent down to them in the Torah and the Gospel which include the command to believe in the Messenger of God (ﷺ). According to the opinions concerning that estimated genitive and what follows it, they differed about the referent of "a small price." Whoever said that the omitted noun is "teaching" said: the small price is the wage for teaching, and that was forbidden in their law; or the stipend allotted to them for teaching, and they were forbidden from it. Whoever said it is "altering" said: the small price is the leadership that they had among their people, which they feared losing if they became followers of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Whoever made the signs a metonym for commands and prohibitions made the small price what they obtained of worldly desires, with which they were occupied instead of carrying out what God commanded and avoiding what He forbade. He described the price as "small" because whatever is obtained in exchange for God's signs, whatever it is, can only be small, however great it may be, as God the Exalted said: ﴿Say: The enjoyment of this world is small﴾ [al-Nisa': 77]. Therefore describing the price as small is not one of the descriptions that specify indefinites; rather it is one of the descriptions necessarily inherent in the price obtained through the signs, since it can only be small. It is possible that there is a coordinated element estimated as: "a small price and not a great one," which has been omitted because the meaning indicates it. Some scholars have used the verse ﴿And do not exchange My signs for a small price﴾ as evidence for prohibiting taking a wage for teaching the Book of God and knowledge. Some traditions have been transmitted on this, but they are not authentic. It is established that they said: "O Messenger of God, we take a wage for the Book of God," and he said: "The best of what you take a wage for is the Book of God." The scholars have concurred on the permissibility of taking a wage for teaching the Qur'an and knowledge. The only reported disapproval is from al-Zuhri and Abu Hanifah, because that is a bodily act of worship, and there is no evidence for that view in this verse, and its interpretation has already passed.

(And fear Me alone): The grammatical analysis of this is like the analysis of "And fear Me" (wa-iyyaya farhabūn), and the meaning of taqwa (God-consciousness/guarding oneself) is close to the meaning of rahbah (awe/fear). The author of al-Muntakhab said: The difference is that rahbah is an expression for fear, while ittiqa' (guarding oneself) is needed when there is certainty of the occurrence of what one guards against. So it is as if God commanded them to have awe because the possibility of punishment exists, then commanded them to have taqwa because the certainty of punishment is established. The words of that author end. The meaning of the possibility of punishment there and its certainty here is this: abandoning mention of the blessing and fulfilling the covenant apparently belongs to the sins that make punishment possible, since it is possible that pardon may occur for that. But abandoning belief in what God the Exalted sent down, and exchanging God's signs for a meager price, are among the sins that necessitate punishment and make it certain, since pardon cannot occur for that. Thus it was said regarding the first: ﴿And fear Me [farhabūn]﴾, and regarding the second: ﴿And fear Me [ittaqūn]﴾, meaning: take a shield against the punishment of God if you do not comply with what I have commanded you. The best view is that ﴿fear Me and guard yourselves against Me﴾ is not restricted to anything; rather, it is a command to fear God and guard oneself against Him, but what the command was directly followed by clearly enters into it. So the meaning is: fear Me if you do not remember My blessing and do not fulfill My covenant, and guard yourselves against Me if you do not believe in what I have sent down and if you exchange My signs for a small price.

﴿And do not mix the truth with falsehood﴾: That is, the truth with falsehood. Ibn 'Abbas said this. Or Judaism and Christianity with Islam, as Mujahid said. Or the Torah with what they wrote with their own hands in it from other than it, or with what they altered in it regarding mention of Muhammad (ﷺ), as Ibn Zayd said. Or trustworthiness with betrayal, because they were entrusted with declaring what is in the Torah, and they betrayed in that by concealing and altering it. Or acknowledging the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) to others and denying that he was sent to them, as Abu al-'Aliyah said. Or the faith of the hypocritical Jews through concealing their disbelief. Or describing the Prophet (ﷺ) with the description of the Dajjal (Antichrist). The apparent structure of this expression is that the "bi" in "bil-bāṭil" (with falsehood) indicates attachment, like your saying "I mixed the water with the milk." So they were prohibited from mixing the truth with falsehood, such that the truth would not be distinguished from falsehood. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that the "bi" be instrumental, as in "I wrote with the pen." He said: as if the meaning is: do not make the truth ambiguous and confused with your falsehood. But this is far from the structure of this expression, and it diverts from the apparent meaning without any necessity requiring that.

﴿And conceal the truth﴾: It is in the jussive mood as a coordination with "talbisū" (mix), and the meaning is a prohibition against each of the two verbs, as they say: "Do not eat the fish and drink the milk," in the jussive, prohibiting each of the two verbs separately. They also permitted it to be in the subjunctive with an implied "an" (that), and according to the Basrans this is a coordination with an assumed verbal noun (maṣdar mutawahham); the Kufans call this the subjunctive of diversion (al-naṣb 'alā al-ṣarf). Al-Jarmi holds that the subjunctive is by the "wa" itself. This is mentioned in the science of grammar. What they permitted is not apparent, because in that case the prohibition would extend to the combination of the two verbs, as when you say: "Do not eat the fish and drink the milk," meaning the prohibition is against combining them, and by implication it would indicate the permissibility of mixing with one of them, which is forbidden. Therefore the jussive was preferred.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 41–42:

﴿And do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾: The elative (af'al al-tafdil, the comparative/superlative form) when it is added to an indefinite noun that is not a descriptive, remains singular and masculine, and the indefinite noun agrees with what precedes it. If the preceding noun is singular, it is singular; if it is dual, it is dual; if it is plural, it is plural. So you say: Zayd is the best man (afḍalu rajulin), Hind is the best woman (afḍalu imra'atin), al-Zaydan are the best two men (afḍalu rajulayni), and al-Zaydun are the best men (afḍalu rijalin). That indefinite noun to which the elative is added is either a descriptive or not a descriptive. If it is not a descriptive, then agreement is as we have mentioned. Abu al-'Abbas permitted "your brothers are the best man" (ikhwatuka afḍalu rajulin) in the singular, but the majority (al-Jumhur) prohibited this. If it is a descriptive, and the elative is preceded by a plural, then agreement is permitted and singular is also permitted. The poet, whose verse was recited by al-Farra', said:

*And when they eat, the most base of eaters [ṭā'imin, singular]; and when they are hungry, the worst of the hungry [jiyā'in, plural].*

He used the singular in "ṭā'imin" and the plural in "jiyā'in."

When a descriptive indefinite noun is singular, and the elative is preceded by a plural, then according to the grammarians it is interpreted (muta'awwal). Al-Farra' said: its estimate is "man ṭa'ima" (whoever ate). Others said: it is estimated as a descriptive of a singular that carries the meaning of a plural, as if he said: "the most base eater" (fa'lamu ṭā'imin), and the qualified noun is omitted and the descriptive takes its place, so what is added to it is, in the estimate, in accordance with what precedes it. Some people said: the figurative usage (al-tajawwuz) occurs in the plural. So when it is said, for example, "al-Zaydun are the best scholar" (al-Zaydūna afḍalu 'ālimin), the meaning is: each one of the Zaydis is the best scholar. This indefinite noun, according to Sibawayh, originally has the definite article and the plural form, but they abbreviated the alif-lam and the plural formation. According to the Kufans, the elative is itself indefinite in meaning. So when you say "your father is the best scholar" (abūka afḍalu 'ālimin), its estimate for them is: "your father is the most excellent, the scholar" (abūka al-afḍalu al-'ālimu), and "afḍal" is added to what is, in meaning, the same as it. All the rulings of the elative are thoroughly set out in the books of grammar (kutub al-naḥw).

On the basis of what we have established, they interpreted (ta'awwalū) "the first disbeliever" (awwala kāfirin) as "one who disbelieved" (man kafara), or "the first party to disbelieve" (awwala ḥizbin kafara), or "let none of you be the first disbeliever." The prohibition against being the first to disbelieve in it does not indicate that disbelief is permitted for them as second or last; so the implied meaning of the descriptive (mafhūm al-ṣifa) is not intended here. Since the sense of "firstness" here was problematic, some claimed that "first" (awwal) is ṣilah, meaning superfluous, and the estimate is: "do not be disbelievers in it." This is very weak. Some claimed that there is an omitted coordinated element (ma'ṭūf maḥdhūf) whose estimate is: "do not be the first disbeliever in it, nor the last disbeliever," and they considered this to be among cases where the coordinated element is omitted because the meaning indicates it. They singled out firstness for mention because it is more shameful, due to the initiation involved in it. This resembles the words of the poet:

*Among people in whose character there is no immediate indecency nor bad impatience.*

He does not mean that among them there is a delayed indecency; rather, he means there is no indecency among them, neither immediate nor delayed. Some interpreted it by omitting a noun in the genitive construction (muḍāf maḥdhūf), meaning: "do not be like the first disbeliever in it," that is, "do not be, while you know it is mentioned in the Torah and described, like one who does not know it and is a polytheist with no scripture." Some interpreted it by an omitted descriptive: "the first disbeliever in it among the People of the Book," since they are the ones looked at in this matter and are presumed to have knowledge. Some interpreted it by omitting a relative clause (ṣilah) through which the meaning is sound. The estimate: "do not be the first disbeliever in it while having knowledge," because the disbelief of the Quraysh was with ignorance. This view resembles the one before it. Some estimated another relative clause: "do not be the first disbeliever in it upon hearing its mention; rather, be steadfast regarding it and reflect upon it with your intellects." It was said: the mention of firstness is an allusion that they should have been the first to believe in it, because of their knowledge of it and its description, and because they were the ones who gave good news of its time and who sought victory over those who disbelieved in it. When he came, their situation was the reverse. God the Exalted said: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89]. Al-Qushayri said: Do not establish disbelief as a practice (sunnah), for the burden of those who initiate what they establish is greater than the burden of those who follow what they adopt.

The pronoun in "bihi" (in it) refers to the relative pronoun in "bi-mā anzaltu" (in what I have sent down), which is the Qur'an, as Ibn Jurayj said; or it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), the meaning indicating him, since mention of what was sent down indicates mention of the one to whom it was sent down, as Abu al-'Aliyah said; or it refers to the blessing (al-ni'mah) in the sense of kindness, and for this reason the pronoun is masculine, as al-Zajjaj said; or it refers to the relative pronoun in "limā ma'akum" (what is with you), because when they disbelieve in what confirms it, they have disbelieved in it. The strongest is the first, because it is closest, it is explicitly stated, and it is the intended subject of the discourse, unlike the other three views.

﴿And do not exchange My signs for a small price﴾: The word "purchase" (ishtirā') here is metaphorical, meaning exchange (istibdāl), as the poet said:

*As the Muslim purchased when he became Christian.*

Another said:

*Indeed I have purchased dreams after you with ignorance.*

Since the meaning is exchange, it is permissible for the preposition "bi" (with) to enter upon the signs, although the analogy would be for it to enter upon what is the price; because the price in a sale is, in its real meaning, that with which something is bought. But since the discourse has come to have the meaning of exchange, that is permitted; because in exchange the object of the verb is what is obtained, and what the "bi" enters upon is what is lost. This is unlike what some people suppose: that your saying "I replaced or I substituted a dirham with a dinar" means "I took the dinar as a replacement for the dirham." The meaning, and God knows best, is: do not exchange My great signs for base, worthless things. If the "bi" were attached to the price instead of the signs, this meaning would be reversed, for the meaning would become: they themselves offered a small price and took the signs. Al-Mahdawi said: the entry of "bi" upon the signs is like its entry upon the price, and likewise for everything that has no physical substance. And if there are dinars or dirhams in the speech, "bi" enters upon the price, as al-Farra' said. The words of al-Mahdawi end; their meaning is that when there are no dinars or dirhams in the sale, it is correct for each of the things given to be both price and priced item; but the entry of "bi" varies according to the one among the contracting parties who attributes the purchase to himself: if he makes what he obtained the priced item, "bi" does not enter upon it; and if he makes what he gave out the price, he makes "bi" enter upon it. The signs themselves are not what is purchased, so an omitted genitive noun is needed. It was said that the estimate is: "by teaching My signs," as Abu al-'Aliyah said; it was said: "by altering My signs," as al-Hasan said; it was said: "by concealing My signs," as al-Suddi said. It was said: no omitted genitive is needed; rather, the signs are a metonym for commands and prohibitions.

According to the three views before this view, the signs are what was sent down of the scriptures, or the Qur'an, or what clarified the proofs and evidences, or the signs sent down to them in the Torah and the Gospel which include the command to believe in the Messenger of God (ﷺ). According to the opinions concerning that estimated genitive and what follows it, they differed about the referent of "a small price." Whoever said that the omitted noun is "teaching" said: the small price is the wage for teaching, and that was forbidden in their law; or the stipend allotted to them for teaching, and they were forbidden from it. Whoever said it is "altering" said: the small price is the leadership that they had among their people, which they feared losing if they became followers of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Whoever made the signs a metonym for commands and prohibitions made the small price what they obtained of worldly desires, with which they were occupied instead of carrying out what God commanded and avoiding what He forbade. He described the price as "small" because whatever is obtained in exchange for God's signs, whatever it is, can only be small, however great it may be, as God the Exalted said: ﴿Say: The enjoyment of this world is small﴾ [al-Nisa': 77]. Therefore describing the price as small is not one of the descriptions that specify indefinites; rather it is one of the descriptions necessarily inherent in the price obtained through the signs, since it can only be small. It is possible that there is a coordinated element estimated as: "a small price and not a great one," which has been omitted because the meaning indicates it. Some scholars have used the verse ﴿And do not exchange My signs for a small price﴾ as evidence for prohibiting taking a wage for teaching the Book of God and knowledge. Some traditions have been transmitted on this, but they are not authentic. It is established that they said: "O Messenger of God, we take a wage for the Book of God," and he said: "The best of what you take a wage for is the Book of God." The scholars have concurred on the permissibility of taking a wage for teaching the Qur'an and knowledge. The only reported disapproval is from al-Zuhri and Abu Hanifah, because that is a bodily act of worship, and there is no evidence for that view in this verse, and its interpretation has already passed.

(And fear Me alone): The grammatical analysis of this is like the analysis of "And fear Me" (wa-iyyaya farhabūn), and the meaning of taqwa (God-consciousness/guarding oneself) is close to the meaning of rahbah (awe/fear). The author of al-Muntakhab said: The difference is that rahbah is an expression for fear, while ittiqa' (guarding oneself) is needed when there is certainty of the occurrence of what one guards against. So it is as if God commanded them to have awe because the possibility of punishment exists, then commanded them to have taqwa because the certainty of punishment is established. The words of that author end. The meaning of the possibility of punishment there and its certainty here is this: abandoning mention of the blessing and fulfilling the covenant apparently belongs to the sins that make punishment possible, since it is possible that pardon may occur for that. But abandoning belief in what God the Exalted sent down, and exchanging God's signs for a meager price, are among the sins that necessitate punishment and make it certain, since pardon cannot occur for that. Thus it was said regarding the first: ﴿And fear Me [farhabūn]﴾, and regarding the second: ﴿And fear Me [ittaqūn]﴾, meaning: take a shield against the punishment of God if you do not comply with what I have commanded you. The best view is that ﴿fear Me and guard yourselves against Me﴾ is not restricted to anything; rather, it is a command to fear God and guard oneself against Him, but what the command was directly followed by clearly enters into it. So the meaning is: fear Me if you do not remember My blessing and do not fulfill My covenant, and guard yourselves against Me if you do not believe in what I have sent down and if you exchange My signs for a small price.

﴿And do not mix the truth with falsehood﴾: That is, the truth with falsehood. Ibn 'Abbas said this. Or Judaism and Christianity with Islam, as Mujahid said. Or the Torah with what they wrote with their own hands in it from other than it, or with what they altered in it regarding mention of Muhammad (ﷺ), as Ibn Zayd said. Or trustworthiness with betrayal, because they were entrusted with declaring what is in the Torah, and they betrayed in that by concealing and altering it. Or acknowledging the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) to others and denying that he was sent to them, as Abu al-'Aliyah said. Or the faith of the hypocritical Jews through concealing their disbelief. Or describing the Prophet (ﷺ) with the description of the Dajjal (Antichrist). The apparent structure of this expression is that the "bi" in "bil-bāṭil" (with falsehood) indicates attachment, like your saying "I mixed the water with the milk." So they were prohibited from mixing the truth with falsehood, such that the truth would not be distinguished from falsehood. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that the "bi" be instrumental, as in "I wrote with the pen." He said: as if the meaning is: do not make the truth ambiguous and confused with your falsehood. But this is far from the structure of this expression, and it diverts from the apparent meaning without any necessity requiring that.

﴿And conceal the truth﴾: It is in the jussive mood as a coordination with "talbisū" (mix), and the meaning is a prohibition against each of the two verbs, as they say: "Do not eat the fish and drink the milk," in the jussive, prohibiting each of the two verbs separately. They also permitted it to be in the subjunctive with an implied "an" (that), and according to the Basrans this is a coordination with an assumed verbal noun (maṣdar mutawahham); the Kufans call this the subjunctive of diversion (al-naṣb 'alā al-ṣarf). Al-Jarmi holds that the subjunctive is by the "wa" itself. This is mentioned in the science of grammar. What they permitted is not apparent, because in that case the prohibition would extend to the combination of the two verbs, as when you say: "Do not eat the fish and drink the milk," meaning the prohibition is against combining them, and by implication it would indicate the permissibility of mixing with one of them, which is forbidden. Therefore the jussive was preferred.

(p-180) Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) read: "wa-taktumūna al-ḥaqq" (and you conceal the truth). It has been construed as a clause in the position of a circumstantial (ḥāl) clause. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as "kātimīna" (concealing), but this is an estimation of meaning, not of grammatical parsing (i'rab), because an affirmative clause beginning with a present-tense verb, when it occurs as a ḥāl, does not take the particle waw. The grammatical estimation would be to supply, before the present-tense verb here, a subject, estimated as: "wa-antum taktumūna al-ḥaqq" (and you are concealing the truth). The construal of this reading as a ḥāl is not evident, because the ḥāl is a restriction on the preceding clause, and they have been forbidden from confusing the truth with falsehood in any case; therefore this restriction by a ḥāl is not appropriate, unless the ḥāl is necessary (lāzima), meaning: confusing the truth with falsehood occurs only when the truth is concealed. This reading can be construed in another way: that God has censured them for concealing the truth while knowing that it is true, so the declarative clause is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon the prohibitive clause, according to one who holds this to be permissible, namely Sibawayh and a group; and coordination of clauses does not require congruity. Both of these constructions are irregular (shādhdh).

The truth which they concealed is the matter of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatada, Abu al-ʿAliya, al-Suddi and Muqatil; or it is Islam, said by al-Hasan. Or the truth may be general, so that the matter of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), the Qur'an, and what he (ﷺ) brought are included in it. Their concealment was that they knew this and showed the opposite of it.

"Wa-antum taʿlamūn" (while you know) (Q. 2:42) is a circumstantial clause, and the object of "taʿlamūn" is omitted by abbreviation (ḥadhf iqtiṣār), since the intended meaning is: "and you are of those possessing knowledge," so it is not fitting for one who has knowledge to conceal the truth and confuse it with falsehood. They have estimated its omission as an abbreviated omission (ḥadhf ikhtiṣār), and there are six opinions about it. The first: "and you know that he is mentioned, he and his description, in the Torah" (ﷺ). The second: "and you know the resurrection and the recompense." The third: "and you know that he is a prophet sent to all people." The fourth: "and you know the truth from falsehood." Al-Zamakhshari said: "and you know, in the state of your knowledge, that you are confusing and concealing," so he made the object of knowledge the confusion and concealment understood from the two preceding verbs. He said: "and this is worse, because ignorance of an ugly act may excuse its doer." End.

So what he estimated is by omitting a modifier, i.e., "and you know the ugliness or prohibition of confusion and concealment." Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "wa-antum taʿlamūn" is a clause in the position of a ḥāl, and He, the Exalted, did not bear witness to them as having knowledge; rather He forbade them from concealing what they knew. End.

The sense of his speech is that the object of "taʿlamūn" is "al-ḥaqq," as if he said: "and do not conceal the truth while you know it," because what is concealed may be true or untrue; if it is true and one knows it to be true, its concealment is greater (and more grievous) in sin, because the disobedient one with knowledge is more disobedient than the ignorant disobedient one. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it is possible that it is a testimony against them of knowledge of a particular truth regarding the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ), and He did not bear witness for them to knowledge in an absolute sense. He said: the clause on this view is not in the position of a ḥāl. End. He means that the clause is coordinated, even though affirmative, upon the prohibitive clause preceding it, even if it is not congruent in its report, according to what we have established in our construal of the reading of Abdullah "wa-taktumūna."

The most evident of these opinions is what we mentioned first, that the object of knowledge has been omitted by abbreviation, since the intended meaning is that whoever is among the people of knowledge and awareness of what the messengers brought, it is not suitable for him to confuse the truth with falsehood or to conceal it. And this ḥāl, although its apparent function is a restriction of the prohibition against confusion and concealment, does not by its implication indicate the permissibility of confusion and concealment in a state of ignorance, because one ignorant of the state of a thing does not know whether it is true or false; its benefit is rather that undertaking ugly things with knowledge is more heinous than undertaking them in ignorance.

Al-Qushayri said: "Do not imagine that there can be gathered for you the joining of opposites and being in one state in two places: either spread out with truth, or bound with abasement. Do not confuse the truth with falsehood—that is deceit (tadlīs); and do not conceal the truth—that is confusion (talbīs); and you know that the right of the truth is sanctification (taqdīs)." End.

In this verse there is evidence that one who knows the truth is obliged to make it manifest, and it is forbidden for him to conceal it.

"Wa-aqīmū al-ṣalāh wa-ātū al-zakāh" (and establish prayer and give zakat): the discussion of the like of this has preceded at the beginning of the surah, in His saying: "wa-yuqīmūna al-ṣalāh wa-yu'tūna al-zakāh" (Q. 9:71), and by it is meant the prayer and zakat of the Muslims. It has been said: it is the obligatory prayer; and it has been said: the genus of prayer and zakat. It has been said: he intended the obligatory (prayer and zakat); and it has been said: the zakat of fitr. It is an address to the Jews, and this indicates that the disbelievers are addressed with the branches of the Shariah. Al-Qushayri said: "Establish the prayer": observe the courtesy of the presence; the observance of courtesy is for the service, from the service. "Give zakat": the zakat of aspirations, just as the zakat of blessings is paid. One of them said:

"Everything has a zakat that is paid, and the zakat of beauty is mercy to the likes of me."

"Wa-irkaʿū maʿa al-rākiʿīn" (and bow with those who bow) is an address to the Jews. It may be intended by bowing: submission and humility; and it may be intended by it: the well-known bowing in prayer. They were commanded with this although bowing is included in the prayer they were commanded to establish, since it is bowing in their prayer; so the command to it draws attention to the fact that it is required in the prayer of the Muslims. It has been said: bowing is used as a metonym for prayer, i.e., "and pray with those who pray," just as prayer is metonymically referred to by prostration, naming the whole by a part. The word "maʿa" (with) in the phrase indicates performing it in congregation, because the earlier command to establish prayer did not include performing it in congregation. The "rākiʿūn" (those who bow): it has been said they are the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions; and it has been said: he intended the genus of those who bow.

In these clauses, although they are coordinated by "wa-," which does not by its basic meaning require sequence, there is a wonderful sequence, in terms of eloquence and the building of speech upon one another. For He, the Exalted, first commanded them to remember the blessing which He bestowed upon them, since in that is what calls to love of the Benefactor and the obligation to obey Him. Then He commanded them to fulfill the covenant which they undertook with the Benefactor. Then He encouraged them by ordering that He Himself fulfills His covenant with them in fulfilling the covenant. Then He commanded them to fear His retribution if they do not fulfill it. Thus the command to fulfill is framed by a command to remember the blessing and kindness, and a command to fear disobedience. Then He followed this with a command to a particular faith, namely what He sent down of the Qur'an, and encouraged it by saying that it confirms what is with them; so it is not a command contrary to what is in their hands, because transition to what agrees is closer than transition to what contradicts. Then He forbade them from exchanging the base for the precious. Then He commanded them to be mindful of Him. Then He followed that with the prohibition against confusing the truth with falsehood and concealing the truth. So the command to faith was a command to abandon misguidance, and the prohibition of confusing the truth with falsehood and concealing the truth was an abandonment of misleading others.

Since misguidance arises from two matters: either disguising falsehood as truth, if the proofs have reached the one who would be misled, or concealing the proofs, if they have not reached him, He pointed to both matters with "do not confuse" and "do not conceal." Then He censured them for these two attributes despite their having knowledge. Then, after obtaining faith and manifesting the truth, He commanded them to establish prayer and give zakat, since prayer is the most emphatic of the bodily acts of worship and zakat the most emphatic of the financial acts of worship. Then He concluded this by commanding submission and humility to Him, the Exalted, together with the body of humble, obedient ones.

Thus the opening of these verses was with the mention of blessings, and their closing with submission to the Benefactor, and what lies between them consists of doctrinal obligations and bodily and financial acts. With the like of what these verses contain of opening, sequence and closing, the excellence of God's speech over all other speech becomes evident. And these commands and prohibitions, although specific in form to the Children of Israel—since they are the ones addressed by them—are general in meaning, so every responsible person is obliged to remember God's blessing, to fulfill the covenant, and the rest of the obligations mentioned after this.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 44:**

﴿Do you enjoin righteousness on the people while you forget yourselves, though you recite the Scripture? Will you not then use your reason?﴾ ﴿Seek help through patience and prayer, and indeed it is a heavy burden except for the humble (al-khashi'in)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 45] ﴿Those who are certain that they will meet their Lord and that to Him they will return﴾ [al-Baqarah: 46]

**Al-amr** (command): a request to bring an act into being. It is also used to mean "matter" or "affair." Its verb is amara, yaamuru, on the pattern of fa'ala, yaf'ulu. In the imperative, its first radical (the hamza) is dropped without a lam, so one says *mur Zaydan* ("command Zayd"). Keeping the hamza (*ii'tamam*, "completing it") is rare. If a waw or fa' precedes the imperative, then keeping the hamza is better (*fa-ithbat al-hamza ajwad*). The verb is transitive to two objects: the first directly, and the second by means of a preposition (*harf jarr*). It is permissible to omit that preposition. This is among a set of limited verbs from which the preposition is omitted from the second object optionally; such usages are to be memorised and not extended by analogy (*la yuqas*) to other cases. [p. 182]

**Al-birr** (righteousness): it means *al-silah* (kindness toward kin) and also *al-ta'ah* (obedience). The rajaz poet said:

*O Lord, indeed Bakr is behind you (dunaka),*
*the people are dutiful to you (yabarrukum) and boast of you (yafkharunaka).*

Al-birr also means "the heart" (al-fu'ad), and "the young of a fox or cat (al-hirr)." One says *barra walidahu*, meaning he honoured and magnified him; the present tense is *yabarruhu*, on the pattern fa'ala, yaf'alu. A man is *barr* or *barr*. *Barrat yaminuhu* means his oath was fulfilled. *Barra hajjuhu* means his pilgrimage was accepted, that is, he magnified it and combined in it many kinds of good. Al-birr is the abundance of goodness and benevolence, and from it come *al-barr* (the land) and *al-bariyyah* (the wilderness), because of their vastness. It encompasses every kind of good. *Al-ibrar* means overcoming. The poet said:

*And they overcome the one who resists (al-abi al-mubirr).*

**Al-nisyan** (forgetting): it is the opposite of remembrance. It is the lapse that occurs after knowledge has been acquired. It is also used to mean abandonment (al-tark), whose opposite is action (al-fi'l). The verb is nasiya, yansa, on the pattern fa'ila, yaf'alu, and it is transitive to one object. Sometimes *nasiya* is used with a suspended (ta'liq) construction, by analogy with *'alima* (to know). The poet said:

*And who are you? Indeed we have forgotten who you are,*
*and what is your scent, from which wind of the storm winds?*

There is an ambiguity in this line.

**Al-tilawah** (recitation): it means *al-qira'ah* (reading). It is so named because verses, words, or letters follow one another in remembrance (yatlu ba'duha ba'dan). *Al-talw* means following. A she-camel is *matl* when her young one follows her.

**Al-aql** (reason): it is the perception that prevents error. From it comes *iqal al-ba'ir* (the camel's tether), which prevents the animal from moving freely. *Al-ma'qil* is a place of refuge. *Al-aql* also means the blood-money (diyah), because its type is camels that are tied (ta'qil) in the courtyard of the guardian, or because it restrains the killer from being killed. *Al-aql* also means a striped garment. The poet said:

*A striped garment and a patterned one that birds keep following,*
*as if it were stained with the blood of the bellies.*

*Al-iqal* also means the zakah of the year. The poet said:

*He (Amr) took the zakah (iqal) and left us no herd (sabad),*
*so how much more would he take if Amr took two zakahs?*

*Raml 'aqanqal* is sand that holds firm against collapse.

**Al-sabr** (patience): it is restraining the self in the face of what is disliked. The verb is sabara, yasbiru, on the pattern fa'ala, yaf'ilu. Originally it is transitive to one object. The poet said:

*So I was patient, knowing that, a free woman*
*who settles (tarsu) when the coward's soul rises up.*

The omission of its object has become so common that it seems intransitive.

**(La-kabirah)** (a heavy burden): from kabura, yakburu. It may refer to physical bulk or to measure. One says *kabura 'alayya kadha*, meaning it was hard upon me. Kabura, yakburu, also describes a man who has advanced in age. The poet said:

*Two young children grazing the goats, O would that we*
*had not grown up until this day, nor had the goats grown up!*

**Al-khushu'** (humility): it is close to al-khudu' (submission). Its origin is softness and ease. It is also said to mean meekness and humbling oneself. Al-Layth said: *al-khudu'* is in the body, while *al-khushu'* is in the body, the gaze, and the voice. *Al-khush'ah* is a low, flat expanse of sand. A ḥadīth says: "The Ka'bah was a low mound above the water."

**Al-zann** (supposition/conviction): it is the inclination toward one of two sides. This is what the grammarians express by doubt (al-shakk). It may also be used for certainty. In both usages it enters upon what originally consists of a subject and predicate, under the conditions mentioned in grammar, contrary to Abu Zayd al-Suhayli, who claimed that it is not one of the abrogators of the inchoative (*min nawasikh al-ibtida'*). Al-zann is also used in the sense of accusation (tuhmah), and in that case it is transitive to one object. Al-Farra' said: *al-zann* may occur in the sense of lying, though the Basrans do not recognise this.

**(A-ta'muruna al-nasa bi-l-birr)** (Do you enjoin righteousness on the people): the hamza here is an interrogative in its original form, but here it carries the sense of rebuke and reproach. The meaning is disapproval and rebuke of them for a person commanding good while neglecting himself. A parallel in prohibition is the saying of Abu al-Aswad:

*Do not forbid a trait while you do the like of it:*
*it is a great shame upon you if you do it.*

and the saying of another:

*Begin with yourself and restrain it from its error;*
*if it desists from it, then you are wise.*

It is ugly to reason that a person should command good while not doing it, or forbid evil while doing it. Concerning the meaning of *al-birr* here, there are several views: steadfastness upon the religion of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), while they do not follow him; or following the Torah, while they contradict it by denying his description. It is narrated from Qatadah, Ibn Jurayj and al-Suddi: or it means charity while they are stingy; or truthfulness while they are not truthful; or urging their companions to prayer and zakah while they do not perform them themselves. Al-Sulami said: "Do you demand of people the realities of meanings while your hearts are empty of the outward forms of their marks?" Al-Qushayri said: "Do you urge people to hasten while you are content to lag behind?" and he also said: "Do you call the creation to us while you stay away from us?" and other expressions of this meaning.

He used the present tense in *ata'murun* (Do you enjoin), although this had occurred from them in the past, because in common usage the present tense conveys in many contexts continuity and frequent engagement in the act, as in the saying "Zayd gives and withholds." He expressed their abandonment of the act with forgetting, as an intensification of abandonment, as though it never came to their minds. He attached forgetting to the selves as an emphasis on the extreme of heedlessness.

**(Wa-tansawna)** (while you forget): it is conjoined with *ta'murun*. The censure is directed at their combining these two states: commanding the people to righteousness, the performance of which brings everlasting salvation, while abandoning its performance until it became forgotten and neglected with respect to themselves. **(Anfusakum)** (yourselves): here *al-anfus* means their persons. It is also said to mean their communities and the people of their religion. Then this occurrence from them is restricted by His saying: **﴿while you recite the Scripture﴾**, meaning: you are directly engaged with the Book, you read it, and you know what it contains. How then did you comply with it with respect to others while you contravened it with respect to yourselves? This is like His saying: **﴿and conceal the truth while you know﴾** [al-Baqarah: 42]. The clause is a circumstantial clause (*hal*). The effect of beginning it with **(wa-antum)** ("while you") is not hidden: it is a rebuke, a reproach, and a censure of them, which is more forceful than if it were a single noun. The Scripture here means the Torah and the Gospel, and both prohibit this blameworthy attribute. This is the view of the majority. It is also said that the Scripture here is the Qur'an. They said: then the address has shifted from addressing the People of the Book to addressing the believers, and this is a shift in address (*talwin al-khitab*), like His saying: **﴿Joseph, turn away from this, and you (wife), ask forgiveness for your sin﴾** [Yusuf: 29]. But this view is remote, since the apparent meaning is that all of this is addressed to the People of the Book.

**(Afala ta'qilun)** (Will you not then use your reason?): the position of Sibawayh and the grammarians is that the original structure of such a sentence was the conjunction preceding the hamza, as in this case, and in *awa-lam yasiru* and *athumma idha ma waqa'*. But since the hamza has the front position in the sentence, it is placed before the conjunction. This differs from *hal*. Al-Zamakhshari claimed that the wa', fa' and thumma after the hamza occupy their position, with no advancing or delaying, and that one posits between the hamza and the conjunction an implied clause to which the conjunction can correctly connect. It seems that he regarded omission as preferable to advancing and delaying. He retracted this view in some of his works in favour of the view of the majority. I have discussed this question in my commentary on the *Tashil*. According to the view of the majority, the sense is: *fa-ala ta'qilun* ("so will you not use your reason?"). According to al-Zamakhshari's view, the sense is: *a-ta'qilun fa-la ta'qilun* ("do you reason, and so do not reason?"), or: *amakathu fa-lam yasiru fi al-ard* ("did they remain and so did not travel in the land?"), or whatever is similar to this verb, to which the clause following the conjunction may correctly be connected. By His saying **(afala ta'qilun)** He alerted them that among them is a noble perception that restrains them from the ugly act they committed, namely commanding others to good while forgetting themselves. This is the condition of one who has been deprived of reason, for the reasonable person strives first to attain what brings his own salvation and deliverance, and only after that strives for the deliverance of others: "Begin with yourself, then with those you support." It is fixed in reason that if a person does not secure a benefit for himself, how will he secure it for others? Do you not see the saying of the poet:

*If a man does not guard his tongue upon himself,*
*he is not a guardian over anything else.*

When a person secures benefit for others but withholds it from himself, that conduct falls outside the actions of the wise, especially in matters through which salvation from the punishment of Allah and success in everlasting bliss are hoped for.

They have explained His saying **(afala ta'qilun)** in several ways: (Will you not then use your reason?) Will you not restrain yourselves from entering this ruinous condition that destroys you? Or: Will you not understand the ugliness of what you do in disobeying your Lord by following Muhammad (ﷺ) and believing in him? Or: Will you not desist, because reason forbids what is ugly? Or: Will you not return, because reason is directed toward what is better? Or: Will you not realise that it is the truth, so that you follow it? Or: Will you not realise that the burden of this falls back upon you? Or: Will you not refrain from acts of disobedience? Or: Will you not reason, since it is not within the matter of reason that you command the good and do not do it? Or: Will you not perceive the ugliness of what you have undertaken, so that its ugliness prevents you from committing it? It is as though you were deprived of reason, since the intellects reject it and repel it.

Similar to this verse is His saying **﴿Why do you say what you do not do?﴾** [al-Saff: 2]. The purpose of commanding good and forbidding evil is guidance to what is beneficial and warning against what is corrupting. This is known through the evidence of reason. Whoever admonishes but does not heed admonition has performed an act that contradicts itself and that reason does not accept. That admonition becomes a cause of desire for disobedience, because it is said: "Were it not that the admonisher knows there is no basis for these warnings, he would not have engaged in disobedience." Thus the soul is repelled from accepting the admonition of one who does not heed it. They recited:

*The admonitions of the admonisher will never be accepted*
*until his own heart first takes them in.*

'Ali, may Allah honour his face, said: "Two men have broken my back: a scholar who is openly immoral, and an ignorant man who is excessively devout."

There is no evidence in the verse for those who argue from it that a sinner may not command good and forbid evil. Nor is there evidence in His saying **﴿Why do you say what you do not do?﴾** [al-Saff: 2], nor for the Mu'tazilah in their claim that the act of the servant is not created by Allah, the Exalted. They said: rebuke is only appropriate if they are the agents of their own acts. This is a difficult question, discussed in the science of kalam.

This denunciation, rebuke and censure, although it is addressed to the Children of Israel, is general in meaning. It is narrated from Muhammad ibn Wasi': "It has reached me that some people of Paradise looked down upon some people of the Fire and said to them: 'You used to command us to do things, and we did them, and so we entered Paradise.' They said: 'We used to command you to them, but we would oppose them and turn to other things.'"

﴿Seek help through patience and prayer﴾. The meanings of the form *istaf'ala* (the form X verb, which can denote seeking) were already mentioned when discussing the root in the verse ﴿It is You we worship, and You we ask for help﴾ (al-Fatihah 1:5). Among those meanings is seeking, and *istaʿāna* means seeking aid. The apparent sense of *al-ṣabr* (patience) is what the word denotes in the language. Mujahid said: *al-ṣabr* is fasting, and fasting is patience, since it is restraint from food. Ramadan is called the month of patience.

*Al-ṣalah* (prayer) is the obligatory prayer together with the Sunnah and voluntary prayers that accompany it, as Mujahid said. It was also said that *al-ṣalah* means supplication. The commentators have supplied for *al-ṣabr* a complement that restricts it. It was said: patience in what your souls dislike of obedience and action. Or patience in performing the obligations; this was narrated from Ibn Abbas. Or patience in refraining from sins. Or patience in forsaking leadership. Or patience in acts of obedience and in abstaining from desires. Or patience regarding your needs from Allah. Or patience in the prayer itself.

When this supplied reading was adopted, namely patience in (ʿalā) the prayer, some who have spoken on the Qur'an thought that the *wāw* in *al-ṣalah* here carries the meaning of ʿalā (upon). The one who holds this view means that they were commanded to seek help through patience with the prayer, by means of the prayer, because the *wāw* means ʿalā. He has in mind the verse ﴿Enjoin prayer upon your family, and be steadfast in it﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:132). They were commanded to seek help through prayer because in it is recited what encourages longing for the Hereafter and renounces the world, or because of the erasure of sins and softening of hearts it brings, or because of the removal of anxieties it effects. From this is the hadith: "Whenever a matter distressed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he would turn to prayer." It has been narrated that when Ibn Abbas was informed of the death of his brother Qutham, he stood and prayed, reciting ﴿Seek help through patience and prayer﴾. Or it is because in it is the prohibition of indecency and wrongdoing. All these aspects have been mentioned by the commentators. Patience was placed before prayer. It was said: because the effect of patience is in removing what is not fitting, and the effect of prayer is in attaining what is fitting, and negation precedes affirmation. It appears that he placed seeking help through patience before seeking help through prayer, because a set of great and demanding obligations had preceded, obligations difficult to leave for one accustomed to them: remembering what they had forgotten, fulfilling what they had broken, believing in a new Book, abandoning their taking of bribes in exchange for the signs of Allah, abandoning their mixing of truth with falsehood and concealing the truth, which for them carried leadership in this world and command over their common people, and establishing the prayer and giving zakat. These are great matters, so beginning with patience was fitting for this reason. Since the pillar of Islam is prayer, and by it the Muslim is distinguished from the polytheist, he followed patience with prayer; (in it occurs withdrawal from worldly concerns, and through the recitation in it one comes to understand what Allah's Book contains of promise and threat, admonitions and ethics, and that creation's destiny is the abode of recompense), so the one occupied with it inclines toward the Hereafter and turns away from this world. And how excellent is an act of worship repeated for a person five times a day and night, in which he confides to his Lord and seeks forgiveness for his sin. By what we have mentioned, the wisdom in being commanded to seek help through patience and prayer becomes clear. The claim of one who said that this is an address to the believers in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is far-fetched, since one who denies him is hardly told, "Seek help through patience and prayer." He said: It is not unlikely that the address was initially to the Children of Israel and then after that it became addressed to the believers. What appears is that all of it is an address to the Children of Israel, because diverting the address to others without a reason, and then it would depart from the structure of eloquence.

﴿And it is indeed heavy﴾: The pronoun refers to prayer. This is the apparent sense of the speech and the rule in the science of Arabic grammar: a pronoun of the third person does not return to other than the nearest referent unless there is evidence. It was said it returns to seeking help, which is the verbal noun understood from "seek help." It would be like ﴿Be just, that is nearer to piety﴾ (al-Ma'idah 5:8), i.e., justice is nearer. This was said by al-Bajali. It was said it returns to the response of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), since patience and prayer were among what he used to call to; this was said by al-Akhfash. It was said it returns to the worship that is implied in meaning by the mention of patience and prayer. It was said it returns to the Ka'bah, since the command to pray was directed toward it. It was said it returns to all the matters the Children of Israel were commanded and forbidden, from the words ﴿Remember My favour﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:47) up to "seek help." It was said the meaning is in the dual, and he suffices with its return to one of the two, as if he said "and they both are" (*wa-innahumā*), like his saying ﴿Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them﴾ (al-Tawbah 9:34) in some interpretations, and like his saying ﴿Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ (al-Tawbah 9:62), and the saying of the poet:

*If the prime of youth and black hair, so long as they are not disobeyed, is madness.*

So these are seven opinions regarding what the pronoun returns to, and the most apparent is the one with which we began. Mu'arrij said regarding the return of the pronoun: because prayer is more important and more prevalent, like his saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They dispersed toward it﴾ (al-Jumu'ah 62:11). He ended. He means that the inclination of those who dispersed during the Friday prayer toward trade was more important and more prevalent than their inclination toward amusement, so the pronoun returned to it. He does not mean that the two pronouns are equal in return, because coordination with *wa* (and) differs from coordination with *aw* (or). With *wa*, the basic rule is that the pronoun agrees with what precedes it in dual and plural, whereas with *aw* the pronoun returns only to one of what has preceded. The meaning of the heaviness of prayer is its weight and difficulty for the one who performs it, like the verse ﴿Hard upon the polytheists is what you call them to﴾ (al-Shura 42:13), i.e., it was hard and burdensome.

﴿Except for the humble﴾: This is an exceptive construction lacking its complement (*istithnāʾ mufarragh*), because the meaning is: it is indeed heavy for everyone, except for the humble (*al-khāshiʿīn*), who are the lowly and submissive. They are not burdened because it encompasses qualities they possess through their humility: standing before Allah, bowing to Him, prostrating to Him, and hoping for what He has of reward. Since the outcome of their deeds is eternal happiness, what is difficult for others, such as the hypocrites and the show-offs who do not hope for any benefit from their deeds, is easy for them. The word *alladhīna* may be in the following form, or cut off to the nominative or accusative, and that is a description of praise; so cutting off is more appropriate for it. *Yaẓunnūn* means "they are certain"; this was said by the majority, because one described as humble does not doubt that he will meet his Lord. This is supported by the fact that in the codex of Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) the reading is *alladhīna yaʿlamūn* ("those who know"). It was also said its meaning is "they suppose," in which case it needs a qualifier for this meaning, which is what they supplied as an omission, namely "with their sins," so that they expect to meet their Lord as sinners. The correct view is the first, and similar to it is ﴿Indeed I thought that I would meet my account﴾ (al-Haqqah 69:20), i.e., they thought they would encounter it. Durayd said:

*I said to them: "Attack two thousand armored men, their chiefs in the coats of mail, in the woven and tightly woven."*

Ibn Atiyyah said: The verb *al-ẓann* may be used in the place of certainty regarding matters that are established, but it is not used regarding what has already come into sensory perception. The Arabs do not say of a man who is present and seen, "I think this is a human being"; rather, they only use it for what has not come into sensory perception. He ended.

Regarding both of its usages, *al-ẓann* (to think/suppose), whether it means certainty or doubt, is transitive to two objects. After *al-ẓann* come *an* (that), which governs the verb, and *inna* (indeed), which governs the noun and makes the predicate nominative. So you say: *ẓanantu an taqūma* (I thought that you would stand), and *ẓanantu annaka taqūmu* (I thought that you stand). On the analysis of this there is disagreement. The school of Sibawayh holds that each of *an* and *inna*, together with what it governs, stands in place of the two objects, because the subject and predicate in this construction are in a relation. The view of Abu al-Hasan and Abu al-Abbas is that *inna* and what it governs occupy the position of one first object, and the second object is implied. So when you say *ẓanantu anna Zaydan qāʾimun* (I thought that Zayd is standing), its implied form is: *ẓanantu qiyāma Zaydin kāʾinan aw wāqiʿan* (I thought Zayd's standing was occurring or existing). The preference between the two views is mentioned in the science of grammar.

﴿That they are meeting their Lord﴾: *al-mulāqāh* (meeting) is a reciprocal form (*mufāʿalah*) that occurs between two parties, because whoever meets you, you have met him. Al-Mahdawi, al-Mawardi and others said: *al-mulāqāh* here, although its form implies sharing, is from one party, like the expressions "I struck the sandal" (*ṭāraqtu al-naʿl*), "I punished the thief" (*ʿāqabtu al-liṣṣ*), and "God granted you well-being" (*ʿāfāka Allāh*). Ibn Atiyyah said: This is weak, because *laqiya* (to meet) includes the meaning of *lāqā* (to meet mutually), and not all verbs are like this; rather, the basic form *faʿala* differs in meaning from *fāʿala*. He ended his speech, which needs explanation. He weakened it on the ground that the root *laqiya*, whether in basic or *fāʿala* form, is by its nature a term denoting the mutual act, in that whoever met you, you met him. The root for this specific act requires sharing and it is impossible for it to belong to one party. This indicates that *fāʿala* may be used to agree with the basic verb, and this is one of the meanings of *fāʿala*, namely that it agrees with the basic verb. Ibn Atiyyah's statement "not all verbs are like this" is correct, meaning that the basic forms of verbs are not all used with the meaning of *fāʿala*; rather, *fāʿala* in them indicates sharing, while his saying "rather the basic *faʿala* is the opposite of *fāʿala*" means that the basic form in them indicates individuality, which is the opposite of *fāʿala*, since *fāʿala* indicates sharing. So it was weakened that *fāʿala* from the root of encounter is of the type of *ʿāqabtu al-liṣṣ*, since the root of encounter requires sharing, whether in the basic or in the *fāʿala* form. This construction (*iḍāfah*, the genitive construction in *mulāqū rabbihim*) is not a pure construction, because it is the construction of an active participle with future meaning. We have previously discussed the active participle when it has present or future meaning in relation to its governing of the object. Its construction to it, and its construction to the Lord, and the construction of the Lord to them, are of the highest eloquence, because the Lord, in whatever sense you take Him, indicates kindness toward the one He nurtures and a clear tenderness that no word other than "the Lord" conveys. The commentators differed on the meaning of "meeting their Lord." Some took it at face value, without omission or metaphor, holding that the encounter is the seeing of the Creator, the Exalted, and there is no encounter greater or more noble than it. It has been established by widespread Sunnah, and most Muslims hold this belief. It was said that this is by omission of a noun, meaning "the reward of their Lord," since meeting in the sense of essences is impossible except in seeing. It was said that this is a metaphor for the end of their term, as is said of one who has died, "he has met Allah." From this is the poet's saying:

*Tomorrow we will meet the Beloved, Muhammad and his companions.*

He used "meeting" as a metaphor for death, because meeting Allah is a consequence of death, so it is an expression of the effect for the cause, and what is meant is the cause. The one who thought of death every moment would not have his heart free of humility. It was said that this is by omission of a more specific noun than reward, namely "the recompense," i.e., "the recompense of their Lord." According to this view and the first view, *ẓanna* keeps its basic meaning of inclining toward a probability. Based on the interpretation of reward or the view that the encounter means the end of the term, *ẓanna* is used in the sense of certainty. The Mu'tazilah disputed whether the word "encounter" is not used to mean seeing and does not convey it. Consider His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts until the Day they meet Him﴾ (al-Tawbah 9:77), and the hypocrite does not see his Lord. And ﴿Know that you will meet Him﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:223). Does it not include the disbeliever and the believer? In the hadith: "He met Allah while He was angry with him," and beyond that from what they have mentioned. Our companions have spoken on this, and the question of seeing is discussed in the principles of religion.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿وأنَّهم إلَيْهِ راجِعُونَ﴾ = ﴿And that they will return to Him﴾.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 45–46 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And that they will return to Him﴾: Scholars differed over what the pronoun in (ilayhi, "to Him") refers back to. The apparent meaning of the speech and the eloquent construction is that it refers to the Lord, and the meaning is: "And that they will return to their Lord," and this is the closest antecedent mentioned. It has been said that it refers to the meeting (liqa') implied by "those who meet their Lord." It has been said that it refers to death. It has been said that it refers to the re-creation (i'adah), and both of these are indicated by "those who meet" (mulaqu). The explanation of "return" (ruju') has already been given, so there is no need to repeat it here. It has been said, according to the first view, that the pronoun refers to the Lord, so the return is not realized, and to realize it one needs to delete a noun (mudaf): the estimate is "they will return to the command of their Lord." It has been said that what is meant by "return" is death. It has been said that "they will return" means they will be restored in the Hereafter; this is the view of Abu al-'Aliyah. It has been said that "they will return" means that none of them will possess harm or benefit for anyone else, just as they were at the beginning of creation. It has been said that "they will return" means that He will recompense them for their deeds. The words "And that they will return to Him" give no proof to the anthropomorphists (mujassimah) or the metempsychosists (tanasukhiyyah) that souls are eternal; rather they were existing in the world of spiritual realities (ruhaniyyat). They said: because return is to a thing that was preceded by existence in it.

It appears that he placed seeking help through patience before seeking help through prayer, because a set of great and demanding obligations had preceded, obligations difficult to leave for one accustomed to them: remembering what they had forgotten, fulfilling what they had broken, believing in a new Book, abandoning their taking of bribes in exchange for the signs of Allah, abandoning their mixing of truth with falsehood and concealing the truth, which for them carried leadership in this world and command over their common people, and establishing the prayer and giving zakat. These are great matters, so beginning with patience was fitting for this reason. Since the pillar of Islam is prayer, and by it the Muslim is distinguished from the polytheist, he followed patience with prayer; (in it occurs withdrawal from worldly concerns, and through the recitation in it one comes to understand what Allah's Book contains of promise and threat, admonitions and ethics, and that creation's destiny is the abode of recompense), so the one occupied with it inclines toward the Hereafter and turns away from this world. And how excellent is an act of worship repeated for a person five times a day and night, in which he confides to his Lord and seeks forgiveness for his sin. By what we have mentioned, the wisdom in being commanded to seek help through patience and prayer becomes clear. The claim of one who said that this is an address to the believers in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is far-fetched, since one who denies him is hardly told, "Seek help through patience and prayer." He said: It is not unlikely that the address was initially to the Children of Israel and then after that it became addressed to the believers. What appears is that all of it is an address to the Children of Israel, because diverting the address to others without a reason, and then it would depart from the structure of eloquence.

﴿And it is indeed heavy﴾: The pronoun refers to prayer. This is the apparent sense of the speech and the rule in the science of Arabic grammar: a pronoun of the third person does not return to other than the nearest referent unless there is evidence. It was said it returns to seeking help, which is the verbal noun understood from "seek help." It would be like ﴿Be just, that is nearer to piety﴾ (al-Ma'idah 5:8), i.e., justice is nearer. This was said by al-Bajali. It was said it returns to the response of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), since patience and prayer were among what he used to call to; this was said by al-Akhfash. It was said it returns to the worship that is implied in meaning by the mention of patience and prayer. It was said it returns to the Ka'bah, since the command to pray was directed toward it. It was said it returns to all the matters the Children of Israel were commanded and forbidden, from the words ﴿Remember My favour﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:47) up to "seek help." It was said the meaning is in the dual, and he suffices with its return to one of the two, as if he said "and they both are" (*wa-innahumā*), like his saying ﴿Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them﴾ (al-Tawbah 9:34) in some interpretations, and like his saying ﴿Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ (al-Tawbah 9:62), and the saying of the poet:

*If the prime of youth and black hair, so long as they are not disobeyed, is madness.*

So these are seven opinions regarding what the pronoun returns to, and the most apparent is the one with which we began. Mu'arrij said regarding the return of the pronoun: because prayer is more important and more prevalent, like his saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They dispersed toward it﴾ (al-Jumu'ah 62:11). He ended. He means that the inclination of those who dispersed during the Friday prayer toward trade was more important and more prevalent than their inclination toward amusement, so the pronoun returned to it. He does not mean that the two pronouns are equal in return, because coordination with *wa* (and) differs from coordination with *aw* (or). With *wa*, the basic rule is that the pronoun agrees with what precedes it in dual and plural, whereas with *aw* the pronoun returns only to one of what has preceded. The meaning of the heaviness of prayer is its weight and difficulty for the one who performs it, like the verse ﴿Hard upon the polytheists is what you call them to﴾ (al-Shura 42:13), i.e., it was hard and burdensome.

﴿Except for the humble﴾: This is an exceptive construction lacking its complement (*istithnāʾ mufarragh*), because the meaning is: it is indeed heavy for everyone, except for the humble (*al-khāshiʿīn*), who are the lowly and submissive. They are not burdened because it encompasses qualities they possess through their humility: standing before Allah, bowing to Him, prostrating to Him, and hoping for what He has of reward. Since the outcome of their deeds is eternal happiness, what is difficult for others, such as the hypocrites and the show-offs who do not hope for any benefit from their deeds, is easy for them. The word *alladhīna* may be in the following form, or cut off to the nominative or accusative, and that is a description of praise; so cutting off is more appropriate for it. *Yaẓunnūn* means "they are certain"; this was said by the majority, because one described as humble does not doubt that he will meet his Lord. This is supported by the fact that in the codex of Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) the reading is *alladhīna yaʿlamūn* ("those who know"). It was also said its meaning is "they suppose," in which case it needs a qualifier for this meaning, which is what they supplied as an omission, namely "with their sins," so that they expect to meet their Lord as sinners. The correct view is the first, and similar to it is ﴿Indeed I thought that I would meet my account﴾ (al-Haqqah 69:20), i.e., they thought they would encounter it. Durayd said:

*I said to them: "Attack two thousand armored men, their chiefs in the coats of mail, in the woven and tightly woven."*

Ibn Atiyyah said: The verb *al-ẓann* may be used in the place of certainty regarding matters that are established, but it is not used regarding what has already come into sensory perception. The Arabs do not say of a man who is present and seen, "I think this is a human being"; rather, they only use it for what has not come into sensory perception. He ended.

Regarding both of its usages, *al-ẓann* (to think/suppose), whether it means certainty or doubt, is transitive to two objects. After *al-ẓann* come *an* (that), which governs the verb, and *inna* (indeed), which governs the noun and makes the predicate nominative. So you say: *ẓanantu an taqūma* (I thought that you would stand), and *ẓanantu annaka taqūmu* (I thought that you stand). On the analysis of this there is disagreement. The school of Sibawayh holds that each of *an* and *inna*, together with what it governs, stands in place of the two objects, because the subject and predicate in this construction are in a relation. The view of Abu al-Hasan and Abu al-Abbas is that *inna* and what it governs occupy the position of one first object, and the second object is implied. So when you say *ẓanantu anna Zaydan qāʾimun* (I thought that Zayd is standing), its implied form is: *ẓanantu qiyāma Zaydin kāʾinan aw wāqiʿan* (I thought Zayd's standing was occurring or existing). The preference between the two views is mentioned in the science of grammar.

﴿That they are meeting their Lord﴾: *al-mulāqāh* (meeting) is a reciprocal form (*mufāʿalah*) that occurs between two parties, because whoever meets you, you have met him. Al-Mahdawi, al-Mawardi and others said: *al-mulāqāh* here, although its form implies sharing, is from one party, like the expressions "I struck the sandal" (*ṭāraqtu al-naʿl*), "I punished the thief" (*ʿāqabtu al-liṣṣ*), and "God granted you well-being" (*ʿāfāka Allāh*). Ibn Atiyyah said: This is weak, because *laqiya* (to meet) includes the meaning of *lāqā* (to meet mutually), and not all verbs are like this; rather, the basic form *faʿala* differs in meaning from *fāʿala*. He ended his speech, which needs explanation. He weakened it on the ground that the root *laqiya*, whether in basic or *fāʿala* form, is by its nature a term denoting the mutual act, in that whoever met you, you met him. The root for this specific act requires sharing and it is impossible for it to belong to one party. This indicates that *fāʿala* may be used to agree with the basic verb, and this is one of the meanings of *fāʿala*, namely that it agrees with the basic verb. Ibn Atiyyah's statement "not all verbs are like this" is correct, meaning that the basic forms of verbs are not all used with the meaning of *fāʿala*; rather, *fāʿala* in them indicates sharing, while his saying "rather the basic *faʿala* is the opposite of *fāʿala*" means that the basic form in them indicates individuality, which is the opposite of *fāʿala*, since *fāʿala* indicates sharing. So it was weakened that *fāʿala* from the root of encounter is of the type of *ʿāqabtu al-liṣṣ*, since the root of encounter requires sharing, whether in the basic or in the *fāʿala* form. This construction (*iḍāfah*, the genitive construction in *mulāqū rabbihim*) is not a pure construction, because it is the construction of an active participle with future meaning. We have previously discussed the active participle when it has present or future meaning in relation to its governing of the object. Its construction to it, and its construction to the Lord, and the construction of the Lord to them, are of the highest eloquence, because the Lord, in whatever sense you take Him, indicates kindness toward the one He nurtures and a clear tenderness that no word other than "the Lord" conveys. The commentators differed on the meaning of "meeting their Lord." Some took it at face value, without omission or metaphor, holding that the encounter is the seeing of the Creator, the Exalted, and there is no encounter greater or more noble than it. It has been established by widespread Sunnah, and most Muslims hold this belief. It was said that this is by omission of a noun, meaning "the reward of their Lord," since meeting in the sense of essences is impossible except in seeing. It was said that this is a metaphor for the end of their term, as is said of one who has died, "he has met Allah." From this is the poet's saying:

*Tomorrow we will meet the Beloved, Muhammad and his companions.*

He used "meeting" as a metaphor for death, because meeting Allah is a consequence of death, so it is an expression of the effect for the cause, and what is meant is the cause. The one who thought of death every moment would not have his heart free of humility. It was said that this is by omission of a more specific noun than reward, namely "the recompense," i.e., "the recompense of their Lord." According to this view and the first view, *ẓanna* keeps its basic meaning of inclining toward a probability. Based on the interpretation of reward or the view that the encounter means the end of the term, *ẓanna* is used in the sense of certainty. The Mu'tazilah disputed whether the word "encounter" is not used to mean seeing and does not convey it. Consider His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts until the Day they meet Him﴾ (al-Tawbah 9:77), and the hypocrite does not see his Lord. And ﴿Know that you will meet Him﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:223). Does it not include the disbeliever and the believer? In the hadith: "He met Allah while He was angry with him," and beyond that from what they have mentioned. Our companions have spoken on this, and the question of seeing is discussed in the principles of religion.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿وأنَّهم إلَيْهِ راجِعُونَ﴾ = ﴿And that they will return to Him﴾.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 45–46 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And that they will return to Him﴾: Scholars differed over what the pronoun in (ilayhi, "to Him") refers back to. The apparent meaning of the speech and the eloquent construction is that it refers to the Lord, and the meaning is: "And that they will return to their Lord," and this is the closest antecedent mentioned. It has been said that it refers to the meeting (liqa') implied by "those who meet their Lord." It has been said that it refers to death. It has been said that it refers to the re-creation (i'adah), and both of these are indicated by "those who meet" (mulaqu). The explanation of "return" (ruju') has already been given, so there is no need to repeat it here. It has been said, according to the first view, that the pronoun refers to the Lord, so the return is not realized, and to realize it one needs to delete a noun (mudaf): the estimate is "they will return to the command of their Lord." It has been said that what is meant by "return" is death. It has been said that "they will return" means they will be restored in the Hereafter; this is the view of Abu al-'Aliyah. It has been said that "they will return" means that none of them will possess harm or benefit for anyone else, just as they were at the beginning of creation. It has been said that "they will return" means that He will recompense them for their deeds. The words "And that they will return to Him" give no proof to the anthropomorphists (mujassimah) or the metempsychosists (tanasukhiyyah) that souls are eternal; rather they were existing in the world of spiritual realities (ruhaniyyat). They said: because return is to a thing that was preceded by existence in it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 47–48 (part 1 of 2):

﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds.﴾ ﴿And guard yourselves against a Day when no soul will avail another soul in anything, nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will any compensation be taken from it, nor will they be helped.﴾ ﴿And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with the worst torment, slaughtering your sons and sparing your women; and in that was a tremendous trial from your Lord.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 49].

Al-fadl (favour, excellence): increase, and its use is in good. Its verb is fa'ala yaf'ulu. Its original construction is to take the preposition ʿala (over), and then ʿala is omitted, in the manner of the poet's saying, who combined both forms:
"We found Nahshal excelled Faqim as the excess of the son of the she-camel excels over the weaned calf."
As for fadlah (surplus) of a thing, meaning the remainder, one says fadala yafdulu, like what we have mentioned, and fadila yafdalu, like sami'a yasma'u, and fadila yafdulu, with the kasra in the past tense and the damma in the present. Some grammarians have been fond of permitting both the fath and the kasra of the ḍād in fadaltu in the line, and the correct reading is the fath.

Al-jaza' (recompense): to suffice for the one owed and to requite. The rajiz said:
"May the Lord of the Throne reward him on my behalf for what he rewarded: the gardens of Eden in the highest heights."
Al-ijza' means sufficiency.

Qabul al-shay' (acceptance of a thing): turning towards it. The verb is qabila yaqbalu. Al-qibal is what faces you. Al-Qutami said:
"I said to the riders when they rose with them, from the right of al-Hubayya, a glance, qibal."

Al-shafa'ah (intercession): adding another to one's means. Al-shuf'ah (pre-emption) is adding ownership. Al-shaf' is the pair, and intercession is from it, because intercession and the one interceded for form a pair. Al-Ahwas said:
"Whoever blamed me for abandoning her, they interceded for Layla by their blame."
A she-camel shafu' is one with a young one following it; it is said: one with a young one following it and a young one in its belly.

Al-akhdh (taking): the opposite of leaving. Al-akhdh is seizing and holding. From it the captive is called akhidh. Its initial hamza is dropped in the imperative without a lam, and completion is rare.

Al-ʿadl (ransom): al-ʿadl is that which equals it in value and measure, even if not of its kind. With a kasra on the ʿayn: that which equals it in kind and bulk. Some Arabs say ʿidl with a kasra in the sense of ransom, and the singular of a'dal is only with a kasra. Al-ʿadl also means one whose word is accepted among people, and a kasra on the ʿayn is also reported for it. Tha'lab said: al-ʿadl is a guarantor and a bribe. The poet said:
"In it the money-changer does not accept the exchange of al-ʿadl."

Al-nasr (help): aid. Ard mansurah: land watered by rain. The poet said:
"Your father, who benefited me by his help, and after him every killer withheld from me."
And another said:
"When the sacred month bids farewell, then bid farewell to the lands of Tamim and let the land of ʿAmir be watered."
Al-nasr is also giving, and al-intisar is retaliation.

Al-najah (deliverance): rescue from destruction after falling into it. The original meaning is casting into a safe height. The poet said:
"Did you not see that al-Nuʿman was in a safe place from evil, had a man been one who was delivered?"
