Al-al: it is said to mean "family" (ahl). It is claimed that its alif is a substitution for a hā', and its diminutive is uhayl. Some have held that its alif is a substitution for a quiescent hamza, and that hamza is a substitution for hā'. It is also said: it is not in the sense of ahl, because ahl is kinship, whereas al is whoever returns (yaʾūl) through kinship, or a patron, or a school of thought; so its alif is a substitution for a wāw, and for this reason Yunus said its diminutive is uwayl, and al-Kisa'i transmitted it explicitly from the Arabs. This is the choice of Abu al-Hasan ibn al-Badhish. Sibawayh did not mention in the chapter on substitution that hā' is replaced by hamza, as he mentioned that hamza is replaced by hā' in: haraqtu, haya, harahtu, and hiyyaka. They have restricted āl to being added to a famous, distinguished proper name of one who is generally known; so one does not say: āl al-iskaf or āl al-hajjam. The poet said:
"We are the family of God in our land; we have not ceased to be a family since the time of Iram."
Al-Akhfash said: āl is only added to the supreme chief, such as: āl Muhammad (ﷺ) and āl Fir'awn, because he is their chief in misguidance. It was said: there is scrutiny in this, because it has been heard from the people of language regarding cities, so they said: āl al-Madinah and āl al-Basrah. Al-Kisa'i said: it is not permissible to say: so-and-so is of the family of Basrah or of the family of Kufah; rather one says: of the people of Basrah and of the people of Kufah. End of his words. It has also been heard added to a common noun and to a pronoun. The poet said:
"Help against the family of the cross and its worshippers today, your family."
Hudbah said:
"I am the horseman who protects the reality of my father and my family, as you protect the reality of your family."
There has been disagreement regarding the permissibility of its addition to a pronoun: al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas and Abu Bakr al-Zubaydi forbade it, while others permitted it. It is pluralised with the wāw and nūn in the nominative, and with the yā' and nūn in the genitive and accusative, just as ahl is pluralised, so they say: ālūn. Al-āl is also the mirage, pluralised on the pattern af'āl; they said: a'wāl. Al-āl is also the pole of a tent, al-āl is the person, and al-ālah is a severe state.

Fir'awn is not declined because of definiteness and foreignness, and discussion of it will come. Sāmahu: he assigned him a hard task. The poet said:
"When the king imposed on the people humiliation, we refused to accept humiliation among us."
It was also said: its meaning is: they teach you from al-simā', which is the mark, and from it is taswim of horses. It was said: they demand from you in the manner of bargaining in a sale. It was said: they send against you, from the sending of camels to pasture. Abu ʿUbaydah said: they appoint you; one says: sāmahu khuttata khasf, meaning he gave him it.

Al-sū': the verbal noun of asā'a. One says sā'a yasū'u, and it is transitive. Asā'a al-rajul: meaning he became one with evil. The poet said:
"If it grieves me that you have touched me with an evil, it has gladdened me that I came to your mind."
The meaning of sā'ahu: grieved him, this is its origin; then it is used for everything that is considered ugly. It is said: "I seek refuge in God from the evil of character and the evil of deed," meaning their ugliness.

Al-dhabh (slaughter): its origin is splitting. The poet said:
"As if between its jaw and the jaw was a musk mouse slaughtered in a container."
And he said:
"As if aloes were slaughtered in your two eyes."
Al-dhabhah is a disease of the throat; from it one says: dhabahahu yadhbahuhu dhabhan. Al-dhibh is the slaughtered animal.

Al-istihya' here is leaving alive, and istaf'ala here has the sense of af'ala. Istahyahu and ahyahu have one meaning, like their saying: aballa and istaballa. Or it means seeking modesty, which is the private part, so istaf'ala here is for seeking, like istaghfara, meaning he sought forgiveness. The discussion of istahya from ḥayā' (modesty) has already passed in His words: ﴿Indeed, God is not ashamed to strike an example﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26]. Nisa' is a noun that applies to the young and the old, and it is a broken plural of niswah, and niswah is on the pattern fi'lah, and it is a plural of paucity, contrary to Ibn al-Sarraj, who claimed that fi'lah is a collective noun, not a broken plural. On both views, no singular is pronounced from its own form; the singular is imra'ah.

Al-balā': testing. Balāhu yablūhu balā'an: he tested him. Then it came to be applied to what is disliked and to hardship. One says: a trial afflicted so-and-so, meaning hardship. It returns to the meaning of wear (bilā), as if the one tried comes to wear out, which is destruction and perishing. One says: abla-hu with blessing, and balāhu with hardship; one may sometimes replace the other, so one says: balāhu bil-khayr, and ablāhu bil-sharr. The poet said:
"May God reward with good what the two did to you, so He tried them with the best trial, which tests."
He used them with one meaning. From it the form ifta'ala is built, so one says: ubtuliya.

* *

﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾: the discussion of this has already been explained. Their address is repeated a second time for emphasis, and so that they attend to what comes after it of enumerating the blessings which God bestowed upon them, detailing them blessing by blessing. The first address is to alert them to obeying the Benefactor, and the second address is to alert them to thanking the blessings. (And that I preferred you): then preference is conjoined to the blessing, and this is conjunction of the specific to the general, because the blessing includes the mentioned preference within it. This is what the waw alone does, to the exclusion of the other particles of conjunction. Our teacher, the scholar Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn Ibrahim ibn al-Zubayr al-Thaqafi, used to mention to us this kind of conjunction, and that it is called tajrid (abstraction), as if it were stripped from the sentence and singled out for mention by way of distinction. The poet said:
"I charge against them on a sturdy horse, and its chest, when it feels the impact of the spear, neighs."
Da'laj here is the name of a horse, and labanuhu is its chest. Abu al-Fath ibn Jinni has a discussion on this which reveals the secret of the craft regarding it.

(Over the worlds): that is, the worlds of their time, as said by al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah, Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Zayd and others; or over all the worlds, by virtue of the prophets He placed among them, and by making them kings and giving them what He had not given any one of the worlds; and this is specific to them to the exclusion of others, so the scope is general while the blessing is particular. They said: what refutes this view is: "You are the best nation" [Al 'Imran: 110]. Or [it means] over the great multitude of people; one says: I saw a 'alam of people, meaning a multitude. On each of these three views, preference over this nation does not follow; for whoever holds the generality restricts the blessing, and preference over every world in some specific respect does not necessitate preference in all respects. As for whoever holds the particularity, the reason for absence of absolute preference is clear.

Al-Qushayri said: He made the Children of Israel witness the excellence of themselves, so He said: "And that I preferred you over the worlds," and He made the Muslims witness the excellence of Himself, so He said: "Say: By the bounty of God and His mercy, so in that let them rejoice" [Yunus: 58]. How far apart is one whose witness is the bounty of his Lord from one whose witness is the bounty of himself: the first implies praise, and the second implies self-admiration. End of his words, and its ending is a summary of his speech.

(And guard yourselves against a Day): an command to guard oneself. As if, when they were commanded to remember the blessings and their preference, it is fitting that one upon whom blessing is bestowed and who is preferred should be one who attains piety. So they were commanded to persist in piety, or to attain piety if any defect befalls them. The accusative of (a Day) is either as an adverbial of time, with the object of guarding omitted, its estimate being: guard against the punishment on a day; or as a direct object by extension, or by omitting a genitive, meaning the punishment of a day, or the terror of a day. It was also said: its meaning is: come as those who guard; and it seems that on this estimate he did not consider the object of guarding, so in that case (a Day) is accusative as an adverbial. Al-Qushayri said: the common people He frightened with His punishment, so He said: "And guard yourselves against a Day," "and guard yourselves against the Fire." The elect He frightened with His attributes, so He said: "And say: Act, and God will see your deed, and His Messenger" [al-Tawbah: 105], "And you are not in any matter" [Yunus: 61], etc. The elect of the elect He frightened with Himself, so He said: "And God warns you of Himself" [Al 'Imran: 28]. Ibn al-Sammak al-'Adawi read: "la tajzi" from ajza'a, meaning sufficed; it was also said jaza and ajza'a have one meaning. This sentence is an attribute of the Day, and the connecting pronoun is omitted, so the estimate may be: la tajzi fihi (no soul will avail in it), the preposition was dropped, the pronoun attached to the verb, then the pronoun was dropped; so the omission is gradual, or he transferred the verb to the pronoun first by extension. This is the choice of Abu 'Ali, and it is what we choose. Al-Mahdawi said: both estimates, namely: la tajzi fihi and la tajzihi, are permissible according to Sibawayh, al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj. Al-Kisa'i said: the omitted pronoun is only for it (the verb with a preposition), he said: it is not permissible to say: hadha rajulun qasadtu (this is a man I intended), nor ra'aytu rajulan arghabu (I saw a man I desire), while you mean qasadtu ilayhi and arghabu fihi. End of his words. Omission of the pronoun from a clause functioning as an attribute is permissible, and from it is his saying:
"I do not know whether it is they who have become distant, and the length of the time, or the wealth they obtained."

He means they hit the mark. As for the view that the connecting pronoun is the one stated, or that the pronoun is apparent: according to the opinion of the Kufans (the grammarians of Kufa), it is also possible that there is a connecting pronoun, and the clause is not a qualifier. Instead, a noun governing the clause, *yawma* (the day), is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it. The intended meaning is: "And fear a day, the day when [no soul] will avail," so *yawm* is omitted because *yawman* (a day) indicates it. The omitted element in the construct phrase then resembles the expressed element in such a phrase as His words, may He be exalted: ﴿This is a day when they will not speak﴾ [al-Mursalat: 35]. In the same way, for *yawma lā tamliku* (the day when no soul will own anything), the clause does not need a pronoun, and the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of the omitted element is as a substitute (*badal*), specifically a substitute of the whole from the whole (*badal kull min kull*). From this is the poet's saying:

May God have mercy on the bones they buried
in Sijistan: Talha, the Talha of Talhas.

In the version where the word is in the genitive, the implied meaning is: "the bones of Talha." The Arabs have also said: "The honoring of you pleases me, Sa'd," meaning: "The honoring of Sa'd pleases me." Al-Kisa'i reported from the Arabs: "They fed us fat meat, a sheep they slaughtered," meaning: "meat of a sheep." Al-Farra' reported from the Arabs: "Indeed, by God, if you knew the knowledge of one whose age is great, whose bones are fine," on the assumption: "if you knew the knowledge of one whose age is great." Thus the second word is omitted, relying on the first. The Basrans (the grammarians of Basra) did not permit what the Kufans permitted, namely omitting the governing noun and leaving the governed noun in the genitive, as in: "The standing of Zayd pleases me." It is not far-fetched to prefer omitting *yawma* because of what precedes it, supported by this heard usage which al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' reported from the Arabs. This interpretation is strengthened by the fact that the noun governed is a clause, which does not show i'rab, so it would clash with the i'rab of what precedes it. If that is permitted in their prose despite the clash, then it is even more permissible where there is no clash. I have not seen any of the grammarians or exegetes who analysed this clause in this way. Rather, they are all agreed that the clause is a qualifier of *yawm* (day). It necessarily follows from this that the connecting element is also omitted from the clauses conjoined to *lā tajzī* (no soul will avail), that is: "and no intercession will be accepted from it [on that day]; and no ransom will be taken from it [on that day]; and they will not be helped [on that day]." According to this interpretation, there is no need to supply these connecting elements.

﴿A soul for another soul, anything﴾: both are indefinite nouns in a negative context, so they are general. The meaning of the indefiniteness is that a soul of the souls will not avail for a soul of the souls in anything of the things. Al-Zamakhshari said: "In it is a complete, decisive despair of all hopes," and this is according to his position that there is no intercession. Some said: the implied meaning is "for a disbelieving soul," so he restricted it to disbelief. In this is an indication that a soul may avail for a believing soul, and this is by the implication of the qualifier. The discussion of that will come, God willing, when we discuss His words: ﴿nor will intercession be accepted from it﴾. Abu al-Sirar al-Ghanawi recited: "No soul will avail for another soul."

The accusative of *shay'an* (anything) is that it is the direct object, meaning: it will not settle anything, that is, any right of the rights. It is also possible that its accusative is as a verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning: "and it will not avail any of the recompense." This was said by al-Akhfash, and in it is an indication of small quantity, like your saying: "I struck a bit of striking."

﴿And no intercession will be accepted from it﴾: Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited *wa-lā tuqbalu* with the *ta'* (feminine prefix), and this is the analogical and more common form. Whoever recited with the *ya'* (masculine prefix) is also correct and eloquent, because of the metaphorical feminine (*majāz al-ta'nīth*), and the separation between the verb and its subject also makes it good. Sufyan recited *wa-lā yaqbalu* with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and *shafā'atan* in the accusative, in the active voice. In this there is a *iltifāt* (shift) from the first-person pronoun to the third-person pronoun, because before it there is "remember My blessing" and "that I preferred you." The passive form is more eloquent, because it is more general in wording, even though it is known that the one who does not accept is God, Exalted. The pronoun in *minhā* (from it) refers to the later *nafs* (soul), because it is the nearest mentioned noun, meaning: "He does not accept from the soul seeking intercession any intercession of an intercessor." It is also possible that the pronoun refers to the first *nafs*, meaning: "and He does not accept from the soul which does not avail for another soul any intercession, being on the verge of that, if it had interceded, it would not have been accepted from it." It may appear preferable that it refers to the first soul, because it is the one spoken about in His words: ﴿No soul will avail for another soul﴾, while the second soul is mentioned as a complement, not as the main element. The apparent meaning of His words: ﴿nor will intercession be accepted from it﴾ is the negation of acceptance and of the existence of intercession. It is also possible that it belongs to the type of the poet's line:

On a faint track, whose landmarks cannot be followed,

where the negation applies to acceptance while the intended meaning is the negation of intercession, as if it were said: "There is no intercession so that it might be accepted."

The exegetes have differed in understanding this in six opinions. The first: it is a general expression for a specific meaning, and the intended meaning is those of the Children of Israel who said: "We are the sons of God and the sons of His prophets, and they will intercede for us with God." So this was rejected and they were despaired of it because of their disbelief. According to this, the first soul is a believer and the second is a disbeliever, and a disbeliever is not benefited by intercession, as in His words: ﴿So the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 48]. The second: its meaning is that they will not find an intercessor whose intercession is accepted, because the one interceded for is unable to obtain it; this is the view of al-Hasan. The third: its meaning is that the intercessor will not grant the one interceded for the intercession, even if he would have been granted it had he interceded. The fourth: its meaning is that since God has not permitted intercession for the disbelievers, and there must be permission from God for the intercessor to intercede, as in His words: ﴿and intercession with Him will not benefit except for one whom He has permitted﴾ [Saba': 23], and ﴿they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya': 28]. The fifth: its meaning is that there is no intercession for it, so that there would be acceptance of it, and this view has already been mentioned. The sixth: that it is a general negation, meaning that it is not accepted for anything other than it, neither for a believing soul nor a disbelieving soul; this was said by al-Zamakhshari.

The People of the Sunna agreed that the intercession of the prophets and the righteous is accepted for the sinful believers, contrary to the Mu'tazila (the Mu'tazilites). They said: a grave sin makes its doer eternal in the Fire, and they denied intercession. They are of two kinds. One group denied intercession entirely and said: the intercession of no one is accepted for anyone, and they used as evidence the apparent meanings of verses. Our companions (the Ash'aris) restricted those apparent meanings to disbelievers, because of the authentic hadiths concerning intercession.

Another group denied intercession for the people of grave sins. They said: it is accepted only for minor sins. In *al-Muntakhab* it is said: the community is agreed that Muhammad (ﷺ) has an intercession in the Hereafter, but they differed as to for whom it is. The Mu'tazila held that it is for those who deserve reward, and its effect is to bring about an increase in benefits beyond what they have deserved. Our companions said: its effect is to remove punishment from those who deserve it, either by their not entering the Fire, or by their coming out of it after entering and entering Paradise. They agreed that it is not for the disbelievers. Then he mentioned about six pages of argument for both groups and refutations of some against others, which can be consulted in that book.

﴿Nor will any ransom be taken from it﴾: *al-'adl* (the ransom) is the compensation (*fidya*). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-'Aliya. It was called *'adl* because the one ransomed is equalled by it, that is, it equals it; or it is the substitute, that is, a man in place of a man. It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "Or a good deed along with polytheism." Three opinions.

﴿And they will not be helped﴾: He used the pronoun in the plural in consideration of the meaning of *nafs* (soul), because it is indefinite in a negative context, so it is general, as in His words: ﴿So there is none of you who could withhold him from it﴾ [al-Haqqa: 47]. He used it in the masculine because the souls are intended as persons, as in their saying: "three souls." The negative particle was made to extend over a nominal sentence, so that the pronoun is mentioned twice, and thus the mention of the one from whom help is negated is emphasized by mentioning it twice. Interpreting it according to meaning is made good by its being at the end of a verse-ending, so that there is harmony among the verse-endings, unlike if it had come as *wa-lā tunṣaru*, which would have lost that harmony.

The pronoun in this position may have two possible i'rab (grammatical analyses). The first, which is the most immediately obvious to the minds of the grammarians, is that it is a subject (*mubtada'*), and the clause after it is in the position of a predicate (*khabar*). The second possibility, which is the most obscure and strangest of the two, is that it is an object of a verb whose subject is not named (*maf'ūl lam yusamma fā'iluhu*), and the verb that follows it explains its verb, and the matter is of the type of *ishtighāl* (the verb being occupied with the pronoun). This is because *lā* is among the particles that come first with the verb, like the interrogative hamza. Just as in *a-Zaydun qā'imun* and *a-Zaydun yadribu* the nominative is permitted by *ishtighāl*, so also here. What strengthens this possibility is that it is preceded by a verbal clause.

The rule in the case of *ishtighāl* is that when a verbal clause precedes, and something is conjoined to it with the conditions of conjunction mentioned in that section, the more eloquent is to apply the case to the verb, though beginning with the noun is permitted as we mentioned first. What strengthens the return of the pronoun to the second *nafs* is the passive construction of the verb, since if it referred to the first *nafs* it would have been active, as in His words: *lā tajzī* (no soul will avail). Some exegetes made the pronoun in *wa-lā hum* (and they) refer to both souls together, saying: "because the dual is a plural." They said: "On the meaning of *naṣr* (help), the exegetes have three opinions here: the first: its meaning is that they will not be prevented from God's punishment. The second: they will not find a helper to help them, nor an intercessor to intercede for them. The third: they will not be assisted in their deliverance and release from the destructive results of their deeds." These three opinions are close in meaning.

The negation of these clauses here came with *lā*, which is used mostly for negating the future, and likewise these four things are future, because that day has not yet come. The arrangement of these clauses is in the utmost eloquence, and it corresponds to what happens in this world, because the one seized by right either has the right discharged on his behalf so that he is freed, or it is not settled on his behalf so that intercession is sought for him, or intercession is not granted for him so that ransom is offered, or ransom is not offered so that the brothers help in securing his release.

These are stages, each following the other. Therefore, and God knows best, they came in this order in the mention. And since people differ regarding intercession and ransom, the one whose love of leadership predominates puts intercession before ransom, and the one whose love of wealth predominates puts ransom before intercession. These clauses came here with intercession put first, while in another passage ransom came before intercession, to show that the two matters differ. Here it began with intercession, because that is more fitting to the loftiness of the soul. Here it came with the word *qabūl* (acceptance), while there it came with the word *naf'* (benefit), to indicate the negation of the very root of the thing and the negation of what follows from it. Here it began with *qabūl* because it is the root of the thing that follows from it; so the item mentioned first is given existence first, and there the benefit was delayed, giving the later-mentioned item existence later.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 47–48 (part 1 of 2):

﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds.﴾ ﴿And guard yourselves against a Day when no soul will avail another soul in anything, nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will any compensation be taken from it, nor will they be helped.﴾ ﴿And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with the worst torment, slaughtering your sons and sparing your women; and in that was a tremendous trial from your Lord.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 49].

Al-fadl (favour, excellence): increase, and its use is in good. Its verb is fa'ala yaf'ulu. Its original construction is to take the preposition ʿala (over), and then ʿala is omitted, in the manner of the poet's saying, who combined both forms:
"We found Nahshal excelled Faqim as the excess of the son of the she-camel excels over the weaned calf."
As for fadlah (surplus) of a thing, meaning the remainder, one says fadala yafdulu, like what we have mentioned, and fadila yafdalu, like sami'a yasma'u, and fadila yafdulu, with the kasra in the past tense and the damma in the present. Some grammarians have been fond of permitting both the fath and the kasra of the ḍād in fadaltu in the line, and the correct reading is the fath.

Al-jaza' (recompense): to suffice for the one owed and to requite. The rajiz said:
"May the Lord of the Throne reward him on my behalf for what he rewarded: the gardens of Eden in the highest heights."
Al-ijza' means sufficiency.

Qabul al-shay' (acceptance of a thing): turning towards it. The verb is qabila yaqbalu. Al-qibal is what faces you. Al-Qutami said:
"I said to the riders when they rose with them, from the right of al-Hubayya, a glance, qibal."

Al-shafa'ah (intercession): adding another to one's means. Al-shuf'ah (pre-emption) is adding ownership. Al-shaf' is the pair, and intercession is from it, because intercession and the one interceded for form a pair. Al-Ahwas said:
"Whoever blamed me for abandoning her, they interceded for Layla by their blame."
A she-camel shafu' is one with a young one following it; it is said: one with a young one following it and a young one in its belly.

Al-akhdh (taking): the opposite of leaving. Al-akhdh is seizing and holding. From it the captive is called akhidh. Its initial hamza is dropped in the imperative without a lam, and completion is rare.

Al-ʿadl (ransom): al-ʿadl is that which equals it in value and measure, even if not of its kind. With a kasra on the ʿayn: that which equals it in kind and bulk. Some Arabs say ʿidl with a kasra in the sense of ransom, and the singular of a'dal is only with a kasra. Al-ʿadl also means one whose word is accepted among people, and a kasra on the ʿayn is also reported for it. Tha'lab said: al-ʿadl is a guarantor and a bribe. The poet said:
"In it the money-changer does not accept the exchange of al-ʿadl."

Al-nasr (help): aid. Ard mansurah: land watered by rain. The poet said:
"Your father, who benefited me by his help, and after him every killer withheld from me."
And another said:
"When the sacred month bids farewell, then bid farewell to the lands of Tamim and let the land of ʿAmir be watered."
Al-nasr is also giving, and al-intisar is retaliation.

Al-najah (deliverance): rescue from destruction after falling into it. The original meaning is casting into a safe height. The poet said:
"Did you not see that al-Nuʿman was in a safe place from evil, had a man been one who was delivered?"

Al-al: it is said to mean "family" (ahl). It is claimed that its alif is a substitution for a hā', and its diminutive is uhayl. Some have held that its alif is a substitution for a quiescent hamza, and that hamza is a substitution for hā'. It is also said: it is not in the sense of ahl, because ahl is kinship, whereas al is whoever returns (yaʾūl) through kinship, or a patron, or a school of thought; so its alif is a substitution for a wāw, and for this reason Yunus said its diminutive is uwayl, and al-Kisa'i transmitted it explicitly from the Arabs. This is the choice of Abu al-Hasan ibn al-Badhish. Sibawayh did not mention in the chapter on substitution that hā' is replaced by hamza, as he mentioned that hamza is replaced by hā' in: haraqtu, haya, harahtu, and hiyyaka. They have restricted āl to being added to a famous, distinguished proper name of one who is generally known; so one does not say: āl al-iskaf or āl al-hajjam. The poet said:
"We are the family of God in our land; we have not ceased to be a family since the time of Iram."
Al-Akhfash said: āl is only added to the supreme chief, such as: āl Muhammad (ﷺ) and āl Fir'awn, because he is their chief in misguidance. It was said: there is scrutiny in this, because it has been heard from the people of language regarding cities, so they said: āl al-Madinah and āl al-Basrah. Al-Kisa'i said: it is not permissible to say: so-and-so is of the family of Basrah or of the family of Kufah; rather one says: of the people of Basrah and of the people of Kufah. End of his words. It has also been heard added to a common noun and to a pronoun. The poet said:
"Help against the family of the cross and its worshippers today, your family."
Hudbah said:
"I am the horseman who protects the reality of my father and my family, as you protect the reality of your family."
There has been disagreement regarding the permissibility of its addition to a pronoun: al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas and Abu Bakr al-Zubaydi forbade it, while others permitted it. It is pluralised with the wāw and nūn in the nominative, and with the yā' and nūn in the genitive and accusative, just as ahl is pluralised, so they say: ālūn. Al-āl is also the mirage, pluralised on the pattern af'āl; they said: a'wāl. Al-āl is also the pole of a tent, al-āl is the person, and al-ālah is a severe state.

Fir'awn is not declined because of definiteness and foreignness, and discussion of it will come. Sāmahu: he assigned him a hard task. The poet said:
"When the king imposed on the people humiliation, we refused to accept humiliation among us."
It was also said: its meaning is: they teach you from al-simā', which is the mark, and from it is taswim of horses. It was said: they demand from you in the manner of bargaining in a sale. It was said: they send against you, from the sending of camels to pasture. Abu ʿUbaydah said: they appoint you; one says: sāmahu khuttata khasf, meaning he gave him it.

Al-sū': the verbal noun of asā'a. One says sā'a yasū'u, and it is transitive. Asā'a al-rajul: meaning he became one with evil. The poet said:
"If it grieves me that you have touched me with an evil, it has gladdened me that I came to your mind."
The meaning of sā'ahu: grieved him, this is its origin; then it is used for everything that is considered ugly. It is said: "I seek refuge in God from the evil of character and the evil of deed," meaning their ugliness.

Al-dhabh (slaughter): its origin is splitting. The poet said:
"As if between its jaw and the jaw was a musk mouse slaughtered in a container."
And he said:
"As if aloes were slaughtered in your two eyes."
Al-dhabhah is a disease of the throat; from it one says: dhabahahu yadhbahuhu dhabhan. Al-dhibh is the slaughtered animal.

Al-istihya' here is leaving alive, and istaf'ala here has the sense of af'ala. Istahyahu and ahyahu have one meaning, like their saying: aballa and istaballa. Or it means seeking modesty, which is the private part, so istaf'ala here is for seeking, like istaghfara, meaning he sought forgiveness. The discussion of istahya from ḥayā' (modesty) has already passed in His words: ﴿Indeed, God is not ashamed to strike an example﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26]. Nisa' is a noun that applies to the young and the old, and it is a broken plural of niswah, and niswah is on the pattern fi'lah, and it is a plural of paucity, contrary to Ibn al-Sarraj, who claimed that fi'lah is a collective noun, not a broken plural. On both views, no singular is pronounced from its own form; the singular is imra'ah.

Al-balā': testing. Balāhu yablūhu balā'an: he tested him. Then it came to be applied to what is disliked and to hardship. One says: a trial afflicted so-and-so, meaning hardship. It returns to the meaning of wear (bilā), as if the one tried comes to wear out, which is destruction and perishing. One says: abla-hu with blessing, and balāhu with hardship; one may sometimes replace the other, so one says: balāhu bil-khayr, and ablāhu bil-sharr. The poet said:
"May God reward with good what the two did to you, so He tried them with the best trial, which tests."
He used them with one meaning. From it the form ifta'ala is built, so one says: ubtuliya.

* *

﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾: the discussion of this has already been explained. Their address is repeated a second time for emphasis, and so that they attend to what comes after it of enumerating the blessings which God bestowed upon them, detailing them blessing by blessing. The first address is to alert them to obeying the Benefactor, and the second address is to alert them to thanking the blessings. (And that I preferred you): then preference is conjoined to the blessing, and this is conjunction of the specific to the general, because the blessing includes the mentioned preference within it. This is what the waw alone does, to the exclusion of the other particles of conjunction. Our teacher, the scholar Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn Ibrahim ibn al-Zubayr al-Thaqafi, used to mention to us this kind of conjunction, and that it is called tajrid (abstraction), as if it were stripped from the sentence and singled out for mention by way of distinction. The poet said:
"I charge against them on a sturdy horse, and its chest, when it feels the impact of the spear, neighs."
Da'laj here is the name of a horse, and labanuhu is its chest. Abu al-Fath ibn Jinni has a discussion on this which reveals the secret of the craft regarding it.

(Over the worlds): that is, the worlds of their time, as said by al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah, Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Zayd and others; or over all the worlds, by virtue of the prophets He placed among them, and by making them kings and giving them what He had not given any one of the worlds; and this is specific to them to the exclusion of others, so the scope is general while the blessing is particular. They said: what refutes this view is: "You are the best nation" [Al 'Imran: 110]. Or [it means] over the great multitude of people; one says: I saw a 'alam of people, meaning a multitude. On each of these three views, preference over this nation does not follow; for whoever holds the generality restricts the blessing, and preference over every world in some specific respect does not necessitate preference in all respects. As for whoever holds the particularity, the reason for absence of absolute preference is clear.

Al-Qushayri said: He made the Children of Israel witness the excellence of themselves, so He said: "And that I preferred you over the worlds," and He made the Muslims witness the excellence of Himself, so He said: "Say: By the bounty of God and His mercy, so in that let them rejoice" [Yunus: 58]. How far apart is one whose witness is the bounty of his Lord from one whose witness is the bounty of himself: the first implies praise, and the second implies self-admiration. End of his words, and its ending is a summary of his speech.

(And guard yourselves against a Day): an command to guard oneself. As if, when they were commanded to remember the blessings and their preference, it is fitting that one upon whom blessing is bestowed and who is preferred should be one who attains piety. So they were commanded to persist in piety, or to attain piety if any defect befalls them. The accusative of (a Day) is either as an adverbial of time, with the object of guarding omitted, its estimate being: guard against the punishment on a day; or as a direct object by extension, or by omitting a genitive, meaning the punishment of a day, or the terror of a day. It was also said: its meaning is: come as those who guard; and it seems that on this estimate he did not consider the object of guarding, so in that case (a Day) is accusative as an adverbial. Al-Qushayri said: the common people He frightened with His punishment, so He said: "And guard yourselves against a Day," "and guard yourselves against the Fire." The elect He frightened with His attributes, so He said: "And say: Act, and God will see your deed, and His Messenger" [al-Tawbah: 105], "And you are not in any matter" [Yunus: 61], etc. The elect of the elect He frightened with Himself, so He said: "And God warns you of Himself" [Al 'Imran: 28]. Ibn al-Sammak al-'Adawi read: "la tajzi" from ajza'a, meaning sufficed; it was also said jaza and ajza'a have one meaning. This sentence is an attribute of the Day, and the connecting pronoun is omitted, so the estimate may be: la tajzi fihi (no soul will avail in it), the preposition was dropped, the pronoun attached to the verb, then the pronoun was dropped; so the omission is gradual, or he transferred the verb to the pronoun first by extension. This is the choice of Abu 'Ali, and it is what we choose. Al-Mahdawi said: both estimates, namely: la tajzi fihi and la tajzihi, are permissible according to Sibawayh, al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj. Al-Kisa'i said: the omitted pronoun is only for it (the verb with a preposition), he said: it is not permissible to say: hadha rajulun qasadtu (this is a man I intended), nor ra'aytu rajulan arghabu (I saw a man I desire), while you mean qasadtu ilayhi and arghabu fihi. End of his words. Omission of the pronoun from a clause functioning as an attribute is permissible, and from it is his saying:
"I do not know whether it is they who have become distant, and the length of the time, or the wealth they obtained."

He means they hit the mark. As for the view that the connecting pronoun is the one stated, or that the pronoun is apparent: according to the opinion of the Kufans (the grammarians of Kufa), it is also possible that there is a connecting pronoun, and the clause is not a qualifier. Instead, a noun governing the clause, *yawma* (the day), is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it. The intended meaning is: "And fear a day, the day when [no soul] will avail," so *yawm* is omitted because *yawman* (a day) indicates it. The omitted element in the construct phrase then resembles the expressed element in such a phrase as His words, may He be exalted: ﴿This is a day when they will not speak﴾ [al-Mursalat: 35]. In the same way, for *yawma lā tamliku* (the day when no soul will own anything), the clause does not need a pronoun, and the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of the omitted element is as a substitute (*badal*), specifically a substitute of the whole from the whole (*badal kull min kull*). From this is the poet's saying:

May God have mercy on the bones they buried
in Sijistan: Talha, the Talha of Talhas.

In the version where the word is in the genitive, the implied meaning is: "the bones of Talha." The Arabs have also said: "The honoring of you pleases me, Sa'd," meaning: "The honoring of Sa'd pleases me." Al-Kisa'i reported from the Arabs: "They fed us fat meat, a sheep they slaughtered," meaning: "meat of a sheep." Al-Farra' reported from the Arabs: "Indeed, by God, if you knew the knowledge of one whose age is great, whose bones are fine," on the assumption: "if you knew the knowledge of one whose age is great." Thus the second word is omitted, relying on the first. The Basrans (the grammarians of Basra) did not permit what the Kufans permitted, namely omitting the governing noun and leaving the governed noun in the genitive, as in: "The standing of Zayd pleases me." It is not far-fetched to prefer omitting *yawma* because of what precedes it, supported by this heard usage which al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' reported from the Arabs. This interpretation is strengthened by the fact that the noun governed is a clause, which does not show i'rab, so it would clash with the i'rab of what precedes it. If that is permitted in their prose despite the clash, then it is even more permissible where there is no clash. I have not seen any of the grammarians or exegetes who analysed this clause in this way. Rather, they are all agreed that the clause is a qualifier of *yawm* (day). It necessarily follows from this that the connecting element is also omitted from the clauses conjoined to *lā tajzī* (no soul will avail), that is: "and no intercession will be accepted from it [on that day]; and no ransom will be taken from it [on that day]; and they will not be helped [on that day]." According to this interpretation, there is no need to supply these connecting elements.

﴿A soul for another soul, anything﴾: both are indefinite nouns in a negative context, so they are general. The meaning of the indefiniteness is that a soul of the souls will not avail for a soul of the souls in anything of the things. Al-Zamakhshari said: "In it is a complete, decisive despair of all hopes," and this is according to his position that there is no intercession. Some said: the implied meaning is "for a disbelieving soul," so he restricted it to disbelief. In this is an indication that a soul may avail for a believing soul, and this is by the implication of the qualifier. The discussion of that will come, God willing, when we discuss His words: ﴿nor will intercession be accepted from it﴾. Abu al-Sirar al-Ghanawi recited: "No soul will avail for another soul."

The accusative of *shay'an* (anything) is that it is the direct object, meaning: it will not settle anything, that is, any right of the rights. It is also possible that its accusative is as a verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning: "and it will not avail any of the recompense." This was said by al-Akhfash, and in it is an indication of small quantity, like your saying: "I struck a bit of striking."

﴿And no intercession will be accepted from it﴾: Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited *wa-lā tuqbalu* with the *ta'* (feminine prefix), and this is the analogical and more common form. Whoever recited with the *ya'* (masculine prefix) is also correct and eloquent, because of the metaphorical feminine (*majāz al-ta'nīth*), and the separation between the verb and its subject also makes it good. Sufyan recited *wa-lā yaqbalu* with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and *shafā'atan* in the accusative, in the active voice. In this there is a *iltifāt* (shift) from the first-person pronoun to the third-person pronoun, because before it there is "remember My blessing" and "that I preferred you." The passive form is more eloquent, because it is more general in wording, even though it is known that the one who does not accept is God, Exalted. The pronoun in *minhā* (from it) refers to the later *nafs* (soul), because it is the nearest mentioned noun, meaning: "He does not accept from the soul seeking intercession any intercession of an intercessor." It is also possible that the pronoun refers to the first *nafs*, meaning: "and He does not accept from the soul which does not avail for another soul any intercession, being on the verge of that, if it had interceded, it would not have been accepted from it." It may appear preferable that it refers to the first soul, because it is the one spoken about in His words: ﴿No soul will avail for another soul﴾, while the second soul is mentioned as a complement, not as the main element. The apparent meaning of His words: ﴿nor will intercession be accepted from it﴾ is the negation of acceptance and of the existence of intercession. It is also possible that it belongs to the type of the poet's line:

On a faint track, whose landmarks cannot be followed,

where the negation applies to acceptance while the intended meaning is the negation of intercession, as if it were said: "There is no intercession so that it might be accepted."

The exegetes have differed in understanding this in six opinions. The first: it is a general expression for a specific meaning, and the intended meaning is those of the Children of Israel who said: "We are the sons of God and the sons of His prophets, and they will intercede for us with God." So this was rejected and they were despaired of it because of their disbelief. According to this, the first soul is a believer and the second is a disbeliever, and a disbeliever is not benefited by intercession, as in His words: ﴿So the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 48]. The second: its meaning is that they will not find an intercessor whose intercession is accepted, because the one interceded for is unable to obtain it; this is the view of al-Hasan. The third: its meaning is that the intercessor will not grant the one interceded for the intercession, even if he would have been granted it had he interceded. The fourth: its meaning is that since God has not permitted intercession for the disbelievers, and there must be permission from God for the intercessor to intercede, as in His words: ﴿and intercession with Him will not benefit except for one whom He has permitted﴾ [Saba': 23], and ﴿they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya': 28]. The fifth: its meaning is that there is no intercession for it, so that there would be acceptance of it, and this view has already been mentioned. The sixth: that it is a general negation, meaning that it is not accepted for anything other than it, neither for a believing soul nor a disbelieving soul; this was said by al-Zamakhshari.

The People of the Sunna agreed that the intercession of the prophets and the righteous is accepted for the sinful believers, contrary to the Mu'tazila (the Mu'tazilites). They said: a grave sin makes its doer eternal in the Fire, and they denied intercession. They are of two kinds. One group denied intercession entirely and said: the intercession of no one is accepted for anyone, and they used as evidence the apparent meanings of verses. Our companions (the Ash'aris) restricted those apparent meanings to disbelievers, because of the authentic hadiths concerning intercession.

Another group denied intercession for the people of grave sins. They said: it is accepted only for minor sins. In *al-Muntakhab* it is said: the community is agreed that Muhammad (ﷺ) has an intercession in the Hereafter, but they differed as to for whom it is. The Mu'tazila held that it is for those who deserve reward, and its effect is to bring about an increase in benefits beyond what they have deserved. Our companions said: its effect is to remove punishment from those who deserve it, either by their not entering the Fire, or by their coming out of it after entering and entering Paradise. They agreed that it is not for the disbelievers. Then he mentioned about six pages of argument for both groups and refutations of some against others, which can be consulted in that book.

﴿Nor will any ransom be taken from it﴾: *al-'adl* (the ransom) is the compensation (*fidya*). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-'Aliya. It was called *'adl* because the one ransomed is equalled by it, that is, it equals it; or it is the substitute, that is, a man in place of a man. It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "Or a good deed along with polytheism." Three opinions.

﴿And they will not be helped﴾: He used the pronoun in the plural in consideration of the meaning of *nafs* (soul), because it is indefinite in a negative context, so it is general, as in His words: ﴿So there is none of you who could withhold him from it﴾ [al-Haqqa: 47]. He used it in the masculine because the souls are intended as persons, as in their saying: "three souls." The negative particle was made to extend over a nominal sentence, so that the pronoun is mentioned twice, and thus the mention of the one from whom help is negated is emphasized by mentioning it twice. Interpreting it according to meaning is made good by its being at the end of a verse-ending, so that there is harmony among the verse-endings, unlike if it had come as *wa-lā tunṣaru*, which would have lost that harmony.

The pronoun in this position may have two possible i'rab (grammatical analyses). The first, which is the most immediately obvious to the minds of the grammarians, is that it is a subject (*mubtada'*), and the clause after it is in the position of a predicate (*khabar*). The second possibility, which is the most obscure and strangest of the two, is that it is an object of a verb whose subject is not named (*maf'ūl lam yusamma fā'iluhu*), and the verb that follows it explains its verb, and the matter is of the type of *ishtighāl* (the verb being occupied with the pronoun). This is because *lā* is among the particles that come first with the verb, like the interrogative hamza. Just as in *a-Zaydun qā'imun* and *a-Zaydun yadribu* the nominative is permitted by *ishtighāl*, so also here. What strengthens this possibility is that it is preceded by a verbal clause.

The rule in the case of *ishtighāl* is that when a verbal clause precedes, and something is conjoined to it with the conditions of conjunction mentioned in that section, the more eloquent is to apply the case to the verb, though beginning with the noun is permitted as we mentioned first. What strengthens the return of the pronoun to the second *nafs* is the passive construction of the verb, since if it referred to the first *nafs* it would have been active, as in His words: *lā tajzī* (no soul will avail). Some exegetes made the pronoun in *wa-lā hum* (and they) refer to both souls together, saying: "because the dual is a plural." They said: "On the meaning of *naṣr* (help), the exegetes have three opinions here: the first: its meaning is that they will not be prevented from God's punishment. The second: they will not find a helper to help them, nor an intercessor to intercede for them. The third: they will not be assisted in their deliverance and release from the destructive results of their deeds." These three opinions are close in meaning.

The negation of these clauses here came with *lā*, which is used mostly for negating the future, and likewise these four things are future, because that day has not yet come. The arrangement of these clauses is in the utmost eloquence, and it corresponds to what happens in this world, because the one seized by right either has the right discharged on his behalf so that he is freed, or it is not settled on his behalf so that intercession is sought for him, or intercession is not granted for him so that ransom is offered, or ransom is not offered so that the brothers help in securing his release.

These are stages, each following the other. Therefore, and God knows best, they came in this order in the mention. And since people differ regarding intercession and ransom, the one whose love of leadership predominates puts intercession before ransom, and the one whose love of wealth predominates puts ransom before intercession. These clauses came here with intercession put first, while in another passage ransom came before intercession, to show that the two matters differ. Here it began with intercession, because that is more fitting to the loftiness of the soul. Here it came with the word *qabūl* (acceptance), while there it came with the word *naf'* (benefit), to indicate the negation of the very root of the thing and the negation of what follows from it. Here it began with *qabūl* because it is the root of the thing that follows from it; so the item mentioned first is given existence first, and there the benefit was delayed, giving the later-mentioned item existence later.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 49 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And [remember] when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾: The discussion of (idh) has already been given in His words: ﴿And [remember] when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I will make upon the earth a successive authority"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. As for the one who permits the accusative of (idh) there as an object by the implied (udhkuru, "remember"), and claims that it is extra (ziyadah, "superfluous"), the analogy of his statement there is to permit it here, since nothing precedes it that it could coordinate with, unless someone claims that (idh) is coordinated with the object of (udhkuru), as if he had said: "Remember My blessing and My preferring you, and the time of My delivering you," and the parenthetical clause, which is: (and fear a Day), would come between the coordinated and what it is coordinated with. We have previously stated that we do not choose that it be an object of (udhkur), neither apparent nor implied, because that would be a treatment of it as a verb's object, whereas in our view it is one of the adverbial nouns (zuruf) which may not be treated in this way except by adding a noun of time to it, as established in grammar. Since this is the case, what we choose is that it be in the accusative as an adverb (zarf), and the verb that governs it be an implied verb indicated by what precedes it, its estimate being: "And We blessed you when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh." The estimate of this verb is preferable to all that we have mentioned before. It has come out, with His words (anjaynakum, "We delivered you"), from the pronoun of the first person of one who magnifies himself, to the pronoun of the first person that does not indicate magnification, in His words: ﴿My blessing which I bestowed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 47], because this act, which is the deliverance from their enemy, is among the greatest of blessings, or greater, so it was fitting to attribute the greatest to the One who magnifies Himself. It was read: (anjaynakum), with the hamzah for transitivity to the object, like the doubling in (najjaynakum). This reading is attributed to al-Nakha'i. Some have mentioned that he read (anjaytukum), so the pronoun would agree with the pronoun in (ni'mati, "My blessing"), and the meaning is: "I rescued you from the people of Pharaoh." The rescue from them is attributed to them because they were the ones who directly carried out these evil acts, even though Pharaoh was the one who commanded them. The people of Pharaoh here are the people of Egypt, as said by Muqatil, or specifically his household, as said by Abu 'Ubayd, or his followers in his wrongdoing, as said by al-Zajjaj. Among this usage is: ﴿And We drowned the people of Pharaoh﴾ [al-Baqarah: 50], and they are his followers in his wrongdoing, since he had no father, no daughter, no son, no paternal uncle, no brother, and no kinsmen (asabah). And admit the people of Pharaoh to the most severe punishment. It is narrated that it was said to the Messenger of God, ﷺ: "Who are your family (al?)?" He said: "Every pious person." The second view is supported by: "Charity is not lawful for Muhammad and the family of Muhammad." The meaning of "family" here is: the family of 'Aqil, the family of 'Abbas, the family of al-Harith ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib and their clients. It is also reported that his family (al) are his wives and his descendants, (p-193) so this indicates that for the Messenger of God, ﷺ, there is a general family and a specific family.

And Fir'awn (Pharaoh) is a title (alam) for whoever ruled the 'Amaliqah, just as it was said: Qayṣar for whoever ruled the Romans, Kisra for whoever ruled the Persians, al-Najashi for whoever ruled Abyssinia, and Tubba' for whoever ruled Yemen. Al-Suhayli said: it is a name for everyone who ruled the Copts and Egypt, and from it was derived: tafarʿana al-rajul, meaning when a man became tyrannical and insolent. His name was al-Walid ibn Mus'ab, as said by Ibn Ishaq and most of the exegetes; or Funtus, as said by Muqatil; or Mus'ab ibn al-Rayyan, related by Ibn Jarir; or Mughith, mentioned by some exegetes; or Qabus, whose kunyah was Abu Murrah, and he was from the descendants of 'Amliq ibn Lawidh ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh. It is narrated that he was from the people of Istakhr, and was returned to Egypt, where he became a king.

It is not known that Pharaoh has an Arabic etymology, as said by al-Mas'udi. Ibn Wahb said: the Pharaoh of Moses is the Pharaoh of Joseph. They said: this is not correct, because between Joseph's entry into Egypt and Moses's entry there are more than four hundred years, and the correct view is that he is other than him. It was also said: the name of the Pharaoh of Joseph was al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid.

﴿They inflicted upon you﴾ (yasumunakum): It is possible that this sentence is a new clause, narrating a past state, and it is possible that it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning "tormenting you," and it is a circumstantial clause from the people of Pharaoh. (And the evil of the punishment): the most severe and harshest of it. Its accusative is governed by the intended meaning of (yasumunakum), and on it the exegetes have several views. (al-sawm) has the meaning of imposing or afflicting, so (suwa' al-'adhab) on this view is a second object of (sama), meaning "they impose upon you" or "they assign you the evil of the punishment." Or it has the meaning of sending, or continuing, or directing, meaning: they send you, or they keep you, or they direct you to hard labour. Or it has the meaning of raising, meaning: they raise you to the evil of the punishment. Or it has the meaning of marking (al-wasm), meaning: they mark you, from the sign (al-'alamah), and the meaning is that hard labour, because of its long practice, becomes a sign upon them through its effect on their skins and clothing, as with blacksmithing, carpentry and the like, which becomes a mark for them; the estimate being: "they mark you with the evil of the punishment." This view was weakened from the standpoint of derivation, since if it were so it would be (yasimunakum). But this weakening is weak, since he did not say that it is derived from wasm; rather its meaning is the meaning of wasm, and it is from al-simiya' and al-sima'. And (musawwimin) in one of its interpretations means "marked." The roots of this are sin, waw and mim, and these are the roots of (yasumunakum). The base form (fa'ala) would then be in the meaning of (fa'ila), and it, together with wasm, is among those whose meanings agree while their roots differ, like damith and damthara, and sabita and sabtara. Or it has the meaning of seeking by increase from the sawm in sale, meaning: they seek from you by increasing hard labours.

On these views, other than the first two, (suwa' al-'adhab) is an object with the preposition omitted. Some people said: (suwa' al-'adhab) is in the accusative like a verbal noun, and then they estimated it as (sawman shadidan, "a severe imposing"). The evil of the punishment: the vile labours, as said by al-Suddi; or tilling, farming, building and other things, as said by some. He said: their people were soldiers and kings. Or it is slaughter, or the abandoning of the newborn to live (istihya') mentioned for both, as said by al-Zajjaj; this was refuted by the affirmation of the conjunction waw in (Ibrahim), where he said: "and they slaughter", which indicates that he tormented them with slaughter and with other than slaughter. It is related that Pharaoh made the children of Israel servants in labours of building, demolition, farming and service, and whoever did not work was subject to the poll tax. Those of strength would hew pillars from the mountains until their necks and hands were sore and their backs were wounded from cutting and carrying them; a group would carry stones and clay for him and build him palaces; a group would mould bricks and fire baked bricks; and a group were carpenters and blacksmiths. As for the weak, a levy was imposed on them as a tax which they paid each day. Whoever the sun set upon before he had paid it, his hand would be chained to his neck for a month. The women would spin flax and weave. The origin of the settlement of the children of Israel in Egypt was the descent of Israel there in the time of his son Joseph, upon our Prophet and upon them both be peace.

﴿They slaughter your sons﴾: the reading of the majority is with the shaddah (yudhabbihuna), and this is preferable because of the evident repetition of the verb in relation to its objects. al-Zuhri and Ibn Muhaysin read (yadhbahuna) without the shaddah, from the base (dhabaha), being content with the general verb and, for knowledge of its repetition from its objects. 'Abd Allah read (yuqattiluna) with the shaddah in place of (yudhabbihuna), and slaughter is killing. (yudhabbihuna) is a substitute for (yasumunakum), a verb substituted from a verb, like His words, exalted is He: ﴿He shall meet a penalty; the punishment will be doubled for him﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], and the words of the poet:

"When you come to us, you will gather us in our homes, and you will find firewood, thick, and a fire blazing."

It is possible that it is one of those from which the conjunction has been omitted, since it is affirmed in (Ibrahim). The view of those who held that the waw is extra because it is omitted here is weak.

al-Farra' said: the place where the waw is omitted is an explanation of the attributes of the punishment, and the place where the waw is present shows that the punishment touched them, other than slaughter. It is permissible for (yudhabbihuna) to be in the position of a circumstantial clause from the nominative pronoun in (yasumunakum), and it is permissible for it to be a new clause. On the cause of the slaughter and of the abandonment of the newborn there are various reports and stories, God knows best their soundness, and most of them indicate Pharaoh's fear that his kingship would be lost at the hand of a boy from the children of Israel.

(al-abna'): the male children, it is said that he killed forty thousand boys. It was also said: by "the sons" he meant the men, and they were called sons in consideration of what they had been before; and the first is more famous. (al-nisa') here: the girls, and they were called women in consideration of what they would become, or by the name by which they are used and debased at that time. It was also said: he meant the grown women, and the first is more famous.

﴿And they spare your women alive﴾: (istihya') has been explained by the two meanings we mentioned when we spoke on the vocabulary, namely that the meaning is: they leave your daughters alive for service, or they search the wombs of your women. On this view, the apparent meaning is that the people of Pharaoh were the ones who directly did this. It has been mentioned that he appointed for every ten women a man to watch whoever of them became pregnant; and it was said: he appointed midwives for this. It has also been said that (istihya') here is from hayaʾ, which is the opposite of shamelessness, and its meaning is that they would approach the women in acts that brought them shame. The slaughter is mentioned before the sparing alive because it is the more difficult and harder of the matters: it is that the son of the man and the woman, who were hoping for offspring from him, be slaughtered; and slaughter is the hardest of pains. The sparing alive of the women on the first view is not in itself a punishment, but punishment occurs through it, by way of leaving them as servants and making them taste the grief of the slaughter of sons, if by women are meant the grown women, or the slaughter of brothers, if by them are meant the children, and by the attachment of shame to them, since they remain women without men and so become sexually possessed by their enemies. Some scholars have used this verse to show that the one who commands killing without right and the one who directly carries it out are partners in retaliation, since God drowned Pharaoh, who commanded it, and his household, who carried it out. This is a question discussed in the science of jurisprudence, and there is disagreement among the people of knowledge about it.

﴿And in that was a great trial from your Lord﴾: (that) is a reference to the slaughter of sons and the sparing alive of women, and it is the verbal noun indicated by the verb, like His words: ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives, indeed that is﴾ [al-Shura: 43]; and it is the nearest thing mentioned, so the meaning of the trial is hardship and something disliked. It was also said: it refers to the sentence (they inflict upon you) together with what follows it, so the meaning of the trial is as previously stated. It was also said: it refers to the deliverance, which is the verbal noun understood from His words: "We delivered you," so the trial here is a blessing, and (that) is then a reference to the furthest thing mentioned; this is weaker than the view before it, while the more evident and nearest in mention is the first view.

His words: ﴿from your Lord, a great﴾ are evidence that good and evil are from God, in the sense that He is their creator. In this there is a refutation of the Christians and of whoever says in accordance with their view: that good is from God and evil is from Satan.

Describing it as great is evident: if (that) is a reference to the deliverance from the people of Pharaoh, then the greatness of the blessing and the abundance of the favour is clear; and if it is a reference to what came after the deliverance, namely the imposing, or the slaughter and the sparing alive, then that is a great, severe trial upon souls. It is said that he subjected them, so they built seven walls, their livers hungry and their bodies naked, and he slaughtered forty thousand of their boys; what trial is greater than this? Its being great is relative to the addressee and the hearer, not relative to God, exalted is He, since it is impossible for Him to be described with regarding something as great.

al-Qushayri said: whoever is patient for God under the trial of God, God will compensate him with the companionship of His friends. These, (p-195) the children of Israel, endured the suffering of hardship from Pharaoh and his people, so He made among them prophets, made among them kings, and gave them what He had not given anyone of the worlds. End of quotation. Blessings do not cease to erase the traces of afflictions; the poet said:

"We wipe away with our wealth the traces of our hands."

Since the command to remember the blessings had been given in summary earlier, He commanded them to remember them a second time in detail. He began with them by mentioning the preference (given to them), then commanded them to guard against a Day in which there is no escape, neither by a just judge, nor an intercessor, nor a ransom, nor help, for those who did not remember His blessings, did not comply with His command, and did not avoid His prohibition. The command to guard (against that Day) is especially important here, because whoever is informed that he has been preferred over the worlds may become complacent in this preference. So it was made known to them that, along with this, it is necessary to attain taqwa (God-consciousness, piety) and not to rely merely on the preference, for whoever has begun to favor you with his earlier blessings, it is incumbent upon you to guard against the consequences of his punishments. Then He repeated the mention of the deliverance, through which was the cause of survival after severe hardship, and after that He mentioned the details of the favors, of what He specified up to His saying: ﴿Go down to a city, for indeed you will have what you ask for﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61]. So enumerating the blessings is among what necessitates good remembrance and great praise. The discussion of the arrangement of these blessings, blessing by blessing, will come, God Most High willing.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 50 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And when We parted the sea for you and saved you and drowned the people of Pharaoh while you were looking on.﴾ ﴿And when We appointed Moses forty nights, then you took the calf after him while you were wrongdoers.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 51] ﴿Then We pardoned you after that, that you might be grateful.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 52] ﴿And when We gave Moses the Book and the Criterion, that you might be guided.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 53] . .

*al-Farq* (separation): *al-fasl* (division). *Faraqa bayna kadha wa kadha* means he separated them; *farraqa kadha* means he separated part of it from another part. From this come *al-farq* (the parting in the hair of the head), *al-fariq* (a group), *al-furqan* (the criterion), *al-tafarruq* (dispersal), and *al-farq al-mafruq*, like grinding. Its opposite is *al-jam'* (gathering). Its near synonyms are *al-fasl* (separation), whose opposite is *al-wasl* (joining); *al-shiqq* (splitting) and *al-sad'* (cleaving), whose opposite is *al-la'm* (mending); and *al-tamyiz* (distinguishing), whose opposite is *al-ikhtilat* (mixing). It has been said that one says *faraqa* for meanings and *farraqa* for physical bodies, but this is not correct.

*al-Bahr* (the sea): a low place of the earth that gathers water. Its plural in the paucity form is *abhur*, and in the abundance form *buhur* and *bihar*. Its origin is said to be "splitting," and it is said to be "breadth." From the first comes *al-bahira*, the she-camel whose ear is split. From the second comes *al-buhayra*, a wide city, and *faras bahr*, a horse of wide stride. *Tabahhara fi al-'ilm* means he expanded in knowledge, i.e. became broad. He said:

*Drive your sheep into pasture that you spread wide, from the valley floors, and hold them back with Bahlandan.*

Its use extends to both sweet water and salt water. God the Exalted says: ﴿And the two seas are not alike: this one is sweet, palatable, pleasant to drink, and that one is salty and bitter.﴾ [Fatir: 12]. It is also used for salt, and it is said that this is its original meaning. Ahmad ibn Yahya recited:

*Sweet water has become a sea, and it added to me, over an illness, that the sweet drink became brackish.*

That is, it became salt.

*al-Gharaq* (drowning) is well known. Its verb is *fa'ila* with a kasra on the 'ayn, in the form *yaf'alu* with a fatha. He said:

*And at times it surges and drowns.*

*Al-taghriq*, *al-ta'wis*, *al-tarsib* and *al-taghyib* have the same meaning.

*al-Nazar* (looking): directing the eye toward the seen thing. It is also used for seeing. It takes *ila* after it, and it may be used with a dependent clause even though it is not a verb of the heart, as in ﴿then let him see which of them is purer in food﴾. *Nazara*, *intazara* and *anzara* (to delay) all mean to postpone. *Al-nazirah* is delay.

*Wa'ada*: used for good and for evil. *Al-wa'd* is used for good, and *awada* for evil. *Al-i'ad* and *al-wa'id* are used for evil.

*Musa* (Moses) is a non-Arabic name that does not take tanwin, because of its foreignness and its being a proper noun. It is said that it is compounded of *mu*, which is water, and *shaw*, which is tree. When it was Arabized, they changed its shin to sin. Since it is foreign, no Arabic derivation applies to it. The scholars differed about its derivation. Makki said: Musa is *mufal* from *awsaytu*. Others said it is derived from *masa yamis*, and its pattern is *fu'la*, and the ya was changed to waw because of the damma before it, as they said *tuba*, though it is from the ya-roots, since it is from *taba yatiba*. That its pattern is *fu'la* is the view of the grammarians of i'rab, but Sibawayh stated explicitly that the pattern of Musa is *mufal*, and that applies to what does not take tanwin. Sibawayh argued in the matter of patterns for this, that the prefixing of mim is more frequent than the suffixing of alif. Al-Farisi argued that it is *mufal* and not *fu'la* by the consensus that it takes tanwin when indefinite; if it were *fu'la*, it would not take tanwin when indefinite, because the alif would be the feminine alif, and the feminine alif alone prevents tanwin in both definite and indefinite forms.

*Al-Arba'un* (forty) is not a sound plural. It is rather of the category of singular nouns that are collective nouns (*ism jam'*); its referent is known, and it is inflected like the sound masculine plural.

*al-Laylah* (night): its referent is known. It is broken irregularly into *fa'ali*, so one says *al-layali*. Its parallel is *al-kaykah* and *al-kayaki*, as if it were the plural of *laylah* and *kaykah*, and of *ahl* and *ahali*. They also deviated in the diminutive as they deviated in the broken plural, saying *luyayla*.

*al-Ittikhadh* (taking): an *ifti'al* form from *al-akhdh* (taking). The analogical expectation was that the hamza should be changed only to ya, so one says *iytakhadha*, like the hamza of *iman*, since its original form was *i'man*. Likewise they say *i'tazara* (to wear a waist-wrap), from *al-izar*. So when the first radical of the root is waw or ya, and one forms *ifta'ala* from it, the standard dialect changes it to ta and assimilates it into the ta of the *ifti'al* form. So one says *ittasala* and *ittasara*, from *al-wasl* (joining) and *al-yusr* (ease). If the first radical of the root is a hamza and one forms *ifta'ala*, one changes that hamza to ya and keeps it. This is the analogy. The ya may be changed to ta and assimilated, as they said *ittaman* (he trusted), whose origin is *i'tamana*. On this basis came *ittakhadha*.

Among the benefits that have remained in my memory from the teachings of the Imam, Shaykh Baha' al-Din Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Ibrahim ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr al-Halabi, known as Ibn al-Nahhas, may God have mercy on him, who was the most renowned in the science of grammar in the lands of Egypt, is that *ittakhadha* is among those in which the waw was changed to ta according to the standard dialect, because there is a dialect in which one says *wakhadha* with waw. So this came according to the original rule of substitution, even though it is built on a rare dialect. This is better, because they stated explicitly that *ittaman* is a poor dialect. He, may God have mercy on him, would mention the rarity of this dialect.

Al-Farisi analyzed the question of *ittakhadha* on the basis that the first ta is original, when one says: the Arabs said *takhidha* with a kasra on the kha', meaning *akhadha* (took). God the Exalted says: (*latakhidhta 'alayhi ajran*, "you would surely have taken a reward for it") in the reading of those who read so. Al-Farisi recited, may God have mercy on him:

*And my leg has taken, beside its saddle-strap, a crouching like the crouching of a collared sandgrouse.*

According to his view, the ta is original, and one forms *ifta'ala* from it, so one says *ittakhadha*, just as one says *ittaba'a*, formed from *taba'a*. Al-Zajjaji disputed the case of *takhidha*, and he claimed that its origin is *ittakhadha*, and that it was deleted as *ittaqa* was deleted, so they said *taqaya*. He cited as evidence their saying *takhidha* with a fatha on the ta and light (without shadda), as they said *yattaqi* and *yattasi'* with the deletion of the ta which is a substitute for the first radical of the root. Al-Sirafi rejected this view and said: if it were deleted from it, the kha' would not be kasra; it would be fatha, like the qaf in *taqaya*. As for *yattakhidhu*, it is deleted like *yattasi'*, deleted from the present tense and not the past tense, and *takhidha* is an original pattern. End of quotation.

What al-Farisi and al-Sirafi held, that it is an original pattern in its own right, is the correct view, based on what Abu Zayd related: *takhidha yatkhadhu takhdhan*. The poet said:

*And do not make excessive the taking (*takhdh*) of the pregnant camels, for they desire pastures whose structures are wide.*

Al-Mahdawi mentioned in the commentary on *al-Hidaya* that the original is a waw substituted for a hamza; then the waw was changed to ta and assimilated into the ta. So there are several opinions about *ittakhadha*: First, the first ta is original. Second, it is a substitute for an original waw. Third, it is a substitute for a ta which was substituted for a hamza. Fourth, it is a substitute for a waw which was substituted for a hamza. *Ittakhadha* sometimes takes one object, as in God's saying: ﴿she took a house﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 41]. Sometimes it takes two, as in God's saying: ﴿Have you seen him who takes his desire as his god?﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 23], meaning "made."

*Al-'Ijl* (calf): well known; it is the young male offspring of a cow. *Ba'da* (after) is an adverb of time. Its origin is as an adjective, like *qabla* (before). Its ruling is like its ruling in that it is built on damma when it is cut off from an annexation to a definite noun, and it is inflected with two movements. When you say *ji'tu ba'da Zayd* (I came after Zayd), the implied meaning is: I came at a time after the time of Zayd's coming. Its genitive case is only preserved with *min* alone.

*'Afa*: in the sense of "to increase," it is intransitive and does not take an object, as in ﴿until they multiplied﴾. In the sense of "to efface," it is both intransitive and transitive, as in: *'afati al-diyar* (the abodes were effaced), and *'afahā al-rih* (the wind effaced them). *'Afa 'an Zayd* means he did not hold him accountable for his offense. *I'fu 'an al-lihā* means leave the beards alone, that is, leave them and do not take anything from them. A *'afuww* man, its plural *'ufw* on the pattern *fu'l* with a sukun on the 'ayn, is an irregular plural. *Al-'ifa'* is abundant hair. The poet said:

*Upon it, from its birth-hair, is abundant hair.*

They say in prayer against a person: *'alayhi al-'afa'* (may he be effaced). He said:

*Upon the traces of those who departed is effacement.*

He means the ruins. *'Afa* may also mean "to be easy," from their saying: *khudh ma 'afa wa safa* (take what is easy and clear), and *akhadhtu 'afwahu*, that is, what was easy for him. ﴿They ask you what they should spend; say: the surplus﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219], that is, the surplus that is easy to give. From it: *khudh al-'afw*, that is, the easy, according to one of the opinions. *Al-'afiyah* is the easy and gentle condition.

*Al-shukr* (gratitude): praise for the bestowal of blessings. Its verb is *shakara yashkuru shukran wa shukuran*. It takes one object sometimes directly and sometimes with a preposition. It is among the words which are heard and must be memorized, and no analogy is drawn from them. It is a category of its own: sometimes it takes the object directly and sometimes with a preposition, equally, contrary to one who claimed that this is impossible. Our shaykh Abu al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Rabi' used to hold that the original usage of *shakara* is to take a preposition, and then it was dropped for breadth of usage. It has been said: *al-shukr* is the manifestation of the blessing, from their saying: *shakarat al-ramakah muhrahā* (the mare showed her foal), that is, when she displayed it. *Al-shakir* is the small leaves that appear from the effect of water. The poet said:

*While the youth was swaying in life, fresh, like a shoot whose small leaves sway from it.*

It is also the first gray hair. The rajaz poet said:

*Night-travel with you has made the camel-herd lax, and the head, when it has become gray.*

A *shakur* she-camel is one that yields more milk than what it grazed.

*Al-furqan*: the verbal noun of *farraqa*; the discussion of *faraqa* has already preceded.

﴿And when We parted the sea for you﴾ is coordinated with (*wa-idh najjaynakum*, "and when We delivered you"). The governing element of it is what was mentioned as the governing element of that *idh*, through the intermediary of the particle. Al-Zuhri read *farraqna* with shadda, which indicates intensification, because the paths were twelve, according to the number of the tribes of the children of Israel.
