Whoever reads *faraqna* without shadda suffices with the unqualified form, and intensification is understood from the enumeration of the tribes. *Bikum* (for you): attached to *faraqna*. The ba' has the meaning of cause, that is, because of your entering; or accompaniment, that is, while being joined with you, as in the saying: *tadus bina al-jamajima wa al-tarība* (it tramples us upon the skulls and the dust), that is, joined with us. Or it means: We made it a parting for you, as one separates two things by what lies between them. This is close to the meaning of instrumentality. Or its meaning is the *lam*: that is, We parted the sea for you, that is, for your sake, and its meaning returns to cause. The parting may be a width from one bank to the other, and it may be a length. Both have been reported. On this second view, they said: that was near the place of deliverance, and one would not reach the land except after many days, because of mountains and rough intervening terrain. Al-'Amiri mentioned that the place where they came out of the sea was near the desert of Palestine, and that was their route.

*al-Bahr* (the sea): it is said that it is the Sea of Qulzum, one of the seas of Persia, and between its two shores was a distance of four farsakhs. It is said that it is from a sea of Egypt called Asaf, now known as the Sea of Qulzum. It has been said that this is the correct view. They did not differ that the parting of the sea was according to the number of the tribes, twelve paths. They differed about the number of those who were parted and the number of Pharaoh's people, in opinions which contradict one another. They related accounts about the manner of the departure of the children of Israel, their obstinacy while they were plunging into the sea, and the manner of Pharaoh's departure with his soldiers, very lengthy narratives which neither the Qur'an nor sound hadith indicates. So God knows best which of them is correct.

﴿Then We saved you﴾: meaning from drowning, and from Pharaoh's overtaking you. The day on which the parting, the deliverance and the drowning took place was the Day of 'Ashura'. They digressed into discussion of the Day of 'Ashura' and its fasting, which is a question mentioned in jurisprudence.

Between His saying ﴿We parted the sea for you﴾ and His saying (*fa-anjaynakum*, "so We saved you") there is an omitted element which the meaning indicates. Its implied meaning is: And when We parted the sea for you, and Pharaoh and his soldiers pursued you into its plunging, so We saved you.

**And We drowned the family of Pharaoh.** The *hamza* in *aghraqnā* is for *ta'diya* (making the verb transitive, i.e. "to cause to drown"). It can also be made transitive by *tad'if* (doubling the middle radical). Pharaoh himself is not mentioned among those who drowned, because his presence with them is firmly established, so the text suffices with mention of "the family" here. They are the ones mentioned in the verse before it, and the ugly deeds were attributed to them: they subjected the Children of Israel to torment, slaughtered their sons, and spared their women. Therefore it was fitting to single them out for drowning. God Most High mentions the drowning of Pharaoh in other verses, among them: ﴿So We seized him and his hosts, and threw them into the sea﴾ [al-Qasas: 40]; ﴿until, when drowning overtook him﴾ [Yunus: 90]; ﴿Then Pharaoh followed them with his hosts, and there overwhelmed them of the sea that which overwhelmed them﴾ [Ta-Ha: 78]. Their deliverance from Pharaoh, by being cast into the sea and emerging from it safe, corresponds to the deliverance of their prophet Musa, upon our Prophet and upon him be peace, from slaughter, by being cast into the sea as an infant and emerging from it safe. Every nation has its share of its prophet. The destruction of Pharaoh and his people by drowning also corresponds to the destruction of the Children of Israel at their hands by slaughter, because slaughter brings death swiftly through the flow of blood, whereas drowning delays death and no blood flows out. And that by which there is life, ﴿and We made from water every living thing﴾ [al-Anbiya: 30], became a means of their annihilation from existence. Since drowning is among the most difficult of deaths and the most severe in intensity, God Most High made it a deterrent for whoever claims lordship, so He said: ﴿"I am your Lord, the Most High"﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 24]. For punishment is proportionate to the sin, and claims of lordship and exaltation are fittingly matched by the abasement of the claimant and his being submerged in the depths of the water.

**And you were looking on:** this is a circumstantial clause (*jumla ḥaliyya*), and *nazar* here means seeing (*ibṣār*). The meaning, and God knows best, is that these great marvels, the parting of the sea for you, your deliverance from drowning and from your enemies, and the destruction of your enemies by drowning, occurred while you were witnessing and observing them. This was not conveyed to you by report, but by direct observation, which necessitates the necessary knowledge that this was a miracle from God Most High through the hand of the Prophet who came to you. It has been said: "and you were looking on" means looking at them, because they were close to one another. It has also been said: it means looking at their floating on the surface of the water as drowned corpses. It has also been said: it means looking at them after the sea had cast them out, and they were an uncountable multitude; the sea did not keep a single one of them in its depths. It has also been said: "you were looking on" means some of you looking at others while you were travelling in the sea. It was reported that some of the people of Musa said to him: "Where are our companions?" He said: "Go on, for they are on a path like your path." They said: "We will not be content until we see them." So God revealed to him: "Strike the walls with your staff in this manner." He did so, and it became openings in them, so they saw one another and heard one another's speech. These five statements understand *nazar* in the sense of *ru'ya* (sight). It has also been said: *nazar* is used figuratively for nearness, meaning "while you were near them," that is, in a state where, had you looked at them, you would have seen them, like the saying: "You are within sight and earshot of me," meaning near enough that I see you and hear you. This was said by Ibn al-Anbari. It has also been said: it is from the *nazar* of insight and reason, and its meaning is: "while you were taking lessons from their downfall and heeding the places of the vengeance that was sent upon them." It has also been said: *nazar* here means knowledge, because knowledge comes from looking, so it is used as a metonymy for it. This was said by al-Farra', and it is the meaning of the statement of Ibn Abbas.

(p-199)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 51–53 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And when We appointed for Moses forty nights﴾. The majority read *wa'adna* (we appointed), while Abu 'Amr read *wa'adna* without an alif here, and in al-A'raf and Ta-Ha. *Wa'adna* (with the alif) may mean the same as *wa'adna* (without it), in which case it proceeds from one party. It may also be from two parties according to the original sense of the form *mufa'ala* (reciprocal action), so that God promised Moses the revelation, and Moses promised God that he would come at the appointed time. Or the promise came from God and its acceptance came from Moses, and accepting a promise resembles making one. Al-Qaffal said: "It is not far-fetched that a human being may promise God, meaning that he binds himself to Him by covenant." It has also been said: *wa'ada* is used when there is no request, and *wa'ada* (with the alif) when there is a request. Abu 'Ubayd preferred the reading without the alif and rejected the reading with the alif. Abu Hatim and Makki agreed with him in meaning. Abu 'Ubayd said: "*al-muwa'ada* (mutual promising) is only from humans." Abu Hatim said: "Mutual promising is most often between equal created beings, each of whom promises the other." The derivation of *wa'ada* according to those aspects mentioned earlier has already been given. There is no basis for preferring one reading over the other, because each of them is *mutawatir* (transmitted through so many chains that its authenticity is certain), so both are equally sound. Most reciters read with the alif, and this is the reading of Mujahid, al-A'raj, Ibn Kathir, Nafi', al-A'mash, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i.

*Musa* (Moses) is Musa son of 'Imran son of Yashhar son of Qahith son of Lawi son of Ya'qub son of Ishaq son of Ibrahim, the Friend of the Most Merciful. Al-Sharif Abu al-Barakat Muhammad ibn As'ad ibn 'Ali al-Hiwwani, the genealogist, mentioned that Musa, upon our Prophet and upon him be peace, is Musa son of 'Imran son of Qahith. The discussion of the word *Musa* as a proper name has already been given. As for *Musa* (the razor) with which hair is shaved, it is an Arabic feminine noun derived from *asawtu al-shay'* (I set the thing right) when you repair it. Its pattern is *maf'al*, and its original root is hamza. It has also been said that its derivation is from *awsaytu* (I shaved), and this derivation is more fitting for it, and on this view the waw has no root in the hamza.

*Arba'in laylatan* (forty nights): these are Dhu al-Hijjah and ten days of Muharram, or Dhu al-Qa'dah and ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. This was said by Abu al-'Aliyah and most of the exegetes. 'Ali and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read *arba'in* with a kasrah on the ba' (*arbi'in*), which is an irregular reading, through assimilation to the following sound. *Arba'in* is in the accusative as the second object of *wa'adna*, either because it is itself the thing promised, or by omitting a modifier, the implied sense being "the completion of forty" or "the end of forty." The modifier is omitted and the thing modified is put in its place and takes its case endings. This was said by al-Akhfash, and it is like the line of poetry:

> "So promise him the two trees of Malik, or the sand-hill between them, that they be easy."

That is, the coming of the two trees of Malik.

It is not permissible for *arba'in* to be in the accusative as an adverb of time, because it is a counted time-noun, which would require the verb to fall on each part of it, and the promising did not happen in that way. *Laylatan* (nights) is in the accusative as a specifier (*tamyiz*, a noun that clarifies an ambiguity) coming after the completion of the numeral. The governing element in this type of specifier is the numeral before it. *Arba'in* is treated as if it were a participle of the form of "hitting" (*dharibin*). It is agreed that this type of specifier may not precede the numeral, and that it may not be separated from it by a prepositional phrase except in poetic necessity, as in the line:

> "Thirty years have passed since then, a complete year of separation, and twenty of them, a finger's breadth behind us."

There is no definiteness for the specifier, contrary to some of the Kufans and Abu al-Husayn ibn al-Taraawah. Our companions interpreted what Abu Zayd al-Ansari related from the Arabs, saying: "*Ma fa'alat al-'ishrun al-dirham?*" (What did the twenty do with the dirham?), and similar expressions that indicate definiteness. This is mentioned in the science of grammar. The explanation of the forty as nights rather than days is because the beginning of the month is the night of the crescent, and for this reason time was dated by nights. The Arabs relied on the crescents, so days became subordinate to nights. Or it is because darkness precedes light, as shown by the verse ﴿And a sign for them is the night; We strip from it the day﴾ [Ya-Sin 37]. Or it indicates that he continued the fast by night and by day without interruption, because if the explanation had been by days, one might think he broke the fast at night. When the nights were specified, the force of the speech required that he continued for forty nights with their days.

(p-200) This promise was for speaking with God, or for the sending down of the Torah. Al-Mahdawi said: This happened after Moses had crossed the sea, when his people asked him to bring them a Book from God. He went out to the mountain (Tur) with seventy men from the best of the Children of Israel. He ascended the mountain and promised them until the completion of forty nights. They then waited, as the exegetes mention, twenty days and ten nights, and they said: "He has broken his promise to us." The end of his speech. Al-Zamakhshari said: When the Children of Israel entered Egypt after the destruction of Pharaoh, and they had no Book to refer to, God promised to send down the Torah to them, and He appointed a time for it. The end.

* *

﴿Then you took the calf﴾. The majority read with assimilation of the dhal into the ta' (*ittakhadhtum*). Ibn Kathir and Hafs, among the Seven, read with clear pronunciation (*idh-har*). The verb *ittakhadha* here may be transitive to one object, meaning "you made a calf," as in His saying: ﴿And the people of Moses took after him from their ornaments a calf, a body that lowed﴾ [al-A'raf 148], according to one of the two interpretations. On this reckoning there is an omitted clause indicated by the sense, and its estimate would be: "and you worshipped it as a god." It may also be that the verb is one that takes two objects, in which case the second object is omitted, its meaning being indicated: "you took the calf as a god." The first view is more likely, because if the verb took two objects in this story, it would state the second one, at least in one place. Do you not see that it is not given two objects in this place, but one, and in ﴿the people of Moses took﴾ [al-A'raf 148], and in ﴿they took it, and they were wrongdoers﴾ [al-A'raf 148], and in ﴿Indeed, those who took the calf﴾ [al-A'raf 152], and in His saying in this same surah: ﴿Indeed you have wronged yourselves by your taking of the calf﴾ [al-Baqarah 54]? Nevertheless the second view is preferred, because the first view would require the omission of a clause in these verses, whereas the second requires only the omission of an object, and omitting a single word is easier than omitting a clause. According to the first view, there is condemnation of the group for the act of one man, because the one who made the calf was the Samiri, and his story, his name, and the account of his misleading will come, God willing, when His saying is reached: ﴿and the Samiri misled them﴾ [Ta-Ha 85]. This is the custom of the Arabs in their speech, praising or blaming a tribe for what was done by some of its members. According to the second view, the blame falls upon them for what proceeded from them. The definite article in *al-'ijl* (the calf), on the first view, is for defining the quiddity (the nature of the thing), since no previous reference had been mentioned. On the second view it is for the prior known reference, since they had made a calf and then took that calf as a god. That it is a calf is clear evidence that it became flesh and blood, so it is a calf in reality and the attribution of lowing to it is literal. This was said by al-Hasan. It has also been said that this is metaphorical, meaning a calf in form and shape, because the Samiri fashioned it in the shape of a calf, and according to what they mentioned he was a goldsmith. The attribution of lowing to it would then be metaphorical. This was said by the majority. The discussion of this matter will come in al-A'raf, God willing. Among the strangest things said about this calf is that it was named a calf because they hastened (*'ajjalu*) to it before Moses' arrival and took it as a god. This was said by Abu al-'Aliyah. Or it was called a calf because of the shortness of its duration.

﴿From after him﴾. *Min* indicates the beginning of a limit (*ibtida' al-ghayah*), and its meaning conflicts with the meaning of *thumma* (then). This is because *thumma* requires that the taking happened after an interval following the promise, while *min* requires that the transitive action following the promise begins immediately. Since the pronoun obviously refers back to Moses, and the act of transitivity cannot be conceived of in the essence, it is necessary to supply an omitted element. The nearest element to omit is a verbal noun indicated by the word *wa'adna*, meaning "after his promising." Therefore it is necessary to commit a figurative usage in one of the two particles, unless one supplies an omitted element other than the promising, namely that the estimate is "after his going off to the mountain." In that case the conflict disappears, because the interval lies between the promising and the taking, and the beginning of the limit comes right after going to the mountain. The interval is made clear by the story in al-A'raf, where between the promising and the taking there are many sentences. The beginning of the limit occurs immediately after going to the mountain, so the interval and the beginning do not apply to one and the same thing, and the conflict disappears. It has also been said that the pronoun in *ba'dihi* (after him) refers to the going, meaning "after the going," and this is indicated by the fact that the promising implies the going. It then refers to something not mentioned, but understood from the context of speech, as in His saying: ﴿until it was hidden by the veil﴾ [Sad 32], and ﴿and raised thereby a cloud of dust﴾ [al-'Adiyat 4], meaning "the sun was hidden," since the evening (*al-'ashiyy*) indicates it in His saying, and "they raised dust in the place," since the place is indicated by ﴿by the charging ones﴾ [al-'Adiyat 1], ﴿by the striking sparks﴾ [al-'Adiyat 2], ﴿and the raiders at dawn﴾ [al-'Adiyat 3], since these actions can occur only in a place, so the speech required it and indicated it. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the rescue, meaning "after the rescue," and it has been said that it refers to the guidance, meaning "after the guidance." Both of these views are weak.

﴿And you were wrongdoers﴾. This is a circumstantial clause (*jumla haliyya*). As for the object of the wrongdoing, it has been said: they were wrongdoers by placing worship in other than its proper place. It has also been said: by engaging in the means of their own destruction. It has been said: by your consent to the deed of the Samiri in his making of the calf, since you did not object to it. It is also possible that the clause is not circumstantial, but is rather a report from God that they are wrongdoers, meaning that wrongdoing is their disposition, and wrongdoing is the placing of things in other than their proper place. The meaning would then be: "Then you took the calf after him, while you were wrongdoers," like His saying: ﴿they took it, and they were wrongdoers﴾ [al-A'raf 148]. This clause has been put in the form of a nominal sentence with a predicate, because it is more eloquent and emphatic than the verbal clause, and in order to agree with the verse endings (*fawasil*). The apparent sense of His saying "then you took" is generality, that they all worshipped the calf except Aaron. It has been said that those who devoted themselves to its worship from the people of Moses were eight thousand men. It has been said that all of them worshipped it except Aaron together with twelve thousand. It has been said: this is the correct view. It has been said: except Aaron and the seventy men who were with Moses. As for the Samiri's choice of a calf rather than other animals, it has been said: because they passed by a people who devoted themselves to idols of theirs, which were in the forms of cows. They said: "Make for us a god as they have gods." So the idea occurred to the Samiri's mind to tempt them from this direction, and he made for them the calf. It has also been said that he was from a people who worshipped cows, and that he was a hypocrite who outwardly professed faith in Moses, so he made a calf of the same kind as what he had worshipped. In their taking the calf as a god there is evidence that they were anthropomorphists (*mujassima*) or incarnationists (*hulliyya*), because whoever believes in God's transcendence above that, and the impossibility of that for Him, by necessity would immediately see the invalidity of the claim that the calf is a god. The exegetes have reported from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi and others many varied stories concerning the cause of the taking of the calf and the manner of its making, and many reports have accompanied these. God knows best their soundness, since no book and no sound hadith has attested to their authenticity. Therefore we have left the transmission of these in accordance with our custom in this book.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 51–53 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Then We pardoned you after that﴾: The meanings of ʿafā (to pardon) have already been discussed. It may be that ʿafā here carries the sense of erasing and removing, or the sense of leaving alone, or the sense of making easy. ʿAfw (pardon) and ṣafḥ (overlooking) are close in meaning. Some scholars said: ʿafw is used in the sense of ṣafḥ only with regard to a sin. If ʿafw here means leaving alone or making easy, then ʿankum ("you") is general in wording but specific in meaning, because the pardon was granted only to those among them who remained. If it means erasing, then it is general in both wording and meaning, for God accepted the repentance of those who were killed and of those who remained. God says: ﴿So kill yourselves; that is better for you in the sight of your Creator, and He turned to you [in forgiveness]﴾ [al-Baqara 2:54]. It is related that after they killed themselves, God revealed to Moses: "I have accepted their repentance. Whoever was killed is a martyr, and whoever was not killed, I have turned to him and forgiven him." The Mu'tazila (a theological school) said: "We pardoned you" means because of your bringing about repentance, which was the killing of some of them by others. ﴿after that﴾ refers to the taking of the calf, and it was said that it refers to their killing themselves. The first view is more evident.

﴿la-llakum (so that you may)﴾: The discussion of la-ʿalla (perhaps, so that) has already been given in His saying ﴿so that you may be God-fearing﴾, linguistically and in its semantic implication with regard to God Most High, so there is no need to repeat it. ﴿tashkurūn (you may give thanks)﴾: that is, you praise Him for bestowing His blessings upon you, and you manifest the blessing by praising Him. They said: thanks is by the tongue, which is speaking of the Benefactor's blessing and praising Him for it; and by the heart, which is believing in the rightful due of the Benefactor from the one who is benefited; and by action, ﴿Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude﴾ [Saba' 34:13]; and through God, that is, thanks to God through God, because none can give Him thanks as He deserves except Himself. Someone said:

Gratitude to those who do good is at times by speech, at times by the heart, and then by action, the most noble.

And my gratitude to my Lord is not by my heart or my obedience alone, nor by my tongue, but rather His thanks is by Him on our behalf.

The meaning of ﴿so that you may give thanks﴾ is: [so that you may give thanks for] God's pardon of you, because pardon requires gratitude. This is what the majority said. Or: you may show God's blessing upon you in the pardon. Or: you may acknowledge My blessing. Or: you may persist in My obedience. Or: you may confess your inability to thank Me. These are four opinions. Ibn ʿAbbas said: thanks is the obedience of the limbs. Al-Junayd said: thanks is the admission of inability to give thanks. Al-Shibli said: humility under the vision of the favour. Al-Fudayl said: that you do not disobey God. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: that you recognise the blessing as coming from God. Dhu l-Nun said: thanks to one above you is through obedience, to your equal through reciprocation, and to one below you through kindness. Al-Qushayri said: swiftness in pardoning a grave offence indicates the lowliness of the one pardoned, as is witnessed by His saying: ﴿Whoever of you commits a manifest immorality, her punishment will be doubled﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:30]. These were the Children of Israel who worshipped the calf, and God said: ﴿Then We pardoned you after that﴾, and to this Ummah He said: ﴿Whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [al-Zalzala 99:8]. The end of his words.

The hope of gratitude is appropriate immediately after the mention of pardon, because pardon for such a great slip, namely taking the calf as a god, is among the greatest, or the greatest, bestowal of blessings. Therefore He said: ﴿so that you may give thanks﴾.

﴿And when We gave Musa the Book﴾: It is the Torah, by the consensus of the exegetes.

﴿and the Furqan﴾: It is the Torah. The meaning is that He gave it to him combining being a Book and being a criterion (furqan) distinguishing truth from falsehood. The "and" would then be a conjunction of attributes, because the Book in reality means the written, as said by al-Zajjaj and preferred by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn ʿAtiyya began with this view and said: the meaning is repeated with a change of wording, and because it adds the sense of distinction between truth and falsehood, which the word kitab does not express. Or the wa is superfluous (muqhama), that is, extra, and the furqan is an epithet of the Book. A poet said:

To the mighty king and the son of the noble, and the lion of the battalion in the throng.

This was said by al-Kisa'i, but it is weak. Rather, his words "and the son of the noble and the lion" are a conjunction of attributes one upon another, and this requires that the attributes differ in meaning.

Or the furqan is victory, because it distinguished between the enemy and the ally in drowning and salvation. From this it was said of the day of Badr: the Day of the Furqan. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Or all the signs with which Musa was given, of the staff, the hand, and other things, because they distinguished between truth and falsehood.

Or the furqan is the distinction between truth and falsehood; this was said by Abu l-ʿAliya and Mujahid.

Or the furqan is the sacred law which distinguishes between the lawful and the unlawful.

Or it is the proof which distinguishes between disbelief and belief; this was said by Ibn Bahr and Ibn Zayd.

Or it is the relief from distresses, because they were enslaved along with the Copts. From this is His saying: ﴿He will grant you a furqan﴾ [al-Anfal 8:29], that is, a relief and a way out. This view returns to the meaning of victory.

Or it is the Qur'an. The meaning would be that God gave Musa the mention of the descent of the Qur'an upon Muhammad (ﷺ), so that he believed in it; this was related by Ibn al-Anbari.

Or the furqan is the Qur'an with an omitted object, the estimated meaning being: and Muhammad the Furqan. This is reported from al-Farra', Qutrub and Tha'lab, and they said: it is like the saying of the poet:

And they adorned the brows and the eyes.

The estimated meaning is: and they applied kohl to the eyes. This view was rejected by Makki, al-Nahhas and a group, because there is no evidence for this omitted element, and it would become like the saying: "I fed Zayd bread and meat," where the meat would be something you fed other than Zayd. Also, the basic principle of coordination is that the conjoined element shares the preceding ruling with what it is conjoined to, when the particle of coordination is one that shares in that. The example they cited, "and they adorned the brows and the eyes," is not like this, for reasons mentioned in grammar.

It has come in: ﴿And We gave Musa and Harun the Furqan and a light﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:48]. They also mentioned all the signs which God Most High gave Musa, because they distinguished between truth and falsehood.

Or the furqan is the splitting of the sea; this was said by Yaman and Qutrub. This view is weakened by the prior mention of the parting of the sea in His saying ﴿when We parted [the sea]﴾, and by the mention of hoping for guidance immediately after the furqan, which fits only the Book.

It is answered that, although the splitting was mentioned earlier, it is repeated here and stated explicitly, as a sign given to Musa specifically. The mention of guidance after the parting of the sea is appropriate because it is among the proofs by which the existence of the Creator and the truthfulness of Musa (upon our Prophet and upon him be peace) are established, and that is guidance. Or because the intended guidance is salvation and success, and by the parting of the sea they obtained this, so He has mentioned to them the blessing of the Book, which is the foundation of their religion, and the blessing of salvation from their enemies. These are twelve statements of the exegetes concerning the intended meaning of furqan here.

[p. 203] ﴿so that you may be guided﴾: a hope for their guidance. The discussion of la-ʿalla has already been given. Ibn ʿAtiyya's wording here, and his earlier wording on ﴿so that you may give thanks﴾, shows that it expresses expectation. What is established in grammar is that if the object of la-ʿalla is beloved, it is for hope (tarajjī); if it is feared, it is for anticipation (tawaqquʿ), as in your saying: "Perhaps the enemy will advance." Gratitude and guidance are beloved things, so the meaning of la-ʿalla here should be expressed only as hope.

Al-Qushayri said: the furqan of this Ummah, with which they are distinguished, is a light in their hearts by which they distinguish between truth and falsehood. "Consult your heart," "Beware the discernment of the believer, for the believer sees by the light of God," and "If you fear God, He will grant you a furqan." The end of his words.

That furqan is what they have put forward of goodness.

The hope for guidance comes right after the mention of Musa's being given the Book and the Furqan, because by the Book guidance is attained: ﴿Indeed, We revealed the Torah, in which is guidance and light﴾ [al-Ma'ida 5:44]; ﴿That is the Book, there is no doubt in it, a guidance﴾ [al-Baqara 2:2]; ﴿And We gave him the Gospel, in which is guidance and light﴾ [al-Ma'ida 5:46].

These noble verses contain several sections of the mention of God's favour upon the Children of Israel. Among them: the parting of the sea for them in the manner mentioned, so that it became twelve paths according to the number of the tribes, with a partition between each tribe preventing them from crowding, without any sense of alienation befalling them in that, because in each partition there were openings so that some could see others, as is reported. This is among the greatest signs indicating the truthfulness of Musa (upon our Prophet and upon him be peace). This parting is the third blessing. The first blessing was their being preferred, the second was their deliverance from the people of Pharaoh, and the third was this parting and what followed from it, namely their deliverance from drowning and the drowning of their enemies while they looked on, so that they had no doubt of their destruction. Then he digressed after that to the mention of the fourth blessing, which is the pardon for the great sin they committed by worshipping the calf. So He mentioned the cause of this, that it happened because of Musa's absence from them for intimate conversation with his Lord, and that despite the short duration of his absence, they were deceived by what this Samiri did, and time did not lengthen for them, and their successor for Musa among them was his brother Harun, who forbade them, but they did not desist. And despite this great slip, He pardoned them and turned to them. What blessing is greater than this? Then He mentioned the fifth blessing, which is the fruit of the promise, namely Musa's bringing the Torah, by which they were guided, and in which are the benefits of their worldly and otherworldly life.

The arrangement of these blessings came in a coherent sequence, each part taking hold of the next, and it is a chronological arrangement, one of the five arrangements that have been mentioned in this book. This is because preference is a matter of judgment, so it is first, and then the blessings came after it, and they are acts following one another. The first of them is deliverance from the evil torment, the slaughter of the sons and the sparing of the women, by Musa bringing them out of Egypt, such that neither Pharaoh nor his people had any power over them after this departure and deliverance. Then came the parting of the sea for them and their being shown this great marvel with their own eyes. Then God's promise to Musa of intimate conversation with Him, and his going to it. Then their taking of the calf. Then the pardon of them. Then the giving of the Torah to Musa. Consider the excellence of these sections, which are arranged like pearls on their strings and blossoms on their branches, each section concluded with its fitting close, and rising to the height of eloquence in its loftiest station, sent down by God upon the tongue of Muhammad, His trustworthy one, the tongue of one who had not recited a Book before it nor written it with his right hand.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 51–53 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And when We appointed for Moses forty nights﴾. The majority read *wa'adna* (we appointed), while Abu 'Amr read *wa'adna* without an alif here, and in al-A'raf and Ta-Ha. *Wa'adna* (with the alif) may mean the same as *wa'adna* (without it), in which case it proceeds from one party. It may also be from two parties according to the original sense of the form *mufa'ala* (reciprocal action), so that God promised Moses the revelation, and Moses promised God that he would come at the appointed time. Or the promise came from God and its acceptance came from Moses, and accepting a promise resembles making one. Al-Qaffal said: "It is not far-fetched that a human being may promise God, meaning that he binds himself to Him by covenant." It has also been said: *wa'ada* is used when there is no request, and *wa'ada* (with the alif) when there is a request. Abu 'Ubayd preferred the reading without the alif and rejected the reading with the alif. Abu Hatim and Makki agreed with him in meaning. Abu 'Ubayd said: "*al-muwa'ada* (mutual promising) is only from humans." Abu Hatim said: "Mutual promising is most often between equal created beings, each of whom promises the other." The derivation of *wa'ada* according to those aspects mentioned earlier has already been given. There is no basis for preferring one reading over the other, because each of them is *mutawatir* (transmitted through so many chains that its authenticity is certain), so both are equally sound. Most reciters read with the alif, and this is the reading of Mujahid, al-A'raj, Ibn Kathir, Nafi', al-A'mash, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i.

*Musa* (Moses) is Musa son of 'Imran son of Yashhar son of Qahith son of Lawi son of Ya'qub son of Ishaq son of Ibrahim, the Friend of the Most Merciful. Al-Sharif Abu al-Barakat Muhammad ibn As'ad ibn 'Ali al-Hiwwani, the genealogist, mentioned that Musa, upon our Prophet and upon him be peace, is Musa son of 'Imran son of Qahith. The discussion of the word *Musa* as a proper name has already been given. As for *Musa* (the razor) with which hair is shaved, it is an Arabic feminine noun derived from *asawtu al-shay'* (I set the thing right) when you repair it. Its pattern is *maf'al*, and its original root is hamza. It has also been said that its derivation is from *awsaytu* (I shaved), and this derivation is more fitting for it, and on this view the waw has no root in the hamza.

*Arba'in laylatan* (forty nights): these are Dhu al-Hijjah and ten days of Muharram, or Dhu al-Qa'dah and ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. This was said by Abu al-'Aliyah and most of the exegetes. 'Ali and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read *arba'in* with a kasrah on the ba' (*arbi'in*), which is an irregular reading, through assimilation to the following sound. *Arba'in* is in the accusative as the second object of *wa'adna*, either because it is itself the thing promised, or by omitting a modifier, the implied sense being "the completion of forty" or "the end of forty." The modifier is omitted and the thing modified is put in its place and takes its case endings. This was said by al-Akhfash, and it is like the line of poetry:

> "So promise him the two trees of Malik, or the sand-hill between them, that they be easy."

That is, the coming of the two trees of Malik.

It is not permissible for *arba'in* to be in the accusative as an adverb of time, because it is a counted time-noun, which would require the verb to fall on each part of it, and the promising did not happen in that way. *Laylatan* (nights) is in the accusative as a specifier (*tamyiz*, a noun that clarifies an ambiguity) coming after the completion of the numeral. The governing element in this type of specifier is the numeral before it. *Arba'in* is treated as if it were a participle of the form of "hitting" (*dharibin*). It is agreed that this type of specifier may not precede the numeral, and that it may not be separated from it by a prepositional phrase except in poetic necessity, as in the line:

> "Thirty years have passed since then, a complete year of separation, and twenty of them, a finger's breadth behind us."

There is no definiteness for the specifier, contrary to some of the Kufans and Abu al-Husayn ibn al-Taraawah. Our companions interpreted what Abu Zayd al-Ansari related from the Arabs, saying: "*Ma fa'alat al-'ishrun al-dirham?*" (What did the twenty do with the dirham?), and similar expressions that indicate definiteness. This is mentioned in the science of grammar. The explanation of the forty as nights rather than days is because the beginning of the month is the night of the crescent, and for this reason time was dated by nights. The Arabs relied on the crescents, so days became subordinate to nights. Or it is because darkness precedes light, as shown by the verse ﴿And a sign for them is the night; We strip from it the day﴾ [Ya-Sin 37]. Or it indicates that he continued the fast by night and by day without interruption, because if the explanation had been by days, one might think he broke the fast at night. When the nights were specified, the force of the speech required that he continued for forty nights with their days.

(p-200) This promise was for speaking with God, or for the sending down of the Torah. Al-Mahdawi said: This happened after Moses had crossed the sea, when his people asked him to bring them a Book from God. He went out to the mountain (Tur) with seventy men from the best of the Children of Israel. He ascended the mountain and promised them until the completion of forty nights. They then waited, as the exegetes mention, twenty days and ten nights, and they said: "He has broken his promise to us." The end of his speech. Al-Zamakhshari said: When the Children of Israel entered Egypt after the destruction of Pharaoh, and they had no Book to refer to, God promised to send down the Torah to them, and He appointed a time for it. The end.

* *

﴿Then you took the calf﴾. The majority read with assimilation of the dhal into the ta' (*ittakhadhtum*). Ibn Kathir and Hafs, among the Seven, read with clear pronunciation (*idh-har*). The verb *ittakhadha* here may be transitive to one object, meaning "you made a calf," as in His saying: ﴿And the people of Moses took after him from their ornaments a calf, a body that lowed﴾ [al-A'raf 148], according to one of the two interpretations. On this reckoning there is an omitted clause indicated by the sense, and its estimate would be: "and you worshipped it as a god." It may also be that the verb is one that takes two objects, in which case the second object is omitted, its meaning being indicated: "you took the calf as a god." The first view is more likely, because if the verb took two objects in this story, it would state the second one, at least in one place. Do you not see that it is not given two objects in this place, but one, and in ﴿the people of Moses took﴾ [al-A'raf 148], and in ﴿they took it, and they were wrongdoers﴾ [al-A'raf 148], and in ﴿Indeed, those who took the calf﴾ [al-A'raf 152], and in His saying in this same surah: ﴿Indeed you have wronged yourselves by your taking of the calf﴾ [al-Baqarah 54]? Nevertheless the second view is preferred, because the first view would require the omission of a clause in these verses, whereas the second requires only the omission of an object, and omitting a single word is easier than omitting a clause. According to the first view, there is condemnation of the group for the act of one man, because the one who made the calf was the Samiri, and his story, his name, and the account of his misleading will come, God willing, when His saying is reached: ﴿and the Samiri misled them﴾ [Ta-Ha 85]. This is the custom of the Arabs in their speech, praising or blaming a tribe for what was done by some of its members. According to the second view, the blame falls upon them for what proceeded from them. The definite article in *al-'ijl* (the calf), on the first view, is for defining the quiddity (the nature of the thing), since no previous reference had been mentioned. On the second view it is for the prior known reference, since they had made a calf and then took that calf as a god. That it is a calf is clear evidence that it became flesh and blood, so it is a calf in reality and the attribution of lowing to it is literal. This was said by al-Hasan. It has also been said that this is metaphorical, meaning a calf in form and shape, because the Samiri fashioned it in the shape of a calf, and according to what they mentioned he was a goldsmith. The attribution of lowing to it would then be metaphorical. This was said by the majority. The discussion of this matter will come in al-A'raf, God willing. Among the strangest things said about this calf is that it was named a calf because they hastened (*'ajjalu*) to it before Moses' arrival and took it as a god. This was said by Abu al-'Aliyah. Or it was called a calf because of the shortness of its duration.

﴿From after him﴾. *Min* indicates the beginning of a limit (*ibtida' al-ghayah*), and its meaning conflicts with the meaning of *thumma* (then). This is because *thumma* requires that the taking happened after an interval following the promise, while *min* requires that the transitive action following the promise begins immediately. Since the pronoun obviously refers back to Moses, and the act of transitivity cannot be conceived of in the essence, it is necessary to supply an omitted element. The nearest element to omit is a verbal noun indicated by the word *wa'adna*, meaning "after his promising." Therefore it is necessary to commit a figurative usage in one of the two particles, unless one supplies an omitted element other than the promising, namely that the estimate is "after his going off to the mountain." In that case the conflict disappears, because the interval lies between the promising and the taking, and the beginning of the limit comes right after going to the mountain. The interval is made clear by the story in al-A'raf, where between the promising and the taking there are many sentences. The beginning of the limit occurs immediately after going to the mountain, so the interval and the beginning do not apply to one and the same thing, and the conflict disappears. It has also been said that the pronoun in *ba'dihi* (after him) refers to the going, meaning "after the going," and this is indicated by the fact that the promising implies the going. It then refers to something not mentioned, but understood from the context of speech, as in His saying: ﴿until it was hidden by the veil﴾ [Sad 32], and ﴿and raised thereby a cloud of dust﴾ [al-'Adiyat 4], meaning "the sun was hidden," since the evening (*al-'ashiyy*) indicates it in His saying, and "they raised dust in the place," since the place is indicated by ﴿by the charging ones﴾ [al-'Adiyat 1], ﴿by the striking sparks﴾ [al-'Adiyat 2], ﴿and the raiders at dawn﴾ [al-'Adiyat 3], since these actions can occur only in a place, so the speech required it and indicated it. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the rescue, meaning "after the rescue," and it has been said that it refers to the guidance, meaning "after the guidance." Both of these views are weak.

﴿And you were wrongdoers﴾. This is a circumstantial clause (*jumla haliyya*). As for the object of the wrongdoing, it has been said: they were wrongdoers by placing worship in other than its proper place. It has also been said: by engaging in the means of their own destruction. It has been said: by your consent to the deed of the Samiri in his making of the calf, since you did not object to it. It is also possible that the clause is not circumstantial, but is rather a report from God that they are wrongdoers, meaning that wrongdoing is their disposition, and wrongdoing is the placing of things in other than their proper place. The meaning would then be: "Then you took the calf after him, while you were wrongdoers," like His saying: ﴿they took it, and they were wrongdoers﴾ [al-A'raf 148]. This clause has been put in the form of a nominal sentence with a predicate, because it is more eloquent and emphatic than the verbal clause, and in order to agree with the verse endings (*fawasil*). The apparent sense of His saying "then you took" is generality, that they all worshipped the calf except Aaron. It has been said that those who devoted themselves to its worship from the people of Moses were eight thousand men. It has been said that all of them worshipped it except Aaron together with twelve thousand. It has been said: this is the correct view. It has been said: except Aaron and the seventy men who were with Moses. As for the Samiri's choice of a calf rather than other animals, it has been said: because they passed by a people who devoted themselves to idols of theirs, which were in the forms of cows. They said: "Make for us a god as they have gods." So the idea occurred to the Samiri's mind to tempt them from this direction, and he made for them the calf. It has also been said that he was from a people who worshipped cows, and that he was a hypocrite who outwardly professed faith in Moses, so he made a calf of the same kind as what he had worshipped. In their taking the calf as a god there is evidence that they were anthropomorphists (*mujassima*) or incarnationists (*hulliyya*), because whoever believes in God's transcendence above that, and the impossibility of that for Him, by necessity would immediately see the invalidity of the claim that the calf is a god. The exegetes have reported from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi and others many varied stories concerning the cause of the taking of the calf and the manner of its making, and many reports have accompanied these. God knows best their soundness, since no book and no sound hadith has attested to their authenticity. Therefore we have left the transmission of these in accordance with our custom in this book.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 51–53 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Then We pardoned you after that﴾: The meanings of ʿafā (to pardon) have already been discussed. It may be that ʿafā here carries the sense of erasing and removing, or the sense of leaving alone, or the sense of making easy. ʿAfw (pardon) and ṣafḥ (overlooking) are close in meaning. Some scholars said: ʿafw is used in the sense of ṣafḥ only with regard to a sin. If ʿafw here means leaving alone or making easy, then ʿankum ("you") is general in wording but specific in meaning, because the pardon was granted only to those among them who remained. If it means erasing, then it is general in both wording and meaning, for God accepted the repentance of those who were killed and of those who remained. God says: ﴿So kill yourselves; that is better for you in the sight of your Creator, and He turned to you [in forgiveness]﴾ [al-Baqara 2:54]. It is related that after they killed themselves, God revealed to Moses: "I have accepted their repentance. Whoever was killed is a martyr, and whoever was not killed, I have turned to him and forgiven him." The Mu'tazila (a theological school) said: "We pardoned you" means because of your bringing about repentance, which was the killing of some of them by others. ﴿after that﴾ refers to the taking of the calf, and it was said that it refers to their killing themselves. The first view is more evident.

﴿la-llakum (so that you may)﴾: The discussion of la-ʿalla (perhaps, so that) has already been given in His saying ﴿so that you may be God-fearing﴾, linguistically and in its semantic implication with regard to God Most High, so there is no need to repeat it. ﴿tashkurūn (you may give thanks)﴾: that is, you praise Him for bestowing His blessings upon you, and you manifest the blessing by praising Him. They said: thanks is by the tongue, which is speaking of the Benefactor's blessing and praising Him for it; and by the heart, which is believing in the rightful due of the Benefactor from the one who is benefited; and by action, ﴿Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude﴾ [Saba' 34:13]; and through God, that is, thanks to God through God, because none can give Him thanks as He deserves except Himself. Someone said:

Gratitude to those who do good is at times by speech, at times by the heart, and then by action, the most noble.

And my gratitude to my Lord is not by my heart or my obedience alone, nor by my tongue, but rather His thanks is by Him on our behalf.

The meaning of ﴿so that you may give thanks﴾ is: [so that you may give thanks for] God's pardon of you, because pardon requires gratitude. This is what the majority said. Or: you may show God's blessing upon you in the pardon. Or: you may acknowledge My blessing. Or: you may persist in My obedience. Or: you may confess your inability to thank Me. These are four opinions. Ibn ʿAbbas said: thanks is the obedience of the limbs. Al-Junayd said: thanks is the admission of inability to give thanks. Al-Shibli said: humility under the vision of the favour. Al-Fudayl said: that you do not disobey God. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: that you recognise the blessing as coming from God. Dhu l-Nun said: thanks to one above you is through obedience, to your equal through reciprocation, and to one below you through kindness. Al-Qushayri said: swiftness in pardoning a grave offence indicates the lowliness of the one pardoned, as is witnessed by His saying: ﴿Whoever of you commits a manifest immorality, her punishment will be doubled﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:30]. These were the Children of Israel who worshipped the calf, and God said: ﴿Then We pardoned you after that﴾, and to this Ummah He said: ﴿Whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [al-Zalzala 99:8]. The end of his words.

The hope of gratitude is appropriate immediately after the mention of pardon, because pardon for such a great slip, namely taking the calf as a god, is among the greatest, or the greatest, bestowal of blessings. Therefore He said: ﴿so that you may give thanks﴾.

﴿And when We gave Musa the Book﴾: It is the Torah, by the consensus of the exegetes.

﴿and the Furqan﴾: It is the Torah. The meaning is that He gave it to him combining being a Book and being a criterion (furqan) distinguishing truth from falsehood. The "and" would then be a conjunction of attributes, because the Book in reality means the written, as said by al-Zajjaj and preferred by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn ʿAtiyya began with this view and said: the meaning is repeated with a change of wording, and because it adds the sense of distinction between truth and falsehood, which the word kitab does not express. Or the wa is superfluous (muqhama), that is, extra, and the furqan is an epithet of the Book. A poet said:

To the mighty king and the son of the noble, and the lion of the battalion in the throng.

This was said by al-Kisa'i, but it is weak. Rather, his words "and the son of the noble and the lion" are a conjunction of attributes one upon another, and this requires that the attributes differ in meaning.

Or the furqan is victory, because it distinguished between the enemy and the ally in drowning and salvation. From this it was said of the day of Badr: the Day of the Furqan. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Or all the signs with which Musa was given, of the staff, the hand, and other things, because they distinguished between truth and falsehood.

Or the furqan is the distinction between truth and falsehood; this was said by Abu l-ʿAliya and Mujahid.

Or the furqan is the sacred law which distinguishes between the lawful and the unlawful.

Or it is the proof which distinguishes between disbelief and belief; this was said by Ibn Bahr and Ibn Zayd.

Or it is the relief from distresses, because they were enslaved along with the Copts. From this is His saying: ﴿He will grant you a furqan﴾ [al-Anfal 8:29], that is, a relief and a way out. This view returns to the meaning of victory.

Or it is the Qur'an. The meaning would be that God gave Musa the mention of the descent of the Qur'an upon Muhammad (ﷺ), so that he believed in it; this was related by Ibn al-Anbari.

Or the furqan is the Qur'an with an omitted object, the estimated meaning being: and Muhammad the Furqan. This is reported from al-Farra', Qutrub and Tha'lab, and they said: it is like the saying of the poet:

And they adorned the brows and the eyes.

The estimated meaning is: and they applied kohl to the eyes. This view was rejected by Makki, al-Nahhas and a group, because there is no evidence for this omitted element, and it would become like the saying: "I fed Zayd bread and meat," where the meat would be something you fed other than Zayd. Also, the basic principle of coordination is that the conjoined element shares the preceding ruling with what it is conjoined to, when the particle of coordination is one that shares in that. The example they cited, "and they adorned the brows and the eyes," is not like this, for reasons mentioned in grammar.

It has come in: ﴿And We gave Musa and Harun the Furqan and a light﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:48]. They also mentioned all the signs which God Most High gave Musa, because they distinguished between truth and falsehood.

Or the furqan is the splitting of the sea; this was said by Yaman and Qutrub. This view is weakened by the prior mention of the parting of the sea in His saying ﴿when We parted [the sea]﴾, and by the mention of hoping for guidance immediately after the furqan, which fits only the Book.

It is answered that, although the splitting was mentioned earlier, it is repeated here and stated explicitly, as a sign given to Musa specifically. The mention of guidance after the parting of the sea is appropriate because it is among the proofs by which the existence of the Creator and the truthfulness of Musa (upon our Prophet and upon him be peace) are established, and that is guidance. Or because the intended guidance is salvation and success, and by the parting of the sea they obtained this, so He has mentioned to them the blessing of the Book, which is the foundation of their religion, and the blessing of salvation from their enemies. These are twelve statements of the exegetes concerning the intended meaning of furqan here.

[p. 203] ﴿so that you may be guided﴾: a hope for their guidance. The discussion of la-ʿalla has already been given. Ibn ʿAtiyya's wording here, and his earlier wording on ﴿so that you may give thanks﴾, shows that it expresses expectation. What is established in grammar is that if the object of la-ʿalla is beloved, it is for hope (tarajjī); if it is feared, it is for anticipation (tawaqquʿ), as in your saying: "Perhaps the enemy will advance." Gratitude and guidance are beloved things, so the meaning of la-ʿalla here should be expressed only as hope.

Al-Qushayri said: the furqan of this Ummah, with which they are distinguished, is a light in their hearts by which they distinguish between truth and falsehood. "Consult your heart," "Beware the discernment of the believer, for the believer sees by the light of God," and "If you fear God, He will grant you a furqan." The end of his words.

That furqan is what they have put forward of goodness.

The hope for guidance comes right after the mention of Musa's being given the Book and the Furqan, because by the Book guidance is attained: ﴿Indeed, We revealed the Torah, in which is guidance and light﴾ [al-Ma'ida 5:44]; ﴿That is the Book, there is no doubt in it, a guidance﴾ [al-Baqara 2:2]; ﴿And We gave him the Gospel, in which is guidance and light﴾ [al-Ma'ida 5:46].

These noble verses contain several sections of the mention of God's favour upon the Children of Israel. Among them: the parting of the sea for them in the manner mentioned, so that it became twelve paths according to the number of the tribes, with a partition between each tribe preventing them from crowding, without any sense of alienation befalling them in that, because in each partition there were openings so that some could see others, as is reported. This is among the greatest signs indicating the truthfulness of Musa (upon our Prophet and upon him be peace). This parting is the third blessing. The first blessing was their being preferred, the second was their deliverance from the people of Pharaoh, and the third was this parting and what followed from it, namely their deliverance from drowning and the drowning of their enemies while they looked on, so that they had no doubt of their destruction. Then he digressed after that to the mention of the fourth blessing, which is the pardon for the great sin they committed by worshipping the calf. So He mentioned the cause of this, that it happened because of Musa's absence from them for intimate conversation with his Lord, and that despite the short duration of his absence, they were deceived by what this Samiri did, and time did not lengthen for them, and their successor for Musa among them was his brother Harun, who forbade them, but they did not desist. And despite this great slip, He pardoned them and turned to them. What blessing is greater than this? Then He mentioned the fifth blessing, which is the fruit of the promise, namely Musa's bringing the Torah, by which they were guided, and in which are the benefits of their worldly and otherworldly life.

The arrangement of these blessings came in a coherent sequence, each part taking hold of the next, and it is a chronological arrangement, one of the five arrangements that have been mentioned in this book. This is because preference is a matter of judgment, so it is first, and then the blessings came after it, and they are acts following one another. The first of them is deliverance from the evil torment, the slaughter of the sons and the sparing of the women, by Musa bringing them out of Egypt, such that neither Pharaoh nor his people had any power over them after this departure and deliverance. Then came the parting of the sea for them and their being shown this great marvel with their own eyes. Then God's promise to Musa of intimate conversation with Him, and his going to it. Then their taking of the calf. Then the pardon of them. Then the giving of the Torah to Musa. Consider the excellence of these sections, which are arranged like pearls on their strings and blossoms on their branches, each section concluded with its fitting close, and rising to the height of eloquence in its loftiest station, sent down by God upon the tongue of Muhammad, His trustworthy one, the tongue of one who had not recited a Book before it nor written it with his right hand.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 51–53 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And when We appointed for Moses forty nights﴾. The majority read *wa'adna* (we appointed), while Abu 'Amr read *wa'adna* without an alif here, and in al-A'raf and Ta-Ha. *Wa'adna* (with the alif) may mean the same as *wa'adna* (without it), in which case it proceeds from one party. It may also be from two parties according to the original sense of the form *mufa'ala* (reciprocal action), so that God promised Moses the revelation, and Moses promised God that he would come at the appointed time. Or the promise came from God and its acceptance came from Moses, and accepting a promise resembles making one. Al-Qaffal said: "It is not far-fetched that a human being may promise God, meaning that he binds himself to Him by covenant." It has also been said: *wa'ada* is used when there is no request, and *wa'ada* (with the alif) when there is a request. Abu 'Ubayd preferred the reading without the alif and rejected the reading with the alif. Abu Hatim and Makki agreed with him in meaning. Abu 'Ubayd said: "*al-muwa'ada* (mutual promising) is only from humans." Abu Hatim said: "Mutual promising is most often between equal created beings, each of whom promises the other." The derivation of *wa'ada* according to those aspects mentioned earlier has already been given. There is no basis for preferring one reading over the other, because each of them is *mutawatir* (transmitted through so many chains that its authenticity is certain), so both are equally sound. Most reciters read with the alif, and this is the reading of Mujahid, al-A'raj, Ibn Kathir, Nafi', al-A'mash, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i.

*Musa* (Moses) is Musa son of 'Imran son of Yashhar son of Qahith son of Lawi son of Ya'qub son of Ishaq son of Ibrahim, the Friend of the Most Merciful. Al-Sharif Abu al-Barakat Muhammad ibn As'ad ibn 'Ali al-Hiwwani, the genealogist, mentioned that Musa, upon our Prophet and upon him be peace, is Musa son of 'Imran son of Qahith. The discussion of the word *Musa* as a proper name has already been given. As for *Musa* (the razor) with which hair is shaved, it is an Arabic feminine noun derived from *asawtu al-shay'* (I set the thing right) when you repair it. Its pattern is *maf'al*, and its original root is hamza. It has also been said that its derivation is from *awsaytu* (I shaved), and this derivation is more fitting for it, and on this view the waw has no root in the hamza.

*Arba'in laylatan* (forty nights): these are Dhu al-Hijjah and ten days of Muharram, or Dhu al-Qa'dah and ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. This was said by Abu al-'Aliyah and most of the exegetes. 'Ali and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read *arba'in* with a kasrah on the ba' (*arbi'in*), which is an irregular reading, through assimilation to the following sound. *Arba'in* is in the accusative as the second object of *wa'adna*, either because it is itself the thing promised, or by omitting a modifier, the implied sense being "the completion of forty" or "the end of forty." The modifier is omitted and the thing modified is put in its place and takes its case endings. This was said by al-Akhfash, and it is like the line of poetry:

> "So promise him the two trees of Malik, or the sand-hill between them, that they be easy."

That is, the coming of the two trees of Malik.

It is not permissible for *arba'in* to be in the accusative as an adverb of time, because it is a counted time-noun, which would require the verb to fall on each part of it, and the promising did not happen in that way. *Laylatan* (nights) is in the accusative as a specifier (*tamyiz*, a noun that clarifies an ambiguity) coming after the completion of the numeral. The governing element in this type of specifier is the numeral before it. *Arba'in* is treated as if it were a participle of the form of "hitting" (*dharibin*). It is agreed that this type of specifier may not precede the numeral, and that it may not be separated from it by a prepositional phrase except in poetic necessity, as in the line:

> "Thirty years have passed since then, a complete year of separation, and twenty of them, a finger's breadth behind us."

There is no definiteness for the specifier, contrary to some of the Kufans and Abu al-Husayn ibn al-Taraawah. Our companions interpreted what Abu Zayd al-Ansari related from the Arabs, saying: "*Ma fa'alat al-'ishrun al-dirham?*" (What did the twenty do with the dirham?), and similar expressions that indicate definiteness. This is mentioned in the science of grammar. The explanation of the forty as nights rather than days is because the beginning of the month is the night of the crescent, and for this reason time was dated by nights. The Arabs relied on the crescents, so days became subordinate to nights. Or it is because darkness precedes light, as shown by the verse ﴿And a sign for them is the night; We strip from it the day﴾ [Ya-Sin 37]. Or it indicates that he continued the fast by night and by day without interruption, because if the explanation had been by days, one might think he broke the fast at night. When the nights were specified, the force of the speech required that he continued for forty nights with their days.

(p-200) This promise was for speaking with God, or for the sending down of the Torah. Al-Mahdawi said: This happened after Moses had crossed the sea, when his people asked him to bring them a Book from God. He went out to the mountain (Tur) with seventy men from the best of the Children of Israel. He ascended the mountain and promised them until the completion of forty nights. They then waited, as the exegetes mention, twenty days and ten nights, and they said: "He has broken his promise to us." The end of his speech. Al-Zamakhshari said: When the Children of Israel entered Egypt after the destruction of Pharaoh, and they had no Book to refer to, God promised to send down the Torah to them, and He appointed a time for it. The end.

* *

﴿Then you took the calf﴾. The majority read with assimilation of the dhal into the ta' (*ittakhadhtum*). Ibn Kathir and Hafs, among the Seven, read with clear pronunciation (*idh-har*). The verb *ittakhadha* here may be transitive to one object, meaning "you made a calf," as in His saying: ﴿And the people of Moses took after him from their ornaments a calf, a body that lowed﴾ [al-A'raf 148], according to one of the two interpretations. On this reckoning there is an omitted clause indicated by the sense, and its estimate would be: "and you worshipped it as a god." It may also be that the verb is one that takes two objects, in which case the second object is omitted, its meaning being indicated: "you took the calf as a god." The first view is more likely, because if the verb took two objects in this story, it would state the second one, at least in one place. Do you not see that it is not given two objects in this place, but one, and in ﴿the people of Moses took﴾ [al-A'raf 148], and in ﴿they took it, and they were wrongdoers﴾ [al-A'raf 148], and in ﴿Indeed, those who took the calf﴾ [al-A'raf 152], and in His saying in this same surah: ﴿Indeed you have wronged yourselves by your taking of the calf﴾ [al-Baqarah 54]? Nevertheless the second view is preferred, because the first view would require the omission of a clause in these verses, whereas the second requires only the omission of an object, and omitting a single word is easier than omitting a clause. According to the first view, there is condemnation of the group for the act of one man, because the one who made the calf was the Samiri, and his story, his name, and the account of his misleading will come, God willing, when His saying is reached: ﴿and the Samiri misled them﴾ [Ta-Ha 85]. This is the custom of the Arabs in their speech, praising or blaming a tribe for what was done by some of its members. According to the second view, the blame falls upon them for what proceeded from them. The definite article in *al-'ijl* (the calf), on the first view, is for defining the quiddity (the nature of the thing), since no previous reference had been mentioned. On the second view it is for the prior known reference, since they had made a calf and then took that calf as a god. That it is a calf is clear evidence that it became flesh and blood, so it is a calf in reality and the attribution of lowing to it is literal. This was said by al-Hasan. It has also been said that this is metaphorical, meaning a calf in form and shape, because the Samiri fashioned it in the shape of a calf, and according to what they mentioned he was a goldsmith. The attribution of lowing to it would then be metaphorical. This was said by the majority. The discussion of this matter will come in al-A'raf, God willing. Among the strangest things said about this calf is that it was named a calf because they hastened (*'ajjalu*) to it before Moses' arrival and took it as a god. This was said by Abu al-'Aliyah. Or it was called a calf because of the shortness of its duration.

﴿From after him﴾. *Min* indicates the beginning of a limit (*ibtida' al-ghayah*), and its meaning conflicts with the meaning of *thumma* (then). This is because *thumma* requires that the taking happened after an interval following the promise, while *min* requires that the transitive action following the promise begins immediately. Since the pronoun obviously refers back to Moses, and the act of transitivity cannot be conceived of in the essence, it is necessary to supply an omitted element. The nearest element to omit is a verbal noun indicated by the word *wa'adna*, meaning "after his promising." Therefore it is necessary to commit a figurative usage in one of the two particles, unless one supplies an omitted element other than the promising, namely that the estimate is "after his going off to the mountain." In that case the conflict disappears, because the interval lies between the promising and the taking, and the beginning of the limit comes right after going to the mountain. The interval is made clear by the story in al-A'raf, where between the promising and the taking there are many sentences. The beginning of the limit occurs immediately after going to the mountain, so the interval and the beginning do not apply to one and the same thing, and the conflict disappears. It has also been said that the pronoun in *ba'dihi* (after him) refers to the going, meaning "after the going," and this is indicated by the fact that the promising implies the going. It then refers to something not mentioned, but understood from the context of speech, as in His saying: ﴿until it was hidden by the veil﴾ [Sad 32], and ﴿and raised thereby a cloud of dust﴾ [al-'Adiyat 4], meaning "the sun was hidden," since the evening (*al-'ashiyy*) indicates it in His saying, and "they raised dust in the place," since the place is indicated by ﴿by the charging ones﴾ [al-'Adiyat 1], ﴿by the striking sparks﴾ [al-'Adiyat 2], ﴿and the raiders at dawn﴾ [al-'Adiyat 3], since these actions can occur only in a place, so the speech required it and indicated it. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the rescue, meaning "after the rescue," and it has been said that it refers to the guidance, meaning "after the guidance." Both of these views are weak.

﴿And you were wrongdoers﴾. This is a circumstantial clause (*jumla haliyya*). As for the object of the wrongdoing, it has been said: they were wrongdoers by placing worship in other than its proper place. It has also been said: by engaging in the means of their own destruction. It has been said: by your consent to the deed of the Samiri in his making of the calf, since you did not object to it. It is also possible that the clause is not circumstantial, but is rather a report from God that they are wrongdoers, meaning that wrongdoing is their disposition, and wrongdoing is the placing of things in other than their proper place. The meaning would then be: "Then you took the calf after him, while you were wrongdoers," like His saying: ﴿they took it, and they were wrongdoers﴾ [al-A'raf 148]. This clause has been put in the form of a nominal sentence with a predicate, because it is more eloquent and emphatic than the verbal clause, and in order to agree with the verse endings (*fawasil*). The apparent sense of His saying "then you took" is generality, that they all worshipped the calf except Aaron. It has been said that those who devoted themselves to its worship from the people of Moses were eight thousand men. It has been said that all of them worshipped it except Aaron together with twelve thousand. It has been said: this is the correct view. It has been said: except Aaron and the seventy men who were with Moses. As for the Samiri's choice of a calf rather than other animals, it has been said: because they passed by a people who devoted themselves to idols of theirs, which were in the forms of cows. They said: "Make for us a god as they have gods." So the idea occurred to the Samiri's mind to tempt them from this direction, and he made for them the calf. It has also been said that he was from a people who worshipped cows, and that he was a hypocrite who outwardly professed faith in Moses, so he made a calf of the same kind as what he had worshipped. In their taking the calf as a god there is evidence that they were anthropomorphists (*mujassima*) or incarnationists (*hulliyya*), because whoever believes in God's transcendence above that, and the impossibility of that for Him, by necessity would immediately see the invalidity of the claim that the calf is a god. The exegetes have reported from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi and others many varied stories concerning the cause of the taking of the calf and the manner of its making, and many reports have accompanied these. God knows best their soundness, since no book and no sound hadith has attested to their authenticity. Therefore we have left the transmission of these in accordance with our custom in this book.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 51–53 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Then We pardoned you after that﴾: The meanings of ʿafā (to pardon) have already been discussed. It may be that ʿafā here carries the sense of erasing and removing, or the sense of leaving alone, or the sense of making easy. ʿAfw (pardon) and ṣafḥ (overlooking) are close in meaning. Some scholars said: ʿafw is used in the sense of ṣafḥ only with regard to a sin. If ʿafw here means leaving alone or making easy, then ʿankum ("you") is general in wording but specific in meaning, because the pardon was granted only to those among them who remained. If it means erasing, then it is general in both wording and meaning, for God accepted the repentance of those who were killed and of those who remained. God says: ﴿So kill yourselves; that is better for you in the sight of your Creator, and He turned to you [in forgiveness]﴾ [al-Baqara 2:54]. It is related that after they killed themselves, God revealed to Moses: "I have accepted their repentance. Whoever was killed is a martyr, and whoever was not killed, I have turned to him and forgiven him." The Mu'tazila (a theological school) said: "We pardoned you" means because of your bringing about repentance, which was the killing of some of them by others. ﴿after that﴾ refers to the taking of the calf, and it was said that it refers to their killing themselves. The first view is more evident.

﴿la-llakum (so that you may)﴾: The discussion of la-ʿalla (perhaps, so that) has already been given in His saying ﴿so that you may be God-fearing﴾, linguistically and in its semantic implication with regard to God Most High, so there is no need to repeat it. ﴿tashkurūn (you may give thanks)﴾: that is, you praise Him for bestowing His blessings upon you, and you manifest the blessing by praising Him. They said: thanks is by the tongue, which is speaking of the Benefactor's blessing and praising Him for it; and by the heart, which is believing in the rightful due of the Benefactor from the one who is benefited; and by action, ﴿Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude﴾ [Saba' 34:13]; and through God, that is, thanks to God through God, because none can give Him thanks as He deserves except Himself. Someone said:

Gratitude to those who do good is at times by speech, at times by the heart, and then by action, the most noble.

And my gratitude to my Lord is not by my heart or my obedience alone, nor by my tongue, but rather His thanks is by Him on our behalf.

The meaning of ﴿so that you may give thanks﴾ is: [so that you may give thanks for] God's pardon of you, because pardon requires gratitude. This is what the majority said. Or: you may show God's blessing upon you in the pardon. Or: you may acknowledge My blessing. Or: you may persist in My obedience. Or: you may confess your inability to thank Me. These are four opinions. Ibn ʿAbbas said: thanks is the obedience of the limbs. Al-Junayd said: thanks is the admission of inability to give thanks. Al-Shibli said: humility under the vision of the favour. Al-Fudayl said: that you do not disobey God. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: that you recognise the blessing as coming from God. Dhu l-Nun said: thanks to one above you is through obedience, to your equal through reciprocation, and to one below you through kindness. Al-Qushayri said: swiftness in pardoning a grave offence indicates the lowliness of the one pardoned, as is witnessed by His saying: ﴿Whoever of you commits a manifest immorality, her punishment will be doubled﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:30]. These were the Children of Israel who worshipped the calf, and God said: ﴿Then We pardoned you after that﴾, and to this Ummah He said: ﴿Whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾ [al-Zalzala 99:8]. The end of his words.

The hope of gratitude is appropriate immediately after the mention of pardon, because pardon for such a great slip, namely taking the calf as a god, is among the greatest, or the greatest, bestowal of blessings. Therefore He said: ﴿so that you may give thanks﴾.

﴿And when We gave Musa the Book﴾: It is the Torah, by the consensus of the exegetes.

﴿and the Furqan﴾: It is the Torah. The meaning is that He gave it to him combining being a Book and being a criterion (furqan) distinguishing truth from falsehood. The "and" would then be a conjunction of attributes, because the Book in reality means the written, as said by al-Zajjaj and preferred by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn ʿAtiyya began with this view and said: the meaning is repeated with a change of wording, and because it adds the sense of distinction between truth and falsehood, which the word kitab does not express. Or the wa is superfluous (muqhama), that is, extra, and the furqan is an epithet of the Book. A poet said:

To the mighty king and the son of the noble, and the lion of the battalion in the throng.

This was said by al-Kisa'i, but it is weak. Rather, his words "and the son of the noble and the lion" are a conjunction of attributes one upon another, and this requires that the attributes differ in meaning.

Or the furqan is victory, because it distinguished between the enemy and the ally in drowning and salvation. From this it was said of the day of Badr: the Day of the Furqan. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Or all the signs with which Musa was given, of the staff, the hand, and other things, because they distinguished between truth and falsehood.

Or the furqan is the distinction between truth and falsehood; this was said by Abu l-ʿAliya and Mujahid.

Or the furqan is the sacred law which distinguishes between the lawful and the unlawful.

Or it is the proof which distinguishes between disbelief and belief; this was said by Ibn Bahr and Ibn Zayd.

Or it is the relief from distresses, because they were enslaved along with the Copts. From this is His saying: ﴿He will grant you a furqan﴾ [al-Anfal 8:29], that is, a relief and a way out. This view returns to the meaning of victory.
