Or it is the Qur'an. The meaning would be that God gave Musa the mention of the descent of the Qur'an upon Muhammad (ﷺ), so that he believed in it; this was related by Ibn al-Anbari.

Or the furqan is the Qur'an with an omitted object, the estimated meaning being: and Muhammad the Furqan. This is reported from al-Farra', Qutrub and Tha'lab, and they said: it is like the saying of the poet:

And they adorned the brows and the eyes.

The estimated meaning is: and they applied kohl to the eyes. This view was rejected by Makki, al-Nahhas and a group, because there is no evidence for this omitted element, and it would become like the saying: "I fed Zayd bread and meat," where the meat would be something you fed other than Zayd. Also, the basic principle of coordination is that the conjoined element shares the preceding ruling with what it is conjoined to, when the particle of coordination is one that shares in that. The example they cited, "and they adorned the brows and the eyes," is not like this, for reasons mentioned in grammar.

It has come in: ﴿And We gave Musa and Harun the Furqan and a light﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:48]. They also mentioned all the signs which God Most High gave Musa, because they distinguished between truth and falsehood.

Or the furqan is the splitting of the sea; this was said by Yaman and Qutrub. This view is weakened by the prior mention of the parting of the sea in His saying ﴿when We parted [the sea]﴾, and by the mention of hoping for guidance immediately after the furqan, which fits only the Book.

It is answered that, although the splitting was mentioned earlier, it is repeated here and stated explicitly, as a sign given to Musa specifically. The mention of guidance after the parting of the sea is appropriate because it is among the proofs by which the existence of the Creator and the truthfulness of Musa (upon our Prophet and upon him be peace) are established, and that is guidance. Or because the intended guidance is salvation and success, and by the parting of the sea they obtained this, so He has mentioned to them the blessing of the Book, which is the foundation of their religion, and the blessing of salvation from their enemies. These are twelve statements of the exegetes concerning the intended meaning of furqan here.

[p. 203] ﴿so that you may be guided﴾: a hope for their guidance. The discussion of la-ʿalla has already been given. Ibn ʿAtiyya's wording here, and his earlier wording on ﴿so that you may give thanks﴾, shows that it expresses expectation. What is established in grammar is that if the object of la-ʿalla is beloved, it is for hope (tarajjī); if it is feared, it is for anticipation (tawaqquʿ), as in your saying: "Perhaps the enemy will advance." Gratitude and guidance are beloved things, so the meaning of la-ʿalla here should be expressed only as hope.

Al-Qushayri said: the furqan of this Ummah, with which they are distinguished, is a light in their hearts by which they distinguish between truth and falsehood. "Consult your heart," "Beware the discernment of the believer, for the believer sees by the light of God," and "If you fear God, He will grant you a furqan." The end of his words.

That furqan is what they have put forward of goodness.

The hope for guidance comes right after the mention of Musa's being given the Book and the Furqan, because by the Book guidance is attained: ﴿Indeed, We revealed the Torah, in which is guidance and light﴾ [al-Ma'ida 5:44]; ﴿That is the Book, there is no doubt in it, a guidance﴾ [al-Baqara 2:2]; ﴿And We gave him the Gospel, in which is guidance and light﴾ [al-Ma'ida 5:46].

These noble verses contain several sections of the mention of God's favour upon the Children of Israel. Among them: the parting of the sea for them in the manner mentioned, so that it became twelve paths according to the number of the tribes, with a partition between each tribe preventing them from crowding, without any sense of alienation befalling them in that, because in each partition there were openings so that some could see others, as is reported. This is among the greatest signs indicating the truthfulness of Musa (upon our Prophet and upon him be peace). This parting is the third blessing. The first blessing was their being preferred, the second was their deliverance from the people of Pharaoh, and the third was this parting and what followed from it, namely their deliverance from drowning and the drowning of their enemies while they looked on, so that they had no doubt of their destruction. Then he digressed after that to the mention of the fourth blessing, which is the pardon for the great sin they committed by worshipping the calf. So He mentioned the cause of this, that it happened because of Musa's absence from them for intimate conversation with his Lord, and that despite the short duration of his absence, they were deceived by what this Samiri did, and time did not lengthen for them, and their successor for Musa among them was his brother Harun, who forbade them, but they did not desist. And despite this great slip, He pardoned them and turned to them. What blessing is greater than this? Then He mentioned the fifth blessing, which is the fruit of the promise, namely Musa's bringing the Torah, by which they were guided, and in which are the benefits of their worldly and otherworldly life.

The arrangement of these blessings came in a coherent sequence, each part taking hold of the next, and it is a chronological arrangement, one of the five arrangements that have been mentioned in this book. This is because preference is a matter of judgment, so it is first, and then the blessings came after it, and they are acts following one another. The first of them is deliverance from the evil torment, the slaughter of the sons and the sparing of the women, by Musa bringing them out of Egypt, such that neither Pharaoh nor his people had any power over them after this departure and deliverance. Then came the parting of the sea for them and their being shown this great marvel with their own eyes. Then God's promise to Musa of intimate conversation with Him, and his going to it. Then their taking of the calf. Then the pardon of them. Then the giving of the Torah to Musa. Consider the excellence of these sections, which are arranged like pearls on their strings and blossoms on their branches, each section concluded with its fitting close, and rising to the height of eloquence in its loftiest station, sent down by God upon the tongue of Muhammad, His trustworthy one, the tongue of one who had not recited a Book before it nor written it with his right hand.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 54 (part 1 of 3):**

﴿And when Moses said to his people, "O my people, you have wronged yourselves by taking the calf [for worship]. So turn in repentance to your Creator and kill yourselves. That is better for you in the sight of your Creator." Then He accepted your repentance. Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿And when you said, "O Moses, we will never believe you until we see Allah openly," the thunderbolt seized you while you were looking on.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 55] ﴿Then We revived you after your death, so that you might be grateful.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 56] ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds and sent down to you manna and quails: "Eat of the good things with which We have provided you." They did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 57]

*al-Qawm* (the people): a collective noun (*ism jam'*) that has no singular from its own form; its singular is *imru'*. Analogically it should not be pluralized, but its plural is irregularly formed: they said *aqwam*, and the plural of that is *aqawim*. It has been said that it is restricted to men. God, the Exalted, says: ﴿Let not a people ridicule another people﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11], and for this reason He set it against: ﴿nor let women ridicule other women﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11]. Zuhayr said:

*Are they a people, the family of Hisn, or women?*

Another said:

*My people are the ones who killed Umayyim, my brother; so when I shoot, my arrow strikes me.*

Another said:

*Let not my people be far away, those who are the poison of enemies and the calamity of the slaughtered camels.*

It has also been said: it is not restricted to men but applies to both men and women. God says: ﴿Indeed, We sent Noah to his people﴾ [Nuh: 1], and ﴿O my people, what is [the matter] with me that I call you to salvation﴾ [Ghafir: 41]. Every prophet was sent specifically to his own people. The speaker of this view said: if there is an indication restricting it, then the general meaning is nullified and the intended meaning is that restricted thing. The first view is more correct. The inclusion of women within *qawm* is by way of following (*istitba'*) and giving precedence to men (*taghlib*), and metaphor is better than homonymy (*ishtirak*). Men were called *qawm* because they "stand up" (*yaqumuna*) with affairs.

*al-Bari'* (the Creator): the one who creates. *Bara'a yabra'u* means "he created." The combination of *al-Khaliq* and *al-Bari'* in God's words ﴿He is Allah, the Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner﴾ [al-Hashr: 24] indicates a distinction, unless it is taken as emphasis.

Some people distinguished between them, saying: *al-Bari'* is the one who originates and innovates, while *al-Khaliq* is the one who determines and moves [things] from one state to another. Some scholars said: *bara'a*, *ansha'a*, and *abda'a* are synonyms. Al-Mahdawi and others said, and the wording is his: its origin is from *tabarra'a al-shay' min al-shay'*, meaning that it separates from it. Thus the created things have been separated from non-existence into existence. End of quote. Umayya said: "The Creator, the Originator, the one who fashions in the wombs water until it becomes blood."

*al-Qatl* (killing): the taking of life by the action of someone, through stabbing, striking, slaughtering, strangling, or what resembles these. If it is without an action, it is death by perishing (*mawt halak*). *al-Muqattal* means "the humbled." Imru' al-Qays said:

*With your two arrows in the parts of a humbled heart.*

They explained it as "humbled."

*Khayr* (better): it is the comparative form (*af'al al-tafdil*) whose hamza has been omitted irregularly in speech, so its form is shortened and it becomes diptotic. Just as they omitted it irregularly in poetry from *ahabb*, which is also comparative. Al-Ahwas said:

*Love increased my passion when I was denied, and the thing most beloved to man is that which is denied.*

They have also pronounced the hamza in poetry. A poet said:

*Bilal is the best of people, and the son of the best.*

*Khayr* also comes not in the sense of comparison: you say, "In Zayd there is *khayr*," meaning by it a beautiful quality. And as a lightened form of *khayyir*: "a man who is *khayr*," i.e., one who has goodness in him. It is possible that God's words ﴿therein are good, beautiful [women]﴾ [al-Rahman: 70] are of this type.

*Hatta* (until): a particle whose meaning is mostly the end point. It can also indicate causation. Replacing its *ha'* with *ayn* is the dialect of Hudhayl, and inclination (*imalah*) in it has been heard rarely. Its rulings are fully treated in grammar.

*al-Ru'ya* (seeing) is sight. The past tense is *ra'a*, whose middle radical is a hamza that is dropped in its present tense, its imperative, the pattern *af'ala* and its imperative, the active participle, and the passive participle. You say: *yara*, *tara*, *nara*, *ara Zayd*, *arayt Zayd*, *ri Zayd*, *mari Zayd*, *mariya*. It remains in *al-ru'ya*, *al-ra'y*, *al-ru'ya* (dream), *al-mar'a*, *al-mar'iyy*, *al-mar'ah*, *istar'a*, *ar'a min kadha*, and in *ma arha* and *ar'ih* in exclamation. This omission that we have mentioned applies when the meaning of *ra'a* is sight, whether awake, asleep, or in belief. If *ra'a* means "struck his lung" (*asaba ri'atahu*), then the hamza is not dropped, and you say: *ra'ahu yar'ahu*, meaning he struck his lung. The author of the book *al-Amr* transmitted this. The dialect of Tamim is to keep the hamza in forms where others drop it, so they say *yar'a* and *ar'i*. Some Arabs combined dropping and keeping the hamza, saying:

*Have you not seen what I have met, while time is grinding? Whoever seeks a living sees and hears.*

*al-Jahra* (openness): the manifest, and from it *al-jahr*, the opposite of secrecy. The opening of the ayn in this pattern is attested according to the Basrans and analogical according to the Kufans, and some of this has been mentioned before. It is said: *jahara al-rajul al-amr*, meaning he uncovered it. *Jaharat al-rakiyya* means the well brought out what was in it of mud and revealed the water. He said:

*When we came to brackish water we made it open, or [if it was] empty of its people we made it populous.*

*al-Jahwari* means "loud-voiced," *sawt jahir* means "loud voice," and *wajh jahir* means "clearly radiant face." *Al-ajhar* means "the blind," named by the opposite.

*al-Ba'th* (raising): revival, and its original sense is stirring up. The poet said:

*I make her kneel when I wish, then I rouse her, as if she were a falcon in the air, a broad-winged one.*

Another said:

*And young men of truth, I roused them at dawn, and they all stood up between staggering and intoxicated.*

It has been said its origin is sending. From it: ﴿And We certainly sent in every nation a messenger﴾ [al-Nahl: 36]. It also comes in the sense of recovering from a faint or sleep: ﴿And thus We roused them that they might question one another﴾ [al-Kahf: 19]. The common element among these meanings is the removal of what prevents free action.

*Zallala* (to shade): on the pattern *fa''ala*, derived from *al-zill* (shade). *Al-zill* originally means benefit, and a cloud is a *zulla* because of the shade that occurs beneath it. From this it is said: "The sultan is the shadow of God on earth." The poet said:

*Even if you were the lord of glory or in its shadow, you would have wronged; but you have no hand in wrongdoing.*

*al-Ghamam* (clouds): a collective noun whose singular is formed with the feminine *ha'*: *ghamama* and *ghamam*, like *hamama* and *hamam*. It means clouds. It has been said: that which is white among the clouds. Mujahid said: it is colder and thinner than clouds. It is named *ghamam* because it covers (*yaghummu*) the face of the sky, meaning it veils it. From this: *al-ghamm*, *al-ghamam*, *al-aghamm*, *al-ghumma*, *al-ghumma*, *al-ghamma'*. *Ghumma al-hilal* means the crescent was concealed. The *ghamim* plant is that which conceals what is adjacent to it on the surface of the earth.

*al-Manna*: the verbal noun of *mannantu*, meaning I cut. *Al-mann* also means kindness. *Al-mann* is also a sweet gum that falls on trees. The views on what is meant by it in the verse are many, and they will come, God willing.

*al-Salwa*: a collective noun, its singular is *salwah*, as al-Khalil said. The *alif* in it is for assimilation (*ilhaq*), not for the feminine, as in *'alqa* and *'alqah*, since if it were for the feminine it would not have been feminized with the *ha'*. The poet said:

*Indeed, when I remember you, a *salwa* comes over me, as the *salwa* shakes off the wetness of the rain.*

Al-Kisa'i said: *salwa* is singular, and its plural is *salawa*. Al-Akhfash said: its plural and singular have one form. It has also been said: a collective with no singular from its own form. Mu'arrij al-Sadusi said: *salwa* is honey in the dialect of Kinana. The poet said:

*He swore to her by God with effort that you are sweeter than *salwa* when its honey is poured.*

Others said: it is a bird. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the Hudhali erred in his words:

*Sweeter than *salwa* when its [honey] is poured*

and thought *salwa* was honey. There are two answers showing that this is not an error. One is what we transmitted from Mu'arrij, that it is honey in the dialect of Kinana. The second is that in his words *nashuruha* there is a figurative usage for the sake of rhyme, where eating is expressed by *shawr*, by way of metaphor.

They said: the derivation of *salwa* is from *salwa* (consolation), because by its goodness it consoles one from other things.

*al-Tayyib* (good): on the pattern *fay'al*, from *taba yatibu*, meaning delicious. The discussion of this pattern's restriction to weak-lettered roots, except for rare cases, and the lightening of this type, has preceded. From its lightened form the city of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was named *Taybah*.

﴿And when Moses said to his people, "O my people, you have wronged yourselves"﴾: The author of *al-Muntakhab* counted this as the fifth blessing. It has been said: this verse and what follows are disconnected from what preceded of reminders of blessings, because he commanded killing, and killing is not a blessing. This was refuted: among the greatest blessings is alerting them to what allows them to escape the punishment of a great sin, and that is repentance. Since He enumerated for them the worldly blessings, then it is more fitting that He enumerate for them the religious blessings. Since this blessing is not complete in its description except with an introduction of what caused it, He mentioned that first. This address is the dialogue of Moses with his people when he returned from the appointed time and found them having worshipped the calf.

The *lam* in His words "to his people" is for conveying the message and for Moses' turning toward them with the call. His calling them with the words "O my people" indicates tenderness toward them, and that he is of them and they are of him. For this reason he attributed them to himself, as a man says, "O my brother" or "O my friend," so that this becomes a reason for accepting what he conveys to them, unlike if he had called them by name or by a vile description coming from them. In this also is a stirring of them toward accepting the command to repent, after rebuking them that they wronged themselves. And what greater wrong is there than taking a god other than Him? ﴿Indeed, associating others with Allah is a great injustice﴾ [Luqman: 13]. He specified that they wronged themselves by this because it is the most foul wrong, since a person's own soul is the most beloved thing to him. So when he wrongs it, that is more foul than wronging another.

*Ya qawm* (O people): a vocative noun attached to the first-person pronoun *ya'* (of the speaker). The *ya'* has been dropped and the kasra is used instead of it, and this dialect is the most common in the Qur'an. Its retention has also come, like the reading of the one who read: *ya 'ibadi fattaquni* ("O My servants, then fear Me"), with the *ya'* retained as sukun. It is permissible to make it fatha: you say *ya ghulami*, and making the preceding letter fatha and converting the *ya'* into an *alif*: *ya ghulaman*. Al-Akhfash permitted dropping the *alif* and using the fatha in its place: *ya ghulam*. He also permitted making it damma, and this is with the intention of the idafa: *ya ghulam*, meaning *ya ghulami*. Upon this is the reading of the one who read: "*qala rabbi uhkum bil-haqq*" and ﴿He said, "My Lord, prison is more beloved to me"﴾ [Yusuf: 33]. They stated this without qualification. Some distinguished between whether it is a verb or a noun: if it is a verb, its building on damma is not permitted, and he gave as an example of a verb *ya daribi* (O one who strikes me), so he does not permit *ya dharib* here. The apparent meaning of the address is that it is specific to those who took the calf. It has been said: it is permissible that it be meant for those who worshipped and those who did not, and they are described as wrongdoers because they did not prevent them and did not fight them.

The *ba'* in ﴿by your taking the calf﴾ is causal. The two possibilities mentioned earlier regarding His words ﴿then you took the calf﴾ [al-Baqarah: 51] occur here too: that is, "by your action of the calf and its worship," or "by your taking the calf as a god." Al-Sulami said: each person's calf is his own self, so whoever sets aside his desire and opposes his caprice has been freed from his wrongdoing.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 54 (part 2 of 3):

﴿So repent to your Creator.﴾ The fa' in (fatubu) carries the sense of causation (tasbib), because wrongdoing is the cause of repentance. Since al-Samiri had made for them a calf from their ornaments, they were told: "Repent to your Creator," meaning the one who brings you into being and originates you from non-existence, for the true originator of substances is the one who truly creates them. As for the making and fashioning of the calf, it did not bring the essences out of non-existence. It was only a compositional arrangement (ta'lif tarkibi), not the creation of substances. So they were alerted through the word al-Bari' (the Originator) to the Fashioner, meaning that the one who brought you into being is the one deserving of worship, not the one who made something, himself a made thing like it. For this reason, and God knows best, the mention of al-Bari' is made here.

The majority of reciters pronounced the vowel of i'rab (grammatical case ending, i'rab being the system of case inflection in Arabic) clearly in bari'ikum. It is narrated from Abu 'Amr that he used ikhtilas (ikhtilas, a rapid, reduced articulation of a short vowel), which Sibawayh narrated from him, and it is also narrated from him that he used sukun (pausal silence of the vowel). This is treating the separated word of two words in the manner of the joined word of one word, for it is permissible to make sukun in a form like ibil (camels). Thus the two kasras in bari'ikum were treated in the manner of ibil. Al-Mubarrad prohibited sukun in the vowel of i'rab and claimed that the reading of Abu 'Amr is a solecism (lahn). What he held is not valid, for Abu 'Amr only recited on the basis of a transmission (athar) from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The Arabic language also agrees with him in this, so al-Mubarrad's rejection of it is itself objectionable. A poet said:

"Today I drink without incurring a sin from God, nor as an uninvited guest."

Another said:

"You came with your two legs in what state they were, and your private parts were exposed from the loincloth."

Another said:

"Or the stream of Tayra, so the Arabs do not recognise you."

The exegetes have confused matters here in refuting Abu al-'Abbas, for they cited what indicates sukun from cases where the vowel is not an i'rab vowel. Al-Farisi said: As for the vowel of construction (harakat al-bina'), the grammarians have not differed over the permissibility of making it sukun. Among what indicates the soundness of Abu 'Amr's reading is what Abu Zayd related from the saying of the Exalted: "And Our messengers are with them, recording" (43:80). Also the reading of Maslama ibn Muharib: "And their husbands have more right to take them back in that [period]" (2:228). Abu 'Amr mentioned that the dialect of Tamim is the sukun of the nominative in forms like ya'lamuhu and similar. Like the sukun of bari'ikum is the reading of Hamza: "and the evil plotting" (35:43).

Al-Zuhri read (bariyyikum), with a kasra on the ya' without hamza, and this reading is narrated from Nafi'. This reading has two explanations. The first: the original is the hamza, and it is from bara'a, and the hamza was lightened by full substitution (al-ibdal al-mahd) without analogy, since the analogical lightening of this would be to make it between-between (bayn bayn). The second: the original is bariyyukum, with ya' and without hamza, and it is derived from the saying "I sharpened the pen" (bara'tu al-qalam) when you improved it, or from al-bariy, meaning dust. Then the letter of weakness (harf al-'illa) was given a vowel, although its analogical treatment in such a case, in the nominative and genitive, would be to assume a vowel. A poet said:

"And one day we met in desire, not passing."

Another said:

"And the spears' tips were not dyed with blood."

Another said:

"Corrupt in the soil like Abu al-Azid."

All of this is an explanation of an anomaly (shudhudh). Al-Zamakhshari has mentioned, regarding the specific mention of al-Bari' here, a good statement, and this is its text: "If you say: from where is this place singled out for the mention of al-Bari'? I say: al-Bari' is the one who created creatures free (bari'an) of disparity, ﴿You see in the creation of the Most Merciful no inconsistency﴾ (67:3), and distinct, one from another, by their differing shapes and varied forms. So there is in it a rebuke for what they did in abandoning the worship of the All-Knowing, the Wise, who originated them by His subtle wisdom in differing forms, free of disparity and discord, in favour of worshipping the cow, which is a proverb for stupidity and dullness. The Arabs have a saying: 'more stupid than a bull.' They thus exposed themselves to the wrath of God and the descent of His command, that He should unravel what He had composed of their creation and scatter what He had arranged of their forms and shapes, since they did not thank Him for that blessing and envied it by worshipping one who has no power over any of it." End of his statement.

﴿Then kill yourselves.﴾ The apparent meaning of this is the well-known killing that takes away the soul. Its outward sense is that they themselves carry out the killing of their own selves. The command to kill from Moses, upon our Prophet and upon him be peace, could only have been by revelation from God Most High, either because the Torah in his law already established the killing of a soul, or because he commanded this by a new command as a punishment for those who worshipped the calf. The one commanded to kill themselves are the worshippers of the calf, or both those who worshipped and those who did not. The meaning is: kill those among your own people who worshipped the calf, like His saying: "There has certainly come to you a messenger from among yourselves" (9:128), meaning from among your own families and kin. Or all were commanded to kill themselves. There are three opinions. Ibn Ishaq said: they were commanded to surrender to being killed, and the surrender to killing was called killing by way of metaphor (majaz). It was also said: the meaning of "kill yourselves" is: subdue your desires. We have already mentioned that killing (taqtil) can mean subduing (tadhlil), and from this also is the saying of Hassan:

"The one you offered me, which I returned, was killed. You were killed, so bring her; she did not kill."

Thus there emerge three opinions regarding His saying "kill": the first is the command to kill themselves; the second is surrender to being killed; the third is subduing the desires. The first is the apparent meaning, and it is what most people have transmitted. The apparent sense of the speech is that they are the ones commanded to kill themselves. It was said: the killing occurred in this way, they killed themselves with their own hands. It was also said: some of them killed others without any killer or killed being specified. It was said: the killers were those who withdrew with Aaron, and the killed were the worshippers of the calf. It was said: the killers were those who were with Moses at the secret conversation at Mount Sinai, and the killed were the rest.

If we say that some of them killed others, they differed over the manner of the killing. It was said: they lined up in two rows and struck each other with swords and daggers, until some killed others, until it was said to them: "Stop!" That was a martyrdom for the slain and a repentance for the slayer. It was said: God sent upon them a darkness, and they did this. It was said: the worshippers of the calf stood in a row, and those who had not worshipped it came upon them with weapons and killed them. It was said: the worshippers of the calf sat with their knees hugged in the courtyards of their houses, or in some other place, and Yusha' ibn Nun came out to them while they were sitting thus and said: "Cursed is whoever unclasps his hold, or lifts his gaze toward his killer, or shields himself with a hand or a foot." They would say: "Amen." None of them unclasped his hold until seventy thousand of them were killed. In another narration, he said to them: "Whoever unclasps his hold, his repentance will not be accepted," and he did not mention the curse. It was also said: a man would see his son, his father, his neighbour, and his relative, and they could not proceed in obedience to God's command, so God sent a haze and a black cloud under which they could not see one another, and they were commanded to sit with their knees hugged at the courtyards of their houses, and those who had not worshipped the calf took up their swords, and it was said to them: "Be patient." So God cursed whoever lifted his gaze, or unclasped his hold, or shielded himself with a hand or a foot, and they would say: "Amen." They kept killing them until evening, until Moses and Aaron prayed and said: "O Lord, the Children of Israel are being destroyed, the remnant, the remnant!" The cloud was lifted and repentance descended, the blades fell from their hands, and the slain were seventy thousand. End of what we have transmitted from some of what the exegetes have reported regarding the manner of the killing and regarding the slayers and the slain. In that there is enough admonition and lesson to necessitate hastening to refrain from opposing the Mighty King.

And consider God's gentleness toward this Muhammadan community, in that He made its repentance consist in giving up sin, regretting it, and resolving not to return to it.

As for the fa' in His saying "Then kill yourselves": if we say that repentance is itself the killing, and that God made their repentance the killing of themselves, then this clause is a substitute (badal) for His saying "so repent," and the fa' is, as in "so repent," a fa' of causation. If we say that the killing is the completion of their repentance, then the fa' is for sequence (li al-ta'qib), and the meaning is: "so follow the repentance with the killing as a completion of your repentance." In al-Muntakhab, it was denied that killing could be repentance, and killing was made a condition of repentance, so it was applied to it figuratively, as one says to the usurper who intends to repent: "Your repentance is the return of what you usurped," meaning that your repentance is not complete except by it. So it is here too. Transitivity of repentance with "to" (ila) means ending with it to God, so that it is free of showing off (riya') in the repentance, because if they showed off with it, it would not be to God. It should not be heeded that what occurred in al-Muntakhab, that the exegetes unanimously agreed they did not kill themselves with their own hands, since we have transmitted that some of them said so, and so it is not a consensus. As for 'Abd al-Jabbar's prohibition of that on rational grounds, that killing is the dissolution of the structure which he holds, which must cause it to cease being alive, and anything other than that is called killing only figuratively, he said: "This is not something God may command, because legal acts of worship are good only because they are benefits for that responsible person, and there is no benefit except in future matters. After killing there is no state of obligation so that killing could be a benefit for him. This differs from what God does by causing death, because that is an act of God Most High, so it is good that He does it when it is a benefit for another responsible person. It also differs from God commanding someone to wound himself or cut off a limb of his, without death occurring immediately after, because since he remained alive after that act, it is not impossible that that act could be a benefit for future acts." End of his statement. It is grounded in their Mu'tazilite principle of observing benefit (maslaha). The discussion with them on this is mentioned in the principles of religion (usul al-din). Yet it can be said here, in terms of benefit, that the command to kill is only a matter of deterrents and restraints, and it is not a condition of that to consider the state of the responsible person. Rather, one establishes deterrents so that others may be restrained, and when such a great act as killing is carried out against those who worshipped the calf, others take warning from it and refrain from falling into what cannot be repented of except by killing.

Qatadah recited, as al-Mahdawi, Ibn 'Atiyyah, al-Tabrizi and others reported: (فَأقِيلُوا أنْفُسَكم) ("then ask your selves for reprieve"). al-Tha'labi said: Qatadah recited (فاقْتالُوا أنْفُسَكم) ("then kill your selves"). As for (فَأقِيلُوا), it is an imperative from *al-iqalah* (cancellation or reprieve). The meaning seems to be that your souls have plunged into the punishment of God through this grave act you committed, the worship of the calf, and they have perished. So ask them back to life through repentance and commitment to obedience, and remove the traces of those sins by displaying acts of obedience. As for (فاقْتالُوا أنْفُسَكم), they said: it is *ifta'ala* used in the sense of *istaf'ala*, meaning (فاسْتَقِيلُوها), "then seek their reprieve." The well-known form is *istaqala*, not *iqtala*. Ibn Jinni said: it is weak for its middle radical to be a *waw*, as in *iqtadu*, but it may be a *ya'*, as in *aqyas*. Morphology makes it weak that it derives from *al-istiqalah*, as Ibn Jinni said. Yet this word is undoubtedly attested, as shown by Qatadah's transmission of it, and it would be one of the cases where *ifta'ala* carries the meaning of *istaf'ala*. This is one of the meanings for which *ifta'ala* is used, like *i'tasama* and *ista'sama* (both meaning "to hold fast" or "to seek protection").

al-Sulami said: (فَتُوبُوا إلى بارِئِكم) means return to Him with your secrets and your hearts. (فاقْتُلُوا أنْفُسَكم) means slay your selves by disavowing them, for they are not fit for the carpet of intimacy.

al-Wasiti said: The repentance of the Children of Israel was the killing of their selves, and for this community it is harder, namely the annihilation of their selves from their desires while the outward forms of the bodies remain.

Fares said: Repentance is the effacement of human nature through the contrasts of divinity.

It was also said: Repent to Him from your actions, your words, and your acts of obedience, and slay your selves in His obedience. Slaying the self from what is other than God and from God consists of being free from seeking recompense, until it returns to the origin of non-existence, and the Truth remains as it always was.

Some people of subtle insight said: The repentance by slaying the self is not abrogated (*naskh*, abrogation by a later ruling), because the Children of Israel slew their selves openly, whereas this community slays its selves within themselves. The first step toward God is to come out of the self. People imagined that the repentance of the Children of Israel was harder, but it is not as they imagined. That was enduring the killing once, whereas for the people of special spiritual rank (*ahl al-khusus*) there is killing at every moment. The poet said:

*He who dies and finds rest is not truly dead;*
*the true dead are the dead among the living.*

(ذَلِكم) is a reference to the verbal noun implied by His words (فاقْتُلُوا), since it is the nearest thing mentioned, meaning the killing: (خَيْرٌ لَكم) "is better for you." Some said it refers to the two verbal nouns implied by His words (فَتُوبُوا واقْتُلُوا), so the singular has been used in place of the dual, meaning repentance and killing are better for you. This is like their statement regarding God's words: ﴿عَوانٌ بَيْنَ ذَلِكَ﴾ ("neither old nor young, but between that" [2:68]), meaning between those two, that is, between the aged and the virgin. Likewise is the poet's line:

*Indeed for good and for evil there is a limit,*
*and both of those have a direction and a source.*

Meaning: both of those two. This depends on what we stated earlier, namely whether His words (فاقْتُلُوا) are an explanation of the repentance, in which case repentance is the killing. Then (ذَلِكم) should be singular, referring to a singular, namely killing. Or killing is distinct from repentance, and what this speaker said is possible. But the more probable reading is that (خَيْرٌ) is comparative. It was said: the meaning is better than disobedience and persistence in sin. It was also said: better than the fruit of disobedience, which is the destruction that awaits them, since a limited destruction is better than unlimited destruction, because death is inevitable, so there is only advancement and delay. Both of these interpretations do not treat the comparative in its literal sense, since disobedience and unlimited destruction have no good in them, so it cannot be said that the other is more good than them. Rather it is like the saying: honey is sweeter than vinegar. It is also possible that it is not comparative at all, but rather means a good thing among goods.

(لَكم) is connected to (خَيْرٌ) if it is comparative. If it means a good among goods, it is connected to an omitted element, meaning "a good that is for you." The two analyses also apply to the accusative of (عِنْدَ بارِئِكُمْ) ("with your Creator"). The use of *'indiyyah* ("with") here is figurative, since it is a noun of place, and it has been used figuratively to mean the attainment of their reward from God. He repeated (البارِئَ) explicitly for emphasis, and because it is an independent sentence, so explicit mention is appropriate, and to draw attention to the fact that this act is preferable in the sight of the One who brought you into being. Just as He saw that your creation was preferable, He saw that your annihilation by this way of killing is preferable, so submission to Him is required in every state, and what comes from Him must be received with acceptance and compliance.

﴿فَتابَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ ("then He accepted your repentance"): its apparent meaning is that it is a report from God that He accepted their repentance. There must be an omitted element to which this sentence is joined, meaning: you complied with that, so He accepted your repentance. These two sentences fall under the scope of the temporal clause (إذْ, "when"), in His words ﴿وإذْ قالَ مُوسى لِقَوْمِهِ﴾ ("And when Moses said to his people"). al-Zamakhshari allowed that it falls under Moses' statement, on the assumption of an omitted conditional, as if he said: "If you do it, then He has accepted your repentance." In that case the *fa'* would be linking the response clause to the omitted conditional clause together with its particle. What al-Zamakhshari went to is not permissible, because the response may often be omitted when there is evidence for it. As for the verb of the condition alone without its particle, it may be omitted in eloquent speech when it is negated with *la*, as in the poet's line:

*So divorce her, for you are not her equal,*
*and if the sword does not reach your forehead.*

The estimate is: "and if you do not divorce her, it will reach." If it is not negated with *la*, its omission is not permissible except in poetic necessity, as in the poet's line:

*The thunderclouds of summer watered it, and if*
*from autumn, it will not be lacking.*

The estimate is: "and if they watered it in autumn, it will not lack." This is one of the two analyses of the line. Similarly, omitting both the verb of the condition and the verb of the response is permissible only in poetic necessity, as in the line:

*The daughters of my uncle said, "O Salma, even if"*
*he is incapable and poor, she said, "even if."*

The estimate is: "even if he is incapable and poor, I will marry him." As for omitting both the verb and particle of the condition while keeping the response, it is not permissible, since this is not attested in Arabic speech. As for the jussive after the imperative and prohibition and their like, it has another place in the science of grammar, where its basis and the rationale for the rulings we have mentioned are explained.

The apparent meaning of ﴿فَتابَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾, as we have said, is a report about those who were commanded to kill and who complied. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: its meaning is about those who remained, and God made the killing a martyrdom for those who were slain, and He accepted the repentance of those who remained and pardoned them. End of his words.

﴿إنَّهُ هو التَّوّابُ الرَّحِيمُ﴾ ("Indeed He is the Accepting of repentance, the Most Merciful"): the discussion of this sentence has already preceded at His words in the story of Adam: ﴿فَتابَ عَلَيْهِ إنَّهُ هو التَّوّابُ الرَّحِيمُ﴾ ("Then He accepted his repentance; indeed He is the Accepting of repentance, the Most Merciful" [2:37]), so that suffices and it need not be repeated here.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 55–57 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And when you said, "O Moses..."﴾: This is the dialogue of the Children of Israel with Moses, after his dialogue with them in the verse before this. The pronoun in (qultum, "you said") is said to refer to the seventy chosen men (al-sab'in al-mukhtarin), as related by Ibn Mas'ud and Qatadah, and the manner of the choosing of the seventy will come, God willing, in its place in al-A'raf. It is also said that the pronoun refers to the rest of the Children of Israel except those whom God protected, as related by Ibn Zayd. It is also said that it refers to those who stood apart with Harun and did not worship the calf. One of those who compiled tafsir said: The sayings of the leading exegetes agree that those who were struck by the thunderbolt (al-sa'iqah) were the seventy men whom Moses chose and took with him to the appointed time (miqat) of his Lord and his intimate conversation (munajah). What has been mentioned cannot be reconciled with the mention in His words, ﴿And when you said﴾, because the apparent meaning is that those who said it are the ones seized by the thunderbolt, unless this is a shift in address (talwin al-khitab), and that is far-fetched here. In the Children of Israel calling their prophet by his name there is an impropriety on their part toward him, since they did not say, "O Prophet of God," or "O Messenger of God," or "O Interlocutor of God," or any other of the expressions that convey honour. This was their habit with him: ﴿O Moses, we will not be patient with one kind of food﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61], ﴿O Moses, make for us a god﴾ [al-A'raf: 138], ﴿O Moses, call upon your Lord for us﴾ [al-A'raf: 134]. And God has said to this community: ﴿Do not make the calling of the Messenger among you like the calling of some of you to others﴾ [al-Nur: 63].

﴿We will not believe you﴾: It is said that its meaning is: we will not affirm you concerning what you brought of the Torah. They did not intend the negation of faith in him, as evidenced by their saying (laka, "to you") and not saying (bika, "in you"), as in: ﴿And you will not be a believer to us﴾ [Yusuf: 17], meaning, one who affirms. It is also said that its meaning is: we will not acknowledge you, so he expressed acknowledgment by faith and transitivized it with the lam, and it has come in: ﴿You shall certainly believe in him and certainly support him. He said: Do you acknowledge, and take upon that My covenant? They said: We acknowledge﴾ [Al 'Imran: 81]; so the meaning would be: we will not acknowledge to you that the Torah is from God. It is also said: the lam may be for causation, i.e., we will not believe because of your saying about the Torah. It is also said: it is possible that what is intended is the negation of perfection, i.e., our faith in you is not complete, as was said regarding his saying, ﷺ: "A servant does not believe until I am more beloved to him than his self, his family, and all people" (ﷺ).

﴿until we see God manifestly﴾: (Hatta, "until") here is a particle of limit (harf ghayah). They informed of the negation of their faith extended up to this limit, and its implication is that if they saw God manifestly, they would believe. The seeing here is ocular seeing (al-ru'yah al-basariyyah), which has no veil or screen between. The accusative of (jahratan, "manifestly") is as an emphatic infinitive (masdar mu'akkad) removing the possibility that the seeing be a dream or knowledge by the heart. The meaning is: until we see God with our own eyes (ʿiyanan). It is a verbal noun from your saying: he "jahara" with the recitation and with the supplication, i.e., he made it public. So by it is meant a kind of seeing, and its accusative is like their saying: he sat "al-qurfusa'" (in a squatting manner). On the question of the accusative of this type there is a disagreement mentioned in grammar. The more correct view is that it is governed by the preceding verb, which extends to the type, as it extends to the verbal noun cognate with the verb (al-masdar al-mulaqa ma'a al-fi'l) in derivation. It is also said that its accusative is as a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial (hal) by way of an omitted supposition, i.e., "possessors of manifestness," or in the sense of "openly declaring the seeing," not in the manner of hyperbole as in: "a man ṣawm" (a man who fasts constantly), because hyperbole is not intended here. So according to the first view, the manifestness is an attribute of the seeing, and according to this view, it is an attribute of the seers. There is a third view, which is that it refers back to the meaning of the saying or the sayers, so the meaning is: "when you said such-and-such a saying manifestly," or "declaring that saying openly," not concealing it or whispering about it among themselves, but stating it plainly and declaring openly that they were reporting the negation of faith limited by seeing. The view that manifestness refers back to the meaning of the saying is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Abu 'Ubaydah, but the apparent connection is with the seeing, not with the saying, and this is what the eloquent construction requires.

Ibn 'Abbas, Sahl ibn Shu'ayb and Humayd ibn Qays read (jahratan) with a fatha on the ha'. This reading admits two possibilities. One is that (jahratan) is a verbal noun like al-ghalabah, so its meaning and the meaning of (jahratan) with a sukun on the ha' are the same, and the grammatical possibilities mentioned for (jahratan) apply to it. The second is that it is the plural of (jahir), as you say: fasiq and fasaqah, so its accusative is as a circumstantial, i.e., "declaring the seeing openly." Al-Zamakhshari said: In this statement there is evidence that Moses, upon him be peace, rejected them, and made known to them that the seeing of what is not permissible for Him to be in a direction is impossible, and that whoever permits the seeing of God has made Him among the categories of the bodies or the accidents. So they rejected him after the proof was explained and the evidence made clear, and they persisted in obstinacy, and they were in disbelief like the worshippers of the calf, so God sent upon them the thunderbolt, as He sent the killing upon those, equating between the two disbeliefs and indicating their greatness by the greatness of the trial. End of his words. This expressly states the impossibility of seeing God with the eyes. This question is one on which Muslims differ.

The Qadariyyah, the Mu'tazilah, the Najjariyyah, the Jahmiyyah and those who share with them among the Kharijites went to the impossibility of this with respect to the Creator, glorified and exalted is He. Most Muslims went to affirming the seeing. The Karramiyyah said: He is seen in the direction above, and He has a below, and He is seen as a body. The Mushabbihah said: He is seen in a form. The People of the Sunnah said: not facing, nor opposite, nor settled, nor in a place, nor coloured, nor in a form or shape, nor in aggregation or corporeality; rather, the believers will see Him, knowing that He is unlike created things, as they knew Him to be so before. The sound, established hadiths concerning the seeing of God are abundant, so it is obligatory to adhere to them. This question is among the most difficult questions of the principles of religion (usul al-din). I have seen a large volume on it by Abu Ja'far al-Tusi, one of the eminent scholars of the Imamiyyah. There is nothing in the verse that indicates what al-Zamakhshari went to regarding the impossibility of seeing, but his habit is to load words with what they do not indicate, especially what leads to his Mu'tazilite doctrine. We seek God's refuge from partisanship in what is not fitting. Likewise they differed regarding the seeing of the Truth Himself: most of the Mu'tazilah went to the view that He does not see Himself; a group of them went to the view that He sees Himself; al-Ka'bi went to the view that He sees neither Himself nor others, and this is the doctrine of al-Najjar. All of this is mentioned in the science of the principles of religion.

﴿Then the thunderbolt seized you﴾: that is, it overcame you and encompassed you. The original meaning of akhdh (seizing) is grasping with the hand. The sa'iqah (thunderbolt) here: is it a fire from the sky that burned them, or death, or a heavenly host whose sound they heard and so died, or terror which persisted until they died, or they fainted, or the punishment from which they die, or a heavenly cry? These are sayings; the most correct of them is that it is the cause of death, not death itself, even if they differed about the cause, as the verifying scholars (al-muhaqqiqun) said, in view of His words: ﴿So when the quake seized them﴾ [al-A'raf: 155]. The exegetes agreed that the duration from the death or the swooning was a day and a night. It is said: what befell them also befell Moses; and it is said he fainted and did not die. They said: this is the sound view, because it came: "when he recovered" concerning Moses, and it came: "then We raised you" concerning them, and most of the use of ba'th (raising) in the Qur'an is the raising of the dead. It is said: they fainted as he did, and did not die; and the verb sa'q is applied to other than death. Jarir said:

Was al-Farazdaq anything but an ape struck by thunderbolts so that he turned round?

(p-212) The apparent cause of the thunderbolt seizing them is their saying: ﴿We will not believe you until we see God manifestly﴾, since they did not say that and ask for the seeing except by way of obstinacy. It is also said that the cause of the thunderbolt seizing them was other than this saying: their disbelief in Moses, or their denial of him when he brought them the Torah, or the worship of the calf. 'Amr read (al-sa'qah, "the thunderclap") with the definite article, and he regarded the request for seeing as grave wherever it occurs, because His seeing is not attained except in the Hereafter, so seeking it in this world is reprehensible; or because God's ruling is to remove obligation from the servant at the moment he sees Him, so seeking it is seeking the removal of obligation; or because when the proofs have indicated the truthfulness of the claimant, seeking additional proofs is obstinacy; and because withholding the seeing in this world contains a kind of important benefit for creation, therefore it was deemed reprehensible.

﴿And you were looking on﴾: a circumstantial clause (jumlah hāliyyah). The object of the looking is the seizing by the thunderbolt, i.e., while you were looking at what had befallen you from it, or some of you looking at others, how they fell dead; or at the living; or you knew that it was seizing you. So he expressed by looking the knowing; or at the traces of the thunderbolt on your bodies after you were raised; or each one of you looking at the revival of himself, as happened in the story of 'Uzayr, they said: he came to life member by member; or at the first signs of what used to descend of the thunderbolt before death; or "you" in which some of you face others, from the Arab saying: the houses of the family of so-and-so "face each other" (tatarra'a), i.e., some of them face others. And if someone went to the meaning "and you were looking on" as the answer to their request for the occurrence of the seeing for them, it would be a possibility from their saying: "I looked at the man," meaning "I waited for him," as the poet said:

So if you two would wait for me a while of time, it would benefit me with Umm Jundab.

But this possibility is not transmitted, so I do not venture to say it, even though the wording admits it. The author of al-Muntakhab counted this as a sixth favour, and in explaining why it is a favour he mentioned aspects, some of which relate to others than the Children of Israel and some to them. The point intended is mention of what relates to this being a favour, namely that their revival was so that they would repent of obstinacy, and so that they would escape painful punishment and win abundant reward, which are among the greatest blessings. This verse does not indicate whether their saying was after the worshippers of the calf were commanded to be killed or before it. Both views have been said, because these clauses are joined with "and," and "and" by its form does not indicate temporal sequence.

Some said: When God placed them in the station of His intimate conversation and made them hear the sweetness of His address, their souls were raised up toward pride and elevation of rank, so God dealt with them in the opposite of what had arisen in their souls, by the thunderbolt, which is humility and abasement, as discipline for them and a lesson for others: ﴿Indeed in that is a lesson for those of insight﴾ [Al 'Imran: 13].

﴿Then We raised you from after your death﴾: It is joined to His words: ﴿Then the thunderbolt seized you﴾. The joining with "then" (thumma) indicates that between the seizing by the thunderbolt and the raising there is a time in which delay and postponement are conceivable, which is the time of what resulted from the thunderbolt of death or swooning, according to the disagreement that has passed. The raising here is revival. It is mentioned that when they died, Moses continued to plead with his Lord for their revival, saying: "O Lord, the Children of Israel say: You killed our best." Until God revived them all, man after man, while some looked at others to see how they came to life. It is also said: the meaning of raising is sending, i.e., We sent you. It was narrated that when God revived them they asked that He raise them as prophets, and He raised them as prophets. It is also said: the meaning of raising is recovering from the swoon, and this follows the view of those who said they were struck senseless and did not die. It is also said: the raising here is rising quickly from their places of fall, and from it: ﴿They said: Woe to us, who has raised us from our sleeping place?﴾ [Ya Sin: 52]. It is also said the meaning of raising here is teaching, i.e., then We taught you after your ignorance. The death here, its apparent meaning is the separation of the soul from the body, and this is the real meaning, and their revival was for the sake of completing their lifespans. Whoever says that it was a swoon and stupor makes death figurative, as God says: ﴿And death comes to him from every place, but he is not dead﴾ [Ibrahim: 17], and what came to him were its preliminaries, which were called death by way of metaphor. The poet said:

**Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 2, verses 55–57 (part 2 of 3)**

؎Say to them: "Hasten to make your excuse, and seek a word that will clear you, for I am Death."

He made himself Death because he was the cause of death. Likewise, when death is taken to mean ignorance, it is a metaphor (majaz). He has used life as a metaphor for knowledge and death as a metaphor for ignorance. The Exalted said: ﴿Is one who was dead and We brought him to life?﴾ [al-An'am: 122]. And al-Shafi'i said:

؎Indeed the soul is like a glass lamp-cover, and knowledge is the lamp, and God's wisdom is the oil.
؎So when you see clearly, you are alive, and when you are in darkness, you are dead.

Ibn al-Sayyid said:

؎The man of knowledge is alive and eternal after his death, though his bones lie beneath the dust, decayed.
؎The man of ignorance is dead while he walks upon the earth, thought to be among the living, yet he is nothing.

Moses, upon our Prophet and upon him be peace, is not included in the address ﴿then We raised you up﴾, because it is a direct address to those who said: ﴿We will not believe you until we see God openly﴾ [al-Baqarah: 55], and because of His saying: ﴿when he regained consciousness﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]. This expression is not used for death. Ibn Qutaybah erred in his claim that Moses had died.

﴿so that you may give thanks﴾: There are several views regarding the object of the thanks, and most of them depend on what is meant by the raising up and by death. Whoever holds that these are literal says: the meaning is "so that you may give thanks for His favour of bringing you to life after death," or "for this favour and all the other favours He bestowed upon them." Whoever takes this as a metaphor for sending them prophets, or for reviving them from unconsciousness (al-ghashy), or for teaching them after ignorance, makes the object of the thanks one of these metaphorical meanings. Whoever makes the object of thanks the sending down of the Torah, in which is mention of His forgiveness of them and the details of His laws, when no laws had existed before, is far from the truth. It has also been said: the meaning is "so that you may give thanks for God's favour after you had disbelieved in it, when you saw the might of God in His striking you with the thunderbolt and His making you taste death." Al-Razi (in al-Muntakhab) said: He only raised them after death in this world so that they might be obligated, and so that they might be able to attain faith and to make amends for the sins they had committed. As for His having obligated them, it is from His saying: ﴿so that you may give thanks﴾. The word "thanks" encompasses all acts of obedience, due to His saying: ﴿Work, O family of Dawud, in thankfulness﴾ [Saba': 13]. End of his words.

Al-Mawardi said: Scholars differed about whether the obligation (taklif) remains on one who is restored after death and after witnessing the terrors which compel him and force him to acknowledge what he has done. Some said: the obligation fell from them, so that their obligation would be based on reasoning rather than compulsion. Others said: their obligation remains, so that no adult sane person is left without worship, and the ruling of obligation is not prevented, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿And when We lifted the mountain above them as though it were a canopy﴾ [al-A'raf: 171]. That was when they refused to accept the Torah; when He lifted the mountain above them, they believed and accepted it. Their faith in it was therefore a faith of compulsion, and the obligation did not fall from them. The people of Yunus were similar in their faith. End of his words.

﴿And We shaded you with the clouds﴾. (al-ghamam): it is an object with the preposition dropped, i.e., "with the clouds," as you would say: "I shaded so-and-so with the cloth." Or it is a direct object, not with the preposition dropped, and the meaning would be "We made them shade over you." In accordance with this second view, the form fa''ala (here, ẓallala) is used in the sense of making something into what is derived from it, as in the saying "I made Zayd just (ʿadala Zaydan)," meaning "I made him just." Likewise here, the meaning is: We made the clouds a shade over you. In accordance with the first view, fa''ala is used in the sense of af'ala, so the doubling originally serves to make the verb transitive. Then it was given the meaning of a verb that takes ʿalā, so the original would have been: "and We shaded you (ẓallalnākum)," i.e., "We gave you shade with the clouds," like what is reported in the hadith: "Seven will be shaded by God in His shade." Then ẓallala was given the meaning of kallala (to surround) or something similar that can take ʿalā, and so it took ʿalā. The meanings of fa''ala have been mentioned before. The meaning is not what the apparent wording requires, since its apparent sense implies that the clouds were shaded, so that something would have been placed above the clouds to shade them, which is not the case. Rather, the meaning, and God knows best, is what the exegetes have mentioned. The meaning of "clouds" has been discussed before. It has been said that it is the cloud in which the angels came on the day of Badr, and the one in which the angels of the Merciful will come, which is referred to in His saying: ﴿in canopies of clouds, with the angels﴾ [al-Baqarah: 210]. It is not literally a cloud; it was called a cloud only because it resembles one. It has also been said: those who were shaded by the cloud were some of the Children of Israel. God had established the custom among the Children of Israel that whoever worshipped God for thirty years without committing a sin in that time would be shaded by a cloud.

It is related that a man worshipped for thirty years and was not shaded by a cloud. He came to the people of the clouds and told them of this, and they said: "Perhaps you have committed a sin." He said: "I know of nothing, except that I once raised my gaze to the sky and lowered it again without thinking." They said to him: "That is your sin." There was among them a group called the People of the Clouds, and God bestowed favour upon them by their being among those who have this manifest and striking honour. The place where the cloud shaded them was in the wilderness (al-tih) between Syria and Egypt, when they complained of the heat of the sun, and the account of this will come in their story. It has also been said: it was a white, dusty land with no water and no shade. They came to it when they came out of the sea, and God shaded them with the cloud and protected them from the heat of the sun.

﴿And We sent down upon you the manna and the quails﴾. Al-manna is a collective noun with no singular from its own root. Concerning the manna which God sent down to the Children of Israel, there are several views: it is what falls upon the trees, sweeter than honey and whiter than snow; this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Shaʿbi. Or it is a good, sweet resin; this is the view of Mujahid. Or it is a drink that would descend upon them, which they would drink after mixing it with water; this is the view of al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas and Abu al-ʿAliyah. Or it is honey that would descend upon them; this is the view of Ibn Zayd. Or it is thin bread made of millet or of clarified butter; this is the view of Wahb. Or it is ginger; this is the view of al-Suddi. Or it is turanjabin (a sweet, cleansing confection); this is the view of most exegetes. Or it is sour honey; this was said by ʿAmr ibn ʿIsa. Or it is everything God bestowed upon them in the wilderness that came to them effortlessly without toil; this was said by al-Zajjaj, and its evidence is his (ﷺ) saying: "The mushroom is of the manna which God bestowed upon the Children of Israel." In another narration: "upon Musa."

Concerning the quails (al-salwa) which God sent down upon the Children of Israel, there are several views: a bird resembling the quail (al-sumana), or the quail itself; or red birds which God sent by means of a cloud, which rained down in an area a mile wide and a spear's length high in the sky, one upon another; this was said by Abu al-ʿAliyah and Muqatil. Or a bird found in India, larger than a sparrow; this was said by ʿIkrimah. Or a fat bird like a pigeon. Or honey in the dialect of Kinanah. The quails used to come to them from the sky, and they would choose the fat ones and leave the lean ones. It has also been said: the south wind would drive them to them, and they would take what they needed and the rest would go away. It has also been said: they would descend upon the trees, so that half of them would be cooked and half roasted. The manna used to descend upon them from dawn until sunrise, and the quails in the morning and evening. It has also been said: continually. It has also been said: whenever they wished.

The exegetes have related accounts concerning the shading and the descent of the manna and quails, and their reports agree that this took place in the open plain of the wilderness. Its story will come in Surah al-Ma'idah, God willing. They said: "Who will shield us from the movement of the sun?" and the clouds shaded them. They said: "Who will provide us with food?" and God sent down the manna and quails. They said: "Who will provide us with water?" and God commanded Musa to strike the rock. This is indicated by the Qur'an. It has been added to these accounts that they said: "With what shall we light our lamps?" and a pillar of light was set up for them in the middle of their encampment; it has also been said it was of fire. They said: "Who will provide us with clothing?" and they were granted that their garments would not wear out, nor decay, nor become soiled, and that their young would grow as children grow.

(kulū), "eat": it is an imperative of permission and license, like His saying: ﴿then hunt﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2], ﴿then disperse through the land﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 10]. This is according to the view of those who say that the default ruling for things is prohibition (al-hazr). Or it means "keep on eating," according to the view of those who say that the default ruling for things is permissibility (al-ibahah). Here there is an omitted saying, i.e., "and We said: Eat." The saying is often omitted while the content remains, and this is because the meaning is understood. From this is His saying: "Did you disbelieve?", i.e., "it will be said: Did you disbelieve?" Omitting the content while retaining the verb of saying is rare, and this too is because the meaning is understood. The poet said:

؎It is we of whom you said, so how were you filled with terror at our sight before you had concerned yourselves with fighting you?

The estimated meaning is: you said, "We will fight them."

﴿from the good things﴾: "min" here is partitive (lil-tab'id), because the manna and quails are part of the good things. Whoever claimed that it is superfluous is far from the truth, and this would only be correct according to the view of al-Akhfash. Even further from this is the view of one who claimed that it denotes the genus (lil-jins), because the one which denotes genus is disputed as to its establishment, and there must be something before it which could be taken as antecedent to a relative clause describing it. The view of one who claimed that it is for substitution (lil-badal) is also weak, since that meaning is disputed as to its establishment, and nothing here calls for or favours this. The good things (al-tayyibat) here (p-215) have been said to mean the lawful, and it has been said they mean the delicious and desirable. Whoever claimed that this is by omission of a noun, namely "eat from the substitute for the good things of what We have provided for you," his view is weak. He compensated them, in place of all their delicious foods, with the manna and quails, so these two became a substitute for the good things. Some scholars have inferred from His saying: ﴿Eat from the good things We have provided for you﴾ that merely placing food before a person by its owner is not sufficient for permission to eat it; rather, it is not permissible to dispose of it except with the owner's permission. This is one view. It has also been said: it becomes owned merely by placement; it has been said: by taking and receiving; and it has been said: it is never owned, but is benefited from while remaining in the owner's possession.

The "mā" in His saying "what We have provided for you" is a relative pronoun, and the returning pronoun is omitted, i.e., "what We have provided you with it." The conditions for omitting it are present. It is not far-fetched that someone might allow that it is a verbal noun (maṣdariyyah), in which case no pronoun needs to be estimated, and the verbal noun would be used in the sense of the object. But the first is more immediate to the mind.

﴿and they did not wrong Us﴾: this is a negation that they had not committed wrong against God the Exalted. In this is evidence that it is not a condition of negating a thing that its occurrence be possible, since a person's wronging God the Exalted is absolutely impossible. It has been said: the meaning is "they did not wrong Us by their saying: 'Show us God openly' [al-Nisa': 153]; rather they wronged themselves by what We met them with, the thunderbolt." It has been said: "they did not wrong Us by hoarding the manna and quails; rather they wronged themselves by the spoiling of their food and the curtailing of their provision." It has been said: "they did not wrong Us by their refusal to enter the city of the tyrants at Moses' command." It has been said: "they did not wrong Us by preferring punishment and cutting off the source of their provision from themselves; rather they wronged themselves thereby." It has been said: "they did not wrong Us by ingratitude for the favours; rather they wronged themselves by bringing down vengeance upon themselves." It has been said: "they did not wrong Us by worshipping the calf; rather they wronged themselves by killing one another."

Ibn ʿAtiyyah and al-Zamakhshari agreed that something omitted must be estimated before this sentence. Ibn ʿAtiyyah estimated it as: "so they disobeyed and did not respond to the favours with thanks." He said: "The meaning is: they did not place their action in a position of harm to Us, but they placed it in a position of harm to themselves, since it was not due." Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "so they wronged themselves by disbelieving these favours, and they did not wrong Us." He said: "The speech was abridged by omitting it, because of the indication of 'and they did not wrong Us' upon it." End of his words. It is not necessary to estimate an omitted element, as they claimed, since there were indeed committed from them the commission of abominable acts, such as taking the calf as a god, and asking to see God as a challenge, and other things not related here. So His saying "and they did not wrong Us" is a negated sentence indicating that what they committed of those abominations did not reach Us with any deficiency or harm; rather, the consequence of that returns to themselves and is specific to them, and nothing from it reaches Us.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 55–57 (part 3 of 3):

﴿But they were wronging themselves.﴾ Here *lakin* (but, a corrective particle) is used in the best possible position, because a negation comes before it and an affirmation follows it, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves﴾. The reverse also occurs, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Surely it is they who are the foolish, but they do not know﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:13]. That is, an affirmation comes first and is followed by a negation. This is because the corrective (*istidrak*) that *lakin* brings always relates in some way to what precedes it. Since it has been established that wrongdoing did occur from them, and since that wrongdoing has been negated from reaching God, the soul remains eager and attentive to hear who was harmed by it. So the correction is made: that wrongdoing which came from them was in fact inflicted upon themselves. The best placements of *lakin* are between two opposites (*mutadaddan*), next between two contradictories (*naqidan*), and next between two differing statements (*khilafan*). Scholars of grammar disagree about the last of these: is it a valid Arabic construction or not? An example is your saying: "Zayd is not standing, but he is laughing." This has been discussed in the science of grammar. They agreed that *lakin* does not occur between two identical items, as in: "Zayd did not go out, but 'Amr did not go out."

The correspondence of the statement (*tibaq al-kalam*) is that what follows *lakin* is affirmed in the manner of what was negated before it, as in His saying: ﴿And We did not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves﴾ [Hud 11:101]. Here *kanu* (they were) is inserted to indicate that this was among their characteristics and their way of life. Also, *lakin* in many contexts is used where the predicate does not separate from the subject, as in His saying: ﴿And God has always been Knowing of all things﴾. The meaning therefore is: "But they were continually wronging themselves by the abundance of transgressions that proceeded from them."

The form of *yazlimun* (they wrong) is that of the present tense, but in meaning it is past. This is one of the instances in which the present tense carries the meaning of the past [p. 216]. Ibn Malik did not mention this in *al-Tashil*, nor in any of his works that we have examined, though others did mention it. The object of the predicate, *anfusahum* (themselves), is placed first here, so that the endings of the verses (*ra'us al-ayat*) and the closing units (*fawasil*) correspond, and to show concern for reporting the one upon whom the action fell. Also, in terms of meaning, the verb governing the object has become an emphasis (*tawkid*) of what the preceding words already indicate. Therefore its mention is not necessary. Moreover, emphasis may come after the item it emphasizes. You can say: "I did not strike Zayd, but I struck 'Amr." Here the second mention of "I struck" serves as emphasis, because *lakin* is designed so that what follows it is contrary to what precedes it. For this reason you may also say: "I did not strike Zayd, but 'Amr," and you are not obliged to mention the governing verb. Since the meaning of His saying, ﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾, is equivalent to "but they wronged themselves," mentioning the governing verb for the object is not necessary. For if one said: "They did not wrong us, but themselves," it would be proper Arabic. The meaning is sufficiently indicated by the function of *lakin*, that what follows it is contrary to what precedes it. Since these embellishments combined to justify placing the object first, its placement here is the most eloquent.

These noble verses have included, among the accounts of the Children of Israel, several sections. Among them: the command of Moses, upon our Prophet and him be peace, to them to repent to God from committing this great sin, which is the worship of the calf apart from God, and that repentance is accepted for a sin as great as this. There is also the gentleness shown to them in addressing them with "O my people," and the alerting of them to the cause of the wrong, the consequence of which returned upon them. There is the announcement that their repentance would be by killing themselves. Then the report that God's forgiveness of them was realized, and that this was due to His preceding mercy. Then the rebuke to them for asking what they should not have asked, namely seeing God openly, since that was a request made out of obstinacy. Then the mention of what followed from this request: the thunderbolt seized them. Then the favor bestowed upon them by raising them up again, which is among the great miraculous events: a human being is brought back to life in this world after having died. Then the granting of what they asked, since they fell into the wilderness (*tih*) and needed something to remove the harm and need caused by the scorching of the sun and to nourish their bodies with what suits them. So He shaded them with the cloud. This is among the greatest things and the most magnificent miracles, in which the upper world is made subject to the lower world according to its request. It is said that it used to shade them by day and depart by night so that the moon would illuminate them. He sent down upon them the manna and the quails, and these are among the noblest foods, for they combined nourishment and medicine, with the sweetness that is in the manna and the richness that is in the quail, and both of them restrain heat and stimulate strength in the body. Then the command to them to partake of these things was not restricted by time or place; rather it was an absolute command. Then the explicit statement that these were among the good things, and truly so. Then the mention that this was a provision from Him for them, which they did not toil to obtain, extract, or increase, but came to them as a provision pleasant and free of labor. Then the joining of these sentences with the final sentence, since that sentence reinforces the opening of these preceding sentences: for He opened them by reporting that they wronged themselves, and He closed them with that, namely His saying: ﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾.

Thus these sentences came in the utmost eloquence in wording and the greatest rhetorical force in meaning, for they combined chosen words and abundant meanings, with the beginnings of their endings linked to the endings of their beginnings, together with a gentle manner of reporting about Himself. Where He mentioned the blessings, He explicitly attributed them to Himself, saying: ﴿Then We raised you up﴾, and: ﴿And We shaded you﴾, and: ﴿And We sent down﴾. Where He mentioned the punishments, He did not attribute them to Himself, saying: ﴿So the thunderbolt seized you﴾. The secret of this is that it is a place for enumerating blessings, so it was fitting to attribute them to Him so as to remind them of His bounties, whereas He did not attribute the punishments to Himself, even though they truly came from Him, because attributing them to Him would produce a great fear that might outweigh the joy of the blessings. The purpose is the expansion of their souls through remembering what God bestowed upon them, although the speech contains both warning and encouragement, with encouragement predominating.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 55–57 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And when you said, "O Moses..."﴾: This is the dialogue of the Children of Israel with Moses, after his dialogue with them in the verse before this. The pronoun in (qultum, "you said") is said to refer to the seventy chosen men (al-sab'in al-mukhtarin), as related by Ibn Mas'ud and Qatadah, and the manner of the choosing of the seventy will come, God willing, in its place in al-A'raf. It is also said that the pronoun refers to the rest of the Children of Israel except those whom God protected, as related by Ibn Zayd. It is also said that it refers to those who stood apart with Harun and did not worship the calf. One of those who compiled tafsir said: The sayings of the leading exegetes agree that those who were struck by the thunderbolt (al-sa'iqah) were the seventy men whom Moses chose and took with him to the appointed time (miqat) of his Lord and his intimate conversation (munajah). What has been mentioned cannot be reconciled with the mention in His words, ﴿And when you said﴾, because the apparent meaning is that those who said it are the ones seized by the thunderbolt, unless this is a shift in address (talwin al-khitab), and that is far-fetched here. In the Children of Israel calling their prophet by his name there is an impropriety on their part toward him, since they did not say, "O Prophet of God," or "O Messenger of God," or "O Interlocutor of God," or any other of the expressions that convey honour.
