The alif after it is the ya' which was a ya' after the plural alif, which was a lengthening in the singular, according to al-Khalil's opinion. We have explained this issue in depth in our book "Kitāb al-Takmīl li-Sharḥ al-Tashīl."

Al-iḥsān, al-in'ām and al-ifḍāl are synonyms. Aḥsana al-rajul means he did good; aḥsana al-shay' means he did it well; aḥsana ilā 'Amr means he conferred goodness upon him. Al-tabdīl means changing a thing for another. You say: "This is the replacement (badal) of this," that is, its substitute. It is transitive to two objects, the second of which originally has a preposition. "I exchanged a dinar for a dirham," meaning: I made the dinar a substitute for the dirham. It may also be transitive to three objects, so you say: "I exchanged Zayd a dinar for a dirham," meaning: I obtained for him a dinar in exchange for a dirham. The omission of the preposition is permitted when the meaning is understood. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿fa-ulā'ika yubaddilu Allāhu sayyi'ātihim﴾ [al-Furqan: 70], meaning: good deeds will be made for them in place of their bad deeds. Many people have erred and made what the preposition ba' entered upon the thing obtained, and the accusative object the thing removed, to the extent that they said: "If he substituted ḍād for ẓā', his prayer would not be valid." The correct statement is: "If ẓā' were substituted for ḍād."

Al-rijz means punishment; its rā' may be kasra or damma, and the damma is the dialect of the Banu al-Ṣa'adat, and both have been recited in some places. Ru'bah said:

*"How many a one of great number, who had defeated us,*
*until we were protected from his plot by the rijz."*

Al-rujz with a damma is the name of a well-known idol. Al-rajzā' is a she-camel whose hindquarters are afflicted with a disease, so that when she rises her thighs tremble. The poet said:

*"You resolved on good, then fell short of it,*
*as the rajzā' strains when its hobble is tied."*

It was said: al-rijz is derived from al-rijazah, which is wool with which litters are adorned, as if it marked them. The poet said:

*"And if they had overtaken them, they would have been dyed with their blood,*
*as the rajā'iz (wool) are dyed with the red of the lean she-camel."*

Al-istisqā' is seeking water, and seeking is one of the meanings previously mentioned for the form istaf'ala in His statement: ﴿iyyāka na'budu wa iyyāka nasta'īn﴾ [al-Fatiha: 5]. Al-'aṣā (staff) is feminine, and its alif is changed from a waw. They say: 'aṣawān (two staffs). 'Aṣawtuhu means I struck him with the staff. It is pluralized irregularly as a'ṣin, whose origin is a'ṣuw. It is pluralized regularly as 'iṣiyy on the pattern fi'il, whose origin is 'iṣiwwu, and the sād follows the vowel of the ayn. The poet said:

*"Unless there are camels, then goats,*
*whose horns are the 'iṣiyy (staves)."*

Al-ḥajar (stone) is this solid body well known among people. It is pluralized as aḥjār and ḥijār, and both are analogical plurals for it. They say ḥijārah with a tā' marker, and they derived from it: istaḥjara al-ṭīn (the mud hardened into stone). Derivation from concrete nouns is very rare.

Al-infijār (bursting forth) is the splitting of one thing from another, and from it comes infajara. Al-fujūr, which is the rushing into disobedience like water, is the reflexive (muṭāwi') of the verb fajara, so that: fajarahu fa-infajara (he burst it and it burst open). Reflexivity (al-muṭāwaʿah) is one of the meanings for which the form infa'ala came, and it has been previously mentioned.

Ithnatā (two, feminine) is the feminine of ithnān, and both have the case inflection of the dual. It is not truly a dual, because it is not singular: one does not say ithnun or ithnatun. Their final letter is deleted, and it is a ya', because it is from thannaytu al-'ashrah (I doubled the ten), with a sukūn on the shīn: this is the dialect of the Ḥijāz; with a kasra it is the dialect of Tamīm; a fatha on it is an irregular and unknown form. It is the first of the decades. They derived from it: 'asharahum yu'ashshiruhum (he made them ten, one of ten). From it come al-'ashr and al-'asharu, and al-'ashr is a soft tree, and al-a'shār are pieces without a singular, and a singular has been attached to them: they say birmatu a'shār (a pot of pieces).

Al-'ayn is a homonymous term shared between the source of water, the seeing organ, a cloud that approaches from the direction of the qiblah, rain that falls five or six days without ceasing, a person of honour among people, and a hole in a waterskin or gold or other things. Its plural is a'yun irregularly, or 'uyūn by analogy. They used a'yān for the nobles of people, and it came rarely for the seeing organ. The poet said:

*"Bleary-eyed (asmal) of eyes, and their inner corners."*

Unās is a collective noun with no singular from its own form. If a masculine is named by it, it takes tanwīn. The poet's statement:

*"And to the son of Umm Unās I transport my she-camel,"*

is without tanwīn, either because it is a proper name for a feminine referent, or as a poetic necessity according to the view of the Kufans.

Mashrab (drinking place) is a mafʿal from al-sharāb (drink), which may be a verbal noun, a time noun, or a place noun. It is regular from every unaugmented, inflected triliteral whose present-tense ayn is not kasra, whether its lam is sound, as in kasirta and dakhala, or defective, as in ramā and ghazā. Some words that the grammarians mention are irregular.

Al-'utuww and al-'athy mean the worst corruption. It is said: 'athā yaʿthū 'utuwwan, and 'athā yaʿthī 'athiyyan, and 'athā yaʿthī 'athyan is an irregular dialect. The poet said:

*"Were it not for shame, and that my head has been corrupted*
*by gray hair, I would visit Umm al-Qasim."*

The occurrence of al-'athy is evidence that 'athā does not have the origin 'athawa, like raḍiya whose origin is raḍawa, contrary to the one who claims so. 'Āthā ya'īthu 'aythan and ma'ātha, and 'aththā ya'itthu likewise. From it is 'uththat al-ṣūf, which is the moth that gnaws it.

Al-ṭaʿām (food) is a noun for what is eaten, like al-ʿaṭāʾ, a noun for what is given; and it is a generic noun.

* *

Al-wāḥid (one) is that which is not divisible and to which no second is added. It is said: waḥida yaḥidu waḥdan and waḥdatan, when he was alone. Al-duʿāʾ (supplication) is calling out the name of the one called upon in the manner of an address, and its verb is daʿā yadʿū duʿāʾan. Al-inbāt (causing to grow): the hamzah in it is for transitivity, and it is the bringing forth of what by nature grows. Al-baql (herbs) is a genus including fresh plants that people and animals eat. From it one says baqalat al-arḍ and abqalat, meaning the land became full of herbs. From the same root: al-bāqilāʾ (broad beans), as Ibn Durayd said. Al-qiththāʾ (cucumber) is a collective noun whose singular is qiththāʾah, with a damma or kasra on the qāf; it is this well-known thing. Al-Khalil said: it is the khiyār (cucumber variety), and one says arḍ maqthaʾah, meaning land abundant in cucumbers. Al-fūm: al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl and others said: it is garlic (thūm), the thā' being changed to fā', as they said maghthūr to maghfūr, jaddatha to jaddafa, and ʿāthūr to ʿāfūr. Al-Ṣalt said:

*"Their dwellings at that time were visible,*
*in them were the qarādīs, the fūm and the onions."*

Muʾarrij recited for Ḥassān:

*"And you are a people of base origins,*
*your food is the fūm and the ḥawqal."*

He means the fūm and the onion. This is just as they replaced the fā' with thā', saying al-athāthī for al-afāfī. Both substitutions are not analogical: I mean changing thā' into fā' and fā' into thā'. Abu Malik and a group said: al-fūm is wheat, and from it is the statement of Uḥayḥah ibn al-Julāḥ:

*"I used to think myself the wealthiest of anyone*
*who came to Medina from cultivating fūm."*

It was said: this is the dialect of Egypt, and this is the opinion favoured by al-Mubarrad. Al-Farra' said: it is an ancient dialect. Ibn Qutaybah and al-Zajjaj said: it is the grains that are eaten. Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn Durayd said: it is the ear of grain; Abu 'Ubaydah added: in the dialect of Asad. It was said: the grains that are baked into bread. It was said: bread. The Arabs say: "fūmū lanā" (bake bread for us), that is, bake; and Ibn Qutaybah preferred this, saying:

The first verse of the poem is a line of verse with a rhyme. Its sense is rendered below as it stands:

*"He gulps the fūm, not having chewed it, / a gulping that exceeded the gulping."*

Qutrub said: al-fūm (garlic, or a grain-like food; see below) is every knot in an onion, every large piece of meat, and every large mouthful. It was also said that it is chickpeas (al-himmaṣ), and this is a Levantine dialect usage. Its seller is called *fāmiyy*, which is changed from *fūmiyy* by the relative suffix, as they say *shahliyy* and *dahriyy*. Al-ʿadas is lentil, a known thing. ʿUdas and ʿUdus are proper names. ʿAdas is a command to a mule to stop. Al-baṣal is onion, a known thing.

*Adnā* is the comparative-superlative form (*af‘al al-tafḍīl*, the elative) from *al-dunuww*, which is nearness; it is said: *dana yadnū dunuwwan*. ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān al-Akhfash said: it is an elative from *al-danāʾa*, which is baseness and inferiority; the hamza was lightened by changing it into an alif. Abu Zayd said, regarding the hamzated root: *danuʾa al-rajul, yadnaʾu danāʾatan wa dināʾan*, and *danaʾa yadnaʾu*. Another said: it is an elative from *al-dūn*, meaning lower in rank; its original form was *adwan*, and its pattern became *af‘al* as in *awlā* ("more fitting"). It is an elative from *al-wayl* (woe); its original form was *awyal*, and it was transposed.

Al-miṣr: the town (*al-balad*), derived from *maṣartu al-shāh amṣuruhā maṣran*, "I milked all that was in her udder." It was also said that *al-miṣr* is the boundary between two lands. The people of Hajar say: "He bought the house with its *muṣūr*," meaning with its boundaries. ʿAdī ibn Zayd said:

*"And the one who made the sun a miṣr, with no concealment in it, / a separator between day and night."*

Al-suʾāl: the request (*al-ṭalab*). It is said: *saʾala yasʾalu suʾālan*. Al-suʾl is the thing requested. *Sāla yasāl* follows the pattern of *khāfa yakhāf*. Its verb may govern a clause even though it is not a verb of the heart, as in: *salhum ayyuhum bi-dhālika zaʿīm* ("ask them which of them is surety for that"). They said: this is because the question is a means to knowledge, so it is treated as knowledge.

Al-dhilla: the verbal noun of *dhalla yadhillu dhilletan wa dhullan*. It was said: *al-dhilla* is as if it were a form (*hay'a*) of *al-dhull*, like *al-jilsa* (a manner of sitting). *Al-dhull* is submission and the removal of difficulty.

Al-maskana: a *maf‘ala* form from *al-sukūn* (stillness). From it the *miskīn* (poor person) is named, because of the scarcity of his movements and the slackness of his energy. A verb has been formed from its root, *fa‘‘ala*: they say *tamaskana*, as they say *tamadraʿa* from *al-madraʿa* (coat of mail). This transmission has been criticized, and it was said: it is not sound; what is sound is *tasakkana* and *tadarraʿa*.

*Bāʾa bi-kadha*: meaning he returned (*raja‘a*), said by al-Kisāʾī; or he confessed, said by Abu ʿUbayda; or he deserved, said by Abu Ruq; or he settled and established himself, said by al-Mubarrad; or he was equal, said by al-Zajjāj. They cited for each opinion what could be used as evidence from the speech of the Arabs, but we have omitted that here.

Al-nabiyy: hamzated, from *anbaʾa* (to inform). It is a *fa‘īl* in the sense of *muf‘il*, like *samīʿ* from *asmaʿa*. Its plural is *al-nubaʾ*, and its verbal noun is *al-nubūʾa*. Musaylima "claimed prophethood" (*tanabba'a*). All of this is evidence that the *lām* (of the root) is a hamza. Al-Zahrāwī related that it is said: *nabuʾa*, when it becomes evident, and so one is *nabīʾ*; and by this the evident road was named *nabīʾan*. On this view it is a *fa‘īl* in the sense of an active participle from *fa‘ula*, like *sharīf* from *sharufa*. Whoever does not hamzate it said its original form is with hamza, then it was eased. It was also said: it is derived from *nabā yanbū*, when it becomes evident and elevated. They said: *al-nabī* is the evident road. The poet said:

*"When they reached a nabī, and we were settled, / a fiercely striding one, of the traces of the wiping, loose-limbed."*

Al-Kisāʾī said: *al-nabī* is the road; it was named so because one is guided by it. They said: by this also the Messenger (*al-rasūl*) was named, because he is a road to God, exalted is He.

Al-ʿiṣyān: non-submission to command and prohibition. Its verb is *ʿaṣā yaʿṣī*, and *al-ʿaṣy* has come in the sense of *al-ʿiṣyān*. Ibn Hammād, in his commentary, cited from Abu al-Hasan ibn al-Badhish, from what al-Farrāʾ cited:

*"In obedience to the Lord and disobedience to the Devil."*

Al-iʿtidāʾ: an *iftiʿāl* form from *al-ʿadw*; its explanation has already passed at His words: ﴿Some of you are enemies to others﴾ [al-Baqara 36].

﴿And when We said: Enter this town﴾. The speaker is God, exalted is He. Whether this was on the tongue of Moses or of Joshua, peace be upon them both, there are two opinions. The accusative of *hādhihi* is as an adverb of place, because it refers to a place-adverb, just as demonstrative nouns are put in the accusative as a verbal noun or as an adverb of time, when they refer to these: you say *ḍarabtu hādhā al-ḍarb* ("I struck this blow") and *ṣumtu hādhā al-yawm* ("I fasted this day"). This is the view of Sibawayh regarding *dakhala*: that it transitively takes a definite place-adverb without the mediation of *fī*. If the adverb is figurative, it is transitive with *fī*, as in *dakhaltu fī ghimār al-nās* ("I entered into the crowd of people") and *dakhaltu fī al-amr al-mushkil* ("I entered into the difficult matter"). The view of al-Akhfash and al-Jarmī is that *dakhaltu al-bayt* is an object, not an adverb of place; this is a question treated in the science of grammar. The *alif-lām* in *al-qarya* is for presence (deixis), and the accusative of *al-qarya* is as an adjective or as an appositive (*ʿaṭf al-bayān*), as already passed in the i'rab of *al-shajara* in His words: ﴿Do not approach this tree﴾ [al-Baqara 35]. Although the two aspects of i'rab differ for *hādhihi*, in ﴿do not approach this﴾ [al-Baqara 35] it is an object, and here it is in the disagreement we have mentioned.

The town here is Jerusalem (*bayt al-maqdis*) according to the majority, as said by Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, al-Suddī, al-Rabīʿ and others. It was said: Jericho (Arīḥā), said also by Ibn ʿAbbās, and it is in the land of Jerusalem. Abu Zayd ʿUmar ibn Shabba al-Numayrī said: it was a capital and the dwelling of kings, and in it is a mosque, which is Jerusalem, and in the mosque is a house called Īlyā. Al-Kawāshī said: Jericho is the town of the giants (*al-jabbārīn*); they were remnants of ʿĀd, called the ʿAmālaqa, and their head was ʿŪj ibn ʿUnuq. It was said: al-Ramla, said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk; it was said: Aylah; it was said: al-Urdunn; it was said: Palestine; it was said: al-Balqāʾ; it was said: Tadmur; it was said: Egypt; it was said: a town near Jerusalem, not specified, that they were ordered to enter; it was said: Syria. This was related from Ibn Kaysān. The first opinion has been preferred because of His words in al-Māʾida: ﴿Enter the holy land﴾ [al-Māʾida 21]. It was said: there is no disagreement that the reference in the two verses is one. This view was refuted by His words "so he substituted" (*fa-baddala*), because that requires that the change happened in Moses' lifetime; but he died in the wilderness of al-Tīh and did not enter Jerusalem. Those who said it is Jerusalem replied that the verse contains nothing indicating that the speech was on the tongue of Moses. This reply is a mistake, because it has already been said that the reference in this verse and in the verse of al-Māʾida, His words ﴿Enter the holy land﴾ [al-Māʾida 21], is one; and the speaker in the verse of al-Māʾida is certainly [Moses]. Do you not see His words: ﴿O my people, enter the holy land﴾ [al-Māʾida 21], and their words: ﴿They said: O Moses, in it are a people of giants﴾ [al-Māʾida 22]? Wahb said: they had committed sins, so it was said to them: ﴿Enter﴾, and the verse follows. Another said: they grew weary of the manna and the quails, so it was said to them: ﴿Go down to a town﴾ [al-Baqara 61], and the first place they reached was Jericho.

In His words ﴿this town﴾ is evidence that they approached it and saw it, because *hādhihi* is a reference to a present, near thing. It was said: the one who said this to them was Joshua son of Nun, for it is related from them that they did not enter the holy house (Jerusalem) until after returning from fighting the giants, and Moses was not with them when they entered it, for he and his brother died in the wilderness. It was also said: the two did not enter the wilderness, because it is a punishment, and God does not punish His prophets.

﴿So eat from it wherever you wish, plentifully﴾: the discussion of the parallel of this clause has already passed in the story of Adam, in His words: ﴿And eat from it plentifully wherever you both wish﴾ [al-Baqara 35], except that there the conjunction is *wa* (and) and here it is *fa* (so); there *raghadan* (plentifully) is placed before the adverb, and here the adverb is placed before *raghadan*. The meaning in both is one, except that the *wa* there came with the meaning of *fa*. It was said: this is its most common meaning, namely that the one preceding in time is what comes first and what is conjoined with it is what comes later in time, though it may occur the other way round, but rarely; it also has the meanings of accompaniment and time, but these are weaker than the first. That *wa* means *fa* is shown by what came in al-Aʿrāf with His words *fa-kulā* (so eat), with *fa*, and the matter is the same. As for the fronting of *raghadan* there, it is clear: it is an attribute of the eating or the eater, so it fits that it be near the governing element and not postponed from it, and it is not separated from it by an adverb; though a non-blocking intervening element would not prevent it, since both are objects of one governing verb. Here, however, it was postponed for the sake of the rhyme (*munāsabat al-fāṣila*) that follows it. Do you not see that His words ﴿so eat from it wherever you wish, plentifully﴾ and His words ﴿and enter the gate prostrating﴾ are two rhymed-prose units (*sajʿatān*) that correspond? For this reason, and God knows best, these two constructions were in these two arrangements.

﴿And enter the gate﴾: the dispute over the accusative of *al-bāb* is like the dispute over the accusative of *al-qarya*. The gate is one of the gates of Jerusalem, which is now called the Gate of Ḥiṭṭa, said by Ibn ʿAbbās; or it is the eighth of the gates of Jerusalem, which is called the Gate of Repentance, said by Mujāhid and al-Suddī; or the gate of the town they were ordered to enter; or the gate of the dome in which Moses and Aaron used to worship; or a gate in the mountain on which God spoke to Moses.

﴿Prostrating﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun in *udkhulū* (enter). Ibn ʿAbbās said: its meaning is bowing (*rukkaʿan*), and bowing was expressed by prostration, as prostration is sometimes expressed by bowing. It was said: because the gate was small and narrow, so the one entering needed to bend. This view is weak, because if it were narrow they would have been compelled to enter bowing, and then no command would be needed; but this does not follow, because the state could be a necessary one, in the sense that entry could only occur in this state, and necessary states exist in the speech of the Arabs. It was also said: its meaning is humbly and lowly, and this was chosen by Abu ʿAbd Allāh Muḥammad ibn Abī al-Faḍl in *al-Muntakhab*; we will mention the reason for his choosing it. It was also said: its meaning is the well-known prostration of placing the forehead on the ground, and the meaning is: enter prostrating in thanks to God, exalted is He, for He returned you to it. This is the apparent sense of the wording. Abu ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī al-Faḍl said: this is far-fetched, because the apparent sense requires that entry occur while prostrating, and if we take it on its apparent sense, that would be impossible; so, since the literal prostration was impossible, it must be taken as humility, because those who repent of a sin must be humble and submissive. What he proposed is not necessary, because accompanying (*muqārana*) is one kind of state, and that was impossible in his view; but it is not impossible, since it is not far-fetched that they were ordered to enter while prostrating, placing their foreheads on the ground while entering. The accompanying state is fulfilled by placing the forehead on the ground when they enter. If we make the state anticipated (*muqaddara*), that too is correct, because the prostration then would be after the entry; and the anticipated state exists in the language of the Arabs. Among examples is what is in Sibawayh's book: *marartu bi-rajulin maʿahu ṣaqrun ṣāʾidan bihi ghadan* ("I passed by a man with him a falcon, hunting with it tomorrow"). Since it is possible to take prostration in its commonly used sense, which is very frequent, namely placing the forehead on the ground, with the state being accompanying or anticipated, this is preferable. Al-Zamakhsharī said: they were ordered to prostrate upon reaching the gate, in thanks to God and humility. What he mentioned is not the implication of the verse, for they were not ordered in the verse to prostrate upon reaching the gate; rather they were ordered to enter in the state of prostration. So prostration is not what is commanded; it is a restriction on the occurrence of the commanded act, namely entering. States are relational restrictions (*nisab taqyīdiyya*), and commands are predicative relations (*nisab isnādiyya*), so the two contradict, since a thing cannot be both restrictive and predicative: in terms of restriction it does not form a complete utterance, and in terms of predication it does; so the contradiction is evident.

Regarding the manner of their entering the gate, there are several opinions. Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿIkrima said: they entered from their backsides (*min qibali astāhim*). Ibn Masʿūd said: they entered with their heads covered (*muqanniʿī ru'ūsihim*). Mujāhid said: they entered on the edges of their eyes (*ʿalā ḥurūf aʿyunihim*). Muqātil said: they entered lying on their backs (*mustalqīna*). It was said: they entered crawling on their knees, out of obstinacy and arrogance. What is established in al-Bukhārī and Muslim is that they entered the gate crawling on their backsides. These interpretations have thus collapsed, and it became necessary to turn to the interpretation of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

Its statement: "And say, 'Ḥiṭṭah'" — ḥiṭṭah means "remission" (a request for remission). Something reported as speech must necessarily be a sentence, so a corrective element is needed to make it a sentence, and it is therefore supplied as "our request is ḥiṭṭah." This is the estimate of al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan. Al-Ṭabarī said the estimate is "our entering the gate as we were commanded is ḥiṭṭah." Others said the estimate is "your command is ḥiṭṭah." It was also said that the estimate is "our command is ḥiṭṭah," meaning that we should lay down (ḥaṭṭa) in this town and settle in it. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "The original form is the accusative, in the sense of 'Remit our sins, a remission (ḥiṭṭah),' but it was put in the nominative to convey the sense of permanence, as in his saying:

ṣabrun jamīlun fakilānā mubtalā
(Patience is beautiful, and each of us is tested),

where the original is ṣabran." End of his words, and they are good. This derivation is confirmed by the reading of Ibrāhīm ibn Abī ʿAbla: (ḥiṭṭatan) in the accusative, as is reported in:

ṣabran jamīlan fakilānā mubtalā
(Patience, beautiful patience, and each of us is tested)

in the accusative. Of the earlier estimates for the omitted subject, the first opinion is the most apparent, because the fitting context for linking forgiveness to it is the request to remove sins, not any of the other estimates. A parallel to this omission is the poet's saying:

idhā dhuqtu fāhan qultu ṭaʿmu mudāmatin ∗∗∗ muʿattaqatin mimmā tajīʾu bihi al-tujur
(When I taste her mouth I say: the flavor of wine, aged, of what the merchants bring),

which is related with the nominative "ṭaʿmu" as an estimate of "this is the flavor of wine," and with the accusative as an estimate of "I tasted the flavor of wine." Al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you ask, may ḥiṭṭatun be put in the accusative in the reading of the one who reads it so, with qūlū taking the sense of 'say this word'?" I say: "It is not far." End of his words. What he permitted is not permissible, because qawl does not govern single words; it enters only upon sentences for quotation, and so it occupies the position of the direct object, except if the single word is a verbal noun (maṣdar), as in qultu qawlan, or an adjective of a verbal noun, as in qultu ḥaqqan, or an expression for a sentence, as in qultu shiʿran and qultu khuṭbatan. Even this category may be taken to return to the verbal noun, since poetry and sermon are two kinds of speech. But ḥiṭṭah is none of these. Also, if you make ḥiṭṭah accusative by the wording of "qūlū," that would be a verbal (lafẓī) predication, stripped of meaning-based (maʿnawī) predication, and the original is the meaning-based predication. When it is a verbal predication, no benefit at all follows from uttering it, except the mere compliance with the command to utter a word, so there is no difference between it and meaningless words that were not set to signify any meaning. It is also far-fetched that forgiveness of sins should be made to follow the utterance of a bare single word that signifies no sense of speech. As for what Abū ʿUbayda held, that his saying "ḥiṭṭah" is a single word, and that it is nominative by quotation and not excerpted from a sentence, but they were commanded to say it this way in the nominative, this is far from correct, because it leaves ḥiṭṭah nominative without a governing agent, and because qawl was placed in the chapter of quotation only to quote sentences, not single words; that is why the grammarians needed an interpretation for His saying: "It is said of him, Abraham" (Q. al-Anbiyāʾ 21:60). As for his comparing it to the saying:

samiʿtu al-nāsa yantajiʿūna ghaythan
(I heard people seeking rain),

and to:

wajadnā fī kitābi banī Tamīmin ∗∗∗ aḥaqqu al-khayli bi-l-rakḍi al-muʿāri
(We found in the book of the Banū Tamīm: the horse most worthy of the lent gallop),

this is not sound, because "heard" and "found" each relate to single words and sentences, since what is heard and what is found in a book may be a single word or a sentence. But qawl falls only upon sentences, and it falls upon single words only in what has been mentioned earlier, and ḥiṭṭah is not among them.

The statements of the exegetes differ regarding ḥiṭṭah. Al-Ḥasan said its meaning is "remit our sins." Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jubayr and Wahb said: they were commanded to seek forgiveness. ʿIkrima said its meaning is "There is no god but Allah." Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said its meaning is "and say this true command." It was also said: its meaning is "we shall always remain under your rule, obeying your command," as one says "I have set down my saddle-bags in your courtyard." The estimates for the omitted subject before ḥiṭṭah have already been given, and these are the sayings of the people of exegesis. It has been related from Ibn ʿAbbās that they were commanded with this very word, but it was said: the closer view is otherwise, because this word is Arabic and they did not speak with it, and because the closer view is that they were commanded to say a statement signifying repentance, regret and humility; even if they had said, "O Allah, we ask You for forgiveness and repent to You," humility would have been achieved, since the purpose of repentance is, on the part of the heart, regret, and on the part of the tongue, the utterance of a word indicating that regret has arisen in the heart; and that does not depend on a particular word being uttered.

(yaghfir) — Nāfiʿ: with a yāʾ, damma; Ibn ʿĀmir: with a tāʾ — Abū Bakr through al-Juʿfī's route: (yaghfar); the rest: naghfir. Whoever reads with yāʾ and damma does so because khaṭāyā is feminine. Whoever reads with yāʾ and fatḥa, the pronoun refers to God Most High, and it is an instance of iltifāt (shift of person), because the opening of the verse is "and when We said," then He said "yaghfir," so it shifts from the first person plural of one magnifying Himself to the third person singular. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to the saying implied by "qūlū," i.e., "the saying is forgiven," and forgiveness is ascribed to it metaphorically, since it was a cause of forgiveness. Whoever reads with nūn, which is the reading of the rest of the seven, it is in line with what precedes it, "and when We said," and what follows it, "and We shall increase," so the discourse is in a single style. None of the seven read anything other than khaṭāyākum, and al-Kisāʾī imāla'd it. A group read (taghfir) with fatḥa of the tāʾ; it was said: as if ḥiṭṭah were the cause of forgiveness — by which he means the speaker of this, Ibn ʿAṭiyya — so the pronoun would refer to ḥiṭṭah. This is not good, because the word itself, by its bare form, is not a cause of forgiveness. We have explained this before, so the pronoun refers to the understood utterance from "qūlū," and forgiveness is ascribed to it metaphorically, since it was a cause of forgiveness. Al-Jaḥdarī and Qatāda read tughfar with damma of the tāʾ and singular khaṭīʾa. It is reported from Qatāda: yughfar with damma of the yāʾ. al-Aʿmash read yaghfir with fatḥa of the yāʾ and singular khaṭīʾa. al-Ḥasan read yaghfir with fatḥa of the yāʾ and the sound plural. Abū Ḥaywa read tughfar with damma of the tāʾ and the sound plural. al-Ahwāzī related that he read khaṭa'ayākum with hamza on the alif and sukūn on the final alif; and the reverse is also related from him. The justification for this hamza is that the speakers found it burdensome to pronounce two alifs, since the separator is a letter with fatḥa, and the fatḥa gives rise to an alif, so it was as though three alifs had gathered; so they made hamza of one of the two alifs to remove this burden. Since they had already made hamza of a lone alif after fatḥa in the saying:

wakhindifin hāmatu hādhā al-ʿaʾlami
(and Khindif, the chief of this great one),

it is all the more fitting that they make hamza here; this is a justification of an anomaly. Whoever reads with damma of the yāʾ or the tāʾ, then khaṭāyākum or khaṭīyātikum or khaṭīyatikum is the object of a passive verb whose agent is not named; whoever reads with fatḥa of the tāʾ or yāʾ or with nūn, then that is the object, and this verb is in the jussive because it is the answer to the imperative. The discussion of its counterpart has already been given in His saying: "And fulfil My covenant, I shall fulfil your covenant" (Q. al-Baqara 2:40), and we mentioned the disagreement on that. Here four commands have preceded: "Enter" (Q. 2:58), "and eat," "and enter the gate," "and say, ḥiṭṭah." The apparent view is that it is an answer only to the last two, and the meaning is upon that, because the forgiveness is not consequent upon entering the town nor upon eating from it, but it is consequent upon entering the gate, since that is restricted to the state which is an act of worship, namely prostration, and to His saying "and say ḥiṭṭah," because it contains the request for the removal of sins, owing to the strength of the connection and the proximity. What shows that this forgiveness is consequent upon these is what is in al-Aʿrāf in His saying: "And say ḥiṭṭah, and enter the gate prostrating" (Q. 7:161), and "We shall forgive" — and the story is one. There He made forgiveness consequent upon their saying ḥiṭṭah and upon entering the gate prostrating, because entering includes prostration. In the difference between these two clauses in order of mention and delay, there is evidence that the particle wa does not establish sequence, and that it is for mere conjunction. Most reciters recite the idghām-less form, idhhār of the rāʾ in naghfir before the lām, while a group assimilated it, and they said this is weak.

(wasanazīdu): here with the wāw; in al-Aʿrāf: "sanazīdu" (Q. 7:161), and the one in al-Aʿrāf is abridged. Do you not see the omission of raghadan and of the wāw in "wasanazīdu"? And His saying "fa-arsalnā ʿalayhim" (Q. 7:162) is in place of "fa-anzalnā ʿalā alladhīna ẓalamū" (Q. 2:59), and the affirmation of that here; the elaboration fits here, and the brevity there.

Ziyāda is elevation above a known measure, and its opposite is nuqṣān (deficiency). (al-muḥsinīn): it was said: those among them who had not been of the people of that wrongdoing; and it was said: the muḥsinīn from among them. It was said: the meaning is whoever among them does good after that, We increase his reward and ranks; and it was said: the meaning is whoever among them was a doer of good, We increase his good; and whoever among them was a wrongdoer after that, We increase his reward and ranks; and it was said: the meaning is whoever among them was a doer of good, We increase his good, and whoever among them was a wrongdoer, erring, We forgive him his sin; and they were of these two categories, so God informed them that when they did what they were commanded — entering the gate prostrating and saying ḥiṭṭah — He would forgive and multiply the reward of their doers of good. It was said: the muḥsinīn are those who entered as commanded and said, "There is no god but Allah." So it is established that the muḥsinīn are either from others or from among them. Those from among them are either those who were characterized by goodness in the past, i.e., were doers of good, or in the future, i.e., whoever among them does good hereafter, or in the present, i.e., "We shall increase you for your goodness in your obedience to what you were commanded: entering the gate prostrating and saying ḥiṭṭah." This clause is conjoined to "And say ḥiṭṭah; We shall forgive you your sins," and it is not conjoined to "naghfir," so that it would be an answer; do you not see that it came disconnected from conjunction in al-Aʿrāf in His saying "sanazīdu"? Even though in meaning, though not in grammatical structure, it follows upon entering the gate prostrating and saying ḥiṭṭah, it is treated as a pure report that is not consequent upon anything before it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 59:

﴿So those who did wrong substituted﴾: Its apparent meaning is that they were divided into wrongdoers and non-wrongdoers, and that the wrongdoers are the ones who substituted. If all of them substituted, then this is the placing of the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun, to signal the cause. It is as if it had been said: "So they substituted," but He made it explicit to draw attention to the cause of the substitution, which is wrongdoing. That is, had it not been for their wrongdoing, they would not have substituted. The thing substituted is omitted, and its estimated form is: "So those who did wrong substituted, by their saying hitta (a word meaning 'remission' or 'release'), ﴿a saying other than what had been said to them﴾." Since it is omitted, it was appropriate for (غَيْرَ, ghayra, "other than") to be followed by the apparent noun. What was said to them was that they should say hitta. Had it not been omitted, the sentence would have been: "So those who did wrong substituted, by their saying hitta, a saying other than it." But when it was omitted, the explicit noun was put in the genitive after (غَيْرَ), to show that the omitted element is this explicit noun, namely what was said to them. This estimate we have made is in the form of a substitution (badal), since the genitive is what is removed and the accusative is what is obtained.

The exegetes differed concerning the saying they uttered in place of "hitta." Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, Mujahid, Wahb and Ibn Zayd said: "ḥinṭa" (wheat). al-Suddi said, on the authority of his teachers: "ḥinṭa ḥamrā'" (red wheat). It was also said: "ḥinṭa bayḍā' mathqūba fīhā sha'ra sawdā'" (white wheat with a black hair pierced through it). Abu Salih said: "sunbula" (an ear of grain). al-Suddi and Mujahid also said: "hiṭā shamhāthā," and it was said: "ḥiṭā sham'āthā." Their meaning, according to these two sayings, is "red wheat," and it was said: "white wheat pierced with a hair." It was also said: "a grain in a barley-corn," and Ibn Mas'ud said: "red wheat in which there is barley." It was said: "wheat in barley," narrated by Ibn Abbas from the Prophet (ﷺ). It was said: "a grain of wheat rolled in a hair." It was also said: "they spoke in the language of the Nabataeans, by way of mockery and contempt." It was further said: "They altered what had been prescribed for them, and did not act upon what Allah had sent down to them."

What is established in the Sahih of al-Bukhari and Muslim is that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained it: they said, "a grain in a hair." Therefore, it is obligatory to adopt this saying and to discard those other sayings. Even if any of the previous sayings were authentic, the difference in wording would be attributed to the difference among the speakers, so some said this and some said that, and there would be no contradiction among them. The meaning of the verse is that they put in place of what they were commanded, which was repentance and seeking forgiveness, a different saying that indicated their mockery of what they had been commanded, and their turning away from that by which their sins would be forgiven. All of this reflects indifference to the commands of Allah, and so they deserved the punishment.

﴿So We sent down upon those who did wrong a punishment (rijz)﴾: He repeated the earlier apparent noun to add to the condemnation of their state and to signal that the descent of the punishment was caused by it. It was left implicit in al-A'raf, where He said: ﴿so We sent upon them﴾ (Al-A'raf: 162), because the implicit is the explicit. Ibn Muhaysin read rujzan with a damma on the rā', and it has already been mentioned that this is a dialectal form of rijz. The exegetes differed concerning rijz here. Abu al-Aliyah said it is the anger of Allah, the Exalted. Ibn Zayd said it is a plague which destroyed seventy thousand of them in one hour. Wahb said it is a plague with which they were punished for forty nights, after which they died. Ibn Jubayr said it is snow, by which seventy thousand of them perished. Ibn Abbas said it is darkness and death: twenty-four thousand of them died in one hour, and seventy thousand perished as a punishment. What the Qur'an indicates is that a punishment was sent down upon them, without its kind being specified, since there is no great benefit in specifying the type.

﴿from the heaven﴾: If rijz is interpreted as snow, then its being from the sky is clear. If it is interpreted otherwise, then it is an indication of the direction from which the judgment against them came, or an exaggeration of its height through domination and conquest.

(بِما كانُوا)، ما: is a verbal-source particle (maṣdariyya), with the estimate: بِكَوْنِهِمْ (because of their being). (يَفْسُقُونَ) (they were defiantly disobedient). Some have permitted that ما be understood as الَّذِي (the one which), but this is far-fetched. al-Nakha'i, Ibn Wathhab and others read (يَفْسُقُونَ) with a kasra on the sīn, and this is a dialectal form. Abu Muslim said: this defiance (fisq) is the wrongdoing mentioned in the words ﴿those who did wrong﴾. The purpose of the repetition is emphasis, because the description indicates causation. So the apparent meaning is that the substitution was caused by wrongdoing, and the sending down of the punishment was also caused by wrongdoing. Others besides Abu Muslim said: it is not a repetition in two respects. The first is that wrongdoing may be of minor sins (﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾ (Al-A'raf: 23)), and of major sins (﴿Indeed, associating others with Allah is a great wrongdoing﴾ (Luqman: 13)), whereas defiance (fisq) can only be of major sins. So when He first described them as wrongdoers, then described them as defiant, which must be of major sins. The second is that it is possible that they deserved the name of wrongdoers because of that substitution and the sending down of the punishment upon them from the sky, not because of the substitution itself, but because of the defiance they committed before that substitution. On this view, the repetition disappears. End of quotation.

Some people have argued from His words, ﴿So those who did wrong substituted﴾, and from the ordering of the punishment upon this substitution, that what has been revealed as a fixed utterance (tawqīf) may not be altered or replaced with another wording. Others said that this is permissible if the word fills the same role, and on this basis the disagreement arose concerning recitation of the Qur'an by its meaning, concerning the opening takbir (takbīr al-iḥrām), concerning the validity of marriage using the words "gift," "sale," or "transfer of ownership," and concerning transmitting a hadith by its meaning.

They mentioned that there are questions regarding the verse. The first: here He says (وإذْ قُلْنا) ("and when We said"), while in al-A'raf He says ﴿وإذْ قِيلَ﴾ ("and when it was said") (Al-A'raf: 161). It was answered that the agent is stated explicitly in al-Baqarah to remove ambiguity, and it is omitted in al-A'raf because it is known from surah al-Baqarah. The second: here He says (ادْخُلُوا) ("enter"), and there (اسْكُنُوا) ("dwell"). It was answered that entering precedes dwelling, so entering is mentioned in the earlier surah and dwelling in the later one. The third: here (خَطاياكم) ("your sins," plural of abundance), and there (خَطِيئاتِكم) ("your sins," plural of paucity). It was answered that khaṭāyā is a plural of abundance, so it suited the context in which He joined it with what befits His generosity, namely forgiveness of the abundant. Khaṭī'āt is a plural of paucity, and since He did not attribute the forgiveness to Himself there, He used it. The fourth: here (رَغَدًا) ("abundantly") is mentioned, and there it is omitted. It was answered with the answer given previously. The fifth: here the entering of the gate is placed before the saying, and there it is reversed. It was answered that the conjunction (الواو) indicates joint action, and those addressed here are sinners, so their occupation with removing sin takes precedence over their occupation with worship. So they were commanded to say hitta first, then to enter. But those addressed there are not sinners, so their occupation first with worship, then with mentioning repentance second, is by way of humbling the self and removing self-admiration. And since the division was possible, the ruling for each of the two was mentioned in a surah, beginning with whichever of them. The sixth: the conjunction (و) is affirmed in (وسَنَزِيدُ) ("and We will increase") here, and omitted there. It was answered that since two matters preceded, bringing the conjunction indicates that the combined forgiveness and increase is a single reward for the combination of the two matters. Where it is left out, it indicates that each one is distributed against each of the two matters: the forgiveness corresponds to the saying, and the increase corresponds to (ادْخُلُوا) ("enter").

The seventh: here He did not mention (مِنهم) ("from among them"), but He did there. It was answered that the beginning of the story in al-A'raf is built on specification by the word (مِن), He said: ﴿And among the people of Musa is a community﴾ (Al-A'raf: 159). So He mentioned the word (مِن) at the end to match its end with its beginning. Here the story is not built on specification. The eighth: here (فَأنْزَلْنا) ("so We sent down"), and there (فَأرْسَلْنا) ("so We sent"). It was answered that sending down indicates its occurrence at the beginning of the matter, while sending indicates His domination over them and their complete eradication, and this occurs only at the end. The ninth: here (يَفْسُقُونَ) ("they defy"), and there (يَظْلِمُونَ) ("they wrong"). It was answered that since He clarified here that this wrongdoing is defiance, He was content to mention wrongdoing in surah al-A'raf, because of the clarification that preceded here. Some people said: the Children of Israel opposed Allah in both word and deed, and the Exalted informed of the requital for opposition by word alone, not by deed, namely their refusal to enter with the attitude of prostration. It was answered that action is not required except by a command, and a command is a word. So the requital for the word yields the requital for both together. The requital here, if it fell upon this particular opposition, then (يَفْسُقُونَ) admits of the present sense; and if it fell upon the earlier oppositions by which they defied, then it is a present-tense verb standing in the place of the past tense, which is common in the Qur'an and in eloquent speech.

﴿And when Musa asked for water for his people﴾ (al-Baqarah: 60): This is the ninth favour, and it encompasses the blessings of this world and the next. As for this world, it removed from them the severe need for water. Had it not been for this, they would have perished in the wilderness. This is more eloquent than ordinary water for livestock, because they were in a remote, cut-off desert. As for the religion, it is among the clearest proofs of the existence of the Creator, His power, and His knowledge, and of the truthfulness of Musa (peace be upon him). Istisqā' is seeking water when it is absent or scarce. It was said: the object of istasqā is omitted, meaning Musa asked his Lord for water, so the one from whom water is sought is the omitted element, and the verb has been transitive to it, as it was transitive to it in His words, ﴿when his people asked him for water﴾ (Al-A'raf: 160), meaning they asked him for drink. Some said: the omitted object is estimated as "he asked for water," and in this view the omitted element is the thing sought, and the verb has been transitive to it, as it was in the line of poetry:

*"And a fair one by whose face the clouds are sought for rain."*

The claim that the verb is transitive to two objects requires evidence from Arabic speech. It was heard in their speech: "Zayd was asked for water and was given to drink." It has been established that it is transitive once to the one from whom water is sought and once to the water sought, so its transitivity to both requires a firm basis from the language of the Arabs. Allah mentioned this blessing of watering without restricting it to a place. This has been disputed. Abu Muslim said: this was according to the customary practice of people when they suffered drought, and what Allah did by making water gush from the stone exceeded a mere answer to prayer for rain and sending down rain. Most exegetes said: this istisqā' took place in the wilderness, when they said: "Who will provide us with such-and-such?" until they said: "Who will provide us with water?" So Allah commanded Musa to strike the stone. It was also said that this occurred when they came out of the sea that had split, and they arrived at a white land with no shade and no water, so they asked him to ask for water for them. The lām in (لِقَوْمِهِ) ("for his people") is the lām of cause, meaning for the sake of his people. There is an omitted element that completes the meaning of the sentence: that is, for his people when they were thirsty. Or it is not with this meaning, and there is another omitted element: that is, "so We answered him."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 60 (part 1 of 2):

﴿So We said: Strike the rock with your staff.﴾ They said: This staff is the one referred to in His words: ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 17], and it had properties that will be mentioned in their proper place. It was said: it was of nabk (nabk, a type of wood) wood; it was said: it was of 'ulayqi (ulayqi, a thorny tree); and it was said: it was of the myrtle of Paradise. Its length was ten cubits, the height of Musa, peace be upon him. It had two branches that gave light in darkness. Adam had carried it with him from Paradise to the earth, and it was inherited by the younger from the elder until it reached Shu'ayb, and he gave it to Musa, upon our Prophet and upon them both be blessings and peace. That was because when he (Shu'ayb) hired him (as a shepherd), he said to him: "Go and take a staff." So he went to (p-227) the house, and this one flew into his hand. He commanded him to return it, so he took another, and it flew into his hand, and he left it to him. It was also said: an angel from among the angels handed it to him on the road to Madyan.

(The rock): al-Hasan said: it was not a specific rock; rather, whichever rock he struck, water gushed forth from it, and this is more eloquent in terms of miraculousness, since water gushes from whatever rock he strikes. It is narrated that they said: "If Musa were to lose his staff, we would die of thirst." So Allah revealed to him: "Do not strike the stones; speak to them, and they will obey you, perhaps they will take heed." So they (the stones) obeyed him, but they did not take heed. Wahb said: he would strike for them the nearest rock and it would gush forth. According to this, the alif and lam in (al-hajar, "the rock") are for the genus. It was also said: the alif and lam are for a known reference, and it is a specific rock which he carried with him from Mount Tur, square-shaped, having four faces, from each face three springs gush forth, for each tribe a spring that flows in a channel to the tribe that you were commanded to water. They were six hundred thousand, besides their animals, and the width of the camp was twelve miles. It was also said: it is a rock that Adam brought down with him from Paradise, and they inherited it until it came to Shu'ayb, and he gave it to Musa along with the staff. It was also said: it is the rock upon which Musa placed his garment when he bathed, when they accused him of having a swollen testicle (udra), and he fled. Jibril, peace be upon him, said to him: "By the command of Allah, lift this rock, for it has a power from Me and a miracle for you in it," so he carried it in a sack. This was reported by Ibn 'Abbas. It was also said: it is a light, square rock that he took from the bottom of the sea, the size of a man's head, having four faces, from each face three springs gush forth, for each tribe a spring that flows in a channel to it, and he would place it in his sack, and whenever they needed water he would place it down and strike it with his staff. It was also said: it was marble with twelve holes, from each hole a spring of sweet water gushes forth, which they would take, and when they were finished, Musa would strike it with his staff and the water would go away. It was also said: it is a rock he took from Mount Zabid, four cubits long, reported by al-Dahhak. It was also said: a rock the size of a sheep's head, which they would throw into the side of the saddlebag when they set out, and in it from every side three springs would remain after its water was retained following their journey; when they alighted, Musa would strike it with his staff and the springs would return according to their number, reported by Ibn Zayd. It was also said: a rock he carried in his sack, which he took when they said: "How will we be when we come to a land that has no stones?" So wherever they alighted he would cast it down and it would gush forth water. It was also said: a rock of kadhdhan (a type of soft stone) having twelve springs, which would supply six hundred thousand each day, reported by Abu Rawq. It was also said: a rock one dhira' by one dhira', reported by al-Suddi. It was also said: a rock the size of a bull's head. It was also said: a rock from which water gushed for them, which they did not carry; rather, wherever they alighted they would find it there. That is greater in miraculousness and more eloquent as an extraordinary sign. Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: whenever they had satisfied their need for water, those springs would vanish, and whenever they needed water, they would gush forth again.

These are the statements of the exegetes concerning the rock, and their apparent meaning, or the apparent meaning of most of them, is contradictory. Some of those who compiled works on the interpretation of the Qur'an said: the most fitting view is that it is the rock that fled with Musa's garment, peace be upon him, for Allah placed in it the motion of moving and running, or entrusted an angel to carry it, and that is not to be deemed strange. For it is authentically reported that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed I know a rock that used to greet me with salam." This man attempted to reconcile these statements by saying that the rock is not specific, but rather whatever rock he found, he struck it; so once he found it square, once kadhdhan, once marble, and so on in it. He said: so the narrator related the description of that rock which he struck in that station, and thus the differences in the descriptions disappear and the narrations are reconciled. This statement is as you see. The apparent meaning of the Qur'an is that the rock is not specific, since no rock was previously mentioned so that this one would be known; that the seeking of water was not repeated, neither it nor the striking nor the gushing; and that these modes which they mentioned are not addressed by the wording of the Qur'an, so it is possible that this was repeated, and it is possible that it happened once, and the once is the established one.

﴿Then gushed forth﴾: the fa' is for coordination upon an omitted clause; the estimate is: "So he struck, and it gushed forth," like His words: ﴿Strike with your staff the sea, and it parted﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 63], meaning: "So he struck, and it parted." What indicates this omitted element is the occurrence of the gushing as consequent upon his striking, for if it were to gush without striking, the command would have no purpose, and his abandoning it would be disobedience, which is not permissible for the Prophets, peace be upon them. As for what some people have claimed, that the fa' in such as "fa-infalaqa" is the fa' in "fa-daraba," and that the omitted element is the coordinated element, with the coordinating particle taken from the coordinated element, so that the omitted element still retains an indicator, since its fa' was retained and the fa' of "infalaqa" was omitted, and the fa' of "fa-daraba" was joined to "infalaqa" — this is an artificial construction and a fabrication upon the Arabs without evidence. It is established in the language of the Arabs to omit the coordinated element where a coordinated particle exists, where no fa'-coordinated element is present. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So send me forth﴾ [Yusuf: 45], ﴿Yusuf, O truthful one﴾ [Yusuf: 46]; the estimate is: "So they sent him, and he said." So both the coordinated element and the coordinating particle were omitted, and if omitting both together is permissible, then omitting each one alone is more so. Al-Zamakhshari claimed that the fa' is not for coordination, but is the response to an omitted conditional, saying: "If you strike, then it has gushed forth," as we mentioned in His words: ﴿So He turned to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 54], and it is on this basis an eloquent fa' that occurs only in eloquent speech. End of his words.

We have already given a response to al-Zamakhshari in this estimate in His words: ﴿So He turned to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 54], that the omission of such a condition is not permissible, and we explained that there. And in his words also is the omission of (qad), for it is estimated: "So He has indeed turned to you, and it has indeed gushed forth," and such a thing is hardly preserved from their language; rather it occurs without fa', or if the fa' enters, then qad must be made explicit. And that which qad enters must necessarily be past in wording and meaning, such as His words: ﴿And if they deny you, then indeed messengers before you were denied﴾ [Fatir: 4]. And if it is past in wording and meaning, it is impossible for it to itself be the response of the condition, so an interpretation and the omission of a conditional response becomes necessary.

It is known that the gushing, according to what is estimated, would be consequent upon his being struck; and if it is consequent upon a future matter, it must be future; and if it is future, it is impossible for (qad) to enter upon it, since qad by its nature does not enter in the position resembling a conditional response upon the past except that its meaning is past, as in the verse and as in their saying: "If you do good to me, then I have indeed done good to you," and it requires an interpretation as we mentioned. And this verb is not a supplication such that the fa' enters upon it only and its meaning becomes future, even if it is in the past form, such as: "If you visit me, then may Allah forgive you." Furthermore, what is understood from the verse is that the gushing has occurred and been realized, and for this reason He said: ﴿Each people has indeed known its drinking place; eat and drink﴾. Making it the response of an omitted condition, as this man went, would render it unrealized, since it would become future, for it is contingent upon the existence of a future matter, and what is contingent upon the existence of a future matter does not imply its possibility, let alone its existence. So what he went to is corrupt in Arabic structure and corrupt in terms of meaning, and therefore it must be discarded. Where is this from his words: "And it is on this basis an eloquent fa' that occurs only in eloquent speech"?

Here (the verse) has (infajarat, "gushed forth"), while in al-A'raf it has (inbajasat, "burst forth"). It was said: they are the same; infajara, inbajasa and inshaqqa are synonyms. It was also said: there is a difference between them, which is that inbijas is the first emergence of water, and infijar is its spreading and abundance. It was also said: inbijas is its coming out from hard ground, and infijar is its coming out from soft ground. It was also said: inbijas is seepage, and infijar is flowing. The apparent usage of the Qur'an is that they are used with one meaning, because the two verses are one story.

(Minhu, "from it"): it is connected to His words "fa-infajarat," and min here is for the beginning of the limit (ibtida' al-ghaya). The pronoun refers to the rock that was struck, so the gushing of the water was from the rock, not from the place, as He, the Exalted, says: ﴿And indeed among stones there are those from which rivers gush forth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 74]. Had this construction been in speech other than the speech of Allah the Exalted, it would have been possible for the pronoun to refer to the striking, which is the verbal noun understood from the preceding speech, and for (min) to be causal, meaning: "it gushed forth because of the striking." But it is not permissible to resort to such a thing in the speech of Allah the Exalted, for it should only be understood according to the finest of expressions in both structure and meaning, since it is the most eloquent of speech. In this gushing there is miraculousness: the appearance of water itself from a rock that has no connection to the earth, so that its material would be from it; its emerging in abundance from a small rock; its emerging according to their need; its emerging at the striking with the staff; and its stopping when they no longer need it.

(Ithnata 'ashrata, "twelve"): the ta' in (ithnata) is for the feminine, and in (thintā) it is for assimilation (al-ilhaq), and these are like ibnatun and bintun. The majority read (ashrata) with a sukun on the shin. Mujahid, Talha, 'Isa, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Ibn Abi Layla and Yazid read it with a kasra on the shin. Nu'aym al-Sa'idi related this from Abu 'Amr, but the well-known reading from him is the sukun. It has been mentioned that it is the dialect of Tamim, and their kasra on it is rare by their analogy, since they lighten (fa'il) forms, saying of namir: nimr. Ibn al-Fadl al-Ansari and al-A'mash read it with a fatha on the shin. It is related from al-A'mash that he read it with sukun and also with kasra. Al-Zamakhshari said: the fatha is a dialect. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is a weak dialect. Al-Mahdawi said: the fatha of the shin is not well-known, though it may be a dialect; and some grammarians have stated that the fatha of the shin is anomalous. (Ashrata) is in the position of a genitive by the idafa, and it is indeclinable because it occupies the position of the nun, so it is among those in which the first element is inflected and the second element is indeclinable. Do you not see that (ithnata) is inflected like the dual, since its alif is retained in the nominative and changes to ya' in the accusative and genitive, while (ashrata) is indeclinable? And since it occupies the position of the nun of ithnatayn, its idafa is not valid, so one does not say: ithnata 'ashratak. In my memory, Ibn Darastawayh held that ithna, ithnata and ithnat together with 'ashr are indeclinable, and he did not take the alternation as evidence of inflection.

('Ayna, "a spring"): it is accusative as a specification (tamyiz), and the singularity of the accusative specification in the category of numbers is obligatory according to the majority; al-Farra' permitted that it be plural. This number was specified over others because they were twelve tribes, and there was enmity and rivalry among them, so Allah caused for each tribe among them a spring to which it would come, none of the other tribe sharing it with it. Mentioning this number rather than others is called takhsis (specification) by the scholars of rhetoric, which is that a type from among many types is mentioned for a meaning in it that none other shares with it. From this is His words: ﴿And that He is the Lord of Sirius﴾ [al-Najm: 49], and the explanation of that specification will come in its place, if Allah the Exalted wills. And the words of al-Khansa':

"The rising of the sun reminds me of Sakhr, and I lament him at every setting of the sun."

Abu Hayyan's commentary on surah 2, verse 60 (part 2 of 2):

They were singled out from all other times for raiding and for hospitality. Some people of subtle insight (ahl al-lata'if) said: God created stone and placed in it a hardness by which many parts of hard solid things are split apart. He created trees with pliant branches, which lack the strength of stones, so they do not affect the breaking of things by their parts, nor do they make water gush from springs; rather, stones affect them. When the stone was strengthened by the power of prophethood, the seas were split by it, parts of stones were separated by it, and rivers flowed from it. ﴿Indeed in that is a lesson for those with insight﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:13).

﴿Every people knew their drinking place﴾: this is a resumptive clause (jumla istinafiyya, a clause that begins a new sentence without grammatical dependence on what precedes it), indicating that each tribe among them had a drinking place that it recognized, so it did not go beyond it to the drinking place of another. It appears to be an explanation of the wisdom behind the division into twelve springs, and an alert to it. Here ('alima, "to know") is transitive to one object, treated as 'arafa ("to recognize"), and its use in this way is common in the Qur'an and in the Arabic language. ﴿Every people﴾ is specified by an omitted qualifier, meaning: from among their own people for whom he (Moses) had asked water. The word mashrab (drinking place) here means the place of drinking and its direction from which the water flows. Some have taken it to mean the thing drunk, which is water, but the first meaning is preferable, because its indication of place is by its basic lexical form, whereas its indication of water is metaphorical, being the naming of a thing by the name of its place. The drinking places are attributed to them because, since each drinking place was assigned to those specifically assigned to it, it became as though it were their property. The pronoun in (their drinking place) refers to the sense of (every), not to its wording, and it is not permissible for it to refer to its wording, so that one would say "his drinking place," because observing the sense is obligatory here. This is because (every) has been placed in apposition to an indefinite noun, and whenever it is added to an indefinite noun, observing the sense is obligatory, so that it agrees with what it is added to in the reference of a pronoun and otherwise. God Most High said: ﴿On the day We shall call every people with their leader﴾ (Al-Isra 17:71). The poet said:

*And every people has approached the tether of its stallion,*
*but we have untied its tether, so it has fled.*

And he said:

*And every people will surely enter among them*
*a Duwayhiyya (a calamity) from which the fingertips turn yellow.*

(p. 230) God Most High said: ﴿Every soul shall taste death﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:185). You may say: "Every two men say that," and in none of this is it permissible to observe the wording of (every), while there is an omitted element whose estimate is: "their drinking place from them," that is, from the twelve springs. The drinking place is singled out to draw attention to the great benefit that is the cause of life. Although the plain statement would be "every people knew their spring," the mention of the drinking place contains what we have mentioned about the permissibility of drinking from them for them. It was established for them the command to eat the manna and quails and to drink from these springs, or they were commanded to continue in that, because permission was known from other than this command, and a command concerning something existing is a command to its continuation, like your saying to someone standing: "Stand."

﴿Eat and drink﴾: it is by the omission of a verb of saying, meaning: and We said to them. This command is a command of permission. Al-Sulami said: The drinking place of each person is where his guide (ra'id) has brought him down. So whoever's guide is his self, his drinking place is this world; or his heart, then his drinking place is the Hereafter; or his inner secret, then his drinking place is Paradise; or his spirit, then his drinking place is Salsabil; or his Lord, then his drinking place is the presence in witnessing, as He says: ﴿And their Lord gave them a pure drink﴾ (Al-Insan 76:21), purifying them thereby from everything other than Him. Eating was mentioned first because it is the primary aim, and drinking was mentioned second because the need for it arises after eating, and because the mention of the manna and quails precedes the bursting forth of water.

﴿from the provision of God﴾: (min) here indicates the starting point, and it may also be partitive. Since their food and drink were obtained by them without fatigue or effort, they were attributed to God Most High. This is an iltifat (a shift in grammatical person), since previously there was ﴿So We said: Strike﴾. Had it followed one consistent pattern, it would have said: "from Our provision." Unless you make the implied subject before "eat" refer to Moses, meaning: and Moses said: ﴿Eat and drink﴾, in which case there is no iltifat. Then ﴿from the provision of God﴾ is connected to "drink," and this is an instance of applying the second verb (i'mal al-thani, the grammatical principle that the nearer of two verbs governs the shared complement) according to the preference of the Basran school, for if it were an instance of applying the first verb, a pronoun would have been supplied in the second for what it needs, so it would have been: "eat and drink from it from the provision of God." It is not permissible to delete (from it) except in a poetic necessity, according to what some have stated, and poetic necessity and what is rare are not to be used to interpret the speech of God. Here "provision" means that which is provided, namely food from the manna and quails, and drink from the water of the springs. It was said that it is the water from which crops and fruits grow, so it is a provision from which one eats and drinks. In this view, ﴿from the provision of God﴾ combines the literal and the metaphorical, because drinking from water is literal, and eating is only of what arose from water, not that eating from water is literal. So taking "provision" to mean the common quality between food and water is preferable to this view.

Since their food and drink involved no burden or effort in obtaining it, it was fitting to attribute it to God Most High. Although all provisions are attributed to God Most High, whether or not the servant had a hand in earning them, the attribution was specifically to the name God, since it is the proper name that no one shares with Him, comprising all the other names. ﴿God is He who created you, then provided for you﴾ (Ar-Rum 30:40). ﴿Say: Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth? Say: God﴾ (Saba 34:24). ﴿Or who originates creation then repeats it﴾ (An-Naml 27:64). ﴿Who provides for you from the sky and the earth﴾ (Yunus 10:31). ﴿Is there a god with God?﴾ (An-Naml 27:60).

The Mu'tazila used this verse to argue that provision is only what is lawful, because the minimum level of this command is that it be permission, and so it required that provision be permitted. Hence, if an unlawful provision existed, then provision would be both permitted and forbidden, which is impermissible. The answer: provision here is not general, if what is meant by it is the manna, the quails, and the water gushing from the rock. The lawfulness of a particular kind of provision does not entail the lawfulness of all provision. This verse contains evidence for the permissibility of eating good foods and drinking pleasant beverages, and combining two kinds of food or two foods, all on condition that they are lawful. It is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) loved halwa and honey, that he drank cold, sweet water, that dates were soaked in water for him, that he combined cucumber with fresh dates, and that he gave some of his wives water to drink. It has also been reported from a group of the Companions and the Successors that they used to abstain from delicious food and appealing drink out of desire for what is with God Most High.

﴿And do not commit corruption on the earth, causing mischief﴾: when they were commanded to eat and drink from the provision of God, and that was not restricted for them by time, place, or quantity of food or drink (p. 231), this was a great favor and bounty to them, and it called for expansiveness in foods and drinks, and from this arises the force of anger and the force of domineering self-exaltation. He forbade them from what could arise from this, which is corruption, lest they meet those blessings with what nullifies them, which is corruption on the earth. Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-'Aliyah said: its meaning is "do not strive." Qatadah said: "do not travel." It was said: do not wrong one another regarding the drinking places among yourselves, since each tribe among you has been assigned a known drinking place. It was said: its meaning is: do not delay the midday meal, for when they delayed it, it spoiled. It was said: its meaning is: do not mix with the corrupters. It was said: its meaning is: do not persist in your corruption. It was said: do not transgress; this was said by Ibn Zayd. All these sayings are close to one another.

﴿on the earth﴾ (Al-Baqara 2:11): the majority hold that it is the land of the wandering (al-tih), though it is permissible that it refers to it and to other lands they might reach, where their corruption would reach, and it is permissible that it refers to all the lands. The article (al-) is for the generalization of the genus, and their corruption in it is in that the abundance of disobedience, insistence on transgressions, and insolence signal the cutting off of rain, the drought of lands, and the removal of blessings, and that is a retribution that encompasses the earth through corruption.

(causing mischief) is an emphatic circumstantial clause (hal mu'akkada, a circumstantial qualifier that reinforces the meaning of the main verb).

Al-Qushayri said, regarding God's words ﴿And when Moses asked for water﴾, the verse: the One who was able to bring water out of the hard rock was able to satisfy them without water, but this was to manifest the effect of the miracle in it, and to connect the place of seeking help with Him, and so that Moses, peace be upon him, would have some occupation with the excellence of the stone together with himself, and because his being commanded to strike with the staff was a kind of treatment. Then He willed that each tribe should proceed according to its own custom, without crowding out its companion. When He sufficed them for what they had asked, He commanded them to give thanks, to keep the command, and to avoid accumulating burdens, so He said: ﴿And do not commit corruption﴾. The watering places are different, and each one approaches its own drinking place: there is a sweet drinking place, a salty drinking place, a clear drinking place, and a turbid drinking place. Each people's own course leads them. Souls approach the watering places of desire, hearts approach the drinking places of piety, spirits approach the watering places of unveiling, and witnesses and secrets approach the watering places of realities by being snatched away from the reality of unity and of the Essence. The end of his words, summarized.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 61 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And when you said, "O Musa, we will not endure one kind of food"﴾: When they grew weary of remaining in the wilderness (al-tih) and of persisting on one single food, being far from the land they had been accustomed to and from the customs they had known, they reported what they found of their inability to endure this and their longing for what they used to be familiar with, and they asked Musa to ask God on their behalf. Most of the exegetes of the outward meaning (ahl al-zahir) hold that this request was a act of disobedience. They said: because they disliked the sending down of the manna (al-mann) and the quails (al-salwa), and that dislike is disobedience; and because Musa described what they asked for as "lesser" (adna) and what they were upon as "better" (khayr), and because his saying, "Would you exchange...?" (﴿أتَسْتَبْدِلُونَ﴾), is in the manner of rebuke.
The answer is that their saying, "we will not endure one kind of food," does not indicate only dissatisfaction with it, but they craved other things. As for the rebuke, it may be because of what it entails of losing what is more beneficial in this world or what is more beneficial in the Hereafter. As for the matter of "better," the discussion of it will come. Rather, it was a permissible request, and the evidence for this is that His saying, ﴿Eat and drink﴾ [al-Baqarah: 60], which came before this verse, at the sending down of the manna and the gushing forth of the spring, is not an obligation but a permission. Since this is so, their saying, "we will not endure one kind of food," was not disobedience, because one to whom various kinds of food have been permitted may well ask for other than them, either himself or through the messenger. And since asking the Prophet is closer to permission, they asked him about it. Also, one kind of food for forty years becomes tiresome, and other kinds are desired at that time; and also because they had not become accustomed to that kind. A person's desire for what he has become accustomed to, even if it is base, is greater than his desire for what he has not become accustomed to, even if it is noble. Also, that would be a cause of their moving away from the wilderness which they had grown weary of, because those foods are not found there, so they wished to settle elsewhere. Also, persistence on one food is a cause of diminished appetite, weakness of digestion and lack of desire, while abundance of kinds is the opposite. Thus it is established by this that exchanging one kind for another is fit to be an aim of sensible people, and it is established that there is nothing in the Qur'an indicating that they were forbidden from it; so it is established that it cannot be disobedience. And what confirms (p-232) this is His saying: ﴿Go down to a city, for you will have what you asked﴾, which is like an answer to what they requested. Had they been disobedient in that request, granting it would have been disobedience, and that is impermissible for the prophets, upon them be prayer and peace. He described the food as one, though it was two, because it was the manna and the quails which they were provided with in the wilderness; and because they meant by "one" what does not vary and does not change. Had a man's table had many dishes which he persisted upon every day without changing them, it would be said: "So-and-so eats only one food," meaning by the unity the negation of change and variation. It is also possible that they meant that the two are of one kind, since both together are of the food of the people of luxury and extravagance, whereas we are a people of farming, people of cultivation, so we want only what we are accustomed to and what we have been trained in of varied things, such as grains, herbs and the like. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned these two interpretations of "one."
It was also said: he referred to the word "food" in terms of its being singular, not its meaning. It was said: they used to eat the manna and the quails mixed together, so it becomes like a color that gathers things together and is called one color; this was said by Ibn Zayd. It was said: their food used to come with the attribute of unity; the manna descended upon them, and they ate of it for a period until they grew weary and tired of it; then it ceased from them, and the quails were sent down upon them, and they ate them for a period alone. It was said: by "one food" they meant the quails, because the manna was a drink or something they sweetened with, and they did not count anything as food except the quails. It was said: he expressed both by "one," just as "two" is used for "one," as in His saying: ﴿From them come out the pearl and the coral﴾ [al-Rahman: 22], whereas it comes out only from one of them, which is the salt and not the fresh. It was said: they said that at the sending down of one of them. It was said: its meaning is, "we will not endure that we are all rich, so that none of us seeks help from another," and he has used "one food" as a metaphor for their being of one kind, namely being people of wealth, so that none of them serves another; and so they were in the wilderness, and when they came out of it they returned to what they had been upon of the poverty of some and the wealth of others. These are nine sayings concerning the meaning of His saying: ﴿upon one food﴾.
