﴿So call upon your Lord for us﴾: its meaning: ask Him for us, and the object of the supplication is omitted, that is, "call upon your Lord for us that He bring forth such-and-such." The dialect of Banu 'Amir is (fad'i) with a kasra on the 'ayn, making "da'a" from the defective verbs of ya', like "rama yarmi." They asked Musa to supplicate for them with what they proposed, and he did not supplicate for them; because the answering of prophets is closer than the answering of others. Therefore they said "your Lord" and did not say "our Lord," because in that there is a specialness to him that they do not share, of intimate conversation with Him, His speaking to him, and His bringing him the Torah. It is as if they said: "Call upon for us the One who is good to you; as He has been good to you in things, so we hope that He will be good to us in answering your supplication."
﴿He will bring forth for us﴾: its jussive mood is on the answer to the imperative "ud'u" (call), and its like has passed in ﴿Fulfil My covenant, and I will fulfil your covenant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 40]. It was said: there is an omitted element whose estimate is: "Say to him, 'Bring forth,' and He will bring forth," jussive as an answer to this imperative "akhrij" (bring forth). It was said: "yukhrij" is jussive by a hidden lam, the lam of request, meaning "li-yukhrij," and this is not permitted according to the Basrans.
﴿of what the earth grows﴾: the object of "yukhrij" is omitted, and "min" is partitive: that is, edible things from what the earth grows; this is according to the view of Sibawayh. Al-Akhfash said: "min" is superfluous, the estimate being "what the earth grows," and "ma" is a relative pronoun, and the returning pronoun is omitted, its estimate being "tunbituhu" (it grows), and it has the conditions for permitting the omission. Some permitted that "ma" be a verbal noun, its estimate being "from the growth of the earth." Abu al-Baqa' said: that is not permitted, because the omitted object is a substance and cannot be described by growth, since growth is a verbal noun; and the attribution of growth to the earth is figurative, since the one who causes growth is God Most High, but when He placed in it the capacity for growth, He attributed the growth to it.
﴿from its herbs﴾: this is a substitute for His saying ﴿of what the earth grows﴾, by repeating the preposition, which is eloquent in speech, I mean that the preposition is repeated in the substitute. So "min" according to this estimate is partitive, as it is in "mimma tunbitu." It is connected to "yukhrij": either the first, or another one estimated, according to the disagreement over the governing element of the substitute: is it the first governing element, or is it a repetition of the governing element? The well-known view is the second. Al-Mahdawi and Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu al-Baqa' also permitted that "min" in His saying "min baqlihā" be for specifying the kind, and al-Mahdawi expressed it as being for specification. Then they differed: Abu al-Baqa' said its position is accusative as a circumstantial element (hal) from the omitted pronoun, its estimate being "what the earth grows, being from its herbs," and he mentioned this view first, saying: it is also permitted that it be a substitute for the first "ma" by repeating the preposition. As for al-Mahdawi and Ibn 'Atiyya, they maintained, together with their saying that "min" in "min baqlihā" is a substitute for "mimma tunbitu," that "min" in "mimma tunbitu" is partitive, while "min" in "min baqlihā" according to their claim is for specifying the kind, so the meanings of the two particles differ, and the difference of meaning is like the difference of the particles, so substitution is not permitted, unless one holds that "min" in His saying "mimma tunbitu al-ard" is for specifying the kind, in which case the view of substitution could be built upon its being for specifying the kind. The preferred view is what we have set forth: that "min" in both places is partitive. As for its being for specifying the kind, our companions (the Basrans) have rejected it and interpreted what those who affirm it cite as evidence. The meaning of "baql" here is: the choice herbs that people eat, such as mint, celery, leek and the like; this was said by al-Zamakhshari. Yahya ibn Wathhab, Talha ibn Musarrif and others read "wa-quthta'ihā" with a dammah on the qaf, and it has already been mentioned that this is a dialect.
﴿and its garlic (fūmihā)﴾: its discussion has passed, and the exegetes have six sayings concerning it. The first: that it is garlic (al-thawm), and the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, "wa-thawmihā" with the letter thā', clarifies it, and it is the fitting one with herbs, lentils and onions. The second: said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Suddi: that it is wheat. The third: that it is all grains. The fourth: that it is bread; said by Mujahid, Ibn 'Ata' and Ibn Zayd. The fifth: that it is chickpeas. The sixth: that it is the ear of grain.
﴿and its lentils and its onions﴾: The conditions of these five which they mentioned differ. They mentioned first what combines heat, cold, moisture and dryness, for herbs include what is cold and moist, like endive, and what is hot and dry, like celery and dill, and what is hot and has a transverse moisture, like mint. Second: the cucumber, which is cold and moist. Third: garlic, which is hot and dry. Fourth: lentils, which are cold and dry. Fifth: onions, which are hot and moist, and when cooked become cold and moist. Accordingly, this is the order of mention of these five.
﴿He said: Would you exchange﴾: the pronoun in "qāla" (he said) is apparently returning to Musa, and it is possible that it returns to the Lord Most High, and this is supported by ﴿Go down to a city, for you will have what you asked﴾. The hamza in ﴿Would you exchange?﴾ is for denunciation, and al-istibdal is taking in exchange (al-i'tiyad). Ubayy read "atubaddilūna" (do you cause to exchange), and this is figurative, because the exchanging is not theirs; it belongs to God Most High; but since the exchange came about by their request, they were treated as exchangers, and the meaning was: "Do you ask for an exchange of..."
﴿that which is lesser for that which is better﴾: "alladhī" is the object of "tastabdilūna," and it is the acquired thing, and the "alladhī" to which the "ba'" entered is the thing relinquished, as we have established in more than one place.
﴿huwa adnā﴾ is a relative clause for "alladhī," and here "huwa" must be affirmed according to the view of the Basrans, since there is no lengthening in the relative clause; "adnā" is the predicate of "huwa," and it is the comparative form, and "min" and "ma" entered upon it with omission, because it is known; the omission of both was made good by the comparative form being a predicate, and if it occurred other than as a predicate, like being a circumstantial element or an attribute, the omission would be rare. Its estimate is: "lesser than that one food." The omission of both was also made good by the mention after it of the thing compared against, namely His saying ﴿for that which is better﴾. He used the singular in ﴿alladhī huwa adnā﴾ because he referred by it to the food which is "of what the earth grows," and to "ma" in His saying ﴿mimma tunbitu﴾; so he took account of the thing substituted-from; for had he taken account of the substitute, he would have said, "Would you exchange those which are lesser?" The discussion of "adnā" has already passed when speaking of the vocabulary, and we mentioned the three sayings concerning it.
Zuhayr al-Furqubi, who is also called Zuhayr al-Kisa'i, read "adna'" with a hamza. Some compilers of tafsir made an error in attributing this reading to al-Kisa'i; he said: "Zuhayr and al-Kisa'i read anomalously 'adna'," and he thought this was the reading of al-Kisa'i and made Zuhayr and al-Kisa'i two persons, whereas he is Zuhayr al-Kisa'i, known by that and by al-Furqubi, so he is one man.

Regarding the meaning of "al-adnā" (the lesser) and "al-khayr" (the better) here, there are several opinions. The first: al-Zajjaj said: the excellence of things is by their value, and these herbs have no worth or high value, whereas the manna and the quails are higher in value and greater in worth. Al-Zamakhshari chose this view, saying: "closer in rank and lesser in measure. Nearness and proximity are used to express lowness of value, so one says: 'he is of the lowest place (adna al-mahall) and near in rank,' just as distance is used to express the opposite, so one says: 'far of place, far in rank,' meaning elevation and loftiness." The end of his words; and it is from the words of al-Zajjaj. The second: that the manna and quails are what Allah bestowed as a favour and commanded them to eat, and in continuing what Allah commanded and in thanking His blessing there is reward and treasure in the Hereafter, whereas what they asked for is devoid of these qualities, so it was lesser in this respect. The third: that the preference occurs in terms of goodness and pleasure, and the manna and quails are undoubtedly better in taste than the herbs they requested. The fourth: that the manna and quails involve no burden, effort or hardship in obtaining them, whereas herbs are obtained only after the hardship of ploughing, sowing, tending and watering; and what is obtained without hardship is better than what is obtained with hardship. The fifth: that the manna and quails are undoubtedly lawful and pure, since they descend from Allah, whereas grains and land are subject to defects and usurpation, and haram and doubtful matters may enter them; and what is purely lawful is better than what haram and doubt may enter. The sixth: that the manna and quails surpass what they asked for in the kind of nourishment and its benefit. The summary of these opinions: is the lowness and goodness relative to value, or to obeying the command and what follows from it, or to pleasure, or to burden, or to lawfulness, or to kind? Six opinions. As for the reading of Zuhayr, it is from "al-dinā'" (baseness).

It has been mentioned that "adnā" without hamza is said to have originally had a hamza, and was eased, as in this reading; and whoever says it is by transposition (qalb), and that its origin is "adwan," then "al-dana'a" (baseness) and "al-dun" (lowness) return to one meaning, which is lowliness; and in terms of meaning it is a better counterpart to His words: ﴿with that which is better﴾. And whoever makes "adnā" mean "aqrab" (nearer), because "al-adwan" and "al-adna'" are opposed by "al-khayr," and "adnā" in the sense of "aqrab" is opposed by "al-ab'ad" (farther). The "min" and its complement were omitted after His words ﴿He is better﴾, for the reason we mentioned concerning His words "he is adnā," owing to the superlative form occurring as a predicate, and its estimate is: "than it," i.e., than ﴿that which is adnā﴾. These two relative clauses are nominal sentences because of the permanence of the nominal sentence, and "al-khayr" is the superlative form, because it carries no indication of a specific time; rather, in it is the affirmation of lowness and goodness without restriction to a time, unlike the verbal sentence, in which time would be specified or stretched into metaphor if one did not intend specification. So linking with what is literally indicative of non-specification of time was more eloquent. And the relative clause of "mā" in His words "from what the earth produces" (mimmā tunbitu) is a verbal sentence, because the verb in their view conveys renewal and occurrence, and growing is continually renewed, so each place suited what fits it of relative clauses.

* *

﴿Go down to a city﴾: In the speech there is an omission, on the estimate that the speaker of ﴿Do you exchange﴾ is Moses; and the estimate of the omitted part: so Moses called upon his Lord and He answered him, ﴿He said: Go down﴾ [al-A'raf: 24]. The meaning of descending has been mentioned, and it is said: "he descended into the valley": he settled in it; and "he descended from it": he came out of it; as if the one arriving at a land falls upon it. It was read "uhbutū" with a ḍamma on the bā', and both are dialects, and the more eloquent is the kasra; and the majority read "miṣran" here with tanwīn. Al-Hasan, Talha, al-A'mash and Aban ibn Taghlib read it without tanwīn, and it is clear thus in the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, the codex of Abdullah, and some codices of Uthman. As for those who read it with tanwīn, they mean a city of the cities, unspecified, and they argued from the command to enter the town, and from their settling in Syria after the wandering, and from the fact that what they asked for of herbs and other things would only be found in cities. This is the view of Qatada, al-Suddi, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd. It was said: it is an unspecified city, but it is one of the cities of the Holy Land, by the evidence of ﴿Enter the Holy Land﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 21]. It was said: by His words "miṣran," though indefinite, He meant Egypt, the city of Pharaoh; and this is from the use of an indefinite noun intended as a definite, as you say: "bring me a man," meaning Zayd. Ashhab said: Malik told me: "it is Misr, your town, the dwelling of Pharaoh." And those among the grammarians and exegetes whose words we have reviewed permitted that this tanwīn-marked "Miṣr" be the proper noun. The meaning of His words ﴿that you settle your people in Egypt with houses﴾ [Yunus: 87] — they said: it was declined although it has both proper-nounness and feminine gender, just as "Hind" and "Da'd" are declined, to balance one of the two causes, owing to the lightness of the name because its middle is quiescent; so said al-Akhfash; or it was declined because it treated the word in the manner of a place, making it masculine, so only one cause remained and it was declined. Al-Zamakhshari compared it, regarding the prohibition of declension, to the proper names Nuh and Lut, which were declined, although both have proper-nounness and foreignness, owing to the lightness of the name by being triliteral with quiescent middle. This is not as they have claimed, that it resembles Hind or resembles Nuh; for Misr combines three causes, namely: feminine gender, proper-nounness, and foreignness, so its non-declension is obligatory, unlike Hind, which has only proper-nounness and feminine gender. Moreover, some grammarians disagreed regarding Hind, claiming that it is permissible only to prohibit its declension, and claimed there is no evidence for what the grammarians assert of its declension in the verse:

Da'd did not wrap herself in the excess of her waist-wrapper, nor was Da'd given to drink in the cups.

And unlike Nuh: foreignness is not considered except in what is other than triliteral with quiescent middle; but when it is triliteral with quiescent middle, it is declined. Isa ibn Umar permitted prohibiting its declension by analogy with Hind, though it was not heard from the Arabs except declined; so it is analogy upon a disputed point opposed to Arab usage, and therefore it must be discarded.

Al-Hasan ibn Bahr said: the meaning of His words ﴿miṣran﴾ is the Holy House, meaning that the word, though indefinite, refers to a specific one, as we said regarding the view of one who said he meant by it, though indefinite, the specific Egypt. As for one who reads "Miṣra" without tanwīn, the meaning is the proper noun Misr, which is the house of Pharaoh. Some people considered unlikely the view of one who said it is Pharaoh's Egypt; he said: because they went out from Egypt, and were commanded to descend to the Holy Land to fight the tyrants, but they refused, so they were punished with wandering for forty years for their failure to fight the tyrants, and for their saying: ﴿Go you and your Lord and fight, for we are sitting here﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 24]; so they all died in the wandering, and their children remained, and they obeyed Allah's command and descended to Syria, fought the tyrants, then returned to the Holy House; and no exegete or historian has stated explicitly that they descended from the wandering to Egypt. End of his words. So it is concluded from the tanwīn reading that the meaning is an unspecified city, neither from Syria nor from elsewhere; or an unspecified city among the cities of Syria; or a specified one, which is the Holy House; or Pharaoh's Egypt. These are four opinions.

﴿For you shall have what you asked﴾: this sentence is the answer to the command, as it is answered by a jussive verb; and the disagreement that applies there applies here too: whether "uhbiṭū miṣran" was implicitly given the sense of "tahubbū" (you should descend), or a condition with its verb was implied after the verb of command, as if he said: "if you descend to a city, then for you is what you asked." In that there are two omissions: the first: what connects this sentence to what precedes it, its estimate: "then for you therein is what you asked." The second: the pronoun returning to "mā," its estimate: "what you asked for," and the conditions for permitting the omission are present. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and Yahya ibn Wathhab read "sa'altum" with a kasra on the sīn, and this is from the mixing of dialects; for in "sa'ala" there are two dialects: one in which the 'ayn is a hamza, so its pattern is fa'ala; and the second in which the 'ayn is a waw, you say: "sa'ala yas'alu," so the alif is converted from a waw, and what indicates that it is from waw is their saying: "they two exchange requests (yatasāwalān)," just as you say: "yatajāwabān." When he gave the sīn a kasra, he imagined that he had opened it, and so brought the 'ayn as a hamza. The poet said:

When you come to them and ask them, you find in them a present excuse.

The original is sā'altahum, and the well-known usage is to convert the hamza into a yā', so you say sāyaltahum; so he combined the substitute, which is the yā', with what was substituted, which is the hamza; but when compelled he put the hamza before the alif of fā'il. Ibn Jinni said: it is possible that the hamza in "sa'altum" was converted into a yā', as it was converted into an alif in His words:

Hudhayl asked the Messenger of Allah about an indecency,

so the sīn took a kasra before the yā', then he noticed the hamza and made it a hamza.

The meaning: what you asked for of herbs and grains which you chose over the manna and quails. It was said: what you asked for of relying on your own management in the interests of your livelihood and the affairs of your sustenance.

﴿And humiliation and wretchedness were stamped upon them﴾: The meaning of "ḍarb" here is imposition and decree upon them, from "daraba al-amīr al-ba'th 'alā al-jaysh" (the commander imposed the dispatch upon the army), and like the Arab saying: "ḍarbatu lāzib" (an inevitable blow); and it is said: "daraba al-ḥākim 'alā al-yad" (the judge imposed a restriction on the hand), and "daraba al-dahr ḍarabātih" (time struck its blows), i.e., imposed its impositions. It was said: its meaning is encompassing them and enveloping them, taken from "ḍaraba al-qibāb" (he pitched the tents), and from it the words of al-Farazdaq:

The spider wove its web over you, and the revealed Book decreed upon you with it.

It was said: its meaning is that they clung to them, from "ḍarabtu al-ḥā'iṭ bi al-ṭīn" (I plastered the wall with clay): I stuck it to it. It was said: its meaning is: were placed, from "ḍarabtu al-ṭīn kharazan" (I shaped the clay into pottery), i.e., humiliation and wretchedness were placed upon them. As for "al-dhilla" (humiliation): it was said: it is their disgrace through what was imposed upon them of the poll-tax which they pay "from a position of submission, while they are humbled" (ʿan yadin wa hum ṣāghirūn). It was said: it is what they were obliged to in displaying a distinctive dress, so that it would be known they are Jews and not mingle with the Muslims. It was said: it is poverty of soul and its avarice; for you see no community among the communities more abject and more covetous than the Jews. As for "al-maskana" (wretchedness): it is humility, so no Jew is seen without visible humility; or it is the tribute, which is the poll-tax, said by al-Hasan and Qatada; or destitution and need, said by Abu al-'Aliya; or what they display of their poor condition for fear that the poll-tax be multiplied upon them; or weakness, so you see him with still movements and little rising. The author of al-Muntakhab considered unlikely the view of one who explained "al-dhilla" as the poll-tax, because the poll-tax was not imposed upon them from the beginning of their affair. It was said: this is among the miracles, because he (ﷺ) reported it, and it was as he reported. The ones upon whom humiliation and wretchedness were stamped are the Jews contemporary with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); this is said by the majority; or those who disbelieved in the signs of Allah and killed the prophets without right. And those who said: ﴿Ask your Lord for us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 68], and whoever followed them among their descendants. Three opinions.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 61 (part 3 of 3):

﴿And they incurred wrath from Allah﴾: The explanation of (bā'a) has already been given. According to the one who says (bā'a) means "returned," the bā' is for circumstance (ḥāl), meaning "accompanied by wrath." According to the one who says it means "deserved" (istaḥaqqa), the bā' is an extra particle (ṣila), as in: lā yuqra'anna bil-suwar (meaning: they deserved wrath). According to the one who says it means "descended and settled" or "were equal," the bā' is adverbial of place (ẓarfiyya): on the first view it is linked to an omitted element, on the second it is not linked to anything, and on the third it is linked to (bā'a) itself. Al-Akhfash claimed that the bā' in His saying (bi-ghaḍab) is for causation (sabab), so on this view it is linked to (bā'a), and the object of (bā'a) is omitted, meaning: they deserved punishment because of Allah's wrath upon them. (Bā'a) is also used for good: ﴿We will surely settle them in the Garden in lofty chambers﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 58], ﴿And We had certainly settled the Children of Israel in a truthful settlement﴾ [Yunus: 93], ﴿We settle in the Garden wherever we will﴾ [al-Zumar: 74]. And for evil: ﴿And they incurred wrath from Allah﴾, ﴿that you should bear the sin of me and your sin﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 29], ﴿so they incurred wrath upon wrath﴾ [al-Baqarah: 90]. The use of both meanings has come in the hadith: "I acknowledge Your blessing upon me and I acknowledge my sin." Some people said: bā' only comes for evil.

The wrath here is the affliction and retributions that befell them in this world, or the punishment that will befall them in the Hereafter. (Bā'ū) is in the sense of yabū'ūn, as in ﴿The approaching one has drawn near﴾ [al-Najm: 57], ﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾ [al-Qamar: 1].

(min Allah) may be linked to (bā'ū) if (bā'a) means "returned," as if they had been turning toward Allah the Exalted, so by their disobedience they returned from Him, i.e., from His presence, with wrath. It may also be linked to an omitted element and be in the position of a qualifier (ṣifa), meaning: with wrath coming from Allah. This latter view is evident if (bā'a) means "deserved" or "descended and settled," and the first view is remote. Describing the wrath as coming from Allah is a magnification of the wrath and an exaltation of its status.

﴿That is because they﴾: the demonstrative refers to the incurring of wrath, or to the incurring and the humiliation, and it is the subject (mubtada'), and the prepositional phrase after it is the predicate (khabar); the bā' is for causation, meaning: that is by their disbelief and killing.

﴿They used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah﴾: the signs (āyāt) are the nine miracles and others that Moses brought, or the Torah, or some of its verses, such as the verses that describe the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or those containing stoning, or the Qur'an, or all the signs of Allah sent down upon the messengers; these are five opinions. The attribution of the signs to Allah is because they come from Him, the Exalted.

﴿And they killed the prophets﴾: they killed Yahya, Sha'ya and Zakariyya. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that the Children of Israel killed seventy prophets, and in another narration three hundred prophets, in the early part of the day, and the market of their killing was established at its end. On this basis the reading of one who reads (yuqattilūn) with the emphatic doubling is explained, due to the apparent intensification in the killing; this is the reading of 'Ali. Al-Hasan read (wa-taqtulūn) with the letter tā', and this would be an iltifāt (shift of grammatical person). It is narrated from him with the letter yā' like the majority.

There is no difference in meaning between (al-nabiyyīn) and (al-anbiyā'), because when both plurals are preceded by the definite article they are equal, unlike their situation when they are indefinite, since the sound plural then clearly indicates paucity, while the broken plural on the pattern af'ilā' clearly indicates abundance. Nafi' read with hamza: al-nabiyyīn, al-nabī', al-anbiyā' and al-nubū'a, except that Qalun substituted and assimilated in al-Ahzab in: ﴿if a woman gives herself to the Prophet﴾ [al-Ahzab: 50] if he intends it, and in ﴿do not enter the houses of the Prophet unless﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53], in connected speech. The majority read without hamza, and the discussion of it has already been given in the section on vocabulary.

﴿without right﴾: it is linked to His saying (wa-taqtulūn), and it is in the position of an accusative as a circumstantial element (ḥāl) from the pronoun in (taqtulūn), meaning: you kill them with emphasis. It has been said: it may also be a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: killing without right. On both views it is an emphasis. This does not conflict with the fact that the killing of prophets divides into killing with right and killing without right; rather, whatever killing of them occurred was only without right, because a prophet is protected from committing any act that would deserve killing for him; this qualifier came as a way of reproaching their killing and denouncing their deed with their prophets, meaning: without right according to them, i.e., they did not claim in their killing any justification by which they deserved to kill them in their view. It has been said: that came as an emphasis, like His saying: ﴿but it is the hearts within the breasts that go blind﴾ [al-Hajj: 46], since the killing of a prophet occurs only without right, and no prophet ever came with anything that would require his killing; rather, whoever of them was killed was killed out of hatred for him and an increase in his station. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: no prophet among the prophets was ever killed except one who had not been commanded to fight, and everyone who was commanded to fight was given victory. It has been said: "the right" (al-ḥaqq) is definite here because it refers to what is known in His saying, peace be upon him: "The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except in one of three cases." As for the indefinite, what is intended by it is emphasis of generality, meaning: there was no right there at all, neither what the Muslims know nor anything else.

﴿That is because they disobeyed and used to transgress﴾: (dhālika) is a response to the first and a repetition of it, so the same demonstrative is used for what the first (dhālika) pointed to. It may also be that it is a reference to the disbelief and killing mentioned, in which case it is neither a repetition nor an emphasis. Its meaning: what led them to deny the signs of Allah and kill the prophets was only the prior occurrence of their disobedience and transgression, which emboldened them toward that, since sins are the courier of disbelief.

﴿Rather, their hearts have been sealed by what they used to earn﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 14], ﴿And they said, "Our hearts are uncovered." Rather, Allah has cursed them for their disbelief﴾ [al-Baqarah: 88], ﴿and their saying, "Our hearts are closed." Rather, Allah has sealed them for their disbelief﴾ [al-Nisa': 155].

The linguistic explanation of disobedience (iṣyān) and transgression (i'tidā') has already been given. Transgression here has been explained as their going beyond what Allah had set as right for them to falsehood. It has been said: persistence in opposition and the killing of prophets. It has been said: disobedience by breaking the covenant and transgression by the frequent killing of prophets. It has been said: transgression through the cause of opposition and persistence in that for a long time, transmitted from Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The Children of Israel differed after Moses by five hundred years, when the children of captives multiplied among them, and they differed after Jesus by one hundred years." It has been said: it is transgression regarding the Sabbath, as He the Exalted said: ﴿And We said to them, "Do not transgress regarding the Sabbath"﴾ [al-Nisa': 154].

The (mā) in His saying ﴿by what they disobeyed﴾ is verbal-source (maṣdariyya), meaning: that is by their disobedience. Transgression was not conjoined to disobedience, lest the harmony of the verse-endings be lost, and to indicate that transgression had become like something that continually proceeded from them. When the Exalted mentioned the descent of punishment upon them, namely the striking of humiliation and poverty and the incurring of wrath, and explained its cause, He began with the greatest of the causes, which is their disbelief in the signs of Allah, then followed it with what comes next in magnitude, which is the killing of prophets, then followed that with what results of sins and what extends of injustice. The author of al-Muntakhab said this is the meaning of it.

It appears that His saying: "That is because they used to disbelieve and kill" is a cause for the striking of humiliation and poverty and the incurring of wrath, and that the demonstrative in His saying "That is by what they disobeyed" refers to disbelief and killing, and "by what" is a cause for both; thus disobedience returns to disbelief and transgression returns to killing. He has mentioned two things and matched them with two things, just as He first mentioned two things, the striking and the incurring, and matched them with two things, disbelief and killing. This is a figure of "wrapping and spreading" (laff wa-nashr) in both places, and this is among the beauties of speech and the excellence of its composition. It goes out thereby from emphasis, which is not resorted to except when needed, when the speech is too remote to be taken as introducing new information.

These verses contained, among the subtle favors and wondrous kindnesses toward the Children of Israel, several points. Among them: they were commanded to enter the town where they could take refuge and eat from its fruits whatever they desired; then they were charged with a small act and word, namely entering its gate prostrating, and their saying one word repentantly; and forgiveness of their great crimes and grave sins was made to follow from this small deed. They opposed both commands, in deed and in word, following their custom of not complying, so He punished them for that with the severest punishment.

Then the Exalted mentioned what Moses, peace be upon him, was upon of compassion toward them and seeking good for them, namely that he prayed to Allah for them for water. He left it to Allah's own action, so He produced for them from striking the rock with the staff springs through which flowed what sufficed them of water, abundant, in accordance with the description the Exalted mentioned, that these springs were according to the number of the tribes, so that no rivalry or contention would occur among them. He informed them that this was a provision from Him, and they were commanded to eat from it and drink, then they were forbidden from corruption, since that is a cause for cutting off provision.

Then the Exalted mentioned their weariness with the provision with which He had favored them, so they persisted in seeking what had been familiar to them, saying to their prophet: "Call upon your Lord for us." This was in accordance with his custom with them, for he used to commune with his Lord regarding what returned to them of the good of their religion and their worldly affairs. He mentioned His reproof of them for what they asked of him, namely the exchange of the base for the precious, and by what involves no toil in acquiring it, since what they sought required the spending of their appointed times for worshipping their Lord in obtaining it. Despite that, these became harmful, injurious foods, bringing bad humors, from which the light of sight and insight is extinguished, unlike what Allah had provided them, which is one good thing, from which bodily health and quality of perception arise.

Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, used to sip barley flour and drink fresh water over it; his intellect was the brightest of the minds of his time, and he was physically strong, campaigning one year and performing Hajj the next.

Then they were commanded to settle where their aim lay and to descend to the source of what they had asked for. Then the Exalted informed of what He punished them with, namely making them humiliated and poor and incurring His wrath upon them, and that this was a consequence of their disbelief in the signs, which are the cause of faith, because of the supernatural things they contained that made humans and jinn incapable, and of their killing those who were a cause of their guidance, namely the prophets, since by following them comes honor in this world and success in the next; and that what drew disbelief and killing upon them was disobedience and transgression, which had preceded from them before engaging in disbelief and killing.

And he said:
Indeed, matters, even small ones, are such that the great is stirred by them.
And he said:
You belittle evil, yet it may grow.

﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Christians, and the Sabians, whoever believes in God and the Last Day and does righteous deeds, for them is their reward with their Lord, and no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve.﴾ ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised the mount above you: "Hold firmly to what We have given you, and remember what is in it, that you may be mindful of God."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 63] ﴿Then you turned away after that, and but for the grace of God upon you and His mercy, you would have been among the losers.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 64] ﴿And you certainly knew those among you who transgressed on the Sabbath, so We said to them: "Be apes, despised and driven away."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 65] ﴿So We made it a deterrent for what lay before it and what lay after it, and an admonition for the God-conscious.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 66].

**Hada (هادَ):** Its alif is converted from a waw, and its present tense is yahud, meaning "he repented." Alternatively, it is from a ya', with present tense yahid, meaning "he moved." The first is preferable, because of God's words: ﴿Indeed, we have turned back to You﴾ [al-A'raf: 156]. The discussion of the word "al-Yahud" will come when we reach it in the Qur'an, God willing.

**Al-Nasara (النَّصارى):** This is the plural of nasran and nasranah, like nadman and nadmanah. Sibawayh said, and he recited:

*"Both of them fell down, and her head was made to prostrate, as a Christian woman prostrates, not inclining."*

Al-Tabari recited:

*"He stays, when the evening turns, bent over, and in the morning he is by it, and he is a Christian, sunburnt."*

The word *nasran* (نَصْرانًا) is not declined (lit. it is prevented from tanwin) out of necessity, though it is a diptote in principle; its feminine is *nasranah*. Sibawayh said: however, it is not used in speech except with the ya' of relation, so it is said *kalihyan*, *lihyani*, and *ka-ahmari*. Al-Khalil said: the singular of al-Nasara is *nasri*, like *mahri* and *mahara*. It has been said that it is a relative noun derived from *Nasrah*, a village where Jesus dwelt. Qatadah said: they were attributed to *Nasirah*, a village where they settled. On this view, it is among the changes in the relative form.

**Al-Sabi'in (الصّابِئِينَ):** This is the plural of *al-sa'ibun*. It has been said that they are those who leave a well-known religion for another, from *subu'* of the tooth and the star. It is said: *sabaʾat al-nujum*, meaning the stars rose; *sabaʾat thaniyyat al-ghulam*, meaning the boy's front tooth came out; and *sabaʾat ʿala al-qawm*, meaning it came upon them suddenly. A poet said:

*"When the forward horses turn away from us, I think of their necks as the eastern side of a camel."*

As for the one who reads it without a hamza, we will discuss his reading later. Al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: they are between the Jews and the Magians. Qatadah and al-Kalbi said: they are between the Jews and the Christians; they shave the middle of their heads and castrate themselves. Al-Khalil said: they are similar to the Christians; their qiblah is the direction of the south wind; they acknowledge Noah, recite the Psalms, and worship the angels. ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn Yahya said: there is neither trace nor sign of them. Al-Maghribi, quoting al-Sabi, author of the *Rasa'il*, said: they are close to the Mu'tazilah, and they believe in the governance of the stars. Mujahid said: they are a people with no religion; they are neither Jews nor Christians. Ibn Abi Najih said: a people whose religion is a mixture of Judaism and Magianism; their slaughtered animals are not eaten. Ibn Zayd said: a people who say, "There is no god but God," but who have no works and no book; they were in al-Jazirah and Mosul. It is also narrated from al-Hasan and Qatadah that they are a people who worship the angels, pray the five prayers facing the qiblah, and recite the Psalms. Ziyad ibn Abi Sufyan saw them and wished to remove the jizyah (poll tax) from them, until he learned that they worship the angels. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they are a people from among the Jews and Christians whose marriage is not permitted and whose slaughtered animals are not eaten. Abu al-ʿAliyah said: a people from among the People of the Book, whose slaughtered animals are like those of the People of the Book; they recite the Psalms and differ from them in the rest of their practices. Al-Hasan and al-Hakam said: a people like the Magians. It has been said: a monotheist people who believe in the influence of the stars and that they are the agents of action.

Abu Sa'id al-Istakhri gave a fatwa, when al-Qadir billah asked him about them, declaring them disbelievers. It has also been said: a people who worship the stars. They have two opinions. The first is that the Creator of the world is God, but He commanded the glorification of the stars and taking them as a qiblah for prayer, glorification, and supplication. The second is that God created the spheres and the stars, and the stars are the ones who govern what is in this world of good and evil, health and sickness; therefore it is obligatory on mankind to glorify them, because they are the gods who govern this world, and they worship God. This doctrine is attributed to the people to whom Abraham, peace be upon him, was sent, refuting them.

**Al-Ajr (الأجْرُ):** This is the verbal noun of *ajara* (أجَرَ), *ya'juru*, and it is used for the thing by which one is rewarded, which is the reward. *Al-ujur* means the setting of a crooked break. *Al-ijar* means a roof. The poet said:

*"Its forward parts appear through the dust like an army in rows upon the roofs."*

**Al-Raf' (الرَّفْعُ):** This is well known; it means the highest part of a thing. Its verb is *rafa'a*, *yarfa'u*.

**Al-Tur (الطُّورُ):** This is a name for every mountain, according to Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, and Qatadah. Or it is the mountain that grows plants, as opposed to one that does not, said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Dahhak. Or it is the mountain upon which Moses conversed with God, upon our Prophet and him be blessings and peace. Al-ʿAjjaj said:

*"Its wings draw near from the Tur, so the falcon swoops, when the falcon strikes."*

Another said:

*"If Salma's jinn see her and become familiar with her, and if the companion of the Tur sees Salma, he will descend."*

Its root meaning is "side," and from it comes *tawar al-dar*, the side of the house. Mujahid said: it is the general term for mountain in Syriac.

**Al-Quwwah (القُوَّةُ):** This means strength, and it is the verbal noun of *qawiya* (قَوِيَ), *yaqwa*. The Tayy tribe say *qawa*, pronouncing the ʿayn with fatha and the ya' with fatha, so it converts into an alif. They say in *baqiya*: *baqa*, and in *zahiya*: *zaha*. This also occurs in the speech of others. ʿAlqamah ibn ʿAbdah al-Tamimi said:

*"Longing has increased until the pupil of his eye keeps overflowing with tears, abundant and flowing."*

This root is rare: its ʿayn and lam are both waws (or both are weak letters of the same kind).

**Al-Tawalli (التَّوَلِّي):** This means turning away after turning toward.

**Law la (لَوْلا):** This is used for urging, in the sense of *hallā*, and a verb follows it, either explicitly or implicitly. It is also a particle of prohibition for the existence of something, so it has an answer clause. After it comes a noun in the nominative governed by it according to al-Farra', by an omitted verb according to al-Kisa'i, and by the inchoative (mubtada') according to the Basrans. The predicate is omitted according to most of them. According to some of them there is a distinction which we mentioned in *Manhaj al-Salik*, our work. The answer clause is not the predicate, contrary to Abu al-Husayn ibn al-Tarawah. If a pronoun occurs after it, it is a nominative pronoun of an inchoative according to the Basrans. It is also permissible for a genitive pronoun to follow it, so you say: *lawlani*, *lawlaka*, *lawlahu*, and so on to the end. It is in the genitive position with *law la* according to Sibawayh, and in the nominative position according to al-Akhfash. The genitive pronoun is borrowed for the nominative, just as they borrowed the nominative pronoun for the genitive in their saying: *ma ana kanat*, and *la anta kana*. The preference between the two views is mentioned in grammar.

* *

Whoever holds that *law la* is negative, and takes from this the verse ﴿Why was there not a town that believed?﴾ [Yunus: 98], his statement is far from correct.

**Al-Sabt (السَّبْتَ):** This is the name of a known day. It is derived either from *al-sabt*, which means cutting, or from *al-subat*, which means rest and ease. Abu al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzi said: this is an error; it is not known in the speech of the Arabs that *sabata* means "he rested." *Al-sabt* also means shaving and travelling. The poet said:

*"With a camel whose straps are taut: its day is sabt, and its night is dhamil."*

*Al-sabt* also means a sandal, because it is cut, like threshing and grazing. Ibn Juraij said: the day was called Saturday because it is a piece of time. Labid said:

*"I sang the sabt before the race of Dahis, if the stubborn soul had immortality."*

**Al-Qird (القِرْدُ):** This is well known. Its plural follows the analogical pattern *fu'ul*, like *qird* and *qurud*, and *jism* and *jusum*. Rarely it follows *fi'alah*, like *qird* and *qiradah*, and *hisl* and *hisalah*.

**Al-Khasʾ (الخَسْءُ):** This means humiliation and expulsion. Its verb is *khasa'a*, and it can be intransitive or transitive. It is said: *khasa'a al-kalb khusuwwan*, meaning the dog was humiliated and driven away; and *khasa'tuhu*, meaning I drove him away and expelled him. *Khasa'a* is like *raja'a rujuʿan*, and *raja'tuhu raj'an*.

**Al-Nakal (النَّكالُ):** This means a lesson. Its root meaning is prevention, and *al-nakl* means a shackle. Muqatil said: *al-nakal* means punishment.

**Al-Yad (اليَدُ):** This is a well-known limb, whose root is *yadayy*, and this root has been made explicit. They have replaced its ya' with a hamza, and they say: *qata'a Allahu adayhi*, meaning "may God cut off his two hands." It is pluralized on the pattern *af'il*, and they say *aydin*, whose root is *aydi*. It has been used for blessing and kindness. As for *al-ayadi*, it is in reality a plural of a plural. Its use for blessing is more frequent than its use for the limb, just as its use for the limb is more frequent than its use for blessing.

**Khalf (خَلْفَ):** This is an adverb of indefinite place, of intermediate flexibility, and it can also be a descriptive word. It is said: *rajulun khalf*, meaning a bad man; and *sakata alfan wa nataqa khalfan*, meaning he was silent for a thousand and spoke badly.

**Mawʿizah (مَوْعِظَةٌ):** This is a *maf'alah* form from *al-wa'z*. *Al-wa'z* means reminding with what is good in a way that softens the heart. Breaking the ʿayn of a word of this pattern, and of the pattern *maf'il*, is the analogical rule, though some irregular forms, such as *mu'alah* and *kalim*, which the grammarians mentioned, came with a fatha on the ʿayn.

* *

God's words: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and those who were Jews﴾, and so on the verse.

It was revealed concerning the companions of Salman. He accompanied some Christian worshippers, and one of them said to him: "The time of a prophet has drawn near. If you reach him, believe in him." He saw from them great devotion. When the Prophet ﷺ came, he told him of their situation and asked him about them, and this verse was revealed. Ibn Ishaq, al-Tabari, and al-Bayhaqi narrated this story at length. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that it was revealed at the beginning of Islam, and God decreed through it that whoever believed in Muhammad ﷺ, and whoever remained upon his Judaism, Christianity, or Sabianism while believing in God and the Last Day, would have his reward. Then He abrogated what He had decreed of this by His words: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 85].

All the laws were brought back to the law of Muhammad ﷺ. Others besides Ibn ʿAbbas said: it is not abrogated, and it refers to those who remained steadfast in their faith in the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Wahidi narrated, with a connected chain to Mujahid, that he said: when Salman related to the Prophet ﷺ the story of his companions and told him they were in the Fire, Salman said: "The earth became dark upon me, so I descended until the words 'they shall grieve,' and it was as if a mountain had been lifted from me."

The connection of this verse to what precedes it is this: when God mentioned the disbelieving People of the Book and the punishment that befell them, He informed of the great reward for the believers, indicating that He recompenses each for his deed. "Those who believed" refers to the hypocrites of this community, meaning those who believed outwardly. For this reason He joined them with those mentioned after them. Then He explained the ruling for those who believed outwardly and inwardly, as said by Sufyan al-Thawri. Or "those who believed" refers to the believers in the Messenger.

"Whoever believed" means whoever persevered in his faith. Among the other groups it means whoever entered into it. Or it refers to the Hanifs who did not meet the Messenger, such as Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl, Qays ibn Sa'idah, and Waraqah ibn Nawfal; and to those who met him, such as Abu Dharr, Salman, and Bahira; and to the delegation of the Negus, who were awaiting the mission (*al-mab'ath*). Some of them reached it and followed, and some did not reach it. "Those who were Jews" is likewise, among those who did not meet him except those who disbelieved in Jesus, upon our Prophet and him be blessings and peace. The Christians are likewise, and the Sabians likewise, as said by al-Suddi. Or they refer to the companions of Salman, whose story has already passed. Or the believers in Jesus before the Messenger was sent, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas. Or the believers in Moses who acted upon his law until Jesus came, and they believed in him and acted upon his law, until Muhammad came, as said by al-Suddi on the authority of his teachers. Or the believers among the earlier nations. Or the believers in God, His angels, His books, and His messengers among all the nations. These are eight opinions concerning those meant by "those who believed" and "those who were Jews," who are the Jews.

Al-Jumhur read *hadu* with a dammah on the dal. Abu al-Sammak al-ʿAdawi read it with a fatha on it, from *al-muhadah*, which it is said means that some of them inclined toward others. The first reading's root consists of ha', waw, and dal, or ha', ya', and dal. The second reading's root consists of ha', dal, and ya'. The verb would be *fa'ala* from *al-hidayah*, and *fa'ala* has come in this form in agreement with *fa'ala*, as if it were said: *wa'l-ladhina hadaw*, meaning they guided themselves, like *jawaztu al-shay'*, meaning I passed the thing.

(And the Christians): The alif is for the feminine, and for this reason the word is not declined (diptotic) in His saying ﴿Those who say, "Indeed, we are Christians"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 14]. This pattern, namely fa'alā, comes both as a broken plural with the alif shortened (maqsur) and as a singular with the alif lengthened (mamdud), and its alif is likewise for the feminine, as in buraka' (a kind of bird) ... 

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "wa-al-Sabi'in" with a hamza, and likewise "wa-al-Sabi'un," and the meaning of the hamzated verb sabaa has already been discussed. Nafi' read it without a hamza, and this may have two possible meanings. The more apparent is that it derives from sabaa, meaning "to incline," and from this is the saying of the poet:

"To Hind my heart inclined, and Hind is one who causes inclination."

The second possibility is that its original form has a hamza, which was eased by converting the hamza into an alif in the verb and into a ya' in the noun, as the poet said:

"Indeed the predators are guided within their lairs, while people are never guided by their evil ones forever."

And another said:

"And I was more humiliated than a peg in a plain, whose head is struck with the mallet."

And another said:

"So pasture Fazarah; may its pasture not be pleasant for you."

Except that converting the hamza into an alif is transmitted and not used as a basis for analogy. As for converting the hamza into a ya', that is the domain of poetry, which is why the first possibility is more apparent. Some exegetes mentioned issues of rulings concerning the Jews and the Christians.

(And the Sabi'in): The wording of the Qur'an here does not indicate them, so it does not mention them, and their place is in the books of jurisprudence (fiqh).

﴿Whoever believes in God and the Last Day﴾: "man" (whoever) is a subject (mubtada'), and it may be conditional (shartiyyah), in which case the predicate is the verb after it. If it is relative (mawsulah), the predicate is His saying ﴿then for them is their reward﴾, and the fa' entered the predicate because the relative subject has fulfilled the conditions for the fa' to enter the predicate, which have been mentioned earlier. The grammarians and the exegetes agree that the clause ﴿whoever believes﴾ is in the position of the predicate of inna when man is a subject, and that the connecting pronoun is omitted, its estimate being: "whoever of them believes." What they said is not complete except on the basis that the two beliefs are different, namely the one that is the relative clause of alladhina and the one that is the relative clause of man, either in the conditionality, or in time, or in the act and its continuation. But if they are not different, that does not hold, because the meaning would become: "Indeed those who believed, whoever of them believes, and whoever were believers," and one would not say "whoever of them believes" except on the basis of the difference between the two beliefs. Some people held that this is by omission, and that the estimate is: "Indeed those who believed, for them is their reward with their Lord; and those who were Jews, and the Sabi'in, and the Christians, whoever of them believes, that is, of the three categories, then for them is their reward," and this is because "whoever believes" could not be a predicate about "those who believed" and what follows them for him. Whoever made man a subject considered it conditional.

We have mentioned the permissibility of its being relative. They also parsed man as an appositive (badal), in which case it is in the accusative and relative. They said: it is an appositive of the noun of inna and what follows it, and this too does not hold except on the estimate of the difference between the two beliefs, as we mentioned, when it is a subject. What we prefer is that it is an appositive of the conjoined nouns that follow the noun of inna, so the meaning is sound then, and it is as if it were said: "Indeed those who believed from outside the three categories, and whoever believed from the three categories, then for them is their reward." The fa' entered the predicate because the relative pronoun was given the meaning of the conditional, and the entry of inna upon the relative was not counted, and that is permissible in the speech of the Arabs; and no regard is paid to the one who disagrees on this. As for the one who claims that "whoever believes" is conjoined to what precedes it, with the conjunction particle omitted, the estimate being: "and whoever believes in God," his saying is far from the correct, and there is no need for that. Belief in the Last Day already includes belief in the messengers, since resurrection is known only through the messengers.

﴿And does righteous deeds﴾: it is general over all acts and statements of righteousness and the performance of obligations, or the affirmation of Muhammad (ﷺ); there are opinions. The second is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. The relative clause or the verb of the condition and the conjoined word were carried over to the wording of "man," so the pronoun in "believes and does" is singular. Then He said: ﴿then for them is their reward﴾ to the end of the verse, so it is plural, carrying the meaning. These two carryings do not hold except by parsing man as a subject; as for parsing man as an appositive, there is only carrying on the wording alone. For carrying on wording and meaning there are conditions mentioned in grammar. Abu Muhammad ibn 'Atiyyah said: "When what follows man proceeds on the wording, it is permissible afterward to shift to the meaning; but when what follows it proceeds on the meaning, it is not permissible afterward to shift to the wording, because confusion enters the speech." End of his words. It is not as he said; rather, if you observe the meaning, it is permissible afterward to observe the wording, but the Kufans require a separation when combining these two carryings, so they say: "man yaqumuna fi ghayri shay'in, wa-yanzuru fi umurina qawmuka" (whoever stand for nothing, and your people look into our affairs). The Basrans do not require that, and this is as established in the science of Arabic:

"Traditions are related from every tolerant one, but their meanings are according to their meanings."

And "ajruhum" (their reward) is nominative by the inchoative, and "lahum" (for them) is in the position of the predicate. According to al-Akhfash and the Kufans, "ajrahum" is nominative by the prepositional phrase.

﴿with their Lord﴾: an adverbial complement, governed by the settledness that governs "lahum," and it may be accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), the governing element being omitted, its estimate being: "being with their Lord."

The majority read ﴿and no fear﴾ with a raised nominative and tanwin. al-Hasan read "wa-la khawfu" without tanwin. The discussion of His saying ﴿no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾ has already been made at the end of the story of Adam, upon our Prophet and upon him be blessings and peace, so it is sufficient not to repeat it here.

The appropriateness of concluding this verse with it is evident, since whoever has his reward established with his Lord will not be touched by grief over what has passed, nor by fear for what is to come. Al-Qushayri said: The difference of paths together with the unity of the origin does not prevent acceptance; whoever is truthful toward God in his faith, and believes in what He has informed of His right and His attributes, the difference in the occurrence of the name does not undermine entitlement to good pleasure.

﴿And when We took your covenant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 63]: this is the tenth blessing, since He took their covenant only for their benefit. The discussion of the word "covenant" has already been made in His saying: ﴿Those who break the covenant of God after its binding﴾ [al-Baqarah: 27]. The mithaq is what God placed in the intellects of proofs for His existence, His power, His wisdom, and the truthfulness of His prophets and messengers; or what was taken from the descendants of Adam in His saying: ﴿Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes﴾ [al-A'raf: 172]; or the obligation of people to follow the prophets; or the belief in Muhammad (ﷺ); or the pledge from them that they would act by what is in the Torah, but when Moses came they read what was in it of burdens and refused to take it; or His saying: ﴿Do not worship except God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83]. These are six opinions. Al-Qaffal said: He said "your covenant" and did not say "your covenants," because He intended the covenant of each one of you, as in His saying: ﴿Then He brings you forth as a child﴾ [Ghafir: 67]; or because what He took from one of them He took from the others, so it was one covenant, whereas if it were plural it would allow for difference. End of his words, summarized.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 63:**

﴿And We raised the mount above you.﴾ The reason for its being raised was their refusal to enter the Holy Land, or to prostrate, or to take the Torah and commit to it. There are three opinions. It is narrated that when Musa (Moses) came to the Children of Israel from Allah with the tablets, in which was the Torah, he said to them: "Take it and commit to it." They said: "No, unless Allah speaks to us with it as He spoke to you." So they were struck senseless, then they were revived. He said to them: "Take it." They said: "No." So Allah the Exalted commanded the angels, who uprooted a mountain from the mountains of Palestine, its length a farsakh (a league, a unit of distance) by the same in width, and their camp was like that. It was placed over them like a canopy. Allah the Exalted also brought out the sea behind them and kindled a fire before them, so that His wrath encompassed them. It was said to them: "Take it, and upon you is the covenant that you will not neglect it; otherwise the mountain will fall upon you, the sea will drown you, and the fire will burn you." So they prostrated in repentance to Allah, took the Torah with the covenant, and prostrated on one side (of the face), because they were watching the mountain out of fear. When Allah showed them mercy, they said: "There is no prostration better than a prostration which Allah accepted and with which He showed mercy." So they made their prostration on one side only.

Al-Tha'labi mentioned that the height of the mountain above their heads was the stature of a man. The verse does not indicate this prostration mentioned in this narrative.

The waw in His saying (﴿And We raised﴾) is the waw of conjunction according to the tafsir of Ibn 'Abbas, because the taking of the covenant was prior; when they broke it by refusing to accept the Book, the mountain was raised over them. As for the tafsir of Abu Muslim, it is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), meaning that the taking of the covenant took place while the mountain was raised above them, like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Noah called out to his son, and he was apart﴾ [Hud: 42], meaning: while he was apart.

﴿Take what We have given you﴾: this is with an implied verb of speech, meaning: "And We said to you: take what We have given you." Some of the Kufan grammarians (al-Kufiyyin) said: there is no need to imply a verb of speech, because the taking of the covenant is itself a saying, and the meaning is: "And when We took your covenant that you would take what We have given you." Here (ma) is a relative pronoun, and its returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: "what We have given you of it (ma atainakumuhu)," referring to the Book. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿and remember what is in it﴾. It was also read as ma ataytukum (what I have given you), which is a kind of iltifat (shift of person), because it moved from the speech of the Majestic speaking of Himself to another.

The meaning of His saying (bi-quwwah, "with strength") is with earnestness and striving, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Suddi; or with action, as said by Mujahid; or with truthfulness and right, as said by Ibn Zayd; or with acceptance, as said by Ibn Bahr; or with obedience, as said by Abu al-'Aliya and al-Rabi'; or with intention and sincerity; or with frequent study and understanding; or with earnestness, resolve, desire and action; or with power. Al-quwwah means power and ability. All these opinions are close in meaning. The ba' here is for circumstance (lil-hal) or for seeking help (lil-isti'anah).

﴿and remember what is in it﴾. Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) read it as an imperative from dhakara ("remember"). Ubayy read (wa-ddakkaru ma fihi), an imperative from iddakkara, whose original form is wa-dhtakkaru; then the ta' was changed into a dal, then the dhal was assimilated into the dal. Most assimilation involves the first letter becoming like the second, but in this case it is permissible for the second to become like the first and be assimilated into it, so one says iddakkara; and it is also permissible to leave it unassimilated, so you say iddhakkara. Ibn Mas'ud read (wa-tadhakkaru), as a present verb in the jussive mood, governed as the answer to the imperative "take" (khudhu). On both readings it has been said that this is an imperative to remember. On this reading, remembering is consequent upon taking with strength, meaning: if you take with strength, you will remember what is in it.

Al-Zamakhshari mentioned that it was read as (wa-tadhakkaru), an imperative from tadhakkur (remembering). I do not think it unlikely that this reading is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, and the one who transmitted from his book "tadhakkaru" erred in omitting the waw. What is in it (the Book) is the reward it contains, as said by Ibn 'Abbas; or: "Memorize what is in it, do not forget it, and study it," as said by al-Zajjaj; or: what is in it of Allah's commands and prohibitions and the description of Muhammad (ﷺ); or: "Take warning from it, so that you may be saved from destruction in this world and from punishment in the Hereafter." Remembrance may be by the tongue, and it may be by the heart as mentioned earlier, and it may be by both. By the tongue its meaning is: study; by the heart its meaning is: reflect; by both its meaning is: study its words and reflect upon its meanings. Or remembrance may be intended as its fruit, which is action, so its meaning is: act upon what is in it of rulings and laws. The pronoun in (fihi, "in it") refers to (ma). And al-Muntakhab says: it should not be understood as remembrance itself, because remembrance, which is the opposite of forgetfulness, is an act of Allah the Exalted, so how is it permissible to command it? End of quote.

﴿so that you may be mindful of God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21]: that is, in hope that piety (taqwa) may be attained by you through remembering what is in it. It has been said: its meaning is "so that you may refrain from what you are engaged in." What is understood from the context of the speech is that they complied with the command and carried out its requirement. This is shown by His saying: ﴿Then you turned away after that﴾ [al-Baqarah: 64]. This indicates acceptance and commitment to what they were commanded. In some narratives it is said that when the mountain was removed, they said: "O Musa, we have heard and we obey; had it not been for the mountain, we would not have obeyed you." And in some narratives: "They believed unwillingly," and the apparent meaning of this is compulsion. The preferred view among the scholars is that Allah the Exalted created faith and obedience in their hearts at the time of the prostration, so that their faith was willing, not unwilling.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 64:

﴿Then you turned away after that.﴾ That is, you turned away from the covenant and from acting upon what it contains. The original meaning of *tawalli* (turning away, "tawallā") is a bodily turning, and then it was used, by extension and figuratively, for turning away from matters, religions and beliefs. The presence of *thumma* (then) indicates a lapse of time, and *min* (from) indicates the starting point of an action. However, between the two clauses there is an omitted statement, and the estimated meaning, Allah knows best, is: "So you took what We had given you, you remembered what is in it, and you acted according to its requirements." Therefore a figurative usage must be admitted in the signification of *min*, namely that because of the speed with which they turned away and their unanimity in doing so, it is as if nothing intervened between what they were commanded to do and their turning away. It is known that after they accepted the Torah, they turned away from it in various ways: they distorted it, abandoned acting by it, killed the prophets, disbelieved in Allah and disobeyed His command. Among these were matters peculiar to some of them, what their early generations did, and what their later generations did. They continued in the wandering (in the wilderness), despite witnessing marvels, opposing Musa and openly committing sins in their camp, until some of them were swallowed up by the earth, fire burned some of them, and they were punished with plague. All of this is mentioned in the translations of the Torah that they read. Then their sorcerers did what is not hidden, until they were punished with the destruction of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem's Temple), they disbelieved in the Messiah and resolved to kill him. Although the Qur'an does not explain what they turned away from in the Torah, the matter is well known, and this is a report from Allah about their predecessors. Therefore it is not strange that they deny what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought, and their condition regarding his Book is as He mentioned.

The demonstrative *dhalika* (that) in His saying ﴿min ba'di dhalika﴾ [al-Baqarah: 52] refers either to the acceptance of what they were given, or to taking the covenant and fulfilling it, and the lifting of the mountain, or the departure of Musa from among them, or to faith. These are opinions.

﴿Had it not been for Allah's favour upon you and His mercy...﴾ The *fadl* (favour) is Islam, and the *rahmah* (mercy) is the Qur'an, as said by Abu al-'Aliyah. Or the *fadl* is the acceptance of repentance, and the *rahmah* is pardoning the slip. Or the *fadl* is granting the success of repenting, and the *rahmah* is acceptance. Or the *fadl* is the mercy itself, and Allah informs about them. Or the *fadl* and the *rahmah* are the sending of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and their living to see his time. On this opinion there is a shift in address (*talwin al-khitab*, the change of addressee), since this becomes directed at those present. The opinions before it indicate that the one addressed is those who preceded, because it came within the context of their story. The *fadl* of Allah, according to the school of the Basran grammarians, is in the nominative case as a subject (*mubtada'*), and the predicate is omitted, its estimated form being "existing" (*mawjud*), or something similar that fits the context. *'Alaykum* (upon you) is connected to *fadl* (favour), or is an object of it, and so it is not in the position of a predicate. The estimate is: ﴿Had it not been for Allah's favour upon you and His mercy﴾ both existing.

*Lakuntum* (you would have been): this is the response (*jawab*) of *lawla* (had it not been). The most common usage is that when it is affirmative it takes the particle *lam* (la), and in the Qur'an it has not come affirmative except with *lam*, except for what some claim regarding His saying ﴿wa-hamma bihā﴾ [Yusuf: 24], where the response of *lawla* is placed first, so there is no *lam* with it. It has come in Arabic speech without *lam*, and some grammarians restrict that to poetry. The poet said:

*Had it not been for modesty and religion, I would have reproached you both for some of what is in you, since you reproached me for my flaw.*

It has also come in their speech with *qad* after the *lam*. The poet said:

*Had it not been for the commander, and the right of obedience to him, I would have drunk blood sweeter than honey.*

It has also come in their speech with the omission of *lam* and the retention of *qad*, as in: *lawla Zaydun qad akramtuka* (had it not been for Zayd, I would have honoured you).

﴿among the losers﴾: It has been previously stated that *khusran* (loss) is deficiency, and its meaning is among those who perish in this world and the next. It is possible that *kana* (was) here means *sara* (became). Al-Qushayri said: Allah, glorified is He, took the covenant of the responsible people, but some people answered Him willingly, because He made Himself known to them, so they affirmed His unity, and some people answered Him unwillingly, because He concealed Himself from them, so they denied Him. There is no proof stronger than the direct witnessing of what was raised above them of the mountain, but they lacked the light of insight, so the direct seeing of the eyes did not benefit them. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Then you turned away﴾, that is, you returned to disobedience after witnessing faith with your own eyes. Were it not for His judgment of granting respite, and His judgment of bestowing favour, He would have hastened punishment upon you, and a great calamity would have befallen you.

Some people of subtle insight said: The souls of the Children of Israel, because of the darkness of their disobedience, were stumbling in a blind night, dark in its cloak, and strutting from their arrogance and loftiness, wearing garments of pride and self-admiration. When they were commanded to take the Torah, and saw in it the weight of its obligations, their proud souls were stirred, so Allah raised the mountain over them, and they found it heavier than what they had been charged with. So carrying the Torah, with its obligations and fatigue, became easier for them, for that was less than destruction. The poet said:

*To Allah are called, by proofs, those who refuse; and if he does not answer, the white swords call him.*

﴿Indeed, you certainly knew those among you who transgressed concerning the Sabbath﴾. The lam in *laqad* is the lam of emphasis (*lam al-tawkid*), which is also called the lam of initiation (*lam al-ibtida'*), as in *la-Zaydun qa'imun* ("Indeed Zayd is standing"). One of its rules is that what falls within its scope may not precede it, except when it enters upon the predicate of *inna*, as established in grammar. Some grammarians have authored a book on these lams, mentioning them and their rules.

It is possible that it is the response to an omitted oath, but it came in the form of emphasis, because such a story might be denied by them. This is because what befell those transgressors in their outcome, of being transformed into apes, is something that requires emphasis, and that they knew it as a certainty. *'Alima* here is like *'arafa* (to know), so it takes one object. The apparent meaning is that they knew the very persons who transgressed. Some have supposed a deleted element: "you knew the rulings concerning those who..." and some have supposed: "the transgression of those who...". The transgression was, as is related, that Moses had been commanded by God to fast on Friday, and was informed of its excellence, just as all the prophets were commanded. He mentioned that to the Children of Israel and commanded them to legislate it for themselves, but they refused and transgressed it to Saturday. God revealed to Moses: "Leave them with what they have chosen," and He tested them in it by commanding them to abstain from work, and forbade them the hunting of fish on it. So the fish would come on Saturday until they came out to the open areas. This was said by al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan. It was also said: until they put their snouts out of the water. The matter of the Children of Israel was at Aylah on the sea. When the Sabbath passed, the fish would depart, and they would not appear until the next Sabbath. They remained in this state for a time until they desired fish. A man deliberately, on the Sabbath, tied a fish with a cord and drove a peg for it at the shore. When the Sabbath had passed, he came and took it. A group heard of his deed and did the same. It was also said: rather, a man dug in a pit, not on the Sabbath, a hollow through which the sea would enter. When the Sabbath came, the fish came out and got into the hollow. When the sea receded, the water left by the channel of the hollow and the fish remained. He came after the Sabbath and took it. A group did as he did. It multiplied until they hunted it openly on the Sabbath and sold it in the markets. This was among the greatest transgressions. Additional details regarding the manner of the transgression have been related, but God knows the soundness of that. What is sound in this matter is what God mentioned in His Book and what is authentically transmitted from His Prophet.

*Minkum* is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), so it is linked to an omitted element, its estimate being: "being among you." *Min* is partitive (*lil-tab'id*).

*Fi al-Sabt* is linked to *i'tadaw*, either by supposing *yawm* (day) or by a ruling. What drove them to transgress was said to be: Satan whispered to them and said, "You were only forbidden to take them on the Sabbath; you were not forbidden to hold them," so they obeyed him and did that. It was also said: when some of them did that and no punishment was hastened upon him, and some people among them imitated him and did as he did, they thought the Sabbath had been made lawful for them, so a large group conspired in that, and what befell them befell them. It was also said: they proceeded in it interpreting in a way of their own, because He had commanded them to abstain from work on the Sabbath, and they said: "God only forbade us the means of earning that distract us from worship, and He did not forbid us light work." It was also said: their rabble did that out of defiance and disobedience, so God encompassed all of them with the punishment.

*Faqulna lahum kunu*: it is an imperative from *al-kawn* (being), but it is not an imperative in reality, because their becoming what was mentioned involved no acquisition on their part, since they were not capable of transforming their own persons into apes. Rather, what is meant is the swiftness of their becoming in this description, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [al-Nahl: 40]. Its figurative meaning is that when He intended that of them, they became so. The apparent meaning of the Qur'an is that they were transformed into apes. It was also said: they were not transformed into apes; rather, it is a parable God struck for them, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿like the example of a donkey carrying books﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 5]. This was said by Mujahid. It was also said: their hearts were transformed until they became like the hearts of apes, accepting no admonition and comprehending no reproof. This too is reported from Mujahid. The first view is the view of the majority, and it is permissible that God leaves them the faculty of human understanding after their becoming apes. It is related in some of their stories that one of them would be approached by a person from among his relatives who had forbidden them, and he would say to him: "Did I not forbid you?" and he would indicate with his head: "Yes," and tears would flow down his cheek. No mention was made in this transformation of any of them becoming swine. It is related from Qatadah that the young among them became apes, and the elders became swine, and none were saved except those who had been forbidden, while the rest perished. It is related in their stories that God transformed the disobedient into apes at night. The saved rose in the morning to their mosques and gathering places, and they did not see anyone of the perished, so they said: "Surely something has happened to the people." They opened the doors upon them as they had been closed at night, and they found them apes who recognized the man and the woman. It was also said: the saved had divided the town between themselves and the disobedient by a wall, disavowing them, so in the morning the city of the perished was not opened, and they climbed over the wall, and behold, they were apes leaping upon one another. Qatadah said: they became apes that bark, with tails, after they had been men and women.

*Qiradatan khasi'in*: both are predicates of *kana*, and the meaning is that they would have combined apehood and abasement. It is permissible that *khasi'in* be an attribute of *qiradatan*, and it is permissible that it be a circumstantial clause from the subject of *kunu*. The meaning of *khasi'in* is: distanced. Abu Rawq said: "losing," as though he explained it by its necessary consequence, because whoever God distances has indeed lost. The majority of the exegetes hold that those whom God transformed did not eat, did not drink, and did not reproduce, but all died, and that they did not live more than three days. Muqatil claimed that they lived seven days and died on the eighth day, and that this was in the time of David, upon our Prophet and upon him be the best of blessings and peace, and that they were in a town called Aylah. It was also said: Madyan. Muslim related from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to one who asked him about apes and swine: "Are they among those who were transformed?" He said: "God does not destroy a people, or punish a people, and then grant them offspring. The apes and swine existed before that." Al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi preferred that they lived, and that the apes existing now are their descendants.

The pronoun in *fa-jaʿalnāhā* refers to the town, the nation, the state, the transformation, the fish, or the punishment. What appears to be the correct reading is that the pronoun refers to the verbal noun (*maṣdar*) understood from *kūnū* (be), meaning: So We made their being (*kaynūnatahum*) into apes, despised.

*Nakālan* means a deterrent, i.e., a lesson, and it is the second object (*maf ʿūl thānin*) of *jaʿala* (to make).

﴿For what lies before it and what lies behind it﴾: that is, of the towns. The pronoun refers to the town. This is said by ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbas. Or it refers to those who came after them of the nations. (*Wa mā khalfahā*): that is, those who were remaining with them. This is narrated by al-Ḍaḥḥāk, from Ibn ʿAbbas. Or *mā bayna yadayhā* means what is below it, and *mā khalfahā* means for those who come after them of the nations. The pronoun refers to the nation; this is said by al-Suddi.
