Or *mā bayna yadayhā* means the sins of the people, and *mā khalfahā* refers to the fish which they caught; this is said by Qatadah. Or *(li-mā bayna yadayhā)* means what passed of their wrongdoings by which they were destroyed; this is said by Mujahid. Or *li-mā bayna yadayhā* refers to those who witnessed it, and *mā khalfahā* to those who did not witness it; this is said by Qutrub. Or *mā bayna yadayhā* means the sins of the people, and *mā khalfahā* refers to whoever sins after them with the same sins. Or *(li-mā bayna yadayhā)* means those among the rescued who were present, and *(mā khalfahā)* refers to those who come after them. Or *li-mā bayna yadayhā* refers to the punishment of the Hereafter that lies before them, and *(mā khalfahā)* to their worldly life, so that they are remembered by it until the Hour. Or *(li-mā bayna yadayhā)* means what is around it of towns, and *(mā khalfahā)* means what happens after it of towns that did not exist; for their transformation was mentioned in the books of the earlier people, so they took warning from it, and those of later generations who learned of it also took warning from it. Or there is inversion (*taqdīm wa-ta khīr*) in the verse, meaning: We made it, and what follows it of the punishment prepared for them in the Hereafter, a deterrent and a recompense, not for what lies before it, that is, for what preceded of their sins through their transgression on the Sabbath. These are eleven opinions. Some said: The closest to correctness is the view of the one who said: *(mā bayna yadayhā)* refers to those who come after it of the nations, and *(mā khalfahā)* refers to those among them and others who remained and were not struck by the punishment. As for the one who said the pronoun refers to the town, what is meant is its people.

﴿And an admonition for the God-fearing﴾: He specified the God-fearing because they are the ones who benefit from admonition and reminder. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, the reminder benefits the believers﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 55], and ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 45]. It has been said: He meant a deterrent for the Children of Israel and an admonition for the God-fearing of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). It has been said: The God-fearing are the community of Muhammad (ﷺ); this is said by al-Suddi, from his teachers. It has been said: The wording is general for every God-fearing person of every nation; this is said by Ibn ʿAbbas. It has been said: They are those who were forbidden and were saved.

These noble verses have included the equality between believing Jews, Christians, and Sabians, and believers of other communities, in the reality of the reward for them, and that this is with the One who sees them; and that their faith in this world produced for them security in the Hereafter, so there is no fear of what lies ahead, nor grief over what has passed, for whoever has his reward secured with his Lord has reached the utmost goal of honor. He placed this verse between the stories of the Children of Israel to make clear that success belongs only to whoever obeys. This verse came between two verses of punishment: one includes the striking of humiliation and wretchedness upon the Children of Israel, and the other includes what they were punished with, namely the lifting of the mountain over them, the taking of the covenant, and then their turning away after that. So this verse informed of the good end of whoever believes, even from this category which was punished with these two punishments, as an encouragement to faith and a facilitation for entering the most noble of religions, and as an explanation that Islam (submission to God) erases what came before it, and that obedience to Allah brings His goodness and bounty.

His saying ﴿And when We took your covenant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 63] included a reminder of the covenant that was taken from them, that fulfilling it was obligatory, that He raised the mount above them so that they would repent and return, and that despite witnessing this great marvel they turned away and refused to accept the truth; and that had He not overtaken them with His bounty and mercy, they would have been lost. Then He began to remind them of what is within their knowledge of the punishment of the disobedient and the outcome of the transgression of transgressors, and that by persisting in disobedience and transgression, in permitting what the Most Merciful has forbidden, He punishes the disobedient by taking him out of the stage of humanity to the stage of apehood. So while he rejoices at being counted among the people of intellect, and delights in the pleasure of being addressed with favor, his name has been erased from the register of perfection, and his form has been altered into the most hideous likeness, and in addition to this, a deterrent has been prepared for him in the Hereafter. Punishments for crimes proceed according to measure, arising from the will of the Sovereign, the Subduer; they are not something known by analogy, so that the minds of people should struggle to define them. Such a punishment serves as an alert to the heedless and an admonition to the wise.

[p. 247]

﴿And when Moses said to his people, "Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow," they said, "Do you take us in ridicule?" He said, "I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant."﴾ ﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is." He said, "Indeed, He says it is a cow neither old nor young, but median between that, so do what you are commanded."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 68] ﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what its color is." He said, "Indeed, He says it is a yellow cow, bright in color, pleasing to the observers."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 69] ﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is, for cattle have become confusing to us, and we, if Allah wills, will be guided."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 70] ﴿He said, "Indeed, He says it is a cow not trained to plow the earth or water the field, sound and without blemish." They said, "Now you have brought the truth." So they slaughtered it, though they had nearly not done so.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 71] ﴿And when you killed a soul and disputed over it, while Allah was to bring out that which you were concealing.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 72] ﴿So We said, "Strike him with part of it." Thus Allah brings the dead to life and shows you His signs that you may reason.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 73] ﴿Then your hearts hardened after that, so they were like stones or even harder. And indeed, among stones are those from which rivers gush forth, and indeed, among them are those that split and water emerges from them, and indeed, among them are those that fall down out of fear of Allah. And Allah is not unaware of what you do.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 74] (p. 248)

**al-baqarah** (the cow): the female of this well-known animal, and it may also apply to the male. Al-bāqir, al-baqīr, al-bayqūr and al-bāqūr (all forms meaning a cow or one who splits). They said: it was named "baqarah" because it "tabqur" the earth, meaning it splits it for tilling. From this root Muhammad ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib was named al-Bāqir. He and his brother Zayd ibn ʿAlī were among the eloquent scholars.

**al-ʿiyādh and al-maʿādh** (seeking protection): seeking refuge. Its verb is ʿādha, yaʿūdhu.

**al-jahl** (ignorance): well known. Its verb is jahila, yajhalu. It is said it has been pluralized as ajhāl, which is anomalous.

Al-Shanfarā said:
"Let not the ignorant (ajhāl) be vain toward my forbearance, nor do I see one who asks with the edges of words."

It may also be that ajhāl is the plural of jāhil, like aṣḥāb as the plural of ṣāḥib.

**al-fāriḍ**: the aged cow whose calving has ceased due to old age. It is said farida and farura, yafriḍu, with the vowel of the past tense being fatḥa or ḍamma, and the verbal noun is furūḍ. Al-faraḍ means cutting. The poet said:
"A bay dark-colored, not fāriḍ, nor ʿawān with a spotted color."

It is also said of anything that has been old and whose matter is long: fāriḍ. The poet said:
"O many a one with an old grudge against me, who has cycles like the cycles of a menstruating woman."

It seems the aged one was called fāriḍ because she has "faraḍat" her teeth, meaning she has cut them and reached their end. Khufāf ibn Nudbah said:
"By my life, you have given your guest a fāriḍ, one led to him that cannot stand on one foot."
"And you did not give him a young cow so that he would be pleased with its fatness, so how will you be repaid with affection and favor?"

**al-bikr**: a young cow who has not given birth from youth. Ibn Qutaybah said: one who has given birth to one offspring. Bikr among women is one whom a man has not touched. Ibn Qutaybah said: one who has not conceived. Bikr among offspring means the first, and among needs means the first.

The rājiz (rajaz poet) said:
"O firstborn of firstborns, and O tender of the liver, you have become from me like an arm from the upper arm."

Al-bakr, with a fatḥa on the bāʾ, is a young male camel; its female is bakrah. Its root is from precedence in time, and from it come al-bakrah and al-bākūrah.

**al-ʿawān**: the middle one, the one who has given birth to one or two litters. It is also said: the one who has given birth once. The Arabs said: the ʿawān does not know the virgin's bashfulness. It is said: ʿawanat the woman, and ḥarbun ʿawān, the war that has been fought in repeatedly. It is pluralized as ʿuwun on the pattern fuʿul, which is the analogical form for a weak-lettered noun of the pattern faʿal. In poetry it is permissible to vowel the second radical with ḍamma, as in:
"And in the hands, the gleaming bracelets (suwar)."

**bayna** (between): an adverb of place with medial syntactic range. You say: he is far between the shoulders, and clear between the eyebrows. Allah said: ﴿This is parting between me and you﴾ [al-Kahf: 78]. Its use when it is an adverb is between what can have betweenness, as in "the wealth is between Zayd and ʿAmr", which is heard in their speech. It moves from the spatial to the temporal when mā or alif is attached to it, and then it loses its specialization with nouns, so the nominal and verbal sentences follow it. Sometimes bayna is idafa to a verbal noun. In the science of the Kufans (grammarians), bayna has a large dedicated chapter.

**al-lawn** (color): well known, and its analogical plural is alwān. Lawn also means type, and from it come alwān al-ṭaʿām, meaning its kinds. They say: so-and-so is mutalawwin if he does not remain on one character and one state. From it: "he changes like the chameleon (ḥirbāʾ)," because the chameleon, due to the clarity of its body, takes on whatever color it faces, so it changes from one color to another.

**al-ṣufrah** (yellowness): a well-known color. The analogical verb from this verbal noun is ṣafira, so he is aṣfar, and she is ṣafrāʾ, like the saying shahuba: he is ashhab, and she is shahbāʾ.

**al-fuqūʿ**: the most intense and most emphatic degree of yellowness. It is said: aṣfar fāqiʿ and wāris, aswad ḥālik and ḥāyik, abyad naqqu and lamaq, aḥmar qāniʾ and zinjī, akhḍar nāḍir and mudhāmm, azraq khuṭbānī, and armak rādinī.

**al-surūr** (joy): a pleasure in the heart upon obtaining benefit or expecting it, or seeing a pleasing and delightful matter. Some said: surūr, farah, ḥubūr and jadhal are synonyms, and the opposite of surūr is ghamm (grief).

**al-dhalūl**: the tamed one whose wildness has departed. It is said: a dābbah dhalūl means one clearly "docile" (dhill, with a kasrah on the dhāl), and a man dhalīl means one clearly abased (dhull, with a ḍamma on the dhāl). The verb: dhalla, yadhillu.

**al-ithārah** (stirring): extracting and agitating from one place to another. Imru' al-Qays said:
"It pours it out and scatters its dust and stirs it, the stirring of a searcher of the hot noon, one who digs up."

al-Nābighah said:
"They stir up the pebbles until they touch the dust, when the sun spits its saliva upon the breasts."

**al-ḥarth** (tilling): the verbal noun of ḥaratha, yaḥruthu, which is cleaving the earth so that seed may be sown in it. It is also applied to what has been plowed and sown. It is metaphorical in: ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 223]. Al-ḥarth also means crops, and al-ḥarth also means earning. Al-ḥarāʾith are camels, the singular being ḥarīthah. In a hadith: "The truest of names is Ḥārith," because the ḥārith is the earner. Iḥtirāth al-māl means acquiring wealth.

**al-musallamah** (sound): the one purified and free from defects. Sallama lahu kadhā means he purified it, with salām and salāmah, like al-lidhādh and al-ladhādhah.

**al-shiyah** (blemish): the verbal noun of washā al-thawb, yashīhi, washyan and shiyah: he beautified and adorned it with lines of differing colors. From this is called the one who sows discord among people wāshin, because he beautifies his lie in their eyes until it is accepted. Al-shiyah is also a streak contrary to the color, and from this comes a bull with marked legs (mawshiyy al-qawāʾim). The poet said:
"From the wild cattle of Wajrah, marked in its legs, lean in its belly, like the sword of the polisher, single."

**al-ān** (now): an adverb of time, in which all or part of it is present, and its alif and lam are for presence. It is said they are extra, and it is indeclinable because it contains the meaning of pointing. Al-Farrāʾ claimed it is derived from the verb: āna yaʾīnu aynan, meaning ḥāna (it has come).

**al-darʾ** (repelling): defense, and "yadraʾu ʿanhā al-ʿadhāb" (he repels punishment from her). The poet said:
"So he turned aside from them the repelling of enemies."

**Idda ʾara** (disputed): a tafāʿul form from it, and its verbal noun has a rule that differs from the verbal nouns of verbs whose first letter is a hamzat al-waṣl, which is mentioned in grammar (nahw).

**al-qasāwah** (hardness): hardness and toughness of the heart. It is said: qasā yaqsū qaswan, qaswah and qasāwah. Qasā, jasā and ʿasā are close in meaning.

**al-shaqq**: to make a thing two halves, and taqashshaqa from it means it split.

**al-khashyah** (awe): fear together with great reverence for the one feared. It is said: khashiya yakhshā.

**al-ghaflah, al-sahw and al-nisyān** (heedlessness, inattention and forgetfulness) are close in meaning. It is said from it: ghafala yaghfulu, and a place ghufl means one that is not known.

* *

﴿And when Moses said to his people, "Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow"﴾, the verse. A slain man was found among the Children of Israel named ʿĀmīl, and they did not know his killer, and they disputed about him and about the cause of his killing. ʿAṭāʾ and al-Suddī said: the killer was the cousin of the slain man, and he was poor, while the slain man had much wealth. It was said: he was his brother, and it was said: his nephew, and he had no heir except him, so when his life was prolonged he killed him in order to inherit from him. ʿAṭāʾ also said: under ʿĀmīl was a cousin, a girl with no equal among the Children of Israel in beauty and grace, so he killed him in order to marry her. The commentators elaborated on this story with what is found in their books. The one who asked Moses for clarification was the killer, as said by Abū al-ʿĀliyah. Others said: rather, the people gathered and asked Moses. The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that the mention of their opposition to their prophets and their denial of them in most of their reports has preceded, so it was fitting to mention this verse, because it includes repeated back-and-forth, stubbornness and obstinacy.

His saying "(And when he said)" is coordinated with his saying: ﴿And when We took your covenant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 63]. The people of Moses are his followers and partisans.

The majority read yaʾmurukum with a ḍamma on the rāʾ. From Abū ʿAmr: sukūn, ikhtilās, and replacing the hamzah with an alif. This explanation has already been mentioned in the discussion of bāriʾukum. Yaʾmurukum is in the present form, so it may mean the present, and it may mean the past if the command to slaughter the cow was by what Allah revealed in the Torah, or by what Moses reported. And an tadhbaḥū is in the position of the second object of yaʾmuru, and it is with the preposition dropped, meaning "bi-an tadhbaḥū" (to slaughter). For the omission of the preposition here there are two justifications. One: it is permissible when the object is affected by a prepositional particle that the particle be omitted, as he said: "I commanded you the good, so do what you were commanded," (p. 250) when the object is with inna, and it is permissible with inna to omit the prepositional particle if it causes no confusion. The indication of the speech that the commanded act is "that you slaughter a cow" is that whichever cow they slaughtered would fulfill the obligation. Al-Ḥasan narrated, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muḥammad, if they had merely taken any cow and slaughtered it, it would have sufficed for them, but they made it strict, so Allah made it strict upon them." The cow was singled out from among all other animals because they used to revere cattle and worship them besides Allah, so they were tested with that, since this is among the great trials, namely that a person is commanded to kill one whom he loves and reveres. Or because Allah, exalted is He, wished that good would reach the boy who had been dutiful to his mother. Ṭalḥah ibn Muṣarrif said: it was not of the cattle of this world, but came down from heaven. Some scholars said: cattle are the master of domesticated animals.

And he read: (atattakhidhunā) ? The majority read with a tāʾ, taking the pronoun as referring to Moses. ʿĀṣim al-Jaḥdarī and Ibn Muḥaysin read with a yāʾ, taking the pronoun as referring to Allah, exalted is He, and it is an interrogative in the manner of denunciation.

(هُزُوًا)، Hamzah, Isma'il, Khalaf in his selection, al-Qazzaz from Abd al-Warith, and al-Mufaddal read it with the zay (ز) sukun (ـْ), i.e., *huzwan*. Hafs read it with a damma on the zay and a waw (و) in place of the hamza, i.e., *huzuwan*. The rest read it with a damma on the zay and a hamza, i.e., *huzuan*. There are three dialectal forms in the recitations (*qira'at*, the authorized Qur'anic readings). Its grammatical position is as a second object (*maf'ul thani*) of the verb in ﴿Do you take us in mockery?﴾. It may be intended as an active participle in the sense of a passive, meaning *mahzu'an* (mocked), as in the saying "a dirham is the minting of the amir" and "this is the creation of Allah." Or it may be used as an intensive (*mubalaghah*) form, meaning "Do you take us as mockery itself?" This is because of the great amount of mockery directed at one who is ignorant. Or it may be understood with an elided genitive construction, meaning "in place of mockery" or "those who mock." Their reply, when their prophet informed them of the command of Allah to slaughter a cow, was ﴿Do you take us in mockery?﴾. This is evidence of the corruption of their belief concerning their prophet and of their denial of him. For if they had known that this was a true report from Allah the Exalted, their response would have been nothing but compliance with the command, and their reply was thus disbelief in Musa (Moses). Some people said: they were believers who affirmed the truth, but this occurred in keeping with the harshness of their natures, their coarseness, and their disobedience. The excuse for them is that when they asked Musa to specify the killer, and he said to them ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter [a cow]﴾, they saw a wide gap between the question and the answer, and they imagined that Musa was joking with them. It may be that he had not informed them at that time that the slain man would be struck with part of the slaughtered cow, come back to life, and name his killer. Or he may have informed them of this, and they were amazed that a dead person should be brought to life by part of a dead animal, so they thought this was a kind of mockery. It was also said: there is an elided element in the speech, its implied meaning being: "Did Allah command you to make us a mockery?" It was also said: it is a genuine question with no denial in it, a question of seeking guidance (*istirshad*), not a question of denial and obstinacy.

﴿He said, "I seek refuge in Allah that I should be among the ignorant."﴾ When Musa, peace be upon him, understood from them that this statement issued from them only because they believed that he had reported from Allah something He had not commanded, he sought refuge in Allah, the One from whom he had reported, lest he be among those ignorant of Allah, who would report about Him a matter He had not commanded. For reporting about Allah the Exalted what Allah has not reported is only done out of ignorance of Allah the Exalted. His saying "among the ignorant" explicitly indicates that there are ignorant people, and he sought refuge in Allah from being one of them. It also implicitly indicates that they are ignorant, as if he had said: "lest I be among you." For they permitted [the attribution of error] to one who is protected from lying (*ma'sum*, protected from error), especially in conveying from Allah, that he would report lies about Allah. They said: ignorance is of two kinds, simple (*basit*) and compound (*murakkab*). Simple ignorance is general and specific. General simple ignorance is lacking knowledge of anything among the knowable things; specific simple ignorance is lacking knowledge of some of the knowable things. Compound ignorance is when one is ignorant and is also ignorant that he is ignorant. General and compound ignorance cannot be attributed to one who has some knowledge, let alone to a prophet who was honored with messengerhood and direct speech from Allah, and that is impossible for him. Therefore it is impossible for him to seek refuge from it except as a matter of courtesy (*adab*). What Musa sought refuge from is the specific kind, which would lead to his reporting about Allah the Exalted while mocking, or which is the opposite of their ignorance. So they said: ﴿Do you take us in mockery?﴾ toward one who reports to them about Allah, or its meaning is mockery of the believers. That would be ignorance. Or [he sought refuge from being] among the ignorant (p-251) in the answer, not in accordance with the question, for that would be ignorance, and [it would mean] the command comes from my own self while I attribute it to Allah, and departing from the answer of the seeking inquirer toward mockery is ignorance. These six aspects are impossible for Musa. It was said: he sought refuge from them only as a matter of courtesy, just as Nuh, peace be upon him, said ﴿I seek refuge in You from asking You about that of which I have no knowledge﴾ [Hud: 47], and as in ﴿And say, "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the incitements of the devils"﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 97]. They only said this as a matter of courtesy with Allah and humility before Him.

﴿They said: Call upon your Lord for us, that He may make clear to us what it is.﴾ When Moses said to them, ﴿I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 67], and they knew that what Moses had told them of Allah's command to slaughter a cow was a binding command (ʿazīma) and a demand, their saying this to him was permissible. This statement also contains from them obstinacy (taʿnīt) and little compliance (qillat tawāʿiya), for had they obeyed and slaughtered a cow, they would have fulfilled what was commanded. Instead, they made it difficult, so Allah made it difficult for them. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbās, Abu al-ʿĀliya and others.

The kasra on the ʿayn of ادع (udʿu) is the dialect of the Banu ʿĀmir, and this was mentioned previously in ﴿So call upon your Lord for us, that He may bring forth for us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61]. The jazm on يبين (yubayyin) is because it is the answer to the imperative. ما هي (mā hiya) is a mubtada' (subject) and khabar (predicate). ʿAbdullah (Ibn Masʿud) recited: سل لنا ربك يبين ما هي. The object of يبين (yubayyin) is the clause consisting of the mubtada' and khabar, and the verb is suspended (muʿallaq), because the meaning of يبين لنا is يعلمنا ما هي (informs us what it is), since clarification (tabyīn) entails informing. The pronoun in هي (hiya) refers back to the cow previously mentioned. It is as if they said: "Make clear to us what the cow is that He has commanded us to slaughter." They did not intend to clarify the essence (māhiyya) of the cow; rather, the question concerned its attribute, so there is an omitted modifier (ḥadhf muḍāf), the estimate being: "What is its attribute?" For this reason they were answered with the attribute, which is His saying: ﴿Neither old nor virgin﴾.

They asked in the manner of obstinacy, as we have stated, or in the manner of wonder at a dead cow with which a dead man is struck so that he comes to life, for that is in the extreme of strangeness and departure from the familiar. Or they thought that His saying ﴿that you slaughter a cow﴾ [al-Baqarah: 67] was of the category of the ambiguous (mujmal), so they asked for its clarification, since clarifying the ambiguous is obligatory. Or they hoped that the obligation of slaughtering would be abrogated (naskh) for them, owing to its heaviness upon them, because they did not know the purpose for which they had been commanded to do it.

The meaning of their saying ﴿Call upon your Lord for us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 69] has already been explained, namely how they singled out the word "Lord" (rabb) as attached to Moses. That is because they knew his special status and lofty rank with Allah. It has also been said: they asked Moses for guidance, not out of stubbornness, for had it been stubbornness they would have disbelieved in him and their punishment would have been hastened, as it was hastened in their saying ﴿Show us Allah openly﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 153], and in their worship of the calf, and in their refusal to accept the Torah, and their saying ﴿So go you and your Lord and fight﴾ [al-Māʾida: 24]. In the speech there is an omission, its estimate being: So Moses called upon his Lord, and He answered him.

﴿He said: Indeed He says it is a cow neither old nor virgin﴾: this is an attribute (ṣifa) of بقرة (baqara, "cow"). When an attribute is negated with لا (lā), its repetition is obligatory, as the poet said:

*And youths of truth, neither weak nor unarmed*

If it comes without repetition, then that is a matter of poetry. Whoever makes this a description by the ambiguous, estimating an omitted mubtada', meaning "it is neither old nor virgin," has gone too far, because the original is description by a single word (mufrad), and the original is that there is no omission.

(ʿawān): an explanation of what is contained in His saying ﴿neither old nor virgin﴾.

(bayna dhālika, "between that"): بين (bayna) requires that it enter upon something that can take the dual, yet after it came only a singular demonstrative, so it is said: the demonstrative bi-dhālika refers to a singular, as if it were said: "a middle [cow] between what has been mentioned." Its form is that of the singular, but in meaning it is dual, because the dual and plural of the demonstrative are not truly dual or plural. Rather, analogy would require that the demonstrative not be made dual, plural or feminine. They said: the pronoun has been treated like the demonstrative. Ru'ba said:

*In them are lines of blackness and whiteness, as if on the skin is the spotting of leprosy*

It was said to him: How do you say "as if it" (kaʾannahu)? Why did you not say "as if they" (kaʾannahā), which would refer back to the lines, or "as if they two" (kaʾannahumā), which would refer back to the blackness and the whiteness? He said: "I intended: that was."

And Labid said:

*Indeed for good and for evil there is a limit, and both that and a before-time are a way*

It was said: he meant "both those two," so he used the singular and meant the dual. It is possible that the verse is of this kind, so that ذلك (dhālika) is used and is meant to be "those two," though this is a different ambiguity from the first. What I hold to is other than what they mentioned: that it is a case where the conjoined element has been omitted because the meaning indicates it. The estimate is: "a middle between that and this," i.e., between the old and the virgin. This is like the saying of the poet:

*There was not between the good, had he come safe, and Abu Ḥajar, except a few nights*

That is: "there was not between the good and its seeker," with the seeker omitted because the meaning is understood. From this is His saying ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Naḥl: 81], meaning "and the cold." It was made a "middle" (ʿawān) because it is the most complete of its states; the young one is deficient, having passed its state.

﴿So do what you are commanded﴾: that is, of slaughtering the cow, and do not repeat the question, and do not be obstinate concerning what you have been commanded to slaughter. It is possible that this sentence is from the speech of Allah, and it is possible that it is from the speech of Moses, and the latter is more apparent. He urged them to comply with what they had been commanded, out of compassion. Mā (ما) is a relative pronoun (mawṣūla), and its returning pronoun is omitted, the estimate being: "what you are commanded to do (tu'marūnahu)." The agent was omitted because it is known, since it was previously stated that Allah commands you, and for the harmony of the endings of the verses, just as the harmony of the case-endings at the ends of verses was intended in the poet's saying:

*And there is no escape, one day the deposits will be returned*

Because the last word of the line before this is his saying:

*And they do not know where the places of fall are*

Some have permitted that ما (mā) be a verbal noun (maṣdariyya), meaning: "so do your command," and that the verbal noun would have the sense of the passive participle, meaning "what is commanded of you." But this is far-fetched.

[p. 252]

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 69–70 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us, that He may make clear to us what its color is."﴾ When they had learned its age, they began to inquire about its color. All of this indicates the weakness of their natural disposition and their intellects, since God had already commanded them to slaughter a cow, and the one who conveyed God's command, who advised them and was concerned for them, had said: ﴿So do what you are commanded﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:68]. Despite this, they did not refrain from asking about its color. The discussion of ﴿Call upon your Lord for us﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:68], of the jussive in (yubayyin), and of the interrogative construction and the element omitted after it has already been covered in the preceding verse, so there is no need to repeat it here.

﴿He said, "Indeed He says it is a yellow cow"﴾: The majority of scholars said that this refers to the well-known color, and for this reason it is emphasized with "bright and pleasing" (al-fuqu' wa-l-surur), so it is yellow even in its horns and hooves. Al-Hasan and Abu 'Ubayda said that what is meant here is black, and a poet said:

*"A yellow one, not yellowish, but black like the coals of the fire."*

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it is yellow only in its horns and hooves.

(faqi'): that is, intensely yellow. This was stated by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan. Or it means purely yellow, as stated by Qutrub. Or it means clear, as stated by Abu al-'Aliyah and Qatadah.

(lawnuha) [its color]: They mentioned several possibilities for its i'rab (grammatical analysis, inflection). The first: it is a subject (fa'il) in the nominative, governed by "fāqiʿ," and "fāqiʿ" is an adjective of the cow. The second: it is a subject (mubtada') and its predicate (khabar) is "fāqiʿ." The third: it is a subject (mubtada'), and ﴿tasurru al-nazirin﴾ [it pleases the beholders] is its predicate. The feminine form is used according to one of two meanings. The first: because it is attached to a feminine noun, as they say: "some of his fingers went." The second: it is meant as a feminine, since it is the yellowness itself, so it is as if he said: "its yellowness pleases the beholders," and the word is construed according to the meaning, as in their saying: "his letter reached him, so he belittled it," meaning the letter. The better option is the first i'rab, because treating "lawnuha" as a subject and "fāqiʿ" as a fronted predicate is not permitted by the Kufans, or treating "tasurru al-nazirin" as its predicate involves the feminine marking of the predicate, which requires interpretation, as we have explained. That "lawnuha" is the subject (fa'il) of "fāqiʿ" follows the natural arrangement of the speech and requires no fronting, delaying, or interpretation. He did not make "fāqiʿ" feminine even though it is an adjective of a feminine noun, because it refers to the causal noun (al-sababi), which is masculine, so the construction becomes like: "a woman came to me whose father is good." It is not valid here for it to be a follower of "ṣafrāʾ" as an emphatic (tawkid), because that would require agreement with the noun it follows. Do you not see that you say: "black, intensely black (aswad hālik)," and "black [f.] intensely black [f.] (sawdāʾ hālikah)," but it is not permitted to say "sawdāʾ hālik"? As for his saying:

*"Indeed I pour the drink, yellow and intensely so, as if the fine musk within it is being crushed."*

its basis is poetry, since the usual wording would be "ṣafrāʾ fāqiʿah." The Qur'anic wording ﴿ṣafrāʾ fāqiʿun lawnuha﴾ [yellow, intensely yellow is its color] was not limited to "ṣafrāʾ fāqiʿah," because he intended to emphasize the attribution of yellowness. He judged of it that it is yellow, then judged of the color that it is intensely yellow. So he began first by describing the cow as yellow, then emphasized that by describing its color with it, as if he said: "It is yellow, and its color is intensely yellow." Thus the two ways in which yellowness is related differ in wording: first it is related to the essence itself, then secondly to the accident which is the color, and the object of the relation also differs, because mere yellowness differs from intense yellowness. Despite this clear difference, it does not require emphasis. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, why was it not said: 'ṣafrāʾ fāqiʿah'? And what is the benefit of that word 'color'? I say: its benefit is emphasis, because 'color' is a name for the appearance, which is the yellowness; so it is as if it was said: 'Its yellowness is intensely yellow,' and this is like your saying: 'his diligence is diligence,' and 'your madness is madness.'" End of his words. Wahb said: "When you look at it, it seems to you that the rays of the sun come out from its skin."

﴿tasurru al-nazirin﴾ [it pleases the beholders]: that is, it delights those who look at it because of its fatness, its appearance, and its color. This clause is an adjective of the cow, although the one who made it a predicate has been mentioned, as in his saying "lawnuha," and there is strain in that, which we have mentioned. This description came with a verb and not with the active participle, because the verb indicates occurrence and renewal. Since its color is among the stable things that do not renew, the description of it came with a noun and not with a verb. This description is placed after the one before it, because it arises from the preceding description, or is almost arising from it, since when the color is bright and beautiful, the eyes are amazed by it and the insights marvel at its beauty. The plural is used for "the beholders" to make clear that the eyes of people are drawn to it and delight in looking at it. It is not something that pleases one person without another, and for this reason the definite article (al-) is used which indicates totality, that is: it is ready to please whoever looks at it. Even if the looking here is the looking of the heart, which is reflection, then the pleasure arises from contemplating the wonders of God's creation, in the beautifying of its color and the perfecting of its form. The pronoun in "tasurru" refers to the cow, if we assume it is an adjective; if it is a predicate, it refers to the color about which "tasurru" is predicated. The feminine form has already been explained, and for this reason whoever reads "yasurru" with the yāʾ, it refers to the color; so it may be that "lawnuha" is a subject (mubtada'), "yasurru" is its predicate, and "fāqiʿ" is an adjective following "ṣafrāʾ" according to the pattern of this line of verse that we cited:

*"Indeed I pour the drink, yellow and intensely so."*

despite the rarity of that. It may also be that "lawnuha" is the subject (fa'il) of "fāqiʿ," and "yasurru" is a new independent statement. The majority of the commentators indicate that yellow is among the colors that bring joy, and for this reason 'Ali, may God honor his face, used to prefer yellow sandals. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Yellow expands the soul and removes worry," and Ibn 'Abbas also encouraged wearing yellow sandals. Ibn al-Zubayr and Yahya ibn Abi Kathir forbade wearing black sandals, because they cause anxiety.

﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us, that He may make clear to us what it is"﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:68]. Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Abi al-Fadl al-Mursi said in Ri al-Zam'an: The reason for their confusion was that they thought no cow could be a sign, because of what they knew about the she-camel of Salih and the marvels it contained. So they supposed that an animal would not be a sign unless it was in that manner. When they were told that it was a sign, they asked about its essence and its manner. For this reason they did not ask Musa about this, but asked him to ask God on their behalf, since God, exalted is He, is the one who knows the signs; they only asked about specification, even though the wording implies generality, because if they had acted on its generality, they would not have been certain of fulfilling the command. End of his words. Another said: When complete similarity in every respect was impossible, and confusion arose, it became permissible for them to ask. So they were informed of its age, and they found many like it in age, so they asked about its color, and were informed of that, but the confusion was not removed by this. So they asked about the work it was to do, and were informed of that, and about some of its particular qualities, and the confusion was removed by specifying its age, its color, its work, and some of its attributes, since the existence of many cows with these attributes is rare. This is the reason which emboldened them to repeat the question: ﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us, that He may make clear to us what it is"﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:68]. The discussion of this clause has already been covered.

﴿Surely, if God wills, we shall indeed be guided.﴾ That is, we shall indeed be guided to the exact cow that is commanded to be slaughtered, or to what was hidden of the matter of the killer, or to the wisdom for which we were commanded to slaughter the cow. The attachment of their guidance to God's will indicates submission, humility, and an acknowledgment of their regret for having failed to comply with the command. A hadith has come in this regard: "Had they not made the exception (saying 'if God wills'), they would never have been shown it until the end of time." The apodosis (jawab) of this conditional clause is omitted, and its meaning is indicated by the sense of the sentence: that is, "if God wills, we will be guided." When the apodosis is omitted, the verb of the conditional (fi'l al-shart) is past in form and negated with lam. By analogy, the conditional whose apodosis is omitted should come after the evidence for the apodosis. Thus the normal word order in speech would be: "Inna Zaydan la-qa'imun in sha'a Allah" (Indeed Zayd is standing, if God wills), meaning: "if God wills, then he is standing." However, here the conditional has been placed between the subject of inna (ism inna) and its predicate (khabar inna), in order to achieve harmony of the verse-endings (tawafuq ru'us al-ayy, the correspondence of the verses' final sounds), and for the emphasis of attaching the guidance to God's will. The predicate of inna came as a noun (ism), because it indicates more firmly the establishment (thubut) of the matter and that guidance is actually attained by them. It was emphasized by the two particles of emphasis, inna and the lam. They used this conditional only as a matter of courtesy (adab) toward God the Exalted, since they reported the establishment of guidance for themselves, and they emphasized that attribution. Had it been a pure conditional (ta'liq mahd), no emphasis would have been needed. Rather, it is like the speaker's saying: "I am doing such-and-such, if God wills," while he is actually engaged in doing it; he mentions "if God wills" by way of courtesy. Al-Maturidi said: The people of Musa, despite the coarseness of their understanding and the weakness of their intellects, were more knowing of God and more complete in tawhid than the Mu'tazila, because they said: ﴿Surely, if God wills, we shall indeed be guided.﴾ The Mu'tazila say: "God has willed that they be guided, and they have willed that they not be guided, so their will overcame the will of God the Exalted, since the matter is according to what they willed and not as God the Exalted willed." Thus the verse is a proof for us against the Mu'tazila. End of his words.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 69–70 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us, that He may make clear to us what its color is."﴾ When they had learned its age, they began to inquire about its color. All of this indicates the weakness of their natural disposition and their intellects, since God had already commanded them to slaughter a cow, and the one who conveyed God's command, who advised them and was concerned for them, had said: ﴿So do what you are commanded﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:68]. Despite this, they did not refrain from asking about its color. The discussion of ﴿Call upon your Lord for us﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:68], of the jussive in (yubayyin), and of the interrogative construction and the element omitted after it has already been covered in the preceding verse, so there is no need to repeat it here.

﴿He said, "Indeed He says it is a yellow cow"﴾: The majority of scholars said that this refers to the well-known color, and for this reason it is emphasized with "bright and pleasing" (al-fuqu' wa-l-surur), so it is yellow even in its horns and hooves. Al-Hasan and Abu 'Ubayda said that what is meant here is black, and a poet said:

*"A yellow one, not yellowish, but black like the coals of the fire."*

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it is yellow only in its horns and hooves.

(faqi'): that is, intensely yellow. This was stated by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan. Or it means purely yellow, as stated by Qutrub. Or it means clear, as stated by Abu al-'Aliyah and Qatadah.

(lawnuha) [its color]: They mentioned several possibilities for its i'rab (grammatical analysis, inflection). The first: it is a subject (fa'il) in the nominative, governed by "fāqiʿ," and "fāqiʿ" is an adjective of the cow. The second: it is a subject (mubtada') and its predicate (khabar) is "fāqiʿ." The third: it is a subject (mubtada'), and ﴿tasurru al-nazirin﴾ [it pleases the beholders] is its predicate. The feminine form is used according to one of two meanings. The first: because it is attached to a feminine noun, as they say: "some of his fingers went." The second: it is meant as a feminine, since it is the yellowness itself, so it is as if he said: "its yellowness pleases the beholders," and the word is construed according to the meaning, as in their saying: "his letter reached him, so he belittled it," meaning the letter. The better option is the first i'rab, because treating "lawnuha" as a subject and "fāqiʿ" as a fronted predicate is not permitted by the Kufans, or treating "tasurru al-nazirin" as its predicate involves the feminine marking of the predicate, which requires interpretation, as we have explained. That "lawnuha" is the subject (fa'il) of "fāqiʿ" follows the natural arrangement of the speech and requires no fronting, delaying, or interpretation. He did not make "fāqiʿ" feminine even though it is an adjective of a feminine noun, because it refers to the causal noun (al-sababi), which is masculine, so the construction becomes like: "a woman came to me whose father is good." It is not valid here for it to be a follower of "ṣafrāʾ" as an emphatic (tawkid), because that would require agreement with the noun it follows. Do you not see that you say: "black, intensely black (aswad hālik)," and "black [f.] intensely black [f.] (sawdāʾ hālikah)," but it is not permitted to say "sawdāʾ hālik"? As for his saying:

*"Indeed I pour the drink, yellow and intensely so, as if the fine musk within it is being crushed."*

its basis is poetry, since the usual wording would be "ṣafrāʾ fāqiʿah." The Qur'anic wording ﴿ṣafrāʾ fāqiʿun lawnuha﴾ [yellow, intensely yellow is its color] was not limited to "ṣafrāʾ fāqiʿah," because he intended to emphasize the attribution of yellowness. He judged of it that it is yellow, then judged of the color that it is intensely yellow. So he began first by describing the cow as yellow, then emphasized that by describing its color with it, as if he said: "It is yellow, and its color is intensely yellow." Thus the two ways in which yellowness is related differ in wording: first it is related to the essence itself, then secondly to the accident which is the color, and the object of the relation also differs, because mere yellowness differs from intense yellowness. Despite this clear difference, it does not require emphasis. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, why was it not said: 'ṣafrāʾ fāqiʿah'? And what is the benefit of that word 'color'? I say: its benefit is emphasis, because 'color' is a name for the appearance, which is the yellowness; so it is as if it was said: 'Its yellowness is intensely yellow,' and this is like your saying: 'his diligence is diligence,' and 'your madness is madness.'" This clause is an adjective of the cow, although the one who made it a predicate has been mentioned, as in his saying "lawnuha," and there is strain in that, which we have mentioned. This description came with a verb and not with the active participle, because the verb indicates occurrence and renewal. Since its color is among the stable things that do not renew, the description of it came with a noun and not with a verb. This description is placed after the one before it, because it arises from the preceding description, or is almost arising from it, since when the color is bright and beautiful, the eyes are amazed by it and the insights marvel at its beauty. The plural is used for "the beholders" to make clear that the eyes of people are drawn to it and delight in looking at it. It is not something that pleases one person without another, and for this reason the definite article (al-) is used which indicates totality, that is: it is ready to please whoever looks at it. Even if the looking here is the looking of the heart, which is reflection, then the pleasure arises from contemplating the wonders of God's creation, in the beautifying of its color and the perfecting of its form. The pronoun in "tasurru" refers to the cow, if we assume it is an adjective; if it is a predicate, it refers to the color about which "tasurru" is predicated. The feminine form has already been explained, and for this reason whoever reads "yasurru" with the yāʾ, it refers to the color; so it may be that "lawnuha" is a subject (mubtada'), "yasurru" is its predicate, and "fāqiʿ" is an adjective following "ṣafrāʾ" according to the pattern of this line of verse that we cited:

*"Indeed I pour the drink, yellow and intensely so."*

despite the rarity of that. It may also be that "lawnuha" is the subject (fa'il) of "fāqiʿ," and "yasurru" is a new independent statement. The majority of the commentators indicate that yellow is among the colors that bring joy, and for this reason 'Ali, may God honor his face, used to prefer yellow sandals. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Yellow expands the soul and removes worry," and Ibn 'Abbas also encouraged wearing yellow sandals. Ibn al-Zubayr and Yahya ibn Abi Kathir forbade wearing black sandals, because they cause anxiety.

﴿He said, "Indeed, He says it is a cow"﴾. The discussion of this is like the discussion of its counterpart.

﴿Unbroken, neither ploughing the earth nor watering the tilth﴾. "Unbroken" (dhalul) is an attribute of "a cow." It is a single-word attribute, though whoever says it is a clause-attribute, with the implied sense "neither is she unbroken," is far from correct. "Ploughing the earth" is an attribute of "unbroken," and it is a relative clause (sila) that falls within the scope of negation. The intended meaning is the negation of her ploughing the earth, that is, she does not plough and thereby become tractable. This is of the type of the line:

*"Over a faded road whose landmarks cannot be followed"*

The wording negates tractability, while the intended meaning is the negation of ploughing. Thus it follows that she is not tractable. "Nor watering the tilth" negates something equivalent to his saying "unbroken." The clause is an attribute, and both attributes are negated in meaning, just as "nor watering" is also negated in meaning. The sense of the statement is that she was not made tractable through work, neither in tilling nor in irrigating, and for this reason both ploughing the earth and watering it were negated of her.

Al-Hasan said: that cow was wild, and for this reason she was described as one that does not plough the earth through tilling, nor is she yoked to a water-wheel so that she might irrigate.

Some people held that His saying "ploughing the earth" is a verb affirmed both in wording and in meaning, and that He affirmed of the cow that she ploughs the earth and tills it, while He negated of her the watering of the tilth. This view was rejected on the level of meaning, because one who tills does not thereby fail to be tractable.

Some exegetes said: the meaning of "ploughing the earth" without tilling is through insolence and exuberance. It is a habit of cows, when they are insolent, to strike with their horns and hooves, thereby stirring the dust of the earth, and the dust gathers upon them. Thus this meaning completes His saying "unbroken," because describing her as exuberant and insolent is evidence that she is not tractable.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "unbroken" is an attribute of "a cow," meaning: a cow that is not broken, that is, she has not been trained for ploughing and stirring the earth, nor is she among the water-camels upon which one is yoked to irrigate the tilth. The first "la" is for negation, and the second is superfluous, emphasizing the first, because the meaning is: "unbroken, ploughing and watering." The two verbs are attributes of "unbroken," as if it were said: "unbroken, stirring and watering." That is the end of his words. The author of al-Muntakhab agreed with him in treating the second "la" as superfluous. But what they both held is not correct, because His saying "unbroken" is an attribute negated by "la," and when the attribute has been negated by "la," the repetition of the negating "la" is required for what it governs. You say: "I passed by a man who is neither generous nor brave" (la karim wa-la shuja'). He, exalted, said: ﴿having three branches﴾ [al-Mursalat 30], ﴿neither shady nor sparing from the blaze﴾ [al-Mursalat 31], ﴿and a shadow of black smoke﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 43], ﴿neither cool nor generous﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 44], ﴿neither old nor virgin﴾ [al-Baqarah 68]. It is not permissible to omit the repetition, because what is conveyed by them is negation, except in a case of poetic necessity. When their estimated form returns to "unbroken, stirring and watering," it is impermissible, for the reason we have mentioned, namely the obligation to repeat the negating "la." And upon their estimate it becomes like: "a man came to me, neither generous," and that is not permissible except in poetry, as we have pointed out.

Ibn Atiyyah said: this clause cannot be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), because it is from an indefinite noun (nakirah). That is the end of his words.

The clause he referred to is His saying "ploughing the earth," and the indefinite noun is either His saying "unbroken" or His saying "a cow." If by the indefinite noun he means "a cow," then it has been described, and a circumstantial clause from a described indefinite noun is permissible, quite acceptably. If by the indefinite noun he means "unbroken," then this is the view of the majority of those who did not grasp the doctrine of Sibawayh and did not examine his book closely. Indeed Sibawayh, in his book, in several places permitted the coming of a circumstantial clause from an indefinite noun even when it is not described, though agreement (ittiba') is the more apparent and better form. Sibawayh said in the chapter on what the noun cannot be except indefinite: "It may also be put in the accusative in the manner of: 'this is a man, departing' (hadha rajulun muntaliqan)," meaning as a circumstantial clause from an indefinite noun. Then he said: "This is the view of 'Isa." Then he said: "al-Khalil claimed that this is permissible, and he put it in the accusative as he would put a definite noun in the accusative, making it a circumstantial clause and not an attribute." Similar to this: "I passed by a man standing," when you make the passing occur in a state of standing. It may also be permitted here: "there is in it a man standing." Similar to this: "upon him is a hundred, white" (alayhi mi'atun bayda'), and the nominative is the preferred form; "upon him is a hundred, as debt" (alayhi mi'atun dayna), and the nominative is the preferred form. Yunus claimed that some Arabs say: "I passed by water, the sitting of a man" (qa'data rajulin), and the preferred form is the genitive. Similarly Sibawayh said in the chapter on what is put in the accusative because it is unsuitable to be an attribute, and he said: "a jar of ghee" (raquduun khala) and "upon you a jar of ghee" (nihyun samnan). He said in the chapter on "na'am": "If you say to me, 'honey, a jar's worth' (asalun mil'u jarratin), and 'upon him is a debt, the hair of two dogs' (shi'ru kalbayn), then the preferred form is the nominative, since it is an attribute, and the accusative is permitted as in 'upon him is a hundred, white'." These are the texts of Sibawayh. Had it been impermissible, as Ibn Atiyyah claimed, Sibawayh would not have analogized from it, for what is impermissible is not stated, let alone analogized. And though agreement with the indefinite noun is better, it is avoided in this issue because what Abu Muhammad (Ibn Atiyyah) held is the view of the weak in the craft of i'rab (grammatical inflection), who did not grasp the words of the Imam.

Some grammarians of i'rab permitted that "ploughing the earth" be in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun concealed in "unbroken," its estimate being: "she is not made tractable while ploughing." But the preferable reading is what we began with first.

Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read: "la dhalula" (with the fatha). Al-Zamakhshari said: in the sense of "la dhalula hunaka," that is, wherever she is, and it is a negation of her being tractable, and so that she may be described by it, so one says: "she is tractable." Similar to this is your saying: "I passed by a people, neither stingy nor cowardly," meaning: among them, or wherever they are. That is the end of his words. According to his estimate, the predicate is omitted, and His saying "ploughing the earth" is an attribute of the noun of "la," and it is negated in meaning, and for this reason a negated clause is conjoined to it, namely His saying "nor watering the tilth." Given this, "ploughing the earth and not watering the tilth" cannot be the predicate, because this construction would be discordant with what precedes it, since His saying "He says it is a cow" [al-Baqarah 68] would remain a statement cut off from what follows, as the meaning would not be complete except on the estimate that this clause is a parenthetical interposed between the attribute and the thing described, and the focal point of the predicate would be His saying "a sound one with no blemish in it," because it is an attribute in wording and a predicate in meaning. That parenthetical would, in meaning, negate the tractability of this cow, since she is one individual of the kind negated by "la" which was built with it. It is not permissible that this clause, I mean "la dhalula," in the reading of al-Sulami, be in the position of an attribute on the estimate that "ploughing" and what follows it is the predicate, because there is in it no resumptive pronoun referring back to the described noun, which is "a cow," for the resumptive pronoun in "ploughing" and in "watering" is the pronoun of the noun of "la." It cannot be imagined that His saying "unbroken, ploughing the earth and not watering the tilth" on the estimate that "ploughing" and what follows it is a predicate would indicate negation of tractability together with a predicate about existence, because that would not match what exists. Rather, the meaning is the negation of that in relation to their land and their tilth, and the alif and lam are for prior reference (al-'ahd). Just as the negation of "unbroken" is conceived while one believes that "ploughing" and what follows it is an attribute, because you restricted the predicate by your estimate "wherever she is," so this negation is apt. Likewise, the negation of "unbroken" is conceived together with the predicate about it, when it is believed that the referent of the two predicates is specific, namely the land and the tilth. And just as you estimate "there is no unbroken one ploughing and not watering wherever that cow is," so you estimate "there is no unbroken one ploughing their land and not watering their tilth." Both are negations that have been restricted, either by the omitted predicate or by the referent of the affirmative predicate.

Thus the description of the cow as "unbroken" and what follows it has been negated, either by the clause being an attribute with the omitted predicate as the linking element, or by the clause being a parenthetical between the attribute and the thing described, since it does not contain a linking element connecting it with what precedes it when you make "ploughing" a predicate. It should not be said that the linking element here is generality (al-'umum), since the cow is an individual of the generic noun, because linking by generality has only been said of constructions like "Zayd is the best of men" (na'ima al-rajul), and that is disputed, though the sounder view is the opposite. The "na'am" construction is an anomalous pattern not to be analogized from. If you said, "Zayd is not a man in the house" and "I passed by a man, not sensible, in the house," meaning the predicate and the attribute, and you made generality the linking element, that would not be permissible, because if you negate "not a man in the house," Zayd is negated from it, and if you say "not sensible in the house," the sense is negated from passing by him. For this reason we chose, in this reading, on the estimate that "ploughing" and "watering" are predicates of "unbroken," that the clause be a parenthetical between the attribute and the thing described, and that it indicate the negation of ploughing and the negation of watering in meaning, not in the sense that the two clauses are attributes of the cow. As for al-Zamakhshari's illustration with "I passed by a people, neither stingy nor cowardly among them, or wherever they are," it is a sound illustration, because the clause functioning as an attribute of "a people" does not have generality as its linking element; the linking element there is this pronoun. Likewise what he established has a pronoun as its linking element, since he estimated "unbroken there," that is, wherever she is, so this pronoun refers back to the cow, and the linking was accomplished by it, just as it was accomplished in his illustration with "among them" or "wherever they are."

From what we have established, it follows that His exalted saying "unbroken" in the reading of al-Sulami may be construed in two ways: first, that it is parenthetical, on the estimate of an omitted predicate; second, that it is parenthetical, on the estimate that it is the predicate of "neither ploughing the earth nor watering the tilth." The reading of the majority is preferable, because describing by a single word is better than describing by a clause, and because in the reading of Abu Abd al-Rahman, on one of its two constructions, you would have described with a clause and placed it before the single-word description, and this is restricted to necessity according to some of our companions, since "la dhalula," whose negation is a clause, and "musallamah," a single word, means that you placed the clause-description before the single-word description.

The second object of "watering" (tasqi) is omitted, because saqa is transitive to two objects. Some read "tusqi" with a damma on the ta', from "asqa," and the two have one meaning. It is also read "nasqikum" with a fatha and with a damma on the nun.

"Sound" (musallamah): free from defects. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, Abu al-Aliyah and Muqatil. Or: free from colours and markings, said by Mujahid and Ibn Zayd. Or: free from labour in tilling, watering and all other kinds of use, said by al-Hasan and Ibn Qutaybah. The meaning is that its owners had exempted it from that, as another poet said:

*"Or a beast whose back is unladen, bearing witness to its turned-away flank, that never performed the Hajj to its Lord in this world nor the umrah."*

Or: free from the unlawful, with no usurpation, no theft, and nothing else of the kind, but purified from all that. Or: sound in its limbs and its make, said by Ata al-Khurasani. Or: sound from all that has been mentioned before, so that it is free from defects, innocent of usurpation, perfect in creation, strong in its build, complete in its qualities, and fit for the manifestation in it of the sign of God, exalted, and the miracle of His Messenger.

Abu Muhammad ibn 'Atiyya said: "Musallama" is a form of intensification (mubalagha) from "salama" (free from defect). Someone else said the same, claiming that it is one of the forms of intensification, since its pattern is mufa''ala from salama. This is not as he mentioned, because the doubling (tadh'if) in "musallama" is not for the sake of intensification. Rather, it is the doubling of transitivity (naql wa-ta'diya): one says sallama kadha, and when you make it transitive by doubling, the doubling here is like its use in the phrase "farrahtu Zaydan" (I made Zayd happy), since the original is "fariha Zayd" (Zayd was happy), and similarly this one originally is "sallama Zaydan," which is then doubled and becomes transitive. So there is no intensification here, but rather it is synonymous with the transitive pattern formed with the hamza.

"La shiyata fiha": that is, without any white (la bayad), as said by al-Suddi; or "without any mixture" (la wadah), which is the combination of two colours of black and white; or "without any defect" (la 'ayb fiha); or "without any colour that contradicts its colour, whether black or white"; or "without any black on the face and legs," which is the shiya in cattle. It is said that a bull is musawwa when there is black on its face and legs. It is also said that "shiyata fiha" explains "musallama," meaning its yellowness is pure, free from the admixture of other colours, as said by Ibn Zayd. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "And the bull that is ashyah is the one whose piebald marks are apparent. One says: a horse is abqa', a ram is akhraj, a he-goat is abraq, a dog is abqa', and a bull is ashyah. All of these have the same meaning as baligha (piebald)." End of quote. But ashyah is not derived from shiya, because the two roots differ.

* *

﴿Qalu al-Ana ji'ta bil-haqq﴾ (They said: "Now you have brought the truth"): The majority read "al-" with a sukun on the lam and a hamza after it. Nafi' read it by omitting the hamza and transferring its vowel to the lam. He has two transmitted versions: in one, the waw of "qalu" is dropped, since the vowel transfer is considered incidental; in the other, the waw is kept, taking account of the transfer and the incidental vowelling, because the waw was dropped only on account of the sukun of the lam after it. When the cause of deletion is removed, the waw returns to its original state of being present. "Al-An" is in the accusative as an adverb of time, denoting the present time, which is their statement to him: ﴿Innaha baqaratun la dhulul﴾ up to ﴿la shiyata fiha﴾. The governing verb is "ji'ta," and "ji'ta" is not meant to imply that he was absent and then came; rather its figurative sense is "you spoke the truth." On this meaning, "bil-haqq" is connected to "ji'ta." Alternatively, the ba' is for transitivity, as if he said: "You have brought the truth" meaning that the truth had not come to us and you brought it. Here there is an omitted qualifier, whose estimated form is "bil-haqqi al-mubin," that is, the clear truth which leaves no ambiguity. The qualifier had to be estimated because in every discussion he had with them he brought the truth, so unless this qualifier is supposed, their restricting his coming with the truth to this particular occasion would have no benefit.

Qatada went to the view that there is no omitted qualifier here, and said: they disbelieved by this statement because the Prophet of God (ﷺ), may the best prayers and peace be upon our Prophet, never came to them except with the truth at every time. They said: the meaning of "bil-haqq" is "with the reality of the description of the cow, and no ambiguity remained in it."

﴿Fa-dhabahuha﴾ (So they slaughtered it): Before this clause there is an omitted element, the estimated sense being: "So they sought it and obtained it," that is, this cow (p-258) that combines the previously mentioned attributes. Its obtaining happened either by God sending it down from heaven, or by it having been wild and they captured it, or by buying it from the young man who was dutiful to his parents. This is what the sayings of most of the exegetes agree upon. They mentioned in this a great deal of disagreement and confused narratives, which we have passed over without citing, as is our habit with most of the stories they transmit, since only what is authentically reported from God Most High, or from His Messenger, in the Qur'an or the Sunna should be transmitted in this matter.

﴿Wa-ma kadu yaf'alun﴾ (And they nearly did not do it): He referred to the slaughtering by the verb "fa'ala," because the verb is used as a euphemism for every act. "Kada" in affirmative form indicates approximation. When you say "kada Zayd yaqumu," its meaning is that standing was nearly approached but he did not actually undertake it. When you say "ma kada Zayd yaqumu," its meaning is the negation of approximation. It behaves like other verbs in being obligatory and negated. Some people have held that when it is affirmed it indicates the negation of the predicate, and when negated it indicates the affirmation of the predicate, citing this verse, since God's statement ﴿fa-dhabahuha﴾ indicates this. The correct view is the first. As for the verse, the time of the negation of approximation and the time of the slaughter differs, since the meaning is: "They did not even approach slaughtering it before that," that is, the slaughter occurred after its approach was negated. So the meaning is that they found it difficult to slaughter it, then they slaughtered it afterward. It is said that the reason why they nearly did not slaughter it was either the high price of it, or fear of the exposure of the killer, or the scarcity of compliance and obstinacy toward the prophets, as was known of them. They differed regarding this slaughtered cow: was it the one they were first commanded to slaughter, specified in the first command, such that if the slaughter had first occurred on it, it would have occurred only on this specific one? Or was the cow first commanded an unspecified cow, which then became specified by a colour and attributes, so they slaughtered the specified one? In that case the first command was specified by the transfer of the ruling from a cow in general to a specific cow. Abrogation before the act is permitted, on the basis that this specific cow falls under the command to slaughter a cow, so if the slaughter had been performed on it under the first address, they would have complied, and likewise after the specification. Then those who hold this second view differed: is it obligatory that it be with the final attribute only, namely that it is not a dhalul, and so on to the end? Or must it, in addition to these attributes, in the answers to the two earlier questions, be neither fariq nor bikr, and yellow with a bright colour? The view we choose is this second one, because the apparent reading is that these attributes are combined, since His saying "ma hiya" and "ma lawnuha" and "ma hiya" indicate this. This is what has become well known in the reports, that it had all these attributes together. And since clarification must not be delayed beyond the time of need, that would be a command after a command, and this indicates the abrogation of the easier by the more difficult, and the permissibility of abrogation before the act.

﴿Wa-idh qatalتم nafsan﴾ (And when you killed a soul): This is conjoined to His saying: ﴿Wa-idh qala Musa li-qawmihi﴾ [al-Baqara: 67]. It is possible that the order of their occurrence and revelation follows the order of their recitation, so that God commanded them to slaughter the cow, and they slaughtered it without knowing the secret God had in it. Then after that came the matter of the slain man, and He revealed to them what He had hidden from them of wisdom in His saying: "Strike him with part of it." Nothing compels us to believe that the killing of the slain occurred earlier. Then they asked about identifying his killer, since they had differed over that, so God commanded them to slaughter a cow. In that case the command to slaughter is earlier in revelation and recitation but later in occurrence, and the killing of the slain is later in revelation and recitation but earlier in occurrence. Nor are we compelled to believe that the command to slaughter and what follows it is later in revelation but earlier in recitation, with the report of their killing earlier in revelation but later in recitation, without addressing the time of occurrence of the two stories. Those who turned the verses away from their apparent meaning did so out of consideration of the stories they transmitted that are not authentic, since no book or Sunna has reported them. Whenever a matter can be understood according to its apparent meaning, that is preferable, since departing from the apparent meaning to what is not apparent occurs only with a preponderant reason, and there is no preponderance here. Rather, the profound wisdom appears in their being first commanded to slaughter a cow: would they comply or not? And compliance with commands whose wisdom does not appear at first sight is greater than compliance with commands whose wisdom is apparent, because it is pure obedience, complete servitude, and sincere submission. This is unlike a command for which wisdom appears, since in the intellect there is a motive to comply with it and an incitement to act upon it.

The author of al-Muntakhab said: the occurrence of that killing must be prior to God's command to slaughter. As for the report of that killing, and that the slain must be struck with part of that cow, it is not required that it be prior to the report about the story of the cow. So the statement of one who says that this story must be prior to the first is an error, since this story in itself must be prior to the first in occurrence. But precedence in mention is not required, since sometimes the mention of the cause precedes the mention of the ruling, and sometimes the reverse. So it is as if, when that incident befell them, He commanded them to slaughter the cow, and when they had slaughtered it, He said: ﴿Wa-idh qatalتم nafsan﴾ earlier, and you disputed, so I will reveal to you the killer whom you concealed, by striking the slain with part of this slaughtered cow. The story of the command to slaughter the cow was placed before the mention of the slain, because if the order were reversed it would not be a single story, and the purpose of repeated reproach would be lost. End of his words. This is based on the premise that the killing occurred first and then they were commanded afterward to slaughter the cow, and he has no evidence for that except transmitting some stories that are not established in any book or Sunna. We have already shown how the two verses are to be read: the command to slaughter is earlier, and the killing is later, just as their recitation is.

Some people said: inversion of order is acceptable, because it is found in the Qur'an, in phrases and in words, and in Arab speech. They cited many examples, among them the story of Noah (peace be upon him) concerning the destruction of his people, and His saying ﴿Wa-qala irkabu fiha﴾ [Hud: 41]; and in the ruling on the widow whose husband has died, the waiting period of four months and ten days, and the provision for a year, since the abrogating ruling is earlier and the abrogated is later. He mentioned many instances on his view of inversion of words in the Qur'an and poetry. Our scholars have mentioned that inversion of order is one of the poetic licences (darurat), so the Qur'an should be exempt from it. The attribution of the slain to a group is either because the killers were a group, namely the heirs of the slain, and it has been reported that they gathered together to kill him; or because the killer was one person, and the act was attributed to them since it existed among them, following the Arab manner of attributing things to a tribe when something blameworthy or praiseworthy is found in some of its members.

﴿Fa-idda'ra'tum fiha﴾ (Then you disputed about it): The majority read it with idgham (assimilation). Abu Haywa read "fa-tadara'tum," on the pattern of tafa'altum, which is the original form; this was transmitted by one of the compilers of the tafsir. Ibn 'Atiyya said: Abu Haywa and Abu al-Sawwar al-Ghanawi read "wa-idh qatalتم nafsan fa-idda'ra'tum," and a group read "fa-tadara'tum" on the original form. End of his words. One of the compilers of the tafsir reported that Abu al-Sawwar read "fa-dara'tum" without an alif before the ra'. This tadara'u, meaning mutual repelling, may be literal, namely that some of them push others with their hands because of the intensity of the dispute; or figurative, namely that one of them shifted his killing onto another, and the one on whom it was shifted pushed it back to the one who shifted it; or that some of them pushed others with accusation and exoneration. The pronoun in "fiha" refers to the soul, which is the apparent reading. It is also said to refer to the killers, so it returns to the verbal noun understood from the verb. It is also said to refer to the accusation, so it returns to what the sense of the speech indicates.

Allah is the One who brings forth what you were concealing.

"Ma" (what) is in the accusative, governed by the active participle (ism al-fa'il, the active participle form), and it is a known relative pronoun (mawsul ma'hud, a relative with a definite, known antecedent). Therefore He used the active participle, because it indicates permanence (thubut), and He did not use the verb, which indicates renewal (tajaddud) and repetition (takrar). There is no repetition here, since there is no renewal in it, because this is one single, well-known story. Therefore, and Allah knows best, the verb was not used.

The active participle came functioning as a verb governing its object, and it was not made into a construct (lam yudaf), even though in meaning it refers to the past. This is because it narrates what was future at the time of the dispute (al-tada'u), and this is like the way the present tense narrates the present state in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And their dog stretching forth its forelegs at the threshold﴾ [al-Kahf: 18]. The verb "kana" (was) entered here to indicate that the concealment came earlier, and the returning pronoun referring to "ma" is omitted, its estimated form being: "ma kuntum taktumunahu" (what you were concealing it).

The apparent meaning is that it refers to what you were concealing concerning the matter of the slain man and his killer, and this is the view of the majority (al-jumhur). It has been said that it is permissible for it to be general, covering the slain man and other matters, so that the slain man would be among its particulars. There is consideration in this, since not everything they concealed from the people did Allah make manifest.

﴿He said, "Indeed, He says it is a cow"﴾. The discussion of this is like the discussion of its counterpart.

﴿Unbroken, neither ploughing the earth nor watering the tilth﴾. "Unbroken" (dhalul) is an attribute of "a cow." It is a single-word attribute, though whoever says it is a clause-attribute, with the implied sense "neither is she unbroken," is far from correct. "Ploughing the earth" is an attribute of "unbroken," and it is a relative clause (sila) that falls within the scope of negation. The intended meaning is the negation of her ploughing the earth, that is, she does not plough and thereby become tractable. This is of the type of the line:

*"Over a faded road whose landmarks cannot be followed"*

The wording negates tractability, while the intended meaning is the negation of ploughing. Thus it follows that she is not tractable. "Nor watering the tilth" negates something equivalent to his saying "unbroken." The clause is an attribute, and both attributes are negated in meaning, just as "nor watering" is also negated in meaning. The sense of the statement is that she was not made tractable through work, neither in tilling nor in irrigating, and for this reason both ploughing the earth and watering it were negated of her.

Al-Hasan said: that cow was wild, and for this reason she was described as one that does not plough the earth through tilling, nor is she yoked to a water-wheel so that she might irrigate.

Some people held that His saying "ploughing the earth" is a verb affirmed both in wording and in meaning, and that He affirmed of the cow that she ploughs the earth and tills it, while He negated of her the watering of the tilth. This view was rejected on the level of meaning, because one who tills does not thereby fail to be tractable.

Some exegetes said: the meaning of "ploughing the earth" without tilling is through insolence and exuberance. It is a habit of cows, when they are insolent, to strike with their horns and hooves, thereby stirring the dust of the earth, and the dust gathers upon them. Thus this meaning completes His saying "unbroken," because describing her as exuberant and insolent is evidence that she is not tractable.
