Al-Zamakhshari said: "unbroken" is an attribute of "a cow," meaning: a cow that is not broken, that is, she has not been trained for ploughing and stirring the earth, nor is she among the water-camels upon which one is yoked to irrigate the tilth. The first "la" is for negation, and the second is superfluous, emphasizing the first, because the meaning is: "unbroken, ploughing and watering." The two verbs are attributes of "unbroken," as if it were said: "unbroken, stirring and watering." That is the end of his words. The author of al-Muntakhab agreed with him in treating the second "la" as superfluous. But what they both held is not correct, because His saying "unbroken" is an attribute negated by "la," and when the attribute has been negated by "la," the repetition of the negating "la" is required for what it governs. You say: "I passed by a man who is neither generous nor brave" (la karim wa-la shuja'). He, exalted, said: ﴿having three branches﴾ [al-Mursalat 30], ﴿neither shady nor sparing from the blaze﴾ [al-Mursalat 31], ﴿and a shadow of black smoke﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 43], ﴿neither cool nor generous﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 44], ﴿neither old nor virgin﴾ [al-Baqarah 68]. It is not permissible to omit the repetition, because what is conveyed by them is negation, except in a case of poetic necessity. When their estimated form returns to "unbroken, stirring and watering," it is impermissible, for the reason we have mentioned, namely the obligation to repeat the negating "la." And upon their estimate it becomes like: "a man came to me, neither generous," and that is not permissible except in poetry, as we have pointed out.

Ibn Atiyyah said: this clause cannot be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), because it is from an indefinite noun (nakirah). That is the end of his words.

The clause he referred to is His saying "ploughing the earth," and the indefinite noun is either His saying "unbroken" or His saying "a cow." If by the indefinite noun he means "a cow," then it has been described, and a circumstantial clause from a described indefinite noun is permissible, quite acceptably. If by the indefinite noun he means "unbroken," then this is the view of the majority of those who did not grasp the doctrine of Sibawayh and did not examine his book closely. Indeed Sibawayh, in his book, in several places permitted the coming of a circumstantial clause from an indefinite noun even when it is not described, though agreement (ittiba') is the more apparent and better form. Sibawayh said in the chapter on what the noun cannot be except indefinite: "It may also be put in the accusative in the manner of: 'this is a man, departing' (hadha rajulun muntaliqan)," meaning as a circumstantial clause from an indefinite noun. Then he said: "This is the view of 'Isa." Then he said: "al-Khalil claimed that this is permissible, and he put it in the accusative as he would put a definite noun in the accusative, making it a circumstantial clause and not an attribute." Similar to this: "I passed by a man standing," when you make the passing occur in a state of standing. It may also be permitted here: "there is in it a man standing." Similar to this: "upon him is a hundred, white" (alayhi mi'atun bayda'), and the nominative is the preferred form; "upon him is a hundred, as debt" (alayhi mi'atun dayna), and the nominative is the preferred form. Yunus claimed that some Arabs say: "I passed by water, the sitting of a man" (qa'data rajulin), and the preferred form is the genitive. Similarly Sibawayh said in the chapter on what is put in the accusative because it is unsuitable to be an attribute, and he said: "a jar of ghee" (raquduun khala) and "upon you a jar of ghee" (nihyun samnan). He said in the chapter on "na'am": "If you say to me, 'honey, a jar's worth' (asalun mil'u jarratin), and 'upon him is a debt, the hair of two dogs' (shi'ru kalbayn), then the preferred form is the nominative, since it is an attribute, and the accusative is permitted as in 'upon him is a hundred, white'." These are the texts of Sibawayh. Had it been impermissible, as Ibn Atiyyah claimed, Sibawayh would not have analogized from it, for what is impermissible is not stated, let alone analogized. And though agreement with the indefinite noun is better, it is avoided in this issue because what Abu Muhammad (Ibn Atiyyah) held is the view of the weak in the craft of i'rab (grammatical inflection), who did not grasp the words of the Imam.

Some grammarians of i'rab permitted that "ploughing the earth" be in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun concealed in "unbroken," its estimate being: "she is not made tractable while ploughing." But the preferable reading is what we began with first.

Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read: "la dhalula" (with the fatha). Al-Zamakhshari said: in the sense of "la dhalula hunaka," that is, wherever she is, and it is a negation of her being tractable, and so that she may be described by it, so one says: "she is tractable." Similar to this is your saying: "I passed by a people, neither stingy nor cowardly," meaning: among them, or wherever they are. That is the end of his words. According to his estimate, the predicate is omitted, and His saying "ploughing the earth" is an attribute of the noun of "la," and it is negated in meaning, and for this reason a negated clause is conjoined to it, namely His saying "nor watering the tilth." Given this, "ploughing the earth and not watering the tilth" cannot be the predicate, because this construction would be discordant with what precedes it, since His saying "He says it is a cow" [al-Baqarah 68] would remain a statement cut off from what follows, as the meaning would not be complete except on the estimate that this clause is a parenthetical interposed between the attribute and the thing described, and the focal point of the predicate would be His saying "a sound one with no blemish in it," because it is an attribute in wording and a predicate in meaning. That parenthetical would, in meaning, negate the tractability of this cow, since she is one individual of the kind negated by "la" which was built with it. It is not permissible that this clause, I mean "la dhalula," in the reading of al-Sulami, be in the position of an attribute on the estimate that "ploughing" and what follows it is the predicate, because there is in it no resumptive pronoun referring back to the described noun, which is "a cow," for the resumptive pronoun in "ploughing" and in "watering" is the pronoun of the noun of "la." It cannot be imagined that His saying "unbroken, ploughing the earth and not watering the tilth" on the estimate that "ploughing" and what follows it is a predicate would indicate negation of tractability together with a predicate about existence, because that would not match what exists. Rather, the meaning is the negation of that in relation to their land and their tilth, and the alif and lam are for prior reference (al-'ahd). Just as the negation of "unbroken" is conceived while one believes that "ploughing" and what follows it is an attribute, because you restricted the predicate by your estimate "wherever she is," so this negation is apt. Likewise, the negation of "unbroken" is conceived together with the predicate about it, when it is believed that the referent of the two predicates is specific, namely the land and the tilth. And just as you estimate "there is no unbroken one ploughing and not watering wherever that cow is," so you estimate "there is no unbroken one ploughing their land and not watering their tilth." Both are negations that have been restricted, either by the omitted predicate or by the referent of the affirmative predicate.

Thus the description of the cow as "unbroken" and what follows it has been negated, either by the clause being an attribute with the omitted predicate as the linking element, or by the clause being a parenthetical between the attribute and the thing described, since it does not contain a linking element connecting it with what precedes it when you make "ploughing" a predicate. It should not be said that the linking element here is generality (al-'umum), since the cow is an individual of the generic noun, because linking by generality has only been said of constructions like "Zayd is the best of men" (na'ima al-rajul), and that is disputed, though the sounder view is the opposite. The "na'am" construction is an anomalous pattern not to be analogized from. If you said, "Zayd is not a man in the house" and "I passed by a man, not sensible, in the house," meaning the predicate and the attribute, and you made generality the linking element, that would not be permissible, because if you negate "not a man in the house," Zayd is negated from it, and if you say "not sensible in the house," the sense is negated from passing by him. For this reason we chose, in this reading, on the estimate that "ploughing" and "watering" are predicates of "unbroken," that the clause be a parenthetical between the attribute and the thing described, and that it indicate the negation of ploughing and the negation of watering in meaning, not in the sense that the two clauses are attributes of the cow. As for al-Zamakhshari's illustration with "I passed by a people, neither stingy nor cowardly among them, or wherever they are," it is a sound illustration, because the clause functioning as an attribute of "a people" does not have generality as its linking element; the linking element there is this pronoun. Likewise what he established has a pronoun as its linking element, since he estimated "unbroken there," that is, wherever she is, so this pronoun refers back to the cow, and the linking was accomplished by it, just as it was accomplished in his illustration with "among them" or "wherever they are."

From what we have established, it follows that His exalted saying "unbroken" in the reading of al-Sulami may be construed in two ways: first, that it is parenthetical, on the estimate of an omitted predicate; second, that it is parenthetical, on the estimate that it is the predicate of "neither ploughing the earth nor watering the tilth." The reading of the majority is preferable, because describing by a single word is better than describing by a clause, and because in the reading of Abu Abd al-Rahman, on one of its two constructions, you would have described with a clause and placed it before the single-word description, and this is restricted to necessity according to some of our companions, since "la dhalula," whose negation is a clause, and "musallamah," a single word, means that you placed the clause-description before the single-word description.

The second object of "watering" (tasqi) is omitted, because saqa is transitive to two objects. Some read "tusqi" with a damma on the ta', from "asqa," and the two have one meaning. It is also read "nasqikum" with a fatha and with a damma on the nun.

"Sound" (musallamah): free from defects. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, Abu al-Aliyah and Muqatil. Or: free from colours and markings, said by Mujahid and Ibn Zayd. Or: free from labour in tilling, watering and all other kinds of use, said by al-Hasan and Ibn Qutaybah. The meaning is that its owners had exempted it from that, as another poet said:

*"Or a beast whose back is unladen, bearing witness to its turned-away flank, that never performed the Hajj to its Lord in this world nor the umrah."*

Or: free from the unlawful, with no usurpation, no theft, and nothing else of the kind, but purified from all that. Or: sound in its limbs and its make, said by Ata al-Khurasani. Or: sound from all that has been mentioned before, so that it is free from defects, innocent of usurpation, perfect in creation, strong in its build, complete in its qualities, and fit for the manifestation in it of the sign of God, exalted, and the miracle of His Messenger.

Abu Muhammad ibn 'Atiyya said: "Musallama" is a form of intensification (mubalagha) from "salama" (free from defect). Someone else said the same, claiming that it is one of the forms of intensification, since its pattern is mufa''ala from salama. This is not as he mentioned, because the doubling (tadh'if) in "musallama" is not for the sake of intensification. Rather, it is the doubling of transitivity (naql wa-ta'diya): one says sallama kadha, and when you make it transitive by doubling, the doubling here is like its use in the phrase "farrahtu Zaydan" (I made Zayd happy), since the original is "fariha Zayd" (Zayd was happy), and similarly this one originally is "sallama Zaydan," which is then doubled and becomes transitive. So there is no intensification here, but rather it is synonymous with the transitive pattern formed with the hamza.

"La shiyata fiha": that is, without any white (la bayad), as said by al-Suddi; or "without any mixture" (la wadah), which is the combination of two colours of black and white; or "without any defect" (la 'ayb fiha); or "without any colour that contradicts its colour, whether black or white"; or "without any black on the face and legs," which is the shiya in cattle. It is said that a bull is musawwa when there is black on its face and legs. It is also said that "shiyata fiha" explains "musallama," meaning its yellowness is pure, free from the admixture of other colours, as said by Ibn Zayd. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "And the bull that is ashyah is the one whose piebald marks are apparent. One says: a horse is abqa', a ram is akhraj, a he-goat is abraq, a dog is abqa', and a bull is ashyah. All of these have the same meaning as baligha (piebald)." End of quote. But ashyah is not derived from shiya, because the two roots differ.

* *

﴿Qalu al-Ana ji'ta bil-haqq﴾ (They said: "Now you have brought the truth"): The majority read "al-" with a sukun on the lam and a hamza after it. Nafi' read it by omitting the hamza and transferring its vowel to the lam. He has two transmitted versions: in one, the waw of "qalu" is dropped, since the vowel transfer is considered incidental; in the other, the waw is kept, taking account of the transfer and the incidental vowelling, because the waw was dropped only on account of the sukun of the lam after it. When the cause of deletion is removed, the waw returns to its original state of being present. "Al-An" is in the accusative as an adverb of time, denoting the present time, which is their statement to him: ﴿Innaha baqaratun la dhulul﴾ up to ﴿la shiyata fiha﴾. The governing verb is "ji'ta," and "ji'ta" is not meant to imply that he was absent and then came; rather its figurative sense is "you spoke the truth." On this meaning, "bil-haqq" is connected to "ji'ta." Alternatively, the ba' is for transitivity, as if he said: "You have brought the truth" meaning that the truth had not come to us and you brought it. Here there is an omitted qualifier, whose estimated form is "bil-haqqi al-mubin," that is, the clear truth which leaves no ambiguity. The qualifier had to be estimated because in every discussion he had with them he brought the truth, so unless this qualifier is supposed, their restricting his coming with the truth to this particular occasion would have no benefit.

Qatada went to the view that there is no omitted qualifier here, and said: they disbelieved by this statement because the Prophet of God (ﷺ), may the best prayers and peace be upon our Prophet, never came to them except with the truth at every time. They said: the meaning of "bil-haqq" is "with the reality of the description of the cow, and no ambiguity remained in it."

﴿Fa-dhabahuha﴾ (So they slaughtered it): Before this clause there is an omitted element, the estimated sense being: "So they sought it and obtained it," that is, this cow (p-258) that combines the previously mentioned attributes. Its obtaining happened either by God sending it down from heaven, or by it having been wild and they captured it, or by buying it from the young man who was dutiful to his parents. This is what the sayings of most of the exegetes agree upon. They mentioned in this a great deal of disagreement and confused narratives, which we have passed over without citing, as is our habit with most of the stories they transmit, since only what is authentically reported from God Most High, or from His Messenger, in the Qur'an or the Sunna should be transmitted in this matter.

﴿Wa-ma kadu yaf'alun﴾ (And they nearly did not do it): He referred to the slaughtering by the verb "fa'ala," because the verb is used as a euphemism for every act. "Kada" in affirmative form indicates approximation. When you say "kada Zayd yaqumu," its meaning is that standing was nearly approached but he did not actually undertake it. When you say "ma kada Zayd yaqumu," its meaning is the negation of approximation. It behaves like other verbs in being obligatory and negated. Some people have held that when it is affirmed it indicates the negation of the predicate, and when negated it indicates the affirmation of the predicate, citing this verse, since God's statement ﴿fa-dhabahuha﴾ indicates this. The correct view is the first. As for the verse, the time of the negation of approximation and the time of the slaughter differs, since the meaning is: "They did not even approach slaughtering it before that," that is, the slaughter occurred after its approach was negated. So the meaning is that they found it difficult to slaughter it, then they slaughtered it afterward. It is said that the reason why they nearly did not slaughter it was either the high price of it, or fear of the exposure of the killer, or the scarcity of compliance and obstinacy toward the prophets, as was known of them. They differed regarding this slaughtered cow: was it the one they were first commanded to slaughter, specified in the first command, such that if the slaughter had first occurred on it, it would have occurred only on this specific one? Or was the cow first commanded an unspecified cow, which then became specified by a colour and attributes, so they slaughtered the specified one? In that case the first command was specified by the transfer of the ruling from a cow in general to a specific cow. Abrogation before the act is permitted, on the basis that this specific cow falls under the command to slaughter a cow, so if the slaughter had been performed on it under the first address, they would have complied, and likewise after the specification. Then those who hold this second view differed: is it obligatory that it be with the final attribute only, namely that it is not a dhalul, and so on to the end? Or must it, in addition to these attributes, in the answers to the two earlier questions, be neither fariq nor bikr, and yellow with a bright colour? The view we choose is this second one, because the apparent reading is that these attributes are combined, since His saying "ma hiya" and "ma lawnuha" and "ma hiya" indicate this. This is what has become well known in the reports, that it had all these attributes together. And since clarification must not be delayed beyond the time of need, that would be a command after a command, and this indicates the abrogation of the easier by the more difficult, and the permissibility of abrogation before the act.

﴿Wa-idh qatalتم nafsan﴾ (And when you killed a soul): This is conjoined to His saying: ﴿Wa-idh qala Musa li-qawmihi﴾ [al-Baqara: 67]. It is possible that the order of their occurrence and revelation follows the order of their recitation, so that God commanded them to slaughter the cow, and they slaughtered it without knowing the secret God had in it. Then after that came the matter of the slain man, and He revealed to them what He had hidden from them of wisdom in His saying: "Strike him with part of it." Nothing compels us to believe that the killing of the slain occurred earlier. Then they asked about identifying his killer, since they had differed over that, so God commanded them to slaughter a cow. In that case the command to slaughter is earlier in revelation and recitation but later in occurrence, and the killing of the slain is later in revelation and recitation but earlier in occurrence. Nor are we compelled to believe that the command to slaughter and what follows it is later in revelation but earlier in recitation, with the report of their killing earlier in revelation but later in recitation, without addressing the time of occurrence of the two stories. Those who turned the verses away from their apparent meaning did so out of consideration of the stories they transmitted that are not authentic, since no book or Sunna has reported them. Whenever a matter can be understood according to its apparent meaning, that is preferable, since departing from the apparent meaning to what is not apparent occurs only with a preponderant reason, and there is no preponderance here. Rather, the profound wisdom appears in their being first commanded to slaughter a cow: would they comply or not? And compliance with commands whose wisdom does not appear at first sight is greater than compliance with commands whose wisdom is apparent, because it is pure obedience, complete servitude, and sincere submission. This is unlike a command for which wisdom appears, since in the intellect there is a motive to comply with it and an incitement to act upon it.

The author of al-Muntakhab said: the occurrence of that killing must be prior to God's command to slaughter. As for the report of that killing, and that the slain must be struck with part of that cow, it is not required that it be prior to the report about the story of the cow. So the statement of one who says that this story must be prior to the first is an error, since this story in itself must be prior to the first in occurrence. But precedence in mention is not required, since sometimes the mention of the cause precedes the mention of the ruling, and sometimes the reverse. So it is as if, when that incident befell them, He commanded them to slaughter the cow, and when they had slaughtered it, He said: ﴿Wa-idh qatalتم nafsan﴾ earlier, and you disputed, so I will reveal to you the killer whom you concealed, by striking the slain with part of this slaughtered cow. The story of the command to slaughter the cow was placed before the mention of the slain, because if the order were reversed it would not be a single story, and the purpose of repeated reproach would be lost. End of his words. This is based on the premise that the killing occurred first and then they were commanded afterward to slaughter the cow, and he has no evidence for that except transmitting some stories that are not established in any book or Sunna. We have already shown how the two verses are to be read: the command to slaughter is earlier, and the killing is later, just as their recitation is.

Some people said: inversion of order is acceptable, because it is found in the Qur'an, in phrases and in words, and in Arab speech. They cited many examples, among them the story of Noah (peace be upon him) concerning the destruction of his people, and His saying ﴿Wa-qala irkabu fiha﴾ [Hud: 41]; and in the ruling on the widow whose husband has died, the waiting period of four months and ten days, and the provision for a year, since the abrogating ruling is earlier and the abrogated is later. He mentioned many instances on his view of inversion of words in the Qur'an and poetry. Our scholars have mentioned that inversion of order is one of the poetic licences (darurat), so the Qur'an should be exempt from it. The attribution of the slain to a group is either because the killers were a group, namely the heirs of the slain, and it has been reported that they gathered together to kill him; or because the killer was one person, and the act was attributed to them since it existed among them, following the Arab manner of attributing things to a tribe when something blameworthy or praiseworthy is found in some of its members.

﴿Fa-idda'ra'tum fiha﴾ (Then you disputed about it): The majority read it with idgham (assimilation). Abu Haywa read "fa-tadara'tum," on the pattern of tafa'altum, which is the original form; this was transmitted by one of the compilers of the tafsir. Ibn 'Atiyya said: Abu Haywa and Abu al-Sawwar al-Ghanawi read "wa-idh qatalتم nafsan fa-idda'ra'tum," and a group read "fa-tadara'tum" on the original form. End of his words. One of the compilers of the tafsir reported that Abu al-Sawwar read "fa-dara'tum" without an alif before the ra'. This tadara'u, meaning mutual repelling, may be literal, namely that some of them push others with their hands because of the intensity of the dispute; or figurative, namely that one of them shifted his killing onto another, and the one on whom it was shifted pushed it back to the one who shifted it; or that some of them pushed others with accusation and exoneration. The pronoun in "fiha" refers to the soul, which is the apparent reading. It is also said to refer to the killers, so it returns to the verbal noun understood from the verb. It is also said to refer to the accusation, so it returns to what the sense of the speech indicates.

Allah is the One who brings forth what you were concealing.

"Ma" (what) is in the accusative, governed by the active participle (ism al-fa'il, the active participle form), and it is a known relative pronoun (mawsul ma'hud, a relative with a definite, known antecedent). Therefore He used the active participle, because it indicates permanence (thubut), and He did not use the verb, which indicates renewal (tajaddud) and repetition (takrar). There is no repetition here, since there is no renewal in it, because this is one single, well-known story. Therefore, and Allah knows best, the verb was not used.

The active participle came functioning as a verb governing its object, and it was not made into a construct (lam yudaf), even though in meaning it refers to the past. This is because it narrates what was future at the time of the dispute (al-tada'u), and this is like the way the present tense narrates the present state in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And their dog stretching forth its forelegs at the threshold﴾ [al-Kahf: 18]. The verb "kana" (was) entered here to indicate that the concealment came earlier, and the returning pronoun referring to "ma" is omitted, its estimated form being: "ma kuntum taktumunahu" (what you were concealing it).

The apparent meaning is that it refers to what you were concealing concerning the matter of the slain man and his killer, and this is the view of the majority (al-jumhur). It has been said that it is permissible for it to be general, covering the slain man and other matters, so that the slain man would be among its particulars. There is consideration in this, since not everything they concealed from the people did Allah make manifest.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 73–74 (part 1 of 4):

﴿So We said: "Strike him with part of it."﴾: This clause is conjoined (ma'tuf) to His saying: ﴿You killed a soul and then disputed about it﴾ (2:72). The clause ﴿Allah will bring forth what you were concealing﴾ (2:72) is a parenthetical clause (i'tiradiyyah) between the conjoined and the element it is conjoined to. It indicates that the disputing was futile, since Allah brings to light what was hidden about the slain man's affair. The pronoun in "uḍribūhu" (strike him) refers to the soul (nafs). This is based on treating the soul as masculine, although its grammatical gender is feminine, and that feminine treatment is the more well-known usage. Alternatively, the first mention is elliptical, meaning "and when you killed one possessing a soul" (dhā nafs). The modifier was omitted and the modified term was placed in its position. Thus the pronoun in ﴿disputed about it﴾ (2:72) is feminine, respecting the explicit term, while the pronoun in ﴿strike him﴾ is masculine, respecting the omitted term. Or the pronoun refers to the slain man, meaning: "So We said: strike the slain man with part of it." The apparent meaning is that they were commanded to strike him with any part of it. It has been said they struck him with its tongue, or its right thigh, or its tail, or the cartilage, or the bone adjacent to the cartilage, which is the base of the ear, or the piece of flesh between the shoulders, or the 'ajb (the base of the tail), or with the heart and tongue together, or with one of its bones. This was related from Abu al-'Aliyah. The "bi" in "bi-ba'ḍihā" (with part of it) denotes instrument, as you say "I struck with the adze." The pronoun refers to the cow, meaning: with part of the cow. In the speech there is an ellipsis indicated by what precedes and follows it. The estimated sense is: "So they struck him, and he came to life." What indicates "they struck him" is His saying ﴿Strike him with part of it﴾, and what indicates "he came to life" is His saying ﴿Thus Allah brings the dead to life﴾ (2:73). It has been related that the striking was on the neck of the slain man, and this was before his burial. Whoever says they remained seeking it for forty years, or whoever says they were commanded to seek it while it was not in a loin or a womb, the striking cannot be except after his burial. It has been said it was upon his grave. The more apparent view is that the one who struck was the one who performed the striking, not the grave. It is related that he rose while his veins were gushing blood, and he informed them of his killer, saying: "My nephew killed me." His nephews said: "By Allah, we did not kill him." They denied the truth after witnessing it, then he died on the spot. In some narrations he said: "So-and-so and so-and-so killed me," naming two of his cousins; then he fell dead. They were seized and killed, and no killer inherited from him after that. Al-Mawardi said: the striking was with a dead body that had no life in it, lest it be confused for one who has doubt that life was transferred to him from what he was struck with, so that doubt is removed and the proof is confirmed.

﴿Thus Allah brings the dead to life﴾: If this is an address to those who witnessed the bringing to life of the slain man, then there is an implied saying, meaning: "And We said to them: Thus Allah brings the dead to life on the Day of Resurrection." Al-Mawardi estimated it as an address from Moses, upon our Prophet and upon him be peace. If it is for those who deny resurrection during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then it is a shift of address (talwin al-khitab). The meaning is: just as the slain man of the Children of Israel was brought back to life in this world, so Allah brings the dead to life on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Tabari went in this direction. The first view is more apparent, for the verses flow in one consistent order, and so that the address in ﴿so that you may understand﴾ does not differ from the address in ﴿then your hearts hardened﴾ (2:74), since the apparent sense of "your hearts" is an address to the Children of Israel. The kaf in "kadhālika" (thus) is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun (maṣdar) governed by His saying ﴿Allah brings the dead to life﴾, meaning: a bringing to life like that bringing to life, by which Allah brings the dead to life. The similarity lies only in the general act of bringing to life, not in the manner of bringing to life. Thus this refers to the bringing to life of the slain man. The author of al-Muntakhab made it a reference to the slain man himself, which requires an omitted modifier to be correct, meaning: "like the bringing to life of that slain man, Allah brings the dead to life." Making it a reference to the verbal noun is preferable and less forced. If this is an address to the Children of Israel who witnessed the bringing to life of the slain man, then the wisdom in witnessing it, even though they were believers in resurrection, is the reassurance of their hearts and the removal of doubt from them, since what they believed in through inference, they now believed in through direct witnessing.

﴿And He shows you His signs﴾: The apparent sense of this statement is that it is a resumption (isti'naf). It is also permissible that it be conjoined to "yuḥyī" (brings to life). The apparent sense is that "āyāt" (signs) is plural in both form and meaning. They are what He showed them: the bringing of the dead to life, the staff, the stone, the cloud, the manna and the quails, the magic, the sea, the mount, and other things. Yet despite this, they were the most blind of people in heart, and the most hard and denying toward their prophet at those times when they witnessed those marvels and miracles. The author of al-Muntakhab said: "And He shows you His signs," even though it is one sign, because it indicates (p. 261) the existence of the Creator who is capable of all things possible, knowing of all things known, choosing in originating and innovating; and it indicates the truthfulness of Moses, upon him be peace; and the innocence of one who was not a killer; and the specific identification of the accusation against the one who actually committed that killing. End of his words.

﴿So that you may understand﴾: That is, so that you may refrain from disobeying Him, and act according to what your intellects dictate, namely that whoever is capable of bringing one soul to life is capable of bringing all souls to life, since there is no distinction. ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are but as a single soul﴾ (31:28), meaning: like the creation of one soul and its resurrection. Al-Zamakhshari said: in the causes and conditions there are wisdoms and benefits. That condition was stipulated because of what the slaughter of the cow contains: nearness (to Allah), the fulfillment of obligation, the earning of reward, and an indication of the goodness of giving precedence to the act of drawing near over the request. Also what is in the strictness upon them, due to their strictness, of kindness to them and to others in not being strict, and of hastening to comply with the commands of Allah, and of accepting them immediately without searching and excessive questioning; and the benefit to the orphan through profitable trade; and the indication of the blessing of kindness to the two parents, and compassion toward children; and the making ignorant of the mocker who mocks what he does not know the reality of and does not grasp the truth of it, from the words of the wise; and the clarification that it is incumbent upon one who draws near to his Lord to be exacting in choosing what he draws near with, and to choose a young animal, neither fat nor milk-producing, of good color, free from defects, that delights the one who looks at it, and to pay a high price for it, as was related from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he sacrificed a noble she-camel for three hundred dinars. Also that the addition to the command is an abrogation (naskh) of it. (Naskh here means abrogation, the removal of a previously established ruling by a later revelation.) Also that abrogation before the act is permissible, though it is not permissible before the time of the act and its possibility, because that would lead to a beginning without purpose. And so that one would know what he was commanded: touching the dead with the dead, and the occurrence of life immediately after it; and that the effective cause is the One who causes, not the means. For the two deaths present in the two bodies, it is not conceivable that life could be produced from them both. End of his words, and it is good.

Scholars have mentioned legal rulings (fiqhiyyah) which they derived and proved from the story of this slain man, but the deduction of these from this verse is not apparent. They said: this verse is evidence that the killer is barred from inheriting from the one he killed, even if he would otherwise be one of his heirs. I say: this verse does not indicate that, but rather the story, if it is authentic, indicates it, since at its end is: "No killer inherited from him after that, from the one he killed." It was related from Umar, Ali, Ibn Abbas, and Ibn al-Musayyib that there is no inheritance for him, whether the killing was intentional or by mistake, neither from his blood money nor from the rest of his property. This is also the view of Abu Hanifah, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, and Abu Yusuf, except that the companions of Abu Hanifah said: if he was a minor or insane, he inherits. Uthman al-Laythi said: the killer by mistake inherits. Ibn Wahb said, from Malik: the killer by intention does not inherit from his blood money nor from his property. If he killed by mistake, he inherits from his property but not from his blood money. Similar is related from al-Hasan, Mujahid, and al-Zuhri, and it is the view of al-Awza'i. Al-Muzani said, from al-Shafi'i: if the rebel kills the just, or the just kills the rebel, they do not inherit from each other, because they are both killers. They also said: Malik, in the narration of Ibn al-Qasim and Ibn Wahb, used this story as evidence for the validity of the qasamah (the procedure of oaths in homicide cases) based on the statement of the slain man: "My blood is with so-and-so," or "so-and-so killed me." The majority held otherwise. They said regarding the description of the cow that it is evidence for those who say that the law of those before us is law for us, which is the position of Malik and a group of jurists. They said: in these verses is the strongest proof that an animal can be described by its attributes; that when it is specified by a describing attribute by which it is known, a salam (advance-payment sale) for it is permissible. This is the view of Malik, al-Awza'i, al-Layth, and al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifah said: salam in animals is not permissible. The proofs of these issues are mentioned in the books of jurisprudential disagreement, and the deduction of any of this from this story is not apparent. Al-Qushayri said: Allah willed to bring their dead back to life so that he would clearly testify against his killer, so He commanded the slaughter of an animal belonging to them. He made the cause of the life of their slain man the slaughter of an animal of theirs. The indication in this is that whoever wishes the life of his heart cannot reach it except by slaughtering his own self. Whoever slaughters his self through striving, his heart is brought to life by the lights of witnessing. Likewise, whoever desires an everlasting life causes his remembrance to die in this world through obscurity.

﴿Then your hearts hardened after that﴾: Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning of "then they hardened" is the denunciation of hardness after what was mentioned that necessitates softness and tenderness of hearts and the like, then you still doubt. End of his words. It is related from him that the conjunction with "thumma" (then) implies denunciation, and for this reason it was said of him regarding His saying ﴿Then those who disbelieve in their Lord ascribe equals (to Him)﴾ (6:1). (p. 262) This denunciation is not derived from the conjunction with "thumma," but rather from the occurrence of these sentences after what preceded them, which does not necessitate their occurrence. Also, the emergence of this great extraordinary marvel beyond the measure of humans contains lessons and admonitions that necessitate softness of hearts, repentance to Allah the Exalted, and submission to His decrees. Yet what came from them was other than that: hardness of hearts, failure of hearts to benefit from what they witnessed, obstinacy, and denial, to the point that it is related that after the slain man came back to life and informed them of his killer, they said: "He lied." The pronoun in "qulūbukum" (your hearts) refers to the heirs of the slain man, as said by Ibn Abbas, and they are the ones who killed him and denied killing him. It was also said: the hearts of all the Children of Israel hardened through their disobedience and what they committed; this was related from Abu al-'Aliyah and others. Hardness is used as a metaphor for the heart's inability to take lessons, and that admonitions do not move within it. He used "min" in His saying ﴿after that﴾ to indicate that the hardening began immediately after witnessing that extraordinary event. But the conjunction with "thumma" implies a delay, so the meaning of "thumma" and the meaning of "min" conflict, and there must be some figurative usage (tajawwuz) in one of them. The figurative usage is more appropriate in "thumma," because their dispositions incline them to hasten toward disobedience, to the point that they witness the great sign and then immediately turn to disobedience out of obstinacy and denial. As for the reference of "dhālika" (that), it was said to refer to the bringing of the slain man back to life. It was also said to refer to the speech of the slain man. It was said to be a reference to the signs mentioned earlier: their transformation into apes and swine, the lifting of the mountain, the gushing of water, and the bringing of the slain man back to life. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 73–74 (part 2 of 4):

﴿Like stones﴾: he means in hardness. This is a nominal sentence in which the hearts of these people are likened to stones, since a stone is not affected by admonition, and it means that their hearts are hard, not loosened by miracles, just as the stone was created hard. In this there is an indication that the stubbornness of their hearts is not due to an accidental cause, but that it was created in them as an original creation, just as the hardness of the stone is so. The kaf (ك) that conveys the meaning of comparison is a particle (ḥarf), in agreement with Sibawayh and the majority of the grammarians, in contrast to those who claimed that it occurs as a noun in speech, and this is reported from al-Akhfash. Its attachment here is therefore to an omitted element, the estimate being: "So they are existing like stones," in contrast to Ibn 'Usfur, who claimed that the kaf of comparison is not attached to anything; the proofs for this are mentioned in the books of grammar. The alif and lam in al-ḥijārah (الحجارة) are for the definition of the genus. The word ḥijārah is used in the plural and not in the singular, so one would not say ka-l-ḥajr (كالحجر), which would have been more concise, since the indication of the singular for the genus is like the indication of the plural; the plural is matched with the plural, since their hearts are plural, so it is fitting to match it with the plural. Also, their hearts vary in hardness, just as stones vary in firmness. Had it been said ka-l-ḥajar (كالحجر), that would have conveyed lack of variation, since that could be imagined from the singular form.

﴿Or harder in hardness﴾. Or: in the sense of waw (and), or in the sense of "or" for indefiniteness, or for permissibility, or for doubt, or for choice, or for variety: these are opinions. The commentators mentioned examples for these meanings, and the best is the last opinion. It is as if their hearts were of two kinds: hearts like stones in hardness, and hearts harder than stones. He summarized this in His saying: ﴿Then your hearts hardened﴾, then He detailed and diversified it into what is likened to stones and what is harder than them, since whatever is harder shares in absolute hardness and then is distinguished by being harder. The accusative of "qaswah" (قسوة) is as a specification (tamyīz), and in meaning it is required by the kaf and required by the comparative form (af'al al-tafḍīl), since each of them takes a specification after it. You say: Zayd is like 'Amr in forbearance (zaydun ka-'amrin ḥilman). This specification, which comes after the comparative form, is transferred from the subject, and this is a rare transfer; you postpone this specification and place in its position what was the genitive complement. You say: Zayd is better in face than 'Amr (zaydun aḥsanu wajhan min 'amrin), and its estimate is: the face of Zayd is better than the face of 'Amr; you postponed "wajhan" and placed in its position what was the complement, so it takes the nominative by being the subject, as "wajh" was the subject; and when it was postponed, it led to the omission of "wajh" from your saying "min wajhi 'Amr," and the placement of "'Amr" in its position, so you said "min 'Amr." The original was that, because what is truly characterized by increase in beauty is not the man but the face. A parallel to this is: "I passed by the man whose face is handsome" (marartu bi-l-rajuli l-ḥasani l-wajhi), or the face is the origin of this nominative, since what is truly characterized by beauty is not the man but the face. We have clarified this because mentioning the coming of the specification transferred from the subject is rare. And "ashaddu" (أشد) is used in the singular, although it is a predicate about a plural, because its use here is with "min," but it has been omitted, and this is a place that makes its omission good, since the comparative form occurs as a predicate of the subject, and "aw ashaddu" (أو أشد) is conjoined to His saying "like stones," so it is conjunction of predicate to predicate of the type of conjoining a single term, as you say: Zayd is on a journey, or resident. The pronoun in "ashaddu" refers to the hearts. There is no need for what al-Zamakhshari permitted, that its nominative may have two other possibilities: one of them: that the estimate be "or they are harder in hardness," so that it becomes conjunction of sentences. The second: that the estimate be "or like something harder," so "mithl" (مثل) is omitted and "ashaddu" placed in its position, and the pronoun in "ashaddu" then does not refer to the hearts, since the original would be "or like something harder in hardness than stones," so the pronoun in "ashaddu" refers to that described thing omitted with "ashaddu." This second possibility is supported by the reading of al-A'mash, with the dal in the accusative as a conjunction to "ka-l-ḥijārah," as al-Zamakhshari said. This should not be resorted to except in this reading alone. As for the reading in the nominative, it has the previous explanation that we mentioned, with no omitted element in it, so it is preferable.

Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Abi l-Faḍl in his Muntakhab refuted al-Zamakhshari's statement that it is conjoined to the kaf, saying: "It is according to the position of al-Akhfash, not according to the position of Sibawayh, since he does not permit it to be a noun except in poetry, and does not permit that in speech, so how in the Qur'an?" So it is more fitting that "ashaddu" be the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "wa-hiya ashaddu" (and they are harder). End of his speech. What al-Zamakhshari held is correct, and by his saying "conjoined to the kaf" he does not mean that the kaf is a noun; he means conjoined to the prepositional phrase, since it is in a nominative position, so he sufficed with mentioning the kaf instead of the prepositional phrase. As for his saying "the more fitting is that 'ashaddu' is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., 'hiya ashaddu'", we have already shown that the more fitting is other than this, since it is an estimate for which there is no need. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: why did He say "ashaddu qaswah" (harder in hardness), when the verb of hardness is among those from which the comparative form and the verb of wonder are derived? I say: because it is clearer and more indicative of extreme hardness. Another aspect: that the meaning of "more hard" (al-aqsa) is not intended, but the description of hardness with intensity is intended, as if it was said: the hardness of stones has intensified, and their hearts are harder in hardness. End of his speech. The meaning of his saying "the verb of hardness is among those from which the comparative form and the verb of wonder are derived" is that qasa (قسا) may have the comparative form and the verb of wonder built from it, by the fulfilment of the conditions that permit building these: that it is from a triliteral, unaugmented, active, complete verb, capable of increase and decrease, affirmative. Regarding whether it comes from af'ala, or from kawn, or from a passive form, there is disagreement. Abu Haywah read: "aw ashaddu qasawah" (أو أشد قساوة), and this is also a verbal noun of qasa.

﴿And indeed among stones there are those from which rivers gush forth﴾: when He, exalted is He, likened their hearts to stones in hardness, then mentioned that they are harder in hardness, according to the people's differing about the meaning of "aw" (or), He clarified that this comparison is only in relation to what the addressee knows of the hardness of rocks, and began to mention the aspect in which their hearts are harder in hardness. The meaning: the hearts of these people are rigid and hard, not softened by admonitions, and not affected by warnings; and indeed among stones there is that which accepts splitting, and they vary in accepting that, according to the division that He, exalted is He, pointed to, and we will speak about it. Thus the stones are preferred over their hearts in that some of them accept splitting, while the hearts of these people are at the extreme of hardness.

The commentators differed about this verse. Some said: His saying "And indeed among stones" to the end is by way of example, meaning that if the stone were of those who understand, it would fall down from fear of God, exalted is He, and split from awe of Him; and you, God has placed in you the intellect by which matters are perceived and the consequences of things considered, and despite that your hearts are harder and further from good. Others said: this is not by way of example; rather He informed about the stones themselves, divided them into these categories, and by this division it became clear that their hearts are harder than stones. The majority read "wa-inna" with the shadda (وإنّ مُشَدَّدَةً), and Qatadah read "wa-in" with the light form (وإنْ مُخَفَّفَةً), and likewise in the two places after that; it is the light form of the heavy one, and it may have two aspects: one of them: that it is operative, with "min al-ḥijārah" in the position of its predicate, "mā" in the position of accusative governed by it, which is its subject, and the lam is the lam of initiation (lām al-ibtidā'), placed on the postponed subject, and the subject when postponed may take the lam, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed for you is a reward﴾ [al-Qalam: 3]. Its operation when light is not permitted by the Kufans, and they are refuted by the established hearing from the Arabs, which is their saying: "in 'amran la-munṭaliqun" (إن عمراً لمنطلق) with the nun quiescent, except that when it is lightened it does not govern a pronoun of 'la', so you say: "innaka munṭaliqun," except if it occurs in poetry.

The second aspect: that it is not operative, but rather nullified, and "mā" is in the position of nominative by initiation, and the predicate is the prepositional phrase before it. The lam in "lamā" is disputed: some went to the view that it is the lam of initiation which is obligatory to distinguish between the emphatic inna and the negative in, and this is the view of Abu l-Ḥasan 'Ali ibn Sulayman al-Akhfash al-Saghir, and most of the Baghdadi grammarians, and Abu l-Ḥasan ibn al-Akhḍar of our lands said so too. Others went to the view that it is a lam that was stolen for distinction, and not the lam of initiation, and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said so, and among the great men of our lands Ibn Abi l-'Aliyah; and the discussion on this is mentioned in the science of grammar.

The commentators and grammarians did not mention regarding the light "in" here except this second aspect, namely that it is nullified, and that the lam in "lamā" is obligatory for distinction. Al-Mahdawi said: whoever reads "in" lightly, it is the light form of the heavy one, and the lam is obligatory for distinction between it and the in that means mā. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the lam of emphasis in "lamā" distinguished it from the negative. Al-Zamakhshari said: it was read "wa-in" lightly, and it is the light in of the heavy one, which is accompanied by the distinguishing lam, and from it is His saying: ﴿And indeed all of them are, all of them, present before Us﴾ [Ya-Sin: 32]. Their taking in as the light form of the heavy is the view of the Basrans. As for al-Farra', he claimed about what came of that that in is the negative, and the lam means "illa"; so when you say "in zaydun la-qā'imun," its meaning for him is "mā zaydun illa qā'imun" (Zayd is only standing). As for al-Kisa'i, he claimed that if a verb follows it, in is negative and the lam means illa; and if a noun follows it, it is the light form of the heavy. Qutrub went to the view that if a verb follows it, it has the meaning of qad, and the discussion on this view is in the books of grammar.

The commentator, Muhammad ibn Yusuf Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit), on Surah al-Baqarah, verses 73–74 (part 3 of 4):

Al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read *lamma* with a light *mim* (*mukhaffafah*), and it is a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*). Talhah ibn Musarrif read *lamma* with a doubled *mim* (*lamma*, *bi-l-tashdid*), and he recited it that way in both places. Probably a *waw* has dropped out here, so that the sense is "and in both places." Muhammad ibn Atiyyah said: "This is a reading that does not hold together (*ghayr muttajihah*)." What Ibn Atiyyah said, that it does not hold together, only stands if it is reported from Talhah that he read *inna* with a doubled *nun*. In that case it is difficult to justify this reading. But if he read *inna* with a light *nun*, which is the more likely assumption about him, then its justification becomes somewhat clear. *Inna* would be a negation particle, and *lamma* would have the function of *illa* ("except"), as in the Almighty's words: ﴿There is no soul but that over it there is a guardian﴾ [al-Tariq: 4], ﴿And all of them will be brought before Us [for judgment]﴾ [Ya-Sin: 32], and ﴿And all that is but the enjoyment of the life of this world﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 35], according to the reading of the one who reads *lamma* with a doubled *mim*. The subject (*mubtada'*) is omitted here because the meaning points to it. The sense is: "And there is no stone but that rivers gush forth from it." The same applies to *ma* in it, as in the Almighty's words: (p. 265) ﴿There is none of us but that he has a known station﴾ [al-Saffat: 164], meaning: "There is none of us who does not have a known station." And ﴿There is none of the People of the Book but that he will surely believe in him before his death﴾ [al-Nisa': 159], meaning: "There is none of the People of the Book." Omitting this subject is better, because the meaning points to it. However, it creates a sense of restriction (*hasr*), since by this distinction it appears that the stones are of several kinds: some of them rivers gush forth from, some of them split so that water comes out of them, and some of them descend out of fear of God. When a restriction is made, the sense understood from what precedes it is that every single stone has all of these attributes: rivers gush forth from it, it splits and water comes out of it, and it descends out of fear of God. This is not far-fetched if the wording is understood as referring to potentiality (*al-qabiliyyah*), since every stone is capable of this, and it is not impossible for it, if God wills it. When all of this has been clarified, the reading is justified on the assumption that Talhah reads *inna* with a light *nun*. But if it is confirmed from him that he reads *inna* with a doubled *nun*, then justifying that is difficult. As for the one who claims that the doubled *inna* means the same as the negating *ma*, his statement is not correct, and this usage is not established in the language of the Arabs. Talhah's reading *lamma* with a doubled *mim* can be justified together with the reading of *inna* with a doubled *nun*, by taking the subject of *inna* to be omitted because the meaning makes it understood, as it is omitted in the poet's line:

"But there is a black man with thick lips"

and in the line:

"So would that you had removed my worry for a moment"

*Lamma* may mean "when" (*hina*) according to the view of al-Farisi, or it may be a particle of obligation for an obligation according to the view of Sibawayh. The sense is: "And indeed, of them is one that is submissive, or soft, and what resembles this." Since they have omitted both the subject and the predicate, as one of them has interpreted the statement "God curse a she-camel that carried me to you," where he said: "*Inna* and its companion," then omitting the subject alone is easier.

Al-Jumhur read *yatafajjaru* with a *ya'* (the imperfect of *tafajjara*). Malik ibn Dinar read *yanfajiru* with a *ya'* (the imperfect of *infajara*). Both are *mutawi'* forms (verbs of reflexive effect). *Yatafajjaru* is the reflexive of *tafajjara*, and *yanfajiru* is the reflexive of *fajara* in its light form. *Al-tafajjur* means opening up with breadth and abundance, while *al-infijar* is less than that. The meaning is: among stones there are some with wide openings from which a great quantity of water pours out in a flood.

Ubayy and al-Dahhak read *minha al-anhar* ("from them the rivers"). Al-Jumhur read *minhu* ("from it"). The first reading is an accommodation to the meaning (*hamlun 'ala al-ma'na*), and the reading of the majority is an accommodation to the wording (*'ala al-lafz*). This is because *ma* here has both form and meaning, since what is intended by it is stones, and it is not possible for it to be intended as a singular for a meaning, so that its wording and its meaning would be one. The meaning is not "And indeed, from the stone that water gushes forth from," but rather "from the stones from which rivers gush forth." The discussion of rivers has already been given in the Almighty's words: ﴿And give good tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 25], and so on.

Some have held that the stone from which rivers gush forth is the stone that Moses struck with his staff, so that twelve springs gushed out of it.

﴿And indeed, of them is that which splits and water comes out of it﴾. *Al-tashaqquq* is splitting open lengthwise or widthwise, so that water wells out of it in a small amount, not to the extent of becoming a river. Al-Jumhur read *yashsha??aqu* (*yashsha??aqu*, with the *shin* doubled), and its origin is *yatashaqqaqu*, so the *ta'* was assimilated into the *shin*. Al-A'mash read *tashaqqaqu* with a *ta'* and a light *shin*, according to the original form. I have seen this attributed to Ibn Musarrif. In the copy of Ibn Atiyyah's tafsir that I consulted, its text reads: "Ibn Musarrif read *yanshaqqu*, with a *nun* and two *qafs*. What the language requires is that it be with one doubled *qaf*. The *fakk* (unassimilated form) may occur in poetry. If the imperfect is jussive, the *fakk* is permitted in eloquent speech, but here it is in the nominative, so the *fakk* is not permitted. However, it is an irregular reading (*shadhdhah*), so it is possible that this occurs in it. As for the imperfect with a *nun* together with two *qafs* and doubling of the first of them, this is not permitted." Abu Hatim said: "It should be *lama tatafajjaru* with a *ta'*, but *tatashaqqaqu* with a *ta'* is not permitted, because if he says *tatafajjaru* he makes it feminine to agree with *al-anhar* (the rivers), and that does not apply to *tashaqqaqu*." Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: "What Abu Hatim rejected is permitted, by accommodation to the meaning, because the meaning is: 'And indeed, from them are the stones that split,' but *yashsha??aqu* with a *ya'* is accommodated to the wording." End of quotation, and it is a sound statement. It has not been reported here that anyone read *minha al-ma'* ("from them the water"), so that it would agree with the meaning. It is only reported in the Almighty's words: ﴿From which the rivers gush forth﴾, where the plural suits the plural. Also, rivers in terms of being a plural are, by custom, unlikely to come out of a single stone, rather they come out of stones. For this reason, accommodation to the meaning is appropriate here. As for ﴿from which water comes out﴾, *al-ma'* (water) is not a plural, so it is not suitable to accommodate *minhu* to the meaning. Rather, *yashsha??aqu* and *minhu* are kept in accordance with the wording.

﴿And indeed, of them is that which descends out of fear of God﴾. *Al-huburu* here means falling headlong from a height to a low place. Al-A'mash read *yahbutu* with a *damma* on the *ba'*, and it has already been mentioned that this is a dialect form. *Khashyat Allah* means His fear. The exegetes differed in interpreting this. Some held that *khashyah* here is literal. They differed among themselves. One group said its meaning is: out of the stones' fear of God the Exalted, so it is a verbal noun (*masdar*) with the object (*maf'ul*) in the genitive, and God the Exalted made for these stones that descend out of fear of God the Exalted a discernment (*tamyiz*) that stood in for the action placed in one who has intellect. They supported this by the fact that God the Exalted described some of the stones with fear, and some with will, and described all of them with speech, glorification, sanctification, returning in praise, and splitting. All of these are attributes that proceed only from those who have discernment and knowledge. The Almighty said: ﴿Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain﴾ [al-Hashr: 21], to the end of the verse; ﴿And there is nothing but that it glorifies His praise﴾ [al-Isra': 44]; ﴿O mountains, sing back praises with him, and the birds﴾ [Saba': 10]. In the authentic hadith: "I know a stone that used to greet me with peace before I was sent as a prophet." And that after his mission, he did not pass by any stone or clod of earth except that it greeted him with peace. And concerning the Black Stone, that it bears witness for whoever touches it. And in the hadith of the stone that fled with the garment of Moses, peace be upon him, and began to run after him, saying: "My garment, stone! My garment, stone!" And in the hadith about Uhud: "This is a mountain that loves us and we love it." And in the hadith of Hira' when it trembled: "Be still, Hira'." And in the hadith of small pebbles glorifying God in the palm of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). This sentence and other hadiths indicate that animals and inanimate things speak, and that trees submit, and other such things. If God had not placed in them a distinguishing power, a speaking attribute, and a voluntary movement, nothing of that would proceed from them, nor would describing them with it be fitting. This is the view of Mujahid, Ibn Juraij, and a group. Others said: *khashyah* here is literal, and it is a verbal noun attributed to the agent. The stone that descends out of fear of God is hail (*al-barad*), and by "fear of God" is meant that He causes His servants to fear, so He used *khashyah* while meaning *ikhsha'* (causing fear), that is, the descent of hail by which God frightens His servants and deters them from disbelief and sins. This is a strained view, and it contradicts the apparent meaning. Hail is not stone, and although it hardens when it falls, it is in reality water. Others said: *khashyah* here is literal, and it is a verbal noun attributed to the object, with its agent omitted, which is the servants. The meaning is: that among stones are those that some of them fall from others at the time of an earthquake out of the fear of God's servants of Him.

The verification of this is: since what was intended by them is the fear of God the Exalted, that fear became like the effective cause of that descending, so the meaning is: it descends in order that it may come about for the servants of God the Exalted. Abu Muslim held that *khashyah* is literal, and that the pronoun in the Almighty's words ﴿And indeed, of them is that which descends out of fear of God﴾ refers to hearts. The meaning is: among hearts there are hearts that become calm and still and return to God the Exalted, so he used descent as a metaphor for this meaning, and by it he means the hearts of the sincere. This is a very distant interpretation, because it began with the Almighty's words ﴿And indeed, of the stones﴾, then said ﴿And indeed, of them﴾, so the apparent sense of the speech is a division of the stones, and one does not depart from the apparent sense except by clear evidence. Descending does not befit hearts, rather it befits stones. And interpreting descent is no more preferable than interpreting fear, if we interpret it. It is possible in the views that include taking it as literal, though some of those views are stronger than others. Some held that what descends out of fear of God is the mountain upon which God spoke to Moses, peace be upon him, when He made it crumble (*dakk*). Others held that *khashyah* here is a metaphor of a metaphor (*majaz min majaz al-isti'arah*), just as will (*iradah*) was used metaphorically for a wall in the Almighty's words: ﴿Which is about to collapse﴾ [al-Kahf: 77], and as Zayd al-Khayl said:

"With a host in whose tents the spotted horses go astray; you see the hills prostrate to its hooves"

and as another said:

"When the news of al-Zubayr came, the walls of Medina and the stern mountains were shaken"

Its meaning: whoever sees the stone falling down from a height to a lower place imagines in it fear (khashyah), so he uses khashyah metaphorically (istiʿarah) as a figure of speech (kinayah) for its submission (inqiyad) to the command of Allah, and that it does not refuse what Allah the Exalted wills concerning it. So whoever sees it thinks that this rapid reaction is the fear of Allah the Exalted. This is the view of those who hold that life and speech do not inhere in inanimate things (jamadat), and that is impossible in their opinion. They interpreted what came in the Qur'an and the hadith, which indicates that, as meaning that Allah the Exalted has joined angels to them, and it is these who greet and speak, just as it is reported that the womb (rahim) is suspended from the Throne, calling out: "O Allah, join whoever joins me, and sever whoever severs me." The wombs are not a body, nor do they have perception, and it is impossible that meanings should prostrate or speak; rather Allah the Exalted has joined to them an angel who says that statement. They also interpreted: "This is a mountain that loves us and we love it," meaning its people love us and we love its people, like His saying the Exalted: "And ask the town" (Yusuf 12:82). The preference of Ibn ʿAtiyyah, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, is that Allah creates for the stones some measure of perception, by which fear and movement occur. The preference of al-Zamakhshari is that khashyah is a metaphor for submission to the command of Allah the Exalted and for not refusing. The arrangement of the division of these stones is a very good arrangement, and it is according to ascending gradation. He began first with that from which rivers gush forth, meaning it was created with wide openings, so no act or action is attributed to it in itself; that is, they were created with openings such that there is no need to attribute to them the issuing of an act from them. Then he ascended from this stone to the stone that undergoes a slight reaction, which is that a crack issues from it such that water springs from it. Then he ascended from this stone to the stone that undergoes a great reaction, such that it moves and rolls down from a height to a lower place. Then he reinforced this complete reaction by saying that this is from the fear of Allah the Exalted, from its obedience and submission to what Allah the Exalted wills from it, so he used khashyah as a metaphor (kinayah) for obedience and submission, because whoever fears obeys and submits.

﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾: This contains a warning. That is because when He said: ﴿Then your hearts hardened after that﴾, it implied that from the hardness of hearts arise corrupt deeds and ugly actions, from disobedience to Allah the Exalted and opposition to His messengers. So He followed that with a threat to them that Allah the Exalted is not unaware of their deeds, but rather He the Exalted counts them against them, and when He is not unaware of them, He will recompense for them. As for heedlessness (ghaflah): if by it is meant forgetfulness (sahw), forgetfulness is not permissible for Allah the Exalted; and if by it is meant leaving off deliberately, they mentioned that it is among what may be ascribed to Allah the Exalted. In either case, Allah the Exalted negated heedlessness from Himself. And the negation of a thing from a thing may be because it is not possible for it rationally, and because it does not occur from it although it is possible. The judge (al-Qadi) held that it is not valid to describe Allah the Exalted as "not unheedful," he said: because it creates the impression that heedlessness is permissible for Him; but the matter is not as he held, because negating a thing from a thing does not entail its possibility. Do you not see His saying the Exalted: ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:255]? And His saying: ﴿He feeds and is not fed﴾ [al-Anʿam 6:14]? So He negated from Himself the Exalted what does not entail its possibility for Him.

And "bi-ghafilin" (unheedful): it is in the accusative position, on the basis that "ma" is Hijazi (i.e., operates like "laysa"). It may also be in the nominative position, on the basis that "ma" is Tamimi, so the "ba" (bi-) entered the predicate of the subject, and the negation justified that. Do you not see that it does not enter in an affirmative sentence? You do not say: "Zayd bi-qa'imin" (Zayd is standing), nor: "ma Zayd illa bi-qa'imin" (Zayd is only standing)? Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "Bi-ghafilin" is in the accusative position as the predicate of "ma," because it is the Hijazi form, and this is strengthened by the entry of "ba" into the predicate, though "ba" may come anomalously with the Tamimi form. End of his words. As for what Abu Muhammad ibn ʿAtiyyah held, that "ba" with the Tamimi form may come anomalously, no grammarian we know of has held it; rather the sayers are two: one says that the Tamimi form does not admit "ba" into the predicate after it, which is the position of Abu ʿAli al-Farisi in one of his two views, and al-Zamakhshari followed him; and another says that it is permissible to govern it with "ba," and this is the correct view. al-Farazdaq said:

*By your life, Maʿn does not abandon his right*

The poetry of the Banu Tamim contains the governing of the predicate with "ba" frequently. The majority read "taʿmalun" with the "ta" (you do), which follows the pattern of His saying: ﴿Then your hearts hardened﴾. Ibn Kathir read it with "ya" (they do), so it may be that the address is with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and it may be that the address is with the Children of Israel, and this would be a shift (iltifat), as it departed from address in His saying: ﴿Then your hearts hardened﴾ to the third person in His saying: (yaʿmalun). The wisdom of this shift is that He turned away from addressing them and presented them in the form of those to whom one does not turn with address, and made them like absent ones, because addressing a person and confronting him with speech is an turning toward him by the speaker and a befriending of him; so He cut off from them the confrontation with address, because of the abundance of the transgressions that came from them. These noble verses contain great lessons and many dialogues. Moses, upon our Prophet and upon him be prayers and peace, told them directly that Allah the Exalted commands them to slaughter the cow, and that was a trial from Allah the Exalted for them; but they did not hasten to comply with Allah's command, and they treated that as mockery, since they did not understand the secret of the command. They should have hastened to comply, so Moses answered them by seeking refuge in Allah from being among those who are ignorant, so that he would report about Allah what He did not command him; he thus replied to them that using mockery in conveying from Allah the Exalted, and in other matters, is something he seeks refuge from. So they returned to his words, and were obstinate about the cow and its attributes; it would have sufficed them to slaughter any cow, since what was commanded was an unspecified cow; so they asked what it was, and asked Moses to supplicate to Allah the Exalted to make it clear to them, since his supplication was closer to being answered than theirs; so he reported from Allah the Exalted its age. Then he feared from their excessive questioning and their obstinacy, as came in the report: "What destroyed the Children of Israel was their excessive questioning and their disagreement with their prophets," so he hastened to command them to do what they were commanded, to cut off their questioning; but they did not heed his command, and asked that he ask Allah the Exalted again about its color, since they had been told its age; so he reported to them from Allah the Exalted about its color, and did not command them a second time to do what they were commanded, since he knew their obstinacy, because they had opposed Allah's command first in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:67], and opposed Moses' command a second time in His saying: ﴿So do what you are commanded﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:68]. So there was nothing for it but that he left them to their nature of excessive questioning. They asked a third time that he ask Allah about it, so he reported to them from Allah the Exalted about its condition in relation to the action and the rest of the attributes he had mentioned; then they stated plainly that Moses had brought the clear truth which explained the matter of this cow, so they searched for it until they obtained it and slaughtered it in compliance with Allah's command the Exalted; and that was after much hesitation and great delay, and before that they had not come close to slaughtering it, but remained seeking things so that obtaining them and slaughtering it would be delayed for them.

Then Allah the Exalted reported about them the killing of a soul, and their pushing blame onto one another regarding who killed it, and their disagreement about that; so they were commanded to strike that slain person with part of this slaughtered cow, and they struck him and he came to life by Allah's permission, and the secret of Allah's command to slaughter the cow was revealed to them, and that there resulted from it an extraordinary miraculous matter by which the necessary knowledge is attained, indicating the truthfulness of Moses, peace be upon him, and of our Prophet, the best of prayers and peace.

Then Allah the Exalted explained that a similar revival revives the dead, since there is no difference between the two revivals in the general sense of reviving. Then Allah the Exalted reported that He shows them His signs, so that from that showing there results that they become people of intellect, reflecting on the outcomes of affairs, pondering the return. Then Allah the Exalted reported after that that they, despite witnessing this great extraordinary matter and seeing the signs before that, were not affected by it; rather there resulted the opposite of its requirement of severe hardness, to the point that He likened their hearts to stones, or they are harder than stones. Then He digressed to mention the stones with the division He mentioned, to show that the stones surpass their hearts in that some of them are affected by a great effect, such that they move and roll down, and some of them split and are affected by a slight effect, so water springs from them, and some of them were created split open, from which rivers flow; while their hearts are of one disposition, accepting no admonition, not affected by reminder, and not moved to obedience. Then He concluded that by saying that He the Exalted is not unaware of what they committed in the worldly abode, but rather He will recompense them for that in the Hereafter. The opening of these verses was that Allah the Exalted commands, and their closing is that Allah is not unaware. So He is the Knower of who complied and who neglected, so He recompenses the one who complies with His command with abundant reward, and the one who neglects His command with severe punishment.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 73–74 (part 1 of 4):

﴿So We said: "Strike him with part of it."﴾: This clause is conjoined (ma'tuf) to His saying: ﴿You killed a soul and then disputed about it﴾ (2:72). The clause ﴿Allah will bring forth what you were concealing﴾ (2:72) is a parenthetical clause (i'tiradiyyah) between the conjoined and the element it is conjoined to. It indicates that the disputing was futile, since Allah brings to light what was hidden about the slain man's affair. The pronoun in "uḍribūhu" (strike him) refers to the soul (nafs). This is based on treating the soul as masculine, although its grammatical gender is feminine, and that feminine treatment is the more well-known usage. Alternatively, the first mention is elliptical, meaning "and when you killed one possessing a soul" (dhā nafs). The modifier was omitted and the modified term was placed in its position. Thus the pronoun in ﴿disputed about it﴾ (2:72) is feminine, respecting the explicit term, while the pronoun in ﴿strike him﴾ is masculine, respecting the omitted term. Or the pronoun refers to the slain man, meaning: "So We said: strike the slain man with part of it." The apparent meaning is that they were commanded to strike him with any part of it. It has been said they struck him with its tongue, or its right thigh, or its tail, or the cartilage, or the bone adjacent to the cartilage, which is the base of the ear, or the piece of flesh between the shoulders, or the 'ajb (the base of the tail), or with the heart and tongue together, or with one of its bones. This was related from Abu al-'Aliyah. The "bi" in "bi-ba'ḍihā" (with part of it) denotes instrument, as you say "I struck with the adze." The pronoun refers to the cow, meaning: with part of the cow. In the speech there is an ellipsis indicated by what precedes and follows it. The estimated sense is: "So they struck him, and he came to life." What indicates "they struck him" is His saying ﴿Strike him with part of it﴾, and what indicates "he came to life" is His saying ﴿Thus Allah brings the dead to life﴾ (2:73). It has been related that the striking was on the neck of the slain man, and this was before his burial. Whoever says they remained seeking it for forty years, or whoever says they were commanded to seek it while it was not in a loin or a womb, the striking cannot be except after his burial. It has been said it was upon his grave. The more apparent view is that the one who struck was the one who performed the striking, not the grave. It is related that he rose while his veins were gushing blood, and he informed them of his killer, saying: "My nephew killed me." His nephews said: "By Allah, we did not kill him." They denied the truth after witnessing it, then he died on the spot. In some narrations he said: "So-and-so and so-and-so killed me," naming two of his cousins; then he fell dead. They were seized and killed, and no killer inherited from him after that. Al-Mawardi said: the striking was with a dead body that had no life in it, lest it be confused for one who has doubt that life was transferred to him from what he was struck with, so that doubt is removed and the proof is confirmed.
