The preferable course is to take the wording in its apparent sense without rearrangement or reordering, when that is possible. It is possible, by making ﴿ʿinda rabbikum﴾ fit some of the meanings we have mentioned. As for the view of this one who holds that position, it is very remote, because لِيُحاجُّوكم (*liyuḥājjūkum*) is connected to the verb أَتُحَدِّثُونَهم, and ʿinda rabbikum is connected to the phrase بِما فَتَحَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْكم, so you would have separated ʿinda rabbikum from its governing element, which is فَتَحَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْكم, by the phrase لِيُحاجُّوكم, which is foreign to both, since it is connected to أَتُحَدِّثُونَهم according to the more apparent view. It is far-fetched that this structure would occur thus in eloquent speech; how then would it occur in the speech of God, which is the most eloquent speech?

﴿أَفَلا تَعْقِلُونَ﴾ (*afalā taʿqilūn*, "Will you not then reason?"): its apparent meaning is that it falls under the statement of the one who said: "Do you report to them what will be a proof against you? Will you not reason, so that you do not report that to them?" It has also been said that it is an address from God to the believers, meaning: "Will you not reason that these Jews will not believe, while they have these blameworthy attributes: following their predecessors who distorted the words of God, imitating them in what they distorted, showing hypocrisy, and other things for which He censured them?"

(p-٢٦٩)﴿Do you hope that they will believe you, when a group of them used to hear the words of Allah and then distort them after they had understood them, while they knew?﴾ ﴿When they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe." But when they are alone with one another, they say, "Do you tell them what Allah has disclosed to you, so that they may argue with you about it before your Lord? Do you not understand?"﴾ ﴿Do they not know that Allah knows what they keep secret and what they make public?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 77] ﴿Among them are unlettered people who know not the Scripture except wishful fancies, and they do nothing but conjecture.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 78] ﴿So woe to those who write the Scripture with their own hands and then say, "This is from Allah," to trade it for a small price. Woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they earn.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 79] ﴿And they say, "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days." Say, "Have you taken a covenant with Allah, so that Allah will not break His covenant? Or do you say about Allah what you do not know?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80] ﴿Yes! Whoever earns an evil deed and his sin surrounds him, those are the companions of the Fire; therein they will abide forever.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 81]

*al-tam'* (طَّمَع, greed/hope): the soul's strong attachment to attaining a desired thing. It is stronger than *al-raja'* (hope), because it arises only from intense desire and strong will. When it intensifies it becomes *tam'*, and when it weakens it is *raghbah* (desire) and *raja'* (hope). One says: *tami'a yat'amu tam'an wa tama'atan wa tama'iyatan* (with the lightened form, like *tawa'iyah*). The poet says:

﻿*Tama'iyatun an yaghfira al-dhamba ghafiruh*
(a greedy hope that the Forgiver will forgive the sin)

The active participle is *tama'* and *ta'mi'*. It is transitive by means of the hamzah: *ta'ma'ahu mut'amatan*. One says *tami'a* with a damma on the mim (*tamu'a*), meaning his greed increased. The opposite of *tam'* is *al-ya's* (despair). Kuthayyir says:

﻿*La khayra fi al-hubbi waqfan la yuharrikuhu*
*'awaridu al-ya'si aw yartajuhu al-tama'u*
(There is no good in love that is a stationary halt, which is not moved by the passing winds of despair, or which is not closed up by greed.)

One says *imra'atun mit'am*, meaning a woman who hopes [for a suitor] but is not allowed [to be approached]. The word has also been extended: *al-tam'* is used to name soldiers' pay. One says: *amara lahumu al-amir bi-at'amihim*, meaning the commander ordered their stipends, i.e., their provisions. This is the verbal noun placed in the position of the object (*maf'ul*).

*al-kalam* (كَلَام, speech): speech is the utterance that signifies a predicative relation intended for its own sake. The term is also applied to the single word, and it is used to express writing, a sign, and what is understood from the state of a thing. Is it applied to the meanings present in the mind that are expressed by speech? On this there is disagreement. Its six permutations are established and return to the meaning of strength and intensity: *kalama, kamala, lakama, lamaka, malaka, makala*.

*al-tahrif* (تَحْرِيف, distortion): turning a thing from one state to another. *al-harf* is the inclined edge.

*al-tahdith* (تَحْدِيث, narrating): reporting about an occurrence. From it one says *yahduth*. Its origin is from *al-huduth* (occurrence). The basic form of the verb is to be transitive to one object directly, to another by *'an*, and to a third by *bi*. One says *haddathtu Zaydan 'an Bakrin bi-kadha* (I told Zayd about Bakr such-and-such).

Then it may be used with the meaning of *a'lama* (to inform), which is derived from *'allama*, which is transitive to two objects, so it becomes transitive to three. These are from the extension by others (not Sibawayh) to *a'lama*. Sibawayh did not mention, among verbs transitive to three objects, other than *a'lama*, *ara* and *naba'a*. As for *haddatha*, they cited the verse of al-Harith ibn Hilliza:

﻿*Aw man'tum ma tus'aluna fa-man*
*haddathtumuhu lahu 'alayna al-'ala'u*
(Or you refuse what is asked of you, then whoever you inform of it, for him there is a hold upon us.)

They made *haddatha* in it transitive to three objects. It is possible that the implied meaning is *haddathtumu 'anhu* (you narrated about it), and the clause after it is a state (*hal*). As Sibawayh interpreted his saying *nubbi'tu 'Abdallah*, meaning *'an 'Abdillah* (about 'Abdullah), while there is the possibility that *nubbi'tu* includes the meaning of *u'limtu* (I was informed), but for him omitting the preposition was preferred over implying a meaning. If it is possible that the verse of al-Harith is explained as one in which the preposition is omitted, there is no proof in it that *hadatha* is transitive to three objects directly. Therefore it should not be taken that way, unless it is established from the speech of the Arabs.

*al-fath* (فَتْح, opening/judgment): judgment in the dialect of Yemen. ﴿He is the Opener, the All-Knowing﴾ [Saba': 26]. *Al-adhkar*: opening (of a verse) for the imam. *Al-zafar* (victory): ﴿Then there has come to you the victory﴾ [al-Anfal: 19]. Al-Kalbi said it also means narrating. Al-Kisa'i said it means clarifying. Al-Akhfash said it means bestowing. The basic meaning of *al-fath* is breaking open a thing, and *al-sadd* (closing) is its opposite.

*al-muhajjah* (مُحَاجَّة, disputation): from *al-ihtijaj* (argumentation), which is the intention to prevail. *Hajjahu*: he intended to overcome him. *Al-hujjah*: sound speech, derived from *mahajjat al-tariq* (the straight path of the road).

*asarra al-shay'*: he concealed it; *a'lanahu*: he made it manifest.

*al-ummi* (أُمِّيّ, unlettered): one who neither reads a book nor writes. It is attributed to *al-umm* (mother) because it is not the business of women to write or to read in a book; or because he is in the state in which his mother bore him, not having moved from it; or it is attributed to *al-umma* (nation), which means stature and form; or to *al-amma* (the maidservant), since she is simple before she knows knowledge.

*al-amani* (أَمَانِيّ, wishful fancies): the plural of *umniyyah*, which is *uf'uwlah*. Its origin is *umnuwiyah*. A *ya'* and a *waw* came together, and the first of them was preceded by a sukun, so the *waw* was changed to a *ya'*, and the *ya'* was assimilated into the *ya'*. It is from *manna*, meaning to estimate, because the one who wishes estimates in his soul and conjectures what he desires. Or it is from *tamanna*, meaning he lied. A Bedouin said to Ibn Da'ab about something he had narrated: "Is this something you have related, or have you fabricated it?" That is, have you invented it. 'Uthman said: "I have neither wished nor sung since I embraced Islam." Or it is from *tamanna*, meaning he recited. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Except when he recites, Satan casts into his recitation﴾ [al-Hajj: 52], meaning when he recites and reads. The poet says:

﻿*Tamanna kitaba Allahi awwala laylihi*
*wa-akhirahu laqa himama al-maqadiri*
(He recited the Book of Allah at the beginning of his night, and at its end he met the death decreed.)

Recitation and falsehood both return to the meaning of estimating, so estimating is the root. The poet says:

﻿*Wa la taqulanna li-shay'in sawfa af'aluhu*
*hatta tabayyana ma yamnI laka al-mani*
(And do not say to a thing, "I will surely do it," until there becomes clear what the one who estimates estimates for you.)

That is, estimates. Its plural is with the shadda on the ya' because it is *afa'il*. When it is pluralized on the pattern *af'il*, the ya' is lightened, while the original is the shadda, because the first ya' in the plural is the waw that was in the singular, which changed into a ya' there. Do you not see that the plural of *umluwd* is *amalid*?

*Wayl* (وَيْل, woe): *al-wayl* is a verbal noun with no verb of its own from its own form. What is mentioned from their saying *wa'l* is fabricated. No word from this root whose first radical is waw and middle radical is ya' came except: *wayl*, *wayh*, *ways*, *wayb*. It is not dualized nor pluralized. It is said *waylahu*, and it is pluralized as *wayilat*. The poet says:

﻿*Fa-qalat laka al-waylatu innaka murjili*
(So she said to you, "Woes! You are the one who makes me walk on foot.")

When *wayl* is annexed, the better form in it is the accusative. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Woe to you! Do not fabricate a lie against Allah﴾ [Ta-Ha: 61]. Some claim that when it is annexed, only the accusative is permissible; and when you use it unannexed, the nominative is preferred. He said: ﴿So woe to those who [...]﴾ [al-Baqarah: 79]. The accusative is also permissible. The poet says:

﻿*Fa-waylan li-Taymin min sarabilih al-khudr*
(So woe to Taym from their green garments.)

*Al-wayl* means disgrace and regret. Al-Khalil said: *al-wayl* is the intensity of evil. Al-Mufaddal and Ibn 'Arafah said: *al-wayl* is sorrow; one says *tawayyala al-rajulu*, meaning the man called out "woe," and that is only said at sorrow and hardship. Others said: *al-wayl* is destruction, and whoever falls into destruction calls out "woe." Al-Asma'i said: it is a word of lamentation, and it may be compassion. From it:

﻿*Waylu ummihi mis'ara harbin*
(Woe to his mother, the kindler of war!)

*Al-aydi*: the plural of *yad* (hand). *Yad* is among those from which the lam has been omitted; its pattern is *fa'l*, and the original has been made explicit. They said *yadyun*, and they replaced the first ya' with a hamzah, saying *qata'a Allahu adyahu* (may Allah cut off his hand). They also replaced it with a jim, saying *la af'alu dhalika jadda al-dahr*, meaning *yada al-dahr* (the hand of time). It is real in the limb and metaphorical in other things. As for *al-ayadi*, it is the plural of the plural, and most of its use is for blessings. The original is *al-aydi*. They found the damma on the ya' heavy, so it was dropped, the ya' became quiescent, and before it there was a damma, so it changed into a waw, and it became *al-aydu*. As it was said of *muyqin* that it became *muqin*. Then in their language there is no quiescent waw preceded by a damma in a noun; and when analogy leads to that, that waw is changed to a ya', and the damma before it becomes a kasra, so it became *al-aydi*. The discussion of *yad* has already preceded at the discussion of His saying: ﴿for what is before its hands﴾ [al-Baqarah: 66].

*Al-kasb* (كَسْب, earning): its origin is acquiring benefit, though it has also come for acquiring harm. From it: ﴿Yes! Whoever earns an evil deed﴾. Its verb is transitive to one object: you say *kasabtu malan* (I earned wealth); and to two objects: you say *kassabtu Zaydan malan* (I made Zayd earn wealth). Ibn al-A'rabi said: one says *kasaba* (he himself) and *aksaba ghayrahu* (he caused another to earn). He recited:

﻿*Fa-aksabani malan wa-aksabtuhu hamdan*
(So he gained me wealth, and I gained him praise.)

*Al-mass* (مَسّ, touching): attainment. *Al-mass* is the bringing together of two things at the utmost nearness; *al-lams* is similar but with perception. *Al-mass* may come with perception. The real meaning of *al-mass* and *al-lams* is with the hand. It has been transferred from perception to meanings, like: ﴿That Satan has touched me﴾ [Sad: 41], ﴿The one whom Satan has confounded by his touch﴾ [al-Baqarah: 275]. From it madness is called *mass*. It was said: *al-mass*, *al-lams* and *al-jass* are close; except that *al-jass* is general for sensible things, while *al-mass* is for what is hidden and subtle, like the pulse of the veins. *Al-mass* and *al-lams* are with the outer surface of the skin. *Al-mass* is also a metaphor for intercourse and for madness.

*Al-ma'dud* (مَعْدُود, numbered): the passive participle from *'adda*, in the sense of *hasiba* (to reckon). *Al-'adad* is the reckoning.

*Al-ikhlaf* (إخْلاف, breaking a promise): not fulfilling a promised thing.

*Bala* (بَلَى, yes/indeed): a particle of answer that occurs only after a negation, either in wording or in meaning. Its meaning is to reject it, whether an interrogative particle accompanies it or not. It has occurred as an answer to a question in such a case as: "Can Zayd withstand me?" when he denies Zayd's ability to withstand him, because its meaning is negation. Among what it occurred in as an answer to a question is the saying of al-Hujaf ibn Hakim:

﻿*Bal sawfa nubkihim bi-kulli muhannadin*
*wa-nubki Numayran bi-al-rimahi al-khawatiri*
(Rather, we will make them weep with every Indian sword, and we will make Numayr weep with the quivering spears.)

It occurred as an answer to the one who said to him, and he is al-Akhtal:

﻿*Ala fas'al al-Hujafa hal huwa*
*ha'irun bi-qatla unsibat min Numayri ibn 'Amir*
(Ask al-Hujaf, is he avenging those slain from Numayr ibn 'Amir?)

According to us, *bala* is a triliteral in its formation, and its origin is not *bal*, so an alif was added to it, contrary to the Kufans.

*Al-sayyi'ah* (سَيِّئَة, evil deed): on the pattern *fay'ilah*, from *sa'a yasu'u masa'atan*, when he grieved. It is the feminine of *al-sayyi'* (evil). The discussion of this pattern has already preceded at the discussion of His saying: ﴿or like a downpour﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19], so it is sufficient and need not be repeated.

* *

﴿Do you hope that they will believe you?﴾ Regarding the cause of revelation of this verse, they mentioned several sayings. First: it was revealed about the Ansar, who were allies of the Jews, and between them there was neighborliness and fosterage, and they used to wish that the Jews would embrace Islam. It was also said: the Prophet ﷺ and the believers used to wish for the Islam of those Jewish children who were in their presence, because they were people of Scripture and law, and they used to be angry on their behalf and treat them gently, hoping for their Islam. It was also said: it was revealed about those of the sons of the seventy who were with Musa (peace be upon him) at the Mount, who heard the speech of Allah, but did not comply with His command, and distorted the saying in their reports to their people, and said: "We heard Him say: if you are able to do these things, then do them, and if you wish, do not do them." It was also said: it was revealed about the scholars of the Jews who distort the Torah, making the lawful unlawful and the unlawful lawful, following their desires. It was also said: the Prophet ﷺ said: "No one enters upon us the town (qasabat) of Medina except a believer." Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Wahb ibn Yahudha and their likes said: "Go and spy on the news of those who believe, and tell them, 'We believe,' and disbelieve when you return," so it was revealed. It was also said: it was revealed about a people of the Jews who said to some of the believers: "We affirm that he is a prophet, but he is not to us; he is only to you specifically." When they were alone, some of them said: "Do you acknowledge his prophethood when we used to seek victory through him before?" This is what Allah opened upon them of His knowledge. It was also said: it was revealed about a people of the Jews who used to hear the revelation, and then distort it after they had understood it.

This commentary's opinions all come back to one point: the passage is about the Jews who were alive in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because they are the ones for whom hoping that they would believe is actually possible, since hope only applies to the future. The pronoun in ﴿أن يؤمنوا لكم﴾ ("that they would believe [in] you") refers to the Jews. The meaning is to regard the belief of the Jews as unlikely, since their forebears had already committed deeds of this kind and their descendants followed in their footsteps. Thus it is far-fetched that belief should come from these people.

If it is asked: how does it follow that, because some of them deliberately distorted the text, the rest have lost hope of believing? It is answered: al-Qaffal (al-Qaffal) said: it is possible that the meaning is, "How could these people believe, when they take their religion and learn it only from a people who distort it out of obstinacy? They teach them only what they have distorted and altered from its proper form, and the imitators accept that from them, so they do not turn towards the truth." It has also been said: the loss of hope concerns a specific group of them by name.

The hamza in ﴿أفتطمعون﴾ is an interrogative particle, and it carries the sense of affirmation (taqrir), as if he had said: "You have hoped for the belief of these people, while their condition is as has been mentioned." It has also been said: it contains a kind of disapproval of the desire for the belief of those whose signs of refusal are established. Their belief is regarded as unlikely because they disbelieved Moses, despite the miracles they witnessed at his hands; because they did not acknowledge the truth despite their knowledge; and because they are not fit for reflection and reasoning. The address in ﴿أفتطمعون﴾ is to the Prophet (ﷺ) alone; he is addressed in the plural form as a mark of honour. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Muqatil. Or it is addressed to the believers; this was said by Abu al-Aliyah and Qatadah. Or it is addressed to the Helpers (al-Ansar); this was said by al-Naqqash. Or it is addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers, or to a group of the believers, or to a group of the Helpers.

The fa' (the particle "then") after the hamza originally comes before it, and the underlying form is: fa-atatma'una ("so do you hope"). The fa' is for coordination, but the interrogative hamza has been given precedence and placed before it. Al-Zamakhshari claims that there is an elided verb between the hamza and the fa', and he leaves the fa' in its place, so that the clause following it is coordinated with the elided clause before it. This is contrary to the school of Sibawayh, and it is refuted by instances where it is impossible to assume a verb, such as His saying: ﴿أو من ينشأ في الحلية﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 18] ("Is one who is brought up amid ornaments...?"), ﴿أفمن يعلم أنما أنزل إليك﴾ [al-Ra'd: 19] ("Is one who knows that what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth like one who is blind?"), and ﴿أفمن هو قائم﴾ [al-Ra'd: 33] ("Is then He who stands over every soul...?").

﴿أن يؤمنوا﴾ ("that they would believe") is the object of ﴿تطمعون﴾ ("you hope"), with the preposition dropped; the underlying form is "in that they would believe." It is therefore in the accusative position according to the school of Sibawayh, and in the genitive position according to the school of al-Khalil and al-Kisa'i. ﴿لكم﴾ ("for you"), as a complement, is connected to ﴿يؤمنوا﴾, on the basis that the lam here has the meaning of the bi' (the preposition "in/with"); but this is weak. It may also be the lam of cause, meaning: that they would believe on account of your call to them.

﴿وقد كان فريق منهم يسمعون كلام الله﴾ ("And there was a group of them who would hear the words of Allah"). The "group" (al-fariq): it has been said that they are the rabbis who distorted the Torah concerning the description of Muhammad (ﷺ). This was said by Mujahid and al-Suddi. It has also been said: a group of Jews who used to hear the revelation when it came down upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and then they would distort it, intending to introduce into the religion what is not in it, and so create contradiction in its rulings. It has also been said: everyone who distorted a ruling or altered it, as in their conduct regarding the verse of stoning and similar matters. It has also been said: they are the seventy who heard the words of Allah together with Moses (peace be upon him), and then changed after that; but it has been denied that they heard the words of Allah, the Exalted. Ibn al-Jawzi said: the scholars denied this, among them al-Tirmidhi, the author of Al-Nawadir, who said: Moses (peace be upon him) alone was singled out for speech.

The words of Allah which they distorted: it has been said they are the Torah, and they distorted it by changing its wording of their own accord; this is the view of the majority. It has also been said: by interpretation, while the wording of the Torah remained; this was said by Ibn Abbas. It has also been said: it is the words of Allah which they heard at the Mount (al-Tur). It has also been said: what they used to hear of the revelation sent down upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Al-A'mash recited kalima Allah ("the word of Allah") in the singular, as the plural of kalima (word). The word kalima may be used for speech, in which case the two readings have one meaning. It may also be used for individual words, so that they distort the individual words, and thus the compound sentences and their construction change with the change of the individual words.

﴿ثم يحرفونه﴾ ("then they distort it"). The distortion that occurred: it has been said it concerned the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for they described him with a description other than the one he actually had, so that the proof would not be established against them through it. It has also been said: it concerned his description and the verse of stoning.

﴿من بعد ما عقلوه﴾ ("after they had understood it"), that is, after they had memorised it and comprehended it, and its correctness had not been obscure to them. The ma is verbal (masdariyya), meaning: after their understanding of it. The pronoun in ʿaqalūhu refers to the words of Allah. It has also been said: the ma is a relative pronoun and the pronoun refers back to it, but this is far-fetched.

﴿وهم يعلمون﴾ ("while they knew"). The object of the knowledge is omitted, meaning: that they had distorted it; or the punishment that is due for distorting it; or that it is the truth; or that they are false and lying. The waw in His saying ﴿وقد كان فريق﴾ and in His saying ﴿وهم يعلمون﴾ is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal). It is possible that the governing element of the circumstantial clause is His saying ﴿أفتطمعون﴾ ("do you hope?"), and it is possible that it is ﴿أن يؤمنوا﴾ ("that they would believe").

On the first possibility, the meaning is: "Would there be any hope on your part for the belief of the Jews and their forebears, who are accustomed to distorting the words of Allah, and who follow their ways and their misguidance?" The circumstantial clause then serves as a qualifier of the hoped-for expectation, meaning: the hope for the belief of these people is regarded as unlikely, given this description of them. On the second possibility, the meaning is: the hope that belief would come from these people is regarded as unlikely, while their forebears were, as has been established, distorting the words of Allah, the Exalted. In this case the circumstantial clause is a qualifier of their belief. On both analyses, each of "do you hope" and "that they would believe" is qualified by this circumstance in meaning. What we have mentioned is what the grammatical construction requires. The explanation of the qualification in meaning is this: when you say, "Do you hope that Zayd will follow you?" while he follows the way of his father, the disapproval of the hope is qualified by this circumstance, and the object of the hope, which is the following that is supposed to happen, is also qualified by this circumstance. The upshot is that the presence of this circumstance is incompatible with following, and does not suit hope; rather, hope and expectation of following would fit only if this circumstance were absent.

As for the governing element of ﴿وهم يعلمون﴾, it is His saying ﴿ثم يحرفونه﴾: that is, the distortion occurs from them after they have understood and comprehended it, knowing what severe punishment is due for distorting it, and yet they proceed to do so and act boldly in it. Condemnation of one who knows is more severe than condemnation of one who is ignorant, because the knowing person has the motives for obedience, since he knows its reward, and the restraint from disobedience, since he knows its punishment. Some have held that the governing element of ﴿وهم يعلمون﴾ is His saying ﴿عقلوه﴾ ("they understood it"), but the apparent view is the first, which is His saying ﴿يحرفونه﴾ ("they distort it").

﴿وإذا لقوا الذين آمنوا قالوا آمنا﴾ ("And when they meet those who believe, they say, 'We believe'"). Ibn al-Sumayqa' recited laqaw (with the verb in the form lāqaw, "they met") and qālū ("they said"), in the form of intensification. The intensification does not appear, for it is from the form fa'ala, which has the same meaning as the simple form. So the meaning of laqaw and the meaning of laqu is one, and the explanation of the individual words of this conditional sentence has already been given. This sentence may be taken as a new independent statement, indicating a kind of the vices of the Jews who were in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and revealing what they concealed of hypocrisy. It may also be a circumstantial clause, coordinated with His saying ﴿وقد كان فريق منهم﴾ and the verse that follows, meaning: how can one hope for their belief, when among their forebears there were those who distorted the words of Allah, and these are following their path, and in their own selves they are hypocrites, showing agreement with you when they meet you, claiming to be of you, while inwardly they are disbelievers? Whoever combines these two conditions, following their misguided forebears and being hypocritical toward the believers, is not to be hoped to believe.

The ones who believe here are Abu Bakr, Umar, and a group of the believers; this is the view of the majority of the commentators. Some have said: the believers here are a group of Jews who believed and were sincere in their belief. The pronoun in laqaw refers to a group of the Jews who were unspecified, remaining upon their religion; or to a group of them who had embraced Islam and then became hypocrites; or to the Jews whose leaders from the Banu Qurayza ordered them to enter Medina and spy on the news of the Prophet (ﷺ), and said: "Enter Medina and display belief, for he (ﷺ) has forbidden anyone to enter Medina except a believer."

﴿وإذا خلا بعضهم إلى بعض﴾ ("And when some of them are alone with others"), that is: when some of them are alone with each other, meaning when those who did not become hypocrites are alone with those who did. The word ilā ("to") has been said to carry the sense of ma'a ("with"), meaning: when some of them are alone with some. The better view is that the verb khalā ("was alone") is construed as containing the sense of a verb that takes ilā, meaning: "withdrew to" or "submitted to," or "became calm with," or something similar, because the implying of verbs is preferable to the implying of particles.

(qālū): that is, that part which was alone with the others said:

﴿أتحدثونهم﴾ ("Do you speak to them?"): meaning, they said reproachfully to them: "Do you speak to the believers?" ﴿بما فتح الله عليكم﴾ ("of what Allah has disclosed to you"): ma is a relative pronoun, and the returning pronoun is omitted, its underlying form being: "that which Allah has disclosed to you." It has been permitted that ma be an indefinite qualifying noun (nakira mawsufa), or a verbal noun (masdariyya), meaning: "by the opening of Allah to you." The first form is preferable. What they spoke of was what a group of the Jews said about the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); this was said by Abu al-Aliyah and Qatadah. Or it is what Allah punished their forebears with; this was said by al-Suddi. Mujahid said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to the Banu Qurayza: 'O brothers of the apes and the swine!'" So the rabbis said to their followers: "He knew this only from you." Ibn Zayd said: whenever they were asked about something, they would say, "In the Torah it is so-and-so," and their rabbis disliked this, and forbade it in private.

According to what Abu al-Aliyah said, fath ("opening") means informing and reminding, meaning: "Do you speak to them of what Allah has informed you of concerning their prophet?" This was also narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas. According to al-Suddi, it means judgment and decree, meaning: "Do you speak to them of what Allah has judged and decreed against your forebears, of their punishment?" According to Ibn Zayd, it means sending down, meaning: "Do you speak to them of what Allah has sent down to you in the Torah?" Al-Kalbi said: the meaning is what Allah has decreed upon you, which returns to the meaning of sending down. It has also been said: the meaning is what Allah has made clear to you concerning the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ), his description, his law, what he has called you to of belief in him, and of taking covenants from your prophets to confirm and support him. It has also been said: the meaning is what Allah has bestowed upon you of victory over your enemy, and of the interpretation of your Book.

﴿ليحاجوكم﴾ ("so that they may argue with you"): this is the lam of purpose (lam kay), and the verb is in the subjunctive by an elided "an" after it. Eliding it is permissible, unless after it comes "la" (not), in which case it must be stated. The lam is connected to His saying ﴿أتحدثونهم﴾, so it is a lam of the genitive (jarr), and it is called lam kay in the sense that it indicates cause, just as kay indicates cause. They do not mean that the subjunctive after it is by an elided kay, although it is correct to state kay after it, saying "li-kay ukrimaka" ("so that I may honour you"), because what is elided is "an," not "kay." Ibn Kaysan and al-Sirafi permitted that the elided particle after this lam be either kay or an. The Kufans held that the subjunctive after this lam is by the lam itself, and that what appears after it of kay or an is only for emphasis. A full discussion of this is found in the extended works of grammar.

[p. 272]

Some grammarians held that the lām (ل) is connected to the verb فَتَحَ (*fataha*, "opened/disclosed"). This is not apparent, because the argument (*muḥājjah*) is not the cause of the disclosure. Rather, the argument arises from the reporting (*taḥdīth*). The exception is if the lām is the lām of consequence (*lām al-ṣayrūra*, "the lām indicating outcome") according to those who affirm that meaning for it. Then the meaning could be: "What God disclosed to you, they reported, so the matter ended with them arguing with you about it." This is like the verse ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 8]. They did not pick him up for this purpose; rather, the matter ended in that outcome. [p-274]

As for the one who does not affirm the lām of consequence, he makes it the lām of purpose (*lām kay*, "the lām of 'in order that'"), by way of metaphorical extension, because what results from something, even if not intended, is like a cause.

There is no difference between making it connected to the verb أَتُحَدِّثُونَهم (*ataḥaddithūnahum*, "Do you report to them?") and connecting it to بِما فَتَحَ (*bimā fataḥa*, "with what He disclosed"). However, connecting it to the first is closer in mediation, as if he said: "Do you report to them so that they argue with you?" On the second, it is more remote, since the meaning becomes: "God disclosed to you with it, so you reported it to them, so they argued with you." Therefore, it is better to connect it to the nearer mediation. The pronoun in بِهِ (*bihi*, "with it") refers to *mā* (ما, "what") in the phrase ﴿with what God disclosed﴾.

With this, the view of those who held that the lām is verbal-nominal (*maṣdariyyah*, introducing a verbal noun) becomes weak, because a pronoun does not refer back to a verbal-nominal lām.

﴿عِنْدَ رَبِّكُمْ﴾ (*ʿinda rabbikum*, "before your Lord") is the object-complement of the verb لِيُحاجُّوكم (*liyuḥājjūkum*, "that they may argue with you"). The meaning is: "that they may argue with you about it in the Hereafter." So by his saying ﴿before your Lord﴾ he alludes to their gathering with them in the Hereafter, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord you will dispute﴾ [al-Zumar: 31].

It has been said that the meaning of ʿinda rabbikum is "in your Lord," that is, they will have more right to it, with ʿinda taken in the sense of fī (في, "in"). It has also been said that it is by omission of a modifier, meaning: "that they may argue with you about it by mentioning your Lord." It has also been said that its meaning is: He made the argument in your Book an argument before God. Do you not see that you say, "It is in God's Book thus," and "It is before God thus," with one meaning?

It has also been said that it is the object-complement of the verb بِما فَتَحَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْكم (*bimā fataḥa Allāhu ʿalaykum*, "with what God disclosed to you") — ʿinda rabbikum — meaning: from before your Lord, that they may argue with you. This is the sending of the Prophet ﷺ and the taking of their covenant to affirm him. Ibn Abi al-Fadl said: "This view is the correct one, because the argument against them is with what was in the world." End of quotation.

The preferable course is to take the wording in its apparent sense without rearrangement or reordering, when that is possible. It is possible, by making ﴿ʿinda rabbikum﴾ fit some of the meanings we have mentioned. As for the view of this one who holds that position, it is very remote, because لِيُحاجُّوكم (*liyuḥājjūkum*) is connected to the verb أَتُحَدِّثُونَهم, and ʿinda rabbikum is connected to the phrase بِما فَتَحَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْكم, so you would have separated ʿinda rabbikum from its governing element, which is فَتَحَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْكم, by the phrase لِيُحاجُّوكم, which is foreign to both, since it is connected to أَتُحَدِّثُونَهم according to the more apparent view. It is far-fetched that this structure would occur thus in eloquent speech; how then would it occur in the speech of God, which is the most eloquent speech?

﴿أَفَلا تَعْقِلُونَ﴾ (*afalā taʿqilūn*, "Will you not then reason?"): its apparent meaning is that it falls under the statement of the one who said: "Do you report to them what will be a proof against you? Will you not reason, so that you do not report that to them?" It has also been said that it is an address from God to the believers, meaning: "Will you not reason that these Jews will not believe, while they have these blameworthy attributes: following their predecessors who distorted the words of God, imitating them in what they distorted, showing hypocrisy, and other things for which He censured them?"

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 77–78:

﴿Do they not know that Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal?﴾ This is a rebuke from Allah to them. The meaning is: if Allah's knowledge encompasses all their deeds, and they know this, how is it proper for them to be hypocritical and to display to the believers something that Allah knows to be the opposite of what is in them? The state of their hypocrisy does not coincide with their knowledge that Allah knows about it. The preferable interpretation of "what they conceal and what they reveal" is that it is general, since that is the apparent sense of the wording. It has been said: what they concealed is disbelief, and what they revealed is faith. It has been said: enmity and friendship. It has been said: their saying to their devils, "We are with you," and their saying to the believers, "We believe." It has been said: the description of the Prophet (ﷺ) and their changing of his description to another description, so that the proof would not be established against them.

Ibn Muhaysin recited ﴿أوَلا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ with the ta' (you), "Do you not know?" They said: in that case it is an address to the believers, and in it is an alert to them about their ignorance of the One who knows the secret and the open. It is possible that it is an address to them, and its benefit is to alert them to listen to what comes after it. Then he turned away from addressing them and returned the pronoun to the third person, neglecting them. This is of the type of iltifat (a shift in grammatical person), and its wisdom in both cases is what we have mentioned.

It has previously been established for us that, like ﴿أفَلا تَعْقِلُونَ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 76] and ﴿أوَلا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾, the fa' and the waw in them are for coordination (ʿatf), and that their original position is to be at the beginning of the speech, but the interrogative hamzah received priority, so it was placed first. We have also mentioned al-Zamakhshari's approach to this, so there is no need to repeat it.

﴿That Allah knows﴾ (anna Allaha yaʿlamu): it may be one of the cases in which anna occupies the position of a single noun (a verbal noun), if we say that yaʿlamuna is transitive to one object, like ʿarafa. It may also be one of the cases in which anna occupies the position of two objects, if we say that yaʿlamuna is transitive to two, like ẓanantu; this is according to the view of Sibawayh. As for al-Akhfash, according to him it occupies the position of one object, and he takes the second as omitted. We have previously mentioned this disagreement. The returning pronoun to "ma" is omitted; its estimated form is: yusirruna-hu wa yuʿlinuna-hu ("they conceal it and they reveal it").

The apparent sense of this interrogation is that it is an affirmation to them that they know this, that is, that Allah knows the secret and the open. In other words, they have indeed known this, so hypocrisy and denial of what they know to be the truth do not suit them. It has been said: this is a reproach to them and an urging to reflect, so that by reflection they would know it. That is because when they acknowledged the authenticity of the Torah, in which there is what points to the prophethood of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the acknowledgment of Lordship (rububiyyah) became binding upon them. It also shows that disobedience with knowledge of it is more abominable.

In this verse and in those similar to it there is evidence that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to overlook the hypocrites, even though Allah had revealed their hypocrisy to him, hoping that they would believe. So he overlooked them, until Allah accepted from those whom He accepted and destroyed those whom He destroyed. It has been disputed whether this ruling remains in force or has been abrogated (naskh, the lifting of a ruling by a later one). Some said: it has been abrogated, because he (ﷺ) used to do that to win hearts (taʾlif al-qulub, a term for conciliating people to Islam). Allah has since honoured Islam and made them unnecessary, so there is no need for winning hearts. Others said: it remains in force until now, because the people of disbelief are more numerous than the people of faith, so they need an increase in supporters and in numbers. The first view is the more well known.

In His saying ﴿knows what they conceal and what they reveal﴾ there is a proof against whoever claims that Allah does not know particulars (juziyyat) but only universals (kulliyyat).

﴿Among them are unlettered ones (ummiyyun)﴾: the apparent sense of the speech is that this was revealed about the Jews mentioned in the verse before it, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas. It has been said: it was revealed about the Magians, as said by ʿAli ibn Abi Talib. It has been said: about the Jews and the hypocrites. ʿIkrimah and al-Dahhak said: about the Christians of the Arabs, for they did not write well. It has been said: about a people of the People of the Book whose book was lifted from them because of sins they committed, so they became unlettered. It has been said: about a people who did not believe in a book or a messenger, so they wrote their own book and said, "This is from Allah," and so they were named ummiyyun, for their denial of the Book, and they became like one who does not do anything well. The first view is the most apparent, because the context of the speech is with the Jews, so the pronoun refers to them.

The connection of this verse is as follows: when Allah clarified the matter of the misguided sect that distorted the Book of Allah, while they had understood it and knew the evil of what they had done, then clarified the second sect, the hypocrites, and the third sect, the disputers, He began to clarify the fourth sect, which is the common people, whose way is taqlid (blind imitation) and acceptance of what is said to them. Abu al-ʿAliyah, Mujahid and others said: among these are the Jews mentioned, so the verse alerts to their common people and followers, meaning that their faith is not to be hoped for.

Abu Haywah and Ibn Abi ʿAblah read ﴿أُمِيُّونَ﴾ with a lightened mim. It has previously been established that the ummi is one who does not write and does not read in a book, meaning they do not know books well enough to study the Torah and to verify what is in it.

﴿They do not know the Book﴾: this clause is in the position of a descriptive qualifier (ṣifah). The Book is the Torah.

﴿Except wishful thinking (amani)﴾: this is a disjunctive exception (istithnaʾ munqatiʿ, an exception where the excluded item is not of the same kind as what precedes). Amani is not of the kind of the Book, nor included under its meaning. It is one of the two types of disjunctive exception, the type to which the governing verb applies. Do you not see that if it were said, "They do not know except wishful thinking," it would be correct? This type of exception permits two readings. The first is the accusative (naṣb) as an exception, which is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. The second is following (itbaʿ) as a substitute (badal), with the condition that it comes after, which is the dialect of Tamim. So the accusative of amani is valid under both analyses. The meaning is: except what they have of their wishes. Their wishful thinking is that Allah will pardon them, have mercy on them, and not hold them accountable for their sins, and that their forefathers, the Prophets, will intercede for them. Or it is what their rabbis give them to hope for, that the Fire will not touch them except for a number of days. Or it means they know nothing but fabricated lies they heard from their scholars and transmitted by taqlid. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid, and chosen by al-Farraʾ. It has been said: its meaning is "except recitation," that is, they do not know the understanding (fiqh) of the Book; they restrict themselves to what they hear recited to them. Abu Muslim said: taking it to mean the wishful thinking of the heart is preferable, because of His saying, ﴿And they said, "None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian." Those are their wishful thinking﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111].

The majority read amaniyy with a shaddah (the doubled yaʾ). Abu Jaʿfar, Shaybah, al-Aʿraj, and Ibn Jammaz, from Nafiʿ, and Harun, from Abu ʿAmr, read amani with the shaddah removed, pluralised on the pattern afaʿil, without counting the long vowel of the singular. Abu Hatim said: everything of this kind whose singular is doubled may be read both with the shaddah and without it, like: ananiyy, aghaniyy, amaniyy, and the like. Al-Akhfash said this, just as one says in the plural of miftah: mafatih and mafatih. Al-Nahhas said: deletion is more common in the defective (muʿtall) forms, as the poet said:

Has the greeting returned, or can the blind be made to see?
The three hearthstones remain, and the desolate traces of the camp.

﴿And they are not but assuming (yazunnun)﴾: here in (in) is the negating particle, meaning "ma." Hum is the subject (mubtadaʾ), and illa yazunnun is in the position of the predicate, and it is from the "exception from an unstated element" (mufarragh) type. When in is negating and enters upon a subject and predicate, it does not function like the Hijazi ma. Some permitted that, and whoever permitted it stipulated that the predicate be negated and postponed. The correct view is that this is not permitted, because nothing of that kind has been preserved except a rare line of poetry:

If he is dominant over anyone, except over the weakest of the madmen...

Al-Suhayli and others attributed to Sibawayh the permission of in functioning like ma, but there is no explicit text to that effect in his book. As for the meaning of yazunnun: Mujahid said they lie; others said they speak; others said they doubt, which is hesitation between two matters, neither of which is preferred by the one who considers them. The preferable interpretation is to take it in its original sense, which is preferring one of two matters over the other, since it cannot be taken to mean certainty, and preference in their view does not necessarily mean preference in reality. Muqatil said: its meaning is that they are not certain, whether the leaders lie or tell the truth; they pledge allegiance to them. End of his words.

He gave the predicate as a present-tense verb and not as an active participle (ism al-fāʿil), because the present tense indicates that the assumption occurs and renews itself for them moment by moment. They are not steadfast on a single assumption; rather, new assumptions keep arising for them, indicating the instability of their beliefs and the divergence of their desires.

In this verse there is evidence that knowledge is acquired (kasbi), that taqlid is invalid, that one who is deceived by the misguidance of a misleader is blameworthy, that relying on conjecture in the fundamentals of belief is impermissible, that speech without evidence is void, and that for something whose existence and non-existence are equally probable, one may not incline to either of them except on the basis of textual evidence (samʿi). Those who reject analogical reasoning (qiyas) and the report of a single transmitter (khabar al-wahid) also cling to this verse, since those two do not produce certain knowledge.

Abu Haywah and Ibn Abi ʿAblah read ﴿أُمِيُّونَ﴾ with a lightened mim. It has previously been established that the ummi is one who does not write and does not read in a book, meaning they do not know books well enough to study the Torah and to verify what is in it.

﴿They do not know the Book﴾: this clause is in the position of a descriptive qualifier (ṣifah). The Book is the Torah.

﴿Except wishful thinking (amani)﴾: this is a disjunctive exception (istithnaʾ munqatiʿ, an exception where the excluded item is not of the same kind as what precedes). Amani is not of the kind of the Book, nor included under its meaning. It is one of the two types of disjunctive exception, the type to which the governing verb applies. Do you not see that if it were said, "They do not know except wishful thinking," it would be correct? This type of exception permits two readings. The first is the accusative (naṣb) as an exception, which is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. The second is following (itbaʿ) as a substitute (badal), with the condition that it comes after, which is the dialect of Tamim. So the accusative of amani is valid under both analyses. The meaning is: except what they have of their wishes. Their wishful thinking is that Allah will pardon them, have mercy on them, and not hold them accountable for their sins, and that their forefathers, the Prophets, will intercede for them. Or it is what their rabbis give them to hope for, that the Fire will not touch them except for a number of days. Or it means they know nothing but fabricated lies they heard from their scholars and transmitted by taqlid. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid, and chosen by al-Farraʾ. It has been said: its meaning is "except recitation," that is, they do not know the understanding (fiqh) of the Book; they restrict themselves to what they hear recited to them. Abu Muslim said: taking it to mean the wishful thinking of the heart is preferable, because of His saying, ﴿And they said, "None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian." Those are their wishful thinking﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111].

The majority read amaniyy with a shaddah (the doubled yaʾ). Abu Jaʿfar, Shaybah, al-Aʿraj, and Ibn Jammaz, from Nafiʿ, and Harun, from Abu ʿAmr, read amani with the shaddah removed, pluralised on the pattern afaʿil, without counting the long vowel of the singular. Abu Hatim said: everything of this kind whose singular is doubled may be read both with the shaddah and without it, like: ananiyy, aghaniyy, amaniyy, and the like. Al-Akhfash said this, just as one says in the plural of miftah: mafatih and mafatih. Al-Nahhas said: deletion is more common in the defective (muʿtall) forms, as the poet said:

Has the greeting returned, or can the blind be made to see?
The three hearthstones remain, and the desolate traces of the camp.

﴿And they are not but assuming (yazunnun)﴾: here in (in) is the negating particle, meaning "ma." Hum is the subject (mubtadaʾ), and illa yazunnun is in the position of the predicate, and it is from the "exception from an unstated element" (mufarragh) type. When in is negating and enters upon a subject and predicate, it does not function like the Hijazi ma. Some permitted that, and whoever permitted it stipulated that the predicate be negated and postponed. The correct view is that this is not permitted, because nothing of that kind has been preserved except a rare line of poetry:

If he is dominant over anyone, except over the weakest of the madmen...

Al-Suhayli and others attributed to Sibawayh the permission of in functioning like ma, but there is no explicit text to that effect in his book. As for the meaning of yazunnun: Mujahid said they lie; others said they speak; others said they doubt, which is hesitation between two matters, neither of which is preferred by the one who considers them. The preferable interpretation is to take it in its original sense, which is preferring one of two matters over the other, since it cannot be taken to mean certainty, and preference in their view does not necessarily mean preference in reality. Muqatil said: its meaning is that they are not certain, whether the leaders lie or tell the truth; they pledge allegiance to them. End of his words.

He gave the predicate as a present-tense verb and not as an active participle (ism al-fāʿil), because the present tense indicates that the assumption occurs and renews itself for them moment by moment. They are not steadfast on a single assumption; rather, new assumptions keep arising for them, indicating the instability of their beliefs and the divergence of their desires.

In this verse there is evidence that knowledge is acquired (kasbi), that taqlid is invalid, that one who is deceived by the misguidance of a misleader is blameworthy, that relying on conjecture in the fundamentals of belief is impermissible, that speech without evidence is void, and that for something whose existence and non-existence are equally probable, one may not incline to either of them except on the basis of textual evidence (samʿi). Those who reject analogical reasoning (qiyas) and the report of a single transmitter (khabar al-wahid) also cling to this verse, since those two do not produce certain knowledge.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 79–80:**

﴿So woe to those who write the Book with their own hands﴾, and so on. It is said: this was revealed concerning those who altered the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and changed his attributes. They made him dark-skinned with straight hair and tall, whereas in their Book he was described as he truly is. They said to their companions and followers: "Look at the description of this Prophet who will be sent at the end of time. He does not resemble the description of this man." The rabbis of the Jews feared that their livelihood would be lost if the description of the Prophet (ﷺ) were left as it was, so they changed it. It is also said: their kings feared for their kingship if all the people believed. So they came to the rabbis of the Jews and gave them bribes and provisions from the people, and they erased that from the Torah and wrote a book with their own hands, declaring lawful what they chose and forbidding what they chose. It is also said: this was revealed concerning those who did not believe in any prophet and did not follow any Book, but wrote a book with their own hands, declared lawful what they chose and forbade what they chose, and said: "This is from Allah." Abu Malik said: this was revealed concerning Abdullah ibn Sa'd ibn Sarh, the scribe of the Prophet (ﷺ), who used to alter (the revelation) and then apostatised.

The explanation of *wayl* (woe, a word of denunciation; transliterated *wayl*) has already been given in the discussion of the vocabulary. It is reported from Uthman, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that it is a mountain of the Fire of Hell. It is also mentioned that Abu Sa'id narrated that it is a valley in Hell between two mountains, into which the one who falls will plunge. It is mentioned that Sufyan and Ata ibn Yasar narrated that it is a valley running through the courtyard of Hell, from the pus of the people of the Fire. Al-Zahrawi and a group have related that it is a gate of the gates of Hell. It is also said that it is a cistern in Hell. And it is said, on the authority of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that it is a valley in Hell, which if the mountains of this world were set ablaze in it, would melt from its heat. Yet if anything had been authentically transmitted from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explaining *wayl*, it would have been necessary to adopt it. The Arabs used the word *wayl* in their poetry and prose before the Qur'an came, and they did not apply it to any of these explanations. Its meaning is rather what the lexicographers have explained. It is an indefinite noun carrying the sense of supplication (invocation of harm), and for this reason it is permissible to begin a sentence with it, since supplication is one of the justifications for beginning a sentence with an indefinite noun. These justifications number nearly thirty, and we have mentioned them in our book *Manhaj al-Salik* (The Method of the Traveller).

*Kitaba* (writing) is well known. It is said: the first to write with the pen was Idris, and it is also said: Adam. As for "the Book" here, it is said: they wrote things they had invented, and rulings they had altered from the Torah, until their rulings became established among them. It is also said: they wrote in the Torah what indicates the opposite of the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and spread it among their foolish ones and among the Arabs. They hid those copies that were with them, which were unaltered. Their foolish ones, and whoever among the idolaters of the Arabs came to them, when they asked them about the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), would say: "Is this the one described in our Torah, the altered and changed one?" They would recite it to them and say to them: "This is the Torah which was sent down from Allah," in order to exchange it for a small price.

*Bi-aydihim* (with their own hands) is an emphasis that removes the suspicion of metaphor (*majaz*). For when you say "Zayd writes," the apparent meaning is that he himself does the writing, but it may also be attributed to him in a figurative way, as when he orders it be done. It is narrated in a hadith that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) "wrote," but the meaning is that he commanded writing. This is because Allah the Exalted has informed us that he was the unlettered Prophet, one who neither writes nor reads a book. Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿You did not recite before it any Book, nor did you write it with your right hand; otherwise the falsifiers would have had cause for doubt﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 48]. A parallel to this emphasis is ﴿flies with its two wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38], and (they say with their mouths), and the poet's words:

*"You looked, but you did not look with your eyes at a sight."*

All of these were brought to emphasise what the apparent wording requires, and to remove the figurative meaning it might bear. In this emphasis there is also a censure of their deed, for they were not content merely to order the fabrication and alteration; rather, they themselves undertook it and committed it with their own hands. Ibn al-Sarrah said: the mention of hands is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for their having invented that of their own accord and from themselves, without it being sent down to them. End of his words. But this does not indicate what has been mentioned, because handling a thing with the hand does not necessarily imply fabrication. There must be an omitted circumstantial clause (*hal*) indicated by what follows. The estimate is: they write the Book with their own hands, altered, or something similar that conveys this meaning, as shown by His saying afterwards: ﴿Then they say: this is from Allah﴾. For there is no censure against one who handles a book with his hand unless he places it in other than its proper place. For this reason we have estimated this circumstantial clause.

﴿Then they say﴾: that is, to their unlettered followers, who know nothing except what is read to them. The object of the saying is this sentence: ﴿this is from Allah, that they may exchange it﴾. The *li* here is the *lam* of purpose (*lam kay*), and its discussion has been given earlier. It is vowelled with a kasra because it is a preposition, so it is connected to (they say). Whoever claimed that it is connected to the sense of settledness (*istiqrar*) has gone too far. The Banu al-'Anbar pronounce the *lam* of purpose with a fatha; this is what Makki said in his *I'rab al-Qur'an*.

﴿for a small price﴾: *bihi* (with it) is connected to His saying *li-yashtaru* (that they may exchange). The pronoun refers to what they pointed to with their saying "this is from Allah," namely the written, altered text. The discussion of "purchasing" (*ishtira*) has already been given in His saying: ﴿they purchased error in exchange for guidance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16]. The *thaman* (price) here is the worldly goods, or the bribes and provisions they had. It is described as small either because it is perishable, or unlawful, or contemptible, or because nothing can balance it, neither a price nor a priced thing. In this act they combined going astray and leading others astray, lying against Allah, and adding to that the love of this world. This threat is directed at the writing of the altered Book and at attributing it to Allah the Exalted. Both are reprehensible, and their combination is even more reprehensible. This indicates the prohibition of taking wealth through falsehood, even if the giver gives it willingly.

﴿So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they earn﴾: their writing is the preliminary, and its outcome is the acquisition of unlawful wealth. For this reason *wayl* is repeated with each of the two, lest it be supposed that the threat applies only to the combination. Each of these two (p-278) is a matter for which destruction is threatened. The apparent meaning of "what they earn" is what they took as wealth through their altering of the Book, which is unlawful. This is the most fitting reading in the context of the verse. It is also said that what they earn refers to their evil deeds. Both views require a restriction, since "what they earn" is general, and the better course is to restrict it to what we have mentioned.

﴿And they said: The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days﴾. The occasion of revelation of this verse: they claimed that they had found written in the Torah that the distance between the two edges of Hell is a journey of forty years, until one reaches the tree of Zaqqum. They said: "We will only be punished until we reach the tree of Zaqqum, and then Hell will pass away and perish." This is reported from Ibn 'Abbas. It is also said that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The Jews are among the people of the Fire." They said: "We, and then you will succeed us." He said: "You have lied; you know that we will not succeed you." Then this verse was revealed. It is also reported from them that they would be punished for seven days, the number of the days of the world, seven thousand years, a day for each thousand, and then the punishment would end. It is reported from them that they would be punished for forty days, the number of their worship of the calf. It is also said: forty days, as a fulfilment of an oath (*tahillat al-qasam*). It is also said: forty nights, after which a call would go out: "Bring out every circumcised one from the Children of Israel." Then this verse was revealed. The pronoun in "and they said" refers to those who write the Book. They combined with the altering and distortion of the Book of Allah, and their taking unlawful wealth through it, and their lie that it was from Allah, the report of a pure falsehood concerning the length of their stay in the Fire. The meaning of *massa* (to touch) has already been given: it is to reach or afflict. That is, the Fire will not reach us except for days. This is a *mustathna mufarragh* (an exception from an unstated general), meaning: the Fire will never touch us, except for a number of days. The number of days has already been mentioned: seven or forty. It is also said: by His saying *ma'dudatan* (numbered) he meant "few in number, which can be counted," because they are determined in their number in themselves.

Then He proceeded to refute this claim and these false reports, saying: ﴿Say: Have you taken a covenant from Allah?﴾ That is, a report of this kind. A firm assertion is made only by one who has taken a covenant with Allah concerning it, and you have not taken any covenant concerning it. So it is a lie and a fabrication. He commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to respond to them with this interrogative, which indicates the denial of what they said. The *hamzat al-wasl* (connecting hamza) in *man ittakhadhtum* was elided on account of the interrogative *hamza*. Whoever softens it by transferring its vowel to the *lam* and eliding it says: *qul ittakhadhtum* with a fatha on the *lam*, because the hamza was originally fatha. *'Inda Allah* (with Allah) is an adverbial phrase of place (*zarf*) in the accusative, governed by *ittakhadhtum*. Here the verb is transitive to one object, but it may also be transitive to two, in which case the second is the adverbial phrase, and it is then connected to an omitted verb. The word *'ahd* (covenant) here means a pledge and a promise. Ibn 'Abbas said its meaning is: "Have you said: there is no god but Allah, and believed and obeyed, so that by this you are guided and know your exit from the Fire?" According to the first interpretation the meaning is: "Has Allah made a covenant with you concerning what you claim?" According to the second: "Have you sent forward deeds with Allah that necessitate what you claim?"

﴿Then Allah will not break His covenant, or do you say about Allah what you do not know?﴾ This sentence is the answer to the interrogative which has the sense of a condition, like your saying: "Does Zayd intend us? Then we will not answer him out of our kindness." The difference over the answer to these matters has already been discussed: is it by way of implication, so that the interrogative, the optative, the imperative and the prohibitive are all given the sense of a condition, or is the condition omitted after them? For this reason al-Zamakhshari said: *fa-lan yukhlifa* (then He will not break) is connected to an omitted element, its estimate being: "If you have taken a covenant with Him, then Allah will not break His covenant." It seems he chose the second view, that the condition is implied after these matters. Ibn 'Atiyya said: ﴿then Allah will not break His covenant﴾ is a parenthetical interjection in the midst of the speech. It is as though he means that His saying ﴿or do you say﴾ is equivalent (*mu'adil*) to His saying ﴿Say: Have you taken a covenant from Allah?﴾ So this sentence, placed between the two sentences which stand in equivalence, becomes a parenthetical sentence and has no place in the grammar. It is as though he says: "Which of these two has occurred: your taking a covenant from Allah, or your saying about Allah what you do not know?" He presented this in the manner of one uncertain about its specification, by way of affirmation, even though it is known that one of them has occurred, namely their saying about Allah what they do not know. A parallel is: ﴿And indeed we or you are upon guidance or in manifest error﴾ [Saba': 24]. It is known which of them is upon guidance and which is in error. It is also said: *am* here is disjunctive (*munqati'a*), so it is estimated as *bal* (rather) together with the *hamza*. As if he said: "Rather, do you say about Allah what you do not know?" This is an interrogative of denial, because they had said about Allah what they did not know, and so their denial was against their own utterance. In His saying ﴿then Allah will not break His covenant﴾ there is evidence that Allah does not break His promise. Scholars differed concerning His threat. The majority held that He does not break it, just as He does not break His promise. Others held that it is permissible for Him to break His threat, arguing that breaking a promise is ugly, whereas breaking a threat is good. This is a question discussed in the principles of religion (*usul al-din*).

Ibn 'Abbas said its meaning is: "Have you said: there is no god but Allah, and believed and obeyed, so that by this you are guided and know your exit from the Fire?" According to the first interpretation the meaning is: "Has Allah made a covenant with you concerning what you claim?" According to the second: "Have you sent forward deeds with Allah that necessitate what you claim?"

﴿Then Allah will not break His covenant, or do you say about Allah what you do not know?﴾ This sentence is the answer to the interrogative which has the sense of a condition, like your saying: "Does Zayd intend us? Then we will not answer him out of our kindness." The difference over the answer to these matters has already been discussed: is it by way of implication, so that the interrogative, the optative, the imperative and the prohibitive are all given the sense of a condition, or is the condition omitted after them? For this reason al-Zamakhshari said: *fa-lan yukhlifa* (then He will not break) is connected to an omitted element, its estimate being: "If you have taken a covenant with Him, then Allah will not break His covenant." It seems he chose the second view, that the condition is implied after these matters. Ibn 'Atiyya said: ﴿then Allah will not break His covenant﴾ is a parenthetical interjection in the midst of the speech. It is as though he means that His saying ﴿or do you say﴾ is equivalent (*mu'adil*) to His saying ﴿Say: Have you taken a covenant from Allah?﴾ So this sentence, placed between the two sentences which stand in equivalence, becomes a parenthetical sentence and has no place in the grammar. It is as though he says: "Which of these two has occurred: your taking a covenant from Allah, or your saying about Allah what you do not know?" He presented this in the manner of one uncertain about its specification, by way of affirmation, even though it is known that one of them has occurred, namely their saying about Allah what they do not know. A parallel is: ﴿And indeed we or you are upon guidance or in manifest error﴾ [Saba': 24]. It is known which of them is upon guidance and which is in error. It is also said: *am* here is disjunctive (*munqati'a*), so it is estimated as *bal* (rather) together with the *hamza*. As if he said: "Rather, do you say about Allah what you do not know?" This is an interrogative of denial, because they had said about Allah what they did not know, and so their denial was against their own utterance. In His saying ﴿then Allah will not break His covenant﴾ there is evidence that Allah does not break His promise. Scholars differed concerning His threat. The majority held that He does not break it, just as He does not break His promise. Others held that it is permissible for Him to break His threat, arguing that breaking a promise is ugly, whereas breaking a threat is good. This is a question discussed in the principles of religion (*usul al-din*).

**﴿Bala﴾**: a particle of response (ḥarf jawāb) by which what follows a negation is affirmed. If you say, "Zayd did not stand," and the reply is "Naʿam" (yes), it is a confirmation of the negation of Zayd's standing. If you say "Bala" (on the contrary), it is a nullification of that negation. When they said, "The Fire will not touch us except for a few days" (lan tamassanā al-nār), they were answered with His words "Bala," and its meaning is: "The Fire will touch you." The meaning is eternity, and this is clarified by "khulūd" (abiding).

**﴿Man kasaba sayyiʾatan﴾**: "Man" may be conditional (sharṭiyyah) and may be relative (mawṣūlah). The factors permitting the entry of the fāʾ into the predicate when the subject is a relative pronoun (mawṣūl) are present here, and what makes it preferable is the use of "alladhīna" in both cases, which is a relative pronoun. "Sayyiʾah" (evil deed): it is disbelief and polytheism (shirk), so said Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid. It was also said: that which necessitates the Fire, so said al-Suddi, and upon this is the interpretation of those who explained "sayyiʾah" as the major sins (kabāʾir), because they are what necessitate the Fire, meaning its doer deserves the Fire if it is not forgiven for him.

**﴿Wa-aḥāṭat bihi khaṭīʾatuh﴾**: al-Jumhur read it in the singular (khaṭīʾah). Nafiʿ read "khaṭīʾātuh" (sound plural), and some readers read "khaṭāyāh" (broken plural). The meaning is that it has seized him from all his sides. The meaning of encompassing him is that he dies upon disbelief and polytheism; this is if "khaṭīʾah" is interpreted as shirk. Whoever interprets it as the major sin, then the meaning of encompassing him is that he dies while persisting in it. Thus, the abiding according to the first view means remaining, not until an end; and according to the second view, the intended meaning of abiding is remaining a long age, since its outcome is departure from the Fire. Al-Kalbi said: his sins have bound him. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they have nullified his good deeds. Mujahid said: they have covered his heart. Muqatil said: he persisted in them. al-Rabiʿ said: he died upon polytheism. al-Hasan said: every matter for which God has threatened the Fire is the encompassing sin.

Man, as mentioned previously, has both wording and meaning. He first treated it according to its wording, saying, "Whoever earns an evil deed and his sin encompasses him," and then treated it according to its meaning, which is His words, "Those are..." to the end. He used the singular "sayyiʾah" because it refers to a singular thing, which is polytheism. Whoever used the singular "khaṭīʾah" intended by it the genus and as a counterpart to "sayyiʾah," since "sayyiʾah" is singular; whoever used the plural did so because the major sins are many, observing the meaning and matching the wording to it.

A group held that "sayyiʾah" and "khaṭīʾah" are one and the same, and that "khaṭīʾah" is a description of "sayyiʾah." Some distinguished between them, saying: "sayyiʾah" is disbelief, and "khaṭīʾah" is what is below disbelief of sins; so said Mujahid, Abu Wail, and al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas. It was also said: "khaṭīʾah" is polytheism, and "sayyiʾah" here is what is below polytheism of sins. al-Zamakhshari said: "And his sin encompassed him, that, and it dominated him, as an enemy encircles, and he was not freed from it by repentance." End of his words. This is among his subtle insertions which he included in his book, for the belief of the Muʿtazilah is that whoever commits a major sin and does not repent of it, and dies, is abiding in the Fire forever.

In His words, **﴿Ulāʾika aṣḥābu al-nār hum fīhā khālidūn﴾** ("Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever"): there is an indication that the intended are the disbelievers, and this is supported by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "As for the people of the Fire who are its people, they will neither die nor live." Their being companions of the Fire has been ordered upon the existence of two matters: one of them, earning an evil deed; the other, the encompassing of sin. What is ordered upon the existence of two conditions does not follow from the existence of only one of them. This indicates that whoever does not earn an evil deed, which is polytheism, even if his sin encompasses him, which is the major sins, will not be among the companions of the Fire, nor among those who abide therein. By "companions of the Fire" is meant those who are truly its people, not one who entered it and then left it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 82:

﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds, they are the companions of Paradise; therefore they will abide in it.﴾ After mentioning the people of the Fire and the destruction prepared for them, He followed this with mention of the people of faith and the eternal abiding in the Gardens prepared for them. What is meant by "those who believe" is the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the believers of the nations before him. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and others, and it is the apparent meaning of the wording. Ibn Zayd said it is specific to the Prophet (ﷺ) and his community. Rarely is a verse of threat mentioned in the Qur'an without a verse of promise being mentioned alongside it. The benefit of this is the manifestation of God's justice, (p-280) and the balance between the believer's hope and fear, and the completeness of His mercy in His promise and His wisdom in His warning. These noble verses also contain a rejection of the believers' hope for the faith of those among their forefathers who were honoured by hearing the speech of God, and then the contrast of that with their great distortion, and this was done with knowledge on their part of the ugliness of what they committed. Those whose faith was hoped for are the sons of those distorters, so they follow the path of their forefathers in disbelief. Then they concealed, inwardly, the flattery of the believers, such that when they met them they made them understand that they were believers, and when some of them were alone with others, they denied to them what they had said to the believers of the reports of some things in their books. That was out of fear that the believers would argue against them with what was in their book. Then God denied them that, because they knew that God knows their secrets and their private talk. Nothing suits that except submission to the Book of God, reporting what is in it, and following what it contains of commands, by following the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and believing in what they find written with them in the Tawrah (Torah) and the Injil (Gospel). But they disbelieved out of obstinacy, ﴿and they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance﴾ (Surah al-Naml 27:14).

Then, when He mentioned the condition of these people who are among the learned, and did not benefit from their knowledge, He also mentioned their followers and common people, and that they know nothing of the Book except audible words, and that their way regarding the foundations of their religions is only their good opinion of their scholars, who distort and alter. Then God threatened with destruction and regret whoever distorts the speech of God and claims that it is from God, in order to obtain a trivial, meagre, and non-lasting worldly aim. So he sold what remains for what perishes.

Then He repeated the threat for what they did. Then He informed about them of the pure lie they uttered, that their staying in the Fire would be "﴿a number of days﴾" (Surah al-Baqarah 2:80), and that this report did not proceed from a covenant they had made with God, but rather was a saying about God for which they have no knowledge. Then He refuted their claim with His saying: "Bala" (Yes, [you will abide in the Fire]), that is, a affirmation of the negation they had made. Then He divided people into two categories: the disbeliever, who is the companion of the Fire, and the believer, who is the companion of Paradise. They were included in the category of the disbeliever, because they earned evil deeds, and their sins encompassed them. And sufficient is what God related about them from the beginning of the surah up to here, and what He relates after that of the disbelief and violations they committed.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 83 (part 1 of 4):

﴿And [remember] when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: "Worship none but Allah, and be good to parents, and to kinsfolk, orphans, and the needy, and speak kindly to people, and establish prayer, and give zakat." Then you turned away, except for a few of you, and you were [habitually] averse.﴾ ﴿And [remember] when We took your covenant: "Do not shed your blood, nor expel yourselves from your homes." Then you acknowledged it, while you were witnesses.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 84] ﴿Yet you are those who kill yourselves and expel a group of you from their homes, backing one another against them in sin and aggression. But if they come to you as captives, you ransom them, while their expulsion was itself forbidden to you. Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part? So what is the recompense of those among you who do that, except disgrace in the worldly life? And on the Day of Resurrection they will be returned to the most severe punishment. And Allah is not unaware of what you do.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 85] ﴿Those are the ones who have bought the worldly life in exchange for the Hereafter. So the punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be helped.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 86].

al-Walidani (the two parents): the father and the mother. Each of them is called a walid (parent), and the apparent, literal sense of the term applies. The poet said:
"And one who has a child whom two parents did not beget"
It is also said that the mother may be called walid and walidah. It was said that al-walid refers to the father alone, and the dual was used as a predominance of the masculine form.

al-Ihsan (goodness): benefiting others in every good way.
