Dhu: meaning "possessor of," and it is among the Six Nouns, which take a waw in the nominative, an alif in the accusative, and a ya' in the genitive. Its original form, according to Sibawayh, is dhawy, and its morphological pattern according to him is fa'l. According to al-Khalil, it is dhuwwah, from the pattern of khuwwah and quwwah, and its pattern according to him is fu'l. It is always construed with a noun (idafah), and its idafah to a common noun is regular. Its idafah to a pronoun is disputed. It may be construed with a proper noun obligatorily when the two are conjoined by lexical usage, as in the expressions dhu Jadan, dhu Yazan, dhu Ru'ayn, and dhu al-Kula'. If they are not conjoined by lexical usage, it may still be permitted, as in their saying of 'Amr and Qatari: dhu 'Amr and dhu Qatari, meaning the possessor of this name. Its idafah to a proper noun in its usual direction is attested, as is: "I am dhu Makkah," and "O Allah, bless Muhammad and his dhawi (family)." Among what is construed with a proper noun and intended in the sense of "possessor of wealth," and among what is construed with the pronoun of a proper noun and also with the pronoun of the addressee, the poet said:
"Indeed we hope for swiftly from you the like of what we hoped for from your noble kinsmen of old"
Dhu has also come in the dialect of Tayy as a relative pronoun, and it has rules in grammar.

al-Qurba: a verbal noun like al-ruj'a, and the alif in it is the feminine marker. It denotes kinship of blood and lineage. Tarafah said:
"And I drew near through kinship and your grandfather, that when a matter of [tribal] breach arises, I will bear witness"
He also said:
"And the oppression of kinsmen is more painful to the free man than the impact of the polished sword"

al-Yatama: the pattern fa'ala, and it is a plural that does not take tanwin, because the alif in it is the feminine marker. Its singular is yatim, like nadim, and it is a plural not conforming to analogy; likewise its plural yetama (ayta'm) is irregular. al-Asma'i said: orphanhood among the children of Adam is from the father's side, and among other creatures from the mother's side. al-Mawardi related that orphanhood among the children of Adam is said of one who has lost the mother, but the first is the well-known usage, and its root meaning is isolation. Thus the meaning of "a young orphan" is: isolated from his father. The unique pearl that has no equal was called yatimah for its singularity, as Tha'lab said. It was said: the root of orphanhood is heedlessness, and a child was called yatim because he is neglected in terms of kindness. It was said: the root of orphanhood is delay, and from it the word yatim is derived, because kindness is delayed toward him; this was said by Abu 'Amr.

al-Masakin: the plural of miskin, which is derived from sukun (stillness), so the mim is augmentative, like mihdir from hadar. It is related: "tamaskana fulan" (he became needy), but the more correct form in the language is tasakkana, meaning he became a miskin. It is synonymous with faqir, one who has nothing. It was said: it is one who has some small thing.

al-Hasan and al-Husn: it was said they are two dialectal forms, like al-bukhl and al-bakhal. Al-husn is the verbal noun of hasuna, as al-qubh is the verbal noun of qabuha, the opposite of hasuna.

al-Qalil: an active participle from qalla, just as kathir, its opposite, is an active participle from kathura. It is said: qalla yaqillu qillatan, qallan, and qullan.

al-I'rad: turning away. It was said: turning away with the body, and i'rad with the heart. Al-'Ard means side, so it is possible that your saying "a'rada Zayd 'an 'Amr" means he went to one side of him, and the hamzah in it then indicates becoming.

al-Dam: well known; it is defective in its final radical, which is ya' according to the verse:
"The two bloods flowed with the certain good"
or waw, according to their saying damawan. Its pattern is fa'l. It was said: fil. It has been heard as a shortened form, the poet said:
"She was heedless, then came seeking him, and behold, [there were] bones and blood"
And he said:
"But on our heels blood drips"
according to the narration of one who transmitted it so. It has also been heard with a doubled mim, the poet said:
"He humiliated your blood, empty, after its honor, O 'Amr, your reproach stubbornly persisting in envy"

al-Diyar: plural of dar. This is the regular pattern for a noun of the form fi'l when it is neither doubled nor defective in its final radical, such as talal and fata. The ya' in this plural is changed from waw, for its original form is duwar. This substitution is regular when the plural is of a form with a defective middle radical, like thawb, hawd, and dar, on condition that the pattern is fi'al with a sound final radical. If it is defective in its final radical, it is not changed, as in rawa. They said for the plural of tawil: tuwal and tiyal.

aqarra bi'l-shay': acknowledged it, admitted to it.

Tazahirun: you cooperate, as if each of those backing one another leans his back on his companion; al-zahr means helper.

al-Ithm: sin, its plural is athām.

al-Usara: plural of asir, and fa'la is regular for fa'il in the sense of "dead" or "afflicted," like qatil and jarih. As for al-usara, it was said to be the plural of asir, and the form asara with an open hamzah has been heard, though it is not the most common. It was said: asara is the plural of usra, so it is a plural of a plural; this was said by al-Mufaddal. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: al-usra are those in hand, and al-usara are those in bonds, and al-asir is one taken by compulsion and overpowering.

al-Fida': its initial letter may be kasrah with a long vowel, as al-Nabighah said:
"Enough, may all peoples be ransom for you, and whatever I gain of wealth and offspring"
It may also be shortened, he said:
"Ransom for you from a Lord, my possessions and my heritage"
If its initial letter is fatha, it is shortened, as one says: "Stand, ransom you, my father." This was said by al-Jawhari. The meaning of "fada fulan fulanan" is: he gave his equivalent.

al-Muharram: the passive participle of harrama, and it returns to the meaning of prohibition. You say: harramahu yahrimuhu, if he forbade him.

al-Jaza': recompense, requital, and it is used for both good and evil.

al-Khizy: disgrace. Al-Jawhari said: khazia, with a kasrah, yakhza khizyan. Ibn al-Sikkit said: the meaning of khazia is that he fell into a trial; Allah also made him disgraced (akhzahu). Khaza al-rajul fi nafsihi yakhza khaza'atan, when he felt shame, and he is khazyan; the people are khaza ya, or a woman khazya.

al-Dunya: the feminine of al-adna, and it goes back to dunuw, meaning nearness. The alif in it is the feminine marker, and the alif and lam are not dropped from it except in poetry, as in his saying:
"In the striving of a world that has long been stretched out"
Al-dunya is sometimes used as an adjective and sometimes used as a noun. When it is an adjective, the ya' is changed from waw, since it is derived from dunuw, like al-'ulya. Therefore it is used as an adjective for "the life" in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the example of the life of this world is like rain which We send down from the sky﴾ [Yunus: 24]. As for al-quswa and al-hulwa, they are anomalous. When it is used as a noun, the same applies. Abu Bakr ibn al-Sarraj said, regarding the shortened and extended forms: al-dunya is feminine and shortened, written with an alif. This is the dialect of Najd and Tamim specifically; however, the people of the Hijaz and Banu Asad append it and its counterparts to verbal nouns with a waw, so they say dunwa, like shar wa. They do the same with every fu'la whose final radical is waw: they open its first letter and change the waw into ya', because they find the damma and the waw burdensome.

﴿And [remember] when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: "Worship none but Allah"﴾ — this verse is connected to the verses before it in its reproach and rebuke of the Children of Israel, and in clarifying what was taken from them of the covenant to worship Allah, to single Him out for worship, and what He commanded them of noble character, such as maintaining the ties of kinship, being good to the needy, and persevering in the two pillars of Islam, the bodily and the financial. Then it mentions their turning away from that and their breaking of that covenant, in keeping with their earlier habit and their familiar way. Idh (when) is conjoined to the earlier temporal clauses before it. The covenant is that which Allah took from them while they were in the loins of their fathers like particles, as Makki said; this was criticized on the ground that the address has been restricted to the Children of Israel, and the covenant of the verse concerns them. Or it is a covenant taken from them while they were sane in their lives through the tongue of Musa, peace be upon him, and other of their prophets, as Ibn 'Atiyyah said. It was also said: it is a covenant taken from them in the Torah, that they would worship Him, and so on to the end of the verses. Ibn Kathir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "la ya'budun" with the ya'. The rest read it with the ta' from above. Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read "la ta'budu," in the prohibitive. As for "la ya'budun," they mentioned several possibilities for its parsing:

The first: it is a negated sentence in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the Children of Israel, meaning: not worshipping except Allah, that is, affirming the oneness of Allah and singling Him out for worship. It is a circumstantial clause from the genitive-attached noun, and that is not permitted according to the correct view. It cannot be said that the noun in the genitive could be semantically the agent of "covenant," since it may be a verbal noun, or its rule is the rule of a verbal noun. If that is so, the noun in the genitive after it could be an agent or an object in meaning; for what is analyzed as a verbal particle plus verb is what supposedly carries the action, and here the meaning does not allow it to be analyzed in that way. Therefore one may not judge its position as nominative or accusative, for if you assumed that "akhadhna" means "we covenanted with the Children of Israel," or "the Children of Israel covenanted with us," it would not be valid. Indeed, even if we posit it as a true verbal noun, it would not permit that. Do you not see that if you said "I took the knowledge of Zayd," it would not be analyzed as a particle plus verb: one does not say "I took that Zayd should know." When the verbal noun cannot be analyzed as a verbal particle plus verb, nor is it like "darban Zaydan," it does not govern, though there is disagreement about the latter. For this reason Ibn al-Tarawah prohibited, in the translation of Sibawayh's "This is the chapter on the knowledge of what words are in Arabic," that the verbal noun be analyzed as a verbal particle plus verb, and he refuted those who permitted it. Among those who permitted the sentence to be a circumstantial clause were al-Mubarrad and Qutrub. They said: it may be a circumstantial clause that is concomitant, and a circumstantial clause that is prospective.

The second: the sentence is a response to an omitted oath indicated by His saying: "We took the covenant of the Children of Israel," meaning: we made them swear by Allah, "they will not worship," attributed to Sibawayh, and permitted by al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', and al-Mubarrad.

The third: "an" is omitted, and "an" with what follows it is taken as governed by an omitted preposition. The estimate is: "bi-an la ta'budu illa Allah," the preposition is omitted, since omitting it with "an" and "anna" is permitted and regular, when it causes no ambiguity. Then "an" is omitted after that, so the verb becomes nominative: "la ta'budun." This was said by al-Akhfash, and its parallel in prose of the Arabs is: "Order him to dig it," and in their verse is his saying:
"Ala ayyuhadha al-zajiri ahdhur al-waghi"

Its original form is: "Command him to dig it." And (the construction) "'an an uhdara al-waghā" (that I attend the battle), in which the verb has taken the same governance as what we mentioned. This type of omitting *an* (the infinitive particle "that") in such a context is disputed. Among the grammarians, some prohibited it, and our later Shafi'i (companions) follow this view. A group of grammarians held that it is permissible to delete it in this position. Then they disagreed. It was said: the verb must then be in the nominative (*raf'*), and this is the view of Abu al-Hasan (al-Akhfash). Others said the verb loses its governance altogether, and this is the view of al-Mubarrad and the Kufans. The sound position is to restrict what has been transmitted of this to the attested usage (*samā'*, what is heard from the Arabs), and what is of this kind should not be used to explain the verse, because it involves deleting a verbal particle (*harf maṣdarī*) while retaining its complement in positions where such deletion is not regularly permitted.

The fourth possibility: the intended meaning is "that you not worship," so *an* is deleted and the verb is in the nominative. This would be in the accusative position as a substitute (*badal*) for His words: ﴿the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾. The same objection applies to this possibility as to the previous one: the sound view is that deleting *an*, and making the verb nominative or accusative, is not a regular (analogical) usage.

The fifth possibility: the clause is related with an omitted circumstantial phrase (*ḥāl maḥdhūfa*), meaning "saying: you do not worship except Allah." Its wording is that of a statement, but its meaning is a prohibition. That is, "saying to them: do not worship except Allah." This was stated by al-Farra'. It is supported by the reading of Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud, and the next phrase, ﴿and speak to people kindly﴾, is coordinated with it.

The sixth possibility: the omitted element is the verb of saying, meaning: "And We said to them: ﴿You do not worship except Allah﴾," and this is also a negation with the sense of a prohibition. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Just as one says 'you go to so-and-so, say such-and-such to him,' meaning a command. It is more eloquent than an explicit command or prohibition, because they were quick to comply and desist, so He reports about them." End of his words. This is good.

The seventh possibility: the intended meaning is "that you not worship," and *an* is explanatory (*mufassira*) of the content of the sentence, because in His words ﴿We took the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾ there is the sense of saying. So the explanatory *an* was deleted and what it explains was retained. There is an issue with whether the explanatory *an* may be deleted.

The eighth possibility: the sentence is explanatory (*tafsīriyya*), so it has no place in the grammatical structure (*i'rāb*). This is because when He mentioned that He took the covenant of the Children of Israel, there was an ambiguity about what the covenant was. So He brought this sentence to explain the covenant. As for the one who read it with *yā'* (the third-person form, "they do not worship"), this is because "Children of Israel" is a third-person expression. As for the one who read it with *tā'* (the second-person form, "you do not worship"), this is an *iltifāt* (shift from third person to second person), and its wisdom is turning toward them with direct address, so that it is more likely to be accepted and closer to compliance, since it involves Allah turning toward the addressee directly. Even when the sentence is taken as explanatory, the negation is still one intended as a prohibition, since the literal sense of a report is remote here.

﴿Illā Allāh﴾ (except Allah): this is an exceptive construction with a missing object (*istithnā' mufarragh*), because "you do not worship" has not taken its object. There is also an *iltifāt* here, as it shifts from the first-person pronoun to the explicit third-person name. Do you not see that if it had continued in one pattern, the wording would have been "you do not worship except Us"? But the shift to the explicit noun carries grandeur, indicates all the attributes, and singles out the name, which the pronoun does not do. Also, what comes after it of names are explicit nouns, so it is fitting for an explicit noun to be adjacent to an explicit noun.

﴿And to parents, kindness﴾: the meaning is the command to be kind to one's parents, to be dutiful to them, and to honour them. Many verses of the Qur'an and numerous hadiths contain this, to the point that disobedience to parents (*ʿuqūq*) was counted among the major sins. Consider the importance given to them in that Allah joined it with His worship, may He be exalted. Among the strange narratives is that Umar saw a woman carrying her father on her back around the Ka'ba, having brought him on her back from Yemen. He said to her: "May Allah reward you well; you have fulfilled his right." She said: "I have not fulfilled it, nor have I been fair to him; for he used to carry me and wished for my life, while I carry him and wish for his death."

They differed about what the preposition *bi-* in His words ﴿and to parents﴾ is connected to, and about the accusative case of *iḥsānan* (kindness), with several possibilities:

The first: it is coordinated with "do not worship," meaning with the infinitive construction formed from the infinitival particle and the verb. According to this speaker, the implied meaning is: "devoting worship to Allah alone, and to parents" — that is, "and to the dutifulness toward parents," or "to kindness toward parents." *Iḥsānan* is accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) of the omitted genitive construction (*muḍāf maḥdhūf*) from that. The governing element for it is the covenant (*mīthāq*), because the prepositional phrase depends on it, and verbal nuances (*rawā'iḥ al-af'āl*) govern adverbials and prepositional phrases.

The second possibility (p. 284): the preposition is attached to *iḥsānan*, and *iḥsānan* is a verbal noun placed in the position of the imperative verb, as if he had said: "And be kind to parents." They said: *bā'* (bi-) is synonymous with *ilā* (to) in this verb; one says *aḥsantu bihi* and *ilayhi* with one meaning. On this interpretation it may also be by omission of a genitive construction, meaning: "And be kind to parents by being dutiful to them," so the sense is: "Be kind to parents through being dutiful to them." On both of these possibilities, the governing element of the prepositional phrase is the word pronounced. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This view may be objected to on the grounds that the verbal noun has had its own complement (*ma'mūl*) placed before it." End of his words. This objection is complete only according to the view of Abu al-Hasan, who prohibited placing an object before the verbal noun, as in "a beating Zayd," but this is not valid. The prohibition holds only when the verbal noun is linked to *an* and a verb, but when it is not so linked, placing its complement before it is not forbidden. So it is permissible to say "a beating Zayd" and "Zayd a beating," whether the governance is for the omitted verb governing the verbal noun, or for the verbal noun substituting for the verb, because that omitted verb is a command, and the verbal noun substituting for it also has the sense of a command. So, given the disagreement between the two schools about the governing element, placing it first is permissible.

The third possibility: the governing element is omitted and is estimated as "and be kind," or "and they be kind to parents." *Iḥsānan* is accusative as a verbal noun emphasizing that omitted verb. Its estimate is: "And be kind," in consideration of the meaning, since the meaning of "do not worship" is "do not worship" (in the sense of a command); or its estimate is "and they be kind," in consideration of the wording "do not worship." With these two estimates al-Zamakhshari estimated this omitted element.

The fourth possibility: the governing element is omitted and is estimated as "and enjoin strongly regarding the parents," and *iḥsānan* is accusative as the object. This was stated by al-Mahdawi.

The fifth possibility: the governing element is omitted and is estimated as "And We enjoined on them regarding the parents," and *iḥsānan* is accusative as an object of purpose (*maf'ūl min ajlihi*), meaning: "And We enjoined on them regarding the parents, out of kindness from Us," that is, for the sake of Our kindness. That is, the reason for enjoining regarding them is Our kindness, either because it is part of Our nature to be kind, or as kindness from Us toward those enjoined, since by complying with it they receive a great reward and immense recompense, or as kindness from Us toward those enjoined about. This verb has come explicitly in His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And We enjoined upon man regarding his parents, goodness﴾ [al-'Ankabūt: 8].

The preferred view is the second, because there is no omission in it, and because the verbal noun regularly occurs in the sense of the imperative verb.

﴿And to the near of kin, and the orphans, and the needy﴾: this is coordinated with His words "and to parents." The parents were mentioned first because they are the most emphatic in dutifulness and kindness, and the prepositional object was placed before the governing element to give attention to the object of the preposition, which is the two parents, and out of concern for their matter. This order came to give priority to the most emphatic. So He began with the parents, since their precedence over everyone in kindness toward them is not hidden. Then with the near of kin, because maintaining ties of kinship is also emphatic, and because he shares the parents' kinship. Then with orphans, because they do not have full ability to earn a living. There has come: "I and the one who sponsors an orphan will be like these two in Paradise," along with other reports. Then with the needy, because of the reward for being kind to them. The needy were ranked later because they can look after themselves by taking employment and setting their livelihood right, unlike orphans, who, because of their youth, cannot be relied upon, and who need someone to benefit them.

The first of these obligations is devoting worship to Allah alone, then kindness to parents, then to the near of kin, then to orphans, then to the needy. These are five obligations which together comprise worship of Allah, encouragement toward kindness to parents, and support for the near of kin, orphans, and the needy. He made *dhū al-qurbā* (the near of kin) singular because He intended it as a category, and because its being attached to the verbal noun includes every relative.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 83 (part 3 of 4):

﴿And speak to people kindly﴾: When He mentioned, after the worship of God, kindness to those mentioned, and most of what was demanded in that was action (of maintaining ties, feeding, and checking on people), He followed it with good speech, so that those upon whom the covenant was taken would combine obedience to God's command in deeds and in words. So the Exalted said: ﴿And speak to people kindly﴾. Since speech is easy to achieve, being a substitute of utterance and not of wealth, its object with respect to people is general, since there is no harm to a person in doing good to people with good speech.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read ḥasanan (حَسَنًا) with a fatḥah on the ḥā' and the sīn. ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abi Rabah and ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read ḥusunan (حُسُنًا) with a ḍammah on both. Ubayy and Talhah ibn Musarrif read ḥusnā (حُسْنى), on the pattern fuʿlā. Al-Jahdari read iḥsānan (إحْسانًا).

As for the reading of the majority, ḥasanan, its apparent sense is that it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and that originally it was "a good speech," either by omitting a modified noun, meaning "possessing goodness," or by describing it with the verbal noun for the sake of its excessive goodness. It was also said that it may be an adjective, not because its origin is a verbal noun, but like "sweet" and "bitter," so that ḥusn and ḥasan are two dialect forms, like ḥuzn and ḥazan, and ʿurb and ʿarab. It was also said that it is accusative as a verbal noun from the meaning, because the meaning is: "let your speech be good in goodness." As for one who reads ḥasanan with two fatḥahs, it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "and speak to people a good speech." As for one who reads with two ḍammahs, the ḍammah on the sīn is assimilation to the ḍammah of the ḥā'.

As for one who reads ḥusnā, Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: Sibawayh rejected it, because afʿal and fuʿlā do not come except as definite, unless the meaning of preference is removed from them and they remain a verbal noun, like al-ʿUqbā, and then that is permissible, and that is the basis of the reading with it. End of his words. In his words there is confusion, because he said: "because afʿal and fuʿlā do not come except as definite," and it is not as he mentioned. As for afʿal, it has uses: one of them is that it has min (مِن) apparent or implied, or is annexed to an indefinite noun; this never becomes definite, but remains indefinite. The second use is that it has the definite article al-, and then it is definite by it. The third is that it is annexed to a definite noun, and there is disagreement about whether this annexation makes it definite, as in afḍal al-qawm ("the best of the people"). As for fuʿlā, it has two uses: one is with the definite article, and it is definite by it. The second is annexed to a definite noun, as in fuḍlā al-nisāʾ ("the most excellent of women"). With regard to this annexation there is the same disagreement as with afʿal. So Ibn ʿAṭiyyah's statement, "because afʿal and fuʿlā do not come except as definite," is not correct. And his statement, "unless the meaning of preference is removed from them and they remain a verbal noun, so that fuʿlā, which is the feminine of afʿal, when you remove from it the meaning of preference it remains a verbal noun," is not so; rather, the coming of fuʿlā as a verbal noun is not regular, but only a few words came from it. So it is not permissible to believe that fuʿlā, whose masculine is afʿal, becomes a verbal noun when the meaning of preference is removed from it. Do you not see that kubrā, ṣughrā, jullā, fuḍlā, and what is similar to them, are not regularly made verbal nouns after the removal of the meaning of preference? Rather, what is regular in one view is that when you remove from them the meaning of preference they become in meaning kabīrah, ṣaghīrah, jalīlah, and fāḍilah. Just as, when you remove from their masculines the meaning of preference, akbar becomes in meaning kabīr, afḍal becomes in meaning fāḍil, and aṭwal becomes in meaning ṭawīl.

It is possible that the pronoun in ʿanhā ("from it") refers to ḥusnā, not to fuʿlā, and that the exception is disjunctive, as if he said: "except that the meaning of preference be removed from ḥusnā, which is the word that Ubayy and Talhah read, and it remains a verbal noun," and the meaning of the statement would be "except if it is a verbal noun, like al-ʿUqbā." His words "and that is the basis of the reading with it" mean: and the verbal noun is the basis of the reading with it. This reading has two possible analyses. The first: it is a verbal noun, like al-Bushrā, and this requires the transmission that the Arabs say ḥasuna ḥusnā, just as they say rajaʿa rujʿā and bashshara bushrā, since the coming of fuʿlā as a verbal noun, as we mentioned, is regular. The second: it is an adjective of an omitted modified noun, meaning "and speak to people a word that is ḥusnā" or "a statement that is ḥusnā." Regarding describing with it there are two views. The first: that it remains as it is for preference, and its use without the definite article or annexation to a definite noun is rare, and this has occurred in poetry; the poet said:

"And if you call upon noble deeds and honour, on a day of the generous chiefs of the people, then call us."

So this reading may be from this, since it is a irregular (shādh) reading. The second view: that it is not for preference, so ḥusnā means ḥasanah ("good"), that is, "and speak to people a good statement," just as they analysed Yūsuf as aḥsan ikhwatihi ("the best of his brothers") in the sense of ḥasan ikhwatihi.

As for one who reads iḥsānan, it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a speech of goodness," and iḥsānan is a verbal noun of aḥsana, whose hamzah is for becoming, meaning "a speech that possesses goodness," just as you say aʿshabat al-arḍu iʿshāban, meaning "the land became possessing herbage."

The exegetes differed about the meaning of His words: ﴿And speak to people kindly﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: say to them "there is no god but God," and command them with it. Ibn Jurayj said: speak to them kindly in informing them of what is in your Book about the description of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Abu al-ʿAliyah said: speak to them the good word, and answer them with the best that you would like to be answered with. Sufyan al-Thawri said: command them with what is right and forbid them from what is wrong. Ibn ʿAbbas also said: be truthful about the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ). They differed about who is addressed by His words "And speak to people kindly"; who is it?

The apparent sense is that it is part of the covenant taken from the Children of Israel: that you should not worship except God, and that you should speak to people kindly. On the reading of one who reads lā yaʿbudūna with the yāʾ, it is an iltifāt (shift), since it went from the third person absence to the second person address. It was said: the addressee is the community (of Muhammad). The first is closer, so that the narrative is one, comprising noble character, and so that it suits the address that follows it, His words ﴿then you turned away﴾ to the end of the verses, for it is not possible that it refers to the Children of Israel. The apparent sense of the verse indicates that kindness to the two parents and whoever is joined to them, and good speech to people, were obligatory upon the Children of Israel in their religion, since the taking of the covenant indicates obligation, and so does the apparent form of the command, and it is as if He blamed them for turning away from that. It is related from Qatadah that His words ﴿And speak to people kindly﴾ are abrogated (mansūkh) by the verse of the sword. This cannot be realized except if we say that the addressee is this community. Some people specified this generality as applying to believers, or to calling to God through what is in the command to good, so that it is a specification according to the addressee, or according to the address. Abu Jaʿfar Muhammad ibn ʿAli al-Baqir claimed that this generality remains on its apparent sense, and that there is no need for specification. It was said: and this is the stronger view. The evidence for it: that Harun and Musa, upon our Prophet and upon them both be prayers and peace, were commanded to be gentle with Fir'awn, and likewise the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was told: ﴿Call to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good admonition﴾ [al-Nahl 16:125], and the Exalted said: ﴿And do not revile those who call upon other than God﴾ [al-Anʿam 6:108], ﴿and when they pass by vain talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan 25:72], ﴿and turn away from the ignorant﴾ [al-Aʿraf 7:199]. And whoever said: good speech is not with disbelievers and sinners, argued that we are commanded to curse them, to condemn them, and to fight them, and by His words: ﴿God does not love the public utterance of evil speech except by one who has been wronged﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:148].

﴿And establish the prayer and give the zakat﴾: If this address is to the believers, then it is a shift of address. The discussion of the interpretation of these two clauses has already passed. If this address is to the Children of Israel, and this is the apparent sense because what precedes it and what follows it indicates it, then the prayer is what they were commanded in the Torah, and they continue to observe it until now. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that the zakat of their wealth used to be an offering: a fire would descend upon them and carry it away, and that was its acceptance; what the fire did not do with it was not accepted. It was said: the prayer is this one enjoined upon us, and the address is to the sons of the Jews who were in the presence of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). This possibility has two aspects. The first: that their command to prayer and zakat is a command to Islam. The second: according to the view of those who say that the disbelievers are addressed concerning the branches of faith, and zakat is this one that is enjoined. It was also said: the prayer and zakat here mean obedience to God alone. The meaning of this view is that obedience to God, the Exalted, was referred to by prayer and zakat, which are the greatest pillars of Islam.

﴿Then you turned away, except a few of you, while you were averse﴾: Its apparent sense is that it is an address to the Children of Israel upon whom God took the covenant. It was said: it is an address to the contemporaries of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) from the Children of Israel, and turning away is ascribed to them for their predecessors, since they are all on that same path. Ibn ʿAbbas and others said similarly. The meaning: then you turned away from what the covenant had taken from you. What is meant by "the few" is the few in number of persons. It was said: this few is ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and his companions. It was said: those who believed early from their predecessors, and recently like ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and others. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: it is possible that the fewness is in faith, meaning: when they disobeyed and their last generation disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ), there remained only a little faith, since it would not benefit them; and the first is stronger. End of his words. This is a far possibility from the wording, since what the understanding grasps first is the exception of a few persons from the agent, which is the pronoun in tawallaytum. The accusative of qalīlan is by exception, and this is the more eloquent, since before it there is an affirmative statement. It is related from Abu ʿAmr that he read illā qalīlun (إلّا قَلِيلٌ) with a ḍammah (raf'). Some people also read so, and Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: this is as a substitute (badal) of qalīlun from the pronoun in tawallaytum, and this was permitted, meaning the substitution, even though no negation preceded in the statement, because tawallaytum means negation, as if he said: "none fulfilled the covenant except a few." End of his words. What the grammarians mentioned is that a substitute after an affirmative statement is not permissible: if you say qāma al-qawm illā Zayd ("the people stood except Zayd") with a ḍammah as a substitute, it is not permitted. They said: because the substitute stands in the place of what it substitutes, so if you say qāma illā Zayd, it is not permitted, because illā does not enter an affirmative statement. As for what was offered as a justification for allowing this, that the meaning of tawallaytum is negation, as if it were said: "none fulfilled except a few," this is nothing, because every affirmative statement, when you proceed to negate its contradictory or opposite, becomes like this, so let it be permitted: qāma al-qawm illā Zayd, since it is interpreted as your saying lam tajlisū illā Zayd ("you did not sit except Zayd"). Yet the Arabs did not take this interpretation into account to build their speech upon it; rather the grammarians permitted qāma al-qawm illā Zayd with a ḍammah, in the sense of an adjective (ṣifah). Sibawayh set a section in his book about this and said: this is a section on what illā and what follows it is an adjective, in the position of ghayr ("other than") and mithl ("like"). He mentioned among the examples of this section: "If there were with us a man, except Zayd, we would have prevailed," and ﴿If there had been in them gods except God, they would have been corrupted﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:22], and the poet's line:

"And few are the voices with it, except its bugham (the bleating of a calf)."

He equated this with the reading of one who read ﴿Those who sit at home among the believers, other than those with a harm﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:95] with ghayr in the raf'; and in the case of mā qāma al-qawm illā Zayd ("none of the people stood except Zayd") both the substitute and the adjective are permitted with the raf'. And upon this was interpreted the verse of ʿAmr ibn Maʿdi Karib:

"And every brother whom his brother leaves, by the life of your father, except the two Farqads."

He said: it is as if he said: "and every brother other than the two Farqads whom his brother leaves," just as al-Shammakh said:

"And every close friend, other than one who suppresses his own self for the joining of a friend, is a sharp one or one who..."

And among what the grammarians recited:

"A lost blood, whose nearest kin have moved away from it, except the east wind and the south wind."

And they also recited:

"And in al-Sarima, among them, is a dwelling, worn out, effaced, changed, except the stone-marker and the tent-peg."

---

The teacher Abu al-Hasan ibn 'Usfur said: The description with *illa* (ʾillā, "except") differs from description with other words, in that it describes both indefinite and definite nouns, both apparent and pronominal ones. He also said: The grammarians mean by describing with *illa* only ʿatf al-bayan (appositive, a clarifying apposition). Others said: One is not described with *illa* except when the described noun is indefinite, or definite with the generic *al-* (lām al-jins). Al-Mubarrad said: One is not described with *illa* except when the description occupies a position in which a substitute (badal) could stand. The full discussion of this belongs to the science of grammar. We have only pointed out that what Ibn ʿAṭiyya said in explaining this reading was not held by any grammarian. Among the confusions of some who analyse the grammatical structure (iʿrab, the case-endings and syntactic analysis of words) is that one of them permitted the nominative *qalīlun* to be governed by a deleted verb, as if he said: "Only a few refrained" should be an emphasis of the nominative pronoun in the excepted-from clause. Had these two statements not been recorded in books, I would not have mentioned them. Some also permitted that *qalīlun* be nominative as a subject (mubtadaʾ), with a deleted predicate, as if he said: "Except a few of you who did not turn away," just as they said: "I did not pass by anyone except a man from the Banu Tamim who is better than him." These are the analyses of those who did not reflect deeply on grammar.

*Wa-antum muʿriḍūn* (and you are turning away) is a circumstantial clause (jumla ḥāliyya). Some said it is emphatic. This is the view of those who make *tawallī* (turning away) identical with *iʿrāḍ* (aversion) itself. Whoever distinguishes between them makes the circumstantial clause explanatory. It is likewise explanatory when the object of *tawallī* and of *iʿrāḍ* differs, as some said its meaning is: "Then you turned away from the covenant of your pact, while you are averse to this Prophet ﷺ." The circumstantial clause came as a nominal sentence beginning with *antum* because it is more emphatic, and the predicate was a noun because it indicates stability more clearly. It is as if it were said: "Turning away from the truth and aversion to it are your habit." Addressing them directly with *antum* is a rebuke of their conduct, and of their having committed that ugly act which should not have occurred, like your saying: "Zayd treats you well, while you mistreat him." The meaning is: whoever God has bound by a covenant and taken a pledge from in matters through which his religion and worldly life are ordered, is worthy to remain steadfast in the covenant, not to break it, and not to turn away from it.

It was also said: *tawallī* and *iʿrāḍ* are derived from walking a path. Whoever abandons the path has two states: one is that he returns on his own tracks, and this is *tawallī*; the second is that he takes to the side of the road, and this is *iʿrāḍ*. According to this explanation of *tawallī* and *iʿrāḍ*, there is no proof in the verse of a difference, unless it is intended that some people turned away and others were averse, and it gathers this for them; or that they turn away at one time and are averse at another time.

Al-Qushayri said: Worship through these qualities is obtained for us in our law. The first of them is tawhid (monotheism), which is singling out God for worship and obedience. Then he directs you to observe the right of one like you, showing that whoever is not fit for the companionship of a person like himself, how can he fulfil the right of the One to Whom nothing is like? If upbringing, which includes the rights of the two parents, necessitates the greatness of this right, then what is the right of the upbringing your Master gave you? How do you render thanks for it? Then he mentioned the general mercy toward the kinsfolk, the orphans and the needy, and that one should speak kindly to people. The reality of servanthood is sincerity with the Truth and gentleness with creation. End of quotation, and some of it is abridged.

Some of the people of allusive interpretation (ahl al-ishārāt) said: The means by which one draws near to God, exalted is He, are: belief, speech, action and intention. By His saying: "You shall worship none but God," He alerted to the station of tawhid and to the belief in what is due to Him from His servants of acts of obedience and submission, singling Him out alone for this. Then (came) purely financial worship, which is zakat (almsgiving); purely bodily worship, which is prayer (ṣalāt); and worship that is both bodily and financial, which is kindness to the two parents and benevolence toward the orphan and the needy.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 84–86 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And when We took your covenant: "You shall not shed your blood"﴾: The discussion of ﴿tasfikūna﴾ is like the discussion of ﴿lā taʿbudūna illā Allāh﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83] in terms of its i'rab (grammatical analysis). The majority recited it with a fatha on the ta', sukun on the sin, and a kasra on the fa'. Talha ibn Musarrif and Shu'ayb ibn Abi Hamza recited it likewise, except that they put a damma on the fa'. Abu Nahik and Abu Mijlaz recited it with a damma on the ta', a fatha on the sin, and a kasra on the shaddated fa'. Ibn Abi Ishaq recited it likewise, except that he made the sin sakin and lightened the fa'. The apparent meaning of ﴿You shall not shed your blood﴾ is: do not do this to yourselves due to the severe hardship that afflicts you and the rage that overtakes you. There has come in a hadith the story of the man who placed the blade of his sword in the ground with its point between his breasts, then leaned on it and killed himself, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) informed that he is among the people of the Fire. And it is authentically reported: "Whoever kills himself with an iron implement, his implement will be in his hand, stabbing himself in his belly in the Fire of Hell, abiding therein forever and ever." The religious communities have concurred on the prohibition of taking a human life. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 29]. It has been said that its meaning is: do not shed the blood of people, for whoever sheds their blood, their blood will be shed. One said:

"We gave them a cup, and they gave us its like in return, but they were more patient in the face of death."

It has been said: its meaning is: do not kill yourselves by committing what necessitates that, such as apostasy, adultery after being married, waging war, killing a soul without right, and the like of what removes the sanctity of blood. It has been said: its meaning is: let not some of you shed the blood of others, and to this he alluded with his saying: "Do not revert after me to disbelief, striking one another's necks." The people of one religion were like a single soul, as said by Qatada, and al-Zamakhshari chose it. Ibn 'Atiyya said: Allah took a covenant from the Children of Israel in the Torah that none of them should kill another, nor expel him, nor enslave him, nor allow him to be enslaved, along with other acts of obedience. The address in "We took your covenant" is to the scholars of the Jews who were in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or with their forefathers.

﴿And do not expel yourselves from your homes﴾: its meaning is: let not some of you expel others, or: do not mistreat the neighbour who is your neighbour so that you force them to leave their homes, or: do not do what would expel you from Paradise, which is your home, or: do not expel yourselves, that is, your brothers, because you are like a single soul, or: do not cause corruption which would be the cause of your expulsion from your homes, as if it alludes to the exile of the offender, or: do not cause corruption and oppose the prophets and the believers, so that exile is prescribed for you. These are six opinions. Then ﴿you acknowledged﴾: that is, to the covenant, and admitted its obligation, or you acknowledged its acceptance, or you were content with it, as al-Bu'ayth said:

"I am not a Kulaybī, when he is branded with a disgrace, who acquiesces like a wife acquiescing to her husband."

﴿And you bear witness﴾: that is, you know that Allah took it from you. He meant upon the early Children of Israel, if the address is directed at them; and if it is directed at his contemporaries (ﷺ) among their descendants, its meaning is: "And you bear witness against your forefathers to what Allah took from them of covenant," either through mutawatir transmission or through what you recite from the Torah. If the meaning of witnessing is presence, then the address must be to their forefathers. Some exegetes said: "Then you acknowledged" refers to the later generation, and "and you bear witness" refers to the earlier generation, because they witnessed the shedding of one another's blood. And it was said: "and you bear witness" because the earlier and later ones became like one thing, therefore the address of presence was applied to them. It has also been said: his saying "and you bear witness" is for emphasis, like your saying: "So-and-so admits against himself to such-and-such, bearing witness against it."

﴿Then you are these, killing yourselves﴾: this is an expression of astonishment at what He informed about them of killing, expulsion and transgression, after the taking of the covenant from them, and their acknowledgement and testimony. The grammarians differed on the i'rab of this clause. The preferred view is that ﴿antum﴾ is the subject, ﴿hā'ulā'﴾ is the predicate, and ﴿taqtulūna﴾ is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause). The Arabs have said: "Here you are standing (hā anta dhā qā'iman)," and "Here I am standing (hā ana dhā qā'iman)," and also: "This is me standing (hadhā anā qā'iman)," and "Here he is standing (hā huwa dhā qā'iman)." The demonstrative is applied to the pronoun in wording, as if he said: "You are the present one, I am the present one, he is the present one." The intended meaning is the informing of the state. What indicates that the clause is a ḥāl is that the singular noun comes in the accusative as a ḥāl, in accordance with what we have said, in their saying: "hā anta dhā qā'iman" and the like. Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is: "Then you, after that, are these witnesses," meaning that you are other people, not those who acknowledged, treating the change of attribute as the change of essence, as you say: "I returned by other than the way I went out." His saying "taqtulūna" is an explanation of "Then you are these." End of his words. The apparent view is that what is indicated by "Then you are these" are the ones originally addressed, so they are not other people. Do you not see that this estimation which al-Zamakhshari made of treating the change of attribute as the change of essence cannot be realised in the like of "hā anā dhā qā'iman" nor in "hā antum ulā'"? Rather, the addressee is the one indicated, without change.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: Al-Ustadh al-Ajall Abu al-Hasan ibn Ahmad, our shaykh, said: "Hā'ulā'" is raised as the subject, "antum" is the fronted predicate, and "taqtulūna" is a ḥāl; with it the meaning is complete, and it was the intended part, so it is not dispensable, and it came only after the sentence had been completed in its predicate and its subject, as you say: "This is Zayd, departing," while you intended to inform of his departure, not of the fact that this is Zayd. End of what Ibn 'Atiyya transmitted from his shaykh, who is Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn Ahmad ibn Khalaf al-Ansari, from the people of our town Granada, known as Ibn al-Bādhish, and he is the father of the Imam Abu Ja'far Ahmad, author of the book al-Iqna' in the readings, and he has preferences in grammar. He transmitted Sibawayh's book from the Vizier Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Hisham al-Mus-hafi, and he commented on it in grammar on the book al-Jumal and al-Idah and some issues from Sibawayh's book. He died in the year 528 AH. I do not know what the reason is for deviating from making "antum" the subject and "hā'ulā'" the predicate to the reverse of this. The governing element of this ḥāl is the demonstrative with what is in it of the meaning of the verb. They said: it is a ḥāl from it, so the ṣāḥib al-ḥāl and its governing element would then be one. We have discussed this issue in our book Manhaj al-Sālik, which is our composition, so consult it there. Some grammarians held that "hā'ulā'" is a vocative with the particle of address omitted, and this is not permitted according to the Basrians, because a demonstrative may not have the vocative particle omitted from it; its permissibility is reported from al-Farra', and al-Zajjaj and others interpreted the verse according to it, inclining to the view of al-Farra', so according to this view "taqtulūna" is a predicate about "antum." The separation between subject and predicate is by the vocative, and separation by the vocative is permitted. Those who took this view in this verse did so because it was difficult for them that a sentence consisting of subject and predicate could be formed from the addressee pronoun and a demonstrative. We have explained how this sentence is formed. Verses have been cited in which the vocative particle is omitted with the demonstrative, among them the saying of a man of Tayy:

"Indeed the first ones described my people to them, so by them, hadha i'tasim, you will meet whoever opposes you humiliated."

Ibn Kaysan and others held that "antum" is the subject, "yaqtulūna" is the predicate, and "hā'ulā'" is a specification of the addressees, when they were alerted to the state they were persisting in; so in that case it is accusative by "a'nī." The grammarians have stated that specification does not occur with indefinite nouns or demonstratives. What is established from Arabic usage is that it comes as "ayyuhā" (e.g., "O Allah, forgive us, O band"), or definite with "al-" (e.g., "we Arabs are the most generous of people toward guests"), or with an annexation (e.g., "we, the company of the prophets, are not inherited from"), and it may be a proper name, as they recited:

"By us Tamim, the haze is cleared."

End. It most often comes after a first-person pronoun, as we have illustrated. It has also come after a second-person pronoun, as in their saying: "By you, Allah, we hope for grace." Some held that "hā'ulā'" is a relative pronoun meaning "alladhī," and it is the predicate about "antum," and "taqtulūna" is its relative clause; this is not permitted according to the Basrians, while the Kufans permitted it, and it is a disputed question mentioned in the science of grammar. The majority recited "taqtulūna" from qatala, lightened. Al-Hasan recited "tuqattilūna" from qattala, shaddated. This is so in some tafsirs; in the tafsir of al-Mahdawi it is said that it is the reading of Abu Nahik, and he said that al-Zuhri and al-Hasan recited "tuqattilūna anbiyā'a Allāh," from qattala, meaning shaddated. Allah knows best the correctness of that.

﴿And you expel a party of you from their homes﴾: this was revealed concerning the Banu Qaynuqa', the Banu Qurayza and al-Nadir among the Jews. The Banu Qaynuqa' were enemies of Qurayza and al-Nadir; the Aws and the Khazraj were brothers, and al-Nadir and Qurayza were also brothers, then they separated. So al-Nadir became allies of the Khazraj, and Qurayza allies of the Aws. They would fight one another, then the war would cease, and they would ransom their captives. Allah reproached them for this, as al-Mahdawi said. Al-Zamakhshari said: Each party would fight with its allies, and when they prevailed, they would ruin their homes and expel them; and when a man from either party was captured, they would gather to ransom him. The Arabs reproached them and said: "How do you fight them and then ransom them?" They would say: "We have been commanded to ransom them, and fighting them has been forbidden to us, but we are ashamed that our allies be humiliated."

﴿Supporting one another against them in sin﴾: ʿAsim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read with a lightened ẓā', and its origin is "tatazāhirūna," so the ta' was dropped; and it is, in our view, the second ta' and not the first, contrary to Hisham, who claimed that the one dropped is the one of the present tense, which in such a case indicates address. Much has come in the Qur'an of dropping the ta'. He said:

"You sneeze all together around your house, so every one of you, O sons of Hamdan, has a cold."

He means "tatatāsaṭūna" [i.e., tatatā'asūna]. The rest of the seven read with a shaddated ẓā', that is, by assimilating the ẓā' into the ta'. Abu Haywa recited "tuzāhirūna," with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the ha'. Mujahid and Qatada, with variation from them, recited "tazzahharūna," with a fatha on the ta', ẓā' and ha', all shaddated, without an alif; and it is narrated from Abu 'Amr. Some recited "tatazāhirūna" according to the origin. These are five readings, and their meanings are all cooperation and support. Abu al-'Aliya narrated that he said: When the Children of Israel oppressed a people, they would expel them from their homes. "Against them in sin": there are two views concerning it. One: it is the act for which its doer deserves blame and reproach. The second: it is what the soul recoils from and the heart is not at ease with. In the hadith of al-Nawwas: "Sin is what troubles your breast." It has been said: the meaning is "supporting one another against them in what necessitates sin," and this is the mention of the cause for its effect; that is why wine is called sin, as one said:

"I drank sin until my reason strayed."

(And transgression) is exceeding the limit in wrongdoing.

﴿And if they come to you as captives﴾: the reading of the majority is on the pattern fu'ālā, and of Hamza on the pattern fa'lā.

﴿تُفادُوهُمْ﴾ (ʾtufādūhum): Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim and al-Kisāʾī read it from fādā. The rest read it from fadā.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: The good wording of "ʾitāʾ" (coming/bringing), in that it stands opposite "ʾikhrāj" (expulsion), makes the contrast apparent, which denounces their action in the expulsion. That is, it is not fitting that you should treat well with ransom those whom you have wronged by expelling them from their homes. The meaning of ﴿تُفادُوهم﴾ (tufādūhum) is "tafdūhum" (you ransom them), since the form "mufāʿala" (the pattern fāʿala) occurs with two parties and with one. So fāʿala here has the meaning of the bare form faʿala, which is one of its meanings. It was also said: the meaning of "fādā" is "bādala" (to exchange) a captive for a captive, and the meaning of "fadā" is "dafaʿa al-fidāʾ" (to pay the ransom). The first is supported by the words of al-ʿAbbās: "I ransomed myself and I ransomed ʿAqīl." It is known that he did not exchange one captive for another. It was also said: the meaning is "tafdūhum" (you ransom them) by peace, and "tufādūhum" (you exchange them) by violence. It was also said: "tufādūhum" means that you seek the ransom from the captive who is in your hands from your enemies. From this is his saying:

"Stay, O ransomer of your captive, for my people
and your people, I do not see them coming together."

"Tafdūhum" means you give their ransom. Abū ʿAlī said: the meaning of "tufādūhum" linguistically is that you release them after you take something from them. "Fādaytu nafsī" means I released myself after I paid something. Both "fādā" and "fadā" take two objects, the second with a preposition, and here that object is omitted.

﴿وهُوَ مُحَرَّمٌ عَلَيْكم إخْراجُهُمْ﴾ (wa-huwa muḥarramun ʿalaykum ʾikhrājuhum; "and it is forbidden for you, their expulsion"): Four things have preceded: killing the self, expulsion from the homes, backing one another (ẓāhara), and ransoming, and all of them are forbidden. This category was singled out for emphasis of the prohibition, even though all of them are forbidden, because expulsion from homes carries the disgrace of exile and banishment, whose harm does not end except with death. This is unlike killing, since killing, although in itself it is the destruction of the structure (of life), is greater, yet in it the evil comes to an end. Unlike ransoming them with it, for it arises from the crime of expulsion from homes and of backing one another, since had it not been for the expulsion from homes and the backing against them, they would not have fallen into the bonds of captivity. It may also be that, as in every sentence, the mention of the prohibition is omitted, and the sense is: "You kill your selves, and it is forbidden for you," and likewise the rest. The word ﴿هو﴾ (huwa, "it") is in the nominative as a subject (mubtadaʾ). It is either a pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), and the sentence after it is its predicate, and its analysis is that "ʾikhrājuhum" is the subject and "muḥarram" is the predicate, with a pronoun in it referring back to "ʾikhrāj," since the intended order is the delayed one. The Kufans do not permit fronting the predicate when it carries a raised pronoun. So they do not permit "qāʾimun Zaydun" (standing is Zayd) with "qāʾim" as a fronted predicate. Therefore they chose that it be the predicate of "huwa" is "muḥarramun," and "ʾikhrājuhum" is in the nominative as a passive subject (nāʾib al-fāʿil), and al-Mahdawī followed them in this. The Basrans do not permit this view, because according to them a pronoun of the matter may only be explained by a full sentence with both its parts stated. If you make "muḥarramun" a predicate of "huwa," and "ʾikhrājuhum" is raised by it, then the pronoun of the matter would have been explained by something other than a sentence, which is not permitted according to the Basrans as we have mentioned. They also permitted that "huwa" be a subject which is not a pronoun of the matter, but refers back to "ʾikhrāj," with "muḥarram" being its predicate, and "ʾikhrājuhum" an apposition (badal). On this there is disagreement. Some permitted that an unexpressed pronoun, for which nothing has preceded to which it refers, be explained by an apposition, and some forbade it. Al-Kisāʾī permitted it, and it is so in some reports. The Kufans permitted that "huwa" be a separator (ʿimād), which the Basrans call a "faṣl" (a separating pronoun), and this has already been mentioned along with the predicate. The sense is: "And their expulsion, it is forbidden for you," so when the predicate of the subject was fronted before the subject, the separator was fronted with it. Al-Farrāʾ said: "Because the conjunction 'wa' here requires a noun, and wherever it requires a noun, the separator is permitted." This analysis is not permitted according to the Basrans, because in it there are two things which they do not permit: first, the occurrence of a separator between a definite and an indefinite that is not close to the definite, since the sense is "and their expulsion, it is forbidden," and "muḥarram" is an indefinite not close to the definite. Second, that it involves fronting the separator, whose condition according to the Basrans is that it stand between the subject and the predicate, or between the two of which they were originally composed. All these are matters that are verified in the science of grammar (naḥw).

In Ibn ʿAṭiyya's book, at this point, there are statements that are open to criticism. He said: "It was said regarding 'huwa' that it is a pronoun of the matter, its sense being: 'and the matter is forbidden for you,' and 'ʾikhrājuhum' in this view is an apposition of 'huwa.'" End of what he transmitted on this view. This is an error from two aspects. First: he informed of a pronoun of the matter with a single noun, and no Basran or Kufan permits that. As for the Basran: because the explainer of a pronoun of the matter must necessarily be a sentence. As for the Kufan: because he permits a sentence, and he permits a single noun if it has combined with what follows it into a predication and a subject in meaning, as in your saying: "I thought him standing, Zayd and ʿAmr." Second: he made "ʾikhrājuhum" an apposition of a pronoun of the matter, but a pronoun of the matter is not conjoined to, nor is it replaced by an apposition, nor is it emphasised. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "It was said: it is a separator (fāṣila), and this is the view of the Kufan, but it is not here the one that is a separator (ʿimād), and 'muḥarram' according to this is the subject, and 'ʾikhrājuhum' is the predicate." End of what he transmitted on this view. What is transmitted from the Kufans is the reverse of this analysis, which is that the separator has been fronted with the predicate before the subject, so the analysis of "muḥarram" according to them is a fronted predicate, and "ʾikhrājuhum" is the subject. This is the one suitable to the rules, since one does not begin with an indefinite noun when there is no justification for it, and the predicate would be definite. Rather, the established usage in their language is the reverse of this, except that if it occurs in poetry, it is heard but not used as an analogy. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "It was said: it is the pronoun implied in 'muḥarram,' fronted and made explicit." End of what he transmitted on this view. This view is very weak, since there is no reason for fronting the pronoun, nor for its surfacing after being concealed, and because it leads to a passive participle (ismu al-mafʿūl) being empty of a pronoun, since according to this view "muḥarram" would be a fronted predicate and "ʾikhrājuhum" the subject, and no active or passive participle is found without a pronoun, except when it raises an explicit noun. Here it is not possible that it raise an explicit noun, because the detached fronted pronoun "huwa" was the pronoun raised by "muḥarram," and then this pronoun would remain of unknown analysis, since it is not permitted that it be the subject, nor that it be a fronted agent. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "It was said: it is the pronoun of the expulsion; its sense: 'and their expulsion is forbidden for you.'" End of what he transmitted on this view. He did not explain the nominative case of "ʾikhrājuhum," and it cannot be made to work with "huwa" being its pronoun, with "ʾikhrājuhum" as an explanation of that concealed pronoun, except by making "ʾikhrājuhum" an apposition of the pronoun. It has already been mentioned that there is disagreement on this, some permitting it and some forbidding it.

﴿أفَتُؤْمِنُونَ بِبَعْضِ الكِتابِ وتَكْفُرُونَ بِبَعْضٍ﴾ (ʾafa-tuʾminūna biʿḍi al-kitābi wa-takfurūna biʿḍin; "Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?"): This is an interrogative whose meaning is rebuke and denunciation. He did not blame them for the ransom, but for the inconsistency, since they performed part of what was obligatory and left out part. The inconsistency is more emphatic in censure. It may be said: expulsion is a sin, so why did He call it disbelief? We say: perhaps they declared that leaving off expulsion was not obligatory, even though the clear text of the Torah indicated its obligation. The part they believed in, if by "the Book" is meant the Torah, then it is general in what they believed of its rulings, and the ransoming of the captive is among them. The part they disbelieved in is the killing of some of them by others, the expulsion of some of them from their homes, and backing one another in sin and aggression, all of which is among what they disbelieved of the Torah. It was also said: the meaning is that they use part and abandon part; you ransom the captives of your own tribe and abandon the captives of the people of your religion, not ransoming them. It was also said: ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām passed by the head of the exilarch (Raʾs al-Jālūt, the leader of the Jewish community) in Kufa, while he was ransoming from among the women whoever had not been struck by war, and not ransoming whoever had been struck by war. He said: Ibn Salām said: "Surely it is written for you in your Book that you ransom all of them." Mujāhid said: its meaning is: if you find him in the hand of another, you ransom him, while you yourself kill him with your hand. It was also said: the purpose is to alert that they, in their adherence to the prophethood of Mūsā, peace be upon him and upon our Prophet, while denying Muḥammad ﷺ, though the proof in the matter of both is the same, have followed the course of their predecessors, in believing in part and disbelieving in part. They said: it is also permitted that "the Book" here mean what was prescribed for them of these four rulings, that is, what was obligated, and what they believed in of them is the ransoming of captives, and what they disbelieved in is the remaining four.

﴿فَما جَزاءُ مَن يَفْعَلُ ذَلِكَ مِنكم إلّا خِزْيٌ في الحَياةِ الدُّنْيا﴾ (fa-mā jazāʾu man yafʿalu dhālika minkum illā khizyun fī al-ḥayāti al-dunyā; "So what is the recompense of those among you who do that, except disgrace in the life of this world"): The word "jazāʾ" (recompense) is used for good and evil. He said: ﴿وجَزاهم بِما صَبَرُوا﴾ (wa-jazāhum bimā ṣabarū; "and He will recompense them for what they endured") [al-Insān: 12], and He said: ﴿فَجَزاؤُهُ جَهَنَّمُ﴾ (fa-jazāʾuhu jahannamu; "then his recompense is Hell") [al-Nisāʾ: 93]. "Khizy" here means disgrace, punishment, and retaliation against whoever is killed, or the imposition of the poll-tax (jizya) for all time, or the killing of the Qurayẓa, and the expulsion of the Naḍīr from their dwellings to Ariḥā (Jericho) and Adhriʿāt, or the victory of the enemy: five views. The view of the poll-tax and of exile is not feasible unless we take the verse as applying to those who were contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The better view is that the meaning is great censure and profound contempt, without restriction. "Illā khizyun" (except disgrace) is an exceptive construction with the exception omitted in full (istithnāʾ mufarragh), and it is the predicate of the subject. Breaking the negation here is a breaking of the working of "mā" (the negative particle), which is a matter of difference of opinion and detail. That is: when the predicate comes after and "illā" is placed upon it, it is either the first (the subject) or it takes its place, or it is an adjective, if it is the first in meaning, or takes its place. If it is the first, or takes its place, then only the nominative is permitted according to the majority. The Kufans permitted the accusative where the second is in place of the first. If it is an adjective, al-Farrāʾ permitted the accusative in it, and the Basrans forbade it. It is transmitted from Yūnus that he permitted the accusative in the predicate after "illā," "whatever it may be" (kāʾinan mā kāna). This contradicts what Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās transmitted; he said: "There is no disagreement among the grammarians about your saying: mā Zaydun illā akhūka (Zayd is nothing but your brother), that it is not permitted except with the nominative." He said: "If you say: mā anta illā liḥyatuka (you are nothing but your beard), the Basrans use the nominative, and the meaning according to them is: there is nothing in you but your beard," and likewise: mā anta illā ʿaynāka (you are nothing but your eyes). The Kufans permitted the accusative in this, and the Basrans do not permit the accusative except with verbal nouns (maṣādir), unless the meaning is known, so that one supposes a governing verb, such as: mā anta illā liḥyataka marratan wa-ʿaynaka ukhrā (you are nothing but your beard at one time and your eyes at another), and mā anta illā ʿimāmataka taḥsīnan wa-ridāʾaka tazyīnan (you are nothing but your turban for beautifying and your cloak for adorning).

﴿ويَوْمَ القِيامَةِ يُرَدُّونَ إلى أشَدِّ العَذابِ﴾ (wa-yawma al-qiyāmati yuraddūna ʾilā ashaddi al-ʿadhābi; "And on the Day of Resurrection they will be returned to the most severe punishment"): "The Day of Resurrection" is an expression for an extended time until judgment is made between the servants, and the people of Paradise enter Paradise and the people of the Fire enter the Fire. The meaning of "yuraddūna" (they will be returned) is "yaṣīrūna" (they will become), so it does not necessarily follow that they were in the most severe punishment before that. Or "radd" may mean returning to something they were in, as He said: ﴿فَرَدَدْناهُ إلى أُمِّهِ﴾ (fa-radadnāhu ʾilā ʾummihi; "So We returned him to his mother") [al-Qaṣaṣ: 13]. It is as if they were also in the most severe punishment in this world, since they were punished in this world by killing, captivity, exile, and various kinds of punishment. The majority read "yuraddūna" with the yāʾ (third person), which fits what precedes it, the saying: "man yafʿalu" (whoever does). It may be a shift (iltifāt) back to His saying ﴿أفَتُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ (ʾafa-tuʾminūna; "Do you believe"), so that it moves from the pronoun of address to the pronoun of absence. al-Ḥasan and Ibn Hurmuz, with a difference transmitted from them, read "turaddūna" with the tāʾ (second person), which fits His saying ﴿أفَتُؤْمِنُونَ﴾. It may be a shift in relation to His saying ﴿مَن يَفْعَلُ ذَلِكَ﴾, so that it moves from the pronoun of absence to the pronoun of address. "Ashaddu al-ʿadhābi" (the most severe punishment) is: abiding in the Fire, and its severity is because it has no end; or the kinds of punishment of Hell, since its levels are varied, and in it are valleys and serpents; or the punishment in which there is no joy nor spirit, with despair of escape; or the severity is in comparison with the punishment of this world; or the severity is in comparison with the punishment of their common people, since they are the ones who misled them and deceived them. Five views.

This is the final part of Abu Hayyan's commentary on verses 84–86 of Surah al-Baqarah.

﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾ [al-Baqarah: 74]: The discussion of the interpretation (tafsir) of this statement has already been given, since it occurred before ﴿Do you then hope...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 75]. Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr read it with the ya' (yaʿmalūna, "they do"), while the rest read it with the ta' from above (taʿmalūna, "you do"). With the ya', it corresponds to the reading of the majority for yuraddūna ("they are returned"). With the ta', it corresponds to the reading of turaddūna with the ta' ("you are returned"), so the addressees are those who were addressed in the verse. It has been said that the address may also be to the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ). It is related from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab that he said: "The Children of Israel have passed away, and you are the ones intended by this, O Ummah of Muhammad, and by what is similar to it." This verse is among the most admonishing of verses, since its meaning is that Allah is lying in wait for every disbeliever and sinner.

﴿Those are the ones who have bought the worldly life at the price of the Hereafter. So the punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be helped﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas said: It was revealed concerning the Jews, those whose mention preceded, who believed in part of the Book and disbelieved in part. The demonstrative noun ("those") is evidence that it refers to those who combined the previously mentioned blameworthy attributes. The discussion of this has already been given when discussing ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5], and that when a number of attributes are enumerated for a subject, the demonstrative is used to refer to that subject, as an alert that he is the one who combines those attributes. "Those who" (alladhīna) is the predicate of "those" (ulāʾika). The discussion of ﴿bought﴾ (ishtarawū) has already been given, and it was stated that buying and selling require a consideration and a thing exchanged, which are concrete. So the Arabs extended this usage to abstract meanings, and their preferring the splendour and adornment of this world over everlasting bliss was called "buying", as a preference of the transient and perishing over the enduring and lasting. For the buyer is not the one who prefers obtaining it, and the price paid for it is something he himself is averse to. None does this except one who is deceived in judgement and corrupt in intellect.

Some scholars of the meanings (ahl al-maʿānī) said: The "world" (dunyā) is that which is near to the desires of the heart, and the "Hereafter" (ākhira) is that which is connected to the pleasure of the Lord. ﴿So it will not be lightened﴾ (fa-lā yukhaffafu) is conjoined to the relative clause (ṣila). It is permissible for a relative pronoun to be connected to two relative clauses differing in time, as you say: "The one who killed Zayd yesterday came to me, and will kill his brother tomorrow." For the relative clauses are sentences, and whoever stipulates the unity of the time of their verbs, in contrast to what functions as individual words, they have explicitly stipulated the unity of tense, whether past or otherwise, and the preference for agreement in form.

It is also permissible that "those" (ulāʾika) is the subject (mubtadaʾ) and "who" (alladhīna) with its relative clause is the predicate (khabar). "So it will not be lightened" (fa-lā yukhaffafu) is a predicate following a predicate. The insertion of the fa' (so) is explained by the fact that "who", when its relative clause is a verb, carries the meaning of a conditional. This is an error, because here the relative pronoun is parsed by him as a predicate of "those", so the statement "so it will not be lightened" is not a predicate of the relative pronoun; rather, it is a predicate of "those", and the conditional quality does not transfer to the subject from the relative pronoun which serves as its predicate.

It is also permissible that "those" (ulāʾika) is the subject, "who" (alladhīna) is a second subject, and "so it will not be lightened" (fa-lā yukhaffafu) is the predicate of "who". The "who" with its predicate is a predicate of "those". It was said: A resumptive pronoun (ʿāʾid) was not needed, because "those who" are "those", just as you say: "This is Zayd, departing." This is an error, because every sentence that serves as a predicate of a subject must contain a connective (rābiṭ), unless it is itself the subject in meaning, in which case that connective is not needed. You have predicated "those" by means of the relative subject and its predicate, so a connective is necessary. This is not similar to the example he gave, "This is Zayd, departing", because "Zayd departing" are two predicates of "this", and they are two single words, or "Zayd" is an apposition (badal) of "this" and "departing" is the predicate. Or "this" is the subject, "Zayd" is a second subject, "departing" is the predicate of "Zayd", and "Zayd departing" is a sentence in the position of the predicate of "this", which is not permissible for lack of a connective. Furthermore, if there were a connective here, this parsing would not be valid, because "who" is restricted by the pointing to it, so it does not resemble a conditional noun, since its generality disappears through its specification. And because the relative clause of "who" is past in both wording and meaning. With these two points, it is not permissible to insert the fa' into the sentence functioning as a predicate.

Lightening (takhfīf) is facilitation (tasḥīl). The negation of lightening has been interpreted as the cessation of it, and it has also been interpreted as intensification. The preferable interpretation is that it negates lightening by cessation, or by reduction of it, or at a particular time, or at all times, since it is a negation of the essence, which necessarily entails the negation of its individual instances and forms. The apparent meaning of negation with "lā" and its common usage in it is that it negates in the future. Al-Zamakhsharī interpreted the negation of lightening as applying to this world and the Hereafter: in this world by reducing the poll-tax (jizya), and likewise the negation of help in this world and the Hereafter. The meaning of the negation of help is that they will not find anyone to repel from them what has befallen them of the punishment of Allah.

﴿Nor will they be helped﴾ (wa-lā hum yunṣarūn): a nominal sentence conjoined to a verbal sentence. It is also permissible for it to be verbal, and the matter to be one of ishtighāl (the verb being occupied with an object pronoun), so that "they" (hum) is in the nominative by a verb omitted which is explained by what follows it, in accordance with the statement of the poet:

"And if he does not bear its injustice upon himself..."

This reading is strengthened and made better by the fact that the statement "so it will not be lightened" preceded it, and it is a verbal sentence. For if the verbal sentence had not preceded, the preferable reading would have been the nominative by inception (ibtidāʾ). That is because "lā" (not) is not one of the particles that demand a verb, neither exclusively nor preferentially, so that it is like "kāna" (was) and the interrogative hamza, unlike Abu Muhammad ibn al-Sayyid, who claimed that placing the verb on the object in what the particle precedes is no better than inception, and that the passive voice is preferable to the active because it is more general, unless the agent is made general, in which case it would be: "nor will anyone help them", and that would forfeit the closing of the verse-endings with what they were closed with before and after, and would forfeit the conciseness, even though the statement "nor will they be helped" conveys that, namely generality.

These noble verses have contained Allah's reports: that He took the covenant from the Children of Israel to worship Allah alone, to do good to the two parents, to kinsmen, orphans and the needy, to speak good to people, to establish prayer and give zakat. And that they broke the covenant by their turning away and aversion. And that He took from them that they would not shed their blood, nor expel themselves from their homes, and that they acknowledged and committed to that. So the first covenant contained commands, and the second covenant contained prohibitions, since divine obligations are built upon commands and prohibitions. The beginning with commands was more emphatic, because they contain actions, while prohibitions contain abstentions, and actions are more burdensome than abstentions.
