Among the commands was the command to worship Allah alone, which is the head of faith, since its object is the most noble of objects, so beginning with it was preferable. Then He reproached them for being entangled with what they were forbidden, though His report had already preceded that they had disobeyed in the command, by His saying: ﴿Then you turned away﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83]. For committing what is forbidden is more ugly than abandoning what is commanded, since those are abstentions, as we have mentioned.

Then He rebuked them for opposing Allah's prohibitions, and that they seek help in that from other than the truth, but rather from sin and aggression. Then He mentioned the contradiction of their opinions and the foolishness of their intellects, in ransoming those among them who came to them as captives, although they themselves were the cause of their expulsion and captivity, while knowing that their expulsion was forbidden. And by mentioning that they believed in part of the Book and disbelieved in part. This is despite the fact that all of it is truth and sincerity, so disbelieving in part and believing in part is not fitting for that. Then He mentioned that the recompense for the doer of that is humiliation in this world and the severest punishment in the Hereafter, and that Allah, exalted is He, is not unaware of what they did, so He will requite them for that. Then He indicated those who adorned themselves with these blameworthy attributes and opposed Allah's command and prohibition: they have bought the immediate, trivial, at the price of the lasting, great, and preferred the transient, troubled over the enduring, pure. The result of this buying is that the punishment that has befallen them will not be lightened for them, and they will not find a helper to repel from them the evil of the punishment. They have indeed lost the transaction, and in exchange for everlasting bliss they have been given a fire whose fuel is people and stones. And if lightening has been negated, then elevation (of the punishment) is more fitting. Is this not from the category of alerting to the higher by means of the lower?

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 84–86 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And when We took your covenant: "You shall not shed your blood"﴾: The discussion of ﴿tasfikūna﴾ is like the discussion of ﴿lā taʿbudūna illā Allāh﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83] in terms of its i'rab (grammatical analysis). The majority recited it with a fatha on the ta', sukun on the sin, and a kasra on the fa'. Talha ibn Musarrif and Shu'ayb ibn Abi Hamza recited it likewise, except that they put a damma on the fa'. Abu Nahik and Abu Mijlaz recited it with a damma on the ta', a fatha on the sin, and a kasra on the shaddated fa'. Ibn Abi Ishaq recited it likewise, except that he made the sin sakin and lightened the fa'. The apparent meaning of ﴿You shall not shed your blood﴾ is: do not do this to yourselves due to the severe hardship that afflicts you and the rage that overtakes you. There has come in a hadith the story of the man who placed the blade of his sword in the ground with its point between his breasts, then leaned on it and killed himself, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) informed that he is among the people of the Fire. And it is authentically reported: "Whoever kills himself with an iron implement, his implement will be in his hand, stabbing himself in his belly in the Fire of Hell, abiding therein forever and ever." The religious communities have concurred on the prohibition of taking a human life. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 29]. It has been said that its meaning is: do not shed the blood of people, for whoever sheds their blood, their blood will be shed. One said:

"We gave them a cup, and they gave us its like in return, but they were more patient in the face of death."

It has been said: its meaning is: do not kill yourselves by committing what necessitates that, such as apostasy, adultery after being married, waging war, killing a soul without right, and the like of what removes the sanctity of blood. It has been said: its meaning is: let not some of you shed the blood of others, and to this he alluded with his saying: "Do not revert after me to disbelief, striking one another's necks." The people of one religion were like a single soul, as said by Qatada, and al-Zamakhshari chose it. Ibn 'Atiyya said: Allah took a covenant from the Children of Israel in the Torah that none of them should kill another, nor expel him, nor enslave him, nor allow him to be enslaved, along with other acts of obedience. The address in "We took your covenant" is to the scholars of the Jews who were in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or with their forefathers.

﴿And do not expel yourselves from your homes﴾: its meaning is: let not some of you expel others, or: do not mistreat the neighbour who is your neighbour so that you force them to leave their homes, or: do not do what would expel you from Paradise, which is your home, or: do not expel yourselves, that is, your brothers, because you are like a single soul, or: do not cause corruption which would be the cause of your expulsion from your homes, as if it alludes to the exile of the offender, or: do not cause corruption and oppose the prophets and the believers, so that exile is prescribed for you. These are six opinions. Then ﴿you acknowledged﴾: that is, to the covenant, and admitted its obligation, or you acknowledged its acceptance, or you were content with it, as al-Bu'ayth said:

"I am not a Kulaybī, when he is branded with a disgrace, who acquiesces like a wife acquiescing to her husband."

﴿And you bear witness﴾: that is, you know that Allah took it from you. He meant upon the early Children of Israel, if the address is directed at them; and if it is directed at his contemporaries (ﷺ) among their descendants, its meaning is: "And you bear witness against your forefathers to what Allah took from them of covenant," either through mutawatir transmission or through what you recite from the Torah. If the meaning of witnessing is presence, then the address must be to their forefathers. Some exegetes said: "Then you acknowledged" refers to the later generation, and "and you bear witness" refers to the earlier generation, because they witnessed the shedding of one another's blood. And it was said: "and you bear witness" because the earlier and later ones became like one thing, therefore the address of presence was applied to them. It has also been said: his saying "and you bear witness" is for emphasis, like your saying: "So-and-so admits against himself to such-and-such, bearing witness against it."

﴿Then you are these, killing yourselves﴾: this is an expression of astonishment at what He informed about them of killing, expulsion and transgression, after the taking of the covenant from them, and their acknowledgement and testimony. The grammarians differed on the i'rab of this clause. The preferred view is that ﴿antum﴾ is the subject, ﴿hā'ulā'﴾ is the predicate, and ﴿taqtulūna﴾ is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause). The Arabs have said: "Here you are standing (hā anta dhā qā'iman)," and "Here I am standing (hā ana dhā qā'iman)," and also: "This is me standing (hadhā anā qā'iman)," and "Here he is standing (hā huwa dhā qā'iman)." The demonstrative is applied to the pronoun in wording, as if he said: "You are the present one, I am the present one, he is the present one." The intended meaning is the informing of the state. What indicates that the clause is a ḥāl is that the singular noun comes in the accusative as a ḥāl, in accordance with what we have said, in their saying: "hā anta dhā qā'iman" and the like. Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is: "Then you, after that, are these witnesses," meaning that you are other people, not those who acknowledged, treating the change of attribute as the change of essence, as you say: "I returned by other than the way I went out." His saying "taqtulūna" is an explanation of "Then you are these." End of his words. The apparent view is that what is indicated by "Then you are these" are the ones originally addressed, so they are not other people. Do you not see that this estimation which al-Zamakhshari made of treating the change of attribute as the change of essence cannot be realised in the like of "hā anā dhā qā'iman" nor in "hā antum ulā'"? Rather, the addressee is the one indicated, without change.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: Al-Ustadh al-Ajall Abu al-Hasan ibn Ahmad, our shaykh, said: "Hā'ulā'" is raised as the subject, "antum" is the fronted predicate, and "taqtulūna" is a ḥāl; with it the meaning is complete, and it was the intended part, so it is not dispensable, and it came only after the sentence had been completed in its predicate and its subject, as you say: "This is Zayd, departing," while you intended to inform of his departure, not of the fact that this is Zayd. End of what Ibn 'Atiyya transmitted from his shaykh, who is Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn Ahmad ibn Khalaf al-Ansari, from the people of our town Granada, known as Ibn al-Bādhish, and he is the father of the Imam Abu Ja'far Ahmad, author of the book al-Iqna' in the readings, and he has preferences in grammar. He transmitted Sibawayh's book from the Vizier Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Hisham al-Mus-hafi, and he commented on it in grammar on the book al-Jumal and al-Idah and some issues from Sibawayh's book. He died in the year 528 AH. I do not know what the reason is for deviating from making "antum" the subject and "hā'ulā'" the predicate to the reverse of this. The governing element of this ḥāl is the demonstrative with what is in it of the meaning of the verb. They said: it is a ḥāl from it, so the ṣāḥib al-ḥāl and its governing element would then be one. We have discussed this issue in our book Manhaj al-Sālik, which is our composition, so consult it there. Some grammarians held that "hā'ulā'" is a vocative with the particle of address omitted, and this is not permitted according to the Basrians, because a demonstrative may not have the vocative particle omitted from it; its permissibility is reported from al-Farra', and al-Zajjaj and others interpreted the verse according to it, inclining to the view of al-Farra', so according to this view "taqtulūna" is a predicate about "antum." The separation between subject and predicate is by the vocative, and separation by the vocative is permitted. Those who took this view in this verse did so because it was difficult for them that a sentence consisting of subject and predicate could be formed from the addressee pronoun and a demonstrative. We have explained how this sentence is formed. Verses have been cited in which the vocative particle is omitted with the demonstrative, among them the saying of a man of Tayy:

"Indeed the first ones described my people to them, so by them, hadha i'tasim, you will meet whoever opposes you humiliated."

Ibn Kaysan and others held that "antum" is the subject, "yaqtulūna" is the predicate, and "hā'ulā'" is a specification of the addressees, when they were alerted to the state they were persisting in; so in that case it is accusative by "a'nī." The grammarians have stated that specification does not occur with indefinite nouns or demonstratives. What is established from Arabic usage is that it comes as "ayyuhā" (e.g., "O Allah, forgive us, O band"), or definite with "al-" (e.g., "we Arabs are the most generous of people toward guests"), or with an annexation (e.g., "we, the company of the prophets, are not inherited from"), and it may be a proper name, as they recited:

"By us Tamim, the haze is cleared."

End. It most often comes after a first-person pronoun, as we have illustrated. It has also come after a second-person pronoun, as in their saying: "By you, Allah, we hope for grace." Some held that "hā'ulā'" is a relative pronoun meaning "alladhī," and it is the predicate about "antum," and "taqtulūna" is its relative clause; this is not permitted according to the Basrians, while the Kufans permitted it, and it is a disputed question mentioned in the science of grammar. The majority recited "taqtulūna" from qatala, lightened. Al-Hasan recited "tuqattilūna" from qattala, shaddated. This is so in some tafsirs; in the tafsir of al-Mahdawi it is said that it is the reading of Abu Nahik, and he said that al-Zuhri and al-Hasan recited "tuqattilūna anbiyā'a Allāh," from qattala, meaning shaddated. Allah knows best the correctness of that.

﴿And you expel a party of you from their homes﴾: this was revealed concerning the Banu Qaynuqa', the Banu Qurayza and al-Nadir among the Jews. The Banu Qaynuqa' were enemies of Qurayza and al-Nadir; the Aws and the Khazraj were brothers, and al-Nadir and Qurayza were also brothers, then they separated. So al-Nadir became allies of the Khazraj, and Qurayza allies of the Aws. They would fight one another, then the war would cease, and they would ransom their captives. Allah reproached them for this, as al-Mahdawi said. Al-Zamakhshari said: Each party would fight with its allies, and when they prevailed, they would ruin their homes and expel them; and when a man from either party was captured, they would gather to ransom him. The Arabs reproached them and said: "How do you fight them and then ransom them?" They would say: "We have been commanded to ransom them, and fighting them has been forbidden to us, but we are ashamed that our allies be humiliated."

﴿Supporting one another against them in sin﴾: ʿAsim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read with a lightened ẓā', and its origin is "tatazāhirūna," so the ta' was dropped; and it is, in our view, the second ta' and not the first, contrary to Hisham, who claimed that the one dropped is the one of the present tense, which in such a case indicates address. Much has come in the Qur'an of dropping the ta'. He said:

"You sneeze all together around your house, so every one of you, O sons of Hamdan, has a cold."

He means "tatatāsaṭūna" [i.e., tatatā'asūna]. The rest of the seven read with a shaddated ẓā', that is, by assimilating the ẓā' into the ta'. Abu Haywa recited "tuzāhirūna," with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the ha'. Mujahid and Qatada, with variation from them, recited "tazzahharūna," with a fatha on the ta', ẓā' and ha', all shaddated, without an alif; and it is narrated from Abu 'Amr. Some recited "tatazāhirūna" according to the origin. These are five readings, and their meanings are all cooperation and support. Abu al-'Aliya narrated that he said: When the Children of Israel oppressed a people, they would expel them from their homes. "Against them in sin": there are two views concerning it. One: it is the act for which its doer deserves blame and reproach. The second: it is what the soul recoils from and the heart is not at ease with. In the hadith of al-Nawwas: "Sin is what troubles your breast." It has been said: the meaning is "supporting one another against them in what necessitates sin," and this is the mention of the cause for its effect; that is why wine is called sin, as one said:

"I drank sin until my reason strayed."

(And transgression) is exceeding the limit in wrongdoing.

﴿And if they come to you as captives﴾: the reading of the majority is on the pattern fu'ālā, and of Hamza on the pattern fa'lā.

﴿تُفادُوهُمْ﴾ (ʾtufādūhum): Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim and al-Kisāʾī read it from fādā. The rest read it from fadā.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: The good wording of "ʾitāʾ" (coming/bringing), in that it stands opposite "ʾikhrāj" (expulsion), makes the contrast apparent, which denounces their action in the expulsion. That is, it is not fitting that you should treat well with ransom those whom you have wronged by expelling them from their homes. The meaning of ﴿تُفادُوهم﴾ (tufādūhum) is "tafdūhum" (you ransom them), since the form "mufāʿala" (the pattern fāʿala) occurs with two parties and with one. So fāʿala here has the meaning of the bare form faʿala, which is one of its meanings. It was also said: the meaning of "fādā" is "bādala" (to exchange) a captive for a captive, and the meaning of "fadā" is "dafaʿa al-fidāʾ" (to pay the ransom). The first is supported by the words of al-ʿAbbās: "I ransomed myself and I ransomed ʿAqīl." It is known that he did not exchange one captive for another. It was also said: the meaning is "tafdūhum" (you ransom them) by peace, and "tufādūhum" (you exchange them) by violence. It was also said: "tufādūhum" means that you seek the ransom from the captive who is in your hands from your enemies. From this is his saying:

"Stay, O ransomer of your captive, for my people
and your people, I do not see them coming together."

"Tafdūhum" means you give their ransom. Abū ʿAlī said: the meaning of "tufādūhum" linguistically is that you release them after you take something from them. "Fādaytu nafsī" means I released myself after I paid something. Both "fādā" and "fadā" take two objects, the second with a preposition, and here that object is omitted.

﴿وهُوَ مُحَرَّمٌ عَلَيْكم إخْراجُهُمْ﴾ (wa-huwa muḥarramun ʿalaykum ʾikhrājuhum; "and it is forbidden for you, their expulsion"): Four things have preceded: killing the self, expulsion from the homes, backing one another (ẓāhara), and ransoming, and all of them are forbidden. This category was singled out for emphasis of the prohibition, even though all of them are forbidden, because expulsion from homes carries the disgrace of exile and banishment, whose harm does not end except with death. This is unlike killing, since killing, although in itself it is the destruction of the structure (of life), is greater, yet in it the evil comes to an end. Unlike ransoming them with it, for it arises from the crime of expulsion from homes and of backing one another, since had it not been for the expulsion from homes and the backing against them, they would not have fallen into the bonds of captivity. It may also be that, as in every sentence, the mention of the prohibition is omitted, and the sense is: "You kill your selves, and it is forbidden for you," and likewise the rest. The word ﴿هو﴾ (huwa, "it") is in the nominative as a subject (mubtadaʾ). It is either a pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), and the sentence after it is its predicate, and its analysis is that "ʾikhrājuhum" is the subject and "muḥarram" is the predicate, with a pronoun in it referring back to "ʾikhrāj," since the intended order is the delayed one. The Kufans do not permit fronting the predicate when it carries a raised pronoun. So they do not permit "qāʾimun Zaydun" (standing is Zayd) with "qāʾim" as a fronted predicate. Therefore they chose that it be the predicate of "huwa" is "muḥarramun," and "ʾikhrājuhum" is in the nominative as a passive subject (nāʾib al-fāʿil), and al-Mahdawī followed them in this. The Basrans do not permit this view, because according to them a pronoun of the matter may only be explained by a full sentence with both its parts stated. If you make "muḥarramun" a predicate of "huwa," and "ʾikhrājuhum" is raised by it, then the pronoun of the matter would have been explained by something other than a sentence, which is not permitted according to the Basrans as we have mentioned. They also permitted that "huwa" be a subject which is not a pronoun of the matter, but refers back to "ʾikhrāj," with "muḥarram" being its predicate, and "ʾikhrājuhum" an apposition (badal). On this there is disagreement. Some permitted that an unexpressed pronoun, for which nothing has preceded to which it refers, be explained by an apposition, and some forbade it. Al-Kisāʾī permitted it, and it is so in some reports. The Kufans permitted that "huwa" be a separator (ʿimād), which the Basrans call a "faṣl" (a separating pronoun), and this has already been mentioned along with the predicate. The sense is: "And their expulsion, it is forbidden for you," so when the predicate of the subject was fronted before the subject, the separator was fronted with it. Al-Farrāʾ said: "Because the conjunction 'wa' here requires a noun, and wherever it requires a noun, the separator is permitted." This analysis is not permitted according to the Basrans, because in it there are two things which they do not permit: first, the occurrence of a separator between a definite and an indefinite that is not close to the definite, since the sense is "and their expulsion, it is forbidden," and "muḥarram" is an indefinite not close to the definite. Second, that it involves fronting the separator, whose condition according to the Basrans is that it stand between the subject and the predicate, or between the two of which they were originally composed. All these are matters that are verified in the science of grammar (naḥw).

In Ibn ʿAṭiyya's book, at this point, there are statements that are open to criticism. He said: "It was said regarding 'huwa' that it is a pronoun of the matter, its sense being: 'and the matter is forbidden for you,' and 'ʾikhrājuhum' in this view is an apposition of 'huwa.'" End of what he transmitted on this view. This is an error from two aspects. First: he informed of a pronoun of the matter with a single noun, and no Basran or Kufan permits that. As for the Basran: because the explainer of a pronoun of the matter must necessarily be a sentence. As for the Kufan: because he permits a sentence, and he permits a single noun if it has combined with what follows it into a predication and a subject in meaning, as in your saying: "I thought him standing, Zayd and ʿAmr." Second: he made "ʾikhrājuhum" an apposition of a pronoun of the matter, but a pronoun of the matter is not conjoined to, nor is it replaced by an apposition, nor is it emphasised. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "It was said: it is a separator (fāṣila), and this is the view of the Kufan, but it is not here the one that is a separator (ʿimād), and 'muḥarram' according to this is the subject, and 'ʾikhrājuhum' is the predicate." End of what he transmitted on this view. What is transmitted from the Kufans is the reverse of this analysis, which is that the separator has been fronted with the predicate before the subject, so the analysis of "muḥarram" according to them is a fronted predicate, and "ʾikhrājuhum" is the subject. This is the one suitable to the rules, since one does not begin with an indefinite noun when there is no justification for it, and the predicate would be definite. Rather, the established usage in their language is the reverse of this, except that if it occurs in poetry, it is heard but not used as an analogy. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "It was said: it is the pronoun implied in 'muḥarram,' fronted and made explicit." End of what he transmitted on this view. This view is very weak, since there is no reason for fronting the pronoun, nor for its surfacing after being concealed, and because it leads to a passive participle (ismu al-mafʿūl) being empty of a pronoun, since according to this view "muḥarram" would be a fronted predicate and "ʾikhrājuhum" the subject, and no active or passive participle is found without a pronoun, except when it raises an explicit noun. Here it is not possible that it raise an explicit noun, because the detached fronted pronoun "huwa" was the pronoun raised by "muḥarram," and then this pronoun would remain of unknown analysis, since it is not permitted that it be the subject, nor that it be a fronted agent. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "It was said: it is the pronoun of the expulsion; its sense: 'and their expulsion is forbidden for you.'" End of what he transmitted on this view. He did not explain the nominative case of "ʾikhrājuhum," and it cannot be made to work with "huwa" being its pronoun, with "ʾikhrājuhum" as an explanation of that concealed pronoun, except by making "ʾikhrājuhum" an apposition of the pronoun. It has already been mentioned that there is disagreement on this, some permitting it and some forbidding it.

﴿أفَتُؤْمِنُونَ بِبَعْضِ الكِتابِ وتَكْفُرُونَ بِبَعْضٍ﴾ (ʾafa-tuʾminūna biʿḍi al-kitābi wa-takfurūna biʿḍin; "Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?"): This is an interrogative whose meaning is rebuke and denunciation. He did not blame them for the ransom, but for the inconsistency, since they performed part of what was obligatory and left out part. The inconsistency is more emphatic in censure. It may be said: expulsion is a sin, so why did He call it disbelief? We say: perhaps they declared that leaving off expulsion was not obligatory, even though the clear text of the Torah indicated its obligation. The part they believed in, if by "the Book" is meant the Torah, then it is general in what they believed of its rulings, and the ransoming of the captive is among them. The part they disbelieved in is the killing of some of them by others, the expulsion of some of them from their homes, and backing one another in sin and aggression, all of which is among what they disbelieved of the Torah. It was also said: the meaning is that they use part and abandon part; you ransom the captives of your own tribe and abandon the captives of the people of your religion, not ransoming them. It was also said: ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām passed by the head of the exilarch (Raʾs al-Jālūt, the leader of the Jewish community) in Kufa, while he was ransoming from among the women whoever had not been struck by war, and not ransoming whoever had been struck by war. He said: Ibn Salām said: "Surely it is written for you in your Book that you ransom all of them." Mujāhid said: its meaning is: if you find him in the hand of another, you ransom him, while you yourself kill him with your hand. It was also said: the purpose is to alert that they, in their adherence to the prophethood of Mūsā, peace be upon him and upon our Prophet, while denying Muḥammad ﷺ, though the proof in the matter of both is the same, have followed the course of their predecessors, in believing in part and disbelieving in part. They said: it is also permitted that "the Book" here mean what was prescribed for them of these four rulings, that is, what was obligated, and what they believed in of them is the ransoming of captives, and what they disbelieved in is the remaining four.

﴿فَما جَزاءُ مَن يَفْعَلُ ذَلِكَ مِنكم إلّا خِزْيٌ في الحَياةِ الدُّنْيا﴾ (fa-mā jazāʾu man yafʿalu dhālika minkum illā khizyun fī al-ḥayāti al-dunyā; "So what is the recompense of those among you who do that, except disgrace in the life of this world"): The word "jazāʾ" (recompense) is used for good and evil. He said: ﴿وجَزاهم بِما صَبَرُوا﴾ (wa-jazāhum bimā ṣabarū; "and He will recompense them for what they endured") [al-Insān: 12], and He said: ﴿فَجَزاؤُهُ جَهَنَّمُ﴾ (fa-jazāʾuhu jahannamu; "then his recompense is Hell") [al-Nisāʾ: 93]. "Khizy" here means disgrace, punishment, and retaliation against whoever is killed, or the imposition of the poll-tax (jizya) for all time, or the killing of the Qurayẓa, and the expulsion of the Naḍīr from their dwellings to Ariḥā (Jericho) and Adhriʿāt, or the victory of the enemy: five views. The view of the poll-tax and of exile is not feasible unless we take the verse as applying to those who were contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The better view is that the meaning is great censure and profound contempt, without restriction. "Illā khizyun" (except disgrace) is an exceptive construction with the exception omitted in full (istithnāʾ mufarragh), and it is the predicate of the subject. Breaking the negation here is a breaking of the working of "mā" (the negative particle), which is a matter of difference of opinion and detail. That is: when the predicate comes after and "illā" is placed upon it, it is either the first (the subject) or it takes its place, or it is an adjective, if it is the first in meaning, or takes its place. If it is the first, or takes its place, then only the nominative is permitted according to the majority. The Kufans permitted the accusative where the second is in place of the first. If it is an adjective, al-Farrāʾ permitted the accusative in it, and the Basrans forbade it. It is transmitted from Yūnus that he permitted the accusative in the predicate after "illā," "whatever it may be" (kāʾinan mā kāna). This contradicts what Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās transmitted; he said: "There is no disagreement among the grammarians about your saying: mā Zaydun illā akhūka (Zayd is nothing but your brother), that it is not permitted except with the nominative." He said: "If you say: mā anta illā liḥyatuka (you are nothing but your beard), the Basrans use the nominative, and the meaning according to them is: there is nothing in you but your beard," and likewise: mā anta illā ʿaynāka (you are nothing but your eyes). The Kufans permitted the accusative in this, and the Basrans do not permit the accusative except with verbal nouns (maṣādir), unless the meaning is known, so that one supposes a governing verb, such as: mā anta illā liḥyataka marratan wa-ʿaynaka ukhrā (you are nothing but your beard at one time and your eyes at another), and mā anta illā ʿimāmataka taḥsīnan wa-ridāʾaka tazyīnan (you are nothing but your turban for beautifying and your cloak for adorning).

﴿ويَوْمَ القِيامَةِ يُرَدُّونَ إلى أشَدِّ العَذابِ﴾ (wa-yawma al-qiyāmati yuraddūna ʾilā ashaddi al-ʿadhābi; "And on the Day of Resurrection they will be returned to the most severe punishment"): "The Day of Resurrection" is an expression for an extended time until judgment is made between the servants, and the people of Paradise enter Paradise and the people of the Fire enter the Fire. The meaning of "yuraddūna" (they will be returned) is "yaṣīrūna" (they will become), so it does not necessarily follow that they were in the most severe punishment before that. Or "radd" may mean returning to something they were in, as He said: ﴿فَرَدَدْناهُ إلى أُمِّهِ﴾ (fa-radadnāhu ʾilā ʾummihi; "So We returned him to his mother") [al-Qaṣaṣ: 13]. It is as if they were also in the most severe punishment in this world, since they were punished in this world by killing, captivity, exile, and various kinds of punishment. The majority read "yuraddūna" with the yāʾ (third person), which fits what precedes it, the saying: "man yafʿalu" (whoever does). It may be a shift (iltifāt) back to His saying ﴿أفَتُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ (ʾafa-tuʾminūna; "Do you believe"), so that it moves from the pronoun of address to the pronoun of absence. al-Ḥasan and Ibn Hurmuz, with a difference transmitted from them, read "turaddūna" with the tāʾ (second person), which fits His saying ﴿أفَتُؤْمِنُونَ﴾. It may be a shift in relation to His saying ﴿مَن يَفْعَلُ ذَلِكَ﴾, so that it moves from the pronoun of absence to the pronoun of address. "Ashaddu al-ʿadhābi" (the most severe punishment) is: abiding in the Fire, and its severity is because it has no end; or the kinds of punishment of Hell, since its levels are varied, and in it are valleys and serpents; or the punishment in which there is no joy nor spirit, with despair of escape; or the severity is in comparison with the punishment of this world; or the severity is in comparison with the punishment of their common people, since they are the ones who misled them and deceived them. Five views.

This is the final part of Abu Hayyan's commentary on verses 84–86 of Surah al-Baqarah.

﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾ [al-Baqarah: 74]: The discussion of the interpretation (tafsir) of this statement has already been given, since it occurred before ﴿Do you then hope...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 75]. Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr read it with the ya' (yaʿmalūna, "they do"), while the rest read it with the ta' from above (taʿmalūna, "you do"). With the ya', it corresponds to the reading of the majority for yuraddūna ("they are returned"). With the ta', it corresponds to the reading of turaddūna with the ta' ("you are returned"), so the addressees are those who were addressed in the verse. It has been said that the address may also be to the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ). It is related from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab that he said: "The Children of Israel have passed away, and you are the ones intended by this, O Ummah of Muhammad, and by what is similar to it." This verse is among the most admonishing of verses, since its meaning is that Allah is lying in wait for every disbeliever and sinner.

﴿Those are the ones who have bought the worldly life at the price of the Hereafter. So the punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be helped﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas said: It was revealed concerning the Jews, those whose mention preceded, who believed in part of the Book and disbelieved in part. The demonstrative noun ("those") is evidence that it refers to those who combined the previously mentioned blameworthy attributes. The discussion of this has already been given when discussing ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5], and that when a number of attributes are enumerated for a subject, the demonstrative is used to refer to that subject, as an alert that he is the one who combines those attributes. "Those who" (alladhīna) is the predicate of "those" (ulāʾika). The discussion of ﴿bought﴾ (ishtarawū) has already been given, and it was stated that buying and selling require a consideration and a thing exchanged, which are concrete. So the Arabs extended this usage to abstract meanings, and their preferring the splendour and adornment of this world over everlasting bliss was called "buying", as a preference of the transient and perishing over the enduring and lasting. For the buyer is not the one who prefers obtaining it, and the price paid for it is something he himself is averse to. None does this except one who is deceived in judgement and corrupt in intellect.

Some scholars of the meanings (ahl al-maʿānī) said: The "world" (dunyā) is that which is near to the desires of the heart, and the "Hereafter" (ākhira) is that which is connected to the pleasure of the Lord. ﴿So it will not be lightened﴾ (fa-lā yukhaffafu) is conjoined to the relative clause (ṣila). It is permissible for a relative pronoun to be connected to two relative clauses differing in time, as you say: "The one who killed Zayd yesterday came to me, and will kill his brother tomorrow." For the relative clauses are sentences, and whoever stipulates the unity of the time of their verbs, in contrast to what functions as individual words, they have explicitly stipulated the unity of tense, whether past or otherwise, and the preference for agreement in form.

It is also permissible that "those" (ulāʾika) is the subject (mubtadaʾ) and "who" (alladhīna) with its relative clause is the predicate (khabar). "So it will not be lightened" (fa-lā yukhaffafu) is a predicate following a predicate. The insertion of the fa' (so) is explained by the fact that "who", when its relative clause is a verb, carries the meaning of a conditional. This is an error, because here the relative pronoun is parsed by him as a predicate of "those", so the statement "so it will not be lightened" is not a predicate of the relative pronoun; rather, it is a predicate of "those", and the conditional quality does not transfer to the subject from the relative pronoun which serves as its predicate.

It is also permissible that "those" (ulāʾika) is the subject, "who" (alladhīna) is a second subject, and "so it will not be lightened" (fa-lā yukhaffafu) is the predicate of "who". The "who" with its predicate is a predicate of "those". It was said: A resumptive pronoun (ʿāʾid) was not needed, because "those who" are "those", just as you say: "This is Zayd, departing." This is an error, because every sentence that serves as a predicate of a subject must contain a connective (rābiṭ), unless it is itself the subject in meaning, in which case that connective is not needed. You have predicated "those" by means of the relative subject and its predicate, so a connective is necessary. This is not similar to the example he gave, "This is Zayd, departing", because "Zayd departing" are two predicates of "this", and they are two single words, or "Zayd" is an apposition (badal) of "this" and "departing" is the predicate. Or "this" is the subject, "Zayd" is a second subject, "departing" is the predicate of "Zayd", and "Zayd departing" is a sentence in the position of the predicate of "this", which is not permissible for lack of a connective. Furthermore, if there were a connective here, this parsing would not be valid, because "who" is restricted by the pointing to it, so it does not resemble a conditional noun, since its generality disappears through its specification. And because the relative clause of "who" is past in both wording and meaning. With these two points, it is not permissible to insert the fa' into the sentence functioning as a predicate.

Lightening (takhfīf) is facilitation (tasḥīl). The negation of lightening has been interpreted as the cessation of it, and it has also been interpreted as intensification. The preferable interpretation is that it negates lightening by cessation, or by reduction of it, or at a particular time, or at all times, since it is a negation of the essence, which necessarily entails the negation of its individual instances and forms. The apparent meaning of negation with "lā" and its common usage in it is that it negates in the future. Al-Zamakhsharī interpreted the negation of lightening as applying to this world and the Hereafter: in this world by reducing the poll-tax (jizya), and likewise the negation of help in this world and the Hereafter. The meaning of the negation of help is that they will not find anyone to repel from them what has befallen them of the punishment of Allah.

﴿Nor will they be helped﴾ (wa-lā hum yunṣarūn): a nominal sentence conjoined to a verbal sentence. It is also permissible for it to be verbal, and the matter to be one of ishtighāl (the verb being occupied with an object pronoun), so that "they" (hum) is in the nominative by a verb omitted which is explained by what follows it, in accordance with the statement of the poet:

"And if he does not bear its injustice upon himself..."

This reading is strengthened and made better by the fact that the statement "so it will not be lightened" preceded it, and it is a verbal sentence. For if the verbal sentence had not preceded, the preferable reading would have been the nominative by inception (ibtidāʾ). That is because "lā" (not) is not one of the particles that demand a verb, neither exclusively nor preferentially, so that it is like "kāna" (was) and the interrogative hamza, unlike Abu Muhammad ibn al-Sayyid, who claimed that placing the verb on the object in what the particle precedes is no better than inception, and that the passive voice is preferable to the active because it is more general, unless the agent is made general, in which case it would be: "nor will anyone help them", and that would forfeit the closing of the verse-endings with what they were closed with before and after, and would forfeit the conciseness, even though the statement "nor will they be helped" conveys that, namely generality.

These noble verses have contained Allah's reports: that He took the covenant from the Children of Israel to worship Allah alone, to do good to the two parents, to kinsmen, orphans and the needy, to speak good to people, to establish prayer and give zakat. And that they broke the covenant by their turning away and aversion. And that He took from them that they would not shed their blood, nor expel themselves from their homes, and that they acknowledged and committed to that. So the first covenant contained commands, and the second covenant contained prohibitions, since divine obligations are built upon commands and prohibitions. The beginning with commands was more emphatic, because they contain actions, while prohibitions contain abstentions, and actions are more burdensome than abstentions. Among the commands was the command to worship Allah alone, which is the head of faith, since its object is the most noble of objects, so beginning with it was preferable. Then He reproached them for being entangled with what they were forbidden, though His report had already preceded that they had disobeyed in the command, by His saying: ﴿Then you turned away﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83]. For committing what is forbidden is more ugly than abandoning what is commanded, since those are abstentions, as we have mentioned.

Then He rebuked them for opposing Allah's prohibitions, and that they seek help in that from other than the truth, but rather from sin and aggression. Then He mentioned the contradiction of their opinions and the foolishness of their intellects, in ransoming those among them who came to them as captives, although they themselves were the cause of their expulsion and captivity, while knowing that their expulsion was forbidden. And by mentioning that they believed in part of the Book and disbelieved in part. This is despite the fact that all of it is truth and sincerity, so disbelieving in part and believing in part is not fitting for that. Then He mentioned that the recompense for the doer of that is humiliation in this world and the severest punishment in the Hereafter, and that Allah, exalted is He, is not unaware of what they did, so He will requite them for that. Then He indicated those who adorned themselves with these blameworthy attributes and opposed Allah's command and prohibition: they have bought the immediate, trivial, at the price of the lasting, great, and preferred the transient, troubled over the enduring, pure. The result of this buying is that the punishment that has befallen them will not be lightened for them, and they will not find a helper to repel from them the evil of the punishment. They have indeed lost the transaction, and in exchange for everlasting bliss they have been given a fire whose fuel is people and stones. And if lightening has been negated, then elevation (of the punishment) is more fitting. Is this not from the category of alerting to the higher by means of the lower?

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 84–86 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And when We took your covenant: "You shall not shed your blood"﴾: The discussion of ﴿tasfikūna﴾ is like the discussion of ﴿lā taʿbudūna illā Allāh﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83] in terms of its i'rab (grammatical analysis). The majority recited it with a fatha on the ta', sukun on the sin, and a kasra on the fa'. Talha ibn Musarrif and Shu'ayb ibn Abi Hamza recited it likewise, except that they put a damma on the fa'. Abu Nahik and Abu Mijlaz recited it with a damma on the ta', a fatha on the sin, and a kasra on the shaddated fa'. Ibn Abi Ishaq recited it likewise, except that he made the sin sakin and lightened the fa'. The apparent meaning of ﴿You shall not shed your blood﴾ is: do not do this to yourselves due to the severe hardship that afflicts you and the rage that overtakes you. There has come in a hadith the story of the man who placed the blade of his sword in the ground with its point between his breasts, then leaned on it and killed himself, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) informed that he is among the people of the Fire. And it is authentically reported: "Whoever kills himself with an iron implement, his implement will be in his hand, stabbing himself in his belly in the Fire of Hell, abiding therein forever and ever." The religious communities have concurred on the prohibition of taking a human life. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 29]. It has been said that its meaning is: do not shed the blood of people, for whoever sheds their blood, their blood will be shed. One said:

"We gave them a cup, and they gave us its like in return, but they were more patient in the face of death."

It has been said: its meaning is: do not kill yourselves by committing what necessitates that, such as apostasy, adultery after being married, waging war, killing a soul without right, and the like of what removes the sanctity of blood. It has been said: its meaning is: let not some of you shed the blood of others, and to this he alluded with his saying: "Do not revert after me to disbelief, striking one another's necks." The people of one religion were like a single soul, as said by Qatada, and al-Zamakhshari chose it. Ibn 'Atiyya said: Allah took a covenant from the Children of Israel in the Torah that none of them should kill another, nor expel him, nor enslave him, nor allow him to be enslaved, along with other acts of obedience. The address in "We took your covenant" is to the scholars of the Jews who were in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or with their forefathers.

﴿And do not expel yourselves from your homes﴾: its meaning is: let not some of you expel others, or: do not mistreat the neighbour who is your neighbour so that you force them to leave their homes, or: do not do what would expel you from Paradise, which is your home, or: do not expel yourselves, that is, your brothers, because you are like a single soul, or: do not cause corruption which would be the cause of your expulsion from your homes, as if it alludes to the exile of the offender, or: do not cause corruption and oppose the prophets and the believers, so that exile is prescribed for you. These are six opinions. Then ﴿you acknowledged﴾: that is, to the covenant, and admitted its obligation, or you acknowledged its acceptance, or you were content with it, as al-Bu'ayth said:

"I am not a Kulaybī, when he is branded with a disgrace, who acquiesces like a wife acquiescing to her husband."

﴿And you bear witness﴾: that is, you know that Allah took it from you. He meant upon the early Children of Israel, if the address is directed at them; and if it is directed at his contemporaries (ﷺ) among their descendants, its meaning is: "And you bear witness against your forefathers to what Allah took from them of covenant," either through mutawatir transmission or through what you recite from the Torah. If the meaning of witnessing is presence, then the address must be to their forefathers. Some exegetes said: "Then you acknowledged" refers to the later generation, and "and you bear witness" refers to the earlier generation, because they witnessed the shedding of one another's blood. And it was said: "and you bear witness" because the earlier and later ones became like one thing, therefore the address of presence was applied to them. It has also been said: his saying "and you bear witness" is for emphasis, like your saying: "So-and-so admits against himself to such-and-such, bearing witness against it."

﴿Then you are these, killing yourselves﴾: this is an expression of astonishment at what He informed about them of killing, expulsion and transgression, after the taking of the covenant from them, and their acknowledgement and testimony. The grammarians differed on the i'rab of this clause. The preferred view is that ﴿antum﴾ is the subject, ﴿hā'ulā'﴾ is the predicate, and ﴿taqtulūna﴾ is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause). The Arabs have said: "Here you are standing (hā anta dhā qā'iman)," and "Here I am standing (hā ana dhā qā'iman)," and also: "This is me standing (hadhā anā qā'iman)," and "Here he is standing (hā huwa dhā qā'iman)." The demonstrative is applied to the pronoun in wording, as if he said: "You are the present one, I am the present one, he is the present one." The intended meaning is the informing of the state. What indicates that the clause is a ḥāl is that the singular noun comes in the accusative as a ḥāl, in accordance with what we have said, in their saying: "hā anta dhā qā'iman" and the like. Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is: "Then you, after that, are these witnesses," meaning that you are other people, not those who acknowledged, treating the change of attribute as the change of essence, as you say: "I returned by other than the way I went out." His saying "taqtulūna" is an explanation of "Then you are these." End of his words. The apparent view is that what is indicated by "Then you are these" are the ones originally addressed, so they are not other people. Do you not see that this estimation which al-Zamakhshari made of treating the change of attribute as the change of essence cannot be realised in the like of "hā anā dhā qā'iman" nor in "hā antum ulā'"? Rather, the addressee is the one indicated, without change.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: Al-Ustadh al-Ajall Abu al-Hasan ibn Ahmad, our shaykh, said: "Hā'ulā'" is raised as the subject, "antum" is the fronted predicate, and "taqtulūna" is a ḥāl; with it the meaning is complete, and it was the intended part, so it is not dispensable, and it came only after the sentence had been completed in its predicate and its subject, as you say: "This is Zayd, departing," while you intended to inform of his departure, not of the fact that this is Zayd. End of what Ibn 'Atiyya transmitted from his shaykh, who is Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn Ahmad ibn Khalaf al-Ansari, from the people of our town Granada, known as Ibn al-Bādhish, and he is the father of the Imam Abu Ja'far Ahmad, author of the book al-Iqna' in the readings, and he has preferences in grammar. He transmitted Sibawayh's book from the Vizier Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Hisham al-Mus-hafi, and he commented on it in grammar on the book al-Jumal and al-Idah and some issues from Sibawayh's book. He died in the year 528 AH. I do not know what the reason is for deviating from making "antum" the subject and "hā'ulā'" the predicate to the reverse of this. The governing element of this ḥāl is the demonstrative with what is in it of the meaning of the verb. They said: it is a ḥāl from it, so the ṣāḥib al-ḥāl and its governing element would then be one. We have discussed this issue in our book Manhaj al-Sālik, which is our composition, so consult it there. Some grammarians held that "hā'ulā'" is a vocative with the particle of address omitted, and this is not permitted according to the Basrians, because a demonstrative may not have the vocative particle omitted from it; its permissibility is reported from al-Farra', and al-Zajjaj and others interpreted the verse according to it, inclining to the view of al-Farra', so according to this view "taqtulūna" is a predicate about "antum." The separation between subject and predicate is by the vocative, and separation by the vocative is permitted. Those who took this view in this verse did so because it was difficult for them that a sentence consisting of subject and predicate could be formed from the addressee pronoun and a demonstrative. We have explained how this sentence is formed. Verses have been cited in which the vocative particle is omitted with the demonstrative, among them the saying of a man of Tayy:

"Indeed the first ones described my people to them, so by them, hadha i'tasim, you will meet whoever opposes you humiliated."

Ibn Kaysan and others held that "antum" is the subject, "yaqtulūna" is the predicate, and "hā'ulā'" is a specification of the addressees, when they were alerted to the state they were persisting in; so in that case it is accusative by "a'nī." The grammarians have stated that specification does not occur with indefinite nouns or demonstratives. What is established from Arabic usage is that it comes as "ayyuhā" (e.g., "O Allah, forgive us, O band"), or definite with "al-" (e.g., "we Arabs are the most generous of people toward guests"), or with an annexation (e.g., "we, the company of the prophets, are not inherited from"), and it may be a proper name, as they recited:

"By us Tamim, the haze is cleared."

End. It most often comes after a first-person pronoun, as we have illustrated. It has also come after a second-person pronoun, as in their saying: "By you, Allah, we hope for grace." Some held that "hā'ulā'" is a relative pronoun meaning "alladhī," and it is the predicate about "antum," and "taqtulūna" is its relative clause; this is not permitted according to the Basrians, while the Kufans permitted it, and it is a disputed question mentioned in the science of grammar. The majority recited "taqtulūna" from qatala, lightened. Al-Hasan recited "tuqattilūna" from qattala, shaddated. This is so in some tafsirs; in the tafsir of al-Mahdawi it is said that it is the reading of Abu Nahik, and he said that al-Zuhri and al-Hasan recited "tuqattilūna anbiyā'a Allāh," from qattala, meaning shaddated. Allah knows best the correctness of that.

﴿And you expel a party of you from their homes﴾: this was revealed concerning the Banu Qaynuqa', the Banu Qurayza and al-Nadir among the Jews. The Banu Qaynuqa' were enemies of Qurayza and al-Nadir; the Aws and the Khazraj were brothers, and al-Nadir and Qurayza were also brothers, then they separated. So al-Nadir became allies of the Khazraj, and Qurayza allies of the Aws. They would fight one another, then the war would cease, and they would ransom their captives. Allah reproached them for this, as al-Mahdawi said. Al-Zamakhshari said: Each party would fight with its allies, and when they prevailed, they would ruin their homes and expel them; and when a man from either party was captured, they would gather to ransom him. The Arabs reproached them and said: "How do you fight them and then ransom them?" They would say: "We have been commanded to ransom them, and fighting them has been forbidden to us, but we are ashamed that our allies be humiliated."

﴿Supporting one another against them in sin﴾: ʿAsim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read with a lightened ẓā', and its origin is "tatazāhirūna," so the ta' was dropped; and it is, in our view, the second ta' and not the first, contrary to Hisham, who claimed that the one dropped is the one of the present tense, which in such a case indicates address. Much has come in the Qur'an of dropping the ta'. He said:

"You sneeze all together around your house, so every one of you, O sons of Hamdan, has a cold."

He means "tatatāsaṭūna" [i.e., tatatā'asūna]. The rest of the seven read with a shaddated ẓā', that is, by assimilating the ẓā' into the ta'. Abu Haywa recited "tuzāhirūna," with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the ha'. Mujahid and Qatada, with variation from them, recited "tazzahharūna," with a fatha on the ta', ẓā' and ha', all shaddated, without an alif; and it is narrated from Abu 'Amr. Some recited "tatazāhirūna" according to the origin. These are five readings, and their meanings are all cooperation and support. Abu al-'Aliya narrated that he said: When the Children of Israel oppressed a people, they would expel them from their homes. "Against them in sin": there are two views concerning it. One: it is the act for which its doer deserves blame and reproach. The second: it is what the soul recoils from and the heart is not at ease with. In the hadith of al-Nawwas: "Sin is what troubles your breast." It has been said: the meaning is "supporting one another against them in what necessitates sin," and this is the mention of the cause for its effect; that is why wine is called sin, as one said:

"I drank sin until my reason strayed."

(And transgression) is exceeding the limit in wrongdoing.

﴿And if they come to you as captives﴾: the reading of the majority is on the pattern fu'ālā, and of Hamza on the pattern fa'lā.

﴿تُفادُوهُمْ﴾ (ʾtufādūhum): Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim and al-Kisāʾī read it from fādā. The rest read it from fadā.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: The good wording of "ʾitāʾ" (coming/bringing), in that it stands opposite "ʾikhrāj" (expulsion), makes the contrast apparent, which denounces their action in the expulsion. That is, it is not fitting that you should treat well with ransom those whom you have wronged by expelling them from their homes. The meaning of ﴿تُفادُوهم﴾ (tufādūhum) is "tafdūhum" (you ransom them), since the form "mufāʿala" (the pattern fāʿala) occurs with two parties and with one. So fāʿala here has the meaning of the bare form faʿala, which is one of its meanings. It was also said: the meaning of "fādā" is "bādala" (to exchange) a captive for a captive, and the meaning of "fadā" is "dafaʿa al-fidāʾ" (to pay the ransom). The first is supported by the words of al-ʿAbbās: "I ransomed myself and I ransomed ʿAqīl." It is known that he did not exchange one captive for another. It was also said: the meaning is "tafdūhum" (you ransom them) by peace, and "tufādūhum" (you exchange them) by violence. It was also said: "tufādūhum" means that you seek the ransom from the captive who is in your hands from your enemies. From this is his saying:

"Stay, O ransomer of your captive, for my people
and your people, I do not see them coming together."

"Tafdūhum" means you give their ransom. Abū ʿAlī said: the meaning of "tufādūhum" linguistically is that you release them after you take something from them. "Fādaytu nafsī" means I released myself after I paid something. Both "fādā" and "fadā" take two objects, the second with a preposition, and here that object is omitted.

﴿وهُوَ مُحَرَّمٌ عَلَيْكم إخْراجُهُمْ﴾ (wa-huwa muḥarramun ʿalaykum ʾikhrājuhum; "and it is forbidden for you, their expulsion"): Four things have preceded: killing the self, expulsion from the homes, backing one another (ẓāhara), and ransoming, and all of them are forbidden. This category was singled out for emphasis of the prohibition, even though all of them are forbidden, because expulsion from homes carries the disgrace of exile and banishment, whose harm does not end except with death. This is unlike killing, since killing, although in itself it is the destruction of the structure (of life), is greater, yet in it the evil comes to an end. Unlike ransoming them with it, for it arises from the crime of expulsion from homes and of backing one another, since had it not been for the expulsion from homes and the backing against them, they would not have fallen into the bonds of captivity. It may also be that, as in every sentence, the mention of the prohibition is omitted, and the sense is: "You kill your selves, and it is forbidden for you," and likewise the rest. The word ﴿هو﴾ (huwa, "it") is in the nominative as a subject (mubtadaʾ). It is either a pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), and the sentence after it is its predicate, and its analysis is that "ʾikhrājuhum" is the subject and "muḥarram" is the predicate, with a pronoun in it referring back to "ʾikhrāj," since the intended order is the delayed one. The Kufans do not permit fronting the predicate when it carries a raised pronoun. So they do not permit "qāʾimun Zaydun" (standing is Zayd) with "qāʾim" as a fronted predicate. Therefore they chose that it be the predicate of "huwa" is "muḥarramun," and "ʾikhrājuhum" is in the nominative as a passive subject (nāʾib al-fāʿil), and al-Mahdawī followed them in this. The Basrans do not permit this view, because according to them a pronoun of the matter may only be explained by a full sentence with both its parts stated. If you make "muḥarramun" a predicate of "huwa," and "ʾikhrājuhum" is raised by it, then the pronoun of the matter would have been explained by something other than a sentence, which is not permitted according to the Basrans as we have mentioned. They also permitted that "huwa" be a subject which is not a pronoun of the matter, but refers back to "ʾikhrāj," with "muḥarram" being its predicate, and "ʾikhrājuhum" an apposition (badal). On this there is disagreement. Some permitted that an unexpressed pronoun, for which nothing has preceded to which it refers, be explained by an apposition, and some forbade it. Al-Kisāʾī permitted it, and it is so in some reports. The Kufans permitted that "huwa" be a separator (ʿimād), which the Basrans call a "faṣl" (a separating pronoun), and this has already been mentioned along with the predicate. The sense is: "And their expulsion, it is forbidden for you," so when the predicate of the subject was fronted before the subject, the separator was fronted with it. Al-Farrāʾ said: "Because the conjunction 'wa' here requires a noun, and wherever it requires a noun, the separator is permitted." This analysis is not permitted according to the Basrans, because in it there are two things which they do not permit: first, the occurrence of a separator between a definite and an indefinite that is not close to the definite, since the sense is "and their expulsion, it is forbidden," and "muḥarram" is an indefinite not close to the definite. Second, that it involves fronting the separator, whose condition according to the Basrans is that it stand between the subject and the predicate, or between the two of which they were originally composed. All these are matters that are verified in the science of grammar (naḥw).

In Ibn ʿAṭiyya's book, at this point, there are statements that are open to criticism. He said: "It was said regarding 'huwa' that it is a pronoun of the matter, its sense being: 'and the matter is forbidden for you,' and 'ʾikhrājuhum' in this view is an apposition of 'huwa.'" End of what he transmitted on this view. This is an error from two aspects. First: he informed of a pronoun of the matter with a single noun, and no Basran or Kufan permits that. As for the Basran: because the explainer of a pronoun of the matter must necessarily be a sentence. As for the Kufan: because he permits a sentence, and he permits a single noun if it has combined with what follows it into a predication and a subject in meaning, as in your saying: "I thought him standing, Zayd and ʿAmr." Second: he made "ʾikhrājuhum" an apposition of a pronoun of the matter, but a pronoun of the matter is not conjoined to, nor is it replaced by an apposition, nor is it emphasised. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "It was said: it is a separator (fāṣila), and this is the view of the Kufan, but it is not here the one that is a separator (ʿimād), and 'muḥarram' according to this is the subject, and 'ʾikhrājuhum' is the predicate." End of what he transmitted on this view. What is transmitted from the Kufans is the reverse of this analysis, which is that the separator has been fronted with the predicate before the subject, so the analysis of "muḥarram" according to them is a fronted predicate, and "ʾikhrājuhum" is the subject. This is the one suitable to the rules, since one does not begin with an indefinite noun when there is no justification for it, and the predicate would be definite. Rather, the established usage in their language is the reverse of this, except that if it occurs in poetry, it is heard but not used as an analogy. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "It was said: it is the pronoun implied in 'muḥarram,' fronted and made explicit." End of what he transmitted on this view. This view is very weak, since there is no reason for fronting the pronoun, nor for its surfacing after being concealed, and because it leads to a passive participle (ismu al-mafʿūl) being empty of a pronoun, since according to this view "muḥarram" would be a fronted predicate and "ʾikhrājuhum" the subject, and no active or passive participle is found without a pronoun, except when it raises an explicit noun. Here it is not possible that it raise an explicit noun, because the detached fronted pronoun "huwa" was the pronoun raised by "muḥarram," and then this pronoun would remain of unknown analysis, since it is not permitted that it be the subject, nor that it be a fronted agent. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "It was said: it is the pronoun of the expulsion; its sense: 'and their expulsion is forbidden for you.'" End of what he transmitted on this view. He did not explain the nominative case of "ʾikhrājuhum," and it cannot be made to work with "huwa" being its pronoun, with "ʾikhrājuhum" as an explanation of that concealed pronoun, except by making "ʾikhrājuhum" an apposition of the pronoun. It has already been mentioned that there is disagreement on this, some permitting it and some forbidding it.

﴿أفَتُؤْمِنُونَ بِبَعْضِ الكِتابِ وتَكْفُرُونَ بِبَعْضٍ﴾ (ʾafa-tuʾminūna biʿḍi al-kitābi wa-takfurūna biʿḍin; "Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?"): This is an interrogative whose meaning is rebuke and denunciation. He did not blame them for the ransom, but for the inconsistency, since they performed part of what was obligatory and left out part. The inconsistency is more emphatic in censure. It may be said: expulsion is a sin, so why did He call it disbelief? We say: perhaps they declared that leaving off expulsion was not obligatory, even though the clear text of the Torah indicated its obligation. The part they believed in, if by "the Book" is meant the Torah, then it is general in what they believed of its rulings, and the ransoming of the captive is among them. The part they disbelieved in is the killing of some of them by others, the expulsion of some of them from their homes, and backing one another in sin and aggression, all of which is among what they disbelieved of the Torah. It was also said: the meaning is that they use part and abandon part; you ransom the captives of your own tribe and abandon the captives of the people of your religion, not ransoming them. It was also said: ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām passed by the head of the exilarch (Raʾs al-Jālūt, the leader of the Jewish community) in Kufa, while he was ransoming from among the women whoever had not been struck by war, and not ransoming whoever had been struck by war. He said: Ibn Salām said: "Surely it is written for you in your Book that you ransom all of them." Mujāhid said: its meaning is: if you find him in the hand of another, you ransom him, while you yourself kill him with your hand. It was also said: the purpose is to alert that they, in their adherence to the prophethood of Mūsā, peace be upon him and upon our Prophet, while denying Muḥammad ﷺ, though the proof in the matter of both is the same, have followed the course of their predecessors, in believing in part and disbelieving in part. They said: it is also permitted that "the Book" here mean what was prescribed for them of these four rulings, that is, what was obligated, and what they believed in of them is the ransoming of captives, and what they disbelieved in is the remaining four.

﴿فَما جَزاءُ مَن يَفْعَلُ ذَلِكَ مِنكم إلّا خِزْيٌ في الحَياةِ الدُّنْيا﴾ (fa-mā jazāʾu man yafʿalu dhālika minkum illā khizyun fī al-ḥayāti al-dunyā; "So what is the recompense of those among you who do that, except disgrace in the life of this world"): The word "jazāʾ" (recompense) is used for good and evil. He said: ﴿وجَزاهم بِما صَبَرُوا﴾ (wa-jazāhum bimā ṣabarū; "and He will recompense them for what they endured") [al-Insān: 12], and He said: ﴿فَجَزاؤُهُ جَهَنَّمُ﴾ (fa-jazāʾuhu jahannamu; "then his recompense is Hell") [al-Nisāʾ: 93]. "Khizy" here means disgrace, punishment, and retaliation against whoever is killed, or the imposition of the poll-tax (jizya) for all time, or the killing of the Qurayẓa, and the expulsion of the Naḍīr from their dwellings to Ariḥā (Jericho) and Adhriʿāt, or the victory of the enemy: five views. The view of the poll-tax and of exile is not feasible unless we take the verse as applying to those who were contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The better view is that the meaning is great censure and profound contempt, without restriction. "Illā khizyun" (except disgrace) is an exceptive construction with the exception omitted in full (istithnāʾ mufarragh), and it is the predicate of the subject. Breaking the negation here is a breaking of the working of "mā" (the negative particle), which is a matter of difference of opinion and detail. That is: when the predicate comes after and "illā" is placed upon it, it is either the first (the subject) or it takes its place, or it is an adjective, if it is the first in meaning, or takes its place. If it is the first, or takes its place, then only the nominative is permitted according to the majority. The Kufans permitted the accusative where the second is in place of the first. If it is an adjective, al-Farrāʾ permitted the accusative in it, and the Basrans forbade it. It is transmitted from Yūnus that he permitted the accusative in the predicate after "illā," "whatever it may be" (kāʾinan mā kāna). This contradicts what Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās transmitted; he said: "There is no disagreement among the grammarians about your saying: mā Zaydun illā akhūka (Zayd is nothing but your brother), that it is not permitted except with the nominative." He said: "If you say: mā anta illā liḥyatuka (you are nothing but your beard), the Basrans use the nominative, and the meaning according to them is: there is nothing in you but your beard," and likewise: mā anta illā ʿaynāka (you are nothing but your eyes). The Kufans permitted the accusative in this, and the Basrans do not permit the accusative except with verbal nouns (maṣādir), unless the meaning is known, so that one supposes a governing verb, such as: mā anta illā liḥyataka marratan wa-ʿaynaka ukhrā (you are nothing but your beard at one time and your eyes at another), and mā anta illā ʿimāmataka taḥsīnan wa-ridāʾaka tazyīnan (you are nothing but your turban for beautifying and your cloak for adorning).

﴿ويَوْمَ القِيامَةِ يُرَدُّونَ إلى أشَدِّ العَذابِ﴾ (wa-yawma al-qiyāmati yuraddūna ʾilā ashaddi al-ʿadhābi; "And on the Day of Resurrection they will be returned to the most severe punishment"): "The Day of Resurrection" is an expression for an extended time until judgment is made between the servants, and the people of Paradise enter Paradise and the people of the Fire enter the Fire. The meaning of "yuraddūna" (they will be returned) is "yaṣīrūna" (they will become), so it does not necessarily follow that they were in the most severe punishment before that. Or "radd" may mean returning to something they were in, as He said: ﴿فَرَدَدْناهُ إلى أُمِّهِ﴾ (fa-radadnāhu ʾilā ʾummihi; "So We returned him to his mother") [al-Qaṣaṣ: 13]. It is as if they were also in the most severe punishment in this world, since they were punished in this world by killing, captivity, exile, and various kinds of punishment. The majority read "yuraddūna" with the yāʾ (third person), which fits what precedes it, the saying: "man yafʿalu" (whoever does). It may be a shift (iltifāt) back to His saying ﴿أفَتُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ (ʾafa-tuʾminūna; "Do you believe"), so that it moves from the pronoun of address to the pronoun of absence. al-Ḥasan and Ibn Hurmuz, with a difference transmitted from them, read "turaddūna" with the tāʾ (second person), which fits His saying ﴿أفَتُؤْمِنُونَ﴾. It may be a shift in relation to His saying ﴿مَن يَفْعَلُ ذَلِكَ﴾, so that it moves from the pronoun of absence to the pronoun of address. "Ashaddu al-ʿadhābi" (the most severe punishment) is: abiding in the Fire, and its severity is because it has no end; or the kinds of punishment of Hell, since its levels are varied, and in it are valleys and serpents; or the punishment in which there is no joy nor spirit, with despair of escape; or the severity is in comparison with the punishment of this world; or the severity is in comparison with the punishment of their common people, since they are the ones who misled them and deceived them. Five views.

This is the final part of Abu Hayyan's commentary on verses 84–86 of Surah al-Baqarah.

﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾ [al-Baqarah: 74]: The discussion of the interpretation (tafsir) of this statement has already been given, since it occurred before ﴿Do you then hope...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 75]. Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr read it with the ya' (yaʿmalūna, "they do"), while the rest read it with the ta' from above (taʿmalūna, "you do"). With the ya', it corresponds to the reading of the majority for yuraddūna ("they are returned"). With the ta', it corresponds to the reading of turaddūna with the ta' ("you are returned"), so the addressees are those who were addressed in the verse. It has been said that the address may also be to the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ). It is related from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab that he said: "The Children of Israel have passed away, and you are the ones intended by this, O Ummah of Muhammad, and by what is similar to it." This verse is among the most admonishing of verses, since its meaning is that Allah is lying in wait for every disbeliever and sinner.

﴿Those are the ones who have bought the worldly life at the price of the Hereafter. So the punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be helped﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas said: It was revealed concerning the Jews, those whose mention preceded, who believed in part of the Book and disbelieved in part. The demonstrative noun ("those") is evidence that it refers to those who combined the previously mentioned blameworthy attributes. The discussion of this has already been given when discussing ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5], and that when a number of attributes are enumerated for a subject, the demonstrative is used to refer to that subject, as an alert that he is the one who combines those attributes. "Those who" (alladhīna) is the predicate of "those" (ulāʾika). The discussion of ﴿bought﴾ (ishtarawū) has already been given, and it was stated that buying and selling require a consideration and a thing exchanged, which are concrete. So the Arabs extended this usage to abstract meanings, and their preferring the splendour and adornment of this world over everlasting bliss was called "buying", as a preference of the transient and perishing over the enduring and lasting. For the buyer is not the one who prefers obtaining it, and the price paid for it is something he himself is averse to. None does this except one who is deceived in judgement and corrupt in intellect.

Some scholars of the meanings (ahl al-maʿānī) said: The "world" (dunyā) is that which is near to the desires of the heart, and the "Hereafter" (ākhira) is that which is connected to the pleasure of the Lord. ﴿So it will not be lightened﴾ (fa-lā yukhaffafu) is conjoined to the relative clause (ṣila). It is permissible for a relative pronoun to be connected to two relative clauses differing in time, as you say: "The one who killed Zayd yesterday came to me, and will kill his brother tomorrow." For the relative clauses are sentences, and whoever stipulates the unity of the time of their verbs, in contrast to what functions as individual words, they have explicitly stipulated the unity of tense, whether past or otherwise, and the preference for agreement in form.

It is also permissible that "those" (ulāʾika) is the subject (mubtadaʾ) and "who" (alladhīna) with its relative clause is the predicate (khabar). "So it will not be lightened" (fa-lā yukhaffafu) is a predicate following a predicate. The insertion of the fa' (so) is explained by the fact that "who", when its relative clause is a verb, carries the meaning of a conditional. This is an error, because here the relative pronoun is parsed by him as a predicate of "those", so the statement "so it will not be lightened" is not a predicate of the relative pronoun; rather, it is a predicate of "those", and the conditional quality does not transfer to the subject from the relative pronoun which serves as its predicate.

It is also permissible that "those" (ulāʾika) is the subject, "who" (alladhīna) is a second subject, and "so it will not be lightened" (fa-lā yukhaffafu) is the predicate of "who". The "who" with its predicate is a predicate of "those". It was said: A resumptive pronoun (ʿāʾid) was not needed, because "those who" are "those", just as you say: "This is Zayd, departing." This is an error, because every sentence that serves as a predicate of a subject must contain a connective (rābiṭ), unless it is itself the subject in meaning, in which case that connective is not needed. You have predicated "those" by means of the relative subject and its predicate, so a connective is necessary. This is not similar to the example he gave, "This is Zayd, departing", because "Zayd departing" are two predicates of "this", and they are two single words, or "Zayd" is an apposition (badal) of "this" and "departing" is the predicate. Or "this" is the subject, "Zayd" is a second subject, "departing" is the predicate of "Zayd", and "Zayd departing" is a sentence in the position of the predicate of "this", which is not permissible for lack of a connective. Furthermore, if there were a connective here, this parsing would not be valid, because "who" is restricted by the pointing to it, so it does not resemble a conditional noun, since its generality disappears through its specification. And because the relative clause of "who" is past in both wording and meaning. With these two points, it is not permissible to insert the fa' into the sentence functioning as a predicate.

Lightening (takhfīf) is facilitation (tasḥīl). The negation of lightening has been interpreted as the cessation of it, and it has also been interpreted as intensification. The preferable interpretation is that it negates lightening by cessation, or by reduction of it, or at a particular time, or at all times, since it is a negation of the essence, which necessarily entails the negation of its individual instances and forms. The apparent meaning of negation with "lā" and its common usage in it is that it negates in the future. Al-Zamakhsharī interpreted the negation of lightening as applying to this world and the Hereafter: in this world by reducing the poll-tax (jizya), and likewise the negation of help in this world and the Hereafter. The meaning of the negation of help is that they will not find anyone to repel from them what has befallen them of the punishment of Allah.

﴿Nor will they be helped﴾ (wa-lā hum yunṣarūn): a nominal sentence conjoined to a verbal sentence. It is also permissible for it to be verbal, and the matter to be one of ishtighāl (the verb being occupied with an object pronoun), so that "they" (hum) is in the nominative by a verb omitted which is explained by what follows it, in accordance with the statement of the poet:

"And if he does not bear its injustice upon himself..."

This reading is strengthened and made better by the fact that the statement "so it will not be lightened" preceded it, and it is a verbal sentence. For if the verbal sentence had not preceded, the preferable reading would have been the nominative by inception (ibtidāʾ). That is because "lā" (not) is not one of the particles that demand a verb, neither exclusively nor preferentially, so that it is like "kāna" (was) and the interrogative hamza, unlike Abu Muhammad ibn al-Sayyid, who claimed that placing the verb on the object in what the particle precedes is no better than inception, and that the passive voice is preferable to the active because it is more general, unless the agent is made general, in which case it would be: "nor will anyone help them", and that would forfeit the closing of the verse-endings with what they were closed with before and after, and would forfeit the conciseness, even though the statement "nor will they be helped" conveys that, namely generality.

These noble verses have contained Allah's reports: that He took the covenant from the Children of Israel to worship Allah alone, to do good to the two parents, to kinsmen, orphans and the needy, to speak good to people, to establish prayer and give zakat. And that they broke the covenant by their turning away and aversion. And that He took from them that they would not shed their blood, nor expel themselves from their homes, and that they acknowledged and committed to that. So the first covenant contained commands, and the second covenant contained prohibitions, since divine obligations are built upon commands and prohibitions. The beginning with commands was more emphatic, because they contain actions, while prohibitions contain abstentions, and actions are more burdensome than abstentions. Among the commands was the command to worship Allah alone, which is the head of faith, since its object is the most noble of objects, so beginning with it was preferable.
