Had it been treated with *i'lal* (inflectional modification) according to the pattern of *uqqitat* and *uhhidat*, with the vowel of the ʿayn moved to the *fa'* and the ʿayn deleted, the *fa'* would have had to become *waw* because it is moved and preceded by an open vowel, as it became in *awadim*, the plural of *adam* on the pattern *afa'il*. Then the *waw* would become *alif* because it is moved and preceded by an open vowel. When analogy led to modifying both the *fa'* and the ʿayn, it was rejected and the ʿayn was kept sound.

*Al-ruh* (الرُّوحُ) of the animal: a name for the part by which life is obtained. Al-Raghib said this. People differed regarding it and regarding *al-nafs* (soul): are they both of the shared (*mushtarak*) category or of the distinct (*mutabayin*) category? And regarding the reality of the *nafs* and the *ruh*, and works have been written on this.

*Al-qudus* (القُدُسُ): purity. It is said: blessing. This has been discussed before, at the discussion of His saying, ﴿ونُقَدِّسُ لَكَ﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 30).

*Al-rasul* (الرَّسُولُ): on the pattern *fa'ul* with the meaning of *maf'ul*, that is, the sent one. This is rare, and from it come *al-halub* and *al-rakub*, meaning the milked and the ridden.

*Tahwa* (تَهْوى): loves and chooses. Its past tense is on the pattern *fa'ila*, and its verbal noun is *al-hawa*.

*Ghulf* (غُلْفٌ): plural of *aghlaf*, like *ahmar* and *humr*, meaning the one who does not understand. Or it is the plural of *ghilaf*, which is a covering. In that case its original form is with doubling, and it was lightened.

*Al-laʿn* (اللَّعْنُ): expulsion and distancing. It is said: *shaʾwun laʿin*, meaning far away. Al-Shammakh said:

*"I frightened the sandgrouse with it and removed from it the place of the wolf, like the cursed man."*

*Al-maʿrifa* (المَعْرِفَةُ): knowledge that is connected to particulars, and it is preceded by ignorance. This is unlike the basic knowledge (*ʿilm*), which is connected to relation, and which may not be preceded by ignorance. For this reason Allah the Exalted is not described as *ʿarif* (one who recognises), but He is described as *ʿalim* (knowing).

*Bi'sa* (بِئْسَ): a verb made for dispraise. Its original form is *fa'ila*. For it and for *ni'ma* there is a chapter devoted to it in grammar.

*Al-baghy* (البَغْيُ): injustice. Its original meaning is corruption, from the saying: *baghā al-jurh*, meaning the wound became corrupt. Al-Asmaʿi said this. It is also said its original sense is intense seeking. From this come *ma nabghi* (what we seek), and the words of the rajaz poet:

*"He recited, while the seeker loves finding, she-camels of various colours."*

From this the adulteress was called *baghiyy*, because of her intense seeking of fornication.

*Al-ihana* (الإهانَةُ): humiliation. *Hana hawanan*: he was not regarded. This is the meaning of abasement, which is that a person is not valued nor paid attention to.

*Wara'* (وراءَ): one of the adverbs of place of moderate usage, and it can mean "in front of" and "behind." The more common meaning in it is "behind."

*Al-khalis* (الخالِصُ): that which is not mixed with anything. It is said: *khalasa yakhlusu khulusan*.

*Tamanna* (تَمَنّى): from the pattern *tafa'ala*, from *al-munya*, which is the desired thing. The wished-for may also be what is recited, in the sense of recitation. From it: *tamanna ʿala Zayd minhu hajatan*.

*Wajada* (وَجَدَ): shared between finding, knowledge, wealth, and distress, and it varies by its verbal nouns, such as *al-wijdan*, *al-wajd*, and *al-mawjida*.

*Al-hirs* (الحِرْصُ): intense seeking.

*Al-widd* (الوِدُّ): love for a thing and preference for it. Its verb is *wadda*, which is on the pattern *fa'ala yaf'alu*. Al-Kisa'i reported *waddidtu*, and according to this it is permissible to kasra the *waw*, since it would then be *fa'ila yaf'alu*. Also, unmerging the doubled letters in His saying:

*"What is in their hearts for us of mawadda..."*

is a necessity of poetry.

*ʿAmmara* (عَمَّرَ): the doubling in it is for transitivity, since it is from *ʿammara al-rajul*, meaning his life lengthened, and *ʿammarahu Allah*, meaning Allah lengthened his life. *Al-ʿumr* is the duration of remaining.

*Al-alf* (الألْفُ): ten hundreds. It may be exceeded in use, and then it indicates a large quantity. It is from *al-ulfa* (familiarity), since it gathers the types of numbers: the tens gather the units, the hundreds gather the tens, and the thousand gathers the hundreds.

*Al-zahzaha* (الزَّحْزَحَةُ): removal and displacement from a place of stability.

*Basir* (بَصِيرٌ): on the pattern *fa'il*, from *basura bihi* when he saw it, as in ﴿فَبَصُرَتْ بِهِ عَنْ جُنُبٍ﴾ (Al-Qasas: 11). Then it is used figuratively for the sight of the heart, which is knowledge. *Basir bi-kadha* means knowing of such and such.

﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book﴾: the discussion of this lam has been mentioned before, and it may be for emphasis, and it may be the answer to an oath. The connection of this with what precedes is that giving Moses the Book is a blessing for them, since in it are their rulings and their laws. Then they met that blessing with ingratitude, and this followed their established habit, since they were commanded with things and forbidden from things, so they opposed the command and prohibition of Allah. So the mention of this verse fits what precedes it. *Al-itaʾ* means giving. It may mean sending down, because He sent it down to him all at once. It may also mean: We made him understand what it contained of limits, rulings, reports, stories and other matters. Then it would be by omitting a modifier: We gave Moses the knowledge of the Book, or the understanding of the Book.

Moses: he is the Prophet of Allah, Musa ibn ʿImran, may Allah's blessings be upon him, upon our Prophet and upon him, and peace.

*Al-Kitab* here is the Torah, according to the view of the majority. The *alif* and *lam* in it are for definiteness, since it is associated with Moses. Its being in the accusative is because it is the second object of *atayna*. It was mentioned before that it is the first object according to al-Suhayli, and Moses is the second according to him.

(*Wa-qaffayna*) (وقَفَّيْنا): the *ya'* in it originally is a *waw*, except that whenever it occurs in the fourth position it is replaced with a *ya'*, as you say: *ghazaytu* from *al-ghazw*. The doubling in *qaffayna* is not for transitivity, because if it were for transitivity it would be transitive to two objects, since *qafawta* is transitive to one object. You say: *qafawtu Zayda*, meaning I followed him. If it came in the transitive form it would be: *wa-qaffaynahu min baʿdihi al-rusul*. That it did not come like this in the Qur'an makes it unlikely that the *ba'* is extra in the first object while the second object is omitted. Do you not see His saying: ﴿ثُمَّ قَفَّيْنا عَلى آثارِهِمْ بِرُسُلِنا وقَفَّيْنا بِعِيسى ابْنِ مَرْيَمَ﴾ (Al-Hadid: 27)? But it is taken as containing the meaning of *ji'na* (we came), as if He said: and We came after him with the messengers, some following others. And *min* in *min baʿdihi* is for the beginning of the end, and this is clear, because it is reported that Moses did not die until Yushaʿ was made a prophet.

*Bi-al-rusul* (بِالرُّسُلِ): Allah sent after the trace of Moses messengers, namely: Yushaʿ, Shamwil, Shamʿun, Dawud, Sulayman, Sha'ya, Armiya, ʿUzayr, Hazqil, Ilyas, al-Yasaʿ, Yunus, Zakariyya, Yahya, and others. The *ba'* in *bi-al-rusul* is connected to *qaffayna*. The *alif* and *lam* may be for the specific class, and they may be for definiteness, because of what is derived from the Qur'an and other sources, that these were sent after him. And the following may be metaphorical, which is that they follow him in acting by the Torah and its rulings, and they are commanded to follow it and to remain committed to it.

The majority read *al-Rusul* with a *damma* on the *sin*. Al-Hasan and Yahya ibn Yaʿmar read it with sukun, and it has been mentioned before that these are two dialects. Abu ʿAmr agreed with them if it is annexed to a plural pronoun, such as *rusulihim*, *rusulikum*, and *rusulina*, because the succession of four moving vowels is heavy, so it is made sukun for lightness.

*Wa-atayna ʿIsa ibn Maryam* (وآتَيْنا عِيسى ابْنَ مَرْيَمَ): he attributed ʿIsa to his mother as a refutation of the Jews, regarding what they attributed to him.

**(al-bayyinat)**: These are the clear proofs that point to his prophethood. This includes every miracle that Jesus, peace be upon him, was given, and this is the apparent meaning. It was also said: the Gospel. It was also said: the proofs that God established against the Jews. It was also said: healing the blind and the leper, informing of the unseen, and raising the dead. They were four: Sam, son of Noah; al-'Azir; the son of the old woman; and the daughter of al-'Ishar. And from among the birds: the bat. It was said: this was not before Jesus, but was a figure, and God breathed the spirit into it. It was also said: it existed before him, and Jesus shaped it after its likeness. They said: this particular kind of bird was singled out because no bird is more intricately formed than it, for its body is entirely flesh. God mentioned the messengers in general terms and detailed the mention of Jesus, because those before him followed the law of Moses, whereas Jesus abrogated much of the law of Moses.

**(wa-ayyadnahu)**: The majority read it in the form *fa'-'alnahu*. Mujahid, al-A'raj, Humayd, Ibn Muhaysin, Husayn, and (from Abu 'Amr) read *a'yadnahu*, in the form *af'alnahu*. The discussion of this has preceded in the section on vocabulary. Some scholars distinguished between them, saying: the form with the long vowel means "strength," while the short form means "support and victory." The more correct view is that both mean "we strengthened him," and both derive from *al-ayd*, which means strength.

* *

**(bi-ruh al-qudus)**: The reading of the majority is with a *damma* on the *qaf* and the *dal*. Mujahid and Ibn Kathir read it with a sukun on the *dal* wherever it occurs, and there is a dialect that reads it with a *fatha*. Abu Haywa read *al-quddus* with a *waw*. The "spirit" here is: the Greatest Name of God, by which Jesus, peace be upon him, used to revive the dead, as said by Ibn 'Abbas; or the Gospel, just as God named the Qur'an a spirit, as He said: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a spirit of Our command﴾ [al-Shura: 52], as said by Ibn Zayd; or the spirit that God breathed into Jesus, peace be upon him; or Jibril, peace be upon him, as said by Qatada, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak and al-Rabi'. This view is attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, as Ibn 'Atiyya said, and this is the most correct of the opinions. The Prophet ﷺ said to Hassan ibn Thabit: "Satirize the Quraysh, and the Holy Spirit is with you," and at another time he said to him: "And Jibril is with you." The end of his words. They said: this is strengthened by His saying: ﴿when I supported you with the Holy Spirit﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 110]. Hassan said:

*"Jibril is the messenger of God among us, and the Holy Spirit, for whom there is no equal."*

The naming of Jibril by this is because the predominant quality of his body is spirituality, and likewise all the angels; or because religion is revived through him, just as the body is revived by the spirit, for he is the one entrusted with bringing down revelation; or because God created him as a spirit without birth. God's support of Jesus through Jibril, peace be upon them both, was to make his proof and the matter of his religion manifest, or to repel the Jews from him when they intended to kill him, or it was throughout all his circumstances. Al-Zamakhshari chose that its meaning is: "with the holy spirit," and said: just as one says "Hatim of generosity" and "a man of truth." He described it as holy just as He said: "and a spirit from Him," thus describing it with exclusivity and nearness for honor. The end of his words. The meaning of *al-quds* has already been mentioned: that it is purity or blessing. Mujahid and al-Rabi' said: *al-quds* is one of the names of God, like *al-Quddus*. They said: the application of the word "spirit" to Jibril, to the Gospel, and to the Greatest Name of God is figurative, because the spirit is the wind that moves through the openings and passages of a human being. It is known that these three were not like that, but each of them was called "spirit" by way of comparison, in that the spirit is the cause of life: Jibril is the cause of the life of hearts through knowledge; the Gospel is the cause of the manifestation and life of the laws; and the Greatest Name is the cause of reaching the attainment of aims through it. The resemblance between Jibril and the spirit is more complete, and this naming is more evident in him; and because what is meant by "We supported him" is: We strengthened him and aided him, and the attribution of it to Jibril is literal, while its attribution to the Gospel and to the Greatest Name is figurative. And because the particularity of Jesus with Jibril is among the most emphatic forms of particularity, since no other prophet had the like of it: for he is the one who gave Maryam the good news of her son's birth, and Jesus was born by his breath, and he nurtured him in all circumstances, and he traveled with him wherever he went, and was with him when he ascended to heaven.

﴿Is it that whenever a messenger came to you with what your souls did not desire, you became arrogant?﴾: The *hamza* originally is for interrogation, and here it is for reproach and rebuke. The *fa'* is for connecting the sentence to what precedes it, and the particle of interrogation was given priority and placed first; the original is *fa-a-kullama*. It is possible that nothing is presumed before it, but rather the conjunction is with the sentences that precede it, as if he said: "And We certainly gave, O Children of Israel, what We gave you. Then whenever a messenger came to you..." It is also possible that something is presumed before it, meaning: you did what you did of denying one group and killing another group. The discussion of *kullama* has already been presented in His saying: ﴿Whenever they were provided with fruit from it﴾ [al-Baqara: 25], so there is no need to repeat it. The governing element for it is His saying: "you became arrogant." The address in "came to you" may be general to all the Children of Israel, since they shared one nature of bad character, denying the messengers, excessively questioning their prophets, and doubting and suspecting what they brought; or it may refer to their ancestors who did that, and the context of the verses indicates this; or it may refer to their descendants present in the presence of the Messenger of God ﷺ, because they were content with their deeds, and one who is content is like the doer. They denied the Messenger of God ﷺ regarding what he brought, they gave him poison to kill him, and they bewitched him. The *bi-ma* is connected to His saying "came to you"; *ma* is a relative pronoun, and the returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: "you do not desire it." Most of the usage of *al-hawa* (desire) is for what is not true, and this verse is of that kind. Desire is attributed to the souls and not to the pronoun of the addressees, so it would have been "what you do not desire," indicating that the souls are typically attributed bad deeds: ﴿Indeed, the soul is ever inciting to evil﴾ [Yusuf: 53]; ﴿So his soul permitted him the killing of his brother﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 30]; ﴿He said, "Rather, your souls have beautified for you a matter"﴾ [Yusuf: 18]. *Istakbartum* (you became arrogant): *istaf'ala* here means *tafa''ala*, which is one of the meanings of the *istaf'ala* form. The Messenger of God ﷺ defined pride as "rejecting the truth and looking down on people." The meaning is said to be: "you became arrogant regarding responding to him, out of contempt for the messenger," or "out of considering the message far-fetched." This includes the nature of arrogance that they had, which is the location of defects and the result of self-admiration. It is the result of ignorance of the self, which goes together with ignorance of the Creator. This used to recur among them as messengers came to them repeatedly. It is, as we have mentioned, arrogance in the sense of pride, and it implies affectation and effort for that, not that they become truly great and magnificent by it; rather, they practice it and do not attain its reality, because greatness belongs only to God Most High, so it is impossible for anyone else to be truly characterized by it.

﴿So a group you denied﴾: Its apparent meaning is that it is conjoined to His saying "you became arrogant," so from arrogance arose a group of messengers being hastily denied only, when they could not be killed, and a group being killed when they could be killed and the opportunity presented itself. It is implied that whoever they killed, they had also denied. He dispensed with explicitly mentioning their denial because it was known, so he mentioned their most heinous act toward him, which is killing him. Abu al-Qasim al-Raghib permitted that ﴿so a group you denied﴾ be conjoined to His saying "And We supported him," and that "Is it that whenever" together with what follows it be a separation between them in the manner of denunciation. The more apparent arrangement of the speech is the first, though this is also possible. The governing element was delayed and the object was placed first in order to harmonize the ends of the verses. There is an omitted element, its estimate being: "so a group of them you denied." He began with denial because it is the first evil they do, and because it is shared between the two groups: the denied and the killed.

﴿And a group you kill﴾: He used the verb of killing in the present tense, either because by it the past state was narrated, if it is intended and brought vividly to minds and depicted as though it were being undertaken and in progress, and because of the correspondence with the ends of verses which are the rhyming endings; or because it refers to the future, since they intended to kill the Messenger of God ﷺ, and for that reason they bewitched him and poisoned him. The Prophet ﷺ said at his death: "The morsel of Khaybar kept recurring to me, and now is the time for the severing of my aorta." In this form there is an alert that their custom was killing their prophets, because this Prophet is written among them in the Torah and the Gospel, and they were commanded to believe in him and support him, yet they intended to kill him. So how about one about whom there was no prior covenant from God? Killing him is therefore more fitting among them. Ibn 'Atiyya said concerning the Children of Israel: they used to kill three hundred prophets in a single day, and then their marketplace would be set up at the end of the day. It is narrated: seventy prophets, and then their marketplace for transporting goods would be set up at the end of the day.

﴿And they said, "Our hearts are wrapped"﴾: The pronoun in *qalu* refers to the Jews, namely the descendants of the Children of Israel who were present in the presence of the Messenger of God ﷺ. They said this out of slander and repelling, when the proofs were established against them, the clear signs appeared to them, and the miracles left them unable to resist the truth. They descended from the rank of humanity to the rank of animality. The majority read *ghulf* with a sukun on the *lam*. The discussion of the sukun on the *lam* has preceded: is it an original sukun, so that it is the plural of *aghlaf* (wrapped)? Or is it a sukun of lightening, so that it is the plural of *ghilaf* (covering), whose original is with a *damma*, like *himar* and *humur*? Ibn 'Atiyya said: here it indicates that lightening from heaviness is rarely used except in poetry. Ibn Malik stated explicitly that the sukun is permissible in forms like *humur*, the plural of *himar*, without necessity. Ibn 'Abbas, al-A'raj, Ibn Hurmuz, and Ibn Muhaysin read *ghulufun* with a *damma* on the *lam*, and it is transmitted from Abu 'Amr. It is the plural of *ghilaf*, and it cannot be in this reading the plural of *aghlaf*, because making the middle radical of the form *fu'l* heavy (with a *damma*) for a sound middle radical is permissible only in poetry. It is said: *ghallaftu al-sayf* (I covered the sword), meaning I made a sheath for it. As for the one who read *ghulfun* with sukun, its meaning is that they are concealed from understanding and discernment. Mujahid said: meaning there is a veil over them. 'Ikrima said: there is a seal upon them. Al-Zajjaj said: *dhawat ghulf*, meaning upon them are coverings which admonition cannot reach. It was also said: they were created wrapped, not reflecting and not taking heed. It was also said: they are veiled from hearing what you say and understanding what is made clear. In this reading it is possible that their saying this is by way of slander and repelling, so that they silence the Messenger of God ﷺ; and it is possible that it is a report from them about the state of their hearts, because the first would involve blaming themselves with what is not in them, whereas they were repelling by other means, and the causes of repelling are many. As for the one who read with a *damma* on the *lam*, its meaning is that they are receptacles of knowledge: they placed knowledge in the position of a tangible thing, and made the barriers that prevent them into wrappings for it, so that the sensible would be used as evidence for the intelligible. It is possible that they intended by this that they are receptacles of knowledge, so if what you say were true and sincere they would have retained it; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, and al-Suddi. It is possible that the meaning is: our hearts are wrapped, that is, filled with knowledge, so they have no room for anything, and do not need knowledge other than it, for a wrapped thing cannot have its covering receive anything else. It is possible that the meaning is: their hearts are wrapped over what is in them of their religion and their law and their belief that the permanence of their creed is until the Day of Resurrection; and they, because of its firmness and strength, prevent anything other than what is in them from reaching them, like the covering that protects the wrapped object so that what belongs to something else cannot reach it. It was also said: the meaning is like an empty covering with nothing in it.

**Bal** (indicating a shift of meaning, *al-idrab*): this is a shift away not from the statement that was made, since that statement is undeniably true and so cannot be rejected, but from the relation contained in their saying, "Their hearts are *ghulf*" (enveloped). Their hearts were created capable of accepting the truth and naturally disposed to perceive what is right, yet they described them as having a nature God did not give them. Then God informed them that they were cursed because of their previous disbelief, and He requited them with banishment from His mercy, which is the curse that results from the sin of disbelief.

**Fa-qalilan ma yu'minun** (So few do they believe): The accusative of *qalilan* (few) may be parsed in several ways.

- It is an adjective (*na't*) of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning "so they believe with a little belief." This is the view of Qatadah.
- According to Sibawayh's school, it is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*), with the implied sense "so they believe it (faith) in a state of scarcity."
- It is permitted to take it as an adjective of an omitted time expression, meaning "so for a little time they believe," based on God's words: ﴿Believe in what has been sent down to those who believed at the beginning of the day, and reject it at its end﴾ (3:72).
- It is also permitted to take it as governed by *yu'minun* itself, on the basis that the original was *fa-qalilun yu'minun*. Then, when the preposition *ba'* was dropped, the verb reached the noun directly. This is the view of Ma'mar.
- It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial accusative of the subject, the pronoun in *yu'minun*, meaning "so as a few group they believe," that is, the believers among them are few. This meaning is held by Ibn Abbas and Qatadah.

To summarise: the scarcity may refer to the verbal action itself (the *masdar*), in which case it is measured by its object, since faith is not truly described as few or many; or to the time, since before the Prophet's (ﷺ) mission it was small, being the period of seeking victory (*al-istiftah*), after which they disbelieved; or to the object of belief, since they retained only the affirmation of God in a distorted form, as they anthropomorphised Him, and they denied the Messenger and the Torah; or to the agent, since those among them who believed in the Messenger were few.

Al-Waqidi said: the meaning is "not few and not many." It is said *qalla ma yaf'alu*, meaning "he hardly does it," that is, he does not do it at all. Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning is "so they do not believe, few or many." Al-Mahdawi said: Qatadah's view is that the meaning is "so a few of them believe," and the grammarians rejected this, saying that if it were so, *qalil* would have to be nominative. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible for scarcity to mean non-existence. What they said, that *qalilan* may be used to mean pure negation, is correct, but not in this construction, namely God's words *fa-qalilan ma yu'minun*. This is because *qalilan* is governed by an affirmative verb, making it comparable to *qumtu qalilan* ("I stood a little," that is, "a brief standing"). No one should think that when you use an affirmative verb and make *qalilan* an accusative adjective of its verbal noun, the affirmative verb describes a state in which the action is entirely negated and never occurs at all. What the grammarians have transmitted is that scarcity may indeed mean pure negation, as in their sayings: *aqallu rajulin yaqulu dhalik* ("hardly any man says that"), *qalla rajulun yaqulu dhalik*, *qallama yaqumu Zayd* ("Zayd hardly ever stands"), *qalilun min al-rijal yaqulu dhalik* ("few of the men say that"), and *qalilatun min al-nisa' taqulu dhalik* ("few of the women say that").

Given this, taking scarcity here to mean pure negation is not correct. As for what al-Mahdawi reported of Qatadah's view, and the grammarians' rejection of it and their claim that it would require *qalilun* in the nominative, Qatadah's view is correct and the grammarians' objection does not apply. Qatadah was only explaining the meaning and clarifying it; he did not intend to give a grammatical analysis (*sharh al-i'rab*), so that the objection would not bind him. In his view, *qalilan* is a circumstantial accusative of the pronoun in *yu'minun*, and the meaning is: "so they believe as a small group," that is, in a state of scarcity. This means: "so few of them believe."

The *ma* in *ma yu'minun* is a superfluous, emphasising particle (*za'idah mu'akkidah*), inserted between the governed element and the governing verb. It is comparable to the Arab saying *ruwaydan ma al-shi'r* ("slowly, the poetry"), and the line *kharraja ma anifa khatibun bidam* ("the speaker, who was disdainful, brought out what had been blood" [in a poetic usage]). It is not permissible for *ma* to be a verbal (*masdariyya*) particle, because then *qalilun* would have to be nominative so that the two together would form a nominal sentence with subject and predicate.

Of all these meanings, the best is the first: that the meaning is "so they believe with a little belief," because the verb indicates its verbal noun more strongly than it indicates time, state, object, or agent. It also agrees with the apparent sense of God's words: ﴿So they do not believe, except a few﴾ (4:46).

As for the Arabic saying *marartu bi-ardin qalilan ma tunbitu* ("I passed by a land that hardly produces anything") and the claim that they mean "it produces nothing," this is because *qalilan* is a circumstantial accusative of *ardin* (land), even though *ardin* is indefinite, and *ma* is verbal, with the implied sense "its producing being few," that is, it produces nothing at all. *Ma* is not superfluous here, and *qalil* is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun. The implied construction is "it produces a little [production]." If the construction were this, then scarcity could not mean pure negation, because your saying "it produces a little" does not indicate the total absence of production. Similarly, if we said "I struck a little striking," it would not mean "I did not strike at all."

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 90–91 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And when there came to them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89]: The pronoun refers to the Jews. It was revealed concerning them when Ghatafan were fighting and defeating them, or when they were suffering much harm from the Arabs, or when al-Aws and al-Khazraj fought them and overcame them.

(*Kitab*): It is the Qur'an, and attributing the "coming" to it is a figurative usage (*majaz*, a non-literal expression).

﴿from Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89]: This is in the position of a qualifier. Describing it as "from Allah" makes it worthy of being accepted, followed, and acted upon in its content, since it has come from their Creator and their God, who watches over their interests.

(p-303) (*Musaddiq*, "confirming"): This is a second qualifier, and the first was placed before it, because describing it by its being from Allah is more emphatic, while describing it as confirming arises from its being from Allah. It cannot be said that "from Allah" [al-Baqarah: 89] may be connected to "came to them," so that it would not be a qualifier, since that would place something that belongs to neither of the two between the qualifier and the qualified. In the codex of Ubayy it is *musaddiqan* (in the accusative), and Ibn Abi Abla recited it so. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from *kitab*, even though *kitab* is indefinite. Sibawayh permitted this without condition, since it has been specified by the qualifier and has thus come close to being definite.

﴿confirming what is with them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89]: This refers to the Torah and the Gospel. Its confirmation is either by both being from Allah, or by what they both contain of the mention of the sending of the Messenger and his description.

(*Wa kanu*, "and they had been"): It is permissible for it to be coordinated with *ja'ahum* ("came to them"), so that the answer to *lamma* ("when") is ordered upon the coming and the being. It is also possible that it is a circumstantial nominal clause, meaning "and they had already been," so that the answer is ordered upon the coming with a restriction on its object, namely their state of seeking victory. The apparent meaning of al-Zamakhshari's words is that his statement *wa kanu* is not coordinated with the verb after *lamma*, nor is it a circumstantial clause, because he estimated the answer of *lamma* to be an omitted element before its explanation, *yastaftihuna* ("seeking victory"). This indicates that his statement *wa kanu* is a clause coordinated with the whole clause beginning with *wa lamma*.

(*Min qablu*, "before"): That is, before the coming. It is built (on the final vowel) because it has been cut off from being added to a definite noun.

﴿seeking victory﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89]: That is, seeking to be firmly established, or seeking knowledge, or seeking help. These are three opinions. When the enemy attacked them, they would say: "O Allah, give us victory over them through the Prophet sent at the end of time, whose description we find in the Torah." They differed concerning the answer of the first *lamma*. Al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj held that it is omitted because the meaning indicates it, and al-Zamakhshari chose this view and estimated it as something like: "They denied him and treated the coming of him lightly." Others estimated it as: "They disbelieved," so that it was omitted because of the indication of "they disbelieved in it." The meaning is close in this. Al-Farra' held that the *fa'* in His words ﴿So when there came to them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89] is the answer of the first *lamma*, and *kafaru* ("they disbelieved") is the answer to His words *fa-lamma ja'ahum* ("so when there came to them"). In his view, this is similar to His words ﴿Then if there comes to you guidance from Me, whoever follows My guidance will have no fear﴾ [al-Baqarah: 38]. He said: What indicates that the *fa'* here is not coordinating is that the *wa* ("and") cannot fit in its place. Al-Mubarrad held that the answer of the first *lamma* is *kafaru bihi* ("they disbelieved in it"), and *lamma* was repeated because of the length of the speech. This repetition confirms and emphasizes the sin. This view would be the best, were it not that the *fa'* prevents emphasis. As for al-Farra's view, it has not been established in their speech: "*lamma ja'a Zayd, fa-lamma ja'a Khalid aqbala Ja'far*" is a structure not found in their language, so we do not affirm it, and there is no proof in this disputed matter. The best view is that the answer is omitted because the meaning indicates it, and the estimate is: "And when there came to them a Book from Allah confirming what is with them, they denied it," and the denial takes place by the very coming of the Book, without reflection or deliberation, but they hastened to deny it. Then He, exalted, said: ﴿And they had been seeking victory before﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89], that is, seeking victory over the polytheists when they fought them, or opening (the way) against them and informing them that a prophet was going to be sent, whose time of being sent had drawn near, and so they would give this news.

﴿So when there came to them what they recognized﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89]: And what had previously been made known to them of it, to the polytheists.

﴿they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89]: They concealed it and denied it. This is more forceful in censuring them, because the thing that is known to them, settled in their hearts and in the hearts of those whom they informed of it, its existence and description, they deliberately conceal it and deny it. Allah, exalted, said: ﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of injustice and arrogance﴾ [al-Naml: 14]. Abu al-Qasim al-Raghib said, in a summary of what he said: *al-istiftah* is the seeking of opening, and it is of two kinds: divine, which is victory by reaching the knowledge that leads to reward, and from it is His words ﴿Indeed, We have opened for you﴾ [al-Fath: 1], and (*fa-'asa an ya'ti bil-fath*, "perhaps He will bring the victory"). And worldly, which is victory by reaching bodily pleasures, and from it is His words ﴿Then We opened for them the gates of everything﴾ [al-An'am: 44]. So the meaning of *yastaftihuna* is that they would know its news from people at one time, and they would derive its mention from the books at another time. It was also said: they would ask Allah for victory by mentioning it. It was also said: they would say, "We will be given victory through Muhammad ﷺ over the worshippers of idols." All of these are included in the generality of *al-istiftah*. End of quotation. The apparent meaning of His words *ma 'arafu* ("what they recognized") is that it is the Book, since He used the word *ma*. It is possible that what is meant is the Prophet ﷺ, for *ma* may be used to express the attributes of one who has intellect. It is also permissible that the meaning is: what they recognized of the truth, so that the recognition of his prophethood, his law, his book, and what it contains is included in it.

﴿So the curse of Allah is upon the disbelievers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89]: Since the Book came to them from Allah, and they denied it and concealed what they had previously recognized, this amounted to treating both the sender and what was sent with contempt. Allah met them with contempt and expulsion. He attributed the curse to Allah, exalted, as a form of emphasis, because the one whom Allah, exalted, curses is truly the one cursed.

﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that as a recompense from Allah? Whom Allah has cursed﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 60]? ﴿And whoever Allah curses, you will not find for him a helper﴾ [al-Nisa': 52]. Then He did not suffice with the curse until He made it dominant over them, as if it were something that came down upon them from above, and so He covered them with it. Then He drew attention to the cause and reason for the curse, which is disbelief, as He said before: ﴿Rather, Allah has cursed them for their disbelief﴾ [al-Baqarah: 88]. He placed the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun for this meaning. Thus the *alif* and *lam* (of *al-kafirin*) is either for previous reference (*al-'ahd*), or for generality (*al-'umum*), so that these people are one individual among the individuals of the generality. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that it is for the genus (*al-jins*), and that they enter into it as the first entrants. By "genus" we mean the generality. His imagining that they enter it as the first entrants is nothing, because the indication of the cause on its individuals does not favor some individuals over others; rather, it indicates each and every individual equally. When the indication is equal, there is nothing that is first or prior to another.

﴿Evil is that for which they sold themselves﴾: The discussion of *bi'sa* ("evil is") has already preceded. As for *ma* in it, scholars have differed about whether it has a place in grammatical structure (*i'rab*) or not. Al-Farra' held that the whole thing with *bi'sa* is one unit that has been compounded, like *habbadha* ("how excellent"). This is the report of Ibn 'Atiyyah from him. Al-Mahdawi said: Al-Farra' said: It is permissible that *ma* with *bi'sa* is in the position of *kullama* ("whenever"). The apparent meaning of these two reports is that *ma* has no place in grammatical structure. The majority held that it has a place in grammatical structure. They differed over whether its place is in the accusative or the nominative. Al-Akhfash held that its place is in the accusative as a specification (*tamyiz*, a noun clarifying an ambiguity), and the clause after it is in the position of the accusative as a qualifier, and the subject of *bi'sa* is a pronoun explained by *ma*. The estimate is: "Evil is it, a thing that they sold themselves for," and *an yakfuru* ("that they disbelieve") is the one praised or censured. Al-Farisi, in one of his two views, said this too, and al-Zamakhshari chose it. It is possible on this view that the one censured is an omitted element, and *ishtaraw* is a qualifier of it, and the estimate is: "Evil is a thing, a thing that they sold themselves for," and *an yakfuru* is an apposition (*badal*) from that omitted element, so it is in the position of the nominative, or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, whose estimate is: "It is that they disbelieve." Al-Kisa'i, in one of his two views, went to what these scholars went to, that *ma* has the place of the accusative as a specification, and there is another omitted *ma*, a relative pronoun, which is the one censured, and the estimate is: "Evil is a thing, the one that they sold themselves for." So the clause after the omitted *ma* is a relative clause (*silah*) for it, and so it has no place in grammatical structure (p-305). *An yakfuru*, on this view, is an apposition, and it is permissible on this view that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, that is, "it is their disbelief." So three views are summarized concerning the accusative reading of the clause after *ma*: that it is a qualifier of this *ma* which is a specification, so its place is the accusative; or that it is a relative clause of an omitted relative *ma*, so it has no place; or that it is a qualifier of the omitted thing that is the object of the censure, so its place is the nominative. Sibawayh went to the view that its place is the nominative, on the basis that it is the subject of *bi'sa*. Sibawayh said: it is a complete definite noun, and the estimate is: "Evil is the thing," and the one censured on this view is omitted, that is, "a thing that they sold themselves for." This view, namely that *ma* is a complete definite noun and not a relative pronoun, has been attributed to al-Kisa'i. Al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i said, as is reported from them, that *ma* is a relative pronoun with the meaning of *alladhi* ("that which"), and *ishtaraw* is the relative clause, and al-Farisi said this in one of his views. Ibn 'Atiyyah attributed this view to Sibawayh, and said: So the estimate on this view is: "Evil is that which they sold themselves for, that they disbelieve," like your saying: "Evil is the man Zayd," and *ma* in this view is a relative pronoun. End of his words. This is a mistake on the part of Sibawayh. Al-Kisa'i, as al-Mahdawi and Ibn 'Atiyyah reported from him, went to the view that *ma* and what follows it have the place of the nominative, on the basis that it is a verbal noun (*masdariyyah*). The estimate is: "Evil is their buying." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is objectionable, because *bi'sa* does not come before a specific noun that is defined by being added to a pronoun. End of his words. What he said applies only if it is stated that it is in the nominative as the subject of *bi'sa*. But if it is made the one censured, and the subject of *bi'sa* is made a pronoun and the specification is omitted, the meaning is understood. The estimate is: "Evil is a buying, their buying," so the objection does not apply. However, the second view is refuted by the return of the pronoun in *bihi* ("by it") to *ma*, while the verbal *ma* does not have a pronoun returning to it, because according to the majority's view it is a particle, since al-Akhfash claims that it is a noun. The discussion of these views, in establishing or refuting them, is mentioned in the science of grammar (*nahw*).

*Ishtaraw* ("they sold") here means "they sold." It has already been mentioned that he said: *shara* and *ishtara* mean *baa'a* ("sold"), and this is the view of most scholars. In al-Muntakhab: The purchasing here is in its ordinary sense, because the obligated person, when he fears punishment for himself, performs deeds that he thinks will save him, and it is as if he has bought himself by them. These Jews, when they believed about what they had done that it would save them, thought that they had bought themselves, so Allah censured them for it. He said: This view is closer to the meaning and the wording than the first, meaning by the first that it means "sold." What the author of al-Muntakhab chose is refuted by His words, exalted: ﴿out of envy that Allah should send down of His bounty upon whomever He wills of His servants﴾, which indicates that what is meant is not their purchasing themselves by disbelief, thinking that they would escape punishment, but rather that this was out of rebellion and envy, because He, exalted, placed that (Revelation) in Muhammad ﷺ. It has become clear that the view of the majority is more preferable.

﴿that they disbelieve﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89]: It has preceded that its place is the nominative, either as a predicate of an omitted subject, or as the one censured according to the one who makes what precedes it, His words ﴿Evil is that for which they sold﴾, incomplete. Among its grammatical views are those that apply to the one censured when it comes after: is it a subject (*mubtada'*) with the clause before it as the predicate of an omitted subject, as was established earlier? Al-Farra' permitted, on this estimate, that it be an apposition for the pronoun in *bihi*, so it has the place of a predicate.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 90–91 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Bi-mā anzala Allāh﴾ (with what Allah has sent down): This refers to the Book previously mentioned, which is the Qur'an. In this there is a degree of magnification, even though no pronoun is used. Rather, it is stated explicitly as a relative clause with the verb anzala (sent down), which conveys that it comes from the higher realm, and its attribution is made to Allah, so that there is agreement in meaning between His words ﴿a Book from Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:89] and His words ﴿with what Allah has sent down﴾. It is also possible that what is meant is the Torah and the Gospel, since they disbelieved in ʿIsā and in Muhammad (peace and blessings of Allah be upon them both), and disbelief in either of them is disbelief in the Torah. It is also possible that what is meant is all of them: the Qur'an, the Gospel and the Torah, since disbelief in part of them is disbelief in all of them.

(baghyan): That is, out of envy, since they were not from the Children of Israel. This was said by Qatadah, Abu al-ʿĀliyah and al-Suddi. It was also said that its meaning is injustice (ẓulman). Its accusative case is as an object of purpose (mafʿūl min ajlihi), and its apparent governing verb is yakfurū, meaning their disbelief was on account of envy. al-Zamakhshari said: it is the cause of ishtarau, so according to his view the governing word is ishtarau. It was also said: it is an accusative as an infinitive absolute (maṣdar), not an object of purpose, and the estimated form is baghaw baghyan, with the verb omitted (p-306) because the context indicates it.

﴿An yunazzila Allāh﴾ (that Allah should send down): an-with the verb forms a verbal noun (maṣdar) by interpretation, and that estimated verbal noun is in the accusative as an object of purpose, meaning they transgressed for the sake of Allah's sending down. It was also said: the estimate is baghyan ʿalā an yunazzila Allāh, because its meaning is envy at Allah's sending down, that is, at what Allah bestowed upon His Prophet of revelation; so ʿalā was omitted. Here arises the disagreement regarding anna and an, when the preposition is omitted from them: are they in a position of accusative or of genitive? It was also said: an yunazzila is in the genitive position as a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) for mā in His words bi-mā anzala Allāh, meaning bi-tanzīl Allāh, and this is like the saying of the poet:

Amin dhikri Salmā an nataka tanūṣ?

Abu ʿAmr and Ibn Kathir recited all the imperfect forms from anzala with a light (takhfīf) pronunciation, except those on which there is consensus regarding their doubling (tashdīd), which is in al-Hijr: ﴿wa-mā nunazziluhu﴾ [al-Hijr 15:21]. However, Abu ʿAmr doubled "ʿalā an nunazzila āyatan" in al-Anʿām, and Ibn Kathir doubled ﴿wa-nunazzilu min al-Qurʾān mā huwa shifāʾ﴾ [al-Isra' 17:82] and ﴿ḥattā tunazzila ʿalaynā kitāban﴾ [al-Isra' 17:93]. The rest doubled the imperfect wherever it occurs, except Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī, who lightened, in ﴿wa-yunazzilu al-ghayth﴾ [Luqman 31:34] at the end of Luqman, and ﴿wa-huwa alladhī yunazzilu al-ghayth﴾ [al-Shura 42:28] in al-Shura. Both the hamzah and the doubling are, each of them, for causative transitivity. They have mentioned correspondences for the readings of the reciters and their choices, but these are not sound.

﴿min faḍlihi﴾ (from His bounty): min indicates the starting point (ibtidāʾ al-ghāya), and faḍl here means revelation and prophethood. Some have permitted that min be extra (zāʾidah) according to the view of al-Akhfash, so that it is in the position of the object, meaning that Allah sends down His bounty.

﴿ʿalā man yashāʾ﴾ (upon whomever He wills): ʿalā is connected to yunazzilu. What is meant by man yashāʾ is Muhammad (ﷺ), because they envied him when he was not from them and was from the Arabs. The honour of prophethood from Yaʿqub to ʿIsā (peace be upon them) was in Ishaq, so it was concluded with ʿIsā, and there was no prophet from the descendants of Isma'il other than our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), so prophethood was sealed for others, and they lost honour and bounty. Here man is a relative pronoun, and it was said to be an indefinite qualified noun. yashāʾ according to the first view is a relative clause, so it has no place in the grammar, and according to the second view it is a qualifier, so it is in the genitive position, and the returning pronoun to the relative or qualified noun is omitted, its estimate being yashāʾūhu.

﴿min ʿibādihi﴾ (from among His servants): a prepositional phrase in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), its estimate being "being from among His servants." He attributed the servants to Himself as an honour to them, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and He does not approve for His servants disbelief﴾ [al-Zumar 39:7], and ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:23].

﴿fa-bāʾū﴾ (so they returned): that is, they went, and the meaning of bāʾū has already been mentioned.

﴿bi-ghaḍabin ʿalā ghaḍab﴾ (with wrath upon wrath): that is, successive and multiplied, and this indicates the intensification of the state upon them. It was also said that what is meant by this is two angers, each explained by two stories: the first anger was for the worship of the calf, and the second for their disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ); this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. Or the first is their disbelief in the Gospel, and the second their disbelief in the Qur'an; this was said by Qatadah. Or the first is their disbelief in ʿIsā, and the second their disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ); this was said by al-Hasan and others. Or the first is their saying "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah" and their saying "the hand of Allah is chained," and other kinds of their disbelief, and the second is their disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿wa-li-l-kāfirīna ʿadhābun muhīn﴾ (and for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment): The alif and lam in al-kāfirīn are for specific reference (ʿahd), and the explicit noun was placed in the position of the pronoun, to indicate the reason why the humiliating punishment is for them; for if it had said "and for them is a humiliating punishment," there would be no indication of the cause. Or the alif and lam are for generality, so that they are included among the disbelievers. He described the punishment with humiliation, which is abasement, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and let a group of the believers witness their punishment﴾ [al-Nur 24:2]. It came in the Sahih, in the hadith of ʿUbadah, when he mentioned forbidden things and said: "Whoever commits any of these and is punished for it, then it is an expiation for him." So this punishment is only for the expiation of misdeeds, or because it entails eternal abiding that never ends, or because of its severity, greatness and variety of kinds, or because it is a recompense for their arrogance in not following the truth. The Kharijites have argued by this verse that the grave sinner is a disbeliever, since his punishment is established; and the Murji'ah have argued by it that the grave sinner is not punished, since he is not a disbeliever.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 90–91 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And when there came to them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89]: The pronoun refers to the Jews. It was revealed concerning them when Ghatafan were fighting and defeating them, or when they were suffering much harm from the Arabs, or when al-Aws and al-Khazraj fought them and overcame them.

(*Kitab*): It is the Qur'an, and attributing the "coming" to it is a figurative usage (*majaz*, a non-literal expression).

﴿from Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89]: This is in the position of a qualifier. Describing it as "from Allah" makes it worthy of being accepted, followed, and acted upon in its content, since it has come from their Creator and their God, who watches over their interests.

(p-303) (*Musaddiq*, "confirming"): This is a second qualifier, and the first was placed before it, because describing it by its being from Allah is more emphatic, while describing it as confirming arises from its being from Allah. It cannot be said that "from Allah" [al-Baqarah: 89] may be connected to "came to them," so that it would not be a qualifier, since that would place something that belongs to neither of the two between the qualifier and the qualified. In the codex of Ubayy it is *musaddiqan* (in the accusative), and Ibn Abi Abla recited it so. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from *kitab*, even though *kitab* is indefinite. Sibawayh permitted this without condition, since it has been specified by the qualifier and has thus come close to being definite.

﴿confirming what is with them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89]: This refers to the Torah and the Gospel. Its confirmation is either by both being from Allah, or by what they both contain of the mention of the sending of the Messenger and his description.

(*Wa kanu*, "and they had been"): It is permissible for it to be coordinated with *ja'ahum* ("came to them"), so that the answer to *lamma* ("when") is ordered upon the coming and the being. It is also possible that it is a circumstantial nominal clause, meaning "and they had already been," so that the answer is ordered upon the coming with a restriction on its object, namely their state of seeking victory. The apparent meaning of al-Zamakhshari's words is that his statement *wa kanu* is not coordinated with the verb after *lamma*, nor is it a circumstantial clause, because he estimated the answer of *lamma* to be an omitted element before its explanation, *yastaftihuna* ("seeking victory"). This indicates that his statement *wa kanu* is a clause coordinated with the whole clause beginning with *wa lamma*.

(*Min qablu*, "before"): That is, before the coming. It is built (on the final vowel) because it has been cut off from being added to a definite noun.

﴿seeking victory﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89]: That is, seeking to be firmly established, or seeking knowledge, or seeking help. These are three opinions. When the enemy attacked them, they would say: "O Allah, give us victory over them through the Prophet sent at the end of time, whose description we find in the Torah." They differed concerning the answer of the first *lamma*. Al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj held that it is omitted because the meaning indicates it, and al-Zamakhshari chose this view and estimated it as something like: "They denied him and treated the coming of him lightly." Others estimated it as: "They disbelieved," so that it was omitted because of the indication of "they disbelieved in it." The meaning is close in this. Al-Farra' held that the *fa'* in His words ﴿So when there came to them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89] is the answer of the first *lamma*, and *kafaru* ("they disbelieved") is the answer to His words *fa-lamma ja'ahum* ("so when there came to them"). In his view, this is similar to His words ﴿Then if there comes to you guidance from Me, whoever follows My guidance will have no fear﴾ [al-Baqarah: 38]. He said: What indicates that the *fa'* here is not coordinating is that the *wa* ("and") cannot fit in its place. Al-Mubarrad held that the answer of the first *lamma* is *kafaru bihi* ("they disbelieved in it"), and *lamma* was repeated because of the length of the speech. This repetition confirms and emphasizes the sin. This view would be the best, were it not that the *fa'* prevents emphasis. As for al-Farra's view, it has not been established in their speech: "*lamma ja'a Zayd, fa-lamma ja'a Khalid aqbala Ja'far*" is a structure not found in their language, so we do not affirm it, and there is no proof in this disputed matter. The best view is that the answer is omitted because the meaning indicates it, and the estimate is: "And when there came to them a Book from Allah confirming what is with them, they denied it," and the denial takes place by the very coming of the Book, without reflection or deliberation, but they hastened to deny it. Then He, exalted, said: ﴿And they had been seeking victory before﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89], that is, seeking victory over the polytheists when they fought them, or opening (the way) against them and informing them that a prophet was going to be sent, whose time of being sent had drawn near, and so they would give this news.

﴿So when there came to them what they recognized﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89]: And what had previously been made known to them of it, to the polytheists.

﴿they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89]: They concealed it and denied it. This is more forceful in censuring them, because the thing that is known to them, settled in their hearts and in the hearts of those whom they informed of it, its existence and description, they deliberately conceal it and deny it. Allah, exalted, said: ﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of injustice and arrogance﴾ [al-Naml: 14]. Abu al-Qasim al-Raghib said, in a summary of what he said: *al-istiftah* is the seeking of opening, and it is of two kinds: divine, which is victory by reaching the knowledge that leads to reward, and from it is His words ﴿Indeed, We have opened for you﴾ [al-Fath: 1], and (*fa-'asa an ya'ti bil-fath*, "perhaps He will bring the victory"). And worldly, which is victory by reaching bodily pleasures, and from it is His words ﴿Then We opened for them the gates of everything﴾ [al-An'am: 44]. So the meaning of *yastaftihuna* is that they would know its news from people at one time, and they would derive its mention from the books at another time. It was also said: they would ask Allah for victory by mentioning it. It was also said: they would say, "We will be given victory through Muhammad ﷺ over the worshippers of idols." All of these are included in the generality of *al-istiftah*. End of quotation. The apparent meaning of His words *ma 'arafu* ("what they recognized") is that it is the Book, since He used the word *ma*. It is possible that what is meant is the Prophet ﷺ, for *ma* may be used to express the attributes of one who has intellect. It is also permissible that the meaning is: what they recognized of the truth, so that the recognition of his prophethood, his law, his book, and what it contains is included in it.

﴿So the curse of Allah is upon the disbelievers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89]: Since the Book came to them from Allah, and they denied it and concealed what they had previously recognized, this amounted to treating both the sender and what was sent with contempt. Allah met them with contempt and expulsion. He attributed the curse to Allah, exalted, as a form of emphasis, because the one whom Allah, exalted, curses is truly the one cursed.

﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that as a recompense from Allah? Whom Allah has cursed﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 60]? ﴿And whoever Allah curses, you will not find for him a helper﴾ [al-Nisa': 52]. Then He did not suffice with the curse until He made it dominant over them, as if it were something that came down upon them from above, and so He covered them with it. Then He drew attention to the cause and reason for the curse, which is disbelief, as He said before: ﴿Rather, Allah has cursed them for their disbelief﴾ [al-Baqarah: 88]. He placed the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun for this meaning. Thus the *alif* and *lam* (of *al-kafirin*) is either for previous reference (*al-'ahd*), or for generality (*al-'umum*), so that these people are one individual among the individuals of the generality. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that it is for the genus (*al-jins*), and that they enter into it as the first entrants. By "genus" we mean the generality. His imagining that they enter it as the first entrants is nothing, because the indication of the cause on its individuals does not favor some individuals over others; rather, it indicates each and every individual equally. When the indication is equal, there is nothing that is first or prior to another.

﴿Evil is that for which they sold themselves﴾: The discussion of *bi'sa* ("evil is") has already preceded. As for *ma* in it, scholars have differed about whether it has a place in grammatical structure (*i'rab*) or not. Al-Farra' held that the whole thing with *bi'sa* is one unit that has been compounded, like *habbadha* ("how excellent"). This is the report of Ibn 'Atiyyah from him. Al-Mahdawi said: Al-Farra' said: It is permissible that *ma* with *bi'sa* is in the position of *kullama* ("whenever"). The apparent meaning of these two reports is that *ma* has no place in grammatical structure. The majority held that it has a place in grammatical structure. They differed over whether its place is in the accusative or the nominative. Al-Akhfash held that its place is in the accusative as a specification (*tamyiz*, a noun clarifying an ambiguity), and the clause after it is in the position of the accusative as a qualifier, and the subject of *bi'sa* is a pronoun explained by *ma*. The estimate is: "Evil is it, a thing that they sold themselves for," and *an yakfuru* ("that they disbelieve") is the one praised or censured. Al-Farisi, in one of his two views, said this too, and al-Zamakhshari chose it. It is possible on this view that the one censured is an omitted element, and *ishtaraw* is a qualifier of it, and the estimate is: "Evil is a thing, a thing that they sold themselves for," and *an yakfuru* is an apposition (*badal*) from that omitted element, so it is in the position of the nominative, or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, whose estimate is: "It is that they disbelieve." Al-Kisa'i, in one of his two views, went to what these scholars went to, that *ma* has the place of the accusative as a specification, and there is another omitted *ma*, a relative pronoun, which is the one censured, and the estimate is: "Evil is a thing, the one that they sold themselves for." So the clause after the omitted *ma* is a relative clause (*silah*) for it, and so it has no place in grammatical structure (p-305). *An yakfuru*, on this view, is an apposition, and it is permissible on this view that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, that is, "it is their disbelief." So three views are summarized concerning the accusative reading of the clause after *ma*: that it is a qualifier of this *ma* which is a specification, so its place is the accusative; or that it is a relative clause of an omitted relative *ma*, so it has no place; or that it is a qualifier of the omitted thing that is the object of the censure, so its place is the nominative. Sibawayh went to the view that its place is the nominative, on the basis that it is the subject of *bi'sa*. Sibawayh said: it is a complete definite noun, and the estimate is: "Evil is the thing," and the one censured on this view is omitted, that is, "a thing that they sold themselves for." This view, namely that *ma* is a complete definite noun and not a relative pronoun, has been attributed to al-Kisa'i. Al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i said, as is reported from them, that *ma* is a relative pronoun with the meaning of *alladhi* ("that which"), and *ishtaraw* is the relative clause, and al-Farisi said this in one of his views. Ibn 'Atiyyah attributed this view to Sibawayh, and said: So the estimate on this view is: "Evil is that which they sold themselves for, that they disbelieve," like your saying: "Evil is the man Zayd," and *ma* in this view is a relative pronoun. End of his words. This is a mistake on the part of Sibawayh. Al-Kisa'i, as al-Mahdawi and Ibn 'Atiyyah reported from him, went to the view that *ma* and what follows it have the place of the nominative, on the basis that it is a verbal noun (*masdariyyah*). The estimate is: "Evil is their buying." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is objectionable, because *bi'sa* does not come before a specific noun that is defined by being added to a pronoun. End of his words. What he said applies only if it is stated that it is in the nominative as the subject of *bi'sa*. But if it is made the one censured, and the subject of *bi'sa* is made a pronoun and the specification is omitted, the meaning is understood. The estimate is: "Evil is a buying, their buying," so the objection does not apply. However, the second view is refuted by the return of the pronoun in *bihi* ("by it") to *ma*, while the verbal *ma* does not have a pronoun returning to it, because according to the majority's view it is a particle, since al-Akhfash claims that it is a noun. The discussion of these views, in establishing or refuting them, is mentioned in the science of grammar (*nahw*).

*Ishtaraw* ("they sold") here means "they sold." It has already been mentioned that he said: *shara* and *ishtara* mean *baa'a* ("sold"), and this is the view of most scholars. In al-Muntakhab: The purchasing here is in its ordinary sense, because the obligated person, when he fears punishment for himself, performs deeds that he thinks will save him, and it is as if he has bought himself by them. These Jews, when they believed about what they had done that it would save them, thought that they had bought themselves, so Allah censured them for it. He said: This view is closer to the meaning and the wording than the first, meaning by the first that it means "sold." What the author of al-Muntakhab chose is refuted by His words, exalted: ﴿out of envy that Allah should send down of His bounty upon whomever He wills of His servants﴾, which indicates that what is meant is not their purchasing themselves by disbelief, thinking that they would escape punishment, but rather that this was out of rebellion and envy, because He, exalted, placed that (Revelation) in Muhammad ﷺ. It has become clear that the view of the majority is more preferable.

﴿that they disbelieve﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89]: It has preceded that its place is the nominative, either as a predicate of an omitted subject, or as the one censured according to the one who makes what precedes it, His words ﴿Evil is that for which they sold﴾, incomplete. Among its grammatical views are those that apply to the one censured when it comes after: is it a subject (*mubtada'*) with the clause before it as the predicate of an omitted subject, as was established earlier? Al-Farra' permitted, on this estimate, that it be an apposition for the pronoun in *bihi*, so it has the place of a predicate.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 90–91 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Bi-mā anzala Allāh﴾ (with what Allah has sent down): This refers to the Book previously mentioned, which is the Qur'an. In this there is a degree of magnification, even though no pronoun is used. Rather, it is stated explicitly as a relative clause with the verb anzala (sent down), which conveys that it comes from the higher realm, and its attribution is made to Allah, so that there is agreement in meaning between His words ﴿a Book from Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:89] and His words ﴿with what Allah has sent down﴾. It is also possible that what is meant is the Torah and the Gospel, since they disbelieved in ʿIsā and in Muhammad (peace and blessings of Allah be upon them both), and disbelief in either of them is disbelief in the Torah. It is also possible that what is meant is all of them: the Qur'an, the Gospel and the Torah, since disbelief in part of them is disbelief in all of them.

(baghyan): That is, out of envy, since they were not from the Children of Israel. This was said by Qatadah, Abu al-ʿĀliyah and al-Suddi. It was also said that its meaning is injustice (ẓulman). Its accusative case is as an object of purpose (mafʿūl min ajlihi), and its apparent governing verb is yakfurū, meaning their disbelief was on account of envy. al-Zamakhshari said: it is the cause of ishtarau, so according to his view the governing word is ishtarau. It was also said: it is an accusative as an infinitive absolute (maṣdar), not an object of purpose, and the estimated form is baghaw baghyan, with the verb omitted (p-306) because the context indicates it.

﴿An yunazzila Allāh﴾ (that Allah should send down): an-with the verb forms a verbal noun (maṣdar) by interpretation, and that estimated verbal noun is in the accusative as an object of purpose, meaning they transgressed for the sake of Allah's sending down. It was also said: the estimate is baghyan ʿalā an yunazzila Allāh, because its meaning is envy at Allah's sending down, that is, at what Allah bestowed upon His Prophet of revelation; so ʿalā was omitted. Here arises the disagreement regarding anna and an, when the preposition is omitted from them: are they in a position of accusative or of genitive? It was also said: an yunazzila is in the genitive position as a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) for mā in His words bi-mā anzala Allāh, meaning bi-tanzīl Allāh, and this is like the saying of the poet:

Amin dhikri Salmā an nataka tanūṣ?

Abu ʿAmr and Ibn Kathir recited all the imperfect forms from anzala with a light (takhfīf) pronunciation, except those on which there is consensus regarding their doubling (tashdīd), which is in al-Hijr: ﴿wa-mā nunazziluhu﴾ [al-Hijr 15:21]. However, Abu ʿAmr doubled "ʿalā an nunazzila āyatan" in al-Anʿām, and Ibn Kathir doubled ﴿wa-nunazzilu min al-Qurʾān mā huwa shifāʾ﴾ [al-Isra' 17:82] and ﴿ḥattā tunazzila ʿalaynā kitāban﴾ [al-Isra' 17:93]. The rest doubled the imperfect wherever it occurs, except Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī, who lightened, in ﴿wa-yunazzilu al-ghayth﴾ [Luqman 31:34] at the end of Luqman, and ﴿wa-huwa alladhī yunazzilu al-ghayth﴾ [al-Shura 42:28] in al-Shura. Both the hamzah and the doubling are, each of them, for causative transitivity. They have mentioned correspondences for the readings of the reciters and their choices, but these are not sound.

﴿min faḍlihi﴾ (from His bounty): min indicates the starting point (ibtidāʾ al-ghāya), and faḍl here means revelation and prophethood. Some have permitted that min be extra (zāʾidah) according to the view of al-Akhfash, so that it is in the position of the object, meaning that Allah sends down His bounty.

﴿ʿalā man yashāʾ﴾ (upon whomever He wills): ʿalā is connected to yunazzilu. What is meant by man yashāʾ is Muhammad (ﷺ), because they envied him when he was not from them and was from the Arabs. The honour of prophethood from Yaʿqub to ʿIsā (peace be upon them) was in Ishaq, so it was concluded with ʿIsā, and there was no prophet from the descendants of Isma'il other than our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), so prophethood was sealed for others, and they lost honour and bounty. Here man is a relative pronoun, and it was said to be an indefinite qualified noun. yashāʾ according to the first view is a relative clause, so it has no place in the grammar, and according to the second view it is a qualifier, so it is in the genitive position, and the returning pronoun to the relative or qualified noun is omitted, its estimate being yashāʾūhu.

﴿min ʿibādihi﴾ (from among His servants): a prepositional phrase in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), its estimate being "being from among His servants." He attributed the servants to Himself as an honour to them, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and He does not approve for His servants disbelief﴾ [al-Zumar 39:7], and ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:23].

﴿fa-bāʾū﴾ (so they returned): that is, they went, and the meaning of bāʾū has already been mentioned.

﴿bi-ghaḍabin ʿalā ghaḍab﴾ (with wrath upon wrath): that is, successive and multiplied, and this indicates the intensification of the state upon them. It was also said that what is meant by this is two angers, each explained by two stories: the first anger was for the worship of the calf, and the second for their disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ); this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. Or the first is their disbelief in the Gospel, and the second their disbelief in the Qur'an; this was said by Qatadah. Or the first is their disbelief in ʿIsā, and the second their disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ); this was said by al-Hasan and others. Or the first is their saying "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah" and their saying "the hand of Allah is chained," and other kinds of their disbelief, and the second is their disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿wa-li-l-kāfirīna ʿadhābun muhīn﴾ (and for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment): The alif and lam in al-kāfirīn are for specific reference (ʿahd), and the explicit noun was placed in the position of the pronoun, to indicate the reason why the humiliating punishment is for them; for if it had said "and for them is a humiliating punishment," there would be no indication of the cause. Or the alif and lam are for generality, so that they are included among the disbelievers. He described the punishment with humiliation, which is abasement, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and let a group of the believers witness their punishment﴾ [al-Nur 24:2]. It came in the Sahih, in the hadith of ʿUbadah, when he mentioned forbidden things and said: "Whoever commits any of these and is punished for it, then it is an expiation for him." So this punishment is only for the expiation of misdeeds, or because it entails eternal abiding that never ends, or because of its severity, greatness and variety of kinds, or because it is a recompense for their arrogance in not following the truth. The Kharijites have argued by this verse that the grave sinner is a disbeliever, since his punishment is established; and the Murji'ah have argued by it that the grave sinner is not punished, since he is not a disbeliever.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 92–94 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And when it is said to them﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91]: This is a report about the Jews who were in the presence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The context of the verse shows that the intended people are their forefathers, because they were the ones who killed the prophets. What justifies this is that one who is content with a thing is like its doer, that they are one kind, that they follow them and believe in that, and that they support them, so they are of them.

﴿Believe in what Allah has sent down﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91]. The majority of scholars say it refers to the Qur'an. Al-Zamakhshari (d. 538 AH) said it is unrestricted, so "what Allah has sent down" includes whatever He sent down in every Book.

﴿They say: We believe in what was sent down to us﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91]: They mean the Torah and the messages that came through Musa (Moses, peace be upon him) and the prophets after him among them. The subject is omitted here because it is known, since it is known that no one sends down divine books except Allah. Alternatively, it is omitted because it is carried over from His words ﴿Believe in what Allah has sent down﴾, so it is omitted for brevity since it has already been mentioned. They were blamed for this statement because they were commanded to believe in every Book that Allah sent down, but they answered by saying they believe in a restricted one, while the command is general, so their belief did not match the command.

﴿And they reject﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91]: This is a sentence that begins a new report about them, or it is a circumstantial clause (hal, a phrase describing the state of the subject at the time of the action), whose governing verb is "they say." That is, while they reject.

﴿What is beyond it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91]: That is, what is other than it. It is explained this way in ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾ [al-Nisa 4:24] and ﴿Then whoever seeks beyond that﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:7]. Qatadah said it means "what comes after it," that is, they reject what comes after the Torah, which is the Qur'an. Or it means "what is beyond it," that is, the inner meanings that lie beyond its wording, and in that case their belief is in the outward wording only.

﴿And it is the truth﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91]: The pronoun "it" refers to the Qur'an, or to the Qur'an and the Gospel, since the Books of Allah confirm one another.

(Confirming): a circumstantial clause of emphasis, since the Qur'an's confirmation is a necessary attribute that does not change.

﴿Confirming what is with them﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91]: This is the Torah, or the Torah and the Gospel, because both were sent down to the Children of Israel. Neither of them contradicts the Qur'an. In this there is a refutation of them, because whoever does not confirm what agrees with the Torah does not truly believe in it. When proof establishes that a thing was sent down from Allah, believing in it is obligatory. So believing in some parts and rejecting others is self-contradictory.

(Say): that is, say, O Muhammad, and say, O you who wish to dispute with them.

(Then why): the fa' (then) is the answer to an implied condition. The estimated meaning is: if you have believed in what was sent down to you, then why...

﴿do you kill the prophets of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91]? Because believing in the Torah and considering the killing of prophets lawful cannot coexist. So your claim that you believe in the Torah is a lie and a slander, and no one who makes its prohibitions lawful believes in the Qur'an. "Ma" is an interrogative (istifhamiyyah, a question word) whose alif has been dropped because of the preposition lam that precedes it. Al-Bazzi stops with a ha' and says "falimah," while others stop with "fa-lima" without a ha'. This pause is not permitted except for testing or when breath runs out. The verb "yaqtulun" (kill) is in the form of the present tense, but the intended meaning is the past, since the sense is: say, why did you kill? What clarifies this is that those present in the presence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not themselves kill the prophets, and it is restricted by His words ﴿from before﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91], which indicates that the killing happened in the past.

Ibn Atiyya said: The purpose of using the future form to express the past is to inform that the matter is continuous. Do you not see that the contemporaries of Muhammad ﷺ, because they were content with the deeds of their forefathers, still had a share in killing the prophets? Attributing "prophets" to Allah is a great honor for them, and it indicates that whoever comes from Allah should be honored with the highest honor and supported, not killed.

﴿If you are believers﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91]: It has been said that "in" (in) is a negation, meaning you were not believers, because whoever kills the prophets of Allah cannot be a believer. So Allah informs that belief does not coexist with the killing of prophets, that is, no one with this description is characterized by belief. It has been said that the more apparent view is that "in" is conditional, and its answer is omitted. The estimated meaning is: then why did you do that? The condition and its answer have been repeated twice for emphasis, but the condition was dropped from the first and its answer kept, which is "why do you kill?", and the answer was dropped from the second and its condition kept. Ibn Atiyya said: "If you are" is the condition, and the answer comes before it. This statement can only stand according to the view of those who permit placing the answer of a condition before it, and among the Basrans only Abu Zayd al-Ansari and al-Mubarrad held this view. The meaning of "believers" is: in what was sent down to you, or truly established in belief and sincere in it, or believers according to your own claim. This statement was treated as mockery and ridicule of them, just as you say to someone whose behavior is unfitting: you did such-and-such while you are sensible, meaning by your own claim.

﴿And Musa came to you with clear proofs﴾: that is, with clear signs, which are the manifest miracles indicating his truthfulness. It has been said these are the nine: the staff, the years of drought, the hand, the blood, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the splitting of the sea. This is what is meant by His words ﴿And We gave Musa nine clear signs﴾ [al-Isra 17:101].
