﴿And Musa came to you with clear proofs, then you took the calf after him while you were wrongdoers﴾ ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised the mountain above you: Take what We have given you with strength﴾: The explanation of these sentences has already been given. They are repeated here because of their claim that they believe in what was sent down to them, while they are lying in that. Do you not see that taking the calf is not in the Torah? Rather, the Torah says that Allah alone is to be worshipped. Also, worshipping other than Allah is the greatest sin, so the worship of the calf is repeated to emphasize the enormity of their crime. Also, mention of that before was followed by a listing of blessings with His words ﴿Then We pardoned you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:52] and ﴿Had it not been for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:64]. Here it is followed by rebuke and reproach. Also, in the story of the mountain there is mention of their turning away from what they were commanded, namely accepting the Torah, and their unwillingness to accept its rulings by choice, until they were forced to accept it under compulsion, so their claim of believing in what was sent down to them is not accepted. Furthermore, the story of the mountain contains a concluding statement that was not mentioned before. When the Arabs wish to call attention to the ugliness or greatness of something, they repeat it. In this repetition there is also the benefit of reminding them of Allah's blessings upon them and His punishments against them, so that the later generations may be restrained by what befell the earlier ones.

(And listen): that is, accept what you have heard, like His saying "Allah hears whoever praises Him." Or it means "listen while reflecting on what you have heard," or "listen and obey." This is because the benefit of hearing is obedience, as al-Mufaddal said. The meanings of these three opinions are close. Al-Maturidi (d. 333 AH) said: The meaning of "listen" is "understand." It has been said: "act." Its justification is that hearing is by means of which one hears, then it is imagined, then it is understood, then acted upon if it requires action. Since hearing is the beginning and action is the goal, and what is between them are intermediate steps, it is valid to mean some of the intermediate steps, and it is valid to mean the goal.

(They said): this is a shift (iltifat, a sudden change of grammatical person), since if it had come in the second person it would have said "you said."

﴿We hear and we disobey﴾: Its apparent meaning is that both clauses are spoken, and they uttered them as an exaggeration of obstinacy and disobedience. This is supported by the statement of Ibn Abbas: When they looked at the mountain they said, ﴿We hear and we obey﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:285], and when they looked at the Book they said, ﴿We hear and we disobey﴾. It has been said that "said" here is figurative, and they did not speak either clause, but since they did not accept any of what they were commanded, they were treated as though they had spoken these words. It has also been said that "saying" for a thing can express what is understood from its state, even without actual speech. It has also been said that the meaning is: we hear with our ears and we disobey with our hearts. This returns to what al-Zamakhshari said. He said: They said, "We hear your words and we disobey your command." If you ask: how did his statement match their reply? I say: it matches because he told them, "Listen, and let your hearing be the hearing of acceptance and obedience," and they said, "We hear, but not the hearing of obedience." That ends his words. But the first view is better, because we do not turn to interpretation when it is possible to take the statement in its apparent sense, especially when no proof contradicts it.

﴿And they were made to drink﴾: This is conjoined to "they said: we hear and we disobey." So it is conjoined to "they said," meaning: take what We have given you with strength; you said such-and-such and you were made to drink. Or it is a new conjunction that is not part of the shift, but a report from Allah about them concerning what they did in worshipping the calf. Or the "wa" (and) is for the circumstantial state, meaning "while they had been made to drink," with the governing verb being "they said." The Kufans do not need to estimate "qad" before a past verb that functions as a circumstantial clause. The first view is the apparent one.

﴿In their hearts﴾: He mentioned the place of the drinking, as in His saying ﴿They only eat fire into their bellies﴾ [al-Nisa 4:10].

(The calf): this is by omission of two words, meaning "the love of worshipping the calf," from your saying: "I made Zayd drink water." Drinking (ishrab) is the mixing of a liquid with a solid, and the word was extended until it was used for colors. They say: "I made the whiteness drink redness," meaning I mixed it with redness. Its meaning is that the love of its worship entered them, just as dye enters cloth. They recited:

"When the heart is made to drink the love of something, do not hope it will turn away from it."

Ibn Arafa said: It is said, "his heart was made to drink the love of such-and-such," meaning it took the place of the drink and mixed with it. That ends his words. Drinking was used for the love of the calf rather than eating, because drinking water permeates the limbs until it reaches their inner parts. For this reason one of them said:

"Her love flows through my joints like my blood, so that for me every other concern has become a concern with her."

As for food, they said it is adjacent to the body but does not permeate it, and only a little of it reaches the heart. One of them said:

"The love of Athma has permeated my heart, so what is evident of it and what is hidden of it is small."

The omission of those two words is good, and the act of drinking is attributed to the very calf in an exaggerated way, as though they were made to drink its image, although the meaning according to what we have mentioned is by omission. It has been said that the meaning of "they were made to drink" is that the love of the calf was firmly fixed in their hearts because of their infatuation with it, from "I made the camel drink" when you tie a rope around its neck. It has also been said that it is literally from drinking. It is reported that Musa, peace be upon him, ground the calf with a file, threw it into the water, and said to them, "Drink," and they all drank. So whoever loved the calf had its filings on his lips. This view is rejected by His words "in their hearts." It is also reported that those in whom the love of the calf became evident were afflicted with cowardice from that water. The passive form in "they were made to drink" is evidence that this was done to them, and no one does it except Allah, Exalted. The Mu'tazilah said: it came in the passive form because of their excessive eagerness for worshipping it, as one says "impressed with his own opinion." Or because al-Samiri, Iblis, and the devils of mankind and jinn invited them to it. Since drinking is the source of the life of what the earth produces, the act was attributed to love, because love is the source of all the actions that proceeded from them.

(Because of their disbelief): The apparent meaning is that the "ba'" (because of) indicates cause, that is, what led them to worship the calf was their earlier disbelief. It has been said that the "ba'" may have the meaning of "with," indicating a circumstance, that is, accompanied by their disbelief, so that this would be disbelief upon disbelief.

(Say): O Muhammad, or say, O you who dispute with them.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 92–94 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿Say: "Evil is what your faith commands you, if you are believers."﴾ The discussion of *bi'sa* (evil, a verb of blame) has already passed, and so have the positions on *ma*, so there is no need to repeat it. Al-Hasan and Muslim ibn Jundub read *bihu* ("by it" with a *u* vowel on the *ha'*) *īmānukum*, with a *ḍamma* on the *ha'* and joined to a *wāw*. This is a dialect form. The *ḍamma* is the original vowel, but in most dialects it was changed to *kasra* because of the *kasra* on the *bā'*. By "your faith" is meant the faith they claimed in their words, ﴿We believe in what was sent down to us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91]. The command is attributed to their faith ironically, as the companions of Shu'ayb said: "Does your prayer command you that we leave...?" It has also been said that there is an omitted word here, with the sense "the companion of your faith," meaning Iblis. It has also been said that there is an omitted adjective, with the sense "your false faith." The faith is attributed to them because it is not sound faith, and for this reason it does not say "the faith." This was said by some of our contemporaries, may God have mercy on them.

The object of the blame is omitted after *ma*. If *ma* is in the accusative, the sense is: "Evil is a thing that your faith commands you to do, which is the killing of the prophets, disobedience, and the worship of the calf." In that case *yaʾmurukum* is an adjective of the specifier (*tamyīz*). Or the sense is: "Evil is a thing, a thing that your faith commands you to do," in which case *yaʾmurukum* is an adjective of the omitted object of blame. Or the sense is: "Evil is a thing, what it commands you," that is, "the thing which commands you," in which case *yaʾmurukum bihi īmānukum* ("your faith commands you by it") is the clause. The object of blame is then supplied after that, meaning "the killing of the prophets, and so on." In this case *ma* is a relative pronoun. Or the sense is: "The evil thing is a thing that your faith commands you to do," in which case *ma* is complete (*tāmma*). All of this is a set of consequences of the view of those who gave *ma* alone a place in the *i'rab* (grammatical analysis).

﴿if you are believers﴾: it has been said that *in* is a negative particle, and it has been said that it is conditional. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is a casting of doubt on their faith and a discrediting of the soundness of their claim." End of his words. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The conditional may come while the speaker knows that the matter is one of two directions, as God said about Jesus, peace be upon him: ﴿If I had said it, You would have known it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116]. Jesus, peace be upon him, knew that he had not said it. Likewise ﴿if you are believers﴾, and the speaker knows that they are not believers, but he has set up an argument by a clear analogy." End of his words. Its meaning ultimately reverts to negating faith from them. The answer of the condition is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it, meaning: "If you are believers, then do not kill the prophets, do not deny the messengers, and do not conceal the truth." The first omitted supposition is more correct and stronger in *i'rab*.

﴿Say: "If the last abode with God is yours alone, to the exclusion of others..."﴾: It was revealed concerning what Ibn al-Jawzi reported, when the Jews said: "God did not create Paradise except for Israel and his sons." Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Rabi' said: "The reason for the revelation of these two verses is their saying: ﴿None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111], and ﴿We are the sons of God﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18], and ﴿The Fire will not touch us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80], and the verses." The same was related from Qatadah. The pronoun in *qul* ("say") refers either to the Prophet ﷺ, or to whoever is appropriate to establish the proof against them, from him and from others. They explained *al-dar al-akhirah* ("the last abode") as Paradise, and said: "This is familiar in its use for Paradise." God the Exalted said: ﴿That abode of the Hereafter We shall give to those who do not desire haughtiness on earth or corruption﴾ [al-Qasas: 83]. It is known that what is given to these is Paradise. ﴿And the abode of the Hereafter is better for those who fear God﴾ [al-An'am: 32]. The best view is that this is by omission of a modifier which the meaning indicates, meaning: "the bliss of the last abode, its favour, and its good." This is because the last abode is the place of residence after the end of this world. It was called "the last" because it comes after this world, or because it is the last thing that is inhabited. The discussion of this has already passed in His saying: ﴿and they are certain of the Hereafter﴾ [al-Naml: 3]. The meaning of "with God" is "in the judgment of God," as in His saying: ﴿Those are with God...﴾ [al-Nur: 13], that is, in His judgment, ﴿they are the defiantly disobedient﴾ [Al 'Imran: 82]. It has been said that what is meant by "with" here is standing, rank, and honour, not place. The meaning of "exclusively" (*khālisah*) is: specifically for you, with no share of its bliss for others.

They differed over the *i'rab* of *khālisah*. It has been said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*). Al-Zamakhshari did not report any other view. In that case *lakum* ("for you") is the predicate of *kānat*, and the element governing the circumstantial state is the element governing the prepositional phrase. The adverbial phrase cannot be the predicate in that case, because it does not complete the meaning of the sentence by itself. Al-Mahdawi and Ibn 'Atiyya erred in this, when they said: "It is also permissible that *khālisah* be accusative as a state, and *'inda Allah* ("with God") be the predicate of *kāna*." It has been said that the accusative *khālisah* is the predicate of *kānat*. Then *lakum* may be connected to *kānat*, since the prepositional particle can be connected to *kāna*, and it may be connected to *khālisah*. It may also be explanatory (*li-l-tabyīn*), in which case it is connected to an omitted element whose supposition is *lakum*, meaning "I mean for you," like their saying *saqyan laka* ("watering to you") when the supposition is "to you I call."

﴿to the exclusion of mankind﴾: it is connected to *khālisah*. *Dūn* ("to the exclusion of") here is a term used for exclusivity and cutting off partnership. You say: "This is a guardian to the exclusion of you," and you mean there is no right to it for you with me, nor a share. In other places it comes with the meaning of inferiority in rank, place, or amount. What is meant by "mankind" is the category, and this is the apparent sense, because of the indication of the wording and of His saying *khālisah*. It has been said that what is meant is the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims. It has been said that what is meant by it is the Prophet ﷺ, as Ibn 'Abbas said. They said: "People" is used, and what is meant by it is one man, and this would not occur except as a figure of speech, treating one man as a group.

﴿then wish for death﴾: that is, ask for it with the tongue alone, even if not with the heart, as Ibn 'Abbas said. Or: wish for it with your hearts and ask for it with your tongues, as a group said. Or: ask for it with your hearts, against the worse of the two parties, whether of the believers or of them. This was related from Ibn 'Abbas and others. The majority read *fa-tamannaw al-mawt* with a *ḍamma* on the *wāw*, which is the well-known dialect for forms like *ikhshaw al-qawm* ("fear the people"). The *kasra* is permissible, by analogy of this *wāw* with the *wāw* of *wa-law istaṭa'nā* ("and if we were able"), just as they made the *wāw* of *law* analogous to the *wāw* of *ikhshaw*, and so they used *ḍamma* and said *law istaṭa'nā*. Ibn Abi Ishaq read *fa-tamannaw al-mawt* with a *kasra*. Abu 'Ali al-Hasan ibn Ibrahim ibn Yazdad related from Abu 'Amr that he read *fa-tamannaw al-mawt* with a *fatḥa* on the *wāw*, and he gave it a *fatḥa* seeking lightness, since the *ḍamma* and *kasra* on the *wāw* are heavy. It is also related from Abu 'Amr that he elided the *ḍamma* of the *wāw* (*ikhtilās*).

﴿if you are truthful﴾ in your claim that Paradise is yours to the exclusion of others. The answer of the condition is omitted, meaning "then wish for death." Their wishing is made dependent on a condition that is absent, which is their being truthful. They are not truthful in the claim that Paradise is exclusively theirs to the exclusion of mankind, so the wish does not take place. (p-311) The purpose of this is a challenge and the exposure of their lie. Whoever is certain that he is among the people of Paradise chooses to move to it, to be freed from dwelling in the abode of troubles, and to reach the abode of rest. As was related about those to whom the Messenger of God ﷺ testified of Paradise, such as 'Uthman, 'Ali, 'Ammar, and Hudhayfah, that they used to choose death, and likewise the Companions used to choose martyrdom. In the authentic hadith he ﷺ said: "I wish that I might live, then be killed, then live, then be killed," because of what he knew of the excellence of martyrdom. And when news reached him of the killing of those slain at Bir Ma'unah, he said: "Would that I had been left with them in the cloak of the mountain." It was related from Hudhayfah that he used to wish for death, and when he was dying he said: "A beloved has come upon poverty." And from 'Ammar, when he was at Siffin, he said: "Tomorrow we shall meet the beloved, Muhammad and his companions." And from 'Ali that he used to walk between the two lines in a light shirt, and his son al-Hasan said to him: "This is not the dress of those who fight," and he said: "My son, your father does not care whether he falls upon death or death falls upon him." 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah used to recite, while he fought the Romans:

> "How good is Paradise, and its nearness,
> Pleasant and cool is its drink,
> And the Romans are Romans, whose punishment has drawn near."

In the accounts of the killing of 'Uthman and of Sa'id ibn Jubayr there is what indicates their choosing martyrdom. 'Uthman was approached by a group of the Companions, who said to him: "Shall we fight on your behalf?" He said to them: "No." He had about a thousand slaves, and when the attackers came upon them they drew their swords, and he said: "Whoever sheathes his sword is free." So he endured until he was killed. As for Sa'id, when al-Hajjaj sought him, those assigned to him saw the wild beasts seeking refuge with him and rubbing against him, and they said: "We will not take part in shedding the blood of this righteous man." They said to him: "He seeks you to kill you, so go wherever you wish, and we will be a ransom." He said: "No, by God, I asked my Lord for martyrdom, and He has granted it to me. By God, I will not leave."

It was related from the Prophet ﷺ: "If they wished for death, every person would choke on his saliva and die in his place, and no Jew would remain on the face of the earth." That is because God commanded His Prophet to call them to wish for death, and to inform them that whoever among them wished for it would die. The Prophet ﷺ did so, and the Jews knew his truthfulness, so they refrained from wishing for it, out of fear of God.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 92–94 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And when it is said to them﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91]: This is a report about the Jews who were in the presence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The context of the verse shows that the intended people are their forefathers, because they were the ones who killed the prophets. What justifies this is that one who is content with a thing is like its doer, that they are one kind, that they follow them and believe in that, and that they support them, so they are of them.

﴿Believe in what Allah has sent down﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91]. The majority of scholars say it refers to the Qur'an. Al-Zamakhshari (d. 538 AH) said it is unrestricted, so "what Allah has sent down" includes whatever He sent down in every Book.

﴿They say: We believe in what was sent down to us﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91]: They mean the Torah and the messages that came through Musa (Moses, peace be upon him) and the prophets after him among them. The subject is omitted here because it is known, since it is known that no one sends down divine books except Allah. Alternatively, it is omitted because it is carried over from His words ﴿Believe in what Allah has sent down﴾, so it is omitted for brevity since it has already been mentioned. They were blamed for this statement because they were commanded to believe in every Book that Allah sent down, but they answered by saying they believe in a restricted one, while the command is general, so their belief did not match the command.

﴿And they reject﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91]: This is a sentence that begins a new report about them, or it is a circumstantial clause (hal, a phrase describing the state of the subject at the time of the action), whose governing verb is "they say." That is, while they reject.

﴿What is beyond it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91]: That is, what is other than it. It is explained this way in ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾ [al-Nisa 4:24] and ﴿Then whoever seeks beyond that﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:7]. Qatadah said it means "what comes after it," that is, they reject what comes after the Torah, which is the Qur'an. Or it means "what is beyond it," that is, the inner meanings that lie beyond its wording, and in that case their belief is in the outward wording only.

﴿And it is the truth﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91]: The pronoun "it" refers to the Qur'an, or to the Qur'an and the Gospel, since the Books of Allah confirm one another.

(Confirming): a circumstantial clause of emphasis, since the Qur'an's confirmation is a necessary attribute that does not change.

﴿Confirming what is with them﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91]: This is the Torah, or the Torah and the Gospel, because both were sent down to the Children of Israel. Neither of them contradicts the Qur'an. In this there is a refutation of them, because whoever does not confirm what agrees with the Torah does not truly believe in it. When proof establishes that a thing was sent down from Allah, believing in it is obligatory. So believing in some parts and rejecting others is self-contradictory.

(Say): that is, say, O Muhammad, and say, O you who wish to dispute with them.

(Then why): the fa' (then) is the answer to an implied condition. The estimated meaning is: if you have believed in what was sent down to you, then why...

﴿do you kill the prophets of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91]? Because believing in the Torah and considering the killing of prophets lawful cannot coexist. So your claim that you believe in the Torah is a lie and a slander, and no one who makes its prohibitions lawful believes in the Qur'an. "Ma" is an interrogative (istifhamiyyah, a question word) whose alif has been dropped because of the preposition lam that precedes it. Al-Bazzi stops with a ha' and says "falimah," while others stop with "fa-lima" without a ha'. This pause is not permitted except for testing or when breath runs out. The verb "yaqtulun" (kill) is in the form of the present tense, but the intended meaning is the past, since the sense is: say, why did you kill? What clarifies this is that those present in the presence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not themselves kill the prophets, and it is restricted by His words ﴿from before﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91], which indicates that the killing happened in the past.

Ibn Atiyya said: The purpose of using the future form to express the past is to inform that the matter is continuous. Do you not see that the contemporaries of Muhammad ﷺ, because they were content with the deeds of their forefathers, still had a share in killing the prophets? Attributing "prophets" to Allah is a great honor for them, and it indicates that whoever comes from Allah should be honored with the highest honor and supported, not killed.

﴿If you are believers﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91]: It has been said that "in" (in) is a negation, meaning you were not believers, because whoever kills the prophets of Allah cannot be a believer. So Allah informs that belief does not coexist with the killing of prophets, that is, no one with this description is characterized by belief. It has been said that the more apparent view is that "in" is conditional, and its answer is omitted. The estimated meaning is: then why did you do that? The condition and its answer have been repeated twice for emphasis, but the condition was dropped from the first and its answer kept, which is "why do you kill?", and the answer was dropped from the second and its condition kept. Ibn Atiyya said: "If you are" is the condition, and the answer comes before it. This statement can only stand according to the view of those who permit placing the answer of a condition before it, and among the Basrans only Abu Zayd al-Ansari and al-Mubarrad held this view. The meaning of "believers" is: in what was sent down to you, or truly established in belief and sincere in it, or believers according to your own claim. This statement was treated as mockery and ridicule of them, just as you say to someone whose behavior is unfitting: you did such-and-such while you are sensible, meaning by your own claim.

﴿And Musa came to you with clear proofs﴾: that is, with clear signs, which are the manifest miracles indicating his truthfulness. It has been said these are the nine: the staff, the years of drought, the hand, the blood, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the splitting of the sea. This is what is meant by His words ﴿And We gave Musa nine clear signs﴾ [al-Isra 17:101].

﴿And Musa came to you with clear proofs, then you took the calf after him while you were wrongdoers﴾ ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised the mountain above you: Take what We have given you with strength﴾: The explanation of these sentences has already been given. They are repeated here because of their claim that they believe in what was sent down to them, while they are lying in that. Do you not see that taking the calf is not in the Torah? Rather, the Torah says that Allah alone is to be worshipped. Also, worshipping other than Allah is the greatest sin, so the worship of the calf is repeated to emphasize the enormity of their crime. Also, mention of that before was followed by a listing of blessings with His words ﴿Then We pardoned you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:52] and ﴿Had it not been for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:64]. Here it is followed by rebuke and reproach. Also, in the story of the mountain there is mention of their turning away from what they were commanded, namely accepting the Torah, and their unwillingness to accept its rulings by choice, until they were forced to accept it under compulsion, so their claim of believing in what was sent down to them is not accepted. Furthermore, the story of the mountain contains a concluding statement that was not mentioned before. When the Arabs wish to call attention to the ugliness or greatness of something, they repeat it. In this repetition there is also the benefit of reminding them of Allah's blessings upon them and His punishments against them, so that the later generations may be restrained by what befell the earlier ones.

(And listen): that is, accept what you have heard, like His saying "Allah hears whoever praises Him." Or it means "listen while reflecting on what you have heard," or "listen and obey." This is because the benefit of hearing is obedience, as al-Mufaddal said. The meanings of these three opinions are close. Al-Maturidi (d. 333 AH) said: The meaning of "listen" is "understand." It has been said: "act." Its justification is that hearing is by means of which one hears, then it is imagined, then it is understood, then acted upon if it requires action. Since hearing is the beginning and action is the goal, and what is between them are intermediate steps, it is valid to mean some of the intermediate steps, and it is valid to mean the goal.

(They said): this is a shift (iltifat, a sudden change of grammatical person), since if it had come in the second person it would have said "you said."

﴿We hear and we disobey﴾: Its apparent meaning is that both clauses are spoken, and they uttered them as an exaggeration of obstinacy and disobedience. This is supported by the statement of Ibn Abbas: When they looked at the mountain they said, ﴿We hear and we obey﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:285], and when they looked at the Book they said, ﴿We hear and we disobey﴾. It has been said that "said" here is figurative, and they did not speak either clause, but since they did not accept any of what they were commanded, they were treated as though they had spoken these words. It has also been said that "saying" for a thing can express what is understood from its state, even without actual speech. It has also been said that the meaning is: we hear with our ears and we disobey with our hearts. This returns to what al-Zamakhshari said. He said: They said, "We hear your words and we disobey your command." If you ask: how did his statement match their reply? I say: it matches because he told them, "Listen, and let your hearing be the hearing of acceptance and obedience," and they said, "We hear, but not the hearing of obedience." That ends his words. But the first view is better, because we do not turn to interpretation when it is possible to take the statement in its apparent sense, especially when no proof contradicts it.

﴿And they were made to drink﴾: This is conjoined to "they said: we hear and we disobey." So it is conjoined to "they said," meaning: take what We have given you with strength; you said such-and-such and you were made to drink. Or it is a new conjunction that is not part of the shift, but a report from Allah about them concerning what they did in worshipping the calf. Or the "wa" (and) is for the circumstantial state, meaning "while they had been made to drink," with the governing verb being "they said." The Kufans do not need to estimate "qad" before a past verb that functions as a circumstantial clause. The first view is the apparent one.

﴿In their hearts﴾: He mentioned the place of the drinking, as in His saying ﴿They only eat fire into their bellies﴾ [al-Nisa 4:10].

(The calf): this is by omission of two words, meaning "the love of worshipping the calf," from your saying: "I made Zayd drink water." Drinking (ishrab) is the mixing of a liquid with a solid, and the word was extended until it was used for colors. They say: "I made the whiteness drink redness," meaning I mixed it with redness. Its meaning is that the love of its worship entered them, just as dye enters cloth. They recited:

"When the heart is made to drink the love of something, do not hope it will turn away from it."

Ibn Arafa said: It is said, "his heart was made to drink the love of such-and-such," meaning it took the place of the drink and mixed with it. That ends his words. Drinking was used for the love of the calf rather than eating, because drinking water permeates the limbs until it reaches their inner parts. For this reason one of them said:

"Her love flows through my joints like my blood, so that for me every other concern has become a concern with her."

As for food, they said it is adjacent to the body but does not permeate it, and only a little of it reaches the heart. One of them said:

"The love of Athma has permeated my heart, so what is evident of it and what is hidden of it is small."

The omission of those two words is good, and the act of drinking is attributed to the very calf in an exaggerated way, as though they were made to drink its image, although the meaning according to what we have mentioned is by omission. It has been said that the meaning of "they were made to drink" is that the love of the calf was firmly fixed in their hearts because of their infatuation with it, from "I made the camel drink" when you tie a rope around its neck. It has also been said that it is literally from drinking. It is reported that Musa, peace be upon him, ground the calf with a file, threw it into the water, and said to them, "Drink," and they all drank. So whoever loved the calf had its filings on his lips. This view is rejected by His words "in their hearts." It is also reported that those in whom the love of the calf became evident were afflicted with cowardice from that water. The passive form in "they were made to drink" is evidence that this was done to them, and no one does it except Allah, Exalted. The Mu'tazilah said: it came in the passive form because of their excessive eagerness for worshipping it, as one says "impressed with his own opinion." Or because al-Samiri, Iblis, and the devils of mankind and jinn invited them to it. Since drinking is the source of the life of what the earth produces, the act was attributed to love, because love is the source of all the actions that proceeded from them.

(Because of their disbelief): The apparent meaning is that the "ba'" (because of) indicates cause, that is, what led them to worship the calf was their earlier disbelief. It has been said that the "ba'" may have the meaning of "with," indicating a circumstance, that is, accompanied by their disbelief, so that this would be disbelief upon disbelief.

(Say): O Muhammad, or say, O you who dispute with them.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 92–94 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿Say: "Evil is what your faith commands you, if you are believers."﴾ The discussion of *bi'sa* (evil, a verb of blame) has already passed, and so have the positions on *ma*, so there is no need to repeat it. Al-Hasan and Muslim ibn Jundub read *bihu* ("by it" with a *u* vowel on the *ha'*) *īmānukum*, with a *ḍamma* on the *ha'* and joined to a *wāw*. This is a dialect form. The *ḍamma* is the original vowel, but in most dialects it was changed to *kasra* because of the *kasra* on the *bā'*. By "your faith" is meant the faith they claimed in their words, ﴿We believe in what was sent down to us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91]. The command is attributed to their faith ironically, as the companions of Shu'ayb said: "Does your prayer command you that we leave...?" It has also been said that there is an omitted word here, with the sense "the companion of your faith," meaning Iblis. It has also been said that there is an omitted adjective, with the sense "your false faith." The faith is attributed to them because it is not sound faith, and for this reason it does not say "the faith." This was said by some of our contemporaries, may God have mercy on them.

The object of the blame is omitted after *ma*. If *ma* is in the accusative, the sense is: "Evil is a thing that your faith commands you to do, which is the killing of the prophets, disobedience, and the worship of the calf." In that case *yaʾmurukum* is an adjective of the specifier (*tamyīz*). Or the sense is: "Evil is a thing, a thing that your faith commands you to do," in which case *yaʾmurukum* is an adjective of the omitted object of blame. Or the sense is: "Evil is a thing, what it commands you," that is, "the thing which commands you," in which case *yaʾmurukum bihi īmānukum* ("your faith commands you by it") is the clause. The object of blame is then supplied after that, meaning "the killing of the prophets, and so on." In this case *ma* is a relative pronoun. Or the sense is: "The evil thing is a thing that your faith commands you to do," in which case *ma* is complete (*tāmma*). All of this is a set of consequences of the view of those who gave *ma* alone a place in the *i'rab* (grammatical analysis).

﴿if you are believers﴾: it has been said that *in* is a negative particle, and it has been said that it is conditional. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is a casting of doubt on their faith and a discrediting of the soundness of their claim." End of his words. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The conditional may come while the speaker knows that the matter is one of two directions, as God said about Jesus, peace be upon him: ﴿If I had said it, You would have known it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116]. Jesus, peace be upon him, knew that he had not said it. Likewise ﴿if you are believers﴾, and the speaker knows that they are not believers, but he has set up an argument by a clear analogy." End of his words. Its meaning ultimately reverts to negating faith from them. The answer of the condition is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it, meaning: "If you are believers, then do not kill the prophets, do not deny the messengers, and do not conceal the truth." The first omitted supposition is more correct and stronger in *i'rab*.

﴿Say: "If the last abode with God is yours alone, to the exclusion of others..."﴾: It was revealed concerning what Ibn al-Jawzi reported, when the Jews said: "God did not create Paradise except for Israel and his sons." Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Rabi' said: "The reason for the revelation of these two verses is their saying: ﴿None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111], and ﴿We are the sons of God﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18], and ﴿The Fire will not touch us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80], and the verses." The same was related from Qatadah. The pronoun in *qul* ("say") refers either to the Prophet ﷺ, or to whoever is appropriate to establish the proof against them, from him and from others. They explained *al-dar al-akhirah* ("the last abode") as Paradise, and said: "This is familiar in its use for Paradise." God the Exalted said: ﴿That abode of the Hereafter We shall give to those who do not desire haughtiness on earth or corruption﴾ [al-Qasas: 83]. It is known that what is given to these is Paradise. ﴿And the abode of the Hereafter is better for those who fear God﴾ [al-An'am: 32]. The best view is that this is by omission of a modifier which the meaning indicates, meaning: "the bliss of the last abode, its favour, and its good." This is because the last abode is the place of residence after the end of this world. It was called "the last" because it comes after this world, or because it is the last thing that is inhabited. The discussion of this has already passed in His saying: ﴿and they are certain of the Hereafter﴾ [al-Naml: 3]. The meaning of "with God" is "in the judgment of God," as in His saying: ﴿Those are with God...﴾ [al-Nur: 13], that is, in His judgment, ﴿they are the defiantly disobedient﴾ [Al 'Imran: 82]. It has been said that what is meant by "with" here is standing, rank, and honour, not place. The meaning of "exclusively" (*khālisah*) is: specifically for you, with no share of its bliss for others.

They differed over the *i'rab* of *khālisah*. It has been said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*). Al-Zamakhshari did not report any other view. In that case *lakum* ("for you") is the predicate of *kānat*, and the element governing the circumstantial state is the element governing the prepositional phrase. The adverbial phrase cannot be the predicate in that case, because it does not complete the meaning of the sentence by itself. Al-Mahdawi and Ibn 'Atiyya erred in this, when they said: "It is also permissible that *khālisah* be accusative as a state, and *'inda Allah* ("with God") be the predicate of *kāna*." It has been said that the accusative *khālisah* is the predicate of *kānat*. Then *lakum* may be connected to *kānat*, since the prepositional particle can be connected to *kāna*, and it may be connected to *khālisah*. It may also be explanatory (*li-l-tabyīn*), in which case it is connected to an omitted element whose supposition is *lakum*, meaning "I mean for you," like their saying *saqyan laka* ("watering to you") when the supposition is "to you I call."

﴿to the exclusion of mankind﴾: it is connected to *khālisah*. *Dūn* ("to the exclusion of") here is a term used for exclusivity and cutting off partnership. You say: "This is a guardian to the exclusion of you," and you mean there is no right to it for you with me, nor a share. In other places it comes with the meaning of inferiority in rank, place, or amount. What is meant by "mankind" is the category, and this is the apparent sense, because of the indication of the wording and of His saying *khālisah*. It has been said that what is meant is the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims. It has been said that what is meant by it is the Prophet ﷺ, as Ibn 'Abbas said. They said: "People" is used, and what is meant by it is one man, and this would not occur except as a figure of speech, treating one man as a group.

﴿then wish for death﴾: that is, ask for it with the tongue alone, even if not with the heart, as Ibn 'Abbas said. Or: wish for it with your hearts and ask for it with your tongues, as a group said. Or: ask for it with your hearts, against the worse of the two parties, whether of the believers or of them. This was related from Ibn 'Abbas and others. The majority read *fa-tamannaw al-mawt* with a *ḍamma* on the *wāw*, which is the well-known dialect for forms like *ikhshaw al-qawm* ("fear the people"). The *kasra* is permissible, by analogy of this *wāw* with the *wāw* of *wa-law istaṭa'nā* ("and if we were able"), just as they made the *wāw* of *law* analogous to the *wāw* of *ikhshaw*, and so they used *ḍamma* and said *law istaṭa'nā*. Ibn Abi Ishaq read *fa-tamannaw al-mawt* with a *kasra*. Abu 'Ali al-Hasan ibn Ibrahim ibn Yazdad related from Abu 'Amr that he read *fa-tamannaw al-mawt* with a *fatḥa* on the *wāw*, and he gave it a *fatḥa* seeking lightness, since the *ḍamma* and *kasra* on the *wāw* are heavy. It is also related from Abu 'Amr that he elided the *ḍamma* of the *wāw* (*ikhtilās*).

﴿if you are truthful﴾ in your claim that Paradise is yours to the exclusion of others. The answer of the condition is omitted, meaning "then wish for death." Their wishing is made dependent on a condition that is absent, which is their being truthful. They are not truthful in the claim that Paradise is exclusively theirs to the exclusion of mankind, so the wish does not take place. (p-311) The purpose of this is a challenge and the exposure of their lie. Whoever is certain that he is among the people of Paradise chooses to move to it, to be freed from dwelling in the abode of troubles, and to reach the abode of rest. As was related about those to whom the Messenger of God ﷺ testified of Paradise, such as 'Uthman, 'Ali, 'Ammar, and Hudhayfah, that they used to choose death, and likewise the Companions used to choose martyrdom. In the authentic hadith he ﷺ said: "I wish that I might live, then be killed, then live, then be killed," because of what he knew of the excellence of martyrdom. And when news reached him of the killing of those slain at Bir Ma'unah, he said: "Would that I had been left with them in the cloak of the mountain." It was related from Hudhayfah that he used to wish for death, and when he was dying he said: "A beloved has come upon poverty." And from 'Ammar, when he was at Siffin, he said: "Tomorrow we shall meet the beloved, Muhammad and his companions." And from 'Ali that he used to walk between the two lines in a light shirt, and his son al-Hasan said to him: "This is not the dress of those who fight," and he said: "My son, your father does not care whether he falls upon death or death falls upon him." 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah used to recite, while he fought the Romans:

> "How good is Paradise, and its nearness,
> Pleasant and cool is its drink,
> And the Romans are Romans, whose punishment has drawn near."

In the accounts of the killing of 'Uthman and of Sa'id ibn Jubayr there is what indicates their choosing martyrdom. 'Uthman was approached by a group of the Companions, who said to him: "Shall we fight on your behalf?" He said to them: "No." He had about a thousand slaves, and when the attackers came upon them they drew their swords, and he said: "Whoever sheathes his sword is free." So he endured until he was killed. As for Sa'id, when al-Hajjaj sought him, those assigned to him saw the wild beasts seeking refuge with him and rubbing against him, and they said: "We will not take part in shedding the blood of this righteous man." They said to him: "He seeks you to kill you, so go wherever you wish, and we will be a ransom." He said: "No, by God, I asked my Lord for martyrdom, and He has granted it to me. By God, I will not leave."

It was related from the Prophet ﷺ: "If they wished for death, every person would choke on his saliva and die in his place, and no Jew would remain on the face of the earth." That is because God commanded His Prophet to call them to wish for death, and to inform them that whoever among them wished for it would die. The Prophet ﷺ did so, and the Jews knew his truthfulness, so they refrained from wishing for it, out of fear of God.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 92–94 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And when it is said to them﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91]: This is a report about the Jews who were in the presence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The context of the verse shows that the intended people are their forefathers, because they were the ones who killed the prophets. What justifies this is that one who is content with a thing is like its doer, that they are one kind, that they follow them and believe in that, and that they support them, so they are of them.

﴿Believe in what Allah has sent down﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91]. The majority of scholars say it refers to the Qur'an. Al-Zamakhshari (d. 538 AH) said it is unrestricted, so "what Allah has sent down" includes whatever He sent down in every Book.

﴿They say: We believe in what was sent down to us﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91]: They mean the Torah and the messages that came through Musa (Moses, peace be upon him) and the prophets after him among them. The subject is omitted here because it is known, since it is known that no one sends down divine books except Allah. Alternatively, it is omitted because it is carried over from His words ﴿Believe in what Allah has sent down﴾, so it is omitted for brevity since it has already been mentioned. They were blamed for this statement because they were commanded to believe in every Book that Allah sent down, but they answered by saying they believe in a restricted one, while the command is general, so their belief did not match the command.

﴿And they reject﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91]: This is a sentence that begins a new report about them, or it is a circumstantial clause (hal, a phrase describing the state of the subject at the time of the action), whose governing verb is "they say." That is, while they reject.

﴿What is beyond it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91]: That is, what is other than it. It is explained this way in ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾ [al-Nisa 4:24] and ﴿Then whoever seeks beyond that﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:7]. Qatadah said it means "what comes after it," that is, they reject what comes after the Torah, which is the Qur'an. Or it means "what is beyond it," that is, the inner meanings that lie beyond its wording, and in that case their belief is in the outward wording only.

﴿And it is the truth﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91]: The pronoun "it" refers to the Qur'an, or to the Qur'an and the Gospel, since the Books of Allah confirm one another.

(Confirming): a circumstantial clause of emphasis, since the Qur'an's confirmation is a necessary attribute that does not change.

﴿Confirming what is with them﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91]: This is the Torah, or the Torah and the Gospel, because both were sent down to the Children of Israel. Neither of them contradicts the Qur'an. In this there is a refutation of them, because whoever does not confirm what agrees with the Torah does not truly believe in it. When proof establishes that a thing was sent down from Allah, believing in it is obligatory. So believing in some parts and rejecting others is self-contradictory.

(Say): that is, say, O Muhammad, and say, O you who wish to dispute with them.

(Then why): the fa' (then) is the answer to an implied condition. The estimated meaning is: if you have believed in what was sent down to you, then why...

﴿do you kill the prophets of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91]? Because believing in the Torah and considering the killing of prophets lawful cannot coexist. So your claim that you believe in the Torah is a lie and a slander, and no one who makes its prohibitions lawful believes in the Qur'an. "Ma" is an interrogative (istifhamiyyah, a question word) whose alif has been dropped because of the preposition lam that precedes it. Al-Bazzi stops with a ha' and says "falimah," while others stop with "fa-lima" without a ha'. This pause is not permitted except for testing or when breath runs out. The verb "yaqtulun" (kill) is in the form of the present tense, but the intended meaning is the past, since the sense is: say, why did you kill? What clarifies this is that those present in the presence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not themselves kill the prophets, and it is restricted by His words ﴿from before﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91], which indicates that the killing happened in the past.

Ibn Atiyya said: The purpose of using the future form to express the past is to inform that the matter is continuous. Do you not see that the contemporaries of Muhammad ﷺ, because they were content with the deeds of their forefathers, still had a share in killing the prophets? Attributing "prophets" to Allah is a great honor for them, and it indicates that whoever comes from Allah should be honored with the highest honor and supported, not killed.

﴿If you are believers﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91]: It has been said that "in" (in) is a negation, meaning you were not believers, because whoever kills the prophets of Allah cannot be a believer. So Allah informs that belief does not coexist with the killing of prophets, that is, no one with this description is characterized by belief. It has been said that the more apparent view is that "in" is conditional, and its answer is omitted. The estimated meaning is: then why did you do that? The condition and its answer have been repeated twice for emphasis, but the condition was dropped from the first and its answer kept, which is "why do you kill?", and the answer was dropped from the second and its condition kept. Ibn Atiyya said: "If you are" is the condition, and the answer comes before it. This statement can only stand according to the view of those who permit placing the answer of a condition before it, and among the Basrans only Abu Zayd al-Ansari and al-Mubarrad held this view. The meaning of "believers" is: in what was sent down to you, or truly established in belief and sincere in it, or believers according to your own claim. This statement was treated as mockery and ridicule of them, just as you say to someone whose behavior is unfitting: you did such-and-such while you are sensible, meaning by your own claim.

﴿And Musa came to you with clear proofs﴾: that is, with clear signs, which are the manifest miracles indicating his truthfulness. It has been said these are the nine: the staff, the years of drought, the hand, the blood, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the splitting of the sea. This is what is meant by His words ﴿And We gave Musa nine clear signs﴾ [al-Isra 17:101].

﴿And Musa came to you with clear proofs, then you took the calf after him while you were wrongdoers﴾ ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised the mountain above you: Take what We have given you with strength﴾: The explanation of these sentences has already been given. They are repeated here because of their claim that they believe in what was sent down to them, while they are lying in that. Do you not see that taking the calf is not in the Torah? Rather, the Torah says that Allah alone is to be worshipped. Also, worshipping other than Allah is the greatest sin, so the worship of the calf is repeated to emphasize the enormity of their crime. Also, mention of that before was followed by a listing of blessings with His words ﴿Then We pardoned you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:52] and ﴿Had it not been for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:64]. Here it is followed by rebuke and reproach. Also, in the story of the mountain there is mention of their turning away from what they were commanded, namely accepting the Torah, and their unwillingness to accept its rulings by choice, until they were forced to accept it under compulsion, so their claim of believing in what was sent down to them is not accepted. Furthermore, the story of the mountain contains a concluding statement that was not mentioned before. When the Arabs wish to call attention to the ugliness or greatness of something, they repeat it. In this repetition there is also the benefit of reminding them of Allah's blessings upon them and His punishments against them, so that the later generations may be restrained by what befell the earlier ones.

(And listen): that is, accept what you have heard, like His saying "Allah hears whoever praises Him." Or it means "listen while reflecting on what you have heard," or "listen and obey." This is because the benefit of hearing is obedience, as al-Mufaddal said. The meanings of these three opinions are close. Al-Maturidi (d. 333 AH) said: The meaning of "listen" is "understand." It has been said: "act." Its justification is that hearing is by means of which one hears, then it is imagined, then it is understood, then acted upon if it requires action. Since hearing is the beginning and action is the goal, and what is between them are intermediate steps, it is valid to mean some of the intermediate steps, and it is valid to mean the goal.

(They said): this is a shift (iltifat, a sudden change of grammatical person), since if it had come in the second person it would have said "you said."

﴿We hear and we disobey﴾: Its apparent meaning is that both clauses are spoken, and they uttered them as an exaggeration of obstinacy and disobedience. This is supported by the statement of Ibn Abbas: When they looked at the mountain they said, ﴿We hear and we obey﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:285], and when they looked at the Book they said, ﴿We hear and we disobey﴾. It has been said that "said" here is figurative, and they did not speak either clause, but since they did not accept any of what they were commanded, they were treated as though they had spoken these words. It has also been said that "saying" for a thing can express what is understood from its state, even without actual speech. It has also been said that the meaning is: we hear with our ears and we disobey with our hearts. This returns to what al-Zamakhshari said. He said: They said, "We hear your words and we disobey your command." If you ask: how did his statement match their reply? I say: it matches because he told them, "Listen, and let your hearing be the hearing of acceptance and obedience," and they said, "We hear, but not the hearing of obedience." That ends his words. But the first view is better, because we do not turn to interpretation when it is possible to take the statement in its apparent sense, especially when no proof contradicts it.

﴿And they were made to drink﴾: This is conjoined to "they said: we hear and we disobey." So it is conjoined to "they said," meaning: take what We have given you with strength; you said such-and-such and you were made to drink. Or it is a new conjunction that is not part of the shift, but a report from Allah about them concerning what they did in worshipping the calf. Or the "wa" (and) is for the circumstantial state, meaning "while they had been made to drink," with the governing verb being "they said." The Kufans do not need to estimate "qad" before a past verb that functions as a circumstantial clause. The first view is the apparent one.

﴿In their hearts﴾: He mentioned the place of the drinking, as in His saying ﴿They only eat fire into their bellies﴾ [al-Nisa 4:10].

(The calf): this is by omission of two words, meaning "the love of worshipping the calf," from your saying: "I made Zayd drink water." Drinking (ishrab) is the mixing of a liquid with a solid, and the word was extended until it was used for colors. They say: "I made the whiteness drink redness," meaning I mixed it with redness. Its meaning is that the love of its worship entered them, just as dye enters cloth. They recited:

"When the heart is made to drink the love of something, do not hope it will turn away from it."

Ibn Arafa said: It is said, "his heart was made to drink the love of such-and-such," meaning it took the place of the drink and mixed with it. That ends his words. Drinking was used for the love of the calf rather than eating, because drinking water permeates the limbs until it reaches their inner parts. For this reason one of them said:

"Her love flows through my joints like my blood, so that for me every other concern has become a concern with her."

As for food, they said it is adjacent to the body but does not permeate it, and only a little of it reaches the heart. One of them said:

"The love of Athma has permeated my heart, so what is evident of it and what is hidden of it is small."

The omission of those two words is good, and the act of drinking is attributed to the very calf in an exaggerated way, as though they were made to drink its image, although the meaning according to what we have mentioned is by omission. It has been said that the meaning of "they were made to drink" is that the love of the calf was firmly fixed in their hearts because of their infatuation with it, from "I made the camel drink" when you tie a rope around its neck. It has also been said that it is literally from drinking. It is reported that Musa, peace be upon him, ground the calf with a file, threw it into the water, and said to them, "Drink," and they all drank. So whoever loved the calf had its filings on his lips. This view is rejected by His words "in their hearts." It is also reported that those in whom the love of the calf became evident were afflicted with cowardice from that water. The passive form in "they were made to drink" is evidence that this was done to them, and no one does it except Allah, Exalted. The Mu'tazilah said: it came in the passive form because of their excessive eagerness for worshipping it, as one says "impressed with his own opinion." Or because al-Samiri, Iblis, and the devils of mankind and jinn invited them to it. Since drinking is the source of the life of what the earth produces, the act was attributed to love, because love is the source of all the actions that proceeded from them.

(Because of their disbelief): The apparent meaning is that the "ba'" (because of) indicates cause, that is, what led them to worship the calf was their earlier disbelief. It has been said that the "ba'" may have the meaning of "with," indicating a circumstance, that is, accompanied by their disbelief, so that this would be disbelief upon disbelief.

(Say): O Muhammad, or say, O you who dispute with them.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 92–94 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿Say: "Evil is what your faith commands you, if you are believers."﴾ The discussion of *bi'sa* (evil, a verb of blame) has already passed, and so have the positions on *ma*, so there is no need to repeat it. Al-Hasan and Muslim ibn Jundub read *bihu* ("by it" with a *u* vowel on the *ha'*) *īmānukum*, with a *ḍamma* on the *ha'* and joined to a *wāw*. This is a dialect form. The *ḍamma* is the original vowel, but in most dialects it was changed to *kasra* because of the *kasra* on the *bā'*. By "your faith" is meant the faith they claimed in their words, ﴿We believe in what was sent down to us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91]. The command is attributed to their faith ironically, as the companions of Shu'ayb said: "Does your prayer command you that we leave...?" It has also been said that there is an omitted word here, with the sense "the companion of your faith," meaning Iblis. It has also been said that there is an omitted adjective, with the sense "your false faith." The faith is attributed to them because it is not sound faith, and for this reason it does not say "the faith." This was said by some of our contemporaries, may God have mercy on them.

The object of the blame is omitted after *ma*. If *ma* is in the accusative, the sense is: "Evil is a thing that your faith commands you to do, which is the killing of the prophets, disobedience, and the worship of the calf." In that case *yaʾmurukum* is an adjective of the specifier (*tamyīz*). Or the sense is: "Evil is a thing, a thing that your faith commands you to do," in which case *yaʾmurukum* is an adjective of the omitted object of blame. Or the sense is: "Evil is a thing, what it commands you," that is, "the thing which commands you," in which case *yaʾmurukum bihi īmānukum* ("your faith commands you by it") is the clause. The object of blame is then supplied after that, meaning "the killing of the prophets, and so on." In this case *ma* is a relative pronoun. Or the sense is: "The evil thing is a thing that your faith commands you to do," in which case *ma* is complete (*tāmma*). All of this is a set of consequences of the view of those who gave *ma* alone a place in the *i'rab* (grammatical analysis).

﴿if you are believers﴾: it has been said that *in* is a negative particle, and it has been said that it is conditional. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is a casting of doubt on their faith and a discrediting of the soundness of their claim." End of his words. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The conditional may come while the speaker knows that the matter is one of two directions, as God said about Jesus, peace be upon him: ﴿If I had said it, You would have known it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116]. Jesus, peace be upon him, knew that he had not said it. Likewise ﴿if you are believers﴾, and the speaker knows that they are not believers, but he has set up an argument by a clear analogy." End of his words. Its meaning ultimately reverts to negating faith from them. The answer of the condition is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it, meaning: "If you are believers, then do not kill the prophets, do not deny the messengers, and do not conceal the truth." The first omitted supposition is more correct and stronger in *i'rab*.

﴿Say: "If the last abode with God is yours alone, to the exclusion of others..."﴾: It was revealed concerning what Ibn al-Jawzi reported, when the Jews said: "God did not create Paradise except for Israel and his sons." Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Rabi' said: "The reason for the revelation of these two verses is their saying: ﴿None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111], and ﴿We are the sons of God﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18], and ﴿The Fire will not touch us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80], and the verses." The same was related from Qatadah. The pronoun in *qul* ("say") refers either to the Prophet ﷺ, or to whoever is appropriate to establish the proof against them, from him and from others. They explained *al-dar al-akhirah* ("the last abode") as Paradise, and said: "This is familiar in its use for Paradise." God the Exalted said: ﴿That abode of the Hereafter We shall give to those who do not desire haughtiness on earth or corruption﴾ [al-Qasas: 83]. It is known that what is given to these is Paradise. ﴿And the abode of the Hereafter is better for those who fear God﴾ [al-An'am: 32]. The best view is that this is by omission of a modifier which the meaning indicates, meaning: "the bliss of the last abode, its favour, and its good." This is because the last abode is the place of residence after the end of this world. It was called "the last" because it comes after this world, or because it is the last thing that is inhabited. The discussion of this has already passed in His saying: ﴿and they are certain of the Hereafter﴾ [al-Naml: 3]. The meaning of "with God" is "in the judgment of God," as in His saying: ﴿Those are with God...﴾ [al-Nur: 13], that is, in His judgment, ﴿they are the defiantly disobedient﴾ [Al 'Imran: 82]. It has been said that what is meant by "with" here is standing, rank, and honour, not place. The meaning of "exclusively" (*khālisah*) is: specifically for you, with no share of its bliss for others.

They differed over the *i'rab* of *khālisah*. It has been said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*). Al-Zamakhshari did not report any other view. In that case *lakum* ("for you") is the predicate of *kānat*, and the element governing the circumstantial state is the element governing the prepositional phrase. The adverbial phrase cannot be the predicate in that case, because it does not complete the meaning of the sentence by itself. Al-Mahdawi and Ibn 'Atiyya erred in this, when they said: "It is also permissible that *khālisah* be accusative as a state, and *'inda Allah* ("with God") be the predicate of *kāna*." It has been said that the accusative *khālisah* is the predicate of *kānat*. Then *lakum* may be connected to *kānat*, since the prepositional particle can be connected to *kāna*, and it may be connected to *khālisah*. It may also be explanatory (*li-l-tabyīn*), in which case it is connected to an omitted element whose supposition is *lakum*, meaning "I mean for you," like their saying *saqyan laka* ("watering to you") when the supposition is "to you I call."

﴿to the exclusion of mankind﴾: it is connected to *khālisah*. *Dūn* ("to the exclusion of") here is a term used for exclusivity and cutting off partnership. You say: "This is a guardian to the exclusion of you," and you mean there is no right to it for you with me, nor a share. In other places it comes with the meaning of inferiority in rank, place, or amount. What is meant by "mankind" is the category, and this is the apparent sense, because of the indication of the wording and of His saying *khālisah*. It has been said that what is meant is the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims. It has been said that what is meant by it is the Prophet ﷺ, as Ibn 'Abbas said. They said: "People" is used, and what is meant by it is one man, and this would not occur except as a figure of speech, treating one man as a group.

﴿then wish for death﴾: that is, ask for it with the tongue alone, even if not with the heart, as Ibn 'Abbas said. Or: wish for it with your hearts and ask for it with your tongues, as a group said. Or: ask for it with your hearts, against the worse of the two parties, whether of the believers or of them. This was related from Ibn 'Abbas and others. The majority read *fa-tamannaw al-mawt* with a *ḍamma* on the *wāw*, which is the well-known dialect for forms like *ikhshaw al-qawm* ("fear the people"). The *kasra* is permissible, by analogy of this *wāw* with the *wāw* of *wa-law istaṭa'nā* ("and if we were able"), just as they made the *wāw* of *law* analogous to the *wāw* of *ikhshaw*, and so they used *ḍamma* and said *law istaṭa'nā*. Ibn Abi Ishaq read *fa-tamannaw al-mawt* with a *kasra*. Abu 'Ali al-Hasan ibn Ibrahim ibn Yazdad related from Abu 'Amr that he read *fa-tamannaw al-mawt* with a *fatḥa* on the *wāw*, and he gave it a *fatḥa* seeking lightness, since the *ḍamma* and *kasra* on the *wāw* are heavy. It is also related from Abu 'Amr that he elided the *ḍamma* of the *wāw* (*ikhtilās*).

﴿if you are truthful﴾ in your claim that Paradise is yours to the exclusion of others. The answer of the condition is omitted, meaning "then wish for death." Their wishing is made dependent on a condition that is absent, which is their being truthful. They are not truthful in the claim that Paradise is exclusively theirs to the exclusion of mankind, so the wish does not take place. (p-311) The purpose of this is a challenge and the exposure of their lie. Whoever is certain that he is among the people of Paradise chooses to move to it, to be freed from dwelling in the abode of troubles, and to reach the abode of rest. As was related about those to whom the Messenger of God ﷺ testified of Paradise, such as 'Uthman, 'Ali, 'Ammar, and Hudhayfah, that they used to choose death, and likewise the Companions used to choose martyrdom. In the authentic hadith he ﷺ said: "I wish that I might live, then be killed, then live, then be killed," because of what he knew of the excellence of martyrdom. And when news reached him of the killing of those slain at Bir Ma'unah, he said: "Would that I had been left with them in the cloak of the mountain." It was related from Hudhayfah that he used to wish for death, and when he was dying he said: "A beloved has come upon poverty." And from 'Ammar, when he was at Siffin, he said: "Tomorrow we shall meet the beloved, Muhammad and his companions." And from 'Ali that he used to walk between the two lines in a light shirt, and his son al-Hasan said to him: "This is not the dress of those who fight," and he said: "My son, your father does not care whether he falls upon death or death falls upon him." 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah used to recite, while he fought the Romans:

> "How good is Paradise, and its nearness,
> Pleasant and cool is its drink,
> And the Romans are Romans, whose punishment has drawn near."

In the accounts of the killing of 'Uthman and of Sa'id ibn Jubayr there is what indicates their choosing martyrdom. 'Uthman was approached by a group of the Companions, who said to him: "Shall we fight on your behalf?" He said to them: "No." He had about a thousand slaves, and when the attackers came upon them they drew their swords, and he said: "Whoever sheathes his sword is free." So he endured until he was killed. As for Sa'id, when al-Hajjaj sought him, those assigned to him saw the wild beasts seeking refuge with him and rubbing against him, and they said: "We will not take part in shedding the blood of this righteous man." They said to him: "He seeks you to kill you, so go wherever you wish, and we will be a ransom." He said: "No, by God, I asked my Lord for martyrdom, and He has granted it to me. By God, I will not leave."

It was related from the Prophet ﷺ: "If they wished for death, every person would choke on his saliva and die in his place, and no Jew would remain on the face of the earth." That is because God commanded His Prophet to call them to wish for death, and to inform them that whoever among them wished for it would die. The Prophet ﷺ did so, and the Jews knew his truthfulness, so they refrained from wishing for it, out of fear of God.

﴿And they will never wish for it, because of what their hands have sent forward﴾: This is one of the miracles, since it is a report of the unseen. Its counterpart among reports of the unseen is His saying: ﴿But if you do not, and you will never do it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:24]. Its apparent meaning is that whoever claims the Garden is exclusively his, to the exclusion of other people, from among those addressed in His saying: ﴿Say: If the last abode with Allah is exclusively for you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:94], could never wish for death at all. For this reason the particle of negation here is "lan" (will never), which some claim indicates negation extending over all time. Thus the word "abadan" (at all), according to the view of those who claim this, serves for emphasis. As for those who claim that it means "la" (not), then "abadan" in that case conveys the encompassing of all periods of time. By "the abad" (eternity) here is meant what lies ahead of the lifetimes of these people.

In al-Muntakhab, its text reads: "He said here, ﴿and they will never wish for it﴾, and in al-Jumu'ah, ﴿and they will never wish for it﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 62:7], because their claim here is greater than their claim there, since the highest happiness is above the rank of guardianship (wilayah), because the second is desired for the sake of obtaining the first. And "lan" is more emphatic in negation than "la," so He made it the greatest negation." End of his words.

Al-Mahdawi said in his book al-Tahsil, which he authored: "This miracle existed in the time of the Prophet ﷺ and then ended with his death ﷺ. A parallel to this is a man who says to a people, after telling them a narrative: The sign of my truthfulness is that I will move my hand, and none of you can move his hand, and then he does so, and this will be a proof of his truthfulness, and it will not be invalidated if they move their hands after that." End of his words. Other exegetes have said the same.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The correct view is that this incident, the death of the one who wishes for death, was only for many days at the time the verse was revealed, and it is comparable to his calling the Christians of Najran to mubahalah (mutual cursing prayer)." End of his words.

Both statements, I mean the statement of al-Mahdawi and of Ibn 'Atiyyah, contradict the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, since "abadan" apparently extends over the entire duration of their lifetimes, as we have explained. Was their refraining from wishing for death due to their knowledge that every prophet who presented a matter to his people and threatened them with destruction for it, and they rejected him as a denial, that what he threatened them with would certainly come to pass? Or was it due to their knowledge of the truthfulness of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and that he does not speak about Allah except the truth? Or was it because Allah diverted them from it, as has been said regarding the absence of an opposition to the Qur'an through "al-sarfah" (divine diversion)? These are three views. The apparent meaning is that this is grounded in ﴿what their hands have sent forward﴾. What their hands sent forward is their denial of the prophets, their killing of them, their saying ﴿Show us Allah openly﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:153], their saying ﴿Make for us a god﴾ [al-A'raf 7:138], their saying ﴿So go, you and your Lord﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:24], their transgression regarding the Sabbath, and the rest of the major sins which no nation before them or after them committed. This wishing for death that was demanded of them and negated for them never actually occurred from them, for had it occurred it would have been transmitted, and the motives of those opposed to Islam would have been strong to transmit it.

The views regarding the meaning of "tamanni" (wishing) have already been mentioned. The apparent meaning is that it does not refer here to an inner act of the heart, since that is not perceived, and so it is not challenged by it. Rather it refers to verbal speech, like your saying: "Would that the matter were so." Do you not see that the one who says that is said to have "wished" (tamanna)? And "layta" (would that) is called a word of wishing. Nor has it been transmitted that they said: "We wished that in our hearts." And it is not possible that their refraining from reporting was because they wished in their hearts, since they would not be believed in that, because they had contended with the Muslims over things they would not be believed in, such as slandering Allah, distorting His Book, and other things.

Al-Maturidi said, in summary: The believer says that the Garden is his, and yet he does not wish for death. He answered: The believer has not made for himself, in relation to Allah, a status like that claimed by the Jews, of sonship and beloved standing with Allah, because all believers, other than the prophets, are not free from fear of the final outcome, and the one among them who errs needs time in which to make up for the expiation of his error. Therefore the believers did not wish for death. For this reason, those given the good news of the Garden would wish for it. They mentioned regarding "ma" in His saying ﴿because of what﴾ that it may be a verbal (masdariyyah) particle, but the apparent view is that it is a relative pronoun (mawsul), with the returning pronoun omitted, and it is an allusion to what they committed of past sins. The "sending forward" is attributed to the hand metaphorically, and the meaning is "because of what they sent forward," since the hand is the limb most active in good and evil. This usage is frequent in the Qur'an: ﴿That is because of what your two hands have sent forward﴾ [al-Hajj 22:10], ﴿because of what your hands have sent forward﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:182], ﴿then because of what your hands have earned﴾ [al-Shura 42:30]. It has also been said that the hand is meant literally here, and that what their hands sent forward is the altering of the description of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and that this was done by the writing of their hands.

﴿And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾: This is a declarative sentence, and its meaning is threat and warning. Allah's knowledge pertains to the wrongdoer and to the non-wrongdoer. So restricting the mention to the wrongdoer indicates the occurrence of the warning. It has also been said that its meaning is: He will recompense them for their wrongdoing, so He used knowledge as an allusion to requital, and knowledge was tied to the attribute to indicate causation. The "al" in "al-zalimin" (the wrongdoers) is either for specific reference, so it is restricted to the Jews already mentioned, or for the category, so it encompasses every wrongdoer. He mentioned the wrongdoers because wrongdoing is transgressing what Allah has set as limits, and nothing is more emphatic in transgression than claiming the exclusive ownership of the Garden for one who has not clothed himself in any of its requirements, and singling himself out for it to the exclusion of people.

﴿And you will surely find them the most greedy of people for life﴾: The address here is to the Prophet ﷺ. "Wajada" (found) here is transitive to two objects: the first is the pronoun, and the second is "the most greedy of people." When it is transitive to two objects, it has the meaning of "alima" (knew) which is transitive to two, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if We found most of them to be defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-A'raf 7:102]. That it is transitive to two objects here is the view of those whose statements among the exegetes we have come across. It is possible that "wajada" here means "laqiya" (met) and "asaba" (encountered), and that the accusative "ahrasa" (most greedy) is a circumstantial state (hal). But this only holds according to the view of those who hold that the annexation (idafah) of the elative form is not definite, which is the view of al-Farisi. Among our companions, Ustadh Abu al-Hasan ibn 'Asfur went this way. As for those who hold that the annexation is definite and do not permit a circumstantial state to be definite, then the accusative of "ahras" as a circumstantial state is not permitted in their view. Here "ahras" is the elative form, and it is interpreted as meaning "min" (more than), and it is annexed to a definite noun, so both possibilities are permitted: One: that its masculine singular form be used, even though it follows a singular, dual, or plural, masculine or feminine. Two: that it agrees with what precedes it. From the first possibility is "ahras al-nas" (most greedy of people). Had it come in agreement, it would have been "ahariss al-nas" or "ahrasi al-nas." From the second possibility is His saying: ﴿the greatest of its criminals﴾ [al-An'am 6:123]. Both forms are eloquent. Abu Mansur al-Jawaliqi mentioned that agreement is more eloquent than the singular. Ibn al-Sarraj held that the singular is mandatory, and this is not correct. When it is annexed to a definite noun, as in these two places, the condition is that what is annexed is part of what it is annexed to. For this reason the Basrans prohibited "Yusuf is the best of his brothers," taking "ahsan" as the elative, and they interpreted what came similar to it. Rare is his saying:

"O Lord of Musa, I have done wrong, and he has done more wrong."

He means: "We wronged, since the one who was not astray would not wrong" to what is part of it. The accusative pronoun in "and you will surely find them" refers either to the Jews about whom He reported that they do not wish for death, or to all the Jews, or to the scholars of the Children of Israel, in three views. He used the form of the elative from "greed" to emphasize the intensity of their seeking to remain and the continuance of life.
