As for "al-nas" (people): the "al" is for the category, so it encompasses, or for specific reference, either because the intended meaning is a known group of people overwhelmed by greed for life, or because the intended meaning is the Magians or the polytheists of the Arabs, since those do not have certainty of resurrection, so they have only the pleasures or miseries of this world. For this reason one of them said:

"Enjoy the world, for you are perishable, of its delights and beautiful women."

Another said:

"When the world ends and its pleasure vanishes, then for me there is no hope in anything other than that."

﴿for life﴾: They estimated that there is an omitted noun here, meaning "for a long life," or an omitted adjective, meaning "for a long life." If no omission were estimated, the meaning would still be sound, namely that they are the most greedy of people for life in general, since whoever is most greedy for life in general, meaning its being realized even for the briefest time, is all the more greedy for a long life. They had been denounced as being the most intense of people in greed for life, even for a single hour. Ubayy recited "ʿalā al-ḥayāh" with the definite article. Al-Zamakhshari said, in substance: The indefinite reading is more emphatic than Ubayy's reading, because it intends a specific life, namely the prolonged life. End of his words. We have already shown that this description is not necessary.

﴿And among those who associated partners﴾: It is possible that this is connected and included under the elative, so that would be a case of construing according to meaning, since the meaning of "the most greedy of people" is "more greedy than people." It is also possible that this is an instance of ellipsis, meaning "and more greedy than those who associated partners," so the first "ahras" is omitted because the first "ahras" indicates it. "Those who associated partners" are the Magians, because of their worship of light and darkness. It has also been said: fire. Or the polytheists of the Arabs, because of their worship of idols and their taking deities alongside Allah. Or a group of polytheists who denied resurrection, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They say: Shall we indeed be returned to our former state?﴾ [al-Nazi'at 79:10] ﴿When we are decayed bones?﴾ [al-Nazi'at 79:11]. According to these views, ﴿and among those who associated partners﴾ is a specification after a generalization, if we say that His saying "the most greedy of people" is general. In that case it is a greater rebuke to the Jews, since they are People of the Book who hope for reward and fear punishment, and yet they are more greedy than those who do not hope for that and do not believe in resurrection. Their greed was more eloquent because of their knowledge that they are heading toward punishment, so they were the people most eager to be far from it. For whoever expects evil is the most averse to it. So when life was the cause of distance from punishment, they were the most greedy of people for it. On this view, where it is connected and "among those who associated partners" is linked to the elative, the word "min" must be mentioned, because "the most greedy of people" applies to the Jews, so if you joined it without "min" it would be in apposition to "people," and the meaning would be: "and you will find them more greedy than those who associated partners," so the elative would be annexed to something outside what it is part of, since the Jews are not among the polytheists, I mean the polytheists who were explained by "those who associated partners" here. This is not the case if we say that the subsequent items in a conjunction may take what the first items may not take, for then it would be correct. As for the view of one who claimed that His saying "and among those who associated partners" is conjoined to the pronoun in "and you will surely find them," meaning "and you will surely find them and a group of those who associated partners the most greedy of people for life," so that there would be inversion in the speech: this is a meaning that can be correct, but the wording and construction reject it and remove it from eloquence, and there is no necessity compelling that this be a case of inversion, especially according to the view of one who restricts inversion to necessity.

This whole discussion holds on the assumption that the conjunction (*wāw*) in ﴿And among those who associated partners﴾ is coordinating a single noun with a single noun (*ʿaṭf mufrad ʿalā mufrad*). If it is coordinating whole clauses (*ʿaṭf al-jumal*), then the phrase is cut off from being included under the elative form (*afʿal al-tafḍīl*). It then begins a fresh statement about a group of polytheists who likewise wish to live a long time. Earlier it was noted that the intended referents of "those who associated partners" are: the Magians (*al-Majūs*), the polytheists of the Arabs, or a group of the polytheists in the first case. If it is a resumptive statement (*istiʾnāf ikhbār*), Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "They are the Magians, because their way of blessing the one who sneezes in their language means: 'Live a thousand years.'" In this view there is an implicit comparison of the Children of Israel with this group of polytheists. End of his words. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "And those who associated partners, according to this (i.e., that it is a new statement), are referred to as the Jews, because they said, 'ʿUzayr is the son of God.'" End of his words.

According to this view, he has informed us that among this group, who are intensely greedy for life, there is one who *wishes* (*yawaddu*) that he might be given a thousand years of life. This is the utmost in wishing for a long life. The phrase "those who associated partners" would then be an apparent noun placed in the position of a pronoun (*waqʿ al-ẓāhir mawqiʿ al-muḍmar*), which indicates the cause, since the meaning is: "Among them is a group, one of whom wishes..." The phrase *yawaddu aḥaduhum* ("one of whom wishes") is a description (*ṣifa*) of an omitted subject: i.e., "and among those who associated partners is a group, one of whom wishes." This is one of the places where it is permissible to omit the modified noun, as in the verse ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 37:164], and ﴿And there is none of the People of the Scripture but that he will surely believe in it before his death﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 4:159], and as in the Arab saying: "Some of us departed, and some of us stayed."

If the *wāw* in ﴿And among those who associated partners﴾ is coordinating a single noun with a single noun, they say: *yawaddu aḥaduhum* is then a clause in the position of a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*), meaning "one of them wishing." They say it is a state of *alladhīna* (the relative), so that the governing element is the omitted "more greedy" (*aḥraṣa*), or it is a state of the pronoun in *ashrakū*, so that the governing element is *ashrakū*. It is also permissible for it to be a state of the object pronoun in ﴿you will surely find them﴾, meaning "you will surely find them the most greedy for life, one of them wishing." It is also permissible for it to be a new statement about them, explaining the state of their affair in their increasing greed for life.

*Aḥaduhum*: "any one of them." This is not the *aḥad* found in the expression *mā qāma aḥad* ("no one stood up"), because that is used in negation or what is similar to negation. The difference between them is that this *aḥad* is originally *hamza + ḥāʾ + dāl*, whereas the root of that one is *wāw + ḥāʾ + dāl*. So the *hamza* in *aḥaduhum* is a replacement for a *wāw*. The phrase ﴿one of them wishes﴾ does not mean one specific individual among them to the exclusion of the rest. Rather, *aḥaduhum* here is general in the sense of distributive generality (*ʿumūm al-badal*), meaning this ruling against them, that each one of them wishes to be granted a thousand years, applies to each individual in turn. The meaning is that if you look at the greed of any one of them, and at the intensity of his heart's attachment to a long life, you will find that if he were granted a thousand years he would wish for more.

﴿If he were granted a thousand years﴾: the object of the wishing (*al-wadda*) is omitted, its estimated form being: "one of them wishes for long life." The answer to *law* (the conditional particle "if/would that") is also omitted, its estimated form being: "If he were granted a thousand years, he would be delighted by that." So the object of *yawaddu* is omitted because *law yuʿammar* indicates it, and the answer to *law* is omitted because *yawaddu* indicates it. This is what follows the rules of the Basran grammarians in such a place. Some of the Kufan grammarians and others held in such a place that *law* here is a verbal particle (*maṣdariyya*) with the meaning of *an* ("that"), so it has no answer, and from it a verbal noun is formed which is the object of *yawaddu*, as if he had said: "One of them wishes the lengthening of a thousand years." According to this view there is no omission in the sentence. According to the first view, *law yuʿammar alfa sana* has no grammatical position (*maḥall ʿirāb*). According to the second view its position is accusative as an object, as we have mentioned. The preference between the two views is discussed in the science of grammar (*ʿilm al-naḥw*).

Al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you ask: how is *law yuʿammar* connected to *yawaddu aḥaduhum*?" I say: it is a quotation of their wishing, and *law* carries the meaning of wishing. The analogy would have been *law uʿammar* ("if I were granted..."), but it follows the third-person form because of *yawaddu aḥaduhum*, as in their saying: "He swore by God that he would surely do it." End of his words. There is some vagueness in this, because *yawaddu* is a verb of the heart (*fiʿl qalbī*), not a verb of speech, and its meaning is not the meaning of speech. If that is so, how can you say it is a quotation of their wishing? It is only permissible by way of a figurative extension (*tajawwuz*): one treats *yawaddu* as if it were *yaqūlu* ("says"), because speech arises from matters of the heart. So it is as if he had said: "One of them says, out of his own inner wish, 'If I were granted a thousand years...'" And *law*, when it expresses wishing, does not need an answer clause, because its meaning is the meaning of "Oh, would that I were granted life," and in that case the clause stands in the position of an object by way of quotation.

So, by what we have established concerning *law*, there are three views: that it is a particle for what would have happened because of the occurrence of something else; that it is a verbal particle (*maṣdariyya*); and that it expresses a wish, in quoted form. The meaning of "a thousand years" is a long life among the sons of its kind, so "a thousand years" is a metonymy (*kināya*) for a long period of time. It is also possible that it means a literal thousand years, even though he knows he will not live a thousand years, because wishing may be directed at what is possible and at what is customarily or rationally impossible. So the meaning would be that, because of their intense greed for increased life, their wishing in this regard attaches itself to what customarily cannot occur.

﴿And he is not one to remove him from punishment by being granted long life﴾: the pronoun in the phrase *wa mā huwa* ("and he is not") refers to *aḥaduhum*, and it is the subject (*ism*) of *mā*, while *bi-muzaḥzihihi* ("one to remove him") is the predicate (*khabar*) of *mā*, so it is in the accusative position, and this is according to the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz. On this basis, what occurs in the Qur'an of this kind should be interpreted. *An yuʿammar* ("that he be granted long life") is the subject (*fāʿil*) of *bi-muzaḥzihihi*, meaning: "And none of them will remove him from punishment through his being granted long life." They also permitted, in this view, namely that the pronoun refers to *aḥaduhum*, that *huwa* be the subject and *bi-muzaḥzihihi* the predicate, and that *an yuʿammar* be the subject of *bi-muzaḥzihihi*, in which case *mā* is of the Tamīmī dialect. This latter view, namely that *mā* is Tamīmī, is the one with which Ibn ʿAṭiyya began. They also permitted that *huwa* be a pronoun referring to the verbal noun implied by *law yuʿammar* ("if he were granted long life"), and that *an yuʿammar* be a substitute (*badal*) for it. The *huwa* then has its nominative case in either of two ways: as the subject of *mā* or as a subject (*mubtadaʾ*). It has also been said: *huwa* is a metonymic reference to the lengthening of life (*al-taʿmīr*), and *an yuʿammar* is a substitute for it, and *huwa* does not refer back to anything before it. The difference between this view and the preceding one is that in this view the element explaining the pronoun is the substitute, whereas in the first view the element explaining it is the verbal noun indicated by the verb in *law yuʿammar*. Whether a substitute can explain a pronoun within it is disputed, but there is no dispute that a pronoun may be explained by a verbal noun derived from a preceding verb. The first explains it by what precedes, the latter by what follows. This is what al-Zamakhsharī meant by his words: "It is also permissible for *huwa* to be ambiguous (*mubham*), with *an yuʿammar* clarifying it." He means that *huwa* does not refer back to anything before it, and *an yuʿammar* is a substitute for it that explains it.

Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī permitted in *al-Ḥalabiyyāt* that *huwa* be the pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr al-shaʾn*), and this is an inclination on his part toward the view of the Kufans: that the explanation of the pronoun of the matter, which they call "the unknown" (*al-majhūl*), may be something other than a clause when it forms a semantic predication, as in: "I thought him standing, Zayd," and *mā huwa bi-qāʾimin Zaydun* ("He is not standing, Zayd"). Here, according to them, *huwa* is the subject, a pronoun they call "unknown"; *bi-qāʾimin* is in the position of the predicate, and *Zaydun* is the subject of *qāʾim*. Their meaning was: "He is not one standing, Zayd." For this reason they parse, in "I thought him standing, Zayd," the *hāʾ* as the pronoun of the unknown, which is the object of *ẓanantu* ("I thought"), *qāʾiman* as the second object, and *Zaydun* as the subject of *qāʾim*. According to the view of the Basrans, it is not permissible for it to be explained except by a clause whose two parts are explicitly stated and free from a preposition. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "al-Ṭabarī reported from a group that they said: it is an *ʿimād* (separator)." End of his words. This needs explanation, because the *ʿimād* in the view of some Kufans may precede the predicate before the subject. So when you say *mā Zaydun huwa al-qāʾimu* ("Zayd is not the one standing"), they permit you to say *mā huwa al-qāʾimu Zaydun*. So according to them the underlying sentence is: "And its lengthening is not one to remove him..." Then the predicate was placed before the separator, giving: "And he is not one to remove him from punishment by being granted long life," i.e., "its lengthening." This is not permitted according to the Basrans, because their condition for the separator is that it be in the middle position.

To summarize the views on this pronoun: Does it refer to *aḥaduhum*? Or to the verbal noun implied by *yuʿammar*? Or to what follows it, namely *an yuʿammar*? Or is it the pronoun of the matter? Or is it a separator? Five views, the most apparent of which is the first.

﴿And God is Seeing of what they do﴾: The majority read *yaʿmalūna* with the *yāʾ* ("they do"), in line with the preceding discourse. Al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, al-Aʿraj, and Yaʿqūb read it with the *tāʾ* ("you do"), as a shift (*iltifāt*) from the third-person absence to the second-person address. This sentence contains a threat and a warning. Here he uses the attribute *baṣīr* ("Seeing"), although God is exalted above having organs, to inform that His knowledge of all deeds is a knowledge of comprehensive encompassment and perception of hidden things. In *bimā*, the *mā* is a relative pronoun, and the returning pronoun is omitted, meaning *yaʿmalūnahu* ("they do it"). They also permitted that it be a verbal particle, meaning "by their deed." He used the form of the present tense, even though His knowledge encompasses their past and future deeds, for the sake of the harmony of the verse-endings (*tawākhī al-fawāṣil*).

These noble verses have contained a reminder to the Children of Israel and a recollection of them of the blessings of God: when He gave Moses the Torah, which contains guidance and light, and then followed him with messengers to renew the religion of God and His laws; and when He gave Jesus extraordinary matters: the raising of the dead, the healing of the blind and the leper, the creation of a living being and the breathing of the spirit into it, the reporting of unseen things, and other things. He supported him with the one who brings down revelation at his hands, namely Gabriel, peace be upon him. Yet, despite these miracles and blessings, they were the furthest of people from accepting what came to them from God. They were such that whenever a messenger came to them with what did not agree with them, they hastened to deny him or killed him, while being unconcerned with the crimes that issued from them. It is related that in the wake of their killing of a group of prophets, the vegetable market (*sūq al-baql*) was held among them, which is the basest of markets. How then about the markets in which precious things are sold? Then God rebuked them for remaining upon that habit of denying what came from God, even though before His coming they used to mention that he would come to them from God. So when what they had been awaiting and recognizing came to them, they disbelieved in it, and God sealed upon them with the curse. The reason for their expulsion from the mercy of God is what preceded of their disbelief, and their faith was meagre, since before the coming of the Book they used to believe that a Book would come. Then he began to censure them, that they sold their precious selves for what resulted for them from their disbelief in the signs of God, namely foods and leaderships which end in a short time. The factor driving them to this was envy and transgression, because God singled out with His bounty whomever He willed of His servants. They were not content with His judgment or His choice, so they incurred wrath from God, and He prepared for them in the Hereafter the punishment that will humiliate and degrade them. Since their refusal to believe was only out of arrogance, envy, and non-acceptance of the decree, it was fitting that they be punished with the punishment that contains for them disgrace, abasement, and humiliation.

Then God, exalted is He, informed about them that when faith in what God has sent down is presented to them, they reply that they believe in the Torah and that they disbelieve in whatever is other than it. Yet the revealed books that come from God are equal, since all of them are truth, each confirming the others. So disbelief in some of them is disbelief in all of them.

Then God, exalted is He, informed of their lying in their statement: ﴿We believe in what was sent down to us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91]. That is because they killed the prophets, while the Torah speaks explicitly of following the prophets and taking them as examples. Thus their action contradicted their words.

Then He repeated to them, as a rebuke, that Moses, to whom the Torah was sent down, and whom they claim they believed in, came to them with clear signs and extraordinary miracles, such as their deliverance from Pharaoh, the splitting of the sea, and other things. Despite this, after his departure to converse with his Lord, they took as a god the calf made from their ornaments, the most dull-witted and stupid of animals, whose fashioning and making were witnessed, while Moses had not yet died and the Book of God was recently sent down to them, its time not long past.

God repeated the mention of lifting the mountain (Tur) over them so that they would accept what was in (p-317) the Torah. They were commanded to listen and obey, but they responded with disobedience. Moreover, they were compelled to faith, or were as those who are compelled, because such a terrifying thing as a mountain being raised over them, to crush them with it, is sufficient to make a person do what he is commanded and accept the obligations laid upon him. Their refusal and failure to accept was due to the fact that the worship of the calf had permeated their hearts and mixed with them, so that they did not hear acceptance of anything of the truth. When the heart is filled with love of something, it hears nothing else and does not listen to blame. They recited:

*You have filled my whole heart with a portion of your love,*
*so if you seek more, bring a heart.*

Then God censured them for what their faith commanded them, though they have no real faith. Rather, He attributed it to them sarcastically, [namely] the worship of the calf and taking it as a god besides God.

Then He refuted them in their claim that Paradise is exclusively theirs, that no one other than them will enter it. So He commanded them to wish for death, because whoever believes that he will arrive at joy, delight and lasting pleasure that never ends, prefers to reach that and to have the humiliation and misery he is in come to an end.

God informed that their wishing for death will never occur from them, and that their abstention from it is due to the crimes their hands have committed. Thus their claim to be the people of Paradise is shown to be false. Then, as a corroboration of what came before concerning their not wishing for death, He informed that they are the most eager of people for life, even more eager than those who do not believe in the Last Abode, and do not hope for reward or fear punishment. Then He mentioned that one of them wishes to be granted a thousand years of life, yet even with that, his long life, however long, will not save him from God's punishment.

Then He concluded the verses by stating that God, exalted is He, is aware of the ugliness of their deeds and will recompense them for them. The totality of these verses makes clear what the Jews are disposed to: excessive lying, contradiction between their actions and their words, deficiency of intellect, and abundant slander. May God protect us from that, and guide us along the most upright paths.

﴿And they will never wish for it, because of what their hands have sent forward﴾: This is one of the miracles, since it is a report of the unseen. Its counterpart among reports of the unseen is His saying: ﴿But if you do not, and you will never do it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:24]. Its apparent meaning is that whoever claims the Garden is exclusively his, to the exclusion of other people, from among those addressed in His saying: ﴿Say: If the last abode with Allah is exclusively for you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:94], could never wish for death at all. For this reason the particle of negation here is "lan" (will never), which some claim indicates negation extending over all time. Thus the word "abadan" (at all), according to the view of those who claim this, serves for emphasis. As for those who claim that it means "la" (not), then "abadan" in that case conveys the encompassing of all periods of time. By "the abad" (eternity) here is meant what lies ahead of the lifetimes of these people.

In al-Muntakhab, its text reads: "He said here, ﴿and they will never wish for it﴾, and in al-Jumu'ah, ﴿and they will never wish for it﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 62:7], because their claim here is greater than their claim there, since the highest happiness is above the rank of guardianship (wilayah), because the second is desired for the sake of obtaining the first. And "lan" is more emphatic in negation than "la," so He made it the greatest negation." End of his words.

Al-Mahdawi said in his book al-Tahsil, which he authored: "This miracle existed in the time of the Prophet ﷺ and then ended with his death ﷺ. A parallel to this is a man who says to a people, after telling them a narrative: The sign of my truthfulness is that I will move my hand, and none of you can move his hand, and then he does so, and this will be a proof of his truthfulness, and it will not be invalidated if they move their hands after that." End of his words. Other exegetes have said the same.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The correct view is that this incident, the death of the one who wishes for death, was only for many days at the time the verse was revealed, and it is comparable to his calling the Christians of Najran to mubahalah (mutual cursing prayer)." End of his words.

Both statements, I mean the statement of al-Mahdawi and of Ibn 'Atiyyah, contradict the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, since "abadan" apparently extends over the entire duration of their lifetimes, as we have explained. Was their refraining from wishing for death due to their knowledge that every prophet who presented a matter to his people and threatened them with destruction for it, and they rejected him as a denial, that what he threatened them with would certainly come to pass? Or was it due to their knowledge of the truthfulness of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and that he does not speak about Allah except the truth? Or was it because Allah diverted them from it, as has been said regarding the absence of an opposition to the Qur'an through "al-sarfah" (divine diversion)? These are three views. The apparent meaning is that this is grounded in ﴿what their hands have sent forward﴾. What their hands sent forward is their denial of the prophets, their killing of them, their saying ﴿Show us Allah openly﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:153], their saying ﴿Make for us a god﴾ [al-A'raf 7:138], their saying ﴿So go, you and your Lord﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:24], their transgression regarding the Sabbath, and the rest of the major sins which no nation before them or after them committed. This wishing for death that was demanded of them and negated for them never actually occurred from them, for had it occurred it would have been transmitted, and the motives of those opposed to Islam would have been strong to transmit it.

The views regarding the meaning of "tamanni" (wishing) have already been mentioned. The apparent meaning is that it does not refer here to an inner act of the heart, since that is not perceived, and so it is not challenged by it. Rather it refers to verbal speech, like your saying: "Would that the matter were so." Do you not see that the one who says that is said to have "wished" (tamanna)? And "layta" (would that) is called a word of wishing. Nor has it been transmitted that they said: "We wished that in our hearts." And it is not possible that their refraining from reporting was because they wished in their hearts, since they would not be believed in that, because they had contended with the Muslims over things they would not be believed in, such as slandering Allah, distorting His Book, and other things.

Al-Maturidi said, in summary: The believer says that the Garden is his, and yet he does not wish for death. He answered: The believer has not made for himself, in relation to Allah, a status like that claimed by the Jews, of sonship and beloved standing with Allah, because all believers, other than the prophets, are not free from fear of the final outcome, and the one among them who errs needs time in which to make up for the expiation of his error. Therefore the believers did not wish for death. For this reason, those given the good news of the Garden would wish for it. They mentioned regarding "ma" in His saying ﴿because of what﴾ that it may be a verbal (masdariyyah) particle, but the apparent view is that it is a relative pronoun (mawsul), with the returning pronoun omitted, and it is an allusion to what they committed of past sins. The "sending forward" is attributed to the hand metaphorically, and the meaning is "because of what they sent forward," since the hand is the limb most active in good and evil. This usage is frequent in the Qur'an: ﴿That is because of what your two hands have sent forward﴾ [al-Hajj 22:10], ﴿because of what your hands have sent forward﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:182], ﴿then because of what your hands have earned﴾ [al-Shura 42:30]. It has also been said that the hand is meant literally here, and that what their hands sent forward is the altering of the description of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and that this was done by the writing of their hands.

﴿And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾: This is a declarative sentence, and its meaning is threat and warning. Allah's knowledge pertains to the wrongdoer and to the non-wrongdoer. So restricting the mention to the wrongdoer indicates the occurrence of the warning. It has also been said that its meaning is: He will recompense them for their wrongdoing, so He used knowledge as an allusion to requital, and knowledge was tied to the attribute to indicate causation. The "al" in "al-zalimin" (the wrongdoers) is either for specific reference, so it is restricted to the Jews already mentioned, or for the category, so it encompasses every wrongdoer. He mentioned the wrongdoers because wrongdoing is transgressing what Allah has set as limits, and nothing is more emphatic in transgression than claiming the exclusive ownership of the Garden for one who has not clothed himself in any of its requirements, and singling himself out for it to the exclusion of people.

﴿And you will surely find them the most greedy of people for life﴾: The address here is to the Prophet ﷺ. "Wajada" (found) here is transitive to two objects: the first is the pronoun, and the second is "the most greedy of people." When it is transitive to two objects, it has the meaning of "alima" (knew) which is transitive to two, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if We found most of them to be defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-A'raf 7:102]. That it is transitive to two objects here is the view of those whose statements among the exegetes we have come across. It is possible that "wajada" here means "laqiya" (met) and "asaba" (encountered), and that the accusative "ahrasa" (most greedy) is a circumstantial state (hal). But this only holds according to the view of those who hold that the annexation (idafah) of the elative form is not definite, which is the view of al-Farisi. Among our companions, Ustadh Abu al-Hasan ibn 'Asfur went this way. As for those who hold that the annexation is definite and do not permit a circumstantial state to be definite, then the accusative of "ahras" as a circumstantial state is not permitted in their view. Here "ahras" is the elative form, and it is interpreted as meaning "min" (more than), and it is annexed to a definite noun, so both possibilities are permitted: One: that its masculine singular form be used, even though it follows a singular, dual, or plural, masculine or feminine. Two: that it agrees with what precedes it. From the first possibility is "ahras al-nas" (most greedy of people). Had it come in agreement, it would have been "ahariss al-nas" or "ahrasi al-nas." From the second possibility is His saying: ﴿the greatest of its criminals﴾ [al-An'am 6:123]. Both forms are eloquent. Abu Mansur al-Jawaliqi mentioned that agreement is more eloquent than the singular. Ibn al-Sarraj held that the singular is mandatory, and this is not correct. When it is annexed to a definite noun, as in these two places, the condition is that what is annexed is part of what it is annexed to. For this reason the Basrans prohibited "Yusuf is the best of his brothers," taking "ahsan" as the elative, and they interpreted what came similar to it. Rare is his saying:

"O Lord of Musa, I have done wrong, and he has done more wrong."

He means: "We wronged, since the one who was not astray would not wrong" to what is part of it. The accusative pronoun in "and you will surely find them" refers either to the Jews about whom He reported that they do not wish for death, or to all the Jews, or to the scholars of the Children of Israel, in three views. He used the form of the elative from "greed" to emphasize the intensity of their seeking to remain and the continuance of life. As for "al-nas" (people): the "al" is for the category, so it encompasses, or for specific reference, either because the intended meaning is a known group of people overwhelmed by greed for life, or because the intended meaning is the Magians or the polytheists of the Arabs, since those do not have certainty of resurrection, so they have only the pleasures or miseries of this world. For this reason one of them said:

"Enjoy the world, for you are perishable, of its delights and beautiful women."

Another said:

"When the world ends and its pleasure vanishes, then for me there is no hope in anything other than that."

﴿for life﴾: They estimated that there is an omitted noun here, meaning "for a long life," or an omitted adjective, meaning "for a long life." If no omission were estimated, the meaning would still be sound, namely that they are the most greedy of people for life in general, since whoever is most greedy for life in general, meaning its being realized even for the briefest time, is all the more greedy for a long life. They had been denounced as being the most intense of people in greed for life, even for a single hour. Ubayy recited "ʿalā al-ḥayāh" with the definite article. Al-Zamakhshari said, in substance: The indefinite reading is more emphatic than Ubayy's reading, because it intends a specific life, namely the prolonged life. End of his words. We have already shown that this description is not necessary.

﴿And among those who associated partners﴾: It is possible that this is connected and included under the elative, so that would be a case of construing according to meaning, since the meaning of "the most greedy of people" is "more greedy than people." It is also possible that this is an instance of ellipsis, meaning "and more greedy than those who associated partners," so the first "ahras" is omitted because the first "ahras" indicates it. "Those who associated partners" are the Magians, because of their worship of light and darkness. It has also been said: fire. Or the polytheists of the Arabs, because of their worship of idols and their taking deities alongside Allah. Or a group of polytheists who denied resurrection, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They say: Shall we indeed be returned to our former state?﴾ [al-Nazi'at 79:10] ﴿When we are decayed bones?﴾ [al-Nazi'at 79:11]. According to these views, ﴿and among those who associated partners﴾ is a specification after a generalization, if we say that His saying "the most greedy of people" is general. In that case it is a greater rebuke to the Jews, since they are People of the Book who hope for reward and fear punishment, and yet they are more greedy than those who do not hope for that and do not believe in resurrection. Their greed was more eloquent because of their knowledge that they are heading toward punishment, so they were the people most eager to be far from it. For whoever expects evil is the most averse to it. So when life was the cause of distance from punishment, they were the most greedy of people for it. On this view, where it is connected and "among those who associated partners" is linked to the elative, the word "min" must be mentioned, because "the most greedy of people" applies to the Jews, so if you joined it without "min" it would be in apposition to "people," and the meaning would be: "and you will find them more greedy than those who associated partners," so the elative would be annexed to something outside what it is part of, since the Jews are not among the polytheists, I mean the polytheists who were explained by "those who associated partners" here. This is not the case if we say that the subsequent items in a conjunction may take what the first items may not take, for then it would be correct. As for the view of one who claimed that His saying "and among those who associated partners" is conjoined to the pronoun in "and you will surely find them," meaning "and you will surely find them and a group of those who associated partners the most greedy of people for life," so that there would be inversion in the speech: this is a meaning that can be correct, but the wording and construction reject it and remove it from eloquence, and there is no necessity compelling that this be a case of inversion, especially according to the view of one who restricts inversion to necessity.

This whole discussion holds on the assumption that the conjunction (*wāw*) in ﴿And among those who associated partners﴾ is coordinating a single noun with a single noun (*ʿaṭf mufrad ʿalā mufrad*). If it is coordinating whole clauses (*ʿaṭf al-jumal*), then the phrase is cut off from being included under the elative form (*afʿal al-tafḍīl*). It then begins a fresh statement about a group of polytheists who likewise wish to live a long time. Earlier it was noted that the intended referents of "those who associated partners" are: the Magians (*al-Majūs*), the polytheists of the Arabs, or a group of the polytheists in the first case. If it is a resumptive statement (*istiʾnāf ikhbār*), Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "They are the Magians, because their way of blessing the one who sneezes in their language means: 'Live a thousand years.'" In this view there is an implicit comparison of the Children of Israel with this group of polytheists. End of his words. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "And those who associated partners, according to this (i.e., that it is a new statement), are referred to as the Jews, because they said, 'ʿUzayr is the son of God.'" End of his words.

According to this view, he has informed us that among this group, who are intensely greedy for life, there is one who *wishes* (*yawaddu*) that he might be given a thousand years of life. This is the utmost in wishing for a long life. The phrase "those who associated partners" would then be an apparent noun placed in the position of a pronoun (*waqʿ al-ẓāhir mawqiʿ al-muḍmar*), which indicates the cause, since the meaning is: "Among them is a group, one of whom wishes..." The phrase *yawaddu aḥaduhum* ("one of whom wishes") is a description (*ṣifa*) of an omitted subject: i.e., "and among those who associated partners is a group, one of whom wishes." This is one of the places where it is permissible to omit the modified noun, as in the verse ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 37:164], and ﴿And there is none of the People of the Scripture but that he will surely believe in it before his death﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 4:159], and as in the Arab saying: "Some of us departed, and some of us stayed."

If the *wāw* in ﴿And among those who associated partners﴾ is coordinating a single noun with a single noun, they say: *yawaddu aḥaduhum* is then a clause in the position of a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*), meaning "one of them wishing." They say it is a state of *alladhīna* (the relative), so that the governing element is the omitted "more greedy" (*aḥraṣa*), or it is a state of the pronoun in *ashrakū*, so that the governing element is *ashrakū*. It is also permissible for it to be a state of the object pronoun in ﴿you will surely find them﴾, meaning "you will surely find them the most greedy for life, one of them wishing." It is also permissible for it to be a new statement about them, explaining the state of their affair in their increasing greed for life.

*Aḥaduhum*: "any one of them." This is not the *aḥad* found in the expression *mā qāma aḥad* ("no one stood up"), because that is used in negation or what is similar to negation. The difference between them is that this *aḥad* is originally *hamza + ḥāʾ + dāl*, whereas the root of that one is *wāw + ḥāʾ + dāl*. So the *hamza* in *aḥaduhum* is a replacement for a *wāw*. The phrase ﴿one of them wishes﴾ does not mean one specific individual among them to the exclusion of the rest. Rather, *aḥaduhum* here is general in the sense of distributive generality (*ʿumūm al-badal*), meaning this ruling against them, that each one of them wishes to be granted a thousand years, applies to each individual in turn. The meaning is that if you look at the greed of any one of them, and at the intensity of his heart's attachment to a long life, you will find that if he were granted a thousand years he would wish for more.

﴿If he were granted a thousand years﴾: the object of the wishing (*al-wadda*) is omitted, its estimated form being: "one of them wishes for long life." The answer to *law* (the conditional particle "if/would that") is also omitted, its estimated form being: "If he were granted a thousand years, he would be delighted by that." So the object of *yawaddu* is omitted because *law yuʿammar* indicates it, and the answer to *law* is omitted because *yawaddu* indicates it. This is what follows the rules of the Basran grammarians in such a place. Some of the Kufan grammarians and others held in such a place that *law* here is a verbal particle (*maṣdariyya*) with the meaning of *an* ("that"), so it has no answer, and from it a verbal noun is formed which is the object of *yawaddu*, as if he had said: "One of them wishes the lengthening of a thousand years." According to this view there is no omission in the sentence. According to the first view, *law yuʿammar alfa sana* has no grammatical position (*maḥall ʿirāb*). According to the second view its position is accusative as an object, as we have mentioned. The preference between the two views is discussed in the science of grammar (*ʿilm al-naḥw*).

Al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you ask: how is *law yuʿammar* connected to *yawaddu aḥaduhum*?" I say: it is a quotation of their wishing, and *law* carries the meaning of wishing. The analogy would have been *law uʿammar* ("if I were granted..."), but it follows the third-person form because of *yawaddu aḥaduhum*, as in their saying: "He swore by God that he would surely do it." End of his words. There is some vagueness in this, because *yawaddu* is a verb of the heart (*fiʿl qalbī*), not a verb of speech, and its meaning is not the meaning of speech. If that is so, how can you say it is a quotation of their wishing? It is only permissible by way of a figurative extension (*tajawwuz*): one treats *yawaddu* as if it were *yaqūlu* ("says"), because speech arises from matters of the heart. So it is as if he had said: "One of them says, out of his own inner wish, 'If I were granted a thousand years...'" And *law*, when it expresses wishing, does not need an answer clause, because its meaning is the meaning of "Oh, would that I were granted life," and in that case the clause stands in the position of an object by way of quotation.

So, by what we have established concerning *law*, there are three views: that it is a particle for what would have happened because of the occurrence of something else; that it is a verbal particle (*maṣdariyya*); and that it expresses a wish, in quoted form. The meaning of "a thousand years" is a long life among the sons of its kind, so "a thousand years" is a metonymy (*kināya*) for a long period of time. It is also possible that it means a literal thousand years, even though he knows he will not live a thousand years, because wishing may be directed at what is possible and at what is customarily or rationally impossible. So the meaning would be that, because of their intense greed for increased life, their wishing in this regard attaches itself to what customarily cannot occur.

﴿And he is not one to remove him from punishment by being granted long life﴾: the pronoun in the phrase *wa mā huwa* ("and he is not") refers to *aḥaduhum*, and it is the subject (*ism*) of *mā*, while *bi-muzaḥzihihi* ("one to remove him") is the predicate (*khabar*) of *mā*, so it is in the accusative position, and this is according to the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz. On this basis, what occurs in the Qur'an of this kind should be interpreted. *An yuʿammar* ("that he be granted long life") is the subject (*fāʿil*) of *bi-muzaḥzihihi*, meaning: "And none of them will remove him from punishment through his being granted long life." They also permitted, in this view, namely that the pronoun refers to *aḥaduhum*, that *huwa* be the subject and *bi-muzaḥzihihi* the predicate, and that *an yuʿammar* be the subject of *bi-muzaḥzihihi*, in which case *mā* is of the Tamīmī dialect. This latter view, namely that *mā* is Tamīmī, is the one with which Ibn ʿAṭiyya began. They also permitted that *huwa* be a pronoun referring to the verbal noun implied by *law yuʿammar* ("if he were granted long life"), and that *an yuʿammar* be a substitute (*badal*) for it. The *huwa* then has its nominative case in either of two ways: as the subject of *mā* or as a subject (*mubtadaʾ*). It has also been said: *huwa* is a metonymic reference to the lengthening of life (*al-taʿmīr*), and *an yuʿammar* is a substitute for it, and *huwa* does not refer back to anything before it. The difference between this view and the preceding one is that in this view the element explaining the pronoun is the substitute, whereas in the first view the element explaining it is the verbal noun indicated by the verb in *law yuʿammar*. Whether a substitute can explain a pronoun within it is disputed, but there is no dispute that a pronoun may be explained by a verbal noun derived from a preceding verb. The first explains it by what precedes, the latter by what follows. This is what al-Zamakhsharī meant by his words: "It is also permissible for *huwa* to be ambiguous (*mubham*), with *an yuʿammar* clarifying it." He means that *huwa* does not refer back to anything before it, and *an yuʿammar* is a substitute for it that explains it.

Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī permitted in *al-Ḥalabiyyāt* that *huwa* be the pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr al-shaʾn*), and this is an inclination on his part toward the view of the Kufans: that the explanation of the pronoun of the matter, which they call "the unknown" (*al-majhūl*), may be something other than a clause when it forms a semantic predication, as in: "I thought him standing, Zayd," and *mā huwa bi-qāʾimin Zaydun* ("He is not standing, Zayd"). Here, according to them, *huwa* is the subject, a pronoun they call "unknown"; *bi-qāʾimin* is in the position of the predicate, and *Zaydun* is the subject of *qāʾim*. Their meaning was: "He is not one standing, Zayd." For this reason they parse, in "I thought him standing, Zayd," the *hāʾ* as the pronoun of the unknown, which is the object of *ẓanantu* ("I thought"), *qāʾiman* as the second object, and *Zaydun* as the subject of *qāʾim*. According to the view of the Basrans, it is not permissible for it to be explained except by a clause whose two parts are explicitly stated and free from a preposition. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "al-Ṭabarī reported from a group that they said: it is an *ʿimād* (separator)." End of his words. This needs explanation, because the *ʿimād* in the view of some Kufans may precede the predicate before the subject. So when you say *mā Zaydun huwa al-qāʾimu* ("Zayd is not the one standing"), they permit you to say *mā huwa al-qāʾimu Zaydun*. So according to them the underlying sentence is: "And its lengthening is not one to remove him..." Then the predicate was placed before the separator, giving: "And he is not one to remove him from punishment by being granted long life," i.e., "its lengthening." This is not permitted according to the Basrans, because their condition for the separator is that it be in the middle position.

To summarize the views on this pronoun: Does it refer to *aḥaduhum*? Or to the verbal noun implied by *yuʿammar*? Or to what follows it, namely *an yuʿammar*? Or is it the pronoun of the matter? Or is it a separator? Five views, the most apparent of which is the first.

﴿And God is Seeing of what they do﴾: The majority read *yaʿmalūna* with the *yāʾ* ("they do"), in line with the preceding discourse. Al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, al-Aʿraj, and Yaʿqūb read it with the *tāʾ* ("you do"), as a shift (*iltifāt*) from the third-person absence to the second-person address. This sentence contains a threat and a warning. Here he uses the attribute *baṣīr* ("Seeing"), although God is exalted above having organs, to inform that His knowledge of all deeds is a knowledge of comprehensive encompassment and perception of hidden things. In *bimā*, the *mā* is a relative pronoun, and the returning pronoun is omitted, meaning *yaʿmalūnahu* ("they do it"). They also permitted that it be a verbal particle, meaning "by their deed." He used the form of the present tense, even though His knowledge encompasses their past and future deeds, for the sake of the harmony of the verse-endings (*tawākhī al-fawāṣil*).

These noble verses have contained a reminder to the Children of Israel and a recollection of them of the blessings of God: when He gave Moses the Torah, which contains guidance and light, and then followed him with messengers to renew the religion of God and His laws; and when He gave Jesus extraordinary matters: the raising of the dead, the healing of the blind and the leper, the creation of a living being and the breathing of the spirit into it, the reporting of unseen things, and other things. He supported him with the one who brings down revelation at his hands, namely Gabriel, peace be upon him. Yet, despite these miracles and blessings, they were the furthest of people from accepting what came to them from God. They were such that whenever a messenger came to them with what did not agree with them, they hastened to deny him or killed him, while being unconcerned with the crimes that issued from them. It is related that in the wake of their killing of a group of prophets, the vegetable market (*sūq al-baql*) was held among them, which is the basest of markets. How then about the markets in which precious things are sold? Then God rebuked them for remaining upon that habit of denying what came from God, even though before His coming they used to mention that he would come to them from God. So when what they had been awaiting and recognizing came to them, they disbelieved in it, and God sealed upon them with the curse. The reason for their expulsion from the mercy of God is what preceded of their disbelief, and their faith was meagre, since before the coming of the Book they used to believe that a Book would come. Then he began to censure them, that they sold their precious selves for what resulted for them from their disbelief in the signs of God, namely foods and leaderships which end in a short time. The factor driving them to this was envy and transgression, because God singled out with His bounty whomever He willed of His servants. They were not content with His judgment or His choice, so they incurred wrath from God, and He prepared for them in the Hereafter the punishment that will humiliate and degrade them. Since their refusal to believe was only out of arrogance, envy, and non-acceptance of the decree, it was fitting that they be punished with the punishment that contains for them disgrace, abasement, and humiliation.

Then God, exalted is He, informed about them that when faith in what God has sent down is presented to them, they reply that they believe in the Torah and that they disbelieve in whatever is other than it. Yet the revealed books that come from God are equal, since all of them are truth, each confirming the others. So disbelief in some of them is disbelief in all of them.

Then God, exalted is He, informed of their lying in their statement: ﴿We believe in what was sent down to us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91]. That is because they killed the prophets, while the Torah speaks explicitly of following the prophets and taking them as examples. Thus their action contradicted their words.

Then He repeated to them, as a rebuke, that Moses, to whom the Torah was sent down, and whom they claim they believed in, came to them with clear signs and extraordinary miracles, such as their deliverance from Pharaoh, the splitting of the sea, and other things. Despite this, after his departure to converse with his Lord, they took as a god the calf made from their ornaments, the most dull-witted and stupid of animals, whose fashioning and making were witnessed, while Moses had not yet died and the Book of God was recently sent down to them, its time not long past.

God repeated the mention of lifting the mountain (Tur) over them so that they would accept what was in (p-317) the Torah. They were commanded to listen and obey, but they responded with disobedience. Moreover, they were compelled to faith, or were as those who are compelled, because such a terrifying thing as a mountain being raised over them, to crush them with it, is sufficient to make a person do what he is commanded and accept the obligations laid upon him. Their refusal and failure to accept was due to the fact that the worship of the calf had permeated their hearts and mixed with them, so that they did not hear acceptance of anything of the truth. When the heart is filled with love of something, it hears nothing else and does not listen to blame. They recited:

*You have filled my whole heart with a portion of your love,*
*so if you seek more, bring a heart.*

Then God censured them for what their faith commanded them, though they have no real faith. Rather, He attributed it to them sarcastically, [namely] the worship of the calf and taking it as a god besides God.

Then He refuted them in their claim that Paradise is exclusively theirs, that no one other than them will enter it. So He commanded them to wish for death, because whoever believes that he will arrive at joy, delight and lasting pleasure that never ends, prefers to reach that and to have the humiliation and misery he is in come to an end.

God informed that their wishing for death will never occur from them, and that their abstention from it is due to the crimes their hands have committed. Thus their claim to be the people of Paradise is shown to be false. Then, as a corroboration of what came before concerning their not wishing for death, He informed that they are the most eager of people for life, even more eager than those who do not believe in the Last Abode, and do not hope for reward or fear punishment. Then He mentioned that one of them wishes to be granted a thousand years of life, yet even with that, his long life, however long, will not save him from God's punishment.

Then He concluded the verses by stating that God, exalted is He, is aware of the ugliness of their deeds and will recompense them for them. The totality of these verses makes clear what the Jews are disposed to: excessive lying, contradiction between their actions and their words, deficiency of intellect, and abundant slander. May God protect us from that, and guide us along the most upright paths.

**Abu Hayyan, *al-Bahr al-Muhit*, on Surah al-Baqarah 2:97–98 (Part 1 of 3)**

﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel, for he has brought it down upon your heart by God's permission, confirming what is before it, and as guidance and good tidings for the believers.﴾ ﴿Whoever is an enemy to God, His angels, His messengers, Gabriel and Michael, then God is an enemy to the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿And We have sent down to you clear signs, and none disbelieve in them except the defiantly disobedient.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 99] ﴿Is it not that whenever they make a covenant, a party of them throws it aside? Rather, most of them do not believe.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 100] ﴿And when there came to them a messenger from God, confirming what they possess, a party of those who were given the Book threw the Book of God behind their backs, as if they did not know.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 101] ﴿And they followed what the devils recited during the reign of Solomon. Solomon did not disbelieve, but the devils disbelieved, teaching people magic, and what was sent down to the two angels at Babylon, Harut and Marut. They would not teach anyone until they had said, "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve." Yet they learned from them that by which they would separate a man from his wife, though they could harm no one by it except by God's permission. They learned what would harm them and not benefit them. And they certainly knew that whoever purchased it would have no share in the Hereafter. How evil is what they sold their souls for, if only they knew.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102] ﴿And if they had believed and been mindful of God, a reward from God would have been better, if only they knew.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 103]

**Jibril (Gabriel):** a proper noun for an angel, the one who brought the Qur'an down to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It is a non-Arabic name and is diptote (*mamnu' al-sarf*, not declinable with tanwin), due to being a proper noun and being foreign in origin. He who claimed it is derived from *jabarut* (the majesty) of God is far from correct, as is he who claimed it is a compound of the *idafa* (genitive construction) type. The meaning of *Jibr* is "servant," and *Il* is one of the names of God, because a non-Arabic word does not admit Arabic derivation, and because if it were a compound of the *idafa* type it would be declinable.

Al-Mahdawi said: "Whoever says *Jibr*, like *'abd*, and *Il* is one of the names of God, has made it like *Hadramawt*." End of his words. He means that he makes it a compound of the *mazj* (blended) type, so it is diptote due to being a proper noun and a compound. What he mentioned is not correct, because either a sense of *idafa* is considered in it, in which case the second element would have to be declinable and the first would be inflected by the forms of *i'rab* (grammatical inflection), or it is not considered, in which case it is a compound of the *mazj* type. What is compounded in the *mazj* manner may take indeclinability (*bina'*), *idafa*, or being diptote. The fact that *idafa* has not been heard for it, nor indeclinability, is no proof that it is not a compound of the *mazj* type.

The Arabs have modified it according to their custom of changing foreign names, until it reached thirteen dialects. They said: *Jibril*, like *qindil*, which is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and it is the reading of Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, Nafi' and Hafs. Waraqah ibn Nawfal said:

*And Jibril comes to him, and Michael with them both,*
*From God, a revelation that expands the breast, sent down.*

Imran ibn Hittan said:

*And the Spirit, Jibril, among them, having no equal,*
*And Jibril was trusted with God.*

Hassan said:

*Jibril is the messenger of God among us,*
*And the Holy Spirit has no equal.*

It is the same, except that the *jim* is vocalized with a fatha (*Jabril*), and this is the reading of al-Hasan, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muhaysin. Al-Farra' said: "I do not like it, because there is no *fa'il* pattern in speech." What he said is not right, because what the Arabs have introduced into their speech falls into two categories: some of it they assimilate to the patterns of their speech, like *lijam*, and some of it they do not assimilate, like *Ibrisam*. *Jibril*, with a fatha on the *jim*, is of this kind. It was also said: *Jibril* is like *Shamwil*, which is a bird. *Jibra'il*, like *'Antaris*, is the dialect of Tamim, Qays, and many of the people of Najd. Al-Farra' transmitted it, and al-Zajjaj chose it and said: "It is the best of the dialects." Hassan said:

*We witnessed, and you find before us no host*
*For all time, except Jibra'il in front of it.*

Jarir said:

*They worshipped the cross and denied Muhammad,*
*And Jibra'il, and they denied Mika'il.*

This is the reading of al-A'mash, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hammad ibn Abi Ziyad, from Abu Bakr, from 'Asim. Al-Kisa'i also transmitted it from 'Asim, and likewise, except that there is no *ya'* after the *hamza*. This is the transmission of Yahya ibn Adam, from Abu Bakr, from 'Asim. It is also related from Yahya ibn Ya'mar, and likewise, except that the *lam* is doubled. This is the reading of Aban, from 'Asim and Yahya ibn Ya'mar.

*Jibra'il* and *Jibra'iyil*, read by Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah. *Jibral* and *Jibra'il* with a *ya'* and shortened, and Talhah read with it. *Jibra'iyil*, with an *alif* after the *ra'*, followed by two *ya's*, the first of which is kasra, and al-A'mash and Ibn Ya'mar also read with it. *Jibrin* and *Jibrin*, and this is the dialect of Asad. *Jibra'in*.

Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: *Jibril* was made into a broken plural as *Jaraybil*, according to the high dialect.

*Adhina bihi*: he informed of it; *adhanahu*: he made him know. *Adhantukum 'ala sawa'*: I informed you. Then it is applied to enablement: *adhina li fi kadhā*: he enabled me to do it. And by way of choice: *fa'altahu bi-idhnika*: I did it by your choice.

**Mika'il (Michael):** the discussion of it is like the discussion of Jibril, meaning regarding its being diptote. Those who said it is derived from *malakut* (the kingdom) of God are far off, and so are those who said the meaning of *Mika* is "servant" and *Il* is one of God's names. The Arabs have modified it: *Mikal*, like *mifal*, and Abu 'Amr and Hafs read with it, and it is the dialect of the Hijaz. The poet said:

*And on the day of Badr we met you, a reinforcement for us in it,*
*With victory, Mikal and Jibril.*

It is the same, except that after the *alif* there is a *hamza*, and this was read by Nafi' and Ibn Shanabudh for Qunbul. It is the same, except that it has a *ya'* after the *hamza*, and this was read by Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr, and other than Ibn Shanabudh for Qunbul and al-Bazzi. *Mikayil*, like *Mika'il*, and this was read by Ibn Muhaysin, and likewise, except that there is no *ya'* after the *hamza*. It was also read as *Mikayyil* with two *ya's* after the *alif*, the first of which is kasra, and al-A'mash read with it.

*Nabadha al-shay'*, *yanbidhuhu nabdhan*: he threw it and cast it away. *Al-Zahr*: well-known, and the plural of the *fi'l* form of a noun that is not weak in its middle radical, *fu'ul*, is analogical, like *zuhur*, and *fa'lan*, like *zahran*, and it is derived from *al-zuhur*. You say: *zahara al-shay'u zuhuran* when it appeared.

*Talā yatlū*: he followed. *Talā al-Qur'an*: he recited it. *Talā 'alayhi*: he lied, said by Abu Muslim. He also said: *talā 'anhu*: he turned away from it. When he does not mention the two complements, it admits both meanings.

**Sulayman (Solomon):** a non-Arabic name, and it is diptote due to being a proper noun and foreign. Its parallel among foreign names, in having an *alif* and *nun* at the end, is *Haman*, *Mahan*, and *Saman*. Its being diptote is not due to being a proper noun with the addition of *alif* and *nun* like *'Uthman*, because the addition of *alif* and *nun* depends on derivation and morphological conjugation, and Arabic derivation and conjugation do not enter foreign names.

**Sihr (magic):** the verbal noun of *sahara yashaharu sihran*. No verbal noun of the *fa'ala yaf'alu* pattern occurs in the form *fi'l* except *sahara* and *fa'ala*, as some scholars have said. Al-Jawhari said: "Everything that is subtle and fine is *sihr*. One says *sahara-hu*: he revealed to him a matter that is subtle and hidden." End of his words. He also said:

*A gift that came upon me from your gifts, or is it magic?*

It is said: *sahara-hu*: he deceived him, and from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*We see ourselves as those who are placed before an unseen matter,*
*And we are bewitched with food and drink.*

That is: we are distracted and deceived. The discussion of the meaning of magic in the verse will come later.

**Babil (Babylon):** a non-Arabic name, the name of a land, and its identification will come later.

**Harut and Marut:** two non-Arabic names, and the discussion of their meaning will come later. They are pluralized as *hawarit* and *mawarit*. It is said: *hawarita* and *mawarita*, and likewise: *Talut* and *Jalut*.

**Fitna (trial):** testing and examination. *Fatana yaftinu futunan wa fitnatan*.

**Mar' (man):** a man. The most eloquent form is to open the *mim* in all cases. The *damma* on the *mim* in all cases is also reported, and the *mim* taking the vowel of its grammatical position is also reported, so you say: *qama al-mar'u* (with *damma* on the *mim*), *ra'aytu al-mar'a* (with *fatha* on the *mim*), and *marartu bi-l-mir'i* (with *kasra* on the *mim*). Its feminine is *al-mar'a*. Its plural has come with the *waw* and *nun* ending: they said *al-mar'un*.

**Darar and nafa' (harm and benefit):** both are well known. It is said: *darra yadurru*, with *damma* on the *dad*, which is the analogical form for the doubled transitive verb. Its verbal noun is *al-durr*, *al-darr* and *al-darar*. It is also said: *dara yadir*, as he said:

*Some people say: its distance does not harm you,*
*But everything that wears down souls harms them.*

It is said: *nafa'a yanfa'u nafan*.

I saw in the commentary on *al-Muwajaz* by al-Rummani on grammar, which is the composition of a man called al-Ahwazi, not Abu 'Ali al-Ahwazi the reciter, that a passive participle is not formed from it, such as *manfu'*, and grammatical analogy requires it.

**Khalaq (portion):** in the language, it means "share," as said by al-Zajjaj. He said: "But it is most used for good." He said:

*They call out for woe therein; they have no portion,*
*Except garments of tar and shackles.*

*Khalaq* also means "measure." The poet said:

*So for you there is no house near the lofty ones,*
*And for you among Ghalib there is no measure.*

**Mathubah (reward):** a *maf'alah* form from *thawab*. The vowel of the *waw* was moved to the *tha'*. It is also said *mathubah*. Its analogical form would be the weakened form, so you say *mathabah*, but they made it sound, as they made the sound form in proper names with the *kawr* (*mukawwarah*). Its parallels in the sound pattern are *maqbarah* and *maqburah*.

﴿Say: whoever is an enemy to Gabriel﴾: The exegetes (*ahl al-tafsir*, the people of tafsir, meaning Qur'anic exegesis) agree that the Jews said: "Gabriel is our enemy." It is disputed how this occurred, and whether the cause of revelation was their dialogue with the Prophet (ﷺ) or their dialogue with Umar. The summary of the enmity is that it was because he comes with destruction, sinking of the earth, and drought. Had Michael been the companion of Muhammad, we would have followed him, because he comes with abundance and peace. It was also because he defended Bukhtnassar when we wanted to kill him, so he destroyed the House of al-Maqdis and destroyed us, and because he informs Muhammad (ﷺ) of our secret.

The address in His words "Say" is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the object of the verb "say" is the clause that follows. *Man* here is conditional. Al-Raghib said: "*Al-'adawa* (enmity) is transgression and opposition to harmony. With the heart it is called *'adawa*; with walking it is called *'aduww*; with a deviation from justice it is called *'udwan*; and with place or lineage it is called *qawm 'idan*, that is, strangers."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 97–98 (part 2 of 3):

﴿Then indeed, he has sent it down﴾: This is not the response (jawab al-shart, the apodosis of the conditional) to the condition, because it is established in the science of Arabic grammar that the conditional noun (ism al-shart) must have in its response a pronoun referring back to it. So if you say, "Whoever honours me? Zayd is standing," it is not permissible. His saying ﴿then indeed, he has sent it down upon your heart﴾ contains no pronoun referring back to "whoever." Al-Zamakhshari explicitly stated that it is the response to the condition, and this is an error, for the reason we have mentioned, namely the absence of a returning pronoun, and because the verb of sending down is in the past tense, so the clause cannot be the response. Rather, the response is [p. 320] omitted, its omission being indicated by what follows it. The estimate is: "then his enmity has no basis," or something similar to this estimate. The pronoun in ﴿fa-innahu﴾ refers to Jibril, and the pronoun in ﴿nazzalahu﴾ refers to the Qur'an, by the indication of the meaning. Do you not see His saying: ﴿confirming what was before it, and as guidance and good tidings for the believers﴾? All of these are attributes of the Qur'an. And [there is] His saying ﴿by the permission of Allah﴾, meaning: indeed Jibril sent down the Qur'an upon your heart by the permission of Allah. It has also been said: the pronoun in ﴿fa-innahu﴾ refers to Allah, and the pronoun in ﴿nazzalahu﴾ refers to Jibril, the estimate being: indeed Allah sent down Jibril with the Qur'an upon your heart. In each of these two estimates there is an implied element that refers to what the context of the meaning indicates. However, the first estimate is preferable, for the reason we have mentioned, and so that it agrees with His saying: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit brought it down upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 193]. The second estimate is supported by the reading of those who read nazzala with a shadda (intensive form) and al-ruha (the Spirit) in the accusative. The connection of the proof of the response to the condition is that whoever is an enemy of Jibril, his enmity has no basis, because he is the one who brought down the Qur'an that confirms the (previous) Books, and [is] the guide and the bearer of good tidings, just as whoever believed. Whoever is in this position ought to be loved and thanked, since through him came the cause of guidance and the affirmation of what is in their hands of the Books of Allah. Or [the meaning is]: whoever is an enemy of Jibril, the cause of his enmity is that he sent down the Qur'an confirming their Book and obligating them to follow you, and they do not want that; for this reason they distorted what is in their Books of your attributes and of the covenants taken from them concerning them, that they should follow you. The difference between each of these two estimates is that the first estimate necessitates the absence of enmity, while the second estimate is as if it were an excuse for them in their enmity, like your saying: "If Zayd is hostile to you, then you have harmed him and wronged him."

﴿upon your heart﴾: He used the word ʿalā (upon), because the Qur'an is elevated over the heart, since the heart hears it and obeys it, carrying out what it commands and avoiding what it forbids. And ʿalā is more eloquent than ilā (to), because ilā indicates only the endpoint, whereas ʿalā indicates elevation. Whatever is elevated over a thing necessarily reaches it. The heart was singled out, and he did not say "upon you," because the heart is the place of intellect and knowledge and the receiving of inspirations; or because it is his page upon which things are inscribed, and his treasury in which things are preserved; or because it is the sovereign of the body. In the hadith: "Indeed, in the body there is a lump of flesh," then he said afterward: "Behold, it is the heart." Or because the heart is the choicest and most noble part of a thing; or because it is the House of Allah; or because by it he meant the intellect, using the place for what resides in it; or he meant the whole human being, since sending down upon it is mentioned in several places: ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an upon you that you should be distressed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 2], ﴿And Allah sent down upon you the Book and the wisdom﴾ [al-Nisa: 113]; or it is the use of a part for the whole. These are seven opinions. He attributed the heart to the kaf of address (the "you" pronoun), and did not attribute it to the ya' of the speaker, even though the structure of the speech apparently requires it; because His saying ﴿whoever is an enemy to Jibril﴾ is governed by an implied verb of speaking, the estimate being: "Say, O Muhammad: Allah says: 'Whoever is an enemy to Jibril, then indeed he sent it down upon your heart.'" Al-Zamakhshari inclined to this with his statement: "It came as a quotation of the speech of Allah, Exalted, as if it had been said: 'What I spoke of, my saying: "Whoever is an enemy to Jibril, then indeed he sent it down upon your heart."'" His discourse on this is confused. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "It is good in the speech of the Arabs that the word spoken by the one commanded to speak should be preserved, and it is good that the meaning of his speech be intended, so he narrates it in direct address to him, as you say: 'Say to your people: Do not humiliate you,' and so this verse is likewise. A similar example is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

Did you not see that on the day of Jaww Suwayqa, I called out and Hunayda called to me: "What is wrong with you?"

So he preserved the meaning and departed from the calling of Hunayda, [which is] 'What is wrong with you?'" End of his statement. This is a good interpretation, and in that case the conditional clause is governed by the word "say," not by an implied verb of speaking, and this is the apparent sense of the speech.

﴿by the permission of Allah﴾: That is, by the command of Allah. He chose this in al-Muntakhab, and from it [comes] His saying: ﴿No soul speaks except by His permission﴾ [Hud: 105], ﴿Who is it that intercedes with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqara: 255]. This has been stated explicitly in: ﴿We do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾ [Maryam: 64]. Or [it means] by His knowledge and His enabling him to this rank, as Ibn ʿAtiyya said; or by His choice, as al-Mawardi said; or by His facilitation and making it easy, as al-Zamakhshari said.

﴿confirming what was before it﴾: The accusative of muṣaddiqan (confirming) is a state (ḥāl) from the pronoun in nazzalahu if it refers to the Qur'an. If it refers to Jibril, it allows two possibilities: One: it is a state from the implied genitive noun, because the meaning is: "Indeed Allah sent down Jibril with the Qur'an, confirming." The second: it is a state from Jibril. The "mā" in "limā" is a relative pronoun, and by it he meant the Books that Allah sent down to the nations before its sending down, or the Torah and the Gospel. The pronoun in "bayna yadayhi" may refer to the Qur'an, and it may refer to Jibril. So the meaning is: confirming what is before it of the messengers and the Books.

﴿and as guidance and good tidings﴾: These two are conjoined to muṣaddiqan, so they are states, and this would be an instance of placing the verbal noun in the position of the active participle, as if he said: "guiding and bringing good tidings"; or it is from the sphere of hyperbole (mubalagha), as if, since guidance and good tidings were achieved through it, it was made the very essence of guidance and good tidings. The alif in bushrā is for the feminine, as in ruj'ā, and it is a verbal noun. The discussion of its meaning has already been presented in His saying: ﴿And give good tidings to those who believe﴾ [al-Baqara: 25], at the beginning of this surah. The meaning is that He described the Qur'an as confirming what preceded it of the divine Books, and that it is guidance, since in it is the explanation of what the obligations of the deeds of the hearts and the limbs are, and that it is good tidings to whoever attains guidance. Thus this verbal order in these states arose because their referents are arranged in an existential order. The first: its confirming the Books, because all the Books are from one spring. The second: that guidance was achieved through it after its sending down in this state of confirmation. The third: that it is good tidings to whoever attains guidance through it. Al-Raghib said: "And guidance from error, and good tidings of Paradise."

﴿for the believers﴾: He singled out guidance and good tidings for the believers, because guidance and good tidings through it do not belong to non-believers, as He said: ﴿And it is for them a blindness﴾ [Fussilat: 44]; and because the believers are the ones given good tidings: ﴿So give good tidings to My servants﴾ [al-Zumar: 17], ﴿Their Lord gives them good tidings of mercy from Him﴾ [al-Tawba: 21]. This verse indicates the exaltation of Jibril and the honouring of his rank, in that He made him the intermediary between Himself and the noblest of His creation, and the one who brought down the Book that combines the attributes mentioned. It also indicates the reproach of the Jews, in that they hated the one who held this exalted position with Allah, Exalted. They said: The Batiniyya have clung to this verse, and they said: "The Qur'an is an inspiration, and the letters are the expression of the Messenger." It was answered against them: that it is a manifest miracle in its composition, that Allah named it revelation, Book and Arabic, that Jibril descended with it, and that the one inspired (mulham) does not need Jibril.

﴿whoever is an enemy to Allah﴾: Enmity between Allah and the servant is not literal; the servant's enmity to Allah, Exalted, is figurative, and its meaning is opposition to the command. Allah's enmity to the servant is His requiting him for his opposition.

﴿and His angels and His messengers and Jibril and Mika'il, then indeed Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers﴾. He emphasized, with His saying "and His angels," the matter of Jibril, since the Jews had reported that he was their enemy among the angels, because he brings destruction and punishment. So He answered them in the previous verse, that he brought the essence of all goods, which is the Qur'an, comprising those noble attributes, from its agreement with their Books, and its being guidance and good tidings, so love for him was obligatory. And He answered them in this verse by joining him to His own Name, falling under the generality of His angels, then secondly under the generality of His messengers, because the messengers include the angels and others from among the sons of Adam who were sent; then thirdly by explicitly mentioning him singly alongside the one whom they claim to love, namely Mika'il. Thus he is mentioned three times in this verse. All of this is a refutation of the Jews and a reproach to them, and a dignifying of Jibril. The verse indicates that Allah, Exalted, is an enemy to whoever opposes Allah, His angels, His messengers, Jibril and Mika'il. This does not mean that the intended one is whoever combines enmity toward all of them, so that Allah would be his enemy; rather the meaning is that whoever is hostile to one of those mentioned, Allah is his enemy, since hostility toward one of those mentioned is hostility toward all. The Muslims have agreed that whoever hates a messenger or an angel has disbelieved. Some people said: the "wa" (and) here means "or," and it is not for conjunction. Others said: the "wa" is for detailing, and it is not intended that he be an enemy to all the angels, nor to all the messengers; rather this is from the category of attaching the ruling to the genus in the form of a plural, as when you say: "If you speak to men, then you are divorced," you do not mean by it "if you speak to every man," nor the least that the plural applies to; rather he attached it to the genus, even if it is in the form of a plural. So if she spoke to one man, she would be divorced; likewise this plural in the angels and the messengers. The meaning is that whoever is hostile to Allah, or to one of His angels, or to one of His messengers, then Allah is an enemy to him.

Al-Maturidi said: It is possible that the opening with the Name of Allah is in the manner of exalting the one mentioned after it, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then to Allah belongs one-fifth of it﴾ [al-Anfal: 41]. And He singled out Jibril and Mikal for mention to honour and distinguish them.
