We have also related from our teacher Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn Ibrahim ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah sanctify his spirit, that he used to call this type for us "al-tajrid" (isolating a particular item for mention), which is when a thing falls under a general category and then you single it out by name, and that is for a meaning specific to it, not shared with the other members of that general category. Thus Jibril and Mikal are treated as if they were of another kind, and the difference in description is treated like the difference in kind, so they are conjoined by "and". This type of conjunction, namely the conjunction of the particular to the general for the sake of distinction, is one of the rulings that are unique to the particle "wa" (and), so it is not permissible with the other coordinating particles.

It has also been said: they were singled out for mention because the Jews mentioned them, and the verse was revealed concerning them. Had they not been mentioned, the Jews would have had a pretext to say: "We did not oppose Allah," or "nor all His angels"?

It has also been said: they were singled out for mention to remove the objection that what makes disbelief obligatory is enmity toward all the angels, not toward one of them. So it is as if it were said: "or any one of them."

This order is in the utmost beauty: it begins with the mention of Allah, then with the intermediaries between Him and the Messengers, then with the intermediaries between the angels and those to whom they were sent. This is an order according to the transmission of revelation. The mention of the angels first does not indicate their superiority over the Messengers of the children of Adam, because the order we have mentioned is an order in relation to the intermediaries, not in relation to superiority.

The statement of al-Zamakhshari will come, that the angels are nobler than the prophets, God willing. They said: the singling out of Jibril and Mikal for mention indicates that they are nobler than all the angels. They also said: Jibril is superior to Mikal, because he is mentioned first, and because he descends with revelation and knowledge, which is the substance of spirits, whereas Mikal descends with fertility and rain, which is the substance of bodies, and the nourishment of spirits is nobler than the nourishment of bodies. End of quotation. But the preference of Jibril over Mikal requires a clear and explicit text, and precedence in mention does not indicate preference, since it may be by way of ascent (from lesser to greater).

The "man" in His saying ﴿whoever is an enemy﴾ is conditional (shart). The commentators differ regarding the answer (jawab) of the condition. It is said: it is omitted, its estimate being: "then he is a disbeliever," and it was omitted because the meaning points to it. It is also said the answer is: ﴿then indeed Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers﴾. He used the apparent Name of Allah and did not say "He is an enemy," lest it be understood that the pronoun refers to the conditional noun, which would change the meaning, or that it refers to the nearest mentioned item, Mikal. So he made the Name apparent to remove the ambiguity, or for glorification and emphasis, since the Arabs, when they wish to magnify something, repeat it by the name that preceded it. Among examples is: ﴿Allah will surely help him; indeed Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving﴾ [al-Hajj: 60], and the saying of the poet:
"I do not see that death outstrips death, anything..."

This sentence, which stands as the predicate of the conditional, requires a link (rabit) between the clause of the answer and the conditional noun. The link here is the apparent noun, which is "the disbelievers." The apparent noun has been placed in the position of the pronoun to harmonise the endings of the verses, and to state explicitly the cause of the enmity, which is disbelief, since whoever is an enemy of one of those mentioned, or of any one of them, is a disbeliever. Or it may be intended that "the disbelievers" is general, so the link is generality, since disbelief takes many forms, and these disbelievers with this particular thing are one instance of the general category, so the connection is achieved thereby.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "an enemy to the disbelievers" means he intended "an enemy to them," and he brought the apparent noun to show that Allah opposes them because of their disbelief, and that enmity toward the angels is disbelief. If enmity toward the prophets is disbelief, what of the angels? And they are nobler. The meaning: whoever opposes them, Allah opposes him and punishes him with the most severe punishment. End of his words. This is the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah, who hold that the angels are superior to the special ones among the children of Adam. The words of al-Zamakhshari indicate that the apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun, and that generality was not intended in it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The expression came with the generality of "the disbelievers," because the return of the pronoun to "man" would be ambiguous, whether you make it singular or plural, and even if one were not concerned with the ambiguity. We say: the meaning guides the hearer to the intended sense, and it would necessitate specifying a group as the object of Allah's enmity. It is possible that Allah knew some of them would believe, so it is not appropriate to apply the enmity of Allah to them as a final state. It is narrated that Umar uttered this verse in reply to some Jews who said: "That is our enemy," meaning Jibril, so the verse was revealed upon the tongue of Umar. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this report is weak.

**Abu Hayyan, *al-Bahr al-Muhit*, on Surah al-Baqarah 2:97–98 (Part 1 of 3)**

﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel, for he has brought it down upon your heart by God's permission, confirming what is before it, and as guidance and good tidings for the believers.﴾ ﴿Whoever is an enemy to God, His angels, His messengers, Gabriel and Michael, then God is an enemy to the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿And We have sent down to you clear signs, and none disbelieve in them except the defiantly disobedient.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 99] ﴿Is it not that whenever they make a covenant, a party of them throws it aside? Rather, most of them do not believe.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 100] ﴿And when there came to them a messenger from God, confirming what they possess, a party of those who were given the Book threw the Book of God behind their backs, as if they did not know.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 101] ﴿And they followed what the devils recited during the reign of Solomon. Solomon did not disbelieve, but the devils disbelieved, teaching people magic, and what was sent down to the two angels at Babylon, Harut and Marut. They would not teach anyone until they had said, "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve." Yet they learned from them that by which they would separate a man from his wife, though they could harm no one by it except by God's permission. They learned what would harm them and not benefit them. And they certainly knew that whoever purchased it would have no share in the Hereafter. How evil is what they sold their souls for, if only they knew.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102] ﴿And if they had believed and been mindful of God, a reward from God would have been better, if only they knew.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 103]

**Jibril (Gabriel):** a proper noun for an angel, the one who brought the Qur'an down to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It is a non-Arabic name and is diptote (*mamnu' al-sarf*, not declinable with tanwin), due to being a proper noun and being foreign in origin. He who claimed it is derived from *jabarut* (the majesty) of God is far from correct, as is he who claimed it is a compound of the *idafa* (genitive construction) type. The meaning of *Jibr* is "servant," and *Il* is one of the names of God, because a non-Arabic word does not admit Arabic derivation, and because if it were a compound of the *idafa* type it would be declinable.

Al-Mahdawi said: "Whoever says *Jibr*, like *'abd*, and *Il* is one of the names of God, has made it like *Hadramawt*." End of his words. He means that he makes it a compound of the *mazj* (blended) type, so it is diptote due to being a proper noun and a compound. What he mentioned is not correct, because either a sense of *idafa* is considered in it, in which case the second element would have to be declinable and the first would be inflected by the forms of *i'rab* (grammatical inflection), or it is not considered, in which case it is a compound of the *mazj* type. What is compounded in the *mazj* manner may take indeclinability (*bina'*), *idafa*, or being diptote. The fact that *idafa* has not been heard for it, nor indeclinability, is no proof that it is not a compound of the *mazj* type.

The Arabs have modified it according to their custom of changing foreign names, until it reached thirteen dialects. They said: *Jibril*, like *qindil*, which is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and it is the reading of Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, Nafi' and Hafs. Waraqah ibn Nawfal said:

*And Jibril comes to him, and Michael with them both,*
*From God, a revelation that expands the breast, sent down.*

Imran ibn Hittan said:

*And the Spirit, Jibril, among them, having no equal,*
*And Jibril was trusted with God.*

Hassan said:

*Jibril is the messenger of God among us,*
*And the Holy Spirit has no equal.*

It is the same, except that the *jim* is vocalized with a fatha (*Jabril*), and this is the reading of al-Hasan, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muhaysin. Al-Farra' said: "I do not like it, because there is no *fa'il* pattern in speech." What he said is not right, because what the Arabs have introduced into their speech falls into two categories: some of it they assimilate to the patterns of their speech, like *lijam*, and some of it they do not assimilate, like *Ibrisam*. *Jibril*, with a fatha on the *jim*, is of this kind. It was also said: *Jibril* is like *Shamwil*, which is a bird. *Jibra'il*, like *'Antaris*, is the dialect of Tamim, Qays, and many of the people of Najd. Al-Farra' transmitted it, and al-Zajjaj chose it and said: "It is the best of the dialects." Hassan said:

*We witnessed, and you find before us no host*
*For all time, except Jibra'il in front of it.*

Jarir said:

*They worshipped the cross and denied Muhammad,*
*And Jibra'il, and they denied Mika'il.*

This is the reading of al-A'mash, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hammad ibn Abi Ziyad, from Abu Bakr, from 'Asim. Al-Kisa'i also transmitted it from 'Asim, and likewise, except that there is no *ya'* after the *hamza*. This is the transmission of Yahya ibn Adam, from Abu Bakr, from 'Asim. It is also related from Yahya ibn Ya'mar, and likewise, except that the *lam* is doubled. This is the reading of Aban, from 'Asim and Yahya ibn Ya'mar.

*Jibra'il* and *Jibra'iyil*, read by Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah. *Jibral* and *Jibra'il* with a *ya'* and shortened, and Talhah read with it. *Jibra'iyil*, with an *alif* after the *ra'*, followed by two *ya's*, the first of which is kasra, and al-A'mash and Ibn Ya'mar also read with it. *Jibrin* and *Jibrin*, and this is the dialect of Asad. *Jibra'in*.

Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: *Jibril* was made into a broken plural as *Jaraybil*, according to the high dialect.

*Adhina bihi*: he informed of it; *adhanahu*: he made him know. *Adhantukum 'ala sawa'*: I informed you. Then it is applied to enablement: *adhina li fi kadhā*: he enabled me to do it. And by way of choice: *fa'altahu bi-idhnika*: I did it by your choice.

**Mika'il (Michael):** the discussion of it is like the discussion of Jibril, meaning regarding its being diptote. Those who said it is derived from *malakut* (the kingdom) of God are far off, and so are those who said the meaning of *Mika* is "servant" and *Il* is one of God's names. The Arabs have modified it: *Mikal*, like *mifal*, and Abu 'Amr and Hafs read with it, and it is the dialect of the Hijaz. The poet said:

*And on the day of Badr we met you, a reinforcement for us in it,*
*With victory, Mikal and Jibril.*

It is the same, except that after the *alif* there is a *hamza*, and this was read by Nafi' and Ibn Shanabudh for Qunbul. It is the same, except that it has a *ya'* after the *hamza*, and this was read by Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr, and other than Ibn Shanabudh for Qunbul and al-Bazzi. *Mikayil*, like *Mika'il*, and this was read by Ibn Muhaysin, and likewise, except that there is no *ya'* after the *hamza*. It was also read as *Mikayyil* with two *ya's* after the *alif*, the first of which is kasra, and al-A'mash read with it.

*Nabadha al-shay'*, *yanbidhuhu nabdhan*: he threw it and cast it away. *Al-Zahr*: well-known, and the plural of the *fi'l* form of a noun that is not weak in its middle radical, *fu'ul*, is analogical, like *zuhur*, and *fa'lan*, like *zahran*, and it is derived from *al-zuhur*. You say: *zahara al-shay'u zuhuran* when it appeared.

*Talā yatlū*: he followed. *Talā al-Qur'an*: he recited it. *Talā 'alayhi*: he lied, said by Abu Muslim. He also said: *talā 'anhu*: he turned away from it. When he does not mention the two complements, it admits both meanings.

**Sulayman (Solomon):** a non-Arabic name, and it is diptote due to being a proper noun and foreign. Its parallel among foreign names, in having an *alif* and *nun* at the end, is *Haman*, *Mahan*, and *Saman*. Its being diptote is not due to being a proper noun with the addition of *alif* and *nun* like *'Uthman*, because the addition of *alif* and *nun* depends on derivation and morphological conjugation, and Arabic derivation and conjugation do not enter foreign names.

**Sihr (magic):** the verbal noun of *sahara yashaharu sihran*. No verbal noun of the *fa'ala yaf'alu* pattern occurs in the form *fi'l* except *sahara* and *fa'ala*, as some scholars have said. Al-Jawhari said: "Everything that is subtle and fine is *sihr*. One says *sahara-hu*: he revealed to him a matter that is subtle and hidden." End of his words. He also said:

*A gift that came upon me from your gifts, or is it magic?*

It is said: *sahara-hu*: he deceived him, and from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*We see ourselves as those who are placed before an unseen matter,*
*And we are bewitched with food and drink.*

That is: we are distracted and deceived. The discussion of the meaning of magic in the verse will come later.

**Babil (Babylon):** a non-Arabic name, the name of a land, and its identification will come later.

**Harut and Marut:** two non-Arabic names, and the discussion of their meaning will come later. They are pluralized as *hawarit* and *mawarit*. It is said: *hawarita* and *mawarita*, and likewise: *Talut* and *Jalut*.

**Fitna (trial):** testing and examination. *Fatana yaftinu futunan wa fitnatan*.

**Mar' (man):** a man. The most eloquent form is to open the *mim* in all cases. The *damma* on the *mim* in all cases is also reported, and the *mim* taking the vowel of its grammatical position is also reported, so you say: *qama al-mar'u* (with *damma* on the *mim*), *ra'aytu al-mar'a* (with *fatha* on the *mim*), and *marartu bi-l-mir'i* (with *kasra* on the *mim*). Its feminine is *al-mar'a*. Its plural has come with the *waw* and *nun* ending: they said *al-mar'un*.

**Darar and nafa' (harm and benefit):** both are well known. It is said: *darra yadurru*, with *damma* on the *dad*, which is the analogical form for the doubled transitive verb. Its verbal noun is *al-durr*, *al-darr* and *al-darar*. It is also said: *dara yadir*, as he said:

*Some people say: its distance does not harm you,*
*But everything that wears down souls harms them.*

It is said: *nafa'a yanfa'u nafan*.

I saw in the commentary on *al-Muwajaz* by al-Rummani on grammar, which is the composition of a man called al-Ahwazi, not Abu 'Ali al-Ahwazi the reciter, that a passive participle is not formed from it, such as *manfu'*, and grammatical analogy requires it.

**Khalaq (portion):** in the language, it means "share," as said by al-Zajjaj. He said: "But it is most used for good." He said:

*They call out for woe therein; they have no portion,*
*Except garments of tar and shackles.*

*Khalaq* also means "measure." The poet said:

*So for you there is no house near the lofty ones,*
*And for you among Ghalib there is no measure.*

**Mathubah (reward):** a *maf'alah* form from *thawab*. The vowel of the *waw* was moved to the *tha'*. It is also said *mathubah*. Its analogical form would be the weakened form, so you say *mathabah*, but they made it sound, as they made the sound form in proper names with the *kawr* (*mukawwarah*). Its parallels in the sound pattern are *maqbarah* and *maqburah*.

﴿Say: whoever is an enemy to Gabriel﴾: The exegetes (*ahl al-tafsir*, the people of tafsir, meaning Qur'anic exegesis) agree that the Jews said: "Gabriel is our enemy." It is disputed how this occurred, and whether the cause of revelation was their dialogue with the Prophet (ﷺ) or their dialogue with Umar. The summary of the enmity is that it was because he comes with destruction, sinking of the earth, and drought. Had Michael been the companion of Muhammad, we would have followed him, because he comes with abundance and peace. It was also because he defended Bukhtnassar when we wanted to kill him, so he destroyed the House of al-Maqdis and destroyed us, and because he informs Muhammad (ﷺ) of our secret.

The address in His words "Say" is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the object of the verb "say" is the clause that follows. *Man* here is conditional. Al-Raghib said: "*Al-'adawa* (enmity) is transgression and opposition to harmony. With the heart it is called *'adawa*; with walking it is called *'aduww*; with a deviation from justice it is called *'udwan*; and with place or lineage it is called *qawm 'idan*, that is, strangers."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 97–98 (part 2 of 3):

﴿Then indeed, he has sent it down﴾: This is not the response (jawab al-shart, the apodosis of the conditional) to the condition, because it is established in the science of Arabic grammar that the conditional noun (ism al-shart) must have in its response a pronoun referring back to it. So if you say, "Whoever honours me? Zayd is standing," it is not permissible. His saying ﴿then indeed, he has sent it down upon your heart﴾ contains no pronoun referring back to "whoever." Al-Zamakhshari explicitly stated that it is the response to the condition, and this is an error, for the reason we have mentioned, namely the absence of a returning pronoun, and because the verb of sending down is in the past tense, so the clause cannot be the response. Rather, the response is [p. 320] omitted, its omission being indicated by what follows it. The estimate is: "then his enmity has no basis," or something similar to this estimate. The pronoun in ﴿fa-innahu﴾ refers to Jibril, and the pronoun in ﴿nazzalahu﴾ refers to the Qur'an, by the indication of the meaning. Do you not see His saying: ﴿confirming what was before it, and as guidance and good tidings for the believers﴾? All of these are attributes of the Qur'an. And [there is] His saying ﴿by the permission of Allah﴾, meaning: indeed Jibril sent down the Qur'an upon your heart by the permission of Allah. It has also been said: the pronoun in ﴿fa-innahu﴾ refers to Allah, and the pronoun in ﴿nazzalahu﴾ refers to Jibril, the estimate being: indeed Allah sent down Jibril with the Qur'an upon your heart. In each of these two estimates there is an implied element that refers to what the context of the meaning indicates. However, the first estimate is preferable, for the reason we have mentioned, and so that it agrees with His saying: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit brought it down upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 193]. The second estimate is supported by the reading of those who read nazzala with a shadda (intensive form) and al-ruha (the Spirit) in the accusative. The connection of the proof of the response to the condition is that whoever is an enemy of Jibril, his enmity has no basis, because he is the one who brought down the Qur'an that confirms the (previous) Books, and [is] the guide and the bearer of good tidings, just as whoever believed. Whoever is in this position ought to be loved and thanked, since through him came the cause of guidance and the affirmation of what is in their hands of the Books of Allah. Or [the meaning is]: whoever is an enemy of Jibril, the cause of his enmity is that he sent down the Qur'an confirming their Book and obligating them to follow you, and they do not want that; for this reason they distorted what is in their Books of your attributes and of the covenants taken from them concerning them, that they should follow you. The difference between each of these two estimates is that the first estimate necessitates the absence of enmity, while the second estimate is as if it were an excuse for them in their enmity, like your saying: "If Zayd is hostile to you, then you have harmed him and wronged him."

﴿upon your heart﴾: He used the word ʿalā (upon), because the Qur'an is elevated over the heart, since the heart hears it and obeys it, carrying out what it commands and avoiding what it forbids. And ʿalā is more eloquent than ilā (to), because ilā indicates only the endpoint, whereas ʿalā indicates elevation. Whatever is elevated over a thing necessarily reaches it. The heart was singled out, and he did not say "upon you," because the heart is the place of intellect and knowledge and the receiving of inspirations; or because it is his page upon which things are inscribed, and his treasury in which things are preserved; or because it is the sovereign of the body. In the hadith: "Indeed, in the body there is a lump of flesh," then he said afterward: "Behold, it is the heart." Or because the heart is the choicest and most noble part of a thing; or because it is the House of Allah; or because by it he meant the intellect, using the place for what resides in it; or he meant the whole human being, since sending down upon it is mentioned in several places: ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an upon you that you should be distressed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 2], ﴿And Allah sent down upon you the Book and the wisdom﴾ [al-Nisa: 113]; or it is the use of a part for the whole. These are seven opinions. He attributed the heart to the kaf of address (the "you" pronoun), and did not attribute it to the ya' of the speaker, even though the structure of the speech apparently requires it; because His saying ﴿whoever is an enemy to Jibril﴾ is governed by an implied verb of speaking, the estimate being: "Say, O Muhammad: Allah says: 'Whoever is an enemy to Jibril, then indeed he sent it down upon your heart.'" Al-Zamakhshari inclined to this with his statement: "It came as a quotation of the speech of Allah, Exalted, as if it had been said: 'What I spoke of, my saying: "Whoever is an enemy to Jibril, then indeed he sent it down upon your heart."'" His discourse on this is confused. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "It is good in the speech of the Arabs that the word spoken by the one commanded to speak should be preserved, and it is good that the meaning of his speech be intended, so he narrates it in direct address to him, as you say: 'Say to your people: Do not humiliate you,' and so this verse is likewise. A similar example is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

Did you not see that on the day of Jaww Suwayqa, I called out and Hunayda called to me: "What is wrong with you?"

So he preserved the meaning and departed from the calling of Hunayda, [which is] 'What is wrong with you?'" End of his statement. This is a good interpretation, and in that case the conditional clause is governed by the word "say," not by an implied verb of speaking, and this is the apparent sense of the speech.

﴿by the permission of Allah﴾: That is, by the command of Allah. He chose this in al-Muntakhab, and from it [comes] His saying: ﴿No soul speaks except by His permission﴾ [Hud: 105], ﴿Who is it that intercedes with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqara: 255]. This has been stated explicitly in: ﴿We do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾ [Maryam: 64]. Or [it means] by His knowledge and His enabling him to this rank, as Ibn ʿAtiyya said; or by His choice, as al-Mawardi said; or by His facilitation and making it easy, as al-Zamakhshari said.

﴿confirming what was before it﴾: The accusative of muṣaddiqan (confirming) is a state (ḥāl) from the pronoun in nazzalahu if it refers to the Qur'an. If it refers to Jibril, it allows two possibilities: One: it is a state from the implied genitive noun, because the meaning is: "Indeed Allah sent down Jibril with the Qur'an, confirming." The second: it is a state from Jibril. The "mā" in "limā" is a relative pronoun, and by it he meant the Books that Allah sent down to the nations before its sending down, or the Torah and the Gospel. The pronoun in "bayna yadayhi" may refer to the Qur'an, and it may refer to Jibril. So the meaning is: confirming what is before it of the messengers and the Books.

﴿and as guidance and good tidings﴾: These two are conjoined to muṣaddiqan, so they are states, and this would be an instance of placing the verbal noun in the position of the active participle, as if he said: "guiding and bringing good tidings"; or it is from the sphere of hyperbole (mubalagha), as if, since guidance and good tidings were achieved through it, it was made the very essence of guidance and good tidings. The alif in bushrā is for the feminine, as in ruj'ā, and it is a verbal noun. The discussion of its meaning has already been presented in His saying: ﴿And give good tidings to those who believe﴾ [al-Baqara: 25], at the beginning of this surah. The meaning is that He described the Qur'an as confirming what preceded it of the divine Books, and that it is guidance, since in it is the explanation of what the obligations of the deeds of the hearts and the limbs are, and that it is good tidings to whoever attains guidance. Thus this verbal order in these states arose because their referents are arranged in an existential order. The first: its confirming the Books, because all the Books are from one spring. The second: that guidance was achieved through it after its sending down in this state of confirmation. The third: that it is good tidings to whoever attains guidance through it. Al-Raghib said: "And guidance from error, and good tidings of Paradise."

﴿for the believers﴾: He singled out guidance and good tidings for the believers, because guidance and good tidings through it do not belong to non-believers, as He said: ﴿And it is for them a blindness﴾ [Fussilat: 44]; and because the believers are the ones given good tidings: ﴿So give good tidings to My servants﴾ [al-Zumar: 17], ﴿Their Lord gives them good tidings of mercy from Him﴾ [al-Tawba: 21]. This verse indicates the exaltation of Jibril and the honouring of his rank, in that He made him the intermediary between Himself and the noblest of His creation, and the one who brought down the Book that combines the attributes mentioned. It also indicates the reproach of the Jews, in that they hated the one who held this exalted position with Allah, Exalted. They said: The Batiniyya have clung to this verse, and they said: "The Qur'an is an inspiration, and the letters are the expression of the Messenger." It was answered against them: that it is a manifest miracle in its composition, that Allah named it revelation, Book and Arabic, that Jibril descended with it, and that the one inspired (mulham) does not need Jibril.

﴿whoever is an enemy to Allah﴾: Enmity between Allah and the servant is not literal; the servant's enmity to Allah, Exalted, is figurative, and its meaning is opposition to the command. Allah's enmity to the servant is His requiting him for his opposition.

﴿and His angels and His messengers and Jibril and Mika'il, then indeed Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers﴾. He emphasized, with His saying "and His angels," the matter of Jibril, since the Jews had reported that he was their enemy among the angels, because he brings destruction and punishment. So He answered them in the previous verse, that he brought the essence of all goods, which is the Qur'an, comprising those noble attributes, from its agreement with their Books, and its being guidance and good tidings, so love for him was obligatory. And He answered them in this verse by joining him to His own Name, falling under the generality of His angels, then secondly under the generality of His messengers, because the messengers include the angels and others from among the sons of Adam who were sent; then thirdly by explicitly mentioning him singly alongside the one whom they claim to love, namely Mika'il. Thus he is mentioned three times in this verse. All of this is a refutation of the Jews and a reproach to them, and a dignifying of Jibril. The verse indicates that Allah, Exalted, is an enemy to whoever opposes Allah, His angels, His messengers, Jibril and Mika'il. This does not mean that the intended one is whoever combines enmity toward all of them, so that Allah would be his enemy; rather the meaning is that whoever is hostile to one of those mentioned, Allah is his enemy, since hostility toward one of those mentioned is hostility toward all. The Muslims have agreed that whoever hates a messenger or an angel has disbelieved. Some people said: the "wa" (and) here means "or," and it is not for conjunction. Others said: the "wa" is for detailing, and it is not intended that he be an enemy to all the angels, nor to all the messengers; rather this is from the category of attaching the ruling to the genus in the form of a plural, as when you say: "If you speak to men, then you are divorced," you do not mean by it "if you speak to every man," nor the least that the plural applies to; rather he attached it to the genus, even if it is in the form of a plural. So if she spoke to one man, she would be divorced; likewise this plural in the angels and the messengers. The meaning is that whoever is hostile to Allah, or to one of His angels, or to one of His messengers, then Allah is an enemy to him.

Al-Maturidi said: It is possible that the opening with the Name of Allah is in the manner of exalting the one mentioned after it, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then to Allah belongs one-fifth of it﴾ [al-Anfal: 41]. And He singled out Jibril and Mikal for mention to honour and distinguish them. We have also related from our teacher Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn Ibrahim ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah sanctify his spirit, that he used to call this type for us "al-tajrid" (isolating a particular item for mention), which is when a thing falls under a general category and then you single it out by name, and that is for a meaning specific to it, not shared with the other members of that general category. Thus Jibril and Mikal are treated as if they were of another kind, and the difference in description is treated like the difference in kind, so they are conjoined by "and". This type of conjunction, namely the conjunction of the particular to the general for the sake of distinction, is one of the rulings that are unique to the particle "wa" (and), so it is not permissible with the other coordinating particles.

It has also been said: they were singled out for mention because the Jews mentioned them, and the verse was revealed concerning them. Had they not been mentioned, the Jews would have had a pretext to say: "We did not oppose Allah," or "nor all His angels"?

It has also been said: they were singled out for mention to remove the objection that what makes disbelief obligatory is enmity toward all the angels, not toward one of them. So it is as if it were said: "or any one of them."

This order is in the utmost beauty: it begins with the mention of Allah, then with the intermediaries between Him and the Messengers, then with the intermediaries between the angels and those to whom they were sent. This is an order according to the transmission of revelation. The mention of the angels first does not indicate their superiority over the Messengers of the children of Adam, because the order we have mentioned is an order in relation to the intermediaries, not in relation to superiority.

The statement of al-Zamakhshari will come, that the angels are nobler than the prophets, God willing. They said: the singling out of Jibril and Mikal for mention indicates that they are nobler than all the angels. They also said: Jibril is superior to Mikal, because he is mentioned first, and because he descends with revelation and knowledge, which is the substance of spirits, whereas Mikal descends with fertility and rain, which is the substance of bodies, and the nourishment of spirits is nobler than the nourishment of bodies. End of quotation. But the preference of Jibril over Mikal requires a clear and explicit text, and precedence in mention does not indicate preference, since it may be by way of ascent (from lesser to greater).

The "man" in His saying ﴿whoever is an enemy﴾ is conditional (shart). The commentators differ regarding the answer (jawab) of the condition. It is said: it is omitted, its estimate being: "then he is a disbeliever," and it was omitted because the meaning points to it. It is also said the answer is: ﴿then indeed Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers﴾. He used the apparent Name of Allah and did not say "He is an enemy," lest it be understood that the pronoun refers to the conditional noun, which would change the meaning, or that it refers to the nearest mentioned item, Mikal. So he made the Name apparent to remove the ambiguity, or for glorification and emphasis, since the Arabs, when they wish to magnify something, repeat it by the name that preceded it. Among examples is: ﴿Allah will surely help him; indeed Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving﴾ [al-Hajj: 60], and the saying of the poet:
"I do not see that death outstrips death, anything..."

This sentence, which stands as the predicate of the conditional, requires a link (rabit) between the clause of the answer and the conditional noun. The link here is the apparent noun, which is "the disbelievers." The apparent noun has been placed in the position of the pronoun to harmonise the endings of the verses, and to state explicitly the cause of the enmity, which is disbelief, since whoever is an enemy of one of those mentioned, or of any one of them, is a disbeliever. Or it may be intended that "the disbelievers" is general, so the link is generality, since disbelief takes many forms, and these disbelievers with this particular thing are one instance of the general category, so the connection is achieved thereby.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "an enemy to the disbelievers" means he intended "an enemy to them," and he brought the apparent noun to show that Allah opposes them because of their disbelief, and that enmity toward the angels is disbelief. If enmity toward the prophets is disbelief, what of the angels? And they are nobler. The meaning: whoever opposes them, Allah opposes him and punishes him with the most severe punishment. End of his words. This is the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah, who hold that the angels are superior to the special ones among the children of Adam. The words of al-Zamakhshari indicate that the apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun, and that generality was not intended in it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The expression came with the generality of "the disbelievers," because the return of the pronoun to "man" would be ambiguous, whether you make it singular or plural, and even if one were not concerned with the ambiguity. We say: the meaning guides the hearer to the intended sense, and it would necessitate specifying a group as the object of Allah's enmity. It is possible that Allah knew some of them would believe, so it is not appropriate to apply the enmity of Allah to them as a final state. It is narrated that Umar uttered this verse in reply to some Jews who said: "That is our enemy," meaning Jibril, so the verse was revealed upon the tongue of Umar. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this report is weak.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 2, Verse 99**

﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you clear signs (āyāt bayyināt)﴾: The occasion of its revelation, as al-Tabarani mentioned, was that Ibn Suriya said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "You have not brought us any clear sign," so this was revealed. Al-Zamakhshari said: He said, "You have not brought us anything we recognise, and no sign has been sent down to you that we might follow you by it," and so it was revealed. The连接 (munasabah, the connection) of this verse with what precedes it is evident. When God, exalted is He, mentioned a number of the ugly deeds of the Jews and censured them for them, and among what He mentioned was their enmity toward Gabriel, this matched their denial of what Gabriel had brought. So God informed that the Messenger, peace be upon him, had been sent down clear signs, and that none denies their revelation except every wicked person (fāsiq), because of their clarity. As for "the clear signs" (al-āyāt al-bayyināt), that is, the Qur'an, or the miracles accompanied by the challenge (al-tahaddi), or the informing of what was hidden and concealed in the earlier scriptures, or the laws (al-sharā'i'), or the obligations (al-farā'id), or the totality of all that has preceded: these are five opinions. The apparent meaning is the unrestricted sense of whatever "clear signs" indicates, without specifying any one of them. The arrival of these at the Messenger of God (ﷺ) is expressed by "sending down," because that was from a higher position to a lower one.

﴿And none disbelieve in them except the wicked (al-fāsiqūn)﴾: What is meant by "the wicked" here is "the disbelievers," because disbelief in the signs of God, exalted is He, belongs to the category of wickedness of belief, not the category of wickedness of deeds. Al-Hasan said: When the term fisq (wickedness) is used for any sin, it refers to its greatest form, whether disbelief or otherwise. End of quotation. The word "clear" (bayyinat) matches the word "disbelief" (kufr), which means covering. For what is clear admits no confusion, so failure to believe in it is not due to doubt, since it is clear; rather it is a covering and concealment of what is evident and plain. Concealing what is evident occurs only from one who is obstinate in his wickedness. The definite article in "al-fāsiqūn" is either generic (li-l-jins) or referential (li-l-'ahd), because the context of the verses indicates that this refers to the Jews. Here wickedness is used as a metaphor for disbelief, because fisq is the going out of a person beyond what is prescribed for him. Al-Hasan's statement has already been mentioned, that it indicates the greatest of what the term applies to, so it is as if it were said: "None disbelieve in them except those who go to the extreme in their disbelief, reaching its ultimate limit." As for "except the wicked," this is an exceptive construction (istithna' mufarragh, an open exception with no stated subject), since its underlying sense is: "None disbelieve in them," and so it negates that anyone disbelieves in the manifest signs. Then he excepted the wicked from "anyone," and that they disbelieve in them. According to the school of al-Farra', it is permissible in this kind of exception to put the noun in the accusative, so he permitted: "No one stood except Zayd" (mā qāma illā Zaydan), considering that deleted element, since if it had not been deleted the accusative would be permitted. The Basrans do not permit this.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 100:

﴿Is it that whenever they make a covenant, a party of them casts it aside?﴾: It was revealed concerning Malik ibn al-Sayf, who said: "By God, no covenant was taken from us in our Scripture that we should believe in Muhammad (ﷺ), nor any pledge." And it was said concerning the Jews: they made a covenant that if he (ﷺ) went forth they would surely believe in him and surely stand with him against the polytheists of the Arabs, but when he was sent they disbelieved in him. ʿAṭāʾ said: it refers to the covenants between him (ﷺ) and the Jews, which they broke, like the conduct of Qurayẓa and al-Naḍīr. God the Exalted said: ﴿those with whom you made a covenant, then they break their covenant each time﴾ [al-Anfal: 56]. The majority read: ﴿أوَكُلَّما﴾ (awakullamā) with a fatḥah on the waw. Regarding this waw there is difference: it was said that it is superfluous (zā'idah), as stated by al-Akhfash. It was said that it is "aw" (or), whose waw was silent and was vocalized with a fatḥah, and it means "bal" (rather), as stated by al-Kisa'i. Both opinions are weak. It was said that it is the conjunctive waw (wāw al-ʿaṭf), and this is the correct view. It has already been mentioned that the position of Sibawayh and the grammarians is that the original order is to place this waw, the fa', and thumma before the interrogative hamzah, and the hamzah was placed first because it has the front of the sentence. As for al-Zamakhshari, he holds that there is an omitted element conjoined with it, estimated between the hamzah and the conjunctive particle, and for that reason he estimated it here as: ﴿أكَفَرُوا بِالآياتِ البَيِّناتِ؟ وكُلَّما عاهَدُوا﴾ ("Did they disbelieve in the clear signs? And whenever they made a covenant..."). Al-Zamakhshari retracted his preference and returned to the view of the majority. We have discussed this at length in our book called al-Takmil li-Sharh al-Tashil. The purpose of this interrogative is denunciation and magnification of what they undertake of repeatedly making covenants and breaking them, until this became a habit and a disposition for them. Therefore one should not be concerned with their affair, nor should that be difficult, and this is a consolation to the Messenger (ﷺ) when they disbelieved in what was sent down to him, because what has become a person's habit and character should not be made much of. Abu al-Sammal al-ʿAdawi and others read: ﴿أوْ كُلَّما﴾ (aw kullamā) with a sukun on the waw, and al-Zamakhshari explained this as conjoined to "the wicked (al-fasiqin)," estimating: "None disbelieve in them except those who are defiant, or who have broken the covenant of God many times." Al-Mahdawi and others explained it as "aw" being for transition from one speech to another, like the disconnected "am," so it is as if he said: "Rather, whenever they make a covenant..." like a man saying to another, "I will punish you," and he replies, "Or may God improve your opinion," meaning "rather, may He improve your opinion." This explanation is according to the view of the Kufans, for "aw" is with them equivalent to "bal." They cited as evidence for this claim the poet's verse:

"She appeared like the horn of the sun in the brightness of the forenoon, and her form, or you are more graceful in the eye."

Also "aw" has come in the sense of waw in his saying:

"From between one who bridles his colt, or one who seizes it,"

and his saying:

"Spear-points that were lifted, or chains,"

meaning: "and one who seizes it," and "and chains."

It has been said regarding ﴿خَطِيئَةً أوْ إثْمًا﴾ [al-Nisa': 112] that the meaning is "and," so this irregular reading may be explained as "aw" being in the sense of waw, as if it were said: "And whenever they make a covenant..." Al-Hasan and Abu Rajaʾ read: ﴿أوَكُلَّما عُوهِدُوا﴾ in the passive form, and this reading contradicts the script of the Mushaf. The accusative of ʿahdan is either as a verbal noun of an unusual form, meaning "mu'ahadah," or as an object with "ʿāhada" being taken to mean "aʿṭā" (gave), meaning they gave a covenant. It was also read: ﴿عَهِدُوا﴾, in which case ʿahdan is a verbal noun. The meaning of the covenant has already been mentioned in the occasion of revelation, so there is no need to repeat it.

﴿نَبَذَهُ﴾ (nabadhahu): threw it away, or broke it, or abandoned acting upon it, or set it aside, or cast it. Five opinions, which are close in meaning. Attributing "nabdh" (casting) to a covenant is metaphorical, because a covenant is an abstract meaning, while casting is literal and applies only to tangible things: ﴿So We seized him and his soldiers, and cast them into the sea﴾ [al-Qasas: 40], ﴿when she withdrew from her family to a place toward the east﴾ [Maryam: 16], so he cast his ring, and the people cast their rings, ﴿he would surely have been cast out into the wasteland﴾ [al-Qalam: 49].

﴿فَرِيقٌ مِنهُمْ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 75]: "Fariq" (party) is a collective noun with no singular, applying to both the few and the many. ʿAbd Allah read: ﴿نَقَضَهُ فَرِيقٌ مِنهم﴾, and this reading contradicts the text of the Mushaf, so it is better to take it as an explanation.

﴿بَلْ أكْثَرُهم لا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ ("Rather, most of them do not believe"): It is possible that this is conjunction of sentences, which is the apparent reading, so "aktharuhum" is the subject and "la yu'minun" is its predicate, and the pronoun in "aktharihim" refers to those to whom the pronoun in "ʿahadu" refers, namely the Jews. The sense of this transition (idrab) is a shift from one statement to another, and "most" in this case covers what "party" covers, as if it were more general, since whoever cast off the covenant is included among those who do not believe. It is as if he said: "Rather, the party that cast off the covenant, and other than that party, are judged as not believing." It was also said: it is possible that this is conjunction of single words, with "aktharuhum" conjoined to "fariq," meaning "a party of them cast it aside, rather most of them," and "la yu'minun" is a circumstantial clause, its governing element being "nabadhahu," and its circumstantial referent being "aktharuhum." Since "fariq" applies to both the few and the many, and the casting was attributed to it, it might be thought that the casters are few, so He clarified that the casters are the majority, and mentioning the majority became evidence that "fariq" here does not mean a small number of them; this is an idrab from what the word "fariq" might imply of meaning the few. The pronoun in "aktharuhum" refers either to the party or to all the Children of Israel. On both possibilities, He mentioned the majority as the subject of the judgment of casting off, or of not believing, because some of them did believe, and whoever believed did not cast off the covenant. The Muslims have agreed that whoever disbelieves in a single verse of the Book of God, or breaks the covenant of God which He took from His servants in His scriptures, is a disbeliever.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 101:

﴿When there came to them a messenger﴾: The pronoun in *jaa'ahum* (came to them) refers to the Children of Israel, or to their scholars. The "messenger" (*rasul*) is Muhammad (ﷺ), or Jesus, upon our Prophet and upon him be the best of prayers and peace. Or its meaning is *risalah* (the message), in which case it is a verbal noun (*masdar*), as they explained the words of the poet:

*"The slanderers have lied; I did not confide my secret to her about Layla, nor did I send them as a messenger (bi-rasul)."*

That is, "with a message." There are three opinions. The apparent one is the first, because the address to the Jews was directed in relation to Muhammad (ﷺ). Do you not see His saying: "Say" (*qul*), "Say," and ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel – indeed, he has brought it down upon your heart﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 97], and ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 99]? So this is like an *iltifat* (shift of address), as it is a movement from direct address to a third-person name. He is described by His saying: ﴿from Allah, confirming﴾, to magnify his station, since the messenger is according to the rank of the one who sent him. Then he is also described as confirming what is with them. They said: his confirming is that he was created with the description mentioned in the Torah; or his confirming is by the foundations of monotheism, the principles of religion, the reports of the nations, and the admonitions and wisdoms; or his confirming is his informing that what is with them is the speech of Allah, and that it was revealed to Moses; or his confirming is his manifesting what they asked about of the obscure matters of the Torah. These are four opinions. If it is interpreted as Jesus, then his confirming is of the Torah. If it is interpreted as the message, then the attribution of coming and confirming to the message is by way of extension and metaphor (*majaz*). Ibn Abi Abla read *musaddiqan* (confirming) in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*), and its coming from an indefinite noun is made acceptable by its being qualified by His saying: ﴿from Allah﴾.

﴿confirming what is with them﴾: This is the Torah. It is also said: all the books that were revealed to them, such as the Psalms of David and the scrolls of the prophets, which they believe in.

﴿a party of those who were given the Book threw away﴾: The Book that they were given is the Torah, and it is the second object of *utu* (were given), according to the view of the majority, and the first object according to the view of al-Suhayli. This was discussed previously.

﴿the Book of Allah﴾: It is the object of *nabadha* (threw away). It is said: the Book of Allah is the Torah. The meaning of their throwing it away is abandoning its rulings, or abandoning what is in it of the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), since disbelief in part is disbelief in all. It is also said: it is the Gospel, and their throwing it away is abandoning it entirely. It is also said: it is the Qur'an, and this is more apparent, since the discourse is with the Messenger. So the meaning becomes: he confirms what is before them of the Torah, while they, on the contrary, deny and cast aside what he brought of the Qur'an. He attributed the Book to Allah to glorify it, just as he attributed the Messenger to Him with the description mentioned earlier. Thus this becomes the utmost in blaming them, since it came to them from Allah with His Book confirming their Book, and it is a witness to the Messenger and the Book, yet they threw it away.

﴿behind their backs﴾: This is an allegory used for one who turns away from a thing entirely. The Arabs say: "He put this matter behind his back and the back of his ear." Al-Farazdaq said:

*"O Tamim ibn Murr, let not my need be behind a back, and let its answer not be hard for you."*

The Arabs said this because what is placed behind the back cannot be looked at. From it is His saying: ﴿and you took it behind your backs, cast away﴾ [Hud: 92]. In *al-Muntakhab* it is said: *nabdh* (throwing), *tarh* (casting), and *ilqa'* (flinging) are close in meaning, but *nabdh* is most often said of what is discarded as worthless, *tarh* is most often said of what is spread out and similar things, and *ilqa'* is used where there is a meeting between two things.

﴿as if they did not know﴾: This is a circumstantial clause (*jumla haliyya*), its subject (*sahib al-hal*) is *fariq* (party), and the governing element of the state is *nabadha* (threw away). It is a comparison of one who knows with one who is ignorant, because the one ignorant of a thing does not regard it or value it, since he has no awareness of the benefit in it. The object of knowledge is omitted, meaning: as if they did not know that it is the Book of Allah, with no doubt entering them concerning it, because its truth is established and verified for them, and they only threw it away out of obstinacy and defiance. Al-Sha'bi said: it is among them, they read it, but they abandoned acting by it. And from Sufyan: they wrapped it in brocade and silk, and adorned it with gold, but did not make lawful what it made lawful, nor make unlawful what it made unlawful. The end of his speech. The saying of al-Sha'bi and Sufyan indicates that the Book of Allah is the Torah. Al-Mawardi said: as if they did not know what they were commanded of following Muhammad (ﷺ). It is also said: its meaning is as if they did not know that he is a truthful prophet. It is also said: its meaning is as if they did not know that the Qur'an, the Torah, and the Gospel are books of Allah, and that each of them is true, and that acting by it is obligatory.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 102 (part 1 of 4):**

﴿And they followed what the devils recited over the kingdom of Solomon﴾. The meaning of *ittaba'u* (followed): that is, they took it as a model (*iqtada'u*) (imam), or they preferred it, because whoever follows something prefers it. Or the *waw* of the pronoun in *ittaba'u* is intended to refer to the Jews. Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi said: it refers to those who were in the time of Solomon. Ibn Abbas said: it refers to those in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. It was also said: it refers to all the Jews. The clause beginning with *wa-ittaba'u* is conjoined to the whole preceding clause, from His words *wa-lamma ja'ahum* (and when there came to them) to its end, and it is a report about their condition in following what should not be followed (p. 326). This is the apparent meaning, not that it is conjoined to His words *nabadhahu fariqun minhum* (a party of them cast it away), because following did not result from the coming of the Messenger, since they were following that before the coming of the Messenger. This is unlike the casting away of the Book of Allah, which does result from the coming of the Messenger.

*Tatlu* (recite): it means *tattabi'u* (follow), as said by Ibn Abbas; or it means *tadda'i* (claim), or *taqra'u* (read), or *tuhaddithu* (narrate), as said by Ata; or *tarwi* (transmit), as said by Yaman; or *ta'malu* (practice), or *takdhibu* (lie), as said by Abu Muslim. These statements are close in meaning.

*Ma* is a relative (*mawsula*) whose relative clause is *tatlu*, and it is a present verb with the meaning of the past, i.e., *ma talat* (what they recited). The Kufans said: the meaning is *ma kanat tatlu* (what they used to recite). They do not mean that the relative clause of *ma* is omitted, namely *kanat*, with *tatlu* in the position of the predicate. Rather, they mean that the present verb has taken the place of the past, just as when you say *kana Zaydun yaqumu* (Zayd used to stand), it is a report about Zayd's standing, and it is past because of the indication of *kana* upon it.

*Al-shayatin* (the devils): its apparent meaning is that they are the devils of the jinn, because when the word *shaytan* is used without qualification, the mind immediately goes to it being from the jinn. It was also said: what is intended is the devils of mankind.

Al-Hasan and al-Dahhak read *al-shayatuna* with a *raf'* (nominative) using the *waw*. This is anomalous; he analogized it to the Arab saying: *bustan fulan hawlahu basatun* (the garden of so-and-so has gardens around it), which was transmitted by al-Asma'i. They said: the correct view is that this *jinn* is an abomination. Abu al-Baqa' said: he made the *ya'* before the *nun* resemble the *ya'* of the sound masculine plural, and this is close to an error. Al-Sajawandi said: al-Kharazbaji rejected it as an error.

*Ala mulk* (over the kingdom): it is connected to *tatlu*. *Talā* is transitive with *ala* when its object is that over which something is recited, as in *yutlā ala Zaydin al-Qur'anu* (the Qur'an is recited to Zayd). The kingdom here is not in this sense, because it is not a person over whom something is recited. Therefore some grammarians claimed that *ala* has the meaning of *fi* (in), i.e., *tatlu fi mulk Sulayman* (they recite in the kingdom of Solomon). Our companions said: *ala* does not have the meaning of *fi*; rather this is *tadmin* (implicit meaning) in the verb, where *tataqawwalu* (to fabricate) is implied, so it takes *ala*, because *taqawwala* is used with it. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us﴾ [al-Haqqah: 44]. The meaning of ﴿over the kingdom of Solomon﴾ is: over his law, his prophethood, and his state. It was also said: over his time, and in his era, which is close. It was also said: over the throne of Solomon after his death, because it was one of the instruments of his kingdom.

They interpreted *ma tatlu al-shayatin* (what the devils recited) as magic. They said: this is the most well-known and most apparent view, based on what was transmitted in the reports on the occasions of revelation, that the devils wrote magic, fabricated it, and attributed it to Solomon and Asif. It was also said: what they recited is the lie that they attribute to what they steal of the news of the heavens, and they attributed that to Solomon to glorify the matter of what they recited. This is because what Solomon had of miracles, displaying extraordinary acts, subjugating the jinn and mankind, bringing distant things near, joining hearts, and speaking with dumb animals was a great matter. The magician claims things of this kind: subjugating the jinn, attaining desires, influencing hearts, and even claiming the transformation of things, as will come in the discussion of magic in His words: ﴿They teach people magic﴾. Or because they used to claim that the kingdom of Solomon was achieved only by magic. The commentators have mentioned many stories about the ways in which they arranged what they recited, but Allah knows best about them. Neither the noble verse nor any authentic, connected hadith addresses any of it, so we have not mentioned it.

﴿And Solomon did not disbelieve﴾: this is an exoneration of Solomon from disbelief. That is, what the jinn fabricated, attributing to Solomon what they claim, was not practiced by Solomon, because it is disbelief, and the one whom Allah has made a prophet is free from major and minor sins, let alone disbelief. In this is evidence for the validity of denying a thing of one who could not possibly do it, because a prophet cannot possibly commit disbelief. This does not indicate that what they attributed to Solomon of magic would be disbelief, since it is possible that they attributed disbelief to him along with magic. It is narrated that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ mentioned Solomon among the prophets, some of the Jews said: Look at Muhammad, he mentions Solomon among the prophets, and he was only a magician. The verses did not previously mention that anyone attributed disbelief to Solomon, but this is a verse revealed concerning the earlier cause, that the Jews attributed to him magic and practicing it.

﴿But the devils disbelieved﴾: their disbelief is either by teaching magic, or by learning it, or by declaring Solomon a disbeliever because of it. It is possible that their disbelief was for other than that. The use of *lakinna* (but) here is good, because it comes between negation and affirmation. It is read *wa-lakinna* with the *tashdid* (doubling of the nun), in which case it must be operative (i.e., governing the accusative of its noun), and this is the reading of Nafi', Asim, Ibn Kathir, and Abu Amr. (p. 327) It is also read with the *takhfif* (lightening of the nun) and the raising of what follows it as the subject and predicate, and this is the reading of Ibn Amir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i. When it is lightened, is it permissible to make it operative? This is a matter of disagreement. The majority hold that it is not permissible, and Abu al-Qasim ibn al-Rimak transmitted from Yunus that it is permissible to make it operative, and others transmitted that from al-Akhfash, but the correct view is that it is not permissible. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: the preferred view is the *tashdid* when a *waw* precedes it, and the *takhfif* when no *waw* accompanies it, because when lightened it is a conjunction and does not need a *waw* with it, like *bal*. When a *waw* precedes it, it is not like *bal*, because *bal* does not take a *waw* before it; but when *lakinna* is doubled, it operates like *inna* and is not a conjunction. End of the speech. All of this is on the assumption that *lakinna* is a conjunction, which is a matter of disagreement. The majority hold that *lakinna* is a conjunction. Yunus went to the view that it is not one of the conjunctive particles, and this is the correct view, because that is not preserved in the language of the Arabs. Rather, when what follows it gives the impression of conjunction, it is accompanied by the *waw*, as in His words: ﴿Muhammad is not the father of any one of your men, but he is the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 40]. As for when a clause follows it, sometimes it is with the *waw* and sometimes without the *waw*, as Zuhayr said:

*Indeed the son of Warqa', his sudden assaults are not feared,*
*but his encounters in war are awaited.*

As for what is found in the books of the grammarians, such as their saying: *ma qama Zaydun lakin Amrun* (Zayd did not stand, but Amr did), *ma darabtu Zaydan lakin Amran* (I did not strike Zayd, but Amr), and *ma marartu bi-Zaydin lakin Amrin* (I did not pass by Zayd, but Amr), this is from their illustration, not something heard from the Arabs. Among the strange things said about *lakinna* is that it is composed of three words: *la* for negation, the *ka* for address, and *anna* for affirmation and confirmation, and the *hamza* was dropped for heaviness. This is a corrupt view, and the correct view is that it is simple.

﴿They teach people magic﴾: the pronoun in *yu'allimuna* (they teach) has been disputed as to what it refers to. The apparent view is that it refers to the devils, intending by it their seduction and misguidance, and this is the choice of al-Zamakhshari. On this view, the clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of the pronoun in *kafaru*. They said: or it is a second predicate. It was also said: it is a circumstantial clause of the devils, and this was refuted on the grounds that *lakinna* does not govern a circumstantial clause. It was also said: it is a substitute for *kafaru*, a substitution of verb for verb, because the devils teaching magic is disbelief in meaning. The apparent view is that it is a resumed report about them. It was also said: the pronoun refers to those who followed what the devils recited, according to the disagreement of the commentators about whom the pronoun *ittaba'u* refers to, so the meaning would be: those who followed what the devils recited teach people magic, and the people are teachers of the followers. On the first view they are teachers of the devils.

The reality of magic has been disputed, with several views:

The first: it is the transformation of things and their invention, and the alteration of people's forms, of the kind that resembles miracles and marvels, such as flying and covering distances in a night.

The second: it is trickery, deception, sleight of hand, and charlatanry with no reality. The evidence for this is His words: ﴿It will appear to him from their magic that they are moving﴾ [Ta-Ha: 66]. And in the hadith, when Labid ibn al-A'sam practiced magic upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "It appeared to him that he was doing a thing when he was not doing it." This is the view of the Mu'tazila, who hold that magic has no reality, and Abu Ishaq al-Isfarayini (al-Istirabadhi) of the Shafi'is agreed with them.

The third: it is a matter that takes hold of the eye by way of trickery, and from it is His words: ﴿They bewitched the eyes of the people﴾ [al-A'raf: 116], as it is narrated that their ropes and staffs were filled with mercury, so they kindled a fire beneath them, the ropes and staffs grew hot, moved, and slithered. Practitioners of tricks, sleight of hand, and charlatanry have many things of this sort, much of which is explained in the book called *Kashf al-Dakk wa al-Sha'wadha wa Idah al-Shakk* (Revealing Sleight of Hand and Charlatanry and Clarifying Doubt), and in the book *Irkha' al-Sutur wa al-Kalal fi al-Sha'wadha wa al-Hiyal* (Lowering the Curtains and Obstacles in Charlatanry and Tricks). In the hadith, when the moon split into two halves at Mecca, Abu Jahl said: wait until the people of the desert come; if they do not report this, then Muhammad has bewitched our eyes. They came and reported it, and he said: This is nothing but great magic.

The fourth: it is a kind of service of the jinn, who extracted it from the kind of their subtle bodies and their forms, so it became subtle, fine, and hidden.

The fifth: it is composed of bodies that are gathered and burned, and from them are made ashes and ink, and names and incantations are recited over them, and then they are used for what magic needs.

The sixth: its origin is talismans and *qalfatriyyat* (occult formulas), built on the influence of the properties of the stars, such as the influence of the sun on the mercury of Pharaoh's staff, or the employment of devils to facilitate what is difficult.

The seventh: it is composed of words mixed with disbelief.

One of our contemporary scholars said: All these views that have been stated regarding the reality of magic are types of magic, and other types have been added to them, of sleight of hand, charlatanry, *narinjiyyat* (conjuring), talismans, incantations, varieties of *mandal* (aloe incense) and seizures, and what is similar to that. End of his speech. There is no doubt that magic existed, due to the explicit statement of the Qur'an and the authentic hadith. As for our time now, whatever we come across in books about it is a lie and fabrication, from which nothing follows, and nothing from it is valid at all. Likewise, incantations and the burning of *mandal*, and the people who are believed to be intelligent and believe in these things and listen attentively to them. I have seen some who claim to be of knowledge, when he becomes bankrupt, write books and mention things from his own head, and sell them in the markets for good silver coins.

Some scholars have applied the name of magic to spreading discord among people through tale-bearing, because in it a friend is turned into an enemy and a beloved into a hated one. It has also been applied to the beautiful use of eloquent, sweet speech, because of the attraction it contains, and it has been called lawful magic. It is narrated: "Indeed, there is magic in eloquence." And someone said:

*Her speech is lawful magic; if only it had not
caused the killing of a Muslim who was on guard.*

Abu Hayyan's commentary on al-Bahr al-Muhit, 2:102 (part 2 of 4):

The apparent meaning of His words ﴿they teach people magic﴾ is that they make people understand it through reading and instruction. It has also been said that the meaning is that they guide people to those books, so "teaching" is applied to "guiding," by naming the effect after its cause. It has also been said that the meaning is that they instil in their hearts the belief that it is true, that it harms and benefits, and that Solomon's rule was established only through it. This too is naming the effect after its cause. It has also been said that *yu'allimun* means *yu'limun* (to inform), that is, they inform people of the means by which they learn magic, or of the one from whom they learn it, without actually teaching it to them. In that case it belongs to the category of informing, not of teaching.

As for the ruling on magic, whatever of it involves exalting other than Allah, such as the stars and the devils, or attributing to them what Allah brings about, is unbelief by consensus (*ijma'*, the consensus of scholars). Learning it and acting upon it are not permitted. Likewise, whatever is learnt with the aim of shedding blood or separating spouses or friends. If nothing of that is known from it, but it is merely possible, the apparent view is that learning it and acting upon it are not permitted. As for what belongs to the category of trickery, illusion, sleight of hand and conjuring: if one intends by learning it to practise it and deceive people, then it is not fitting to learn it, because it belongs to falsehood. If one intends by it to know it so that the deceptions and tricks of sorcerers do not succeed against him, there is no harm in learning it. Or (if one intends) amusement, play and entertaining people with the ease of its performance, then it is disliked. It is narrated: "I am not of the frivolous, nor is the frivolous of me." As for the magic of eloquence, whatever is intended by it is the softening of hearts towards good is the lawful magic, while concealing the truth is not permitted to learn or act upon. As for the legal ruling on the sorcerer, both the punishment and repentance, the exegetes have addressed this, but the verse does not address it. It is a matter whose subject is the science of jurisprudence (*fiqh*), so it is to be mentioned there.

﴿And what was sent down﴾: The apparent meaning is that *ma* is a noun-relative (*ism mawsul*, relative pronoun) in the accusative, and that it is conjoined to His words "magic." The apparent sense of conjunction is difference, so what was sent down upon the two angels is not magic. It has been said that it is conjoined to *ma tatlu al-shayatin* (what the devils recited), meaning: and they followed what the devils recited and what was sent down. The apparent meaning here is that what they taught people, or what they followed, was something sent down. Regarding this sent-down matter, which was taught or followed, it has been disputed. It has been said: the science of magic was sent down upon the two angels as a trial from Allah for people. Whoever learnt it from them and acted upon it became an unbeliever, and whoever avoided it, or learnt it without acting upon it, but in order to guard against it and so as not to be deceived by it, was a believer, just as the people of Talut were tested by the river. This is the view chosen by al-Zamakhshari. Mujahid and others said: what was sent down is the thing by which a man is separated from his wife, and it is lesser than magic. It has been said: magic was sent down so that it might be known for the purpose of warning against it and forbidding it, and on this view the teaching is merely a brief acquaintance with its basics. It has been said: *ma* is in the position of the genitive, conjoined to "the kingdom of Solomon," and the meaning is: a fabrication against the kingdom of Solomon, and a fabrication against what was sent down (p-329) upon the two angels. This is the view chosen by Abu Muslim, who denied that magic was sent down upon the two angels. He said: because it is unbelief, and angels are infallible; and because it is not fitting for Allah to send it down or for it to be attributed to Him, since Allah nullifies it. What was sent down upon the two angels is the Law (*shar'*), and they were teaching people that. It has been said: *ma* is a negative particle, and the clause is conjoined to "And Solomon did not disbelieve." This is because the Jews said that Allah sent down Gabriel and Michael with magic, and Allah negated that.

﴿upon the two angels﴾: The reading of the majority is with a fatha on the *lam*, and the apparent meaning is that they are two of the angels. The discussion of the angel has already preceded in His words ﴿And when We said to the angels﴾ [al-Baqarah: 34]. It has been said that they are Gabriel and Michael, as we mentioned in this last view. It has been said that they are two other angels, namely Harut and Marut. It has been said that they are two other angels, and the grammatical analysis of Harut and Marut according to these views will come, God willing. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali, al-Dahhak and Ibn Abza read *al-malakayni* with a kasra on the *lam*. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are two magicians who were in Babylon, because the angels do not teach people magic. Al-Hasan said: they are two non-Arab men of Babylon of Iraq. Abu al-Aswad said: they are Harut and Marut, which is consistent with the view of al-Hasan. Ibn Abza said: they are Dawud and Sulayman, upon our Prophet and upon both of them be blessings and peace. It has been said: they are two devils. So on the view of Ibn Abza, *ma* is a negative particle, and on the other views in this reading, *ma* is a relative pronoun. The meaning of "sending down" here is the casting into their hearts.

The exegetes have mentioned, regarding the reading of those who read *al-malakayni* with a fatha on the *lam*, many stories. They include that the angels marvelled at the children of Adam for their disobedience to what Allah had commanded, and that Allah rebuked them by saying: choose two angels to descend to the earth. So they chose Harut and Marut, and Allah placed desire in them. They judged between people, and they were tempted by a woman called in Arabic al-Zuhra, and in Persian Mid-dakht. They sought her, but she refused unless they worshipped an idol, drank wine and killed. They feared for their affair, so they taught her what she could ascend to the sky by and what she could descend by. She ascended and forgot what she could descend by, and so she was transformed (into a star). They also interceded with Idris before Allah, and He gave them the choice between the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter. They chose the punishment of this world, so they are in Babylon, being punished. They differed about the manner of their punishment. None of this is sound. The angels are infallible: ﴿they do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6]; ﴿they do not disdain His worship, nor do they tire﴾ [al-Anbiya': 19]; ﴿they glorify Him night and day, and do not slacken﴾ [al-Anbiya': 20]. It is not sound that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cursed al-Zuhra, nor Ibn 'Umar. It has been said that the cause of sending down the two angels was that sorcerers had multiplied in that era, claimed prophethood, and challenged people with magic. So the two came to teach people magic, so that they might be able to counter magic, and so that the falsehood of their claim to prophethood would become clear. Or because miracle and magic are two distinct realities, and confusion arises between them. So they came to clarify the two realities. Or because the magic which brings about separation between the enemies of Allah and His friends was permissible, or even recommended, so they were sent for that purpose, and then the people used it to separate the friends of Allah. Or because the jinn possessed among them kinds of magic that humans could not match, so the two were sent down with it for the purpose of counter-argument. It has been said: they were sent down upon Idris, because angels cannot be messengers to all of mankind, and there must be a messenger from among humans.

﴿at Babylon﴾: Ibn Mas'ud said: it is in the outskirts of Kufa. Qatadah said: it lies between Nasibin and Ras al-'Ayn. It has been said: it is the mountain of Damawand. It has been said: it is in the west. It has been said: it is in an unknown land, in which Harut and Marut are. It was named Babylon. Al-Khalil said: it is because of the confusion (*tabalbul*) of tongues, when God willed to divide their languages. A wind came and gathered the people to Babylon, and no one understood what the other said. Then the wind scattered them throughout the lands. It has been said: it is because of the confusion of tongues there when the palace of Nimrod fell.

﴿Harut and Marut﴾: The majority read them with a fatha on the *ta'*, and they are in apposition (*badal*, substitution) for the two angels. The fatha is the sign of the genitive because they are not declined, on the basis that we say they are two proper names for them. It has been said that they are in apposition to "the people," so the fatha is the sign of the accusative, and Harut and Marut are not names for the two angels. It has been said that they are two tribes of devils. On this view they are in apposition to the devils, and the fatha is the sign of the accusative, according to the reading of one who puts "the devils" in the accusative. As for one who puts "the devils" in the nominative, their accusative is by way of dispraise, as if he said: I dispraise Harut and Marut, meaning these two tribes, as the poet said:

*"I contend with Awf, I seek no other, / faces of apes seeking whom they deceive."*

This is on the reading of *al-malakayni* with a fatha on the *lam*. As for one who reads it with a kasra, they are in apposition to "the two angels," unless the two are interpreted as Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them both. Then Harut and Marut are not in apposition to them, but they are connected to the devils on the two aspects we mentioned concerning the nominative and accusative of "the devils." Al-Hasan and al-Zuhri read "Harut and Marut" with a damma, so they may be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are Harut and Marut, if they are two angels. It is also permissible that they be in apposition to the first or the second "devils," on the reading of one who puts it in the nominative, if they are two devils. The discussion of Harut and Marut has already preceded, and that they are non-Arabic names. Some claimed that they derive from *al-hurt* and *al-mart*, which means breaking. But this statement is wrong, as evidenced by their being prevented from declension. Had they been as he claimed, they would have been declined, just as "jamus" (buffalo) is declined when you name someone with it. Babylon was singled out for the sending down because it was the land with the most magic.

﴿And they do not teach anyone﴾: The majority read it with a shadda, from *'allama*, in its original sense of teaching. A group said: here it has the meaning of *yu'allimani* (they teach), and the doubling and the hamza have the same meaning, so it belongs to the category of informing. This is supported by the reading of Talhah ibn Musarrif. *Wa ma yu'allimani* (from *a'lama*): he said, because the two angels only came down to teach magic and to forbid it. The pronoun in *yu'allimani* refers to the two angels, that is, "and the two angels do not teach." This is also the reading of Ubayy, that is, by making the subject explicit rather than implicit. It has been said that it refers to Harut and Marut. On the first view it refers to the substituted noun, and on the second view to the substitute. *Min* is extra, to emphasise the comprehensiveness of the category, because *ahad* (anyone) is among the words used for comprehensiveness in general negation, so it is added here to emphasise that. This differs from your saying "no man stood," where *min* is added for the comprehensiveness of the category. The condition for its addition here exists according to the majority of the Basran grammarians, because they stipulated that a noun indefinite must follow it and that it be preceded by a non-affirmative context. I have thoroughly discussed the addition of *min* in my book *Manhaj al-Salik*. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that *ahad* here has the same meaning, but the first is more apparent.

﴿until they say﴾: Here *hatta* is a particle of limit (*harf ghayah*, a particle marking an endpoint). The meaning is the negation of their teaching or informing, depending on the two views regarding *yu'allimani*, until they say: ﴿We are only a trial﴾. Abu al-Baqa' said: *hatta* here means *illa an* (except that). This is a meaning of *hatta* which I know of no earlier scholar having mentioned. Ibn Malik mentioned it in *al-Tashil* and cited for it in another work:

*"Generosity is not the surplus of giving, / until you give, while what you have is little."*

He said: he means "except that you give." And *ma* in *innama* is a particle that prevents *inna* from governing, so it becomes one of the particles of the beginning of a sentence. Some grammarians have permitted the governing of *inna* despite the presence of *ma*, as in: *innama Zayd qa'im* (Zayd is only standing).
