﴿We are only a trial﴾: that is, a test and an examination.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 102 (part 3 of 4):

﴿فَلا تَكْفُرْ﴾: ʿAli (raḍiya Allahu ʿanhu) said: "They were teaching it as a warning, not as a call to it. It was as if they were saying: Do not do such-and-such, just as if someone asked about the description of adultery or murder and was told its description so that he might avoid it." So the meaning of yuʿallimān is yuʿlimān (they inform). Al-Zamakhshari said: "Fa-la takfur": do not learn it believing it to be true, lest you disbelieve. Al-Mahdawi related that their saying ﴿innamā naḥnu fitnatun fa-la takfur﴾ was mockery, because they said it only to one whose misguidance they had already confirmed. Al-Mahdawi also said in al-Muntakhab: their saying ﴿innamā naḥnu fitnatun﴾ is an emphasis on accepting the law and holding fast to it, so one group complied and another opposed it. It was also said: "fa-la takfur" means: do not use it for what you have been forbidden, but when you learn of it, be on guard lest a sorcerer's deception take effect on you. It was also said: "fa-la tafʿalhu" means: do not practise it in order to act upon it. This is according to the view of those who say that learning it is permissible but acting upon it is disbelief. It was also said: "fa-la takfur" means do not disbelieve by teaching sorcery, and this is according to the view of those who say that learning it is disbelief. It was also said: "fa-la takfur" means do not disbelieve by [following] us, and this is according to the view that the two angels descended from the sky with sorcery, and that whoever learned it at that time became a disbeliever, while whoever abandoned it remained a believer, as came in the account of the river of Talut. It has already been mentioned what al-Mahdawi related, that their saying "fa-la takfur" was by way of mockery, not by way of advice. As for His saying "ḥattā yaqūlā", it is unrestricted in the saying, and what is minimally achieved is by a single instance. It was said once; it was said seven times; it was said nine times; it was said three times. That requires a sound transmission, and if none is found, it remains conjectural, while what is established is a single instance.

The manner in which that knowledge was received from them differed. Mujahid said: Harut and Marut cannot be reached by anyone, and two devils come to them once a year, learning from them what they use to separate a man from his wife. The apparent view is that Harut and Marut are the ones who directly carry out the teaching, given His saying ﴿wa-mā yuʿallimān﴾. The exegetes have mentioned stories concerning the dialogue that takes place between the two angels and whoever comes to learn from them, and in each of these stories they command him to urinate into an oven. They differed concerning the light that comes out of him: did he see a horseman armored in iron come out of him until he disappeared into the sky? Or a light that emerged from ashes, shining until it entered the sky? Or a bird that came out from between his garments and flew toward the sky? They explained that departing thing as being faith. All of this is something that is not sound in any way at all, so we have summarized some of it, though it is not sound, so that our book is not left empty of what they mentioned.

﴿fa-yataʿallamūna﴾: this was said by al-Farraʾ and preferred by al-Zajjaj, and it is conjoined to something indicated by the beginning of the speech, as if he said: "fa-yaʾbawna fa-yataʿallamūna" (so they refuse, and so they learn). Al-Farra' also said: it is conjoined to ﴿yuʿallimūna al-nās al-siḥr﴾, ﴿fa-yataʿallamūna minhumā﴾. Al-Zajjaj rejected this because of the plural form in yuʿallimūna, while he said "minhumā" (from the two). Abu ʿAli and others permitted it, since there is no obstacle to conjoining fa-yataʿallamūna to yuʿallimūna, even if the teaching is from the two angels alone, and the pronoun in minhumā refers back to them, because His saying fa-yataʿallamūna minhumā came only after mention of the two angels. Sibawayh said: it is conjoined to kafarū. He said: fa-yataʿallamūna is marfūʿ because He did not report of the two angels that they said "do not disbelieve", so that they [the people] learn [it], making their disbelief a cause for others' learning; rather it is conjoined to kafarū, fa-yataʿallamūna. Sibawayh means: fa-yataʿallamūna is not an answer to His saying fa-la takfur, so that it would be put in the subjunctive as in ﴿wayλkum lā taftarū ʿalā Allāhi kadhiban fa-yushḥitakum bi-ʿadhāb﴾ [Ta-Ha: 61], because the disbelief of the one forbidden to disbelieve in the verse is not a cause for the learning of the one who learns. And kafarū is in the position of a verb in the nominative, so a nominative is conjoined to it. There is no basis for the objection of those who objected to conjoining it to kafarū or to yuʿallimūna, on the grounds that this involves an implied reference to the two angels. It was said: He mentioned them for the sake of the sense: "But the devils disbelieved, teaching people sorcery, and [people] learn from them", since His saying fa-yataʿallamūna minhumā came only after mention of the two angels, as already stated. It has been transmitted from Sibawayh that His saying fa-yataʿallamūna is by implicit "hum", meaning fa-hum yataʿallamūna (so they learn), so that it is an independent sentence conjoined to what precedes it as conjunction of sentences. According to these views, the pronoun in fa-yataʿallamūna refers to the people. It is also permissible that fa-yataʿallamūna be conjoined to yuʿallimān, with the pronoun in fa-yataʿallamūna referring to someone, and it is put in the plural by consideration of meaning, as He, exalted, said: ﴿fa-mā minkum min aḥadin ʿanhu ḥājizīn﴾ [al-Haqqa: 47]. Although this conjunction is to a negated verb, that negated thing is affirmative in meaning, because its meaning is that the two teach each one, when they say to him: "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve." Al-Zajjaj mentioned this view. Al-Zajjaj also said: the better view is that it is conjoined to yuʿallimān, fa-yataʿallamūna, and the mention of yuʿallimān is dispensed with, owing to the indication in the speech. Abu ʿAli said: there is no basis for al-Zajjaj's saying that mention of yuʿallimān is dispensed with, because it is present in the text. End of Abu ʿAli's words; and this is speech containing sophistry, because al-Zajjaj did not intend that fa-yataʿallamūna is conjoined to yuʿallimān which is preceded by the negating mā in His saying "wa-mā yuʿallimān", so that yuʿallimān would be present in the text; rather he meant that yuʿallimān is an implied affirmative, not negated. This which al-Zajjaj supposed is not present in the text. Abu ʿAli's desire to refute al-Zajjaj and correct him led him to this sophistry, for he was fond of that. The enmity between them has a cause that people have mentioned. End of what we have found people saying about this conjunction, most of which is the words of al-Mahdawi, because he is the one who expounded the discussion at length. What is summed up regarding this conjunction is that it is conjoined to an omitted element, estimated as fa-yaʾbawna fa-yataʿallamūna, or yuʿallimān fa-yataʿallamūna, that is, to an affirmative; or yataʿallamūna is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning fa-hum yataʿallamūna, conjoining a nominal sentence to a verbal one; or conjoined to yuʿallimūna al-nās; or conjoined to kafarū; or conjoined to the negated yuʿallimān, because it is affirmative in meaning. These are six views, the nearest of them to the wording being this last view.

﴿minhumā﴾: The pronoun in the apparent sense refers to the two angels, that is, fa-yataʿallamūna min al-malakayn (they learn from the two angels), whether al-lām is read with fatha or kasra. It was said: it refers to the sorcery, and to what was sent down upon the two angels. It was also said: it refers to the trial and the disbelief, which is a verbal noun understood from His saying fa-la takfur; this is the view of Abu Muslim, and the estimate according to him is: fa-yataʿallamūna min al-fitnah wa-al-kufr miqdāra mā yufarriqūna bihi bayna al-mar' wa-zawjihi (they learn from the trial and disbelief the amount with which they separate a man from his wife).

﴿mā yufarriqūna bihi﴾: mā is a relative pronoun. It is permitted that it be an indefinite qualified noun, but it is not permitted that it be a verbal (ḥarf maṣdariyya) particle, because of the return of the pronoun to it. The verbal particle is not referred back to by a pronoun, since according to the majority it is a particle; and what is separated by it is sorcery. By separation is meant the separation of affection and love, such that enmity and hatred occur and they part; or separation of religion, such that when one learns it he disbelieves and becomes an apostate, and that thereby separates the two.

﴿bayna al-mar'﴾: the reading of the majority is with fatha on the mīm, sukūn on the rāʾ, and hamza. Al-Hasan, al-Zuhri and Qatada read al-mar without hamza, lightened. Ibn Abi Ishaq read al-mur' with ḍamma on the mīm and hamza. Al-Ashhab al-ʿUqayli read al-mir' with kasra on the mīm and hamza, and this was transmitted from al-Hasan. Al-Zuhri also read al-marr with fatha on the mīm, dropping the hamza and doubling the rāʾ. As for fatha, kasra and ḍamma on the mīm, these are dialectal forms. As for al-mar with kasra on the rāʾ, its explanation is that he transferred the vowel of the hamza to the rāʾ and dropped the hamza; as for doubling it after dropping, its explanation is that he intended pausal form and doubled it, as was transmitted from ʿAsim: mustaṭarr with doubled rāʾ in pause, then the connected reading was treated like the pause, so he kept it doubled in it.

﴿wa-zawjihi﴾: Its apparent sense is that he means by it the man's wife. It was said that zawj here means relatives and companions, who are the kind suitable to a person; and from this: ﴿min kulli zawjin bahīj﴾ [al-Hajj: 5], ﴿uḥshurū alladhīna ẓalamū wa-azwājahum﴾ [al-Saffat: 22].

﴿wa-mā hum bi-ḍārrīna bihi﴾: The pronoun in hum refers back to the sorcerers, to whom the pronoun of fa-yataʿallamūna referred. It was also said: it refers to the Jews, to whom the pronoun of wa-ittabaʿū referred. It was also said: it refers to the devils. As for bi-ḍārrīna, it is in the accusative position if mā is Ḥijāzī, or in the nominative position if mā is Tamīmī. The pronoun in bihi refers back to what is in His saying "mā yufarriqūna". The majority read with the nūn kept in bi-ḍārrīna. Al-Aʿmash read with it dropped, and this was explained on two grounds: first, that it was dropped for lightening, even though the active participle is in the relative clause of the alif-lām; second, that its dropping is due to the annexation to aḥad, with a separation between the annexed and annexed-to by the prepositional phrase bihi, as in the verse:

"They two are brothers in war to one who has no brother"

and as in the verse:

"As the book is inscribed by the hand of a Jewish man one day"

This is al-Zamakhshari's preference. Then this was challenged, because aḥad is genitive by min, so how can it be held that it is genitive by annexation? He said: "If you say, how is it annexed to aḥad when it is genitive by min?" I say: the preposition was made part of the genitive noun. End of quote. This explanation is not good, because separation between the annexed and annexed-to by an adverb or prepositional phrase is among the poetic necessities, and worse than that is that there is no annexed-to at all, since it is occupied by a governing genitive particle, so that it is the particle that governs it, not the annexation. As for making the preposition part of the genitive noun, this is nothing, since it governs it, and part of a thing does not govern the thing. The first explanation is better, because it has a parallel in Arabic verse and prose. From prose is the Arab saying: qaṭāqaṭā bayḍuki thintā wa-bayḍī mi'tā (qaṭāqaṭā, your eggs are two and my eggs are two hundred), meaning: thintāni wa-mi'tāni.

﴿min aḥad﴾: min is extra, and aḥad is the object of ḍārrīn. Min may be inserted into the object, though the familiar practice is its insertion into the object which is the operand of the subject directly preceded by the negative particle, such as: mā ḍaraba min rajul and mā ḍaraba Zayd min rajul. Here the nominal clause without the verb and subject was treated as the verbal clause with verb and subject, because the meaning is: wa-mā yaḍurrūna min aḥad (and they do not harm anyone).

﴿illā bi-idhni Allāh﴾: an exceptive phrase emptied from the states (mustathnā mufarraghun min al-aḥwāl). It is possible that it is a state of the pronoun subject in bi-ḍārrīn; it is possible that it is a state of the object min aḥad; it is possible that it is a state of bihi, meaning the sorcery by which separation is made; it is possible that it is a state of the harm, the definite verbal noun omitted. The idhn here explains the aspects mentioned when speaking of the vocabulary. Al-Hasan said: idhn here is letting the bewitched person be subject to the harm of sorcery. Al-Asamm said: it is knowledge. Others said: it is creation, and it is attributed to His permission as in His saying "Be, and it is" [al-Baqara: 117]. It was said: it is command. It was said: idhn is literally that, and this was deemed unlikely, because God does not command sorcery, and because He condemned them for it. The meaning of command in it was interpreted as the separation being the becoming of a disbeliever, for this is a legal ruling, and that can only occur by God's command. In this sentence there is evidence that what they learn has an effect and harm, but that harm occurs only by God's permission, because He may bring about something in him, or may not.

﴿And they learn what harms them and does not benefit them.﴾ Having mentioned that harm comes to those who cause separation between a man and his wife through it, he also mentions that its harm is not confined to those against whom it is practised, but also harms the one who learns it. And since affirming that a thing causes harm does not negate benefit, because a thing may cause both harm and benefit, he negated benefit from it altogether, using the particle *lā*, because it negates the present and the future. The apparent reading is that ﴿and does not benefit them﴾ is conjoined to ﴿harms them﴾, and both verbs are the relative clause (ṣilah) of *mā*, so it has no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis). Some permitted that *lā yanfaʿuhum* be taken with an implied *huwa* (he), meaning "and he does not benefit them", so that it would be in the place of a nominative, and the *wāw* would be for the circumstantial (ḥāl), making it a circumstantial clause. This is weak. It has been said that the harm and the lack of benefit are specific to the Hereafter. It has been said that it applies both in this world and the Hereafter: if learning it is unlawful, it leads to acting upon it, to punishment for it if one is caught, and to the fact that what one takes for it is unlawful; this is in this world. As for the Hereafter, it is for the punishment that results from it.

﴿And they certainly knew﴾: The pronoun refers, it has been said, to the Jews who were in the time of Solomon, peace be upon him, and who were present at the extraction of the devils' magic and its burial, or at Solomon's taking the magic and burying it beneath his throne. When they extracted it after his death, they said: "By God, this is not from Solomon's work or from his treasures." It has been said that it refers to those Jews present in the presence of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It has been said that it refers to all the Jews, meaning they knew this in the Torah. It has been said that it refers to the scholars of the Jews. It has been said that it refers to the devils. It has been said that it refers to the two angels, because they used to say to whoever learned magic: "So do not disbelieve," so they knew that he had no portion in the Hereafter. The plural pronoun was used according to the view of the one who holds this. As for *ʿalima* (knew) here, it may be the one transitive to two objects, and it has been suspended from the clause; it may also be the one transitive to a single object, and it has likewise been suspended, as in *ʿarafta* (you knew). The difference between these two interpretations appears in conjunction with its place (of i'rab). The *lām* in ﴿for whoever purchased it﴾ is the *lām* of the beginning (lām al-ibtidāʾ), and it is what prevents *ʿalima* from governing, and it is one of the causes that require suspension. They permitted its omission, and it remains preventing action. On this they cited:

*Indeed I have found the foundation of character to be good manners*

meaning *li-mala'ik al-shīmah* (for the foundation of character). *Man* here is a relative pronoun, in the nominative as subject (mubtadaʾ). The clause ﴿he has no portion in the Hereafter﴾ is in the place of the predicate (khabar). The *lām* in *laqad* is for oath. This is the view of Sibawayh and most grammarians. The clause ﴿And they certainly knew﴾ is the one sworn upon, the implied meaning being: "By God, they certainly knew." The second clause, in his view, is not sworn upon. Al-Farrāʾ permitted that both clauses be sworn upon, and that *man* be a conditional particle, and al-Ḥawfī and Abu al-Baqāʾ followed him in this. Abu al-Baqāʾ said: The *lām* in ﴿for whoever purchased it﴾ is the one with which the oath is introduced, like ﴿if you do not desist﴾ [Maryam: 46], and *man* is in the place of the nominative as subject, and it is the condition, and the answer of the oath is ﴿he has no portion in the Hereafter﴾. End of his words. So *ishtarāhu* in the first view is a relative clause, and in this view it is the predicate of *man*; in that case the answer of the condition is omitted, indicated by the answer of the oath, because an oath and a condition came together, and neither was preceded by something with a predicate, so the answer belongs to the earlier one, which is the oath; that is why the verb of the condition is in the past form in wording. This is the statement and clarification of this view. In both views, *li-man ishtarāhu* is in the place of the accusative, governed by *yaʿlamūna* (they know). It has been reported from al-Zajjāj that he rejected the view of those who said *man* is a conditional, and said: "This is not a place of condition." Nothing has been reported from him explaining why it is not a place of condition. I think the obstacle to this is that the verb following *man* is past in wording and meaning, because the purchasing has already occurred, and making it a condition is not valid, because when the verb of the condition is past in wording, it must be future in meaning. Since that is the case, it is not a place of condition. The pronoun object in *ishtarāhu* refers to the magic, or to disbelief, or to their Book which they sold for magic, or to the Qur'an, because they exchanged it for books of magic; these are four views. *Khalāq* means portion, said Mujāhid; or religion, said al-Ḥasan; or sustenance/stability, said Ibn ʿAbbās; or deliverance, or destiny, said Qatādah; five views.

﴿And wretched is what they sold their souls for﴾: The discussion of *biʾsa* (wretched) and of the *mā* that follows it has already been given, and its meaning is: blame for what they sold their souls for. The pronoun in *bihi* refers to the magic or to disbelief. The thing being censured is omitted, its implied form being the best of the aspects mentioned earlier regarding *biʾsa mā* (wretched is what): the magic or disbelief. The pronoun in *sharaw* (they sold) and *yaʿlamūna* (they know) refers by agreement to the Jews. So whenever the pronoun in ﴿And they certainly knew﴾ is interpreted as referring to the devils, or to the Jews who were in the presence of Solomon and in his time, or to the two angels with a *fatḥa* on the *lām* or with a *kasra*, there is no difficulty in the differing subjects of the knowing. If the subject is unified, the second knowing is interpreted as intellect, because knowledge is its fruit; since the root was removed, its fruit was also removed. Or it is interpreted as action, because it is the fruit of knowledge; since the fruit was removed, what arises from it is also negated. Or the object of the knowing is interpreted, namely the omitted one, meaning: they knew its harm in the Hereafter, but did not know its benefit in this world; or they knew the negation of reward, but did not know the deserving of punishment. The answer of *law* (if) is omitted, its implied form being:

﴿If only they had known﴾. This is censured, since they sold their souls.

﴿ولَوْ أنَّهم آمَنُوا واتَّقَوْا﴾: The discussion of *law* (لَوْ, a conditional particle) and its categories has already been given. Here it is a particle indicating that something would have occurred because something else would have occurred. The discussion of its response (jawab) will come, God willing. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also possible that His saying ﴿ولَوْ أنَّهم آمَنُوا واتَّقَوْا﴾ is an expression of wishing for their faith, figuratively referring to God's will for their faith and their choosing it, as if it were said: 'Would that they had believed.' Then the sentence begins: ﴿لَمَثُوبَةٌ مِن عِنْدِ اللَّهِ خَيْرٌ﴾." End of quotation. According to this, the response would not be obligatory, because *law* may take a response with *fa'* when it is used for wishing, just as *layta* (would that) does. However, al-Zamakhshari slipped into his statement here, and his Mu'tazili doctrine embarrasses him, since he made the wish a metaphor for God's will. The meaning would then be: God willed their faith, but His will was not fulfilled. This is exactly the doctrine of the Mu'tazila, and of the group who named themselves "the Justice people" ('Adliyya):

؎ They said: He wills, yet His will does not come to pass. They deviated, but from the path of knowledge.

And *annahum amanu* (أنَّهم آمَنُوا) is construed as a verbal noun (maṣdar), as if it were said: "if their faith" (law imanuhum), and it is in the nominative case. Sibawayh said it is nominative as a subject of an inchoative sentence (mubtada'), meaning: "if their faith is established." Al-Mubarrad said it is nominative as an agent (fa'il), meaning: "if their faith had occurred." In each of the two views there is an omission of the predicate and retention of the subject. The preference between the two views is mentioned in the science of grammar (naḥw). The pronoun in *annahum* refers either to the Jews or to those who teach sorcery; there are two opinions. *Al-iman* and *al-taqwa*: *al-iman* is complete faith, and *al-taqwa* is that which encompasses its kinds (taqwa, God-consciousness); or *al-iman* is faith in Muhammad and in what he brought, and *taqwa* is avoidance of disbelief and sorcery. These are two closely related opinions.

﴿لَمَثُوبَةٌ﴾: the *lam* is the *lam* of inception (lam al-ibtida'), not the *lam* that falls in the response of *law*. The response of *law* is omitted because the meaning is understood, i.e. "they would have been rewarded." Then it begins as an informative, resumptive statement, not as a conditional linked to their faith and God-consciousness and consequent upon them. This is the view of al-Akhfash, namely that the response is omitted. It was also said that the *lam* is the one that falls in the response of *law*, and the response is the phrase ﴿لَمَثُوبَةٌ﴾, i.e. the nominal sentence. The first is the preference of al-Raghib, and the second is the preference of al-Zamakhshari, who said: "The nominal sentence was preferred over the verbal one in the response because it indicates the establishment and permanence of the reward, just as one turns from the accusative to the nominative in ﴿سَلامٌ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ [al-An'am 6:54] for this reason." End of his words. But his preferred view is not accepted, because it is not known in the language of the Arabs for an inceptive sentence to fall as a response to *law*; this has only occurred in what is disputed in its interpretation. Universal rules are not established on the basis of what is merely possible. And it is not like *salamun 'alaykum*, because the nominative *salamun 'alaykum* is established in the language of the Arabs. Those who permitted it argued that *mathūba* is a verbal noun that can refer to the past and the future, so it is suitable for this, insofar as it can refer to the past. We have discussed this issue in our book *al-Takmil*, more fully than this. The majority read *lamathūbatun* with a *ḍamma* on the *tha'*, like *al-mashūra*. Qatada, Abu al-Sammal and Abdullah ibn Buraydah read it with a sukun on the *tha'*, like *mashwura*. The meaning of His saying *lamathūba* is "indeed a reward," and it is the recompense and the wage for faith and God-consciousness, with all kinds of goodness. It was also said: *lamathūba*: "indeed a return to God is better."

﴿مِن عِنْدِ اللَّهِ﴾: this prepositional phrase is in the position of an attribute, i.e. "existing from God." This attribute is what permits beginning with an indefinite noun. Describing the reward as coming from God glorifies and magnifies it, and it fits the context of faith and God-consciousness. For this reason the meaning is: the One in whom you believed and whose prohibitions you guarded is the One from whom your reward for that comes; He is the one who guarantees it for you. The indefiniteness here is used because the meaning is "some reward."

*Qalīluka lā yuqālu lahu qalīl*
(Your little is not called little.)

﴿خَيْرٌ﴾ is the predicate of His saying *lamathūba*. *Khayr* here is not the elative (af'al al-tafḍīl), but it is for preference (tafḍīl) and not for superiority (al-afḍaliyya). It is like His saying: ﴿أفَمَن يُلْقى في النّارِ خَيْرٌ﴾ [Fuṣṣilat 41:40], and ﴿وخَيْرٌ عُقْبًا﴾ [al-Kahf 18:44].

*Fa-sharruhumā li-khayrikumā al-fidā'*
(So your evil is the ransom for your good.)

﴿لَوْ كانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾: the response of *law* is omitted. The estimate: "If they knew, the attaining of the reward would have been better," meaning the cause of the reward, which is faith and God-consciousness. For this reason some estimated it as "they would have believed," because whoever has knowledge and insight does not have the truth hidden from him, so he hastens to follow it, and the falsehood is not hidden from him, so he strives to avoid it. The object of *ya'lamūn* is omitted for brevity, so the meaning is: "If they were among those possessing knowledge." Or it is omitted for abridgement, and some estimated it as: "If they knew the preference in that," and some estimated it as: "If they knew that what is with God is better and more lasting." It was also said: knowledge here is a metaphor for action, i.e. "if they had known by their knowledge." Since the fruit of knowledge, which is action, is absent, knowledge is made here a metaphor for action, i.e. "if they had acted by their knowledge." And since the fruit of knowledge, which is action, is absent, knowledge is treated as absent.

These noble verses contain what the Jews had of corrupt inner dispositions, lack of success, lack of submissiveness toward the prophets of God, and their taking enmity towards them. This reached the point of their being hostile to one who is not harmed by their enmity, and who should not be opposed, because he is the envoy between God and His creation: Gabriel. He brought the Qur'an, which confirms their scripture and contains guidance and good tidings for whoever believes in it, so it was fitting to hasten to his allegiance and love. Then He followed that by saying that whoever is an enemy to God, i.e. opposes His command, His angels and His messengers, i.e. hates them, then God is his enemy, i.e. treats him in a way that suits his foul deed. Then He turned to His Messenger with direct address, and informed him that He had sent down to him clear signs, and that because of their clarity, none disbelieves in them except a rebel in his wickedness. Then He began to console him, that the custom of these people is breaking their covenants, so do not care about one whose way is this, and that they followed this same way with you when you came to them from God with the message, so they cast His Book behind their backs, to the point that they no longer looked into it, nor paid attention to what it contained of the good news about you and of obligating them to follow you, as though they had never looked at the Book, nor had any knowledge of you from it. Then He mentioned among their disgraces that they abandoned the Book of God and followed what the devils recited of the books of sorcery in the time of Solomon. Then He exonerated His prophet Solomon from disbelief, and that the devils were the ones who disbelieved. Then He digressed into the account of Harut and Marut, and that they do not teach anyone until they advise him, that they were made a trial and a test, and that because of their great sincerity they forbid disbelief. Then He mentioned that the most they teach is causing separation between a man and his wife. Then He mentioned that the harm of this does not occur except by God's permission, because He is the one who harms and benefits. Then He established that what they learn is harmful to its practitioner and learner. Then He informed that they had known the reality of the harm, and that whoever practices it has no share in the Hereafter. Then He emphasized the condemnation of what they sold their souls for, since what they received in exchange ends in loss.

Then He concluded all this with what they would have obtained had they followed it, namely faith and God-consciousness: they would have received from God an abundant reward for that, and that all the sins they committed and the crimes they earned would be effaced by the trailing hem of faith, and bad deeds would be replaced by beautiful goodness. Since the preceding verses contain threat, such as His saying: ﴿فَإنَّ اللَّهَ عَدُوٌّ لِلْكافِرِينَ﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:98] ("God is an enemy to the disbelievers"), and His saying: ﴿وما يَكْفُرُ بِها إلّا الفاسِقُونَ﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:99] ("None disbelieve in them except the defiantly wicked"), and the mention of breaking covenants, breaking the Book of God, following devils, learning what harms and does not benefit, and informing about them that they knew they had no share in the Hereafter, He followed this with a verse containing the beautiful promise for whoever believes and is God-conscious. Thus these verses combined threat and promise, encouragement and warning, admonition and good tidings. Within them is digression from one matter to another, and information about the unseen after another unseen, arranged harmoniously like pearls in their strings, clear like stars in the rising of their auspicious positions, making known the truthfulness of the one who brought them, who did not read books, nor studied, nor travelled, nor associated with rabbis, nor practised: ﴿وما يَنْطِقُ عَنِ الهَوى إنْ هو إلّا وحْيٌ يُوحى عَلَّمَهُ شَدِيدُ القُوى﴾ [al-Najm 53:3–5] ("Nor does he speak from desire. It is not but a revelation revealed; taught to him by one mighty in power"). May God bless him (ﷺ) and convey the purest greeting to him.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 104 (part 1 of 2):

﴿O you who believe, do not say "Ra'ina" but say "Unzurna" and listen. For the disbelievers there is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book, and the polytheists, do not wish that any good should be sent down to you from your Lord. But Allah singles out for His mercy whom He wills, and Allah is the Possessor of great bounty.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 105] ﴿Whatever sign We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring a better one than it or its like. Do you not know that Allah is capable of everything?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 106] ﴿Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and that you have, besides Allah, no protector and no helper?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 107] ﴿Or do you wish to question your Messenger as Musa was questioned before? Whoever exchanges disbelief for faith has strayed from the right way.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 108] ﴿Many of the People of the Book wish that they could turn you back to disbelief after your faith, out of envy from themselves, after the truth has become clear to them. So pardon and overlook until Allah brings His command. Indeed Allah is capable of everything.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 109] ﴿And establish the prayer and give zakat. Whatever good you send forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah. Indeed Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 110] ﴿And they say: "None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians." Those are their wishful thoughts. Say: "Produce your proof, if you are truthful."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111] ﴿Rather, whoever submits his face to Allah while being a doer of good will have his reward with his Lord, and no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 112] ﴿And the Jews say: "The Christians are not upon anything," and the Christians say: "The Jews are not upon anything," while they recite the Book. Likewise said those who have no knowledge, the like of their words. So Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that about which they used to differ.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 113].

[p. 337] Al-ri'aya (care, attention) and al-mura'a: looking into the interests of a person and managing his affairs. Al-ru'una and al-ra'an: ignorance and foolishness. Dhu: it has the meaning of "possessor of" (ṣāḥib); it is dualized, pluralized and feminized, and it must be followed by an annexed noun (iḍāfa) to an apparent common noun. Regarding its annexation to a pronoun of a common noun there is a difference of opinion; the well-known view is prohibition, and there is no disagreement that it is attested, but whoever prohibits it restricts it to necessity (ḍarūra, poetic license). Its annexation to a proper noun that is by origin associated with it, or to one that is not originally associated with it, is attested. From the first category are the sayings: Dhu Yazan, Dhu Jadan, Dhu Ru'ayn, Dhu al-Kala'. In these cases the annexation is obligatory. From the second category are the sayings: in Tabuk, 'Amr and Qatari: Dhu Tabuk, Dhu 'Amr, Dhu Qatari. The most common practice is that the word dhu is not taken into account, and the noun is pronounced bare without dhu. What came of its annexation to the pronoun of a proper noun, or to the pronoun of an addressee, is not analogically extended, such as the saying: "O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad and upon those of his" (dhawiyhi), and the poet's verse:

"Indeed we hope for a quick favor from you, like what we hoped for in the past from your excellent kin (dhawika)."

The school of Sibawayh holds that its measure is faʿal, with the ʿayn vowelled with a fatha; the school of al-Khalil holds that its measure is faʿl, with the ʿayn sukun. They agreed that in its broken plural it takes the pattern afʿāl. They said: adhwāʾ. Dhu is among the Six Nouns (al-asmāʾ al-sitta), which in the nominative take waw, in the accusative take alif, and in the genitive take ya. The i'rab (grammatical inflection) of dhu in this manner is obligatory, unlike the other of those nouns, so that is by way of permissibility. Concerning what these nouns are inflected by, there are ten doctrines mentioned in grammar. Dhu has also come as a relative pronoun (mawsula), and that is in the dialect of Tayy, and it has its own rules, but it does not occur in the Qur'an.

Al-naskh (abrogation): the removal of a thing without a replacement following it, as in: "the sun abrogated the shade" (nasakhat al-shams al-zill), and "the wind abrogated the trace" (nasakhat al-rih al-athar). Or the transfer of a thing without removal, as in: "I copied the book" (nasakhtu al-kitab), when you transfer what is in it to another place. Al-nasi'a: postponement; nasa'a yan'a'u, and nasa'a comes with the meaning of "he let the thing pass." The poet said:

"Strong like the boards of the mill-stone, I let her pass over a broad road, as if its back were the back of a Burjud (a kind of camel)."

Al-wali: fa'il in the intensive form, from waliya al-shay': he bordered it and clung to it. Al-hasad (envy): wishing for the removal of a blessing from a person; hasada yahsudu hasadan wa hasadah. Al-safh: its meaning is close to that of pardon (al-'afw), and it is turning away from holding someone accountable for a sin, derived from turning the face-side (tawliyat safhat al-wajh) away in aversion. It was also said: it is passing over, from your saying: "I scanned the page" (tasaffahtu al-waraqa), meaning you passed over what was in it. Al-Safuh: it was said that it is among the names of Allah. Al-safuh also means a woman who covers part of her face in aversion. He said:

"She is aloof, and you do not meet her except as a stingy one; whoever tires of this union with her, she too becomes weary."

Tilka: a demonstrative pronoun used for a feminine item at a distance. It is said: talka, tilka (with kasra and ya), and taluka (with fatha and alif), with fatha on the ta and sukun on the lam, and with kasra on the ta and ya after it and kasra on the lam, and with fatha on it and alif after it and kasra on the lam. He said:

"Until it became a stone-mass at al-Judi, and the subsidence of that great flood came."

Hati: its meaning is "bring here." The ha' is original, not a substitute for the hamza of ata (to come), because it transitively governs one object, and because the alif is fixed; for if it were a hamza it would have appeared, since the cause of its substitution, which is the hamza before it, has disappeared. Therefore its measure is not af'al, contrary to whoever claimed that; rather its measure is fa'il, like karam. It is a verb (fi'l), contrary to whoever claimed that it is a verb-noun (ism fi'l), and the proof of its verbhood is the attachment of pronouns to it. And contrary to whoever claimed that it is a sound (sawt) of the same status as ha' in the meaning of "bring," and that was al-Zamakhshari; it is an imperative and its verb is inflected. You say: hati yuhati muhataʾatan. The only part of its verbal forms that has become obsolete is the imperative from it, contrary to whoever claimed that. And ha is not for alerting (tanbih) that entered upon ata, so that the hamza of ata was obligatorily deleted; because the original principle is that there is no deletion, and because the meaning of hati and the meaning of i'ti are different. The meaning of hati is "bring here," and the meaning of i'ti is "come." You say: hati, hati, hatiya, hatu, hatina, and you inflect it like karam.

Al-burhan (proof): evidence for the validity of a claim. It was said: it is derived from al-baraha, which is cutting off, so the nun is an augmentation. It was said: from al-barhana, which is clarification; they said: barhana if he clarified, so the nun is an augmentation because of the absence of fa'lan and the presence of fa'lal. Based on this derivation, the question arises regarding the naming "Burhan": does it take tanwin (is it diptote) or not (is it triptote, i.e., non-diptote)? Al-wajh (the face/aspect): well known; its paucal plural is awjuh, and its plural of multitude is wujuh. So af'ul is analogically applied to the form of a noun whose middle radical is sound, and fu'ul is analogically applied to the form of a noun whose middle radical is not waw.

Al-yahud (the Jews): a known religious community; the ya' is original, so the root of the word is not the root h-w-d from His saying: ﴿hudan aw nasara﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111], because it is confirmed in conjugation as yahdihi. As for hawwadahu, it is from the root h-w-d.

Al-Ustadh Abu 'Ali al-Shalawbin, who was the imam to whom the science of language ended in his time, said: "Yahud has two aspects: one, that it be the plural of Yahudi, so it is indefinite and triptote (masrufa). The second, that it be a proper name for this tribe, so it is diptote (mamnu' al-sarf)." End of his words. According to the first aspect, the definite article alif-lam entered upon it, so they said al-yahud; for if it were a proper name, it would not have taken it. According to the second, the poet said:

"Those are more worthy of praise than Yahud, when you say it one day, you will not be blamed."

Laysa: a past-tense verb, contrary to Abu Bakr ibn Shuqayr and to one of al-Farisi's two opinions, for they claimed it is a negative particle like ma, and its measure is fa'ila with kasra on the ʿayn. Whoever says lusta with damma on the lam, its measure according to him is fu'ula with damma on the ʿayn, and it is a rare pattern in triliteral verbs with a ya' ʿayn; nothing has been heard from it except the saying: hay'a al-rajul, so he is hayyi', if his appearance was good. The rulings of laysa are many and explained in the grammar books. Al-hukm (judgment): separation; from it the judge is called hakim, because he separates between the two litigants. Al-ikhtilaf (disagreement): the opposite of agreement.

* *

﴿O you who believe﴾: this is the first address directed to the believers in this surah, with the vocative that indicates direct attention to them. The first vocative came general: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21]; the second came specific: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember﴾ [al-Baqarah: 122], and they are the great group that comprised both religions, Judaism and Christianity; and the third vocative was for the believers of the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ). So the first vocative was general, in which they were commanded with the foundation of Islam, which is the worship of Allah. The second vocative reminded them of the abundant blessings, they were made to worship through the great obligations, and they were warned of the arrival of grievous retributions. The third vocative: they were taught in it a courtesy from the courtesies of the Shari'ah towards their Prophet, since the worship of Allah, the reminder of blessings, the warning of retributions, and taking admonition from the nations that preceded had already been achieved for them. So nothing remained except what they were commanded with by way of completion, namely the exaltation of the one through whose hands their guidance came. The honoring and address with "O you who believe" is directed to the believers in Madinah. It was said: it may be that it is directed to every believer in his era. It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that wherever this address occurs, the intended meaning is the people of Madinah, and wherever "O mankind" occurs, the intended meaning is the people of Makkah.

﴿Do not say Ra'ina and say Unzurna﴾: it begins with the prohibition because it is among the matters of abstention (al-turuk), so it is easier. Then the command came after it, which is more difficult, because familiarity is achieved before the prohibition. Furthermore, it was not a prohibition against something whose prohibition had preceded; but since the form of the verb of mutual action (mufa'ala) generally indicates participation, the meaning became: let there occur from you a care (ri'an) for us and from us a care for you. This includes what is not hidden in the case of someone who is esteemed. They were forbidden from this expression for this reason, and they were commanded to say: "Unzurna" (look upon us), since it is a verb coming from the Prophet (ﷺ) in which they have no participation with him. The reading of the majority is: (Ra'ina). In the Mushaf of 'Abd Allah and his recitation, and the recitation of Ubayy: Ra'unā, with the verb attributed to the plural pronoun. It was also mentioned that in the Mushaf of 'Abd Allah: Ar'awna. They addressed him with that out of reverence and exaltation, since they placed him in the position of the plural. This prohibition includes a prohibition against everything in which there is equality with the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Layla, Abu Haywa and Ibn Muhaysin recited: Ra'inan with tanwin, making it an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a saying: Ra'inan," and it is according to the pattern of the relative adjective (nisba), like Labin and Tamir. Since saying (qawl) is a cause of reviling (sabb), it was described with ru'un (foolishness). So in this recitation they were forbidden from addressing the Messenger with a word that contains, or implies, something of disparagement from what he deserves of honor, gentleness of speech and courtesy.

It has been mentioned that the cause of the revelation of this verse was that "the Jews used to intend by that, when they addressed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), foolishness." And likewise it was said regarding Ra'unan, that it is fa'ulan from al-ru'una, like 'ashuran. It was said: the Jews had a Hebrew or Syriac word which they used to revile one another, and it was: Ra'ina. When they heard the believers' saying Ra'ina, they borrowed it and addressed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with it, meaning that reviling. So the believers were forbidden from it, and they were commanded with what has its meaning. As for whoever claimed that Ra'ina is a dialect specific to the Ansar, his saying is nothing, because that is preserved in all the language of the Arabs. Likewise is the saying of whoever said that this verse abrogates an act that had been permissible, because the former was not an established legal ruling beforehand. It has been said about its cause of revelation other than that. In sum, as Muhammad ibn Jarir said, it is a word that Allah disliked for His Prophet to be addressed with, just as he (ﷺ) said: "Do not say 'my slave' and 'my female slave'; say 'my young man' and 'my young woman,' and do not call the grape 'the vine'."

Several aspects have been mentioned regarding the prohibition: that its meaning is "listen" (isma') and not "may you not hear" (sami'ta), or that the people of the Hijaz used to say it when they fled (al-mafarr), as said by Qutrub; or that the Jews used to say: Ra'ina, meaning "our shepherd of goats"; or that it is a verb of mutual action and so it implies equality; or its meaning is: attend to our speech and do not neglect it; or because it may be assumed to derive from ru'una (foolishness).

His saying: Unzurna, is the reading of the majority, with a connected hamza, a damma on the zay, from al-nazra (delay/respite), which is postponement, i.e., wait for us and be patient with us, as in the saying of the poet:

"Indeed if you two grant me a respite (tunzirani) for a moment of time, you will benefit me with Umm Jundab."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 104 (part 2 of 2):

Or from "al-nazar" (looking/regarding). It is extended in its usage, so it is transitive without a preposition, whereas its original form is to be transitive with "ila" (to), as the poet said:

"Manifest in beauty and grace, they look (yanzur-na)
As the gazelles look upon the arak trees."

He means: "ila al-arak" (to the arak trees), and its meaning is: "Attend to us with your gaze" (tafaqqadna bi-nazarika).

Mujahid said: its meaning is "make us understand and explain to us." It is interpreted by what is necessarily implied in the original, namely "unzurna" (look at us, i.e., "regard us"), because kindness, patience with the questioner, and a gentle pace with him necessarily result in his understanding. It is said: it is from the looking of insight (nazar al-basira), through reflection and contemplation on what is suitable for the thing being looked into. Its usage is also extended, since its original form is to be transitive with "fi" (in). It may also be by omission of a modifier, i.e., "unzur fi amrina" (consider our affair).

Ibn 'Atiyya said: This is a word free of any defect for honouring the Prophet (ﷺ). In my view the apparent meaning is requesting the looking of the eye combined with contemplation of the situation, and this is the meaning of "raina" (do not say "ra'ina"), so the word was replaced for the believers in order to remove the Jews' exploitation of it. End of quotation.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' (not) — rather, Ubayy and al-A'mash read "anzirna" with a hamza and a kasra on the zay, from "al-in-zar" (granting respite). Its meaning is: "Delay us and give us time until we receive from you." This reading supports the first opinion in the reading of the majority.

"Wa-asma'u" (and listen): that is, listen with acceptance and obedience. It is said: its meaning is "accept." It is said: "Empty your ears so that you need not ask again." It is said: "Listen to what you have been commanded, so that you do not return to it again." He stressed to them the abandonment of that word. It is narrated that Sa'd ibn Mu'adh heard it from them and said: "O enemies of Allah, may the curse of Allah be upon you! By Him in whose hand is my soul, if I hear it from any man of you saying it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), I will surely strike his neck."

"Wa-lil-kafirina 'adhabun alim" (And for the disbelievers is a painful punishment): its apparent meaning is generality, so the Jews are included. It is said: the intended meaning is the Jews, that is, "and for the Jews who treated the Messenger lightly and reviled him." When He first forbade, and then commanded, and commanded listening and urged it, since obedience is implied in it, He began to mention those who opposed His command and disbelieved: "So let those who oppose His command beware lest a trial strike them or a painful punishment strike them" (al-Nur: 63).

"Ma yawaddu alladhina kafaru min ahl al-kitab wa-la al-mushrikin" (Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book nor the polytheists do not wish) (al-Baqara: 105): The commentators mention that the Muslims said to their allies among the Jews: "Believe in Muhammad (ﷺ)." They said: "We would wish that it were better than what we are upon, so that we might follow him." Allah refuted them with His saying: "Those who disbelieve do not wish" (al-Baqara: 105). According to this, the intended meaning of "ahl al-kitab" is those present in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The apparent meaning is generality regarding the People of the Book, who are the Jews and Christians, and regarding the polytheists, who are the polytheists of the Arabs and others. He negated with "ma," because it is for negating the present state; they are engaged in hatred and dislike that anything good should descend upon you. The "min" in His saying "min ahl al-kitab" is partitive, so it is connected to an omitted element, meaning "being from the People of the Book." Whoever affirms that "min" can be explanatory (li-bayan al-jins) says so here, and al-Zamakhshari said this, but our companions do not affirm that it has the explanatory sense.

﴿وَلَا الْمُشْرِكِينَ﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to ﴿مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ﴾ (from the People of the Book).

I saw in a book by Abu Ishaq al-Shirazi, the author of al-Tanbih, a passage refuting the Shi'a and those who share their view that the prescribed method for the feet in ablution (wudu') is wiping (masḥ), on the basis that the conjunction in His saying ﴿وَأَرْجُلَكُمْ﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6] is conjoined to His saying ﴿بِرُءُوسِكُمْ﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6]. In that book, Abu Ishaq gave the reading وأرجلِكم with the genitive (jarr) an explanation: that it is a case of khafḍ 'ala al-jiwar (genitive by proximity), and that its original form is the accusative (naṣb), so it was put in the genitive by attraction to the adjacent word. In the same book he indicated that the Qur'an and the Arabic language both attest to the permissibility of this, and he cited as an example of it His saying in this verse, ﴿وَلَا الْمُشْرِكِينَ﴾, and His saying ﴿لَمْ يَكُنِ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ وَالْمُشْرِكِينَ مُنْفَكِّينَ﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 1], holding that the original form is the nominative, that is, ﴿وَلَا الْمُشْرِكُونَ﴾, conjoined to ﴿الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾. This is the talk of one who falls short in Arabic grammar, who presumes to speak on it without knowledge, and who turns away from carrying the wording on its correct meaning and its eloquent construction.

The particle ﴿لَا﴾ in His saying ﴿وَلَا الْمُشْرِكِينَ﴾ is there for emphasis (li'l-ta'kid), and had this been outside the Qur'an, it would have been permissible to omit it. It does not appear in His saying ﴿لَمْ يَكُنِ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ وَالْمُشْرِكِينَ مُنْفَكِّينَ﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 1] for a reason that will be mentioned there, God willing.

﴿أَنْ يُنَزَّلَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾: this is in the position of the object of ﴿يَوَدُّ﴾ (wishes). It is built in the passive (mabni li'l-maf'ul), and the agent is omitted because it is known, and because it is made explicit in His saying ﴿مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ﴾. Had it been built in the active, the phrase ﴿مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ﴾ would not have appeared.

(﴿مِنْ خَيْرٍ﴾): ﴿مِنْ﴾ is extra (za'idah), and the sense is: "good from your Lord." Its addition here is acceptable, although ﴿يُنَزَّلَ﴾ is not directly preceded by the negative particle. It is not like the phrase "ma yukrimu min rajul" (no man honours…), because the negation extends to it in meaning: when wishing (widdad) is negated, it is as if its object (the sending down) were negated. There are parallels to this in the speech of the Arabs. Among them is His saying: ﴿أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا أَنَّ اللَّهَ الَّذِي خَلَقَ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ وَلَمْ يَعْيَ بِخَلْقِهِنَّ بِقَادِرٍ﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 33]. Since the negation precedes, the insertion of the particle ﴿بِ﴾ is acceptable. Similarly the Arabs say: "ma zanantu ahadan yaqulu dhalika illa Zayd" (I did not think anyone said that except Zayd), with Zayd in the nominative as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun concealed in ﴿يَقُولُ﴾, although the negative particle does not directly precede it, because the meaning is: "No one says that except Zayd, as far as I think."

This explanation follows the view of Sibawayh and al-Khalil. As for the view of al-Akhfash and the Kufans in this place, the insertion is permissible, because they do not require that the judgement be negated from what the particle enters upon; rather they permit its insertion in affirmative statements and otherwise. Al-Akhfash adds that he permits its insertion before a definite noun (ma'rifah). A group held that ﴿مِنْ﴾ is partitive (li'l-tab'id), and on this view the object that was not named as agent is ﴿عَلَيْكُمْ﴾, and the meaning is: "that there be sent down upon you some good from your Lord."

(﴿مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ﴾): ﴿مِنْ﴾ here marks the starting point (li-ibtida' al-ghayah), as when you say "this good is from Zayd." It is also permissible for it to be partitive. The meaning is "good that comes from the goods of your Lord." When it marks the starting point, it is connected to ﴿يُنَزَّلَ﴾; when it is partitive, it is connected to an omitted element, and this involves the omission of a modifying noun (mudaf), as we have estimated. The "good" here is the Qur'an, or revelation (al-wahy), since it encompasses the Qur'an and other things; or what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was singled out for in terms of honour; or wisdom, the Qur'an and victory; or prophethood and Islam; or knowledge, jurisprudence and wisdom; or it is general here, covering all kinds of good. They wish that these would not be bestowed upon the believers. There are seven opinions, the last of which is the most apparent.

The reason for their not wishing this: as for the Jews, it is because prophethood was among the children of Isma'il, and because they feared for their leadership. As for the Christians, it is because of their denial of the claim that Jesus is divine and the Son of God, and because they feared for their leadership. As for the polytheists, it is because of their reviling of their gods and their belittling of their intellects, and out of envy that a man from among them should be singled out for the message and that people should follow him.

* *

﴿وَاللَّهُ يَخْتَصُّ بِرَحْمَتِهِ مَنْ يَشَاءُ﴾: that is, He singles it out for them (yufrid bi-ha). The opposite of ikhtisas (singling out) is ishtirak (sharing). It is possible that ﴿يَخْتَصُّ﴾ here is intransitive, meaning "is singled out," or transitive, meaning "singles out," since the verb occurs in both ways. One says: "ikhtassa Zayd bi-kadha" and "akhtassu-hu bi-hi" (I singled him out for it). Its being transitive here is not necessary, as some have mentioned, since the sentence is also valid as "God singles out with His mercy whom He wills," in which case ﴿مَنْ﴾ is the agent. It is the form ifta'ala derived from khassastu Zayd bi-kadha. When it is intransitive, it denotes the action of the subject upon itself, as in: "idturartu" (I was compelled). When it is transitive, it agrees with the bare form, as in: "kasaba Zayd malan" and "iktasaba Zayd malan" (Zayd earned wealth). Mercy here is general, encompassing all its kinds; or it means prophethood, wisdom and victory, with which Muhammad (ﷺ) was singled out, as said by 'Ali, al-Baqir, Mujahid and al-Zajjaj; or it means Islam, as said by Ibn 'Abbas; or the Qur'an; or the Prophet (ﷺ), as in His saying ﴿وَمَا أَرْسَلْنَاكَ إِلَّا رَحْمَةً لِلْعَالَمِينَ﴾ [al-Anbiya': 107], he being the Prophet of mercy. These are five opinions, the first of which is the most apparent.

﴿وَاللَّهُ ذُو الْفَضْلِ الْعَظِيمِ﴾: it has already been stated that ﴿ذُو﴾ means "possessor of" (sahib). The mention of a number of the rules concerning ﴿ذُو﴾: describing with ﴿ذُو﴾ is considered by them more noble than describing with ﴿صَاحِب﴾, because they stated that ﴿ذُو﴾ is always used only in construct with a noun, so what it denotes is more noble. That is why one finds Dhu Ru'ayn, Dhu Yazan and Dhu al-Kala', whereas they did not hear of "Sahib Ru'ayn" or "Sahib Yazan" and the like. It is not permitted to say, of a companion named Abu Sa'id or Jabir, "Dhu Rasul Allah (ﷺ)," though it is permitted to say "Sahib Rasul Allah (ﷺ)." For this reason God described Himself with His saying ﴿ذُو الْجَلَالِ﴾ [al-Rahman: 27] and ﴿ذُو الْفَضْلِ﴾. The difference between His saying ﴿وَذَا النُّونِ إِذْ ذَهَبَ مُغَاضِبًا﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87] and His saying ﴿وَلَا تَكُنْ كَصَاحِبِ الْحُوتِ﴾ [al-Qalam: 48] will come, God willing.

The explanation of ﴿الْفَضْلِ الْعَظِيمِ﴾ has already been given. It is permissible that what is meant here is all kinds of bounties, in which case the ﴿الْ﴾ is for comprehensiveness (li'l-istighraq), and its greatness is due to its breadth and abundance; or it means the bounty of prophethood. God has described this as great in His saying ﴿وَكَانَ فَضْلُ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكَ عَظِيمًا﴾ [al-Nisa': 113]; or it means the Sharia, and its greatness is due to its explanation of rulings: the lawful, the unlawful, the recommended, the disliked and the permissible; or it means reward and recompense, and its greatness is due to its breadth and abundance: ﴿فَلَا تَعْلَمُ نَفْسٌ مَا أُخْفِيَ لَهُمْ مِنْ قُرَّةِ أَعْيُنٍ﴾ [al-Sajdah: 17], and the hadith: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived." On these interpretations the ﴿الْ﴾ is for definiteness (li'l-'ahd), and the most apparent opinion is the first.

﴿مَا نَنْسَخْ مِنْ آيَةٍ﴾: the occasion of its revelation, as they mention, is that when the Jews envied the Muslims for facing the Ka'bah in prayer and disparaged Islam, they said: "Muhammad orders his companions to do one thing today and forbids them from it tomorrow, says one thing today and retracts it tomorrow. This Qur'an is nothing but from Muhammad, and it contradicts itself, one part against another." So this was revealed.

The commentators have spoken here about the reality of the legal abrogation (naskh shar'i) and its types, what is agreed upon concerning it and what is disputed, its rational permissibility, its occurrence in the Sharia, what it abrogates by, and other rulings on abrogation and the proofs for those rulings, and they have gone at length. All of this is the subject matter of the science of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), where all of it is discussed. This has been our custom: every principle in any science is referred to that science for its establishment, and in the science of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis) we take it as settled from that science, and we do not lengthen the discussion of it in the science of tafsir, lest we depart from the method of tafsir, as Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn 'Umar al-Razi, known as Ibn Khatib al-Ray, did. He gathered in his tafsir many lengthy matters that have no need in the science of tafsir. For this reason it is reported of some extreme scholars that he said: "It contains everything except tafsir."

We have already mentioned in the introduction what the science of tafsir requires. Whoever goes beyond that is superfluous in this science. The parallel to what al-Razi and others did is this: a grammarian begins to write a book on grammar, then starts discussing the altered alif (al-alif al-munqalibah), and says: is the alif in "Allah" converted from a ya' or a waw? Then he digresses from this into speech about God Most High, what is necessary for Him, what is permissible for Him and what is impossible for Him. Then he digresses into the permissibility of God sending messengers to people. Then he digresses into the attributes of the Messenger (ﷺ). Then he digresses from that into the inimitability of what the Qur'an brought and the truth of what it contains. Then he digresses into the fact that among its contents are resurrection and recompense with reward and punishment, and that the rewarded in Paradise will not have their bliss cut off, nor the punished in Hell have their torment cut off. While he is in the midst of discussing the altered alif, he suddenly speaks about Paradise and Hell. Whoever follows this course in knowledge is at the extreme of confusion and muddle. Our teacher, the great scholar Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn Ibrahim ibn al-Zubayr al-Thaqafi, may God sanctify his dust, used to say something to the effect of: "Whenever you see a man moving from one discipline to another in his research or writing, know that this is either because of the deficiency of his knowledge of that discipline, or because of the muddling of his mind and his failure to grasp, as he supposes that things that differ are alike."

I have only gone into such detail in this section so that whoever reads it may benefit, and so that no one thinks that we were unaware of what people have placed in their books of tafsir. Rather, we deliberately left that aside and limited ourselves to what befits the science of tafsir. I ask God for success in what is right.

And regarding His saying ﴿ما نَنْسَخْ﴾ (whatever We abrogate), it is a conditional construction (shart), and it is a fronted object (maf'ul muqaddam). In ﴿نَنْسَخْ﴾ there is an iltifat (a shift in grammatical person), since it moves from the third-person absent to the first-person plural speaker. Do you not see His saying ﴿واللَّهُ يَخْتَصُّ﴾ (And Allah specially chooses) and ﴿واللَّهُ ذُو الفَضْلِ﴾ (And Allah is the possessor of great bounty)?

The majority read ﴿نَنْسَخْ﴾ from nasakha, meaning "to remove" (azala). It is therefore general, covering the removal of both the wording and the ruling together, or the removal of the wording alone, or the removal of the ruling alone.

A group, and Ibn 'Amir among the Seven, read ﴿ما نُنْسِخْ﴾ from al-insakh (causing abrogation). Abu 'Ali al-Farisi objected to this reading, saying: "It is not a valid usage, because one does not say nasakha and ansakha with the same meaning. Nor is the hamza here for transitivity, because the meaning would then be: 'whatever verse is written down', i.e. 'whatever verse is sent down', and then the entire Qur'an would be abrogated by this, and that is not the case. So it only remains that the meaning is: 'whatever we find to be abrogated', as one says: aḥmadtu al-rajul (I found the man praiseworthy) when you find him praiseworthy, and abkhaltuhu (I found him stingy) when you find him stingy." Abu 'Ali said: "We would find it abrogated only by its being abrogated, so the readings agree in meaning even though they differ in wording." End of his words.

So he made the hamza in naskh not for transitivity, but for indicating that a thing exists in the sense of what is derived from the root, and this is one of the meanings of af'ala mentioned in the Fatiha. Al-Zamakhshari, however, made the hamza in it for transitivity, saying: "Its causing abrogation (insakhuha) is the commanding of its abrogation, namely that he commands Jibril (peace be upon him) to make it abrogated, by informing him of its abrogation." This is a confused expression of the meaning that the hamza is for transitivity. Its clarification is that nasakha is transitive to one object, so when the hamza of transfer (hamzat al-naql) enters, it becomes transitive to two. You say: nasakha Zayd al-shay' (Zayd abrogated the thing), meaning he removed it; and ansakhahu iyyahu 'Amr (ʿAmr caused it to be abrogated for him), meaning ʿAmr made Zayd abrogate the thing, that is, remove it.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The estimate is ﴿ما نَنْسَخْكَ مِن آيَةٍ﴾, that is, "whatever verse We cause you to abrogate", i.e. "whatever We permit you to abrogate." It is as if, when God abrogated it, He permitted His Prophet (ﷺ) to leave it, by that abrogation, and so He named that permission insakh (causing abrogation). This which Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned is also the making of the hamza for transitivity, but he and al-Zamakhshari differed regarding the omitted first object: is it Jibril or the Prophet (ﷺ)? Al-Zamakhshari made insakh the commanding of abrogation, while Ibn 'Atiyyah made insakh the permission to leave something by abrogation.

Ibn 'Atiyyah also explained this reading by another explanation, namely that the hamza here is also for transitivity, and that it is from the copying of a book (naskh al-kitab), which is transferring it without removing it. He said: The meaning would be: "whatever We write down and send down from the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), or whatever We delay in it and leave, so We do not send it down, in whichever way We do it, We bring something better than what was delayed and left, or like it." Thus the pronouns in ﴿مِنها﴾ and ﴿بِمِثْلِها﴾ refer back to the pronoun in ﴿نَنْسَأْها﴾. End of his words.

He overlooked a grammatical rule, namely that the conditional noun (ism al-shart) must have a resumptive pronoun in its response (jawab) referring back to it. In His saying ﴿ما نَنْسَخْ﴾, ma is conditional, and His saying ﴿أوْ نَنْسَأْها﴾ refers back to the verse. Although the meaning does not refer back to it in itself in terms of wording and meaning, it refers back to it in wording only, not in meaning. This is like the saying: "I have a dirham and half of it" (ʿindi dirham wa niṣfuh), which in reality is with the implicit ma of the conditional, the estimate being: "or whatever We delay of a verse." This is because the abrogated is not the delayed. But the statement ﴿ما نَنْسَخْ مِن آيَةٍ﴾ remains detached from the response, since there is no resumptive pronoun in it to link it to the response, and that is not permitted. Therefore this meaning is invalid.

﴿مِن آيَةٍ﴾ (of a verse): min here is partitive (lil-tab'id), and āya is singular but stands in the place of the plural, similar to fāris in your saying: hadha awwal fāris (this is the first knight), the estimate being awwal al-fawaris (the first of the knights). The meaning is: "whatever of the verses." The same applies to what comes in this manner in the Qur'an and in the speech of the Arabs, which is analysed in this way, such as His saying ﴿ما يَفْتَحِ اللَّهُ لِلنّاسِ مِن رَحْمَةٍ﴾ (Whatever mercy Allah opens to the people) [Fatir: 2], ﴿وما بِكم مِن نِعْمَةٍ﴾ (And whatever blessing is upon you) [al-Nahl: 53], and the saying: man yaḍrib min rajul aḍribhu (whoever strikes from among men, I will strike him). This prepositional phrase clarifies what was the object of the conditional verb, since it particularises it, for the conditional noun carries generality. If you had not brought the prepositional phrase, it would be understood as general. If you say: "man yaḍrib aḍrib" (whoever strikes, I strike), it is general in the signification of man. But when you say min rajul, the category of men is particularised by this, and women are not included in it, although the signification of min is general for both kinds.

For this reason some grammarians made min āya and what resembles it in the position of accusative (naṣb) as a specification (tamyiz). He said: "The specified noun is what he said, and the estimate is: 'whatever thing was abrogated of a verse.'" He said: "It is not good to estimate it as ayyu āya nansakh (which verse We abrogate), because you do not combine āya with a specifier in āya. You do not say: ayya āya nansakh min āya, nor ayyu rajul yaḍrib min rajul aḍribhu."

They also permitted that min be superfluous (zā'ida), and that āya be a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). The meaning is: "whatever thing We abrogate, little or much." They said: The word āya has come as a ḥāl in His exalted saying ﴿ناقَةُ اللَّهِ لَكم آيَةً﴾ (This is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you) [al-A'raf: 73]. But this is corrupt, because the ḥāl is not put in the genitive by min.

They also permitted that ma be a verbal noun (maṣdar), and āya be the direct object (maf'ul bihi), the estimate being: "whatever kind of abrogation We abrogate a verse with." The coming of the conditional ma as a maṣdar is permitted. You say: ma taḍrib Zaydan aḍrib mithlahu (whatever manner of striking you strike Zayd with, I strike him with its like). The estimate is: "whatever kind of striking you strike Zayd with, I strike with its like." The poet said:

"The crow cawed, so I said: 'Imminent separation, whatever you wish, when they departed for separation, then caw!'"

But this is corrupt, because if you make ma as the abrogation (li-l-naskh), the response is left bereft of a pronoun referring back to it, and there must be a pronoun referring back to the conditional noun. Do you not see that if you said: ayya ḍarb yaḍrib Hindan aḍrib aḥsana minha (whatever kind of striking one strikes Hind with, I strike with a better kind than it), it would not be permitted, because the response clause would be bereft of a pronoun referring back to the conditional noun? The pronoun in minha refers back to the object which is Hind, not to ayya ḍarb, which is the conditional noun. Also, the direct object may not have the superfluous min unless two conditions are met: that a negative precedes it, and that what min enters upon is indefinite. This is according to the well-known school of the Basran grammarians. And the conditional is not of the category of the negative, so it is not permitted to say: in qama min rajul aqum ma'ahu (if a man should stand up, I will stand with him). There is a weak disagreement on this among some Basran grammarians.

(أوْ نَنْسَأْها) (or We cause it to be forgotten, or We delay it): ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Nakha'i, ʿAta', Mujahid, ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read it, and among the Seven, Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read: aw nanskha'ha, with the opening of the nun of the present tense and the sin, and the hamza being silent. A group also read it like this, except without a hamza. Abu ʿUbayd al-Bakri mentioned in his book al-Lali' that this reading is from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, and I think it is a mistake, and Ibn ʿAtiyyah said the same. He said: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas read tansaha with a ta' that is open, the nun silent, and the sin open, without a hamza, and this is the reading of al-Hasan and Ibn Ya'mar. A group read likewise, except that they used a hamza. Abu Haywa read likewise, except that he raised the ta'. Sa'id read likewise, except without a hamza. The rest of the Seven read nunsiha, with the nun raised, the sin lowered, without a hamza. A group read likewise, except that they put a hamza after the sin. al-Dahhak and Abu Raja' read with the first nun raised, the second nun opened, the sin doubled, and without a hamza. Ubayy read aw nunsika, with the first nun raised, the second nun silent, the sin lowered, without a hamza, and with the kaf of address instead of the third-person pronoun. In the codex of Salim the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfa, it is like this, except that he combined the two pronouns, and this was the reading of Abu Hudhayfa. al-A'mash read: ma nunsika min aya aw nansakh-ha najji' bi-mithliha. Thus it is established in the codex of ʿAbd Allah. So there are eleven readings for this word, apart from the reading of al-A'mash: with the hamza: nanse'ha, nunsi'ha, nunsi'ha (hmm)...

[Note: the list in the original is: with hamza: nansa'ha, nansi'ha, nunsa'ha, tansa'ha; without hamza: nansaha, nunsiha, tansaha, tunsiha, nunsika, nunsikaha.]

The naskh here has been explained as tabdil (replacement), said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Zajjaj, or the replacement of the ruling while the writing remains, said by ʿAbd Allah and also Ibn ʿAbbas, or raf' (lifting), said by al-Suddi.

As for His saying ﴿أوْ نُنْسِها﴾ without a hamza: if it is from forgetting, the opposite of remembering, then the meaning is "We cause you to forget it" if it is from the form af'ala, or "We cause it to be forgotten" if it is from the form fa'ala. This was said by Mujahid and Qatada. If it is from leaving, then the meaning is: "or We leave off sending it down," said by al-Dahhak; or "We erase it, so We do not leave for it a wording that is recited nor a ruling that is binding," said by Ibn Zayd; or "We command leaving it," as one says: ansaytuhu al-shay' (I made him forget the thing), meaning I commanded him to leave it, and nasiytuhu (I forgot him), meaning I left him. The poet said:

"Indeed upon me is a debt I will pay; I am not forgetting it, nor will I make it forgotten."

That is, I do not command its abandonment.

Al-Zajjaj said: The reading nunsiha, with the nun raised, the second nun silent, and the sin lowered, has no meaning of abandonment, because one does not say unsiya in the sense of "he left". Abu ʿAli al-Farisi and others said: That is valid, because it means "We make you leave it". Al-Zajjaj similarly weakened the view that the verse should be understood as forgetting, the opposite of remembrance, and he said: This did not happen to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he never forgot any Qur'an. Abu ʿAli and others said: That is permissible, and it has occurred, and there is no difference between the verse being lifted by abrogation or by causing it to be forgotten. Al-Zajjaj cited His saying exalted: ﴿ولَئِنْ شِئْنا لَنَذْهَبَنَّ بِالَّذِي أوْحَيْنا إلَيْكَ﴾ (And if We willed, We would surely take away what We revealed to you) [al-Isra': 86], meaning: We did not do it. Abu ʿAli said: Its meaning is: We did not take away all of it. Al-Tabari related al-Zajjaj's view from one earlier than him.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: The correct view in this is that the Prophet (ﷺ) forgetting what God willed to make him forget, and He did not intend to establish it as Qur'an, is permissible. As for forgetting which is a human defect, the Prophet (ﷺ) is protected from it before the conveying and after the conveying, as long as no one among the Companions has memorised it. But after it has been memorised, what is permissible for humans is permissible for him, because he has conveyed and fulfilled the trust. From this is the hadith, when he omitted a verse. When he finished the prayer he said: "Is Ubayy among the people?" He said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Then why did you not remind me?" He said: "I feared that it had been lifted." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It was not lifted, but I forgot it." End of the words of Ibn ʿAtiyyah.

As for the one who read with the hamza, it is from delay. The Arabs say: nasa'tu al-ibil ʿan al-hawd (I delayed the camels from the watering trough), and ansa'a al-ibil ʿan dhama'iha yawman aw yawmayn aw akthar (he delayed the camels from their thirst a day or two days or more), meaning he delayed them from the watering. In the verse, the meaning is: "We delay its abrogation or its sending down," said by ʿAta' and Ibn Abi Najih; or "We erase it in wording and ruling," said by Ibn Zayd; or "We let it stand, so We do not abrogate it," said by Abu ʿUbayda. This is weakened by His saying ﴿نَأْتِ بِخَيْرٍ مِنها﴾ (We bring something better than it), because what is allowed to stand and remain is not described as "We bring something better than it."

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that in the verse there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), its estimate being: "What We replace of the ruling of a verse, We bring something better than it for you, or like it. Then He said: aw nansa'ha, i.e. We delay it, so We do not abrogate it nor replace it." This report is not sound from that scholar Ibn ʿAbbas, because it contradicts the arrangement of the Qur'an's wording.

(نَأْتِ) (We bring): this is the response of the conditional, and the conditional noun here is followed by a conditional and a response both in the present tense. This is the best construction for the two verbs of condition and response, namely that both be in the present tense.

(بِخَيْرٍ مِنها) (with something better than it): Apparently khayran here is the elative (af'al al-tafdil), and the superiority is evident, because what is brought, if it is lighter than the abrogated or the delayed, its superiority is with respect to the lifting of the burdens of obligation; and if it is heavier, its superiority is with respect to the increase of reward.

(Or one like it): or one equal to it in obligation and reward, as in the abrogation of facing Bayt al-Maqdis by facing the Ka'bah. Some people held that khayr here is not an elative (af'al al-tafdil, comparative form) but is one of the kinds of good (khayr min al-khuyur), like khayr in His saying: ﴿that there should be sent down to you any good from your Lord﴾. According to them it is a verbal noun (masdar), and min denotes the starting point of the limit (min li-ibtida' al-ghayah). The meaning becomes: whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring a better one of the goods from the standpoint of the abrogated or forgotten verse. But this meaning is weakened by His saying "or one like it," for on this meaning it is not valid to coordinate it with His saying "a better," unless khayr is applied to the absence of obligation, so that the meaning becomes: We bring one of the goods, which is the absence of obligation, or We bring one like the abrogated or forgotten verse. It is as if He is saying: whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, [it is replaced] with no substitute, or with an equivalent substitute. The one with no substitute is a good that reaches you from the standpoint of the abrogated or forgotten verse, since it is relief for you from obligations. As for coordinating "one like it" with the pronoun in "than it" that is governed by a preposition, this is weak because the preposition is not repeated.

﴿Do you not know that God is powerful over everything?﴾ Ibn 'Atiyyah said: its apparent sense is a pure interrogative, so the corresponding (mu'adil) element here, according to a group, is "or do you want." Others said: here "am" is disjunctive (munqati'ah), so the corresponding element according to them is omitted, its estimate being "or do you know." All of this is on the basis that addressing the Prophet ﷺ intends addressing his community. But if he alone is addressed, the corresponding element is omitted and nothing else, and both opinions are transmitted. End of his words and his citation. What they said is not good. Rather, this is an interrogative whose meaning is affirmation (taqrir), so it needs no corresponding element at all.
