The better view is that the addressee is the hearer, and the interrogative in the sense of affirmation is very common in their speech, especially when it enters upon a negation: ﴿Is not God the most knowing of what is in the breasts of the worlds?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 10]? ﴿Is not God the most just of judges?﴾ [al-Tin: 8]? ﴿Did We not raise you among us as a child?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 18]? ﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?﴾ [al-Duha: 6]? ﴿Did We not expand your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh: 1]? All of this is interrogative in which no corresponding element is needed, because only affirmation is intended. The meaning: you have already known, O addressee, that God is capable of everything, so He has the disposal of His servants' obligations, by erasing, affirming, and replacing one ruling with another, and by bringing for you the better or the like. The reason for addressing a single addressee is that no person fails to imagine that he is the one addressed by this, the one alerted by it, and the one affirmed on a fact established in his mind, namely that God's power relates to all things, so nothing can frustrate Him. When this is so, abrogation is not denied, because God does what He wills and rules what He desires; none repels His command and none overturns His judgment. In His saying ﴿Do you not know that God﴾ there is a shift from a plural addressed pronoun, in ﴿from your Lord﴾, to a singular addressed pronoun for the wisdom we have explained, and a shift from a first-person speaker who magnifies himself to an apparent third-person noun, God, since it is the proper name comprising all attributes, so within it is the attribute of power. It is more emphatic in attributing power to Him than the magnifying first-person pronoun. For this reason He turned from "Do you not know that We" to "Do you not know that God." The explanation of His saying ﴿Indeed God is powerful over everything﴾ [al-Baqarah: 20] has already passed at the beginning of this surah, so that suffices and it need not be repeated.

﴿وَلَا الْمُشْرِكِينَ﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to ﴿مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ﴾ (from the People of the Book).

I saw in a book by Abu Ishaq al-Shirazi, the author of al-Tanbih, a passage refuting the Shi'a and those who share their view that the prescribed method for the feet in ablution (wudu') is wiping (masḥ), on the basis that the conjunction in His saying ﴿وَأَرْجُلَكُمْ﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6] is conjoined to His saying ﴿بِرُءُوسِكُمْ﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6]. In that book, Abu Ishaq gave the reading وأرجلِكم with the genitive (jarr) an explanation: that it is a case of khafḍ 'ala al-jiwar (genitive by proximity), and that its original form is the accusative (naṣb), so it was put in the genitive by attraction to the adjacent word. In the same book he indicated that the Qur'an and the Arabic language both attest to the permissibility of this, and he cited as an example of it His saying in this verse, ﴿وَلَا الْمُشْرِكِينَ﴾, and His saying ﴿لَمْ يَكُنِ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ وَالْمُشْرِكِينَ مُنْفَكِّينَ﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 1], holding that the original form is the nominative, that is, ﴿وَلَا الْمُشْرِكُونَ﴾, conjoined to ﴿الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾. This is the talk of one who falls short in Arabic grammar, who presumes to speak on it without knowledge, and who turns away from carrying the wording on its correct meaning and its eloquent construction.

The particle ﴿لَا﴾ in His saying ﴿وَلَا الْمُشْرِكِينَ﴾ is there for emphasis (li'l-ta'kid), and had this been outside the Qur'an, it would have been permissible to omit it. It does not appear in His saying ﴿لَمْ يَكُنِ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ وَالْمُشْرِكِينَ مُنْفَكِّينَ﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 1] for a reason that will be mentioned there, God willing.

﴿أَنْ يُنَزَّلَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾: this is in the position of the object of ﴿يَوَدُّ﴾ (wishes). It is built in the passive (mabni li'l-maf'ul), and the agent is omitted because it is known, and because it is made explicit in His saying ﴿مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ﴾. Had it been built in the active, the phrase ﴿مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ﴾ would not have appeared.

(﴿مِنْ خَيْرٍ﴾): ﴿مِنْ﴾ is extra (za'idah), and the sense is: "good from your Lord." Its addition here is acceptable, although ﴿يُنَزَّلَ﴾ is not directly preceded by the negative particle. It is not like the phrase "ma yukrimu min rajul" (no man honours…), because the negation extends to it in meaning: when wishing (widdad) is negated, it is as if its object (the sending down) were negated. There are parallels to this in the speech of the Arabs. Among them is His saying: ﴿أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا أَنَّ اللَّهَ الَّذِي خَلَقَ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ وَلَمْ يَعْيَ بِخَلْقِهِنَّ بِقَادِرٍ﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 33]. Since the negation precedes, the insertion of the particle ﴿بِ﴾ is acceptable. Similarly the Arabs say: "ma zanantu ahadan yaqulu dhalika illa Zayd" (I did not think anyone said that except Zayd), with Zayd in the nominative as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun concealed in ﴿يَقُولُ﴾, although the negative particle does not directly precede it, because the meaning is: "No one says that except Zayd, as far as I think."

This explanation follows the view of Sibawayh and al-Khalil. As for the view of al-Akhfash and the Kufans in this place, the insertion is permissible, because they do not require that the judgement be negated from what the particle enters upon; rather they permit its insertion in affirmative statements and otherwise. Al-Akhfash adds that he permits its insertion before a definite noun (ma'rifah). A group held that ﴿مِنْ﴾ is partitive (li'l-tab'id), and on this view the object that was not named as agent is ﴿عَلَيْكُمْ﴾, and the meaning is: "that there be sent down upon you some good from your Lord."

(﴿مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ﴾): ﴿مِنْ﴾ here marks the starting point (li-ibtida' al-ghayah), as when you say "this good is from Zayd." It is also permissible for it to be partitive. The meaning is "good that comes from the goods of your Lord." When it marks the starting point, it is connected to ﴿يُنَزَّلَ﴾; when it is partitive, it is connected to an omitted element, and this involves the omission of a modifying noun (mudaf), as we have estimated. The "good" here is the Qur'an, or revelation (al-wahy), since it encompasses the Qur'an and other things; or what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was singled out for in terms of honour; or wisdom, the Qur'an and victory; or prophethood and Islam; or knowledge, jurisprudence and wisdom; or it is general here, covering all kinds of good. They wish that these would not be bestowed upon the believers. There are seven opinions, the last of which is the most apparent.

The reason for their not wishing this: as for the Jews, it is because prophethood was among the children of Isma'il, and because they feared for their leadership. As for the Christians, it is because of their denial of the claim that Jesus is divine and the Son of God, and because they feared for their leadership. As for the polytheists, it is because of their reviling of their gods and their belittling of their intellects, and out of envy that a man from among them should be singled out for the message and that people should follow him.

* *

﴿وَاللَّهُ يَخْتَصُّ بِرَحْمَتِهِ مَنْ يَشَاءُ﴾: that is, He singles it out for them (yufrid bi-ha). The opposite of ikhtisas (singling out) is ishtirak (sharing). It is possible that ﴿يَخْتَصُّ﴾ here is intransitive, meaning "is singled out," or transitive, meaning "singles out," since the verb occurs in both ways. One says: "ikhtassa Zayd bi-kadha" and "akhtassu-hu bi-hi" (I singled him out for it). Its being transitive here is not necessary, as some have mentioned, since the sentence is also valid as "God singles out with His mercy whom He wills," in which case ﴿مَنْ﴾ is the agent. It is the form ifta'ala derived from khassastu Zayd bi-kadha. When it is intransitive, it denotes the action of the subject upon itself, as in: "idturartu" (I was compelled). When it is transitive, it agrees with the bare form, as in: "kasaba Zayd malan" and "iktasaba Zayd malan" (Zayd earned wealth). Mercy here is general, encompassing all its kinds; or it means prophethood, wisdom and victory, with which Muhammad (ﷺ) was singled out, as said by 'Ali, al-Baqir, Mujahid and al-Zajjaj; or it means Islam, as said by Ibn 'Abbas; or the Qur'an; or the Prophet (ﷺ), as in His saying ﴿وَمَا أَرْسَلْنَاكَ إِلَّا رَحْمَةً لِلْعَالَمِينَ﴾ [al-Anbiya': 107], he being the Prophet of mercy. These are five opinions, the first of which is the most apparent.

﴿وَاللَّهُ ذُو الْفَضْلِ الْعَظِيمِ﴾: it has already been stated that ﴿ذُو﴾ means "possessor of" (sahib). The mention of a number of the rules concerning ﴿ذُو﴾: describing with ﴿ذُو﴾ is considered by them more noble than describing with ﴿صَاحِب﴾, because they stated that ﴿ذُو﴾ is always used only in construct with a noun, so what it denotes is more noble. That is why one finds Dhu Ru'ayn, Dhu Yazan and Dhu al-Kala', whereas they did not hear of "Sahib Ru'ayn" or "Sahib Yazan" and the like. It is not permitted to say, of a companion named Abu Sa'id or Jabir, "Dhu Rasul Allah (ﷺ)," though it is permitted to say "Sahib Rasul Allah (ﷺ)." For this reason God described Himself with His saying ﴿ذُو الْجَلَالِ﴾ [al-Rahman: 27] and ﴿ذُو الْفَضْلِ﴾. The difference between His saying ﴿وَذَا النُّونِ إِذْ ذَهَبَ مُغَاضِبًا﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87] and His saying ﴿وَلَا تَكُنْ كَصَاحِبِ الْحُوتِ﴾ [al-Qalam: 48] will come, God willing.

The explanation of ﴿الْفَضْلِ الْعَظِيمِ﴾ has already been given. It is permissible that what is meant here is all kinds of bounties, in which case the ﴿الْ﴾ is for comprehensiveness (li'l-istighraq), and its greatness is due to its breadth and abundance; or it means the bounty of prophethood. God has described this as great in His saying ﴿وَكَانَ فَضْلُ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكَ عَظِيمًا﴾ [al-Nisa': 113]; or it means the Sharia, and its greatness is due to its explanation of rulings: the lawful, the unlawful, the recommended, the disliked and the permissible; or it means reward and recompense, and its greatness is due to its breadth and abundance: ﴿فَلَا تَعْلَمُ نَفْسٌ مَا أُخْفِيَ لَهُمْ مِنْ قُرَّةِ أَعْيُنٍ﴾ [al-Sajdah: 17], and the hadith: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived." On these interpretations the ﴿الْ﴾ is for definiteness (li'l-'ahd), and the most apparent opinion is the first.

﴿مَا نَنْسَخْ مِنْ آيَةٍ﴾: the occasion of its revelation, as they mention, is that when the Jews envied the Muslims for facing the Ka'bah in prayer and disparaged Islam, they said: "Muhammad orders his companions to do one thing today and forbids them from it tomorrow, says one thing today and retracts it tomorrow. This Qur'an is nothing but from Muhammad, and it contradicts itself, one part against another." So this was revealed.

The commentators have spoken here about the reality of the legal abrogation (naskh shar'i) and its types, what is agreed upon concerning it and what is disputed, its rational permissibility, its occurrence in the Sharia, what it abrogates by, and other rulings on abrogation and the proofs for those rulings, and they have gone at length. All of this is the subject matter of the science of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), where all of it is discussed. This has been our custom: every principle in any science is referred to that science for its establishment, and in the science of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis) we take it as settled from that science, and we do not lengthen the discussion of it in the science of tafsir, lest we depart from the method of tafsir, as Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn 'Umar al-Razi, known as Ibn Khatib al-Ray, did. He gathered in his tafsir many lengthy matters that have no need in the science of tafsir. For this reason it is reported of some extreme scholars that he said: "It contains everything except tafsir."

We have already mentioned in the introduction what the science of tafsir requires. Whoever goes beyond that is superfluous in this science. The parallel to what al-Razi and others did is this: a grammarian begins to write a book on grammar, then starts discussing the altered alif (al-alif al-munqalibah), and says: is the alif in "Allah" converted from a ya' or a waw? Then he digresses from this into speech about God Most High, what is necessary for Him, what is permissible for Him and what is impossible for Him. Then he digresses into the permissibility of God sending messengers to people. Then he digresses into the attributes of the Messenger (ﷺ). Then he digresses from that into the inimitability of what the Qur'an brought and the truth of what it contains. Then he digresses into the fact that among its contents are resurrection and recompense with reward and punishment, and that the rewarded in Paradise will not have their bliss cut off, nor the punished in Hell have their torment cut off. While he is in the midst of discussing the altered alif, he suddenly speaks about Paradise and Hell. Whoever follows this course in knowledge is at the extreme of confusion and muddle. Our teacher, the great scholar Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn Ibrahim ibn al-Zubayr al-Thaqafi, may God sanctify his dust, used to say something to the effect of: "Whenever you see a man moving from one discipline to another in his research or writing, know that this is either because of the deficiency of his knowledge of that discipline, or because of the muddling of his mind and his failure to grasp, as he supposes that things that differ are alike."

I have only gone into such detail in this section so that whoever reads it may benefit, and so that no one thinks that we were unaware of what people have placed in their books of tafsir. Rather, we deliberately left that aside and limited ourselves to what befits the science of tafsir. I ask God for success in what is right.

And regarding His saying ﴿ما نَنْسَخْ﴾ (whatever We abrogate), it is a conditional construction (shart), and it is a fronted object (maf'ul muqaddam). In ﴿نَنْسَخْ﴾ there is an iltifat (a shift in grammatical person), since it moves from the third-person absent to the first-person plural speaker. Do you not see His saying ﴿واللَّهُ يَخْتَصُّ﴾ (And Allah specially chooses) and ﴿واللَّهُ ذُو الفَضْلِ﴾ (And Allah is the possessor of great bounty)?

The majority read ﴿نَنْسَخْ﴾ from nasakha, meaning "to remove" (azala). It is therefore general, covering the removal of both the wording and the ruling together, or the removal of the wording alone, or the removal of the ruling alone.

A group, and Ibn 'Amir among the Seven, read ﴿ما نُنْسِخْ﴾ from al-insakh (causing abrogation). Abu 'Ali al-Farisi objected to this reading, saying: "It is not a valid usage, because one does not say nasakha and ansakha with the same meaning. Nor is the hamza here for transitivity, because the meaning would then be: 'whatever verse is written down', i.e. 'whatever verse is sent down', and then the entire Qur'an would be abrogated by this, and that is not the case. So it only remains that the meaning is: 'whatever we find to be abrogated', as one says: aḥmadtu al-rajul (I found the man praiseworthy) when you find him praiseworthy, and abkhaltuhu (I found him stingy) when you find him stingy." Abu 'Ali said: "We would find it abrogated only by its being abrogated, so the readings agree in meaning even though they differ in wording." End of his words.

So he made the hamza in naskh not for transitivity, but for indicating that a thing exists in the sense of what is derived from the root, and this is one of the meanings of af'ala mentioned in the Fatiha. Al-Zamakhshari, however, made the hamza in it for transitivity, saying: "Its causing abrogation (insakhuha) is the commanding of its abrogation, namely that he commands Jibril (peace be upon him) to make it abrogated, by informing him of its abrogation." This is a confused expression of the meaning that the hamza is for transitivity. Its clarification is that nasakha is transitive to one object, so when the hamza of transfer (hamzat al-naql) enters, it becomes transitive to two. You say: nasakha Zayd al-shay' (Zayd abrogated the thing), meaning he removed it; and ansakhahu iyyahu 'Amr (ʿAmr caused it to be abrogated for him), meaning ʿAmr made Zayd abrogate the thing, that is, remove it.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The estimate is ﴿ما نَنْسَخْكَ مِن آيَةٍ﴾, that is, "whatever verse We cause you to abrogate", i.e. "whatever We permit you to abrogate." It is as if, when God abrogated it, He permitted His Prophet (ﷺ) to leave it, by that abrogation, and so He named that permission insakh (causing abrogation). This which Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned is also the making of the hamza for transitivity, but he and al-Zamakhshari differed regarding the omitted first object: is it Jibril or the Prophet (ﷺ)? Al-Zamakhshari made insakh the commanding of abrogation, while Ibn 'Atiyyah made insakh the permission to leave something by abrogation.

Ibn 'Atiyyah also explained this reading by another explanation, namely that the hamza here is also for transitivity, and that it is from the copying of a book (naskh al-kitab), which is transferring it without removing it. He said: The meaning would be: "whatever We write down and send down from the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), or whatever We delay in it and leave, so We do not send it down, in whichever way We do it, We bring something better than what was delayed and left, or like it." Thus the pronouns in ﴿مِنها﴾ and ﴿بِمِثْلِها﴾ refer back to the pronoun in ﴿نَنْسَأْها﴾. End of his words.

He overlooked a grammatical rule, namely that the conditional noun (ism al-shart) must have a resumptive pronoun in its response (jawab) referring back to it. In His saying ﴿ما نَنْسَخْ﴾, ma is conditional, and His saying ﴿أوْ نَنْسَأْها﴾ refers back to the verse. Although the meaning does not refer back to it in itself in terms of wording and meaning, it refers back to it in wording only, not in meaning. This is like the saying: "I have a dirham and half of it" (ʿindi dirham wa niṣfuh), which in reality is with the implicit ma of the conditional, the estimate being: "or whatever We delay of a verse." This is because the abrogated is not the delayed. But the statement ﴿ما نَنْسَخْ مِن آيَةٍ﴾ remains detached from the response, since there is no resumptive pronoun in it to link it to the response, and that is not permitted. Therefore this meaning is invalid.

﴿مِن آيَةٍ﴾ (of a verse): min here is partitive (lil-tab'id), and āya is singular but stands in the place of the plural, similar to fāris in your saying: hadha awwal fāris (this is the first knight), the estimate being awwal al-fawaris (the first of the knights). The meaning is: "whatever of the verses." The same applies to what comes in this manner in the Qur'an and in the speech of the Arabs, which is analysed in this way, such as His saying ﴿ما يَفْتَحِ اللَّهُ لِلنّاسِ مِن رَحْمَةٍ﴾ (Whatever mercy Allah opens to the people) [Fatir: 2], ﴿وما بِكم مِن نِعْمَةٍ﴾ (And whatever blessing is upon you) [al-Nahl: 53], and the saying: man yaḍrib min rajul aḍribhu (whoever strikes from among men, I will strike him). This prepositional phrase clarifies what was the object of the conditional verb, since it particularises it, for the conditional noun carries generality. If you had not brought the prepositional phrase, it would be understood as general. If you say: "man yaḍrib aḍrib" (whoever strikes, I strike), it is general in the signification of man. But when you say min rajul, the category of men is particularised by this, and women are not included in it, although the signification of min is general for both kinds.

For this reason some grammarians made min āya and what resembles it in the position of accusative (naṣb) as a specification (tamyiz). He said: "The specified noun is what he said, and the estimate is: 'whatever thing was abrogated of a verse.'" He said: "It is not good to estimate it as ayyu āya nansakh (which verse We abrogate), because you do not combine āya with a specifier in āya. You do not say: ayya āya nansakh min āya, nor ayyu rajul yaḍrib min rajul aḍribhu."

They also permitted that min be superfluous (zā'ida), and that āya be a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). The meaning is: "whatever thing We abrogate, little or much." They said: The word āya has come as a ḥāl in His exalted saying ﴿ناقَةُ اللَّهِ لَكم آيَةً﴾ (This is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you) [al-A'raf: 73]. But this is corrupt, because the ḥāl is not put in the genitive by min.

They also permitted that ma be a verbal noun (maṣdar), and āya be the direct object (maf'ul bihi), the estimate being: "whatever kind of abrogation We abrogate a verse with." The coming of the conditional ma as a maṣdar is permitted. You say: ma taḍrib Zaydan aḍrib mithlahu (whatever manner of striking you strike Zayd with, I strike him with its like). The estimate is: "whatever kind of striking you strike Zayd with, I strike with its like." The poet said:

"The crow cawed, so I said: 'Imminent separation, whatever you wish, when they departed for separation, then caw!'"

But this is corrupt, because if you make ma as the abrogation (li-l-naskh), the response is left bereft of a pronoun referring back to it, and there must be a pronoun referring back to the conditional noun. Do you not see that if you said: ayya ḍarb yaḍrib Hindan aḍrib aḥsana minha (whatever kind of striking one strikes Hind with, I strike with a better kind than it), it would not be permitted, because the response clause would be bereft of a pronoun referring back to the conditional noun? The pronoun in minha refers back to the object which is Hind, not to ayya ḍarb, which is the conditional noun. Also, the direct object may not have the superfluous min unless two conditions are met: that a negative precedes it, and that what min enters upon is indefinite. This is according to the well-known school of the Basran grammarians. And the conditional is not of the category of the negative, so it is not permitted to say: in qama min rajul aqum ma'ahu (if a man should stand up, I will stand with him). There is a weak disagreement on this among some Basran grammarians.

(أوْ نَنْسَأْها) (or We cause it to be forgotten, or We delay it): ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Nakha'i, ʿAta', Mujahid, ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read it, and among the Seven, Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read: aw nanskha'ha, with the opening of the nun of the present tense and the sin, and the hamza being silent. A group also read it like this, except without a hamza. Abu ʿUbayd al-Bakri mentioned in his book al-Lali' that this reading is from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, and I think it is a mistake, and Ibn ʿAtiyyah said the same. He said: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas read tansaha with a ta' that is open, the nun silent, and the sin open, without a hamza, and this is the reading of al-Hasan and Ibn Ya'mar. A group read likewise, except that they used a hamza. Abu Haywa read likewise, except that he raised the ta'. Sa'id read likewise, except without a hamza. The rest of the Seven read nunsiha, with the nun raised, the sin lowered, without a hamza. A group read likewise, except that they put a hamza after the sin. al-Dahhak and Abu Raja' read with the first nun raised, the second nun opened, the sin doubled, and without a hamza. Ubayy read aw nunsika, with the first nun raised, the second nun silent, the sin lowered, without a hamza, and with the kaf of address instead of the third-person pronoun. In the codex of Salim the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfa, it is like this, except that he combined the two pronouns, and this was the reading of Abu Hudhayfa. al-A'mash read: ma nunsika min aya aw nansakh-ha najji' bi-mithliha. Thus it is established in the codex of ʿAbd Allah. So there are eleven readings for this word, apart from the reading of al-A'mash: with the hamza: nanse'ha, nunsi'ha, nunsi'ha (hmm)...

[Note: the list in the original is: with hamza: nansa'ha, nansi'ha, nunsa'ha, tansa'ha; without hamza: nansaha, nunsiha, tansaha, tunsiha, nunsika, nunsikaha.]

The naskh here has been explained as tabdil (replacement), said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Zajjaj, or the replacement of the ruling while the writing remains, said by ʿAbd Allah and also Ibn ʿAbbas, or raf' (lifting), said by al-Suddi.

As for His saying ﴿أوْ نُنْسِها﴾ without a hamza: if it is from forgetting, the opposite of remembering, then the meaning is "We cause you to forget it" if it is from the form af'ala, or "We cause it to be forgotten" if it is from the form fa'ala. This was said by Mujahid and Qatada. If it is from leaving, then the meaning is: "or We leave off sending it down," said by al-Dahhak; or "We erase it, so We do not leave for it a wording that is recited nor a ruling that is binding," said by Ibn Zayd; or "We command leaving it," as one says: ansaytuhu al-shay' (I made him forget the thing), meaning I commanded him to leave it, and nasiytuhu (I forgot him), meaning I left him. The poet said:

"Indeed upon me is a debt I will pay; I am not forgetting it, nor will I make it forgotten."

That is, I do not command its abandonment.

Al-Zajjaj said: The reading nunsiha, with the nun raised, the second nun silent, and the sin lowered, has no meaning of abandonment, because one does not say unsiya in the sense of "he left". Abu ʿAli al-Farisi and others said: That is valid, because it means "We make you leave it". Al-Zajjaj similarly weakened the view that the verse should be understood as forgetting, the opposite of remembrance, and he said: This did not happen to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he never forgot any Qur'an. Abu ʿAli and others said: That is permissible, and it has occurred, and there is no difference between the verse being lifted by abrogation or by causing it to be forgotten. Al-Zajjaj cited His saying exalted: ﴿ولَئِنْ شِئْنا لَنَذْهَبَنَّ بِالَّذِي أوْحَيْنا إلَيْكَ﴾ (And if We willed, We would surely take away what We revealed to you) [al-Isra': 86], meaning: We did not do it. Abu ʿAli said: Its meaning is: We did not take away all of it. Al-Tabari related al-Zajjaj's view from one earlier than him.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: The correct view in this is that the Prophet (ﷺ) forgetting what God willed to make him forget, and He did not intend to establish it as Qur'an, is permissible. As for forgetting which is a human defect, the Prophet (ﷺ) is protected from it before the conveying and after the conveying, as long as no one among the Companions has memorised it. But after it has been memorised, what is permissible for humans is permissible for him, because he has conveyed and fulfilled the trust. From this is the hadith, when he omitted a verse. When he finished the prayer he said: "Is Ubayy among the people?" He said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Then why did you not remind me?" He said: "I feared that it had been lifted." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It was not lifted, but I forgot it." End of the words of Ibn ʿAtiyyah.

As for the one who read with the hamza, it is from delay. The Arabs say: nasa'tu al-ibil ʿan al-hawd (I delayed the camels from the watering trough), and ansa'a al-ibil ʿan dhama'iha yawman aw yawmayn aw akthar (he delayed the camels from their thirst a day or two days or more), meaning he delayed them from the watering. In the verse, the meaning is: "We delay its abrogation or its sending down," said by ʿAta' and Ibn Abi Najih; or "We erase it in wording and ruling," said by Ibn Zayd; or "We let it stand, so We do not abrogate it," said by Abu ʿUbayda. This is weakened by His saying ﴿نَأْتِ بِخَيْرٍ مِنها﴾ (We bring something better than it), because what is allowed to stand and remain is not described as "We bring something better than it."

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that in the verse there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), its estimate being: "What We replace of the ruling of a verse, We bring something better than it for you, or like it. Then He said: aw nansa'ha, i.e. We delay it, so We do not abrogate it nor replace it." This report is not sound from that scholar Ibn ʿAbbas, because it contradicts the arrangement of the Qur'an's wording.

(نَأْتِ) (We bring): this is the response of the conditional, and the conditional noun here is followed by a conditional and a response both in the present tense. This is the best construction for the two verbs of condition and response, namely that both be in the present tense.

(بِخَيْرٍ مِنها) (with something better than it): Apparently khayran here is the elative (af'al al-tafdil), and the superiority is evident, because what is brought, if it is lighter than the abrogated or the delayed, its superiority is with respect to the lifting of the burdens of obligation; and if it is heavier, its superiority is with respect to the increase of reward.

(Or one like it): or one equal to it in obligation and reward, as in the abrogation of facing Bayt al-Maqdis by facing the Ka'bah. Some people held that khayr here is not an elative (af'al al-tafdil, comparative form) but is one of the kinds of good (khayr min al-khuyur), like khayr in His saying: ﴿that there should be sent down to you any good from your Lord﴾. According to them it is a verbal noun (masdar), and min denotes the starting point of the limit (min li-ibtida' al-ghayah). The meaning becomes: whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring a better one of the goods from the standpoint of the abrogated or forgotten verse. But this meaning is weakened by His saying "or one like it," for on this meaning it is not valid to coordinate it with His saying "a better," unless khayr is applied to the absence of obligation, so that the meaning becomes: We bring one of the goods, which is the absence of obligation, or We bring one like the abrogated or forgotten verse. It is as if He is saying: whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, [it is replaced] with no substitute, or with an equivalent substitute. The one with no substitute is a good that reaches you from the standpoint of the abrogated or forgotten verse, since it is relief for you from obligations. As for coordinating "one like it" with the pronoun in "than it" that is governed by a preposition, this is weak because the preposition is not repeated.

﴿Do you not know that God is powerful over everything?﴾ Ibn 'Atiyyah said: its apparent sense is a pure interrogative, so the corresponding (mu'adil) element here, according to a group, is "or do you want." Others said: here "am" is disjunctive (munqati'ah), so the corresponding element according to them is omitted, its estimate being "or do you know." All of this is on the basis that addressing the Prophet ﷺ intends addressing his community. But if he alone is addressed, the corresponding element is omitted and nothing else, and both opinions are transmitted. End of his words and his citation. What they said is not good. Rather, this is an interrogative whose meaning is affirmation (taqrir), so it needs no corresponding element at all. The better view is that the addressee is the hearer, and the interrogative in the sense of affirmation is very common in their speech, especially when it enters upon a negation: ﴿Is not God the most knowing of what is in the breasts of the worlds?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 10]? ﴿Is not God the most just of judges?﴾ [al-Tin: 8]? ﴿Did We not raise you among us as a child?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 18]? ﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?﴾ [al-Duha: 6]? ﴿Did We not expand your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh: 1]? All of this is interrogative in which no corresponding element is needed, because only affirmation is intended. The meaning: you have already known, O addressee, that God is capable of everything, so He has the disposal of His servants' obligations, by erasing, affirming, and replacing one ruling with another, and by bringing for you the better or the like. The reason for addressing a single addressee is that no person fails to imagine that he is the one addressed by this, the one alerted by it, and the one affirmed on a fact established in his mind, namely that God's power relates to all things, so nothing can frustrate Him. When this is so, abrogation is not denied, because God does what He wills and rules what He desires; none repels His command and none overturns His judgment. In His saying ﴿Do you not know that God﴾ there is a shift from a plural addressed pronoun, in ﴿from your Lord﴾, to a singular addressed pronoun for the wisdom we have explained, and a shift from a first-person speaker who magnifies himself to an apparent third-person noun, God, since it is the proper name comprising all attributes, so within it is the attribute of power. It is more emphatic in attributing power to Him than the magnifying first-person pronoun. For this reason He turned from "Do you not know that We" to "Do you not know that God." The explanation of His saying ﴿Indeed God is powerful over everything﴾ [al-Baqarah: 20] has already passed at the beginning of this surah, so that suffices and it need not be repeated.

﴿وَلَا الْمُشْرِكِينَ﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to ﴿مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ﴾ (from the People of the Book).

I saw in a book by Abu Ishaq al-Shirazi, the author of al-Tanbih, a passage refuting the Shi'a and those who share their view that the prescribed method for the feet in ablution (wudu') is wiping (masḥ), on the basis that the conjunction in His saying ﴿وَأَرْجُلَكُمْ﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6] is conjoined to His saying ﴿بِرُءُوسِكُمْ﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6]. In that book, Abu Ishaq gave the reading وأرجلِكم with the genitive (jarr) an explanation: that it is a case of khafḍ 'ala al-jiwar (genitive by proximity), and that its original form is the accusative (naṣb), so it was put in the genitive by attraction to the adjacent word. In the same book he indicated that the Qur'an and the Arabic language both attest to the permissibility of this, and he cited as an example of it His saying in this verse, ﴿وَلَا الْمُشْرِكِينَ﴾, and His saying ﴿لَمْ يَكُنِ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ وَالْمُشْرِكِينَ مُنْفَكِّينَ﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 1], holding that the original form is the nominative, that is, ﴿وَلَا الْمُشْرِكُونَ﴾, conjoined to ﴿الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾. This is the talk of one who falls short in Arabic grammar, who presumes to speak on it without knowledge, and who turns away from carrying the wording on its correct meaning and its eloquent construction.

The particle ﴿لَا﴾ in His saying ﴿وَلَا الْمُشْرِكِينَ﴾ is there for emphasis (li'l-ta'kid), and had this been outside the Qur'an, it would have been permissible to omit it. It does not appear in His saying ﴿لَمْ يَكُنِ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ وَالْمُشْرِكِينَ مُنْفَكِّينَ﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 1] for a reason that will be mentioned there, God willing.

﴿أَنْ يُنَزَّلَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾: this is in the position of the object of ﴿يَوَدُّ﴾ (wishes). It is built in the passive (mabni li'l-maf'ul), and the agent is omitted because it is known, and because it is made explicit in His saying ﴿مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ﴾. Had it been built in the active, the phrase ﴿مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ﴾ would not have appeared.

(﴿مِنْ خَيْرٍ﴾): ﴿مِنْ﴾ is extra (za'idah), and the sense is: "good from your Lord." Its addition here is acceptable, although ﴿يُنَزَّلَ﴾ is not directly preceded by the negative particle. It is not like the phrase "ma yukrimu min rajul" (no man honours…), because the negation extends to it in meaning: when wishing (widdad) is negated, it is as if its object (the sending down) were negated. There are parallels to this in the speech of the Arabs. Among them is His saying: ﴿أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا أَنَّ اللَّهَ الَّذِي خَلَقَ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ وَلَمْ يَعْيَ بِخَلْقِهِنَّ بِقَادِرٍ﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 33]. Since the negation precedes, the insertion of the particle ﴿بِ﴾ is acceptable. Similarly the Arabs say: "ma zanantu ahadan yaqulu dhalika illa Zayd" (I did not think anyone said that except Zayd), with Zayd in the nominative as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun concealed in ﴿يَقُولُ﴾, although the negative particle does not directly precede it, because the meaning is: "No one says that except Zayd, as far as I think."

This explanation follows the view of Sibawayh and al-Khalil. As for the view of al-Akhfash and the Kufans in this place, the insertion is permissible, because they do not require that the judgement be negated from what the particle enters upon; rather they permit its insertion in affirmative statements and otherwise. Al-Akhfash adds that he permits its insertion before a definite noun (ma'rifah). A group held that ﴿مِنْ﴾ is partitive (li'l-tab'id), and on this view the object that was not named as agent is ﴿عَلَيْكُمْ﴾, and the meaning is: "that there be sent down upon you some good from your Lord."

(﴿مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ﴾): ﴿مِنْ﴾ here marks the starting point (li-ibtida' al-ghayah), as when you say "this good is from Zayd." It is also permissible for it to be partitive. The meaning is "good that comes from the goods of your Lord." When it marks the starting point, it is connected to ﴿يُنَزَّلَ﴾; when it is partitive, it is connected to an omitted element, and this involves the omission of a modifying noun (mudaf), as we have estimated. The "good" here is the Qur'an, or revelation (al-wahy), since it encompasses the Qur'an and other things; or what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was singled out for in terms of honour; or wisdom, the Qur'an and victory; or prophethood and Islam; or knowledge, jurisprudence and wisdom; or it is general here, covering all kinds of good. They wish that these would not be bestowed upon the believers. There are seven opinions, the last of which is the most apparent.

The reason for their not wishing this: as for the Jews, it is because prophethood was among the children of Isma'il, and because they feared for their leadership. As for the Christians, it is because of their denial of the claim that Jesus is divine and the Son of God, and because they feared for their leadership. As for the polytheists, it is because of their reviling of their gods and their belittling of their intellects, and out of envy that a man from among them should be singled out for the message and that people should follow him.

* *

﴿وَاللَّهُ يَخْتَصُّ بِرَحْمَتِهِ مَنْ يَشَاءُ﴾: that is, He singles it out for them (yufrid bi-ha). The opposite of ikhtisas (singling out) is ishtirak (sharing). It is possible that ﴿يَخْتَصُّ﴾ here is intransitive, meaning "is singled out," or transitive, meaning "singles out," since the verb occurs in both ways. One says: "ikhtassa Zayd bi-kadha" and "akhtassu-hu bi-hi" (I singled him out for it). Its being transitive here is not necessary, as some have mentioned, since the sentence is also valid as "God singles out with His mercy whom He wills," in which case ﴿مَنْ﴾ is the agent. It is the form ifta'ala derived from khassastu Zayd bi-kadha. When it is intransitive, it denotes the action of the subject upon itself, as in: "idturartu" (I was compelled). When it is transitive, it agrees with the bare form, as in: "kasaba Zayd malan" and "iktasaba Zayd malan" (Zayd earned wealth). Mercy here is general, encompassing all its kinds; or it means prophethood, wisdom and victory, with which Muhammad (ﷺ) was singled out, as said by 'Ali, al-Baqir, Mujahid and al-Zajjaj; or it means Islam, as said by Ibn 'Abbas; or the Qur'an; or the Prophet (ﷺ), as in His saying ﴿وَمَا أَرْسَلْنَاكَ إِلَّا رَحْمَةً لِلْعَالَمِينَ﴾ [al-Anbiya': 107], he being the Prophet of mercy. These are five opinions, the first of which is the most apparent.

﴿وَاللَّهُ ذُو الْفَضْلِ الْعَظِيمِ﴾: it has already been stated that ﴿ذُو﴾ means "possessor of" (sahib). The mention of a number of the rules concerning ﴿ذُو﴾: describing with ﴿ذُو﴾ is considered by them more noble than describing with ﴿صَاحِب﴾, because they stated that ﴿ذُو﴾ is always used only in construct with a noun, so what it denotes is more noble. That is why one finds Dhu Ru'ayn, Dhu Yazan and Dhu al-Kala', whereas they did not hear of "Sahib Ru'ayn" or "Sahib Yazan" and the like. It is not permitted to say, of a companion named Abu Sa'id or Jabir, "Dhu Rasul Allah (ﷺ)," though it is permitted to say "Sahib Rasul Allah (ﷺ)." For this reason God described Himself with His saying ﴿ذُو الْجَلَالِ﴾ [al-Rahman: 27] and ﴿ذُو الْفَضْلِ﴾. The difference between His saying ﴿وَذَا النُّونِ إِذْ ذَهَبَ مُغَاضِبًا﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87] and His saying ﴿وَلَا تَكُنْ كَصَاحِبِ الْحُوتِ﴾ [al-Qalam: 48] will come, God willing.

The explanation of ﴿الْفَضْلِ الْعَظِيمِ﴾ has already been given. It is permissible that what is meant here is all kinds of bounties, in which case the ﴿الْ﴾ is for comprehensiveness (li'l-istighraq), and its greatness is due to its breadth and abundance; or it means the bounty of prophethood. God has described this as great in His saying ﴿وَكَانَ فَضْلُ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكَ عَظِيمًا﴾ [al-Nisa': 113]; or it means the Sharia, and its greatness is due to its explanation of rulings: the lawful, the unlawful, the recommended, the disliked and the permissible; or it means reward and recompense, and its greatness is due to its breadth and abundance: ﴿فَلَا تَعْلَمُ نَفْسٌ مَا أُخْفِيَ لَهُمْ مِنْ قُرَّةِ أَعْيُنٍ﴾ [al-Sajdah: 17], and the hadith: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived." On these interpretations the ﴿الْ﴾ is for definiteness (li'l-'ahd), and the most apparent opinion is the first.

﴿مَا نَنْسَخْ مِنْ آيَةٍ﴾: the occasion of its revelation, as they mention, is that when the Jews envied the Muslims for facing the Ka'bah in prayer and disparaged Islam, they said: "Muhammad orders his companions to do one thing today and forbids them from it tomorrow, says one thing today and retracts it tomorrow. This Qur'an is nothing but from Muhammad, and it contradicts itself, one part against another." So this was revealed.

The commentators have spoken here about the reality of the legal abrogation (naskh shar'i) and its types, what is agreed upon concerning it and what is disputed, its rational permissibility, its occurrence in the Sharia, what it abrogates by, and other rulings on abrogation and the proofs for those rulings, and they have gone at length. All of this is the subject matter of the science of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), where all of it is discussed. This has been our custom: every principle in any science is referred to that science for its establishment, and in the science of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis) we take it as settled from that science, and we do not lengthen the discussion of it in the science of tafsir, lest we depart from the method of tafsir, as Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn 'Umar al-Razi, known as Ibn Khatib al-Ray, did. He gathered in his tafsir many lengthy matters that have no need in the science of tafsir. For this reason it is reported of some extreme scholars that he said: "It contains everything except tafsir."

We have already mentioned in the introduction what the science of tafsir requires. Whoever goes beyond that is superfluous in this science. The parallel to what al-Razi and others did is this: a grammarian begins to write a book on grammar, then starts discussing the altered alif (al-alif al-munqalibah), and says: is the alif in "Allah" converted from a ya' or a waw? Then he digresses from this into speech about God Most High, what is necessary for Him, what is permissible for Him and what is impossible for Him. Then he digresses into the permissibility of God sending messengers to people. Then he digresses into the attributes of the Messenger (ﷺ). Then he digresses from that into the inimitability of what the Qur'an brought and the truth of what it contains. Then he digresses into the fact that among its contents are resurrection and recompense with reward and punishment, and that the rewarded in Paradise will not have their bliss cut off, nor the punished in Hell have their torment cut off. While he is in the midst of discussing the altered alif, he suddenly speaks about Paradise and Hell. Whoever follows this course in knowledge is at the extreme of confusion and muddle. Our teacher, the great scholar Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn Ibrahim ibn al-Zubayr al-Thaqafi, may God sanctify his dust, used to say something to the effect of: "Whenever you see a man moving from one discipline to another in his research or writing, know that this is either because of the deficiency of his knowledge of that discipline, or because of the muddling of his mind and his failure to grasp, as he supposes that things that differ are alike."

I have only gone into such detail in this section so that whoever reads it may benefit, and so that no one thinks that we were unaware of what people have placed in their books of tafsir. Rather, we deliberately left that aside and limited ourselves to what befits the science of tafsir. I ask God for success in what is right.

And regarding His saying ﴿ما نَنْسَخْ﴾ (whatever We abrogate), it is a conditional construction (shart), and it is a fronted object (maf'ul muqaddam). In ﴿نَنْسَخْ﴾ there is an iltifat (a shift in grammatical person), since it moves from the third-person absent to the first-person plural speaker. Do you not see His saying ﴿واللَّهُ يَخْتَصُّ﴾ (And Allah specially chooses) and ﴿واللَّهُ ذُو الفَضْلِ﴾ (And Allah is the possessor of great bounty)?

The majority read ﴿نَنْسَخْ﴾ from nasakha, meaning "to remove" (azala). It is therefore general, covering the removal of both the wording and the ruling together, or the removal of the wording alone, or the removal of the ruling alone.

A group, and Ibn 'Amir among the Seven, read ﴿ما نُنْسِخْ﴾ from al-insakh (causing abrogation). Abu 'Ali al-Farisi objected to this reading, saying: "It is not a valid usage, because one does not say nasakha and ansakha with the same meaning. Nor is the hamza here for transitivity, because the meaning would then be: 'whatever verse is written down', i.e. 'whatever verse is sent down', and then the entire Qur'an would be abrogated by this, and that is not the case. So it only remains that the meaning is: 'whatever we find to be abrogated', as one says: aḥmadtu al-rajul (I found the man praiseworthy) when you find him praiseworthy, and abkhaltuhu (I found him stingy) when you find him stingy." Abu 'Ali said: "We would find it abrogated only by its being abrogated, so the readings agree in meaning even though they differ in wording." End of his words.

So he made the hamza in naskh not for transitivity, but for indicating that a thing exists in the sense of what is derived from the root, and this is one of the meanings of af'ala mentioned in the Fatiha. Al-Zamakhshari, however, made the hamza in it for transitivity, saying: "Its causing abrogation (insakhuha) is the commanding of its abrogation, namely that he commands Jibril (peace be upon him) to make it abrogated, by informing him of its abrogation." This is a confused expression of the meaning that the hamza is for transitivity. Its clarification is that nasakha is transitive to one object, so when the hamza of transfer (hamzat al-naql) enters, it becomes transitive to two. You say: nasakha Zayd al-shay' (Zayd abrogated the thing), meaning he removed it; and ansakhahu iyyahu 'Amr (ʿAmr caused it to be abrogated for him), meaning ʿAmr made Zayd abrogate the thing, that is, remove it.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The estimate is ﴿ما نَنْسَخْكَ مِن آيَةٍ﴾, that is, "whatever verse We cause you to abrogate", i.e. "whatever We permit you to abrogate." It is as if, when God abrogated it, He permitted His Prophet (ﷺ) to leave it, by that abrogation, and so He named that permission insakh (causing abrogation). This which Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned is also the making of the hamza for transitivity, but he and al-Zamakhshari differed regarding the omitted first object: is it Jibril or the Prophet (ﷺ)? Al-Zamakhshari made insakh the commanding of abrogation, while Ibn 'Atiyyah made insakh the permission to leave something by abrogation.

Ibn 'Atiyyah also explained this reading by another explanation, namely that the hamza here is also for transitivity, and that it is from the copying of a book (naskh al-kitab), which is transferring it without removing it. He said: The meaning would be: "whatever We write down and send down from the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), or whatever We delay in it and leave, so We do not send it down, in whichever way We do it, We bring something better than what was delayed and left, or like it." Thus the pronouns in ﴿مِنها﴾ and ﴿بِمِثْلِها﴾ refer back to the pronoun in ﴿نَنْسَأْها﴾. End of his words.

He overlooked a grammatical rule, namely that the conditional noun (ism al-shart) must have a resumptive pronoun in its response (jawab) referring back to it. In His saying ﴿ما نَنْسَخْ﴾, ma is conditional, and His saying ﴿أوْ نَنْسَأْها﴾ refers back to the verse. Although the meaning does not refer back to it in itself in terms of wording and meaning, it refers back to it in wording only, not in meaning. This is like the saying: "I have a dirham and half of it" (ʿindi dirham wa niṣfuh), which in reality is with the implicit ma of the conditional, the estimate being: "or whatever We delay of a verse." This is because the abrogated is not the delayed. But the statement ﴿ما نَنْسَخْ مِن آيَةٍ﴾ remains detached from the response, since there is no resumptive pronoun in it to link it to the response, and that is not permitted. Therefore this meaning is invalid.

﴿مِن آيَةٍ﴾ (of a verse): min here is partitive (lil-tab'id), and āya is singular but stands in the place of the plural, similar to fāris in your saying: hadha awwal fāris (this is the first knight), the estimate being awwal al-fawaris (the first of the knights). The meaning is: "whatever of the verses." The same applies to what comes in this manner in the Qur'an and in the speech of the Arabs, which is analysed in this way, such as His saying ﴿ما يَفْتَحِ اللَّهُ لِلنّاسِ مِن رَحْمَةٍ﴾ (Whatever mercy Allah opens to the people) [Fatir: 2], ﴿وما بِكم مِن نِعْمَةٍ﴾ (And whatever blessing is upon you) [al-Nahl: 53], and the saying: man yaḍrib min rajul aḍribhu (whoever strikes from among men, I will strike him). This prepositional phrase clarifies what was the object of the conditional verb, since it particularises it, for the conditional noun carries generality. If you had not brought the prepositional phrase, it would be understood as general. If you say: "man yaḍrib aḍrib" (whoever strikes, I strike), it is general in the signification of man. But when you say min rajul, the category of men is particularised by this, and women are not included in it, although the signification of min is general for both kinds.

For this reason some grammarians made min āya and what resembles it in the position of accusative (naṣb) as a specification (tamyiz). He said: "The specified noun is what he said, and the estimate is: 'whatever thing was abrogated of a verse.'" He said: "It is not good to estimate it as ayyu āya nansakh (which verse We abrogate), because you do not combine āya with a specifier in āya. You do not say: ayya āya nansakh min āya, nor ayyu rajul yaḍrib min rajul aḍribhu."

They also permitted that min be superfluous (zā'ida), and that āya be a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). The meaning is: "whatever thing We abrogate, little or much." They said: The word āya has come as a ḥāl in His exalted saying ﴿ناقَةُ اللَّهِ لَكم آيَةً﴾ (This is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you) [al-A'raf: 73]. But this is corrupt, because the ḥāl is not put in the genitive by min.

They also permitted that ma be a verbal noun (maṣdar), and āya be the direct object (maf'ul bihi), the estimate being: "whatever kind of abrogation We abrogate a verse with." The coming of the conditional ma as a maṣdar is permitted. You say: ma taḍrib Zaydan aḍrib mithlahu (whatever manner of striking you strike Zayd with, I strike him with its like). The estimate is: "whatever kind of striking you strike Zayd with, I strike with its like." The poet said:

"The crow cawed, so I said: 'Imminent separation, whatever you wish, when they departed for separation, then caw!'"

But this is corrupt, because if you make ma as the abrogation (li-l-naskh), the response is left bereft of a pronoun referring back to it, and there must be a pronoun referring back to the conditional noun. Do you not see that if you said: ayya ḍarb yaḍrib Hindan aḍrib aḥsana minha (whatever kind of striking one strikes Hind with, I strike with a better kind than it), it would not be permitted, because the response clause would be bereft of a pronoun referring back to the conditional noun? The pronoun in minha refers back to the object which is Hind, not to ayya ḍarb, which is the conditional noun. Also, the direct object may not have the superfluous min unless two conditions are met: that a negative precedes it, and that what min enters upon is indefinite. This is according to the well-known school of the Basran grammarians. And the conditional is not of the category of the negative, so it is not permitted to say: in qama min rajul aqum ma'ahu (if a man should stand up, I will stand with him). There is a weak disagreement on this among some Basran grammarians.

(أوْ نَنْسَأْها) (or We cause it to be forgotten, or We delay it): ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Nakha'i, ʿAta', Mujahid, ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read it, and among the Seven, Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read: aw nanskha'ha, with the opening of the nun of the present tense and the sin, and the hamza being silent. A group also read it like this, except without a hamza. Abu ʿUbayd al-Bakri mentioned in his book al-Lali' that this reading is from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, and I think it is a mistake, and Ibn ʿAtiyyah said the same. He said: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas read tansaha with a ta' that is open, the nun silent, and the sin open, without a hamza, and this is the reading of al-Hasan and Ibn Ya'mar. A group read likewise, except that they used a hamza. Abu Haywa read likewise, except that he raised the ta'. Sa'id read likewise, except without a hamza. The rest of the Seven read nunsiha, with the nun raised, the sin lowered, without a hamza. A group read likewise, except that they put a hamza after the sin. al-Dahhak and Abu Raja' read with the first nun raised, the second nun opened, the sin doubled, and without a hamza. Ubayy read aw nunsika, with the first nun raised, the second nun silent, the sin lowered, without a hamza, and with the kaf of address instead of the third-person pronoun. In the codex of Salim the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfa, it is like this, except that he combined the two pronouns, and this was the reading of Abu Hudhayfa. al-A'mash read: ma nunsika min aya aw nansakh-ha najji' bi-mithliha. Thus it is established in the codex of ʿAbd Allah. So there are eleven readings for this word, apart from the reading of al-A'mash: with the hamza: nanse'ha, nunsi'ha, nunsi'ha (hmm)...

[Note: the list in the original is: with hamza: nansa'ha, nansi'ha, nunsa'ha, tansa'ha; without hamza: nansaha, nunsiha, tansaha, tunsiha, nunsika, nunsikaha.]

The naskh here has been explained as tabdil (replacement), said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Zajjaj, or the replacement of the ruling while the writing remains, said by ʿAbd Allah and also Ibn ʿAbbas, or raf' (lifting), said by al-Suddi.

As for His saying ﴿أوْ نُنْسِها﴾ without a hamza: if it is from forgetting, the opposite of remembering, then the meaning is "We cause you to forget it" if it is from the form af'ala, or "We cause it to be forgotten" if it is from the form fa'ala. This was said by Mujahid and Qatada. If it is from leaving, then the meaning is: "or We leave off sending it down," said by al-Dahhak; or "We erase it, so We do not leave for it a wording that is recited nor a ruling that is binding," said by Ibn Zayd; or "We command leaving it," as one says: ansaytuhu al-shay' (I made him forget the thing), meaning I commanded him to leave it, and nasiytuhu (I forgot him), meaning I left him. The poet said:

"Indeed upon me is a debt I will pay; I am not forgetting it, nor will I make it forgotten."

That is, I do not command its abandonment.

Al-Zajjaj said: The reading nunsiha, with the nun raised, the second nun silent, and the sin lowered, has no meaning of abandonment, because one does not say unsiya in the sense of "he left". Abu ʿAli al-Farisi and others said: That is valid, because it means "We make you leave it". Al-Zajjaj similarly weakened the view that the verse should be understood as forgetting, the opposite of remembrance, and he said: This did not happen to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he never forgot any Qur'an. Abu ʿAli and others said: That is permissible, and it has occurred, and there is no difference between the verse being lifted by abrogation or by causing it to be forgotten. Al-Zajjaj cited His saying exalted: ﴿ولَئِنْ شِئْنا لَنَذْهَبَنَّ بِالَّذِي أوْحَيْنا إلَيْكَ﴾ (And if We willed, We would surely take away what We revealed to you) [al-Isra': 86], meaning: We did not do it. Abu ʿAli said: Its meaning is: We did not take away all of it. Al-Tabari related al-Zajjaj's view from one earlier than him.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: The correct view in this is that the Prophet (ﷺ) forgetting what God willed to make him forget, and He did not intend to establish it as Qur'an, is permissible. As for forgetting which is a human defect, the Prophet (ﷺ) is protected from it before the conveying and after the conveying, as long as no one among the Companions has memorised it. But after it has been memorised, what is permissible for humans is permissible for him, because he has conveyed and fulfilled the trust. From this is the hadith, when he omitted a verse. When he finished the prayer he said: "Is Ubayy among the people?" He said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Then why did you not remind me?" He said: "I feared that it had been lifted." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It was not lifted, but I forgot it." End of the words of Ibn ʿAtiyyah.

As for the one who read with the hamza, it is from delay. The Arabs say: nasa'tu al-ibil ʿan al-hawd (I delayed the camels from the watering trough), and ansa'a al-ibil ʿan dhama'iha yawman aw yawmayn aw akthar (he delayed the camels from their thirst a day or two days or more), meaning he delayed them from the watering. In the verse, the meaning is: "We delay its abrogation or its sending down," said by ʿAta' and Ibn Abi Najih; or "We erase it in wording and ruling," said by Ibn Zayd; or "We let it stand, so We do not abrogate it," said by Abu ʿUbayda. This is weakened by His saying ﴿نَأْتِ بِخَيْرٍ مِنها﴾ (We bring something better than it), because what is allowed to stand and remain is not described as "We bring something better than it."

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that in the verse there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), its estimate being: "What We replace of the ruling of a verse, We bring something better than it for you, or like it. Then He said: aw nansa'ha, i.e. We delay it, so We do not abrogate it nor replace it." This report is not sound from that scholar Ibn ʿAbbas, because it contradicts the arrangement of the Qur'an's wording.

(نَأْتِ) (We bring): this is the response of the conditional, and the conditional noun here is followed by a conditional and a response both in the present tense. This is the best construction for the two verbs of condition and response, namely that both be in the present tense.

(بِخَيْرٍ مِنها) (with something better than it): Apparently khayran here is the elative (af'al al-tafdil), and the superiority is evident, because what is brought, if it is lighter than the abrogated or the delayed, its superiority is with respect to the lifting of the burdens of obligation; and if it is heavier, its superiority is with respect to the increase of reward.

(Or one like it): or one equal to it in obligation and reward, as in the abrogation of facing Bayt al-Maqdis by facing the Ka'bah. Some people held that khayr here is not an elative (af'al al-tafdil, comparative form) but is one of the kinds of good (khayr min al-khuyur), like khayr in His saying: ﴿that there should be sent down to you any good from your Lord﴾. According to them it is a verbal noun (masdar), and min denotes the starting point of the limit (min li-ibtida' al-ghayah). The meaning becomes: whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring a better one of the goods from the standpoint of the abrogated or forgotten verse. But this meaning is weakened by His saying "or one like it," for on this meaning it is not valid to coordinate it with His saying "a better," unless khayr is applied to the absence of obligation, so that the meaning becomes: We bring one of the goods, which is the absence of obligation, or We bring one like the abrogated or forgotten verse. It is as if He is saying: whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, [it is replaced] with no substitute, or with an equivalent substitute. The one with no substitute is a good that reaches you from the standpoint of the abrogated or forgotten verse, since it is relief for you from obligations. As for coordinating "one like it" with the pronoun in "than it" that is governed by a preposition, this is weak because the preposition is not repeated.

﴿Do you not know that God is powerful over everything?﴾ Ibn 'Atiyyah said: its apparent sense is a pure interrogative, so the corresponding (mu'adil) element here, according to a group, is "or do you want." Others said: here "am" is disjunctive (munqati'ah), so the corresponding element according to them is omitted, its estimate being "or do you know." All of this is on the basis that addressing the Prophet ﷺ intends addressing his community. But if he alone is addressed, the corresponding element is omitted and nothing else, and both opinions are transmitted. End of his words and his citation. What they said is not good. Rather, this is an interrogative whose meaning is affirmation (taqrir), so it needs no corresponding element at all. The better view is that the addressee is the hearer, and the interrogative in the sense of affirmation is very common in their speech, especially when it enters upon a negation: ﴿Is not God the most knowing of what is in the breasts of the worlds?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 10]? ﴿Is not God the most just of judges?﴾ [al-Tin: 8]? ﴿Did We not raise you among us as a child?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 18]? ﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?﴾ [al-Duha: 6]? ﴿Did We not expand your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh: 1]? All of this is interrogative in which no corresponding element is needed, because only affirmation is intended. The meaning: you have already known, O addressee, that God is capable of everything, so He has the disposal of His servants' obligations, by erasing, affirming, and replacing one ruling with another, and by bringing for you the better or the like. The reason for addressing a single addressee is that no person fails to imagine that he is the one addressed by this, the one alerted by it, and the one affirmed on a fact established in his mind, namely that God's power relates to all things, so nothing can frustrate Him. When this is so, abrogation is not denied, because God does what He wills and rules what He desires; none repels His command and none overturns His judgment. In His saying ﴿Do you not know that God﴾ there is a shift from a plural addressed pronoun, in ﴿from your Lord﴾, to a singular addressed pronoun for the wisdom we have explained, and a shift from a first-person speaker who magnifies himself to an apparent third-person noun, God, since it is the proper name comprising all attributes, so within it is the attribute of power. It is more emphatic in attributing power to Him than the magnifying first-person pronoun. For this reason He turned from "Do you not know that We" to "Do you not know that God." The explanation of His saying ﴿Indeed God is powerful over everything﴾ [al-Baqarah: 20] has already passed at the beginning of this surah, so that suffices and it need not be repeated.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 108–109 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Do you not know that to God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 107]? This is also an interrogative (istifham) that enters upon a negation, so it is an affirmation (taqrir), and it has no counterpart (mu'adil), because the meaning of taqrir is affirmation. That is, you have already known, O addressee, that God has authority over the heavens and the earth and control over them. He manages your affairs and directs them as He chooses, including abrogation (naskh) and other things. He singled out the heavens and the earth for dominion because they are among the greatest of created things, and because they encompass all created things. Since His control extends over both extremes, He is in control of all that they contain. Or it may be that He refers to His higher creatures by "the heavens" and His lower creatures by "the earth."

These two sentences include an affirmation of the two attributes by which the complete exercise of authority is achieved: power (qudrah) and control (istila'). A person may be able, in the sense that he has the capability to do something, but he may lack control over that thing, so that he cannot carry out what he is capable of doing. When capability and the absence of any impediment come together, the exercise of authority is complete, along with the will. He began with the affirmation of the attribute of power, because it is more emphatic than the attribute of control and authority.

﴿And you have no protector or helper besides God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 107]: He shifted from the singular form of address to the plural form of the group. The plural suits the context here, because the negated item becomes explicit in generality through the entry of min upon it. So it fits that what is negated should also be general. The meaning is: for each one of you there is no single protector.

﴿Protector (wali) or helper﴾ [al-Baqarah: 107]: He used the form walī, which is fa'īl, for emphasis (mubalaghah), and because it is more common in usage. For this reason, the word wali (wāl) did not occur in the Qur'an except in surah al-Ra'd, for the sake of matching the closing rhyme (fawasil). He used naṣīr, in the pattern fa'īl, to match walī in being of the pattern fa'īl, to match the endings of the verses, and because it is more intensive than fā'il. The min in "min waliyy" is extra (za'idah), so it is not connected to anything. The min in "min dun Allah" is connected to what the genitive phrase "lakum" is connected to, and that is attached to something omitted (mahdhuf), since it occupies the position of the predicate. The word mā here may be Tamimi (i.e., it does not operate as the Hijazi negative), and it may be Hijazi, according to the view of those who permit the predicate of mā to precede it when it is an adverbial phrase or a prepositional phrase. As for those who prohibit this, mā cannot be Hijazi. The first min denotes the starting point (ibtida' al-ghayah). The name of God is repeated explicitly in these three sentences and is not replaced by a pronoun, to indicate the independence of each sentence and that they are not linked to one another in a way that would require a pronoun.

Since the first two sentences are for affirmation, which in meaning is an assertion, it fits that the third sentence be a negation of a protector and a helper. That is, the things that are under God's power, authority, and control cannot restrain Him from what He wills concerning them, and no one can overpower Him in what He wills.

﴿Or do you wish to question your Messenger as Moses was questioned before?﴾: There is disagreement about the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of this verse. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that it was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Umayya and a group of Quraysh, who said: "O Muhammad, make al-Safa into gold, widen the land of Mecca for us, and make rivers gush forth through it in a gushing, and we will believe in you." It was also said: The Jews and other polytheists made wishes. Some of them said: "Bring us a Book from heaven all at once, as Moses brought the Torah." Others said: "Bring me a Book from heaven that contains, from the Lord of the worlds, to 'Abd Allah ibn Umayya: I have sent Muhammad to the people." Others said: "We will not believe you until you bring God and the angels before us as a group." It was also said: Rafi' ibn Khuzayma and Wahb ibn Zayd said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Bring us a Book from heaven, and make rivers gush forth for us, and we will follow you." It was also said: A group of the Companions said to the Prophet ﷺ: "I wish our sins had the same course as the sins of the Children of Israel, in hastening punishment in this world." He said: "The Children of Israel, when a sin befell them, would find it written on the door of the sinner. If he atoned for it, it would be a disgrace for him in this world, and if he did not atone for it, it would be a disgrace for him in the Hereafter." It was also said: The Jews and the disbelievers of Quraysh asked that al-Safa be returned to gold, and it was said to them: "Take it, like the table for the Children of Israel," but they refused and drew back. It was also said: A people asked that a Dhat Anwat be made for them, as there was for the polytheists. It was a tree they worshipped, on which they hung fruit and other food and their weapons. Just as the Children of Israel asked Moses and said: "Make for us a god as they have gods." It is possible that all of these were causes of the revelation of this verse. We have been lengthy in mentioning these causes, contrary to our purpose in this book.

Here, am (أم) is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and the disjunctive am is estimated as bal (بل, "rather") plus the hamzah of interrogation. The meaning is: "Rather, do you wish...?" So bal indicates a turning away from what precedes it. The turning away here means a transition from one sentence to another, not a cancellation of the first. The view of those who made am here connective (mu'adilah) to the first interrogative has already been mentioned, and we have shown its weakness. A group said: am is an interrogative cut off from the first, as if he said: "Do you wish?" Both of these views are weak. What is established is that am is of two kinds: connective (muttasilah) and disjunctive (munfasilah). The connective am requires that it be preceded by the interrogative hamzah and that what follows it be a single noun, or something equivalent to a single noun. The disjunctive am is one in which one or both of these conditions are absent, and in that case it is estimated as bal and hamzah together. As for its coming in the sense of the hamzah alone, or in the sense of bal alone, or as an extra particle, these views are weak.

Depending on the disagreement about the addressees, the discussion of "your Messenger" (rasulakum) follows. If the address is to the believers, as is the view of al-Asamm, al-Jubba'i, and Abu Muslim, then "your Messenger" comes according to the reality of the matter and according to what they acknowledged of his messengership. If the address is to the disbelievers, the attribution of the Messenger to them is according to the reality as it is in itself, not according to their acknowledgment of it. The view that the address is to the believers is preferred on the basis of God's words: ﴿And whoever exchanges disbelief for faith﴾, since this statement is valid only with regard to a believer. It is also preferred because the verse is coordinated with His words: ﴿Do not say: "Ra'ina"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 104], meaning: "Will you do what you have been commanded, or do you wish (to do something else)?" The view that they are the Jews is also preferred, because the discussion has already preceded concerning what they said in the narratives about them, and because a believer in the Messenger hardly asks him something that would be disbelief.

"As he was questioned" (kama su'ila): The kaf is in the accusative position. According to the view of Sibawayh, it is a circumstantial clause (hal). According to the well-known view of the grammarians (mu'rabun), it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), so it is estimated as: "a questioning as he was questioned." According to the view of Sibawayh, it is estimated as: "that you ask him," i.e., the questioning as he was questioned. Here ma is verbal (masdariyyah), and the estimate is: "like the questioning of." Al-Hawfi permitted that ma be a relative pronoun (mawsulah) in the sense of alladhi (which), the estimate being: "that which Moses was asked." Abu Ja'far, Shayba, and al-Zuhri read su'ila with a vowel of the sound of ś. Al-Hasan and Abu al-Sammal read it with a kasra on the sin and a ya. Some readers read it with the hamzah softened between-between and a damma on the sin. These readings are based on the two dialects regarding sa'ala: that the hamzah is retained and fatha is pronounced, so one says sa'ala. According to this dialect, the reading of the majority is the reading of one who softens the hamzah between-between. The second dialect is that the middle radical of the root is a waw, and the form is fa'ila with kasra on the middle radical, so one says: silt asal, like khiftu akhaf. Its original is su'iltu. According to this dialect, the reading of al-Hasan and the reading of one who gives a mixed vowel (ishmam) are valid. Explaining these two readings according to this dialect is more preferable than explaining them as if the original of the alif were the hamzah, which was changed to an alif so that it became like qala and baa'a, so that it was said of it: sīla with pure kasra or ishmam. This is because this substitution is anomalous and not analogical. The second dialect is a second language, and so it is better to apply what is an established dialect than to apply the anomalous, non-regular one. The subject is omitted here because it is known, the estimate being: "as the people of Moses asked Moses before."

﴿Moses before (min qabl)﴾: This prepositional phrase is connected to the verb su'ila. Qabl is cut off from its genitive construction in form, because the noun it is attached to is a definite noun which has been omitted. For this reason qabl is built on damma, and the estimate is: "from before your questioning." This is emphasis, because it is known that the questioning of the Children of Israel of Moses, upon our Prophet and upon him be blessings and peace, preceded the questioning of these people of the Messenger of God ﷺ. The questioning of the people of Moses, peace be upon him, is their saying: ﴿Show us God openly﴾ [al-Nisa': 153], ﴿Make for us a god﴾ [al-A'raf: 138]. God intended to rebuke them for the fact that their desire was attached to asking the Messenger of God ﷺ and proposing demands to him, since what has been revealed to them is sufficient for them. He compared their questioning to the questioning of what the ancestors of the Jews proposed, of things whose outcome is calamity. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that the questioning did not actually take place from them. Do you not see that He said: ﴿Or do you wish to ask﴾? He rebuked them for their desire being attached to asking. If the questioning had taken place, the rebuke would have been for it, not for their desire. The wording would have been: "Do you ask your Messenger?" or something similar that expresses the occurrence of the questioning. But the reports about the occasion of revelation of this verse have agreed, even though they differ in specifying the cases, that the questioning did take place.

* *

﴿And whoever exchanges disbelief for faith?﴾ The discussion of exchange (tabdil) has already preceded, meaning: whoever takes disbelief instead of faith. This is a metaphor (kinayah) for turning away from faith and turning towards disbelief, as in God's words: ﴿They bought error in exchange for guidance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16]. Al-Zamakhshari explained this by saying: whoever abandons trust in the revealed signs, doubts them, and asks for other than them. Abu al-'Aliyah said: disbelief here means hardship, and faith means ease. This is weak, unless he means that these two terms are used figuratively for hardship upon oneself and ease in exchange for torment and blessing. As for the well-known hardships and ease of the affairs of this world, the verse is not interpreted that way. The apparent meaning is to take disbelief and faith in their true legal (shar'i) senses. This is because whoever asked the Messenger what he asked, despite the manifest miracles and the clear evidences of his truthfulness, his question was one of obstinacy and denial, and that is disbelief.

﴿Then he has certainly strayed from the right way﴾: This is the answer of the conditional clause. The discussion of straying (dalal) has already preceded in God's words: ﴿nor of those who are astray﴾ [al-Fatihah: 7], and of "sawa'" (equal, evenly-balanced) in God's words: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6], and that sawa' can mean "equal" (mustawin). For this reason, it bears a pronoun in the saying: "I passed by a man, sawa' (equal), he and nothing," and it is used as a qualifier in: ﴿Come to a word (kalimah) that is equal (sawa') between us and you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 64]. It is also explained in the sense of justice and fairness, because that is even. Zuhayr said:

"Show us a course with no fault in it, in which fairness (al-sawa') levels us all equally."

It is also explained in the sense of the middle. God said: ﴿So he saw him in the midst (sawa') of the Hellfire﴾ [al-Saffat: 55], meaning in its middle. 'Isa ibn 'Umar said: "I wrote until my sawa' (middle finger/side) was cut off." Hassan said:

"Alas for the Helpers of the Prophet and his kin, after he was hidden in the midst of the grave-niche (sawa' al-mulhad)."

Abu 'Ubayda interpreted al-sawa' in the verse in this sense, and al-Farra' interpreted it as "the middle path" (al-qasd).

Since the Sharia leads its follower to the good pleasure of Allah the Exalted, He referred to it as "the Way" (al-sabil), and made whoever deviates from it like one who has lost his way. He alluded to their asking of their Prophet what it was not permissible for them to ask, by exchanging disbelief for faith, and He expressed this in the form of a conditional sentence. The apodosis of the condition has not yet occurred, as a warning against it and as a distancing from it. So He first rebuked them for their desire to ask what they were not entitled to ask, and addressed them with that, then included them in the general scope of the conditional sentence. Such a thing should not occur, because it is straying from the straight method, so the beginning of the verse becomes a denunciation and rebuke, and its end a warning and a declaration of misguidance. Whatever leads to this, no aim, request or desire should be attached to it. The assimilation (idgham) of the dal into the dad is a permissible assimilation (idgham). It has been read as (fa-qad dalla) with assimilation and with clear pronunciation (izhar) among the Seven Readings.

﴿Many of the People of the Book wish⦆: The one meant by "many" is Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, or Huyayy ibn Akhtab and his brother Abu Yasir, or a group of Jews who attempted, after the Battle of Uhud, to make the Muslims return to their religion, or Finhas ibn 'Awarua, Zayd ibn Qays and a group of Jews who tried to make Huzayfa and 'Ammar return to their religion. These are sayings. The Qur'an did not specify anyone; it only reported the wishing of many of the People of the Book.
