The disagreement over the occasion of revelation is based on the disagreement over the interpretation of "many of the People of the Book," and the qualifier was particularized by His words "of the People of the Book," so the omission of the modified noun and the placing of the qualifier in its position was good. The Book here is the Torah.

﴿If they could turn you back after your faith into disbelievers⦆: The discussion of "law" (law) here is like the discussion of it in His words: ﴿each one of them wishes he could be given a life of a thousand years﴾ [al-Baqara: 96]. Whoever says it is a verbal (masdariyya) particle, says that law with the verb in the sense of a verbal noun is the object of "wish," meaning: they wish your returning. Whoever makes it a particle for what would have happened because of the occurrence of something else, makes the answer omitted and makes the object of "wish" omitted, the estimate being: they wish your returning you as disbelievers; if they were to turn you back as disbelievers they would be delighted by that. Some people said its estimate is: if they were to turn you back as disbelievers they would wish that. So "wish" indicates the answer, and the first "wish" cannot be the answer, because the condition of law is that it precedes the answer. End of quote. What he estimated is not valid, because if you make the answer of law his words "they would wish that," that would indicate that the wishing did not occur, since it is an answer to law, which is for what would have happened because of the occurrence of something else, so the occurrence of the wishing is prevented because the occurrence of the returning is prevented. The point is that the wishing has indeed occurred. Do you not see the sayings of the exegetes on the occasion of revelation of this verse? Although they differed, they agreed on the occurrence of the wishing, although their sayings differed as to who it occurred from. The estimate of the answer of law as "they would wish that" indicates that the wishing did not occur, so the estimate of its answer as "they would be delighted by that" or "they would rejoice at that" is the one that is determined, if you make law require an answer. Here "yaruddu" means "makes (someone) become," so it takes two objects: the first is the pronoun of address, and the second is "kuffaran." Some have parsed it (i'rab) as a circumstantial accusative (hal), and this is weak, because the circumstantial accusative is dispensable in most of its occurrences, while here it is indispensable. "Min" is connected to "yaruddu" and is for the starting point of the end (ibtida' al-ghaya). The apparent meaning of the waw in "yaruddunakum" is that it is for the plural. Whoever interprets "kathiran" as one or two, and makes the waw for him or for them, has not kept to the original usage.

﴿out of envy from themselves⦆: "Hasadan" is in the accusative as an object of cause (maf'ul min ajlihi), and its governing element is "wadda," meaning: what drives them to wish your returning as disbelievers is envy. They allowed it to be an infinitive (masdar) in the accusative as a circumstantial, meaning "envious," and it is not pluralized because it is an infinitive, and this is weak, because making an infinitive a circumstantial is not analogical. They also allowed its accusative to be as an absolute object (masdar), with a verb governing it that is omitted and indicated by the meaning, the estimate being: they envied you with envy. The first view is more evident, because the conditions of the object of cause are gathered in it. The prepositional phrase "min 'indi anfusihim" is connected either to the word that is pronounced, which is "wadda," meaning: they wished that from the side of their desire, not that their wishing that was from the direction of religiosity and following the truth. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He: ﴿after the truth has become clear to them⦆? Or it is connected to an estimated element, so it is in the place of a qualifier, the estimate being: envy existing from their own selves. On both estimates it is an emphasis, meaning: their wishing or their envy is from their own initiative. Do you not see that the wishing of disbelief and envy toward faith can only be from their own selves? So it is like His words: ﴿nor a bird that flies with its two wings⦆ [al-An'am: 38]. It has been said: the prepositional phrase is connected to His words "yaruddunakum," and "min" is causal, meaning the returning is from their own initiative and by their misleading and their embellishment.

﴿after the truth has become clear to them⦆: "Min" here is connected to His words "wadda," meaning: their wishing your disbelief is due to the envy arising from their own selves. That wishing began from the time the truth became evident and clear to them, so they are not among the heedless ones to whom the clarity of the truth may be obscure, rather it is by way of envy and stubbornness. This indicates that disbelief occurs out of obstinacy. Do you not see the apparent sense of His words: ﴿after the truth has become clear to them⦆? Ibn 'Atiyya said: The People of the Sunna (ahl al-Sunna) differed over the permissibility of that. The correct view according to me is its permissibility by reason, and its remoteness in occurrence, and it follows in every verse that requires it that knowledge is removed from the one who is in a second state of stubbornness. End of his words. The "al" in "al-haqq" is either for the known (al-'ahd), and by it is meant faith, and its preceding context indicates this, or the "al" is for totality (al-istighraq), meaning: after the aspects and kinds of the truth have become clear to them.

﴿So pardon and overlook⦆: Ibn 'Abbas said: it is abrogated (mansukha) by His words: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah⦆ [al-Tawba: 29]. It has been said: by His words: ﴿kill the polytheists⦆ [al-Tawba: 5]. Some people said: this is not the definition of abrogation (naskh), because this, in reality, was for the purpose of specifying its time limit.

﴿until Allah brings His command⦆: He made pardoning and overlooking end at this limit, and this was a truce until the command of Allah came with the killing of the Banu Qurayza, the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir and their humiliation by the jizya, and other things that came from the rulings of the Sharia concerning them, and the abandonment of pardon and overlooking. Al-Kalbi said: it is the Islam of some and the destruction of others. It has been said: the terms of the children of Adam. It has been said: the Resurrection. It has been said: the requital on the Day of Resurrection. It has been said: the strength of the message and the multiplication of the community. The majority hold that it is the command to fight. From al-Baqir: he was not commanded to fight until there was revealed: ﴿Permission is given to those who are being fought⦆ [al-Hajj: 39]. The command to pardon and overlook is that they should not be fought, and that one should turn away from their reply, so that this is more effective in quieting the uproar, extinguishing the strife, and the Islam of some of them, not that this occurs with approval, because that would be disbelief.

﴿Indeed Allah is over all things competent⦆: The interpretation of this verse has passed, and in it is an indication of retribution against the disbelievers and a promise to the believers of victory and empowerment. Do you not see that He commanded truce by pardoning and overlooking, and made that end at the point where Allah brings His command, then informed that He is capable of all things?

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 108–109 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Do you not know that to God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 107]? This is also an interrogative (istifham) that enters upon a negation, so it is an affirmation (taqrir), and it has no counterpart (mu'adil), because the meaning of taqrir is affirmation. That is, you have already known, O addressee, that God has authority over the heavens and the earth and control over them. He manages your affairs and directs them as He chooses, including abrogation (naskh) and other things. He singled out the heavens and the earth for dominion because they are among the greatest of created things, and because they encompass all created things. Since His control extends over both extremes, He is in control of all that they contain. Or it may be that He refers to His higher creatures by "the heavens" and His lower creatures by "the earth."

These two sentences include an affirmation of the two attributes by which the complete exercise of authority is achieved: power (qudrah) and control (istila'). A person may be able, in the sense that he has the capability to do something, but he may lack control over that thing, so that he cannot carry out what he is capable of doing. When capability and the absence of any impediment come together, the exercise of authority is complete, along with the will. He began with the affirmation of the attribute of power, because it is more emphatic than the attribute of control and authority.

﴿And you have no protector or helper besides God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 107]: He shifted from the singular form of address to the plural form of the group. The plural suits the context here, because the negated item becomes explicit in generality through the entry of min upon it. So it fits that what is negated should also be general. The meaning is: for each one of you there is no single protector.

﴿Protector (wali) or helper﴾ [al-Baqarah: 107]: He used the form walī, which is fa'īl, for emphasis (mubalaghah), and because it is more common in usage. For this reason, the word wali (wāl) did not occur in the Qur'an except in surah al-Ra'd, for the sake of matching the closing rhyme (fawasil). He used naṣīr, in the pattern fa'īl, to match walī in being of the pattern fa'īl, to match the endings of the verses, and because it is more intensive than fā'il. The min in "min waliyy" is extra (za'idah), so it is not connected to anything. The min in "min dun Allah" is connected to what the genitive phrase "lakum" is connected to, and that is attached to something omitted (mahdhuf), since it occupies the position of the predicate. The word mā here may be Tamimi (i.e., it does not operate as the Hijazi negative), and it may be Hijazi, according to the view of those who permit the predicate of mā to precede it when it is an adverbial phrase or a prepositional phrase. As for those who prohibit this, mā cannot be Hijazi. The first min denotes the starting point (ibtida' al-ghayah). The name of God is repeated explicitly in these three sentences and is not replaced by a pronoun, to indicate the independence of each sentence and that they are not linked to one another in a way that would require a pronoun.

Since the first two sentences are for affirmation, which in meaning is an assertion, it fits that the third sentence be a negation of a protector and a helper. That is, the things that are under God's power, authority, and control cannot restrain Him from what He wills concerning them, and no one can overpower Him in what He wills.

﴿Or do you wish to question your Messenger as Moses was questioned before?﴾: There is disagreement about the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of this verse. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that it was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Umayya and a group of Quraysh, who said: "O Muhammad, make al-Safa into gold, widen the land of Mecca for us, and make rivers gush forth through it in a gushing, and we will believe in you." It was also said: The Jews and other polytheists made wishes. Some of them said: "Bring us a Book from heaven all at once, as Moses brought the Torah." Others said: "Bring me a Book from heaven that contains, from the Lord of the worlds, to 'Abd Allah ibn Umayya: I have sent Muhammad to the people." Others said: "We will not believe you until you bring God and the angels before us as a group." It was also said: Rafi' ibn Khuzayma and Wahb ibn Zayd said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Bring us a Book from heaven, and make rivers gush forth for us, and we will follow you." It was also said: A group of the Companions said to the Prophet ﷺ: "I wish our sins had the same course as the sins of the Children of Israel, in hastening punishment in this world." He said: "The Children of Israel, when a sin befell them, would find it written on the door of the sinner. If he atoned for it, it would be a disgrace for him in this world, and if he did not atone for it, it would be a disgrace for him in the Hereafter." It was also said: The Jews and the disbelievers of Quraysh asked that al-Safa be returned to gold, and it was said to them: "Take it, like the table for the Children of Israel," but they refused and drew back. It was also said: A people asked that a Dhat Anwat be made for them, as there was for the polytheists. It was a tree they worshipped, on which they hung fruit and other food and their weapons. Just as the Children of Israel asked Moses and said: "Make for us a god as they have gods." It is possible that all of these were causes of the revelation of this verse. We have been lengthy in mentioning these causes, contrary to our purpose in this book.

Here, am (أم) is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and the disjunctive am is estimated as bal (بل, "rather") plus the hamzah of interrogation. The meaning is: "Rather, do you wish...?" So bal indicates a turning away from what precedes it. The turning away here means a transition from one sentence to another, not a cancellation of the first. The view of those who made am here connective (mu'adilah) to the first interrogative has already been mentioned, and we have shown its weakness. A group said: am is an interrogative cut off from the first, as if he said: "Do you wish?" Both of these views are weak. What is established is that am is of two kinds: connective (muttasilah) and disjunctive (munfasilah). The connective am requires that it be preceded by the interrogative hamzah and that what follows it be a single noun, or something equivalent to a single noun. The disjunctive am is one in which one or both of these conditions are absent, and in that case it is estimated as bal and hamzah together. As for its coming in the sense of the hamzah alone, or in the sense of bal alone, or as an extra particle, these views are weak.

Depending on the disagreement about the addressees, the discussion of "your Messenger" (rasulakum) follows. If the address is to the believers, as is the view of al-Asamm, al-Jubba'i, and Abu Muslim, then "your Messenger" comes according to the reality of the matter and according to what they acknowledged of his messengership. If the address is to the disbelievers, the attribution of the Messenger to them is according to the reality as it is in itself, not according to their acknowledgment of it. The view that the address is to the believers is preferred on the basis of God's words: ﴿And whoever exchanges disbelief for faith﴾, since this statement is valid only with regard to a believer. It is also preferred because the verse is coordinated with His words: ﴿Do not say: "Ra'ina"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 104], meaning: "Will you do what you have been commanded, or do you wish (to do something else)?" The view that they are the Jews is also preferred, because the discussion has already preceded concerning what they said in the narratives about them, and because a believer in the Messenger hardly asks him something that would be disbelief.

"As he was questioned" (kama su'ila): The kaf is in the accusative position. According to the view of Sibawayh, it is a circumstantial clause (hal). According to the well-known view of the grammarians (mu'rabun), it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), so it is estimated as: "a questioning as he was questioned." According to the view of Sibawayh, it is estimated as: "that you ask him," i.e., the questioning as he was questioned. Here ma is verbal (masdariyyah), and the estimate is: "like the questioning of." Al-Hawfi permitted that ma be a relative pronoun (mawsulah) in the sense of alladhi (which), the estimate being: "that which Moses was asked." Abu Ja'far, Shayba, and al-Zuhri read su'ila with a vowel of the sound of ś. Al-Hasan and Abu al-Sammal read it with a kasra on the sin and a ya. Some readers read it with the hamzah softened between-between and a damma on the sin. These readings are based on the two dialects regarding sa'ala: that the hamzah is retained and fatha is pronounced, so one says sa'ala. According to this dialect, the reading of the majority is the reading of one who softens the hamzah between-between. The second dialect is that the middle radical of the root is a waw, and the form is fa'ila with kasra on the middle radical, so one says: silt asal, like khiftu akhaf. Its original is su'iltu. According to this dialect, the reading of al-Hasan and the reading of one who gives a mixed vowel (ishmam) are valid. Explaining these two readings according to this dialect is more preferable than explaining them as if the original of the alif were the hamzah, which was changed to an alif so that it became like qala and baa'a, so that it was said of it: sīla with pure kasra or ishmam. This is because this substitution is anomalous and not analogical. The second dialect is a second language, and so it is better to apply what is an established dialect than to apply the anomalous, non-regular one. The subject is omitted here because it is known, the estimate being: "as the people of Moses asked Moses before."

﴿Moses before (min qabl)﴾: This prepositional phrase is connected to the verb su'ila. Qabl is cut off from its genitive construction in form, because the noun it is attached to is a definite noun which has been omitted. For this reason qabl is built on damma, and the estimate is: "from before your questioning." This is emphasis, because it is known that the questioning of the Children of Israel of Moses, upon our Prophet and upon him be blessings and peace, preceded the questioning of these people of the Messenger of God ﷺ. The questioning of the people of Moses, peace be upon him, is their saying: ﴿Show us God openly﴾ [al-Nisa': 153], ﴿Make for us a god﴾ [al-A'raf: 138]. God intended to rebuke them for the fact that their desire was attached to asking the Messenger of God ﷺ and proposing demands to him, since what has been revealed to them is sufficient for them. He compared their questioning to the questioning of what the ancestors of the Jews proposed, of things whose outcome is calamity. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that the questioning did not actually take place from them. Do you not see that He said: ﴿Or do you wish to ask﴾? He rebuked them for their desire being attached to asking. If the questioning had taken place, the rebuke would have been for it, not for their desire. The wording would have been: "Do you ask your Messenger?" or something similar that expresses the occurrence of the questioning. But the reports about the occasion of revelation of this verse have agreed, even though they differ in specifying the cases, that the questioning did take place.

* *

﴿And whoever exchanges disbelief for faith?﴾ The discussion of exchange (tabdil) has already preceded, meaning: whoever takes disbelief instead of faith. This is a metaphor (kinayah) for turning away from faith and turning towards disbelief, as in God's words: ﴿They bought error in exchange for guidance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16]. Al-Zamakhshari explained this by saying: whoever abandons trust in the revealed signs, doubts them, and asks for other than them. Abu al-'Aliyah said: disbelief here means hardship, and faith means ease. This is weak, unless he means that these two terms are used figuratively for hardship upon oneself and ease in exchange for torment and blessing. As for the well-known hardships and ease of the affairs of this world, the verse is not interpreted that way. The apparent meaning is to take disbelief and faith in their true legal (shar'i) senses. This is because whoever asked the Messenger what he asked, despite the manifest miracles and the clear evidences of his truthfulness, his question was one of obstinacy and denial, and that is disbelief.

﴿Then he has certainly strayed from the right way﴾: This is the answer of the conditional clause. The discussion of straying (dalal) has already preceded in God's words: ﴿nor of those who are astray﴾ [al-Fatihah: 7], and of "sawa'" (equal, evenly-balanced) in God's words: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6], and that sawa' can mean "equal" (mustawin). For this reason, it bears a pronoun in the saying: "I passed by a man, sawa' (equal), he and nothing," and it is used as a qualifier in: ﴿Come to a word (kalimah) that is equal (sawa') between us and you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 64]. It is also explained in the sense of justice and fairness, because that is even. Zuhayr said:

"Show us a course with no fault in it, in which fairness (al-sawa') levels us all equally."

It is also explained in the sense of the middle. God said: ﴿So he saw him in the midst (sawa') of the Hellfire﴾ [al-Saffat: 55], meaning in its middle. 'Isa ibn 'Umar said: "I wrote until my sawa' (middle finger/side) was cut off." Hassan said:

"Alas for the Helpers of the Prophet and his kin, after he was hidden in the midst of the grave-niche (sawa' al-mulhad)."

Abu 'Ubayda interpreted al-sawa' in the verse in this sense, and al-Farra' interpreted it as "the middle path" (al-qasd).

Since the Sharia leads its follower to the good pleasure of Allah the Exalted, He referred to it as "the Way" (al-sabil), and made whoever deviates from it like one who has lost his way. He alluded to their asking of their Prophet what it was not permissible for them to ask, by exchanging disbelief for faith, and He expressed this in the form of a conditional sentence. The apodosis of the condition has not yet occurred, as a warning against it and as a distancing from it. So He first rebuked them for their desire to ask what they were not entitled to ask, and addressed them with that, then included them in the general scope of the conditional sentence. Such a thing should not occur, because it is straying from the straight method, so the beginning of the verse becomes a denunciation and rebuke, and its end a warning and a declaration of misguidance. Whatever leads to this, no aim, request or desire should be attached to it. The assimilation (idgham) of the dal into the dad is a permissible assimilation (idgham). It has been read as (fa-qad dalla) with assimilation and with clear pronunciation (izhar) among the Seven Readings.

﴿Many of the People of the Book wish⦆: The one meant by "many" is Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, or Huyayy ibn Akhtab and his brother Abu Yasir, or a group of Jews who attempted, after the Battle of Uhud, to make the Muslims return to their religion, or Finhas ibn 'Awarua, Zayd ibn Qays and a group of Jews who tried to make Huzayfa and 'Ammar return to their religion. These are sayings. The Qur'an did not specify anyone; it only reported the wishing of many of the People of the Book. The disagreement over the occasion of revelation is based on the disagreement over the interpretation of "many of the People of the Book," and the qualifier was particularized by His words "of the People of the Book," so the omission of the modified noun and the placing of the qualifier in its position was good. The Book here is the Torah.

﴿If they could turn you back after your faith into disbelievers⦆: The discussion of "law" (law) here is like the discussion of it in His words: ﴿each one of them wishes he could be given a life of a thousand years﴾ [al-Baqara: 96]. Whoever says it is a verbal (masdariyya) particle, says that law with the verb in the sense of a verbal noun is the object of "wish," meaning: they wish your returning. Whoever makes it a particle for what would have happened because of the occurrence of something else, makes the answer omitted and makes the object of "wish" omitted, the estimate being: they wish your returning you as disbelievers; if they were to turn you back as disbelievers they would be delighted by that. Some people said its estimate is: if they were to turn you back as disbelievers they would wish that. So "wish" indicates the answer, and the first "wish" cannot be the answer, because the condition of law is that it precedes the answer. End of quote. What he estimated is not valid, because if you make the answer of law his words "they would wish that," that would indicate that the wishing did not occur, since it is an answer to law, which is for what would have happened because of the occurrence of something else, so the occurrence of the wishing is prevented because the occurrence of the returning is prevented. The point is that the wishing has indeed occurred. Do you not see the sayings of the exegetes on the occasion of revelation of this verse? Although they differed, they agreed on the occurrence of the wishing, although their sayings differed as to who it occurred from. The estimate of the answer of law as "they would wish that" indicates that the wishing did not occur, so the estimate of its answer as "they would be delighted by that" or "they would rejoice at that" is the one that is determined, if you make law require an answer. Here "yaruddu" means "makes (someone) become," so it takes two objects: the first is the pronoun of address, and the second is "kuffaran." Some have parsed it (i'rab) as a circumstantial accusative (hal), and this is weak, because the circumstantial accusative is dispensable in most of its occurrences, while here it is indispensable. "Min" is connected to "yaruddu" and is for the starting point of the end (ibtida' al-ghaya). The apparent meaning of the waw in "yaruddunakum" is that it is for the plural. Whoever interprets "kathiran" as one or two, and makes the waw for him or for them, has not kept to the original usage.

﴿out of envy from themselves⦆: "Hasadan" is in the accusative as an object of cause (maf'ul min ajlihi), and its governing element is "wadda," meaning: what drives them to wish your returning as disbelievers is envy. They allowed it to be an infinitive (masdar) in the accusative as a circumstantial, meaning "envious," and it is not pluralized because it is an infinitive, and this is weak, because making an infinitive a circumstantial is not analogical. They also allowed its accusative to be as an absolute object (masdar), with a verb governing it that is omitted and indicated by the meaning, the estimate being: they envied you with envy. The first view is more evident, because the conditions of the object of cause are gathered in it. The prepositional phrase "min 'indi anfusihim" is connected either to the word that is pronounced, which is "wadda," meaning: they wished that from the side of their desire, not that their wishing that was from the direction of religiosity and following the truth. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He: ﴿after the truth has become clear to them⦆? Or it is connected to an estimated element, so it is in the place of a qualifier, the estimate being: envy existing from their own selves. On both estimates it is an emphasis, meaning: their wishing or their envy is from their own initiative. Do you not see that the wishing of disbelief and envy toward faith can only be from their own selves? So it is like His words: ﴿nor a bird that flies with its two wings⦆ [al-An'am: 38]. It has been said: the prepositional phrase is connected to His words "yaruddunakum," and "min" is causal, meaning the returning is from their own initiative and by their misleading and their embellishment.

﴿after the truth has become clear to them⦆: "Min" here is connected to His words "wadda," meaning: their wishing your disbelief is due to the envy arising from their own selves. That wishing began from the time the truth became evident and clear to them, so they are not among the heedless ones to whom the clarity of the truth may be obscure, rather it is by way of envy and stubbornness. This indicates that disbelief occurs out of obstinacy. Do you not see the apparent sense of His words: ﴿after the truth has become clear to them⦆? Ibn 'Atiyya said: The People of the Sunna (ahl al-Sunna) differed over the permissibility of that. The correct view according to me is its permissibility by reason, and its remoteness in occurrence, and it follows in every verse that requires it that knowledge is removed from the one who is in a second state of stubbornness. End of his words. The "al" in "al-haqq" is either for the known (al-'ahd), and by it is meant faith, and its preceding context indicates this, or the "al" is for totality (al-istighraq), meaning: after the aspects and kinds of the truth have become clear to them.

﴿So pardon and overlook⦆: Ibn 'Abbas said: it is abrogated (mansukha) by His words: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah⦆ [al-Tawba: 29]. It has been said: by His words: ﴿kill the polytheists⦆ [al-Tawba: 5]. Some people said: this is not the definition of abrogation (naskh), because this, in reality, was for the purpose of specifying its time limit.

﴿until Allah brings His command⦆: He made pardoning and overlooking end at this limit, and this was a truce until the command of Allah came with the killing of the Banu Qurayza, the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir and their humiliation by the jizya, and other things that came from the rulings of the Sharia concerning them, and the abandonment of pardon and overlooking. Al-Kalbi said: it is the Islam of some and the destruction of others. It has been said: the terms of the children of Adam. It has been said: the Resurrection. It has been said: the requital on the Day of Resurrection. It has been said: the strength of the message and the multiplication of the community. The majority hold that it is the command to fight. From al-Baqir: he was not commanded to fight until there was revealed: ﴿Permission is given to those who are being fought⦆ [al-Hajj: 39]. The command to pardon and overlook is that they should not be fought, and that one should turn away from their reply, so that this is more effective in quieting the uproar, extinguishing the strife, and the Islam of some of them, not that this occurs with approval, because that would be disbelief.

﴿Indeed Allah is over all things competent⦆: The interpretation of this verse has passed, and in it is an indication of retribution against the disbelievers and a promise to the believers of victory and empowerment. Do you not see that He commanded truce by pardoning and overlooking, and made that end at the point where Allah brings His command, then informed that He is capable of all things?

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 110–112 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And establish the prayer and give the zakah﴾: When He commanded pardon and forgiveness, He commanded persistence in the two pillars of Islam: bodily worship and financial worship. In prayer there is intimate conversation with Allah Most High and the delight of standing before Him, and in zakah there is kindness to creation through preferring others to oneself. So they were commanded to stand before the Truth and to be kind to creation. Al-Tabari said: "Allah commanded here the prayer and the zakah only to remove what had preceded of their inclination toward the statement of the Jews, 'Ra'ina' (Do not say ra'ina), because that is a prohibition of its kind. Then He commanded the believers with what removes it." End of his words. But this does not have that clarity.

﴿And whatever good you put forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah﴾: When He had put first the command to pray and give zakah, He followed it with this conditional sentence, general to all kinds of good, so that the prayer, the zakah, and other things are included in it. The discussion of the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of mā and min khayr is like the discussion of the analysis of mā nansakh min āyah (Whatever verse We abrogate). They said: mā may be the object (maf'ūlah); min khayr may be a circumstantial (ḥāl) or a verbal noun (maṣdar); min khayr may be the object (maf'ūl) or the object (maf'ūlah); min khayr may be a specifier (tamyīz) or an object (maf'ūlah); and min khayr is partitive (tab'īḍiyyah), attached to an omitted element. This is the view we have chosen. Li-anfusikum (for your own selves) is attached to tuqaddimū, and it is with an omitted modifier, meaning for the salvation of your selves and their life, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿He will say, "Oh, I wish I had sent forward for my life"﴾ [al-Fajr: 24]. Khayr has been explained here as zakah and charity, but the more apparent meaning is generality. Tajidūhu is the answer of the condition, and the pronoun refers to mā. The goods that were sent forward are completed actions, and that very completed action does not exist again; so it is with an omitted modifier, meaning you will find its reward. He made the necessity of what is consequent upon it a form of its existence. Tajidūhu is transitive to one object, because it means "to attain." The element governing ʿinda Allāh is either the verb itself or an omitted element, in which case it is in the sense of a circumstantial (ḥāl) from the pronoun, meaning you will find it stored up and prepared with Allah. The locative sense of "with" in the meaning of physical presence is impossible here; it is rather a metaphor meaning "before," as you say: "You have a favor with me (ʿindī yad)," meaning "in my prior dealings"; or in the meaning of "in the knowledge of Allah," as in ﴿And indeed a day with your Lord is like a thousand years﴾ [al-Hajj: 47], meaning in His knowledge and decree; or in the meaning of exclusivity through attribution to Allah Most High, as an honour, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord do not disdain His worship﴾ [al-A'raf: 206].

﴿Indeed Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾: The use of the apparent noun (Allah) indicates the independence of the sentences; therefore it came as "Indeed Allah" and not "Indeed He," although that was possible in the speech. This is a declarative sentence, and there is evident coherence in ending what precedes with it. It contains both promise and warning. By His saying "Seeing" he meant knowledge of the observed, meaning that the deed of any doer is not hidden from Him and He does not waste it. Whoever is seeing your action is not hidden from him whether it is good or bad. He used the word "Seeing" (baṣīr) rather than "one who sees" (mubṣir), either because it derives from baṣura, which indicates firmness and natural disposition with regard to a human being, or because it is an intensive form (fa'īl) in the meaning of mufʿil, which is for multiplicity. It may also be that fa'īl is in the meaning of mufʿil, like samīʿ in the meaning of musmiʿ. Some Sufis said: The seeker must maintain connections and persist in seeking means through various kinds of acts of drawing near to Allah, confident that what he has sent forward of truthful struggles will bear fruit in the final states. They recited:

*Hasten to good and be quick to it, for behind you is only what you know.*
*And put forward good, for every man will come to what he has put forward.*

﴿And they said, "None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian"﴾: The occasion of its revelation was the dispute between the Christians of Najran and the Jews of Madinah, and their argument before the Messenger ﷺ. The Jews said: ﴿The Christians are not on anything﴾ [al-Baqarah: 113], and the Christians said: ﴿The Jews are not on anything﴾ [al-Baqarah: 113], and they denied the Torah and Moses. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The pronoun in "and they said" refers to the People of the Book, Jews and Christians, and the saying "None will enter Paradise" is attributed to them collectively, because the statement came from all of them in the sense that each group said it, not that every single individual said it, judging that the restriction of entry into Paradise applies to every individual Jew and Christian. For this reason "or" (aw) is used, which is for specification and classification. The enmity between the two groups, and their misguiding of one another, made clear that this is so, and it was impossible for each group to judge the other as entering Paradise. Similar to this in the gathering of the pronoun, and in "or" being for specification, is His saying: ﴿And they said, "Be Jews or Christians and you will be guided"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 135], since it is known that a Jew does not command Christianity, nor does a Christian command Judaism. Since entry into Paradise is later, the negation came with "lan" (never), the particle that makes the future definite (al-mukhallisah li-l-istiqbāl). Man is the subject of yadkhula, and this is from the emptied exception (istithnāʾ mufarragh), and the meaning is: "No one will enter Paradise except one who is..." It is permissible, according to the view of al-Farra', for it to be a substitute (badal), or for it to be in the accusative as an exception, since he permits that the omitted element be taken into account and made the subject while being omitted. Had it been pronounced, a substitute or the accusative of exception would have been permissible; likewise when it is omitted and first carried to the wording of man, so the pronoun in kāna is singular, then it is carried to the meaning, so it is plural in the predicate of kāna, and He said: ﴿Jews or Christians﴾. Hūd is the plural of hāʾid, like ʿāʾid and ʿūd. The singular of al-Naṣārā has already been discussed, whether it is anṣarān or naṣrī. There is disagreement about the permissibility of such two kinds of agreement, namely that the predicate be other than a verb, but an adjective whose masculine and feminine are distinguished by the ta' marker, as in: "Whoever was standing (man kāna qāʾimīn), the men (al-zaydūn)," and "Whoever was standing, the two men (al-zaydān)." The view of the Kufans and many of the Basrans is that this is permissible. A group went to prohibition, and to this went Abu al-ʿAbbas (al-Mubarrad), but they are refuted by the occurrence of this in the speech of the Arabs, as in this verse, for hūdan in its most apparent sense is the plural of hāʾid, which is among the adjectives whose masculine and feminine are distinguished by the ta' marker, and like the saying of the poet:

*And he woke those among you who were sleeping.*

So niyām is the plural of nāʾim, which is among the adjectives whose masculine and feminine are distinguished by the ta' marker. He put Hūd before Naṣārā because of its precedence in time. Ubayy recited: "Illā man kāna yahūdiyyan aw naṣrāniyyan," so he carried both the noun and the predicate to the wording, which is singular and masculine.

﴿Those are their wishful thinkings﴾: This is a nominal sentence of subject and predicate, inserted between their statement and the demand for proof of the validity of their claim. Tilka is used to point to a single item and to a plural that is not a sound masculine or feminine plural, and al-Zamakhshari carried it to the plural. He said: "It refers to the wishes mentioned: their wish that no good from their Lord descend upon the believers, their wish to return them as disbelievers, and their wish that no one other than them enter Paradise. That is, those vain wishes are their wishes." End of his words. What he went to in the first aspect is not apparent, because every sentence in which their desire for something is mentioned has been separated, completed, and independent in its revelation, so it is far-fetched to refer to it. As for what he went to in the second aspect, it contains metaphorical omission, and it contains an inversion of the structure, since the original is that tilka should be the subject (mubtada') and amāniyyuhum the predicate (khabar). He inverted the structure, saying that their wishes in their falsity are like this wish of theirs. In it also is that when the predicate is the one likened to the subject, it is not permissible to place it first, as in "Zayd, Zuhayr"; the grammarians stated this. When that which is the origin for being likened to something is placed first, it is of the reverse of likening and of the category of exaggeration, since the branch is made the origin and the origin a branch, as in your saying: "The lion is Zayd in courage." The more apparent view is that tilka is a reference to their statement, "None will enter Paradise." That is, that statement is their wishful thinking, meaning this is not based on verification or proof from the Book of Allah, nor from reports from a Messenger, but rather it is by way of wishing. Although they themselves were certain of their statement, since it was not based on evidence, it was wishful thinking, and wishing occurs with the possible and the impossible. This is among the impossible, and for this reason the word amāniyy was used and not "what they hope for," since hope (rajāʾ) is related to the possible. You say: "Would that I were a bird (layta-nī ṭāʾir)," and it is not permissible to say "Perhaps I am a bird (laʿallanī ṭāʾir)." The subject was made singular in wording because it is a metonym for the statement, and the statement is a verbal noun that may be used for few or many. So here it is intended to mean many, with regard to those who say it; for this reason the predicate was made plural (khayr?), so that it agreed in meaning in plurality. The explanation of amāniyy has already been discussed in His saying: ﴿They know not the Book except wishful recitations﴾ [al-Baqarah: 78]. It may be that the meaning is: "Those are their lies and falsehoods," or "Those are their chosen preferences and desires," or "Those are their recitations."

﴿Say, "Bring your proof, if you should be truthful"﴾: When their claim was put forward that none would enter Paradise except those they named, they were asked for evidence for the validity of their claim. In this is evidence that whoever claims a negation or an affirmation must have proof. The verse indicates the invalidity of taqlīd (blind imitation), which is accepting something without evidence. Al-Zamakhshari said: "This is the most destructive thing to the position of the imitators, and that every statement for which there is no evidence is false. If you are truthful, then bring your proof, that is, make your claim clear." The apparent meaning of the verse is that the object of truthfulness is their claim that they are specially entitled to enter Paradise. It was said: "Truthful in your faith." It was said: "Truthful in your wishes." It was said that the meaning of ṣādiqīn is ṣāliḥīn (righteous), as you claim, and everything that is attributed to righteousness and good is attributed to truthfulness. You say: "A man of truth (rajul ṣidq)," "a true friend (ṣadīq ṣidq)," "a true guide (dālla ṣidq)." From this is His saying: ﴿This is a day when their truthfulness will benefit the truthful﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 119]. It was said: the meaning of ﴿This is a day when their truthfulness will benefit the truthful﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 119] is: if you are certain of what Allah took as His covenant and pledges. From this is His saying: ﴿Among the believers are men who were true to what they pledged to Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 23].

(Balā): It is a rejection of their statement, "None will enter Paradise," and the discussion of it is like the discussion that preceded in His saying: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil﴾ [al-Baqarah: 81], and before that: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80]. Both of them contain negation and affirmation, except that the former is an emptied exception with respect to times, and this is an emptied exception with respect to agents. He is far off who went to the view that balā is a rejection of the negation contained in His saying: ﴿Say, "Bring your proof"﴾, because its meaning is: "You have no proof for the truth of your claim," so with balā he affirmed that for whoever submits his face there is a proof. This view is repudiated by the wording.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 110–112 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Whoever submits his face to Allah﴾: The discussion concerning *man* (مَن, "whoever") is like the discussion concerning *man* in His words: ﴿whoever earns an evil deed﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 81]. The more evident view is that it is a *mubtada'* (the inchoative, or subject of a nominal sentence). Some grammarians allowed that it could be a *fa'il* (agent), meaning that the one who submits enters [Paradise]. If it is a *mubtada'*, it is not necessarily a conditional (*shartiyyah*) construction. Then the sentence after it is the *khabar* (predicate), and the response of the conditional is (﴿then he has his reward﴾). If it is a relative (*mawsulah*), then the sentence after it is a *silah* (relative clause) that has no place in *i'rab* (grammatical analysis), and the *khabar* is the part of the nominal sentence to which the *fa'* (fa of consequence) is attached. If *man* is an agent, then His words (﴿then he has his reward﴾) form a nominal sentence conjoined to that verb which raises *man*.

The word *wajh* (face) here may refer to the organ itself, singled out for mention because it is the most honourable of the limbs, or because it contains most of the senses, or because it is used to refer to the essence, as in His words: ﴿Everything will perish except His face﴾ [Al-Qasas: 88]. It may also mean the direction, and the meaning would then be: he sincerely devoted his way in religion to Allah. Muqatil said: he sincerely devoted his religion. Ibn Abbas said: he sincerely devoted his deed to Allah. It was also said: his intention. It was also said: he entrusted his affair to Allah, the Exalted. It was also said: he humbled himself and showed humility. These statements are close in meaning. The early scholars (*salaf*) said them as examples, not as though each one were a fixed meaning contradicting the others. This is like the grammarian who says: "The agent is Zayd" in your saying "Zayd stood," while another says: "Ja'far" in "Ja'far went out," and another says: "'Amr" in "'Amr set off." This is the best that may be assumed of the early scholars, may God have mercy on them, regarding what has been transmitted from them of this kind.

﴿and he is a doer of good﴾: This is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah haliyyah*), and it is emphatic in meaning, because whoever submits his face to Allah is a doer of good. Al-Zamakhshari restricted *ihsan* (doing good) to action, and he understood His words ﴿whoever submits his face to Allah﴾ to mean: whoever sincerely devotes himself to Him, not associating anything with Him, and he is a doer of good in his action. Thus the circumstantial clause here becomes explanatory, since one who does not associate has two kinds: one who is a doer of good in his action, and one who is not. This is a leaning on his Mu'tazili doctrine that action is indispensable, and that by both of these one deserves to enter Paradise. For this reason he explained His words ﴿then he has his reward﴾ as the reward that he deserves. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained the reality of legal *ihsan* when he was asked about its nature, and he said: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you." Here *ihsan* has been explained as sincerity, and it has been explained as faith, and it has been explained as carrying out the commands and refraining from the prohibitions.

﴿then he has his reward with his Lord﴾: The governing element of *'inda* (with) is the same as the governing element of *lahu* (for him), meaning: his reward is established for him with his Lord. Since He referred his reward to Allah, He attached the adverbial expression to the word *Rabb* (Lord), meaning the One who looks after his interests, nurtures him, and manages his affairs, so that this would be more encouraging to him. For this reason He used the attribute of *Rabb* and did not use a pronoun referring back to Allah in the preceding clause, nor the explicit noun "Allah." He did not say "then he has his reward with Him," for the reason we have mentioned, and because of the awkwardness of using these pronouns. Nor did He say "then he has his reward with Allah," for the meaning we have mentioned, which the word *Rabb* indicates.

﴿No fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾: The pronoun in His words ﴿upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾ is in the plural, taking the meaning of *man* (whoever). Earlier, He took it in the singular according to the wording, in His words ﴿whoever submits his face to Allah and is a doer of good, then he has his reward with his Lord﴾. This is the more eloquent usage, namely to begin first with agreement according to the wording, and then with agreement according to the meaning. The explanation of this sentence has already been given.

The reading of Ibn Muhaysin is *fala khawfu* (with a raised *fa'*, without tanwin), with variation transmitted from him. The reading of al-Zuhri, Isa al-Thaqafi, Ya'qub, and others is *fala khawfa* (with a fathah, without tanwin). Its justification has been given, so there is no need to repeat it here.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 110–112 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And establish the prayer and give the zakah﴾: When He commanded pardon and forgiveness, He commanded persistence in the two pillars of Islam: bodily worship and financial worship. In prayer there is intimate conversation with Allah Most High and the delight of standing before Him, and in zakah there is kindness to creation through preferring others to oneself. So they were commanded to stand before the Truth and to be kind to creation. Al-Tabari said: "Allah commanded here the prayer and the zakah only to remove what had preceded of their inclination toward the statement of the Jews, 'Ra'ina' (Do not say ra'ina), because that is a prohibition of its kind. Then He commanded the believers with what removes it." End of his words. But this does not have that clarity.

﴿And whatever good you put forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah﴾: When He had put first the command to pray and give zakah, He followed it with this conditional sentence, general to all kinds of good, so that the prayer, the zakah, and other things are included in it. The discussion of the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of mā and min khayr is like the discussion of the analysis of mā nansakh min āyah (Whatever verse We abrogate). They said: mā may be the object (maf'ūlah); min khayr may be a circumstantial (ḥāl) or a verbal noun (maṣdar); min khayr may be the object (maf'ūl) or the object (maf'ūlah); min khayr may be a specifier (tamyīz) or an object (maf'ūlah); and min khayr is partitive (tab'īḍiyyah), attached to an omitted element. This is the view we have chosen. Li-anfusikum (for your own selves) is attached to tuqaddimū, and it is with an omitted modifier, meaning for the salvation of your selves and their life, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿He will say, "Oh, I wish I had sent forward for my life"﴾ [al-Fajr: 24]. Khayr has been explained here as zakah and charity, but the more apparent meaning is generality. Tajidūhu is the answer of the condition, and the pronoun refers to mā. The goods that were sent forward are completed actions, and that very completed action does not exist again; so it is with an omitted modifier, meaning you will find its reward. He made the necessity of what is consequent upon it a form of its existence. Tajidūhu is transitive to one object, because it means "to attain." The element governing ʿinda Allāh is either the verb itself or an omitted element, in which case it is in the sense of a circumstantial (ḥāl) from the pronoun, meaning you will find it stored up and prepared with Allah. The locative sense of "with" in the meaning of physical presence is impossible here; it is rather a metaphor meaning "before," as you say: "You have a favor with me (ʿindī yad)," meaning "in my prior dealings"; or in the meaning of "in the knowledge of Allah," as in ﴿And indeed a day with your Lord is like a thousand years﴾ [al-Hajj: 47], meaning in His knowledge and decree; or in the meaning of exclusivity through attribution to Allah Most High, as an honour, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord do not disdain His worship﴾ [al-A'raf: 206].

﴿Indeed Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾: The use of the apparent noun (Allah) indicates the independence of the sentences; therefore it came as "Indeed Allah" and not "Indeed He," although that was possible in the speech. This is a declarative sentence, and there is evident coherence in ending what precedes with it. It contains both promise and warning. By His saying "Seeing" he meant knowledge of the observed, meaning that the deed of any doer is not hidden from Him and He does not waste it. Whoever is seeing your action is not hidden from him whether it is good or bad. He used the word "Seeing" (baṣīr) rather than "one who sees" (mubṣir), either because it derives from baṣura, which indicates firmness and natural disposition with regard to a human being, or because it is an intensive form (fa'īl) in the meaning of mufʿil, which is for multiplicity. It may also be that fa'īl is in the meaning of mufʿil, like samīʿ in the meaning of musmiʿ. Some Sufis said: The seeker must maintain connections and persist in seeking means through various kinds of acts of drawing near to Allah, confident that what he has sent forward of truthful struggles will bear fruit in the final states. They recited:

*Hasten to good and be quick to it, for behind you is only what you know.*
*And put forward good, for every man will come to what he has put forward.*

﴿And they said, "None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian"﴾: The occasion of its revelation was the dispute between the Christians of Najran and the Jews of Madinah, and their argument before the Messenger ﷺ. The Jews said: ﴿The Christians are not on anything﴾ [al-Baqarah: 113], and the Christians said: ﴿The Jews are not on anything﴾ [al-Baqarah: 113], and they denied the Torah and Moses. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The pronoun in "and they said" refers to the People of the Book, Jews and Christians, and the saying "None will enter Paradise" is attributed to them collectively, because the statement came from all of them in the sense that each group said it, not that every single individual said it, judging that the restriction of entry into Paradise applies to every individual Jew and Christian. For this reason "or" (aw) is used, which is for specification and classification. The enmity between the two groups, and their misguiding of one another, made clear that this is so, and it was impossible for each group to judge the other as entering Paradise. Similar to this in the gathering of the pronoun, and in "or" being for specification, is His saying: ﴿And they said, "Be Jews or Christians and you will be guided"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 135], since it is known that a Jew does not command Christianity, nor does a Christian command Judaism. Since entry into Paradise is later, the negation came with "lan" (never), the particle that makes the future definite (al-mukhallisah li-l-istiqbāl). Man is the subject of yadkhula, and this is from the emptied exception (istithnāʾ mufarragh), and the meaning is: "No one will enter Paradise except one who is..." It is permissible, according to the view of al-Farra', for it to be a substitute (badal), or for it to be in the accusative as an exception, since he permits that the omitted element be taken into account and made the subject while being omitted. Had it been pronounced, a substitute or the accusative of exception would have been permissible; likewise when it is omitted and first carried to the wording of man, so the pronoun in kāna is singular, then it is carried to the meaning, so it is plural in the predicate of kāna, and He said: ﴿Jews or Christians﴾. Hūd is the plural of hāʾid, like ʿāʾid and ʿūd. The singular of al-Naṣārā has already been discussed, whether it is anṣarān or naṣrī. There is disagreement about the permissibility of such two kinds of agreement, namely that the predicate be other than a verb, but an adjective whose masculine and feminine are distinguished by the ta' marker, as in: "Whoever was standing (man kāna qāʾimīn), the men (al-zaydūn)," and "Whoever was standing, the two men (al-zaydān)." The view of the Kufans and many of the Basrans is that this is permissible. A group went to prohibition, and to this went Abu al-ʿAbbas (al-Mubarrad), but they are refuted by the occurrence of this in the speech of the Arabs, as in this verse, for hūdan in its most apparent sense is the plural of hāʾid, which is among the adjectives whose masculine and feminine are distinguished by the ta' marker, and like the saying of the poet:

*And he woke those among you who were sleeping.*

So niyām is the plural of nāʾim, which is among the adjectives whose masculine and feminine are distinguished by the ta' marker. He put Hūd before Naṣārā because of its precedence in time. Ubayy recited: "Illā man kāna yahūdiyyan aw naṣrāniyyan," so he carried both the noun and the predicate to the wording, which is singular and masculine.

﴿Those are their wishful thinkings﴾: This is a nominal sentence of subject and predicate, inserted between their statement and the demand for proof of the validity of their claim. Tilka is used to point to a single item and to a plural that is not a sound masculine or feminine plural, and al-Zamakhshari carried it to the plural. He said: "It refers to the wishes mentioned: their wish that no good from their Lord descend upon the believers, their wish to return them as disbelievers, and their wish that no one other than them enter Paradise. That is, those vain wishes are their wishes." End of his words. What he went to in the first aspect is not apparent, because every sentence in which their desire for something is mentioned has been separated, completed, and independent in its revelation, so it is far-fetched to refer to it. As for what he went to in the second aspect, it contains metaphorical omission, and it contains an inversion of the structure, since the original is that tilka should be the subject (mubtada') and amāniyyuhum the predicate (khabar). He inverted the structure, saying that their wishes in their falsity are like this wish of theirs. In it also is that when the predicate is the one likened to the subject, it is not permissible to place it first, as in "Zayd, Zuhayr"; the grammarians stated this. When that which is the origin for being likened to something is placed first, it is of the reverse of likening and of the category of exaggeration, since the branch is made the origin and the origin a branch, as in your saying: "The lion is Zayd in courage." The more apparent view is that tilka is a reference to their statement, "None will enter Paradise." That is, that statement is their wishful thinking, meaning this is not based on verification or proof from the Book of Allah, nor from reports from a Messenger, but rather it is by way of wishing. Although they themselves were certain of their statement, since it was not based on evidence, it was wishful thinking, and wishing occurs with the possible and the impossible. This is among the impossible, and for this reason the word amāniyy was used and not "what they hope for," since hope (rajāʾ) is related to the possible. You say: "Would that I were a bird (layta-nī ṭāʾir)," and it is not permissible to say "Perhaps I am a bird (laʿallanī ṭāʾir)." The subject was made singular in wording because it is a metonym for the statement, and the statement is a verbal noun that may be used for few or many. So here it is intended to mean many, with regard to those who say it; for this reason the predicate was made plural (khayr?), so that it agreed in meaning in plurality. The explanation of amāniyy has already been discussed in His saying: ﴿They know not the Book except wishful recitations﴾ [al-Baqarah: 78]. It may be that the meaning is: "Those are their lies and falsehoods," or "Those are their chosen preferences and desires," or "Those are their recitations."

﴿Say, "Bring your proof, if you should be truthful"﴾: When their claim was put forward that none would enter Paradise except those they named, they were asked for evidence for the validity of their claim. In this is evidence that whoever claims a negation or an affirmation must have proof. The verse indicates the invalidity of taqlīd (blind imitation), which is accepting something without evidence. Al-Zamakhshari said: "This is the most destructive thing to the position of the imitators, and that every statement for which there is no evidence is false. If you are truthful, then bring your proof, that is, make your claim clear." The apparent meaning of the verse is that the object of truthfulness is their claim that they are specially entitled to enter Paradise. It was said: "Truthful in your faith." It was said: "Truthful in your wishes." It was said that the meaning of ṣādiqīn is ṣāliḥīn (righteous), as you claim, and everything that is attributed to righteousness and good is attributed to truthfulness. You say: "A man of truth (rajul ṣidq)," "a true friend (ṣadīq ṣidq)," "a true guide (dālla ṣidq)." From this is His saying: ﴿This is a day when their truthfulness will benefit the truthful﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 119]. It was said: the meaning of ﴿This is a day when their truthfulness will benefit the truthful﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 119] is: if you are certain of what Allah took as His covenant and pledges. From this is His saying: ﴿Among the believers are men who were true to what they pledged to Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 23].

(Balā): It is a rejection of their statement, "None will enter Paradise," and the discussion of it is like the discussion that preceded in His saying: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil﴾ [al-Baqarah: 81], and before that: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80]. Both of them contain negation and affirmation, except that the former is an emptied exception with respect to times, and this is an emptied exception with respect to agents. He is far off who went to the view that balā is a rejection of the negation contained in His saying: ﴿Say, "Bring your proof"﴾, because its meaning is: "You have no proof for the truth of your claim," so with balā he affirmed that for whoever submits his face there is a proof. This view is repudiated by the wording.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 110–112 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Whoever submits his face to Allah﴾: The discussion concerning *man* (مَن, "whoever") is like the discussion concerning *man* in His words: ﴿whoever earns an evil deed﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 81]. The more evident view is that it is a *mubtada'* (the inchoative, or subject of a nominal sentence). Some grammarians allowed that it could be a *fa'il* (agent), meaning that the one who submits enters [Paradise]. If it is a *mubtada'*, it is not necessarily a conditional (*shartiyyah*) construction. Then the sentence after it is the *khabar* (predicate), and the response of the conditional is (﴿then he has his reward﴾). If it is a relative (*mawsulah*), then the sentence after it is a *silah* (relative clause) that has no place in *i'rab* (grammatical analysis), and the *khabar* is the part of the nominal sentence to which the *fa'* (fa of consequence) is attached. If *man* is an agent, then His words (﴿then he has his reward﴾) form a nominal sentence conjoined to that verb which raises *man*.

The word *wajh* (face) here may refer to the organ itself, singled out for mention because it is the most honourable of the limbs, or because it contains most of the senses, or because it is used to refer to the essence, as in His words: ﴿Everything will perish except His face﴾ [Al-Qasas: 88]. It may also mean the direction, and the meaning would then be: he sincerely devoted his way in religion to Allah. Muqatil said: he sincerely devoted his religion. Ibn Abbas said: he sincerely devoted his deed to Allah. It was also said: his intention. It was also said: he entrusted his affair to Allah, the Exalted. It was also said: he humbled himself and showed humility. These statements are close in meaning. The early scholars (*salaf*) said them as examples, not as though each one were a fixed meaning contradicting the others. This is like the grammarian who says: "The agent is Zayd" in your saying "Zayd stood," while another says: "Ja'far" in "Ja'far went out," and another says: "'Amr" in "'Amr set off." This is the best that may be assumed of the early scholars, may God have mercy on them, regarding what has been transmitted from them of this kind.

﴿and he is a doer of good﴾: This is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah haliyyah*), and it is emphatic in meaning, because whoever submits his face to Allah is a doer of good. Al-Zamakhshari restricted *ihsan* (doing good) to action, and he understood His words ﴿whoever submits his face to Allah﴾ to mean: whoever sincerely devotes himself to Him, not associating anything with Him, and he is a doer of good in his action. Thus the circumstantial clause here becomes explanatory, since one who does not associate has two kinds: one who is a doer of good in his action, and one who is not. This is a leaning on his Mu'tazili doctrine that action is indispensable, and that by both of these one deserves to enter Paradise. For this reason he explained His words ﴿then he has his reward﴾ as the reward that he deserves. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained the reality of legal *ihsan* when he was asked about its nature, and he said: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you." Here *ihsan* has been explained as sincerity, and it has been explained as faith, and it has been explained as carrying out the commands and refraining from the prohibitions.

﴿then he has his reward with his Lord﴾: The governing element of *'inda* (with) is the same as the governing element of *lahu* (for him), meaning: his reward is established for him with his Lord. Since He referred his reward to Allah, He attached the adverbial expression to the word *Rabb* (Lord), meaning the One who looks after his interests, nurtures him, and manages his affairs, so that this would be more encouraging to him. For this reason He used the attribute of *Rabb* and did not use a pronoun referring back to Allah in the preceding clause, nor the explicit noun "Allah." He did not say "then he has his reward with Him," for the reason we have mentioned, and because of the awkwardness of using these pronouns. Nor did He say "then he has his reward with Allah," for the meaning we have mentioned, which the word *Rabb* indicates.

﴿No fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾: The pronoun in His words ﴿upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾ is in the plural, taking the meaning of *man* (whoever). Earlier, He took it in the singular according to the wording, in His words ﴿whoever submits his face to Allah and is a doer of good, then he has his reward with his Lord﴾. This is the more eloquent usage, namely to begin first with agreement according to the wording, and then with agreement according to the meaning. The explanation of this sentence has already been given.

The reading of Ibn Muhaysin is *fala khawfu* (with a raised *fa'*, without tanwin), with variation transmitted from him. The reading of al-Zuhri, Isa al-Thaqafi, Ya'qub, and others is *fala khawfa* (with a fathah, without tanwin). Its justification has been given, so there is no need to repeat it here.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 110–112 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And establish the prayer and give the zakah﴾: When He commanded pardon and forgiveness, He commanded persistence in the two pillars of Islam: bodily worship and financial worship. In prayer there is intimate conversation with Allah Most High and the delight of standing before Him, and in zakah there is kindness to creation through preferring others to oneself. So they were commanded to stand before the Truth and to be kind to creation. Al-Tabari said: "Allah commanded here the prayer and the zakah only to remove what had preceded of their inclination toward the statement of the Jews, 'Ra'ina' (Do not say ra'ina), because that is a prohibition of its kind. Then He commanded the believers with what removes it." End of his words. But this does not have that clarity.

﴿And whatever good you put forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah﴾: When He had put first the command to pray and give zakah, He followed it with this conditional sentence, general to all kinds of good, so that the prayer, the zakah, and other things are included in it. The discussion of the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of mā and min khayr is like the discussion of the analysis of mā nansakh min āyah (Whatever verse We abrogate). They said: mā may be the object (maf'ūlah); min khayr may be a circumstantial (ḥāl) or a verbal noun (maṣdar); min khayr may be the object (maf'ūl) or the object (maf'ūlah); min khayr may be a specifier (tamyīz) or an object (maf'ūlah); and min khayr is partitive (tab'īḍiyyah), attached to an omitted element. This is the view we have chosen. Li-anfusikum (for your own selves) is attached to tuqaddimū, and it is with an omitted modifier, meaning for the salvation of your selves and their life, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿He will say, "Oh, I wish I had sent forward for my life"﴾ [al-Fajr: 24]. Khayr has been explained here as zakah and charity, but the more apparent meaning is generality. Tajidūhu is the answer of the condition, and the pronoun refers to mā. The goods that were sent forward are completed actions, and that very completed action does not exist again; so it is with an omitted modifier, meaning you will find its reward. He made the necessity of what is consequent upon it a form of its existence. Tajidūhu is transitive to one object, because it means "to attain." The element governing ʿinda Allāh is either the verb itself or an omitted element, in which case it is in the sense of a circumstantial (ḥāl) from the pronoun, meaning you will find it stored up and prepared with Allah. The locative sense of "with" in the meaning of physical presence is impossible here; it is rather a metaphor meaning "before," as you say: "You have a favor with me (ʿindī yad)," meaning "in my prior dealings"; or in the meaning of "in the knowledge of Allah," as in ﴿And indeed a day with your Lord is like a thousand years﴾ [al-Hajj: 47], meaning in His knowledge and decree; or in the meaning of exclusivity through attribution to Allah Most High, as an honour, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord do not disdain His worship﴾ [al-A'raf: 206].

﴿Indeed Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾: The use of the apparent noun (Allah) indicates the independence of the sentences; therefore it came as "Indeed Allah" and not "Indeed He," although that was possible in the speech. This is a declarative sentence, and there is evident coherence in ending what precedes with it. It contains both promise and warning. By His saying "Seeing" he meant knowledge of the observed, meaning that the deed of any doer is not hidden from Him and He does not waste it. Whoever is seeing your action is not hidden from him whether it is good or bad. He used the word "Seeing" (baṣīr) rather than "one who sees" (mubṣir), either because it derives from baṣura, which indicates firmness and natural disposition with regard to a human being, or because it is an intensive form (fa'īl) in the meaning of mufʿil, which is for multiplicity. It may also be that fa'īl is in the meaning of mufʿil, like samīʿ in the meaning of musmiʿ. Some Sufis said: The seeker must maintain connections and persist in seeking means through various kinds of acts of drawing near to Allah, confident that what he has sent forward of truthful struggles will bear fruit in the final states. They recited:

*Hasten to good and be quick to it, for behind you is only what you know.*
*And put forward good, for every man will come to what he has put forward.*

﴿And they said, "None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian"﴾: The occasion of its revelation was the dispute between the Christians of Najran and the Jews of Madinah, and their argument before the Messenger ﷺ. The Jews said: ﴿The Christians are not on anything﴾ [al-Baqarah: 113], and the Christians said: ﴿The Jews are not on anything﴾ [al-Baqarah: 113], and they denied the Torah and Moses. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The pronoun in "and they said" refers to the People of the Book, Jews and Christians, and the saying "None will enter Paradise" is attributed to them collectively, because the statement came from all of them in the sense that each group said it, not that every single individual said it, judging that the restriction of entry into Paradise applies to every individual Jew and Christian. For this reason "or" (aw) is used, which is for specification and classification. The enmity between the two groups, and their misguiding of one another, made clear that this is so, and it was impossible for each group to judge the other as entering Paradise. Similar to this in the gathering of the pronoun, and in "or" being for specification, is His saying: ﴿And they said, "Be Jews or Christians and you will be guided"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 135], since it is known that a Jew does not command Christianity, nor does a Christian command Judaism. Since entry into Paradise is later, the negation came with "lan" (never), the particle that makes the future definite (al-mukhallisah li-l-istiqbāl). Man is the subject of yadkhula, and this is from the emptied exception (istithnāʾ mufarragh), and the meaning is: "No one will enter Paradise except one who is..." It is permissible, according to the view of al-Farra', for it to be a substitute (badal), or for it to be in the accusative as an exception, since he permits that the omitted element be taken into account and made the subject while being omitted. Had it been pronounced, a substitute or the accusative of exception would have been permissible; likewise when it is omitted and first carried to the wording of man, so the pronoun in kāna is singular, then it is carried to the meaning, so it is plural in the predicate of kāna, and He said: ﴿Jews or Christians﴾. Hūd is the plural of hāʾid, like ʿāʾid and ʿūd. The singular of al-Naṣārā has already been discussed, whether it is anṣarān or naṣrī. There is disagreement about the permissibility of such two kinds of agreement, namely that the predicate be other than a verb, but an adjective whose masculine and feminine are distinguished by the ta' marker, as in: "Whoever was standing (man kāna qāʾimīn), the men (al-zaydūn)," and "Whoever was standing, the two men (al-zaydān)." The view of the Kufans and many of the Basrans is that this is permissible. A group went to prohibition, and to this went Abu al-ʿAbbas (al-Mubarrad), but they are refuted by the occurrence of this in the speech of the Arabs, as in this verse, for hūdan in its most apparent sense is the plural of hāʾid, which is among the adjectives whose masculine and feminine are distinguished by the ta' marker, and like the saying of the poet:

*And he woke those among you who were sleeping.*

So niyām is the plural of nāʾim, which is among the adjectives whose masculine and feminine are distinguished by the ta' marker. He put Hūd before Naṣārā because of its precedence in time. Ubayy recited: "Illā man kāna yahūdiyyan aw naṣrāniyyan," so he carried both the noun and the predicate to the wording, which is singular and masculine.

﴿Those are their wishful thinkings﴾: This is a nominal sentence of subject and predicate, inserted between their statement and the demand for proof of the validity of their claim. Tilka is used to point to a single item and to a plural that is not a sound masculine or feminine plural, and al-Zamakhshari carried it to the plural. He said: "It refers to the wishes mentioned: their wish that no good from their Lord descend upon the believers, their wish to return them as disbelievers, and their wish that no one other than them enter Paradise. That is, those vain wishes are their wishes." End of his words. What he went to in the first aspect is not apparent, because every sentence in which their desire for something is mentioned has been separated, completed, and independent in its revelation, so it is far-fetched to refer to it. As for what he went to in the second aspect, it contains metaphorical omission, and it contains an inversion of the structure, since the original is that tilka should be the subject (mubtada') and amāniyyuhum the predicate (khabar). He inverted the structure, saying that their wishes in their falsity are like this wish of theirs. In it also is that when the predicate is the one likened to the subject, it is not permissible to place it first, as in "Zayd, Zuhayr"; the grammarians stated this. When that which is the origin for being likened to something is placed first, it is of the reverse of likening and of the category of exaggeration, since the branch is made the origin and the origin a branch, as in your saying: "The lion is Zayd in courage." The more apparent view is that tilka is a reference to their statement, "None will enter Paradise." That is, that statement is their wishful thinking, meaning this is not based on verification or proof from the Book of Allah, nor from reports from a Messenger, but rather it is by way of wishing. Although they themselves were certain of their statement, since it was not based on evidence, it was wishful thinking, and wishing occurs with the possible and the impossible. This is among the impossible, and for this reason the word amāniyy was used and not "what they hope for," since hope (rajāʾ) is related to the possible. You say: "Would that I were a bird (layta-nī ṭāʾir)," and it is not permissible to say "Perhaps I am a bird (laʿallanī ṭāʾir)." The subject was made singular in wording because it is a metonym for the statement, and the statement is a verbal noun that may be used for few or many. So here it is intended to mean many, with regard to those who say it; for this reason the predicate was made plural (khayr?), so that it agreed in meaning in plurality. The explanation of amāniyy has already been discussed in His saying: ﴿They know not the Book except wishful recitations﴾ [al-Baqarah: 78]. It may be that the meaning is: "Those are their lies and falsehoods," or "Those are their chosen preferences and desires," or "Those are their recitations."

﴿Say, "Bring your proof, if you should be truthful"﴾: When their claim was put forward that none would enter Paradise except those they named, they were asked for evidence for the validity of their claim. In this is evidence that whoever claims a negation or an affirmation must have proof. The verse indicates the invalidity of taqlīd (blind imitation), which is accepting something without evidence. Al-Zamakhshari said: "This is the most destructive thing to the position of the imitators, and that every statement for which there is no evidence is false. If you are truthful, then bring your proof, that is, make your claim clear." The apparent meaning of the verse is that the object of truthfulness is their claim that they are specially entitled to enter Paradise. It was said: "Truthful in your faith." It was said: "Truthful in your wishes."
