It was said that the meaning of ṣādiqīn is ṣāliḥīn (righteous), as you claim, and everything that is attributed to righteousness and good is attributed to truthfulness. You say: "A man of truth (rajul ṣidq)," "a true friend (ṣadīq ṣidq)," "a true guide (dālla ṣidq)." From this is His saying: ﴿This is a day when their truthfulness will benefit the truthful﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 119]. It was said: the meaning of ﴿This is a day when their truthfulness will benefit the truthful﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 119] is: if you are certain of what Allah took as His covenant and pledges. From this is His saying: ﴿Among the believers are men who were true to what they pledged to Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 23].

(Balā): It is a rejection of their statement, "None will enter Paradise," and the discussion of it is like the discussion that preceded in His saying: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil﴾ [al-Baqarah: 81], and before that: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80]. Both of them contain negation and affirmation, except that the former is an emptied exception with respect to times, and this is an emptied exception with respect to agents. He is far off who went to the view that balā is a rejection of the negation contained in His saying: ﴿Say, "Bring your proof"﴾, because its meaning is: "You have no proof for the truth of your claim," so with balā he affirmed that for whoever submits his face there is a proof. This view is repudiated by the wording.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 110–112 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Whoever submits his face to Allah﴾: The discussion concerning *man* (مَن, "whoever") is like the discussion concerning *man* in His words: ﴿whoever earns an evil deed﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 81]. The more evident view is that it is a *mubtada'* (the inchoative, or subject of a nominal sentence). Some grammarians allowed that it could be a *fa'il* (agent), meaning that the one who submits enters [Paradise]. If it is a *mubtada'*, it is not necessarily a conditional (*shartiyyah*) construction. Then the sentence after it is the *khabar* (predicate), and the response of the conditional is (﴿then he has his reward﴾). If it is a relative (*mawsulah*), then the sentence after it is a *silah* (relative clause) that has no place in *i'rab* (grammatical analysis), and the *khabar* is the part of the nominal sentence to which the *fa'* (fa of consequence) is attached. If *man* is an agent, then His words (﴿then he has his reward﴾) form a nominal sentence conjoined to that verb which raises *man*.

The word *wajh* (face) here may refer to the organ itself, singled out for mention because it is the most honourable of the limbs, or because it contains most of the senses, or because it is used to refer to the essence, as in His words: ﴿Everything will perish except His face﴾ [Al-Qasas: 88]. It may also mean the direction, and the meaning would then be: he sincerely devoted his way in religion to Allah. Muqatil said: he sincerely devoted his religion. Ibn Abbas said: he sincerely devoted his deed to Allah. It was also said: his intention. It was also said: he entrusted his affair to Allah, the Exalted. It was also said: he humbled himself and showed humility. These statements are close in meaning. The early scholars (*salaf*) said them as examples, not as though each one were a fixed meaning contradicting the others. This is like the grammarian who says: "The agent is Zayd" in your saying "Zayd stood," while another says: "Ja'far" in "Ja'far went out," and another says: "'Amr" in "'Amr set off." This is the best that may be assumed of the early scholars, may God have mercy on them, regarding what has been transmitted from them of this kind.

﴿and he is a doer of good﴾: This is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah haliyyah*), and it is emphatic in meaning, because whoever submits his face to Allah is a doer of good. Al-Zamakhshari restricted *ihsan* (doing good) to action, and he understood His words ﴿whoever submits his face to Allah﴾ to mean: whoever sincerely devotes himself to Him, not associating anything with Him, and he is a doer of good in his action. Thus the circumstantial clause here becomes explanatory, since one who does not associate has two kinds: one who is a doer of good in his action, and one who is not. This is a leaning on his Mu'tazili doctrine that action is indispensable, and that by both of these one deserves to enter Paradise. For this reason he explained His words ﴿then he has his reward﴾ as the reward that he deserves. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained the reality of legal *ihsan* when he was asked about its nature, and he said: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you." Here *ihsan* has been explained as sincerity, and it has been explained as faith, and it has been explained as carrying out the commands and refraining from the prohibitions.

﴿then he has his reward with his Lord﴾: The governing element of *'inda* (with) is the same as the governing element of *lahu* (for him), meaning: his reward is established for him with his Lord. Since He referred his reward to Allah, He attached the adverbial expression to the word *Rabb* (Lord), meaning the One who looks after his interests, nurtures him, and manages his affairs, so that this would be more encouraging to him. For this reason He used the attribute of *Rabb* and did not use a pronoun referring back to Allah in the preceding clause, nor the explicit noun "Allah." He did not say "then he has his reward with Him," for the reason we have mentioned, and because of the awkwardness of using these pronouns. Nor did He say "then he has his reward with Allah," for the meaning we have mentioned, which the word *Rabb* indicates.

﴿No fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾: The pronoun in His words ﴿upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾ is in the plural, taking the meaning of *man* (whoever). Earlier, He took it in the singular according to the wording, in His words ﴿whoever submits his face to Allah and is a doer of good, then he has his reward with his Lord﴾. This is the more eloquent usage, namely to begin first with agreement according to the wording, and then with agreement according to the meaning. The explanation of this sentence has already been given.

The reading of Ibn Muhaysin is *fala khawfu* (with a raised *fa'*, without tanwin), with variation transmitted from him. The reading of al-Zuhri, Isa al-Thaqafi, Ya'qub, and others is *fala khawfa* (with a fathah, without tanwin). Its justification has been given, so there is no need to repeat it here.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 113:

﴿The Jews say, "The Christians have nothing [valid] to stand on," and the Christians say, "The Jews have nothing [valid] to stand on."﴾ It has been said: the intended meaning is most Jews and most Christians. This is then information about past nations, and the alif-lam (al) is for the category (li-l-jins), and in this there is a rebuke to those from both groups who were in the presence of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and a consolation for him (ﷺ), since they had denied the messengers and the scriptures before him. It has also been said: the intended meaning is the Jews of Medina and the Christians of Najran, when they disputed in the presence of the Messenger and reviled one another. The Jews denied the Gospel and the prophethood of Jesus, and the Christians denied the Torah and the prophethood of Moses. In this case it is a report of a particular situation, and the alif-lam is for a known reference (li-l-ahd). Or the intended meaning is two men: a man from the Jews, called Nafi' ibn Harmala, said to the Christians of Najran, "You have nothing [valid] to stand on," and a man from the Christians of Najran said to the Jews, "You have nothing [valid] to stand on." Thus this is attributed to all of them, since it occurred from some of them, as one says, "The Banu Tamim killed so-and-so," when in fact only one of them killed him. This is by way of metaphor, extension, and attributing a judgment issued by one person to the group. This is a well-known method among the Arabs in their speech, both prose and verse. (p. 353) When He had grouped them in the first statement, which is: ﴿And they say, "None will enter Paradise except those who are Jewish or Christian."﴾ [al-Baqara: 111], He separated them in this verse and explained the statement of each group about the other.

"ʿAla shay'in" (on anything [valid]) is in the position of the predicate of laysa (the negative verb "is not"). It is possible that the meaning is "on anything that is considered valid in religion," in which case it is an instance of omitting the qualifier, comparable to the poet's saying:

*"Indeed I have fallen upon meat,"*

meaning "upon meat that is forbidden" (or "unattainable"). And [the Qur'anic statement is] "he is not of your family" meaning "not of your saved family," since it is known that each of them is "on something." Or this may be negation by way of great exaggeration, since what they are upon, though it is something, is made as if it were nothing. Furthermore, the word "shay'" (thing) is applied by some to the non-existent and the impossible. So when the name "thing" is negated of what they are upon, this is an exaggeration in not considering it valid, and it becomes like the saying "less than nothing."

﴿While they recite the Book﴾: this is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya), meaning: while they know what is in their books and recite them. This is a reproach against them for that statement, since the Book speaks against what they are saying. Their Torah bears witness to the good news of Jesus and Muhammad, peace be upon them both, and to the truth of their prophethood. Their Gospel bears witness to the truth of the prophethood of Moses and Muhammad (ﷺ), since the books of God confirm one another. In this there is a warning to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ): whoever knows the Qur'an should stand by it, act upon what is in it, and speak according to what it contains, and not contradict its word with what it itself testifies against. Otherwise he would be like the Jews and Christians. It has been said that "the Book" here is the Torah and the Gospel. It has also been said that it is the Torah alone, since the Christians rely on it.

* *

﴿Likewise said those who do not know, the like of their statement﴾: "those who do not know" are, according to the majority, the polytheists of the Arabs. It has been said they are the polytheists of Quraysh. ʿAtaʾ said they are nations that existed before the Jews and Christians. Some said the intended meaning is the Jews, and it is as if their statement were repeated, meaning: the Jews said the like of what the Christians said, and they were denied knowledge because they did not benefit from it, so they were made to be as those who do not know. The apparent view is the first opinion. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, like that which you heard, in that same manner. Said the ignorant ones who have no knowledge and no book, such as the idol-worshippers and the deniers (al-mu'attila) and their like: "Every people of a religion are not upon anything." This is a great rebuke against them, since they placed themselves, despite their knowledge, in the same row as those who do not know. The apparent view is that the kaf in *kadhalika* (likewise) is in the accusative position, either as an adjective to an omitted verbal noun whose estimated form is: "a statement like that statement," [and then] ﴿those who do not know the like of their statement﴾; or as an accusative circumstantial element (hal) from the omitted definite verbal noun indicated by "said." The estimate is: "like that statement, he said it," meaning: those who do not know said the statement. This is according to the opinion of Sibawayh. In both of these readings the kaf is governed by "said," and "the like of their statement" is in the accusative as an apposition (badal) to the position of the kaf. It has been said that "the like of their statement" is accusative as an object of "they know," meaning: those who do not know the like of the statement of the Jews and Christians said the like of their statement, meaning: those who do not know the statements of the Christians and Jews agreed with the Jews and Christians in that statement, since whoever is ignorant of what the Jews and Christians say agrees with them in such a statement. They also allowed that the kaf could be in the nominative position as the subject, with the clause after it as the predicate, and the returning pronoun omitted, its estimated form being: "like that, those who said it." It is not permissible for *qala* to govern "the like of their statement" as its direct object, because *qala* has already taken its object, namely the omitted pronoun referring back to the subject. Thus "the like of their statement" would be accusative as an adjective to an omitted verbal noun, or as an object of "they know," meaning: the like of their statement, that is, the statement of the Jews and Christians, said by those who do not know, the belief of the Jews and Christians. That is the end of what they said regarding this reading, and it is weak, because it uses the kaf as a noun, which in our view is not permitted except in cases of poetic necessity, even though what has come of that has been interpreted. He permitted it (i.e., that it be a noun in ordinary speech) and that the pronoun referring back to the subject be omitted when the subject is accusative governed by a verb which, if it were supposed to be free of that pronoun, would govern the noun before it and make it accusative. This is like: "Zayd, I struck him." Our companions explicitly stated that this pronoun may not be omitted except in poetry, and they cited:

*"Khalid praises our masters for truth; he does not praise them for falsehood,"*

meaning: our masters praise him. Regarding the permissibility of omitting such a pronoun, some of the Kufans have a detailed position mentioned in the grammar books.

* *

﴿So God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ﴾: that is, He will decide between them. The "decision" (faṣl) is the judgment; or He will show them, face to face, who enters Paradise and who enters the Fire, as al-Zajjaj said; or He will declare them all false and cast them into the Fire; or He will reward those who were upon the truth and punish those who were upon falsehood. All of these views are close in meaning. The two adverbials, the first being the object of "will judge," and the second being the object of "they differ," are both governed by "will judge" [in the sense of the first adverbial], and the prepositional phrase concerning it is governed by "differ."

These noble verses contain several matters. Among them: they begin with a fine form of address; they affirm for them the attribute of faith; and they alert them to learn one of the manners of the sacred law, namely that they are forbidden to say a word that creates an ambiguous impression, and are instead to use a word more explicit about the intended meaning and clearer about what is sought. Then He mentioned the punishment for the opponent, which humiliates and degrades him. Then He pointed out that what you have been commanded is good, and that the disbelievers do not wish that any good be sent down upon you. Then He mentioned that this is not subject to their desires or wishes, but is a divine matter specific to whomever He wills, and that He, exalted is He, is the Lord of immense bounty. Since the beginning of the verse involved a shift from one wording to another, and the second wording became more explicit about the intended meaning, He clarified that what God does of abrogation (naskh, the replacement of one ruling by another) is for a wisdom from Him; He brings something better than what was abrogated or something equivalent to it. And whoever is capable of everything has the right to dispose of things as He wills, whether by abrogation or otherwise. He also alerted the addressee to his knowledge of the power of God, the Exalted, and of His all-encompassing dominion over all creatures, and that we have no protector apart from Him who could prevent us from Him. "Who then will help us against the might of God if it comes upon us?" Then He reproached those whose will is set on asking the Messenger of God (ﷺ) an impermissible question, like the questions the people of Moses put to him. Then He mentioned that whoever prefers disbelief to faith has strayed from the right path. Then He mentioned that many of the People of the Book wish to make you apostatize, and that what drives them to this is envy. Then you were commanded to forbear and to pardon, and this was limited by the command of God: when the command of God comes, the command to pardon and forgive is lifted.

Then He concluded the verse by mentioning the power of God over everything, because before it there was a promise to change a state, so the mention of power was appropriate. Then He commanded them with what cuts off the disbelievers' statements from them, namely prayer and zakat, and He informed them that whatever good you have sent forward, it is not lost with God, but you will find it stored up for you. Then He concluded this by alerting that what good is done is with God, by mentioning the attribute of sight, which indicates direct witnessing and observation of things. Then He condemned the Jews and Christians for their claim that they alone are destined for Paradise, and that this is one of their well-known falsehoods, and that they were required to produce proof for their claim of exclusivity. Then He mentioned that whoever submits outwardly and inwardly to God, the Exalted, will have his reward and will be secure, neither fearing what is to come nor grieving over what has passed. Then He began to mention the statements of the Christians and Jews about one another, and that these are the statements of those who openly disavow what the messengers brought and what the revealed books made clear. All of this is in a manner of obstinacy, because they recite the books and know what they contain. Thus they are in this worldly life in the same state as they will be in the Hereafter, as God, the Exalted, informed about them in His saying: ﴿On the Day of Resurrection some of you will disavow others, and some of you will curse others﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 25].

Then He mentioned that their statement, even though they are knowledgeable, is similar to the statement of one who does not know. Then He concluded this with the warning which includes the judgment and the separation of falsehood from truth, and that He, the Exalted, is the One who takes charge of that, in order to recompense them for their disbelief.

(p-355)﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned in them and strives for their ruin? Those would not have entered them except in fear. For them in this world is disgrace, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment.﴾ ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west, so wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah. Indeed, Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 115] ﴿And they say, "Allah has taken a son." Glory be to Him! Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth; all are devoutly obedient to Him.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 116] ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 117] ﴿Those who do not know say, "Why does Allah not speak to us, or a sign come to us?" Likewise said those before them, similar to their saying. Their hearts are alike. We have certainly made the signs clear for a people who are certain.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 118] ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good news and a warner, and you will not be questioned about the companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 119] ﴿The Jews will never be pleased with you, nor the Christians, until you follow their religion. Say, "Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the [true] guidance." And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, you would have against Allah no protector and no helper.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 120] ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recite it with its true recitation. Those believe in it, and whoever disbelieves in it, those are the losers.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 121]

Al-Manʿ (prevention): preventing the one who wills from what he wills. Since a thing may be withheld for protection, al-manʿ became commonly used for what is competed over; this is what al-Raghib said. Its verb is manaʿa yamnaʿu, with a fatha on the nun, which is the regular form, because the final radical of the verb is one of the throat letters (ḥurūf al-ḥalq). Al-masājid (mosques): a known term; discussion of the singular will come, God willing, at the first place it is mentioned in the Qur'an. Al-saʿy (striving): walking quickly, less than running, and then it is used for seeking, as Imru' al-Qays said:

"Had what I strive for been enough for a modest livelihood, it would have sufficed me, and I would not seek much wealth.
But I strive for lasting glory, and those like me do attain lasting glory."

The commentators explained it as seeking (al-talab). Al-kharab (ruin): the opposite of cultivation (al-ʿimarah). It is the verbal noun of kharaba al-shayʾ yakhrabu kharaban, and it is used as an adjective, so one says manzil kharab (a ruined dwelling). The active participle is kharib, as Abu Tammam said:

"The abode of Mayya, when inhabited and visited by Ghaylan, is no finer in its gardens than its ruined abode."

Al-kharab also denotes the male bustard, whose plural is khirbān. Al-mashriq and al-maghrib: the place of sunrise and sunset. Both are among the words that came in the pattern maf‘il with a kasra on the ʿayn irregularly; the analogical form is with a fatha, because every triliteral verb whose present-tense ʿayn is not kasra forms its verbal noun, noun of time and noun of place on the pattern mafʿal with a fatha on the ʿayn. Ayna (where): one of the adverbs of place. It is built (mabniy) because it contains in interrogation the meaning of its particle, and in conditional sentences the meaning of its particle. When it is conditional, it is permissible to add mā after it. Among what came in conditional use without mā is the line:

"Wherever the enemies drive us, you will find us [there]."

Some claimed that the original sense of ayna is asking about places. Thamma (there): an adverb of place used to point to a distant location. It is built because it contains the meaning of indication, and it is necessarily adverbial; it is not used in any other way except that one says min thamma kāna kadhā (from there such-and-such happened). Whoever parsed it as a direct object in His saying ﴿And when you look there, you will see bliss and a great dominion﴾ [Al-Insan: 20] has erred; rather, the object of "you see" is omitted. Wāsiʿ (All-Encompassing): an active participle from wasiʿa yasaʿu saʿatan and wus‘an; its opposite is ḍāqa. However, wasiʿa also occurs transitively: ﴿His Throne extends over the heavens and the earth﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 255], and ﴿My mercy encompasses all things﴾ [Al-A'raf: 156]. Al-walad (child): a known term; it is on the pattern faʿal in the sense of maf‘ūl, like qabḍ and naqḍ, and the pattern faʿal in the sense of maf‘ūl is not productive. Its verb is walada yalidu, widāḥah and walīdiyyah; this second verbal noun is unusual. Al-qunūt: standing, and from it the best prayer is the long qunūt, meaning standing; and it also means obedience, worship and supplication. Qanata shahran: he supplicated for a month. Al-badīʿ (the Originator): the rare, unusual in form. One says badaʿa yabdaʿu badāʿah, so he is badīʿ, when he is rare and strange in beautiful appearance. It returns to the meaning of innovation (al-ibtidāʿ), which is creation and bringing into being. Qaḍā: to decree; it also comes in the sense of to execute. Qaḍā yaqḍī qaḍā'an. He said:

"I will wash the shame from myself with the sword, bringing upon myself what God has decreed, whatever it brings."

Al-Azhari said: qaḍā has several usages, all returning to the ending and completion of a thing. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

"Upon them two are two coats of mail, which Dawud completed, or the makers of the ample ones, the Tubba'."

Al-Shammakh said about ʿUmar:

"I completed matters, then I left after them calamities whose sheaths were not yet split open."

So it means "created" in ﴿and He completed them as seven heavens﴾ [Fussilat: 12]; "informed" in ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Book﴾ [Al-Isra': 4]; "commanded" in ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾ [Al-Isra': 23]; "obligated," from which qaḍā al-qāḍī (the judge ruled); "fulfilled" in ﴿So when Musa had fulfilled the term﴾ [Al-Qasas: 29]; and "willed" in ﴿When He decrees a matter﴾ [Al-Imran: 47]. (p-356) Law (lawlā): a particle of urging; it occurs often in the Qur'an, and its rule is the rule of hallā. It also comes as a particle of prohibition due to existence. Its rules in both meanings are mentioned in the books of grammar. Among them: the urging type is followed only by a verb, explicit or implicit, while the other type is followed only by a noun, with disagreement about its grammatical status. Al-Jahim (the Blazing Fire): one of the levels of the Fire, may God protect us from it. Al-Farra' said: al-Jahim is fire upon fire. Abu ʿUbayd said: a fire that is intense and blazing. Al-Zajjaj said: a fire of intense fuel; one says jaḥamati al-nār tajḥamu, meaning its fuel became intense. These statements are all close to one another. Ibn Faris said: al-jāḥim is a place of intense heat; the eye of a lion is called juḥmah because of its intense blaze; and intense heat is called jāḥim. He said:

"War does not leave for its sheltering the imagination and the fancy."

Al-Ridā (contentment): a known term, and its opposite is anger. Its verb is raḍiya yarḍā ridā with shortened form, and riḍā' with a long form, and riḍwān. Its yā' is converted from a wāw, as shown by riḍwān. Most often it takes ʿan as its complement, but it has also been construed with ʿalā. He said:

"When the Banu Qushayr are pleased with me..."

This has been explained either as ʿalā being in the sense of ʿan, or as raḍiya being implicitly used in the sense of ʿaṭafa (to incline toward), so it takes ʿalā just as ʿaṭafa does. Al-millah (religion): the path. It came to be used frequently in the sense of the sacred law (sharīʿah). It was said that it derives from amlaltu (I dictated), because the sacred law is founded on what is recited and heard. It was also said that it derives from their saying "a worn road" (ṭarīq mumallu), meaning that walking has worn it. Al-khusrān and al-khasārah (loss): it is the decrease from the capital in trade; this is its origin. Then it is used for loss in general, and its verb is transitive, just as its opposite, al-ribḥ (profit), is transitive. One says khasira dirhaman (he lost a dirham), just as one says rabiḥa dirhaman (he gained a dirham). He said: ﴿They have lost their souls and their families﴾ [Al-Zumar: 15].

* *

﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned in them﴾: It was revealed about Natus ibn Isbisyanus al-Rumi, who destroyed Bayt al-Maqdis, and it remained in ruins until it was rebuilt in the time of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab. It was also said concerning the polytheists of the Arabs: they prevented the Muslims from mentioning God in the Sacred Mosque; this was said by ʿAṭāʾ, from Ibn ʿAbbas, (p-357) or concerning the Christians, who wished for the ruin of Bayt al-Maqdis and cast filth into it. It was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Qatadah and al-Suddi said: it concerns the Romans who helped Bukht Nasr (Nebuchadnezzar) in destroying Bayt al-Maqdis, when the Children of Israel killed Yahya ibn Zakariyya, upon our Prophet and upon him be peace. Abu Bakr al-Razi said: there is no disagreement among the scholars of history that the era of Bukht Nasr was long before the birth of the Messiah, peace be upon him. It was also said concerning Bukht Nasr, as Qatadah said. Ibn Zayd and Abu Muslim said: the intended ones are the disbelievers of Quraysh when they barred the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from the Sacred Mosque. Based on the differences among these statements, there arises a difference in the interpretation of the preventer and of the mosques.

The apparent meaning of the verse is generality, covering every preventer and every mosque. Although the cause of its revelation is specific, the lesson drawn is from the general wording, not from the particular cause.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 114 (part 2 of 3):

The connection (munasabah) of this verse with what precedes it is that mention was made of the Christians in His words: ﴿And the Christians say: "The Jews are not on anything"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 113], and mention was made of the polytheists in His words: ﴿Thus say those who do not know, the like of their words﴾ [al-Baqarah: 113]. Whether it was revealed concerning them or not, this is suitable as a link to what comes before it. "Man" (من, man) is an interrogative, and it is in the nominative case as the subject (mubtada'). "Azlamu" (أظلم, adhlam) is an elative form (af'al al-tafdil), and it is the predicate (khabar) of "man." The interrogative is not meant here in its literal sense; rather it has the meaning of negation, as He said: ﴿Will anyone be destroyed except the defiantly disobedient people?﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35], meaning: none is destroyed. The meaning of this is: there is no one more unjust than the one who prevents. This expression is repeated in the Qur'an, and this is its first occurrence. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah?﴾ [al-An'am: 21]. And He said: ﴿So who is more unjust than one who denies the signs of Allah?﴾ [al-An'am: 157] And: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who has been reminded of the signs of his Lord but turns away from them?﴾ [al-Kahf: 57], and other verses besides these.

Since this interrogative means negation, it is a statement (khabar). Since it is a statement, some people imagined that if these verses are taken at face value, a contradiction arises in them, because the one who interprets this says: "There is no one more unjust than the one who prevents the mosques of Allah," and in another place He says: "There is no one more unjust than the one who fabricates," and in another: "There is no one more unjust than the one who was reminded of the signs of his Lord and turned away from them." So he interpreted this by restricting each one to the meaning of its relative clause, as if He had said: "There is no one among the preventers more unjust than the one who prevented the mosques of Allah, and no one among the fabricators more unjust than the one who fabricated against Allah," and so on for the rest. When they are restricted by their relative clauses, the contradiction disappears for him. Another said: the restriction is with respect to precedence; since no one had preceded to the like of it, they are judged to be more unjust than whoever came after them following their way in that matter, and this returns in meaning to precedence in preventing or in fabricating. All of this is far from the indication of the speech and its Arabic usage, and is a kind of foreignness in the language followed by obscurity of meaning. Rather, this is a negation of being "more unjust," and negating "more unjust" does not require negating "unjust," because negating the qualified does not indicate negating the unqualified. If you say: "There is no clever man in the house," that does not indicate the negation of any man at all. And if it does not indicate the negation of being unjust, there is no contradiction, because in it there is an affirmation of equality in being most unjust. When equality in being most unjust is established, none of those described by it exceeds the other, because they are equal in being most unjust. The meaning becomes: there is no one more unjust than the one who prevents, and than the one who fabricates, and than the one who was reminded. There is no difficulty in these being equal in being most unjust, and it does not indicate that one of them is more unjust than another. Just as when you say: "No one is more knowledgeable than Zayd, 'Amr and Khalid," this does not indicate that one of them is more knowledgeable than another; rather it is a negation that anyone be more knowledgeable than them. It cannot be said: whoever prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned in them and strives to ruin them, and does not fabricate lies against Allah, is less unjust than the one who combines both, so he is not equal in being most unjust; because all these verses are only about the disbelievers, so they are equal in being most unjust, even though the paths of being most unjust differ. All of them lead to disbelief, so it is one thing in which there is no possibility of excess relative to the individuals who are characterized by it. Excess in injustice is possible only relative to them and to the sinful believers, by the common ground of what they share of opposition. So we say: the disbeliever is more unjust than the believer, and we say: no one is more unjust than the disbeliever. Its meaning is: the injustice of the disbeliever exceeds the injustice of others. "Man" in His words "than one who prevents" is a relative pronoun (mawsulah) with the meaning of "alladhi." Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be an indefinite qualified noun (nakirah mawsufah). "An yudhkara" (that His name be mentioned): it may be a second object of "mana'a" (prevented), or an object for the sake of which (maf'ul min ajlihi), in which case the deletion of a genitive-governing element (mudaf) is necessary, i.e., entry into the mosques of Allah, or what resembles that; or it may be a substitute (badal) for "masajid" in the sense of inclusion (badal ishtimal), i.e., the mention of the name of Allah in them; or it may be an object with the preposition dropped, i.e., from its being mentioned. When "man" is deleted, it is in the accusative according to one opinion, or remains in the genitive according to another opinion. He used the mention of the name of Allah as a metonym for what takes place in the mosques of prayers and acts of drawing near to Allah, exalted is He, through the acts of the heart and of the body, from the recitation of His books, and bodily movements of standing, bowing, prostrating and sitting, which He has made an act of worship. Or the connection of the prevention with the mention of the name of Allah is mentioned only to draw attention to the fact that they prevented the easiest of things, which is uttering the name of Allah. So their preventing other than it is all the more so. The subject was deleted here for brevity, because they are a multitude that cannot be counted. The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the passive verb's unnamed agent is because the topic of discussion before was "the mosques of Allah," which are mentioned in the wording before the name of Allah, so fronting the prepositional phrase suits that. The mosques are ascribed to Allah as an honour, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And that the mosques belong to Allah﴾ [al-Jinn: 18]. It is specified with the word "masjid," even though what takes place in it includes many acts of standing, bowing, sitting and staying in seclusion. All of this is acts of worship, and He did not say "maqam," "marka'," "maq'ad," or "ma'kaf," because prostration is the greatest of postures indicating humility, reverence and complete obedience. Do you not see His words, may blessings and peace be upon him: "The closest a servant is to his Lord is when he is prostrating"? It is a state in which a person casts himself down for complete submission, and he places in direct contact with the dust, which is the place his feet tread, the most noble and highest part of himself, which is the face.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This verse covers everyone who prevents a mosque until the Day of Resurrection, or ruins a city of Islam, because they are mosques, even if they are not endowed, since the whole earth is a mosque. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: how is it said "mosques of Allah," when the prevention and destruction only fell upon one mosque, namely Bayt al-Maqdis or al-Masjid al-Haram? I say: there is no harm in the ruling coming in general terms even if the cause is specific, just as you say to one who harmed a single righteous person: "Who is more unjust than the one who harmed the righteous?" And as Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Woe to every slanderer, backbiter﴾ [al-Humazah: 1], and the one concerning whom it was revealed was al-Akhnas ibn Shariq. End of his words. Another said: it was put in the plural because it is the qibla of all mosques, meaning the Ka'bah for the Muslims and Bayt al-Maqdis for others.

﴿And strove for their ruin﴾: either literally, as in the destruction of Bayt al-Maqdis, or figuratively, by the cessation of remembrance in them and the prevention of those who intend them from them, since that leads them to ruin. So prevention was made ruin, just as maintaining remembrance and prayer in them was made building (imarah), and this is a metaphor. Al-Marwazi said: He said "and who is more unjust" to make known that the ugliness of belief results in the destruction of mosques, just as the goodness of belief results in the building of mosques.

﴿It was not for them to enter them except in fear﴾: this is a declarative sentence, which they said indicates what will happen in the future, and that is one of the miraculous features of the Qur'an, since it is information of the unseen. In it there is good news for the believers of the elevation of the word of Islam and the subjugation of whoever opposes it. "Except in fear" (إلا خائفين, illa kha'ifin): an accusative of state (hal), and it is an exceptive construction with the exception left open (istithna' mufarragh) from the states. Ubayy read "illa khuyyafan," which is the plural of "kha'if," like "na'im" and "nuwwam," and he did not make it a rhyme-ending (fasilah), so it was made into a broken plural. The changing of the waw into ya' (khuyyaf from khawf) is because the original is "khawf," and that is permissible, as in their saying "suyyam" for "suwwam." Their fear is: what befalls them of humiliation, abasement and the poll-tax (jizyah); or that the believers might seize them; or in a trial, which includes fear; or a painful beating, because the Christians do not enter Bayt al-Maqdis except in fear of being beaten. These are opinions. The apparent meaning is: it is not fitting for them to enter the mosques of Allah except while they are fearful of Allah and trembling before His punishment. How then could they engage in preventing His remembrance and striving to ruin them, when they are houses that Allah has permitted to be raised and in which His name is mentioned, glorifying Him in them morning and evening? And a place of which this is the way should be honoured by remembering Allah in it, and people should strive to build it, and a person should not enter it except trembling and fearful, since it is the House of Allah, and He commanded standing before Him in it for worship. A parallel to the verse would be to say: "And who is more unjust than one who killed a friend of Allah, the Exalted?" It was not for him to meet him except honouring and esteeming him. That is, this is the condition of one who meets a friend of Allah, not that he should attack him with killing. In this there is a great censure of what he did, since its opposite should have occurred, which is reverence and magnification. Since this meaning that we have mentioned did not occur to the exegetes, they differed about the verse according to those opinions we have mentioned from them. Had what they mentioned been intended, the wording would have been: "They do not enter them except in fear," and He would not have used the expression "it was not for them," which indicates the negation of seeking. It was said the meaning is: "It was not for them in the judgment of Allah," meaning that Allah has decreed and written in the Preserved Tablet that He will support the believers and strengthen them so that no disbelievers enter the mosques except in fear. Some people said: in it is evidence for the permissibility of disbelievers entering mosques in a state of fear; but this is not as he said, since we have already mentioned what the apparent meaning of the verse indicates. It was also said concerning His words: ﴿It was not for them to enter them﴾: its wording is that of a statement but its meaning is a command to us to frighten them, and this view was taken because Allah, exalted is He, has informed that they will enter Bayt al-Maqdis by way of subjugation and conquest, in His words: ﴿So when the promise of the Hereafter came, they would disfigure your faces and enter the mosque as they had entered it the first time, and destroy what they had conquered with complete destruction﴾ [al-Isra': 7]; and because the Prophet, may blessings and peace be upon him, reported that a man with two small legs from Abyssinia would demolish the Ka'bah stone by stone. When he saw that this conflicts with the verse if we take it as a statement both in wording and meaning, he interpreted it as a command; but its indication of a command to us to frighten them is very remote. If we interpret the verse as we have mentioned, these views are invalidated. As for His words: ﴿Then when the promise of the Hereafter comes﴾ [al-Isra': 7], that is not a metaphor for the Day of Resurrection, and the discussion of it will come in its proper place, God willing, exalted is He. As for His words "Ula'ika" (those), it is taken in terms of the meaning of "man" in His words "and who is more unjust," and the taking of it in terms of wording and meaning is not restricted to its being a relative pronoun; rather it is so in all its other meanings of conditional, interrogative and connective, and both aspects exist in all its meanings in Arabic speech. As for when it is a qualifying noun, like: "I passed by a man who is good to you," there is in what I have memorized of Arabic speech no observance of meaning in it. We have discussed earlier its being a qualifying noun. Some people said concerning His words, exalted is He: "And who is more unjust" – the verse – that it is evidence for prohibiting disbelievers from entering the mosque; then he mentioned the disagreement of the jurists on this, which is a question mentioned in the science of jurisprudence (fiqh). There is nothing in the verse indicating what he mentioned, according to what we understood from the verse ourselves.

* *

This recompense corresponds to what they did. As for disgrace (khizy) in this world, it is humiliation and degradation. It corresponds to the first attribute, because it involves the desolation of the mosques through the non-mention of God and their being left empty of it. Accordingly, they were requited with degradation and humiliation. As for the great punishment in the Hereafter, it is punishment by the Fire, which destroys their bodies and forms and ruins them after they were already ruined: ﴿Whenever their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins so that they may taste the punishment﴾ [al-Nisa: 56]. This corresponds to the second attribute, which is their striving to ruin the mosques. Accordingly, they were requited with the ruin of their forms and their being torn apart by punishment.

Since the disgrace that befalls them in this world does not differ among them in ruling, whether you interpret it as killing or taking captive the combatant (harbi), or the poll tax (jizya) imposed on the protected non-Muslim (dhimmi), no description was needed. Since punishment varies, I mean the punishment of the unbeliever and the punishment of the believer, the punishment of the unbeliever was described as great so that it would be distinguished from the punishment of the believer.

It has been said: the disgrace is the Islamic conquest, such as Constantinople, Amorium and Rome. It has been said: it is the jizya of the dhimmi, as Ibn Abbas said. It has been said: it is their expulsion from the Sacred Mosque. It has been said: it is the killing of them by the Mahdi when he emerges, as al-Marwazi said. It has been said: it is their being barred from the mosques.

One of our contemporary scholars said: for every group of unbelievers there is disgrace in this world. As for the Jews and the Christians, there is the killing of Qurayza, the expulsion of Banu al-Nadir, the killing of the Christians, the conquest of their fortresses and lands, the imposition of the jizya upon them, the marks they committed to, and what Umar stipulated upon them. As for the polytheists of the Arabs, there is the killing of their champions and chieftains, the breaking of their idols, the mocking of their reason, their expulsion from the Arabian Peninsula which was their abode and the place of their origin, and the obligation upon them of the path of ruin, namely killing, unless they embrace Islam.

Al-Farra' said: its meaning is at the end of the world, which is what God promised the Muslims of the conquest of Rome, and it had not yet occurred. Al-Qushayri said: in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And who is more unjust﴾ the verse, there is an allusion to the wrong done by one who ruins the homelands of knowledge of God with desires and attachments, which are the hearts of the gnostics; and the homelands of worship with appetites, which are the souls of the servants; and the homelands of love with fortunes and dwellings, which are the spirits of those who find; and the homelands of contemplation with turning toward acts of nearness, which are the secrets of the monotheists.

﴿For them in this world is disgrace﴾: the humiliation of the veil; and in the Hereafter punishment, for their contentment with the ranks. End of quotation, and part of it has been summarized. This is a strange interpretation, which the wording of the Qur'an repudiates, and so too most of what these people say.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 115–116 (part 1 of 2):

﴿To Allah belong the east and the west; so wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: He had permitted them at the beginning to pray wherever they wished, and that was abrogated (naskh). Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: its meaning is an indication toward the Ka'bah, that is, wherever you are, from east or west, you are able to face the Ka'bah. Accordingly, it abrogates the (ruling concerning) Bayt al-Maqdis. Abu al-'Aliyah and Ibn Zayd said: it was revealed as a reply to those among the Jews who reproached (the Muslims) for the change of the qiblah from Bayt al-Maqdis to the Ka'bah. Ibn 'Umar said: it was revealed concerning the prayer of the traveller, wherever his mount turns him. It has also been said: it is a reply to someone who said: "Is our Lord near so that we may whisper to Him, or far so that we must call out to Him?" This was reported by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. It has also been said: it concerns the prayer over al-Najashi, when they said: "He did not pray toward our qiblah." It has also been said: it concerns one whose qiblah became uncertain on a cloudy night, so they prayed by ijtihad (taharri) toward different directions. This has been related in a hadith from Jabir, that this happened to a sariyyah (detachment), and from 'Amir ibn Rabi'ah, that this occurred with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ during a journey. Even if that is authentic, one should not turn from it to any other of these varying and conflicting statements. Al-Nakha'i said: the verse is general, (meaning) wherever you turn in your dealings and undertakings. It has also been said: it was revealed when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came back from the House.

These are many statements concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse, and its apparent meaning is contradictory. Nothing should be accepted from them except what is authentic, and the exegetes have filled their books with transmitting them. Al-Wahidi composed a book on this matter in which almost nothing is authentic, and he should not have occupied himself with transmitting anything except what is authentic. What appears to be the connection of this verse with what precedes it is this: when He mentioned the prevention of the mosques from the remembrance of Allah and the effort to ruin them, He drew attention to the fact that this does not prevent the performance of prayers or the remembrance of Allah, since the east and the west belong to Allah the Exalted; whichever direction you perform worship in, it is for Allah, who rewards for it, and the place of performance is not restricted to the mosque. The meaning is: to Allah belong the lands of the east and the west and what lies between them; this would be by omission of a modifier (muda'f mahdhuf), or the meaning is: to Allah belong the east and the west and what lies between them, this would be by omission of a conjoined element (ma'tuf mahdhuf), or He mentioned only the two of them to honour them, since they are attributed to Allah, although all things belong to Allah, just as He honoured the Sacred House and other places by attributing them to Himself, the Exalted. All of this is on the assumption that al-mashriq and al-maghrib are (names of) places.

Some exegetes held that they are verbal nouns (ism masdar), and the meaning is that Allah has charge of the rising of the sun from its rising-point and its setting from its setting-point, so that they (the words) would mean "rising" (shuruq) and "setting" (ghurub). What weakens this view is His saying afterward: "so wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah." The singular form of al-mashriq and al-maghrib is used with regard to the direction, or with regard to the verbal noun occurring in the direction. As for the plural, it is by consideration of the differing settings and risings each day. As for the dual, it is by consideration of the risings and settings of winter and summer. The meaning of tawliyah is turning the faces toward (istiqbal). It has also been said that its meaning is turning one's back (istidbar), from your saying: "I turned away from so-and-so" when you turned your back on him; so the sense would be: "Whichever direction you turn away from and face another, there is the Face of Allah." It has also been said: it is not about prayer; rather it is an address to those who ruin the mosques, meaning: wherever you turn fleeing from Me, I am watching you. This is strengthened by al-Hasan's reading: ﴿fa-aynama tuwallū﴾ (with the verb in the third person plural), making it third-person, so that it accords with His saying: ﴿For them in this world is disgrace﴾ [al-Baqarah: 114], and with His saying: ﴿and they say: Allah has taken a son﴾, so the pronouns follow one pattern. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Wherever you perform the tawliyah, meaning the turning of your faces toward the qiblah, as is shown by His saying: ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144]," (p-361) end of quote. He thus restricted the general tawliyah to the tawliyah which is toward the qiblah, and this is a fine statement. Some exegetes, in connection with His saying ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west﴾, have mentioned issues whose subject is the science of fiqh, among them: one who prayed in darkness, striving (ijtihad) toward a direction, and then it became clear that he prayed other than toward the qiblah; the issue of one who prays on the back of a mount, whether an obligatory prayer due to illness or a voluntary prayer; and the issue of the funeral prayer over an absent deceased, if we say the verse was revealed about al-Najashi. He filled his book with mention of these issues, the disagreement concerning them, some of their proofs and their subject matter, which is, as we have mentioned, the science of fiqh.

﴿then there is the Face of Allah﴾: this is the answer of the conditional, and it is a nominal sentence (jumlah ibtida'iyyah). It has been said: its meaning is "then there is the qiblah of Allah," so the word "face" means "direction," and it was attributed to Allah because He commanded facing it; it is the direction in which is the good pleasure of Allah the Exalted. This was said by al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah and Muqatil. It has also been said: "face" here is superfluous (silah), and the meaning is "then Allah is there," that is, His knowledge and His judgment. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil: or the Essence is expressed by the word "face," as in His saying: ﴿and there remains the Face of your Lord﴾ [al-Rahman: 27], and ﴿everything perishes except His Face﴾ [al-Qasas: 88]. It has also been said: the meaning is "the deed is for Allah," said by al-Farra', who said:

I seek the forgiveness of Allah for a sin I cannot count,
Lord of the servants, to Him is the face and the deed.

It has also been said: it is possible that "face" here is meant as standing or rank (jah), as one says: "So-and-so is the face of the people," meaning the place of their honour, and "so-and-so has a face among people," meaning standing and dignity. The sense would be: "then there is the majesty and greatness of Allah," said by Abu Mansur in al-Muqni'. Wherever the word "face" comes attributed to Allah the Exalted, it has a sound basis in the language of the Arabs, since it is a word applied to many meanings, and it is impossible to take it as the organ, although that is most well known in it. Some people held that this is an attribute of Allah established by revelation, additional to what reason necessitates regarding the attributes of the Eternal, the Exalted. Abu al-'Aliyah and others weakened this view, because in it there is a definite affirmation of an attribute of Allah the Exalted by an ambiguous term, an attribute whose reality is not known and whose meaning is not understood in the Arabic language; therefore this view must be discarded, and one should rely on what has a basis in the language of the Arabs. If a word carries an indication of anthropomorphism (tajsim), we take it either in the sense of literal reality that may rightly be attributed to Allah the Exalted, if the word is homonymous (mushtarak), or in the sense of metaphor (majaz), if the word is not homonymous. Metaphor in the speech of the Arabs is more abundant than the sand of Yabrin and the river of Filastin.

So to hold to the apparent sense of a word that indicates anthropomorphism is stupidity and ignorance of the Arabic language, its idioms and its usages in speech, and of the rational proofs to which the interpretation of obscure words must return. We seek refuge in Allah from being like the Karramiyyah and those who follow their path in affirming anthropomorphism and attributing organs to Allah. Exalted is Allah above what the slanderers say, a great exaltation. In His saying ﴿wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾ there is a refutation of those who say that He is in a space and a direction, because when He gave the choice of facing all the directions, this shows that He is not in a direction nor a space; for had He been in a space, facing Him and turning toward Him would have been more worthy than all places. Since He did not specify a place, we know that He is neither in a direction nor in a space; rather, all directions are in His dominion and under His dominion. So whichever direction we turn toward Him in, in a manner of humility, we are glorifying Him and obeying His command.

* *

﴿Indeed Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾: He described Himself with the attribute of "the All-Encompassing" (al-Wasi'). It has been said that this is for the vastness of His forgiveness; there came: ﴿Indeed your Lord is vast in forgiveness﴾ [al-Najm: 32], and this is the meaning of al-Kalbi's statement: no sin is too great for Him. It has been said: "All-Encompassing in bounty," and this is the meaning of Abu 'Ubaydah's statement: "Rich (ghani)," and the meaning of al-Farra's statement: "Generous (jawwad)." It has been said: its meaning is "All-Knowing," from His saying: ﴿His Throne encompasses the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255], according to one of the interpretations, and it is combined with "All-Knowing" for emphasis. It has been said: "All-Encompassing in power." It has been said: its meaning is that He widens for His servants in judgment; His religion is ease. "All-Knowing": that is, of their welfare, or of the intentions of the hearts, which are the foundation of the deed, even if their outward forms differ in the qiblah and other matters. These interpretations accord with the view of those who say the verse was revealed concerning the matter of the qiblah. Al-Qaffal said: it contains no mention of the qiblah or prayer; rather, Allah the Exalted informed them of His knowledge of them and of His authority encompassing them wherever they were, as in His saying: ﴿If you are able to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Rahman: 33], and His saying: ﴿There is no private conversation of three but He is their fourth﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 7], and in this there is a threat to whoever prevented the mosques of Allah from remembrance and strove to ruin them: that there is no escape from Allah and no refuge, as He the Exalted said: ﴿Where is the escape?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 10] ﴿No! There is no refuge﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 11] ﴿To your Lord on that Day is the place of rest﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 12], and as the poet said:

So you are like the night which will overtake me, even if I imagine that the place far from you is vast.

And he said:

The one deluded by Allah when he travelled did not intend to escape,
and the one made mighty by Allah, His seeker is he.

And he said:

Where is the escape? There is no escape for the fugitive,
and to Him belong the two expanses, the dry land and the water.

On this meaning the address is general, including whoever prevented the mosques from remembrance and other things. This sentence came emphasized by "inna" with the name of Allah explicitly stated in it, indicating independence. We have already discussed this in His saying: ﴿you will find it with Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 110], and like His saying: ﴿and seek the forgiveness of Allah; indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 199]. That is more majestic and more eloquent than the pronoun, because the pronoun indicates strength of connection, while the apparent noun indicates independence. Do you not see that it is valid to begin with it even if what precedes it is not considered? Unlike the pronoun, which links the sentence it is in to the sentence before it. Do you not see that most of what occurs in the Qur'an of this kind came with the apparent noun, as we have illustrated, and like His saying: ﴿So establish the prayer; indeed the prayer has been for the believers a decreed obligation﴾ [al-Nisa: 103], ﴿And if Allah willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight; indeed Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 20]. And the poet said:

Would that I knew, and where for me is "would that"? Indeed "layta" and indeed "law" are a weariness.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 115–116 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And they say, "Allah has taken a son," Exalted is He﴾: It was revealed concerning the Jews, when they said, "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah" [al-Tawba: 30], or concerning the Christians, when they said, "The Messiah is the son of Allah" [al-Tawba: 30], or concerning the polytheists, when they said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah," or concerning the Christians and the polytheists together. These are four opinions, and the last was stated by al-Zajjaj. Because they differ regarding the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul), they differ regarding the pronoun in "and they say" (waqalu): to whom does it refer? It was said that it refers to all of them without specification, for each of them has attributed a son to Allah; this was stated by Ibn Ishaq. The majority read it with the conjunction "wa" (وقالوا), and it is more emphatic in linking, so that it is a declarative clause conjoined to a similar declarative clause. It was also said that it is conjoined to His saying: ﴿and who strives for their ruin﴾ [al-Baqara: 114], so that it would be conjoined to something conjoined to the relative clause (al-silah), with many clauses intervening between them; and this is very far-fetched, the Qur'an being exalted above the like of it. Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿAmir and others read it without "wa": qalu (قالوا), and this would be either a resumption of speech (istiʾnaf), or one in which the sense of conjunction is intended, the pronoun and the connection through it being sufficient in place of connection by "wa." al-Farisi said: "Without 'wa' is what appears in the codices of the people of Syria."

It has been established that "ittakhadha" (اتخذ) is a form of "iftaʿala" from "akhadha" (to take), and that it sometimes takes one object, as in His saying: ﴿has taken a house﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 41]; they said its meaning is "made" and "did." And it takes two objects, in which case it means "made/rendered" (sayyara). Both meanings are possible here, and each of the two meanings requires conceiving it as impossible for there to be a son, because a son is of the same kind as the father. If you take ittakhadha to mean "did" and "made," it is impossible, because the Creator, exalted, is exempt from coming into being; He is eternal, having no beginning to His eternity, and what He makes is originated, so it is impossible that He should have a son. And if you take ittakhadha to mean "rendered," it is also impossible, because "rendering" is the transfer from one state to another, and this occurs only in what accepts change; the supposition of a son by it requires that it be of the same kind as the father, not that it involve change, so this too is impossible. When ittakhadha is taken to mean "rendered," one of the two objects is omitted; the estimate is: "And they say, 'Allah has taken some of the existents as a son.'" What has come in the Qur'an apparently takes one object, as He, exalted, said: ﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son"﴾ [Maryam: 88]; ﴿Allah has not taken any son﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 91]; ﴿It is not befitting for the Most Merciful that He take a son﴾ [Maryam: 92]. al-Qushayri said: "He mentioned the son, while He is singular in His essence; there is no part to His essence, and desire is not permissible in His attributes." End.

Since this statement is among the most corrupt and clearest in its impossibility, He brought the word that requires declaring Him free of and absolved from the things that are not permissible for Allah, exalted, before turning away from their statement and arguing against the falsity of their claim. Mention of the declaration of transcendence came first, because in it there is a rebuke to the one who makes such a claim, and because they claimed a matter from which Allah is exalted and sanctified. Then He began to refute that statement, saying: (p-363) ﴿Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾: that is, all of that is owned by Him, and among them are those whom they claimed to be a son of Allah. Begetting contradicts ownership, for a father does not own his son. Some commentators have mentioned here the question of one who buys his father, or his son, or any of his relatives, whose subject belongs to the science of jurisprudence (fiqh). When He mentioned that all belong to Allah, exalted, He mentioned that they are all obedient to Him (qanitun), that is, submissive and humbly subjected to Him. This is the custom of the owned: that he be obedient to his owner, complying with what he wills from him. The result of obedience was used as evidence for establishing ownership. Whoever has this attribute is not of the same kind as the father, since a son is of the same kind as the father. He used the word "mā" in His saying: ﴿Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, though it is for what does not reason, because when what does not reason is mixed with what reasons, it is permissible to refer to the whole by "mā." For this reason Sibawayh said: "As for mā, it is ambiguous and applies to everything." That those who reason are included under the connotation of "mā" is shown by the plural of the sound masculine type with "wa" and "nun," which is literally for those who reason, while what does not reason is included in it by the rule of giving precedence to those who reason. So when He mentioned ownership, He used the word mā, and when He mentioned obedience, He used the plural form for those who reason, which indicates that this is inclusive of those who reason and those who do not.

al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: how did He use 'mā,' which is for non-rational beings, together with His saying 'qanitun'? I say: it is like His saying: 'Glory be to Him who subjected these to us' (subhana ma sakhkharakunna lana), and it is as if He used 'mā' rather than 'man,' belittling them and diminishing their status, like His saying: ﴿and they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾ [al-Saffat: 158]." End of his words. This is an inclination on his part to the view that "mā" is applied to one who knows, and for this reason he made it like His saying "mā sakhkharakunna lana," meaning: "Glory be to Him who subjected you to us," since it is intended thereby Allah, exalted. According to us, "mā" applies only to what does not reason, unless it is mixed with those who reason, in which case it applies to both, as we have mentioned; or it applies to the attributes of those who reason, in which case it is expressed thereby. But that it apply to those who reason exclusively, whether singly or otherwise, is not so. Some grammarians permitted this, but it is a view for which there is no proof, since everything adduced for this view is open to more than one interpretation and may be interpreted otherwise. Thus His saying "subhana ma sakhkharakunna" is interpreted on the basis that "subhana" is not in a construct state and is a proper name for the meaning of glorification, so it is like the saying:

"Glory be to him of ʿAlqama the proud (subhana min ʿAlqama al-fakhir)"

And "mā" here is a temporal verbal particle (ẓarfiyya maṣdariyya), meaning: "for the duration of your subjection to us." The agent of "sakhkhara" is an implied pronoun, which the meaning and the context of speech explain, since it is known that the one who subjected them is Allah, exalted. As for al-Zamakhshari's statement, "as if He used mā rather than man, belittling them and diminishing their status," the "mā" here is not restricted to what reasons, so that one could say He expressed them by "mā," which is for what does not reason, as a belittling of them; rather it is general, applying to those who reason and to what does not reason.

The meaning of "qanitun": standing in witness, said al-Hasan; or standing for reckoning on the Day of Resurrection, said al-Rabiʿ; or obedient, said Qatada; or affirming servitude, said ʿIkrima. It was also said: standing by Allah. An objection was raised against the one who says "qunut means standing for Allah in witness and servitude": how is it generalized by this statement while many are not obedient? It was answered: its apparent meaning is generality, but the intended meaning is specificity, i.e., the people of every obedience are obedient to Him; and because the disbelievers, their misguided ones, prostrate; and because the effect of craftsmanship appears in it, and the rulings of Allah apply to it, and that is a proof of its humbling itself to Allah, exalted; this was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

(And each of them belongs to Him): "kull" is in the nominative as the subject of the nominal sentence, and the genitive complement is omitted; it is an expression for those in the heavens and the earth, that is, every one who is in the heavens and the earth, and these are the ones judged to be owned. al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also permissible that it refers to each one whom they made a son for Allah." This is very far-fetched, because the one made a son for Allah has not been mentioned, and because the predicate is shared by the one made a son and others.

And ﴿qanitun﴾ is the predicate concerning "kull," and it is put in the plural by consideration of the meaning. When "kull" is detached from what it is attached to, it is permissible to observe the meaning, so it takes the plural, or to observe the wording, so it takes the singular. The observance of the plural is good here because it is the end-of-verse rhyme (fasila), and because in their speech it is more common and better, when "kull" is detached from the genitive, to observe the meaning. He, exalted, said: ﴿and each of them were wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anfal: 54]; ﴿and each of them comes to Him humbled﴾ [al-Naml: 87]; ﴿each in an orbit they swim﴾ [al-Anbiya: 33]. The predicate has also come singular, as in His saying: (p-364) ﴿Say: each acts according to his manner﴾ [al-Isra: 84], and, if Allah, exalted, wills, the reason for the singular predicate as an embellishment will come there.
