﴿then there is the Face of Allah﴾: this is the answer of the conditional, and it is a nominal sentence (jumlah ibtida'iyyah). It has been said: its meaning is "then there is the qiblah of Allah," so the word "face" means "direction," and it was attributed to Allah because He commanded facing it; it is the direction in which is the good pleasure of Allah the Exalted. This was said by al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah and Muqatil. It has also been said: "face" here is superfluous (silah), and the meaning is "then Allah is there," that is, His knowledge and His judgment. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil: or the Essence is expressed by the word "face," as in His saying: ﴿and there remains the Face of your Lord﴾ [al-Rahman: 27], and ﴿everything perishes except His Face﴾ [al-Qasas: 88]. It has also been said: the meaning is "the deed is for Allah," said by al-Farra', who said:

I seek the forgiveness of Allah for a sin I cannot count,
Lord of the servants, to Him is the face and the deed.

It has also been said: it is possible that "face" here is meant as standing or rank (jah), as one says: "So-and-so is the face of the people," meaning the place of their honour, and "so-and-so has a face among people," meaning standing and dignity. The sense would be: "then there is the majesty and greatness of Allah," said by Abu Mansur in al-Muqni'. Wherever the word "face" comes attributed to Allah the Exalted, it has a sound basis in the language of the Arabs, since it is a word applied to many meanings, and it is impossible to take it as the organ, although that is most well known in it. Some people held that this is an attribute of Allah established by revelation, additional to what reason necessitates regarding the attributes of the Eternal, the Exalted. Abu al-'Aliyah and others weakened this view, because in it there is a definite affirmation of an attribute of Allah the Exalted by an ambiguous term, an attribute whose reality is not known and whose meaning is not understood in the Arabic language; therefore this view must be discarded, and one should rely on what has a basis in the language of the Arabs. If a word carries an indication of anthropomorphism (tajsim), we take it either in the sense of literal reality that may rightly be attributed to Allah the Exalted, if the word is homonymous (mushtarak), or in the sense of metaphor (majaz), if the word is not homonymous. Metaphor in the speech of the Arabs is more abundant than the sand of Yabrin and the river of Filastin.

So to hold to the apparent sense of a word that indicates anthropomorphism is stupidity and ignorance of the Arabic language, its idioms and its usages in speech, and of the rational proofs to which the interpretation of obscure words must return. We seek refuge in Allah from being like the Karramiyyah and those who follow their path in affirming anthropomorphism and attributing organs to Allah. Exalted is Allah above what the slanderers say, a great exaltation. In His saying ﴿wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾ there is a refutation of those who say that He is in a space and a direction, because when He gave the choice of facing all the directions, this shows that He is not in a direction nor a space; for had He been in a space, facing Him and turning toward Him would have been more worthy than all places. Since He did not specify a place, we know that He is neither in a direction nor in a space; rather, all directions are in His dominion and under His dominion. So whichever direction we turn toward Him in, in a manner of humility, we are glorifying Him and obeying His command.

* *

﴿Indeed Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾: He described Himself with the attribute of "the All-Encompassing" (al-Wasi'). It has been said that this is for the vastness of His forgiveness; there came: ﴿Indeed your Lord is vast in forgiveness﴾ [al-Najm: 32], and this is the meaning of al-Kalbi's statement: no sin is too great for Him. It has been said: "All-Encompassing in bounty," and this is the meaning of Abu 'Ubaydah's statement: "Rich (ghani)," and the meaning of al-Farra's statement: "Generous (jawwad)." It has been said: its meaning is "All-Knowing," from His saying: ﴿His Throne encompasses the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255], according to one of the interpretations, and it is combined with "All-Knowing" for emphasis. It has been said: "All-Encompassing in power." It has been said: its meaning is that He widens for His servants in judgment; His religion is ease. "All-Knowing": that is, of their welfare, or of the intentions of the hearts, which are the foundation of the deed, even if their outward forms differ in the qiblah and other matters. These interpretations accord with the view of those who say the verse was revealed concerning the matter of the qiblah. Al-Qaffal said: it contains no mention of the qiblah or prayer; rather, Allah the Exalted informed them of His knowledge of them and of His authority encompassing them wherever they were, as in His saying: ﴿If you are able to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Rahman: 33], and His saying: ﴿There is no private conversation of three but He is their fourth﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 7], and in this there is a threat to whoever prevented the mosques of Allah from remembrance and strove to ruin them: that there is no escape from Allah and no refuge, as He the Exalted said: ﴿Where is the escape?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 10] ﴿No! There is no refuge﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 11] ﴿To your Lord on that Day is the place of rest﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 12], and as the poet said:

So you are like the night which will overtake me, even if I imagine that the place far from you is vast.

And he said:

The one deluded by Allah when he travelled did not intend to escape,
and the one made mighty by Allah, His seeker is he.

And he said:

Where is the escape? There is no escape for the fugitive,
and to Him belong the two expanses, the dry land and the water.

On this meaning the address is general, including whoever prevented the mosques from remembrance and other things. This sentence came emphasized by "inna" with the name of Allah explicitly stated in it, indicating independence. We have already discussed this in His saying: ﴿you will find it with Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 110], and like His saying: ﴿and seek the forgiveness of Allah; indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 199]. That is more majestic and more eloquent than the pronoun, because the pronoun indicates strength of connection, while the apparent noun indicates independence. Do you not see that it is valid to begin with it even if what precedes it is not considered? Unlike the pronoun, which links the sentence it is in to the sentence before it. Do you not see that most of what occurs in the Qur'an of this kind came with the apparent noun, as we have illustrated, and like His saying: ﴿So establish the prayer; indeed the prayer has been for the believers a decreed obligation﴾ [al-Nisa: 103], ﴿And if Allah willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight; indeed Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 20]. And the poet said:

Would that I knew, and where for me is "would that"? Indeed "layta" and indeed "law" are a weariness.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 115–116 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And they say, "Allah has taken a son," Exalted is He﴾: It was revealed concerning the Jews, when they said, "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah" [al-Tawba: 30], or concerning the Christians, when they said, "The Messiah is the son of Allah" [al-Tawba: 30], or concerning the polytheists, when they said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah," or concerning the Christians and the polytheists together. These are four opinions, and the last was stated by al-Zajjaj. Because they differ regarding the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul), they differ regarding the pronoun in "and they say" (waqalu): to whom does it refer? It was said that it refers to all of them without specification, for each of them has attributed a son to Allah; this was stated by Ibn Ishaq. The majority read it with the conjunction "wa" (وقالوا), and it is more emphatic in linking, so that it is a declarative clause conjoined to a similar declarative clause. It was also said that it is conjoined to His saying: ﴿and who strives for their ruin﴾ [al-Baqara: 114], so that it would be conjoined to something conjoined to the relative clause (al-silah), with many clauses intervening between them; and this is very far-fetched, the Qur'an being exalted above the like of it. Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿAmir and others read it without "wa": qalu (قالوا), and this would be either a resumption of speech (istiʾnaf), or one in which the sense of conjunction is intended, the pronoun and the connection through it being sufficient in place of connection by "wa." al-Farisi said: "Without 'wa' is what appears in the codices of the people of Syria."

It has been established that "ittakhadha" (اتخذ) is a form of "iftaʿala" from "akhadha" (to take), and that it sometimes takes one object, as in His saying: ﴿has taken a house﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 41]; they said its meaning is "made" and "did." And it takes two objects, in which case it means "made/rendered" (sayyara). Both meanings are possible here, and each of the two meanings requires conceiving it as impossible for there to be a son, because a son is of the same kind as the father. If you take ittakhadha to mean "did" and "made," it is impossible, because the Creator, exalted, is exempt from coming into being; He is eternal, having no beginning to His eternity, and what He makes is originated, so it is impossible that He should have a son. And if you take ittakhadha to mean "rendered," it is also impossible, because "rendering" is the transfer from one state to another, and this occurs only in what accepts change; the supposition of a son by it requires that it be of the same kind as the father, not that it involve change, so this too is impossible. When ittakhadha is taken to mean "rendered," one of the two objects is omitted; the estimate is: "And they say, 'Allah has taken some of the existents as a son.'" What has come in the Qur'an apparently takes one object, as He, exalted, said: ﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son"﴾ [Maryam: 88]; ﴿Allah has not taken any son﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 91]; ﴿It is not befitting for the Most Merciful that He take a son﴾ [Maryam: 92]. al-Qushayri said: "He mentioned the son, while He is singular in His essence; there is no part to His essence, and desire is not permissible in His attributes." End.

Since this statement is among the most corrupt and clearest in its impossibility, He brought the word that requires declaring Him free of and absolved from the things that are not permissible for Allah, exalted, before turning away from their statement and arguing against the falsity of their claim. Mention of the declaration of transcendence came first, because in it there is a rebuke to the one who makes such a claim, and because they claimed a matter from which Allah is exalted and sanctified. Then He began to refute that statement, saying: (p-363) ﴿Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾: that is, all of that is owned by Him, and among them are those whom they claimed to be a son of Allah. Begetting contradicts ownership, for a father does not own his son. Some commentators have mentioned here the question of one who buys his father, or his son, or any of his relatives, whose subject belongs to the science of jurisprudence (fiqh). When He mentioned that all belong to Allah, exalted, He mentioned that they are all obedient to Him (qanitun), that is, submissive and humbly subjected to Him. This is the custom of the owned: that he be obedient to his owner, complying with what he wills from him. The result of obedience was used as evidence for establishing ownership. Whoever has this attribute is not of the same kind as the father, since a son is of the same kind as the father. He used the word "mā" in His saying: ﴿Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, though it is for what does not reason, because when what does not reason is mixed with what reasons, it is permissible to refer to the whole by "mā." For this reason Sibawayh said: "As for mā, it is ambiguous and applies to everything." That those who reason are included under the connotation of "mā" is shown by the plural of the sound masculine type with "wa" and "nun," which is literally for those who reason, while what does not reason is included in it by the rule of giving precedence to those who reason. So when He mentioned ownership, He used the word mā, and when He mentioned obedience, He used the plural form for those who reason, which indicates that this is inclusive of those who reason and those who do not.

al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: how did He use 'mā,' which is for non-rational beings, together with His saying 'qanitun'? I say: it is like His saying: 'Glory be to Him who subjected these to us' (subhana ma sakhkharakunna lana), and it is as if He used 'mā' rather than 'man,' belittling them and diminishing their status, like His saying: ﴿and they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾ [al-Saffat: 158]." End of his words. This is an inclination on his part to the view that "mā" is applied to one who knows, and for this reason he made it like His saying "mā sakhkharakunna lana," meaning: "Glory be to Him who subjected you to us," since it is intended thereby Allah, exalted. According to us, "mā" applies only to what does not reason, unless it is mixed with those who reason, in which case it applies to both, as we have mentioned; or it applies to the attributes of those who reason, in which case it is expressed thereby. But that it apply to those who reason exclusively, whether singly or otherwise, is not so. Some grammarians permitted this, but it is a view for which there is no proof, since everything adduced for this view is open to more than one interpretation and may be interpreted otherwise. Thus His saying "subhana ma sakhkharakunna" is interpreted on the basis that "subhana" is not in a construct state and is a proper name for the meaning of glorification, so it is like the saying:

"Glory be to him of ʿAlqama the proud (subhana min ʿAlqama al-fakhir)"

And "mā" here is a temporal verbal particle (ẓarfiyya maṣdariyya), meaning: "for the duration of your subjection to us." The agent of "sakhkhara" is an implied pronoun, which the meaning and the context of speech explain, since it is known that the one who subjected them is Allah, exalted. As for al-Zamakhshari's statement, "as if He used mā rather than man, belittling them and diminishing their status," the "mā" here is not restricted to what reasons, so that one could say He expressed them by "mā," which is for what does not reason, as a belittling of them; rather it is general, applying to those who reason and to what does not reason.

The meaning of "qanitun": standing in witness, said al-Hasan; or standing for reckoning on the Day of Resurrection, said al-Rabiʿ; or obedient, said Qatada; or affirming servitude, said ʿIkrima. It was also said: standing by Allah. An objection was raised against the one who says "qunut means standing for Allah in witness and servitude": how is it generalized by this statement while many are not obedient? It was answered: its apparent meaning is generality, but the intended meaning is specificity, i.e., the people of every obedience are obedient to Him; and because the disbelievers, their misguided ones, prostrate; and because the effect of craftsmanship appears in it, and the rulings of Allah apply to it, and that is a proof of its humbling itself to Allah, exalted; this was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

(And each of them belongs to Him): "kull" is in the nominative as the subject of the nominal sentence, and the genitive complement is omitted; it is an expression for those in the heavens and the earth, that is, every one who is in the heavens and the earth, and these are the ones judged to be owned. al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also permissible that it refers to each one whom they made a son for Allah." This is very far-fetched, because the one made a son for Allah has not been mentioned, and because the predicate is shared by the one made a son and others.

And ﴿qanitun﴾ is the predicate concerning "kull," and it is put in the plural by consideration of the meaning. When "kull" is detached from what it is attached to, it is permissible to observe the meaning, so it takes the plural, or to observe the wording, so it takes the singular. The observance of the plural is good here because it is the end-of-verse rhyme (fasila), and because in their speech it is more common and better, when "kull" is detached from the genitive, to observe the meaning. He, exalted, said: ﴿and each of them were wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anfal: 54]; ﴿and each of them comes to Him humbled﴾ [al-Naml: 87]; ﴿each in an orbit they swim﴾ [al-Anbiya: 33]. The predicate has also come singular, as in His saying: (p-364) ﴿Say: each acts according to his manner﴾ [al-Isra: 84], and, if Allah, exalted, wills, the reason for the singular predicate as an embellishment will come there.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 117:**

﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾: When He mentioned that He owns all who are in the heavens and the earth, and that they are all obedient to Him (*qanitun*), and that they are contained within the heavens and the earth, He mentioned the two containers and singled them out for origination, because they are the greatest of the created things we witness. The word *badi'* (بَدِيعُ) is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, and it is of the category of the *sifa mushabbaha* (the attributive adjective resembling the active participle). The genitive noun that follows is thus like the object, and its original form was *badi' samawatihi* (the originator of His heavens). Then the adjective was made to resemble a verb, so a pronoun was concealed in it and it governed the accusative *al-samawat*, and then the genitive was given to the one that was in the accusative. In it there is also a pronoun that refers back to God, Exalted, and the meaning in its original form is that His heavens were originated (*bud'it*), meaning they came into creation in a novel form that had no precedent. This view was initiated by al-Zamakhshari, except that he said: "The originator of the heavens is an attribution of the *sifa mushabbaha* to its agent." But this is not our view. Rather, it is an attribution of the *sifa mushabbaha* to its object. In our view, an adjective does not become *mushabbaha* unless it governs something in the accusative or genitive. When it raises what follows it, then in our view it is not a *sifa mushabbaha*, because the function of raising the agent is shared by transitive and intransitive adjectives. So when we say: *Zayd qa'imun abuhu* (Zayd, his father is standing), *qa'im* raises *abu* as *darib* raises its object. If you say: *Zayd daribun abuhu 'amran* (Zayd, his father is striking Amr), you do not say that *qa'iman* here, in its function of raising, was made to resemble *darib*. And if this is so, then the attribution of the active participle to its nominative noun is not permissible, according to what is established in the science of Arabic grammar (*'ilm al-'arabiyya*), unless we take al-Zamakhshari's statement as figurative, in which case it is possible, and the meaning would be an attribution of the *sifa mushabbaha* to what was its agent before it was made to resemble a verb. Al-Zamakhshari also related a second view, in which he said: "It was said that *al-badi'* has the meaning of *al-mubdi'* (the one who originates), just as *al-sami'* in the words of Amr:

*Amin raybanata al-da'i al-sami'*
(Is it from Rayhana, the caller, the one who hears?)

has the meaning of *al-musmi'* (the one who makes hear). And in this there is consideration." End of his words. Ibn 'Atiyya did not mention any other view besides this one. He said: "*Badi'* is derived from *mubdi'*, like *basir* from *mubsir* (the one who sees), and from it is the verse of Amr ibn Ma'di Karib:

*Amin raybanata al-da'i al-sami' ∗∗∗ yu'arriquni wa-ashabi huju'*
(Is it from Rayhana, the caller, the one who hears, that keeps me awake while my companions sleep?)

He means: *al-musmi'*, *al-mubdi'*, and *al-mun'ši'* (the one who creates). From it also is *ashab al-bida'* (the people of innovations), and from it is the statement of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab about the prayer of Ramadan: 'What a fine innovation (*bid'a*) this is.' End of his words. The consideration that al-Zamakhshari mentioned, and God knows best, is that *fa'il* in the sense of *muf'il* is not a regular pattern, although the verse of Amr is open to interpretation. On this view it is of the category of the attribution of the active participle to its object. The reciter al-Mansur read *badi'an* in the accusative as a form of praise, and it was also read in the genitive as an apposition to the pronoun in *lahu* (to Him).

* *

﴿And when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾: When He mentioned what indicates invention (*al-ikhtira'*), He mentioned what indicates the obedience of the inventor and the speed of His bringing into being. The meaning of *qada* (decreed) here is *arada* (willed), that is, when He wills the bringing into existence and invention of a matter. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "*Qada* means *qaddara* (determined), and it may come with the meaning of *amda* (executed). Both meanings are suitable in this verse. According to the view of the People of the Sunna (*Ahl al-Sunna*), He determined it in eternity and executed it therein; according to the view of the Mu'tazila, He executed it at the moment of creation and bringing into existence." And *al-amr* (the matter) is the singular of *al-umur* (affairs), and here it is not the verbal noun of *amara yamuru* (to command). The belief regarding this verse is that God has never ceased commanding the non-existent things upon the condition of their existence, being capable even though the things decreed are delayed, and knowing even though the known things' occurrence is delayed. Everything in the verse that requires the future tense is according to what is commanded, since the originated things come after they were not. Everything ascribed to God, from power and knowledge, is eternal and has never ceased." End of what we have transmitted here from his words. Al-Mahdawi said: "*And when He decrees a matter*, that is, He perfects it, makes it firm, and finishes with it. The meaning of *fa-innama yaqulu lahu kun fa-yakun* (He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is) is that He says on account of it. It was also said: He says to it 'Be' while it is non-existent, because it is like something existing, since it is known to Him. Al-Tabari said: His command to a thing 'Be' does not precede its existence nor follow it, so a thing is not commanded to exist unless it already exists by the command, and it does not exist by the command unless it is commanded to exist. He said: A parallel to this is the rising of the dead from their graves, which does not precede God's call nor follow it, as He said: ﴿Then when He calls you with a call from the earth, behold, you will come out﴾ [al-Rum: 25]. So the pronoun in *lahu* refers to the command, or to the decree indicated by *qada*, or to the intended object indicated by the context." End of what we have transmitted from his book. Makki said: "The meaning of the verse is that He knows what will be and what is existing, so His saying 'Be' is only for what exists in His knowledge, in order to bring it out into the open for us." End of his words. Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Kun fa-yakun* (Be, and it is) is from *kana* in its complete sense, meaning 'come into being, and it comes into being.' This is a figurative speech, an illustration, and not an actual saying, just as in the words of the poet:

*Idh qalat al-anse'u li-l-batni al-haqi*
(When the ribs said to the belly, 'Be steadfast')

the meaning is that whatever He decreed of matters and willed to be, it comes into being and enters existence without any hindrance or delay, just as an obedient servant who is commanded and complies does not delay, does not refuse, and does not show reluctance. By this he emphasized the improbability of childbirth, because whoever has this degree of power, his state is different from the states of bodies in their reproduction." End of his words. Al-Sajawandi said: "*Kun* (Be) is by way of illustration for the execution of the command." He said:

*Fa-qalat lahu al-'aynani sam'an wa-ta'atan ∗∗∗ wa-illa fa-al-ma'dumu kayfa yukhatabu*
(So the two eyes said to him, 'We hear and obey,' otherwise how would a non-existent be addressed?)

Or it is a sign to the angels of the existence of the thing that has come into being, or it is according to the supposition of what was conceived of its existence in His knowledge, or it is specific to the transformation of an existent from one state to another. And if *kun* were created, it would need another *kun*, and so on without end, which shows that the Qur'an is uncreated." End of his words. Al-Mahdawi said: "In this verse there is evidence that the speech of God is uncreated, because if it were created, He would be speaking to it, 'Be,' and would be speaking, 'Be' to the 'Be,' until that goes on infinitely. That is impossible, and what leads to it is that no act at all would proceed from God, since there must be acts before it that are sayings without end, and that is impossible. It is not permissible to take it as figurative, because figurative use occurs with inanimate things, and does not occur with one who is capable of speech except with evidence. What strengthens this is that the verbal noun in it, which is 'our saying' from His words: ﴿Our word to a thing, when We desire it, is only that We say to it, 'Be,' and it is﴾ [al-Nahl: 40], is emphasized by another verbal noun, which is *an naqula* (that We say), and the Arabic grammarians (*Ahl al-'Arabiyya*) agree that when they emphasize the verb with a verbal noun, it is literal. That is why His words came: ﴿And God spoke to Moses directly (*taklimā*)﴾ [al-Nisa': 164], since God was the one who directly addressed him. It has been said that the meaning of *fa-innama yaqulu lahu kun fa-yakun* is 'by His being.'" End of al-Mahdawi's words. In *al-Muntakhab* (al-Razi's Muntakhab?) it is said: "*Kun fa-yakun* does not mean that He says 'Be' and then that thing becomes; that is corrupt from several aspects, so it must be interpreted. There are several interpretations: The first, which is the strongest, is that the meaning is the speed of God's power in forming things, and He creates them not from deliberation. A parallel is: ﴿They both said, 'We come obedient'﴾ [Fussilat: 11]. The second: it is a sign that the angels understand, and when they hear it they know that He has brought a matter into being, as Abu al-Hudhayl said. The third: it was addressed to those existing ones to whom He said: ﴿Be apes, despised﴾ [al-Baqara: 65], and whoever is like them, and this is the view of al-Asamm. The fourth: it is a command to the living to die, and to the dead to live. All of these are weak, and the strongest is the first." End of his words.

This is what we have transmitted from the words of the commentators on this verse. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that when God wills to bring a thing into being, He says to it, "Be," as another verse explains: ﴿Our word to a thing, when We desire it, is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [al-Nahl: 40], and His words: ﴿And Our command is but one, like the blink of an eye﴾ [al-Qamar: 50]. However, rational proof prevents belief in addressing the non-existent, and prevents God from being a locus of temporal events, because the expression "Be" is originated, and whoever understands the meaning of the expression and that its letters come one after another does not doubt its originatedness. If this is so, there is no address and no verbal speech; rather, it is an expression of the speed of bringing into existence and its ease, so it is of the figurative illustration, and it is as if He supposed that the non-existent is existent, accepting the command and complying with speed, such that it does not delay in executing what it was commanded.

*Fa-yakunu* (and it is) was read by the majority with the nominative, and this was explained as being a new sentence, meaning "so it is," and this was attributed to Sibawayh. Others said: *fa-yakunu* is coordinated with *yaqulu* (He says), and al-Tabari chose and affirmed this. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is an error from the perspective of meaning, because it implies that the saying together with the bringing into being is temporal, and Ibn 'Atiyya's refutation ends there." The meaning of his refutation is that the command, in his view, is already complete, and the coming into being is temporal, and it has been coordinated with it by *fa-* (then), so it is concomitant with it, that is, it follows it immediately; so this is not valid, because the eternal is not followed immediately by the temporal. Al-Tabari's affirmation of it is what preceded at the beginning of the discussion on this issue, that the command does not precede existence nor follow it. What Ibn 'Atiyya refuted it with is only complete if the verse is taken to mean that there is a saying and an eternal command. But if that is by way of figurative speech and illustration, then it is permissible to coordinate it with *naqulu* (We say). Ibn 'Amir read *fa-yakuna* with the accusative, and in Al 'Imran: ﴿Be, and it is﴾ and *nu'allimuhu* (and We teach him); and in al-Nahl, and in Maryam, and in Ya-Sin, and in al-Mu'min. Al-Kisa'i agreed with him in al-Nahl and Ya-Sin, and there was no disagreement regarding ﴿Be, and it is﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59] and ﴿the truth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 60] in Al 'Imran.

﴿Be, and it is; His word is the truth﴾ [al-An'am: 73] in al-An'am is read with the nominative. The reason for the accusative is that it is an answer to the wording of *kun* (Be), since it came in the form of a command, and so it is treated like a real command. It is not valid to put it in the accusative as the answer to a real command, because that happens only with two verbs which form a condition and a consequence, such as: *i'tini fa-ukrimka* (come to me, and I will honor you), the meaning being: "If you come to me, I will honor you." Here that does not apply, because the meaning would become: "If it be, it will be," so there must be a difference between the condition and the consequence, either with respect to the agent, or with respect to the verb itself, or in some aspect of its related elements. Ibn 'Atiyya related, from Ahmad ibn Musa, regarding Ibn 'Amir's reading, that it is *lahn* (a grammatical error), and this is a wrong statement, because this reading is among the seven, so it is a widely transmitted reading. Moreover, it is the reading of Ibn 'Amir, who was an Arab who would not commit a grammatical error. And al-Kisa'i's reading in some places, and he is the imam of the Kufans in the science of Arabic grammar. So the claim that it is *lahn* is among the most grievous errors that make the one who says it sinful, and that may lead him to disbelief, since it is an attack on what is known to have been transmitted through widespread transmission from the Book of God, Exalted.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 2, Verse 118:**

﴿Those who do not know say, "Why does Allah not speak to us, or a sign come to us?"﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, al-Rabiʿ and al-Suddi said: it was revealed concerning the disbelievers of the Arabs, when ʿAbd Allah ibn Umayya and others made this demand. Mujahid said: it refers to the Christians, and al-Tabari preferred this view, because they are the ones mentioned in the verse first. Ibn ʿAbbas also said: it refers to the Jews who lived in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Rafiʿ ibn Khuzayma, one of the Jews, said: "If you are a messenger from Allah, then ask Allah to speak to us until we hear His speech." So Allah revealed the verse. Qatada said: it refers to the polytheists of Mecca. It has also been said that the reference of the phrase ﴿those who do not know﴾ is to all of these groups, since they all made this same statement, and the difference among them about the relative pronoun is based on their difference about the occasion of revelation. If the relative pronoun refers to the ignorant Arabs, then knowledge is denied of them because they had no scripture and were not followers of any prophethood. If the relative pronoun refers to the Jews and Christians, then knowledge is denied of them because its fruit is absent, and that fruit is following it and acting in accordance with its requirements. The object of the verb "to know" is omitted here for brevity, because the intended meaning is only to deny that knowledge is attributed to them, not to deny that they know any particular thing. It is as if it were said: "and those who are not people who have any disposition toward knowledge, due to their extreme dullness." This is a statement that issued from one who is not characterized by discernment or perception. The object of the verb "say" is the specifying clause: ﴿Those who do not know say, "Why does Allah not speak to us, or a sign come to us?"﴾, as in "Allah speaks to the angels, and as He spoke to Musa, peace be upon him." They said this in a manner of arrogance and rebelliousness. ﴿Or a sign come to us﴾ means: "Would that one of these two things happened: either that He speak, or that a sign come?" They said this out of denial that what had come to them was a sign, and in contempt for it. When Allah related their attribution of a son to Him, He followed it with another of their statements, which shows their obstinacy and their ignorance of the reverence due to Allah the Exalted and of not making demands upon His prophets.

﴿Thus said those before them, the like of their saying﴾: The discussion of the grammatical analysis (iʿrab) of "thus" (kadhalika) has already passed, as has the explanation of how "from before them" (min qablihim) functions as a relative clause for "those" in His words: ﴿and those before you, that you may be righteous﴾ [al-Baqara 2:21], and "those before them." If the relative pronoun in "those who do not know" is interpreted as the disbelieving Arabs or the polytheists of Mecca, then "those before them" are the disbelieving nations from their ancestors and others. If it is interpreted as the Jews or Christians, then "those before them" are their forefathers. (p-367) The accusative of "the like of their saying" is a substitute (badal) for the position of the particle "kaf" (in "thus"). Similarity does not necessarily mean identity in the very content of what was said; it is possible that those before them proposed something other than this, and that the similarity lies in proposing what is not fitting to ask for, even if it was not that very statement, since "similarity" applies in this sense.

﴿Their hearts have become alike﴾: The pronoun refers to ﴿those who do not know﴾ and ﴿those before them﴾ [Ali ʿImran 3:11]. When He mentioned the similarity of their statements, which proceed from desires and hearts, He mentioned the similarity of their hearts in blindness and ignorance, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿Did they bequeath it to one another?﴾ [al-Dhariyat 51:53]. It has been said: their hearts became alike in disbelief. It has been said: in hardness. It has been said: in obstinacy and making demands. It has been said: in impossibility. Ibn Abi Ishaq and Abu Haywa read "tashabbahat" with a doubled shin (tashdid). Abu ʿAmr al-Dani said: this is not permissible, because it is a past-tense verb, meaning that the gathering of the two added letters (taʾs) does not occur in the past tense; it occurs only in the present tense, as in "tatashabbahu," and in that case assimilation (idghaam) is permitted. As for the past tense, its original form is not "tatashabbaha." The parallel of this reading has already occurred in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the cows have become confused for us﴾ [al-Baqara 2:70], and we explained it by an interpretation that is not possible here, so an interpretation for this reading must be sought here.

﴿We have already made the signs clear for a people who are certain﴾: That is, We have clarified the signs. Therefore, demanding a sign after signs have already come and been made clear is merely a form of obstinacy. Moreover, these are clear signs, with no ambiguity and no uncertainty, due to the intensity of their clarity. However, their being signs is not apparent except to one who is certain. As for one who is in doubt, or suspicion, or heedlessness, or ignorance, the signs do not benefit him, even if they were in the utmost clarity. Do you not see their saying: ﴿Our eyes have only been dazzled; rather, we are a people bewitched﴾ [al-Hijr 15:15]? And the saying of Abu Jahl, when he asked the desert people who came to Mecca about the splitting of the moon, and they informed him of it, he then said: "This is continuous magic." When He mentioned that the demanding of what was previously mentioned comes only from the desires of those who do not know, He said at its end: ﴿for a people who are certain﴾. Certainty (iyqan) is a quality in knowledge by which one reaches the utmost firmness in knowledge; that is, whoever is certain, We have made the signs clear to him, so he believes in them, they become evident to him, and the proof is established against others by them. In all the signs there is a refutation of whoever demands a sign, since the signs have been made clear, and so they are not a single sign which could be claimed to be ambiguous. Rather, this is a collection of clear signs, but only one who is among the people of knowledge, insight and certainty benefits from them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 119:

﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good news and a warner.﴾ "A bringer of good news" to those who believe, and "a warner" to those who disbelieve. This verse is a consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for he would feel distress at their persistence in their misguidance. The connection of this verse to what precedes it: when Allah mentioned that He had made the signs clear, He mentioned those through whose hands they were made clear. So He turned to him and addressed him (ﷺ), so that he would know that he is the bearer of the signs, and said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth﴾, meaning with the clear signs. The word "truth" here has been interpreted as truthfulness, as the Qur'an, and as Islam. "With the truth" is in the position of a hal (circumstantial clause), meaning: We sent you while the truth is with you and does not leave you. The accusative of "bashiran wa nadhiran" (as a bringer of good news and a warner) is a hal from the kaf (the pronoun "you"). It is also possible that it is a hal from "the truth", because what he brought of the truth is also characterized by good news and warning. But the first is more apparent. He shifted to the pattern fa'il for intensification (mubalagha), because fa'il is among the patterns of inherent qualities. The shift to the intensive form in "bashir" is regular according to Sibawayh, if we take it from bashsharа, because they said bishr with the lightened form. It is not regular in "nadhir", because it is from anzara. The likely reason for the shift in it is that it is coordinated with what permits that form, because a word may be permissible in conjunction with its counterpart when it is not permissible if it stood alone, as they said: akhadhahu ma qaddama wa ma hadatha, and the like.

﴿And you will not be questioned about the companions of the Hellfire.﴾ The reading of the majority is with a damma on the ta' and the lam: "tus'alu". Ubayy read: "wa ma tus'alu". Ibn Mas'ud read: "wa lan tus'ala". All of this is a statement (khabar). In the first reading and in Ubayy's reading, the sentence may be a new sentence (isti'naf), which is the more apparent, and it may be in the position of a hal. As for Ibn Mas'ud's reading, the isti'naf is necessarily determined in it, and the meaning on the basis of the isti'naf is that you will not be questioned about the disbelievers regarding why they did not believe, because that is not up to you: ﴿If upon you is only the conveyance [of the message]﴾ [Ash-Shura: 48], ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ [Al-Qasas: 56], ﴿You are only a warner﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 7]. In this there is consolation for him (ﷺ) and lightening of what he would feel of their obstinacy, so it is as if it was said: You are not responsible for them, so their disbelief should not grieve you. In this is evidence that no one is questioned about the sin of another: ﴿and no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾ [Al-An'am: 164]. As for the hal, it is coordinated with what precedes it of the hal, meaning: and not responsible for the disbelievers regarding why they do not believe. Thus it becomes a restriction on the sending, unlike the isti'naf.

Nafi' and Ya'qub read: "wa la tas'al" with a fatha on the ta' and a jazm on the lam, and that is in the form of a prohibition (nahy). Its apparent meaning is that it is a prohibition in reality: "He (ﷺ) was forbidden to ask about the conditions of the disbelievers." Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I wish I knew what my two parents did," and then it was revealed. This was considered unlikely in al-Muntakhab, because he knows what their affair came to. 'Iyad mentioned that they were brought back to life for him and they embraced Islam. It is also established that Allah permitted him to visit them, and this too was considered unlikely, because the context of the speech indicates that this refers to the Jews, the Christians, and the idolaters of the Arabs, who denied his prophethood, disbelieved out of obstinacy, and persisted in their disbelief. Likewise what came after it: ﴿And the Jews will never be pleased with you, nor the Christians﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 120], unless this is in the sense of a break from the first speech, and it would be a shift of address (talwin al-khitab), and that is far-fetched. It has been said: it is possible that it is not a prohibition in reality, but this came in the sense of magnifying what the people of disbelief have fallen into of punishment, as you say: "How is so-and-so?" when he has fallen into a calamity, and it is said to you: "Do not ask about him." The aspect of magnification is that the one asking recoils from letting on his tongue what that person is in, because of its horror, so do not ask him and do not burden him with what would distress him. Or, "you, O questioner, are not able to hear his news, because it would distress the listener and trouble him, so do not ask." So the meaning of magnification is either in relation to the one answering or in relation to the one being asked about, and the literal meaning of prohibition is not intended by this.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 120:

﴿And the Jews will never be pleased with you, nor the Christians, until you follow their religion.﴾ It is related that the Jews and the Christians asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for a truce (hudnah), and promised that after a period they would follow him, as a deception on their part. Allah informed him of the secret of their deception, and so this was revealed. Allah negated their being pleased with him unless he followed their religion. This is a statement that they are the companions of the Blazing Fire (al-Jahim), who are its companions, and there is no hope of their accepting Islam. The apparent meaning of His words, ﴿And the Jews will never be pleased with you﴾, is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), in which their being pleased with him is made conditional upon something impossible for him (ﷺ) to do, namely following their religion. Whatever is conditional upon something impossible is itself impossible, whether we interpret the millah (religious community/creed) as the sharia, or as the qiblah, or as the Qur'an. It has also been said that this is an address to him, but its purpose is to discipline his community, since they know his standing with his Lord. This is so that the believers may learn manners from it and not take the disbelievers as allies, for they will not be satisfied with them unless they follow their religion. It has also been said that this is an address to him, but what is meant is his community, because the one addressed cannot possibly do what he is addressed about, so it is directed to those who are able to do it, like His words: ﴿If you were to associate partners with Allah, your deeds would surely be nullified﴾ (Az-Zumar 39:65). This serves as an alert from Allah that the Jews and the Christians will deceive you with what they show of inclination, their seeking of a truce, and their promise of agreement, but their being pleased will not occur except by following their religion. The word millah is in the singular, even though they have two religions, because both are united by disbelief (kufr), so it is one in this respect. Or it is for brevity, and it is then a case of collective pronominal reference, like the words: ﴿And they say: Be Jews or Christians﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:135). For it is known that the Christians will never be pleased until you follow their religion, and the Jews will never be pleased until you follow their religion. The scholars have differed regarding disbelief: is it one religion or several religions? The fruit of this disagreement appears in apostasy from one religion to another, and in inheritance, and this is mentioned in fiqh (jurisprudence).

﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the guidance﴾: He commanded him to address them by saying that the guidance of Allah, that is, what is attributed to Allah, which is Islam, the religion you follow, is the guidance, that is, the beneficial and complete one beyond which there is no guidance. What you are commanded to follow is desire, not guidance: ﴿And who is more astray than one who follows his own desire without guidance from Allah?﴾ (Al-Qasas 28:50). He emphasized the sentence with inna and with the separating pronoun (al-fasl) that precedes it, and so it indicates exclusivity and restriction (al-ikhtisas wa al-hasr). The word al-huda is definite with the article (al-), and it has been said that this indicates restriction: when you say "Zayd is the scholar," it is as if it were said that he is the one specifically characterized by knowledge and confined to it. Then Allah mentioned that what they are upon is only desires and misguidance arising from their appetites and inclinations (p-369), so He said:

﴿And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, you would have from Allah no protector or helper﴾: This is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), according to the views expressed regarding His words: ﴿And the Jews will never be pleased﴾. The lam in la'in is called al-muwatti'ah and al-mu'dhinah (the lam that prepares for or announces an oath), and it indicates an oath implied before it. For this reason, what follows the condition is built upon the oath and not upon the condition, since if it were built upon the condition, the fa' would have entered in His words: ﴿you would have﴾. Al-ahwa' is the plural of hawa (desire), and the plural indicates the multitude of their disagreements, since if they were upon the truth, it would be one path: ﴿And if it had been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much discrepancy﴾ (An-Nisa' 4:82). He attributed the desires to them because they are their innovations (bida') and misguidance, and for this reason the people of innovations are called "lords of desires."

﴿After the knowledge that has come to you﴾: that is, from the religion. He called it knowledge because it is known through sound proofs. This verse indicates several matters. Among them: whoever Allah knows will not do a thing, it is permissible for him to be addressed with a threat, because it is possible that this threat is what turns him away, or that this threat is one of the turning-away factors. Its parallel is: ﴿If you were to associate partners with Allah, your deeds would surely be nullified﴾ (Az-Zumar 39:65). Among them: His words, ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾, indicate that a threat is not permissible except after a prior excuse (ma'dhirah), and thus the imposition of what cannot be borne is invalidated. Among them: following desire is invalid, and this indicates the invalidity of taqlid (blind imitation). The knowledge here has been interpreted as the Qur'an, and as knowledge of the misguidance of the people, and as the clarification that the religion of Allah is Islam, and as the turning toward the Ka'bah; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. In His words, ﴿you would have from Allah no protector or helper﴾, there is a cutting off of their hopes that you would follow their desires, since whoever knows that he has no protector and no helper who benefits him if he commits something is further from committing it. This is a despairing (iya's) of them that anyone would follow their desires. The discussion of the protector (wali) and the helper (nasir) has already passed, and so its repetition here is unnecessary.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 121:**

﴿Those to whom We have given the Book recite it with its true recitation. It is they who believe in it.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: It was revealed concerning the people of the ship who came with Jaʿfar ibn Abi Talib, who were thirty-two men from the people of Abyssinia (al-Habasha) and eight monks from al-Sham. It was also said: some of them were from the people of Najran, some from the people of Abyssinia and from the Romans, and eight sailors, the companions of the ship, came with Jaʿfar. Al-Dahhak said: they are those among the Jews who believed, such as Ibn Salam, Ibn Suriya, Ibn Yamin, and others. It was said: they are the scholars of the Jews and the rabbis of the Christians. Ibn Kaysan said: they are the prophets and messengers. It was said: they are the believers. It was said: they are the Companions, as reported by ʿIkrima and Qatada. Based on this difference, the difference over the Book also arises: is it the Torah or the Gospel, or both of them together with the Qur'an, or the category (of scripture)? So it means "the written," and thus includes the earlier scriptures.

﴿They recite it with its true recitation﴾: that is, they read it and recite it with its i'rab (grammatical inflection). ʿIkrima said: they follow its rulings. al-Hasan said: they act upon its clear (muhkam) verses and entrust its ambiguous (mutashabih) verses to Allah. ʿUmar said: they ask from His mercy and seek refuge from His punishment. al-Zamakhshari said: they do not distort it, nor change what is in it concerning the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

*Alladhina* (those who): it is a subject (mubtada'). If it is intended specifically for those who were guided, then *yatluna-hu* (they recite it) may be its predicate, and it may also be a circumstantial clause (hal muqaddara, a clause understood to describe a state at a future time), either from the pronoun of the object or from *al-Kitab* (the Book), because at the time it was given they were not reciting it, nor was it recited to them. In that case the predicate would be, in the sentence as a whole, the statement *ulaʾika yu'minuna bihi* (it is they who believe in it). al-Hawfi permitted that *yatluna-hu* be the predicate, and *ulaʾika* and what follows it be a second predicate after a predicate. He said it is like their saying: *hadha hulwun hamid* (this is sweet and sour). This is based on whether one subject can take two predicates or not. It is only permitted if they are in the sense of one predicate, as in their saying: *hadha hulwun hamid*, meaning *mazz* (pleasant to taste), and there is a difference of opinion on this. If *alladhina atayna-hum al-Kitab* (those to whom We have given the Book) is meant in a general sense, the predicate is *ulaʾika yu'minuna bihi* (it is they who believe in it). They said, among them Ibn ʿAtiyya: *wa-yatluna-hu* (and they recite it) is a circumstantial clause that cannot be dispensed with, and it carries the benefit, and it is not permissible for it to be a predicate, because then every believer would be a reciter of the Book, and that is not so under any interpretation of recitation. We say: whatever applies to preventing it from being a predicate applies to it as a circumstantial clause too, because not every believer is in a state of recitation under any interpretation of it.

*Haqqa tilawatihi* (with its true recitation) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), as you say: *darabtu Zaydan haqqa darbihi* (I struck Zayd with its true striking). Its original form was *tilawatan haqqan* (a recitation, a true one). Then the adjective was placed first and was made into an annexed construction with the verbal noun, and it became like: *darabtu shadida al-darb* (I struck a severe striking), since its original form was *darban shadidan* (a striking, a severe one). They permitted that it be a description of an omitted verbal noun, and that it be in the accusative as a circumstantial clause of the subject, meaning: they recite it while being sincere (muhiqqin). Ibn ʿAtiyya said: *haqq* is a verbal noun, and the governing element is a suppressed verb, and it has the same meaning. It is not permissible to annex it to a single definite noun, but it is permitted here because the definiteness of *tilawa* (recitation) by its annexation to the pronoun is not pure definiteness; it is rather like their saying: *rajulun wahidu ummihi* (a man who is the only son of his mother) and *nasiju wahdihi* (one unique of his kind). End of his words.

*Ulaʾika yu'minuna bihi* (it is they who believe in it): its apparent meaning is that the pronoun in *bihi* (in it) refers to what the pronoun in *yatluna-hu* refers to, which is the Book, according to the differing views of people about the Book. It was also said that it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ). They said: even though he has not been mentioned before, the strength of the speech points to him. But this is not so; rather, he has been mentioned before in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth﴾ [al-Baqara: 119], but this becomes an iltifat (a shift from direct address to third person) and a movement from address to absence. It was also said that it refers to Allah, the Exalted, and this too is an iltifat, and a movement from the first-person pronoun of the Majestic Speaker who glorifies Himself to the third-person singular pronoun. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: In my view it is possible that the pronoun refers to the guidance that was mentioned before, because He mentioned the disbelieving Jews and Christians in the verse, and warned His Messenger against following their desires, and informed him that the guidance of Allah is the guidance that He gave him and sent him with. Then He mentioned to him that the believers who recite the Book of Allah are those who believe in that guidance and follow its lights. End of his words. It is open to what has been mentioned. But the apparent meaning is that it refers to the Book, so that the pronouns agree and do not differ, and so that there is no complication in the wording and no ambiguity in the meaning. For when making agreeing pronouns refer to one thing, with a sound meaning and correct construction, is better than making them discordant, and we do not turn away from that except by a factor that diverts from the first sense, either verbal or semantic. al-Zamakhshari went to the view that it refers to the Book.

﴿Whoever disbelieves in it, it is they who are the losers﴾: the pronoun in *bihi* (in it) in this sentence has the same disagreement as in the preceding sentence, and the apparent meaning, as we have said, is that it refers to the Book. He did not make the two sentences parallel in the declarative non-conditional or conditional structure. Rather, in the first he intended to mention the ruling without attaching a condition to it, and the contrast with loss indicates the profit of those who believed in it, their success, and the abundance of their share with Allah. So he was content with the establishment of the cause instead of mentioning what it causes. In the second sentence he intended to mention the result on the assumption that the cause has occurred, so that this carries a warning against engaging in the cause because of the consequence that follows from it, which is loss and the diminishing of one's share. He expressed this in a conditional sentence in which the condition is shaped according to the wording of *man* (whoever), and the response according to its meaning. *Hum* (they) may be a subject (mubtada') or a separating pronoun (fasl). On both assessments there is emphasis. In al-Muntakhab: the description that fits this is the Qur'an. *Ulaʾika* (those) the first refers to the believers, and the second refers to the disbelievers. The evidence for this is that those mentioned before are the People of the Book, so when He censured their way and related the evil of their deeds, He followed that with praise of those who abandoned their way, by reflecting upon the Torah and leaving off its distortion, and recognizing from it the truth of the Prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ). End.

*Al-tilawa* (recitation) has two meanings: recitation in words, and following in deeds. The views transmitted about the interpretation of recitation here have already been mentioned, and it is better to take it in all those senses, because they share a common meaning, which is that among all of them there is a shared quality. So it is appropriate to take it in that sense, because of the abundance of its benefits.

(p-370)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 122–123:

﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds.﴾ ﴿And guard yourselves against a Day when no soul will avail another in anything, nor will any compensation be accepted from it, nor will intercession benefit it, nor will they be helped.﴾: He repeated the address to the Children of Israel here and reminded them of His blessings emphatically, since after that address there follows mention of a second address, which comes after the mention of the two groups, those who follow guidance and the disbelievers who denied the signs. And this address follows the mention of those two groups, the believers and the disbelievers. Between the two addresses lay the narratives of the Children of Israel, what God bestowed upon them, what proceeded from them of actions unbefitting one upon whom God had bestowed favours, of transgressions, lying and obstinate demands, what they were recompensed with in this world for that, and what has been prepared for them in the Hereafter, placed between the two reminders and set between the two admonitions and the two warnings concerning the Day of Resurrection. The parallel to this in speech is that you command a person with something in general terms, then you elaborate that thing into many numerous particulars, which you recount one after another, each of which falls under that earlier command. The speech lengthens until you nearly forget that earlier command, so you restate it a second time, so that you remember that command, and those details become enclosed by the two mentioned matters.

This verse does not differ from the previous one except in His saying there: ﴿nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will any ransom be taken from it, nor will they be helped﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48], whereas here He said: ﴿nor will any compensation be accepted from it, nor will intercession benefit it, nor will they be helped﴾. We have already mentioned there the reason for placing intercession before ransom there and delaying it here, and for attributing acceptance there to intercession and benefit here to it; so refer to it there.

These noble verses contain information about exceeding the limit in wrongdoing by one who obstructs the houses of God from remembrance and strives to ruin them, although they, insofar as they are attributed to God, are places of His remembrance and the sheltering of His righteous servants; they should not enter them except in fear and trembling, mindful of Him for whom they were built and of what is mentioned in them. Then He informed that for those there is disgrace in this world and a great punishment in the Hereafter. Then He mentioned that to Him, exalted is He, belong the east and the west, so the mosques are included in that; and whatever direction you face, God, exalted is He, encompasses it and owns it, so He is not confined to any place or location. He concluded this sentence with the all-encompassing power that contradicts the power of decrees, and with the knowledge which is the proof of encompassing.

Then He informed of them with the most heinous statement, which is ascribing a son to God, exalted is He. He declared His holy essence free of that, and informed that all who are in the heavens and the earth belong to Him, submissive and obedient. Then He mentioned the originating of the heavens and the earth, and that they were created without a pattern. Just as there is no pattern for them, so too the One who originated them has no pattern. In this is an indication that a son is impossible, for if He had a son, he would be of His kind, while the Originator has nothing resembling Him, so He has no son. Then He mentioned that whenever His will is related to what He wishes to bring into being, there is no delay for it. In this is also an indication of the negation of a son, because that would only come about through procreation, which requires the succession of times; God is exalted above that.

Then He mentioned a type of their statements by which they were obstinate with the prophets of God, such as demanding that He speak to them directly or that a sign descend. Many signs had descended, yet they did not heed them. And they followed the footsteps of those who preceded them in this statement, and their desires are alike in their obstinacy toward the prophets. He, exalted is He, has made the signs clear and manifest, but for the one who has understanding, he is certain of their truth and believes in them.

Then He mentioned, exalted is He, that He sent him as a bearer of good tidings to whoever believes, of bliss in the Hereafter and triumph in this world, and as a warner to whoever disbelieves, of the opposite of that; and that you should not grieve over one who was sealed with wretchedness and so became one of the people of the Fire, nor be distressed by his not believing, for you have conveyed and given excuse. Then He mentioned the extent of the Jews' and Christians' blindness to the truth, that they will not be pleased with you until you abandon the guidance that has come to you, which is the guidance of God, for what they follow of the creed of disbelief and the pursuit of desires. Then He informed that whoever follows their desires after the clarity of the religion and Islam that has reached him, no one will support him or protect him from the punishment of God. And that those to whom We have given the Book and whom We have chosen for it follow the Book and pursue its meanings; they confirm what it contains of matters whose knowledge is hidden from them, and the benefit of it has not been obtained by them except from Him, whether of a past or future report, of promise and threat, of reward and punishment. And whoever disbelieves in it, the loss is due upon him.

Then He concluded these verses with the command to the Children of Israel by mentioning His previous blessings and their preference over the worlds of their time. This was the third address with which the Children of Israel were addressed, in addition to their forefather, and an honouring of them by their being born of him. Then in the majority of the Qur'an He turned away from addressing them by this name, and the light of this mark was effaced from them. The number three is the beginning of multiplicity, and one who alerts you and calls you once, and again, and again, has been concerned for you:

*Indeed you have made them hear, had you called a living one; but there is no life for one you call.*

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 122–123:

﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds.﴾ ﴿And guard yourselves against a Day when no soul will avail another in anything, nor will any compensation be accepted from it, nor will intercession benefit it, nor will they be helped.﴾: He repeated the address to the Children of Israel here and reminded them of His blessings emphatically, since after that address there follows mention of a second address, which comes after the mention of the two groups, those who follow guidance and the disbelievers who denied the signs. And this address follows the mention of those two groups, the believers and the disbelievers. Between the two addresses lay the narratives of the Children of Israel, what God bestowed upon them, what proceeded from them of actions unbefitting one upon whom God had bestowed favours, of transgressions, lying and obstinate demands, what they were recompensed with in this world for that, and what has been prepared for them in the Hereafter, placed between the two reminders and set between the two admonitions and the two warnings concerning the Day of Resurrection. The parallel to this in speech is that you command a person with something in general terms, then you elaborate that thing into many numerous particulars, which you recount one after another, each of which falls under that earlier command. The speech lengthens until you nearly forget that earlier command, so you restate it a second time, so that you remember that command, and those details become enclosed by the two mentioned matters.

This verse does not differ from the previous one except in His saying there: ﴿nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will any ransom be taken from it, nor will they be helped﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48], whereas here He said: ﴿nor will any compensation be accepted from it, nor will intercession benefit it, nor will they be helped﴾. Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 124 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And when Abraham was tried by his Lord with words, and he fulfilled them, He said: "Indeed, I will make you an imam (leader) for the people." He said: "And from my offspring?" He said: "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿And when We made the House a place of return for the people and a sanctuary, and [said]: "Take the station of Abraham as a place of prayer," and We charged Abraham and Ishmael: "Purify My House for those who circumambulate, those who stay in devotion, and those who bow and prostrate."﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 125] ﴿And when Abraham said: "My Lord, make this a secure land and provide its people with fruits, those of them who believe in Allah and the Last Day." He said: "And whoever disbelieves, I will grant him enjoyment for a little, then I will drive him to the torment of the Fire, and wretched is the destination."﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 126] ﴿And when Abraham and Ishmael were raising the foundations of the House: "Our Lord, accept from us. Indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing."﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 127] ﴿"Our Lord, make us submissive to You, and of our descendants a Muslim community submissive to You, and show us our rites, and turn to us in forgiveness. Indeed You are the Ever-Relenting, the Most Merciful."﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 128] ﴿"Our Lord, send among them a messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses, teach them the Book and wisdom, and purify them. Indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise."﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 129] ﴿And who would turn away from the creed of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself? We chose him in this world, and in the Hereafter he is surely among the righteous.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 130].

Ibrahim (Abraham): a non-Arabic (a'jami) proper name. It is said that its meaning in Syriac, before it was transferred to be a proper noun, was "compassionate father." It has six dialectal forms: Ibrahim with an alif and a ya', which is the famous and common form; with an alif in place of the ya'; with the ya' dropped and the ha' vowelled with a kasra, a fatha or a damma; and with both the alif and the ya' dropped and the ha' with a fatha. 'Abd al-Muttalib said:

"We are the family of Allah in His Ka'bah; we have not ceased to be so since the covenant of Ibrahim (Ibrahim pronounced as Ibrahim)."

And Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl said:

"I have taken refuge in what Ibrahim took refuge in, when he said: my face is submitted to You, humbled."

Al-itmam (completion): al-iklam (perfecting). The hamzah in it is for transfer (naql). Then "al-shay' yatimmu" means it became complete; it is the opposite of deficiency. Al-imam: the model who is followed, and from it is said of the line of a building: imam, and of a road: imam. It is a singular on the pattern fi'al, like al-izar for that with which one wraps oneself. It may also be the plural of amm, the active participle of amma yaummu, like jai' and jiya', qa'im and qiyam, na'im and niyam. Al-dhurriyyah (offspring): descendants, derived from dharawtu, or dharaytu, or dhara'a Allah al-khalq, or al-dhárr. Its dhal may be vowelled with a damma, a kasra or a fatha. As for the damma, it may be that dhurriyyah is fu'ayilah from dhara'a Allah al-khalq, its original form being dhurri'iyah. The hamzah was lightened by changing it into a ya', as they lightened the hamzah of al-nasi' and said al-nasiyy, then they assimilated the ya' which is the lam of the verb and which serves for the prolongation. It may also be fu'ulah from dharawtu, its original form being dhuruwah, the lam of the verb being changed into a ya'. There gathered a waw and a ya': the waw of prolongation and the ya' which had changed from the waw that is the lam of the verb, and one of them was preceded by a sukun, so the waw of prolongation was changed into a ya' and assimilated into the ya', and the letter before it was given a kasra, because the ya' requires a kasra. It may also be fu'ayilah from dharraytu, its original form being dhurrayawah; the ya' of prolongation and the waw which is the lam of the word gathered, and one of them was preceded by a sukun, so the waw was changed into a ya' and the ya' of prolongation was assimilated into it. It may also be fu'ulah or fu'aylah from dharaytu, a dialectal form of dharawtu; its original form, if it is fu'ulah, is dhuruwiyah, and if it is fu'aylah, dhurayyiyah, and then it was assimilated. It may also be fa'ilah from al-dharr, relative (mansubah), or fi'liyyah from al-dharr, unrelated, or fa'ilah like mariqah, or fu'ul like subbuh and quddus, or fa'lulah like qardudat al-zahr. Its first letter is vowelled with a damma if it is a noun, like qumriyyah, and if it is a relative noun, as they said in the relative form of al-dahr: duhriyy, and of al-sahl: suhliyy. The original of fa'ilah from al-dharr is dhariyrah, of fa'ulah from al-dharr is dharurah, and likewise fa'lulah; the last ra' in these was changed into a ya' out of dislike of gemination, as they said in tasarrartu: tasarraytu. As for the one who vowelled the dhal of dhurriyyah with a kasra, it is possible that it is fa'ilah from dhara'a Allah al-khalq, like bitti'khah, so the hamzah was changed into a ya' and assimilated into the ya' of prolongation; or fi'liyyah from al-dharr, relative by an irregular analogy; or fi'iilah from al-dharr, its original being dhariyrah; or fi'lil like hiltit. It is possible that it is dhiriwah from dharawtu, or fi'ilah: dhiri'ah from dharaytu. As for the one who opened the dhal of dhurriyyah, it is possible that it is fa'ilah from dhara'a, like sakinah, or fa'ulah from this also, like kharubah. The original is dharu'ah, the hamzah was changed into a ya' as a heard substitution, and the waw was changed into a ya' and assimilated. It is possible that it is fa'ilah from al-dharr, unrelated, like barniyyah, or relative to al-dharr, or fa'ulah like kharubah from al-dharr, its original being dharurah, and what was mentioned was done to it; or fa'lulah like bakkulah, its original also being dharurah; or fa'ilah like sakinah: dhariyrah, the ra' being changed into a ya' in all of that. It is possible that it is from dharawtu fa'ilah like sakinah, its original being dhariwah, or from dhuraytu: dhariyyah, or fu'ulah from dharawtu or dharaytu. As for the one who formed it on fa'lah like jafnah, and said dhurriyyatan, it is from dhurriyt.

Al-nayl: attainment. Naltu al-shay' analuhu nayalan; al-nayl also means giving. Al-bayt (the house): a known thing, and it became a proper name by predominance for the Ka'bah, like al-najm for al-Thurayya (the Pleiades). Al-amn: the verbal noun of amina yamanu, when one is not afraid and his soul becomes at rest. Al-maqam: maf'al from al-qiyam; it may denote the verbal noun, the time or the place. Isma'il: a non-Arabic proper name, and it is said Isma'il with a lam and Isma'in with a nun. He said:

"The neighbours of the tribe said when we came: this, by the Lord of the House, is Isma'in."

Among the strange things said about his naming is that Ibrahim used to pray that Allah would grant him a child, and say: "Isma' il," and Il is Allah, Exalted. Al-tathhir (purification): the verbal noun of tahhara, and the doubling in it is for transitivity. It is said: tahhara al-shay' tahharatan: he cleaned it. Al-ta'if: the active participle from taafa bihi, when he went around it; it is also said atafa, with the same meaning as taafa. He said:

"The Jiyal surrounded him at his weaning."

Al-'akif: the active participle from 'akafa bi-al-shay': he stayed with it and kept to it. He said:

"Birds watching him in devotion."

And "they cling (ya'kufun) to idols of theirs" means: they persist in worshipping them. Al-balad: a known thing; al-balad also means the chest, and from it the city was named, because it is the chest of the towns. It is said: the she-camel placed her balad (chest) when she knelt. It is also said that balad means a trace, and from it is said "baleed" for ignorance's effect upon him; and from it the kneeling of the camel is called "balda," for its effect upon the ground when it kneels. He said:

"She was made to kneel and cast a balda after a balda, few are the voices in it except her bugham."

Al-barik: the one who kneels in the land. Al-idtirar: it is being compelled to something and forced into it. It is ifta'ala from al-darr; its original is idtirar, and the ta' was changed into a ta' as a necessary substitution. Its verb is transitive, and so it is used in the Qur'an and in the speech of the Arabs. He said:

"The hirz from Salma compelled you to Ajaa."

Al-masir (destination): maf'il from sara yasiru, and it denotes time and place. As for the verbal noun, its analogy is maf'al with a fatha on the 'ayn, because what has a kasra on the 'ayn of its present tense has as its analogy what we have mentioned. However, the grammarians differed about what has a ya' as its 'ayn in this, according to three positions: the first, that it is like the sound form, so it is vowelled with a fatha in the verbal noun and with a kasra in the time and place. The second, that it is optional. The third, that it is restricted to what is heard, so what the Arabs vowelled with a fatha we vowel with a fatha, and what they vowelled with a kasra we vowel with a kasra; and this is the preferred position. Al-qawa'id (the foundations): al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: they are the walls. Abu 'Ubaydah said: the foundations. He said:

"On a height of a hill, its first ones adorned its high points, its foundations."

Ibn 'Atiyyah first interpreted it as the foundations, and so did al-Zamakhshari, and he said: it is a predominant adjective, and its second meaning is: "qa''adaka Allah," i.e., I ask Allah to make you sit, that is, to make you firm. That is the end of his words.

Al-qawa'id from women means the plural of qa'id, those who have ceased to bear children. The discussion of why qa'id is without the taa' in its place will come, Allah willing. Al-ummah: the community; it is a homonymous word (lafz mushtarak, a word with several meanings), applied to a group, to a single leader who is greatly honoured and followed, to one who stands alone in a matter, in religion, and in a period of time. Al-umm: "this is the ummah of Zayd," i.e., his mother. Also the wound that reaches the brain's membrane, the followers of the messengers, the straight path, and a generation. Al-manasik: the plural of mansak and mansik; the kasra on the sin of mansik is irregular, because the verbal noun, the time and the place of yaf'ulu, with a damma or a fatha on the 'ayn, is maf'al with a fatha on the 'ayn, except what is irregular from that. Al-nasik: the one who worships. Al-ba'th: sending, reviving, and waking from sleep. Al-'Aziz (the Mighty): it is said 'azza ya'uzzu, with a damma on the 'ayn, meaning: he overcame; and from it: "wa 'azzani fi al-khitab" (he overpowered me in speech). And 'azza ya'azzu, with a fatha, meaning: he became strong; and from it: "'azza 'alayya hadha al-amr," meaning: it was difficult for me; and ta'azzaza lahm al-naqah: the meat of the she-camel became firm. And 'azza ya'izzu, from preciousness, meaning: there is no like of him, or his like is rare. Al-raghbah 'an al-shay' (aversion to a thing): renunciation of it; al-raghbah fihi (desire for it): preferring it and choosing it; and the origin of raghbah is seeking. Al-istifa' (choosing): selecting and choosing; it is ifti'al from al-safw, which is what is pure of turbidity and impurities. The ta' of it was changed into a ta'; its triliteral form is intransitive, and the ifti'al came from it transitively. Safa al-shay' yasfu, and the meaning of ifti'al here is: choosing, which is one of the meanings that came for ifta'ala.

﴿And when Abraham was tried by his Lord with words, and he fulfilled them, He said: "Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people." He said: "And from my offspring?"﴾: The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when the mention of the Ka'bah and the qiblah was made, and the Jews reproached the believers for turning towards the Ka'bah and leaving Bayt al-Maqdis, as He said: ﴿What turned them away from their qiblah?﴾, He mentioned the story of Abraham and what Allah tried him with. He digressed to the mention of the House and how it was built, and that since they were of Abraham's lineage, they ought to be the people most in following his law and tracing his footsteps. So the honouring of the House was binding upon them. Allah thereby drew attention to their poor reliance and their frequent opposition, and their departure from the examples of those who ought to be followed among their forefathers; and that although they were of his offspring, they would not attain any of his covenant because of their wrongdoing. The governing element (al-'amil) in idh, according to what they mentioned, is omitted, and they estimated it as: "udhkur" (remember), meaning: remember when Abraham was tried; so it is an object. Or: when He tried him, it was such and such. The discussion of this has already passed at His saying: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 30].
