The preferred position is that the governing element is explicitly stated, which is: ﴿He said: Indeed, I will make you﴾. Al-ibtila' (trial): testing, and its meaning is that He imposed on him commands and prohibitions. The Creator, Exalted, knows what will come from him. It is said: its meaning is that He commanded. Al-Zamakhshari said: Allah's testing of His servant is a metaphor for enabling him to choose one of two matters: what Allah wills and what the servant desires, as if He tests him to see what will come from him, so that He may requite him according to that. That is the end of his words, and in it is the subtle hint of Mu'tazilism. In Rayy al-Zam'an: al-ibtila' is the manifestation of the act, and al-ikhtibar is the seeking of information, and the two are mutually implying.

Abraham (Ibrahim) here, and throughout the Qur'an, is the thirty-first ancestor (al-jadd al-hadi wa'l-thalathun) of our Prophet, the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he is Khalil Allah (the Friend of God). He is the son of Tarah, son of Nahur, son of Sarugh, son of Arghu, son of Falagh, son of Abir, and he is Hud the Prophet (peace be upon him). His birthplace was in the land of al-Ahwaz. It is said: Kuthaa; it is said: Babylon; it is said: Najran. His father transported him to Babylon, the land of Nimrod ibn Kan'an.

The six dialects (al-lughat al-sitt) concerning his name have already been mentioned in its pronunciation.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read Ibrahim with an alif and a ya'. Ibn 'Amir, according to one variant, transmitted from Ibn Dhakwan, read it in al-Baqarah with two alifs. Hisham added that he recited it likewise in: Ibrahim, al-Nahl, Maryam, al-Shura, al-Dhariyat, al-Najm, al-Hadid, the beginning of al-Mumtahanah, the three final verses of al-Nisa', the other (verse) of al-Tawbah, the end of al-An'am, and al-'Ankabut. Al-Mufaddal read Ibraham with two alifs, except in al-Mawaddah and al-A'la. Ibn al-Zubayr read Ibraham. Abu Bakrah read Ibrahm with an alif, with the ya' omitted and the ha' vowelled with kasra.

The majority read: with the accusative of Ibrahim and the nominative of Rabbuhu. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-Sha'tha' (p-375) and Abu Hanifah read with the nominative of Ibrahim and the accusative of Rabbahu. The reading of the majority is that the agent (al-fa'il) is the Lord, and the meaning of His testing him has already been discussed.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: He placed the object first for the sake of emphasis on the one upon whom the testing fell, since it is known that God, exalted is He, is the One who tests. Attaching the pronoun of the object to the agent necessitates placing the object first. End of his words, and there is some abridgment in it.

That it is one of those cases in which the agent must be placed first is the view of the majority. Similar constructions have occurred in the speech of the Arabs, such as: "darab ghulamuhu Zaydan" (his servant struck Zayd). Some grammarians analogised upon it, and the majority interpreted some of it or considered it an anomaly (shudhudh). Al-Zamakhshari has elaborated on this question, to the extent of what may be found in his words in al-Kashshaf, but it is not among the matters that are elaborated upon, given its fame in Arabic.

Ibn 'Abbas read: its meaning is that he asked his Lord with words of supplication, seeking an answer in them, and so that was called a testing by way of metaphor, because in supplication there is a request to uncover what the decrees will bring upon the human being.

The words were not specified in the Qur'an, nor in the authentic hadith, and the commentators have various opinions about them.

First: Tawus narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that they are the ten of the fitrah: rinsing the mouth, sniffing water into the nose, trimming the moustache, letting the beard grow, parting the hair, plucking the armpit hair, clipping the nails, shaving the pubic area, istinjaa (cleansing after the toilet), and circumcision. This is also the view of Qatadah.

Second (twelve): They are: shaving the pubic area, plucking the armpit hair, clipping the nails, trimming the moustache, the ghusl of Friday, circling the House (tawaf), sa'y (between Safa and Marwah), stoning the pillars (ramy al-jimar), and ifadah. This was also related from Ibn 'Abbas.

Third: thirty portions (sahm) in Islam, which no one completed except Ibrahim: ten in Bara'ah (al-Ta'ibun) the verse, ten in al-Ahzab "Inna al-muslimin" [al-Ahzab: 35] the verse, and ten in "Qad aflaha" [al-Mu'minun: 1] and in al-Ma'arij. This was also related from Ibn 'Abbas.

Fourth: They are the six traits by which the star, the moon, the sun, the fire, the migration (hijrah) and circumcision were tested. It was said: in place of the migration is the sacrifice of his son; this was said by al-Hasan.

Fifth: The rites of Hajj; narrated by Qatadah from Ibn 'Abbas.

Sixth: Every request that Ibrahim made in the Qur'an, such as: "Rabb aj'al hadha al-balada aminan" [Ibrahim: 35]; this was said by Muqatil.

Seventh: They are the words: Subhan Allah, al-Hamdu lillah, la ilaha illa Allah, Allahu akbar, and la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah al-'Aliyy al-'Azim. And His words: "Rabbana taqabbal minna" (Our Lord, accept from us); this was said by Ibn Jubayr.

Eighth: It is His, exalted is He, saying: "Wa hajjahu qawmuhu" [al-An'am: 80]; this was said by Yaman.

Ninth: They are His words: "Alladhi khalaqani fahuwa yahdin" [al-Shu'ara': 78] and the verses that follow; this was said by Abu Rawq.

Tenth: They are what He tested him with in his wealth, his offspring and his self: he gave his wealth to the guests, his son to the sacrifice, his self to the fire, and his heart to the Most Merciful; so God took him as a Friend (khalil).

Eleventh: It is that God revealed to him: be pure, so he rinsed his mouth; then be pure, so he sniffed water into his nose; then be pure, so he used the siwak; then be pure, so he trimmed his moustache; then be pure, so he parted his hair; then be pure, so he cleansed himself after the toilet; then be pure, so he shaved his pubic area; then be pure, so he plucked his armpit hair; then be pure, so he clipped his nails; then be pure, so he turned to his body, looking at what he would do, and he was circumcised after a hundred and twenty years. In al-Bukhari, it is that he was circumcised at the age of eighty with an adze (qadum). God revealed to him: "Inni ja'iluka li'l-nasi imaman" [al-Baqarah: 124], that people would follow you in these traits and the righteous would take you as an exemplar. If that report is sound, then the interpretation is that he was circumcised after a hundred and twenty years from his birth, and at the age of eighty from the time of his prophethood, so the two dates agree, and God knows best.

Twelfth: They are ten: the testimony that there is no god but God, which is the creed (al-milla) and the prayer (al-salah); which is the fitrah and the zakah; which is the purification (al-tuhrah) and the fasting; which is the Garden and the Hajj; which is the sacred rite (al-sha'irah) and the holy war (al-ghazw); which is the victory (al-nusrah) and obedience; which is the protection (al-'isma) and the community (al-jama'ah); which is the affection (al-ulfah) and enjoining good; which is fidelity (al-wafa') and forbidding evil; and which is the proof (al-hujjah).

Thirteenth: They are: "make me an imam," "make the House a place of return and a sanctuary," "show us our rites," "relent towards us," "make this land secure," and "provide its people with fruits." God answered him in all that he asked; this is the meaning of the statement of Mujahid and al-Dahhak.

These opinions should be understood as meaning that each speaker mentioned a portion of what God tested Ibrahim with, since all of them were tests for him; and this should not be taken as restricted to a specific number, nor as definitive, lest that lead to contradiction.

If these things by which the words were explained are statements, then the application of the term "words" to them is clear. If they are actions, then applying the term "words" to them is metaphorical, because the actions of obligation proceeded from commands, and commands are words. The Essence (al-dhat) was called a word (kalimah) because of its manifestation from the word "Be" (kun). God, exalted is He, says: "Wa kalimatuhu alqaha ila Maryam" [al-Nisa': 171].

Some commentators have discussed the rulings concerning what the words were explained as: rinsing the mouth, sniffing water into the nose, trimming the moustache, letting the beard grow, parting the hair, sadl (letting the hair hang loose), the siwak, plucking the armpit hair, shaving the pubic area, clipping the nails, istinja', circumcision, greying and dyeing the hair, tharid (a dish of bread and meat), and hospitality. This is discussed in the science of jurisprudence (fiqh), and our book is not devoted to that, so we have left aside discussion of it.

Fa-atammahunna: The concealed pronoun in "fa-atammahunna" shows that it refers to God, exalted is He, because He is the one to whom the verb before it is ascribed in the manner of agency. "Fa-atammahunna" is conjoined to "ibtala" (tested), so the pronoun should agree. On this basis the meaning is: that is, He perfected them for him without deficiency, or clarified them, and clarification by them completes and makes the meaning manifest; or He facilitated for him the work of them and strengthened him to complete them; or He completed for him their rewards; or He made them a lasting custom (sunnah) in him and in his posterity until the Day of Religion. These are five opinions.

It is also possible that the concealed pronoun refers to Ibrahim. The meaning on this basis is: He sustained them, or he established them, said by al-Dahhak; or he acted upon them, said by Yaman; or he fulfilled them, said by al-Rabi'; or he discharged them, said by Qatadah. Five opinions that come close to being synonyms, since their outcome is that he carried them out in the manner commanded.

They differed over this testing: was it before his prophethood or after it? al-Qadi said: it was before prophethood, because He indicated that his carrying them out was a cause, since He made him an imam, and a cause precedes what it causes, so the testing must necessarily be prior in existence to his becoming an imam. Others said: it was after prophethood, because he would not know that he was obligated with those duties except through revelation, so revelation must precede his knowledge that he was thus. al-Qadi replied: it is possible that these burdensome obligations were revealed to him through Gabriel, and when he had completed them, He made him a prophet sent to creation.

"Qala inni ja'iluka": It has been stated that the preferred view regarding "qala" is that it governs "idh," and if we take the governing element of "idh" to be omitted, then "qala" is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), as if it were said: what did his Lord say to him when he completed the words? So it is said: "Qala inni ja'iluka li'l-nasi imaman." On the view that "qala" itself governs "idh," "qala" is a clause conjoined to what precedes it, meaning: and He said, "I am making you an imam for the people," when He tested him; and it is also possible that it is an explanation of "ibtala" and an elaboration of it.

"Li'l-nas": It is possible that by them is meant his community who followed him, and it is possible that by it is meant all believers among the nations, and this would be in matters of the creed of monotheism and in what agrees with their laws. "Li'l-nas" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), since it is a qualifier of an indefinite noun that precedes it; the estimate being: an imam existing for the people. They said: it is possible that it is connected to "ja'iluka," meaning: for the sake of the people. "Ja'il" here means "musayyir" (one who makes), so it takes two objects: the first is the kaf to which the active participle is attached, and the second is "imaman." It has been said: the scholars of verification (ahl al-tahqiq) said: by imam here is meant the prophet, that is, the bearer of a law to be followed, because if he were a follower of a messenger, he would be one who is led by that messenger, not an imam for him. Also, the word imam indicates that he is an imam in everything, and whoever is so is only a prophet. Also, prophets, inasmuch as obedience to them is obligatory upon creation, are imams, as God, exalted is He, says: "Wa ja'alna minhum a'immatan yahduna bi-amrina" [al-Sajdah: 24]. Caliphs are also imams, as are judges, jurists, the one who leads the people in prayer, and whoever is followed in falsehood. God, exalted is He, says: "Wa ja'alnahum a'immatan yad'una ila al-nar" [al-Qasas: 41]. Since the term encompasses all of these, it must be understood here as referring to the most noble and highest rank, because He mentioned it in the context of favour, so it must be the greatest blessing, and nothing is greater than prophethood.

"Qala wa min dhurriyyati": Al-Zamakhshari said: it is conjoined to the kaf, as if he said: and making some of my offspring [imams], just as one says to you: "I will honour you," and you reply: "and Zayd." End of his words. But conjunction to the kaf is not valid, because it is in the genitive, so conjunction to it can only occur with the repetition of the preposition, and "man" cannot be estimated as a preposition governing it, because it is a particle, so estimating it as synonymous with "some of" until one estimates an active participle governing it is not valid. Nor is it valid that the estimate of conjunction be of the type of conjunction to the position (mahall) of the kaf, because it is in the accusative, so "man" would be placed in the accusative position; that is not one of the cases in which conjunction is made to the position according to the school of Sibawayh, due to the loss of the restrictive element; and it is not like "sa-ukrimuka, fa-taqulu: wa Zaydan," because the kaf here is in the accusative position. What the meaning requires is that "min dhurriyyati" be connected to an omitted element, the estimate being: and make from my offspring an imam; because Ibrahim understood from His words "inni ja'iluka li'l-nasi imaman" the restriction, so he asked God, exalted is He, to make from his offspring an imam.

Zayd ibn Thabit read "dhirriyyati" with kasra on the dhal. Abu Ja'far read it with fath. The majority read it with damma, and we have mentioned that these are dialects of it, and from what it is derived when we spoke about the individual vocabulary items.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 124 (part 3 of 3):

﴿Said: My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers.﴾ The pronoun in the second qāla (said) refers to Ibrahim, while the pronoun in the first qāla refers to God, exalted is He. The ʿahd (covenant) here is leadership (imamah). Mujahid said: or prophethood, as said by al-Suddi; or security (amān), as said by Qatadah. It is also narrated from al-Suddi, and chosen by al-Zajjaj: or reward, also said by Qatadah; or mercy, said by ʿAta'; or religion, said by al-Dahhak and al-Rabi'; or: there is no covenant for you with a wrongdoer that you should obey him in his wrongdoing, said by Ibn ʿAbbas; or the command, from His saying: ﴿Indeed, God has enjoined upon us﴾ [Al ʿImran: 183], ﴿Did I not enjoin upon you﴾ [Ya Sin: 60]; or His admitting him to Paradise, from the saying: (He had with God a covenant), that He would admit him to Paradise; or My obedience, said by al-Dahhak also; or the pledge, or the trust.

Of these views, the apparent one is that the covenant is leadership, because the verse opens with it, so He informed Ibrahim that leadership does not reach the wrongdoers. Some scholars have mentioned that His saying ﴿and from my offspring﴾ is a question, as if it were said: Will You make from my offspring a leader? We have already mentioned that the apparent meaning is that it is in the form of a request, i.e., "and make from my offspring [leaders]." This answer with which God answered Ibrahim is of the kind that exceeds the question, because Ibrahim asked God and requested that He make from his offspring a leader, so He answered him that his covenant does not reach the wrongdoers, and by the implication of the attribute it indicates that his covenant reaches one who is not a wrongdoer. This is evidence that his offspring are divided into wrongdoers and non-wrongdoers. What shows that the covenant is leadership is that the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ is that it is an answer to Ibrahim's saying ﴿and from my offspring﴾ [Ibrahim: 40] in the sense of appointment, for if it were in the sense of prohibition he would have said "no," or "My covenant does not reach your offspring," and would not have restricted the prohibition to the wrongdoers.

Abu Rajaʾ, Qatadah and al-Aʿmash read al-ẓālimūna (the wrongdoers) with a nominative ending (ḍamma), since the covenant is "reached" as in ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾, or: the wrongdoers do not reach it and do not attain it. The wrongdoing (ẓulm) here has been interpreted as disbelief (kufr), which is the view of Ibn Jubayr, and as wrongdoing of sins other than disbelief, which is the view of ʿAta' and al-Suddi. From this it has been deduced that when a wrongdoer is given a covenant, fulfilment of that covenant is not obligatory. Al-Hasan said: God did not make a covenant for them.

Ibn Abi al-Fadl said: What the exegetes have mentioned, that he asked for leadership for his offspring and was granted his request, does not appear from the wording, because he said ﴿and from my offspring﴾, and this is open to possibility: "and making from my offspring," or "You will make from my offspring," or "make from my offspring." And if all of this is possible and not explicitly stated, then from where do they know that he asked? As for their saying "he was granted his request," the wording does not indicate that, but rather indicates the opposite, for its apparent meaning is: your descendants are wrongdoers. But evidence points against that, namely: ﴿And We placed in his offspring prophethood and the Book﴾ and other verses indicating that prophethood is among his offspring. And if he had said "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers among them," that would indicate what they say; but the wording does not clearly descend to that. End of what he mentioned, summarized in part.

Concerning what Ibn Abi al-Fadl mentioned there is room for examination, because those assumed readings whose apparent meaning is a question: as for one who assumes "and make from my offspring a leader," it is a request; and as for one who assumes "and You make" or "making," it is an interrogative with the interrogative elided, for its meaning is: "Are You, O Lord, making?" or "Will You make, O Lord, from my offspring?" The interrogative ultimately returns in meaning to a request, and it is not permissible that the assumed phrase be "and making" or "you make from my offspring a leader" as a statement, because it would be a report from a prophet, and if it were a report from a prophet it would necessarily be true. No prior announcement from God to Ibrahim of this had been made; He only informed him that He would make him a leader for the people. So from where would he report this, and to whom would he address it, if God had informed him of it? Rather, that assumption is in the form of interrogation and seeking to know: will leadership be attained by some of his offspring or not? So God answered him: whoever is a wrongdoer, his covenant does not reach him. As for his saying that the apparent wording is that your offspring are wrongdoers, this is not so; rather its apparent meaning is that whoever among his offspring and others does wrong will not attain it, and by the implication of the attribute it indicates that one who is not a wrongdoer attains it. If it were as Ibn Abi al-Fadl said, the wording would mean that your offspring do not attain it because of their wrongdoing; and it is possible that the definite article in al-ẓālimīn is a substitute for the pronoun, i.e., "their wrongdoers," or the pronoun is omitted, i.e., "among them."

Among the strangest deductions from His saying ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ is what some Imamiyyah told me: they deduced from it that Abu Bakr cannot be an imam. They said: because the term "wrongdoer" applies to him, since he prostrated to idols, and so he wronged; and God has said ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾; and this is unlike ʿAli, for he never prostrated to an idol. I said to him: then it would follow that every Companion who embraced Islam would be called a wrongdoer, such as Salman, Abu Dharr, Ibn Masʿud, Hudhayfah, and ʿAmmar. And no one holds this, so he had no answer.

Al-Zamakhshari said: They said in this a proof that the sinner is not fit for leadership. How can one be fit for it whose judgment is not valid, whose testimony is not accepted, whose obedience is not obligatory, whose report is not accepted, and who may not lead the prayer? Abu Hanifa, may God be pleased with him, used to issue fatwas secretly that it was obligatory to support Zayd ibn ʿAli, to bring money to him, and to go out with him against the usurping tyrant who named himself imam and caliph, like al-Dawaniqi and his like. A woman said to him: You advised my son to go out with Ibrahim and Muhammad, the two sons of ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Husayn, until he was killed; he said: I wish I were in place of your son. He used to say of al-Mansur and his partisans: If they intended to build a mosque and asked me to count its bricks, I would not do it. And from Ibn ʿUyaynah: The wrongdoer is never an imam. And how is it permissible to appoint a wrongdoer to leadership, when the imam is only to repel injustice? If one who is a wrongdoer in himself is appointed, then the well-known proverb has come true: "Whoever entrusts the wolf with the flock has wronged." End of his words.

Zayd ibn ʿAli whom he mentioned is Zayd ibn ʿAli Zayn al-ʿAbidin ibn al-Husayn ibn ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may God honour his face, and he is the brother of Muhammad al-Baqir ibn ʿAli, and to him the Zaydiyyah trace their lineage today. He was among the people of knowledge, jurisprudence, understanding of the Qur'an and courage. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned him because he was residing in Mecca as a neighbour to the Zaydiyyah and in their company, and he composed his book al-Kashshaf for their sake. The usurping tyrant who named himself imam and caliph, whom al-Zamakhshari mentioned, is Hisham ibn ʿAbd al-Malik; Zayd ibn ʿAli rebelled against him. He had said to his brother al-Baqir: Why do you not rise and call people to rise with you? He turned away from him and said to him: For this there is a time that will not be exceeded. Zayd then called people to himself and said: The imam from among us is only one who unsheathes his sword and stands to seek the right of the family of Muhammad, not one who lets down his curtains and sits in his house. Al-Baqir said to him: O Zayd, the likeness of the one who rises from this family before the rising of their Mahdi is the likeness of a chick that leaves its nest before its wings are fully grown; when it does so it falls, and children take it and play with it. So fear God for yourself, lest you be the one crucified tomorrow at al-Kunasah. Zayd did not heed al-Baqir's words, went out against Hisham, was overcome, and crucified him at the Kunasah of Kufa, and burned him with fire, just as al-Baqir had warned.

As for al-Dawaniqi, he is al-Mansur, brother of al-Saffah; he was so named, it is said, for his stinginess. Some authors have mentioned that he was not stingy, and have recorded many reports of his giving and generosity. As for Ibrahim and Muhammad, whom al-Zamakhshari mentioned, they are the two sons of ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Hasan ibn al-Hasan ibn ʿAli ibn Abi Talib. Both had gone into hiding during the days of al-Saffah and the early days of al-Mansur. Then Muhammad appeared on the first day of Rajab in the year 145 AH, entered the mosque of Medina before dawn, delivered a sermon until the prayer time arrived, then descended and led the people in prayer, and was pledged allegiance in Medina willingly, appointed governors, gained control of Medina and Basra, and collected revenues. His brother Ibrahim had gone to Basra calling people to him. In the end, al-Mansur sent armies against them both, and they were killed.

Some exegetes have mentioned here the rulings of the Great Imamate, though its proper subject is the principles of religion, and it is discussed there; yet I do not leave my book free of a summary of it without evidence. So we say: What the people of hadith and Sunnah hold is that appointing an imam is an obligation, in contrast to a group of the Kharijites, the followers of Najdah al-Harurī, who claimed that leadership is not an obligation, and that people are only required to establish the Book of God and the Sunnah of His Messenger, and have no need of an imam; and a group of the Ibadiyyah claimed that it is voluntary. The obligation of appointing an imam is grounded in the Law, not in reason, in contrast to the Rafidah, who made it obligatory by reason. The imam must be of the pure stock of Quraysh, in contrast to a group of the Mu'tazilah, who said: if there is found someone fit for it who is Qurashi and someone who is Nabati, it is obligatory to appoint the Nabati rather than the Qurashi. All the clans of Quraysh are equal in this, in contrast to those who restricted it to the descendants of ʿAli or al-ʿAbbas, whether by explicit designation or by ijtihad. He must be the most excellent of the people, so a less excellent person is not validly installed while an excellent one exists, in contrast to Abu al-ʿAbbas al-Qalanisi, who says that it is valid for the less excellent if he possesses the qualities of imamate, even with an excellent one present. Its conditions: he must be just, a mujtahid in the rulings of the Sharia, brave, and courage must be in the heart such that he can manage the affair and preserve the protection of Islam. It is not permissible to appoint from the outset one who has lost his justice. If the office is conferred on a person who meets all the conditions and then he falls into wickedness, Abu al-Hasan said: rebellion against him is permitted if the people are secure. Many scholars have gone this way. Abu al-Hasan also said, and the judge Abu Bakr ibn al-Tayyib: rebellion against him is not permitted even if the people are secure from it, unless he disbelieves or calls to error and innovation. Its appointment is referred to the choice of the people of ijtihad in religion; the common folk follow them in this, and their opinion carries no weight. It is not a condition that all mujtahids gather, and no number is required; rather, if one of the people who loose and bind (ahl al-hall wa-l-ʿaqd) concludes it, allegiance is binding upon all, in contrast to one who restricted the pledging body to four, or who said it is not valid with fewer than that, or with forty, or with seventy. Whoever opposes this is then a rebel, or a considerer, or one mistaken, and each has a ruling mentioned in the science of jurisprudence. It is not valid for two imams in one age, in contrast to the Karramiyyah, who permitted it and claimed that ʿAli and Muʿawiyah were two imams at one time. The doctrine of taqiyyah is false, in contrast to the Imamiyyah; its meaning is that the person who combines the conditions of imamate is an imam in concealment, hiding himself for fear of one who has seized power and is not fit for imamate. Infallibility is not a condition of the imam, in contrast to the Rafidah, who say that infallibility is obligatory for the imam, both secretly and openly. Knowledge of all things is not a condition, in contrast to the Imamiyyah. The imam is to be obeyed in what his ijtihad leads him to. No one may rise against him with the sword, and likewise it is not permitted to rebel against a ruler who has prevailed, in contrast to those among the Mu'tazilah, Kharijites, Rafidah and others who held otherwise. Some people have spoken here about the lesser imamate, which is leadership in prayer, and its subject is the science of jurisprudence.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 125 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And when We made the House a place of return (mathaba) for the people and a sanctuary (amn)﴾: When he (Allah) refuted the Jews in their denial of facing the Ka'bah (in prayer), and the Ka'bah was the building of Ibrahim, their father, they were more entitled to honouring it, because it is one of the glories of their father. And there is another aspect of showing its excellence, which is that it is a place of return for the people and a sanctuary, and that in it is the Station of Ibrahim, and that He, exalted is He, revealed to him and to his son to build it and purify it, and to make it a place for those who circumambulate, those who remain in devotion (al-'akifin), those who bow and those who prostrate, and He commanded him to proclaim to the people its pilgrimage. Here "the House" means the Ka'bah according to the view of the majority (al-Jumhur). It has been said: what is meant is the Sacred House (al-Bayt al-Haram), not the Ka'bah itself, because He described it as a sanctuary, and this is the attribute of the whole Haram, not of the Ka'bah alone. It is permissible to use the term "the House" and mean by it the entire Haram. As for "the Ka'bah," it is applied only to the structure around which one circumambulates, and it is not applied to the whole Haram. The "ta'" in mathaba is for emphasis (lil-mubalaghah), because of the large number of those who return to it; this is what al-Akhfash said. Or it is for the feminine form of the verbal noun, or for the feminine form of the locality (al-buqah), as one says maqam and maqamah. The poet said:
"Did you not see that the earth is wide and spacious, so will a single plot of its plots defeat me?"
He described it as "wide" (rahb) with regard to the meaning of "place" (al-makan), and made "spacious" (fasihah) feminine with regard to the wording. Al-A'mash and Talhah read "mathabat" in the plural. Waraqah ibn Nawfal said:
"A place of return for the tribes of every kind, to which the swift camels hasten, the she-camels that are lean from travel."
It is also narrated as "al-dhawabil." The reading in the plural has the sense that it is a place of return for every one of the people, none of them being specific to it, the one who resides in it and the one who comes from the desert alike. As for "mathabatan," Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr said its meaning is: they return to it from every side, that is, they make pilgrimage to it every year; they disperse, then return to it, themselves or their likes, and none of them ever fulfils his need (wataran) there. The poet said:
"He made the House a place of return for them, from which they never, through time, fulfil their need."
Ibn 'Abbas said: a refuge and a shelter. Qatadah and al-Khalil said: a gathering place. Some of the lexicographers said, as related by al-Mawardi: that is, a place of reward (ithabah), one of the rewards; Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned this view as a possibility. The alif and lam in His words "lil-nas" (for the people) are either for the generalization of the genus (istighraq al-jins), according to the view of one who holds that all people are addressed with the branches of faith, or for a specific genus, according to the view of one who does not hold that. "Ja'alna" here means "sayyarna" (We made), so "mathabah" is the second object. It has been said: "ja'ala" here means "khalaqa" (created) or "wada'a" (placed), and "lil-nas" is attached to an omitted element, its estimate being: "mathabah ka'innah" (a place of return existing), since it occupies the position of a qualifier. It has been said: it is attached to the word "ja'alna," that is, for the sake of the people. "Amn" is a verbal noun; He made the House that very thing, by way of emphasis, because of the great amount of security that occurs in it; or by omitting a modifier, that is, possessing security; or it is used figuratively in place of the active participle, that is, secure, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Make this city secure﴾ [Ibrahim: 35]. They differed: is that in this world or in the Hereafter? As for one who says it is in this world, it has been said that its meaning is: people used to fight and raid one another around Makkah, while it was safe from that; a man would meet the killer of his father and not stir him, because He, exalted is He, placed in souls a sanctity for it, and made it a sanctuary for the people, the birds and the beasts, except the five harmful creatures (al-fawasiq al-khams), and this was specified through the words of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). As for one who committed an offence outside the Haram and then entered the Haram, whether he is safe from being molested in it is a disputed matter mentioned in jurisprudence. It has been said that its meaning is: it is secure for its people, so that one of them travels to distant places and no one terrifies him. It has been said: its meaning is: it is protected from tyrants preventing between it and those who intend it. As for one who says this security is in the Hereafter, it has been said: from the deception at death; it has been said: from the punishment of the Fire; it has been said: from the diminishing of the reward of one who intends it. Some people said: this security is specific to the House. It has been said: it includes the House and the Haram. And in Ri Al-Zam'an he said its meaning is: possessing security for its residents from what befalls the inhabitants of the deserts and all the other lands of the Arabs. The apparent meaning is that His words "wa-amnan" (and a sanctuary) are conjoined to His words "mathabah," and "amn" is explained by what has already been mentioned. Some have gone to the view that the meaning is in the form of a command, the estimate being: "wa-jʿaluhu aminan" (and make it secure), that is: We made it a place of return for the people, so make it secure, that none transgresses against another in it. So its meaning is that God commanded the people to make that place secure from raids and killing, and the House was made sacred by God's ruling. This interpretation may perhaps be supported by the reading of one who read "wa-ittakhidhu" in the imperative; on this view the conjunction is one of sentences, a imperative sentence being conjoined to a declarative sentence, while on the apparent view it is a conjunction of single words.
* *
﴿And take, from the Station of Ibrahim, a place of prayer﴾: Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and the majority read "wa-ittakhidhu" with a kasrah on the kha' as an imperative. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read it with a fathah, making it a past-tense verb. As for the reading "wa-ittakhidhu" as an imperative, it is disputed who is addressed by it. It has been said: Ibrahim and his descendants, that is, God said to Ibrahim and his descendants: take. It has been said: (p-381) the Prophet (ﷺ) and his community, that is: We said, take. This is supported by what is narrated from 'Umar, that he said: "I agreed with my Lord in three matters," and he mentioned among them, and I said: "O Messenger of Allah, if only you would take the Station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer." It is also narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he took 'Umar by the hand and said: "This is the Station of Ibrahim." 'Umar said: "Should we not take it as a place of prayer?" He said: "I have not been commanded with that." And the sun had not set before it was revealed. On these two views "ittakhidhu" is an object governed by an omitted saying. It has been said: the one addressed is the Children of Israel, and it is conjoined to His words: ﴿Remember My favour﴾ [al-Baqarah: 122]. It has been said: it is conjoined to His words: ﴿And when We made the House a place of return﴾, and they said: because the meaning is: "return to the House," so it is conjoined by way of meaning. These two views are remote. As for the reading "wa-ittakhadhu" with a fathah on the kha', it is conjoined to what precedes it: either to the whole of "when We made," in which case the "idh" must be supposed, or to "ja'alna" itself, in which case it need not be estimated but is within the relative clause of "idh." The meaning is: the people took, from the place of Ibrahim, by which he was marked for his concern with it and the settling of his descendants by it, a qiblah which they face in prayer; so said al-Zamakhshari. "Min maqam": they permitted "min" to be partitive, or meaning "in," or superfluous according to the view of al-Akhfash; the first is more apparent. Al-Qaffal said: it is like "I took a friend from so-and-so," and "God gave me a righteous brother from so-and-so": "min" introduces the thing taken or given, and specifies it in that sense. "Maqam" is a noun of place from "qiyam" (standing), meaning the place where he stood, namely the stone upon which Ibrahim rose when he was too weak to lift the stones which Isma'il was handing him in building the House, and his feet sank into it; so said Ibn 'Abbas, Jabir, Qatadah and others, and al-Bukhari transmitted it. It is now the place of that stone, and it is called the Station of Ibrahim. 'Umar asked al-Mutallib ibn Abi Rifa'ah: "Do you know where its first place was?" He said: "Yes," and showed him its place today. Anas said: "I saw in the Maqam the trace of his fingers, his heel, and the soles of his feet, except that people's rubbing with their hands had removed it." Al-Qushayri related it. Or it is a stone which Umm Isma'il brought to him while he was riding, and he stood upon it while washing, and his feet sank into it when he leaned upon it; so said al-Rabi' ibn Anas. Or it is all the stations of the Hajj; so said Ibn 'Abbas also, 'Ata' and Mujahid. Or 'Arafat, Muzdalifah and the jamarat; so said 'Ata' and al-Sha'bi, because he stood in these places and supplicated in them. Or the whole Haram; so said al-Nakha'i and Mujahid. Or the Sacred Mosque; so said a group. The scholars agreed upon the first view, and it was preferred by the hadith of 'Umar: "Should we not take it as a place of prayer?" etc., and by the recitation of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he finished circumambulating and came to the Maqam: ﴿And take, from the Station of Ibrahim, a place of prayer﴾, which shows that what is meant is that place. Also, this name by custom is specific to that place; also, the stone came under his feet in the softness of mud when his feet sank into it, and in that is a miracle for him, so his being specifically associated with it is stronger than the association of others, so applying this name to it is more fitting; also, the Maqam is the place of standing, and his standing on the stone is established, while it is not established upon anything else. "Musalla": qiblah, so said al-Hasan; a place of prayer, so said Qatadah; a place of supplication, so said Mujahid. The preferable interpretation is to take it as the legal prayer, not the prayer in its linguistic sense. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "a place of prayer" according to the view of one who says "al-Maqam is the stone"; and one who says otherwise says: "musalla," a figurative use based on the root meaning of prayer, that is, in the lexical sense. End.
* *
﴿And We enjoined upon Ibrahim and Isma'il﴾: that is, We commanded, or charged, or revealed, or said; sayings close in meaning.
﴿that purify﴾: "an" may be explanatory, meaning "purify," so that the covenant is explained by it; or it may be verbal (masdariyyah), meaning "that you purify." On the first, it has no place in the grammar; on the second it may be in the genitive or accusative according to the grammarians' disagreement. When the preposition is omitted from "an," is its position accusative or genitive? We have previously discussed the connection of "an" with the imperative verb, and Sibawayh and others explicitly stated this; but there is room for doubt, since all that has been mentioned is possible, and I do not recall from their speech: "I was amazed at an-adriba Zaydan," or "I do not like an-adriba Zaydan," with the imperative linked by "an"; and because the verbal-noun construction alters the meaning of the imperative, making it attributed to it and nullifying that imperative. The purification commanded is cleansing from everything unbecoming to it. They explained purification as building and founding upon purity and monotheism; said al-Suddi, and this is remote; and as purification from idols. They mentioned that it was inhabited in the time of Nuh, and that there were idols in it in the shapes of its righteous people, and that the time lengthened, so they were worshipped besides God, so God commanded its purification from those idols; so said Jubayr, Mujahid, 'Ata' and Muqatil. The meaning is that no idol is set up in it and no one other than God is worshipped in it. Yaman said: its meaning is: fumigate it, cleanse it and make it pure. It has been said: from calamities and suspicion. It has been said: from unbelievers. It has been said: from the dung and blood that used to be cast in it. It has been said: its meaning is: keep it sincere for these people, that no one else approach it. The preferable approach is to take it as purification from what is not fitting for God's houses, so that idols and impurities and all abominations are included, and whatever is forbidden by the law, such as a menstruating woman.
﴿My House﴾: this is an idafah of honour, not that a place is a dwelling of God, exalted is He; but since He commanded its building, its purification, and that people be brought to it from every deep ravine, it acquired a special relation through this, so its attribution to God became fitting, and it is like His words: ﴿the she-camel of Allah﴾ [al-A'raf: 73] and ﴿the spirit of Allah﴾ [Yusuf: 87], in that each has a particularity not found in other things, so attribution to Him, exalted is He, is appropriate. The command to purify it requires that it already existed, unless we take "purification" to mean building and founding upon purity and piety. It has been mentioned earlier that it was built in the time of Nuh.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 125 (part 2 of 2):

﴿for those who circumambulate and those who stay there devoutly﴾: Its apparent meaning is that it refers to everyone who circumambulates, whether a resident or a nomad; this is what ʿAṭāʾ and others said. Ibn Jubayr said: "The strangers (al-ghurabāʾ) who arrive at Mecca as pilgrims and visitors, who then depart soon after." This is supported by the fact that it is mentioned after it, "and those who stay there" (al-ʿākifīn). He said: "They are the permanent residents of the Sacred City, and the resident (al-muqīm) is the opposite of the traveller (al-musāfir)." ʿAṭāʾ said: "Those who stay there (al-ʿākifūn) are those who sit without circumambulating, whether local or foreign." Mujāhid said: "Those who dwell near it from among the strangers." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The worshippers in prayer (al-muṣallūn), because the one who enters the House enters only for circumambulation or prayer." It was also said: "They are those in seclusion (al-muʿtakifūn)." Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also permissible that by al-ʿākifīn is meant al-wāqifīn, that is, those who stand, just as He said: 'for those who circumambulate and those who stand and bow and prostrate,' and the meaning is 'for those who circumambulate and those who pray,' because standing, bowing and prostration are the postures of the one who prays." End of quotation. If he had said: "al-qāʾim here means al-ʿākif, from His words: ﴿as long as you stand over him﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 75]," it would have been good, and in that case it would combine the states of everyone who enters the House for worship, because at that time he is never without circumambulation, seclusion or prayer, so interpreting it in that way is most comprehensive for what the House was prepared for.

﴿and those who bow and prostrate﴾: They are those who pray at the Kaʿba; this is what ʿAṭāʾ and others said. Al-Hasan said: "They are all the believers." The bowing and prostration were singled out for mention from all the states of the one who prays, because they are the closest states of his to God. Bowing was placed before prostration because it precedes it in time. Both were put in the broken plural (jamʿ taksīr) to contrast them with the sound plurals (jamʿ salāmah) that precede them, and this was a variation in eloquence. The patterns of their broken plurals were varied as well, another variation in eloquence. The last of them was in the form fuʿūl rather than fuʿʿal for the sake of its being a closing rhyme (fāṣila), and the rhyme before it and after it ends with a long vowel of madd and līn. These two descriptions were joined by a conjunction because of the great contrast between them, under whatever interpretation you explained them from what has preceded. Prostration was not joined by a conjunction to bowing, because what is intended by both is "those who pray." Although bowing and prostration differ in their postures, one act encompasses them both, namely prayer. So the meaning of al-rukkaʿ al-sujūd is "those who pray," and it was appropriate not to join them with a conjunction, lest it be thought that each of them is a separate act of worship on its own, and they are not combined in a single act of worship; and that is not the case. In His words ﴿and those who bow and prostrate﴾ there is evidence for the permissibility of prayer in the House, both obligatory and voluntary, since no restriction was specified.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 126 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And when Abraham said: "My Lord, make this a secure land"﴾: They mention that the governing element (al-'amil) of *idh* (when) is omitted. *Rabb* (Lord) is a vocative noun (munada) annexed to the *ya'* (my), and the vocative particle has been dropped from it. There are several dialectal forms for a noun annexed to the *ya'*. The best of them is that the *ya'* of annexation is dropped and indicated by a *kasra* (vowel i), which is then relied upon, because the vocative is a place of lightening. Do you not see that the apocope (tarkhim, truncation) is permissible in it? These forms are mentioned in grammar, and some of them will occur in the Qur'an, and we will discuss them in their place, God willing. He addressed Him with the word *Lord* annexed to him, because in that there is gentleness in the request and in the address, through a description that indicates the acceptance of the petitioner and the answering of his supplication. *Ij'al* (make) here means *sayyir* (render, make into), and its form is an imperative, but it expresses a request and a desire. *Hadha* (this) is a reference to the valley in which he supplicated for its people when he settled them there, which is His saying: ﴿in a valley without cultivation, by Your Sacred House﴾ [Ibrahim: 37]. Or it refers to the place that became a city, and for this reason he made it indefinite, saying: ﴿a secure city﴾. And when it became a city, he said: ﴿My Lord, make this city secure and keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾ [Ibrahim: 35], and He said: ﴿I swear by this city﴾ [al-Balad: 1]. This is if the supplication was twice at two different times. It was also said: the two verses are the same, so the indefinite form (in this verse) may admit that before it there is an omitted definite noun, meaning: make this the city, a secure city, and the indefinite *baladan* (city) serves as a preparatory introduction (tawti'a) to what comes after it, just as you say: "This day was a hot day," so the reference to it in the two verses would be after it had become a city. It may also admit another possibility, which is: that it is not omitted, and at that time it was not yet "a city," but he prayed for it to be so; and the definite form that came in his saying *this city* [Ibrahim: 35] is according to what it will become, so he called it a city. The description of *balad* (city) as *amin* (secure) is either in the sense of attribution (nisba), meaning possessing security, like their saying: ﴿in a pleasing life﴾ [al-Haqqah: 21], meaning possessing pleasure; or by figurative extension (ittisa'), since security occurs in it, he made it secure, like their saying: "Your day is fasting and your night is standing." Is the supplication that He make it secure from tyrants and oppressors, or from its sacred precinct becoming lawful, or from being emptied of its people, or secure from killing, or from being swallowed up and stoned, or from famine and drought, or from the entry of the Dajjal, or from the People of the Elephant? These are sayings. As for one who interprets *amin* as meaning secure from tyrants, reality refutes it, since tyrants have entered it and killed, such as Amr ibn Luhayy al-Jurhumi, al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, the Qaramita, and others. Likewise one who says secure from famine and drought, for it is among the most famine-stricken and drought-stricken lands of God. Al-Qaffal said: its meaning is "a place where one is safe," and before the Arabs invaded them they were in the utmost security, to the extent that one of them, if he found himself in a desert or wilderness, would not be attacked when he knew that he was from the inhabitants of the Sacred Precinct.
* *
﴿And provide its people with fruits, those of them who believe in God and the Last Day﴾: When Abraham built the House in an barren land, and the condition of anyone who settles in places requires flowing water and farmland by which settlement in a city is possible, he prayed to God for the city's security and that provisions be gathered to it. For when the city is secure, merchants can come to it seeking profit. When he heard in the matter of the imamate His saying: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124], he restricted here those for whom he asked provision, saying: ﴿those of them who believe in God and the Last Day﴾. The pronoun in *minhum* (of them) refers to its people. He prayed for its believers with security and abundance, because the disbeliever is not prayed for with that. Do you not see that when the Quraysh became insolent, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) prayed against them: "O God, tighten Your grip on Mudar, and make it upon them as years like the years of Joseph," and Mecca at that time was a desert with no water and no vegetation, as He said: ﴿in a valley without cultivation﴾ [Ibrahim: 37], so God blessed what was around it, such as al-Ta'if and others, and God caused various kinds of fruit to grow in it. It is narrated that when Abraham supplicated, God commanded Gabriel, who uprooted Palestine, and it was said: a piece of al-Urdunn, and carried it around the House seven times, then set it down at Wajj, and al-Ta'if was named for that circumambulation. Some of them said:
"Every place, out of reverence for its sanctity, strives toward it, and in its striving there is honor for it."
He mentioned the object of faith, which is God Most High and the Last Day, because in faith in God there is faith in the Creator, the Necessarily Existent, and in what befits Him of attributes; and in faith in the Last Day there is faith in reward and punishment, which are ordained upon obedience and disobedience, the basis of the obligation that requires a truthful informer about it, and they are the prophets. Thus faith in the Last Day includes faith in the prophets and in what they brought. And since faith in God and the Last Day includes faith in all that must be believed, he limited himself to these, because the rest is included within them. Abraham's supplication for the people of the House encompasses whoever is called by this name, and it is not restricted to his offspring, even though the apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿and provide them with fruits﴾ [Ibrahim: 37] is restricted to his offspring, because of His saying: ﴿I have settled some of my offspring﴾ [Ibrahim: 37], (p-384) since the pronoun in *warzuqhum* (and provide them) refers to it. So it is possible that these are two requests. The *min* (from) in His saying *min al-thamarat* (of the fruits) is partitive, because they were only given some of the fruits. It was also said that it is explanatory of the genus, and *man* (those who) is a substitute (badal) for *ahlihi* (its people): a substitute of part from whole (badl ba'd min kull), or a substitute of inclusion (badl ishtimal) specifying what the substituted noun indicates. Its benefit is that it is mentioned twice: once by the general term in the substituted noun that preceded it, and a second time by explicit specification of it, and it becomes clear that the substituted noun was only meant and intended as the substitute, so it becomes figurative, since the specific is intended by the general. This is the benefit of these two substitutions, and in this there is emphasis and confirmation for the element to which the ruling is attached, which is the substitute, since it is mentioned twice.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 126 (part 2 of 3):**

﴿He said: "As for him who disbelieves, I will let him enjoy [life] for a little, then I will compel him to the punishment of the Fire, and what an evil destination!"﴾: The majority of the Seven [Readers] (al-Sab'a, the seven canonical readers) read *fa-umatti'uhu* (فَأُمَتِّعُهُ) with a shaddah on the *ta'*, as a report (khabar). Ibn 'Amir read *fa-umti'uhu* (فَأُمْتِعُهُ) without the shaddah, as a report. These same readers read *thumma adtarruhu* (ثُمَّ أضْطَرُّهُ) as a report. Yahya ibn Wathhab read *fa-umti'uhu* without the shaddah, and *thumma idtarruhu* (ثُمَّ إضْطَرُّهُ) with a kasrah on the hamzah, and both are reports. Ibn Muhaysin read *thumma adtarruhu* with the *dad* assimilated into the *ta'* (إدغام), as a report. Yazid ibn Abi Habib read *thumma udtarruhu* (ثُمَّ أضْطُرُّهُ) with a dammah on the *ta'*, as a report. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read *fa-numatti'uhu thumma nadtarruhu* (فَنُمَتِّعُهُ ثُمَّ نَضْطَرُّهُ) with the *nun* in both. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others read *fa-umatti'uhu qalilan thumma adtarruhu* in the imperative form (صِيغَةِ الأمْرِ) in both places. On this reading, it is necessary that the pronoun in *qal* (قالَ) refers to Ibrahim, since when he prayed for the believers for provision, he prayed against the disbelievers for brief enjoyment and for being driven (al-ilzaz) to the punishment.

*Man* (مَنْ): on this reading it may be in the nominative position, either as a relative pronoun (مَوْصُولَة) or as a conditional (شَرْطِيَّة), and in the accusative position by the grammatical construction of *ishtighal* (الِاشْتِغال, where a verb is "occupied" with a pronoun referring back to the noun), also in the case of conjunction (الوَصْل).

On the reading of the rest [of the Seven], the pronoun in *qal* necessarily refers to Allah, the Exalted. *Man* may be in the accusative position, by assuming a verb that is omitted, its implied sense being: "Allah said, and I provide for whoever disbelieves, so I let him enjoy," with *fa-umatti'uhu* conjoined to that omitted verb which governs *man*. It may also be that *man* is in the nominative position as an inceptive (مُبْتَدَأ), either as a relative or as a conditional, with the *fa'* (الفاء) being the response of the conditional, or the *fa'* being inserted into the predicate of the relative because of its resemblance to the conditional particle. It is not permissible for *man* to be in the accusative position by *ishtighal* if it is a conditional, because only the conditional verb explains the governing element of *man*, not the verb that occurs as the response. Nor if it is a relative, because the predicate is a present-tense verb into which the *fa'* has entered, by analogy of the relative pronoun to the conditional particle. Just as the response is not explained, so the predicate that is made analogous to the response is not explained either. As for when it is an imperative, that is, the predicate in the form such as *zaydan fa-idribhu* (زَيْدًا فاضْرِبْهُ, "Zayd, so strike him"), then it is permissible for it to be explained, but it is not permissible to say *zaydan fa-tadribuhu* (زَيْدًا فَتَضْرِبُهُ) by *ishtighal*. The reason for the permissibility of *zaydan fa-idribhu* in the imperative is mentioned in books of grammar.

Abu al-Baqa' said: It is not permissible for *man* to be the inceptive (مُبْتَدَأ) and *fa-umatti'uhu* the predicate, because *alladhi* (الَّذِي) does not take the *fa'* in its predicate unless the predicate deserves its relative clause, as in your saying: "Whoever comes to me, then for him is a dirham." Disbelief does not merit enjoyment. If the *fa'* were made superfluous (زَائِدَة), according to the opinion of al-Akhfash, it would be permissible, or if the predicate were omitted and *fa-umatti'uhu* were evidence for it, it would be permissible, its implied sense being: "Whoever disbelieves, I provide for him, so I let him enjoy." It is also permissible for *man* to be a conditional with the *fa'* as its response. It was also said that the response is omitted, its implied sense being: "And whoever disbelieves, I provide." On this view *man* is in the nominative by being an inceptive, and it is not permissible for it to be in the accusative, because the conditional particle is not governed by its response, but by the condition. End of his words.

His earlier statement that "it is not permissible" and his reasoning for it are not correct, because the predicate deserves the relative clause, since brief enjoyment and the arrival at the Fire both deserve disbelief. Furthermore, Abu al-Baqa' contradicted himself in permitting *man* to be a conditional with the *fa'* as its response. Is the response anything other than something that deserves and follows from the condition? So likewise the predicate that is analogous to it. If brief enjoyment does not deserve the relative clause, and what deserves the relative clause is conjoined to it, it is fitting that it should be a predicate, insofar as it occurs as a response, and he himself permitted that.

As for positing a superfluous *fa'*, an omitted predicate, or an omitted response of the conditional when we make *man* a conditional, there is no need for that, because the speech is arranged in utmost eloquence without this omission. Abu al-Baqa' proceeded in his parsing of the Qur'an in the manner of the poetry of al-Shanfara and al-Shammakh, permitting remote possibilities and unnecessary assumptions, and we exempt the Qur'an from that.

Al-Zamakhshari said: *Wa-man kafara* (وَمَن كَفَرَ) is conjoined to *man amana* (مَن آمَنَ), just as *wa-min dhurriyyati* (وَمِن ذُرِّيَّتِي) was conjoined to the *kaf* in *ja'iluka* (جاعِلُكَ). End of his words. Our refutation of his claim that *wa-min dhurriyyati* is conjoined to the *kaf* in *ja'iluka* has already been given. As for conjoining *man kafara* to *man amana*, it is not correct, because it is contrary to the structure of the speech, since it would make the meaning: "Ibrahim said: Provide for whoever disbelieves." It is not conjoined to it until it shares its governing element, and *man amana* is governed by the imperative verb, which is also the governing element of *wa-man kafara*. If you assume it to be an imperative, it contradicts His saying *fa-umatti'uhu*, because the apparent sense of this is a report from Allah that He attributes the enjoyment to Himself and compels them towards it, and that each of the two verbs takes as its subject the pronoun of Allah, the Exalted. That is not permissible except by a remote interpretation, by positing after the *fa'* a omitted saying containing a pronoun for Allah, the Exalted, that is: "Ibrahim said: Provide for whoever disbelieves, and Allah said: I let him enjoy briefly, then I compel him to the punishment of the Fire."

Then al-Zamakhshari contradicted this statement of his, that he conjoined to *man*, just as he conjoined *wa-min dhurriyyati* to the *kaf* in *ja'iluka*. He said: "If you ask: Why did Ibrahim specify the believers, such that he was answered?" I answer: He analogized provision to the imamate, and so he knew the difference between them, because appointment as a successor is a trust specific to one who gives sincere counsel to the one entrusted. The people furthest from sincere counsel are the wrongdoers. Provision differs, for it may be a gradual leading on for the one provided for and a establishing of proof against him. The meaning is: "And I provide for whoever disbelieves, so I let him enjoy." End of his words.

The apparent sense of his words "and the meaning is: And I provide for whoever disbelieves, so I let him enjoy" indicates that the pronoun in *qal* and in *wa-man kafara* refers to Allah, and that *man kafara* is in the accusative governed by *arzuqu* (أرْزُقُ), which is a present-tense verb attributed to Allah, the Exalted. This contradicts what was stated earlier, that *man kafara* is conjoined to *man amana*.

In his statement that Ibrahim "specified the believers such that he was answered," there is a breach of courtesy towards the prophets, since he [Ibrahim] was not answered, because he did not claim, nor desire, that he should provide for the disbeliever. Rather, His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He said: "And whoever disbelieves"﴾ is a report from Allah, the Exalted, about what the disbeliever's end will be: brief enjoyment and arrival at the Fire. Here there is neither analogy of provision to the imamate, nor any distinction made between them, as he claimed.

The meaning of *mata'* (مَتاع) has already been explained, that it is everything by which one benefits. Here *tamti'* (التَّمْتِيع) and *imta'* (الإمْتاع) are explained as "maintaining" (بِالإبْقاءِ) or "facilitating benefits" (بِتَيْسِيرِ المَنافِعِ), from which is *mata' al-hayat al-dunya* (مَتاعُ الحَياةِ الدُّنْيا), that is, its benefit which does not last; or as "providing" (بِالتَّزْوِيدِ), from which is *fa-matti'uhunna* (فَمَتِّعُوهُنَّ), that is, provide them with sustenance. *Al-mut'ah* (المُتْعَةُ) is what one is provided with for the journey of provision, and its plural is *mutaq*, from which is *matagan lakum wa-lil-sayyarah* (مَتاعًا لَكم ولِلسَّيّارَةِ, "a provision for you and for the travelling caravan"). The *hamzah* in *amta'a* (أمْتَعَ) makes the thing the possessor of what is derived from it: *amta'tu Zaydan* (أمْتَعْتُ زَيْدًا), "I made Zayd the possessor of provision," like their saying *aqbartuhu* (أقْبَرْتُهُ, "I made him a grave") and *an'altuhu* (أنْعَلْتُهُ, "I made him shod"). Likewise the doubling in *matta'a* (مَتَّعَ) makes the thing [take on] the meaning of what is derived from it, like their saying *addaltuhu* (عَدَّلْتُهُ, "I made him equal"). The doubling in *matta'a* does not require multiplicity, so the apparent sense of this is not contradicted by the smallness [of the enjoyment], which would then require interpretation, as some have thought, who interpreted the multiplicity as the addition of some parts to others and the smallness as relative to the bliss of the Hereafter. The two directions of multiplicity and smallness differ, so they do not contradict each other.

*Qalilan* (قَلِيلًا) is in the accusative either as an attribute of an omitted adverbial noun (ظَرْف), meaning "a brief time" (زَمانًا قَلِيلًا), or as an attribute of an omitted verbal noun (مَصْدَر), meaning "brief enjoyment" (تَمْتِيعًا قَلِيلًا), according to the reckoning of the majority, or as a circumstantial state (حال) from the omitted pronoun of the verbal noun indicated by the verb, and that is according to the school of Sibawayh. The description as "brief" is because of its swift ending, either by the arrival of the appointed term, or by the appearance of Muhammad (ﷺ) who kills him or expels him from this land, if he persists in disbelief. Or [it is brief] in comparison with enjoyment through bliss and adornment, or through respite from hastening the retribution therein, or through provision, or through remaining in this world. These are the opinions of the commentators.

The reading of Yahya ibn Wathhab is *thumma idtarruhu* with a kasrah on the hamzah. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is according to the dialect of Quraysh in their saying *la ikhalu* (لا إخالُ, "I do not think")," meaning with a kasrah on the hamzah. The apparent sense of this transmission is that this, that is, the kasrah of the hamzah which is for the speaker in such words as *idtarru* (إضْطَرُّ), which is the one whose initial hamzah is a connecting hamzah (هَمْزَةُ وَصْلٍ), and in such words as *ikhalu* (إخالُ), which is *af'ala* (إفْعَلَ) with a fatha on the 'ayn, from *fa'ila* (فَعِلَ) with a kasrah on the 'ayn, is contrary to what the grammarians have transmitted. For they transmitted from the people of the Hijaz the fatha on the letter of the present-tense prefix in what begins with a connecting hamzah, and in what is of the pattern *fa'ila* with a kasrah on the 'ayn, *yaf'alu* with a fatha on it, or with a yā' added at its beginning, such as *'alima ya'lamu* (عَلِمَ يَعْلَمُ), *intalaqa yantaliqu* (انْطَلَقَ يَنْطَلِقُ), and *ta'allama yata'allamu* (تَعَلَّمَ يَتَعَلَّمُ). Except if the present-tense prefix is a yā', then the majority of the Arabs other than the people of the Hijaz do not take a kasrah on the yā', but a fatha. As for the like of *yawjilu* (يَوْجِلُ) with a yā' as the present-tense of *wajila* (وَجِلَ), there are positions mentioned in the science of grammar. What is intended here is that the statement of Ibn 'Atiyya contradicts what the grammarians have related, unless he transmitted that *ikhalu*, in its particularity in the dialect of Quraysh, has a kasrah on the hamzah and not its like, so they would have followed in that the dialect of other Arabs, and in that case the statement of Ibn 'Atiyya could be correct.

Earlier, in the Surah al-Hamd (al-Fatihah), at His words "nasta'in" (نَسْتَعِينُ), we noted that the kasra (vowel i) is the dialect of Qays, Tamim, Asad and Rabi'ah. We have fully explained this point in our book "al-Takmil li-Sharh Kitab al-Tashil" (كِتابِ التَّكْمِيلِ لِشَرْحِ كِتابِ التَّسْهِيلِ).

The reading of Ibn Muhaysin is: ﴿ثُمَّ أطَّرُّهُ﴾ (thumma adtarruhu), with the dad assimilated into the ta' (إدْغامِ الضّادِ في الطّاءِ). Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is a rejected dialect (lughah marthulah), because the dad is one of the five letters into which the letters adjacent to it are assimilated, and it is not itself assimilated into what is adjacent to it. These are the letters of the phrase 'ḍumma shufr' (ضُمَّ شُفْرٌ)." End of his words.

When the dad meets the ta' in a word such as mudtarib (مُضْطَرِبٍ), the preferred form is clarification (al-bayan), and if it is assimilated, the second letter is changed to match the first, so it is said mudarrib (مُضَّرِبٍ), just as it is said musabbir (مُصَّبِرٍ) for mustabir (مُصْطَبِرٍ).

Sibawayh said: "Some of them have said mutta'ji' (مُطَّجِعٍ) for mudtaji' (مُضْطَجِعٍ), while madda'ji' (مَضَّجِعٍ) is more common." The form mutta'ji' is permitted, although mutabbir is not permitted for mustabir, because the dad is not in hearing like the sad: the sibilance (al-safir) in the sad is more audible than the elongation (istitalah) of the dad. The apparent meaning of Sibawayh's words is that it is not a rejected dialect. Do you not see how he cites it from some Arabs as mutta'ji', and how he says "madda'ji' is more common", which indicates that mutta'ji' is frequent? Do you not see his explanation, that the dad was changed into the ta' and assimilated, while this was not done with the sad, and that he points out the differences between them? All of this from Sibawayh indicates permissibility.

The dad has been assimilated into the dhal in His words, exalted is He: ﴿الأرْضَ ذَلُولًا﴾ (al-ard dhalulan) [al-Mulk: 15], as transmitted by al-Yazidi from Abu 'Amr, but it is weak. It has also been assimilated into the shin in His words: ﴿لِبَعْضِ شَأْنِهِمْ﴾ (li-ba'di sha'nihim) [al-Nur: 62] and ﴿والأرْضِ شَيْئًا﴾ (wa-l-ard shay'an) [al-Nahl: 73], and this too is weak.

As for the shin, it has been assimilated into the sin. This was narrated from Abu 'Amr in His words: ﴿إلى ذِي العَرْشِ سَبِيلًا﴾ (ila dhi al-'arsh sabilan) [al-Isra': 42], but the Basrans do not permit this from Abu 'Amr, and he is one of the leading Basran scholars.

As for the fa', it has been assimilated into the ba' in the reading of al-Kisa'i: ﴿إنْ نَشَأْ نَخْسِفْ بِهِمُ﴾ (in nasha' nakhsif bihim) [Saba': 9], and he is the imam of the Kufans.

As for the ra', al-Khalil, Sibawayh and his companions held that it is not permissible to assimilate the ra' into the lam because of its repetition (takriruha), nor into the nun. Yaqub, Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', and Abu Ja'far al-Ru'asi permitted it into the lam; these three are leading Kufan scholars, and they related it as heard from the Arabs.

I have only addressed the assimilation of these letters into what is adjacent to them and mentioned the disagreement about them, so that it is not assumed from al-Zamakhshari's statement, "they are not assimilated into what is adjacent to them," that this is impermissible by consensus of the grammarians. I have therefore cited this disagreement to alert that it is not a consensus, since his absolute statement indicates prohibition without exception.

The reading of Ibn Abi Habib with a damma on the ta' (bi-dammi al-ta'): its explanation is that he made the vowel of the ta' follow the vowel of the ra', and it is shadhdh (anomalous).

As for the reading of Ubayy with the nun in both places, it contradicts the orthography of the Mushaf, so it is shadhdh.

As for the reading of Ibn 'Abbas in the imperative form (bi-sigha al-amr), the repetition of "qala" (قالَ) may be for emphasis, or so that it becomes two sentences: one sentence with the supplication for those who believe, and another sentence with the supplication against those who disbelieve. Thus they are not governed by one operator; rather he has made each one a separate saying. Its form on this reading is ad-tarrhu with a fathah on the shaddah of the ra', as you say 'addahu (عَضَّهُ) with a fathah. This assimilation is in the dialect of non-Hijazis, because the dialect of the Hijazis in such a case is to unassimilate (al-fakk). Had he read in the dialect of his people, it would be "adtarruhu ila 'adhab" (أضْطَرُّهُ إلى عَذابٍ), with "ila 'adhab" connected to His words "thumma adtarruhu."

The meaning of compulsion (al-idtirar) here is that he is driven and forced toward the punishment, such that he finds no escape from it, since no one prefers or chooses to enter the Fire.

The conditional concept here is cancelled (mulgha), since some of the sinful believers may enter the Fire.

﴿وبِئْسَ المَصِيرُ﴾ (wa-bi'sa al-masir): the object of dispraise is omitted because the meaning is understood, i.e., "and wretched is the destination, the Fire," if al-masir is a noun of place. If it is a verbal noun (masdar), according to the view of those who permit that, the estimate is: "and wretched is the becoming, its becoming toward the punishment."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 127–128 (part 1 of 2):

﴿وإذْ يَرْفَعُ إبْراهِيمُ﴾: This clause is conjoined (*ma'tuf*) to what precedes it, so the governing element (*al-'amil*) of *idh* here is the same as the one mentioned for the *idh* before it. *Yarfa'u* has the sense of *rafa'a* (past tense). *Idh* is one of the particles that convert the present tense into the past, because it is an adverb of time referring to past time. The act of raising (*al-raf'*) had already taken place at the time of address. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is a narration of a past state (*hikayat hal madiyah*)," but this requires examination.

﴿مِنَ البَيْتِ﴾: "The House" is the Ka'bah. The commentators mentioned many stories about the nature of this House, its antiquity and origin, what its foundations were made of, how many times Adam performed the pilgrimage, what Ibrahim built it from, and who helped him in the construction. They digressed from this into discussions of the Frequented House (*al-Bayt al-Ma'mur*), the height of Adam, the baldness that afflicted him and his offspring, and the Black Stone. They went at length on matters which neither the Qur'an nor an authentic hadith contains, and some of these contradict one another. This happened because of their custom of transmitting whatever circulated and whatever was current. One should rely only on what is authenticated in the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Ibn Atiyyah said: "What is sound from all of this is that Allah commanded Ibrahim to raise the foundations of the House." We dispute him over his saying "commanded," since the text does not state that Allah commanded this.

﴿القَواعِدَ﴾ (*al-qawa'id*, "foundations"): Its meaning was explained earlier in the discussion of vocabulary. Are they the foundations (*al-asas*) or the walls (*al-judur*)? If they are the foundations, then raising them means building upon them, moving them from a state of lowness to a state of height, and lengthening them after they had been short. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also possible that what is meant is the supports (*saqat*) of the building, and it is possible that the meaning is what was set down (*qu'id*) of the House, i.e., what was made into a level base (*istuwti'a*), meaning he made the form of the level base high and elevated by building upon it."

﴿مِنَ البَيْتِ﴾ (*min al-bayt*): It may be connected to *yarfa'u*, or it may be in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) for *al-qawa'id*, in which case it is tied to a deleted element whose estimated form is *ka'innah* ("being from the House"). The foundations were not made grammatically dependent (*lam tudaf*) to "the House," which would have made the phrase "foundations of the House." The absence of the construct (*idafah*) provides clarification after ambiguity and magnifies the status of what is specified.

﴿وإسْماعِيلُ﴾ (*wa-Isma'il*): It is conjoined to Ibrahim, so both share in the act of raising. It was said that Ibrahim was building while Isma'il handed him the stones. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: "Ibrahim and Isma'il raised it together," and this is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. It is related from Ibn Abbas that Isma'il was then a small child, who would hand him the stones. It is also related from Ali that Isma'il was then a small child, but this report from Ali is not authentic.

Whoever makes the *waw* in "wa-Isma'il" a *waw* of circumstance (*waw al-hal*) parses Isma'il as a subject (*mubtada'*) and deletes the predicate. The estimated sense is: "And Isma'il was saying, 'Our Lord, accept from us,'" so that Ibrahim is specialized in the building and Isma'il is specialized in the supplication. Whoever takes the view of conjunction makes "﴿Our Lord, accept from us﴾" an object (*ma'mul*) of a deleted saying that refers to both Ibrahim and Isma'il together, in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*nasb 'ala al-hal*). Its estimated form is: "And when the two of them were raising the foundations, saying: Our Lord, accept from us." This interpretation is supported by the fact that the conjunction in "wa-Isma'il" is more evident than that the *waw* is a *waw* of circumstance. The reading of Ubayy and Abd Allah, "yaqulani" ("the two of them say"), makes this clause explicit. It is also possible that the deleted saying is the governing element of *idh*, so that it is not in the position of a circumstance. The meaning would then be that they made that supplication at the moment they began raising the foundations. In calling out with the word "Our Lord" there is a gentle and pleading tone, through mention of this attribute which indicates nurturing and reform, in keeping with the state of the one supplicating.

﴿رَبَّنا تَقَبَّلْ مِنّا﴾ ("Our Lord, accept from us"): That is, our deeds which we intended for Your obedience. *Taqabbal* has the sense of *aqbal* (accept), so the form *tafa''ala* here has the sense of the unaugmented root, as in the saying: "*ta'adda al-shay'* and *'addahu*" (the thing passed over and someone passed it over), which is one of the meanings for which the form *tafa''ala* comes. The meaning of acceptance here is recompense (*al-ithabah*). He expressed it by one of two mutually implying things in place of the other, because acceptance (*taqabbul*) is when a man accepts from another man what he gives to him. So the act of the servant is likened to a gift, and the good pleasure of Allah, exalted is He, is likened to acceptance, by extension. Some commentators related from some people a distinction between *qabul* and *taqabbul*, saying: "*Taqabbul* is the effort to accept, which is when the deed is deficient and does not deserve to be accepted." He said: "So this is an acknowledgment by Ibrahim and Isma'il of shortcoming in the deed." The intention was not to give reward, because the act being placed in the position of acceptance from the one served is more pleasurable to the intelligent servant than receiving a reward for it. Their request for acceptance (*taqabbul*) in this manner, and the fact that the arrangement of reward upon deeds is not obligatory upon Allah, exalted is He, ends here in summary. We say: *Taqabbul* and *qabul* are the same with respect to Allah, exalted is He, since it is not possible to conceive of obligation (*taklif*) in relation to Him, exalted is He. We have already stated that *tafa''ala* here is equivalent to the unaugmented verb which is *qabila*.

﴿إنَّكَ أنْتَ السَّمِيعُ العَلِيمُ﴾ ("Indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing"): *Anta* may be a subject (*ibtida'*), a separator (*fasl*, also called *damir al-fasl*, a pronoun of separation), or an emphasis (*ta'kid*). The discussion of the separator and its function has already been covered. It is one of the matters on which I gathered the discussion in about seven pages, presenting rulings without argumentation. These two attributes are extremely appropriate here, since a deed and a humble plea for acceptance have come from them. So He is the All-Hearing of their humble supplication and their asking for acceptance, and He is the All-Knowing of their intentions in sincerely performing their deed. The attribute of hearing is mentioned first, even though the request for acceptance comes after the deed, by way of proximity, as in His saying: ﴿On the day when some faces turn white and some faces turn black﴾ [Al 'Imran: 106]. As for the attribute of "the All-Knowing," it is placed later because it is the closing word of the verse (*fasilah*) and because of its generality, since it encompasses knowledge of what is heard and what is not heard.

﴿رَبَّنا واجْعَلْنا مُسْلِمَيْنِ لَكَ﴾ ("Our Lord, make us submissive to You"): That is, compliant, or those who devote our faces to You, derived from His saying: "whoever submits his face" (*man aslama wajhahu*), meaning sincerely devotes his deed. The meaning is: Continue this for us, because they were already submitting. The preposition *lak* indicates the direction of submission, meaning to You and not to another. Ibn Abbas and Awf al-A'rabi read *muslimin* in the plural, as a supplication for the two of them and for those of their family who were present, such as Hajar. This is better than making a plural form refer to the dual, although that has been said here.
