﴿ومِن ذُرِّيَّتِنا أُمَّةً مُسْلِمَةً لَكَ﴾ ("And from our offspring a nation that submits to You"): When the answer to him had been given in His saying: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124], they knew that among their offspring there would be both the wrongdoer and the non-wrongdoer. So here they supplicated with partitive *min* (indicating a part) and not with generality, saying: ﴿and from our offspring﴾. They specified their offspring in the supplication out of compassion and tenderness toward them, and because the righteousness of the offspring of the righteous brings much benefit to those who follow them, since they become a cause of righteousness for those who come after them. "Offspring" here is said to mean the Community of Muhammad (ﷺ), by the evidence of His saying: ﴿and send among them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 129]. It is also said that they are the Arabs, since they are from their offspring. Al-Qaffal said: "There has never ceased to be among their offspring those who worship Allah alone without associating anything with Him, and the Messengers, peace and blessings be upon them, have never ceased to be from their offspring. In the pre-Islamic era there were Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl and Qass ibn Sa'idah al-Iyadi. It is also said that 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim, grandfather of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and 'Amr ibn al-Zarib were upon the religion of Islam."

Al-Zamakhshari permitted that *min* in "and from our offspring" is explanatory (*lil-tabyin*), saying: "like His saying: ﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe﴾ [al-Nur: 55]." It has already been stated earlier that our companions (the scholars of our school) reject that *min* is explanatory, and they interpret what is understood from its apparent meaning as being otherwise.

The explanation of *ummah* has already been given. What is meant by it here is the group or the generation. The meaning, on the basis that "from our offspring" is in the position of the first object (*maf'ul awwal*) of *ij'al*, since the making (*ja'l*) here means transformation (*tasyir*), is: "Make a group of people from our offspring a nation that submits to You." It is impossible that what is estimated in the phrase *ij'al* from "from our offspring" means "create" or "bring into existence." Even if this were sound in terms of meaning, the verb would then be transitive to one object only. "From our offspring" is connected to the estimated *ij'al*, because if it is of the type of coordination of single words (*'atf al-mufradat*), then it shares the first governing element, and the first governing element does not carry the meaning of creating and bringing into existence. If it is of the type of coordination of clauses (*'atf al-jumal*), then nothing is deleted except what is indicated by the stated speech, and the stated speech does not have the meaning of bringing into existence, so the deleted element is likewise. Do you not see that they prohibited, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who sends blessings upon you, and His angels﴾ [al-Ahzab: 43], that the estimate be: "and His angels send blessings," because the two blessings differ in meaning: from Allah it is mercy, and from the angels it is supplication. They interpreted this and took it to refer to the common element between the two blessings, not as a deletion. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that the first object be *ummah*, and "from our offspring" be a circumstance (*hal*), because it is a qualifier of an indefinite noun that was placed before it, so it became accusative as a circumstance, and *muslimah* is the second object. The original would then be: "Make a nation from our offspring submissive to You." He said: "So the *waw* is inserted in the original before *ummah*, and it has been separated from it by His saying 'from our offspring,' which is permissible because it is part of the speech conjoined by the adverbial phrase." They regarded the poet's verse:

*Yawman tarahā kashibhi ardiyat al-khims*
*wa-yawman adīmuhā naghila*

(Sometimes you see her like the mottled cloaks of the Khims, and sometimes her hide is marked with stains)

as a poetic necessity. The separation by a circumstance is further removed than separation by an adverbial phrase, so it becomes like the example "I struck the man," and "*mutajarridah* the woman," meaning "and the woman is stripped." It should be restricted to necessity alone.

﴿وأرِنا مَناسِكَنا﴾ ("And show us our rites"): Qatadah said: "the landmarks of the pilgrimage." 'Ata' and Ibn Jurayj said: "our places of slaughter," meaning the places of sacrifice. It was said: "every act of worship by which Allah, exalted is He, is worshipped." Taj al-Qurra' al-Kirmani said: "If what is meant is the acts of the pilgrimage and what is done at the standing-places, such as circumambulation (*tawaf*), running between Safa and Marwah (*sa'y*), standing at 'Arafah (*wuquf*), and prayer, then *manasik* is the plural of *mansak*, which is the verbal noun, pluralized because its forms differ. If he meant the places where the rules of the pilgrimage are carried out, such as Mina, 'Arafah, and Muzdalifah, then it is the plural of *mansak*, which is the place of worship." It is related from Ali that when Ibrahim had finished building the House and made this supplication, Allah sent Gabriel (peace be upon him) to him, and he performed the pilgrimage with him.

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "wa-arihim manasikahum" (and show them their rites), referring the pronoun back to the offspring. The meaning of *arina* is: "make us see" (*basir*), if it is from the sight of the eye (*ru'yah basariyyah*). Transitivity here to two objects is clear, because it is transferred by the *hamzah* (causative) from a verb that is transitive to one object. If it is from the sight of the heart (*ru'yat al-qalb*), then what is transmitted is that it is transitive to two objects, as in the saying of the poet:

*Wa-inna la-qawmun ma narā al-qatla subbatan*
*idha ma ra'athu 'amirun wa-salūl*

(Indeed we are a people who do not regard killing as a shame, when 'Amir and Salul see it)

and the verse of al-Kumayt:

*Bi-ayyi kitabin am bi-ayyati sunnatin*
*yura hubbuhum 'aran 'alayya wa-yuhsabu*

(By what book, or by what sunnah, is their love seen as a disgrace upon me, and reckoned as such?)

When the *hamzah* of transfer is added to it, it becomes transitive to three objects, but here there are only two, so it must be held that it is from the sight of the eye. Al-Zamakhshari made it from the sight of the heart and explained it with the saying "make known" ('arrif), so in his view it comes with the meaning of "make known," meaning it is of the heart type and transitive to one object, then the *hamzah* of transfer was added so it became transitive to two. This requires a hearing from the speech of the Arabs. Ibn Atiyyah related from a group that it is from the sight of the eye, and from a group that it is from the sight of the heart. Ibn Atiyyah said: "This is the more sound view, and it entails that its verb be transitive to three objects. It is resolved by the fact that there is found, transitive by the *hamzah* from the sight of the heart, the same as the non-transitive form." Ha'ta'it ibn Ya'fur, brother of al-Aswad, said:

*Arini jawadan mata hazlan li-annani*
*ara ma tarina aw bakhilan mukhalladan*

(Show me a horse that died of emaciation, for I see what you see, or a stingy man who lives forever.)

The Commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya ends here. Its words and his are as follows. It would necessarily follow for the one who says this that it transitively takes three objects. That is necessary only according to what we have mentioned, that the established usage is: when *ra'a* (to see) is a heart-verb, it transitively takes two objects, and with the causative hamza (*hamzat al-naql*, the hamza of transfer) it becomes transitive to three. As for his statement, "It is distinguished by the fact that there is found a verb made transitive by the hamza from the sight of the heart, as with the non-transitivized form," he means that it has been used in the Arabic language transitively to two objects together with the causative hamza, just as it has been used transitively to two objects without the hamza. Since this is so, it is established that *ra'a* when it is a heart-verb has two usages: first, that it means *ʿalima* (to know), transitive to one object, in the sense of *ʿarafa* (to recognize); and second, that it means *ʿalima* transitive to two objects.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya's use of the verse of Ibn Yaʿfur as evidence that *arā* is a heart-verb is not conclusive. Rather, the apparent meaning is that it is a verb of sight, and the meaning is "Let me see the horse." Do you not see his saying, "He died of emaciation"? Indeed this belongs to the things related to sight, so establishing *ra'a* as a heart-verb transitive to one object requires a transmitted usage (*samaʿ*).

Ibn Mālik, who was a gatherer of language and a preserver of rare usages, when he enumerated what is transitive to two objects, said in *al-Tashil*: "*Ra'a*, not for seeing, nor for opinion, nor for striking." So if *ra'a* meant *ʿarafa*, he would have negated that just as he negated for *ra'a* (in the sense of opinion) that it is transitive to two objects, its being used for seeing, for *ra'a*, or for *daraba*.

Some people said: The meaning here of "seeing" is the seeing of sight and of the heart together, because the Hajj is not complete except by matters some of which are known and not seen, and some of which the purpose of is not complete except by seeing. So it is obligatory to take the word in both meanings together. This is weak, because it involves combining the literal and the figurative, or applying a homonymous word to more than one established meaning in one instance, and that is not permitted in our view.

Ibn Kathir read *wa-arna* and *arini khamsatan* with the vowel of the *rāʾ* being sukun (silent). It is related from Abu ʿAmr: *al-iskan* (silencing) and *al-ikhtilas* (the rapid, partial vowel). It is also related from him: *al-ishbaʿ* (full vowel), like the rest. Except that Abu ʿĀmir and Abu Bakr silenced the *rāʾ* in *arna* in both places. So *al-ishbaʿ* is the original, *al-ikhtilas* is a good and well-known feature in Arabic, and *al-iskan* is an assimilation of the separated to the connected, as they said *fakhdh* (thigh), and it was made easier by the fact that the vowel in it is not a case-ending.

Some people rejected the silencing on the ground that the kasra indicates what has been elided, so it is ugly to delete it. They mean that the original was *arʾa*, so the vowel of the hamza was transferred to the *rāʾ* and the hamza was deleted; so retaining it indicates the deleted element. This is nothing, because this is a rejected principle, and the vowel becomes as if it were the vowel of the *rāʾ*.

Al-Fārisī said: What this speaker said is nothing. Do you not see that they assimilated in *lakinna huwa Allahu rabbi*, the original being *lakin*; then they transferred the vowel and deleted, then they assimilated? So the loss of the vowel in *arna* is no less than its loss in assimilation. Furthermore, the silencing of this letter has been heard explicitly from the Arabs. The poet said:

*Arna adawata ʿAbdi Allahi namlaʾuha*
*min maʾi zamzama inna al-qawma qad ẓamiʾu*

*Show us the water-vessel of ʿAbd Allah, that we may fill it*
*with the water of Zamzam, for indeed the people have become thirsty.*

Furthermore, it is a mutawatir (widely transmitted) reading, so rejecting it is nothing.

The commentators mentioned, regarding how Ibrahim and Isma'il performed these rites, seven opinions with conflicting transmissions. They also mentioned who among the prophets performed the Hajj to this House, and who died in Makkah among them. They said that Nuh, Hud, Salih, Shu'ayb, Isma'il and others died there. The noble verse did not address any of that, so we left transmitting it, according to our custom.

﴿And accept our repentance﴾: They said that repentance (*tawba*) varies in its legal aspect according to the variation of those who repent. The repentance of the general Muslims is regret in the heart, turning away from the sin, resolve not to return to it, returning wrongful gains where possible, and intention to return them when it is not possible. The repentance of the elite is turning away from disliked things, from evil thoughts, from laxity in deeds, and from performing worship without its perfection. The repentance of the elite of the elite is for raising ranks and advancing in stations. So if Ibrahim and Isma'il prayed for themselves to repent, and the pronoun in His saying "And accept our repentance" was specific to the two of them, then it is possible that the repentance here is of this last category. They said: It is also possible that he intends steadfastness upon that state, like His saying: ﴿Our Lord, and make us submissive to You﴾. If the pronoun included them and their descendants, the supplication for repentance would be directed to those who are among the people of repentance. If the pronoun before it is elided and understood, the estimate is "upon our disobedient ones", and he prayed for repentance for the disobedient. This verse does not indicate the permissibility of the occurrence of sin from the prophets, peace be upon them, because of the possibility we have mentioned, unlike the one who claimed that and said: repentance is conditioned upon a prior sin, since otherwise requesting repentance would be impossible.

What strengthens that the intended ones are the disobedient descendants is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾ [Ibrahim: 35], up to His saying: ﴿And whoever disobeys me, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [Ibrahim: 36], meaning: then You are able to accept his repentance and forgive him. Also the reading of ʿAbd Allah: "Show them their rites and accept their repentance," and the possibility that it is "Show us our rites" with an elided genitive, meaning "show our descendants our rites," like His saying: ﴿And We created you﴾, meaning "We created your father."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Accept our repentance for what has passed from us of minor sins," or they both sought repentance for their descendants. End. So his saying "for what has passed from us of minor sins" is according to the doctrine of the Mu'tazila, since they say that minor sins are permissible for the prophets. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: He mentioned the two opinions of firmness or that this is a supplication for the descendants. He said: It was said, and it is the best in my view, that when they knew the rites, built the House, and obeyed, they wished to establish for the people that that standing and those places are places of disavowal of sins and seeking repentance. Al-Tabari said: There is no one among God's creation except that between him and God, exalted is He, are meanings he loves to be better than they are. End of Ibn ʿAṭiyya's words. In it is a departure of the statement "And accept our repentance" from its apparent meaning to a distant interpretation: that is, the supplication with His saying "And accept our repentance" does not mean that they both sought repentance, but rather by that request they indicated that others in those places seek repentance, so they did not literally intend the request themselves; they only mentioned it to legislate for others to seek it. This is very far-fetched.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: The community has agreed upon the *ʿisma* (infallibility) of the prophets in respect of conveying the message, and from the major sins and from those minor sins which contain baseness; and it has been disputed regarding other minor sins. End of his words.

Imam Fakhr al-Din Abu ʿAbd Allah Muhammad ibn ʿUmar ibn al-Hasan al-Razi said in his book *al-Mahsul*, what is summarized of it: The Shi'a said: It is not permissible that any sin occur from them, neither minor nor major, neither intentionally nor by forgetfulness, nor from the perspective of interpretation. Then he mentioned the agreement that it is not permissible from them to commit disbelief, nor alteration in conveying the message, nor error in giving rulings. He mentioned disagreement on other matters. Then he said: What he who holds this view says is that no sin occurs from them deliberately, neither major nor minor. As for forgetfulness, it may occur, but on condition that they remember it at once and alert others that that was forgetfulness.

﴿Indeed You, You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾: The word *anta* permits three grammatical functions: the separating pronoun (*fasl*), emphasis (*ta'kid*), and the subject of a nominal sentence (*ibtida'*). These two attributes are appropriate, because they both prayed that He make them and from their descendants a Muslim community submitting to Him, and that He show them their rites, and that He accept their repentance. So mention of accepting repentance from them, or mercy upon them, is appropriate. And putting the mention of repentance before mercy is appropriate, due to the proximity of the last supplication in His saying "And accept our repentance." The attribute of mercy was delayed because of its generality, since repentance is among mercy; but it is the closing word (*fasila*) of the verse. And *al-Tawwab* (the Accepting of repentance) is not suitable to be the closing word here, because before it is ﴿Indeed You, You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾, and after it: ﴿Indeed You, You are the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾ [al-Baqara: 129].

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 127–128 (part 1 of 2):

﴿وإذْ يَرْفَعُ إبْراهِيمُ﴾: This clause is conjoined (*ma'tuf*) to what precedes it, so the governing element (*al-'amil*) of *idh* here is the same as the one mentioned for the *idh* before it. *Yarfa'u* has the sense of *rafa'a* (past tense). *Idh* is one of the particles that convert the present tense into the past, because it is an adverb of time referring to past time. The act of raising (*al-raf'*) had already taken place at the time of address. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is a narration of a past state (*hikayat hal madiyah*)," but this requires examination.

﴿مِنَ البَيْتِ﴾: "The House" is the Ka'bah. The commentators mentioned many stories about the nature of this House, its antiquity and origin, what its foundations were made of, how many times Adam performed the pilgrimage, what Ibrahim built it from, and who helped him in the construction. They digressed from this into discussions of the Frequented House (*al-Bayt al-Ma'mur*), the height of Adam, the baldness that afflicted him and his offspring, and the Black Stone. They went at length on matters which neither the Qur'an nor an authentic hadith contains, and some of these contradict one another. This happened because of their custom of transmitting whatever circulated and whatever was current. One should rely only on what is authenticated in the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Ibn Atiyyah said: "What is sound from all of this is that Allah commanded Ibrahim to raise the foundations of the House." We dispute him over his saying "commanded," since the text does not state that Allah commanded this.

﴿القَواعِدَ﴾ (*al-qawa'id*, "foundations"): Its meaning was explained earlier in the discussion of vocabulary. Are they the foundations (*al-asas*) or the walls (*al-judur*)? If they are the foundations, then raising them means building upon them, moving them from a state of lowness to a state of height, and lengthening them after they had been short. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also possible that what is meant is the supports (*saqat*) of the building, and it is possible that the meaning is what was set down (*qu'id*) of the House, i.e., what was made into a level base (*istuwti'a*), meaning he made the form of the level base high and elevated by building upon it."

﴿مِنَ البَيْتِ﴾ (*min al-bayt*): It may be connected to *yarfa'u*, or it may be in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) for *al-qawa'id*, in which case it is tied to a deleted element whose estimated form is *ka'innah* ("being from the House"). The foundations were not made grammatically dependent (*lam tudaf*) to "the House," which would have made the phrase "foundations of the House." The absence of the construct (*idafah*) provides clarification after ambiguity and magnifies the status of what is specified.

﴿وإسْماعِيلُ﴾ (*wa-Isma'il*): It is conjoined to Ibrahim, so both share in the act of raising. It was said that Ibrahim was building while Isma'il handed him the stones. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: "Ibrahim and Isma'il raised it together," and this is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. It is related from Ibn Abbas that Isma'il was then a small child, who would hand him the stones. It is also related from Ali that Isma'il was then a small child, but this report from Ali is not authentic.

Whoever makes the *waw* in "wa-Isma'il" a *waw* of circumstance (*waw al-hal*) parses Isma'il as a subject (*mubtada'*) and deletes the predicate. The estimated sense is: "And Isma'il was saying, 'Our Lord, accept from us,'" so that Ibrahim is specialized in the building and Isma'il is specialized in the supplication. Whoever takes the view of conjunction makes "﴿Our Lord, accept from us﴾" an object (*ma'mul*) of a deleted saying that refers to both Ibrahim and Isma'il together, in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*nasb 'ala al-hal*). Its estimated form is: "And when the two of them were raising the foundations, saying: Our Lord, accept from us." This interpretation is supported by the fact that the conjunction in "wa-Isma'il" is more evident than that the *waw* is a *waw* of circumstance. The reading of Ubayy and Abd Allah, "yaqulani" ("the two of them say"), makes this clause explicit. It is also possible that the deleted saying is the governing element of *idh*, so that it is not in the position of a circumstance. The meaning would then be that they made that supplication at the moment they began raising the foundations. In calling out with the word "Our Lord" there is a gentle and pleading tone, through mention of this attribute which indicates nurturing and reform, in keeping with the state of the one supplicating.

﴿رَبَّنا تَقَبَّلْ مِنّا﴾ ("Our Lord, accept from us"): That is, our deeds which we intended for Your obedience. *Taqabbal* has the sense of *aqbal* (accept), so the form *tafa''ala* here has the sense of the unaugmented root, as in the saying: "*ta'adda al-shay'* and *'addahu*" (the thing passed over and someone passed it over), which is one of the meanings for which the form *tafa''ala* comes. The meaning of acceptance here is recompense (*al-ithabah*). He expressed it by one of two mutually implying things in place of the other, because acceptance (*taqabbul*) is when a man accepts from another man what he gives to him. So the act of the servant is likened to a gift, and the good pleasure of Allah, exalted is He, is likened to acceptance, by extension. Some commentators related from some people a distinction between *qabul* and *taqabbul*, saying: "*Taqabbul* is the effort to accept, which is when the deed is deficient and does not deserve to be accepted." He said: "So this is an acknowledgment by Ibrahim and Isma'il of shortcoming in the deed." The intention was not to give reward, because the act being placed in the position of acceptance from the one served is more pleasurable to the intelligent servant than receiving a reward for it. Their request for acceptance (*taqabbul*) in this manner, and the fact that the arrangement of reward upon deeds is not obligatory upon Allah, exalted is He, ends here in summary. We say: *Taqabbul* and *qabul* are the same with respect to Allah, exalted is He, since it is not possible to conceive of obligation (*taklif*) in relation to Him, exalted is He. We have already stated that *tafa''ala* here is equivalent to the unaugmented verb which is *qabila*.

﴿إنَّكَ أنْتَ السَّمِيعُ العَلِيمُ﴾ ("Indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing"): *Anta* may be a subject (*ibtida'*), a separator (*fasl*, also called *damir al-fasl*, a pronoun of separation), or an emphasis (*ta'kid*). The discussion of the separator and its function has already been covered. It is one of the matters on which I gathered the discussion in about seven pages, presenting rulings without argumentation. These two attributes are extremely appropriate here, since a deed and a humble plea for acceptance have come from them. So He is the All-Hearing of their humble supplication and their asking for acceptance, and He is the All-Knowing of their intentions in sincerely performing their deed. The attribute of hearing is mentioned first, even though the request for acceptance comes after the deed, by way of proximity, as in His saying: ﴿On the day when some faces turn white and some faces turn black﴾ [Al 'Imran: 106]. As for the attribute of "the All-Knowing," it is placed later because it is the closing word of the verse (*fasilah*) and because of its generality, since it encompasses knowledge of what is heard and what is not heard.

﴿رَبَّنا واجْعَلْنا مُسْلِمَيْنِ لَكَ﴾ ("Our Lord, make us submissive to You"): That is, compliant, or those who devote our faces to You, derived from His saying: "whoever submits his face" (*man aslama wajhahu*), meaning sincerely devotes his deed. The meaning is: Continue this for us, because they were already submitting. The preposition *lak* indicates the direction of submission, meaning to You and not to another. Ibn Abbas and Awf al-A'rabi read *muslimin* in the plural, as a supplication for the two of them and for those of their family who were present, such as Hajar. This is better than making a plural form refer to the dual, although that has been said here.

﴿ومِن ذُرِّيَّتِنا أُمَّةً مُسْلِمَةً لَكَ﴾ ("And from our offspring a nation that submits to You"): When the answer to him had been given in His saying: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124], they knew that among their offspring there would be both the wrongdoer and the non-wrongdoer. So here they supplicated with partitive *min* (indicating a part) and not with generality, saying: ﴿and from our offspring﴾. They specified their offspring in the supplication out of compassion and tenderness toward them, and because the righteousness of the offspring of the righteous brings much benefit to those who follow them, since they become a cause of righteousness for those who come after them. "Offspring" here is said to mean the Community of Muhammad (ﷺ), by the evidence of His saying: ﴿and send among them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 129]. It is also said that they are the Arabs, since they are from their offspring. Al-Qaffal said: "There has never ceased to be among their offspring those who worship Allah alone without associating anything with Him, and the Messengers, peace and blessings be upon them, have never ceased to be from their offspring. In the pre-Islamic era there were Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl and Qass ibn Sa'idah al-Iyadi. It is also said that 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim, grandfather of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and 'Amr ibn al-Zarib were upon the religion of Islam."

Al-Zamakhshari permitted that *min* in "and from our offspring" is explanatory (*lil-tabyin*), saying: "like His saying: ﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe﴾ [al-Nur: 55]." It has already been stated earlier that our companions (the scholars of our school) reject that *min* is explanatory, and they interpret what is understood from its apparent meaning as being otherwise.

The explanation of *ummah* has already been given. What is meant by it here is the group or the generation. The meaning, on the basis that "from our offspring" is in the position of the first object (*maf'ul awwal*) of *ij'al*, since the making (*ja'l*) here means transformation (*tasyir*), is: "Make a group of people from our offspring a nation that submits to You." It is impossible that what is estimated in the phrase *ij'al* from "from our offspring" means "create" or "bring into existence." Even if this were sound in terms of meaning, the verb would then be transitive to one object only. "From our offspring" is connected to the estimated *ij'al*, because if it is of the type of coordination of single words (*'atf al-mufradat*), then it shares the first governing element, and the first governing element does not carry the meaning of creating and bringing into existence. If it is of the type of coordination of clauses (*'atf al-jumal*), then nothing is deleted except what is indicated by the stated speech, and the stated speech does not have the meaning of bringing into existence, so the deleted element is likewise. Do you not see that they prohibited, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who sends blessings upon you, and His angels﴾ [al-Ahzab: 43], that the estimate be: "and His angels send blessings," because the two blessings differ in meaning: from Allah it is mercy, and from the angels it is supplication. They interpreted this and took it to refer to the common element between the two blessings, not as a deletion. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that the first object be *ummah*, and "from our offspring" be a circumstance (*hal*), because it is a qualifier of an indefinite noun that was placed before it, so it became accusative as a circumstance, and *muslimah* is the second object. The original would then be: "Make a nation from our offspring submissive to You." He said: "So the *waw* is inserted in the original before *ummah*, and it has been separated from it by His saying 'from our offspring,' which is permissible because it is part of the speech conjoined by the adverbial phrase." They regarded the poet's verse:

*Yawman tarahā kashibhi ardiyat al-khims*
*wa-yawman adīmuhā naghila*

(Sometimes you see her like the mottled cloaks of the Khims, and sometimes her hide is marked with stains)

as a poetic necessity. The separation by a circumstance is further removed than separation by an adverbial phrase, so it becomes like the example "I struck the man," and "*mutajarridah* the woman," meaning "and the woman is stripped." It should be restricted to necessity alone.

﴿وأرِنا مَناسِكَنا﴾ ("And show us our rites"): Qatadah said: "the landmarks of the pilgrimage." 'Ata' and Ibn Jurayj said: "our places of slaughter," meaning the places of sacrifice. It was said: "every act of worship by which Allah, exalted is He, is worshipped." Taj al-Qurra' al-Kirmani said: "If what is meant is the acts of the pilgrimage and what is done at the standing-places, such as circumambulation (*tawaf*), running between Safa and Marwah (*sa'y*), standing at 'Arafah (*wuquf*), and prayer, then *manasik* is the plural of *mansak*, which is the verbal noun, pluralized because its forms differ. If he meant the places where the rules of the pilgrimage are carried out, such as Mina, 'Arafah, and Muzdalifah, then it is the plural of *mansak*, which is the place of worship." It is related from Ali that when Ibrahim had finished building the House and made this supplication, Allah sent Gabriel (peace be upon him) to him, and he performed the pilgrimage with him.

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "wa-arihim manasikahum" (and show them their rites), referring the pronoun back to the offspring. The meaning of *arina* is: "make us see" (*basir*), if it is from the sight of the eye (*ru'yah basariyyah*). Transitivity here to two objects is clear, because it is transferred by the *hamzah* (causative) from a verb that is transitive to one object. If it is from the sight of the heart (*ru'yat al-qalb*), then what is transmitted is that it is transitive to two objects, as in the saying of the poet:

*Wa-inna la-qawmun ma narā al-qatla subbatan*
*idha ma ra'athu 'amirun wa-salūl*

(Indeed we are a people who do not regard killing as a shame, when 'Amir and Salul see it)

and the verse of al-Kumayt:

*Bi-ayyi kitabin am bi-ayyati sunnatin*
*yura hubbuhum 'aran 'alayya wa-yuhsabu*

(By what book, or by what sunnah, is their love seen as a disgrace upon me, and reckoned as such?)

When the *hamzah* of transfer is added to it, it becomes transitive to three objects, but here there are only two, so it must be held that it is from the sight of the eye. Al-Zamakhshari made it from the sight of the heart and explained it with the saying "make known" ('arrif), so in his view it comes with the meaning of "make known," meaning it is of the heart type and transitive to one object, then the *hamzah* of transfer was added so it became transitive to two. This requires a hearing from the speech of the Arabs. Ibn Atiyyah related from a group that it is from the sight of the eye, and from a group that it is from the sight of the heart. Ibn Atiyyah said: "This is the more sound view, and it entails that its verb be transitive to three objects. It is resolved by the fact that there is found, transitive by the *hamzah* from the sight of the heart, the same as the non-transitive form." Ha'ta'it ibn Ya'fur, brother of al-Aswad, said:

*Arini jawadan mata hazlan li-annani*
*ara ma tarina aw bakhilan mukhalladan*

(Show me a horse that died of emaciation, for I see what you see, or a stingy man who lives forever.)

The Commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya ends here. Its words and his are as follows. It would necessarily follow for the one who says this that it transitively takes three objects. That is necessary only according to what we have mentioned, that the established usage is: when *ra'a* (to see) is a heart-verb, it transitively takes two objects, and with the causative hamza (*hamzat al-naql*, the hamza of transfer) it becomes transitive to three. As for his statement, "It is distinguished by the fact that there is found a verb made transitive by the hamza from the sight of the heart, as with the non-transitivized form," he means that it has been used in the Arabic language transitively to two objects together with the causative hamza, just as it has been used transitively to two objects without the hamza. Since this is so, it is established that *ra'a* when it is a heart-verb has two usages: first, that it means *ʿalima* (to know), transitive to one object, in the sense of *ʿarafa* (to recognize); and second, that it means *ʿalima* transitive to two objects.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya's use of the verse of Ibn Yaʿfur as evidence that *arā* is a heart-verb is not conclusive. Rather, the apparent meaning is that it is a verb of sight, and the meaning is "Let me see the horse." Do you not see his saying, "He died of emaciation"? Indeed this belongs to the things related to sight, so establishing *ra'a* as a heart-verb transitive to one object requires a transmitted usage (*samaʿ*).

Ibn Mālik, who was a gatherer of language and a preserver of rare usages, when he enumerated what is transitive to two objects, said in *al-Tashil*: "*Ra'a*, not for seeing, nor for opinion, nor for striking." So if *ra'a* meant *ʿarafa*, he would have negated that just as he negated for *ra'a* (in the sense of opinion) that it is transitive to two objects, its being used for seeing, for *ra'a*, or for *daraba*.

Some people said: The meaning here of "seeing" is the seeing of sight and of the heart together, because the Hajj is not complete except by matters some of which are known and not seen, and some of which the purpose of is not complete except by seeing. So it is obligatory to take the word in both meanings together. This is weak, because it involves combining the literal and the figurative, or applying a homonymous word to more than one established meaning in one instance, and that is not permitted in our view.

Ibn Kathir read *wa-arna* and *arini khamsatan* with the vowel of the *rāʾ* being sukun (silent). It is related from Abu ʿAmr: *al-iskan* (silencing) and *al-ikhtilas* (the rapid, partial vowel). It is also related from him: *al-ishbaʿ* (full vowel), like the rest. Except that Abu ʿĀmir and Abu Bakr silenced the *rāʾ* in *arna* in both places. So *al-ishbaʿ* is the original, *al-ikhtilas* is a good and well-known feature in Arabic, and *al-iskan* is an assimilation of the separated to the connected, as they said *fakhdh* (thigh), and it was made easier by the fact that the vowel in it is not a case-ending.

Some people rejected the silencing on the ground that the kasra indicates what has been elided, so it is ugly to delete it. They mean that the original was *arʾa*, so the vowel of the hamza was transferred to the *rāʾ* and the hamza was deleted; so retaining it indicates the deleted element. This is nothing, because this is a rejected principle, and the vowel becomes as if it were the vowel of the *rāʾ*.

Al-Fārisī said: What this speaker said is nothing. Do you not see that they assimilated in *lakinna huwa Allahu rabbi*, the original being *lakin*; then they transferred the vowel and deleted, then they assimilated? So the loss of the vowel in *arna* is no less than its loss in assimilation. Furthermore, the silencing of this letter has been heard explicitly from the Arabs. The poet said:

*Arna adawata ʿAbdi Allahi namlaʾuha*
*min maʾi zamzama inna al-qawma qad ẓamiʾu*

*Show us the water-vessel of ʿAbd Allah, that we may fill it*
*with the water of Zamzam, for indeed the people have become thirsty.*

Furthermore, it is a mutawatir (widely transmitted) reading, so rejecting it is nothing.

The commentators mentioned, regarding how Ibrahim and Isma'il performed these rites, seven opinions with conflicting transmissions. They also mentioned who among the prophets performed the Hajj to this House, and who died in Makkah among them. They said that Nuh, Hud, Salih, Shu'ayb, Isma'il and others died there. The noble verse did not address any of that, so we left transmitting it, according to our custom.

﴿And accept our repentance﴾: They said that repentance (*tawba*) varies in its legal aspect according to the variation of those who repent. The repentance of the general Muslims is regret in the heart, turning away from the sin, resolve not to return to it, returning wrongful gains where possible, and intention to return them when it is not possible. The repentance of the elite is turning away from disliked things, from evil thoughts, from laxity in deeds, and from performing worship without its perfection. The repentance of the elite of the elite is for raising ranks and advancing in stations. So if Ibrahim and Isma'il prayed for themselves to repent, and the pronoun in His saying "And accept our repentance" was specific to the two of them, then it is possible that the repentance here is of this last category. They said: It is also possible that he intends steadfastness upon that state, like His saying: ﴿Our Lord, and make us submissive to You﴾. If the pronoun included them and their descendants, the supplication for repentance would be directed to those who are among the people of repentance. If the pronoun before it is elided and understood, the estimate is "upon our disobedient ones", and he prayed for repentance for the disobedient. This verse does not indicate the permissibility of the occurrence of sin from the prophets, peace be upon them, because of the possibility we have mentioned, unlike the one who claimed that and said: repentance is conditioned upon a prior sin, since otherwise requesting repentance would be impossible.

What strengthens that the intended ones are the disobedient descendants is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾ [Ibrahim: 35], up to His saying: ﴿And whoever disobeys me, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [Ibrahim: 36], meaning: then You are able to accept his repentance and forgive him. Also the reading of ʿAbd Allah: "Show them their rites and accept their repentance," and the possibility that it is "Show us our rites" with an elided genitive, meaning "show our descendants our rites," like His saying: ﴿And We created you﴾, meaning "We created your father."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Accept our repentance for what has passed from us of minor sins," or they both sought repentance for their descendants. End. So his saying "for what has passed from us of minor sins" is according to the doctrine of the Mu'tazila, since they say that minor sins are permissible for the prophets. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: He mentioned the two opinions of firmness or that this is a supplication for the descendants. He said: It was said, and it is the best in my view, that when they knew the rites, built the House, and obeyed, they wished to establish for the people that that standing and those places are places of disavowal of sins and seeking repentance. Al-Tabari said: There is no one among God's creation except that between him and God, exalted is He, are meanings he loves to be better than they are. End of Ibn ʿAṭiyya's words. In it is a departure of the statement "And accept our repentance" from its apparent meaning to a distant interpretation: that is, the supplication with His saying "And accept our repentance" does not mean that they both sought repentance, but rather by that request they indicated that others in those places seek repentance, so they did not literally intend the request themselves; they only mentioned it to legislate for others to seek it. This is very far-fetched.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: The community has agreed upon the *ʿisma* (infallibility) of the prophets in respect of conveying the message, and from the major sins and from those minor sins which contain baseness; and it has been disputed regarding other minor sins. End of his words.

Imam Fakhr al-Din Abu ʿAbd Allah Muhammad ibn ʿUmar ibn al-Hasan al-Razi said in his book *al-Mahsul*, what is summarized of it: The Shi'a said: It is not permissible that any sin occur from them, neither minor nor major, neither intentionally nor by forgetfulness, nor from the perspective of interpretation. Then he mentioned the agreement that it is not permissible from them to commit disbelief, nor alteration in conveying the message, nor error in giving rulings. He mentioned disagreement on other matters. Then he said: What he who holds this view says is that no sin occurs from them deliberately, neither major nor minor. As for forgetfulness, it may occur, but on condition that they remember it at once and alert others that that was forgetfulness.

﴿Indeed You, You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾: The word *anta* permits three grammatical functions: the separating pronoun (*fasl*), emphasis (*ta'kid*), and the subject of a nominal sentence (*ibtida'*). These two attributes are appropriate, because they both prayed that He make them and from their descendants a Muslim community submitting to Him, and that He show them their rites, and that He accept their repentance. So mention of accepting repentance from them, or mercy upon them, is appropriate. And putting the mention of repentance before mercy is appropriate, due to the proximity of the last supplication in His saying "And accept our repentance." The attribute of mercy was delayed because of its generality, since repentance is among mercy; but it is the closing word (*fasila*) of the verse. And *al-Tawwab* (the Accepting of repentance) is not suitable to be the closing word here, because before it is ﴿Indeed You, You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾, and after it: ﴿Indeed You, You are the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾ [al-Baqara: 129].

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 129–130 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Our Lord, and raise up among them a messenger from among them﴾. When he had asked his Lord for security for Makkah, provision for its people, and that He make from his offspring a Muslim community (ummah muslimah), he concluded his supplication for them with what would bring them happiness in this world and the next, namely the sending of Muhammad (ﷺ) among them. His supplication for them thus included security, fertility, and guidance. The meaning of *al-ba'th* (sending forth) has already been explained in His words: ﴿then We resurrected you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 56]. What is meant here is sending (*al-irsal*) to them. The pronoun in *fihim* ("among them") may refer to the offspring, or to "a Muslim community," or to the people of Makkah. The last is supported by His words: ﴿It is He who sent among the unlettered ones a messenger from among them﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 2]. There is no disagreement that he is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It is also authentically reported from him that he said: "I am the supplication of my father Abraham." Allah did not send anyone to Makkah and its surroundings except him (ﷺ).

Ubayy read *wa-ab'ath fihim fi akhirihim* ("and raise up among them at their end"). Ibn ʿAbbas said: All the prophets were from the Children of Israel except ten: Noah, Hud, Salih, Shu'ayb, Lot, Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, and Muhammad (ﷺ), and [the tenth is not named in the transmission]. *Minhum* ("from among them") is in the position of a qualifier (*sifah*) of *rasulan* ("a messenger"), meaning: one who is from them and not from others. Thus they know his face, his lineage, and his upbringing, as He said: ﴿Allah certainly conferred favour upon the believers when He sent among them a messenger from among themselves﴾ [Aal ʿImran: 164]. He asked that the messenger be sent among them and from them, because he would be more compassionate toward his people, they would be more honoured and exalted through him, and they would be more inclined to respond, since they knew his origin, truthfulness, and trustworthiness. Al-Rabiʿ said: When Abraham made his supplication, it was said to him: "It has been answered for you," and that is at the end of time.

﴿who recites to them Your verses﴾: this clause is in the position of a qualifier of *rasulan*. It is also said that it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from him, since he has already been described by *minhum*. Abraham described the messenger as one who would recite to them the verses of Allah, that is, read them, and so it was. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was given the Qur'an, which is the greatest of miracles. Allah accepted Abraham's supplication and brought the one for whom he prayed with the most perfect of the qualities Abraham had asked for. Here "verses" means the verses of the Qur'an. It is also said that they are the reports of those who passed and the reports of those who will come until the Day of Resurrection. Al-Fadl said: its meaning is that he explains to them their religion.

﴿and teaches them the Book﴾: this is the Qur'an. The meaning is that he makes them understand it and conveys its meanings to them. The order places teaching after recitation, because recitation and pronouncing the Qur'an are what first strike the hearing, and after that its meanings are learned and its implications contemplated. Teaching is ascribed to the Messenger because he is the one who conveys the speech to the learner, who understands it, who gently works to bring the meanings to the learner's understanding, and who causes that to happen. *Al-taʿlim* (teaching) can mean making someone understand and the learner acquiring knowledge, and it can mean supplying the means of knowledge without knowledge necessarily being attained. For this reason it accepts two opposites: you say ʿallamtuhu fa-taʿallama ("I taught him, so he learned") and ʿallamtuhu fa-ma taʿallama ("I taught him, but he did not learn"), because of the difference in the meanings of *taʿallama*.

Al-Zamakhshari said: *yatlu ʿalayhim ayatika* means he reads to them and conveys to them what is revealed to him of the proofs of Your oneness and the truthfulness of Your prophets. *Wa-yuʿallimuhumu al-kitab* means the Qur'an. *Wa-al-hikmah* means the law and the explanation of the rulings. Qatadah said: *al-hikmah* is the Sunnah, and the Prophet's explanation of the laws. Malik and Abu Razin said: *al-hikmah* is understanding of the religion, and the comprehension that is a disposition and a light from Allah, the Exalted. Mujahid said: *al-hikmah* is understanding of the Qur'an. Muqatil said: it is knowledge together with acting upon it; a man is not wise until he combines the two. It is also said: it is judgment and decision. It is also said: it is what can only be known through the Messenger. Ibn Zayd said: every word that admonishes you, or calls you to nobility, or forbids you from ugliness, is *hikmah*. Some said: *al-hikmah* here is the Book, and it is repeated for emphasis. Abu Jaʿfar Muhammad ibn Yaʿqub said: every correct statement that produces a correct action is *hikmah*. Yahya ibn Muʿadh said: *hikmah* is one of the soldiers of Allah, which Allah sends into the hearts of the knowers until it cools them from the heat of this world. It is also said: it is placing things in their proper places. It is also said: it is every saying whose enactment is obligatory. All these statements about *hikmah* are close in meaning, and two statements gather them: one is that it is the Qur'an, and the other that it is the Sunnah, because the Sunnah clarifies what is ambiguous in the Book and manifests the aspects of the rulings.

The meaning, and Allah knows best, of His words *yatlu ʿalayhim ayatika* is that he clarifies its wording for them and, by reciting it, makes them aware of the manner of its recitation, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Ubayy: "Allah has commanded me to recite the Qur'an to you," so that Ubayy might learn from him (ﷺ) the manner of reciting the Qur'an, its pauses and its continuities. In His words *wa-yuʿallimuhumu al-kitab*, that is, he explains to them the aspects of its rulings: its lawful and unlawful, its obligatory and recommended, its admonitions and parables, its encouragements and warnings, the gathering, the scattering, the punishment, the reward, Paradise, and Hell. In His words *wa-al-hikmah*, that is, the Sunnah explains what is general in the Book, clarifies what is ambiguous in the difficult, discloses measures and preparations not addressed by the Book, and establishes rulings not contained in the Book.

﴿and purifies them﴾: inwardly from the filth of polytheism and the impurities of doubt, and outwardly through the obligations that refine sins and bring about blessings. Ibn ʿAbbas said: *al-tazkiyah* is obedience and sincerity. Ibn Juraij said: he purifies them from polytheism. It is also said: he takes from them the zakat, which is a cause of their purification. It is also said: he calls to what makes them pure. It is also said: he testifies for them to their purity, as with the testimony of trustworthy witnesses. The meaning of *zakah* does not go beyond purification or growth.

* *

﴿Indeed You, You are the Mighty, the Wise﴾. *Al-ʿAziz* is the Victorious or the Invincible who cannot be approached, as said by al-Mufaddal ibn Salamah; or the One whom nothing can overpower, as said by Ibn Kaysan; or the One who has no equal, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas; or the Avenger, as said by al-Kalbi; or the Strong, from which comes His words: ﴿so We strengthened [them] with a third﴾ [Yasin: 14]; or the Bestower of might, from which comes His words: ﴿and You bestow might upon whom You will﴾ [Aal ʿImran: 26]. *Al-Hakim* (the Wise): the explanation of *al-Hakim* has already been given in the story of the angels and Adam, in His words: ﴿Except what You have taught us. Indeed You, You are the Knowing, the Wise﴾ [al-Baqarah: 32]. As for *anta* ("You") here, what was permissible in ﴿You are the Hearing, the Knowing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 127] earlier of the grammatical analyses (*iʿrab*, grammatical parsing) is permissible here too. These two attributes are fitting to what precedes them, because sending a messenger endowed with the qualities Abraham asked for can only proceed from one characterized by might, which is dominance or strength or having no peer, and by wisdom, which is placing an action in its right place. Thus He places the message with the noblest of His creation and the most honoured of them before Him. Allah knows best where He places His messages. The attribute *al-ʿAziz* is placed before *al-Hakim* because the former is an attribute of the Essence while the latter is an attribute of the Acts, and because *al-Hakim* is a closing word (*fasilah*) like the closing words before it.

In al-Muntakhab: *yatlu ʿalayhim ayatika* means the verses are the Qur'an. It is also said: they are the signs indicating the existence of the Creator and His attributes. The meaning of recitation is reminding them of these, calling them to them, and urging them to believe in them. The wisdom of recitation is that its wording remains upon the tongues, so that it remains preserved from distortion and alteration; that its composition and wording are miraculous; and that its recitation in the prayers and other acts of worship is a kind of worship. Yet the greatest wisdom is the teaching of what it contains of proofs and rulings. Al-Qaffal said: some philosophers defined wisdom as assimilation to God to the extent of human capacity. It is also said that *al-hikmah* refers to the ambiguous verses. It is also said: the Book is the rulings of the laws, and the wisdom is the aspects of the benefits and advantages in them. It is also said: all of these are attributes of the Qur'an: it is verses, it is a Book, and it is wisdom. End of what was summarized from al-Muntakhab.

﴿And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself﴾. It is narrated that ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam invited his two nephews, Salamah and Muhajir, to Islam, and said to them: "You know that Allah said in the Torah: 'I will raise up from the offspring of Ishmael a prophet whose name is Ahmad; whoever believes in him has been guided and has found the right path, and whoever does not believe in him is cursed.'" Salamah then embraced Islam, but Muhajir refused, and Allah revealed this verse. *Man* here is an interrogative noun in the nominative position as a subject (*mubtada'*), and it is an interrogative whose meaning is denial, which is why *illa* ("except") comes after it. The meaning is: no one turns away. Thus the meaning is general negation. *Man safiha* ("one who makes a fool of himself") is in the nominative position as a substitute (*badal*) for the concealed pronoun in *yarghabu* ("turns away"). It may also be in the accusative position as an exception (*istithna'*). The nominative is preferable as a substitute, because it is an exception after a negative clause that is not affirmative. The *man* in *man safiha* is a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*). It is also said it is an indefinite antecedent with a qualifying clause (*nakirah mawsufah*). The accusative of *nafsahu* ("himself") is, according to some Kufans, namely al-Farra', a specifier (*tamyiz*, accusative of specification), or it is something resembling the object according to some others, or it is a direct object (*maf'ul bihi*), either because *safiha* is transitive by itself like the doubled *saffaha*, or because the verb has absorbed the meaning of a verb that takes an object, namely *jahila* ("was ignorant of"), which is the view of al-Zajjaj and Ibn Jinni, or *ahlaka* ("destroyed"), which is the view of Abu ʿUbaydah, or because the preposition has been dropped, which is the view of some Basrans, or as an emphatic (*tawkid*) for an emphasized noun that is omitted, the estimated form being *safiha qawluhu nafsahu* ("his statement made a fool of himself"), reported by Makki.

As for the specifier, the Basrans do not permit it, because it is definite, and their condition for a specifier is that it be indefinite. As for it being like the object, that according to the majority is restricted to the adjective and is not permitted with the verb. You say: *Zayd hasan al-wajh* ("Zayd is good-looking"), and you do not say *hassana al-wajh* or *yuhsinu al-wajh*. As for dropping the preposition, whose original form is *man safiha fi nafsihi* ("one who makes a fool of himself"), this is not a regular rule. As for it being an emphatic with its emphasized noun omitted, there is disagreement about it; some have affirmed that this is not permissible, namely that the emphasized noun be omitted while the emphatic remains. As for absorption of meaning, this is not regular. As for taking it as a direct object with the verb transitive by itself, this is what we prefer, because Tha'lab and al-Mubarrad reported that *safiha* with a kasra on the fa' is transitive, like *saffaha* with a fatha on the fa' and a shadda. It is reported from Abu al-Khattab that this is a dialect. Al-Zamakhshari said: *saffaha nafsahu* means he degraded it and treated it lightly, and the root meaning of *safah* is lightness, from which comes *zimam safih* ("a loose rein"). It is also said that the accusative of *nafs* is a specifier, like *ghubina ra'yahu* ("his opinion was defrauded") and *alima ra'suhu* ("his head ached"). It may also be a rare definite specifier, like the verse:

*"Nor to the Fazarah, the men with hairy necks,
With humped backs, having no hump."*

It is also said that the meaning is *safiha fi nafsihi* and the preposition was dropped, like the expression *Zayd zanni muqim* ("Zayd is my assumption resident"), meaning "in my assumption." The first view is preferable, and sufficient as evidence for it is what came in the hadith: "Pride is to disdain the truth and to belittle people." End of his words. He thus permitted its accusative as a direct object. However, his statement "It may be a rare definite specifier, like the verse" is not correct, because *al-riqab* ("necks") falls under the category of the object of an adjective in the form of the attributive adjective (*sifah mushabbahah*). *Al-shuʿr* is the plural of *ashʿar* ("hairy"), and likewise *ajabb al-zahr* ("with a humped back") is also of the form of the attributive adjective, and *ajabb* is a noun of the pattern *afʿal*, not a verb. Before the first half of the verse is the line: *"So my people are not with Tha'labah ibn Sa'da,"* and before the second half is the line: *"And we take after him by the tail of life."* Neither of these is comparable to it, because *nafsahu* in the accusative came after a verb, whereas *al-riqab* and *al-zahr* came in the accusative after a noun, and both are of the form of the attributive adjective. The meaning of the verse is that he does not hold himself in low regard or lift himself above the way of Abraham, who is the prophet whose love is agreed upon by all the sects, except one who humiliates himself and makes himself contemptible.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: the meaning of *safiha nafsahu* is that he lost himself. Abu Rawq said: his opinion was too weak for himself. Yaman said: his opinion became foolish. Al-Kalbi said: he killed himself. Ibn Bahr said: he was ignorant of it and did not know what proofs it contains. It is reported from some that the meaning is: he was ignorant of the truth of himself. As for *safuha* with a damma on the fa', its meaning is: he became foolish, (p-395) like *faqiha* when he became a jurist. He said: [the poem follows; the text breaks off here]

The Knowing one has no knowledge when he is ignorant, * and there is no right guidance when the forbearing one acts foolishly.

﴿And We indeed chose him in this world﴾: that is, We made him pure from impurities. His being chosen includes his receiving the message, his being taken as a close friend (khullah), the words he fulfilled and with which he charged his descendants, the building of the House, his leadership (imamah), taking his station as a place of prayer, the purification of the House, his deliverance from the fire of Nimrod, his contemplation of the stars, his proclaiming the pilgrimage, and his being shown the rites of pilgrimage, along with other things that Allah mentioned in His Book of his special qualities and the aspects of his being chosen.

﴿And indeed, in the Hereafter he is among the righteous﴾: Allah, exalted is He, mentioned Ibrahim's honour in both abodes: in this world he was among the chosen elite, and in the Hereafter he is among those attested to be steadfast in goodness. Whoever has this quality, it is obligatory upon everyone not to turn away from his creed (millah). These two sentences are emphasised: the first by the lam (al-lam, the emphatic lam), and the second by inna (inna, the emphatic particle) and the lam. Since this was information about a state that is unseen in the Hereafter, it required greater emphasis, unlike the situation in this world, since the people of the later generations knew of Allah's choosing him in this world through what they witnessed of him and what they transmitted generation after generation. As for his being among the righteous in the Hereafter, this is a matter unseen by them, which requires information from Allah, exalted is He. So Allah informed of it with great emphasis.

"Fi al-akhirah" (in the Hereafter) is connected to a deleted verb that is indicated by what follows it, meaning: "And indeed he is righteous in the Hereafter." Some said: it is governed by an implied "a'ni" (I mean), so it is for specification (al-tabyin), like the expression *kalaka ba'du suqyan* (lit. "to you after, watering," i.e., may you be watered). It was not connected to *al-salihin* (the righteous) because the active participle (ism al-fa'il) is within the relative clause (silah) of the alif-lam (al-alif wa-l-lam, the definite article), and the governed element (ma'mul) of an adjective cannot precede it in that case. Some of our shaykhs permitted this when the governed element was an adverb of time or place (zarf) or a prepositional phrase (jar wa-majrur), saying: "Because in these two, latitude is allowed that is not allowed in others." They also permitted that the alif-lam be not a relative marker but a definite article (ma'rifah), as in *al-rijl* (the man), and that the prepositional phrase be connected to the active participle in that case.

It was said: "fi al-akhirah" means "in the works of the Hereafter," so it is by omitting a construct noun (hadhf mudaf). It was also said: "al-akhirah" here means the barzakh (the intermediate state), and righteousness is the good praise that follows him in this world. It was said: "al-akhirah" is the Day of Resurrection, and this is the most apparent view.

Ibn Abbas said: "among the righteous" means among the prophets. It was said: among those who deserve the good reward; this was the view of al-Hasan. It was also said: those who arrive at the places of His holiness and dwell in the stations of His intimacy.

Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: there is inversion and displacement (taqdim wa-ta'khir) in the speech, the intended meaning being: "And We indeed chose him in this world, and in the Hereafter, and indeed he is among the righteous." This view that he adopted is an error, and the Book of Allah is free from it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 129–130 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Our Lord, and raise up among them a messenger from among them﴾. The last is supported by His words: ﴿It is He who sent among the unlettered ones a messenger from among them﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 2]. There is no disagreement that he is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It is also authentically reported from him that he said: "I am the supplication of my father Abraham." Allah did not send anyone to Makkah and its surroundings except him (ﷺ).

Ibn ʿAbbas said: All the prophets were from the Children of Israel except ten: Noah, Hud, Salih, Shu'ayb, Lot, Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, and Muhammad (ﷺ), and [the tenth is not named in the transmission]. *Minhum* ("from among them") is in the position of a qualifier (*sifah*) of *rasulan* ("a messenger"), meaning: one who is from them and not from others. Thus they know his face, his lineage, and his upbringing, as He said: ﴿Allah certainly conferred favour upon the believers when He sent among them a messenger from among themselves﴾ [Aal ʿImran: 164]. He asked that the messenger be sent among them and from them, because he would be more compassionate toward his people, they would be more honoured and exalted through him, and they would be more inclined to respond, since they knew his origin, truthfulness, and trustworthiness. Al-Rabiʿ said: When Abraham made his supplication, it was said to him: "It has been answered for you," and that is at the end of time.

﴿who recites to them Your verses﴾: this clause is in the position of a qualifier of *rasulan*. It is also said that it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from him, since he has already been described by *minhum*. Abraham described the messenger as one who would recite to them the verses of Allah, that is, read them, and so it was. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was given the Qur'an, which is the greatest of miracles. Allah accepted Abraham's supplication and brought the one for whom he prayed with the most perfect of the qualities Abraham had asked for. Here "verses" means the verses of the Qur'an. It is also said that they are the reports of those who passed and the reports of those who will come until the Day of Resurrection. Al-Fadl said: its meaning is that he explains to them their religion.

﴿and teaches them the Book﴾: this is the Qur'an. The meaning is that he makes them understand it and conveys its meanings to them. The order places teaching after recitation, because recitation and pronouncing the Qur'an are what first strike the hearing, and after that its meanings are learned and its implications contemplated. Teaching is ascribed to the Messenger because he is the one who conveys the speech to the learner, who understands it, who gently works to bring the meanings to the learner's understanding, and who causes that to happen. *Al-taʿlim* (teaching) can mean making someone understand and the learner acquiring knowledge, and it can mean supplying the means of knowledge without knowledge necessarily being attained. For this reason it accepts two opposites: you say ʿallamtuhu fa-taʿallama ("I taught him, so he learned") and ʿallamtuhu fa-ma taʿallama ("I taught him, but he did not learn"), because of the difference in the meanings of *taʿallama*.

Al-Zamakhshari said: *yatlu ʿalayhim ayatika* means he reads to them and conveys to them what is revealed to him of the proofs of Your oneness and the truthfulness of Your prophets. *Wa-yuʿallimuhumu al-kitab* means the Qur'an. *Wa-al-hikmah* means the law and the explanation of the rulings. Qatadah said: *al-hikmah* is the Sunnah, and the Prophet's explanation of the laws. Malik and Abu Razin said: *al-hikmah* is understanding of the religion, and the comprehension that is a disposition and a light from Allah, the Exalted. Mujahid said: *al-hikmah* is understanding of the Qur'an. Muqatil said: it is knowledge together with acting upon it; a man is not wise until he combines the two. It is also said: it is judgment and decision. It is also said: it is what can only be known through the Messenger. Ibn Zayd said: every word that admonishes you, or calls you to nobility, or forbids you from ugliness, is *hikmah*. Some said: *al-hikmah* here is the Book, and it is repeated for emphasis. Abu Jaʿfar Muhammad ibn Yaʿqub said: every correct statement that produces a correct action is *hikmah*. Yahya ibn Muʿadh said: *hikmah* is one of the soldiers of Allah, which Allah sends into the hearts of the knowers until it cools them from the heat of this world. It is also said: it is placing things in their proper places. It is also said: it is every saying whose enactment is obligatory. All these statements about *hikmah* are close in meaning, and two statements gather them: one is that it is the Qur'an, and the other that it is the Sunnah, because the Sunnah clarifies what is ambiguous in the Book and manifests the aspects of the rulings.

The meaning, and Allah knows best, of His words *yatlu ʿalayhim ayatika* is that he clarifies its wording for them and, by reciting it, makes them aware of the manner of its recitation, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Ubayy: "Allah has commanded me to recite the Qur'an to you," so that Ubayy might learn from him (ﷺ) the manner of reciting the Qur'an, its pauses and its continuities. In His words *wa-yuʿallimuhumu al-kitab*, that is, he explains to them the aspects of its rulings: its lawful and unlawful, its obligatory and recommended, its admonitions and parables, its encouragements and warnings, the gathering, the scattering, the punishment, the reward, Paradise, and Hell. In His words *wa-al-hikmah*, that is, the Sunnah explains what is general in the Book, clarifies what is ambiguous in the difficult, discloses measures and preparations not addressed by the Book, and establishes rulings not contained in the Book.

﴿and purifies them﴾: inwardly from the filth of polytheism and the impurities of doubt, and outwardly through the obligations that refine sins and bring about blessings. Ibn ʿAbbas said: *al-tazkiyah* is obedience and sincerity. Ibn Juraij said: he purifies them from polytheism. It is also said: he takes from them the zakat, which is a cause of their purification. It is also said: he calls to what makes them pure. It is also said: he testifies for them to their purity, as with the testimony of trustworthy witnesses. The meaning of *zakah* does not go beyond purification or growth.

* *

﴿Indeed You, You are the Mighty, the Wise﴾. *Al-ʿAziz* is the Victorious or the Invincible who cannot be approached, as said by al-Mufaddal ibn Salamah; or the One whom nothing can overpower, as said by Ibn Kaysan; or the One who has no equal, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas; or the Avenger, as said by al-Kalbi; or the Strong, from which comes His words: ﴿so We strengthened [them] with a third﴾ [Yasin: 14]; or the Bestower of might, from which comes His words: ﴿and You bestow might upon whom You will﴾ [Aal ʿImran: 26]. *Al-Hakim* (the Wise): the explanation of *al-Hakim* has already been given in the story of the angels and Adam, in His words: ﴿Except what You have taught us. Indeed You, You are the Knowing, the Wise﴾ [al-Baqarah: 32]. As for *anta* ("You") here, what was permissible in ﴿You are the Hearing, the Knowing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 127] earlier of the grammatical analyses (*iʿrab*, grammatical parsing) is permissible here too. These two attributes are fitting to what precedes them, because sending a messenger endowed with the qualities Abraham asked for can only proceed from one characterized by might, which is dominance or strength or having no peer, and by wisdom, which is placing an action in its right place. Thus He places the message with the noblest of His creation and the most honoured of them before Him. Allah knows best where He places His messages. The attribute *al-ʿAziz* is placed before *al-Hakim* because the former is an attribute of the Essence while the latter is an attribute of the Acts, and because *al-Hakim* is a closing word (*fasilah*) like the closing words before it.

In al-Muntakhab: *yatlu ʿalayhim ayatika* means the verses are the Qur'an. It is also said: they are the signs indicating the existence of the Creator and His attributes. The meaning of recitation is reminding them of these, calling them to them, and urging them to believe in them. The wisdom of recitation is that its wording remains upon the tongues, so that it remains preserved from distortion and alteration; that its composition and wording are miraculous; and that its recitation in the prayers and other acts of worship is a kind of worship. Yet the greatest wisdom is the teaching of what it contains of proofs and rulings. Al-Qaffal said: some philosophers defined wisdom as assimilation to God to the extent of human capacity. It is also said that *al-hikmah* refers to the ambiguous verses. It is also said: the Book is the rulings of the laws, and the wisdom is the aspects of the benefits and advantages in them. It is also said: all of these are attributes of the Qur'an: it is verses, it is a Book, and it is wisdom. End of what was summarized from al-Muntakhab.

﴿And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself﴾. It is narrated that ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam invited his two nephews, Salamah and Muhajir, to Islam, and said to them: "You know that Allah said in the Torah: 'I will raise up from the offspring of Ishmael a prophet whose name is Ahmad; whoever believes in him has been guided and has found the right path, and whoever does not believe in him is cursed.'" Salamah then embraced Islam, but Muhajir refused, and Allah revealed this verse. *Man* here is an interrogative noun in the nominative position as a subject (*mubtada'*), and it is an interrogative whose meaning is denial, which is why *illa* ("except") comes after it. The meaning is: no one turns away. Thus the meaning is general negation. *Man safiha* ("one who makes a fool of himself") is in the nominative position as a substitute (*badal*) for the concealed pronoun in *yarghabu* ("turns away"). It may also be in the accusative position as an exception (*istithna'*). The nominative is preferable as a substitute, because it is an exception after a negative clause that is not affirmative. The *man* in *man safiha* is a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*). It is also said it is an indefinite antecedent with a qualifying clause (*nakirah mawsufah*). The accusative of *nafsahu* ("himself") is, according to some Kufans, namely al-Farra', a specifier (*tamyiz*, accusative of specification), or it is something resembling the object according to some others, or it is a direct object (*maf'ul bihi*), either because *safiha* is transitive by itself like the doubled *saffaha*, or because the verb has absorbed the meaning of a verb that takes an object, namely *jahila* ("was ignorant of"), which is the view of al-Zajjaj and Ibn Jinni, or *ahlaka* ("destroyed"), which is the view of Abu ʿUbaydah, or because the preposition has been dropped, which is the view of some Basrans, or as an emphatic (*tawkid*) for an emphasized noun that is omitted, the estimated form being *safiha qawluhu nafsahu* ("his statement made a fool of himself"), reported by Makki.

As for the specifier, the Basrans do not permit it, because it is definite, and their condition for a specifier is that it be indefinite. As for it being like the object, that according to the majority is restricted to the adjective and is not permitted with the verb. You say: *Zayd hasan al-wajh* ("Zayd is good-looking"), and you do not say *hassana al-wajh* or *yuhsinu al-wajh*. As for dropping the preposition, whose original form is *man safiha fi nafsihi* ("one who makes a fool of himself"), this is not a regular rule. As for it being an emphatic with its emphasized noun omitted, there is disagreement about it; some have affirmed that this is not permissible, namely that the emphasized noun be omitted while the emphatic remains. As for absorption of meaning, this is not regular. As for taking it as a direct object with the verb transitive by itself, this is what we prefer, because Tha'lab and al-Mubarrad reported that *safiha* with a kasra on the fa' is transitive, like *saffaha* with a fatha on the fa' and a shadda. It is reported from Abu al-Khattab that this is a dialect. Al-Zamakhshari said: *saffaha nafsahu* means he degraded it and treated it lightly, and the root meaning of *safah* is lightness, from which comes *zimam safih* ("a loose rein"). It is also said that the accusative of *nafs* is a specifier, like *ghubina ra'yahu* ("his opinion was defrauded") and *alima ra'suhu* ("his head ached"). It may also be a rare definite specifier, like the verse:

*"Nor to the Fazarah, the men with hairy necks,
With humped backs, having no hump."*

It is also said that the meaning is *safiha fi nafsihi* and the preposition was dropped, like the expression *Zayd zanni muqim* ("Zayd is my assumption resident"), meaning "in my assumption." The first view is preferable, and sufficient as evidence for it is what came in the hadith: "Pride is to disdain the truth and to belittle people." End of his words. He thus permitted its accusative as a direct object. However, his statement "It may be a rare definite specifier, like the verse" is not correct, because *al-riqab* ("necks") falls under the category of the object of an adjective in the form of the attributive adjective (*sifah mushabbahah*). *Al-shuʿr* is the plural of *ashʿar* ("hairy"), and likewise *ajabb al-zahr* ("with a humped back") is also of the form of the attributive adjective, and *ajabb* is a noun of the pattern *afʿal*, not a verb. Before the first half of the verse is the line: *"So my people are not with Tha'labah ibn Sa'da,"* and before the second half is the line: *"And we take after him by the tail of life."* Neither of these is comparable to it, because *nafsahu* in the accusative came after a verb, whereas *al-riqab* and *al-zahr* came in the accusative after a noun, and both are of the form of the attributive adjective. The meaning of the verse is that he does not hold himself in low regard or lift himself above the way of Abraham, who is the prophet whose love is agreed upon by all the sects, except one who humiliates himself and makes himself contemptible.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: the meaning of *safiha nafsahu* is that he lost himself. Abu Rawq said: his opinion was too weak for himself. Yaman said: his opinion became foolish. Al-Kalbi said: he killed himself. Ibn Bahr said: he was ignorant of it and did not know what proofs it contains. It is reported from some that the meaning is: he was ignorant of the truth of himself. As for *safuha* with a damma on the fa', its meaning is: he became foolish, (p-395) like *faqiha* when he became a jurist. He said: [the poem follows; the text breaks off here]

The Knowing one has no knowledge when he is ignorant, * and there is no right guidance when the forbearing one acts foolishly.

﴿And We indeed chose him in this world﴾: that is, We made him pure from impurities. His being chosen includes his receiving the message, his being taken as a close friend (khullah), the words he fulfilled and with which he charged his descendants, the building of the House, his leadership (imamah), taking his station as a place of prayer, the purification of the House, his deliverance from the fire of Nimrod, his contemplation of the stars, his proclaiming the pilgrimage, and his being shown the rites of pilgrimage, along with other things that Allah mentioned in His Book of his special qualities and the aspects of his being chosen.

﴿And indeed, in the Hereafter he is among the righteous﴾: Allah, exalted is He, mentioned Ibrahim's honour in both abodes: in this world he was among the chosen elite, and in the Hereafter he is among those attested to be steadfast in goodness. Whoever has this quality, it is obligatory upon everyone not to turn away from his creed (millah). These two sentences are emphasised: the first by the lam (al-lam, the emphatic lam), and the second by inna (inna, the emphatic particle) and the lam. Since this was information about a state that is unseen in the Hereafter, it required greater emphasis, unlike the situation in this world, since the people of the later generations knew of Allah's choosing him in this world through what they witnessed of him and what they transmitted generation after generation. As for his being among the righteous in the Hereafter, this is a matter unseen by them, which requires information from Allah, exalted is He. So Allah informed of it with great emphasis.

"Fi al-akhirah" (in the Hereafter) is connected to a deleted verb that is indicated by what follows it, meaning: "And indeed he is righteous in the Hereafter." Some said: it is governed by an implied "a'ni" (I mean), so it is for specification (al-tabyin), like the expression *kalaka ba'du suqyan* (lit. "to you after, watering," i.e., may you be watered).
