It was not connected to *al-salihin* (the righteous) because the active participle (ism al-fa'il) is within the relative clause (silah) of the alif-lam (al-alif wa-l-lam, the definite article), and the governed element (ma'mul) of an adjective cannot precede it in that case. Some of our shaykhs permitted this when the governed element was an adverb of time or place (zarf) or a prepositional phrase (jar wa-majrur), saying: "Because in these two, latitude is allowed that is not allowed in others." They also permitted that the alif-lam be not a relative marker but a definite article (ma'rifah), as in *al-rijl* (the man), and that the prepositional phrase be connected to the active participle in that case.

It was said: "fi al-akhirah" means "in the works of the Hereafter," so it is by omitting a construct noun (hadhf mudaf). It was also said: "al-akhirah" here means the barzakh (the intermediate state), and righteousness is the good praise that follows him in this world. It was said: "al-akhirah" is the Day of Resurrection, and this is the most apparent view.

Ibn Abbas said: "among the righteous" means among the prophets. It was said: among those who deserve the good reward; this was the view of al-Hasan. It was also said: those who arrive at the places of His holiness and dwell in the stations of His intimacy.

Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: there is inversion and displacement (taqdim wa-ta'khir) in the speech, the intended meaning being: "And We indeed chose him in this world, and in the Hereafter, and indeed he is among the righteous." This view that he adopted is an error, and the Book of Allah is free from it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 131:

﴿When his Lord said to him, "Submit," he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds."﴾ This is an instance of *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person). Had it continued in the preceding style, it would have read: "When We said to him, 'Submit.'" The reverse, a shift from the second person to the third, is found in the poet's words:

؎باتَتْ تَشَكّى إلَيَّ النَّفْسُ مُجْهِشَةً وقَدْ حَمَلْتُكِ سَبْعًا بَعْدَ سَبْعِينا

*"The soul spent the night complaining to me in distress, though I had carried you seven and after seven and seventy."*

The governing verb of *idh* (when) is "he said, 'I have submitted.'" It has also been said that it is governed by "We indeed chose him," meaning "We chose him at that time." Some have allowed that it is a substitute (*badal*) for "in this world." One who made "idh qala" a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of "We indeed chose him," and made the governing element of the *hal* "We chose him," went too far. It has also been said that the governing element is a deleted verb whose implied meaning is "remember." On the assumption that the governing element is "We chose him," or the implied "remember," the words "he said, 'I have submitted'" do not connect with what precedes them, unless it is supposed that the conjunction has been deleted, or that the clause serves as the answer to an implied statement, meaning: "What was his answer? He said, 'I have submitted.'" 

Is the word *qala* (said) here in its literal sense, so that it entails a revelation from God and a demand, or is it a metaphor (*kinaya*) for what God placed in his nature of the proofs leading to Divine Unity and to the law of Islam? In the latter case the "proof" is treated figuratively as if it were speech. If *qala* is taken literally, scholars have disagreed about when this was said to him. Most hold that it was said to him before prophethood and before puberty, at the time when he reasoned from the star, the moon, and the sun, perceived in them signs of having been created, and realized that they depended on a governor who differs from them in their corporeality (p-396) and in the signs of createdness. When he recognized his Lord, God said to him: "Submit." It has also been said that it occurred after prophethood, and that the command to submit is interpreted as a command to persevere and remain constant, since he was already adorned with it at the time of the command, and that "submission" here retains its usual sense, meaning submission to the law of Islam. 

It has also been said that "submission" here is not in its well-known sense, and it has been interpreted in several ways. ʿAtaʾ said: its meaning is "surrender yourself." al-Kalbi and Ibn Kaysan said: "make your religion sincere (for God)." It has also been said: "be humble and submissive before God." It has been said: "act with the limbs," because faith is a quality of the heart, while submission is a quality of the limbs. Since he was a believer in his heart, he was then charged with the work of the limbs. In his words "he submitted," there is an implied element, meaning: "submit to your Lord." He answered that he submitted to the Lord of the worlds, which includes that he submitted to his own Lord, since he is one of the individuals of the general category. There is in generality a grandeur that is not found in particularity. For this reason he departed from saying "I have submitted to my Lord." Whoever is Lord of the worlds deserves that all of them be submitting to him and obedient to him.

These noble verses also contain, at the outset, the stories of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). First He mentioned his being tested with the words, his fulfilling them, and his deserving the imamate over all people of his time because of this. Then came Ibrahim's request for the imamate for his descendants, out of compassion for them and love for them, and from his preference that among his descendants there be one who would succeed him in the imamate. God answered him that His covenant does not reach the wrongdoers, and implicit in this is that one who is just may attain it. At the beginning of the stories of Ibrahim, his sons and descendants were mentioned, among the Children of Israel and others, to show his excellence and special status with God Most High, so that this would move them to follow him. For when a person has a father endowed with the qualities of perfection, his son is likely to follow him and take his path, because human nature inclines to follow fathers and trace their footsteps. Do you not see His words: ﴿Indeed we found our fathers upon a religion﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 22]?

Then God Most High mentioned the nobility of the Sacred House, and that He made it a destination for people who come toward it, and a refuge in which they are secure. He commanded people to take the Station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer, so that they would follow his example, by making his station a place of worship and a locus of answered supplication. Then He mentioned His covenant with Ibrahim and Ismaʿil to purify the House, since it became a place of worship for God Most High. A place of worship of God must be purified of filth and impurities. By purifying the place, He pointed to purifying the state of the one present in it, outwardly and inwardly, and to purifying what takes place in it of worship, through sincerity toward God Most High, so that it is not defiled by any show-off (riya'). Rather, it is purified by sincerity of it to God Most High. Then He pointed to those for whose sake the House was purified, namely those who circumambulate, those who remain in seclusion, and those who pray. Thus He drew attention to these acts of worship that take place in the House, and indicated that the House is not suitable for any worldly affairs, such as buying and selling, practicing crafts and trades, or disputes, and that it was prepared only for the performance of acts of worship in it. 

Then He mentioned Ibrahim's supplication to his Lord to make this House a place of safety, and his supplication for its people for abundance and provision, and the restriction of that supplication to believers, since safety and abundance are two causes for the flourishing of this House and for people's resorting to it. Then God Most High informed that whoever disbelieves, his enjoyment is little and his destination is the Fire, so that the warning would move one to adhere to faith and submission to acts of obedience. It also shows that provision in this world is not reserved for those who believe; rather, God's provision is shared by the righteous and the wicked. Then He mentioned Ibrahim and Ismaʿil raising the foundations of the House, and what they supplicated at that time: asking that their work be accepted, that they remain steadfast in Islam, that their descendants be Muslims, that the rites be shown to them, that they be forgiven, and that a messenger from their community be sent who would guide them to the path of Islam through what is revealed to him from God, and purify them from sins and transgressions. This shows the legitimacy of good supplications when one is engaged in acts of worship and deeds of obedience, that such a time is a likely occasion for answered prayer, and that it is permissible to supplicate for one who is engaged in obedience and for anyone one wishes to supplicate for. He concluded each supplication with what suits what precedes it. There was nothing in this supplication concerning the affairs of this world; rather, all of it was supplication for matters related to religion. This shows that Ibrahim and his son Ismaʿil were not concerned with worldly affairs during the building of this House and the raising of its foundations.

His supplication for safety and abundance has already been mentioned, but it occurred (p-397) after he had completed the House and finished the act of worship of building it and raising its foundations. Then He mentioned Ibrahim's nobility and his obedience to his Lord, his being singled out in his time for the imamate, and his becoming one to be followed. He stated that none turns away from his path except one who has foolishly ruined himself, because he was chosen in this world and is righteous in the Hereafter. He concluded this by his submission to God Most High's command. Thus the beginning of his story is his completing what God charged him with, and its end is his submission to God and his obedience to Him. May God's blessings and peace be upon our Prophet (ﷺ) and upon him.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 132 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Abraham enjoined it upon his sons, and so did Jacob: "O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except as Muslims."﴾ ﴿Or were you witnesses when death came to Jacob, when he said to his sons, "What will you worship after me?" They said, "We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Abraham and Ismail and Isaac, one God, and to Him we are Muslims."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 133] ﴿That is a nation that has passed away. For it is what it earned, and for you is what you have earned, and you will not be asked about what they used to do.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 134] ﴿And they say, "Be Jews or Christians and you will be guided." Say, "Rather, the religion of Abraham, a hanif, and he was not of the polytheists."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 135] ﴿Say, "We have believed in Allah and what has been revealed to us and what was revealed to Abraham and Ismail and Isaac and Jacob and the Tribes, and what was given to Moses and Jesus and what was given to the prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we are Muslims."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 136] ﴿So if they believe in the like of what you have believed, then they are [rightly] guided. But if they turn away, they are only in dissension, and Allah will suffice you against them, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 137] ﴿The baptism of Allah. And who is better than Allah in baptism? And we are worshippers of Him.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 138].

Al-wasiyyah (the bequest) means al-ahd (the covenant). "Wassa banihi" means he made a covenant with them and informed them of what is to be acted upon, accompanied by admonition. Wassa and awsa are two dialectal forms, except that they said the intensive form (wassa, with the doubled letter) indicates emphasis and multiplication.

Ya'qub (Jacob) is a non-Arabic proper name, diptote (mamnu' al-sarf) because of being a proper noun and personal foreignness (al-'ujmah al-shakhsiyyah). Ya'qub is also an Arabic word, meaning the male partridge (dhakar al-qabj), and it is declinable (masruf). Had it been named by this, it would have been declinable. Whoever claims that the prophet Jacob was named Ya'qub because he and his twin brother Esau were twins, so that Esau came out first and then he came out following him ('ya'qubuhu'), or that he was named so because of the abundance of his descendants ('aqib), his statement is corrupt, for if it were so, it would have an Arabic derivation and therefore would have been declinable.

Al-hudur (presence) means al-shuhud (witnessing). From it one says ḥaḍara with a fatḥah on the ʿayn; in the present tense, yaḥḍuru with a ḍammah on both letters. It is also said ḥaḍira with a kasrah on the ʿayn. The regular present form should be with a fatḥah, so it would be yaḥḍaru, but the Arabs dispensed with that by using the present of faʿala with a fatḥah on the ʿayn, saying ḥaḍara yaḥḍuru with ḍammah. These are words in which the Arabs deviated (shadhdhat). The present of faʿila with a kasrah on the ʿayn came to be yafʿulu with ḍammah, as they said niʿma yanʿumu, faḍila yafḍulu, ḥaḍara yaḥḍuru, mitta tamūtu, dumta tadūmu. All of these came with faʿala with fatḥah on the ʿayn, so for this reason they dispensed with its present in place of the present of faʿila, just as they dispensed with yafʿilu with kasrah on the ʿayn in place of yafʿalu with fatḥah. They said ḍalila with kasrah on the ʿayn, taḍillu with kasrah, because it is permissible to say ḍalalta with fatḥah on the ʿayn.

Ishaq (Isaac) is a non-Arabic proper name, diptote because of being a proper noun and personal foreignness. Ishaq is also a verbal noun of asḥaqa. Had it been named by it, it would have been declinable. In the plural they said asāḥiqah and asāḥīq; in the plural of Ya'qub: ya'āqibah and ya'āqīb; in the plural of Isra'il: asārilah. The Kufans permitted for Ibrahim and Ismail: barāhimah and salāmilah (plural forms), the hā' being a replacement for the yā', as in zanādiqah for zanādīq. Abu al-Abbas said: this plural is wrong, because the hamzah is not an added letter; the plural is abārah and asāmi', and it is permissible: abārīh and asāmī'. The proper way is to pluralize these with the sound masculine plural: Ibrahimūn, Ismā'ilūn, Ishaqūn, and Ya'qūbūn. The Kufans also related: barāhim, salāmil, asāḥiq, and ya'āqib, without yā' or hā'. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: Birahim and Isma'il. Abu al-Abbas rejected those who dropped the hamzah, because this is not a place for its addition. Tha'lab permitted: barāh, as it is said in diminutive: buraye'h. Abu Ja'far al-Saffar said: As for Isra'il, we do not know of anyone who permits deleting the hamzah from its beginning; rather it is said asārīl. The Kufans related: asārilah and asāril. End of quotation. The discussion of such plurals has already passed for us, and the transmission has been fully covered here.

Al-ḥanaf (inclination): linguistically it is al-mayl (inclination), and from it al-Ahnaf was named, because of an inclination that was in one of his feet relative to the other. The poet said:
By God, were it not for a crookedness in his leg, there would not be among your children one like him.
Ibn Qutaybah said: al-ḥanaf is uprightness (al-istiqamah), and al-Ahnaf was named by way of optimism, as the one stung (al-ladigh) was named Salim (the safe one). Al-Qaffal said: al-ḥanaf is a title for whoever adheres to Islam, like the other titles of religions. Umar said:
I praised God when He guided my heart to Islam and the upright religion.
Al-Zajjaj said: al-ḥanif is one who inclines away from what the common people are upon toward what he has adhered to, and he recited:
And we were created, when we were created, with our religion being upright (ḥanīf), apart from every religion.

Al-asbāt (the Tribes) is the plural of sibt. Among the Children of Israel they are like the tribes among the Children of Ismail. They are the twelve sons of Jacob, for each of whom there is a nation of people, and their names will come later. They were called this from al-sabat, which is succession, so they are a group in succession. It is said sabata 'alayhi al-'aṭa' when he followed up with the gift. It is also said it is the inverse of basata, and from it come al-subāṭah and al-sābāṭ. It is said of al-Hasan and al-Husayn: "the two grandsons (sibṭā) of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." They were so called for their multitude, their expansion and their dispersal. Then the use of sibṭ became applied to the son of a daughter, so it is said: sibṭ Abi 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr, sibṭ Husayn ibn Mandah, and sibṭ al-Silafi, among the children of their daughters. It was also said: the origin of al-asbāt is from al-sibṭ, which is an intertwined tree, and al-sibṭ is a group returning to one origin.

Al-shiqaq (dissension) is the verbal noun of shāqqahu, as you say ḍāraba ḍirāban and khālafa khilāfan. Its meaning is hostility and opposition. Its root is from al-shiqq, meaning this one is on one side and that one is on another side. Al-shiqq is the side, as the poet said:
When she weeps behind her, she turns toward him on one side and another side, and by us it is not changed.
It was also said it is from al-mashaqqah (hardship), because each of the two is eager for what burdens the other.

Al-kifayah (sufficiency) is al-iḥsab (reckoning/enough). "Kafānī kadhā" means it reckoned enough for me. The poet said:
Even if what I strive for were for a lowly livelihood, a little of wealth would have sufficed me, and I would not have sought more.
That is, a little of wealth made me sufficient.

Al-ṣibghah (the dye/baptism) is a form (fi'lah) from ṣabagha, like jilsah from jalasa. Its origin is the state (hay'ah) in which dyeing occurs. Al-ṣabgh is what is dyed with, and al-ṣabgh as a verbal noun is changing a thing into one of the colors. Its verb is on faʿala with fatḥah on the ʿayn, and its well-known present is yafʿulu with ḍammah, while the analogical form is fatḥah since its final radical is a guttural letter. My teacher Abu al-Abbas Ahmad ibn Yusuf ibn ʿAli al-Fihri, known as al-Laythi, the commentator of al-Faṣīḥ, was reported to me as having mentioned in it the ḍammah, the fatḥah and the kasrah on the bā' in the present tense.

﴿Abraham enjoined it upon his sons, and so did Jacob: "O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you the religion"﴾: Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read awṣā, and the rest read wassā. Tha'lab said: Khalaf ibn Hisham al-Bazzar dictated to me, saying: the codex of the people of Medina and the people of Iraq differed in twelve letters. The people of Medina wrote: awṣā, sāri'ū, yaqūlu, alladhīna āmanū, man yartadid, alladhīna ittakhadhū, masjidan, khayran minhumā, fatawakkal, wa-an yazhara, bimā kasabat aydīkum, mā tashtahīhi al-anfus, fa-inna Allāha al-ghaniyy, and wa-lā yakhāfu 'uqbāhā. And the people of Iraq wrote: wassā, sāri'ū, yaqūlu, man yartadd, alladhīna ittakhadhū, khayran minhā, fatawakkal, an yazhara, fīmā kasabat aydīkum, mā tashtahī, fa-inna Allāha huwa, and fa-lā yakhāfu.

"Bihā" is related to awṣā, and the pronoun refers to the religion (millah) in His saying: "And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham?" [al-Baqarah: 130], and with this al-Zamakhshari began. Al-Mahdawi did not mention anything other than this. Or it refers to the word which is His saying: "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds" [al-Baqarah: 131], and its like, and he made it "a word that remains among his descendants" [az-Zukhruf: 28], since before it came: "Indeed, I am free of what you worship" [az-Zukhruf: 26]. With this view Ibn 'Atiyyah began and said: it is more correct, because it is the nearest thing mentioned. He preferred the reference to the religion because the explicit antecedent is then stated, whereas if it refers to the word it is not explicitly stated, and returning to what is explicitly stated is better than returning to what is implied. Also, its return to the religion is more comprehensive than its return to the word, since the word is part of the religion. It is known that he (Abraham) would only bequeath what is most comprehensive for success and triumph in the Hereafter. It was said: it refers to the nearest subsequent word, which is His saying: "So do not die except as Muslims." It was said: it refers to the word of sincerity, which is: there is no god but Allah, even if no mention of it has preceded; it is pointed to in meaning, since it is the greatest pillar of Islam. It was said: it refers to the bequest indicated by "wassā." It was said: it refers to obedience.

"Banīhi" (his sons): the sons of Abraham, Ismail, whose mother was Hajar the Copt, and Isaac, whose mother was Sarah. Madyan, Madyan (variant), Naqshan, Zamran, Nashaq, and Naqash Surj, were mentioned by the noble genealogist Abu al-Barakat Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Ma'mar al-Husayni al-Jawwani and others. The mother of these six was Qatura bint Yaqtan al-Kan'aniyyah. These eight are his offspring by his own loins, and the remaining line among them is two: Ismail and Isaac, and no others.

The majority read "wa-Ya'qūbu" in the nominative (raf'), while Isma'il ibn 'Abd Allah al-Makki, al-Darir, and 'Amr ibn Fa'id al-Aswari read it in the accusative (nasb). As for the nominative reading, it allows two possibilities. One is that it is coordinated with Ibrahim, and it falls under the ruling of the bequest concerning his sons, meaning: "and Jacob enjoined his sons." The other is that it is nominative as a new sentence (mubtada'), with its predicate omitted, its estimated form being: "He said, O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen," and the first is more evident. As for the accusative reading, it is coordinated with "banīhi," meaning: "and he enjoined with it his grandson Ya'qub," who is the son of his son Isaac. The sons of Jacob, whose names will come up when speaking about the Tribes.

"Yā banī": whoever reads "wa-Ya'qūba" in the accusative, "yā banī" is among the sayings of Abraham. Whoever reads it in the nominative by coordination is the same, or by new sentence, then it is part of Jacob's speech. If we make it part of Abraham's speech, then according to the Basrans it has an implied verb of saying, and according to the Kufans it does not need that, because the bequest has the meaning of saying, so it is as if he said: "Abraham said to his sons, O my sons." A similar example is the saying of the rajiz (rajaz poet):
Two men from Dabba informed us: "Did we see a naked man?"
with the hamzah in kasrah, either by implying the verb of saying, or as an object of "akhbaranā" according to both views. The address is to one present before the speaker. That the address uses the word "sons" with a pronoun attached is an odd gentleness, a delaying of acceptance, and a stirring and shaking, for what is being conveyed to them concerning the matter of dying upon the religion of Islam, which ought to be sought with gentleness. For this reason he began his speech with His saying: "Indeed Allah has chosen for you the religion," and whatever Allah has chosen, the sensible person does not turn away from. Ubayy, 'Abd Allah and al-Dahhak read "anna yā banī," in which case "an" here must be explanatory with the meaning of "ay," and it cannot be verbal (maṣdariyyah), because it is not possible for a verbal noun to be formed from it and what follows it. Whoever does not affirm the explanatory meaning, because he considers it here as extra (zā'idah), these are the Kufans.

﴿Indeed Allah has chosen for you the religion﴾: meaning He singled it out for you and selected for you the purest of religions. The "al-" in "al-dīn" is for prior knowledge (al-'ahd), because they had already known it, and it is the religion of Islam.

Verse 2:132, part 2 of 2:

﴿Do not die except while you are Muslims.﴾ This is an exception concerning states: that is, "except in this state." The meaning is steadfastness upon Islam, and the prohibition is in reality only against their being in a condition contrary to Islam. However, this is a prohibition against death itself. A parallel in command is "Die while you are a martyr" (mut wa anta shahid), which is not a command to die but a command to be martyred; it is as if he said: "Seek martyrdom in the way of Allah," and mention of death is by way of preparing for martyrdom. This statement contains eloquent concision, admonition and reminder, for a person is certain of death but does not know when it will overtake him. So when he is commanded to be in a state in which death will come upon him only, he is constantly mindful of death, since he is constantly commanded to be in that state. This, in truth, is a prohibition against engaging in things that would be a cause of meeting Allah in a state other than Islam. A parallel to this is their saying: "I must not see you here" (laareynaka huna), where the speaker does not forbid himself from seeing, but the meaning is a prohibition against the other's presence in this place, so that he sees him; it is as if he said: "Go away from this place." Do you not see that the addressee has no way to keep the speaker from perceiving him except by leaving that place? He thus conveyed the intended meaning with a expression that indicates anger and disapproval, because a person only forbids what he dislikes occurring.

This sentence includes (p-400) subtle points. Among them: the bequest (wasiyyah), which occurs only at the approach of death. In this there is the concern Abraham had for the matter of religion, to the extent that he bequeathed it to those connected with him, since his sons were upon the religion of Islam. Among them also is his singling out his sons, and he singles out only what secures their final outcome. Among them also is that he included all his sons and did not single out any one of them, as came in the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, when his father gave him a gift and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: "Do you wish that they all be equal to you in kindness?" and he returned the gift to him, saying: "I will not bear witness to injustice." Among them also is the absoluteness of the bequest, for he did not restrict it by time or place. Then he concluded it with the most forceful deterrence: that they should die not as Muslims. Then the preparation for this prohibition and deterrence: that Allah the Exalted is the One who chose Islam for you, so do not depart from what Allah has chosen for you.

The historians said: Abraham brought his son Isma'il to Makkah when he was a suckling infant, and it is said: when he was two years old, and it is said: when he was fourteen years old. Isma'il was born fourteen years before Isaac, and Abraham died at the age of one hundred and thirty. When Abraham died, Isma'il was eighty-nine years old. Isaac lived one hundred and eighty years and died in the Holy Land and was buried beside his father Abraham. The interval between the death of his father Abraham and the birth of Muhammad ﷺ was about two thousand six hundred years, while the Jews reckon it about four hundred years less than that.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 133 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Or were you witnesses when death came to Ya'qub?﴾ It was revealed concerning the Jews. They said: "Do you not know that when Ya'qub died he enjoined his sons to be Jews?" Al-Kalbi said: "When Ya'qub entered Egypt, he saw them worshipping idols and the two luminaries (al-nayyirayn, the sun and the moon). He gathered his sons, fearing this for them, and said to them: 'What will you worship after me?' So Allah revealed this verse, informing His Prophet of what Ya'qub had enjoined, and refuting the Jews." Here *am* (أم) is *munqati'a* (disjunctive, introducing a new topic), carrying the meaning of *bal* (بل, "rather") together with the interrogative hamza that indicates denial. The implied sense is: "Rather, were you witnesses?" The meaning of *idrab* (إضراب, shift) is the transition from one matter to another, not that this cancels what came before. The interrogation here is rebuke and reproach, and it has the sense of negation: "You were not witnesses, so how do you attribute to him what you do not know? Neither you nor your forefathers witnessed it." It has also been said that *am* here means *bal*, and the meaning is "Rather, you were," that is, your forefathers were, or he (the Prophet) was placed in the position of their forefathers, since their forefathers had transmitted that to them. Affirming this is a rebuke to them for what they attributed to Ya'qub of Judaism. The address in *kuntum* (كنتم, "you were") is to those present with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) among the rabbis and chiefs of the Jews and Christians. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "He said to them, by way of confirmation and reproach: 'Were you present with Ya'qub, and did you know what he enjoined, so that you claim it on the basis of knowledge?' That is, you did not witness it; rather, you are inventing." And *am* may have the meaning of the interrogative *alif* (ألف, the interrogative particle) at the beginning of a sentence, a Yemeni dialect usage. End of what he mentioned. I have not found any of the grammarians stating that *am* is used interrogatively at the beginning of a sentence. Where is that? If the transmission is sound, there is no objection to it and no reproach. Al-Tabari related that *am* is used interrogatively in the middle of a speech whose beginning has already preceded, and this verse is an example of that. Among examples is: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ [Yunus: 38]. End of what he said, and this too is a strange view. The result is that *am* here has three views: the best-known is that it is disjunctive here, meaning *bal* and the hamza. The second is that it is only for *idrab*, meaning *bal*. The third is that it means only the interrogative hamza.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The address is to the believers, in the sense: "You did not witness that; rather, you came to know it through revelation." It has also been said that the address is to the Jews, because they used to say: "No prophet died except upon Judaism." But had they witnessed it, and had they heard what he said to his sons, and what they said, it would have become clear to them how eager he was for the religion of Islam, and they would not have claimed Judaism for him. So the verse contradicts their claim; how then can it be said to them: ﴿Or were you witnesses?﴾ But the better view is that *am* is connected (*muttasila*), with some omitted element assumed before it, as if it were said: "Do you claim Judaism for the prophets? Or were you witnesses when death came to Ya'qub?" He means that your early ancestors among the Children of Israel were present with him when he enjoined his sons upon monotheism and the religion of Islam, so why do you claim against the prophets what they are free of? End of his words. In summary: he made *am* connected, and he omitted before it what would balance it. We know of no one who permitted the omission of this construction, nor is it attested in poetry or otherwise. So it is not permitted to say *am Zaydun?* ("or Zayd?") meaning "Did 'Amr stand, or Zayd?" nor *am qama Khalid?* meaning "Did Zayd go out, or did Khalid stand?" The reason omission is not permitted is that the sentence means: "Which of the two matters occurred?" So they are in reality one sentence. The element coordinated with (*al-ma'tuf 'alayh*) is omitted only and the coordinated element remains with *wa* (و, "and") or *fa* (ف, "then") when a clear indication shows it, such as your saying, in reply to someone who said, "Did you not strike Zayd?": *Bala wa-'Amran* ("Yes, and 'Amr"). Similarly His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Strike with your staff the rock﴾ [al-A'raf: 160], "so it burst forth," meaning: "So he struck, and it burst forth." Omitting the coordinated element with *aw* (أو, "or") is rare, as in the poet's words:

"Is there for you, or a father of yours before us?"

He meant: "Is there for you a brother, or a father?" With *hatta* (حتى, "until/even") it is also attested, though with some dispute, in the words:

"O wonder, even Kulayb reviles me!"

That is, "People revile me, even Kulayb." But what is heard in the speech of the Arabs is the omission of the connected *am* with its coordinated element. The poet said:

"Desire called me to it, and I am attentive to its matter, yet I do not know whether its pursuit is right guidance."

He means: "Or is it not right guidance?" It was omitted because the sentence indicates it. This was permitted because the one who asks about an affirmative matter implies its opposite. So the meaning is: "Did Zayd stand, or did he not stand?" For this reason the answer may be *ni'am* (نعم, "yes") or *la* (لا, "no"), and therefore this is permitted in the line in the phrase "is it right guidance, its pursuit?" meaning "or is it not right guidance?" It is also permitted to omit the second of paired opposites when the meaning indicates it. Do you not see His saying: ﴿It protects you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81], where He omitted "and the cold"? 

*Idh hadara* (إذ حضر, "when death came"): the governing element of *idh* (إذ, "when") is *shuhada'* (شهداء, "witnesses"), and this is in the manner of an adverbial of time, not as an object. It is as if it were said: "Present at his speech at the time of the coming of death." He used death as a metonym for its preliminaries, because when death itself arrives, the dying person says nothing. From this is His saying: ﴿Death comes to him from every place, yet he is not dead﴾ [Ibrahim: 17], meaning that its causes and occasions come to him. The poet said:

"Say to them: hasten to make excuses, and seek a word that clears you; I am indeed Death."

In His saying *hadara* (حضر, "came"), there is a strange metaphor: the one who is absent must certainly arrive, and for this reason it is said in supplication: "Make death the best absent one we await."

It has been read as *hadira* (حَضِرَ) with the *dad* vowelled with a kasra, and we have mentioned that this is a dialect form, and that its present tense with a *dammah* on the *dad* is anomalous. The object is placed first here for emphasis (*al-i'tina'*).

*Idh qala li-baniyhi* (إذ قال لبنيه, "when he said to his sons"): *idh* is a *badal* (بدل, substitution) from *idh* in His saying *idh hadara*. The governing element for it is either *shuhada'*, which governs the first *idh*, according to the view of those who hold that the governing element of the substitute is the governing element of the substituted, or *shuhada'* is repeated, according to the view of those who hold that the substitution is by repetition of the governing element. Al-Qaffal claimed that *idha* is a time for the presence, so the governing element is *hadara*, and this amounts to the unity of the two temporal adverbs, even if their governing elements differ.

*Ma ta'buduna min ba'di* (ما تعبدون من بعدي, "What will you worship after me?"): *ma* (ما) is interrogative about what does not reason, and it is a complete noun in the accusative, governed by the verb after it. According to the view that *ma* is generic for everything, it here applies to both rational and non-rational beings, since human beings, angels, the sun, the moon, some stars, and carved idols have been worshipped. As for those who hold that *ma* is restricted to non-rational beings, it has been said that the question is about the attribute of the one worshipped, since *ma* is used to ask about attributes: you say *ma Zayd, afaqih am sha'ir?* ("What is Zayd, a jurist or a poet?"). It has also been said that he used *ma* because the commonly worshipped objects of that time were inanimate, such as idols, fire, the sun, and stones, so he asked with *ma*, the particle used for what does not reason. His sons understood him and answered: "We do not worship any of these." It has also been said that he asked with *ma* about the one worshipped as a test for them, and did not say *man* (من, "who"), so that they would not be led to guidance; he only wanted to test them and see whether they would hold firm to what they were upon. The apparent sense is that he asked about what they worship, that is, the prescribed worship? Al-Qaffal said: he called them not to seek anything in their deeds other than the face of Allah, Exalted is He. He did not fear that they would be occupied with worshipping idols; he feared that their worldly affairs would occupy them. In this is evidence that the compassion of the prophets, upon them be prayers and peace, toward their children was within the domain of religion, and their concern was directed toward that.

*Min ba'di* (من بعدي, "after me"): he means after my death. It is reported that Ya'qub, peace be upon him, when he was given the choice, as prophets are given the choice, chose death, and said: "Give me time until I enjoin my sons and my family," and he gathered them and said these words to them.

﴿They said: We shall worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq﴾: this is the reading of the majority. Ubayy read: "and the God of Ibrahim," omitting *aba'ika* (آبائك, "your fathers"). Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Ibn Ya'mar, al-Jahdari, and Abu Raja' read: "and the God of your father" (*wa-ilaha abika*). As for the reading of the majority, Ibrahim and what follows it are a *badal* (substitution) from *aba'ika*, or an *'atf bayan* (explanatory apposition). When it is a substitution, it is a detailed substitution (*badal tafsili*), and if it were read with a break (in the sense of *qat'*, making them separate in case), that would be permitted. Al-Mahdawi permitted that Ibrahim and what follows it be in the accusative by an implied *a'ni* ("I mean"). In this is evidence that the paternal uncle is also called "father," and it has come in the case of al-'Abbas: "This is the remnant of my fathers," and "Return my father to me," and "I am the son of the two sacrificed ones," according to the well-known view that the one sacrificed was Ishaq. In this is evidence that the grandfather is called "father," by His saying: ﴿and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim﴾, and Ibrahim was the grandfather of Ya'qub. Ibn 'Abbas used this, together with His saying: ﴿and I followed the religion of my fathers, Ibrahim and Ishaq and Ya'qub﴾ [Yusuf: 38], as evidence for the inheritance of the grandfather to the exclusion of the brothers, and for placing him in the position of the father in inheritance when the father is absent, and that his ruling and the father's ruling regarding inheritance should not differ when there is no father. This is the view of al-Siddiq (Abu Bakr) and a group of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all, and it is the view of Abu Hanifa. Zayd ibn Thabit said: he is in the position of the brothers, so long as sharing does not reduce him below a third, in which case he receives a third and nothing is reduced from him; this is the view of Malik, Abu Yusuf, and al-Shafi'i. Ali said: he is in the position of one of the brothers, so long as sharing does not reduce him below a sixth, in which case he receives a sixth and nothing is reduced from him; this is the view of Ibn Abi Layla. The proofs for these views are in the books of jurisprudence. As for the reading of Ubayy, it is clear. As for the reading of Ibn 'Abbas and those mentioned with him, the apparent sense is that the word *abika* is intended in the singular, and Ibrahim is a substitution from it or an explanatory apposition. It has been said that it is a plural from which the *nun* was dropped because of the annexation (*idafa*): *ab* has been pluralized as *abin* in the accusative and genitive and *abun* in the nominative. Sibawayh reported this, and the poet said:

"When they recognized our voices, they wept, and we ransomed them with our fathers."

On this view, the i'rab (إعراب, grammatical inflection) of Ibrahim is like its inflection when it is a broken plural.

In their answering him by expressing the verb (*izhar al-fi'l*) there is emphasis on what they answered, since it was permissible to say: "They said: your God," so their explicit statement of the verb is an emphasis in the answer that it corresponds to the question, namely in the governing element pronounced in the question. The annexation of God to Ya'qub is evidence that the object of worship of the questioner and the answerer is one in words. In His saying: (and the God of your fathers) is evidence that the object of worship is also one in terms of wording. The word *wa-ilaha* was repeated only because it is not correct to coordinate with a pronominal suffix in the genitive without repeating its governing preposition, except in poetry, or according to the view of one who permits it, which is rare in his view. If the coordinated element were a noun, omitting the preposition would be preferable to repeating it, because repeating it would imply difference, whereas omitting it indicates unity. He began first with annexing God to Ya'qub, because he was the questioner. He placed Ibrahim first because he is the origin. He placed Isma'il before Ishaq because he was older or more excellent, given that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was among his descendants and in the main line of his lineage. He limited the mention to these, because they were the best of people in their times, and he did not generalize, because people had many other objects of worship besides Allah.

﴿One God﴾ (*ilahan wahidan*): it may be a substitution, a substitution of an indefinite qualified noun from a definite one, and it may be a circumstantial accusative (*hal*), and it would be a *hal muwatti'a* (preparatory circumstantial), like your saying: "I saw you a righteous man." The intention is only the description, and the proper noun is brought as a preparation for the description. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be in the accusative by specification (*ikhtisas*), meaning: "We intend by your God one God." But the grammarians have stated that what is in the accusative by specification cannot be indefinite or ambiguous. The benefit of this circumstantial element or substitution is to state explicitly that their object of worship is one, a single unit, since the annexation of a thing to many may suggest the multiplicity of that annexed thing, so this circumstantial element or substitution serves to remove that suggestion.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 133 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And We are submitting to Him﴾: That is, We are obedient to Him. He mentioned the answer with the verb "we worship" (na'budu), because worship is continuous and constantly renewed. He stated this nominal clause, whose predicate is the active participle (ism al-fa'il), which indicates permanence, because submission (al-inqiyad) is something they never cease to have, and worship arises from it. So His saying ﴿And We are submitting to Him﴾ is one of the two parts of the answer. Thus they answered him with two things: the first is what he asked about, and the second confirms what they had answered, so this is from the category of the answer that reinforces the question. Some scholars permitted that the clause be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "na'budu," but the first view is more eloquent, namely that the clause is conjoined to His saying "na'budu," so it is one of the two halves of the answer. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be a parenthetical clause (jumla i'tiradiyya) that emphasizes, meaning: "And it is part of our state that We are submitting to Him, sincere in monotheism, or submissive." What the grammarians have stated is that the parenthetical clause (al-jumla al-i'tiradiyya) is the clause that provides reinforcement between the two parts of a relative pronoun and its relative clause, like the saying:

> "What then — and there is no blame in what is decreed — I have sought, whether it misses you with success or with loss and misguidance"

(p-404) (And he said):

> "That is the one, by your father, who knows Malik, and truth repels the nonsense of falsehood"

Or between the two parts of a predication, like His saying:

> "Misfortunes have already overtaken me, many as they are, the spear-points of a people who are neither weak nor unarmed"

Or between a conditional verb and its response, or between an oath and its answer, or between a noun modified and its adjective, or whatever is similar to that, of which there is some mutual implication. This clause, which is His saying ﴿And We are submitting to Him﴾, is not from this category, because before it there is an independent statement and after it there is an independent statement, which is His saying ﴿That is a community that has passed away﴾ [al-Baqarah: 134]. It cannot be said that between the referent and what is predicated of it there is a mutual implication by which the clause could be parenthetical, because what precedes it is the speech of the children of Ya'qub, which God related from them, and what follows it is the speech of God Most High, who informed about them what He informed. The parenthetical clause that falls between two mutually implying elements can only come from the speaker of the two mutually implying elements, by which he emphasizes and strengthens what his speech contains. From all of this it becomes clear that His saying ﴿And We are submitting to Him﴾ is not a parenthetical clause.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: ﴿And We are submitting to Him﴾ is a subject and predicate, meaning: "Thus We were, and thus We shall be." It may be in the position of a circumstantial clause, and the governing element is "na'budu." The first interpretation is more praiseworthy. End of his words. It appears from this that he made the clause conjoined to an omitted clause, which is his saying "Thus We were." There is no need to burden oneself with this implied elision, because it is correct to conjoin it to "na'budu ilahaka" (we worship your God), as we mentioned and established before. Whenever it is possible to interpret the speech without an elision while the meaning remains sound, that is preferable to interpreting it with an elision.

In al-Muntakhab (a summary, ministering to the summary we noted) it is said: The advocates of imitation (al-muqallida) held onto this verse and said: The children of Ya'qub were content with imitation, and he did not object to them about it, which indicates that imitation is sufficient. The Ta'limiyya (the school that holds that knowledge of God comes only through instruction) also cited it as evidence and said: There is no way to know God Most High except through instruction from the Messenger and the Imam, for they did not say, "We worship the God whom reason indicates," but rather said: "We worship only the One whom you worship and your fathers worshipped," and this indicates that the method of knowing is learning. But what they went to has no proof in the verse, because the verse contains only the affirmation of worship of God. The affirmation of worship for God does not indicate that this arises from imitation or instruction, nor that it also arises from reasoning by the intellect, so their use of the verse as evidence is invalid. The verse did not address rational inference only because it did not come in that context, since he asked them only about what they would worship after his death, so they referred him to their object of worship and the object of worship of their fathers, namely God Most High. That was more concise in speech than explaining His attributes, such as oneness, knowledge, power and other attributes, and closer to calming the soul of Ya'qub. It is as if they said: "We only follow your way." It may be said that in His saying ﴿We worship your God and the God of your fathers﴾ there is an allusion to rational inference for the existence of the Creator, because it was previously stated at the beginning of the surah: ﴿O people, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21]. So their meaning here by their saying ﴿We worship your God and the God of your fathers﴾ is the God whose existence is indicated by the existence of your fathers, and this is an allusion to inference.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 134:

﴿That was a nation that has passed away﴾. "That" refers to Ibrahim, Ya'qub and their descendants. The meaning of "passed away" (khalat) is that they died, ended, and went to the khala' (the desolate land, the place with no one to keep company). The addressees are the Jews and Christians who claimed for Ibrahim and his sons Judaism and Christianity. The clause "qad khalat" is a description (sifah) of "ummah."

﴿To them is what they earned, and to you is what you have earned﴾: That is, that nation is singled out for the recompense of what it earned, just as you are likewise singled out for the recompense of what you earned of good and evil. No one benefits from the earnings of another. The apparent reading of "ma" is that it is a relative pronoun (mawsulah) with the returning pronoun omitted, i.e., "what it earned." They also permitted that "ma" be a verbal noun (masdariyyah), i.e., "its earning," and likewise the "ma" in His words ﴿and to you is what you have earned﴾. It is also permissible that the clause "laha ma kasabat" be a new independent sentence (isti'naf), and it is permissible that it be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "khalat," meaning "having passed away, established and fixed, to them is what they earned." The first is more evident, because the phrase "wa lakum ma kasabtum" is conjoined (ma'tuf) to "laha ma kasabat." It is not valid for "wa lakum ma kasabtum" to be conjoined to the circumstantial clause before it, because the time of the establishment of their earning for them differs from the time of the establishment of the earning of the addressees, and conjoining a circumstance to a circumstance requires the unity of time. They boasted of their forefathers, so they were informed that no one benefits anyone, whether earlier or later. It is narrated: "O children of Hashim, people will not come to me with their deeds while you come to me with your lineages; O Fatimah, I will not avail you anything before Allah." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: In this verse there is a refutation of the Jabriyyah, who say: there is no acquisition (iktisab) for the servant. End of quote.

This is a question discussed in the principles of the religion (usul al-din), and it is one of the difficult questions, and the doctrines of the people of Islam concerning it are four. The first: the view of the Jabriyyah (determinists), which is that the servant is compelled in his action, that he has no choice in that, but is forced to it, and that the attribution of the act to him is like the attribution of the movement of a branch to it when a mover moves it. The second: the view of the Qadariyyah, which is that they are not compelled in the act, but they have power to bring the act into existence. The third: the view of the Mu'tazilah, that the servant has a power which Allah creates for him before the act, and he is able to perform it or not perform it. The fourth: the doctrine of the Ahl al-Sunnah wa'l-Jama'ah, that Allah creates for the servant an enablement (tamkin) and power together with the act, by which he does good and evil, not by way of compulsion and forcing; and this enablement is the basis of moral responsibility (taklif), upon which punishment and reward are based. Then, after their agreement on this principle, they differed in its explanation into three interpretations. The first: the saying of Abu'l-Hasan (al-Ash'ari): that power is an attribute related to the object of power without any effect on the object, rather the power and its object both come about by the creation of Allah; but the thing that comes about by the creation of Allah, which is the object of the originated power, is the acquisition (kasb). The second: the saying of al-Baqillani: that the act's essence does not by itself acquire the attribute of being obedience or disobedience, rather this attribute comes to it through the originated power. The third: the saying of Abu Ishaq al-Isfara'ini: that the eternal and the originated powers, when they relate to one object, take effect through both together, so that the servant's act is brought about with assistance, and this is the acquisition.

﴿And you will not be asked about what they used to do﴾: a clause emphasizing what precedes it, because He has informed that each person is singled out for his own earning of good; and if that is so, no one is asked about another's deed. Just as their good deeds do not benefit you, likewise you will not be asked about, nor held to account for, the misdeeds of those who earned them.

﴿And no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164]: "Every sheep is hung by its own leg." They said: in this verse and what precedes it there is evidence that a person may argue against another with what amounts to a contradiction of his position, to confound him, even if that is not itself a proof in its own right; because it is known that he (peace and blessings be upon him) did not argue for his prophethood with such sayings, but rather argued with the manifest miracles. Yet when he had established the proof with them and removed the excuse, he found them obstinate, persisting in their falsehood. At that point he presented against them an argument matching what they held, saying: if religion is by imitation, then what is agreed upon is more fitting. In His words ﴿To them is what they earned﴾ to the end, there is evidence against the view of one who holds that it is permissible to punish the children of polytheists for the sins of their fathers. And in the verse before it there is evidence that children are rewarded for the obedience of their fathers.

﴿وقالوا كونوا هودًا أو نصارى تهتدوا﴾: They say, "Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided." The pronoun in "قالوا" (they said) refers to the leaders of the Jews who were in Medina, and to the Christians of Najran. The verse was revealed about them: Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Malik ibn al-Sayf, Wahb, Ubayy ibn Yas ibn Akhtab, al-Sayyid, al-Aqib, and their companions. Each of these groups disputed with the Muslims about the religion, each claiming that it had a better right to the religion of God than the other. So God reported their words and refuted them. Here "أو" (or) is used for distribution (li-al-tafsil), like the "أو" in His words, ﴿And they say, "None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111]. The meaning is: the Jews said, "Be Jews," and the Christians said, "Be Christians." So the statement is made collectively to the collective, not to each individual, as if each one were commanded to follow either of the two religions. This has already been explained and discussed at length in His words, ﴿And they say, "None will enter Paradise"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111].

﴿قل بل ملة إبراهيم﴾: Say, "Rather, the religion of Abraham." The majority of readers read "ملةَ" in the accusative, by supposing a verb to be omitted (idmar fi'l). It may be in the accusative as the object: "Rather, we follow a religion," because the meaning of His words, ﴿Be Jews or Christians﴾, is "follow Judaism or Christianity." It may also be the predicate of "kāna" (was): "Rather, let there be the religion of Abraham," meaning "the people of the religion of Abraham," as 'Adi ibn Hatim said, "Innī min dīn," meaning "I am from the people of a religion." This was said by al-Zajjaj. It may also be in the accusative as an incitement (al-ighra'), meaning "Adhere to the religion of Abraham." This was said by Abu 'Ubayd. It may also be in the accusative by dropping the preposition, meaning "we follow a religion," i.e., "by a religion." This may be addressed to the disbelievers, so the omitted verb would be "follow" or "be." It may also be part of the believers' speech, so it would be estimated as "we follow," or "be," or "we adhere to," as the earlier estimate stated.

Ibn Hurmuz al-A'raj and Ibn Abi 'Abla read "ملةُ" in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject: "Rather, guidance is the religion," or "our affair is his religion," or "we are his religion," meaning "we are the people of his religion." Or it is the subject with an omitted predicate: "Rather, the religion of Abraham, as a ḥanīf, is our religion."

(ḥanīfan): They mentioned that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of Abraham, meaning "in the state of his being a ḥanīf." This was said by al-Mahdawi, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari, and others. Al-Zamakhshari said, "Like your saying, 'I saw the face of Hind, standing'." It is also said that it is in the accusative by an omitted verb, as Ibn 'Atiyya reported, because the state is linked to the object of the genitive (al-muḍāf ilayhi). Its estimated verb would be "we follow ḥanīfan," and it is also said to be in the accusative as an independent qualifier (al-qaṭ'), reported by al-Sajawandi. This is a Kufan explanation, since the accusative as an independent qualifier is the view of the Kufans. We have already discussed this, along with the disagreement between al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i. The original was, "Rather, the religion of Abraham the ḥanīf," but when it was made indefinite, it could not agree with it, so it was put in the accusative as an independent qualifier. As for the state being from the object of the genitive, when the governing noun does not govern the object of the genitive before the construction, we do not permit it, whether it is part of what is added or like a part, or otherwise. We have fully discussed this in our book *Minhaj al-Masalik*. As for the accusative as an independent qualifier, the Basrans have rejected this principle. As for the omitted verb, it is close, and it is possible that it is in the accusative as a state of the governing noun. "Ḥanīfan" is mentioned without the feminine ending, though "milla" is feminine, because it was construed according to meaning, since the "milla" is the "dīn" (religion). So it is as if it were said, "We follow the religion of Abraham, ḥanīfan." On this basis, Hibat Allah ibn al-Shajari explained it in the third session of his *Amali*. He said, "It has been said that ḥanīfan is a state of Abraham, but in my view it is more likely that it is a state of the milla, even though it disagrees with it in gender, because the milla has the meaning of dīn. Do you not see that it was put in apposition to dīn in His words, ﴿a upright religion, the religion of Abraham﴾ [al-An'am: 161]? So if you make ḥanīfan a state of the milla, then its governing word is the same as that of the milla, and the estimate is: 'Rather, we follow the religion of Abraham ḥanīfan.' The state of the object of the genitive is weak only because the governing word of the state must be the same as the governing word of the thing it qualifies." End of his words. This would be a necessary state, because the religion of Abraham never separated from ḥanīfiyya, and similarly, if ḥanīfan is made a state of Abraham, it would be a necessary state, because Abraham never separated from ḥanīfiyya.

The ḥanīf is the one who inclines away from all religions, as Ibn 'Abbas said. Or the one who inclines away from what the common people are upon, as al-Zajjaj said. Or the upright one, as Ibn Qutaybah said. Or the pilgrim, as Ibn 'Abbas also said. Or the son of the ḥanīfiyya (a title). Or the follower, as Mujahid said. Or the one who purifies, as al-Suddi said. Or the one who opposes everything, as Ibn Bahr said. Or the Muslim, as al-Dahhak said. He said, "When ḥanīf is combined with Muslim, it means the pilgrim." Or the one who is circumcised. Or al-Hanaf: it is circumcision, performing the rites of pilgrimage, and forbidding the mothers, daughters, sisters, paternal aunts, and maternal aunts. These are ten sayings close in meaning. Abraham was singled out from among the other prophets, even though all of them inclined toward the truth, were upright in their way, and were ḥunafā', because God singled out Abraham for leadership (al-imama) on account of what he established of the rites of pilgrimage, circumcision, and other laws of Islam, which are followed until the Hour. The ḥanīfiyya became a distinct mark between the believer and the disbeliever. The name "ḥanīf" is given to whoever follows him and stays upright on his guidance. Whoever breaks from his religion is given the names of other religions, so he is called a Jew, a Christian, a Magian, and other kinds of sects.

﴿وما كان من المشركين﴾: God, may He be exalted, reported that he (Abraham) did not worship an idol, nor the sun, nor the moon, nor a star, nor anything other than God, the Exalted. In His words, ﴿Rather, the religion of Abraham﴾, there is evidence that his religion differs from the religion of the Jews and the Christians. That is why "بل" (rather) turns away from both of them, so it is established that he was neither a Jew nor a Christian. The Arabs were among those who adhered to some things of the religion of Abraham, then they associated partners with God. So God denied of Abraham that he was among the polytheists. It has been said that the verse contains an allusion to the People of the Book and others, because each of them claims to follow Abraham while being on polytheism. This was said by al-Zamakhshari. So the Jews' association of partners is in their saying, ﴿Uzayr is the son of God﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30], the Christians' association of partners is in their saying, ﴿The Messiah is the son of God﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30], and the association of partners by others is in worshipping idols and other things.

(p-408) ﴿Say: "We believe in God and in what has been sent down to us"﴾ - the verse - Al-Bukhari transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The People of the Book used to read the Torah in Hebrew and explain it to the People of Islam in Arabic. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do not believe the People of the Book, nor disbelieve them, but say: 'We believe in God and what has been sent down to us' - the verse - If it is true, you have not disbelieved it, and if it is false, you have not believed it." The pronoun in His saying "Say" refers to those who said "Be Jews or Christians" (Al-Baqarah 2:135). They were commanded to be upon the truth and to declare it. It is also possible that it refers to the believers, and this is more apparent. This verse is connected to what precedes it, because when He mentioned, in His saying "Rather, the creed of Abraham" (Al-Baqarah 2:135), a binding response (jawab ilzami, a reply that forces the opponent to accept a conclusion from his own premises), which is that they were not commanded to follow Judaism or Christianity, and that their adherence to them was by way of imitation (taqlid). Moreover, each of the two groups declares the other to be unbelievers. They were answered that the better course in imitation is to follow Abraham, because they, that is the two differing groups, have agreed on the validity of the religion of Abraham. And adhering to what is agreed upon is better than adhering to what is disputed, if religion is to be taken by imitation. So when He mentioned here a binding response, He mentioned after it a proof in this verse, which is the manifestation of the miracle upon them through the sending down of the signs. It has appeared at the hand of Muhammad (ﷺ), so belief in his prophethood is obligatory. For singling out some for acceptance and others for rejection entails contradiction in the argument, and that is impossible by reason.

﴿and what has been sent down to us﴾: If the pronoun in "Say" refers to the believers, then what is sent down to them is the Qur'an, and it is correct to attribute its sending down to them, because they are those addressed by its obligations, through commands, prohibitions and other things. The construction of "sent down" with "to" (ila) is an indication of the endpoint of what was sent down to them. If the pronoun in "Say" refers to the Jews and Christians, then what was sent down to the Jews is the Torah, and what was sent down to the Christians is the Gospel, and belief in both entails belief in the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It is also valid that by what was sent down to them is meant the Qur'an, because they were commanded to follow it, to believe in it, and in the one through whose hands it came.

﴿and what was sent down to Abraham﴾: What was sent down to Abraham was ten scrolls. He said: ﴿Indeed, this is in the former scrolls﴾ (Al-A'la 87:18) ﴿the scrolls of Abraham and Moses﴾ (Al-A'la 87:19). The relative pronoun (al-mawsul, the relative word) is repeated, because what was sent down to us, which is the Qur'an, is other than those scrolls that were sent down to Abraham. For if the relative pronoun were omitted, it would give the false impression that what was sent down to us is what was sent down to Abraham. They said: It was not sent down to Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes, but they are joined to Abraham, because they were charged with acting upon it and calling to it, so the sending down was attributed to them, as it was attributed in His saying: "and what has been sent down to us."

The Tribes (al-asbat) are the sons of Jacob, and they were twelve tribes. The noble genealogist Abu al-Barakat al-Jawani said: The son of Jacob the Prophet (ﷺ) was Joseph the Prophet (ﷺ), lord of Egypt and its ruler, and he was the first of the twelve tribes of Jacob (peace be upon him). The tribes other than Joseph were: Kaadh, Binyamin, Yahudha, Yaftali, Zabulun, Shim'un, Ruwbin, Yasakha, Lawi, Dan, and Yashirkha, from Judah son of Jacob, and Solomon the Prophet (ﷺ). From Solomon (peace be upon him) the Prophet came Mary daughter of Imran, mother of the Messiah (peace be upon them both). From Levi son of Jacob came Moses, the one who spoke with God, and his brother Aaron (peace be upon them both). End of his words.

Ibn Atiyyah said: The Tribes are the sons of Jacob. They are: Rubil, Shim'un, Lawi, Yahudha, Rafalun, Bishjar, and their sister Dhaynah, and their mother was Layatim, who was married after her sister Rachel, and she bore him Joseph and Binyamin. And he had from two concubines: Dani, Naftali, Jad, and Ashir. End of his words. This differs from the words of al-Jawani in some of the names. It has been said that Rubil was his eldest son. Al-Husayn ibn Ahmad ibn Abd al-Rahim al-Bayyani said: Rubil is more sound and more established, meaning with the lam. He said: His grave is in the cemetery of Egypt, in the slope of the mountain, in the tomb of al-Yasa' (peace be upon them both).

(p-408) ﴿and what was given to Moses and Jesus﴾: That is, and we believe in what was given to Moses from the Torah and the signs, and to Jesus from the Gospel and the signs. Moses here is Moses son of Imran, the one who spoke with God. Al-Husayn ibn Ahmad al-Bayyani said: And among the sons of Mesha son of Joseph, meaning the truthful Moses son of Mesha son of Joseph. The People of the Torah claim that God made him a prophet and that he was the companion of al-Khidr. The historians mention that when Jacob died, sorcery (kihanah) spread among the Tribes, so God sent Moses son of Mesha to call them to the worship of God, and he was a hundred years before Moses son of Imran. God knows best the soundness of that. End of his words. He specified Moses and Jesus because they are the two whom the Jews and Christians follow by their claim, and the discourse is with them. The relative pronoun was not repeated with Jesus, because Jesus came only as a confirmer of what is in the Torah; he abrogated (nasakha, cancelled) from it only a small part. So what was given to Jesus is what was given to Moses, even if he differed in a small part. And "what has been sent down to us" came, and "what was given to Moses and Jesus" came, as variation in speech and variation in its wording, even though the meaning is one. This would be so if all of it were in the word "giving," or in the word "sending down," for there would be no sweetness of variety in the words. Do you not see that they did not admire the saying of Abu al-Tayyib:

Plundering the souls of plunderers is more fitting for the plunderers than plundering cloth.

When He mentioned the sending down first in a specific form, He followed it with a general plural. Likewise when He mentioned the giving in a specific form, He followed it with a general plural. And when He expressed the relative pronoun with the sending down in the conjunction, He expressed it with the giving, saying: ﴿and what was given to the prophets from their Lord﴾, which is generalization after specification. The apparent sense of His saying "and what was given" requires generality in the books and the laws.

In a hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: "I said: O Messenger of God, how many books did God send down? He said: 'One hundred books and four books. He sent down to Seth fifty scrolls, He sent down to Enoch thirty scrolls, He sent down to Abraham ten scrolls, He sent down to Moses before the Torah ten scrolls, then He sent down the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms and the Furqan.'"

As for the number of prophets, it is narrated from Ibn Abbas and Wahb ibn Munabbih that they are one hundred and twenty-four thousand prophets, all of them from the Children of Israel, except twenty thousand prophets. The number of messengers is three hundred and thirteen, all of them from the sons of Jacob, except twenty messengers. Of them, twenty-five are mentioned in the Qur'an, whose names are expressly stated: Adam, Idris, Nuh, Hud, Salih, Ibrahim, Lut, Shu'ayb, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub, Yusuf, Musa, Harun, al-Yasa', Ilyas, Yunus, Ayyub, Dawud, Sulayman, Zakariyya, Uzayr, Yahya, Isa, and Muhammad (ﷺ). In a narration from Ibn Abbas: all the prophets are from the Children of Israel, except ten: Nuh, Hud, Shu'ayb, Salih, Lut, Ibrahim, Ishaq, Ya'qub, Isma'il, and Muhammad (ﷺ), all of them.

It began first with belief in God, because that is the root of the laws. And He put forward "and what has been sent down to us," even though its sending down was later than what follows it, because it is more deserving of mention, since people after the sending of Muhammad (ﷺ) are called to believe in what was sent down to him, in its entirety and in its details. He put forward "and what was sent down to Abraham" before "and what was given to Moses and Jesus," for the sake of chronological precedence, or because what was sent down to Moses and those mentioned with him is what was sent down to Abraham, since they are included under his law.

﴿and what was given to Moses﴾: Its apparent sense is conjunction with what precedes it of the prepositional phrases connected with belief. They allowed that "and what was given to Moses and Jesus" could be in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada', subject of a nominal sentence), and the second "and what was given" is conjoined to "what was given," so it is in the nominative position. The predicate (khabar, the predicate of a nominal sentence) is in His saying "from their Lord," or "we make no distinction." Or "and what was given to Moses and Jesus" is conjoined to the preceding genitive phrase, and "and what was given to the prophets" is nominative as subject, and "from their Lord" is the predicate, or "we make no distinction" is the predicate. The apparent view is that "from their Lord" is in the accusative position, and "from" indicates the starting point, so it is connected to the second "what was given," or to the first "what was given," and the second is an emphatic repetition (tawkid, emphasis). Do you not see its omission in Al 'Imran in His saying: ﴿and what was given to Moses and Jesus and the prophets from their Lord﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:84)? It is also permissible that it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal, a clause describing the state of the subject) from the pronoun referring to the relative pronoun, (p-409) so it is connected to an omitted word, meaning: and what the prophets were given, being from their Lord.

﴿we make no distinction between any one of them﴾: Its apparent sense is a resumptive new sentence (isti'naf, a new sentence not grammatically dependent on what precedes). The meaning is: We believe in all of them, so we do not believe in some and disbelieve in others, as the Jews and Christians did. For the Jews believed in all the prophets and disbelieved in Muhammad and Jesus - may God's blessings be upon all of them. The Christians believed in the prophets and disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ). It has been said: its meaning is that we do not say that they differ in the principles of the religions. It has been said: its meaning is that we do not split their unity, as it is said "he split the staff of the Muslims" when he separated from their community. As for "one" (ahad) here, it has been said: it is used in negation, its roots are the hamza, the ha and the dal, and it is general, so for that reason "between" (bayn) did not require a conjoined word after it, since it is a general noun under which there are individuals, so it is correct for "between" to be attached to it, just as it is attached to a plural, so you say: "the wealth is between the two Zaids." Al-Zamakhshari did not mention any view other than this one. It has been said: "ahad" here means "wāḥid" (one), and the hamza is a substitution for the waw, since its original form is waḥad, and the conjoined word was omitted because the listener understands it, and the estimate is: between one of them and his counterpart, so it was abridged, or between one of them and the other, and it is like the saying of the poet:

"There was not between the good, had Abu Hajar come back safe, except a few nights."

He means: between the good and me, so he omitted it because the meaning indicates it, since it is known that "between" must enter between two things, just as the conjoined word is omitted in His saying: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ (Al-Nahl 16:81). It is known that what protects from heat protects from cold, so the omission of "and the cold" is because the meaning is understood. Ibn Atiyyah did not mention any view other than this one. Other than al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyyah mentioned both views, and the first view is more preferable, because there is no omission in it.

﴿and to Him we are Muslims﴾: All of this falls under His saying "Say." And when He first mentioned belief, which is affirmation and is connected to the heart, He concluded by mentioning submission (islam), which is the compliance arising from belief and manifest in the limbs. So He combined belief and submission, so that the root and what arises from the root would be joined together. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) explained belief and submission when he was asked about them, and that is in the hadith of Jibril (peace be upon him). They explained His saying "Muslims" with close meanings: it was said "humbled," it was said "obedient," it was said "submitting to servanthood," it was said "submitting to His command and prohibition by reason and action," it was said "entering under the rule of Islam," it was said "submissive," it was said "sincere." The word "to Him" (lahu) is connected to "Muslims," and the governing word was placed after it for the sake of the verse endings (fawasil, the rhyme endings of verses), or it was placed before it for the sake of attention to the pronoun referring to God Most High. When His saying "Say: We believe in God..." was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited it to the Jews and Christians and said: "God commanded me with this." When they heard the mention of Jesus, they denied it and disbelieved. The Christians said: Jesus is not in the rank of the other prophets, but he is the son of God Most High. So God revealed: ﴿If they believe﴾ - the verse. The pronoun in "they believe" refers to the one to whom it referred in His saying: ﴿and they said, "Be Jews or Christians"﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:135). It is also possible that the address is specific, and what is meant by it is generality, and it is also possible that it refers to every disbeliever, and the meaning will explain it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 136–137 (part 2 of 2):

The majority (al-Jumhur) read: ﴿bi-mithli mā āmantum bihi﴾ ("in the like of that which you believed in"). ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās read: "bi-mā āmantum bihi" ("in that which you believed in"). Ubayy read: "bi-alladhī āmantum bihi" ("in that which you believed in"). Ibn ʿAbbās said: "There is no like unto Allah." This indicates the retention of the preposition bāʾ in its original sense, as in "āmantu bi-llāh" (I believed in Allah), and the use of mā for Allah, the Exalted, as one of the scholars held in His saying: ﴿wa-s-samāʾi wa-mā banāhā﴾ [al-Shams: 5], meaning "and He who built it." The reading of Ubayy is evident, and it encompasses everything that the believers believed in. As for the reading of the majority, the bāʾ is considered superfluous (ziyādah), and the estimate is: "a belief like your belief," just as it was made superfluous in His saying: ﴿wa-huzzī ilayki bi-jidhʿi an-nakhlah﴾ [Maryam: 25].

*(Verse of poetry)*
"And black-eyed ones do not recite with the suwar"

﴿wa-lā tulqū bi-aydīkum ilā at-tahlukah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 195], and mā is then a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah). It has been said: it is not superfluous, and it has the meaning of ʿalā (upon), meaning: "If they believe upon the like of what you believed in." That the bāʾ carries the meaning of ʿalā has been stated, and among those who said so is Ibn Mālik, who said this regarding His saying: ﴿man in tathmanhu bi-qinṭār﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 75], meaning "upon a qinṭār." It has also been said: it is for instrumentality (istiʿānah), like your saying: "I worked with the adze (qadūm)," and "I wrote with the pen," meaning: "If they enter into belief with a testimony like your testimony." This is an escape from the superfluity of the bāʾ, since it is not, by analogy, among the places where bāʾ is made superfluous.

The object of belief (al-muʾmin bihi) in these three possibilities is omitted; the estimate is: "If they believe in Allah." The pronoun in "bihi" returns to what the phrase ﴿wa-naḥnu lahu﴾ refers to, namely Allah, the Exalted. It has been said that it returns to mā, in which case mā is a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah). As for mithl, it has been said that it is superfluous, and the estimate is: "If they believe in what you believed in." They said: it is like His saying: ﴿laysa ka-mithlihi shayʾ﴾ [ash-Shūrā: 11], meaning "there is nothing like Him," and like His saying:

*(Verse of poetry)*
"Then they became like stubble eaten up"

and like His saying:

*(Verse of poetry)*
"O my blamer, leave me from your blame, / my like does not accept from your like"

It has been said: it is not superfluous. The likeness here is connected to belief (iʿtiqād), meaning: "If they hold a belief like your belief," or it is connected to the Book, meaning: "If they believe in a book like the Book in which you believed." The meaning is: "If they believe in your Book, which is like their Book," that is, "If they believe in the Qurʾan, which confirms what is in the Torah and the Gospel." On this interpretation, the bāʾ is not superfluous, but is like it in His saying: "I believed in the Book." A group said: this is a figure of speech (majāz), one says: "This is a matter that someone like you does not do," meaning: "you do not do it." The meaning is: "If they believe in that which you believed in," and this leads to nullifying "mithl" and making it superfluous in meaning.
