Az-Zamakhsharī said: "bi-mithli mā āmantum bihi" is a rebuke (tabkīt), because the religion of truth is one and has no like, and it is the religion of Islam.

﴿wa-man yabtaghi ghayra al-Islāmi dīnan fa-lan yuqbala minhu﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 85]. Thus there is no other religion that resembles the religion of Islam in being true, so that even if they believe in that religion which is like it, they would be guided. It has been said: "If they believe" is an expression of doubt, by way of presentation, and the estimate is: "If they obtain another religion like your religion, equal to it in soundness and rectitude."

﴿fa-qad ihtadaw﴾: In this is the indication that their religion in which they are, and every religion other than it, is different from it and not like it, because it is truth and guidance, and what is other than it is falsehood and misguidance. Similar to this is your saying to the man to whom you give advice: "This is the correct opinion; if you have an opinion more correct than it, then act upon it." You know that there is no more correct opinion than yours, but you want to rebuke your companion and make him acknowledge that what you hold has no opinion beyond it. End of his words, and it is good. The response of the conditional is His saying: ﴿fa-qad ihtadaw﴾, and the response is not omitted, as it is in His saying: ﴿wa-in yukadhdhibūka fa-qad kudhdhibat rusul﴾ [Fāṭir: 4], for the meaning of the denial of the messengers is certain, whereas guidance here is future, because it is conditional upon a future event and had not yet occurred.

﴿wa-in tawallaw﴾: that is, if they turn away from entering into belief.

﴿fa-innamā hum fī shiqāq﴾: He emphasized the clause that stands as the condition with "innamā," and the meaning of the predicate was strengthened so that it became a container for them, while they are contained within it. Thus, opposition (shiqāq) overpowers them from all sides and encompasses them as a house encompasses whoever is in it. This is an intensification of the opposition that results for them from turning away. This is like His saying: ﴿innā lanarāka fī ḍalālin mubīn﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 60], ﴿innā lanarāka fī safāhah﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 66]; it is more eloquent than your saying: "Zayd opposes ʿAmr, Zayd is astray, and Bakr is foolish." Shiqāq here means: opposition (khilāf), said Ibn ʿAbbās; or enmity (ʿadāwah); or separation (firāq); or contention (munāzaʿah), said Zayd ibn Aslam; or disputation (mujādalah); or misguidance and disagreement; or the removal of obedience (khalʿ al-ṭāʿah), said al-Kisāʾī; or distance and separation until the Day of Resurrection. These are interpretations of shiqāq that are close in meaning. We have mentioned the root of this in al-Mufradāt on two meanings: either from hardship (mashaqqah), or that one becomes on one side (shiqq) while his companion is on another side, meaning that disagreement arises between them. Al-Qāḍī said: "Shiqāq is hardly said of enmity in the true sense, because shiqāq is in a great opposition that brings its doer into the enmity and wrath of Allah." And this is a warning to them. End of his words.

﴿fa-sa-yakfīkahumu Allāh﴾: When He mentioned that their turning away results in shiqāq, which is great enmity, He informed that this enmity will not reach you with anything of it, because Allah, the Exalted, has sufficed you against their evil. This announcement is a guarantee from Allah to His Messenger of His sufficiency and protection from them, and it guarantees his victory over his enemies and his overpowering them, because whoever is in utmost opposition to you is striving to harm you; if he cannot reach that, it is only because of your supremacy over him and the strength of your defense against him. This is similar to His saying: ﴿wa-llāhu yaʿṣimuka mina an-nās﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 67]. Allah sufficed him in their affair through the taking captive and killing in Qurayẓah and Banū Qaynuqāʿ, the expulsion in Banū an-Naḍīr, and the jizyah from the Christians of Najrān. The conjunction of the clause with "fa" indicates the immediate sequence of sufficiency following their opposition, and the use of "sa" (sīn) indicates nearness of the future, since sīn in its usage is closer in extension than "sawfa." The one sufficed is not the essence, so it is by elision of a modifier, meaning: "He will suffice you against their opposition." The means by which one is sufficed is omitted, meaning: by those among the believers whom Allah guides, or by the dispersal of the word of the opponents, or by destroying their persons and humiliating the remainder through captivity, expulsion, and jizyah, as we have explained.

﴿wa-huwa as-Samīʿu al-ʿAlīm﴾: The suitability of these two attributes: each of belief and its opposite comprises sayings and actions, and creeds from which those sayings and actions arise. It was fitting that this be concluded with them, that is: He is the Hearer of your sayings, the Knower of your intentions and beliefs. Since sayings are what is apparent to us and indicative of what is within, the attribute "the Hearer" is placed before "the Knower." Also, "al-ʿAlīm" is likewise a closing word (fāṣilah). These two attributes contain a warning, because the meaning is: He is the Hearer, the Knower, so He will requite you for what proceeds from you.

(p-408) ﴿Say: "We believe in God and in what has been sent down to us"﴾ - the verse - Al-Bukhari transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The People of the Book used to read the Torah in Hebrew and explain it to the People of Islam in Arabic. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do not believe the People of the Book, nor disbelieve them, but say: 'We believe in God and what has been sent down to us' - the verse - If it is true, you have not disbelieved it, and if it is false, you have not believed it." The pronoun in His saying "Say" refers to those who said "Be Jews or Christians" (Al-Baqarah 2:135). They were commanded to be upon the truth and to declare it. It is also possible that it refers to the believers, and this is more apparent. This verse is connected to what precedes it, because when He mentioned, in His saying "Rather, the creed of Abraham" (Al-Baqarah 2:135), a binding response (jawab ilzami, a reply that forces the opponent to accept a conclusion from his own premises), which is that they were not commanded to follow Judaism or Christianity, and that their adherence to them was by way of imitation (taqlid). Moreover, each of the two groups declares the other to be unbelievers. They were answered that the better course in imitation is to follow Abraham, because they, that is the two differing groups, have agreed on the validity of the religion of Abraham. And adhering to what is agreed upon is better than adhering to what is disputed, if religion is to be taken by imitation. So when He mentioned here a binding response, He mentioned after it a proof in this verse, which is the manifestation of the miracle upon them through the sending down of the signs. It has appeared at the hand of Muhammad (ﷺ), so belief in his prophethood is obligatory. For singling out some for acceptance and others for rejection entails contradiction in the argument, and that is impossible by reason.

﴿and what has been sent down to us﴾: If the pronoun in "Say" refers to the believers, then what is sent down to them is the Qur'an, and it is correct to attribute its sending down to them, because they are those addressed by its obligations, through commands, prohibitions and other things. The construction of "sent down" with "to" (ila) is an indication of the endpoint of what was sent down to them. If the pronoun in "Say" refers to the Jews and Christians, then what was sent down to the Jews is the Torah, and what was sent down to the Christians is the Gospel, and belief in both entails belief in the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It is also valid that by what was sent down to them is meant the Qur'an, because they were commanded to follow it, to believe in it, and in the one through whose hands it came.

﴿and what was sent down to Abraham﴾: What was sent down to Abraham was ten scrolls. He said: ﴿Indeed, this is in the former scrolls﴾ (Al-A'la 87:18) ﴿the scrolls of Abraham and Moses﴾ (Al-A'la 87:19). The relative pronoun (al-mawsul, the relative word) is repeated, because what was sent down to us, which is the Qur'an, is other than those scrolls that were sent down to Abraham. For if the relative pronoun were omitted, it would give the false impression that what was sent down to us is what was sent down to Abraham. They said: It was not sent down to Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes, but they are joined to Abraham, because they were charged with acting upon it and calling to it, so the sending down was attributed to them, as it was attributed in His saying: "and what has been sent down to us."

The Tribes (al-asbat) are the sons of Jacob, and they were twelve tribes. The noble genealogist Abu al-Barakat al-Jawani said: The son of Jacob the Prophet (ﷺ) was Joseph the Prophet (ﷺ), lord of Egypt and its ruler, and he was the first of the twelve tribes of Jacob (peace be upon him). The tribes other than Joseph were: Kaadh, Binyamin, Yahudha, Yaftali, Zabulun, Shim'un, Ruwbin, Yasakha, Lawi, Dan, and Yashirkha, from Judah son of Jacob, and Solomon the Prophet (ﷺ). From Solomon (peace be upon him) the Prophet came Mary daughter of Imran, mother of the Messiah (peace be upon them both). From Levi son of Jacob came Moses, the one who spoke with God, and his brother Aaron (peace be upon them both). End of his words.

Ibn Atiyyah said: The Tribes are the sons of Jacob. They are: Rubil, Shim'un, Lawi, Yahudha, Rafalun, Bishjar, and their sister Dhaynah, and their mother was Layatim, who was married after her sister Rachel, and she bore him Joseph and Binyamin. And he had from two concubines: Dani, Naftali, Jad, and Ashir. End of his words. This differs from the words of al-Jawani in some of the names. It has been said that Rubil was his eldest son. Al-Husayn ibn Ahmad ibn Abd al-Rahim al-Bayyani said: Rubil is more sound and more established, meaning with the lam. He said: His grave is in the cemetery of Egypt, in the slope of the mountain, in the tomb of al-Yasa' (peace be upon them both).

(p-408) ﴿and what was given to Moses and Jesus﴾: That is, and we believe in what was given to Moses from the Torah and the signs, and to Jesus from the Gospel and the signs. Moses here is Moses son of Imran, the one who spoke with God. Al-Husayn ibn Ahmad al-Bayyani said: And among the sons of Mesha son of Joseph, meaning the truthful Moses son of Mesha son of Joseph. The People of the Torah claim that God made him a prophet and that he was the companion of al-Khidr. The historians mention that when Jacob died, sorcery (kihanah) spread among the Tribes, so God sent Moses son of Mesha to call them to the worship of God, and he was a hundred years before Moses son of Imran. God knows best the soundness of that. End of his words. He specified Moses and Jesus because they are the two whom the Jews and Christians follow by their claim, and the discourse is with them. The relative pronoun was not repeated with Jesus, because Jesus came only as a confirmer of what is in the Torah; he abrogated (nasakha, cancelled) from it only a small part. So what was given to Jesus is what was given to Moses, even if he differed in a small part. And "what has been sent down to us" came, and "what was given to Moses and Jesus" came, as variation in speech and variation in its wording, even though the meaning is one. This would be so if all of it were in the word "giving," or in the word "sending down," for there would be no sweetness of variety in the words. Do you not see that they did not admire the saying of Abu al-Tayyib:

Plundering the souls of plunderers is more fitting for the plunderers than plundering cloth.

When He mentioned the sending down first in a specific form, He followed it with a general plural. Likewise when He mentioned the giving in a specific form, He followed it with a general plural. And when He expressed the relative pronoun with the sending down in the conjunction, He expressed it with the giving, saying: ﴿and what was given to the prophets from their Lord﴾, which is generalization after specification. The apparent sense of His saying "and what was given" requires generality in the books and the laws.

In a hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: "I said: O Messenger of God, how many books did God send down? He said: 'One hundred books and four books. He sent down to Seth fifty scrolls, He sent down to Enoch thirty scrolls, He sent down to Abraham ten scrolls, He sent down to Moses before the Torah ten scrolls, then He sent down the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms and the Furqan.'"

As for the number of prophets, it is narrated from Ibn Abbas and Wahb ibn Munabbih that they are one hundred and twenty-four thousand prophets, all of them from the Children of Israel, except twenty thousand prophets. The number of messengers is three hundred and thirteen, all of them from the sons of Jacob, except twenty messengers. Of them, twenty-five are mentioned in the Qur'an, whose names are expressly stated: Adam, Idris, Nuh, Hud, Salih, Ibrahim, Lut, Shu'ayb, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub, Yusuf, Musa, Harun, al-Yasa', Ilyas, Yunus, Ayyub, Dawud, Sulayman, Zakariyya, Uzayr, Yahya, Isa, and Muhammad (ﷺ). In a narration from Ibn Abbas: all the prophets are from the Children of Israel, except ten: Nuh, Hud, Shu'ayb, Salih, Lut, Ibrahim, Ishaq, Ya'qub, Isma'il, and Muhammad (ﷺ), all of them.

It began first with belief in God, because that is the root of the laws. And He put forward "and what has been sent down to us," even though its sending down was later than what follows it, because it is more deserving of mention, since people after the sending of Muhammad (ﷺ) are called to believe in what was sent down to him, in its entirety and in its details. He put forward "and what was sent down to Abraham" before "and what was given to Moses and Jesus," for the sake of chronological precedence, or because what was sent down to Moses and those mentioned with him is what was sent down to Abraham, since they are included under his law.

﴿and what was given to Moses﴾: Its apparent sense is conjunction with what precedes it of the prepositional phrases connected with belief. They allowed that "and what was given to Moses and Jesus" could be in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada', subject of a nominal sentence), and the second "and what was given" is conjoined to "what was given," so it is in the nominative position. The predicate (khabar, the predicate of a nominal sentence) is in His saying "from their Lord," or "we make no distinction." Or "and what was given to Moses and Jesus" is conjoined to the preceding genitive phrase, and "and what was given to the prophets" is nominative as subject, and "from their Lord" is the predicate, or "we make no distinction" is the predicate. The apparent view is that "from their Lord" is in the accusative position, and "from" indicates the starting point, so it is connected to the second "what was given," or to the first "what was given," and the second is an emphatic repetition (tawkid, emphasis). Do you not see its omission in Al 'Imran in His saying: ﴿and what was given to Moses and Jesus and the prophets from their Lord﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:84)? It is also permissible that it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal, a clause describing the state of the subject) from the pronoun referring to the relative pronoun, (p-409) so it is connected to an omitted word, meaning: and what the prophets were given, being from their Lord.

﴿we make no distinction between any one of them﴾: Its apparent sense is a resumptive new sentence (isti'naf, a new sentence not grammatically dependent on what precedes). The meaning is: We believe in all of them, so we do not believe in some and disbelieve in others, as the Jews and Christians did. For the Jews believed in all the prophets and disbelieved in Muhammad and Jesus - may God's blessings be upon all of them. The Christians believed in the prophets and disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ). It has been said: its meaning is that we do not say that they differ in the principles of the religions. It has been said: its meaning is that we do not split their unity, as it is said "he split the staff of the Muslims" when he separated from their community. As for "one" (ahad) here, it has been said: it is used in negation, its roots are the hamza, the ha and the dal, and it is general, so for that reason "between" (bayn) did not require a conjoined word after it, since it is a general noun under which there are individuals, so it is correct for "between" to be attached to it, just as it is attached to a plural, so you say: "the wealth is between the two Zaids." Al-Zamakhshari did not mention any view other than this one. It has been said: "ahad" here means "wāḥid" (one), and the hamza is a substitution for the waw, since its original form is waḥad, and the conjoined word was omitted because the listener understands it, and the estimate is: between one of them and his counterpart, so it was abridged, or between one of them and the other, and it is like the saying of the poet:

"There was not between the good, had Abu Hajar come back safe, except a few nights."

He means: between the good and me, so he omitted it because the meaning indicates it, since it is known that "between" must enter between two things, just as the conjoined word is omitted in His saying: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ (Al-Nahl 16:81). It is known that what protects from heat protects from cold, so the omission of "and the cold" is because the meaning is understood. Ibn Atiyyah did not mention any view other than this one. Other than al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyyah mentioned both views, and the first view is more preferable, because there is no omission in it.

﴿and to Him we are Muslims﴾: All of this falls under His saying "Say." And when He first mentioned belief, which is affirmation and is connected to the heart, He concluded by mentioning submission (islam), which is the compliance arising from belief and manifest in the limbs. So He combined belief and submission, so that the root and what arises from the root would be joined together. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) explained belief and submission when he was asked about them, and that is in the hadith of Jibril (peace be upon him). They explained His saying "Muslims" with close meanings: it was said "humbled," it was said "obedient," it was said "submitting to servanthood," it was said "submitting to His command and prohibition by reason and action," it was said "entering under the rule of Islam," it was said "submissive," it was said "sincere." The word "to Him" (lahu) is connected to "Muslims," and the governing word was placed after it for the sake of the verse endings (fawasil, the rhyme endings of verses), or it was placed before it for the sake of attention to the pronoun referring to God Most High. When His saying "Say: We believe in God..." was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited it to the Jews and Christians and said: "God commanded me with this." When they heard the mention of Jesus, they denied it and disbelieved. The Christians said: Jesus is not in the rank of the other prophets, but he is the son of God Most High. So God revealed: ﴿If they believe﴾ - the verse. The pronoun in "they believe" refers to the one to whom it referred in His saying: ﴿and they said, "Be Jews or Christians"﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:135). It is also possible that the address is specific, and what is meant by it is generality, and it is also possible that it refers to every disbeliever, and the meaning will explain it.

A group said: this is a figure of speech (majāz), one says: "This is a matter that someone like you does not do," meaning: "you do not do it." The meaning is: "If they believe in that which you believed in," and this leads to nullifying "mithl" and making it superfluous in meaning. Az-Zamakhsharī said: "bi-mithli mā āmantum bihi" is a rebuke (tabkīt), because the religion of truth is one and has no like, and it is the religion of Islam.

﴿wa-man yabtaghi ghayra al-Islāmi dīnan fa-lan yuqbala minhu﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 85]. Thus there is no other religion that resembles the religion of Islam in being true, so that even if they believe in that religion which is like it, they would be guided. It has been said: "If they believe" is an expression of doubt, by way of presentation, and the estimate is: "If they obtain another religion like your religion, equal to it in soundness and rectitude."

﴿fa-qad ihtadaw﴾: In this is the indication that their religion in which they are, and every religion other than it, is different from it and not like it, because it is truth and guidance, and what is other than it is falsehood and misguidance. Similar to this is your saying to the man to whom you give advice: "This is the correct opinion; if you have an opinion more correct than it, then act upon it." You know that there is no more correct opinion than yours, but you want to rebuke your companion and make him acknowledge that what you hold has no opinion beyond it. End of his words, and it is good. The response of the conditional is His saying: ﴿fa-qad ihtadaw﴾, and the response is not omitted, as it is in His saying: ﴿wa-in yukadhdhibūka fa-qad kudhdhibat rusul﴾ [Fāṭir: 4], for the meaning of the denial of the messengers is certain, whereas guidance here is future, because it is conditional upon a future event and had not yet occurred.

﴿wa-in tawallaw﴾: that is, if they turn away from entering into belief.

﴿fa-innamā hum fī shiqāq﴾: He emphasized the clause that stands as the condition with "innamā," and the meaning of the predicate was strengthened so that it became a container for them, while they are contained within it. Thus, opposition (shiqāq) overpowers them from all sides and encompasses them as a house encompasses whoever is in it. This is an intensification of the opposition that results for them from turning away. This is like His saying: ﴿innā lanarāka fī ḍalālin mubīn﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 60], ﴿innā lanarāka fī safāhah﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 66]; it is more eloquent than your saying: "Zayd opposes ʿAmr, Zayd is astray, and Bakr is foolish." Shiqāq here means: opposition (khilāf), said Ibn ʿAbbās; or enmity (ʿadāwah); or separation (firāq); or contention (munāzaʿah), said Zayd ibn Aslam; or disputation (mujādalah); or misguidance and disagreement; or the removal of obedience (khalʿ al-ṭāʿah), said al-Kisāʾī; or distance and separation until the Day of Resurrection. These are interpretations of shiqāq that are close in meaning. We have mentioned the root of this in al-Mufradāt on two meanings: either from hardship (mashaqqah), or that one becomes on one side (shiqq) while his companion is on another side, meaning that disagreement arises between them. Al-Qāḍī said: "Shiqāq is hardly said of enmity in the true sense, because shiqāq is in a great opposition that brings its doer into the enmity and wrath of Allah." And this is a warning to them. End of his words.

﴿fa-sa-yakfīkahumu Allāh﴾: When He mentioned that their turning away results in shiqāq, which is great enmity, He informed that this enmity will not reach you with anything of it, because Allah, the Exalted, has sufficed you against their evil. This announcement is a guarantee from Allah to His Messenger of His sufficiency and protection from them, and it guarantees his victory over his enemies and his overpowering them, because whoever is in utmost opposition to you is striving to harm you; if he cannot reach that, it is only because of your supremacy over him and the strength of your defense against him. This is similar to His saying: ﴿wa-llāhu yaʿṣimuka mina an-nās﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 67]. Allah sufficed him in their affair through the taking captive and killing in Qurayẓah and Banū Qaynuqāʿ, the expulsion in Banū an-Naḍīr, and the jizyah from the Christians of Najrān. The conjunction of the clause with "fa" indicates the immediate sequence of sufficiency following their opposition, and the use of "sa" (sīn) indicates nearness of the future, since sīn in its usage is closer in extension than "sawfa." The one sufficed is not the essence, so it is by elision of a modifier, meaning: "He will suffice you against their opposition." The means by which one is sufficed is omitted, meaning: by those among the believers whom Allah guides, or by the dispersal of the word of the opponents, or by destroying their persons and humiliating the remainder through captivity, expulsion, and jizyah, as we have explained.

﴿wa-huwa as-Samīʿu al-ʿAlīm﴾: The suitability of these two attributes: each of belief and its opposite comprises sayings and actions, and creeds from which those sayings and actions arise. It was fitting that this be concluded with them, that is: He is the Hearer of your sayings, the Knower of your intentions and beliefs. Since sayings are what is apparent to us and indicative of what is within, the attribute "the Hearer" is placed before "the Knower." Also, "al-ʿAlīm" is likewise a closing word (fāṣilah). These two attributes contain a warning, because the meaning is: He is the Hearer, the Knower, so He will requite you for what proceeds from you.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 2, verse 138:**

﴿صِبْغَةَ اللَّهِ﴾ (*sibghat Allah*, "the dye of God"): that is, the religion of God. This is what Ibn 'Abbas said. It is called *sibgha* (dye) because the effect of the religion becomes visible on its adherent, as the effect of dye becomes visible on a garment, and because it clings to him and does not leave him, as dye clings to cloth. Or it means the *fitra* (natural disposition) of God, as Mujahid and Muqatil said. Or the *khilqa* (creation) of God, as al-Zajjaj and Abu 'Ubayd said. Or the *sunna* (way) of God, as Abu 'Ubayda said. Or Islam, also said by Mujahid. Or the *jiha* (direction) of God, meaning the *qibla* (prayer direction), as Ibn Kaysan said. Or the *hujja* (proof) of God against His servants, as al-Asamm said. Or circumcision, because it dyes its owner with blood. The Christians, when a child was born to them, would immerse him on the seventh day in water called *al-ma'mudiyya* (baptism), and he would become pure in their view and become a Christian. They thus dispensed with circumcision, and God answered them with His words: ﴿the dye of God﴾. Or it means the ritual bath for entering Islam in place of the water of baptism, as al-Mawardi related. Or it means drawing near to God, as Ibn Faris related in *al-Mujmal*. Or it means instruction (*talqin*). It is said: "So-and-so dyes so-and-so in a thing," meaning he makes him enter it and binds him to it, just as dye makes the color cling to the cloth.

These statements are close in meaning, and the closest of them is that it means religion and creed (*milla*), because before it comes God's words: ﴿Say: We believe in God and in what has been sent down to us﴾ (2:136), and so on. This verse contains the essence of the *hanifiyya* (the pure monotheistic religion), and so the dye is used as a metaphor for it. Its figurative sense is the visibility of the effect, or its constant attachment to the one who adopts it. It is like dye in these two respects, as was said. Likewise is faith, when its gladness mixes into the hearts.

The Arabs call a person's religious affiliation to something, and his being characterized by it, a *sibgha*. One of their poets, from among their kings' poets, said:

*Every people has a dye (sibgha) of their own, and the dye of Hamdan is the best of dyes.*

*Upon that we dyed our sons, so how honorable is our dye among dyes!*

It has been related from Ibn 'Abbas that the origin of calling religion a *sibgha* is that 'Isa (Jesus), when he came to Yahya ibn Zakariyya (John, son of Zechariah) and said: "I came to be dyed by you and to bathe in the river Jordan (*al-Urdunn*)." When he came out, the Holy Spirit (*ruh al-qudus*) descended upon him. So the Christians began doing this with their children in their churches, imitating 'Isa, and they say: "Now he has truly become a Christian." They claim that in the Gospel (*al-Injil*) 'Isa is mentioned as "the Dyer." They call the water in which they immerse their children *al-ma'mudiyya* (with a *dal*), and it is also said *al-ma'murriyya* (with a *ra'*). He said: They call that act *al-taghmis* (immersion), and some of them call it *al-sabgh* (dyeing). God rejected this with His words: ﴿the dye of God﴾.

Al-Raghib said: *Sibgha* is an indication of what God placed in people of the primary intellects (*bada'ih al-'uqul*) by which He distinguished us from the beasts, and by which He guided us toward knowing Him and seeking the truth, which is what is indicated by *fitra*. This was called *sibgha* because the faculties of a human being, when considered, function like dye on the thing dyed. And since the Christians, when they instructed their children in Christianity, would say, "We have made him Christian" (*nassarnahu*), He said: "Indeed, faith like what you have believed in is the dye of God."

The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read ﴿*sibghata Llah*﴾ with the accusative (*naṣb*). Whoever reads *milla* in the nominative (*raf'*) reads *sibgha* in the nominative as well, as al-Tabari said. It has already been mentioned that this is the reading of al-A'raj and Ibn Abi 'Abla. As for the accusative, it has several possible analyses. The most apparent is that it is in the accusative as a *masdar mu'akkad* (emphatic verbal noun) of God's words: ﴿Say: We believe in God﴾ (2:136). It was also said that it is in the accusative as an emphatic verbal noun of His words: ﴿and to Him we are submitting﴾ (2:136). And it was said that it is an emphatic verbal noun of His words: ﴿then they are rightly guided﴾ (2:137). It was also said that it is in the accusative as an *ighra'* (incitement or urging), meaning: "Hold fast to the dye of God." And it was said that it is a *badal* (substitute) for His words: ﴿the creed of Ibrahim﴾ (2:135). As for the incitement interpretation, the end of the verse rejects it, which is His words: ﴿and to Him we are worshippers﴾, unless one supposes there a verb of saying, and that is an implied element for which there is no need, and no indication in the discourse. As for the substitute interpretation, it is remote, and the distance between the substituted noun and the substitute is long, with several sentences between them, and such a thing is not permissible. The best is that it is in the accusative as an emphatic verbal noun of His words: ﴿Say: We believe﴾ (2:136). If the command is addressed to the believers, the meaning is: God dyed us with faith as a dye, and did not dye us with your dye. And if the command is addressed to the Jews and Christians, the meaning is: God dyed us with faith as a dye, not like your dye, and purified us with it with a purification, not like your purification. A parallel to the accusative of this verbal noun is the accusative in His words: ﴿the handiwork of God, who has perfected everything﴾ (27:88), since before it comes: ﴿And you see the mountains, you think them fixed, while they pass away like clouds﴾ (27:88). Its meaning is: "The handiwork of God is that handiwork." The word *sibgha* was used here by way of *mushakala* (matching of wording), as you would say to a man who plants trees: "Plant as so-and-so plants," meaning a man who cultivates vineyards. As for the nominative reading, it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "That faith is the dye of God."

﴿And who is better than God in dye?﴾: This is an interrogative with the meaning of negation, that is: "No one is better than God in dye." The word "better" (*ahsan*) here does not mean literal preference, since the dye of other than God has no goodness at all. Or preference is intended with regard to those who think there is goodness in the dye of other than God, not that this is relative to the reality of the thing. The *sibgha* here is in the accusative as a *tamyiz* (specification), and it is of the type of *tamyiz* transferred from the subject (*mubtada'*). We have mentioned that this is rare, I mean the grammarians' explicit statement that among the *tamyiz* is a *tamyiz* transferred from the subject, and the underlying sense is: "Whose dye is better than the dye of God?" So the comparison takes place only between the two dyes, not between the dyers.

﴿and to Him we are worshippers﴾: This is connected to His words: ﴿We believe in God﴾ (2:136), and is coordinated with it. Al-Zamakhshari said: This coordination refutes the view of whoever claims that *sibghat Allah* is a substitute for *milla*, or that it is in the accusative as an incitement, in the sense of "upon you is the dye of God," because of what it involves of breaking the structure of the composition and removing the speech from its coherence and consistency. Its accusative, meaning *sibghat Allah* as an emphatic verbal noun, is the view mentioned by Sibawayh, and "the saying is what Hadhdham said" (a proverb). End of quotation. As for the estimate in the incitement, "upon you the dye of God," it is not good, because when the incitement is with an adverbial phrase or a prepositional phrase, that phrase cannot be omitted. That is why, when we mentioned the incitement interpretation, we estimated it as "Hold fast to the dye of God."

The discussion of worship (*'ibada*) has already been given in His words: ﴿You alone we worship﴾ (1:5). Here it was said: "worshippers" means monotheists, and from this is His words: ﴿I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me﴾ (51:56), meaning that they should affirm My oneness. It was also said: obedient, following the creed of Ibrahim and the dye of God. And it was said: humbly submissive, submitting in following the creed of Ibrahim, not arrogant. These statements are close in meaning.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 139:

﴿Say: Do you argue with us about God, when He is our Lord and your Lord?﴾: The occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul). It is said: the Jews and the Christians said, "O Muhammad, the prophets were from among us and were upon our religion. You were not from the Arabs. If you were a prophet, you would be from among us and upon our religion." It is also said: they argued with the Muslims, saying, "We are the sons of God and His beloved, and the people of the first Scripture, and our qibla (direction of prayer) is older, so we have a greater claim to God than you," and so this was revealed.

The majority of reciters read أتُحاجُونَنا (atuḥājjūnanā) with two nūns, one being the nūn of the nominative (nūn al-rafʿ) and the other the pronoun. Zayd ibn Thabit, al-Hasan, al-Aʿmash and Ibn Muḥaysin read it with the assimilation (idgham) of the nūn into the nūn. Some scholars permitted the deletion of one nūn. As for the reading of the majority, it is clear. As for the reading of Zayd and those mentioned with him, its justification is that when two identical letters come together, and there is a long vowel letter (ḥarf madd wa-līn) before the first, assimilation is permitted, as in your saying: هَذِهِ دارُ راشِدٍ (this is the house of Rashid). This is because the lengthening (madd) takes the place of the vowel (ḥaraka), as in: جَعَلَ لَكَ (he made for you). As for the permissibility of deleting the first nūn, the justification of those who permitted it is based on the reading of the one who read: فَبِمَ تُبَشِّرُونَ (fa-bi-ma tubashshirūn, Q. 15:54) with a kasra on the nūn, and they cited the verse:

*You see him like the thughām (a white-flowered plant), perfuming himself with musk, which displeases the lice-pickers when they crush me.*

He intends: فَلَيْنَنِي (falaynanī). The address in His saying "Say" is to the Messenger, or to the listener. The hamza is an interrogative particle accompanied by reproach directed at them. The wāw is the pronoun of the Jews and the Christians. It is also said that it refers to the polytheists of the Arabs, when they said: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from the two towns?" (Q. 43:31). It is also said that it refers to the Jews, the Christians and the polytheists.

Al-muḥājjah here means al-mujādalah (dispute). The meaning is: Do you dispute with us concerning the affair of God and His choosing of the Prophet from among the Arabs rather than from you? You say: "If God had sent down (revelation) to anyone, He would have sent it down to us," and you consider yourselves more deserving of prophethood than us?

﴿And He is our Lord and your Lord﴾: This is a circumstantial clause (jumla ḥāliyya). It means that He is the owner of all of them, so they share in servitude, and He may therefore single out whomever He wills with whatever honour He wills. The meaning is: together with our all acknowledging that we are all servants of one Lord, it is not fitting to dispute over whatever acts He wills, or over the nobility and nearness that He has bestowed on some of His creatures, because He disposes of all of them as an owner disposes of his property. It is also said that the meaning is: Do you dispute with us concerning the religion of God, and say that your religion is the best of religions and your Scripture the best of books?

The apparent meaning is the denial of disputing about God, since the Christians claimed that God is the Messiah, and some of them claimed that God is the third of three, and the Jews claimed that God has a son, and they claimed that He is an old man with white hair and beard, along with what they ascribe to Him of the signs of createdness (ḥudūth) and deficiency. Exalted is God far above that. So He denounced them: how can they claim this, when the Lord is one for all of them? Therefore belief concerning Him must be one, namely that His lofty attributes be affirmed and that He be declared free of createdness and deficiency.

﴿And to us are our deeds, and to you are your deeds﴾: The meaning is: for us is the recompense of our deeds, if good then good, and if evil then evil. The meaning is that the Lord is one, and He is the one who recompenses for deeds, so disputing about Him or quarrelling about Him is not appropriate.

﴿And we are sincere to Him﴾: Having explained the common share of lordship and recompense, He mentions that by which the believers are distinguished: sincerity (ikhlāṣ) to God, the Exalted, in action and belief, and the absence of associating partners (shirk), which exists among the Christians and among the Jews. This is because whoever worships one described with the attributes of createdness and deficiency has associated another god with God. The meaning is: we have not tainted our beliefs and our actions with anything of associating partners, as the Jews claimed regarding the calf and the Christians regarding Jesus. This sentence is of the type of indirect reproach (taʿrīḍ bi-l-dhamm), because mentioning what is specific after mentioning what is shared is a negation of that specific attribute from those who share in the shared matter. It is appropriate that it be a digression (istiṭrād), which is to mention a meaning that implies praise for its doer and blame for its abandoner, such as his saying:

*Indeed we are a people who do not regard killing as a disgrace, when Amir and Salul see it.*

It is a reminder that whoever is sincere to God is worthy that the prophets and the people of nobility be from among them. The sayings of the masters of meanings concerning sincerity are numerous. It is related that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I asked Gabriel about sincerity, what is it? He said: I asked the Lord of Might about sincerity, what is it? He said: It is one of My secrets, which I have deposited in the heart of whoever I love among My servants."

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Sincerity is that one does not associate anyone in his religion and does not show off (riyāʾ) to anyone in his action.

Al-Fudayl said: Abandoning action for the sake of people is showing off, and acting for the sake of people is associating partners, and sincerity is that God protects you from both of them.

Ibn Muʿadh said: Distinguishing the action from the sins is like distinguishing milk from between the dung and the blood.

Al-Bushanji said: It is a meaning that the two angels do not record, the devil does not corrupt, and a human being does not perceive, meaning that no one perceives it except God.

Ruwaym said: It is the elevation of your action above seeing it.

Hudhayfa al-Mar'ashi said: That the actions of the servant be equal in the outward and the inward.

Abu Yaʿqub al-Makfuf said: That the servant conceal his good deeds as he conceals his bad deeds.

Sahl said: It is poverty (iflās), and its meaning is that one returns to belittling the action.

Abu Sulayman al-Darani said: The showy person has three signs: he is lazy when he is alone, he is energetic when he is among people, and he increases in action when he is praised.

This saying, which he (ﷺ) was commanded to say, was said in the manner of compassion and sincere advice in religion, so that they would be alerted to the fact that this dispute from you is not placed in its proper position, nor is it something that ought to be. Our aim in this alert is not to repel harm from you, but our aim is your advice and guidance to purifying your belief from associating partners, and that you be sincere as we have been sincere, so that we are equal in that.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 2, verse 140:**

﴿Or do you say that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes were Jews or Christians?﴾ Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read *taqulūna* with a *tā'* (you say). The rest read it with a *yā'* (they say). As for the reading with *tā'*, the *am* in it may bear two interpretations. The first is that *am* is *muttasilah* (connected, i.e., *am* that links two alternatives, a grammatical term meaning "connected *am*"). The question then concerns which of two matters has occurred: disputing about God, or the claim against Abraham and those mentioned with him that they were Jews and Christians. This is a question accompanied by denial, rebuke and reproach, because each of the two things asked about is untrue. The second interpretation is that *am* is *munqati'ah* (disconnected, a grammatical term meaning "disconnected *am*"), and it is estimated as *bal* plus the interrogative hamzah. The sense is: "Rather, do you say...?" He turns away from the previous sentence and moves to questioning this following sentence, also in denial. That is, the attribution of Judaism and Christianity to Abraham and those mentioned with him is not correct, as witnessed by the true statement that the Truthful One brought in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian﴾ [3:67]; by the testimony of the Torah and the Gospel that they were upon monotheism (*tawhid*) and *hanifiyyah* (pure monotheistic faith); by the testimony that Judaism and Christianity belong to those who followed the path of Jesus; and because what they claim in this regard is a statement without proof, and so it is false.

As for the reading with *yā'*, the apparent view is that *am* here is disconnected. Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari related from some grammarians that it is not disconnected, because when you say: "Do you stand, or does 'Amr stand?" the meaning is: "Would this be or that?" Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this example, namely "Do you stand, or does 'Amr stand?", is not good, because the speaker in it is one and the addressee is one, whereas the statement in the verse comes from two, and the addressees are two different parties. The equation of *am* with the *alif* is only appropriate on the semantic judgment; the meaning would be: Say, "Do you dispute with us?" Would they dispute with you, O Muhammad, or do they say...? End of quotation. The meaning of his words "because the speaker in it is one" refers to the example "Would he stand, or would 'Amr stand?", where the one who utters both clauses is one person. His words "and the addressee is one" refers to the one who is addressed by this speech, and the equation occurred between the standing of the one present in the address and the standing of 'Amr. His words "and the statement in the verse comes from two" mean that "Do you dispute with us?" is from the speech of the Messenger, since he was commanded to address them with it, while "Do you say?" with *tā'* is from the speech of God, exalted is He. His words "and the addressees are two different parties": the first is in "Do you dispute with us?", and the second is the Messenger and his community, who are addressed in "Or do they say?" Al-Zamakhshari said: as for the one who reads with *yā'*, it can only be disconnected. End of quotation. It is possible for it to be connected with the reading of *tā'* as well, and this would be a case of *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person, here from second-person address to third-person reference), since there is a movement from address to absence, and the pronoun refers to specific people. The better view is that *am* in both readings is disconnected. It seems that He denounced them for their disputing about God and for attributing His prophets to Judaism and Christianity, and what He denounced them for had actually occurred. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O People of the Book, why do you dispute about Abraham?﴾ [3:65], and the verses that follow. When we make it connected, this does not include the occurrence of both sentences but only one of them, and the question becomes about specifying one of them; but the matter is not like that, since both occurred together. As for the discussion of *aw* in His saying: ﴿Jews or Christians﴾ [2:111], it has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿And they said: None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾ [2:111]; and His saying: ﴿Be Jews or Christians﴾ [2:135]. It is for distribution (*al-tafdil*, a grammatical term meaning "giving alternatives"), meaning: the Jews said, "They are Jews," and the Christians said, "They are Christians."

﴿Say: Are you more knowing, or is God?﴾ The discussion of the readings of *a-antum* (are you), is as it is in His saying: ﴿Whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [2:6]. The one about whom the question is asked has been placed in the middle here, and this is better than placing it first or last, since in Arabic it is permissible to say: "Are you more knowing, or God?" and it is permissible to say: "Are you, or God, more knowing?" There is no shared knowledge between them and God such that one would ask: "Are they more knowledgeable, or God?" Rather, this is in the manner of mockery and derision toward them, on the assumption that they might be credited with knowledge. This is like the saying of Hassan:

﴿So the evil of you both is the ransom for the better of you both.﴾

He knew that the one who is entirely good is the Messenger, peace be upon him, and that the one who is entirely evil is his satirist. In this there is a refutation of the Jews and the Christians, because God has informed us in His saying: ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was a *hanif*, a Muslim, and he was not of the polytheists﴾ [3:67] [p. 415]; and because Judaism and Christianity only came into existence after Abraham; and because He informed us in the Torah and the Gospel that they were Muslims, distinguished from Judaism and Christianity. This sentence came in the form of something about which there is doubt, because the followers of their rabbis may have imagined or supposed that those ancestors were Jews or Christians, having heard this from them. Thus it would be a refutation from God against them. Or, because their rabbis knew the falsehood of their claim about Abraham and those mentioned with him, but they concealed that and attributed them to what they mentioned. So for their concealment they were placed in the position of one who wavers about the matter, and He refuted them with His saying: "Are you more knowing, or is God?", because whoever is addressed with this speech would hasten to say: "God is more knowing," and so this would be the decisive end of the dispute.

﴿And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from God?﴾ This indicates that they were aware that Abraham and those with him were distinct from Judaism and Christianity, but they concealed this. The discussion of this interrogative form has already been given, and that it is intended as negation. So the meaning is: no one is more unjust than one who conceals. The discussion of the superlative (*af'al al-tafdil*) that comes after *man* in the interrogative has already been given, in His saying: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of God﴾ [2:114]. The one from whom superiority in concealment is negated is the Jews, and it has been said: the hypocrites followed the Jews in concealment. The testimony is that the prophets of God are protected from the false Judaism and Christianity; this was said by al-Hasan, Mujahid and al-Rabi'. Or, it is what is in the Torah concerning the description of Muhammad (ﷺ), his prophethood, and the command to believe in him; this was said by Qatadah and Ibn Zayd. Or, it is Islam, and they knew that it is the truth. The first view is more similar to the context of the verse.

*Min Allah* (from God): It is possible that *min* is connected to the word *katama* (concealed), and this would involve an omitted *mudaf* (a word understood, "servants"), meaning: he concealed from the servants of God a testimony that he had from Him. Its meaning is that He blamed them for preventing it from reaching the servants of God, and for not delivering to them the testimony of truth. It is also possible that *min* is connected to the operator in the adverbial phrase, since the adverbial phrase is in the position of a qualifier, and the estimate is: a testimony that is with him from God, meaning God had made him witness that testimony, and it was with him from God's side, and He entrusted it to him. This is His saying: ﴿And when God took the covenant of those who were given the Book: you must make it clear to the people and not conceal it﴾ [3:187], and so on. Ibn 'Atiyyah said regarding this view: so *min* in this case is connected to *'indahu* (with him), and the accurate position is what we have mentioned, that the operator in the adverbial phrase is what the prepositional phrase depends on, and attributing the dependence to the adverbial phrase is a metaphor. Al-Zamakhshari said: meaning he concealed God's testimony which was with him, that He bore witness to it, and it is His testimony to Abraham regarding *hanifiyyah*. *Min* in His saying "a testimony from God" is like it in your saying: "This is a testimony from me to so-and-so," when you bear witness for him; and similar to it is: ﴿A disavowal from God and His Messenger﴾ [9:1]. End of quotation. The apparent meaning of his words is that "from God" is in the position of a qualifier of "testimony", meaning "which is from God", and this is a third view regarding the operator of *min*. The difference between it and what came before is that in the previous view the operator of the adverbial phrase and of the prepositional phrase is one, while in this view there are two. Making *min* a complement of the operator in the adverbial phrase, or in the position of a qualifier of "testimony", is better than making *min* dependent on *katama*, because it is more emphatic in the superlative of injustice that God should have entrusted the testimony to him and he concealed it. If it depends on *katama*, the superlative of injustice would apply to one who conceals from the servants of God a testimony in an unrestricted sense and hides it from them, and the superlative would not then be valid, because above this testimony there is something in which the superlative of injustice is greater, namely concealing a testimony that God entrusted to him. Therefore we chose that *min* not be connected to *katama*. Al-Zamakhshari said: it can bear two meanings: first, that the People of the Book are not more unjust than them, because they concealed this testimony while knowing it. Second, that if we concealed this testimony, no one would be more unjust than us, so we should not conceal it; and in this there is an allusion to their concealment of God's testimony to Muhammad's prophethood in their books and in all their other testimonies. End of his words. The first meaning is the apparent one, because the verse was preceded by denial concerning what they attributed to Abraham and those with him. What suits is that the speech is with the People of the Book, not with the Messenger (ﷺ) and his followers, because the latter acknowledge what God has informed of, and they know it with certain knowledge, so concealment of that cannot be imagined regarding them.

It is mentioned in *Rayy al-Zam'an* that in the verse there is an inversion, and the estimate is: "And who is more unjust than one who concealed a testimony that came to him?", like your saying: "And who is more unjust than Zayd?", being among the group of those who conceal the testimony. The meaning: if Abraham and his sons were Jews and Christians, then if God concealed this testimony, no one among those who conceal testimony would be more unjust than Him. But since that is impossible given His justice and His being exalted above lying, we know the matter is not so. End of quotation. This view is very forced, both in terms of construction and in terms of meaning. As for construction: its proponent claims the verse is in inverted order, and this would not be found in our view except in poetic necessity. Furthermore, the phrase "of those who conceal" remains dependent either on *azlam* (more unjust), so that it is in the manner of apposition, and in that case it would be an apposition of a general noun from a specific one, and this type is not established in the language of the Arabs according to the majority, although some have claimed that they found apposition of a whole from a part in the language of the Arabs. The majority has interpreted what its apparent meaning would lead to proving such, and treated it as placing the general in the place of the specific, due to the rarity of what has come of that; or it is dependent on something omitted, so it would be in the position of a circumstantial phrase, meaning being from among those who conceal the testimony. As for meaning: the superlative of injustice attached to one who is introduced by *min* would be on the estimate: that is, if he concealed it, then no one is more unjust than him. All of this is a meaning that does not befit God, exalted is He, and the Book of God must be exempt from that.

﴿And God is not unaware of what you do﴾: The discussion of the interpretation of this sentence has already been given at His saying: ﴿And God is not unaware of what you do﴾ [2:74]; "Do you hope" [2:75]. It only comes after the commission of disobedience, so it includes a threat and informs that God does not leave their affair neglected, but rather He records their deeds and will requite them for them.

﴿Those are a nation that has passed away. They shall have what they earned, and you shall have what you earned. And you will not be questioned about what they used to do.﴾: The discussion of the explanation of these clauses has already preceded. They contain the meaning of warning and threat, and this is not a repetition, because that [clause] came after something different from what the first clauses came after. Since that is so, the context differs, so there is no repetition. The clarification of this is that the first [verse] came after the mention of the Prophets, so the demonstrative "those" refers to them. This [second] came after the forefathers of the Jews and Christians, so the one referred to is they. Thus the subject of the statement and the context differ. The meaning is: if the Prophets, despite their excellence and precedence, are repaid for what they earned, then you are more deserving of that. It has been said: the demonstrative "those" refers to Abraham and those mentioned with him. It is considered unlikely that this refers to the forefathers of the Jews and Christians, because no explicit mention of them has preceded. If the demonstrative "those" refers to Abraham and those with him, then the repetition is fine because the statements and the context differ.

These noble verses have included what the Prophets, peace and blessings be upon them, were upon, of calling to God Most High, to the extent that they made this a bequest which they bequeathed one after another. God Most High informed us that Abraham bequeathed his upright religion (al-hanifiyya, the pure monotheistic faith) to his sons, and that Jacob bequeathed the same. He preceded his bequest with God's choosing of this religion for them, so as to ease for them the following of what God had chosen for them, and to encourage them to it. He also commanded them that they should not die except upon it, because actions are judged by their endings. Then He mentioned Jacob's question to his sons about what they would worship after his death, and they answered him with what delighted his eye, namely agreement with him and with his forefathers, the Prophets, in worshipping God alone and submitting to His rulings. The wisdom of this question is that, when he enjoined upon them the upright faith, he asked them to clarify what their hearts harboured, and whether they would accept the bequest. They answered him by accepting it and agreeing with what he loved from them, so that his heart might be at rest and he might know that he had left behind one who would stand in his place in calling to God Most High. Jacob's question came with a rebuke to the Jews and Christians, that they had not witnessed Jacob's bequest, since the signs of death came upon him suddenly. Therefore their claim of Judaism and Christianity regarding Abraham, Jacob and their sons is false, since they were not present at the time of the bequest, and neither their Torah nor their Gospel informed them of it. So their claim is invalid, since it was not obtained either by direct witness or by transmission, nor is it of the kind of matters that can be established by reason.

Then God Most High informed us that that nation has passed on its way, and that it is held accountable for what it earned, just as you are held accountable for your deeds, and that you will not be questioned about them. Then He mentioned what they were upon of false claims, calling to them, and their assumption that guidance lies in following Judaism and Christianity. (p-417) Then He turned away from their speech and began to follow the religion of Abraham, the upright faith, which is distinct from Judaism, Christianity and idolatry. Then He commanded them to declare plainly that they believe in what was sent down to them and to Abraham and those mentioned with him, for belief in that is the upright religion, and that they submit to God in belief and in actions. Then He informed us that if the Jews and Christians agree with you in that belief, then guidance has been attained by them. He made guidance follow from that belief, thereby alerting to the corruption of the arrangement that makes guidance follow from Judaism and Christianity, in His saying: ﴿And they say: Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided.﴾ [al-Baqara 2:135].

Then God Most High informed us that if they turn away, then they are the enemies who oppose you, and that you should not care about their opposition, because God Most High is sufficient for you against them, and whoever God suffices is the victorious one. In this there is an indication of his triumph over them. Then He mentioned that the dye (sibgha) of the upright religion is the dye of God, and if it is the dye of God, then there is no dye better than it. The effect of this dye is its manifestation upon them through worship of God Most High, so He said: ﴿And we are worshippers of Him.﴾ [al-Baqara 2:138]. Then He also questioned them, by way of reproach and rebuke, about their disputing concerning God, while disputing about Him is not becoming, because God is the Lord of us all, and what reason requires is that one should not dispute about Him. Then He mentioned that He is the Lord of all, and indicated that He will recompense all, by His saying: ﴿For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds.﴾ [al-Baqara 2:139]. Then He mentioned what they were singled out for, namely sincerity toward Him, because the Jews and Christians are not sincere toward Him in worship. Then He questioned them again, by way of reproach and rebuke, about their statement concerning Abraham and those mentioned with him, that they were Jews and Christians, while their habit is disputation without right, sometimes concerning God and sometimes concerning the Prophets of God. Then He made clear that they have no knowledge in this, rather God is the most knowing of it. Then He made clear that that statement was not based on evidence or doubt, but was mere obstinacy, and that they were concealers of the truth and deniers of it. So He said, in meaning: none is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony that God has entrusted to him. The meaning is: none is more unjust than you in disputing about God, and in ascribing Judaism and Christianity to Abraham and those mentioned with him, since with them is the testimony from God about their conditions. Then He threatened them that God Most High is not heedless of what they do.

Then He concluded that matter by saying that that nation has passed on, standing alone with its deeds, just as you are so, and that you are not responsible for what they did. These clauses, from the beginning of the mention of Abraham to the end of the discussion about him, despite the variety of its meanings and the multiplicity of its constructions, came as though they were a single sentence, in the beauty of their arrangement and the harmony of their order, rising in eloquence to the summit of excellence, clearly showing that their eloquence is beyond the nature of man, recalling His saying: ﴿Say: If mankind and the jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Qur'an, they would not produce its like.﴾ [al-Isra' 17:88]. May God make us among those who are guided to act by it and to understand it, who are granted the largest share of its reflection, and who are protected in their contemplation from error and delusion.

[p. 418]

**Al-qiblah** (the direction a person faces in prayer): it is the direction that a person faces, and the word derives from *al-muqabalah* (facing). Qutrub said: "They say in their speech, *laysa lahu qiblah*," meaning he has no direction to which he turns. Another said: when two men face each other, each one is the *qiblah* of the other. The word *qiblah* has come, when it is meant as "direction," in the pattern of states (*al-hay'at*), like *al-qi'dah* and *al-jilsah*.

**Al-wasat** (the middle): a noun for what lies between two extremes, and it is applied as an attribute, so it is used for the choicest part of a thing, because the extremities are quickly subject to defect. Because it is a noun, it is used with one form for the singular, the plural, the masculine and the feminine. Habib said: "It was the protected middle, so events surrounded it until it became an extremity."

The middle of a valley (*wasat al-wadi*) is the best place in it, and the one with the most pasture and water. It is said: "So-and-so is among the most central of his people" (*min awsat qawmihi*), and "he is indeed the intermediary of his people" (*lawasitatu qawmihi*), and "the middle of his people" (*wasatu qawmihi*) means among their best and among the people of nobility in them. Zuhayr said:

"They are the middle, whom people are content to have judge them,
when one of the nights of hardship descends upon the great."

And it is said: *wasata* (he was in the middle), *sitatan* and *wasatatan*. He also said:

"Be among people, all of them, a middle one."

As for *wast* (with the *sin* sukun), it is the extremity of a place, and it has rulings mentioned in grammar.

**Adaa'a** (to lose, to neglect): *a-dha'a al-rajulu al-shay'* means he neglected it and did not preserve it. The *hamzah* in it is for causing to transitive from *dha'a yadi'u dada'an*. *Dha'a al-misk yadu'u* means it gave off fragrance.

**Al-inqilab** (turning back): the turning away and the reverting, and it is for reflexive action: "I turned it over, so it turned over."

**'Aqib al-rajul** is well known, and *al-'aqab* means offspring. It is said *'aqib* with the *qaf* sukun.

**Al-ra'fah and al-rahmah** are close in meaning. It is said that *al-ra'fah* is a more intense mercy. The active participle comes for intensity in the pattern *fa'ul* like *darub*, and in the pattern *fa'il* like *hadhir*, and in the pattern *fa'l* like *nads*, and in the pattern *fa'l* like *sa'b*.

**Al-taqallub** (turning over, fluctuation): *al-taraddud*, and it is for reflexive action: "I turned it, so it turned."

**Al-shatr**: the half, a part of a thing, and direction. The poet said:

"Is there anyone who will convey from me a message,
though the message does not avail, toward Amr (*shatra 'Amr*)?"

That is, toward him. Another poet said:

"I say to Umm Zinbaʿ: 'Keep the camels' chests facing toward Banu Tamim.'"

And he said:

"There has overshadowed you from the direction of your frontier
a terror whose darkness covers you in pieces."

Ibn Ahmar said:

"She runs with us toward Najd, while she is tied,
the rope has cut through, from its tightening, the long period."

Another said:

"And I depart with the people toward the kings,"

that is, toward them. And he said:

"Indeed the cattle there has a disease that mixes with it,
and its direction is a gaze of two eyes, bewitched."

It is said *shatara 'anhu* means he went far away, and *shatara ilayhi* means he came toward it. *Al-shatir* among young men is the one far from the neighbors, absent from his home. It is said *shatara shuturan*. *Al-shatir* is the far one; *manzil shatir* means a distant dwelling.

**Al-haram, al-haram and al-hurum**: forbidden, prohibited. The discussion of this was already mentioned in His saying: ﴿And it is forbidden to you to expel them﴾ [2:85].

**Al-imtira'**: a *iftiʿal* form from *al-mirya*, which is doubt. *Amtara fi al-shay'* means he doubted it, and from it comes *al-mira'* (dispute). *Maraytuhu* means I argued with him and cast doubt upon him regarding what he claims. *Iftaʿala* is in the sense of *tafaʿala*. You say: *tamaraynaa* and *imtaraynaa* regarding it, as you say *tahawarna* and *ihtawarna*.

**Wijhah**: some people, among them al-Mazini, al-Mubarrad and al-Farisi, said: *wijhah* is a noun for the place toward which one turns. According to this, the presence of the *waw* is original, since it is a noun and not a verbal noun. Sibawayh said: "If you formed *fi'lah* from the promise, you would say *wi'dah*; if you formed a verbal noun, you would say *'idah*." Some people, among them al-Mazini, as transmitted by al-Mahdawi, went to the view that it is a verbal noun, and this is what appears from Sibawayh's speech. He said, after mentioning the omission of the *waw* from verbal nouns, and they have confirmed it, so they said *wijhah* for *jihah*: according to this, the presence of the *waw* is anomalous, serving as a reminder of the original that has been dropped in verbal nouns. What, in my view, permits the retention of the *waw*, even if it is a verbal noun, is that it is a verbal noun that is not derived from its verb, since *wajaha yajihu* is not known; so the verbal noun is *jihah*. They said: *wa'ada ya'idu 'iddah*, because the reason for dropping the *waw* from *'iddah* is the analogy with the imperfect, for its omission in the imperfect is due to a cause absent in the verbal noun. Since *yajih* is absent and has not been heard, the *waw* was not dropped from *wijhah*, even if it is a verbal noun; because it is not a verbal noun of *yajiha*, but it is a verbal noun with the augments removed, for the verb from it is *tawajjaha* and *ittajaha*. The verbal noun in use is *al-tawajjuh* and *al-ittijah*, and its application to the place toward which one turns is from the category of applying the verbal noun to the noun of the object.

**Al-istibaq** (racing): an *iftiʿal* form from *al-sabq*, which is reaching a thing first. The form *iftaʿala* from it may be either to agree with the bare form, so its meaning and the meaning of *sabaqa* are one, or to agree with *tafaʿala*, so *istabaqa* and *tasabaqa* have one meaning.

**Al-khayrat**: the plural of *khayrah*. It may be built on the pattern *fi'lah* or on the pattern *fay'ilah*, with the letter dropped from it, like *al-mayyitah* and *al-layyinah*. This omission was discussed before. They said: "a man, *khayyir* (good), and a woman, *khayyirah*," just as they said: "a man, *sharr* (evil), and a woman, *sharrah*." These two, in that case, are not the comparative form (*af'al al-tafdil*).

**Al-ju'** (hunger): drought. As for the need for food, its name is *al-gharath*. It is said: *gharitha yaghrathu gharthan*, so he is *gharith* and *gharthan*. The poet said:

"Lean, bluish-eyed, as if their eyes
from the fatigue and the signaling are the flowers of *'adrasan*."

Later scholars have used *al-gharth* to mean hunger in an extended sense.

* *

﴿The foolish among the people will say: "What has turned them away from their qiblah which they were facing?"﴾: The occasion of revelation of this verse is what al-Bukhari transmitted from al-Bara' ibn Azib, who said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to Madinah, he prayed facing Bayt al-Maqdis for sixteen or seventeen months. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ loved to face the Ka'bah, so Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿We see the turning of your face toward the heaven﴾ [2:144], and so on. Then the foolish among the people, and they are the Jews, said: "What has turned them away from their qiblah which they were facing?" So Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: To Allah belong the east and the west﴾, and so on.

(The connection of this verse) with what precedes it: the Jews and the Christians said that Abraham and those mentioned with him were Jews and Christians. They mentioned that as a slander against Islam, because abrogation (*naskh*, the replacement of one ruling by another) is false according to the Jews, so they said: "turning away from our qiblah is false and foolishness." Allah the Exalted refuted that against them by His saying: ﴿Say: To Allah belong the east and the west﴾, and so on, so He made clear what was guidance and what was foolishness.

"Will say" (*sayaqulu*) is apparent in the future, and it is a report from Allah the Exalted to His Prophet ﷺ that this statement will proceed from them in the future, and that is before they were commanded to face the Ka'bah. This verse will be revealed before the verse containing the command to face the Ka'bah, so it will be from the category of reporting a thing before it occurs, so that it is a miracle, since it is a report of the unseen. It also serves so that the soul may prepare itself for what comes from the enemies and be ready for it, so that it will have less effect than when it comes suddenly without prior knowledge; and so that the answer will be ready for one who denies it, which is His saying: ﴿Say: To Allah belong the east and the west﴾. This view was held by al-Zamakhshari and others.

Some people went to the view that it precedes in recitation but follows in revelation, and that His saying ﴿We see the turning of your face﴾ [2:144] and so on was revealed first, then ﴿The foolish among the people will say﴾ was revealed. Ibn Abbas and others stated this. The hadith of al-Bara' mentioned earlier, which al-Bukhari transmitted, indicates and confirms this. If that is so, then the meaning of His saying "will say" is that they continue upon this statement, and although they had already said it, the wisdom of the future tense is that, just as this statement proceeded from them in the past, so they will also say it in the future. We do not have anyone who placed the future in the position of the past. The meaning of "will say" is not "said," as some claimed, because that is not possible with the *sin*, due to the remoteness of the metaphor in it. Had it been without the *sin*, that would have been closer, and it would have been a narration of a past state.

The foolish (*al-sufaha'*) are the Jews, as said by al-Bara' ibn Azib, Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr. The people of Makkah said: "Muhammad has longed for his birthplace, and soon he will return to your religion," narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas, and al-Zajjaj preferred it. Or the hypocrites said it, as a mockery of the Muslims, mentioned by al-Suddi from Ibn Mas'ud. The naming of the hypocrites as foolish has occurred in His saying: ﴿Surely it is they who are the foolish﴾ [2:13]. Or they are the three groups mentioned before among the people.

Ibn Atiyyah and others said: He specified with His saying "from among the people," because *safah* (foolishness) originally means lightness, and it is used to describe inanimate things. They said: "a *thawb safih*," meaning a garment of light weave and thin texture, and "a *rumh safih*," meaning light and swift in penetration. It is also used to describe animals other than people. So if it were restricted to it without specification, it would include people and others, because speech is attributed to people in the literal sense and to others metaphorically. The metaphor is removed by His saying: ﴿from among the people, what turned them away﴾, that is, what turned them, and the pronoun refers to the Prophet ﷺ and the believers, away from their qiblah. He attributed the qiblah to them because they had faced it for a long time, so the attribution is valid.

The scholars of tafsir are unanimous that this change of direction was from Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) to the Ka'bah. Some exegetes have related it thus, but it is not a consensus. Rather, a group has held that the qiblah from which the change was criticised, the one he was turned away from to another, is the Ka'bah itself, and that he used to pray towards it when prayer was prescribed, because it was the qiblah of his father Ibrahim (Abraham). When he turned towards Bayt al-Maqdis, the people of Makkah said, criticising and reproaching him: ﴿What has turned them away from their qiblah which they were upon?﴾ This is an elision of a modifier, i.e. "from facing it." The use of "ista'la" (over, upon) here is metaphorical, and its wisdom for them is their constancy in carrying out God's command to observe the prayers. The qiblah became for them like a thing one is upon, constantly attached. In describing the qiblah with the words ﴿which they were upon﴾ there is an indication of the firmness of facing it and their perseverance in that. The pronoun in "qiblatihim" (their qiblah) and "kanu" (they were) refers to the believers. It has also been said that the pronoun may refer to the foolish ones (al-sufaha'), for they knew only the qiblah of the Jews, which was towards the west, and the qiblah of the Christians, which was towards the east, while the Arabs had no prayer, so they would face none of the directions. When he turned towards the Ka'bah, they found this strange and said: "How does he turn to other than these two well-known directions?" They differed regarding the facing of Bayt al-Maqdis: was it by a recited revelation? Or by a command from God that was not recited? Or by God giving His Messenger the choice among the directions? He chose Bayt al-Maqdis; this is the view of al-Rabi'. Or was it by his own ijtihad (independent reasoning) without revelation; this is the view of al-Hasan, Ikrimah and Abu al-'Aliyah. Sayings: the first, from Ibn 'Abbas, who is related to have said: "The first thing abrogated (nusikha) of the Qur'an was the qiblah." Likewise they differed regarding the period during which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) prayed towards Bayt al-Maqdis: it is said sixteen months, or seventeen months. It is said nine, or ten months. It is said thirteen months. It is said: from the time the five prayers were prescribed and he led them behind Jibril, following the Night Journey, and that was on the night of the seventeenth of Rabi' al-Akhir, one year before the Hijrah; then he migrated in Rabi' al-Awwal, and he continued praying towards Bayt al-Maqdis until Rajab of the second year. It is said: until Jumada. It is said: until the middle of Sha'ban. It has been related that "he (ﷺ) prayed two rak'ahs of Dhuhr, then turned with the last two towards the Ka'bah." This verse has been cited as evidence for the permissibility of the abrogation of the Sunnah by the Qur'an, since his prayer towards Bayt al-Maqdis is not based on any Qur'anic text. It has also been cited as evidence against the view of those who claim that abrogation is a change of mind (bada'). ﴿Say: To God belong the east and the west﴾: the command is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and in it is an instruction to him (ﷺ) on how to refute their claim and reject their objection. The meaning: all directions belong to God, Exalted, who obligates His servants to face whichever of them He wills and to make it a qiblah. The discussion of the phrase ﴿To God belong the east and the west﴾ has already preceded, so it suffices here without repetition. He explained "the east" as Bayt al-Maqdis and "the west" as the Ka'bah, because the Ka'bah is west of Bayt al-Maqdis, so necessarily Bayt al-Maqdis is east of it. ﴿He guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾: that is, whom He wills to guide. The discussion of something resembling this sentence has already preceded in His words ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fatihah: 6], so it suffices without repeating it. It has been established that "huda" (guide) takes the preposition "li-", "ila" and directly, and here it is construed with "ila." They differed regarding the prayer in which the qiblah was changed: it is said Subh (dawn), it is said Zuhr (midday), it is said 'Asr (afternoon). Likewise they have multiplied discussion of the wisdom for which the change of qiblah occurred, with matters for which no evidence stands in their soundness, and they have ascribed it to causes the Shari'ah did not indicate, nor did sound reason lead to. We have therefore left the transmission of that out of this book, in keeping with our custom in this. Whoever seeks rationalisations for conventional matters is more likely to have little correctness and much error. As for what the Shari'ah has stated the wisdom of, or indicated, or what sound reflection leads to, that is what one must not deviate from, and no benefit is to be drawn except from it. His words "a straight path" have been explained as the qiblah, which is the Ka'bah. The apparent meaning is the religion of Islam and its laws, and the Ka'bah is among its prescribed matters.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 143 (part 1 of 3):**

﴿وكَذَلِكَ جَعَلْناكم أُمَّةً وسَطًا﴾ ("And thus We made you a justly balanced community"): الكافُ (al-kaf) is for comparison, and ذَلِكَ is a demonstrative. The كاف is in the accusative position, either because it is an adjective (نَعْت) of a deleted verbal noun (مَصْدَر), or because it is a circumstantial qualifier (حال). The meaning is: "And We made you a justly balanced community, making it in the manner of that." The demonstrative ذَلِكَ does not refer to anything previously mentioned explicitly, since no noun preceding this sentence is pointed to by ذَلِكَ.
