However, the verb يَهْدِي ("guides") has preceded, and it indicates a verbal noun, which is الهُدى (guidance). It has become clear that the meaning of ﴿يَهْدِي مَن يَشاءُ إلى صِراطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:142: "He guides whom He wills to a straight path") is: He makes him upon a straight path, as He said: ﴿مَن يَشَأِ اللَّهُ يُضْلِلْهُ ومَن يَشَأْ يَجْعَلْهُ عَلى صِراطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ﴾ (Al-An'am 6:39: "Whomever Allah wills to leave astray, He leaves him astray; and whomever He wills, He puts him upon a straight path"). He contrasted misguidance with being placed upon the straight path, because that placing is itself the guidance; so the meaning of guidance here is that very placing. It has also become clear from His saying: ﴿قُلْ لِلَّهِ المَشْرِقُ والمَغْرِبُ﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:142: "Say: To Allah belong the east and the west") to the end, that Allah made their qibla better than the qibla of the Jews and Christians, or made it a middle (وَسَط) qibla. Given these possibilities, the scholars differed over what ذَلِكَ refers to.

It was said: the meaning is that He compared their being made a justly balanced community to His guiding them to the straight path. That is: We have bestowed upon you by making you a justly balanced community, just as We previously bestowed upon you by guiding you to the straight path. In this case, the demonstrative ذَلِكَ refers to the verbal noun indicated by يَهْدِي, meaning: We made you a community of the best, just as We guided you by following Muhammad (ﷺ) and what he brought of the truth.

It was said: the meaning is that He compared their being made a justly balanced community to their being placed upon the straight path. That is: We made you a justly balanced community, in the manner of that remarkable placing in which lies your being singled out for guidance, because He said: "He guides whom He wills," so guidance does not occur except for whom Allah wills.

It was said: the meaning is: just as We made your qibla the best of qiblas, We made you the best of nations.

It was said: the meaning is: just as We made your qibla intermediate between the east and the west, We made you a justly balanced community.

It was said: the meaning is: just as We made the Ka'bah the center of the earth, so too We made you a justly balanced community, below the prophets and above the (other) nations.

And the one who went furthest in saying that this demonstrative refers to His saying: ﴿ولَقَدِ اصْطَفَيْناهُ في الدُّنْيا﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:130: "And We had certainly chosen him in this world") — that is, "In the manner of that choosing, We made you a justly balanced community" — is the most distant of interpretations.

The meaning of وَسَطًا ("justly balanced") is: upright (عُدُولًا). This was narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the wording of the commentators is unanimous on it. When this is authentically reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), it is obligatory to rely upon it in explaining the word وَسَط.

It was also said: "best" (خِيارًا), or: "balanced in religion, between the excessive and the deficient, who did not take any of the prophets as a deity as the Christians did, nor did they kill them as the Jews did."

The majority of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist theological school) used this verse to argue that the consensus (إجْماع, ijma') of the community is a proof. They said: Allah informed us of the uprightness of this community and of its excellence; so if they undertake something, their view must be a proof.

﴿لِتَكُونُوا شُهَداءَ عَلى النّاسِ﴾ ("That you may be witnesses over the people"): The explanation of testimony (الشَّهادَة) was already given in His saying: ﴿وادْعُوا شُهَداءَكُمْ﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:23: "And call your witnesses"). Regarding their testimony here, there are several opinions:

The first: what the majority hold, that it is in the Hereafter, namely the testimony of this community for the prophets against their peoples who denied them. This has been narrated explicitly in a hadith in al-Bukhari and others. The author of al-Muntakhab said: "The qadi (judge) has attacked the hadith from several angles, and they mentioned weak aspects." I suspect that by "the qadi" here he means the qadi ʿAbd al-Jabbar the Mu'tazilite, because attacking an authentic, sound hadith does not suit the doctrines of Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah).

It was said: the testimony takes place in this world. Those who said this differed. It was said: the meaning is that some of you testify against others when they die, as came in the hadith that a funeral bier passed by, and good was said about it, and another passed by, and bad was said about it; so the Messenger said: "It is obligatory" — meaning Paradise and Hell — "You are the witnesses of Allah on earth." This is established in Muslim.

It was said: testimony means argumentation (الِاحْتِجاج), that is, that you may be those who argue against the people; this was related by al-Zajjaj.

It was said: its meaning is that you may convey to them what you have known of the revelation and the religion, as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conveyed it.

The particle عَلى ("over") may have the meaning of لِ ("for"), as in His saying: ﴿وما ذُبِحَ عَلى النُّصُبِ﴾ (Al-Ma'idah 5:3: "and what is slaughtered on the stone altars"), meaning "for the stone altars."

It was said: its meaning is that your consensus may be a proof, and that the Messenger may be a witness over you, that is, one who argues against you through the conveying (of the message).

It was said: that you may be witnesses for Muhammad (ﷺ) over the nations, the Jews, the Christians, and the Magians; this was said by Mujahid.

It was said: witnesses over the people in this world, concerning matters that are not valid except by the testimony of upright, good people. The causes of this testimony, that is, the testimony of these upright people, are four: by direct observation, like testimony regarding fornication; by the report of a truthful person, like testimony upon testimony; by widespread reputation, like testimony regarding lineages; and by indication, like testimony regarding ownership of property, and like the vouching for a witness and the impeaching of him.

Ibn Duraid said: the causes of "calling to witness" are four: the angels, by recording the deeds of the servants; the prophets; the community of Muhammad; and the limbs (of the body). End of quotation.

Since there is a strong resemblance between seeing with the eye and perceiving with insight, the perception of insight was called "witnessing" (مُشاهَدَة) and "shuhud," and the one who has gnosis was called "witness" (شاهِد) and "one who witnesses" (مُشاهِد). Then indicating something was called "testimony" over it, because it is what makes the witness a witness. This term has become specialized in the usage of the Sharia for one who reports on the rights of people using specific wordings in specific ways.

They said: in this verse there is evidence that the basic position regarding Muslims is uprightness (ʿadalah). This is the position of Abu Hanifah, and he argued from His saying: ﴿أُمَّةً وسَطًا﴾ ("a justly balanced community"), that is, upright and excellent. The rest of the scholars said: uprightness is an accidental attribute that is not established except by evidence. The later scholars among the companions of Abu Hanifah chose what the majority held, because the conditions of people had changed and because of what prevailed among them at this time. This disagreement applies outside of the hudud (fixed punishments) and qisas (retaliation).

﴿ويَكُونَ الرَّسُولُ عَلَيْكم شَهِيدًا﴾ ("And that the Messenger may be a witness over you"): There is no disagreement that the Messenger here is Muhammad (ﷺ). Regarding his testimony there are several opinions:

The first: his testimony over them that he conveyed the message of his Lord to them.

The second: his testimony over them concerning their faith.

The third: he will be a proof over them.

The fourth: his vouching for them and his declaring them upright; this was said by ʿAta'. He said: "This community are witnesses over whoever among the people abandoned the truth, all of them, and the Messenger is a witness who declares them upright and vouches for them." A hadith has been related regarding this. The hadith that al-Bukhari related on this has also been mentioned earlier.

The lam in His saying "that you may be" (لِتَكُونُوا) is the lam of purpose (لامُ كَيْ), or, according to those who hold that view, the lam of result (لامُ الصَّيْرُورَة). So the coming of what follows it is a cause for making them the best or upright in a clear way. As for the testimony of the Messenger over them being a cause for making them the best, this is also clear, because if the testimony means vouching, or whatever meaning it is explained by, then there is in that complete honor for them, since the most noble of creatures is the one who testifies over them.

Since the witness is like a watcher over the one for whom he testifies, the word عَلى ("over") was used, and the prepositional phrase عَلى النّاسِ ("over the people") was placed after what it governs. This is according to the original order, since the governing element should originally precede what it governs. As for His saying: ﴿عَلَيْكم شَهِيدًا﴾ ("a witness over you"), the prepositional phrase was placed before it as a stylistic broadening for eloquence, and also because شَهِيدًا resembles the rhyme-endings and final sounds of عَلَيْكم, so شَهِيدًا completes the sentence, and its final sound is not عَلَيْكم.

As for what al-Zamakhshari held, that the placing of عَلى first is because the purpose there is to establish their testimony over the nations, and the delaying of عَلى is for singling them out by the Messenger being a witness over them, this is based on his doctrine that the fronting of the object and the prepositional phrase indicates restriction (الِاخْتِصاص). [p. 423] We have already mentioned the invalidity of that earlier, and that it is a claim for which no proof stands.

The reason for making them balanced by their being witnesses was mentioned earlier, and the causal clause about the testimony of the Messenger was placed later, because that is how it occurs. Do you not see that they testify over the nations, and then the Messenger testifies over them? This is according to what is stated in the hadith: when the nations deny their messengers, and the community of Muhammad testifies against them that the message was conveyed, Muhammad (ﷺ) will be brought and asked about the condition of his community, and he will vouch for them and testify to their truthfulness.

If the two testimonies are interpreted in other ways than this, in ways in which the Messenger's testimony could be earlier in time, then the delaying of the mention of the Messenger's testimony is for ascending in rank, since the Messenger's testimony over them is more noble than their testimony over the people.

He used the word "the Messenger" because of what the designation by the word "Messenger" indicates of his being characterized by the mission from Allah to his community.

He used the plural form فُعَلاء, which is the plural of فَعِيل, together with شَهِيد, because that is for emphasis (المُبالَغَة), unlike saying شاهِدِينَ ("witnesses"), or إشْهادًا, or شاهِدًا.

His saying "and that the Messenger may be a witness over you" has been used as evidence that vouching (التَّزْكِيَة) requires the acceptance of testimony, for most of the commentators said: the meaning of شَهِيدًا is "vouching for you," and they said: عَلَيْكم here means "for you" (لَكم).

* *

﴿وما جَعَلْنا القِبْلَةَ الَّتِي كُنْتَ عَلَيْها إلّا لِنَعْلَمَ مَن يَتَّبِعُ الرَّسُولَ مِمَّنْ يَنْقَلِبُ عَلى عَقِبَيْهِ﴾ ("And We did not make the qibla which you were upon except that We might know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels"): جَعَلَ ("made") here has the meaning of صَيَّرَ ("transformed into"), so it takes two objects: the first is القِبْلَة ("the qibla"), and the second is ﴿الَّتِي كُنْتَ عَلَيْها﴾ ("which you were upon"). The meaning is: We did not transform your present qibla, the direction which you were upon at first, except that We might know, that is, we did not transform your current orientation in prayer from the orientation you had at first; for he used to pray at first toward the Ka'bah, then he prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis, then he again began to pray toward the Ka'bah.

According to this reading, القِبْلَة is the second object and الَّتِي كُنْتَ عَلَيْها is the first object, since transformation is a movement from one state to another. So the one who is clothed in the first state is the first object, and the one clothed in the second state is the second object. Do you not see that you say: "I made the clay into pottery," and "I made the ignorant one into a scholar"? The meaning here according to this interpretation is: We did not make the Ka'bah, which was your qibla at first, and then you were turned away from it toward Bayt al-Maqdis, your qibla now, except that We might know.

Al-Zamakhshari erred in this, claiming that الَّتِي كُنْتَ عَلَيْها is the second object of جَعَلَ. He said: "الَّتِي كُنْتَ عَلَيْها" is not an adjective of the qibla; rather it is the second of the two objects of جَعَلَ. He means: "We did not make the qibla, the direction which you were upon, which is the Ka'bah, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to pray in Makkah toward the Ka'bah, then after the Hijrah he was commanded to pray toward the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis, to win over the Jews, then he was turned back to the Ka'bah." So he says: "We did not make the qibla which you must face the direction which you were upon at first in Makkah," meaning: "We did not return you to it except as a test and a trial for the people." End of what he mentioned.

[p. 423]

Abu Hayyan has already explained that the phrase ﴿that which you were upon﴾ is the first object (al-maf'ul al-awwal, the first direct object of the verb). It has also been said that this verse explains the wisdom behind making Bayt al-Maqdis the qibla (the direction of prayer). The meaning is: "We did not make the direction you faced, Bayt al-Maqdis, except so that We might know," so that your facing Bayt al-Maqdis is a temporary matter, by which the one who is firm in his religion is distinguished from the apostate. Each of the Ka'bah and Bayt al-Maqdis is suitable to be described by the phrase ﴿that which you were upon﴾, because he had faced each of them at two different times. It has also been said that ﴿that which you were upon﴾ is an adjective (sifah) of the qibla. On this reading, the scholars differ about the second object. It has been said that its estimated form is: "We did not make the qibla that you were upon a qibla except so that We might know." It has also been said that the estimated form is: "We did not make the qibla that you were upon abrogated except so that We might know." It has also been said that this is by omitting a modifier (hadhf mudaf), meaning: "We did not make the turning away from the qibla that you were upon except so that We might know," and in this case the second object is the phrase ﴿so that We might know﴾, just as you say: "The striking of Zayd is for discipline," meaning "it exists and is present for discipline," i.e., because of discipline.

When ﴿that which﴾ is an adjective, it is possible that by the qibla is meant the Ka'bah, and it is possible that by it is meant Bayt al-Maqdis, since each of them is described as being the one he was upon. Ibn 'Abbas said: The qibla in the verse is the Ka'bah, and the word "kuntа" (you were) means "anta" (you are), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿you are the best nation﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:110), meaning "antum" (you are). End of quotation. This statement from Ibn 'Abbas, if it is authentic, is an explanation of meaning, not an explanation of grammatical analysis (i'rab), because it would amount to the addition of "kana" (was), which raises the subject and governs the predicate, and no one has held this view. The grammatical explanation under this reading is what the grammarians have transmitted: that "kana" can mean "sara" (became). Whoever has become something and has taken on its attribute, it is correct in meaning to ascribe that thing to him. So when you say, "I became knowledgeable," it is correct to say, "You are knowledgeable," because you are informing about him with something that he has become. Thus Ibn 'Abbas's explanation, that "kuntа" means "anta," is of this type; it is an explanation of meaning, not of i'rab. Likewise, whoever has become "the best nation," it is correct to say of him, "You are the best nation."

﴿so that We might know﴾: this is an exceptive construction (istithna' mufarragh) from the object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), and it contains a restriction of the cause, meaning: the cause of changing the qibla was nothing but this. The apparent meaning of "so that We might know" is the beginning of knowledge, but this is not the intended meaning, since the occurrence of God's knowledge is impossible. So it is interpreted by omitting a modifier, meaning: "so that Our Messenger and the believers might know," and the knowledge of them is attributed to Himself, because they are His elect and those brought near to Him. This is then either figurative omission (majaz al-hadhf), or omission, or the use of "knowledge" in the sense of "distinguishing," since distinguishing takes place through knowledge, meaning: "so that We might distinguish the follower from the one who turns back," as He said, exalted is He: ﴿until He separates the wicked from the good﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:179). In this case it is figurative usage of mentioning the cause while meaning the effect (majaz idlaq al-sabab, wa yurad bihi al-musabbab). This interpretation has been related from Ibn 'Abbas. Or it is said that he intended to mention His knowledge at the time they conform to obedience or disobedience, since reward and punishment depend on that time. So the meaning is not "that We might bring about knowledge," but "that We might know that to be existent," for God had already known from eternity who would follow the Messenger. The knowledge continued until their actual occurrence, continued at the time of following and turning back, and continued after that. God, exalted is He, is described in all of that as knowing. In this case, the word "knowledge" is a metonymy (kinayah) for the attachment of knowledge, meaning: "so that Our knowledge might be attached to that at the time of its existence." Or it is said that by knowledge he intended confirmation, meaning: "so that We might confirm the follower," and this is the mention of the cause while meaning the effect, because whoever God knows to be a follower of the Messenger is firm in following. Or it is said that by knowledge is intended the recompense, meaning: "so that We might recompense the obedient and the disobedient." The threat is very often expressed in the Qur'an and in the speech of the Arabs by mentioning knowledge, as when you say: "Zayd knows what you did," and the meaning is: "I will requite him for that." Or it is said that the future tense here is intended as the past, the estimated form being: "since We knew," or "for Our knowledge of who follows the Messenger among those who oppose." All of these are interpretations of ﴿so that We might know﴾, to avoid the occurrence and renewal of knowledge, since that is impossible for God. Every occurrence in the Qur'an that indicates this is interpreted in the way that suits it from among these interpretations.

Here "na'lam" (we know) is transitive to one object, which is the relative pronoun, so it is in the accusative position, and the verb after it is its relative clause (silah). Some people have said: here "na'lam" is suspended (mu'allaqah), as when you say: "I knew whether Zayd is in the house or 'Amr," as related by al-Zamakhshari. On this view, "man" is an interrogative in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), and it governs in the genitive position, and the clause is in the position of the object of "na'lam." This grammatical view has been rejected on the grounds that if "na'lam" is suspended, nothing remains for the phrase ﴿who turns back﴾ to be connected with, because what follows an interrogative cannot be connected to what precedes it, and its connection to "yattabi'" (follows), which is the predicate of the interrogative "man," is not valid, because the meaning does not lie that way. The meaning is that it is connected to "na'lam," as when you say: "I knew who had done good to you from among those who had done evil to you." This strengthens the view that by knowledge is meant distinguishing and separating, since knowledge is not transitive with "min" (from) unless distinguishing is intended, because it is distinguishing that is transitive with "min."

Al-Zuhri read ﴿li-yu'lam﴾ (so that it might be known), with the verb in the passive form whose subject is unnamed. This needs no interpretation, since the agent may be other than God, exalted is He. It is omitted and the verb is built in the passive, and the knowledge of other than God is created (hadith), so it is correct to give the reason for the making with a created knowledge. The estimated form would be: "so that the Messenger and the believers might know." He used the word "the Messenger" and did not continue in the same address as in His saying ﴿that which you were upon﴾, so the speech would have been "whoever follows you," because of what the word "messenger" contains of the indication of the message. The address came enclosing the mention of the Messenger twice, for what that contains of eloquence and variety in rhetoric, and so that it be known that the one addressed is the one described with the message. Since witnessing and being followed are among the divine matters specifically, He used the word "the Messenger" to show that this is specific to pure conveyance. Since facing the Ka'bah is facing a place to which a person is accustomed, and he has an inclination toward it, He used the address without the word "messenger," so it was said: ﴿that which you were upon﴾. So this, God knows best, is the wisdom of the iltifat (shift of address) here.

His saying ﴿turns back on his heels﴾ is a metonymy (kinayah) for returning from what he had been in of faith or occupation. Turning back on one's heels is the worst state of one returning while walking on his face, so the apostate in religion is likened to it. The meaning is: he had been clothed in faith, but when the qibla was changed, he doubted and returned to disbelief. This is a figurative turning back (inqilab ma'nawi), while the literal turning back is returning to the place from which one came out.

* *

His saying ﴿on his heels﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: turning back on his heels. Its meaning is that he returned to what he had been upon; in his return he did not fail to go back from where he came to the first state in which he had been. He has turned away from what he had turned toward, and walked back along the path he had previously taken. That is an intensification of being entangled with the thing that leads him to the state in which he had been first. They said: The scholars have differed about whether this trial occurred because of the appointment of the qibla or because of its change. It has been said the first: since he used to pray toward the Ka'bah, then he prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis, and that was hard for the Arabs because he had abandoned their qibla, then he prayed toward the Ka'bah, and that was hard for the Jews because he had abandoned their qibla. Most scholars held the second view, and they said: If Muhammad had been certain of his matter, his opinion would not have changed. It is related that some people who had embraced Islam returned and said: "One time here, one time there." This view is more likely, because the doubt concerning the matter of abrogation (naskh) is greater than the doubt occurring from the appointment of the qibla, and God has described it as great in His saying: ﴿and indeed it was a great matter﴾.

Ibn Abi Ishaq read ﴿'ala 'aqibayhi﴾ with the qaf (q) sukun, and the sukun of the 'ayn of the pattern fa'ila, whether a noun or a verb, is a Tamimi dialect form, and this has been mentioned previously.

﴿And indeed it was a great matter, except for those whom God guided﴾: the subject of "kanat" (it was) is a pronoun referring to the turning away from Bayt al-Maqdis toward the Ka'bah, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Qatadah. Its verification from the standpoint of Arabic grammar is that it refers to the verbal noun (masdar) understood from His saying ﴿We did not make the qibla﴾, meaning: "and indeed the making was a great matter." Or it refers to the qibla that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to face, which was Bayt al-Maqdis before the change, as said by Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Akhfash. It has been said that it refers to the prayer that they had prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis. The meaning of "great" (kabirah) is difficult and hard, and the reason for its difficulty is that this is contrary to custom, since whoever is accustomed to something and then moves away from it finds the moving difficult, or that it requires knowledge of abrogation, its permissibility, and its occurrence.

Here "in" (inn, if) is the lightened form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy "inna," and it enters upon the nominal clause that has been abrogated (al-jumlah al-nasikhah, i.e., the clause introduced by "inna"). The lam is the lam of distinction between the negative "in" and the lightened form of the heavy "inna," and whether it is the lam of the beginning (lam al-ibtida') that was made obligatory for the distinction, or is a lam brought in for the distinction, is a matter of disagreement. This is the view of the Basrans, al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', and Qutrub regarding "inna," which the Basrans say is a lightened form of the heavy one, and it is a known disagreement in grammar. The reading of the majority is ﴿kabirah﴾ in the accusative, on the basis that it is the predicate of "kanat." Al-Yazidi read ﴿kabirah﴾ in the nominative, and al-Zamakhshari explained this as an additional "kanat," with the estimated form: "and indeed it is great." This is weak, because the superfluous "kana" has no governing effect, and here the pronoun is attached to it, so it governs it, which is why it has a hidden pronoun in it. Abu Sa'id disagreed, claiming that when it is superfluous it governs the pronoun referring to the verbal noun understood from it, meaning that it is "huwa" (he), i.e., the being. This has been refuted in the science of grammar. Likewise, one disputes the view of whoever claims that "kana" is superfluous in the saying:

"And neighbors of ours, who were noble,"

because the pronoun is attached to it and the verb governs it. What should be adopted for this reading is that ﴿kabirah﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, the estimated form being: "lahi kabirah" (indeed it is great). The lam of distinction has entered upon a clause in estimation, and that clause is the predicate of "kanat." This explanation is also weak, and it is an explanation of anomaly (shudhdh).

﴿except for those whom God guided﴾: this is an exception from an omitted antecedent of exception, since the estimated form is: "and indeed it was a great matter for people, except for those whom God guided." It is not said of this that it is an exceptive construction of the mufarragh type, because no negation or implied negation has preceded it; rather, an affirmative has preceded it. The meaning of "God guided" is: He guided them to follow the Messenger, or He preserved them and they were guided by His guidance, or He created for them the guidance which is faith in their hearts, or He enabled them to the truth and made them firm in faith. These are closely related statements. It involves ascribing guidance to God, meaning that the absence of difficulty in that comes only by God's enabling, not from their own selves, for He is the one who enabled them to His guidance.

[p. 424]

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 143 (part 3 of 3):

﴿And Allah would never let your faith be lost﴾: It was said: the occasion of revelation of this is that a group died before the change of the qibla (direction of prayer), so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about them, and this was revealed. It was also said: the questioners were As'ad ibn Zurarah and al-Bara' ibn Ma'rur with a group, and this is problematic, because it has been narrated that As'ad ibn Zurarah and al-Bara' ibn Ma'rur died before the change of the qibla. "Faith" has been interpreted as prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), and al-Bukhari and al-Tirmidhi mentioned this, and Ibn 'Abbas, al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, Qatadah, al-Suddi, al-Rabi' and others said so. He referred to prayer by "faith" because it proceeds from faith, and it is among its great branches. It is also possible that "faith" is kept to its literal meaning, since it includes belief during the time of prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis and during the time of the change. He mentioned faith, although the question was about the prayer of those who prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis, because it is the pillar and that by which deeds are valid. Faith had been established for them during their orientation toward Bayt al-Maqdis and otherwise, so Allah, exalted is He, informed that He does not let their faith be lost, and under it fall its related matters, which are not valid except by it. Mentioning faith was preferable to mentioning prayer, lest one imagine that the prayer of the hypocrites toward Bayt al-Maqdis is included. He used the address form, although the question was about those who died, by way of predominance (taghlib), because not all who prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis had died. Al-Dahhak read "liyudayyi'a" (with a fatha on the dad and a shadda on the ya'), and "adha'a" and "day-ya'a" are both (from) the hamza and the doubling for transitivity (naql), since the root of the word is "da'a". Al-Muntakhab said: "Were it not for mentioning the occasion of revelation of this verse, the speech would not be connected, part to part." The point of the difficulty is this: those who do not allow naskh (abrogation) except with bada' (a change of divine decision) say: when the ruling changed, it must be that the ruling was either corrupt or void; so there came into their hearts, based on this question, that those prayers they performed while facing Bayt al-Maqdis were lost. Allah, exalted is He, answered this difficulty and showed that abrogation is a transfer from one benefit to another and from one obligation to another, and the first is like the second in that the one who adheres to it is upright. End of quotation.

If the doubt arose only from those who permit bada' upon Allah, how is that fitting for the Companions? The answer is that it arises only from a hypocrite, so He informed about the answer to the hypocrite's question; or it is answered on the assumption that such a thought might pass through the mind of a Companion, or on the assumption that he believed facing the Ka'bah to be superior. As for what al-Muntakhab mentioned, that were it not for mentioning the occasion of revelation of this verse the speech would not be connected, it is not correct; rather, the speech is connected, whether or not the occasion of revelation is authentic. That is because when His saying was mentioned, ﴿so that We may know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels﴾, this was a division of people at the time of the change into two groups: one who follows the Messenger and one who turns back. So He informed that He does not let the faith of the follower be lost, rather his action and his belief, both before the qibla was changed and after it was changed; Allah does not waste it, since He is the one who imposes whatever obligations He wills, so whoever complies with them, He does not waste his reward. Since it may come to mind to inquire about the state of faith of those who followed the Messenger in both states, He informed that He does not waste it, and He used "kana" negated with "ma", followed by the lam of denial (lam al-juhud), because that is more emphatic than not using the lam of denial. So your saying, "ma kana Zaydun liyaqum" (Zayd was not about to stand), is more emphatic than "kana Zaydun yaqumu" (Zayd used to stand); because in the first example it is a negation of readiness and intention to stand, and in the second it is a negation of standing. The negation of readiness and intention for an act is more emphatic than the negation of the act, because negating the act does not necessitate negating the intention to do it, whereas negating readiness, suitability and intention for the act necessitates negating the act. Therefore the negation with the lam of denial is more emphatic. The same applies to what occurs of this kind in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech. This emphasis holds only according to the doctrine of the Basrans, for they claim that the predicate of "kana" that is followed by the lam of denial is omitted, and that the lam after it is a hidden "an" from which, together with the verb after it, a verbal noun is formed, and that this particle is connected to that omitted particle. This predicate has been stated explicitly in the verse of one of them:

"You rose high, though you were not fit to rise high."

The doctrine of the Kufans is that the lam is the governing particle (al-nasibah), not a hidden "an" after it, and that the lam after it is for emphasis, and that the very verb governed by this lam is the predicate of "kana"; so there is no difference between "ma kana Zaydun yaqumu" and "ma kana Zaydun liyaquma" except the mere emphasis of the lam. The discussion of these two doctrines is mentioned in the science of grammar.

﴿Indeed Allah is, toward the people, Most Kind, Most Merciful﴾: Ending this verse with this sentence is evident; it runs as a reason (ta'lil) for what precedes it, that is, for the subtlety of His compassion and the breadth of His mercy: He moved you from one law to another that is more beneficial for you and more useful in religion, or He did not place hardship upon those whom He guided, or He does not waste the faith of one who believes; and this last is the most apparent. The alif and lam in "bil-nas" (toward the people) may be generic, as in His saying: ﴿Allah is Subtle with His servants﴾ [al-Shura: 19], ﴿and My mercy encompasses all things﴾ [al-A'raf: 156], ﴿You have encompassed all things in mercy and knowledge﴾ [Ghafir: 7]; and it may be definite by prior reference, so that "the people" means the believers. The two Haramayn (Makki and Madani), Ibn 'Amir and Hafs read "la-ra'uf" with a hamza, on the pattern of "fa'ul" wherever it occurs. The poet said:

"We obey our Messenger and we obey a Lord, who is the Merciful, who has been Compassionate to us."

The rest of the seven read "la-ra'uf" with a hamza, on the pattern of "nadus". The poet said:

"He sees for the Muslims upon himself a right, like the right of the compassionate, merciful father."

And al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah said:

"And the worst of the wrongdoers, do not be like him, who faces his uncle, the compassionate, merciful one."

Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' read "la-rawuf", without a hamza, and similarly he eased every hamza in the Book of Allah, whether it was quiescent or vowelled. Since the negation in the preceding sentence was emphasized by the lam of denial, it was fitting to affirm the concluding sentence with emphasis, so it was emphasized with "inna" (indeed), with the lam, and with the pattern "fa'ul" and "fa'il". All of this points to the breadth of mercy and the abundance of compassion. The attribute of mercy is delayed because it is the closing rhyme (fasilah), and the prepositional phrase is fronted out of concern for those toward whom He is compassionate.

Al-Qushayri said: whoever views the matter with the eye of distinction, the change is difficult for him; whoever views it with the eye of reality, the face of rightness becomes manifest to his insight.

﴿And Allah would never let your faith be lost﴾: That is, whoever is with Allah in all states, upon one heart, then the differing states are one for him. So whether He changes, or confirms, or establishes, or replaces, or verifies, or turns, they are with Him in all states. One of them said:

"Wherever the cup turns, we turn; the ignorant suppose that we have gone mad."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 144 (part 1 of 2):

﴿We see you turning your face about in the sky.﴾ The hadith of al-Bara' has already been mentioned, and the disagreement regarding this verse has already been discussed. And regarding His saying: ﴿The foolish among the people will say﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:142): which of the two was revealed first? Here, *naraa* (we see) is an imperfect verb with the meaning of a perfect verb. Some grammarians have mentioned that *qad* (indeed) can, in some contexts, turn the imperfect into the past, and among its examples are: ﴿He certainly knows what you are upon﴾ (al-Nur 24:64); ﴿And We certainly know that your breast is constricted﴾ (al-Hijr 15:97); ﴿Allah certainly knows those among you who hinder others﴾ (al-Ahzab 33:18). And the poet said:

*By my life, indeed there was a people whom we used to see, yesterday, among them tethers for horses and the thick-herded camels.*

Al-Zamakhshari said: *qad naraa* means *rubba naraa* (perhaps we see), and its meaning is the frequency of seeing, like his saying:

*Indeed I leave the opponent with fingertips yellowed...*

End of quotation. His explanation here is contradictory upon verification, because he explained *qad naraa* as *rubba naraa*. According to the verifying grammarians, *rubba* is used only to indicate the paucity of a thing in itself or the paucity of its counterpart. Then he said: its meaning is the frequency of seeing, so it contradicts the meaning of *rubba* according to the majority position. Furthermore, this meaning he claimed, namely the frequency of seeing, is not indicated by the wording, because the word was not coined for the meaning of frequency. This construction, meaning the combination of *qad* with an imperfect verb intended as a past, indicates only past time, and not anything other than the past. Frequency is understood only from what the seeing is attached to, namely the turning, because whoever raises his gaze to the sky once is not said to have *qallaba basarahu fi al-sama'* (turned his gaze about in the sky); rather it is said *qallaba* only when he repeats it. So the intensity is understood from the turning, which is the *mutawa'a* (reflexive form) of *taqlib* (turning about), like *qatta'tuhu fa-taqatta'a* (I cut it and it was cut) and *kassartuhu fa-takassara* (I broke it and it broke), and whatever receives the action of an intensive form carries intensity.

As for *al-wajh* (the face) here, it has been said: what is intended is its apparent meaning. Qatadah, al-Suddi and others said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to turn his face in supplication to Allah the Exalted that He would turn him to the *qibla* (direction of prayer) of Makkah. It was also said: he used to turn his face so that he would be given permission in supplication. Al-Zamakhshari said: He was expecting from his Lord that He would turn him toward the Ka'ba, because it was the *qibla* of his father Ibrahim, and it was more persuasive to the Arabs to embrace faith, because it was their pride, their place of visitation and their place of circumambulation, and to oppose the Jews. So he would watch for the descent of Jibril (peace be upon him) and the revelation of the change. End of his words, and they are the words of the people before him. The first is the saying of Ibn Abbas, that it was to reach the *qibla* of Ibrahim. The second is the saying of al-Suddi and al-Rabi', that it was to win over the Arabs through their love of the Ka'ba. The third is the saying of Mujahid, and it is the saying of the Jews: "Muhammad did not know his religion until he followed us," so he wished to oppose them.

It has also been said: He used the word "face" as a metonymy for the eye, because it is more noble, and it is the thing used in seeking desires. You say: *badhalat wajhi fi kadha* (I spent my face on such-and-such), and *fa'altu li-wajhi fulan* (I did it for the face of so-and-so). And the poet said:

*She returned with what I sought, and my face with its water.*

This is from the figure of speech of the whole for the part (*al-kinaya bi-al-kull 'an al-juz'*). It is not good to say that it is by omission of a modifier, so that the estimate would be *basar wajhika* (the sight of your face), because this is hardly ever used; one says *basaruka*, *'aynuka* and *anfuka* (your sight, your eye, your nose); one hardly says *anf wajhika* (the nose of your face) or *khadd wajhika* (the cheek of your face).

*Fi al-sama'* (in the sky): it is attached to the verbal noun *taqlib* (turning about), and it is transitive with *fi*, so it is on its apparent sense. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Let not the turning about of those who disbelieve in the lands deceive you﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:196), meaning in the regions of the sky, in this direction and in that direction. It has been said: *fi* means *ila* (to). It has been said: *fi al-sama'* is attached to *tara* (see), and *fi* means *min* (from), meaning: we see from the sky the turning of your face, although Allah the Exalted sees from every place, and His seeing is not confined to one place rather than another. The seeing from the sky is mentioned to magnify the turning of his face, because the sky is specialized in magnifying what is attributed to it, and it is as came in the report: that Allah hears from above seven heavens. The first explanation is the apparent one, namely that the prepositional phrase is attached to the verbal noun, and that *fi* retains its literal meaning. The turning is specifically attributed to the sky because the sky is a direction from which mercy returns, such as rain, lights and revelation; so they make their desire toward the direction in which blessings keep coming, and because the sky is the *qibla* of supplication, and because he was awaiting Jibril, and Jibril used to descend from the sky.

﴿So We will surely turn you to a qibla that you will be pleased with﴾: This indicates that in the preceding sentence there is an omitted circumstantial phrase; the estimate is: *qad naraa taqallaba wajhika fi al-sama'* (we see your face turning about in the sky) seeking a *qibla* other than the one you face. This promise came with an implied oath, for emphasis in its occurrence, because an oath confirms the content of the sentence sworn to. The promise came before the command, so that the soul would rejoice at the answer, and then at the fulfilment of the promise, so that joy would come twice; and because reaching the sought object after being promised it is more pleasing in arriving than the sudden occurrence of the object. He made *qibla* indefinite, because nothing preceding it required that it be known, so that it would be defined by the article *al-*. The wording contains nothing indicating that he was asking for a specific *qibla* by speech. He described it as one that is pleasing to him, because it is close to specification, since the object of pleasure is the heart, and he preferred that it be the Ka'ba, although he did not state this explicitly. They said: his pleasure with it is either due to the inclination of his nature or because it encompasses the interests of the religion. The meaning is: We will make you face a *qibla* pleasing to you, and We will empower you to do so.

﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾: that is, face with your face toward the Ka'ba during prayer. By this command the orientation toward Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) was abrogated (*naskh*, meaning the lifting of a earlier ruling by a later one). They said: The reason it did not mention prayer is that the verse was revealed while he was in prayer, so being engaged in prayer made its mention unnecessary. And whoever says it was revealed outside prayer, the omission of mention of prayer is because what was required was none other than that, namely facing in prayer. I say: In His saying ﴿So We will surely turn you to a qibla that you will be pleased with﴾ there is an indication that the intent is during prayer, because the *qibla* is that which one faces in prayer. By "face" he meant the whole body, because what is obligatory is facing it with the whole body. He used "face" as a metonymy for the whole, because it is the most noble of the limbs, and by it some people are distinguished from others. It may be used with the meaning of the thing itself. And the antithesis requires this: he set His saying ﴿We see your face turning about﴾ against His saying ﴿so turn your face﴾. It has already been mentioned that *shatr* may be used to mean half, and may be used to mean direction. Most of the exegetes hold that what is meant by *shatr* is its facing and its side, and this is the choice of al-Shafi'i. Al-Jubba'i, and it is the choice of al-Qadi, said: what is meant by it is the middle of the mosque and its center, because *shatr* is half, and the Ka'ba is a spot in the middle of the mosque. What is obligatory is facing the Ka'ba, and it was in the middle of the mosque, so it is good to say ﴿turn your face toward the mosque﴾, meaning half from every direction, and it is as if it were an expression for the spot of the Ka'ba. And what supports the validity of what we have mentioned is that if one who is outside the mosque faces the mosque, not the middle of the mosque which is the Ka'ba, his prayer is not valid. And if we interpret *shatr* as the side, there would be no benefit in mentioning it, and it would not indicate the obligation of facing its middle, which is the Ka'ba. Ibn Abbas and others said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was directed toward the whole House. Ibn Umar said: He himself and his community were directed opposite the spout of the Ka'ba, and the spout is the *qibla* of Madinah and Syria, and there is approximately the *qibla* of the people of al-Andalus there. There is no disagreement that the Ka'ba is the *qibla* from every horizon. And in the reading of Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud): ﴿So turn your faces in the direction of the Sacred Mosque﴾.

Those who hold that the meaning of *shatr* is direction disagreed. Ibn Abbas said: The House is the *qibla* for the people of the mosque, the mosque is the *qibla* for the people of the Haram, and the Haram is the *qibla* for the people of the east and the west. This is the saying of Malik. Others said: The *qibla* is the Ka'ba itself, and the apparent meaning is that what is intended by *shatr* is direction and orientation, because facing the exact Ka'ba entails great hardship for one who is far from it, so that it is opposite to it. And in mentioning the Sacred Mosque, not mentioning the Ka'ba, there is an indication that what is obligatory is observing the direction of the Ka'ba, not observing its exact spot. Malik derived from His saying ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾ that the one praying looks in front of him, not at the place of his prostration, contrary to al-Thawri, al-Shafi'i and al-Hasan ibn Hayy, who held that it is recommended to look at the place of prostration, and contrary to Sharik al-Qadi, who held that the one standing looks at the place of prostration, in bowing at the place of his feet, in prostration at the place of his nose, and in sitting at the place of his lap. The hafiz Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: We only said he looks in front of him, because if he bends his head he forfeits part of the standing that is required of the head, which is the most noble of the limbs; and if he holds his head upright and strains his sight toward the ground, that is great hardship and difficulty: ﴿and He has not placed upon you any difficulty in the religion﴾ (al-Hajj 22:78).

﴿And wherever you are﴾: this is a generality over the places a person may occupy, in whichever place you are. It is a conditional sentence with its answer, the *fa'* being the response of the condition, and *kuntum* is in the place of a jussive. *Haythu* is an adverb of place, attached to a clause, so it requires the genitive after it; and what requires the genitive does not require the jussive, because the operators of nouns do not operate on verbs. The attachment clarifies what is attached, just as the relative clause clarifies, which contradicts the conditional noun, because the conditional is indefinite. So when *haythu* is joined with *ma*, its meaning of attachment disappears, it takes on the meaning of a condition, is used as a conditional, and at that point becomes one of the operators of verbs. What is required for its use as a conditional was mentioned earlier, and al-Farra's disagreement on this point.

﴿So turn your faces toward it﴾: This is a command to the community of Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), since his command was mentioned earlier. He intended to make clear that his ruling and the ruling of his community in this matter are one, with greater generality regarding places, lest it be supposed that this *qibla* is specific to the people of Madinah. So He made clear that wherever they are on the earth, they must face the direction of the mosque. Since the Prophet (ﷺ) was the one eager for the change, He began with his command first, then followed it with the command for his community second, because they follow him in that, and lest it be supposed that this was something specific to him (ﷺ). In the reading of Abd Allah: ﴿So turn your faces toward it﴾ (*qibalahu*). And Ibn Abi Abla recited: ﴿So turn your faces in the direction of it﴾ (*tilqa'ahu*). All of this indicates that the intent of *shatr* is direction.

﴿And indeed those who were given the Scripture﴾: that is, the leaders of the Jews and the Christians and their rabbis. Al-Suddi said: They are the Jews.

Their knowing that it (ﷺ)... [see note below]

Let me correct that: I must not add notes, so here is the translation only.

﴿That they may know that it﴾: i.e., turning toward the Sacred Mosque, (the truth): which God prescribed for Abraham and his descendants. Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: the qiblah is the Ka'bah. Al-Kisa'i said: the pronoun refers to the direction (al-shatr), which is close to the second view, because al-shatr is the direction. It was also said: it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning they recognize his truthfulness and prophethood; this was also said by Qatadah and Mujahid. The referent of these pronouns precedes them. The referent of the pronoun of transfer and turning is His saying: ﴿So turn your face﴾, so it refers to the verbal noun understood from His saying: (they turned, fa-walloo). The referent of the pronoun of the qiblah is His saying: ﴿a qiblah that you will be pleased with﴾; the referent of the pronoun of the direction is His saying: ﴿toward the direction of the Sacred Mosque﴾; and the referent of the pronoun of the Messenger is the pronoun of his address (ﷺ). According to this view there are two shifts of pronoun (iltifat). Knowledge here may be taken to be of the kind that transitively governs two objects, or of the kind that governs one object, since its object is "an" and its complement, so both possibilities are allowed. Their knowledge of this is either because the turning toward the Ka'bah is in their Book, as Abu al-'Aliyah said; or because their Book states that Muhammad (ﷺ) is a truthful prophet who commands only the truth; or because abrogation is permissible; or because the good tidings of the prophets state that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would pray toward both qiblahs. (from their Lord): a prepositional phrase in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning established from their Lord. This indicates that the transfer from Bayt al-Maqdis to the Ka'bah was not by personal reasoning (ijtihad) but by a command from God Most High. The attribution of the Lord to them is a reminder that the truth must be followed, which is established by the One who cares for your reform, as God Most High said: ﴿The truth is from your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 147].

﴿And God is not unaware of what they do﴾: Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read with the ta' (second person address). It may mean the believers, given His saying: ﴿so turn your faces toward it﴾, or it may mean the People of the Book, in which case it is an iltifat. Its reasoning is that addressing them with the statement that God is not heedless of their deeds is a stirring for them to act upon what they know of the truth, since being addressed directly with a matter implies intense denunciation and the great magnitude of what is denounced. As for the one who reads with the ya' (third person), the apparent reference is to the People of the Book, since this occurs in a single sequence of third-person address. On both readings, it is an announcement that God Most High does not neglect the deeds of His servants nor is unaware of them, and it contains a warning (wa'id).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 145 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And if you were to bring to those who were given the Book every sign, they would not follow your qibla﴾. This is a consolation to the Messenger concerning the failure of the People of the Book to follow him. He first informed him that they know it is the truth, yet they conceal it and do not act upon their knowledge of it as it requires. Then he consoled him regarding their refusal to accept the truth, by stating that they have reached such a degree of obstinacy and open enmity that, even if you brought them every one of the miracles, each of which would necessitate accepting the truth, they would not follow you nor take your path. And if they do not follow you even when you bring them all the miracles, then it is all the more fitting that they would not follow you if you brought them a single miracle. The meaning is: with every sign that indicates that your turning toward the Ka'bah is the truth. The lam in "wa-la'in" (and if indeed) is the one that signals an omitted preceding oath. The preceding omitted oath and the conditional clause have come together, with the conditional clause being later than it, so the answer belongs to the oath, which is his saying: ﴿they would not follow﴾, and for this reason the fa' (then) did not enter it. The answer of the condition is omitted, due to the answer of the oath indicating it, and it is negated with "ma" with a past verb meaning the future. The meaning: i.e., they do not follow your qibla; because the condition was restricted within the sentence, and the condition is future, so the content of the sentence must be future, necessarily, since the future cannot be a condition in the past. A parallel of this construction in the affirmative is his saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if We were to send a wind and they saw it turned yellow, they would surely remain after it disbelieving﴾ [al-Rum: 51]. The estimation: "la-yazallanna" (they would surely remain). The past verb preceded by the lam was placed as an answer to the omitted oath, and for this reason the lam entered upon it in the place of the future. So it is past in terms of wording, future in terms of meaning, because the condition was restricted in it, as we have mentioned. The answer of the condition in both verses is omitted, and the answer of the oath has taken its place. For this reason the conditional verb came in the past in wording, because when the answer is omitted, the past form of the conditional verb is required in wording, except in the necessity of poetry, where it may come in the present. Al-Farra' went to the view that "in" here means "law" (if), and for this reason "ma" is in the answer; so he made "ma tabi'u" the answer of "in", because "in" means "law", and just as "law" is answered by "ma", so "in" which means "law" is answered in the same way. And if "in" does not mean "law", its answer is not introduced by "ma" but must have a fa'. You say: "in tazurni fa-ma azuruka" (if you visit me, then I will not visit you), and it is not permitted to say: "ma azuruka". On this view the answer of the oath is omitted, due to the answer of "in" indicating it. This view of al-Farra' is built on his doctrine that if the oath precedes the condition, the answer may belong to the condition rather than the oath. This is not the doctrine of the Basrans; rather the answer belongs to the oath under its conditions stated in grammar. The use of "in" in the sense of "law" is rare, so it should not be read that way when its retention in its original meaning is possible. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The answer of "la'in" came like the answer of "law", and it is its opposite in that "law" requires past and occurrence, while "in" requires the future; because both are preceded by an oath. So the answer is in fact for the oath, because one of the two particles takes the place of the other; this is the statement of Sibawayh. End of his words.

This speech contains confusion and does not state the intended meaning clearly; for its beginning implies that the answer belongs to "in", while his saying afterward: "so the answer is in fact for the oath" indicates that the answer does not belong to "in". The justification he gives afterward, "because one of the two particles takes the place of the other", cannot serve as a justification for his statement "so the answer is in fact for the oath"; rather it could serve as a justification for the claim that the answer belongs to "la'in" and is treated in that matter like "law". As for his saying "this is the statement of Sibawayh", there is nothing in the book of Sibawayh except that "ma tabi'u" is the answer of the oath, and that the past is placed in the position of the future. Sibawayh said: They say "la'in fa'alta ma fa'ala" (if you were to do what he did), meaning what he is doing and what he will do. And he also said, and God the Exalted said: ﴿And if they were to cease, none could hold them after Him﴾ [Fatir: 41], i.e., none holds them. Some people said: each of "la'in" and "law" takes the place of the other, and is answered by what the other is answered by, and from it: ﴿And if We were to send a wind and they saw it turned yellow, they would surely remain﴾ [al-Rum: 51], because its meaning is: "and if We had sent a wind". Likewise the answer of "la'in" may be answered as the answer of "law", as in your saying: "law ahsanta ilayya uhsinu ilayka" (if you were to do good to me, I would do good to you). This is the view of al-Akhfash, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. Sibawayh said: one of them is not answered with the answer of the other, because their meanings differ, and the past verb that occurs after "la'in" is in the sense of the future; its estimation: "la yattabi'una" (they will not follow), and "la-yazallanna" (they will surely remain). End of his words.

It results from all of this that regarding his saying ﴿they would not follow﴾ there are two views: the first is that it is the answer of an omitted oath, which is the view of Sibawayh. The second is that it is the answer of "in", because it is treated as "law", which is the view of al-Akhfash, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj.

The apparent sense of "those who were given the Book" is generality, and some have held this here. Al-Asamm said: the intended are their scholars, who were described in the previous verse as "those who were given the Book", and in the later verse. The specification is indicated by the specificity of what precedes and the specificity of what follows, so likewise the middle one, and the report of their persistence, which is the condition of the obstinate, and that many of the People of the Book have believed in him and followed his qibla. They differed regarding his saying: ﴿they would not follow your qibla﴾. Al-Hasan and al-Jubba'i said: He meant all of them, as if He said: they will not unite upon following your qibla, in the manner of: ﴿And if God had willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 35]; and in that case it is a report about the collective as a collective, not a judgment upon the individuals. Al-Asamm said: rather the intended is that none of them believes. It has already been mentioned that among al-Asamm's views is that the People of the Book here refers to a specific group; so it is as if he said: each individual of those specifically devoted to obstinacy, persisting in denying the truth, does not believe and does not follow your qibla. Abu Muslim argued from this verse that God's knowledge of His servants and of what they do is not a proof for them regarding what they commit, and that they are able to do the good that they were commanded, and to leave its opposite that they were forbidden. It was said: our companions also argued from it for the view of charging with what is not within capacity, namely that He informed about them that they do not follow his qibla; so if they followed his qibla, the truthful report of God would turn into a lie, and His knowledge into ignorance, and that is impossible, and whatever entails the impossible is impossible. God, the Exalted, attributed the qibla to Himself because He is the one worshipped by it and the one followed in facing it. God made His Prophet despair of their following his qibla, because they did not abandon following him on account of a clear proof they had, nor on account of a doubt that arose, but rather it was by way of obstinacy, and whoever disputes out of obstinacy, there is no hope of his being drawn back.

﴿And you are not a follower of their qibla﴾: this is a declarative sentence. It was said: its meaning is a prohibition, i.e., do not follow their qibla, and its meaning is continuance upon what you are upon; otherwise he is protected from following their qibla after the command came. It was also said: it remains in the sense of a report, namely that by this report He showed that this qibla will not be abrogated, so this sentence came to remove the possibility of abrogation, or it decided that matter, cutting off the hope of the People of the Book, for they said: "O Muhammad, return to our qibla, and we will believe in you and follow you," as deception from them; so God made them despair of his following their qibla. Or He showed by it the establishment of his protection. Or He reported it by way of impossibility, because their qiblas differ. Or it came by way of contrast, i.e., they will not abandon their falsehood, and you will not abandon your truth. He used the singular "qibla" in his saying "qiblatahum" (their qibla), although they are two, since the Jews have a qibla and the Christians have a qibla different from that one; because the two share being false, so the two became one from the aspect of falsehood, and the contrast in wording made it good; because before it is ﴿they would not follow your qibla﴾. This sentence is more emphatic in negation, inasmuch as it is nominal, in which the noun is repeated twice, and inasmuch as it emphasized the negation with the "bi-" in his saying "bi-tabi'in". It is a resumed sentence conjoined to the speech before it, not to the answer alone, since it cannot take its place; because the negation of their following his qibla is restricted by a condition that cannot be a restriction on the negation of his following their qibla. Some readers read "bi-tabi'i qiblatihim" with the genitive construction, and both are eloquent, I mean applying the active participle here and its annexation, and it has already been mentioned which of the two is more analogical.

﴿And some of them are not followers of the qibla of others﴾: the pronoun in "ba'duhum" (some of them) refers to the People of the Book. The meaning: the Jews do not follow the qibla of the Christians, nor do the Christians follow the qibla of the Jews; this is an indication that Jews do not become Christian, and that Christians do not become Jewish, because of the extreme enmity and mutual hatred between them. We have seen that Jews and Christians very often enter the religion of Islam, but no Jew has been observed to become Christian, nor any Christian to become Jewish. The intended by the two parts is: whoever remains upon his religion among the People of the Book; this is the statement of al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd, and it is the apparent meaning. It was said: one of the two parts is those among the People of the Book who believed, and the second part is those who remained upon their religion among them; because each of them demeans the forbearance of the other and declares it unbelief, since their ways differ. Do you not see the Jews praising 'Abd Allah ibn Salam before they knew of his Islam, and then slandering him after that? These sentences include: that the People of the Book, although they agree in opposing you, are divided in the qibla; the qibla of the Jews is Bayt al-Maqdis, and the qibla of the Christians is the rising of the sun.

﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾: the lam here also indicates an omitted oath, and for this reason the answer came with his saying: "innaka" (indeed you...). The conditioning of the occurrence of a thing upon a condition does not imply the possibility of that condition. A man says to his wife: "If you climb to the sky, you are divorced," and it is known that her climbing to the sky is impossible. God, the Exalted, said of the angels whom He reported: that they ﴿do not disobey God in what He commands them and do what they are commanded﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6]; He said: ﴿And whoever among them should say, "I am a god besides Him," that We would recompense with Hell; thus We recompense the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anbiya': 29]. When this is clear, what came of this type becomes easy. From this is understood impossibility, because what is conditioned upon the impossible is impossible. The meaning of this sentence, whose outward form implies occurrence, becomes on the assumption of the impossibility of occurrence; the meaning becomes: he is not counted a wrongdoer, nor will he become one, because you do not follow their desires; likewise your deeds will not be nullified, because your associating partners is impossible; and likewise no angel will be recompensed with Hell, because he does not claim to be a god. They said: what is addressed to one who is protected from what cannot occur from him, is understood as addressed to his community, and to whoever can commit that; and the address to him came by way of exalting that matter and magnifying its importance, so that distance from it may be achieved. A parallel to this is the saying: "Iyyaki a'ni, wasma'i ya jarah" (It is you I mean, and listen, O neighbor).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 145 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Zamakhshari said: His saying, ﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾, after the clarification of the reality of his state, which is known to him in His saying, ﴿Nor are you a follower of their qibla﴾, is a statement given by way of supposition and assumption, meaning: "And if you were, for example, to follow them after the clarity of the proof and the full knowledge of the reality of the matter, then you would indeed be among those who commit gross wrongdoing." In this there is gentleness toward the listeners, an increase in warning, a expression of horror at the state of one who abandons the proof after it has been made clear and follows his desire, and an incitement to steadfastness upon the truth. End of his words. And in al-Muntakhab he said: They differed regarding this address. Some said: it is addressed to the Messenger. Some said: it is addressed to the Messenger and others. Some said: it is addressed to other than the Messenger, because God, exalted is He, knew that the Messenger would not do that, so it is not permissible to single him out with this address.

﴿Ahwa'a-hum﴾ (their desires): It has been stated that it is the plural of hawa (desire), and it is not pluralized as ahwiya. The usage of hawa is mostly for what has no good in it, though it may be used for good. Its origin is inclination and love. It was pluralized, although its origin is the verbal noun, because of the variety of their aims, their objects, and their differences.

﴿Min ba'di ma ja'aka min al-'ilm﴾ (after the knowledge that has come to you): That is, from the proofs and signs which give you knowledge and bring it about. So the name of the effect is applied to the cause. He called those proofs "knowledge," for emphasis, magnification, and to draw attention to the fact that knowledge is among the most noble and exalted of created things. The verse indicates that the threat directed at the scholars is more severe than that directed at others. Knowledge here has been interpreted as "the truth," meaning that what came to him of the change of the qibla is the truth. Muqatil said: "knowledge" here means "clear explanation." In this place it came as "min ba'di ma ja'aka" and before this as "ba'da alladhi ja'aka" [al-Baqarah: 120], and in al-Ra'd as "ba'di ma ja'aka" [al-Ra'd: 37]. So one place is specific with alladhi and two places with ma, and this place with min. What we say about this is that it is from the breadth of expression and the mention of synonyms, because ma and alladhi are both relative pronouns, so whichever of them you mention is eloquent and good. As for bringing min, it indicates the beginning of the "after" of the coming. As for his saying "ba'da," it has the meaning of min, and the "after" is restricted by it in meaning, though the general sense of ba'da does not necessarily require it. Some said in answer to this: the use of ma in place of alladhi, because alladhi is more specific and ma is more ambiguous; so where it is specified with alladhi, it refers to knowledge of the correctness of the religion, which is Islam, which prevents one from the creeds of the Jews and Christians, and so the more specific and well-known word is preferable there, because it is knowledge of all the foundations of the religion. And it is specified with the word ma, which refers to knowledge of one of the pillars of the religion, one of which is the qibla and the other the Book, because it refers to His saying: ﴿And among the factions are those who deny part of it﴾ [al-Ra'd: 36]. He said: As for the presence of min, its benefit is clear, namely indicating the first time at which it became obligatory upon the Prophet ﷺ to oppose the People of the Book regarding the matter of the qibla, that is, that time at which God commanded you to turn toward the qibla. If you follow their desires, you would be a wrongdoer, placing falsehood in the place of truth. End of his words.

﴿Innaka idhan lamina al-zalimin﴾ (Indeed, you would then be among the wrongdoers): We have mentioned that this sentence is the answer to the omitted oath, which the lam in la'in indicates by its presence, and it indicates the answer to the condition. It is not said that it is an answer to both, because that is impossible both verbally and in meaning. As for meaning, the requirement of the oath differs from the requirement of the condition: the oath is requisite in that it has no effect upon it, because the oath is brought only as emphasis for the sentence sworn to, and what comes by way of emphasis is not suitable to be operative; and the requirement of the condition is that it operates upon it, so the sentence is in the place of a jussive, and the condition operates because of the strength of its demand for it. As for wording, when this sentence is the answer to an oath, it does not need an additional connector; when it is the answer to a condition, it needs an additional connector, which is the fa'. It is not permissible for it to be free of the fa' while the fa' is present in it, so it is impossible to say that the sentence is the answer to the oath and the condition together. ﴿Idhan﴾ entered between the subject of inna and its predicate to establish the relation between them, and its proper place is to come first or last. It did not come first, because an oath and a condition preceded it, and the answer belongs to the oath. If it had come first, it would have been mistakenly taken as establishing the relation between the condition and the omitted answer. Nor did it come last, lest the harmony of the endings and the closing of the verses be lost; so it came in the middle, intending by it delay to establish the relation. The precise meaning of idhan is difficult, and people have disagreed about its meaning. Sibawayh explicitly stated that its meaning is response and consequence. Grammarians differed in understanding Sibawayh's words, and we have discussed this at length in our book "al-Takmil." What has been established about it is that it does not occur at the beginning of speech; rather, it must be preceded by speech, verbally or by implication, and what follows it, verbally or by implication, though it is caused by what precedes it, is in that regard of two kinds. The first: that it indicates the establishing of the connection and condition, such that the connection is not understood without it. An example: "I will visit you" — you say: "Idhan uzurka" (then I will visit you), by which you now intend to make its action a condition for your action. The establishing of causation, in its second state, necessarily occurs in the answer, and with the verb in a future time; in this kind it operates, and its operation is mentioned in grammar. The second kind: that it is emphasizing an answer connected to a preceding statement, or alerting to a conditioned cause that has occurred at present, and in both states it does not operate, because emphases are not relied upon, whereas the operator is relied upon. An example: "in ta'tini idhan atika" (if you come to me, then I will come to you), and "wallahi idhan la'af'alanna" (by God, I will surely do it). If you drop idhan, the connection is still understood. Since in this kind it is not relied upon, it is permissible for it to enter upon a plain nominal sentence, as in: "uzurka fa-taqulu: idhan ana ukrimuka" (I visit you, so you say: then I honour you), and it is permissible for it to come in the middle, as in: "ana idhan ukrimuka" (I, then, honour you), and to come last. Having established this, idhan in the verse comes as emphasis for the answer connected to what preceded it. We have established its meaning here only because it recurs frequently in the Qur'an, so in every place it is to be understood in accordance with what suits this which we have established.

[p. 435]

**Those to whom We gave the Book** (*alladhina ataynahum al-kitab*): This refers either to the scholars of the Jews and Christians, or to those Jews who believed in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), such as Ibn Salam and others, or to whoever believed in him without restriction. These are the opinions. As for "the Book" (*al-kitab*): it is the Torah, or the Gospel, or both together, or the Qur'an. These are opinions that depend on who is meant by "those to whom We gave." The wording *atayna-hum* (We gave them) is more eloquent than *utu* (they were given), because it attributes the giving to Allah, the Exalted, expressing it with the plural of majesty (*nun al-'azama*, the royal "We"). The same applies to similar forms such as *hadayna* (We guided), *ijtaba-yna* (We chose), and *istafayna* (We selected), intended as honour. It has been said: also because *utu* may be used of things that are not acceptable, whereas *atayna-hum* is most often used of what is acceptable, as in ﴿those to whom We gave the Book, the judgment and the prophethood﴾ [al-An'am: 89]. If more than one is meant by "the Book," it is stated in the singular because it refers to the written text, expressed by the verbal noun.

**They recognise him** (*ya'rifunahu*): This sentence is in the position of the predicate of the subject, which is *alladhina atayna-hum*. It is also permissible that *alladhina* be in the genitive, as an adjective of *al-zalimin* (the wrongdoers), or as an apposition to *al-zalimin*, or as an apposition to *alladhina utu al-kitab* (those who were given the Book) in the preceding verse [al-Baqarah: 145]. It may be in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "they are those who," or in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning "I mean." On these parsings, *ya'rifunahu* is a sentence in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), either from the first object of *atayna-hum* or from the second object, which is "the Book," since *ya'rifunahu* contains two pronouns referring back to them both. The apparent parsing is the first, because the speech is complete in itself as a nominal sentence, and because the speech evidently ends at ﴿Indeed, if you did so, you would surely be among the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 145].

The object pronoun in *ya'rifunahu* refers to the Prophet (ﷺ). This is the view of Mujahid, Qatadah and others. It is also transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, chosen by al-Zajjaj, preferred by al-Tibrizi, and al-Zamakhshari began with it, saying: "They recognise him with a clear recognition, distinguishing him from others by the specific, identifying attribute." Al-Zamakhshari and others said, and the wording is al-Zamakhshari's: "The pronoun is permissible even though no antecedent has preceded it, because the context indicates it and it is not ambiguous to the hearer. Such a pronoun carries exaltation and the implication that he is so famous, and so known as a recognised sign, that he needs no introduction." End of quotation. I say: it is not as they have said, that it is a pronoun before its antecedent. Rather, this is an instance of *iltifat* (a shift of grammatical person), because Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven; so We will surely turn you to a qiblah that you will like. So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144], then He said: ﴿And if you were to bring to those who were given the Book every sign, they would not follow your qiblah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 145], to the end of the verse. All of these are second-person pronouns addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then He shifted from the second-person pronoun to the third-person pronoun. The wisdom of this shift is that, when He had finished addressing him directly, He turned to the people and said: ﴿those to whom We gave the Book﴾, and We chose them to bear knowledge and revelation. They recognise this one whom We addressed in the preceding verses, and whom We commanded and forbade. They have no doubt about his identity, nor about the truth of his reports, concerning the obligations We imposed upon him, among which was the abrogation (*naskh*, the replacing of one ruling by another) of Bayt al-Maqdis by the Ka'bah, because their Book contains mention of him, his description, and an explicit statement about him. They find him written with them in the Torah and the Gospel. It is therefore clear from what we have mentioned that this is not a pronoun before its antecedent, but an instance of *iltifat*, and the wisdom of the shift has become evident.

What supports the pronoun referring to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is what is reported: that 'Umar asked 'Abdullah ibn Salam, may Allah be pleased with them both, and said: "Allah has sent down to His Prophet: ﴿those to whom We gave the Book recognise him﴾, the verse. So what is this recognition?" 'Abdullah said: "O 'Umar, I recognised him when I saw him, as I recognise my son, and my recognition of Muhammad (ﷺ) is firmer than my recognition of my son."
