'Umar said: "And how is that?" He said: "I testify that he is truly the Messenger of Allah, and Allah has described him in our Book, but I do not know what women may do." 'Umar said: "May Allah grant you success, O son of Salam, for you have spoken the truth." This report has also been transmitted in an abbreviated form, with words close in meaning to these, and in it: "'Umar kissed his head." If the pronoun refers to the Messenger, then it has been said that what is meant is the recognition of his face and the distinguishing of him, not knowledge of the reality of his lineage. It has also been said: the meaning is that they recognise his truthfulness and his prophethood. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the truth, which is the turning to the Ka'bah, as stated by Ibn 'Abbas and also Qatadah, Ibn Jurayj and al-Rabi'. It has been said that it refers to the Qur'an. It has been said that it refers to knowledge. It has been said that it refers to the fact that the Sacred House is the qiblah of Abraham and of the prophets before him. This recognition is specific to the scholars, because He said: ﴿those to whom We gave the Book﴾. If the recognition relates to the Prophet (ﷺ), then it arises through seeing and description, or through the Qur'an, so it is obtained from the confirmation of their Book of the Qur'an, and from the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his description; or through the qiblah, or the turning, so it is obtained through the report of the Qur'an and the report of the Messenger, supported by extraordinary signs.

**As they recognise their sons** (*kama ya'rifuna abna'ahum*): The *kaf* (as) is in the accusative position, either as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun whose estimate is "a recognition like their recognition of their sons," or in the accusative as a circumstantial clause from the omitted pronoun of recognition, the estimate being: "They recognise him with a recognition similar to the recognition of their sons." The apparent sense of this comparison is that recognition here means recognition of the face and form, and the comparison with the recognition of sons strengthens this, and also strengthens that the pronoun refers to the Messenger (ﷺ), so that both kinds of recognition relate to the perceptible and seen. It is more emphatic in comparison than if the comparison were between a recognition whose object is a meaning and a recognition whose object is perceptible. The apparent meaning of *abna'* (sons) is restricted to males, so they would be singled out for this, because they are most in contact and company with their fathers, and cling more closely to the hearts of fathers. It is also possible that *abna'* means children in general, in which case it is by way of *taghlib* (the dominance of the masculine). The comparison with the recognition of sons is more emphatic than the comparison with the recognition of oneself, because a person may pass through a period of time in which he does not know himself, unlike sons, for no time passes upon a person without his knowing his son.

**Indeed, a group of them conceal the truth** (*wa inna fariqan minhum la-yaktumuna al-haqq*): That is, of those to whom We gave the Book, namely those who persist in disbelief and obstinacy, from the scholars of the Jews and Christians. This is the best interpretation of "those to whom We gave the Book." Those who went far (in their interpretation) claimed that this group means the ignorant among the Jews and Christians, concerning whom it was said: ﴿And among them are unlettered people who know not the Book except wishful thinking﴾ [al-Baqarah: 78], which would be to inform that this group conceals the truth while knowing it, and to describe the unlettered there as those who know not the Book except as wishful thinking. The truth concealed here is the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This is the view of Qatadah and Mujahid, and also the turning to the Ka'bah, or that the Ka'bah is the qiblah, or it is more general than that, so that every truth is included in it.

**While they know** (*wa hum ya'lamun*): A circumstantial clause, meaning: knowing that it is true. It is close to being an emphatic circumstantial clause, because the wording *yaktumuna al-haqq* (they conceal the truth) already indicates their knowledge of it, since concealment is the hiding of what is known. It has been said that the object of the knowledge is the punishment that falls upon the one who conceals the truth, meaning: while they know the punishment prescribed for the concealer of the truth. In that case it is an explanatory circumstantial clause.

**The truth is from your Lord** (*al-haqqu min rabbika*): Al-Jumhur read *al-haqq* with a nominative *damma*, as the subject, with the predicate being *min rabbika*, so the prepositional phrase is in the position of a predicate. Or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "it is the truth from your Lord," and the pronoun refers to the concealed truth, meaning: what they concealed is the truth from your Lord. In that case the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause, or a predicate after a predicate. Those who went far (in their parsing) claimed it is the subject with an omitted predicate, estimated as "the truth from your Lord, they recognise it." The definite article in *al-haqq* is either for a known referent (*'ahd*), namely the truth on which the Messenger stands, or the truth they concealed; or it is for the genus, meaning that truth is from Allah and not from anyone else, i.e. whatever is established as true is from Allah, like that on which the Messenger stands, and whatever its reality is not established is not from Allah, like the falsehood held by the People of the Book. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib read *al-haqqa* with a *fatha*, and it is parsed as an apposition to the concealed truth, so the estimate is: "they conceal the truth from your Lord," as al-Zamakhshari said; or as an object of *ya'lamun* (they know), as Ibn 'Atiyyah said, in which case it is one of the cases where the apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun, meaning: "while they know it being from your Lord." This is fine and good in places of exaltation and emphasis, like the poet's words:

*I see no thing outpacing death*

meaning: "no thing outpaces it." Ibn 'Atiyyah also permitted that it is in the accusative by an omitted verb, estimated as: "adhere to the truth from your Lord," and this is indicated by the address that follows: ﴿So never be among the doubters﴾. The address in meaning is to the community. The prohibition indicates that they exist, and forbids that he be among them, and the prohibition of being among them is more eloquent than the prohibition of the act itself. Your saying "do not be a wrongdoer" is more eloquent than your saying "do not wrong," because "do not wrong" forbids becoming involved in wrongdoing, whereas "do not be a wrongdoer" forbids being in that state. The prohibition against being in a state is more eloquent than the prohibition against that quality, because forbidding being in a state indicates by its form the generality of all future states in that quality, and entails the generality of that quality. The prohibition against a quality indicates by its form the generality of that quality. There is a difference between what indicates generality and entails generality, and what indicates generality only; therefore the first is more eloquent, and for this reason the prohibition against being (*al-kawn*) is common. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿So never be among the ignorant﴾ [al-An'am: 35] and ﴿And never be among those who denied the signs of Allah﴾ [Yunus: 95], and ﴿So never be in doubt about it﴾. The "being" (*al-kaynunah*) is in reality not the object of the prohibition. The meaning is: "Do not wrong in all your states," that is, in every individual state of yours, so that no time passes upon you in which wrongdoing is found from you. Thus *takun* (be) is an explicit statement covering all states, unlike "do not wrong," which entails the states. He emphasised the prohibition with the energetic *nun* (*nun al-tawkid*), for intensity in the prohibition, and the heavy form was used because it is more emphatic than the light form. The meaning is: "So never be among those who doubt the truth," because what comes from Allah, the Exalted, cannot admit doubt or dispute, since it is the pure truth, into which no suspicion or doubt can enter.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 146–148 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Each has a direction toward which it turns﴾, when he mentioned the qibla toward which the Muslims were commanded to face, which is the Ka'bah, and mentioned the determination of the People of the Book not to follow it, and that each of the two groups, the Jews and the Christians, was determined not to follow the other's qibla, he informed that this is by His doing, that He is the One who decrees it, and that He is the One who directs each of them to their qibla. In this there is a reminder to thank God, for He guided the Muslims to follow what He commanded of them regarding facing the qibla, and chose them for it. The majority read: "wa-li-kullin" (with tanwin on kullin), "wijhatun" (in the nominative), "huwa muwalliyha" with a kasra on the lam as an active participle (ism fa'il). Ibn 'Amir read: "huwa muwalliha" with a fatha on the lam as a passive participle (ism maf'ul), and this is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas. A group read irregularly (shadhdh): "wa-li-kulli wijhatin", with a kasra on the lam of "kulli" without tanwin, and "wijhatin" with a kasra and tanwin, on the basis of the idafa (construction of annexation). The tanwin on "kullin" is the tanwin of compensation (tanwin 'iwad) for the annexed noun, and the omitted noun annexed to "kullin" has been disputed in its estimation. It is said: the meaning is "and for each group among the people of the religions". It is said: the meaning is "and for each people of a region among the Muslims there is a direction from the people of all the horizons toward the direction of the Ka'bah, behind it, in front of it, to its right and to its left; no direction of its directions is more deserving to be a qibla than another". It is said: the meaning is "and for each prophet there is a qibla", said by Ibn 'Abbas. It is said: the meaning is "and for each angel and messenger, bearer of a law, there is a direction of qibla; the qibla of those brought near is the Throne, the qibla of the spiritual beings is the Kursi, the qibla of the Karubiyyin is the Bayt al-Ma'mur, and the qibla of the prophets before you is Bayt al-Maqdis, and your qibla is the Ka'bah". Included in what we have mentioned is that the intended meaning of "wijhah" is "qibla", and this is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the reading of Ubayy, who read: "wa-li-kullin qiblatun". 'Abdullah read: "wa-li-kullin ja'alna qiblatan". Al-Hasan said: "wijhatan" means "tariqah" (way, path), as He said: ﴿For each of you We have appointed a law and a method﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48], i.e., for each prophet there is a way. Qatadah said: "wijhatan" means: a prayer they pray, and it is from His saying: "huwa muwalliha" referring to "kullin" according to its wording, not its meaning; i.e., he faces it and directs toward it his prayer by which he draws near (to God). The second object of "muwalliha" is omitted for understanding of the meaning, i.e., he turns it (his) face or himself, said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' and al-Rabi'. This is corroborated by the fact that "huwa" refers to "kull" in the reading of the one who read: "huwa muwalliha". It is said: "huwa" refers to God, the Most High, said by al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj, i.e., God is the One who turns it (the direction) toward them; whoever followed it followed it, and whoever abandoned it abandoned it. So the meaning of "huwa muwalliha" on this interpretation is: its legislator and the one who obligates them with it. The nominal sentence in the position of a description (sifah) for "wijhatun". As for the reading of the one who read "wa-li-kulli wijhatin" in the idafa, Muhammad ibn Jarir said: it is an error, and one should not rush to judge it as an error, especially since it is attributed to Ibn 'Amir, one of the seven readers, and this reading has been given a grammatical justification. Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is "and for each direction, God is the One who turns it", so the lam was added for the fronting of the object, as in your saying: "li-Zayd darabtu" (for Zayd I struck), and "li-Zayd abuhu daribuhu". End of his words. This is corrupt, because when the governing word transitively reaches a pronoun of the noun, it does not extend to its apparent noun governed by the lam. It is not permissible to say: "li-Zayd darabtuhu" nor "li-Zayd ana daribuhu". Moreover, when the verb is transitive to a pronoun without an intermediary, it is strong, and the lam only enters upon the apparent noun when it is fronted in order to strengthen it, because its reaching it when fronted is weak; the governing word cannot be strong and weak in one state, and because it would entail that what is transitive to one becomes transitive to two. For this reason the grammarians interpreted his saying:
Suraqah li-l-Qur'an yadrusuhu [the poetic example]
and it is not similar to what he exemplified with his saying: "li-Zayd darabtu", i.e., Zayd I struck, because "darabtu" in this example did not govern the pronoun of Zayd, and it is not permissible to estimate a governing word in "li-kulli wijhatin" that its saying "muwalliha" explains, like our estimate "Zaydan ana daribuhu", i.e., "I strike Zayd, I am the one striking him", for then the matter would be of the type of al-ishtighal (the verb occupied with a pronoun), because the topicalized element (al-mushtaghal 'anhu) cannot be introduced by a preposition. You say: "Zaydan marartu bihi" (I passed by him), i.e., "I accompanied Zayd", and it is not permissible: "bi-Zaydin marartu bihi", so the estimate would be "marartu bi-Zaydin marartu bihi"; rather, every verb that is transitive with a preposition, when it governs the pronoun of a preceding noun in the case of al-ishtighal, that preceding noun cannot be introduced by a preposition, and that verb is estimated so that the preposition attaches to it; rather, when you intend al-ishtighal you put it in the accusative, and so the speech of the Arabs proceeds. God the Most High said: ﴿And the wrongdoers, He has prepared for them a painful punishment﴾ [al-Insan: 31]. And the poet said:
Atha'labata al-fawaris am Rabahan ... 'adalta bihim Tuhayyata wal-Khishaba
As for his exemplification: "li-Zayd abuhu daribuhu", it is a non-Arabic construction. If you say: why does this reading not work on the basis that "li-kulli wijhatin" is in the position of the second object of "muwalliha", and the first object is the pronoun attached to the active participle "muwalli", which is the ha', and it refers to the groups of the qiblas and the sects, and it is feminine in view of the meaning of "tawa'if" (groups), whose mention has already preceded, and the estimate would be: "and every direction, God is the One who turns the groups, the owners of the qiblas"? The answer: the explicit statement of the grammarians prevents this estimate, that the verb transitive to one object is the one whose object may take the lam when fronted. As for what is transitive to two, neither of its objects may take the lam, whether fronted or delayed. Likewise what is transitive to three. "Muwalli" here is an active participle from a verb transitive to two, so this estimate is not permissible. Ibn 'Atiyyah, in directing this reading, said: i.e., "so race to the good deeds, for every direction, and be attentive to them, and do not object in what He commanded you between this and that, i.e., obedience in all of it is what is incumbent on you." He put his saying "li-kulli wijhatin" before the command in his saying "fastabiqu al-khayrat" for the concern with the direction, as the object was fronted. End of Ibn 'Atiyyah's words, and this is (p.439) a direction that is not objectionable.

﴿So race to the good deeds﴾: this is a command to hasten to doing good and righteous deeds. It fits that whoever God has given a law, or a qibla, or a prayer, it is fitting to be concerned with hastening to it. Qatadah said: the racing in the matter of the Ka'bah is in defiance of the Jews by opposing them. Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is: hasten to righteous deeds, including facing the qibla and other things. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is also possible that the meaning is: "race to the most excellent of the directions, which are the directions parallel to the Ka'bah, even if they differ." We mentioned that "istabiq" means "tasabaq" (race one another), so it indicates reciprocity.
﴿Indeed We went, racing﴾ [Yusuf: 17], i.e., racing one another, as you say "tadarabu" (they struck one another). "Istabaqa" is not transitive, because "tasabaqa" is not transitive; for a transitive verb, when you form from a root whose meaning is "tafa'ala" for reciprocity, it becomes intransitive. You say: "darabtu Zaydan" (I struck Zayd), then you say "tadarabna" (we struck one another). Therefore it was said that "ila" (to) here is omitted, the estimate being: "fastabiqu ila al-khayrat" (race toward the good things). The poet Al-Ra'i said:
Thana'i 'alaykum Al Harb wa-man yamil ... siwakum fa-inni muhtadin ghayru ma'il
He means: and whoever inclines toward other than you.
﴿Wherever you are, God will bring you all together﴾: this sentence contains admonition, warning, and a display of His power. The meaning of "God will bring you all together" is: He will resurrect you and gather you for reward and punishment; you cannot escape Him, whether you comply or oppose. Accordingly Ibn 'Abbas said: i.e., on the Day of Resurrection. It is said: the meaning is: wherever you are from the different directions, God will bring you all together, i.e., He will gather you and make all your prayers toward one direction, and it is as if you were praying in the presence of the Sacred Mosque, said by al-Zamakhshari.
﴿Indeed God is powerful over everything﴾: the explanation of this sentence has been given before. It came after the conditional sentence containing the resurrection and recompense, i.e., the bringing together of the scattered remains in the many dispersed directions is not to be deemed unlikely, for God's power relates to possibilities, and this is one of them. We have previously explained that a sentence introduced by "inna" comes as a reason for what precedes it, so the meaning is: God's bringing you together all of you is because of His power over that.

[p. 435]

**Those to whom We gave the Book** (*alladhina ataynahum al-kitab*): This refers either to the scholars of the Jews and Christians, or to those Jews who believed in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), such as Ibn Salam and others, or to whoever believed in him without restriction. These are the opinions. As for "the Book" (*al-kitab*): it is the Torah, or the Gospel, or both together, or the Qur'an. These are opinions that depend on who is meant by "those to whom We gave." The wording *atayna-hum* (We gave them) is more eloquent than *utu* (they were given), because it attributes the giving to Allah, the Exalted, expressing it with the plural of majesty (*nun al-'azama*, the royal "We"). The same applies to similar forms such as *hadayna* (We guided), *ijtaba-yna* (We chose), and *istafayna* (We selected), intended as honour. It has been said: also because *utu* may be used of things that are not acceptable, whereas *atayna-hum* is most often used of what is acceptable, as in ﴿those to whom We gave the Book, the judgment and the prophethood﴾ [al-An'am: 89]. If more than one is meant by "the Book," it is stated in the singular because it refers to the written text, expressed by the verbal noun.

**They recognise him** (*ya'rifunahu*): This sentence is in the position of the predicate of the subject, which is *alladhina atayna-hum*. It is also permissible that *alladhina* be in the genitive, as an adjective of *al-zalimin* (the wrongdoers), or as an apposition to *al-zalimin*, or as an apposition to *alladhina utu al-kitab* (those who were given the Book) in the preceding verse [al-Baqarah: 145]. It may be in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "they are those who," or in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning "I mean." On these parsings, *ya'rifunahu* is a sentence in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), either from the first object of *atayna-hum* or from the second object, which is "the Book," since *ya'rifunahu* contains two pronouns referring back to them both. The apparent parsing is the first, because the speech is complete in itself as a nominal sentence, and because the speech evidently ends at ﴿Indeed, if you did so, you would surely be among the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 145].

The object pronoun in *ya'rifunahu* refers to the Prophet (ﷺ). This is the view of Mujahid, Qatadah and others. It is also transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, chosen by al-Zajjaj, preferred by al-Tibrizi, and al-Zamakhshari began with it, saying: "They recognise him with a clear recognition, distinguishing him from others by the specific, identifying attribute." Al-Zamakhshari and others said, and the wording is al-Zamakhshari's: "The pronoun is permissible even though no antecedent has preceded it, because the context indicates it and it is not ambiguous to the hearer. Such a pronoun carries exaltation and the implication that he is so famous, and so known as a recognised sign, that he needs no introduction." End of quotation. I say: it is not as they have said, that it is a pronoun before its antecedent. Rather, this is an instance of *iltifat* (a shift of grammatical person), because Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven; so We will surely turn you to a qiblah that you will like. So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144], then He said: ﴿And if you were to bring to those who were given the Book every sign, they would not follow your qiblah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 145], to the end of the verse. All of these are second-person pronouns addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then He shifted from the second-person pronoun to the third-person pronoun. The wisdom of this shift is that, when He had finished addressing him directly, He turned to the people and said: ﴿those to whom We gave the Book﴾, and We chose them to bear knowledge and revelation. They recognise this one whom We addressed in the preceding verses, and whom We commanded and forbade. They have no doubt about his identity, nor about the truth of his reports, concerning the obligations We imposed upon him, among which was the abrogation (*naskh*, the replacing of one ruling by another) of Bayt al-Maqdis by the Ka'bah, because their Book contains mention of him, his description, and an explicit statement about him. They find him written with them in the Torah and the Gospel. It is therefore clear from what we have mentioned that this is not a pronoun before its antecedent, but an instance of *iltifat*, and the wisdom of the shift has become evident.

What supports the pronoun referring to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is what is reported: that 'Umar asked 'Abdullah ibn Salam, may Allah be pleased with them both, and said: "Allah has sent down to His Prophet: ﴿those to whom We gave the Book recognise him﴾, the verse. So what is this recognition?" 'Abdullah said: "O 'Umar, I recognised him when I saw him, as I recognise my son, and my recognition of Muhammad (ﷺ) is firmer than my recognition of my son." 'Umar said: "And how is that?" He said: "I testify that he is truly the Messenger of Allah, and Allah has described him in our Book, but I do not know what women may do." 'Umar said: "May Allah grant you success, O son of Salam, for you have spoken the truth." This report has also been transmitted in an abbreviated form, with words close in meaning to these, and in it: "'Umar kissed his head." If the pronoun refers to the Messenger, then it has been said that what is meant is the recognition of his face and the distinguishing of him, not knowledge of the reality of his lineage. It has also been said: the meaning is that they recognise his truthfulness and his prophethood. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the truth, which is the turning to the Ka'bah, as stated by Ibn 'Abbas and also Qatadah, Ibn Jurayj and al-Rabi'. It has been said that it refers to the Qur'an. It has been said that it refers to knowledge. It has been said that it refers to the fact that the Sacred House is the qiblah of Abraham and of the prophets before him. This recognition is specific to the scholars, because He said: ﴿those to whom We gave the Book﴾. If the recognition relates to the Prophet (ﷺ), then it arises through seeing and description, or through the Qur'an, so it is obtained from the confirmation of their Book of the Qur'an, and from the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his description; or through the qiblah, or the turning, so it is obtained through the report of the Qur'an and the report of the Messenger, supported by extraordinary signs.

**As they recognise their sons** (*kama ya'rifuna abna'ahum*): The *kaf* (as) is in the accusative position, either as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun whose estimate is "a recognition like their recognition of their sons," or in the accusative as a circumstantial clause from the omitted pronoun of recognition, the estimate being: "They recognise him with a recognition similar to the recognition of their sons." The apparent sense of this comparison is that recognition here means recognition of the face and form, and the comparison with the recognition of sons strengthens this, and also strengthens that the pronoun refers to the Messenger (ﷺ), so that both kinds of recognition relate to the perceptible and seen. It is more emphatic in comparison than if the comparison were between a recognition whose object is a meaning and a recognition whose object is perceptible. The apparent meaning of *abna'* (sons) is restricted to males, so they would be singled out for this, because they are most in contact and company with their fathers, and cling more closely to the hearts of fathers. It is also possible that *abna'* means children in general, in which case it is by way of *taghlib* (the dominance of the masculine). The comparison with the recognition of sons is more emphatic than the comparison with the recognition of oneself, because a person may pass through a period of time in which he does not know himself, unlike sons, for no time passes upon a person without his knowing his son.

**Indeed, a group of them conceal the truth** (*wa inna fariqan minhum la-yaktumuna al-haqq*): That is, of those to whom We gave the Book, namely those who persist in disbelief and obstinacy, from the scholars of the Jews and Christians. This is the best interpretation of "those to whom We gave the Book." Those who went far (in their interpretation) claimed that this group means the ignorant among the Jews and Christians, concerning whom it was said: ﴿And among them are unlettered people who know not the Book except wishful thinking﴾ [al-Baqarah: 78], which would be to inform that this group conceals the truth while knowing it, and to describe the unlettered there as those who know not the Book except as wishful thinking. The truth concealed here is the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This is the view of Qatadah and Mujahid, and also the turning to the Ka'bah, or that the Ka'bah is the qiblah, or it is more general than that, so that every truth is included in it.

**While they know** (*wa hum ya'lamun*): A circumstantial clause, meaning: knowing that it is true. It is close to being an emphatic circumstantial clause, because the wording *yaktumuna al-haqq* (they conceal the truth) already indicates their knowledge of it, since concealment is the hiding of what is known. It has been said that the object of the knowledge is the punishment that falls upon the one who conceals the truth, meaning: while they know the punishment prescribed for the concealer of the truth. In that case it is an explanatory circumstantial clause.

**The truth is from your Lord** (*al-haqqu min rabbika*): Al-Jumhur read *al-haqq* with a nominative *damma*, as the subject, with the predicate being *min rabbika*, so the prepositional phrase is in the position of a predicate. Or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "it is the truth from your Lord," and the pronoun refers to the concealed truth, meaning: what they concealed is the truth from your Lord. In that case the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause, or a predicate after a predicate. Those who went far (in their parsing) claimed it is the subject with an omitted predicate, estimated as "the truth from your Lord, they recognise it." The definite article in *al-haqq* is either for a known referent (*'ahd*), namely the truth on which the Messenger stands, or the truth they concealed; or it is for the genus, meaning that truth is from Allah and not from anyone else, i.e. whatever is established as true is from Allah, like that on which the Messenger stands, and whatever its reality is not established is not from Allah, like the falsehood held by the People of the Book. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib read *al-haqqa* with a *fatha*, and it is parsed as an apposition to the concealed truth, so the estimate is: "they conceal the truth from your Lord," as al-Zamakhshari said; or as an object of *ya'lamun* (they know), as Ibn 'Atiyyah said, in which case it is one of the cases where the apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun, meaning: "while they know it being from your Lord." This is fine and good in places of exaltation and emphasis, like the poet's words:

*I see no thing outpacing death*

meaning: "no thing outpaces it." Ibn 'Atiyyah also permitted that it is in the accusative by an omitted verb, estimated as: "adhere to the truth from your Lord," and this is indicated by the address that follows: ﴿So never be among the doubters﴾. The address in meaning is to the community. The prohibition indicates that they exist, and forbids that he be among them, and the prohibition of being among them is more eloquent than the prohibition of the act itself. Your saying "do not be a wrongdoer" is more eloquent than your saying "do not wrong," because "do not wrong" forbids becoming involved in wrongdoing, whereas "do not be a wrongdoer" forbids being in that state. The prohibition against being in a state is more eloquent than the prohibition against that quality, because forbidding being in a state indicates by its form the generality of all future states in that quality, and entails the generality of that quality. The prohibition against a quality indicates by its form the generality of that quality. There is a difference between what indicates generality and entails generality, and what indicates generality only; therefore the first is more eloquent, and for this reason the prohibition against being (*al-kawn*) is common. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿So never be among the ignorant﴾ [al-An'am: 35] and ﴿And never be among those who denied the signs of Allah﴾ [Yunus: 95], and ﴿So never be in doubt about it﴾. The "being" (*al-kaynunah*) is in reality not the object of the prohibition. The meaning is: "Do not wrong in all your states," that is, in every individual state of yours, so that no time passes upon you in which wrongdoing is found from you. Thus *takun* (be) is an explicit statement covering all states, unlike "do not wrong," which entails the states. He emphasised the prohibition with the energetic *nun* (*nun al-tawkid*), for intensity in the prohibition, and the heavy form was used because it is more emphatic than the light form. The meaning is: "So never be among those who doubt the truth," because what comes from Allah, the Exalted, cannot admit doubt or dispute, since it is the pure truth, into which no suspicion or doubt can enter.

The answer: the explicit statement of the grammarians prevents this estimate, that the verb transitive to one object is the one whose object may take the lam when fronted. As for what is transitive to two, neither of its objects may take the lam, whether fronted or delayed. Likewise what is transitive to three. "Muwalli" here is an active participle from a verb transitive to two, so this estimate is not permissible. Ibn 'Atiyyah, in directing this reading, said: i.e., "so race to the good deeds, for every direction, and be attentive to them, and do not object in what He commanded you between this and that, i.e., obedience in all of it is what is incumbent on you." He put his saying "li-kulli wijhatin" before the command in his saying "fastabiqu al-khayrat" for the concern with the direction, as the object was fronted. End of Ibn 'Atiyyah's words, and this is (p.439) a direction that is not objectionable.

﴿So race to the good deeds﴾: this is a command to hasten to doing good and righteous deeds. It fits that whoever God has given a law, or a qibla, or a prayer, it is fitting to be concerned with hastening to it. Qatadah said: the racing in the matter of the Ka'bah is in defiance of the Jews by opposing them. Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is: hasten to righteous deeds, including facing the qibla and other things. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is also possible that the meaning is: "race to the most excellent of the directions, which are the directions parallel to the Ka'bah, even if they differ." We mentioned that "istabiq" means "tasabaq" (race one another), so it indicates reciprocity.
﴿Indeed We went, racing﴾ [Yusuf: 17], i.e., racing one another, as you say "tadarabu" (they struck one another). "Istabaqa" is not transitive, because "tasabaqa" is not transitive; for a transitive verb, when you form from a root whose meaning is "tafa'ala" for reciprocity, it becomes intransitive. You say: "darabtu Zaydan" (I struck Zayd), then you say "tadarabna" (we struck one another). Therefore it was said that "ila" (to) here is omitted, the estimate being: "fastabiqu ila al-khayrat" (race toward the good things). The poet Al-Ra'i said:
Thana'i 'alaykum Al Harb wa-man yamil ... siwakum fa-inni muhtadin ghayru ma'il
He means: and whoever inclines toward other than you.
﴿Wherever you are, God will bring you all together﴾: this sentence contains admonition, warning, and a display of His power. The meaning of "God will bring you all together" is: He will resurrect you and gather you for reward and punishment; you cannot escape Him, whether you comply or oppose. Accordingly Ibn 'Abbas said: i.e., on the Day of Resurrection. It is said: the meaning is: wherever you are from the different directions, God will bring you all together, i.e., He will gather you and make all your prayers toward one direction, and it is as if you were praying in the presence of the Sacred Mosque, said by al-Zamakhshari.
﴿Indeed God is powerful over everything﴾: the explanation of this sentence has been given before. It came after the conditional sentence containing the resurrection and recompense, i.e., the bringing together of the scattered remains in the many dispersed directions is not to be deemed unlikely, for God's power relates to possibilities, and this is one of them. We have previously explained that a sentence introduced by "inna" comes as a reason for what precedes it, so the meaning is: God's bringing you together all of you is because of His power over that.

[p. 435]

**Those to whom We gave the Book** (*alladhina ataynahum al-kitab*): This refers either to the scholars of the Jews and Christians, or to those Jews who believed in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), such as Ibn Salam and others, or to whoever believed in him without restriction. These are the opinions. As for "the Book" (*al-kitab*): it is the Torah, or the Gospel, or both together, or the Qur'an. These are opinions that depend on who is meant by "those to whom We gave." The wording *atayna-hum* (We gave them) is more eloquent than *utu* (they were given), because it attributes the giving to Allah, the Exalted, expressing it with the plural of majesty (*nun al-'azama*, the royal "We"). The same applies to similar forms such as *hadayna* (We guided), *ijtaba-yna* (We chose), and *istafayna* (We selected), intended as honour. It has been said: also because *utu* may be used of things that are not acceptable, whereas *atayna-hum* is most often used of what is acceptable, as in ﴿those to whom We gave the Book, the judgment and the prophethood﴾ [al-An'am: 89]. If more than one is meant by "the Book," it is stated in the singular because it refers to the written text, expressed by the verbal noun.

**They recognise him** (*ya'rifunahu*): This sentence is in the position of the predicate of the subject, which is *alladhina atayna-hum*. It is also permissible that *alladhina* be in the genitive, as an adjective of *al-zalimin* (the wrongdoers), or as an apposition to *al-zalimin*, or as an apposition to *alladhina utu al-kitab* (those who were given the Book) in the preceding verse [al-Baqarah: 145]. It may be in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "they are those who," or in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning "I mean." On these parsings, *ya'rifunahu* is a sentence in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), either from the first object of *atayna-hum* or from the second object, which is "the Book," since *ya'rifunahu* contains two pronouns referring back to them both. The apparent parsing is the first, because the speech is complete in itself as a nominal sentence, and because the speech evidently ends at ﴿Indeed, if you did so, you would surely be among the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 145].

The object pronoun in *ya'rifunahu* refers to the Prophet (ﷺ). This is the view of Mujahid, Qatadah and others. It is also transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, chosen by al-Zajjaj, preferred by al-Tibrizi, and al-Zamakhshari began with it, saying: "They recognise him with a clear recognition, distinguishing him from others by the specific, identifying attribute." Al-Zamakhshari and others said, and the wording is al-Zamakhshari's: "The pronoun is permissible even though no antecedent has preceded it, because the context indicates it and it is not ambiguous to the hearer. Such a pronoun carries exaltation and the implication that he is so famous, and so known as a recognised sign, that he needs no introduction." End of quotation. I say: it is not as they have said, that it is a pronoun before its antecedent. Rather, this is an instance of *iltifat* (a shift of grammatical person), because Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven; so We will surely turn you to a qiblah that you will like. So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144], then He said: ﴿And if you were to bring to those who were given the Book every sign, they would not follow your qiblah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 145], to the end of the verse. All of these are second-person pronouns addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then He shifted from the second-person pronoun to the third-person pronoun. The wisdom of this shift is that, when He had finished addressing him directly, He turned to the people and said: ﴿those to whom We gave the Book﴾, and We chose them to bear knowledge and revelation. They recognise this one whom We addressed in the preceding verses, and whom We commanded and forbade. They have no doubt about his identity, nor about the truth of his reports, concerning the obligations We imposed upon him, among which was the abrogation (*naskh*, the replacing of one ruling by another) of Bayt al-Maqdis by the Ka'bah, because their Book contains mention of him, his description, and an explicit statement about him. They find him written with them in the Torah and the Gospel. It is therefore clear from what we have mentioned that this is not a pronoun before its antecedent, but an instance of *iltifat*, and the wisdom of the shift has become evident.

What supports the pronoun referring to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is what is reported: that 'Umar asked 'Abdullah ibn Salam, may Allah be pleased with them both, and said: "Allah has sent down to His Prophet: ﴿those to whom We gave the Book recognise him﴾, the verse. So what is this recognition?" 'Abdullah said: "O 'Umar, I recognised him when I saw him, as I recognise my son, and my recognition of Muhammad (ﷺ) is firmer than my recognition of my son." 'Umar said: "And how is that?" He said: "I testify that he is truly the Messenger of Allah, and Allah has described him in our Book, but I do not know what women may do." 'Umar said: "May Allah grant you success, O son of Salam, for you have spoken the truth." This report has also been transmitted in an abbreviated form, with words close in meaning to these, and in it: "'Umar kissed his head." If the pronoun refers to the Messenger, then it has been said that what is meant is the recognition of his face and the distinguishing of him, not knowledge of the reality of his lineage. It has also been said: the meaning is that they recognise his truthfulness and his prophethood. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the truth, which is the turning to the Ka'bah, as stated by Ibn 'Abbas and also Qatadah, Ibn Jurayj and al-Rabi'. It has been said that it refers to the Qur'an. It has been said that it refers to knowledge. It has been said that it refers to the fact that the Sacred House is the qiblah of Abraham and of the prophets before him. This recognition is specific to the scholars, because He said: ﴿those to whom We gave the Book﴾. If the recognition relates to the Prophet (ﷺ), then it arises through seeing and description, or through the Qur'an, so it is obtained from the confirmation of their Book of the Qur'an, and from the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his description; or through the qiblah, or the turning, so it is obtained through the report of the Qur'an and the report of the Messenger, supported by extraordinary signs.

**As they recognise their sons** (*kama ya'rifuna abna'ahum*): The *kaf* (as) is in the accusative position, either as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun whose estimate is "a recognition like their recognition of their sons," or in the accusative as a circumstantial clause from the omitted pronoun of recognition, the estimate being: "They recognise him with a recognition similar to the recognition of their sons." The apparent sense of this comparison is that recognition here means recognition of the face and form, and the comparison with the recognition of sons strengthens this, and also strengthens that the pronoun refers to the Messenger (ﷺ), so that both kinds of recognition relate to the perceptible and seen. It is more emphatic in comparison than if the comparison were between a recognition whose object is a meaning and a recognition whose object is perceptible. The apparent meaning of *abna'* (sons) is restricted to males, so they would be singled out for this, because they are most in contact and company with their fathers, and cling more closely to the hearts of fathers. It is also possible that *abna'* means children in general, in which case it is by way of *taghlib* (the dominance of the masculine). The comparison with the recognition of sons is more emphatic than the comparison with the recognition of oneself, because a person may pass through a period of time in which he does not know himself, unlike sons, for no time passes upon a person without his knowing his son.

**Indeed, a group of them conceal the truth** (*wa inna fariqan minhum la-yaktumuna al-haqq*): That is, of those to whom We gave the Book, namely those who persist in disbelief and obstinacy, from the scholars of the Jews and Christians. This is the best interpretation of "those to whom We gave the Book." Those who went far (in their interpretation) claimed that this group means the ignorant among the Jews and Christians, concerning whom it was said: ﴿And among them are unlettered people who know not the Book except wishful thinking﴾ [al-Baqarah: 78], which would be to inform that this group conceals the truth while knowing it, and to describe the unlettered there as those who know not the Book except as wishful thinking. The truth concealed here is the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This is the view of Qatadah and Mujahid, and also the turning to the Ka'bah, or that the Ka'bah is the qiblah, or it is more general than that, so that every truth is included in it.

**While they know** (*wa hum ya'lamun*): A circumstantial clause, meaning: knowing that it is true. It is close to being an emphatic circumstantial clause, because the wording *yaktumuna al-haqq* (they conceal the truth) already indicates their knowledge of it, since concealment is the hiding of what is known. It has been said that the object of the knowledge is the punishment that falls upon the one who conceals the truth, meaning: while they know the punishment prescribed for the concealer of the truth. In that case it is an explanatory circumstantial clause.

**The truth is from your Lord** (*al-haqqu min rabbika*): Al-Jumhur read *al-haqq* with a nominative *damma*, as the subject, with the predicate being *min rabbika*, so the prepositional phrase is in the position of a predicate. Or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "it is the truth from your Lord," and the pronoun refers to the concealed truth, meaning: what they concealed is the truth from your Lord. In that case the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause, or a predicate after a predicate. Those who went far (in their parsing) claimed it is the subject with an omitted predicate, estimated as "the truth from your Lord, they recognise it." The definite article in *al-haqq* is either for a known referent (*'ahd*), namely the truth on which the Messenger stands, or the truth they concealed; or it is for the genus, meaning that truth is from Allah and not from anyone else, i.e. whatever is established as true is from Allah, like that on which the Messenger stands, and whatever its reality is not established is not from Allah, like the falsehood held by the People of the Book. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib read *al-haqqa* with a *fatha*, and it is parsed as an apposition to the concealed truth, so the estimate is: "they conceal the truth from your Lord," as al-Zamakhshari said; or as an object of *ya'lamun* (they know), as Ibn 'Atiyyah said, in which case it is one of the cases where the apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun, meaning: "while they know it being from your Lord." This is fine and good in places of exaltation and emphasis, like the poet's words:

*I see no thing outpacing death*

meaning: "no thing outpaces it." Ibn 'Atiyyah also permitted that it is in the accusative by an omitted verb, estimated as: "adhere to the truth from your Lord," and this is indicated by the address that follows: ﴿So never be among the doubters﴾. The address in meaning is to the community. The prohibition indicates that they exist, and forbids that he be among them, and the prohibition of being among them is more eloquent than the prohibition of the act itself. Your saying "do not be a wrongdoer" is more eloquent than your saying "do not wrong," because "do not wrong" forbids becoming involved in wrongdoing, whereas "do not be a wrongdoer" forbids being in that state. The prohibition against being in a state is more eloquent than the prohibition against that quality, because forbidding being in a state indicates by its form the generality of all future states in that quality, and entails the generality of that quality. The prohibition against a quality indicates by its form the generality of that quality. There is a difference between what indicates generality and entails generality, and what indicates generality only; therefore the first is more eloquent, and for this reason the prohibition against being (*al-kawn*) is common. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿So never be among the ignorant﴾ [al-An'am: 35] and ﴿And never be among those who denied the signs of Allah﴾ [Yunus: 95], and ﴿So never be in doubt about it﴾. The "being" (*al-kaynunah*) is in reality not the object of the prohibition. The meaning is: "Do not wrong in all your states," that is, in every individual state of yours, so that no time passes upon you in which wrongdoing is found from you. Thus *takun* (be) is an explicit statement covering all states, unlike "do not wrong," which entails the states. He emphasised the prohibition with the energetic *nun* (*nun al-tawkid*), for intensity in the prohibition, and the heavy form was used because it is more emphatic than the light form. The meaning is: "So never be among those who doubt the truth," because what comes from Allah, the Exalted, cannot admit doubt or dispute, since it is the pure truth, into which no suspicion or doubt can enter.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 146–148 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Each has a direction toward which it turns﴾, when he mentioned the qibla toward which the Muslims were commanded to face, which is the Ka'bah, and mentioned the determination of the People of the Book not to follow it, and that each of the two groups, the Jews and the Christians, was determined not to follow the other's qibla, he informed that this is by His doing, that He is the One who decrees it, and that He is the One who directs each of them to their qibla. In this there is a reminder to thank God, for He guided the Muslims to follow what He commanded of them regarding facing the qibla, and chose them for it. The majority read: "wa-li-kullin" (with tanwin on kullin), "wijhatun" (in the nominative), "huwa muwalliyha" with a kasra on the lam as an active participle (ism fa'il). Ibn 'Amir read: "huwa muwalliha" with a fatha on the lam as a passive participle (ism maf'ul), and this is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas. A group read irregularly (shadhdh): "wa-li-kulli wijhatin", with a kasra on the lam of "kulli" without tanwin, and "wijhatin" with a kasra and tanwin, on the basis of the idafa (construction of annexation). The tanwin on "kullin" is the tanwin of compensation (tanwin 'iwad) for the annexed noun, and the omitted noun annexed to "kullin" has been disputed in its estimation. It is said: the meaning is "and for each group among the people of the religions". It is said: the meaning is "and for each people of a region among the Muslims there is a direction from the people of all the horizons toward the direction of the Ka'bah, behind it, in front of it, to its right and to its left; no direction of its directions is more deserving to be a qibla than another". It is said: the meaning is "and for each prophet there is a qibla", said by Ibn 'Abbas. It is said: the meaning is "and for each angel and messenger, bearer of a law, there is a direction of qibla; the qibla of those brought near is the Throne, the qibla of the spiritual beings is the Kursi, the qibla of the Karubiyyin is the Bayt al-Ma'mur, and the qibla of the prophets before you is Bayt al-Maqdis, and your qibla is the Ka'bah". Included in what we have mentioned is that the intended meaning of "wijhah" is "qibla", and this is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the reading of Ubayy, who read: "wa-li-kullin qiblatun". 'Abdullah read: "wa-li-kullin ja'alna qiblatan". Al-Hasan said: "wijhatan" means "tariqah" (way, path), as He said: ﴿For each of you We have appointed a law and a method﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48], i.e., for each prophet there is a way. Qatadah said: "wijhatan" means: a prayer they pray, and it is from His saying: "huwa muwalliha" referring to "kullin" according to its wording, not its meaning; i.e., he faces it and directs toward it his prayer by which he draws near (to God). The second object of "muwalliha" is omitted for understanding of the meaning, i.e., he turns it (his) face or himself, said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' and al-Rabi'. This is corroborated by the fact that "huwa" refers to "kull" in the reading of the one who read: "huwa muwalliha". It is said: "huwa" refers to God, the Most High, said by al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj, i.e., God is the One who turns it (the direction) toward them; whoever followed it followed it, and whoever abandoned it abandoned it. So the meaning of "huwa muwalliha" on this interpretation is: its legislator and the one who obligates them with it. The nominal sentence in the position of a description (sifah) for "wijhatun". As for the reading of the one who read "wa-li-kulli wijhatin" in the idafa, Muhammad ibn Jarir said: it is an error, and one should not rush to judge it as an error, especially since it is attributed to Ibn 'Amir, one of the seven readers, and this reading has been given a grammatical justification. Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is "and for each direction, God is the One who turns it", so the lam was added for the fronting of the object, as in your saying: "li-Zayd darabtu" (for Zayd I struck), and "li-Zayd abuhu daribuhu". End of his words. This is corrupt, because when the governing word transitively reaches a pronoun of the noun, it does not extend to its apparent noun governed by the lam. It is not permissible to say: "li-Zayd darabtuhu" nor "li-Zayd ana daribuhu". Moreover, when the verb is transitive to a pronoun without an intermediary, it is strong, and the lam only enters upon the apparent noun when it is fronted in order to strengthen it, because its reaching it when fronted is weak; the governing word cannot be strong and weak in one state, and because it would entail that what is transitive to one becomes transitive to two. For this reason the grammarians interpreted his saying:
Suraqah li-l-Qur'an yadrusuhu [the poetic example]
and it is not similar to what he exemplified with his saying: "li-Zayd darabtu", i.e., Zayd I struck, because "darabtu" in this example did not govern the pronoun of Zayd, and it is not permissible to estimate a governing word in "li-kulli wijhatin" that its saying "muwalliha" explains, like our estimate "Zaydan ana daribuhu", i.e., "I strike Zayd, I am the one striking him", for then the matter would be of the type of al-ishtighal (the verb occupied with a pronoun), because the topicalized element (al-mushtaghal 'anhu) cannot be introduced by a preposition. You say: "Zaydan marartu bihi" (I passed by him), i.e., "I accompanied Zayd", and it is not permissible: "bi-Zaydin marartu bihi", so the estimate would be "marartu bi-Zaydin marartu bihi"; rather, every verb that is transitive with a preposition, when it governs the pronoun of a preceding noun in the case of al-ishtighal, that preceding noun cannot be introduced by a preposition, and that verb is estimated so that the preposition attaches to it; rather, when you intend al-ishtighal you put it in the accusative, and so the speech of the Arabs proceeds. God the Most High said: ﴿And the wrongdoers, He has prepared for them a painful punishment﴾ [al-Insan: 31]. And the poet said:
Atha'labata al-fawaris am Rabahan ... 'adalta bihim Tuhayyata wal-Khishaba
As for his exemplification: "li-Zayd abuhu daribuhu", it is a non-Arabic construction. If you say: why does this reading not work on the basis that "li-kulli wijhatin" is in the position of the second object of "muwalliha", and the first object is the pronoun attached to the active participle "muwalli", which is the ha', and it refers to the groups of the qiblas and the sects, and it is feminine in view of the meaning of "tawa'if" (groups), whose mention has already preceded, and the estimate would be: "and every direction, God is the One who turns the groups, the owners of the qiblas"? The answer: the explicit statement of the grammarians prevents this estimate, that the verb transitive to one object is the one whose object may take the lam when fronted. As for what is transitive to two, neither of its objects may take the lam, whether fronted or delayed. Likewise what is transitive to three. "Muwalli" here is an active participle from a verb transitive to two, so this estimate is not permissible. Ibn 'Atiyyah, in directing this reading, said: i.e., "so race to the good deeds, for every direction, and be attentive to them, and do not object in what He commanded you between this and that, i.e., obedience in all of it is what is incumbent on you." He put his saying "li-kulli wijhatin" before the command in his saying "fastabiqu al-khayrat" for the concern with the direction, as the object was fronted. End of Ibn 'Atiyyah's words, and this is (p.439) a direction that is not objectionable.

﴿So race to the good deeds﴾: this is a command to hasten to doing good and righteous deeds. It fits that whoever God has given a law, or a qibla, or a prayer, it is fitting to be concerned with hastening to it. Qatadah said: the racing in the matter of the Ka'bah is in defiance of the Jews by opposing them. Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is: hasten to righteous deeds, including facing the qibla and other things. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is also possible that the meaning is: "race to the most excellent of the directions, which are the directions parallel to the Ka'bah, even if they differ." We mentioned that "istabiq" means "tasabaq" (race one another), so it indicates reciprocity.
﴿Indeed We went, racing﴾ [Yusuf: 17], i.e., racing one another, as you say "tadarabu" (they struck one another). "Istabaqa" is not transitive, because "tasabaqa" is not transitive; for a transitive verb, when you form from a root whose meaning is "tafa'ala" for reciprocity, it becomes intransitive. You say: "darabtu Zaydan" (I struck Zayd), then you say "tadarabna" (we struck one another). Therefore it was said that "ila" (to) here is omitted, the estimate being: "fastabiqu ila al-khayrat" (race toward the good things). The poet Al-Ra'i said:
Thana'i 'alaykum Al Harb wa-man yamil ... siwakum fa-inni muhtadin ghayru ma'il
He means: and whoever inclines toward other than you.
﴿Wherever you are, God will bring you all together﴾: this sentence contains admonition, warning, and a display of His power. The meaning of "God will bring you all together" is: He will resurrect you and gather you for reward and punishment; you cannot escape Him, whether you comply or oppose. Accordingly Ibn 'Abbas said: i.e., on the Day of Resurrection. It is said: the meaning is: wherever you are from the different directions, God will bring you all together, i.e., He will gather you and make all your prayers toward one direction, and it is as if you were praying in the presence of the Sacred Mosque, said by al-Zamakhshari.
﴿Indeed God is powerful over everything﴾: the explanation of this sentence has been given before. It came after the conditional sentence containing the resurrection and recompense, i.e., the bringing together of the scattered remains in the many dispersed directions is not to be deemed unlikely, for God's power relates to possibilities, and this is one of them. We have previously explained that a sentence introduced by "inna" comes as a reason for what precedes it, so the meaning is: God's bringing you together all of you is because of His power over that.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 2, Verse 149:**

﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque.﴾ When the Exalted One mentioned that every people has a direction (*wijhah*) toward which it turns, He commanded His Prophet to turn his face toward the Sacred Mosque from whatever place he set out from. This is because His saying, ﴿So We shall surely turn you to a qiblah (direction of prayer) with which you will be pleased; so turn your face﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144], apparently means a command to him to face the Ka'bah while he was residing in Medina. Thus this second command made clear that the two states, residence and travel, are equal in that he is commanded to face the Sacred House. Then He joined to it, ﴿And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 150], to make clear their equality in this matter, meaning in the state of travel, while the first refers to the state of residence. ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmayr read "wa-min ḥaythu" with a fatḥah (ḥaythu), lightening it. The discussion of *ḥaythu* has already been presented in His saying, ﴿Eat from it wherever you wish (ḥaythu shi'tumā)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 35].

﴿And indeed, it is the truth from your Lord.﴾ This is a report from Allah the Exalted that facing this qiblah is the truth, meaning the established matter to which abrogation (*naskh*, the cancellation of a ruling by a later one) or alteration does not apply. In the first passage He said, ﴿And indeed, those who were given the Scripture know that it is the truth from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144], since the discourse was with their foolish ones who objected to changing the qiblah. He responded to them with several points, among them that their scholars know that changing the qiblah is a truth from Allah. He concluded the end of this verse with what He concluded the end of that one with, His saying, ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾, regarding compliance with this great obligation, which is the change from one direction to another, and this is purely an act of worship (*taʿabbud*). All directions are equal with respect to the Creator, the Exalted, so His specifying this direction for facing during a period of time, and then abrogating that by facing another direction that is permanent, does not appear, at first glance, to be anything other than pure worship. Nothing remains in this but compliance with what Allah has commanded. So He informed the Exalted that He is not heedless of your deeds, but rather He is the One who observes them, rewarding with reward the one who complies with His command, and with punishment the one who opposes it.

The phrase ﴿the truth from your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 147] occurs in both places, and the phrase "And Allah is not" (*wa-mā Allāhu*) occurs in both places. Where He draws attention to deriving His wisdom by reflecting on His acts, He mentions the Lord (*Rabb*), who necessitates blessings, so that we may look through them to the Benefactor and infer Him from them. And when He reached the mention of the threat (*waʿīd*), He mentioned the name Allah, which necessitates worship, whoever neglects which deserves painful punishment. (p-440)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 150 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it.﴾ The apparent sense of this sentence is that it is repeated as an emphasis only for what precedes it in the verse that follows, not that it is an emphasis for the first verse, because we have already explained that the first is concerning residence (al-iqamah), the second concerning travel (al-safar), and the third is concerning travel, so it is an emphasis for the second. The wisdom of this emphasis is to fix this ruling and to confirm the abrogation (naskh) of facing Bayt al-Maqdis, because abrogation is one of the places of trial (fitnah), doubt (shubhah), and Satan's adorning [of falsehood] for the purpose of slandering the change of one qiblah for another, since that was difficult for them. Thus He emphasized the matter of abrogation with this and affirmed it. The emphasis on what we have established was by repeating these sentences twice, because that is the most common usage in the Arabic language, which is that a sentence is repeated once. Al-Mahdawi said: these commands were repeated because not everyone memorizes the Qur'an, so something would be found with some people that was not with others if it were not repeated. This meaning of repetition is narrated from Ja'far al-Sadiq, and for this same reason repetition was removed in the stories. It has also been said: since this event was the first of the occurrences in which abrogation appeared in our law, it was repeated for emphasis, affirmation, and the removal of doubt. The scholars have mentioned in these verses specifying factors that take them out of the category of emphasis. It was said: the first, from His saying "So turn your face," is the abrogation of the first qiblah; the second is for the uniformity of the ruling in all places; and the third is for its permanence in all times. It was said: the first is in the Sacred Mosque, the second is outside the Mosque, and the third is outside the city. It was said: the first departure is to a place where the Ka'bah can be seen, and the second is to a place where it cannot be seen, so He equated the two situations. It was said: the first departure is connected to the mention of the cause, which is: ﴿And indeed it is the truth from your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 149], and the second is connected to the removal of argument, which is: ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾. It was said: the first is for all conditions, the second for all places, and the third for all times. It was said: the first is that the person is in the Sacred Mosque, the second that he is outside it but still in the city, and the third that he leaves the city for the regions of the earth, so He equated these situations, lest it be supposed that the nearer has a sanctity that does not hold for the farther. It was said: the specification occurred in each of the three through a matter: the first clarifies that the People of the Book know the matter of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ and the matter of this qiblah, to the extent that they witnessed that in the Torah and the Gospel; the second contains God's testimony that this is true; and the third clarifies that He did this ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾, thereby cutting off the words of the obstinate. It was said: the first is coupled with God's honoring them with the qiblah they loved, which is the qiblah of Abraham, upon our Prophet and him be the best of prayers and peace, by His saying: ﴿And for each there is a direction toward which he turns﴾ [al-Baqarah: 148], meaning: for every possessor of a call there is a qiblah he turns toward; so turn you toward the most noble of directions, which God knows to be the truth. The third is coupled with God cutting off the argument of those Jews who disputed with Him. It was said: perhaps it occurred to an ignorant person that He did this for the pleasure of His Prophet, because of His saying: ﴿So We will surely turn you to a qiblah that you will be pleased with﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144]; so He removed this illusion by His saying: ﴿And indeed it is the truth from your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 149], meaning: We did not turn you merely for pleasure, but because this turning is the truth; so it is not like the qiblah of the Jews, which they follow merely out of desire. Then He repeated a third time, and the meaning is: persist upon this qiblah in all times. It was said: He repeated "and wherever you are," so with one of them He urged turning toward the qiblah with the heart and body, wherever a person may be, whether far from it or near to it, and that is in a state of ability and choice; and with the other He urged turning toward it in the heart when the qiblah is uncertain, in a state of competition, in voluntary prayer during travel, and on the mount during travel.
