(so that not): This is the lam of purpose (lam kay), and "an" after it is followed by the negative "la", and he has placed it as a barrier between "an" and its operand, which is "yakūna", just as they placed it as a barrier between the conditional particle and the jussive in their saying: "a-in la taf'al af'al" [Is it if you do not do it that I will do it?]. In the Mushaf it was written: "la" with no following "ya" [i.e., the hamzah was given the form of a yā'], followed by an alif-lam, so they made the form of the hamzah a yā', in accordance with the lightening (al-takhfif) which Nafi' recited in the Qur'an by substituting this hamzah with a yā'.

Al-Jumhur recited with full articulation (al-tahqiq): and this "an" must be made clear (wajibat al-izhar) here, because of their disliking the juxtaposition of the lam of genitive (lam al-jarr) with the negative "la", since in that there is an awkwardness in pronunciation; and it is permissible to make it clear in other than this position. So when they retained it, that is the original, and it is the less common in their speech; and when they omitted it, that is because the meaning requires it, the necessity being that the lam is not the nasb-governing particle, since it has been established that it governs nouns in the genitive, and the governors of nouns do not govern verbs.

﴿for the people, an argument against you﴾: i.e., a contention (ihtijaj). As for "the people": it has been said it is general, including the Jews, the Arabs, and others. It has been said: the Jews, and their argument is their saying: "Muhammad opposes us in our qiblah, and he used to follow it," or "he did not turn away from Bayt al-Maqdis while knowing it was the truth, except by his own opinion, and he claims that he was commanded to it," or "Muhammad and his companions did not know where their qiblah was until We guided them." It has been said: the polytheist Arabs, and their argument is their saying: "Muhammad has returned to our qiblah, and he will return to our religion since he has begun to face the qiblah." It has been said: "the people" is general, and the meaning is that God promised them that no argument would stand against them except a false argument, which is their saying: "He agrees with the Jews while saying: I am a ḥanīf, following the religion of Abraham," or "you have no certainty and you do not hold firmly to any religion," or they said: "What is wrong with you that you abandoned Bayt al-Maqdis? If it was misguidance, then you practised it; and if it was guidance, then you departed from it," or their saying: "The man longed for his father's house and his people's religion," or their saying in the Torah: "He will turn to the qiblah of his father Abraham," so God turned him so that they would not say: "We find him in the Torah turning, yet he did not turn," and that would be an argument for them; so God removed their argument by that.

The lam in "li-allā" is the lam of genitive, which entered upon "in" and what follows it, so it is interpreted as a verbal noun, i.e., "for the absence of an argument against you." This lam is connected, it has been said, to an omitted element, i.e., "We have made you know the correct direction in your qiblah, and the argument in that is so that there will not be..." It has been said: it is connected to "wallū," and the reading with the yā' is because the feminine of "ḥujjah" is not real, and the separation between the verb and its subject by two prepositional phrases made the masculine very easy. The predicate of "kāna" is His saying "li-l-nās," and "'alaykum" is in the position of an accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl); originally it was an attribute of "ḥujjah," but when it preceded it, it became accusative as a ḥāl, and the governing element is omitted. "Wa-lā" is not permissible to be connected to "ḥujjah," because it carries the sense of contention, and the complement of a masdar that is resolved into a particle and a verb may not precede its governor. Some permitted that "'alaykum" be connected to "ḥujjah," so they reported, and it is possible that "'alaykum" is the predicate, and "li-l-nās" is connected to the word "yakūn," because "kāna" as a defective verb may govern adverbial and prepositional phrases.

﴿except those of them who did wrong﴾. Al-Jumhur read "illā," taking it as the particle of exception. Ibn 'Amir, Zayd ibn 'Ali, and Ibn Zayd read "alā," with a fatḥah on the hamzah and the lightening of the lam of "allā," treating it as the particle of alerting and opening. According to the reading of these, "alladhīna ẓalamū" is a subject (mubtada'), and the sentence "fa-lā takhshawhum wa-khshawnī" [So do not fear them, but fear Me] is in the position of the predicate, and the fa' entered because he treated "alladhīna" in the manner of a conditional, and the past verb serving as the relative clause is in the future sense. The meaning: as if it were said: whoever of the people does wrong, then do not fear their attacks upon your qiblah. "Wa-khshawnī": do not oppose My command. Were it not for the entry of the fa', the accusative of "alladhīna ẓalamū" would be preferred, on the basis that the matter is from the chapter of ishtighāl, i.e., "do not fear those who did wrong; do not fear them." But that is permissible according to the view of al-Akhfash on the addition of the fa'. Ibn 'Aṭiyyah permitted that "alladhīna" be accusative by an implied verb in the sense of incitement (al-ighrā'). Al-Sajawandi reported from Abu Bakr ibn Mujahid that he read "ilā alladhīna," making it a preposition and interpreting it with the sense of "maʿa" [with]. As for the reading of al-Jumhur, the exception is connected (muttasil), as said by Ibn 'Abbas and others, and chosen by al-Tabari, and Ibn 'Aṭiyyah began with it, and al-Zamakhshari mentioned no other; for whenever a connected exception is possible in a good manner, it is preferable to other than it. Al-Zamakhshari said: its meaning is: so that there will be no argument for anyone among the Jews, except for the obstinate among them who say: "He did not abandon our qiblah for Ka'bah except out of inclination toward the religion of his people and love for his land; and if he were upon the truth, he would have adhered to the qiblah of the prophets." (If you say): what argument would there have been for those of them who were fair, had he not turned, so that he avoided that argument and did not care for the argument of the obstinate? I say: they would say: "Why does he not turn toward the qiblah of his father Abraham, as is mentioned of him in the Torah?" (If you say): how did he apply the name "argument" to the saying of the obstinate? I say: because they present it in the manner of an argument. The end of his words. Ibn 'Aṭiyyah said: the meaning is that there is no argument against you except the futile argument of those who did wrong among the Jews and others, from everyone who spoke about this event, in their saying: "What turned them from their qiblah which they were upon?" [al-Baqarah: 142] mockingly, and in their saying: "Muhammad has become confused in his religion," and other sayings that did not arise except from a worshipper of idols, or from a Jew, or from a hypocrite. God called them "argument" and judged their invalidity when they came from wrongdoers. The end of his words. With this explanation the connection of the exception has become clear. Some people went to the view that it is a disconnected exception (istithnā' munqaṭiʿ), i.e., "but those who did wrong, they will attach themselves to you with doubt, placing it in the position of argument, while it is not an argument." The point of disagreement is: is the argument the valid proof and demonstration, or is the argument the act of contending and dispute? If it is the first, then it is a disconnected exception; if it is the second, then it is a connected exception. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, God made you know the matter of contention regarding the qiblah in His saying: ﴿And for each there is a direction toward which he turns﴾ [al-Baqarah: 148]: "so that there will be no argument for the people against you, except from those who did wrong by their contention regarding what had become clear to them," as you say: "You have no argument against me except injustice, or except that you wrong me," meaning: you have no argument at all, but you are wronging me. Qutrub permitted that "alladhīna" be in the genitive position as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun of address in "'alaykum," the sense being: "so that no argument may be established for the people against those of them who are not wrongdoers, namely you, the addressed, by turning your faces to the qiblah." Al-Sajawandi reported that Qutrub read: "illā ʿalā alladhīna ẓalamū," and it is also a substitute by making the preposition explicit, like His saying: ﴿to those who were deemed weak, to those of them who believed﴾ [al-A'raf: 75]. But this is weak, because it involves substituting an apparent noun for a pronoun of address, a substitution of one thing for another while they are of one referent, and that is not permissible except according to the view of al-Akhfash. Abu 'Ubayd Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna asserted that "illā" in the verse has the meaning of "wa" [and], and he cited as an instance of that the verse:

"In Medina there is no house other than one: the house of the caliph, except the house of Marwan."

And his saying:

"Every brother will be parted from his brother... by your father's life, except the two stars [al-Farqadan]."

**Estimated sense:** Its (the commentary's) estimation: "with Him are those who did wrong," and "the house of Marwan" and "al-Farqadan." Affirming that *illa* (except) means *wa* (and) is not supported by any evidence. The exception is permissible in the case where he claimed that *illa* means *wa*, and Abu 'Ubayda was considered weak in grammar (*nahw*). Al-Zajjaj said: "This is an error according to the skilled grammarians (*hudhdhaq al-nahwiyyin*). Even weaker than this is the claim that *illa* means *ba'da* (after), i.e., after those who did wrong." He cited as examples *(illa ma qad salaf)*, meaning "after what has already passed," and *﴿illa al-mawtata al-ula﴾* [al-Dukhan 44:56], meaning "after the first death." Had some exegetes (*mufassirin*) not mentioned these two opinions, I would not have mentioned them, because of their weakness.

**﴿So do not fear them, but fear Me﴾:** This contains a belittling of their status, a command to disregard them, and an observance of God's command. The pronoun of the object in *fala takhshawhum* may refer to the people, meaning "do not fear the people," or it may refer to those who did wrong, meaning "do not fear the wrongdoers." He forbade fearing them regarding the false speech they embellish, for they have no power to benefit or harm. He commanded fear of Him in abandoning what He commanded them of turning toward the Sacred Mosque. It was also said: the meaning of "do not fear them" is in opposition (*mubayana*), and "fear Me" is in opposition to disobedience (*mukhalafa*), and this meaning is close to the first. We have already explained these two clauses in mentioning the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, with something close to this. Al-Suddi said: its meaning is "do not fear that I will return you to your religion, and fear Me." But what he said is not supported by His saying "so do not fear them." Some said: He mentioned *khashya* (awe-fear) here and did not mention *khawf* (fear), because *khashya* is caution regarding a matter that has already occurred, while *khawf* is caution regarding a matter that has not yet occurred. What language and usage indicate is that *khashya* and *khawf* are synonyms. God the Exalted said: ﴿So do not fear them, but fear Me﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:175], just as He said here: ﴿So do not fear them, but fear Me﴾.

**﴿And that I may complete My favor upon you﴾:** The apparent view is that it is coordinated (*ma'tuf*) with His saying "so that there will not be" (*li'alla yakuna*). The meaning would be: We informed you of the correct direction of your qibla and gave you the proof against the people's arguments, and in order to complete the favor, so the guidance is motivated by these two causes. The separation by the exception and what follows it is no separation at all, since it belongs to the scope of the first cause. It was also said: it is coordinated with a deleted cause, and both of them have as their motive the earlier fear, as if it were said: "fear Me so that I may grant you success, and so that I may complete My favor upon you." It was also said: the *lam* is attached to a delayed verb, the estimated sense being: "And so that I may complete My favor upon you, I informed you of My qibla." Whoever claims that the *waw* is superfluous, his statement is weak. The completion of the favor is through what He guided them to of the qibla, or through what He prepared for them of the reward of obedience, or through what came to the Arabs of honor by changing the qibla to the Ka'ba, or through the nullification of the arguments of those who argued against them, or through their entry into Paradise, or through dying in Islam, or the favor is the way (*sunna*) of Islam, the Qur'an, Muhammad (ﷺ), concealment, well-being, and independence from people; or through the laws of the true primordial religion (*al-milla al-hanifiyya*). These are eight opinions, which came as examples and not as a definitive specification, and each of them is a favor.

**﴿And that you may be guided﴾:** The discussion of *la'alla* has preceded regarding its coming from God the Exalted in His saying ﴿those before you, that you may be mindful﴾ [al-Baqara 2:183], at the beginning of al-Baqara, and this is its first occurrence there. The meaning: that you may be in hope of the continuation of My guidance of you toward facing the Ka'ba, or that you may be guided to the qibla of your father Ibrahim. The apparent meaning is the hope of guidance in general.

**﴿كَما أرْسَلْنا فِيكُمْ﴾** ("as We sent among you"): The *kaf* here is for comparison (*tashbih*), and it is in the accusative position as an adjective (*na't*) of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*). Scholars differ on how to supply that omitted noun. One view says the sense is: "and that I may complete My favour upon you with a completion like the completion of sending the Messenger among you." The two instances of "completion" have different objects: the first completion is by reward in the Hereafter, and the second is by sending the Messenger to us in this world. Or, the first completion is by the answering of Abraham's first supplication in His words, ﴿ومِن ذُرِّيَّتِنا أُمَّةً مُسْلِمَةً لَكَ﴾ (2:128), and the second is by the answering of his second supplication in His words, ﴿رَبَّنا وابْعَثْ فِيهِمْ رَسُولًا مِنهُمْ﴾ (2:129).

Another view says the sense is: "and that you may be guided with a guidance like Our sending a Messenger among you," so that the comparison of guidance with sending is in its certainty and firmness, meaning a guidance that is established and realised, just as the realisation and establishment of Our sending is. Another view says it is connected to His words, ﴿وكَذَلِكَ جَعَلْناكم أُمَّةً وسَطًا﴾ (2:143), meaning "a making like what We sent," and this is the view of Abu Muslim. But this is very far-fetched, because of the long separation, which indicates a break in the connection.

Another view says the *kaf* is in the accusative position as a state (*hal*) of "My favour," meaning ﴿ولِأُتِمَّ نِعْمَتِي عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ (2:150) "likening Our sending among you of a Messenger," that is, likening the favour of sending, so this involves an omitted *mudaf* (governed noun). Another view says the *kaf* is cut off from the speech before it and connected to what follows it. Al-Zamakhshari said: "As (p-444) I reminded you by sending the Messenger, so remember Me by obedience, and I will remember you by reward," end of quote. On this view it is an omitted verbal noun and an omitted *mudaf*, meaning: "remember Me with a remembrance like Our remembrance of you by sending," and then "like the remembrance of Our sending," then the *mudaf* was omitted and the *mudaf ilayh* was put in its place. This is like saying: "As so-and-so came to you, go to him with your generosity." This is the view of Mujahid, Ata, al-Kalbi and Muqatil, and it is the choice of al-Akhfash, al-Zajjaj, Ibn Kaysan and al-Asamm. The meaning is that you were in a state in which you did not read a Book and did not know a Messenger, and Muhammad (ﷺ) was a man from among you, who came to you with the most wondrous of signs indicating his truthfulness. So He said: "As I have bestowed this favour upon you and made it a proof for you, remember Me with thankfulness, and I will remember you with My mercy." This is confirmed by ﴿لَقَدْ مَنَّ اللَّهُ عَلى المُؤْمِنِينَ إذْ بَعَثَ فِيهِمْ رَسُولًا مِن أنْفُسِهِمْ﴾ (3:164). This sense is possible, indeed it is apparent, and it is when *an* is attached to what follows it. In that case the *kaf* is not for comparison but for causation (*ta'lil*), which is a meaning said to be attributed to it, and this is the interpretation of His words, ﴿واذْكُرُوهُ كَما هَداكُمْ﴾ (2:198), and the verse of the poet:

*"Do not revile people as you are not reviled."*

That is: "remember Him for His guidance of you," and "do not revile people because you are not reviled," meaning refrain from reviling people because people refrain from reviling you. The *ma* in *kama* is verbal (*masdariyya*). Whoever claimed that it is relative in the sense of *alladhi* ("who"), with an omitted returning pronoun and *rasulan* as an apposition to it, is far off the mark, since the sense "like him whom We sent as a messenger" is hard to sustain with the speech before it and the speech after it, and because it involves using *ma* for individuals who have intellect. Likewise, the one who made *ma* a restrictive particle (*kaffa*) was going there only where a verbal noun cannot be formed from it together with what follows it, because it governs nominal sentences, as in the poet's words:

*"By your life, I and Abu Humayd are like the drunkard and the forbearing man."*

As for the view of one who said that "as We sent" is connected to what follows it, Abu Muhammad Makki ibn Abi Talib rejected it. He said: because when the command has an answer, what precedes it is not connected to it, since it is occupied with its answer. He said: If you said, "As I have been good to you, honour me, and I will honour you," the *kaf* of *kama* would not be connected to "honour me," because it has an answer. Rather it would be connected to something else or to a hidden element. Likewise, "remember Me, and I will remember you" is a command that has an answer, so *kama* is not connected to it, and this is not permissible except by analogy with the conditional which takes two answers, which is your saying: "If so-and-so comes to you, go to him and you will please him," so *kama* and "remember Me" would be two answers to the command. The first is more eloquent and more well-known. You may say: "As I have been good to you, honour me," and it is correct to make the *kaf* connected to "honour me," since it has no answer. End of his words.

Makki preferred the view that it is connected to what precedes it, namely ﴿ولِأُتِمَّ نِعْمَتِي عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ (2:150), because the context of the wording indicates that the meaning is: "and that I may complete My favour upon you by clarifying the creed of your father Abraham, as We answered his supplication concerning you, so We sent to you a Messenger from among you who recites." What Makki went to, namely invalidating the connection of *kama* to what follows it for the reason mentioned, is not a valid argument, because the *kaf* is either for comparison or for causation. If it is for comparison, then it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, and it is permissible for that verbal noun to precede the verb. An example: "Honour me with the honour I previously gave you, and I will honour you," so this verbal noun may be placed first. If it is for causation, then it is also permissible for that to precede the verb. An example: "Honour me for my honouring you, and I will honour you." We know of no disagreement about the permissibility of placing this verbal noun and this cause before the verb that governs them. Makki's permitting that by analogy with the conditional that takes two answers, and his calling "as" and "remember Me" two answers to the command, is not correct, because *kama* is not an answer, and because that analogy is invalid: a verbal noun of comparison does not resemble an answer, and likewise causation. As for the comparative verbal noun, it is a description of the action commanded, so it is not consequent upon the mere occurrence of the act; rather the act occurs only with that description. On this basis it does not resemble an answer, because an answer is consequent upon the very occurrence of the act. As for causation, it likewise is not consequent upon the occurrence of the act; rather the act is consequent upon the existence of the cause. So it is the opposite of an answer, because an answer is consequent upon the occurrence of the act, while the cause is that upon which the existence of the act is consequent. There is thus no resemblance between them. In my view, what is really weak is the connection of *kama* to "remember Me," because of the *fa'* (the particle "so"), since what follows the *fa'* does not govern what precedes it. Were it not for the *fa'*, the connection would be clear, but the *fa'* being superfluous is unlikely. Thus the connection of *kama* to what precedes it becomes apparent, and in it is a comparison of the completion of this favour, which came about through guidance to facing the direction of prayer, which is the pillar of Islam.

The most excellent of deeds and the strongest indicators of adherence to the Islamic law is the completion of the prior favour, by sending the Messenger who has the quality of being from among them, along with the other qualities which He described him with. He made that a completion of the favour in both states, because facing the Ka'ba a second time is a matter to which nothing is added that abrogates it (*naskh*, abrogation), since it is the last of the directions faced in prayer. Just as the sending of Muhammad (ﷺ) is the last of the sendings of the prophets, peace be upon them, since there is no prophet after him, and he is the Seal of the Prophets. So He likened the completion of that favour, which is the perfection of the favour of facing the qiblas, to this completion, which is the perfection of the sending of the messengers. In the completion of these two favours is honour for the Arabs, and nobility, and the winning of their hearts, since the Messenger was from among them, and the qibla they face in prayer is among them, the one they perform the pilgrimage to, anciently and in modern times, and venerate.

**﴿رَسُولًا مِنكُمْ﴾** ("a Messenger from among you"): In it is special regard for the Arabs, since the sending was among them, and the Messenger is from them, although his message is universal. Likewise, ﴿هُوَ الَّذِي بَعَثَ في الأُمِّيِّينَ﴾ (62:2) came. This gratitude indicates that no Messenger was previously sent or raised among the Arabs other than our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). That is why He made it singular, saying "a Messenger from among them," and described him with qualities which are all a miracle for them: that he is from among them, reciting to them the signs of Allah, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and the wisdom and what they did not know. He mentioned first that he is from among them, meaning they know him in person, lineage, birth and upbringing, because knowing the person himself precedes knowing what proceeds from his actions. Second, he mentioned the quality of reciting the signs to Him, may He be exalted, because they are the miracle indicating his truthfulness, which remains forever. He attributed the signs to Him, may He be exalted, because they are His speech, and from their recitation are derived the acts of worship and the comprehensive noble morals, and from them the sciences spring forth. Third, he mentioned the quality of purification, which is cleansing from the impurities of misguidance, because that arises from the manifestation of the miracle to whomever Allah, may He be exalted, wills to grant success and acceptance of the truth. Fourth, he mentioned the quality of teaching the Book and the wisdom, because that arises from the purification of the human being through following the Prophet (ﷺ), so he then teaches him and makes him understand what the Book of Allah, may He be exalted, contains, and what the divine wisdom requires. He stated these qualities as present-tense verbs to indicate renewal, because recitation, purification and teaching are continually renewed. As for the first quality, namely that he is from among them, it is not renewed; rather it is a fixed description of him. The discussion of these qualities was already covered, in more detail, in His words, ﴿رَبَّنا وابْعَثْ فِيهِمْ رَسُولًا مِنهُمْ﴾ (2:129), so refer back there.

He concluded this with His words, ﴿ويُعَلِّمُكم ما لَمْ تَكُونُوا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ ("and teaches you what you did not know"), which is a general mention after a specific one, because they did not know the Book or the wisdom. Some explained what they did not know as: the stories of those who came before, and the stories of the unseen that will come. In this verse He placed purification before teaching, whereas in Abraham's supplication He placed teaching before purification, and that is because the intended meaning of purification differs. Apparently the intended meaning here is purification from disbelief, as we explained, while there it is the testimony that they are the best and the purest, and that comes after teaching the laws and acting upon them.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 151–152 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿Remember Me, and I will remember you﴾: That is, remember Me with obedience, and I will remember you with reward and forgiveness. This is the view of Ibn Jubayr. Or it means remember Me with supplication, glorification and the like. This is the view of al-Rabi' and al-Suddi. ʿIkrimah said: Allah says, "O son of Adam, remember Me for a while after the Dawn prayer and for a while after the ʿAsr prayer, and I will suffice you for what is between them," or "Praise Me, and I will praise you." (p-446) This meaning has come in the long hadith (prophetic tradition), where the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah has angels who roam the roads seeking the people of remembrance." In it: "What do My servants say?" They said: "They glorify You, praise You and magnify You."

It has also been said that this is an elided construction, meaning: remember My blessing and I will remember you with increase. The mention of the blessing appears in His words: ﴿Remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:122].

It has been said: remembrance is by the tongue and by the heart at the commands and prohibitions. It has been said: remember Me by affirming My oneness and by confirming My Prophet. It has been said: by what I have made obligatory upon you or recommended to you; I will remember you, that is, I will reward you for it. The meaning of this has already been discussed, and it is the view of Saʿid: remember Me with obedience and I will remember you with reward. It has been said: remember Me in ease with obedience and supplication, and I will remember you in hardship with gift and bounty. This was stated by Ibn Hajar. It has been said: remember Me by asking, and I will remember you by bestowing. Or: remember Me by repentance, and I will remember you by pardoning your sin. Or: remember Me in this world, and I will remember you in the Hereafter. Or: remember Me in solitude, and I will remember you in the wilderness. Or: remember Me with My praises, and I will remember you with My guidance. Or: remember Me with sincerity and devotion, and I will remember you with deliverance and an increase in special closeness. Or: remember Me through agreement with Me, and I will remember you with honours. Or: remember Me by abandoning every portion of your own, and I will remember you by establishing you in My right after your passing away from yourselves. Or: remember Me by cutting off attachments, and I will remember you with the description of realities. Or: remember Me before those you meet, and I will remember you before everyone You address. He said: whoever remembers Me in an assembly, I will remember him in an assembly better than it. Or: remember Me and I will remember you; love Me and I will love you. Or: remember Me with humility, and I will remember you with grace. Or: remember Me with your hearts, and I will remember you by fulfilling your aim. Or: remember Me at the door by way of service, and I will remember you on the carpet of nearness by completing the blessing. Or: remember Me by purifying the inner flow, and I will remember you by fulfilling righteousness. Or: remember Me in your state of joy, and I will remember you in your graves. Or: remember Me while you are in a state of safety, and I will remember you on the Day of Resurrection, the day when regret will not benefit. Or: remember Me with fear together with hope.

al-Qushayri said: "So remember Me, and I will remember you." Dhikr is the absorption of the one who remembers in witnessing the One remembered, then his being consumed in the existence of the One remembered, until nothing remains of him except a trace that is mentioned, so it is said: "So-and-so existed." He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, they had been before that doers of good﴾ [al-Dhariyat 51:16]. Indeed, this world is a good tale, so be a good tale for whoever is attentive. The poet said:

*The world is only its good qualities,*
*and the best of what remains is the good report.*

In the Al-Muntakhab (a summary work) there is what may be summarised as follows: remembrance occurs by the tongue, which is praise, glorification, exalting Him, and the recitation of the books of Allah; and by the heart, which is reflection on the proofs that indicate the obligations, rulings, commands, prohibitions, promise and warning, and reflection on the divine attributes, and reflection on the secrets of Allah's creatures, until every atom becomes like a polished mirror facing the world of holiness. When the servant looks at it, the ray of his sight is reflected from it to the world of majesty. And by the limbs, by being wholly engaged in the commanded acts and free of the forbidden acts. On this understanding Allah called the prayer "remembrance," in His words: ﴿Then hasten to the remembrance of Allah﴾ [al-Jumuʿah 62:9]. End of quotation. They said: remembrance is the alerting of the heart to the One remembered and being awake to Him, and it is applied to the tongue because it indicates that. Since it became frequently applied to the tongue, it became the first to come to mind. So remembrance by the tongue is silent and audible, and remembrance by the heart is continuous and intermittent, and with both together it is also continuous and intermittent. By the tongue is the remembrance of the general body of believers, which is the lowest rank of remembrance, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called it "remembrance." Ibn Majah related that a Bedouin said: "O Messenger of Allah, the laws of Islam have become too many for me, so inform me of something to which I may cling." He said: "Let your tongue remain moist with the remembrance of Allah." He also related: Allah, exalted is He, says: "I am with My servant when he remembers Me and his lips move with Me." Abu ʿUthman was asked, and it was said to him: "We remember Allah but we find no sweetness in our hearts." He said: "Praise Allah that He has adorned one of your limbs with His obedience." By the heart is the remembrance of the knowers and the elite of the believers, which the Prophet (ﷺ) called "remembrance." Its meaning is the settling of the remembrance within it, so that nothing other than the One remembered comes to mind. The poet said:

*Other than You does not occur to my mind;*
*if I forget You, whom would I remember?*

And by both together: this is the remembrance of the elite of the believers. These are three stations, and the most enduring of them is the most excellent. End of quotation.

We have spoken at length on this phrase and have left out many things that people have mentioned. These qualifications and explanations by which remembrance has been interpreted are not indicated by the wording itself. It should be understood that these are the interpretations of the exegetes, given by way of illustration and as possibilities of what is meant. As for the indication of the wording, it is the demand for remembrance in general, and what the mind immediately grasps is verbal remembrance. Verbal remembrance cannot be merely the remembrance of the name of Majesty (Allah) on its own without any predication; there must be a predicate. The best of these are the remembrances transmitted in the reports and those alluded to in the Qur'an. Encouragement to recite a number of them has come, along with promise of great reward for reciting them. These remembrances include: praise of Allah, giving Him thanks, extolling His majesty, and seeking good from Him. He expressed this as "remembrance" and commanded the servant to it, so it is as if it were said: "Magnify Allah and praise Him with words that indicate that." The reward that follows from this has been called "remembrance," so He said: ﴿So remember Me, and I will remember you﴾, by way of correspondence, since it is the result of remembrance and arises from it, so He called it remembrance.

﴿And be grateful to Me﴾: The explanation of gratitude has already been given. Here it takes the preposition *li* (to), and likewise in ﴿Give thanks to Me and to your parents﴾ [Luqman 31:14]. It is one of the verbs said to sometimes take a preposition and sometimes take its object directly, as ʿAmr ibn La'ja' al-Tamimi said:

*They gathered my misery and my blessings upon you,*
*so why did you not thank the people, when you did not repay them?*

Whether this kind of verb is correctly established as sometimes transitive directly and sometimes through a preposition is a matter of disagreement. They said: when you say "I thanked Zayd," the implied meaning is "I thanked Zayd for his deed," so they made it a verb that takes one object with a preposition and another directly. For this reason al-Zamakhshari explained this passage by saying: "and be grateful to Me for what I have bestowed upon you." Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "*Wa-shkuru li* and *wa-shkurūnī* have one meaning, though *li* is more eloquent and more common with *shukr* (gratitude), and its meaning is: My blessings and My favours. Likewise, when you say 'I thanked you,' the meaning is 'I thanked you for your deed and mentioned it,' so the object is elided, since the meaning of gratitude is the mention of the favour and the mention of its giver together. What is elided of that is an abbreviation, since what remains indicates what is elided." End of his words. But the claim that it takes one object directly and another through a preposition, as in "I thanked Zayd for his deed," needs to be supported by Arab usage, and then it may be accepted.

﴿And do not be ungrateful to Me﴾: This is ingratitude for blessings (*kufr al-niʿmah*), and it is an elision: that is, "do not be ungrateful for My blessing." Had it been disbelief, the opposite of faith, it would have said "do not disbelieve" or "do not disbelieve in Me." This *nūn* is the *nūn al-wiqāyah* (the protective nūn, which separates the verb's ending from the first person pronoun), and the first-person *yā'* after it has been dropped for lightness, to match the rhyme of the verse endings. It has been said: the meaning is "be grateful to Me by obedience and do not be ungrateful to Me by disobedience." It has also been said: the meaning of gratitude here is acknowledging the right of the benefactor and praising Him, and for this reason He opposed it with His words "and do not be ungrateful to Me."

Here there are three clauses: the clause commanding remembrance, the clause commanding gratitude, and the clause forbidding ingratitude. It begins first with the clause of remembrance, because it is intended as praise, general commendation and giving thanks to Him, exalted is He, and a reward that follows from it is mentioned. It follows with the clause of gratitude, because it is praise of a particular thing, and it is already included under the first, so it is like emphasis and does not need a separate response. It ends with the clause of prohibition, because when He commanded gratitude, the wording could not indicate all times, and it is not possible to obligate the presence of gratitude at every time, since a person may be heedless of it at many times. He forbade ingratitude because a prohibition requires abstention from what is forbidden at all times, and that is possible, since it belongs to the category of abstentions. We have already discussed that when there is a command and a prohibition, the command is mentioned first. We mentioned the wisdom behind that in His words: ﴿And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you, and do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:41], so there is no need to repeat it here.

**﴿كَما أرْسَلْنا فِيكُمْ﴾** ("as We sent among you"): The *kaf* here is for comparison (*tashbih*), and it is in the accusative position as an adjective (*na't*) of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*). Scholars differ on how to supply that omitted noun. One view says the sense is: "and that I may complete My favour upon you with a completion like the completion of sending the Messenger among you." The two instances of "completion" have different objects: the first completion is by reward in the Hereafter, and the second is by sending the Messenger to us in this world. Or, the first completion is by the answering of Abraham's first supplication in His words, ﴿ومِن ذُرِّيَّتِنا أُمَّةً مُسْلِمَةً لَكَ﴾ (2:128), and the second is by the answering of his second supplication in His words, ﴿رَبَّنا وابْعَثْ فِيهِمْ رَسُولًا مِنهُمْ﴾ (2:129).

Another view says the sense is: "and that you may be guided with a guidance like Our sending a Messenger among you," so that the comparison of guidance with sending is in its certainty and firmness, meaning a guidance that is established and realised, just as the realisation and establishment of Our sending is. Another view says it is connected to His words, ﴿وكَذَلِكَ جَعَلْناكم أُمَّةً وسَطًا﴾ (2:143), meaning "a making like what We sent," and this is the view of Abu Muslim. But this is very far-fetched, because of the long separation, which indicates a break in the connection.

Another view says the *kaf* is in the accusative position as a state (*hal*) of "My favour," meaning ﴿ولِأُتِمَّ نِعْمَتِي عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ (2:150) "likening Our sending among you of a Messenger," that is, likening the favour of sending, so this involves an omitted *mudaf* (governed noun). Another view says the *kaf* is cut off from the speech before it and connected to what follows it. Al-Zamakhshari said: "As (p-444) I reminded you by sending the Messenger, so remember Me by obedience, and I will remember you by reward," end of quote. On this view it is an omitted verbal noun and an omitted *mudaf*, meaning: "remember Me with a remembrance like Our remembrance of you by sending," and then "like the remembrance of Our sending," then the *mudaf* was omitted and the *mudaf ilayh* was put in its place. This is like saying: "As so-and-so came to you, go to him with your generosity." This is the view of Mujahid, Ata, al-Kalbi and Muqatil, and it is the choice of al-Akhfash, al-Zajjaj, Ibn Kaysan and al-Asamm. The meaning is that you were in a state in which you did not read a Book and did not know a Messenger, and Muhammad (ﷺ) was a man from among you, who came to you with the most wondrous of signs indicating his truthfulness. So He said: "As I have bestowed this favour upon you and made it a proof for you, remember Me with thankfulness, and I will remember you with My mercy." This is confirmed by ﴿لَقَدْ مَنَّ اللَّهُ عَلى المُؤْمِنِينَ إذْ بَعَثَ فِيهِمْ رَسُولًا مِن أنْفُسِهِمْ﴾ (3:164). This sense is possible, indeed it is apparent, and it is when *an* is attached to what follows it. In that case the *kaf* is not for comparison but for causation (*ta'lil*), which is a meaning said to be attributed to it, and this is the interpretation of His words, ﴿واذْكُرُوهُ كَما هَداكُمْ﴾ (2:198), and the verse of the poet:

*"Do not revile people as you are not reviled."*

That is: "remember Him for His guidance of you," and "do not revile people because you are not reviled," meaning refrain from reviling people because people refrain from reviling you. The *ma* in *kama* is verbal (*masdariyya*). Whoever claimed that it is relative in the sense of *alladhi* ("who"), with an omitted returning pronoun and *rasulan* as an apposition to it, is far off the mark, since the sense "like him whom We sent as a messenger" is hard to sustain with the speech before it and the speech after it, and because it involves using *ma* for individuals who have intellect. Likewise, the one who made *ma* a restrictive particle (*kaffa*) was going there only where a verbal noun cannot be formed from it together with what follows it, because it governs nominal sentences, as in the poet's words:

*"By your life, I and Abu Humayd are like the drunkard and the forbearing man."*

As for the view of one who said that "as We sent" is connected to what follows it, Abu Muhammad Makki ibn Abi Talib rejected it. He said: because when the command has an answer, what precedes it is not connected to it, since it is occupied with its answer. He said: If you said, "As I have been good to you, honour me, and I will honour you," the *kaf* of *kama* would not be connected to "honour me," because it has an answer. Rather it would be connected to something else or to a hidden element. Likewise, "remember Me, and I will remember you" is a command that has an answer, so *kama* is not connected to it, and this is not permissible except by analogy with the conditional which takes two answers, which is your saying: "If so-and-so comes to you, go to him and you will please him," so *kama* and "remember Me" would be two answers to the command. The first is more eloquent and more well-known. You may say: "As I have been good to you, honour me," and it is correct to make the *kaf* connected to "honour me," since it has no answer. End of his words.

Makki preferred the view that it is connected to what precedes it, namely ﴿ولِأُتِمَّ نِعْمَتِي عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ (2:150), because the context of the wording indicates that the meaning is: "and that I may complete My favour upon you by clarifying the creed of your father Abraham, as We answered his supplication concerning you, so We sent to you a Messenger from among you who recites." What Makki went to, namely invalidating the connection of *kama* to what follows it for the reason mentioned, is not a valid argument, because the *kaf* is either for comparison or for causation. If it is for comparison, then it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, and it is permissible for that verbal noun to precede the verb. An example: "Honour me with the honour I previously gave you, and I will honour you," so this verbal noun may be placed first. If it is for causation, then it is also permissible for that to precede the verb. An example: "Honour me for my honouring you, and I will honour you." We know of no disagreement about the permissibility of placing this verbal noun and this cause before the verb that governs them. Makki's permitting that by analogy with the conditional that takes two answers, and his calling "as" and "remember Me" two answers to the command, is not correct, because *kama* is not an answer, and because that analogy is invalid: a verbal noun of comparison does not resemble an answer, and likewise causation. As for the comparative verbal noun, it is a description of the action commanded, so it is not consequent upon the mere occurrence of the act; rather the act occurs only with that description. On this basis it does not resemble an answer, because an answer is consequent upon the very occurrence of the act. As for causation, it likewise is not consequent upon the occurrence of the act; rather the act is consequent upon the existence of the cause. So it is the opposite of an answer, because an answer is consequent upon the occurrence of the act, while the cause is that upon which the existence of the act is consequent. There is thus no resemblance between them. In my view, what is really weak is the connection of *kama* to "remember Me," because of the *fa'* (the particle "so"), since what follows the *fa'* does not govern what precedes it. Were it not for the *fa'*, the connection would be clear, but the *fa'* being superfluous is unlikely. Thus the connection of *kama* to what precedes it becomes apparent, and in it is a comparison of the completion of this favour, which came about through guidance to facing the direction of prayer, which is the pillar of Islam.

The most excellent of deeds and the strongest indicators of adherence to the Islamic law is the completion of the prior favour, by sending the Messenger who has the quality of being from among them, along with the other qualities which He described him with. He made that a completion of the favour in both states, because facing the Ka'ba a second time is a matter to which nothing is added that abrogates it (*naskh*, abrogation), since it is the last of the directions faced in prayer. Just as the sending of Muhammad (ﷺ) is the last of the sendings of the prophets, peace be upon them, since there is no prophet after him, and he is the Seal of the Prophets. So He likened the completion of that favour, which is the perfection of the favour of facing the qiblas, to this completion, which is the perfection of the sending of the messengers. In the completion of these two favours is honour for the Arabs, and nobility, and the winning of their hearts, since the Messenger was from among them, and the qibla they face in prayer is among them, the one they perform the pilgrimage to, anciently and in modern times, and venerate.

**﴿رَسُولًا مِنكُمْ﴾** ("a Messenger from among you"): In it is special regard for the Arabs, since the sending was among them, and the Messenger is from them, although his message is universal. Likewise, ﴿هُوَ الَّذِي بَعَثَ في الأُمِّيِّينَ﴾ (62:2) came. This gratitude indicates that no Messenger was previously sent or raised among the Arabs other than our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). That is why He made it singular, saying "a Messenger from among them," and described him with qualities which are all a miracle for them: that he is from among them, reciting to them the signs of Allah, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and the wisdom and what they did not know. He mentioned first that he is from among them, meaning they know him in person, lineage, birth and upbringing, because knowing the person himself precedes knowing what proceeds from his actions. Second, he mentioned the quality of reciting the signs to Him, may He be exalted, because they are the miracle indicating his truthfulness, which remains forever. He attributed the signs to Him, may He be exalted, because they are His speech, and from their recitation are derived the acts of worship and the comprehensive noble morals, and from them the sciences spring forth. Third, he mentioned the quality of purification, which is cleansing from the impurities of misguidance, because that arises from the manifestation of the miracle to whomever Allah, may He be exalted, wills to grant success and acceptance of the truth. Fourth, he mentioned the quality of teaching the Book and the wisdom, because that arises from the purification of the human being through following the Prophet (ﷺ), so he then teaches him and makes him understand what the Book of Allah, may He be exalted, contains, and what the divine wisdom requires. He stated these qualities as present-tense verbs to indicate renewal, because recitation, purification and teaching are continually renewed. As for the first quality, namely that he is from among them, it is not renewed; rather it is a fixed description of him. The discussion of these qualities was already covered, in more detail, in His words, ﴿رَبَّنا وابْعَثْ فِيهِمْ رَسُولًا مِنهُمْ﴾ (2:129), so refer back there.

He concluded this with His words, ﴿ويُعَلِّمُكم ما لَمْ تَكُونُوا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ ("and teaches you what you did not know"), which is a general mention after a specific one, because they did not know the Book or the wisdom. Some explained what they did not know as: the stories of those who came before, and the stories of the unseen that will come. In this verse He placed purification before teaching, whereas in Abraham's supplication He placed teaching before purification, and that is because the intended meaning of purification differs. Apparently the intended meaning here is purification from disbelief, as we explained, while there it is the testimony that they are the best and the purest, and that comes after teaching the laws and acting upon them.

*The world is only its good qualities,*
*and the best of what remains is the good report.*

In the Al-Muntakhab (a summary work) there is what may be summarised as follows: remembrance occurs by the tongue, which is praise, glorification, exalting Him, and the recitation of the books of Allah; and by the heart, which is reflection on the proofs that indicate the obligations, rulings, commands, prohibitions, promise and warning, and reflection on the divine attributes, and reflection on the secrets of Allah's creatures, until every atom becomes like a polished mirror facing the world of holiness. When the servant looks at it, the ray of his sight is reflected from it to the world of majesty. And by the limbs, by being wholly engaged in the commanded acts and free of the forbidden acts. On this understanding Allah called the prayer "remembrance," in His words: ﴿Then hasten to the remembrance of Allah﴾ [al-Jumuʿah 62:9]. End of quotation. They said: remembrance is the alerting of the heart to the One remembered and being awake to Him, and it is applied to the tongue because it indicates that. Since it became frequently applied to the tongue, it became the first to come to mind. So remembrance by the tongue is silent and audible, and remembrance by the heart is continuous and intermittent, and with both together it is also continuous and intermittent. By the tongue is the remembrance of the general body of believers, which is the lowest rank of remembrance, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called it "remembrance." Ibn Majah related that a Bedouin said: "O Messenger of Allah, the laws of Islam have become too many for me, so inform me of something to which I may cling." He said: "Let your tongue remain moist with the remembrance of Allah." He also related: Allah, exalted is He, says: "I am with My servant when he remembers Me and his lips move with Me." Abu ʿUthman was asked, and it was said to him: "We remember Allah but we find no sweetness in our hearts." He said: "Praise Allah that He has adorned one of your limbs with His obedience." By the heart is the remembrance of the knowers and the elite of the believers, which the Prophet (ﷺ) called "remembrance." Its meaning is the settling of the remembrance within it, so that nothing other than the One remembered comes to mind. The poet said:

*Other than You does not occur to my mind;*
*if I forget You, whom would I remember?*

And by both together: this is the remembrance of the elite of the believers. These are three stations, and the most enduring of them is the most excellent. End of quotation.

We have spoken at length on this phrase and have left out many things that people have mentioned. These qualifications and explanations by which remembrance has been interpreted are not indicated by the wording itself. It should be understood that these are the interpretations of the exegetes, given by way of illustration and as possibilities of what is meant. As for the indication of the wording, it is the demand for remembrance in general, and what the mind immediately grasps is verbal remembrance. Verbal remembrance cannot be merely the remembrance of the name of Majesty (Allah) on its own without any predication; there must be a predicate. The best of these are the remembrances transmitted in the reports and those alluded to in the Qur'an. Encouragement to recite a number of them has come, along with promise of great reward for reciting them. These remembrances include: praise of Allah, giving Him thanks, extolling His majesty, and seeking good from Him. He expressed this as "remembrance" and commanded the servant to it, so it is as if it were said: "Magnify Allah and praise Him with words that indicate that." The reward that follows from this has been called "remembrance," so He said: ﴿So remember Me, and I will remember you﴾, by way of correspondence, since it is the result of remembrance and arises from it, so He called it remembrance.

﴿And be grateful to Me﴾: The explanation of gratitude has already been given. Here it takes the preposition *li* (to), and likewise in ﴿Give thanks to Me and to your parents﴾ [Luqman 31:14]. It is one of the verbs said to sometimes take a preposition and sometimes take its object directly, as ʿAmr ibn La'ja' al-Tamimi said:

*They gathered my misery and my blessings upon you,*
*so why did you not thank the people, when you did not repay them?*

Whether this kind of verb is correctly established as sometimes transitive directly and sometimes through a preposition is a matter of disagreement. They said: when you say "I thanked Zayd," the implied meaning is "I thanked Zayd for his deed," so they made it a verb that takes one object with a preposition and another directly. For this reason al-Zamakhshari explained this passage by saying: "and be grateful to Me for what I have bestowed upon you." Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "*Wa-shkuru li* and *wa-shkurūnī* have one meaning, though *li* is more eloquent and more common with *shukr* (gratitude), and its meaning is: My blessings and My favours. Likewise, when you say 'I thanked you,' the meaning is 'I thanked you for your deed and mentioned it,' so the object is elided, since the meaning of gratitude is the mention of the favour and the mention of its giver together. What is elided of that is an abbreviation, since what remains indicates what is elided." End of his words. But the claim that it takes one object directly and another through a preposition, as in "I thanked Zayd for his deed," needs to be supported by Arab usage, and then it may be accepted.

﴿And do not be ungrateful to Me﴾: This is ingratitude for blessings (*kufr al-niʿmah*), and it is an elision: that is, "do not be ungrateful for My blessing." Had it been disbelief, the opposite of faith, it would have said "do not disbelieve" or "do not disbelieve in Me." This *nūn* is the *nūn al-wiqāyah* (the protective nūn, which separates the verb's ending from the first person pronoun), and the first-person *yā'* after it has been dropped for lightness, to match the rhyme of the verse endings. It has been said: the meaning is "be grateful to Me by obedience and do not be ungrateful to Me by disobedience." It has also been said: the meaning of gratitude here is acknowledging the right of the benefactor and praising Him, and for this reason He opposed it with His words "and do not be ungrateful to Me."

Here there are three clauses: the clause commanding remembrance, the clause commanding gratitude, and the clause forbidding ingratitude. It begins first with the clause of remembrance, because it is intended as praise, general commendation and giving thanks to Him, exalted is He, and a reward that follows from it is mentioned. It follows with the clause of gratitude, because it is praise of a particular thing, and it is already included under the first, so it is like emphasis and does not need a separate response. It ends with the clause of prohibition, because when He commanded gratitude, the wording could not indicate all times, and it is not possible to obligate the presence of gratitude at every time, since a person may be heedless of it at many times. He forbade ingratitude because a prohibition requires abstention from what is forbidden at all times, and that is possible, since it belongs to the category of abstentions. We have already discussed that when there is a command and a prohibition, the command is mentioned first. We mentioned the wisdom behind that in His words: ﴿And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you, and do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:41], so there is no need to repeat it here.

(p. 448) ﴿O you who believe, seek help through patience and prayer﴾. It is said that the occasion of revelation of this verse is that the polytheists said: "Muhammad will return to our religion, just as he returned to our qiblah." He (God) shook them with this call, which includes this noble description, namely faith, expressed as a past-tense verb in the relative clause of "those who" (alladhīna), indicating its firm establishment and their being characterized by it in past time, so that they would be more ready to accept what comes to them of commands and arduous obligations. This is because patience (ṣabr) and prayer (ṣalāh) are the two pillars of Islam. Patience is restraining the self upon hardships and arduous obligations, and it is an inward matter; prayer is its fruit, and it is among the most difficult obligations because of its repetition. The connection of this verse to what precedes it is evident, for they had heard from the disbelievers' criticism of turning toward the Kaʿbah and praying toward it a great deal of harm, so they were commanded at that point to seek help through patience and prayer. Some have restricted the patience mentioned here to patience over the harm of the disbelievers through their criticism of the change of direction and of praying toward the Kaʿbah, and others to patience in performing the obligatory duties. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, and some said, that it is a metonym for fasting, and from this Ramadan was called "the month of patience." Some said it is a metonym for jihad (struggle in the way of God), because of His later words: ﴿And do not say of those who are killed in the way of God...﴾. This is the view of Abū Muslim. The preferable view is what we have mentioned earlier, namely the generality of the wording, so these individual instances fall under it. It is narrated from ʿAlī, may God ennoble his face, that he said: "Patience in faith is like the head to the body, and there is no good in a body that has no head." The explanation of this sentence has already been discussed in connection with His words: ﴿seek help through patience and prayer﴾.

﴿Indeed God is with the patient﴾: that is, with aid and support, as the poet said: "Satirise them, and the Holy Spirit is with you." And He, exalted, said: ﴿Do not grieve; indeed God is with us﴾ [At-Tawbah: 40]. Whoever God is with is the victor. Since prayer arises from patience, and patience has become the root of all arduous obligations, He said: ﴿Indeed God is with the patient﴾, so those who pray are subsumed under the patient, just as a branch is subsumed under its root. As for His saying there: ﴿And indeed it is difficult, except for the humble﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 45], He returned the pronoun to it according to the apparent sense of the speech, because it is the most noble and most arduous of the fruits of patience.

﴿And do not say of those who are killed in the way of God, "They are dead." Rather, they are alive, but you do not perceive﴾. It is said that the occasion of revelation of this verse is that it was said of one who was killed in the way of God: "So-and-so has died, and the delights and pleasures of this world have departed from him," so it was revealed. They were forbidden from saying of the martyrs that they are dead, and God informed that they are alive. The nominative status of "dead" and "alive" is as the predicate of an elided subject, meaning: "They are dead"; rather, "They are alive." It is possible that "rather, alive" is subsumed under a hidden saying, meaning: "Rather, say: they are alive." However, the first possibility is preferred, namely that it is an informative statement from God, the Exalted, and His words: ﴿but you do not perceive﴾ support this, because its meaning is that their life is something you have no awareness of. The apparent meaning is that the intended sense is the literal reality of death and life. It is also said that this is figurative. They differed: some said they are "dead" through the cessation of remembrance, and "alive" through its continuation and the permanence of reward. The Arabs used to call one who leaves no remembrance after his death, such as a child and others, "dead." Some said they are "dead" in misguidance and "alive" in obedience and guidance, as He said: ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life...﴾ [Al-Anʿām: 122]. If death and life are taken in their literal sense, then they differed. Some people said its meaning is a prohibition against the saying of the Jāhiliyyah (the pre-Islamic age) that they will not be raised, so the meaning is: they will be made alive by resurrection, and they will receive the reward of the martyrs who were killed in the way of God. Most scholars hold that they are alive at present. The meaning of this life is that their spirits remain while their bodies do not; for we witness the decay and perishing of bodies. They used as evidence for the survival of spirits the punishment of the grave, and His words: ﴿but you do not perceive﴾, meaning: you do not perceive the manner of their life. If the meaning of "they will be made alive" were that they will be made alive on the Day of Resurrection, or that they are upon guidance and light, then the negation of perception would have no sense, since this is addressed to the believers, and they already knew of the resurrection and that they were upon guidance. It would not be said of them: "but you do not perceive," because they already perceived this, and His words: ﴿They rejoice in those who have not yet joined them from behind them﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 170] also show this.

Some people have held that the martyr is alive in both body and spirit, and that the absence of perception of this by other living beings does not undermine it. Thus we see them in the state of the dead while they are alive, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them fixed, while they pass like clouds﴾ [An-Naml: 88] (p. 449), and as you see a sleeper in his position while he sees in his dream what delights or pains him. Al-Suhaylī, in his book *Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwah* (Proofs of Prophethood), narrated by way of a report from some of the Companions that he dug in a place and an opening appeared, and behold, a person was sitting on a couch with a copy of the Qur'an in front of him, reading in it, and before him was a green garden. That was at Uhud, and he knew that the man was one of the martyrs, because he saw a wound on the surface of his face. When it is established that the martyrs are alive, whether their spirits alone or their bodies and spirits together, then it is disputed where they reside. It is said: their graves, where they are provided for. It is said: in white domes in Paradise, where they are provided for; this was said by Abū Bashshār al-Sulamī. It is said: in white birds that eat from the fruits of Paradise, and their dwellings are the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntahā); this was said by Qatādah. It is said: they eat from the fruit of Paradise and smell its fragrance, without being in it; this was said by Mujāhid. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "The martyrs are at a river at the gate of Paradise, in a green dome." It is also narrated: "In a green garden, where their provision comes to them from Paradise morning and evening." And it is narrated from him (ﷺ): "The spirits of the martyrs are in green birds that hang from the fruit of Paradise, and they are in lamps of gold, and they are in a green dome." If these reports are sound, then they describe the states of different groups of martyrs, or different states at different times. The majority hold that they are in Paradise, and his (ﷺ) saying to the mother of Ḥārithah supports this: "They are in al-Firdaws." The doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah, i.e., Sunni orthodoxy) is that spirits do not perish, and that they remain after their departure from the body. So the spirits of the people of felicity are blessed until the Day of Judgment, and the spirits of the people of wretchedness are punished until the Day of Judgment.

The difference between the martyr and other believers is only in provision, which God has favoured them with. God, the Exalted, said regarding the disbelievers: ﴿The Fire, to which they are exposed morning and evening﴾ [Ghāfir: 46]. Al-Ḥasan said: "The martyrs are alive with God; their provisions are presented to their spirits, so joy and happiness reach them, just as the Fire is presented to the family of Pharaoh morning and evening, so suffering reaches them." They said: it is possible that God gathers from the parts of a martyr a whole and gives it life and brings bliss to it, even if it is the size of an atom. The noble verse does not address the provision of the spirits of the martyrs nor their abode; rather, mention of this came by way of digression, following the commentators, since they spoke about this in this verse. Otherwise, the proper place for discussing this is His words: ﴿Rather, they are alive with their Lord, receiving provision﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 169], where He mentioned "with" (ʿindiyyah) and provision. The apparent sense of His words: ﴿those who are killed in the way of God﴾ is generality. It is said that it was revealed concerning the martyrs of Badr, who were fourteen; but this generality is not restricted by this occasion, for what matters is the generality of the wording, not the particularity of the occasion. In this verse there is consolation for the relatives of the martyrs and their brothers among the believers, by mentioning that they are alive; so they are to be envied, not grieved over.

﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger, and a loss of wealth, lives, and fruits﴾. It has been previously stated that testing (ibtilāʾ) is examination, in order to know what will be the state of the one examined; but this is impossible with respect to God, the Exalted. Its meaning here is rather "to make manifest" (ijābah), and the pronoun of address refers to: it is said that it refers only to the Companions; this was said by ʿAṭāʾ. He addressed them with this after the Hijrah (migration), and informed them of it before its occurrence in order to reassure their hearts, since when knowledge of what will happen precedes it, one has prepared for it, unlike sudden matters, which are harder on the soul. There is also an increase in reward and recompense for what they experience through awaiting the calamity; and it is an informing of the unseen that happens exactly as it was foretold; and it distinguishes those who embraced Islam seeking the face of God from those who were hypocrites; and it increases sincerity in the state of trial above their sincerity in the state of well-being; and it prompts the one who has not embraced Islam to reflect on the signs of Islam, since he sees these afflicted people patient upon their religion, steadfast in heart, despite what they have been afflicted with. It is also said: they are the people of Makkah, and He addressed them with this to inform them that He answered the supplication of His Prophet (ﷺ) concerning them, and so that they would remain expecting calamity, so that calamities would be multiplied upon them. It is also said: it is an address to the Ummah, and it refers to the end of time. Kaʿb said: "A time will come upon people when the palm tree will bear only one fruit." This informing is a warning and an admonition against inclining toward this world and its splendour, and it is an informing of unseen matters. It is also said: the address is not directed at a specific person, but is general, not restricted to a particular time or a particular addressee (p. 450); so it is as if it were said: "We will surely afflict with such-and-such," and in this there is a warning, and it is for the Companions and others.

This verse is connected to His words: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 45] and the verse, and before it: ﴿And be grateful to Me﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 152]. Gratitude necessitates an increase of blessings, and being tested with what has been mentioned apparently contradicts this. Its explanation is that the completion of the laws is a completion of the blessing, and for this reason it necessitates gratitude; and carrying out those laws is not possible except by bearing hardships, so He commanded patience therein. He blessed him first, so he was grateful, and was tested second, so he was patient, in order that he might attain the two degrees of gratitude and patience, and thus his faith would be perfected. As was narrated from him (peace be upon him): "Faith is in two halves: a half is patience, and a half is gratitude." The phrase "with something" (bi-shayʾin) is connected to His words: ﴿We will surely test you﴾, and the bāʾ in it denotes attachment. He used the singular to indicate paucity, for if He had used the plural and said "with things" (bi-ashyāʾ), it might have meant kinds of each of what follows. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk read "bi-ashyāʾ," so there would be no elision in what follows, and "min" would be in the position of a qualifier. This contrasts with the reading of the majority, "bi-shayʾin," where an elision must be assumed, meaning "something of fear, and something of hunger, and something of loss." The meaning in this reading is: "We will surely test you with a portion of such-and-such." Fear is the fear of the enemy; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, and intense fear occurred at the Battle of the Confederates (al-Aḥzāb). Al-Shāfiʿī said it is the fear of God, the Exalted. Hunger is drought; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, using the effect to denote the cause. It is also said: hunger is poverty, again using the effect to denote the cause. Al-Shāfiʿī said it is the fasting of the month of Ramadan. "Loss of wealth" means through ruin and destruction. Al-Shāfiʿī said it means through charity. "Lives" means through killing and death. Al-Shāfiʿī said it means through illnesses; it is also said through grey hair. "Fruits" means the calamities that strike the fruits, scarcity of produce, and the cessation of blessings. Al-Qaffāl said its loss may be through drought, or through leaving the cultivation of lands because of engagement in jihad, or through spending on those who come as delegations to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It is also said: through the enemy's dominance over them. Al-Shāfiʿī said: "The fruits" are the death of children, because a man's child is the fruit of his heart. In the hadith of Abū Mūsā: "God says to the angels, when the servant's child dies: 'Have you seized the fruit of his heart?'"

Some scholars said: What is meant in this verse is the burdens and hardships of jihad. So fear of the enemy, hunger caused by it and by the journeys to it, loss of wealth through the expenses it requires, loss of lives through killing, and loss of fruits through the enemy's reaching them, or through neglect of them because of jihad. End of his words. He coordinated "and loss" (*wa-naqs*) with his statement "with something" (*bi-shay'*), meaning: "We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and loss." The indefinite form of the noun is suitable for this coordination. It is also possible that it is coordinated with "fear and hunger," so that its implied meaning would be "and something of loss." "From the wealth" (*min al-amwal*) is connected to "loss," because it is a verbal noun from *naqasa*, which is transitive to one object, and that object has been omitted, meaning "and the loss of something." It is also possible that it is in the position of a qualifier for "loss," and *min* would then indicate the starting point. It is also possible that it is in the position of a qualifier for that omitted noun, meaning "and the loss of something from the wealth," and *min* would then be partitive. They said: according to al-Akhfash, *min* may be additional (*za'idah*), meaning "and the loss of wealth, lives and fruits." He introduced the declarative sentence with an oath upon it, to emphasize that the trial will certainly occur. Attributing the verb to Him explicitly indicates that the causes of afflictions are ascribed to Him, and that these trials come from God, Exalted is He. His promise of them to the believers indicates that they are not punishments; rather, when patience accompanies them, they bring a high rank in religion. This order in the coordination follows a progression: He first informed of the trial with "something of fear," which is the anticipation of what hateful thing may come. Then he moved from it to the trial with "something of hunger," which is more severe than fear, whatever interpretation it is given: drought, poverty, or the need for food. The exception is the interpretation of al-Shafi'i, which is fasting in Ramadan. There is no progression between "loss" and "something," according to his preferred coordination of "loss" with "with something." Rather, the progression in the coordination occurs after "and loss": it begins first with the wealth, then rises to the lives. As for "and the fruits," it comes as a specification after a generalization, because they fall under the wealth, so there is no progression in them.

**﴿And give good tidings to the patient﴾**: an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), or to everyone who is capable of giving good tidings. That is, [good tidings of] victory for jihad, or of reward for obedience, or of recompense for calamities. These are the opinions. The best view is not to restrict it: whoever is patient in a praiseworthy manner according to the Shari'ah is included among the patient. They said: patience is a distinctive human quality, because reason and desire conflict within it, and it is physical. It is either active, such as undertaking arduous works, or endurance, such as enduring severe beating, and it is psychological, which is restraining the soul from what the natural disposition desires. If it concerns the desire of the private parts and the stomach, it is called chastity (*iffah*). If it concerns enduring something hateful, its names differ according to the hateful thing. In the case of a calamity, it is restricted to the name "patience," and its opposite is "impatience" (*jaza'*). If it concerns wealth, it is called self-control (*dabt al-nafs*), and its opposite is arrogance (*bataru*). If it concerns war, it is called courage (*shaja'ah*), and its opposite is cowardice (*jubn*). If it concerns a tiresome adversity, it is called breadth of chest (*sa'at sadr*), and its opposite is distress (*dajar*). If it concerns the concealing of speech, it is called secrecy (*kitman*), and its opposite is proclamation (*i'lan*). If it concerns the superfluities of this world, it is called asceticism (*zuhd*), and its opposite is greed (*hirs*). If it concerns a small amount of wealth, it is called contentment (*qana'ah*), and its opposite is avarice (*shurah*). God has gathered all these categories and named all of them patience, saying: ﴿and the patient in adversity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177], that is, in calamity, ﴿and in hardship﴾, that is, in poverty, ﴿and in the time of battle﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177], that is, in fighting. Al-Qaffal said: patience is not that a person does not feel the pain of the hateful thing, nor that he does not dislike it. Rather, it is compelling the soul to refrain from showing impatience, even if tears appear in the eye or the color changes. If he first displays what does not count as patience, and then he becomes patient, that is not counted except as consolation.

**﴿Who, when a calamity strikes them﴾**: regarding "those who" (*alladhina*), it may be in the accusative as a qualifier of "the patient," which is the apparent grammatical reading; or in the accusative by way of praise, in which case it is detached; or in the nominative by implying "they," in two ways: either by detachment or by resumption, as if it were an answer to an implied question, meaning: "Who are the patient?" It was said: "They are those who, when..." They also permitted that "those who" be the subject (*mubtada'*), with "upon them" (*'alayhim*) as its predicate, and this is possible. "Calamity" (*musibah*) is an active participle from *asabat*, and it has acquired a specific connection to a hateful thing; it became a metaphor for the great disaster, so it functioned like nouns and governed the operators. "Asabathum: musibah" is a case of paronomasia of different types (*tajnis mughayir*), which is when one of the two words is a noun and the other is a verb. From it: ﴿The Imminent Event has drawn near﴾ [al-Najm: 57]; ﴿When the Event occurs﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 1]. A calamity is anything that harms the believer in his soul, wealth, or family, whether small or great, to the extent that the extinguishing of a lamp is called a calamity for one who needs it. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said the words of recitation (*istirja'*) when his lamp went out. The meaning of "when" (*idha*) here is repetition and generality. We have previously mentioned the disagreement about *idha*: does it indicate repetition, or was it established for a single occurrence? There are two views among the grammarians.

**﴿they say: Indeed we belong to God﴾**: "they say" (*qalu*) is the answer to "when" (*idha*), and the conditional clause with its answer is a relative clause for "those who." "Indeed we" (*inna-na*): its original form is *innana*, because when *inna* enters upon the attached accusative pronoun, one *nun* of *inna* is dropped. The one that should be dropped is the second, because it is the one that is a place-holder, and because deletion is known in it when it is lightened; they say: *in Zayd la-qa'im*. This is deletion here for the sake of the coincidence of identical sounds, and that is why it operates; if it were a deletion without this reason, the pronoun would be separated and would be in the nominative and it would not operate; because when it is lightened in this way, it does not operate on the pronoun. "To God" (*li-Llah*): its meaning is affirmation of ownership and servitude to God, for He is the One who disposes of us as He wills in matters.

**﴿and indeed to Him we are returning﴾**: an affirmation of resurrection and an alert to the calamity of death, which is the greatest of calamities, and a reminder that whatever befalls a person short of it is near and must come to an end for him. Regarding these two spoken clauses, the exegetes have several opinions. First: our souls, our wealth, and our families belong to God, and He does not wrong us in what He does to us.
