The connection of this verse to what precedes it is evident, for they had heard from the disbelievers' criticism of turning toward the Kaʿbah and praying toward it a great deal of harm, so they were commanded at that point to seek help through patience and prayer. Some have restricted the patience mentioned here to patience over the harm of the disbelievers through their criticism of the change of direction and of praying toward the Kaʿbah, and others to patience in performing the obligatory duties. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, and some said, that it is a metonym for fasting, and from this Ramadan was called "the month of patience." Some said it is a metonym for jihad (struggle in the way of God), because of His later words: ﴿And do not say of those who are killed in the way of God...﴾. This is the view of Abū Muslim. The preferable view is what we have mentioned earlier, namely the generality of the wording, so these individual instances fall under it. It is narrated from ʿAlī, may God ennoble his face, that he said: "Patience in faith is like the head to the body, and there is no good in a body that has no head." The explanation of this sentence has already been discussed in connection with His words: ﴿seek help through patience and prayer﴾.

﴿Indeed God is with the patient﴾: that is, with aid and support, as the poet said: "Satirise them, and the Holy Spirit is with you." And He, exalted, said: ﴿Do not grieve; indeed God is with us﴾ [At-Tawbah: 40]. Whoever God is with is the victor. Since prayer arises from patience, and patience has become the root of all arduous obligations, He said: ﴿Indeed God is with the patient﴾, so those who pray are subsumed under the patient, just as a branch is subsumed under its root. As for His saying there: ﴿And indeed it is difficult, except for the humble﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 45], He returned the pronoun to it according to the apparent sense of the speech, because it is the most noble and most arduous of the fruits of patience.

﴿And do not say of those who are killed in the way of God, "They are dead." Rather, they are alive, but you do not perceive﴾. It is said that the occasion of revelation of this verse is that it was said of one who was killed in the way of God: "So-and-so has died, and the delights and pleasures of this world have departed from him," so it was revealed. They were forbidden from saying of the martyrs that they are dead, and God informed that they are alive. The nominative status of "dead" and "alive" is as the predicate of an elided subject, meaning: "They are dead"; rather, "They are alive." It is possible that "rather, alive" is subsumed under a hidden saying, meaning: "Rather, say: they are alive." However, the first possibility is preferred, namely that it is an informative statement from God, the Exalted, and His words: ﴿but you do not perceive﴾ support this, because its meaning is that their life is something you have no awareness of. The apparent meaning is that the intended sense is the literal reality of death and life. It is also said that this is figurative. They differed: some said they are "dead" through the cessation of remembrance, and "alive" through its continuation and the permanence of reward. The Arabs used to call one who leaves no remembrance after his death, such as a child and others, "dead." Some said they are "dead" in misguidance and "alive" in obedience and guidance, as He said: ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life...﴾ [Al-Anʿām: 122]. If death and life are taken in their literal sense, then they differed. Some people said its meaning is a prohibition against the saying of the Jāhiliyyah (the pre-Islamic age) that they will not be raised, so the meaning is: they will be made alive by resurrection, and they will receive the reward of the martyrs who were killed in the way of God. Most scholars hold that they are alive at present. The meaning of this life is that their spirits remain while their bodies do not; for we witness the decay and perishing of bodies. They used as evidence for the survival of spirits the punishment of the grave, and His words: ﴿but you do not perceive﴾, meaning: you do not perceive the manner of their life. If the meaning of "they will be made alive" were that they will be made alive on the Day of Resurrection, or that they are upon guidance and light, then the negation of perception would have no sense, since this is addressed to the believers, and they already knew of the resurrection and that they were upon guidance. It would not be said of them: "but you do not perceive," because they already perceived this, and His words: ﴿They rejoice in those who have not yet joined them from behind them﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 170] also show this.

Some people have held that the martyr is alive in both body and spirit, and that the absence of perception of this by other living beings does not undermine it. Thus we see them in the state of the dead while they are alive, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them fixed, while they pass like clouds﴾ [An-Naml: 88] (p. 449), and as you see a sleeper in his position while he sees in his dream what delights or pains him. Al-Suhaylī, in his book *Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwah* (Proofs of Prophethood), narrated by way of a report from some of the Companions that he dug in a place and an opening appeared, and behold, a person was sitting on a couch with a copy of the Qur'an in front of him, reading in it, and before him was a green garden. That was at Uhud, and he knew that the man was one of the martyrs, because he saw a wound on the surface of his face. When it is established that the martyrs are alive, whether their spirits alone or their bodies and spirits together, then it is disputed where they reside. It is said: their graves, where they are provided for. It is said: in white domes in Paradise, where they are provided for; this was said by Abū Bashshār al-Sulamī. It is said: in white birds that eat from the fruits of Paradise, and their dwellings are the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntahā); this was said by Qatādah. It is said: they eat from the fruit of Paradise and smell its fragrance, without being in it; this was said by Mujāhid. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "The martyrs are at a river at the gate of Paradise, in a green dome." It is also narrated: "In a green garden, where their provision comes to them from Paradise morning and evening." And it is narrated from him (ﷺ): "The spirits of the martyrs are in green birds that hang from the fruit of Paradise, and they are in lamps of gold, and they are in a green dome." If these reports are sound, then they describe the states of different groups of martyrs, or different states at different times. The majority hold that they are in Paradise, and his (ﷺ) saying to the mother of Ḥārithah supports this: "They are in al-Firdaws." The doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah, i.e., Sunni orthodoxy) is that spirits do not perish, and that they remain after their departure from the body. So the spirits of the people of felicity are blessed until the Day of Judgment, and the spirits of the people of wretchedness are punished until the Day of Judgment.

The difference between the martyr and other believers is only in provision, which God has favoured them with. God, the Exalted, said regarding the disbelievers: ﴿The Fire, to which they are exposed morning and evening﴾ [Ghāfir: 46]. Al-Ḥasan said: "The martyrs are alive with God; their provisions are presented to their spirits, so joy and happiness reach them, just as the Fire is presented to the family of Pharaoh morning and evening, so suffering reaches them." They said: it is possible that God gathers from the parts of a martyr a whole and gives it life and brings bliss to it, even if it is the size of an atom. The noble verse does not address the provision of the spirits of the martyrs nor their abode; rather, mention of this came by way of digression, following the commentators, since they spoke about this in this verse. Otherwise, the proper place for discussing this is His words: ﴿Rather, they are alive with their Lord, receiving provision﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 169], where He mentioned "with" (ʿindiyyah) and provision. The apparent sense of His words: ﴿those who are killed in the way of God﴾ is generality. It is said that it was revealed concerning the martyrs of Badr, who were fourteen; but this generality is not restricted by this occasion, for what matters is the generality of the wording, not the particularity of the occasion. In this verse there is consolation for the relatives of the martyrs and their brothers among the believers, by mentioning that they are alive; so they are to be envied, not grieved over.

﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger, and a loss of wealth, lives, and fruits﴾. It has been previously stated that testing (ibtilāʾ) is examination, in order to know what will be the state of the one examined; but this is impossible with respect to God, the Exalted. Its meaning here is rather "to make manifest" (ijābah), and the pronoun of address refers to: it is said that it refers only to the Companions; this was said by ʿAṭāʾ. He addressed them with this after the Hijrah (migration), and informed them of it before its occurrence in order to reassure their hearts, since when knowledge of what will happen precedes it, one has prepared for it, unlike sudden matters, which are harder on the soul. There is also an increase in reward and recompense for what they experience through awaiting the calamity; and it is an informing of the unseen that happens exactly as it was foretold; and it distinguishes those who embraced Islam seeking the face of God from those who were hypocrites; and it increases sincerity in the state of trial above their sincerity in the state of well-being; and it prompts the one who has not embraced Islam to reflect on the signs of Islam, since he sees these afflicted people patient upon their religion, steadfast in heart, despite what they have been afflicted with. It is also said: they are the people of Makkah, and He addressed them with this to inform them that He answered the supplication of His Prophet (ﷺ) concerning them, and so that they would remain expecting calamity, so that calamities would be multiplied upon them. It is also said: it is an address to the Ummah, and it refers to the end of time. Kaʿb said: "A time will come upon people when the palm tree will bear only one fruit." This informing is a warning and an admonition against inclining toward this world and its splendour, and it is an informing of unseen matters. It is also said: the address is not directed at a specific person, but is general, not restricted to a particular time or a particular addressee (p. 450); so it is as if it were said: "We will surely afflict with such-and-such," and in this there is a warning, and it is for the Companions and others.

This verse is connected to His words: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 45] and the verse, and before it: ﴿And be grateful to Me﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 152]. Gratitude necessitates an increase of blessings, and being tested with what has been mentioned apparently contradicts this. Its explanation is that the completion of the laws is a completion of the blessing, and for this reason it necessitates gratitude; and carrying out those laws is not possible except by bearing hardships, so He commanded patience therein. He blessed him first, so he was grateful, and was tested second, so he was patient, in order that he might attain the two degrees of gratitude and patience, and thus his faith would be perfected. As was narrated from him (peace be upon him): "Faith is in two halves: a half is patience, and a half is gratitude." The phrase "with something" (bi-shayʾin) is connected to His words: ﴿We will surely test you﴾, and the bāʾ in it denotes attachment. He used the singular to indicate paucity, for if He had used the plural and said "with things" (bi-ashyāʾ), it might have meant kinds of each of what follows. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk read "bi-ashyāʾ," so there would be no elision in what follows, and "min" would be in the position of a qualifier. This contrasts with the reading of the majority, "bi-shayʾin," where an elision must be assumed, meaning "something of fear, and something of hunger, and something of loss." The meaning in this reading is: "We will surely test you with a portion of such-and-such." Fear is the fear of the enemy; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, and intense fear occurred at the Battle of the Confederates (al-Aḥzāb). Al-Shāfiʿī said it is the fear of God, the Exalted. Hunger is drought; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, using the effect to denote the cause. It is also said: hunger is poverty, again using the effect to denote the cause. Al-Shāfiʿī said it is the fasting of the month of Ramadan. "Loss of wealth" means through ruin and destruction. Al-Shāfiʿī said it means through charity. "Lives" means through killing and death. Al-Shāfiʿī said it means through illnesses; it is also said through grey hair. "Fruits" means the calamities that strike the fruits, scarcity of produce, and the cessation of blessings. Al-Qaffāl said its loss may be through drought, or through leaving the cultivation of lands because of engagement in jihad, or through spending on those who come as delegations to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It is also said: through the enemy's dominance over them. Al-Shāfiʿī said: "The fruits" are the death of children, because a man's child is the fruit of his heart. In the hadith of Abū Mūsā: "God says to the angels, when the servant's child dies: 'Have you seized the fruit of his heart?'"

Some scholars said: What is meant in this verse is the burdens and hardships of jihad. So fear of the enemy, hunger caused by it and by the journeys to it, loss of wealth through the expenses it requires, loss of lives through killing, and loss of fruits through the enemy's reaching them, or through neglect of them because of jihad. End of his words. He coordinated "and loss" (*wa-naqs*) with his statement "with something" (*bi-shay'*), meaning: "We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and loss." The indefinite form of the noun is suitable for this coordination. It is also possible that it is coordinated with "fear and hunger," so that its implied meaning would be "and something of loss." "From the wealth" (*min al-amwal*) is connected to "loss," because it is a verbal noun from *naqasa*, which is transitive to one object, and that object has been omitted, meaning "and the loss of something." It is also possible that it is in the position of a qualifier for "loss," and *min* would then indicate the starting point. It is also possible that it is in the position of a qualifier for that omitted noun, meaning "and the loss of something from the wealth," and *min* would then be partitive. They said: according to al-Akhfash, *min* may be additional (*za'idah*), meaning "and the loss of wealth, lives and fruits." He introduced the declarative sentence with an oath upon it, to emphasize that the trial will certainly occur. Attributing the verb to Him explicitly indicates that the causes of afflictions are ascribed to Him, and that these trials come from God, Exalted is He. His promise of them to the believers indicates that they are not punishments; rather, when patience accompanies them, they bring a high rank in religion. This order in the coordination follows a progression: He first informed of the trial with "something of fear," which is the anticipation of what hateful thing may come. Then he moved from it to the trial with "something of hunger," which is more severe than fear, whatever interpretation it is given: drought, poverty, or the need for food. The exception is the interpretation of al-Shafi'i, which is fasting in Ramadan. There is no progression between "loss" and "something," according to his preferred coordination of "loss" with "with something." Rather, the progression in the coordination occurs after "and loss": it begins first with the wealth, then rises to the lives. As for "and the fruits," it comes as a specification after a generalization, because they fall under the wealth, so there is no progression in them.

**﴿And give good tidings to the patient﴾**: an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), or to everyone who is capable of giving good tidings. That is, [good tidings of] victory for jihad, or of reward for obedience, or of recompense for calamities. These are the opinions. The best view is not to restrict it: whoever is patient in a praiseworthy manner according to the Shari'ah is included among the patient. They said: patience is a distinctive human quality, because reason and desire conflict within it, and it is physical. It is either active, such as undertaking arduous works, or endurance, such as enduring severe beating, and it is psychological, which is restraining the soul from what the natural disposition desires. If it concerns the desire of the private parts and the stomach, it is called chastity (*iffah*). If it concerns enduring something hateful, its names differ according to the hateful thing. In the case of a calamity, it is restricted to the name "patience," and its opposite is "impatience" (*jaza'*). If it concerns wealth, it is called self-control (*dabt al-nafs*), and its opposite is arrogance (*bataru*). If it concerns war, it is called courage (*shaja'ah*), and its opposite is cowardice (*jubn*). If it concerns a tiresome adversity, it is called breadth of chest (*sa'at sadr*), and its opposite is distress (*dajar*). If it concerns the concealing of speech, it is called secrecy (*kitman*), and its opposite is proclamation (*i'lan*). If it concerns the superfluities of this world, it is called asceticism (*zuhd*), and its opposite is greed (*hirs*). If it concerns a small amount of wealth, it is called contentment (*qana'ah*), and its opposite is avarice (*shurah*). God has gathered all these categories and named all of them patience, saying: ﴿and the patient in adversity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177], that is, in calamity, ﴿and in hardship﴾, that is, in poverty, ﴿and in the time of battle﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177], that is, in fighting. Al-Qaffal said: patience is not that a person does not feel the pain of the hateful thing, nor that he does not dislike it. Rather, it is compelling the soul to refrain from showing impatience, even if tears appear in the eye or the color changes. If he first displays what does not count as patience, and then he becomes patient, that is not counted except as consolation.

**﴿Who, when a calamity strikes them﴾**: regarding "those who" (*alladhina*), it may be in the accusative as a qualifier of "the patient," which is the apparent grammatical reading; or in the accusative by way of praise, in which case it is detached; or in the nominative by implying "they," in two ways: either by detachment or by resumption, as if it were an answer to an implied question, meaning: "Who are the patient?" It was said: "They are those who, when..." They also permitted that "those who" be the subject (*mubtada'*), with "upon them" (*'alayhim*) as its predicate, and this is possible. "Calamity" (*musibah*) is an active participle from *asabat*, and it has acquired a specific connection to a hateful thing; it became a metaphor for the great disaster, so it functioned like nouns and governed the operators. "Asabathum: musibah" is a case of paronomasia of different types (*tajnis mughayir*), which is when one of the two words is a noun and the other is a verb. From it: ﴿The Imminent Event has drawn near﴾ [al-Najm: 57]; ﴿When the Event occurs﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 1]. A calamity is anything that harms the believer in his soul, wealth, or family, whether small or great, to the extent that the extinguishing of a lamp is called a calamity for one who needs it. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said the words of recitation (*istirja'*) when his lamp went out. The meaning of "when" (*idha*) here is repetition and generality. We have previously mentioned the disagreement about *idha*: does it indicate repetition, or was it established for a single occurrence? There are two views among the grammarians.

**﴿they say: Indeed we belong to God﴾**: "they say" (*qalu*) is the answer to "when" (*idha*), and the conditional clause with its answer is a relative clause for "those who." "Indeed we" (*inna-na*): its original form is *innana*, because when *inna* enters upon the attached accusative pronoun, one *nun* of *inna* is dropped. The one that should be dropped is the second, because it is the one that is a place-holder, and because deletion is known in it when it is lightened; they say: *in Zayd la-qa'im*. This is deletion here for the sake of the coincidence of identical sounds, and that is why it operates; if it were a deletion without this reason, the pronoun would be separated and would be in the nominative and it would not operate; because when it is lightened in this way, it does not operate on the pronoun. "To God" (*li-Llah*): its meaning is affirmation of ownership and servitude to God, for He is the One who disposes of us as He wills in matters.

**﴿and indeed to Him we are returning﴾**: an affirmation of resurrection and an alert to the calamity of death, which is the greatest of calamities, and a reminder that whatever befalls a person short of it is near and must come to an end for him. Regarding these two spoken clauses, the exegetes have several opinions. First: our souls, our wealth, and our families belong to God, and He does not wrong us in what He does to us. Second: we have submitted the matter to God and we are content with His decree; "and indeed to Him we are returning" means: to the resurrection, for the reward of the good-doer and the punishment of the evil-doer. Third: we are returning to Him for the compensation of the affliction and the bestowal of great reward. Fourth: its meaning is an affirmation of ownership in His saying "indeed we belong to God," and an affirmation of destruction in His saying "and indeed to Him we are returning." In al-Muntakhab there is a summary of the following: the attribution of the affliction to the calamity, not to God, Exalted is He, is so that it may include what comes from God and what comes from others. What comes from God is included under His saying "indeed we belong to God," because in affirming servitude there is a committing of affairs to Him; and what comes from others, its obligation is to return to God for justice regarding it, and not to transgress. It is as if in the first, "indeed we belong to God," He manages as He wills; and in the second, "and indeed to Him," He does justice for us as He wills. It was said: "indeed we belong to God" is evidence of contentment with what has descended at the present moment; "and indeed to Him we are returning" is evidence of contentment at the present moment with everything that will descend afterward. The verse contains an obligation and a voluntary act. The obligation is submission to God's command, contentment with His decree, and patience in performing His obligations. The voluntary act is the utterance "indeed we belong to God and indeed to Him we are returning," and in uttering it there are benefits, among them: enraging the disbelievers, because they know the earnestness of the believers in obedience to God.

**﴿Upon them are blessings from their Lord and mercy﴾**: "those" (*ula'ika*) is the subject; "blessings" (*salawat*) is in the nominative as the agent of the prepositional phrase, meaning: "those upon whom blessings are established." Thus he has informed about the subject with a singular noun, and this is better than making "blessings" the subject, with the prepositional phrase in the position of its predicate. The sentence is in the position of the predicate of the first subject, because it is information about the subject with a sentence. The blessing (*salah*) from God is forgiveness, according to Ibn Abbas; or praise, according to Ibn Kaysan; or forgiveness and good praise, according to al-Zajjaj. Mercy (*rahmah*): it was said that it is the blessings themselves, repeated for emphasis when the wording differs, like His saying ﴿tenderness and mercy﴾ [al-Hadid: 27]. It was also said: "mercy" is the relief of distress and the fulfilment of need. Umar said: "What excellent two portions, and what excellent addition," and he recited: ﴿those who, when a calamity strikes them﴾, the verse; by the two portions he meant the blessings and the mercy, and by the addition: guidance. In His saying "those" (*ula'ika*), the demonstrative pronoun is used for distance, which is to indicate the distance of this rank, as came in ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5]. The allusion to attaining forgiveness and praise through His saying "upon them are blessings," with the particle "upon" (*'ala*), indicates that they are immersed in that, that it has covered them and enveloped them, and this is more eloquent than saying "for them." He made "blessings" plural to indicate that this is not merely any blessing, but blessing after blessing; and it is indefinite because generality is not intended. He described them as "from their Lord" so that *min* would indicate that they originate from God; that is, those blessings arise and begin from God, Exalted is He. It is possible that *min* is partitive, in which case there is an omitted genitive, meaning "blessings from the blessings of their Lord." He used the word "Lord" because it indicates nurturing, and looking after the servant in what sets him right and rears him. If by "mercy" the blessings are meant, then it does not need to be qualified by an omitted attribute, because it has already been qualified. If by it is meant something other than the blessings, then it is estimated as "and mercy from Him," and the attribute has been omitted because of what preceded. It is possible that "from their Lord" is connected to His saying "upon them," so it is not an attribute, but rather a complement governed by the operator that raises "blessings." This great reward and beautiful praise follow from the station of patience and from the speech of these words that indicate entrusting the matter to God, Exalted is He.

It has come in the Sunnah that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says the words of recitation at a calamity, God will remedy his calamity, make its outcome good for him, and give him a righteous successor whom he will be pleased with." In another hadith: "Whoever remembers his calamity and renews the recitation of *istirja'*, even if its time has long passed, God will write for him the same reward as on the day he was afflicted." The hadith of Umm Salamah is well known, in which God gave her a successor to Abu Salamah: the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Ibn Jubayr said: No one has been given in calamity what this nation has been given; if anyone had been given it before it, Ya'qub would have been given it. Do you not see how he said when he lost Yusuf? ﴿Alas for Yusuf!﴾ [Yusuf: 84].

**﴿And those are the rightly guided﴾**: this is information from God about them regarding guidance, and whoever God informs about being guided will never go astray. This is a firm sentence that indicates concern for the matter of the one about whom it is reported, since every attribute of his appears in an independent sentence. The first sentence was begun with because it is more important for obtaining the reward that follows from the attribute before it; this one was placed later because, relative to what precedes it, it stands in the position of a cause, since that statement, upon which that great reward follows, comes only from one whose guidance has preceded. It was emphasized by His saying "they" (*hum*), and by the definite article, as if guidance were restricted to them; and by the active participle, to indicate permanence, because guidance is not one of the actions that renew from time to time so that it would be reported by a verb; rather, it is a stable attribute. It was said: "the rightly guided" concerns the deserving of reward and the bestowal of great recompense. It was said: it refers to the facilitation of the calamity and the lightening of grief. It was said: it refers to *istirja'*. It was said: it refers to the truth and the correct path. These restrictions have no indication in the wording, so the preferable reading is to take it as guidance which is faith. A parallel to these two sentences is His saying: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5]. The discussion of the grammar of "they are the rightly guided" is like the discussion of "they are the successful," and it has been mentioned before.

This passage contains further emphasis on the command to turn one's face toward the direction from which the Prophet (ﷺ) emerged, toward the Sacred Mosque, and on the command to them to turn their faces toward it, for the sake of attending to the matter of the change of the qibla (naskh, abrogation), since abrogation was difficult for souls: they had become accustomed to one matter and were commanded to abandon it and move to another, especially among those who do not accept abrogation. Therefore it was repeated, and that He, exalted is He, commanded this and did it, so that people would have no arguments. For when it comes by a command from Him, exalted is He, no one has any proof against one who complies with God's command, since God's command the second time is like His command the first time. He had commanded first the facing of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), and then commanded the facing of the Ka'bah. There is no difference between the two commands, and there is no argument for the one who opposes them. He excepted from the people those who did wrong, because their arguments never cease, even though they are false, nor do their confusions and deceptions, because there is a quality in them that prevents them from perceiving the truth and being illuminated by it. Then He, exalted is He, commanded them to fear Him, and forbade them from fearing people, because when they fear God, exalted is He, they comply with His commands and avoid His prohibitions. He joined to that reason another reason, namely the completion of the blessing by facing the Ka'bah, for in that is the following of your father Ibrahim (Abraham), and a return to what is familiar, and the attainment of guidance. He likened this completion to the completion of the blessing of sending a Messenger from among them to them, since this blessing is the foundation, and it is the source of blessings and guidance. Then He described the addressees with those sublime qualities by which they were granted the most complete portion, which is the recitation of the Book to them: [Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book which is recited to them?] [Al-'Ankabut: 51]. How then (would it be) with the increase of purification and teaching, through which purity from impurities is attained, and everlasting life among people?

A brother of knowledge lives forever after his death, though his bones are dust beneath the soil and decayed.

And another said:

The place of knowledge does not return to dust, nor wears away with the ancient ages.

Then He, exalted is He, commanded them to remember these blessings, lest they forget them, and to give thanks for them, so that He would increase them in blessings. Then He forbade them from ingratitude for them, because ingratitude for blessings requires their removal and the deserving of a severe punishment. Then He called out to those characterized by faith, and this is the second call to the believers in this surah, so that they would attend to what He commands them. He commanded them to seek help through patience and prayer, because seeking help through both achieves the happiness of this world and the Hereafter. Then God, exalted is He, informed that He is with those who are patient. Then He forbade them from saying of the martyrs that they are dead, and informed that they are living, so it is obligatory to affirm what He informed of, and He mentioned that we do not perceive their life. Then God, exalted is He, informed that He tests them with what manifests in them patience, and it is a part of the trials that God, exalted is He, mentioned. Then He commanded His Prophet to give good news to the patient ones who are tested with it, those who submit to God's decree in belief and explicit statement, that they are the servants and slaves of God, and to Him is their return and their destination; He disposes of them as He wills. Then He concluded that for whoever is characterized by this quality, there are prayers and mercy from God upon him, and he is the one who is guided, whose guidance is established and firmly rooted.

(p. 448) ﴿O you who believe, seek help through patience and prayer﴾. It is said that the occasion of revelation of this verse is that the polytheists said: "Muhammad will return to our religion, just as he returned to our qiblah." He (God) shook them with this call, which includes this noble description, namely faith, expressed as a past-tense verb in the relative clause of "those who" (alladhīna), indicating its firm establishment and their being characterized by it in past time, so that they would be more ready to accept what comes to them of commands and arduous obligations. This is because patience (ṣabr) and prayer (ṣalāh) are the two pillars of Islam. Patience is restraining the self upon hardships and arduous obligations, and it is an inward matter; prayer is its fruit, and it is among the most difficult obligations because of its repetition. The connection of this verse to what precedes it is evident, for they had heard from the disbelievers' criticism of turning toward the Kaʿbah and praying toward it a great deal of harm, so they were commanded at that point to seek help through patience and prayer. Some have restricted the patience mentioned here to patience over the harm of the disbelievers through their criticism of the change of direction and of praying toward the Kaʿbah, and others to patience in performing the obligatory duties. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, and some said, that it is a metonym for fasting, and from this Ramadan was called "the month of patience." Some said it is a metonym for jihad (struggle in the way of God), because of His later words: ﴿And do not say of those who are killed in the way of God...﴾. This is the view of Abū Muslim. The preferable view is what we have mentioned earlier, namely the generality of the wording, so these individual instances fall under it. It is narrated from ʿAlī, may God ennoble his face, that he said: "Patience in faith is like the head to the body, and there is no good in a body that has no head." The explanation of this sentence has already been discussed in connection with His words: ﴿seek help through patience and prayer﴾.

﴿Indeed God is with the patient﴾: that is, with aid and support, as the poet said: "Satirise them, and the Holy Spirit is with you." And He, exalted, said: ﴿Do not grieve; indeed God is with us﴾ [At-Tawbah: 40]. Whoever God is with is the victor. Since prayer arises from patience, and patience has become the root of all arduous obligations, He said: ﴿Indeed God is with the patient﴾, so those who pray are subsumed under the patient, just as a branch is subsumed under its root. As for His saying there: ﴿And indeed it is difficult, except for the humble﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 45], He returned the pronoun to it according to the apparent sense of the speech, because it is the most noble and most arduous of the fruits of patience.

﴿And do not say of those who are killed in the way of God, "They are dead." Rather, they are alive, but you do not perceive﴾. It is said that the occasion of revelation of this verse is that it was said of one who was killed in the way of God: "So-and-so has died, and the delights and pleasures of this world have departed from him," so it was revealed. They were forbidden from saying of the martyrs that they are dead, and God informed that they are alive. The nominative status of "dead" and "alive" is as the predicate of an elided subject, meaning: "They are dead"; rather, "They are alive." It is possible that "rather, alive" is subsumed under a hidden saying, meaning: "Rather, say: they are alive." However, the first possibility is preferred, namely that it is an informative statement from God, the Exalted, and His words: ﴿but you do not perceive﴾ support this, because its meaning is that their life is something you have no awareness of. The apparent meaning is that the intended sense is the literal reality of death and life. It is also said that this is figurative. They differed: some said they are "dead" through the cessation of remembrance, and "alive" through its continuation and the permanence of reward. The Arabs used to call one who leaves no remembrance after his death, such as a child and others, "dead." Some said they are "dead" in misguidance and "alive" in obedience and guidance, as He said: ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life...﴾ [Al-Anʿām: 122]. If death and life are taken in their literal sense, then they differed. Some people said its meaning is a prohibition against the saying of the Jāhiliyyah (the pre-Islamic age) that they will not be raised, so the meaning is: they will be made alive by resurrection, and they will receive the reward of the martyrs who were killed in the way of God. Most scholars hold that they are alive at present. The meaning of this life is that their spirits remain while their bodies do not; for we witness the decay and perishing of bodies. They used as evidence for the survival of spirits the punishment of the grave, and His words: ﴿but you do not perceive﴾, meaning: you do not perceive the manner of their life. If the meaning of "they will be made alive" were that they will be made alive on the Day of Resurrection, or that they are upon guidance and light, then the negation of perception would have no sense, since this is addressed to the believers, and they already knew of the resurrection and that they were upon guidance. It would not be said of them: "but you do not perceive," because they already perceived this, and His words: ﴿They rejoice in those who have not yet joined them from behind them﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 170] also show this.

Some people have held that the martyr is alive in both body and spirit, and that the absence of perception of this by other living beings does not undermine it. Thus we see them in the state of the dead while they are alive, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them fixed, while they pass like clouds﴾ [An-Naml: 88] (p. 449), and as you see a sleeper in his position while he sees in his dream what delights or pains him. Al-Suhaylī, in his book *Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwah* (Proofs of Prophethood), narrated by way of a report from some of the Companions that he dug in a place and an opening appeared, and behold, a person was sitting on a couch with a copy of the Qur'an in front of him, reading in it, and before him was a green garden. That was at Uhud, and he knew that the man was one of the martyrs, because he saw a wound on the surface of his face. When it is established that the martyrs are alive, whether their spirits alone or their bodies and spirits together, then it is disputed where they reside. It is said: their graves, where they are provided for. It is said: in white domes in Paradise, where they are provided for; this was said by Abū Bashshār al-Sulamī. It is said: in white birds that eat from the fruits of Paradise, and their dwellings are the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntahā); this was said by Qatādah. It is said: they eat from the fruit of Paradise and smell its fragrance, without being in it; this was said by Mujāhid. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "The martyrs are at a river at the gate of Paradise, in a green dome." It is also narrated: "In a green garden, where their provision comes to them from Paradise morning and evening." And it is narrated from him (ﷺ): "The spirits of the martyrs are in green birds that hang from the fruit of Paradise, and they are in lamps of gold, and they are in a green dome." If these reports are sound, then they describe the states of different groups of martyrs, or different states at different times. The majority hold that they are in Paradise, and his (ﷺ) saying to the mother of Ḥārithah supports this: "They are in al-Firdaws." The doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah, i.e., Sunni orthodoxy) is that spirits do not perish, and that they remain after their departure from the body. So the spirits of the people of felicity are blessed until the Day of Judgment, and the spirits of the people of wretchedness are punished until the Day of Judgment.

The difference between the martyr and other believers is only in provision, which God has favoured them with. God, the Exalted, said regarding the disbelievers: ﴿The Fire, to which they are exposed morning and evening﴾ [Ghāfir: 46]. Al-Ḥasan said: "The martyrs are alive with God; their provisions are presented to their spirits, so joy and happiness reach them, just as the Fire is presented to the family of Pharaoh morning and evening, so suffering reaches them." They said: it is possible that God gathers from the parts of a martyr a whole and gives it life and brings bliss to it, even if it is the size of an atom. The noble verse does not address the provision of the spirits of the martyrs nor their abode; rather, mention of this came by way of digression, following the commentators, since they spoke about this in this verse. Otherwise, the proper place for discussing this is His words: ﴿Rather, they are alive with their Lord, receiving provision﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 169], where He mentioned "with" (ʿindiyyah) and provision. The apparent sense of His words: ﴿those who are killed in the way of God﴾ is generality. It is said that it was revealed concerning the martyrs of Badr, who were fourteen; but this generality is not restricted by this occasion, for what matters is the generality of the wording, not the particularity of the occasion. In this verse there is consolation for the relatives of the martyrs and their brothers among the believers, by mentioning that they are alive; so they are to be envied, not grieved over.

﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger, and a loss of wealth, lives, and fruits﴾. It has been previously stated that testing (ibtilāʾ) is examination, in order to know what will be the state of the one examined; but this is impossible with respect to God, the Exalted. Its meaning here is rather "to make manifest" (ijābah), and the pronoun of address refers to: it is said that it refers only to the Companions; this was said by ʿAṭāʾ. He addressed them with this after the Hijrah (migration), and informed them of it before its occurrence in order to reassure their hearts, since when knowledge of what will happen precedes it, one has prepared for it, unlike sudden matters, which are harder on the soul. There is also an increase in reward and recompense for what they experience through awaiting the calamity; and it is an informing of the unseen that happens exactly as it was foretold; and it distinguishes those who embraced Islam seeking the face of God from those who were hypocrites; and it increases sincerity in the state of trial above their sincerity in the state of well-being; and it prompts the one who has not embraced Islam to reflect on the signs of Islam, since he sees these afflicted people patient upon their religion, steadfast in heart, despite what they have been afflicted with. It is also said: they are the people of Makkah, and He addressed them with this to inform them that He answered the supplication of His Prophet (ﷺ) concerning them, and so that they would remain expecting calamity, so that calamities would be multiplied upon them. It is also said: it is an address to the Ummah, and it refers to the end of time. Kaʿb said: "A time will come upon people when the palm tree will bear only one fruit." This informing is a warning and an admonition against inclining toward this world and its splendour, and it is an informing of unseen matters. It is also said: the address is not directed at a specific person, but is general, not restricted to a particular time or a particular addressee (p. 450); so it is as if it were said: "We will surely afflict with such-and-such," and in this there is a warning, and it is for the Companions and others.

This verse is connected to His words: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 45] and the verse, and before it: ﴿And be grateful to Me﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 152]. Gratitude necessitates an increase of blessings, and being tested with what has been mentioned apparently contradicts this. Its explanation is that the completion of the laws is a completion of the blessing, and for this reason it necessitates gratitude; and carrying out those laws is not possible except by bearing hardships, so He commanded patience therein. He blessed him first, so he was grateful, and was tested second, so he was patient, in order that he might attain the two degrees of gratitude and patience, and thus his faith would be perfected. As was narrated from him (peace be upon him): "Faith is in two halves: a half is patience, and a half is gratitude." The phrase "with something" (bi-shayʾin) is connected to His words: ﴿We will surely test you﴾, and the bāʾ in it denotes attachment. He used the singular to indicate paucity, for if He had used the plural and said "with things" (bi-ashyāʾ), it might have meant kinds of each of what follows. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk read "bi-ashyāʾ," so there would be no elision in what follows, and "min" would be in the position of a qualifier. This contrasts with the reading of the majority, "bi-shayʾin," where an elision must be assumed, meaning "something of fear, and something of hunger, and something of loss." The meaning in this reading is: "We will surely test you with a portion of such-and-such." Fear is the fear of the enemy; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, and intense fear occurred at the Battle of the Confederates (al-Aḥzāb). Al-Shāfiʿī said it is the fear of God, the Exalted. Hunger is drought; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, using the effect to denote the cause. It is also said: hunger is poverty, again using the effect to denote the cause. Al-Shāfiʿī said it is the fasting of the month of Ramadan. "Loss of wealth" means through ruin and destruction. Al-Shāfiʿī said it means through charity. "Lives" means through killing and death. Al-Shāfiʿī said it means through illnesses; it is also said through grey hair. "Fruits" means the calamities that strike the fruits, scarcity of produce, and the cessation of blessings. Al-Qaffāl said its loss may be through drought, or through leaving the cultivation of lands because of engagement in jihad, or through spending on those who come as delegations to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It is also said: through the enemy's dominance over them. Al-Shāfiʿī said: "The fruits" are the death of children, because a man's child is the fruit of his heart. In the hadith of Abū Mūsā: "God says to the angels, when the servant's child dies: 'Have you seized the fruit of his heart?'"

Some scholars said: What is meant in this verse is the burdens and hardships of jihad. So fear of the enemy, hunger caused by it and by the journeys to it, loss of wealth through the expenses it requires, loss of lives through killing, and loss of fruits through the enemy's reaching them, or through neglect of them because of jihad. End of his words. He coordinated "and loss" (*wa-naqs*) with his statement "with something" (*bi-shay'*), meaning: "We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and loss." The indefinite form of the noun is suitable for this coordination. It is also possible that it is coordinated with "fear and hunger," so that its implied meaning would be "and something of loss." "From the wealth" (*min al-amwal*) is connected to "loss," because it is a verbal noun from *naqasa*, which is transitive to one object, and that object has been omitted, meaning "and the loss of something." It is also possible that it is in the position of a qualifier for "loss," and *min* would then indicate the starting point. It is also possible that it is in the position of a qualifier for that omitted noun, meaning "and the loss of something from the wealth," and *min* would then be partitive. They said: according to al-Akhfash, *min* may be additional (*za'idah*), meaning "and the loss of wealth, lives and fruits." He introduced the declarative sentence with an oath upon it, to emphasize that the trial will certainly occur. Attributing the verb to Him explicitly indicates that the causes of afflictions are ascribed to Him, and that these trials come from God, Exalted is He. His promise of them to the believers indicates that they are not punishments; rather, when patience accompanies them, they bring a high rank in religion. This order in the coordination follows a progression: He first informed of the trial with "something of fear," which is the anticipation of what hateful thing may come. Then he moved from it to the trial with "something of hunger," which is more severe than fear, whatever interpretation it is given: drought, poverty, or the need for food. The exception is the interpretation of al-Shafi'i, which is fasting in Ramadan. There is no progression between "loss" and "something," according to his preferred coordination of "loss" with "with something." Rather, the progression in the coordination occurs after "and loss": it begins first with the wealth, then rises to the lives. As for "and the fruits," it comes as a specification after a generalization, because they fall under the wealth, so there is no progression in them.

**﴿And give good tidings to the patient﴾**: an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), or to everyone who is capable of giving good tidings. That is, [good tidings of] victory for jihad, or of reward for obedience, or of recompense for calamities. These are the opinions. The best view is not to restrict it: whoever is patient in a praiseworthy manner according to the Shari'ah is included among the patient. They said: patience is a distinctive human quality, because reason and desire conflict within it, and it is physical. It is either active, such as undertaking arduous works, or endurance, such as enduring severe beating, and it is psychological, which is restraining the soul from what the natural disposition desires. If it concerns the desire of the private parts and the stomach, it is called chastity (*iffah*). If it concerns enduring something hateful, its names differ according to the hateful thing. In the case of a calamity, it is restricted to the name "patience," and its opposite is "impatience" (*jaza'*). If it concerns wealth, it is called self-control (*dabt al-nafs*), and its opposite is arrogance (*bataru*). If it concerns war, it is called courage (*shaja'ah*), and its opposite is cowardice (*jubn*). If it concerns a tiresome adversity, it is called breadth of chest (*sa'at sadr*), and its opposite is distress (*dajar*). If it concerns the concealing of speech, it is called secrecy (*kitman*), and its opposite is proclamation (*i'lan*). If it concerns the superfluities of this world, it is called asceticism (*zuhd*), and its opposite is greed (*hirs*). If it concerns a small amount of wealth, it is called contentment (*qana'ah*), and its opposite is avarice (*shurah*). God has gathered all these categories and named all of them patience, saying: ﴿and the patient in adversity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177], that is, in calamity, ﴿and in hardship﴾, that is, in poverty, ﴿and in the time of battle﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177], that is, in fighting. Al-Qaffal said: patience is not that a person does not feel the pain of the hateful thing, nor that he does not dislike it. Rather, it is compelling the soul to refrain from showing impatience, even if tears appear in the eye or the color changes. If he first displays what does not count as patience, and then he becomes patient, that is not counted except as consolation.

**﴿Who, when a calamity strikes them﴾**: regarding "those who" (*alladhina*), it may be in the accusative as a qualifier of "the patient," which is the apparent grammatical reading; or in the accusative by way of praise, in which case it is detached; or in the nominative by implying "they," in two ways: either by detachment or by resumption, as if it were an answer to an implied question, meaning: "Who are the patient?" It was said: "They are those who, when..." They also permitted that "those who" be the subject (*mubtada'*), with "upon them" (*'alayhim*) as its predicate, and this is possible. "Calamity" (*musibah*) is an active participle from *asabat*, and it has acquired a specific connection to a hateful thing; it became a metaphor for the great disaster, so it functioned like nouns and governed the operators. "Asabathum: musibah" is a case of paronomasia of different types (*tajnis mughayir*), which is when one of the two words is a noun and the other is a verb. From it: ﴿The Imminent Event has drawn near﴾ [al-Najm: 57]; ﴿When the Event occurs﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 1]. A calamity is anything that harms the believer in his soul, wealth, or family, whether small or great, to the extent that the extinguishing of a lamp is called a calamity for one who needs it. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said the words of recitation (*istirja'*) when his lamp went out. The meaning of "when" (*idha*) here is repetition and generality. We have previously mentioned the disagreement about *idha*: does it indicate repetition, or was it established for a single occurrence? There are two views among the grammarians.

**﴿they say: Indeed we belong to God﴾**: "they say" (*qalu*) is the answer to "when" (*idha*), and the conditional clause with its answer is a relative clause for "those who." "Indeed we" (*inna-na*): its original form is *innana*, because when *inna* enters upon the attached accusative pronoun, one *nun* of *inna* is dropped. The one that should be dropped is the second, because it is the one that is a place-holder, and because deletion is known in it when it is lightened; they say: *in Zayd la-qa'im*. This is deletion here for the sake of the coincidence of identical sounds, and that is why it operates; if it were a deletion without this reason, the pronoun would be separated and would be in the nominative and it would not operate; because when it is lightened in this way, it does not operate on the pronoun. "To God" (*li-Llah*): its meaning is affirmation of ownership and servitude to God, for He is the One who disposes of us as He wills in matters.

**﴿and indeed to Him we are returning﴾**: an affirmation of resurrection and an alert to the calamity of death, which is the greatest of calamities, and a reminder that whatever befalls a person short of it is near and must come to an end for him. Regarding these two spoken clauses, the exegetes have several opinions. First: our souls, our wealth, and our families belong to God, and He does not wrong us in what He does to us. Second: we have submitted the matter to God and we are content with His decree; "and indeed to Him we are returning" means: to the resurrection, for the reward of the good-doer and the punishment of the evil-doer. Third: we are returning to Him for the compensation of the affliction and the bestowal of great reward. Fourth: its meaning is an affirmation of ownership in His saying "indeed we belong to God," and an affirmation of destruction in His saying "and indeed to Him we are returning." In al-Muntakhab there is a summary of the following: the attribution of the affliction to the calamity, not to God, Exalted is He, is so that it may include what comes from God and what comes from others. What comes from God is included under His saying "indeed we belong to God," because in affirming servitude there is a committing of affairs to Him; and what comes from others, its obligation is to return to God for justice regarding it, and not to transgress. It is as if in the first, "indeed we belong to God," He manages as He wills; and in the second, "and indeed to Him," He does justice for us as He wills. It was said: "indeed we belong to God" is evidence of contentment with what has descended at the present moment; "and indeed to Him we are returning" is evidence of contentment at the present moment with everything that will descend afterward. The verse contains an obligation and a voluntary act. The obligation is submission to God's command, contentment with His decree, and patience in performing His obligations. The voluntary act is the utterance "indeed we belong to God and indeed to Him we are returning," and in uttering it there are benefits, among them: enraging the disbelievers, because they know the earnestness of the believers in obedience to God.

**﴿Upon them are blessings from their Lord and mercy﴾**: "those" (*ula'ika*) is the subject; "blessings" (*salawat*) is in the nominative as the agent of the prepositional phrase, meaning: "those upon whom blessings are established." Thus he has informed about the subject with a singular noun, and this is better than making "blessings" the subject, with the prepositional phrase in the position of its predicate. The sentence is in the position of the predicate of the first subject, because it is information about the subject with a sentence. The blessing (*salah*) from God is forgiveness, according to Ibn Abbas; or praise, according to Ibn Kaysan; or forgiveness and good praise, according to al-Zajjaj. Mercy (*rahmah*): it was said that it is the blessings themselves, repeated for emphasis when the wording differs, like His saying ﴿tenderness and mercy﴾ [al-Hadid: 27]. It was also said: "mercy" is the relief of distress and the fulfilment of need. Umar said: "What excellent two portions, and what excellent addition," and he recited: ﴿those who, when a calamity strikes them﴾, the verse; by the two portions he meant the blessings and the mercy, and by the addition: guidance. In His saying "those" (*ula'ika*), the demonstrative pronoun is used for distance, which is to indicate the distance of this rank, as came in ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5]. The allusion to attaining forgiveness and praise through His saying "upon them are blessings," with the particle "upon" (*'ala*), indicates that they are immersed in that, that it has covered them and enveloped them, and this is more eloquent than saying "for them." He made "blessings" plural to indicate that this is not merely any blessing, but blessing after blessing; and it is indefinite because generality is not intended. He described them as "from their Lord" so that *min* would indicate that they originate from God; that is, those blessings arise and begin from God, Exalted is He. It is possible that *min* is partitive, in which case there is an omitted genitive, meaning "blessings from the blessings of their Lord." He used the word "Lord" because it indicates nurturing, and looking after the servant in what sets him right and rears him. If by "mercy" the blessings are meant, then it does not need to be qualified by an omitted attribute, because it has already been qualified. If by it is meant something other than the blessings, then it is estimated as "and mercy from Him," and the attribute has been omitted because of what preceded. It is possible that "from their Lord" is connected to His saying "upon them," so it is not an attribute, but rather a complement governed by the operator that raises "blessings." This great reward and beautiful praise follow from the station of patience and from the speech of these words that indicate entrusting the matter to God, Exalted is He.

It has come in the Sunnah that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says the words of recitation at a calamity, God will remedy his calamity, make its outcome good for him, and give him a righteous successor whom he will be pleased with." In another hadith: "Whoever remembers his calamity and renews the recitation of *istirja'*, even if its time has long passed, God will write for him the same reward as on the day he was afflicted." The hadith of Umm Salamah is well known, in which God gave her a successor to Abu Salamah: the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Ibn Jubayr said: No one has been given in calamity what this nation has been given; if anyone had been given it before it, Ya'qub would have been given it. Do you not see how he said when he lost Yusuf? ﴿Alas for Yusuf!﴾ [Yusuf: 84].

**﴿And those are the rightly guided﴾**: this is information from God about them regarding guidance, and whoever God informs about being guided will never go astray. This is a firm sentence that indicates concern for the matter of the one about whom it is reported, since every attribute of his appears in an independent sentence. The first sentence was begun with because it is more important for obtaining the reward that follows from the attribute before it; this one was placed later because, relative to what precedes it, it stands in the position of a cause, since that statement, upon which that great reward follows, comes only from one whose guidance has preceded. It was emphasized by His saying "they" (*hum*), and by the definite article, as if guidance were restricted to them; and by the active participle, to indicate permanence, because guidance is not one of the actions that renew from time to time so that it would be reported by a verb; rather, it is a stable attribute. It was said: "the rightly guided" concerns the deserving of reward and the bestowal of great recompense. It was said: it refers to the facilitation of the calamity and the lightening of grief. It was said: it refers to *istirja'*. It was said: it refers to the truth and the correct path. These restrictions have no indication in the wording, so the preferable reading is to take it as guidance which is faith. A parallel to these two sentences is His saying: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5]. The discussion of the grammar of "they are the rightly guided" is like the discussion of "they are the successful," and it has been mentioned before.

This passage contains further emphasis on the command to turn one's face toward the direction from which the Prophet (ﷺ) emerged, toward the Sacred Mosque, and on the command to them to turn their faces toward it, for the sake of attending to the matter of the change of the qibla (naskh, abrogation), since abrogation was difficult for souls: they had become accustomed to one matter and were commanded to abandon it and move to another, especially among those who do not accept abrogation. Therefore it was repeated, and that He, exalted is He, commanded this and did it, so that people would have no arguments. For when it comes by a command from Him, exalted is He, no one has any proof against one who complies with God's command, since God's command the second time is like His command the first time. He had commanded first the facing of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), and then commanded the facing of the Ka'bah. There is no difference between the two commands, and there is no argument for the one who opposes them. He excepted from the people those who did wrong, because their arguments never cease, even though they are false, nor do their confusions and deceptions, because there is a quality in them that prevents them from perceiving the truth and being illuminated by it. Then He, exalted is He, commanded them to fear Him, and forbade them from fearing people, because when they fear God, exalted is He, they comply with His commands and avoid His prohibitions. He joined to that reason another reason, namely the completion of the blessing by facing the Ka'bah, for in that is the following of your father Ibrahim (Abraham), and a return to what is familiar, and the attainment of guidance. He likened this completion to the completion of the blessing of sending a Messenger from among them to them, since this blessing is the foundation, and it is the source of blessings and guidance. Then He described the addressees with those sublime qualities by which they were granted the most complete portion, which is the recitation of the Book to them: [Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book which is recited to them?] [Al-'Ankabut: 51]. How then (would it be) with the increase of purification and teaching, through which purity from impurities is attained, and everlasting life among people?

A brother of knowledge lives forever after his death, though his bones are dust beneath the soil and decayed.

And another said:

The place of knowledge does not return to dust, nor wears away with the ancient ages.

Then He, exalted is He, commanded them to remember these blessings, lest they forget them, and to give thanks for them, so that He would increase them in blessings. Then He forbade them from ingratitude for them, because ingratitude for blessings requires their removal and the deserving of a severe punishment. Then He called out to those characterized by faith, and this is the second call to the believers in this surah, so that they would attend to what He commands them. He commanded them to seek help through patience and prayer, because seeking help through both achieves the happiness of this world and the Hereafter. Then God, exalted is He, informed that He is with those who are patient. Then He forbade them from saying of the martyrs that they are dead, and informed that they are living, so it is obligatory to affirm what He informed of, and He mentioned that we do not perceive their life. Then God, exalted is He, informed that He tests them with what manifests in them patience, and it is a part of the trials that God, exalted is He, mentioned. Then He commanded His Prophet to give good news to the patient ones who are tested with it, those who submit to God's decree in belief and explicit statement, that they are the servants and slaves of God, and to Him is their return and their destination; He disposes of them as He wills. Then He concluded that for whoever is characterized by this quality, there are prayers and mercy from God upon him, and he is the one who is guided, whose guidance is established and firmly rooted.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 158 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah. So whoever performs the Hajj to the House or the 'umrah, there is no blame upon him for going around between them. And whoever volunteers good, indeed Allah is Appreciative and Knowing.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what We have sent down of clear proofs and guidance, after We have made it clear for the people in the Book, those are cursed by Allah, and cursed by those who curse.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 159] ﴿Except for those who repent, make amends, and make things clear. Those I accept their repentance, and I am the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 160] ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers, upon them is the curse of Allah, and of the angels, and of mankind, all together.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 161] ﴿Abiding therein; the punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be reprieved.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 162] ﴿And your God is One God; there is no god but He, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 163] ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, the alternation of night and day, the ship that sails in the sea with what benefits people, the water that Allah sends down from the sky, giving life thereby to the earth after its death and scattering therein every kind of creature, the changing of the winds, and the clouds subjected between the sky and the earth, are indeed signs for a people who reason.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164] ﴿And among the people are those who take rivals besides Allah, loving them as they love Allah. But those who believe are stronger in love for Allah. If only those who did wrong could see, when they behold the punishment, that power belongs entirely to Allah, and that Allah is severe in punishment.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 165] ﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed, and they see the punishment, and their bonds are cut off.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 166] ﴿And those who followed say: "If only we had another return, we would disown them as they have disowned us." Thus Allah shows them their deeds as regrets upon them, and they will not come out of the Fire.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 167].

(p. 454) **al-Safa**: its alif (ألف) is changed from a waw, as shown by their saying ṣafwān, and it is derived from al-ṣafw, which means "the pure, the unmixed." It was also said: it is a generic noun (ism jins), differentiated from its singular by the feminine ending (tā' al-ta'nīth), and its singular is ṣafāh. It was also said: it is a singular noun that forms its plural on the patterns fu'ūl and af'āl; they said ṣafiyy and aṣfā', like qafiyy and aqfā'. The ṣād may be pronounced with ḍamm or kasrah in the pattern fu'ūl, as in ʿiṣiyy, and it means the smooth stone. It was also said: the stone not mixed with anything else, such as mud or dust attached to it, and this is what the derivation indicates. It was also said: it is a large rock.

**al-Marwah**: the singular of al-marw, which is a generic noun. The poet said:

*"You see the marw when she sweeps it aside with her hands, like a moth fluttering."*

They also said marawāt as the plural of marwah, and this is the regular sound plural of marwah. It is small stones in which there is softness. It was also said: hard stones. It was also said: small stones with sharp edges. It was also said: black stones. It was also said: white stones. It was also said: hard white stones.

In the verse, al-Safa and al-Marwah are proper names for two known hills, and the definite article (al-) has become fixed in them through dominance (al-ghalabah), just as it is in al-Bayt for the Kaʿbah, and al-Najm for al-Thurayyā.

**al-Sha'a'ir**: the plural of sha'īrah or sha'ārah. Al-Harawī said: "I heard al-Azhari say: they are the signs that Allah has urged people toward and commanded them to uphold." Al-Zajjaj said: "Everything that is a station (mawqif), a place of witness (mashhad), a place of running (mas'a), or a place of slaughter (madhbah)." This root, sh-ʿ-r, has been discussed before, meaning "to perceive and to know." The Arabs say: "Our house is a shi'ar," meaning a sign, and from it comes ish'ār al-hady (marking the sacrificial animal).

**al-Hajj**: intending (al-qaṣd) repeatedly. The reciter said:

*"Truly a monk goes on pilgrimage to Jerusalem, in a wrap, a cloak, and a hooded cape."*

**al-I'timar**: visiting. It was also said: intending. Then al-Hajj and al-ʿUmrah became fixed names for intending the House and visiting it for the two known rites. In meaning, they are like al-Bayt and al-Najm in reference. These two roots have been discussed before, in yuḥājjūkum and in yaʿmuru.

**al-Junah**: inclining toward sin, then it was applied to sin itself. One says: janaḥa ilā kadhā junūḥan, meaning he inclined. From it comes junḥ al-layl, its inclining with its darkness, and janāḥ al-ṭā'ir, the bird's wing.

**Tatawwa'a**: tafa''ala from al-ṭawʿ, which is submission.

**Al-layl**: it was said to be a generic noun, like tamrah and tamr. The correct view is that it is a singular noun, and no plural for al-layl is known. Whoever thought that al-layāl (nights) is the plural of al-layl was mistaken; rather, al-layālī is the plural of laylah, and it is an irregular plural. Its parallel is kaykah and al-kayākī, and kaykah means an egg. As if they imagined that the two were laylāh and kaykāh. This imagined form is indicated by their diminutive of laylah: luyayylah. They have also explicitly used laylāh in poetry. The poet said:

*"Every day and every night."*

It is possible that this alif is an extension of vowel (ishbā'), like in:

*"I seek refuge in Allah from the scorpion."*

Ibn Fāris said: some birds are called layl, and it is said that it is the young of the bustard (ḥubārā).

As for **al-nahār**: its plural is nahr and anhirah, like qadhal and aqdhilah, and both are regular plurals for it. It was also said: al-nahār is a singular that has no plural, because it is like a verbal noun (maṣdar), as you say: al-ḍiyā' (light) applies to the little and the much. This is not correct. The poet said:

*"Were it not for the two sops, we would have perished from the lean ones; a sop of night and a sop of day."*

It is said: a man is nahr if he works during the day, and there is in it the meaning of a relative adjective (nisbah). They said: the day is from the rising of dawn to the setting of the sun. The Prophet (ﷺ) indicated this when he said to ʿAdī: "It is only the whiteness of the day and the blackness of the night," meaning in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread at dawn﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187]. The apparent meaning in the language is that it begins from the time of brightening (al-isfār). Al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl said: the beginning of the day is usually the rising of the sun. Al-Naḍr added: what comes before that is not counted as day. Al-Zajjaj said, in (the books on the star-risings, kutub al-anwā'): the beginning of the day is the first light of the sun, and he cited the saying of Umayyah ibn Abī al-Ṣalt:

*"The sun rises every other night, red, its color turning rosy."*

ʿAdī ibn Zayd said:

*"And the one who makes the sun a clear boundary, without doubt, separating day from night."*

Al-miṣr means a cut. Al-Kisā'ī recited:

*"When the sun of day rises, it is a sign of my farewell to you, so bid me farewell."*

Ibn al-Anbārī said: from the rising of the sun to its setting is day, and from dawn to its rising is shared between night and day. The root nahara has been discussed before in the saying: (rivers flow beneath them).

**Al-Fulk**: ships. It can be singular and plural. They claimed that its vowels in the plural are not its vowels in the singular, and when it is used in the singular it is dualized: falakān. It was also said: when it is meant as a plural, it is an ism jam' (collective noun). What we hold is that it is a word shared between the singular and the plural, and its vowels in the plural are its vowels in the singular, and they are not to be estimated otherwise. When it is singular, it is masculine, as He said: ﴿in the laden ship﴾ [al-Shu'arā': 119]. They also said that it is feminine like the feminine singular, and he said: ﴿and the ship that runs﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164]. There is no proof in this, since here it is used as a plural, and it is feminine of a plural, and a plural is described by allatī, just as a feminine is described by it. It was also said: the singular of al-fulk is falak, like usd and asad, and its origin is rotation (al-dawarān). From it comes falak al-samā', the sphere in which the stars revolve, and falakat al-mighzal (the whorl of the spindle), and falakat al-jāriyah, meaning the roundness of her breast.

**Baththa**: spread, scattered, and made apparent. The poet said:

*"And on the earth, scattered, is a snake and a scorpion."*

Its present form is yabuththu, according to the regular pattern for every triliteral doubled transitive verb: that it is yafʿulu, except what is anomalous.

**Al-dābbah**: a name for every living animal. The view of those who excluded birds from it is rejected by the verse of ʿAlqamah:

*"As if a cloud had struck them, its thunderbolts for their birds were a crawling."*

Al-A'shā says:

*"The crawling of the sand-grouse in the valley, at every watering place."*

Its verb is dabba yadibbu. This is its regular pattern, because it is intransitive. It is also heard as yadubbu, with ḍamm on the middle radical. The hāʾ in al-dābbah is for the feminine, either to mean the very individual creature, or for emphasis, because this action occurs frequently. It is used for male and female alike.

**Al-taṣrīf**: a verbal noun of ṣarafa, and its meaning goes back to turning (al-ṣarf), which is returning. I turned Zayd away from such-and-such: I returned him.

**Al-riyāḥ**: the plural of rīḥ, a broken plural. Its waw is a waw, because it is from rāḥa yarūḥu. It was changed to yāʾ because of the kasrah before it. When the cause of the change disappeared, which is the kasrah, the waw appeared again. They said arwāḥ, like the plural of rūḥ. The poet said:

*"The winds have passed over them every evening, and nothing remains but the trace of a piled-up stone enclosure."*

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: ʿUmārah ibn ʿAqīl ibn Bilāl ibn Jarīr made a grammatical error in this word; he used al-aryāḥ in his poetry, and he erred in that. Abū Ḥātim said: al-aryāḥ is not permissible. ʿUmārah said to him: "Have you not heard their saying: riyāḥ?" Abū Ḥātim said to him: "This is different from that." He said: "You are right," and he retracted. End of quotation. But in my memory from long ago, al-aryāḥ came in the poetry of some eloquent Arabs whose speech is cited as evidence. It is as if they built it on the singular, even though the cause of the change (ʿillat al-qalb) is absent in the plural, as they said: ʿīd and aʿyād. This is from al-ʿawd (return), but since it always takes the substituted letter, it treated it like an original radical.

**Al-saḥāb**: a generic noun, its singular is saḥābah. It was so named because it drags along (yansaḥibu). It is also called ḥabā, because it moves gently (yaḥbū). This was said by Abū ʿAlī.

**Al-taskhīr**: is making something subdued and placing it under obedience. Al-Rāghib said: al-taskhīr is compulsion upon an action, and it is stronger than coercion (al-ikrāh).

**Al-ḥubb**: a verbal noun of ḥabba yaḥibbu. The regular present form is yuḥibbu with ḍamm, because it is from a doubled transitive verb. The regular verbal noun is al-ḥabb with a fatḥah on the ḥāʾ. It is said: aḥabba, meaning the same as ḥabba, and it is more common than it. Maḥbūb is more common than muḥibb, and muḥibb is more common than ḥābb. The plural of al-ḥubb has come because of the variety of its kinds. The poet said:

*"Three kinds of loves: the love of attachment, the love of stinginess, and a love which is killing."*

Al-ḥubb is also a vessel in which water is placed.

**Al-jamīʿ**: fa'īl from al-jamʿ (gathering). It is as if it were an ism jam', and therefore it is sometimes followed by the singular: ﴿We are a united group, victorious﴾ [al-Qamar: 44], and sometimes by the plural: ﴿all of them brought before Us﴾ [Yā-Sīn: 32]. It is put in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier: zayd and ʿamr came together (jamīʿan). It is used for emphasis in the sense of "all of them": the people came, all of them (jamīʿuhum), meaning all of them. It does not indicate togetherness in time; it only indicates inclusion in the attribution of the action.

**Tabarra'a**: tafa''ala, from their saying: "I am free of religion" (bari'tu min al-dīn). Barā'ah means purity, separation, and distance.

**Taqaṭṭaʿa**: tafa''ala from al-qaṭʿ (cutting), which is well known.

**Al-asbāb**: plural of sabab, which is the means of reaching a place or a need, by way of a link, or affection, or other than that. It was said: al-asbāb may also apply to events (ḥawādith). The poet said:

*"Whoever fears the causes of death will meet it, even if he tries to reach the causes of the heavens with a ladder."*
