The origin of sabab is a rope. It was said: it is what one climbs with. It was said: the connecting tie.

**Al-karrah**: return to the state in which one was. The verb is karra yakirru karran. The poet said:

*"I charge against the battalion, not caring whether my death is in it or in something else."*

**Al-ḥasrah**: intense regret. It is the pain of the heart at the loss of what it hoped for.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 158 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah﴾. The occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul): the Ansar used to perform the Hajj for Manat, and Manat was a idol of clay and iron. They felt uneasy (yataharrajun) about circumambulating between al-Safa and al-Marwah. When Islam came, they asked about it, and this verse was revealed. This occasion of revelation is related in the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others. Various opinions have been mentioned regarding the uneasiness about going around between them.

(And the connection (munasabah) of this verse with what precedes it): when Allah the Exalted praised those who are patient, and Hajj is among the arduous acts that consume wealth and body, and it is one of the pillars of Islam, it was appropriate to mention it after that. As we mentioned, al-Safa and al-Marwah are said to be proper names (a'lam) for these two mountains, and proper names are not considered for grammatical masculinity or femininity of the word; do you not see the saying: Talhah and Hind? It has been transmitted that some people said: al-Safa is masculine because Adam stood upon it, and al-Marwah is feminine because Eve stood upon it. Al-Sha'bi said: on al-Safa there was an idol called Isaf, and on al-Marwah there was an idol called Na'ilah. Thus the masculine and feminine pattern was consistent, and the masculine was given precedence. Ibn Atiyyah related both opinions, and said: were it not that this has been recorded in a book, I would not have mentioned it. Some of the Sufis and some of the People of the House have statements transmitted from them about al-Safa and al-Marwah, which we have preferred to refrain from mentioning.

The two mountains themselves are not, in their essence, among the symbols of Allah; rather, this is by omission of a modifier (hadhf mudaf), i.e., the circumambulation of al-Safa and al-Marwah. And the meaning of "among the symbols of Allah" is: its markers (ma'alimihi). If we say the meaning of "among the symbols of Allah" is "among the places of His worship," then there is no need to omit a modifier in the first case; rather, that would be in the genitive case. Since circumambulating between them is not an independent act of worship, and it becomes an act of worship only when it is part of Hajj or Umrah, Allah the Exalted clarified this by His saying: ﴿So whoever performs Hajj to the House or performs Umrah﴾, and "man" here is conditional.

﴿there is no blame upon him for going around between them﴾. The majority read: an yattawwafa. Anas, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Sirin and Shahr read: an la, and likewise it is in the codices of Ubayy and Abdullah, and this is explained as an extra la, as in: "What prevented you from not prostrating?" and the saying of the poet:
"I do not blame the fair ones for not being tamed when they see the white-haired, shriveled old man."
Thus the meanings of the two readings coincide, and this does not necessarily follow; because lifting blame from doing a thing is lifting blame from leaving it, since it is an option between doing and not doing, as in the Exalted saying: ﴿there is no blame upon them both if they return to one another﴾ [al-Baqarah: 230]. Accordingly, la remains in its original function of negation, and the majority's reading explicitly lifts blame from performing the circumambulation, while this reading explicitly lifts blame from leaving it; both readings indicate choice between doing and not doing. Therefore circumambulating between them is not obligatory. This is related from Ibn Abbas, Anas, Ibn al-Zubayr, Ata', Mujahid, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal, according to what Abu Talib transmitted from him, and that there is no penalty upon one who leaves it, whether intentionally or forgetfully, though one should not leave it. As for those who hold that it is a pillar, like al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Malik in his well-known school, or an obligatory act that is compensated by a sacrifice, like al-Thawri and Abu Hanifah, or that if one leaves more than three rounds, a sacrifice is due, and if three or fewer, then for each round the feeding of a poor person, as in some narrations of Abu Hanifah, they require a clear text that abrogates this Qur'anic text.

As for the saying of Aisha to Urwah when he said to her: "Have you considered the saying of Allah: ﴿there is no blame upon him for going around between them﴾? So we see no obligation upon anyone?" She said: "O nephew, no! Had it been so, it would have said: 'there is no blame upon him that he not go around between them.'" This statement does not take the wording out of what it indicates regarding lifting sin from the one who circumambulates between them, and this does not indicate the obligation of the circumambulation; because what the wording indicates is the permissibility of the act, and when it is permissible you are free between doing it and leaving it. The apparent sense of this circumambulation is that it should be between al-Safa and al-Marwah; so whoever runs between them without ascending upon them is not considered to have circumambulated. The verse indicates the general circumambulation, not a particular manner or number. The scholars of the regions agreed that ramal during the sa'y is a Sunnah. Ata' related from Ibn Abbas: whoever wishes may run in the valley's course of Makkah, and whoever wishes need not run; he meant only ramal in the bottom of the valley. Umar used to walk between al-Safa and al-Marwah and said: if I walk, I have seen the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) walk, and if I run, I have seen the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) run. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ran between them to show the polytheists his strength. It is possible that the ruling ceases with the cessation of its cause, and it is possible that its legislation is perpetual even if the cause has ceased. Riding during the sa'y between them is disliked according to Abu Hanifah and his companions, and riding during the sa'y is not permitted according to Malik, nor during the circumambulation of the House, except for an excuse, and in that case there is a sacrifice upon him. If one circumambulates while riding without an excuse, he repeats it if he is near the House, and otherwise sends a sacrifice. Umm Salamah complained to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "Circumambulate behind the people while you are riding." This hadith does not state that he ordered her to offer a sacrifice. Some scholars made a distinction and said: if one circumambulates on the back of a camel it suffices, but if on the back of a person it does not suffice.

That the pronoun is dual in His saying "bihima" (with them both) does not indicate starting with al-Safa; rather the apparent meaning is that if one begins the sa'y with al-Marwah, it suffices. The legislation of the sa'y, according to the consensus of all scholars, is to begin with al-Safa. If one begins with al-Marwah, the position of Malik and the well-known position of Abu Hanifah is that this round is nullified, and if he does not repeat it, it does not suffice him. It is also related from Abu Hanifah: if he does not nullify it, there is nothing upon him; he treated it as the order in the parts of wudu'.

The majority read "yattawwafa," whose origin is yatatawwafu, and in the past tense its origin was tatawwafa, then the ta' was assimilated into the ta', so a hamzat al-wasl had to be introduced, because what is assimilated into something must be vowelled at rest, so it became ittawwafa; its present form came as yattawwafu, and the hamzat al-wasl was dropped to secure the assimilated letter with the letter of the present tense. Abu Hamzah read: an yatuwwafa bihima, from taafa yatuwfu, and this is an evident reading. Ibn Abbas and Abu al-Sammal read: yutafu bihima, and its origin is yattawifu, yaftaʻilu, and its past is ittawafa (iftaʻala); the waw moved and what preceded it was open, so it changed to an alif, and the ta' was assimilated into the ta' after the ta' changed to a ta', as they did in ittalaba, so he is muttalib; it became ittafa, and its present became yattafu, as yattalibu came. The verbal noun of ittawwafa is ittiwafan, and the verbal noun of ittafa is ittiyafan; the waw returned to its origin because the cause of its alteration had ceased, then it changed to a ya' because of the kasrah before it, as they said: i'tadda i'tiyadan.

The original of "an yattawwafa," in "an yattawwafa," means: there is no sin upon him in circumambulating between them; so the letter was deleted together with "an," and deletion with it is analogical when there is no ambiguity, and in it lies the earlier disagreement: is its position after the deletion genitive or accusative? Some who do not have good knowledge of grammar permitted that "an yattawwafa" be in a nominative position, as a predicate also, the estimate being: "there is no blame: the circumambulation between them," and that it be in an accusative position as a circumstantial clause, the estimate being: "there is no blame upon him in the state of his circumambulating between them," and he said: the governing element of the circumstantial clause is the governing element of the genitive, and it is a circumstantial clause of the ha' in 'alayhi. These two opinions are untenable, and were it not for their being recorded in some books of tafsir, I would not have mentioned them.

﴿And whoever volunteers good﴾: al-tatawwu' is what you undertake of your own accord from what is not obligatory upon you; do you not see his saying in the hadith of Dimam: "Is there anything else obligatory upon me?" He said: "No, unless you volunteer," meaning you give voluntarily. This is the apparent meaning, so the intended sense is voluntary giving of any act of obedience, and this is the saying of al-Hasan; or it is supererogatory performance (al-nafl) upon the obligatory circumambulation, said by Mujahid; or it is Umrah, said by Ibn Zayd; or it is Hajj and Umrah after fulfilling what is obligatory upon him; or it is the sa'y between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and this is the view of one who dropped the obligation of the sa'y, since he understood permissibility in circumambulating between them from His saying: ﴿there is no blame upon him for going around between them﴾, and took this to mean circumambulating between them, as if it were said: and whoever volunteers to circumambulate between them, or to run in the second Hajj which is not obligatory. There are six opinions.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu Amr, Asim and Ibn Amir read "tatawwa'a" as a past verb here, and in His saying: ﴿And whoever volunteers good, it is better for him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184]; it may be understood as meaning "the one who," and it may be conditional. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "yatawwa'" as a jussive present after the conditional "man"; Zayd and Ruways agreed with them in the first of these. The accusative of "khayran" is as an object after the omission of the preposition, i.e., "with good," and this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, who read: "yatatawwa'u bikhayrin." "Yattawwa'" originally is "yatatawwa'," as in the reading of Abdullah, and it was assimilated. They permitted making "khayran" an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, i.e., "and whoever volunteers a good volunteering."

﴿Indeed Allah is Appreciative, All-Knowing﴾: this sentence is the answer of the conditional. And when "man" is a relative pronoun, in the possibility of one of the two aspects of "man" in the reading of one who reads "tatawwa'a" as a past verb, then it is a sentence in the place of the predicate of the subject, because "tatawwa'a" then is a relative clause. Allah's appreciation of His servant is in one of two meanings: either by reward, or by praise. His knowledge here is His knowledge of the measure of the recompense which the servant has for performing the obedience, or of his intention and sincerity in the deed. The two attributes have come here in a fine position, because volunteering good includes the act and the intention, so mention of appreciation corresponds to the act, and mention of knowledge corresponds to the intention; and the attribute of knowledge was placed later, though it precedes, before appreciation, just as the intention precedes the act, for the harmony of the verse-endings (ra'us al-ayy).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 159–160:

﴿Indeed, those who conceal what We sent down of clear proofs and guidance﴾: The verse was revealed concerning the People of the Book and their concealment of the verse of stoning and the matter of the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn ʿAbbas mentioned that Muʿadh asked the Jews about what was in the Torah concerning the mention of the Prophet ﷺ, and they concealed it from him, so God revealed this verse. Those who conceal are the rabbis of the Jews and the scholars of the Christians; most of the exegetes hold this view, and the rabbis of the Jews include Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf, Kaʿb ibn Asad, Ibn Suriya, and Zayd ibn al-Tabut. "What We sent down" contains a shift from the third person to the first person (plural speaker). "Clear proofs" (al-bayyinat) are the arguments indicating his prophethood ﷺ. "And guidance" (al-huda) is the command to follow him, or "clear proofs and guidance" are one and the same, and combining them is for emphasis; it is that which made clear his prophethood and guided to following him. Or "clear proofs" are stoning, the penal provisions, and all the other rulings, while "guidance" is the matter of Muhammad ﷺ, his description, and following him. The word "min" (from) is linked to an omitted element, because it is in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning: existing from among the clear proofs and guidance.

﴿After We had made it clear to the people in the Book﴾: The pronoun in the accusative in bayyanahu refers back to the relative pronoun which is "what We sent down," and the relative pronoun's referent is omitted, meaning: what We sent down. The majority read "bayyanahu," agreeing with His saying "We sent down." Talha ibn Musarrif read "bayyanahu," making it a third-person singular masculine pronoun, which is an iltifat (shift) from first-person pronoun to third-person pronoun. The word "the people" here means the People of the Book, and "the Book" means the Torah and the Gospel. It has also been said: "the people" are the community of Muhammad ﷺ, and "the Book" is the Qur'an. The preferable and more evident view is that the verse is general in its reference to the concealers, to "the people," and to "the Book." Although it was revealed on a specific occasion, it encompasses every person who conceals a piece of knowledge of God's religion that needs to be disseminated and spread. This is explained by his saying ﷺ: "Whoever is asked about a piece of knowledge and conceals it will be bridled on the Day of Resurrection with a bridle of fire," and this applies when he does not fear for himself in spreading it. The Companions understood this verse as general, and they were eloquent Arabs, to whom recourse is had in understanding the Qur'an, as is related from ʿUthman, Abu Hurayra, and others: "Were it not for a verse in the Book of God, I would not have narrated to you." Abu Hurayra refrained from narrating some matters for which he feared, saying: "If I were to disseminate it, this throat would be cut." The apparent meaning of the verse is that the one who conceals what God has sent down deserves the curse, even if he is not asked about it; rather, teaching and clarification are obligatory even if they do not ask: "And when God took the covenant of those given the Book: you shall make it clear to the people and not conceal it" [Al ʿImran: 187]. The Imam Abu Muhammad ʿAli ibn Ahmad ibn Hazm al-Qurtubi said, as heard from him by Abu ʿAbd Allah Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr al-Humaydi, the memorizer (al-Hafiz): The portion of one who prefers knowledge and recognizes its excellence is that he should exert his effort in employing it, teach it according to his capacity, and verify it as much as he can. Indeed, even if he were able to proclaim it at the crossroads of passersby, call to it in the thoroughfare of travelers, and announce it in the gatherings of the caravans, and even if he were able to give money to its students, pay wages to those who seek from it, honor the rewards for those who search after it, and arrange the ranks of its people, patiently enduring hardship and harm in this, that would be a great portion, a good deed, a noble felicity, and a revival of knowledge; otherwise it will be effaced, obliterated, and nothing will remain of it but subtle traces and scattered signs. End of his words.

﴿Those—God curses them, and those who curse curse them﴾: This sentence is the predicate of "inna." They deserve this terrible matter, the curse of God and the curse of those who curse, for this great sin, which is the concealment of what God the Exalted sent down, and He had made it clear and explained it to the people such that no confusion occurs in it; yet they deliberately concealed this clear and manifest matter, and thereby deserved this punishment. The demonstrative "those" (ulaʾika), the distal demonstrative, was used to draw attention to that ugly attribute, and the predicate was presented in the form of two sentences for emphasis and magnification. The verb in the present tense was used, which implies renewal, because its cause is renewed. This is also His saying the Exalted: "Indeed, those who conceal," where the relative clause "those who" is a present-tense verb, likewise to indicate renewal, since their continuing in concealment is a renewal of concealment. The sentence in which the verb is attributed to God was used because He is the one who recompenses for the sin they committed. The second sentence came because the curse of those who curse follows upon God's curse on the concealers. The name of God was made explicit as "God" by way of iltifat (shift), for if it had followed the pattern of the preceding speech, it would have been "those—He curses them," but the explicit mention of this name carries a majesty not found in a pronoun. "Those who curse" means everyone from whom cursing can proceed: they are the angels and the believers of the two species (humans and jinn); this was said by al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas. Or everything among animals and inanimate things other than the two species, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Bara ibn ʿAzib: when he is placed in his grave and is punished, and he cries out, since everything hears it except the two species. Or the beasts and creeping things, said by Mujahid and ʿIkrima, and this is because of the drought that befalls them on account of the sins of the evil scholars who conceal. Or those who drive them away to the Fire when they drive them toward it, because cursing is driving away. Or the angels; said by Qatada. Or those who curse one another: when none of them deserves the curse, it turns toward the Jews; said by Ibn Masʿud. The more evident view is the first. Whoever applies "those who curse" to what does not reason treats it as one that reasons, since the curse proceeds from it, and cursing is the act of one who reasons; this is indicated by the plural with the waw and nun. In His saying "and those who curse curse them" there is a type of rhetorical ornament called the distinct paronomasia (al-tajnis al-mughayir), which is when one of the two words is a noun and the other a verb.

(Except those who repent): This is an exception of the contiguous kind. "Repented" means turning from disbelief to Islam, or from concealment to disclosure. (And amend) what they corrupted of their hearts by mixing disbelief into them, or what they corrupted of their states with God, or they amend their people by guiding them to Islam after misguiding them. (And make clear): that is, the truth they concealed, or the sincerity of their repentance by breaking the wine jars and pouring them out, or what is in the Torah and the Gospel concerning the description of Muhammad ﷺ, or they acknowledged their deception and falsehood, or what they newly did of their repentance, so that they may erase the evil of disbelief from them and be known by the opposite of what they were known for, and so that others of the corrupters may follow them. (Then those): a reference to those who combined these attributes of repentance, amendment, and clarification.

﴿I turn back to them﴾: that is, I incline toward them, and whoever God turns to is not touched by the curse.

﴿And I am the Ever-Relenting, the Most Merciful﴾: The discussion of these two attributes has preceded, and He concluded with them as an encouragement to repentance and an indication that these two attributes are His; whoever returns to Him, He inclines toward him and shows him mercy.

They have mentioned in this verse a number of rulings, among them: concealing knowledge is forbidden, meaning the knowledge of the Sharia, on the basis of His saying "of the clear proofs," and on condition that the teacher does not fear for himself and that he is specifically designated for it. If it is not from the matters of the sacred law, there is no blame in withholding it. It is related from ʿAbd Allah that he said: "You are not one who speaks to a people with a saying their minds cannot reach without it becoming a trial for some of them." It is also related from him ﷺ that he said: "Speak to people in what they understand; do you love that God and His Messenger be denied?" They said: What is explicitly stated in the sacred law and what is derived from it in ruling are equal. If he fears for himself, he is not obligated, as Abu Hurayra did; and if it is not specifically obligatory for him, the same applies, so long as he is not asked, whereupon it becomes specifically obligatory for him. Among them: the prohibition of taking a wage for teaching knowledge, though some scholars have permitted it. Among them: a disbeliever may not be taught the Qur'an until he becomes Muslim, nor may an opponent's evidence be taught against his opponent so as to seize his property by it, nor may a ruler be taught an interpretation by which he reaches the hardships of the subjects, nor may dispensations be taught when it is known that they will be made a path to committing forbidden acts and abandoning obligatory duties. Among them: the obligation to accept the report of a single transmitter, since clarification is obligatory on him only if acceptance of his word has also become obligatory for them, because his word "of the clear proofs and guidance" encompasses both the explicit and the derived. Among them: the permissibility of cursing one who died a disbeliever. Some of the early scholars said: there is no benefit in cursing one of the disbelievers who has died or gone insane; the majority of scholars hold that cursing disbelievers in general, without specification, is permissible, and some have held it obligatory. As for a specific disbeliever, the majority of scholars hold that it is not permissible to curse him, though the Messenger of God ﷺ cursed certain people by name. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: "The correct view in my opinion is the permissibility of cursing him." Ibn al-ʿArabi also reported a consensus that it is not permissible to curse a Muslim who disobeys or openly commits major sins; some scholars mentioned a difference of opinion on this, and some made a distinction, permitting it before the prescribed punishment is carried out against him. Among them: the repentance that is legally valid is for the repentant to manifest the opposite of what he was upon formerly: if he was an apostate, by returning to Islam and manifesting its laws; if a sinner, by returning to righteous action and avoiding the people of corruption. As for repentance by the tongue alone, or repentance from a single sin, that is not repentance. The discussion of repentance has been treated at length earlier.

This is also His saying the Exalted: "Indeed, those who conceal," where the relative clause "those who" is a present-tense verb, likewise to indicate renewal, since their continuing in concealment is a renewal of concealment. The sentence in which the verb is attributed to God was used because He is the one who recompenses for the sin they committed. The second sentence came because the curse of those who curse follows upon God's curse on the concealers. The name of God was made explicit as "God" by way of iltifat (shift), for if it had followed the pattern of the preceding speech, it would have been "those—He curses them," but the explicit mention of this name carries a majesty not found in a pronoun. "Those who curse" means everyone from whom cursing can proceed: they are the angels and the believers of the two species (humans and jinn); this was said by al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas. Or everything among animals and inanimate things other than the two species, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Bara ibn ʿAzib: when he is placed in his grave and is punished, and he cries out, since everything hears it except the two species. Or the beasts and creeping things, said by Mujahid and ʿIkrima, and this is because of the drought that befalls them on account of the sins of the evil scholars who conceal. Or those who drive them away to the Fire when they drive them toward it, because cursing is driving away. Or the angels; said by Qatada. Or those who curse one another: when none of them deserves the curse, it turns toward the Jews; said by Ibn Masʿud. The more evident view is the first. Whoever applies "those who curse" to what does not reason treats it as one that reasons, since the curse proceeds from it, and cursing is the act of one who reasons; this is indicated by the plural with the waw and nun. In His saying "and those who curse curse them" there is a type of rhetorical ornament called the distinct paronomasia (al-tajnis al-mughayir), which is when one of the two words is a noun and the other a verb.

(Except those who repent): This is an exception of the contiguous kind. "Repented" means turning from disbelief to Islam, or from concealment to disclosure. (And amend) what they corrupted of their hearts by mixing disbelief into them, or what they corrupted of their states with God, or they amend their people by guiding them to Islam after misguiding them. (And make clear): that is, the truth they concealed, or the sincerity of their repentance by breaking the wine jars and pouring them out, or what is in the Torah and the Gospel concerning the description of Muhammad ﷺ, or they acknowledged their deception and falsehood, or what they newly did of their repentance, so that they may erase the evil of disbelief from them and be known by the opposite of what they were known for, and so that others of the corrupters may follow them. (Then those): a reference to those who combined these attributes of repentance, amendment, and clarification.

﴿I turn back to them﴾: that is, I incline toward them, and whoever God turns to is not touched by the curse.

﴿And I am the Ever-Relenting, the Most Merciful﴾: The discussion of these two attributes has preceded, and He concluded with them as an encouragement to repentance and an indication that these two attributes are His; whoever returns to Him, He inclines toward him and shows him mercy.

They have mentioned in this verse a number of rulings, among them: concealing knowledge is forbidden, meaning the knowledge of the Sharia, on the basis of His saying "of the clear proofs," and on condition that the teacher does not fear for himself and that he is specifically designated for it. If it is not from the matters of the sacred law, there is no blame in withholding it. It is related from ʿAbd Allah that he said: "You are not one who speaks to a people with a saying their minds cannot reach without it becoming a trial for some of them." It is also related from him ﷺ that he said: "Speak to people in what they understand; do you love that God and His Messenger be denied?" They said: What is explicitly stated in the sacred law and what is derived from it in ruling are equal. If he fears for himself, he is not obligated, as Abu Hurayra did; and if it is not specifically obligatory for him, the same applies, so long as he is not asked, whereupon it becomes specifically obligatory for him. Among them: the prohibition of taking a wage for teaching knowledge, though some scholars have permitted it. Among them: a disbeliever may not be taught the Qur'an until he becomes Muslim, nor may an opponent's evidence be taught against his opponent so as to seize his property by it, nor may a ruler be taught an interpretation by which he reaches the hardships of the subjects, nor may dispensations be taught when it is known that they will be made a path to committing forbidden acts and abandoning obligatory duties. Among them: the obligation to accept the report of a single transmitter, since clarification is obligatory on him only if acceptance of his word has also become obligatory for them, because his word "of the clear proofs and guidance" encompasses both the explicit and the derived. Among them: the permissibility of cursing one who died a disbeliever. Some of the early scholars said: there is no benefit in cursing one of the disbelievers who has died or gone insane; the majority of scholars hold that cursing disbelievers in general, without specification, is permissible, and some have held it obligatory. As for a specific disbeliever, the majority of scholars hold that it is not permissible to curse him, though the Messenger of God ﷺ cursed certain people by name. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: "The correct view in my opinion is the permissibility of cursing him." Ibn al-ʿArabi also reported a consensus that it is not permissible to curse a Muslim who disobeys or openly commits major sins; some scholars mentioned a difference of opinion on this, and some made a distinction, permitting it before the prescribed punishment is carried out against him. Among them: the repentance that is legally valid is for the repentant to manifest the opposite of what he was upon formerly: if he was an apostate, by returning to Islam and manifesting its laws; if a sinner, by returning to righteous action and avoiding the people of corruption. As for repentance by the tongue alone, or repentance from a single sin, that is not repentance. The discussion of repentance has been treated at length earlier.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 161–162:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved and died while they were disbelievers — upon them is the curse of Allah﴾: When He mentioned the state of those who concealed knowledge and the state of those who repented, He mentioned the state of those who died persisting in disbelief, and He intensified the curse by making it superior over them, as though it had enveloped and covered them, so they are beneath it. It is general to everyone who is in that state. Abu Muslim said: It is specific to those who conceal what Allah has sent down in the verse before it, because He mentioned the state of the concealers, then the state of the repentant, then the state of those who died without repenting from among them. Also, because He mentioned that the concealers are cursed in this world during their lifetime, He mentioned that they are also cursed after death. The clause "and they were disbelievers" (وهم كفار) is a circumstantial clause (جملة حالية), and the waw of circumstance (واو الحال) in such a clause, its being stated is more eloquent than its being omitted, unlike the one who considered its omission anomalous, namely al-Farra', and az-Zamakhshari followed him. The explanation of that is in the science of grammar (ʿilm al-nahw). The clause "upon them is the curse of Allah" (عليهم لعنة الله) is the predicate of inna, and "the curse of Allah" (لعنة الله) is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is "upon them" (عليهم). The clause "upon them is the curse of Allah" is a predicate concerning "those" (أولئك). It is better for "the curse" (لعنة) to be a subject (فاعل) of the preceding prepositional phrase, because it has relied on being in a position of a predicate, so what follows it is raised as a subject; thus you have given information about "those" with a single noun, unlike the first parsing, where you gave information about it with a clause.

The majority (الجمهور) read: ﴿والملائكة والناس أجمعين﴾, in the genitive, as a conjunction with the name of Allah. Al-Hasan read: "والملائكةُ والناسُ أجمعونَ", in the nominative. All of those whose words on this we have found among the grammarians and exegetes explained this reading as being conjoined to the place (موضع) of the name of Allah, because it is in a place of nominative as a verbal noun (مصدر), and they estimated it as: that Allah curses them, or that Allah should curse them.

What they permitted is not permissible according to what has been established regarding conjunction to the place, that its condition is that there be an operator (طالب) and that it secure the place without change. This is if we accept that "la'nah" here is among the verbal nouns that govern, and that it can be resolved into "an" and the verb. What appears is that this verbal noun does not resolve into "an" and the verb, because it is not intended for treatment. The meaning was: that the curse established from Allah upon the disbelievers is upon them; it is attributed to Allah in the manner of specification, not in the manner of occurrence. An analogue of that: ﴿ألا لعنة الله على الظالمين﴾ [Hud: 18]; the meaning is not "Allah's cursing upon the wrongdoers," and their saying "له ذكاء الحكماء" (he has the intelligence of the wise). The meaning here is not occurrence, and the estimation of the two verbal nouns as resolved into "an" and the verb; rather it is in the sense of their saying: "له وجه وجه القمر" (he has a face like the moon's face), and "له شجاعة شجاعة الأسد" (he has courage like the courage of the lion), so you attributed the courage for specification and definition, not in the sense that the lion would be brave.

And even if we accept that this verbal noun, namely "la'nat Allah," is estimated with "an" and the verb, it is, as we have mentioned, without a securing of the place, because it has no operator. Do you not see that if you raised the agent after mentioning the verbal noun, it would not be permissible unless you make the verbal noun indefinite with tanwin? Then the verbal noun has changed by its tanwin. For this reason Sibawayh took their saying "هذا ضارب زيد غدا وعمرا" to be by supposing a verb: i.e., "and he strikes ʿAmr," and it was not permissible to take it as conjoined to the place of Zayd, because there is no securing of the place. Do you not see that if you put Zayd in the accusative you would say "هذا ضارب زيدا" with tanwin? This too is on the assumption that the agent comes in the nominative after the tanwinated verbal noun; it is a matter of disagreement. The Basrans permit that, so they say: "عجبت من ضرب زيد عمرا" (I marvelled at Zayd's striking ʿAmr). Al-Farra' says: That is not permissible; rather, when the verbal noun is made indefinite, no nominative agent comes after it. The correct view is the view of al-Farra', and the Basrans have no proof for establishing their claim from transmitted usage; rather they established it by analogy with "an" and the verb. So the rejection of this interpretation that they mentioned is evident, because we say: We do not accept that it is a verbal noun that resolves into "an" and the verb, so that it would govern. Even if we grant that, we do not accept that the genitive noun after it has a place. Even if we grant that, we do not accept that conjunction to it is permissible.

This reading can be explained by ways other than the one they mentioned. The first of them: it is on the supposition of a verb, since conjunction was not possible; the estimate is: "and the angels curse them," just as Sibawayh explained "هذا ضارب زيد وعمرا" as being on the supposition of a verb: "and he strikes ʿAmr." The second: it is conjoined to "la'nat Allah" by omitting a genitive modifier (مضاف), i.e., "the curse of Allah and the curse of the angels," so when the modifier was omitted, the modified noun took the case of its own, as in ﴿واسأل القرية﴾ [Yusuf: 82]. The third: that it is a subject (مبتدأ) whose predicate is omitted for understanding of the meaning, i.e., "and the angels and the people, all of them, curse them." The apparent sense of "and the people, all of them" is generality. It was said that this will occur on the Day of Resurrection, when some of them curse others, and Allah, the angels and the believers curse them, so it became general; this is the view of Abu al-ʿAliyah. It was also said: by "the people" he meant those whose curse is counted, namely the believers only; this is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Qatadah, al-Rabi' and Muqatil. It was also said: the disbelievers curse themselves without realizing it, so they say in the world, "May Allah curse the disbeliever," and so generality is achieved by this consideration. He—exalted is He—began with Himself, and that is enough as expulsion and distancing.

﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that as a recompense from Allah? Whoever Allah has cursed﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 60]. So the curse of Allah is what draws the curse of the angels and the people. Do you not see the saying of one of the Companions: "What is wrong with me that I do not curse whom Allah has cursed upon the tongue of His Messenger?" And as is narrated from Ahmad, that his son asked him: "Does he curse," mentioning a specific person? He said to his son: "My son, have you ever seen me curse anything at all?" Then he said: "What is wrong with me that I should not curse whom Allah has cursed in His Book?" He said: I said: "Father, where is the curse of Allah?" He said: Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Ala la'nat Allah ʿala al-zalimin﴾ [Hud: 18]. Then He mentioned the angels second, because of the greatness of their status, the height of their rank and their purity in souls. Then He mentioned the people third, because they are of their kind, so it is harder for them; because the surprise of a like from one who claims likeness with what is hateful is more grievous, unlike such a thing coming from the higher ones.

(خالدين فيها): i.e., in the curse, and this is the apparent meaning, since nothing preceding in wording referring back to it except the curse. It was said: it refers to the Fire, which is implied by the meaning, and because of the frequency of what comes in the Qur'an, "abiding therein," which refers to the Fire, and because the curse indicates the Fire, since everyone whom Allah has cursed is in the Fire.

﴿The punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be reprieved﴾: The discussion of similar of these two clauses has already passed after His saying ﴿Those are the ones who bought the life of this world at the price of the Hereafter, so it will not be lightened﴾ [al-Baqarah: 86], the verse, so it suffices from repeating it here. Except that the clause "la yukhaffafu" (it will not be lightened) is in a position of accusative from the pronoun hidden in "khalidin," i.e., not lightened for them is the punishment. So it is an interlocking circumstantial clause (حال متداخلة), i.e., a circumstance of a circumstance, since "khalidin" is a circumstance of the pronoun in "ʿalayhim." Whoever permits the governing word to reach two circumstances for one possessor of circumstance permits the clause "la yukhaffafu" to be a circumstance of the pronoun in "ʿalayhim," and it is permissible that "la yukhaffafu" be a resumptive clause (جملة استئنافية), in which case it has no place in grammatical parsing. And at the end of the second clause there is: "wa la hum yunsarun" (nor will they be helped), which negates help from them; and here: "wa la hum yunzarun" (nor will they be reprieved), which negates respite, meaning the delay of punishment.
