Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 163:

﴿And your God is one God﴾ – to the end of the verse. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that it was revealed concerning the disbelievers of Quraysh, who said: "O Muhammad, describe your Lord for us and state His lineage," so the surah of al-Ikhlas and this verse were revealed. It is also related from him that there were, in the Kaʿbah, or around it, three hundred and sixty idols which they worshipped besides Allah, and then this was revealed. The apparent sense of the address is that it is addressed to all created beings capable of worship, and so it is an informing of them about the oneness of Allah, the Exalted. It may also be an address to those who said, "Describe your Lord for us and state His lineage," or an address to those who worship alongside Allah another deity, such as an idol, an image, or fire.

"Ilah" (god) is the predicate of "ilahukum" (your god), and "wahid" (one) is its attribute. In meaning, it is the predicate, because one may dispense with "ilah" (as a predicate) while it cannot be restricted to it. It is therefore like the qualifying circumstantial accusative (al-hal al-muwattiʾah), as in your saying: "I passed by Zayd, a righteous man." The "one" intended here denotes the negation of a like or equal, or the eternal being with whom nothing existed in pre-eternity, or the being who has no parts or components, or the one who is unique in deserving worship. These are four opinions, the first of which is the most evident. One says: "So-and-so is unique (wahid) in his age," meaning he has no equal or like; the meaning here is not "one" as the origin of number.

﴿There is no god but He﴾: this confirms the meaning of oneness and negates divinity from anything other than Him. It is a sentence that came to negate every individual of the gods, and then it restricted that meaning to Him, exalted is He. Thus the first verse establishes the attribute of oneness for Him, the Exalted, and the second establishes the restriction of divinity to Him from the explicit wording, even though the first verse implies that, since whoever has oneness has divinity.

The discussion of the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of the noun after "la" (no) in His saying "there is no doubt in it" has already passed. The predicate is omitted, and it is a substitute (badal) for the noun of "la" according to its position, and it cannot be a predicate, as is permitted in your saying: "Zayd is none but the one who is the scholar." This is because "la" does not govern definites. This holds if we take the view that the predicate after "la," by which the noun is made indeclinable, is raised by it. But if we take the view that the predicate is not raised by it, rather it is the predicate of the subject which is "la" with what is built with it, and this is the position of Sibawayh, then this also is not permitted, because it would entail making the subject indefinite and the predicate definite, which is the reverse of what is established in the Arabic language. The explanation of the substitution here is also problematic according to their saying that it is a substitute for "ilah," because it is not possible for it to be on the assumption of repeating the governing element: you do not say, "There is no man but Zayd." What appears to me is that it is not a substitute for "ilah," nor for "rajul" in your saying "there is no man but Zayd." Rather, it is a substitute for the pronoun concealed in the omitted predicate. So when we say "there is no man but Zayd," the implied sense is: "There is no man existing or present but Zayd." Just as you say: "No one stands but Zayd," where Zayd is a substitute for the pronoun in "stands," not for "one." On this basis, what occurs of this type is understood: it is not a substitute for the position of the noun of "la," but rather a substitute in the nominative from a nominative pronoun, which pronoun refers back to the noun of "la." Were it not for the grammarians' explicit statement that it is a substitute according to the position from the noun of "la," we would interpret their words as meaning by "a substitute from the noun of la" the pronoun referring back to the noun of "la." Some of them said: It has been mentioned that "huwa" is a substitute for "ilah" according to its place. He said: The accusative is not permitted here, because the nominative indicates reliance on the second element, and the meaning of the verse is according to that, whereas the accusative indicates that the reliance is on the first. End of his words.

There is no difference in meaning between "No people stood but Zayd" and "but Zayd" (in the accusative), in that Zayd is excepted in meaning. However, they distinguished them in terms of i'rab: they parsed what follows the preceding element as a substitute, and they parsed this as an accusative of exception. Yet agreement is preferable for verbal harmony, and the accusative is permissible, and we know of no disagreement about that.

In al-Muntakhab, he said: When the Exalted said, "And your God is one God," it was possible that someone would think: "Granted that our god is one, perhaps the god of others is different from ours." So he removed that illusion by stating absolute monotheism, saying: "There is no god but He." His saying "there is no god" requires comprehensive general negation, and when he adds after it "but Allah," it conveys complete, absolute, and established monotheism. It is not permissible that there be an omission in the speech, as the grammarians claim, the implied sense being "there is no god for us," or "in existence," but for Allah; because this does not conform to true monotheism. For if the omitted element is "for us," it would be monotheism of our god, not monotheism of the absolute god, and then there would be no distinction between His saying "And your God is one God" and His saying "There is no god but He," and that would be pure repetition, which is not permissible. And if the omitted element is "in existence," this would be a negation of the existence of a second god. However, if nothing is implied, it is a negation of the quiddity (mahiyyah) of a second god, and it is known that negation of quiddity is stronger in pure monotheism than negation of existence. So it is better to keep the speech on its apparent sense and to refrain from this implication. He placed the negation before the affirmation only for the purpose of establishing monotheism and negating partners and equals. End of the discussion.

Abu ʿAbd Allah Muhammad ibn Abi al-Fadl al-Mursi said in (Ray al-Zamʾan): These are the words of one who does not know the language of the Arabs. For "la ilaha" is in the position of the subject according to the view of Sibawayh, and according to others it is the noun of "la." In either case there must be a predicate for the subject or for "la," so what he said about dispensing with the implied element is invalid. As for his saying that if nothing is implied, it is a negation of quiddity, we say: negation of quiddity is negation of existence, because for us the negation of quiddity cannot be conceived except together with existence. So there is no difference in his view between "no quiddity" and "no existence." This is the position of the People of the Sunnah, unlike the Mu'tazilah (a theological school), who affirm quiddity as free from existence, and the evidence refutes that. End of his words. What he said about the necessity of implying a predicate for "la" is valid, because his saying "la ilaha" is a sentence, and as a sentence it must contain a predicated element and a predicated-of element. The predicated-of element is "ilah," and the predicate is the unrestricted existence (al-kawn al-mutlaq). For this reason its omission is allowed, just as it is allowed after their saying "Were it not for Zayd, I would have honored you," for its implied sense is "Were it not for Zayd existing," since it is a conditional sentence, or a conditional clause according to those who apply that term to it; so it must contain a predicated element and a predicated-of element. For this reason they related that the predicate after "la," when it is known, is frequently omitted according to the Hijazis, and its omission is obligatory according to the Tamimis. When the predicate is unrestricted existence, it is known, because when negation enters with the intention of general negation, what comes to mind immediately is negation of existence, since quiddity is not negated except by the negation of its existence. This differs from restricted existence, for the mind does not immediately settle on specifying it. Therefore its omission is not permitted, as in: "There is no man who enjoins good except Zayd," unless an external indication points to it, in which case it is known and its omission is then permitted.

(The Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate): He mentioned these two attributes as a reminder that worship is due to Him, because He who began you with mercy by creating you as a human being, sound and rational, and by nurturing you in the abode of this world, and who promised you the true promise of a good outcome in the Hereafter, is worthy of your worship, of standing at His command and prohibition, and by these two attributes He made you hopeful of the vastness of His mercy. This verse came after a verse that concludes with the curse and punishment for whoever dies without affirming His oneness, the Exalted. For it is the general pattern of the Qur'an that when a verse of punishment is mentioned, a verse of mercy is mentioned, and when a verse of mercy is mentioned, a verse of punishment is mentioned. The explanation of these two attributes has already preceded, so there is no need to repeat it. "Al-Rahman" may be read in the nominative as a substitute for "huwa," or by supposing an omitted subject, meaning "He is the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate," or as a second predicate after the predicate "your god," so that this subject has three predicates: "one god" is a predicate; "there is no god but He" is a second predicate; and "the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate" is a third predicate. It is not permissible that it be a predicate of this "huwa" mentioned here, because the exception here is not a sentence, unlike your saying: "I did not pass by a man but he is better than Zayd." They said: It is also not permissible that it be raised as an attribute of "huwa," because the pronoun cannot be described. End of his words. However, it is permissible according to the view of al-Kisa'i, when the attribute is for praise and the pronoun is for the absent third person. Ibn Malik omitted the first condition and stated without restriction that al-Kisa'i permits describing the absent pronoun.

It is related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed these two verses are the Greatest Name of Allah: 'And your God is one God, there is no god but He, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.'"

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 164 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾: It is narrated that when the verse ﴿And your God is one God﴾ was revealed, the disbelievers of Quraysh said: "How can one God suffice for all the people?" So there was revealed: ﴿Indeed, in the creation﴾. When His description with oneness and His exclusive divinity had been mentioned earlier, He argued from this wondrous creation and marvellous structure, arguing from the effect to the one who produced it, and from the work to the maker. He taught them the method of reflection and what they should reflect upon. He began first by mentioning the upper world, saying: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens﴾. Its creation means its bringing into existence and its origination, or its creation, the composition of its bodies and the harmony of its parts, from the expression "the creation (khalq) of so-and-so is good", meaning his form and shape. It has been said that khalq here is superfluous, and the meaning is "Indeed, in the heavens and the earth", because khalq is the will to bring a thing into existence. The signs are in the observable aspects of the heavens and the earth, not in the will. This view is weak, because the addition of nouns is not established in the language, and because khalq is not the will itself; rather, khalq arises from the will.

They said: He used the plural "heavens" because they are kinds, each heaven being of a kind different from the others, and He used the singular "earth" because it is all of one kind, being all of dust. He began with mention of the heaven because of its nobility and the greatness of what it contains of spheres (aflak), angels (amlak), the Throne ('Arsh), the Footstool (Kursi) and other things. Its signs are its elevation without pillars beneath it and without attachments above it. Then [there are the signs in] what is in it of the two luminaries, the sun and the moon, the wandering planets and the shining stars, rising and setting, bright and effaced, and the greatness of their bodies and their height. So much so that the astronomers (ahl al-hay'a, the specialists in celestial science) said: the sun is one hundred and sixty-four times the size of the earth, and the smallest star in the sky is seven times the size of the earth, and the spheres are of great bodily size. The specialists in the science of celestial configuration have mentioned their measurements, and that they are seven spheres, encompassed by the all-encompassing sphere (al-falak al-muhit).

It is authentically related from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "The heaven has creaked, and it has the right to creak, for there is no place the width of a foot in it but there is an angel prostrating in it." And it is also authentically related (p-465) that: "The Bayt al-Ma'mur (the frequented house) is entered every day by seventy thousand [angels], who do not return to it until the Day of Resurrection."

The sign of the earth is its expanse, with no support beneath it and no attachments above it, and its rivers, waters, mountains, firm hills, trees, plains, rugged lands and minerals, and the specialisation of each place of it for what has been prepared for it, and the benefits and harms of its plants. The astronomers mentioned that the earth is a point in the middle of a circle having no direction, that the seas surround it, the air surrounds the water, the fire surrounds the air, and the spheres lie beyond that. The judge Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn al-Tayyib al-Baqillani has mentioned, in his well-known book (called al-Daqa'iq), a disagreement among the earlier people: is the earth stationary or moving? For each of these two views there are many doctrines concerning the cause that necessitates its stillness or its motion. Likewise they spoke about the body of the heavens, their colour, their greatness and their zodiacal constellations, and he mentioned doctrines of the astrologers (munajjimin) and the Manichaeans, and many confusions. What the astronomers spoke about is something they argued for with their intellects, and there is nothing of that in the Shari'ah. What is relied upon is that the true nature of these things is known only to God, Exalted is He, and whomever God has informed of something of them through revelation. ﴿He has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾ [al-Talaq: 12], and ﴿and He has enumerated everything by number﴾ [al-Jinn: 28].

﴿And the alternation of the night and the day﴾: Their alternation is by the coming of this and the going of that; or their alternation is by their attributes in light and darkness, length and shortness, or their equality. This was said by Ibn Kaysan. The night was placed before the day because of its precedence in creation, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And a sign for them is the night; We strip from it the day﴾ [Ya-Sin: 37]. Some people said that light precedes darkness, and on this disagreement is built the disagreement about the "night of the day". According to the first view, the night of a day is the night that precedes it, which is the view of the majority; according to the second view, the night of a day is the night that follows it. Likewise, on their disagreement about the day is built their disagreement in the question: if someone swears that he will not speak to Zayd by day (nahar)...

﴿And the ship that runs in the sea﴾: The first to build a ship was Noah, upon our Prophet and upon him be the best of prayers and peace, and Gabriel, peace be upon him, said to him: "Place it on the breast of the bird." So the ship is an inverted bird, and the water beneath it is like the air above it. This was said by Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi. Its sign is God's subjecting it so that it runs on the surface of the water, and its standing upon it despite its weight, and its carrying of goods to their destinations. Were you to throw a pebble into the sea, it would sink. He described it with this attribute of running because that is its greatest sign. He made the attribute a relative clause whose predicate is "runs", a present-tense verb indicating the renewal of that attribute for it at every time that it is needed. He mentioned that attribute in place of [a more specific description] for emphasis, since it is known that it runs only in the sea. The definite article here is for the genus, and the running is attributed to the ship in a broad sense, for it has from its own nature an attribute that calls for running.

﴿With what benefits mankind﴾: It is possible that "mā" is a relative pronoun, meaning it runs accompanied by the goods that benefit people, such as various kinds of merchandise and commodities transported from one land to another, so the bā' (with) is for accompaniment. It is also possible that "mā" is a verbal-source particle (maṣdariyya), meaning people profit in their trade and travels, for raiding, pilgrimage and other purposes, so the bā' is for causation. He restricted himself to mentioning the benefit, even though it runs with what harms, because He mentioned it in the context of divine favour.

﴿And what God sends down from the sky of water﴾: That is, from the direction of the sky. The first "min" (from) is for the starting point and is connected to "sent down". In "sent down" there is an object pronoun returning to "mā", meaning "and that which God sent down from the sky". The second "min" together with what follows it is a substitute for "from the sky", a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), so it is on the intention of repeating the governing word; or it is for specifying the kind according to those who affirm this meaning for it; or it is partitive, and it is connected to "sent down". It is not said: how is the first "min" connected to "sent down" and the second as well, since their meanings differ?

﴿And with it He revived the earth after its death﴾: It is conjoined to the relative clause of "mā", which is "sent down", by the fā' (so), which implies sequence and the swiftness of plant growth, and the pronoun "with it" returns to the relative. He used "reviving" as a metaphor for the emergence of what He deposited in it of plants, and "death" as a metaphor for the settling of that within it and its non-appearance. These are two strange metaphors, because what emerged from it by the rain, God placed in it the nourishing, growing and moving power, and what did not appear is hidden in it, as if it were buried in it, and it is a grave for it (p-466).

﴿And He scattered in it from every creature﴾: If this clause is considered conjoined to the relative clauses preceding it, it needs a pronoun returning to the relative, because the pronoun in "in it" returns to the earth, and its estimate is "and He scattered in it from every creature". But the omission of this pronoun, when it is governed by a preposition, has a condition: that a preposition enters upon the relative, or upon the thing described by the relative, or upon what is attached to the relative, similar to what enters upon the pronoun in form and meaning; that the thing governed by the two prepositions be identical in form and meaning; that the governed noun returning to the relative and its preposition not be in the nominative position; that it not be restricted, nor in the sense of a restricted thing; and that it be specifically designated for the connection. This condition is missing here. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: is His saying 'and He scattered in it' conjoined to 'sent down' or to 'revived'? I say: the apparent is that it is conjoined to 'sent down', falling under the ruling of the relative clause, because His saying 'and with it He revived the earth' is conjoined to 'sent down', so it is connected to it and both become like one thing; as if it were said: 'and what He sent down in the earth of water and scattered in it from every creature.' It is permissible to conjoin it to 'revived', in the sense of 'and with rain He revived the earth and scattered in it from every creature', because they flourish by fertility and live by life." End of his words, and there is no benefit in them. Whichever of his two estimates you take, it is necessary that in His saying ﴿and He scattered in it from every creature﴾ there be a pronoun returning to the relative, whether you conjoin it to "sent down" or to "revived", since both clauses are within the relative clause. What appears from the verse is that it is by omitting a relative for the sake of understanding the meaning, conjoined to what is in "and what He sent down", and the estimate is: "and what He scattered in it from every creature". This would be greater as a sign, because what God scattered in the earth of every creature contains great signs in their forms, attributes, states, movements, harms, benefits and wonders, and what He placed in each form of them of wondrous secrets and strange subtleties of craftsmanship, from the elephant to the atom, and what God brought into existence in the sea of wondrous creatures unlike the forms of the land. Such a thing should be mentioned separately, not made a part of something else in the course of a sentence. The omission of the nominal relative, however, is according to those who hold that "al" (the definite article) is a noun, for understanding the meaning, a common and permissible practice in Arabic speech, although the Basrans do not treat it as analogous, while others have analogized it. A poet of the tribe of Tayy said:

"What is it whose habit is caution and prudence, and whose desire obeyed two equal things?"

That is: "the one who obeyed". Hassan said:

"Whoever among you satirizes the Messenger of God, and whoever praises him and supports him is the same."

That is: "and whoever praises him". Another said:

"By God, what you gained and what was gained from you is not with one who is balanced and guided, nor with one who is close."

He means: "What you gained and what was gained from you". The saying of the Exalted has been interpreted as the omission of the relative: ﴿And say: We believe in what was sent down to us and what was sent down to you﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 46], that is, "and what was sent down to you", to match His saying: ﴿and the Book which He sent to His Messenger and the Book which He sent down before﴾ [al-Nisa': 136]. The first estimate may also work out with the omission of the pronoun for the sake of understanding the meaning, even if the condition for permitting its omission is not present, and this has come in their poetry. He said:

"Indeed my tongue is a sweetness by which one is healed, and it is bitter to whomever God pours it upon."

He means: "upon whomever God poured it". And he said:

"Perhaps the one who raised me up, so that she would return me to the earth, if the Capable does not decree good."

(p-467) He means: "the one with whom she raised me up." According to this view, "from every creature" is in the place of the object, and "min" is partitive. According to the school of al-Akhfash, it is permissible for it to be superfluous, and "every creature" is the object itself. With the omission of the relative, the object of "scattered" is elided, meaning "and He scattered it", and "min" is circumstantial, meaning "being from every creature". It is then partitive, or for specifying the kind according to whoever holds that.

﴿And the turning of the winds﴾: in their blowing, as favourable and as east wind, south and north, and in their attributes, hot and cold, gentle and violent, barren, fertilising, and the sort called nakba', which comes between the directions of two winds. It has been said: sometimes with mercy, and sometimes with punishment. It has been said: their turning is that they come to large ships with the measure of what carries them, and to small ones likewise, and He turns away from them what harms them, and there is no regard for the largeness or smallness of the sails, for if [the winds] came as a single body, they would strike the sails and drown [the ships].

Abu Hayyan's commentary on surah 2, verse 164 (part 2 of 2):

Scholars have discussed the types of wind, the derivation of their names, and their natures, along with the reports (āthār) and poetry that have been transmitted about them. But that is not our purpose. The wind (al-rīḥ) is a subtle, transparent body that cannot be seen. Among its signs is the power God placed in it: it uproots trees, effaces traces, levels dwellings, and destroys unbelievers. It also nurtures crops, makes them grow, and strengthens them, and it drives clouds to a barren land.

The readers (qurrāʾ) differed on whether "wind" (al-rīḥ) should be read in the singular or the plural in eleven places. In the Law and in common usage, it is "He sends the winds" (yursilu al-riyāḥ). Other instances include ﴿the wind blew violently against him﴾ [Ibrahim: 18], ﴿We sent the winds fertilizing﴾ [al-Hijr: 22], ﴿which the winds scatter﴾ [al-Kahf: 45]. In al-Furqan: ﴿He sent the winds﴾ [al-Furqan: 48] and ﴿who sends the winds﴾ [al-Naml: 63]. In al-Rum: ﴿God is He who sends the winds﴾ [al-Rum: 48]. In Fatir: ﴿He sent the winds﴾ [Fatir: 9]. In al-Shura: ﴿If He wills, He stills the wind﴾ [al-Shura: 33].

Ḥamza read it in the singular except in al-Furqan. al-Kisāʾī read it in the singular except in al-Hijr. Nāfiʿ read all of them in the plural. The two al-ʿArabiyyān read the plural except in Ibrahim and al-Shura. Ibn Kathīr read the plural only in al-Baqara, al-Hijr, al-Kahf, and al-Sharīʿa. In the codex of Ḥafṣa, this verse reads "wa-taṣrīf al-arwāḥ" (and the turning of the spirits). They did not differ on the singular form where there is no definite article (alif and lām).

The word appears in the Qur'an in the plural when it accompanies mercy, and in the singular when it accompanies punishment, except in Yunus in God's words: ﴿and they sailed with them on a good wind﴾ [Yunus: 22].

A hadith reads: "O God, make them winds (riyāḥan) and do not make them a wind (rīḥan)." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: because the wind of punishment is violent and its parts are tightly joined, as if it were a single body, whereas the wind of mercy is gentle and its parts are separated; therefore it is called "riyāḥ," and this is the meaning of "spreading" (yanshuru). It was made singular with the ship (al-fulk), because the wind that moves ships is a single, continuous wind. Then it was described as "good," which removed the shared meaning between it and the wind of punishment. End of quote.

Whoever reads it in the singular intends the genus, so it is like the plural reading.

Al-riyāḥ is in the nominative position, so "taṣrīf" (turning) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the genitive construction, meaning: "the turning of the winds, the clouds, or anything else on which they have an effect, by God's permission." It may also be in the accusative position, so the verbal noun is in meaning attached to the agent, and in form attached to the object, meaning: "God's turning of the winds."

﴿and the clouds subjected (al-musakhkhar)﴾. Subjection (taskhīr) means sending it from one place to another. It has also been said that subjection means its remaining between heaven and earth without any tie holding it up. The clouds are described here as "subjected" in the singular, because the word is a collective noun (ism jins). It has two forms: the masculine, as in this verse and as in God's words: ﴿trunks of uprooted palm trees﴾ [al-Qamar: 20]; and the feminine, according to the sense of a feminine plural. Sometimes it is described with what describes a single feminine noun, and sometimes with what describes a plural, as in God's words: ﴿until, when they carry heavy clouds﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 57].

Kaʿb al-Aḥbār said: the cloud is the sieve of rain; if not for the cloud, the rain would ruin what falls upon it from the earth. It has been said: the cloud takes the rain from the sky; it has been said: it scoops it from the seas of the earth; it has been said: God creates it within it. The philosophers have various opinions about it. It is called "subjected" in view of its holding the water, since water is heavy, so its remaining in the air is contrary to its natural disposition. Its measure, which contains benefit, is determined by God, who brings it at the time of need and returns it when the need passes. Or (its subjection is) its being driven by the movement of the wind to wherever God wills. Each of these aspects contains evidence of God's oneness.

﴿between the heaven and the earth﴾: "between" (bayna) is in the accusative as an adverb of place (ẓarf), and its governing element is "subjected": it was subjected between such and such. Or it is governed by an implied verb, meaning "being between," in which case it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun hidden in "subjected."

﴿(there are signs for a people who reason)﴾: the lām entered upon the subject of inna because the predicate intervenes between them. Had it directly followed inna, the lām could not have entered. It is the emphatic lām (lām al-tawkīd), so the sentence contains two emphatic particles: inna and the lām. "For a people" (li-qawmin) is in the position of a qualifier, meaning "existing for a people." The clause is a qualifier of "a people," because no one reflects on these great signs except someone who is rational. Such a person witnesses from this verse what serves as evidence for God's oneness, His unique divinity, the greatness of His power, and the wonder of His wisdom. It has been transmitted in a report: "Woe to whoever recites this verse and then casts it aside," meaning he did not reflect upon it or take a lesson from it.

As for the connection (munāsaba) of this verse to what precedes it: when God mentioned that He is one and that He alone is divine, He did not stop at stating it, but presented proofs for reflection. Furthermore, these proofs are not merely evidence; they are blessings from God upon His servants. Therefore they are clearest to whoever contemplates and most striking to whoever reasons, since calling attention to what is beneficial inspires thought. However, these proofs benefit only one who is capable of looking and reasoning with the intellect bestowed by the King, the Bestower. The things God mentions here are eight. If we take "and He spread in it" as dependent on an omitted relative (as we posited in one of the two analyses), they become nine. In terms of categories they reduce to four: creation, alternation, sending down water, and turning (taṣrīf).

He began first with creation, because it is the greatest sign and the most significant proof of divinity, since it is the bringing forth and origination of something existent from pure non-existence:

﴿Is He who creates like He who does not create?﴾ [al-Nahl: 17]. ﴿And those they call upon besides God create nothing, and they are themselves created﴾ [al-Nahl: 20].

The proof of creation establishes all the essential attributes: necessary existence, unity, life, knowledge, power, and will. He placed the heavens before the earth because of the greatness of their creation, or because (the heavens) precede the earth in creation according to those who hold that view.

Then he followed the mention of the creation of the heavens and the earth with the alternation of night and day, which arises from some of the luminous celestial bodies contained in the heavens. Then he followed that with the mention of the ship (al-fulk). It is conjoined to "the night and the day," as if he had said "and the alternation of the ship," meaning its going at one time in one way and at another time in another way, according to the divine measures that move it. This arises from some of the lower, solid bodies contained in the earth.

Then he followed that with matters shared by the upper world and the lower world: the sending down of water from the sky, and the bringing forth of what was hidden in the earth through life. This shared matter presents the cause before the effect, and therefore it is followed by "fa-" (then), which some hold indicates causation.

Finally he concluded with what the previous mention of the course of ships, the sending down of water, and the reviving of dead land cannot be complete without, namely the turning of the winds and the clouds. He placed the winds before the clouds because the mention of the ship came earlier, and the clouds came later because the sending down of water came after the course of ships in the mention.

Look at this remarkable order of mention: he began first with the origination of the heavens and the earth; then he mentioned as a second item what arises from the upper world; then he came in third place with what arises from the lower world; then he came with what is shared. Then he concluded with what the blessing is not complete for humans without, namely the explained turning.

God mentioned these signs in two categories: one perceived by insight, and one perceived by sight. The creation of the heavens and the earth is perceived by the intellect, and what follows it is witnessed by the eyes. What is witnessed by the eyes is attributed to Necessary Existence, which is inferred by the intellect. Therefore God said: ﴿there are signs for a people who reason﴾, and He did not say "for a people who see," giving precedence to the judgment of the intellect, since the final outcome of what is witnessed by sight returns, through the intellect, to its attribution to God.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 165 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And among the people are those who take, besides Allah, equals (rivals)﴾: When Allah Most High established tawhid (monotheism) through clear proofs, He followed this with mention of those who were not granted success, namely those who take equals besides Allah, in order to show the difference between the two ways. Opposites reveal the beauty of each other. Despite the clarity of these signs, this misguided person did not witness any of them. The word "people" (al-nas) is general, and it is best to understand it as referring to two groups: the People of the Book and the worshippers of idols. As for the People of the Book, the "equals" are their leaders and rabbis, whom they followed in what those leaders prescribed for them of commands and prohibitions, even when these contradicted the command and prohibition of Allah. Allah Most High said: ﴿They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 31]. As for the worshippers of idols, the "equals" are the idols, which they took as gods and worshipped besides Allah. It has also been said that the intended meaning of "people" is specific. It was said: the People of the Book. It was said: the worshippers of idols. The first view is the better one. That they are the People of the Book is preferred on the basis of His saying "they love them," where He uses the pronoun for rational beings, and on the basis of the improbability of idols being loved, and on the basis of His saying: ﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed, and they see the punishment﴾ [al-Baqarah: 166], since disowning is only fitting for rational beings. "Min" (from/among) is either a relative (mawsul) subject, or an indefinite qualified noun (nakirah mawsufah). The verb "yattakhidhu" (takes) is singular in agreement with the form of "min." "Min dun Allah" (besides Allah) is attached to "yattakhidhu." "Dun" here means "ghayr" (other than), and its original usage is as a noun of place, though it was then rarely used in this way. Ibn Atiyyah said: "Min dun" is a term that indicates the absence of what is annexed to it, "dun" being away from the matter under discussion, and interpreting "dun" as "siwa" (besides) or "ghayr" (other than) is not consistently valid. End of quotation. You say: "I did this min dunika," meaning while you were absent. And you say: "I took a friend from you" and "I took a friend min dunika." What is understood from this is that he took a friend from the person of another. And you say: "The people stood dun Zayd," and what is understood from this is that Zayd did not stand; so its meaning in this is that of "ghayr." What the grammarians have mentioned is what I have described to you, that it is used as a noun of place, and that its usage is limited and rare in that sense. Sibawayh also related that it can mean "inferior (radi')," as you say: "This is a garment dun," meaning inferior. When it is a noun of place, it indicates the lowness of the place, so you say: "Zayd sat dunaka," meaning: Zayd sat in a place lower than your place. Likewise, when you intend "dun" in the figurative locative sense, you say: "Zayd dun Amr in nobility," meaning in status and not in place. (The manner of its use in the sense of "ghayr," through its shift from the locative sense, is obscure, so we clarify it.) We say: when you say "I took a friend min dunika," its original form is: "I took a friend from a direction and place lower than your direction and place," so it is a figurative locative. If the place from which the friend was taken is your place, and your direction is lower than it, and it is "dun" it, it necessarily follows that it is "ghayr," since it is not it. Then you deleted the first term of the annexation and placed the second term in its position, while it is "ghayr," so its indication becomes the indication of "ghayr" by this arrangement, not because it was originally assigned to that meaning in the language. "Andadan" (equals) is in the accusative here as the object of "yattakhidhu," and here it is transitive to one object, as in your saying: "I took a friend from you," and it is of the form "ifta'ala" from "akhadha" (to take). The discussion of "nidd" (equal) and of "ittakhadha" has already preceded, so it is not repeated here. Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi said: "al-andad" are the followed leaders, whom they obey in disobedience to Allah Most High. Mujahid and Qatadah said: "al-andad" are the idols. The pronoun in "yuhibbunahum" (they love them) is the pronoun of rational beings. We have previously stated that it is preferable for "al-andad" to be the collective of idols and leaders, and for the verse to be general. The predominance of rational beings is applied in the pronoun in "yuhibbunahum," meaning they exalt them and submit to them. The clause "yuhibbunahum" is either a qualifier of "al-andad," or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the concealed pronoun in "yattakhidhu." It is also permissible for it to be a qualifier of "man," if you make it an indefinite qualified noun. This is permissible because in "yuhibbunahum" there is a pronoun referring to "andad" or to "man," and the pronoun has been returned to "man" in the plural according to meaning, since the agreement with the wording was already made in "yattakhidhu," where the pronoun was singular. A separation has occurred between the two clauses, and that is a condition according to the view of the Kufans.

﴿kahubb Allah (as the love of Allah)﴾: The kaf (ka) is in the accusative position, either as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the omitted pronoun of the love, according to the opinion of Sibawayh, or as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), according to the opinion of the majority of grammatical analysts (mu'rabun). The estimated sense: according to the first view, "yuhibbunahumuhu," meaning the love resembling the love of Allah; and according to the second view, its estimate is: "love like the love of Allah." The verbal noun is annexed to the object in the accusative, and the subject is omitted; the estimate is: "like their love of Allah," or "like the love of the believers for Allah." The meaning is that they equated the two loves, the love of the rivals and the love of Allah. Ibn Atiyyah said: "Hubb" is a verbal noun annexed to the object in form, and it is, by estimate, annexed to the concealed subject; its estimate is: "like your love of Allah," or "like their love," according to whichever estimate each group adopted. End of his statement. His saying "annexed to the concealed subject" does not mean that the subject is concealed within the verbal noun; rather, he called it "concealed" because of what he estimated, "like your love" or "like their love," and so he made it explicit as a concealed pronoun when he revealed its estimate. Or by "concealed" he means the omitted, which exists in the terminology of the grammarians, that is, calling an omission a concealment. I say this because some grammarians claimed that the subject with the verbal noun is not omitted, but rather is a concealed pronoun within the verbal noun. This was refuted on the ground that the verbal noun is a generic noun, like "oil" or "wheat," and generic nouns do not have concealed pronouns in them. Al-Zamakhshari said: "kahubb Allah" means "like the glorification of Allah and submission to Him," that is, as Allah loves, on the basis that it is a verbal noun from the passive form, and He only dispensed with mentioning who loves Him because it does not cause ambiguity. It has been said: "like their love of Allah," meaning they equate between Him and themselves in their love, because they used to acknowledge Allah and draw near to Him: ﴿And when they board ships, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 65]. End of his statement. He chose that the verbal noun be in the passive form, with the agent not named, and this is a point of disagreement. Can it be held that the verbal noun is in the passive form? So it is permissible to say: "I was amazed at the striking of Zayd," considering it an object of a passive construction whose agent is not named, and then it is annexed to it; or is that not permissible? There are three views on this. The third view distinguishes between a verbal noun from a verb that is only used in the passive, such as: "I was amazed at the madness of Zayd by knowledge," since it derives from "junnat," which is only used in the passive with an unnamed agent, and a verb that can be used in both the active and the passive form. It is permissible in the first case and prohibited in the second, and the soundest view is the absolute prohibition. The detailed explanation of all this belongs to grammar. Al-Zajjaj rejected the view of those who estimated the agent of the verbal noun as "the believers," or "their pronoun," which is narrated from Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, Abu al-Aliyah, Ibn Zayd, Muqatil, al-Farra', and al-Mubarrad, and he said: "It is nothing." The proof that it is invalid is His saying afterwards: ﴿But those who believe are stronger in love for Allah﴾. It was preferred that the agent of the verbal noun is the pronoun of those who take the equals, meaning they love the idols as they love Allah, because they associated them with Allah Most High, so they equated between Allah and their idols in love, despite the perfection of His power, the subtlety of His nature, and the humility and paucity of the idols. Abu Rajaa al-Utaridi read "yahibbunahum" with a fatha on the ya', and this is a dialect; and in the well-known proverb: "Whoever loves, becomes ill (min habba tabba)." Its present tense came in the form "yahibbu" with a kasra on the 'ayn, as an anomaly, since it is doubled and transitive, and its analogical form should be with a damma on the 'ayn, as in: "madda-hu yamuddu-hu" and "jarra yajurru-hu."

﴿But those who believe are stronger in love for Allah﴾: Al-Raghib said: "Love (hubb) originally derives from affection (mahabbah). 'Habbabtu-hu' means: I reached the core (habbah) of his heart, and I struck him with the core of the heart. In wording it is a form (fu'l), and in reality it is a state of being affected (infi'al). When it is used of Allah, the meaning is: He reached the core of His servant's heart and made it protected from desire, from Satan, and from all the enemies of Allah." End of his statement. 'Abd al-Jabbar said: "The servant's love for Allah is his exalting Him and holding fast to His obedience, and Allah's love for the servant is His desire to praise him and reward him. The original meaning of love in the language is attachment, because the lover clings to his beloved as much as he can." End. The object of comparison is omitted, and they are those who take the equals. There is a difference of opinion regarding the second object of love. It was said: The meaning of "ashaddu hubban li-Allah" is: stronger in love for Allah than they are, because their love for Allah is mediated; this was said by al-Hasan. Or it means: stronger in their love than they are for their idols; this was said by others. The requirement of the superlative comparison is the believers' singling Him out for love, or because they know what necessitates love, or because of their love for Him in the unseen, or because of Allah Most High's testimony to them of love, when He said: ﴿He loves them and they love Him﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 54], or because of the believer's turning to his Lord in ease and hardship, in tightness and in plenty, or because of his not shifting away from his master and not choosing anything other than Him over Him, or because he knows that Allah is the creator of the idol, while He is the one who harms and benefits, or because his love is by intellect and proof, or because of his obeying His command even on the Day of Resurrection, when Allah Most High commands those who worshipped Him and associated nothing with Him to enter the Fire, and they hasten to it, so the Fire becomes cool for them, and a caller under the Throne calls out: ﴿But those who believe are stronger in love for Allah﴾, and He commands those who worshipped idols to enter the Fire with them, and they lament. This was said by Ibn Jubayr. These are nine statements whose opposites and counterparts are established for those who take equals. All of these are characteristics by which Allah distinguished the believers in their love for Him over the disbelievers, and each of the commentators mentioned one characteristic. The totality is what necessitates the distinction of love, so there is no contradiction among the statements on this basis, since each one of them is not restrictive; rather, each is an example of what the requirement of distinction entails.

And the author of al-Muntakhab said, "The majority of the theologians (mutakallimun) said: Love is a kind of will (iradah), which only relates to possible things (al-ja'izat), so it is impossible for love to relate to the essence of Allah and His attributes. When we say 'Allah loves,' its meaning is: He wills the obedience to Allah, His service, His reward, and His benevolence. He related from a group whom he called 'the knowers' (al-'arifun) that they said: 'We love Allah for His own sake, just as we love pleasure for its own sake, because He Most High is described with perfection, and perfection is loved for its own sake.'" End of his statement. In the superlative form, he deviated from "ahabb" to "ashaddu hubban," because it is established in the science of Arabic that the superlative form (af'al al-tafdil) and the verb of wonder (fi'l al-ta'ajjub) are of one pattern. If you say: "Ma ahabba Zaydan" (How much Zayd is loved!), this would not be an expression of wonder at the act of the doer; rather, it would be an expression of wonder at the act of the object, and it is not permissible to express wonder at an act that falls upon the object, so that the object would be in the accusative as the doer is. You do not say: "Ma adraba Zaydan" (How much Zayd is struck!) meaning that the striking befell Zayd. Given this, "Zayd ahabbu li-Amr" is not permissible, since the meaning would be: Zayd is the one loved by Amr. Since that was not permissible, one turns to the expression of wonder and the superlative form with what is permissible from it, so you say: "Ma ashadda hubba Zaydin li-Amr" (How intense is Zayd's love for Amr!) and "Zayd ashaddu hubban li-Amr min Khalid li-Ja'far" (Zayd loves Amr more intensely than Khalid loves Ja'far). Yet they have an anomaly, for they said: "Ma ahabbahu ilayya" (How beloved he is to me!), so they expressed wonder at the act of the object as an anomaly; and the Qur'an would not come with the anomalous in usage and analogy, and turn away from the correct and eloquent. The accusative of "hubban" is as a specification (tamyiz), and it is of the specification transferred from the subject (mubtada'), its estimate: "Their love for Allah is stronger than the love of those for Allah, or for their rivals, according to the difference of the two views."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 165 (part 2 of 2):

﴿If only those who have done wrong could see, when they see the punishment, that all power belongs to God, and that God is severe in punishment.﴾ Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read *wa-idh tarawna* (with *ta'* at the beginning) for *idh yaraw*, and *anna* in both places with a fatha. Ibn 'Amir also read *idh yurawna* (with a *damma* on the *ya'*). The rest read it with a fatha. al-Hasan, Qatada, Shayba, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read *wa-law tara* (with *ta'* at the beginning) before *inna al-quwwata*, and *inna* with a kasra in both places. The Kufans, Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read *wa-law yara* (with *ya'* at the beginning) before *anna al-quwwata*, and *anna* with a fatha in both places. A group read *wa-law yara* (with *ya'* at the beginning) before *inna al-quwwata*, and *inna* with a kasra in both places.

Here *law* (if only, a particle of counterfactual condition) is a particle for what would have happened had something else occurred. It therefore requires an answer (*jawab*), and scholars have differed about its implied form. Some estimated it to come before *anna al-quwwata*, so that *anna al-quwwata* is the object (*ma'mul*) of that answer. The estimate is: according to the reading of whoever reads with *ta'* at the beginning, "you would have known, O listener, that all power belongs to God," or "you would have known, O Muhammad," if the addressee in *wa-law tara* is him. The Prophet ﷺ already knew this, but he was addressed while the intended audience was his community, since among them are people who need to strengthen their knowledge by witnessing the like of this. Whoever reads with a kasra estimates the answer as: "you would have said that power..." — with the difference of opinion about the addressee of *wa-law tara*: is he the listener or the Prophet ﷺ? Or the estimate is: "you would have considered their condition enormous." Although *inna al-quwwata* is with a kasra, it carries the sense of causation, like: "If you came to Zayd, he would be good to you, for he is a generous host to guests." Ibn 'Atiyya said: the estimate of this is: "If you could see those who have done wrong, at the time of their seeing the punishment and their terror of it and their magnifying of it, they would acknowledge that power belongs to God." So the answer is implied in this sense, and it is the governing element of *inna*. End of quotation. There is an objection to this: his phrase "at the time of their seeing the punishment." It should have been estimated with a synonym, namely "at the time of their seeing the punishment." Also, he estimated the answer of *law*, which does not follow from what comes after *law*, because the listener's or the Prophet's ﷺ seeing the wrongdoers at the time of their seeing does not result in their acknowledging that all power belongs to God. It becomes like your saying: "O Zayd, if you saw 'Amr at the time of striking him, he would acknowledge that God is capable of it," and his acknowledgment of God's power is not a consequence of Zayd's seeing. (p. 472) As for whoever reads *wa-law yara* with *ya'* at the beginning and a fatha on *anna*, the estimate of the answer may be: "they would have known that all power belongs to God," even if the subject of *yara* is those who have done wrong. If the pronoun in *yara* refers to the listener, that is, the listener, the estimate is: "he would have known that all power belongs to God."

Others estimated the answer as omitted after His words ﴿and that God is severe in punishment﴾. This is the view of Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash and Abu al-'Abbas al-Mubarrad. Its estimate is: according to the reading of "*wa-law tara*" with the second-person address, "you would have magnified what befell them." According to the reading of "*wa-law yara*" with the third person, if the listener is the implied subject, the estimate is: "he would have magnified that"; and if those who have done wrong are the subject, the estimate is: "they would have magnified what befell them."

When the answer is estimated at the end of the sentence and *anna* is with a fatha, its grammatical justification has two possibilities. One is that it is the object of *yara* in the reading of whoever reads with *ya'*, meaning: "and if those who have done wrong saw that all power belongs to God." As for whoever reads with *ta'*, *anna* is an object for the sake of which (*maf'ul min ajlihi*), meaning: "because all power belongs to God." Whoever reads *inna* with a kasra alongside the reading *tara* with *ta'*, and estimates the answer at the end of the sentence, then although it is with a kasra, it has the meaning of the fatha form and indicates causation. You say: "Do not humiliate Zayd, for he is a scholar; and do not honor 'Amr, for he is ignorant." It carries the meaning of the fatha form in causation, and this sentence is as if it were an interposition between *law* and its omitted answer.

As for the reading of whoever reads with *ya'* at the beginning and a kasra on the two hamzas, it may be governed by an omitted saying which is the answer of *law*, meaning: "they would have said that power..." Or it is in the form of a resumption (*isti'naf*), and the answer is omitted, meaning: "they would have magnified that." The object of *tara* is omitted, meaning: "and if the wrongdoers saw their condition."

*Tara* in His words "*wa-law tara*" may be visual (*basariyyah*, seeing with the eyes), according to the view of Abu 'Ali, and it may be cognitive (*irfaniyyah*, knowing by recognition). When *anna* is made the object of *yara*, it may be in the sense of *'alima* (to know), transitive to two objects, which *anna* fills the place of both, according to the school of Sibawayh.

"Those who have done wrong" is a reference to those who take rivals (to God), and it draws attention to the causal reason. Or it may be general, including these and other unbelievers. But the context of what follows points to the fact that they are those who take rivals.

Ibn 'Amir's reading *idh yarawna*, in the passive form, is from *aryta*, which is the causative of *ra'ayta* in the sense of *abşarta* (you saw). *Idh*, which is for a past time, has entered into the midst of these future verbs, to bring the matter near and to affirm its occurrence, just as the past tense takes the place of the future in His words: ﴿And the companions of the Fire will call out﴾ [al-A'raf: 50]. And as the poet said:

*I have left my wealth and turned away from exaltation, and I have met my guests with a frowning face.*

This is because he attached that to a future condition, which is his saying:

*If I do not raid the son of Hind with a raid, then he will not be free one day from the plundering of souls.*

Omitting the answer of *law*, for the understanding of the meaning, is frequent in the Qur'an and in the speech of the Arabs. God the Exalted says: ﴿If only you could see when they are terrified, and there is no escape﴾ [Saba': 51]; ﴿If only you could see when they are made to stand over the Fire﴾ [al-An'am: 27]; ﴿If only a Qur'an by which the mountains were set in motion...﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31]. And Imru' al-Qays said:

*By your grandfather, if something came to us from a messenger other than you, but we did not find for you a means of repelling it.*

This is what the study of this verse requires in terms of its grammatical analysis (*i'rab*). We will now mention from the words of the exegetes. 'Ata' said: the meaning is: "If only those who have done wrong could see on the Day of Resurrection, when they see the punishment, when Hell comes out toward them from a distance of five hundred years, snatching them as the dove picks up the seed, they would know that the power and the might belong entirely to God." It was said: "If only they knew in this world what they will know when they see the punishment, they would have acknowledged that all power belongs to God," that is, they would have disavowed the rivals; and the second (sight) is from sight with the eyes. al-Tabrizi said: "If they believed that God is capable and powerful to punish them on the Day of Resurrection, they would have refrained from what brings the penalty of punishment." az-Zamakhshari said: "If those who committed the great wrong by their association (of others with God) knew that all power, over everything, in punishment and reward, belongs to God alone and not to their rivals, and knew the severity of His punishment for the wrongdoers, when they witnessed the punishment on the Day of Resurrection, there would have arisen in them what cannot be described, of regret and anguish (p. 473) and the falling of the wrong upon them because of their wrongdoing and their misguidance." End of his words.

al-Raghib related that some of them claimed that *al-quwwah* (power) is a substitute (*badal*) for *alladhina* (those who), and he said: "this is weak." The meaning would become: "If you saw the power of God and His might over those who have done wrong."

In *al-Muntakhab* it is said: the reading with *ya'* is, according to some of them, preferable to the reading with *ta'*, because the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims already know the measure of what the unbelievers witness and see of the punishment on the Day of Resurrection, whereas those who were threatened did not know that, so the verb had to be attributed to them. End of quotation.

For us there is no difference between the two readings, I mean the *ta'* and the *ya'*, because both are *mutawatir* (transmitted through multiple reliable chains).

The accusative of *jami'an* is a circumstantial state (*hal*) from the concealed pronoun in the governing element of the prepositional phrase. *Al-quwwah* here is a verbal noun intended in the sense of a genus, the estimate being: "that the powers are established entirely for God." It is not permissible for it to be a circumstantial state of *al-quwwah*, because the governing element of *al-quwwah* is *anna*, and *anna* does not govern circumstantial states. This construction is more eloquent here than if you said: "Indeed God is strong," since here it indicates an informing about Him with this attribute. The saying "*anna al-quwwata li-llah*" indicates that all kinds of powers are established and firmly held by Him, the Exalted. His description as "severe in punishment" is placed after that, because the severity of the punishment is one of the effects of power.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 166–167 (part 1 of 2):

﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed, and they see the punishment, and the means of connection are severed from them﴾: When he mentioned those who take rivals (andad) to God, he mentioned that their worship of them and their spending of their lives in obedience to them, believing that they were the cause of their salvation, benefited them nothing, and that when they became most in need of them, they disowned them. And "idh" (when) is a substitute (badal) for "idh yaraw al-'adhab" (when they see the punishment). It was also said that it is governed by His saying "shadid al-'adhab" (severe in punishment). It was also said that it is due to an omitted element whose estimate is "remember those who were followed": they are their leaders and chiefs whom they followed in their sayings and actions. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', Abu al-'Aliyah, Qatadah, al-Rabi', Muqatil and al-Zajjaj. Or they are the devils who used to whisper to them and make the good appear ugly to them and the ugly appear good to them; this was said by al-Hasan, Qatadah also, and al-Suddi. Or it is general to every one who is followed, which is what the apparent wording indicates.

The reading of the majority is "ittubi'u" the first (passive) and the second (active). The reading of Mujahid is the reverse. According to the reading of the majority, the followed disown the followers through remorse for disbelief, or through inability to repel, or through the statement: "We did not lead these astray; rather they disbelieved by their own will, and the punishment is attached to them because of their disbelief," and what they attempted, namely attaching their sins to those who misled them, did not succeed. There are three opinions, the last of which is the most apparent, namely that the disowning is by speech. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿We disown You; they did not worship us﴾ [al-Qasas: 63]. The disowning of the followers is their separation from their followed and their remorse over their worship, since it did not avail them anything on the Day of Resurrection and did not repel from them any of the punishment of God. "And they see the punishment": the apparent meaning is that this clause, and what follows it, are coordinated with "tabarra'a" (disowned), so both fall within the scope of the time expression. It was also said: the waw is for the circumstantial (hal) in both, and the governing element is "tabarra'a," meaning they disowned while seeing the punishment and the means being severed from them, because this is a state in which fear and disavowal of the one who was the cause of the punishment increase. It was also said: the waw is circumstantial in "wa ra'aw al-'adhab" and coordinating in "wa taqatta'at," upon "tabarra'a." This is the choice of al-Zamakhshari.

﴿And the means were severed from them﴾: a metonymy for the fact that there is no escape for them from the punishment, no deliverer, and no attachment to anything that would deliver them from the punishment of God. It is general to everything to which one could attach oneself. The commentators have several opinions on "al-asbab" (the means): the bonds of kinship according to Qatadah; the ties of blood (relatives) according to Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jurayj; or the obligations that are binding (al-a'mal al-multazima) according to Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi; or the covenants according to Mujahid and Abu Rawq; or the bonds of disbelief; or their positions of worldly rank according to Ibn 'Abbas; or the causes of salvation; or the affections. The apparent meaning is that all of these enter into "al-asbab," since it is a general word.

In these clauses there is a type of rhetorical ornament called tarsi' (parallel rhyming), which is that the speech is rhymed (masju') such as His saying: ﴿And you would not accept it except by closing your eyes to it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 267]. It is abundant in the Qur'an, and it occurs in this verse in two places. The first: ﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed﴾, and it makes the omission of the relative pronoun in "ittaba'u" (those who followed) beautiful, since if it had come as "ittaba'uhum," this type of ornament would have been lost. The second place: ﴿And they see the punishment and the means are severed from them﴾. An example of this in poetry is the saying of Abu al-Tayyib:

*In his crown is a moon, in his garment a man, in his armour a lion whose claws drip with blood.*

And our saying from an ode we composed in response to his "Bānat Su'ād":

*So the throat is marble, the scent is ambergris, the teeth are a jewel, and the saliva is sweet.*

﴿And those who followed will say: If only we had a return, we would disown them as they disowned us﴾. The meaning: they wish for a return to the world so that they might obey God and disown them in the Hereafter when they are all gathered, just as the followed first disowned them. "Law" (if only) here is for wishing. It was said: it is not the "law" that denotes what would have happened because something else happened; therefore its answer came with the fa' in His saying "fa-natabarra'u" (so we would disown), just as the answer of "layta" (would that) came in His saying: ﴿Would that I had been with them so that I might achieve a great success﴾ [al-Nisa': 73], and as it came in the saying of the poet:

*If the graves were dug up for Kulayb, he would tell us by the Dhunaib which one is the Zir.*

The correct view is that this "law" is the one denoting what would have happened because something else happened, and it has taken on the meaning of wishing; for this reason its answer came after this verse, namely His saying:

*On the day of al-Sha'thamayn, the eye would have been comforted; but how can one meet those beneath the graves?*

And that the word after "law" is fathah (opened), just as it is opened after "layta" in such a saying as:

*Would that we had joined his ship until the sea returns to its former state.*

It should be excepted from the positions in which the verb is put in the subjunctive by an implied "an" after the answer introduced by fa', and that when the fa' is dropped the verb becomes jussive in this position; for the grammarians only excepted the answer to negation. So this position should also be excepted, because the jussive has not been heard in a verb that is the answer to "law" which has taken on the meaning of wishing when the fa' is dropped. The reason is that its having the meaning of wishing is not its original sense; rather it is by analogy with the wishing particle "layta." The jussive in the answer to "layta" after dropping the fa' is only because it includes the meaning of a condition, or because it indicates that a condition is omitted after it, according to the two views; thus "law" became a branch of a branch, and so this usage is weak in it.

The kaf in "kama" is in the accusative position, either as an adjective (na't) of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), or as a circumstantial (hal) from the pronoun of the omitted verbal noun according to the two earlier views, as discussed in more than one place in this book. The ma in "kama" is verbal (masdariyyah), the estimate being: "disown as their disowning," or "fa-natabarra'uhu," meaning we would disown the disowning resembling their disowning.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the kaf in His saying "kama" is in the accusative position as an adjective, either of a verbal noun or of a circumstantial, its estimate being "mutabarri'in kama" (disowning as). End of his words. As for his saying "as an adjective of a verbal noun," this is clear, and it is the well-known parsing for such a construction. As for his saying "or of a circumstantial, its estimate being mutabarri'in kama," this is not clear, because if we explicitly stated this circumstantial, "kama" would not be in the accusative as an adjective of "mutabarri'in"; for the kaf that enters on the verbal ma is one of the attributes of the verb, not of the agent. When this is so, it cannot be in the accusative as an adjective of the circumstantial, because the circumstantial here is an attribute of the agent. There is no need to estimate this circumstantial, since it would then be an emphatic circumstantial, and we do not posit a circumstantial as emphatic unless it is pronounced explicitly; as for estimating it as a circumstantial and making it emphatic, there is no need for that. Moreover, emphasis contradicts omission, because what is brought for strengthening a thing cannot be omitted either. So if this circumstantial were stated explicitly, it would not be permissible for "kama" to be anything but an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, or a circumstantial of the pronoun hidden in the explicitly stated circumstantial. An example: "they are good to me as they were good to Zayd"; here "kama ahsanu" is not an attribute of "muhsinin" (doers of good), but an attribute of the good-doing; the estimate according to the well-known parsing is "good-doing like their good-doing to Zayd."

﴿Thus God will show them their deeds as regrets upon them﴾: the kaf, according to some, is in the nominative position, and they estimated it as "the matter is thus," or "their gathering is thus," and this is weak, because it requires the addition of the kaf and the omission of the subject, and both are contrary to the original. The apparent meaning is that the kaf is in its own sense of similitude, and that the estimate is: (p-475) "like their being shown those terrors," ﴿Thus God will show them their deeds as regrets upon them﴾; so it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, and it is in the accusative position. The author of al-Muntakhab took "kadhalika" here as a reference to the disowning of some of them by others. The better view is to liken the showing to the showing. They permitted in "yuriyhim" that it be visual, transitivized by the hamza, so "hasarat" (regrets) is accusative as a circumstantial; and that it be mental, so it is a third object. They said: there is an omitted genitive construction here, meaning "over their neglect." "Tahassara" is transitive with "'ala": you say "I regretted over such-and-such," so "'ala" here is attached to "hasarat." It may also be in the position of an attribute, the governing element being omitted, meaning "regrets existing upon them," and "'ala" indicates that the regrets are above them.

"Their deeds": it was said these are the deeds they performed, and they are attributed to them from the standpoint that they did them and are held accountable for them. This is according to the view of those who say that disbelievers are addressed with the branches of the Sharia. This is the meaning of the saying of al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd that they are the evil deeds they committed, for which the Fire became obligatory for them. Ibn Mas'ud and al-Suddi said: the meaning is their righteous deeds which they abandoned, so Paradise escaped them, and they are attributed to them from the standpoint that they were commanded to do them. Al-Suddi said: Paradise is raised up for them and they look at their houses in it, had they obeyed God the Exalted; then it is said to them: "These are your dwellings had you obeyed God the Exalted," then they are divided among the believers who inherit them; this is when they regret. This is the meaning of the saying of some that their deeds, whose reward their disbelief has nullified, because the disbeliever is not rewarded while in disbelief. Do you not see the saying of the Prophet ﷺ, when it was mentioned to him that Ibn Ju'dan used to maintain ties of kinship and feed the poor, and he was asked: "Will that benefit him?" He said: "It will not benefit him, for he never said one day: My Lord, forgive me my sin on the Day of Judgment." And from this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan: 23]. It was also said: the meaning is their deeds by which they drew near to their leaders through honouring them and submitting to their command. The apparent meaning is that they are the deeds in which they followed their leaders and chiefs, namely disbelief and sins. They were a regret for them, because they saw them recorded in their books, and were certain of the recompense for them, and it was possible for them to abandon them and turn away from them, had God willed.

﴿And they will not come out of the Fire﴾: this indicates entry into the Fire, since one does not say "Zayd is not coming out of such-and-such" except after entering. No explicit text on their entry preceded in the verse; what preceded was their seeing the punishment and the exchange caused by the disowning of the followed from the followers, and the report came accompanied by the particle "bi" which indicates emphasis. Al-Zamakhshari said: they are in the same position as in His saying: "They spread the rug, every ... " in indicating the strength of their matter in what is ascribed to them, not as exclusivity. End of his words. In it there is a hint of Mu'tazilism, because if it does not indicate exclusivity, it contains no refutation of the Mu'tazilah, who say that the grave sinner abides forever in the Fire and does not come out of it.
