Is negation anything other than built upon affirmation? When you say "Zayd is going," there is in this no indication of exclusivity or sharing; likewise negation, and its being capable of both exclusivity and sharing shows this. Do you not see that you say "Zayd is going and no other," and "Zayd is going together with another"?

[p. 476] These noble verses include God's report that al-Safa and al-Marwa are among His landmarks, which He made a place for His worship, although the polytheists had previously frequented them and drawn near to idols upon them. He explicitly removed sin from whoever circumambulates between them, whether performing Hajj or 'Umrah. Then He mentioned that whoever volunteers a good deed, God is Appreciative of his action and Knowing of his intention. Since voluntary worship involves both an act and an intention, He concluded with these two fitting attributes.

Then God reported concerning those who concealed what God had sent down of the divine ruling after He had made it clear in His Book: God curses them, and so do the angels and whoever among the righteous of His servants it is permissible to curse. Then He excepted those who repent, make amends, and clarify what they had concealed. He did not suffice with repentance alone until He added amendment to it, because concealing what God has sent down is among the greatest forms of corruption, since it leads people away from the legislated path. He added clarification of what was concealed so that it would become clear to the people, plainly showing the misguidance they had been upon and that he had abandoned it and adopted the opposite of his former conduct. This is more effective in removing what was previously established of concealing the truth, for things are distinguished by their opposites.

Then God reported concerning these excepted people that He turns in forgiveness to them, and that no sin is too great for Him when the servant repents from it, however grave it may be. Then God reported that He is At-Tawwab (the Ever-Returning in forgiveness) and Ar-Rahim (the Most Merciful), by the two intensive forms found in fa''al (التَّوّابُ) and fa'il (الرَّحِيمُ).

When God mentioned the condition of the believers, who are characterized by patience, prayer, Hajj, and other acts of righteousness, and the condition of those who committed sins and then abandoned them and turned to God, He mentioned the condition of those who died in disbelief: they are under the curse of God, His angels, and mankind, and they will abide forever in the curse, their punishment will not be lightened, and they will not be reprieved.

Then, since the disbelief of most disbelievers consists only in taking gods alongside God, ﴿Has He made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a strange thing!﴾ [38:5]; ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides God"?﴾ [5:116]; ﴿And the Jews say, "Ezra is the son of God"﴾ [9:30]. And in the hadith: "They will be asked, and they will say, 'We used to worship Ezra.'"

God reported that the God is one; He is not plural, not divisible, and has no like in His attributes. Then He restricted divinity to Himself, which entails that He is the One who rewards and punishes. He described Himself with these two attributes of ar-Rahmaniyya (the attribute of being Ar-Rahman) and ar-Rahimiyya (the attribute of being Ar-Rahim). Then He began to mention what indicates His oneness and His exclusive divinity. He began by mentioning the creation of the upper spheres and the dense earthly body, and what occurs in them of the variation of that by which there is rest and motion, such as night and day, which arise from what God has placed in the upper world; and the alternation of ships going and returning with what benefits mankind, which arises from what has been placed in the lower world; and what is shared between the two worlds, such as the sending down of water, the splitting of the earth with plants, and the spreading of living creatures upon it. When He mentioned things in the heavenly bodies and things in the earthly body, He mentioned something that lies between the two bodies, namely the directing of the winds and the clouds, since through this the blessing is completed, which is required for the welfare of the world in their maritime and terrestrial benefits.

Then He mentioned that all of this consists of signs for the one who has reason, guiding him to God's oneness and His exclusive right to divinity. For those whom they worshipped besides God know with certainty that it is not possible for them to have power over anything of what these verses contain, and that they are only some of what is contained within the upper circle and the lower circle. Their relation to whoever does not worship them among the rest of the created beings is one and the same in need and change. So they have no superiority over others, except in the view of one who has been deprived of the light of reason and covered by the darkness of ignorance.

Then God mentioned, after mentioning these clear proofs that indicate His oneness and that He alone deserves worship, that among mankind are those who take rivals (to God), and that they prefer and love them as the love of God. So they equate the Creator with the created in love: ﴿Is then He who creates like one who does not create?﴾ [16:17]. Then He mentioned that among the believers are those who love God more intensely than these people love their idols. Then He addressed whoever He addressed with His words: ﴿And if only those who did wrong could see﴾ [2:165], when they witness the outcome of their taking rivals, which is the punishment descending upon them; that is, you would see a tremendous matter.

Then He alerted that their rivals have no capacity or power to repel the punishment from those who took them. This is because all powers and abilities belong to God, the Exalted. Then God mentioned the disavowal of the leaders by the followers at the time of seeing the punishment, when the affections that had existed between them ceased. The followers wished to return to the world so that they might believe and disavow their leaders. But wishing is of no benefit here, and it cannot happen; this wish is impossible, because God has decreed and ordained that there is no return to the world. Then God mentioned that after they see the punishment and all means are cut off, He will show them their deeds as regrets, when regret will not benefit them, so that their pain may be multiplied. Then He concluded this with what He has decreed for them of everlasting punishment and endless wretchedness. We seek refuge in God from the assault of His vengeance, and we ask from His abundant generosity to bestow upon us the spreading of His mercies.

And "idh" (when) is a substitute (badal) for "idh yaraw al-'adhab" (when they see the punishment). It was also said that it is governed by His saying "shadid al-'adhab" (severe in punishment). It was also said that it is due to an omitted element whose estimate is "remember those who were followed": they are their leaders and chiefs whom they followed in their sayings and actions. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', Abu al-'Aliyah, Qatadah, al-Rabi', Muqatil and al-Zajjaj. Or they are the devils who used to whisper to them and make the good appear ugly to them and the ugly appear good to them; this was said by al-Hasan, Qatadah also, and al-Suddi. Or it is general to every one who is followed, which is what the apparent wording indicates.

The reading of the majority is "ittubi'u" the first (passive) and the second (active). The reading of Mujahid is the reverse. According to the reading of the majority, the followed disown the followers through remorse for disbelief, or through inability to repel, or through the statement: "We did not lead these astray; rather they disbelieved by their own will, and the punishment is attached to them because of their disbelief," and what they attempted, namely attaching their sins to those who misled them, did not succeed. There are three opinions, the last of which is the most apparent, namely that the disowning is by speech. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿We disown You; they did not worship us﴾ [al-Qasas: 63]. The disowning of the followers is their separation from their followed and their remorse over their worship, since it did not avail them anything on the Day of Resurrection and did not repel from them any of the punishment of God. "And they see the punishment": the apparent meaning is that this clause, and what follows it, are coordinated with "tabarra'a" (disowned), so both fall within the scope of the time expression. It was also said: the waw is for the circumstantial (hal) in both, and the governing element is "tabarra'a," meaning they disowned while seeing the punishment and the means being severed from them, because this is a state in which fear and disavowal of the one who was the cause of the punishment increase. It was also said: the waw is circumstantial in "wa ra'aw al-'adhab" and coordinating in "wa taqatta'at," upon "tabarra'a." This is the choice of al-Zamakhshari.

﴿And the means were severed from them﴾: a metonymy for the fact that there is no escape for them from the punishment, no deliverer, and no attachment to anything that would deliver them from the punishment of God. The apparent meaning is that all of these enter into "al-asbab," since it is a general word.

In these clauses there is a type of rhetorical ornament called tarsi' (parallel rhyming), which is that the speech is rhymed (masju') such as His saying: ﴿And you would not accept it except by closing your eyes to it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 267]. It is abundant in the Qur'an, and it occurs in this verse in two places. The first: ﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed﴾, and it makes the omission of the relative pronoun in "ittaba'u" (those who followed) beautiful, since if it had come as "ittaba'uhum," this type of ornament would have been lost. The second place: ﴿And they see the punishment and the means are severed from them﴾. An example of this in poetry is the saying of Abu al-Tayyib:

*In his crown is a moon, in his garment a man, in his armour a lion whose claws drip with blood.*

And our saying from an ode we composed in response to his "Bānat Su'ād":

*So the throat is marble, the scent is ambergris, the teeth are a jewel, and the saliva is sweet.*

﴿And those who followed will say: If only we had a return, we would disown them as they disowned us﴾. The meaning: they wish for a return to the world so that they might obey God and disown them in the Hereafter when they are all gathered, just as the followed first disowned them. It was said: it is not the "law" that denotes what would have happened because something else happened; therefore its answer came with the fa' in His saying "fa-natabarra'u" (so we would disown), just as the answer of "layta" (would that) came in His saying: ﴿Would that I had been with them so that I might achieve a great success﴾ [al-Nisa': 73], and as it came in the saying of the poet:

*If the graves were dug up for Kulayb, he would tell us by the Dhunaib which one is the Zir.*

*On the day of al-Sha'thamayn, the eye would have been comforted; but how can one meet those beneath the graves?*

Then He mentioned that all of this consists of signs for the one who has reason, guiding him to God's oneness and His exclusive right to divinity. For those whom they worshipped besides God know with certainty that it is not possible for them to have power over anything of what these verses contain, and that they are only some of what is contained within the upper circle and the lower circle. Their relation to whoever does not worship them among the rest of the created beings is one and the same in need and change. So they have no superiority over others, except in the view of one who has been deprived of the light of reason and covered by the darkness of ignorance.

Then God mentioned, after mentioning these clear proofs that indicate His oneness and that He alone deserves worship, that among mankind are those who take rivals (to God), and that they prefer and love them as the love of God. So they equate the Creator with the created in love: ﴿Is then He who creates like one who does not create?﴾ [16:17]. Then He mentioned that among the believers are those who love God more intensely than these people love their idols. Then He addressed whoever He addressed with His words: ﴿And if only those who did wrong could see﴾ [2:165], when they witness the outcome of their taking rivals, which is the punishment descending upon them; that is, you would see a tremendous matter.

Then He alerted that their rivals have no capacity or power to repel the punishment from those who took them. This is because all powers and abilities belong to God, the Exalted. Then God mentioned the disavowal of the leaders by the followers at the time of seeing the punishment, when the affections that had existed between them ceased. The followers wished to return to the world so that they might believe and disavow their leaders. But wishing is of no benefit here, and it cannot happen; this wish is impossible, because God has decreed and ordained that there is no return to the world. Then God mentioned that after they see the punishment and all means are cut off, He will show them their deeds as regrets, when regret will not benefit them, so that their pain may be multiplied. Then He concluded this with what He has decreed for them of everlasting punishment and endless wretchedness. We seek refuge in God from the assault of His vengeance, and we ask from His abundant generosity to bestow upon us the spreading of His mercies.

[p. 477]

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 168 (part 1 of 2):

﴿O mankind, eat of what is on the earth, lawful and good, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.﴾ ﴿He only commands you to evil and immorality and to say about Allah that which you do not know.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 169] ﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has revealed," they say, "Rather, we will follow that upon which we found our fathers." Even though their fathers did not reason at all, nor were they guided?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 170] ﴿And the example of those who disbelieve is like that of one who shouts to that which hears nothing but a call and cry—deaf, dumb and blind, so they do not reason.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 171] ﴿O you who have believed, eat from the good things We have provided for you, and be grateful to Allah, if it is Him you worship.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 172] ﴿He has only forbidden you dead animals, blood, the flesh of swine, and that which has been dedicated to other than Allah. But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, there is no sin upon him. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 173] ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has revealed of the Book and purchase with it a small price—those eat into their bellies only the Fire, and Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them, and they will have a painful punishment.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 174] ﴿Those are the ones who have purchased error in exchange for guidance and punishment in exchange for forgiveness. So how patient they are for the Fire!﴾ [al-Baqarah: 175] ﴿That is because Allah has sent down the Book with truth, and indeed, those who differ concerning the Book are in extreme dissension.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 176].

Al-ḥalāl (lawful): the opposite of al-ḥarām (forbidden) and of al-muḥarram (prohibited). One says "a thing is ḥalāl," meaning its benefit is permissible; "a thing is ḥarām," meaning it is prohibited; and "a man is ḥalāl," meaning he is not in a state of iḥrām. It is said: it was named ḥalāl because the bond of prohibition concerning it has been loosened (infaḥala), and its verb is ḥalla, yaḥillu (with kasra of the ḥā' in the present tense), according to the pattern of the intransitive doubled verb. One says: "this is ḥall," meaning ḥalāl; one says "ḥalla, ballа" for emphasis; "ḥalla bi-l-makān" means he alighted in the place, and its present tense is yaḥullu and yaḥillu; "ḥalla 'alayhi al-dayn" means the debt became due for payment. Al-khuṭwah, with a ḍammah on the khā' (khuṭwah): the distance between the two feet of a walker on the ground; and al-khaṭwah, with a fatḥah (khaṭwah): the single instance from the verbal noun. One says: khaṭā yakhṭu khaṭwan, meaning he walked. One says: he has a wide stride (wāsi' al-khaṭw). So al-khuṭwah with ḍammah is an expression for the distance one steps across, like al-ghurfah and al-qabḍah, which are expressions for the known thing and the amount grasped. In its plural with alif and yā', there are three dialectal forms: keeping the ṭā' quiet as in its singular state, which is the dialect of Tamīm and some of Qays; a ḍammah on the ṭā' in imitation of the ḍammah on the khā'; and a fatḥah on the ṭā'. It is also broken into the plural khuṭan, which is a regular pattern for the noun of the form fiʻlah.

Al-faḥshā' (immorality): a verbal noun like al-ba'sā', and it is fa'lā' from al-fuḥsh, which is ugliness of appearance. From it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

A neck like the neck of a gazelle, not ugly when she adorns it, nor bare of ornament.

Then it was extended so that it came to be used for what is considered repugnant in meanings.

Alfā: means "found." There is disagreement about its transitivity to two objects. Whoever prohibits it makes the second an adjective (ḥāl), but the more correct view is that it is an object (maf'ūl), because it comes definite, and its interpretation rests on adding the alif and lām contrary to the original form.

Al-naʻīq: the herdsman's call and his shouting to the sheep. The poet said:

So call out to your sheep, O Jarīr, for indeed your soul has deluded you into error in the wilderness.

It is said: naʻaqa al-mu'adhdhin (the muezzin called out). One says: naʻaqa yanʻaqu naʻīqan, nuʻāqan, and naʻqan. As for naghaqa al-ghurāb (the crow cawed), it is with the ghayn marked with a dot. It is also said: it is said with the unmarked ḥā'... (as stated) for the crow.

Al-nidā': the verbal noun of nādā, like al-qitāl is the verbal noun of qātala, and it is with a kasra on the nūn, though it may be given a ḍammah. It is said: it is synonymous with al-du'ā'. It is said: it is specific to loud calling. It is said: to distance. It is said: to an unspecified person. One says: so-and-so is andā ṣawtan than so-and-so, meaning stronger, more intense, and farther-reaching in its course.

Al-laḥm: known (flesh). One says: laḥuma al-rajul laḥāmatan, so he is laḥīm, meaning large-bodied. And laḥima yalḥamu, so he is laḥim, meaning he longed for meat. And laḥama al-nās yulḥimuhum: he fed them meat, so he is lāḥim. And alḥama, so he is mulḥim: meat became abundant with him.

Al-khinzīr (swine): a known animal, its nūn is original, so it is fi'līl. Some claim its nūn is extra and that it is derived from khazar al-ʻayn (squint of the eye), because it looks that way. One says: takhāzara al-rajul, meaning he narrowed his eyelid to sharpen his gaze. Al-khazar is narrowness and smallness of the eye. One says: a man is akhzar, meaning clearly squinting. It is said: it is looking with the back of the eye, so it resembles confusion.

Al-ihlāl: raising the voice, and from it the ihlāl of the talbiyah (pilgrim's chant). From it the crescent (al-hilāl) was named for the raising of the voice at seeing it. One says: ahalla al-hilāl and istahalla, and one says: ahalla bi-kadhā, meaning he raised his voice. Ibn Aḥmar said:

Our riders raise their voices in the wilderness, as the pilgrim in ihram raises his voice.

Al-Nābigha said:

Or a pearl of the Ṣadaf, whose diver is delighted; when you see it, it raises its voice and prostrates.

From it: the ihlāl and istihlāl of a child, which is its crying at birth. The poet said:

The wolf laughs at the slain of Hudhayl, and you see the wolf crying out over them.

Al-baṭn (belly): known. Its plural on fu'ūl is regular, and it is also plural as biṭnān. One says: baṭana al-amr yabṭunu, when it became hidden. And baṭuna al-rajul, so he is baṭīn, meaning his belly became large. Al-biṭnah: the filling of the belly with food. One says: "Excess of belly removes sharpness of mind."

﴿O mankind, eat of what is on the earth, lawful and good, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.﴾: This is the second address that occurs in Surat al-Baqarah with the words "O mankind," and its wording is general. Al-Ḥasan said: it was revealed concerning everyone who prohibited for himself something that Allah had not prohibited for him. Al-Kalbī, Muqātil and others narrated that it was revealed concerning Thaqīf, Khuzāʻah and the Banū al-Ḥārith ibn Kaʻb, as stated by al-Naqqāsh. It is said: concerning Thaqīf, Khuzāʻah and ʻĀmir ibn Ṣaʻṣaʻah. It is said: and the Banū Mudlij, who prohibited for themselves from the tilth and livestock, and prohibited the baḥīrah, the sawā'ib, the waṣīlah and the ḥām. If this is sound, then the cause is specific and the wording general, and what counts is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause. (As for the connection with what precedes it): when He clarified tawḥīd and its proofs, and what awaits those who repent and those who disobey, He followed that with mention of His favour upon both the disbeliever and the believer, to show that disbelief does not cut off His favour. Al-Marwazī said: when He warned the believers about the state of one whose deeds become a source of regret for him, He commanded them to eat what is lawful, because the basis of obedience rests upon it. "Eat" (kulū) is an imperative of permission and allowance, because He, Exalted, is the one who brought things into existence, so He is the one who disposes of them as He wills.

"﴿of what is on the earth﴾": min is partitive, mā is a relative pronoun, and min is in the place of the object, as in: "I ate from the loaf." "Ḥalālan" is a ḥāl from the pronoun residing in the relative clause, transferred from the governing verb to it. Makkī ibn Abī Ṭālib said: "ḥalālan" is an epithet of an omitted object, its estimate being "shay'an ḥallālan" (a lawful thing). Ibn ʻAṭiyyah said: this is far-fetched, and he did not explain the reason for its remoteness. Its remoteness is that it is among the cases where the qualified noun is omitted while its qualifier is not specific, because "ḥalāl" is predicated of both the edible and the non-edible. When the qualifier is of this kind, it is not permissible to omit the qualified noun and let the qualifier stand in its place. Some scholars permitted that "ḥalālan" be in the accusative as an object of "kulū," and al-Zamakhsharī began with this. On this view, min denotes the starting point and is connected to "kulū," or connected to an omitted element, making it a ḥāl, the estimate being: "eat lawful things of what is on the earth." When the qualifier is placed first, it becomes a ḥāl, connected to an omitted element, just as it was an epithet connected to an omitted element. Ibn ʻAṭiyyah said: the purpose of the speech does not allow "ḥalālan" to be an object of "kulū"; reflect. End.

"ṭayyiban": is accusative as an epithet of "ḥalālan," either emphatic, because its meaning and the meaning of "ḥalālan" are one, and this is the view of Mālik and others; or specifying, because its meaning differs from the meaning of "ḥalāl," namely what is pleasant to the taste, and this is the view of al-Shāfiʻī and others. For this reason, the eating of a filthy animal and everything that is foul is forbidden. It is said: "ṭayyiban" is accusative as an epithet of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a good eating," which is against the apparent sense. Ibn ʻAṭiyyah said: "ṭayyiban" may also be a ḥāl from the pronoun in "kulū," the estimate being "seeking good things (mustaṭyibīn)," and this is corrupt both in wording and in meaning. As for wording: "ṭayyib" is an active participle and does not agree with the pronoun, because the pronoun is plural and "ṭayyib" is singular, and "ṭayyib" is not a verbal noun, so it is said: agreement is not required. As for meaning: "ṭayyib" differs in meaning from "mustaṭyib," because the good is an attribute of the food, while the one who finds it good is an attribute of the eater. You say: "the food was good for Zayd," and you do not say: "Zayd found the food good" in the sense of "istaṭābahu." Al-Zamakhsharī said regarding "ṭayyiban": pure from every doubt. Al-Sajāwandī said: "ḥalālan" is the absolute of the Law, "ṭayyiban" is what the nature finds delightful. In al-Muntakhab (p-479) he said, in summary: the lawful is that from which the knot of danger has been loosened, whether because it is intrinsically prohibited like carrion, or not intrinsically prohibited like another's property, since its eating has not been permitted. The good, linguistically, is the pure. The lawful is described as good, just as the forbidden is described as wicked. The basic sense of goodness is what is pleasant, and the pure and the lawful are described with it by way of analogy, because the soul dislikes what is impure, and what is forbidden is not pleasant because the Law has prohibited it. End. What is established in the language is that "ṭayyib" is the pure, free of filth. One poet said:

"And the good ones are the knots of the waistwrappers."

Another said:

"For me is the origin, which in such a case the pure one improves the seed of the one who sows." 

"The good in marriage are easy, and for them are paths, if you wish, in wilderness and rough terrain."

Al-Ḥasan said: the lawful and good is that for which one will not be questioned on the Day of Resurrection. Ibn ʻAbbās said: the lawful is that which carries no accountability in this world and no burden in the Hereafter. It is said: the lawful is what the mufti permits, and the good is what the heart testifies is permissible. Whoever holds that the basic ruling concerning things is prohibition has used this verse as evidence, because things belong to Allah, Exalted, so permission is needed for whatever is taken from them, and whatever He has not permitted remains under prohibition. The apparent sense of the verse is that whatever combines the two qualities, lawful and good, of what is on the earth, is permitted to be eaten. As for owning it and giving it in charity, or storing it, or any other use besides eating, the verse does not indicate it. Such things are permitted either by another text, or by consensus according to those who reject analogy, or by analogy to eating according to those who accept analogy.

﴿And do not follow the footsteps of Satan﴾. Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Kisāʾī, Qunbul, Ḥafṣ, and ʿAbbās, on the authority of Abū ʿAmr and al-Barjamī, on the authority of Abū Bakr, read *khuṭuwāt* with a *ḍamma* on the *khāʾ* and the *ṭāʾ* and with a *wāw*. The rest of the Seven read it with a *ḍamma* on the *khāʾ*, a *sukūn* on the *ṭāʾ*, and a *wāw*. Abū al-Sammāl read *khaṭawāt* with a *ḍamma* on the *khāʾ*, a *fatḥa* on the *ṭāʾ*, and a *wāw*. It has already been mentioned that these are three dialectal forms (*lughā*) for the plural of *khuṭwa* (step). Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Sajāwandī relate that Abū al-Sammāl read *khaṭawāt*, with a *fatḥa* on the *khāʾ* and the *ṭāʾ* and a *wāw*, as the plural of *khaṭwa*, which is a single step taken from *al-khaṭw* (stepping). ʿAlī, Qatāda, al-Aʿmash, and Salām read *khuṭuʾāt*, with a *ḍamma* on the *khāʾ* and the *ṭāʾ* and a *hamza*. The explanation of this reading has been disputed. It has been said that the *hamza* is original and that the word is from *khaṭaʾ* (error), the plural of *khaṭaʾa*, if this form is attested, and otherwise it is assumed. Among those who said it derives from *khaṭaʾ* is Abū al-Ḥasan al-Akhfash, and Mujāhid explained it as "his sins." This explanation may be giving a synonym or may be giving the meaning. It has also been said that it is the plural of *khuṭwa*, but the reader mistakenly thought the *ḍamma* on the *ṭāʾ* was a *wāw*, so he added a *hamza*, since such forms are sometimes given a *hamza*. Al-Zamakhsharī said the same in meaning: the prohibition against following the footsteps of Satan is a metaphor (*kināya*) for not taking him as a model and for not following what he has established of sins. It is said: "Zayd followed the footsteps of ʿAmr and trod in his tracks," when he took his course in his conduct. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "His footsteps are his deeds." Mujāhid said: "His sins." al-Suddī said: "His obedience." Abū Mijlaz said: "Vows made in sin." It has also been said: "What he leads them to of disobedience after disobedience, until they cover all sins," derived from the stepping of the foot from one place to another. al-Zajjāj and Ibn Qutayba said: "His paths." Abū ʿUbayda said: "The lesser sins." al-Muʾarrikh said: "His traces." ʿAṭāʾ said: "His slips." These statements are close in meaning, and each was given by its speaker as an example (*tamthīl*). All of them aim at the same thing: the prohibition against disobeying God. It is as if God, having permitted them to eat the lawful and good, forbade them to disobey Him and to step over into eating the unlawful, because Satan casts into a person what resembles doubt, and so adorns what is not lawful; therefore God forbade this. Satan here is Iblīs, and the prohibition here is against following each individual act of disobedience, not that the plural form implies a collective, so it is not a prohibition only against the singular.

﴿Indeed, he is a clear enemy to you﴾: this is the reason given for the warning against following Satan, because whoever's enmity is manifest and evident is deserving of not being followed in anything and of being fled from, for he has no thought except to bring about the ruin of his enemy.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 169–170:**

﴿He only commands you to evil and immorality﴾: When He informed them that it (the Shaytan) is an enemy, he began to mention the fruit of the enmity and what arises from it, which is his commanding them to what was mentioned.

The discussion of *innama* (a particle meaning "only" or "indeed") has already been covered in His words: ﴿We are only reformers﴾ (2:11). Among the scholars' disagreements about it is whether it indicates restriction (*al-hasr*, exclusivity) or not. The Shaytan's command is either by his speech in the time of the soothsayers (*kahana*), where that is conceivable, or by his whisperings and misguidance. When he is obeyed, his command to evil takes effect, meaning to what will harm them in the afterlife. Ibn 'Abbas said: "*al-su'*" (evil) is what has no limit. As for *al-fahsha'* (immorality), al-Suddi said it is fornication. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is everything that reaches one of the prescribed limits (*hudud*), because it is then gross indecency. It was also said: it is what its mention is gross. It was said: it is what is ugly in word or deed. Tawus said: it is what is not recognized in any law or sunnah. 'Ata' said: it is stinginess.

﴿and that you say about God what you do not know﴾: al-Tabari said: He means by it what they forbade of the *bahira* (a she-camel whose ear was split), the *sa'iba* (a freed animal), and the like, which they made into law. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is their saying "this is lawful and this is unlawful" without knowledge, and it includes everything that is attributed to God that is not permissible for Him. End of quotation. It has been said: the apparent meaning of this is the prohibition of speaking about the religion of God with what the speaker does not know of the religion of God, so that includes opinion (*ra'y*), analogical reasoning (*aqyisa*), resemblance-based reasoning (*shabahiyya*), and juristic preference (*istihsan*). They said: in this verse there is an indication of the blame of one who follows the ignorant and adopts his ruling. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: how could the Shaytan be a commander when He says, ﴿You have no authority over them﴾ (15:42)? I say: he likened his adornment of evil and his urging to it to the command of one who commands, as you say: "my soul commanded me to such-and-such." His urging signifies that you, in this matter, are in the position of those who are commanded, because of your obedience to him and your acceptance of his whisperings. For this reason He said: ﴿I will surely command them, and they will surely cut the ears of the cattle﴾ (4:119), ﴿and I will surely command them, and they will surely change the creation of God﴾ (4:119). And God the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the soul is one that commands to evil﴾ (12:53), because the human being feeds it and gives it what it desires. End of his words.

﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what God has sent down"﴾: The pronoun in *lahum* (to them) refers to the disbelievers of the Arabs, because this was their description, namely their imitation of their fathers. For this reason they said to Abu Talib, when he was dying: "Do you turn away from the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib?" They reminded him of his father's religion and creed. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed concerning the Jews. On this view the pronoun refers to something not previously mentioned, and they are the people most strictly following their forebears. It was said: it refers to "people" in His words: ﴿And among the people are those who take, besides God, equals﴾ (2:165), but this is distant. Al-Tabari said: it refers to "people" in His words: ﴿O people, eat﴾ (2:168), and this is the apparent meaning, and it would be an instance of *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person or address). Its wisdom is that they are presented in the form of an absent party whose action is to be wondered at, when they are called to follow the law of God, which is guidance and light. They answered by following the religion of their fathers, as if it were said: Have you seen anyone with a more foolish opinion and blinder insight than one who is called to follow the Qur'an sent down from God, yet rejects that and turns away from it, and affirms that he follows what he found his fathers upon? In this is an indication of the blame of *taqlid* (blind imitation), which is accepting a matter without evidence or proof. Ibn 'Atiyya reported that there is a consensus (*ijma'*) on its invalidity in matters of belief. In the verse there is evidence that what their fathers were upon was opposed to what God sent down, so the following of their sons of their fathers is blind imitation in error. In this is evidence that the religion of God is the following of what God sent down, because they were not commanded except with it. The meaning of His words "and when" is repetition. The verb *qila* (it is said) was put in the passive form (without naming its agent) because it is more concise, for if those who command were mentioned the speech would be lengthened, since the one who commands this is the Messenger and those believers who follow him. In His words "what God has sent down" there is an announcement of the magnification of what they were commanded to follow, in that its sending down is attributed to God, who is the lawgiver of the laws. So it should have been received with acceptance and not opposed by following their fathers, who were the heads of error. Al-Kisa'i assimilated the *lam* of *bal* into the *nun* of *nattabi'u* (we follow), while others made it clear. *Bal* here is conjunctive, linking a sentence to an omitted sentence. The estimate is: "We do not follow what God has sent down, but we follow what we found our fathers upon" (2:170). It is not permissible for it to be conjoined to His words "Follow what God has sent down." *'Alayhi* (upon it) is connected to the verb *alfayna* (we found), and it is not here transitive to two objects, because it has the meaning of *wajada* (to find) which means *asaba* (to come upon).

﴿Even though their fathers did not understand anything and were not guided?﴾: The *hamza* is an interrogative with reproach, denunciation, and wonder at their condition. As for the *waw* after the *hamza*, al-Zamakhshari said: the *waw* is for the circumstantial (*hal*), and its meaning is: would they follow them even though their fathers understood nothing of the religion and were not guided to the right? Ibn 'Atiyya said: the *waw* is for conjoining one sentence to another, because the utmost corruption in the commitment is that they say: "We follow our fathers even if they did not understand," so they were settled in the commitment to this, that is, this is the condition of their fathers. End of his words. The apparent meaning of al-Zamakhshari's statement that the *waw* is circumstantial contradicts Ibn 'Atiyya's statement that it is for conjunction, because the circumstantial *waw* is not a conjunctive *waw*.

The reconciliation between them is that this sentence accompanied by *law* (even if) in such a context is a conditional sentence. When one says: "Strike Zayd even if he does good to you," the meaning is "even if he does good to you." Likewise: "Give to the beggar even if he comes on a horse," or "Return the beggar even with half a date," the meaning in them is "even if." Here *law* comes as an alert that what follows it did not fit what precedes it, but it has come to exhaust the states in which the action occurs, and to show that the intent of this is the existence of the action in every state, even in this state which is not fitting for the action. For this reason it is not permissible to say: "Strike Zayd even if he wronged you," nor "Give to the beggar even if he were in need," nor "Return the beggar even with a hundred dinars." When this is established, the *waw* in *wa-law* in the examples we mentioned is conjunctive, joining to an estimated circumstance, and conjoining to a circumstance is a circumstance. So it is correct to say that it is for the circumstantial because it conjoins a circumstantial sentence to an estimated circumstance. And the conjoined sentence to the circumstance is a circumstance. And it is correct to say that it is for conjunction because of that conjunction. The meaning, and God knows best, is a denial of following their fathers in every state, even in the state which is not fitting for them to be followed in, namely their being characterized by lack of understanding and lack of guidance. For this reason it is not permissible to delete this *waw* which enters upon *law*, when it is an alert that what follows it did not fit what precedes it. Even if the sentence that is a circumstance contains a pronoun referring back to the bearer of the circumstance, because its coming bare of the *waw* indicates the restriction of the preceding sentence by this circumstance, and that contradicts the comprehensiveness of states, including this state. So these are two different meanings, and the difference is evident between: "Honor Zayd even if he was harsh to you," meaning "if he was harsh to you," and "Honor Zayd even though he was harsh to you."

The accusative of *shay'an* (anything) is on two aspects. The first: as the direct object, so it encompasses all intelligibles, because it is indefinite in the context of negation and so it generalizes. It is not possible that the intent is the negation of unity, so that the meaning would be "they do not understand one thing but rather several things." The second: that it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning "any understanding." When that is negated, all other understandings are negated. He put the negation of understanding first, because it is the source from which all actions proceed, and He delayed the negation of guidance, because that is consequent upon the negation of understanding, since guidance to the right arises from understanding, and the absence of understanding is the absence of guidance.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 169–170:**

﴿He only commands you to evil and immorality﴾: When He informed them that it (the Shaytan) is an enemy, he began to mention the fruit of the enmity and what arises from it, which is his commanding them to what was mentioned.

The discussion of *innama* (a particle meaning "only" or "indeed") has already been covered in His words: ﴿We are only reformers﴾ (2:11). Among the scholars' disagreements about it is whether it indicates restriction (*al-hasr*, exclusivity) or not. The Shaytan's command is either by his speech in the time of the soothsayers (*kahana*), where that is conceivable, or by his whisperings and misguidance. When he is obeyed, his command to evil takes effect, meaning to what will harm them in the afterlife. Ibn 'Abbas said: "*al-su'*" (evil) is what has no limit. As for *al-fahsha'* (immorality), al-Suddi said it is fornication. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is everything that reaches one of the prescribed limits (*hudud*), because it is then gross indecency. It was also said: it is what its mention is gross. It was said: it is what is ugly in word or deed. Tawus said: it is what is not recognized in any law or sunnah. 'Ata' said: it is stinginess.

﴿and that you say about God what you do not know﴾: al-Tabari said: He means by it what they forbade of the *bahira* (a she-camel whose ear was split), the *sa'iba* (a freed animal), and the like, which they made into law. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is their saying "this is lawful and this is unlawful" without knowledge, and it includes everything that is attributed to God that is not permissible for Him. End of quotation. It has been said: the apparent meaning of this is the prohibition of speaking about the religion of God with what the speaker does not know of the religion of God, so that includes opinion (*ra'y*), analogical reasoning (*aqyisa*), resemblance-based reasoning (*shabahiyya*), and juristic preference (*istihsan*). They said: in this verse there is an indication of the blame of one who follows the ignorant and adopts his ruling. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: how could the Shaytan be a commander when He says, ﴿You have no authority over them﴾ (15:42)? I say: he likened his adornment of evil and his urging to it to the command of one who commands, as you say: "my soul commanded me to such-and-such." His urging signifies that you, in this matter, are in the position of those who are commanded, because of your obedience to him and your acceptance of his whisperings. For this reason He said: ﴿I will surely command them, and they will surely cut the ears of the cattle﴾ (4:119), ﴿and I will surely command them, and they will surely change the creation of God﴾ (4:119). And God the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the soul is one that commands to evil﴾ (12:53), because the human being feeds it and gives it what it desires. End of his words.

﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what God has sent down"﴾: The pronoun in *lahum* (to them) refers to the disbelievers of the Arabs, because this was their description, namely their imitation of their fathers. For this reason they said to Abu Talib, when he was dying: "Do you turn away from the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib?" They reminded him of his father's religion and creed. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed concerning the Jews. On this view the pronoun refers to something not previously mentioned, and they are the people most strictly following their forebears. It was said: it refers to "people" in His words: ﴿And among the people are those who take, besides God, equals﴾ (2:165), but this is distant. Al-Tabari said: it refers to "people" in His words: ﴿O people, eat﴾ (2:168), and this is the apparent meaning, and it would be an instance of *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person or address). Its wisdom is that they are presented in the form of an absent party whose action is to be wondered at, when they are called to follow the law of God, which is guidance and light. They answered by following the religion of their fathers, as if it were said: Have you seen anyone with a more foolish opinion and blinder insight than one who is called to follow the Qur'an sent down from God, yet rejects that and turns away from it, and affirms that he follows what he found his fathers upon? In this is an indication of the blame of *taqlid* (blind imitation), which is accepting a matter without evidence or proof. Ibn 'Atiyya reported that there is a consensus (*ijma'*) on its invalidity in matters of belief. In the verse there is evidence that what their fathers were upon was opposed to what God sent down, so the following of their sons of their fathers is blind imitation in error. In this is evidence that the religion of God is the following of what God sent down, because they were not commanded except with it. The meaning of His words "and when" is repetition. The verb *qila* (it is said) was put in the passive form (without naming its agent) because it is more concise, for if those who command were mentioned the speech would be lengthened, since the one who commands this is the Messenger and those believers who follow him. In His words "what God has sent down" there is an announcement of the magnification of what they were commanded to follow, in that its sending down is attributed to God, who is the lawgiver of the laws. So it should have been received with acceptance and not opposed by following their fathers, who were the heads of error. Al-Kisa'i assimilated the *lam* of *bal* into the *nun* of *nattabi'u* (we follow), while others made it clear. *Bal* here is conjunctive, linking a sentence to an omitted sentence. The estimate is: "We do not follow what God has sent down, but we follow what we found our fathers upon" (2:170). It is not permissible for it to be conjoined to His words "Follow what God has sent down." *'Alayhi* (upon it) is connected to the verb *alfayna* (we found), and it is not here transitive to two objects, because it has the meaning of *wajada* (to find) which means *asaba* (to come upon).

﴿Even though their fathers did not understand anything and were not guided?﴾: The *hamza* is an interrogative with reproach, denunciation, and wonder at their condition. As for the *waw* after the *hamza*, al-Zamakhshari said: the *waw* is for the circumstantial (*hal*), and its meaning is: would they follow them even though their fathers understood nothing of the religion and were not guided to the right? Ibn 'Atiyya said: the *waw* is for conjoining one sentence to another, because the utmost corruption in the commitment is that they say: "We follow our fathers even if they did not understand," so they were settled in the commitment to this, that is, this is the condition of their fathers. End of his words. The apparent meaning of al-Zamakhshari's statement that the *waw* is circumstantial contradicts Ibn 'Atiyya's statement that it is for conjunction, because the circumstantial *waw* is not a conjunctive *waw*.

The reconciliation between them is that this sentence accompanied by *law* (even if) in such a context is a conditional sentence. When one says: "Strike Zayd even if he does good to you," the meaning is "even if he does good to you." Likewise: "Give to the beggar even if he comes on a horse," or "Return the beggar even with half a date," the meaning in them is "even if." Here *law* comes as an alert that what follows it did not fit what precedes it, but it has come to exhaust the states in which the action occurs, and to show that the intent of this is the existence of the action in every state, even in this state which is not fitting for the action. For this reason it is not permissible to say: "Strike Zayd even if he wronged you," nor "Give to the beggar even if he were in need," nor "Return the beggar even with a hundred dinars." When this is established, the *waw* in *wa-law* in the examples we mentioned is conjunctive, joining to an estimated circumstance, and conjoining to a circumstance is a circumstance. So it is correct to say that it is for the circumstantial because it conjoins a circumstantial sentence to an estimated circumstance. And the conjoined sentence to the circumstance is a circumstance. And it is correct to say that it is for conjunction because of that conjunction. The meaning, and God knows best, is a denial of following their fathers in every state, even in the state which is not fitting for them to be followed in, namely their being characterized by lack of understanding and lack of guidance. For this reason it is not permissible to delete this *waw* which enters upon *law*, when it is an alert that what follows it did not fit what precedes it. Even if the sentence that is a circumstance contains a pronoun referring back to the bearer of the circumstance, because its coming bare of the *waw* indicates the restriction of the preceding sentence by this circumstance, and that contradicts the comprehensiveness of states, including this state. So these are two different meanings, and the difference is evident between: "Honor Zayd even if he was harsh to you," meaning "if he was harsh to you," and "Honor Zayd even though he was harsh to you."

The accusative of *shay'an* (anything) is on two aspects. The first: as the direct object, so it encompasses all intelligibles, because it is indefinite in the context of negation and so it generalizes. It is not possible that the intent is the negation of unity, so that the meaning would be "they do not understand one thing but rather several things." The second: that it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning "any understanding." When that is negated, all other understandings are negated. He put the negation of understanding first, because it is the source from which all actions proceed, and He delayed the negation of guidance, because that is consequent upon the negation of understanding, since guidance to the right arises from understanding, and the absence of understanding is the absence of guidance.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 171 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And the likeness of those who disbelieve is like that of one who shouts to that which hears nothing but calls and cries. Deaf, dumb, and blind, so they do not understand.﴾: When the Exalted mentioned that these disbelievers, when they were commanded to follow what Allah had sent down, turned away from that and returned to what they were accustomed to of following falsehood, in which they had grown up and upon which they found their fathers, and did not reflect upon what was said to them, and were deaf to hearing the truth, mute in uttering it, and blind to seeing the radiant prophetic light, He mentioned this wondrous comparison in this verse, drawing attention to the state of the disbeliever in his imitation of his father and belittling him, since he has become in the rank of the beast, or in the rank of its caller, according to the disagreement that will come regarding this comparison.

In understanding the meaning of this verse, a omitted element must be supposed. They differed: some said the parable is coined by comparing the disbeliever to the one who shouts. Others said it is coined by comparing the disbeliever to the one being shouted at. Others said it is coined by comparing the caller of the disbeliever to the one who shouts. Others said it is coined by comparing the caller and the disbeliever to the one who shouts and the one being shouted at. As for the view that the parable is coined by comparing the disbeliever to the one who shouts, it has been said that the implied sense is: "And the likeness of those who disbelieve, in their lack of understanding and intellect, is like the likeness of shepherds who speak to sheep, and sheep understand nothing." It has also been said that the implied sense is: "And the likeness of those who disbelieve, in their calling upon their gods who do not comprehend their calling, is like the likeness of one who shouts at his flock, so he gains nothing from his shouting except fatigue and calling, and likewise the disbeliever gets from his calling upon the gods and his worship of idols nothing but weariness." Al-Zamakhshari said: This view has been mentioned, but His saying: ﴿except calling and crying﴾ does not support it, because idols hear nothing. End of his words. Al-Zamakhshari noticed in this view the completeness of the comparison from every aspect: just as the one being shouted at hears only calling and crying, so too the one the disbeliever calls upon, the idol, does not hear, so this view was weak in his eyes. We say: the comparison occurred in the general act of calling, not in the particulars of the one called, so the disbeliever in his calling upon the idol is compared to the one who shouts at the beast, not to the particulars of the one being shouted at. It has been said regarding this view, I mean the view of those who said the implied sense is: "And the likeness of those who disbelieve, in their calling upon their gods and idols," that the one who shouts here is not meant as one who shouts at cattle of sheep or others, but rather the one who calls out in the hollows of mountains, and an echo answers him from them, called the echo, which answers him but does not benefit him. So the meaning is: with that which hears from the one who shouts nothing but his calling and crying, said by Ibn Zayd. According to the two previous views, the subject of "hears" is a pronoun referring to "what," which is the one being shouted at. According to this view, the subject is a pronoun referring to "the one who shouts," and the pronoun referring to "what," which links the relative clause to the relative pronoun, is omitted for the sake of understanding its meaning; its implied form is: "with that which does not hear from it." There is no condition permitting this omission, because the pronoun is governed by a preposition of the relative clause with a different thing. The two prepositions differ in what they are attached to: the first preposition, the bā', is attached to "yanʿiq" (shouts), and the second, min, is attached to "yasmaʿu" (hears). Similar to this has come in their speech. It has been said that by "those who disbelieve" is meant the leaders, not the followers, and its meaning is: the likeness of those who disbelieve in their calling their followers, and that their followers obtain from them nothing but loss and ruin, is like the likeness of one who shouts at the sheep. As for the view that the parable is coined by comparing the disbeliever to the one being shouted at, namely the animals that do not understand, such as camels, cattle, sheep, and donkeys, this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrima, ʿAta', Mujahid, Qatada, al-Hasan, al-Rabiʿ, and al-Suddi. Most of the commentators differed about the element that makes this comparison correct. It was said the implied sense is: "And the likeness of those who disbelieve, in their calling to Allah the Exalted and their not hearing it, is like the likeness of the beasts of the one who shouts," so there is the omission of a qualifier in the first and the omission of a genitive construction in the second. It was said the implied sense is: "And the likeness of those who disbelieve, in their not understanding from Allah and from His Messenger, is like the likeness of the one being shouted at among the beasts, which understand nothing of command and prohibition except the sound." Thus by "the one who shouts" is meant "the one who is shouted at," and this is, in their view, an inversion. They said: as you say, "the ring entered my hand and the shoe my foot," and as they say, "he presented the basin to the she-camel." They cited as an example of what they claimed to be an inversion of a sentence. This interpretation was adopted by Abu ʿUbayda, al-Farra', and a group. The Qur'an should be exonerated from it, because the correct view is that inversion occurs only in poetry, or if it comes in speech it is so rare that it cannot be used as a basis for analogy. As for the view that the parable is coined by comparing the caller of the disbeliever to the one who shouts, then His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the likeness of those who disbelieve﴾ is according to the implied sense: "And the likeness of the caller of those who disbelieve." This involves an omitted genitive construction, so it is not a comparison of the disbeliever to the one who shouts, nor to the one being shouted at, but rather a comparison of the disbeliever's caller, in his calling to him, to the one who shouts at the beasts, in that the disbeliever understands from what his caller addresses him with nothing but the sound of the voice without attention of mind or thought. So he is like the beast that, when shouted at, hears nothing from the one shouting at it except his calling and crying, and understands nothing else. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that by "that which does not hear" is meant the deaf and deaf-of-one-ear, who hears from the speech of one raising his voice with his speech only the calling and the sound, without understanding the letters. As for the view that the parable is coined by comparing the caller and the disbeliever to the one who shouts and the one being shouted at, this is the view preferred by Sibawayh regarding the verse, that the meaning is: "Your likeness, O Muhammad, and the likeness of those who disbelieve, is like the likeness of the one who shouts and the one being shouted at." Sibawayh's words have been disputed: it was said that this is an explanation of meaning, not an explanation of grammatical construction. It was also said that it is an explanation of grammatical construction, namely that there are two omissions in the sentence: an omission from the first part, which is the omission of "their caller," whose counterpart has been affirmed in the second; and an omission from the second part, which is the omission of "the one being shouted at," whose counterpart has been affirmed in the first. Thus he compared the caller of the disbelievers to the shepherd of goats in addressing one who does not understand him, and compared the disbelievers to goats in that they hear from what they are called to nothing but sounds, and do not know what lies beyond them. In this aspect there is much omission, for it involves the omission of two coordinated elements, since the grammatical construction would be: "And the likeness of those who disbelieve and their caller is like the likeness of the one who shouts and the one being shouted at." A group of our companions adopted this aspect, among them the master Abu Bakr ibn Tahir and his pupil Abu al-Hasan ibn Kharuf, and the master Abu ʿAli al-Shalaubin, and they said: the Arabs find it admirable, and it is among the excellent features of their speech. An example of it is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And put your hand into your bosom; it will come out white﴾ [al-Naml: 12]. The implied sense is: "Put your hand into your bosom; it will enter, and bring it out; it will come out white," so "it will enter" is omitted because of the indication of "it will come out," and "and bring it out" is omitted because of the indication of "put." They said: similar to this is the saying of the poet:

"And indeed, when I remember you, a torpor seizes me, as a sparrow shivers when the rain wets it."

He did not intend to compare his torpor to the shivering of a sparrow when rain wets it, because the two are motion and stillness, which are opposites; rather, his meaning is: "When I remember you, a trembling seizes me, then I become torpid, just as the sparrow, when the rain wets it, is seized by torpor, then shivers; except that the pounding and agitation of his heart come before the torpor, and the sparrow's torpor comes before its shivering." All these views regarding the comparison are only according to the consideration of comparing a single word to a single word, and the matching of a part of the preceding speech with a part of the speech compared to. But if the comparison is of the type of comparing a sentence to a sentence, then the matching of individual words is not observed in it; rather the meaning is considered. Abu al-Qasim al-Raghib interpreted the verse in this type of comparison. Al-Raghib said: When He compared the story of the disbelievers in their turning away from the caller to them to the truth with the story of the one who shouts, He placed mention of the one who shouts first, so as to build upon it what proceeds from him and from the one being shouted at. On this line goes ﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Baqara: 261], and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The likeness of what they spend in this worldly life﴾ [Al ʿImran: 117]. These are nine views on the interpretation of this verse.

Some discussion of it remains, so we say: "The likeness of those who" is the subject, its predicate is "like," and the kaf is for comparison. It compares the attribute with the attribute, that is, their attribute is like the attribute of the one who shouts. As for one who holds that the kaf is extra, his words are nothing, because an attribute is not the same as an attribute, so the kaf that gives comparison is necessary. Indeed, even if it came without the kaf we would suppose it omitted, because it is by it that the meaning is made correct. "The one who shouts" does not refer to a singular individual, but the intended meaning is a genus. It has been stated that the intended meaning is: like the one who shouts at the beasts, or like the one who calls out in the mountains from whom only the echo answers, or like the one who calls out at the deaf-and-deaf-of-one-ear, or like the one being shouted at, in which case it is an inversion. It was said: like the one who calls out to something far from him, which does not hear because of the distance, so the caller gets from that only the calling which tires and wearies him. It was said: the comparison was struck with the shepherd of sheep, because they are among the most foolish of animals, so they make their shepherd look foolish. In the proverb: "More foolish than the shepherd of eighty sheep." And Durayd ibn al-Simma said to Malik ibn ʿAwf on the day of Hawazin: "Shepherd of sheep, by Allah!" because when he came to fight the Prophet ﷺ, he ordered Hawazin and those with them to bring along their wealth and women. When Durayd met him, he said: "I see you have driven the wealth and the women?" He said: "They fight for their wealth and their sacred women." Durayd said to him: "Are you not afraid that you will be a shepherd of sheep? By Allah, I will not accompany you." And the poet said:

"I have become a mockery to the shepherd of sheep, who mocks me; what makes you doubt me, O shepherd of sheep?"

"Except calling and crying": this is an exceptive construction that is incomplete, because before it is an active transitive verb that has not taken its object. Some went to the view that it is not an incomplete exception and that "except" is extra, and that calling and crying are negated as to their hearing, the meaning being: "with that which does not hear calling or crying." This is weak, because the claim that "except" is extra is a claim without evidence. Al-Asmaʿi, may Allah have mercy on him, held this view in his verse:

"Swift camels that never cease except kneeling on the hardship, or we throw them toward a barren land."

His view in this was weak, and one does not affirm the extra use of "except" except in a place definitely established, so we affirm its extra use there. Some raised a question here, saying: If it is said that His saying, "does not hear except calling and crying," the only thing heard is calling and crying, so how does He blame them for not hearing except calling? It is as if it were said: they do not hear except what is heard, and this is not permissible. The answer: there is brevity in the speech, and the meaning is: they do not understand the meanings of what is said to them, just as beasts do not distinguish between the meanings of words that they do not make a sound with; rather they understand something slight, which they attain through long practice and frequent repetition. So it is as if it were said: they have nothing but hearing of the call without grasping the meanings and the purposes. End of his words. ʿAli ibn ʿIsa said: He only made it a dual, saying "calling and crying," because calling is the request for action and crying is the answering of a voice.

﴿Deaf, dumb, and blind﴾: the discussion of these words has already preceded.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 171 (part 2 of 2):

﴿So they do not understand﴾: Once their lack of the meanings of these senses was established, He decreed that they do not understand (ya'qilun). As Abu al-Ma'ali (al-Juwayni) and others said: "Reason (al-'aql) consists of necessary knowledges which these senses give, since acquiring them necessarily requires the senses." End of quote. It has been said: the intended meaning is acquired reason (al-'aql al-iktisabi), because innate reason (al-'aql al-matbu') was already present in them, and reason is of two kinds: innate (matbu') and acquired (maksub). Since the path to acquiring acquired reason is to make use of these three faculties, their turning away from them amounted to a lack of acquired reason. For this reason it was said: "Whoever lacks a sense has lacked a kind of reason."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 172:

﴿O you who have believed, eat from the good things We have provided for you﴾: When Exalted Allah permitted His servants to eat what is in the earth of the lawful and good, and the aspects of the lawful are many, He explained to them what He had forbidden, because it is fewer. When He explained what He had forbidden, everything other than that remained permitted until another prohibition comes. This is like the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) when he was asked about what the muhrim (one in the state of ihram) may wear, and he said: "He should not wear a shirt or trousers." He turned away from mentioning what is permitted to mentioning what is prohibited, because the permitted is abundant and the prohibited is scarce, and this is from eloquent concision (al-ijaz al-baligh). "Those who have believed" means those who believed in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and it is possible that the people of Madinah are intended, so the wording is general and the intended meaning is specific. It was also said that this address emphasizes His saying: ﴿O people, eat from what is in the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 168]. Since the word "people" includes the believer and the disbeliever, Allah distinguished the believers with this call, to honour them and to draw attention to their special status. The apparent meaning of "eat" is the command to the customary eating. It was also said that what is intended is benefiting from it, and by "eating" He pointed to the aspects of benefit, since eating is the greatest of them, for by it the body is sustained. It was said: this is closer to the meaning, because Exalted Allah did not restrict lawfulness and unlawfulness to foods only, but extended them to everything from which one benefits, such as eating, drinking, wearing and other things. "The good things" (al-tayyibat): it was said they are the lawful, and it was said they are the pleasant and agreeable, but on condition that (p-485) it be lawful. This condition has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿Eat from what is in the earth, lawful and good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 168], so this second command is like the first in that its object is the pleasant that is lawful. "What We have provided for you": here the provision is attributed to the first-person speaker with the plural of majesty (nun al-azamah), because of the favour and kindness in provision. If "the good things" is interpreted as the lawful, this indicates that what Allah provides is divided into lawful and unlawful, unlike the view of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school), who held that provision is only ever lawful. The discussion of provision (rizq) has already been treated at the beginning of the surah, so there is no need to repeat it here. Whoever prevents provision from being unlawful says: the meaning is "eat from the pleasant of what We have provided for you," and that is the lawful. He commanded it and permitted it, Exalted, to repel the one who imagines that variety in foods and refinement in making them pleasant is forbidden. So the mention of "the pleasant" was specified for this meaning.

﴿And give thanks to Allah﴾: This is an iltifat (shift in grammatical person), for it moves from the first-person speaker to the third-person name. The wisdom in this is clear, because this explicit name includes all the attributes, among them the attributes of bestowing, providing and being thanked. It is not limited to this particular favour; rather one gives thanks for all the blessings and favours, of which this particular favour is one. The verb "give thanks" (ishkuru) is here followed by the preposition lam, and the discussion of this has already been given.

This verse contains two commands. The first: "eat." They said: it is obligatory when averting harm, recommended when with a guest, and when free of external circumstances it is permissible, and so it is in the verse. The second: ﴿and give thanks to Allah﴾, which is a command and not a permission. It was said: it is not possible to hold that giving thanks is obligatory, because it is either by the heart, or by the tongue, or by the limbs. By the heart it is knowledge of the blessing's coming from the Benefactor, or resolve to honour Him; by the tongue or the limbs it is the act. As for that knowledge, it is one of the necessary consequences of the perfection of the intellect, for the sane person does not forget it; and if that knowledge is necessary (darurī), how can it be made obligatory? As for the resolve to honour Him by tongue and limbs, that resolve of the heart follows from verbal affirmation and action by the limbs. So if we have shown that neither of them is obligatory, then the resolve not to make them obligatory is more appropriate. As for thanking by the tongue, it may be interpreted either as acknowledging Him as the Benefactor or as praising Him. This is not obligatory by consensus; rather it belongs to the category of recommended acts. As for thanking by the limbs and members, it is to perform actions that indicate honouring Him, and that too is not obligatory. Another speaker, other than this one, said, summarising: it is obligatory to believe that He deserves honour, and to manifest that by the tongue or other actions where they are present. This discussion of whether giving thanks is obligatory or not would have been more fitting at the first mention of a command to give thanks, which is His saying: ﴿And give thanks to Me and do not be ungrateful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 152].

﴿If you are indeed those who worship Him﴾: Whoever holds that its meaning is the meaning of idh (when), his statement is weak; this is a Kufan view. The conditional here is not intended except to establish and to stir the souls. It is as though the meaning is: worship of Him is obligatory, so giving thanks to Him is obligatory. This is like saying to one who is truly a servant: "If you are my servant, then obey me," not intending a pure condition, but presenting it in the form of a condition so that it will be more compelling for obedience and more stirring to it. It was also said: "worship" is used to mean recognition (irfan), as He said: ﴿I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56]. It was said: its meaning is "that they should know Me," so the meaning becomes: give thanks to Allah if you are those who know Him and His blessings, and this is the use of the effect for the cause (idlaq al-athar ala al-mu'aththir). It was also said: "worship" is used to mean the intention of worship, that is: give thanks to Allah if you intend to worship Him, because giving thanks is the head of the acts of worship. Al-Zamakhshari said: if it is correct that you single Him out for worship and acknowledge that He is the master of blessings. And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Allah, Exalted, says: 'I, and the jinn and mankind, are in a great matter: I create and others are worshipped; I provide and others are thanked.'" End of his words. Here iyyaha (him, as the object) is a preceding object, and it was placed first because the governing verb fell at the end of the verse, for emphasis and to magnify its status, since it refers back to Allah, Exalted, as in your saying: ﴿You alone do we worship, and You alone do we ask for help﴾ [al-Fatihah: 5]. This is one of the positions in which the pronoun must be detached, and when it precedes the governing verb or follows it, it is detached only in cases of necessity. He said:

"ilayka hatta balaghtu iyyaka"
(To you, until I reached iyyaka)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 173 (part 1 of 3):

﴿He has only forbidden you carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which any name other than God's has been invoked.﴾: The discussion of *innama* (a particle of restriction, "only") has already been given under His words: ﴿We are only reformers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 11]. The majority of readers recited *harrama* (He has forbidden) with a verb whose subject is the pronoun referring to the Name of God, and what follows it is in the accusative. Thus *ma* is a *muhayyi'a* (the particle that "prepares" the verb, so that *inna* is followed by a verbal sentence). *Inna* took the verbal sentence because of this preparing *ma*. Ibn Abi Ablah recited *al-maytata* and what follows it in the nominative. In this case *ma* is a *mawsula* (relative pronoun) serving as the subject of *inna*, and its returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: "What God has forbidden is carrion," and what follows it is the predicate of *inna*. Abu Ja'far recited *hurrima* (passive, with doubled *r*). Accordingly *ma* can have two readings. The first: it is a relative pronoun serving as the subject of *inna*, its returning pronoun being the hidden pronoun in *hurrima*, and *al-maytatu* is the predicate of *inna*. The second: *ma* is a *muhayyi'a* and *al-maytatu* is the nominative subject of *hurrima*. Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami recited *innama harama* with a fatha on the *ha'* and a damma on the *ra'*, lightened, making the verb intransitive, and *al-maytatu* and what follows it are in the nominative. Here too *ma* may be either a *muhayyi'a* or a *mawsula*: *al-maytatu* is the subject of *yahrumu* if *ma* is a *muhayyi'a*, and the predicate of *inna* if *ma* is a *mawsula*. Abu Ja'far recited *al-mayyitatu* with the *ya'* doubled throughout the Qur'an. This is the original form, from which the lightened form derives. The discussion of this lightening has already been given under His words: ﴿or like a downpour﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19]. Both are sound dialectal forms, and a poet combined them in his verse:

*"He who has died and found rest is not a dead man (mayyit); the true dead man (al-mayt) is the dead man among the living."*

It is said that Abu Mu'adh related from the early grammarians that *al-mayt* (lightened) refers to one whose soul has departed, while *al-mayyit* (doubled) refers to one who has not yet died but has witnessed the causes of death. The discussion of death has already been given.

(When He, exalted is He, commanded) eating what is lawful in the preceding verse, He here detailed the kinds of what is unlawful, and attributed the prohibition to carrion. The apparent meaning is that the omitted element is eating, because prohibition does not attach to the substance itself, and because what was previously permitted was eating, in His words: ﴿Eat of what is in the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 168], ﴿Eat of the good things We have provided you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 172]. Therefore what is prohibited here is eating. Likewise, the omission of a modifying element (*hadhf al-mudaf*) is to be estimated according to what fits the context. So in His words: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ [al-Nisa': 23], the omitted element is intercourse, as if it were said: "intercourse with your mothers." And in His words: ﴿and lawful to you is what lies beyond that﴾ [al-Nisa': 24], meaning intercourse with what lies beyond that. Accordingly, all other kinds of benefiting from these mentioned substances are forbidden, either by analogy to eating according to those who accept analogy (*qiyas*), or by a revealed textual proof according to those who do not accept it.

Some people said, in substance: When God, exalted is He, attributed the prohibition to carrion and what is conjoined with it, and tied it to their substances, this was evidence of the emphasis of the ruling of prohibition and its inclusion of all kinds of benefit. Thus no part of them is particularized except by a proof that permits benefiting from it. This view thus inferred from the wording the prohibition of all kinds of benefiting. The more evident view is what we have mentioned, namely that the omitted modifying element is particularized as eating. The apparent meaning of the word carrion includes all of it in generality, and no part of it is particularized except by a proof.

Some said: This generality was particularized by His words: ﴿Lawful to you is the game of the sea and its food, as a provision for you and for the travelers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 96], and by what is narrated from His saying (ﷺ): "Two kinds of carrion have been made lawful for us." Ibn Atiyyah said: The fish and the locust never entered into this generality. End of his words. If he means that they did not enter into the indication of the wording, we do not grant him that. If he means that they did not enter into the intention, then he is right, because the particularizing text shows that the speaker did not intend their inclusion in the general wording that was particularized.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): Among carrion there is what is lawful, namely fish and locusts. (I answer): He intended what people understand and customarily recognize. Do you not see that when one says, "So-and-so ate carrion," understanding does not leap to fish and locusts? Just as when one says, "He ate blood," understanding does not leap to liver and spleen. Out of regard for custom and common usage, they have said: whoever swears not to eat meat and then eats fish does not break his oath, even though in reality it is meat. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿that you may eat from it fresh meat﴾ [al-Nahl: 14]. And they compared this to one who swears not to ride a beast and then rides an unbeliever; he does not break his oath, even though God called him a beast in His words: ﴿Indeed the worst of beasts in God's sight are those who disbelieve﴾ [al-Anfal: 55]. End of his words.

The summary of what he says is that fish and locusts are not included in the generality of carrion in terms of indication, and this is not as he said. How could that be, when it is narrated from him (ﷺ) that he said: "Two kinds of carrion have been made lawful for us"? If they were not included in the indication, there would have been no need for a legislative statement of their lawfulness, since they would remain indicated as lawful by His words: ﴿Eat of what is in the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 168], ﴿Eat of the good things We have provided you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 172]. The condition of generality is not what people understand and customarily recognize, as al-Zamakhshari said. Rather, even if the addressees had no awareness at all, and no knowledge of some individual members of the general term, and the ruling was attached to the general term, that individual member of which the addressees were unaware would be included in it.
