An example of this is what occurs in a hadith: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) forbade eating every animal with fangs from among the predators." Here the ruling was attached to every animal with fangs. The addressees, who were the Arabs, had no knowledge of some individual kinds of fanged animals, and that individual kind is included in the generality and is judged by the prohibition. As in our land, the land of al-Andalus, there is a predatory animal called among them the *dubb* and the *sam'*, which has fangs, preys upon a man and eats him, does not resemble the lion, nor the wolf, nor the panther, nor anything that the Arabs know, and we know of no creature of its kind created outside the land of al-Andalus. No one holds that it is not included in the generality of the prohibition on eating every animal with fangs. Rather, the prohibition covers it just as it covers others the Arabs were acquainted with and recognized, because the ruling was tied to the generality and attached to it. It is therefore attached to each of its individual members, even to one that was not created at all at the time of address, and was afterward created in a form distinct from all other fanged forms, and so it is included and judged by the prohibition. Al-Zamakhshari's illustration with faith is different: faith has rulings attached to it, and the verification of this ultimately amounts to a particularization of the generality by the intention to exclude some individual members from it.

The word *al-maytah* (carrion) means what died without ritual slaughter (*dhakah*) of an animal that has a flowing blood (*nafs sa'ilah*). There is disagreement about the floating fish, which is what died in water and then floated. Malik and others held it to be lawful. The school of the Iraqis holds that eating it is forbidden. In the words of some Hanafis, Abu Hanifa held it to be disliked. As for locusts that die without any cause, Malik and the majority of his followers hold them to be forbidden; Ibn Abd al-Hakam and Ibn Nafi' hold them to be lawful; and Ibn al-Qasim, Ibn Wahb, Ashhab and Sahnun have qualifications regarding locusts, mentioned in the books of the Malikis. This is the ruling on carrion with respect to eating. As for benefiting from any part of it, such as the hide, hair, feathers, milk, eggs, rennet, fetus, fat, bone, horn, tooth, and sinew, that is mentioned in the books of jurisprudence (*fiqh*), and they have much disagreement and qualification on these, which may be consulted in their works.

"And blood": its apparent meaning is generality, and it is particularized to flowing blood by the verse in al-An'am. When it is flowing, there is no disagreement about its impurity and prohibition. Regarding the blood of fish that separates from it, in the school of Malik there are two views: one, that it is pure, and this implies that it is not forbidden. They agreed on the permissibility of eating blood that is absorbed into the veins and the flesh, which is difficult to extract, and likewise the liver and the spleen. The exegetes mentioned, regarding a small amount of flowing blood, the disagreement about pardoning it and about the measure of what is small, and the disagreement about the blood of fleas, bedbugs, and flies. All of this belongs to the science of jurisprudence and is to be sought in its books.

God, exalted is He, did not mention a wisdom for the prohibition of eating carrion and blood, nor did any explicit text come from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on this. Had God, exalted is He, imposed upon us the permissibility of eating carrion and blood, that would have been a law that must be followed. People have mentioned that the wisdom in the prohibition of carrion is that its blood congeals in it through death, and that it causes harm to the eater. And the wisdom in the prohibition of blood is that after it flows out it congeals, so it is like the congealed matter in carrion in causing harm. This is nothing, because sense contradicts it. We have found people from among the nations who eat carrion and drink blood, whose appearances and complexions are among the finest and most beautiful that can be seen, and no harm befalls them from it.

* *

"The flesh of swine": its apparent meaning is that what is forbidden of it is its flesh alone. Dawud, the head of the Zahiris, held this view and said: What is forbidden is the flesh, not the fat. Other scholars said: What is forbidden is its flesh and all its parts. The flesh was singled out for mention, while the intended meaning is all its parts, because flesh is the greatest of what is benefited from. Just as He specified killing game for the one in the state of ihram, while the intended meaning is the prohibition of all acts regarding game. And just as He specified abandoning trade ﴿when the call is made to prayer on the day of Friday﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 9], because trade was what they most sought for their benefit, and so it was the most distracting to them from other things, while the intended meaning is all matters that distract from prayer. Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): Why did He mention the flesh of swine and not its fat? (I answer): Because the fat is included in the mention of the flesh, as shown by the expression "lean meat," meaning that it is fatty. End of his words.

This saying of theirs is not evidence that fat is included in the mention of flesh, because describing a thing as mixed with something else does not indicate that the other thing is subsumed under the meaning of that thing. Do you not see that you say, for example, "a man who is a milk-drinker," or "a man who is a scholar"? This does not indicate that milk or knowledge is included in the mention of the man, nor that the mention of the man alone, stripped of the two attributes, indicates them. Ibn Atiyyah said: The mention of flesh of swine was singled out to indicate the prohibition of its substance, whether slaughtered or not, and to include fat and what is there of cartilage and other things. The community agreed on the prohibition of its fat. End of his words. This is not as he stated, because the mention of flesh does not include fat and the cartilage present there, since each of flesh, fat, and the cartilage or other things present there has no name peculiar to it. When one name is applied, the other does not enter into it, nor does it indicate it, neither by correspondence (*mutabaqa*) nor by inclusion (*tadammun*). So singling it out in mention indicates singling it out for the ruling, for if the whole were intended, it would have been expressed by a word that indicates the whole. And his words, "The community agreed on the prohibition of its fat," are not as he stated. Do you not see that Dawud prohibits only what God mentioned, which is the flesh and not the fat? Unless Ibn Atiyyah means what is reported from Abu al-Ma'ali Abd al-Malik al-Juwayni, that disagreement from Dawud is not taken into account in consensus, so that this would be consensus in his view. But the scholars who had complete understanding and independent reasoning, centuries before al-Juwayni was born, took Dawud into account and transmitted his opinions in their books, just as they transmitted the opinions of the imams, such as al-Awza'i, Abu Hanifa, Malik, al-Thawri, al-Shafi'i, and Ahmad. Peoples, lands, judges, and rulers over long periods adhered to his school, his view, and his method. But in our age this school has been carried in a different way. Since flesh, according to Malik, includes fat, he held that if someone swore not to eat meat and then ate fat, he would break his oath. Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i disagreed with him and said: He does not break his oath, just as if he swore not to eat fat and then ate meat. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿We forbade them their fats﴾ [al-An'am: 146]. And the consensus is that meat is not forbidden to the Jews. So the truth is that neither of the two is included under the wording of the other.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 173 (part 2 of 3):

They differed concerning benefiting from its (the pig's) bristles, for making beads and other things. Malik, Abu Hanifa and al-Awza'i permitted that, while al-Shafi'i did not permit it. Abu Yusuf said: "I dislike stringing beads with it." It is also narrated from him that it is permitted. And does the term "pig" (khinzir) include the sea-pig (khinzir al-bahr)? Abu Hanifa and his companions held that it does, so they prohibited eating it. Ibn Abi Layla, al-Awza'i and al-Shafi'i said: "There is no harm in eating it." Al-Layth said: "The water-pig is not eaten, nor its human-like (creature), nor its dog." Malik was asked about the water-pig, and he hesitated and said: "You call it a pig." Ibn al-Qasim said: "I avoid it, but I do not declare it forbidden."

As for the reason for the prohibition of pork, they said: the Christians alone eat it, so the Muslims were forbidden to eat it, so that this would be a means to make you cut off from them, since the pig was among their most prized foods. It was also said: because it is a transformed (mamsukh) creature, so the prohibition of eating it was made more severe because of the corruption of its origin. And it was said: because it severs jealousy and removes self-respect, so people become lax in violating what is forbidden and in permitting fornication. But the noble verse does not point to any of these causes that they mentioned.

﴿"And that over which a name other than God's has been invoked"﴾: that is, what is slaughtered for idols and tyrants (taghut). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Dahhak. Or it means that over which the name of other than God has been mentioned; this was said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas and others. Or it means that over which the name of al-Masih has been mentioned; this was said by al-Zuhri. Or it means what is intended by other than the face of God, Exalted, for boasting and vainglory; this was said by 'Ali and al-Hasan. It is narrated that 'Ali said concerning the camels which Ghalib, the father of al-Farazdaq, slaughtered: "They are among what was invoked for other than God," so people abandoned them; 'Ali took the intention into account in that. al-Hasan forbade eating a camel that a woman slaughtered for her amusement, and said: "She slaughtered it for an idol." 'A'isha was asked about eating what the non-Arabs slaughter for their festivals and send as gifts to the Muslims, and she said: "Do not eat it, but eat from their trees." What appears from the verse is the prohibition of what is slaughtered for other than God, so it falls under the wording "other than God": the idol, al-Masih, boasting and amusement. This is called "ihlal" (invocation) because they raise their voices with the name of the one to whom the slaughtered animal is dedicated at the time of slaughter. Then the usage was broadened and became common until it became the name for every slaughter over which a voice is raised or not raised, just as "ihlal" with the talbiya became a designation for every pilgrim who raises his voice or does not. Whoever takes that to mean what is slaughtered at the altar stones (nusub), which are idols, permits the slaughter of a Christian if he mentions the name of al-Masih over it. This was the view of 'Ata', Makhul, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Ibn al-Musayyib, al-Awza'i and al-Layth. Abu Hanifa, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad, Zufar, Malik and al-Shafi'i said: their slaughter is not eaten if they mention the name of al-Masih over it, and this is the apparent meaning of His saying "for other than God," as we have mentioned, because invoking for other than God is the proclaiming of a name other than God's name, and he did not distinguish between the name of al-Masih and the name of others. It is narrated from 'Ali that he said: "If you hear the Jews and Christians invoking for other than God, do not eat."

"Uhilla" is in the passive voice, the subject of which is not named. The subject that is not named is the prepositional phrase "bihi" in His saying "bihi," and the pronoun in "bihi" refers back to "ma," since it is a relative pronoun meaning "alladhi." The meaning of "ahalla bi-kadha" is "he cried out," so the meaning is: "that over which was cried out," i.e., in its slaughter, for other than God. Then this became a metaphor for everything slaughtered for other than God, whether a cry was raised in its slaughter or not, as we have mentioned before. There is a difference of opinion regarding the slaughter of a Magian. The same applies to what is forbidden to Jews and Christians by the Book. As for what they have forbidden by their own reasoning, it is lawful for us. Ibn 'Atiyya transmitted from Malik: disapproval concerning what a People of the Book has invoked over with the name of al-Masih, or slaughtered for a church, but it does not reach the level of prohibition.

* *

﴿"Whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, there is no sin upon him"﴾. And He said: ﴿"Whoever is compelled by hunger, not inclining to sin"﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 3]. And He said: ﴿"He has already detailed for you what He has forbidden to you, except what you are compelled to"﴾ [al-An'am: 119]. So in this verse He did not restrict the compulsion, while He restricted it in what came before, for the one who is compelled is not inclining to sin. In the first verse, by His saying: ﴿"neither desiring nor transgressing"﴾. Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr and others said: "neither desiring (against) the Muslims nor transgressing against them." So the "rebel" (baghi) and the "transgressor" (adi) include: highway robbers, one who rebels against the ruler, one who travels to sever family ties, and raiding the Muslims and what resembles it. For others than these, the concession applies. This is the view of al-Shafi'i: that if he did not go out rebelling against the Imam of the Muslims, and his journey was not in disobedience, he may eat of these prohibited things when compelled. But if his journey was in disobedience, or he was rebelling against the Imam, it is not permitted for him to eat. 'Ikrima, Qatada, al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd and others said: "not intending corruption and aggression, by finding an alternative to these prohibited things." Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said: "not rebelling in eating carrion, nor transgressing by eating it, while he finds other than it." This returns to the meaning of the statement before it. Abu Hanifa and Malik said likewise, and these permitted the rebels who go out against the Muslims to eat these prohibited things under compulsion, just as they permitted it for the people of justice. al-Suddi said: "'neither desiring'" means exceeding what keeps his life and preserves his strength, so that eating it becomes for pleasure; "'nor transgressing'" means taking provision from it. It was also said: "'neither desiring'" means regarding them as lawful, and "'nor transgressing'" means taking provision from them. Shahr ibn Hawshab said: "'neither desiring'" means exceeding the amount which is lawful for him, and "'nor transgressing'" means not intending it in what is not lawful for him.

The apparent meaning of these statements, as understood from the apparent meaning of the verse, is that there is no sin in consuming any of these prohibited things for the one who is compelled and is neither a rebel nor a transgressor. And His saying: ﴿"except what you are compelled to"﴾ [al-An'am: 119] necessarily requires the restriction mentioned here and in His saying: ﴿"not inclining to sin"﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 3], because the verse of al-An'am contains a reference to these two verses, since He said: ﴿"He has already detailed for you what He has forbidden to you, except what you are compelled to"﴾ [al-An'am: 119]. The detailing of the prohibited things is in these two verses, and the compulsion in them is restricted, so it is necessarily restricted in the verse that refers to others. The apparent meaning of "baghy" and "'udwan" is that they arise from acts of disobedience, for when the two are mentioned without qualification, the mind immediately turns to that. Regarding the permissible quantity of carrion one may eat, and regarding taking provision from it, and regarding drinking wine in necessity, the reasoning is by analogy to these prohibited things. There is a disagreement regarding eating human flesh, mentioned in the books of jurisprudence. They said: if he finds carrion and pork, he eats the carrion, for it was permitted to him in a state of necessity, while pork is never lawful in any circumstance. This is not as they said, because His saying: "whoever is compelled" comes after the mention of the prohibition of carrion, blood and pork flesh. The meaning is: whoever is compelled to eat any of these prohibited things, their rank in permissibility for eating is equal, so none of them is more entitled than the other to be permitted, and the compelled person chooses among what he eats of them. Therefore their statement that pork is never lawful in any circumstance is not correct.

Some commentators mentioned that they unanimously agreed that whoever travels for raiding, pilgrimage or trade, and is at the same time rebelling in seizing wealth, or transgressing in abandoning prayer or zakat, the rebellion and transgression he is engaged in does not prevent him from permitting carrion in necessity. They also unanimously agreed on the permissibility of granting the concession to the rebel or transgressor who is present. But the transmission of these two consensus claims is open to scrutiny.

The readers differed concerning the vowel of the nun in His saying "fa-man-idturra" (fa-manidturra), "wa-an uhkum," "wa-lakini-nzur" and similar forms, and the vowel of the dal in "wa-laqadi-stuhzi'a," the ta' in "wa-qalati-khruj 'alayhinna" [Yusuf: 31], the vowel of the tanwin in "fatilan" [al-Nisa': 49], "unzur" [al-Nisa': 50] and similar, and the vowel of the lam in forms such as "quli-d'u Allah" [al-Isra': 110], and the waw in forms such as "awi-d'u al-Rahman" [al-Isra': 110]. 'Asim and Hamza read these with kasra; Abu 'Amr vocalized them, except at the lam and the waw; 'Abbas and Ya'qub did so except at the waw; and the rest of the seven read with damma, except that Ibn Dhakwan read the tanwin with kasra. Regarding "bi-rahmatin udkhulu" [al-A'raf: 49] and "khabithatin ijtutht" [Ibrahim: 26] there is a difference from him. The rule for this is that the damma of these verbs is fixed; if it is incidental, then the kasra is used, as in "an imshu" [Sad: 6]. The justification for kasra is that it is the vowel of the meeting of two quiescent letters, and for damma that it is a following vowel (ittiba'). They did not count the quiescent letter, because it is a weak barrier, or to show that the vowel of the deleted hamzat al-wasl was a damma. Abu Ja'far and Abu al-Sammal read "fa-manidturra" with kasra on the ta', and its origin is "idtarara"; when it was assimilated, the vowel of the ra' was transferred to the ta'. Ibn Muhaysin read "fa-manittarra," assimilating the dad into the ta', wherever it occurs. The meaning of "idtirar" is being compelled by lack of food and hunger; this is the view of the majority. It was also said its meaning is: being forced and overpowered into eating these prohibited things. The accusative of "ghayra baghin" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun hidden in "idturra," and some made it a circumstantial clause from the hidden pronoun in the omitted verb coordinated with His saying "idturra," and they estimated it: "whoever is compelled and eats, neither desiring nor transgressing." al-Qadi and Abu Bakr al-Razi estimated it thus, so as to make that a condition on the eating, not on the compulsion. What they met is not necessarily fixed, since it is possible that this estimated element comes after "neither desiring nor transgressing," and indeed this is the apparent and the preferable view, because estimating it before "neither desiring nor transgressing" creates a separation between what is apparently connected to what follows, and there is no such separation in estimating it after "neither desiring nor transgressing." "'Adin" is the active participle of "'adá" and not the active participle of "'ada," which would make it inverted or elided in the pattern of shaka and lata, as some have claimed, because inversion is not regular and we do not resort to it except for a reason, and there is no reason here to claim inversion. The root of "baghy," as already stated, is seeking corruption, though it has also been used for seeking in general, so it was employed for seeking good, as the poet said:

"Is the good that I seek / or the evil which seeks me?"

And it is said:

"Let not the tying of amulets prevent you from seeking good."

"There is no sin upon him": "ithm" is bearing the burden of a sin, and by this He negated blame from him. The omitted element we estimated, "fa-akala" (then he ate), is necessary, because it does not negate sin from one in whom compulsion has not occurred, and this consequence is not based on compulsion alone, but on the eating that follows compulsion, while the one compelled is neither a rebel nor a transgressor. The apparent meaning of this structure is that whenever one is disobedient in his journey and eats, sin is upon him, since he is described as a rebel, unlike Abu Hanifa and those who agree with him, who permit him to eat in necessity. The apparent meaning of the form "idturra" is the occurrence of necessity in general, by oppression or coercion, whether the compulsion occurs while travelling or at home. The apparent meaning of His saying "there is no sin upon him" is the negation of every kind of sin from him if he eats, not the obligation to eat. al-Tabari said: eating in necessity is not a concession but a binding obligation, and if he refrains from eating he would be disobedient. Masruq said: "It has reached me that whoever is compelled to carrion and does not eat until he dies enters the Fire," as though he indicated that he is a killer of himself by abandoning what God has permitted him.

(إنَّ اللَّهَ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ): Since (Allah) had mentioned forbidden things and thereby required abstention from them, and then mentioned their permissibility for the one compelled (al-mudtarr) in that restricted circumstance, He followed this with an announcement about Himself that He is Forgiving (Ghafur) and Merciful (Rahim). This is because the addressee is liable to disobey and fall into eating some of these prohibited things. So He informed them that He is Forgiving to the disobedient when they repent, and Merciful to them.

Or, because the addressee, when compelled, eats more than the measure of need, and so He, the Exalted, is Forgiving to him for that, and Merciful in that He permitted him the measure of need.

Or, because the ruling of prohibition persists in these forbidden things, and then He granted a concession (rukhsah) to consume them despite the existence of the prohibiting factor. He expressed this concession and permission by the term forgiveness (maghfirah), and then after forgiveness He mentioned the attribute of mercy, meaning: for the sake of My mercy toward you I have permitted you that.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 174–176 (part 1 of 3):**

﴿Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has sent down of the Book﴾: It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that it was revealed concerning the scholars of the Jews. They used to receive gifts from their inferiors, and they hoped that the Prophet who was to be sent would be from among them. When he was sent from among others, they altered his description and said: "This is the description of the Prophet who will emerge at the end of time," so that they would not follow him. It is also related from him that he said: The kings asked their scholars before the mission (baʿth): "What do you find in the Torah?" They said: "We find that Allah will send a Prophet after the Messiah, called Muhammad, (who will forbid) usury, wine, frivolity and the shedding of blood." When he was sent, the kings said to the Jews: "Is this the one you find in your Book?" They said, out of greed for the kings' wealth: "This is not that Prophet." So the kings gave them wealth, and the verse was revealed as a refutation of them. It has also been said: it was revealed concerning every one who conceals the truth in order to obtain some aim or to fulfil some aim, whether a Muslim, a Jew, a polytheist, or a denier (muʿattil). And if the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) is authentic, the ruling is general (ʿumum) and the ruling applies generally. And if the occasion is specific, it still encompasses those scholars of the Muslims who knowingly conceal the truth for the sake of a worldly benefit they obtain.

﴿What Allah has sent down of the Book﴾: Its apparent meaning is that it was sent down from above to below, and that Allah, may He be exalted, sent an angel with it, that is, with the Book, to His Messenger. It has also been said that the meaning of "Allah sent down" is "Allah manifested," as in His saying: ﴿I will send down the like of what Allah has sent down﴾ [al-Anʿam: 93], meaning: "I will manifest." So the meaning becomes: those who conceal what Allah has manifested, so that manifesting stands in contrast to concealing. Regarding what is meant by "the Book" here there are several views. The first is that it is the Torah, so the concealers are the rabbis of the Jews, who concealed and altered the description of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and concealed verses in the Torah, such as the verse of stoning and the like. It has also been said: the Torah and the Gospel, and the singular is used for the written text; the concealers are then the Jews and the Christians. Allah described His Prophet in both Books, gave his attributes in them, and named him, saying: ﴿They find him written down with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 157], and He said: ﴿And a messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad﴾ [al-Saff: 6]. Both groups denied the description of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The Torah and the Gospel bear witness to this, and the texts are present in them now, in several places, including in the Torah in the ninth chapter, in the tenth chapter of the first book, and in the twentieth chapter of the fifth book. And in the Gospel there are passages that indicate this, all of which have been mentioned by those who have dealt with this subject. It has also been said: the Book is the written text, which is more general than the Torah and the Gospel, so it encompasses everyone who conceals what Allah has sent down of matters pertaining to the rulings, past and present, and every concealer of truth and hider of a lawful matter.

﴿And sell it for a small price﴾: Since they received in exchange for the concealment some of the unlawful gain (suḥt) of this world, this resembled buying and selling, since both involve a consideration and something given in return. Therefore it was described as purchase (ishtiraʾ). As for "it" (bihi): the pronoun refers either to the concealment, or to the Book, or to the relative pronoun "what" (mā). There are three views, the most apparent of which is the last, and it would then involve an omitted noun, that is: "by concealing what Allah has sent down." The difference between this view and the view that the pronoun refers to the concealment is that in the latter case it refers to the verbal noun implied by "they conceal," whereas in this case it refers to an omitted noun. The discussion of His saying ﴿in order to purchase with it a small price﴾ [al-Baqara: 79] has already preceded, so it suffices and needs no repetition, except that the act of purchasing was made a cause there, while here it is made coordinate with "they conceal." The report is attributed to the combination of the two matters, concealment and purchase (p. 492), because the causes of concealment are not restricted to purchase; rather, purchase is only one of its causes. The concealment of what Allah has sent down of the Book, which is the command of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the denial of his prophethood and the alteration of his description, was due to several matters, among them envy (baghy): ﴿out of envy that Allah should send down His bounty upon whom He wills of His servants﴾ [al-Baqara: 90]. Among them is the loss they feared because he was from the Arabs and not from them. Among them is the pursuit of leadership and the desire to make the people of their religion follow them. And among them is the acquisition of their wealth and the bribes (rishaʾ) of their kings and commoners.

﴿Those—they eat nothing into their bellies but the Fire﴾: He used a whole sentence as the predicate of "indeed" because a sentence is more emphatic than a single word, and He began with "those" (ulāʾika), since it is a demonstrative indicating that the subject has the aforementioned attributes. This matter has already been discussed concerning His saying: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqara: 5]. Then He gave four predicates about "those": The first is: ﴿they eat nothing into their bellies but the Fire﴾. Some took it in its apparent sense and said: this occurs in this world, and the bribes they eat turn into fire in their bellies, and they do not perceive it except after death, and Allah, may He be exalted, prevented them from realising that it is fire, as a means of luring them on and giving them respite. In this view there is some figurative usage, because at the time of eating it was not fire; rather, afterwards it became fire in their bellies. It has also been said that this occurs in the Hereafter, and so it is also literal. And they differed: it was said: all that they ate of the unlawful gain and bribes in this world will be turned into fire in the Hereafter, and then Allah will feed it to them in the Fire. It was also said: He will command the guardians of Hell (al-zabaniya) to feed them the Fire, so that the punishment for eating will be of the same kind as the eating. Most scholars interpret His saying: ﴿they eat nothing into their bellies but the Fire﴾ to mean that they will be recompensed with the Fire for what they committed of concealing what Allah has sent down and buying a small price with it, and that what they acquired with these blameworthy attributes will end in the Fire. He expressed it by "eating," because eating is the greatest of the benefits for which wealth is spent. And His mention of "into their bellies" is either for emphasis, since it is known that eating occurs only in the belly, so it becomes like His saying: ﴿nor a bird that flies with its two wings﴾ [al-Anʿam: 38]; or it is a metaphor for filling the belly, since one says: "So-and-so ate in his belly," and "So-and-so ate in part of his belly"; or it is to remove the suspicion of figurative usage, since one says: "So-and-so ate his property" when he squandered it, even though he did not eat it. And He made the thing eaten "the Fire," naming it by what it will lead to, because it is the cause of the Fire. This is like their saying: "So-and-so ate blood," meaning the blood-money (diya), because it is a substitute for blood. A poet said:

*If there were a living man who would accept wealth as ransom, we would drive wealth to him like a full flood.*
*But we are a people whose brother was struck, and they chose disgrace contentedly, and preferred blood to milk.*

Another said:

*I have eaten blood, if I do not make you fall with a blow, far-reaching at the earring's place, fragrant in its scent.*

Another said:

*She eats every night an akaf.*

meaning the price of an akaf (a saddle-pad). The sense of being clothed with the thing is present in all of this. Naming a thing by what it will lead to is common, and among it is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly only consume into their bellies a Fire﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 10]. And among it is the one who drinks from vessels of gold and silver, who only drags into his belly the Fire of Hell. He mentioned "into their bellies" as a warning about their evil and a condemnation of their squandering the greatest blessing for the sake of the food that is the best thing to consume, as al-Raghib said. Ibn ʿAtiyya said something similar, saying: In the mention of the belly there is a warning about their path, that they sold their Hereafter for their share of food which has no value, and about their vileness in obeying their bellies.

﴿And Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection﴾: This is the second predicate about "those." Its apparent meaning is the negation of speech absolutely, meaning direct speech with them. Therefore whatever comes in the Qur'an or the Sunnah whose apparent meaning is that He, may He be exalted, converses with them is interpreted as meaning that He commands whoever says it to them, like His saying: ﴿He said: "Begone therein, and do not speak to Me"﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 108]. And the negation of His speaking to them (p. 493) indicates anger against them. Do you not see that whoever is angry with a person cuts him off and ends speaking to him? For in speaking—even if it is with evil—there is some intimacy and some attention to the one addressed. It has also been said: the meaning of "Allah will not speak to them" is: He will be angry with them. The intended meaning is not the negation of speech, since in other places there are things whose apparent meaning is that He speaks to the disbelievers, as reported by al-Hasan. It has also been said: the meaning is not general, since the Qur'an contains things whose apparent meaning is that He speaks to them, such as His saying: ﴿By your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ [al-Hijr: 92], and questioning can only occur by speech, and He said: ﴿He said: "Begone therein, and do not speak to Me"﴾. So the meaning is: He will not speak to them with words of goodness, favour and greeting; rather, He will speak to them with words that distress them. It has also been said: the meaning is that He will not send the angels to them with greetings. It has also been said: "And Allah will not speak to them" is an allusion to their deprivation of the honour enjoyed by the people of Paradise, in that Allah honours them with His speech. It has also been said: the meaning is that He will not compel them to speak, since whoever you speak to, you have invited his speech; so it is as if He said: their speech will not be solicited, like His saying: ﴿nor will they be permitted to offer excuses﴾ [al-Mursalat: 36]. So He negated speech, while meaning what necessarily follows from it, which is the soliciting of speech.

﴿And will not purify them﴾: This is the third predicate, and the meaning is: He will not accept their deeds as He accepts the deeds of the pure (azkiyaʾ), or He will not place them in the station of the pure. It has also been said: the meaning is that He will not correct their wicked deeds. It has also been said: the meaning is that He will not praise them, from the usage "zakka fulanan," meaning he praised him, as al-Zajjaj said. It has also been said: He will not cleanse them from the filth of their disbelief, and this is the meaning of some people's saying: He will not cleanse them of the causes of punishment, as Ibn Jarir said. It has also been said: the meaning is that He will not call them pure.

(﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾): This is the fourth predicate about "those," and the interpretation of His saying "And for them is a painful punishment" has already been given at the beginning of the surah. These four predicates follow from the concealment and the purchase of a small price, and they are joined by the conjunctive "and" which gathers them. He coordinated the predicates with "and," and there is no disagreement about its permissibility, unlike the case where they are not coordinated, for in that there is disagreement and detail. The mention of these predicates is appropriate to what precedes them, and the coordination of some of them with others is appropriate, for what we shall mention. We say: When an attribute is mentioned and a matter is made to follow upon it, the Arabs have two methods in this. One is that those matters that follow from the attributes are set in correspondence with them, the first of them corresponding to the first of those attributes and the second to the second, so that the correspondence is achieved both in meaning and in verbal order, where the first is matched with the first and the second with the second. And sometimes the first of those matters is adjacent to the attribute that follows it, so the correspondence is achieved in meaning but not in verbal order. This verse came in this category.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 174–176 (part 2 of 3):

When the Exalted mentioned their buying the small price, and that this was an allusion to their base and fleeting provisions (*maṭāʿim*), He first began the report with His saying: ﴿They consume nothing into their bellies but the Fire﴾. Then the Exalted set against their concealment of the religion (and concealment is that they do not speak of it but hide it) His saying: ﴿And Allah will not speak to them﴾. So they were recompensed, for preventing speech about the religion, by being denied God's speaking to them. Built upon their concealment of the religion, and their buying with what Allah sent down a small price, is that they are false witnesses and bearers of evil reports, in that they altered the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and claimed that the prophet who was sent was other than this. All of that was answered by His saying: ﴿And will not purify them﴾. Then He mentioned last what has been prepared for them of painful punishment. He ordered upon the buying of the small price His saying: ﴿They consume nothing into their bellies but the Fire﴾; upon the concealment His saying: ﴿And Allah will not speak to them﴾; and upon the combined two attributes His saying: ﴿And will not purify them, and for them is a painful punishment﴾. So He began first with what corresponds to each individually, and second with what corresponds to the whole. Since the first sentence contained a verb ascribed to Allah, the statement that corresponds to it contained a verb ascribed to Allah. Since the second was ascribed to them, and contains no ascription to Allah, the sentence corresponding to it was ascribed to them, and there did not come "what Allah feeds them into their bellies but the Fire."

(The mention of) this verse is appropriate to what precedes it, because in the verse before it the Exalted mentioned the permission of good things, then specified some prohibited things. It was therefore fitting to mention the recompense of whoever concealed something of Allah's religion and of what He sent down to His prophets. This was a warning that believers should not fall into what the People of the Book fell into: concealing what Allah sent down to them and buying a small price with it.

﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾. "Those" (*ulāʾika*) is a demonstrative referring to the concealers mentioned earlier and to what they were threatened with. The explanation of ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾ was given in full at the beginning of the surah, so there is no need to repeat it.

﴿And punishment in exchange for forgiveness﴾: Since he had first presented their state in this world, that they exchanged error for guidance, he mentioned the result of that in the Hereafter, which is that they exchanged forgiveness, which is the result of guidance and the cause of the longer, everlasting bliss, for the longer, everlasting punishment, which is the result of error. This is because they knew the truth and concealed it for a base worldly purpose. If that is so, it is the buying of punishment in exchange for forgiveness. The wording "they bought" (*ishtaraw*) implies their preference for error and punishment, because a person does not buy except what he has desire for, affection for, and choice in. This indicates the utmost loss and the disregard of consequences.

﴿How patient they are in (the pursuit of) the Fire!﴾ Scholars differ concerning *mā*. The most evident view is that it is exclamatory (*taʿajjub*, expressing wonder), and this is the view of the majority of exegetes. There have come: ﴿Woe to man, how ungrateful he is!﴾ [80:17], and ﴿Hear them and see them!﴾ [19:38]. The grammarians agreed that the exclamatory *mā* is in the nominative position as a subject (*mubtadaʾ*), but they differed: Is it an indefinite complete noun (*nakira tāmma*) with the verb after it in the position of the predicate (*khabar*)? Or an interrogative that carries the meaning of wonder, with the verb after it in the position of the predicate? Or a relative pronoun whose verb after it is a relative clause (*ṣila*) and whose predicate is omitted? Or a qualifying noun whose verb after it is a qualifier (*ṣifa*) and whose predicate is omitted? These are four views mentioned in grammar. The first is the view of Sibawayh and the majority; the second is the view of al-Farra' and Ibn Darastawayh; the third and fourth are of al-Akhfash. Likewise they differed concerning *afʿal* after the exclamatory *mā*: is it a verb (the view of the Basrans), or a noun (the view of the Kufans)? On this difference depends the question of the object after it: is it a direct object (*mafʿūl bihi*) or something resembling a direct object? If we say that the statement is an exclamation, then wonder is the amazement at a thing while the cause of its occurrence is hidden, and this is impossible with respect to Allah the Exalted. So it refers to someone to whom such a thing is possible; that is, they are among those of whom an observer says: "How patient they are in (the pursuit of) the Fire!"

Those who held the statement to be an exclamation differed: Is it patience that actually occurs for them when they are in the Fire? Al-Asamm held this, and said: When it is said to them, ﴿Be silent therein, and do not speak to Me﴾ [23:108], they fall silent and their speech ceases, and they endure the Fire because they have despaired of deliverance. The view of al-Asamm is weak, because the apparent sense of the wonder is that it concerns their patience at the present moment, not that they will be patient, and because the people of the Fire may well express anguish. It was also said: "patience" is a metaphor for remaining in the Fire, meaning: how long He has kept them in the Fire. Or is it patience for which they are described in this world? This is the view of the majority. There is a difference as to whether it is literal or metaphorical. Those who held it to be literal said: its meaning is "how patient they are in an action that leads them to the Fire," because they were knowledgeable that whoever opposed the Prophet (ﷺ) would go to the Fire; this was said by al-Mu'arrij. It was also said: the implied meaning is "how patient they are in the deeds of the people of the Fire," as you say: "How similar your generosity is to Hatim!", meaning: to the generosity of Hatim. So the genitive noun was omitted and the noun in the genitive was placed in its position. This is the view of al-Kisa'i and Qutrub, and it is close to the view of al-Mu'arrij. It was also said: "asbara" here means "ajra'a" (to be bold), which is a Yemeni dialect usage. Thus the word "asbara" at that point would be shared between its more immediate meaning, restraining oneself upon a disliked thing, and the meaning of boldness: "how bold they are in the action that brings them near the Fire." This was said by al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Rabi' and Ibn Jubayr. Al-Farra' said: al-Kisa'i informed me, saying: the judge of Yemen informed me that two litigants came before him, and an oath became incumbent upon one of them, so his opponent swore to him, and he said to him: "How bold you are against Allah!" (*mā aṣbarak ʿalā Allāh*, in the sense of *mā ajra'ak*).

Those who held it to be metaphorical: It was said: it is a metaphor intended to mean action, that is, "how much they act like the people of the Fire." This was said by Mujahid. It was also said: it is a metaphor intended to mean little anguish, that is, "how little they are distressed about the Fire." It was also said: it is a metaphor intended to mean contentment. Its explanation is that one who is content with a thing is content with its consequence and its necessary result, once that necessity is known. When they proceeded to what necessitates the Fire while knowing this, they became like those content with the punishment of Allah and patient under it. This is like what one says to someone who has exposed himself to the anger of the ruler: "How patient you are under the shackles and the prison!"

Al-Zamakhshari said: "How patient they are in (the pursuit of) the Fire!" is an expression of wonder at their state in being engaged in the things that bring about the Fire, without any concern on their part. End of his words. The discussion that the statement is an exclamation ends here.

Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna and al-Mubarrad held that *mā* is interrogative, not exclamatory, and that it is a question in the sense of rebuke directed at them: "What made them patient in the Fire, so that they abandoned the truth and followed falsehood?" This is the view of Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi. It is said: *ṣabbarahu* and *aṣbarahu* have the same meaning, that is, he made him patient. Not that *aṣbara* here means "he restrained and compelled," so that *afʿala* would mean *faʿala*, contrary to al-Mubarrad, who claimed that *aṣbara* means *ṣabbara*. We do not know this in the language. The *hamza* is only for causation, that is, making someone possessed of patience.

Some people held that *mā* is negative, and the meaning is: "God does not make them patient in the Fire," that is, He does not make them endure the punishment. Thus the following are gathered in the meaning of His saying ﴿How patient they are in (the pursuit of) the Fire!﴾: the exclamatory, the interrogative, and the negative. And it is established concerning the exclamatory: is it literal or metaphorical? And both: is that in this world or in the Hereafter?

﴿That is because Allah has sent down the Book with the truth﴾. "That" (*dhālika*) is a reference to the threat mentioned earlier; this was said by al-Zajjaj. Or it refers to the ruling against them that they are among the people who abide eternally in the Fire; this was said by al-Hasan. Or to the punishment; this was said by al-Zamakhshari. Or to the buying; this was said by Ibn Attiyya, following one of the interpretations of His saying "sent down the Book" that will be mentioned. That is, that buying, with what was already decreed for them in the knowledge of Allah and what His reports announced concerning them, or the concealment. The least likely of these is that it refers to what preceded of Allah's reports: that He sealed their hearts, their hearing and their sight, and that they are deaf, dumb and blind, so they do not understand.

The grammatical analysis of *dhālika* has been disputed. It was said: it is in the accusative, governed by an omitted verb whose implied meaning is "We did that," and the *bā'* in *bi-anna Allāh* is connected to that omitted verb. It was said: it is in the nominative, and they differed: is it the subject (*fāʿil*), with the implied meaning "that was due for them"? Or the predicate of an omitted subject, with the implied meaning "the matter is that"; that is, what they were promised of punishment is because Allah sent down the Book with the truth. So they differed. Or is it the subject (*mubtadaʾ*), with the predicate being His saying "because Allah sent down": that is, "that is established and fixed, because Allah sent down the Book with the truth." In that case "that" refers to the nearest thing mentioned, which is the punishment, and the predicate is not merely Allah's sending down of the Book with the truth, but what follows from His sending it down: its opposition and its concealment. Here the cause is put in the place of the effect. The interpretation in meaning: that punishment is theirs by concealing what Allah sent down of the Book accompanied by the truth, or of the Book which He sent down with the truth. Al-Akhfash said: the predicate is omitted; its implied meaning is "that is known because Allah...," so the *bā'* is connected to this implied predicate. The Book is the Torah and the Gospel, or the Qur'an, or the Books of Allah sent down to His prophets, or what He wrote for them of wretchedness by His saying "deaf, dumb, blind." Then the Book would mean judgment and decree. These are four views.

"With the truth": Ibn Abbas said: with justice. Muqatil said: the opposite of falsehood. Makki said: with what is necessary. Wherever "with the truth" is mentioned, it means what is necessary.

﴿Indeed, those who differ concerning the Book﴾: It was said: they are the Jews, and the Book is the Torah, and their disagreement is their concealment of the mission of Jesus and then the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ). They believed in part of it, which is what they made apparent, and disbelieved in part of it, which is what they concealed. It was also said: they are the Jews and the Christians; this was said by al-Suddi. Their disbelief in disagreement is with what Allah the Exalted related of the stories of Jesus and his mother, peace be upon them both, and by denying the Gospel. Disagreement arose among them to the point that they cursed one another and fought. It was also said: they are the disbelieving Arabs, and the Book is the Qur'an. Some of them said it is sorcery, some said it is "tales of the ancients," some said it is fabrication, and so on. It was also said: they are the People of the Book and the polytheists. The People of the Book said: it is a statement of Muhammad (ﷺ), and is not the speech of Allah. They said: only a human teaches him; they said: "You have studied (it)"; they said: "This is nothing but a fabrication," and so on. The polytheists said: some said it is sorcery, some said it is poetry, some said it is soothsaying, some said it is tales, some said it is fabrication, and so on.

The apparent meaning is the report about those from whom disagreement concerning what Allah sent down of the Book proceeded, that they were in hostility and enmity, because disagreement is the setting for mutual hatred and divergence, just as agreement is the setting for mutual love and unity.

In al-Muntakhab: The closer view is to take the Book as the Torah and the Gospel, in which the good news of Muhammad (ﷺ) is mentioned, because the people had known that and concealed it, and they knew its interpretation. When the Exalted presents what functions as the reason for sending down punishment upon them, the closer view is that the intended Book is their own Book, which is the basis among them, not the Qur'an. End of his words.

"Within a far-reaching schism" (*lafi shiqaqin ba'id*): It was previously mentioned that this is derived either from the fact that each party moves to one side (*shiqq*) while the other is on the opposite side, or from the fact that each one causes hardship (*yashuqqu*) to the other. He used *shiqaq* (schism, opposition) as a metaphor for enmity, and described the schism as "far" either because it is far from the truth or because it is far from harmony. Or he used it as a metaphor for length, meaning: in a lengthy enmity that does not end. This disagreement is the reason each group believes that its own Book is the truth and that others are fabrications, and in this they have lied. The Books of God resemble one another and confirm one another.

These noble verses contain the second call to people, commanding them to eat of what is lawful and good, and forbidding them to follow Satan. They mention his "steps" (*khutuwat*), as though people were tracing his footprints and treading in his tracks. So whenever he takes a step, they place their feet upon it, and this is an exaggeration of following him. Then He explained that He forbade them to follow him only because he is the enemy who openly displays his enmity. Then He did not suffice with mentioning enmity until He mentioned that he commands them to commit sins. Since he was their leader (*matbu'*) and they followed him, the mention of commanding is appropriate, since they are obeying what he adorned for them and whispered to them. Then He mentioned what he commands them with, which is commanding them to fabricate against God and to speak about God what they do not know about Him. Then He mentioned the severity of their turning away from what God revealed, and their insistence on following the ways of their forefathers, to the extent that if their forefathers had been deprived of reason and guidance, they would still have followed them, as an exaggeration of blind imitation (*taqlid*, following without evidence) and of turning away from the Book of God, and as a continuation of the later generation upon the practices of the earlier generation, without reflection or reasoning.

Then He mentioned that the likeness of the disbelievers and of their caller to what God revealed is the likeness of one who shouts at what hears nothing except mere sounds. Then He mentioned their condition of deafness, dumbness, and blindness, which prevent knowledge from reaching a person. Therefore He concluded with His saying, "so they do not reason," because the paths of reason and knowledge are corrupted for them. Then He called out to the believers with a special call, and commanded them to eat of the good and to thank God. Then He mentioned some of the things He prohibited, and permitted eating them in a state of necessity, and stipulated in taking that that the one in necessity should be neither rebellious nor transgressing. And when He made lawful the eating of good things and prohibited what He prohibited here, He mentioned the states of those who concealed what God revealed and sold it for a small price, so that this community might take heed from the condition of one who concealed knowledge and sold it for the lowest price. For He, exalted is He, informed that such a person does not eat in his belly except fire, meaning that which necessitates eating fire. And that God will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection, nor purify them, when He speaks to the believers with the speech of mercy and kindness. And He mentioned that, with the absence of instruction, which is the highest rank for a subordinate from a superior, since He qualified him for intimate communication and conversation, and with the absence of praise for them, there is for them a painful punishment. Then He exaggerated in their blame, that these are the ones who preferred misguidance over guidance, and punishment over bliss. Then He mentioned that they are on the verge of being marveled at for their endurance of the fire, and that what befell them of punishment is because of what God revealed in the Book, which they opposed. Then He mentioned that those who disagreed about what God revealed are in an enmity that does not end.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 174–176 (part 1 of 3):**

﴿Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has sent down of the Book﴾: It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that it was revealed concerning the scholars of the Jews. They used to receive gifts from their inferiors, and they hoped that the Prophet who was to be sent would be from among them. When he was sent from among others, they altered his description and said: "This is the description of the Prophet who will emerge at the end of time," so that they would not follow him. It is also related from him that he said: The kings asked their scholars before the mission (baʿth): "What do you find in the Torah?" They said: "We find that Allah will send a Prophet after the Messiah, called Muhammad, (who will forbid) usury, wine, frivolity and the shedding of blood." When he was sent, the kings said to the Jews: "Is this the one you find in your Book?" They said, out of greed for the kings' wealth: "This is not that Prophet." So the kings gave them wealth, and the verse was revealed as a refutation of them. It has also been said: it was revealed concerning every one who conceals the truth in order to obtain some aim or to fulfil some aim, whether a Muslim, a Jew, a polytheist, or a denier (muʿattil). And if the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) is authentic, the ruling is general (ʿumum) and the ruling applies generally. And if the occasion is specific, it still encompasses those scholars of the Muslims who knowingly conceal the truth for the sake of a worldly benefit they obtain.

﴿What Allah has sent down of the Book﴾: Its apparent meaning is that it was sent down from above to below, and that Allah, may He be exalted, sent an angel with it, that is, with the Book, to His Messenger. It has also been said that the meaning of "Allah sent down" is "Allah manifested," as in His saying: ﴿I will send down the like of what Allah has sent down﴾ [al-Anʿam: 93], meaning: "I will manifest." So the meaning becomes: those who conceal what Allah has manifested, so that manifesting stands in contrast to concealing. Regarding what is meant by "the Book" here there are several views. The first is that it is the Torah, so the concealers are the rabbis of the Jews, who concealed and altered the description of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and concealed verses in the Torah, such as the verse of stoning and the like. It has also been said: the Torah and the Gospel, and the singular is used for the written text; the concealers are then the Jews and the Christians. Allah described His Prophet in both Books, gave his attributes in them, and named him, saying: ﴿They find him written down with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 157], and He said: ﴿And a messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad﴾ [al-Saff: 6]. Both groups denied the description of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The Torah and the Gospel bear witness to this, and the texts are present in them now, in several places, including in the Torah in the ninth chapter, in the tenth chapter of the first book, and in the twentieth chapter of the fifth book. And in the Gospel there are passages that indicate this, all of which have been mentioned by those who have dealt with this subject. It has also been said: the Book is the written text, which is more general than the Torah and the Gospel, so it encompasses everyone who conceals what Allah has sent down of matters pertaining to the rulings, past and present, and every concealer of truth and hider of a lawful matter.

﴿And sell it for a small price﴾: Since they received in exchange for the concealment some of the unlawful gain (suḥt) of this world, this resembled buying and selling, since both involve a consideration and something given in return. Therefore it was described as purchase (ishtiraʾ). As for "it" (bihi): the pronoun refers either to the concealment, or to the Book, or to the relative pronoun "what" (mā). There are three views, the most apparent of which is the last, and it would then involve an omitted noun, that is: "by concealing what Allah has sent down." The difference between this view and the view that the pronoun refers to the concealment is that in the latter case it refers to the verbal noun implied by "they conceal," whereas in this case it refers to an omitted noun. The discussion of His saying ﴿in order to purchase with it a small price﴾ [al-Baqara: 79] has already preceded, so it suffices and needs no repetition, except that the act of purchasing was made a cause there, while here it is made coordinate with "they conceal." The report is attributed to the combination of the two matters, concealment and purchase (p. 492), because the causes of concealment are not restricted to purchase; rather, purchase is only one of its causes. The concealment of what Allah has sent down of the Book, which is the command of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the denial of his prophethood and the alteration of his description, was due to several matters, among them envy (baghy): ﴿out of envy that Allah should send down His bounty upon whom He wills of His servants﴾ [al-Baqara: 90]. Among them is the loss they feared because he was from the Arabs and not from them. Among them is the pursuit of leadership and the desire to make the people of their religion follow them. And among them is the acquisition of their wealth and the bribes (rishaʾ) of their kings and commoners.

﴿Those—they eat nothing into their bellies but the Fire﴾: He used a whole sentence as the predicate of "indeed" because a sentence is more emphatic than a single word, and He began with "those" (ulāʾika), since it is a demonstrative indicating that the subject has the aforementioned attributes. This matter has already been discussed concerning His saying: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqara: 5]. Then He gave four predicates about "those": The first is: ﴿they eat nothing into their bellies but the Fire﴾. Some took it in its apparent sense and said: this occurs in this world, and the bribes they eat turn into fire in their bellies, and they do not perceive it except after death, and Allah, may He be exalted, prevented them from realising that it is fire, as a means of luring them on and giving them respite. In this view there is some figurative usage, because at the time of eating it was not fire; rather, afterwards it became fire in their bellies. It has also been said that this occurs in the Hereafter, and so it is also literal. And they differed: it was said: all that they ate of the unlawful gain and bribes in this world will be turned into fire in the Hereafter, and then Allah will feed it to them in the Fire. It was also said: He will command the guardians of Hell (al-zabaniya) to feed them the Fire, so that the punishment for eating will be of the same kind as the eating. Most scholars interpret His saying: ﴿they eat nothing into their bellies but the Fire﴾ to mean that they will be recompensed with the Fire for what they committed of concealing what Allah has sent down and buying a small price with it, and that what they acquired with these blameworthy attributes will end in the Fire. He expressed it by "eating," because eating is the greatest of the benefits for which wealth is spent. And His mention of "into their bellies" is either for emphasis, since it is known that eating occurs only in the belly, so it becomes like His saying: ﴿nor a bird that flies with its two wings﴾ [al-Anʿam: 38]; or it is a metaphor for filling the belly, since one says: "So-and-so ate in his belly," and "So-and-so ate in part of his belly"; or it is to remove the suspicion of figurative usage, since one says: "So-and-so ate his property" when he squandered it, even though he did not eat it. And He made the thing eaten "the Fire," naming it by what it will lead to, because it is the cause of the Fire. This is like their saying: "So-and-so ate blood," meaning the blood-money (diya), because it is a substitute for blood. A poet said:

*If there were a living man who would accept wealth as ransom, we would drive wealth to him like a full flood.*
*But we are a people whose brother was struck, and they chose disgrace contentedly, and preferred blood to milk.*

Another said:

*I have eaten blood, if I do not make you fall with a blow, far-reaching at the earring's place, fragrant in its scent.*

Another said:

*She eats every night an akaf.*

meaning the price of an akaf (a saddle-pad). The sense of being clothed with the thing is present in all of this. Naming a thing by what it will lead to is common, and among it is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly only consume into their bellies a Fire﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 10]. And among it is the one who drinks from vessels of gold and silver, who only drags into his belly the Fire of Hell. He mentioned "into their bellies" as a warning about their evil and a condemnation of their squandering the greatest blessing for the sake of the food that is the best thing to consume, as al-Raghib said. Ibn ʿAtiyya said something similar, saying: In the mention of the belly there is a warning about their path, that they sold their Hereafter for their share of food which has no value, and about their vileness in obeying their bellies.

﴿And Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection﴾: This is the second predicate about "those." Its apparent meaning is the negation of speech absolutely, meaning direct speech with them. Therefore whatever comes in the Qur'an or the Sunnah whose apparent meaning is that He, may He be exalted, converses with them is interpreted as meaning that He commands whoever says it to them, like His saying: ﴿He said: "Begone therein, and do not speak to Me"﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 108]. And the negation of His speaking to them (p. 493) indicates anger against them. Do you not see that whoever is angry with a person cuts him off and ends speaking to him? For in speaking—even if it is with evil—there is some intimacy and some attention to the one addressed. It has also been said: the meaning of "Allah will not speak to them" is: He will be angry with them. The intended meaning is not the negation of speech, since in other places there are things whose apparent meaning is that He speaks to the disbelievers, as reported by al-Hasan. It has also been said: the meaning is not general, since the Qur'an contains things whose apparent meaning is that He speaks to them, such as His saying: ﴿By your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ [al-Hijr: 92], and questioning can only occur by speech, and He said: ﴿He said: "Begone therein, and do not speak to Me"﴾. So the meaning is: He will not speak to them with words of goodness, favour and greeting; rather, He will speak to them with words that distress them. It has also been said: the meaning is that He will not send the angels to them with greetings. It has also been said: "And Allah will not speak to them" is an allusion to their deprivation of the honour enjoyed by the people of Paradise, in that Allah honours them with His speech. It has also been said: the meaning is that He will not compel them to speak, since whoever you speak to, you have invited his speech; so it is as if He said: their speech will not be solicited, like His saying: ﴿nor will they be permitted to offer excuses﴾ [al-Mursalat: 36]. So He negated speech, while meaning what necessarily follows from it, which is the soliciting of speech.

﴿And will not purify them﴾: This is the third predicate, and the meaning is: He will not accept their deeds as He accepts the deeds of the pure (azkiyaʾ), or He will not place them in the station of the pure. It has also been said: the meaning is that He will not correct their wicked deeds. It has also been said: the meaning is that He will not praise them, from the usage "zakka fulanan," meaning he praised him, as al-Zajjaj said. It has also been said: He will not cleanse them from the filth of their disbelief, and this is the meaning of some people's saying: He will not cleanse them of the causes of punishment, as Ibn Jarir said. It has also been said: the meaning is that He will not call them pure.

(﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾): This is the fourth predicate about "those," and the interpretation of His saying "And for them is a painful punishment" has already been given at the beginning of the surah. These four predicates follow from the concealment and the purchase of a small price, and they are joined by the conjunctive "and" which gathers them. He coordinated the predicates with "and," and there is no disagreement about its permissibility, unlike the case where they are not coordinated, for in that there is disagreement and detail. The mention of these predicates is appropriate to what precedes them, and the coordination of some of them with others is appropriate, for what we shall mention. We say: When an attribute is mentioned and a matter is made to follow upon it, the Arabs have two methods in this. One is that those matters that follow from the attributes are set in correspondence with them, the first of them corresponding to the first of those attributes and the second to the second, so that the correspondence is achieved both in meaning and in verbal order, where the first is matched with the first and the second with the second. And sometimes the first of those matters is adjacent to the attribute that follows it, so the correspondence is achieved in meaning but not in verbal order. This verse came in this category.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 174–176 (part 2 of 3):

When the Exalted mentioned their buying the small price, and that this was an allusion to their base and fleeting provisions (*maṭāʿim*), He first began the report with His saying: ﴿They consume nothing into their bellies but the Fire﴾. Then the Exalted set against their concealment of the religion (and concealment is that they do not speak of it but hide it) His saying: ﴿And Allah will not speak to them﴾. So they were recompensed, for preventing speech about the religion, by being denied God's speaking to them. Built upon their concealment of the religion, and their buying with what Allah sent down a small price, is that they are false witnesses and bearers of evil reports, in that they altered the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and claimed that the prophet who was sent was other than this. All of that was answered by His saying: ﴿And will not purify them﴾. Then He mentioned last what has been prepared for them of painful punishment. He ordered upon the buying of the small price His saying: ﴿They consume nothing into their bellies but the Fire﴾; upon the concealment His saying: ﴿And Allah will not speak to them﴾; and upon the combined two attributes His saying: ﴿And will not purify them, and for them is a painful punishment﴾. So He began first with what corresponds to each individually, and second with what corresponds to the whole. Since the first sentence contained a verb ascribed to Allah, the statement that corresponds to it contained a verb ascribed to Allah. Since the second was ascribed to them, and contains no ascription to Allah, the sentence corresponding to it was ascribed to them, and there did not come "what Allah feeds them into their bellies but the Fire."

(The mention of) this verse is appropriate to what precedes it, because in the verse before it the Exalted mentioned the permission of good things, then specified some prohibited things. It was therefore fitting to mention the recompense of whoever concealed something of Allah's religion and of what He sent down to His prophets. This was a warning that believers should not fall into what the People of the Book fell into: concealing what Allah sent down to them and buying a small price with it.

﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾. "Those" (*ulāʾika*) is a demonstrative referring to the concealers mentioned earlier and to what they were threatened with. The explanation of ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾ was given in full at the beginning of the surah, so there is no need to repeat it.

﴿And punishment in exchange for forgiveness﴾: Since he had first presented their state in this world, that they exchanged error for guidance, he mentioned the result of that in the Hereafter, which is that they exchanged forgiveness, which is the result of guidance and the cause of the longer, everlasting bliss, for the longer, everlasting punishment, which is the result of error. This is because they knew the truth and concealed it for a base worldly purpose. If that is so, it is the buying of punishment in exchange for forgiveness. The wording "they bought" (*ishtaraw*) implies their preference for error and punishment, because a person does not buy except what he has desire for, affection for, and choice in. This indicates the utmost loss and the disregard of consequences.

﴿How patient they are in (the pursuit of) the Fire!﴾ Scholars differ concerning *mā*. The most evident view is that it is exclamatory (*taʿajjub*, expressing wonder), and this is the view of the majority of exegetes. There have come: ﴿Woe to man, how ungrateful he is!﴾ [80:17], and ﴿Hear them and see them!﴾ [19:38]. The grammarians agreed that the exclamatory *mā* is in the nominative position as a subject (*mubtadaʾ*), but they differed: Is it an indefinite complete noun (*nakira tāmma*) with the verb after it in the position of the predicate (*khabar*)? Or an interrogative that carries the meaning of wonder, with the verb after it in the position of the predicate? Or a relative pronoun whose verb after it is a relative clause (*ṣila*) and whose predicate is omitted? Or a qualifying noun whose verb after it is a qualifier (*ṣifa*) and whose predicate is omitted? These are four views mentioned in grammar. The first is the view of Sibawayh and the majority; the second is the view of al-Farra' and Ibn Darastawayh; the third and fourth are of al-Akhfash. Likewise they differed concerning *afʿal* after the exclamatory *mā*: is it a verb (the view of the Basrans), or a noun (the view of the Kufans)? On this difference depends the question of the object after it: is it a direct object (*mafʿūl bihi*) or something resembling a direct object? If we say that the statement is an exclamation, then wonder is the amazement at a thing while the cause of its occurrence is hidden, and this is impossible with respect to Allah the Exalted. So it refers to someone to whom such a thing is possible; that is, they are among those of whom an observer says: "How patient they are in (the pursuit of) the Fire!"

Those who held the statement to be an exclamation differed: Is it patience that actually occurs for them when they are in the Fire? Al-Asamm held this, and said: When it is said to them, ﴿Be silent therein, and do not speak to Me﴾ [23:108], they fall silent and their speech ceases, and they endure the Fire because they have despaired of deliverance. The view of al-Asamm is weak, because the apparent sense of the wonder is that it concerns their patience at the present moment, not that they will be patient, and because the people of the Fire may well express anguish. It was also said: "patience" is a metaphor for remaining in the Fire, meaning: how long He has kept them in the Fire. Or is it patience for which they are described in this world? This is the view of the majority. There is a difference as to whether it is literal or metaphorical. Those who held it to be literal said: its meaning is "how patient they are in an action that leads them to the Fire," because they were knowledgeable that whoever opposed the Prophet (ﷺ) would go to the Fire; this was said by al-Mu'arrij. It was also said: the implied meaning is "how patient they are in the deeds of the people of the Fire," as you say: "How similar your generosity is to Hatim!", meaning: to the generosity of Hatim. So the genitive noun was omitted and the noun in the genitive was placed in its position. This is the view of al-Kisa'i and Qutrub, and it is close to the view of al-Mu'arrij. It was also said: "asbara" here means "ajra'a" (to be bold), which is a Yemeni dialect usage. Thus the word "asbara" at that point would be shared between its more immediate meaning, restraining oneself upon a disliked thing, and the meaning of boldness: "how bold they are in the action that brings them near the Fire." This was said by al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Rabi' and Ibn Jubayr. Al-Farra' said: al-Kisa'i informed me, saying: the judge of Yemen informed me that two litigants came before him, and an oath became incumbent upon one of them, so his opponent swore to him, and he said to him: "How bold you are against Allah!" (*mā aṣbarak ʿalā Allāh*, in the sense of *mā ajra'ak*).

Those who held it to be metaphorical: It was said: it is a metaphor intended to mean action, that is, "how much they act like the people of the Fire." This was said by Mujahid. It was also said: it is a metaphor intended to mean little anguish, that is, "how little they are distressed about the Fire." It was also said: it is a metaphor intended to mean contentment. Its explanation is that one who is content with a thing is content with its consequence and its necessary result, once that necessity is known. When they proceeded to what necessitates the Fire while knowing this, they became like those content with the punishment of Allah and patient under it. This is like what one says to someone who has exposed himself to the anger of the ruler: "How patient you are under the shackles and the prison!"

Al-Zamakhshari said: "How patient they are in (the pursuit of) the Fire!" is an expression of wonder at their state in being engaged in the things that bring about the Fire, without any concern on their part. End of his words. The discussion that the statement is an exclamation ends here.

Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna and al-Mubarrad held that *mā* is interrogative, not exclamatory, and that it is a question in the sense of rebuke directed at them: "What made them patient in the Fire, so that they abandoned the truth and followed falsehood?" This is the view of Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi. It is said: *ṣabbarahu* and *aṣbarahu* have the same meaning, that is, he made him patient. Not that *aṣbara* here means "he restrained and compelled," so that *afʿala* would mean *faʿala*, contrary to al-Mubarrad, who claimed that *aṣbara* means *ṣabbara*. We do not know this in the language. The *hamza* is only for causation, that is, making someone possessed of patience.

Some people held that *mā* is negative, and the meaning is: "God does not make them patient in the Fire," that is, He does not make them endure the punishment. Thus the following are gathered in the meaning of His saying ﴿How patient they are in (the pursuit of) the Fire!﴾: the exclamatory, the interrogative, and the negative. And it is established concerning the exclamatory: is it literal or metaphorical? And both: is that in this world or in the Hereafter?

﴿That is because Allah has sent down the Book with the truth﴾. "That" (*dhālika*) is a reference to the threat mentioned earlier; this was said by al-Zajjaj. Or it refers to the ruling against them that they are among the people who abide eternally in the Fire; this was said by al-Hasan. Or to the punishment; this was said by al-Zamakhshari. Or to the buying; this was said by Ibn Attiyya, following one of the interpretations of His saying "sent down the Book" that will be mentioned. That is, that buying, with what was already decreed for them in the knowledge of Allah and what His reports announced concerning them, or the concealment. The least likely of these is that it refers to what preceded of Allah's reports: that He sealed their hearts, their hearing and their sight, and that they are deaf, dumb and blind, so they do not understand.

The grammatical analysis of *dhālika* has been disputed. It was said: it is in the accusative, governed by an omitted verb whose implied meaning is "We did that," and the *bā'* in *bi-anna Allāh* is connected to that omitted verb. It was said: it is in the nominative, and they differed: is it the subject (*fāʿil*), with the implied meaning "that was due for them"? Or the predicate of an omitted subject, with the implied meaning "the matter is that"; that is, what they were promised of punishment is because Allah sent down the Book with the truth. So they differed. Or is it the subject (*mubtadaʾ*), with the predicate being His saying "because Allah sent down": that is, "that is established and fixed, because Allah sent down the Book with the truth."
