In that case "that" refers to the nearest thing mentioned, which is the punishment, and the predicate is not merely Allah's sending down of the Book with the truth, but what follows from His sending it down: its opposition and its concealment. Here the cause is put in the place of the effect. The interpretation in meaning: that punishment is theirs by concealing what Allah sent down of the Book accompanied by the truth, or of the Book which He sent down with the truth. Al-Akhfash said: the predicate is omitted; its implied meaning is "that is known because Allah...," so the *bā'* is connected to this implied predicate. The Book is the Torah and the Gospel, or the Qur'an, or the Books of Allah sent down to His prophets, or what He wrote for them of wretchedness by His saying "deaf, dumb, blind." Then the Book would mean judgment and decree. These are four views.

"With the truth": Ibn Abbas said: with justice. Muqatil said: the opposite of falsehood. Makki said: with what is necessary. Wherever "with the truth" is mentioned, it means what is necessary.

﴿Indeed, those who differ concerning the Book﴾: It was said: they are the Jews, and the Book is the Torah, and their disagreement is their concealment of the mission of Jesus and then the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ). They believed in part of it, which is what they made apparent, and disbelieved in part of it, which is what they concealed. It was also said: they are the Jews and the Christians; this was said by al-Suddi. Their disbelief in disagreement is with what Allah the Exalted related of the stories of Jesus and his mother, peace be upon them both, and by denying the Gospel. Disagreement arose among them to the point that they cursed one another and fought. It was also said: they are the disbelieving Arabs, and the Book is the Qur'an. Some of them said it is sorcery, some said it is "tales of the ancients," some said it is fabrication, and so on. It was also said: they are the People of the Book and the polytheists. The People of the Book said: it is a statement of Muhammad (ﷺ), and is not the speech of Allah. They said: only a human teaches him; they said: "You have studied (it)"; they said: "This is nothing but a fabrication," and so on. The polytheists said: some said it is sorcery, some said it is poetry, some said it is soothsaying, some said it is tales, some said it is fabrication, and so on.

The apparent meaning is the report about those from whom disagreement concerning what Allah sent down of the Book proceeded, that they were in hostility and enmity, because disagreement is the setting for mutual hatred and divergence, just as agreement is the setting for mutual love and unity.

In al-Muntakhab: The closer view is to take the Book as the Torah and the Gospel, in which the good news of Muhammad (ﷺ) is mentioned, because the people had known that and concealed it, and they knew its interpretation. When the Exalted presents what functions as the reason for sending down punishment upon them, the closer view is that the intended Book is their own Book, which is the basis among them, not the Qur'an. End of his words.

"Within a far-reaching schism" (*lafi shiqaqin ba'id*): It was previously mentioned that this is derived either from the fact that each party moves to one side (*shiqq*) while the other is on the opposite side, or from the fact that each one causes hardship (*yashuqqu*) to the other. He used *shiqaq* (schism, opposition) as a metaphor for enmity, and described the schism as "far" either because it is far from the truth or because it is far from harmony. Or he used it as a metaphor for length, meaning: in a lengthy enmity that does not end. This disagreement is the reason each group believes that its own Book is the truth and that others are fabrications, and in this they have lied. The Books of God resemble one another and confirm one another.

These noble verses contain the second call to people, commanding them to eat of what is lawful and good, and forbidding them to follow Satan. They mention his "steps" (*khutuwat*), as though people were tracing his footprints and treading in his tracks. So whenever he takes a step, they place their feet upon it, and this is an exaggeration of following him. Then He explained that He forbade them to follow him only because he is the enemy who openly displays his enmity. Then He did not suffice with mentioning enmity until He mentioned that he commands them to commit sins. Since he was their leader (*matbu'*) and they followed him, the mention of commanding is appropriate, since they are obeying what he adorned for them and whispered to them. Then He mentioned what he commands them with, which is commanding them to fabricate against God and to speak about God what they do not know about Him. Then He mentioned the severity of their turning away from what God revealed, and their insistence on following the ways of their forefathers, to the extent that if their forefathers had been deprived of reason and guidance, they would still have followed them, as an exaggeration of blind imitation (*taqlid*, following without evidence) and of turning away from the Book of God, and as a continuation of the later generation upon the practices of the earlier generation, without reflection or reasoning.

Then He mentioned that the likeness of the disbelievers and of their caller to what God revealed is the likeness of one who shouts at what hears nothing except mere sounds. Then He mentioned their condition of deafness, dumbness, and blindness, which prevent knowledge from reaching a person. Therefore He concluded with His saying, "so they do not reason," because the paths of reason and knowledge are corrupted for them. Then He called out to the believers with a special call, and commanded them to eat of the good and to thank God. Then He mentioned some of the things He prohibited, and permitted eating them in a state of necessity, and stipulated in taking that that the one in necessity should be neither rebellious nor transgressing. And when He made lawful the eating of good things and prohibited what He prohibited here, He mentioned the states of those who concealed what God revealed and sold it for a small price, so that this community might take heed from the condition of one who concealed knowledge and sold it for the lowest price. For He, exalted is He, informed that such a person does not eat in his belly except fire, meaning that which necessitates eating fire. And that God will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection, nor purify them, when He speaks to the believers with the speech of mercy and kindness. And He mentioned that, with the absence of instruction, which is the highest rank for a subordinate from a superior, since He qualified him for intimate communication and conversation, and with the absence of praise for them, there is for them a painful punishment. Then He exaggerated in their blame, that these are the ones who preferred misguidance over guidance, and punishment over bliss. Then He mentioned that they are on the verge of being marveled at for their endurance of the fire, and that what befell them of punishment is because of what God revealed in the Book, which they opposed. Then He mentioned that those who disagreed about what God revealed are in an enmity that does not end.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 174–176 (part 1 of 3):**

﴿Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has sent down of the Book﴾: It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that it was revealed concerning the scholars of the Jews. They used to receive gifts from their inferiors, and they hoped that the Prophet who was to be sent would be from among them. When he was sent from among others, they altered his description and said: "This is the description of the Prophet who will emerge at the end of time," so that they would not follow him. It is also related from him that he said: The kings asked their scholars before the mission (baʿth): "What do you find in the Torah?" They said: "We find that Allah will send a Prophet after the Messiah, called Muhammad, (who will forbid) usury, wine, frivolity and the shedding of blood." When he was sent, the kings said to the Jews: "Is this the one you find in your Book?" They said, out of greed for the kings' wealth: "This is not that Prophet." So the kings gave them wealth, and the verse was revealed as a refutation of them. It has also been said: it was revealed concerning every one who conceals the truth in order to obtain some aim or to fulfil some aim, whether a Muslim, a Jew, a polytheist, or a denier (muʿattil). And if the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) is authentic, the ruling is general (ʿumum) and the ruling applies generally. And if the occasion is specific, it still encompasses those scholars of the Muslims who knowingly conceal the truth for the sake of a worldly benefit they obtain.

﴿What Allah has sent down of the Book﴾: Its apparent meaning is that it was sent down from above to below, and that Allah, may He be exalted, sent an angel with it, that is, with the Book, to His Messenger. It has also been said that the meaning of "Allah sent down" is "Allah manifested," as in His saying: ﴿I will send down the like of what Allah has sent down﴾ [al-Anʿam: 93], meaning: "I will manifest." So the meaning becomes: those who conceal what Allah has manifested, so that manifesting stands in contrast to concealing. Regarding what is meant by "the Book" here there are several views. The first is that it is the Torah, so the concealers are the rabbis of the Jews, who concealed and altered the description of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and concealed verses in the Torah, such as the verse of stoning and the like. It has also been said: the Torah and the Gospel, and the singular is used for the written text; the concealers are then the Jews and the Christians. Allah described His Prophet in both Books, gave his attributes in them, and named him, saying: ﴿They find him written down with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 157], and He said: ﴿And a messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad﴾ [al-Saff: 6]. Both groups denied the description of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The Torah and the Gospel bear witness to this, and the texts are present in them now, in several places, including in the Torah in the ninth chapter, in the tenth chapter of the first book, and in the twentieth chapter of the fifth book. And in the Gospel there are passages that indicate this, all of which have been mentioned by those who have dealt with this subject. It has also been said: the Book is the written text, which is more general than the Torah and the Gospel, so it encompasses everyone who conceals what Allah has sent down of matters pertaining to the rulings, past and present, and every concealer of truth and hider of a lawful matter.

﴿And sell it for a small price﴾: Since they received in exchange for the concealment some of the unlawful gain (suḥt) of this world, this resembled buying and selling, since both involve a consideration and something given in return. Therefore it was described as purchase (ishtiraʾ). As for "it" (bihi): the pronoun refers either to the concealment, or to the Book, or to the relative pronoun "what" (mā). There are three views, the most apparent of which is the last, and it would then involve an omitted noun, that is: "by concealing what Allah has sent down." The difference between this view and the view that the pronoun refers to the concealment is that in the latter case it refers to the verbal noun implied by "they conceal," whereas in this case it refers to an omitted noun. The discussion of His saying ﴿in order to purchase with it a small price﴾ [al-Baqara: 79] has already preceded, so it suffices and needs no repetition, except that the act of purchasing was made a cause there, while here it is made coordinate with "they conceal." The report is attributed to the combination of the two matters, concealment and purchase (p. 492), because the causes of concealment are not restricted to purchase; rather, purchase is only one of its causes. The concealment of what Allah has sent down of the Book, which is the command of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the denial of his prophethood and the alteration of his description, was due to several matters, among them envy (baghy): ﴿out of envy that Allah should send down His bounty upon whom He wills of His servants﴾ [al-Baqara: 90]. Among them is the loss they feared because he was from the Arabs and not from them. Among them is the pursuit of leadership and the desire to make the people of their religion follow them. And among them is the acquisition of their wealth and the bribes (rishaʾ) of their kings and commoners.

﴿Those—they eat nothing into their bellies but the Fire﴾: He used a whole sentence as the predicate of "indeed" because a sentence is more emphatic than a single word, and He began with "those" (ulāʾika), since it is a demonstrative indicating that the subject has the aforementioned attributes. This matter has already been discussed concerning His saying: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqara: 5]. Then He gave four predicates about "those": The first is: ﴿they eat nothing into their bellies but the Fire﴾. Some took it in its apparent sense and said: this occurs in this world, and the bribes they eat turn into fire in their bellies, and they do not perceive it except after death, and Allah, may He be exalted, prevented them from realising that it is fire, as a means of luring them on and giving them respite. In this view there is some figurative usage, because at the time of eating it was not fire; rather, afterwards it became fire in their bellies. It has also been said that this occurs in the Hereafter, and so it is also literal. And they differed: it was said: all that they ate of the unlawful gain and bribes in this world will be turned into fire in the Hereafter, and then Allah will feed it to them in the Fire. It was also said: He will command the guardians of Hell (al-zabaniya) to feed them the Fire, so that the punishment for eating will be of the same kind as the eating. Most scholars interpret His saying: ﴿they eat nothing into their bellies but the Fire﴾ to mean that they will be recompensed with the Fire for what they committed of concealing what Allah has sent down and buying a small price with it, and that what they acquired with these blameworthy attributes will end in the Fire. He expressed it by "eating," because eating is the greatest of the benefits for which wealth is spent. And His mention of "into their bellies" is either for emphasis, since it is known that eating occurs only in the belly, so it becomes like His saying: ﴿nor a bird that flies with its two wings﴾ [al-Anʿam: 38]; or it is a metaphor for filling the belly, since one says: "So-and-so ate in his belly," and "So-and-so ate in part of his belly"; or it is to remove the suspicion of figurative usage, since one says: "So-and-so ate his property" when he squandered it, even though he did not eat it. And He made the thing eaten "the Fire," naming it by what it will lead to, because it is the cause of the Fire. This is like their saying: "So-and-so ate blood," meaning the blood-money (diya), because it is a substitute for blood. A poet said:

*If there were a living man who would accept wealth as ransom, we would drive wealth to him like a full flood.*
*But we are a people whose brother was struck, and they chose disgrace contentedly, and preferred blood to milk.*

Another said:

*I have eaten blood, if I do not make you fall with a blow, far-reaching at the earring's place, fragrant in its scent.*

Another said:

*She eats every night an akaf.*

meaning the price of an akaf (a saddle-pad). The sense of being clothed with the thing is present in all of this. Naming a thing by what it will lead to is common, and among it is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly only consume into their bellies a Fire﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 10]. And among it is the one who drinks from vessels of gold and silver, who only drags into his belly the Fire of Hell. He mentioned "into their bellies" as a warning about their evil and a condemnation of their squandering the greatest blessing for the sake of the food that is the best thing to consume, as al-Raghib said. Ibn ʿAtiyya said something similar, saying: In the mention of the belly there is a warning about their path, that they sold their Hereafter for their share of food which has no value, and about their vileness in obeying their bellies.

﴿And Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection﴾: This is the second predicate about "those." Its apparent meaning is the negation of speech absolutely, meaning direct speech with them. Therefore whatever comes in the Qur'an or the Sunnah whose apparent meaning is that He, may He be exalted, converses with them is interpreted as meaning that He commands whoever says it to them, like His saying: ﴿He said: "Begone therein, and do not speak to Me"﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 108]. And the negation of His speaking to them (p. 493) indicates anger against them. Do you not see that whoever is angry with a person cuts him off and ends speaking to him? For in speaking—even if it is with evil—there is some intimacy and some attention to the one addressed. It has also been said: the meaning of "Allah will not speak to them" is: He will be angry with them. The intended meaning is not the negation of speech, since in other places there are things whose apparent meaning is that He speaks to the disbelievers, as reported by al-Hasan. It has also been said: the meaning is not general, since the Qur'an contains things whose apparent meaning is that He speaks to them, such as His saying: ﴿By your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ [al-Hijr: 92], and questioning can only occur by speech, and He said: ﴿He said: "Begone therein, and do not speak to Me"﴾. So the meaning is: He will not speak to them with words of goodness, favour and greeting; rather, He will speak to them with words that distress them. It has also been said: the meaning is that He will not send the angels to them with greetings. It has also been said: "And Allah will not speak to them" is an allusion to their deprivation of the honour enjoyed by the people of Paradise, in that Allah honours them with His speech. It has also been said: the meaning is that He will not compel them to speak, since whoever you speak to, you have invited his speech; so it is as if He said: their speech will not be solicited, like His saying: ﴿nor will they be permitted to offer excuses﴾ [al-Mursalat: 36]. So He negated speech, while meaning what necessarily follows from it, which is the soliciting of speech.

﴿And will not purify them﴾: This is the third predicate, and the meaning is: He will not accept their deeds as He accepts the deeds of the pure (azkiyaʾ), or He will not place them in the station of the pure. It has also been said: the meaning is that He will not correct their wicked deeds. It has also been said: the meaning is that He will not praise them, from the usage "zakka fulanan," meaning he praised him, as al-Zajjaj said. It has also been said: He will not cleanse them from the filth of their disbelief, and this is the meaning of some people's saying: He will not cleanse them of the causes of punishment, as Ibn Jarir said. It has also been said: the meaning is that He will not call them pure.

(﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾): This is the fourth predicate about "those," and the interpretation of His saying "And for them is a painful punishment" has already been given at the beginning of the surah. These four predicates follow from the concealment and the purchase of a small price, and they are joined by the conjunctive "and" which gathers them. He coordinated the predicates with "and," and there is no disagreement about its permissibility, unlike the case where they are not coordinated, for in that there is disagreement and detail. The mention of these predicates is appropriate to what precedes them, and the coordination of some of them with others is appropriate, for what we shall mention. We say: When an attribute is mentioned and a matter is made to follow upon it, the Arabs have two methods in this. One is that those matters that follow from the attributes are set in correspondence with them, the first of them corresponding to the first of those attributes and the second to the second, so that the correspondence is achieved both in meaning and in verbal order, where the first is matched with the first and the second with the second. And sometimes the first of those matters is adjacent to the attribute that follows it, so the correspondence is achieved in meaning but not in verbal order. This verse came in this category.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 174–176 (part 2 of 3):

When the Exalted mentioned their buying the small price, and that this was an allusion to their base and fleeting provisions (*maṭāʿim*), He first began the report with His saying: ﴿They consume nothing into their bellies but the Fire﴾. Then the Exalted set against their concealment of the religion (and concealment is that they do not speak of it but hide it) His saying: ﴿And Allah will not speak to them﴾. So they were recompensed, for preventing speech about the religion, by being denied God's speaking to them. Built upon their concealment of the religion, and their buying with what Allah sent down a small price, is that they are false witnesses and bearers of evil reports, in that they altered the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and claimed that the prophet who was sent was other than this. All of that was answered by His saying: ﴿And will not purify them﴾. Then He mentioned last what has been prepared for them of painful punishment. He ordered upon the buying of the small price His saying: ﴿They consume nothing into their bellies but the Fire﴾; upon the concealment His saying: ﴿And Allah will not speak to them﴾; and upon the combined two attributes His saying: ﴿And will not purify them, and for them is a painful punishment﴾. So He began first with what corresponds to each individually, and second with what corresponds to the whole. Since the first sentence contained a verb ascribed to Allah, the statement that corresponds to it contained a verb ascribed to Allah. Since the second was ascribed to them, and contains no ascription to Allah, the sentence corresponding to it was ascribed to them, and there did not come "what Allah feeds them into their bellies but the Fire."

(The mention of) this verse is appropriate to what precedes it, because in the verse before it the Exalted mentioned the permission of good things, then specified some prohibited things. It was therefore fitting to mention the recompense of whoever concealed something of Allah's religion and of what He sent down to His prophets. This was a warning that believers should not fall into what the People of the Book fell into: concealing what Allah sent down to them and buying a small price with it.

﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾. "Those" (*ulāʾika*) is a demonstrative referring to the concealers mentioned earlier and to what they were threatened with. The explanation of ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾ was given in full at the beginning of the surah, so there is no need to repeat it.

﴿And punishment in exchange for forgiveness﴾: Since he had first presented their state in this world, that they exchanged error for guidance, he mentioned the result of that in the Hereafter, which is that they exchanged forgiveness, which is the result of guidance and the cause of the longer, everlasting bliss, for the longer, everlasting punishment, which is the result of error. This is because they knew the truth and concealed it for a base worldly purpose. If that is so, it is the buying of punishment in exchange for forgiveness. The wording "they bought" (*ishtaraw*) implies their preference for error and punishment, because a person does not buy except what he has desire for, affection for, and choice in. This indicates the utmost loss and the disregard of consequences.

﴿How patient they are in (the pursuit of) the Fire!﴾ Scholars differ concerning *mā*. The most evident view is that it is exclamatory (*taʿajjub*, expressing wonder), and this is the view of the majority of exegetes. There have come: ﴿Woe to man, how ungrateful he is!﴾ [80:17], and ﴿Hear them and see them!﴾ [19:38]. The grammarians agreed that the exclamatory *mā* is in the nominative position as a subject (*mubtadaʾ*), but they differed: Is it an indefinite complete noun (*nakira tāmma*) with the verb after it in the position of the predicate (*khabar*)? Or an interrogative that carries the meaning of wonder, with the verb after it in the position of the predicate? Or a relative pronoun whose verb after it is a relative clause (*ṣila*) and whose predicate is omitted? Or a qualifying noun whose verb after it is a qualifier (*ṣifa*) and whose predicate is omitted? These are four views mentioned in grammar. The first is the view of Sibawayh and the majority; the second is the view of al-Farra' and Ibn Darastawayh; the third and fourth are of al-Akhfash. Likewise they differed concerning *afʿal* after the exclamatory *mā*: is it a verb (the view of the Basrans), or a noun (the view of the Kufans)? On this difference depends the question of the object after it: is it a direct object (*mafʿūl bihi*) or something resembling a direct object? If we say that the statement is an exclamation, then wonder is the amazement at a thing while the cause of its occurrence is hidden, and this is impossible with respect to Allah the Exalted. So it refers to someone to whom such a thing is possible; that is, they are among those of whom an observer says: "How patient they are in (the pursuit of) the Fire!"

Those who held the statement to be an exclamation differed: Is it patience that actually occurs for them when they are in the Fire? Al-Asamm held this, and said: When it is said to them, ﴿Be silent therein, and do not speak to Me﴾ [23:108], they fall silent and their speech ceases, and they endure the Fire because they have despaired of deliverance. The view of al-Asamm is weak, because the apparent sense of the wonder is that it concerns their patience at the present moment, not that they will be patient, and because the people of the Fire may well express anguish. It was also said: "patience" is a metaphor for remaining in the Fire, meaning: how long He has kept them in the Fire. Or is it patience for which they are described in this world? This is the view of the majority. There is a difference as to whether it is literal or metaphorical. Those who held it to be literal said: its meaning is "how patient they are in an action that leads them to the Fire," because they were knowledgeable that whoever opposed the Prophet (ﷺ) would go to the Fire; this was said by al-Mu'arrij. It was also said: the implied meaning is "how patient they are in the deeds of the people of the Fire," as you say: "How similar your generosity is to Hatim!", meaning: to the generosity of Hatim. So the genitive noun was omitted and the noun in the genitive was placed in its position. This is the view of al-Kisa'i and Qutrub, and it is close to the view of al-Mu'arrij. It was also said: "asbara" here means "ajra'a" (to be bold), which is a Yemeni dialect usage. Thus the word "asbara" at that point would be shared between its more immediate meaning, restraining oneself upon a disliked thing, and the meaning of boldness: "how bold they are in the action that brings them near the Fire." This was said by al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Rabi' and Ibn Jubayr. Al-Farra' said: al-Kisa'i informed me, saying: the judge of Yemen informed me that two litigants came before him, and an oath became incumbent upon one of them, so his opponent swore to him, and he said to him: "How bold you are against Allah!" (*mā aṣbarak ʿalā Allāh*, in the sense of *mā ajra'ak*).

Those who held it to be metaphorical: It was said: it is a metaphor intended to mean action, that is, "how much they act like the people of the Fire." This was said by Mujahid. It was also said: it is a metaphor intended to mean little anguish, that is, "how little they are distressed about the Fire." It was also said: it is a metaphor intended to mean contentment. Its explanation is that one who is content with a thing is content with its consequence and its necessary result, once that necessity is known. When they proceeded to what necessitates the Fire while knowing this, they became like those content with the punishment of Allah and patient under it. This is like what one says to someone who has exposed himself to the anger of the ruler: "How patient you are under the shackles and the prison!"

Al-Zamakhshari said: "How patient they are in (the pursuit of) the Fire!" is an expression of wonder at their state in being engaged in the things that bring about the Fire, without any concern on their part. End of his words. The discussion that the statement is an exclamation ends here.

Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna and al-Mubarrad held that *mā* is interrogative, not exclamatory, and that it is a question in the sense of rebuke directed at them: "What made them patient in the Fire, so that they abandoned the truth and followed falsehood?" This is the view of Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi. It is said: *ṣabbarahu* and *aṣbarahu* have the same meaning, that is, he made him patient. Not that *aṣbara* here means "he restrained and compelled," so that *afʿala* would mean *faʿala*, contrary to al-Mubarrad, who claimed that *aṣbara* means *ṣabbara*. We do not know this in the language. The *hamza* is only for causation, that is, making someone possessed of patience.

Some people held that *mā* is negative, and the meaning is: "God does not make them patient in the Fire," that is, He does not make them endure the punishment. Thus the following are gathered in the meaning of His saying ﴿How patient they are in (the pursuit of) the Fire!﴾: the exclamatory, the interrogative, and the negative. And it is established concerning the exclamatory: is it literal or metaphorical? And both: is that in this world or in the Hereafter?

﴿That is because Allah has sent down the Book with the truth﴾. "That" (*dhālika*) is a reference to the threat mentioned earlier; this was said by al-Zajjaj. Or it refers to the ruling against them that they are among the people who abide eternally in the Fire; this was said by al-Hasan. Or to the punishment; this was said by al-Zamakhshari. Or to the buying; this was said by Ibn Attiyya, following one of the interpretations of His saying "sent down the Book" that will be mentioned. That is, that buying, with what was already decreed for them in the knowledge of Allah and what His reports announced concerning them, or the concealment. The least likely of these is that it refers to what preceded of Allah's reports: that He sealed their hearts, their hearing and their sight, and that they are deaf, dumb and blind, so they do not understand.

The grammatical analysis of *dhālika* has been disputed. It was said: it is in the accusative, governed by an omitted verb whose implied meaning is "We did that," and the *bā'* in *bi-anna Allāh* is connected to that omitted verb. It was said: it is in the nominative, and they differed: is it the subject (*fāʿil*), with the implied meaning "that was due for them"? Or the predicate of an omitted subject, with the implied meaning "the matter is that"; that is, what they were promised of punishment is because Allah sent down the Book with the truth. So they differed. Or is it the subject (*mubtadaʾ*), with the predicate being His saying "because Allah sent down": that is, "that is established and fixed, because Allah sent down the Book with the truth." In that case "that" refers to the nearest thing mentioned, which is the punishment, and the predicate is not merely Allah's sending down of the Book with the truth, but what follows from His sending it down: its opposition and its concealment. Here the cause is put in the place of the effect. The interpretation in meaning: that punishment is theirs by concealing what Allah sent down of the Book accompanied by the truth, or of the Book which He sent down with the truth. Al-Akhfash said: the predicate is omitted; its implied meaning is "that is known because Allah...," so the *bā'* is connected to this implied predicate. The Book is the Torah and the Gospel, or the Qur'an, or the Books of Allah sent down to His prophets, or what He wrote for them of wretchedness by His saying "deaf, dumb, blind." Then the Book would mean judgment and decree. These are four views.

"With the truth": Ibn Abbas said: with justice. Muqatil said: the opposite of falsehood. Makki said: with what is necessary. Wherever "with the truth" is mentioned, it means what is necessary.

﴿Indeed, those who differ concerning the Book﴾: It was said: they are the Jews, and the Book is the Torah, and their disagreement is their concealment of the mission of Jesus and then the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ). They believed in part of it, which is what they made apparent, and disbelieved in part of it, which is what they concealed. It was also said: they are the Jews and the Christians; this was said by al-Suddi. Their disbelief in disagreement is with what Allah the Exalted related of the stories of Jesus and his mother, peace be upon them both, and by denying the Gospel. Disagreement arose among them to the point that they cursed one another and fought. It was also said: they are the disbelieving Arabs, and the Book is the Qur'an. Some of them said it is sorcery, some said it is "tales of the ancients," some said it is fabrication, and so on. It was also said: they are the People of the Book and the polytheists. The People of the Book said: it is a statement of Muhammad (ﷺ), and is not the speech of Allah. They said: only a human teaches him; they said: "You have studied (it)"; they said: "This is nothing but a fabrication," and so on. The polytheists said: some said it is sorcery, some said it is poetry, some said it is soothsaying, some said it is tales, some said it is fabrication, and so on.

The apparent meaning is the report about those from whom disagreement concerning what Allah sent down of the Book proceeded, that they were in hostility and enmity, because disagreement is the setting for mutual hatred and divergence, just as agreement is the setting for mutual love and unity.

In al-Muntakhab: The closer view is to take the Book as the Torah and the Gospel, in which the good news of Muhammad (ﷺ) is mentioned, because the people had known that and concealed it, and they knew its interpretation. When the Exalted presents what functions as the reason for sending down punishment upon them, the closer view is that the intended Book is their own Book, which is the basis among them, not the Qur'an. End of his words.

"Within a far-reaching schism" (*lafi shiqaqin ba'id*): It was previously mentioned that this is derived either from the fact that each party moves to one side (*shiqq*) while the other is on the opposite side, or from the fact that each one causes hardship (*yashuqqu*) to the other. He used *shiqaq* (schism, opposition) as a metaphor for enmity, and described the schism as "far" either because it is far from the truth or because it is far from harmony. Or he used it as a metaphor for length, meaning: in a lengthy enmity that does not end. This disagreement is the reason each group believes that its own Book is the truth and that others are fabrications, and in this they have lied. The Books of God resemble one another and confirm one another.

These noble verses contain the second call to people, commanding them to eat of what is lawful and good, and forbidding them to follow Satan. They mention his "steps" (*khutuwat*), as though people were tracing his footprints and treading in his tracks. So whenever he takes a step, they place their feet upon it, and this is an exaggeration of following him. Then He explained that He forbade them to follow him only because he is the enemy who openly displays his enmity. Then He did not suffice with mentioning enmity until He mentioned that he commands them to commit sins. Since he was their leader (*matbu'*) and they followed him, the mention of commanding is appropriate, since they are obeying what he adorned for them and whispered to them. Then He mentioned what he commands them with, which is commanding them to fabricate against God and to speak about God what they do not know about Him. Then He mentioned the severity of their turning away from what God revealed, and their insistence on following the ways of their forefathers, to the extent that if their forefathers had been deprived of reason and guidance, they would still have followed them, as an exaggeration of blind imitation (*taqlid*, following without evidence) and of turning away from the Book of God, and as a continuation of the later generation upon the practices of the earlier generation, without reflection or reasoning.

Then He mentioned that the likeness of the disbelievers and of their caller to what God revealed is the likeness of one who shouts at what hears nothing except mere sounds. Then He mentioned their condition of deafness, dumbness, and blindness, which prevent knowledge from reaching a person. Therefore He concluded with His saying, "so they do not reason," because the paths of reason and knowledge are corrupted for them. Then He called out to the believers with a special call, and commanded them to eat of the good and to thank God. Then He mentioned some of the things He prohibited, and permitted eating them in a state of necessity, and stipulated in taking that that the one in necessity should be neither rebellious nor transgressing. And when He made lawful the eating of good things and prohibited what He prohibited here, He mentioned the states of those who concealed what God revealed and sold it for a small price, so that this community might take heed from the condition of one who concealed knowledge and sold it for the lowest price. For He, exalted is He, informed that such a person does not eat in his belly except fire, meaning that which necessitates eating fire. And that God will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection, nor purify them, when He speaks to the believers with the speech of mercy and kindness. And He mentioned that, with the absence of instruction, which is the highest rank for a subordinate from a superior, since He qualified him for intimate communication and conversation, and with the absence of praise for them, there is for them a painful punishment. Then He exaggerated in their blame, that these are the ones who preferred misguidance over guidance, and punishment over bliss. Then He mentioned that they are on the verge of being marveled at for their endurance of the fire, and that what befell them of punishment is because of what God revealed in the Book, which they opposed. Then He mentioned that those who disagreed about what God revealed are in an enmity that does not end.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 177 (part 1 of 3):

﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east or the west, but righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets, and gives wealth, in spite of love for it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveler, those who ask, and for [freeing] slaves; and [who] establishes prayer and gives zakah; and those who fulfill their promise when they promise, and the patient in poverty and hardship and during battle. Those are the ones who have been true, and it is those who are the righteous.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, there is prescribed for you retaliation for those murdered: the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female. But whoever is pardoned by his brother [i.e., the victim's heir] in any [degree], then grant [him] reasonable compensation and pay him with good conduct. That is an alleviation from your Lord and a mercy. So whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178] ﴿And for you in retribution is life, O people of understanding, that you may become righteous.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 179] ﴿Prescribed for you when death approaches one of you, if he leaves wealth, is a bequest to parents and relatives in an acceptable manner, [as] a duty upon the righteous.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180] ﴿So whoever alters it after he has heard it, then its sin is only upon those who alter it. Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 181] ﴿But whoever fears from a testator injustice or sin and brings about reconciliation between them, there is no sin upon him. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 182].

(p-497) Qibal (قِبَلُ): a noun of place. You say: "Zayd is qibalaka," meaning he is in the place in front of you. The explanation of the meaning is that he is in the place which is opposite you. It may be extended so that it means "with" in a figurative sense. You say to me: "Qibala Zayd dayn" (I have a debt owed by Zayd). Al-Riqab (الرِّقابُ): the plural of raqabah, and the raqabah is the back of the neck. Its derivation is from al-muraqabah (watching), because its place in the body is that of the watchman overlooking the people. For this meaning it is said: "A'taqa Allahu raqabatahu" (Allah freed his neck), and it is not said: "A'taqa Allahu 'unuqahu" (Allah freed his neck, using 'unuq). Because it was named raqabah, it is as if it watches over punishment. From this, the woman whose child does not survive is called raqub, because of her watching over (muraa'at) the death of her child. In al-Muntakhab it is said: fi'al is a plural that is regular for fa'lah, whether it is a noun, like raqabah and riqab, or an adjective, like hasanah and hisan. The raqabah may be used to refer to the person in his entirety.

Al-Ba'sa' (البَأْساءُ): a noun derived from al-bu's (distress), except that it is feminine and is not an adjective. It is said that it is an adjective that has been placed in the position of the noun it modifies. Al-bu's and al-ba'sa' mean poverty. From it one says: "ba'isa al-rajul" when the man became poor. The poet said:

> "He was not in distress when he spent a night, / Flirting with a gazelle of drowsy gaze, dark-eyed."

Al-ba's (البَأْسُ): the intensity of fighting. From it is the hadith of 'Ali: "When the battle intensified, we took refuge with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." It is also said: "ba'usa al-rajul," meaning he became brave. Al-darra' (الضَّرّاءُ): from al-darr (harm). It is said that it is not an adjective; and it is said that it is an adjective placed in the position of the noun it modifies. In the hadith: "And I seek refuge in You from harm (darr) or detriment (madarrah)." The lexicographers said: al-darra', with a fatha, is the opposite of benefit, and al-durr, with a damma, is affliction (zamanah). Al-qisas (القِصاصُ): the verbal noun of qasas, yuqassu, muqassah, and qisas, like qatala, yuqatilu, muqatalah, and qital. Al-qisas is equalizing one thing with its like, and from it is the killing of one who killed with the one who was killed. Its origin is from qassatu al-athar, meaning I followed the trace, because it is a pursuit for the blood of the one who was killed. From it is qass al-sha'r (cutting hair), which is following its trace. Al-hurr (الحُرُّ): well known. You say: "harra al-ghulam yahurru hurriyyah fahuwa hurr." Its plural, i.e., the form fa'l as an adjective, is preserved as ahrar. They said "marru mirara." If fa'l is an adjective for human beings, the plural is formed with the waw and nun. Just as ahrar is preserved in the plural, so too hara'ir is preserved in the plural of the feminine hurrah.

Al-qatla (القَتْلى): the plural of qatil, and it is regular for fa'il, the adjective meaning dead or wounded. Al-untha (الأُنْثى): well known; it is fu'la, the alif in it is for feminine marking, and it is the counterpart of the male, who is the counterpart of the woman. It is said of the two testicles: unthayan. This pattern does not have an alif except for feminine marking, and it is not for assimilation (ilhaq), because fu'lal is absent from their speech.

Al-ada' (الأداءُ): with the meaning of ta'diyah. "Addaytu al-dayn" means I paid the debt, and "adda 'anka risalah" means he conveyed it. "Innahu la yu'addi 'anni illa rajul min ahl baiti," meaning he does not convey (on my behalf) except a man from my family.

Ulu (أُولُوا): one of the nouns that is in the nominative with the waw, and in the genitive and accusative with the ya'. The meaning of ulu is "possessors of," and its singular is from a different root, which is dhu, meaning possessor. This is inflected in an irregular manner. Its feminine is ulat, meaning possessors (feminine), and its inflection is like its inflection: it takes a damma in the nominative and a kasrah in the genitive and accusative. Both are obligatorily attached to a following apparent noun of a class, and both are written in the Mushaf with a waw after the alif. If you name someone "Ulu," you add a nun and say: "Ja'a min Ulun, wa ra'aytu Ulina, wa marartu bi Ulin." Sibawayh stated this, because in the state of its annexation, the omission of a nun from it is presumed for the sake of annexation, as you say: "darib-u Zayd" and "daribina Zaydan."

Al-Albab (الألْبابِ): the plural of lubb, which is intellect free from desire. It was named thus either from its formation from their saying "alabba bi al-makan" and "labba bihi," meaning he stayed, or from al-lubab, meaning the pure essence. This plural is regular: that is, a noun of the form fu'l is pluralized as af'al. The verb from it is of the form fa'ula with a damma or kasrah on the 'ayn. They said: "lababta," "labibta." The coming of the geminate in fa'ula with a damma on the 'ayn is anomalous; they dispensed with it by using fa'la, such as 'azza ya'izzu and khaffa yakhiffu. So what came of this anomalously is: labibtu, sarirtu, fallilu, dammamtu, and 'azizt. The fatha has been heard for them, except for labibtu, for which the kasrah is heard as mentioned.

Al-janaf (الجَنَفُ): injustice (al-jawr). Janifa, with a kasrah on the nun, yajnafu, so he is janif and janif, according to al-Nahhas. The poet said:

> "I am a man whose lineage of 'Amir has protected / my oppression, though the adversaries have been unjust toward me."

It is also said: al-janaf means inclination. From it is the saying of al-A'sha:

> "My she-camel has inclined away from the enclosure of Yamamah, / and she did not head toward anyone from its people other than you."

Another said:

> "They are the patron, even if they are unjust toward us, / and we are visitors for their meeting."

It is said: "ajnafa al-rajul," meaning he brought injustice, just as "alama al-rajul" means he did what is blameworthy, and "akhassa" means he did something base.

* *

(p-2) ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east or the west﴾. Qatadah, al-Rabi', Muqatil, and 'Awf al-A'rabi said: it was revealed concerning the Jews and the Christians. The Jews used to pray toward the west, and the Christians toward the east, and each group claimed that righteousness was that.

Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and Sufyan said: it was revealed concerning the believers. A man asked the Prophet (ﷺ), and then this was revealed, so he called him and recited it to him.

Some exegetes said: when a man pronounced the two testimonies and prayed toward any direction and then died, Paradise was obligatory for him. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) emigrated, and the obligations were revealed, the prescribed punishments were established, and the qiblah was turned toward the Ka'bah, Allah revealed this.

It was also said: the occasion of its revelation was the denial of the disbelievers against the believers for changing their direction from Bayt al-Maqdis to the Ka'bah. The connection of this verse with what precedes it is evident: for if it concerns the People of the Book, then their mention has preceded with the most reprehensible mention, concealing what Allah had revealed and exchanging it for a small price, and mention of what has been prepared for them. Nothing remained by which they might display the emblem of their religion except their prayer and their claim that this is righteousness, so He refuted them with this verse.

If it concerns the believers, then it is a prohibition for them against clinging to the easiest part of their law, as the People of the Two Books clung, but rather they must act upon all that is within their capacity of the obligations of the Law, as Allah the Exalted has explained them.

Hamzah and Hafs read: ﴿Laysa al-birra﴾ with a fatha on the ra', and the rest of the seven read with a damma on the ra'.

Al-A'mash said, regarding the Codex of 'Abd Allah: "La tahsabanna al-birra." In the Codex of Ubayy and also of 'Abd Allah: "Laysa al-birra bi-an tuwallu." Whoever reads with the fatha on "al-birra" makes it the predicate of laysa, and "an tuwallu" is in the position of the subject. The preferred way is that it should be placed after the nominative, since it functions like a transitive verb. This reading is preferable in one respect, which is that its subject is "an tuwallu" and the predicate is "al-birra," and "an" with its clause is more definite than what is defined by al-alif wa al-lam. The reading of the majority is preferable in one respect, which is that the placement of the predicate of laysa between it and its subject is rare. Ibn Darastawayh held that this is prohibited, likening it to ma: he intended to judge that it is a particle, just as it is not permitted to place the predicate of ma in the middle. This is refuted by this mutawatir reading and by the occurrence of this in the speech of the Arabs.

The poet said:

> "Ask, if you do not know the people about us and about them, / and the knowledgeable and the ignorant are not equal."

Another said:

> "Is it not great that a calamity should befall, / and we have no one to depend upon in calamities?"

The reading "bi-an tuwallu" is with the addition of the ba' in the predicate, just as they added it to its subject when it is "an" and its clause. The poet said:

> "Is it not strange that the young man / is struck by some of what is in his hands?"

He placed the ba' on the subject of laysa, though its proper place is the predicate, and this is acceptable in the verse because of the mention of "strange" together with the affirmation that the hamzah conveys. The meaning of the speech becomes: "I am amazed that the young man..." If you said "alaysa qa'iman bi-Zayd," it would not be permitted.

Al-birr (البِرُّ): a comprehensive noun for good, and its discussion has preceded. The accusative of "qibala" is as an adverb of place, and its governing element is "tuwallu." The meaning is: when they had extensively argued about the matter of the qiblah, until the change to the Ka'bah took place, each of the two groups claimed that righteousness is turning toward its qiblah, so Allah refuted them. It was also said: "Laysa al-birra" means: in what you are upon, for it is abrogated (mansukh) and outside of righteousness (naskh, abrogation, here meaning the earlier direction was abrogated).

It was also said: it is not the great righteousness, which requires that they be preoccupied with its importance, away from all other kinds of righteousness, the matter of the qiblah. Qatadah said: the qiblah of the Christians is the east of Bayt al-Maqdis, because it is the birthplace of 'Isa, upon our Prophet and him be peace, due to the saying of the Exalted: ﴿a place toward the east﴾ [Maryam: 16]. The Jews' qiblah is its west, and the verse is a refutation of both groups.

* *

﴿But righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah﴾. Al-birr is a meaning among meanings, so its predicate cannot be a substance except figuratively. Either al-birr is made to be the very person who believes, as an exaggeration, said by Abu 'Ubaydah, and the meaning is: "But the righteous one (al-barr)." Or it is by omission from the first part, meaning: "But the possessor of righteousness," said by al-Zajjaj. Or from the second part, meaning: "The righteousness of one who believes," said by Qutrub. Sibawayh also derived it this way; in his book he said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿But righteousness is [in] one who believes﴾, and it is only: "But righteousness is the righteousness of one who believes in Allah." End of quote. Sibawayh chose this because the preceding statement is the negation that righteousness is turning the face toward the east or the west, so what is excepted is of the same kind as what is negated. A parallel is: "It is not generosity that you give a dirham, but generosity is giving thousands." It would not fit to say: "But the generous one is the one who gives thousands" unless what precedes it is: "The generous one is not one who gives a dirham."

Al-Mubarrad said: "If I were one of those who recite the Qur'an, I would read: 'Wa lakinna al-barra' with a fatha on the ba'," and he said this because it would be an active participle. You say: "barartu, abarru, fa-ana barr and barr," it is said: it is formed sometimes on the pattern fa'l, like kahl and sa'b, and sometimes on the pattern fa'il. The better view is to claim that the alif has been omitted from al-barr, and like it: sarr, qarr, and rabb, meaning sarr (happy), qarr (settled), barr (righteous), and rabb (lord).

Al-Farra' said: "man amana" means belief (al-iman). Since "man" has taken the position of the verbal noun, it is made a predicate of the first part, as if he said: "But righteousness is belief in Allah." The Arabs make a noun the predicate of a verb. Al-Farra' recited:

> "By your life, youths are not those whose beards have grown, / but youths are every man who is generous."

He made the growth of the beard the predicate of "youth," and the meaning is: "By your life, chivalry is not that beards grow."

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read: "wa lakin" with a sukun on the nun, lightened, and a damma on al-birr. The rest read with a fatha on the nun, doubled, and a fatha on al-birr. The grammar is clear. The parallel of the two readings has already been mentioned in: ﴿But the devils disbelieved﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102].

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 177 (part 2 of 3):

﴿And the Last Day, and the angels, and the Book, and the prophets﴾. In this verse He mentions the pillars of faith explicitly, as came in the hadith of Jibril when he asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about faith, and he said: "That you believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the divine decree (qadar), its good and its bad." The verse does not explicitly mention belief in the qadar, because belief in the Book includes it. The meaning of the verse is that righteousness is not attained by facing east and west, but by a combination of matters. The first of them: belief in Allah. The People of the Book failed in this: as for the Jews, due to anthropomorphism (tajsim) and their saying: ﴿Ezra is the son of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30]; as for the Christians, due to their saying: ﴿The Messiah is the son of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30].

The second: belief in Allah and the Last Day. The Jews failed in this when they said: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80], and the Christians denied the bodily resurrection (al-ma'ad al-jusmani).

The third: belief in the angels. The Jews were hostile to Jibril.

The fourth: belief in the Books of Allah. The Christians and the Jews denied the Qur'an.

The fifth: belief in the prophets. The Jews killed them, and both groups among the People of the Book attacked the prophethood of Muhammad.

The sixth: giving wealth in accordance with the command of Allah. The Jews cast doubts in order to take wealth.

The seventh: establishing the prayer and giving the zakat. The Jews refrain from them.

The eighth: fulfilling the covenant. The Jews broke it.

This preceding negation and the exception (istidrak) are not to be taken at face value, because it negated that turning toward the qibla is righteousness, then ruled that righteousness consists of matters, the first of which is prayer, and in prayer facing the qibla is necessary. So the negation of righteousness is understood as negating the totality of righteousness, not as negating its essence; that is, righteousness is not all of this, but righteousness is what has been mentioned. It may also be understood as negating the essence of righteousness, because their facing east and west after the abrogation was sin and wickedness, so it is not counted as righteousness; or because facing the qibla is not righteousness unless it is accompanied by knowledge of Allah the Exalted, and it becomes righteousness only with faith and those conditions.

He placed the angels and the Books before the messengers, although belief in the existence of the angels and the truthfulness of the Books is attained only through the messengers, because this is considered in terms of the existential order (al-tartib al-wujudi): the angel exists first, then through his conveying the revelation of the Books arises, then that Book reaches the Messenger. So the external existential order was observed, not the mental order (al-tartib al-dhihni). Belief in Allah and the Last Day was placed before belief in the angels, Books and messengers, because the mukallaf (responsible person) has a beginning, a middle, and an end; knowledge of the beginning and the end is the primary aim, and this is what is meant by belief in Allah and the Last Day. As for knowing the benefits of the middle, it is not complete except through the messengership, and that is not complete except through three things: the angels who bring the revelation, the thing revealed, which is the Book, and the one to whom it is revealed, who is the Messenger. He placed faith before the actions of the limbs, namely giving wealth, prayer and zakat, because the actions of the heart are nobler than the actions of the limbs, and because the limb-actions that are beneficial in the sight of Allah the Exalted arise only from faith. By these five, which are the objects of faith, the reality of faith is achieved, because belief in Allah requires belief in His existence, His eternity (qidam), His permanence (baqa'), His knowledge of all that is known, the connection of His power to all possible things and His will, His being All-Hearing, All-Seeing, and Speaking, and His being exalted above indwelling (hulul), being a locus (mahalliyya), spatial confinement (tahayyuz), and accidentality ('aradiyya). Belief in the Last Day achieves knowledge of what is required of the rulings of the resurrection, the reward, the punishment, and what is connected to them. Belief in the angels requires the soundness of their conveying the message to the prophets and other states of the angels. Belief in the Book requires affirming the books of Allah that were sent down. Belief in the prophets requires affirming the soundness of their prophethood and their laws.

Al-Raghib said: If it is asked why he mentioned the Last Day first here and delayed it in His saying: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in Allah and His angels and His Books and His messengers and the Last Day﴾ [al-Nisa': 136], it is answered: this is permissible, although the waw does not require order, because the disbeliever does not know the Hereafter and is not concerned with it, and it is the furthest of things from realities in his view, so He delayed its mention. And when He mentioned the state of the believers, and the nearest thing to the believer is the matter of the Hereafter, and everything he does and seeks he intends by it the face of Allah the Exalted, then the matter of the Hereafter, so He mentioned it first, as an alert that righteousness is observance of Allah and observance of the Hereafter, then observance of other than these two. End of his words.

* *

﴿And gave wealth despite loving it﴾. The giving of wealth here: it was said that it was obligatory, then abrogated by zakat, but this is weakened because He combined it here with zakat. It was said: it is zakat itself, and by this He explained its recipients; this is weakened by the conjunction of zakat after it, which indicates that it is other than it. It was said: it is voluntary charity and optional gifts (al-mabarr), and this is weakened by His saying at the end of the verse: ﴿And those are the God-fearing﴾, which made taqwa dependent on it; had it been recommended, taqwa would not depend on it. This weakening is not valid, because those referred to with taqwa are those who possess the totality of the preceding attributes, which include the obligatory and the recommended, so taqwa was not singled out, nor did he possess only the recommended and make taqwa dependent on it. Rather, if mention of taqwa were made for one who performs the recommended, it would be acceptable, because if he obeys Allah in the recommended, then obeying Him in the obligatory is more fitting and more appropriate. It was also said: it is a due right (haqq wajib) other than zakat.

Al-Sha'bi said: Indeed there is a right in wealth besides zakat, and he recited this verse. It was said: it is meeting essential needs, such as feeding the food to the one in dire need. As for what is narrated that zakat abolishes every right, it is understood as referring to the rights that are specified. As for what is not specified, it is not abrogated, by evidence of the obligation of charity in cases of necessity and the obligation of maintenance for relatives and for the slave, and all of that is unspecified. ("despite loving it") is connected to (gave) and is a circumstantial clause (hal), and the meaning is: he gives wealth while loving it, that is, in a state of his love for wealth, his choosing and preferring it. This is a great quality: that a person's soul be attached to something as the lover is attached to his beloved, and then he prefers it to others seeking the face of Allah, as came: "That you give charity while you are healthy and stingy, fearing poverty and hoping for wealth." The apparent view is that the pronoun in (hubbihi, its love) refers to wealth, because it is the nearest mentioned thing, and among the rules of the grammarians is that a pronoun does not refer to other than the nearest except with evidence. The apparent view is also that the verbal noun's agent is the giver, as we explained, and it was said the agent is the recipients, i.e., their love for it, their need for it and their poverty. To the first view Ibn 'Abbas went, meaning he gave wealth in a state of his health and love for it, so he preferred others with it. The statement of Ibn al-Fadl, that it refers back to the verbal noun implied by "gave," i.e., "love of giving," is far-fetched both lexically and semantically: lexically, because it refers back to something not explicitly mentioned and to something farther than wealth; semantically, because one who does something while loving to do it is hardly praised for it, since in doing so there is the desire of his soul and its aim. Zuhayr said:

"You find him, when you come to him, radiant, as if you were giving him what you yourself are asking for."

The statement of one who referred it back to Allah the Exalted is even farther, because it refers back to a distant term despite the good reference to a near term. In all three of these views the verbal noun is attached to the agent, and this too is far-fetched. Ibn 'Atiyya said: His saying "despite loving it" comes as an eloquent parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) within the speech. If he meant by parenthetical insertion the technical term in grammar, that is not so, because the condition for that is that it be a sentence, and that it have no place in the i'rab, and this is not a sentence, and it has a place in the i'rab. If he meant by parenthetical insertion a separation between the two objects by the circumstantial clause, that is valid, but it creates ambiguity, so he should have said a separating insertion, eloquent, between the parts of the speech.

﴿The near of kin, the orphans, the needy, the wayfarer, and the beggars, and for the freeing of slaves﴾. As for the near of kin, it is better to take it in its general sense, which is whoever is related to you by birth, and there is no basis for restricting it to the forbidden kin (al-rahm al-muharram), as some have held, because prohibition (hurma) is a legal ruling, whereas kinship is a lexical term established for kinship by lineage, even though those to whom it applies vary in nearness and distance. Many hadiths have been related about maintaining kinship, and we have already discussed the near of kin, the orphans and the needy in His saying: ﴿And to parents do good, and to the near of kin, the orphans, and the needy, and speak kindly to people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83], so we need not repeat it. ﴿The near of kin﴾ and what follows it of conjoined terms are the first object according to the view of the majority, and (the wealth) is the second object. Since the greatest intended aim is giving wealth despite loving it, He placed the second object first, out of concern for this meaning. As for according to the view of al-Suhayli, (the wealth) is the first object, and ﴿the near of kin﴾ and what follows is the second object, so the arrangement is in its original order according to him. (The orphans) is conjoined to ﴿the near of kin﴾; some have taken it to involve an elision, i.e., the near of kin of the orphans. He said: it is not good for the giver to hand wealth to an orphan who cannot distinguish and does not know the ways of benefiting from it, and if he does so he errs; but if he is an adolescent who knows the proper placement of his right, and the charity is something to be eaten or worn, it is permissible to give it to him. This is according to the view of one who restricts the orphan to one who is not yet of age; but for one who holds that both the adult and the minor are called orphans, it is given to the adult and to the guardian of the minor. End of his words.

It is not necessary to posit this elided term, since "I gave Zayd wealth" is true even if he did not take it himself but through his agent. (And the wayfarer) is the guest, as said by Qatadah, Ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, Muqatil, al-Farra', Ibn Qutaybah and al-Zajjaj; or the traveler who passes by you from one land to another, as said by Mujahid and also Qatadah and al-Rabi' ibn Anas. He was called ibn al-sabil (son of the road) because he remains on the sabil, which is the path, just as a bird that stays by water is called ibn al-ma' (son of water), and one over whom ages have passed is called ibn al-layali wal-ayyam (son of nights and days). It was also said he was called ibn sabil because the road brings him forth; the bringing-forth of him by the road was likened to birth, so sonship was applied to him metaphorically. Or it is the one stranded in a land other than his own, with a great distance between the land where he was stranded and his own land, as said by Abu Hanifa, Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi and the judge Abu Ya'la. Or it is one who intends a journey and does not find provision, as said by al-Mawardi and others from al-Shafi'i. The beggars (al-sa'ilun) are those who ask for food, namely one whom necessity drives to ask in order to fill his need, since asking is not permitted to him except in that case. As for one who holds that the giving of wealth to these is not zakat, he permits giving it to both the Muslim and the disbeliever. There is in the hadith what indicates the blame of begging, and it is understood as applying to a state other than necessity.

(p-7 markers are retained in place.)

**Ar-riqab** (the slaves): these are the *mukatabun* (slaves who have contracted with their masters to buy their own freedom), who are helped to free their necks. This is the view of ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and al-Shafiʿi. Or they are slaves who are bought and then freed. This is the view of Mujahid, Malik, Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Thawr. It is also reported from Ahmad that both of the preceding opinions apply. Or they are captives who are ransomed, so that their necks are freed from captivity. It has been said that these are the three categories mentioned, and this is the apparent meaning. If this giving is the *zakat* (obligatory almsgiving), then the scholars differ. It has been said that it is permitted only to help the *mukatabun*. It has also been said that it is permitted for that purpose, and also for someone who buys a slave and then frees him. If it is other than *zakat*, then both are permitted. This ordering, in the case of one who gives wealth, is by way of precedence, going from the most to the next most deserving: the poor relative is more deserving of charity than others, since it combines the bond of kinship (*silah*) with charity (*sadaqah*). Moreover, kinship is among the most emphatic grounds for directing wealth toward someone, and for this reason inheritance is due through it. Therefore He mentioned relatives first, then followed them with orphans, because the orphan is cut off from every means of support on account of his youth. Then He followed them with the needy (*masakin*), because their need may become severe. Then the wayfarer (*ibn al-sabil*), because his need may become acute in returning to his family. Then the beggars, and then the slaves, because their need is less than that of those already mentioned. Al-Raghib said: this ordering was chosen because a person's kindness should first be directed to his relatives, so mentioning them first is appropriate. Then He followed them with orphans. People in their means of livelihood are of three kinds: one who supports himself and is not supported, one who both supports and is supported, and one who is supported but does not support. The orphan is one who is supported but does not support, so helping him comes after relatives. Then He mentioned the needy who have no property, either present or absent. Then He mentioned the wayfarer, who has property elsewhere. Then He mentioned the beggars, among whom some are truthful and some are liars. Then He mentioned the slaves, who have masters who support them. Thus each one whose mention is delayed is less poor than the one mentioned before it. End of his words.

The Muslims have reached consensus (*ijma'*) that when need and dire necessity afflict the Muslims after the payment of *zakat*, it is obligatory to spend wealth on them. Malik said: it is obligatory on people to free their captives, even if this consumes all their wealth. The scholars have differed concerning the orphan: is he to be given from voluntary charity (*sadaqat al-tatawwu'*) merely by virtue of being an orphan, as an act of kindness, even if he is wealthy? Or is he not given unless he is poor? There are two opinions among the people of knowledge.

* *

﴿and who establish prayer and give zakat﴾: The discussion of the parallel of these two clauses has already occurred. If by the earlier "giving" zakat is meant, then mentioning it here is for emphasis. Otherwise, the opinions about it have already been presented when it is not meant as zakat. This is the apparent meaning, because the recipients of zakat include things not mentioned among the recipients of this giving. The precedence of prayer over zakat has been discussed: prayer is the most excellent of bodily acts of worship, is repeated every day and night, and is obligatory on every sane person under the stated conditions. For this reason it is mentioned first.

He coordinated His saying ﴿and who establish prayer and give zakat﴾ with the relative clause of "man" (*man*, "whoever"). The relative clause of "man" consists of "believed" and "gave." The relative clause that came first, "believed," takes precedence because faith is the most excellent thing enjoined in worship, the head of religious deeds, and the first thing sought. He mentioned giving wealth second, in the one who is described by it, because this is among the most cherished qualities of the Arabs and one of their clear virtues. They have many reports and poems about this, and take pride in it, to the extent that they do good to relatives even if relatives do them wrong, and tolerate from them what they would not tolerate from non-relatives. Do you not see the saying of Tarafa al-ʿAbdi:

*Why do I see myself and my cousin Malik,*
*when I approach him, he distances himself from me and keeps away.*

Sufficient in regard to kindness to near relatives is the ode of al-Muqannaʿ al-Kindi, whose opening is:

*My people blame me over debts, though my debts*
*are for things that bring them praise.*

And among its lines:

*For them is most of my wealth, if wealth follows me,*
*and if my wealth is little, I do not burden them with generosity.*

They were also kind to orphans and treated them gently. Concerning this one of them says:

*When some years wear us down,*
*the orphans are sufficed by the loss of the orphan's father.*

They take pride in kindness to the needy and to the wayfarer among guests and travelers, as Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma said:

*To those who have much is the provision of whoever comes to them,*
*and among those who have little is generosity and giving.*

Al-Muqannaʿ said:

*And I am a servant of the guest as long as he is staying.*

Another said:

*How many a guest who came to the tribe at night*
*found provision and conversation as he desired.*

Murra ibn Mahkan said:

*Do not blame me for pursuing an honor,*
*which I have seized when I saw praise being plundered.*

*In the grip of a fang, and I have no wealth more generous to give,*
*and praise is better for whoever seeks it in its aftermath.*

Iyas ibn al-Artt said:

*Indeed I am one who speaks welcome to the one who asks,*
*and to the seeker of kindness: you will find it with me.*

*Indeed, when I extend my hand in generosity,*
*while the hand and arm of the miser are clenched.*

Since this was among their noble traits, He made it part of the righteousness that the believer embraces, and made it a prelude to the giving of zakat, urging it by this means. For whoever's way is to spend his wealth on relatives, orphans, the needy and wayfarers, out of nobility, then it is all the more fitting that he should give what God has made obligatory upon him, namely zakat, which is his purification, and hope thereby for a great reward from Him, which is more emphatic and more beloved to him.

* *

﴿and those who fulfill their covenant when they make it﴾: ﴿and those who fulfill﴾ is coordinated with "whoever believed." It has been said that its nominative case is by implying "and they are those who fulfill." The governing element of "idha" (when) is "those who fulfill." The meaning is that the fulfilling of the covenant does not come later than the time of the agreement. The discussion of fulfilling and covenant has already occurred in His saying: ﴿Fulfill My covenant and I will fulfill your covenant﴾ [2:40]. In the codex of Abd Allah it reads "and the fulfillers," in the accusative as a form of praise. (And) al-Jahdari read "bi-ʿuhudihim" (with their covenants) in the plural.

﴿and the patient in misfortune and adversity and in the time of battle﴾: "the patient" (*al-sabirin*) is in the accusative by way of praise. Shifting to the nominative or accusative in attributes of praise, blame, or compassion, and the coordination of attributes with one another, is discussed in the science of grammar (*nahw*).

(And) al-Hasan, al-Aʿmash and Yaʿqub read "al-sabiruna" (the patient, in the nominative), coordinating it with "al-mufuna" (the fulfillers). Al-Farisi said: when many attributes are mentioned in a context of praise or blame, the best course is to vary their grammatical case, and not to make them all follow the noun they describe. This is because this is a place of extended description and of conveying the message thoroughly. When the attributes differ in case, the meaning becomes more complete, since the speech, when it varies, seems like different kinds of speech and varieties of exposition, whereas when it is uniform in case, it is one aspect and one sentence. End of his words.

(He said) al-Raghib: He did not say "wa-wafa" (and he fulfilled) as He said "wa-aqama" (and he established), for two reasons. The first concerns wording: when the relative clause is long, it is better to coordinate with the relative noun rather than with the clause, so that it does not become long and awkward. The second is that in the first case He mentioned what falls within the domain of the Law and is known only from it, while rational wisdom requires justice rather than injustice. When He mentioned fulfilling the covenant, which bare contracts also require, coordinating it with the first was better. Since patience is in one respect the origin of virtues and in another comprehensive of all virtues, for there is no virtue in which patience does not have a profound effect, He changed its grammatical case to draw attention to this purpose. End of his words.

They agreed on interpreting His saying ﴿in a time, then he received﴾ [2:36] as referring to the state of fighting. The commentators differed about "al-basaʾ" and "al-darraʾ." Most of them held that al-basaʾ is poverty and al-darraʾ is affliction in the body, though their expressions differ on this. This is the view of Ibn Masʿud, Qatada, al-Rabiʿ and al-Dahhak.

It has been said: al-basaʾ is fighting and al-darraʾ is siege. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. This is an instance of ascending in the degrees of patience from the lesser to the greater. He first mentioned patience in poverty, then patience in sickness, which is more severe than poverty, then patience in fighting, which is more severe than both poverty and sickness. Al-Raghib said: this encompasses all types of patience, because one either lacks what he needs for sustenance, which is "al-basaʾ"; or he suffers pain and illness in his body, which is "al-darraʾ"; or he defends against one who harms him, which is "in the time of battle." End of his words.

He made "al-sabirin" govern "fi al-basaʾ wa al-darraʾ" with "fi," because a person is not praised for patience in these circumstances unless poverty and sickness have become, as it were, his container. As for poverty or sickness at some time, a person is hardly praised for being patient with them, because rarely does anyone escape them. As for fighting, He made "al-sabirin" govern the time of the battle, because it is a state that does not last long, and it may last a long time in most circumstances of fighting. So the state of fighting was not governed by "fi," which indicates sensory containment as in a physical body, on which the abstract meaning is applied. The coordination of these attributes in this verse with "wa" (and) indicates that among the conditions of righteousness is their completion and gathering together. Whoever embodies only one of them is not described as righteous. For this reason some scholars restricted this description to the prophets, peace be upon them, saying that no one other than them combines all these attributes. This has been discussed previously.

﴿Those are the ones who are truthful, and those are the God-fearing﴾: "Those" (*ulaʾika*) refers to those who combined those well-known attributes, namely faith and what follows it.
