It has been mentioned that the demonstrative is used for this meaning, meaning, it refers to those who combine a number of earlier attributes, as in His saying: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [2:5].

Truthfulness here may mean truthfulness in speech, opposite to lying. The meaning is that their words correspond to what their hearts harbor of faith and report. So when they report something, it is true and cannot be falsified. From it is the hadith: "A man continues to speak the truth and seek the truth until he is recorded before God as truthful, and a man continues to lie and seek lying until he is recorded before God as a liar."

It may also mean truthfulness in states, which is the opposite of showing off, meaning they sincerely directed their deeds to God Most High without ostentation or reputation, but intended the face of God Most High, and were as expected when tested, as you say: "The spear proved me truthful," meaning I found it, when tested, as I chose and as I expected of it. Piety here means guarding against the punishment of God by avoiding His disobedience and complying with His obedience.

The predicate concerning "those" varies here. He described the first "those" with "who are truthful," which is separated by a past-tense verb to indicate that their having this quality is established, that it has occurred from them, is confirmed and firmly settled. He described the second "those" with a relative clause whose predicate is an active participle, to indicate permanence, that this is a quality of theirs that does not renew, but has become their natural disposition and a fixed attribute. It also occurs as the closing word of a verse, because if it were a past-tense verb it would not fall as a closing word.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 178 (part 1 of 3):

﴿O you who have believed, prescribed for you is qisas (legal retribution) for the murdered﴾: Al-Bukhari narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Among the Children of Israel there was qisas, but there was no diyah (blood-money) among them. So Allah, the Exalted, revealed this verse." Qatadah and al-Shaʿbi said: It was revealed concerning a people among the Arabs who were mighty and powerful, and they would not kill a slave of theirs except a master, nor a woman except a man. Al-Suddi and Abu Malik said: It was revealed concerning two groups, one of which was Muslim and the other a covenanted disbeliever, between whom there had been fighting during the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and a number of men, women and slaves were killed from both groups. So the verse was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ made the diyah of a man equal to qisas with the diyah of a man, the diyah of a woman equal to qisas with the diyah of a woman, and the diyah of a slave equal to qisas with the diyah of a slave, and then he reconciled between them.

It was said: It was revealed concerning two tribes of the Arabs who fought one another before Islam, and there were killings and wounds between them for which neither side took retribution from the other. Ibn Jubayr said: They were al-Aws and al-Khazraj. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: They were Qurayzah and al-Nadir, and one of them had superiority over the other in number and nobility, and they would marry their women without bridal gifts, and they swore that they would kill a free man for a slave, and they made their wounds double the wounds of those others. This is how they dealt with them in the Jahiliyyah. So they brought their matter to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the verse was revealed, and he commanded them to equality, and they agreed. Concerning this one of them said:

"They killed among you one who was worth eight, then they persisted, and we took four."

It is narrated that a man from Ghani killed Shas ibn Zuhayr, so his father Zuhayr ibn Khuzaymah gathered against them, and they spoke to him, and one of those who defended them said to him: Ask for the killing of Shas. He said: "One of three things, nothing else will satisfy me." They said: "What are they?" He said: "You bring Shas back to life, or you fill my house with the stars of the sky, or you hand over to me a Ghani entirely so I may kill him, and then I will not consider that I have taken a substitute."

The connection of this verse with what precedes it: when Allah made lawful what He made lawful before, and forbade what He forbade, then followed it with mention of those who take wealth unjustly, and that they eat nothing into their bellies but the Fire, and this implied the inclusion of all forbidden wealth, then He followed that with mention of those who are characterized by righteousness and praised them with the commendable qualities that they embody, He began to mention the prohibition of blood and to call for its preservation and protection. So by the prescription of qisas He drew attention to its prohibition, and He drew attention to the permissibility of taking property on account of it, and that it is not of the wealth that is taken unjustly. The priority given to explaining what Allah made lawful and unlawful of food over explaining the prescription of qisas was because of the general need for food, for by it the body is sustained and the form of the human being is preserved. Then He mentioned the ruling on the one who destroys that form, because one who is a believer rarely commits killing, so for one characterized by the qualities mentioned earlier, such an act is far from him. The mention of what is of general concern was given priority as being more comprehensive. He also drew attention to the fact that, although such a grievous matter may befall one who is characterized by righteousness, that does not remove him from righteousness or from faith. For this reason He addressed them with the description of faith, saying: ﴿O you who have believed, prescribed for you is qisas for the murdered﴾.

The original meaning of kitabah (writing) is the script that is read, and here it is used to express the meaning of obligation and establishment, i.e., it was made obligatory and established, because what is written is worthy of being firmly established and lasting.

It was said: it is in its literal sense, and it is a report about what was written in the Preserved Tablet and what preceded in divine decree. It was said: the meaning of kutiba is "he was commanded," like His saying: ﴿Enter the holy land which Allah has prescribed for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 21], i.e., the one you were commanded to enter. It was said: kataba may come in the sense of ja'ala (made), and from it: ﴿Those — He has written faith in their hearts﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 22], ﴿So I will prescribe it for those who fear Me﴾ [al-A'raf: 156]. The construction of kutiba here with ʿala indicates obligation and necessity. And ﴿in the murdered﴾ — the fi here is for causation, i.e., because of the murdered, like the saying: "A woman entered the Fire because of a cat." The meaning is: O believers, it has become obligatory upon you to carry out qisas against the killer on account of the killing of the murdered without right. The obligation is directed at the imam or whoever takes his place in carrying out rights when the blood-relative wishes to exact it; or the address is to the killer, and the implied meaning is: O killers, it is prescribed for you to surrender yourselves when the guardian of the blood demands qisas. That is because it is obligatory upon the killer, when the guardian wishes to kill him, to submit to the command of Allah and to comply with his lawful qisas, and he has no right to refuse, unlike the adulterer and the thief, for they may flee from the hadd (prescribed punishment) (p-10) and may conceal themselves with the concealment of Allah, and they may choose not to confess. And the guardian is obligated to stop at the killer of his relative and not to transgress against others, as the Arabs used to do by killing someone other than the killer of their slain from among his people. This writing of qisas is restricted to the case where the guardian does not accept blood-money or pardon; qisas is the final recourse only when there is enmity, but if he accepts something less than qisas, whether blood-money or pardon, then there is no qisas. Al-Raghib said: If it is asked, upon whom does this obligation fall? It is said: upon people in general. Some of them are bound to surrender themselves, namely the killer; some are bound to carry it out, namely the imam when the guardian requests it; some are bound to assist and to consent; and some are bound not to transgress, but either to exact qisas or to take blood-money. The purpose of the verse is to prevent transgression, for the people of the Jahiliyyah used to transgress in killing, and one of them, if his slave was killed, would not be satisfied except by killing a free man. End of his words.

From His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, prescribed for you is qisas for the murdered﴾ three views emerge: the first is that the addressees are the rulers and those who stand in their place; the second is that they are the killers; the third is that they are all the believers, as we have explained.

This verse has been the subject of disagreement: is it abrogating (nasikh) or abrogated (mansukh)? Al-Hasan said: it was revealed concerning the abrogation of the retaliatory practice they used to follow: if a man killed a woman, her guardian had the choice between killing him while paying half the diyah, or taking half the diyah of a man and leaving him; and if the killer of a man was a woman, the guardians of the slain had the choice between killing the woman and taking half the diyah of a man, or if they wished they could take the full diyah and not kill her. He said: this verse abrogated what they used to do. End of his words. But this is not abrogation, because their practice is not one of the rulings of Allah that could be abrogated by this verse. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it is abrogated by the verse of al-Ma'idah, and the discussion of this will come.

* *

When the Exalted mentioned the prescription of qisas for killing, He clarified who falls under qisas between them, and said: ﴿The free for the free, and the slave for the slave, and the female for the female﴾. The scholars differed over the implication of these phrases. It was said: it indicates observing equality in freedom, slavery and femaleness, so it is only legislated between two free persons, between two slaves, and between two females. The alif and lam indicate restriction, as if it were said: a free person is not taken except for a free person, a slave is not taken except for a slave, and a female is not taken except for a female. This meaning is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, and that this was abrogated by the verse of al-Ma'idah; and it is also narrated from him that the verse is muhkam (definitive) and contains generality which the verse of al-Ma'idah explained. Among those who held that it is abrogated were Ibn al-Musayyab, al-Nakhaʿi, al-Shaʿbi, Qatadah and al-Thawri. It was said: it does not indicate restriction, but indicates the legitimacy of qisas between those mentioned. Do you not see that the generality of ﴿and the female for the female﴾ requires qisas for a free woman against a slave woman? So if His saying ﴿the free for the free and the slave for the slave﴾ prevented that, the two generalities would clash. His saying ﴿prescribed for you is qisas for the murdered﴾ is a self-standing sentence, and His saying ﴿the free for the free﴾ is a mention of one of its particulars, so it does not prevent the ruling from applying to the rest of its particulars.

Malik said: The best I have heard concerning this verse is that it is meant as a genus, so male and female are alike in it, and the mention of the female was repeated for emphasis and concern, to remove the matter of the Jahiliyyah. It is narrated from ʿAli and al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan that the verse was revealed clarifying the ruling on those mentioned, so that this would indicate the distinction between them and a free person killing a slave, or a slave killing a free person, or a male and a female. They said: if a man kills a woman, then if her guardians wish, they may kill his companion and give his guardians half the diyah; and if they wish, they may spare him and take from him the diyah of a woman. And if a woman kills a man, then if his guardians wish, they may kill her and take half the diyah; otherwise they may take the diyah of their companion and spare her. And if a free person kills a slave, then if the master of the slave wishes, he may kill him and give the diyah of a free person minus the value of the slave; and if he wishes, he may spare him and take the value of the slave. This has been denied as being from ʿAli and al-Hasan. The consensus is on killing a man for a woman and a woman for a man. The majority do not hold that there is any return of compensation, while a group holds that there is pursuit for the excess of the diyahs. The consensus is that a free Muslim is killed if he kills a free Muslim with a sharp instrument. The apparent generality of "the free for the free" is that a father is killed if he kills his son, and this is the view of ʿUthman al-Batti, who said: if he kills his son intentionally, he is killed for him. Malik said: if he intends to kill him, such as by laying him down and slaughtering him, or other kinds of killing in which there is no doubt about his claim of mistake, he is killed for him; but if he kills him by throwing something or by striking, then in the school of Malik there are two opinions: one that he is killed, and the other that he is not killed. The general body of scholars said: a father is not killed for his child, and he owes blood-money for what is his own, as held by Abu Hanifah, al-Awza'i and al-Shafi'i, who equated father and grandfather. This is narrated from ʿAta' and Mujahid. Al-Hasan ibn Salih said: a grandfather is subject to qisas for his son's son, and he used to accept the testimony of a grandfather for his son's son, but did not accept the testimony of a father for his son. The apparent meaning of "the free for the free" also requires that the one who would be killed if he acted alone is killed when he partners with one who is not liable to be killed, such as one who errs, a minor, an insane person, or a father according to those who say he is not killed for his son. Abu Hanifah said: there is no qisas upon either of them; the killing father owes half the diyah from his own property, and the minor and the one who errs and the insane person are upon their aqilah (paternal kin), and this is the view of al-Hasan ibn Salih. Al-Awza'i said: the diyah is upon the aqilah of those who participated among those mentioned. Al-Shafi'i said: the minor killer who participates owes half the diyah from his property; likewise the diyah of a free person and a slave if they kill a slave, and a Muslim and a Christian if they kill a Christian; and if a killer by mistake participates with him, then the intentional killer owes half the diyah, and the mistaken killer's offence is upon his aqilah.

Ibn al-Musayyab, Qatadah, al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi, al-Thawri, Abu Hanifah, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad said: a free person is killed for a slave. Malik, al-Layth and al-Shafi'i said: he is not killed for him. They agreed that a Muslim is not killed for a hostile disbeliever. Abu Hanifah said: a Muslim is killed for a dhimmi. Ibn Shubrumah, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i and al-Shafi'i said: he is not killed for him. Malik and al-Layth said: if he kills him by treachery, he is killed for him, otherwise he is not killed for him. All of them agreed on killing a slave for a free person.

The apparent meaning of the noble verse is that retaliation (qisas) for killing is legislated regardless of the instrument used, whether a heavy stone, a piece of wood, a stick, or something similar that usually kills. This is the position of Malik, al-Shafi'i and the majority (al-Jumhur). Abu Hanifa said that one who kills with a heavy object is not to be killed. The apparent position of the imams is that the instrument with which a person deserving death is killed is not specified. Abu Hanifa, Muhammad, Abu Yusuf and Zufar said: he is not to be killed except by the sword. Ibn al-Ghunaym reported from Malik: if he kills with a stone, a stick, fire or drowning, he is killed by the same means. If he does not die from that, the same kind of act is repeated upon him until he dies, even if this exceeds what the killer did.

Ibn Mansur reported from Ahmad that he is killed with the same means by which he killed.

It was reported from al-Shafi'i that if he killed with wood or by strangulation, he is killed by the sword. It was also reported from him that if he struck him with a stone until he died, the same is done to him. If he confined him without food or drink until he died, then if he does not die within a similar period...

Ibn Shubrumah said: he is struck with the same blow, and he is not struck more than that. They used to dislike mutilation (al-muthla) and say: the sword suffices for all of that. He said: if he dipped him in water until he died, then he is dipped in water until he dies.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that retaliation is legislated only for lives, because of His saying ﴿in the matter of the slain﴾. This was the view of Abu Hanifa, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad and Zufar, namely that there is no retaliation between free persons and slaves except in lives.

Ibn al-Musayyab, al-Nakha'i, Qatada, al-Hakam and Ibn Abi Layla said: retaliation is obligatory between them in all injuries. This was reported from Ibn Mas'ud. Al-Layth said: a free person may be retaliated against on behalf of a slave, but a free person is not retaliated against for a slave in offences. Al-Shafi'i said: whoever is subject to retaliation for a life is subject to it for injuries, but a free person is not retaliated against on behalf of a slave for anything short of a life.

﴿And a female for a female﴾. They agreed to set aside its apparent meaning, and they agreed, as previously mentioned, that a man is killed for a woman and a woman for a man, except for an isolated dissenting view from al-Hasan al-Basri, Ata, Ikrima and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, that a man is not killed for a woman. It was reported that Umar killed a group of men from San'a' for a woman. A woman is killed for a man, and a free person for a slave, and a slave for a free person. Al-Zamakhshari erred in attributing to the school of Malik and al-Shafi'i the view that a male is not killed for a female, whereas there is no disagreement from them that he is killed for her. Uthman al-Batti said: if a woman kills a man, she is killed for him, and half the blood money is taken from her property. If he kills her, then retribution (al-qawd) is due from him and nothing is returned to him.

They differed regarding retaliation for injuries between men and women. Abu Hanifa, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad, Zufar and Ibn Shubrumah held that there is no retaliation between men and women except in lives. Malik, al-Awza'i, al-Thawri, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Layth, al-Shafi'i and Ibn Shubrumah in one report held that retaliation applies between men and women in life and in what is less than life. However, al-Layth said: if a man injures his wife, he pays the compensation (al-'aql) and is not subjected to retaliation.

The grammarians parsed these clauses as a subject and predicate. They are complete clauses that begin with the subject, and the prepositional phrase is the predicate about it. The bā' cannot be locative (ẓarfiyya), so it is not like the saying of people "Zayd is in Basra". Rather, it indicates cause, and it relates to a specific verb (kawn khāṣṣ), not a general verb (kawn muṭlaq). The prepositional phrase takes the place of the specific verb because the meaning indicates it, since a specific verb may only be omitted in a case like this, where the indication for its omission is strong, given that retaliation was already mentioned in ﴿the matter of the slain﴾. So the estimate is: a free person is killed for a free person, that is, by his killing a free person. On this estimate the bā' is causal. It is not valid to estimate the governing element as a general verb. If you said "the free person is existing for the free person", it would not be a complete statement unless the subject is an omitted annexed noun (muḍāf) whose annexed complement has taken its place, in which case it is permissible. The estimate would then be: the killing of a free person is for a free person, that is, by his killing a free person. It is also permissible for "al-ḥurr" (the free person) to be nominative, by supposing an implied verb that the preceding phrase explains. The estimate would then be: a free person is killed by his killing a free person, since in His saying ﴿retaliation in the matter of the slain﴾ there is an indication of this verb.

* *

﴿Whoever is pardoned something by his brother, then pursuit with fairness and payment to him with good conduct﴾. The scholars of tafsir said: the meaning of this is that the People of the Torah had retaliation and had nothing other than that, while the People of the Gospel had pardon and had no retaliation. Allah made for this community, for whoever wills, killing, for whoever wills, taking blood money (diyya), and for whoever wills, pardon. Qatada said: blood money was not permitted to anyone other than this community. It was also reported from Qatada that the ruling among the People of the Torah was retaliation or pardon, with no compensation (arsh) between them, and among the People of the Gospel it was blood money or pardon, with no compensation between them. So Allah gave this community a choice among the three options.

The nominative "man" (man) is the subject, and it is either conditional or relative. The apparent view is that "man" is the killer, and the pronoun in "lahu" (for him) and "min akhihi" (from his brother) refer to him. "Shay'" (something) is the object that has not been named as the agent, and it has the meaning of a verbal noun. "'Ufiya" (was pardoned) is built in the passive, even though it is intransitive, because the intransitive verb can reach a verbal noun, as in His saying ﴿When the Horn is blown with a single blast﴾ [al-Haqqa: 13]. The brother is the one killed, that is, from the blood of his brother or from the guardian of the blood. He called him a brother to the killer on account of the brotherhood of Islam, or to win his sympathy, or because the killer is connected to him through being the guardian of the blood and its claimant, just as you say "say to your companion such and such" to someone with whom you have the slightest connection. This that has taken the place of the agent, although it is a verbal noun, is intended to mean the blood that is pardoned. The meaning is that when the killer is pardoned, the matter reverts to taking blood money. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and a group of the people of knowledge. It has been used as evidence that the obligation of the agreement is one of two things: either retaliation or blood money, because blood money involves a pardoner and one pardoned, and there is none but the guardian of the blood and the killer, and pardon can only come from the guardian. Thus the estimate of the verse becomes: if the guardian of affairs pardons something connected to the killer, then the killer shall follow that pardon with fairness.

"'Afā" (to pardon) takes "'an" (from) to indicate the offender and the offence. You say "'afawtu 'an Zayd" (I pardoned Zayd) and "'afawtu 'an dhanbi Zayd" (I pardoned Zayd's offence). When you transitive it to both together, it reaches the offender with the preposition "li-" and the offence with "'an": "'afawtu li-Zayd 'an dhanbihi" (I pardoned Zayd for his offence). His saying ﴿whoever is pardoned for him﴾ belongs to this pattern, meaning: whoever is pardoned for him for his offence. "'An jinayatihi" (for his offence) was omitted because the meaning is understood. "'Ufiya" is not to be explained as meaning "turuka" (left alone), because this is not established as a transitive usage except with the hamza, as in the saying "a'fū al-liḥā" (let the beards grow) [a hadith], meaning to let them grow. It is not permissible to imply the meaning of "taraka" in "'afā", even though the one who pardons an offence leaves it without holding the offender accountable, because implication (tadmīn) is not a regular process.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, it has been established that they say "'afā athārahu" (he erased its trace) when he effaced and removed it, so why not take its meaning to be: whoever has something erased for him from his brother? I say: this is an expression said in its place, and pardon in matters of offences is a commonly used and well-known expression in the Book, the Sunna and people's usage. So one should not turn away from it to another expression that is strained and far from its place. You will find many who take up this discipline, when a problem becomes difficult for them, boldly deriving the obscure from the words of Allah by inventing a language and attributing to the Arabs what they do not know. This is an audacity from which we seek refuge in Allah. End of his words.

When it is established that "'afā" can mean "maḥā" (erase), it is not far-fetched to read the verse according to it, and the attribution of "'afiya" to its nominative would be a true attribution, because in that case it is a direct object. When it is intransitive, its attribution to it is metaphorical, treating the verbal noun as an object. The two readings are thus balanced: "'afā" as intransitive, due to its fame for offences, and "'afā" as transitive meaning "maḥā", due to its direct connection to its nominative in a true sense.

Al-Zamakhshari's words "and you see many of those who take up this discipline..." to the end: what he mentioned is the act of those who are not trusted in the religion of Allah nor relied upon in transmitting the Sharia. Lying is among the worst sins and the most destructive to a person's standing, especially when it is about Allah and His Messenger. Ibn Hazm said, in substance, that a person may keep company with someone even in an undesirable condition, except for a liar, who is the first to be parted from. But Al-Zamakhshari's words here are not suitable, "and you see many..." through the end of his speech following his saying "If you say..." to its end, because this kind of statement is to take pardon in the sense of erasure, and this is a sound reading and an established usage in the language. So it is not from the category of audacity or inventing a language.

The verb is built here in the passive so that it includes the pardoner whether he is one or more. This applies if "brother" means the one killed, that is, from the blood of his brother. It has also been said that "shay'" (something) means "something of the pardon", so it makes no difference whether he pardons some of the blood or all of it, or whether some of the heirs or all of them pardon. Then the pardon is complete and retaliation falls away, and only blood money is due. It has also been said: the one pardoned is the guardian of the blood, "'Ufiya" here means "yusṣṣira" (made easy), not in its usual meaning of pardon, "min akhihi" means the killer, "shay'" means the blood money, and brotherhood means the brotherhood of Islam. On this interpretation, "akh" (brother) may be understood to mean the one killed, that is, on the part of his brother who was killed. This is the view of Malik, who interpreted the one pardoned as the guardian of the blood, the brother as the killer, and the pardon as facilitation. On this basis Malik said: if the guardian inclines toward pardon in exchange for blood money, the killer is given the choice between paying it or surrendering himself.

Others than Malik say: if the guardian is content with blood money, the killer has no choice and the blood money is binding. This was reported from Malik and was preferred by many of his companions. This view is weakened by the fact that "'ufiya" in the sense of "yusṣṣira" (made easy) is not established.

It has been said: these expressions in both of the two meanings for which this entire verse was revealed, and they cancelled blood money between them by mutual settlement. So the meaning of the verse is: whoever of the two groups has a surplus over the other of some of those blood monies. "'Afā" here means "faḍala" (exceed), from the saying "'afā al-shay'" when it increased, meaning the circumstance, the reckoning or the measure became abundant for him. It has also been said: according to the view of Ali and al-Hasan, it refers to the surplus in blood money between the man and the woman, and between the free person and the slave. That is, whoever has that surplus, then pursuit with fairness, and "'ufiya" here means "ufḍila" (made to have a surplus). It seems that the verse first explained the ruling when the categories do not overlap, then explained the ruling when they overlap. The first view is more apparent, as we have said. Ibn Atiyya permitted that "'ufiya" means "turika" (left), so that "shay'" is the direct object that took the place of the agent. He said: the first is better, in the sense that "'ufiya" does not take a direct object, and that the nominative "shay'" is because it is a verbal noun that has taken the place of the agent. Al-Zamakhshari's statement that "'afā" meaning "turika" is not established has already preceded.

﴿فاتِّباعٌ بِالمَعْرُوفِ وأداءٌ إلَيْهِ بِإحْسانٍ﴾. The word "ittiba'un" (in the sense of "pursuit") is in the nominative because it is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), meaning: "so the ruling, or the obligation, is pursuit." This is how Ibn 'Atiyya estimated it, while al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "so the matter is pursuit." They also permitted its nominative case by supposing an omitted verb, whose estimate is: "so let there be pursuit." They also permitted that it be a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, and its estimate is: "so upon the guardian (wali) is the pursuit of the killer for the blood-money." They also estimated the predicate as delayed, its estimate being: "so pursuit with kindness is incumbent upon him." Ibn 'Atiyya said after estimating it: "So the ruling, or the obligation, is pursuit. This is the way of obligatory matters, like His saying ﴿فَإمْساكٌ بِمَعْرُوفٍ﴾ [al-Baqara: 229] ('then retention in kindness'). As for what is recommended, it comes in the accusative, like His saying ﴿فَضَرْبَ الرِّقابِ﴾ [Muhammad: 4] ('then the striking of necks')." (p-14) End of quote. I do not understand this distinction between the obligatory and the recommended, except for what they mention, that the nominal sentence is more firm and emphatic than the verbal sentence, as in His saying ﴿قالُوا سَلامًا قالَ سَلامٌ﴾ [Hud: 69] ('They said, "Peace." He said, "Peace."'). So it is possible that this is what Ibn 'Atiyya had in mind from this. As for supposing the verb that al-Zamakhshari estimated, "so let there be," it is weak, since it is generally not omitted except after the conditional particle "in" or "law," where evidence indicates its omission. "Bil-ma'ruf" (with what is customary) is connected to the word "fa-ittiba'un." The nominative of ﴿وأداءٌ﴾ is because it is conjoined to "ittiba'un," so it has the same grammatical analysis as what they estimated for "fa-ittiba'un." "Bi-ihsanin" (with goodness) is connected to the word "wa-ada'un." They also permitted that "wa-ada'un" be a subject (mubtada'), with "bi-ihsanin" as its predicate (khabar), but this is remote. The "fa" in "fa-ittiba'un" is the response of the condition if "man" is a conditional, and it is part of the predicate of the subject if "man" is a relative pronoun. If "man" is a metaphor for the killer and "akhuhu" (his brother) is a metaphor for the guardian, which is the apparent meaning, then the sentence is an exhortation to the one who is pardoned and the one who pardons, to good settlement from the one who pays, and good demanding from the claimant. If "the brother" is a metaphor for the slain, then the pronoun in His saying ﴿وأداءٌ إلَيْهِ﴾ ("and payment to him") refers to what is understood from "yuṣāḥibu" (is accompanied) in some way, because in His saying "ʿufiya" (was pardoned) there is an indication of the pardoner. This is like His saying ﴿حَتّى تَوارَتْ بِالحِجابِ﴾ [Sad: 32] ('until it was hidden behind the veil'), since in "al-ʿashiyy" (the evening) there is an indication of the sun's setting, and like the poet's saying:

"Like a man driving camels when the forenoon has been prevented, and birds of death are hovering above them."

That is, above the camels, because in his saying "al-ḥādī" (the driver) there is an indication of them. If "man" is a metaphor for the killer, then it is also an exhortation to him and to the guardian with good settlement and good demanding. That is: "pursuit from the guardian with what is customary, and payment from the killer to him with goodness." The "pursuit with what is customary" is that he not harass him, and not demand from him except in a gentle demand, and not hasten him to three years, which is made the end of collection. The "payment with goodness" is that he not delay him and not cheat him of anything. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas in explaining "pursuit" and "payment."

It was said: the guardian's pursuit with what is customary is that he not demand from the killer more than his right. It has been narrated in a hadith: "Whoever adds a camel to the camels of the blood-money and its prescribed shares, it is from the matter of the Jahiliyya." It was said: pursuit and payment together are from the killer. Pursuit with what is customary is that he not diminish it, and payment with goodness is that he not postpone it. It was said: "al-ma'ruf" is protecting the side (of the other party) and gentleness of speech, and "al-ihsan" is pleasant speech. It was said: "al-ma'ruf" is what God has made obligatory. It was said: "al-ma'ruf" is what the Arabs customarily observe among themselves regarding the blood-money for the slain.

The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿فَمَن عُفِيَ لَهُ مِن أخِيهِ شَيْءٌ﴾ ("whoever is pardoned by his brother in anything") and the rest of the verse is that it prohibits compelling the killer to retaliation (qawad) if he chooses that, and the rightful claimant chooses the blood-money. The killer must pay the blood-money if the guardian chooses it. This is the view of Sa'id, 'Ata', al-Hasan, al-Layth, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, and it was related by Ashhab from Malik.

Abu Hanifa and his companions, Ahmad in one of his two reports, Malik in one of his two reports, al-Thawri, and Ibn Shubruma said: the guardian has nothing but retaliation (qisas), and he does not take the blood-money except with the killer's consent. According to the view of these, it is estimated with an omitted element, meaning: "whoever is pardoned by his brother in anything, and the pardoned party agrees and pays the blood-money, then pursuit with what is customary." We have already mentioned an indication of this disagreement when we explained His saying ﴿فَمَن عُفِيَ﴾ and the people's disagreement about it.

* *

﴿ذَلِكَ تَخْفِيفٌ مِن رَبِّكم ورَحْمَةٌ﴾ ("That is an alleviation from your Lord and a mercy"). By "that" He refers to what God has legislated of pardon and blood-money, since the People of the Torah had as their legislation only retaliation, and the People of the Gospel had as their legislation only pardon. It was said: pardon did not exist in any community before this community. Some chains of this transmission have already been mentioned. This community was given the choice between retaliation and pardon with blood-money. Pardon and blood-money were an alleviation from God, since in it the guardian benefits from the blood-money, he obtains reward through pardon, and the killer's life is preserved, and giving up something other than the soul is easy in order to preserve it. He attributed this alleviation to the Lord because He is the one who sets right the affairs of His servants, the one who looks after them in securing what brings them religious and worldly happiness. The conjunction of "wa-raḥma" (and a mercy) with "takhfīf" (alleviation) is because whoever spares your life after you deserved its destruction has shown you mercy. And what mercy is greater than that? Perhaps the pardoned killer, in the period he lives after deserving his execution, will accumulate good deeds that wipe away this terrible act, so granting him respite is part of the mercy, perhaps he will set his deeds right.

﴿فَمَنِ اعْتَدى بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ فَلَهُ عَذابٌ ألِيمٌ﴾ ("Whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment"). That is: whoever exceeds God's law after the agreement and taking of the blood-money, by killing the killer after the blood has been dropped, or by killing someone other than the killer. In the Jahiliyya they used to do this, killing for one person two, three, or ten. It was said: the meaning is: whoever is killed after taking the blood-money. It was said: after pardon. It was said: whoever takes the blood-money after pardoning it. The first view is the most apparent, because pardon and taking the property come first.

"Al-i'tida'" (transgression), which is exceeding the limit, includes all of that. Al-Zamakhshari said: "after that alleviation," making "dhalika" (that) refer to the alleviation. But it is not evident that "dhalika" refers to the alleviation. The apparent meaning is what we explained, namely pardon and taking the blood-money, and that being an alleviation is like the reason for the legislation of pardon and taking the blood-money. The "man" in His saying ﴿فَمَنِ اعْتَدى﴾ may be conditional or may be relative.

﴿فَلَهُ عَذابٌ ألِيمٌ﴾ ("then he will have a painful punishment") is the response of the condition, or the predicate concerning the relative pronoun. The apparent meaning of this punishment is that it is in the Hereafter, because most of what has come of such threats is for the Hereafter. It was said: the painful punishment is in this world, which is his being killed by retaliation. This was said by 'Ikrima, Ibn Jubayr, and al-Dahhak. It was said: it is his being killed outright as a hadd (prescribed punishment), and the judge does not allow the guardian to pardon. This was also said by 'Ikrima, Qatada, and al-Suddi. It was said: his punishment is that he returns the blood-money and his sin remains for the punishment of the Hereafter. This was said by al-Hasan. It was said: his punishment is the ruler's authority over him to do with him as he sees fit. This was said by 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz. The view of a group of scholars is that if he kills after the blood has been dropped, he is like one who killed from the start: if the guardian wishes, he kills him, and if he wishes, he pardons him.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 179:

﴿And for you in retaliation there is life, O people of understanding, that you may become righteous﴾. The life that is in retaliation is that when a person knows that if he kills, he will be killed, he refrains from killing, and that becomes a life for him and for the one whom he refrained from killing. Thus the legislation of retaliation (qisas) is a general benefit (maslahah 'ammah), while the preservation of the killer and pardoning him is a particular benefit (maslahah khassah) pertaining to him. So the general benefit is given precedence, due to the impossibility of combining the two.

Or the meaning is: "And for you in the legislation of retaliation there is life." The Arabs, when a man killed, his tribe would become incensed and demand retaliation from them, and they would fight one another, and this would lead to the killing of a great number. But when retaliation was legislated, they accepted it, handed over the killer to be retaliated against, agreed on blood-money (diyah), and abandoned fighting. Thus there was life for them in that. How many did Muhalhil kill for his brother Kulayb, until he nearly annihilated Bakr ibn Wa'il?

It has also been said: it is a life for others than the killer, because no one other than him is killed, contrary to what the people of the Jahiliyyah used to do. And it has been said: it is a life for the killer himself. And it has been said: it is a life in the Hereafter, by deterring whoever intends it, since if retaliation is carried out upon him in this world, then in the Hereafter he will not be retaliated against; and if it is not carried out, retaliation will be carried out upon him in the Hereafter. Thus that life is not attained by him that the one who has been retaliated against attains.

Abu al-Jawza', Aws ibn 'Abd Allah al-Rabi'i, recited: "And for you in the qasas", meaning: in what He has related to you of the ruling on killing and retaliation. It has also been said: al-qasas is the Qur'an, meaning: for you in the Qur'an is life of the hearts, like His saying: ﴿a spirit from Our command﴾ [al-Shura: 52], and His saying: ﴿Is one who was dead and We brought him to life﴾ [al-An'am: 122]. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it may be a verbal noun (masdar) like qisas, meaning: that when the trace of the killer is followed (qassa athar al-qatil qasasan), he is killed as he killed. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿And for you in retaliation there is life﴾ is an eloquent statement because of its strangeness, namely that retaliation is killing and a removal of life, yet it has been made a place and a container for life. And of the hitting of the mark of eloquence is the definiteness given to retaliation and the indefiniteness given to life: the meaning is, "And for you in this genus of ruling, which is retaliation, is a great life, or a type of life," namely the life attained through deterrence from killing, due to the certainty of retaliation against the killer. End of his words.

The Arabs said, in something close to this meaning: "Killing is more protective against killing" (al-qatl awqa li-l-qatl); and they said: "more repelling of killing" (anfa li-l-qatl); and they said: "more restraining from killing" (akaff li-l-qatl). The scholars have mentioned the difference in eloquence between the two statements from several aspects. The first: the apparent meaning of the Arabs' statement requires that the existence of a thing be the cause of the negation of itself, and that is impossible. The second: the repetition of the word "killing" in one sentence. The third: the restriction to the claim that killing is more repelling of killing. The fourth: that killing unjustly is (also) killing, and would not be repelling of killing. The Arabs' statement "killing is more repelling of killing" has been included within this, whereas the noble verse is contrary to that.

As for the first aspect: in it there is that a type of killing, namely retaliation, is a cause for a type of life, not for life absolutely; and when it is taken with an elided modifier, i.e., "for you in the legislation of retaliation," it becomes clear that the legislation of retaliation is a cause of life. As for the second aspect: it is evident from the sweetness of the words and the goodness of the construction, and from not needing to posit an ellipsis; for in the speech of the Arabs, as we have said, there is repetition of the word, and the elision is therefore more repelling, or more restraining, or more protective. "Afal" (the elative form) requires that the comparative object be stated, so there must be an assumed comparison: "more repelling of killing than leaving killing."

As for the third aspect: retaliation is more general than killing, because retaliation may be for a soul and for something other than a soul, whereas killing applies only to the soul. So the verse is more general and more beneficial in attaining life. As for the fourth aspect: because retaliation implies entitlement, so that the existence of life is consequent upon its legislation. Then, in the noble verse there is the contrasting of retaliation with life, which is contrasting a thing with its opposite, a kind of rhetorical device called tibaq (antithesis), and it is similar to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that it is He who causes to die and gives life﴾ [al-Najm: 44]. This sentence is a subject and predicate; "in retaliation" is connected to what "for you" is connected to, and it stands in the position of the predicate. The fronting of this predicate justifies beginning with an indefinite noun. The meaning explained: there will be for you in retaliation a life. By addressing those endowed with minds and insight, He draws attention to the general benefit, namely the legislation of retaliation, since only the people of understanding know its true outcome, those who obey God's commands and avoid His prohibitions, and they are those whom God has singled out for address: ﴿Only the people of understanding take heed﴾ [al-Ra'd: 19]; ﴿Surely there are signs for a people who reason﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164]; ﴿Surely there are signs for people of understanding﴾ [Al 'Imran: 190]; ﴿Surely there are signs for people of restraint﴾ [Ta-Ha: 54]; ﴿Surely in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart﴾ [Qaf: 37]. The people of understanding are those who know the consequences and recognize the grounds of fear, for one without intellect does not experience fear; therefore it was specified for the people of understanding.

(﴿that you may become righteous﴾) i.e., retaliation, so that you refrain from killing and guard against killing out of fear of retaliation or of persisting in killing; or you guard yourselves against God by avoiding His disobediences; or you act as the righteous act in upholding retaliation and ruling by it. It is an address that has a particular excellence concerning the leaders (a'immah). There are five opinions; the first of them is what the verse was brought forth for, namely the legislation of retaliation.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 180 (part 1 of 3):**

﴿It is prescribed for you, when death approaches any one of you﴾, and so on. The connection of this verse with what precedes it is evident. When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned killing in retaliation (qisas) and blood-money (diyah), He followed this with a reminder of the bequest (wasiyyah) and an explanation that it is among what Allah has prescribed for His servants, so that everyone will take heed and make a bequest before death comes suddenly and he dies without having made one. There is no necessity to say that "kutiba" (it is prescribed) is originally a conjunction with ﴿It is prescribed for you retaliation for the slain﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178] and "it is prescribed for you," and that the waw was deleted because of length. Rather, this is a new sentence (jumlah mustanifah) whose connection with what precedes it is evident, because whoever is about to be subjected to retaliation is one of those whom death has approached. The meaning of "the approach of death" is the approach of its preliminaries and causes, such as illnesses, diseases and dangerous conditions. The Arabs apply the name "death" to the causes of death by way of metaphor (tajawwuz). Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And death will come to him from every place, but he will not die﴾ [Ibrahim: 17]. 'Antarah said:

*"And death is subservient to my hand when I strike with the Hindi sword."*

(Jarir said):

*"I am the death of which you have been told, so there is no escape for the fleer from me."*

(And another said):

*"Say to them: Hasten to make your excuse, and seek a word that will clear you, for I am death."*

The address in "ʿalaykum" (to you) is to the believers, restricted to what is possible, on the assumption of metaphor in the approach of death. Had the wording of the speech followed the address to the believers, it would have been "when death approaches you." But the generality implied by "ʿalaykum" was observed in meaning, since the meaning is: "It is prescribed upon each one of you," and then that implicit element was made explicit, since it is the one to whom death approaches. So it was said: "when death approaches any one of you." A parallel to observing meaning in generality is the verse of the poet:

*"I shall not ask the neighbour-women of my house: are your men absent or present?"*

He used the singular pronoun in "rijaluki" (your men) because he observed the sense of generality, for the meaning is: "I shall not ask every neighbour-woman among the neighbours of my house," so his saying "are your men absent" comes in observance of this meaning. This is a strange and remarkable point from the science of Arabic. It has also been said: the intended meaning of "death" here is its literal reality, not its preliminaries. In that case the address is directed to the executors and heirs, and there is an elision of a modifier, meaning: "It is prescribed for you, when one of you dies, to carry out the bequest and act upon it." On this view, the verse does not indicate the obligation of the bequest; rather, its obligation is established by another proof.

﴿If he leaves behind wealth﴾: this means property (mal), according to the consensus. Mujahid said: "Good" (khayr) throughout the Qur'an means wealth, as in ﴿And indeed he is intense in his love of wealth﴾ [al-ʿAdiyat: 8], ﴿Indeed, I have preferred the love of good (wealth)﴾ [Sad: 32], ﴿So make a contract with them if you know any good in them﴾ [al-Nur: 33], ﴿Indeed, I see you in prosperity﴾ [Hud: 84]. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates good in general, and this is the view of al-Zuhri, Abu Mijlaz and others, who said: it is obligatory whether the amount is small or large. Aban said: two hundred silver dirhams. Al-Nakha'i said: from a thousand dirhams down to five hundred. ʿAli and Qatadah said: a thousand dirhams or more. Al-Jassas said: four thousand dirhams. This is the view of those who determined "good" by wealth. As for those who determined it by mere abundance, this differs according to the condition of the man and the number of his dependants, whether many or few. It is reported from ʿAisha that she said: "I do not consider it a surplus if a man who has a dependant wishes to make a bequest of four hundred dinars." And she said on another occasion, about a man who had four dependants and three thousand [dinars]: "Allah only said: ﴿if he leaves behind good﴾, and this amount is small, so leave it for your dependants."

And from ʿAli: a client of his wished to make a bequest, and he had seven hundred [dirhams], so he forbade him, saying: "Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿if he leaves behind good﴾, and good is wealth, and you have no wealth." End of quotation.

The absence of a quantified amount does not indicate that the bequest is not obligatory, since the apparent sense is that the obligation is conditional on the existence of good in general. Even if the intended meaning is other than the apparent one, it is possible to make the obligation conditional upon the exertion of effort (ijtihad) regarding the good. In calling it "good" here, and making it so, there is a subtle indication that it is good wealth, not wicked wealth, for wicked wealth must be returned to its owners, and one would be sinful for making a bequest of it.

They differed. A group said: the verse is muhkam (unabrogated/clear), and bequests to parents and near relatives are obligatory, and the heir combines the bequest and the inheritance by the ruling of the two verses. Another group said: it is muhkam in the matter of voluntary (tatawwuʿ) bequests. Another group said: it is muhkam and the meaning of bequest does not contradict inheritance; rather the meaning is: "It is prescribed for you what Allah has enjoined (awsa) concerning the inheritance of parents and near relatives," as in His saying: ﴿Allah enjoins you concerning your children﴾ [al-Nisa': 11]. Al-Zamakhshari said: or it is prescribed for the dying person to make a bequest to parents and near relatives, by fully providing what Allah has enjoined for them upon them, and not diminishing their shares. End of his words.

It has also been said: it is muhkam, and "parents and near relatives" is restricted to those who are not heirs, but are slaves or disbelievers, just as the bequest is restricted to a third or less. This was said by al-Hasan, Tawus and al-Dahhak. Ibn al-Mundhir said: all those from whom knowledge is transmitted among the people of knowledge agree that a bequest to parents and relatives who do not inherit is permissible. Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah said: the verse is general, and the ruling by it remained for a time, and from it every heir was abrogated (nusikha, naskh/abrogation) by the verse of the shares of inheritance. Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbas also, and Ibn Zayd said: the whole verse is abrogated, and the bequest remained as a recommendation (nadb). This is also the view of al-Shaʿbi, al-Nakhaʿi and Malik.

Al-Rabiʿ ibn Khaythum and others said: there is no bequest. It has been said: it existed at the beginning of Islam, then it was abrogated by the verse of inheritances, and by his saying (ﷺ): "Indeed Allah has given everyone who has a right his right; no bequest is valid for an heir." The community's acceptance of it has made it reach the level of the mutawatir, even though it is of the single-transmission type (ahad), because they only accept with acceptance that which has a sound transmission. Others said: the bequest is first for relatives, and if it is for a stranger, it is with them, and it is not permitted for others while they are left out. When Abu al-ʿAliyah died, people said: "How strange! A woman of the Riyah tribe freed him, and he bequeathed his wealth to the Banu Hashim." Al-Shaʿbi said: that was not his, nor an honour for him. Tawus said: if he makes a bequest to someone other than his relatives, the bequest is returned to his relatives and his act is annulled. This was also said by Jabir and Ibn Zayd. The same is reported from al-Hasan, and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh held this view. Al-Hasan, Jabir ibn Zayd also, and ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Yaʿla said: a third of the bequest remains where the deceased placed it. Malik, Abu Hanifah, al-Shafiʿi and Ahmad said: if he makes a bequest to someone other than his relatives and leaves his relatives, that is permissible and is carried out, whether the beneficiary is rich or poor, Muslim or disbeliever. This is also reported from ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿAisha, may Allah be pleased with them.

The apparent meaning of the prescription of the obligation of the bequest is upon the one who leaves behind wealth, and this is the view of al-Thawri. Abu Thawr said: it is not obligatory except upon one who has a debt upon him or has property belonging to people in his keeping. As for one who has no debt upon him and no deposit with him, it is not obligatory upon him. It has also been said: the bequest is not obligatory. They cited the saying of al-Nakhaʿi: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) died without making a bequest," and his saying in the hadith "who wishes to make a bequest," for he made it conditional upon the wish to make a bequest, and if it were obligatory he would not have made it conditional upon his wish. If the beneficiary of the bequest is an heir, and the heirs permit it, it is valid; this is the view of Abu Hanifah and Malik. If the beneficiary is a killer by deliberate killing and the heirs permit it, it is valid according to Abu Hanifah and Muhammad. Abu Yusuf said: it is not valid.

If he makes a bequest of property to some of his heirs and says: "If the heirs permit it, well and good; otherwise it is for the cause of Allah (fi sabil Allah)," then if the heirs permit it, it is valid; otherwise it is an inheritance. This is the view of Malik. Abu Hanifah and Maʿmar said: it is carried out for the cause of Allah. If he makes a bequest to a stranger of more than a third, and the heirs permit it before death, they do not have the right to retract it after death, and it is binding upon them. This was said by Ibn Abi Layla and ʿUthman al-Battti.

Abu Hanifah, Muhammad, Abu Yusuf, Zufar, al-Hasan ibn Salih and Ubayd Allah ibn al-Hasan said: if they permit it during his lifetime, it is not valid until they permit it again after death. This is reported from ʿAbd Allah, Shurayh and Ibrahim. Ibn al-Qasim reported from Malik: if he asks their permission and they grant it, then each heir is separated (by that), so he has no right to retract. As for one who is among his dependants, or is a paternal uncle or paternal cousin, if he cuts off his maintenance from them while he is healthy, they have the right to retract. Ibn Wahb reported from Malik: if they gave him permission in health, they may retract; if in sickness, they may not.

The view of al-Layth is like the view of Malik. There is no disagreement among the jurists that if they permit it after death, they have no right to retract it. It is reported from Tawus and ʿAta': if they permit it during life, it is binding upon them.

There is no disagreement about the validity of the bequest of a sane adult who is not under restriction. It is disputed concerning a child. Abu Hanifah said: his bequest is not valid. Al-Muzani said: this is the analogical view of al-Shafiʿi. Malik and others said: it is valid. There are two opinions from the companions of al-Shafiʿi. The apparent meaning of Allah's saying (kutiba) is prohibition, because he is not among those subject to obligation. They agreed that a person may change his bequest and retract it. They differed concerning the mudabbar (the slave freed upon his master's death). Malik and Abu Hanifah held that he may not change what he has made mudabbar. Al-Shafiʿi, Ahmad and Ishaq said: it is his bequest. This is also the view of al-Shaʿbi, al-Nakhaʿi, Ibn Shubrumah and al-Thawri. It is established that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) "sold a mudabbar," and that ʿAisha sold a mudabbarah.

If he says to his slave: "You are free after my death," he has the right to retract according to Malik in that case. If he says: "So-and-so is mudabbar after my death," he does not have the right to retract it. If he intended mudabbar by his first statement, he also does not retract, according to the majority of Malik's companions. As for al-Shafiʿi, Ahmad, Ishaq and Abu Thawr, all of this is in their view a bequest.

They differed about how retraction of the tadbir (arrangement of freedom upon death) is achieved. Abu Thawr said: if he says "I have retracted concerning my mudabbar," the tadbir is void. Al-Shafiʿi said: it is only by sale or gift, and his saying "I retracted" is not a retraction. And whoever says: "My slave is free after my death," without intending a bequest or tadbir, Ibn al-Qasim said: it is a bequest. Ashhab said: it is a mudabbar.

The form of the bequest which the righteous predecessors used to write was: "This is what so-and-so son of so-and-so bequeathed: that he testifies that there is no god but Allah alone, with no partner, and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger, and ﴿that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt in it, and that Allah will raise those in the graves﴾ [al-Hajj: 7]. And he bequeathed to those of his family whom he leaves behind the fear of Allah, blessed and exalted is He, with the fear due to Him, and that they should set right their affairs among themselves, and obey Allah and His Messenger if they are believers, and he enjoins upon them what ﴿Abraham enjoined upon his sons, and Jacob: O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except as Muslims﴾ [al-Baqarah: 132]." Al-Daraqutni reported it from Anas ibn Malik.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 180 (part 2 of 3):

The verb "kutiba" (it was prescribed) is in the passive voice, and its agent is omitted, both because it is known and for brevity, since it is well known that the agent is God, exalted is He. The subject (marfu') of "kutiba" is apparently "al-wasiyya" (the bequest) [p-19]. The verb does not take the feminine marker, because of the separation (al-fasl) by the prepositional phrase and the two conditional clauses, especially here, as the separation is long. It also does not take it because the noun is feminine but not real (ghayr haqiqi), and because it carries the meaning of "al-iysa'" (the charging with a bequest).

The answer (jawab) of the two conditionals is omitted, since the meaning points to it. It cannot be that it is part of the meaning of "kutiba", because "kutiba" is in the past tense while the two conditionals refer to the future. Rather, the meaning is: "The bequest has been prescribed for one of you when death approaches, if he leaves behind wealth, let him make a bequest." The context and the meaning of the speech indicate this answer. The answer is omitted, and the verb of the condition is in the past form. The verified view is that every condition requires an answer. So that implied element is the answer of the first condition, and the answer of the second condition is omitted, indicated by the omitted answer of the first condition. Thus what is omitted indicates another omitted element. The second condition is a condition within the first, and therefore it must be prior in existence, even though it is later in wording. The combination of two conditionals in which the second is not made the answer of the first by "fa'" (then) is among the most difficult grammatical questions. We have clarified this matter and fully treated it in our book "Kitab al-Takmil" (The Book of Completion), so it should be taken from there.

It has also been said: the answer of the two conditionals is omitted and is to be supplied from the meaning of "kutiba 'alaykum al-wasiyya" (the bequest has been prescribed for you). The expression "kutiba" is used figuratively for "yatawajjahu iyjab al-wasiyya 'alaykum" (the obligation of the bequest is directed at you), so that it becomes future, and then it explains the answer, because it is future.

On this assumption, "idha" may be a pure adverb of time (zarf mahd) and not a conditional. In that case the governing element (al-'amil) of it is "kutiba" under this assumption, and the answer of "in taraka khayran" (if he leaves behind wealth) is omitted, indicated by "kutiba" under this assumption. According to the majority of grammarians (jumhur al-nuhat), it is not permissible for "idha" to be an object (ma'mul) of "al-wasiyya", because the bequest is a verbal noun (masdar) and a relative (mawsul), and the object of the relative may not precede it. Abu al-Hasan (al-Akhfash) permitted this, because according to him the object may precede its governing element if it is an adverb and the governing element is not a pure relative. For him, the verbal noun, and "al" in examples like "al-darib" and "al-marub", is not a pure relative. This condition is present here, and he went to this view in the line: "Abda'li hadha bil-ruhaa al-mutaqa'is?" (Is it for my husband that this one, the one who shrinks back, is set against the millstone?) So he attached "bil-ruha" (against the millstone) to "al-mutaqa'is" (the one who shrinks back).

Abu Muhammad Ibn 'Atiyya said: "In the parsing of this verse, it is possible that 'kutiba' is the governing element of 'idha', and the meaning is: the divine obligation from His Book has been directed at you, when death approaches, so He expressed the directing of the obligation by 'kutiba', so that in this meaning it is also recorded from eternity. 'Al-wasiyya' is the object which has not been named with its agent, governed by 'kutiba'. The answer of the two conditionals, 'idha' and 'in', is omitted, indicated by what preceded it in His words: 'kutiba 'alaykum' (it has been prescribed for you), just as you say: 'I thanked your action that you came to me if it was such-and-such.'" That ends his speech. In it there is a contradiction, because he said the governing element of "idha" is "kutiba", and if the governing element of it is "kutiba", it becomes purely adverbial and not conditional. Then he said: the answer of the two conditionals, "idha" and "in", is omitted, indicated by what preceded, up to the end of his speech. If "idha" is a conditional, then its governing element is either the answer or the verb after it, according to the disagreement concerning its governing element. It is not permissible for its governing element to be what precedes it, except according to the view of one who permits the answer of the condition to precede it and considers the answer to be the governing element of "idha". The words of Ibn 'Atiyya cannot be interpreted according to this view, because he said: the answer of the two conditionals, "idha" and "in", is omitted, indicated by what preceded. What is omitted and indicated by what preceded cannot be the same as what is spoken and precedes. This parsing is according to what the apparent meaning requires, namely that the bequest is the object which has not been named with its agent, and it is in the nominative case (marfu') by "kutiba".

Al-Zamakhshari calls the object which has not been named with its agent an "agent" (fa'il), and this is his terminology. He said in his tafsir: "al-wasiyya" is the agent of "kutiba", and its verb is masculine because of the separation, and because it means "an yuwsiya" (that he should bequeath). That is why the pronoun referring back is masculine in His words: "fa-man baddalahu ba'da ma sami'ahu" (then whoever alters it after he has heard it). End of quote.

I have pointed out his terminology in this matter, so that it is not supposed that calling this object which has not been named with its agent an "agent" is a slip of the copyist.

Some of the grammarians (al-mu'rabin) permitted that "al-wasiyya" be in the nominative case as the subject of an inceptive sentence (mubtada'), with an implied "fa'" (then), and the predicate is either omitted, meaning "fa-'alayhi al-wasiyya" (then upon him is the bequest), or stated, namely His words: "lil-walidayni wal-aqrabin" (for the parents and the near relatives), meaning: "fa-al-wasiyya lil-walidayni wal-aqrabin" (then the bequest is for the parents and the near relatives). This inceptive sentence is the answer to what precedes, and the object which has not been named with its agent, "bi-kutiba", is a hidden pronoun, meaning: the bequeathing, which is explained by what follows. Ibn 'Atiyya said concerning this view: "This bequeathing which is implied, the mention of the bequest after it indicates it, is the governing element of 'idha', and 'al-wasiyya' is raised as an inceptive subject, and in it is the answer of the two conditionals, according to what Sibawayh, may God have mercy on him, cited:

Whoever does good deeds, God will preserve him.

Its raising as an inceptive subject is by the implied 'fa-'alayhi al-wasiyya' (then upon him is the bequest), or by the implied 'fa' alone, as if he said: 'fa-al-wasiyya lil-walidayni' (then the bequest is for the parents)." End of his speech.

In it, he says that "idha" is an object of the implied bequeathing. Then he said that "al-wasiyya" in it is the answer of the two conditionals, and the contradiction of this has already been pointed out, because "idha", inasmuch as it is an object of the bequeathing, is not a condition, and inasmuch as "al-wasiyya" in it is the answer of "idha", it is a condition, so the two statements contradict each other, since one thing cannot be both a condition and not a condition in one and the same state. Nor is it permissible for the implied bequeathing to be the governing element of "idha" either. Because you either suppose that this governing element in "idha" is the word "al-iysa'" (bequeathing) by deletion, or the pronoun of bequeathing. It is not permissible to suppose that the word "al-iysa'" is deleted, because the object which has not been named with its agent may not be deleted. Ibn 'Atiyya supposed the word "al-iysa'", and it is not permissible for him to suppose the pronoun of bequeathing, because if he were to state the pronoun of the verbal noun, it would not be permissible for it to govern, because the verbal noun, according to the Basran grammarians (al-Basriyyun), must be expressed in order to govern, and if it is not permissible to govern through a verbal noun in pronoun form, it is even more so that it should not govern. As for his words: "in it is the answer of the two conditionals", this is not correct, because we have established that every condition requires an answer by its omission, and one thing cannot be the answer of two conditions. As for his words, following the example of what Sibawayh supported:

Whoever does good deeds, God will preserve him.

This is a distortion of Sibawayh. What Sibawayh actually supported in his book is:

Whoever does good deeds, God will thank him, and evil with evil is two equal things before God.

As for his words, "bi-taqdir fa-'alayhi al-wasiyya, aw bi-taqdir al-fa' faqat, ka'annahu qal: fa-al-wasiyya lil-walidayni" (with the implied "then upon him is the bequest", or with the implied "fa" alone, as if he said: "then the bequest is for the parents"), this is the speech of one who has not looked carefully into the speech of Sibawayh, for Sibawayh stated explicitly that such a thing occurs only in poetic necessity (darurat al-shi'r), so the Book of God should be kept free of it.

Sibawayh said: "I asked him, meaning al-Khalil, about the saying: 'in ta'tini ana karim' (if you come to me, I am generous). He said: This only occurs when a poet is compelled, because 'ana karim' is an independent sentence, and the 'fa' and 'idha' only occur joined to what precedes them. They disliked that this should be an answer, since it does not resemble the 'fa'. The poet said it under compulsion." He cited the previous line:

Whoever does good deeds...

It is mentioned from al-Akhfash that this is by the implied "fa", and this is refuted by Sibawayh's report that this occurs only under compulsion.

Some of them permitted that the prepositional phrase "'alaykum", which is the prepositional phrase in question, be placed in the position of the object which has not been named with its agent. This is a view with no harm in it according to what we establish. We say: When He informed that it has been prescribed for one of them when death approaches him, if he leaves behind wealth, the hearer is eager to know what the thing prescribed is. So "al-wasiyya" is an inceptive subject, or the predicate of the inceptive subject according to this assumption, and it is an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "What is prescribed for one of us when death approaches him and he leaves behind wealth?" Then it is said: "The bequest for the parents and the near relatives is what is prescribed," or "What is prescribed is the bequest for the parents and the near relatives." Its parallel is: "He was struck with a whip on Friday, Zayd is the one struck," or "The one struck is Zayd." This is an answer to an implied question, as if he said: "Who is the one struck?" This view is better and less forced than the view before it, which is that the object which has not been named with its agent is the bequeathing, and the pronoun of bequeathing, and "the parents" are both known. The discussion of this was already presented in His words: "wa-bil-walidayni ihsanan" (and to parents, kindness) [al-Baqarah 2:83].

\* \*

"Wal-aqrabin" (and the near relatives) is the plural of "al-aqrab" (the nearest). Its apparent sense is that it is an elative form (af'al tafdil), so everyone who was nearer to the deceased enters into this word [p-21], and the nearest to him are the parents. Thus this becomes generalization after specification, as if the two were mentioned twice: for emphasis and for specification, to make the good reach them. This is what the apparent meaning of this word indicates. According to the exegetes (al-mufassirun), "al-aqrabun" are the children, or all except the children, or all the kin, or those among the relatives who do not inherit. These are the various views.

"Bil-ma'ruf" (in a fair manner) means that he should not bequeath more than one third, nor to the rich while leaving out the poor. Ibn Mas'ud said: "al-akhall fa-al-akhall," meaning the most needy and then the most needy. It is said: "That in which there is no injustice." It is said: this was left to the judgment of the testator, then it was clarified and fixed at one third, and one third is a lot. It is also said: "In the manner that people know, without harm to the heirs, for they used to bequeath all their wealth." It is also said: "In a fair manner from his wealth, not unknown."

These views go back to the amount of what is bequeathed and to the distinguishing of the one to whom the bequest is made. Al-Zamakhshari summarized this and explained it as justice, namely that one does not bequeath to the rich while leaving the poor, and does not exceed one third. "Bil-ma'ruf" may be connected to "al-wasiyya", or to an omitted element, meaning: "being in a fair manner," so that "bil-ma'ruf" is a circumstantial element (hal) of "al-wasiyya".

﴿Haqqan ʿalā al-muttaqīn﴾ (a duty upon the God-fearing). *Haqqan* is in the accusative (naṣb) as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*, the infinitive or verbal noun) that emphasizes the content of the sentence, meaning: "That was due as a [binding] due." This was stated by Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Zamakhsharī. However, the rules of grammar (*al-qawāʿid al-naḥwiyyah*) reject this, because the apparent meaning of His words ﴿ʿalā al-muttaqīn﴾ means that *ʿalā* is then connected to *ḥaqqan*, or that it occupies the position of a qualifier (*ṣifah*) for it. Both of these analyses remove it from being an emphatic (*taʾkīd*). As for connecting it to *ḥaqqan*, that is because an emphatic verbal noun does not govern (*lā yaʿmal*); only a verbal noun that can be resolved into a verb with a verbal particle (*ḥarf maṣdarī*) governs, or a verbal noun that is a substitute (*badal*) for the verb's own form. This is consistent in the case of the imperative and the interrogative, with a difference of opinion regarding the latter, as established in the science of grammar (*ʿilm al-naḥw*). As for making it a qualifier of *ḥaqqan*, meaning "a due that is upon the God-fearing," this removes it from being an emphatic, because in that case it becomes specified by the qualifier.

The grammarians (*al-muʿribūn*, those who analyze the case endings, i.e. *iʿrāb*) permitted that it be an attribute (*naʿt*) of a deleted verbal noun, either a verbal noun derived from ﴿kutiba ʿalaykum﴾, meaning "a binding writing (*katban ḥaqqan*)," or a verbal noun derived from *al-waṣiyyah* (the bequest), meaning "a binding bequeathing (*īṣāʾan ḥaqqan*)." He who held that it is in the accusative governed by *al-muttaqīn* and that the sense is "upon the God-fearing, truly," like His words ﴿ulāʾika humu al-muʾminūna ḥaqqan﴾ [al-Anfāl: 4], was far off the mark, because that is not what comes immediately to mind, and because it precedes its governing word, which is the relative/connected element (*al-mawṣūl*). In my view, the better reading is that it is a verbal noun from the sense of *kutiba*, because the meaning of "the bequest was written" is "it became obligatory and binding." So its accusative case is as a verbal noun of a different root than the verb (*ʿalā ghayr al-ṣadr*), like the saying "I sat sitting" (*qaʿadtu juluwsan*).

The apparent meaning of His words "was written" and "a due" is obligation, since the meaning of that is a binding obligation upon the God-fearing. It has been said: its meaning is that whoever fears God regarding the affairs of the heirs should not be extravagant, and regarding the relatives should give precedence to the most needy, then the next most needy. It has also been said: it means whoever follows the laws of faith, those who act with God-consciousness in speech and deed. He (God) singled them out for mention to honour them and to draw attention to the high station of the God-fearing with Him. It has also been said: it means whoever guards against unbelief and disobedience to the command.

Some have said: His words ﴿ʿalā al-muttaqīn﴾ indicate that bequeathing is recommended (*nadb*), not obligatory, because if it were obligatory He would have said "upon the Muslims." But there is no proof in this, because by "the God-fearing" is meant "the believers," and they are those who guarded against unbelief. So it is possible that this is what is meant here.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 181:

﴿Then whoever alters it after he has heard it﴾. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun refers to the bequest (al-wasiyya) in the sense of the act of bequeathing (al-iṣa', the making of a will). That is, whoever alters the bequeathing from its proper form, if it was in accordance with the Sharia, from among the executors (al-awsiya') and the witnesses, after he has heard it with certainty and assurance. Its referring to the act of bequeathing is preferable to its referring to the bequest, because the feminine gender of "wasiyya" is not true (ḥaqīqī, grammatically genuine) femininity. That is because this is not observed in pronouns that come after a metaphorical (majāzī) feminine noun. Rather, true and metaphorical feminine nouns are equal in this respect. You say: "Hind went out" and "the sun rose." It is not permitted to say "ṭala'a" (masculine) except in poetry. The masculine form in observance of the meaning occurs in their speech, and from it is the line:

"Like the supple shoot of the ban tree that splits open"

Here he took the meaning of "branch" (qaḍīb), as if he had said: "like the branch of the ban tree." From the reverse case is: "His book came to him, so he despised it," in view of the meaning of "page" (ṣaḥīfa). The pronoun in ﴿he had heard it﴾ refers to the bequeathing, as we have explained. It has been said that it refers to the command of God Most High in this verse.

It has been said that the pronoun in ﴿whoever alters it﴾ refers to the obligation and the ruling, and the sense is: whoever alters the matter mentioned before. As for "man" (whoever), the apparent view is that it is conditional (shartiyya, introducing a condition). The answer (jawab, the main clause of the conditional) is ﴿then the sin of it is only upon him﴾. "Man" is general, covering every alterer: whoever is content with other than the bequest in writing, or the division of rights, or a witness who gives other than his testimony, or who conceals it, or others who prevent the wealth from being obtained and reaching its rightful recipient. It has been said that the intended meaning of "man" is the one who undertakes the bequeathing, not the testator or the legatee, for he is the one in whose hand lie justice, injustice, alteration, and execution. It has been said that the intended meaning of "man" is the testator himself. He is forbidden to change his bequest from the situations in which God has forbidden bequeathing to them, because they used to direct it to strangers, so they were commanded to direct it to the nearest relatives. According to this view, the pronoun in His saying ﴿whoever alters it﴾ and in His saying ﴿after he has heard it﴾ must refer to the command of God Most High in the verse. And in His saying ﴿after he has heard it﴾ there is evidence that the sin is not incurred unless the alterer knew of it. He used hearing as a metonymy (kināya) for knowledge, because it is the means by which knowledge is obtained.

﴿then the sin of it is only upon him﴾. The pronoun refers to the altered bequest, or to the verbal noun (maṣdar, the infinitive-like noun) understood from "baddalahu" (he altered it).
