That is: the sin of the alteration is only upon the alterer. In this there is evidence that whoever commits a sin, its burden falls only upon him. If the executor falls short in any part of what the deceased bequeathed, nothing of that falls upon the deceased. He observed the meaning in His saying ﴿upon those who alter it﴾, since if it had followed the pattern of the first wording it would have been "﴿then the sin of it is upon him﴾" or "then the sin of it is upon him upon the one who alters it." In the answer clause he used the explicit noun in place of the pronoun, to indicate the cause of the sin incurred, which is the alteration. He used the relative clause of "those" (alladhīna) in the present-future tense, following the original pattern, since it is future (in reference).

﴿Indeed God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾. In these two attributes there is a threat and a warning to the alterers, for nothing is hidden from Him, Exalted is He, so He will requite them for their alteration with the worst recompense. It has been said: He hears the speech of the testator and knows the deed of the one bequeathed to. It has been said: He hears his bequests and knows his intentions. The apparent view is the first, because it comes right after the mention of the alteration and the sin that follows from it.

(p-23)

﴿فَمَن خافَ مِن مُوصٍ جَنَفًا أوْ إثْمًا فَأصْلَحَ بَيْنَهم فَلا إثْمَ عَلَيْهِ﴾. The apparent meaning is that *khawf* (fear) here means *khashyah* (apprehension), following the basic usage of the word in the language. The meaning is: with the expectation of *janaf* (unintentional deviation) or *ithm* (sin) from the testator. Mujahid said: The meaning is: whoever fears that the testator may deviate, cut off the inheritance of a group, and deliberately harm them, or do so without intent. That is *janaf* without sin. If he does it deliberately, it is *janaf* accompanied by sin. So he admonishes him about this and turns him back, and thereby the matter between him and his heirs is set right, and there is no sin upon him.

﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ غَفُورٌ﴾ toward the testator when the admonition takes effect and he turns back from the intended harm, ﴿رَحِيمٌ﴾ toward him. It has also been said that *khawf* here means *ilm* (knowledge), that is: whoever knows. This is supported by His saying, ﴿إلّا أنْ يَخافا ألّا يُقِيما حُدُودَ اللَّهِ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229], and the saying of Abu Mihjan:

*I fear that when I die I shall not taste it*

The link between *khawf* and *ilm* is such that *khawf* is applied to *ilm*, because a person does not fear something until he knows that it is among the things to be feared. This is therefore the expression of the cause by its effect (*al-tabir bil-musabbab 'an al-sabab*). Al-Razi in *al-Muntakhab* said: *khawf* and *khashyah* are used in the sense of knowledge, because *khawf* is a specific state born of a specific conjecture (*zann*), and between conjecture and knowledge there is resemblance in many respects; therefore each of them may be applied to the other. End of his words.

On the reading of *khawf* as knowledge, Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, Qatadah and al-Rabi' said the meaning of the verse is: whoever knows, that is, after the death of the testator, that the testator has been partial, has deviated, and has deliberately harmed some of his heirs, and then sets right what has occurred among the heirs of disturbance and discord, there is no sin upon him. That is, the sin of the substitution mentioned earlier does not attach to him, even though his act involves a change of the bequest, because it is a change for a benefit. The substitution that carries sin is only the substitution of desire.

Ata' said: The meaning is: whoever fears from a testator *janaf* or *ithm* in his gift to his heirs at the approach of his death, giving some and withholding from others, there is no sin upon him for setting right matters among the heirs in that regard.

Tawus said: The meaning is: whoever fears from a testator *janaf* or *ithm* in his bequest to someone other than his heirs, in a way that returns part of it upon his heirs, and then sets right matters among his heirs, there is no sin upon him. Al-Hasan said: It is that he bequeaths to strangers and leaves out the close relatives, so he returns it to the relatives. He said: This is the setting right. Al-Suddi said: The meaning is: whoever fears from a testator, regarding his fathers and relatives, *janaf* against some of them in favour of others, and then sets right matters between the fathers and relatives, there is no sin upon him.

Ali ibn Isa said: It includes a past event that has occurred and a non-occurring matter. If the bequest is still in effect, the testator is ordered to amend it and to turn from *janaf* toward *nasaf* (fairness). If it has already taken effect, the executor (*al-musa ilayh*) amends it after his death. It has also been said: It is that he bequeaths to the son of his daughter, intending by it the benefit of his daughter. This returns to the saying of Tawus mentioned earlier.

When we interpret *khawf* as *khashyah*, then *khawf* is valid only regarding a matter not yet settled, while the bequest has already taken place. How then can it be linked to *khawf*? The answer: when the one setting things right witnesses the testator making a bequest and signs of *janaf* or of transgression appear in it, such as adding to one who does not deserve, or diminishing from one who does, or turning away from one who does deserve, and he sets things right upon the appearance of these signs, since he has not yet concluded that there is *janaf* and sin, it is fitting that the condition be attached to *khawf*, because the bequest has not yet been enforced or taken place. Or the condition is attached to *khawf* even if the bequest has already taken place, because the testator has the right to abrogate it (*yansakhaha*) or alter it by addition or subtraction, so *janaf* or sin has not become certain, since permitting retraction prevents certainty. Or the condition is attached to *khawf* even if the bequest has been established and the testator has died, because it is permissible that reconciliation take place between the heirs and the beneficiaries in a way that removes inclination and error, so *janaf* and sin were not settled, and therefore the condition is attached to *khawf*. The first answer is stronger.

*Man* is a conditional particle, and its answer is ﴿فَلا إثْمَ عَلَيْهِ﴾. ﴿مِن مُوصٍ﴾ is connected to *khafa*, or to an omitted element whose estimate is: existing from a testator, and it would be a circumstantial clause (*hal*). If it were postponed it would be an attributive (*sifah*), as in His saying ﴿جَنَفًا أوْ إثْمًا﴾, but since it is placed first it becomes a circumstantial clause. In both of these estimates the one who fears is not the testator. It is also permissible that *min* indicates the kind of the one who fears, so that the one who fears is one of the testators, in the manner of: *whoever comes to you from a man, honour him*, meaning: whoever comes to you from among the men, the one who comes is a man. The one who fears here is a testator. The meaning is: whoever fears from the testator *janaf* or *ithm* from his heirs and from those to whom he bequeaths, and then sets right matters between them, there is no sin upon the testator who sets things right. This is a meaning the exegetes did not mention; they only mentioned that the testator is the one feared (*makhuf*) and not the one who fears, and that *janaf* or *ithm* comes from the testator, not from his heirs or from those to whom he bequeaths.

Hamzah read ﴿خافَ﴾ with *imalah* (inclination of the vowel). He, al-Kisai and Abu Bakr read ﴿مُوَصٍّ﴾ (from *wassa*), while the rest read ﴿مُوصٍ﴾ (from *awsa*). It has been mentioned before that both are dialects. The majority read *janafan* with *jim* and *nun*. Ali read *hayfan* with *ha* and *ya*. Abu al-Aliyah said: *al-janaf* is ignorance of the proper place of the bequest, and *al-ithm* is deviation from its proper place. Ata' and Ibn Zayd said: *al-janaf* is inclination, and *al-ithm* is that he has sinned by favouring some heirs over others. Al-Suddi said: *al-janaf* is error, and *al-ithm* is deliberate intent. As for *al-hayf*, its meaning is diminishment, namely that he intends to give some heirs and not others. Al-Farra' said: *tahayyafa malan*, meaning he reduced his property from its edges. It is narrated: Whoever deviates in his bequest will be cast into *Alwa*, and *Alwa* is a valley in Hell.

﴿فَأصْلَحَ بَيْنَهُمُ﴾: the pronoun returns to the testator and the heirs, or to the beneficiaries and the heirs, or to the beneficiaries and the heirs and the beneficiaries together, according to the differing views that preceded. The apparent return is to the beneficiaries, since the word "the testator" implies, by the implicit meaning of the address (*mafhum al-khitab*), that there is a beneficiary. Similarly, in His saying ﴿وأداءٌ إلَيْهِ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178], meaning "to the one who pardons," because of the indication of "the one to whom pardon is granted." From this is what al-Farra', may Allah have mercy on him, recited:

*I do not know, when I set out for a land seeking good, which of the two will befall me*

He said "which of the two" and returned the pronoun to good and evil, though evil was not mentioned before; but good was mentioned, and in it there is an indication of evil. The apparent meaning is that the one who sets things right is the executor, the witness, or whoever takes charge after his death, whether a governor, a guardian, or one who enjoins the good. All of these are included under His saying ﴿فَمَن خافَ﴾ when signs of *janaf* or *ithm* appear to them. There is no reason to restrict the one who fears to the executor. As for the manner of this setting right, it is by addition or subtraction, or by restraining the injustice.

﴿فَلا إثْمَ عَلَيْهِ﴾ means: in altering the bequest, if he does that intending to set things right. The pronoun in ﴿عَلَيْهِ﴾ returns to the one to whom the pronoun in ﴿فَأصْلَحَ﴾ and the pronoun in ﴿خافَ﴾ refer, which is ﴿مَن﴾, that is, the one who fears and sets things right.

Abu Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Umar al-Razi said: When he mentioned the substitute at the beginning of the verse, and this was a form of substitution, he clarified its difference from the first, and that there is no sin upon him, because he returned the bequest to the just measure. Since the one setting things right reduces the bequests, and that is difficult for the beneficiary, he removed the doubt by saying ﴿فَلا إثْمَ عَلَيْهِ﴾, even though there is opposition in it to the testator's bequest, and he diverted his property from the one he loved to the one he disliked. End of his words.

This meaning returns to his first statement. He also said: Setting things right requires much speech, and it may involve some of what is not fitting of word or deed, so He clarified that there is no sin in that if it is for the intention of setting things right. The verse indicates the permissibility of reconciliation between disputing parties when the one wishing reconciliation fears that the dispute will lead to something forbidden in the Sharia. End of his words.

﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾. It has been said: ﴿غَفُورٌ﴾ for what came from the one who fears, and ﴿رَحِيمٌ﴾ toward the one who sets things right, in that He granted a concession. It has also been said: ﴿غَفُورٌ﴾ toward the testator for what he entertained in himself of *janaf*, error, transgression, and sin, when he returned to the truth; ﴿رَحِيمٌ﴾ toward the one who sets things right. Al-Raghib said: That is, He overlooks what may have fallen from the one who sets things right of what was not unjust.

These noble verses have included [page 25] that righteousness (*al-birr*) is not merely turning one's face toward the east or the west, but rather righteousness is carrying out what the person is obligated to do of the obligations of the Sharia, in belief, action, and speech. Of belief: faith in Allah, His angels who are the intermediaries between Him and His prophets, His books which were sent down through the hands of the angels, and His prophets who received those books from His angels. Then He mentioned what the prophets brought from Allah in those books: giving wealth, establishing prayer, paying zakah, fulfilling covenants, and patience in hardships. Then He informed that whoever fulfils these is the patient and the God-fearing. Since He had mentioned before what He made lawful and what He forbade, and then followed that with whoever took wealth unlawfully, promising him the Fire, He thereby indicated all the prohibited kinds of wealth. Then He mentioned those who attained complete righteousness and praised them with the commendable qualities they embodied. He then began to mention what He forbade of blood and called for its protection. The mention of food was placed first because of the general trial with eating.

Then He legislated retaliation (*al-qisas*), and He did not exclude the one who committed the killing and was subjected to retaliation from faith. Do you not see that He addressed him by the name of faith and specified some of the requital, saying ﴿الحُرُّ بِالحُرِّ والعَبْدُ بِالعَبْدِ والأُنْثى بِالأُنْثى﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178]? Then He informed afterward that if pardon is granted by the guardian in return for blood money, then the guardian shall follow up with fairness, and the killer shall pay with goodness, so that by this affection may be sown between the killer and the guardian, and enmities removed. For the legislation of pardon requires, on the third party, mutual love and purity of inner hearts. Then He mentioned that this is a concession from Him, the Exalted, since in it is the preservation of the killer's life through some of the goods of this world. Then He threatened whoever transgresses after that. Then He informed that in the legislation of retaliation there is life, since whoever knows that he will be killed in return for whoever he kills, and is sensible, that knowledge prevents him from advancing to killing, because in it is the destruction of the life of the slain and the destruction of the life of his killer. So by his knowledge of retaliation he becomes cautious lest he kill and be killed, and thereby he preserves the life of the one who intended to kill him, and that was a cause of life for both of them. Then He mentioned the legislation of bequest for the one whom death approaches, and mentioned that the bequest is for parents and close relatives, and He threatened whoever substitutes the bequest after he has known it. Then He mentioned that there is no sin upon the one who sets things right among the beneficiaries when there is *janaf* or *ithm* from the testator, and that this is not counted as the substitution that entails sin. Thus these verses came comprising what is required of the obligated person from the beginning of his state, which is faith in Allah, to the closing of his state, which is the bequest at his departure from this existence, and what lies between them of the paths of obedience and the lapses of disobedience, without exhaustively enumerating their instances, but rather as an alert to the best of deeds after faith, which is establishing prayer and what follows it, and to the greatest of the major sins after polytheism, which is the killing of a soul. Exalted is He whose speech is decisive, and whose judgment is just.

Al-Ṣiyām (fasting) and al-Ṣawm are both verbal nouns (maṣdar) of (ṣāma). The Arabs call anyone who refrains a ṣā'im (one who abstains). From this comes the usage of ṣawm in speech, in the verse ﴿Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast﴾ [Maryam: 26], meaning silence in speech. Also, "ṣāmat al-rīḥ" means the wind stopped blowing, and "ṣāmat al-dābba" means the animal refrained from eating and running. Al-Nābigha al-Dhubyānī said:

*Horses that are ṣiyām (standing still), and other horses that are not ṣā'ima, beneath the dust, while others chew their bits.*

That is, those that refrain from running. The animal that does not turn is called al-ṣā'ima. The rajaz poet said:

*And the young she-camels, the worst of them is the ṣā'ima.*

They also said: "ṣāma al-nahār" means the heat of the day became fixed at midday and intensified. He said:

*A swift (camel) when the day became ṣā'im and grew hot.*

And he said:

*Until, when the day became ṣā'im and moderated, and the sun's saliva inclined and descended.*

Maṣām al-nujūm means their stopping from motion, and from this comes:

*As if al-Thurayyā were hung in its station.*

This is the linguistic meaning of ṣawm. As for its legal (sharʿī) meaning, it is abstention from specific things, at a specific time, and this is explained in jurisprudence (fiqh).

Al-Ṭāqa and al-Ṭawq: power and capacity. It is said: "ṭāqa" and "aṭāqa" something, meaning he was able to do it and had the capacity for it. Abū Dhu'ayb said:

*So I said to him: carry beyond your capacity, for it is sealed; whoever comes to it, it will not harm it.*

Al-Shahr (the month) is a verbal noun of "shahara al-shay'" (he made it apparent): he made it manifest, and from it comes al-shuhra (fame). The month was named after it, and it is the period of time in which the beginning of the crescent is hidden until it becomes concealed, then it appears hidden. It was so named for its prominence in people's need for it in dealings and other affairs. Al-Zajjāj said: al-shahr is the crescent. He said:

*And the month is like the paring of a fingernail.*

It was named so for its clarity (bayān). It was also said: the month was named shahr after the crescent: when the crescent appeared, it was called shahr. The Arabs say: "I saw the shahr," meaning its crescent. Dhū al-Rumma (poetically) said:

*You see the month before the people, and it is slender.*

It is said: "ashharnā," meaning a month came upon us. Al-Farrā' said: I have not heard a verb from it except this. Al-Tha'labī said: it is said "shahara al-hilāl" when it rose. The plural of shahr in the paucity form is on the pattern "af'ul," and in the abundance form on the pattern "fu'ūl," and both are regular for it.

Ramaḍān is a proper name for the month of fasting, and it is a generic proper noun ('alam jins). It is pluralized as ramaḍānāt and armiḍa. The reason for this name is from a period when it occurred during the ramaḍī, which is intense heat, just as the month was named Rabīʿ after the period of Rabīʿ (spring), and Jumādā after the period of jumūd (freezing). It is said: "ramaḍa al-ṣā'im yarmaḍu," meaning his insides burned from intense thirst. "Ramaḍat al-fiṣāl" means the hot sand burned their hooves, so they knelt from intense heat and withdrew to the shade of their mothers. It is also said: "armaḍathu al-ramḍā'," meaning the hot sand burned him, and "armaḍanī al-amr," meaning the matter burned me.

It was said: Ramaḍān was named so because it burns sins (yarmaḍu al-dhunūb), i.e., burns them through righteous deeds. It was also said: because hearts burn from the admonition in it and reflection on the matter of the Hereafter. It was also said: from "ramaḍtu al-naṣl," meaning I thinned the blade between two stones to make it thin, and from this: "naṣl ramīḍ" and "marmūḍ," related from Ibn al-Sikkīt. They used to polish their weapons in this month to fight with them in Shawwāl before the sacred months began. This month was called Nātiq in the pre-Islamic period. Al-Mufaḍḍal recited:

*And in Nātiq, the horsemen of Khath'am were driven away at the zone of battle, and turned their backs.*

Al-Zamakhsharī said: Ramaḍān is a verbal noun of "ramiḍa," meaning he burned from the ramḍā'. End of quote. But establishing that it is a verbal noun requires a sound transmission, because fa'alān is not the verbal noun of the intransitive "fa'ila," rather if it occurs in that form it is anomalous (shādhdh), and the better view is that it is a newly coined (murtajal) name transferred (manqūl).

It was also said: it is derived from al-ramaḍ, which is rain that comes before autumn and purifies the earth from dust.

Al-Qur'ān is the verbal noun of "qara'a qur'ānan" (he recited). Ḥassān (may Allah be pleased with him) said:

*They sacrificed a grey-haired one, whose mark is prostration, who cuts the night with tasbīḥ and qur'ān.*

That is, and recitation. It was applied to what lies between the two covers of the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and it became a proper name for it. This is the application of a verbal noun to the meaning of the object (ism al-maf'ūl) originally. The meaning of qur'ān with a hamza is "gathering," because it gathers the surahs, as was said of the qar' (menstrual blood/ovulation) which is the gathering of blood in the womb initially. The reciter throws it out during recitation, from the Arabs' saying: "This she-camel never threw out a sallah (afterbirth)," meaning she never discharged it. For one who does not hamza it, the more apparent view is that this is from the category of transfer and deletion, or the nūn is original, from "qarantu al-shay' ilā al-shay'," meaning I joined one thing to another: because its surahs, verses and letters are linked to one another, or because its wisdoms and laws are likewise, or because its proofs and correspondences are linked: its verses confirm one another. As for one who claims it comes from "qaraytu al-mā' fī al-ḥawḍ," meaning I collected the water in the basin, his statement is invalid because the two roots differ.

Al-Safar (travel) is derived from their saying: "safarat al-mar'a" when she removed her veil, and the verbal noun is al-sufūr. The poet said:

*And when I came to Layla, she veiled herself, but her unveiling in the morning troubled me.*

You say: "safara al-rajul," meaning he removed his turban, and "asfara al-wajh wa al-ṣubḥ," meaning it lit up. Al-Azharī said: the traveler is called musāfir because he uncovers the shelter from his face and emerges onto open land. Al-Safr with a sukūn on the fā' means travelers, and it is a collective noun like al-ṣaḥb and al-rakb. Al-Sifr among books is the singular of asfār, because it uncovers what it contains.

Al-Yusr is ease. "Yasura" means became easy, "yassara" means facilitated, "aysara" means became rich. "Yasara" (to gamble) comes from al-maysir, which is a well-known gambling. 'Alqama said:

*They do not gamble with a horse I have acquired, and whatever the people gamble with is a loss.*

The left hand was called al-yusrā optimistically, or because the matter is made easy by it through assisting the right hand. Al-ʿUsr is difficulty and constraint, and from it: "a'sara i'sāran" and "dhū 'usra," meaning in constraint.

Al-Ikmāl is completion. Al-Ijāba (response) may mean hearing. In a ḥadīth, a bedouin said: "O Muḥammad." He said: "I have answered you." They also said: "He called upon one who does not answer," meaning one who does not hear. Just as hearing may mean response, from this: "Allah hears whoever praises Him." Ibn al-A'rābī recited where he said:

*I called upon Allah until I feared that Allah would not hear what I say.*

The connection between them is clear: response follows hearing. Ijāba is essentially conveying to the questioner what he asked for. Ajāba and istajāba mean "qaṭaʿa" (cut off), and its alif is converted from a waw. It is said: "jāba yajūbu," meaning he cut through. So the responder cuts off for the questioner what he asked to be given. It is said: "the sky responded with rain" and "the earth responded with plants," as if each asked its companion and it responded with what it asked.

Zuhayr said:

*And rain from al-Wasmī, sweet in its reach, its high ground and its downpours responded to al-najā.*

Al-Rushd is the opposite of error (ghayy). It is said: "rashada" (with fatḥa) rushdan, and "rashida" (with kasra) rashadan. "Arshadtu fulānan" means I guided him. "Ṭarīq arshad" means a direct path. Al-Marāshid are the destinations of the road. "Huwa li-rishda" means he is of lawful birth, which is the opposite of "huwa li-zanya" (of adultery). Umm Rāshid is the mouse. Banū Rushdān is a tribe of the Arabs. Banū Rāshid is a large tribe of the Berbers.

Al-Rafath is a verbal noun of "rafatha," and it is said "arfatha" meaning he spoke obscenely. Al-ʿAjjāj said:

*And the Lord of groups of pilgrims, restrained from idle talk and obscene speech.*

Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Zajjāj and others said: al-rafath is a comprehensive word for everything a man desires from a woman. Ibn ʿAbbās recited:

*And they walk with us softly; if the bird is truthful, we will be with a soft one.*

He was asked: "Do you engage in rafath while you are in iḥrām?" He said: "Rafath is only with women." In a ḥadīth: "Whoever performs this House's pilgrimage and does not engage in rafath or fusūq, comes out like the day his mother bore him." It was also said: al-rafath is intercourse, and this was used as evidence by the verse of the poet:

*They show from the pleasantness of conversation, adulteresses, and from the rafath of men they have aversion.*

And by the saying of another:

*They spent the night engaging in rafath, while among us men spent the night riding in their armor.*

And by the saying of another:

*So we remained there in bliss, and all pleasure except rafath.*

There is no proof in this, since it may mean preliminaries: such as kissing, looking, and playfulness.

Ikhtāna is from khiyāna (betrayal). It is said: "khāna yakhūnu khawnan and khiyāna," when he does not fulfill. That is the opposite of amāna (trust). "Takhawwantu al-shay'" means I diminished it, and from it comes khiyāna, which diminishes the one entrusted. Zuhayr said:

*With a firm-backed one, whom the saddle-straps and the saddle-cloth did not betray.*

"Takhawwanahu" and "takhawwalahu" mean he attended to him.

Al-Khayṭ is well known and its plural is fu'ūl, and this is regular for it, I mean in the "fa'l" noun pattern with a yā' middle radical, such as bayt and buyūt, jayb and juyūb, ghayb and ghuyūb, ʿayn and ʿuyūn. Al-khayṭ with a kasra on the khā' means a group of ostriches. The poet said:

*So he said: Look, this is a herd of wild cattle and a group, and a scattered line of ostriches grazing.*

Al-bayāḍ and al-sawād are two well-known colors. It is said from them: bīḍ and sūd, so he is abyaḍ and aswad. The ʿayn was not altered by transfer and conversion, because it is in the meaning of what is sound: they are abyaḍ and aswad. Al-ʿukūf is residence. "ʿakafa bi-al-makān" means he stayed in it. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They persist in devotion to idols they have﴾ [al-A'rāf: 138]. Al-Farazdaq describing the large bowls said:

*Around them you see the beggars, as if they were on an idol in the pre-Islamic era, devoted.*

And al-Ṭirimmāḥ said:

*The daughters of the night stayed around me, devoted, like weeping women, among them is a fallen one.*

In the Sharʿ it is an expression for a specific ʿukūf, which has been explained in the books of fiqh. Al-Ḥadd: al-Layth said: the ḥadd of a thing is its end and limit. The intended meaning of Allah's ḥudūd is His determinations with specific measures and specific attributes.

Al-Idlā' is sending down a bucket, from which a verb was derived: they said "adlā dalwahu," meaning he lowered his bucket to fill it. It was said: "adlā fulān bi-mālihi ilā al-ḥākim," meaning he brought it forward. The poet said:

*And whenever a need arose, I have made it at the door of your house, I bring it forward with people.*

It is said: "adlā fulān bi-ḥujjatihi," meaning he presented it. And "tadallā min kadhā," meaning he descended. The poet said:

*Like the gazelle's bull, reddish, the eagle swooped down upon him, and descended from the peaks of Thahlān.*

*

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 183 (part 2 of 2):

﴿O you who have believed, fasting has been prescribed for you﴾: The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that He, exalted is He, first informed of the prescription of *qisas* (retaliation), which is the destruction of souls, and it is one of the most burdensome obligations, for the murderer must surrender his own soul to be killed. Second, He informed of the prescription of *wasiyya* (bequest), which is the giving out of wealth, which is the equivalent of the soul. Third, He moved on to the prescription of fasting, which exhausts the body, weakens it, and prevents and cuts off what a person is accustomed to eating during the day. So He began with the most difficult, then with what is more difficult after it, then with what is difficult. This is the progression in what God has prescribed for His servants in this verse. Before this, He had mentioned three of the pillars of Islam: faith, prayer, and almsgiving. So He came with this fourth pillar, which is fasting.

The form *kutiba* (was prescribed) is in the passive voice in these three prescriptions, and the agent is omitted because it is known, namely God, exalted is He. This is because they are difficult burdens for the responsible person, so it is appropriate that they not be attributed to God, exalted is He, even though it is God who prescribed them. When what is prescribed for the responsible person contains ease and good tidings, the verb is built in the active voice, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾ [al-An'am: 54], ﴿God has prescribed: "Surely I and My messengers will overcome"﴾ [al-Mujadila: 21], ﴿Those – He has written faith into their hearts﴾ [al-Mujadila: 22]. This is one of the subtle points of the science of rhetoric (*'ilm al-bayan*).

As for the building of the verb in the active voice in His saying: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the soul is for the soul﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 45], it is appropriate because of the obstinacy of the Jews and the frequency of their opposition to their prophets, unlike this Muhammadan community. So He distinguished between the two addresses because the addressees differ. He called the believers when informing them of this third prescription, which is fasting, in order to alert them to listen to what is conveyed to them of this obligation. He did not need a call with the second prescription, because it is linked with the first in one system, namely the presence of death by retaliation or otherwise. This third obligation differs from them. He placed the prepositional phrase (*al-jar wa-l-majrur*) before the direct object, although the more common Arabic word order is the reverse, as in: *dariba Zayd bi-sawt* (Zayd was struck with a whip). This is because what the verb requires an intermediary to reach is placed before what it reaches without an intermediary. The reason is that beginning with mention of the one upon whom it is prescribed is more important than mentioning the prescription itself, since the prescription is tied to the one who is addressed. So the soul first knows that the one addressed is the responsible person, and then awaits what he is charged with.

The *alif* and *lam* in "﴿al-Siyam﴾" are for a specific reference (*al-'ahd*) if their worship with it had already preceded, or for the category (*al-jins*) if it had not preceded. This verbal noun came in the pattern *fi'al*, which is one of the two common patterns for the verbal noun of this type of verb, namely a verb whose middle radical is *waw* and whose last radical is sound. The two patterns are *fu'ul* and *fi'al*. He turned away from *fu'ul*, although it is the original, because of the heaviness of the two *waws*. Some of it came in the original form, as in *al-fu'ur* (boiling). Because of the heaviness of the two *waws* together, some spoke it with a hamza, saying *al-fu'ur*.

﴿as it was prescribed﴾: Apparently this prepositional phrase is in the position of a qualifier (*sifa*) of an omitted verbal noun, or in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) according to the opinion of Sibawayh, as previously mentioned. That is: a prescription like what was prescribed, or as it was prescribed. Meaning: the prescription from it is a prescription. The causal sense then falls upon the general act of prescribing, which is obligation, even though its object differs in number or otherwise. This meaning is reported from Mu'adh ibn Jabal and 'Ata'. In that case *ma* is a verbal (*masdariyya*) particle. It has also been said that the *kaf* is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause of *al-siyam* (fasting), meaning: resembling what was prescribed upon those before you. Here *ma* is a relative pronoun, meaning: resembling that which was prescribed upon you. The one in the circumstantial position is *al-siyam*, and the governing element of it is the governing element of the verb, namely "was prescribed upon you." Ibn 'Atiyya permitted that the *kaf* be in the position of a qualifier of an omitted *sawm* (fast), the estimate being: a fast like what. This is far-fetched, because comparing fasting to writing is not valid if *ma* is verbal. As for if it is relative, there is also a distance in it, because comparing fasting to the thing fasted is not valid except by a far-fetched interpretation. Some grammarians permitted that the *kaf* be in the nominative position, as a modifier (*na't*) of the word *al-siyam*. He said: its definiteness is not commendable because of the generality that is in it, which the Law has clarified. Therefore it was permitted to modify it with *kama*, since it is only modified by it with indefinite nouns. So it is in the position of: ﴿fasting has been prescribed for you﴾. The end of his speech. This destroys the grammatical rule requiring agreement between the modifier and the modified in definiteness and indefiniteness. Some have gone toward something of this kind, and that when the *alif* and *lam* are generic (*jinsiyya*), it is permitted for what they govern to be described by a clause. They counted as an example of this His saying: ﴿And a sign for them is the night; We strip from it the day﴾ [Ya-Sin: 37]. No proof stands for establishing the destruction of what the grammarians hold. What is summarized regarding *ma* in His saying "*kama*" is two aspects: one is that it is verbal, and this is the apparent meaning; the other is that it is relative in the sense of *alladhi* (which).

﴿upon those before you﴾: Its apparent meaning is the generality of "those before us," from the prophets and their nations, from Adam until our time. 'Ali said: the first of them is Adam, and He did not make it obligatory upon you. He means: fasting is an ancient, original worship. God did not leave any nation free of its prescription upon them, so He did not make it obligatory upon you alone. It has also been said: those before us are the Christians. Al-Sha'bi and others said: the fast that is specified is Ramadan, which was prescribed upon those before us, who are the Christians. They were cautious regarding it by adding a day before it and a day after it, generation after generation, until they reached fifty days. It then became difficult for them in the heat, so they moved it to the solar season. Al-Naqqash said: regarding this there is a report from Daghfal, al-Hasan, and al-Suddi.

It has also been said: rather, one of their kings fell ill, so he vowed that if he recovered he would add ten days to it. Then another added seven, then another three. They saw that adding to it was a good deed in exchange for the error in transferring it. It has been said: the Christians at first used to fast, and when they broke the fast they did not eat, drink, or have intercourse once they slept, until they woke up at night. This was at the beginning of Islam. Then it was abrogated (*naskh*, the cancellation of a ruling by later revelation) through the cause of 'Umar and Qays ibn Sirma. Al-Suddi also said, as did al-Rabi' (p-30) and Abu al-'Aliya.

It has been said: likewise was the fasting of the Jews. So the intended meaning of "those before us" is the Jews and the Christians. It has also been said: "those before us" are specifically the Jews. It was prescribed upon us as it was prescribed upon them, then God abrogated it with the fasting of Ramadan. Al-Raghib said: fasting has two benefits: the training of a person's soul away from what the appetites call him to, and imitating the exalted assembly (the angels) to the extent of one's capacity. The end of his speech. The wisdom of the comparison is that fasting is a difficult worship. When it is mentioned that it was prescribed upon the nations that came before, this worship becomes easier.

﴿so that you may be God-fearing (*tattaqun*)﴾: The apparent meaning is that *la'alla* (so that, perhaps) is connected to *kutiba* (was prescribed). That is: the cause of the obligation of fasting is the hope that God-consciousness (*taqwa*) will be attained for you. It has been said: the meaning is that you enter the company of the God-fearing, because fasting is their emblem. It has been said: you make between yourselves and the Fire a shield (*wiqaya*) by abandoning sins, for fasting weakens and restrains desire, as he, peace be upon him, said: "Then he should fast, for fasting is a shield for him." It has been said: you refrain from eating, drinking, and intercourse during the time of the obligation of fasting, as al-Suddi said. It has been said: you refrain from sins, because fasting restrains from much of what the soul yearns for, as al-Zajjaj said. It has been said: you refrain from the prohibitions of fasting, and this goes back to the saying of al-Suddi.

﴿أيّامًا مَعْدُوداتٍ﴾ If what is prescribed to be fasted here is Ramadan, then the phrase "days numbered" (ayyaman ma'dudat) refers to Ramadan. This is the view of Ibn Abi Layla and the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun). He described them as "numbered" (ma'dudat) to make things easier for the obligated person: these days are limited and countable, not so many that they cannot be counted. For this reason, "counted" is used figuratively to mean "few," as in His saying: ﴿في أيّامٍ مَعْدُوداتٍ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 203], ﴿لَنْ تَمَسَّنا النّارُ إلّا أيّامًا مَعْدُودَةً﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80], and ﴿وشَرَوْهُ بِثَمَنٍ بَخْسٍ دَراهِمَ مَعْدُودَةٍ﴾ [Yusuf: 20].

If what is prescribed to be fasted is three days of every month, and it was said that these are the three days plus the Day of 'Ashura', as that was prescribed for those before us, then His saying ﴿أيّامًا مَعْدُوداتٍ﴾ means these days. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata'.

Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' and Qatada said: they are the "white days" (al-ayyam al-bid), the 13th, 14th and 15th of the lunar month. It was also said: they are the 13th and two days after it. A hadith is narrated on this: "The white days are the 13th and the two days after it." If this is authentic, then it cannot be contradicted.

The exegetes narrated that at the beginning of Islam, fasting three days of every month and fasting the Day of 'Ashura' were obligatory, so they fasted in this way for seventeen months. Then it was abrogated (nusikha) by the fasting of Ramadan. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The first things abrogated after the Hijra were the direction of prayer (qibla) and fasting." It is also said: the fasting of the month of Ramadan was revealed a month and some days before Badr. It was also said: the fasting of those days was voluntary, then it became obligatory, then it was abrogated.

Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Abi al-Fadl al-Mursi said in (Ri al-Zam'an): Those who said that these days are other than Ramadan argued with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The fasting of Ramadan has abrogated every (previous) fast," which indicates that there was another fast before it. Also, He mentioned the sick person and the traveler in this verse, then mentioned their ruling in the following verse. If this fast were the fast of Ramadan, this would be a repetition. Also, His saying ﴿فِدْيَةٌ﴾ indicates choice (takhyir), whereas the fasting of Ramadan is obligatory in a fixed way, so the fast meant must be something other than it.

Most of the careful scholars (muhaqqiqun) held that the "days" means the month of Ramadan, because His saying ﴿كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ الصِّيامُ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183] could mean one day, two days or more. Then He clarified it by His saying ﴿شَهْرُ رَمَضانَ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. When it is possible to interpret it as Ramadan, there is no basis for interpreting it as something else and asserting abrogation. As for the report, it can be understood as the abrogation of every fast that was obligatory in earlier laws, or it may be abrogating a fast that was obligatory for this community. As for the repetition objection, it may be that the mention serves to explain that the ruling for the sick person and the traveler during Ramadan is breaking the fast, in contrast to the choice for the resident, for whom making up (qada') is obligatory. So when the healthy resident was obligated to fast and the ruling was shifted from choice to strict obligation, it was possible to think that the ruling on fasting applies to everyone, so that the sick person and the traveler would be like the resident in terms of the change of the ruling on fasting. Therefore He clarified that the condition of the sick person and the traveler concerning the permission to break the fast and the obligation to make up the days is the same as their condition at first. This is the purpose of the repetition. This is the answer to the third objection, which is their saying: because His saying ﴿فِدْيَةٌ﴾ (p-31) indicates choice, to the end of it. Because the fasting of Ramadan was first obligatory with choice, then it became fixed.

On both views, abrogation (naskh) in the verse is necessary. On the first view it is clear. On the second view, this verse requires that the fasting of Ramadan be obligatory with choice, and the verse that follows indicates strictness, so it abrogates this one. Continuity in recitation does not require continuity in revelation. End of his words.

The accusative of His saying ﴿أيّامًا﴾ is by implying a verb indicated by what precedes it, and its estimate is: "Fast days numbered." They also allowed that it is governed by the word "al-Siyam" (the fasting). This is the choice of al-Zamakhshari, since no one else mentioned it. He said: The accusative of "ayyaman" by "al-siyam" is like your saying: "I intended to leave on Friday." End of his words. This is an error, because the object of the verbal noun (masdar) belongs to its complement, and they are separated by an unrelated element, which is His saying ﴿كَما كُتِبَ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183]. So "kama kutiba" is not an object of the verbal noun; it is the object of something else, whatever estimate you make of it, whether it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun or in the position of a circumstantial (hal). If you assume that it is an adjective of "al-Siyam" according to the view that the definite "al-Siyam" is generic, which is then described by an indefinite, it would still not be permitted, because when the verbal noun is described before its object is mentioned, it cannot govern. If you take the kaf as an adjective of a verbal noun from "al-Siyam," as some have said, and we previously declared it weak, the estimate would be: "a fast as was prescribed." Then "al-Siyam" could govern "ayyaman," because in that case the governing word for "siyaman" is the verbal noun, so no separation occurs between them by something that is not an object of the verbal noun. They also allowed the accusative of "ayyaman" as an adverb of time (zarf), with "kutiba" as its governing word, and that it be a second object by way of extension (ittisa'), with "kutiba" governing it. This is the view of al-Farra' and al-Hawfi. Both views are wrong.

As for the accusative as an adverb of time, it is a place for the verb, but the writing (kitaba) does not occur within the days; rather, what occurs within the days is its complement. If a man said to his son, who was born on Friday: "Your birth pleased me on Friday," it would not be correct for Friday to be governed by "pleased me," because pleasure cannot be located on Friday, since it is not a place for the pleasure he attributed to himself. As for the accusative as an object by extension, that is based on the permissibility of its occurring as an adverb of "kutiba," and we have shown that this is an error.

The fast is either voluntary (nafl) or obligatory (wajib). The obligatory is of fixed time, which is the fast of Ramadan and a specified vow, and what is owed (fi al-dhimma), which is the making up (qada') of Ramadan, an unspecified vow, and the expiation fast (siyam al-kaffara). They agreed on the condition of intention (niyya) in fasting, and differed about its time. The position of Abu Hanifa is that the fast of Ramadan, a specified vow and a voluntary fast are valid with an intention from the night, or with an intention until midday, while the making up of Ramadan and the expiation fast are valid only with an intention from the night specifically. The position of Malik, according to the well-known view, is that the obligatory and the voluntary are not valid except with an intention from the night. The position of al-Shafi'i is that no obligatory fast is valid except with an intention from the night. Malik's position is that one intention suffices for the whole month of Ramadan. It is narrated from Zufar that if he is healthy and resident, and he abstains, then he is fasting even if he did not intend it. Whoever fasts Ramadan with a general intention of fasting, or with the intention of another obligation, Abu Hanifa said: what has a fixed time is valid with a general intention. Malik and al-Shafi'i said: it is not valid except with the intention of the obligatory fast. If a traveler intends another obligation, it falls on what he intended. Abu Yusuf and Muhammad said: it falls on Ramadan. If he, or the sick person, intends voluntary fasting, then according to Abu Hanifa it falls on the obligatory, and according to him also it falls on the voluntary. If the traveler fasts with an intention before midday, it is valid. Zufar said: it is not valid, and a voluntary fast is not valid with an intention after midday. Al-Shafi'i said: it is valid.

If someone obligates fasting for a specific time and then fasts for voluntary purposes, Abu Yusuf said: it falls on what was vowed. If he fasts for another obligation during the time of fasting that he obligated, it falls on what he intended. If he intends voluntary fasting and making up Ramadan, Abu Yusuf said: it falls on the making up, and Muhammad said: it falls on the voluntary. If he intends making up Ramadan and expiation for zihar, it is on the making up according to Abu Yusuf's view, and Muhammad said: it falls on the voluntary. If the fasting person intends to break the fast, then his fast is complete. Al-Shafi'i said: his fast is void. The proofs for these issues are mentioned in the books of jurisprudence (fiqh).

* *

﴿فَمَن كانَ مِنكم مَرِيضًا أوْ عَلى سَفَرٍ فَعِدَّةٌ مِن أيّامٍ أُخَرَ﴾ (p-32) The apparent meaning of the wording is to consider illness in general, such that the term applies to it. Ibn Sirin, 'Ata' and al-Bukhari held this view. The majority said: it is the illness that causes pain and harm, and whose continuation or increase is feared. It was heard from Malik's own words that it is the illness that causes the person hardship and leads to destruction if he fasts. At another time he said: it is severe illness and its increase. Al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i said: if the illness prevents a person from fasting, he breaks the fast. Al-Shafi'i said: no one breaks the fast except one whom the necessity of the illness compels, and whenever fasting is tolerable with the illness, he does not break it. Abu Hanifa said: if he fears that his eye will increase in pain or a severe fever, he breaks the fast. The apparent meaning of the wording is to consider the traveling in general, in time and intent.

They differed about the distance that permits breaking the fast. Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Thawri and Abu Hanifa said: three days. Al-Bukhari narrated that Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas used to break the fast and shorten the prayer at four barids, which is sixteen farsakhs. It is narrated from Ibn Abi Hanifa: two days or more, and three is the minimum. What is considered is the moderate pace, not what is faster or slower. Malik said: the distance for breaking the fast is the distance for shortening the prayer, which is a day and a night. Then he retracted and said: forty-eight miles. At another time he said: forty-two, and at another time forty-six. In his school (al-madhhab) it is thirty miles, and outside his school it is three miles. They agreed that travel for an act of obedience, such as jihad, hajj, maintaining family ties, or seeking necessary livelihood, permits breaking the fast. As for travel for trade and for permissible purposes, there is disagreement. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the view of permission is more apparent. Likewise, travel for sinful purposes is also disputed, and the view of prohibition is stronger. End of his words.

They agreed that a traveler during Ramadan may not intend to break the fast at night. They said: there is no disagreement that it is not permitted for one who intends to travel to break the fast before he leaves. If he breaks the fast, Ashhab said: nothing is incumbent upon him, whether he travels or not. Sahnun said: he owes expiation, whether he travels or not. 'Isa, from Ibn al-Qasim, said: he owes only making up that day. It is narrated from Anas that he broke the fast when he intended to travel, put on travel clothes, saddled his mount, then ate and mounted. Al-Hasan said: he breaks the fast if he wishes, in his house, on the day he wants to leave. Ahmad said: when he goes out from the houses. Ishaq said: no, until he puts his foot in the saddle. Whoever is healthy in the morning and then falls ill breaks the fast for the rest of the day. If he is in his hometown in the morning and then travels, he may break the fast. This is the view of Ibn 'Umar, al-Sha'bi, Ahmad and Ishaq. It was also said: he does not break the fast that day, even if he sets out on his journey. This is the view of al-Zuhri, Yahya al-Ansari, Malik, al-Awza'i, Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr and the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y).

They differed if he does break the fast. All of these said: he makes it up and does not pay expiation. Ibn Kinana said: he makes it up and pays expiation. Al-Baji related this from al-Shafi'i, and Ibn al-'Arabi held it and preferred it. Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: this is nothing, because Allah permitted him to break the fast in the Book and the Sunna, and whoever makes expiation obligatory has made obligatory what Allah did not make obligatory. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿أوْ عَلى سَفَرٍ﴾ is the permission for the traveler to break the fast. If he had intended to fast during the journey, he may break it even if he has no excuse, and there is no expiation for him. This is said by al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i and all the jurists of Kufa. Malik said: he owes making up and expiation. It is also narrated from him that there is no expiation for him, and this is the view of most of his companions.

The position of ﴿or on a journey﴾ is in the accusative, because it is coordinated (ma'tuf) with the predicate (khabar) of *kana* (was). Here *aw* (or) denotes classification (al-tanwi'). He deviated from the active participle, *musafiran* (a traveller), to *ala safar* (on a journey), to indicate that the journey takes hold of the person, because it involves choice on the part of the traveller. Illness is different, since it seizes a person without his choice, so it is compelling, whereas a journey is like a mount that the person rides and controls. That is why it is said *fulanun ala tariq* (so-and-so is on a road) and *rakibu tariq* (a rider of a road), to indicate choice, and that the person is in control of the journey and chooses to ride the road in it.

* *

﴿So a number of other days﴾. The recitation of the majority is *iddatun* in the nominative, as the subject (mubtada') with an omitted predicate (khabar). It is estimated as preceding it, i.e., *fa-alayhi iddatun* (so upon him is a number), or following it, i.e., *amthalu lahu* (the most suitable for him). Or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., *fal-wajibu* (so the obligation is), or *fal-hukmu iddatun* (so the ruling is a number). It was also recited as *fa-iddatan* in the accusative, by implying a verb, i.e., *fal-yasum iddatan* (so let him fast a number). Here *iddah* means *ma'dud* (the counted), like *al-ra'y* (the grazing) and *al-tahn* (the grinding), and this is with an elided annexed term (mudaf), i.e., *fa-sawmu iddati ma aftara* (so the fasting of the number of what he broke). Between the condition and its response there is an omitted element by which the sentence is complete, and the estimate is: *fa-aftara fa-iddatun* (so he broke [it], then a number). A parallel elision is in ﴿Strike the sea with your staff, and it parted﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 63], meaning *fa-darab fa-infalaq* (so he struck, and it parted).

He made *iddatun* indefinite and did not say *fa-iddatuha* (its number), meaning *fa-iddatu al-ayyam allati ufṭirat* (the number of the days that were broken), by way of economy, since it is known that he is not required to make up anything other than what he broke, from among the days he fasted. The *iddah* is the counted, so indefiniteness is more concise. The phrase *min ayyam* (of days) is in the position of a qualifier of *fa-iddatun*, and *ukhar* (other) is a qualifier of *ayyam*. The qualifier of a plural that is not rational (la ya'qilu) is sometimes treated as a feminine singular, and sometimes as the plural of a feminine singular. From the first: ﴿except for a few numbered days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80]. From the second: ﴿except for a few numbered days﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 24], where *ma'dudat* (numbered) is the plural of *ma'dudah*. You do not say *yawmun ma'dudatun* (a numbered day, feminine), but *ma'dud*, because it is masculine. It is permitted in the plural, however, and he deviated from describing the days with the qualifier of a feminine singular, which would have been *min ayyam ukhra*. Although this is permissible and eloquent, as is describing with *ukhar*, it would have been ambiguous, since it could be a qualifier of *iddatun*, so it would not be known whether it describes *iddah* or *ayyam*. This is because the i'rab (grammatical inflection) is hidden due to its being a maqsur (a noun ending in a non-inflecting long vowel). By contrast, *ukhar* is explicit that it qualifies *ayyam*, because its i'rab differs from that of *fa-iddatun*. Does it not diptote (la yanṣarif) for the reason mentioned in grammar, namely that it is the plural of *ukhra* in opposition to *ukhar*, and *ukhar* is the opposite of *akharin* (others), not the plural of *ukhra* in the sense of *akhirah* (the later), which is the opposite of *al-akhar* (the last), as opposed to the first? *Ukhar* is the feminine of *ukhra* in the sense of *akhirah*, which is diptote (ghayr munṣarif). They differ in ruling and in meaning. As for the difference in ruling: that one is not diptote, while this one is. As for the difference in meaning: the meaning of *ukhra*, whose plural is *ukhar* that does not take nunation, is the meaning of *ghayr* (other), while the meaning of *ukhra*, whose plural takes nunation, is *muta'akhkhirah* (later), which is the opposite of the first. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Their first said to their last﴾ [al-A'raf: 39], so *ula* here means *al-akhirah* (the hereafter), as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, to Us belong the hereafter and the first﴾ [al-Layl: 13]. *Ukhar*, whose feminine is *ukhra* and whose singular is *akhar* that is not diptote, in the sense of *ghayr* (other), cannot have anything attached to it except something of the same kind as what precedes it. You say: *marartu bika wa-bi-rajulin akhar* (I passed by you and by another man), but it is not permitted to say *ishtaraytu hadha al-faras wa-himaran akhar* (I bought this horse and another donkey), because a donkey is not of the same kind as a horse. As for his saying:

*Ṣalla ala 'Azzata al-Rahmanu wa-ibnatiha / Layla, wa-ṣalla ala jaratiha al-ukhari*

[May the Merciful bless ʿAzzah and her daughter Layla, and bless her neighbours, the others.]

He made her daughter a neighbour of hers, and without this it would not be permitted. We have explored this question of *ukhra* at length in our book *al-Takmil*.

They said: The Companions and those after them among the Successors (tabi'un), and the jurists of the cities, agreed on the permissibility of fasting for the traveller, and that there is no making up for him if he fasts. This is because, as we have mentioned, they estimated an elision in the verse, while the original principle is that there is no elision. So the apparent meaning is that Allah the Exalted obligated upon the sick and the traveller a number of other days, so if they fast, it does not suffice them, and it is obligatory upon them to fast a number equal to the days in which they were, of the days obligatory to fast for others. They said: It is narrated from Abu Hurayrah that he said: Whoever fasts while travelling must make it up. A few of the people followed him in this. Ibn 'Atiyyah transmitted this from 'Umar and his son 'Abd Allah, and from Ibn 'Abbas that breaking the fast while travelling is an obligation (azimah). Another transmitted from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf: the one who fasts while travelling is like the one who breaks the fast while at home. This was held by a group among the people of the Zahir (literalist school). Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm distinguished between the sick and the traveller. He said, in what we summarised in our book entitled *al-Anwar al-Ajla fi Ikhtisar al-Muhalla*, the following text: It is obligatory upon whoever travels, even if he is disobedient, a mile or more, to break the fast when he leaves the houses, in other than Ramadan. The sick person should break the fast and make it up afterwards. Fasting for him is disliked, but it suffices. The proofs for these opinions are in the books of jurisprudence. It is established by a widely transmitted report (khabar mustafid) that the Prophet (ﷺ) «fasted while travelling». Abu al-Darda', Salamah ibn al-Muhannaq, Abu Sa'id, Jabir, Anas, and Ibn 'Abbas transmitted from him the permissibility of fasting and of breaking the fast while travelling, «by his saying to Hamzah ibn 'Amr al-Aslami when he said: Shall I fast while travelling? He said: "If you wish, fast, and if you wish, break the fast."» According to the view of the majority, there is an elided element there, and its estimate is: *fa-afṭir* (so break the fast), and it is permissible for the traveller to break the fast and to fast.

They differed about which is better. Abu Hanifah and his companions, Malik, and al-Shafi'i in one of what is narrated from them, held that fasting is better. Among the Companions, 'Uthman ibn Abi al-'As al-Thaqafi and Anas ibn Malik held this view. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Anas ibn Malik adopted fasting and said: The dispensation was only revealed when we were hungry, returning to hunger. Al-Awza'i, Ahmad, and Ishaq held that breaking the fast is better. Among the Companions, Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas held this view. Among the Successors: Ibn al-Musayyib, al-Sha'bi, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, Mujahid, and Qatadah. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Mujahid, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, and others said: The easier of the two is the better of the two. Ibn Hanbal disliked fasting while travelling. If someone fasts while travelling and then breaks the fast without an excuse, he must make up the day only, as al-Awza'i and Abu Hanifah said. Al-Layth added expiation (kaffarah) as well. There are two opinions from Malik.

If a traveller breaks the fast and then arrives on the same day, or a menstruating woman breaks the fast and then becomes pure in part of the day, Jabir ibn Yazid, al-Shafi'i, and Malik, according to what Ibn al-Qasim transmitted, said: They eat and do not abstain. Abu Hanifah, al-Awza'i, al-Hasan ibn Salih, and 'Abd Allah ibn al-Hasan said: They abstain for the rest of that day from what the fasting person abstains from. Ibn Shubrumah said, regarding the traveller: he abstains and makes up the day; and regarding the menstruating woman: if she becomes pure, she eats.

The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿a number﴾ is that he must make up the number of days he broke the fast in. So if the month in which he broke the fast had twenty-nine days, he makes up twenty-nine days. The majority of scholars held this. Al-Hasan ibn Salih held that he makes up a month for a month, without regard to the number of days. It is narrated from Malik that he makes up according to the lunar months (al-ahilla). It is narrated from al-Thawri that he makes up a month of twenty-nine days even if Ramadan had thirty. This is contrary to the apparent meaning and contrary to what they agreed upon: that if what he broke the fast in was part of Ramadan, the making up is required by number. Likewise, making up the whole must be by reference to the number. The apparent meaning of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So a number of other days﴾, is that the consecutive sequence is not required. This is the view of the majority of scholars among the Companions and the Successors and the jurists of the cities. It is narrated from 'Ali, Mujahid, and 'Urwah that he does not have to separate them. In the recitation of Ubayy: ﴿a number of other days, consecutive﴾. The apparent meaning of the verse is that the time is not fixed; rather, hastening to make up is recommended. Dawud said: It is obligatory upon him to make up on the second of Shawwal; so if he does not make it up and dies, he is sinful. This view is refuted by the apparent meaning of the verse and by what is established in the Sahih from 'A'ishah, who said: I used to have fasting from Ramadan to make up, and I could not make it up except in Sha'ban, because of the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) business, or with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The apparent meaning of the verse is that whoever delays making up until another Ramadan arrives is required only to make up the first, and he fasts the second. This was held by al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, Abu Hanifah, Dawud, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, and Ishaq, who said that he must give the fidyah in addition to making up.

Yahya ibn Aktham al-Qadi said: The obligation of feeding (ita'am) has been transmitted from six Companions, and I have not found any Companion who opposed them. It is narrated from Ibn 'Umar that there is no making up for someone who neglects the first Ramadan, and he feeds for each day of it one mudd of wheat, and fasts the second Ramadan. Regarding one who delays making up Ramadan until he dies: Malik, al-Thawri, and al-Shafi'i said: No one fasts on behalf of anyone, neither in Ramadan nor in other than it. Al-Layth, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, Abu 'Ubayd, and the people of the Zahir said: Fasting may be done on his behalf, and they restricted this to the vow (nadhr). Ahmad and Ishaq said: Feeding may be done on his behalf for making up Ramadan.

* *

﴿And upon those who are able to do it, a fidyah: the feeding of a poor person﴾. The majority recited *yuṭiqunahu* as the imperfect of *aṭaqa* (to be able). Hamid recited *yuṭawwiqunahu*, from *aṭwaqa*, like their saying *aṭwala* in place of *aṭala* (to lengthen), and this is the original form. The preservation of the weak letter in this type is anomalous, whether from waw or from ya', and what is heard from it is more eloquent: *ajwadu* (better), *a'walu* (to howl), *atwalu* (longer), *aghyamat al-sama'* (the sky clouded over), *akhyalat* (it became cloudy with tanks), *aghyalat al-mar'ah* (the woman nursed while pregnant), *atyabu* (more pleasant). The alteration (i'lal) has occurred in all of them, and this is the analogical form. The preservation, as we have mentioned, is anomalous according to the grammarians, except Abu Zayd al-Ansari, who holds that preservation in such cases is analogical, taking as evidence these rare words in which alteration is heard, with transposition, as being analogical. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas recited, according to the well-known transmission from him: *yuṭawwaqunahu*, in the passive from *ṭawwaqa*, on the pattern of *qaṭṭaʿa* (to cut into pieces). 'A'ishah, Mujahid, Tawus, and 'Amr ibn Dinar recited *yaṭṭawwaqunahu*, from *iṭṭawwaqa*, and its origin is *tatawwaqa* on the pattern of *tafa''ala*, then they assimilated the *ta'* into the *ta'* (*ṭa'*), and so for the past and the imperative they introduced the hamzat al-wasl (connecting hamzah). Some people said: This is an explanation, not a recitation, in disagreement with those who established it as a recitation. What the people said is contrary to the view of this speaker, and they cited it as a recitation.

Recited by a group, among them Ikrimah: "yutiqūnahu" (يُطِيقُونَهُ). This reading is also related from Mujahid and Ibn ʿAbbas. It was also recited thus, but with the first letter of the imperfect verb vowelled with a ḍamma, in the passive form (al-binā' lil-maf'ūl). Some scholars rejected this reading and said: it is invalid, because it is derived from al-ṭawq (the collar, or encircling). They said: it is obligatory in it, and there is no place for the yāʾ in this pattern. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: the shaddah on the yāʾ in this word is weak, end of quote. What made this weak, or impermissible, in the view of these scholars is that they held the verb to be of the form tafaʿʿala, so this presented a difficulty for them. But it is not as they thought; rather it is of the form tafʿīl from al-ṭawq, like their saying: tudīru al-makān wa-mā bihā dayyār. Its original form is tuṭyiwūnahu; a yāʾ and a wāw came together, and one of them was preceded by a sukūn, so the wāw was changed into a yāʾ and the yāʾ was assimilated into it, so it was said: taṭayyaqa yatatayyaqu. This is the grammatical justification of this reading, and it is a clear grammatical justification. (These are six readings.) Their meanings all return (p-36) to the notion of ability and capacity. The form built for the active subject is clear; the form built for the passive object means: he is made capable of that. The reading with shaddah on the wāw and the yāʾ may carry the sense of obligation, i.e. they undertake it or are obligated to it. Its figurative sense may be from al-ṭawq in the meaning of the necklace, as if it were said: they are hung with that, i.e. it is placed on their necks, and it is a metaphor for obligation, i.e. the fast is burdensome for them. On these two meanings the exegetes interpreted His words, exalted is He: ﴿And upon those who are able to [fast] it﴾, the pronoun referring to the fast, and they differed. Muʿādh ibn Jabal, Ibn ʿUmar, Salamah ibn al-Akwaʿ, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, al-Shaʿbī, Ikrimah, Ibn Shihāb and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: fasting was, for the resident who was able, optional; whoever wished fasted, and whoever wished broke the fast and fed [a poor person]. Then this was abrogated by ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. This is the view of most exegetes. It was also said: there is an elided conjunctive element, its estimated sense being: "they are able to it" or "the fast", because they were young and then became incapable of it through old age; this was said by Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab and al-Suddī.

It was said: the meaning is "and upon those who are able to fast," and this refers to the description of the illness in which one is able to fast; so this person was given the choice between fasting and breaking the fast and paying ransom. Then this was abrogated by His saying: (so let him fast it), and the concession was removed except for the one among them who is incapable. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. Some scholars permitted that "lā" (not) be elided, so that the verb would be negated, and they estimated it as: "and upon those who are not able to it." He said: "lā" is elided while it is intended. Ibn Aḥmad said:

*I swore I would praise a base-born man forever, / praise remains and the gift departs.*

(Another said):

*So oppose, for by God you will not descend any valley / of the earth except that you know humiliation.*

(And Imruʾ al-Qays said):

*So I said, by God's oath, I will remain seated / even if they cut off my head and my joints before you.*

The estimate of "lā" is an error, because it is a place of confusion. Do you not see that what the understanding immediately grasps is that the verb is affirmative, and it is not permissible to elide "lā" while intending it except in an oath? The verses by which he argued are of the category of oath, and the reason for this is mentioned in grammar. It was also said: the intended meaning of ﴿those who are able to it﴾ is the decrepit old man and the old woman, i.e. they are able to it with extreme hardship, so God permitted them to break the fast and pay ransom; and the verse, on this view, is muḥkam (not abrogated). This is supported by the reading of whoever read yuṭawwaqūnahu in the sense of "they undertake its fasting and bear it with difficulty." This was related from ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbas, and that the verse was revealed concerning the aged, failing old man and the frail old woman. Zayd, from ʿAlī: and the sick person whose recovery is not expected. According to Mālik, the verse refers only to one who reaches Ramadan while owing the fast of a previous Ramadan; he had been able to fast during that period but left it, so he owes the ransom.

al-Aṣamm said: this refers to the sick person and the traveller, because they have two states: a state in which they are unable to fast, and God has explained its ruling in His saying: ﴿then [an equal] number of other days﴾; and a state in which they are able, namely the condition of illness or travel in which no severe hardship befalls them were they to fast; so they were given the choice between breaking the fast and paying ransom. It is as if it were said: "and upon the sick and the travellers who are able to it." The apparent meaning of these views is the first view, because when God, exalted is He, mentioned the obligation of fasting upon the believers, He divided them into two categories: one characterised by the likelihood of hardship, namely the sick and the traveller, and the ruling for this category is that if they break the fast they must make up the days; and one able to fast, so if they fast they discharge what is owed, and if they break the fast they pay ransom. Then this second ruling was abrogated, and it has already been mentioned that this was so, and then it was abrogated.

As for those who say that "those who are able to it" are the elderly and the infirm, the verse is muḥkam according to their view, and they differed: it was said this ruling is specific to these people; it was said it includes the pregnant and the nursing woman. They agreed that the decrepit old man who breaks the fast owes ransom; this is how some have reported it, but this consensus is not sound, because Ibn ʿAṭiyya reported from Mālik that he said: "I do not consider ransom obligatory upon the weak old man; rather it is recommended for the one who is strong enough for it." Mālik's opinion and view on the verse has already been mentioned. al-Shāfiʿī said: it is obligatory upon the pregnant and the nursing woman (p-37) if they fear for their children, because the verse includes them, and by analogy with the decrepit old man, and [they owe] the making up. It is related in al-Buwayṭī: no feeding is upon them. Abū Ḥanīfa said: ransom is not obligatory, and he rejected the analogy with the decrepit old man, because for him making up is not obligatory, whereas for these two it is obligatory. He said: if we required ransom along with making up, it would be combining two substitutes, which is not permissible. This was also the view of Ibn ʿUmar, al-Ḥasan, Abū Yūsuf, Muḥammad and Zufar. ʿAlī said: ransom without making up. Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbas held that the pregnant woman breaks the fast and pays ransom, with no making up for her. al-Ḥasan, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Zuhrī, Rabīʿa, Mālik and al-Layth held that if the pregnant woman breaks the fast she makes up, with no ransom for her. Mujāhid and Aḥmad held that she makes up and pays ransom. It has already been mentioned that this is al-Shāfiʿī's view. As for the nursing woman, the view of al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Ḥanīfa concerning her if she breaks the fast has already been mentioned. Mālik in the well-known report said: she makes up and pays ransom. In the Mukhtaṣar of Ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥakam he said: no feeding is upon the nursing woman.

They differed about the amount that one who is obligated to feed must give. Ibrāhīm, al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad, Mālik, and al-Shāfiʿī, as related from him by al-Muzanī, said: one mudd for each day. al-Thawrī said: half a ṣāʿ of wheat, and a ṣāʿ of dates or raisins. A group said: an evening meal and a pre-dawn meal. A group said: the staple food of a day. Abū Ḥanīfa and a group said: half a ṣāʿ of wheat for each day. It was related from Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Hurayra, Qays ibn al-Kātib, who was a partner of the Messenger of God ﷺ in the pre-Islamic period, ʿĀʾisha, and Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, concerning the aged old man, that he feeds on his behalf half a ṣāʿ each day. The apparent meaning of the verse is that any kind of food is obligatory, and restriction requires evidence.

If someone becomes insane throughout the whole of Ramadan or during part of it, al-Shāfiʿī said: there is no making up for him, even if he recovers before sunset, since the basis of obligation is reason. Mālik and ʿUbayd Allāh al-ʿAnbarī said: he makes up the fast but does not make up the prayer. Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Thawrī, Muḥammad, Abū Yūsuf and Zufar said: if he becomes insane throughout the whole of Ramadan, there is no making up for him; and if he recovers during any part of it, he makes up the whole of it.

The majority read: ﴿fidyatun ṭaʿāmu miskīn﴾ with tanwīn on "fidyah", raising "ṭaʿām", and singular "miskīn"; Hishām read likewise except that he read "masākīn" in the plural. Nāfiʿ and Ibn Dhakwān read with the fidyah in construct (idāfa) and the plural, and the singular "fidyah" because it is a verbal noun (maṣdar). Whoever applied tanwīn, "ṭaʿām" is in apposition (badal) to "fidyah", and in this there is specification of what the fidyah is. Whoever did not apply tanwīn and used the construct also made a specification through the construct, which is the attribution of a thing to its genus: because "fidyah" is the name of the obligatory measure, while "ṭaʿām" covers the fidyah and other things. In al-Muntakhab it is said that this construct may be of the type of attributing a described noun to its descriptor. He said: because the fidyah has an essence, and its attribute is that it is food. This is not good: because "ṭaʿām" is not an attribute here; and it here is either meant as a verbal noun, as ʿaṭāʾ is meant as "giving", or meant as the object, as sharāb is meant as "what is drunk". On both estimates it cannot appropriately be described. As for when it is a verbal noun, it is not described by it except when intensification is intended, and there is no such sense here; and as for when it is meant as the object, that is because it is not derived from a verb nor is it a regular pattern, so one does not say "a ḍarāb in a maḍrūb" or "a qatāl in a maqtūl"; rather it resembles ra'y, ṭaḥn and duhn, which are not described by any of them and do not function as the object does. Do you not see that it is not permissible to say "I passed by a man whose food is bread and whose drink is water," so that what follows would be raised by it? Given this, it is weak to say that this is the construct of a described noun with its descriptor. As for whoever read "masākīn", he matched plural with plural; and whoever read the singular did so in regard to the singular form of the generic term, meaning: upon each one of those who are able to fast, for each day he breaks the fast, feeding a miskīn. Its parallel is His words: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not produce four witnesses, lash them eighty lashes﴾ [al-Nūr: 4], meaning: lash each one of them eighty lashes. It is clear from the singular "miskīn" that the ruling applies to each day on which a miskīn is fed, and this is not understood from the plural.

* *

﴿So whoever volunteers good, it is better for him﴾. That is: whoever adds to the amount of the fidyah in food for the miskīn; this was said by Mujāhid. Or in the number of those whom he is obliged to feed, so he feeds two miskīns or more; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, Ṭāwūs, ʿAṭāʾ and al-Suddī. Or he combines feeding with fasting; this was said by Ibn Shihāb.

The accusative of "khayran" is as an object with the preposition dropped, meaning: "with good", because "tawwaʿa" does not take an object directly. It is possible that "tawwaʿa" is taken to carry the sense of a transitive verb, so "khayran" is the direct object, and the estimate is: "whoever does, volunteering, good." It is also possible that its accusative is as a qualifier of an elided verbal noun, meaning: "a volunteering good," and the description of the verbal noun as "better" indicates the goodness of what is volunteered. The mention was made earlier of the reading of whoever read "yaṭṭawwaʿ", taking it as the imperfect of "iṭṭawwaʿa", whose original form is "tatawwaʿa", which was assimilated, and a hamzat al-waṣl was brought in. In this reading "man" must be conditional, and that is permissible in the reading of whoever made it a past verb. The pronoun in "fa-huwa" refers to the verbal noun understood from "tatawwaʿa", meaning: "so the volunteering is better for him," like His saying: ﴿Be just; it is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Māʾida: 8], i.e. justice. "Khayrun" is the predicate of "huwa", and here "huwa" is the comparative (af'al al-tafḍīl). The meaning is that the addition above what is obligatory, when it is accepted to be added, is better than limiting oneself to it. The apparent meaning of this verse is general to every volunteering in good, even though it came concerning the ransom in fasting. The apparent sense of "tawwuʿ" is that, in terms of permissibility, there is choice between doing and not doing, and that doing is more excellent. There is no disagreement about this. If someone begins it and then invalidates it, he must make it up according to Abū Ḥanīfa, and there is no making up for him according to al-Shāfiʿī.

﴿And that you fast is better for you﴾. Ubayy read: "wa-al-ṣawmu khayrun lakum." This is how it is reported from Ibn ʿAṭiyya. al-Zamakhsharī reported that his reading was: "wa-al-ṣiyāmu khayrun lakum." The address is to the resident who is able to fast, meaning: better for you than breaking the fast and paying the fidyah; or to the sick person and the traveller, meaning: better for you than breaking the fast and making up; or to whoever is permitted to break the fast in all of these cases. These are three views. And whoever went far off the mark in holding that it is connected to the beginning of the verse, namely ﴿O you who believe, fasting is prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqara: 183], meaning: "and that you fast this prescribed thing is better for you," is mistaken. The first view is the apparent one, and in it there is encouragement toward fasting.

Translation of the passage:

﴿If you knew﴾, that is, if you are of those possessed of knowledge and discernment. It is also permissible that the object be omitted for brevity, the context indicating it; that is: what I have prescribed and made clear to you of the matters of your religion, or the excellence of your deeds and their reward.
