Or he used "knowledge" as a metaphor for "fear" (khashyah), meaning: you fear Allah, because knowledge necessitates fearing Him. ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ [Fatir: 28].

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 185 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Ramadan is the month﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read "shahru" with a nominative vowel (raf'), while Mujahid, Shahr ibn Hawshab, Harun al-A'war, on the authority of Abu 'Amr, and Abu 'Umarah, on the authority of Hafs from 'Asim, read it with an accusative vowel (nasb). The i'rab (grammatical case) of "shahru" becomes clear according to what is meant by His words: ﴿a specified number of days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184]. If what is meant by them is other than the days of Ramadan, then the raf' of "shahru" is as a mubtada' (subject of a nominal sentence), and its khabar (predicate) is His words: ﴿in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾. The mention of this clause serves as an introduction to the obligation of fasting it, by mentioning its virtue, and as an alert that this is the month in which the Qur'an was sent down, and it is the one whose fasting is prescribed for you. They also permitted that "alladhi unzila" be a sifah (adjective), either for "shahru," in which case it is marfu' (nominative), or for "Ramadan," in which case it is majrur (genitive). The khabar of the mubtada' and the clause after it is a sifah from His words: ﴿so whoever of you witnesses the month﴾, and the fa' in "fa-man" would be zā'idah (superfluous) according to the view of Abu al-Hasan (al-Akhfash). It cannot be the fa' that enters the khabar of the mubtada' when that khabar is conditional, because "shahru Ramadan" does not resemble a condition. They said: it is also permissible that the fa' is not superfluous, but rather entered here as it enters the khabar of "alladhi," and similar to it is: ﴿Say: Indeed, the death from which you flee will surely meet you﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 8]. But what they said is not valid, because "alladhi" is a sifah for a definite noun, or for an idafah (construct phrase) to a definite noun, so there is no room to imagine in it any generality, and the verb it contains, which is ﴿was sent down therein, the Qur'an﴾, is both lafz and ma'na. So it is not like His words: ﴿Say: Indeed, the death from which you flee﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 8], because death here is not specific, but rather has generality in it. The silah (relative clause) of "alladhi" is in the future tense, namely "tafirruna" (you flee). And according to the view that the clause from His words "fa-man shahida" is the khabar, the returning pronoun to the mubtada' would be the repetition of the mubtada' by its own wording, i.e., "fa-man shahidahu minkum falyasumhu," so the wording of the mubtada' was placed in the position of the pronoun, and the connection was achieved by it, as in his saying:
"I do not see death overtaking death, anything..."
and that is for its glorification and magnification. If what is meant by His words: ﴿a specified number of days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184] are the days of Ramadan, then they permitted two possibilities in the i'rab of "shahru." (One of them): that it is the khabar of an omitted mubtada', its estimate being "huwa shahru Ramadan," i.e., "the prescribed one is the month of (p-39) Ramadan," as said by al-Akhfash, and al-Farra' estimated it as "dhalikum shahru," and it is close. (The second): that it is a badal (substitute) from His word "al-Siyam," i.e., "the month of Ramadan has been prescribed for you," as said by al-Kisa'i, and it is distant for two reasons: the first is the great separation between the badal and the mubdal minhu (the substituted noun), and the second is that it would then only be badal al-ishtimal (substitution of inclusion), not its reverse, because badal al-ishtimal in most cases occurs with masdars, as in His exalted words: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217], and the saying of al-A'sha:
"Indeed, there was in a year of sojourn that you spent, passing as the milk-times, and the traveller grows weary."
What al-Kisa'i mentioned is the reverse of this. If this structure were: "It has been prescribed for you, the month of Ramadan, its fasting," then the substitution would be sound at that point and reversed. The statement of al-Kisa'i can be justified on the basis that it is by omitting a mudaf (construct noun), so it is a badal of one thing from another, and both refer to one entity; its estimate is "siyamu shahri Ramadan" (the fasting of the month of Ramadan), so the mudaf was omitted and the mudaf ilayhi (the noun in the genitive) was put in its place. But in that there is majaz al-hadhf (figurative omission) and a great separation by many sentences, and it is distant. It is permissible, though remote, that it be a badal of "ayyaman ma'dudat," according to the reading of 'Abd Allah, for he read: "ayyamun ma'dudatun" with the raf', as the khabar of an omitted mubtada', i.e., "what is prescribed for its fasting is a specified number of days." This reading was mentioned by Abu 'Abd Allah al-Husayn ibn Khalawayh in his book (al-Badi') on the Qur'an. The accusative of "shahra Ramadan" according to the reading of whoever read it so is by an implied verb whose estimate is: "Fast the month of Ramadan." They permitted that it be a badal from His words: ﴿a specified number of days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184], said by al-Akhfash and al-Rummani, and it is distant because of the great separation. And that it be accusative as a warning (al-igra'), its estimate being "adhamu shahra Ramadan" (keep to the month of Ramadan), said by Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Hawfi, and it was refuted on the grounds that no mention of the month had preceded. And if it were accusative by His words: ﴿and that you fast﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184], this was related by Ibn 'Atiyyah, and al-Zamakhshari permitted it, saying: "It was read with the accusative: 'Fast the month of Ramadan,' or as a badal from: ﴿a specified number of days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184], or that it is the object of ﴿and that you fast﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184]." End of his words. This is not permissible, because "tasumu" is the silah of "an," and you have separated between the object of the silah and it by the khabar which is "khayrun," because "tasumu" is in the position of a mubtada', i.e., "and your fasting is better for you." If you said: "an yadriba Zaydan shadidun" it would be permissible, but "an tadriba shadidun Zaydan" would not be.

A group read "shahra Ramadan" with idgham (assimilation). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is not required by the principles, because two sakin letters would come together in it. By "the principles" he means the principles established by most of the Basran grammarians, because the letter before the ra' in "shahru" is a sound consonant. If it were a weak letter (harf 'illah), it would be permissible by consensus among them, as in: "hadha thawbu Bakr," because in it, being a weak letter, there is some elongation. The Arabic language has not been restricted to what most of the Basrans transmitted, nor to what they chose; rather, when the transmission is sound, it is obligatory to adopt it.

﴿alladhi unzila fihi al-Qur'an﴾: its i'rab has already been mentioned. Its apparent meaning is that it is a zarf (adverbial of time/place) for the sending down of the Qur'an, and the Qur'an generally encompasses everything, and the place of the sending down has not been specified. From Ibn 'Abbas it is related that the whole of it was sent down to the lowest heaven on the night of the twenty-fourth of Ramadan, and then it was sent down upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in installments. It was said: the sending down here is upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so the Qur'an is among what is expressed by its whole while meaning a part of it, and the meaning is: its sending down upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) began in it, and that was on the twenty-fourth of Ramadan. Or the alif and lam in "al-Qur'an" are for defining the reality (ta'rif al-mahiyyah), as you say: "I ate the meat," not meaning the entirety of its individual pieces, but meaning to define the reality. It was also said that the meaning of ﴿was sent down therein, the Qur'an﴾ is that Jibril used to review with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in Ramadan what Allah had sent down to him, and Allah erases what He wills and affirms what He wills; this was said by al-Sha'bi. So the sending down is an expression for the review.

It was also said: in its obligation of fasting, the Qur'an was sent down, and concerning its matter the Qur'an was sent down, as you say: "a Qur'an was sent down concerning 'A'ishah." The Qur'an that was sent down is His words: ﴿O you who believe, fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183]. This was said by Mujahid and al-Dahhak. Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said: concerning its virtue. It was also said: the meaning of ﴿was sent down therein, the Qur'an﴾ is: it was sent down from the Preserved Tablet to the scribes (safarah) in the lowest heaven on the Night of Power, from twenty months, or Jibril brought it down over twenty years; this was said by Muqatil. Wathilah ibn al-Asqa' (p-40) related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The scrolls of Ibrahim were sent down on the first night of the month of Ramadan, the Torah on the sixth of it, the Gospel on the thirteenth, and the Qur'an on the twenty-fourth." In the narration of Abu Dharr: "The scrolls of Ibrahim were sent down on the third of Ramadan, and the Gospel of 'Isa on the eighteenth." The reconciliation between the two narrations is that the narration of Wathilah informs about the beginning of the sending down of the scrolls and the Gospel, and the narration of Abu Dharr informs about the end of the sending down. Ibn Kathir read "al-Quran" by transferring the vowel of the hamzah to the ra' and dropping the hamzah, and this applies to all instances of the Qur'an, whether it is indefinite or defined with alif and lam, or by idafah. This is the preferred explanation of his reading. The statement of whoever said that the nun in it, even without the hamzah, is original, from qarantu al-shay' fi al-shay' (I joined one thing to another), has already been mentioned.

* *

﴿a guidance for mankind and clear proofs﴾: the accusative of "huda" is as a hal (circumstantial accusative), and it is a masdar placed in the position of the active participle, i.e., "guiding for mankind," so "lil-nas" is connected to the wording "huda," since it occupies the position of "hadin." The dhu al-hal is the Qur'an, and the governing element is "unzila," and this hal is a permanent one (lazimah), because the Qur'an being guidance is a necessary attribute of it. "Wa-bayyinat" is conjoined to "huda," so it is also a hal, and this too is permanent, because the Qur'an being clear, manifest verses is a fixed attribute of it. It is conjunction of the specific upon the general (min 'atf al-khass 'ala al-'amm), because guidance includes what is hidden and what is evident, so he specified "clear proofs" to refer to the evident part of guidance. The Qur'an contains the muhkam and the mutashabih, the nasikh and the mansukh, so he mentioned upon it the noblest of its types, which is that by which the lawful and the unlawful and the admonition are made clear.

﴿from the guidance and the criterion﴾: this is in the position of a sifah to His words "huda" and "bayyinat," i.e., that the Qur'an being guidance and clear proofs is among the totality of Allah's guidance and His clear proofs. "Al-huda" and "al-furqan" encompass the divine books, and this Qur'an is part of them. He expressed "bayyinat" by "furqan," and did not say "min al-huda wa-al-bayyinat" so that the ending would correspond to the beginning, because in it there is an additional necessary meaning for "bayyinat," namely that it distinguishes between truth and falsehood, for whenever a thing is manifest and clear, a distinction is achieved by it. Also, the word "furqan" harmonizes with the rhyme before it, which is His words "Shahru Ramadan," then His words "alladhi unzila fihi al-Qur'an," then His words "huda lil-nas wa-bayyinat min al-huda wal-furqan," so by this the rhymes harmonize, and "furqan" here is more fitting than "bayyinat" both in wording and in meaning, as we established.

It does not appear here what some people said, that "al-huda" and "al-furqan" refer to the Qur'an, because a thing cannot be a part of itself. In "al-Muntakhab" it is mentioned that it is possible to interpret the first "huda" as the principles of the religion, and the second as its branches.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the alif and lam in "al-huda" are for a known reference (al-'ahd), and the intended is the first, end of his words. He means: he first mentioned it indefinitely, then he mentioned it definitely the second time, which indicates that it is the first, like His words: ﴿As We sent to Pharaoh a messenger﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 15] ﴿but Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 16]. It is known that the messenger whom Pharaoh disobeyed is the messenger who was sent to him. From this is the saying: "I met a man, and I struck the man," so the one struck is the one met. This is confirmed by replacing the pronoun for the indefinite noun with this second wording, and the meaning is sound, because if he had said "fa-'asahu Fir'awn" (so Pharaoh disobeyed him), or "laqitu rajulan fa-darabtuhu" (I met a man and struck him), it would be a correct statement. What Ibn 'Atiyyah said cannot apply here, because he and the grammarians mentioned that "huda" is accusative as a hal, a sifah of the dhu al-hal, and conjoined to it is "wa-bayyinat." So the phrase "min al-huda," intended as the first huda, cannot be: either a sifah of "huda," or of "bayyinat," or of both, or connected to the wording "bayyinat." It is not permissible that it be a sifah of "huda," because insofar as it is a sifah it would require being a part, and insofar as it is the first it would require being identical to it, and one thing cannot be a part of itself in relation to its own reality. Nor is it permissible that it be a sifah of "bayyinat" alone, because "wa-bayyinat" is conjoined to "huda," and "huda" is a hal, and what is conjoined to a hal is a hal, and a hal is a sifah of the dhu al-hal; insofar as both are hals, the dhu al-hal would be specified by both, since they are two attributes, and insofar as "bayyinat" is described by "min al-huda," it would specify "bayyinat" by "huda," so the specification of the Qur'an would depend on "huda" and "bayyinat" together, and the specification of "bayyinat" would depend on "huda," so this would require the specification of a thing by itself, which is impossible. Nor is it permissible that it be connected to the wording "wa-bayyinat," because a connected phrase is a restriction of what it is connected to, so it is like a sifah, and it is impossible insofar as a sifah is impossible. Also, if you put a pronoun in place of "huda" here and said "wa-bayyinat minhu" (and clear proofs from it), meaning from that guidance, it would not be correct. Therefore we chose that "huda" and "furqan" be general, so that "huda" and "bayyinat" are partly from them.

* *

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 185 (part 2 of 3):**

﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it.﴾ The alif and lam in *al-shahr* (the month) are for *al-ahd* (a previously known referent, "the" of prior reference), and it means the month of Ramadan. For this reason a pronoun stands in for it. Had it come as *fa-man shahidahu minkum fa-yasumhu*, it would have been correct, but he stated it explicitly to honor it and to magnify it. It was also made more fitting by its being in a second clause. The meaning of witnessing the month is being present in it. The accusative of *al-shahr* is as an *zarf* (adverb of time, a temporal complement). The meaning is that the resident in the month of Ramadan, when he is of the status of being obligated, must fast, since the command implies obligation, and this is his saying *fa-yasumhu*. Others said that *al-shahr* is in the accusative as a direct object (*maf'ul bihi*), and that this involves an omitted *mudaf* (a governed noun), meaning *fa-man shahida* (whoever witnesses), with its object omitted, its estimated sense being *al-misr* (the city) or *al-balad* (the town).

It was also said that *al-shahr* is in the accusative as a direct object, and that this involves an omitted *mudaf*, meaning *fa-man shahida minkum dukhula al-shahr 'alayhi* (whoever of you witnesses the entry of the month upon him) while he is resident, it is obligatory for him to fast. They said: whoever the month of Ramadan enters upon while he is resident fasts in full, whether he is residing or traveling, and only whoever the month of Ramadan enters upon while he is traveling breaks the fast during travel. To this view went 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ubayda al-Salmani, al-Nakha'i, al-Suddi, and the majority, that whoever witnesses the beginning or end of the month, let him fast for as long as he is resident. Al-Zamakhshari said: *al-shahr* is in the accusative as an adverb of time, and likewise the *ha'* in *fa-yasumhu*, and it is not a direct object, as in your saying *shahidtu al-jumu'a* (I attended the Friday), because the resident and the traveler are both present for the month. End of his words. It has already been stated that this would involve an omitted *mudaf*, its estimated sense being *fa-man shahida minkum dukhul al-shahr*, that is, whoever is present. It was also said that the estimate is *hilal al-shahr* (the crescent of the month), but this is weak, because you do not say *shahidtu al-hilal* (I witnessed the crescent); rather you say *shahadtu* (I observed). Also, that would make fasting obligatory for everyone who witnesses the crescent, which is not so.

*Minkum* (of you) is in the position of a circumstantial (*hal*) from the concealed pronoun in *shahida*, so it is attached to an omitted element whose estimate is *ka'inan minkum* (being of you).

Abu al-Baqa' said: *minkum* is a *hal* from the agent, and it is attached to *shahida*, so he is self-contradictory, because making it a *hal* requires that the governing element be omitted, while attaching it to *shahida* requires that it not be a *hal*, so it is contradictory. The *man* in *fa-man shahida* is, on the obvious reading, a conditional (*shartiyya*), and it could be a relative (*mawsula*); its parallels have already passed.

Al-Jumhur read the lam in *fa-yasumhu* with sukun, treating it as *fa'ala* (a pattern in which such vowel-reduction is allowed), so they lightened it, though its original vowel is kasra. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, al-Hasan, al-Zuhri, Abu Haywa, and 'Isa al-Thaqafi read it so, and they likewise read the imperative lam (*lam al-amr*, the jussive particle) throughout the Qur'an, as in ﴿So let him write, and let the one who owes dictate﴾ [al-Baqara: 282] with kasra, and the kasra of the imperative lam is the well-known dialect of the Arabs, and the reason for it is mentioned in grammar. The author of *al-Tashil* (Ibn Malik's work *al-Tashil*) reported that opening the imperative lam is a dialect, and from his son that it is the dialect of Banu Sulaym, and he said: al-Farra' related it. The apparent sense of their words is unrestricted, that opening the lam is a dialect. The author of *Kitab al-I'rab*, who is Abu al-Hakam Ibn 'Udhra al-Khadrawi, reported from al-Farra' that among the Arabs there are those who open this lam for the fatha of the *ya'* after it. He said: so on this view the opening is not present if what follows it is kasra or damma. End of his words. This is like *layunbadhanna* (he will surely be cast out), *latukrim Zaydan* (you shall honor Zayd), *layukram 'Amran wa-Khalidan* (let 'Amr and Khalid be honored), and *wa-qumu fa-la-usalli lakum* (and stand up, so that I may pray for you).

﴿And whoever is ill or on a journey, then a number of other days﴾. The explanation of this sentence has already passed, and the mention of the benefit of its repetition, on the assumption that the month of Ramadan is the phrase ﴿numbered days﴾ [al-Baqara: 184], so that made it unnecessary to repeat it here.

* *

﴿Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you﴾. Discussion of *al-irada* (intention, will) has passed in the words ﴿What did Allah intend by this as an example?﴾ [al-Baqara: 26]. The *irada* here either remains in its basic meaning, in which case it requires an omission, and for this reason the author of *al-Muntakhab* (*al-Muntakhab fi Tafsir al-Qur'an*) estimated it as: Allah intends to command you with what contains ease; or it is used figuratively for *al-talab* (demand), meaning Allah demands ease from you, and *talab* in our view is other than *irada*. These two interpretations were needed because what Allah wills is necessarily existent, according to the doctrine of the people of the Sunna (*ahl al-Sunna*, the Sunni majority), and on the apparent sense of the speech, hardship would not have occurred, yet it does occur. As for the doctrine of the Mu'tazila, the verse is upon its apparent sense. *Arada* is transitive to concrete things with *bi-* and to verbal nouns directly, as in the verse. It also comes transitive to concrete things directly and to verbal nouns with *bi-*. He said:

*She wished 'Irar with humiliation; and whoever wishes 'Irar, by my life, with humiliation has surely wronged.*

They said: *yurid* here means *arada*, so it is a present form used with the sense of the past. The better view is that it refers here to a permanent state, because the present form is what is set for what is existent and not interrupted, and *irada* is an attribute of essence, not an attribute of act, so it is established for Him, exalted is He, perpetually. The apparent sense of ease and hardship is generality in all worldly and otherworldly conditions.

And in the hadith: "The religion of Allah is ease; make things easy and do not make them difficult." And: "He was never given the choice between two matters without choosing the easier of them." And in the Qur'an: ﴿He has not placed upon you in religion any difficulty﴾ [al-Hajj: 78], and ﴿and He relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them﴾ [al-A'raf: 157]. So within the generality of ease falls the breaking of the fast by the sick and the traveler, whose rulings were mentioned before this verse, and within the generality of hardship falls their fasting, because of the hardship and difficulty in the states of illness and travel. It has been related from 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak that ease is breaking the fast during travel and hardship is fasting during it. Their explanation is to be understood as an example of one individual of the general sense, and it was fitting that they exemplified with this because the verse came in the context of what preceded it, so what preceded it entered into it in a way that it cannot exit from. In *al-Muntakhab*: ﴿Allah intends ease for you﴾ suffices in place of His saying ﴿and does not intend hardship for you﴾, and it was repeated only for emphasis. End of his words. Abu Ja'far, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Ibn Hurmuz, and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read *al-yusura* and *al-'usura* with damma on the sin in both, while the rest read them with sukun.

* *

﴿and that you complete the period﴾: Abu Bakr and Abu 'Amr, with a variant from them, read it with a doubled mim and a fatha on the kaf, and it was also related so, while the rest read it with lightening and sukun on the kaf. Regarding the lam there are several views. The first: Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is the lam that enters on the object, like the one in your saying *darabtu li-Zayd* (I struck for Zayd), meaning *wa-yuridu ikmal al-'idda* (and He intends the completion of the period), and it, together with the verb, is estimated with *an* (that), as if the speech were: *wa-yuridu li-an tukmilu al-'idda* (and He intends that you complete the period). This is the view of the Basrans and similar to it, the saying of Abu Sakhr:

*I wish to forget her mention, yet it seems to me that Layla appears to me on every road.*

End of his words. This is as al-Zamakhshari permitted. He said: as if it were said: Allah intends ease for you, and He intends that you complete, by His saying ﴿they intend to extinguish﴾ [al-Saff: 8]. And in his words, it is joined to *al-yusr* (ease). The summary of this view is that the lam came with the object postponed from the verb, and this is among what they stated to be rare, or a poetic necessity, but what makes it fitting here is its distance from the verb by the interposition, so when the verb took its object, which is *al-yusr*, and was separated from it by a sentence, which is ﴿and He does not intend hardship for you﴾, the verb was distanced from its requirement, so it was strengthened by the lam, as is its condition when the object is fronted. For you say *li-Zayd darabtu* (for Zayd I struck), because by fronting and postponing the governor, the governor weakened in reaching it, so it was strengthened by the lam, since the original state of the governor is to come first, and the original state of the governed is to come after it. But in this view there is the implication of *an* after the superfluous lam (*lam al-za'ida*, the extra lam), and there is distance in it. Ibn 'Atiyya's speech contains an error, in his saying "and it" meaning the lam together with the verb, that it is estimated with *an*, and this is not so; rather *an* is hidden after it and the lam is a preposition, and what makes this clear is that he said: as if the speech were *wa-yuridu li-an tukmilu al-'idda*, so he made *an* appear after the lam, so the correctness of his wording is that you say: and it, together with the verb, are both estimated after it. And his saying: this is the view of the Basrans and similar to it, the saying of Abu Sakhr, *uridu li-ansa dhikraha*, is not as he mentioned; rather that is the view of al-Kisa'i and al-Farra', on the claim that the Arabs make the lam of *kay* (in order that) in the place of *an* after *aradtu* and *amartu*. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah intends to make clear to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 26], ﴿they intend to extinguish﴾ [al-Saff: 8], and ﴿that they extinguish﴾ [al-Tawba: 32], ﴿Allah only intends to remove from you the impurity﴾ [al-Ahzab: 33]. And the poet said: *uridu li-ansa dhikraha* (I wish to forget her mention). And Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿and we were commanded to submit﴾ [al-An'am: 71], and ﴿that I submit﴾ [Ghafir: 66]. Sibawayh and his companions went to the view that the lam here remains in its state and *an* is hidden after it, but the verb before it is estimated as a verbal noun, as if he said: *al-irada li-l-tabyin* (the intention is for clarification), and my intention for this. And some people went to the view that the lam is superfluous. We have fully discussed this issue in our book *al-Takmil fi Sharh al-Tashil*, so consult it there.

It is concluded from what we have mentioned that what he said, that it is the view of the Basrans, is not as he said; rather his saying that it, together with the verb, is estimated with *an* is consistent only with the view of al-Kisa'i and al-Farra', not with the view of the Basrans. Ibn 'Atiyya's speech is also self-contradictory, because he said: it is the lam that enters on the object, like the one in your saying *darabtu li-Zayd*, meaning *wa-yuridu ikmal al-'idda*. Then he said: and it, together with the verb, is estimated with *an*. So insofar as he made it the lam that enters on the object, it cannot be a part of the object; and insofar as he estimated it with *an*, it would be a part of the object, because the object is only formed from it together with the verb, so it is a part of it, and a single thing cannot be a part of a thing of which it is not a part, so it is contradictory. As for al-Zamakhshari's permission that it be joined to *al-yusr*, it is impossible except with the superfluous lam and the hiding of *an* after it, or by making the lam carry the meaning of *an*, so that *an* is not hidden after it; and both are weak.

The second view: that the lam in *wa-li-tukmilu al-'idda* is the lam of command (*lam al-amr*). Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is possible that this lam is the lam of command and the waw is conjunctive, joining one sentence to another sentence. End of his words. No one other than Ibn 'Atiyya is known to have mentioned this aspect among what we have come across, and this view is weakened by the grammarians' saying that the imperative of the second-person addressee involves a shift (*iltifat*). They said: one of its forms is a poor, rare dialect, which is the retention of the second-person *ta'* with the lam of command before it, and the other is the good, eloquent dialect, which is that the verb is bare of the present-tense prefix and of the lam. This view is also weakened by the fact that no reciter is reported to have read this lam with sukun, for if it were the lam of command it would be like its counterparts among the readings, read in both ways; so this shows that it is the lam of the *jarr* (preposition), not the lam of command. And Ibn 'Atiyya's saying, "and the waw is conjunctive, joining one sentence to another sentence," means that if the lam is for command, the conjunction is of the type of joining sentences, and if it is like the lam in *darabtu li-Zayd*, the conjunction is of the type of joining single words.

The third view: that the lam is for causation (*lam al-ta'lil*). The proponents of this view differed in several opinions. One of them: that the waw is conjunctive over a suppressed cause, the estimate being *li-ta'maluma ma ta'malun wa-li-tukmilu al-'idda* (so that you may do what you do, and so that you may complete the period), as al-Zamakhshari said. In this view the verb that is caused is the intention for ease. The second: that after the waw there is a suppressed verb that is the caused element, the estimate being *wa-fa'ala hadha li-tukmilu al-'idda* (and He did this so that you may complete the period), as al-Farra' said.

The third (of three) part: [it may be] that it is conjoined to a deleted cause whose effect has also been deleted. The estimated reading is: "God did that so that He might make it easy for you, and so that you might complete [the period]." Al-Zajjaj said this. The fourth: that the act being caused is implied after the causal clause, its estimate being: "And so that you complete the period, He granted you this concession." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is the view of some of the Kufans." The fifth: that the *waw* is superfluous, the estimate being: "God desires ease for you so that you complete the period." This is a weak view. The sixth: that the act being caused is implied after His saying ﴿and that you may be grateful﴾, its estimate being: "He legislated that." Al-Zamakhshari said this, and his exact words are: "He legislated that," meaning the whole of what was mentioned concerning the obligation on the one present to fast the month, the command for the one granted the concession to observe the number of days he broke his fast, and the concession permitting breaking the fast. So His saying ﴿that you complete the period﴾ is the cause of the command to observe the count; ﴿that you magnify God﴾ is the cause of what He taught concerning the manner of making up the fast and of being released from the obligation of breaking it; and ﴿so that you may be grateful﴾ is the cause of the concession and the facilitation. This is a kind of subtle composition, which only a discerning and skilled scholar of rhetoric can perceive. End of his words.

The *alif* and *lam* in His saying ﴿and that you complete the period﴾ apparently denote a known referent, so that this refers back to His saying ﴿then [make up] a number of other days﴾. That is: so that the one who broke his fast during his illness (p-44) or journey may complete the number of days on which he broke his fast, by fasting the equivalent. It was also said that the "period" refers to the lunar month, whether it has twenty-nine days or thirty; in that case, the period refers to the month of Ramadan that was commanded to be fasted.

* *

﴿and that you magnify God for having guided you﴾ is conjoined to "﴿and that you complete the period﴾," and what was said about the *lam* in "﴿and that you complete﴾" applies to the *lam* here. The meaning of *takbir* (magnifying) here is exalting God and praising Him. It is not restricted to the wording of *takbir* alone; rather God is exalted and praised with whatever words of praise and exaltation one wishes. It was also said that it is the *takbir* recited upon sighting the crescent at the end of Ramadan. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "It is incumbent upon the Muslims, when they see the crescent of Shawwal, to say *takbir*." It was also said that it is the *takbir* recommended on the feast day. Sufyan said: it is the *takbir* on the day of breaking the fast (ʿId al-Fitr).

They differed about its duration and its manner. From Ibn 'Abbas: one says *takbir* from the sighting of the crescent until the end of the sermon, and one remains silent at the time the imam emerges, and one says *takbir* along with his *takbir*. It was also said, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i: from the sighting of the crescent until the imam goes out to the prayer. Zayd ibn Aslam and Malik said: from the time one leaves one's home until the imam comes out. Ibn al-Qasim and 'Ali ibn Ziyad transmitted: if one goes out before sunrise, one does not say *takbir* on the way nor while sitting until the sun rises; but if one sets out after sunrise, one should say *takbir* on the way to the place of prayer, and when one sits, until the imam comes out. There is a difference of report from Ahmad: a report from him states that when one arrives at the place of prayer, one stops; Abu Ya'la said: meaning, and the imam has come out. Hanbal transmitted from him that one stops after the imam has finished the sermon.

They differed concerning ʿId al-Adha. Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Abu Yusuf, and Muhammad said: the ʿId al-Fitr and ʿId al-Adha are the same in this regard, and Ibn al-Musayyab, Abu Salama, and 'Urwa said likewise. Abu Hanifa said: one says *takbir* on ʿId al-Adha and does not say it on ʿId al-Fitr.

Its form according to the majority is: "Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar," three times, and this is related from Jabir. It was also said: one says *takbir*, *tahlil* and *tasbih* during the *takbir*. Among them are those who say: "Allahu akbar kabiran, wal-hamdu lillahi kathiran, wa subhan Allahi bukratan wa asila." Ibn al-Mubarak used to say: "Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, la ilaha illa Allah, wa Allahu akbar, wa lillahi al-hamd, Allahu akbar 'ala ma hadana." Ibn al-Mundhir said: Malik did not find a fixed limit for it. Ibn al-'Arabi said: our scholars chose the unrestricted *takbir*, which is the apparent meaning of the Book. Ahmad said: "All of that is ample." The proofs for these sayings are found in the books of jurisprudence.

In (al-Muntakhab) he preferred that the completion of the period is in the fasting of Ramadan, and that the magnifying of God is at the conclusion, for what He guided them to of this act of worship, and it does not mean exalting [in the general sense]. He said: because magnifying God in the sense of exalting Him is obligatory at all times and in every act of worship, so there is no sense in restricting it. End of his words. The "'ala" (upon) is connected to "takabbiru" (you magnify), and it carries an implication of causation, as when you say: "I thank you for what you have bestowed upon me."

Al-Zamakhshari said: The verb of magnifying was made transitive by the preposition of elevation only because it implies the sense of praise, as if it were said: "and that you magnify God, praising Him for what He has guided you to." End of his words. His saying "as if it were said: and that you magnify God praising Him for what He has guided you to" is an explanation of meaning, not an explanation of grammatical construction. For if it were an explanation of grammatical construction, "'ala" would not be connected to "takabbiru" which implies the meaning of praise; rather it would be connected to "hamidin" (praising) which he estimated. The grammatical estimate would be: "as if it were said: and that you praise God by the magnifying, for what He guided you to," just as people estimated in their saying "qatala Allahu Ziyadan a'ni" (God killed Ziyad, I mean: God diverted Ziyad from me by killing him), and in the poet's verse:

"And among us, on the day of terror, there ride horsemen who are discerning in the piercing of the arteries and kidneys,"

meaning: they judge with insight in piercing the arteries. The apparent sense of "ma" is that it is a masdariyya (verbal-noun) particle, meaning "for your being guided." They also allowed that "ma" means "alladhi" (that which), but this is far-fetched, because it requires two deletions. The first is the deletion of the pronoun referring back to "ma," meaning "upon that which He guided you to," which we estimate as accusative, not genitive with "ila" or with the *lam*, so that its deletion is easier than deleting it in the genitive. The second is the deletion of a noun by which the sentence becomes sound, the estimate being: "upon the following of that which He guided you to," and whatever resembles this estimate by which the meaning of the sentence is sound. The apparent sense of "hadakum" (He guided you) is the attainment of guidance for you without restriction. It was also said: the meaning is your guidance regarding what the Christians went astray in, namely altering their fasting. If "ma" is in the sense of "alladhi," the meaning is: "upon what He directed you to of the Islamic law."

﴿and that you may be grateful﴾: this is an expression of hope on the part of humans regarding God's blessing of guidance, as Ibn 'Atiyya said; so gratitude is for the guidance. It was also said: the meaning is that you give thanks for the reward of your acts of obedience that He bestows. Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning of ﴿and that you may be grateful﴾ is the intention that you give thanks, so he interpreted the hope from God as meaning intention. Ibn 'Atiyya took the hope to come from the created being, since hope in its literal sense is impossible for God; therefore al-Zamakhshari interpreted it as intention, while Ibn 'Atiyya attributed it to humans. The two views are equivalent. When the obligation is burdensome, it is fitting that it be followed by the hope of piety; when it is facilitation and concession, it is fitting that it be followed by the hope of gratitude. Therefore this verse is concluded with His saying ﴿so that you may be grateful﴾, because before it comes a concession for the sick and the traveler to break the fast. His saying ﴿God desires ease for you﴾ came after His saying ﴿fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ [2:183] and ﴿so that you may be God-conscious﴾ [2:183], and before it ﴿and in retaliation there is life for you﴾ [2:179]; then He said ﴿so that you may be God-conscious﴾ [2:183], because fasting and retaliation are among the most arduous obligations. Likewise the style of the Qur'an comes in what is difficult, and in what contains concession or elevation, so this should be noted wherever it occurs, for it is among the excellences of the science of rhetoric.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 186 (part 1 of 2):

﴿When My servants ask you about Me, then indeed I am near﴾. The occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul), according to al-Hasan: "A people, it was said the Jews and it was said the believers, said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Is our Lord near, so that we may confide in Him, or far, so that we may call out to Him?'" ʿAṭāʾ said: When the verse ﴿And your Lord said: Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ [Ghafir: 60] was revealed, some people said: "At what hour should we call upon Him?" So this verse was revealed: ﴿When he asks you﴾.

The connection (munasaba) of this verse with what precedes it is that when He, exalted is He, included in His words ﴿and that you may glorify Allah for having guided you, and perhaps you will be grateful﴾ [al-Baqara: 185], He requested that He be glorified and thanked, He clarified that He is aware of the remembrance of one who remembers Him and the gratitude of one who is grateful, that He hears his call and responds to his supplication or his wishes, as an admonition that it must necessarily be preceded by good praise.

The kaf in ﴿sa'alaka﴾ (asks you) is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), even though he has not been mentioned explicitly, but in the phrase ﴿the Qur'an was revealed in it﴾, that is, upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so it is as if it were said: "The Qur'an was revealed to you in it," so this address came in agreement with this omitted element. And "ʿibādī" (My servants), its apparent meaning is generality, though it has been said that it is intended to be particular: either the Jews or the believers, according to the disagreement about the occasion of revelation. As for "ʿibādī" and "ʿannī" (about Me), the pronoun in it refers to Allah, exalted is He, and this is from the category of iltifāt (a shift in grammatical person), because the preceding was ﴿that you may glorify Allah﴾, so it is a movement from the third person (absent) to the first person (speaker). "ʿAnnī" is connected to "sa'alaka," and the intended meaning here is not about His essence, because the answer came with His words ﴿then indeed I am near﴾, and the nearness attributed to Allah, exalted is He, is impossible to be nearness by place. Rather, nearness here is an expression of His being the one who hears His servant's supplication, hastening in granting the requests of whoever asks Him. So He likened the state of facilitating that to the state of one whose place is near to the one who calls him, for due to the nearness of distance he responds to his supplication. A parallel to this nearness here is His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We are nearer to him than the jugular vein﴾ [Qaf: 16], and what is related from His words, peace be upon him: "He is between you and the necks of your mounts." The fa' in His words ﴿then indeed I am near﴾ is the response (jawāb) to "idhā" (when), and there is an omitted statement whose estimation is: "Then say to them: Indeed I am near," because nearness is not a consequence of the condition; rather, what is a consequence is the informing about nearness.

﴿I respond to the supplication of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾. "Ujību" (I respond) is either an attribute of "qarīb" (near), or a predicate after a predicate. The pronoun in "fa-innī" was taken into account, and therefore "ujību" came, and the predicate was not taken into account, so that it would be "yujību" according to the construction of the third person. For the Arabs there are two methods: the more famous of them is taking into account what came before, of speaking or addressing, like this, and like their saying: ﴿Rather, you are a people being tested﴾ [al-Naml: 47], ﴿Rather, you are a people who are ignorant﴾ [al-Naml: 55]. And like the saying of the poet:

"And indeed we are a people who do not consider killing a disgrace."

The second method: taking into account the predicate, like your saying: "I am a man who commands what is good, and you are a person who desires good." The discussion of this issue is extensive in the science of Arabic grammar, and we have spoken about it in our book called (Manhaj al-Salik). The governing element of "idhā" is his saying "ujību." It has been related that when the verse ﴿I respond to the supplication of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾ was revealed, when the verse ﴿then indeed I am near﴾ had been revealed, the polytheists said: "How can He be near to us, between whom and Him, according to your saying, are seven heavens, in thickness, the height of each heaven being five hundred years, and between each heaven and heaven there is the like of that?" So by His saying ﴿I respond﴾ He clarified that this nearness is the responding and the power. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿I respond to the supplication of the supplicant﴾ is the generality of supplications, since He does not intend one single supplication. The ha' in "daʿwata" (supplication) here is not for the single instance (marra); rather, the verbal noun here is patterned on fa'la, like "raḥma" (mercy). The apparent meaning is the generality of "al-dā'ī" (the supplicant), because it does not indicate a specific supplicant, since the alif and lam in it are not for a known referent (ʿahd), but are for generality. The apparent meaning restricts the responding to the time of supplication, and the meaning according to this apparent sense is that Allah, exalted is He, gives to whoever asks Him what he asks.

They mentioned qualifications (quyūd) and particularizations (takhṣīṣāt) in this statement. The responding is qualified by the will of Allah, exalted is He. The estimation: "If I will." This is indicated by the explicit mention of this qualifier in the other verse: ﴿And He removes that for which you call upon Him, if He wills﴾ [al-Anʿām: 41]. It has also been said: "In accordance with the decree," meaning: "I respond if it agrees with My decree," and this returns to the meaning of the will. It has also been said: "What is asked for is good for the asker," meaning: if it is good. It has been said: "What is asked for is not impossible." It may be established by clear reason and sound transmission that some supplicants are not answered by Allah in what they ask, nor does He make them reach what they seek of their request, so they particularized the supplicant as one who is obedient and avoids His disobedience. It has been authentically reported that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said about the man who prolongs the journey, disheveled and dusty, who raises his hands to the sky, saying "O Lord, O Lord," while his food is unlawful, his clothing is unlawful, his drink is unlawful, and he was nourished with the unlawful: "How can it be answered for him?"

They said: Among its conditions is that he not become weary. In the authentic (collections) it is: "Your supplication is answered so long as one does not hasten, saying: 'I have supplicated, but it has not been answered for me.'" And the supplication was particularized to be for what contains no sin, nor severing of kinship, nor disobedience. In the authentic (collections), from Abu Saʿid, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No Muslim supplicates with a supplication in which there is no sin or severing of kinship, except that Allah, blessed and exalted, gives him one of three things: either He hastens his supplication for him, or He stores it for him, or He averts from him evil equal to it." It is fitting that the supplication be with what is transmitted (al-maʾthūr), and that one not intend in it rhymed prose (sajʿ), the rhymed prose of the Jahiliyya, and that it be free from grammatical error (malḥūn).

The responding is hoped for at certain times: at the pre-dawn meal (saḥar), in the last third of the night, at the time of breaking the fast, between the adhan and the iqama, between noon and afternoon prayer on Wednesday, at times of necessity (idṭirār), in the state of travel and illness, at the descent of rain, in the ranks for the sake of Allah, on the two festivals, and the hour which the Prophet (ﷺ) informed about on Friday: it is from the iqama until the completion of the prayer; thus it has come explained in the hadith. It has been said: after the afternoon prayer on Friday, and when the sun declines. And from the places: in the Kaʿba, beneath its spout (mīzāb), in the Sacred Precinct (al-Ḥaram), in the chamber of the Prophet (ﷺ), and in al-Masjid al-Aqṣā. If the supplicant has the qualities mentioned earlier, the acceptance of his supplication is strongly presumed. As for if he is not of those qualities, then he should not despair of the mercy of Allah, nor cut off his hope of His bounty, for Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾ [al-Zumar: 53]. Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna said: Let nothing prevent anyone from supplicating, what he knows of himself, for Allah, exalted is He, has responded to the supplication of the worst of creation, Iblis: ﴿He said: My Lord, reprieve me until the day they are resurrected﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 36].

The Muʿtazila said: The responding is particular to the believers ﴿who believe and do not mix their belief with injustice﴾ [al-Anʿām: 82], because describing a person with the statement that Allah responded to his supplication is an attribute of praise and glorification, and the sinner does not deserve glorification. Rather, the sinner may request something and Allah does it, but it is not called a response. It was said: Supplication is among the greatest stations of servitude, because it is a manifestation of need before Allah, exalted is He, and the Law has come with the command to it, and the prophets and messengers have supplicated, and the divine books have descended with the command to it. In this is a refutation of those among the ignorant who claim that supplication has no benefit, and mention doubts for that, which the people of knowledge of the Law have refuted. They said: The best course for the servant is humble entreaty and asking of Allah, exalted is He, and manifesting his need for Him, because of the texts transmitted that encourage supplication and urge it. Some people, among those whom some people describe as the scholars of the Reality (ḥaqīqa), said: Supplication is recommended in what concerns the matters of the Hereafter, but as for what concerns the matters of this world, Allah has taken responsibility for it, so there is no need for it. Some of them said: If, in the state of supplication, he is more righteous, his heart is more pure, his inner state is clearer, and his soul is more purified, then let him supplicate; but if abstaining from it is more righteous for him, then refraining from supplication is better for him. Some of them said: Abandoning supplication in every state is more righteous, because of the trust in Allah it contains, and the absence of objection; and because it is a choice, and the knower (ʿārif) has no choice. Some of them said: Abandoning sins is supplication, because when he abandons them, Allah takes charge of his affair and sets right his situation; He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever relies upon Allah, He is sufficient for him﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 3]. The responding and the supplication here have been interpreted in several ways:

One of them: that supplication is an expression for monotheism (tawḥīd) and praise of Allah, because you called upon Him and affirmed His unity, and responding is an expression for acceptance. Since monotheism was named supplication, acceptance was named responding, due to the similarity of wording.

The second aspect: that responding is hearing, so it is as if He said: "I hear."

The third aspect: that supplication is repentance from sins, because the penitent calls upon Allah at the time of repentance, and responding is the acceptance of repentance.

The fourth aspect: that supplication is worship, and in the hadith: "Supplication is worship." He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And your Lord said: Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ [Ghafir: 60], then He said: ﴿Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me﴾ [Ghafir: 60]. Responding is an expression for fulfilling what is guaranteed to the obedient of reward.

The fifth aspect: responding is more general than being given what is asked or being denied it, so the meaning is: "I choose for him the better of the two matters, from giving and refusing." All these interpretations go against the apparent meaning.

﴿So let them respond to Me﴾: that is, let them seek (fa-yaṭlubū), that is, let them seek My response to them when they call upon Me. This was said by Thaʿlab, so "istafʿil" has come with the meaning of seeking, like "istaghfir" (seek forgiveness), and this is the common usage of it. Or: "So let them respond to Me," if I call them to faith and obedience, just as I respond to them when they call upon Me for their needs. This was said by Mujāhid, Abu ʿUbayda, and others. Here "istafʿala" is in the sense of "afʿala" (imperative), and this is common in the Qur'an: ﴿So their Lord responded to them: I do not waste﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 195], ﴿So We responded to him and granted him Yaḥyā﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 90]. However, its transitive use in the Qur'an is with the preposition lām, though it has come in Arabic speech transitive without a preposition. He said:

"And a caller who called out, 'O You who answers the call,' / but no answerer answered him at that moment."

That is: "He did not respond to him." Similar to this, namely that "istafʿala" is synonymous with "afʿala," are their sayings: "istaballa" with the meaning of "aballa" (to recover from illness), "istaḥṣada al-zarʿ" and "aḥṣada" (to harvest the crop), "istaʿjala al-shayʾ" and "aʿjala" (to hasten a thing), "istathārahu" and "athārahu" (to stir it up). "Istafʿala" may be synonymous with "afʿala" both transitively and intransitively, and this meaning is one of the meanings we mentioned for "istafʿala" in His words: ﴿It is You we worship, and You we ask for help﴾ [al-Fātiḥa: 5].

Abu Rajāʾ al-Khurasani said: its meaning is "so let them supplicate to Me." Al-Akhfash said: "so let them submit to the responding." Mujāhid also said, and al-Rabīʿ: "so let them obey." It was said: The seeking of response here is the talbiya, which is: "Here I am, O Allah, here I am" (labbayka Allāhumma labbayk). The lām is the lām of command, and it is sukūn (quiescent), and we know of no one who read it with a kasra.

﴿And let them believe in Me﴾: it is conjoined to "so let them respond to Me," and its meaning is the command to belief in Allah. Taking it as a command to create belief in it is remote, because the beginning of the verse requires that they are believers, so for this reason it is interpreted as continuance (dā'ima), or as sincerity of religion, supplication, and action, or as reward for responding to Me by obedience, or by belief and its consequences, or by belief, in that I respond to their supplication: five statements, the last of which is by Abu Rajāʾ al-Khurasani.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 186 (part 2 of 2):

﴿That they may be rightly guided﴾. The reading of the majority (al-jumhur) is with a fathah on the ya' and a dammah on the shin, "yarshudun." Some people read "yurshadun" in the passive voice (mabni li-l-maf'ul). It is also narrated from Abu Haywah and Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Ablah that they read "yarshidun" with a fathah on the ya' and a kasrah on the shin, and this is with a difference of transmission from them both. It was also read "yarshadun" with a fathah on both letters.

The meaning is that when they respond to Allah and believe in Him, they are in hope of attaining rushd (right guidance) for themselves, which is being guided to the interests of their religion and their worldly life. Ending the verse with the hope of rushd is among the most excellent things, because when Allah, exalted is He, commanded them to respond to Him and to believe in Him, He alerted them that the purpose of this obligation is nothing other than your reaching your own rashad (rectitude) through complying with it. None of its benefits reaches Him, exalted is He; rather, that benefit belongs only to you.

Since faith was likened to the path that is travelled in the Qur'an, it was fitting to mention rushad, which is guidance (al-hidayah), as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fatihah: 6], ﴿And indeed, you guide to a straight path﴾ [al-Shura: 52], ﴿And We guided them both to the straight path﴾ [al-Saffat: 118].

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 187 (part 1 of 3):

(p-48) ﴿It is made lawful for you, on the night of the fast, to go in unto your wives.﴾ The occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of this verse is what al-Bukhari narrated from al-Bara': "When the fasting of the whole of Ramadan was prescribed, men used to betray themselves, so this was revealed." It has also been said: a man, when he had finished the evening (maghrib), was permitted eating, drinking and intercourse until he prayed the late night prayer (al-'isha' al-akhira) or slept; but if he prayed it or slept without having broken his fast, what had been lawful for him before became forbidden to him until the following night. Also, 'Umar, Ka'b al-Ansari and a group of the Companions had intercourse with their wives after the late night prayer, and Qays ibn Sirma al-Ansari slept before breaking his fast, and rose in the morning fasting, and fainted at midday. This was mentioned to the Prophet (ﷺ), and so this was revealed. Some scholars said: the verse was revealed concerning a lapse that had occurred, and this was made the cause of a concession (rukhsa) for all Muslims until the Day of Resurrection. This is from the perfection of care (ihkam al-'inaya).

The connection (munasaba) of this verse with what precedes it of the verses is that it is among the complete rulings concerning the states that befall the fasting person. Since the opening of the verses on fasting was: "Fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you," this required general likeness in its prescription, in its number, in its conditions, and in all the obligations of fasting. The People of the Book had been commanded to abstain from lawful eating, drinking and intercourse during their fasts after they slept; it was also said: after the late night prayer. The Muslims were likewise. When what has been mentioned in the occasion of revelation happened to 'Umar and Qays, God permitted them that from the beginning of the night until the break of dawn, out of kindness to them. It also fits His saying at the end of the verse on fasting: ﴿God desires ease for you, and does not desire hardship for you﴾ [al-Baqara: 185], and this is from facilitation (taysir).

His saying "it is made lawful" (uhilla) implies that it was forbidden before that, and its transmission has already been mentioned in the occasion of revelation; but it was not forbidden throughout the whole night. Do you not see that it was lawful for them until the time of sleep, or until after the late night prayer?

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "uhilla" in the passive voice, with the agent omitted because it is known. It was also read "ahalla" in the active voice, with "al-rafath" (the sexual talk/intercourse) in the accusative as its object. Either this is by elision (idmar) because the meaning indicates it, since it is known to the believers that the One who makes lawful and forbids is God; or it is by iltifat (shift), which is the move from the first person pronoun to the third person pronoun, since before it is: ﴿So let them respond to Me and believe in Me﴾ [al-Baqara: 186]. "Lakum" (for you) is connected to "ahalla", and it is an iltifat because before it there is a third person pronoun. "Layla" (night) is in the accusative as an adverb of time, and "layla" is not meant as a single night but as a class (jins). They said: the governing element (al-nasib) of this adverb is "ahalla", but this is not correct, because "layla" is not an adverb of "ahalla"; rather, in meaning it is an adverb of "al-rafath". Although grammatical practice (sina'at al-nahw) rejects that the accusative of "layla" be governed by "al-rafath", because "al-rafath" is a verbal noun (masdar) and here it is a relative (mawsul), so its complement may not precede it. But a governing element is supposed for it, and its supposed form is: al-rafath layla al-siyam (the sexual talk on the night of the fast), and it was deleted, and what is mentioned was made to be dependent on it, as they said in the verse of the poet:

"And part of forbearance in the face of ignorance is submission to humiliation."

Its supposed form is: "submission to humiliation is submission". Similarly they explained His saying: ﴿Indeed I am to you both among the sincere advisers﴾ [al-A'raf: 21] and ﴿Indeed I am of those who hate your deed﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 168], meaning "sincere adviser to you both", and he said "to your deed". So whatever is in the relative clause, what is related to it in meaning is placed before it, and a governing element indicated by that relative clause is supposed for it. It has already been mentioned that some grammarians permit the adverb to precede this kind of verbal noun. "Layla" was made the complement of "al-siyam" by way of extension (ittisa'), because the annexation (idafa) occurs for the slightest connection; and since fasting is intended during the night and is not realized except by fasting a part of it, the annexation is valid.

The majority read "al-rafath", and 'Abd Allah read "al-rufuth". Here it is used as a euphemism for intercourse. They said that "al-rafath" is the plain expression of what should be concealed, like the word "al-nayk" (coition). He expressed it with a word close to "al-nayk" as a reproach for what they had done, since that was forbidden to them, yet they fell into it; as He said about it: ﴿You were betraying yourselves﴾, so He made that betrayal. It was construed with "ila", though its original construction is with "ba'", because it implies the meaning of "ifda'" (reaching/going unto), and the word's use made this implication fitting. Thus it became close to the euphemisms that came in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿When he covered her﴾ [al-A'raf: 189], ﴿And do not approach them﴾ [al-Baqara: 222], ﴿So come to your tillage﴾ [al-Baqara: 223], ﴿And now have relations with them (fa-al-ana basharuhunna)﴾.

"Al-nisa'" (women) is the plural of a plural, namely "niswa," or the plural of "imra'a" according to a non-standard form. He attributed "the women" to the addressees for the sake of specificity, since intercourse is not lawful except for one who is specifically connected to the one he has intercourse with, either by marriage or by ownership.

﴿They are a garment for you and you are a garment for them﴾. "Libas" (garment) originally applies to clothing, then it is used for a woman. Abu 'Ubayda said: it is said of a woman: she is your garment, your bedding, and your wrapper, because of the intermingling between them. Since they embrace and each of them envelops the other in the embrace, each of them is likened to the garment which envelops the human being. Al-Rabi' said: "They are a covering for you, and you are a covering for them." Mujahid and al-Suddi said: "They are a dwelling (sakan) for you," meaning one of you rests in the other, like His saying: ﴿And He it is who made the night a garment for you and sleep a rest﴾ [al-Furqan: 47]. This clause has no place in grammatical analysis (i'rab), rather it is independent (mustanafa), like an explanation of the cause of the permission, which is the inability to be patient away from them, since they are for you in intimacy like a garment. He placed "They are a garment for you" before "you are a garment for them" because the man's need of the woman is more evident and his patience away from her is less, and the man is the one who initiates that act, while a woman hardly initiates that act because of the dominance of modesty over them; so much so that some of them cover their faces at the time of intercourse so as not to look at their husband out of modesty at that time.

The verse combined three kinds of rhetorical expression (bayan): the antithesis of meaning (tibaq ma'nawi) in His saying "it is made lawful for you", since it implies a prior prohibition, as if it were made lawful for you what was forbidden to you, or what was forbidden to those before you; the euphemism (kinaya) in the word "al-rafath", which is a euphemism for intercourse; and the striking metaphor (isti'ara badi'a) in His saying "they are a garment for you". "Libas" is used in the singular because it is like a verbal noun: one says "labastu mulabasa wa libasan".

* *

﴿God knew that you were betraying yourselves﴾. If "'alima" is transitive in the sense of "'arafa" (to know), then "anna" fills the place of the object; or if it is transitive in its original way, then it fills the place of the two objects, according to Sibawayh's view, and a parallel to this has already been discussed. "Takhtanun" is from "khiyana" (betrayal), and "iftaʿala" here has the meaning of "fa'ala", so "ikhtana" means "khana" (betrayed), as "iqtadara" means "qadara" (was able). It has been said that the addition of a letter indicates an addition in meaning. "Ikhtiyan" here is expressed about what they fell into of disobedience by intercourse and by eating after sleep, and that was betrayal of themselves, because the harm of disobedience returns to themselves. So it is as if it were said: you wrong yourselves and diminish their share of good. It was also said: it means you are selfishly keeping yourselves in what you were forbidden, and it was said: it means you are attending to yourselves by approaching your wives. It is said: "takhawwana" and "takhawwala" meaning "ta'ahhada" (to look after), so the nun is a substitute for the lam, since the lam form is more common. Abu Muslim said: it is an expression for not fulfilling what is obligatory of the right of the self; and therefore He said "yourselves" and did not say "God". The apparent meaning of the statement is that the betrayal occurred from them, because of the indication of "kuntum" (you were) and because of the authentic transmission in the hadith about intercourse and other things. It was also said: that is on the assumption of "and it had not yet happened", and the meaning is: you would betray yourselves if that prohibition continued. This view is weak, because of the existence of "kuntum", and because it is an assumed elision for which no indication is present, and because it conflicts with the apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿So He turned to you and pardoned you﴾.

﴿So He turned to you﴾: that is, He accepted your repentance when you repented from what you had committed of the forbidden. It was also said: it means He lightened [the burden] for you by concession and permission, like His saying: ﴿He knew that you would not be able to keep count of it, so He turned to you﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20]; ﴿So fasting for two consecutive months as a repentance from God﴾ [al-Nisa': 92]; ﴿God certainly turned in forgiveness to the Prophet and the Emigrants and the Helpers﴾ [al-Tawba: 117]. All of these mean lightening. It was also said: it means He removed from you what He had obligated of prohibition of eating, drinking and intercourse after the late night prayer, or after sleep, according to the disagreement, and this view returns to the meaning of the previous view. The second: ﴿and pardoned you﴾, that is, for your sins, so He does not take you to account. The acceptance of repentance is the lifting of the sin, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Repentance erases the sin (al-hawba)." Pardon (al-'afw) is the effacing of the trace of the sin; so both return to one meaning, and he combined them for emphasis. It was also said: the meaning is: He made the matter of women easy for you in what is to come, that is, He left the prohibition for you, as you say: "this is a thing pardoned (ma'fu)," meaning left, and it is said: "He gave him 'afw," meaning easily, without requiring him to ask; and "the horse ran two pacings 'afwan," meaning of its own accord, without urging or calling by a whip or spur.

﴿So now have relations with them (fa-al-ana basharuhunna)﴾. The discussion of "al-ana" has already been given at His saying: ﴿They said: now you have brought the truth﴾ [al-Baqara: 71]. That is, "fa-hadha al-zaman", meaning: at this time, that is, the night of the fast, have relations with them. This is a command intended as permission, because it came after a prohibition, and because consensus (ijma') has been reached on it. The "mubasha" (relations) in the view of the majority is intercourse. It was also said: intercourse and what is less than it, and it is derived from the contact of the two skins, so it includes embracing and touching. If we say the intended meaning here is intercourse, because of His saying "al-rafath" and because of the occasion of revelation, then the permission for it includes the permission for what is less than it.

(Part of the verse continues:) ﴿And seek what God has decreed for you﴾: seek. Regarding the interpretation of "what God has decreed" there are several views. First: it is offspring. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrima, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, al-Rabi', al-Suddi, and al-Hakam ibn 'Utayba: when permission for intimacy was granted to them, they were commanded to seek what God had apportioned for them and recorded for them in the Preserved Tablet, namely offspring. It seems that this permission was granted not merely for satisfying desire, but for seeking what God legislated marriage for, namely procreation: "Marry and multiply, for I will boast of you among the nations on the Day of Resurrection." Second: it is the place of intercourse, that is: seek the lawful place for intercourse, not the forbidden place which was not decreed for you, according to His saying: ﴿So come to them from where God has commanded you﴾ [al-Baqara: 222]. Third: it is what He permitted after the prohibition, that is: seek the concession and permission; this was said by Qatada and Ibn Zayd. Fourth: "seek the Night of Power (laylat al-qadr)," said by Mu'adh ibn Jabal, and it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is close to the strange interpretations (bida' al-tafasir). Fifth: it is the Qur'an, said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Zajjaj, that is: seek what is permitted to you and what you are commanded to do; this is preferred by the reading of al-Hasan and Mu'awiya ibn Qurra: "wattabi'u" (follow), from following, and it is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. Sixth: it is the states and times in which intercourse is permitted to you, since intercourse is prohibited during menstruation, postpartum bleeding, the waiting period, and apostasy. Seventh: it is the wife and the female slave, as in His saying: ﴿except from their wives or what their right hands possess﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 6]. Eighth: that this is a prohibition of 'azl (coitus interruptus), because it concerns free women.

"Kataba" here means "ja'ala" (made), as in His saying: ﴿He inscribed faith in their hearts﴾ [al-Mujadila: 22], or means "qada" (decreed), or means "athbata fi al-lawh al-mahfuz" (recorded in the Preserved Tablet), or "in the Qur'an". The apparent meaning is that this clause is an emphasis of what precedes it, and the meaning, and God knows best, is: seek and do what God has permitted you to do of approaching women during the whole night of the fast. This is supported by the reading of al-A'mash: "wa'tu ma kataba Allah lakum" (come to what God has decreed for you). This is an irregular reading, because it contradicts the consonantal text of the codex (sawad al-mushaf).

****[Continuing from the previous part]**

﴿And eat and drink﴾ is also a command of permission. The three things that had been forbidden to them during part of the night of fasting were made lawful for them. ﴿Until﴾ marks the end of the three things, namely sexual intercourse, eating, and drinking. The story of Sirmah ibn Qays has already been mentioned in the occasion of revelation (asbab al-nuzul). Thus the permission for intercourse was due to the case of Umar and others, and the permission for eating was due to the case of Sirmah or others.

﴿The white thread from the black thread﴾: its apparent meaning is the well-known thread, and for this reason a group of the Companions, when they intended to fast, would tie a white thread and a black thread to one of their feet, and would continue eating and drinking until the two became distinct to them. This continued until the words of Allah the Exalted were revealed: ﴿from the dawn﴾, and they understood that He meant by this the night and the day. Sahl ibn Sa'd related this regarding the revelation of this verse. It is also reported that between the revelation of ﴿And eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread﴾ and the revelation of ﴿from the dawn﴾ there was a year, from one Ramadan to the next.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Those who do not permit the delay of clarification (ta'khir al-bayan), and they are the majority of jurists and theologians, and this is the view of Abu Ali and Abu Hashim, do not accept this hadith because of the meaning of the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd. As for those who permit it, they say: It is not pointless, because the addressee benefits from it the obligation of the address, and he resolves to act upon it when he has clarified the intended meaning. End of his words. But this, in my view, is not a case of delaying clarification until the time of need; rather it is a case of abrogation (naskh). Do you not see that the Companions acted upon it, I mean by applying the wording to its apparent sense, until the words ﴿from the dawn﴾ were revealed, so the apparent sense of the white thread and the black thread was abrogated, and these two became figurative (majaz). The white thread was likened to the dawn that appears spreading across the horizon, and the black thread to the darkness of the night that extends with it. They were likened to two threads, white and black. What moved it from metaphor (isti'arah) to simile (tashbih) is His words ﴿from the dawn﴾, like your saying: "I saw a lion from Zayd." If you had not said "from Zayd," it would have been a metaphor, and the simile here is more eloquent than the metaphor, because a metaphor occurs only where the situation or the context indicates it. Here, if ﴿from the dawn﴾ had not been mentioned, the metaphor would not have been known. For this reason the Companions understood the literal sense of the two threads before the revelation of ﴿from the dawn﴾, to the extent that some of them, namely Adi ibn Hatim, neglected this simile and the clarification of the words ﴿from the dawn﴾, and took the two threads in their literal sense. He related that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he laughed and said: "Indeed your pillow must be wide," and it is reported: "Indeed you have a broad nape." That refers only to the whiteness of the day and the blackness of the night. A broad nape is taken as an indication of a man's lack of understanding, and the poet said:

"Broad-napped, his scale leaning to his left,
his moustache clipped short by the measure of the carats."

Everything that is fine, long, and resembles a thread, the Arabs have called a thread.

Al-Zajjaj said: They are two dawns. One of them appears as a black line stretched across the horizon, and it is the black thread; the other rises bright, filling the horizon. So according to him the two threads are the two dawns, named so because of their extension, by way of likening them to threads. His words ﴿from the dawn﴾ indicate that by the white thread is meant the true dawn (al-subh al-sadiq), which is the whiteness spreading across the horizon, not the false dawn (al-subh al-kadhib), which is the elongated whiteness, because dawn (fajr) is the bursting forth of light, and that belongs to the second, not the first. The white thread is likened to it in its initial state, because it appears thin and then rises spreading out. Thus with the rising of its first part on the horizon, abstention becomes obligatory. This is the view of the majority, and people have acted upon it, and it has prevailed through the ages and in the cities. It is also the implication of the hadiths of Ibn Mas'ud and Samurah ibn Jundub. It has been said that abstention becomes obligatory with the appearance of dawn in the roads and on the tops of the mountains. This is reported from Uthman, Hudhayfah, Ibn Abbas, Talq ibn Ali, Ata', al-A'mash, and others. It is reported from Ali that he led the people in the dawn prayer, then said: "Now the white thread has become distinct from the black thread." What led them to this view is that they held that fasting is only during the day, and the day for them is from sunrise to sunset. The disagreement about the day has already been mentioned. The specification, by the appearance of dawn to the fasting person, of the permission of intimacy, eating, and drinking indicates that whoever doubts whether dawn has appeared and does one of these things, and then it becomes clear that dawn had already risen while he was fasting, owes no make-up, because the limit was set by the appearance of dawn to the fasting person, not by its rising. It is reported from Ibn Abbas that he sent two men to watch the dawn for him. One of them said: "Dawn has risen," and the other said: "It has not risen." He said: "You have disagreed." So he ate, and it became clear that there was no make-up for him. Al-Thawri, Ubayd Allah ibn al-Hasan, and al-Shafi'i said so. Malik said: If he ate doubting the dawn, he is obliged to make up the day. There are two views from Abu Hanifah.

In this limit there is also an indication of the permissibility of intimacy up to the appearance of dawn, so it is not obligatory on him to perform ritual washing (ghusl) before dawn, because if intimacy is permitted until dawn, he could not perform ghusl except after dawn. By this the view of Abu Hurayrah is refuted. Al-Hasan holds that if a person in a state of major ritual impurity (junub) reaches the morning before performing ghusl, his fast is invalid. But A'isha reported that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) "used to enter the morning in a state of major impurity from intercourse while fasting." This limit applies only where it is possible to determine dawn by direct observation. If the sky is moonlit or cloudy, or he is in a place from which he cannot see the rising of dawn, then he is commanded to be cautious regarding the entry of dawn, since he has no way of knowing the state of the dawn's rising. Therefore he must abstain until he is certain that the time of dawn has begun, to safeguard his religion.

Abu Muslim held that the fast is broken only by these three: intimacy, eating, and drinking. As for anything beyond these, such as vomiting, an enema, and other things, it remained under the original permission. The jurists, however, said: These three were singled out for mention because the soul inclines toward them, whereas vomiting and enemas are things the soul dislikes, and snuff is rare, so it was not mentioned. As for the first ﴿from﴾, it indicates the starting point of the limit. It has been said that it and what follows it are in the accusative position, because the meaning is: "until the white thread separates from the black thread," just as one says: "the hand separated from its wrist," meaning it parted from it. The second ﴿from﴾ is partitive, because the white thread is a part of the dawn and its beginning. It also relates to ﴿becomes distinct﴾. It is permissible for two particles to relate to one verb when the wording is the same but the meanings differ: so the first ﴿from﴾ indicates the starting point and the second ﴿from﴾ is partitive. It is also possible that it is partitive with respect to both threads together, according to al-Zajjaj's view, since for him dawn consists of two dawns, so "dawn" here is not meant in the singular but as a genus. It has been said that it is also possible for ﴿from the dawn﴾ to be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿the white﴾, so it would relate to an omitted element, meaning: "being from the dawn."
