Whoever permits the first ﴿from﴾ to be explanatory (bayaniyyah) permits it here too, so it is as if it were said: "until the white thread, which is the dawn, becomes distinct to you from the black thread." The explanation of the white thread is sufficient without explaining the black thread, because the explanation of one of them is an explanation of the other. Omitting it was preferable, because what is intended by the distinguishing and what depends on its clarification is the ruling concerning the permission of intimacy, eating, and drinking. Also, to avoid awkwardness of wording, had it been stated explicitly it would have read: "until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread from the dawn from the night," in which "from the dawn" would explain the white thread and "from the night" the black thread. And since the phrase "from the black thread" came as a secondary element, it was fitting to omit its explanation.

* *

﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾. The obligation of fasting has already been mentioned, so it is not commanded here again, and its end had not been mentioned, so the end is mentioned here, namely His words ﴿until the night﴾. An end-point occurs when what follows it is not of the same kind as what precedes it, and it does not fall under the ruling of what precedes it. The night is not of the same kind as the day, so it does not fall under its ruling. However, from the necessity of certainly knowing the end of the day, some part of the night is included. Ibn Abbas said: The People of the Book would break their fast from the evening prayer to the evening prayer, so Allah the Exalted commanded opposition to them, and breaking the fast at sunset. The command to complete here is obligatory, because fasting is obligatory, so completing it is obligatory. This differs from intimacy, eating, and drinking, since these are permissible in origin, so the command concerning them is permission. Al-Raghib said: In it there is evidence for the permissibility of intention during the day, for the permissibility of delaying ghusl until dawn, and for the prohibition of continuous fasting (sawm al-wisal), end of his words.

As for the verse indicating the permissibility of intention during the day, this is not evident, because what is commanded is completing the fast, not beginning the fast. Rather, it implies a previous fast that we are commanded to complete, so there is no reference in the verse to intention during the day.

As for the permissibility of delaying ghusl until dawn, this is not evident from this verse either, but from the statement preceding it. As for the indication of the prohibition of continuous fasting, this is not evident either, because it set the end of the obligation to complete the fast only at the entry of night, and there is no contradiction between this and continuous fasting. It is authentically reported in the hadith that continuous fasting is forbidden. Some interpreted the prohibition as unlawfulness, and others as disliked. Continuous fasting has been reported from a group of the Companions and the Successors, such as Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, Ibrahim al-Taymi, and Abu al-Hawra'. Some permitted it until the pre-dawn meal (suhur), among them Ahmad, Ishaq, and Ibn Wahb.

The apparent sense of the verse is the obligation to complete the fast until night. So if someone thought the sun had set and broke his fast, and then the sun rose, he did not complete it until night, and he must make up the day, but there is no expiation (kaffarah) for him. This is the view of the majority, Abu Hanifah, al-Shafi'i, and others. Ishaq and the Zahiris said: There is no make-up for him, like one who forgot. This is reported from Umar. Malik said: Whoever broke his fast doubting the sunset must make up and expiate. In the Thamaniyah of Abu Zayd: he owes make-up only, by analogy with one who doubts the dawn.

If one who intentionally breaks the fast by intercourse cuts off the completion, there is consensus on the obligation of make-up. If by eating and drinking or what is similar, then according to al-Shafi'i he owes make-up, and according to the rest of the scholars he owes make-up and expiation. If he has intercourse while forgetting, he is treated like one who did it intentionally according to the majority, though there is a disagreement from al-Shafi'i regarding the expiation. If by eating and drinking, then he remains in his fast according to Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i, while according to Malik he must make up the day. If one intends to break the fast during the day but does not actually do so, rather he cancels the intention to fast, he remains in his fast according to the majority and owes no make-up. Ibn Habib said: According to Malik in al-Mudawwanah, he breaks his fast and owes make-up.

The apparent sense of the verse implies that completion is obligatory only upon one who had already begun the fast. So if he entered the morning without fasting, for no valid excuse, abstention is not obligatory on him, because no fast had preceded it for him to complete. They said: However, the Sunnah has made abstention obligatory on him. The apparent sense of the verse implies that completing a voluntary fast is obligatory, according to the position of the Hanafis, because it falls under the general wording "and complete the fasts." The Shafi'is said: What is meant is the obligatory fast, because this was revealed to explain the rulings of the obligatory fast.

Some of the masters of spiritual realities (haqa'iq) said: When Allah the Exalted knew that the servant must have his portions (hudhuz), He divided the night and the day of this month between His right and your portion. So He said, concerning His right: ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾, and concerning your portion: ﴿And eat and drink until it becomes distinct﴾.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 187 (part 3 of 3):

﴿And do not have intercourse with them while you are devoted to worship (i'tikaf) in the mosques.﴾ When He permitted them intimacy during the night of fasting, they used to, when they were in i'tikaf and one of them was driven by need for sexual intercourse, go out to his wife, fulfil his desire, then perform ghusl and come back to the mosque. So they were forbidden from that during their i'tikaf, both inside the mosque and outside it, and this is the apparent meaning of the verse and the context of the intimacy mentioned before it. The occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) was that mubashara means only sexual intercourse, and a group held this view; so what is forbidden is intercourse. The majority said: it applies here to intercourse and to whatever is enjoyed sexually. There is consensus (ijma') that this prohibition is one of prohibition (nahy tahrim), and that i'tikaf is invalidated by intercourse. As for the preliminaries of marriage, such as looking, touching, and kissing with desire, i'tikaf is invalidated by them according to Malik. Abu Hanifa said: if he does so and ejaculates, it is invalidated. Al-Muzani reported from al-Shafi'i: if he does so, it is invalidated. Al-Shafi'i also said: intercourse invalidates it only if the like of it with a non-spouse would require a penalty. It is authentically reported in a hadith that "'A'isha used to comb the head of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was in i'tikaf in the mosque," and there is no doubt that she would touch him. They said: this shows that touching without desire is not prohibited.

And since mubashara is understood as touching, and touching has been forbidden, then intercourse is more fitting and more deserving of prohibition, because it includes touching and more; and mubashara, when understood as touching, is restricted by desire.

I'tikaf in the Shari'ah is an expression for confining oneself to a place for worship and drawing near to Allah, and it is among the ancient laws. Qatada read "wa-antum 'akifun" without an alif, and the clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal), meaning: do not have intercourse with them in this state. The apparent meaning of the verse requires the permissibility of i'tikaf, and there is consensus that it is not obligatory. It is established that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) performed i'tikaf," so it is a sunnah. The verse does not address its recommendation, so we mention its conditions. Among its conditions is fasting; this is reported from 'Ali, Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, and 'A'isha, and Abu Hanifa and his companions, Malik, al-Thawri, and al-Hasan ibn Salih held this view. It is reported from 'A'isha that fasting is a sunnah of the one in i'tikaf. A group of the Successors, including Sa'id and Ibrahim, said fasting is not a condition. Tawus reported the same from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Shafi'i held this view. The apparent meaning of the verse is that no fixed time is required; rather, anything that is called staying (luth) in some period is called i'tikaf, and this is the position of al-Shafi'i. Malik said: one may not perform i'tikaf for less than ten days; this is the well-known position of his school, and it is reported from him that the minimum is one day and night. The apparent unrestricted sense of i'tikaf also requires the permissibility of i'tikaf during the night and the day, or either of them; accordingly, if one vows i'tikaf for only a night, or only a day, it is valid, and this is the position of al-Shafi'i. Sahnun said: if one vows i'tikaf for a night, it is not binding on him. Abu Hanifa said: if one vows i'tikaf for days, it is binding on him along with their nights.

Regarding leaving the place of i'tikaf, occupying oneself in it with other than the intended worship, entering it, and the matters that invalidate it, there are many rulings mentioned in the books of jurisprudence. The apparent meaning of His words "﴿while you are devoted to worship in the mosques﴾" is that being in mosques is not a condition of i'tikaf, because a prohibition against something qualified by a state that has a object of relation does not indicate that, when that state occurs among those being addressed, that object becomes a condition for its occurrence. A parallel: "Do not strike Zayd while you are riding a horse," which does not imply that whenever you ride, your riding must be only on a horse. Thus it becomes clear that using this verse to prove that a mosque is a condition of i'tikaf is weak; the mention of mosques is only because i'tikaf usually occurs only in them, not because it is a condition. The apparent meaning of "﴿in the mosques﴾" is that i'tikaf is not restricted to a particular mosque; rather every mosque is a place for i'tikaf. This was said by Abu Qilaba, Ibn 'Uyayna, al-Shafi'i, Dawud al-Tabari, and Ibn al-Mundhir, and it is one of Malik's two opinions. The other opinion is that there is no i'tikaf except in a mosque where congregational prayer is held, and this was said by 'Abd Allah, 'A'isha, Ibrahim, Ibn Jubayr, 'Urwa, and Abu Ja'far. Some said there is no i'tikaf except in one of the three mosques, reported from 'Abd Allah and Hudhayfa. Some said there is no i'tikaf except in the mosque of a prophet, said by Ibn al-Musayyab, which agrees with the previous view, since these are the mosques of the prophets, upon them be prayers and peace. al-Harith reported from 'Ali that there is no i'tikaf except in the Sacred Mosque and in the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The apparent meaning of the verse indicates the permissibility of i'tikaf for men; as for women, the verse is silent about them. Abu Hanifa said: she performs i'tikaf in the prayer-place of her house and not elsewhere. Malik said: she performs i'tikaf in the mosque of congregation, and he disliked it in her house. al-Shafi'i said: wherever she wishes. Mujahid and al-A'mash read "fi al-masjid" in the singular; al-A'mash said it is the Sacred Mosque. The apparent meaning is that it refers to the category (lil-jins). The reading of the one who read the plural "fi al-masajid" supports this. Some Sufis said concerning "﴿And do not have intercourse with them﴾" and the rest of the verse: Allah informed that the place of devotion is sanctified against the pursuit of worldly desires, end of quote.

* *

﴿These are the limits of Allah﴾. "Tilka" is a subject described by a plural predicate, so it cannot be a reference to what was forbidden in i'tikaf, because that is one thing. Rather it refers to what the verse of fasting contains from its beginning until here. The verse of fasting contained a number of commands, and commanding something is a prohibition of its opposite; so in this sense they were a number of prohibitions. Then the prohibition on intimacy during i'tikaf came at the end, and so the whole is called "limits" by giving precedence to what is stated explicitly, and by considering those prohibitions contained within the commands. It was said: "the limits of Allah," and this interpretation was needed because what is commanded to be done is not described with "﴿so do not approach them﴾." The limits of Allah are His conditions, said by al-Suddi; or His obligations, said by Shahr ibn Hawshab; or His disobediences, said by al-Dahhak. al-Zamakhshari said its meaning is His prohibited matters and His prohibitions. Or the limits are permission and prohibition, said by Ibn 'Atiyya. Attributing the limits to Allah the Exalted here, and wherever they are mentioned, indicates emphasis on not coming near to them, and they were not stated indefinitely or with the definite article for this meaning.

﴿So do not approach them﴾. The prohibition of approaching the limits is more emphatic than the prohibition of coming into contact with them. This is like the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed every king has a sanctuary (hima), and the sanctuary of Allah is His prohibited things; whoever grazes around the sanctuary is near to falling into it." Grazing around the sanctuary and approaching it are the same. Here it came as "fa-la taqrabuha," and elsewhere: "﴿fa-la ta'taduha wa-man yata'adda hudud Allah﴾" [al-Baqara: 229], and His words: "﴿wa-man ya'si Allah wa-rasulahu wa-yata'adda hududahu﴾" [al-Nisa': 14]. This is because here it emphasized the aspect of prohibition, since it follows with His words "These are the limits of Allah." What is forbidden to do, the prohibition against approaching it is more emphatic. As for where "﴿fa-la ta'taduha﴾" [al-Baqara: 229] came, it came after the explanation of the number of divorces and the mention of the rulings on the waiting period, the ila' and menstruation, so it suited to forbid transgression in them, which is exceeding the limit Allah set in them. Likewise His words "﴿wa-man ya'si Allah wa-rasulahu wa-yata'adda hududahu﴾" [al-Nisa': 14] came after the rulings on inheritance, the mention of the heirs' shares, consideration of orphans' property, and the explanation of the number of wives permitted, so it suited to mention after all this transgression, which is exceeding what Allah legislated of these rulings to what He did not legislate. His words "﴿These are the limits of Allah﴾" came after His words "﴿a bequest from Allah﴾" [al-Nisa': 12], then He promised paradise to the one who obeys and threatened the Fire to the one who disobeys and transgresses His limits; so every prohibition of approaching or transgressing falls in the place appropriate to it. Abu Muslim said the meaning of "la taqrabuha" is: do not interfere with them by altering them, like His words: "﴿wa-la taqrabu mal al-yatim illa bi-allati hiya ahsan﴾" [al-An'am: 152].

﴿Thus Allah makes His signs clear﴾: that is, like that clarification previously mentioned in the mention of the rulings of fasting and what is connected to it, in concise and eloquent words, He makes clear His signs indicating the rest of His legislation. Abu Muslim said: by the signs are meant the obligations which He explained, as if He said: thus Allah makes clear to people what He prescribed for them, so that they may be mindful of Him by acting upon what He revealed, end of his words. This is only possible on the assumption that the kaf is extra (za'ida); but if it is for comparison (tashbih), then there must be a thing compared and a thing compared to.

﴿for the people﴾: its apparent meaning is generality. Ibn 'Atiyya said its meaning is particular, concerning those whom Allah has facilitated for guidance, by the evidence of verses which indicate that Allah leads astray whom He wills, end of his words. There is no need to claim particularity; rather Allah makes His signs clear to people and explains them to them, and makes them manifest and plain for them until they become evident and clear. Making them clear does not necessarily mean people become clear about them, because you say: "I explained to him, but he did not understand," just as you say: "I taught him, but he did not learn." Ibn 'Atiyya considered that the meaning of "yubayyin" is making clarity exist in them, so he claimed the meaning is particular; because just as Allah placed guidance in some people, He placed misguidance in others. According to this understanding, particularity must be applied to what we have established, and it remains with its original generality; and according to our interpretation of "making clear," that is a consensus between us and the Mu'tazila, whereas according to his interpretation, the Mu'tazila would dispute it.

﴿So that they may be mindful of Allah (la'allahum yattaqun)﴾: it has been mentioned earlier that wherever piety (taqwa) is mentioned, it comes after a matter involving hardship. Likewise it came here, because preventing a person from something naturally desired with great appetite, to the point that it is among the most delightful bodily pleasures, is burdensome for him, and nothing restrains him from indulging in it except piety. Therefore this verse is concluded with it; that is, they are hopeful of attaining piety through the clarification which Allah has made clear to them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 188 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Do not devour your wealth among yourselves by false means﴾. Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning Imru' al-Qays ibn 'Abis al-Kindi and 'Iddan ibn Ash'a al-Hadrami, who brought a dispute before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) over a piece of land. Imru' al-Qays was the one being sued, and 'Iddan was the claimant. Imru' al-Qays wanted to swear an oath, so the verse was revealed, and 'Iddan took the land from him without contesting it further.

The connection of this verse to what precedes it is clear. The one who worships Allah the Exalted through fasting restrains himself from what he is accustomed to, namely eating, drinking and intimacy during the day. Then he restrains himself by confining himself in a place of worship, fasting for Him, deprived of the greatest pleasure by night and day. It is fitting that his food and drink be only from what is lawful and pure, which illuminates the heart, increases its insight, and leads him to strive in worship. For this reason he is forbidden to consume what is unlawful, since that would prevent his worship, his fasting and his seclusion from being accepted. Between the verses on fasting there also falls the verse on the answering of the supplication of the one who calls, and the supplication of the servants to Allah the Exalted. A hadith has come: "Whoever has unlawful food, unlawful clothing and unlawful drink, and then supplicates Allah, how could it be answered for him?" So the prohibition of consuming unlawful property also fits here.

It is also possible that the connection is this: when He made fasting obligatory upon them, as He had made it obligatory upon those before them, He then differed between them and the People of the Book. He permitted them to eat, drink and have intercourse during the nights of fasting. He commanded them not to agree with the People of the Book in devouring bribes from their kings and lowly folk, and in what they practise of usury, and in what they permit themselves of wealth by falsehood. As the Exalted said: ﴿and sell it for a small price﴾ [al-Baqara: 174], ﴿There is no blame upon us regarding the unlettered﴾ [Al 'Imran: 75], ﴿devourers of unlawful gain﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 42]. They were to oppose them in word and deed, in fasting and breaking the fast, in earning and in belief. For this reason it was reported, when the eating of the pre-dawn meal (suhur) was recommended, "Oppose the Jews." Likewise He commanded them to oppose them regarding menstruating women, when the Companions resolved to separate entirely from menstruating women, since ﴿so keep away from women during menstruation﴾ [al-Baqara: 222] was revealed, in imitation of the Jews' seclusion of them, not eating with them nor sleeping with them in one house. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do everything except intercourse." The Jews said: "This man does not want to leave anything of our affairs without opposing us in it."

What is understood from the Exalted's words ﴿Do not devour﴾ is the ordinary meaning of eating, because it is the literal sense. He mentioned it to the exclusion of the other forms of transgression and seizure because it is the most important of needs, and through it most wealth is destroyed. It is also possible that eating here is a metaphor, used to express taking and seizing. This address and prohibition are directed to the believers, and the attribution of the wealth to those addressed means: "Let not some of you devour the wealth of others," as in His saying: ﴿and do not kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 29], meaning: let not some of you kill others. The pronoun of address is valid for each one among them, so that each may be both forbidden and one forbidden from, both a consumer and one consumed from. Thus the address combines these possibilities. Just as it is forbidden to be consumed, it is forbidden to consume the property of others. Therefore the attribution in that case is not truly to the owners but is an attribution by association (idafa bi'l-mulabasa). Some scholars permitted the attribution to the owners and interpreted "falsehood" as amusements, singing girls, drinking and idleness. The phrase "among yourselves" means in your dealings and your trusts, in accordance with His saying: "you desire it among yourselves." ﴿by false means﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: by injustice. Others said: by any way that is not legitimate, so that seizure, plunder, gambling, a soothsayer's fee, embezzlement, bribery, what the astrologers take, and everything the Law has not permitted taking, all enter into this. Ibn 'Abbas said: this refers to a man who owes property with no proof against him, so he denies the debt and disputes with his creditor while knowing that he is sinful. 'Ikrima said: it is the man who buys a commodity, then returns it and returns with it some dirhams. Ibn 'Abbas also said: it is the taking of property by false testimony. Ibn 'Atiyya said: deception in a sale does not enter into this when the seller knows the true state of what he sells, because the deception is, as it were, a gift. End of his words. This is correct.

The word governing the adverb (al-zarf) is "devour." The "among" (bayniyya) is used figuratively, since its original meaning is a place-adverb; then it was extended and used for persons, and then for meanings. In the phrase "among yourselves" there is a reference to what they practise of that, because what some of them conceal from one another of wrongdoing is more abominable than what they do not conceal from one another. This supports the first view, that the attribution is not to the owners, for had it been so, there would have been no need for this adverb indicating interpenetration and awareness of what is practised of such things. It has been said that "among yourselves" is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "your wealth," so that it is connected to an omitted element, meaning: existing among yourselves. This is weak. The preposition in "by false means" marks cause, and it is connected to "devour." Some permitted that "by false means" be a circumstantial qualifier of the wealth, or of the agent.

﴿and bring them forward to the rulers﴾ is jussive by conjunction to the prohibition (ma'tuf 'ala al-nahy), meaning: and do not bring them forward to the rulers. Likewise it is in the codex of Ubayy, with the prohibitive "la" made explicit: "and do not bring forward." The apparent view is that the pronoun in "by them" refers to the wealth, so they were forbidden from two things: the first, taking the property by falsehood; the second, presenting it to the judges for taking it by falsehood. Al-Akhfash and others permitted that it be in the accusative as an answer to the prohibition with an implied "an" (anna mudmara), and al-Zamakhshari allowed this. Ibn 'Atiyya related that it was said: "tudlu" is in the accusative position as an adverb of time (zarf). He said: this is a Kufan view, that the meaning of time-adverb is what governs the accusative. According to Sibawayh, what governs in such a case is an implied "an." End of his words. No decisive evidence from Arabic usage has been established that an adverb governs the accusative, so we do not say so. As for the parsing of al-Akhfash here, that this is accusative as an answer to the prohibition, and al-Zamakhshari's allowance of it here, that is the case of "do not eat the fish and drink the milk" in the accusative. The grammarians said: if you put it in the accusative, the sentence is a prohibition against combining the two. This meaning is not valid in the verse, for two reasons.

The first: a prohibition against combining two things does not entail a prohibition against each of them separately. A prohibition against each of them does entail a prohibition against combining them, because combining them means each of them occurs with the other necessarily. Do you not see that devouring wealth by falsehood is forbidden whether it stands alone or is combined with other prohibited things?

The second, which is stronger: His saying "so that you may" (li-ta'kulu) is a cause for what precedes it. If the prohibition were against combining, the cause would not be suitable for it, because it is composed of two things, and the cause cannot be suitable for something that is contingent upon the existence of both of them together; rather it is contingent upon the existence of only one of them, namely: bringing forward the wealth to the rulers. As for "tudlu" here, it has been said that its meaning is hastening the dispute over property before the rulers, when you know that proof will stand for you, either because there is no evidence against the denier, or because the property is a trust, such as the property of an orphan and the like, where the word of the one against whom the claim is made is accepted. The preposition on this view marks cause. It has also been said that its meaning is: do not bribe the rulers with the wealth so that they will rule for you in a greater amount. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this view is preferred, because the judge is a likely object of bribery except for one who is protected, and such are few. Also, the two words are cognate: "tudlu" from sending down the bucket (dalw), and bribery (rishwa) from the rope (rishaa), as if it is drawn with it so that the need is fulfilled. End of his words. This is good.

It has also been said: the meaning is: do not incline with them toward the rulers, from the expression "so-and-so brought forward his argument" (adla fulan bi-hujjatihi), meaning he stood up with it. This returns to the meaning of the first view. The pronoun in "by them" refers to the wealth, as we have established. He who went far off and said that it refers to false testimony, meaning: do not bring forward false testimony to the rulers, implies by this view that those forbidden from bringing forward are the witnesses, and the portion of wealth is what they took for false testimony. It is also possible that those forbidden are the ones in whose favour testimony was given, and the portion of wealth is what they take from people's property because of the testimony of those witnesses.

﴿so that you may consume a portion﴾, that is, a piece and a group ﴿of the wealth of people﴾. It has been said: it is the wealth of orphans. It has been said: it is deposits. The better view is generality, and that this is an expression for taking any property that is reached in a judgment without right. The phrase ﴿of the wealth of people﴾ is in the position of a qualifier, meaning: a portion existing from the wealth of people.

﴿through sin﴾ is connected to the saying ﴿so that you may consume﴾. It was interpreted as judging by false testimony, and it has been said: by bribery, and it has been said: by a false oath, and it has been said: by a settlement, with knowledge that the one in whose favour the judgment is given is a wrongdoer. The best view is generality: whatever property is taken by means that lead to sin is sin. The original meaning of sin (ithm) is falling short in a matter. The poet said:

A she-camel that surges with her saddle-cushions when the negligent ones deny the midday heat.

That is, the negligent ones (al-muqassirat). Then the falling short in the command of Allah the Exalted and the offence was called sin. The preposition in "through sin" marks cause, and it may be for circumstance, meaning: involved in sin, which is the offence. ﴿while you know﴾ is a circumstantial clause, meaning: you are wrongdoers and sinners, and aware of what is prepared for you as requital for that. This is an exaggeration of the boldness in disobedience with knowledge of it, especially regarding the rights of servants. A hadith says: "Whoever I give a judgment in his favour concerning a portion of his brother's right, let him not take anything from it, for what I give him is a piece of fire." The apparent meaning of the hadith and the verse is the prohibition of taking what is taken from people's property by sin, and that the judgment of a judge does not make lawful for the litigant what he knows to be unlawful for him. This is agreed upon regarding property. As for contracts and their annulments, scholars differed about the judge's ruling in outward appearance, while the inward reality is contrary to it, by a contract or the dissolving of a contract through false testimony, the beneficiary knowing this. Abu Hanifa said: it is binding, and it is like a new creation, even if they were false witnesses. The majority said: it takes effect outwardly and does not take effect inwardly.

In His saying ﴿while you know﴾ there is an indication that whoever does not know that he is sinful, and the judge rules in his favour to take property, is permitted to take it. For example, if someone finds a debt owed to his father and establishes proof of that debt, and the judge rules for him with it, he is permitted to take it, even if he does not know its validity, since it is possible that his father gave it to him as a gift, or that the debtor paid it, or that the acknowledgment was made under coercion. But he does not know it, nor does he know that he is in the wrong in what he takes. The original state is the non-discharge of the one who acknowledged, and the absence of coercion upon him, so it is permitted for him to take it.

These verses include the address to the believers, to draw them near and stir them to what is being enjoined on them: the obligation of fasting. Allah prescribed it for us just as He prescribed it for those before us, so that we would share this demanding obligation with them. It is therefore not specific to us. He prescribed it in the hope that we would attain taqwa (God-consciousness) of Him, the Exalted. Then He lightened this obligation by making it a number of specified days, or days that can be counted because they are few. He then granted the sick person and the traveller a concession, permitting them to break their fast during their illness or journey, and obligated them to make up the number of days missed once they recover and are settled. He then mentioned that whoever is able to fast but wishes to break it and does so must redeem it by feeding the needy. He then stated that voluntarily doing good is better, and that fasting is better than breaking the fast and paying the ransom. Afterwards He abrogated (naskh, the replacement of one ruling by a later one) this ruling concerning the few days, by making the fasting of Ramadan obligatory. This is how the custom has run in the legal obligations of the Shariah: they begin with the lightest, then the lighter, and proceed to the final limit that is the sought-after goal of the Shariah, at which point the ruling becomes settled.

He drew attention to the excellence of this obligatory month by stating that it is the month in which revelation was sent down to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He commanded whoever witnessed it to fast it, and He excused the sick person and the traveller, mentioning that they must observe a number of days equal to what they broke, once they recover and are settled, in the same condition as when He imposed on them the fasting of those days. Then the Exalted drew attention to the fact that the concession for the sick and the traveller is due to His will for the mukallafun (those under obligation) regarding ease. He then stated that the legislation of fasting the month, the permission to break the fast for the sick and the traveller, and His will for ease for us, are for completing the prescribed number, for magnifying Allah, and in hope of gratitude. Thus He matched each legislated matter with what suits it. Then, when the Exalted mentioned the servants' magnification of their Lord and their praise of Him, He mentioned His nearness to them in station. So when they ask Him, He answers them, and His answer is not delayed beyond the time of their supplication (p. 58). He then asked them to respond to Him when He calls them, just as He responds to them when they call upon Him. Then He commanded them to persevere in faith, because it is the foundation of the acts of worship and their validity depends on it. He then mentioned the hope of their attaining right guidance if they respond to Him and believe in Him. Then the Exalted bestowed His favour upon them by making lawful what they had been forbidden, namely intercourse during all the nights of the fasting days. He then drew attention to the reason for this: that wives are like a garment for you, and you cannot do without them. Then, when some of them fell into some violation, Allah turned to them in forgiveness and pardoned them. Then the Exalted did not suffice with reporting the permission, but permitted it in the form of a command, saying: ﴿So now, have relations with them﴾. Likewise with eating and drinking, and He set the limit of these three by the clarity of the dawn. Then He commanded them with a command of obligation to complete the fast until night.

Since the permission of intercourse during all the nights of fasting had been established, and since one of the states of the fasting person is i'tikaf (seclusion in the mosque), and intercourse with women during i'tikaf is forbidden, He drew attention to this with His words: ﴿And do not have relations with them while you are in seclusion in the mosques﴾. Then He pointed to the limits, which are the boundaries, and attributed them to Himself so that it would be known that the One who set them is Allah, the Exalted. So He forbade them to approach them, let alone to transgress them, in emphasis of keeping far from them. Then He informed that He makes the signs clear and explains them, and these signs are all the evidences and indicators pointing to the Shariah of Allah, the Exalted, like this clear explanation of the preceding rulings, so that they may be hopeful of attaining the taqwa of Allah, which leads its possessor to obedience to Allah, the Exalted. Then He forbade them that some of them consume the wealth of others unjustly, which is the way by which Allah has not permitted acquisition. He also forbade you from offering bribes to corrupt rulers so that they would thereby take some of the wealth that they do not deserve. He qualified the prohibition and the taking with the condition of knowledge of what they commit, as a way of denouncing them and rebuking them, because whoever commits a sin while knowing it and knowing the evil recompense that follows from it is worse in his case, and more reprehensible, than one who commits sin while ignorant of it, and of what follows from it.

Since this noble verse opens with the categorical command to fast, and since fasting is one of the great acts of worship in which one is commanded to avoid the prohibited things, to the point that it came in the hadith: "If someone insults him, let him say, 'I am fasting.'" And it came from Allah, the Exalted: "Fasting is for Me, and I reward for it." And among the greatest of its prohibitions and the most serious of them is eating during it, He concluded these verses with the prohibition of consuming wealth unjustly, so that what the fasting person breaks his fast with would be from what is lawful and free of doubt, and it is hoped that his deed will be accepted, and that he will not be among those who fast and have nothing from their fasting but hunger and thirst. Thus these verses began with an obligation commanded, and concluded with a prohibited matter forbidden, and between the beginning and the end there also intervened a command and a prohibition. All of this is a set of obligations from Allah, the Exalted, to comply with what He has commanded and to avoid what He has forbidden. May Allah help us to them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 189–190 (part 1 of 3):

﴿They ask you about the new moons. Say: They are timings for the people and for the Hajj. Righteousness is not in entering the houses from their backs, but righteousness is in one who fears God. Enter the houses through their doors, and fear God so that you may prosper.﴾ ﴿Fight in the way of God against those who fight you, but do not transgress. God does not love the transgressors.﴾ ﴿Kill them wherever you find them, and expel them from where they expelled you. Persecution is worse than killing. Do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque unless they fight you there. If they fight you, then kill them. Such is the recompense of the disbelievers.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 191] ﴿But if they desist, then God is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 192] ﴿Fight them until there is no persecution and religion is for God. But if they desist, then there is no aggression except against the wrongdoers.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 193] ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month, and sacred things are subject to retribution. Whoever transgresses against you, then transgress against him in the same way as he transgressed against you. Fear God, and know that God is with the God-fearing.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 194] ﴿Spend in the way of God, and do not throw yourselves into destruction with your own hands. Do good, for God loves the good-doers.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 195] ﴿Complete the Hajj and the ʿUmrah for God. But if you are prevented, then [offer] what is easy of the sacrificial animal. Do not shave your heads until the offering reaches its place of sacrifice. Whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of the head, then a ransom of fasting, or charity, or a sacrifice. When you are secure, whoever performs ʿUmrah followed by Hajj [shall offer] what is easy of the sacrificial animal. Whoever does not find [one] shall fast three days during the Hajj and seven when you return, making ten complete. That is for one whose family is not present at the Sacred Mosque. Fear God, and know that God is severe in retribution.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 196] .

﴿al-ahilla﴾ is the plural of hilal (crescent). It is the regular plural pattern of fiʿal for geminate roots, as in ʿinan and aʿinna. The pattern fuʿul is anomalous for it, as in ʿunun for ʿinan and ḥujuj for ḥijaj.

Regarding al-hilal, the author of the book Shajar al-Durr mentioned in lexicography that it is a homonym (mushtarak) applied to: the crescent of the sky; an iron tool shaped like a crescent in the hand of a hunter with which he hamstrings the wild donkey; the tip of a sandal; a piece of dust; the amount of meat that can be taken with the nail of a finger; a piece of a millstone; the skin shed by a snake; an agreement with a hired worker on a monthly basis; competing in the fineness of weaving; competing in saying the tahlil (la ilaha illa Allah); the plural of halla, which is a woman who has a gap between her teeth; a serpent; and the remaining water in a pool. End of what he mentioned, summarized. That which is in the sky is called hilal for two nights, and it was said for three. Abu al-Haytham said: it is called hilal for the first two nights of the month and the last two nights, and what lies between them is called qamar (moon). Al-Asmaʿi said: it is called hilal until it becomes ḥajar, and its ḥajar is when it becomes circled like a thin thread. It was also said: it is called that until its light overcomes the blackness of the night, and that only occurs at seven. They said: it was called hilal because of the raising of voices at the sighting of it, from the expression istahalla al-sabiyy (the child cried out at birth), and al-ihlal bi'l-hajj, which is raising the voice with the talbiyah. Or it was called that because of raising the voice with tahlil at its sighting. The word hilal may be applied to the month, just as the word shahr (month) is applied to the crescent. It is said: ahalla al-hilal and istahalla, and ahlalnahu and istahlalnahu. This is the statement of the majority of lexicographers. Shamir said: it is said istahalla al-hilal also, meaning in the active form, where the subject is the crescent itself, and shahr mustahill (a month beginning). He recited:
"A month beginning after a month, and a year after it, a new year."
It is also said istahalla in the sense of becoming clear (tabayyana), but ahalla is not said in this sense. It is said ahlalna ʿan layilat kadha (we saw the crescent on such-and-such night). Abu Nasr ʿAbd al-Rahim al-Qushayri said in his tafsir: it is said ahalla al-hilal and istahalla, and ahlalna al-hilal and istahlalnahu. End.

The discussion of the root h-l-l was previously mentioned for us, but we repeat it here with regard to the specific usage of the word hilal for the things we have mentioned here.

(mawaqit) is the plural of miqat, meaning time, just as miʿad means promise. Some said: miqat is the end point of a time. God the Exalted said: ﴿So the appointed term of his Lord was completed as forty nights﴾ [Al-Aʿraf: 142].

Thaqifa al-shay': when he found it and came upon it by way of seizing and overpowering. From this comes rajul thiqf (a man quick to seize his opponents). From this: ﴿So if you overtake them in war﴾ [Al-Anfal: 57], and the verse of the poet:
"If you capture me, then kill me; and whoever I capture, there is no eternity for him."
Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: ﴿thaqiftumuhum﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 191] means you firmly established your domination over them. It is said: rajul thiqf laqif when he is firm in handling the matters he takes up. End. It is also said: thaqifa al-shay' thaqafatan when he mastered it. From this: I took skill with the sword (al-thaqafah bi'l-sayf). Al-thiqaf is also an iron tool used by archers and spearmen to straighten what is bent. Thaqifa al-shay' also means he adhered to it. Huwa thiqf means he is quick in knowledge. Thaqqaftuhu means I straightened it, and from this comes al-rimah al-muthaqqafah, meaning straightened spears. The poet said:
"I remembered you while the Khatti (spear) swayed between us, and the straightened dark spears had drunk from us."
He means straightened spears.

﴿al-tahlukah﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 195] is on the pattern taf'ulah, a verbal noun from halaka. The form taf'ulah is a rare verbal noun. Sibawayh recorded from it: al-tadurrah and al-tasurrah. Similar to it among concrete nouns: al-tanṣubah and al-tanfulah. It is said: halaka halakan, halakan, tahlukatan, and halka'a on the pattern fa'la'. The form mafil from halaka comes with dammah, fathah and kasrah, and likewise with the tā' (mahlakah). It has three vowels on the ʿayn. The dammah in mahlik is rare. Halak, for a living being, means death; and for other than it, it means perishing and exhaustion. That tahlukah is a verbal noun was reported by Abu ʿAli from Abu ʿUbaydah, and said by others among the grammarians. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible to say its original form is al-tahlikah, like al-tajribah and al-tabsirah and such, on the basis that it is a verbal noun from halla (with doubled lam), so the kasrah was changed into a dammah, just as al-juwar appears as al-jiwar. End of his statement. What he went to is not good, because it involves analogy with an anomalous form, and a claimed substitution for which there is no evidence. As for analogy with the anomalous, it is based on the claim that the original of taf'ulah with dammah is taf'ilah with kasrah, and making tahlukah a verbal noun of hallaka with doubled lam, while fa''ala with sound non-hamzated lam has its verbal noun on the pattern tafʿil, as in kassara takhsiran, and does not come on the pattern tafʿulah except anomalously. Therefore it is better to make tahlukah a verbal noun, since that is attested in examples like al-tadurrah. As for tahlikah, the best view is also that it is a verbal noun of halaka with light lam, because it has the same meaning as tahlukah with dammah on the lam. The verbal nouns of fa'ala also come on tafʿilah. They said: jalla al-rajul tajillah, meaning jalal (magnificence). Therefore tahlikah in that case is not a verbal noun of hallaka with doubled lam. As for substituting dammah for kasrah without a reason, it is extremely anomalous. As for his giving the example of al-juwar and al-jiwar, no substitution is claimed there; rather the verbal noun is formed on fuʿal with dammah on the fa' as an anomaly.

Tha'lab claimed that tahlukah is a verbal noun with no parallel, since there is nothing else in verbal nouns like it. His claim is not correct, since we have reported from Sibawayh that he recorded al-tadurrah and al-tasurrah as verbal nouns. It was said: al-tahlukah is whatever it is possible to guard against, and al-halak is what it is not possible to guard against. It was said: al-tahlukah is the thing that causes destruction, and halak is the occurrence of loss. It was said: al-tahlukah is anything whose ultimate end is destruction.

* *

• ﴿uhsirtum﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 196]: Yunus ibn Habib said: uhsira al-rajul means he was turned back from a path he wanted. It was said: hasara and uhsira have one meaning. This was said by al-Shaybani, al-Zajjaj, and Ibn ʿAtiyyah reported it from al-Farra'. Ibn Mayyadah said:
"The separation from Layla is not that she has moved far from you, nor that the preoccupations have confined you."
It was said: uhsira due to illness, and hasarahu the enemy (he was besieged by the enemy). This was said by Yaʿqub. Al-Zajjaj also said: the transmission from the scholars concerning knowledge that is prevented by fear and illness is uhsira; and the one imprisoned is husira. Abu ʿUbaydah and al-Farra' also said: uhsira, so he is muhsar. If he is confined in a prison or house, it is said husira, so he is mahsur. Thaʿlab said: the root of hasr and ihsar is confinement, and husira in confinement is stronger than uhsira. Ibn Faris said in al-Mujmal: husira by illness, and uhsira by the enemy. It is said: hasira sadruhu, meaning it was constricted. A rajul hasir is one who does not reveal his secret. Jarir said:
"The informers surrounded me, but they found one who guards your secret, O Tamim, reticent."
Al-hasr is the retention of excrement. Al-hasir means king, because he is like one confined by the curtain. Labid said:
"Until at the gate of the hasir (king) they stand."
Al-hasir is well known: it is a mat of reeds from Baradah, named so because some of it is joined to other parts, like the confinement of a thing together with something else.

(al-hadyi): hady is what is brought as an offering to the House of God the Exalted, seeking nearness to Him, like a gift that a person gives to another. It is said: ahdaytu ila al-bayt al-haram hadiyyan and hadyan, with doubled or single consonant. The doubled form is the plural of hadiyyah, like matiyyah and matiyy. The single form is the plural of hidyah, like jidhyat al-sirj and jidhy. Al-Farra' said: hady has no singular. It was said: the doubled form is the dialect of Tamim, and from it is the verse of Zuhayr:
"I have not seen a people who gave hadiyy, nor seen a neighbor of the house who was reproached."
It was also said: al-hadiyy, with doubled consonant, is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul. It was said: al-hady, with single consonant, is originally a verbal noun, and it means the same as al-hady, like al-rahn and similar, so it applies to singular and plural. In language, whatever is given as a gift, whether dirhams, goods, livestock, or other things, is called hady; but the technical religious meaning (al-haqiqah al-shar'iyyah) restricted hady to livestock. The disagreement has occurred over what is called hady among livestock, as will be mentioned God willing.

al-halq: a verbal noun of halaqa yahliqu, when hair is removed by a razor or other sharp tool or depilatory cream. Al-halq also means the passage of food after the mouth. al-adha: a verbal noun, meaning pain. You say: adhani Zayd idhaʾan, meaning Zayd harmed me.

al-sadaqah: what is given of wealth without compensation, seeking nearness to God the Exalted. al-nusuk: Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: al-nusuk are ingots of silver, each ingot being a nasikah. Then the one who worships is called nasik, because he purified his soul from the filth of sins and cleansed it, like the purified ingot free from impurity. Then the sacrificial animal was called nusuk, because it is among the noblest acts of worship by which one seeks nearness to God the Exalted. It was also said: nusuk is a verbal noun of nasaka yanska, nusukan and nusuk, just as you say halima al-rajul, hulman and hulum. al-amn: the removal of what is feared. It is said: amina yaʾmanu, amnan and amanah.

al-thalathah: a known number. From it one says: thallathtu al-qawm uthallithuhum, meaning I made them three with myself. Al-thalathun is a known number. Al-thulth, with dammah or sukun on the lam, is one of the parts of what is divided into three. Thulth is not declined (mamnuʿ min al-sarf), and the discussion of this will come, God willing. al-ʿiqab: a verbal noun of ʿaqaba, meaning to recompense the wrongdoer for his wrongdoing. It is derived from al-ʿaqibah (outcome), as if it means the outcome of the wrongdoer's act.

* *

﴿They ask you about the new moons. Say: They are timings for the people and for the Hajj.﴾ It was revealed in response to a question from some Muslims to the Prophet (ﷺ) about the crescent: what is the benefit of its waning and waxing, and its difference from the state of the sun? This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah, al-Rabiʿ, and others. It was reported that the ones who asked were Muʿadh ibn Jabal and Thaʿlabah ibn Ghanm al-Ansari, who said: O Messenger of God! What is the matter with the crescent, that it appears thin like a thread, then increases until it becomes full, then continues to decrease until it returns as it began, not being in one state? So it was revealed.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 189–190 (part 2 of 3):

The connection between this verse and what precedes it is clear. The verses before it were revealed about fasting, and the fast of Ramadan is tied to sighting the crescent (hilal), as is the ending of the fast in the month of Shawwal. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Fast when you see it, and break the fast when you see it." Earlier discussion also covered part of the rites of Hajj, namely the circumambulation (tawaf), and Hajj is one of the pillars on which Islam is built. The discussion had already covered the Oneness of Allah, prayer, zakat and fasting, so it came to the fifth pillar, which is Hajj, to complete the pillars on which Islam is built.

It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "No nation has asked fewer questions than the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ). They asked about fourteen matters, and they were answered. Among them, in Surat al-Baqarah, the first is: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near﴾ [al-Baqarah: 186], the second is this verse, and six after it. And in other surahs: ﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 4], ﴿They ask you about the spoils of war﴾ [al-Anfal: 1], ﴿And they ask you about the Spirit﴾ [al-Isra': 85], ﴿And they ask you about Dhul-Qarnayn﴾ [al-Kahf: 83], ﴿And they ask you about the mountains﴾ [Ta-Ha: 105], ﴿They ask you about the Hour﴾ [al-A'raf: 187]." It is said: two of these questions, at the beginning, concern the explanation of the origin (al-mabda'), and two at the end concern the explanation of the return (al-ma'ad). A parallel to this is that two surahs open with "O mankind" (ya ayyuha al-nas): the first, which is the fourth surah in the first half, includes an explanation of the origin, and the second, which is also the fourth surah in the latter half, includes an explanation of the return.

The pronoun in "yas'alunaka" is plural, indicating that the questioners were a group, even though, as is reported, the questioners were two persons. It is possible that this is the attribution of an action to a group when it was in fact done by one or two of them, and this is common in their speech. It is said: or because two is treated as a plural by way of extension and metaphor. The kaf in "ka" ("you") is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), and "yas'alunaka" is a statement. If the verse was revealed before the question, this would be information about the unseen; but if it was revealed after the question, which is what is transmitted in the reports on the occasions of revelation (asbab al-nuzul), then it is a narration of a past situation. "'An" (about) is connected to "yas'alunaka". It is said: "sa'ala bihi" and "sa'ala 'anhu" with the same meaning. The question is not about the essence of the crescents, but about the wisdom in the variation of their states and the benefit of this. For this reason he answered with: ﴿Say: they are times for people﴾. If they were in one unchanging state, no timing would be achieved by them.

Hilal is both singular and plural depending on its times. They said: insofar as it is a crescent in one month, it is different from its being a crescent in another. Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) read "﴿'ani al-ahilla﴾" with a kasra on the nun and a sukun on the lam of al-ahilla, followed by a hamzah. Warsh, according to his method, transposed the vowel of the hamzah and dropped the hamzah. A reader of irregular (shadhdh) reading assimilated the nun of "'an" into the lam of al-ahilla after the transposition and the deletion. (Say: they are) i.e. the crescents (al-ahilla) ﴿are times for people﴾. This is the wisdom in the waxing and waning of the moon, since they are timings for terms (al-ajal), transactions (al-mu'amalat), oaths, prescribed waiting periods (al-'iddah), fasting, breaking the fast, the periods of pregnancy and nursing, vows tied to times, and the merits of fasting on days that are known only by the crescents. The Exalted has mentioned this meaning in His saying: ﴿And He determined it as stations so that you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾ [Yunus: 5], and in His saying: ﴿So We effaced the sign of the night and made the sign of the day illuminating, that you may seek bounty from your Lord and that you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾ [al-Isra': 12]. Al-Raghib said: al-waqt (time) is the period of time appointed for an action. The meaning of "mawaqit li al-nas" is what concerns them of their affairs of transactions and interests, end of quote. Al-Rummani said: al-waqt is a measure of time that is determined in itself, and al-tawqit is the setting of its limit. Whenever you set an end for it, it is muwaqqat (timed). Al-miqat is the endpoint of a time, and the Hereafter is the endpoint of creation. Al-ihlal is the timing of the month, and the places of ihram are the miqat of Hajj because they are measures at which one arrives. Al-miqat is a measure set as a sign for what is to be done, end of his words.

In the variation of the crescent through waning and waxing there is a refutation of the philosophers in their claim that celestial bodies cannot undergo change in their states. The Exalted therefore manifested difference in the moon but did not manifest it in the sun, so that it would be known that this is by His power, the Exalted. "Al-Hajj" is conjoined to His saying "li al-nas". They said: the estimate is "wa mawaqit li al-hajj", so the second was dropped, being sufficed by the first. The meaning is: that by them you may know the months of Hajj and its timings. Since Hajj is among the greatest things whose timing and months are sought by the crescents, it was singled out for mention, as if it were a particularisation after a generalisation. For the saying "mawaqit li al-nas" does not mean timings for the persons of people, but rather timings for the purposes of people, which require a timing for religion and for worldly affairs. So His saying "wa al-Hajj" after that is a particularisation after a generalisation. In reality, it is not conjoined to "al-nas", but to the omitted genitive construct (mudaf mahdhuf) which "al-nas" stands in place of in grammatical case. Since enumerating those purposes would lead to lengthy elaboration, he restricted himself to His saying: ﴿timings for people﴾.

Al-Qaffal said: the singling out of Hajj for mention is to show that Hajj is restricted to the months which Allah the Exalted designated for the obligation of Hajj, and that it is not permitted to shift Hajj from those months to other months. The Arabs used to do this through the nasi' (intercalation), end of his words.

Al-Jumhur read "wa al-Hajji" with a fatha on the ha'. Al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "wa al-Hijji" with a kasra on it in all of the Qur'an, in the phrase "hijj al-bayt". It is said: with a fatha it is the verbal noun (masdar), and with a kasra it is the noun (ism). Sibawayh said: al-Hajj, like al-radd and al-sadd, and al-Hijj, like al-dhikr, are both verbal nouns. The apparent meaning of His saying "﴿mawaqit li al-nas wa al-hajj﴾" is what Abu Hanifah and Malik held: that it is permitted to enter ihram for Hajj at any time of the year, because of the generality of "al-ahilla", contrary to those who said that it is valid only in the months of Hajj. It is said: in it is evidence that a woman who is subject to two waiting periods (iddah) from one man is satisfied by completing one waiting period for both, and does not begin a new menstrual period or months for each of them, because of the generality of His saying: "mawaqit li al-nas". It is also evidence that when the waiting period begins with the crescent and is counted in months, its completion must be by crescents and not by number of days. It is also evidence that the one who makes an oath of abstention (ila') against his wife from the beginning of the month until the four months pass is considered in following up divorce by crescents and not by the reckoning of thirty days, and the Prophet (ﷺ) did likewise when he "made an oath of abstention from his wives for a month." Likewise with hire contracts, oaths and debts: whenever their beginning is with the crescent, all of them are like this, and consideration of number is dropped. The Prophet (ﷺ) judged in this way regarding fasting. It is also a refutation of the people of the apparent meaning (ahl al-zahir). And whoever holds their view that musaqat contracts (irrigation partnerships) are permitted for an unknown term of uncertain years is refuted. It is also evidence for the one who permitted sale until the harvest, or the threshing, or for al-Ghitas (a Christian feast) or similar, and this is the view of Malik, Abu Thawr and Ahmad. Likewise until the return of the warriors. It is reported from Ibn Abbas that he prohibited it, and al-Shafi'i held this view. It is also evidence that the attribute of the crescent being large or small is not taken into account, because it is said: "what is distinguished" (ma fussila), so whether it is seen large or small, it belongs to the night in which it is seen.

* *

﴿It is not righteousness that you enter houses from their backs, but righteousness is [in] one who fears Allah﴾. Al-Bara' ibn Azib, al-Zuhri and Qatadah said: the occasion of its revelation was that the Ansar, when they performed Hajj and 'umrah, would bind themselves by a legal rule that nothing should come between them and the sky, so they would climb onto the roofs of their houses over the walls. It is also said: in the pre-Islamic period and at the start of Islam, whenever one of them entered ihram for Hajj or 'umrah, he would not come to a wall or a house, nor to a dwelling through its door. If he was from the people of Madinah, he would make an opening in the back of his house through which he would enter and exit, or he would set up a ladder by which he would climb. If he was from the people of the wool tents (al-Wabar), he would go out from behind the tent or the pavilion, and would not enter or exit through the door until his ihram ended. They considered this righteousness, except for those who belonged to al-Hums (the Hums), who were: Quraysh, Kinanah, Khuza'ah, Thaqif, Khath'am, the Banu 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah, and the Banu Nasr ibn Mu'awiyah. The Prophet (ﷺ) entered, and with him was a man from them. That man stopped and said: "I am from al-Hums." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "And I am from al-Hums." Then it was revealed. Al-Suddi narrated this in brief.

Al-Rabi' narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) "entered, and behind him was a man from the Ansar. He entered as well, breaking the custom of his people. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'Why did you enter while you are in ihram?' He said: 'You entered, so I entered following your entry.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'I am from al-Hums; I am from a people who do not hold this religion.' The man said: 'And my religion is your religion.'" Then it was revealed. Ibrahim said: some people of the Hijaz used to do what has been mentioned. It is also said: whoever went out for a need would not return through his door, for fear of the omen of failure, and he would remain like that for a full year. The summary of these occasions is that Allah the Exalted revealed this verse: rejecting those who considered entering houses from their backs to be righteousness, and commanding entering houses through their doors. These occasions are in agreement that the houses are meant literally, and that "coming" means arriving at them. Taking the words in their literal sense is preferable to claiming metaphor while contradicting what these occasions agree upon.

The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when He mentioned that the crescents are timings for Hajj, He digressed (istitrad) to mention something they used to do in Hajj while claiming it was righteousness, so He made clear to them that this is not righteousness, and that the custom was established before Hajj that they would do it during Hajj. And when He mentioned their question about the crescents concerning the waxing and waning, and what the wisdom of this is, and it being known that He is Wise, and His acts follow wisdom, He answered them that what they do of entering houses from their backs when they are in ihram is not in any way wisdom, nor righteousness. Or, when the two accounts happened at the same time, the verse was revealed concerning both together, and one was joined to the other.

As for taking "coming" and "houses" in a metaphorical sense, there are several opinions. The first: that this is a parable (darb mathal): the meaning is that righteousness is not that you ask the ignorant, but rather fear Allah and ask the scholars. This is like saying: "I came to the matter from its door," as stated by Abu 'Ubaydah. The second: that He mentioned entering houses through their doors as a parable for violating what is obligatory in Hajj, and that refers to what they did in the nasi', for they used to shift Hajj from the time that Allah the Exalted had appointed for it, making lawful what was forbidden and forbidden what was lawful. So it was used as a parable for violation. It is also said: "and fear Allah" is under the entering of every obligation, in avoiding every prohibition. This was stated by Abu Muslim. The third: that entering houses from their backs is a kinayah (metonymy) for deviating from the correct path, and entering them through their doors is a kinayah for adhering to the correct path. That is because the straight path is to infer the unknown from the known. It has been established that the Creator is Wise and does only what is right, and we know that the variation in the moon's light is from His action, so it is known that there is benefit and wisdom in it. This is inference from the known to the unknown. But to infer from our not knowing the wisdom in it that its Doer is not wise is inference from the unknown to the known. So the meaning is: since you did not know His wisdom in the variation of the moon, you became doubters about the wisdom of the Creator, and thus you have done what you think to be righteousness. Righteousness is only that you come to houses through their doors, and so you infer from the known, which is the wisdom of the Creator, to the unknown, and you conclude that in it there is profound wisdom, even if you do not know it. This was stated in (Ri le al-Zaman) [Ri al-Zaman], and it is an opinion compiled from the words of al-Zamakhshari.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is possible that this is an illustration of their inverting their questions, and that their situation in this is like that of one who leaves the door of a house and enters it from the back. The meaning is: righteousness, and what they ought to be upon, is not that you invert your questions; rather, righteousness is the righteousness of one who is mindful of God (taqwa) of that and avoids it, and does not dare to do the like of it. Then he said: ﴿And come to houses by their doors﴾, that is: and undertake matters from the aspects in which they must be undertaken, and do not invert them. The intended meaning is the obligation of settling the souls and binding the hearts to the conviction that all of God's acts are wisdom and rightness, without the stirring of doubt or the objection of suspicion regarding that, so that He is not questioned about it (p-64), because of the accusation of committing doubt contained in questioning: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾ [al-Anbiya: 23]. End of his words. Ibn Atiyyah related this view in brief, and said: Other than Abu Ubaydah said: Righteousness is not that you deviate in questions about the crescent moons and other things, so that you approach matters in a way other than what the sacred laws love.

He metaphorically used "houses" for women: coming to them is like coming to houses. Its meaning: do not approach women from the place not permitted, from their backs, and approach them from the place that is permitted, from their front. This was said by Ibn Zayd, and Makki and al-Mahdawi related it from Ibn al-Anbari. Ibn Atiyyah said: That it refers to intercourse with women is remote and changes the style of the speech.

The ba' in "bi-an ta'tu" is extra in the predicate of laysa, and "bi-an ta'tu" is the predicate of laysa; it is to be construed as a verbal noun. This is a case of informing about the meaning by means of the meaning, and of the more definite about what is less definite, because "an" and its clause are, in their view, equivalent to a pronoun. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Amir, al-Kisai, Qalun, Abbas (on the authority of Abu Amr), al-Ijli (on the authority of Hamzah), and al-Shammuni (on the authority of al-A'sha, on the authority of Abu Bakr) read "al-biyut" with a kasra wherever it occurs, for the sake of harmony with the ya'; the original form is with a damma, because it is on the pattern fu'ul. The rest of the seven read it with a damma. "Min" is connected to "ta'tu" and indicates the starting point. The pronoun in "abwabiha" refers to "al-buyut." It returns in the manner of a singular feminine pronoun, because "al-buyut" is a plural of paucity... [Note: the original reads "جَمْعُ كَثْرَةٍ", i.e., a plural of abundance.] Because "al-buyut" is a plural of abundance, and the plural of a feminine non-rational noun is distinguished in terms of its few and many, the more eloquent form for its few is that the pronoun be plural, and the more eloquent form for its many is that it be singular, as is the case with the singular feminine pronoun; the reverse is also permissible. As for the plural of a feminine rational noun, the Arabs did not distinguish between its few and many, and the more eloquent is that the pronoun be plural. Therefore it came in the Qur'an: ﴿They are a garment for you and you are a garment for them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187] and similar; it is also permissible that it return as it returns to a singular feminine, which is eloquent.

* *

﴿But righteousness is [the conduct of] one who fears God﴾. The interpretations given for His words ﴿But righteousness is [the conduct of] one who believes in God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177] are valid here too: that the term "righteousness," which is a verbal noun, was applied to the person who performs it, as an intensification; or that there is an ellipsis in the first part, meaning "the one possessing righteousness," and in the second, meaning "the righteousness of one who believes." The preference in this has already been discussed. This verse is as though it were an abridgment of that one: for there he enumerated many attributes, from belief in God through to the rest of those attributes, and concluded with: ﴿It is those who are the mindful [muttaqun]﴾ [al-Zumar: 33]; and here he said: ﴿But righteousness is [the conduct of] one who fears God﴾, and taqwa is not attained except by the attainment of those attributes, so he here referred implicitly to those attributes, since the one who is mindful came along with them. Nafi and Ibn Amir read "wa-lakinna" with a light (takhfif) and "al-birru" with a raised ending, while the rest read it with the doubled nun and the accusative.

﴿And come to houses by their doors﴾: its explanation follows from the views already mentioned regarding His words: ﴿It is not righteousness to come to houses from their backs﴾.

(And be mindful of God): a command to guard against God. Two declarative clauses preceded it, namely ﴿It is not righteousness to come to houses from their backs, but righteousness is [the conduct of] one who fears God﴾, and he joined to them two imperative clauses: the first relates to the first, and the second relates to the second, and this is of the wonders of speech. Since the apparent sense of His words "one who fears [God]" has its object omitted, he specified in His words "and be mindful of God" who is to be feared, so that it became clear in the first that the meaning is "one who fears God." (So that you may prosper): its apparent connection is with the last clause, His words ﴿and be mindful of God﴾, because God-consciousness is the gathering of goodness through carrying out commands and avoiding prohibitions; so he tied taqwa to the hope of success, which is the attainment of one's aim.

﴿And fight in the way of God﴾, the verse. Ibn Abbas said: It was revealed when the polytheists barred the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, and they made a treaty with him that he would return the following year and they would vacate Makkah for him for three days; so he returned for the Umrah of the Qada'. The Muslims feared that Quraysh would not keep faith with them, would bar them, and would fight them in the Sacred Precinct and in the sacred month, and they disliked that, so it was revealed. He permitted them to fight those who fought them within the Sacred Precinct and in the sacred month, and lifted the blame from them in that. By mentioning this occasion, the connection of this verse with what precedes it became apparent, since what precedes it contains some matters related to the Hajj. It also appears that the more fitting connection is that when God Most High commanded taqwa, and the most demanding and arduous forms of taqwa upon the self is fighting God's enemies, He commanded it, saying: ﴿And fight in the way of God﴾. The apparent meaning is that fighting in the way of God is jihad against the unbelievers (p-65) to make the religion of God manifest and to raise His word. Most scholars of tafsir hold that it is the first verse revealed concerning the command to fight, in which He commanded fighting against those who fight, and restraint from those who refrain; so it abrogates the verses of truce. It is related from Abu Bakr that the first verse revealed about fighting was: ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought, because they have been wronged﴾ [al-Hajj: 39]. al-Raghib said: He first commanded gentleness and restriction to exhortation and good argument, then He permitted fighting, then He commanded fighting against those who refuse the truce by war; this was one command after another according to the requirements of policy. End of his words.

It has been said that this verse is abrogated by the command to fight the polytheists. It has been said that it is muhkam (not abrogated). In Ri al-Zaman (sic: Ri al-Zam'an) it is said that it is abrogated by His words: ﴿And fight them until there is no more fitnah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 193]. Its abrogation is weak, given His words: ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191], because that is a matter of specification, not of abrogation. The abrogation of ﴿And do not fight them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191] by His words "and fight them" is also weak, because it is impermissible to initiate fighting in the Sacred Precinct, and this ruling has not been abrogated but remains in force; and because it is far-fetched to combine consecutive verses in which each one abrogates the other. Even more remote is the view of those who held that His words "and fight" are not a command to fight, but that by fighting He meant contention, argument, and rigour in religion, and that this was called fighting because it usually leads to fighting, naming a thing by what it leads to. On this view the verse is muhkam. This view opposes the apparent meaning, and departing from the apparent meaning without a valid reason is not appropriate.

"In the way of God": "sabil" is the road; it has been used metaphorically for God's religion and its laws, since one who follows them reaches by them his religious and worldly goal, so it is likened to the road that conveys a person to what he intends. This is a case of applying the language of concrete bodies to abstract meanings. "In the way of God" is connected to "and fight," and it is a figurative container (zarf majazi), because when fighting occurs on account of supporting the religion, it is as if it occurred within it. It involves an elided genitive: the estimate being "in support of the religion of God." It is also possible that it is a case of tadmin (implicit meaning), as if it were said: "and strive earnestly in fighting in support of the way of God," so "fight" is given the sense of striving earnestly in fighting.

﴿Who fight you﴾: its apparent meaning is: those who engage you in fighting first, or in repelling [aggression] from the truth. It has been said: those who have the capacity for fighting, excluding one who inclines to peace, so women, children, and monks are excluded. It has been said: those who have the power to fight; calling one who has the capacity and power a "fighter" is a metaphor. Further removed metaphorically is the view that the meaning is "those who oppose you," making opposition into fighting because it leads to fighting, so that it becomes a command to fight whoever opposes, whether or not he fights. The prepositional phrase is placed before the direct object because it is the more important, namely that the fighting should be for the sake of making manifest the law of Islam. Do you not see that it is restricted to this in such a verse as: ﴿And fight in the way of God, and know that God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 244].

﴿And do not transgress﴾: a general prohibition against exceeding every limit God has set, so it includes transgression in fighting by what is not permitted. It has been said: the meaning is "and do not transgress in killing women, children, monks, infants, and those who are similar to them." This was said by Ibn Abbas, Umar ibn Abd al-'Aziz, and Mujahid, and a group of exegetes preferred it, such as al-Nahhas and others, because the form of the verb (mufa'alah) generally does not occur except between two parties, and fighting does not occur from these; and because the prohibition was reported concerning this, "the prohibition by the Messenger of God (ﷺ) of killing women and children, and of mutilation"; and in Abu Bakr's charge to Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan there is a prohibition of killing these, and of the aged decrepit man, and of destroying an inhabited place, and of slaughtering a cow or sheep for other than food, and of destroying a fruit-bearing tree by burning or otherwise.

It has been said: "do not transgress" means in fighting those who offer the jizya; this was said by Ibn Bahr. It has been said: in abandoning fighting. It has been said: by launching surprise attacks before the call has reached them. It has been said: by mutilation. It has been said: by initiating hostilities against them in the Sacred Precinct in the sacred month. It has been said: in fighting for other than the sake of God, such as tribal zeal and the pursuit of renown.

﴿Indeed, God does not love transgressors﴾. This is like a causal explanation of what precedes it, as in the saying: "Honour Zayd, for Amr honours him." The true reality of love, which is the inclination of the soul toward what it prefers, is impossible with respect to God Most High; and there is no intermediate between love and hatred with respect to God Most High, because they are both metaphors for desiring His reward and desiring His punishment, or for the objects of desire, namely reward and punishment.

(p-66) This differs from human love and hatred, for between these there is an intermediary, namely the absence of both. Therefore it is not objected to the negation of God's love that one might say: negating love does not entail the existence of hatred; rather, that follows from what we have explained, namely that there is no intermediary between them with regard to Him Most High.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 189–190 (part 1 of 3):

﴿They ask you about the new moons. Say: They are timings for the people and for the Hajj. Righteousness is not in entering the houses from their backs, but righteousness is in one who fears God. Enter the houses through their doors, and fear God so that you may prosper.﴾ ﴿Fight in the way of God against those who fight you, but do not transgress. God does not love the transgressors.﴾ ﴿Kill them wherever you find them, and expel them from where they expelled you. Persecution is worse than killing. Do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque unless they fight you there. If they fight you, then kill them.
