Such is the recompense of the disbelievers.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 191] ﴿But if they desist, then God is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 192] ﴿Fight them until there is no persecution and religion is for God. But if they desist, then there is no aggression except against the wrongdoers.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 193] ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month, and sacred things are subject to retribution. Whoever transgresses against you, then transgress against him in the same way as he transgressed against you. Fear God, and know that God is with the God-fearing.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 194] ﴿Spend in the way of God, and do not throw yourselves into destruction with your own hands. Do good, for God loves the good-doers.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 195] ﴿Complete the Hajj and the ʿUmrah for God. But if you are prevented, then [offer] what is easy of the sacrificial animal. Do not shave your heads until the offering reaches its place of sacrifice. Whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of the head, then a ransom of fasting, or charity, or a sacrifice. When you are secure, whoever performs ʿUmrah followed by Hajj [shall offer] what is easy of the sacrificial animal. Whoever does not find [one] shall fast three days during the Hajj and seven when you return, making ten complete. That is for one whose family is not present at the Sacred Mosque. Fear God, and know that God is severe in retribution.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 196] .

﴿al-ahilla﴾ is the plural of hilal (crescent). It is the regular plural pattern of fiʿal for geminate roots, as in ʿinan and aʿinna. The pattern fuʿul is anomalous for it, as in ʿunun for ʿinan and ḥujuj for ḥijaj.

Regarding al-hilal, the author of the book Shajar al-Durr mentioned in lexicography that it is a homonym (mushtarak) applied to: the crescent of the sky; an iron tool shaped like a crescent in the hand of a hunter with which he hamstrings the wild donkey; the tip of a sandal; a piece of dust; the amount of meat that can be taken with the nail of a finger; a piece of a millstone; the skin shed by a snake; an agreement with a hired worker on a monthly basis; competing in the fineness of weaving; competing in saying the tahlil (la ilaha illa Allah); the plural of halla, which is a woman who has a gap between her teeth; a serpent; and the remaining water in a pool. End of what he mentioned, summarized. That which is in the sky is called hilal for two nights, and it was said for three. Abu al-Haytham said: it is called hilal for the first two nights of the month and the last two nights, and what lies between them is called qamar (moon). Al-Asmaʿi said: it is called hilal until it becomes ḥajar, and its ḥajar is when it becomes circled like a thin thread. It was also said: it is called that until its light overcomes the blackness of the night, and that only occurs at seven. They said: it was called hilal because of the raising of voices at the sighting of it, from the expression istahalla al-sabiyy (the child cried out at birth), and al-ihlal bi'l-hajj, which is raising the voice with the talbiyah. Or it was called that because of raising the voice with tahlil at its sighting. The word hilal may be applied to the month, just as the word shahr (month) is applied to the crescent. It is said: ahalla al-hilal and istahalla, and ahlalnahu and istahlalnahu. This is the statement of the majority of lexicographers. Shamir said: it is said istahalla al-hilal also, meaning in the active form, where the subject is the crescent itself, and shahr mustahill (a month beginning). He recited:
"A month beginning after a month, and a year after it, a new year."
It is also said istahalla in the sense of becoming clear (tabayyana), but ahalla is not said in this sense. It is said ahlalna ʿan layilat kadha (we saw the crescent on such-and-such night). Abu Nasr ʿAbd al-Rahim al-Qushayri said in his tafsir: it is said ahalla al-hilal and istahalla, and ahlalna al-hilal and istahlalnahu. End.

The discussion of the root h-l-l was previously mentioned for us, but we repeat it here with regard to the specific usage of the word hilal for the things we have mentioned here.

(mawaqit) is the plural of miqat, meaning time, just as miʿad means promise. Some said: miqat is the end point of a time. God the Exalted said: ﴿So the appointed term of his Lord was completed as forty nights﴾ [Al-Aʿraf: 142].

Thaqifa al-shay': when he found it and came upon it by way of seizing and overpowering. From this comes rajul thiqf (a man quick to seize his opponents). From this: ﴿So if you overtake them in war﴾ [Al-Anfal: 57], and the verse of the poet:
"If you capture me, then kill me; and whoever I capture, there is no eternity for him."
Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: ﴿thaqiftumuhum﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 191] means you firmly established your domination over them. It is said: rajul thiqf laqif when he is firm in handling the matters he takes up. End. It is also said: thaqifa al-shay' thaqafatan when he mastered it. From this: I took skill with the sword (al-thaqafah bi'l-sayf). Al-thiqaf is also an iron tool used by archers and spearmen to straighten what is bent. Thaqifa al-shay' also means he adhered to it. Huwa thiqf means he is quick in knowledge. Thaqqaftuhu means I straightened it, and from this comes al-rimah al-muthaqqafah, meaning straightened spears. The poet said:
"I remembered you while the Khatti (spear) swayed between us, and the straightened dark spears had drunk from us."
He means straightened spears.

﴿al-tahlukah﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 195] is on the pattern taf'ulah, a verbal noun from halaka. The form taf'ulah is a rare verbal noun. Sibawayh recorded from it: al-tadurrah and al-tasurrah. Similar to it among concrete nouns: al-tanṣubah and al-tanfulah. It is said: halaka halakan, halakan, tahlukatan, and halka'a on the pattern fa'la'. The form mafil from halaka comes with dammah, fathah and kasrah, and likewise with the tā' (mahlakah). It has three vowels on the ʿayn. The dammah in mahlik is rare. Halak, for a living being, means death; and for other than it, it means perishing and exhaustion. That tahlukah is a verbal noun was reported by Abu ʿAli from Abu ʿUbaydah, and said by others among the grammarians. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible to say its original form is al-tahlikah, like al-tajribah and al-tabsirah and such, on the basis that it is a verbal noun from halla (with doubled lam), so the kasrah was changed into a dammah, just as al-juwar appears as al-jiwar. End of his statement. What he went to is not good, because it involves analogy with an anomalous form, and a claimed substitution for which there is no evidence. As for analogy with the anomalous, it is based on the claim that the original of taf'ulah with dammah is taf'ilah with kasrah, and making tahlukah a verbal noun of hallaka with doubled lam, while fa''ala with sound non-hamzated lam has its verbal noun on the pattern tafʿil, as in kassara takhsiran, and does not come on the pattern tafʿulah except anomalously. Therefore it is better to make tahlukah a verbal noun, since that is attested in examples like al-tadurrah. As for tahlikah, the best view is also that it is a verbal noun of halaka with light lam, because it has the same meaning as tahlukah with dammah on the lam. The verbal nouns of fa'ala also come on tafʿilah. They said: jalla al-rajul tajillah, meaning jalal (magnificence). Therefore tahlikah in that case is not a verbal noun of hallaka with doubled lam. As for substituting dammah for kasrah without a reason, it is extremely anomalous. As for his giving the example of al-juwar and al-jiwar, no substitution is claimed there; rather the verbal noun is formed on fuʿal with dammah on the fa' as an anomaly.

Tha'lab claimed that tahlukah is a verbal noun with no parallel, since there is nothing else in verbal nouns like it. His claim is not correct, since we have reported from Sibawayh that he recorded al-tadurrah and al-tasurrah as verbal nouns. It was said: al-tahlukah is whatever it is possible to guard against, and al-halak is what it is not possible to guard against. It was said: al-tahlukah is the thing that causes destruction, and halak is the occurrence of loss. It was said: al-tahlukah is anything whose ultimate end is destruction.

* *

• ﴿uhsirtum﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 196]: Yunus ibn Habib said: uhsira al-rajul means he was turned back from a path he wanted. It was said: hasara and uhsira have one meaning. This was said by al-Shaybani, al-Zajjaj, and Ibn ʿAtiyyah reported it from al-Farra'. Ibn Mayyadah said:
"The separation from Layla is not that she has moved far from you, nor that the preoccupations have confined you."
It was said: uhsira due to illness, and hasarahu the enemy (he was besieged by the enemy). This was said by Yaʿqub. Al-Zajjaj also said: the transmission from the scholars concerning knowledge that is prevented by fear and illness is uhsira; and the one imprisoned is husira. Abu ʿUbaydah and al-Farra' also said: uhsira, so he is muhsar. If he is confined in a prison or house, it is said husira, so he is mahsur. Thaʿlab said: the root of hasr and ihsar is confinement, and husira in confinement is stronger than uhsira. Ibn Faris said in al-Mujmal: husira by illness, and uhsira by the enemy. It is said: hasira sadruhu, meaning it was constricted. A rajul hasir is one who does not reveal his secret. Jarir said:
"The informers surrounded me, but they found one who guards your secret, O Tamim, reticent."
Al-hasr is the retention of excrement. Al-hasir means king, because he is like one confined by the curtain. Labid said:
"Until at the gate of the hasir (king) they stand."
Al-hasir is well known: it is a mat of reeds from Baradah, named so because some of it is joined to other parts, like the confinement of a thing together with something else.

(al-hadyi): hady is what is brought as an offering to the House of God the Exalted, seeking nearness to Him, like a gift that a person gives to another. It is said: ahdaytu ila al-bayt al-haram hadiyyan and hadyan, with doubled or single consonant. The doubled form is the plural of hadiyyah, like matiyyah and matiyy. The single form is the plural of hidyah, like jidhyat al-sirj and jidhy. Al-Farra' said: hady has no singular. It was said: the doubled form is the dialect of Tamim, and from it is the verse of Zuhayr:
"I have not seen a people who gave hadiyy, nor seen a neighbor of the house who was reproached."
It was also said: al-hadiyy, with doubled consonant, is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul. It was said: al-hady, with single consonant, is originally a verbal noun, and it means the same as al-hady, like al-rahn and similar, so it applies to singular and plural. In language, whatever is given as a gift, whether dirhams, goods, livestock, or other things, is called hady; but the technical religious meaning (al-haqiqah al-shar'iyyah) restricted hady to livestock. The disagreement has occurred over what is called hady among livestock, as will be mentioned God willing.

al-halq: a verbal noun of halaqa yahliqu, when hair is removed by a razor or other sharp tool or depilatory cream. Al-halq also means the passage of food after the mouth. al-adha: a verbal noun, meaning pain. You say: adhani Zayd idhaʾan, meaning Zayd harmed me.

al-sadaqah: what is given of wealth without compensation, seeking nearness to God the Exalted. al-nusuk: Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: al-nusuk are ingots of silver, each ingot being a nasikah. Then the one who worships is called nasik, because he purified his soul from the filth of sins and cleansed it, like the purified ingot free from impurity. Then the sacrificial animal was called nusuk, because it is among the noblest acts of worship by which one seeks nearness to God the Exalted. It was also said: nusuk is a verbal noun of nasaka yanska, nusukan and nusuk, just as you say halima al-rajul, hulman and hulum. al-amn: the removal of what is feared. It is said: amina yaʾmanu, amnan and amanah.

al-thalathah: a known number. From it one says: thallathtu al-qawm uthallithuhum, meaning I made them three with myself. Al-thalathun is a known number. Al-thulth, with dammah or sukun on the lam, is one of the parts of what is divided into three. Thulth is not declined (mamnuʿ min al-sarf), and the discussion of this will come, God willing. al-ʿiqab: a verbal noun of ʿaqaba, meaning to recompense the wrongdoer for his wrongdoing. It is derived from al-ʿaqibah (outcome), as if it means the outcome of the wrongdoer's act.

* *

﴿They ask you about the new moons. Say: They are timings for the people and for the Hajj.﴾ It was revealed in response to a question from some Muslims to the Prophet (ﷺ) about the crescent: what is the benefit of its waning and waxing, and its difference from the state of the sun? This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah, al-Rabiʿ, and others. It was reported that the ones who asked were Muʿadh ibn Jabal and Thaʿlabah ibn Ghanm al-Ansari, who said: O Messenger of God! What is the matter with the crescent, that it appears thin like a thread, then increases until it becomes full, then continues to decrease until it returns as it began, not being in one state? So it was revealed.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 189–190 (part 2 of 3):

The connection between this verse and what precedes it is clear. The verses before it were revealed about fasting, and the fast of Ramadan is tied to sighting the crescent (hilal), as is the ending of the fast in the month of Shawwal. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Fast when you see it, and break the fast when you see it." Earlier discussion also covered part of the rites of Hajj, namely the circumambulation (tawaf), and Hajj is one of the pillars on which Islam is built. The discussion had already covered the Oneness of Allah, prayer, zakat and fasting, so it came to the fifth pillar, which is Hajj, to complete the pillars on which Islam is built.

It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "No nation has asked fewer questions than the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ). They asked about fourteen matters, and they were answered. Among them, in Surat al-Baqarah, the first is: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near﴾ [al-Baqarah: 186], the second is this verse, and six after it. And in other surahs: ﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 4], ﴿They ask you about the spoils of war﴾ [al-Anfal: 1], ﴿And they ask you about the Spirit﴾ [al-Isra': 85], ﴿And they ask you about Dhul-Qarnayn﴾ [al-Kahf: 83], ﴿And they ask you about the mountains﴾ [Ta-Ha: 105], ﴿They ask you about the Hour﴾ [al-A'raf: 187]." It is said: two of these questions, at the beginning, concern the explanation of the origin (al-mabda'), and two at the end concern the explanation of the return (al-ma'ad). A parallel to this is that two surahs open with "O mankind" (ya ayyuha al-nas): the first, which is the fourth surah in the first half, includes an explanation of the origin, and the second, which is also the fourth surah in the latter half, includes an explanation of the return.

The pronoun in "yas'alunaka" is plural, indicating that the questioners were a group, even though, as is reported, the questioners were two persons. It is possible that this is the attribution of an action to a group when it was in fact done by one or two of them, and this is common in their speech. It is said: or because two is treated as a plural by way of extension and metaphor. The kaf in "ka" ("you") is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), and "yas'alunaka" is a statement. If the verse was revealed before the question, this would be information about the unseen; but if it was revealed after the question, which is what is transmitted in the reports on the occasions of revelation (asbab al-nuzul), then it is a narration of a past situation. "'An" (about) is connected to "yas'alunaka". It is said: "sa'ala bihi" and "sa'ala 'anhu" with the same meaning. The question is not about the essence of the crescents, but about the wisdom in the variation of their states and the benefit of this. For this reason he answered with: ﴿Say: they are times for people﴾. If they were in one unchanging state, no timing would be achieved by them.

Hilal is both singular and plural depending on its times. They said: insofar as it is a crescent in one month, it is different from its being a crescent in another. Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) read "﴿'ani al-ahilla﴾" with a kasra on the nun and a sukun on the lam of al-ahilla, followed by a hamzah. Warsh, according to his method, transposed the vowel of the hamzah and dropped the hamzah. A reader of irregular (shadhdh) reading assimilated the nun of "'an" into the lam of al-ahilla after the transposition and the deletion. (Say: they are) i.e. the crescents (al-ahilla) ﴿are times for people﴾. This is the wisdom in the waxing and waning of the moon, since they are timings for terms (al-ajal), transactions (al-mu'amalat), oaths, prescribed waiting periods (al-'iddah), fasting, breaking the fast, the periods of pregnancy and nursing, vows tied to times, and the merits of fasting on days that are known only by the crescents. The Exalted has mentioned this meaning in His saying: ﴿And He determined it as stations so that you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾ [Yunus: 5], and in His saying: ﴿So We effaced the sign of the night and made the sign of the day illuminating, that you may seek bounty from your Lord and that you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾ [al-Isra': 12]. Al-Raghib said: al-waqt (time) is the period of time appointed for an action. The meaning of "mawaqit li al-nas" is what concerns them of their affairs of transactions and interests, end of quote. Al-Rummani said: al-waqt is a measure of time that is determined in itself, and al-tawqit is the setting of its limit. Whenever you set an end for it, it is muwaqqat (timed). Al-miqat is the endpoint of a time, and the Hereafter is the endpoint of creation. Al-ihlal is the timing of the month, and the places of ihram are the miqat of Hajj because they are measures at which one arrives. Al-miqat is a measure set as a sign for what is to be done, end of his words.

In the variation of the crescent through waning and waxing there is a refutation of the philosophers in their claim that celestial bodies cannot undergo change in their states. The Exalted therefore manifested difference in the moon but did not manifest it in the sun, so that it would be known that this is by His power, the Exalted. "Al-Hajj" is conjoined to His saying "li al-nas". They said: the estimate is "wa mawaqit li al-hajj", so the second was dropped, being sufficed by the first. The meaning is: that by them you may know the months of Hajj and its timings. Since Hajj is among the greatest things whose timing and months are sought by the crescents, it was singled out for mention, as if it were a particularisation after a generalisation. For the saying "mawaqit li al-nas" does not mean timings for the persons of people, but rather timings for the purposes of people, which require a timing for religion and for worldly affairs. So His saying "wa al-Hajj" after that is a particularisation after a generalisation. In reality, it is not conjoined to "al-nas", but to the omitted genitive construct (mudaf mahdhuf) which "al-nas" stands in place of in grammatical case. Since enumerating those purposes would lead to lengthy elaboration, he restricted himself to His saying: ﴿timings for people﴾.

Al-Qaffal said: the singling out of Hajj for mention is to show that Hajj is restricted to the months which Allah the Exalted designated for the obligation of Hajj, and that it is not permitted to shift Hajj from those months to other months. The Arabs used to do this through the nasi' (intercalation), end of his words.

Al-Jumhur read "wa al-Hajji" with a fatha on the ha'. Al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "wa al-Hijji" with a kasra on it in all of the Qur'an, in the phrase "hijj al-bayt". It is said: with a fatha it is the verbal noun (masdar), and with a kasra it is the noun (ism). Sibawayh said: al-Hajj, like al-radd and al-sadd, and al-Hijj, like al-dhikr, are both verbal nouns. The apparent meaning of His saying "﴿mawaqit li al-nas wa al-hajj﴾" is what Abu Hanifah and Malik held: that it is permitted to enter ihram for Hajj at any time of the year, because of the generality of "al-ahilla", contrary to those who said that it is valid only in the months of Hajj. It is said: in it is evidence that a woman who is subject to two waiting periods (iddah) from one man is satisfied by completing one waiting period for both, and does not begin a new menstrual period or months for each of them, because of the generality of His saying: "mawaqit li al-nas". It is also evidence that when the waiting period begins with the crescent and is counted in months, its completion must be by crescents and not by number of days. It is also evidence that the one who makes an oath of abstention (ila') against his wife from the beginning of the month until the four months pass is considered in following up divorce by crescents and not by the reckoning of thirty days, and the Prophet (ﷺ) did likewise when he "made an oath of abstention from his wives for a month." Likewise with hire contracts, oaths and debts: whenever their beginning is with the crescent, all of them are like this, and consideration of number is dropped. The Prophet (ﷺ) judged in this way regarding fasting. It is also a refutation of the people of the apparent meaning (ahl al-zahir). And whoever holds their view that musaqat contracts (irrigation partnerships) are permitted for an unknown term of uncertain years is refuted. It is also evidence for the one who permitted sale until the harvest, or the threshing, or for al-Ghitas (a Christian feast) or similar, and this is the view of Malik, Abu Thawr and Ahmad. Likewise until the return of the warriors. It is reported from Ibn Abbas that he prohibited it, and al-Shafi'i held this view. It is also evidence that the attribute of the crescent being large or small is not taken into account, because it is said: "what is distinguished" (ma fussila), so whether it is seen large or small, it belongs to the night in which it is seen.

* *

﴿It is not righteousness that you enter houses from their backs, but righteousness is [in] one who fears Allah﴾. Al-Bara' ibn Azib, al-Zuhri and Qatadah said: the occasion of its revelation was that the Ansar, when they performed Hajj and 'umrah, would bind themselves by a legal rule that nothing should come between them and the sky, so they would climb onto the roofs of their houses over the walls. It is also said: in the pre-Islamic period and at the start of Islam, whenever one of them entered ihram for Hajj or 'umrah, he would not come to a wall or a house, nor to a dwelling through its door. If he was from the people of Madinah, he would make an opening in the back of his house through which he would enter and exit, or he would set up a ladder by which he would climb. If he was from the people of the wool tents (al-Wabar), he would go out from behind the tent or the pavilion, and would not enter or exit through the door until his ihram ended. They considered this righteousness, except for those who belonged to al-Hums (the Hums), who were: Quraysh, Kinanah, Khuza'ah, Thaqif, Khath'am, the Banu 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah, and the Banu Nasr ibn Mu'awiyah. The Prophet (ﷺ) entered, and with him was a man from them. That man stopped and said: "I am from al-Hums." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "And I am from al-Hums." Then it was revealed. Al-Suddi narrated this in brief.

Al-Rabi' narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) "entered, and behind him was a man from the Ansar. He entered as well, breaking the custom of his people. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'Why did you enter while you are in ihram?' He said: 'You entered, so I entered following your entry.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'I am from al-Hums; I am from a people who do not hold this religion.' The man said: 'And my religion is your religion.'" Then it was revealed. Ibrahim said: some people of the Hijaz used to do what has been mentioned. It is also said: whoever went out for a need would not return through his door, for fear of the omen of failure, and he would remain like that for a full year. The summary of these occasions is that Allah the Exalted revealed this verse: rejecting those who considered entering houses from their backs to be righteousness, and commanding entering houses through their doors. These occasions are in agreement that the houses are meant literally, and that "coming" means arriving at them. Taking the words in their literal sense is preferable to claiming metaphor while contradicting what these occasions agree upon.

The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when He mentioned that the crescents are timings for Hajj, He digressed (istitrad) to mention something they used to do in Hajj while claiming it was righteousness, so He made clear to them that this is not righteousness, and that the custom was established before Hajj that they would do it during Hajj. And when He mentioned their question about the crescents concerning the waxing and waning, and what the wisdom of this is, and it being known that He is Wise, and His acts follow wisdom, He answered them that what they do of entering houses from their backs when they are in ihram is not in any way wisdom, nor righteousness. Or, when the two accounts happened at the same time, the verse was revealed concerning both together, and one was joined to the other.

As for taking "coming" and "houses" in a metaphorical sense, there are several opinions. The first: that this is a parable (darb mathal): the meaning is that righteousness is not that you ask the ignorant, but rather fear Allah and ask the scholars. This is like saying: "I came to the matter from its door," as stated by Abu 'Ubaydah. The second: that He mentioned entering houses through their doors as a parable for violating what is obligatory in Hajj, and that refers to what they did in the nasi', for they used to shift Hajj from the time that Allah the Exalted had appointed for it, making lawful what was forbidden and forbidden what was lawful. So it was used as a parable for violation. It is also said: "and fear Allah" is under the entering of every obligation, in avoiding every prohibition. This was stated by Abu Muslim. The third: that entering houses from their backs is a kinayah (metonymy) for deviating from the correct path, and entering them through their doors is a kinayah for adhering to the correct path. That is because the straight path is to infer the unknown from the known. It has been established that the Creator is Wise and does only what is right, and we know that the variation in the moon's light is from His action, so it is known that there is benefit and wisdom in it. This is inference from the known to the unknown. But to infer from our not knowing the wisdom in it that its Doer is not wise is inference from the unknown to the known. So the meaning is: since you did not know His wisdom in the variation of the moon, you became doubters about the wisdom of the Creator, and thus you have done what you think to be righteousness. Righteousness is only that you come to houses through their doors, and so you infer from the known, which is the wisdom of the Creator, to the unknown, and you conclude that in it there is profound wisdom, even if you do not know it. This was stated in (Ri le al-Zaman) [Ri al-Zaman], and it is an opinion compiled from the words of al-Zamakhshari.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is possible that this is an illustration of their inverting their questions, and that their situation in this is like that of one who leaves the door of a house and enters it from the back. The meaning is: righteousness, and what they ought to be upon, is not that you invert your questions; rather, righteousness is the righteousness of one who is mindful of God (taqwa) of that and avoids it, and does not dare to do the like of it. Then he said: ﴿And come to houses by their doors﴾, that is: and undertake matters from the aspects in which they must be undertaken, and do not invert them. The intended meaning is the obligation of settling the souls and binding the hearts to the conviction that all of God's acts are wisdom and rightness, without the stirring of doubt or the objection of suspicion regarding that, so that He is not questioned about it (p-64), because of the accusation of committing doubt contained in questioning: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾ [al-Anbiya: 23]. End of his words. Ibn Atiyyah related this view in brief, and said: Other than Abu Ubaydah said: Righteousness is not that you deviate in questions about the crescent moons and other things, so that you approach matters in a way other than what the sacred laws love.

He metaphorically used "houses" for women: coming to them is like coming to houses. Its meaning: do not approach women from the place not permitted, from their backs, and approach them from the place that is permitted, from their front. This was said by Ibn Zayd, and Makki and al-Mahdawi related it from Ibn al-Anbari. Ibn Atiyyah said: That it refers to intercourse with women is remote and changes the style of the speech.

The ba' in "bi-an ta'tu" is extra in the predicate of laysa, and "bi-an ta'tu" is the predicate of laysa; it is to be construed as a verbal noun. This is a case of informing about the meaning by means of the meaning, and of the more definite about what is less definite, because "an" and its clause are, in their view, equivalent to a pronoun. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Amir, al-Kisai, Qalun, Abbas (on the authority of Abu Amr), al-Ijli (on the authority of Hamzah), and al-Shammuni (on the authority of al-A'sha, on the authority of Abu Bakr) read "al-biyut" with a kasra wherever it occurs, for the sake of harmony with the ya'; the original form is with a damma, because it is on the pattern fu'ul. The rest of the seven read it with a damma. "Min" is connected to "ta'tu" and indicates the starting point. The pronoun in "abwabiha" refers to "al-buyut." It returns in the manner of a singular feminine pronoun, because "al-buyut" is a plural of paucity... [Note: the original reads "جَمْعُ كَثْرَةٍ", i.e., a plural of abundance.] Because "al-buyut" is a plural of abundance, and the plural of a feminine non-rational noun is distinguished in terms of its few and many, the more eloquent form for its few is that the pronoun be plural, and the more eloquent form for its many is that it be singular, as is the case with the singular feminine pronoun; the reverse is also permissible. As for the plural of a feminine rational noun, the Arabs did not distinguish between its few and many, and the more eloquent is that the pronoun be plural. Therefore it came in the Qur'an: ﴿They are a garment for you and you are a garment for them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187] and similar; it is also permissible that it return as it returns to a singular feminine, which is eloquent.

* *

﴿But righteousness is [the conduct of] one who fears God﴾. The interpretations given for His words ﴿But righteousness is [the conduct of] one who believes in God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177] are valid here too: that the term "righteousness," which is a verbal noun, was applied to the person who performs it, as an intensification; or that there is an ellipsis in the first part, meaning "the one possessing righteousness," and in the second, meaning "the righteousness of one who believes." The preference in this has already been discussed. This verse is as though it were an abridgment of that one: for there he enumerated many attributes, from belief in God through to the rest of those attributes, and concluded with: ﴿It is those who are the mindful [muttaqun]﴾ [al-Zumar: 33]; and here he said: ﴿But righteousness is [the conduct of] one who fears God﴾, and taqwa is not attained except by the attainment of those attributes, so he here referred implicitly to those attributes, since the one who is mindful came along with them. Nafi and Ibn Amir read "wa-lakinna" with a light (takhfif) and "al-birru" with a raised ending, while the rest read it with the doubled nun and the accusative.

﴿And come to houses by their doors﴾: its explanation follows from the views already mentioned regarding His words: ﴿It is not righteousness to come to houses from their backs﴾.

(And be mindful of God): a command to guard against God. Two declarative clauses preceded it, namely ﴿It is not righteousness to come to houses from their backs, but righteousness is [the conduct of] one who fears God﴾, and he joined to them two imperative clauses: the first relates to the first, and the second relates to the second, and this is of the wonders of speech. Since the apparent sense of His words "one who fears [God]" has its object omitted, he specified in His words "and be mindful of God" who is to be feared, so that it became clear in the first that the meaning is "one who fears God." (So that you may prosper): its apparent connection is with the last clause, His words ﴿and be mindful of God﴾, because God-consciousness is the gathering of goodness through carrying out commands and avoiding prohibitions; so he tied taqwa to the hope of success, which is the attainment of one's aim.

﴿And fight in the way of God﴾, the verse. Ibn Abbas said: It was revealed when the polytheists barred the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, and they made a treaty with him that he would return the following year and they would vacate Makkah for him for three days; so he returned for the Umrah of the Qada'. The Muslims feared that Quraysh would not keep faith with them, would bar them, and would fight them in the Sacred Precinct and in the sacred month, and they disliked that, so it was revealed. He permitted them to fight those who fought them within the Sacred Precinct and in the sacred month, and lifted the blame from them in that. By mentioning this occasion, the connection of this verse with what precedes it became apparent, since what precedes it contains some matters related to the Hajj. It also appears that the more fitting connection is that when God Most High commanded taqwa, and the most demanding and arduous forms of taqwa upon the self is fighting God's enemies, He commanded it, saying: ﴿And fight in the way of God﴾. The apparent meaning is that fighting in the way of God is jihad against the unbelievers (p-65) to make the religion of God manifest and to raise His word. Most scholars of tafsir hold that it is the first verse revealed concerning the command to fight, in which He commanded fighting against those who fight, and restraint from those who refrain; so it abrogates the verses of truce. It is related from Abu Bakr that the first verse revealed about fighting was: ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought, because they have been wronged﴾ [al-Hajj: 39]. al-Raghib said: He first commanded gentleness and restriction to exhortation and good argument, then He permitted fighting, then He commanded fighting against those who refuse the truce by war; this was one command after another according to the requirements of policy. End of his words.

It has been said that this verse is abrogated by the command to fight the polytheists. It has been said that it is muhkam (not abrogated). In Ri al-Zaman (sic: Ri al-Zam'an) it is said that it is abrogated by His words: ﴿And fight them until there is no more fitnah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 193]. Its abrogation is weak, given His words: ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191], because that is a matter of specification, not of abrogation. The abrogation of ﴿And do not fight them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191] by His words "and fight them" is also weak, because it is impermissible to initiate fighting in the Sacred Precinct, and this ruling has not been abrogated but remains in force; and because it is far-fetched to combine consecutive verses in which each one abrogates the other. Even more remote is the view of those who held that His words "and fight" are not a command to fight, but that by fighting He meant contention, argument, and rigour in religion, and that this was called fighting because it usually leads to fighting, naming a thing by what it leads to. On this view the verse is muhkam. This view opposes the apparent meaning, and departing from the apparent meaning without a valid reason is not appropriate.

"In the way of God": "sabil" is the road; it has been used metaphorically for God's religion and its laws, since one who follows them reaches by them his religious and worldly goal, so it is likened to the road that conveys a person to what he intends. This is a case of applying the language of concrete bodies to abstract meanings. "In the way of God" is connected to "and fight," and it is a figurative container (zarf majazi), because when fighting occurs on account of supporting the religion, it is as if it occurred within it. It involves an elided genitive: the estimate being "in support of the religion of God." It is also possible that it is a case of tadmin (implicit meaning), as if it were said: "and strive earnestly in fighting in support of the way of God," so "fight" is given the sense of striving earnestly in fighting.

﴿Who fight you﴾: its apparent meaning is: those who engage you in fighting first, or in repelling [aggression] from the truth. It has been said: those who have the capacity for fighting, excluding one who inclines to peace, so women, children, and monks are excluded. It has been said: those who have the power to fight; calling one who has the capacity and power a "fighter" is a metaphor. Further removed metaphorically is the view that the meaning is "those who oppose you," making opposition into fighting because it leads to fighting, so that it becomes a command to fight whoever opposes, whether or not he fights. The prepositional phrase is placed before the direct object because it is the more important, namely that the fighting should be for the sake of making manifest the law of Islam. Do you not see that it is restricted to this in such a verse as: ﴿And fight in the way of God, and know that God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 244].

﴿And do not transgress﴾: a general prohibition against exceeding every limit God has set, so it includes transgression in fighting by what is not permitted. It has been said: the meaning is "and do not transgress in killing women, children, monks, infants, and those who are similar to them." This was said by Ibn Abbas, Umar ibn Abd al-'Aziz, and Mujahid, and a group of exegetes preferred it, such as al-Nahhas and others, because the form of the verb (mufa'alah) generally does not occur except between two parties, and fighting does not occur from these; and because the prohibition was reported concerning this, "the prohibition by the Messenger of God (ﷺ) of killing women and children, and of mutilation"; and in Abu Bakr's charge to Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan there is a prohibition of killing these, and of the aged decrepit man, and of destroying an inhabited place, and of slaughtering a cow or sheep for other than food, and of destroying a fruit-bearing tree by burning or otherwise.

It has been said: "do not transgress" means in fighting those who offer the jizya; this was said by Ibn Bahr. It has been said: in abandoning fighting. It has been said: by launching surprise attacks before the call has reached them. It has been said: by mutilation. It has been said: by initiating hostilities against them in the Sacred Precinct in the sacred month. It has been said: in fighting for other than the sake of God, such as tribal zeal and the pursuit of renown.

﴿Indeed, God does not love transgressors﴾. This is like a causal explanation of what precedes it, as in the saying: "Honour Zayd, for Amr honours him." The true reality of love, which is the inclination of the soul toward what it prefers, is impossible with respect to God Most High; and there is no intermediate between love and hatred with respect to God Most High, because they are both metaphors for desiring His reward and desiring His punishment, or for the objects of desire, namely reward and punishment.

(p-66) This differs from human love and hatred, for between these there is an intermediary, namely the absence of both. Therefore it is not objected to the negation of God's love that one might say: negating love does not entail the existence of hatred; rather, that follows from what we have explained, namely that there is no intermediary between them with regard to Him Most High.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 191–192:**

﴿And kill them wherever you find them﴾. The pronoun of the object refers back to "﴿those who fight you﴾" (al-Baqarah 2:190). This is a command to kill them. "﴿Wherever you find them﴾" is general, covering every place, whether sacred or not, and it therefore implies the generality of times, both in the sacred months and outside them. In (al-Muntakhab) [a tafsir by al-Tantawi? (no added notes)] it is said: in the first verse he commanded jihad on condition that the disbelievers initiate the fighting, while in this verse he added to the obligation and commanded jihad with them whether or not they fight, and he excepted from this the fighting at the Sacred Mosque, end of quotation. But this is not as he said. He said that he added to the obligation and commanded jihad whether or not they fight, because the pronoun refers back to "those who fight you," so the description remains. The meaning is: "Kill those who fight you wherever you find them." Therefore it is not a command to jihad whether or not they fight. Ibn Ishaq said: this verse was revealed concerning the matter of Amr ibn al-Hadrami, when Waqid ibn Abdullah al-Tamimi killed him, and that was in the expedition of Abdullah ibn Jahsh.

﴿And expel them from where they expelled you﴾, that is, from the place from which they expelled you, meaning Makkah. It is a command of expulsion in the sense of granting empowerment (amr tamkin), as though it were a promise from God of the conquest of Makkah. He fulfilled what He promised, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did this on the day of the conquest of Makkah with those who had not become Muslim along with them. "From where" is connected to his saying "﴿and expel them﴾." The word "where" (haythu) may be used with prepositions attached to it, such as min (from), the ba' (with/in), fi (in), and with the addition of la-da (at) to it. The pronoun of the object in "﴿expelled you﴾" refers to those commanded to be killed and expelled. In reality it refers to some of them: the expulsion of some of them, namely the most honored of them in rank, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the Muhajirun, was made as the expulsion of all of them.

﴿And persecution is worse than killing﴾. Regarding "fitnah" (persecution, trial) here there are several opinions.

The first: returning to disbelief is worse than a believer being killed. This is said by Mujahid. They had tortured a group of the believers so that they would return to disbelief, but God protected them. Disbelief in God entails punishment forever, whereas killing is not like that. Some of the Companions had killed in the sacred month, and so the Muslims regarded that as grave. The second: polytheism, that is, their associating partners with God is a greater violation than the killing for which they reproached you concerning the matter of Ibn al-Hadrami. The third: the violation of God's sanctities by them is worse than the killing that was permitted for you, O believers, to inflict upon them. The fourth: the punishment of the Hereafter for them is worse than their killing of the Muslims in the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram). From this usage is "﴿Taste your persecution﴾" (al-Dhariyat 51:14) and "﴿Indeed, those who persecuted the believing men and believing women﴾" (al-Buruj 85:10), meaning: those who tortured them. The fifth: expulsion from one's homeland, because of what it contains of separation from what is familiar and from loved ones, and the constant spoiling of life. From this is the saying of the poet:

*Death by the edge of the sword is lighter in its effect on the soul*
*than killing by the edge of separation.*

The sixth: that their persecution of you, by barring you from the Sacred Mosque, is meant as worse than your killing of them in the Sacred Precinct, or than their killing of you. If they kill you, then do not mind fighting them. This is said by al-Zamakhshari, and it returns to the meaning of the third opinion. The seventh: their torture of the Muslims in order to make them apostatize. This is said by al-Kisa'i.

The original sense of "fitnah" is the placing of gold over fire to extract it from its impurities. Then it came to be used for testing (imtihan), and its application to what was explained in these opinions is common. The words "fitnah" and "qatl" (killing) are verbal nouns whose agent and object are not mentioned. What is affirmed is that the reality of persecution is worse than the reality of killing. So every place where this relation is realized falls within the generality of these statements, whether the verbal noun's agent or its object is the believers or the disbelievers. Specifying a particular kind among the instances of the general requires evidence.

﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque until they fight you therein﴾. This means that you should not initiate the fighting at this site until it occurs from them there. Mujahid said: this verse is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated), and it is not permitted to fight anyone in the Sacred Mosque unless they have first fought. Tawus and Abu Hanifa also said this. Al-Rabi' said: it is mansukh (abrogated) by his saying: "﴿And fight them until there is no persecution﴾" (al-Baqarah 2:193). Qatadah said: it is abrogated by his saying: "﴿Then when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists﴾" (al-Tawbah 9:5). Abrogation (naskh) is the view of the majority, and some of the discussion of this abrogation has already been mentioned in this verse.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and al-A'mash read "﴿wa-la taqtuluhum﴾" (do not kill them), and likewise "﴿hatta yaqtulukum﴾" (until they kill you), and "﴿fa-in qatalukum﴾" (if they kill you), from killing. So the metaphor may be in the verb, meaning: do not begin their killing until they begin your killing. The metaphor may also be in the object, meaning: do not kill some of them until they kill some of you. If they kill some of you, one says: "the sons of so-and-so killed us," meaning they killed some of us. The poet said:

*If you kill us, we will kill you,*
*and if you aim at blood, we will aim at blood.*

A parallel is "﴿Many prophets fought along with Him, and they did not weaken﴾" (Al 'Imran 3:146), meaning: some of the Rabbiyyun were killed along with them, yet the rest did not weaken.

The governing element for "ʿinda" (at) is "wa-la tuqatiluhum" (do not fight them). "Hatta" (until) here indicates a limit (ghayah). The phrase "fihi" (therein) is connected to "yuqatiluukum" (they fight you). The pronoun refers back to "ʿinda," and the verb has been transitive to the pronoun of the adverbial noun, so "fi" (in) was needed to reach it. It did not take the expanded form (ittisa'), so the verb was transitive to the pronoun of the adverbial noun in the same way it is transitive to a direct object. It cannot be said that if the adverbial noun is not inflected (ghayr mutasarrif), then the verb may not extend to its pronoun by ittisa', because its apparent form does not allow this; rather, ittisa' is permissible in that case. Do you not see that it differs from the apparent form in its being governed by "fi," although the apparent form does not allow that? Likewise it differs from it in ittisa'. So the ruling for the pronoun in that case is not the ruling for the noun in its apparent form.

﴿Then if they fight you, kill them﴾. This is an explicit statement of the implied sense (mafhum) of the limit, and it contains an omitted element. That is: if they fight you therein, then kill them therein. The context of the speech indicates that this is intended. There is no disagreement that "fa-qtuluhum" (kill them) is a command to kill them under that supposition, and in it is a great good tiding of victory over them. That is, they are so bereft of support and help that you are commanded to kill them, not to fight them. Thus you are empowered over them, such that they require only that the killing be inflicted upon them, when they engage you in battle, not that you fight them.

﴿Such is the recompense of the disbelievers﴾. The particle "ka-dhalika" (such) is in the nominative position, because it is the predicate of the subject which is the predicate of "al-kafirin" (the disbelievers). The meaning is: the recompense of the disbelievers is like that recompense, which is killing. That is, whoever disbelieves in God Most High, his recompense is killing. In attributing the recompense to the disbelievers there is an indication of killing being the cause (illiyyah).

﴿But if they desist, then indeed God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. That is, from disbelief, and they enter Islam. For this reason forgiveness and mercy are tied to it, and these cannot exist together with disbelief: "﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they desist, what has passed will be forgiven them﴾" (al-Anfal 8:38). What indicates this from the wording has already been mentioned: the recompense of the disbelievers, and the context of the speech is only with the disbelievers. It is said: "if they desist" means from fighting and from polytheism, because both have been mentioned earlier in the speech, and this is a good view. It is said: from fighting only, not from disbelief. On this view, forgiveness is not for them. Rather the meaning is: indeed God is Forgiving to you and Merciful to you, in that He removed from you the obligation of fighting them. It is said: the answer (jawab) is omitted, that is: then forgive them, for God is Forgiving and Merciful to you. On the view that desisting is only from fighting, the verse is abrogated, while on the two views before it, the verse is muhkam. The meaning of "intaha" (desisted) is ceased, and it is of the form "if'tala" derived from "nahy" (prohibition). Its meaning is the action of the agent upon himself, like the saying "idtarraba" (he was agitated). This is one of the meanings for which the form "if'tala" comes. They say: in His saying "﴿But if they desist, then indeed God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾" there is an indication of accepting the repentance of one who has committed deliberate killing, since disbelief is a greater sin than killing, and God Most High has informed us that He accepts repentance from disbelief.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 191–192:**

﴿And kill them wherever you find them﴾. The pronoun of the object refers back to "﴿those who fight you﴾" (al-Baqarah 2:190). This is a command to kill them. "﴿Wherever you find them﴾" is general, covering every place, whether sacred or not, and it therefore implies the generality of times, both in the sacred months and outside them. In (al-Muntakhab) [a tafsir by al-Tantawi? (no added notes)] it is said: in the first verse he commanded jihad on condition that the disbelievers initiate the fighting, while in this verse he added to the obligation and commanded jihad with them whether or not they fight, and he excepted from this the fighting at the Sacred Mosque, end of quotation. But this is not as he said. He said that he added to the obligation and commanded jihad whether or not they fight, because the pronoun refers back to "those who fight you," so the description remains. The meaning is: "Kill those who fight you wherever you find them." Therefore it is not a command to jihad whether or not they fight. Ibn Ishaq said: this verse was revealed concerning the matter of Amr ibn al-Hadrami, when Waqid ibn Abdullah al-Tamimi killed him, and that was in the expedition of Abdullah ibn Jahsh.

﴿And expel them from where they expelled you﴾, that is, from the place from which they expelled you, meaning Makkah. It is a command of expulsion in the sense of granting empowerment (amr tamkin), as though it were a promise from God of the conquest of Makkah. He fulfilled what He promised, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did this on the day of the conquest of Makkah with those who had not become Muslim along with them. "From where" is connected to his saying "﴿and expel them﴾." The word "where" (haythu) may be used with prepositions attached to it, such as min (from), the ba' (with/in), fi (in), and with the addition of la-da (at) to it. The pronoun of the object in "﴿expelled you﴾" refers to those commanded to be killed and expelled. In reality it refers to some of them: the expulsion of some of them, namely the most honored of them in rank, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the Muhajirun, was made as the expulsion of all of them.

﴿And persecution is worse than killing﴾. Regarding "fitnah" (persecution, trial) here there are several opinions.

The first: returning to disbelief is worse than a believer being killed. This is said by Mujahid. They had tortured a group of the believers so that they would return to disbelief, but God protected them. Disbelief in God entails punishment forever, whereas killing is not like that. Some of the Companions had killed in the sacred month, and so the Muslims regarded that as grave. The second: polytheism, that is, their associating partners with God is a greater violation than the killing for which they reproached you concerning the matter of Ibn al-Hadrami. The third: the violation of God's sanctities by them is worse than the killing that was permitted for you, O believers, to inflict upon them. The fourth: the punishment of the Hereafter for them is worse than their killing of the Muslims in the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram). From this usage is "﴿Taste your persecution﴾" (al-Dhariyat 51:14) and "﴿Indeed, those who persecuted the believing men and believing women﴾" (al-Buruj 85:10), meaning: those who tortured them. The fifth: expulsion from one's homeland, because of what it contains of separation from what is familiar and from loved ones, and the constant spoiling of life. From this is the saying of the poet:

*Death by the edge of the sword is lighter in its effect on the soul*
*than killing by the edge of separation.*

The sixth: that their persecution of you, by barring you from the Sacred Mosque, is meant as worse than your killing of them in the Sacred Precinct, or than their killing of you. If they kill you, then do not mind fighting them. This is said by al-Zamakhshari, and it returns to the meaning of the third opinion. The seventh: their torture of the Muslims in order to make them apostatize. This is said by al-Kisa'i.

The original sense of "fitnah" is the placing of gold over fire to extract it from its impurities. Then it came to be used for testing (imtihan), and its application to what was explained in these opinions is common. The words "fitnah" and "qatl" (killing) are verbal nouns whose agent and object are not mentioned. What is affirmed is that the reality of persecution is worse than the reality of killing. So every place where this relation is realized falls within the generality of these statements, whether the verbal noun's agent or its object is the believers or the disbelievers. Specifying a particular kind among the instances of the general requires evidence.

﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque until they fight you therein﴾. This means that you should not initiate the fighting at this site until it occurs from them there. Mujahid said: this verse is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated), and it is not permitted to fight anyone in the Sacred Mosque unless they have first fought. Tawus and Abu Hanifa also said this. Al-Rabi' said: it is mansukh (abrogated) by his saying: "﴿And fight them until there is no persecution﴾" (al-Baqarah 2:193). Qatadah said: it is abrogated by his saying: "﴿Then when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists﴾" (al-Tawbah 9:5). Abrogation (naskh) is the view of the majority, and some of the discussion of this abrogation has already been mentioned in this verse.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and al-A'mash read "﴿wa-la taqtuluhum﴾" (do not kill them), and likewise "﴿hatta yaqtulukum﴾" (until they kill you), and "﴿fa-in qatalukum﴾" (if they kill you), from killing. So the metaphor may be in the verb, meaning: do not begin their killing until they begin your killing. The metaphor may also be in the object, meaning: do not kill some of them until they kill some of you. If they kill some of you, one says: "the sons of so-and-so killed us," meaning they killed some of us. The poet said:

*If you kill us, we will kill you,*
*and if you aim at blood, we will aim at blood.*

A parallel is "﴿Many prophets fought along with Him, and they did not weaken﴾" (Al 'Imran 3:146), meaning: some of the Rabbiyyun were killed along with them, yet the rest did not weaken.

The governing element for "ʿinda" (at) is "wa-la tuqatiluhum" (do not fight them). "Hatta" (until) here indicates a limit (ghayah). The phrase "fihi" (therein) is connected to "yuqatiluukum" (they fight you). The pronoun refers back to "ʿinda," and the verb has been transitive to the pronoun of the adverbial noun, so "fi" (in) was needed to reach it. It did not take the expanded form (ittisa'), so the verb was transitive to the pronoun of the adverbial noun in the same way it is transitive to a direct object. It cannot be said that if the adverbial noun is not inflected (ghayr mutasarrif), then the verb may not extend to its pronoun by ittisa', because its apparent form does not allow this; rather, ittisa' is permissible in that case. Do you not see that it differs from the apparent form in its being governed by "fi," although the apparent form does not allow that? Likewise it differs from it in ittisa'. So the ruling for the pronoun in that case is not the ruling for the noun in its apparent form.

﴿Then if they fight you, kill them﴾. This is an explicit statement of the implied sense (mafhum) of the limit, and it contains an omitted element. That is: if they fight you therein, then kill them therein. The context of the speech indicates that this is intended. There is no disagreement that "fa-qtuluhum" (kill them) is a command to kill them under that supposition, and in it is a great good tiding of victory over them. That is, they are so bereft of support and help that you are commanded to kill them, not to fight them. Thus you are empowered over them, such that they require only that the killing be inflicted upon them, when they engage you in battle, not that you fight them.

﴿Such is the recompense of the disbelievers﴾. The particle "ka-dhalika" (such) is in the nominative position, because it is the predicate of the subject which is the predicate of "al-kafirin" (the disbelievers). The meaning is: the recompense of the disbelievers is like that recompense, which is killing. That is, whoever disbelieves in God Most High, his recompense is killing. In attributing the recompense to the disbelievers there is an indication of killing being the cause (illiyyah).

﴿But if they desist, then indeed God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. That is, from disbelief, and they enter Islam. For this reason forgiveness and mercy are tied to it, and these cannot exist together with disbelief: "﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they desist, what has passed will be forgiven them﴾" (al-Anfal 8:38). What indicates this from the wording has already been mentioned: the recompense of the disbelievers, and the context of the speech is only with the disbelievers. It is said: "if they desist" means from fighting and from polytheism, because both have been mentioned earlier in the speech, and this is a good view. It is said: from fighting only, not from disbelief. On this view, forgiveness is not for them. Rather the meaning is: indeed God is Forgiving to you and Merciful to you, in that He removed from you the obligation of fighting them. It is said: the answer (jawab) is omitted, that is: then forgive them, for God is Forgiving and Merciful to you. On the view that desisting is only from fighting, the verse is abrogated, while on the two views before it, the verse is muhkam. The meaning of "intaha" (desisted) is ceased, and it is of the form "if'tala" derived from "nahy" (prohibition). Its meaning is the action of the agent upon himself, like the saying "idtarraba" (he was agitated). This is one of the meanings for which the form "if'tala" comes. They say: in His saying "﴿But if they desist, then indeed God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾" there is an indication of accepting the repentance of one who has committed deliberate killing, since disbelief is a greater sin than killing, and God Most High has informed us that He accepts repentance from disbelief.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 193:**

﴿And fight them until there is no fitnah﴾. The object pronoun refers to those who fought you, namely the disbelievers of Makkah. Here *fitnah* (trial, persecution, discord) means shirk and the harm that follows from it against the Muslims. They were commanded to fight them until nothing is worshipped besides God, and until the practice of the People of the Book, in accepting the *jizyah* (poll tax), is not applied to them. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, al-Rabīʿ and al-Suddī. That is, *fitnah* here means shirk and the harm that accompanies it. It was also said that the pronoun refers to all disbelievers. They were commanded to fight and kill them everywhere, so the verse is general and includes every disbeliever, whether a polytheist or otherwise. From among them, those whom the evidence indicates are exempted by the *jizyah*. The view of those who said that this verse abrogates (*nāsikhah*, abrogating) the verse ﴿and do not fight them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191] has already been mentioned. In *al-Muntakhab* it is said: the correct position is that it is not so; rather, this expression is general and what precedes it is specific, namely ﴿and do not fight them at al-Masjid al-Ḥarām﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191]. The position of al-Shāfiʿī is the specification of the general, whether the specifier comes before it or after it. Abū Muslim said: *fitnah* here means fighting within the Sacred Precinct. He said: God commanded them to fight them so that there would no longer be fighting from them, which, when they initiated it, would be a *fitnah* for the believers because of the various kinds of harm they feared. *Ḥattā* (until) here indicates a limit or a reason. If *fitnah* is interpreted as disbelief, and disbelief does not necessarily cease through fighting, then how is the command to fight made conditional upon its cessation? The answer is that this is according to the usual and actual state of affairs: whoever is killed, his disbelief has ended and ceased, and whoever survives fears remaining steadfast in his disbelief, so he accepts Islam. Or the meaning is: fight them intending the cessation of disbelief, because the obligation in fighting disbelievers is that the aim be the cessation of disbelief. For this reason, if one thinks that they will desist from disbelief without fighting, it becomes obligatory for him to refrain from it.

﴿and religion is for God﴾. *Dīn* (religion, submission) here means obedience, i.e., submission should be sincerely for God. It was also said that *dīn* here means prostration and humility before God alone, so that none is prostrated to other than Him. Here the command to fight is limited by two things: first, the absence of *fitnah*; second, the establishment of religion for God. This is the conjunction of an affirmative with a negative, and the two have one meaning and are mutually entailed: for when shirk against God is removed, He, Exalted is He, is the one worshipped and obeyed. According to Abū Muslim's interpretation of *fitnah*, the command is limited by two different matters: first, the absence of fighting in the Sacred Precinct; second, the exclusivity of religion for God, Exalted is He. It was said that in al-Anfāl the expression ﴿and religion entirely is for God﴾ [al-Anfāl: 39] occurs, while the word *kulluhu* (entirely) does not occur here, because the verse in al-Anfāl concerns disbelievers in general, while here it concerns the polytheists of Makkah. Generality was appropriate there, and it was not needed here. It was said: this does not hold except according to the view of those who take the pronoun in ﴿and fight them﴾ as referring to the people of Makkah, according to one of the two views. A man argued with Ibn ʿUmar about going out in the *fitnah* of Ibn al-Zubayr, citing as evidence the verse ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight﴾ [al-Ḥujurāt: 9]. Ibn ʿUmar countered him with the verse ﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 93]. The man said: Did He not say, ﴿And fight them until there is no fitnah﴾? Ibn ʿUmar replied that we did that during the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) when Islam was few, and a man would be put to trial concerning his religion by being killed or tortured. When Islam became numerous, there was no more *fitnah*, and religion was for God. But you fight until there is *fitnah* and religion is for other than God.

﴿But if they desist, then there is no hostility except against the wrongdoers﴾. The object of *intahā* (desist) is omitted; the estimated meaning is: from shirk by entering Islam, or from fighting. Or they submit to paying the *jizyah* from those for whom it is prescribed, or from shirk and from torturing the Muslims and putting them to trial so that they return from their religion. This depends on the difference over the pronoun: if it is general to disbelievers, or specific to the disbelievers of Makkah.

*ʿUdwān* (hostility, aggression) is a verbal noun of *ʿadā*, meaning *iʿtadā* (to transgress). It is a general negation, meaning: no single instance of any kind of it is taken at all except against the one who has done wrong. The *ʿudwān* that is wrongdoing is here taken to mean the requital. It is called hostility because it is the requital of hostility, and punishment is named after the sin, by way of correspondence, as in His words: ﴿and the requital of an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shūrā: 40]; ﴿so whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in like manner﴾ [al-Baqarah: 194]; ﴿and they schemed, and God schemed﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 54]. The poet said:

*We repaid those who had transgressed against us yesterday, their injury in full, equal, as you match sandal to sandal.*

Al-Rummānī said: the word *ʿudwān* was used for the requital without verbal correspondence, because verbal correspondence is correspondence of meaning. It is as if He were saying: desist from hostility, so there is no hostility except against the wrongdoers. End of his words. This general negation is intended as a prohibition, i.e., do not transgress. This is by way of emphasis: when they wish to emphasize refraining from a thing, they turn from the prohibition to a pure general negation, and it becomes more binding in prohibition, since it becomes one of the things that do not occur at all. It is not valid to take this as a literal negation, because hostility does occur against someone other than a wrongdoer. Then it would be a non-conforming report, which is not permissible with respect to God, Exalted is He. The wrongdoers here were interpreted as those who initiated the fighting. It was also said: those who remain in disbelief and *fitnah*. ʿIkrimah and Qatādah said: the wrongdoer here is one who refuses to say, "There is no god but God." (p-69) Al-Akhfash said the meaning is: if some of them desist, then there is no hostility except against those who do not desist, who are the wrongdoers.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: do not transgress against those who desist, because fighting those who desist is hostility and wrongdoing. So the words ﴿except against the wrongdoers﴾ were placed in the position of "against those who desist." End of his words. What he said is not valid except on the interpretation of meaning. As for the interpretation of i'rab (grammatical analysis), it is not valid, because "against those who desist" is not synonymous with ﴿except against the wrongdoers﴾. The negation of hostility against those who desist does not indicate its affirmation against the wrongdoers except through implicit meaning, the *mafhūm al-ṣifa* (implication drawn from a qualifier). In the Qur'anic construction, it indicates its affirmation against the wrongdoers through explicit meaning (*manṭūq*), which is restricted by negation and *illā* (except). There is a difference between the two indications. It appears from his words that he intended the interpretation of i'rab. Do you not see his words: "the words ﴿except against the wrongdoers﴾ were placed in the position of 'against those who desist'"? This substitution occurs only in the interpretation of i'rab, and it is not so, because of the difference between the two indications that we have explained. Do you not see the difference between your saying, "How noble is the ignorant one!" and "None is noble except the knowledgeable one"?

﴿except against the wrongdoers﴾ is an exceptive construction (*istithnāʾ mufarragh*) from the report, "against the wrongdoers," in a position of nominative case as the predicate of *lā* (no), according to the view of al-Akhfash, or as the predicate of the subject that is the whole phrase "lā ʿudwāna" (there is no hostility), according to the view of Sībawayh. This has been noted before. The use of *ʿalā* (against) indicates the imposition of the requital upon them and its dominance over them.

It was also said: the meaning of "lā ʿudwāna" is "lā sabīl" (no way, no path), as in His words: ﴿Whichever of the two terms I fulfil, there shall be no hostility against me﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 28], i.e., there is no way against me. This is a metaphor for domination and attack, and it goes back to the meaning of the requital of the wrongdoer by which we explained *ʿudwān*. The link of the requital to the condition is either by an omitted estimate, i.e., "except against the wrongdoers among them," or by inclusion within the general sense of "the wrongdoers," so the link is through generality.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 194–195:

﴿The sacred month for the sacred month, and sacred things demand retaliation.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, Miqsam, al-Suddi, al-Rabi', al-Dahhak and others said: It was revealed concerning the 'Umrat al-Qada' (the make-up 'Umrah) in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah. The polytheists had fought them that year in the sacred month, which is Dhu al-Qa'dah. So it was said to them when they set out for the make-up 'Umrah, and they were averse to fighting, and that was in Dhu al-Qa'dah: ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month﴾, meaning: its violation for its violation. You violate its sanctity against them, just as they violated its sanctity against you.

Al-Hasan said: The unbelievers asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Do you fight in the sacred month?" He told them that he would not fight in it. So they resolved to attack him and kill those with him, when they thought he would not fight. Then it was revealed.

"Al-shahr" (the month) is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is the prepositional phrase following it. Lexically it cannot be the predicate, so an ellipsis is necessary. The estimated meaning is: the violation of the sanctity of the sacred month occurs through the violation of the sanctity of the sacred month. The alif and lam in "al-shahr" are, in wording, for prior reference (al-'ahd). So the first month is Dhu al-Qa'dah of the seventh year, at the 'Umrat al-Qada', and the second month is that of the sixth year, the year of al-Hudaybiyyah. ﴿And sacred things demand retaliation﴾: the alif and lam in "al-hurumat" are for prior reference. That is: the sanctity of the month, the sanctity of those in ihram (muhrimin) when you were barred, and the sanctity of the land (al-balad), the month, and fighting when you entered. This interpretation follows the occasion of revelation reported from Ibn 'Abbas and those with him. As for the occasion reported from al-Hasan, the alif and lam are for generality, covering life, property and honor. That is: every sanctity in which retaliation applies, so those earlier sanctities and others are included. It has also been said that ﴿and sacred things demand retaliation﴾ is a separate sentence, cut off from what precedes it, not concerning the matter of Hajj and 'Umrah. Rather, it is the start of a ruling that existed at the beginning of Islam. That is: whoever violates your sanctity, you may inflict upon him the same as he inflicted upon you. Then this was abrogated (naskh) by fighting.

A group said: Whatever transgression occurs in property or injury has not been abrogated. One may transgress against the offender in the same way he transgressed, and may do so secretly if he is able, without the judge, and he does not sin by this. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, and it is a narration in the school of Malik. Another group, including Malik, said: retaliation (qisas) is reserved for the rulers, so none may exact it except them.

Al-Hasan recited "﴿wal-hurumatu﴾" with a sukun on the ra' (ḥurmāt), according to the original form, since it is the plural of ḥurmah. The ḍamma in the plural is an assimilation (ittiba').

﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you.﴾ This confirms what came before it, His words: ﴿and sacred things demand retaliation﴾. There is disagreement about it: is it abrogated or not? (p-70) According to what preceded from the school of al-Shafi'i and the school of Malik. Ibn 'Abbas said: this verse and what is similar to it were revealed in Mecca, when Islam was not yet strong. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) emigrated and his religion became strong, the Muslims were commanded to refer their affairs to their rulers, and they were commanded to fight the unbelievers. Mujahid said: rather, this verse was revealed in Medina after the 'Umrat al-Qada', and it is part of the gradual progression in the command to fight.

His words ﴿fa'taduu﴾ (transgress) are not a command of obligation, since pardon is permissible. The act was called "transgression" by way of reciprocity. The preposition bi in "bi-mithli" (in the same manner) is connected to ﴿fa'taduu 'alayhi﴾, and the meaning is: with a punishment equal to the offence of his transgression. It has also been said that the bi is superfluous, meaning "like his transgression," and it is an adjective of a deleted verbal noun, meaning: a transgression equal to his transgression.

﴿And fear Allah﴾ is a command to be mindful of Allah, and it includes being mindful of Him by not transgressing in retaliation beyond what is lawful.

﴿And know that Allah is with the righteous﴾ with help, empowerment and support. The word "ma'a" (with), which indicates companionship and constancy, is used here to urge people to piety at all times, for whoever has Allah with him is the victorious one who prevails. Do you not see what came in the hadith: "Shoot, and I am with the sons of so-and-so," and they held back, so he said: "Shoot, and I am with you all," or words to this effect? Likewise his saying to Hassan: "Satirize them, and the Holy Spirit is with you."

﴿And spend in the way of Allah﴾: this is a command to spend on the path of Islam. Whatever is a path to Allah and a law from Him is one in which spending is commanded. It has been said that the meaning is a command to spend on the price of weapons of war. It has also been said that it is for the poor among the fighters. Ibn 'Abbas said this, saying: It was revealed concerning some Bedouins who asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), saying: "With what should we equip ourselves? By Allah, we have no provisions." It has also been said that it refers to striving with oneself and with others. It has been said that it refers to striving (jihad) with oneself and others. And it has been said the meaning is: offer your souls in striving in the way of Allah.

The giving of one's soul in the way of Allah has been called "spending" by way of metaphor and extension, like the saying of the poet:

"I spent my life in idleness and youth, so no life remains for me, and no reward remains for me."

The more apparent view is the first opinion, which is the command to direct wealth to acts of righteousness: whether Hajj, or 'Umrah, or striving with one's self, or equipping another, or maintaining kinship ties, or charity, or supporting dependents, or zakat, or expiation, or building roads, or other than these.

Since this verse follows what precedes it, which indicates fighting and the command to it, the spending in jihad came to mind for the sake of this connection.

﴿And do not cast yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾. 'Ikrimah said: It was revealed concerning the Ansar, who withheld from spending in the way of Allah. Al-Nu'man ibn Bashir said: A man would commit a sin and say: "Allah will not forgive me," so it was revealed.

In a long hadith it is related that a man among the Muslims charged into the ranks of the Romans, entered among them and came out. The people said: "He has thrown himself into destruction." Abu Ayyub al-Ansari said: You have interpreted the verse other than its proper interpretation. This verse was only revealed concerning us, the assembly of the Ansar, when Allah strengthened His religion. We said: "If we stay behind and set right what was lost of our wealth," so it was revealed. There are several views on the interpretation of "destruction" (al-tahlukah).

The first: abandoning jihad and inclining to ease and setting right one's wealth. This was said by Abu Ayyub.

The second: abandoning spending in the way of Allah out of fear of poverty. This was said by Hudhayfah, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, 'Ata', 'Ikrimah, and Ibn Jubayr.

The third: rushing into the enemy without inflicting harm. This was said by Abu al-Qasim al-Balkhi.

The fourth: giving charity from what is wicked. This was said by 'Ikrimah.

The fifth: extravagance by spending all of one's wealth. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy﴾ [al-Furqan: 67], and ﴿Do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it fully outstretched﴾ [al-Isra': 29]. This was said by Abu 'Ali.

The sixth: indulging in sins out of despair of the acceptance of one's repentance. This was said by al-Bara' and 'Ubaydah al-Salmani.

The seventh: despair of repentance. This was said by a group.

The eighth: setting out for jihad without provisions. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam. Some people did this, and it led them to being cut off on the road, or to becoming a burden on people.

The ninth: the nullifying of reward, either through reminding (of favors) or showing off and seeking reputation, as in His words: ﴿And do not nullify your deeds﴾ [Muhammad: 33].

All these views are possible readings of this verse. The apparent meaning is that they were forbidden from everything that leads them to destruction in other than obedience to Allah the Exalted. For striving in the way of Allah leads to destruction, which is killing, yet it was not forbidden. Rather it is a sought-after command, with the promise of Paradise upon it, and it is among the best deeds by which one draws near to Allah the Exalted. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) himself desired that, namely that he be killed in the way of Allah and then brought to life, and then fight and be killed again, or as came in the hadith.
