It is said: "He cast his hand into such-and-such, and to such-and-such," when he surrendered, because one who surrenders in battle casts his weapon with his two hands, and likewise for every helpless person in any action. From this is the saying of 'Abd al-Muttalib: "By Allah, our casting ourselves with our own hands to death is indeed weakness."

Alqa (to cast) is transitive by itself, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So Musa cast down his staff﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 45], and the poet said:

"Until, when its darkness cast a hand upon an unbeliever, and concealed the nakedness of the frontiers."

It also comes used with the bi (preposition), as in this verse, and like the saying of the poet:

"The young man cast with his two palms in submission, from hunger, in weakness, neither bitter nor sweet."

When alqa is used in these two ways, Abu 'Ubaydah and a group said: the bi is superfluous, the estimated meaning being: "and do not cast your hands into destruction," and the hand is used to refer to the self, as if it were said: "and do not cast your selves into destruction." The bi has been added to the object, as in His saying:

"Black-eyed, they do not read the suwar."

That is: they do not read the suwar. But the addition of bi to the object is not analogous (not a general rule). It has also been said that the object of alqa is deleted, the estimated meaning being: "do not cast your selves with your hands into destruction," and the bi is connected to tulqu, and the bi is for causation, as you say: "Do not ruin your condition by your opinion."

What we choose in this is that the object in meaning is "with your hands," but alqa has been given the meaning of what is transitive by bi, so it was made transitive by it, as if it were said: "do not extend your hands to destruction." Like His saying: "I laid my side upon the earth," meaning: I placed my side on the earth. In that case the selves are referred to by the hands, because by them is movement, grasping and defense. It is as if He says: the thing whose nature is to be defended from destruction, and not neglected from what it was made for, and led to destruction by it. The meanings of af'ala were discussed at the beginning of al-Baqarah; there are twenty-four meanings. I presented them against the form alqa and found that the closest thing said about it is that af'ala is for making (al-ja'l). According to what the morphologists (al-tasrifiyyun) inferred, it divides into three categories.

The first category: that you make something do what it does, like your saying akhrajtuhu, meaning: I made him go out. In this type the hamza is for transitivity.

The second category: that you make something have a certain attribute, like your saying atradtuhu. Here the hamza is not for transitivity, because the verb was already transitive without it, and the meaning is: I made him an outcast (tarid).

The third category: that you make something the possessor of a thing in some respect. From this: ashfaytu fulanan, meaning I made for him a medicine by which he is cured, and asqaytuhu, meaning I made him one who has water with which he waters what needs watering. From this category: aqbartuhu (I buried him), an'altuhu (I shod him), arkabtuhu (I mounted him), akhdamtuhu (I gave him a servant), and a'badtuhu (I made him a slave): I made for him a grave, a shoe, a mount, a servant, a slave.

As for alqa, it is from the second category. The meaning of alqaytu al-shay' is: I made the thing a laqiy, and laqiy is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, just as tarid is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul. So it is as if it were said: "Do not make yourselves a laqiy (something cast) into destruction, so that you perish." Al-Zamakhshari approached this meaning which we have supported, but he did not succeed in clarifying it. He said: The bi in "bi-aydikum" is like its use in a'ta bi-yadihi (he gave with his hand) to the one who is submissive. The meaning is: "do not let destruction seize your hands," that is, do not make it grasping with your hands, possessing you. End of his words.

In his statement, the bi is superfluous, and we have mentioned that this is not analogous.

(Wa-ahsinu) This is a command to goodness. It is better to take it as a request for goodness without restricting it to a specific object. 'Ikrimah said: the meaning is: "and think well of Allah." Zayd ibn Aslam said: "and do good by spending in the way of Allah and in charities." It has also been said: "and do good in your deeds by carrying out acts of obedience." Some of the Companions said this. It has been said that the meaning of "and do good" is: strive in the way of Allah, and the one who strives is a doer of good.

﴿Indeed, Allah loves the good-doers.﴾ This is an incitement to goodness, because in it is an announcement that Allah loves those whose attribute is goodness. Whoever is loved by Allah for this attribute should have the attribute of goodness constantly, such that Allah's love never ceases to be with him.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 194–195:

﴿The sacred month for the sacred month, and sacred things demand retaliation.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, Miqsam, al-Suddi, al-Rabi', al-Dahhak and others said: It was revealed concerning the 'Umrat al-Qada' (the make-up 'Umrah) in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah. The polytheists had fought them that year in the sacred month, which is Dhu al-Qa'dah. So it was said to them when they set out for the make-up 'Umrah, and they were averse to fighting, and that was in Dhu al-Qa'dah: ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month﴾, meaning: its violation for its violation. You violate its sanctity against them, just as they violated its sanctity against you.

Al-Hasan said: The unbelievers asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Do you fight in the sacred month?" He told them that he would not fight in it. So they resolved to attack him and kill those with him, when they thought he would not fight. Then it was revealed.

"Al-shahr" (the month) is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is the prepositional phrase following it. Lexically it cannot be the predicate, so an ellipsis is necessary. The estimated meaning is: the violation of the sanctity of the sacred month occurs through the violation of the sanctity of the sacred month. The alif and lam in "al-shahr" are, in wording, for prior reference (al-'ahd). So the first month is Dhu al-Qa'dah of the seventh year, at the 'Umrat al-Qada', and the second month is that of the sixth year, the year of al-Hudaybiyyah. ﴿And sacred things demand retaliation﴾: the alif and lam in "al-hurumat" are for prior reference. That is: the sanctity of the month, the sanctity of those in ihram (muhrimin) when you were barred, and the sanctity of the land (al-balad), the month, and fighting when you entered. This interpretation follows the occasion of revelation reported from Ibn 'Abbas and those with him. As for the occasion reported from al-Hasan, the alif and lam are for generality, covering life, property and honor. That is: every sanctity in which retaliation applies, so those earlier sanctities and others are included. It has also been said that ﴿and sacred things demand retaliation﴾ is a separate sentence, cut off from what precedes it, not concerning the matter of Hajj and 'Umrah. Rather, it is the start of a ruling that existed at the beginning of Islam. That is: whoever violates your sanctity, you may inflict upon him the same as he inflicted upon you. Then this was abrogated (naskh) by fighting.

A group said: Whatever transgression occurs in property or injury has not been abrogated. One may transgress against the offender in the same way he transgressed, and may do so secretly if he is able, without the judge, and he does not sin by this. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, and it is a narration in the school of Malik. Another group, including Malik, said: retaliation (qisas) is reserved for the rulers, so none may exact it except them.

Al-Hasan recited "﴿wal-hurumatu﴾" with a sukun on the ra' (ḥurmāt), according to the original form, since it is the plural of ḥurmah. The ḍamma in the plural is an assimilation (ittiba').

﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you.﴾ This confirms what came before it, His words: ﴿and sacred things demand retaliation﴾. There is disagreement about it: is it abrogated or not? (p-70) According to what preceded from the school of al-Shafi'i and the school of Malik. Ibn 'Abbas said: this verse and what is similar to it were revealed in Mecca, when Islam was not yet strong. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) emigrated and his religion became strong, the Muslims were commanded to refer their affairs to their rulers, and they were commanded to fight the unbelievers. Mujahid said: rather, this verse was revealed in Medina after the 'Umrat al-Qada', and it is part of the gradual progression in the command to fight.

His words ﴿fa'taduu﴾ (transgress) are not a command of obligation, since pardon is permissible. The act was called "transgression" by way of reciprocity. The preposition bi in "bi-mithli" (in the same manner) is connected to ﴿fa'taduu 'alayhi﴾, and the meaning is: with a punishment equal to the offence of his transgression. It has also been said that the bi is superfluous, meaning "like his transgression," and it is an adjective of a deleted verbal noun, meaning: a transgression equal to his transgression.

﴿And fear Allah﴾ is a command to be mindful of Allah, and it includes being mindful of Him by not transgressing in retaliation beyond what is lawful.

The word "ma'a" (with), which indicates companionship and constancy, is used here to urge people to piety at all times, for whoever has Allah with him is the victorious one who prevails. Do you not see what came in the hadith: "Shoot, and I am with the sons of so-and-so," and they held back, so he said: "Shoot, and I am with you all," or words to this effect? Likewise his saying to Hassan: "Satirize them, and the Holy Spirit is with you."

It has been said that the meaning is a command to spend on the price of weapons of war. It has also been said that it is for the poor among the fighters. Ibn 'Abbas said this, saying: It was revealed concerning some Bedouins who asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), saying: "With what should we equip ourselves? By Allah, we have no provisions." It has also been said that it refers to striving with oneself and with others. It has been said that it refers to striving (jihad) with oneself and others. And it has been said the meaning is: offer your souls in striving in the way of Allah.

The giving of one's soul in the way of Allah has been called "spending" by way of metaphor and extension, like the saying of the poet:

"I spent my life in idleness and youth, so no life remains for me, and no reward remains for me."

The more apparent view is the first opinion, which is the command to direct wealth to acts of righteousness: whether Hajj, or 'Umrah, or striving with one's self, or equipping another, or maintaining kinship ties, or charity, or supporting dependents, or zakat, or expiation, or building roads, or other than these.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 196 (part 1 of 5):**

﴿And complete the Hajj (pilgrimage) and the ʿUmrah (lesser pilgrimage) for Allah﴾. Completion (al-itmam), as mentioned earlier, is the opposite of deficiency. The meaning is: perform both of them complete, and do not perform them deficient in any of their conditions or their acts, those on which the existence of their reality (mahiyyah) depends, as Ghaylan said:

*The completion of the Hajj is that the mounts stop
at the one with the split (lip) and loose veil.*

He made the stopping of the mounts at his beloved, who is Mayy, like some of the rites of the Hajj, which is not complete except by it. This is the apparent meaning of the wording. "Completion" has been interpreted otherwise than what the apparent meaning requires. Al-Shaʿbi and Ibn Zayd said: its completion is that it is not interrupted, and that you complete both of them once you have begun them.

ʿAli, Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, Saʿid and Tawus said: its completion is that you enter the state of ihram (ritual consecration) for them separately from the dwelling of your family, and ʿImran ibn Husayn did so. Al-Thawri said: its completion is that you set out intending them only, not for trade or anything else, and this is supported by His saying "for Allah." Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad and Qatadah said: its completion is that you enter ihram for the ʿUmrah and perform it outside the months of Hajj, and that you complete the Hajj without deficiency and without compensation by a sacrifice. A group said: its completion is that you perform each one of Hajj or ʿUmrah separately and do not combine them (qiran), and separate performance (ifrad) is better according to these.

Some people said: its completion is that you combine them (qiran), and combining is better according to these. Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAlqamah, Ibrahim and others said: its completion is that you perform their rites fully, along with what is due in them of sacrifices, and this is close to the first opinion. Some people said: it is that one sets out a separate journey for each of them. It was said: it is that the expenses are lawful. Muqatil said: its completion is that you do not make lawful in them what is not permitted, and they used to associate in their ihram, saying: "Here I am, O Allah, here I am, You have no partner, except a partner who belongs to You, You possess him and what he possesses." So He said: complete them and do not mix anything with them.

Al-Maturidi said: He only said ﴿And complete the Hajj and the ʿUmrah for Allah﴾ because the disbelievers used to perform the Hajj for Allah and the ʿUmrah for the idol. Al-Marwazi said: the disbelievers used to make Hajj to the idols.

ʿAlqamah recited: "Wa-aqimu al-hajja" (and establish the Hajj). Talhah ibn Musarrif recited "al-Hijja" with a kasrah (vowel i) here and in Al ʿImran, and with a fathah (vowel a) in the rest of the Qur'an. The recitation of Ibn Ishaq "al-Hijja" with a kasrah in the whole Qur'an has already been mentioned, and the difference concerning His saying "hajja al-bayt" (performed the pilgrimage to the House) will come in its place.

Ibn Masʿud recited: "And complete the Hajj and the ʿUmrah to the House for Allah." ʿAli, Ibn Masʿud, Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar, al-Shaʿbi and Abu Haywah recited: "wal-ʿumratu lillah" with a raf (nominative ending), as a subject and predicate, so the ʿUmrah goes out of the command and the Hajj stands alone with it. It was also narrated from him: "Wa-aqimu al-hajja wal-ʿumrata ila al-bayt." All of this should be taken as explanation (tafsir), because it contradicts the consonantal text of the codex (mushaf) on which the Muslims have agreed.

"Lillah" is connected to "atimmu," and it is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlih). It may also be in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal), with the governing word omitted, its estimated form being: "being for Allah." There is no disagreement that the Hajj is obligatory (fard), and that it is one of the pillars on which Islam is built. Its obligatory elements (furud) are: the intention (niyyah), the ihram, the tawaf (circumambulation) connected to the sa'y (running) between al-Safa and al-Marwah, contrary to Abu Hanifah, standing at ʿArafah, and the stoning of the jamrah according to the opinion of Ibn al-Majishun, and standing at Muzdalifah according to the opinion of al-Awzaʿi.

As for the acts of the ʿUmrah: they are intention, ihram, tawaf and sa'y. The command to complete the Hajj and the ʿUmrah does not indicate the obligation of the ʿUmrah, nor that it is a sunnah (recommended practice), for the fasting of Ramadan and some of Shawwal may be valid, by the common ground in what they share of being sought, even if the aspects of the request differ. For this reason the opinion of those who argued that the ʿUmrah is obligatory from His saying "and complete" is weak. This was narrated from ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar, Masruq, ʿAta, Tawus, Mujahid, Ibn Sirin, al-Shaʿbi, Ibn Jubayr, Abu Burdah, and ʿAbd Allah ibn Shaddad. Among the scholars of the regions were al-Shafiʿi, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu ʿUbayd, and Ibn Hamim among the Malikis.

A group of the Companions went to the view that the ʿUmrah is a sunnah, among them Ibn Masʿud and Jabir; among the Successors, al-Nakhaʿi; and among the scholars of the regions, Malik and Abu Hanifah, except that when one begins it, its completion becomes obligatory according to them both. Some of the Qazwinis and Baghdadis related two opinions from Abu Hanifah, and the proofs are recorded in the books of jurisprudence.

* *

﴿Then if you are prevented (uhsirtum)﴾. Its apparent meaning is that this ruling applies to the community, and that one exits the state of ihram by being prevented (ihsar).

It was narrated from ʿAʾishah and Ibn ʿAbbas that one does not exit one's ihram except by performing one's rite and remaining in ihram until the prevention is lifted. It is not permitted for a muhrim (one in ihram) to exit by ihsar after the Prophet (ﷺ). If his ihram was for ʿUmrah, it is not lost; if it was for Hajj and he missed it, he makes it up by the missing (qada' bil-fawat) after exiting from it. The discussion of ihsar has already preceded.

It is established by the transmission of those who transmitted from the lexicographers that ihsar and hasr are the same, and that both are used for prevention by an enemy, by illness, and by other impediments. So the verse is taken to cover that, and the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) came in response to one of the absolute applications of ihsar. There is no restriction in the verse. Qatadah, al-Hasan, ʿAta, al-Nakhaʿi, Mujahid and Abu Hanifah said this. ʿAlqamah and ʿUrwah said: the verse was revealed concerning one prevented by illness, not by an enemy. Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn al-Zubayr, Malik and al-Shafiʿi said: ihsar is only by an enemy alone. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the verse was revealed concerning one prevented by an enemy, not by illness. Malik and al-Shafiʿi said: even if one is prevented by illness, only the House releases him, and he remains until he recovers, even if it takes years.

The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿if you are prevented﴾ is equality between the Makkan and the one from outside in this. ʿUrwah, al-Zuhri and Abu Hanifah said: there is no ihsar for the people of Makkah.

The apparent meaning of the wording "uhsirtum" is absolute ihsar, whether one knows that the enemy remains there, with his strength and numbers, so that the one prevented exits at once where he is according to the majority, or whether his departure is expected. It was said: he is not permitted to exit except after there remains between him and the Hajj the amount of time he knows that, were the enemy to depart, he would not reach the Hajj; then he exits at that time. Ibn al-Qasim and Ibn al-Majishun said this.

It was said: whoever is prevented from the Hajj by an excuse until the day of sacrifice (yawm al-nahr), he does not cut off the talbiyah (the chant of "Here I am") until the people set out for ʿArafah. The absolute ihsar includes before ʿArafah and after it, contrary to Abu Hanifah, for whoever is prevented in Makkah, or after standing at ʿArafah, is not considered prevented. The building of the verb in the passive form indicates that being prevented by a Muslim or by a disbeliever is the same.

﴿Then what is easy of the sacrificial animal (hady)﴾. It is a sheep, said ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAta, Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, Ibrahim, al-Dahhak and Mughirah. It has been called hady in His saying: ﴿an offering reaching the Kaʿbah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95]. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: the best of it is a camel, its middle is a cow, and its least is a sheep. Malik said this too.

Abu Yusuf and Zufar said: it may be from any of the three, the "easy" being according to the condition of the one offering and according to what is available.

Tawus narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that it is according to the measure of one's means. Ibn ʿUmar, ʿAʾishah, al-Qasim and ʿUrwah said: it is a camel but not just any camel, and a cow but not just any cow, and the hady is only from these two, and a sheep is not from the hady. Abu Hanifah said this. Ibn Shubrumah said: only from camels. Al-Awzaʿi said: males of camels and cattle are offered. If the one prevented does not find the hady, is there a substitute to which he moves? Abu Hanifah said: it remains in his obligation forever, and he does not exit until he finds a hady and slaughters it on his behalf. Ahmad said: there is a substitute. There are two opinions from al-Shafiʿi. According to the first view, he remains in his ihram or exits, two opinions. According to the second, the hady is valued in dirhams, and food is bought with them. All agree that there is no substitute for the hady.

The apparent meaning is that the ʿUmrah is like the Hajj in the ruling of ihsar, and this is what most jurists said. Ibn Sirin said there is no ihsar in ʿUmrah, because it is not time-bound.

The apparent meaning is that no age is required for the hady. Abu Hanifah and al-Shafiʿi said: only a thaniyy (one who has shed his milk teeth) and older is acceptable. Malik said: only a thaniyy and older of camels is acceptable. It is permitted for seven to share one cow or one camel, and this is the view of Abu Hanifah, al-Awzaʿi and al-Shafiʿi.

Malik said: this is permitted in voluntary (tatawwuʿ) offerings, not in obligatory ones. The apparent meaning is the obligation of ﴿what is easy of the sacrificial animal﴾. Ibn al-Qasim said: one does not offer anything unless he has a hady with him. The majority hold that one exits where he is prevented, and performs his hady immediately if there is a hady there, and shaves his head.

Qatadah and Ibrahim said: he sends his hady if he is able, and when it reaches its place of sacrifice (mahall), he becomes lawful.

Abu Hanifah said: if he is a pilgrim (hajj), then in the Haram whenever he wishes. Abu Yusuf and Muhammad said, regarding the days of sacrifice: and if he is a ʿUmrah pilgrim, then in the Haram at any time, according to all of them, "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) slaughtered his hady where he was prevented," and the edge of al-Hudaybiyah was the hills below Makkah, and it is part of the Haram. It was narrated from al-Zuhri that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) [p. 74] "slaughtered his hady in the Haram." Al-Waqidi said: al-Hudaybiyah is the edge of the Haram, nine miles from Makkah.

They differed regarding stipulation (ishtirat) in Hajj if one fears being prevented by an enemy or by illness. The formula of stipulation is that one says when he declares the talbiyah: "Here I am, O Allah, here I am, and my release is where You hold me back." Al-Thawri, Abu Hanifah, Malik and their companions went to the view that stipulation does not benefit him. Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Thawr and al-Shafiʿi, in the old opinion, said: there is no harm in stipulating, and there are conditions for it. There is a hadith on it recorded in the Sahih. There is no qada' (make-up) obligation upon him according to all, except for one who had not performed Hajj; upon him is the Hajj of Islam. Ibn al-Majishun deviated and said: he is not obligated to the Hajj of Islam, since he performed it when he was prevented.

The "ma" in His saying ﴿fa-ma istaysara﴾ is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), and it is a subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is omitted, its estimated form being: "upon him is what is easy." This was said by al-Akhfash. Or it is in the accusative position: "then let him offer," said by Ahmad ibn Yahya. It may also be the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimated form being: "then the obligation for him is what is easy." The verb "istaysara" has the meaning of the bare verb, i.e., "yasura" (to be easy), in the sense of "istaghna wa-ghaniya" (to be sufficient) and "istasʿaba wa-saʿuba" (to be difficult), and it is one of the meanings for which the form "istaf'ala" came.

"Min" here is partitive (tabʿidiyyah), and it is in the circumstantial position from the hidden pronoun in "istaysara," which refers back to "ma," so it is connected to an omitted element, the estimated form being: "being from the hady." Whoever permits "min" to be explanatory of the kind (li-bayan al-jins) permits that here. The "al" in "al-hady" is for generality.

Mujahid, al-Zuhri, Ibn Hurmuz and Abu Haywah recited "al-Hadiyyi" with a kasrah on the dal and a shaddah on the ya in both places, meaning here in the genitive and nominative cases. ʿIsmah narrated that from ʿAsim.

* *

﴿And do not shave your heads until the hady reaches its place of sacrifice﴾. This is a prohibition of shaving the head, limited by the arrival of the hady at its place of sacrifice. Its implied meaning (mafhum): when the hady reaches its place of sacrifice, then shave your heads. The pronoun in "tahliquu" may refer to those addressed by the completion, so it includes the one prevented and others. It may also refer to those prevented. Both possibilities were held by a group. It may also be an address to those prevented, and this is the view of al-Zamakhshari, who said: that is, do not exit until you know that the hady that you sent to the Haram has reached its place of sacrifice, meaning the place where it must be slaughtered, and the place of a debt is the time when its payment is due. This is according to the apparent doctrine of Abu Hanifah. End of his words.

Abu Hayyan's commentary on al-Bahr al-Muhit, Surah 2, verse 196 (part 2 of 5):

It seems he preferred that it refers to those who are prevented (al-muhsarin), because it is the closest thing mentioned. The apparent meaning of Ibn 'Atiyya's statement is that he prefers the address to be to the whole community, whether the muhrim (the one in the state of ihram) is prevented or free, because he put this view first and then related the other view. He said: "Some scholars hold that it is for those who are prevented only, in His words: ﴿And do not shave your heads﴾. It is a metaphor (majaz) in both the agent and the object. As for the agent, the shaving is attributed to all of them, although only some of them shave the heads of others. This is a common and widespread metaphor. You say: 'I shaved my head,' and the meaning is that someone else shaved it for you. As for the metaphor in the object, the estimate is: 'the hair of your heads,' so it is an elision of a modifier (hadhf mudaf). The address is specific to the men, and shaving for women is similar to it in the Hajj and elsewhere; what is prescribed for women in the Hajj is only shortening (taqsir)."

Abu Dawud related from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no shaving for women; for them there is only shortening." The scholars have agreed upon this, but they differed over the amount of hair to be shortened, with many estimates mentioned in fiqh (jurisprudence). This verse does not address shortening, so we will not address it here; we digressed to it from His words: ﴿And do not shave﴾.

The apparent meaning of the prohibition is prohibition and forbiddance until the hady (sacrificial animal) reaches its place of sacrifice (mahill). So if someone forgets and shaves before the sacrifice, Abu Hanifa and Ibn al-Majishun said: he is like one who did it deliberately. Ibn al-Qasim said: there is nothing upon him. If he does it deliberately, Abu Hanifa and Malik said: it is not permitted. Al-Shafi'i said: it is permitted. They said: this contradicts the apparent meaning of the verse.

The verse indicates that shaving the head is among the rites (nusuk) of the Hajj, and this indicates its permissibility outside the Hajj, contrary to those who said that shaving the head outside the Hajj is mutilation (muthla), because if it were mutilation it would not be permitted either in the Hajj or elsewhere.

It has been related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) "shaved the heads of the sons of Ja'far three days after the news of his death reached him." 'Ali used to shave. Abu 'Umar Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: the scholars have agreed on the permissibility of shaving. The apparent general meaning of ﴿And do not shave﴾, or its specific application to those who are prevented, is that shaving for them is a rite (nusuk). This is the view of Malik and Abu Yusuf.

Abu Hanifa and Muhammad said: there is no shaving for the one who is prevented (al-muhsar), and there are two views from al-Shafi'i.

﴿Until the hady reaches its place of sacrifice﴾: the place where he was prevented, whether in the hill (outside the sacred precinct) or the haram (the sacred precinct). This was said by 'Umar, al-Miswar ibn Makhrama, and Marwan ibn al-Hakam. Or it means the muhrim, as said by 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', al-Hasan, and Mujahid. Their explanation indicates that the mahall here means the place. It has not been read except with a kasra on the ha' (mahill), as far as we know, though a fatha (mahall) is permissible when it is intended to mean the place. Al-Kisa'i distinguished here, saying: the kasra refers to the release from ihram (ihlal), and the fatha refers to the place of alighting (mawdi' al-hulul) in the case of being prevented. A portion of the discussion about the mahall of the hady has already been mentioned. The verse does not address what is due from the one who is prevented in the Hajj when he exits the state by means of the hady. Concerning the one who is prevented, there is a view that it is a Hajj (to be made up) upon him. Al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin, Ibrahim, 'Alqama, al-Qasim, Ibn Mas'ud as related from him by Mujahid, and Ibn 'Abbas as related from him by Ibn Jubayr, said: upon him is a Hajj and an 'Umra. If he combines the two in the months of Hajj, then upon him is a dam (sacrificial animal) and he is a mutamatti' (one who performs tamattu'). If he does not combine them in the months of Hajj, then there is no dam upon him. If the one prevented by illness or by an enemy was in the state of ihram for a voluntary Hajj or a voluntary 'Umra, and he exited by the hady, then upon him is the obligation of making up (qada') according to Abu Hanifa. Malik and al-Shafi'i said: there is no qada' upon the one prevented by an enemy, neither in Hajj nor in 'Umra.

* *

﴿So whoever among you is ill or has an injury from his head﴾. The occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) is "the well-known hadith of Ka'b ibn 'Ujra, that he (ﷺ) saw him while lice were falling from his head." It was also said: he saw him when his head had sores. Since the prohibition on shaving had been mentioned up to the limit, which is the arrival of the hady at its place, that prohibition was comprehensive, and so it was specified for the one who is not ill and does not have an injury from his head. As for these two, shaving was permitted for them. There is an elided element through which the speech is correct. The estimate is: "So whoever among you is ill, and thus does what is forbidden to the muhrim, such as shaving or other things, or has an injury from his head and so shaves." The apparent meaning of the prohibition is general. Some scholars said: it is specific to the one who is prevented, because shaving before the hady reaches its place is not permitted, and so he may be afflicted by illness or an injury in his head if he endures, so he was permitted to remove that by way of the requirement of ransom (fidya). Most scholars hold that it is general, and the story of Ibn 'Ujra indicates this.

"Minkum" (from among you) is connected to an elided element and is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). Before it was placed first, it was an attribute of "marida" (ill), so when it was placed first it became in the accusative as a circumstantial clause. The "min" here is partitive. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be connected to "marida," but this is hardly conceivable. As for "aw bihi adha min ra'sihi" (or has an injury from his head), it is possible that it is of the type of coordinating single words (min bab 'atf al-mufradat), so it is coordinated with His words "marida," and "adha" is in the nominative as the agent of the preposition-phrase "bihi," the estimate being: "or there is in him an injury from his head." It may also be of the type of coordinating a clause with a single word, because that clause is in the position of a single word, so this clause is coordinated with His words "marida," and it is in the position of a single word, because a coordinated element after a single word is a single word in estimation when it is a clause. "Adha" is then nominative as a subject of a predicate in the position of the predicate, so it is in the nominative position, and in the previous parsing it is in the accusative position. They also permitted that it be coordinated with an elided "kana" (was), because the first "kana" indicates it. The estimate: "or there was in him an injury from his head." The subject of "kana" in this case is either a pronoun referring to "man" (whoever), "wa bihi adha" being a subject and predicate in the position of the predicate of "kana"; or "adha wa bihi" is in the position of the predicate of "kana." Abu al-Baqa' also permitted that "aw bihi adha min ra'sihi" be coordinated with "kana," and "adha" is nominative by the inchoative, and "bihi" is the predicate related to the stable (al-istiqrar), and the "ha'" in "bihi" refers back to "man." Abu al-Baqa' had earlier stated that "man" is conditional, and on this estimate what he said is an error, because a coordinated element following the conditional clause must be a verbal clause, since the conditional clause must be verbal, and the element coordinated with the condition is a condition, so what must apply to the condition applies to it. What Abu al-Baqa' said is not permitted on the estimate that "man" is relative, because in that case it implies the meaning of the conditional noun, so it cannot be connected to a nominal clause according to the well-known view. The "ba'" in "bihi" is for attachment, and it may be locative. "Min ra'sihi" may be connected to what "bihi" is connected to, and it may be in the position of an attribute of "adha." On both estimates, "min" is for the beginning of the limit.

﴿Then a ransom of fasting, or charity, or a sacrifice﴾. The "fidya" is nominative as an inchoative, the estimate being "then upon him is a ransom," or as a predicate, meaning "then the obligation is a ransom." Some exegetes mentioned that it was read in the accusative by implying a verb, the estimate being: "then let him ransom with a ransom." "Min siyam" (of fasting) is in the position of an attribute, and "aw" here is for choice, so the one who ransoms is free to choose any of the three he wishes.

Al-Hasan and al-Zuhri read "aw nusk" with a sukun on the sin. The apparent meaning is the unrestricted application of fasting, charity, and sacrifice, but the Sunna established in the hadith of Ibn 'Ujra restricts this: fasting is three days, charity is feeding six poor people, and the sacrifice is a sheep. Those who held that fasting is three days include 'Ata', Mujahid, Ibrahim, 'Alqama, al-Rabi', and others. Malik and the majority held the same. It was related from al-Hasan, 'Ikrima, and Nafi' that it is ten days. Its place and time are wherever and whenever he chooses. As for feeding, some of them mentioned the consensus on six poor people, and this is not as they mentioned; rather al-Hasan and 'Ikrima said: he feeds ten poor people. There is disagreement about the quantity of food and the place of feeding. As for the quantity, the reports about the hadith of 'Ujra are inconsistent, and the jurists differ about it. Abu Hanifa said: for each poor person, a sa' of dates, or half a sa' of wheat. Malik and al-Shafi'i said: the food in that is two mudd for each person, by the Prophetic mudd (mudd al-nabawi). This is the view of Abu Thawr and Dawud. It is related from al-Thawri: half a sa' of wheat, and a sa' of dates, barley, or raisins. Ahmad said once with a view like that of Malik, and once he said: two mudd of wheat for each poor person, and half a sa' of dates. Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf said: it suffices for him to give them lunch and dinner. Malik, al-Thawri, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, and al-Shafi'i said: this does not suffice until he gives each poor person two mudd each, by the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ).

As for the place, 'Ali, Ibrahim, and 'Ata' in some of what is related from him, and Malik and his companions except Ibn al-Jahm, and the companions of opinion (ashab al-ra'y), said: wherever he wishes. Al-Hasan, Tawus, Mujahid, also 'Ata', and al-Shafi'i said: the feeding is in Mecca. As for the sacrifice, it is a sheep. They said by consensus that whoever sacrifices something better than it, then it is better. As for its place, it is wherever he wishes, as said by 'Ali, Ibrahim, Malik, and his companions except Ibn al-Jahm. He said: the sacrifice is only in Mecca. 'Ata' in some of what is related from him, al-Hasan, Tawus, Mujahid, Abu Hanifa, and al-Shafi'i said likewise.

The apparent meaning of the ransom is that it is not required except after shaving, since the estimate is: "if he shaves, then a ransom." Al-Awza'i said: it suffices for him to expiate by the ransom before shaving, so the meaning becomes: "then a ransom of fasting, or charity, or sacrifice, if he intends to shave." The apparent meaning of the condition is that the ransom is only attached to the one who has an illness or an injury and shaves. So if he shaves, or cuts, or removes his hair with depilatory cream (nura) without necessity, or wears sewn clothing, or applies perfume without an excuse, knowingly, then Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i and his companions, and Abu Thawr said: there is no option in other than necessity, and upon him is a dam only. Malik said: he has the option. Deliberate and mistaken acts, whether with necessity or otherwise, are the same according to him. If he did it forgetfully, Ishaq and Dawud said: there is nothing upon him. Abu Hanifa, al-Thawri, Malik, and al-Layth said: the forgetful one is like the deliberate one regarding the obligation of that amount. There are two views from al-Shafi'i. Most scholars require the ransom for wearing sewn clothing, covering the head or part of it, wearing leather socks, trimming nails, applying perfume, removing harm, shaving body hair, or the places of cupping (hijama). For man and woman in this matter, it is the same. Some of them make a dam upon both of them for each of these things. Dawud said: there is nothing upon them for shaving body hair.

* *

﴿Then when you are secure﴾, meaning: from being prevented. This security's interpretation is ordered upon the interpretation of being prevented. So whoever interpreted it there as being prevented by illness and not by an enemy, takes the security here to be from illness and not from an enemy, and this is the view of 'Alqama and 'Urwa. The meaning is: "then when you are cured of your illness."

Whoever interprets it as being prevented by an enemy and not by illness says here: the security is from the enemy and not from illness. The meaning is: "then when you are secure from your fear of the enemy."

Whoever interprets being prevented as being from an enemy, illness, and the like, the security here for him is from all of that. Security is a tranquility that arises in the heart after its agitation. It has come in the hadith: "The cold (zukam) is a security from leprosy (judham)." Ibn Majah related it. It also came: whoever "precedes the one sneezing with praise is secured from al-shaws, al-lawsh, and al-'ilwas," meaning: from toothache, earache, and stomach pain.

The address, apparently, is general to the one who is prevented and to others. That is: "when you are in a state of security and ease." This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and a group. 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, 'Alqama, and Ibrahim said: the verse is about those who are prevented, not about those whose way is free.

﴿Whoever performs Umrah and then Hajj (in tamattu')﴾. The discussion of enjoyment (matā') has already been covered in His words: ﴿and provision for a time﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36]. Tamattu' is explained here as dropping one of the two journeys, because the proper form of Umrah is to be performed on a journey separate from the journey of Hajj. It was also said that it is called tamattu' because the pilgrim enjoys everything that is otherwise unlawful, from the time he exits the state of ihram for Umrah until the time he enters into ihram for Hajj.

Scholars differed about the form of this tamattu' mentioned in the verse. Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr said: it refers to the one who was prevented (from completing his pilgrimage) until he missed Hajj. Then he arrived in Mecca and exited his ihram by performing an Umrah, and he enjoyed his release from ihram through that Umrah until the following year, then he performs Hajj and offers a sacrifice.

Ibn Jubayr, 'Alqama and Ibrahim said its meaning is: "So when you are secure and you have been released from your ihram after being prevented, and you have not performed an Umrah by which you exit your ihram with your Hajj, but rather you were released where you were prevented, by the offering, and you postponed the Umrah until the coming year, and you performed Umrah in the months of Hajj, and thus you enjoyed your release until your Hajj, then upon you is what is easy of the offering." 'Ali said: that is, if he postpones the Umrah until he combines it with Hajj, then upon him is an offering. Al-Suddi said: whoever converts his Hajj into an Umrah, making it an Umrah, and enjoys his Umrah until his Hajj. Ibn Abbas, 'Ata' and a group said: it is the man who precedes (the months) as a pilgrim (for Umrah) from a distant horizon during the months of Hajj; when he completes his Umrah he remains in a state of release in Mecca until he begins Hajj from there in that same year. So he is enjoying the release until he enters ihram for Hajj. Thus the meaning of tamattu' is the assuming of ihram for Umrah; he remains in a state of release, doing what a person in a state of release does, and then he performs Hajj after his release from Umrah without returning to the miqat.

The verse is capable of all these opinions. There is no disagreement among scholars that Hajj occurs in three forms: tamattu', ifrad, and qiran. This has been explained in the books of jurisprudence. The prohibition of tamattu' attributed to 'Umar is perhaps not authentic; some have interpreted it as referring to the cancelling of Hajj into Umrah, but as for tamattu' with Umrah until Hajj, then it is not (prohibited).

﴿then what is easy of the offering﴾. The discussion of this clause, both its exegesis and its i'rab (grammatical analysis), has already been given in His words: ﴿but if you are prevented, then what is easy of the offering﴾, so it suffices without repeating it. The fa' in "fa-idha amintum" (then when you are secure) is for coordination (ataf); in "fa-man tamatta'a" (then whoever performs tamattu') it is the response of the conditional; and in "fa-ma" it is the response to the second conditional. A conditional and its response may serve as the response to a conditional introduced by fa', and we know of no disagreement about this, as in the example: "If you enter the house, then if you speak to Zayd, then you are divorced."

The offering of tamattu' is an act of worship (nusuk) according to Abu Hanifa, because it combines the two acts of worship during one journey, and he (the pilgrim) eats from it. According to al-Shafi'i, it is treated as a penalty (jinayat) for abandoning one of the two journeys, and he does not eat from it. It is slaughtered on the Day of Sacrifice according to Abu Hanifa, and according to al-Shafi'i it is permissible to slaughter it once he has entered ihram for his Hajj. The apparent position is that slaughter is obligatory upon the occurrence of tamattu', immediately after it.

The form of tamattu' according to the one who makes the phrase "So when you are secure, then whoever performs tamattu'" specific to those who were prevented, has already been presented in the opinion of Ibn al-Zubayr and the opinion of Ibn Jubayr and those with him. As for the one who makes it general to the one who was prevented and others, then tamattu' has forms. The first: that a non-Meccan enters ihram for Umrah first, during the months of Hajj, in a single journey in one year; he arrives in Mecca, completes the Umrah, then remains in a state of release until he begins Hajj from Mecca in the year of the Umrah, before he returns to his own land or before he sets out to the miqat of the people of his region. The Hajj and Umrah are then on behalf of one person.

The second: that he combines Hajj and Umrah in one ihram, which is called qiran (combination). He says: "Labbayka with Hajj and Umrah together." When he arrives in Mecca, he performs tawaf and sa'y for his Hajj and Umrah. It was narrated from 'Ali and Ibn Mas'ud that he performs two tawafs and two sa'ys. This was the view of al-Sha'bi, Jabir ibn Zayd and Ibn Abi Layla. It was narrated from Abdullah ibn Umar and Jabir ibn Abdullah that there is one tawaf and one sa'y for both. This was also the view of 'Ata', al-Hasan, Mujahid, Tawus, Malik, al-Shafi'i and their companions, Ishaq, and Abu Thawr. Qiran has been classed under tamattu' because of the avoidance of the hardship of travelling to Umrah once and to Hajj another time, and because of combining them, and because he did not enter ihram separately at each miqat. So this is an aspect of tamattu' about whose permissibility there is no disagreement. It has been said: the people of Mecca do not permit combining Umrah and Hajj except with the driving of the offering, which for you is a camel (badanah) that may not be less than that. Malik said: I have not heard that a Meccan performed qiran; if he did, there is no offering upon him nor fasting. The majority of jurists follow this view. Ibn al-Majishun said: if a Meccan combines Hajj with Umrah, the offering of qiran is upon him. Abdullah ibn Umar said: if a Meccan performs tamattu' or qiran, there is upon him neither the offering of qiran nor of tamattu'.

(p-78)

The third: that he enters ihram for Hajj, and when he enters Mecca he cancels his Hajj into an Umrah, then he exits (ihram) and remains in a state of release until he enters ihram for Hajj on the Day of Tarwiyah. The majority of scholars refrain from acting upon this. It was narrated from Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Suddi that it is permissible, and this is the view of Ahmad.

The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that the offering is obligatory for the one (who performs tamattu'), or fasting for the one who does not find (an offering), when he performs tamattu' with Umrah in the months of Hajj, then returns to his own land, then performs Hajj in the same year. This is narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and al-Hasan. It has been narrated from al-Hasan that he is not considered a tamattu' performer, so there is neither offering nor fasting; this is the view of the majority. The apparent meaning of the verse is that if he performs Umrah after the Day of Sacrifice, he is not a tamattu' performer; on this they said there is consensus (ijma'), because tamattu' is limited (ghayah) to Hajj and the thing limited was not realised. Al-Hasan was an outlier and said: it is mut'ah (enjoyment). The apparent meaning is that if he performs Umrah outside the months of Hajj, then remains until the months of Hajj, then performs Hajj in the same year, he is a tamattu' performer; this is the view of Tawus. The majority said: he is not a tamattu' performer.

* *

(fa-man lam yajid) The object of "yajid" (find) is omitted, understood from the meaning. The intended sense is: "whoever does not find what is easy of the offering." The negation of finding is either because it is absent or because its price is absent.

﴿then fasting three days﴾. The word "sawm" is in the nominative as the subject, meaning: "then upon him (is fasting)," or as the predicate, meaning: "then obligatory (is fasting)." It was also read as "fa-sawma" in the accusative, meaning: "then let him fast the fast of three days," and the verbal noun (masdar) is annexed to "thalathah" (three) after the expansion (of the grammar), because if it remained in the sense of a time adverb (zarfiyyah), the annexation would not be permissible. (fi al-Hajj) means: in the months of Hajj. So he may fast them during this period between the two ihrams, the ihram of Umrah and the ihram of Hajj. This was said by 'Ikrimah and 'Ata'. Abu Hanifa said: the best is that he fasts the day of Tarwiyah, the day of Arafat, and the day before them. If this period passes, only the offering suffices for him. 'Ata' also said, along with Mujahid: he does not fast them except during the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah; this was the view of al-Thawri and al-Awza'i. Ibn Umar, al-Hasan and al-Hakam said: he fasts the day before Tarwiyah, the day of Tarwiyah, and the day of Arafat. All of these say: it is not permissible to delay them beyond the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah, because with their end the Hajj ends. 'Ali and Ibn Umar said: if he misses fasting them before the Day of Sacrifice, he fasts them during the days of tashriq, because they are days of Hajj. It is reported from 'A'isha, 'Urwah, and Ibn Umar in the narration of his son Salim from him, that they are the days of tashriq. It has been said: their time is after his ihram. It has been said: it is the Day of Sacrifice; this was said by 'Ali, Ibn Umar, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, Tawus, 'Ata', and al-Suddi. Malik also said this. Al-Shafi'i and Ahmad said: he fasts them from the time he enters ihram for Hajj until the Day of Arafat; this is the view of Ibn Umar and 'A'isha.

This was narrated from Malik, and it is his view in al-Muwatta', so that the Day of Arafat is a non-fasting day. From Ahmad: it is permissible to fast the three days before he enters ihram. Some said: he may postpone them initially until the days of tashriq, because fasting is only obligatory upon him if he does not find the offering on the Day of Sacrifice. 'Urwah said: he fasts them as long as he is in Mecca; this was also said by Malik and a group from the people of Medina. All these opinions need evidence to support them.

The apparent meaning of His words "in the Hajj" is that the omitted element is a time (zaman), because it is the counterpart in His words "and seven when you return" (2:196), since its meaning is "at the time of returning," and the time of Hajj is its months. The slaughter of the offering for the tamattu' performer has not been stipulated with a time; rather it should follow the tamattu', since it is the response of the conditional. So when he does not find it, then it is obligatory upon him to fast three days in Hajj, i.e., during its time. Whoever considers only this omitted element permits fasting before and after entering ihram for Hajj, and permits it until the end of the days of tashriq, because they are part of the time of Hajj. Whoever supposes a different omitted element, i.e., "at the time of the acts of Hajj," does not permit fasting except after entering ihram for Hajj. The first opinion is more apparent because of the paucity of omission. Whoever does not consider the months of Hajj, and permits that it is "as long as he is in Mecca," then if he believes the omitted element is a place adverb (zarf makan), meaning: "fasting three days in the places of Hajj."

The apparent meaning is that he must move to fasting when he does not find the offering. So if he began fasting and then found the offering, he continues the fasting, which is his obligation. This was said by al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr, and it was chosen by Ibn al-Mundhir. Malik said: I prefer that he offers, but if he fasts, it suffices him. Abu Hanifa said: if he becomes able (to offer) on the third day of his fasting, the fast is nullified and the offering becomes obligatory upon him; but if he becomes able after completing them, he may fast the seven days. This was said by al-Thawri, Ibn Abi Najih, and Hammad.

﴿and seven when you return﴾. Zayd ibn Ali and Ibn Abi Abla read "wa-sab'atan" in the accusative. Al-Zamakhshari said: (it is) coordinated (ataf) on the position (mahall) of "thalathat ayyam" (three days), as if it were said: "fasting three days" like your saying: "or feeding in a day of hunger an orphan" [al-Balad 90:14], end of quote. Al-Hawfi and Ibn 'Atiyyah took it as an implied verb, meaning: "so let them fast," or "fast seven," and this is the explanation from which one should not depart, because we have established that coordination upon the position requires a governing factor (muhriz), and the coming of "wa-sab'ah" with the taa' (feminine) is the eloquent form, treating the omitted element as if it were pronounced, as it is said: "wa-sab'at ayyam" (and seven days), so it is omitted because what precedes indicates it, and because it is known that fasting is only the days. It is permissible in speech to omit the taa' when the specified noun is omitted, and upon this came: "then he followed it with six (days) of Shawwal" [Muslim], and al-Kisa'i related: "we fasted five (days) of the month." The governing element of "idha" is "fasting three days," and "in the Hajj" is attached to it. It is not said that "idha" (when) governs both of them, because this would make the governing element extend to two time adverbs; that is permissible with coordination and apposition, and here he coordinated two things upon two things, as you say: "I honoured Zayd on Thursday and 'Amr on Friday." Here "idha" is purely an adverb of time, with no conditional force; and in "raja'tum" (you returned) there is a shift (iltifat), and a construction according to the sense of "man" (whoever). As for the shift, His words "whoever performs tamattu'" and "whoever does not find" are third-person nouns, and for this reason the pronoun of the third person is concealed in both verbs; had it come according to this arrangement, the speech would have been "idha raja'a" (when he returned). As for construction according to the sense, He used the plural pronoun, whereas if He had observed the wording He would have used the singular. The word "return" (raj'ah) is ambiguous, and its clarification has come in the Sunnah.

It is established in Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Ibn Umar, in another wording: "And let him offer a sacrifice. Whoever cannot find one, then [he fasts] three days during the Hajj and seven when he returns to his family." In Sahih al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Ibn Abbas: "And seven when he returns to his family, to your cities." This is also the view of Qatadah, 'Ata', Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, and al-Rabi'. They said: "This is a concession from Allah, Exalted. The meaning is: when you return to your homelands. No one is obliged to fast the seven except once he reaches his homeland, unless someone chooses to be stricter, as one who fasts while traveling during Ramadan does." Ahmad and Ishaq said: "It suffices for him to fast on the road." Mujahid, 'Ata', and Ibrahim said: "The meaning is: when you return, that is, when you depart [from Mina] and finish the rites of the Hajj." This is the position of Abu Hanifa. So whoever remains in Makkah fasts them there, and whoever sets out for his country fasts them on the road. Malik said in al-Kitab (al-Mudawwana): "If he returns from Mina, there is no harm in his fasting."

* *

﴿Those are ten complete.﴾ "Those" refers to the total of the days previously commanded to be fasted. It is known that three and seven make ten. Al-Ustadh Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn Ahmad al-Badhish said, in substance: "[The number] ten was mentioned as a preparation for the information that follows it, and it is not itself the news whose benefit is the predication. It was brought for emphasis, as when you say: 'Zayd is a righteous man.'" Ibn 'Arafah said: "It is the way of the Arabs, when they mention two numbers, to combine them." al-Zamakhshari endorsed this view, saying: "The benefit of the summation (fadhlakah) in every calculation is that the number is known as a whole, just as it was known in detail, so that it is grasped from two angles and knowledge is reinforced. In the proverbs of the Arabs: 'Two kinds of knowledge are better than one.'" Ibn 'Arafah said: "The Arabs only do this because of their scant knowledge of arithmetic. It has been reported: 'He neither reckons nor writes.' This occurs in many of their poems." al-Nabighah said:

"I imagined signs for her, then I recognised them after six years, and this year is the seventh."

al-A'sha said:

"Three in the morning are enough for me, and six when the evening overtakes me.
So that is nine in a day, my satisfaction, and a man's drinking beyond satisfaction is a disease."

al-Farazdaq said:

"Three, and two, and they are five, and a sixth that leans toward a sip of drink."

Another said:

"I travelled to them for twenty months, and four, so that is two years."

al-Mufaddal said: "When [the number] was separated by an interruption (of fasting), he restricted them to ten so that it would be known that they are, in reward, as if connected." al-Zajjaj said: "He combined the two numbers because it might be supposed that he owes three or seven, since the wa (and) may stand in place of aw (or). Compare ﴿two, or three, or four﴾ [al-Nisa': 3]. Thus he removed the possibility of choice." Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned only this view, and it is an opinion in line with the school of the Kufans, not with that of the Basrans, because wa does not mean aw. al-Zamakhshari said: "Wa may come to express permissibility, as in your saying: 'Sit with al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin.' Do you not see that if he sat with both of them together, or with either one of them, he would have complied? So it was made a summation to negate the supposition of permissibility." End of his words. There is a problem with this: permissibility is not supposed here, because the context is one of obligation, and obligation contradicts permissibility but does not contradict choice, since choice may occur in obligatory matters. The grammarians have explained the difference between choice and permissibility. It has also been said: this is an inversion of order, its implied meaning being: "Those are ten: three during the Hajj and seven when you return." This view is attributed to Abu al-'Abbas al-Mubarrad, but such a view cannot be authentically ascribed to him, and we exalt the Qur'an above anything like it. It has also been said: He mentioned the ten so that it would not be supposed that the seven are together with the three, like His saying: ﴿and He determined in it its sustenance in four days﴾ [Fussilat: 10], meaning together with the two days that follow in His saying: ﴿He created the earth in two days﴾ [Fussilat: 9]. It has been said: He mentioned the ten to remove the supposition that seven is not intended as a number but as a multitude. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and Ibn al-A'rabi transmitted from the Arabs: "May Allah multiply your reward for you (sabba'a Allahu laka al-ajr)," meaning: increase it. They intended multiplication, and this occurs in the reports: "For him seven, and for him seventy, and for him seven hundred." al-Azhari said, regarding His saying: ﴿seventy times﴾ [al-Tawbah: 80], that it is the plural of sab' (seven), which is used for multitude. It is also reported from al-Mubarrad that he said: "Those are ten, because the listener might suppose that there is something else after the seven, so he removed the supposition." It has also been said: He mentioned ten to remove the ambiguity that arises from a copying error in the script, since seven and nine look alike. It has also been said: He mentioned ten so that it would not be supposed that completeness is restricted to the three fasted during the Hajj, or to the seven which he fasts upon returning. The ten is the one described as complete. The best of these opinions is the first.

al-Hasan said: "Complete in reward, in that it fills the place of the sacrificial animal in the meaning for which it was made a substitute." It has also been said: "Complete in purpose and in sequence; had he fasted them out of this order, they would not be complete." It has also been said: "Complete in reward for one who did not perform tamattu'." It has also been said: "'Complete' is an emphasis, as when you say: 'I wrote it with my own hand,' and ﴿the roof fell upon them from above them﴾ [al-Nahl: 26]. al-Zamakhshari said: "In the emphasis there is an added instruction to fast them, and not to be negligent about them or diminish their number, as you say to a man when you have concern for a matter you command him, and he is of such standing with you: 'Allah, Allah, do not fall short!'" It has also been said: "The formula is a statement but its meaning is a command, that is: complete their fasting; that is their obligation. The expression moved from the imperative to the declarative because when an obligation is emphatic, it is contrary to the apparent entry of the one obligated into existence, so it is expressed by a statement which has occurred and become established."

By these benefits we have mentioned, a response is given to the heretics who object that it is known by necessity that three and seven make ten, so this is clarifying the obvious; and that describing the ten as complete implies the existence of an incomplete ten, which is impossible. Completeness is a relative attribute and is not restricted to numbers, as they claimed, may Allah curse them:

"How many a critic has faulted a sound statement, and its flaw is from a sick understanding."

﴿That is for one whose family are not present at the Sacred Mosque.﴾ Tamattu' was mentioned earlier, along with what it requires, which is the sacrifice (hady), and its substitute, which is fasting. They differed about what is referred to by "that." It was said: it refers to the one performing tamattu' and what is required of him. This is the position of Abu Hanifa: there is no tamattu' or qiran (combining Hajj and 'Umrah) for those present at the Sacred Mosque, and whoever of them performs tamattu' or qiran owes a penalty sacrifice of which he may not eat. For the qarin and the mutamatti' from among the people of the distant regions, their sacrifice is a sacrifice of worship, of which they may eat. It was said: it refers to what is required of the mutamatti', namely the sacrifice. This is the position of al-Shafi'i: nothing is obligatory upon those present at the Sacred Mosque; the sacrifice and its substitute are required only of the one from afar. The disagreement about the Makkan, whether he may perform tamattu' in the months of Hajj or not, has already been mentioned. The more apparent meaning in the context is that the reference is to the permissibility of tamattu' and what follows from it, because the appropriate particle for a concession is "li" (for), while the appropriate particle for obligations is "'ala" (upon). Since it came as "li-man" and not "'ala-man," [this indicates the concession]. Some claimed that "li" here means "'ala," as in His saying: ﴿those for them is the curse﴾ [al-Ra'd: 25].

Those present at the Sacred Mosque: Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: the people of the whole Haram. Makhul and 'Ata' said: whoever is within the miqat boundaries from every direction. al-Zuhri said: whoever is a day or two days away. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: the people of Makkah, Dajnan, Dhu Tuwa, and what resembles them. Some said: the people of the miqat and those closer than them to Makkah; this is the position of Abu Hanifa. Some said: the people of the Haram, and whoever of the people of the Haram is at a distance where prayer is shortened; this is the position of al-Shafi'i. Some said: the people of Makkah and the people of Dhu Tuwa; this is the position of Malik. Some scholars said: whoever is at a place where Friday prayer is obligatory in Makkah is a hadari (settled), and whoever is farther than that is a badawi (nomad), taking the word from hadara (settledness) and badawa (desert life).

The apparent meaning is that those present at the Sacred Mosque are only the inhabitants of Makkah, because they are the ones who see the Sacred Mosque. All other opinions require a figurative usage, which is far-fetched, some of it more far-fetched than others. The mention of "the family" being present, while the intended meaning is his presence, is because the usual case is that one lives where his family lives.

﴿And fear Allah.﴾ When a command, a prohibition, and an obligation were mentioned, it was fitting to conclude with the command to be mindful of Allah, so that one does not exceed what Allah has set as limits. Then He emphasized the command to attain taqwa (God-consciousness) by His saying: ﴿And know that Allah is severe in punishment.﴾ For whoever knows the severity of punishment for disobedience will be eager to attain taqwa, since by it one is safe from punishment. "Severe in punishment" is an instance of an attributive construct (idafat al-sifah) to the qualified noun, for the sake of resemblance, and the genitive construction and the accusative are more eloquent than the nominative, because in them the attribute is ascribed to the qualified noun, whereas the nominative only ascribes it to the one to whom it truly belongs, without ascribing it to the qualified noun.

This passage has included noble verses in which the people asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the condition of the crescent moons and their benefit in changing from small to large. This was a matter of information about the unseen, so the question was asked about it, and they were answered that the wisdom behind it is that they were made into timepieces (*mawaqit*) for the benefits and dealings of the servants and for their religious practices. Among the greatest of their benefits is that they are timepieces for the Hajj (pilgrimage). Then He mentioned something of what whoever entered the state of ihram for Hajj used to do, and they considered that to be righteousness, so He rejected it from them. They were commanded to come to the houses (*al-buyut*) through their doors, and they were informed that righteousness lies in the fear of Allah (*taqwa*). Then they were commanded to have taqwa, hoping for success (*al-falah*) upon its attainment. Then they were commanded to fight in support of the religion against whoever fights them, and they were forbidden from transgression (*i'tida'*), and He informed that Allah the Exalted does not love the transgressors. Then they were commanded to kill whoever they overcame and to expel whoever had expelled them from the place from which they had been expelled. Then He informed that persecution (*fitnah*) in the religion, or by expulsion from the homeland, or by torture, is worse than killing, because in killing there is relief from all of this. Then, since the command to expel included that they should expel [the enemy] from the place from which they had been expelled, and the Masjid al-Haram was part of that, they were forbidden from fighting them there unless they fought them first. This is because of the sanctity of the Masjid al-Haram in the pre-Islamic period and in Islam. Then He commanded their killing when they initiated fighting. In this there was good news that we would kill them, since He commanded us to kill them, not merely to fight them, and no one kills a person except one who is capable of killing him. Then He mentioned that whoever disbelieves in Allah, his recompense is like this recompense: fighting him, expelling him from his homeland, and killing him. Then Allah the Exalted informed that He is Forgiving and Merciful to whoever desists from disbelief and enters Islam, for Islam erases what came before it. Since the command to fight had previously been restricted at one time to those who fought, and at another time to a place where fighting would be initiated, He commanded them to fight in every state, whether the enemy fights or does not fight, and whether at the Masjid al-Haram or elsewhere. So this command abrogated (*naskh*) those restrictions, and it became conditioned (*mughayyan*) or given a reason (*mu'allal*) by the cessation of persecution and the purity of the religion for Allah (p. 82). He concluded this command by stating that whoever desists and enters Islam, there is no transgression against him, and transgression is only against the wrongdoers, who are the disbelievers. Just as He concluded the previous command by stating that whoever desists from disbelief and enters Islam, Allah forgives him and has mercy upon him. Then Allah the Exalted informed that violating the sanctity of the Sacred Month by fighting in it, which is the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah, and which they used to dislike fighting in, is permitted for you when they fought you in it, at the time of al-Hudaybiyyah, and when they barred you from the House. This is because of their violation of its sanctity when they fought you in it. Then He reaffirmed this by His saying: ﴿And for the sacred things there is retribution﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:194]. This necessitates that whoever violates any sanctity is retaliated against by having that sanctity violated for him. So just as they violated the sanctity of your month, do not be concerned about violating its sanctity for them. Then He commanded requital against whoever transgresses against us with a punishment like his punishment, as an affirmation of what preceded, and He commanded taqwa, so that one does not inflict upon the one being requited anything other than what He permitted for him. Then He said that Allah the Exalted is with those who have taqwa, and whoever Allah is with, he is the one given victory over his enemy. Then Allah the Exalted commanded spending wealth in His way and in support of His religion, and that one should not incline to ease and desire for improving this world and settling in it. He forbade us from becoming engrossed in ease and comfort, so that we would become weak before our enemies while they become strong against us, and our affair with them would end in destruction for us, because of our weakness and their strength. In this command and this prohibition there is an exhortation to jihad that is not hidden. Then Allah the Exalted commanded them to do good, and that He loves those who do good. Then He commanded the completion of Hajj and 'Umrah, that they should perform both complete and whole, with their rites (*manasik*) and conditions (*shara'it*). And that this action should be for the sake of Allah the Exalted, such that no showing off (*riya'*) or reputation-seeking (*sum'ah*) mixes into its performance. In the pre-Islamic period they used to make Hajj for some of their idols, so they were commanded to make the work in this sincere for Allah the Exalted.

Then He mentioned that whoever is prevented (*uhsira*) and held back from completing the Hajj or 'Umrah, then what is easy (*ma yassara*) of the sacrificial animal (*hady*) becomes obligatory upon him. The hady includes the camel, the cow, and the sheep. Then He forbade shaving the head until the hady reaches its place of sacrifice (*mahalluhu*). What was customary regarding the hady is that its place of sacrifice is the Haram, so they were addressed with what they already knew from before. Since He limited the shaving by the attainment of this end, which is the hady reaching its place, and since a person may encounter something that necessitates shaving his head due to illness, or harm to his head from lice, sores, or other such things, Allah the Exalted made obligatory upon him, because of this, a compensation (*fidyah*): either fasting, or charity, or an act of worship (*nusuk*). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) clarified what was vague in this general statement regarding these three options in the hadith of Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah, as its explanation has already passed. This structure necessitates the choice between these three.

Then Allah the Exalted mentioned that when they are safe (*amin*), and one of them performs tamattu' (combining 'Umrah with Hajj in one journey, *tamattu'* being the term used for this) by means of 'Umrah until the time of entering ihram for Hajj, then what is easy of the hady becomes obligatory upon him. We have already explained what is easy of the hady. If he does not find that, due to the inability to afford the price of the hady or the absence of the hady, then he must fast three days during Hajj, that is, during the period of the Hajj, and seven days when he returns to his family and homeland.

Then He informed that these days, although the time of fasting them differs, some of them are fasted by one who is engaged in this noble act of worship, and some are fasted by one who is not engaged in it. Yet all of it is complete in reward and recompense, since it represents what Allah the Exalted commanded. There is no difference in reward between what He commanded to be performed during Hajj and what He commanded to be performed outside Hajj.

Then He mentioned that this tamattu' and what it necessitates of hady or fasting is prescribed for non-Makkans. Then, since Allah the Exalted had previously in these verses given commands and prohibitions, He repeated the command to have taqwa, and informed that Allah the Exalted is severe in punishment for whoever opposes what Allah the Exalted has legislated.

This verse came with exceptional cohesion and firmly established order, its parts arranged one upon another, not like the arrangement of pearls, its meaning brilliant, not like the brilliance of the sun in its lofty tower. Sublime in eloquence to the highest peaks, inimitable such that no one among mankind could bring its like.

The Hajj is in known months, so whoever undertakes the Hajj in them, there shall be no obscenity, no wickedness, and no quarrelling during the Hajj. Whatever good you do, Allah knows it. Take provision, but the best provision is piety. So fear Me, O people of understanding. ﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord. When you pour forth from ʿArafat, remember Allah at the sacred landmark, and remember Him as He has guided you, though before it you were indeed among the astray.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198] ﴿Then pour forth from where the people pour forth, and seek the forgiveness of Allah. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 199] ﴿When you have completed your rites, remember Allah as you remember your fathers, or with even greater remembrance. Among the people is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world," and he has no share in the Hereafter.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 200] ﴿And among them is one who says, "Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 201] ﴿Those will have a share of what they have earned, and Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 202].

*Al-jidal* (contention), the form *fiʿāl*, is a verbal noun of *jādala*, and it means fierce hostility. It is derived from *al-jadālah*, which means the ground. Each of the two disputants would resist his opponent until he overcame him, so that he was like one who had thrown him down onto the ground. From this is the saying of the poet:

*I bring down the mighty after the mighty, and I bring down the weak with a fall to the ground.*

That is, to the ground. It has also been said that the word is derived from *al-jadl*, which means twisting. From this comes the saying "a twisted rein" (*zimām majdūl*). It has also been said that it has a *jadīl* because of its twisting. It has been said of the falcon, *al-ajdal*, because of its strength and the compactness of its build, as though some of its parts were twisted into others, so it became strong.

*Al-zād* (provision) is well known. It is what a person takes with him for a journey of food, drink, mount, and clothing, if he needs these. Its *alif* is converted from a *wāw*. This is shown by the saying *tazawwada*, which is the *tafaʿʿala* form derived from *al-zād*.

*Al-ifāḍah* means to plunge in, to rush forward, and to go out from a place in large numbers. It is likened to the pouring of water or tears. So *afāḍa* is from *al-fayḍ* (overflow), not from *fawaḍa*, which means the mixing of people without a leader to manage them. The *afʿala* form here has the sense of the bare form, and the *hamzah* is not for causation, because it is not reported that one says *afaḍtu Zaydan* in the sense explained above. Although it is permissible to say *fāḍa al-damʿu* (the tear overflowed) and make it causative with the *hamzah*, as in *afāḍa al-ḥuzn*, meaning "he made it overflow." Al-Zajjaj, and al-Zamakhsharī after him, and the author of *al-Muntakhab* claimed that the *hamzah* in *afāḍa al-nās* (Q. 2:199) is for causation, and said that the original was *afaḍtum anfusakum* ("you poured yourselves forth"). The author of *al-Muntakhab* explained it as rushing forward in the march in large numbers, though he should have explained it with a different wording. He said its meaning is: some of you pushed others, because when people leave crowded, some push others. It has been said that *al-ifāḍah* is returning from where you began. It has been said that it is rapid marching, or dispersing in large numbers, or pushing in large numbers. One says *rajul fayyāḍ*, meaning a man who gives generously. It has been said that it means departing, from the expression *afāḍa bil-qidāḥ* and *ʿalā al-qidāḥ*, where *al-qidāḥ* are the arrows of gambling, and *afāḍa al-baʿīr bi-jirānih* ("the camel let its neck down").

*ʿArafāt* [al-Baqarah: 198] is a proper noun for the mountain on which they stand during the Hajj. It has been said that it is not derived from anything. It has been said that it is derived from *al-maʿrifah* (knowledge), and that this is the reason for its being named by this name. There are several views about the cause of this knowledge. It has been said that it is because Ibrahim knew this place, since it had been described to him before that. It has been said that it is because he knew Hajar and Isma'il in this place, for Sarah had sent Isma'il away in Ibrahim's absence, so he set out to seek him when he lost him, and found him and his mother at ʿArafāt. It has been said that it is because on the night of ʿArafah he knew that the dream he had seen on the night of the Tarwiyah, about slaughtering his son, was from Allah. It has been said that when Jibril came to him at the last of the sacred sites, in order to show Ibrahim its rites, he said to him, "Have you known?" He said, "I have known," so it was named ʿArafah. It has been said that it is because people recognize one another there. It has been said that it is for the recognition of Adam and Eve there, since his descent was in the valley of Sarandib and her descent was at Jeddah, and Allah commanded him to build the Kaʿbah, so he came in obedience, and they recognized one another in this place. It has been said that it is from *al-ʿarf*, which means a pleasant fragrance. It has been said that it is from *al-ʿirf*, which means patience. It has been said that the Arabs call whatever is high *ʿArafāt* and *ʿArafah*, and from this comes *ʿurf al-dīk* (the comb of the rooster), because of its height. ʿArafāt is higher than all the mountains of the Hijaz. Although ʿArafāt is the name of a mountain, it is feminine. Sibawayh reported: "This is ʿArafāt, blessed in it." It is synonymous with ʿArafah. It has been said that it is a plural. If this means in origin, it is correct, but if it means in its state as a proper noun, it is not correct, because plurality contradicts being a proper noun. Some people said: ʿArafah is the name of the day, and ʿArafāt is the name of the place.
