The tanwin in *ʿArafāt* and similar words is the tanwin of correspondence (*tanwīn al-muqābalah*). It has been said that it is the tanwin of declension (*tanwīn al-ṣarf*). Its exemption from declension despite being feminine and a proper noun is explained by the fact that the femininity is only with the *alif* before it, which is the sign of the feminine sound plural. Even if it is by estimation, like *Suʿād*, it is not valid to estimate it in *ʿArafāt*, because this *tā'* (the *tā'* of the plural) is specific to the feminine plural, so it prevents being estimated, just as the *tā'* of femininity is estimated in *bint*, because the *tā'* which is a replacement for a *wāw* is specific to the feminine, like the *tā'* of femininity, so the estimation of its femininity is... This is the end of this reasoning, and most of it is from al-Zamakhsharī. He treated it in the Qur'an in the manner of what is not named as its agent, by retaining the tanwin in the genitive case, and it is permissible to omit it in the case of naming. The Kufans and al-Akhfash reported treating that and similar words in the manner of *Fāṭimah*, and they cited the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*I looked at her from Adhruʿāt, and her people in Yathrib, the near part of her house is a high view.*

With a *fatḥah*.

*Al-naṣīb* is the share, and its plural *afʿilāʾ* is irregular, because it is a noun. They said *anṣibāʾ*, and its regular pattern is *fuʿul*, like *kathīb* and *kuthub*.

*Sarīʿ* is an active participle from *saruʿa yasruʿu surʿatan*, so it is *sarīʿ*. One says *asraʿa*, and both are intransitive.

*Al-ḥisāb* is the verbal noun of *ḥāsaba*. Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā said: *ḥasibtu al-ḥisāb, aḥsubuhu ḥasban wa ḥusbānan*, and *al-ḥisāb* is the noun. It has been said that *al-ḥisāb* is the verbal noun of *ḥasiba al-shayʾ*, and in language *al-ḥisāb* is counting. Al-Layth ibn al-Muẓaffar and Yaʿqūb said: *ḥasaba yaḥsubu ḥusbānan wa ḥisābatan wa ḥisbatan wa ḥasban*, and he recited:

*And she hastened to count in that number.*

From this comes *ḥasuba al-rajul*, which is what he counted of his glorious deeds and merits. *Al-iḥsāb* is relying on something. Al-Zajjaj said: *al-ḥisāb* in language is derived from your saying *ḥasbuka kadhā*, meaning "that suffices you." So reckoning in transactions is called *ḥisāb* because it contains sufficiency, with neither excess nor deficiency.

* *

[al-Baqarah: 197] ﴿The Hajj is in known months.﴾ When Allah commanded the completion of the Hajj and the ʿUmrah, and the ʿUmrah had no known time, He explained that the Hajj has a known time. This is the connection of this verse with what precedes it.

*Al-ḥajju* (the Hajj) is the subject, and *ashhurun* (months) is the predicate. There must be an elision, since the months are not the Hajj. That elision is either in the subject, so the estimate is "the months of the Hajj" or "the time of the Hajj," or in the predicate, meaning "the Hajj is the Hajj of months." Or the original is *fī ashhurin* (in months), and it was extended, and the adverb of time was used to describe the Hajj because it occurs in it, and it was treated as a figurative extension. On this estimate, the accusative would be permissible, and there is nothing in Arabic that prevents it.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: whoever estimates the sentence as *fī ashhurin*, will be obliged, with the dropping of the preposition, to put the months in the accusative, and no one has read it in the accusative. This is the end of his statement. However, the accusative of the months is not obligatory with the dropping of the preposition, as Ibn ʿAṭiyyah claimed, because we have already mentioned that it is put in the nominative by extension. This has no disagreement among the Basrans, meaning that when the adverb of time is an indefinite noun and the predicate about verbal nouns, they permit both the nominative and the accusative, whether the event covers the whole time or not. As for the Kufans, they have a distinction: the event either covers the time, so it is in the nominative and the accusative is not permitted, or it does not cover it. Hisham held that the nominative is obligatory in that case, so one says *mīʿādaka yawmun wa thalāthatu ayyāmin* ("your appointment is a day and three days"). Al-Farrāʾ held that both the accusative and the nominative are permissible, like the Basrans. It is transmitted from al-Farrāʾ in this place that the accusative of *ashhur* is not permissible, because *ashhuran* is an indefinite, unlimited noun. This transmission contradicts what we have reported from him, so it is possible that he had two views: the view of the Basrans and the view of Hisham. The plural of *shahr* is *afʿul*, because it is a paucity plural, unlike His saying: *inna ʿiddata al-shuhūr* (Q. 9:36), which is in *fuʿūl*, the plural of abundance.

The apparent sense of the word *ashhur* is plural, namely Shawwal, Dhu al-Qaʿdah, and the whole of Dhu al-Hijjah. This was said by Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿUmar, ʿAṭāʾ, Ṭāwūs, Mujāhid, al-Zuhrī, al-Rabīʿ, and Mālik. Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn Sīrīn, al-Ḥasan, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Shaʿbī, Ṭāwūs, al-Nakhaʿī, Qatādah, Makḥūl, al-Suddī, Abū Ḥanīfah, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ibn Ḥabīb, from Mālik, said: they are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qaʿdah, and ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. This was transmitted from Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿUmar. Al-Zamakhsharī and the author of *al-Muntakhab* reported from al-Shāfiʿī that the third is nine days of Dhu al-Hijjah with the night of sacrifice, because the Hajj ends by the rising of dawn. These two views contain a figurative usage, since the name of a month was applied to a part of the month.

Al-Farrāʾ said: The Arabs say, "I have not seen him for two days today," and it is really one day and part of another day. They only said that by prioritizing the greater part of the time over the smaller part. It is as reported in the hadith: "The days of Mina are three days," though it is really two days and part of the third. This is of the type of applying a part to the whole. As the poet said:

*Thirty months in three seasons.*

On one of the two interpretations. It has been said: also, because the Arabs use the plural for the dual, since the dual is the least plural. Al-Zamakhsharī said: If you say, how could two months and part of a month be "months"? I say: the collective noun includes what is beyond the singular, as evidenced by His saying: *faqad ṣaghat qulūbukumā* (Q. 66:4). So there is no question about it. Rather, it would be a place for a question only if it were said: *thalāthatu ashhurin maʿlūmātin* ("three known months"). This is the end of his statement.

What he mentioned is a general claim, that the collective noun includes what is beyond the singular, and this is what is disputed. The proof he cited is specific, namely *faqad ṣaghat qulūbukumā* (Q. 66:4), and there is no disagreement about this. The use of the plural in such a case for the dual has conditions mentioned in grammar, and *ashhur* is not of the type *faqad ṣaghat qulūbukumā*, so it cannot be used as evidence for it. His saying "so there is no question about it" is not good, because he assumed the question with his saying "if you say," and his saying "rather, it would be a place for a question only if it were said: three known months." For us there is no difference between *shahr* and the phrase *thalāthat ashhur*, because just as figurative usage enters the word *ashhur*, so figurative usage may enter the numeral. Do you not see what al-Farrāʾ reported: *lahu al-yawma yawmān lam arahu*? He said: it is really one day and part of another day. And the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*Thirty months in three seasons,*

as we mentioned earlier. And what is reported from the Arabs: *mā raʾaytuhu mundhu khamsati ayyāmin* ("I have not seen him since five days"), even though you may have seen him on the first and fifth days. The negation did not cover all five days. Rather, it is taken to mean: I did not see him in part of it, and the seeing was negated in part of it. If there was a full day in which you did not see him, then, since this exists in their speech, there is no difference between *ashhur* and *thalāthat ashhur*. But the figurative usage of the plural is closer than the figurative usage of the numeral.

They said: the fruit of the disagreement between the one who makes the months the three whole months, and the one who makes them two months and part of the third, appears in the obligation of a sacrifice for actions done on the day of sacrifice. On the first view, there is no obligation of a sacrifice for him, because those actions occurred within the months of the Hajj. On the second, there is an obligation, because the Hajj has ended by the day of sacrifice, and he delayed the performance of that act beyond its time.

[p. 85]

The benefit of fixing the time by months is that none of the acts of Hajj is valid except within them. According to Abu Hanifa, Malik and Ahmad, it is disliked to enter into Hajj ihram outside them, and al-Nakha'i said the same. He said: "One does not leave ihram until one has completed one's Hajj." Ata', Mujahid, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr said: it is not valid, and it turns into an 'Umrah, and one exits ihram by means of it. Ibn 'Abbas said: "It is part of the Sunnah of Hajj to enter ihram for it [in these months]." The cause of the disagreement is their differing over the omitted element in the words of Allah, ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months﴾: is the implied meaning "entering ihram for Hajj" or "the acts of Hajj"? Mentioning Hajj in these months does not indicate that 'Umrah cannot occur in them. What is reported from 'Umar and his son 'Abdullah, that 'Umrah is not recommended in them, suggests that these months are reserved exclusively for Hajj. It is reported that 'Umar used to strike people with a whip and forbid them from performing 'Umrah during these months. It is reported from Ibn 'Umar that he said to a man: "If you release me, I will wait until I have begun the month of Muharram, then I will set out to Dhat 'Irq and begin ihram from there for 'Umrah." The meaning of "well-known" (ma'lumat) is "recognized by the people," and the legislation of Hajj in these months came in line with what they knew and what was established among them.

* *

﴿Whoever imposes upon himself the Hajj within them﴾: that is, whoever binds himself to Hajj within them. The root of fard (obligation/imposition) is a notch, such as the one found on arrows, bows and other things, and from it comes farḍat al-nahr and al-jabal (a gap/pass in a river bank or mountain). What is meant by this fard is that by which the one in the state of ihram becomes a muhrim (one in ihram). Ibn Mas'ud said: it is the declaration (ihlal) of Hajj and entering ihram. Ata' and Ta'us said: it is to recite the talbiyah. This was also the view of a group of the Companions and the Successors, may Allah have mercy on them. And this is the report of Sharik from Ibn 'Abbas: that the obligation of Hajj is by the talbiyah. It is reported from 'A'isha: "There is no ihram except for one who declares it and recites the talbiyah." Abu Hanifa and his companions adopted this, as did Ibn Habib, and they, together with the Zahiriyyah, said: it is a pillar (rukn) of Hajj. Abu Hanifa and his companions also said: if one garlands one's camel and drives it, intending ihram, then one has entered ihram. His statement is based on the premise that his school holds the talbiyah to be obligatory, or that what takes its place, namely the sacrificial blood. It is reported from Ibn 'Umar: "If one garlands one's camel and drives it, one has entered ihram." It is reported from 'Ali, Qays ibn Sa'd, Ibn 'Abbas, Ta'us, Ata', Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, Ibn Sirin, Jabir ibn Zayd and Ibn Jubayr that one does not become a muhrim by that. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Hasan said: the obligation of Hajj is entering ihram for it, and al-Shafi'i held this view.

All these statements are given with the condition of intention (niyyah). A summary of this: according to Malik and al-Shafi'i, one becomes a muhrim by intention and ihram; according to Abu Hanifa, by intention and talbiyah or by driving the sacrificial animal; and according to a group of scholars, by intention and marking the sacrificial animal (ish'ar) or garlanding it.

"Man" (من) is either conditional or relative. "Fihinna" (فيهن) is connected to "faraḍa." The pronoun refers back to "ashhur" (months). It did not say "fiha" (in it) because ashhur is a plural of paucity (jam' qillah). This follows the common usage that the plural of paucity for non-rational nouns is treated like the plural for feminine rational nouns, which is also the more common usage. Some said that the two are equivalent in usage.

﴿So there shall be no sexual relations, no wickedness, and no quarreling during Hajj﴾. Regarding "rafath" here, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Qatada, al-Hasan, 'Ikrima, Mujahid, al-Zuhri and al-Suddi said: it is sexual intercourse. Ibn 'Umar, Ta'us, Ata' and others said: it is obscene speech to a woman, such as saying, "When we exit ihram, we will do such-and-such to you," without euphemism. Some said: it is obscenity by mentioning women, whether that is in their presence or not. Some said: rafath is a comprehensive word for everything a man desires from his wife. Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is idle speech. Ibn al-Zubayr said: it is making advances through embracing, promising a tryst, joking or winking.

A summary of these statements is that they revolve between something that would invalidate the Hajj, namely intercourse, and something that is unbecoming for one who is engaged in Hajj, given the sanctity of Hajj.

As for "fusuq" (wickedness): it has been interpreted as doing what is forbidden in ihram, such as killing game or shaving hair. Yet all sins are included, and none is specifically excluded. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ata', al-Hasan, Mujahid and Ta'us. Or it means sacrificing to idols, and from this comes the verse ﴿or that which has been dedicated to other than Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 145]. This was said by Ibn Zayd and Malik. Or it means mutual insulting by nicknames; He said: ﴿Wretched is the name of wickedness﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11]. This was said by al-Dahhak. Or it means cursing, and from this comes the saying: "Cursing a Muslim is wickedness." This was also said by Ibn 'Umar, Mujahid, Ata', Ibrahim and al-Suddi. Muhammad ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) preferred that it refers to what the pilgrim is forbidden during his ihram, because of the words: ﴿Whoever imposes upon himself the Hajj within them﴾.

It is known that all sins are forbidden to everyone, whether in ihram or not, and likewise mutual insulting. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi the exegete, and others preferred the view of the one who said it refers to all sins, because the word covers all sayings and actions. Also, because this is the view of the majority of the Companions and Successors. And also because it has been reported: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, there is no deed between heaven and earth more excellent than jihad in the way of Allah, or a mabrur Hajj (accepted, sincere Hajj) in which there is no rafath, no fusuq, and no jidal." The scholars said: the mabrur Hajj is one in which Allah is not disobeyed during its performance. Al-Farra' said: it is one in which Allah is not disobeyed afterward.

Jidal (quarreling) here means arguing with a Muslim until he becomes angry. As for discussion of knowledge, there is no prohibition on it. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Ata' and Mujahid. Or it means cursing, as said by Ibn 'Umar and Qatada. Or it means disputing over who came upon the standing place (mawqif) of their fathers. They used to do this in the Jahiliyyah: Quraysh would stand at a place other than the standing place of the Arabs, and then they would dispute about it. This was said by Ibn Zayd and Malik. Or some say, "Hajj is today," and others say, "Hajj is tomorrow." This was said by al-Qasim. Or it means disputing over the months, according to what the Arabs did, for they sometimes made Hajj fall outside Dhu al-Hijjah. Some would stand at Jam', others at 'Arafat, and they would argue over which is correct. This was said by Mujahid.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is the most correct and most apparent of the views. The Law has fixed the time of Hajj, and entering ihram for it is decisive and not open to dispute. Or it is the saying of a group: "Our Hajj is more righteous than yours," and the other group says the same. This was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi. Or it is boasting about one's fathers, said by some. Or it is the saying of the Companions to the Prophet (ﷺ), "We began the declaration of Hajj," when he said during the Farewell Pilgrimage: "Whoever does not have a sacrificial animal with him, let him exit ihram and make it an 'Umrah." This was said by Muqatil. Or it is the dispute with companions, servants and hired camel-drivers. This was said by al-Zamakhshari. Or it is everything that is called jidal for the sake of overpowering and self-interest, in which case the nine views mentioned above are included.

The fa' (ف) in "fa-la rafath" (so there is no rafath) is the one that enters into the response of the conditional, if "man" is taken as a conditional, which is the more apparent. Or it is in the predicate (khabar) if "man" is taken as a relative pronoun.

Ibn Mas'ud and al-A'mash read "rufuth," and it has already been mentioned that rafath and rufuth are both verbal nouns (masadir). Abu Ja'far read with raf' (nominative) and tanwin (nunation) in all three words, and this is reported from 'Asim in some transmissions, namely the route of al-Mufaddal from 'Asim. Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi read with nasb (accusative) and tanwin in all three. The Kufans and Nafi' read with fath (vowel "a") in all three without tanwin. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "fa-la rafathun wa la fusuqun" with raf' and tanwin, and "wa la jidal" with fath without tanwin.

As for those who read all three with raf', they treated "la" as not governing, and put what follows it in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'). The predicate for all of them is the phrase "fi al-Hajj" (during Hajj). It is possible that it is the predicate of the first subject, with the predicate of the second and third omitted for indication. It is also possible that it is the predicate of the third, with the predicates of the first and second omitted for indication. It is not permissible that it be the predicate of the second, and that the predicates of the first and third be omitted, because of the ugliness of this construction and the separation. It was said: it is also possible that "la" acts like laysa (is not), so that "fi al-Hajj" is in the accusative position. Ibn 'Atiyya firmly held this view, saying: "la" has the meaning of laysa in the reading with raf'. But this view that Ibn 'Atiyya permitted and firmly adopted is weak, because the operation of "la" like laysa is very rare, and nothing of it has come in the language of the Arabs except for what is of no consequence. What is preserved of that is the verse:

*"Be consoled; there is nothing on earth that remains, nor any refuge against what Allah has decreed."*

Ibn Malik recited this, and I do not know this line except through him. Al-Nabigha al-Ja'di said:

*"She has taken possession of the heart's blackness; I am not one who seeks another, nor one who is slack in her love."*

Another said:

*"I denied her after years had passed; neither is the house a house, nor the neighbors neighbors."*

Sibawayh explained the verse of the poet on this basis:

*"Whoever turns away from its fires, I am the son of Qays; there is no retreat."*

All of this admits of interpretation, and if it were taken at face value, it does not reach the degree of frequency upon which rules are built. Therefore it should not be applied to the Book of Allah, which is the most eloquent and most sublime speech, and one should not depart from the common and eloquent form. As for the reading with nasb and tanwin, they are in the accusative as verbal nouns (masadir), and the governing verbs are of the same root: the estimate is "fa-la yarfuthu rafathan, wa la yafsuqu fusuqan, wa la yujadilu jidalan" (so he should not commit sexual intercourse, nor wickedness, nor quarrel). "Fi al-Hajj" is connected to whichever of these verbs you wish, following the method of operation and contention (tanazu').

As for the reading with fath in all three without tanwin, the disagreement is over the vowel: is it a vowel of i'rab (grammatical declension) or a vowel of bina' (fixed construction)? The second is the view of the majority, and the proofs are mentioned in grammar books. When it is built with fath, is the whole, consisting of "la" and what is built with it, in the nominative position as a subject? And even if "la" governs the noun in the accusative according to its position, and has no predicate? Or is the whole not in the position of a subject, but "la" governs that noun in the accusative according to its position, and what follows it is the predicate of "la," when it is treated like inna in putting the noun in the accusative and the predicate in the nominative? There are two views among the grammarians: the first is the view of Sibawayh, and the second is that of al-Akhfash. On these two views depends the grammatical analysis of "fi al-Hajj": it is in the position of the predicate of the subject according to Sibawayh, and in the position of the predicate of "la" according to al-Akhfash.

As for the reading of the one who read with raf' and tanwin "fa-la rafathun wa la fusuqun," and with fath without tanwin "wa la jidal," then according to our chosen view of raf' as subject, and according to Sibawayh's view that the fathah word with "la" is in the nominative position as subject, "fi al-Hajj" is the predicate of all of them, because there is nothing in it but conjunction, the conjunction of a subject on a subject. As for al-Akhfash's view, "fi al-Hajj" cannot be anything but the predicate of the two subjects, or of "la," or the predicate of "la," because the case of "fi al-Hajj" differs: the subject requires it, or "la" requires it, and since the case differs, it cannot be the predicate of both.

Ibn 'Atiyya said regarding this reading the following text: "'La' has the meaning of laysa in the reading with raf'. The predicate is omitted in the reading of Abu 'Amr, and 'fi al-Hajj' is the predicate of 'la jidal'. The omission of the predicate here is according to the view of Abu 'Ali [al-Farisi], but this has been opposed. Rather, 'fi al-Hajj' is the predicate of everything, since it is in the nominative position in both readings, because 'la' only operates on what follows it, and its predicate is raised by inna in its original state of the predicate of the subject. Abu 'Ali thought that it is like laysa in the accusative of the predicate, and this is not so. Rather, it and the noun are in the position of the subject, and both require a predicate, and 'fi al-Hajj' is the predicate." End of his words. There are objections to this. The first: his statement that "la" has the meaning of laysa. We have already mentioned that the use of "la" with the meaning of laysa is so rare in their speech that rules are not built upon it, and we explained that the raising of such a thing is on the basis of the subject. The second: his statement "the predicate is omitted in the reading of Abu 'Amr." People have stated that the predicate of kana and its sisters, including laysa, may not be omitted, neither by abbreviation nor by brevity. Then they mentioned that the predicate of laysa has been omitted in poetry, in the verse:

*"He hopes for your protection when there is no protector."*

...through the way of necessity or rarity, and what is like this should not be used to interpret the Qur'an.

The third point: his saying, "rather, *fi al-Hajj* ('in the Hajj')" is the predicate (*khabar*) of the whole, since it is in a position of nominative case (*raf'*) according to both possibilities. By the two possibilities he means that *la* is in the sense of *laysa* ("is not"), and that it is built (*mabniyyah*) together with *la*. This is not correct. If it has the meaning of *laysa*, it requires a predicate in the accusative (*manṣūb*). If it is built together with *la*, the predicate must be in the nominative, either because *la* itself is the governing element that gives the nominative case, according to the view of al-Akhfash, or because it, together with what it governs, is in a position of nominative case as a subject (*mubtada'*), which requires that the predicate of the subject be the predicate according to the view of Sibawayh, as we have previously stated regarding the disagreement. Once this is established, it is impossible for *fi al-Hajj* to be in a position of nominative case according to what Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned as the two possibilities.

The fourth point: his saying, "because *la* only works in its own manner on what follows it, and its predicate remains nominative as it was from the predicate of the subject." This is a justification for *fi al-Hajj* being the predicate of the whole, since it is in a position of nominative case in both possibilities, as he claimed. We have already shown that this is not permissible: if it has the meaning of *laysa*, its predicate is in a position of accusative case. This justification fits only if *la* works only like *inna*, according to the view of Sibawayh and not according to the view of al-Akhfash. For according to al-Akhfash, *fi al-Hajj* is in a position of nominative case by *la*, and *la* is the governing element of the nominative, so the grammarian contradicts his own view, because the reading with nominative case is based on the subject, while the reading with fatha in "﴿nor any disputing﴾" is based on *la* working like *inna*.

The fifth point: his saying, "Abu 'Ali thought that it has the status of *laysa* in the accusative of the predicate, and it is not so." This thought is correct, and it is as he thought. What proves it is that the Arabs, when they explicitly stated the predicate to show that *la* has the meaning of *laysa*, used it in the accusative in their poetry. This shows that what Abu 'Ali thought regarding the accusative of the predicate is correct, but it is so rare that rules are not built upon it, as we have mentioned. Therefore Abu 'Ali permitted it, but something like this should not be applied to the Qur'an.

The sixth point: his saying, "rather, it and the noun in the position of a subject both require a predicate, and *fi al-Hajj* is the predicate." What he mentioned is a confirmation of what was established earlier, that when *la* has the meaning of *laysa*, it works on the noun only in the nominative, and it and the noun are in a position of nominative case as a subject, and the predicate is nominative for that subject. We have shown that this is not correct, because the Arabs put the predicate in the accusative when it has the meaning of *laysa*. And even if we accept what he said, we cannot know that it works like *laysa* on the noun only when the predicate is nominative, because we have only the form: *la rajula qa'imun* ("no man is standing") and *wa la imra'atun*. Here *rajul* is the subject, *qa'im* is the predicate about it, and *la* does not govern. What distinguishes its being in the sense of *laysa* is the accusative of the predicate when it has the meaning of *laysa*, and the nominative of the noun from it being a subject, and the nominative of the predicate when what follows it is nominative as a subject. Otherwise it is impossible to know this at all, since it is likely that the noun is the subject and the nominative after it is its predicate. [p. 90] Al-Zamakhshari said: Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read the first two with nominative case and the last with accusative case, because they took the first two to mean a prohibition, as if it were said: "there should not be obscenity or sin," and the third to mean a statement of the absence of disputing, as if it were said: "there is no doubt or disagreement regarding the Hajj." This is because the Quraysh differed from the rest of the Arabs: they would stand at the Sacred Mash'ar, while the rest of the Arabs stood at 'Arafat. They would advance the Hajj one year and delay it another year, which is the *nasi'* (intercalation), so it was returned to one time, and the standing was returned to 'Arafat. So God the Exalted informed that the disagreement regarding the Hajj has been removed.

* *

It has been cited as evidence that what is forbidden is obscenity (*rafath*) and sin (*fusuq*), not disputing, by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever performs the Hajj and does not commit obscenity and does not sin returns like the day his mother bore him." And that he did not mention disputing. End of his statement. There are objections to it.

The first: his interpretation for Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir, that they took the first two to mean a prohibition because of the nominative, and the third to mean a statement because of the built form. The nominative and the built form do not require any of that. Rather, there is no difference between the nominative and the built form in that what they are in is built. As for the claim that the nominative requires a prohibition and the built form requires a predicate, this is not so. Then the reading of all three with nominative and the reading of all of them as built both show this. The only difference between them is that the reading of the built form is an explicit statement of generality, and the reading of the nominative supports it. So their reading of the first two with nominative and the third as built with fatha is only a followed tradition, when this cannot be achieved except in this way, among the permissible ways in Arabic in this kind of construction.

The second: his saying "as if it were said: there is no doubt or disagreement regarding the Hajj." Supporting this with the history he mentioned under this interpretation contradicts what he himself explained for disputing. For he said before: "nor disputing nor quarrelling with companions, servants, or muleteers." This interpretation of disputing contradicts that interpretation.

The third: the history he mentioned consists of two opinions among the earlier scholars regarding the interpretation of "﴿nor any disputing﴾": their disagreement about the standing place, according to Ibn Zayd and Malik, and the *nasi'* according to Mujahid. He made these two one thing, as the cause for the statement that there is no disputing in the Hajj.

The fourth: his saying "It has been cited as evidence that what is forbidden is obscenity and sin, not disputing..." up to the end of his statement. There is no evidence in this. For if disputing is among what is prohibited, it is included in his saying "﴿nor sin﴾" by its generality. And if it is among what is disliked and leaving the better, then it is not made a condition for the forgiveness of sins. Therefore the Prophet (ﷺ) connected the forgiveness of sins to the prohibition of what invalidates the Hajj among the forbidden acts specific to it, which is permissible outside the Hajj, namely intercourse, referred to by obscenity. And among the forbidden acts prohibited absolutely both in the Hajj and outside it is the disobedience of God, expressed by sin. The saying "﴿nor any disputing﴾" comes as a completion of what the pilgrim should be upon, namely devoting his deeds to the Hajj and avoiding quarrelling and arguing. So the purpose of the verse is other than the purpose of the hadith. Therefore the verse combined the three, while the hadith mentioned only two.

The discussion of this sentence remains: is it meant literally as a negation, and so it is a statement? Or is its form that of a negation while what is meant is a prohibition? They differed on this. In *al-Muntakhab*, it is said: the people of the meanings (*ahl al-ma'ani*) said: the apparent meaning of the verse is a negation, but its meaning is a prohibition, i.e., "do not commit obscenity, do not sin, do not dispute," like His saying: "﴿there is no doubt in it﴾" [al-Baqarah 2], i.e., do not doubt in it. The qadi mentioned that its apparent meaning is a report, and it allows the prohibition. If it is taken as a report, its meaning is that his Hajj is not valid with any of these characteristics; rather it is invalidated. So it is like the opposite of them, and they prevent its validity. This meaning does not hold unless obscenity is understood as intercourse, sin as fornication, and disputing as doubt regarding the Hajj and its obligation, because doubt in that is disbelief, and the Hajj is not valid with it. These words are understood in these meanings so that God's report is true, since these things are not found together with the Hajj. And if it is taken as a prohibition, which is contrary to the apparent meaning, it is possible that obscenity means intercourse and its preliminaries, and the speech of indecency, sin, and disputing means all their kinds, by the generality of the word, so it includes all its divisions, since the prohibition of a thing is a prohibition of all its divisions. [p. 91] The verse would then be clear about beautiful morals, pointing to the subduing of the appetitive power by His saying "﴿so there is no obscenity﴾," the subduing of the irascible power by His saying "﴿nor sin﴾," and the subduing of the imaginative power by His saying "﴿nor any disputing﴾." He mentioned these three because the source of evil is confined to them. And since He forbade disputing, He understood disputing as the establishment of falsehood and the seeking of wealth and status, not as the establishment of truth and calling people to God and defending His religion. End of what we have summarized from his statement.

What we choose is that it is a sentence whose form is that of a report, but whose meaning is a prohibition, because if the literal report were intended, the expression conveying this meaning would be a different construction from this one. Do you not see that if a person said, for example: "Whoever enters the prayer, there is no intercourse with his wife, no fornication with others, and no disbelief in the prayer," intending a report that these things invalidate it, this statement would not be in the eloquence of the rank of his saying: "Whoever enters the prayer, he has no prayer with the intercourse with his wife, his fornication, and his disbelief"? So what fits the report's meaning is the negation of the validity of the Hajj together with the presence of obscenity, sin, and disputing, not the negation of them in it. This is the eloquent Arabic arrangement. Rather, the form of a negation is used for the prohibition to indicate that what is forbidden is considered unlikely to occur in the Hajj, as if it were something that does not exist, and something about which it is not valid to report that it does not exist. He also said in *al-Muntakhab*: If what is meant by obscenity is intercourse, then it is a prohibition of what requires the invalidity of the Hajj, and there is consensus (*ijma'*) on this, and it is a negation of validity in its presence. If what is meant by it is conversation with women about the matter of intercourse, or obscene speech, then it is a prohibition for the perfection of virtue. Ibn al-'Arabi said: it is not a negation of the existence of obscenity, but a negation of its legitimacy, because obscenity occurs from some people during it, and God's reports cannot be contrary to what they report. The negation returns only to its existence as legitimate, not to its existence as perceptible. Like His saying: "﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods﴾" [al-Baqarah 228], its meaning is legitimate, not perceptible, since we find divorced women who do not wait. So the negation returns to the legal ruling, not to sensory existence. This is like His saying: "﴿None touches it except the purified﴾" [al-Waqi'ah 79], if we say it refers to human beings, which is the correct view, because its meaning is: none of them touches it legally. If touching occurs, it is contrary to the legal ruling. This is the subtle point that escaped the scholars, who said that the report has the meaning of a prohibition, and that this never existed and cannot exist, since the two differ in reality and are distinct in description. End of Ibn al-'Arabi's statement. Four opinions are summarized regarding this sentence. One: it is a report of the negation of specific things, namely intercourse, fornication, and disbelief. Two: it is a report of the negation of legitimacy, not of existence. Three: it is a report in form, and what is meant is a prohibition. Four: a distinction in the reading of Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Umar, that the first two have the meaning of a prohibition and the third is a report. This sentence is in the position of the response of the conditional if *man* is conditional, and in the position of the predicate if *man* is relative. In both cases it must contain a connecting element (*rabit*) that links the response clause to the condition, when the condition is a noun, and the report clause to the relative subject when it is not the same in meaning. There is no connecting element here pronounced, so it must be implied. It may have two possibilities. One: that *minhu* ("from it") is implied after "﴿nor any disputing﴾," and it is in the position of a qualifier, and the connection is achieved by it, as in the saying: "Butter is two *manas* for a dirham," i.e., two *manas* of it, with *minhu* being a qualifier of the two *manas*. Two: that it is implied after *al-Hajj*, and its implication is: "in the Hajj, from it, or for it," or what resembles it, by which the connection is achieved.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 197 (part 4 of 4):

The Kufans have another interpretation of such a case: the *alif* and *lam* (of "al-Hajj") are a substitute (*'iwad*) for the pronoun. On their view, the implied wording in his saying "in al-Hajj" is "in his Hajj," so the *alif* and *lam* stand in place of the pronoun, and the connection is achieved through them. Some have said: he repeated "al-Hajj," saying "fi al-Hajj" rather than "fihi," following the Arab custom of emphasis by placing the noun in place of the pronoun, as in the words of the poet:

*I do not see death being outpaced by anything*

End of his words. In the verse, however, this is better, because it is further from the first interpretation, because it comes in a different clause from the first, and to remove the suspicion that the pronoun refers to "man" (*man*) and not to Hajj, that is: "in the one who obligates himself (*fariḍ*) (p-92) to Hajj."

According to what we have chosen, that the purpose of these statements is prohibition, these three things are forbidden during Hajj. As for *rafath* (obscene speech or sexual conduct), most scholars, both later and earlier, hold that it here means sexual intercourse, and that it is forbidden by the verse. The scholars have agreed that intercourse invalidates the Hajj, and that its preliminaries require a sacrificial animal (*dam*), except for what was narrated by some unknown transmitters from Abu Hurayrah, that he heard him say: "For the one in ihram, everything from his wife is permitted except intercourse." The community has agreed against this, and that whoever kisses his wife with desire must offer a *dam*. This was narrated from Ali, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Ata, Ikrimah, Ibrahim, Ibn al-Musayyab, and Ibn Jubayr, and it is the view of the jurists of the major cities. Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm held that kissing one's wife and physical contact with her are permitted, while he avoids sexual intercourse.

As for *fusuq* (wickedness) and *jidal* (quarrelling), although they are forbidden outside Hajj too, they were singled out for mention during Hajj to magnify the sanctity of Hajj, and because indulging in sins in such a state is a more flagrant display against this act of worship, and more grievous, than in other circumstances. Do you not see the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the fasting person: "He should not engage in obscenity or act foolishly; if someone insults him, let him say, 'I am fasting'"? And his saying, when he turned the gaze of al-Fadl ibn Abbas away from looking at women during Hajj: "This is a day in which whoever keeps his hearing and his sight under control will be forgiven"? It is well known that such a thing (i.e., the wrong) occurs on other days too, but he singled it out for mention to magnify its sanctity. In His saying "*nor wickedness*" there is an indication that Hajj renews repentance from sins, until a person returns from his sins as on the day his mother bore him.

* *

﴿And whatever good you do, Allah knows it﴾. This is a conditional clause, and the discussion of the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of its counterpart was given earlier, in His saying: ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate﴾ (2:106). Good was singled out, although Allah, may He be exalted, knows both good and evil, to urge doing good. Also, because what preceded of the mention of the obligation of Hajj is good; and so that these forbidden things are replaced by their opposites: obscene speech is replaced by good speech and beautiful conduct, wickedness by obedience, and quarrelling by harmony. Also, so that the hope for the face of Allah, may He be exalted, increases; and so that it is a promise of reward. The answer to the condition is "Allah knows it." Either the recompense for doing good is expressed by knowledge, as if it were said: "Allah will recompense you for it," or the mention of recompense comes after the mention of knowledge, meaning: "Allah knows it, and so He will reward for it." In His saying "*whatever you do*" there is an iltifat (shift in grammatical person), since it is a shift from the third person to the second person (address). It also involves treating the word "*man*" (whoever) in terms of its meaning, since it is a shift from singular to plural. He expressed what proceeds from a person of action, speech and intention by the phrase "*you do,*" either by giving precedence to action, or by applying the term "action" to speech and belief, for it is said: "the actions of the limbs," "the actions of the tongue," and "the actions of the heart." The pronoun in "*knows it*" refers to "*what*" (*ma*) in His saying "*whatever you do*," and "*min*" (of) is in the accusative position and is connected to an omitted element. Some grammarians have erred, saying: "*min khayr*" is connected to "*taf'alu*" and is in the accusative position as a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun, whose implied wording is: "*wa-ma taf'aluhu fi'lan min khayrin ya'lamhu Allah*" (and whatever you do of an act of good, Allah knows it). He made it jussive as the answer to the condition, and the pronoun in "*Allah knows it*" returns to *khayr*. That is the end of his words. Had it not been recorded in the tafsir, I would not have related it. The source of the error in it is that he claimed "*min khayr*" is connected to "*taf'alu*," then he said it is in the accusative position as a qualifier of a verbal noun. If that is so, the governing element is omitted, and this contradicts the claim that "*min*" is connected to "*taf'alu*," because when "*min*" is connected to "*taf'alu*," the governing element is not omitted. His statement that the pronoun returns to *khayr* is a gross error, because the clause is the answer to a conditional clause with a noun (the noun-form condition). So the pronoun returns to the noun, that is, the noun of condition. If you make it return to *khayr*, the answer is devoid of a pronoun referring back to the noun of condition, and that is not permitted. If you say "*man ya'tini yakhruj Khalid*" (whoever comes to me, Khalid will go out), it is not allowed unless a pronoun referring to the condition noun is supposed to be there. However, when the condition is with a particle, it is permitted for the clause to be devoid of a pronoun, as in: "*in ta'tini yakhruj Khalid*" (if you come to me, Khalid will go out).

﴿And take provision, for the best provision is taqwa (God-consciousness)﴾. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that it was revealed about some people from Yemen who would perform Hajj without provisions, saying: "We rely upon God for the Hajj to the House of God, will He not feed us?" They would then depend on people, and sometimes they would oppress and seize property, so they were commanded to take provisions and not to oppress or become a burden on people. It is narrated from Ibn Umar that he said: "When they entered ihram and had with them provisions, they would throw them away and take other provisions, so they were forbidden from that (p-93) and commanded to take care of provisions and to take provisions." According to what is narrated as the occasion of revelation of this verse, it is a command to take provision for worldly journeys. But what the context of what precedes and follows this command indicates is that the command to take provision here is in relation to acquiring righteous deeds, which are for him like provision for his journey to the Hereafter. Do you not see that before it is: ﴿And whatever good you do, Allah knows it﴾, meaning the exhortation and encouragement to do good, for which recompense in the Hereafter is established; and after it: ﴿for the best provision is taqwa﴾? In the usage of the Shari'ah and the Qur'an, taqwa is an expression for that by which the Fire is guarded against. The object of "*tazawwadu*" (take provision) is omitted; its implied wording is: "*wa-tazawwadu al-taqwa*" (and take taqwa as provision), or "*min al-taqwa*" (of taqwa). Because he omitted the object, he brought the predicate of *inna* (indeed) as an explicit noun so as to indicate that the omitted element is this explicit noun. Had the object not been omitted, he would have brought it as a pronoun referring back to the object, or he would have brought it explicitly to glorify the mention of taqwa and to magnify its status. Some have said about taking provision for the Hereafter:

*If you do not travel with provision of taqwa,*
*and meet after death one who has taken provision,*
*You will regret not being like him,*
*and that you did not prepare as he had prepared.*

(And some of the Arabs of the Jahiliyyah said):

*If praise could make people immortal, no one would die,*
*but the praise of people does not grant immortality.*
*Yet from it there are lasting inheritances,*
*so leave to your sons some of it, and take provision.*
*Take provision for the day of death, for it*
*is the last appointment, even if the soul dislikes it.*

Sa'dun al-Majnun (the madman) climbed a hill in a graveyard when a group of people had departed from a funeral, and he called out to them:

*Oh army of the living!*
*This is the army of the dead!*
*They answered the lesser call,*
*while they await the greater.*
*They urge you toward provision,*
*but there is no provision except taqwa.*
*They say to you: strive,*
*for this is the goal of the world.*

It was said: He commanded taking provision for the journey of worship and of livelihood, and its provision is food, drink, mount and wealth; and for the journey to the Return, its provision is the fear of Allah, may He be exalted. This provision is better than the first provision, because of His saying: ﴿for the best provision is taqwa﴾.

From all of this, three opinions emerge. The first: it is a command to take provision for the journeys of this world, so the object of "*tazawwadu*" is what they benefit from, for the best provision is that by which you protect your faces from begging and your selves from injustice. Al-Baghawi said: The exegetes said: taqwa here means cakes, olive oil, roasted flour, dates, raisins, and what resembles these foods. The second: it is a command to take provision for the journey of the Hereafter, and this is what we choose. The third: it is a command to take provision for both journeys, as if the implied meaning is: "Take what you benefit from for the near and the far of your journey." The one who held that the meaning is: "Take as provision the good companion" is far off, unless by it he means righteous deeds, in which case it is not far, for that is the second opinion, which we have chosen.

Abu Bakr al-Razi said: His saying "*take provision*" may include both meanings: provision of food and provision of taqwa. So it is necessary to take it as both, since no evidence has established the restriction of one of the two meanings. He mentioned taking provision of righteous deeds in Hajj because it is the most deserving of the accumulation of acts of righteousness in it, owing to the multiplication of reward for them. Just as He emphasized the gravity of wickedness, though it is forbidden in other places, to magnify the sanctity of the state of ihram, and to inform that it carries a greater sin during it. Then He informed that the provision of taqwa is better than both, because its benefit lasts and its reward endures. This indicates the invalidity of the doctrine of the Sufis and those who travel without provision or mount, because He, may He be exalted, addressed with this those whom He addressed with Hajj. On this basis, the Prophet (ﷺ) said when he was asked about *istita'ah* (ability to perform Hajj): "It is provision and a mount." That is the end of his words.

It was refuted: those who are perfect in the station of tawakkul (trust in God) are not faulted for traveling without provision, because it is authentically reported: "If you truly relied upon Allah, He would provide for you as He provides for the birds: they go out hungry in the morning and return full at evening." And the Most High said: ﴿Whoever relies upon Allah, He is sufficient for him﴾ (65:3). Some people have passed days without food, some have been content with a little sustenance over many days, and some with a sip of water. It is authentically reported in the hadith of Abu Dhar that he was sustained by Zamzam water for a month, and he left it with a bulge in his stomach. Also, a group of the Companions were content for many days, each of them with one date per day. As for breaking customary norms, such as the millstone turning by itself to grind flour, and the oven filling with dough even though there is no food and the like, they have related the occurrence of such things. Sufyan ibn Uyaynah drank the leftover of Sufyan al-Thawri from the water of Zamzam, and found it to be sawiq (roasted flour drink). The breaking of customary norms for non-prophets is authentically established and confirmed, so such a thing does not recur except from one who claims it, and it is not on the path of uprightness, like many of those whom we have witnessed claiming it, and it is claimed for them.

﴿And fear Me﴾. This is a command to fear Allah, may He be exalted. Since what indicates the avoidance of certain things during Hajj has preceded, and they were commanded to take provision for the Return, and He informed about taqwa as the best provision, all of that was fitting with the command to taqwa and the warning against committing what incurs His punishment. Then He said: ﴿O people of understanding﴾, to stir them to comply with the command to taqwa, because no one heeds the consequences except the one who possesses intellect; he is the one upon whom Allah's proof is established, and he is the one who is fit for command and prohibition. If the one of intellect does not fear Allah, it is as if he has no intellect. This form of address has been discussed earlier in His saying: ﴿And in retribution there is life for you, O people of understanding﴾ (2:179), so it suffices without repeating it. The apparent meaning of "intellect" is the intellect that is the basis of legal responsibility (taklif), so it is general, not the intellect acquired through experience, which would make it specific, because those commanded to fear Allah are all those who are legally responsible.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 198 (part 1 of 2):

﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord﴾. The occasion of its revelation (sabab al-nuzul) is that the Arabs, when Islam came, felt uneasy about attending the markets of the Jahiliyyah (the period of ignorance before Islam), such as ʿUkaz, Dhu al-Majaz, and Majanna. So God permitted them to do so. This was said by Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, and ʿAta'. Mujahid also said: Some of the Arabs would not slaughter animals from the time they entered the state of ihram, so this verse was revealed to permit that. It is also narrated from Ibn ʿUmar that it was revealed concerning the one who hires out (his animals or himself) during the Hajj, and that his Hajj remains complete. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn ʿAbbas, and Ibn al-Zubayr read: "bounty from your Lord during the seasons of the Hajj." The better view, however, is to treat this as an explanation (tafsir) and not as part of the text, because it contradicts the written text of the Mushaf upon which the Ummah has agreed.

The word al-junah (blame) means liability for consequence (al-darak), and it is more general than sin (ithm), because it applies to what requires punishment and to what requires only reproof and punishment. By "bounty" (fadl) here is meant the profits that result from trade. Likewise included is what is obtained as payment for hire during the Hajj. Consensus (ijma') has been established on the permissibility of trade and earning of every kind, and of commerce, provided one performs the Hajj in its proper manner. The only exception is what is reported as an anomalous opinion from Saʿid ibn Jubayr: a Bedouin asked him, "I hire out my camels, and I intend to perform the Hajj; will it count for me?" He said, "No, and no honour." This contradicts the apparent sense of the Book and the consensus, so it is not to be relied upon.

The connection (munasabah) of this verse with what precedes it is as follows: when God forbade disputation (jidal), and trade may lead to dispute, it was appropriate that trade be placed under restraint. This is because whatever leads to a forbidden thing is itself forbidden. Alternatively, trade was prohibited among the people of the Jahiliyyah at the time of the Hajj, since one who is occupied with worship should not busy himself with worldly gain. Or again, since many permissible things had become forbidden to the Muslims during the Hajj, trade was likely to be regarded by them as belonging to that category, so God permitted it and informed them that there is no blame upon them for it during the days of the Hajj. This is supported by the reading of those who read "during the seasons of the Hajj." Abu Muslim understood the verse to refer to what comes after the Hajj, and he compared it to the verse: ﴿And when the prayer is concluded, disperse in the land and seek of God's bounty﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 10]. Thus he analogized the Hajj to the prayer. His view is weakened by the presence of the particle "fa" in "﴿When you have finished﴾" [al-Baqarah: 200]. This was made explicit after the seeking of bounty, which indicates that what precedes the outpouring (al-ifadah) occurs during the time of the Hajj. Moreover, the locus of the suspicion of impermissibility is trade during the time of the Hajj, not after its completion, since everyone knows that trade is lawful at that time. Therefore, interpreting the verse in terms of the locus of the suspicion is more appropriate. Also, analogizing the Hajj to the prayer is a faulty analogy, because the acts of prayer are connected to one another, whereas the acts of the Hajj are separate from one another. Within the course of the Hajj, the one performing it remains under the original ruling, in that he is not yet in the state of a pilgrim in the relevant respects. It cannot be said that the ruling of the Hajj extends over him at those times, as evidenced by the prohibition of perfume, sewn clothing, and similar things, because this is an analogy against an explicit text, so it is invalid, and it has been attributed to him.

Indeed, the bounty here is what a person does by which he hopes for God's grace and mercy, such as helping the weak, aiding one in distress, and feeding the hungry. The judge (al-Qadi) objected to this, saying that these things are obligatory or recommended, so one does not say of them "there is no blame upon you." Rather, one says this of permissible acts, and of trade: if it causes a deficiency in obedience, it is not permissible, and if it does not cause a deficiency, then leaving it is better. Thus it is in the category of concessions (rukhas). The grammatical analysis (iʿrab) of the phrase "an tabtaghu" (that you seek) has already been discussed in the verse: ﴿There is no blame upon him that he should go around them both﴾ [al-Baqarah: 158]. The phrase "min rabbikum" (from your Lord) is connected with "tabtaghu," and "min" indicates the starting point (ibtida' al-ghayah). Alternatively, it is connected with a deleted element and is an attribute of "fadl" (bounty). In that case "min" also indicates the starting point, or it indicates partition (al-tab'id), which requires supposing a deleted genitive construction, meaning: "from the surpluses of" (min fudul).

﴿So when you pour forth from ʿArafat﴾. It has been said that this indicates the obligation of standing at ʿArafat, since the outpouring cannot occur except after it. This is what was said, and the conclusion of this statement has been reached. However, obligation does not clearly follow from this condition. It indicates only that one must be present at ʿArafat and stand there. Is that by way of obligation or recommendation? The verse gives no evidence for that, but the established Sunnah and consensus indicate it. In al-Muntakhab it is said: The outpouring from ʿArafat is conditional upon presence at ʿArafat, and whatever is necessary for an obligation to be fulfilled, and which is within the capacity of the responsible person, is itself obligatory. Thus it is established that the verse indicates that presence at ʿArafat is obligatory in the Hajj. So if he does not do it, he has not performed the Hajj that was commanded, and therefore he is not released from the obligation. This implies that standing at ʿArafat is a condition. This is the end of his words.

His statement that "the outpouring from ʿArafat is conditional upon presence at ʿArafat" is ambiguous. If he means that its occurrence is conditional, that is, the occurrence of the outpouring is conditional upon presence at ʿArafat, then it is correct, but occurrence does not indicate obligation. If he means that its obligation is conditional upon presence at ʿArafat, then we do not grant that. Rather we say: if he stood at ʿArafat and made it his dwelling until he died, the outpouring from it would not be obligatory for him, and he would not have neglected an obligation if he died there, and his Hajj is complete if he has performed all its pillars (arkan). His statement "and whatever is necessary for an obligation to be fulfilled" up to the end of the sentence is based on the premise that the outpouring is obligatory, and we have rejected that. His statement "thus it is established that the verse indicates that presence at ʿArafat is obligatory" is built upon what came before, and we have made clear that this does not follow. Moreover, "idha" (when) does not indicate a specific time. Rather it indicates the certainty of occurrence or its likelihood. Its apparent meaning requires that whenever he pours forth from ʿArafat it is permitted for him, and this requires that the standing at ʿArafat which is followed by the outpouring was sufficient.

The time of standing at ʿArafat extends from the decline of the sun on the day of ʿArafat until the break of dawn on the day of sacrifice (yawm al-nahr), without disagreement. They agreed that whoever stands there at night, his Hajj is complete, even if he pours forth before sunset, provided he had stood there after the decline of the sun. They agreed that his Hajj is complete, except Malik, who said: his Hajj is void. Something similar is reported from al-Zubayr. Malik also said: he must perform the Hajj again in the following year, and he must sacrifice a sacrificial animal (hady) during that subsequent Hajj. As for one who says his Hajj is complete: al-Hasan said, he must offer a sacrificial animal; Ibn Jurayj said, a camel (badanah); and ʿAta', al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa, al-Shafiʿi, Ahmad, and Abu Thawr said: he must offer a sheep or goat (dam). If he poured forth before sunset and then returned to ʿArafat, and then departed after sunset, Abu Hanifa, al-Thawri, and Abu Thawr held that the sacrifice is not dropped. Al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, and Dawud al-Tabari held that there is nothing due from him. The hadith of ʿUrwah ibn Mudarris: "Whoever pours forth from ʿArafat before that, whether by night or by day, his Hajj is complete and he has fulfilled his obligations (qada tafathahu)" agrees with the apparent sense of the verse in not requiring any part of the night, except what consensus has excluded, namely that standing before the decline of the sun does not suffice, and that one who pours forth during the day has nothing due upon him. In the phrase "﴿from ʿArafat﴾" the "min" indicates the starting point, and it is connected with "afadtum" (you poured forth). The apparent sense of this expression implies the generality of ʿArafat, so from whichever part of it one pours forth, it suffices for him. This also implies that standing may be performed in whichever part of it one stands. The majority hold that ʿUrana is part of ʿArafat. Al-Bajji related from Ibn Habib that ʿUrana is in the non-sacred area (al-hill), while ʿUrana is in the sacred area (al-haram). It has been said that the western wall of the Mosque of ʿUrana, if it were to fall, would fall into the belly of ʿUrana. Whoever holds that the belly of ʿUrana is part of ʿArafat, then if one stands there: it is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Qasim, and Salim that: "Whoever pours forth from ʿUrana has no Hajj." Ibn al-Mundhir mentioned this from al-Shafi'i, and Abu al-Mus'ab from Malik. Khalid ibn Nawar related from Malik that his Hajj is complete, and he must shed blood (sacrifice). Ibn al-Mundhir also mentioned this from Malik. It is related: "All of ʿArafat is a place of standing (mawqif), but rise above the belly of ʿUrana." Most of the reports do not contain this exception, so they are like the apparent sense of the verse.

The manner of the outpouring is that they proceed with a good gait, and do not trample the weak, and do not harm one who is walking. For when the Prophet (ﷺ) departed from ʿArafat, he would hasten (aʿnaqa), and when he found an open space, he would go at full speed (nassa). The ʿanaq is a swift pace with gentleness, and the nass is a strong pace beyond the ʿanaq. This is what al-Asmaʿi and al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said. If the imam delays without excuse, the people push forward. The ritual of standing in the mosques (al-taʿrif) that people perform, imitating the people of ʿArafat, is not prescribed. Some scholars said: it is nothing. The first to perform the taʿrif was Ibn ʿAbbas in Basra, and ʿAmr ibn Huraith also performed it. Ahmad said: I hope there is no harm in it, and many have done it: al-Hasan, Bakr, Thabit, and Muhammad ibn Wasi' used to attend the mosque on the day of ʿArafat.

As for fasting on the day of ʿArafat for those standing there: Yahya ibn Saʿid al-Ansari said: it is obligatory for them to break the fast. Some permitted it. ʿUthman ibn al-Qadi, Ibn al-Zubayr, and ʿAisha fasted it. ʿAta' said: I fast it in winter and I do not fast it in summer. The majority hold that leaving the fast is better, following the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

* *

﴿So remember God at the sacred monument (al-mashʿar al-haram)﴾. The "fa" is the response to "idha" (when). The remembrance (dhikr) here means supplication, humble entreaty, and praise; or it means the maghrib and ʿisha prayers at Muzdalifah; or it means supplication. There are three views on this prayer, and jurists build upon them whether the command is one of recommendation or of obligation. If remembrance means the prayer, then there is no indication in it of combining the two prayers, so the command to remember, with respect to combining the two prayers, becomes general (mujmal), and it is clarified by the action of the Prophet (ﷺ), which is the Sunnah at Muzdalifah. If one prays maghrib before arriving at Muzdalifah, Abu Hanifa and Muhammad said: it does not suffice for him. ʿAta', ʿUrwah, al-Qasim, Ibn Jubayr, Malik, Ahmad, Ishaq, and Abu Thawr said: combining is not a condition for validity. As for one who has an excuse from pouring forth, among those who stood with the imam, he prays each prayer at its own time. This was said by Ibn al-Mawwaz. Malik said: he combines them when the twilight has disappeared. Ibn al-Qasim said: if he hopes to reach Muzdalifah by the third of the night, he should delay the two prayers until he reaches it; otherwise he prays each prayer at its own time.

Do they pray the two with two iqamahs without an adhan? Or with one adhan for maghrib and two iqamahs? Or with two adhans and two iqamahs? Or with an adhan and iqamah for the first, and no adhan and no iqamah for the second? These are four views.

The first is the view of Salim, al-Qasim, al-Shafi'i, Ishaq, and one of two opinions of Ahmad. The second is the view of Zufar, al-Tahawi, and Ibn Hazm, and it is reported from Abu Hanifa. The third is the view of Malik. The fourth is the view of Abu Hanifa; and the Sunnah is that the one combining them should not perform a voluntary prayer between them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 198 (part 2 of 2):

Al-mash'ar (the sacred landmark) is a mash'al form from sha'ara, meaning "the landmark" or "the marker." Al-Haram (the sacred, inviolable) is so called because it is forbidden to do there what is prohibited of the restrictions of ihram. This mash'ar is also called Jam' (the Gathering), and it is the stretch between the two mountains of Muzdalifah, from the boundary of the passage from 'Arafah to the bottom of Muhassir. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, Ibn Jubayr, and Mujahid. The Arabs call the valley of Muhassir "the Valley of Fire." Neither al-Ma'ziman nor the valley of Muhassir is part of al-Mash'ar al-Haram. Al-Ma'zim (the narrow pass) is a single narrow passage between two mountains; it is called in the dual because of the two mountains. It has also been said that al-Mash'ar al-Haram is Quzah, the mountain on which the imam stands and on which is the fire-place (al-maydaqah). It has been said that this is the correct view, based on the hadith of Jabir: "When the Prophet ﷺ prayed the dawn prayer, that is, at Muzdalifah, in the darkness of the early morning, he mounted his she-camel and came to al-Mash'ar al-Haram, then he supplicated, glorified God (takbir) and declared His oneness (tahlil), and he continued standing until it became light." According to this, the verse mentioned does not refer to the remembrance (p-97) at Muzdalifah, neither as supplication nor as prayer there. Rather, it is a command to remember at this mountain, Quzah, to which the Messenger of God ﷺ rode, where he supplicated, glorified God and declared His oneness, and he stood after his dawn prayer at Muzdalifah in the darkness until it became light. There is then an omitted clause, the implied meaning being: "When you pour forth from 'Arafat and have spent the night at Muzdalifah, then remember God at al-Mash'ar al-Haram." The meaning of "at" (indi) here is nearness to it, and that it is adjacent to it. All of Muzdalifah is a place of standing (waqf), except the valley of Muhassir, and it was made entirely a place of standing because it has the ruling of the mash'ar and is connected to it. It has also been said that Muzdalifah and what the stated boundary contains were called a mash'ar, and it is expressed in the singular because it is uniform in ruling, so it is like a single place. In al-Muntakhab it is said: "This command indicates that presence at al-Mash'ar al-Haram is obligatory, and passing through it suffices, as with 'Arafah. As for standing there, it is sunnah," end of his words. That standing is sunnah is the view of the majority of scholars. Abu Hanifa said: it is obligatory, so whoever abandons it without an excuse must offer a sacrifice (dam); but if he has an excuse, or fears crowding, there is no harm in his leaving early at night, and there is nothing upon him. Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Hasan, 'Alqamah, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, and al-Awza'i said: standing at Muzdalifah is an obligatory pillar (fard), and whoever misses it has missed the Hajj, and he should make his ihram an 'umrah.

The verse indicates only the desirability of remembrance at al-Mash'ar al-Haram, not standing, nor spending the night at Muzdalifah. They agreed that spending the night there is not a pillar (rukn). Malik said: whoever does not spend the night there must offer a sacrifice; and if he remains there for most of the night, there is nothing upon him, because spending the night there is a strongly emphasized sunnah according to Malik. This is also the view of 'Ata', Qatadah, al-Zuhri, al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa, Ahmad, Ishaq, and Abu Thawr. Al-Shafi'i said: if he leaves it after midnight, there is nothing upon him; if before, he must pay a ransom (fidyah), which is a sheep. The absolute command to remember does not indicate a specific remembrance. Some said: the best remembrance is to say, "O God, as You have granted us success in it, grant us success in remembering You as You have guided us, and forgive us and have mercy on us as You promised us," by Your saying, and Your saying is the truth: ﴿When you pour forth﴾, and he recites up to His saying: ﴿Indeed God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 199], and after that he supplicates with whatever he wishes of the good of this world and the Hereafter. What appears to be the case is that the remembrance of God here is praising Him, and extolling Him, and giving Him praise; and by the remembrance of God here is not meant the mere utterance of the word "Allah," but rather the meaning is: remember God with words that indicate His glorification, His praise, and His commendation. "'Inda" (at) is in the accusative governed by "udhkurū" (remember). This shows that the response of "idhā" (when) cannot be the governing element for it, because the place of the pouring forth is not the place of the remembrance: the former is 'Arafat, and the latter is this sacred mash'ar; and when the two places differ, it necessarily follows that the two times differ, so the remembrance at the sacred mash'ar cannot occur at the time of the pouring forth.

﴿And remember Him as He has guided you﴾. This second command is the first, and it is repeated for emphasis and to intensify the command to remember, since remembrance is among the best acts of worship; or it is a different command, and what is meant is its connection to the Oneness of God, that is: remember Him in His oneness as He guided you by His guidance; or the connection of the remembrance has the sense of: remember Him with remembrance after remembrance. This view was held by Muhammad ibn Qasim the grammarian. The remembrance that is performed at standing at Muzdalifah on the morning of Jam' is what is meant; and the first is taken to mean the sunset and night prayers at Muzdalifah, as related by al-Qadi Abu Ya'la. The kaf in "kama" (as) is for comparison, and it is in the accusative position, either as an adjective to an omitted verbal noun or as a circumstantial qualifier (hal). This discussion has been treated in more than one place earlier. The meaning: produce the remembrance in its best state, by resembling God's guidance to you, since His guiding you is the finest of the blessings He has bestowed upon you; so let the remembrance be at the utmost of presence and constancy until it resembles the excellence of the guidance. For this meaning al-Zamakhshari said: remember Him with a good remembrance as He guided you with a good guidance, end of his words. It is possible that the kaf is causal, according to the view of those who affirmed this meaning for the kaf, so the sense would be: "as He guided you," that is: remember Him and magnify Him for the prior guidance from Him, exalted is He, to you. Sibawayh related: "kama annahu la ya'lamu fa-tajawaza Allahu 'anhu," that is, because he does not know, God pardoned him. al-Akhfash and Ibn Burhan affirmed this meaning for it. The "ma" in "kama" is verbal (masdariyyah), that is: like His guidance of you. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah permitted that "ma" be a ma that restrains the kaf from governing. The difference between them is that the verbal "ma" (p-98) makes it and what follows it in the place of a genitive, since a verbal noun is formed from it together with the verb, whereas the kaf cannot have this, since it has no governing power at all. The better reading is to take "ma" as verbal, so that the kaf retains the governance of the genitive that is established for it. Abu Sa'd, and 'Ali ibn Mas'ud ibn al-Farrukhal, author of al-Mustawfi, prohibited that the kaf be restrained by "ma" from governing, and whoever affirmed it argued with the verse of the poet:

"By your life, I and Abu Humayd are like the drunk man and the forbearing man,
I want to satirize him, and I fear my Lord, but I know he is a base slave."

The guidance here is specific, that is: by returning you in the rites of your pilgrimage to the sunnah of Abraham, may God bless our Prophet and him. So "ma" is general, encompassing the kinds of guidance: knowledge of God, knowledge of His angels, His books, His messengers, and His laws.

﴿And indeed you were before it among the astray﴾. "In" here, according to the Basrans, is the emphatic "in" that is the lightened form of the heavy one, and it entered upon the sister-verb as it enters upon the nominal sentence. As for the lam in "lamina" and what resembles it, there is disagreement: is it the lam of the beginning (lam al-ibtida'), obligatory for distinction? Or is it another lam brought in for distinction? The view of al-Farra' on such a construction is: "in" is the negating "in" meaning "ma," and the lam means "illa"; al-Kisa'i held that "in" means "qad" when it enters upon a verbal sentence, and the lam is superfluous; and when it enters upon a nominal sentence it means the negating "ma," and the lam means "illa." The proofs of this question are treated in the science of grammar. According to the view of the Basrans, this sentence is affirmative and emphatic with no restriction; according to the view of al-Farra', it is affirmative with restriction; and according to the view of al-Kisa'i, it is affirmative and emphatic from a different aspect than the Basrans' view. "Min qablihi" (before it) is connected to an omitted element, which is explained by His saying "among the astray," the sense being: "And indeed you were astray before it, among the astray." Whoever among the grammarians permits fronting an adverbial or prepositional phrase over the governing element when it is the complement of the definite article (al-alif wa-l-lam), would connect "min qablihi" according to his view with "among the astray." This has been mentioned before. The pronoun in "qablihi" refers to the guidance understood from His saying "hada-kum" (He guided you), that is: "And indeed you were before the guidance among the astray." God reminded them of the blessing of guidance, which is the most complete of blessings, so that they would keep remembering Him, praising Him, and thanking Him, which is the cause of increased favor. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, and it has been said that it refers to the Prophet ﷺ. The apparent meaning of "error" is the error of disbelief, just as the apparent meaning of "guidance" is the guidance of faith. It has also been said: "among the astray" concerning the rites of the Hajj, or concerning the details of its rituals.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 199 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Then depart from where the people depart﴾. It is authentically reported from ʿĀʾisha that she said: "The Ḥums (the Ḥums being the people of Quraysh and those who followed their religion) were those about whom Allah, the Exalted, revealed: ﴿Then depart from where the people depart﴾. They used to return to ʿArafāt." And in al-Jāmiʿ of al-Tirmidhi, from ʿĀʾisha, she said: "Quraysh and those who followed their religion, who are the Ḥums, used to stand at Muzdalifa, saying, 'We are the people of Allah's sanctuary (qaṭīn Allāh).' Everyone else used to stand at ʿArafa, so Allah revealed: ﴿Then depart from where the people depart﴾." Abu ʿĪsā (al-Tirmidhi) said: "This is a ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ ḥadīth." Muḥammad ibn Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim narrated from his father, who said: "I went out in search of a camel at ʿArafa, and I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) standing at ʿArafa with the people before he was commissioned as a prophet. I said, 'By Allah, this man is from the Ḥums; what is he doing standing here with the people?'" The standing of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at ʿArafa was an inspiration from Allah, the Exalted, and a divine enabling toward what is the legislation of Allah and His intent. Quraysh had invented practices: they would not eat clarified butter (aqiṭ) and would not melt ghee while in ihram; they would not enter a house of hair, and would seek shade only in tents of leather; they would not eat until they had left the sacred precinct (ḥilл) while in the state of ḥurum; no one arriving at the House would circumambulate except in the garments of the Ḥums, and whoever did not find such garments would circumambulate naked; if he circumambulated in his own clothes, he would cast them off and never take them back, neither he nor anyone else. The Arabs called those garments al-laqī. They also permitted a woman to circumambulate wearing her shift, whereas previously she would circumambulate naked with a cord over her private parts, until a woman among them said:
"Today some of it or all of it appears, but what appears of it, I do not make lawful."
When Allah revealed: ﴿Then depart from where the people depart﴾, and revealed: ﴿Take your adornment at every place of worship, and eat and drink, but do not be excessive﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 31], He permitted for them what they had forbidden to themselves, namely standing at ʿArafa, and eating, drinking and clothing. Based on this reported occasion of revelation, the addressees of "departing" here are Quraysh, their allies, and those who followed their religion, who are the Ḥums. This is the view of the majority. It has also been said that the address is general, to Quraysh and others. The departure commanded is from ʿArafāt, except that "thumma" (then), on this reading, departs from its original Arabic function of indicating a delay in time relative to the preceding action. Allah has said: ﴿When you depart from ʿArafāt, remember Allah at the sacred landmark, and remember Him as He has guided you﴾ [al-Baqara: 198], and then ﴿Then depart﴾. The departure has already been mentioned, and they were commanded to remember [Allah] when they depart; so how can they be commanded to it afterward with "thumma," which indicates a delay in time? This has been answered in several ways.

The first: that this is the order of mention, not the order in time in which the actions occur. This is supported by the fact that the earlier departure was not something commanded; what was commanded was remembrance of Allah when it is performed, and a command to remember at the time of performing it does not imply a command to perform it.
