Do you not see that you say: "If Zayd strikes you, then strike him"? Zayd is not thereby commanded to strike. So it is as if it were said: "Then let that departure be from ʿArafāt, not from Muzdalifa as the Ḥums do." Some have claimed that "thumma" here means "wa" (and), indicating no sequence, as if he said: "And depart from where the people depart," so it is for conjoining one statement to another that has been separated from the first. Some grammarians have permitted that "thumma" may come in the sense of "wa," indicating no sequence. Some people have read "thumma" here in its original sense of sequence by positing an inversion of order in the speech, making: ﴿Then depart﴾ coordinated with His statement: ﴿And fear Me, O people of understanding﴾ [al-Baqara: 197]. As if it were said: "Then depart from where the people depart, and ask Allah's forgiveness; indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful. There is no blame upon you in seeking bounty from your Lord. Then when you depart from ʿArafāt..." On this reading, the departure conditioned here is that departure commanded. But inversion of order is something specific to necessity, and we exalt the Qur'an above being interpreted by it. This can be achieved by making "thumma" indicate order in mention rather than in the time of the action, or by making the departure commanded here other than the conditioned departure, this departure being from Jamʿ to Mina. The addressees of "Then depart" are all Muslims. This is what al-Ḍaḥḥāk and a group with him said, and al-Ṭabarī preferred it, and it is what the apparent meaning of the Qur'an requires. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you ask: what is the position of 'thumma'? I say: its position is like its position in your saying: 'Be good to people, then do not be good to an ungenerous person.' 'Thumma' comes to indicate the disparity between being good to the generous and being good to others, and the distance between them. Likewise, when He commanded them to remember Allah at departing from ʿArafāt, He said: 'Then depart,' because of the disparity between the two departures, one of which is correct and the second an error." End of his words.

The verse is not like the example he gave. The summary of what has been mentioned is that "thumma" is stripped of sequence and has another meaning, which he called disparity and distance between what follows and what precedes. He also did not permit in the verse the mention of the erroneous departure, so "thumma" in "﴿Then depart﴾" came to indicate the distance and disparity between the two departures. We know of no one who preceded him in establishing this meaning for "thumma."

* *

"Min ḥaythu" (from where) is connected to "afīḍū" (depart); "min" is for the beginning of the limit, and "ḥaythu" here is in its original use as an adverb of place. Al-Qaffāl said: "From where the people depart" is an expression for the time of departure from ʿArafa. There is no need to remove "ḥaythu" from its original meaning, and it seems he wished to differentiate between the two departures: the first is in place and the second in time. But there is no difference, because each of them requires the other and indicates it, so they are mutually entailing, namely the place of departure from ʿArafāt and its time. Thus this does not provide an answer regarding the coming of the conjunction "thumma."

"Al-nās" (the people), its apparent meaning is generality among those who depart, and its meaning is that it is the ancient matter upon which the people are, as you say: "This is something people do," meaning (p-100) it is their custom. It has been said: "al-nās" refers to the people of Yemen and Rabīʿa. It has been said: all the Arabs except the Ḥums. It has been said: "al-nās" refers to Ibrāhīm and those who departed with him from among his sons and the believers in him. It has been said: Ibrāhīm alone. It has been said: Ādam alone, and this is the view of al-Zuhrī, because he is the father of mankind and they are his offspring and followers, and the Arabs address a great man who has followers with the plural address, and likewise one who has many attributes. From this is the verse of poetry:
"You are all the people, for in you is what all people have gathered of beautiful description."
This is supported by the reading of Ibn Jubayr: "min ḥaythu afāḍa al-nāsī" (with a yāʾ), from His statement: ﴿And We had already taken a covenant from Ādam before, but he forgot﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 115]. The use of "al-nās" for one individual of mankind is contrary to the original usage. This has been preferred on the ground that His statement "min ḥaythu afāḍa al-nās" is a past verb indicating an earlier agent, and the departure proceeded only from Ādam and Ibrāhīm. This preference does not necessarily follow, because "ḥaythu," when it is attached to a clause beginning with a past verb, may have the past verb in its literal sense, as in His statement: ﴿Then come to them from where Allah has commanded you﴾ [al-Baqara: 222]. Sometimes it is meant as the future, as in His statement: ﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face﴾ [al-Baqara: 150]. This is well known with "ḥaythu," so the objection does not follow. Even granting that it is a past verb and indicates an earlier agent, it does not follow that its agent must be one person, because before this command to depart, the departure was either by all who had departed before Quraysh changed that, or by others than Quraysh after their change, from the rest of the Arabs who performed Ḥajj. Therefore it is better to take "al-nās" as the general class of those who depart, or their specific class. Al-Ṭabarī preferred the view that they were the people of Yemen and Rabīʿa, based on the Ḥajj of Abū Bakr with the people when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded him to lead the people out to ʿArafāt and stand there; when the sun set, he would depart with the people until he brought them to Jamʿ and they spent the night there. Abū Bakr set out for ʿArafāt and passed by the Ḥums who were standing at Jamʿ. When he wanted to pass them, the Ḥums said to him: "O Abū Bakr! Where are you passing us to go to others? This is the standing place of your fathers!" But Abū Bakr continued as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had commanded him until he reached ʿArafāt, where the people of Yemen and Rabīʿa were. This is the interpretation of His statement: ﴿From where the people depart﴾. He stood there until the sun set, then departed with the people to the Sacred Landmark (al-Mashʿar al-Ḥarām), where he stood, and when the sun rose he departed from it.

The reading of Ibn Jubayr, "min ḥaythu afāḍa al-nāsī" with a yāʾ, is an anomalous reading (shādhdha), and in it is an alert that departure from ʿArafāt is an ancient legislation, and it contains a reminder that calls to mind the covenant of Allah and that one should not forget. We have mentioned that it is interpreted to mean that the "forgetful one" (al-nāsī) is Ādam, peace be upon him. It is possible that al-nāsī in Saʿīd's reading means "the one who leaves," i.e., who leaves standing at Muzdalifa first, and that it refers to the class, since al-nāsī may be used for one who leaves something. So the meaning, and Allah knows best, is that they were commanded to depart from the same direction from which whoever left departing from Muzdalifa and departed from ʿArafāt departs. The "forgetful one" here denotes the class, so it agrees in meaning with the reading of the majority, because the people whom we are commanded to depart from where they departed are those who leave standing at Muzdalifa and who make departure from ʿArafāt in accordance with the practice of the one who established Ḥajj, namely Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him, unlike Quraysh, who made departure from Muzdalifa and would not stand at ʿArafāt and depart from it. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "It is permitted according to some of them to drop the yāʾ, so one says al-nās, like al-qāḍ and al-hād." He said: "As for its permissibility in Arabic, Sībawayh mentioned it; as for its being recited, I do not know of it." End of his words.

As for his statement, "As for its permissibility in Arabic, Sībawayh mentioned it," the apparent sense of Ibn ʿAṭiyya's words is that this is permissible absolutely, whereas Sībawayh permitted it only in poetry, and al-Farrāʾ permitted it in ordinary speech. (p-101) As for his statement, "As for its being recited, I do not know of it," that he does not know it does not mean that no one else knows it. Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Mahdawī said: "'Afāḍa al-nāsī' is attributed to Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, and also from him: al-nāsi with a kasra and without a yāʾ." End of the words of Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Mahdawī.

﴿And ask Allah for forgiveness﴾. He commanded them to seek forgiveness in places where acceptance is expected and in places of mercy. It is asking Allah for forgiveness with the tongue together with repentance in the heart, since seeking forgiveness with the tongue without repentance in the heart is not beneficial. They were commanded to seek forgiveness even though some of them had committed no sin, such as one who reached puberty shortly before entering ihram and had not committed a sin and entered ihram; so seeking forgiveness is for such a person because perhaps some shortcoming occurred in performing the obligations and in guarding against the prohibited acts. The apparent meaning of this command is that it is not a request for forgiveness of a specific sin, but a request for forgiveness of sins in general. It has also been said that it is a command to seek a specific forgiveness, and the meaning is: "And ask Allah's forgiveness for what occurred from your opposition in standing and departing, for He is Forgiving to you, Merciful regarding what you neglected in your state of ḥill and ihram, and in your travel and your residence."

In the command to seek forgiveness after departure, or together with it, is evidence that that time, and that place from which one departs and to which one goes, are times and places of answered supplication, and of mercy and forgiveness.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 199 (part 2 of 2):

It has been narrated that he (ﷺ) delivered a sermon on the evening of 'Arafah, saying: "O people, indeed Allah, the Exalted, has shown His favour to you in this standing place of yours. He has accepted from your righteous ones, and has pardoned your sinners for the sake of your righteous ones, except for wrongs committed among yourselves. So proceed in the name of Allah." Then, when it was the morning of Jam', he delivered a sermon and said: "O people, indeed Allah has shown His favour to you, and has compensated for the wrongs from His own presence."

Abu 'Amr ibn 'Abd al-Barr (d. 463 AH) cited in (al-Tamhid) three hadiths which indicate that Allah, the Exalted, boasts before His angels of the pilgrims to His House, that He forgives them what sins they had committed before, and that He has guaranteed on their behalf the compensation for wrongs.

"Istaghfara" (to seek forgiveness) takes two objects: the second of them is with a preposition, and it is of the form "fu'ul" (i.e., it is transitive with the preposition). The original usage is: istaghfartu Allah min al-dhanb (I asked Allah's forgiveness for the sin), and it is permissible to omit "min," as the poet said:

"I seek Allah's forgiveness for a sin I cannot count, Lord of the servants, to Him are directed the face and the deed."

Its implied form is: min dhanb (from a sin). Abu al-Hasan ibn al-Tarawah (al-Tarawah) held that "istaghfara" takes two direct objects by itself, and that the saying "istaghfara Allah min al-dhanb" came by way of tadmin (implicit meaning), as if he had said "tubtu ila Allah min al-dhanb" (I repented to Allah from the sin). This view is refuted by Sibawayh's statement and his transmission of it from the Arabs, and this is mentioned in the science of grammar. Here the second object has been omitted because it is known, and it did not come in the Qur'an expressed, neither with "min" nor in the accusative. This contrasts with "ghafara," for its object sometimes comes mentioned in the Qur'an, as in His saying: ﴿And who forgives sins except Allah?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 135], and sometimes omitted, as in His saying, Exalted is He: (He forgives whom He wills). "Istaghfara" also comes governing the particle "li" (for), as Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿So they sought forgiveness for their sins﴾ [Al 'Imran: 135], and ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin﴾ [Ghafir: 55]. It seems that this lam, Allah knows best, is the lam of cause, and that what it governs is a object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlih). The form "istaf'ala" here expresses request, like "istawhaba" (to ask for a gift), "istat'ama" (to ask for food), and "ista'ana" (to seek help), and this is one of the meanings for which the form "istaf'ala" comes. We have mentioned this in His saying: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ [al-Fatihah: 5].

(Indeed Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful): this is as a reason for the command to seek forgiveness, namely that He, Exalted is He, is abundant in forgiveness and abundant in mercy. These two attributes are for emphasis. The most common pattern "fa'ul" comes from "fa'ala," such as ghafur (Forgiving), safuh (Pardoning), sabur (Patient), shakur (Grateful), darub (Striking), qattul (Slayer), tarruk (Leaver), hajum (Assailant), and 'alluk (Glutton). The most common pattern "fa'il" comes from "fa'ila" with a kasra on the 'ayn, such as Rahim (Merciful), 'Alim (Knowing), Hafiz (Preserver), and Sami' (Hearing). The two patterns may overlap. They say: raqaba fa-huwa raqib (he watched, so he is a watcher), qadara fa-huwa qadir (he was able, so he is capable), and jahila fa-huwa jahul (he was ignorant, so he is ignorant). The discussion of such phrases has already passed, namely that the end of the speech is the mention of the name of Allah, then it is repeated with its wording after "inna."

It is preferable that forgiveness and mercy be stated without restriction, and that this is part of His nature, Exalted is He. It has been said that the forgiveness promised in the verse is at the departure from 'Arafah, and it has been said that it is at the departure from Jam' to Mina. The first view that we have mentioned is preferable.

﴿So when you have completed your rites, remember Allah as you remember your fathers, or with a more intense remembrance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 200]. The occasion of its revelation: they used, when they gathered at the season, to boast of their fathers. One of them would say: "He used to host the guest, strike with the sword, feed the food, slaughter the camel, free the captive, and forelock-cut the foes (i.e., hold the forelocks of the enemy), and he did such and such." Then it was revealed.

Al-Hasan said: when they related stories, they swore by their fathers, saying: "By your father," so it was revealed. Al-Suddi said: when they completed the rites and stayed at Mina, a man would stand and ask Allah, saying: "O Allah, indeed my father was great in hospitality and abundant in wealth, so give me the like of that," not mentioning Allah, but mentioning his father, and asking Allah to give him in his worldly life. Abu Wa'il and Ibn Zayd said the same meaning. So it was revealed: "﴿So when you have completed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 200]," meaning: when you have performed and finished. Like His saying: ﴿So when the prayer is concluded﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 10], meaning: when it is performed. The term "qada'" (completion) may be used for acts of worship performed outside the prescribed time. When "qada'" is attached to the action of the self, what is meant is completion and finishing, as in His saying: "And whatever you missed, make up (faqdu)." When it is attached to the action of another, what is meant is obligation, as in His saying: "The judge decided between them (qada al-hakim bayna-huma)." What is meant in the verse is finishing.

Some exegetes said: it is possible that this is a condition and its consequent, like your saying: "When you perform Hajj, then circumambulate and stand at 'Arafah," so that by "qada'" is not meant finishing the Hajj, but entering into it, and by "remembrance" is meant what they were commanded to do of supplication at 'Arafah, at the Sacred Mash'ar, and in the circumambulation and the running (sa'y). The meaning would then be: when you begin the completion of the rites, that is, in performing them, then remember. This is contrary to the apparent sense, for the apparent meaning is finishing the rites, not beginning them, and the fa' in "fa-idha" after the preceding sentences supports this.

"Al-manasik" (the rites) are the places of worship, so this is on the omission of a modifier, meaning: the acts of your rites. Or the acts of worship themselves commanded in Hajj, as al-Hasan said. Or the sacrifices and the shedding of blood, as Mujahid said.

"Fa-udhkuru Allah" (then remember Allah) is the answer to "idha" (when). The meaning: when you have finished standing at 'Arafah and departed from Mina, then glorify Allah and praise Him, since He guided you to this obedience and made it easy and facile for you, until you fulfilled the obligation of your Lord and were freed from the burden of this difficult, arduous matter that cannot be accomplished except with great toil and the exertion of self and wealth. It has been said: the remembrance here is the mention of Allah over the sacrificial animal. It has been said: it is the takbirs after the prayer on the day of sacrifice and the days of tashriq. It has been said: rather, the intent is to turn them from remembering their fathers to remembering Him, Exalted is He: "as you remember your fathers" has already passed. This is the mention of their boasts; or the request from Allah to give them the like of what He gave their fathers; or the oath by their fathers. It has been said: the remembrance of their fathers in childhood, and their clinging to their father, saying "abah abah" (Daddy, Daddy), as their first utterance. It has been said: the meaning of remembrance here is anger for the sake of Allah, as you become angry for your parents when they are reviled; this was said by Abu al-Jawza, from Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn 'Atiyyah transmitted that Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi recited: "kadhikrikum aba'ukum" (with the nominative "aba'ukum"), and others transmitted from Muhammad ibn Ka'b that he recited "abakum" (in the singular). The justification for the nominative is that it is the subject of the verbal noun, and the verbal noun is annexed to the object, the sense being: as your fathers remember you. The meaning: be devoted to the remembrance of Allah and cling to Him as a man clings to the remembrance of his son.

The justification for the singular is that it is sufficient in place of the plural, because the plurality is understood from the annexation to a plural, since it is known that the addressees do not have one father, but fathers.

Regarding "aw" (or) here, it has been said: it is for choice; it has been said: it is for permission; and it has been said: it means "bal" (rather) with "ashadda" (more intense). They allowed for its parsing several possibilities, to which they were compelled, because they believed that "dhikran" after "ashadda," as a specification (tamyiz) after the superlative (af'al al-tafdil), cannot be maintained as a specification except by these estimations that they proposed. The problem with it being a specification is that when the superlative governs what follows, it is other than what precedes it; you say: "Zayd is better in face" (ahsan wajhan), because the face is not Zayd. If it is of the same kind as what precedes it, it takes the genitive, as in: "Zayd is the best man" (afdal rajulin). Accordingly, the construction in the likes of "strike Zayd like the striking of 'Amr, Khalid, or a more intense striking" would be in the genitive, not the accusative, because what follows the superlative is of the same kind as what precedes it. They therefore permitted the accusative in that case on several grounds.

The first: that it is in coordination with the place of the kaf in "dhikrikum," because it is, in their view, an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: a remembrance like your remembrance of your fathers, or more intense. They made the remembrance itself the one who remembers, in a metaphorical sense, as they say: "poetry is a poet" (shi'r sha'ir). This was said by Abu 'Ali and Ibn Jinni.

The second: that it is coordinated with "aba'ikum" (your fathers). This was said by al-Zamakhshari, who said: in the sense of "aw ashadda dhikran min aba'ikum" (or more intense in remembrance than your fathers), on the basis that "dhikran" is from the action of the one mentioned. The end of his words. This is an unsettled statement; its meaning is that if you coordinate "ashadda" with "aba'ikum," the estimate becomes: "aw qawman ashadda dhikran min aba'ikum" (or a people more intense in remembrance than your fathers), so the people become the ones mentioned, and the remembrance that is the specification after "ashadda" is from their action, that is, from the action of the people mentioned, since it came after the superlative that is an attribute of the people. The phrase "min aba'ikum" means: from your remembrance of your fathers.

The third: that it is in the accusative by an implied verb of being, and the speech is carried according to the meaning. The estimate: "aw kunu ashadda dhikran lahu minkum li-aba'ikum" (or be more intense in remembrance of Him than you are of your fathers). This is indicated by the fact that the meaning of "fa-udhkuru Allah" is: be remembering Him. Abu al-Baqa said: this is easier than carrying it on the figurative sense, meaning making remembrance have a remembrance, in the view of Abu 'Ali and Ibn Jinni.

They also permitted the genitive for "ashadd" in two ways. The first: that it is coordinated with "dhikrikum." This was said by al-Zajjaj, Ibn 'Atiyyah, and others. The estimate then is: "aw ka-dhikrin ashadd dhikran" (or like a remembrance more intense in remembrance), so that the remembrance has been made to have a remembrance. The second: that it is coordinated with the pronoun in the genitive attached to the verbal noun in "kadhikrikum." This was said by al-Zamakhshari. He said, in his exact words: "aw ashadd dhikran" is in the genitive position, coordinated with what the remembrance was annexed to in His saying "kadhikrikum," as you say: "like the remembrance of Quraysh of their fathers, or a people more intense in remembrance than them." In al-Zamakhshari's statement there is coordination on the pronoun in the genitive without repeating the preposition. So these are five grammatical possibilities, all of them weak. What comes most readily to mind in the verse is that they were commanded to remember Allah with a remembrance equal to that of their fathers, or more intense. It is possible for us to carry the verse on this meaning with a clear justification which they overlooked: that "ashadd" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), being an adjective of "dhikran" had it come after it. Since it came before, it took the accusative as a state, like their saying: "li-Mayya mūḥishan ṭalalu" (for Mayya, a desolate ruin). Had it come after, it would have been: "li-Mayya ṭalalun mūḥishun" (for Mayya, a ruin, desolate). Likewise, had this come after, it would be: "aw dhikran ashadd" (or a remembrance more intense), meaning: of the remembrance of your fathers. Then "aw ashadd" would be coordinated on the place of the kaf in "kadhikrikum." It is also possible that "dhikran" is a verbal noun for "fa-udhkuru" (remember) in the place of a state, as the estimate is: "fa-udhkuru kadhikrikum" (remember as you remember); it being a noun of indefinite reference which came before its adjective, it took the accusative as a state. And "aw ashadd" is coordinated on the place of the kaf as a coordinated state on a state, and it becomes like the saying: "a-dribu mithla darbi fulanin darban" (I strike a blow like the blow of so-and-so, a blow), the estimate being: "darban mithla darbi fulanin." When it came first, it took the accusative as a state. The delay of its position is made fitting because it is like a closing rhyme in the class of the verse-ending. Had it come first, it would be: "fa-udhkuru dhikran kadhikrikum" (so remember a remembrance like your remembrance), and the wording would repeat, while they avoid excessive repetition of the same wording. For this meaning, and for the goodness of the cadence, it came later.

It should not be said against the first aspect that it requires separating the coordinating particle "aw" and the coordinated term "dhikran" by the state "ashadd," for they have stated that when this is permissible, its condition is that the intervening element be an oath, an adverbial of time or place, or a prepositional phrase, and that the coordinating particle be on more than one letter. This second condition is met, namely that the particle is of more than one letter. The first condition is not met, for the intervening element is neither an oath, nor an adverb, nor a prepositional phrase, but a state. A state is in meaning something acted upon within it, so it resembles a particle, and what is permitted for the adverb is permitted for it. This is better than making "dhikran" a specification of the superlative, which is an attribute in meaning, so that the remembrance has a remembrance by putting it in the accusative in the place of the kaf, or by putting it in the genitive as coordinated on the genitive annexed to the remembrance; or that it is an attribute in meaning of the remembrance by putting it in the accusative by an implied verb, i.e., "kunu ashadd," or for the one remembering the remembrance, by putting it in the accusative coordinated on "aba'akum"; or for the remembering agent by putting it in the genitive coordinated on the noun annexed to the remembrance. The weakness of these aspects is not hidden, and the Qur'an should be exalted above them.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 200–202 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Among people there are those who say, "Our Lord, give us in this world,"﴾. They said: God Most High described the state of those who remember Him before His sending of the Prophet, and the state of the believers after His sending, and their knowledge of reward and punishment. What appears to be the case is that this is a division of those commanded to remember God after completing the rites (manasik), and that in their supplication they divide into those whose love of this world predominates, so they ask for nothing but it, and those who ask for the goodness of their condition in this world and the Hereafter. This is an iltifat (a shift in grammatical person). Had it come in the second person, it would have said: "among you are those who say," and "among you." The wisdom of this iltifat is that they were not directed toward this course which no rational person should take, namely limiting oneself to this world. So they were presented in the form of those not addressed with the remembrance of God, by being placed in the form of absent persons. This is one of the divisions which belong to the modes of eloquent expression (bayan). It is a wonderful division, which the divider confines to these two types, and not as the Sufis hold, that there is a third category which God Most High did not mention for them. They said: they are those who are content with His decree, who submit to His command, who remain silent about every supplication and complaint. The second object of "give us" (ataina) is omitted; its estimated form is: "what we desire," or "our request," or what is similar. And the claim that "fi" is superfluous, making "the world" the second object, is a weak opinion; likewise the claim that "fi" means "min" so that it occupies the position of the object is also (p-105) weak. The omission of both objects of ataa (give) and of one of them is permissible for brevity and for limitation, because this is the category of a'ta (give), and that is permissible in it.

﴿And he has no portion in the Hereafter.﴾ Its explanation has already been given in His words: ﴿And they certainly knew that whoever purchased it would have no share in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102]. This sentence here may carry two meanings. One is the report that he has no share in the Hereafter because he limits himself to this world. The second is that the meaning is a report about the supplicant that he has no seeking of a share in the Hereafter, so this serves as an emphasis for his limiting himself to seeking this world. He used the plural in His words: ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world﴾, whereas if it followed the wording of "man" (whoever), it would have been: "My Lord, give me." The plural was observed here because of the large number of those who desire to limit themselves to the aims of this world and to attaining them; had it been singular, it would have been imagined that this was few.

﴿And among them are those who say, "Our Lord, give us in this world a good [thing]"﴾. "Good" (hasanah) is unrestricted, and the meaning is that they asked God in this world for a good condition. The exegetes have illustrated this in several ways: that it is a righteous wife, as said by Ali; or health and sufficiency of wealth, as said by Qatada; or knowledge, or worship, as said by al-Hasan; or wealth, as said by al-Suddi, Abu Wa'il, and Ibn Zayd; or abundant provision, as said by Muqatil; or blessing in this world, as said by Ibn Qutayba; or contentment with provision, or success and protection from sin, or righteous children, or steadfastness in faith, or the sweetness of obedience, or following the Sunnah, or the praise of people, or health, security, competence and victory over enemies, or understanding of the Book of God Most High, or the companionship of the righteous, as said by Ja'far. Many examples are also reported from the Sufis regarding this.

﴿And in the Hereafter a good [thing]﴾. They illustrated the good of the Hereafter as being Paradise, or pardon, forgiveness, and safety from the terror of the standing place and the evil of reckoning, or blessing, or the wide-eyed houris, or the easing of reckoning, or companionship with the Prophets, or the delight of seeing [God], or contentment (ridan), or meeting [Him].

Ibn Atiyya said: it is "the good" by consensus (ijma', i.e., agreement of the scholars). It has been said: it is fitting that the two goods be health in this world and in the Hereafter, because this is established in the hadith of the man whom the Messenger of God (ﷺ) visited when he had become like a young bird, and the Prophet (ﷺ) asked him what he used to supplicate with. He informed him that he had asked God in this world to hasten what would punish him with in the Hereafter, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "You cannot bear it," and said: "Why did you not say: 'O God, give us in this world…'" to its end. So he supplicated to God with both of them and was healed. It is sound that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to supplicate with it most often, and he used to say it between the Yemeni Corner and the Black Stone, and he would command that the most frequent supplication of the Muslim at the standing place (of Arafat) be this. Abu Bakr was the first to say it at the pilgrimage season in the year of the Conquest, then Ali followed him, and all the people. Anas, when he was asked to supplicate, supplicated with it; then when he was asked for more, he repeated it; then when he was asked for more, he said: "What do you want? I have asked God for the good of this world and the Hereafter."

"And in the Hereafter a good [thing]": the waw in it is for conjoining two things with two things, so "in the Hereafter a good [thing]" is conjoined to "in this world a good [thing]." A particle may conjoin two or more things to two or more things. You say: "I informed Zayd of your brother going out and Amr of his father remaining," unless it stands in for two governing words, in which case there is a disagreement, and on permissibility there is detail. This is not from the separation between the conjunction particle and the conjoined element by an adverbial or prepositional phrase, as some claimed; so he permitted that, citing it as evidence against the weakness of al-Farisi's position that this is specific to poetry. For the verse does not belong to this category, but to conjoining two or more things to two or more things. What al-Farisi (Abu Ali) disagreed about is: "I struck Zayd and Amr in the house." The weakness of Abu Ali's position is only shown by the words of God Most High: ﴿God is He who created seven heavens and of the earth their like﴾ [al-Talaq: 12], and by His words: ﴿Indeed, God commands you to render trusts to their owners, and when you judge between people, to judge with justice﴾ [al-Nisa': 58]. The complete discussion of this question is mentioned in the science of grammar (nahw).

﴿And protect us from the punishment of the Fire.﴾ This is a request for protection from the Fire, that is, that they not enter it; it is the Fire of Hell. It has been said: it is the evil woman who is much harmful. Al-Qushayri said: the lam in "the Fire" is the lam of genus (lam al-jins), so seeking refuge is obtained from the fires of burning and the fires of separation, end quote. The apparent meaning of this supplication is that, since their saying "and in the Hereafter a good [thing]" implies that whoever enters Paradise, even the last of the people, is truly said to have been given a good thing in the Hereafter, they asked God that, together with entering Paradise, He preserve them from the punishment of the Fire. It is as if it is a supplication for entering Paradise first without punishment, and that they would not be among those who enter the Fire because of their sins and come out of it through intercession. It is also possible that it is an emphasis on the request to enter Paradise, as one of the Companions said: "I only say in my supplication: O God, admit me into Paradise and protect me from the Fire, and I do not know what your murmuring is, nor the murmuring of Mu'adh." So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Around it we murmur."

﴿Those will have a share of what they have earned.﴾ The division of people into two groups has already been mentioned: a group limited its supplication to its worldly affairs, and a group associated its Hereafter with its worldly affairs. The apparent meaning is that "those" refers to both groups, since the judgment affirmed, namely that they have a share of what they have earned, is common to both, and the meaning is that each group has a share of what it earned: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil. "Earning" here does not mean supplication; rather this is merely a report from God about what the outcome of each of the two groups will be, and that their shares of good and evil follow their earnings.

It has been said: the intended meaning of earning here is supplication, that is, each one of them has a share of what he supplicated for. Supplication was called earning because it is an act, so this constitutes a guarantee of response, a promise from Him Most High that He gives each of them a share of what their supplication requires, either the world alone, or the world and the Hereafter. This is like His words: ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter﴾ [al-Shura: 20], and ﴿Whoever desires the immediate [world]﴾ [al-Isra': 18], and ﴿Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment﴾ [Hud: 15], and the verses (of this kind). As has come in the Sahih: "As for the unbeliever, he is fed with his good deeds in this world for what he did for God with them; then when he comes to the Hereafter, he will have no good for which he is rewarded." In the first meaning there is no promise of response. The "min" in His words "of what they have earned" may be partitive, that is, a share of the kind of what they earned; it may also be causal. The "ma" may be a relative pronoun in the sense of "that which," or a verbal (masdari) relative, that is, "of their earning." It has been said: "those" is specific to reference to the seekers of the two goods only; Ibn Atiyya mentioned no other, while al-Zamakhshari mentioned it opposite to it. Ibn Atiyya said: He promised upon the earning of righteous deeds in the form of a bare report. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Those who supplicate for the two goods, they have a share of the kind of what they earned of righteous deeds, which is the reward that is the benefits of the good, or on account of what they earned, like His words: 'Because of their sins they were drowned'," then he said after some discussion: "It is also possible that 'those' refers to both groups together, and that each group has a share of the kind of what they earned." End of his words.

What is more evident is what we have already presented, that "those" refers to both groups, and it is supported by His words: ﴿And God is swift in reckoning﴾, and this is not something specific to one group rather than another; rather this applies to all creation, and reckoning encompasses the reckoning of the whole world, not merely the reckoning of this group seeking the two goods. It is reported from Ibn Abbas that the share here is specific to one who performs the pilgrimage on behalf of a deceased person, the reward being shared between him and the deceased. It is also reported from him, concerning the hadith of the man who asked whether he should perform the pilgrimage on behalf of his father, who had died, and at its end he said: "Then do I have a reward?" So this verse was revealed. It has been said: if this is sound, then the verse is separate from the one before it, connected to what precedes it of the mention of the pilgrimage, its rites and rulings, end quote. But it is not as he mentioned, separate; rather it is connected to what precedes it, because what precedes it concerns the pilgrimage, and the division of the two groups is within the pilgrimage: among them is one who asked God for this world alone, and among them one who asked for the world and the Hereafter. The answer was given to the questioner about his pilgrimage on behalf of his father: does he have a reward in it? By the general wording of His words: ﴿Those will have a share of what they have earned﴾. Ibn Abbas answered with this verse the one who asked him whether he could hire his mount to people on condition that they perform the pilgrimage, and whether it suffices on his behalf, by the generality of His words: ﴿Those will have a share of what they have earned﴾.

﴿And God is swift in reckoning.﴾ Its apparent meaning is a report about Him Most High with the swiftness of His reckoning; and His swiftness is by its completion quickly, like the approach of its time. It is reported: as much as the milking of a sheep; it is reported: as much as the interval of a she-camel's milking (fawaq); it is reported: as much as the blinking of the eye. Or because He does not need thought or deliberation, like one who is incapable; this was said by Abu Sulayman. Or because He knows what is for the one reckoned and what is against him before his reckoning; this was said by al-Zajjaj. Or because the reckoning of the whole world is like the reckoning of one man, and because the time of the reckoning is near; this was said by Muqatil. It has been said: "reckoning" is used as a metonymy (kunniya) (p-107) for requital for deeds, since it arises from them, like His words: ﴿And I did not know what my reckoning is﴾ [al-Haqqah: 26], meaning what my recompense is. It has been said: "reckoning" is used as a metonymy for knowledge of the courses of affairs, because reckoning leads to knowledge; this was also said by al-Zajjaj. It has been said: he expressed by reckoning the acceptance of His servants' supplication. It has been said: he expressed by it the power and fulfillment, that is, He does not delay the reward of the doer of good nor the punishment of the evildoer. It has been said: it is by omitting a qualifier, that is, "swift is the coming of the Day of Reckoning." So the purpose of the verse is a warning about the swiftness of the Day of Resurrection. It has been said: "swiftness of reckoning" means that His mercy is great and abundant, so it is not diminished nor cut off. Something close to this is reported from Ibn Abbas.

The apparent context of this discourse indicates that the reckoning applies to both the disbeliever and the believer, since it comes after what appears to be addressed to the obedient. The reckoning of the disbelievers is a rebuke and a censure, because they have no good deed in the Hereafter for which they will be recompensed. This is the apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿And I did not know what my account is﴾ [al-Haqqah 69:26]. The majority (al-jumhur) said: the disbelievers are not called to account. God the Exalted said: ﴿So We will not assign them any weight on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Kahf 18:105], and ﴿And We will advance to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan 25:23]. The apparent meaning of the heaviness and lightness of the scales, and what follows from them in the verses of the Qur'an, is that good deeds include the righteous and the wicked, the believer and the disbeliever.

These noble verses contain the following: the Hajj (pilgrimage) has known months (ashhur ma'lumat). He used the plural "months" (ashhur) because of their small number, and they are: Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, and Dhu al-Hijjah, in their entirety, according to what the apparent sense of the plural requires. He described them as "known" (ma'lumat) because people know them. God the Exalted informed that whoever obliges himself to the Hajj during these months must not commit obscenity (rafath), must not transgress (fusuq), and must not dispute (jidal). Thus He forbade the things that spoil the Hajj, including what was permissible before it, and what was impermissible absolutely, so as to equate between the two prohibitions, even though one of them is time-limited and the other is not time-limited.

Then, having forbidden these spoilers, God the Exalted informed that whatever good a person does, beyond the obligation of the Hajj, God knows it, and He rewards him for it. Then He commanded provision for the Hereafter through acts of obedience, and this included what they were engaged in of the Hajj. He informed that the best provision is that which serves as a protection (wiqayah) between you and the Fire. Then He called out to the people of intellect, who are the addressees of the discourse, and commanded them to guard against His punishment. This is because the prohibitions had already been mentioned, so it was fitting that they be concluded with guarding against God's punishment by refraining from what He forbade.

Then, since the pilgrim is occupied with this arduous worship, engaged in its words and actions, it might be supposed that its time cannot be mixed with anything other than its acts. God the Exalted therefore clarified that there is no blame upon whoever seeks bounty (fadl) during it through trade, hire, or other activities that help with the burdens of worldly life. Then He commanded them to remember Him at the Sacred Landmark (al-Mash'ar al-Haram) when they depart from 'Arafat, so that remembrance would bring them back to occupation with the rites of the Hajj, lest attachment to trade and gain absorb them. Then He commanded them to remember Him in gratitude for the guidance He granted them, when previously they had been in error, and He chose them for guidance. Then He commanded them to depart from where the people depart, which is the place from which the people customarily depart. That place is 'Arafah. The meaning is that they were commanded to make that departure, the earlier one, from 'Arafah and not from anywhere else, as mentioned in the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul).

He used "then" (thumma), not to indicate sequence in time, but to indicate sequence in mention, not in occurrence. Then He commanded seeking forgiveness. Then, after the performance of the rites, He commanded remembrance of God the Exalted. Since a person often mentions his father and praises him for the noble deeds he performed before, and this was for them the utmost form of mention, He likened the remembrance of God to that remembrance. Then He emphasized the desirability of exaggerating in remembrance by His saying "or more intensely" (aw ashadd), so that it would be understood that what He had first used as a comparison is only by way of giving an example to them. The intent is that they should not neglect the remembrance of God the Exalted even for the blink of an eye.

Then He divided the aim of the pilgrim into one that is purely worldly and one that is both worldly and otherworldly, and clarified this in his request, and He mentioned that whoever limits himself to his worldly life has no share in the Hereafter. Then He pointed to the totality of the two categories by saying that each of them has a share of what they earned through deeds: if good, then good; and if evil, then evil. He, the Exalted, is swift in reckoning, so He recompenses the servant for what he earned.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 200–202 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Among people there are those who say, "Our Lord, give us in this world,"﴾. They said: God Most High described the state of those who remember Him before His sending of the Prophet, and the state of the believers after His sending, and their knowledge of reward and punishment. What appears to be the case is that this is a division of those commanded to remember God after completing the rites (manasik), and that in their supplication they divide into those whose love of this world predominates, so they ask for nothing but it, and those who ask for the goodness of their condition in this world and the Hereafter. This is an iltifat (a shift in grammatical person). Had it come in the second person, it would have said: "among you are those who say," and "among you." The wisdom of this iltifat is that they were not directed toward this course which no rational person should take, namely limiting oneself to this world. So they were presented in the form of those not addressed with the remembrance of God, by being placed in the form of absent persons. This is one of the divisions which belong to the modes of eloquent expression (bayan). It is a wonderful division, which the divider confines to these two types, and not as the Sufis hold, that there is a third category which God Most High did not mention for them. They said: they are those who are content with His decree, who submit to His command, who remain silent about every supplication and complaint. The second object of "give us" (ataina) is omitted; its estimated form is: "what we desire," or "our request," or what is similar. And the claim that "fi" is superfluous, making "the world" the second object, is a weak opinion; likewise the claim that "fi" means "min" so that it occupies the position of the object is also (p-105) weak. The omission of both objects of ataa (give) and of one of them is permissible for brevity and for limitation, because this is the category of a'ta (give), and that is permissible in it.

﴿And he has no portion in the Hereafter.﴾ Its explanation has already been given in His words: ﴿And they certainly knew that whoever purchased it would have no share in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102]. This sentence here may carry two meanings. One is the report that he has no share in the Hereafter because he limits himself to this world. The second is that the meaning is a report about the supplicant that he has no seeking of a share in the Hereafter, so this serves as an emphasis for his limiting himself to seeking this world. He used the plural in His words: ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world﴾, whereas if it followed the wording of "man" (whoever), it would have been: "My Lord, give me." The plural was observed here because of the large number of those who desire to limit themselves to the aims of this world and to attaining them; had it been singular, it would have been imagined that this was few.

﴿And among them are those who say, "Our Lord, give us in this world a good [thing]"﴾. "Good" (hasanah) is unrestricted, and the meaning is that they asked God in this world for a good condition. The exegetes have illustrated this in several ways: that it is a righteous wife, as said by Ali; or health and sufficiency of wealth, as said by Qatada; or knowledge, or worship, as said by al-Hasan; or wealth, as said by al-Suddi, Abu Wa'il, and Ibn Zayd; or abundant provision, as said by Muqatil; or blessing in this world, as said by Ibn Qutayba; or contentment with provision, or success and protection from sin, or righteous children, or steadfastness in faith, or the sweetness of obedience, or following the Sunnah, or the praise of people, or health, security, competence and victory over enemies, or understanding of the Book of God Most High, or the companionship of the righteous, as said by Ja'far. Many examples are also reported from the Sufis regarding this.

﴿And in the Hereafter a good [thing]﴾. They illustrated the good of the Hereafter as being Paradise, or pardon, forgiveness, and safety from the terror of the standing place and the evil of reckoning, or blessing, or the wide-eyed houris, or the easing of reckoning, or companionship with the Prophets, or the delight of seeing [God], or contentment (ridan), or meeting [Him].

Ibn Atiyya said: it is "the good" by consensus (ijma', i.e., agreement of the scholars). It has been said: it is fitting that the two goods be health in this world and in the Hereafter, because this is established in the hadith of the man whom the Messenger of God (ﷺ) visited when he had become like a young bird, and the Prophet (ﷺ) asked him what he used to supplicate with. He informed him that he had asked God in this world to hasten what would punish him with in the Hereafter, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "You cannot bear it," and said: "Why did you not say: 'O God, give us in this world…'" to its end. So he supplicated to God with both of them and was healed. It is sound that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to supplicate with it most often, and he used to say it between the Yemeni Corner and the Black Stone, and he would command that the most frequent supplication of the Muslim at the standing place (of Arafat) be this. Abu Bakr was the first to say it at the pilgrimage season in the year of the Conquest, then Ali followed him, and all the people. Anas, when he was asked to supplicate, supplicated with it; then when he was asked for more, he repeated it; then when he was asked for more, he said: "What do you want? I have asked God for the good of this world and the Hereafter."

"And in the Hereafter a good [thing]": the waw in it is for conjoining two things with two things, so "in the Hereafter a good [thing]" is conjoined to "in this world a good [thing]." A particle may conjoin two or more things to two or more things. You say: "I informed Zayd of your brother going out and Amr of his father remaining," unless it stands in for two governing words, in which case there is a disagreement, and on permissibility there is detail. This is not from the separation between the conjunction particle and the conjoined element by an adverbial or prepositional phrase, as some claimed; so he permitted that, citing it as evidence against the weakness of al-Farisi's position that this is specific to poetry. For the verse does not belong to this category, but to conjoining two or more things to two or more things. What al-Farisi (Abu Ali) disagreed about is: "I struck Zayd and Amr in the house." The weakness of Abu Ali's position is only shown by the words of God Most High: ﴿God is He who created seven heavens and of the earth their like﴾ [al-Talaq: 12], and by His words: ﴿Indeed, God commands you to render trusts to their owners, and when you judge between people, to judge with justice﴾ [al-Nisa': 58]. The complete discussion of this question is mentioned in the science of grammar (nahw).

﴿And protect us from the punishment of the Fire.﴾ This is a request for protection from the Fire, that is, that they not enter it; it is the Fire of Hell. It has been said: it is the evil woman who is much harmful. Al-Qushayri said: the lam in "the Fire" is the lam of genus (lam al-jins), so seeking refuge is obtained from the fires of burning and the fires of separation, end quote. The apparent meaning of this supplication is that, since their saying "and in the Hereafter a good [thing]" implies that whoever enters Paradise, even the last of the people, is truly said to have been given a good thing in the Hereafter, they asked God that, together with entering Paradise, He preserve them from the punishment of the Fire. It is as if it is a supplication for entering Paradise first without punishment, and that they would not be among those who enter the Fire because of their sins and come out of it through intercession. It is also possible that it is an emphasis on the request to enter Paradise, as one of the Companions said: "I only say in my supplication: O God, admit me into Paradise and protect me from the Fire, and I do not know what your murmuring is, nor the murmuring of Mu'adh." So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Around it we murmur."

﴿Those will have a share of what they have earned.﴾ The division of people into two groups has already been mentioned: a group limited its supplication to its worldly affairs, and a group associated its Hereafter with its worldly affairs. The apparent meaning is that "those" refers to both groups, since the judgment affirmed, namely that they have a share of what they have earned, is common to both, and the meaning is that each group has a share of what it earned: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil. "Earning" here does not mean supplication; rather this is merely a report from God about what the outcome of each of the two groups will be, and that their shares of good and evil follow their earnings.

It has been said: the intended meaning of earning here is supplication, that is, each one of them has a share of what he supplicated for. Supplication was called earning because it is an act, so this constitutes a guarantee of response, a promise from Him Most High that He gives each of them a share of what their supplication requires, either the world alone, or the world and the Hereafter. This is like His words: ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter﴾ [al-Shura: 20], and ﴿Whoever desires the immediate [world]﴾ [al-Isra': 18], and ﴿Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment﴾ [Hud: 15], and the verses (of this kind). As has come in the Sahih: "As for the unbeliever, he is fed with his good deeds in this world for what he did for God with them; then when he comes to the Hereafter, he will have no good for which he is rewarded." In the first meaning there is no promise of response. The "min" in His words "of what they have earned" may be partitive, that is, a share of the kind of what they earned; it may also be causal. The "ma" may be a relative pronoun in the sense of "that which," or a verbal (masdari) relative, that is, "of their earning." It has been said: "those" is specific to reference to the seekers of the two goods only; Ibn Atiyya mentioned no other, while al-Zamakhshari mentioned it opposite to it. Ibn Atiyya said: He promised upon the earning of righteous deeds in the form of a bare report. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Those who supplicate for the two goods, they have a share of the kind of what they earned of righteous deeds, which is the reward that is the benefits of the good, or on account of what they earned, like His words: 'Because of their sins they were drowned'," then he said after some discussion: "It is also possible that 'those' refers to both groups together, and that each group has a share of the kind of what they earned." End of his words.

What is more evident is what we have already presented, that "those" refers to both groups, and it is supported by His words: ﴿And God is swift in reckoning﴾, and this is not something specific to one group rather than another; rather this applies to all creation, and reckoning encompasses the reckoning of the whole world, not merely the reckoning of this group seeking the two goods. It is reported from Ibn Abbas that the share here is specific to one who performs the pilgrimage on behalf of a deceased person, the reward being shared between him and the deceased. It is also reported from him, concerning the hadith of the man who asked whether he should perform the pilgrimage on behalf of his father, who had died, and at its end he said: "Then do I have a reward?" So this verse was revealed. It has been said: if this is sound, then the verse is separate from the one before it, connected to what precedes it of the mention of the pilgrimage, its rites and rulings, end quote. But it is not as he mentioned, separate; rather it is connected to what precedes it, because what precedes it concerns the pilgrimage, and the division of the two groups is within the pilgrimage: among them is one who asked God for this world alone, and among them one who asked for the world and the Hereafter. The answer was given to the questioner about his pilgrimage on behalf of his father: does he have a reward in it? By the general wording of His words: ﴿Those will have a share of what they have earned﴾. Ibn Abbas answered with this verse the one who asked him whether he could hire his mount to people on condition that they perform the pilgrimage, and whether it suffices on his behalf, by the generality of His words: ﴿Those will have a share of what they have earned﴾.

﴿And God is swift in reckoning.﴾ Its apparent meaning is a report about Him Most High with the swiftness of His reckoning; and His swiftness is by its completion quickly, like the approach of its time. It is reported: as much as the milking of a sheep; it is reported: as much as the interval of a she-camel's milking (fawaq); it is reported: as much as the blinking of the eye. Or because He does not need thought or deliberation, like one who is incapable; this was said by Abu Sulayman. Or because He knows what is for the one reckoned and what is against him before his reckoning; this was said by al-Zajjaj. Or because the reckoning of the whole world is like the reckoning of one man, and because the time of the reckoning is near; this was said by Muqatil. It has been said: "reckoning" is used as a metonymy (kunniya) (p-107) for requital for deeds, since it arises from them, like His words: ﴿And I did not know what my reckoning is﴾ [al-Haqqah: 26], meaning what my recompense is. It has been said: "reckoning" is used as a metonymy for knowledge of the courses of affairs, because reckoning leads to knowledge; this was also said by al-Zajjaj. It has been said: he expressed by reckoning the acceptance of His servants' supplication. It has been said: he expressed by it the power and fulfillment, that is, He does not delay the reward of the doer of good nor the punishment of the evildoer. It has been said: it is by omitting a qualifier, that is, "swift is the coming of the Day of Reckoning." So the purpose of the verse is a warning about the swiftness of the Day of Resurrection. It has been said: "swiftness of reckoning" means that His mercy is great and abundant, so it is not diminished nor cut off. Something close to this is reported from Ibn Abbas.

The apparent context of this discourse indicates that the reckoning applies to both the disbeliever and the believer, since it comes after what appears to be addressed to the obedient. The reckoning of the disbelievers is a rebuke and a censure, because they have no good deed in the Hereafter for which they will be recompensed. This is the apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿And I did not know what my account is﴾ [al-Haqqah 69:26]. The majority (al-jumhur) said: the disbelievers are not called to account. God the Exalted said: ﴿So We will not assign them any weight on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Kahf 18:105], and ﴿And We will advance to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan 25:23]. The apparent meaning of the heaviness and lightness of the scales, and what follows from them in the verses of the Qur'an, is that good deeds include the righteous and the wicked, the believer and the disbeliever.

These noble verses contain the following: the Hajj (pilgrimage) has known months (ashhur ma'lumat). He used the plural "months" (ashhur) because of their small number, and they are: Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, and Dhu al-Hijjah, in their entirety, according to what the apparent sense of the plural requires. He described them as "known" (ma'lumat) because people know them. God the Exalted informed that whoever obliges himself to the Hajj during these months must not commit obscenity (rafath), must not transgress (fusuq), and must not dispute (jidal). Thus He forbade the things that spoil the Hajj, including what was permissible before it, and what was impermissible absolutely, so as to equate between the two prohibitions, even though one of them is time-limited and the other is not time-limited.

Then, having forbidden these spoilers, God the Exalted informed that whatever good a person does, beyond the obligation of the Hajj, God knows it, and He rewards him for it. Then He commanded provision for the Hereafter through acts of obedience, and this included what they were engaged in of the Hajj. He informed that the best provision is that which serves as a protection (wiqayah) between you and the Fire. Then He called out to the people of intellect, who are the addressees of the discourse, and commanded them to guard against His punishment. This is because the prohibitions had already been mentioned, so it was fitting that they be concluded with guarding against God's punishment by refraining from what He forbade.

Then, since the pilgrim is occupied with this arduous worship, engaged in its words and actions, it might be supposed that its time cannot be mixed with anything other than its acts. God the Exalted therefore clarified that there is no blame upon whoever seeks bounty (fadl) during it through trade, hire, or other activities that help with the burdens of worldly life. Then He commanded them to remember Him at the Sacred Landmark (al-Mash'ar al-Haram) when they depart from 'Arafat, so that remembrance would bring them back to occupation with the rites of the Hajj, lest attachment to trade and gain absorb them. Then He commanded them to remember Him in gratitude for the guidance He granted them, when previously they had been in error, and He chose them for guidance. Then He commanded them to depart from where the people depart, which is the place from which the people customarily depart. That place is 'Arafah. The meaning is that they were commanded to make that departure, the earlier one, from 'Arafah and not from anywhere else, as mentioned in the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul).

He used "then" (thumma), not to indicate sequence in time, but to indicate sequence in mention, not in occurrence. Then He commanded seeking forgiveness. Then, after the performance of the rites, He commanded remembrance of God the Exalted. Since a person often mentions his father and praises him for the noble deeds he performed before, and this was for them the utmost form of mention, He likened the remembrance of God to that remembrance. Then He emphasized the desirability of exaggerating in remembrance by His saying "or more intensely" (aw ashadd), so that it would be understood that what He had first used as a comparison is only by way of giving an example to them. The intent is that they should not neglect the remembrance of God the Exalted even for the blink of an eye.

Then He divided the aim of the pilgrim into one that is purely worldly and one that is both worldly and otherworldly, and clarified this in his request, and He mentioned that whoever limits himself to his worldly life has no share in the Hereafter. Then He pointed to the totality of the two categories by saying that each of them has a share of what they earned through deeds: if good, then good; and if evil, then evil. He, the Exalted, is swift in reckoning, so He recompenses the servant for what he earned.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 200–202 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Among people there are those who say, "Our Lord, give us in this world,"﴾. They said: God Most High described the state of those who remember Him before His sending of the Prophet, and the state of the believers after His sending, and their knowledge of reward and punishment. What appears to be the case is that this is a division of those commanded to remember God after completing the rites (manasik), and that in their supplication they divide into those whose love of this world predominates, so they ask for nothing but it, and those who ask for the goodness of their condition in this world and the Hereafter. This is an iltifat (a shift in grammatical person). Had it come in the second person, it would have said: "among you are those who say," and "among you." The wisdom of this iltifat is that they were not directed toward this course which no rational person should take, namely limiting oneself to this world. So they were presented in the form of those not addressed with the remembrance of God, by being placed in the form of absent persons. This is one of the divisions which belong to the modes of eloquent expression (bayan). It is a wonderful division, which the divider confines to these two types, and not as the Sufis hold, that there is a third category which God Most High did not mention for them. They said: they are those who are content with His decree, who submit to His command, who remain silent about every supplication and complaint. The second object of "give us" (ataina) is omitted; its estimated form is: "what we desire," or "our request," or what is similar. And the claim that "fi" is superfluous, making "the world" the second object, is a weak opinion; likewise the claim that "fi" means "min" so that it occupies the position of the object is also (p-105) weak. The omission of both objects of ataa (give) and of one of them is permissible for brevity and for limitation, because this is the category of a'ta (give), and that is permissible in it.

﴿And he has no portion in the Hereafter.﴾ Its explanation has already been given in His words: ﴿And they certainly knew that whoever purchased it would have no share in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102]. This sentence here may carry two meanings. One is the report that he has no share in the Hereafter because he limits himself to this world. The second is that the meaning is a report about the supplicant that he has no seeking of a share in the Hereafter, so this serves as an emphasis for his limiting himself to seeking this world. He used the plural in His words: ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world﴾, whereas if it followed the wording of "man" (whoever), it would have been: "My Lord, give me." The plural was observed here because of the large number of those who desire to limit themselves to the aims of this world and to attaining them; had it been singular, it would have been imagined that this was few.

﴿And among them are those who say, "Our Lord, give us in this world a good [thing]"﴾. "Good" (hasanah) is unrestricted, and the meaning is that they asked God in this world for a good condition. The exegetes have illustrated this in several ways: that it is a righteous wife, as said by Ali; or health and sufficiency of wealth, as said by Qatada; or knowledge, or worship, as said by al-Hasan; or wealth, as said by al-Suddi, Abu Wa'il, and Ibn Zayd; or abundant provision, as said by Muqatil; or blessing in this world, as said by Ibn Qutayba; or contentment with provision, or success and protection from sin, or righteous children, or steadfastness in faith, or the sweetness of obedience, or following the Sunnah, or the praise of people, or health, security, competence and victory over enemies, or understanding of the Book of God Most High, or the companionship of the righteous, as said by Ja'far. Many examples are also reported from the Sufis regarding this.

﴿And in the Hereafter a good [thing]﴾. They illustrated the good of the Hereafter as being Paradise, or pardon, forgiveness, and safety from the terror of the standing place and the evil of reckoning, or blessing, or the wide-eyed houris, or the easing of reckoning, or companionship with the Prophets, or the delight of seeing [God], or contentment (ridan), or meeting [Him].

Ibn Atiyya said: it is "the good" by consensus (ijma', i.e., agreement of the scholars). It has been said: it is fitting that the two goods be health in this world and in the Hereafter, because this is established in the hadith of the man whom the Messenger of God (ﷺ) visited when he had become like a young bird, and the Prophet (ﷺ) asked him what he used to supplicate with. He informed him that he had asked God in this world to hasten what would punish him with in the Hereafter, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "You cannot bear it," and said: "Why did you not say: 'O God, give us in this world…'" to its end. So he supplicated to God with both of them and was healed. It is sound that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to supplicate with it most often, and he used to say it between the Yemeni Corner and the Black Stone, and he would command that the most frequent supplication of the Muslim at the standing place (of Arafat) be this. Abu Bakr was the first to say it at the pilgrimage season in the year of the Conquest, then Ali followed him, and all the people. Anas, when he was asked to supplicate, supplicated with it; then when he was asked for more, he repeated it; then when he was asked for more, he said: "What do you want? I have asked God for the good of this world and the Hereafter."

"And in the Hereafter a good [thing]": the waw in it is for conjoining two things with two things, so "in the Hereafter a good [thing]" is conjoined to "in this world a good [thing]." A particle may conjoin two or more things to two or more things. You say: "I informed Zayd of your brother going out and Amr of his father remaining," unless it stands in for two governing words, in which case there is a disagreement, and on permissibility there is detail. This is not from the separation between the conjunction particle and the conjoined element by an adverbial or prepositional phrase, as some claimed; so he permitted that, citing it as evidence against the weakness of al-Farisi's position that this is specific to poetry. For the verse does not belong to this category, but to conjoining two or more things to two or more things. What al-Farisi (Abu Ali) disagreed about is: "I struck Zayd and Amr in the house." The weakness of Abu Ali's position is only shown by the words of God Most High: ﴿God is He who created seven heavens and of the earth their like﴾ [al-Talaq: 12], and by His words: ﴿Indeed, God commands you to render trusts to their owners, and when you judge between people, to judge with justice﴾ [al-Nisa': 58]. The complete discussion of this question is mentioned in the science of grammar (nahw).

﴿And protect us from the punishment of the Fire.﴾ This is a request for protection from the Fire, that is, that they not enter it; it is the Fire of Hell. It has been said: it is the evil woman who is much harmful. Al-Qushayri said: the lam in "the Fire" is the lam of genus (lam al-jins), so seeking refuge is obtained from the fires of burning and the fires of separation, end quote. The apparent meaning of this supplication is that, since their saying "and in the Hereafter a good [thing]" implies that whoever enters Paradise, even the last of the people, is truly said to have been given a good thing in the Hereafter, they asked God that, together with entering Paradise, He preserve them from the punishment of the Fire. It is as if it is a supplication for entering Paradise first without punishment, and that they would not be among those who enter the Fire because of their sins and come out of it through intercession. It is also possible that it is an emphasis on the request to enter Paradise, as one of the Companions said: "I only say in my supplication: O God, admit me into Paradise and protect me from the Fire, and I do not know what your murmuring is, nor the murmuring of Mu'adh." So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Around it we murmur."

﴿Those will have a share of what they have earned.﴾ The division of people into two groups has already been mentioned: a group limited its supplication to its worldly affairs, and a group associated its Hereafter with its worldly affairs. The apparent meaning is that "those" refers to both groups, since the judgment affirmed, namely that they have a share of what they have earned, is common to both, and the meaning is that each group has a share of what it earned: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil. "Earning" here does not mean supplication; rather this is merely a report from God about what the outcome of each of the two groups will be, and that their shares of good and evil follow their earnings.

It has been said: the intended meaning of earning here is supplication, that is, each one of them has a share of what he supplicated for. Supplication was called earning because it is an act, so this constitutes a guarantee of response, a promise from Him Most High that He gives each of them a share of what their supplication requires, either the world alone, or the world and the Hereafter. This is like His words: ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter﴾ [al-Shura: 20], and ﴿Whoever desires the immediate [world]﴾ [al-Isra': 18], and ﴿Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment﴾ [Hud: 15], and the verses (of this kind). As has come in the Sahih: "As for the unbeliever, he is fed with his good deeds in this world for what he did for God with them; then when he comes to the Hereafter, he will have no good for which he is rewarded." In the first meaning there is no promise of response. The "min" in His words "of what they have earned" may be partitive, that is, a share of the kind of what they earned; it may also be causal. The "ma" may be a relative pronoun in the sense of "that which," or a verbal (masdari) relative, that is, "of their earning." It has been said: "those" is specific to reference to the seekers of the two goods only; Ibn Atiyya mentioned no other, while al-Zamakhshari mentioned it opposite to it. Ibn Atiyya said: He promised upon the earning of righteous deeds in the form of a bare report. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Those who supplicate for the two goods, they have a share of the kind of what they earned of righteous deeds, which is the reward that is the benefits of the good, or on account of what they earned, like His words: 'Because of their sins they were drowned'," then he said after some discussion: "It is also possible that 'those' refers to both groups together, and that each group has a share of the kind of what they earned." End of his words.

What is more evident is what we have already presented, that "those" refers to both groups, and it is supported by His words: ﴿And God is swift in reckoning﴾, and this is not something specific to one group rather than another; rather this applies to all creation, and reckoning encompasses the reckoning of the whole world, not merely the reckoning of this group seeking the two goods. It is reported from Ibn Abbas that the share here is specific to one who performs the pilgrimage on behalf of a deceased person, the reward being shared between him and the deceased. It is also reported from him, concerning the hadith of the man who asked whether he should perform the pilgrimage on behalf of his father, who had died, and at its end he said: "Then do I have a reward?" So this verse was revealed. It has been said: if this is sound, then the verse is separate from the one before it, connected to what precedes it of the mention of the pilgrimage, its rites and rulings, end quote. But it is not as he mentioned, separate; rather it is connected to what precedes it, because what precedes it concerns the pilgrimage, and the division of the two groups is within the pilgrimage: among them is one who asked God for this world alone, and among them one who asked for the world and the Hereafter. The answer was given to the questioner about his pilgrimage on behalf of his father: does he have a reward in it? By the general wording of His words: ﴿Those will have a share of what they have earned﴾. Ibn Abbas answered with this verse the one who asked him whether he could hire his mount to people on condition that they perform the pilgrimage, and whether it suffices on his behalf, by the generality of His words: ﴿Those will have a share of what they have earned﴾.

﴿And God is swift in reckoning.﴾ Its apparent meaning is a report about Him Most High with the swiftness of His reckoning; and His swiftness is by its completion quickly, like the approach of its time. It is reported: as much as the milking of a sheep; it is reported: as much as the interval of a she-camel's milking (fawaq); it is reported: as much as the blinking of the eye. Or because He does not need thought or deliberation, like one who is incapable; this was said by Abu Sulayman. Or because He knows what is for the one reckoned and what is against him before his reckoning; this was said by al-Zajjaj. Or because the reckoning of the whole world is like the reckoning of one man, and because the time of the reckoning is near; this was said by Muqatil. It has been said: "reckoning" is used as a metonymy (kunniya) (p-107) for requital for deeds, since it arises from them, like His words: ﴿And I did not know what my reckoning is﴾ [al-Haqqah: 26], meaning what my recompense is. It has been said: "reckoning" is used as a metonymy for knowledge of the courses of affairs, because reckoning leads to knowledge; this was also said by al-Zajjaj. It has been said: he expressed by reckoning the acceptance of His servants' supplication. It has been said: he expressed by it the power and fulfillment, that is, He does not delay the reward of the doer of good nor the punishment of the evildoer. It has been said: it is by omitting a qualifier, that is, "swift is the coming of the Day of Reckoning." So the purpose of the verse is a warning about the swiftness of the Day of Resurrection. It has been said: "swiftness of reckoning" means that His mercy is great and abundant, so it is not diminished nor cut off. Something close to this is reported from Ibn Abbas.

The apparent context of this discourse indicates that the reckoning applies to both the disbeliever and the believer, since it comes after what appears to be addressed to the obedient. The reckoning of the disbelievers is a rebuke and a censure, because they have no good deed in the Hereafter for which they will be recompensed. This is the apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿And I did not know what my account is﴾ [al-Haqqah 69:26]. The majority (al-jumhur) said: the disbelievers are not called to account. God the Exalted said: ﴿So We will not assign them any weight on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Kahf 18:105], and ﴿And We will advance to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan 25:23]. The apparent meaning of the heaviness and lightness of the scales, and what follows from them in the verses of the Qur'an, is that good deeds include the righteous and the wicked, the believer and the disbeliever.
