These noble verses contain the following: the Hajj (pilgrimage) has known months (ashhur ma'lumat). He used the plural "months" (ashhur) because of their small number, and they are: Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, and Dhu al-Hijjah, in their entirety, according to what the apparent sense of the plural requires. He described them as "known" (ma'lumat) because people know them. God the Exalted informed that whoever obliges himself to the Hajj during these months must not commit obscenity (rafath), must not transgress (fusuq), and must not dispute (jidal). Thus He forbade the things that spoil the Hajj, including what was permissible before it, and what was impermissible absolutely, so as to equate between the two prohibitions, even though one of them is time-limited and the other is not time-limited.

Then, having forbidden these spoilers, God the Exalted informed that whatever good a person does, beyond the obligation of the Hajj, God knows it, and He rewards him for it. Then He commanded provision for the Hereafter through acts of obedience, and this included what they were engaged in of the Hajj. He informed that the best provision is that which serves as a protection (wiqayah) between you and the Fire. Then He called out to the people of intellect, who are the addressees of the discourse, and commanded them to guard against His punishment. This is because the prohibitions had already been mentioned, so it was fitting that they be concluded with guarding against God's punishment by refraining from what He forbade.

Then, since the pilgrim is occupied with this arduous worship, engaged in its words and actions, it might be supposed that its time cannot be mixed with anything other than its acts. God the Exalted therefore clarified that there is no blame upon whoever seeks bounty (fadl) during it through trade, hire, or other activities that help with the burdens of worldly life. Then He commanded them to remember Him at the Sacred Landmark (al-Mash'ar al-Haram) when they depart from 'Arafat, so that remembrance would bring them back to occupation with the rites of the Hajj, lest attachment to trade and gain absorb them. Then He commanded them to remember Him in gratitude for the guidance He granted them, when previously they had been in error, and He chose them for guidance. Then He commanded them to depart from where the people depart, which is the place from which the people customarily depart. That place is 'Arafah. The meaning is that they were commanded to make that departure, the earlier one, from 'Arafah and not from anywhere else, as mentioned in the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul).

He used "then" (thumma), not to indicate sequence in time, but to indicate sequence in mention, not in occurrence. Then He commanded seeking forgiveness. Then, after the performance of the rites, He commanded remembrance of God the Exalted. Since a person often mentions his father and praises him for the noble deeds he performed before, and this was for them the utmost form of mention, He likened the remembrance of God to that remembrance. Then He emphasized the desirability of exaggerating in remembrance by His saying "or more intensely" (aw ashadd), so that it would be understood that what He had first used as a comparison is only by way of giving an example to them. The intent is that they should not neglect the remembrance of God the Exalted even for the blink of an eye.

Then He divided the aim of the pilgrim into one that is purely worldly and one that is both worldly and otherworldly, and clarified this in his request, and He mentioned that whoever limits himself to his worldly life has no share in the Hereafter. Then He pointed to the totality of the two categories by saying that each of them has a share of what they earned through deeds: if good, then good; and if evil, then evil. He, the Exalted, is swift in reckoning, so He recompenses the servant for what he earned.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 203 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And remember God during the counted days. Whoever hastens (to leave) in two days, there is no sin upon him, and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him, for those who are mindful (of God). And fear God, and know that you will be gathered to Him.﴾ ﴿And among people is one whose speech about the life of this world impresses you, and he calls God to witness what is in his heart, yet he is the most contentious of opponents.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 204] ﴿And when he turns away, he strives in the land to cause corruption therein and to destroy the crops and the offspring, and God does not love corruption.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 205] ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear God," pride takes him to sin, so Hell is sufficient for him, and what an evil resting place.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 206] ﴿And among people is one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of God, and God is Kind to the servants.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 207] ﴿O you who have believed, enter into peace (al-silm) completely, and do not follow the steps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 208] ﴿And if you slip after the clear proofs have come to you, then know that God is Mighty and Wise.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 209] ﴿Do they await only that God should come to them in canopies of clouds, with the angels, and the matter be decided? And to God are all matters returned.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 210] ﴿Ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We gave them. And whoever changes the blessing of God after it has come to him, indeed God is severe in punishment.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 211] ﴿The life of this world has been made attractive to those who disbelieve, and they mock those who believe. But those who are mindful (of God) will be above them on the Day of Resurrection. And God provides for whom He wills without reckoning.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 212]. Al-ʿajalah (haste): hurrying in something and rushing toward it. Ta'ajjala is of the form tafaʿʿala from it, and it may be in the sense of istafʿala, which is one of the meanings for which tafaʿʿala comes, so it means istaʿjala (to seek to hasten), like their saying: takabbara and istakbara, tayaqqana and istayqana, taqaḍḍā and istaqḍā, ta'ajjala and ista'jala. It comes intransitive and transitive. You say: "ta'ajjaltu fī al-shay'" and "ta'ajjaltuhu," and "ista'jaltu fī al-shay'" and "ista'jaltu Zaydan." Or it may be in the sense of the bare verb, so it means ʿajila, like their saying: talabbatha in the sense of labitha, and ta'ajjaba and ʿajiba, and tabarra'a and bari'a. This is one of the meanings for which tafaʿʿala came.

Al-ḥashr: gathering the people from every direction. Al-maḥshar is their gathering place. It is said from it: ḥashara yaḥshuru. Ḥashārāt al-arḍ are its small creatures. Al-Rāghib said: al-ḥashr is joining what is scattered and driving it, and it has the meaning of the gathering that we have mentioned. Al-iʿjāb: it is af'āl from al-ʿajab, and its origin is (wonder at) what has not been like it, as al-Mufaḍḍal said. It is approval of something, inclination toward it, and magnifying it. You say: "aʿjabanī Zayd" (Zayd impressed me). The hamzah in it is for transitivity. Al-Rāghib said: ʿajab is a bewilderment that befalls a person because of something, and it is not something that has a state in its own essence; rather, it is according to the relations to one who knows the cause and one who does not. The real meaning of "aʿjabanī kadhā" is: it appeared to me in a manner whose cause I did not know. End of his words. It may also be said: "ʿajibtu min kadhā" in denial, as Ziyād al-Aʿjam said:

"I wondered, though time has many wonders, at a man from ʿAnaza who cursed me, and I did not strike him."

Al-ladad: intensity of contention. It is said: "ladidta taladdu ladadan wa ladādatan," and a man is alladd and a woman is laddāʾ, and men and women are luddun. A man "iltadda" and "yaltaddu" also means intense in contention. When he overcomes his opponent it is said: "laddahu yalladduhu," transitively. The reciter said:

"He overcomes the rivals of men, the most contentious."

Its derivation is from ladīdayi al-ʿunuq, which are its two sides, as al-Zajjāj said. It is also said it is from ladīdayi al-wādī, which are its two banks, and they were named so for their crookedness. It is also said it is from laddahu, he restrained him, as if he restrains his opponent from discussing and contending with him.

Al-khiṣām: the verbal noun of khāṣama. The plural of khaṣm is said: khaṣm, khuṣūm, and khiṣām, like baḥr, bubūr, and biḥār. The original sense of contention is probing deeply into a matter, and for this reason it is said of the corners of containers: khuṣūm, singular khuṣima.

Al-nasl: the verbal noun of nasala yanselu, and its origin is coming out quickly. From it they say: nasala wabar al-baʿīr, and sha'r al-ḥimār, and rīsh al-ṭāʾir: it came out and fell from it. It is also said: al-nasl is coming out in succession, and from it nusāl al-ṭāʾir (the feathers of a bird), which fall one after another. He said:

"So strip my garments from your garments, and they will fall off."

The application of the word nasl to offspring is from the application of the verbal noun to the object, named so because it comes out from the back of the father and falls quickly from the belly of the mother.

Jahannam: a proper name for the Fire. It is also said it is the name of its lowest level. It is Arabic, derived from their saying rakiyyatun jahannām when a well is very deep. The man has also been named Jahannām, so it is a proper name. Both are from al-jahm, which is dislike and harshness. So the nūn in this case is extra, and its measure is faʿannal. Some have stated that jahannām's measure is faʿannāl. Some of our companions held that faʿannal is a pattern absent from their speech, and they made dawannak a faʿallal, like ʿadabbas. The waw is original in quadriliterals, as in warantal, and the correct view is affirming this pattern. Words have come from it: they said ḍaghannaṭ, from al-ḍaghāṭa, which is bulk; and safannaj; and hajannaf for the male ostrich; and al-zawannak, the short one, named so because he struts in his walk, that is, he swaggers. Ḥassān said:

"I have resolved that you are the basest of those who walked in the foulness of an adulterous woman and the strutting of a crow."

Some said in its meaning: zawannakā. All of this indicates the extra nūn in jahannam. It is not declined because of being a proper noun and feminine. It is also said it is non-Arabic, and its original form was kahannām, and it was Arabized by changing the kāf to jīm and dropping the alif. On this view it is not declined because of foreignness and being a proper noun.

Ḥasb: in the sense of "enough." You say: "aḥsabanī al-shay'," meaning it sufficed me. So ḥasb takes the place of muḥsib. It is used as a subject and its predicate is then put in the genitive with a superfluous bā'. When used as a predicate, the bā' is not added. When used as an adjective, it is made an annexed construction, and it does not become definite when annexed to a definite noun. You say: "marartu bi-rajulin ḥasbika." It is accompanied by a specification (tamyīz), as in: "bi-rajulin ḥasbika min rajulin." It is not made dual, plural, or feminine, even if it is an adjective for a dual, plural, or feminine noun, because it is a verbal noun.

Al-mihād: the bedding, which is what is spread out for sleep. It is also said it is the plural of mahd, which is the place prepared for sleep. Al-silm: with a kasra or fatha on the sīn, meaning reconciliation. It may be masculine or feminine, and its origin is from al-istislām, which is submission. The Basrans related from the Arabs: "banū Fulān silm and salm," with one meaning. It is pronounced with fatha and kasra to mean Islam, as said by al-Kisā'ī and a group of lexicographers, and they cited part of Kinda's saying:

"I called my tribe to peace (silm) when I saw them turning their backs."

That is, to Islam. He said this when Kinda apostatized with al-Ash'ath ibn Qays after the death of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Another said regarding the conquest:

"The laws of peace (silm) have become clear in their signs, so no one sees disbelief except one who has madness in him."

He means Islam, because he contrasted it with disbelief. It is also said that with kasra it means Islam, and with fatha it means reconciliation.

(Kāffatan): it is an active participle used in the sense of "all together." Its root derivation is from kaffa al-shay', meaning he prevented him from taking it. Al-kaff means prevention, and from it comes kuffat al-qamīṣ, its border. From it also comes al-kaff, which is the extremity of the hand, because it restrains the rest of the body by it. A man is makfūf when his sight is prevented from looking. From it also comes kiffat al-mīzān, the pan of the balance, because it prevents the weighed item from spreading out. Some lexicographers said: kuffa with a ḍamma is for anything elongated, and with a kasra for anything round. Kāffatan is among what is obligatorily in the accusative as a circumstantial (ḥāl), like qāṭibatan, so removing it from the accusative as a circumstantial is a grammatical error.

Al-tazyīn: embellishment. Al-zīna is what is beautified and adorned by. Faʿʿala from al-zayn has the meaning of the bare verb, and the doubling in it is not for transitivity. Its being in the sense of the bare verb is one of the meanings for which faʿʿala came, like their saying: qaddara Allāh and qadara, mayyaza and māza, bashshara and bashara. From al-zayn one forms iftaʿala: izdāna, with the tā' changed to dāl, and it is intransitive.

﴿And remember God during the counted days.﴾ This is the fourth command to remember in this verse. Remembrance here is either the takbīr at the jamarāt, after the prayers, and at other times of the Hajj, or the takbīr following the obligatory prayers; two views. It is reported from ʿUmar that he used to say the takbīr in his tent at Minā, so those around him would say it until the people said it in the road and during the ṭawāf. The counted days are three days after the day of sacrifice (yawm al-naḥr), and the day of sacrifice is not among the counted days. This is the position of al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, Mālik, and Abū Ḥanīfa, and it was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAṭāʾ, Mujāhid, Ibrāhīm, Qatāda, al-Suddī, al-Rabīʿ, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk. Or they are the day of sacrifice and two days after it, said by Ibn ʿUmar and ʿAlī, and he said: "Slaughter on whichever of them you wish." Or the day of sacrifice and the three days of tashrīq, said by al-Marwazī. Or they are the days of the ten, narrated by Mujāhid from Ibn ʿAbbās. It was said: their saying "the days of the ten" is an error of the transmitters. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: either it is a scribal error in the copy, or he means the ten after the day of sacrifice, and this is a stretch. The commentators spoke here about His saying: ﴿during known days over what He has provided them of the cattle﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 28], and we will defer discussion of that to its place, God willing.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya cited for the first view, that the counted days are the days of tashrīq, which are the three days after the day of sacrifice, and the day of sacrifice is not among them, by saying: "This is supported by the consensus of people that no one departs on the day of qarr, which is the second day after the day of sacrifice. If the day of sacrifice were among the counted days, it would be permissible for whoever wishes to depart hastily on the day of qarr, because he would have taken two days from the counted days." End of his words. What he said is not necessarily binding, because His saying: ﴿whoever hastens in two days﴾ cannot be taken literally. When a temporal adverb is governed by the verb, it must occur in each of the two days. If you say, "I struck Zayd two days," then the striking must occur with him on each of the two days. Here that is not possible, because hastening to depart did not occur on each of the two days. So a metaphor is necessary: either its occurrence on one of them is taken as if it occurred in both, and it becomes like His saying: ﴿they forgot their fish﴾ [al-Kahf: 61], and ﴿from both of them come out the pearl and coral﴾ [al-Raḥmān: 22]; in reality only one of them was forgotten, and likewise they come out of only one of them. Or it is taken as an elision of a noun, the meaning being: "whoever hastens on the second of two days after the day of sacrifice," so the day that follows the day of qarr is the one in which one hastens. It is also possible that the elided word is: "within the completion of two days" or "the fulfilment of two days," so it does not necessarily follow that the hastening occurs on either of the two days, but rather after them. On this view it is valid to count the day of sacrifice among the counted days, and it does not follow that departure is on the day of qarr, as Ibn ʿAṭiyya stated.

The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿And remember God during the counted days﴾ is a command to remember God in general during the counted days, without specifying what these days are. But His saying ﴿whoever hastens in two days﴾ suggests that these are the days in which one departs, namely the days of tashrīq. In (Rayy al-Ẓamʾān), it was said: the commentators agreed that the counted days are the days of tashrīq. End of his words.

(p-108) (p-109) (p-110)

The placement of the days as the time for the remembrance indicates that whenever God is remembered during those days, that is what is sought. It also suggests that, since the stoning of the pillars (al-Jimar) at Mina is not restricted to a specific time, it fits to perform it at any time of the days in which God is remembered. This is supported by His saying: ﴿Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾. It is also evident that the address in His saying "wa-dhkurū" (and remember) is directed to the pilgrims (al-Hujjaj), since the speech is with them, the address preceded for them, and the report follows about them. Therefore, others do not join them in this commanded remembrance. As for one who understands the remembrance here as the remembrance prescribed after the prayer, he is included with them in its time and in its manner. As for its time: it runs from the dawn prayer on the Day of Arafah until the afternoon prayer on the last of the days of Tashriq (the days after the Eid sacrifice). This was said by Umar, Ali, and Ibn Abbas. Or it runs from the morning of Arafah until the afternoon prayer on the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr). This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Alqamah, and Abu Hanifa. Or it runs from the dawn prayer on the Day of Arafah until one prays the dawn prayer on the last of the days of Tashriq, and this is narrated from Malik. Or it runs from the noon prayer on the Day of Sacrifice until the noon prayer of the last of the days of Tashriq, said by Yahya ibn Sa'id. Or it runs from the noon prayer on the Day of Sacrifice until the dawn prayer of the last of the days of Tashriq, said by Malik and al-Shafi'i. Or it runs from noon on the Day of Sacrifice until the afternoon prayer of the last of the days of Tashriq, said by Ibn Shihab. Or it runs from noon on the Day of Arafah until the afternoon prayer of the last of the days of Tashriq, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Or it runs from the noon prayer on the Day of Sacrifice until the noon prayer of the first day of departure (Yawm al-Nafr al-Awwal), said by al-Hasan. Or it runs from the noon prayer on the Day of Arafah until the noon prayer on the Day of Sacrifice, said by Abu Wa'il. Or it runs from noon on the Day of Sacrifice until the last of the days of Tashriq, said by Zayd ibn Thabit, and Abu Yusuf held this in one of his two opinions.

As for its manner: the well-known position of Malik is three takbirs (saying "Allahu akbar"). In his school there is also a narration that one adds after them: "There is no god but Allah, Allah is greatest, and to Allah is the praise." The position of Abu Hanifa is: "Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, there is no god but Allah, and Allahu akbar." The position of al-Shafi'i is: "Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, there is no god but Allah, and Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, and to Allah is the praise." Abu Hanifa said: the takbir is specific to the ends of the obligatory prayers performed in congregation. Malik said: whether one prays alone or in congregation, it is after every obligatory prayer. This was also the view of al-Shafi'i, Abu Yusuf, and Muhammad, and there are two reports from Ahmad. The traveler is like the resident regarding the takbir according to the scholars of the major cities and the renowned Companions and Successors. It is narrated from Abu Hanifa that if travelers pray in congregation, there is no takbir upon them. If a traveler follows a resident (in prayer), he says the takbir. He should say it after the salam. The majority hold that one does something that cuts off the prayer, such as speech and other things. It was said: turning one's back to the qiblah, and the majority hold to this. If he forgets the takbir when he finishes, and he remembers before leaving the gathering, then he should say it. Malik said in (al-Mukhtasar): he says it as long as he is in his place; once he rises from it, there is nothing upon him. He said in (al-Mudawwanah): if he forgets it and was close, he sits and says it; if the time has passed, there is nothing upon him. If the imam leaves while the people are seated, then they should say it. Abu Hanifa said likewise. Whoever forgets a prayer during the days of Tashriq of that year makes it up and says the takbir. If he makes it up after them, he does not say the takbir. The evidences for these issues are mentioned in the books of fiqh (Islamic jurisprudence).

What appears to be correct is what we have previously presented: that this address is to the pilgrims, and that this remembrance is what is specific to the pilgrim among the acts of Hajj (pilgrimage), whether the remembrance is at the stoning or after the prayers. Others do not share with them in the commanded remembrance unless there is evidence. The remembrance during the days of Mina, and on the Day of Sacrifice after the prayers, applies to non-pilgrims as well. Determining the manner of the remembrance, its beginning, and its end requires a transmitted textual proof (dalil sam'i).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 204 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 203] The apparent meaning is that "taʿajjala" (hastened) here is intransitive, because it is paired with an intransitive verb in His words "whoever delays" (man taʾakhkhara). It is then the reflexive form (muṭāwiʿ) of ʿajila, like "kasarahu fa-takassara" (he broke it, so it broke). The object of the hastening is omitted, and the estimated meaning is "with oneself." It is also possible that taʿajjala is transitive, with its object omitted, meaning "whoever hastens the departure (al-nafr)." The phrase "in two days" means two of the counted days. Some have said the meaning is that one departs on the second day of the Days of Tashriq, and we have already discussed the connection of "in two days" with the word "taʿajjala." The apparent generality of "whoever hastens" includes both the people of the outlying regions (al-āfāqī) and the people of Makkah alike; each of them may depart on the second day. This is the view of ʿAṭāʾ. Ibn al-Mundhir said: "It resembles the school of al-Shafiʿi, and we say it," and his words end there. Thus the concession is for all people, both the people of Makkah and others. Mālik and others said: the hastening is permitted only for one whose homeland is far away, not for the Makkan or the one who is near, unless he has an excuse. It is narrated from ʿUmar that he said: "Whoever among all people wishes may depart in the first departure, except the family of Khuzaymah, for they do not depart except in the last departure." Aḥmad and Ishāq took ʿUmar's words "except the family of Khuzaymah" to mean that they are people of the sacred precinct (ḥaram). Aḥmad used to say: whoever departs in the first departure should stay in Makkah.

The apparent meaning of "in two days" is that hastening does not take place at night but during some part of the day: one departs after finishing the stoning of the pillars (al-jimār). This is the school of al-Shafiʿi, and it is narrated from Qatada. Abu Hanifa said: before the break of dawn, meaning of the third day. It is narrated from ʿUmar, Ibn ʿĀmir, Jābir ibn Zayd, al-Ḥasan, and al-Nakhaʿi that they said: whoever is overtaken by the afternoon (ʿaṣr) on the second day of the Days of Tashriq while in Mina does not depart until the morning (al-ghuduw). This contradicts the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, because He said "in two days," and whatever remains of the two days is permissible for him to depart in. Ibn al-Mundhir said: they may be saying this as a recommendation (istiḥbāb).

The apparent meaning of "whoever hastens" is that the stoning on the third day is dropped for him, so he does not stone the pillars of the third day on the day of his departure. Ibn Abi Zamanin said: he stones them on the day of the first departure when he intends to hasten. Ibn al-Mawwāz said: the one who hastens in two days stones twenty-one pebbles, seven for each pillar, so his entire stoning totals forty-nine pebbles, meaning that he has already stoned the Jamrat al-ʿAqabah with seven on the Day of Sacrifice. Ibn al-Mawwāz said: the stoning of the third day is dropped.

The apparent meaning of His words: ﴿And remember God during the counted days. Whoever hastens﴾ [al-Baqarah: 203], to the end of the verse, is the legitimacy of spending the nights in Mina during the Days of Tashriq, because hastening and delaying refer only to departure from Mina. They agreed that no pilgrim may spend the night anywhere but there, except for the herders (al-ruʿāʾ) and whoever is in charge of the water-supply (al-siqāyah) from the family of al-ʿAbbās. Whoever among others leaves the night of Mina for one night is, according to Mālik and Abu Hanifa, liable for a sacrifice (damm). Al-Shafiʿi said: whoever leaves the night-stay during the three nights, if he leaves the stay of one night only, he is liable for one-third of a sacrifice, or a mudd, or a dirham; these are three opinions. The verse does not address the stoning, neither its ruling, nor its time, nor its number, nor its place, because it was well known among them. Its rulings are taken from the Sunnah. It has been said: in His words "and remember God" there is an indication of it, since it is from his Sunnah to say "Allahu akbar" over each pebble from it, so there is no sin upon him.

Salim ibn ʿAbd Allah recited "fa-lā ithma ʿalayhi" with the hamzah of the alif (wasl) dropped. Its explanation is that he eased the hamzah to an intermediate sound (bayna bayna), so it came close to a sukūn, and he therefore dropped it, likening it to the alif; then he dropped the alif because of its being unvoiced and the unvoiced state of the tāʾ. This is the answer of the conditional if we take "man" as conditional, which is the apparent reading. If we take it as relative, it is in the position of the predicate, and its apparent meaning is the negation of sin for him. It has therefore been interpreted as meaning that he is forgiven. Likewise, whoever delays is forgiven and has no sin upon him. This was narrated from ʿAlī, Abu Dharr, Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Shaʿbi, and Mutarrif ibn al-Shikhkhīr. Muʿāwiyah ibn Qurrah said: he comes out of his sins like the day his mother bore him. Something supporting this view is narrated from ʿUmar. Mujāhid said: the meaning is: whoever hastens or delays, there is no sin upon him up to the following year.

What appears to be the meaning is: there is no sin upon him in hastening, and no sin upon him in delaying, because the reward is connected to the condition. The meaning is that there is no blame on one who hastens nor on one who delays. This was said by ʿAṭāʾ. That is because when God commanded them to remember Him during known days, and these days have been explained as the least of plural numbers, which are three days, or four, or ten, then the permission to depart on the second of the Days of Tashriq was granted to them. The command to remember Him during all these days would have required that there be no hastening. So by His words "there is no sin upon him," He negated blame from the one who was granted leniency in not staying until the third day, so he departs on it, and He made him equal in permission and absence of blame to the one who delays. Thus He included the three days in the remembrance. This division indicates choice between hastening and delaying. Choice may follow between the lesser and the better. It has been said: "whoever delays, there is no sin upon him" came in order to correspond with "whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him," so He negated sin from him even though he is better, for that reason. It has also been said: "there is no sin upon him" means there is no sin in leaving the concession. It has been said: the people of the Jahiliyyah were two groups: some of them considered the one who hastens sinful, and some considered the one who delays sinful, so the Qur'an came with lifting sin from both. It has also been said: He expressed by this the forgiveness, as narrated from ʿAlī and those with him. This is a matter in which the one who hastens and the one who delays share. It has also been said: the meaning is: whoever delays beyond the third day to the fourth and does not depart with the general people, there is no sin upon him. It is as if it were said: the days of Mina are three; whoever falls short of them by hastening on the second of them, there is no sin upon him; and whoever exceeds them by delaying, there is no sin upon him.

In these two conditional clauses there is, from the science of rhetorical ornament (ʿilm al-badīʿ), the tibāq (antithesis) in "whoever hastens" and "whoever delays." Tibāq is the mention of a thing and its opposite, like His words: ﴿And that it is He who makes laugh and makes weep﴾ [al-Najm: 43]. Here it is an unusual antithesis, because He mentioned "taʿajjala" as the counterpart of "taʾakhkhara," whereas in reality the counterpart of "taʿajjala" is "taʾannā" (to be deliberate), and the counterpart of "taʾakhkhara" is "taqaddama" (to advance). In "taʿajjala" He expressed the necessary by the consequent (al-malzūm) for the necessary (al-lāzim), and in "taʾakhkhara" He expressed the necessary (lāzim) for the consequent (malzūm). And in them, from the science of exposition (ʿilm al-bayān), there is the verbal correspondence (al-muqābalah al-lafẓiyyah), since the one who delays performs an extra act of worship, so he has an extra reward. He used "there is no sin upon him" as the counterpart to "whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him," like His words: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 194]. This has already been pointed out.

﴿For the one who fears God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 203]. It has been said: it is connected to "and remember God," meaning the remembrance is for the one who fears God. It has also been said: it is connected to the negation of sin, meaning he is forgiven on condition that he fears God in the rest of his life. This was said by Abu al-ʿĀliyah. It has also been said: the meaning is that this granting of choice and the negation of sin from the one who hastens and the one who delays is for the sake of the pilgrim who fears God, so that nothing of either of them stirs in his heart, and he does not suppose that one of them brings sins upon its doer for undertaking it, because the one who has taqwā is cautious and guards against everything that troubles him, and because he is the true pilgrim. This was said by al-Zamakhsharī, and he also said: it is not permissible that what has been mentioned of the rulings of the Hajj and other matters be meant for "the one who fears God," because he is the one who benefits from it and no one else, like His words: ﴿That is better for those who desire His face﴾. His words end there. "Ittaqā" (feared) here is the verb that is attached to "li-man" (for whoever), and it is in the past tense. It has been said: it is past in meaning as well, meaning that forgiveness is attained only by one who was God-fearing and repentant before his pilgrimage, like: ﴿God accepts only from those who fear Him﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 27]. Its reality is that one who persists in sin is not benefited by his pilgrimage, even if he has discharged the obligation outwardly. It has been said: he feared God in every forbidden thing while busy with the pilgrimage. This was said by Qatada and Abu Ṣāliḥ. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "for whoever fears God" means in the state of ihram, from obscene speech (al-rafath), wickedness (al-fusūq), and disputing (al-jidāl). Al-Māturīdī said: "for whoever fears God" means from killing game during the state of ihram. It has been said: the future is meant by it, meaning: for whoever fears God in the rest of his life, as we have mentioned before. The apparent meaning is that it is connected to the latter, which is the negation of sin, because of its nearness to it, and also because the meaning is sound: for whoever is not God-fearing, sin is not lifted from him.

(p-١١٣) The apparent meaning is that the omitted object of "ittaqā" is God, meaning: for whoever fears God. And so it was indeed stated explicitly in the codex of ʿAbd Allah.

(And fear Allah.) When He, exalted is He, mentioned the lifting of sin and that this applies to whoever fears Allah, He commanded taqwa (God-consciousness) in general. He also drew attention to what moves a person to fear Allah: the gathering (hashr) to Him for recompense. This becomes a motive for them to fear Allah, because whoever knows that he will be held to account in the Hereafter for what he committed in this world strives to be saved from the punishment and to have great reward. Since the one commanded to taqwa is described by it, that command is a command to persist in it. In the mention of the gathering there is a warning against sins. The mention of the command together with knowledge ('ilm) indicates that belief in the gathering is not sufficient unless it is a firm certainty that is not mixed with any conjecture (zann). "Ilayhi" (to Him) is placed first for emphasis on the one to whom the gathering is, and for the harmony of the verse endings (fawasil). The meaning is "to His recompense."

The rulings of the Hajj mentioned in this surah have been completed, from the mention of the time of Hajj to the last act, which is the departure (nafar). They began with the command to taqwa and ended with it, and the command to it was interspersed throughout the verses. This indicates the emphasis on its being required. And why would it not be so, when it consists of avoiding what Allah forbids and holding to what He commands? This is the utmost of obedience to Allah, and by it the obedient is distinguished from the disobedient.

﴿And among people is one whose speech impresses you in the life of this world﴾. It was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, whose name was Ubayy. He was sweet of tongue and of appearance. He would sit with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), display his love and his Islam, and swear to that. The Prophet (ﷺ) would bring him close, not knowing what he concealed. He was from Thaqif, an ally of Banu Zuhra. Something happened between him and Thaqif, so he attacked them by night, burned their crops and destroyed their livestock. This was said by ʿAtaʾ, al-Kalbi and Muqatil. Al-Suddi said: He passed by a field of the Muslims and some donkeys, so he burned the crop and slaughtered the donkeys. It is said that concerning him was revealed ﴿And do not obey every man who swears much, contemptible﴾ [68:10], and ﴿Woe to every slanderer, backbiter﴾ [104:1].

Ibn ʿAbbas said: It concerns the unbelievers of Quraysh, who sent to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "We have embraced Islam, so send us someone to teach us your religion." That was a deception from them. He sent to them Khubayb, Marthad, ʿAsim ibn Thabit, Ibn al-Dathinna and others. This is called the Sariyyat al-Raji' (the Expedition of al-Raji'), and al-Raji' is a place between Makkah and Madinah. They were killed, and their story is long and well known in the Sahih collections.

Qatada and Ibn Zayd said: It was revealed concerning every hypocrite who displayed with his tongue what was not in his heart. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that it is about the hypocrites, who said concerning the expedition of al-Raji': "Woe to these men! They did not sit in their houses, nor did they deliver the message of their companion."

The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when Allah divided the askers earlier into those who confine themselves to the matters of this world, and those who ask for the good of this world and the Hereafter and protection from the Fire, He mentioned here both types. From the first type He mentioned the one who is sweet of speech, who shows affection, whose outward is not like his inward. He joined to him the one who seeks the pleasure of Allah and sells himself in seeking it. He placed the first here because there the first mentioned was in His words ﴿Among them is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world"﴾. Here He referred to the impressiveness of his speech specifically, and not to other attributes, because speech is what appears from him first in His words ﴿Among people is one who says, "Our Lord"﴾ [2:200]. So from the standpoint of his addressing Allah in supplication, he should not confine himself to this world, and should ask Him to save him from His punishment. Likewise this second one should not confine himself to the sweetness of his speech, but should match his inward state to his outward state.

The "man" in "man yu'jibuka" (the one who impresses you) is a relative pronoun (mawsul). It is said to be an indefinite noun qualified by a following clause (nakira mawsufa). The kaf in "yu'jibuka" is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) if the verse was revealed concerning a specific person, such as al-Akhnas or another. It is addressed to whoever is a believer if the verse was revealed concerning an unspecified person among those who are hypocrites, whether earlier or later. The meaning of impressing (ijab) by his speech is approving it for its agreement with what you are upon of faith and good.

It occurs in al-Tirmidhi that in some of the books of Allah: "Among the servants of Allah are a people whose tongues are sweeter than honey, and whose hearts are more bitter than aloes" (al-hadith).

"Fi al-hayat" (in the life of this world) is connected to "qawluhu" (his speech). That is, his statement impresses you in the sense of worldly matters, because his false claim of love and following seeks through it a share of the shares of this world. He does not intend the Hereafter, since the Hereafter is not sought except through true faith and sincere love.

Al-Zamakhshari, after mentioning this view, said: "It is permissible that it be connected to yu'jibuka, meaning: his speech is sweet, so it pleases you in this world, and it does not please you in the Hereafter, because of the stammering and incoherence he will suffer in the Standing (on the Day of Judgment), or because they will not be permitted to speak, so he will not speak until his speech pleases you." End of quote. And in it there is remoteness.

What appears is that it is connected to yu'jibuka, not in the meaning he stated. The meaning is that you approve of his speech continuously throughout his life, for nothing issues from him but what is impressive, pleasing and refined. So his outward speech is always impressive. Do you not see that he turns from that good and pleasing speech to a harsh, contrary speech? And despite that, his deeds contradict his outward words, and his inward words also contradict his outward words. For "yu'jibuka qawluhu" (his speech impresses you) and "wa huwa aladdu al-khisam" (while he is the most contentious of opponents) cannot be understood except in two states: he is sweet in speech outwardly, and fierce in contention inwardly.

﴿And he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read it with a damma on the ya and a kasra on the ha, and with the Name of Allah in the accusative from "ashhada" (to call to witness). Abu Haywa and Ibn Muhaysin read it with a fatha on the ya and the ha, and the Name in the nominative, from "shahida". Ubayy and Ibn Masʿud read "wa-yastashhidu Allaha" (and he calls Allah as a witness).

The meaning according to the reading of the majority and their interpretation is that he swears by Allah and calls Him to witness that he is truthful, that he is speaking the truth, and that he loves the Messenger and Islam. Testimony in the sense of an oath came in the story of the mutual curse (mula'ana) in Surat al-Nur.

It is said that the Name of Allah is in the accusative by the dropping of the preposition, and the estimate is: "and he swears by Allah concerning what is in his heart." This is an error, because what is sworn by is the trilateral verb, not the quadrilateral. You say "ashhadu billahi la-af'alanna" (I swear by Allah that I will certainly do it), and you do not say "ashhadu billah" (I bear witness by Allah) in that sense.

My view is that the meaning is: he makes Allah aware of what is in his heart, and no one knows of it because of his intense concealment and his hiding of disbelief. This is apparent in "ʿala ma fi qalbihi" (concerning what is in his heart), because what is in his heart is the opposite of what he expresses by his speech.

On the interpretation of the majority, the word "ma" needs to be deleted for the meaning to be correct. That is: he swears by Allah contrary to what is in his heart, because what is in his heart is disbelief, and he does not swear to it. He swears to its opposite, which is what he is admired for.

This interpretation is strengthened by the reading of Abu Haywa and Ibn Muhaysin, since its meaning is: he makes Allah aware of what is in his heart of disbelief, which is contrary to his speech.

As for the reading "yastashhidu", it may be that istafʿala here has the meaning of afʿala, as in ayqana and istayqana, so it agrees with the reading of the majority, and this is the apparent meaning. It is also possible that istafʿala has the meaning of the bare form, so istashhada means shahida. In that case it becomes apparent that the Name of Allah is in the accusative by dropping the preposition, that is, "wa-yastashhidu billahi" (he calls on Allah as a witness), just as you say "wa-yashhadu billah" (and he bears witness by Allah). The deletion is necessary for the meaning to be correct, that is: "and he calls upon Allah as a witness contrary to what is in his heart."

Apparently, "wa-yushhidu Allaha" is conjoined to "yu'jibuka," so it is a relative clause (silah) or an attributive clause (sifa). It is permissible that the waw is the waw of circumstance (hal) and not the waw of conjunction, so the clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the implicit subject in "yu'jibuka," or from the pronoun in "qawluhu." The estimate is: "while he calls Allah as a witness." This would make it a restriction on the admiration or on the speech. The apparent view is that there is no restriction, and that it is a relative clause. This is because a circumstantial clause introduced by the waw with a present affirmative verb requires a pronoun referring back to the subject. This is necessary since a present affirmative verb with waw can by itself serve as a circumstance, so a pronoun was needed, just as they required it in their saying "qumtu wa-asukku ʿaynahu," meaning "I got up while I was striking his eye," that is, "wa-ana asukku" (and I was striking). Adding a pronoun is against the original form.

﴿And he is the most contentious of opponents﴾. That is, he is the most intense of those who dispute. Here khisam is the plural of khasm (an opponent), as said by al-Zajjaj. If khisam is meant as a verbal noun (masdar), as al-Khalil said, then a word must be deleted to make the predicate apply to the subject. Either the deletion is from the subject, meaning "and his contention is the most intense contention," or it is from the complement of the predicate, meaning "and he is the most intense of those with contention."

It is permitted that khisam here be a verbal noun with the meaning of the active participle, just as a man can be described by a verbal noun, as in "rajul khasim" (a contentious man). It is also permitted that afʿal (in aladd) is not comparative, as if it said: "and he is intensely contentious." It is also permitted that huwa (he) is a pronoun referring to contention, which is explained by the context, meaning "and his contention is the most intense."

The statements of the commentators on "aladd al-khisam" are close in meaning. Ibn ʿAbbas said: its meaning is "one who has much argument." Al-Hasan said: "the liar, the false one." Qatada said: "intensely harsh in disobedience to Allah." Al-Suddi said: "crooked in contention." Mujahid said: "he does not stand firm upon the truth in contention."

It is apparent that this nominal sentence is conjoined to the relative clause of "man," so it is a relative clause. They permitted (p. 115) that it be a circumstantial clause conjoined to "wa-yushhidu," if that is itself a circumstantial clause, or a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "yushhidu."

If khisam is plural, then aladd is of the type of an idafa in which a part is added to the whole. If it is a verbal noun, we have mentioned the correction through the deletion we have described. If you take it in the sense of the active participle, then it is like the plural, in that afʿal is a part of what it is added to. If you interpret afʿal outside its usual pattern, then aladd is of the type of an attributive adjective (sifa mushabbaha) with an idafa.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Al-khisam is contention (al-mukhasama), and the idafa of aladd is in the meaning of fi (in), like their saying: thabtu al-ghadar (steadfast in treachery)." End of quote. He means that afʿal is not of the type of what is added to a part of it, but is an idafa in the meaning of "in." This contradicts what the grammarians claim, that the superlative does not take an idafa except to what is part of it. In it is also an affirmation of the idafa in the meaning of "in," which is a disfavored view in grammar.

They (the scholars) said: In this verse there is evidence of caution in matters relating to religion and worldly affairs, and of the equality of the states of witnesses and judges. The judge does not act on the outward states of people, or on what appears of their faith and righteousness, until he investigates their inward states. This is because Allah explained the states of people, and that among them is one who displays beauty while intending ugliness.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 205:**

﴿When he turns away, he strives in the land to cause corruption therein and to destroy crops and livestock.﴾ The literal meaning of *tawalli* (turning away) is departing with the body. It was then extended to refer to retracting a statement or an action. Its meaning here is as follows. Ibn ʿAbbas said: he became angry, because it is a retraction from the satisfaction that preceded it. Al-Hasan said: he departed from the statement he had made. Muqatil and Ibn Qutaybah said: he departed bodily. Mujahid said: from the *wilayah* (authority), meaning he became a governor (*wali*). *Sa'y* (striving) literally means walking on foot with speed. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi and Ibn ʿAbbas, as reported by Ibn ʿAtiyyah from him, understood it here in this sense. The meaning is: when he rises up from you, O Muhammad, after softening speech and sweetness of expression, he strides on his feet through the land, cuts the roads and corrupts therein, as al-Akhnas did to the Thaqif.

It was also said that *sa'y* here means action (*ʿamal*). This is a permissible figurative usage (*majaz*) in the speech of the Arabs. Examples of it include ﴿And that there is not for man except what he strives for﴾ [al-Najm: 39], and ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it as due striving while he is a believer﴾ [al-Isra: 19]. A poet said:

*"Had what I strive for been enough to meet a lowly livelihood, I would not seek, a little of wealth would suffice me."*

*"But I strive for lasting glory, and those like me may attain lasting glory."*

(Al-Aʿsha said):

*"And Qays strove for Kindah, not the striving of one who depends on others, and it repelled her enemy and built for her."*

(Another said):

*"I strive on behalf of the clan of Banu Malik, each man is striving in his own affair."*

The meaning is: he strives by his tricks and by turning the circles against Islam. Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj inclined to this view, and it is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, and so are those who hold this view. Some of them said: its meaning is that he strives therein with disbelief, and some said with injustice. *Sa'y* may also occur with speech. It is said: "He strove between so-and-so and so-and-so," meaning he conveyed to the two of them a statement that causes separation. From this is the poet's line:

*"I did not say what the slanderers said, those who strove the striving of an enemy between us, spreading rumours."*

As for ﴿in the land﴾: it is known that striving can only be in the land. However, it conveys generality, in the sense of wherever in it he alights, he strives for corruption. The phrase *fi al-ardi* also indicates the great frequency of his striving and his movement across the regions of the land, because the generality of "the land" entails repetition of striving. A similar expression occurred earlier in His words ﴿Do not cause corruption in the land﴾ [al-Baqarah: 11]. If the intended person is al-Akhnas, then "the land" is the land of Madinah, and the definite article *al-* is for prior reference (*ʿahd*).

﴿to cause corruption therein﴾: this is the cause (*ʿillah*) of his striving and what drives him to strive in the land. *Fasad* (corruption) is the opposite of *salah* (righteousness), and it is opposition to God, in His words ﴿and He made you inhabitants of it﴾ [Hud: 61]. Corruption takes the forms of injustice, killing, plundering, and taking captives, and it may also be by disbelief.

﴿and to destroy crops and livestock﴾: he joined this cause to the cause before it, which is "to cause corruption therein." It resembles His words ﴿and His angels and His messengers and Jibril and Mikail﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98], and the line:

*"I charge against them with a bay steed and its chest."*

This is because corruption is all-encompassing, and destroying crops and livestock falls under it. However, He singled out these two for mention because they are the greatest of what is needed for the building of the world, so their corruption was the ultimate form of corruption. Whoever interprets *ifsad* (corruption) as ruin makes this part of the detailed explanation after the general statement.

Regarding ﴿destroy crops﴾: *al-harth* (crops) was mentioned earlier in His words ﴿and you do not water the crops﴾ [al-Baqarah: 71]. *Al-nasl* (livestock/offspring) was mentioned in the discussion of vocabulary. Given what was said earlier, that the verse concerns al-Akhnas, *al-harth* is the crops, and *al-nasl* is the donkeys he killed, so *al-nasl* here means the animals that have offspring. It was also said that here *al-harth* means women, and *al-nasl* means children. He, exalted is He, said ﴿Your women are a tilth for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 223]. Ibn ʿAtiyyah reported this from al-Zajjaj as a possibility, and in that case it is a metonymy (*kinayah*), which is one of the types of rhetorical expression (*bayan*).

The majority of readers recited ﴿wa-yuhlika﴾ (and he destroys) from *ahlaka*, coordinated with *li-yufsida* (to cause corruption). Ubayy recited ﴿wa-li-yuhlika﴾ with the *lam* of cause made explicit. Some readers recited ﴿wa-yuhliku﴾ from *ahlaka*, with the *kaf* in the nominative. This is explained as coordination with the verb *yuʿjibuka* (pleases you), or with *saʿa* (he strives), since it has the meaning of *yasʿa* (strives). It may also be a new sentence (*istiʾnaf*), or the implied subject (*mubtada'*) may be supplied, meaning: "and he is one who destroys." Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu Haywah, and Ibn Muhaysin recited ﴿wa-yahliku﴾ from *halaka*, with the *kaf* in the nominative, and *al-harthu wa-al-naslu* (crops and livestock) as the subject. Hammad ibn Salamah reported this from Ibn Kathir in the same way, and so did ʿAbd al-Warith from Abu ʿAmr. Al-Mahdawi reported that what Hammad transmitted from Ibn Kathir is actually *wa-yuhliku* from *ahlaka* with a *damma* on the *kaf*, and *al-harth* in the accusative. Some readers recited ﴿wa-yahlaku﴾ from *halaka*, with a *fatha* on the *lam*, the *kaf* in the nominative, and *al-harth* in the nominative. This is a rare dialectal form, like *rakana yarkunu*. This reading is attributed to al-Hasan and al-Zamakhshari.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It was also transmitted from him, meaning from al-Hasan, as ﴿wa-yuhlaku﴾ with the passive voice. So this word has six readings: *wa-yuhlika*, *wa-li-yuhlika*, *wa-yuhliku*, with what follows these three in the accusative, because the verb contains the pronoun of the subject; *wa-yahlaku*, *wa-yuhliku*, *wa-yuhlaku*, with what follows these three in the nominative, because it is governed by the verb. This conditional clause is either a new sentence, and the speech is complete at His words ﴿and he is the most contentious of adversaries﴾, or it is coordinated with the relative clause (*silah*) of "whoever" (*man*), or with its descriptive modifier, from His words ﴿that pleases you﴾.

﴿And Allah does not love corruption﴾: two causes have been mentioned, and the second is included under the first. So He, exalted is He, informed that He does not love corruption, and He suffices with mentioning the first because it encompasses the second. Even if love is interpreted as will (*irada*), and it has come in that sense in several places, among them ﴿Indeed, those who love that indecency should spread among those who believe﴾ [al-Nur: 19], there must be a specification, meaning: He does not love corruption from the people of righteousness. In that case, it cannot be taken as general according to our school, because corruption has occurred, and if it were not intended, it would not have occurred.

The Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school) relied on this verse to argue that God does not will corruption, so what occurs of it is not willed by God, the Exalted, nor is it created by Him, because if He did it, He would be willing it, since it is impossible for Him to do what He does not will. They said: What indicates that His love for an act is His willing it, is that it is not permissible for Him to love its existence while not willing that it exist, but rather He would dislike its existence. In this there is what there is of contradiction. The end of what they said. It was also said: the meaning is that Allah does not love corruption as a religion. It was said: it is by omitting a governed noun (*mudaf*), meaning: "does not love the people of corruption." Ibn ʿAbbas said: the meaning is that He does not approve of sins. It was also said: He expressed love in place of command, meaning He does not command corruption. Al-Raghib said: *ifsad* is taking a thing out of a praiseworthy state without a valid purpose, and that does not exist in the acts of Allah, the Exalted. All these interpretations are according to the view of the theologians (*mutakallimun*) that love means will. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: love in His regard denotes a privilege of preference, so if someone said that the corruption willed lacks the privilege of preference, that would be correct, since love from Allah, the Exalted, is only for what is good in all its aspects. The end of his words.

If this is correct, the difference between will and love becomes clear, and it is valid that Allah wills a thing without loving it. Some of them said: the Mu'tazilah equated love and will, and they used this verse as evidence, while the majority of scholars differ from that. The difference between will and love is clear, for a person may will the slow healing of a wound without loving it. When the difference between will and love is evident in reason, their claim of equality between them is invalidated. The meaning of this verse is similar to His words ﴿And He does not approve for His servants disbelief﴾ [al-Zumar: 7]. The end of his words.

The Qur'an contains the negation of Allah's love for several things, since with respect to Him there is no intermediate state between love and its absence, unlike with others, who may be in neither state. So love and its opposite, in relation to Allah, the Exalted, are contradictories (*naqidan*), and in relation to others they are contraries (*didan*). The apparent meaning of corruption covers every kind of corruption, whether in the land, in property, or in religion. ʿAta' derived from His words ﴿And Allah does not love corruption﴾ the prohibition of a person tearing his garment. Ibn ʿAbbas said: corruption here means ruin.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 206:

﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah," pride takes hold of him for sin﴾. This clause may also be taken as a new (independent) sentence (mustaʾnafah), or it may be included within the relative clause (ṣilah). The discussion of this type of construction has already been presented in His words: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Do not cause corruption on the earth"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 11]. As for what has taken the place of the subject (fāʿil) here, it dispenses with mentioning it. And "pride took hold of him" (akhadhathu al-ʿizzah) means it encompassed him and surrounded him, so that he becomes like one who is seized by it, just as one takes hold of a thing with the hand. Al-Zamakhshari said: from your saying "I took him with such-and-such" (akhadhtuhu bi-kadha), when you compel him to it and bind him to it, meaning: pride that is in him, and the zeal of ignorance (ḥamiyyat al-jahiliyyah), compelled him to the sin that is forbidden, and bound him to committing it, and to not leaving it out of harm and obstinacy, or in order to reject the words of the admonisher. End of his speech. So the bāʾ (in bi-l-ithm), according to his words, is for transitivity (lil-taʿdiyah), as if the meaning were: pride bound him to sin. Transitivity by means of bāʾ is characteristic of intransitive verbs, such as: ﴿would have taken away their hearing and their sight﴾ [al-Baqarah: 20], meaning: would have taken away their hearing. Transitivity by means of bāʾ in a verb that is already transitive is rare, as in: "I struck the stone with the stone" (ṣakaktu al-ḥajar bi-l-ḥajar), meaning: I made one of them strike the other. The bāʾ may also be for accompaniment (lil-muṣāḥabah), meaning: it took hold of him accompanied by sin, or accompanied (feminine) by sin, in which case it is a circumstantial (ḥāl) from the object or the subject. It may also be causal (sababiyyah), and the meaning is: his previous sin was the cause for pride taking hold of him, so that he would not accept from one who commands him to fear Allah, the Exalted. In that case the bāʾ here is like min, in the words of the poet:

"Pride took hold of him from his ignorance, so he turned away angry, acting like one annoyed."

On the reading that the bāʾ is causal, al-Hasan explained it, saying: that is, because of the sin that is in his heart, meaning disbelief. Pride (al-ʿizzah) has been explained as strength, as zeal, and as protection, and all of these are close in meaning. In His words ﴿pride took hold of him for sin﴾ there is a type of rhetorical ornament called al-tatmim, which is following a statement with a word that removes ambiguity and brings it closer to understanding, as in His words: ﴿nor any bird that flies with its two wings﴾ [al-Anʿam: 38]. This is because pride (ʿizzah) is praiseworthy and blameworthy: the praiseworthy kind is obedience to Allah, as He said: ﴿humble toward the believers, stern toward the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 54]; ﴿And to Allah belongs honor, and to His Messenger and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]; ﴿For indeed, honor belongs entirely to Allah﴾ [al-Nisa': 139]. When He said "for sin," the meaning became clear and complete, and it became evident that it is the blameworthy pride whose possessor is held accountable for sin.

Ibn Mas'ud said: A man should not become angry when he is told, "Fear Allah," or say, "Does such a one as me get told this?" It was said to ʿUmar: "Fear Allah," so he placed his cheek on the ground in humility. It was also said that he prostrated and said: "This is my capacity." A Jew kept coming to the door of Harun al-Rashid for a year, but he did not grant him his need. So he contrived until he stood before him and said: "Fear Allah, O Commander of the Faithful." Harun dismounted from his mount and fell down prostrate, and granted his need. He was asked about that, and said: "I remembered His words: ﴿And when it is said to him, 'Fear Allah,' pride takes hold of him for sin﴾."

﴿Then Hell is sufficient for him﴾: that is, Hell is sufficient for him as recompense and humiliation. It is a compound sentence consisting of a subject and predicate. Some scholars held that Jahannam is the subject (fāʿil) of "fa-ḥasbuhu," because they treat it as an ism al-fiʿl (verbal noun), either with the meaning of the past verb, that is, "Hell sufficed him," or with the meaning of the imperative verb. The entry of the preposition on it and its use as an adjective, and the operation of the case-endings upon it, nullify its being an ism al-fiʿl. Its pride is matched by the punishment of Hell, which is the utmost degree of humiliation. Since His words "Fear Allah" entailed that what he was commanded to fear would befall him, namely the punishment of Allah, and in His words "Hell is sufficient for him" there is an amplification of the punishment that befell him, just as you say to a man: "What has befallen you is enough for you," when you magnify what has befallen him and make it great.

﴿And wretched is the resting place﴾. The discussion of "biʾsa" has already been presented, and the disagreement concerning the structure of such a sentence is mentioned in the science of grammar. However, the derivation according to the school of the Basrans, that biʾsa and niʿma are rigid verbs, that the noun following them is their subject, and that the one specified by blame (al-makhsus bi-l-dhamm), if it comes first, is a subject (mubtada'), and if it comes later, likewise, is the view of Sibawayh. The one specified by blame is omitted here because it is known, since it has been mentioned before, and the estimate is: "And wretched is the resting place, Hell," or "it." By this omission, the view of those who claim that the one specified by praise or blame, when it comes later, is the predicate of an omitted subject, or an omitted-predicate subject, is invalidated: because it would necessitate omitting the whole sentence entirely without anything standing in for it, for it would remain a sentence detached from the preceding sentence, having no place in the grammatical structure, and being neither parenthetical nor explanatory, since those two are dispensable while this one is not. Thus it becomes connected yet unconnected, and that is not permissible. If we make the omitted element belong to the category of the single noun (mufrad), there is in what precedes it something that indicates its omission, and it becomes one sentence, as its state when it comes first. You do not see any difference between your saying "Zayd is a fine man" (niʿma al-rajul) and "a fine man is Zayd," just as you do not find a difference between "Zayd, his father stood" and "the father of Zayd stood." The omission of the one specified by blame is justified here by the fact that "al-mihad" occurs as a closing rhyme (fasilah). It has been omitted frequently in the Qur'an for this purpose, such as His words: ﴿How excellent a Protector and how excellent a Helper﴾ [al-Hajj: 78]; ﴿So wretched is the abode of the arrogant﴾ [al-Nahl: 29]. He made what was prepared for them a "mihad" (resting-place) in the manner of mockery toward them, since "mihad" is that upon which a person rests and which is spread out for him for sleep. Similar to it is the words of the poet:

"And horses I have advanced against with horses, a greeting among them being a painful blow."

That is: what takes the place of the greeting is the painful blow. Likewise, what takes the place of a resting place for them is the dwelling in the Fire.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 207:**

﴿And among the people is he who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah.﴾ It was said: what is meant by "he who" (*man*) is not a specific person, but applies to everyone who sells himself to Allah, the Exalted, in jihad, or in patience upon the religion, or in speaking a word of truth before a tyrant, or in zeal for Allah, or in defending His law, or what is similar to these. It was also said that it refers to a specific person. It was said: it was about al-Zubayr and al-Miqdad, whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent to Mecca to take Khubayb down from his wooden cross. It was said: it was about Suhayb al-Rumi, who went out as a migrant, and the Quraysh caught up with him. He emptied his quiver, and he was a skilled archer of great strength, to be feared in his aim. They said: "We will not leave you until you show us where your wealth is." So he showed them its location, and they turned back from him. It was also said: he was tortured so that he would abandon his religion, so he ransomed himself with his wealth and went out as a migrant. It was said: it was about Ali, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ left him in Mecca to settle his debts, return the deposits, and ordered him to sleep in his bed the night he went out as a migrant ﷺ. al-Hasan said: it was revealed concerning the Muslim who meets the disbeliever and says to him, "Say: there is no god but Allah," but he does not say it, so the Muslim says, "By Allah, I will sell myself," and he fights until he is killed. Ibn Abbas said: it was about enjoining good and forbidding evil. It was said: it was about Suhayb and Abu Dharr. Abu Dharr had been seized by his family, then he escaped and went out as a migrant. It was said: it was about the Muhajirun and the Ansar. The exegetes mentioned other than this, and long narratives about the reports of these specific persons concerning whom the verse was said to have been revealed. What should be said is this: when Allah, the Exalted, mentioned ﴿And among the people is he whose speech pleases you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 204], and that was general concerning the hypocrite who shows the opposite of what he conceals, it was fitting to mention its counterpart in general: he who gives his soul in obedience to Allah, the Exalted, whatever difficulty it may involve. Thus the hypocrite protects himself through lying, hypocrisy, and sweetness of speech, whereas this one gives his soul to Allah and to seeking His pleasure. The sayings that are in the two verses fall under the generality of these two verses, and the mention of what was specified by those who specified is only by way of giving examples. It is not far-fetched that the cause (of revelation) was specific while the intended meaning is the generality of the wording. Since the separation between the first division and the second division was long here, in the second division he brought the explicit mention of the one divided, saying ﴿And among the people is he who sells﴾, unlike his saying ﴿And among them is he who says: Our Lord, give us in this world good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 201], for when the mention of one of the two parts was close to the divided whole, he left the whole implicit in the second.

The meaning of *yashri* (sells) is "sells," and this is valid in the language. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And they sold him for a low price, a few dirhams﴾ [Yusuf: 20]. The poet said:

*I sold a cloak; would that after the cloak I had been a fool*

And *yashri* is an expression for giving one's soul in (the cause of) Allah, and from it the *Shurat* (those who sell themselves for Allah) are named, as though they had sold their souls to Allah. Some said: *shara* means *ishtara* (bought). If the verse is about Suhayb, then this is present in him, since he bought his soul with his wealth and did not sell it.

The accusative of *ibtighaa'* (seeking) is as an object of purpose (*maf'ul min ajlihi*), meaning: what moves them to sell their souls is only the seeking of Allah's pleasure, and it fulfills the conditions of the object of purpose, being a verbal noun whose agent and time are one. This annexation, I mean the annexation of the object of purpose, is a pure (*mahdah*) annexation, contrary to al-Jurmi, al-Riyashi, al-Mubarrad, and some later grammarians, who claim it is a non-pure annexation. This is mentioned in the books of grammar.

*Mardat* (pleasure) is a verbal noun built with the *ta'* like *mad'aah*, and the analogical form is to strip it of the *ta'*, as you say *marma* and *maghza*. al-Kisa'i inclined *Mardaat* (to *ā*), and regarding Warsh there is a difference in inclining *Mardaat*, and we recited for him with both possibilities. Hamza stopped on it with the *ta'*, and the rest stopped with the *ha'*. As for Hamza's stopping with the *ta'*, it has two possible aspects:

The first: that it is according to the view of those Arabs who stop on *Talha* and *Hamza* with the *ta'*, as in continuation, and this would have been the analogical form rather than substitution. He said:

*A dwelling of Salma after a year has passed, has been effaced, but beyond Tayha' like the back of the Hajfat*

Sibawayh has transmitted this dialect.

The other aspect: that it is intended as an annexed form, as though he intended to indicate the omitted annexed term, wishing to make known that the word is annexed and that the annexed term is intended, like the *ishmam* of one who indicates a vowelled letter at pause, to make known that the *damma* is intended. In His saying ﴿the seeking of the pleasure of Allah﴾ there is an indication of the attainment of the best that is with Allah for the martyrs, which is His pleasure, the Exalted. In the authentic hadith about the residents of Paradise living beside their Lord, the Exalted, when He asks them: "Are you pleased?" They say: "O Lord, how could we not be pleased when You have admitted us to Your Garden and distanced us from Your Fire?" He says: "And for you I have something better than that." They say: "O Lord, and what is better than that?" He says: "I shall cause My pleasure to descend upon you, so I shall never be displeased with you after it."

﴿And Allah is Compassionate toward the servants﴾: in that He charged them with jihad, thereby exposing them to the reward of the martyrs. This was said by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is a *tarji'ah* (a reassurance) that requires encouragement to comply with what the verse praised, as in His saying ﴿Hell is sufficient for him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 206], a warning that requires caution against what the verse blamed. It has already been mentioned that *ra'fah* (compassion) is more emphatic than *rahmah* (mercy).

If *al-'ibad* (the servants) is general, then His compassion toward the disbelievers is granting them respite until the end of their terms and facilitating their provisions, and His compassion toward the believers is preparing them for His obedience and raising their ranks in Paradise. If it is specific, which is the more apparent, then because He concluded the verse with the threat in His saying ﴿Hell is sufficient for him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 206], and that was specific to those disbelievers, He concluded this (verse) with the promise giving good tidings of excellent reward and abundant return, and this is indicated by compassion, which is the cause of that. Thus it becomes an allusion (*kinayah*) to Allah's beneficence toward them, because His compassion toward them requires all kinds of beneficence. Had He mentioned any particular kind of beneficence, it would not have conveyed what the word *ra'fah* conveyed, and for this reason the allusion is more eloquent. In this case, the word *al-'ibad* would be an *iltifat* (shift), since it is a move from a singular absent pronoun to an apparent noun. Had it followed the composition of the preceding speech, it would have been: "And Allah is compassionate toward him" or "toward them." Two things make this apparent noun in the shift fitting: first, that the word *al-'ibad* in the usage of the Qur'an carries honour and distinction, as in His saying ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾ [al-Hijr: 42], ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra': 1], ﴿Then We made to inherit the Book those whom We chose from Our servants﴾ [Fatir: 32], ﴿Rather, they are honoured servants﴾ [al-Anbiya': 26]. Second, the coming of the word as a closing rhyme: because before it is ﴿And Allah does not love corruption﴾ [al-Baqarah: 205], ﴿Hell is sufficient for him, and what an evil resting place﴾ [al-Baqarah: 206], so ﴿And Allah is Compassionate toward the servants﴾ is fitting.

* *

In this verse and the one before it there is, among the figures of rhetorical embellishment (*badi'*), *taqsim* (division). We have mentioned the appropriateness of this division to the preceding division before it, in His saying ﴿So among the people is he who says: Our Lord, give us in this world﴾ [al-Baqarah: 200]. Some people said: in these verses there is a kind of rhetorical embellishment, namely *taqdim* and *ta'khir* (advancing and postponing), which is one of the modes of expression in prose and verse, and an evidence of strength of faculty in various kinds of speech. That is His saying ﴿And remember Allah during the numbered days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 203], which is advanced before His saying ﴿So among the people is he who says﴾ [al-Baqarah: 200], because His saying ﴿And remember Allah during the numbered days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 203] is coordinated with His saying ﴿Then when you have completed your rites, remember Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 200]. His saying ﴿So among the people is he who says﴾ [al-Baqarah: 200] is coordinated with His saying ﴿And among them is he who says﴾ [al-Baqarah: 201], and His saying ﴿And among them is he who says﴾ [al-Baqarah: 201] is coordinated with His saying ﴿And among the people is he whose speech pleases you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 204], and with His saying ﴿And among the people is he who sells﴾. Thus the speech becomes coordinated with the mention, because it is appropriate to what precedes it in meaning, and the division becomes coordinated, part with part, because the first division is in the meaning of the second, so the meaning is unified and the wording is consistent. Then he said: "Similar to this," and he mentioned the story of the cow and the killing of a soul, and the story of the woman whose husband has died in the two verses. He said: "Similar to this is much in the Qur'an," meaning *taqdim* and *ta'khir*. But what he mentioned is not to be followed, and there is no advancing or postponing in the Qur'an, because advancing and postponing, in our view, belong to the category of necessities (of poetry), and the Book of Allah, the Exalted, is exalted above it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 208:

﴿O you who have believed, enter into Islam completely⁠﴾: It was revealed concerning ʿAbdullah ibn Salam and those who embraced Islam with him, who used to avoid the Sabbath, camel meat, and other things that the People of the Book avoided. This was said by ʿIkrimah, and Abu Salih narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbas. Or it was revealed concerning the People of the Book who did not believe in the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; this was said by al-Dahhak. It is also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas: or it was revealed concerning the Muslims, commanding them to enter into the laws of Islam; this was said by Mujahid and Qatadah. Or it was revealed concerning the hypocrites, and this view is supported by the verse's occurrence right after the description of the hypocrites. Based on this difference regarding the occasion of revelation, the opinions of the exegetes have differed.

Nafiʿ, Ibn Kathir and al-Kisa'i read the sin in "al-silm" with a fatha (as-salm), and likewise in al-Anfal: ﴿And if they incline to peace (lil-salm)⁠﴾ [al-Anfal: 61], and in Muhammad: ﴿and call to peace (al-salm)⁠﴾ [Muhammad: 35]. The meaning of "al-silm" here has been disputed. It has been said that it means Islam, since Islam is sometimes called silm with a kasra on the sin, and it is also narrated with a fatha; just as silm meaning reconciliation is narrated with both fatha and kasra, except that the fatha in silm meaning Islam is rare. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi permitted that silm here may mean reconciliation (sulh), because Islam is truly a reconciliation: do you not see that there is no fighting among its adherents, and that they are one hand against others? If the address is to Ibn Salam and his companions, then they were commanded to enter into the laws of Islam and not to retain any of the laws of the People of the Book that do not agree with the laws of Islam. If the address is to the People of the Book who did not believe in the Messenger, then the meaning is: O you who believed in what came before from their prophets, enter into this law, which is for them as well; as if it were said: O you to whom faith in the Torah and the Gospel has been granted, and they both attest to the truth of this law, enter into this law. If the address is to the Muslims, then the meaning is: O you who have believed in your heart and affirmed, enter into the laws of Islam, and join Islam to faith. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ explained faith and Islam in the hadith of Jibril's question, when he asked him about the reality of each of them. If the address is to the hypocrites, then the meaning is: O you who have believed with your tongue, enter into Islam with your heart, so that speech matches belief.

Of these opinions, the apparent one is that it is an address to the believers, who were commanded to adhere to the laws of Islam, or to submission and acceptance without reluctance, or to abandoning retaliation; and they were all commanded to be united and to avoid division. For this reason, the word "kaffah" (completely) was used. The accusative of "kaffah" is a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of the subject in "udkhulū" (enter), and the meaning is: enter into peace all together. It is a ḥāl that emphasizes the sense of generality, so it conveys the meaning of "kull" (all). Thus, when you say: "The people stood kaffah," the meaning is: they all stood. Al-Zamakhshari and others permitted that it be a ḥāl of "al-silm," i.e., in all the laws of Islam; they were commanded not to enter into one obedience while leaving another. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is permissible for kaffah to be a ḥāl of al-silm, because it is feminine just as ḥarb (war) is feminine," and the poet said:

Peace (al-silm) takes from you what you are pleased with, and war suffices you with its breaths, which are sips.

It is also said that the believers were commanded to enter all acts of obedience, and not to enter one obedience while leaving another; or into all branches and laws of Islam, and not to neglect any of them.
