It is narrated from ʿAbdullah ibn Salam that he asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for permission to continue observing the Sabbath and to recite from the Torah in his night prayer. "Kaffah" derives from "kaff" (to restrain), as if they were restrained from anyone leaving them through their unity. This is the end of al-Zamakhshari's words. His justification for permitting kaffah to be a ḥāl of al-silm, by saying "because it is feminine just as ḥarb is feminine," is not valid: the tāʾ in "kaffah," although its original basis is for feminine marking, is not for feminine marking when it is a ḥāl; rather, this has become a pure transfer to the meaning of jamīʿ and kull, just as "qāṭibatan" and "ʿāmmatan," when used as ḥāl, have become pure transfers to the meaning of kull and jamīʿ. So when you say "the people stood kaffah," or "qāṭibatan," or "ʿāmmatan," none of these words indicates feminine gender, just as kull and jamīʿ do not indicate it. His stress by saying "in all branches and laws of Islam" is the first sense of his words "to enter into all acts of obedience," so there is no need for this alternation with "or."

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: A group said: all the believers in Muhammad ﷺ, and the meaning is: He commanded them to persist in it and to increase in adherence to its limits. Then "kaffah" encompasses the believers and all parts of the Law, so the ḥāl is of two things, and that is permissible, like His saying: ﴿So she brought him to her people, carrying him⁠﴾ [Maryam: 27], among other examples. Then, after a statement he mentioned, he said: "Kaffah means jamīʿan (all together), and by kaffah is meant the group that restrains its opponents." This is the end of his words.

His statement "so the ḥāl is of two things" means: of the subject in "udkhulū" and of "al-silm." This is possible, but the more apparent view is that it is a ḥāl of the pronoun of the subject, and that is permissible; that is, a single ḥāl may belong to two things, and this is treated in detail in grammar. His statement, "like His saying: ﴿carrying him⁠﴾," means that "taḥmiluhu" is a ḥāl of the implicit subject in "atat" and of the pronoun in the preposition-governed form; but this example does not match a ḥāl of two things, because the wording "taḥmiluhu" cannot carry two referents, and a ḥāl of two things can occur only if the wording can accommodate both. The test for this is to make the two referents into subjects and predicate the ḥāl of them; whenever this is valid the ḥāl is valid, and whenever it is impossible it is impossible. An example is the poet's words:

I was enamored of Salma, while she was one with a closed tent, and her breast showed no bulk to the maidens.

Two young ones grazing the flock; O that we had not grown up until today, and the flock had not grown up either.

Here "ṣaghīrayn" is a ḥāl of the pronoun in "ʿulliqtu" and of Salma, because one can say: I and Salma are two young ones grazing the flock. Similar is:

I went out with her, walking, dragging behind us.

Here "namshī" is a ḥāl of the tāʾ in "kharajtu" and of the pronoun in "bihā" in the preposition-governed form, and one can say: I and she are walking. Here "taḥmiluhu" cannot be a predicate of both; if you said: she and he are carrying him, "taḥmiluhu" could not be a predicate, as in: Hind and Zayd honor him; because "taḥmiluhu" and "tukrimuhu" can only be construed with a singular noun. Therefore it is impossible for it to be a ḥāl of two referents. This is why grammarians parsed in:

I went out with her, walking, dragging behind us.

that "namshī" is a ḥāl of both of them, and "tajurru" is a ḥāl of the feminine pronoun only, because if you said: I and she are dragging behind us, "tajurru" could not be a predicate of them; since "tajurru" and "taḥmilu" are construed only as singular participles, namely ḥāmilatan and jārratan, and when you state this singular participle explicitly it cannot be a ḥāl of both. And "kaffah," because it signifies the meaning of jamīʿ, can be a ḥāl of the subject in "udkhulū" and of "al-silm," in the sense of the laws of Islam: because if you said: "The men and the women are jamīʿ in such-and-such," it would be valid as a predicate. It cannot be said that kaffah cannot be a predicate; you do not say "the Zayds and the ʿAmrs are kaffah in such-and-such." So it is impermissible for it to be a ḥāl on the basis of what you established; the impossibility of this is only because of the root of "kaffah," since it is not inflected but is obligatorily fixed in the accusative as a ḥāl, whereas its synonym can be used that way. His statement, "and by kaffah is meant the group that restrains its opponents," means that this was its original usage; then its usage came to mean jamīʿan, as he and others said, and "kaffah" means jamīʿan.

* *

﴿And do not follow the footsteps of Satan; indeed, he is to you a clear enemy⁠﴾. The explanation of these two clauses has already been given after His saying: ﴿O mankind, eat of what is on the earth, lawful and good⁠﴾ [al-Baqarah: 168], so that suffices and there is no need to repeat it. The author of al-Kitab al-Muwaddih, Abu ʿAbdullah Nasr ibn ʿAli ibn Muhammad, known as Ibn Maryam, stated that raising the ʿayn of the word in such cases, as in ghurfah and ghurufat, is the position of the people of the Hijaz. He said regarding those who make the tāʾ sukūn: when they pluralized it, they intended the ḍamma on the ṭāʾ, then they made it sukūn for lightness. This, in the sense of being fixed, indicates that the ḍamma is treated as present, because this movement serves to distinguish the noun from the adjective, as it does in the plural of faʿlah with a fatḥa on the first letter; so the ʿayn of the noun is not deleted outright, since it distinguishes it from the adjective, and therefore it is inevitably intended. This is the end of his words. It has become clear from this that in the adjective it is not transferred; so when we pluralize ḥulwah and ḍuḥkah, meaning the feminine adjective, one does not say ḥuluwāt or ḍuḥukāt with a ḍamma on the ʿayn of the word. By this analogy, the pattern fuʿlah for adjectives, such as julfah, is not pluralized as julufāt.

﴿So if you slip after the clear proofs have come to you﴾: that is, you disobey, or disbelieve, or err, or go astray. There are several views. The second, reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, is the apparent meaning, given the verse's words, ﴿Enter into peace﴾, meaning Islam, so that ﴿if you slip﴾ means slipping away from entering it. The root of *zalal* (slipping) is for the foot, as one says, "his foot slipped" (*zallat qadamuhu*), as the poet said:

"Nor let a mocker rejoice if the sandal of ʿAzza has slipped."

Then the word is used for opinion and belief, and it is *zalaq* (slipping). Part of its explanation has already been given in His words, ﴿Then Satan caused them both to slip from it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 36]. Abu al-Simak recited *"fa-in zalilltum"* with a kasra on the lam (*zalilltum*). The two are dialectal variants, like *ḍalaltu* and *ḍalilltu*. "The clear proofs" (*al-bayyinat*) are the proofs and evidences of God, or Muhammad (ﷺ), as He said, ﴿until there comes to them clear evidence﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 1], ﴿a Messenger from God﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 2]. It is plural out of honour for him, because although he is one in person, he is many in meaning. Or it means the Qur'an, as Ibn Jurayj said. Or it means the Torah and the Gospel, as He said, ﴿Moses came to you with clear proofs﴾ [al-Baqarah: 92], and He said, ﴿and We gave ʿIsa son of Maryam clear proofs﴾ [al-Baqarah: 253]. This is derived according to the view of those who said that the addressees are the People of the Book, or Islam, or the miracles that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) brought. These are six views. In *al-Muntakhab*: "The clear proofs encompass all rational and transmitted proofs, since the excuse of the accountable person does not cease except upon the arrival of the clear proofs, not merely the arrival of clarification from the obligation." End of his words. Rational proofs are not described as "coming," because they are fixed in the intellects, so "coming" is attributed to them only metaphorically, and this is a stretch.

* *

﴿Then know that God is Mighty, Wise﴾: that is, persist in knowledge, if the address is to the believers. If the address is to the disbelievers or hypocrites, then it is a command for them to acquire knowledge through correct reflection that leads to it. Describing Him here as *ʿIzza* (Might), which includes the dominance and power by which retribution is carried out, is a severe warning to whoever opposes Him and strays from the path of truth. Describing Him as *Hikma* (Wisdom) indicates the perfection of His acts, and that what He ordains of deterrents for those who oppose Him is required by wisdom. It is reported that a reciter recited "Forgiving, Merciful" (*ghafurun rahim*), and a Bedouin heard him, denied it, and he did not used to recite the Qur'an, and said: "If this is the speech of God, the Wise would not say that. He would not mention forgiveness at the time of slipping, because that would be an incitement to it." Something similar has been reported from Kaʿb. And that the one from whom he was learning had taught him, "Then know that God is Forgiving, Merciful," so he denied it until he heard "Mighty, Wise," and said: "This is how it should be."

(p-124) ﴿Are they waiting for anything but that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds, and the angels?﴾ *Hal* here is for negation. The meaning is: *ma yanzurun* (they are not waiting for anything). For this reason *illa* (except) follows it. When *hal* is used in the sense of negation and is followed by *illa*, it is very common in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech. Allah says: ﴿And do We requite any but the ungrateful?﴾ [Saba: 17]; ﴿Will any be destroyed but the wrongdoing people?﴾ [al-An'am: 47]. The poet says:

*Am I anything but of Ghaziyya? If it goes astray, I go astray, and if Ghaziyya is rightly guided, I am rightly guided.*

*Yanzurun* here means *yantazirun* (they wait). The Arabs say: *nazartu fulanan antaziruhu* (I waited for so-and-so), and the verb does not take a single object directly except with a preposition. Imru' al-Qays says:

*So if you two would give me a little time from the days, you would benefit me in the presence of Umm Jundab.*

The object of *yanzurun* is what follows *illa*, meaning: they wait for nothing except the coming of Allah. This is an *istithna' mufarragh* (exceptive construction in which the object of the verb is absent and must be supplied from what follows *illa*). It was said: *yanzurun* here is not from *nazar* (looking), which is the eye moving over the thing looked at, because if it were from *nazar* it would be followed by *ila* and would be connected to the face. Rather, it is from *intizar* (waiting). This was stated and concluded. This reasoning is worthless, because it is said that it is from *nazar*, which is the movement of the eye. It is followed by *ila*, but *ila* is omitted, and the sense is: "Are they waiting for anything except *ila* that Allah should come to them?" Omitting the preposition with *an* is a regular analogical rule when there is no ambiguity, and there is no ambiguity here, so *ila* was omitted. His statement "and it is connected to the face" refers to the verse ﴿Faces that day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22–23]. This is also not necessary, since looking has often been attributed to essences, as in ﴿Do they not look at the camels?﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 17] and ﴿Show me Yourself, that I may look at You﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]. The pronoun in *yanzurun* refers back to the wrongdoers, and this is an *iltifat* (shift from second-person address to third-person reference).

*Ityan* (coming) is, literally, movement from one place to another, and that is impossible for Allah, the Exalted. Abu Salih reported from Ibn Abbas that this is among the hidden matters which are not explained, and the early generation (*salaf*) always believed in this and similar matters, leaving the understanding of their meaning to the knowledge of the one who spoke them, who is Allah, the Exalted. The later scholars interpreted the *ityan* and its attribution in several ways:

First: it is a coming befitting Allah, the Exalted, without movement from place to place.

Second: it is an expression for His requital of them and His retribution, as He says: ﴿So Allah came at their structure from the foundations﴾ [al-Nahl: 26] and ﴿Allah came at them from where they did not expect﴾ [al-Hashr: 2].

Third: the object of the coming is omitted, meaning: that Allah should bring them what He promised them of reward and punishment. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Fourth: it is by omitting a noun modified by the phrase: the meaning is "the command of Allah," in the sense of what Allah will do to them, not the command whose opposite is prohibition. This is clarified by His statement after it: ﴿and the matter is decided﴾.

Fifth: His power. This was mentioned by al-Qadi Abu Ya'la, from Ahmad.

Sixth: *fi zulal* means *bi zulal* (with canopies), so *fi* carries the sense of *ba'* (with), as in the poet's words:

*Experts in striking the arteries and kidneys*

meaning *bi-ta'n* (by striking). This is because *khabir* (expert) is only followed by *ba'*, as the poet says:

*An expert in the ailments of women, a physician*

This was said by al-Zajjaj and others. The better view is that the meaning is "the command of Allah," since it is stated explicitly in His statement: ﴿Or the command of your Lord comes﴾ [al-Nahl: 33], and it means His might and punishment, because this verse came in the manner of threat and warning. It was also said: the omitted word is "the signs of Allah," so the coming of His signs is treated as His coming, to magnify their importance. This was said in *al-Muntakhab*. It is reported from Ibn Jarir that he said: He comes to them to call them to account, in the clouds, on His throne carried by eight angels. It was also said that the address is to the Jews, who are *mushabbiha* (anthropomorphists). What indicates that it is addressed to the Jews is His statement after it: ﴿Ask the Children of Israel﴾. If that is the case, the meaning is that they will not accept that except if Allah comes to them. So the verse is taken in its apparent sense, since the meaning is that a people wait for the coming of Allah. This does not indicate that they are right or wrong.

﴿in canopies of clouds﴾: discussion of this was already given under His statement: ﴿And We shaded you with clouds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 57]. It is impossible for the Holy Essence to be contained in a canopy. It was said: the intended meaning is to depict the greatness, occurrence, and severity of the Day of Resurrection, because nothing is more severe for sinners, and more terrifying, than the time of their gathering and the presence of the most skilled and most dignified judges to decide the dispute. This is then a figure of speech. If it is interpreted as meaning that the punishment of Allah comes to them in canopies of clouds, then that is because it is greater; or the evil comes to them from the direction of good, as in His statement: ﴿This is a cloud bringing us rain; rather, it is what you were hastening, a wind in which is painful punishment﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 24]. And because, if that is the Day of Resurrection, it is a sign of the greatest terrors of that day. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And the day the sky will be split open by clouds﴾ [al-Furqan: 25]. And because the cloud sends down drops that are not limited, so likewise the punishment is not restricted. It was also said: the punishment does not come in canopies, but the meaning is a comparison of the terrors to canopies of clouds, as He says: ﴿And when a wave covers them like canopies﴾ [Luqman: 32]. So the meaning is that the punishment of Allah comes to them with great terrors, like canopies of clouds.

They differed about this threat. Ibn Juraij said: it is a threat of what will happen in this world. Others said: rather, it is a threat of the Day of Resurrection.

Ubayy, Abdullah, Qatada, and al-Dahhak read *fi zilal* (with the plural *zilal*). Likewise Harun ibn Hatim reported from Abu Bakr, from Asim, here and in the two places in al-Zumar. It is the plural of *zullah*, like *qullah* and *qilal*, and this plural is not regular, unlike *zulal*, which is a regular plural. Or it is the plural of *zill* (shade), like *dill* and *dulal*. *Fi zulal* is connected to *ya'tiyahum* (comes to them). They allowed that it could be a circumstantial phrase (*hal*), and then it is connected to an omitted word. *Min al-ghamam* stands in the position of an adjective for *zulal*. They also allowed that it is connected to *ya'tiyahum*, meaning "from the direction of the clouds," so *min* is then for the starting point. In the first case, *min* is partitive.

Al-Hasan, Abu Haywa, and Abu Ja'far read *wal-malaikati* (and the angels) in the genitive, as a conjunction to *fi zulal*, or as a conjunction to *al-ghamam*. The preposition then varies in its implied form: in the first case the implied preposition is *fi* (in the angels), and in the second it is *min* (from the angels). The majority read it in the nominative as a conjunction to "Allah."

It was also said: in this sentence there is inversion. The coming is in canopies and is attached to the angels, so the meaning is: "Unless Allah and the angels come in canopies." So the coming attached to Allah, the Exalted, is only the coming itself. This is supported by the reading of Abdullah: "Unless Allah comes to them and the angels in canopies."

﴿and the matter is decided﴾: the meaning is that the requital occurred and those who disobeyed were punished. It was said: the matter of their destruction was completed and finished. It was said: the time of waiting ended, and the time of punishment came. It was said: the matter was finished for them, in regard to what they were promised, until the Day of Resurrection. It was said: the reckoning was finished and the punishment became binding. These statements are close in meaning.

﴿and the matter is decided﴾ is connected to His statement "ya'tiyahum" (comes to them). It is therefore the placing of the past tense in the position of the future, and the past tense is used for the future because it is like something already finished that has occurred. The meaning is: "and the matter will be decided." It is possible that this is a report from Allah, the Exalted, meaning: their affair was finished with what preceded in destiny. Then it is a conjunction of sentences, not something still awaited. Mu'adh ibn Jabal read *wa-qada'u al-amr* (and the judgment of the matter). Al-Zamakhshari said: it is in the nominative as a verbal noun, connected to the angels. Others said: it is in the genitive, with the long vowel, connected to the angels. It was said that *fi* in this case means *bi* (with): with canopies of clouds, with the angels, and with the judgment of the matter. Yahya ibn Ma'mar read *wa-qudiya al-umur* (and the matters were decided) in the plural, and the verb is in the passive, the agent being omitted because it is known. Also, if it were expressed and the verb were active, the noun would be repeated three times.

* *

﴿And to Allah all matters are returned﴾: Ibn Amir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read *turja'* (returned), with *ta'* open and *jim* kasra throughout the Qur'an. Ya'qub read it with *ta'* open and *jim* kasra throughout the Qur'an, taking *raja'a* as intransitive. The rest of the seven read *yurja'* with *ya'* and *jim* open, in the passive. Kharija from Nafi' read *yurja'* with *ya'* and *jim* open, taking *raja'a* as transitive. Both usages exist in the language of the Arabs, and the transitive use is a rare dialect. *Arja'a* is the quadriliteral form. Whoever reads with *ta'* does so because the plural noun is feminine, and whoever reads with *ya'* does so because the feminine is not real. The name of Allah is stated explicitly because it is more majestic, greater, and clearer, even though it was already mentioned in His statement: ﴿unless Allah comes to them﴾. It is also because it is in a new independent sentence, which is not included in what is awaited. It is rather an announcement that to Allah all matters return, and no one else, since He alone is the one who requites. It is also to remove the impression of what the kings of this world had, in handing over the affairs of people to them. So He informs that this will not belong to them in the Hereafter, but to Allah alone. Or it is to inform that they have returned to Him in the Hereafter, after He had given some of them as dominion to them in this world, and then all of them belonged to Him in the Hereafter. When the verb is passive, the omitted subject is either Allah, the Exalted, who returns them to Himself by annihilating this world and establishing the Resurrection, or those in charge of affairs. Since their own essences and attributes testify against them that they are created, accountable, and to be requited, they are returning their affairs to their Creator. It was said: or this is according to the manner of the Arabs in their saying: "So-and-so is self-conceited," and a man says to another: "Where is he being taken?" even when no one is taking him. The statement ends.

Its summary: the verb is made passive and there is no agent. This is an error, because a verb must have an agent conceived of. It is not necessary that the agent of the going be someone, nor that the agent of the self-admiration be someone. Rather, the agent is something else. The one who made him admire himself is his opinion and his belief in the beauty of his own self. So the meaning is that his opinion made him admire himself, and his opinion took him away. It is as if it were said: his opinion made him admire himself; where does your opinion or your intellect take you? Then the agent was omitted and the verb was made passive. It was said: in His statement ﴿and the matter is decided, and to Allah all matters are returned﴾ there are two kinds of the sciences of eloquence (*'ilm al-bayan*). The first is *ijaz* (conciseness) in His statement ﴿and the matter is decided﴾, since within these two words are included all the states of the servants from the time they were created until the Day of Calling and from that day until the judgment between the servants. The second is *ikhtisas* (specification) by His statement "and to Allah," so that day is specified for this, since Allah alone has disposal, judgment, and dominion on it. The statement ends.

Al-Sulami said: "And the matter is decided": they reached what was decided for them in eternity, of the two stations. Ja'far said: the reality of the matter and its prohibition was uncovered. Al-Qushayri said: the veil of the unseen was torn away from the clear decree.

(p-124) ﴿Are they waiting for anything but that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds, and the angels?﴾ *Hal* here is for negation. The meaning is: *ma yanzurun* (they are not waiting for anything). For this reason *illa* (except) follows it. When *hal* is used in the sense of negation and is followed by *illa*, it is very common in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech. Allah says: ﴿And do We requite any but the ungrateful?﴾ [Saba: 17]; ﴿Will any be destroyed but the wrongdoing people?﴾ [al-An'am: 47]. The poet says:

*Am I anything but of Ghaziyya? If it goes astray, I go astray, and if Ghaziyya is rightly guided, I am rightly guided.*

*Yanzurun* here means *yantazirun* (they wait). The Arabs say: *nazartu fulanan antaziruhu* (I waited for so-and-so), and the verb does not take a single object directly except with a preposition. Imru' al-Qays says:

*So if you two would give me a little time from the days, you would benefit me in the presence of Umm Jundab.*

The object of *yanzurun* is what follows *illa*, meaning: they wait for nothing except the coming of Allah. This is an *istithna' mufarragh* (exceptive construction in which the object of the verb is absent and must be supplied from what follows *illa*). It was said: *yanzurun* here is not from *nazar* (looking), which is the eye moving over the thing looked at, because if it were from *nazar* it would be followed by *ila* and would be connected to the face. Rather, it is from *intizar* (waiting). This was stated and concluded. This reasoning is worthless, because it is said that it is from *nazar*, which is the movement of the eye. It is followed by *ila*, but *ila* is omitted, and the sense is: "Are they waiting for anything except *ila* that Allah should come to them?" Omitting the preposition with *an* is a regular analogical rule when there is no ambiguity, and there is no ambiguity here, so *ila* was omitted. His statement "and it is connected to the face" refers to the verse ﴿Faces that day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22–23]. This is also not necessary, since looking has often been attributed to essences, as in ﴿Do they not look at the camels?﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 17] and ﴿Show me Yourself, that I may look at You﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]. The pronoun in *yanzurun* refers back to the wrongdoers, and this is an *iltifat* (shift from second-person address to third-person reference).

*Ityan* (coming) is, literally, movement from one place to another, and that is impossible for Allah, the Exalted. Abu Salih reported from Ibn Abbas that this is among the hidden matters which are not explained, and the early generation (*salaf*) always believed in this and similar matters, leaving the understanding of their meaning to the knowledge of the one who spoke them, who is Allah, the Exalted. The later scholars interpreted the *ityan* and its attribution in several ways:

First: it is a coming befitting Allah, the Exalted, without movement from place to place.

Second: it is an expression for His requital of them and His retribution, as He says: ﴿So Allah came at their structure from the foundations﴾ [al-Nahl: 26] and ﴿Allah came at them from where they did not expect﴾ [al-Hashr: 2].

Third: the object of the coming is omitted, meaning: that Allah should bring them what He promised them of reward and punishment. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Fourth: it is by omitting a noun modified by the phrase: the meaning is "the command of Allah," in the sense of what Allah will do to them, not the command whose opposite is prohibition. This is clarified by His statement after it: ﴿and the matter is decided﴾.

Fifth: His power. This was mentioned by al-Qadi Abu Ya'la, from Ahmad.

Sixth: *fi zulal* means *bi zulal* (with canopies), so *fi* carries the sense of *ba'* (with), as in the poet's words:

*Experts in striking the arteries and kidneys*

meaning *bi-ta'n* (by striking). This is because *khabir* (expert) is only followed by *ba'*, as the poet says:

*An expert in the ailments of women, a physician*

This was said by al-Zajjaj and others. The better view is that the meaning is "the command of Allah," since it is stated explicitly in His statement: ﴿Or the command of your Lord comes﴾ [al-Nahl: 33], and it means His might and punishment, because this verse came in the manner of threat and warning. It was also said: the omitted word is "the signs of Allah," so the coming of His signs is treated as His coming, to magnify their importance. This was said in *al-Muntakhab*. It is reported from Ibn Jarir that he said: He comes to them to call them to account, in the clouds, on His throne carried by eight angels. It was also said that the address is to the Jews, who are *mushabbiha* (anthropomorphists). What indicates that it is addressed to the Jews is His statement after it: ﴿Ask the Children of Israel﴾. If that is the case, the meaning is that they will not accept that except if Allah comes to them. So the verse is taken in its apparent sense, since the meaning is that a people wait for the coming of Allah. This does not indicate that they are right or wrong.

﴿in canopies of clouds﴾: discussion of this was already given under His statement: ﴿And We shaded you with clouds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 57]. It is impossible for the Holy Essence to be contained in a canopy. It was said: the intended meaning is to depict the greatness, occurrence, and severity of the Day of Resurrection, because nothing is more severe for sinners, and more terrifying, than the time of their gathering and the presence of the most skilled and most dignified judges to decide the dispute. This is then a figure of speech. If it is interpreted as meaning that the punishment of Allah comes to them in canopies of clouds, then that is because it is greater; or the evil comes to them from the direction of good, as in His statement: ﴿This is a cloud bringing us rain; rather, it is what you were hastening, a wind in which is painful punishment﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 24]. And because, if that is the Day of Resurrection, it is a sign of the greatest terrors of that day. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And the day the sky will be split open by clouds﴾ [al-Furqan: 25]. And because the cloud sends down drops that are not limited, so likewise the punishment is not restricted. It was also said: the punishment does not come in canopies, but the meaning is a comparison of the terrors to canopies of clouds, as He says: ﴿And when a wave covers them like canopies﴾ [Luqman: 32]. So the meaning is that the punishment of Allah comes to them with great terrors, like canopies of clouds.

They differed about this threat. Ibn Juraij said: it is a threat of what will happen in this world. Others said: rather, it is a threat of the Day of Resurrection.

Ubayy, Abdullah, Qatada, and al-Dahhak read *fi zilal* (with the plural *zilal*). Likewise Harun ibn Hatim reported from Abu Bakr, from Asim, here and in the two places in al-Zumar. It is the plural of *zullah*, like *qullah* and *qilal*, and this plural is not regular, unlike *zulal*, which is a regular plural. Or it is the plural of *zill* (shade), like *dill* and *dulal*. *Fi zulal* is connected to *ya'tiyahum* (comes to them). They allowed that it could be a circumstantial phrase (*hal*), and then it is connected to an omitted word. *Min al-ghamam* stands in the position of an adjective for *zulal*. They also allowed that it is connected to *ya'tiyahum*, meaning "from the direction of the clouds," so *min* is then for the starting point. In the first case, *min* is partitive.

Al-Hasan, Abu Haywa, and Abu Ja'far read *wal-malaikati* (and the angels) in the genitive, as a conjunction to *fi zulal*, or as a conjunction to *al-ghamam*. The preposition then varies in its implied form: in the first case the implied preposition is *fi* (in the angels), and in the second it is *min* (from the angels). The majority read it in the nominative as a conjunction to "Allah."

It was also said: in this sentence there is inversion. The coming is in canopies and is attached to the angels, so the meaning is: "Unless Allah and the angels come in canopies." So the coming attached to Allah, the Exalted, is only the coming itself. This is supported by the reading of Abdullah: "Unless Allah comes to them and the angels in canopies."

﴿and the matter is decided﴾: the meaning is that the requital occurred and those who disobeyed were punished. It was said: the matter of their destruction was completed and finished. It was said: the time of waiting ended, and the time of punishment came. It was said: the matter was finished for them, in regard to what they were promised, until the Day of Resurrection. It was said: the reckoning was finished and the punishment became binding. These statements are close in meaning.

﴿and the matter is decided﴾ is connected to His statement "ya'tiyahum" (comes to them). It is therefore the placing of the past tense in the position of the future, and the past tense is used for the future because it is like something already finished that has occurred. The meaning is: "and the matter will be decided." It is possible that this is a report from Allah, the Exalted, meaning: their affair was finished with what preceded in destiny. Then it is a conjunction of sentences, not something still awaited. Mu'adh ibn Jabal read *wa-qada'u al-amr* (and the judgment of the matter). Al-Zamakhshari said: it is in the nominative as a verbal noun, connected to the angels. Others said: it is in the genitive, with the long vowel, connected to the angels. It was said that *fi* in this case means *bi* (with): with canopies of clouds, with the angels, and with the judgment of the matter. Yahya ibn Ma'mar read *wa-qudiya al-umur* (and the matters were decided) in the plural, and the verb is in the passive, the agent being omitted because it is known. Also, if it were expressed and the verb were active, the noun would be repeated three times.

* *

﴿And to Allah all matters are returned﴾: Ibn Amir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read *turja'* (returned), with *ta'* open and *jim* kasra throughout the Qur'an. Ya'qub read it with *ta'* open and *jim* kasra throughout the Qur'an, taking *raja'a* as intransitive. The rest of the seven read *yurja'* with *ya'* and *jim* open, in the passive. Kharija from Nafi' read *yurja'* with *ya'* and *jim* open, taking *raja'a* as transitive. Both usages exist in the language of the Arabs, and the transitive use is a rare dialect. *Arja'a* is the quadriliteral form. Whoever reads with *ta'* does so because the plural noun is feminine, and whoever reads with *ya'* does so because the feminine is not real. The name of Allah is stated explicitly because it is more majestic, greater, and clearer, even though it was already mentioned in His statement: ﴿unless Allah comes to them﴾. It is also because it is in a new independent sentence, which is not included in what is awaited. It is rather an announcement that to Allah all matters return, and no one else, since He alone is the one who requites. It is also to remove the impression of what the kings of this world had, in handing over the affairs of people to them. So He informs that this will not belong to them in the Hereafter, but to Allah alone. Or it is to inform that they have returned to Him in the Hereafter, after He had given some of them as dominion to them in this world, and then all of them belonged to Him in the Hereafter. When the verb is passive, the omitted subject is either Allah, the Exalted, who returns them to Himself by annihilating this world and establishing the Resurrection, or those in charge of affairs. Since their own essences and attributes testify against them that they are created, accountable, and to be requited, they are returning their affairs to their Creator. It was said: or this is according to the manner of the Arabs in their saying: "So-and-so is self-conceited," and a man says to another: "Where is he being taken?" even when no one is taking him. The statement ends.

Its summary: the verb is made passive and there is no agent. This is an error, because a verb must have an agent conceived of. It is not necessary that the agent of the going be someone, nor that the agent of the self-admiration be someone. Rather, the agent is something else. The one who made him admire himself is his opinion and his belief in the beauty of his own self. So the meaning is that his opinion made him admire himself, and his opinion took him away. It is as if it were said: his opinion made him admire himself; where does your opinion or your intellect take you? Then the agent was omitted and the verb was made passive. It was said: in His statement ﴿and the matter is decided, and to Allah all matters are returned﴾ there are two kinds of the sciences of eloquence (*'ilm al-bayan*). The first is *ijaz* (conciseness) in His statement ﴿and the matter is decided﴾, since within these two words are included all the states of the servants from the time they were created until the Day of Calling and from that day until the judgment between the servants. The second is *ikhtisas* (specification) by His statement "and to Allah," so that day is specified for this, since Allah alone has disposal, judgment, and dominion on it. The statement ends.

Al-Sulami said: "And the matter is decided": they reached what was decided for them in eternity, of the two stations. Ja'far said: the reality of the matter and its prohibition was uncovered. Al-Qushayri said: the veil of the unseen was torn away from the clear decree.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 212 (part 1 of 4):**

﴿Ask the Children of Israel﴾ [al-Baqarah: 211]. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Zamakhshari said: "Or it is to everyone." Abu 'Amr, in a narration from Ibn 'Abbas, read *is'al* (اسْألْ). Some read *isal* (اسَلْ). Its origin is *is'al*, so they moved the vowel of the hamza onto the sin and deleted the hamza that is the 'ayn (middle radical). The hamza of wasl (the connecting hamza) was not deleted, because the vowel on the sin was not considered, since it was incidental, as they said *al-hamar* (الَحْمَرَ) for *al-ahmar* (الأحْمَرِ).

The majority read *sal* (سَلْ), which allows two possibilities. The first is that its origin is *is'al*. When he moved the vowel and deleted the hamza, he considered the vowel, so he deleted the hamza because the letter after it was vowelled. The second possibility is that it follows the dialect of those who derive the root from (sin, waw, lam), saying *sa'ala yas'alu*, so he said *sal*, as one says *khaf* (from *khafa*). In such a case no connecting hamza is needed. The 'ayn of the word was deleted because it came together with the silent lam, and for this reason it returns when the first radical (fa') is vowelled, as in *khafa*, *khafu*, *khafi*.

When the previous verse was revealed, *﴿Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies﴾* [al-Baqarah: 210], the meaning of which was a delay in their joining Islam, and that they await only a great sign that compels them to enter Islam, this command came: asking them about the great signs that came to them, which did not benefit them. Thus their not becoming Muslims is linked to their obstinacy and their persistence in their stubbornness. This question is not a question about something unknown, since He knows that Allah gave the Children of Israel clear signs. It is a question about something known, so it is a reproach, a rebuke, and an affirmation to them of what Allah gave them of clear signs, and that these did not benefit them. This is confirmed by His saying afterwards: *﴿And whoever substitutes the favour of Allah after it has come to him﴾* [al-Baqarah: 211].

In this question there is also reassurance and increase, as He, the Exalted, says: *﴿And all We relate to you of the news of the messengers is that by which We strengthen your heart﴾* [Hud: 120]. Or it is an increase in the certainty of the believer. So the address in wording is to him (ﷺ), but the intended audience is his community. Or it is to inform the People of the Book that this statement is from Allah, because the Prophet (ﷺ) and his people knew nothing of the stories of the Children of Israel, nor of the signs that were among them, before Allah revealed that in His Book.

*(Children of Israel)*: whoever was present among them, or whoever believed in him among them, or their scholars, or their prophets. These are four opinions.

*Kam* (كَمْ, "how many") is in the accusative position as a second object of *ataynahum* (آتَيْناهم, "We gave them"), according to the view of the majority. Or it is a first object according to the view of al-Suhayli, as previously mentioned. Ibn 'Atiyya permitted it to be in the accusative position by means of a hidden verb after it, explained by what follows, and he regarded this as falling under *al-ishtighal* (الِاشْتِغال, "the verb being occupied with a pronoun"). He said: "*Kam* is in the accusative position either by a hidden verb after it, because it has precedence in the sentence, its estimate being: how many did We give them, or by their coming," and he finished.

This is not permissible if his saying *min ayah* (مِن آيَةٍ, "of a sign") is a specifier (*tamyiz*, the noun clarifying a number or quantity) for *kam*. The verb that explains this hidden verb did not govern the pronoun of the first noun, which is in the accusative by the hidden verb, nor its causal relation. If that is the case, it is not permissible for it to be of the category of *al-ishtighal*. An analogy is that one may say *zaydan darabtu* (زَيْدًا ضَرَبْتُ, "Zayd, I struck"), making *zaydan* an object of a hidden verb explained by what follows, the estimate being: *zaydan darabtu darabtu* ("Zayd, I struck, I struck"). Likewise: *al-dirham a'tayta zaydan* (الدِّرْهَمَ أعْطَيْتُ زَيْدًا, "the dirham, I gave Zayd"). But we do not know anyone who held what he held. Rather, the texts of the grammarians, from Sibawayh onwards, state that such a structure is a fronted object governed by the verb after it, even when the specifier of *kam* is omitted.

*Kam* was used to refer to a people or a group, so the estimate is: "how many groups did We give them," and this is permissible, since in the sentence explaining that hidden verb there is a pronoun referring back to *kam*. Ibn 'Atiyya and others also permitted *kam* to be in the nominative position as a subject (*mubtada'*, the topic of a nominal sentence), with the clause *ataynahum* as the predicate (*khabar*), and the returning pronoun omitted. The estimate would be: *ataynahumuhu* or *ataynahumuha*. This is not permissible according to the Basrans except in poetry, or in an anomalous reading of the Qur'an, such as the reading of whoever read *﴿Do they seek the judgement of the Jahiliyyah?﴾* [al-Ma'idah: 50] with *al-hukm* in the nominative. Ibn Malik said: "If the subject is other than *kull* (كُلّ, "all"), and the pronoun is a direct object, then according to the Kufans it is not permissible to omit it while keeping the nominative, except in cases of necessity. The Basrans permit it in ordinary usage, but consider it weak," and he finished. If it is only permitted in necessity, or is weak, what motive is there to permit it in the Qur'an, when it can be taken otherwise and is more preferable, namely that it is in the accusative position as we have established?

*Kam* here is interrogative in form, but its meaning is affirmation (*taqrir*), not a true question. The interrogative may leave its real meaning when something precedes it that removes it, as in your saying: *sawa'un 'alayka aqama Zayd am qa'ada* (سَواءٌ عَلَيْكَ أقامَ زَيْدٌ أمْ قَعَدَ, "it is all the same to you whether Zayd stood or sat"), *wa-ma ubali aqama Zayd am qa'ada* (وما أُبالِي أقامَ زَيْدٌ أمْ قَعَدَ, "I do not care whether Zayd stood or sat"), *wa-qad 'alimtu azaydun muntaliqun aw 'amrun* (وقَدْ عَلِمْتُ أزَيْدٌ مُنْطَلِقٌ أوْ عَمْرٌو, "I know whether Zayd is leaving or 'Amr"), and *wa-ma adri aqarib am ba'id* (وما أدْرِي أقَرِيبٌ أمْ بَعِيدٌ, "I do not know whether it is near or far"). All of these have the form of a question and the structure and rules of interrogatives, but they are not true questions.

This clause, *﴿how many We gave them﴾*, is in the position of the second object of *sal* (سَلْ, "ask"), because *sa'ala* (سَألَ, "to ask") takes two objects: one directly, and the other by a preposition, either *'an* (عَنْ, "about") or *ba'* (الباء, "with"). Both have been combined in poetry, as in:

*fa-asbahna la yas'alnahu 'an bi-ma bihi* (فَأصْبَحْنَ لا يَسْألْنَهُ عَنْ بِما بِهِ)
"So they no longer asked him about what was with him."

Here *sa'ala* is suspended (*mu'allaqah*) before the interrogative clause. It governs the meaning but not the wording, because an interrogative is not governed by what precedes it except by a preposition. They said: "*Sal* is suspended even though it is not one of the verbs of the heart (verbs of knowing), because asking is a cause of knowledge, so the cause is treated as the effect in this regard." Allah says: *﴿Ask them which of them will stand surety for that﴾* [al-Qalam: 40]. The poet said:

*sa'il Bani Asad: ma hadhihi as-sawt* (سائِلْ بَنِي أسَدٍ: ما هَذِهِ الصَّوْتُ)
"Ask the Banu Asad: what is this voice?"

And he said:

*wa-as'al bi-Masqalata al-Bikri ma fa'ala* (واسْألْ بِمَصْقَلَةَ البِكْرِيِّ ما فَعَلا)
"And ask Masqalah al-Bakri what he did."

Al-Zamakhshari permitted *kam* here to be declarative (*khabariyyah*, not interrogative), saying: "If you say, is *kam* interrogative or declarative? I say it allows both, and the meaning of interrogation in it is an estimate." This is the end of his words. It is not a good view, because making it declarative separates the clause in which it occurs from the question. The meaning becomes: "Ask the Children of Israel," and the subject of the question is not mentioned. Then he says: "Many of the signs We gave them," so this speech becomes detached from what precedes it, because the clause *kam ataynahum* becomes a pure statement to which *sal* is not connected. Yet you see that the meaning of the speech and the focus of the question rest on this clause. This is only so in the interrogative form. To establish the declarative form one needs to assume an omission, namely the second object of *sal*, and the meaning would be: "Ask the Children of Israel about the signs which We gave them," and then He informs that many of the signs were given to them.

*(min ayah)* (مِن آيَةٍ, "of a sign") is a specifier of *kam*. It is permissible for *min* to enter upon the specifier of both the interrogative and the declarative, whether it directly follows or is separated from it. Separation by a clause, by an adverbial phrase, or by a prepositional phrase is permissible, as we established in grammar. Ibn 'Atiyya permitted *min ayah* to be a second object of *ataynahum*, on the estimate previously stated, that *kam* is in the accusative by a hidden verb explained by *ataynahum*, and on the estimate we established, that *kam* is a reference to a people or group whose specifier is omitted for understanding the meaning. If that is the case, then if *kam* is declarative, *min ayah* cannot be a second object, because the addition of *min* is not permitted in affirmative sentences according to the Basrans other than al-Akhfash. If *kam* is interrogative, then one may say that this is permissible because the interrogative extends to what precedes it. But this is far-fetched, because the focus of the interrogative is the first object, not the second. So if you say, *kam min dirham a'taytuhu min rajul* (كَمْ مِن دِرْهَمٍ أعْطَيْتُهُ مِن رَجُلٍ, "how many dirhams did I give him from a man"), with the addition of *min* in *min rajul*, there would be a problem. We have thoroughly discussed the addition of *min* in our book *Manhaj al-Salik* (مَنهَجِ السّالِكِ).

*The clear signs* (الآياتُ البَيِّناتُ) are: what the Torah and the Gospel contained concerning the description of the Prophet (ﷺ), the confirmation of his prophethood, and the verification of what he brought. Or they are the miracles of Musa (peace be upon our Prophet and upon him), such as the staff, the white hand, and the splitting of the sea. Or they are the Qur'an, in which Allah related the stories of the past nations as they occurred, through one who had not studied the books or the scholars, and who neither wrote nor improvised. Or they are the miracles of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), such as the glorification of the pebbles, the water flowing from between his fingers, the splitting of the moon, and the greeting of the stone. These are four opinions. They estimated a hidden word after *min ayah bayyinah* (مِن آيَةٍ بَيِّنَةٍ, "of a clear sign"). Some estimated: *fa-kadhdhabu biha* (فَكَذَّبُوا بِها, "so they denied them"), and some: *fa-baddalu-ha* (فَبَدَّلُوها, "so they substituted them").

*﴿And whoever substitutes the favour of Allah﴾* [al-Baqarah: 211]. The favour of Allah (*ni'mat Allah*, نِعْمَةُ اللَّهِ) is: the clear proofs that indicate his (ﷺ) matter, with which one substitutes comparison and interpretations. Or it is what came in the Book of Allah describing him (ﷺ), with which one substitutes the description of the Antichrist (al-Dajjal). Or it is the acknowledgement of his prophethood, with which one substitutes denial of it. Or it is the books of Allah revealed to Musa and Isa (peace be upon our Prophet and upon them both), with which one substitutes something other than their rulings, such as the verse of stoning and the like. Or it is Islam, as al-Tabari said. Or it is the thankfulness for the favour, with which one substitutes disbelief. Or it is His signs, which are the greatest favour from Allah, because they are the means of guidance and salvation from error. Their substitution of them is that Allah manifested them so that they would be means of their guidance, but they made them means of their misguidance, as in His saying: *﴿So it increased them in uncleanness to their uncleanness﴾* [al-Tawbah: 125]. This is what al-Zamakhshari said. These are seven opinions.

The wording *man yubaddil* (مَن يُبَدِّلْ, "whoever substitutes") is general, and it is a conditional. So there is included with the Children of Israel every substituter of a favour, such as the disbelieving Quraysh and others. The sending of Muhammad (ﷺ) is a favour to them, and they substituted disbelief for thankfulness for it and its acceptance.

*﴿After it has come to him﴾* [al-Baqarah: 211], that is: after it was bestowed upon him, and he was able to accept it, and after he knew it. This is as in His saying: *﴿Then they distort it after they had understood it﴾* [al-Baqarah: 75]. He used the word *min* (مِن, "after") to indicate the starting point, and that the substitution follows immediately upon *after it has come to him*. In His saying *﴿After it has come to him﴾*, there is emphasis, because the possibility of substitution depends on having reached it.

It was read *wa-man yubdil* (ومَن يُبْدِلْ) with the lightened form. *Yubdil* requires two objects: the substituted (*mubdal*) and the substitute (*mubdal lahu*). The one to which the verb reaches by a preposition is the *mubdal*, and the one to which it reaches directly is the *badal* (substitute). The preposition may be omitted when the meaning is understood. This was discussed previously in His saying: *﴿So those who did wrong substituted﴾* [al-Baqarah: 59]. Given this, the single object here is omitted, which is the substitute. The best estimate is similar to what is said in His saying: *﴿Have you not seen those who substituted the favour of Allah with disbelief?﴾* [Ibrahim: 28]. Here *kufran* (كُفْرًا, "disbelief") is the substitute, and *ni'mat Allah* is the substituted, which originally would be reached by a preposition. So the estimate is: *wa-man yubaddil ni'mat Allah kufran*. The omission of the single object and of the preposition is permitted because the meaning is understood. Also, the order of the response to the condition after what precedes it indicates this, because it is consequent upon the estimate that the favour is the substitute and disbelief is the substituted. The response is: *﴿Indeed, Allah is severe in punishment﴾* [al-Baqarah: 211], a statement containing a warning.

Among the omissions of the preposition for the sake of meaning is His saying: *﴿Those, Allah will change their bad deeds into good deeds﴾* [al-Furqan: 70]. The meaning is: "for their bad deeds" (*bi-sayyi'atihim*), and it cannot be that the estimate is: "their bad deeds for good deeds," so that the bad deeds would be the substitute and the good deeds the substituted, because that would not follow from His saying: *﴿except for those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds﴾* [Maryam: 60].

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 212 (part 2 of 4):

﴿فَإنَّ اللَّهَ شَدِيدُ العِقابِ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 211] is a statement that includes the threat of punishment for those who alter the blessing of God. If it is the response of the conditional clause (jawab al-shart), then it is necessary to posit a returning pronoun (ʿaʾid) in the sentence referring back to the conditional particle, its estimated form being: "Indeed God is severe in punishment for him." Or the alif and lam may serve as a substitute for the pronoun according to the school of the Kufans (al-Kufiyyun), so that it dispenses with the linking element, since they take the place of the pronoun. The preferable view is that the response is omitted, because what follows it indicates it, the estimated form being: "He punishes him." ʿAbd al-Qahir said in the book Dala'il al-I'jaz: "Leaving out this implied element is preferable," meaning by the implied element "severe in punishment for him," because the purpose of the verse is intimidation, by describing him as being severe in punishment, without attention to his being severe in punishment for this reason. For this reason punishment was called ʿiqab, because it follows (yaʿqubu) the crime. Some of those who compiled tafsir mentioned that this verse, ﴿Ask the Children of Israel﴾ [al-Baqarah: 211], is placed later in recitation but earlier in meaning, and the address is to the Prophet ﷺ. He said: The estimated form is: "If you slip..." up to the end of the verse, "Ask, O Muhammad, the Children of Israel how many clear signs We gave them, yet they did not heed them nor submit to them. Do they await only that God should come to them?" That is, they will not believe until God comes to them. End of his words. But there is no need to claim anterior and posterior arrangement; rather this verse, in its own order, has its parts bound together, tightly structured, falling in its proper places. The meaning is: they were commanded to enter Islam, then they were informed that whoever slips, God the Mighty, who is not overcome, the Wise, who places things in their proper places, will requite him. Then it was said: they await in their faith only the appearance of clear signs, out of obstinacy on their part, although the signs had come to them. Then He consoled His Prophet ﷺ regarding their slowness to believe despite the signs he had brought them, with His saying: ﴿Ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We gave them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 211], yet they did not believe in them but altered and changed them. Then He threatened whoever alters the blessing of God with severe punishment. You see these meanings harmonious and ordered in a miraculous arrangement, with eloquent and concise wording. So the claim of anterior and posterior arrangement, specific to the necessities of poetry and to the composition of those of limited capacity, is far removed from the speech of the One, the Subduer.

﴿زُيِّنَ لِلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا الحَياةُ الدُّنْيا﴾ [al-Baqarah: 212]. It was revealed concerning Abu Jahl and his companions, who used to indulge in what God had spread out for them, deny the Hereafter, and mock the poor believers, such as ʿAmmar, Suhayb, Abu ʿUbayda, Salim, ʿAmir ibn Fuhayra, Khabbab, and Bilal, saying: "If our Prophet were truly a prophet, our nobles would follow him." This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, in the narration of al-Kalbi from Abu Salih from him. Muqatil said: it was about ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions, who used to indulge and mock the weak believers, saying: "Look at these whom Muhammad claims he will prevail through." ʿAta' said: it was about the scholars of the Jews of Banu Qurayza, al-Nadir, and Qaynuqaʿ, who mocked the poor emigrants, so God promised them that He would give them the wealth of Banu Qurayza and al-Nadir without fighting, the easiest and least troublesome thing. The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when He mentioned that clear signs from God had come to the Children of Israel and that they altered them, He informed that the cause of that alteration was inclining to this world, delighting in it, its adornment for them, and their mockery of the believers. Therefore the Children of Israel have the greatest share of this verse, for they used to sell the signs of God for a small price, lie against the Book of God, writing whatever they wished in order to obtain a base share of the shares of this world, and say: "This is from God."

The reading of the majority is "zuyyina" with the verb in the passive, and there is no need to mark the feminine sign because of the intervening word and because the feminine here is not of true feminine gender. Ibn Abi ʿAbla read "zuyyinat" with a tāʾ, and its justification is clear: the subject of the verb is feminine, and the agent is omitted because its meaning is understood, namely God Most High. This is supported by the reading of Mujahid, Humayd ibn Qays, and Abu Haywa: "zayyana," in the active voice, whose agent is a pronoun referring to God Most High, since before it stands: ﴿Indeed God is severe in punishment﴾ [al-Baqarah: 211]. His adorning it for them is through what He placed in their natures of love for it, so that inclination and desire for it arise in their souls, or through the desires which He created in them. To this He alluded with His saying: ﴿Beautified for people is the love of desires﴾ [Al ʿImran: 14], and so on. He perfected, made excellent, and beautified it among His creatures, so its radiance pleased them, its appeal won their hearts, and they inclined to it entirely, giving it more desire than it deserves.

Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, when wealth was brought to him, said: "O God, we cannot do otherwise than rejoice in what You have adorned for us." Al-Zamakhshari said: It is possible that God adorned it for them by forsaking them until they found it good and loved it, or that the granting of respite to the one adorned constitutes an adornment. This is supported by the reading of one who read: "zayyana li-l-ladhina kafaru al-hayata al-dunya" in the active voice. End of his words. This is in accordance with the doctrine of the Mu'tazila that God Most High does not create evil, but that is from the creation of the servant; therefore they interpreted the adornment as forsaking or as granting respite. It was also said: the adorner is Satan, and his adornment is by beautifying what is ugly in the Law and making ugly what is good in the Law. The difference between the two adornments: God's adornment is through what He composed and placed in the disposition, while Satan's adornment is through reminding them of what they had neglected, and beautifying it for them by his whisperings. It was also said: the adorner is their own souls, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed the soul commands to evil﴾ [Yusuf: 53], ﴿so his soul facilitated for him the killing of his brother﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 30], ﴿and thus my soul enticed me﴾ [Ta-Ha: 96]. It was also said: their partners from among the jinn and mankind, as He said: ﴿And thus did many of the polytheists have their partners make attractive to them﴾ [al-An'am: 137], and He said: ﴿Satans of mankind and jinn, inspiring one another﴾ [al-An'am: 112]. It was also said: the one adorned is this worldly life, as He said: ﴿The life of this world is only play and amusement and adornment﴾ [al-Hadid: 20]. It was also said: the one adorned is the whole collection. In this statement is an informing of the believers about the feebleness of the minds of the disbelievers, in that they preferred the perishing over the enduring.

﴿ويَسْخَرُونَ مِنَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾ [al-Baqarah: 212]. The pronoun refers to those who disbelieved, whose identity has been mentioned, and likewise the discussion of "those who believed" regarding the occasion of revelation has preceded. The meaning of yaskharun is: they mock, and that is because of their poverty, or because they follow the Messenger of God ﷺ, or because they accuse them of believing the Messenger of God ﷺ, or because of their weakness and small number. Four opinions.

This verbal sentence is conjoined to the verbal sentence in His saying "zuyyina," and it is not considered here as conjoining a verb to a verb, for that would require unity of time, though it does not require unity of form. The first is introduced by the past verb because it is a settled matter, namely the composition of their natures upon love of this world, so it is not a renewed matter. The second is introduced by the present verb because it is a state that renews itself at every time. It was also said: it is by way of resumption, that is, the present verb, and the meaning of resumption is that it stands with them presupposing the estimate "and they mock," so it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and it becomes a conjoining of a nominal sentence to a verbal sentence.

﴿والَّذِينَ اتَّقَوْا فَوْقَهم يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 212]. Fawqa is an adverb of place. It was said: it remains in its own literal sense of spatial locative, since the believers are in ʿIlliyyin in the heaven, and the disbelievers are in Sijjin in the earth. It was also said: the sense of "above" is metaphorical, either with respect to the two blessings: the blessing of the believers in Paradise and the blessing of the disbelievers in this world; or with respect to the proofs of the believers and the doubts of the disbelievers, since proofs are established and doubts vanish; or with respect to what the disbelievers supposed when they said: if there is a return, we shall have a share in it; or with respect to the believers' mockery of them in the Hereafter and the disbelievers' mockery of the believers in this world, so they will be exalted over them, lording it over them and laughing at them, just as those used to lord it over the believers and laugh at them in this world; or with respect to the height of their state, for they are in honor while the disbelievers are in humiliation. This sentence has been introduced with His saying "those who feared God," in order to make clear that the greatest happiness is attained only by the believing God-fearing person, and to move the believer to piety, and so that the unease of repetition would be removed had it been "those who believed," since "those who believed" already precedes it. The accusative of "the Day of Resurrection" is as an adverbial of time, and the governing element in it is the governing element in the adverb that falls as the predicate, that is: they will be, they, on the Day of Resurrection.

When they understood from "fawqa" that it implies a superiority between the one about whom it is reported and the one to whom it is attached, as when you say: "Zayd is above ʿAmr in rank," as if it were said: "Zayd is higher than ʿAmr in rank," they needed to interpret "ʿali" and "aʿla minhu." Ibn ʿAtiyya said: all this is among the stretched interpretations, a preservation of the school of Sibawayh and al-Khalil, that superiority only occurs in what has a share (shirka), while the Kufans permit it where there is no sharing. End of his words.

What he related from Sibawayh and al-Khalil, we do not know; rather the point of disagreement is the elative form (af'al al-tafdil). The Basrans prohibit "Zayd is the best of his brothers," while the Kufans permit it. As for whether that applies to "fawqa," we do not know it; but because it was supposed that it is synonymous with "aʿla," and "aʿla" is an elative, he transferred the disagreement to it. What we say is that "fawqa" does not imply sharing in superiority; it only indicates absolute height. When it is attached to something, it does not necessarily follow that what it is attached to has height. Just as its opposite "taht" does not indicate sharing in lowness, but only indicates its absolute sense, and we do not say that it is synonymous with "asfal," because "asfal" is an elative, which is shown by its use with "min," as in His saying: "The caravan is lower than you (asfala minkum)," just as "aʿla" is likewise. Once this is established, the meaning, and God knows best, is: those who feared God will be above them on the Day of Resurrection, and this does not indicate that the disbelievers are on a height; rather the meaning is that elevation on the Day of Resurrection belongs only to the God-fearing, and others are beneath, the reverse of their state in this world, where they used to mock them.

[p. 131] ﴿And Allah provides for whom He wills without reckoning.﴾ The connection of this clause with what precedes it, namely the superiority of the righteous on the Day of Resurrection, indicates that it relates to them. It has been said that this provision is in the Hereafter, which is the reward the believer receives there, and the meaning of His words "without reckoning" is "without end," since what has no end is beyond reckoning. Or the meaning may be that part of it is reward and part of it is pure grace, so it is "without reckoning." It has also been said that this provision is in this world, and that it refers to the believers, who were mocked, taking possession of the wealth of Banu Qurayza and al-Nadir, which came to them without reckoning, rather they obtained it with the easiest and least effort. This was said by Ibn Abbas, and al-Qaffal said something similar. He said: Allah did this to them by giving them what He bestowed from the wealth of the chiefs of Quraysh and the leaders of the Jews, and by what was conquered after his death at the hands of his Companions. Others have said something to the effect that it is connected to the disbelievers. al-Zamakhshari said: He means that He expands provision for whoever wisdom requires to be expanded for, as He expanded it for Qarun and others. So this expansion upon you is from Allah for the sake of the wisdom in it, and that wisdom is that He is leading you on gradually through blessings. Had it been an honour, His friends the believers would have had a better claim to it than you. End of his words. He mentioned no other opinion regarding the meaning of this clause.

Ibn Atiyya said: It is possible that the meaning is: Allah provides for these disbelievers in this world, so do not consider that great, and do not measure the Hereafter by it, for provision is not according to the measure of disbelief and faith. Rather, this person's deeds are reckoned and that person's deeds are reckoned, and each is provided according to that reckoning. Rather, provision is without reckoning of deeds, while the recompense for deeds is a matter of reckoning and repayment, since the parts of the recompense correspond to the parts of the act for which one is recompensed. So the meaning is: even if the believer is not provided for in this world, he is above the disbeliever on the Day of Resurrection. End of his words.

What appears to be correct is that provision is not restricted to either of the two groups. Rather, when He mentioned their two conditions, namely the mockery of the disbelievers toward them in this world, because of what they were given of power in it, leadership, and abundance, and the elevation of the believers over them in the Hereafter, because of what they were given of success and of being alone in everlasting bliss, He made clear that what He does of that and provides for them is due to His preceding will, and that no one calls Him to account, nor does He call Himself to account for what He gives, because that is only for one who fears the depletion of what he possesses.

They have said regarding the authentic hadith: "The right hand of Allah is full; nothing diminishes it, however much He spends since He created the heavens and the earth, for that has not diminished anything of what is with Him." The object of yashā' (He wills) is omitted; the estimated meaning is: whom He wills to provide for. This is indicated by what precedes it. The phrase bi-ghayri ḥisāb (without reckoning) precedes three things to which it may be attached: the verb, the subject, and the first object, which is man (whom). If it is attached to the verb, it is a qualifier of the verbal noun (maṣdar), and if it is attached to the subject, it is a qualifier of the subject, or if it is attached to the object, it is a qualifier of the object. When it is attached to the verb, the meaning is: He provides for whom He wills with provision that is not reckoned, i.e., not one that has a reckoning. By reckoning is meant counting, so it cannot be enumerated or limited because of its abundance. Or by it is meant the reckoning in the Hereafter, i.e., provision upon which no reckoning will fall in the Hereafter. In this case, the bā' (bā') is a redundant particle (zā'idah).

When it is attached to the subject, it occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). The meaning is: Allah provides without reckoning Him for it, i.e., He is generous in His giving and does not reckon it, or not counting what He gives. This would be a metaphor for scarcity and restriction. In that case, ḥisāb is a verbal noun used in place of the active participle of ḥāsaba, or of the active participle of ḥasiba, and the bā' is redundant in the circumstantial clause. It has been said that the bā' is redundant in a negated circumstantial clause, but this circumstantial clause was not preceded by a negation. Among what has been said that it is redundant in a negated circumstantial clause is the words of the poet:

"The mounts did not return disappointed, / Hakim ibn al-Musayyib is their destination."

That is: they did not return disappointed. It is also possible in this case that ḥisāb is a verbal noun used in place of the passive participle, i.e., not reckoned for what He gives, exalted is He; that is, no one calls Allah to account for what He grants. So His giving is abundant without any limit. When it is attached to man, which is the first object of yarzuq (provides), the meaning is that the one provided for is not called to account for what Allah provides for him. This also becomes a circumstantial clause from him, and the reckoning, which is the verbal noun, falls on the object that is the passive participle of ḥāsaba, or on the object from ḥasiba, i.e., what he is provided with is not counted against him. Or by omitting a genitive, the meaning is: not possessing a reckoning, and by reckoning is meant being called to account or counting. The bā' is also redundant in this circumstantial clause. It is also possible in this case that the meaning is: He is provided for from where he does not expect, i.e., from where he does not suppose or imagine that provision would come to him, as He said: ﴿And He provides for him from where he does not expect﴾ [al-Talaq: 3]. So this is also a circumstantial clause, i.e., not expecting it. All these interpretations are forced, and they include the redundancy of the bā'. The better view is that the bā' indicates accompaniment, which is what is called the bā' of circumstance (bā' al-ḥāl). On this view it may apply to the verbal noun, the subject, or the object, and ḥisāb is meant as calling to account or counting, i.e., He provides for whom He wills and there is no reckoning for the provision, or: and there is no reckoning for the provider, or: and there is no reckoning for the one provided.

That the bā' has a meaning is better than its being redundant, and that the verbal noun remains a verbal noun is better than its being a metaphor for an active or passive participle, and its being attached to something else is better than making it attached to a deleted possessor. There is no contradiction between His words ﴿a recompense from your Lord, a gift reckoned﴾ [al-Naba': 36], i.e., sufficient, from aḥsabanī kadhā, meaning "it sufficed me," and "without reckoning," which means counting or calling to account. Or, if they have the same meaning, the difference is according to the attributes of provision and gift in the Hereafter: so "without reckoning" is in pure grace, and "a gift reckoned" is in the recompense corresponding to the deed. Or the difference is according to their two ends: "without reckoning" is in this world, since He provides for the disbeliever and the believer and does not call the recipients to account for it, while in the Hereafter He does reckon. Or the difference is according to the one who performs it: "without the reckoning of Allah," which is a circumstantial clause from Him, i.e., He provides and does not reckon it against them, or does not count it against them; and "reckoned" is an attribute of the gift. Thus the difference is in terms of who performs it, and the apparent contradiction disappears.

These noble verses contain, at the end of the rulings and acts of the Hajj, the command to remember Allah during numbered days, i.e., a few days. The remembrance indicates the stoning of the pillars (al-ramy), even though it is not stated explicitly, because the remembrance commanded during those days is at the stoning. The command indicates its legislation on days, and it is plural. Then He granted a concession for hastening (leaving early) at the end of two of those days, so the remembrance specific to the third day lapses. He informed that the state of the one who hastens and the one who delays is equal in the absence of sin, although the state of the one who delays is better. Some of the people of the pre-Islamic period believed that whoever hastened had sinned, and some believed that whoever delayed had sinned. Therefore He informed that Allah lifted sin from both of them, since hastening and delaying are among the things Allah has legislated. Then He informed that the lifting of sin only applies to those who fear Allah. Then He commanded taqwa (God-consciousness) and repeated the command to it during the Hajj. Then He mentioned what moves one to adopt taqwa, which is that He is severe in punishment toward those who do not fear Him. Then, since taqwa is divided into those who show it with their tongues while their hearts conceal its opposite, and those whose inner and outer selves are equal in taqwa, Allah divided this into two categories, saying: ﴿And among people is one whose speech in the life of this world pleases you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 204], i.e., it delights you and his words are pleasing. He beautifies what he brings of agreement and obedience outwardly. Then he is not content with what he has adorned and polished of his pleasant speech until he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart of it. So he swears by Allah that his inner self is like his outward self. When he disputes, he is extremely contentious, and when he leaves your presence he roams the land. Then He mentioned the reason for his striving, that it is for corruption in general, and to destroy the crops and the offspring, which are the foundations of existence. Then He informed that He does not love corruption, so this one who turns away and strives in the land does what Allah does not love and is not pleased with. Then He mentioned that, because of the severity of his obstinacy in hypocrisy, when he is commanded to fear Allah, pride and anger overcome him with sin, i.e., accompanied by sin, so his anger is not for Allah, but for other than Allah, and therefore sin accompanies him.

Then He mentioned the outcome of the condition of this one, who is deceived by other than Allah, namely Hell. It is sufficient for him, and it will change his honour after his might into humiliation. Then Allah dispraised what he prepared for himself of Hell, and "wretched" is the utmost dispraise. Then He mentioned the category opposite to this one, namely the one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah, and this noble description suffices, since it indicates that he encompasses all acts of obedience and submission, for he became a servant of Allah, found wherever Allah is pleased. Then He mentioned that whoever is in this position, Allah shows him compassion (ra'fah) and mercy (raḥmah). Allah's compassion for him includes kindness toward him and benefaction to him in all kinds of benefaction. He mentioned ra'fah, which is said to be more tender than raḥmah.

Then He called the believers with His words: "O you who have believed," and commanded them to enter into Islam. He followed it with the prohibition, because the command is harder than the prohibition, since the command is an act while the prohibition is an abstention. It is also because of its proximity to His words: ﴿And among people is one who sells himself﴾ [al-Baqarah: 207], so it became like His words: ﴿On the Day when some faces will be whitened and some faces will be blackened; as for those whose faces are blackened﴾ [Al 'Imran: 106]. When He forbade them to follow the steps of Satan, which is committing the disobedience of Allah, He informed that if they slip after the clear proofs had come to them, proofs that are bright and that should not be accompanied by slipping, because in their clarification there is what removes doubt, then know that Allah is Mighty, not overcome, Wise, placing things in their proper places. So He recompenses slipping after the verses have become clear, which demand firmness in obedience, with what is appropriate to that slipping. By His might He indicates power, and by His wisdom He indicates the recompense of the disobedient and the obedient: ﴿That He may recompense those who did evil according to what they did and recompense those who did good with the best﴾ [al-Najm: 31].

Then Allah turned away from addressing them and spoke of them in the manner of absent persons, consoling His Messenger regarding their slowness in entering Islam. He said: ﴿They are not waiting except for Allah to come to them in the shadows of the clouds, and the angels, and the matter would be decided﴾ [al-Baqarah: 210] … rather: they await nothing except the establishment of the Hour, the Day of Allah's judgment between the servants, the decree of the matter, and the return of all affairs to Him. There the fruit of what they earned against themselves will appear, as came in the hadith: "On the Day of Resurrection Allah will come to them in such and such a form," according to what befits His sanctity above all that resembles created beings, and we declare Him far above what is impossible for Him of the marks of createdness and the attributes of deficiency.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 212 (part 4 of 4):

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Ask the Children of Israel﴾ [al-Baqarah: 211], alerting that the habit of those to whom the prophets were sent, and to whom the miracles became manifest, is turning away from that, not accepting faith, and that they reverse the thing from its required implication, so they deny the signs that came indicating the truth. Then He, exalted is He, informed that whoever changes the blessing of Allah, He will punish him with the most severe punishment; He countered the blessing of Allah, which is the place of thankfulness, with disbelief. Then He, exalted is He, mentioned the factor that drives them to alter the blessings of Allah, which is the adornment of the worldly life, so they desired the perishable and renounced the lasting, preferring the immediate over the deferred. Then He mentioned along with that their mockery of the believers, in that which is imagined in the description of faith and in the desire for what is with Allah, exalted is He. He mentioned that they will be the superior ones on the Day of Resurrection, and by that He indicated that those are the inferior ones. Then He mentioned that He provides for the believers, who are those He loves, without reckoning, indicating the vastness of provision and the absence of restriction and measuring. He repeated their mention with the wording "whom He wills," alerting to His willing for them, His love for them, and their being singled out for Him; for if He had said, "And Allah provides for them without reckoning," the meaning of the will, which is the volition, would have been lost.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 213 (part 1 of 3):**

﴿Mankind was one community.
