Then God sent the prophets as bearers of good tidings and warners, and sent down with them the Book with truth, to judge between people concerning what they differed about. None differed about it except those who had been given it, after clear proofs had come to them, out of rebellion among themselves. So God guided those who believed to the truth concerning what they had differed about, by His permission. And God guides whom He wills to a straight path.﴾ ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise without there having come to you the like of what came to those who passed away before you? Misfortune and hardship touched them, and they were shaken, until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, "When is the help of God?" Unquestionably, the help of God is near.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214] ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: "Whatever good you spend is for parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer. And whatever good you do, God is knowing of it."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 215] ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you, while it is hateful to you. But perhaps you hate a thing while it is good for you, and perhaps you love a thing while it is bad for you. And God knows, while you know not.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 216] ﴿They ask you about fighting in the sacred month. Say: "Fighting therein is great, but averting people from the way of God, disbelieving in Him, and (barring access to) the Sacred Mosque, and expelling its people from it, is greater in the sight of God. And fitnah is greater than killing." And they will not cease fighting you until they turn you back from your religion, if they are able. And whoever of you reverts from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever, those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217] ﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who emigrated and strove in the way of God, those hope for the mercy of God. And God is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 218]

(p-134) *Ḥasiba* (حَسِبَ): with a kasra on the sin, it has the present form *yaḥsabu* with a fatḥa. It is one of the sisters of *ẓanna* (to think/suppose), and it requires two objects. These are, according to the well-known view of the grammarians, a subject and a predicate. Its meaning is the attribution of the predicate, from what is certain, to the subject, and it may occasionally be used for what is certain, as in the verse of poetry:

"I reckoned piety and generosity the best of trade, a profitable one, when a man rises up burdened."

Its verbal noun is *al-ḥusbān*. *Ḥasiba* also comes with the meaning of "to become red," as one says *ḥasiba al-rajulu yaḥsabu*, and he is *aḥsab*, just as one says *shaqira*, and he is *ashqar*. *Ḥasiba* has rulings that are mentioned in grammar.

*Lammā* (لَمّا) as a jussive particle: it is a particle, and they claimed that it is compounded from *lam* and *mā*. It has rulings in which it differs from *lam*. Among them: it is permissible to omit the verb after it when the meaning indicates its omission, and this occurs in eloquent speech. Among them: its negation must be connected to the present. And among them: it does not enter upon a conditional verb or a verb of the apodosis. *Zalzala* (زَلْزَلَ): it means to shake and to move. It is quadriliteral according to the Basran grammarians, like *daḥraja*. This type of quadriliteral is a matter of disagreement with the Kufans and al-Zajjaj, which is mentioned in grammar.

*Mādhā* (ماذا): when each of the two words is used separately in its own state, *mā* is intended as an interrogative, and *dhā* is for indication. If figurative usage enters, then *dhā* is a relative pronoun, with the meaning of *alladhī* and *allatī* and their derivatives, and *mā* remains in its original interrogative sense. In that case *dhā* requires a complement. It is compounded with the interrogative *mā*, so the meaning of the two together becomes the meaning of the interrogative *mā* if it stood alone. For this reason the Arabs said: *'an mādhā tas'alu?* (about what do you ask?) with the alif of *mā* retained, and the preposition has entered upon it. It may also be compounded with the relative *mā* or the indefinite descriptive *mā*, so the meaning of the combination is the meaning of the relative or descriptive *mā* if it stood alone without *dhā*. The other view is from al-Farisi.

*Al-Kurh* (الكُرْهُ), with a damma or fatḥa on the kāf, and *al-karāhiyya* and *al-karāha* are verbal nouns of *kariha*, as stated by al-Zajjaj, meaning "to detest." It was said: *al-kurh* with a damma is what a person dislikes, and *al-karh* with a fatḥa is what one is compelled to. It was also said: *al-kurh* with a damma is the passive participle, like *al-khubr* and *al-naqḍ* in the sense of *al-makhbūr* and *al-manqūḍ*, and *al-karh* with a fatḥa is the verbal noun.

*ʿAsā* (عَسى): it is among the verbs of approximation. It is a verb, contrary to those who said it is a particle. It does not conjugate, and its pattern is *fa'ala*. When it is attached to a first-person or second-person pronoun in the nominative, or to the feminine plural *nūn*, it is permissible to pronounce its sin with a kasra, and the pronoun for the third person is implied in it, as in *ʿasayā* and *ʿasawā*. This is contrary to al-Rummani; Ibn Ziyad al-Baghdadi reported the disagreement from him. The omission of *an* from the present is not restricted to poetry, contrary to the one who claims that. It has many rulings mentioned in the science of grammar, and these are: it occurs frequently in hope, and rarely in apprehension. Al-Raghib said so.

*Al-ṣadd* (الصَّدُّ): the side of a ravine or valley that blocks the traveler. *Ṣaddahu ʿan kadhā* is as if he placed between him and what he wants a barrier that prevents him. End of quote. It is said: *ṣadda yaṣuddu ṣudūdan*, meaning he turned away. Its analogical form, due to its intransitivity, would be *yaṣiddu* with a kasra, and this has been heard. *Ṣaddahu yaṣuddu ṣaddan* means he prevented him. *Tasadda lil-shayʾ* means he confronted something, and its root is *tasaddada*, like *taẓannā* meaning *taẓannana*. Its pattern is *tafaʿʿala*. It is also permissible that it be *tafaʿlā*, like *yaʿalnā*, in which case the alif and lām are for assimilation, and it is from a doubled-lām root.

*Zāla* (زالَ): one of the sisters of *kāna*, whose present form is *yazālu*. It is from the roots with a *yāʾ*, and its pattern is *faʿila* with a kasra on the ʿayn. What al-Kisaʾi reported in its present form indicates that its ʿayn is a *yāʾ*, namely *yuzīlu*. It is only used negated with a negative particle, or with *laysa*, or with *ghayr*, or with *lā* for prohibition or supplication. *Al-ḥubūṭ* (الحُبُوطُ): its root meaning is corruption. *Ḥubūṭ al-ʿamal* is the nullifying of a deed. *Ḥabiṭa baṭnuhu* means his belly swelled. *Al-Ḥabaṭāt* is a tribe of the Banū Tamīm. *Al-Ḥabanṭā* is one with a swollen belly. *Al-muhājara* is moving from one land to another land, and it is a form of *mufāʿala* from *al-hajr*. *Al-mujāhada* is a form of *mufāʿala* from *jahida*, meaning to extract effort and striving. *Al-tajāhud* is exerting one's utmost and effort. *Al-jihād* with a fatḥa is hard ground.

* *

﴿Mankind was one community﴾. The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that the persistence of those people in their disbelief is love of this world, and that this is not specific to this era in which you were sent, but is a matter that existed in ancient times. For they were upon the truth, then they differed out of rebellion, envy, and dispute over seeking (p-135) this world. The people (*al-nās*) were the generations between Adam and Noah, and they were ten, who were upon the truth until they differed. So God sent Noah and those after him. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah. Or: the people of Noah and those in his ark were Muslims. Or: it was Adam alone, according to Mujahid. Or: it was he and Eve. Or: the children of Adam when He brought them forth from his back as souls, and they were upon the natural disposition (*fiṭra*), said by Ubayy and Ibn Zayd. Or: Adam and his children were upon a true religion, and they differed from the time Qabil killed Habil. Or: the children of Adam from the time of his death until the sending of Noah were disbelievers like cattle, said by ʿIkrima and Qatadah. Or: the people of Abraham, who were upon his religion until ʿAmr ibn Yahya changed it. Or: the People of the Book who believed in Moses, upon our Prophet and upon him be peace. Or: the people of Noah when he was sent to them, they being disbelievers, said by Ibn ʿAbbas. Or: the species, they being one community in their being free of the laws, with no command or prohibition upon them; or one kind, so the meaning is that all are of one substance and one father. Then He specified a category of people with the sending of messengers to them and the sending down of Books upon them, as an honor for them, said by al-Maturidi. These are twelve views regarding "people." As for the monotheism of them, there are five views: either in faith, or in disbelief, or in creation upon the natural disposition, or in being free from the laws, or in being of one substance, which is the father. It has been preferred that they were one community in faith, by His saying: ﴿then God sent﴾, and they were only sent when they differed. This is confirmed by the reading of ʿAbd Allah: ﴿a single community, then they differed﴾ [Yunus: 19]. Also by His saying: ﴿to judge between people concerning what they differed about﴾, which indicates that the agreement had occurred before the sending and the sending down. Also by the evidence of reason, since sound reflection leads to the truth. Adam was sent to his offspring and they were Muslims. Also by birth upon the natural disposition. Also by the fact that the people of the ark were upon the truth. Also by their acknowledgment on the Day of the Covenant. It appears that this view is the most preferred, due to the reading of ʿAbd Allah, and for the explicit statement of this omitted element in another verse, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And mankind was not but one community, then they differed﴾ [Yunus: 19]. The Quran explains part of itself by another part. The explanation of "community" has already preceded in His saying: ﴿and from our offspring a Muslim community for You﴾ [al-Baqarah: 128].

In the reading of Ubayy: "*kāna al-bashar*" (mankind was), as an indication that the word "people" does not refer to a specific group. Whoever makes the unity in faith requires the supposition: "then they differed, so God sent." Whoever makes it in disbelief does not need this supposition, since the sending of the prophets was to them. The first of the messengers, according to what is reported in the authentic hadith of the intercession, is Noah, upon our Prophet and upon him be peace, "People will say to him: 'You are the first of the messengers.'" The meaning is: to a people of disbelievers, because Adam came before him, and he was sent to his children to teach them the religion and faith.

* *

﴿So God sent the prophets as bearers of good tidings and warners﴾: that is, He sent the prophets as bearers of good tidings of reward for whoever obeys, and as warners of punishment for whoever disobeys. He put the good tidings first because it is more delightful to the soul and more receptive to what the Prophet conveys. In it is the reassurance of the obligated person and the promise of reward for what he does of obedience. From this is His saying: ﴿So We have only made it easy in your tongue that you may give good tidings thereby to the God-fearing and warn thereby a people contentious﴾ [Maryam: 97]. The accusatives of "bearers of good tidings" and "warners" are as circumstantial accusatives of simultaneity.

﴿And He sent down with them the Book with truth﴾. "With them" is a circumstantial phrase of "the Book," and it is not governed by "sent down," since that would necessitate their sharing in the sending down, and they were not described by it. It is a predicated circumstance, meaning: He sent down the Book accompanying them at the time of sending down; it had not been accompanying them, but it reached them. "The Book" may have the article *al* for the category, or for the known, according to the interpretation of "with them" as "with each one of them," or according to the interpretation that it refers to a single specific book, which is the Torah, said by al-Tabari. It was sent down upon Moses and the prophets after him judged by it, and they relied upon it, such as the tribes and others. It is weak that it is singular placed in the position of plural, although this has been said. It is possible that "with the truth" is connected to "sent down," or to the meaning of what is in the Book of the sense of the verb, since by it is meant what is written. Or it is connected to an omitted element, so it would be in the position of a circumstantial phrase of "the Book," meaning: accompanied by the truth. It would be a confirmatory circumstance, since the books of God that were sent down are accompanied by the truth and do not separate from it. This clause is conjoined to His saying: ﴿So God sent﴾. It should not be said: the good tidings and warning only occur through command and prohibition, and these are only derived from the sending down of books. (p-136) Why then are they placed before the sending down, even though they arise from it? Because that is not necessarily the case, since good tidings and warning may arise from something other than books, from the revelation of God to His prophet without that being a book that is recited and written. Even if that were granted, their placement first would be preferable, because they are two circumstances of the prophets, so it is appropriate for them to be connected to the prophets, even if they arise from the sending down of books.

Al-Qadi said: "For prophets, peace be upon them, promise and warning before the explanation of the Law is possible in matters connected with rational truths, such as knowledge of God, the Exalted, and abstaining from wrongdoing and other things." End of his words. What he mentioned does not hold, because the promise of reward and the warning of punishment are not things that reason alone decides as obligatory. Rather, they are matters of permissibility (*jawaz*). Then the Law came with them, so what was permissible by reason became obligatory by the Law. Something that is rationally possible cannot be attributed to the Prophet as obligatory except after revelation, with certainty. Therefore, revelation of the promise and the warning must precede the manifestation of good tidings and warning to the one to whom it is revealed, with certainty.

Al-Qadi said: "The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that there is no prophet except that he has with him a revealed Book containing the explanation of the truth, whether that Book was long or short, written down or not written down, miraculous or not miraculous, because the fact that the Book was sent down with them does not necessitate any of that." End of his words.

It is possible that the figurative usage (*majaz*) lies in *anzala* (sent down), so that it means *ja'ala* (made), as in His saying: ﴿And We sent down iron﴾ [al-Hadid: 25]. Since the sending down was mostly for them, it is attributed to all of them. It is also possible that the figurative usage lies in *al-kitab* (the Book), so that it means "that which was revealed." Since most of what was revealed came in books, the word "Book" was applied to the whole, naming the collection by the name of many of its parts.

* *

﴿So that He may judge between people concerning that over which they differed﴾. The *lam* is the *lam* of causation (*lam al-'illa*) and is connected to *anzala*. The pronoun in *liyahkum* (that He may judge) refers to God in His saying "then God sent," and it is the implicit subject of *anzala*. This is the apparent meaning. The sense is that God, the Exalted, sent down the Book so that by it He might decide between people. It has also been said that it refers to the Book, meaning: so that the Book may judge between people. Attributing judgment to it is figurative, as He attributed speech to it in His saying: ﴿This Our Book speaks against you with truth﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 29], and as the poet said:

*The spider has spun its web over you,*
*and the revealed Book has decreed against you with it.*

Also, because the Book is the origin of the judgment, it is attributed to it as a way of returning the judgment to its origin. This is the view of the majority. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that the agent be the Prophet. He said: "so that God may judge, or the Book, or the Prophet to whom it was sent down." The singular pronoun weakens this, although it could be argued that it refers to the individual members of the plural, meaning: so that every prophet may judge by his book. But there is no need for this strained reading, given that the pronoun clearly refers back to God, the Exalted. What confirms its reference to God, the Exalted, is the reading of al-Jahdari, which Makki reported: *linahkum* (so that We may judge) with the *nun*. Its reference to God, the Exalted, is then certain, and this would be a shift (*iltifat*) from the third-person pronoun in *anzala* to the first-person pronoun. Ibn 'Atiyya considered this reading a scribal error (*tashif*). He said, in substance, that Makki did not report al-Jahdari's reading as people transmitted it from him, which is *liyuhkama*, with the verb in the passive. Makki reported *linahkum* with the *nun*. In the reading that people transmitted, *wa-liyuhkama*, the agent is omitted because it is known, and the best view is that it is God, the Exalted. They said it could also be the Book or the prophets.

*Bayna* (between) is a locative adverb, and here it is figurative. It is governed by *liyahkum*. *Fima* (concerning) is also connected to *liyahkum*, and *fihi* (over it) is connected to *ikhtalafu* (they differed). The pronoun in *fihi* refers back to the relative *ma*, and what is meant by it is the religion and Islam. The meaning is: that He may judge between people concerning the religion over which they differed after agreement. It has been said that what they differed over may be Muhammad (ﷺ) or his religion, or both, or his Book.

* *

﴿And none differed over it except those who were given it, after the clear proofs had come to them, out of envy among themselves﴾. The pronoun in *wa-ma ikhtalafa fihi* (and none differed over it) refers back to what the first *fihi* refers to. It has already been stated that the pronoun refers to *ma*. As for the explanation of *ma*, is it the religion, or Muhammad (ﷺ), or his religion, or both, or his Book? The pronoun in *utuhu* (who were given it) at that point refers to what the pronoun in *fihi* refers to. It has been said that the pronoun in *fihi* refers to the Book, and *utuhu* also refers to the Book. The implied sense is: "and none differed concerning the Book except those who were given it," that is, those who were given the Book. Al-Zajjaj said: the second pronoun in *fihi* may refer to the Prophet (ﷺ), that is: "and none differed concerning the Prophet (ﷺ) except those who were given it," meaning those who were given knowledge of his prophethood. They did that out of rebellion. According to this view, the Book is the Torah, and "those who were given it" are the Jews. It has been said that the pronoun in *fihi* refers to what they differed over concerning the ruling of the Torah, the qibla, and other matters. It has been said that the pronoun in *fihi* refers to Jesus, may God's blessings be upon our Prophet and upon him. Muqatil said: the pronoun refers to the religion, that is, "and none differed concerning the religion." End of his words.

What appears from the context of the discourse and the excellence of the composition is that all the pronouns in *utuhu* and the first *fihi* refer to the relative *ma* in the phrase "concerning that over which they differed." The second *fihi* refers to the same. The sense of "those who differed over it" is: every matter over which they differed. Its ultimate reference is to God, who explained it by what was sent down in the Book; or to the Book, since it contains everything the responsible person needs; or to the Prophet (ﷺ), who clarifies it through the Book, according to the views mentioned earlier concerning the agent in "so that He may judge."

"Those who were given it" are the masters of knowledge of it and those who studied it. He singled them out for mention to alert the reader to the heinousness of their act and the ugliness of what they did in differing. Also, others followed them in the difference, so they are the root of the evil. He used the word *min* (from), which indicates the starting point of an action, to indicate that their difference connects to the very first time the clear proofs came. No agreement occurred among them on anything after the coming. Rather, with the very coming of the clear proofs they differed. Nothing intervened between the two.

The clear proofs (*bayyinat*) are the Torah and the Gospel. So "those who were given it" are the Jews and the Christians, or all the revealed Books. Thus "those who were given it" are the scholars of every religious community. Or it means what is in the Torah concerning the description of Muhammad (ﷺ), and "those who were given it" are the Jews. Or it means the miracles of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and "those who were given it" are all nations. Or it means Muhammad (ﷺ), and "those who were given it" are those to whom he was sent. What appears is that the clear proofs are what the revealed Books clarified, given to the prophets of the nations, which necessitates agreement and the absence of difference. They made the coming of the clear signs a cause of their difference, and that is more shameful for them, since they placed the opposite of what the thing requires as its consequence.

Then He explained that this difference, which should not have existed, has no cause or motive except mere rebellion, wrongdoing, and transgression. *Baghyan* (out of rebellion) is in the accusative as an object of purpose (*maf'ul min ajlihi*). *Baynahum* (among themselves) is in the position of a qualifier to it, so it is connected to an omitted element, meaning: existing among themselves. Whoever said it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*hal*), meaning "rebelling," is far off. The sense is that what drives the difference is rebellion. The cause of this rebellion is their envy of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) concerning prophethood, or their concealment of his description that is in the Torah, or their pursuit of worldly things and leadership. There are views on this. The first two apply specifically to the people of the Book and others present with the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The third applies to all the differing nations. The sending down of Books occurred after the first difference existed, and for this reason He said: ﴿So that He may judge between people concerning that over which they differed﴾. The second difference is meant as an increase in difference, or the continuation of difference, if we interpret *utuhu* as "those who were given the Book." This difference occurs after the Book was given. It has been said that it is by denying what is in it, and it has been said that it is by distorting it.

In His saying *baghyan* (out of rebellion) there is an indication that the cause is restricted (*hasr al-'illa*). This refutes the view of those who said that the difference after the sending down of the Book was so that the difference that existed before it would disappear through it. In His saying *al-bayyinat* (the clear proofs) there is evidence that both the rational proofs established in sound natures and the revealed proofs that came in the Book have been achieved, and there is no excuse for turning away or disregarding the truth. But what counteracted this decisive proof was what was built into them of rebellion, envy, and greed for monopolizing this world.

Unless (*illa*) "those who were given it" is an exceptive construction with the antecedent omitted (*istithna' mufarragh*, an exception in which the exceptive particle is preceded by no explicit antecedent). It is the subject of *ikhtalafa* (differed). "After what had come to them" is connected to *ikhtalafa*. *Baghyan* is in the accusative and connected to *ikhtalafa*. This is the view of some of them. He said: "It is not prevented except from this, just as you say: 'Zayd did not stand except on Friday.'" End of his words. This is open to question. The meaning of the exception with the antecedent omitted applies to the subject, to the prepositional phrase, and to the object of purpose. The meaning is: "and none differed over it except those who were given it, except after the clear proofs had come to them, except out of rebellion among themselves." So each of the three is restricted. If this is so, then the exceptive particle would have two exceptions after it without a conjunction before the first. That is not permissible. It is permissible only with a conjunction, because the conjunction is understood to be followed by *illa*, so it becomes as if it were pronounced with it. If something appears that seems to contradict this, it is interpreted as having an implied governing element. For this reason, they interpreted His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed; so ask the people of the reminder if you do not know﴾ [al-Nahl: 43], ﴿with the clear proofs and the scriptures﴾ [al-Nahl: 44], as an implied verb of the sense: "We sent them with the clear proofs and the scriptures." They did not make *bil-bayyinat* connected to His saying *wa-ma arsalna* (and We did not send), lest *illa* have two exceptions after it, one being *rijalan* (men) and the other *bil-bayyinat*, without a conjunction.

Abu al-Hasan and Abu 'Ali prohibited: "No one took except Zayd a dirham," and "The people did not strike except some of them some others," and they differed over correcting them. Abu al-Hasan corrected them by placing before the following nominative a noun, so one says: "No one, Zayd, took except a dirham." Then Zayd is a substitute (*badal*) for "no one," and *illa* has one thing excepted by it, namely the dirham. "Except a dirham" is an exception with the antecedent omitted from the omitted object, and the meaning becomes: "Zayd did not take anything except a dirham." Abu 'Ali's correction is by adding an accusative element before *illa*, so one says: "No one took something except Zayd a dirham," and "The people did not strike someone except some of them some others." The nominative is then a substitute for the nominative, and the accusative is a substitute for the accusative. Some of them have so derived it.

Ibn al-Sarraj said: "'I gave the people a dirham except 'Amr' is permissible. But 'I gave the people a dirham except 'Amr the dinars' is not permissible, because only one thing can be excepted by the particle. If you say: 'I did not give the people a dirham except 'Amr a dang,' as an exception, it is not permissible; as a substitute, it is permissible. So you substitute 'Amr for the people and *dang* for *dirham*, as if you said: 'I did not give except 'Amr a dang.'" He means that the meaning is restriction over the two objects. One of our companions said: "What Ibn al-Sarraj said has weakness, because a substitute in an exception must be accompanied by *illa*, so it resembles a conjoined noun with a particle. Just as two conjoined nouns cannot follow it, two substitutes cannot follow *illa*." End of his words.

Some people permitted two exceptions to follow *illa* without a conjunction. The correct view is that it is not permissible, because *illa* in terms of meaning is transitive. Were it not for *illa*, the noun after it could not be connected to what precedes it. So it is like the *waw* of *ma'a* (with), and like the hamza that was made to produce transitivity in the verb's structure. Just as the *waw* of *ma'a* does not transitively extend, nor does the hamza extend to something other than its first intended object except with a conjunction, so likewise is *illa*. Based on what we have prepared, *min ba'di ma jaa'hum al-bayyinat* (after the clear proofs had come to them) is connected, and *baghyan* is in the accusative with an implied governing element indicated by what precedes it. Its estimated form is: "They differed over it after the clear proofs had come to them, out of rebellion among themselves."

* *

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 213 (part 3 of 3):**

﴿So Allah guided those who believed to the truth concerning what they had differed about, by His leave.﴾ "Those who believed" are those who believed in Muhammad (ﷺ). The pronoun in "what they had differed about" refers to "those who were given it" (the Book), meaning: when those who differed about it did so. "Of the truth" specifies what was differed about. The word "min" (of) is attached to an omitted element, since it occupies the position of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of "mā" (what), so it is partitive (li-l-tab'īḍ). It may also be explanatory of the genus (li-bayān al-jins) according to the view of those who hold this, the sense being: "what they differed about, which is the truth." The better view is that what was differed about here is the religion and Islam, and this is supported by the reading of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud): "what they differed about of Islam."

This "matter of difference" has been interpreted in other ways, and there is disagreement about its specification:
- Is it Friday? The Jews made it Saturday and the Christians Sunday, and it had been prescribed for them just as it was prescribed for us. In the two Ṣaḥīḥs (of al-Bukhārī and Muslim) it is narrated: "We are the last (in time) and the first (in merit) on the Day of Resurrection; however, they were given the Book before us, and we were given it after them." So this is the day about which they differed, and Allah guided us to it. He said: "Friday: the day is ours, tomorrow is for the Jews, and the day after tomorrow for the Christians."
- Or is it the prayer? Some of them prayed toward the east and some toward the west, and Allah the Exalted guided the believers to the qiblah (direction of prayer). This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam.
- Or is it Abraham (peace be upon our Prophet and upon him)? The Christians said he was a Christian, and the Jews said he was a Jew, so Allah guided the believers to his religion by His saying: ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:67].
- Or is it Jesus (peace be upon our Prophet and upon him)? The Jews made him a curse, and the Christians made him a god, so Allah the Exalted guided us to the true word about him. This was said by Ibn Zayd.
- Or is it the Books, in which they believed in some and disbelieved in others?
- Or is it fasting? They differed about it, and Allah guided us to the month of Ramadan.

These are six opinions other than the first.

Al-Farrāʾ said: "There is transposition (qalb, inversion of word order) in the speech, and its intended sense is: 'So Allah guided those who believed to the truth from what they differed about.'" Al-Ṭabarī adopted this. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "What led him to this interpretation is the fear that the wording might be understood to mean that they differed about the truth itself, so that Allah guided the believers to some of what they differed about, while that (thing) may not have been the truth in itself." He said: "Claiming transposition in the wording of the Book of Allah without any necessity compelling it is incapacity and poor reasoning, for the speech is understood in its own straightforward form and arrangement: his saying 'so He guided' requires that they attained the truth, the meaning is complete at 'concerning it,' and by 'of the truth' the genus of that concerning which the disagreement occurred is made clear." Al-Mahdawī said: "He placed the word 'difference' before the word 'truth' for emphasis, since the concern is indeed with mentioning the difference." The words of Ibn ʿAṭiyyah end here, and they are good. However, transposition (qalb), according to our companions (the Ḥanbalī/Shāfiʿī scholars of grammar), is restricted to poetic necessity, so we do not interpret the speech of Allah by it.

"By His leave" means: by His knowledge; this was said by al-Zajjāj. Or: by His command and enabling grace (tawfīq), or by His empowerment. These views have already passed, and the discussion of them was extensively explained in His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is He who has sent it down upon your heart by the permission of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:97]. "By His leave" is connected to "so Allah guided." Whoever supposed an implied intransitive verb (muṭāwiʿ, reflexive) for it, with the meaning "so they were guided by His leave," which is the view of Abū ʿAlī (al-Fārisī), has gone too far, since there is no need for this implication.

* *

﴿And Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.﴾ In this sentence and what precedes it there is evidence that the guidance of a servant comes only from Allah, to whomever He wills to grant guidance. This refutes the Muʿtazilah (rationalist school) in their claim that a person independently guides himself. The name of Allah is repeated in His saying "and Allah," which is in the eloquent style in which each sentence stands independently; this is better than making it depend, through a pronoun, on what precedes it for the explanation of that pronoun, and similar examples have been mentioned before for this.

In His saying "whom He wills" there is an indication, indeed a clear proof, that His guidance has its source only in His will, not in an inherent attribute in the one He guides which makes him deserving of guidance. Rather, that is bestowed solely by His will, the Exalted: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ 21:23].

﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise while there has not yet come to you the example of those who passed away before you?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:214]. This was revealed concerning the Battle of the Trench (al-Khandaq), when the Muslims suffered what they suffered of hardship, intense fear, cold, and various kinds of harm, as the Exalted said: ﴿And hearts reached the throats﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 33:10]. This was said by Qatādah and al-Suddī. Or it was revealed concerning the Battle of Uhud, in which a group of the Muslims were killed and hardships occurred, until ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy and his companions said: "How long will you kill yourselves and destroy your wealth? If Muhammad were a prophet, killing and captivity would not have been imposed upon you." So they said: "Indeed, whoever among us is killed enters Paradise." So he (Allah) said: "How long will you claim for yourselves falsely?"

Or it was revealed at the beginning of their migration to Medina, when they entered it without wealth, and left their homes and their property in the hands of the polytheists, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with them. Then the Jews openly showed enmity, and a group concealed hypocrisy. This was said by ʿAṭāʾ.

It has been said: the connection of this verse to what precedes it is that He said "He guides whom He wills," and the intended meaning is the truth whose following leads to Paradise. So He clarified that this is not complete except by bearing hardships and obligations. Or: when He explained that He had guided them, He explained that after that guidance they bore hardships in establishing the truth; so likewise you, companions of Muhammad, do not deserve virtue in the religion except by bearing these trials.

Here "am" (or) is disconnected (munqaṭiʿah), estimated to be equivalent to "bal" (rather) with the hamzah (interrogative particle), so it includes a turning away (iḍrāb), which is a transition from one speech to another. It indicates a question, but it is a question of affirmation (taqrīr). This is what Abū Muḥammad ibn ʿAṭiyyah expressed when he said that "am" may come at the beginning of speech, even without any division or equivalence, as the interrogative alif. So his saying "it may come" as the beginning of speech is not as he stated, because it is estimated as "bal" and the hamzah. Just as "bal" must be preceded by speech so that it falls within the scope of coordinating sentences, so too what contains its meaning.

Some grammarians claimed that it comes in the place of the interrogative hamzah and begins speech with it; this would require that the estimate be: "Did you think?" Al-Zajjāj said it has the meaning of "bal," and he cited:

*"She appeared like the horn of the sun in the brightness of the forenoon; did you shape her, or are you more beautiful in the eye?"*

Some exegetes wished to make it connected (muttaṣilah), and to posit before it an estimated sentence which by that estimate makes "am" connected. So the estimate of the verse becomes: "So Allah guided those who believed to the truth concerning what they differed about, so they endured the mockery of their people toward them. Will you then follow their path? Or do you think that you will enter Paradise without following their path?" Thus there are four views concerning "am" here: disconnection, in the sense of "bal" and the hamzah; connection, by positing a sentence before it; the interrogative sense of the hamzah; and turning away in the sense of "bal." The correct view is the first one.

The two objects of "ḥasibtum" (you thought) are filled by "anna" (that) according to the school of Sībawayh. As for Abū al-Ḥasan (al-Akhfash), "anna" fills the place of the first object, and the second object is omitted. This meaning has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿those who are certain that they will meet their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:46].

﴿Yet there has not come to you the example of those who passed away before you﴾. The clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). The implied sense is: "not yet having come to you is the example of those who passed away before you." That is, entering Paradise necessarily requires being tested with severe hardships and patience in the face of the harm inflicted by the disbelievers, poverty, and striving in the way of God. This is not merely through faith alone; rather, your path in this is the path of those who came before you, the followers of the messengers. God Most High addressed His believing servants with this, turning to them in encouragement and in strengthening them, and informing them that it does no harm that their enemies do not agree with them. The nations differed with their prophets, and they were patient until victory came to them. *Lamma* (not yet) is more emphatic in negation than *lam* (not), because it indicates the negation of the action extending up to the present time; so it is for negating expectation. *Mathal* (example) means resemblance, except that it is used figuratively for a strange situation or a wondrous matter that has importance. It stands by omission of a modified noun, the implied sense being "the like of the ordeal of those who passed away before you," and by omission of a qualified noun, whose implied sense is "the believers." The phrase *alladhīna khalaw min qablikum* (those who passed away before you) is connected to *khalaw* (passed away), and it is as if it were an emphasis, because "those who passed away" already implies precedence.

* *

﴿Hardship and adversity touched them﴾. This clause explains and clarifies the example, so it has no place in the grammatical analysis (i'rab). It is as if someone asked: "What is that example?" and it was said: "Hardship and adversity touched them." The word *massa* (touched) here means "befell," and its literal meaning is touching with the hand, so its use here is figurative. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that the clause, which begins with *massathum* (touched them), be in the position of a circumstantial clause with *qad* (indeed) implied, but this is far-fetched; in that case the circumstantial element would be from the subject pronoun in *khalaw* (passed away). The explanation of *al-ba'sā' wa'l-ḍarrā'* (hardship and adversity) has already been given in the saying of God Most High: ﴿and those patient in hardship and adversity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177].

(And they were shaken), that is, they were disturbed with a severe disturbance by quaking; the verb is in the passive, and the agent is omitted because it is known, that is: "and their enemies shook them."

﴿Until the Messenger says﴾. Al-A'mash read: "and they were shaken and the Messenger says," with *wa* (and) in place of *ḥattā* (until). In the codex of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) it is: "and they were shaken, then they were shaken, and the Messenger says." The majority read *ḥattā* (until), and the verb after it is in the subjunctive, either as an end point (ghāyah) or as a cause (ta'līl). That is: "and they were shaken until the Messenger says," or "and they were shaken so that the Messenger might say." The first meaning is clearer, because the touching and the shaking were not caused by the saying of the Messenger and the believers. Nafi' read *yaqūlu* (says) in the nominative after *ḥattā*. When the present-tense verb after *ḥattā* is a verb of circumstance, it is either a circumstance at the time of narration, as in: "he fell ill until they no longer hoped for him," or it is a circumstance that has already passed, and it narrates it as it occurred, so the verb is put in the nominative according to one of these two aspects. The intended meaning here is past, so it is a narrated circumstance, the sense being: "and they were shaken, so the Messenger said." I have discussed the issues of *ḥattā* in my book *al-Takmīl*, and I have fully treated them there, and the discussion of them has preceded in this book.

﴿And those who believed with him﴾. The word *ma'ahu* (with him) may be in the accusative governed by *yaqūlu* (says), and it may be in the accusative governed by *āmanū* (believed).

﴿When will the help of God come? Indeed, the help of God is near﴾. *Matā* (when) is a question about time. It was said: this is by way of supplication to God Most High and seeking information about the time of help, so God answered them and said: ﴿Indeed, the help of God is near﴾. It was also said: this is by way of asking impatiently, since what befell them of hardship, ordeal and shaking was the utmost extreme, and it grew and persisted upon the believers until they uttered this speech; so this was said to them as a response to their request for hastening the help. What the analysis requires is that the two clauses be included under the saying, and that the first clause is the saying of the believers, who said this out of impatience for the help and weariness at the hardship that had reached them, and the second clause is the saying of their Messenger, responding to them and informing them of the nearness of help. Thus each clause is attributed to the one suited to it, and it is correct to attribute the whole to the whole, not to attribute the whole to each type of speaker. A parallel to this has been mentioned in some of the notes on the saying of God Most High: ﴿They said: "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood, while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. The saying ﴿"Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30] is from the speech of Iblis, and the saying ﴿"while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30] is from the speech of the angels about Iblis. The answer was that, because Iblis was included in the address with the angels in the saying: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels: "Indeed, I am going to place upon the earth a successive authority"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30].

A group said: there is inversion (taqdīm wa ta'khīr) in the speech; the estimate being: "until those who believed say: 'When is the help of God?' Then the Messenger says: 'Indeed, the help of God is near.'" So the Messenger was placed first in rank because of his station, and the saying of the believers was placed first because it came first in time.

Ibn 'Aṭiyyah said: this is arbitrary (taḥakkum), and bringing the speech to its proper sense is not impossible. End of quotation. His statement is good, because inversion and rearrangement are among things that are only resorted to out of necessity.

In His saying "and those who believed" there is an exalting of their status, in that He explicitly named them with this noble attribute, which is faith, and did not say "until the Messenger says, and they," and this indicates the omission of that qualified noun we estimated earlier, like the ordeal of the believers who passed away.

Ibn 'Aṭiyyah said: Most of the interpreters hold that the speech up to the end of the verse is from the saying of the Messenger and the believers, and that this is from the saying of the Messenger, seeking to hasten the help, not out of doubt or suspicion. The Messenger is a generic noun, not a specific individual, and God mentioned him to magnify the calamity that prompted the Messenger to this saying. End of his words. What is fitting for the conditions of the messengers is the saying which we mentioned, which the analysis requires. The Messenger, as Ibn 'Aṭiyyah mentioned, is a generic noun, not a particular individual. It was said: he is Yasa' (Elisha); it was said: he is Shu'ayb (Jethro). On this view, "those who passed away" are a people specifically identified, namely the followers of these messengers.

Some commentators reported that the Messenger here is Muhammad (ﷺ), and that the shaking here is attributed to his community. The context of the speech does not indicate what was mentioned, and some scholars followed this view. In this speech there is a generality, and its detail is that the followers of Muhammad (ﷺ) said: "When is the help of God?" and the Messenger said: "Indeed, the help of God is near."

What emerges from these transmissions is that the whole of both clauses is from the speech of the Messenger and the believers, in detail, or that the Messenger and the believers each said both clauses, so it is as if they said: "We have been patient, trusting in Your promise." Or the first clause is from the speech of the Messenger and the believers, and the second is from the speech of God Most High.

Since the question with *matā* (when) indicates seeking information about nearness, the answer included nearness. The apparent meaning of this information is that the nearness of help is that they will be helped against their enemies in this world and will prevail over them, as in the saying of God Most High: ﴿Our help came to them﴾ [Yusuf: 110], and ﴿When the help of God and the victory come﴾ [al-Nasr: 1]. Ibn 'Abbas said: the help is in the Hereafter, because the believer does not cease from ordeal, and whenever one battle ends another comes to him, so he continues in striving against the enemy, enjoining good, and striving against the self until death. And in the description of the conditions of those who passed away is that which indicates that what happened to them will happen to us, so we take them as an example and await relief and help from God, for they were answered in this regard, quickly.

﴿They ask you what they should spend﴾ [al-Baqarah: 215]. It was revealed concerning Amr ibn al-Jamuh, who was an elderly man of great wealth, who asked: "With what should I give in charity, and upon whom should I spend?" This was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas. In a narration from 'Ata': it was revealed concerning a man who said: "I have a dinar." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Spend it upon yourself." He said: "I have two dinars." He said: "Spend them upon your family." He said: "I have three." He said: "Spend them upon your servant." He said: "I have four." He said: "Spend them upon your parents." He said: "I have five." He said: "Spend them upon your relatives." He said: "I have six." He said: "Spend them in the way of God, and it is the best of them."

It should be understood from this progression that what was mentioned is superior to what came before it. Al-Hasan said: it concerns voluntary charity. Al-Suddi said: it has been abrogated (naskh, i.e., replaced by a later ruling) by the obligation of zakat.

Ibn 'Aṭiyyah said: al-Mahdawi erred against al-Suddi in this, so it was attributed to him that he said: the verse concerns the obligatory zakat, then the parents were abrogated from it. End of his words. And he said: he began with this view, that it concerns obligatory zakat, and on this basis the parents and those in their position among the close relatives were abrogated from it. Ibn Jurayj said: it is a recommendation (nadb), and zakat is other than this spending, so on this view there is no abrogation in it.

The connection (munāsabah) of this verse with what precedes it is that patience in spending and in giving away wealth is among the greatest qualities with which a believer adorns himself, and it is among the strongest means that lead to Paradise, to the extent that it has been related: "Charity extinguishes the anger of the Lord." The pronoun in the nominative in "they ask you" refers to the believers, and the *kāf* (you) is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ). *Mādhā* (what) here may be in the accusative or the nominative. The accusative is on the basis that the whole of *mādhā* is an interrogative, as if he said: "What thing do they spend?" So *mādhā* is in the accusative governed by *yunfiqūna* (they spend). The nominative is on the basis that *mā* alone is the interrogative, and *dhā* is a relative pronoun meaning "that which," and *yunfiqūna* (they spend) is the relative clause of *dhā*, and the returning pronoun is omitted, the estimate being: "What is it that they spend with?" So *mā* is in the nominative as the subject, and *dhā* in the sense of "that which" is its predicate. On both analyses, *yas'alūnaka* (they ask you) is suspended (mu'allaq); it operates in meaning but not in wording, and it is in the position of the second object of *yas'alūnaka*. Its parallel is what preceded in the saying of God Most High: ﴿Ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We gave them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 211], according to what we explained there. *Mādhā* is a question about the one who spends, not about the recipient, and it seems the speech contains an omission, whose estimate is: "And to whom do they give it?" A parallel to the verse in the question and the suspension is the saying of the poet:

*Will you not ask a man what he is striving for?*

But here *mādhā* is a subject and predicate, and it is not permissible for it to be an object of *yuḥāwilu* (strives), because after it comes:

*Is it a death that will be decreed, or error and falsehood?*

It is weak for the whole of *mādhā* to be a subject, with *yuḥāwilu* as the predicate, because of the weakness of omitting the returning pronoun in the accusative from the predicate of the subject, while omitting it from the relative clause is eloquent. Ibn 'Aṭiyyah mentioned that when *mādhā* is a compound noun, it is in the accusative, except what came in the saying of the poet:

*And what may the slanderers hope to say, except that they say that I am in love with you?*

For *'asā* (may) does not govern *mādhā* in the nominative position, and it is compound, since *dhā* has no relative clause. End of his words. The reason *dhā* in the line has no relative clause is that *'asā* does not occur as a relative clause of a nominal relative pronoun, so *dhā* cannot be in the sense of "that which." What Ibn 'Aṭiyyah mentioned, that when it is a compound noun it is in the accusative position, except in that line, we do not recognize; rather it is permissible to say: "What is beloved to you?" and "Who is standing?" on the estimate of the compound, as if you said: "What is beloved? And who is standing?" There is no difference between this and "Whom do you strike?" on the estimate of "Whom do you strike?" with *man* (who) as the subject.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 215:

﴿Say: Whatever wealth you spend, let it be for parents, relatives, orphans, the needy and the wayfarer.﴾ This explains the destination of what they spend, and it has already included the one about whom the question is asked, who is the spender, through His saying "of good" (min khayr). It is possible that "mādhā" (what) is a question about the destination, with an elided noun, the estimated meaning being: "What is the destination of what they spend?" That is, "they direct their spending to..." Then the answer corresponds to the question. It is also possible that the question's element that is the destination was omitted from the first part, and the element that is the spender was omitted from the second part (the answer), and both are intended even though they are elided. This is a type of eloquence (balaghah) whose parallel has already occurred in His saying: ﴿And the likeness of those who disbelieve is like that of one who shouts﴾ [al-Baqarah: 171]. Al-Zamakhshari said: His saying, ﴿whatever wealth you spend﴾, has included the explanation of what they spend, which is every good, and the speech was built on their intention, which is the explanation of the destination, because spending is not counted as such unless it falls in its proper place, like the saying of the poet:

Indeed a kindness is not a kindness until it strikes the path of the cistern.

The end of his words. There is no harm in it. "Of good" (min khayr) covers the little and the much. He began with the destinations in order of nearness, then with the most needy, then the neediest. The discussion of some of this ordering and its like has already passed. This verse has been used as evidence for the obligation of supporting parents and close relatives upon the one who has means. Some of them interpreted the verse as referring to parents who are poor while the child is wealthy.

﴿And whatever good you do, indeed Allah is Knowing of it.﴾ "Mā" in both places is conditional (shartiyyah), governing the verb after it in the accusative. It is permissible for "mā" in His saying ﴿Say: whatever wealth you spend﴾ to be a relative pronoun (mawsūlah), with "anfaqtum" as its relative clause (ṣilah), and "lil-wālidayn" as its predicate. Then the prepositional phrase is in the position of a single word, or in the position of a clause, according to the disagreement about a prepositional phrase functioning as a predicate, or it is a complement of a single word or of a clause. If "mā" in "mā anfaqtum" is conditional, then this prepositional phrase is in the position of the predicate of an elided subject. The estimated meaning: "So it (its destination) is for the parents," or "So its destination is for the parents." 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib read "wa-mā yafʿalū" with the yā (third person), and then this is a case of iltifāt (shift of grammatical person), or of what is concealed because the meaning indicates it, meaning: "and whatever people do," so it is more general than the previously addressed ones, since it includes them and others. In His saying "of good" in the matter of spending, it indicates the goodness of what is spent and that it is lawful, because the corrupt is forbidden by His saying: ﴿and do not aim at the corrupt from it to spend﴾ [al-Baqarah: 267]; and what has come in the report that "Allah is good and accepts only what is good"; and because what is unlawful is not described as "good." His saying "of good" in His saying "and whatever you do" is more general than the "good" intended as wealth, because what is connected to it is the act, and the act is more general than spending, so spending enters into the act. Thus "khayr" here is what is opposite to evil, and the meaning is: "and whatever you do of any kind of piety and acts of obedience." Some of them made "wa-mā taf'alū" here refer to the meaning of spending, meaning: "and whatever you do of spending of good," so the first would be an explanation of the destination, and this an explanation of the reward. The more appropriate is generality, because it includes the spending of wealth and other than it, and it is preferred by taking the wording according to its apparent generality. Since the question at first was about something specific, they were answered with something specific; then after that specific there came the generalization in acts of good, and mention of the reward for doing them. His saying "indeed Allah is Knowing of it" indicates the reward, because when He knows it He rewards it. So it is a declarative sentence that contains the promise of reward.

﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 216]. Ibn ʿAbbās said: When Allah enjoined jihad upon the Muslims, it was hard for them and they disliked it, so this verse was revealed. The apparent meaning of His saying "kutiba" is that it was made obligatory upon individuals (ʿayn), like His saying: ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183]; ﴿Retaliation has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178]; ﴿Indeed prayer has been enjoined upon the believers at fixed times﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 103]. ʿAṭāʾ said this, and he said: Fighting was enjoined upon the individuals of the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), then when the law was established and became firm, it became a communal obligation (kifāyah). The majority said: Its first obligation was only as a communal obligation without specification, then the consensus (ijmāʿ) continued that it is a communal obligation until it reached the territory of Islam, so it becomes an individual obligation (farḍ ʿayn). Al-Mahdawī and others related from al-Thawrī that he said: Jihad is voluntary, and it is interpreted as the answer to a questioner who asked: Has the one who was appointed to jihad been established? So it was answered that for him it is voluntary. The majority read "kutiba" in the passive voice, in the pattern that preceded this, from the word "kutiba." A group read "kataba" in the active voice, with "al-qitāl" in the accusative, and the subject is a pronoun in "kataba" referring to the name of Allah the Exalted. The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when He mentioned what touched those before us from the followers of the messengers of afflictions, and that entering Paradise is known through patience in what the accountable person is tested with, then He mentioned spending upon those who were mentioned, which is jihad of the self with wealth, He moved to something higher than it, which is the jihad by which religion is upheld, and in which is patience in giving up wealth and self.

﴿And it is hateful to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 216]. That is, disliked (makrūh). So it is from the usage of the verbal noun (nagḍ) in the sense of the thing rendered (manqūḍ), or: "possessing hatred" if it is intended as a verbal noun, so it is with an elided modifier, or for emphasis about people's aversion to fighting, its very hatred is made. The apparent reference of "huwa" is to fighting, and it is possible that it refers to the verbal noun understood from "kutiba," meaning: its prescription and its obligation are hard upon you. The clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: it is hateful to you by nature, or it is hateful to you before the command came. As-Sulamī read "kurhun" with a fatḥah on the kāf, and the meaning of hatred has already been mentioned in the discussion of the vocabulary. Al-Zamakhshari said in justifying the reading of as-Sulamī: It is permissible for it to mean the same as the dammah: like "ḍaʿf" and "ḍuʿf," meaning the verbal noun. He said: It is permissible for it to mean compulsion (ikrāh) in a figurative way, as if they were compelled to it because of its intense hatefulness to them and its hardship upon them, and from this is His saying: ﴿His mother bore him with hardship and gave birth to him with hardship﴾ [al-Aḥqāf: 15]. The end of his words. That "kurh" means "ikrāh," where the triliteral form is a verbal noun for the quadriliteral form, is not a regular pattern. If the usage of that has been related from the Arabs, we adopt it.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit, "The Surrounding Ocean") on Surah 2, verse 216:**

﴿And it may be that you dislike a thing and it is good for you﴾. *ʿAsā* (a verb of approximation, meaning "perhaps") here expresses apprehension (*al-ishfāq*) and not hope (*al-tarajjī*). Its use to express apprehension is rare. Here it is *tāmmah* (complete, meaning it needs no predicate), and it does not need a complement (*khabar*). Had it been *nāqisah* (incomplete, requiring a predicate), the construction would be like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Would you, if you turned away, perhaps cause corruption in the land?﴾ [Muhammad: 22]. The phrase *"an takrahū"* is in the nominative position (*fī mawḍiʿ rafʿ*) as the subject of *ʿasā*. Al-Hawfi claimed that it is in the accusative position, but this is not possible except with a far-fetched contrivance.

Included in the word *"shayʾan"* (a thing) is fighting, because it is naturally disliked, due to what it involves of exposure to captivity, killing, the destruction of bodies, and the ruin of wealth. The good in it is victory and booty, by seizing souls and possessions, through captivity, killing, plunder and conquest. The greatest of these is martyrdom, which is the state that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wished for repeatedly. The clause *"wa huwa khayrun lakum"* (and it is good for you) is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) referring back to *"shayʾan"*, which is indefinite. A circumstantial clause from an indefinite noun is less common than one from a definite noun. They also permitted that the clause be in the position of a descriptive (*ṣifah*). They said: the waw was permitted because the form of the clause here is like its form when it is a circumstantial clause. End of quote. But this is weak, because the waw in descriptions is only used for conjunction, as in: "I passed by a learned and generous man," whereas here nothing precedes it to be conjoined to. The claim that the waw is extra is far-fetched, so the clause cannot be a descriptive.

﴿And it may be that you love a thing and it is bad for you﴾. *ʿAsā* here expresses hope (*tarajjī*), and its use for this meaning is common in the language of the Arabs. They said: every *ʿasā* in the Qur'an is for certainty, meaning that it will occur, except the saying of the Exalted: ﴿It may be that his Lord, if he divorced you, would substitute for him wives better than you﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5]. Included in the word *"shayʾan"* is inclining to ease and abandoning fighting, because that is naturally loved, due to what it contains of the opposite of what may be expected of harm in fighting. The harm in it is their humiliation, the weakening of their affair, the uprooting of their strength, the taking captive of their offspring, the plunder of their wealth, and the seizure of their lands. The discussion of this in terms of *iʿrāb* (grammatical analysis) is like the discussion of the previous one.

﴿And Allah knows﴾ what contains the benefit, in that He has obligated you to fight, ﴿while you do not know﴾ what Allah the Exalted knows, because the ends of affairs are hidden from your knowledge. In this statement there is an admonition to contentment with what the decrees have brought about. Al-Hasan said: Do not dislike the calamities that befall you, for perhaps a matter you dislike contains your benefit, and perhaps a matter you love contains your destruction. Abu Saʿid al-Darir said:

*Often a matter you guard against draws you into a matter you approve of,*
*the beloved in it is concealed, and the disliked in it appears.*

Al-Wadahi said:

*Often a young man is given a choice while he hates the good in it.*

Ibn al-Sarhan said:

*How many a joy folded for you amid the folds of calamities,*
*and a delight that has come from where the misfortunes are awaited.*

Another said:

*How many a time disliked things surrounded you, and Allah chose for you while you disliked it.*

﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it.﴾ The exegetes wrote at length about the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of this verse, over several pages. The summary and the most well-known account is that it was revealed concerning the story of ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh al-Asadi, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent him with eight men: Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, ʿUkkasha ibn Miḥṣan, ʿUqba ibn Ghazwan, Abu Ḥudhayfa ibn ʿUtba ibn Rabiʿa, Suhayl ibn Bayḍa, ʿAmir ibn Rabiʿa, Wafid ibn ʿAbd Allah, and Khalid ibn Bukayr, with ʿAbd Allah as their leader. They were lying in wait for the caravan of Quraysh at Batn Nakhla. They reached it, and the caravan passed by. In it were ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥaḍrami, al-Ḥakam ibn Kaysan, ʿUthman ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mughira, and Nawfal ibn ʿAbd Allah. This took place on the last day of Jumada, according to their reckoning, and it was the first day of Rajab. Wafid shot ʿAmr with an arrow and killed him; he was the first of the polytheists to be killed. They captured al-Ḥakam and ʿUthman, and they were the first two prisoners in Islam. Nawfal escaped. They brought the caravan to Medina. Quraysh said, "Muhammad has made the sacred month lawful," and people spoke much about this. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) withheld the caravan, and the companions of the expedition (sariyya) said, "We will not move until our repentance is revealed." Then the verse was revealed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took one-fifth (khums) of the caravan, and it was the first khums in Islam. Quraysh then sent to ransom the two prisoners, but it was said, "Not until Saʿd and ʿUtba arrive." They had lost a camel of theirs before the encounter with the caravan (p-145) and had set out to search for it. They returned, and the two prisoners were ransomed. As for al-Ḥakam, he embraced Islam, remained in Medina, and was killed as a martyr at Bir Maʿuna. As for ʿUthman, he died in Mecca as a disbeliever. As for Nawfal, on the day of the Confederates (al-Aḥzab) he struck his horse's belly so that he would enter the trench against the Muslims; he fell into the trench with his horse, both were crushed, and Allah killed them.

There is disagreement in several details of this story. Al-Sajawandi summarized this occasion, saying: It was revealed concerning the first expedition (sariyya) of Islam, whose leader was ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh. They raided a caravan of Quraysh coming from al-Ta'if, and they killed ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥaḍrami on the last day of Jumada al-Akhira. It was confused with the first day of Rajab, so the people of Mecca reproached them for making it lawful. It was also said: It was revealed when the polytheists criticized fighting in a sacred month in the year of the Conquest (of Mecca). It was also said: It was revealed concerning the killing by ʿAmr ibn Umayya al-Ḍamri of two men of the tribe of Kilab who were with the Prophet (ﷺ), while ʿAmr did not know this; this happened on the first day of Rajab. Quraysh said, "He killed them in the sacred month," and so it was revealed.

The connection (munasaba) of this verse to what precedes it is that when fighting was prescribed, it was not restricted to one time over another. It was an established custom that fighting was not permitted in the sacred month, so He clarified the ruling on fighting in the sacred month. The meaning of His words ﴿Say: fighting in it is a great (sin)﴾ will come later, as well as what He said: ﴿And kill them wherever you encounter them﴾ [al-Baqara: 191], and after it: ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Baqara: 191]. That restriction concerned place, and this one concerns time.

Regarding the subject pronoun in "yas'alūnaka" (they ask you), it was said that it refers to the polytheists, who asked in order to disparage the violation of the sanctity of the martyrs and with the intention of treachery. It was also said that it refers to the believers, who asked out of amazement at what had come from Ibn Jahsh and in order to seek clarity about the ruling.

The sacred month here is Rajab without disagreement, so they say, on the basis that the definite article in it is for previous reference (al-ʿahd). It is possible that the article is for the category (al-jins), in which case it means the sacred months, which are: Dhu al-Qaʿda, Dhu al-Ḥijja, al-Muḥarram, and Rajab. They were called ḥurum because fighting in them is forbidden. Something of this was mentioned in His words: ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month﴾ [al-Baqara: 194].

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "qitālin fīhi" with a kasra, and it is a substitute (badal) for "al-shahr," a badal of inclusion (badal ishtimal). Al-Kisa'i said it is in the genitive by repetition of the governing particle (ʿalā al-takrīr), and this is the meaning of al-Farrā's statement, since he said: it is in the genitive by an elided ʿan. This should not be taken as a disagreement, as some make it, because the view of the Basran grammarians that the substitute is intended with a repeated governing element is the view of al-Kisa'i and al-Farra'; there is no difference between these statements, as all of them go back to one meaning.

Abu ʿUbayda said: "qitālin fīhi" is in the genitive by proximity (al-jiwār). Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: This is an error. If Abu ʿUbayda meant the genitive by proximity as the grammarians have established it, then as Ibn ʿAṭiyya said, the error lies in this: the word would be a follower of what precedes it in the nominative or accusative in both form and meaning, and then it would be shifted from that case to the genitive because it is adjacent to a genitive word to which it cannot be a follower in meaning. Here, no nominative or accusative word has preceded, so that "qitālin" could be its follower and then be shifted from its case to the genitive by proximity. If, however, Abu ʿUbayda meant by the genitive by proximity that it is a follower of a genitive word, so that it was put in the genitive by being adjacent to a genitive word, that is, it became its follower, and we do not mean by it the established term, then this would be permissible and not an error, and would agree with the view of the majority, except that it is more obscure in expression and more ambiguous in terminology.

Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Rabīʿ, and al-Aʿmash read "ʿan qitālin fīhi" with "ʿan" made explicit, and it is thus in the codex of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud). It is read anomalously as "qitālun fīhi" in the nominative. ʿIkrima read "qatlin fīhi, qul qatlun fīhi," without the alif in both. The reasoning for the nominative in the reading "qitālun fīhi" is that, by presupposing the interrogative hamza, it is a subject (mubtada'), and the beginning with an indefinite noun is permitted by the intention of the interrogative hamza. This sentence asked about is in the position of a substitute for "al-shahr al-ḥarām," because "saʾala" has already taken its two objects, so it does not occupy the position of an object, even though it is the focus of the question. Some claimed that it is in the nominative by an elided active participle, its estimated form being: "Is fighting in it permissible?" It was said: The analogue of this is that the questioners did not ask about the existence of fighting in the sacred month; they asked: "Is fighting in the sacred month permissible?" So they asked about its legitimacy, not about its occurrence in it.

* *

﴿Say: fighting in it is a great (sin).﴾ This sentence is a subject and predicate, and "qitālun" is indefinite. The beginning with the indefinite noun is permitted because it is qualified by the prepositional phrase (p-146) "fīhi," so they say. It is also possible that "fīhi" is an object of "qitālun," in which case it is not in the position of a qualifier. Restricting the indefinite noun by a complement is likewise a permission for beginning with an indefinite. The rule is that when a noun is previously mentioned as indefinite and is the same noun, it is repeated with the definite article: you say, "I met a man, so I struck the man," as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿As We sent to Pharaoh a messenger﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 15], ﴿but Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 16]. It was said: The reason it is not repeated with the definite article here is that the intended meaning is not to magnify the mentioned fighting about which they asked, so that it would be repeated with the article; rather, the intended meaning is to magnify any fighting at all in the sacred month. On this basis, the second "qitālun" is other than the first. End of quote. But the definite article in a noun does not indicate magnification, since the earlier noun was indefinite; rather, it indicates prior reference. It was said in (al-Muntakhab): The two were indefinite only because the second indefinite is other than the first. They meant by the first the one they asked about, and ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh's action was for the support of Islam and the humbling of disbelief, so this is not one of the great sins. Rather, what is great is fighting other than this, which is that whose purpose is the destruction of Islam and the strengthening of disbelief. So the indefiniteness in both expressions was chosen for this subtle point, and if the reference to either or both were made with the definite article, this meaning would be lost. End of quote.

The majority agree that the ruling of this verse is the prohibition of fighting in the sacred month, since the meaning is: "Say: fighting in it is a great (sin) for them." Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatada, Ibn al-Musayyab, al-Ḍaḥḥak, and al-Awzaʿi said: It has been abrogated (mansukha) by the verse of the sword: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawba: 5], since general applicability of place entails general applicability of time. It was said: It is abrogated by His words: ﴿And fight the polytheists all together﴾ [al-Tawba: 36], and this was the view of al-Zuhri, Mujahid, and others. It was said: Both were abrogated by the Prophet's (ﷺ) campaign against Thaqif in the sacred month, and his dispatching of Abu ʿAmir to Awtas in the sacred month. It was said: It was abrogated by the Pledge of Ridwan and the fighting in Dhu al-Qaʿda. This view is weak, because that pledge was for defense, not for initiating fighting.

ʿAṭa' said: It was not abrogated. He swore by Allah that it is not lawful for people to raid in the Sanctuary (al-Ḥaram) or in the sacred month, except that they be attacked in it. This view was also reported from Mujahid. Jabir related that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not raid in the sacred months unless he was attacked," and this is His saying: ﴿Say: fighting in it is a great (sin)﴾. The view that it is muhkam (not abrogated) was preferred on the basis of this hadith, and on the basis of what Ibn Wahb related: "that the Prophet (ﷺ) paid blood money for Ibn al-Ḥaḍrami, and returned the booty and the two prisoners." Also, the verses that came after it are general in their applicability to all times, while this one is specific, and the general does not abrogate the specific by consensus.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 217 (part 2 of 3):

﴿And hindering from the way of Allah, and disbelieving in Him, and the Sacred Mosque, and expelling its people from it, is greater with Allah; and fitnah (persecution/disbelief) is greater than killing.﴾ This is a clause consisting of a subject (mubtada', the topic of a nominal sentence) and a predicate (khabar), conjoined to His statement, exalted is He, "in it is a great [sin]." Both clauses are things said, meaning: Say to them, "Fighting in the Sacred Month is a great sin," and say to them, "Hindering from such-and-such, to the end of it, is greater than fighting." It is also possible that it is detached from the speech, being a pure report that hindering from the way of Allah, and such and such, is greater. The meaning is: You, disbelievers of Quraysh, consider fighting in the Sacred Month a great matter from us, yet what you yourselves do of hindering from the way of Allah those who wish to embrace Islam, and of your disbelief in Allah, and your expelling the people of the Mosque from it, as they did to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions, is greater in crime with Allah than what the expedition (sariyyah, a small military detachment) did of fighting in the Sacred Month, on the basis of conjecture.

It has already been mentioned to us that this clause is a subject and predicate. The subject is "hindering" (ṣadd), which is an indefinite noun restricted by the prepositional phrase that follows it, so its use as a subject is permissible. It is a verbal noun (maṣdar) whose agent and object are omitted because they are known: "your hindering the Muslims from the way of Allah," and the way of Allah is Islam, as said by Muqatil; or it is "the Hajj," because they hindered the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from Makkah, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Suddi on the authority of his teachers; or it is "the Hijrah" (emigration), they hindered the Muslims from it. "And disbelief in Him" is conjoined to "and hindering," and it too is an intransitive verbal noun whose agent is omitted; its estimate is "and your disbelief in Him." The pronoun in "Him" refers to the way, since it is the thing spoken of as being hindered from; the meaning is "and disbelief in the way of Allah, which is the religion of Allah and His law." It is said that the pronoun in "Him" refers to Allah, the Exalted, as said by al-Hufi. "The Sacred Mosque" is the Kaʿbah. It was read irregularly (shadhdhan) as "wal-masjidu al-ḥarāmu" in the nominative, and its basis is that it is conjoined to "and disbelief in Him," with an omitted modifier, meaning "and disbelief in the Sacred Mosque"; then the preposition was dropped and the disbelief was annexed to the Mosque, then the annexed noun was dropped and the annexed-to noun was put in its place. It thus returns to the meaning of the majority reading with the genitive "the Sacred Mosque," according to the best of the interpretations we shall mention.

We say: They differed regarding what "and the Mosque" is conjoined to. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, al-Zamakhshari, following al-Mubarrad in this, said: it is conjoined to "the way of Allah." Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: this is the correct view. This view has been rejected on the ground that if it were conjoined to "the way of Allah," it would be connected to the word "hindering," since the estimate would be "hindering from the way of Allah and from the Sacred Mosque," and it would then be part of the verbal noun's governed complement; yet it has been separated from it by "and disbelief in Him," and it is not permissible to separate the relative clause from the relative pronoun. It is also said that it is conjoined to "the Sacred Month." This is weak, because the people did not ask about the Sacred Month, since they did not doubt its sanctity; they asked only about fighting in the Sacred Month, because it had occurred from them without their realising that it had entered (the month), so they feared sin, and the polytheists reproached them for it. End of quotation. This is what made this view weak. On this parsing, the question would concern two things: one, fighting in the Sacred Month; and the other, the Sacred Mosque, which is conjoined to the Sacred Month. The Sacred Month was not asked about in itself; it was asked about only with regard to fighting in it. Likewise, the thing conjoined to it would be asked about with regard to fighting in it. The meaning becomes: "They ask you about fighting in the Sacred Month and in the Sacred Mosque."
