So the answer is: fighting in the Sacred Month is a great [sin], and hindering from the way of Allah, and disbelief in Him. On this view, "and hindering from the way of Allah" is conjoined to the word "great," meaning: fighting in the Sacred Month is what is reported about, that it is a great sin, and that it is hindering from the way of Allah and disbelief in Him.

It is also possible that "and hindering" is a subject, and its predicate is omitted, the predicate of "fighting" indicating it. The estimate is: "and hindering from the way of Allah and disbelief in Him is great," as you say, "Zayd is standing, and ʿAmr," meaning "and ʿAmr is standing." It was answered that fighting in the Sacred Mosque, the expulsion of its people from it, is greater with Allah than fighting in it. Its being conjoined to the Sacred Month is very strained, and the Qur'anic arrangement and the eloquent construction are remote from it. It is also said that it is connected to an omitted verb indicated by the verbal noun, its estimate being: "and they hinder from the Sacred Mosque," as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They are the ones who disbelieved and barred you from the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Fath: 25]. Some of them said: this is the best of the parsings that have been given. And "the Sacred Mosque" (in the genitive) is not good in the view that goes to it, because it contains the genitive by means of an implied preposition, and this is not permissible in such a case except in necessity, as in the poet's words:

"Kulayb pointed with the fingers of their hands"

meaning: to Kulayb. It is also said that it is conjoined to the pronoun in His statement "and disbelief in Him," meaning "and [disbelief in] the Sacred Mosque." This was said by al-Farra', and it was rejected on the ground that this is not permissible except by repeating the preposition, and that is according to the school of the Basrans.

We say: conjoining to an implied pronoun in the genitive has several positions. The first: it is not permissible except by repeating the preposition, except in necessity, in which case it is permissible without repeating the preposition; this is the view of the majority of the Basrans. The second: it is permissible in ordinary speech, and this is the view of the Kufans, Yunus, Abu al-Hasan, and our master Abu ʿAli al-Shalawbin. The third: it is permissible in ordinary speech if the pronoun is emphasised, and otherwise it is not permissible in ordinary speech, as in: "I passed by you yourself and Zayd," and this is the view of al-Jarmi. What we choose is that it is permissible in ordinary speech absolutely, because the attested usage supports it and analogy strengthens it. As for the attested usage, there is what has been transmitted from the Arabs' saying: "There is nothing in it besides him and his horse," with "his horse" in the genitive conjoined to the pronoun in "besides him." The estimate is: "There is nothing in it but him and the non-existence of his horse." The second reading in the seven canonical readings is: ﴿You ask one another by Him and the wombs﴾ [al-Nisa': 1], meaning: "and by the wombs." Interpreting it as not being conjoined to the pronoun pushes the speech outside eloquence, so one should not turn to that interpretation. It was read thus by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Nakhaʿi, Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-Aʿmash, Abu Razin, and Hamzah. Whoever claims a grammatical error or mistake in it, attributing it to Hamzah, has lied. Much of this occurs in the poetry of the Arabs, to an extent that cannot be considered mere necessity. Among it is the poet's saying:

"We hang our swords on pillars like these, / and between them and the earth is a hollow of dust-heaps"

Another said:

"Why did you not ask about Dhu al-Jamajim concerning them, / and about Abu Nuʿaym, bearer of the burning banner?"

Another said:

"Through us alone, never through others, are hopes attained, / and the grim calamities of misfortunes are removed."

Another said:

"When they kindle a fire for the war against their enemy, / he who roasts himself in it and in its blaze has failed."

Another said:

"If there had been for me and for Zuhayr a third, the herds of the wild doves would have come to us, / the worst of watering-times."

A man of Tayy said:

"When we, nay, two companions, guarded a band / it remained secure from those who oppose it."

Al-ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas said:

"I charge against the squadron, unconcerned, / whether my death is in it or in something else."

Sibawayh, may Allah have mercy on him, recited:

"Today you have indeed spent the night insulting us and reviling us, / so go away; what is wrong with you and the days, of wonder!"

Another said:

"Is there a sign in you, or one who is sent back / of the donkeys of the dung-heap, a courageous, bold one?"

You see this attested usage and its abundance, and the Arabs' variety in the conjunctive particle: sometimes they conjoin with "and" (wa), sometimes with "or" (aw), sometimes with "but rather" (bal), sometimes with "or" in questions (am), and sometimes with "no" (la). All this variety indicates permissibility, although the more common usage is to repeat the preposition, as in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And upon them and upon the ship you are carried﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 22]; ﴿He said to it and to the earth: "Come both, willingly or unwillingly"﴾ [Fussilat: 11]; ﴿Say: "Allah delivers you from it and from every distress"﴾ [al-An'am: 64]. There has also come, conjoined without repeating the preposition, His statement: ﴿and for those for whom you are not providers﴾ [al-Hijr: 20], conjoined to His statement ﴿We have provided for you therein means of livelihood﴾ [al-A'raf: 10], meaning "and for whom"; and His statement: ﴿and what is recited to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 127], conjoined to the pronoun in His statement "concerning them" (fihinna), meaning "and concerning what is recited to you."

As for analogy, it is this: just as it is permissible for a noun to be substituted by a pronoun or emphasised by it without repeating the preposition, so likewise it is permissible to conjoin to it without repeating the preposition. As for one who argues for prohibition on the ground that the pronoun is like the tanwin (nunation), so conjoining to it should be impermissible except with repetition, since the tanwin is not conjoined to in any way: once it has been established that conjoining without repeating the preposition is attested in the speech of the Arabs, both in prose and verse, then the conjoining of "and the Sacred Mosque" to the pronoun in "in Him" comes out more probable, indeed it is definite, because the quality of the speech and the eloquence of the construction require it. "And the expulsion of its people" is conjoined to the verbal noun before it, and it is a verbal noun annexed to its object, the estimate being "and your expulsion of its people." The pronoun in "its people" refers to "the Sacred Mosque." They made the believers its people because they are the ones who uphold its rights, or because they will become its people in the end. They did not make the disbelievers who remain in Makkah its people, because their staying is incidental and will pass, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They are not its guardians; its guardians are only the righteous﴾ [al-Anfal: 34]. "From it" is connected to "expulsion," and the pronoun in "from it" refers to the Sacred Mosque. It is also said that it refers to "the way of Allah," which is Islam, but the first is more apparent. "Greater" (akbar) is the predicate of the subject "hindering" and what is conjoined to it. It is possible that it is the predicate of the whole collection, and it is possible that it is the predicate of each of them individually, as you say: "Zayd and ʿAmr and Bakr are better than Khalid," meaning: each one of them is better than Khalid. This apparent sense is what is intended, not the collection. The singular form of the predicate is because it is an elative (af'al al-tafdil) used with "than" (min), which introduces the less-favoured item in the estimate. Its estimate is: "greater than fighting in the Sacred Month," and it has been omitted because it is known. It is also said that "hindering" is the subject, "disbelief" is conjoined to it, and the predicate of both is omitted, indicated by the predicate of "expulsion." The estimate is: "hindering from the way of Allah and disbelief in Him and in the Sacred Mosque is greater." This estimate is not needed, because we have already shown that "greater" is the predicate of all three. "With Allah" is governed by "greater," and "with" (ʿinda) is not intended to mean a place; rather that is a metaphor.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah and al-Sajawandi reported from al-Farra' that he said: "hindering" is conjoined to "great." Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: this is an error, because the meaning leads to the conclusion that His statement "and disbelief in Him" is also conjoined to "great," and it would follow from this that the expulsion of the people of the Mosque from it is greater than disbelief with Allah, and the corruption of this is clear. End of Ibn ʿAṭiyyah's words. It is not as he stated, and it is not required that what he said, that "and disbelief in Him" is conjoined to "great," be the case, since it is possible that the speech was complete at His statement "and hindering from the way of Allah," and that fighting in the Sacred Month was reported about with two predicates: one, that it is great; and the other, that it is hindering from the way of Allah. Then He began: "and disbelief in Allah, and in the Sacred Mosque, and the expulsion of its people from it, is greater with Allah than the fighting which is great, and which is hindering from the way of Allah." This is a sound and good meaning, and there is no doubt that disbelief in Allah and what is conjoined to it is greater than the fighting mentioned. As for his statement, "it would follow from this that the expulsion of the people of the Mosque from it is greater than disbelief with Allah, and the corruption of this is clear," it is not a sound statement, because nothing of what he mentioned follows from it except by a remote strain. Rather, what follows from it is that the expulsion of the people of the Mosque from it is greater with Allah than the fighting which is reported as great and as hindering from the way of Allah. So the thing judged to be greater is the expulsion, and the thing it is measured against is the fighting, not disbelief and persecution. That is, disbelief and polytheism; this was said by Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, and others.

Or the persecution inflicted on the believers to make them turn away from Islam. This is worse in its wrongdoing (ḥurm) than killing. According to the majority of the exegetes (mufassirūn), the meaning is that the trial (fitnah) that was tempting the Muslims away from their religion until they perished is a greater crime (ijtirām) than their killing of you in the Sacred Mosque. It has also been said: the meaning is that the trial is more severe than if they had killed that tempted person. That is, your action against every human being is worse than our action, because the trial is a pain that keeps renewing, whereas killing is a pain that comes to an end. As for one who interprets fitnah as disbelief (kufr), the meaning for him is: your disbelief is worse than our killing of those people. Here he stated the lesser element explicitly, namely his words "than killing," and did not omit it, because there is no indication that it should be omitted. This differs from his words "is greater in the sight of Allah," where the element being compared against was mentioned earlier, namely "fighting" (al-qitāl).

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaḥsh said poetry about this incident:

*You count the killing in the sacred month a great matter,*
*But greater than it is what the rightly guided one would see, were he rightly guided.*
*Your turning away from what Muhammad says, and disbelief in him, while Allah is watching and witnessing.*
*And your expulsion of his people from the mosque of Allah, so that no one may prostrate to Allah in the House.*
*For we, even if you revile us for a killing,*
*And a rebel and an envious one spreads rumours against Islam,*
*We gave the son of al-Ḥaḍramī a drink of our spears at Nakhla, when the one who kindles war kindled it.*
*Blood, while the son of ʿAbd Allāh, ʿUthmān, is between us, contended for by a rancorous, hostile rival of the leather strap.*

* *

﴿And they will not cease fighting you until they turn you back from your religion, if they are able.﴾ The pronoun in "they will not cease" refers to the disbelievers. This indicates that the subject pronoun in His words "they ask you" refers to the disbelievers, while the object pronoun in "they fight you" is addressed to the believers. The address shifted from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to the believers. This is an informing from Allah to the believers about the extreme enmity of the disbelievers, their separation from them, the continuation of that enmity, and that their fighting of you is contingent upon their capacity to do so and their power over it. The phrase "until they turn you back" (ḥattā yaruddūkum) may be read as a limit (ghāyah) or as a cause (taʿlīl). Abū al-Baqāʾ took it in both senses, and in both cases it is connected to "they fight you." Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "until they turn you back" is in the accusative by ḥattā, because it is a pure limit. Al-Zamakhsharī said: ḥattā here has the meaning of causation, like your saying: "So-and-so worships Allah until he enters Paradise," meaning: they fight you in order that they may turn you back. End of quotation. Al-Zamakhsharī's analysis is more acceptable in meaning, since the action proceeding from them that is contrary to the believers, namely "fighting," is given a cause that necessitates it. Thus the time of the action extends for as long as the cause of the action exists. This differs from the limit, which is a restriction on the action without mention of what motivates it. So the time of its occurrence is restricted by its limit, whereas the time of the action that has a cause is restricted by the existence of that cause. There is a difference in strength between what is restricted by a limit and what is restricted by a cause, since restriction by cause includes mention of the motive, whereas restriction by limit does not. "From your religion" (ʿan dīnikum) is connected to "they turn back" (yaruddūkum). Here "religion" (dīn) means Islam. "If they are able" (in istaṭāʿū) is a conditional clause whose response is omitted, indicated by what precedes it. The estimated sense is: if they are able, then they will not cease fighting you. Whoever permits the response of the conditional to precede it says that "they will not cease" is the response. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "if they are able" is a expression of improbability regarding their ability, like a man saying to his enemy: "If you overpower me, then do not spare me," while he is confident that the other will not overpower him. End of quotation. There is no objection to this.

* *

﴿And whoever of you turns back from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever, those are the ones whose deeds have become void in this world and the Hereafter.﴾ "Irtadda" (apostatised) is of the form iftaʿala from "radd," which means returning, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So they both went back, retracing their footsteps﴾ [al-Kahf: 64]. Some grammarians counted it among the verbs that take two objects when it means "made" or "rendered," as in His words: ﴿so he regained his sight﴾ [Yūsuf: 96], meaning he became sighted. There is no disagreement here about the contraction of the two identical consonants (fakk al-mithlayn), and contraction is the dialect of the Ḥijāz. The form iftaʿala here carries the meaning of effort and acquisition (taʿammul and takassub), because it is effortful: whoever has engaged with the religion of truth is unlikely to turn back from it. For this reason the form iftaʿala is used here. This meaning, namely effort and acquisition, is one of the meanings for which the form iftaʿala comes. "Minkum" (from among you) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relative to the concealed pronoun in "yartadid," which refers back to "man" (whoever). The "min" is partitive (lil-tabʿīḍ). "ʿAn dīnihi" (from his religion) is connected to "yartadid." Here "religion" means Islam, because the address is to the Muslims. The thing turned back to is the religion of disbelief, as evidenced by the fact that the opposite of truth is falsehood, and by His words: ﴿and dies while he is a disbeliever﴾. These are two conditions, one of which is conjoined to the other by the particle fa (then), which implies that death follows disbelief immediately after apostasy and is connected to it. He made the voiding of deeds in this world and the Hereafter the consequence of these conditions. The voiding in this world is through the entitlement to his being killed and his being classed with the disbelievers in legal rulings. In the Hereafter it is through what he will ultimately face of everlasting punishment. It has also been said: the voiding of their deeds in this world is their failure to attain what they intend of harm and plotting against the Muslims, so they gain nothing from that, because Allah has honoured His religion through His helpers.

The apparent meaning of this conditional and its consequence is that the voiding of deeds is consequent upon dying in a state of disbelief, not upon mere apostasy. This is the view of a group of scholars, including al-Shāfiʿī. The voiding of deeds is also consequent upon mere disbelief in His words: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in faith, his deed has certainly become void﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 5]; ﴿And if they had associated others with Allah, what they used to do would have been lost from them﴾ [al-Anʿām: 88]; ﴿And those who denied Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter, their deeds have become void﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 147]; ﴿If you associate others with Allah, your deed will surely become void﴾ [al-Zumar: 65]. The address in meaning is to his community. Mālik, Abū Ḥanīfah and others held this view, meaning that his deed is voided by the apostasy itself, without the requirement of dying in that state, even if he returns to Islam. The fruit of this disagreement appears in a Muslim who performed the Hajj, then apostatised, then embraced Islam again. Mālik said: he is obligated to perform the Hajj. Al-Shāfiʿī said: he is not obligated to perform the Hajj. Al-Shāfiʿī argues: an unrestricted (muṭlaq) and a restricted (muqayyad) text have come together, so the unrestricted is restricted. Others say: these are two conditions, each with its own consequence. One condition is apostasy, which leads to the voiding of deeds. The second condition is dying in disbelief, which leads to eternal abiding in the Fire.

The clause "while he is a disbeliever" (wa huwa kāfir) is in the position of a circumstantial clause relative to the concealed pronoun in "fa-yamut" (and dies). It appears to be an emphatic circumstantial clause, because if it were dispensed with, its meaning would still be understood, since what precedes it already implies the immediacy of death after apostasy. That the circumstantial element is a clause contains an intensification of emphasis, since the pronoun is repeated twice in it, unlike a singular adjective, which contains only one pronoun.

The exegetes here addressed the ruling on the apostate, whereas the verse addresses only the voiding of deeds. We have already mentioned the disagreement about it, namely whether dying in disbelief is a condition or whether deeds are voided by apostasy alone. As for his ruling with respect to execution, al-Nakhaʿī and al-Thawrī held that he should be asked to repent while kept imprisoned permanently. Ṭāwūs, ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, al-Ḥasan (in one of the reports from him), ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Abī Salamah, and al-Shāfiʿī in one of his two opinions, held that he is killed without being asked to repent. Something similar is reported from Abū Mūsā and Muʿādh. A group of scholars said that he should be asked to repent. As to whether he should be asked to repent immediately, or within one hour, or a month (this was reported from ʿAlī), or three days (reported from ʿUmar and ʿUthmān, and this is the view of Mālik as transmitted by Ibn al-Qāsim, the view of Aḥmad, Isḥāq, al-Shāfiʿī in one of his two opinions, and the people of opinion), or a hundred times (this is the view of al-Ḥasan).

ʿAṭāʾ said: if he was the son of two Muslim parents, he is killed without being asked to repent; if he had embraced Islam and then apostatised, he is asked to repent. Al-Zuhrī said: he is called to Islam; if he repents, well and good, otherwise he is killed. Abū Ḥanīfah said: Islam is presented to him; if he embraces it, well and good, otherwise he is killed on the spot, unless he asks for a delay, in which case he is granted three days. The well-known view from him and his companions is that he is not killed until he is asked to repent. For them the heretic (zindīq) and the apostate are the same. Mālik said: heretics are killed without being asked to repent. If he apostatised, then returned, then apostatised again, his ruling for the second, third, or fourth apostasy is the same as the first. If he returns after the fourth apostasy, he is beaten and released. It has been said that he is imprisoned until signs of repentance and sincerity appear in him. If a disbeliever moves from one form of disbelief to another, the majority hold that he is not killed. Al-Muzanī and al-Rabīʿ reported from al-Shāfiʿī that a dhimmī (non-Muslim protected subject) who changes his religion is joined by the ruler (imām) to the land of war, is expelled from his city, and his property may be seized along with the property of the people of war if the House (the territory) is overpowered. This is the ruling for a man.

As for a woman who apostatises: Mālik, al-Awzāʿī, al-Layth and al-Shāfiʿī said she is killed just like a man, equally. ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ḥasan, al-Thawrī, Abū Ḥanīfah and his companions, Ibn Shubrumah, and Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said she is not killed. This is reported from ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās.

As for his inheritance: they agreed that his non-Muslim relatives do not inherit from him, except what is reported from Qatādah and ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, that they do inherit from him. Something contrary to this is reported from ʿUmar. ʿAlī, al-Ḥasan, al-Shaʿbī, al-Ḥakam, al-Layth, Abū Ḥanīfah in one of his two opinions, and Ibn Rāhawayh said: his Muslim relatives inherit from him. Mālik, Rabīʿah, Ibn Abī Laylā, al-Shāfiʿī, and Abū Thawr said: his inheritance goes to the public treasury (bayt al-māl). Ibn Shubrumah, Abū Yūsuf, Muḥammad, and al-Awzāʿī in one of the two reports said: what he acquired after apostasy goes to his Muslim heirs. Abū Ḥanīfah said: what he acquired while in Islam before apostasy goes to his Muslim heirs.

Al-Ḥasan read "ḥabaṭat" (with a fatḥah on the bāʾ). Both are dialects. Abū al-Simmāk also read it this way throughout the Qur'an. As for His words: ﴿those are the ones whose deeds have become void﴾, the demonstrative "those" (ulāʾika) indicates the persons who possess the attributes mentioned earlier. It is used in the plural in accordance with the meaning of "man" (whoever), since first the verb was construed according to the wording of "man" in His words "yartadid, fa-yamut wa huwa kāfir," and when one combines the two constructions, the more correct practice is to begin with construction according to the wording, then with construction according to the meaning. This most eloquent arrangement is the one in which this verse came. The phrase "in this world" (fī al-dunyā) is connected to the verb "ḥabaṭat" (have become void).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 218:

﴿And those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217]. The interpretation of this sentence has already been given, so it suffices and there is no need to repeat it. This sentence may be an independent statement from God Most High about the eternal abiding of these people in the Fire, so it is not included in the apodosis (al-jaza', the consequent of the conditional), and it is coordinated with the conditional sentence. It may also be coordinated with His words: ﴿Then those, their deeds have become void﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217], in which case it is included in the apodosis, because what is coordinated with an apodosis is an apodosis. This latter view is preferable, because proximity is a preponderant factor. The first view is given preference because it implies independence.

«﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who emigrated and strove in the way of God, those hope for the mercy of God﴾. The occasion of its revelation (sabab al-nuzul) is that 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh said: "O Messenger of God, suppose that we are punished for what we have done; do we then hope for a reward and recompense from Him?" So it was revealed.» This is because 'Abd Allah was a believer, he was an emigrant, and he was, by reason of this fighting, a striver. Then the verse is general in respect of whoever possesses these attributes.

Al-Zamakhshari said: 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh and his companions, when they killed the man from Hadramawt, some people thought that if they were safe from sin, then they had no reward; so it was revealed. End of his words. (p-152) It is like the first, except that there is a difference regarding the one who held the opinion: in the first it is Ibn Jahsh, and in al-Zamakhshari's statement it is a group of people. On this occasion of revelation, the connection of this verse with what precedes it is clear.

It has been said: when He made jihad obligatory by His words: ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 216], and made clear that abandoning it is a cause of threat, He followed that with mention of those who undertake it, and a threat is hardly ever mentioned without a promise following it. This sentence contains three attributes, and they came in an order according to the events and the reality, because faith comes first, then emigration, then striving in the way of God. And since faith is the root, it was singled out with a separate relative pronoun (al-mawsul) on its own. And since emigration and striving are branches of it, they were singled out with one relative pronoun, because in terms of being branches they are like one thing. The predicate of "inna" (indeed) came as a sentence introduced by "ulaika" (those), because the demonstrative noun (ism al-isharah) is what comprises the preceding attributes of faith, emigration and striving. It is not a repetition of the relative pronoun with a conjunction indicating difference in the essences; rather, it is a repetition with respect to the attributes, while the essences are those characterized by the three attributes. So it returns to the meaning of conjoining some attributes to others for the sake of difference, because "those who believed" are a category by themselves, distinct from "those who emigrated and strove."

He used the word "yarjun" (they hope) because as long as a person is in the bond of life, it cannot be certain that he will go to Paradise, even if he obeys to the utmost degree, since one does not know how his end will be, and he should not rely on his deeds, since he does not know whether they will be accepted or not. Also, because the verse mentions three attributes, and there must alongside them be the rest of the good works, and he hopes that God will grant him success in them just as He granted him success in these three; therefore He said: "then those hope." Or the mention of hope is because they imagine that they have not fulfilled the right of God's support in jihad, nor discharged what was incumbent upon them of that; so they approach God with fear and hope, as He Most High said: ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 60].

It is narrated from Qatadah that he said: it is for the best of this community; then God made them people of hope, as they hear. It has also been said: hope enters here regarding the quantity and timing of the reward, not regarding the principle of the reward, since that is certain and assured by the true promise. The word "rahmat" (mercy) is written here with a "ta'" in accordance with the dialect of those who pause on it with a "ta'" here, or on the basis of continuous recitation, since in continuous recitation it is a "ta'". There are seven places where "rahmat" is written with a "ta'": the first is this one; and in al-A'raf: ﴿Indeed, the mercy of God is near﴾ [al-A'raf: 56]; and in Hud: ﴿The mercy of God and His blessings﴾ [Hud: 73]; and in Maryam: ﴿A mention of the mercy of your Lord﴾ [Maryam: 2]; and in al-Zukhruf: ﴿Do they apportion the mercy of your Lord?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 32], and ﴿But the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 32]; and in al-Rum: ﴿So look at the traces of the mercy of God﴾ [al-Rum: 50].

* *

(And God is Forgiving, Merciful). When He mentioned that they are eager for the mercy of God, God Most High informed that He is characterized by mercy, and He added another attribute, which is that He is characterized by forgiveness. So it is as if it were said: God Most High, when they thought and hoped for His reward, then mercy is established, because it is among His attributes, Exalted is He. These noble verses have included God Most High's report about the past generations, that they were upon one path, and that He sent to them prophets as bearers of good news to whoever obeyed, with reward from God Most High, and as warners to whoever disobeyed, with punishment from God. He placed the good news first because it is what brings joy, and because its outcome is the pleasure of God with whoever follows His commands and avoids His prohibitions. He also sent down with them a Book from Him, accompanied by the manifest truth, so that it would be more precise in preserving what they brought of the laws, because what they brought which is not in a book that is read and studied over the passage of ages may pass away with their passing; so when what was legislated for them is perpetuated in written pages, it is more enduring. Indeed, the fruit of books is to settle disputes among people concerning matters in which they differ, regarding their creeds, their obligations, and the interests of their worldly life. Then He mentioned that those who differed about what they differed about were only those who were given it, that is, were given the Book and it reached them from God; and that was after the verses had become clear and had come to them. So it is as if what was meant to lead to guidance and to settling differences became, for these people, a cause of difference. They placed upon the coming of the clear thing the opposite of its requirement. The factor that drove them to this is only the transgression and injustice that arose among them. Then God guided the believers to follow the truth about which those who differed had differed, and that is by God's facilitation for them. This is without any prior merit of deserving; rather, His guidance of them to the truth is by His granting them power to it, Exalted is He. Then He Most High mentioned that guidance to the straight path (p-153) is only for whomever He wills to guide. Then He Most High mentioned, addressing the believers, since He had informed of the sending of the messengers with the legal obligations, that it is not to be reckoned that you will attain the lofty rank of success by entering Paradise, while the trial has not yet come upon you as it came upon those who were before you. Then He explained the example of the past ones: that adversity and hardship touched them, and that they were shaken, so that they asked their Lord about the time of the coming of victory, so that their souls might endure what He had tried them with, and that they might await relief from God soon. So it was answered them that the help of God is near, and what is near, is it not? The sum is: their souls were calmed from that shaking by waiting for the near victory.

Then they asked the Messenger of God ﷺ about what they should spend of their wealth in the ways of righteousness. He did not clarify to them the kind of what they should spend, nor its amount, but mentioned the recipients of it, because that is the more important part of the answer. It is as if it were said: whatever you spend, of little or much, its recipients are the closest people to you. These are the two parents, who were the cause of your existence and your upbringing from the time you were created until you came to have something of the world, and of their tenderness toward you. Then He mentioned the nearest relatives with the comparative form, because they are the ones who share your lineage, and spending on them is both charity and maintaining kinship. Then He mentioned the orphans, who are those whose fathers have died, so there is no one to take care of their interests; so spending on them is a great kindness. Then He mentioned the needy (al-masakin), who are those poor people who have reached the state of destitution (maskanah), which is the lack of movement and disposal in the affairs of the world and its livelihood. Then God Most High informed that whatever you spend, God knows it and records it, so He will repay for it and reward. Then God Most High informed about the prescription of fighting for the believers, and that it is disliked by natures, because of what it entails of the destruction of lives, the loss of wealth, and the violation of bodies through travel in it and otherwise. Then He mentioned that a person may dislike a thing while it is good for him, because its consequence is toward good; so fighting, although it is disliked by nature, is nevertheless good if one is spared; its good is in victory over the enemies of God, in spoils, in gaining control over them by killing and plunder, and in possessing a home. And if one is killed, its good is that he has with God the rank of the martyrs, and what has come regarding this great rank in the Book of God and in what is authentically reported from the Messenger of God ﷺ will suffice you.

Then He mentioned the opposite of this, which is His words: ﴿But it is possible that you dislike a thing and it is good for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 216]. Among what is loved is abandoning fighting, which leads to ease and rest; but in that is the great evil of the domination of the enemies of God and the striking of the Muslims, and the uprooting of their root by killing, plunder, and seizure of their homelands. Whenever a person inclines to rest, his enemy covets him and reaches his aims from him. Zuhayr has indeed excelled when he said:

Bold: whenever he is wronged, he punishes with his own wrong swiftly; and if he does not initiate wrong, he will wrong.

Then He Most High mentioned that He knows what they do not know, in prescribing fighting. He Most High is Knowing of what the religious and worldly interests are that result for you from the legislation of fighting. Then He Most High mentioned that they asked the Messenger of God ﷺ about fighting in the sacred month, because of what occurred from them in that, not with intent, but on the assumption that the time in which it occurred was not one of the sacred months. So they were told that this is a great sin, since the custom was that the sacred months were not to have fighting in them. Then He mentioned that greater than that is what the disbelievers commit of barring the Muslims from the way of God, and of disbelief in God, and in the Sacred Mosque, and of expelling its people from it. Then He Most High mentioned that the trial (fitnah) is greater than killing, namely, the trial of a Muslim man from his religion, which is greater than killing him while he is upon his religion; because that trial leads him to the Fire, while his being killed leads him to Paradise. Then God Most High informed about the enduring enmity of the disbelievers, and that their aim is only to try you away from your religion and to return you to what they are upon of error; and that whenever they are able to do so and have power over it, they will fight you. Then God Most High informed that whoever turns back from his true religion to his false religion, and dies upon that, then all of his good deeds that preceded have become void in this world, by attaching him to the disbelievers and applying to him the rulings of apostates; and in the Hereafter, so no fruit of them remains for which he might hope for forgiveness of what he committed; rather, his destination is the Fire, abiding therein forever.

Then, after mentioning the state of the one who apostatizes from his religion, He mentioned the state of the one who believed (p-154) in God, remained steadfast in his faith, emigrated from his homeland, which is the place of disbelief, to the abode of Islam, and then strove in the way of God against those who disbelieve in God; and he is hopeful for the mercy of God. Then He Most High mentioned that He is Forgiving of what occurred from him before faith, and of what may intervene during faith of some disobedience; and that He is Merciful to him, so He makes realize for him what he hoped for of His mercy.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 219 (part 1 of 3):

﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: "In both there is great sin and benefit for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit." And they ask you what they should spend. Say: "The surplus." Thus God makes the signs clear to you, so that you may reflect, ﴿on this world and the Hereafter.﴾ They ask you about orphans. Say: "Setting things right for them is good. And if you mix with them, they are your brothers. God knows the corrupter from the reformer. Had God willed, He would have burdened you. Indeed God is Mighty and Wise.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 220]

﴿Do not marry idolatresses until they believe. A believing slave woman is better than an idolatress, even if she pleases you. And do not marry off your women to idolaters until they believe. A believing slave is better than an idolater, even if he pleases you. Those invite to the Fire, but God invites to the Garden and forgiveness by His leave, and He makes His signs clear to people so that they may take heed.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 221]

Khamr (wine): it is the juice pressed from grapes once it boils, becomes strong, and throws off foam. It is so named from kh-m-r, meaning "to cover," and from it comes khimar (a woman's headcover). One says takhammarat and ikhtamarat, and "she has a good khimrah" (a good covering or state of intoxication). Khamr also means whatever covers you of trees and other things. One says "he entered among the people's khimar and ghimar," meaning into a hidden place. Also: "khamr futatikum" (the remnant of your dough/mixture), and "khamiri Umma 'Amir," like a fool. And "khamiri hadajir, ataka ma tuhadhir," where hadajir is a name for both the male and female of the beasts of prey. Its meaning is: "Enter the cover and conceal yourself." Since it covers the intellect, it was named thus. It is also said: it is so named because it "khammara," that is, covers, until it matures and becomes strong. Ibn al-Anbari said: it was named thus because it "khamara" the intellect, that is, mixes with it. One says: "the disease khamara," meaning it mingled. It is also said: it was named thus because it is left (to ferment) until it ripens, as one says "the dough ikhtamara," meaning it reached its ripeness, and "khammara al-ra'y," meaning he left the opinion until its course became clear. According to these derivations, the word is originally a verbal noun (masdar) but is used to mean the active participle (ism al-fa'il) or the passive participle (ism al-maf'ul).

Maysir: gambling (qimar). It is on the pattern mafil from y-s-r, like mawʿid from w-ʿ-d. One says: "yassartu al-maysir," meaning I gambled with him. The poet said:

"Had you gambled with horses that I have gambled with, every gain that people have gained is a loss."

Its derivation is either from yusr, which is ease, or from yasar (wealth), because it strips the player of his wealth, or from yasara, when something became obligatory, or from yasara, when it cut up (the slaughtered animal). The yasir is the one who cuts up the camel (al-jazur), dividing it into portions. The poet said:

"I say to them at the mountain pass, when they gamble over me: Have you not despaired that I am the son of the horseman Zahdam?"

The camel on which the arrows are cast was called maysir, because it is the place of gain (al-yasar). Then the arrows themselves were called maysir, by metonymy (al-mujawara). The yasar is the one who takes part in striking the arrows; its plural is ayʿsar. It is also said that yasar is the plural of yasir, like harris and haras and ahras (guard). The description of the maysir is that it has ten arrows. It is also said eleven, as mentioned in it. These are: the azlam, the aqlam, and the sihām. Seven of them have shares, and for them are portions according to the number of shares: al-qadd, which has one arrow; al-tawʾam, which has two; al-raqib, which has three; al-hils, which has four; al-nafis, which has five; al-musbil, which has six; and al-muʿalla, which has seven. Three arrows with no shares are: al-manih, al-safih, and al-wagh. It is also said there are four: al-masdar, al-mudʿif, al-manih, and al-safih. These three or four are added, according to differing reports, so that the arrows multiply and become confused for the al-hurdah, who is the one who strikes the arrows, so that he cannot find a way to favour anyone. He is also called al-mujil, al-mughid, al-darib, and al-darib, and the plural is duraba'; he is a man trusted among them. It is also said that a raqib is appointed so that he does not favour anyone. Then the striker kneels on his knees, wraps himself in a garment, and puts his head out. He places those arrows in the rababa, which is a bag in which they are put, then shakes it, and puts his hand in and draws out an arrow for each man by name. Whoever draws an arrow of the shares takes the portion marked on that arrow, and whoever draws one of those three gets nothing and must pay for the whole camel.

It was the custom of the Arabs to cast these arrows (p. 155) in the winter season, in hard times and in the cold biting frost, for the poor. They would buy a camel, and the gamblers would guarantee its price. Then it would be slaughtered and divided into ten parts according to the saying of Abu ʿAmr, or twenty-eight according to the number of shares of the arrows according to the saying of al-Asmaʿi. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: al-Asmaʿi erred in dividing the camel into twenty-eight. Whoever drew a share would give it to the poor, and would not eat any of it. They boasted of this, and called the one who did not take part in it "al-barama" (the stingy one), and they reviled him for it. Among their boasting in this is the saying of al-Aʿsha:

"They are those who feed the guest when winter comes, and who place the food in the hands of the gamblers."

Zuhayr said about the barama:

"Until he takes refuge in a shameless, stingy, miserly man, who is not generous when his companions gain."

Sometimes they stood up for themselves (i.e., they refused to be such people).

Tafakkur (reflection) on something: directing the thought toward it and turning it over repeatedly. Fikr is the mind (dhihn). Khalt (mixing): joining one thing with another. Khalaṭa is the form fa'ala from it, and khilt is the mixed thing, like rigy (fodder). Ikhwan is the plural of akh (brother), and the akh is well known; he is the one whom your father and mother bore, or one of them. The plural of fa'l into fi'lan is not regular. Anat (hardship): difficulty, and from it comes ʿanat al-ghurbah (the hardship of exile). ʿAqabah ʿanut is a steep climb. ʿAnata al-baʿir means the camel broke after being set. Nikah (marriage): intercourse, which is copulation. Al-Tabrizi said: its origin among the Arabs is the attachment of one thing to another and clinging to it, and from it the saying "nakaha al-matar al-ard" (the rain covered the earth), related by Tha'lab in al-Amali from Abu Zayd and Ibn al-A'rabi. al-Farra' related from the Arabs: nukh al-mar'ah, with a dammah on the nun, meaning a part between the front and back passages. When they say "nakahaha," it means he reached its nukh, that place of hers. It is seldom said "nakahaha" as one says "bada'aha." It is said that nikah has come in Arabic poetry meaning only the contract. Among that is the saying of a poet:

"Do not approach a neighbour woman, for her secret is forbidden to you, so marry or remain celibate."

That is, contract marriage, or otherwise abstain from women and be solitary, for he said: do not approach a neighbour woman in the way that is forbidden. It has also come with the meaning of intercourse, as he said:

"Those who ride the backs of their women, and who copulate with cows on the banks of the Tigris."

Abu ʿAli said: the Arabs distinguished between the contract and intercourse by a subtle difference. When they say "Fulan nakaha Fulanah," they mean only the contract. When they say "nakaha imra'atahu" or "zawjatahu," they mean nothing but intercourse. Amah (slave-girl): a female owned slave, whose final letter (lam) has been deleted, and it is a waw. The proof of this is its appearing in the plural. al-Kilabi said:

"As for the maidservants, they do not claim me as a son when the sons of the dead are called to account for shame."

In the verbal noun one says "amah bayyinat al-umuwwah," and "she acknowledged the umuwwah," meaning servitude. It is also plural as ima' and a'mi, like akamah, akam, and akam. Its origin is a'mu, and the rules of morphology applied to it. In a hadith: "Do not prevent God's maidservants from God's mosques." And a poet said:

"She walks with her, her steps are short like the walk of the she-camels with worn feet."

Its pattern is amwah, and its lam was deleted without regular analogy, since analogy would require it to become an alif because it is vowelled and the letter before it is open, like qanat. Abu al-Haytham claimed that the plural of amah is amw, and that its pattern is fa'lah with a sukun on the ʿayn, so it is like nakhlah and nakhl, and baqlah and baql. Its origin is amwah, and they deleted its lam because it is a soft letter. When they pluralised it on the pattern of nakhlah and nakhl, they were obliged to say amah and umm, but they disliked making it two letters, and they disliked restoring the deleted waw since it was at the end of the noun, so they put the waw first and made it an alif between the alif and the mim. What Abu al-Haytham claimed is not valid, for if it were as he claimed, the i'rab (grammatical case) would fall on the mim as it falls on the lam of nakhl. But it falls on the deleted ya', which is the lam, since its origin is (p. 156) alamu. Then it was treated as they treated "al-adluww" and "al-ajruww," the plurals of dalw and jarw. The second hamzah was changed into an alif, as it was changed in "Adam." That is why you say "jaʾat al-amiyy" (the amiyy came). If it were as Abu al-Haytham claimed, it would be "jaʾat al-amm," with a damma on the mim.

Mahid (menstruation): the pattern mafil from haydh, suitable for the verbal noun, the place and the time. One says: "hadat al-mar'ah tahid haydan wa mahidan." They formed it on the pattern mafil with the ʿayn vowelled with kasra and with fatha. In the case of this type of verb whose ʿayn is ya' (yā'ī al-ʿayn), of the form fa'ala yaf'ilu, there are three positions. The first: its analogical form is maf'al, with a fatha on the ʿayn when the meaning is the verbal noun, and with a kasra when the meaning is the place or time, so that it becomes like madrab for the verbal noun and madrib with a kasra (on the ra'), that is, for time and place. On this view, mahid is irregular when it means the verbal noun, and regular when it means time and place. The second position: you have the choice between opening its ʿayn or making it kasra, as came in mahid and mahad. The argument for this view is that both forms were common in this, so they became standard. The third position: restriction to what is heard. Whatever the Arabs said as mafil with kasra or maf'al with fatha, we do not go beyond it, and this is the most preferred position. The original meaning of haydh in lexicography is flowing. One says: "hadat al-sayl wa fada" (the torrent flowed and overflowed). al-Farra' said: "hadat al-shajarah" when its gum flowed. al-Azhari said: from this comes the name hawd (basin) for the pool, because water flows (yahid) into it, that is, flows. The Arabs substitute waw for ya' and ya' for waw, and because they are from one region, which is the air.

I'tizal (withdrawal): the opposite of association. It is despair of a thing and distance from it. It is sometimes with the body and sometimes with the heart. It is the ifti'al form from 'azl, which is removing one thing from another. Anna: a noun, used as a conditional adverb of place, and comes as an adverb of time with the meaning of "mata" (when), and as an interrogative with the meaning of "kayfa" (how). It is indeclinable because it includes the meaning of the conditional particle and of the interrogative particle, and it is in the position of the accusative and is never inflected in any other way.

* *

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 219 (part 2 of 3):**

﴿They ask you about wine and gambling.﴾ The occasion of its revelation was the question of ʿUmar and Muʿadh, who said: "O Messenger of Allah, give us a ruling on wine and gambling; for they take away the intellect and strip away wealth." So it was revealed. The connection (munasabah) of this verse to what precedes it is that when they asked, "What should we spend?", He explained to them the outlets for that: parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer. Then He mentioned the obligation of fighting and striving in the way of Allah. The question about wine and gambling fits this context, since these two are also among the outlets of wealth, and with their constant indulgence, little wealth remains to be given in charity or spent in jihad. Therefore the question about them occurred.

Some of those who wrote on *naskh* (abrogation) said: Most scholars hold that this verse abrogated what was permitted of drinking wine. Surat al-Anʿam is Meccan, so what it contains, namely His saying ﴿Say: I do not find﴾ [al-Anʿam: 145], is not to be taken into account. Ibn Jubayr said: When ﴿In them is great sin and benefits for people﴾ was revealed, some people disliked wine because of the sin, while others drank it for its benefits, until ﴿Do not approach the prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 43] was revealed, so they avoided it during the times of prayer, until ﴿So avoid it﴾ [al-Maʾidah: 90] was revealed, and it was then prohibited. Makki said: This indicates that this verse is abrogated by the verse of al-Maʾidah, and there is no doubt that al-Maʾidah was revealed after al-Baqarah. Qatadah said: Allah censured wine through this verse but did not prohibit it.

Some people said: It should not be said that this verse abrogated what was permitted of drinking wine, because it would follow that Allah revealed its permissibility and then abrogated it, and that did not happen. Rather, drinking it was left unaddressed, so they continued drinking it according to their custom, until the prohibition was revealed, just as He was silent about other prohibited matters until the time of their prohibition.

The phrase ﴿They ask you﴾ came with the plural *wāw* (wāw al-jamʿ), although the one who asked, according to the narration of the occasion of revelation, was two people: ʿUmar and Muʿadh. This is because the Arabs attribute an action performed by one person to a group in their speech, and this has been explained.

The question here is not about the substance itself but about the ruling on these two: whether they are lawful, prohibited, or beneficial. Therefore the answer came fitting to that, not as an answer about the substance.

The linguistic meaning of *khamr* (wine) has already been explained. As for its legal meaning, the majority said: Whatever clouds the intellect and corrupts it, of what is drunk, is called *khamr*. Al-Razi reported from Abu Hanifah that *khamr* is the name only of what is made from grapes. Al-Samarqandi reported from him that *khamr*, in his view, is the name of what is made from grapes, raisins, and dates. He said: What is made from maize and wheat is not among the drinks; rather, it is among the foods that disturb the intellect, like henbane and sikrān. It was said: The sound view from Abu Hanifah is that a single drop of these drinks is *khamr*.

*Maysir* (gambling) has already been explained; it is the gambling of the people of the Jahiliyyah. As for its legal meaning, the name *maysir* is applied to all kinds of gambling, and there is consensus on its prohibition. ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAta, Ibn Sirin, al-Hasan, Ibn al-Musayyab, Qatadah, Tawus, Mujahid, and Muʿawiyah ibn Salih said: Everything in which there is gambling, such as dice, chess, or others, is *maysir*, even the children's game with knucklebones and walnuts. Excepted are what is permitted of betting on horses and drawing lots to determine rights.

Malik said: *Maysir* is of two kinds: *maysir* of amusement, which includes backgammon, chess, and all entertainments; and *maysir* of gambling, which is what people stake against one another. He said of chess that it is the *maysir* of the non-Arabs (ʿajam). Al-Qasim said: Everything that distracts from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer is *maysir*.

* *

﴿Say: In them is great sin and benefits for people﴾. Four verses were revealed concerning wine: ﴿And of the fruits of the date-palms and grapes﴾ [al-Nahl: 67], in Mecca; then this verse; then ﴿Do not approach the prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 43]; then ﴿Indeed, wine and gambling…﴾ [al-Maʾidah: 90]. Al-Qaffal said: The prohibition came in this order because Allah knew that the people had become accustomed to drinking it and deriving much benefit from it; so the prohibition came gradually, out of His gentleness, Exalted is He. (End of the summary.)

Al-Rabiʿ said: This verse was revealed after the prohibition of wine. The exegetes (mufassirun) differed on whether this verse indicates the prohibition of wine and gambling or not. The apparent meaning is that it does indicate that. The meaning is: say, concerning their indulgence, there is great sin, that is, the occurrence of great sin. Indulgence in them has thus become among the major sins. Allah, Exalted, has said: ﴿Say: My Lord has only forbidden indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is concealed, and sin﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 33]. Whatever is sin, or contains sin, is prohibited. Sin (*ithm*) is wrongdoing, and when the wrongdoing in committing something is great or large, its commission is not permitted. How could one proceed to it while it is explicitly stated to lead to loss, if the sin is greater than the benefit?

Al-Hasan said: Whatever has sin in it is prohibited. Since drinking it involves sin, it was called *ithm* (sin), in the words of the poet:

*I drank sin until my intellect slipped; thus sin takes away the intellects.*

Whoever said that it does not indicate prohibition relied on His saying ﴿and benefits for people﴾, and what is prohibited would not have any benefit in it. Also, if it indicated prohibition, the Companions would have been content with it, but they were not content until the verse of al-Maʾidah was revealed, and the verse of prohibition during prayer. It was answered that what is prohibited may have an immediate benefit in this world, and that some of the Companions asked that the prohibition come in a clear matter that is not ambiguous to anyone, so that it would be more emphatic in prohibiting it.

The apparent meaning of the verse is a report that in them there is great sin and benefits at the time of the answer. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Rabiʿ said: The sin in them is after the prohibition, and the benefit in them is before the prohibition. On this view, the sin is at one time and the benefit at another. The apparent meaning is that it is a report about the present state. The sin in them is wrongdoing that entails punishment.

A group said: The sin in wine is the loss of the intellect, insulting, slander, and the aggression that comes from its drinker. The benefit in wine: most said it is what is gained from it of profits and earnings, which is the meaning of Mujahid's statement. It was also said that it refers to what the physicians mentioned of its benefits: the removal of worry, the arising of joy, the digestion of food, strengthening the weak, aiding sexual potency, loosening the miserly, clarifying the complexion, encouraging the coward, and other benefits. They have written treatises and books on this, calling it "the fragrant drink" (al-sharab al-rayhani). They have also mentioned many harms of it from the standpoint of medicine.

The benefit in gambling is gaining wealth easily without toil or exertion. It was also said: it is the provision of generosity to the needy; for whoever won among them would not eat from the slaughtered camel but would distribute it to the poor.

The exegetes mentioned here the ruling on what intoxicates in large quantity from drinks other than grape wine, the punishment for the drinker, the manner of beating, and what is protected against in the one being beaten so that he is not struck there. The verse does not address any of that, and it is mentioned in the science of jurisprudence (ʿilm al-fiqh).

Hamzah and al-Kisaʾi read ﴿*ithmun kathīrun*﴾ with the letter *thāʾ*. The sin is described as great either in view of the sinners, as if it were said: in it there are sins for people, that is, each of its indulgers commits sin; or in view of what follows from drinking it of continued punishment and its multiplication, so it was fitting to describe it as great; or in view of the prohibited actions and words that proceed from its drinker; or in view of everyone who handles it from the time it is grown until it is sold and drunk. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cursed wine and cursed with it ten: its seller, its buyer, the one for whom it is bought, its presser, the one for whom it is pressed, its server, its drinker, its carrier, the one for whom it is carried, and the one who eats its price. So describing the sin as great fits this consideration.

The rest read *kabīr* with the letter *bāʾ*, and this is apparent, because drinking wine and gambling are among the major sins. Some people gave preference to each of these two readings over the other, and this is an error, because each of the two readings is the speech of Allah, Exalted; so it is not permissible to prefer one part of it over another from our own opinion, since all of it is the speech of Allah, Exalted.

* *

﴿And their sin is greater than their benefit﴾. In the codex and recitation of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud), it reads *akthar* with the letter *thāʾ*, as in his codex *kathīr* with the three-dotted *thāʾ* in both places. Al-Zamakhshari said: The punishment for sin in indulging in them is greater than their benefit, which is the pleasure of drinking wine and gambling, the delight in them, the means to fellowship and companionship with young men, the seizing of their food, drink, and gifts, the taking of wealth by gambling, and boasting over the paupers. In the recitation of Ubayy it is ﴿*wa-ithmuhuma aqrabu*﴾ ("and their sin is nearer"). The meaning of multiplicity is that those who drink and gamble commit sins in them from many aspects. End of al-Zamakhshari's words.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, and Muqatil said: Their sin after the prohibition is greater than their benefit before the prohibition. It was also said: "greater" because its punishment remains continuous, while the benefits are transient, and the lasting is greater than the perishing.

* *

﴿And they ask you what they should spend. Say: The surplus﴾. This question was previously raised, and here they were answered by mention of the quantity and measure. The questioner in this verse is said to be ʿAmr ibn al-Jamuh; it was also said to be the believers, and this is what is apparent from the *wāw* of the plural. The expenditure here was said to be for jihad, and was said to be for charities. Those who spoke of charities said that it was voluntary charity, which is the view of the majority; and it was said to be obligatory. Those who spoke of the obligatory said that it is the prescribed zakat, and its mention came here in general terms, which the Sunnah then detailed. It was also said that before zakat was prescribed it was obligatory upon them to spend what exceeded their needs from their earnings for their year, and then this was abrogated by the verse of zakat.

*Al-ʿafw* (the surplus) is what remains beyond family and property, as Ibn ʿAbbas said; or what is easy and light that does not diminish wealth, as Tawus said; or the middle course that involves neither extravagance nor shortfall, as al-Hasan said; or the good and best, as al-Rabiʿ said; or the abundant, from His saying ﴿until they multiplied (*ʿafaw*)﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 95], that is, they increased. The poet said:

*But we are such that the sword bites from them into the fleshy, full-bodied thighs.*

Or it means the pure, as in "it came to you *ʿafwan*," that is, pure without turbidity. The poet said:

*Take the pure from me, so that my affection will last, and do not speak in my anger when I am wrathful.*

Or what exceeds a thousand dirhams, or its value in gold. This was an obligation on them before the obligation of zakat, as Qatadah said. Or what exceeds one-third (of one's wealth). Or what exceeds what sustains them for a year, for those who farm, and a month, for those who hunt wild game, or what sustains them for a day, for the one who works at this. They were commanded to do this, but it was burdensome to them, so zakat was made obligatory. Or it means the obligatory charity, as Mujahid said. Or it means what does not exhaust the wealth and leaves its owner needing to ask people, as al-Hasan also said. It has been narrated in the hadith of the man who came to give charity with an egg of gold, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ rejected it from him, and his saying (ﷺ): "One of you comes with all his wealth, gives it in charity, and then sits begging from people. Charity is only what is given from surplus wealth." In the hadith of Sa'd: "It is better for you to leave your heirs wealthy than to leave them destitute, begging from people."

Al-Zamakhshari said: al-'afw is the opposite of al-juhd (exertion), and it means spending what is not so much that it reaches the point of exertion and the exhaustion of one's capacity. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the meaning is, spend what exceeds your needs and do not harm yourselves by it so that you become destitute. Al-Raghib said: al-'afw includes what is obligatory and what is voluntary, and it is the surplus over wealth (ghina). Al-Maturidi said: it is the surplus over sustenance.

The majority of readers recited "al-'afwa" with a fatha, and it is in the accusative governed by a hidden verb whose estimate is "Say: they spend the surplus." On this reading, the better analysis of His saying "mādhā yunfiqūn" (what do they spend) is that "mādhā" is in the accusative position with "yunfiqūn," and both words are interrogative. The estimate is: what thing do they spend? Thus they were answered with the accusative so that the answer matches the question.

It is also permissible for "mā" to be an interrogative in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada'), and "dhā" to be a relative pronoun meaning "alladhī" (who/which), serving as its predicate. In that case the answer does not match the question in wording, but only in meaning, and the returning pronoun to the relative is omitted because the condition for omission is present. Its estimate is: what is it that they spend?

Abu 'Amr recited "qul al-'afw" with a damma. The better option in that case is that it is the predicate of a omitted subject, estimated as "Say: what is spent is the surplus." And "mā" is in the nominative position as a subject, and "dhā" is a relative pronoun, as we have explained, so that the answer matches the question. It is also permissible for "mādhā" as a whole to be an interrogative in the accusative governed by "yunfiqūn," and the matching is then in meaning, not in wording.

It is reported from Ibn Kathir regarding "al-'afw" that it was recited with a fatha like the majority, and also with a damma like Abu 'Amr.

Ibn 'Atiyyah, when he mentioned the two readings of "al-'afw," said the following, and this is his text: "This is built upon 'mā.' Whoever makes 'mā' the subject and 'dhā' its predicate in the sense of 'alladhī,' and estimates the pronoun in 'yunfiqūnahu' as returning to it, recites 'al-'afw' with a damma, so that the correspondence of the answer is sound. Its damma is as the subject, the estimate being: al-'afw is your spending, or: what they spend is al-'afw. Whoever makes 'mādhā' a single word as the object of 'yunfiqūn' recites 'al-'afwa' with a fatha, by hidden verb, and the correspondence is sound for him. Raising 'al-'afw' with the accusative of 'mā' is permissible but weak, and likewise its accusative with its raising." End of his words.

His estimate, "al-'afw is your spending," is not good, because he has brought the verbal noun (maṣdar), and the question is not about a verbal noun. And his saying "permissible, weak," and likewise its accusative with its raising, is not as he mentioned. Rather it is permissible and not weak.

* *

﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you the signs, so that you may reflect﴾ ﴿upon this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:217]. The kaf is for comparison and it is in the position of an adjective for an omitted verbal noun, or in the position of a circumstantial state (hal) according to the school of Sibawayh. The meaning is: a clarification like that, He makes clear. Or it is in the state of His making clear that clarification, meaning: He makes clear the clarification similar to that clarification. The demonstrative "dhālika" most likely refers to the nearest thing, namely the clarification of the condition of the one who spends, as Ibn al-Anbari said.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it refers to what it leads to, which is the clarification that the 'afw is better than exertion in spending, or the ruling on wine and gambling, and the nearby spending. That is: just as He makes clear in this, He makes clear in the future. The meaning is that He makes the signs clear just as He made this clear. It is also permissible that it refers to the clarification of what they asked about, so He made clear for them like the clarification of the destination of what they spend, and the clarification of what is consequently rewarded, indicated by the knowledge of Allah in His saying "fa-inna Allāha bihi 'alīm" (for Allah has knowledge of it), and the clarification of the ruling on fighting, and the clarification of its status in the sacred month, and what the verse mentioning fighting in the sacred month contains, and the clarification of the status of wine and gambling, and the clarification of the amount they spend. Whoever restricts the demonstrative to the clarification of the ruling on wine and gambling alone is mistaken, and more mistaken is whoever makes it refer to the clarification of the rulings previously mentioned in the surah.

The kaf of address (in "dhālika-kum" type forms) may be for the Prophet ﷺ, or for the listener, or for the generic addressee; therefore it is singular. Or it is for the community of believers, in which case it has the meaning of "dhālikum" (plural). This is the language of the Arabs, who address a plural with the address of the singular, and this occurs with demonstratives. What supports this here is His saying "yubayyinu lakum" (makes clear for you), where He uses the plural pronoun, which shows that the address is to the plural.

"Lakum" is connected to "yubayyinu." The lam in it is for conveying (tabligh), as in your saying "qultu laka" (I said to you). Its being for causation (ta'lil) is far-fetched. "Al-āyāt" means the signs and proofs.

"La'allakum tatafakkarūn" (so that you may reflect) is a hope (ta'rijah) for reflection, which occurs at the making clear of the signs, because whenever the sign is clear and manifest with no ambiguity in it, reflection and contemplation follow it regarding that for which that clear sign came, whether it concerns the matters of this world or the matters of the Hereafter.

As for "fī al-dunyā wa-al-ākhirah" (in this world and the Hereafter), the better view is that it is an adverbial complement of time (ẓarf) for reflection and connected to it. The clarification of the signs is then for the hope of reflection on the matters of this world and the Hereafter in general, not specifically concerning some particular aspect of their conditions, but so that reflection occurs on what is meant by their affairs. Al-Zamakhshari first stated this meaning, saying: "you reflect" on what concerns the two abodes, so that you take what is better for you. It was also said: you reflect on the commands and prohibitions of Allah, and you seek obedience to Him in this world and His reward in the Hereafter. Al-Mufaddal ibn Salamah said: you reflect on the matter of spending in this world and the Hereafter, so you retain from your wealth what sustains you in the livelihood of this world, and spend the remainder on what benefits you in the next life. It was also said: you reflect on the passing of this world and the permanence of the Hereafter, so you work for the more lasting of the two. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Zamakhshari said this meaning. It was also said: you reflect on the benefits of wine in this world and its harms in the Hereafter, so do not choose immediate benefit over salvation from continuous punishment. Al-Zamakhshari said something close to this. It was also said: you reflect in this world so that you retain, and in the Hereafter so that you give charity.

They permitted that "fī al-dunyā" be connected to the phrase "yubayyinu lakum" (makes clear for you) the signs, not to "tatafakkarūn," and it is connected to the wording "yubayyinu" (He makes clear), meaning: Allah makes clear in this world and the Hereafter. This was narrated from al-Hasan. On this view there must be an interpretation if the clarification of the signs occurs in this world; then the estimate is "in the matter of this world and the Hereafter." If it occurs in both, then no interpretation is needed, because the signs, which are the indications, are manifested by Allah Most High in this world and the Hereafter.

Some scholars considered this view to be a case of inversion (taqdim wa-ta'khir), since its estimate for them is: "Thus Allah makes clear to you the signs in this world and the Hereafter, so that you may reflect." He said: it is possible to take it according to the apparent sense of the speech, since "fī al-dunyā wa-al-ākhirah" is connected to "tatafakkarūn." So positing inversion, according to what al-Hasan said, would be a departure from the apparent meaning without evidence, and that is impermissible. This is not a case of inversion, because "la'alla" here functions as a causal particle, so it is like something connected to "yubayyinu," and when it is so, it and the adverbial complement are both objectives of "yubayyinu," and the placement of one of the two objectives before the other and the delay of the other is not inversion.

It is possible that "la'allakum tatafakkarūn" is a parenthetical clause (jumlah i'tiradiyyah), in which case this is not inversion, because the condition for a parenthetical clause is that it separates two things that depend on each other. Ibn 'Atiyyah said, and Makki said: the meaning of the verse is that He makes clear to the believers signs in this world and the Hereafter, which indicate them and their status, so that you may reflect on those signs. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: so "fī al-dunyā" on this interpretation is connected to the signs. End of his words.

Makki explained the verse by making the signs indefinite, so that the two adverbial complements are a qualifier of the signs, and the meaning in his view is: signs existing in this world and the Hereafter. This is an explanation of meaning, not an explanation of grammatical analysis (i'rab). What Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned, that on this interpretation it is connected to the signs, if he means the apparent sense that the grammarians intend by "connection" (ta'alluq), then it is corrupt, because no prepositional phrase is connected to "al-āyāt," and it governs nothing at all. If he means that the adverbial complement completes the signs, this is only possible by considering it to be in the position of a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: existing in this world and the Hereafter. Therefore Makki explained it in a way that implies it is a qualifier, since he estimated the signs as indefinite, and the circumstantial state and the qualifier are alike in that the governing element for both is omitted when they are adverbial complements or prepositional phrases. On this view, "fī al-dunyā" is connected to an omitted element, not to "al-āyāt." On the view of the Kufans, the signs would be a relative noun joined to the adverbial complement; the refutation and argument for their position belongs to a different place.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 220–221 (part 1 of 3):

﴿They ask you about orphans﴾. The occasion of its revelation: in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance), they were scrupulous about mixing with orphans in food, drink and other matters, and they avoided their property. This was said by al-Dahhak and al-Suddi. It was also said: when ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan﴾ [6:152] and ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans﴾ [4:10] were revealed, they avoided the orphans and their property and separated them from themselves; so this verse was revealed. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Ibn al-Musayyab.

The connection of this verse to what precedes it: when He mentioned the question about wine and gambling, and abandoning them was a means of developing wealth, and He mentioned the question about spending, and they were answered that they spend what is easy for them, it was fitting to consider the situation of the orphan, the preservation and development of his property, and the reform of the orphan by attending to his upbringing. The common element between the two verses is that abandoning wine and gambling reforms their own states, while attending to the situation of orphans reforms others who are unable to reform themselves; so they combine benefit for themselves and for others. The apparent meaning is that the questioner combined the two matters with the conjunctive waw (واو الجمع), which is for joining, and it was said that this is so.

Muqatil said: the questioner was Thabit ibn Rifa'ah al-Ansari. It was said: Abdullah ibn Rawahah. It was said: the questioner was whoever among the believers was present with the Prophet (ﷺ). The Arabs used to consider it ill-omened to mix the property of orphans with their own. So Allah informed the believers that their mixing was in fact ill-omened because of their improper handling of the property: they would put the lean in place of the fat, and exchange the worthless for the precious. Then He said: ﴿Say: reforming them is best﴾.

Reform of the orphan is by undertaking his reform through teaching and discipline, and reform of his property through development and preservation. "Işlāḥun" (إصلاحٌ, reform) is the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence), and it is indefinite. What permits beginning with an indefinite here is the qualification by the prepositional phrase "lahum" (لهم, "for them"), which is either as a descriptive qualifier or as a complement of the verbal noun. "Khayrun" (خيرٌ, good) is the predicate (khabar) about işlāḥ. As we have said, işlāḥ is a verbal noun whose agent has been omitted, so "khayr" encompasses the reform related both to the agent and to the object. Thus the good is for both sides together: their reform of the orphans is good for the reformer and the reformed. It covers the situation of the orphan and of the guardian. It was said that "khayr" refers to the guardian: his reform of the orphan without compensation or wage is better for him and greater in reward. It was said that "khayr" refers to the orphan: the guardian's reform of the orphan and his mixing with him is better for the orphan than the guardian's turning away from him and isolating himself from him. The word "khayr" is unrestricted, so restricting it to one of the two sides requires a preponderant indicator, and keeping it general is better.

Ṭāwūs read: "Qul işlāḥun ilayhim" (قل إصلاحٌ إليهم), meaning: in caring for their property and other matters, it is better than your scrupulousness, or better in reward than reforming your own property.

﴿And if you mix with them, they are your brothers﴾. This is an iltifat (التفات, a shift in grammatical person) from the third person to the second person, because before it is "wa yas'alūnaka" (ويسألونك, "and they ask you"). The waw (و) is the pronoun of the absent. The wisdom of this iltifat is that addressing the one present directly prepares him to hear what is conveyed, to accept it, and to be careful with it. The waw in "fa-ikhwānukum" (فإخوانكم) refers to the guardians, and "hum" (هم) refers to the orphans. The meaning is that they are your brothers in religion; so you should care for them as you care for your brothers by lineage, with compassion, gentleness, and reform of their persons and their property.

"Mukhālaṭah" (مخالطة, mixing) is a form of mufā'alah (مفاعلة) from al-khalt (الخلط), which is blending. The meaning here concerns food: the orphan's provision is combined with the provision of his dependents with care, since it is difficult to single him out with his own food, so the guardian has no choice but to mix him with his own property for his dependents. Thus the verse brought a concession for that. This was said by Abu Ubayd.

Or it means partnership in property and trading on their behalf, so that you take from the profit what belongs to you and leave for them what belongs to them. Or it means marriage: if the orphan is a boy, he marries his daughter to him, or if the orphan is a girl, he marries her to his son. This view was preferred because this is mixing with the orphan himself, whereas partnership is mixing with his property. Also, partnership is included in His saying "Say: reforming them is best", but mixing through marriage is not included in it, so restricting it to this kind of mixing is closer to the meaning. And there is His saying "they are your brothers in religion": if the orphan is from the children of unbelievers, it is obligatory to seek the reform of his property just as one would for a Muslim. So the reference by "your brothers" must be to another type of mixing. Also His saying afterwards: "do not marry polytheistic women". So it is as if the meaning is that the mixing recommended is with orphans who are your brothers by Islam.

Or it means: drinking from his milk and his drinking from yours, and your eating from his bowl and his eating from yours. This was said by Ibn Abbas.
