Or it means mixing property with property in expenditure, food, dwelling, servants and animals, so that they take from their property compensation for your attending to their affairs, in an amount equal to the customary wage for that work. Among those who hold this view are some who permitted it whether the guardian was rich or poor, and some who said that if he is rich he should not eat from their property. Or it means mudāraba (مضاربة, profit-sharing partnership) by which their property grows.

What appears is that the mixing was not restricted to anything; it did not say "in such-and-such". So it is understood as any mixing that contains reform for the orphan. That is why He said "fa-ikhwānukum", i.e., you look upon them with the same regard as you look upon your brothers, in whatever reforms them. This mixing is framed by reform before and after: before it, by "Say: reforming them is best", and after it, by "And Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer". So the better view is that the intended mixing is whatever contains reform for the orphan by any means whatsoever: mixing in food, dwelling, trade, partnership, mudāraba, marriage, or otherwise.

The response to the conditional is "fa-ikhwānukum" (فإخوانكم), which is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject, i.e., "then they are your brothers". Abu Mijlaz read "fa-ikhwānakum" (فإخوانَكم) with an implied verb, meaning: "then you mix with your brothers".

The answer to the question came in two sentences: one composed of a subject and predicate, and the second of a condition and consequence. The first sentence includes the reform of orphans and that it is good. It was presented affirmatively with an indefinite subject to indicate that it covers every kind of reform by way of substitution. Had it been made definite by annexation (idāfah), it would have been either general, which cannot be realized, or it would refer to a known specific reform, and the known does not encompass others. So indefiniteness came to indicate general substitution. It was predicated with "khayr", which indicates attaining reward, since the Muslim hastens to do what is good seeking Allah's reward.

The second sentence was presented as conditional because it comes to indicate the permissibility of occurrence, not requesting or recommending it.

The first answer indicates various kinds of rulings in which the orphan's interest lies: permissibility of teaching him matters of religion and manners, hiring someone for that on his behalf, spending on him from his property, accepting what is given to him, marrying him off, hiring him out, selling his property on the orphan's behalf, managing his property by buying and selling, working with his property personally on a mudāraba basis, handing it to another on a mudāraba basis, and other dispositions bound up with reform.

The second answer indicates the permissibility of mixing with orphans in what reforms them, so that one mixes him with oneself in marriages, and mixes his property with one's own in maintenance, trade and the like.

It was said that the verse includes the permissibility of mixing, so it indicates the permissibility of munāhadah (مناهدة, pooling provisions), which travellers practise on journeys: this person brings some of his property and that person some of his, so it is mixed, spent, and people eat, even if the amounts eaten differ. And if it is permitted to you in the property of an orphan, it is all the more permitted in the property of an adult with his willing consent. A parallel to the permissibility of munāhadah is the story of the People of the Cave: ﴿So send one of you with this silver of yours﴾ [18:19], and so on.

Some of the rulings we have presented have been disputed. Among them: the guardian's purchase from the orphan's property, his mudāraba with it, the guardian marrying his female orphan to himself, and the orphan marrying his daughter (to the guardian). This is mentioned in the books of jurisprudence.

It was said: He made them brothers for two reasons. The first is brotherhood in religion. The second is that they benefit from them, either in reward from Allah the Exalted, or in what they receive as wages for their work with their property. Everyone who benefits you is your brother.

al-Baqir said to a person: "I saw you among a people I did not know." He said: "They are my brothers." He said: "Among them is someone who, when you are in need, puts his hand into your sleeve and takes from it without asking permission?" He said: "No." He said: "Then you are not brothers."

It was said: in His saying ﴿fa-ikhwānukum﴾ there is evidence that the children of believers are believers in the rulings, since Allah named them our brothers.

﴿And Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer﴾. This is a sentence whose meaning is a warning. In it He informs that He knows who corrupts from among those who reform. The meaning is that He recompenses each of the two according to the attribute that he has. Knowledge is often attributed to Allah the Exalted as a warning, because whoever knows something will recompense for it. It is therefore an expression of the cause by the effect (ta'bīr bil-sabab 'an al-musabbab). "Ya'lamu" (يعلم, knows) here is transitive to one object. The report came here in a verb that implies renewal, although Allah's knowledge does not renew, because He intends reward and punishment for the corrupter and the reformer, two attributes which renew in those who bear them. Therefore the recompense attached to them is repeated as they recur. The action is linked to the corrupter first, so that refraining from corruption takes place.

"Min" (من) is connected to "ya'lamu" by the principle of implied meaning (taḍmīn), as if the meaning were: "Allah distinguishes by His knowledge the corrupter from the reformer."

The apparent meaning of the definite article (al-) is that it is for comprehensiveness over all kinds of corrupter and reformer, and the reformer of an orphan's property is among the things this covers. It is also possible that the article is for a known reference: the corrupter in the orphan's property from the reformer in it, and the corrupter through neglect of his upbringing from the reformer through discipline.

This sentence came with this division because mixing is of two kinds: mixing by corruption and mixing by reform. Also, since it was said "Say: reforming them is best", its opposite was understood, namely that corruption is evil. So this division came with reference to reform.

Its counterpart is ﴿Had Allah willed, He would have distressed you﴾, i.e., He would have made you suffer hardship and imposed strictness upon you. This was said by Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi and others. Or: He would have destroyed you. This was said by Abu Ubaydah. Or: He would have made what you took from the orphans' property a ruin (mawbiq, مَوْبِق, a destruction), said by Ibn Abbas, and this is the meaning of what precedes. Or: He would have imposed upon you what is difficult for you, said by al-Zajjaj. Or: He would have made you sinful through mixing with them. Or: He would have constricted the matter for you in mixing with them, said by 'Ata'. Or: He would have forbidden you to mix with them, said by Ibn Jarir. These sayings are all close in meaning.

The object of "shā'a" (شاء, willed) is omitted, as indicated by the answer, and the intended sense is: "Had Allah willed to distress you." The lām (ل) in an affirmative verb is most commonly used in the speech of the Arabs, and it is employed here. Most readers recited "la-a'natakum" (لأعنتكم) with the hamza lightened, which is the original form. Al-Bazzi, through the transmission of Abu Rabi'ah, recited it with the hamza softened. It was also recited with the hamza dropped and its vowel placed on the lām, like the reading of one who recited "fa-lā ithma 'alayhi" (فلا إثم عليه) with the hamza dropped.

Abu Abdullah Nasr ibn Ali, known as Ibn Maryam, said: Ibn Mujahid did not mention this letter, and Ibn Kathir did not drop the hamza, but softened it and realised it in full, so people assumed it was deleted. For the hamza here is a hamzat al-qat' (همزة القطع, a cutting hamza, i.e., one that is always pronounced), so it does not fall away in connected speech as the hamzat al-wasl (همزة الوصل, the connecting hamza) falls away when connected. End of his words. Thus he considered the dropping of the hamza a mistake, although others transmitted it as a reading, as we have mentioned.

In this conditional sentence is an announcement and a reminder of Allah's kindness and favour toward the guardians of orphans, since He removed from them distress and hardship in mixing with orphans and in attending to their situations and their property.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) on Surah 2, verses 220–221 (part 2 of 3):

﴿Indeed, Allah is Mighty and Wise.﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said: "*'Aziz* (Mighty) means one who prevails, who is able to put His servants in difficulty and distress, but He is *Hakim* (Wise), and does not impose upon them except what their capacity can bear." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "*'Aziz* means that His command cannot be repelled, and *Hakim* means one who makes firm what He executes." End of quotation. In describing Him, exalted is He, with *'izza* (might), which is dominance and control, there is an indication that this belongs to Him alone and that no one shares in it. It is as if, when He gave them guardianship over the orphans, He warned them that they should not oppress them, nor overpower them, nor seize control over them in the manner of a tyrant, for this attribute belongs to Allah alone. In describing Him, exalted is He, with *hikma* (wisdom), there is an indication that He does not exceed what He has permitted regarding them and their wealth. Therefore you have no latitude except within what the Law has permitted you and what Divine wisdom has required, for He is the Wise, the Perfect in what He creates and legislates. Thus the reform of the orphans is not dependent on your opinion; rather, it depends on following what has been legislated concerning them.

﴿And do not marry polytheistic women until they believe﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: It was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Rawaha. He freed a slave-woman and married her, and she was a Muslim. Some Muslims criticized him, saying, "He married a slave-woman," and they wanted to marry into the polytheists out of desire for their lineages, so this was revealed. Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning Abu Marthad al-Ghanawi, whose name was Kannaz ibn al-Husayn. In another report, it was Marthad ibn Abi Marthad, who was an ally of the Banu Hashim. He asked permission to marry 'Anaq, who was a woman of Quraysh, possessing some beauty, and a polytheist. He said: "O Messenger of Allah, she pleases me." This cause is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, in a longer form than this. It has also been said that it was revealed concerning a beautiful black slave-woman belonging to Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman, whom he freed and married. It is possible that the cause includes all these accounts.

The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when He mentioned the ruling on mixing with orphans, which could entail marriage and other things called "mixing" (mukhalata), to the extent that some of them interpreted it as affinity (musaharah) only, and preferred that view as mentioned earlier, and among the orphans there were some who were children of disbelievers, Allah forbade marriage to polytheist women and men. He indicated the cause that makes marriage lawful, which is religious brotherhood (al-ukhuwwa al-diniyya), so He forbade marrying anyone in whom this brotherhood was absent, and the orphans of disbelievers were included in the general scope of those who associate partners with Allah. There is another connection: when the ruling on drinking wine and on consuming the proceeds of gambling (maysir) had come before, and He mentioned the ruling on marriage, then just as He forbade wine among drinks and what gambling leads to among foods, He forbade polytheist women among those one may marry.

The majority of reciters read *wa-la tankihu* with a *fatha* on the *ta'*, from *nakaha*, which is used with the meaning of contracting a marriage and with the meaning of intercourse by ownership or otherwise. Al-A'mash read *wa-la tunkihu* with a *damma* on the *ta'*, from *ankaha*, meaning: do not give your own selves in marriage to polytheist women. The "polytheist women" here means disbelievers, so it includes People of the Book (*kitabiyyat*) and whoever sets up another god with Allah. It has been said that the People of the Book are not included, but the correct view is that they are included, because the Jews worship 'Uzayr and the Christians worship 'Isa, and because of His saying: ﴿Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they associate with Him﴾ [Yunus: 18]. This second view is the view of the majority of the commentators (*mufassirun*). It has also been said that the intended meaning is the polytheist women of the Arabs, which is the view of Qatada.

According to the view of those who say that the People of the Book are included among them, one needs a justification for marrying them. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that this is a general ruling that was abrogated (*naskh*, abrogation), and from Mujahid that it is a general ruling from which the People of the Book were excluded. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the verse is general, covering idolaters, Magians, People of the Book, and everyone who is not upon the religion of Islam, and marrying them is forbidden, and the verse is muhkam (definitive) on this view, abrogating the verse of al-Ma'ida, although the verse of al-Ma'ida was revealed earlier, even though it comes later in the recitation. This is confirmed by the statement of Ibn 'Umar in *al-Muwatta'* (of Malik): "I know of no greater association (*shirk*) than that a woman says her lord is 'Isa."

It is narrated that Talha ibn 'Ubayd Allah married a Jewish woman, that Hudhayfa married a Christian woman, and that 'Umar became extremely angry with them both, to the point that he almost struck them. 'Uthman married Na'ila bint al-Farafisa, who was a Christian. Marrying People of the Book is permissible. This was the view of the majority of the Companions and the Successors: 'Umar, 'Uthman, Jabir, Talha, Hudhayfa, 'Ata', Ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan, Tawus, Ibn Jubayr, and al-Zuhri, and al-Shafi'i held it, as did the general body of the scholars of Madina and Kufa. It has been said that the scholars of the cities (*ulama' al-amsar*) agreed (*ijma'*, consensus) on the permissibility of marrying People of the Book, except that Malik and Ibn Hanbal disliked it while Muslim women were available and one was able to marry them. There is disagreement about marrying Magian women. Hudhayfa married a Magian woman. As for whether the Magians are People of the Book, there is disagreement. It is narrated from a group that they have a prophet called Zaradasht and an ancient scripture that was lifted up. The narration of the scripture is reported from 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas, and a lengthy account is mentioned concerning its lifting and the alteration of their law. Allah knows best its authenticity.

The proofs of these positions are mentioned in the books of jurisprudence (*fiqh*). The apparent meaning of the prohibition in His saying "wa-la tankihu" is prohibition (*tahrim*), though it has been said that it is a prohibition of disapproval (*karaha*). "Until they believe" is a limit (*ghaya*) to the prohibition of marrying them. The meaning of their believing is their affirmation of the two testimonies of faith and their commitment to the laws of Islam.

﴿And a believing slave-woman is better than a polytheist woman﴾. The apparent meaning is that *amah* (slave-woman) is intended in the sense of a female slave. The meaning of "better than a polytheist woman" is: better than a free polytheist woman, so the qualified noun is omitted because its contrast, "slave-woman," indicates it. It has been said that *amah* here means woman in general, so it includes free women and slave-women, and from this comes the hadith: "Do not prevent the female servants of Allah from the mosques of Allah." This is the view of al-Dahhak, and al-Zamakhshari mentioned no other. In this there is evidence for the permissibility of marrying a believing slave-woman. The implication of the qualifier (*mafhum al-sifa*) requires that it is not permissible to marry a disbelieving slave-woman, whether she is a People of the Book or otherwise. This is the position of Malik and others. Abu Hanifa and his companions permitted marrying a slave-woman from the People of the Book. Concerning a Magian slave-woman there is disagreement. The position of Malik and a group is that she may not be had by marriage or by ownership. It is narrated from 'Ata' and 'Amr ibn Dinar that there is no harm in marrying her by ownership (*milk al-yamin*). They interpreted "wa-la tankihu al-mushrikat" as referring to the contract, not to a slave-woman purchased, and they argued from the captives of Awtas, and that the Companions married female captives from them by ownership.

It has been said that in this verse there is evidence for the permissibility of a man who is able to afford a free Muslim woman (*tawl*, means) marrying a Muslim slave-woman. The basis of this inference is that His saying "better than a polytheist woman" means better than a free polytheist woman, and whoever has the means to marry a free polytheist woman also has the means to marry a free Muslim woman, since the means do not differ with respect to faith and disbelief. The amount of wealth needed for the costs of marriage is the same. It follows from this that whoever has the means to marry a free Muslim woman may marry a Muslim slave-woman. This is a subtle inference.

"*Amah*" is the subject (*mubtada'*), the justification for beginning with an indefinite noun is the descriptive phrase, and "*khayr*" (better) is the predicate. It has been argued from His saying "*khayr*" that marrying a polytheist woman is permissible, because the elative form (*af'al al-tafdil*) implies sharing. The prohibition is first in the sense of disapproval. They said: Comparison occurs only between two permissible things. But there is no proof in this, because comparison may be made in terms of belief, not only in terms of actual existence. Among examples is His saying: ﴿The companions of the Garden, on that Day, will have a better abode﴾ [al-Furqan: 24], and "Honey is sweeter than vinegar," and 'Umar said in his letter to Abu Musa: "Returning to the truth is better than persisting in falsehood." It is also possible to retain the meaning of "better" as sharing in actual existence, and this does not prove permissibility of marriage, since marriage to a polytheist woman involves worldly benefits, while marrying a believing slave-woman involves otherworldly benefits. The two benefits share in general benefit, but the benefit of the Hereafter has the supreme excellence. Therefore a ruling based on this worldly benefit does not require permission, just as wine and gambling have benefits, yet this does not imply their permissibility, and there is hardly any prohibited thing that does not contain some benefit.

These interpretations of the elative form are according to the view of Sibawayh and the Basrans, that the word *af'al* used for comparison is not valid where there is no sharing, as in your saying: "Snow is colder than fire," and "Light is brighter than darkness." Al-Farra' and a group of the Kufans said: it is valid where there is sharing, and where there is no sharing. Ibrahim ibn 'Arafa said: the elative form in the speech of the Arabs comes to affirm the first and negate the second. According to one view, it is not valid that there is no good in the polytheist woman, rather the good is in the believing slave-woman.

﴿And even if she pleases you﴾. *Law* (even if) here has the meaning of the conditional *in* (if), like the saying: "Return the beggar even with a burnt sheep's hoof." The *waw* in "wa-law" is for conjunction with an omitted circumstance; the estimated meaning is: "better than a polytheist woman in every state, even in this state." We have mentioned that this serves to exhaust all states, and that what follows *law* in this construction comes in a way that is contrary to what precedes it in some respect. Pleasing (*i'jab*) contradicts the ruling of preference, and requires the permissibility of marriage because of the suitor's desire for her. The pleasing is attributed to the person of the polytheist woman, without specifying who is pleased by her, so the intended meaning is pleasing in general, whether because of beauty, nobility, wealth, or anything else by which one may be pleased. The meaning is: even if the polytheist woman surpasses in beauty, wealth, and lineage, a believing slave-woman is better than her, because what the polytheist woman excels in belongs to this world, while faith belongs to the Hereafter, and the Hereafter is better than this world. Through agreement in religion, love is completed and the benefits of this world are attained, such as companionship, obedience, and the preservation of wealth and children, while through difference in religion, neither love nor any benefit of this world is achieved.

﴿And do not marry polytheistic men until they believe﴾. The reading with a *damma* on the *ta'* is a consensus (*ijma'*) among the reciters. The address is to the guardians (*awliya'*), and the second object is omitted; the estimated meaning is: "Do not marry off the believing women to polytheistic men." The community agreed that a polytheist may not have intercourse with a believing woman in any way, and the prohibition here is for forbiddance (*tahrim*). It has been argued from this address that guardianship is required in marriage, and that this is explicit evidence for it.

﴿And a believing slave is better than an idolater, even though you admire him.﴾ The discussion of this clause is the same as the discussion of the clause before it. There is a disagreement about the meaning of "slave" ('abd): does it mean a bondservant (raqiq) or a man (rajul)? It is used like that in the case of the female slave there. Does the meaning, then, become "better than a free idolater," so that it corresponds to "slave"? Or does it mean "better than an idolater" absolutely, so that it covers both the slave and the free person, as in His saying, "better than an idolatress"?

﴿Those invite to the Fire.﴾ This refers to both categories, the female idolaters and the male idolaters. "Yad'una" (they invite) may mean invitation by speech, as in His saying, "And they say: Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided" [al-Baqarah: 135]. It may also mean that there is no speech, but that through love and association, something of the dispositions of the disbelievers creeps into him, which leads him to agree with them in their religion, and Allah forbid, so he becomes one of the people of the Fire. It was also said: its meaning is that they invite to abandoning fighting and combat, and that abandoning them entails deserving the Fire. The proponent of this interpretation distinguished between a dhimmi woman and others, since a dhimmi woman's husband is not made to fight. It was also said: the meaning is that a child who is born may be invited to disbelief by the disbeliever and may agree, and so become one of the people of the Fire. What the apparent sense of the verse indicates is that the disbelievers are certainly invited to the Fire, either by speech, or by intimacy, close association and intermarriage leading to it. The meaning is that whoever is inviting to the Fire must be shunned, lest by his invitation he constantly sway his companion, who then responds to what he invites him to and perishes. In this verse there is an indication of the cause that prevents marriage with disbelievers: because of their involvement in forbidden things, such as wine, pork, immersion in filth, the raising of offspring, the absorption of their dispositions, and other things in which the desire for marriage is not equal to some of what they are upon. When this cause is considered, it is present in every male and female disbeliever, and so it requires the prohibition of marriage absolutely. The discussion of Surat al-Ma'idah will come, if Allah the Exalted wills, and we will show there, if Allah wills, that it does not contradict this.

"Ila" (to) is connected to "yad'una," as in His saying, "And Allah invites to the abode of peace" [Yunus: 25]. It also takes the particle "li" (for), as in the line of poetry:

"I called out for what befell me, Miswar"

The object of "yad'una" is omitted, either for brevity, since the intention is to establish that it is among their nature to invite to the Fire without considering a specific object; or for abridgement, so the meaning is: "those invite you to the Fire."

﴿And Allah invites to the Garden and forgiveness.﴾ This confirms the prohibition of marrying disbelievers, since two divisions are mentioned: one must be followed, and the other must be avoided, so the two divisions are opposed. It is not possible to answer Allah's call and follow what He has commanded except by avoiding the invitation of the disbelievers and abandoning them entirely. Allah's invitation is to follow His religion, which is the cause of entering the Garden, so He expressed the cause by its result, because it follows from it. The apparent sense of the verse is a report about Allah the Exalted, that He Himself invites to the Garden. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It means: and the friends of Allah, who are the believers, invite to the Garden and forgiveness, and to what leads to them. They are the ones whose friendship and intermarriage must be maintained, and who must be preferred over others." End of quotation. What led him to hold that this is by omitting a modifier is the desire to establish an equivalence between the idolaters and the believers in invitation. When He reported about those who associated partners that they invite to the Fire, He made those who believe invite to the Garden. But there is no need for what he mentioned. Rather, leaving the wording on its apparent sense, by attributing the invitation to Allah the Exalted, is more emphatic in distancing from the idolaters, since He made the Originator of the world opposed to them in invitation. This is more eloquent than establishing an equivalence between the idolaters and the believers.

The majority (al-Jumhur, the main body of reciters) read "wal-maghfirati" with the genitive, coordinated with "al-Jannah," and the meaning is that He the Exalted invites to forgiveness, that is, to the cause of forgiveness, which is repentance and adherence to acts of obedience. Here "al-Jannah" is placed before "forgiveness," while in His saying, "And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden" [Al 'Imran: 133], and His saying, "Race to forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden" [al-Hadid: 21], it comes after. The basic principle is that forgiveness precedes the Garden, because entry into the Garden follows from the attainment of forgiveness. In those two verses it came according to this basic principle. Here, however, the Garden is mentioned before forgiveness for the sake of a fine correspondence, since before it is: "Those invite to the Fire," so: "And Allah invites to the Garden" came. Also, so that it begins with what the soul yearns for when the invitation of Allah is mentioned, He brought the most noble before the most noble, and then followed it with forgiveness by way of completing the favour and preparing the cause of entering the Garden.

Al-Hasan read "wal-maghfiratu" with the nominative, as the subject, and the predicate is His saying "bi-idhnihi" (by His permission), meaning: forgiveness is attained by His facilitating and enabling it. The explanation of permission (idhn) has already been given. According to the readings of the majority, "bi-idhnihi" is connected to "yad'u" (invites).

﴿And He makes His signs clear to the people, that they may remember.﴾ That is, He manifests them and reveals them in such a way that no ambiguity arises in them. This clarification is not restricted to some people rather than others, but He shows His signs to everyone, in the hope that through the manifestation of the signs remembrance and admonition will occur, because whenever a sign is clear and evident, it is apt that remembrance will occur through it, so that compliance with what those signs indicate is achieved, namely conformity with the command and avoidance of what is forbidden. "Lin-nas" (to the people) is connected to "yubayyinu" (makes clear), and the "li" (the particle) means arrival and conveyance, which is one of its meanings mentioned at the beginning of al-Fatihah.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 220–221 (part 1 of 3):

﴿They ask you about orphans﴾. The occasion of its revelation: in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance), they were scrupulous about mixing with orphans in food, drink and other matters, and they avoided their property. This was said by al-Dahhak and al-Suddi. It was also said: when ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan﴾ [6:152] and ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans﴾ [4:10] were revealed, they avoided the orphans and their property and separated them from themselves; so this verse was revealed. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Ibn al-Musayyab.

The connection of this verse to what precedes it: when He mentioned the question about wine and gambling, and abandoning them was a means of developing wealth, and He mentioned the question about spending, and they were answered that they spend what is easy for them, it was fitting to consider the situation of the orphan, the preservation and development of his property, and the reform of the orphan by attending to his upbringing. The common element between the two verses is that abandoning wine and gambling reforms their own states, while attending to the situation of orphans reforms others who are unable to reform themselves; so they combine benefit for themselves and for others. The apparent meaning is that the questioner combined the two matters with the conjunctive waw (واو الجمع), which is for joining, and it was said that this is so.

Muqatil said: the questioner was Thabit ibn Rifa'ah al-Ansari. It was said: Abdullah ibn Rawahah. It was said: the questioner was whoever among the believers was present with the Prophet (ﷺ). The Arabs used to consider it ill-omened to mix the property of orphans with their own. So Allah informed the believers that their mixing was in fact ill-omened because of their improper handling of the property: they would put the lean in place of the fat, and exchange the worthless for the precious. Then He said: ﴿Say: reforming them is best﴾.

Reform of the orphan is by undertaking his reform through teaching and discipline, and reform of his property through development and preservation. "Işlāḥun" (إصلاحٌ, reform) is the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence), and it is indefinite. What permits beginning with an indefinite here is the qualification by the prepositional phrase "lahum" (لهم, "for them"), which is either as a descriptive qualifier or as a complement of the verbal noun. "Khayrun" (خيرٌ, good) is the predicate (khabar) about işlāḥ. As we have said, işlāḥ is a verbal noun whose agent has been omitted, so "khayr" encompasses the reform related both to the agent and to the object. Thus the good is for both sides together: their reform of the orphans is good for the reformer and the reformed. It covers the situation of the orphan and of the guardian. It was said that "khayr" refers to the guardian: his reform of the orphan without compensation or wage is better for him and greater in reward. It was said that "khayr" refers to the orphan: the guardian's reform of the orphan and his mixing with him is better for the orphan than the guardian's turning away from him and isolating himself from him. The word "khayr" is unrestricted, so restricting it to one of the two sides requires a preponderant indicator, and keeping it general is better.

Ṭāwūs read: "Qul işlāḥun ilayhim" (قل إصلاحٌ إليهم), meaning: in caring for their property and other matters, it is better than your scrupulousness, or better in reward than reforming your own property.

﴿And if you mix with them, they are your brothers﴾. This is an iltifat (التفات, a shift in grammatical person) from the third person to the second person, because before it is "wa yas'alūnaka" (ويسألونك, "and they ask you"). The waw (و) is the pronoun of the absent. The wisdom of this iltifat is that addressing the one present directly prepares him to hear what is conveyed, to accept it, and to be careful with it. The waw in "fa-ikhwānukum" (فإخوانكم) refers to the guardians, and "hum" (هم) refers to the orphans. The meaning is that they are your brothers in religion; so you should care for them as you care for your brothers by lineage, with compassion, gentleness, and reform of their persons and their property.

"Mukhālaṭah" (مخالطة, mixing) is a form of mufā'alah (مفاعلة) from al-khalt (الخلط), which is blending. The meaning here concerns food: the orphan's provision is combined with the provision of his dependents with care, since it is difficult to single him out with his own food, so the guardian has no choice but to mix him with his own property for his dependents. Thus the verse brought a concession for that. This was said by Abu Ubayd.

Or it means partnership in property and trading on their behalf, so that you take from the profit what belongs to you and leave for them what belongs to them. Or it means marriage: if the orphan is a boy, he marries his daughter to him, or if the orphan is a girl, he marries her to his son. This view was preferred because this is mixing with the orphan himself, whereas partnership is mixing with his property. Also, partnership is included in His saying "Say: reforming them is best", but mixing through marriage is not included in it, so restricting it to this kind of mixing is closer to the meaning. And there is His saying "they are your brothers in religion": if the orphan is from the children of unbelievers, it is obligatory to seek the reform of his property just as one would for a Muslim. So the reference by "your brothers" must be to another type of mixing. Also His saying afterwards: "do not marry polytheistic women". So it is as if the meaning is that the mixing recommended is with orphans who are your brothers by Islam.

Or it means: drinking from his milk and his drinking from yours, and your eating from his bowl and his eating from yours. This was said by Ibn Abbas. Or it means mixing property with property in expenditure, food, dwelling, servants and animals, so that they take from their property compensation for your attending to their affairs, in an amount equal to the customary wage for that work. Among those who hold this view are some who permitted it whether the guardian was rich or poor, and some who said that if he is rich he should not eat from their property. Or it means mudāraba (مضاربة, profit-sharing partnership) by which their property grows.

What appears is that the mixing was not restricted to anything; it did not say "in such-and-such". So it is understood as any mixing that contains reform for the orphan. That is why He said "fa-ikhwānukum", i.e., you look upon them with the same regard as you look upon your brothers, in whatever reforms them. This mixing is framed by reform before and after: before it, by "Say: reforming them is best", and after it, by "And Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer". So the better view is that the intended mixing is whatever contains reform for the orphan by any means whatsoever: mixing in food, dwelling, trade, partnership, mudāraba, marriage, or otherwise.

The response to the conditional is "fa-ikhwānukum" (فإخوانكم), which is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject, i.e., "then they are your brothers". Abu Mijlaz read "fa-ikhwānakum" (فإخوانَكم) with an implied verb, meaning: "then you mix with your brothers".

The answer to the question came in two sentences: one composed of a subject and predicate, and the second of a condition and consequence. The first sentence includes the reform of orphans and that it is good. It was presented affirmatively with an indefinite subject to indicate that it covers every kind of reform by way of substitution. Had it been made definite by annexation (idāfah), it would have been either general, which cannot be realized, or it would refer to a known specific reform, and the known does not encompass others. So indefiniteness came to indicate general substitution. It was predicated with "khayr", which indicates attaining reward, since the Muslim hastens to do what is good seeking Allah's reward.

The second sentence was presented as conditional because it comes to indicate the permissibility of occurrence, not requesting or recommending it.

The first answer indicates various kinds of rulings in which the orphan's interest lies: permissibility of teaching him matters of religion and manners, hiring someone for that on his behalf, spending on him from his property, accepting what is given to him, marrying him off, hiring him out, selling his property on the orphan's behalf, managing his property by buying and selling, working with his property personally on a mudāraba basis, handing it to another on a mudāraba basis, and other dispositions bound up with reform.

The second answer indicates the permissibility of mixing with orphans in what reforms them, so that one mixes him with oneself in marriages, and mixes his property with one's own in maintenance, trade and the like.

It was said that the verse includes the permissibility of mixing, so it indicates the permissibility of munāhadah (مناهدة, pooling provisions), which travellers practise on journeys: this person brings some of his property and that person some of his, so it is mixed, spent, and people eat, even if the amounts eaten differ. And if it is permitted to you in the property of an orphan, it is all the more permitted in the property of an adult with his willing consent. A parallel to the permissibility of munāhadah is the story of the People of the Cave: ﴿So send one of you with this silver of yours﴾ [18:19], and so on.

Some of the rulings we have presented have been disputed. Among them: the guardian's purchase from the orphan's property, his mudāraba with it, the guardian marrying his female orphan to himself, and the orphan marrying his daughter (to the guardian). This is mentioned in the books of jurisprudence.

It was said: He made them brothers for two reasons. The first is brotherhood in religion. The second is that they benefit from them, either in reward from Allah the Exalted, or in what they receive as wages for their work with their property. Everyone who benefits you is your brother.

al-Baqir said to a person: "I saw you among a people I did not know." He said: "They are my brothers." He said: "Among them is someone who, when you are in need, puts his hand into your sleeve and takes from it without asking permission?" He said: "No." He said: "Then you are not brothers."

It was said: in His saying ﴿fa-ikhwānukum﴾ there is evidence that the children of believers are believers in the rulings, since Allah named them our brothers.

﴿And Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer﴾. This is a sentence whose meaning is a warning. In it He informs that He knows who corrupts from among those who reform. The meaning is that He recompenses each of the two according to the attribute that he has. Knowledge is often attributed to Allah the Exalted as a warning, because whoever knows something will recompense for it. It is therefore an expression of the cause by the effect (ta'bīr bil-sabab 'an al-musabbab). "Ya'lamu" (يعلم, knows) here is transitive to one object. The report came here in a verb that implies renewal, although Allah's knowledge does not renew, because He intends reward and punishment for the corrupter and the reformer, two attributes which renew in those who bear them. Therefore the recompense attached to them is repeated as they recur. The action is linked to the corrupter first, so that refraining from corruption takes place.

"Min" (من) is connected to "ya'lamu" by the principle of implied meaning (taḍmīn), as if the meaning were: "Allah distinguishes by His knowledge the corrupter from the reformer."

The apparent meaning of the definite article (al-) is that it is for comprehensiveness over all kinds of corrupter and reformer, and the reformer of an orphan's property is among the things this covers. It is also possible that the article is for a known reference: the corrupter in the orphan's property from the reformer in it, and the corrupter through neglect of his upbringing from the reformer through discipline.

This sentence came with this division because mixing is of two kinds: mixing by corruption and mixing by reform. Also, since it was said "Say: reforming them is best", its opposite was understood, namely that corruption is evil. So this division came with reference to reform.

Its counterpart is ﴿Had Allah willed, He would have distressed you﴾, i.e., He would have made you suffer hardship and imposed strictness upon you. This was said by Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi and others. Or: He would have destroyed you. This was said by Abu Ubaydah. Or: He would have made what you took from the orphans' property a ruin (mawbiq, مَوْبِق, a destruction), said by Ibn Abbas, and this is the meaning of what precedes. Or: He would have imposed upon you what is difficult for you, said by al-Zajjaj. Or: He would have made you sinful through mixing with them. Or: He would have constricted the matter for you in mixing with them, said by 'Ata'. Or: He would have forbidden you to mix with them, said by Ibn Jarir. These sayings are all close in meaning.

The object of "shā'a" (شاء, willed) is omitted, as indicated by the answer, and the intended sense is: "Had Allah willed to distress you." The lām (ل) in an affirmative verb is most commonly used in the speech of the Arabs, and it is employed here. Most readers recited "la-a'natakum" (لأعنتكم) with the hamza lightened, which is the original form. Al-Bazzi, through the transmission of Abu Rabi'ah, recited it with the hamza softened. It was also recited with the hamza dropped and its vowel placed on the lām, like the reading of one who recited "fa-lā ithma 'alayhi" (فلا إثم عليه) with the hamza dropped.

Abu Abdullah Nasr ibn Ali, known as Ibn Maryam, said: Ibn Mujahid did not mention this letter, and Ibn Kathir did not drop the hamza, but softened it and realised it in full, so people assumed it was deleted. For the hamza here is a hamzat al-qat' (همزة القطع, a cutting hamza, i.e., one that is always pronounced), so it does not fall away in connected speech as the hamzat al-wasl (همزة الوصل, the connecting hamza) falls away when connected. End of his words. Thus he considered the dropping of the hamza a mistake, although others transmitted it as a reading, as we have mentioned.

In this conditional sentence is an announcement and a reminder of Allah's kindness and favour toward the guardians of orphans, since He removed from them distress and hardship in mixing with orphans and in attending to their situations and their property.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) on Surah 2, verses 220–221 (part 2 of 3):

﴿Indeed, Allah is Mighty and Wise.﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said: "*'Aziz* (Mighty) means one who prevails, who is able to put His servants in difficulty and distress, but He is *Hakim* (Wise), and does not impose upon them except what their capacity can bear." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "*'Aziz* means that His command cannot be repelled, and *Hakim* means one who makes firm what He executes." End of quotation. In describing Him, exalted is He, with *'izza* (might), which is dominance and control, there is an indication that this belongs to Him alone and that no one shares in it. It is as if, when He gave them guardianship over the orphans, He warned them that they should not oppress them, nor overpower them, nor seize control over them in the manner of a tyrant, for this attribute belongs to Allah alone. In describing Him, exalted is He, with *hikma* (wisdom), there is an indication that He does not exceed what He has permitted regarding them and their wealth. Therefore you have no latitude except within what the Law has permitted you and what Divine wisdom has required, for He is the Wise, the Perfect in what He creates and legislates. Thus the reform of the orphans is not dependent on your opinion; rather, it depends on following what has been legislated concerning them.

﴿And do not marry polytheistic women until they believe﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: It was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Rawaha. He freed a slave-woman and married her, and she was a Muslim. Some Muslims criticized him, saying, "He married a slave-woman," and they wanted to marry into the polytheists out of desire for their lineages, so this was revealed. Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning Abu Marthad al-Ghanawi, whose name was Kannaz ibn al-Husayn. In another report, it was Marthad ibn Abi Marthad, who was an ally of the Banu Hashim. He asked permission to marry 'Anaq, who was a woman of Quraysh, possessing some beauty, and a polytheist. He said: "O Messenger of Allah, she pleases me." This cause is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, in a longer form than this. It has also been said that it was revealed concerning a beautiful black slave-woman belonging to Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman, whom he freed and married. It is possible that the cause includes all these accounts.

The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when He mentioned the ruling on mixing with orphans, which could entail marriage and other things called "mixing" (mukhalata), to the extent that some of them interpreted it as affinity (musaharah) only, and preferred that view as mentioned earlier, and among the orphans there were some who were children of disbelievers, Allah forbade marriage to polytheist women and men. He indicated the cause that makes marriage lawful, which is religious brotherhood (al-ukhuwwa al-diniyya), so He forbade marrying anyone in whom this brotherhood was absent, and the orphans of disbelievers were included in the general scope of those who associate partners with Allah. There is another connection: when the ruling on drinking wine and on consuming the proceeds of gambling (maysir) had come before, and He mentioned the ruling on marriage, then just as He forbade wine among drinks and what gambling leads to among foods, He forbade polytheist women among those one may marry.

The majority of reciters read *wa-la tankihu* with a *fatha* on the *ta'*, from *nakaha*, which is used with the meaning of contracting a marriage and with the meaning of intercourse by ownership or otherwise. Al-A'mash read *wa-la tunkihu* with a *damma* on the *ta'*, from *ankaha*, meaning: do not give your own selves in marriage to polytheist women. The "polytheist women" here means disbelievers, so it includes People of the Book (*kitabiyyat*) and whoever sets up another god with Allah. It has been said that the People of the Book are not included, but the correct view is that they are included, because the Jews worship 'Uzayr and the Christians worship 'Isa, and because of His saying: ﴿Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they associate with Him﴾ [Yunus: 18]. This second view is the view of the majority of the commentators (*mufassirun*). It has also been said that the intended meaning is the polytheist women of the Arabs, which is the view of Qatada.

According to the view of those who say that the People of the Book are included among them, one needs a justification for marrying them. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that this is a general ruling that was abrogated (*naskh*, abrogation), and from Mujahid that it is a general ruling from which the People of the Book were excluded. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the verse is general, covering idolaters, Magians, People of the Book, and everyone who is not upon the religion of Islam, and marrying them is forbidden, and the verse is muhkam (definitive) on this view, abrogating the verse of al-Ma'ida, although the verse of al-Ma'ida was revealed earlier, even though it comes later in the recitation. This is confirmed by the statement of Ibn 'Umar in *al-Muwatta'* (of Malik): "I know of no greater association (*shirk*) than that a woman says her lord is 'Isa."

It is narrated that Talha ibn 'Ubayd Allah married a Jewish woman, that Hudhayfa married a Christian woman, and that 'Umar became extremely angry with them both, to the point that he almost struck them. 'Uthman married Na'ila bint al-Farafisa, who was a Christian. Marrying People of the Book is permissible. This was the view of the majority of the Companions and the Successors: 'Umar, 'Uthman, Jabir, Talha, Hudhayfa, 'Ata', Ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan, Tawus, Ibn Jubayr, and al-Zuhri, and al-Shafi'i held it, as did the general body of the scholars of Madina and Kufa. It has been said that the scholars of the cities (*ulama' al-amsar*) agreed (*ijma'*, consensus) on the permissibility of marrying People of the Book, except that Malik and Ibn Hanbal disliked it while Muslim women were available and one was able to marry them. There is disagreement about marrying Magian women. Hudhayfa married a Magian woman. As for whether the Magians are People of the Book, there is disagreement. It is narrated from a group that they have a prophet called Zaradasht and an ancient scripture that was lifted up. The narration of the scripture is reported from 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas, and a lengthy account is mentioned concerning its lifting and the alteration of their law. Allah knows best its authenticity.

The proofs of these positions are mentioned in the books of jurisprudence (*fiqh*). The apparent meaning of the prohibition in His saying "wa-la tankihu" is prohibition (*tahrim*), though it has been said that it is a prohibition of disapproval (*karaha*). "Until they believe" is a limit (*ghaya*) to the prohibition of marrying them. The meaning of their believing is their affirmation of the two testimonies of faith and their commitment to the laws of Islam.

﴿And a believing slave-woman is better than a polytheist woman﴾. The apparent meaning is that *amah* (slave-woman) is intended in the sense of a female slave. The meaning of "better than a polytheist woman" is: better than a free polytheist woman, so the qualified noun is omitted because its contrast, "slave-woman," indicates it. It has been said that *amah* here means woman in general, so it includes free women and slave-women, and from this comes the hadith: "Do not prevent the female servants of Allah from the mosques of Allah." This is the view of al-Dahhak, and al-Zamakhshari mentioned no other. In this there is evidence for the permissibility of marrying a believing slave-woman. The implication of the qualifier (*mafhum al-sifa*) requires that it is not permissible to marry a disbelieving slave-woman, whether she is a People of the Book or otherwise. This is the position of Malik and others. Abu Hanifa and his companions permitted marrying a slave-woman from the People of the Book. Concerning a Magian slave-woman there is disagreement. The position of Malik and a group is that she may not be had by marriage or by ownership. It is narrated from 'Ata' and 'Amr ibn Dinar that there is no harm in marrying her by ownership (*milk al-yamin*). They interpreted "wa-la tankihu al-mushrikat" as referring to the contract, not to a slave-woman purchased, and they argued from the captives of Awtas, and that the Companions married female captives from them by ownership.

It has been said that in this verse there is evidence for the permissibility of a man who is able to afford a free Muslim woman (*tawl*, means) marrying a Muslim slave-woman. The basis of this inference is that His saying "better than a polytheist woman" means better than a free polytheist woman, and whoever has the means to marry a free polytheist woman also has the means to marry a free Muslim woman, since the means do not differ with respect to faith and disbelief. The amount of wealth needed for the costs of marriage is the same. It follows from this that whoever has the means to marry a free Muslim woman may marry a Muslim slave-woman. This is a subtle inference.

"*Amah*" is the subject (*mubtada'*), the justification for beginning with an indefinite noun is the descriptive phrase, and "*khayr*" (better) is the predicate. It has been argued from His saying "*khayr*" that marrying a polytheist woman is permissible, because the elative form (*af'al al-tafdil*) implies sharing. The prohibition is first in the sense of disapproval. They said: Comparison occurs only between two permissible things. But there is no proof in this, because comparison may be made in terms of belief, not only in terms of actual existence. Among examples is His saying: ﴿The companions of the Garden, on that Day, will have a better abode﴾ [al-Furqan: 24], and "Honey is sweeter than vinegar," and 'Umar said in his letter to Abu Musa: "Returning to the truth is better than persisting in falsehood." It is also possible to retain the meaning of "better" as sharing in actual existence, and this does not prove permissibility of marriage, since marriage to a polytheist woman involves worldly benefits, while marrying a believing slave-woman involves otherworldly benefits. The two benefits share in general benefit, but the benefit of the Hereafter has the supreme excellence. Therefore a ruling based on this worldly benefit does not require permission, just as wine and gambling have benefits, yet this does not imply their permissibility, and there is hardly any prohibited thing that does not contain some benefit.

These interpretations of the elative form are according to the view of Sibawayh and the Basrans, that the word *af'al* used for comparison is not valid where there is no sharing, as in your saying: "Snow is colder than fire," and "Light is brighter than darkness." Al-Farra' and a group of the Kufans said: it is valid where there is sharing, and where there is no sharing. Ibrahim ibn 'Arafa said: the elative form in the speech of the Arabs comes to affirm the first and negate the second. According to one view, it is not valid that there is no good in the polytheist woman, rather the good is in the believing slave-woman.

﴿And even if she pleases you﴾. *Law* (even if) here has the meaning of the conditional *in* (if), like the saying: "Return the beggar even with a burnt sheep's hoof." The *waw* in "wa-law" is for conjunction with an omitted circumstance; the estimated meaning is: "better than a polytheist woman in every state, even in this state." We have mentioned that this serves to exhaust all states, and that what follows *law* in this construction comes in a way that is contrary to what precedes it in some respect. Pleasing (*i'jab*) contradicts the ruling of preference, and requires the permissibility of marriage because of the suitor's desire for her. The pleasing is attributed to the person of the polytheist woman, without specifying who is pleased by her, so the intended meaning is pleasing in general, whether because of beauty, nobility, wealth, or anything else by which one may be pleased. The meaning is: even if the polytheist woman surpasses in beauty, wealth, and lineage, a believing slave-woman is better than her, because what the polytheist woman excels in belongs to this world, while faith belongs to the Hereafter, and the Hereafter is better than this world. Through agreement in religion, love is completed and the benefits of this world are attained, such as companionship, obedience, and the preservation of wealth and children, while through difference in religion, neither love nor any benefit of this world is achieved.

﴿And do not marry polytheistic men until they believe﴾. The reading with a *damma* on the *ta'* is a consensus (*ijma'*) among the reciters. The address is to the guardians (*awliya'*), and the second object is omitted; the estimated meaning is: "Do not marry off the believing women to polytheistic men." The community agreed that a polytheist may not have intercourse with a believing woman in any way, and the prohibition here is for forbiddance (*tahrim*). It has been argued from this address that guardianship is required in marriage, and that this is explicit evidence for it.

﴿And a believing slave is better than an idolater, even though you admire him.﴾ The discussion of this clause is the same as the discussion of the clause before it. There is a disagreement about the meaning of "slave" ('abd): does it mean a bondservant (raqiq) or a man (rajul)? It is used like that in the case of the female slave there. Does the meaning, then, become "better than a free idolater," so that it corresponds to "slave"? Or does it mean "better than an idolater" absolutely, so that it covers both the slave and the free person, as in His saying, "better than an idolatress"?

﴿Those invite to the Fire.﴾ This refers to both categories, the female idolaters and the male idolaters. "Yad'una" (they invite) may mean invitation by speech, as in His saying, "And they say: Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided" [al-Baqarah: 135]. It may also mean that there is no speech, but that through love and association, something of the dispositions of the disbelievers creeps into him, which leads him to agree with them in their religion, and Allah forbid, so he becomes one of the people of the Fire. It was also said: its meaning is that they invite to abandoning fighting and combat, and that abandoning them entails deserving the Fire. The proponent of this interpretation distinguished between a dhimmi woman and others, since a dhimmi woman's husband is not made to fight. It was also said: the meaning is that a child who is born may be invited to disbelief by the disbeliever and may agree, and so become one of the people of the Fire. What the apparent sense of the verse indicates is that the disbelievers are certainly invited to the Fire, either by speech, or by intimacy, close association and intermarriage leading to it. The meaning is that whoever is inviting to the Fire must be shunned, lest by his invitation he constantly sway his companion, who then responds to what he invites him to and perishes. In this verse there is an indication of the cause that prevents marriage with disbelievers: because of their involvement in forbidden things, such as wine, pork, immersion in filth, the raising of offspring, the absorption of their dispositions, and other things in which the desire for marriage is not equal to some of what they are upon. When this cause is considered, it is present in every male and female disbeliever, and so it requires the prohibition of marriage absolutely. The discussion of Surat al-Ma'idah will come, if Allah the Exalted wills, and we will show there, if Allah wills, that it does not contradict this.

"Ila" (to) is connected to "yad'una," as in His saying, "And Allah invites to the abode of peace" [Yunus: 25]. It also takes the particle "li" (for), as in the line of poetry:

"I called out for what befell me, Miswar"

The object of "yad'una" is omitted, either for brevity, since the intention is to establish that it is among their nature to invite to the Fire without considering a specific object; or for abridgement, so the meaning is: "those invite you to the Fire."

﴿And Allah invites to the Garden and forgiveness.﴾ This confirms the prohibition of marrying disbelievers, since two divisions are mentioned: one must be followed, and the other must be avoided, so the two divisions are opposed. It is not possible to answer Allah's call and follow what He has commanded except by avoiding the invitation of the disbelievers and abandoning them entirely. Allah's invitation is to follow His religion, which is the cause of entering the Garden, so He expressed the cause by its result, because it follows from it. The apparent sense of the verse is a report about Allah the Exalted, that He Himself invites to the Garden. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It means: and the friends of Allah, who are the believers, invite to the Garden and forgiveness, and to what leads to them. They are the ones whose friendship and intermarriage must be maintained, and who must be preferred over others." End of quotation. What led him to hold that this is by omitting a modifier is the desire to establish an equivalence between the idolaters and the believers in invitation. When He reported about those who associated partners that they invite to the Fire, He made those who believe invite to the Garden. But there is no need for what he mentioned. Rather, leaving the wording on its apparent sense, by attributing the invitation to Allah the Exalted, is more emphatic in distancing from the idolaters, since He made the Originator of the world opposed to them in invitation. This is more eloquent than establishing an equivalence between the idolaters and the believers.

The majority (al-Jumhur, the main body of reciters) read "wal-maghfirati" with the genitive, coordinated with "al-Jannah," and the meaning is that He the Exalted invites to forgiveness, that is, to the cause of forgiveness, which is repentance and adherence to acts of obedience. Here "al-Jannah" is placed before "forgiveness," while in His saying, "And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden" [Al 'Imran: 133], and His saying, "Race to forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden" [al-Hadid: 21], it comes after. The basic principle is that forgiveness precedes the Garden, because entry into the Garden follows from the attainment of forgiveness. In those two verses it came according to this basic principle. Here, however, the Garden is mentioned before forgiveness for the sake of a fine correspondence, since before it is: "Those invite to the Fire," so: "And Allah invites to the Garden" came. Also, so that it begins with what the soul yearns for when the invitation of Allah is mentioned, He brought the most noble before the most noble, and then followed it with forgiveness by way of completing the favour and preparing the cause of entering the Garden.

Al-Hasan read "wal-maghfiratu" with the nominative, as the subject, and the predicate is His saying "bi-idhnihi" (by His permission), meaning: forgiveness is attained by His facilitating and enabling it. The explanation of permission (idhn) has already been given. According to the readings of the majority, "bi-idhnihi" is connected to "yad'u" (invites).

﴿And He makes His signs clear to the people, that they may remember.﴾ That is, He manifests them and reveals them in such a way that no ambiguity arises in them. This clarification is not restricted to some people rather than others, but He shows His signs to everyone, in the hope that through the manifestation of the signs remembrance and admonition will occur, because whenever a sign is clear and evident, it is apt that remembrance will occur through it, so that compliance with what those signs indicate is achieved, namely conformity with the command and avoidance of what is forbidden. "Lin-nas" (to the people) is connected to "yubayyinu" (makes clear), and the "li" (the particle) means arrival and conveyance, which is one of its meanings mentioned at the beginning of al-Fatihah.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 222 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They ask you about menstruation.﴾ In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Anas, the Jews used to expel a woman from among them when she menstruated; they would not eat with her, nor drink with her, nor have intercourse with her in the house. They asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it, and Allah the Exalted revealed this verse. It was also said: the Arabs were as is mentioned in this hadith, so Abu al-Dahdah asked about this, saying: "How should we deal with women when they menstruate?" Then it was revealed. Mujahid said: they used to have intercourse with menstruating women, excepting the practice of the Children of Israel in avoiding eating with menstruating women and living with them, so this verse was revealed. It was also said: the Christians used to have intercourse with menstruating women and paid no regard to menstruation, while the Jews avoided them in everything, so Allah commanded moderation between the two matters. It was also said: Usayd ibn Hudayr and Abbad ibn Bishr asked about menstruation, and so it was revealed. It was also said: the Jews used to say, "Whoever comes to his wife from behind, his child will be born squinting," so the women of the Ansar refrained from that, and he was asked about a man's approaching his wife while she is menstruating, and what the Jews had said; so it was revealed.

The pronoun in "They ask you" (wa-yas'aluna-ka) is a plural pronoun, so the apparent meaning is that the questioners on this matter are those to whom the plural applies, neither two nor one. And it came as "They ask you" here, and before it in: "They ask you about orphans" [al-Baqarah: 220], and before that (p-167) "They ask you what they should spend. Say: the surplus" [al-Baqarah: 219], with the conjunctive waw upon "They ask you about wine and gambling" [al-Baqarah: 219]. It was said: because the questioning about the three occurred at one time, so the particle of plurality was used for that, as if it were said: they combined for you the question about wine and gambling and the question about such and such. It was also said: these are three separate questions without a waw: "They ask you about the new moons" [al-Baqarah: 189], "They ask you what they should spend. Say: what you spend" [al-Baqarah: 215], "They ask you about the sacred month" [al-Baqarah: 217], and three: "They ask you about wine" [al-Baqarah: 219]. It was said: they came without the conjunctive waw because their questioning about those events occurred at different, separate times, so no conjunction particle was used in them, since each of them is a fresh question. End of quotation.

The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when He forbade marrying polytheists, and this implied marrying believers and preferring that, He explained a great ruling among the rulings of marriage, namely the ruling on marriage during the time of menstruation. "Al-mahid" (menstruation), as we have established, is a form of the root of menstruation (hayd), and it may linguistically be a verbal noun, a noun of time, or a noun of place. Most of the exegetes among the literati assert that what is meant is the verbal noun, as if it were said: "about menstruation," and Zamakhshari explained it this way, and Ibn Atiyyah began with it, saying: "al-mahid is a verbal noun like al-hayd, and similarly al-maqil from qala yaqil." Al-Ra'i said:

"Their elbows were built above a slippery place where the tick cannot find a resting place."

Al-Tabari said: al-mahid is the name of the menstruation (al-hayd), and similar to it is the saying of Ru'bah about life:

"To you I complain of the hardship of living, and the passing of years that have plucked my feathers."

End of his words. It appears from this that he distinguished between the statement "al-mahid is a verbal noun like al-hayd" and al-Tabari's statement "al-mahid is the name of the menstruation," and there is no difference between them: it may be called a verbal noun, and it may be called a noun of the verbal noun, and the meaning is one. The view that al-mahid is a verbal noun is transmitted from Ibn al-Musayyab. Ibn Abbas said: it is the place of the blood, and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan held the same. Accordingly, the meaning is the place. He preferred that it means the place of the blood by His saying: "So withdraw from women during the menstruation" [al-Baqarah: 222]. For if it were meant as the verbal noun, the apparent meaning would be forbidding enjoyment of them in what is above the navel and below the knee, and that is not established; it would necessitate the claim of abrogation or specification, which is contrary to the basic principle. So when it is taken to mean the place of menstruation, the meaning is: withdraw from women in the place of menstruation. They said: its use for the place is more common and more famous than its use for the verbal noun. End of his words. It is possible to prefer the verbal noun by His saying: "Say: it is an injury" [al-Baqarah: 222], whereas the place of the blood itself is not an injury, because injury is a specific quality, an accident, while the place is a body, and a body cannot be an accident. This is answered by saying that it is elliptical when the place is meant, that is, "possessing injury." The address in "They ask you" and in "Say" is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the pronoun in "it" refers back to menstruation, and the meaning is that a revulsion and disgust arise in a person because of it.

﴿So withdraw from women during menstruation﴾: the disagreement concerning "al-mahid" has preceded, whether it is the place of the blood or the menstruation itself. It is possible that the first is taken as the verbal noun and the second as the place. If we take the second as the verbal noun, then an elided genitive must be supplied: "So withdraw from intercourse with women during the time of menstruation." There is disagreement about this withdrawal. Ibn Abbas, Shurayh, Ibn Jubayr, Malik, Abu Hanifah, Abu Yusuf, and a group of scholars held that it is obligatory to withdraw from what the waist-wrapper covers, and this is supported by what is authentically reported: that she would tie her waist-wrapper on herself and then he would do as he wished above it. Aisha, al-Sha'bi, Ikrimah, Mujahid, al-Thawri, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, and Dawud held that only withdrawal from the vagina is obligatory, and this is the sound view of al-Shafi'i. It is reported from Ibn Abbas and Ubaydah al-Salmani that it is obligatory for a man to withdraw from his wife's bed when she menstruates, taking the apparent meaning of the verse, but this is an anomalous view. Since menstruation is known in the language, it did not need explanation, and the verse does not address its minimum or its maximum; rather, it indicates the obligation of withdrawal from women during menstruation. Its minimum according to Malik has no limit; rather, a single flow of blood is menstruation for him, and yellowness and turbidity are menstruation. The well-known view of Abu Hanifah is that its minimum is three days, and al-Thawri held likewise. Ata' and al-Shafi'i said: one day and one night. As for its maximum, Ata' and al-Shafi'i said: fifteen days; al-Thawri said: ten days, and this is the well-known view of the companions of Abu Hanifah. The school of Malik on this is like the view of Ata', and it was derived from a statement of Nafi' as seventeen days, and it was said eighteen days. Al-Qurtubi said: it is transmitted from Malik that there is no time for little or much menstruation except what is commonly found among women. It is transmitted from al-Shafi'i that this is referred back to the custom of women, like the view of Malik. It is transmitted from Ibn Jubayr: menstruation extends to thirteen days, and if it exceeds that, it is istihadah. All the proofs of this and the remaining rulings of menstruation are mentioned in the books of jurisprudence. The verse does not address what is required of one who has intercourse during menstruation, and the scholars differed on this. Abu Hanifah, Malik, Yahya ibn Sa'id, al-Shafi'i, and Dawud said: he seeks forgiveness from Allah and there is nothing upon him. Muhammad said: he gives charity of half a dinar. Ahmad said: he gives charity of a dinar or half a dinar, and al-Tabari approved this, and it is the view of al-Shafi'i in Baghdad. A group of the people of hadith said: if he has intercourse during the flow of blood, it is a dinar, and if at its cessation, half of it. Ibn Atiyyah transmitted this view from al-Awza'i, and others transmitted from al-Awza'i that if he has intercourse while she is menstruating, he gives charity of fifty dinars. In al-Tirmidhi, from the Prophet (ﷺ) he said: "If it is red blood, a dinar; and if it is yellow blood, half a dinar."

﴿And do not approach them until they are purified﴾: Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal from him read "yattahharna" with shaddah on the ta' and ha' and a fatha, its origin being "yatatahharna," and so it is in the codices of Ubayy and Abdullah. The rest of the seven read "yathurna," the imperfect of tahura. In the codex of Anas: "And do not approach women during their menstruation and withdraw from them until they purify themselves." This should be taken as explanation and not as Qur'an, because of its frequent contradiction of the consonantal text. Al-Farisi preferred "yathurna" with lightness, since it is a triliteral form opposite to "tamisat," which is triliteral. Al-Tabari preferred the shaddah, and said: it has the meaning of "they bathe," since there is consensus that it is forbidden for a man to approach his wife after the blood has ceased until she is purified; he said: the disagreement is only about what purity is. End of his words. It was said: the reading with shaddah means "until they bathe," and the reading with lightness means "until their blood ceases," as Zamakhshari and others said. In the book of Ibn Atiyyah: each of the two readings may be understood to mean washing with water, or the cessation of blood and removal of its harm. He said: what al-Tabari held, that the reading with shaddah implies bathing and the reading with lightness implies cessation of blood, is not a necessary matter; likewise his claim of consensus that there is no disagreement about the disliked nature of intercourse before bathing. End of what is in the book of Ibn Atiyyah. His saying "and do not approach them until they are purified" is a metaphor for intercourse and confirms His saying "So withdraw from women during the menstruation." The apparent meaning of withdrawal and approach is that they do not touch each other, but the Sunnah has clarified that it is a specific withdrawal and approach. From their disagreement about the minimum and maximum of menstruation one knows their disagreement about the minimum and maximum of purity.

﴿And when they have purified themselves﴾: that is, they have bathed with water. Ibn Atiyyah said: the disagreement about its meaning, as already mentioned, is between purification with water and the cessation of blood. Mujahid and a group here said: what is meant is bathing with water, and this is required by the context of the command to come to them; although approaching them before bathing is permissible, the imperative from Allah the Exalted is only expressed in its most perfect form. If purification is bathing with water, then the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, and a group is that it is like the bath of major impurity; this is also the view of Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, and al-Hasan. Tawus and Mujahid said: ablution suffices for permissibility of intercourse. al-Awza'i held that what permits intercourse is washing the place of intercourse with water, and Ibn Hazm held this too. The cause of the disagreement is whether purification with water is taken as legal purification or linguistic purification. Whoever takes it as linguistic says: she washes the place of the harm with water; whoever takes it as legal takes the lighter of the two kinds, which is ablution, for the sake of ease, or the more complete of the two, which is that she bathes as for major impurity, since by it the discharge of obligation is certain. Bathing with water necessarily brings about the cessation of blood, since it is not prescribed except after it. And if we say that bathing like the bath of major impurity is required, then it is disputed concerning a dhimmi woman whether she is compelled to bathe from menstruation. Whoever holds that bathing is an act of worship says she is not obligated, since the intention of worship is not valid from a disbeliever; and whoever does not hold that it is worship, but rather that bathing is a right of the husband in order to make her lawful for intercourse, says: she is compelled to bathe. As for whoever makes bathing obligatory, its description is what is transmitted in the Sahih from Asma' bint Umays, that she asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the bath of menstruation, and he said: "One of you takes her water and her lote-leaves, and purifies herself, performing the purification well; then she pours water over her head and rubs it until it reaches the roots of her hair, then she pours water over the rest of her body."

﴿So come to them﴾: this is a command meant to express permissibility, like His saying: "And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt" [al-Ma'idah: 2], and "And when the prayer is ended, disperse" [al-Jumu'ah: 10]. The command of permissibility is often followed by prohibition, and it is an elliptical expression for intercourse.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 222 (part 2 of 2):

﴿From where Allah has commanded you﴾. "Hayth" (where) is a locative adverb, so the meaning is: from the direction which Allah the Exalted has commanded, namely the front passage (al-qubul), since that is what is forbidden during menstruation. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Rabi'. Or: from the direction of their purity, not from the direction of their menstruation. This was said by 'Ikrimah, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Abu Razin and al-Suddi. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the meaning becomes: "So approach them in purity, not in menstruation." Or: from where it has been made lawful for you to approach them in marriage, not from the direction of immorality. This was said by Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah. Or: from where He has made lawful for you their intimacy, by their not being fasting, nor in i'tikaf (seclusion in the mosque), nor in ihram. This was said by al-Asamm. The first view is the most apparent, because taking "hayth" to mean place and location is the literal meaning, and anything else is figurative. When it is taken in the most apparent sense, it contains a refutation of those who permitted intercourse with women in their posteriors. It has been said: the consensus (ijma') has been established on the prohibition of that, and whatever has been reported permitting it from any of the scholars is disputed and not sound. The meaning of "Allah has commanded you" is to withdraw from them in the vagina, or from the navel to the knees.

﴿Indeed Allah loves those who turn back (tawwabin)﴾, i.e., those who return to good. It came after the command and the prohibition as an announcement of the acceptance of the repentance of one who falls into what has been prescribed against him. It is general in regard to those who repent from sins.

﴿And He loves those who purify themselves (mutatahhirin)﴾, i.e., those who are cleansed of immoralities. Some restricted it to the one who repents from polytheism and the one who purifies himself from sins. This was said by Ibn Jubayr. Or the reverse, as said by 'Ata' and Muqatil. Some restricted it to the one who repents from intercourse during menstruation. Mujahid said: from approaching women in their posteriors during their days of menstruation. Abu al-'Aliyah said: "tawwabin" refers to those who repent from disbelief, and "mutatahhirin" to those who purify themselves through faith.
