Qatadah said: "tawwabin" refers to those who repent from major sins, and "mutatahhirin" to those who purify themselves from minor sins. It was said: "tawwabin" refers to those who repent from sins, and "mutatahhirin" to those who purify themselves from defects. 'Ata' also said: "mutatahhirin" means those who purify themselves with water. It was said: from the posteriors of women, so that they are not defiled by sin after repentance. It is as if this view is parallel to the saying of the Exalted, relating about the people of Lut: ﴿Expel them from your town; indeed they are people who keep themselves pure﴾ [al-A'raf: 82]. What appears to be the case is that the Exalted mentioned at the beginning of the verse: ﴿And they ask you about menstruation﴾, and the cause indicates that they had a practice they committed during menstruation, of intercourse with them during menstruation, in the vagina or in the posterior. Then Allah the Exalted informed of the prohibition of that, during the state of menstruation, in the vagina or in the posterior. Then He permitted intercourse in the vagina after the cessation of blood and the purification which is obligatory upon the woman for the sake of the husband, although it is not explicitly commanded in the wording of the verse. So Allah the Exalted praised the one who complied with the command of Allah the Exalted and returned from the practice of the Jahiliyyah to what He had legislated, and praised the one who complied with His command regarding the legislated purification with water. He expressed this in two general forms, drawing in husbands and wives in this matter. So He said: ﴿Indeed Allah loves those who turn back﴾, i.e., those who return to what He legislated, ﴿and He loves those who purify themselves﴾ with water in what was legislated concerning it. Thus the ending of the verse with the love of Allah encompassed husbands and wives. He mentioned the verb to indicate the difference of the two aspects of repentance and purification, and that each of the two attributes has a love from Allah specific to that attribute; or He repeated it for emphasis. Allah the Exalted praised the people of Quba' by His saying: ﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves, and Allah loves those who purify themselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 108]. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked them about the cause for which Allah praised them, and they said: "We used to combine istijmar and istinja' with water," or words to this effect. Talhah ibn Musarrif recited "al-muttahhirin" with the assimilation of the ta' into the ta', since its original form is "al-mutatahhirin."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 223–224 (part 1 of 4):

﴿Your women are a tilth for you﴾. In al-Bukhari and Muslim: the Jews used to say about one who has intercourse with his wife from behind, in her vagina, that the child would be cross-eyed (ahwal). So this was revealed. It has also been said that the occasion of revelation was the dislike of the women of the Ansar when the Muhajirun married them, for they used to do this in Makkah, enjoying their women both from the front and from behind. Al-Hakim related its meaning in his Sahih. It has also been said that the cause of this was that "some of the Companions said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: 'I am ruined.' He said: 'What has ruined you?' He said: 'I turned my saddle last night.' So it was revealed." Its connection to what precedes is clear, for when there came before it: ﴿So go to them from where Allah has commanded you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 222], and the unrestricted wording required permission to approach them in all manners of intercourse, He emphasized this by stating explicitly what indicates all the modes; and He also specified the locus by making it a tilth, which is the vagina. The tilth, as mentioned in the story of the cow, is the tilling of the earth for planting, then the crop itself was called a tilth: ﴿It struck the tilth of a people﴾ [Al 'Imran: 117], and earning was also called a tilth. The poet said:

"When the locusts eat the tilths of a people, my tilth is their concern: the eating of the locusts."

They said: he means his wife. Ahmad ibn Yahya recited:

"Indeed the wombs are tilled lands for us,
So upon us is the sowing in them, and upon Allah is the growth."

This sentence came as an explanation and clarification of His saying: ﴿So go to them from where Allah has commanded you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 222], which is the place forbidden for use during menstruation. This indicates that the essential aim is seeking offspring: "Marry, for I will boast of you among the nations on the Day of Resurrection," not merely the fulfilment of desire. So come to women by the path to which the essential aim is connected, which is the vagina. "Your women" is the subject (mubtada'), and "a tilth for you" is the predicate (khabar), either by omitting the particle of comparison, i.e., "like a tilth for you," and "your women" with an omitted modifier, i.e., "the intercourse with your women is like a tilth for you," likening intercourse to tilling, since the semen is like the seed, the womb like the earth, and the child like the plant. It has also been said that it is with an omitted modifier, i.e., "a place of tilth for you." This metaphor for marriage is one of the subtle metaphors of the Qur'an. They said: this is like His saying: ﴿eats food﴾ [al-Furqan: 7], and like His saying: ﴿and a land you have not trodden﴾ [al-Ahzab: 27], according to those who interpreted it as women. It is possible that "a tilth for you" means "a thing tilled for you," so it is of the category of using the verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle. In the expression "a tilth for you" there is evidence that it is the vagina and not the anus. Al-Maturidi said: that is, a field sown for you, and in it is evidence of the prohibition of refraining from intercourse with women, for what is sown is wasted if left, and evidence of the permissibility of intercourse for the purpose of seeking offspring and children, not for the fulfilment of desire. End of his words. Al-Raghib distinguished between tilth (harth) and sowing (zar'), saying: tilth is casting the seed and preparing the land, and sowing is tending it and causing it to grow. For this reason He said: ﴿Have you considered what you till?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 63] ﴿Is it you who sow it, or are We the sowers?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 64], attributing to them the tilling and denying them the sowing.

﴿So go to your tilth however you wish﴾. The word "going to" (ityan) is a metaphor for intercourse. "A tilth for you" came indefinite because it is the original form of the predicate, and because it was the unknown; its attribution to the subject conveyed the permissibility of enjoying it under the Law. "Your tilth" came definite because in the idafah there is a reference back to something previously mentioned and a specification of what is added to it. A parallel is your saying: "Zayd is a slave belonging to you, so treat your slave well." When an indefinite noun has preceded and you repeat the word, it must be definite, either with al- as in His saying: ﴿Pharaoh disobeyed the Messenger﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 16], or with idafah as in this verse. "Anna" here means "how" with respect to withdrawal (al-'azl) and non-withdrawal. This was said by Ibn al-Musayyab; so the manner would be restricted to these two states. Or it means "how" in general regarding the conditions of the woman; this was said by Ikrimah and al-Rabi'; so it indicates the permissibility of intercourse with the woman in whatever state the one who penetrates wishes, facing forward or backward, on either side, standing or reclining, and other states; this is in the place of tilth. Or it means "when" (mata); this was said by al-Dahhak; in which case it is a temporal adverb, and the meaning is: go to your tilth at whatever time you wish. A group of exegetes said "anna" means "ayy" (which/whatever), and the meaning is: in whatever manner you wish; so according to this it is a choice among the modes and postures, i.e., face forward, turn around, but avoid the anus and menstruation. This has been explained in some hadiths that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "That is not a concern after being in one single opening." The simam is the mouth of a bottle, then it was used figuratively. Another group said "anna" means "where" (ayna), making it a place, and used this as evidence for the permissibility of intercourse with a woman in her anus. Among those reported to have permitted that: Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, Ibn Abi Mulayka, and 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar among the Companions, and Malik; and it occurred in al-'Utbiyyah. It is reported from Ibn 'Umar that he declared disbelief in one who does this and denounced it; and it is reported from Malik that he denounced it. When he was asked, it was said: "They claim you permit approaching women in their posteriors?" He said: "Allah forbid! Have you not heard the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Your women are a tilth for you﴾? And how can tilth be except in the place of sowing?" Similar to this is reported from al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifah, and permissibility of it is reported from Nafi' and Ja'far al-Sadiq, and it is the choice of al-Murtada among the Shi'i imams. What was cited in (al-Muntakhab) as evidence for this position and what was refuted with, can be consulted there, since our book is not designed to mention the proofs of jurisprudence except to the extent related to the verse. Twelve Companions related from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ the prohibition of this, with varying wordings all indicating prohibition, which Ahmad mentioned in (his Musnad), and Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and others; and Abu al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzi gathered them with their chains in a booklet he named (The Prohibition of the Detested Place). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It is not fitting for one who believes in Allah and the Last Day to take a slip of a scholar as a guide in this matter. He also said: "Anna shi'tum": its meaning according to the majority of scholars, from Companions, Successors, and imams, is: from whatever direction you wish, meaning: facing forward or backward, on one side. "Anna" only comes as a question or report about a matter that has aspects, so it is more general in the language than "how," than "where," than "when." This is the Arabic usage. People have explained "anna" in this verse by these words, and Sibawayh explained it as "how" and "from where" together. The grammarians said: "anna" is for generalizing conditions, and it may come in the sense of "when" and "where," and be interrogative or conditional, and they made it, in the conditional use, only a place adverb. Since its predominant meaning in the language is for conditions, there is no argument for one who holds that it indicates generalization of places of penetration, so that it would mean "where." Al-Zamakhshari said: His saying: ﴿So go to your tilth however you wish﴾ is an analogy: that is, go to them as you go to your fields that you wish to till, from whatever direction you wish, with no direction forbidden to you over another; and the meaning: have intercourse with them from whatever side you wish, provided the place of entry is one, which is the place of tilth. His saying: ﴿It is an injury, so withdraw from women﴾ [al-Baqarah: 222], ﴿from where Allah has commanded you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 222], ﴿So go to your tilth however you wish﴾ are of the subtle metaphors and admirable allusions, and these and similar in the speech of Allah the Exalted are good manners which believers should learn and adopt, and strive to imitate in their conversations and correspondence. End of his words. It is good. They said: the governing element in "anna" is "go." This that they said is not correct, because we have mentioned that it is an interrogative or conditional; it cannot be conditional here, because then it would be a place adverb, which would permit intercourse with women other than in the vagina, and the prohibition of that from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is established; and on the conditional reading the preceding word cannot govern the conditional adverb, because it is an object of the conditional verb, just as the conditional verb is an object of it. Nor can it be interrogative, because when it is interrogative it is complete with what follows it of a verb, as in His saying: ﴿How can I have a son?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 47], or of a noun, as in His saying: ﴿From where is this for you?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 37], and does not require anything else; but here its dependence on what precedes it is evident. And if it were interrogative, what precedes it would not govern it, and it would be governed by the verb after it. Thus it is clear, for both aspects of "anna," that it is not governed by what precedes it, and this is one of the problematic points that require thought and reflection. What appears to me, and Allah knows best, is that it is conditional, because it requires a clause other than the clause after it, and the conditions have been placed within it, like the placing of locative adverbs, and it has been treated like them, likening the condition to the locative adverb. A parallel to this has come with the word "kayfa" (how), which has passed from interrogation to the sense of condition in their saying: "How you do, I will do," and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Rather, both His hands are outstretched; He spends however He wills﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64]; so it cannot be interrogative here, but the sense of condition and the connection of the clause with the other was intended, and the answer of the clause is omitted, indicated by what precedes it. Its estimate: "Anna shi'tum fa'tuhu" (however you wish, then go to it), and "kayfa yasha'u yunfiq" (however He wills, He spends), just as the answer of the conditional is omitted in your saying: "Strike Zayd wherever you meet him," the estimate being: "wherever you meet him, then strike him." If you say: you have removed "anna" from its true locative sense and kept it for generalizing conditions, like "kayfa," and made it require another clause like the conditional clause, then is the past verb "shi'tum" in a jussive position like its state when it is a locative adverb, or is it in a nominative position like it after "kayfa" in their saying: "How do you do, I do?" The answer: it may be either, but the jussive is preferred, because the jussive has been established with it when it is a clear adverb, and the only thing is the likening of conditions to adverbs, and there is a clear connection between them, since each of them carries the meaning of "in"; unlike "kayfa," for the jussive has not been established with it; and whoever permitted jussive with it did so by analogy, while what is transmitted from the Arabs is the nominative for the verb after it, where it requires another clause.

﴿And send ahead for yourselves﴾. The object of "qaddimu" (send ahead) is omitted. It has been said: the estimate is: the mention of Allah at the time of intercourse, or seeking offspring, and excess, as intercessors; said by Ibn 'Abbas. Or: the good; said by al-Suddi. Or: a sure standing (qadama sidq); said by Ibn Kaysan. Or: the reward in avoiding what you were forbidden and carrying out what you were commanded; said by Ibn 'Atiyyah. Or: the mention of Allah upon intercourse, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "If one of you, when he approaches his wife, says: 'O Allah, keep Satan away from us and keep Satan away from what You provide us,' then if a child is decreed between them, it will not harm him." Or the invocation of the name over the intercourse; related by al-Zamakhshari. Or: what must be sent ahead of righteous deeds, which is the opposite of what I forbade you; said by al-Zamakhshari, and this is a saying compounded from the saying of those before him. What appears is that the meaning is: send ahead for yourselves obedience to Allah, compliance with what He commanded, and avoidance of what He forbade; because a command and a prohibition came before, and this is the good He mentioned in His saying: ﴿And whatever good you send ahead for yourselves, you will find it with Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 110]; and for this reason there came after it: "and fear Allah," that is: fear Allah regarding what He commanded you and forbade you, and it is a warning to them against opposition; and because the Great One who has been mentioned requires that you send ahead before Him what you will be approached by, that you will not be disgraced before Him, and that is righteous action.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 223–224 (part 2 of 4):

"And know that you will meet Him" (﴿واعْلَمُوا أنَّكم مُلاقُوهُ﴾). The apparent meaning is that the pronoun attached to "meeting" (﴿مُلاقُوهُ﴾) refers to God the Exalted, and this is by way of omitting a modified noun (mudaf, a noun in a construct phrase), meaning: "those who will meet the recompense for your deeds." It is also permissible that it refers to the omitted object of the verb "send forward" (﴿وقَدِّمُوا﴾), meaning: "you will meet what you have sent forward of good and obedience." This too involves an omitted modified noun, meaning: "those who will meet its recompense." It is also permissible that it refers to the recompense indicated by the omitted object (ma'mul, the grammatical object) of "send forward" (﴿قَدَّمُوا﴾ [Yasin: 12]). In this there is a refutation of those who deny resurrection, reckoning and the return, whether the pronoun refers to God the Exalted, to the object of "send forward," or to the recompense.

"And give good tidings to the believers" (وَبَشِّرِ المُؤْمِنِينَ): that is, of a good outcome in the Hereafter. In it is an indication of the attribute by which one fears God and sends forward good, and deserves the good tidings, which is faith. In the command to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to give good tidings there is great consolation and a generous promise of abundant reward. He did not use a pronoun of absence but used the explicit noun that indicates the attribute, and also because it is, with that, the end of a verse (fasl ayah, a verse-ending).

These noble verses contain God the Exalted's report about the believers that they ask the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about wine and gambling, and what He reported occurred. He commanded His Prophet to inform the one who asked him about these two that they both involve a great sin. This information became an incentive to abandon them, and it indicates their prohibition. The meaning is that drinking wine and playing games of chance produce sin. He did not suffice with mere sin until He described it as "great" in one reading, and as "abundant" in another reading (p-173). God the Exalted has said concerning the forbidden things: ﴿Those who avoid the grave sins of the wrongdoing﴾ [al-Najm: 32]; ﴿If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden﴾ [al-Nisa: 31]; ﴿Indeed, it is a great sin﴾ [al-Nisa: 2]. Since He described the sin as "great," and it is among the greatest sins and the most emphatic in prohibition, He also informed that there are benefits for people in them, such as gaining wealth through trade in wine, and through gambling with arrows, and other things. This is because there is no prohibited thing without some benefit in some respect, especially what the nature inclines toward, or what a person has been raised upon by nature.

Then God the Exalted informed that the harm of sin, which leads to the Fire, is greater than the benefit that ends with the end of its time, to guide the intelligent person to avoid what its punishment is lasting and its benefit is passing. Then God the Exalted informed that they ask Him about what they should spend; they were answered that they should spend what is easy for them to spend, pointing to ﴿and He has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion﴾ [al-Hajj: 78]. Then He mentioned that He makes the signs clear to the believers, as He made clear the matter of wine, gambling and what they spend. Then He mentioned that with this clarification hope is produced for reflecting on the situation of this world and the Hereafter, and when one reflects on both, by reflection one prefers the Hereafter over this world.

Then He digressed from these two questions to the question about the orphans and what they were obligated regarding them, since orphans are not capable of looking after their own affairs, due to their youth and deficiency of intellect. They were answered that reforming them is better than neglecting them, both for the reformer, through obtaining reward, and for the reformer through disciplining, teaching them, and developing their wealth. (Hadith: "My community is like a building, its parts strengthen one another.")

Then He informed that mixing with them is required, because "they are your brothers in Islam," so brotherhood necessitates considering the situation of the brother. He expressed the request in the form of a conditional clause, and the answer came with what requires association, which is that they are your brothers. When He commanded reform for orphans, He mentioned that God the Exalted knows the corrupter from the reformer, so that one would beware of corruption and be called to righteousness. Here the meaning of His knowledge is that He will recompense the one who corrupts and the one who reforms with what suits his action. Then God the Exalted informed that if He willed, He would have burdened you with what is difficult for you; thus He indicated that the previous obligations, such as the prohibition of wine and gambling, the obligation of charity being "what is easy," and the obligation of reforming the orphan, contain no hardship or distress. Then He concluded this by saying that He is the Mighty who cannot be overcome, the Wise who places things in their proper places.

Since He mentioned the prohibition of something of what they used to enjoy, namely drinking wine and eating from it, and gambling with arrows and eating from it, and since marriage is also among the greatest desires and pleasures, He digressed to mention the prohibition of one type of it, namely marrying one who has the attribute contrary to faith, which is polytheism that necessitates aversion and distance. Marriage necessitates association and affection. God the Exalted has said: ﴿And He placed between you affection and mercy﴾ [al-Rum: 21]; ﴿You will not find a people who believe in God and the Last Day loving those who oppose God and His Messenger﴾ [al-Mujadila: 22]. "Their dwellings do not face each other" (a reference to the separation of their homes). So He forbade marriage with one who has the attribute contrary to faith, and He limited that by the attainment of faith. Then He mentioned that a believing slave is better than a polytheist, even if the polytheist would please one by beauty, wealth or position. He also drew attention to the cause that necessitates abandoning it, which is that the polytheist calls to the Fire, and the one who keeps company with someone, mixes with him, and is in contact with him, even in marriage, which calls to intimacy, from every kind of companionship, may respond to him when he invites him to what is in accordance with his desire. They were recent in their acceptance of faith and its newness, so they were prevented from this, as a closing of the path to the Fire.

Then God the Exalted informed that He Himself calls to the Garden and forgiveness; so He is the one who looks out for your interest in prohibiting what He prohibited and permitting what He permitted. He makes His signs clear and explains them so that no confusion appears with them, in order to hope that you remember and take admonition from the signs.

Since He mentioned the prohibition of marrying one who has the attribute of polytheism, He mentioned the prohibition of intercourse with a believing woman who is in menstruation, and He limited that by her purity, just as He limited what came before it by faith. Then He permitted, when she purifies herself, for us to have intercourse with them from the place God commanded, which is the place that was occupied by menstruation, and He commanded us to avoid intercourse with her during menstruation. Then He pointed out the excellence of the one who repents and the one who purifies himself, by His loving him. He did not suffice with that in one sentence, but repeated it in two sentences, and singled out each attribute with love, saying: "Indeed God loves those who repent and loves those who purify themselves" (p-174).

Then God the Exalted mentioned the permissibility of intercourse with a woman whose menstruation has ceased, in whatever manner the husband wishes and chooses, whether she is facing him or turned away, or lying on her side or on her back, and from whichever side he wishes, because of the increased pleasure in changing positions, and the enjoyment of looking at all of her body, and the postures that stimulate desire. By the term "tilth" (harth) He pointed out that it is the place of offspring; this indicates the prohibition of intercourse in the rear passage, because it is not the place of offspring. Since they were prevented from intercourse with a menstruating woman because the place of intercourse contains harm from menstrual blood, then being prevented from the place that is more harmful is more fitting and more appropriate.

Since prohibition and command were mentioned first in the previous verses and in this one, it was concluded with the command to send forward righteous deeds, and that what a person sends forward returns only to the benefit of his own soul. Then he was commanded to fear God the Exalted, and was commanded to know and be certain with the certainty that has no doubt, that we will meet God, and He will recompense us for our deeds. He commanded His Prophet to give good tidings to the believers, who are those who carried out what He commanded and avoided what He forbade. So the beginning of these verses was with a warning against engaging in disobedience, and their conclusion with good tidings to the people of faith. These are verses whose contained wonders the tongues are unable to describe, and before whose eloquence the most skilled and fluent expert submits. They combined eloquence of expression and clarity of meaning, the connection of sentences and refinement of structure, question and answer, warning of punishment, and encouragement toward reward. They guided to the straight path, and were received from the presence of the Wise, the All-Knowing.

﴿And do not make God an obstacle in your oaths that you would be righteous and fear God and make reconciliation among people; and God is Hearing and Knowing﴾ ﴿God will not hold you accountable for what is unintentional in your oaths, but He will hold you accountable for what your hearts have earned; and God is Forgiving and Forbearing﴾ [al-Baqara: 225] ﴿For those who swear abstention from their wives is a waiting period of four months; and if they return, then indeed God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Baqara: 226] ﴿And if they decide upon divorce, indeed God is Hearing and Knowing﴾ [al-Baqara: 227] ﴿Divorced women shall wait by themselves for three menstrual periods. And it is not lawful for them to conceal what God has created in their wombs, if they believe in God and the Last Day. And their husbands have more right to take them back during that period, if they want reconciliation. And due to them is similar to what is expected of them, according to what is reasonable; but the men have a degree over them. And God is Mighty and Wise﴾ [al-Baqara: 228] ﴿Divorce is twice; then either keep [her] in an acceptable manner or release [her] with good treatment. And it is not lawful for you to take anything of what you have given them unless both fear that they will not keep within the limits of God. But if you fear that they will not keep within the limits of God, then there is no blame upon either of them concerning that by which she ransoms herself. These are the limits of God, so do not transgress them. And whoever transgresses the limits of God – it is those who are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqara: 229].

"Al-'Urda" (the obstacle): it is a form (fu'la) from "al-'ard" (presenting), and it has the meaning of the passive participle (maf'ul), like "al-furqa" and "al-qabda." It is said: "So-and-so is an 'urda for such-and-such," and "the woman is an 'urda for marriage," meaning she is presented for it. Ka'b said:

Her path is one whose landmarks are effaced, unknown.

Hassan said:

"God said: 'I have made ready a host; they are the Helpers'; its encounter is..."

Habib said:

When was my hearing a target for my blamers, and how have my resolves become clear to those who blame?

It is said: "He made him an 'urda for calamity," meaning exposed to it. Aws ibn Hajar said:

And a she-camel like a stallion; one day I presented her for my saddle, and in her is boldness and jostling.

It is also said: it is the name of what you place in front of a thing, from placing a stick across a vessel, so that it stands in the way and becomes a barrier and obstacle. It is also said: the original meaning of "'urda" is strength, and from this it is said of a strong camel: "this is an 'urda for travel," meaning strong for it; and of a swift horse: "it is an 'urda for our departure."

"Al-yamin" (the oath, right hand): its original meaning is the limb, and it has been used for swearing an oath because of the custom in the handshake of the two contracting parties. It is pluralized as "ayman" and "aymun," and it is used both for the limb and for the oath. "Al-yamin" is also used for the direction that is on the side of the limb called by that name, so it is put in the accusative as an adverb of place. You say: "Zayd is on the right of 'Amr" (yamin 'Amr). In the sense of the limb it is derived from "al-yumn" (blessing). It is said: "So-and-so is blessed in his appearance, blessed in his counsel, and blessed in his omen."

"Al-laghw" (idle talk): it is what the tongue slips into without intention, as said by al-Farra'. It is derived from their saying for what is not counted in blood-money of young camels: "laghw." It is said: "laga yalghu laghwan" and "lagha yalgha laghan." Ibn al-Muzaffar said: the Arabs say: "al-laghw," "al-laghiya," "al-lawaghi," and "al-lughawi." Ibn al-Anbari said: "al-laghw" for the Arabs is what is discarded from speech as being dispensable; it is also said it is what its wording is not understood. It is said: "laghā al-ta'ir yalghu," meaning it made a sound; and "laghā bi-l-amr," meaning he was fond of it, "yalghā." It is also said that "al-lugha" (language) is derived from this. Ibn 'Isa, having mentioned that "al-laghw" is what is not beneficial, said: "From it comes 'al-lugha,' because to those other than its people it is laghw." He made an error in this derivation, for "al-lugha" is only derived from their saying: "laghā bi-kadha" when one is devoted to it.

"Al-Halim" (the forbearing): the one who pardons sin while having the power to hold one accountable for it. It is said: "halama al-rajul yahlumu hilman," and he is "halim." Al-Nabigha al-Ja'di said:

There is no good in forbearance if it has no sources that protect its purity from being clouded.

It is also said: "halima al-adim yahlamu halman," when the hide becomes perforated and spoiled. He said:

For you and the Book to 'Ali are like one tanning a hide, and the hide has become rotten.

And he dreamed (ḥalama) in sleep, yalamu ḥulman and ḥuluman, and the one who dreams is ḥālim. ﴿And we are not versed in the interpretation of dreams﴾ [Yusuf: 44].

Al-īlāʾ (oath of abstention) is the verbal noun of ālā, meaning he swore. It is also said: ta'allā and i'talā, meaning he swore. An oath is called ulliyya, ulwa, ulwa and ilwa. The plural of ulliyya is alāyā, like ʿashiyya and ʿashāyā. It is also said that ulawwa is pluralized as alāyā, like rakūba and rakāʾib.

At-tarabbuṣ (waiting) means expectation and waiting. It is the verbal noun of tarabbaṣa, and it is a metathesis (qalb) of at-tabaṣṣur. A poet said:

> Wait for her, for the misfortunes of time (rayb al-manūn). Perhaps she will be divorced one day, or her husband will die.

Fāʾa (to return) means yafīʾu fayʾan and fayʾatan: he returned. The shadow after midday is called fayʾ because it returned from the east side to the west. It is quick to return (sarīʿ al-fayʾa), meaning quick to return. ʿAlqama said:

> I said to her, "Return (fīʾī), for you do not shrink from the eyes that are beautiful and the dyed fingertips."

Al-ʿazm (resolve) is that to which the heart is bound and determined. It is said: ʿazama ʿalayhi yaʿzimu ʿazman, ʿazaman, ʿazīma and ʿazāman. It is also said: aʿzama iʿzāman. And ʿazamtu ʿalayka latafʿalanna means: I swore to you that you will certainly do it.

At-ṭalāq (divorce) is the dissolution of the marriage contract. From it it is said: ṭullīqat tuṭallaqu, so she is ṭāliq and ṭāliqa. Al-Aʿshā said:

> O neighbour of mine, separate, for you are divorced.

It is also said: ṭalaqat with a damma on the lām. Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā related this, and al-Akhfash denied it.

Al-qurʾ (menstrual cycle or purity period): its original meaning in the language is the time whose recurrence is customary. The qurʾ of a star is the time of its rising and its setting. It is said from it: aqraʾa an-najm, meaning it rose or it set. The qurʾ of a woman is her menstruation (ḥayḍ) and her purity (ṭuhr). So it is one of the words with opposite meanings (min al-aḍdād), as Abū ʿAmr, Yūnus and Abū ʿUbayd said. It is said from both: aqraʾat al-marʾa (she became one who menstruates or one who is pure). Abū ʿAmr said: Among the Arabs there are those who call menstruation along with purity qurʾ. Some said: al-qurʾ is what is between two menstruations. Al-Akhfash said: aqraʾat means she became one who has menstruation. When she menstruates, you say qarat without an alif. It is said: al-qurʾ originally means gathering, from the saying: qaraʾtu al-māʾ fī al-ḥawḍ, meaning I gathered the water in the pool. From this: mā aqraʾat hādhihi an-nāqa salan qaṭṭu, meaning this she-camel never gathered a fetus in her belly. If it is meant as menstruation, it is the gathering of blood in the womb (raḥim). If it is meant as purity, it is the gathering of blood in the body.

Ar-raḥim (womb) is the vagina of a female, and it may be used metaphorically for kinship. It is said: baynahumā raḥim, meaning there is kinship between them. And he joins the ties of kinship (yaṣilu ar-raḥim).

Al-baʿl (husband) is the spouse. From it: baʿala yabʿalu buʿūlatan, meaning he became a husband. Bāʿala ar-rajul imraʾatahu means he had intercourse with his wife. She is bāʿalahu when she does that with him. A woman who is ḥasanat at-tabʿīl is one who treats her husband well. Al-baʿl also means king, and the idol (ṣanam) was named after it, because it is self-sufficient. From it comes baʿl an-nakhl (the palm tree that needs no irrigation). The plural of al-baʿl is buʿūl and buʿūla, like faḥl and fuḥūla. The tāʾ in it is for the feminine of the plural and is not analogous (lā yanqāsu). So one does not say for kuʿūb, the plural of kaʿb, kuʿūba.

Ar-rajul (man) is well known and is pluralized as rijāl. It is derived from ar-rujla, which is (p-176) strength. It is said: rajul bayyin ar-rujūla wa ar-rujla, and he is arjal ar-rajulayn, meaning the stronger of the two. A horse that is rajīl is strong at walking, and from it the foot (rijl) was named for its strength in walking. Irtajal al-kalām means he was strong in it. Tarajjal an-nahār means the daylight became strong. It is said: rajul and rijla, just as they say امرؤ and امرأة. I copied from the handwriting of our teacher Abū Jaʿfar ibn az-Zubayr, may God have mercy on him:

> Every neighbour remains content, except my neighbours, the Banū Jabala.
> They tore the collar of their young woman, and did not care for the sanctity of the man.

Ad-daraja (degree) is rank. Its origin is from darajtu ash-shayʾa and adraljtuhu, meaning I folded it. Daraja al-qawm means they perished. Allah caused them to pass away (adrajahum), and so it is like folding a thing step by step. The degree is a rank among the ranks of folding. From it is the degree by which one ascends.

Al-imsāk (holding) of a thing is restraining it. From it are two nouns: mask and masāk. It is said: innahu la-dhū maskin wa mīsāk, meaning he is stingy. In it is a remnant (muskatun) of good, meaning strength. Tamāsuk means holding together. Masīk means one who is clearly tight-fisted (bayyin al-masāka).

At-tasrīḥ (release) is sending away. Sarraḥa ash-shaʿr means he separated some of the hair from others. Sarraḥa al-māshiya means he sent the livestock out to graze. As-sarḥ is livestock. Nāqa masraḥ is a she-camel that is easy to walk, because of its ease of movement in it.

﴿And do not make Allah an obstacle (ʿurḍa) for your oaths﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās said: It was revealed about ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥa and his brother-in-law Bashīr ibn an-Nuʿmān. There was something between them. ʿAbd Allāh swore that he would not enter upon him, nor speak to him, nor reconcile between him and his wife. He kept saying: I have sworn by Allah, so it is not permissible for me except to fulfil my oath. Ar-Rabīʿ said: It was revealed about the man who swears that he will not join his ties of kinship and will not reconcile between people. Ibn Jurayj said: It was about Abū Bakr when he swore that he would not spend on Mistaḥ, when he spoke in the slander (al-ifk). Al-Muqātilān, Ibn Ḥayyān and Ibn Sulaymān said: He swore that he would not spend on his son ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān until he became Muslim. It is also said: He swore that he would not eat with the guests, when his son delayed the evening meal from them, and he himself became angry with his son. ʿĀʾisha said: It was revealed about the repetition of oaths by Allah. So He forbade that one swear by Him in righteousness, how much more in wickedness.

The connection of this verse with what precedes it: When He commanded piety toward Allah and warned them of the Day of Meeting, He forbade them to make His name common and to make it a target for what they swear to constantly. Whoever is revered and feared, his name must be preserved and guarded from what is not fitting for it, such as being mentioned in every oath, whether small or great, whether trivial or important. For repetition of that causes disregard for the one sworn by. The connection may also be that when He commanded the believers to be cautious in their earlier actions, concerning wine, gambling, spending the surplus, the affairs of orphans, marrying those who associate others with Allah, and the situation of having intercourse with a menstruating woman, He commanded them to be cautious in their speech. So their command to be cautious in actions and words is united.

They differed in understanding this clause, ﴿And do not make Allah an obstacle for your oaths﴾. This difference is based on the difference about the derivation of ʿurḍa. It is said: They were forbidden to make Allah a target for their oaths, so that they swear by Him in righteousness and wickedness. For breaking the oath along with frequent swearing shows little regard for the right of Allah the Exalted, as it is narrated from ʿĀʾisha that it was revealed about frequent swearing by Allah. It was forbidden that a man swear by Him in righteousness, how much more in wickedness? Allah has censured the one who swears often, in His words: ﴿And do not obey every frequent swearer, contemptible﴾ [al-Qalam: 10], and He said: ﴿And guard your oaths﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 89]. The Arabs praise those who swear little. Kuthayyir said:

> Few are the oaths of one who guards his oath. When an oath comes from him, he is true to it.

The wisdom in forbidding the multiplication of oaths by Allah is that this leaves no weight for the oath in the heart, and one is not safe from proceeding to a false oath. The mention of Allah is too exalted to be invoked for worldly purposes. It is also said: The meaning is: Do not make Allah a strength for your oaths and a confirmation of them. Something close to this meaning is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibrāhīm, Mujāhid, ar-Rabīʿ and others. He said: The meaning concerns what you intend to be firm in, namely abandoning the maintenance of kinship, righteousness and reconciliation. It is also said: The meaning is: Do not make Allah a barrier and a hindrance from righteousness and reconciliation. The saying of the one who said it was revealed about ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥa, or about Abū Bakr, as mentioned in the occasion of revelation, confirms this. So the meaning is that the man would swear regarding some good deeds, such as maintaining kinship, reconciling between people, doing good to someone, or worship, and then he would say: I fear Allah that I break my oath, and so he would abandon righteousness in his oath. So they were forbidden to make Allah a barrier to what they had sworn about.

(p-177) ﴿For your oaths﴾: the lām may be connected to ﴿ʿurḍa﴾, so it is like reinforcing the transitivity, or it is a target and an aim for your oaths. It may also be connected to the saying: (And do not make), so it is for causation, meaning: do not make Allah a target on account of your oaths. The apparent meaning is that by oaths here is meant the act of swearing, not the thing sworn about. Az-Zamakhsharī said: That is, a barrier to what you have sworn about, and the thing sworn about is called an oath because it is connected to the oath, as the Prophet ﷺ said to ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn Samura: "If you swear an oath and then see something else better than it, then do what is better, and expiate your oath." That is, concerning something of what is sworn about. End of his words. There is no need here to depart from the apparent meaning. The hadith was only pressed into this sense because he used the word oath generally and meant by it what it governs, since he said: "If you swear on an oath", where the verb "swear" takes ʿalā. So this interpretation was needed. There is nothing in the verse that requires this interpretation, but az-Zamakhsharī, when he took ʿurḍa to mean barrier and hindrance, was compelled to this interpretation.

﴿That you be righteous, and be mindful of Allah, and make reconciliation between people﴾. Az-Zajjāj, and at-Tibrīzī after him, said: ﴿That you be righteous﴾ is in the place of a nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence. Az-Zajjāj said: The meaning is: your righteousness, your piety and your reconciliation are better and more fitting. He made the speech end at the saying ﴿for your oaths﴾. The meaning of the sentence that contains the prohibition, according to him, is that it concerns a man who is asked to do a good deed or the like, and he makes an excuse by Allah and says: "An oath is upon me," though he has not sworn. At-Tibrīzī estimated the predicate of the omitted subject as meaning: "That you be righteous, be mindful of Allah and make reconciliation between people is better for you than that you make Allah a target for your oaths." What az-Zajjāj and at-Tibrīzī went to is weak, because it separates ﴿that you be righteous﴾ from what precedes it, and connecting it to it is the correct approach. It also involves an omission for which there is no evidence. Az-Zamakhsharī said: ﴿That you be righteous and be mindful of Allah and make reconciliation﴾ is an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to ﴿your oaths﴾, that is, to the matters sworn about, which are righteousness, piety and reconciliation between people. End of his words. This is weak, because it contradicts the apparent meaning: the apparent meaning of oaths is the acts of swearing, while righteousness, piety and reconciliation are the things sworn about, so they are distinct, and it is not permissible for them to be an explanatory apposition to oaths. But since he interpreted oaths as what is sworn about, this became acceptable for him. We have already shown that there is no need to force oaths into the sense of things sworn about. According to his view, ﴿that you be righteous﴾ would be in the genitive position. If he claimed that ﴿that you be righteous﴾ and what follows it is a substitute (badal) for (your oaths), that would be better, because explanatory apposition is most common with proper names. The majority held that his saying ﴿that you be righteous﴾ is an object of purpose (mafʿūl min ajlihi). Then they differed about the estimate: it is said: out of aversion that you be righteous, said by al-Mahdawī. Or: for abandoning that you be righteous, said by al-Mubarrad. It is also said: so that you do not be righteous, nor be mindful of Allah, nor make reconciliation, said by Abū ʿUbayda and aṭ-Ṭabarī, as in his saying:

> He opposed, so no, by Allah, he will not descend into a valley.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 223–224 (part 4 of 4):

He means: "it does not descend" (lā tahbiṭu). It was also said: the implied phrase is "the desire that you be righteous" (irādatu an tabarrū). The first interpretations converge in meaning. This meaning is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, ʿAṭāʾ, Ibn Jurayj, Ibrahim, Qatada, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Suddi, Muqatil, al-Farrāʾ, Ibn Qutayba, and al-Zajjaj, the last of those narrated from. Their view is that the meaning is: "Do not swear by Allah that you will not be righteous," so that it is connected to His words, "and do not make" (wa-lā tajʿalū). This meaning does not appear clearly, because it makes the prohibition of swearing depend on the absence of righteousness, whereas in fact the act of swearing is what is conditioned by the absence of righteousness. Moreover, no conditional and consequent can be formed if you say, regarding the meaning and cause of this prohibition: "If you swear by Allah, you will be righteous," which is not valid. This is like your saying: "Do not strike Zayd, so that he does not harm you." The harm is negated by refraining from striking. The meaning is: if you do not strike him, he will not harm you, and if you strike him, he will harm you. Thus, the absence of righteousness does not follow from refraining from swearing, nor does its existence follow from its existence. Rather, the existence of righteousness follows from refraining from swearing, and the absence of righteousness follows from the occurrence of swearing. What we have mentioned supports the view that the implied phrase is "the desire that you be righteous," because it gives as the cause of refraining from swearing the desire for righteousness to exist, and from this the conditional and consequent are formed. You say: "If you swear, you will not be righteous, and if you do not swear, you will be righteous."

Some scholars have explained this meaning, saying: "that you be righteous, and God-fearing, and make peace" (in tabarrū wa-tattaqū wa-tuṣliḥū) is the cause of this prohibition, that is, the desire that you be righteous. The meaning is: our prohibition of this is only because of what is in avoiding it of righteousness, piety, and reconciliation, so that you, O company of believers, will be righteous, pious, and reformers on earth, not corruptors. If you ask: how does the absence of swearing necessarily bring about righteousness, piety, and reconciliation among people? We say: because whoever abstains from swearing, believing that Allah, blessed and exalted, is greater and more majestic than that His exalted name should be invoked in seeking worldly gain, this is one of the greatest gates of righteousness. As for the meaning of piety, it is clear, because he guards against doing anything that would violate the glorification of Allah, exalted is He. As for reconciliation among people, it is because when people believe that he glorifies Allah to this degree, guarding against violating what is due to Him, they believe that he glorifies Allah and is truthful, far from corrupt aims. So they accept his word, and reconciliation is achieved through his mediation. End of this discussion.

In al-Muntakhab, which is an elaboration of what al-Zamakhshari said, it says: "Its meaning according to the other reading is 'to make it liable to' (ʿurḍah), in the sense of exposed to the matter." He said: "Do not make Allah exposed to your oaths, so that you cheapen Him by frequently swearing by Him." For this reason He censured the one about whom He revealed: "And do not obey every excessive swearer, contemptible" (Qur'an 68:10), with the most abominable reproaches, and made the excessive swearer its prelude. "That you be righteous" (an tabarrū) is the cause of the prohibition, that is, the desire that you be righteous, God-fearing, and reconcilers, because the habitual swearer is bold toward Allah and does not glorify Him. Therefore he is not righteous or God-fearing, and people do not trust him, so they do not admit him into their mediation and the reconciliation of their affairs.

It was also said: the meaning is, "Do not swear by Allah while lying, so that you be righteous toward those to whom you swear, and God-fearing toward them, and reconcile them through lying." This meaning is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. He thus restricted the thing made known to lying, restricted the cause to people, and restricted reconciliation to lying, which is contrary to the apparent meaning.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "That you be righteous" (an tabarrū) is connected either to the verb or to the phrase "liable to" (ʿurḍah). That is: "Do not make Allah, because of your oaths by Him, liable to your being righteous." End of quotation. This implied phrase is not valid, because it involves separation between the governing word and the governed element by an unrelated element. He connected "for your oaths" (li-aymānikum) with "make" (tajʿalū), and connected "that you be righteous" (li-an tabarrū) with "liable to" (ʿurḍah). Thus he separated "liable to" (ʿurḍah) and "that you be righteous" (li-an tabarrū) by his words "for your oaths" (li-aymānikum), which is unrelated to both, since in his view it is governed by "make" (tajʿalū). That is not permissible. A parallel to what he permitted would be your saying: "Pass and strike with Zayd Hind," which is not permissible. They also stated explicitly that it is not permissible to say: "A man with a horse came to me, riding a piebald," because of the separation by an unrelated element.

What appears to me is that "that you be righteous" (an tabarrū) is in the accusative position by dropping the preposition, and the governing element is His words "for your oaths" (li-aymānikum). The implied phrase is: "for your oaths that you be righteous." Thus they were forbidden from degrading the name of Allah, the Exalted, and making it an object for their oaths on righteousness, piety, and reconciliation, which are beautiful qualities. This is because of what we fear in that from breaking the oath (ḥinth). How much more so when the oaths are on what contradicts righteousness, piety, and reconciliation? On this view the speech is coherent, with each word in its proper place that suits it. Thus, in the position of "that you be righteous" (an tabarrū), there are three views. The nominative, on the basis of it being the subject (mubtada'), with dispute about the implied governing element. The genitive, in two ways: as an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf al-bayān) and as a substitution apposition (badal). The accusative, in two ways: either as an object of purpose (al-mafʿūl min ajlihi), depending on the disagreement about its implied element, or as governed by "your oaths" (aymānikum) with the dropping of the preposition.

"And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing" (wa-llāhu samīʿun ʿalīm). He ended this verse with these two attributes because what relates to them was previously mentioned. What relates to hearing is swearing, since it is among the things heard. What relates to knowledge is the desire for righteousness, piety, and reconciliation, since it is something whose locus is the heart, and so it is among the things known. These two attributes came corresponding to the cause and the effect, and came in the order of what preceded, namely the mention of hearing before knowledge, just as He mentioned swearing before the desire.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 223–224 (part 1 of 4):

﴿Your women are a tilth for you﴾. In al-Bukhari and Muslim: the Jews used to say about one who has intercourse with his wife from behind, in her vagina, that the child would be cross-eyed (ahwal). So this was revealed. It has also been said that the occasion of revelation was the dislike of the women of the Ansar when the Muhajirun married them, for they used to do this in Makkah, enjoying their women both from the front and from behind. Al-Hakim related its meaning in his Sahih. It has also been said that the cause of this was that "some of the Companions said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: 'I am ruined.' He said: 'What has ruined you?' He said: 'I turned my saddle last night.' So it was revealed." Its connection to what precedes is clear, for when there came before it: ﴿So go to them from where Allah has commanded you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 222], and the unrestricted wording required permission to approach them in all manners of intercourse, He emphasized this by stating explicitly what indicates all the modes; and He also specified the locus by making it a tilth, which is the vagina. The tilth, as mentioned in the story of the cow, is the tilling of the earth for planting, then the crop itself was called a tilth: ﴿It struck the tilth of a people﴾ [Al 'Imran: 117], and earning was also called a tilth. The poet said:

"When the locusts eat the tilths of a people, my tilth is their concern: the eating of the locusts."

They said: he means his wife. Ahmad ibn Yahya recited:

"Indeed the wombs are tilled lands for us,
So upon us is the sowing in them, and upon Allah is the growth."

This sentence came as an explanation and clarification of His saying: ﴿So go to them from where Allah has commanded you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 222], which is the place forbidden for use during menstruation. This indicates that the essential aim is seeking offspring: "Marry, for I will boast of you among the nations on the Day of Resurrection," not merely the fulfilment of desire. So come to women by the path to which the essential aim is connected, which is the vagina. "Your women" is the subject (mubtada'), and "a tilth for you" is the predicate (khabar), either by omitting the particle of comparison, i.e., "like a tilth for you," and "your women" with an omitted modifier, i.e., "the intercourse with your women is like a tilth for you," likening intercourse to tilling, since the semen is like the seed, the womb like the earth, and the child like the plant. It has also been said that it is with an omitted modifier, i.e., "a place of tilth for you." This metaphor for marriage is one of the subtle metaphors of the Qur'an. They said: this is like His saying: ﴿eats food﴾ [al-Furqan: 7], and like His saying: ﴿and a land you have not trodden﴾ [al-Ahzab: 27], according to those who interpreted it as women. It is possible that "a tilth for you" means "a thing tilled for you," so it is of the category of using the verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle. In the expression "a tilth for you" there is evidence that it is the vagina and not the anus. Al-Maturidi said: that is, a field sown for you, and in it is evidence of the prohibition of refraining from intercourse with women, for what is sown is wasted if left, and evidence of the permissibility of intercourse for the purpose of seeking offspring and children, not for the fulfilment of desire. End of his words. Al-Raghib distinguished between tilth (harth) and sowing (zar'), saying: tilth is casting the seed and preparing the land, and sowing is tending it and causing it to grow. For this reason He said: ﴿Have you considered what you till?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 63] ﴿Is it you who sow it, or are We the sowers?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 64], attributing to them the tilling and denying them the sowing.

﴿So go to your tilth however you wish﴾. The word "going to" (ityan) is a metaphor for intercourse. "A tilth for you" came indefinite because it is the original form of the predicate, and because it was the unknown; its attribution to the subject conveyed the permissibility of enjoying it under the Law. "Your tilth" came definite because in the idafah there is a reference back to something previously mentioned and a specification of what is added to it. A parallel is your saying: "Zayd is a slave belonging to you, so treat your slave well." When an indefinite noun has preceded and you repeat the word, it must be definite, either with al- as in His saying: ﴿Pharaoh disobeyed the Messenger﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 16], or with idafah as in this verse. "Anna" here means "how" with respect to withdrawal (al-'azl) and non-withdrawal. This was said by Ibn al-Musayyab; so the manner would be restricted to these two states. Or it means "how" in general regarding the conditions of the woman; this was said by Ikrimah and al-Rabi'; so it indicates the permissibility of intercourse with the woman in whatever state the one who penetrates wishes, facing forward or backward, on either side, standing or reclining, and other states; this is in the place of tilth. Or it means "when" (mata); this was said by al-Dahhak; in which case it is a temporal adverb, and the meaning is: go to your tilth at whatever time you wish. A group of exegetes said "anna" means "ayy" (which/whatever), and the meaning is: in whatever manner you wish; so according to this it is a choice among the modes and postures, i.e., face forward, turn around, but avoid the anus and menstruation. This has been explained in some hadiths that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "That is not a concern after being in one single opening." The simam is the mouth of a bottle, then it was used figuratively. Another group said "anna" means "where" (ayna), making it a place, and used this as evidence for the permissibility of intercourse with a woman in her anus. Among those reported to have permitted that: Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, Ibn Abi Mulayka, and 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar among the Companions, and Malik; and it occurred in al-'Utbiyyah. It is reported from Ibn 'Umar that he declared disbelief in one who does this and denounced it; and it is reported from Malik that he denounced it. When he was asked, it was said: "They claim you permit approaching women in their posteriors?" He said: "Allah forbid! Have you not heard the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Your women are a tilth for you﴾? And how can tilth be except in the place of sowing?" Similar to this is reported from al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifah, and permissibility of it is reported from Nafi' and Ja'far al-Sadiq, and it is the choice of al-Murtada among the Shi'i imams. What was cited in (al-Muntakhab) as evidence for this position and what was refuted with, can be consulted there, since our book is not designed to mention the proofs of jurisprudence except to the extent related to the verse. Twelve Companions related from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ the prohibition of this, with varying wordings all indicating prohibition, which Ahmad mentioned in (his Musnad), and Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and others; and Abu al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzi gathered them with their chains in a booklet he named (The Prohibition of the Detested Place). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It is not fitting for one who believes in Allah and the Last Day to take a slip of a scholar as a guide in this matter. He also said: "Anna shi'tum": its meaning according to the majority of scholars, from Companions, Successors, and imams, is: from whatever direction you wish, meaning: facing forward or backward, on one side. "Anna" only comes as a question or report about a matter that has aspects, so it is more general in the language than "how," than "where," than "when." This is the Arabic usage. People have explained "anna" in this verse by these words, and Sibawayh explained it as "how" and "from where" together. The grammarians said: "anna" is for generalizing conditions, and it may come in the sense of "when" and "where," and be interrogative or conditional, and they made it, in the conditional use, only a place adverb. Since its predominant meaning in the language is for conditions, there is no argument for one who holds that it indicates generalization of places of penetration, so that it would mean "where." Al-Zamakhshari said: His saying: ﴿So go to your tilth however you wish﴾ is an analogy: that is, go to them as you go to your fields that you wish to till, from whatever direction you wish, with no direction forbidden to you over another; and the meaning: have intercourse with them from whatever side you wish, provided the place of entry is one, which is the place of tilth. His saying: ﴿It is an injury, so withdraw from women﴾ [al-Baqarah: 222], ﴿from where Allah has commanded you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 222], ﴿So go to your tilth however you wish﴾ are of the subtle metaphors and admirable allusions, and these and similar in the speech of Allah the Exalted are good manners which believers should learn and adopt, and strive to imitate in their conversations and correspondence. End of his words. It is good. They said: the governing element in "anna" is "go." This that they said is not correct, because we have mentioned that it is an interrogative or conditional; it cannot be conditional here, because then it would be a place adverb, which would permit intercourse with women other than in the vagina, and the prohibition of that from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is established; and on the conditional reading the preceding word cannot govern the conditional adverb, because it is an object of the conditional verb, just as the conditional verb is an object of it. Nor can it be interrogative, because when it is interrogative it is complete with what follows it of a verb, as in His saying: ﴿How can I have a son?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 47], or of a noun, as in His saying: ﴿From where is this for you?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 37], and does not require anything else; but here its dependence on what precedes it is evident. And if it were interrogative, what precedes it would not govern it, and it would be governed by the verb after it. Thus it is clear, for both aspects of "anna," that it is not governed by what precedes it, and this is one of the problematic points that require thought and reflection. What appears to me, and Allah knows best, is that it is conditional, because it requires a clause other than the clause after it, and the conditions have been placed within it, like the placing of locative adverbs, and it has been treated like them, likening the condition to the locative adverb. A parallel to this has come with the word "kayfa" (how), which has passed from interrogation to the sense of condition in their saying: "How you do, I will do," and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Rather, both His hands are outstretched; He spends however He wills﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64]; so it cannot be interrogative here, but the sense of condition and the connection of the clause with the other was intended, and the answer of the clause is omitted, indicated by what precedes it. Its estimate: "Anna shi'tum fa'tuhu" (however you wish, then go to it), and "kayfa yasha'u yunfiq" (however He wills, He spends), just as the answer of the conditional is omitted in your saying: "Strike Zayd wherever you meet him," the estimate being: "wherever you meet him, then strike him." If you say: you have removed "anna" from its true locative sense and kept it for generalizing conditions, like "kayfa," and made it require another clause like the conditional clause, then is the past verb "shi'tum" in a jussive position like its state when it is a locative adverb, or is it in a nominative position like it after "kayfa" in their saying: "How do you do, I do?" The answer: it may be either, but the jussive is preferred, because the jussive has been established with it when it is a clear adverb, and the only thing is the likening of conditions to adverbs, and there is a clear connection between them, since each of them carries the meaning of "in"; unlike "kayfa," for the jussive has not been established with it; and whoever permitted jussive with it did so by analogy, while what is transmitted from the Arabs is the nominative for the verb after it, where it requires another clause.

﴿And send ahead for yourselves﴾. The object of "qaddimu" (send ahead) is omitted. It has been said: the estimate is: the mention of Allah at the time of intercourse, or seeking offspring, and excess, as intercessors; said by Ibn 'Abbas. Or: the good; said by al-Suddi. Or: a sure standing (qadama sidq); said by Ibn Kaysan. Or: the reward in avoiding what you were forbidden and carrying out what you were commanded; said by Ibn 'Atiyyah. Or: the mention of Allah upon intercourse, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "If one of you, when he approaches his wife, says: 'O Allah, keep Satan away from us and keep Satan away from what You provide us,' then if a child is decreed between them, it will not harm him." Or the invocation of the name over the intercourse; related by al-Zamakhshari. Or: what must be sent ahead of righteous deeds, which is the opposite of what I forbade you; said by al-Zamakhshari, and this is a saying compounded from the saying of those before him. What appears is that the meaning is: send ahead for yourselves obedience to Allah, compliance with what He commanded, and avoidance of what He forbade; because a command and a prohibition came before, and this is the good He mentioned in His saying: ﴿And whatever good you send ahead for yourselves, you will find it with Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 110]; and for this reason there came after it: "and fear Allah," that is: fear Allah regarding what He commanded you and forbade you, and it is a warning to them against opposition; and because the Great One who has been mentioned requires that you send ahead before Him what you will be approached by, that you will not be disgraced before Him, and that is righteous action.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 223–224 (part 2 of 4):

"And know that you will meet Him" (﴿واعْلَمُوا أنَّكم مُلاقُوهُ﴾). The apparent meaning is that the pronoun attached to "meeting" (﴿مُلاقُوهُ﴾) refers to God the Exalted, and this is by way of omitting a modified noun (mudaf, a noun in a construct phrase), meaning: "those who will meet the recompense for your deeds." It is also permissible that it refers to the omitted object of the verb "send forward" (﴿وقَدِّمُوا﴾), meaning: "you will meet what you have sent forward of good and obedience." This too involves an omitted modified noun, meaning: "those who will meet its recompense." It is also permissible that it refers to the recompense indicated by the omitted object (ma'mul, the grammatical object) of "send forward" (﴿قَدَّمُوا﴾ [Yasin: 12]). In this there is a refutation of those who deny resurrection, reckoning and the return, whether the pronoun refers to God the Exalted, to the object of "send forward," or to the recompense.

"And give good tidings to the believers" (وَبَشِّرِ المُؤْمِنِينَ): that is, of a good outcome in the Hereafter. In it is an indication of the attribute by which one fears God and sends forward good, and deserves the good tidings, which is faith. In the command to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to give good tidings there is great consolation and a generous promise of abundant reward. He did not use a pronoun of absence but used the explicit noun that indicates the attribute, and also because it is, with that, the end of a verse (fasl ayah, a verse-ending).

These noble verses contain God the Exalted's report about the believers that they ask the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about wine and gambling, and what He reported occurred. He commanded His Prophet to inform the one who asked him about these two that they both involve a great sin. This information became an incentive to abandon them, and it indicates their prohibition. The meaning is that drinking wine and playing games of chance produce sin. He did not suffice with mere sin until He described it as "great" in one reading, and as "abundant" in another reading (p-173). God the Exalted has said concerning the forbidden things: ﴿Those who avoid the grave sins of the wrongdoing﴾ [al-Najm: 32]; ﴿If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden﴾ [al-Nisa: 31]; ﴿Indeed, it is a great sin﴾ [al-Nisa: 2]. Since He described the sin as "great," and it is among the greatest sins and the most emphatic in prohibition, He also informed that there are benefits for people in them, such as gaining wealth through trade in wine, and through gambling with arrows, and other things. This is because there is no prohibited thing without some benefit in some respect, especially what the nature inclines toward, or what a person has been raised upon by nature.

Then God the Exalted informed that the harm of sin, which leads to the Fire, is greater than the benefit that ends with the end of its time, to guide the intelligent person to avoid what its punishment is lasting and its benefit is passing. Then God the Exalted informed that they ask Him about what they should spend; they were answered that they should spend what is easy for them to spend, pointing to ﴿and He has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion﴾ [al-Hajj: 78]. Then He mentioned that He makes the signs clear to the believers, as He made clear the matter of wine, gambling and what they spend. Then He mentioned that with this clarification hope is produced for reflecting on the situation of this world and the Hereafter, and when one reflects on both, by reflection one prefers the Hereafter over this world.

Then He digressed from these two questions to the question about the orphans and what they were obligated regarding them, since orphans are not capable of looking after their own affairs, due to their youth and deficiency of intellect. They were answered that reforming them is better than neglecting them, both for the reformer, through obtaining reward, and for the reformer through disciplining, teaching them, and developing their wealth. (Hadith: "My community is like a building, its parts strengthen one another.")

Then He informed that mixing with them is required, because "they are your brothers in Islam," so brotherhood necessitates considering the situation of the brother. He expressed the request in the form of a conditional clause, and the answer came with what requires association, which is that they are your brothers. When He commanded reform for orphans, He mentioned that God the Exalted knows the corrupter from the reformer, so that one would beware of corruption and be called to righteousness. Here the meaning of His knowledge is that He will recompense the one who corrupts and the one who reforms with what suits his action. Then God the Exalted informed that if He willed, He would have burdened you with what is difficult for you; thus He indicated that the previous obligations, such as the prohibition of wine and gambling, the obligation of charity being "what is easy," and the obligation of reforming the orphan, contain no hardship or distress. Then He concluded this by saying that He is the Mighty who cannot be overcome, the Wise who places things in their proper places.

Since He mentioned the prohibition of something of what they used to enjoy, namely drinking wine and eating from it, and gambling with arrows and eating from it, and since marriage is also among the greatest desires and pleasures, He digressed to mention the prohibition of one type of it, namely marrying one who has the attribute contrary to faith, which is polytheism that necessitates aversion and distance. Marriage necessitates association and affection. God the Exalted has said: ﴿And He placed between you affection and mercy﴾ [al-Rum: 21]; ﴿You will not find a people who believe in God and the Last Day loving those who oppose God and His Messenger﴾ [al-Mujadila: 22]. "Their dwellings do not face each other" (a reference to the separation of their homes). So He forbade marriage with one who has the attribute contrary to faith, and He limited that by the attainment of faith. Then He mentioned that a believing slave is better than a polytheist, even if the polytheist would please one by beauty, wealth or position. He also drew attention to the cause that necessitates abandoning it, which is that the polytheist calls to the Fire, and the one who keeps company with someone, mixes with him, and is in contact with him, even in marriage, which calls to intimacy, from every kind of companionship, may respond to him when he invites him to what is in accordance with his desire. They were recent in their acceptance of faith and its newness, so they were prevented from this, as a closing of the path to the Fire.

Then God the Exalted informed that He Himself calls to the Garden and forgiveness; so He is the one who looks out for your interest in prohibiting what He prohibited and permitting what He permitted. He makes His signs clear and explains them so that no confusion appears with them, in order to hope that you remember and take admonition from the signs.

Since He mentioned the prohibition of marrying one who has the attribute of polytheism, He mentioned the prohibition of intercourse with a believing woman who is in menstruation, and He limited that by her purity, just as He limited what came before it by faith. Then He permitted, when she purifies herself, for us to have intercourse with them from the place God commanded, which is the place that was occupied by menstruation, and He commanded us to avoid intercourse with her during menstruation. Then He pointed out the excellence of the one who repents and the one who purifies himself, by His loving him. He did not suffice with that in one sentence, but repeated it in two sentences, and singled out each attribute with love, saying: "Indeed God loves those who repent and loves those who purify themselves" (p-174).

Then God the Exalted mentioned the permissibility of intercourse with a woman whose menstruation has ceased, in whatever manner the husband wishes and chooses, whether she is facing him or turned away, or lying on her side or on her back, and from whichever side he wishes, because of the increased pleasure in changing positions, and the enjoyment of looking at all of her body, and the postures that stimulate desire. By the term "tilth" (harth) He pointed out that it is the place of offspring; this indicates the prohibition of intercourse in the rear passage, because it is not the place of offspring. Since they were prevented from intercourse with a menstruating woman because the place of intercourse contains harm from menstrual blood, then being prevented from the place that is more harmful is more fitting and more appropriate.

Since prohibition and command were mentioned first in the previous verses and in this one, it was concluded with the command to send forward righteous deeds, and that what a person sends forward returns only to the benefit of his own soul. Then he was commanded to fear God the Exalted, and was commanded to know and be certain with the certainty that has no doubt, that we will meet God, and He will recompense us for our deeds. He commanded His Prophet to give good tidings to the believers, who are those who carried out what He commanded and avoided what He forbade. So the beginning of these verses was with a warning against engaging in disobedience, and their conclusion with good tidings to the people of faith. These are verses whose contained wonders the tongues are unable to describe, and before whose eloquence the most skilled and fluent expert submits. They combined eloquence of expression and clarity of meaning, the connection of sentences and refinement of structure, question and answer, warning of punishment, and encouragement toward reward. They guided to the straight path, and were received from the presence of the Wise, the All-Knowing.

﴿And do not make God an obstacle in your oaths that you would be righteous and fear God and make reconciliation among people; and God is Hearing and Knowing﴾ ﴿God will not hold you accountable for what is unintentional in your oaths, but He will hold you accountable for what your hearts have earned; and God is Forgiving and Forbearing﴾ [al-Baqara: 225] ﴿For those who swear abstention from their wives is a waiting period of four months; and if they return, then indeed God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Baqara: 226] ﴿And if they decide upon divorce, indeed God is Hearing and Knowing﴾ [al-Baqara: 227] ﴿Divorced women shall wait by themselves for three menstrual periods. And it is not lawful for them to conceal what God has created in their wombs, if they believe in God and the Last Day. And their husbands have more right to take them back during that period, if they want reconciliation. And due to them is similar to what is expected of them, according to what is reasonable; but the men have a degree over them. And God is Mighty and Wise﴾ [al-Baqara: 228] ﴿Divorce is twice; then either keep [her] in an acceptable manner or release [her] with good treatment. And it is not lawful for you to take anything of what you have given them unless both fear that they will not keep within the limits of God. But if you fear that they will not keep within the limits of God, then there is no blame upon either of them concerning that by which she ransoms herself. These are the limits of God, so do not transgress them. And whoever transgresses the limits of God – it is those who are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqara: 229].

"Al-'Urda" (the obstacle): it is a form (fu'la) from "al-'ard" (presenting), and it has the meaning of the passive participle (maf'ul), like "al-furqa" and "al-qabda." It is said: "So-and-so is an 'urda for such-and-such," and "the woman is an 'urda for marriage," meaning she is presented for it. Ka'b said:

Her path is one whose landmarks are effaced, unknown.

Hassan said:

"God said: 'I have made ready a host; they are the Helpers'; its encounter is..."

Habib said:

When was my hearing a target for my blamers, and how have my resolves become clear to those who blame?

It is said: "He made him an 'urda for calamity," meaning exposed to it. Aws ibn Hajar said:

And a she-camel like a stallion; one day I presented her for my saddle, and in her is boldness and jostling.

It is also said: it is the name of what you place in front of a thing, from placing a stick across a vessel, so that it stands in the way and becomes a barrier and obstacle. It is also said: the original meaning of "'urda" is strength, and from this it is said of a strong camel: "this is an 'urda for travel," meaning strong for it; and of a swift horse: "it is an 'urda for our departure."

"Al-yamin" (the oath, right hand): its original meaning is the limb, and it has been used for swearing an oath because of the custom in the handshake of the two contracting parties. It is pluralized as "ayman" and "aymun," and it is used both for the limb and for the oath. "Al-yamin" is also used for the direction that is on the side of the limb called by that name, so it is put in the accusative as an adverb of place. You say: "Zayd is on the right of 'Amr" (yamin 'Amr). In the sense of the limb it is derived from "al-yumn" (blessing). It is said: "So-and-so is blessed in his appearance, blessed in his counsel, and blessed in his omen."

"Al-laghw" (idle talk): it is what the tongue slips into without intention, as said by al-Farra'. It is derived from their saying for what is not counted in blood-money of young camels: "laghw." It is said: "laga yalghu laghwan" and "lagha yalgha laghan." Ibn al-Muzaffar said: the Arabs say: "al-laghw," "al-laghiya," "al-lawaghi," and "al-lughawi."
