Ibn al-Anbari said: "al-laghw" for the Arabs is what is discarded from speech as being dispensable; it is also said it is what its wording is not understood. It is said: "laghā al-ta'ir yalghu," meaning it made a sound; and "laghā bi-l-amr," meaning he was fond of it, "yalghā." It is also said that "al-lugha" (language) is derived from this. Ibn 'Isa, having mentioned that "al-laghw" is what is not beneficial, said: "From it comes 'al-lugha,' because to those other than its people it is laghw." He made an error in this derivation, for "al-lugha" is only derived from their saying: "laghā bi-kadha" when one is devoted to it.

"Al-Halim" (the forbearing): the one who pardons sin while having the power to hold one accountable for it. It is said: "halama al-rajul yahlumu hilman," and he is "halim." Al-Nabigha al-Ja'di said:

There is no good in forbearance if it has no sources that protect its purity from being clouded.

It is also said: "halima al-adim yahlamu halman," when the hide becomes perforated and spoiled. He said:

For you and the Book to 'Ali are like one tanning a hide, and the hide has become rotten.

And he dreamed (ḥalama) in sleep, yalamu ḥulman and ḥuluman, and the one who dreams is ḥālim. ﴿And we are not versed in the interpretation of dreams﴾ [Yusuf: 44].

Al-īlāʾ (oath of abstention) is the verbal noun of ālā, meaning he swore. It is also said: ta'allā and i'talā, meaning he swore. An oath is called ulliyya, ulwa, ulwa and ilwa. The plural of ulliyya is alāyā, like ʿashiyya and ʿashāyā. It is also said that ulawwa is pluralized as alāyā, like rakūba and rakāʾib.

At-tarabbuṣ (waiting) means expectation and waiting. It is the verbal noun of tarabbaṣa, and it is a metathesis (qalb) of at-tabaṣṣur. A poet said:

> Wait for her, for the misfortunes of time (rayb al-manūn). Perhaps she will be divorced one day, or her husband will die.

Fāʾa (to return) means yafīʾu fayʾan and fayʾatan: he returned. The shadow after midday is called fayʾ because it returned from the east side to the west. It is quick to return (sarīʿ al-fayʾa), meaning quick to return. ʿAlqama said:

> I said to her, "Return (fīʾī), for you do not shrink from the eyes that are beautiful and the dyed fingertips."

Al-ʿazm (resolve) is that to which the heart is bound and determined. It is said: ʿazama ʿalayhi yaʿzimu ʿazman, ʿazaman, ʿazīma and ʿazāman. It is also said: aʿzama iʿzāman. And ʿazamtu ʿalayka latafʿalanna means: I swore to you that you will certainly do it.

At-ṭalāq (divorce) is the dissolution of the marriage contract. From it it is said: ṭullīqat tuṭallaqu, so she is ṭāliq and ṭāliqa. Al-Aʿshā said:

> O neighbour of mine, separate, for you are divorced.

It is also said: ṭalaqat with a damma on the lām. Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā related this, and al-Akhfash denied it.

Al-qurʾ (menstrual cycle or purity period): its original meaning in the language is the time whose recurrence is customary. The qurʾ of a star is the time of its rising and its setting. It is said from it: aqraʾa an-najm, meaning it rose or it set. The qurʾ of a woman is her menstruation (ḥayḍ) and her purity (ṭuhr). So it is one of the words with opposite meanings (min al-aḍdād), as Abū ʿAmr, Yūnus and Abū ʿUbayd said. It is said from both: aqraʾat al-marʾa (she became one who menstruates or one who is pure). Abū ʿAmr said: Among the Arabs there are those who call menstruation along with purity qurʾ. Some said: al-qurʾ is what is between two menstruations. Al-Akhfash said: aqraʾat means she became one who has menstruation. When she menstruates, you say qarat without an alif. It is said: al-qurʾ originally means gathering, from the saying: qaraʾtu al-māʾ fī al-ḥawḍ, meaning I gathered the water in the pool. From this: mā aqraʾat hādhihi an-nāqa salan qaṭṭu, meaning this she-camel never gathered a fetus in her belly. If it is meant as menstruation, it is the gathering of blood in the womb (raḥim). If it is meant as purity, it is the gathering of blood in the body.

Ar-raḥim (womb) is the vagina of a female, and it may be used metaphorically for kinship. It is said: baynahumā raḥim, meaning there is kinship between them. And he joins the ties of kinship (yaṣilu ar-raḥim).

Al-baʿl (husband) is the spouse. From it: baʿala yabʿalu buʿūlatan, meaning he became a husband. Bāʿala ar-rajul imraʾatahu means he had intercourse with his wife. She is bāʿalahu when she does that with him. A woman who is ḥasanat at-tabʿīl is one who treats her husband well. Al-baʿl also means king, and the idol (ṣanam) was named after it, because it is self-sufficient. From it comes baʿl an-nakhl (the palm tree that needs no irrigation). The plural of al-baʿl is buʿūl and buʿūla, like faḥl and fuḥūla. The tāʾ in it is for the feminine of the plural and is not analogous (lā yanqāsu). So one does not say for kuʿūb, the plural of kaʿb, kuʿūba.

Ar-rajul (man) is well known and is pluralized as rijāl. It is derived from ar-rujla, which is (p-176) strength. It is said: rajul bayyin ar-rujūla wa ar-rujla, and he is arjal ar-rajulayn, meaning the stronger of the two. A horse that is rajīl is strong at walking, and from it the foot (rijl) was named for its strength in walking. Irtajal al-kalām means he was strong in it. Tarajjal an-nahār means the daylight became strong. It is said: rajul and rijla, just as they say امرؤ and امرأة. I copied from the handwriting of our teacher Abū Jaʿfar ibn az-Zubayr, may God have mercy on him:

> Every neighbour remains content, except my neighbours, the Banū Jabala.
> They tore the collar of their young woman, and did not care for the sanctity of the man.

Ad-daraja (degree) is rank. Its origin is from darajtu ash-shayʾa and adraljtuhu, meaning I folded it. Daraja al-qawm means they perished. Allah caused them to pass away (adrajahum), and so it is like folding a thing step by step. The degree is a rank among the ranks of folding. From it is the degree by which one ascends.

Al-imsāk (holding) of a thing is restraining it. From it are two nouns: mask and masāk. It is said: innahu la-dhū maskin wa mīsāk, meaning he is stingy. In it is a remnant (muskatun) of good, meaning strength. Tamāsuk means holding together. Masīk means one who is clearly tight-fisted (bayyin al-masāka).

At-tasrīḥ (release) is sending away. Sarraḥa ash-shaʿr means he separated some of the hair from others. Sarraḥa al-māshiya means he sent the livestock out to graze. As-sarḥ is livestock. Nāqa masraḥ is a she-camel that is easy to walk, because of its ease of movement in it.

﴿And do not make Allah an obstacle (ʿurḍa) for your oaths﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās said: It was revealed about ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥa and his brother-in-law Bashīr ibn an-Nuʿmān. There was something between them. ʿAbd Allāh swore that he would not enter upon him, nor speak to him, nor reconcile between him and his wife. He kept saying: I have sworn by Allah, so it is not permissible for me except to fulfil my oath. Ar-Rabīʿ said: It was revealed about the man who swears that he will not join his ties of kinship and will not reconcile between people. Ibn Jurayj said: It was about Abū Bakr when he swore that he would not spend on Mistaḥ, when he spoke in the slander (al-ifk). Al-Muqātilān, Ibn Ḥayyān and Ibn Sulaymān said: He swore that he would not spend on his son ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān until he became Muslim. It is also said: He swore that he would not eat with the guests, when his son delayed the evening meal from them, and he himself became angry with his son. ʿĀʾisha said: It was revealed about the repetition of oaths by Allah. So He forbade that one swear by Him in righteousness, how much more in wickedness.

The connection of this verse with what precedes it: When He commanded piety toward Allah and warned them of the Day of Meeting, He forbade them to make His name common and to make it a target for what they swear to constantly. Whoever is revered and feared, his name must be preserved and guarded from what is not fitting for it, such as being mentioned in every oath, whether small or great, whether trivial or important. For repetition of that causes disregard for the one sworn by. The connection may also be that when He commanded the believers to be cautious in their earlier actions, concerning wine, gambling, spending the surplus, the affairs of orphans, marrying those who associate others with Allah, and the situation of having intercourse with a menstruating woman, He commanded them to be cautious in their speech. So their command to be cautious in actions and words is united.

They differed in understanding this clause, ﴿And do not make Allah an obstacle for your oaths﴾. This difference is based on the difference about the derivation of ʿurḍa. It is said: They were forbidden to make Allah a target for their oaths, so that they swear by Him in righteousness and wickedness. For breaking the oath along with frequent swearing shows little regard for the right of Allah the Exalted, as it is narrated from ʿĀʾisha that it was revealed about frequent swearing by Allah. It was forbidden that a man swear by Him in righteousness, how much more in wickedness? Allah has censured the one who swears often, in His words: ﴿And do not obey every frequent swearer, contemptible﴾ [al-Qalam: 10], and He said: ﴿And guard your oaths﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 89]. The Arabs praise those who swear little. Kuthayyir said:

> Few are the oaths of one who guards his oath. When an oath comes from him, he is true to it.

The wisdom in forbidding the multiplication of oaths by Allah is that this leaves no weight for the oath in the heart, and one is not safe from proceeding to a false oath. The mention of Allah is too exalted to be invoked for worldly purposes. It is also said: The meaning is: Do not make Allah a strength for your oaths and a confirmation of them. Something close to this meaning is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibrāhīm, Mujāhid, ar-Rabīʿ and others. He said: The meaning concerns what you intend to be firm in, namely abandoning the maintenance of kinship, righteousness and reconciliation. It is also said: The meaning is: Do not make Allah a barrier and a hindrance from righteousness and reconciliation. The saying of the one who said it was revealed about ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥa, or about Abū Bakr, as mentioned in the occasion of revelation, confirms this. So the meaning is that the man would swear regarding some good deeds, such as maintaining kinship, reconciling between people, doing good to someone, or worship, and then he would say: I fear Allah that I break my oath, and so he would abandon righteousness in his oath. So they were forbidden to make Allah a barrier to what they had sworn about.

(p-177) ﴿For your oaths﴾: the lām may be connected to ﴿ʿurḍa﴾, so it is like reinforcing the transitivity, or it is a target and an aim for your oaths. It may also be connected to the saying: (And do not make), so it is for causation, meaning: do not make Allah a target on account of your oaths. The apparent meaning is that by oaths here is meant the act of swearing, not the thing sworn about. Az-Zamakhsharī said: That is, a barrier to what you have sworn about, and the thing sworn about is called an oath because it is connected to the oath, as the Prophet ﷺ said to ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn Samura: "If you swear an oath and then see something else better than it, then do what is better, and expiate your oath." That is, concerning something of what is sworn about. End of his words. There is no need here to depart from the apparent meaning. The hadith was only pressed into this sense because he used the word oath generally and meant by it what it governs, since he said: "If you swear on an oath", where the verb "swear" takes ʿalā. So this interpretation was needed. There is nothing in the verse that requires this interpretation, but az-Zamakhsharī, when he took ʿurḍa to mean barrier and hindrance, was compelled to this interpretation.

﴿That you be righteous, and be mindful of Allah, and make reconciliation between people﴾. Az-Zajjāj, and at-Tibrīzī after him, said: ﴿That you be righteous﴾ is in the place of a nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence. Az-Zajjāj said: The meaning is: your righteousness, your piety and your reconciliation are better and more fitting. He made the speech end at the saying ﴿for your oaths﴾. The meaning of the sentence that contains the prohibition, according to him, is that it concerns a man who is asked to do a good deed or the like, and he makes an excuse by Allah and says: "An oath is upon me," though he has not sworn. At-Tibrīzī estimated the predicate of the omitted subject as meaning: "That you be righteous, be mindful of Allah and make reconciliation between people is better for you than that you make Allah a target for your oaths." What az-Zajjāj and at-Tibrīzī went to is weak, because it separates ﴿that you be righteous﴾ from what precedes it, and connecting it to it is the correct approach. It also involves an omission for which there is no evidence. Az-Zamakhsharī said: ﴿That you be righteous and be mindful of Allah and make reconciliation﴾ is an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to ﴿your oaths﴾, that is, to the matters sworn about, which are righteousness, piety and reconciliation between people. End of his words. This is weak, because it contradicts the apparent meaning: the apparent meaning of oaths is the acts of swearing, while righteousness, piety and reconciliation are the things sworn about, so they are distinct, and it is not permissible for them to be an explanatory apposition to oaths. But since he interpreted oaths as what is sworn about, this became acceptable for him. We have already shown that there is no need to force oaths into the sense of things sworn about. According to his view, ﴿that you be righteous﴾ would be in the genitive position. If he claimed that ﴿that you be righteous﴾ and what follows it is a substitute (badal) for (your oaths), that would be better, because explanatory apposition is most common with proper names. The majority held that his saying ﴿that you be righteous﴾ is an object of purpose (mafʿūl min ajlihi). Then they differed about the estimate: it is said: out of aversion that you be righteous, said by al-Mahdawī. Or: for abandoning that you be righteous, said by al-Mubarrad. It is also said: so that you do not be righteous, nor be mindful of Allah, nor make reconciliation, said by Abū ʿUbayda and aṭ-Ṭabarī, as in his saying:

> He opposed, so no, by Allah, he will not descend into a valley.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 223–224 (part 4 of 4):

He means: "it does not descend" (lā tahbiṭu). It was also said: the implied phrase is "the desire that you be righteous" (irādatu an tabarrū). The first interpretations converge in meaning. This meaning is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, ʿAṭāʾ, Ibn Jurayj, Ibrahim, Qatada, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Suddi, Muqatil, al-Farrāʾ, Ibn Qutayba, and al-Zajjaj, the last of those narrated from. Their view is that the meaning is: "Do not swear by Allah that you will not be righteous," so that it is connected to His words, "and do not make" (wa-lā tajʿalū). This meaning does not appear clearly, because it makes the prohibition of swearing depend on the absence of righteousness, whereas in fact the act of swearing is what is conditioned by the absence of righteousness. Moreover, no conditional and consequent can be formed if you say, regarding the meaning and cause of this prohibition: "If you swear by Allah, you will be righteous," which is not valid. This is like your saying: "Do not strike Zayd, so that he does not harm you." The harm is negated by refraining from striking. The meaning is: if you do not strike him, he will not harm you, and if you strike him, he will harm you. Thus, the absence of righteousness does not follow from refraining from swearing, nor does its existence follow from its existence. Rather, the existence of righteousness follows from refraining from swearing, and the absence of righteousness follows from the occurrence of swearing. What we have mentioned supports the view that the implied phrase is "the desire that you be righteous," because it gives as the cause of refraining from swearing the desire for righteousness to exist, and from this the conditional and consequent are formed. You say: "If you swear, you will not be righteous, and if you do not swear, you will be righteous."

Some scholars have explained this meaning, saying: "that you be righteous, and God-fearing, and make peace" (in tabarrū wa-tattaqū wa-tuṣliḥū) is the cause of this prohibition, that is, the desire that you be righteous. The meaning is: our prohibition of this is only because of what is in avoiding it of righteousness, piety, and reconciliation, so that you, O company of believers, will be righteous, pious, and reformers on earth, not corruptors. If you ask: how does the absence of swearing necessarily bring about righteousness, piety, and reconciliation among people? We say: because whoever abstains from swearing, believing that Allah, blessed and exalted, is greater and more majestic than that His exalted name should be invoked in seeking worldly gain, this is one of the greatest gates of righteousness. As for the meaning of piety, it is clear, because he guards against doing anything that would violate the glorification of Allah, exalted is He. As for reconciliation among people, it is because when people believe that he glorifies Allah to this degree, guarding against violating what is due to Him, they believe that he glorifies Allah and is truthful, far from corrupt aims. So they accept his word, and reconciliation is achieved through his mediation. End of this discussion.

In al-Muntakhab, which is an elaboration of what al-Zamakhshari said, it says: "Its meaning according to the other reading is 'to make it liable to' (ʿurḍah), in the sense of exposed to the matter." He said: "Do not make Allah exposed to your oaths, so that you cheapen Him by frequently swearing by Him." For this reason He censured the one about whom He revealed: "And do not obey every excessive swearer, contemptible" (Qur'an 68:10), with the most abominable reproaches, and made the excessive swearer its prelude. "That you be righteous" (an tabarrū) is the cause of the prohibition, that is, the desire that you be righteous, God-fearing, and reconcilers, because the habitual swearer is bold toward Allah and does not glorify Him. Therefore he is not righteous or God-fearing, and people do not trust him, so they do not admit him into their mediation and the reconciliation of their affairs.

It was also said: the meaning is, "Do not swear by Allah while lying, so that you be righteous toward those to whom you swear, and God-fearing toward them, and reconcile them through lying." This meaning is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. He thus restricted the thing made known to lying, restricted the cause to people, and restricted reconciliation to lying, which is contrary to the apparent meaning.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "That you be righteous" (an tabarrū) is connected either to the verb or to the phrase "liable to" (ʿurḍah). That is: "Do not make Allah, because of your oaths by Him, liable to your being righteous." End of quotation. This implied phrase is not valid, because it involves separation between the governing word and the governed element by an unrelated element. He connected "for your oaths" (li-aymānikum) with "make" (tajʿalū), and connected "that you be righteous" (li-an tabarrū) with "liable to" (ʿurḍah). Thus he separated "liable to" (ʿurḍah) and "that you be righteous" (li-an tabarrū) by his words "for your oaths" (li-aymānikum), which is unrelated to both, since in his view it is governed by "make" (tajʿalū). That is not permissible. A parallel to what he permitted would be your saying: "Pass and strike with Zayd Hind," which is not permissible. They also stated explicitly that it is not permissible to say: "A man with a horse came to me, riding a piebald," because of the separation by an unrelated element.

What appears to me is that "that you be righteous" (an tabarrū) is in the accusative position by dropping the preposition, and the governing element is His words "for your oaths" (li-aymānikum). The implied phrase is: "for your oaths that you be righteous." Thus they were forbidden from degrading the name of Allah, the Exalted, and making it an object for their oaths on righteousness, piety, and reconciliation, which are beautiful qualities. This is because of what we fear in that from breaking the oath (ḥinth). How much more so when the oaths are on what contradicts righteousness, piety, and reconciliation? On this view the speech is coherent, with each word in its proper place that suits it. Thus, in the position of "that you be righteous" (an tabarrū), there are three views. The nominative, on the basis of it being the subject (mubtada'), with dispute about the implied governing element. The genitive, in two ways: as an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf al-bayān) and as a substitution apposition (badal). The accusative, in two ways: either as an object of purpose (al-mafʿūl min ajlihi), depending on the disagreement about its implied element, or as governed by "your oaths" (aymānikum) with the dropping of the preposition.

"And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing" (wa-llāhu samīʿun ʿalīm). He ended this verse with these two attributes because what relates to them was previously mentioned. What relates to hearing is swearing, since it is among the things heard. What relates to knowledge is the desire for righteousness, piety, and reconciliation, since it is something whose locus is the heart, and so it is among the things known. These two attributes came corresponding to the cause and the effect, and came in the order of what preceded, namely the mention of hearing before knowledge, just as He mentioned swearing before the desire.

﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for the idle oaths in your oaths﴾. The connection of this verse to what precedes it is clear. When Allah forbade making Him an obstacle to oaths, that would have meant abandoning oaths entirely, and this was difficult for them, because swearing oaths had become their custom. So He mentioned that oaths which are idle (al-lagh) are not held against them, because they are not intended as true oaths. They are words that flow over the tongue in conversation without intention. This is the best way to explain al-lagh, because Allah set it in contrast with what the heart has earned, which is what the heart relies on and intends.

The commentators differed in explaining the idle oath (lagh al-yamin). Abu Hurayrah, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, 'Ata', al-Sha'bi, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Qatadah, Muqatil, al-Suddi (from his shaykhs), Malik in his more well-known of two opinions, and Abu Hanifah said: it is swearing on the basis of strong assumption, and then the unseen reveals the opposite of that. 'A'ishah, Ibn 'Abbas also, Tawus, al-Sha'bi, Mujahid, Abu Salih, and al-Shafi'i said: it is what flows over the tongue in the course of speech and haste, such as "No, by Allah" and "Yes, by Allah," without intending an oath. This is one of Malik's two opinions. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn al-Musayyab, Abu Bakr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, and the two sons of al-Zubayr, 'Abd Allah and 'Urwah, said: it is swearing to do an act of disobedience. Except that Ibn Jubayr said: one does not do it, and makes expiation (kaffarah). The rest said: one does not do it, and there is no expiation for it. Ibn 'Abbas also, 'Ali, and Tawus said: it is swearing in a state of anger. Al-Nakha'i said: it is swearing about something one forgets. Ibn 'Abbas also, and al-Dahhak said: it is that for which expiation is due, and if expiation is made, it falls away; Allah does not hold one accountable for making expiation for it and returning to what is better. Makhul, Ibn Jubayr also, and a group said: it is that one forbids for oneself what Allah has made lawful, as in his saying: "My wealth is forbidden to me if I do such and such," or "What is lawful is forbidden to me." Malik held this view except regarding a wife, for whom he imposed the prohibition unless the swearer intends to exclude her in his heart. Zayd ibn Aslam and his son said: it is a man's invocation of curse upon himself: "May Allah blind his sight, take away his wealth, he is a Jew, he is a polytheist, he is an adulterer, if he does such and such." Mujahid said: it is the oath of two sellers, one of whom says: "By Allah, I will not sell you for such and such," and the other says: "By Allah, I will not buy it except for such and such." Masruq said: it is what one is not obliged to guard against. It is narrated from him, and from al-Sha'bi, that it is swearing to an act of disobedience. It has been said: it is the oath of one who is compelled; this was reported by Ibn 'Abd al-Barr. All these opinions are possible meanings of the word lagh, but the most apparent is what we explained first, because it is set in contrast with kasb al-qalb (what the heart has earned), which is the heart's deliberate intention toward something. All the other opinions can be covered by the heart's earning, because the heart has an intention toward them. The negation of the unity (of the oath) indicates that there is no sin and no expiation. Thus the view of one who says that it applies only to sin is weak, and the idle oath is explained as the oath that requires expiation. Al-Hasan was asked about the idle oath and about a captive woman who is married. Al-Farazdaq jumped up and said: "Did you not hear what I said:

"You are not held accountable for anything you say
if you did not intend the binding resolutions."

And what I said:

"And a woman with a husband, our spears made her
lawful for us, and had it not been for her capture, she would not have been divorced."

Al-Hasan said: "How clever you are, were it not for your breaking of the oath."

(p-180) "Bi-al-lagh" is connected to "yu'akhidhukum" (He holds you accountable), and the "ba'" is causal, similar to it in: ﴿And if Allah were to hold people accountable for their wrongdoing﴾ [al-Nahl: 61], and ﴿So each We seized for his sin﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 40]. "Fi aymanikum" (in your oaths) is connected either to the verb, or to the verbal noun, or to an implied element, meaning: existing in your oaths; in which case it is a circumstantial clause (hal). And what supports this is that if you made it part of the relative clause of "alladhi" and described al-lagh with it, it would be sound.

* *

﴿But He will hold you accountable for what your hearts have earned﴾: that is, for the oaths in which the heart has an earning. So every oath that the heart has bound is an earning for it. Likewise Mujahid explained "kasb" as "binding," like the verse of al-Ma'idah: ﴿for what you have bound in oaths﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 89]. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Nakha'i said: it is swearing falsely or on falsehood, and this is al-ghamus (the perjurous oath). Zayd ibn Aslam said: it is binding association in the heart when one says: "He is a polytheist if he does such and such." Qatadah said: it is what the heart intends of sins. What Allah mentioned of being held accountable is punishment in the Hereafter if the oath was a ghamus, or was not a ghamus and one left its expiation undone, and punishment in this world by imposing expiation if it is among the things that can be expiated.

They differed about the perjurous oath (al-yamin al-ghamus). Malik and a group said: it is not expiated, and it is a greater sin than that. 'Ata', Qatadah, al-Rabi', and al-Shafi'i said: it is expiated, and the expiation is itself a holding accountable. Al-ghamus is when a man intends by the oath to lie, and it is also called al-masburah. It was named ghamus because it plunges (taghmis) its swearer into sin, and masburah because its endurance (sabr) is a struggle and a force upon it, as an animal is bound (yusbar) for killing or shooting.

Oaths have been divided into: idle (lagh), binding (mun'aqidah), and perjurous (ghamus). The binding oath is that which concerns the future, in which breaking it (hinth) and keeping it (birr) are valid, and we have explained the idle and the perjurous. They have also been divided into: an oath concerning something forbidden, which is the false oath; and a permissible one, which is the true oath; and concerning a future matter whose binding is an act of obedience and persisting in it is an act of obedience, while undoing it is disobedience or disliked; and its opposite, or what is permissible to bind, to persist in, and to undo. But here (the verse) places them between two opposites with regard to the existence of the oath, because it (the oath) is either not intended by the heart but flows over the tongue, which is idle, or it is intended, which is binding; and these two are contraries with regard to the oath's not existing, since a person may be free of oaths. These two kinds of contradictories and contraries are the best place where "lakin" (but) is used. As for the two disagreements, there is a difference of opinion over whether they may be placed between them, and some of this has been mentioned earlier. The changing of the hamzah into waw in forms like "yu'akhidh" is regular, as in "yu'dhin" and "yu'allif." And in His saying ﴿But He will hold you accountable for what your hearts have earned﴾ there is an omitted element, its estimate being: "But He will hold you accountable in your oaths for what your hearts have earned," and it was omitted because of what precedes it indicating it. The "ma" in "bima" is a relative pronoun, and its returning pronoun is omitted. It is possible that it is a verbal (masdariyyah) "ma," and what makes it good is its contrast with the verbal noun in His saying ﴿idle﴾. It is also permitted that it be an indefinite qualified noun.

﴿And Allah is Forgiving, Forbearing﴾: these two attributes came to indicate Allah's broadening of His favor upon His servants, since He did not hold them accountable for idle oaths. And following the verse with them indicates forgiveness and forbearance toward one whom He threatened with being held accountable, and an encouragement toward the vastness of His mercy; for whoever describes himself with abundant forgiveness and pardon is one who is hoped for in what he has described himself with. Thus this threat that Allah mentioned is conditioned by His will, like all His other threats.

[p. 181]

**Qur'an 2:226:** ﴿For those who swear off their wives, a waiting period of four months.﴾

Ibn al-Musayyab said: The *ila'* (an oath of abstention from intercourse with one's wife) was a form of harm practiced by the people of the Jahiliyya (the pre-Islamic period). A man would neglect his wife and would not want anyone else to marry her, so he would swear that he would not approach her, and he would leave her neither as a widow nor as a married woman. So God sent down this verse.

Ibn Abbas said: The *ila'* of the people of the Jahiliyya was a year or two years or more, so God set a limit for it.

The connection of this verse to what precedes it is clear, because earlier there was a matter concerning the rulings on women and a matter concerning the rulings on oaths, and this verse combined the two.

Abdullah [ibn Mas'ud] read *lilladhina alu* (﴿for those who swore﴾) in the past tense. Ubayy and Ibn Abbas read *lilladhina yuqsimuna* (﴿for those who swear﴾).

The *ila'*, as mentioned earlier, is an oath. We have already mentioned how the *ila'* from women was practiced in the Jahiliyya. As for the legal *ila'* caused by intercourse with women, Ibn Abbas said: it is the oath that one will never have intercourse with her. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Nakha'i, Qatada, al-Hakam, Ibn Abi Layla, Hammad ibn Sulayman and Ishaq said: it is the oath that one will not approach her for a day, or less, or more, and then he does not have intercourse with her for four months; thereby she is separated from him through the *ila'*. Al-Thawri and Abu Hanifa said: it is the oath that one will not have intercourse for four months, and after that period passes the *ila'* lapses and it becomes a divorce; it does not lapse before the period passes except by *fay'* (return), which is intercourse within the period. The majority (al-Jumhur) said: it is the oath that one will not have intercourse for more than four months. So if one swears for four months or less, he is not a *mu'li* (one who swears *ila'*), and it is a pure oath; if he has intercourse during this period, nothing is due from him, like other oaths. This is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Abu Thawr.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that the *ila'* is an oath to abstain from having intercourse with one's wife, without restriction of time. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿For those who swear off﴾ includes the free and the slave, the intoxicated and the foolish, and one under guardianship; it excludes the insane; it includes the eunuch who is not castrated and one from whom intercourse can be expected; and likewise the mute, by whatever is understood from him by allusion or gesture. There is disagreement regarding the one who is castrated (*majbub*): some said his *ila'* is not valid, and some said it is valid. The term of the slave's *ila'* is the same as the free person's term, because he is included in the general sense of His words ﴿For those who swear off﴾; this is the view of al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Thawr and Ibn al-Mundhir. Ata', al-Zuhri, Malik and Ishaq said: his term is two months. Al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i and Abu Hanifa said: the *ila'* of a slave-wife is two months, and of a free wife four months. Al-Sha'bi said: the term of a slave-wife's *ila'* is half the *ila'* of a free wife.

The apparent meaning of His words ﴿swear off﴾ is the *ila'* in general, so it occurs whether or not it was intended to correct a suckling child, and whether or not it was in anger, sulking or secrecy. Ata' and Malik said: if it was for the correction of a suckling child, the ruling of *ila'* does not bind him. This was narrated from Ali, and al-Shafi'i held it in one of his two opinions; in the other opinion he said there is no consideration of nursing, and Abu Hanifa held this. Ali, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Ata', al-Sha'bi and al-Layth said: its condition is that it not be in anger. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Sirin, al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa, Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad said: *ila'* occurs both in anger and not in anger. Ibn al-Mundhir said: this is the more correct view, because of the general sense of the verse, and because they agree that *zihar* (a form of divorce by likening a wife to one's mother), divorce, and all other oaths are the same whether in anger or in contentment; and likewise *ila'*.

The majority understood His words ﴿For those who swear off from their wives﴾ as referring only to an oath to refrain from intercourse. Al-Sha'bi, al-Qasim, Salim and Ibn al-Musayyab said: it is an oath to refrain from having intercourse with her, or not speaking to her, or harming her, or angering her; all of this, according to these scholars, is *ila'*. However, Ibn al-Musayyab said: if he swears not to speak to her while he has intercourse with her, it is not *ila'*; it is *ila'* only when refraining from intercourse is combined with it. The statements of those mentioned along with Ibn al-Musayyab contain what Ibn al-Musayyab said, and what they imply is that the corruption of marital relations is *ila'*; al-Tabari adopted this possibility. The apparent meaning of the verse supports the view of these scholars, because He said ﴿For those who swear off from their wives﴾ and did not specify intercourse or anything else.

The phrase *min* ("from") is connected to His words ﴿swear off﴾, but *alla* (to swear off) does not take *min* as its complement. Some said *min* here means *ala* ("upon"); some said it means *fi* ("in"), and that this is by the omission of a noun, meaning "upon abandoning intercourse with their wives," or "in abandoning intercourse with their wives." Some said *min* is superfluous, and the sense is: "swear off that they will keep away from their wives." Some said it is connected to an omitted element, the sense being: ﴿For those who swear off from their wives, a waiting period of four months﴾, so that it is connected to what "for them" (*lahum*) as an omitted element is connected to; this was stated by al-Zamakhshari. All of this is weak, and the Qur'an is too exalted for it. Rather, it is connected to ﴿swear off﴾ in one of two ways: either *min* indicates cause, meaning "they swear because of their wives"; or *ila'* is given the meaning of abstaining, so that it takes *min*, and it is as if it were said: "for those who abstain through *ila'* from their wives." And ﴿from their wives﴾ is general, covering wives who are free, slave, People of the Book, consummated or not.

Ata', al-Zuhri and al-Thawri said: there is no *ila'* except after consummation. Malik said: there is no *ila'* from a minor girl who has not reached puberty; if one swears *ila'* against her and she then reaches puberty, the *ila'* binds him from the day of her puberty.

The apparent meaning of His words ﴿For those who swear off﴾ is the generality of *ila'* by whatever oath it is made. Al-Shafi'i, in his later view (*al-Jadid*), said: *ila'* occurs only by swearing by God alone. Ibn Abbas said: every oath that prevents intercourse is *ila'*; this was also the view of al-Nakha'i, al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa, the people of Iraq, Malik, the people of the Hijaz, Abu Thawr, Abu Ubayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, the judge Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi, and al-Shafi'i in his final view. Abu Hanifa said: if one says "I swear by God," it is an oath without qualification, and by it he is not a *mu'li*; but if he says, "If I have intercourse with you, then it is incumbent upon me to fast a month or a year," then he is a *mu'li*. Abu Hanifa also said: if that month passes before the four months, then he is not a *mu'li*, and likewise for everything that becomes obligatory upon him, whether pilgrimage, divorce, emancipation, prayer or charity. Abu Hanifa differed in the case where one says, "If I have intercourse with you, then it is incumbent upon me to pray two *raka'at*": he said he is not a *mu'li*. Muhammad [al-Shaybani] said: he is a *mu'li*.

Some commentators mentioned many subsidiary rulings concerning *ila'* here, but we, following our custom, mention only what has some connection to the Qur'an; and tafsir is not intended for the enumeration of every detail of subsidiary rulings. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿For those who swear off﴾ is that the oath occurs from them, whether one swears not to have intercourse in a specific place or in general. This was said by Ibn Abi Layla and Ishaq. Abu Hanifa, Malik, al-Shafi'i and their followers, al-Awza'i and Ahmad said: one who swears not to have intercourse with his wife in this house or this dwelling is not a *mu'li*; but if he swears not to have intercourse with her in his city or town, then he is a *mu'li* according to Malik. The *dhimmi* (non-Muslim subject under protection) is not included in His words ﴿For those who swear off﴾, because of His words ﴿So if they return, then God is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾; this is the view of Malik, just as *zihar* is not valid from him. Abu Hanifa said: if one swears by one of the names of God, or by one of His attributes, or swears by something that is valid for him to bind himself to, such as divorce, then he is a *mu'li*. If the *mu'li* makes an exception (*istithna'*) in his oath, the majority hold that he is not a *mu'li*, like all other oaths accompanied by an exception. Ibn al-Qasim said, on the authority of Malik, that he is a *mu'li*, but if he has intercourse then there is no expiation (*kaffara*) for him; and Ibn al-Majishun said in *al-Mabsut*, on the authority of Malik, that he is not a *mu'li*.

﴿A waiting period of four months﴾. This is of the type of the construction of the verbal noun (*masdar*) with what is originally a time adverb, but it has been extended and made into a direct object; for this reason the construction with it is valid. The original would be: "their waiting [for] four months." The construction with an adverb of time without extension is not the same, so the construction would be understood as "in," contrary to those who held that. The apparent meaning of this is that the beginning of the term of the *ila'* is from the time he swore, not from the time of dispute and referral to the judge. It was said: its ruling is four months, because this is the usual length a woman endures being away from her husband. The story of Umar is well known, when he heard a woman reciting at night:

*Ala tala hadha al-laylu wa-iswaddda janibuhu*
*Wa-arraqani an la habiba ulA'ibuhu*

(Oh, how long this night has been, and its side has grown black,
and it keeps me awake that I have no beloved to play with.)

He asked: "How long can a woman endure being away from her husband?" It was said to him: "She cannot endure more than four months." So he made that the limit for every expedition he sent out.

﴿So if they return﴾, that is, they return by intercourse. This was said by Ibn Abbas and the majority. According to the majority, it suffices for one who is able to do so to have the head of the penis enter. If he has an excuse, or is ill, or imprisoned, or in some similar condition, then his taking her back is valid, and she is still his wife; and if his excuse ends and he refuses to have intercourse, they are separated if the period has already expired. This was stated by Malik in *al-Mudawwana* and *al-Mabsut*. Al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, Ikrimah and al-Awza'i said: it suffices for the one who has an excuse to call witnesses to his return in his heart. Al-Nakha'i also said: the return is valid by words and calling witnesses alone, and the ruling of *ila'* lapses when you see that he has not become aroused. It was said: *fay'* is contentment; it was said: return by the tongue in every case. This was stated by Abu Qilaba, Ibrahim, and those who said the *mu'li* is one who swears to cause his wife distress. Ahmad said: if he has an excuse, he returns in his heart. Ibn Jubayr, Ibn al-Musayyab and a group said: *fay'* occurs only by intercourse, whether one is able or not, or in prison, travel, illness, or otherwise.

Jarya ibn A'idh read *fa'u* with *imala* (an inclined vowel) because of the form *fi'tu*. Abdullah read *fa'in fa'u fihinna* ("if they return in them"). Ubayy read *fa'in fa'u fiha* ("if they return in it"), and it is narrated from him: *fihinna*, like the reading of Abdullah. The pronoun refers to the four months. This reading is supported by the view of Abu Hanifa, that *fay'* occurs only within the months; and if he does not return within them, the divorce takes effect upon him after the four months have passed, without being suspended. This was the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Uthman ibn Affan, Ali, Zayd ibn Thabit, Jabir ibn Zayd, al-Hasan and Masruq. Umar, Uthman, also Ali, Abu al-Darda', Ibn Umar, Ibn Amir, al-Musayyab, Mujahid, Tawus, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq and Abu Ubayd said: when the four months have passed, he is held in suspension; then either he returns, or divorce is imposed upon him. The widely transmitted (*mutawatir*) reading is ﴿fa'in fa'u﴾ without *bi-ghayrihinna* ("with others") and without *fiha* ("in it"); so it is possible that the sense is: "if they return within the months," and it is possible that it is: "if they return after their expiry."

﴿Then God is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾. Those who said that if the *mu'li* returns and has intercourse, there is no expiation for him in his oath, used this as evidence; this was the view of al-Hasan and Ibrahim. The majority—Malik, Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i and their followers—held that the expiation for oaths is obligatory upon the *mu'li* by having intercourse with his wife. Thus the forgiveness here is an indication of the removal of sin through performing the expiation. This is the view of Ali, Ibn Abbas and Ibn al-Musayyab: that it is forgiveness of sin, and upon him is an expiation. According to the preceding view, it means the removal of the expiation. Abu Hanifa said: there is no expiation upon one who is incapable of intercourse if he returns. Ishaq said: some of the interpreters said regarding one who swears to perform righteousness and piety, or some door of goodness, that he should not do it, that he should do it, and there is no expiation upon him; and the evidence for this is ﴿So if they return, then God is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾, without mention of expiation. It was also said: the meaning is "Forgiving of the sins of the oath, Merciful in permitting a way out from it through expiation"; this was stated by Ibn Ziyad, and it returns to the second view. It was also said: the meaning of "Merciful" is that He considered the woman, so that her husband would not harm her; thus the attribute of forgiveness relates to the husband, and the attribute of mercy relates to the wife.

﴿And if they are resolved upon divorce﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas read: "And if they are resolved upon release (al-sarah)." The accusative of "al-talaq" (divorce) is either due to the omission of the preposition, which is "ʿala" (upon), since "ʿazama" (to resolve) takes "ʿala" as in the verse: "I resolved upon holding a morning raid." Or "ʿazama" is taken to mean "nawa" (to intend), so that it takes a direct object. The meaning of "ʿazm" (resolve) here is determination upon divorce. It appears that the response to the condition is omitted, and its estimated form is: "then let them pronounce it," that is, the divorce. In His saying in this division, ﴿then if they return﴾ [al-Baqarah: 226], and ﴿if they are resolved upon divorce﴾, there is evidence that the separation that takes place in iyla' (the oath of abstention from intercourse) does not occur by the passing of the four months without a statement. Rather, a statement is necessary, due to His saying ﴿resolved upon divorce﴾, because resolving to do a thing is not the doing of it. This is confirmed by ﴿indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾, since only utterances are heard. These two attributes came in relation to the condition and its response. Since we estimated the response as: "then let them pronounce it," that is, divorce, ﴿All-Hearing﴾ came in regard to the pronouncing of divorce, because it belongs to the category of things heard, and it is the response of the condition. And ﴿All-Knowing﴾ came in regard to the resolve to divorce, because it belongs to the category of inner intentions, which is the condition, and intentions are not perceived except by knowledge. This attribute was placed later for the sake of harmonizing the ends of the verses (ruʾus al-ayy), and because knowledge is more general than hearing, so its object is more general, while the object of hearing is more specific. Whoever said that ﴿indeed Allah is All-Hearing﴾ refers to His hearing of the iyla' was far off the mark, because of the remoteness of its fit with the condition preceding it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, what do you say about His saying, "indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing," when their resolve to divorce is something that is neither known nor heard? I say: Usually the one resolved upon divorce, and upon abandoning the return and fleeing, is not free from murmuring and mumbling, and he must speak to himself and confide to it about this. That is a speech that only Allah hears, just as He hears the whispering of Satan. End of his words. We have already mentioned that the attribute of hearing came here because the meaning is: "And if they are resolved upon divorce: they pronounce it," that is, the divorce, and pronouncing it can only be by speech. So it belongs to the category of things heard, and the attribute relates to the response, not to the condition, so it does not need the interpretation of al-Zamakhshari.

In His saying, ﴿And if they are resolved upon divorce﴾, there is an indication of divorce in general, so it does not indicate a specific type of divorce as revocable (raj'i) or irrevocable (ba'in). There has been disagreement about the divorce that follows iyla' in this regard. ʿUthman, ʿAli, Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAta', al-Nakhaʿi, al-Awzaʿi and Abu Hanifa said: it is an irrevocable single divorce, with no right of return for him in it. Ibn al-Musayyab, Abu Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman, Makhul, al-Zuhri, Malik and Ibn Shubrumah said: it is revocable.

In the ruling that the one who has made iyla' must choose one of two matters, either return (fayʾa) or divorce, there is evidence that, according to those who require expiation (kaffara), it is not permissible to pay the expiation before the return, because if that were permitted, iyla' would be nullified without a return or a resolve to divorce. For if he breaks the oath, nothing would become binding upon him by the breaking, and whenever nothing becomes binding upon the one who swore by breaking the oath, he is not one who has made iyla'. So permitting the advance payment of expiation would mean dropping the ruling of iyla'. This was stated by Muhammad ibn al-Hasan. The position of Abu Hanifa (p-184) and the well-known position of Malik is that it is permissible to advance the expiation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿And if they are resolved upon divorce, then wait until the term has passed﴾.

﴿Indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ is a warning against their persistence and their abandonment of return. According to the view of al-Shafiʿi, its meaning is: "If they return, then indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful; and if they resolve upon divorce after the term has passed." End of his words.

It had already been stated in the explanation of His saying ﴿then if they return﴾ [al-Baqarah: 226] the following text: "If they return within the four months, as evidenced by the reading of ʿAbd Allah: 'If they return within them, then indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful,' He forgives the believers for whatever they might undertake of seeking to harm women through iyla', which is the common case, although it is also possible that it is with their consent, out of fear for the child from breastfeeding, or for some other reasons, for the sake of the return, which is like repentance." Al-Zamakhshari interpreted the verse according to the view of Abu Hanifa and differentiated between the objects of the two verbs on the two sides, since he made the time after ﴿they return﴾ [al-Baqarah: 226] within the period of the four months, and the time after "they are resolved" after the passing of the period. What the apparent wording indicates is that return and resolve upon divorce can only occur after the four months have passed. When al-Zamakhshari sensed this, he objected to himself, saying: If you ask, how is the placement of the fa' (then) when the return occurs before the end of the waiting period? I say: It is a correct placement, because His saying ﴿then if they return﴾ [al-Baqarah: 226] and "(if they are resolved)" are a detailing of His saying ﴿for those who make iyla' against their wives﴾ [al-Baqarah: 226], and the detail follows what is detailed, as when you say: "I am your guest this month; if I please you, I stay with you," and so on, "and if not, I stay only for as long as it takes me to move on." End of his words.

This is not correct, because what he used as an example does not correspond to what is in the verse. Do you not see that the example in it is a statement about the detailed subject, whose condition is what is said: "I am your guest this month," and after the two conditions there is an explicit response indicating a difference in the object of the verb of the response? The verse is not like that in its structure, because ﴿those who make iyla'﴾ is not a subject about whom something is reported, nor is a judgment attributed to them. What is reported is "their waiting" (tarabbus). So the meaning is: the waiting of the one who has made iyla' for four months is legislated for them after their oath, then He said ﴿then if they return﴾ [al-Baqarah: 226] and ﴿and if they are resolved﴾. The apparent meaning is that it follows the entire legislated waiting period, because the return happens within it, and the resolve happens after it. For this distinct restriction is not indicated by the wording. The correspondence of the verse would be for us to say to the guest: "Hosting for three days is due to the guest; if he stays, we are generous and hospitable, and if he resolves to leave, he may leave." What first comes to the mind is that the two conditions are presumed after his hosting for the three days. As for the meaning being: "If he stays within the three days, and if he resolves to leave after that," this difference between the two sides does not come to mind, even though the wording may allow it. A distinction is made between what is apparent and what is merely possible. No one distinguishes between the verse and al-Zamakhshari's example except one whose mind has been trained in Arabic structures and who is free from forcing the Book of Allah into the legal details of a school, by following the truth and avoiding partisanship.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 228 (part 1 of 3):**

﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods﴾. Some [commentators] mentioned, regarding the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of this verse, things that do not qualify as an occasion. The connection (munasabah) of this verse to what precedes it is very evident, because it is a rule that concerns women in general. Divorce leads to a continuous prohibition of intercourse and enjoyment, whereas through illa' (vow of abstinence) a husband prevents himself from intercourse for a limited period. So it was appropriate to mention what is unlimited after what is limited. The prescribed waiting period for the one who makes illa' is four months, and the prescribed waiting period for these women is three periods (qurū'), so it was appropriate to mention it right after.

The apparent meaning of ﴿And divorced women﴾ is generality (ʿumūm). However, it is restricted (makhsūs) to those who have been consummated with and who have menstrual periods, because the ruling for those not yet consummated with, for the pregnant, and for those past menstruation is stated explicitly and differs from the ruling for these women. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah that the ruling was general for all divorced women, then it was abrogated (nusikha, naskh: abrogation) for all divorced women except the consummated women who have menstrual periods. This [view] is weak. The use of a general expression while meaning a specific subset does not require evidence, because it is common. Nor is it [required] to treat it as a question and answer, as al-Zamakhshari said. He said: "If you say, how is it permissible for the intended meaning to be specifically them while the wording requires generality? I say: rather, the wording is absolute (muṭlaq) in encompassing the category, suitable for all of it and for part of it, so it came in one of the things it is suitable for, like a homonym (mushtarak)." End of quote. What he said is not correct, because the indication (dalalah) of a general term is not the indication of an absolute term, and the general term is not absolute in encompassing the category, suitable for all of it and part of it. Rather, it is an indication of each and every individual, established for this meaning, so it is not suitable for the whole category and part of it, because what is established as general encompasses each individual and covers all individuals, and it is not said of it that it is suitable for the whole and part. So it does not come in one of what it is suitable for, nor is it like the homonym, because the homonym has two or more established meanings, with a separate imposition for each of its referents, so each referent has its own imposition, whereas the general term has only one imposition, as we have clarified. So it is not like the homonym.

﴿And divorced women﴾: a subject (mubtada'), and ﴿shall wait﴾ (yatarabbaṣna) is the predicate (khabar) of the subject. Its form is that of a predicate, but in meaning it is a command. It was said: it is a command both in wording and meaning, with the particle of command (lām) elided, i.e., *li-yatarabbaṣna* (let them wait). This is according to the view of the Kufans. It was said: ﴿divorced women﴾ is with an elided noun (muḍāf), i.e., "and the ruling concerning divorced women is that they wait," with the particle *an* (that) elided, so that it can be a predicate of that elided noun. The estimate is: "and the ruling concerning divorced women is that they wait." This is very far-fetched.

Al-Zamakhshari said, after saying that it is a predicate with the meaning of a command: "Putting the command in the form of a predicate is an emphasis of the command and an indication that it is something that must be received with haste in carrying it out, as if they had already carried out the command to wait, so it reports it as existing. A similar example is their saying in supplication, 'May Allah have mercy on him' (raḥimahu Allah), in which the form of a report is used about God out of confidence in the answer, as if mercy had already occurred, so it reports about it. Its construction on the subject adds an extra emphasis. Had it been said, 'And the divorced women shall wait,' it would not have had that strength." End of quote. This is a good statement. The nominal sentence (jumlah ibtidaʾiyyah) contains extra emphasis over the verbal sentence (verb and subject), because the noun is mentioned twice in it: once by its explicit appearance and once by pronominal reference (iḍmār). In the verbal sentence the noun is mentioned only once.

Ibn ʿAbbas (?) — [see note]. Al-Qurtubi and others said... [continues below]

Ibn Hayyan (?) — [continuing the text]:

Al-Zamakhshari? — [end of passage]

Among those who quoted "Rī al-Ṣamʾān" (Ri al-Zam'an) he said: a verb is used in two ways. The first: restricting that verb to the mention of the matter, as in their saying, "I wrote to the sultan regarding such-and-such matter," meaning a claim of sole performance. The second: that the intention is not that, but rather that placing the subject of the statement first, with a more emphatic statement, establishes that verb for him, as in their saying, "He gives abundantly," not meaning exclusivity, but that the hearer should be convinced that giving abundantly is his habit.

The meaning of *yatarabbaṣna* is: they wait and do not proceed to marry. Al-Qurtubi said: it is a predicate in its proper sense, and it is a report about a ruling of the Sharia. If you find a divorced woman who does not wait, that is not from the Sharia. It was said: treating it as a report is the better option, because the reported matter must occur, whereas a command may or may not be carried out, and because they do not need intention or resolve. *Tarabbaṣa* is transitive, since its meaning is "he waited" (intazara). It came in the Qur'an both with its object elided and with its object stated. Of the elided type is this one, and they estimated its object as "waiting for marriage" or "waiting for husbands." Of the stated type is His saying: ﴿Say: Do you wait for us except for one of the two best outcomes (martyrdom or victory)? And we wait for you that Allah will afflict you with a punishment from Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 52], and ﴿We wait for him for the misfortunes of time﴾ [al-Tur: 30].

*Bi-anfusihinna* (﴿by themselves﴾) is connected to *tarabbaṣa*. The apparent sense of the *bāʾ* with *tarabbaṣa* is that it marks cause, i.e., "for the sake of themselves." It is necessary that there be mention of the selves (anfus), because if it were said in the sentence "it is waited for them" (yutarabbaṣu bihinna), it would not be permissible, since that would involve transferring the verb that takes a pronoun referring to the subject attached to it onto a pronoun in the genitive case, like: "Hind passes by her," and that is not permitted. Here it is permissible for it to be an emphatic addition (zāʾidah li-l-tawkīd), and the meaning is: *yatarabbaṣna anfusahunna* (they wait themselves), just as you say: "Zayd came himself" (bi-nafsihi) and "Zayd came in person" (bi-ʿaynihi), meaning his self and his person. It is not said that emphasis here is not permitted, because it falls under emphasis of the attached pronoun in the nominative case, which is the *nūn* that is the feminine plural pronoun in *tarabbaṣna*, and for which the condition is that it be emphasized with a detached pronoun. The construction would have been: *yatarabbaṣna hunna bi-anfusihinna*, because this emphasis, when put in the genitive with the *bāʾ*, has left being a follower (tābiʿ), and the reason for which emphasizing an attached nominative pronoun requires a detached pronoun has been lost in it, when the intent is emphasis of self and person. Similar to the permissibility of this is: *aḥsin bi-Zaydin wa-ajmil* (how good is Zayd, how beautiful!), the estimate being *wa-ajmil bihi*, so it was elided even though it is the agent (fāʿil). This is the view of the Basrans. Also, because when it is put in the genitive with the *bāʾ* it leaves being an agent in form, and becomes like an adjunct (faḍlah), so its elision is permitted. This holds even though al-Akhfash mentioned in *al-Masāʾil* the permissibility of "they themselves stood" (qāmū anfusuhum) without emphasis. The benefit of the emphasis here is that they themselves carry out the waiting, and the possibility is removed that others carry it out on their behalf, rather they themselves are the ones commanded to wait, since that is more conducive to the act occurring from them. The emphasis is needed because of the aspiration toward men and marriage in their natures, so whenever the statement is emphasized, it indicates the intensity of the desired matter. (p-186)

The accusative of *thalāthah* (three) is as a time adverb (ẓarf), since we estimated that *tarabbaṣa* has already taken its object, and the meaning is: "for a period of three periods (qurū')." It was said: its accusative is as an object (mafʿūl), i.e., they wait for the meaning of three periods. Both parsings are transmitted.

The discussion of the meaning of *qurū'* (periods) in the language of the Arabs has already been covered, and there is disagreement about the intended meaning here. Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthman, ʿAli, Ibn Masʿud, Abu Musa, Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, ʿIkrimah, al-Dahhak, Muqatil, al-Suddi, al-Rabiʿ, Abu Hanifah and his companions, and other jurists of Kufa said: it is menstruation (ḥayḍ). Zayd ibn Thabit, ʿUbadah ibn al-Samit, Abu al-Darda', ʿAʾishah, Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Zuhri, Aban ibn ʿUthman, Sulayman ibn Yasar, al-Awzaʿi, al-Thawri, al-Hasan ibn Salih, Malik, al-Shafiʿi, and other jurists of the Hijaz said: it is the purity period (ṭuhr). Ahmad said: "I used to say that the *qurʾ* is the purity, and now I go to the view that it is menstruation." It is reported from al-Shafiʿi that *qurʾ* is the transition from purity to menstruation, and he did not regard the transition from menstruation to purity as a *qurʾ*. Another view has already been mentioned, that it is the exit from purity to menstruation, or from menstruation to purity. The mention of the arguments of each speaker for what he adopted belongs elsewhere.

The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿three periods﴾ is that the waiting period is completed by three periods. Whoever says that *qurʾ* is menstruation says: if she was divorced during a purity in which she had not been touched, she begins one menstruation, then another, then another, then she performs ghusl, and by the ghusl the waiting period is completed. It is reported from ʿAli, Ibn Masʿud, Abu Musa, and others among the Companions: "Her husband has more right to take her back as long as she has not performed ghusl." Shurayk even said: "If she neglected the ghusl and did not perform it for twenty years, her husband would still have more right to return to her." What appears from the verse is that ghusl has no role in completing the waiting period.

It is reported from Zayd, Ibn ʿAmr, and ʿAʾishah: "If she enters the third menstruation, he has no path over her, and she is not lawful to husbands until she performs ghusl from the third menstruation." This is because these hold that *qurʾ* is purity. So if she was divorced in a purity in which she had not been touched, she counts what remains of it, even if only an hour. Then she begins a second purity after one menstruation, then a third after a second menstruation. When she sees blood from the third menstruation, she becomes lawful to husbands and exits the waiting period with the first drop she sees. This is the view of Malik, al-Shafiʿi, Ahmad, and Dawud.

Ashhab said: the bond of marriage and inheritance is not severed except by verifying that it is blood of menstruation, because of the possibility that it is a single discharge of blood from other than menstruation. Everyone who says that *qurʾ* is the purities counts the purity in which she was divorced. Ibn Shihab was an outlier and said: she counts three *qurʾ* beyond the rest of that purity, and the waiting period is not completed until she enters the fourth menstruation, because God Most High said ﴿three periods﴾, and if she was divorced during menstruation, her waiting period is completed by beginning the fourth menstruation. Abu Hanifah said: her waiting period is not completed until she becomes pure from the fourth menstruation. He said: if she becomes pure for the majority of menstruation, her waiting period is completed before ghusl or at its beginning, so it is not completed until she performs ghusl, or performs tayammum when water is unavailable, or until the time of prayer passes over her.

The apparent generality of "divorced women" includes the slave wife (amah) within the waiting period of three periods. This was held by Dawud, the body of the people of the literal reading (ahl al-ẓāhir), and ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Kaysan al-Asamm. It is reported from Ibn Sirin that he said: "I do not see the waiting period of a slave woman as anything other than that of a free woman, unless a Sunnah has been established about it, and the Sunnah has more right to be followed." The majority said: her waiting period is two *qurʾ*.

The majority read ﴿qurū'﴾ on the pattern *fu'ūl*. al-Zuhri read *qurūw* with shaddah without hamzah, and this is reported from Nafiʿ. al-Hasan read *qarw* with a fatḥah on the *qāf*, a sukūn on the *rāʾ*, and a light *wāw*. The justification for using the plural of multitude (kathrah) in this place, where it did not come as "three *aqrāʾ*" (the plural of paucity), is that it is from the license (tawassuʿ) in placing one of the two plurals in place of the other, namely the plural of paucity in place of the plural of multitude and the reverse, just as ﴿by themselves﴾ (bi-anfusihinna) came, and because marriage multiplies the self into selves in number. Often one of the two plurals becomes more common in usage, which causes it to be used in place of the other, while the other remains nearly neglected. This is like *shusūʿ* being preferred over *ashsāʿ* because *ashsāʿ* is rarely used, though it is not anomalous, since *shiss* is a noun for which the pattern *afʿāl* is regular. It was said: *qurū'* was used with the meaning of multitude, because every divorced woman waits three *qurū'*. It was also said: *qurū'* was preferred over *aqrāʾ* because its singular is *qarʾ* with a fatḥah on the *qāf*, and the plural of *fa'l* on *af'āl* is irregular (shādh). Al-Mubarrad permitted "three donkeys" (thalāthatu ḥamīr) and "three dogs" (thalāthatu kilāb) with the meaning "of dogs" and "of donkeys," so it may be parsed on what he permitted as "three *qurū'*," i.e., "of *qurū'*." The justification for the shaddah on the *wāw* is that the hamzah was changed to a *wāw* and the *wāw* of *fu'ūl* was assimilated into it, and this is a permissible and regular easing. The justification for al-Hasan's reading is that he made the number a qualifier of a collective noun (ism al-jins), since the collective noun is applied to the singular and to the plural, depending on the meaning you intend, and the number indicated that the singular is not meant.

﴿It is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs﴾. What is forbidden to conceal is menstruation (al-haydh). She says, "I am not menstruating," while she is menstruating, or, "I have menstruated," when she has not, in order to lengthen the waiting period (al-'iddah) and hasten the separation. 'Ikrimah, al-Nakha'i, and al-Zuhri said: or pregnancy. This is the view of 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas. Or menstruation and pregnancy together. This is the view of Ibn 'Umar, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd, and al-Rabi'. They have purposes in concealing that. Allah the Exalted informed that concealing it is forbidden. The words ﴿It is not lawful for them to conceal﴾ indicate that they are believers in this matter, and if investigation were permitted, concealment would not be possible. Sulayman ibn Yasar said: "We were not commanded to open women and look at their private parts. Rather, that matter was entrusted to them, since they are trustworthy." End of quotation. The scholars agreed that it is not permissible for a woman to conceal what Allah has created in her womb of pregnancy or menstruation, and this contains severe censure and condemnation. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that what is meant is: those who desire to abort what is in their wombs of fetuses, so they do not acknowledge it and deny it for this reason. Thus the concealment of what is in their wombs was made a metaphor for its abortion. End of his words. The verse can bear this meaning. Ibn al-Mundhir said: Everyone from the scholars whom I have memorized said: if a woman says within ten days, "I have menstruated," she is not believed, and her claim is not accepted unless she says, "I have miscarried a fetus whose form has become clear." They differed regarding the period during which a woman is believed. Malik said: if she claims the end of menstruation within a period in which the waiting period would end in a similar time, her word is accepted; or if it is within a period that occurs rarely, there are two opinions. He said in (al-Mudawwana): if she says, "I have menstruated three menstrual cycles in one month," she is believed if women confirm it. This is also the view of 'Ali and Shurayh. In the book of (Muhammad), he said: she is not believed except in a month and a half. Something close to this is the view of Abu Thawr: the minimum for that is forty-seven days. It was also said: she is not believed for less than sixty days. It was narrated from 'Ali that he made a woman who had not completed her menstruation take an oath, and 'Uthman ruled accordingly. The word "for them" (lahunna) is connected to "lawful" (yahillu), and the lam indicates communication. The "ma" in ﴿what has created﴾ is most evidently a relative pronoun meaning "that which," and the returning pronoun is omitted. It is also permissible for it to be an indefinite qualified noun, with the returning pronoun also omitted; the estimated meaning is: "created it." The phrase ﴿in their wombs﴾ is connected to "created it." It is also permissible for ﴿in their wombs﴾ to be a circumstantial phrase (hal) of the omitted element. It was said: it is a future circumstantial phrase, because at the time of its creation it was not yet a thing until its creation was completed. Mubashshir ibn 'Ubayd recited ﴿in their wombs﴾ and (wa-biraddihinna) with a damma on the ha' in both, and the damma is the original form; it was changed to a kasra only because of the kasra before it.

﴿If they believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾. This is a conditional clause (shart), whose answer is omitted according to the most correct of the views. It was omitted because what precedes it indicates it, and here it is estimated from its own wording. That is: "If they believe in Allah and the Last Day, then it is not lawful for them to do that." The meaning is that whoever has the attribute of faith does not proceed to commit what is not lawful for him. This was made conditional on this condition, even though faith was already present in them, as a warning and to magnify the concealment. This is like their saying: "If you are a believer, do not oppress," and "If you are free, then defend yourself." It makes what exists treated as non-existent, and makes it conditional upon it, even if it exists in reality. The meaning is: "If they are believing women, concealment is not lawful for them," and "You are a believer, so do not oppress," and "You are free, so defend yourself." It was also said: there is an omission in the speech, meaning: "If they believe in Allah and the Last Day with true faith." It was said: "in" (in) has the meaning of "when" (idh), but this is weak. This statement includes a threat. Ibn 'Abbas said: this is for what the man deserved of the right of return. Qatadah said: it is for attributing a child to someone other than its father, as the people of the Jahiliyyah did.

﴿And their husbands have more right to take them back in that period﴾. Maslamah ibn Muharib recited ﴿and their husbands﴾ with a sukun on the ta', to flee from the heaviness of successive vowels. This is like what Abu Zayd reported: "wa-rusulna" with a sukun on the lam. Abu 'Umar mentioned that the dialect of Tamim is to make the nominative ending of "ya'lamhum" and similar words sukun. He called them "husbands" (bu'ulah) with regard to what they had been, or because the revocable divorcee is a wife according to what some of them held. The meaning is that the husbands have more right to take them back. Ubayy recited "bi-riddatihinna" with a ta' after the dal. The ba' and "fi" are connected to the word ﴿more right﴾. It was also said that "fi" is connected to "biraddihinna." By his saying ﴿in that period﴾ he refers to the term in which they were commanded to wait, which is the time of the waiting period. It was also said: it refers to the hidden pregnancy. The pronoun in ﴿their husbands﴾ [al-Nur: 31] returns to the divorced women, and it is specific to the revocable divorcees. In this there is evidence that the specification of the last part of a phrase does not prevent the generality of its first part, nor does it require specifying it. This is because the phrase ﴿and divorced women﴾ is general, including both irrevocably divorced women and revocably divorced women, while ﴿their husbands have more right to take them back﴾ is specific to the revocable divorcees. A parallel to this according to them is ﴿We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 8]. This is general. Then He said ﴿but if they strive with you﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 8], and this is specific to the polytheists. My preferred view is that it is by omitting a qualifying noun (mudaf) indicated by the ruling, its estimate being: "and the husbands of their revocable divorcees." Here "ahaqq" is not used in its usual sense, because a non-husband has no right, and there is no authority over the wife during the waiting period, which belongs only to the husband. She also has no right in that, rather if she refuses, he has the right to take her back. So it is as if it were said: "their husbands are entitled to take them back." The phrase ﴿to take them back﴾ indicates a previous separation. Whoever says that a revocably divorced woman is forbidden to have intercourse, the "return" is literal in its proper sense. Whoever says that she is permitted to have intercourse and her rulings are those of a wife, then since there is a cause upon which the cessation of the marriage depends at the end of the waiting period, it is permissible to apply the term "return" to it, since it removes that cause.

They differed regarding what effects the return. Sa'id, al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin, 'Ata', Tawus, al-Zuhri, al-Thawri, Ibn Abi Layla, and Abu Hanifah said: if he has intercourse with her, he has taken her back, and he should call witnesses. al-Layth and a group of Malik's companions said: his intercourse is a return in every case, whether he intended it or not. Malik said: if he has intercourse with her during the waiting period, intending the return but not knowing that he should call witnesses, it is a return, and the woman should prevent him from intercourse until he calls witnesses. Ishaq also said this. If he has intercourse without intending the return, Malik said: he takes her back during the waiting period, but does not have intercourse until she has been cleansed of his corrupt water (istibra'). Ibn al-Qasim said: if her waiting period ends, neither he nor anyone else may marry her during the remainder of the period of cleansing. If he does, his marriage is annulled, and her prohibition upon him is not permanent, because the water is his. al-Shafi'i said: if he has intercourse with her, it is not a return, whether he intended the return or not, and she has the bride-price of her equivalent (mahr mithlih). Malik said: there is nothing upon him. Abu 'Umar said: I do not know of anyone who required the bride-price of an equivalent except al-Shafi'i. al-Shafi'i said: the return is not valid except by speech. This is also the view of Jabir ibn Zayd, Abu Qilabah, and Abu Thawr. al-Baji said in (al-Muntaqa): there is no disagreement about the validity of taking her back by speech. If he kisses her or touches her skin, he sins according to Malik, and it is not a return. The sunnah is that he should call witnesses before that. Abu Hanifah and al-Thawri said: if he touches her with desire, or looks at her private part with desire, it is a return. According to Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ishaq, Abu 'Ubayd, and Abu Thawr, he should call witnesses. May he travel with her before taking her back? Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah, and his companions forbade it. From al-Hasan ibn Ziyad: he may travel with her before the return. May he enter upon her and see some of her beauty, and she adorns herself for him or makes herself attractive? Abu Hanifah permitted this. Malik said: he may not enter upon her except with permission, and he may not look at her except while she is wearing her clothes, and he may not look at her hair, and there is no harm in his eating with her if others are present with her, and he should not spend the night with her in one room. Ibn al-Qasim said: then Malik retracted this and said: he may not enter upon her, and he may not see her hair. Sa'id said: when he enters upon her he should ask permission and greet her, or let her know of his presence by clearing his throat, and she may wear whatever clothes and jewelry she wishes. If she has only one room, then the two of them should place a screen between them. al-Shafi'i said: she is forbidden to him with the prohibition of an irrevocably divorced woman until she is taken back by speech, as was mentioned earlier.

They agreed that if a divorcing husband says, after the end of the waiting period, to his wife, "I had taken you back during the waiting period," and she denies it, then the word of the wife is accepted with her oath. There is a disagreement with Abu Hanifah about this. If the wife is a slave woman, and the husband claims the return during the waiting period after its end, then the word of the slave wife is accepted, even if her master denies it. This is the view of Abu Hanifah, al-Shafi'i, and Abu Thawr. Abu Yusuf and Muhammad said: the word of the master is accepted, and he has more right to her.

﴿If they intend reconciliation﴾. This is another conditional clause, whose answer is omitted because what precedes it indicates it.
