Its outward meaning is that the permission of the return is tied to the condition of intending reconciliation. There is no disagreement among the scholars that if he takes her back harmfully, intending to lengthen the waiting period against her, his return is valid. They used as evidence the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And do not keep them in marriage to harm them, in order to transgress﴾ [al-Baqarah: 231]. They said: this indicates the validity of the return even if he intends harm, because the return would not be valid if it were done in the manner of harm, since that would be wrongful by his act. Al-Mawardi said: regarding the reconciliation referred to, there are two views. One: reconciling what is corrupt between them through divorce. The second: upholding for each of them what right he has over the other. End of his words. They said: in the return, the husband is exempt from a guardian (wali), from her consent, from naming a bride-price, and from calling witnesses to the return according to the correct view. The remaining waiting period falls away by the return, and intercourse with her becomes lawful immediately. Establishing all of this requires clear evidence from the Shari'ah. What appears to me is that by divorce the woman separates from the man, so it is not permissible for him to return to her except by a second marriage contract. Then, if he divorces her and wants to marry her again, either some of her waiting period remains or none remains. If some of her waiting period remains, he may marry her before her waiting period ends from him if he intends reconciliation, and the implication of the condition is that if he intends other than reconciliation, this is not permitted for him. If her waiting period has ended, he and others are equal in the permissibility of marrying her. Or she may have been divorced while still within her waiting period, and he takes her back without observing the conditions of marriage. Establishing this ruling requires clear evidence, as we have said. If there is clear evidence from a text or consensus, we follow it. It is not objected against us that he has the right of return as they described, and that this is among the fundamental matters of jurisprudence about which dispute is not permissible, and that every ruling requires evidence.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 228 (part 3 of 3):

﴿And they [the women] have rights similar to those they owe, according to what is fair.﴾ This is from the eloquence of the speech: he omitted something from the first part and affirmed its counterpart in the second, and affirmed something in the first and omitted its counterpart in the second. The underlying construction is: "And they have upon their husbands a right similar to that which their husbands have upon them." So "upon their husbands" was omitted because "upon them" was affirmed, and "for their husbands" was omitted because "for them" was affirmed.

Scholars differed about this similarity. It was said: the similarity lies in compliance and obedience; al-Dahhak said this. It was said: the similarity lies in adornment and beautification; Ibn Abbas said this, and said: "I love to adorn myself for the woman as I love her to adorn herself for me," citing this verse. It was said: the similarity lies in fearing God regarding them, just as they are required to fear God regarding them (the men); for this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) indicated by his saying: "Fear God regarding women, for they are with you as 'awan (captives)," meaning prisoners; this was said by Ibn Zayd. It was said: the similarity means that they have, in terms of maintenance, dowry, good companionship and refraining from harm, a right like that which is owed from them regarding command and prohibition. On this view, the similarity lies in the obligation of what the man does of these things, and the obligation of the woman's compliance with his command and prohibition, not in the kind of the act performed or the one who complies, since what the man does is perceptible and intelligible, while what she does is intelligible; but they share in the obligation, so the similarity is realized. It was said: the verse is general, encompassing all the rights of the husband over the wife and the rights of the wife over the husband. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he was asked about the right of a woman over her husband, and he said: "That he feeds her when he eats, clothes her when he clothes himself, does not strike the face, and does not abandon her except within the house." In the hadith of the Hajj from Jabir: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said in the sermon of the day of 'Arafah: "Fear God regarding women, for you have taken them under the trust of God, the Blessed and Exalted, and you have made lawful their private parts by the word of God. Your right over them is that they do not allow anyone you dislike to tread upon your bedding. If they do that, then strike them with a non-severe strike. And their right over you is their provision and their clothing according to what is fair."

"Mithl" (similar) is the subject (mubtada'), "lahunna" is in the position of the predicate (khabar), and "bil-ma'ruf" is connected to "lahunna," meaning: and a similar right to that which their husbands have over them belongs to them over their husbands. It was also said: "bil-ma'ruf" is in the position of an attribute (sifah) to "mithl," so it is in the nominative position, and then it is connected to an omitted element.

The meaning of "bil-ma'ruf" is: in the manner that is not rejected by the Shari'ah and the customs of people, and that one of them does not burden the other with tasks that are not customary for them; rather each of them treats the other in the manner befitting them.

﴿And the men have a degree over them﴾: that is, a superiority and excellence in right. He used the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, since if he had spoken with the pronoun he would have said "and they have a degree over them," in order to highlight the mention of manhood by which the superiority of men over women became manifest. And because the pronoun would have produced a confusion of similar wordings in the speech, and you know what that entails: it would have read "and they have a right similar to what is upon them according to what is fair, and the men have a degree over them." Because of the awkwardness of the pronouns, two pronouns and two possessives were omitted from the first clause. The "degree" here: his excess over her in inheritance and in jihad; this was said by Mujahid and Qatadah. Or by the obligation of her obedience to him, while he is not obliged to obey her; this was said by Zayd ibn Aslam and his son. Or by the dowry, the permissibility of mutual cursing (li'an) if he accuses her, and the punishment for her if she accuses him; this was said by al-Sha'bi, may God be pleased with him. Or by his taking care of her through maintenance and otherwise, even though they share in enjoyment; this was said by Ibn Ishaq. Or by possession of the marital bond and that divorce is in his hand; this was said by Qatadah and Ibn Zayd. Or by what distinguishes him from her, such as the beard; this was said by Mujahid. Or by the right of return (revocation), or by responding to his bed when he calls her; this falls under the second view. Or by reason, or by religious commitment, or by testimony, or by strength in worship, or by maleness, or because the woman was created from the man; this was pointed out by Ibn al-'Arabi. Or by being safe from the harm of menstruation, childbirth and postpartum bleeding. Or by his marrying another woman over her and taking concubines, which is not permitted to her. Or by his bearing the blood-money (diyah) while she does not, unlike her. Or by his being the imam (leader), unlike her. Ibn Abbas said: "That degree" is a reference to urging men toward good companionship and to being generous to women in wealth and character, meaning that the superior should bear hardship upon himself. End of quotation. What appears to me is that the degree is what women desire of goodness, honor, compliance and reverence toward men. This is because when he stated that each of the spouses has over the other a right similar to what the other has over him, this required equality; so he clarified that although they are equal in what each owes the other, women owe their husbands an extra measure of honor and esteem, and he indicated the reason for that: that the man is one who confronts hardships and dangers, and always strives for the welfare of his wife, and spares her the toil of earning. In return for this, a degree over them belongs to the man in the abundance of compliance and in what leads to his comfort with her. The summary of what the exegetes said implies that the man has a degree that entails preference.

"Darajah" (degree) is the subject (mubtada'), "lil-rijal" (for the men) is its predicate (khabar), and this is a predicate that makes it permissible to begin with an indefinite noun. "'Alayhinna" (over them) is connected to what the predicate is connected to of existence and settledness. They also permitted that "'alayhinna" be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), because if it had come later it would have been a qualifier of the indefinite noun; since it came first, it became a circumstantial clause, and then it is connected to an omitted element, which is other than the governing element of the predicate. A parallel is: "fi al-dar qa'iman rajul" (in the house, standing, a man), whose original was "rajul qa'im." It is not permissible that "'alayhinna" be the predicate and "lil-rijal" be in the position of a circumstantial clause, because the governing element of the circumstantial clause would then be implied (ma'nawi), and it has been placed before both parts of the sentence, which is not permitted. A parallel is: "qa'iman fi al-dar zayd" (standing in the house is Zayd), and this is prohibited, not merely weak as some claimed. If the circumstantial clause came in the middle and the predicate came later, as in "Zayd qa'iman fi al-dar," this is the point of disagreement between us and Abu al-Hasan: Abu al-Hasan permits it, and others prohibit it.

﴿And God is Mighty, Wise﴾: the meaning of these two attributes has already been explained, and He concluded the verse with them because the verse contained what implies command in His saying "they shall wait" (yatarabbasna), prohibition in His saying "it is not lawful for them" (la yahillu lahunna), permission in His saying "and their husbands have more right" (wa-bu'ulatuhunna ahaqq), and obligation in His saying "and they have a right similar to what is upon them." The attribute of might, which is dominance and overpowering, suited this, and that corresponds to the imposition of obligations.

The divorce is twice; then either retain her in kindness or release her with good treatment.

The wisdom (ḥikmah), which is the perfecting of things and placing them as they should be, is fitting to mention alongside His description, and it also suits the legal obligations (taklīf).

﴿Divorce is twice; then either retain [them] in an honorable manner or release [them] with kindness﴾. The occasion of revelation of this verse is what Hisham ibn ʿUrwah narrated from his father:

That a man, when he divorced his wife and then took her back before the end of her waiting period (ʿiddah), had the right to do so, even if he divorced her a thousand times over. A man divorced his wife and then took her back before the end of her waiting period. Then he divorced her again, and when she was nearing the end of her waiting period, he took her back, then divorced her again, and then said: "By God, I will not let you come near me, nor will you be free of me." She complained of this to the Prophet (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed.

Its connection with what precedes is clear. The verse before it included revocable divorce (al-ṭalāq al-rajʿī), and they used to divorce and take back without limit or count. So this verse specified that it is twice, thereby restricting revocable divorce to two occurrences. That is, the husband has the right to take her back after he divorces her, and then he has the right to take her back again after he divorces her again. After a third divorce, he does not have the right to take her back.

This is by omitting a modifier (ḥadhf muḍāf), meaning: the number of divorces in which the right of return exists is two, and in the third he has no right of return.

On this reading, the definite article in "al-ṭalāq" (the divorce) is for a known reference (lil-ʿahd), referring to the divorce mentioned previously, which is the one in which return is valid. This is the view of ʿUrwah and Qatadah.

It was also said that it refers to the recommended divorce (ṭalāq al-sunnah), which the verse explains by saying "Divorce is twice." This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid.

It was also said that the meaning is separating the divorces when he intends to divorce three times, and this is what the wording requires, because if he divorced twice together in a single utterance, it would not be correct to say "he divorced her twice," just as if he gave a man two dirhams, it would not be correct to say "he gave him twice" until he separates the giving. Then it would be true of him.

This is how they investigated the matter here, and it is a sound investigation. But something has kept stirring in my mind: if he says "You are divorced twice or three times," only one divorce takes effect, because it is a verbal noun of divorce (maṣdar lil-ṭalāq), and it implies a number, so the action that governs it must necessarily recur in existence, as you say "I struck two blows" or "three strikes," because the verbal noun specifies the number of the action. So whenever the action does not recur in existence, it is impossible for its verbal noun to repeat or to specify ranks of number. Thus if he says "You are divorced three times," this is one utterance with one referent, and the one cannot be three or two. The analogy of this is a person who concludes a sale between himself and a man over something, and then at the time of speaking says "I sold you this three times." His words "three times" are void and do not correspond to what preceded. Also, with performative utterances (inshāʾāt), repetition is impossible in them, unless the summarized term becomes capable of that performative act. This is hard to grasp for one who is accustomed to understanding from the words of someone who says "I divorced you twice or three times" that the divorce takes effect twice or three times, as we will explain.

They said: This verse includes rulings, among them that the recommended form of divorce is to separate the number of the three when he intends to divorce three times, and that whoever divorces three or two times in a single instance has divorced in a manner contrary to the Sunnah.

Among them is that what is less than three is established with the right of return, and that if he divorces two during menstruation, both take effect, even though the surplus over three has been abrogated (naskh).

The verse does not address the recommended time for pronouncing divorce, and we will discuss that in its proper place, God willing.

They divided this divorce into: obligatory (wājib), prohibited (maḥẓūr), recommended (masnūn), disliked (makrūh), and permissible (mubāḥ). This belongs to the science of jurisprudence (ʿilm al-fiqh), so we will discuss it in its books.

The apparent sense of the verse is general, so the free and the slave both fall within "divorce," and their ruling is the same. Abu Bakr al-Razi reported a consensus of the early generation (salaf) and the jurists of the cities that a married couple of slaves are separated by two divorces, and it is not lawful for him to remarry her after them except after another husband.

But something from Ibn ʿAbbas contradicts part of this: that the matter of a slave's divorce rests with his master.

They differed when one of them is free and the other is a slave. It was said: the divorce is according to the woman. So if she is free and under a slave or a free man, her divorce is three; or if she is a slave-woman under a free man or a slave, their divorce is two. This was the view of Abu ʿAli, Abu Hanifah, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad, Zufar, al-Thawri, and al-Hasan ibn Salih.

It was also said: the divorce is according to the man. So if she is a slave-woman under a free man, her divorce is three; or if she is free under a slave, her divorce is two. This was the view of Umar and Uthman al-Batti.

"Al-ṭalāq" is the verbal noun of "the woman was divorced, divorce," and it may also mean the act of divorcing (al-taṭlīq), like salām meaning taslīm. It is the subject (mubtada'), and "twice" (marratān) is its predicate. It involves an omitted modifier, meaning: the number of divorces legislated in which return is valid, or: the legislated divorce that is recommended is twice. The omitted modifier was necessary so that the predicate would be the subject itself, and so that "marratān" is literally a dual, because the revocable divorce, or the recommended one, according to the two views, has the number two by way of separation. We have already shown that it occurs by way of separation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: By "twice" he did not intend the dual and repetition as in His saying: ﴿Then return the gaze twice﴾ [al-Mulk: 4], meaning: one glance after another, not two glances. Similar to this are the expressions of repetition such as their saying: "labbayka" (here I am at Your call), "saʿdayka" (at Your service), "ḥananayka" (compassion), "hadhādhayka," and "dawālayka."

End of his words.

This is apparently self-contradictory with what he said before, and contrary to the reality of the matter.

As for the self-contradiction: he said in explaining "Divorce is twice," meaning: the legislated divorce is one divorce after another by separation, not by combining and sending it all at once. So his saying "one divorce after another" is apparently contradictory to his saying "he did not intend by the two times the dual." For when you say "I struck you one blow after another," it is understood from it only that it is limited to two blows, and it is equivalent in meaning to your saying "I struck you two blows." Also, your saying "two blows" cannot be realized except as one blow after another.

As for its contradiction with the reality of the matter: this is not the dual that is used for repetition, because the dual used for repetition does not necessarily mean two or three when repeated, but indicates repetition many times. So their saying "labbayka" means: a response after a response, and more, and the same with its siblings. Likewise His saying "twice" (karratayn) means: then return the gaze many times over. The dual in His saying ﴿Divorce is twice﴾ is only intended to mean the pair of one (shaf' al-wāḥid), which is the original sense of the dual. Do you not see that here by His saying "twice" is not meant more than two? Because of His subsequent saying: ﴿then either retain [them] in an honorable manner or release [them] with kindness﴾, which is the third divorce? That is why what follows is: ﴿And if he divorces her﴾ [al-Baqarah: 230], meaning: if he releases her the third time.

Having established this, the saying "twice" does not indicate repetition that does not form a pair, but it is intended to mean the pair of one. What misled al-Zamakhshari in this is the possibility of the interpretation in his saying: "the legislated divorce is one divorce after another," so he made this from the category of the dual that does not form a pair of one, and intended by it multiplicity. But what undermines this is that the original sense is the pair of one, and that the dual that does not form a pair of one and is intended for repetition is not restricted to three in repetition. When al-Zamakhshari took His saying (twice) to be from the category of the dual intended for repetition, he had to interpret His saying ﴿then either retain [them] in an honorable manner or release [them] with kindness﴾ as an option for them, after He had taught them how to divorce: either they retain the women with good companionship and fulfilling their rights, or they release them with the gracious release He taught them.

From this discussion it is established that His saying ﴿Divorce is twice﴾ has two views among the early generation:

One: that it is an explanation of the number of divorces after which the husband may take back, without renewing the dower and a guardian. This was the view of ʿUrwah, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd.

The second: that it is a definition of the Sunnah of divorce, meaning: whoever divorces two, let him fear God regarding the third, either by leaving her without wronging her of any part of her right, or by retaining her while treating her well in companionship. This was the view of Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, and others.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: The verse includes both of these meanings, and retention in an honorable manner is the taking back after the second divorce with good companionship and fulfilling the rights of marriage.

End of his words.

Al-Zamakhshari reported the first view, saying: It was also said that its meaning is: the revocable divorce is twice, because there is no return after three. ﴿Then either retain in an honorable manner﴾, meaning by return, or ﴿release with kindness﴾, meaning by not taking her back until she is separated by the waiting period, or by not taking her back in a manner intended to prolong the waiting period against her and to harm her. It was also said: by divorcing her the third time.

It was narrated that a questioner asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Where is the third?" He said, peace be upon him: ﴿or release with kindness﴾.

End of his words.

The interpretation of "release with kindness" as not taking her back until she is separated by the waiting period is the view of al-Dahhak and al-Suddi.

As for his saying: "or by not taking her back in a manner intended to prolong the waiting period against her and to harm her," this is a statement whose construction is not clearly consistent with interpreting His saying ﴿or release with kindness﴾, because it requires that he take her back in a good manner intended for kindness, affection, and marital union. Then this would become the counterpart of His saying ﴿then retain in an honorable manner﴾, so the meaning would be: then retain in an honorable manner or take her back in a good manner. This statement does not fit as an interpretation of ﴿or release with kindness﴾. Had it been interpreted this way for ﴿then retain in an honorable manner﴾, it would have been correct.

As for his saying: "It was also said: by divorcing her the second time," this is the view of Mujahid, ʿAtaʾ, (p-194) and the majority of the early generation and the scholars of the cities.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: This view is strengthened in my judgment by three aspects:

The first: it was narrated that a man said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Messenger of God, this is the mention of the two divorces; where is the third?" He said, peace be upon him: "It is His saying: ﴿or release with kindness﴾."

The second aspect: release (tasrīḥ) is one of the words of divorce. Do you not see that it has been recited: "wa-in ʿazamū al-sarāḥ" (and if they resolve on release)?

The third aspect: that faʿʿala with taf'īl (intensive form) indicates that he has produced a repeated act after the second divorce, and in abstention there is no production of an act that is expressed by the intensive form.

End of his words.

This is a good statement.

What the apparent wording indicates is that "al-ṭalāq" has the article for a known reference, namely the divorce mentioned before His saying ﴿And their husbands have more right to take them back in that [period]﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228], which is the divorce in which return is valid. His saying "twice" is an explanation of the number of this divorce. His saying ﴿then either retain in an honorable manner﴾, with the fāʾ that signifies sequence (taʿqīb) after the issuing and occurrence of the two divorces, is a metaphor for return after the second divorce, and the fāʾ of sequence requires consequence. His saying ﴿or release with kindness﴾ is clearly about the third divorce, because it is conjoined to ﴿then retain in an honorable manner﴾, and whatever is conjoined to what is consequent upon something must be consequent upon that thing. So He made for him two states after the two divorces: either he retains her in an honorable manner, or he divorces her with kindness.

However, the conjunction with "or" (aw) detracts from this meaning, because it indicates one of two things. And it becomes stronger in that case that the release is a metaphor for leaving and abandonment, because the meaning would be: divorce is twice, and after the two there are one of two matters:

(p-195) Either retention (imsak), which is a kinaya (metaphorical allusion) for taking her back, or release (tasrih), which is a kinaya for leaving her alone and continuing the release, not the act of pronouncing the release. Or it indicates that release follows the retention referred to as taking her back. If a omitted condition is assumed and imsak is made the answer to that condition, and imsak is made a kinaya for the continuation of the marriage, then it is possible that tasrih means the pronouncement of divorce (inshaʾ al-talaq). The sense would then be:

If he pronounces the two divorces and takes his wife back, then ﴿either keep her in good manner or release her with kindness﴾, because taking back is followed by one of two things: either continuation of the marriage, which is done in good manner, or the third divorce, which is done with kindness.

In al-Muntakhab, he said, in an abridged form:

"Divorce is twice." Some people said: it is a new sentence (mubtada’) with no connection to what precedes it. Its meaning is that lawful divorce must be one pronouncement after another, separately, not all at once in a single instance. This is the interpretation of those who said: combining the three is forbidden. This is the position of Ubayy and a group of the Companions.

The alif and lam (al-alif wa-l-lam) are for totality (al-istighraq), and the sense is: all divorce is twice, and a third time. This indicates separation, because "times" can only occur after separation from cohabitation. The wording is a report, but its meaning is a command. Those who hold this view said:

If he divorced her three times or two, they differed. Many scholars of the household (of the Prophet) said: only one occurs, because a prohibition indicates that the forbidden act includes a dominant corruption, and saying that it takes effect brings that corruption into existence, which is not permitted.

Abu Hanifa said: what he uttered takes effect, on the basis that a prohibition does not indicate invalidity.

Some people said: it is connected to what precedes it, and the meaning is: revocable divorce is twice, and there is no return after three. This is the interpretation of those who permitted combining the three, and it is the position of al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him. The reason is that the preceding verse mentions that the right of return belongs to the husband, but does not state that it is permanent or limited to a specific term. So this is like a general statement needing specification, or an unspecified statement (mujmal) needing clarification, or a general term (ʿamm) needing a restrictor (mukhassis). He therefore clarified when return is established, which is when there are two divorces. As for the third, return is not established. So the alif and lam in "divorce" refer to the known prior divorce, the one in which return is established. This view is preferred because His saying ﴿and their husbands have more right to take them back in that [period]﴾ [al-Baqara 2:228], if general in all circumstances, requires a restrictor, or if unspecified because the condition under which return is established is not stated, requires clarification. Therefore, connecting it to what precedes it provides the restrictor or clarifier, which is more apt than not doing so. Because delaying clarification from the time of address, though permissible, is less preferred. Also, taking it this way brings in the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul), whereas taking it to refer to a different, unrelated ruling removes it from that context, and the occasion cannot lie outside the scope of the general statement.

In al-Muntakhab also, he said, in an abridged form:

The meaning of release is before the third divorce occurs, and before leaving off return until the waiting period (ʿidda) ends and she is separated. This is the closest meaning, because the fa' (then) in His saying ﴿then if he divorces her﴾ [al-Baqara 2:230] requires that this divorce occur after that release. If the third were meant by release, then ﴿if he divorces her﴾ [al-Baqara 2:230] would be a fourth divorce, which is not permitted. Also, after it comes ﴿and it is not lawful for you to take﴾, and what is meant is khulʿ (divorce by the wife's compensation), and it is known that it is not valid after three. So if the Messenger of Allah ﷺ's interpretation of release here, that it is the third, is correct, then nothing more can be said about it.

End of what was intended to be summarized from al-Muntakhab.

It does not follow from what was mentioned that his saying ("if he divorces her a fourth time") is as he said, because he assumed the release to have occurred. That is not the case, because he mentioned one of two matters after he divorces twice: the first is that he takes her back and retains her in good manner, and the second is that he releases her after taking back with kindness. So the meaning is that the ruling is one of two matters. Then he said: if one of the two matters occurs, namely divorce, then its ruling is such-and-such. So it does not follow that this occurring matter is different from one of the two preceding matters, just as you would say: My opinion is that you should stay or leave, and if you leave, then such-and-such. His saying "if you leave" does not indicate that the leaving is a different one from the one whose occurrence is uncertain, and the uncertainty about the ruling between staying and leaving does not indicate that leaving has occurred, because the thing judged is one of the two matters. Nor does it follow what was mentioned about khulʿ coming after three, which is not valid for the reason we mentioned, that the ruling is one of two matters, so it does not indicate that the third divorce occurred. Rather, He mentioned khulʿ before mentioning the occurrence of the third divorce, because it is after it, which is His saying ﴿then if he divorces her﴾ [al-Baqara 2:230]. Also, even if we grant that the third divorce occurred before it, ﴿and it is not lawful for you to take﴾ does not require that khulʿ be after the third divorce, because the verse came to clarify the ruling of khulʿ and to begin discussion about it. The fact that it was brought for this meaning after mention of the third divorce in recitation does not indicate sequence in existence. So what was mentioned does not follow unless he explicitly stated a qualifier requiring that khulʿ come after the third divorce in existence, and that is not the case, so what he said does not follow.

The nominative (irtifaʿ) of His saying ﴿imsak﴾ is as a beginning (mubtada’), and the predicate is omitted. Ibn ʿAtiyya assumed it as delayed, the sense being: "more fitting and better." Others assumed it as preceding, that is: "upon you is retention in good manner." Ibn ʿAtiyya also permitted that it be the predicate of an omitted subject, the sense being: "so what is obligatory is retention," and "bi-maʿruf" and "bi-ihsan" each attach to what follows of the verbal noun. The bāʾ is for attachment (lil-ilsāq). He also permitted that the prepositional phrase be an attribute of what precedes it, and so attaches to an omitted element. They said: it is permissible in Arabic, and it was not read this way: the accusative (nasb) of imsak or tasrih as a verbal noun (masdar), that is: "so retain them with retention in good manner, or release them with release in kindness."

﴿And it is not lawful for you to take anything of what you have given them﴾, the verse. The occasion of revelation: Jamila bint ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy was married to Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, and she hated him while he loved her. She complained about him to her father, but he did not punish him. Then she complained to him a second and third time, and there was a mark of beating on her, but he did not punish him. So she came to the Prophet ﷺ, complained about him to him, and showed him the mark of the beating, and said: "Neither I nor Thabit—nothing unites my head with his head. By Allah, I will not blame him in religion or character, but I dislike disbelief in Islam. I cannot endure him out of hatred. I lifted the side of the tent and saw him coming in a group, and he was the blackest of them, the shortest in stature, and the ugliest in face." Thabit said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is more beloved to me after you than her. I gave her a garden, let her return it to me, and I release her." So she did that, and he released her. This was the first khulʿ in Islam, and the verse was revealed.

The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned retention in good manner or release in kindness, this required that among kindness is that the husband take from his wife something of what he gave her. He excepted from this case the matter of khulʿ, and so He permitted the man to take from her on the terms we will explain in the verse. As Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿and if you have given one of them a heap of gold, do not take anything back from it﴾ [al-Nisa’ 4:20], the verse. The address in "lakum" (to you) and what follows apparently is to the husbands, because taking and giving from husbands is literal. So they were forbidden to take anything, because custom has it that the soul is stingy and seeks what it gave at the time of discord and separation. Some permitted that the address be to the imams and judges, so that it fits with His saying ﴿if you fear﴾, because it is an address to them and not to the husbands. The taking and giving were attributed to them at the time of litigation, because they are the ones who enforce that. Whoever said it is for the husbands replied that the address may differ between the two clauses, so each address is directed to whom this ruling befits, and such a thing is not objectionable. Also, taking the word in its literal sense is then preferable to taking it metaphorically. ﴿what you have given them﴾ apparently covers the whole of what they gave, whether as dower (ṣadāq) or otherwise, as a gift (hiba). Some interpreted it as the ṣadaqāt (dowers), but the wording is general. ﴿anything﴾ indicates the gravity of taking from them, whether little or much. ﴿anything﴾ is indefinite in the context of a prohibition, so it is general. "Mimma" (of what) attaches to His saying ﴿take﴾, or to an omitted element, in which case it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial (ḥāl) of ﴿anything﴾, because if it were delayed it would be an attribute of it.

﴿Unless they both fear that they will not keep the limits of Allah﴾. The alif and lam in "yakhafa" and "yuqima" refer to the two categories of spouses, and this is an instance of shift in pronoun (iltifat), because when an addressee and an absent party are together and a ruling is attributed to both, the addressee takes precedence. You say: "You and Zayd go out" (antum... takhrujan), and you do not say "yakhrujan." Likewise with the first person: "I and Zayd go out" (nakhruj). Since the exception came after the sentence had finished addressing, the shift was permitted. Had it followed the first pattern, it would have been: "unless you fear that you will not keep," and the pronoun would then refer to the addressees and their wives. The meaning is: "unless both of them, i.e. the two categories of spouses, fear abandoning the keeping of Allah's limits regarding the rights of marriage that bind them, because of the hatred that arises in the woman toward her husband, to the point that the intensity of hatred becomes a cause of falling into disbelief, as in the story of Jamila with her husband Thabit." As for ﴿that they both fear﴾ (an yakhafa), it has been said that it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial, the sense being "unless they are fearful," so it is an exception from the circumstances, as if it were said: "it is not lawful for you to take anything of what you have given them in any circumstance except in the circumstance of fear that they will not keep Allah's limits." This is because "an" with the verb is in the sense of a verbal noun, and the verbal noun stands in the place of the active participle, so it is in the accusative as a circumstantial. But this permission is open to question, because a verbal noun occurring as a circumstantial is not a regular pattern, so what occupies its place, namely "an" plus the verb, is even less so, and it would be a frequent metaphor, since the circumstantial would then be "an" plus the verb standing in place of a verbal noun standing in place of an active participle. Sibawayh prohibited "an" plus the verb from occurring as a circumstantial, and he stated this at the end of the section: "this is a chapter in which the nominative is preferred and is the form in all dialects." What appears to be the case is that it is an exception from the object of purpose (mafʿul lahu), as if it were said: "It is not lawful for you to take on any basis except on the basis of fear of not keeping Allah's limits; that is what permits you to take." The particle of cause has been omitted before "an," and that is permissible and very common in eloquent speech. It does not arise here, against the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh, whether when the preposition is removed from "an" it is in the accusative or in the genitive position. Rather, this is in the accusative, because it is assumed as a verbal noun, and a verbal noun if stated explicitly would be in the accusative, the governing word reaching it directly. Likewise this assumed form. What we have mentioned, that "an" plus the verb when in the position of an object of purpose is in the accusative and nothing else, is explicitly stated by the grammarians, and its reason is evident.

The meaning of fear here is certainty (al-iqan), as Abu ʿUbayda said. Or it is knowledge, i.e. "unless they both know," as Ibn Salama said, and this is what Abu Mihjan meant by his words:

I fear that, if I die, I will not taste her (love).

Therefore the verb after "an" is in the nominative, or "al-zann" (supposition), as al-Farraʾ said. Ubayy also recited it this way: "unless they both suppose," and he recited:

The speech of one whom we would reach came to me with its words, and I did not fear, O Salam, that you would blame me.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 229 (part 3 of 4):

The more appropriate reading is to keep "fear" (khawf) in its basic sense, which is caution about something. The meaning would then be: "unless each of them knows, or suspects, or is certain, or is wary, on their own account, that they will not fulfil the rights of marriage owed to the other as they should be fulfilled, in which case taking the compensation is permitted." ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) recited: "unless they fear that they will not uphold the rights of," meaning: unless the husbands and wives fear. This is a shift of grammatical person (iltifat, a change in the person of address), since if the earlier pattern had continued it would have been with the second person "you" (tāʾ). It is also reported that ʿAbd Allah recited: "unless you fear," with the tāʾ.

Ḥamzah, Yaʿqub and Yazid ibn al-Qaqaʿ recited: "unless they are feared" (yukhāfū), with a ḍamma on the yāʾ, in the passive voice, with the omitted agent being the rulers (al-wulāt). The phrase "that they not uphold" (an lā yuqīmā) is in the nominative case as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun, meaning: unless the non-upholding of the two of them of the limits of God is feared. This is an inclusive apposition (badal al-ishtimal, where the substitute is related to the original by inclusion), as when you say: "The two Zayds pleased me, their beauty," the original being "unless they are feared, that the rulers..., the non-upholding by the two of them of the limits of God."

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: in the recitation yukhāfā with the ḍamma, the verb khāfa has passed on to two objects. One of them is the subject to which the verb was attributed, and the other is a preposition omitted and understood. So the position of an (that) is in the genitive case by the omitted preposition according to Sibawayh and al-Kisaʾi, while according to others it is in the accusative, because when the omitted preposition was dropped, the verb reached the second object, like: "I ask God's forgiveness for a sin" (astaghfiru Allaha dhanban), and "I commanded you the good" (amartuka al-khayr). This is the end of his words. It is the exact text of Abu ʿAli al-Farisi, which he quoted from his book, except for the comparison with astaghfiru. The comparison of khāfa with astaghfiru by Ibn ʿAtiyya is not correct, because khāfa does not pass on to two objects in the way astaghfiru Allah does, and the grammarians did not mention this when they listed verbs that take two objects, one of which originally takes a preposition. Rather, when one says: "I feared Zayd his beating, Amr," this is a substitute (badal), since "from his beating Amr" is an object of purpose, and it is not understood as a second object. Ibn ʿAtiyya has also erred in attributing to Sibawayh's school that the position is genitive. What Abu ʿAli and others transmitted is that Sibawayh's view is that the position after the omission is accusative, and this is also the view of al-Farrāʾ, while the view of al-Khalil is that it is genitive, and this is the view of al-Kisaʾi. Other than Ibn ʿAtiyya, some have estimated the omitted preposition to be ʿalā (on), saying: the estimated meaning is "unless the two fear over that they will not uphold." On this view, Abu ʿAli's statement could be valid, though it is a distant reading.

Some who do not properly understand the constructions of Arabic have criticised this recitation, but it is a sound recitation, correct both in wording and in meaning. What supports it is his later words: "But if you fear" (fa-in khiftum), which indicate that the expected fear is from someone other than the spouses. Abu ʿUbayd also preferred this recitation. Abu Jaʿfar al-Saffar said: I know of no choice by Ḥamzah more remote than this letter, since neither grammatical analysis (iʿrab) nor the wording nor the meaning requires it. As for grammatical analysis, if one argues for it by the recitation of ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, "unless they are feared that they not uphold," this is grammatical in Arabic on the basis of the passive form, but in that case it should have been said: "unless they two are feared that they two not uphold." al-Farrāʾ argued for Ḥamzah's recitation and said that he took into account the recitation of ʿAbd Allah: "unless they are feared." Abu ʿAli rejected this and said: he was not correct, because in the recitation of ʿAbd Allah the fear falls on "that," whereas in the recitation of Ḥamzah it falls on the man and the woman. As for wording, if it is correct, it must be said: "if the two are feared," and if it follows the wording of "if," it must be said: "unless they fear." As for meaning, it is remote to say: "It is not lawful for you to take anything of what you have given them, unless the others fear," and God, exalted and majestic, did not say: "There is no blame on you that they take from her a ransom," which would make the khulʿ dependent on the ruler. It is established from ʿUmar and ʿUthman that they permitted khulʿ without a ruler. This is the end of al-Saffar's words. What he mentioned does not follow. The construction of the recitation with ḍamma is clear, because when He said: "And it is not lawful for you," it became obligatory for the judges to prevent anyone who wanted to take anything of that. Then He said: "unless the two fear," where the pronoun refers to the spouses, and the one who fears is omitted, namely the guardians and judges. The estimate is: "unless the guardians fear for the two spouses that they will not uphold the limits of God, and then the ransom is permitted." The meaning of fear has already been explained here.

As for his statement that "it is therefore obligatory to say: if the two are feared," this does not follow, because this is an iltifat, which is frequent in the Qur'an, and it is among the excellences of the Arabic language. Also, on al-Saffar's view, the opening of the yāʾ would require the reading "if the two fear" (fa-in khāfā), whereas in both recitations it is an iltifat. As for the rejection of al-Farrāʾ, it is not correct, because the recitation of ʿAbd Allah, "unless they are feared," is evidence for it, since the estimate is: "unless they fear them, that they not uphold," and the fear in the recitation of Ḥamzah falls on "that," because it is in the nominative position as a substitute for their pronoun. This is inclusive apposition, as we have established before, so it is not as Abu ʿAli imagined. This is like saying: "Zayd was feared, his evil." As for his statement that it is remote in meaning, the answer to it has already been given: they have the right to prohibit this, so whenever they suspect or are certain that the limits of God will not be upheld, they do not have the right to prohibit it. Abu ʿUbayda preferred the ḍamma recitation because of God's words: "But if you fear," so he made the fear belong to others than the spouses. If He had meant the spouses, He would have said: "if the two fear." It has also been said that His words "And it is not lawful for you" to the end form a parenthetical clause between His words: "Divorce is twice; then either retain with kindness or release with good treatment," and between His words: "But if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him thereafter" [al-Baqarah 2:230].

"But if you fear" (fa-in khiftum): the pronoun refers to the guardians or the ruler. If there are none, then it refers to the righteous Muslims. It has also been said that it refers to the whole group, meaning whoever stands in that role is sufficient.

"That they not uphold the limits of God": the non-upholding of the limits is the manifestation of nushuz (ill-temper, disobedience, or refusal of marital duties) and bad conduct on her part. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Malik and the majority of jurists. It may also mean her not obeying his command and not fulfilling his oath, as said by al-Hasan and al-Shaʿbi. And it may mean showing her dislike of him with her tongue, as said by ʿAta. On these three views it has been said that the dual is used for the singular, or the dislike of each of them for the other, so that neither upholds what God has made obligatory toward the other. This was said by Tawus and Ibn al-Musayyab, and on this view the dual is in its proper sense.

It is narrated that a woman showed nushuz in the time of ʿUmar, so he made her spend three nights in a stable among the dung. Then he called her and said: "How did you find your place?" She said: "I have not seen nights more pleasing to my eye than these, and I have not found rest since I was with him except these nights." ʿUmar said: "By your father, this is nushuz!" and he said to her husband: "Divorce her (khlaʿha), even if it is for her earring. Take a khulʿ from her for less than the hair-clasps on her head, for there is no good for you in her."

"There is no blame on them both for what she gives up to be free": this is the answer to the condition. They said: its implication (mafhum) requires that khulʿ is not permitted except in the presence of the one who has authority, whether ruler or guardian, and the fear of their not upholding the limits of God. What they said about the implication requiring the existence of fear is correct, but as for the presence of the authority, it is not. The apparent meaning of His words "And it is not lawful for you," if it is addressed to the husbands, is that this condition is not required. al-Hasan restricted khulʿ to the presence of the ruler. The pronoun in "on them both" refers to the spouses together: that is, there is no blame on the husband for what he took, nor on the wife for what she gave up to be free. al-Farrāʾ said: "on them both" means "on him," like His words: "There come out of them both the pearl and the coral" [al-Rahman 55:22], meaning only the salt water, and "they forgot their fish" [al-Kahf 18:61], where the one who forgot was Yusha ʿ. The poet said:

"If you two restrain me, O son of ʿAffan, I will be restrained,
And if you leave me, I will protect an honour kept inviolable."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 229 (part 4 of 4):

The apparent meaning of His words ﴿in what she gives up for it﴾ is generality: it covers her dowry, more than it, and all of her property. This was said by Umar, Uthman, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrimah, al-Nakha'i, al-Hasan, Qabisa ibn Dhu'ayb, Malik, Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr, and Umar ruled accordingly. It has also been said that it refers only to the dowry she gives up, without any addition from him. This was said by Ali, Tawus, Amr ibn Shu'ayb, Ata', al-Zuhri, Ibn al-Musayyib, al-Sha'bi, al-Hasan, al-Hakam, Hammad, Ahmad, Ishaq and Ibn al-Rabi'. Al-Hasan and he used to read ﴿in what she gives up for it from him﴾, with the added word "minhu" (from him), meaning: from what you have given them, which is the mahr (bridal payment). Makki reported this opinion from Abu Hanifa. It has also been said that the compensation is only part of her dowry, and that it is not permissible to take all of it if he has consummated the marriage, so that some of it remains to serve as a substitute for his enjoyment of her.

The apparent meaning of His words ﴿if you fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah﴾ is that both of them share in failing to observe the limits, and that the permissibility of taking the compensation depends on this failure occurring from both of them together. Allah has forbidden the husband to take it except after fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah. He reinforced the prohibition with His words ﴿so do not transgress them﴾, then threatened those who transgress. The majority of scholars agree (ijma', scholarly consensus) on the prohibition of taking her property, except where the disobedience (nushuz) and the corruption of the marriage come from her side. Ibn al-Mundhir said: we have related this meaning from Ibn Abbas, al-Sha'bi, Mujahid, Ata', al-Nakha'i, Ibn Sirin, al-Qasim, Urwa, Humayd ibn Abd al-Rahman, Qatada, al-Thawri, Malik, Ishaq and Abu Thawr. Malik, al-Sha'bi and others said: if the corruption and disobedience of the wife are accompanied by corruption on the part of the husband, and the discord between them has worsened, then the ransom (fidya) is permissible for the husband. Abu Muhammad ibn Atiyya said: the meaning of this is that if the husband were to abandon his own corruption, her disobedience would not cease. As for when the husband alone is corrupt, I know of no one who permits him to take the ransom, except what has been related from Abu Hanifa, that he said: if the wrongdoing and disobedience come from him, and she gives up her property to him in exchange for divorce, then it is valid and binding, but he is sinful, it is not lawful for him to do what he did, and he must not return what he took. His companions Abu Yusuf, Muhammad and Zufar agreed with this. Malik said: the divorce takes effect at that time, and he must return her property to her. Al-Awza'i said regarding a man who divorced his wife by khul' while she was ill: if she was disobedient, the payment is taken from her one-third (of the estate), but if she was not disobedient, he must return it to her, and he has the right of return (raj'a) over her. He said: if the two of them agreed to annul the marriage before consummation, and no disobedience appeared from her, I see no harm in that. Al-Hasan ibn Salih and Uthman al-Batti said: if the wrongdoing comes from him, he has no right to seek khul' from her; if it comes from her, he has that right, provided they agree on its terms. The apparent meaning of the verse is that if the fear does not arise, it is not permissible for her to give anything in exchange for separation. Bakr ibn Abd Allah al-Muzani held an anomalous view, saying: it is not permissible for a man to take anything from his wife as khul', neither a little nor a lot. He said: this verse is abrogated (mansukh) by His words ﴿and if you wish to replace one wife with another﴾ [al-Nisa': 20], and the verse. His view is weak, because the community has agreed (ijma') on the permissibility of the ransom, and because the meaning associated with the verse of the ransom is different from the meaning in the verse about wishing to replace a wife.

Scholars differed over whether the general wording of ﴿in what she gives up for it﴾ includes harmful or unknown things, such as dates that have not yet ripened, a runaway camel, a runaway slave, a fetus in the womb, the fruit her palm trees will produce, the offspring her sheep will bear, and her nursing of her child from him. All of this and what scholars derived from it is mentioned in the books of jurisprudence (fiqh). They said: the apparent meaning of His words ﴿in what she gives up for it﴾ shows that khul' is a annulment (faskh) when he does not intend divorce by it, based on His later words ﴿then if he divorces her﴾ [al-Baqarah: 230]. They agreed that this divorce is the third, so if khul' had been a divorce before it, this would be the fourth, which contradicts the consensus. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Tawus, Ikrimah, Ahmad, Ishaq and Abu Thawr. It has been related from Ali, Uthman, Ibn Mas'ud and a group of the Successors (tabi'un) that it is a divorce. The majority held this view: Malik, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, Abu Hanifa and his companions, and al-Shafi'i. The apparent meaning of the verse does not indicate that khul' is an annulment, as they claimed, because the verse was revealed only to explain the rulings of khul', without addressing whether it is an annulment or a divorce. If he intended two or three divorces by it, Malik said: it is what he intended. Abu Hanifa said: if he intended three, then it is three; if he intended two, then it is one irrevocable divorce.

* *

﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them﴾: this refers to the verses that precede it, from His words ﴿and do not marry polytheistic women﴾ [al-Baqarah: 221] up to here. Stating "the limits" with a noun rather than a pronoun is a sign of glorifying the limits of Allah the Exalted. Repeating the attribution (to Allah) specifies them and honors them, and repeating the noun is appropriate because the statements are in different sentences. "Tilka" (these) is the subject (mubtada'), and "hudud Allah" (the limits of Allah) is the predicate (khabar). The meaning of ﴿so do not transgress them﴾ is: do not go beyond them to what He has not commanded you.

﴿And whoever transgresses the limits of Allah, those are the wrongdoers﴾: since He had forbidden transgressing the limits, which means going beyond them, and this address was for those who had been addressed before, He used this general conditional sentence, which includes every single person who exceeds the limits. He judged them to be the wrongdoers (zalimun), and wrongdoing (zulm) means placing a thing in other than its proper place. Thus it included those addressed, and it was said: and others as well. "Man" (whoever) is a conditional particle, and the fa' in "fa-ula'ika" (then those) is the response of the condition. "Yata'adda" is treated according to its wording and so is singular, while "ula'ika" is treated according to its meaning and so is plural. It was emphasized by His words "hum" (they), and the definite article in "al-zalimun" (the wrongdoers), which conveys restriction or emphasis in the description. "Hum" may be a separating pronoun (fasl) and an apposition (badal).

﴿Then if he divorces her﴾ [al-Baqarah: 230]: this means the husband who divorced once after another. It refers back to His words ﴿or release with kindness﴾, as if He had said: if he releases her with the third release that remains from the number of divorces. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Dahhak, Mujahid and al-Suddi. From Ibn Abbas's view that khul' is a severance of the marital bond and not a divorce, this verse is used as evidence: Allah mentioned the two divorces, then mentioned khul', then mentioned the third after the two divorces, and khul' did not have a ruling that counts. As for those who consider it a divorce, they replied: this objection is clear. The two divorces, and the third, in which He stated that it is not lawful to take anything from the wife's property except under the condition mentioned, is a ruling that can apply to every divorce. The placement of the verse of khul' between these two verses is ruling-wise, that reconciliation and khul' are only valid before the third divorce; after it, none of this remains. It is like a conclusion to all the rulings concerning this topic.

[p. 200]

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 230 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Then she is not lawful to him thereafter﴾, i.e., after this third divorce, ﴿until she marries another husband﴾. The word nikah (marriage) is applied both to the contract (al-'aqd) and to sexual intercourse (al-wat'). Ibn al-Musayyab and Ibn Jubayr took it to mean the contract, and al-Nahhas mentioned this in his Ma'ani al-Qur'an, saying: if the second husband contracts marriage with her, she becomes lawful to the first, even if he has not entered her or had intercourse with her. The majority disagreed with him, on account of the well-known hadith of the wife of Rifa'ah. al-Hasan said: she becomes lawful only through intercourse and emission, and this is the "tasting of the honey" (dhawq al-'asaliyah). The rest of the scholars said: the penetration of the glans (taghyib al-hashafah) makes her lawful. Some jurists said: the meeting of the two circumcised parts (iltiqa' al-khitanayn) makes her lawful, and this reverts to the statement before it, since the two do not meet except with the penetration upon which the majority agrees. In His saying ﴿until she marries another husband﴾ there is an indication that the marriage of the muhallil (the one who makes her lawful) is permissible, since the lawfulness is not meant except through marriage to a husband, and this applies to him, that it is a marriage to a husband, so it is permissible. This is the view of Ibn Abi Layla, Abu Hanifa, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad, Dawud, and it is the view of al-Awza'i in one narration, al-Thawri in one narration, and the view of al-Shafi'i in his new Egyptian book, provided he did not stipulate the making-lawful at the time of the contract. al-Qasim, Salim, Rabi'ah, and Yahya ibn Sa'd said: there is no harm in his marrying her in order to make her lawful, provided the two spouses do not know, and he is rewarded. Malik, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i in his old view, and Abu Hanifa in one narration said: it is not permissible, she is not lawful to the first, and it is not allowed to stand, whether they knew or did not know. It is narrated from al-Thawri that if they stipulated, the stipulation is void and the marriage is valid, and this is the view of Ibn Abi Layla regarding that and regarding temporary marriage (nikah al-mut'ah). al-Hasan and Ibrahim said: if any of the three knew of the making-lawful, the marriage is invalid. In His saying ﴿another husband﴾ there is an indication that the one who marries must be a husband. So if she was a slave-woman and was divorced three times, or twice according to those who hold that view, and then her master had intercourse with her, she is not lawful to the first. This was said by Ali, Ubaydah, Masruq, al-Sha'bi, Jabir, Ibrahim, Sulayman ibn Yasar, Hammad, Abu Ziyad, and the body of jurists of the cities. It is narrated from Uthman, Zayd ibn Thabit, and al-Zubayr that he makes her lawful if he has intercourse with her in a manner in which he does not intend deception or making-lawful, and she returns to her husband by proposal and dowry. In His saying "a husband" there is also an indication that if the husband was a slave and she was a slave-woman, and the master gave her to him after the irrevocable divorce, or the husband bought her after the irrevocable divorce, she is not lawful to him in both cases by right of ownership (milk al-yamin) until she marries another husband. Abu 'Umar said: this is the view of the body of scholars and leading jurists: Malik, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, and Abu Thawr. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', Tawus, and al-Hasan said: she becomes lawful by right of ownership. In His saying "a husband other than him" there is an indication that if a Muslim irrevocably divorced a dhimmiyyah (non-Muslim woman) three times, and a dhimmi married her, entered her, and divorced her, she becomes lawful to the first. This was said by al-Hasan, al-Zuhri, al-Thawri, al-Shafi'i, Abu 'Ubayd, and the companions of Abu Hanifa. Malik and Rabi'ah said: she does not become lawful. The apparent meaning of His saying "until she marries a husband" is that it is by a valid marriage; so if she was married by an invalid marriage, she does not become lawful. This is the view of the majority of scholars: Malik, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu 'Ubayd, and the companions of Abu Hanifa. al-Hakam said: he is a husband. They agreed that if the woman told the first husband, "I have married, and my husband has entered me," and her husband confirmed it, she becomes lawful to the first. al-Shafi'i said: the cautious course is that he should not act if it occurs to his mind that she lied to him. In the verse there is evidence that the term "husband" suffices, whether he is strong in marriage or weak, or a boy or an adolescent, or a castrated man who retains what can penetrate, as the non-eunuch can penetrate, and whether he penetrated with his own hand or with hers, and whether she was in ihram or fasting. All of this is according to what al-Shafi'i described as the view of Abu Hanifa and his companions, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, al-Hasan ibn Salih, and some companions of Malik. Malik said in one of his two views: if he had intercourse with her while she was asleep or unconscious, she is not lawful to the one who divorced her. The view of the majority of jurists is that the woman divorced three times is not lawful to that husband except by five conditions: she observes the waiting period (iddah) from him, a contract is made with a second husband, he has intercourse with her, then he divorces her, and she observes the waiting period from him. As for intercourse being a condition, it was said that this is established by the Sunnah, and it was said by the Qur'an, and this is the view of Abu Muslim. It was said: this is the preferred view, because Abu 'Ali related that the Arabs say: "so-and-so married so-and-so" meaning he contracted with her, and "he married his wife" meaning he had intercourse with her. The ways of this have already passed for us. In al-Muntakhab, after much discussion, its substance is that His saying "until she marries another husband" indicates the previously mentioned husbandhood, which is the contract between them, then nikah applied to whoever his wife preceded, so it is necessarily meant as intercourse, so His saying "marries" indicates intercourse and "husband" indicates the contract. What he said is not necessarily so, since it is possible that it does not indicate that husbandhood must precede, by making his being called husband refer to what his state will become, so the meaning is: until he contracts with one who will be a husband. Also in al-Muntakhab: as for the statement of one who says the verse does not indicate intercourse and that it was established only by the Sunnah, it is weak, because the verse requires the prohibition to be negated, extended to a limit, and what is a limit for a thing requires the ruling to end upon its occurrence; so the prohibition is necessarily removed upon the occurrence of marriage. So if nikah were a reference to the contract, the verse would indicate that this prohibition ends upon the occurrence of the contract, and lifting it by a report would be abrogation of the Qur'an by a single report, which is not permissible. But if we take nikah to mean intercourse, and take His saying "husband" to mean the contract, this difficulty does not arise. End. What he mentioned of this difficulty is not necessary, namely that it would entail abrogating the Qur'an by a single report, because the one who says so says: He did not make the negation of lawfulness end at this limit, namely her marrying another husband, only. Although the apparent meaning of the verse is that, rather there are conjunctions before the stated limit in the verse and after it which indicate its intended meaning, and these are also limits. The estimate is: "Then she is not lawful to him thereafter," i.e., after the third divorce, until her waiting period from him ends, and she is contracted to another husband, and he enters her, and divorces her, and her waiting period from him ends; then at that point she is lawful to the husband who divorced her three times, that they return to one another. So the verse has become one of those where the explanation of lawfulness requires estimating these omitted elements and clarifying them, and the Book and the established Sunnah indicate their intended meaning. When this is so, and the Book and the Sunnah clarify these omitted elements, this is not a case of abrogating the Qur'an by a single report. Do you not see that it also necessarily follows from taking nikah here to mean intercourse that there must be implied before it: "until she is contracted to a husband and he has intercourse with her." So there is no difference in the implication between it preceding the stated limit, where intercourse is intended, or following it when the contract is intended; this is an implication that the Book and the Sunnah indicate, so it is not a case of abrogation at all.
* *
﴿And if he divorces her﴾. It was said: the pronoun refers to the husband of the indefinite noun, namely the second. He used the word "if" (in) rather than "when" (idha), as a reminder that his divorce must be according to what occurs to him, not conditional. End. Its meaning is that "idha" is only used for what is certain, though it may also be used for what is uncertain and whose occurrence is either possible or not, or for what is certain but whose time of occurrence is unknown, as in His saying: ﴿Then if you die, will they be the immortals?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 34]. The meaning: if he divorces her and her waiting period from him ends, ﴿there is no blame upon the two of them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229], i.e., upon the husband who divorced her three times and this wife. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. There is no disagreement among the people of knowledge that the wording may refer to the second husband and the woman, and the verse would then convey two rulings. The first: the woman irrevocably divorced three times becomes lawful to the first after marriage to another husband under the conditions mentioned earlier, and this is understood from the beginning of the verse. The second ruling: it is permissible for the second husband who divorced her to take her back, because he takes the place of the first, so it is permissible for both of them to return to one another. This removes what might occur to the mind, that if the second divorced her she would become lawful to the first, so that by her becoming lawful to him she would be exclusive to him, and the second could not take her back. So His saying ﴿there is no blame upon the two of them that they return to one another﴾ clarifies that the ruling for the second is the ruling for the first, and that it is not necessary that the first must take her back. Rather, by the evidence that if her waiting period from the second ends, she is free to choose whichever of them to marry, and if her waiting period has not ended, and the divorce was revocable, then her second husband may take her back. On this view, no omission is needed between His saying ﴿And if he divorces her﴾ and His saying ﴿there is no blame upon the two of them that they return to one another﴾. Omission is needed only if the pronoun in "upon the two of them" refers to the one who divorced three times and the wife, and the omitted element is: "and her waiting period from him has ended," i.e., if the second divorces her and her waiting period from him ends, there is no blame upon the one who divorced three times and the wife in returning to one another.
* *
His saying ﴿if they both think they can keep within the limits of Allah﴾: i.e., if the second husband and the wife think they can keep within the limits of Allah, because divorce generally occurs only at quarreling, enmity, and hatred. All the pronouns run in a single line without any turning or variation, and there is no conflict with deriving these two rulings from taking the pronouns in their apparent sense. What we have mentioned is not transmitted; rather what they understood is the turning and variation of the pronouns.
﴿that they return to one another﴾: i.e., regarding their returning to one another. The pronoun in "upon the two of them" and in "that they return to one another," according to what they explained, refers to the first husband and the wife whom the second husband divorced. Ibn al-Mundhir said: the people of knowledge agreed that if a free man divorced his wife three times, then her waiting period ended, she married another husband who entered her, then the first married her again, she is with him on three divorces, and then she returns to the first. A group said: she remains on whatever remains of her divorces. This was the view of the senior Companions: 'Umar, 'Ali, Ubayy, 'Imran ibn Husayn, Abu Hurayrah, Zayd ibn Thabit, Mu'adh ibn Jabal, and 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As; and among the Successors: 'Abidah al-Salmani, Ibn al-Musayyab, and al-Hasan. Among the imams: Malik, al-Thawri, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Shafi'i, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu 'Ubayd, Abu Thawr, and Ibn Nasr. Another group said: it is a new marriage, because the second husband demolishes it, whether it was one or two divorces just as he demolishes three; this was said by Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', al-Nakha'i, Shurayh, and the companions of 'Abdullah except 'Abidah, and it is the view of Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf. A third view was stated: if the other one entered her, it is a new divorce and a new marriage for the first; and if he did not enter her, it remains on what is left.
* *

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 230 (part 2 of 2):

﴿If they both think that they will keep within the limits of God﴾: that is, if each of them thinks that he or she will treat the other well, and that there will be harmony between them regarding the limits that God has set for each of them. We have already mentioned some of what each of them owes the other in His saying: ﴿And they have rights similar to their obligations, according to what is reasonable﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:228]. Ibn Khuwayz said: Our companions, meaning the companions of Malik, disagreed on whether the wife is obliged to perform housework or not. Some of them said: The wife is not required to do anything other than sexual intercourse. Others said: She is required to do the work of women like her. If she is of noble standing, because of her father's wealth or affluence, then she must manage the household and oversee the servant. If she is of middling circumstances, then she must spread the bedding and the like. If she is from among the women of the Kurds and the Daylam in their lands, then she is charged with what their women are charged with. The practice of the Muslims in their lands, in old times and new, has followed what we have mentioned. Do you not see that the women of the Companions were required to grind grain, bake bread, cook, spread bedding, serve food, and similar tasks, and we do not know of a woman who refused this? Rather, they would beat their wives if they fell short in it.

﴿If they both think﴾ is a conditional clause whose response is omitted, because the preceding context indicates it. So the permissibility of reconciliation is conditional on two things: one is the second husband's divorcing her, and the other is their thinking that they will keep the limits of God. The implication of the second condition is that it is not permissible if they do not think so. The meaning of "thinking" here is the predominance of one of two possibilities. On this basis it becomes clear that the meaning of "fear" in the verse about khul' (divorce by compensation by the wife) is the meaning of "thinking," because the context of "limits" is one and the same. Abu Ubayda and others said: The meaning is "they are certain," so he took "thinking" here to mean "certainty." Their view is weak, on the ground that certainty is known only to God, since it is hidden from both of them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Whoever interprets "knowledge" here as "thinking" has erred in terms of the wording, and in meaning, because you do not say: "I know that Zayd will stand," but rather: "I know that Zayd is standing"; and because a person does not know what will happen tomorrow, but only thinks so. End of his words.

As for his statement that you do not say "I know that Zayd will stand," others have said it too. They said: The subjunctive "an" (that, with the subjunctive) that puts a verb into the subjunctive does not follow a verb of certainty, such as knowledge, certainty, or verification. It only follows "anna" (that, with the emphatic) when it is intensive. Abu Ali al-Farisi said in al-Idah: If you said "I know that Zayd will stand," putting the verb into the subjunctive with "an," it would not be permitted, because this is one of the positions of "anna," since it is something established and fixed, just as it is not good to say "I hope that you will stand." The apparent meaning of Abu Ali al-Farisi's words contradicts what Sibawayh stated, that it is permissible to say: "I do not know except that Zayd will stand," where "knew" governs "an." One of our companions said: The way to reconcile them is that "I know" may be used to mean definite knowledge, in which case "an" cannot follow it, as al-Farisi stated; and it may be used to mean strong thinking, in which case it can govern "an." The use of it to mean something other than definite knowledge is shown by His saying: ﴿If you know them to be believers﴾ [al-Mumtahanah 60:10]. Here "knowledge" means strong thinking, because certainty about their faith is not something that can be reached. And the poet's saying:

"I know with the knowledge of truth, not mere thinking, and the fear of God is the best provision for the Hereafter."

His saying "knowledge of truth" indicates that knowledge may be other than knowledge of truth. Likewise his saying "not mere thinking" indicates that one says "I know" while thinking. And one of the things that proves the soundness of what Sibawayh said, that "knew" may govern "an" when it is meant as something other than definite knowledge, is Jarir's saying:

"We are content with God, that people know that no human from among His creatures will come near us."

Here he used "an," the subjunctive particle, after "I know." End of his words. Jarir's verse and Sibawayh's permission establish that "knew" may take the subjunctive "an," so it is not a mistake, as al-Zamakhshari said, in terms of wording. As for his statement that a person does not know what will happen tomorrow and only thinks so, it is not as he said. Rather, a person knows many things that will happen tomorrow, and is certain of them rather than merely thinking so.

The "fa" in ﴿then it is not lawful﴾ is the response of the conditional. "For him," "after him," and "until" all three are connected to "lawful." The "lam" here means indicating the one to whom something is due; "min" means the starting point of a limit; and "hatta" (until) means causation. [The word "after him" is built on a fixed form] because it has been cut off from the genitive construction, since its full form is "after the third divorce." The word "spouse" was mentioned either as a preparatory element or as a restriction. The more evident of the two is the second. If it was mentioned as a preparatory element and not as a restriction, then its mention is by way of the common case, since people mostly marry free women, and the word "spouse" becomes as if it were dropped. In that case there is an indication that if a slave woman is irrevocably divorced and her master has intercourse with her, she becomes lawful to her first husband, since the word "spouse" is not a restriction. If it was mentioned as a restriction, which is the apparent meaning, then intercourse by her master does not make her lawful.

The "fa" in ﴿then there is no blame﴾ is the response of the conditional before it. "On both of them" is in the position of the predicate. As for the whole "blame" (junah): according to Sibawayh it is the subject, and according to the view of Abu al-Hasan it is the predicate of "la" (there is no). ﴿That they return to each other﴾ means: in returning to one another. The disagreement after the deletion of "fi" (in) regarding whether "an" with what follows it remains in the accusative position or the genitive position has been mentioned earlier by us. ﴿That they keep﴾ is in the position of the two objects, taking the place of both of them, because of the subject and predicate in this sentence according to Sibawayh's view. According to the view of Abu al-Hasan and Abu al-Abbas, the second object is omitted.

* *

﴿These are the limits of God, which He makes clear to a people who know﴾. "These" is the subject, "limits" is the predicate, and "makes clear" may be a second predicate; or it may be in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning "making clear." The governing element in that case is the demonstrative, and the one it describes is "limits of God," as in His saying: ﴿So those are their houses, empty﴾ [al-Naml 27:52]. "For a people" is connected to "makes clear." "These" refers to the rulings mentioned earlier. It is also read as "We make clear" with the "nun," by way of iltifat (a shift in grammatical person), and this reading is transmitted from Asim. The meaning of "making clear" here is explanation. He specified that those for whom it is made clear are people of knowledge as an honor for them, because they are the ones who benefit from what God has made clear through establishing evidence, whether by word or by deed. If "making clear" means creating clarity, then it is necessary to mention by name those for whom it is made clear, namely those who know, because the one whose heart has been sealed will not have clarity created in his heart.

These noble verses also contain God's prohibition to His servants against making His name common and frequently repeated on their tongues in their oaths, whether for righteousness, piety, or reform.
