This indicates that the emphasis of the prohibition against such oaths, when they are in opposition to righteousness, piety, and reform, applies all the more. This is because frequent swearing by God shows carelessness and disregard for the one sworn by, since oaths are liable to be broken by a person very often, and one who swears often is rarely seen without often breaking them.

Then He concluded this verse by stating that He is All-Hearing of their words and All-Knowing of their intentions. Since the prohibition concerning what we have mentioned was stated, God showed them leniency: what slips from their tongues as idle talk, without the intention of swearing, they will not be held to account for. They are held to account only for what the heart harbors and has committed to through a binding pledge. Then He concluded this verse with what indicates leniency toward the idle talk of oaths, namely the attributes of forgiveness and forbearance.

Since many rulings concerning women have been mentioned, He mentioned the ruling on ila' (a husband's oath to abstain from intercourse with his wife), which is swearing to refrain from having intercourse with them. He set a period for this, namely four months, which is the most a woman usually endures being apart from her husband. Then, after waiting this period and its completion, if he returns, then God is All-Forgiving: He does not hold him to account but overlooks that oath. If he resolves on divorce, he is to enact it.

When divorce was mentioned, (p-205) he digressed (istitrad) into mention of a number of its rulings. So He mentioned the waiting period of the divorced woman, which is three menstrual cycles (quru'). The mention of the qur' indicates that the divorced women intended are those who menstruate and are in a state of purity, who have not been divorced before consummation and are not pregnant. Other verses indicate that these specifications are intended. He also mentioned that it is not lawful for them to conceal what God has created in their wombs, which covers both blood and the child, because they used to conceal it for their own purposes. He linked this to faith in God, who is the Creator of what is in their wombs, and to faith in the Last Day, which is the time when reckoning, reward, and punishment take place for what a person does of forbidding what God has permitted, permitting what God has forbidden, and opposing Him in what He has legislated.

Then He mentioned that their husbands who divorced them have more right to take them back during the waiting period, and He made the condition of this greater right the intention of reconciling. This indicates that if one intends by taking her back to harm her, he has no greater right to take her back. Then He mentioned that wives have rights over the husband, just as husbands have rights over wives, so each of them is bound to fulfill what is owed. Then He mentioned that men have an additional degree of preference and rank over women, so the man's right is greater and the woman's obedience to him is more binding. He did not specify what this degree is, but it appears to be what results from much obedience, from taking care to honor him, and from esteeming him. This is because before it is the phrase "according to what is reasonable," meaning what people recognize in their customs: that a wife should be very affectionate toward her husband and comply with what he commands.

He concluded this verse with the attribute of might, which means dominance and power, and wisdom, which means placing a thing in the position that suits it. These are the two attributes that obligation requires.

Then He mentioned that the divorce in which the husband is entitled to take her back during that waiting period is two pronouncements: a first divorce followed by a second. After the two divorces have occurred, he may either take her back and keep her in good manner, or release her with kindness. Then right after this He mentioned the ruling on khul' (divorce initiated by the wife through compensation), because its legitimacy exists only before the third divorce; after it, khul' is not appropriate. For this reason it came between the divorce that allows taking back and the divorce that irrevocably severs the marriage bond. He also mentioned among its rulings that it is not lawful to take anything from the wife's property except on the condition that both of them fear that they will not keep the limits of God. Then He emphasized this by mentioning the fear that they will not keep the limits of God, making it a matter for both of them together. So if only one of them feared, khul' would not be permitted. This is the apparent meaning of the verse.

Then God forbade transgressing the limits of God and exceeding them, and informed that whoever transgresses them is a wrongdoer.

God said: ﴿Then if he divorces her﴾, meaning a third time. The meaning is: if he pronounces the release that was left undecided in His saying: ﴿Then either keep her in good manner or release her with kindness﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:229]. Then she is not lawful to him until after she marries another husband. If the second husband divorces her, and the first husband wishes to take her back, then he may do so; but he has made a condition for this reconciliation, namely that both of them think they will keep the limits of God. So whenever they do not think this, it is not permitted for them to reconcile. This is the apparent meaning of the wording.

Then He mentioned that He clarifies His verses for a people characterized by knowledge. As for one who does not know, he is blind and sees none of the verses and they are not made clear to him: ﴿Is then one who knows that what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth like one who is blind? Only those of understanding take heed﴾ [al-Ra'd 13:19].

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 231 (part 1 of 2):

﴿When you divorce women and they reach their term, then either retain them honourably or release them honourably. And do not retain them to harm them, so that you transgress. Whoever does that has wronged himself. And do not take the signs of Allah in jest. Remember Allah's favour upon you and what He has sent down to you of the Book and wisdom, by which He admonishes you. Fear Allah and know that Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾ ﴿When you divorce women and they reach their term, do not prevent them from marrying their husbands when they agree among themselves in an honourable manner. This is an admonition for whoever among you believes in Allah and the Last Day. That is more virtuous for you and purer. Allah knows, and you do not know.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 232] ﴿Mothers shall breastfeed their children for two complete years, for whoever wishes to complete the nursing. The father is responsible for their provision and clothing in an honourable manner. No soul is burdened beyond its capacity. A mother shall not be harmed through her child, nor a father through his child. The heir bears a like obligation. If both of them desire weaning by mutual consent and consultation, there is no blame upon them. And if you wish to seek a wet-nurse for your children, there is no blame upon you, provided you hand over what you agreed to give in an honourable manner. Fear Allah and know that Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 233]

*balagha* (to reach) – yablughu, bulugh: to arrive at a thing. The poet said:

> And a galloping steed like the spread of the wild ass, reaching the enemy's abodes, of great strength and firm pillars.

The *bulghah* (sufficiency) from it – and *al-balagh* is the original meaning – applies to the entire period and to its end. It is said of a person's lifespan: *ajal*, and of the death that ends it: *ajal*. Likewise the *ghayah* (goal) and the *amad* (term).

*al-'adal*: prevention. *'adala ayyimahu*: he prevented her from a husband, yet ('ya'dulu-ha), with the *dad* vowelled either with a kasra or a damma. Ibn Harmah said:

> Indeed the space of my hand is yours, so make me your prize, noble women who have been prevented from marriage.

It is said: *dajaj mu'dil* (a hen that is egg-bound) when its eggs are held back. Al-Khalil said this and said:

> We have restrained our women with spears, and among you there is no one who restrains for the sake of Allah's sanctity.

It is also said that its origin is narrowness: *'adalat al-mar'ah* (the woman was obstructed) when the child stuck in her womb; *'adalat al-shah* (the sheep was obstructed); *'adalat al-ardu bil-jaysh* (the land was constrained by the army, i.e. it became too narrow for them). Aws said:

> You see the land by our open space as sick, constrained by our army, a dense host.

*A'dala al-da'u al-atibba'*: the disease defeated the physicians, and *da'un 'udal*: a disease whose treatment is narrow and cannot be borne. Layla al-Akhyaliyyah said:

> From the disease that was in her, the grievous malady, a youth healed her when he shook the spear.

*A'dala al-amr*: the matter became severe and narrow, and every problematic matter is *mu'dil* (problematic) among the Arabs. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

> When the problematic matters confront me, I uncover their realities by reflection.

*al-Ruda'*: sucking the breast to drink milk. It is said: *radi'a yarda'u rad'an wa-rada'an wa-rada'atan*, and his mother *arda'at-hu* (nursed him). It is said of a miser: *radi'*, because of his extreme stinginess, he does not milk the sheep for fear that the sound of milking will be heard and he will be asked for milk, so he sucks the sheep's teat until no one notices him.

*al-Hawl*: the year. *Ahwala al-shay'*: it attained a year. The poet said:

> Of the modest-gazed women, if a small ant were to crawl upon the dust of her... the trace would have affected her.

It is pluralised as *ahwal*. *Al-hawl* also means stratagem. *Haala al-shay'*: it turned over. *Tahawwala*: it moved. *Rajul hawal*: a man who turns things over and manages much. It has already been mentioned that *hawl* can be a noun of place. You say: *Zayd hawlaka* and *hawaylaka* and *hawalaka* and *ahwalaka*, meaning: in what is near you of place.

*al-Kiswah*: clothing. From it: *kasa yaksu*. Its verb is transitive to two objects: you say *kasawtu Zaydan thawban* (I clothed Zayd with a garment). It has also come transitive to one object. The poet said:

> And I ride into the terror a mare whose face was covered by a spreading palm frond.

It has been construed with the sense of *ghatta* (to cover), so it takes one object. It is said: *kusiya al-rajul fa-huwa kasin* (the man was clothed, so he is clothed). The poet said:

> And that the women be bare if they are clothed.

And he said:

> Sit, for you are the one who feeds and clothes.

*Al-taklif*: imposition of obligation. Its origin is from *kalaf*, which is a dark mark on the face. *Fulan kalaf bi-kadha*: so-and-so is fond of such a thing, i.e. urged towards it. The poet said:

> By her is led a camel with a mark on both cheeks, tested, abundant in flesh, sturdy.

*Al-warith*: well known. From it: *waritha yarithu*, with the *ra'* vowelled with a kasra, and its analogy in the imperfect is a fatha. It is said: *arratha* and *warrratha*, and it is said *al-irth* as one says *alladahu fi waladihi*. The origin is the *waw*. *Al-fisal*: the verbal noun of *fasala fasalan wa-fisalan*, and the plural of *fasil*, which is the one weaned from his mother's breast. *Futila bayna al-khasmayn*: it was separated between the two litigants and they parted. *Fasalat al-'ir*: the caravan departed. The meaning: it left its place. *Fasilat al-rajul*: the nearest people to him. *Al-fasilah*: a piece of meat from the thigh. *Al-tafsil* in the sense of *al-tabyin* (clarification): ﴿signs made distinct﴾ [al-A'raf: 133]. The *tafsil* of each thing is its clarification, and it returns to the meaning of separating one ruling from another, so clarification is achieved through it. The core of this word is separation and distancing.

*Al-tashawur* in language: it is the extraction of an opinion, from their saying *shirtu al-'asal* [p. 206] *ashuruhu*, when I gathered it (honey). *Al-shawrah* and *al-mashwrah*, and with a damma on the 'ayn with the vowel transferred, like *al-ma'unah*. Hatim said:

> My fire has no screen whose palms cover it for one who seeks a light at night, but I display it.

Abu Zayd said: *shirtu al-dabbah* and *shawwartuha*: I made it run to extract its running. The root's core is manifestation, so that each of the consultants reveals what is in his heart to the other. From it: *al-shuwar*, which is household goods, because they are visible to the viewer. *Sharat al-rajul*: his appearance, because it shows in his dress and begins from his adornment. Some scholars, when mentioning this root, cited the sign (*isharah*) and said: "*al-ishārah* is bringing out what is in your self and making it manifest to the addressee by speech or otherwise." End of quote. If he meant that they are close in meaning, then it is correct; but if he meant that they share the same root, then it is not correct. This issue arose between the Amir Ibn al-Aghlab, the governor of Ifriqiyah, and some scholars of his land: how is it said, when they gesture to the crescent at its rising, and they form from *ishārah* the pattern *tafā'alnā*? Ibn al-Aghlab said: *tashāwarnā* (we consulted). That scholar said: *tashāyarnā*. They asked Qutaybah, the companion of al-Kisa'i, whom Ibn al-Aghlab had brought from Iraq to Ifriqiyah to teach his children, saying to him: "How do you form from *ishārah* the pattern *tafā'alnā*?" He said: *tashāyarnā*, and he recited an Arab verse as evidence for that, whose second half is:

> O how good, O glory of that *tashāyur*!

This shows the difference of the two roots: the one from the *ya'* roots, and the other from the *waw* roots.

﴿When you divorce women and they reach their term﴾: it was revealed concerning Thabit ibn Bashshar, also said to be Asnan al-Ansari, who divorced his wife until two or three days remained of her waiting period and she was about to become irrevocably separated. He took her back, then divorced her, then took her back, then divorced her, until seven months had passed, harming her. Divorce at that time was not restricted. The address in "*tallaqtum*" apparently is to the husbands. It was said that it is addressed to Thabit ibn Yasar. The singular was addressed with the plural form because of sharing the ruling. Whoever said that the address is to the guardians is far removed from the truth, because of His saying: ﴿then either retain them honourably or release them honourably﴾, and attributing divorce, retention and release to the guardians is very far-fetched. *Fa-balaghna*: they approached the completion of the waiting period and the term, which Allah appointed for the women undergoing 'iddah, of menstrual cycles (*iqrā'*), months, and the delivery of the child. He attributed the term to them because it touches them more closely; hence it is said: divorce belongs to men and the waiting period to women. "*Balaghna ajalahunna*" cannot be taken literally, because retention in that case would not be applicable to him, since she would no longer be a wife, her waiting period having ended, so he would have no authority over her.

﴿then either retain them honourably﴾: that is, take them back before the waiting period ends. *Al-ma'ruf* was interpreted as calling witnesses to the return. It was also said: by what is due to her as a right upon him. This is the view of some scholars, and it is the opinion of 'Umar, 'Ali, Abu Hurayrah, Ibn al-Musayyab, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu 'Ubayd, Abu Thawr, Yahya al-Qattan, and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi. They said: retaining honourably means that he provides for her; if he cannot, he divorces her. If he does not do so, he has exceeded the limit of what is honourable, and the ruler (*al-hakim*) divorces her on his behalf because of the harm that befalls her by staying with one who cannot support her. Ibn al-Musayyab even said: this is the Sunnah. In the *Sahih* of al-Bukhari: "The woman says: either you feed me, or you divorce me." 'Ata', al-Zuhri, al-Thawri, Abu Hanifah and his companions said: they are not separated, she must endure it, and the maintenance remains a debt upon him by the judgment of the judge. Those who hold that there is separation differed. Malik said: it is a revocable single pronouncement, because it is a separation after consummation in which the number of divorces is not completed, and it was not for a consideration, nor for harm to the husband; so it is revocable, like the harm of one who makes a vow of abstention (*al-mūlī*). Al-Shafi'i said: it is an irrevocable single pronouncement. It was also said: "with what is honourable," without seeking harm, by taking her back.

﴿or release them honourably﴾: that is, leave them until their waiting period ends and they become separated, without harm. He expressed release as letting go, because its outcome leads to it, since with the completion of the waiting period separation (*bayna*) occurs.

﴿And do not retain them to harm them, so that you transgress﴾: this is like an emphasis on His saying: ﴿then retain them honourably﴾. He forbade that retention be harmful. The wisdom of this prohibition is that the command in His saying ﴿then retain them honourably﴾ [p. 207] is fulfilled by retaining her once honourably; that is the implication of the command, and it does not cover all times. The prohibition came to cover all times, so as to include them, and to draw attention to what they used to do: returning, then divorcing, then returning, then divorcing, as a means of harm. He prohibited this shameful act specifically, to magnify this wicked sin which is the greatest harm to women, so that her waiting period in terms of months would be nine months. The meaning of "*dirar*" is harming, the verbal noun of *darra* (to harm): *darra darran* and *mudarrah*. It was interpreted as prolonging the waiting period, bad companionship, and restricting maintenance, and it is more general than all of these. So every retention for the sake of harm and aggression is forbidden. "*Dirar*" is in the accusative as an object of purpose (*maf'ul min ajlihi*). It was also said: it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*hal*), meaning: harming them, so that you wrong them. It was also said: so that you force them to ransom themselves. The *lam* is the *lam* of *kay* (purpose). If *dirar* is a circumstantial accusative, the *lam* is attached to it, or to "*la tumsikūhunna*" [do not retain them]. If it is an object of purpose, the *lam* is attached to it, and it is a cause for a cause. You say: "I disciplined my son for his benefit." It is not permissible for it to be attached to "*la tumsikūhunna*," because the verb does not govern two objects of purpose except by conjunction or by apposition (*badal*), and apposition is not possible here because of the difference in *i'rab* (case endings). Whoever makes the *lam* express consequence (*al-'aqibah*) permits it to be attached to "*la tumsikūhunna*," so that the verb is transitive to a cause and to a consequence, and these two are different.

His saying: ﴿Whoever does that has wronged himself﴾: "*dhālika*" is a reference to retaining in the manner of harm and transgression, and to wronging oneself by incurring punishment for oneself; or by depriving oneself of the benefits of religion, namely the reward gained through good companionship, and the benefits of this world, namely the desire to marry him being lost because of his notoriety for this shameful act.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 231 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And do not take the signs of Allah in mockery﴾. Abu al-Darda' said: "A man used to divorce in the Jahiliyyah and say, 'I divorced (her) while I was joking,' and he would free (a slave), marry, and say the same. So Allah revealed this verse, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited it and said: 'Whoever divorces, or frees (a slave), or marries, and claims that he was joking, then he is in earnest.'"

Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, be earnest in taking it up, in acting upon what it contains, and in observing it with due observance; otherwise you have taken it in mockery and play. It is said of one who is not earnest in a matter: "You are only playing and mocking." End of his words. A group of commentators (mufassirun, the exegetes) said the same meaning.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: The intended meaning is His signs revealed concerning commands and prohibitions. Al-Kalbi restricted them to His words: ﴿Then either retain them in kindness or release them with good treatment﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:229] and ﴿and do not hold them back﴾.

Al-Hasan said: This verse was revealed concerning the one who divorces while joking or jesting, or who takes back (his wife) in the same way.

What appears to be the case is that when Allah, the Exalted, revealed verses containing rulings on marriage, menstruation, ila' (oath of abstention), divorce, the waiting period, return (ruj'ah), khul' (divorce at the wife's request), and the avoidance of covenant violation, and these rulings concerned the relationship between a man and his wife, and they established rights for the wife over the husband and for the husband over her, while it was the custom of the Arabs to disregard women and to neglect their affairs, regarding them as too insignificant to have any matter or right against the husband, Allah revealed concerning them what He revealed of rulings and set limits that must not be transgressed. He informed them that whoever opposes these is a wrongdoer and a transgressor. He reinforced this by forbidding them from taking the signs of Allah, among which are these verses revealed concerning women, as mockery; rather, they must be accepted and received with earnestness and striving, because they are rulings of Allah. There is therefore no difference between them and the verses revealed about all the obligations between the servant and his Lord and between the servant and people.

"Huzuan" (هُزُوًا) is in the accusative as a second object of "tattakhidhu" (you take). One says: "hazi'a bihi huzuan" meaning he belittled him.

Hamza read "hazan" (هَزْءًا) with the letter zay sukun. When pausing, he eased the hamza according to his own method of tashil al-hamz (easing of the hamza). The scholars mentioned several ways of easing it in his reading, which are discussed in the science of recitations ('ilm al-qira'at). This is from the lightening of the pattern fu'ul, like 'unuq. The discussion of this has already preceded.

'Isa ibn 'Umar said: Every noun of three letters whose first letter is damma and whose second letter is (any) has two dialects: lightening and heavying.

He read "huzuwan" (هُزُوًا) with damma on the zay and replacing the hamza with waw, because of the damma. The majority of readers read "huzu'an" (هُزُؤًا) with two dammas and with the hamza. It was said: this is the original form. The discussion of this has already preceded in His words: ﴿Do you take us in mockery?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:67].

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 232 (part 1 of 2):

(p-209) ﴿And remember the favour of Allah upon you, and what He sent down to you of the Book and the wisdom, by which He admonishes you.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 231] This is a command conjoined in meaning to a previous command, namely: ﴿And do not take the signs of Allah in jest.﴾ The favour (ni'mah) here is not one in which the ta' marks a single instance (wahdah); rather, the verbal noun (masdar) is formed upon it, and it means the favours, both apparent and hidden, the greatest of which is what He bestowed through Islam and the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). The phrase ﴿what He sent down to you﴾ is conjoined to "favour," and it is a particularization after a generalization, since what was sent down is itself of the favour. We have already mentioned that this is called tajrid (specification after generalization), as in His saying: ﴿and Jibril and Mikail﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98] after mention of the angels, and the discussion of it has preceded. He used "upon you" to alert those commanded and to honour them; for in reality nothing was sent down except upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but since we are addressed by its rulings and charged with following it, it is as though it were sent down upon us. "The Book" is the Qur'an, and "the wisdom" is the Sunnah, by which the rulings not contained in the Qur'an are completed, and which clarifies its generalities (ijmal). This indicates that the Sunnah was sent down by Allah upon His Messenger (ﷺ), as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Nor does he speak from desire.﴾ [al-Najm: 3] ﴿It is but a revelation revealed.﴾ [al-Najm: 4] It has been said: in its apparent sense there is a refutation of one who claims that he judges by ijtihad, because what he judges by from the Sunnah descends to him from Allah, so there is no ijtihad. The mention of favours does not mean reciting them by the tongue; rather the intended remembrance is thankfulness for them, because a Muslim's mention of a favour is a cause of thanking for it, so the cause is expressed by the effect. If "favour" is taken to mean that which is bestowed, then "upon you" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), attached to an omitted element, i.e., "existing upon you," and this indicates that His favour extends over us, having risen high, enveloped us, and become like a canopy over us. If "favour" is taken to mean the act of bestowing, then "upon you" is attached to the word "favour," and in that case it is a verbal noun of "an'ama" without regular derivation, like nabat from anbata. The second "upon you" is attached to "anzala," and "min" (from) is in the position of a circumstantial clause, i.e., "being from the Book," and it is a circumstantial clause either of "ma anzala" or of the pronoun returning to the omitted relative pronoun, since its presumed form is: "and what was sent down upon you." Whoever attributes to "min" the meaning of explanation of genus permits this here, as if it were said: "and what He sent down to you, which is the Book and the Sunnah."

﴿He admonishes you thereby﴾ [al-Baqarah: 231]: He reminds you by it. The pronoun returns to "ma" in His saying "and what He sent down," and the clause is a circumstantial clause from the subject concealed in "anzala," and the governing element in it is "anzala." They permitted that "ma" in "and what He sent down" be a subject (mubtada'). "He admonishes you" is a clause in the position of the predicate, as if it were said: "and He who sent it down, Allah, from the Book and the wisdom, admonishes you by it." Its conjunction to "favour" is more apparent.

(And fear Allah): since Exalted is He had mentioned commands and prohibitions, and this was on account of women, who are the locus of neglect and lack of care, Allah commanded taqwa, which is that by whose attainment success is achieved in this world and the Hereafter. Then He conjoined to it what reinforces its pursuit, which is His saying: ﴿And know that Allah is Knower of all things.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 231] The meaning is: by seeking knowledge with constancy upon it, since they know this; and in this there is an alert that He knows your intentions in harm and transgression, so do not deceive yourselves. He repeated the name of Allah in His saying, "(And fear Allah)" and "(And know that Allah)," because it comes from two clauses; its repetition is more majestic and its reverberation in souls is greater.

﴿And when you divorce women and they reach their term, do not prevent them﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Zuhri and al-Dahhak said: it was revealed concerning everyone who prevented a woman of his from marrying another when he had divorced her. It was said: it was revealed concerning the paternal cousin of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, whose husband divorced her, her waiting period (iddah) ended, and he wished to take her back. Jabir came and said: "You divorced our paternal cousin, then you want to marry her?" The woman wanted her husband, so it was revealed. It was also said: it was revealed concerning Ma'qil ibn Yasar and his sister Jumal, and her husband Abu al-Walid 'Asim ibn 'Adi ibn al-'Ajlan, in which there occurred to them what occurred to Jabir in his account; al-Bukhari transmitted its meaning. According to the first cause, the addressees are the husbands; according to this cause, the guardians. There is remoteness in this, because attributing the divorce to them is a distant metaphor, namely that the guardians caused the divorce until it took place, so divorce was attributed to them in this sense. It is very unlikely that the address in "(And when you divorce)" is to the husbands while in "do not prevent them" it is to the guardians, because of the incongruity of the address and the discordance of condition and consequence. Thus the better view, and what the context of speech suits, is that the address in the condition and the consequence is to the husbands, because the address from the beginning of the verses is with the husbands, no mention of guardians has occurred, and because the verse before this is an address to the husbands concerning how to treat women before the end of the waiting period, and this verse is an address to them concerning how to treat them after the end of the waiting period. The divorcing husbands are thereby forbidden from prevention, since they used to do this out of oppression, coercion and jahiliyyah zeal, not letting them marry whomever they wished of husbands. On this view, the meaning of "that they marry their husbands" is: whomever they wish to marry, so they are called husbands in consideration of what they will become. On the view that the address is to the guardians, "their husbands" are the divorcers, and they are called husbands in consideration of what they were, even though after the end of the waiting period they are not husbands in reality. The forms of prevention by the husband are many: by denying the divorce, or claiming a return within the waiting period, or threatening whoever would marry her, or speaking ill of her to deter people from her; so they were forbidden from prevention absolutely, for any reason of those we have mentioned or others. Al-Zamakhshari said: the better view is that it is an address to people in general, i.e., there is no prevention among you, for if it exists among them while they are content, they are in the status of those who prevent. Ibn 'Atiyyah began his speech with something close to this meaning, saying: "And when you divorce women and they reach their term, do not prevent them" — the verse is an address to the believers who are the husbands, and among them are the guardians, because they are intended by "do not prevent them." End of his speech. This interpretation returns to the view that the address in "divorce" is to the husbands and in "do not prevent them" to the guardians, and we have already shown the incongruity in it.

﴿That they marry their husbands﴾: it is in the accusative position as a substitute for the pronoun, a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal), or its original is "from that they marry," and "yankihna" is the imperfect of the triliteral nakaha. In it is the indication that a woman may marry without a guardian, for if he had a right, he would not have been forbidden from it; the prohibition is not used as evidence for establishing the right. Its apparent meaning is the contract. The apparent sense of the verse, if the address in "do not prevent them" is to the guardians, is the prohibition of prevention absolutely, so it is realized by preventing her from a single suitor. Malik said: if he prevents her from one or two suitors, he is not thereby a preventer. Abu Hanifa said: a previously married woman may contract her own marriage and receive the dower, and the guardian has no objection over her; this is also the view of Zufar. If the husband is not a suitable match (kufu'), it is permitted, and the guardians may separate them. Those who permit marriage without a guardian: Ibn Sirin, al-Sha'bi, al-Zuhri, and Qatada. Abu Yusuf said: if the guardian consents to her marriage it is permitted, otherwise not, except if he is a suitable match, in which case the judge permits it if the guardian refuses to consent; this is the view of Muhammad. Something other than this is transmitted from Abu Yusuf. Al-Awza'i said: if she entrusts her affair to a man, and the husband is a suitable match, the marriage is permitted and the guardian has no right to separate them. Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Shubrumah, al-Thawri, and al-Hasan ibn Salih said: marriage is not permitted except with a guardian; this is the school of al-Shafi'i. Al-Layth said: she may marry herself without a guardian. Ibn al-Qasim said, from Malik: if she is a freedwoman, or poor, or of lowly status, there is no harm in her appointing a man to marry her, and the guardians may annul that before consummation; there is a difference of opinion about it after consummation. If she is wealthy, then none may marry her except the guardian or the ruler. The proofs of these schools are in the books of jurisprudence.

﴿When they mutually agree﴾: the pronoun returns to the addressees and the women, and the masculine was predominant, so the pronoun came with the waw. Whoever makes a mention of the guardians in the verse says: it may return to the guardians and the husbands. The governing element of "idha" is "yankihna."

﴿Among themselves in a fair manner﴾: the pronoun in "bayinahum" is a figurative adverbial location whose governing element is ﴿tarada'u﴾ (mutually agreed). (In a fair manner): its apparent sense is that it is attached to "tarada'u," and it has been explained as what is good in religion and honour in the conditions; it was said: the customary dower (mahr al-mithl); it was said: the dower and witnessing. It is permissible that "in a fair manner" be attached to "yankihna," not to "tarada'u," and it is not believed that this is a separation between the governing element and the governed that is not permitted; rather it is an eloquent separation, because it is a separation by a complement of the verb, namely His saying ﴿when they mutually agree﴾; so "idha" is governed by His saying "an yankihna," and "(in a fair manner)" is attached to it; both are complements of the verb.

﴿That is admonished by it whoever among you believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾: "that" addresses the Prophet (ﷺ); it was said: it addresses every hearer; then he returned to the address of the group, saying "among you." It was said: "dhalika" has the meaning of "dhalikum," and by it he pointed to what was mentioned in the verse of the prohibition of prevention. "Dhalika" is for distance and takes the place of the demonstrative for nearness, "hadha," even though the ruling mentioned in the verse is near; this is because of the majesty of the one indicating the thing. The meaning of "is admonished by it" is: is reminded by it and warned. "Among you" is attached to "kana," or to an omitted element in the position of a circumstantial clause from the concealed pronoun in "yu'minu." The belief in Allah is mentioned because He, exalted is He, is the one who imposes obligations on His servants, forbidding them and commanding them. "The Last Day" is mentioned because it is that by which the warning is realized, and the fruit of disobeying the prohibition is reaped in it. He singled out the believers because only the believer benefits from admonition, since the light of faith guides him to acceptance: ﴿Only those who hear respond﴾ [al-An'am: 36], and the soundness of his intellect removes from him the intrusion of desire: ﴿Only those of understanding are reminded﴾ [al-Ra'd: 19].

﴿That is purer for you and more pure﴾: that is, enabling marriage is purer for the one who is about to prevent, because of the reward he has in obeying Allah's command, and more pure for the two spouses, because of the doubt that is feared for them if they are prevented from marriage; and that is due to the attachments between women and men.

Allah knows, and you do not know (﴿وَاللَّهُ يَعْلَمُ وَأَنتُمْ لَا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾). That is: He knows what the hearts of the spouses harbor of inclination of each toward the other; for this reason the Exalted prohibited ʿadl (preventing them from remarrying). Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said this is its meaning.

Or: He knows what it contains of gaining reward and removing punishment.

Or: He knows the inner realities of affairs and their outcomes, while you do not know that; you only know what is apparent.

Or: He knows who acts in accordance with these obligations and who does not act by them. The purpose of this is to affirm the promise and the warning.

It has been said: this verse includes six kinds of eloquence and rhetorical beauty from the science of bayan (rhetoric):

First: ṭibāq (antithesis), which is ṭalāq (divorce) and imsāk (retention), for they are opposites. Tasrīḥ (release) is a second antithesis, because it is the opposite of imsāk (retention). Also knowledge and non-knowledge, for non-knowledge is ignorance (jahl).

Second: muqābalah (contrast) in: ﴿فَأَمْسِكُوهُنَّ بِمَعْرُوفٍ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 231] and ﴿وَلَا تُمْسِكُوهُنَّ ضِرَارًا﴾ [al-Baqarah: 231]. He contrasted ma‘rūf (good) with ḍirār (harm), and ḍirār is indefinite (nakirah), so this is a semantic contrast (muqābalah maʿnawiyyah).

Third: takrār (repetition) in: ﴿فَبَلَغْنَ أَجَلَهُنَّ﴾. He repeated the expression to change the two meanings, and this is the peak of eloquence, since the difference in meaning between the two indicates the difference between the two arrivals at the term (balaghayn).

Fourth: iltifāt (shift of address) in: ﴿وَإِذَا طَلَّقْتُمُ النِّسَاءَ فَبَلَغْنَ أَجَلَهُنَّ﴾, then he turned to the guardians (awliyāʾ) and said: ﴿فَلَا تَعْضُلُوهُنَّ﴾. And in the verse, in His saying "dhālika" (this), if it is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), then he turned to the plural in His saying "minkum" (among you).

Fifth: taqdīm and taʾkhīr (inversion of word order). The intended sense: that they (the women) marry their husbands (azwājahunna) in a proper manner (bil-maʿrūf) if they agree mutually.

Sixth: addressing one person with the plural form, because it is mentioned in the occasions of revelation (asbāb al-nuzūl) that it was revealed concerning Maʿqil ibn Yasar, or concerning the sister of Jabir, and it has been said "his daughter" (ibnatuhu).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 233 (part 1 of 5):

﴿And the mothers shall breastfeed their children for two full years﴾. The connection (munasabah) of this verse to what precedes it is that when God Most High mentioned a group of rulings concerning marriage, divorce, the waiting period ('iddah), reconciliation (raj'ah), and preventing (ʿadl) women from remarrying, He began to mention the rulings that follow from marriage, namely what was legislated concerning breastfeeding and its duration, and the rulings on clothing and maintenance. These are what the discussion in this verse concerns, God willing.

﴿The mothers﴾: this is the plural of wālidah, with the feminine ending. The analogical form would have been wālid, but wālid has been applied to the father as well. Therefore the phrase "the mothers" (al-wālidāt) is used for both him and her. The feminine ta' in wālidah serves to distinguish the feminine from the masculine in linguistic usage. It seems that in this usage it is taken into account that they are both the origins of the child, so the dual wālidān ("the two parents") is applied to them. The apparent meaning of the word "the mothers" (al-wālidāt) is general, so it includes wives and divorced women. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Suddi, and others said: it refers to divorced women. God made this a limit (ḥadd) for when the spouses disagree about the duration of breastfeeding. Whoever of them calls for completing the two years, that is his or her right. He (al-Ṭabarī) preferred this view because His saying "the mothers" comes right after the verse of divorce, so it was part of its completion. This is legislated for them because divorce involves hostility, so it may lead to harming the child, since harming him is harming his father. And because if she desires to marry another man, the child is neglected. It was also said: it refers to wives only, because a divorced woman does not deserve clothing but only payment. ﴿Shall breastfeed their children﴾: its form is a report (khabar), and it may be meant as a report, i.e., according to God's ruling which He legislated, so the mothers have the most right to breastfeed their children, whether they are under the husband's protection or not, since breastfeeding is one of the characteristics of motherhood, not of marriage. It may also be meant as a command, like His saying: ﴿And divorced women shall wait﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228], but it is a recommendation (nadb), not an obligation (ījāb), since if it were obligatory she would not deserve payment. God Most High said: ﴿And if you disagree, then another woman shall breastfeed for him﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 6]. So the obligation of breastfeeding rests on the father, not the mother, and he must hire a wet-nurse (ẓi'r) for him, unless the mother volunteers to breastfeed him. She is encouraged to do so but is not compelled to. If the child does not accept her breast, or no wet-nurse is available, and the father is unable to hire one, then it becomes obligatory upon her to breastfeed him. Accordingly, the command is for obligation in the case of some mothers. The madhhab (school of law) of al-Shafi'i is that breastfeeding is obligatory only upon the father or the grandfather, however far up. The madhhab of Malik is that it is a right upon the wife, since it is like a condition, unless she is noble and of distinguished lineage, in which case her custom is not to breastfeed. There is also a difference of opinion from him on some matters of breastfeeding.

﴿Two full years﴾: the two years are described as "full" to block the figurative usage (majāz) that the phrase "two years" may admit, since one says: "I stayed with so-and-so for two years," even if he did not complete them. This is an emphatic descriptor, like His saying: ﴿ten complete﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196]. God made this period a limit when the spouses disagree about the duration of breastfeeding. Whoever of them calls for completing the two years, that is his or her right. The apparent meaning of His saying "their children" is general, so the two years apply to every child, and this is the view of the majority (al-jumhūr). It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: this refers to a child who remains in the womb for six months; if he remains seven months, his breastfeeding is twenty-three months, or if eight, twenty-two, or if nine, twenty-one. It seems this view was based on God's saying: ﴿His carrying and weaning are thirty months﴾ [al-Aḥqāf: 15], because that is a general ruling on the human being. In His saying "shall breastfeed" there is an indication that the mother has the most right to breastfeeding the child. Some exegetes have discussed here matters that have no connection with the wording of the Qur'an, among them: the period of breastfeeding that establishes prohibition (taḥrīm), the amount of breastfeeding that creates the prohibition, custody (ḥaḍānah), who has the most right to it after the mother, what the ruling is when the mother remarries, and whether a non-Muslim woman (dhimmiyyah) has a right to breastfeed. They extended the discussion by citing the differences of opinion and the evidence, and the subject of this belongs to the science of jurisprudence (fiqh).

﴿For whoever wishes to complete the breastfeeding﴾: this indicates that breastfeeding within the two years is not a limit that cannot be exceeded; rather, that is for whoever wishes to complete it. As for whoever does not wish that, he may wean the child before reaching that, provided there is no harm to the child. It is narrated from Qatadah that he said: the obligation of breastfeeding was imposed upon the mothers, then it was made easy and lightened, and so this was revealed: ﴿for whoever wishes to complete the breastfeeding﴾. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: this view is contradictory (mutadāʿin). Al-Rāghib said: in His saying ﴿two full years for whoever wishes to complete the breastfeeding﴾ there is an indication that it is not permitted to exceed that, and that there is no ruling for breastfeeding after the two years, and a reinforcement of the prohibition of breastfeeding after the two years, and the breastfeeding that establishes prohibition (raḍāʿah min al-majāʿah). What confirms this is that every ruling in the Sharia that is tied to a specific number, where it is permissible to fall short of it at one end, is not permissible to exceed it at the other end, such as the option of three (days) (khiyār al-thalāth), the number of stones for istinjāʾ (cleansing after relieving oneself), and wiping over the leather socks for one day and night or three days. Since breastfeeding may be lessened at one end, which is deficiency, it is not permissible to exceed it. The end of his words. Another said: mentioning the two years is not a binding time limit; rather, it is to end disputes between the two parents. Most jurists hold that it is permissible to increase or decrease it if they both see that.

The lām in ﴿li-man﴾ is said to be connected to ﴿yurḍiʿna﴾, as you say: "So-and-so breastfed so-and-so's child." In this case the lām is for causation (taʿlīl), i.e., for the sake of, so "man" refers to the father, as if it were said: for the sake of whoever among the fathers wishes to complete the breastfeeding. It was also said: the lām is for specification (tabyīn), so it is connected to an omitted element, as in their saying "saqyan laka" (a blessing: "watering for you") and in His saying: ﴿hayta laka﴾ [Yūsuf: 23]. The lām then specifies the one for whom the watering is invoked and the one addressed. This is because when He placed first His saying ﴿shall breastfeed their children for two full years﴾, He made clear that this ruling is for whoever among the mothers wishes to complete the breastfeeding, so "man" refers to the mother, as if it were said: ﴿for whoever among the mothers wishes to complete the breastfeeding﴾. Or "man" may refer to both the mothers and the one to whom the child belongs. All of this the wording allows. The majority read ﴿an yutimma al-raḍāʿah﴾ (p-213) with yā' (from atamma, "to complete") and the accusative for al-raḍāʿah. Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan, Ḥumayd, Ibn Muḥayṣin, and Abū Rajāʾ read ﴿tatimma﴾ with tā' (from tamma) and the nominative for al-raḍāʿah. Abū Ḥanīfah, Ibn Abī ʿAblah, and al-Jārūd ibn Abī Sabrah read it the same way, except that they vocalized the rāʾ of al-raḍāʿah with kasrah, and this is a dialect, like al-ḥaḍārah and al-ḥiḍārah. The Basrans say the rāʾ is vocalized with fatḥah together with the hāʾ, and with kasrah without the hāʾ, while the Kufans reverse this. It is narrated from Mujāhid that he read "al-ruḍʿah" on the pattern of "al-qaṣʿah." It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that he read ﴿an yukmila al-raḍāʿah﴾ with a damma on the yā'. It was also read ﴿an yutimm﴾ with a raf' on the mīm, and the grammarians attributed it to Mujāhid. Raising the verb after "an" has occurred in Arabic speech in poetry. Al-Farrāʾ, may God have mercy on him, recited:

"an tahbiṭīna bilādu qawmin yartaʿūna min al-ṭilāḥ"
(that you descend into the lands of a people who graze on the acacia)

Another said:

"an tuqriʾāni ʿalā Asmāʾa wayḥakumā minnī al-salāma wa-an lā tublighā aḥadā"
(that you two recite to Asma'—woe to you both—my greeting, and that you do not convey it to anyone)

According to the Basrans, this "an" is the particle that puts the present verb into the subjunctive, and its government is left out by analogy with "mā," its sister, since each of them is verbal-nominal (maṣdariyyah). As for the Kufans, it is for them the light form of the heavy "anna" (mukhaffafah min al-thaqīlah), and its occurring in the position of the subjunctive particle is rare, just as the subjunctive particle occurring in the position of the light form is rare in Jarīr's saying:

"naraḍā ʿani Allāhi anna al-nāsa qad ʿalimū ∗∗∗ an lā yudāniyanā min khalqihi bashar"
(We are content with God, since people know that no human being among His creatures comes near us)

What appears is that the retention of the nūn in the present verb with "anna" is restricted to poetic necessity, and "anna" is not preserved as non-governing except in this poetry. The reading attributed to Mujāhid, and whatever is of this kind, does not provide a basis for building a rule.

﴿And upon the one to whom the child belongs is their provision and clothing according to what is customary﴾: "al-mawlūd" is a generic noun, and the lām in it is a relative (mawṣūlah) joined to the passive participle and "al," like "man." The pronoun returns to the wording, singular and masculine, and it is permissible for it to return to the meaning according to what you intend of the meaning, dual, plural, or feminine. Here the pronoun returned to the wording, so it came as "lahu." It is permissible in Arabic for it to return to the meaning, so it would be "lahum," though this was not read that way. The passive element (the object not named as subject) is the prepositional phrase, and the agent has been omitted, which is "the mothers," and the direct object, which is "the children," and the prepositional phrase has been put in the place of the agent. This is according to the Basran school, namely that the prepositional phrase can be put in the place of the agent when the agent is omitted, as in "murra bi-Zaydin" (Zayd was passed by). The Kufans held that this is not permitted except in cases where the preposition is extra (zā'idah), as in "mā ḍuriba min aḥadin" (no one was struck), but if the preposition is not extra, this is not permitted in their view, and by agreement among them the noun in the genitive cannot be in the place of nominative. After this agreement they differed about what was put in the place of the agent. Al-Farrāʾ held that the preposition alone is in the place of nominative, just as "yaqūm" in "Zayd yaqūm" (Zayd stands) is in the nominative place. Al-Kisāʾī and Hishām held that the object of the verb is an unspecified hidden pronoun within the verb, and its indefiniteness is because it may refer to what the verb indicates of a verbal noun, a time adverb, or a place adverb, and there is no evidence that it refers to some of these rather than others. Some held that the subject of the verb is a pronoun referring back to the verbal noun, the intended meaning being "a journey, it" (sayr huwa), meaning "the journey of the journey," and the pronoun refers to the verbal noun understood from the verb. This is permissible according to some Basrans, and prohibited according to the verifying Basrans. The examination of the evidence for these positions, to confirm or refute them, is discussed in the science of grammar (naḥw). Some of our elders erred when he mentioned in his book called (al-Sharḥ al-Kabīr li-Jumal al-Zajjājī) that the grammarians agreed on the permissibility of putting the genitive in the place of the agent, except al-Suhaylī, who forbade it. This is not as he said, since we have mentioned the disagreement of al-Farrāʾ, al-Kisāʾī, and Hishām, and the detail regarding the genitive. Among those who followed al-Suhaylī in his view was his student Abū ʿAlī al-Zaydī, the commentator on (al-Jumal). "Al-mawlūd lahu" is the father, the one who begets. He did not use the word "al-wālid" (the parent) nor the word "al-ab" (the father), but used the expression "al-mawlūd lahu" (the one to whom the child belongs), because of what this contains of informing the father about what God has granted and given him, since the lām in "lahu" has a meaning close to possession, as in His saying: ﴿And He made for you from your spouses children and grandchildren﴾ [al-Naḥl: 72]. This is one of the meanings we mentioned for the lām at the beginning of al-Fātiḥah. For this reason the father disposes of his child as he chooses, and you find the child in most cases obedient to his father, complying with what he commands and carrying out what he enjoins. The children, in reality, belong to the fathers, and they are attributed to them, not to their mothers, as al-Maʾmūn ibn al-Rashīd recited, whose mother was a female slave, a cook named Marājil, he said:

"fa-innamā ummahātu al-nāsi awʿiyatun ∗∗∗ mustawdaʿātun wa-lil-abnāʾi ābāʾu"
(Indeed, people's mothers are but vessels, deposited (for a time), while for children there are fathers.)

Since the word "al-mawlud" (the one born to, i.e. the child's father) conveys the sense of a gift and a kind of ownership, He used it rather than the words "al-walad" (the child) and "al-ab" (the father). Where this meaning is not intended, He used "al-walid" (the parent) and "al-ab," as in His saying: ﴿No parent will avail anything for his child﴾ [Luqman: 33], and His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon them concerning their fathers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 55]. There is another subtle point in His saying: ﴿and upon the one to whom the child is born﴾. It is that, since he is charged with the nursing mother's needs for their child, in provision and clothing, it is fitting that he be consoled that this child is his child, not his mother's, and that you are the one who benefits from him in support and in increasing the clan, and that you have the right to his obedience, just as he was a burden on you, because of him, in the cost of provision and clothing for his nurse. Ibn Atiyyah interpreted "al-rizq" (provision) here as adequate food, making it a name for what is provided, like "al-tahn" (the grinding) and "al-ra'y" (the pasturing). Al-Zamakhshari said: "So it was incumbent upon them to provide for them and clothe them," so he explained "al-rizq" by "an" and the verb, which together form a verbal noun (masdar). "Al-rizq" can carry both meanings: the thing provided, or the verbal noun. We have mentioned that "rizqan" with a kasra on the ra' is reported as a masdar, like "rizqan" with a fatha, earlier. Abu Ali al-Farisi made it a masdar in His saying: ﴿who possesses no provision for them from the heavens or the earth, not at all﴾ [al-Nahl: 73]. Ibn al-Tarawah refuted this against him, and this will come in its place, God willing. The meaning of "bil-ma'ruf" (in a fair and customary manner) is what custom has established of maintenance and clothing for such a person, such that there is neither excess nor shortfall. This was said by al-Dahhak. Ibn Atiyyah said: "'Bil-ma'ruf' comprises the quality of the amount in food, the goodness of the demand for it, and the goodness of the demand from the woman." End of his words. It does not indicate the goodness of the demand from the woman, because the verse is only about what is obligatory upon the one to whom the child is born of provision and clothing. So "bil-ma'ruf" is connected to "rizquhunna" or to "kiswatuhunna" by the principle of operation (i'mal), either to the first or to the second, if both are masdars. If they are meant as the thing provided and the matter, then an omitted noun must be supplied, the estimate being "delivery" or "payment," or something similar that makes the meaning correct, and "bil-ma'ruf" would be in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal) for them, so it is connected to a deleted element. It was said that the governing element in it is the sense of settledness in "ala." Talhah recited ﴿wa-kiswatuhunna﴾ with a damma on the kaf, and both are dialectal forms: it is said "kuswatan" and "kiswatan," with damma and kasra on the kaf.

* *

﴿No soul is burdened except according to its capacity﴾. "Al-taklif" (imposing a burden) is the imposition of what has an effect on hardship, from "kalifa al-wajh" (the face was marked) and "kalifa al-'ishq" (he was afflicted by love), because of the effect of each. "Wus'aha" means its capacity, which is what it can bear. God has explained this in His saying: ﴿Let him who has abundance spend from his abundance﴾ [al-Talaq: 7], and so on. The apparent generality of His saying ﴿No soul is burdened except according to its capacity﴾ covers all obligations. It has been said: the meaning of the verse is that the father of the child is not burdened with spending on him and on his mother except by what his ability can bear. It has also been said: the meaning is that the woman is not burdened to endure a shortfall in the wage, and the husband is not burdened with what is extravagance, but moderation is observed. The reading of the majority is ﴿lā tukallafu nafsun﴾ in the passive voice, with God as the agent, which is omitted because it is known. Abu Rajaa' recited "lā takallafu" with a fatha on the ta', meaning "no soul should take upon itself," and "nafsun" is raised as the subject. One of the two tas is elided, according to the disagreement between us and some of the Kufans. "Takallafa" is on the pattern "tafa''ala," the reflexive (muta'wa'a) of "fa''ala," like "kasartuhu fa-takassara" (I broke it and it broke). Reflexivity is one of the meanings for which the pattern "tafa''ala" comes. Abu al-Ashhab reported from Abu Rajaa' that he recited "lā nukallifu nafsan" with a nun, attributing the verb to God's pronoun, and "nafsan" in the accusative is the object.

﴿Neither a mother should be harmed because of her child, nor a father because of his child.﴾ Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub, and Aban on the authority of 'Asim recited "lā tuḍārru" with a *raf'* (nominative vowel), meaning the first *rā'* is pronounced with a *ḍamma* and is doubled. This reading fits what precedes it, "﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾," because both clauses share the *raf'*, even though their meanings differ. The first clause is declarative in both form and meaning, whereas this one is declarative in form but prohibitive in meaning. (p-215)

The rest of the seven readers recited "lā tuḍārra" with a *fatḥa* on the *rā'*, treating it as a prohibition (*nahy*). The final *rā'* is therefore given a *sukūn* for the apocopate (*jazm*), and the first *rā'* is given a *sukūn* for assimilation (*idghām*). Two consonants with *sukūn* then meet, so the final one is vocalized with a *fatḥa* to harmonize with the *alif* before the *rā'*, since the *alif* and the *fatḥa* are homogeneous. Do you not see that when they apocopated "asḥāran" (a name of a plant), when it was used as a proper name, they dropped the final *rā'* and gave a *fatḥa* to the *rā'* with *sukūn* that had been assimilated into the dropped *rā'*, because of the *alif* before it? They did not vocalize it with a *kasra*, which is the original rule for two consonants meeting. They took the *alif* into account and used a *fatḥa*, departing from the *kasra* even though it is the original form.

It was also recited as "lā yuḍārri" with a *kasra* on the doubled *rā'*, as a prohibition. Abu Ja'far al-Saffar recited "lā tuḍārr" with *sukūn* and doubling, applying the pause form to continuous speech. It is narrated from him: "lā tuḍār" with *sukūn* on the *rā'* and without doubling, and this is the reading of al-A'raj, from *ḍāra yaḍīru*. It is in the nominative, and the continuous speech has been treated as a pause.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "He stole the *ḍamma* (made it faint), so the narrator thought it was a *sukūn*." End of his words. This is in keeping with his habit of faulting and mistaking the readers, and we do not go that way. Some people justified this reading by saying: "He dropped the second *rā'* to avoid doubling a repeated letter, which is the *rā'*. It is permissible to bring together two consonants with *sukūn*, either because he treated the continuous speech as a pause, or because the length of the *alif* functions as a vowel." End of his words.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "lā tuḍārir," with the assimilation undone, the first *rā'* with a *kasra* and the second with *sukūn*. Ibn Mas'ud recited "lā tuḍārir," also with the assimilation undone, the first *rā'* with a *fatḥa* and the second with *sukūn*. It is said that Aban related it on the authority of 'Asim.

Undoing the assimilation in examples like these two is the dialect of the Hijaz. As for the one who recited with a doubled *rā'*, whether nominative, *fatḥa* or *kasra*, it is possible that the verb is active (*mabnī lil-fā'il*), and it is possible that it is passive (*mabnī lil-maf'ūl*), as came in the reading of Ibn 'Abbas and in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud. The *raf'* of "wālidatun" and "mawlūdun" would be as subject (*fā'iliyya*) if the verb is taken as active, and as object (*maf'ūliyya*) if the verb is taken as passive.

If we take the verb as active, the object is omitted, and its estimated form is: "A mother should not harm her husband by demanding of him what he cannot afford of provision and clothing and other kinds of harm. And a father (who is) the one to whom the child belongs should not harm his wife by withholding from her what is due to her of provision and clothing, by taking her child while she prefers to nurse him, and by other kinds of harm." The *bā'* in "bi-waladihā" and in "bi-waladihi" is the *bā'* of cause (*bā' al-sabab*).

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also permissible that 'yuḍārr' means 'taḍurr' (harms), and that the *bā'* belongs to it: 'a mother should not harm her child with it,' so she should not neglect its nourishment and care, nor fail in what is due to it, nor hand it over to the father after she has become attached to it, and the father should not harm it by snatching it from her hand, or fall short in his duty to her, so that she in turn falls short in her duty to the child." End of his words.

By his saying "that the *bā'* belongs to it," he means that it is connected to "tuḍārr," and "ḍārra" means "aḍarra" (to harm), with *fā'ala* used in the sense of *af'ala*, as in "bā'adtuhu" and "abʿadtuhu" (I put him far away) and "ḍā'afto" and "ḍā'ftuhu" (I multiplied). The use of *fā'ala* in the sense of *af'ala* is one of the meanings for which *fā'ala* is coined. You say: "Hunger harmed (aḍarra) so-and-so," so the prepositional phrase is the object in meaning, and the object is not omitted. This differs from the first interpretation, in which the *bā'* indicates cause, so the object is omitted as we estimated.

It is said that the harm may refer back to the infant, meaning: neither of them should harm the infant, so that his nursing is not abandoned until he dies, and the father should not refrain from providing for him, nor snatch him from his mother, so as to harm the infant. In this case the *bā'* is extra, and the meaning is: "A mother should not harm her child, and a father should not harm his child." End of his words. So "ḍārra" would mean "ḍarra" (to harm), and this is one of the instances in which *fā'ala* agrees with the bare verb "ḍarra," as in their saying "jāwaztu al-shay'a wa-juztuhu" (I passed the thing and traversed it) and "wā'adtuhu wa-wa'adtuhu" (I promised him), and this is one of the meanings for which *fā'ala* came.

The apparent meaning is that the *bā'* is of cause. This is shown by the reading of those who recited "lā tuḍārir" with two *rā'*s, the first with a *fatḥa*, which is the reading of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. The interpretation of those who read the assimilated form is that the verb is passive. When the verb is passive, the *bā'* must be of cause, and Zamakhshari's interpretation that "ḍārra bihi" means "aḍarra bihi" is excluded, as is the other interpretation that "ḍārra bihi" means "ḍarrahu" with the *bā'* extra, because the extra *bā'* is not regular with the object. Moreover, both interpretations take *fā'ala* out of its common meaning, which is that the two nouns are partners in the subjecthood and objecthood, though each of them is in the nominative while the other is in the accusative.

These four clauses contain, in meaning and in the clarity of their wording, a rhetorical excellence (*balāgha*) that is not hidden from anyone who has studied the science of eloquence (*'ilm al-bayān*). The first clause is presented in the form of a subject and predicate, and its predicate is a verb, because breastfeeding is something that is constantly renewed. Then the children are attributed to the mothers, as a reminder of their compassion for the children and as an incitement and encouragement to nurse. The nursing is restricted to a period, and this is for the one who wishes to complete it. The word "al-wālidāt" (the mothers) comes in a general form, and "al-awlād" (the children) is attributed to a pronoun of generality so that it generalizes. A plural of paucity, when it takes the definite article or is attributed to a general noun, becomes general. I have discussed some of this in my book called (*al-Tamkīl fī Sharḥ al-Tashīl*, "The Completion in Explaining the Facilitation").

The second clause is also presented in the form of a subject and predicate, and its predicate is a prepositional phrase with "ʿalā" (upon), which indicates figurative elevation and obligation. Thus the content of the clause is emphasized, because it is a person's habit to withhold the property in his hand and to neglect what is obligatory upon him of rights. So this is emphasized, and the predicate is placed first to show concern for it. Provision comes before clothing because it is the more important for the continuation of life, and it recurs every day.

The third clause is presented in the form of a verb and its subject. Its subject comes in indefinite form because it is in the context of negation, so it is general, and it encompasses first what the verse was sent for, namely the ruling on mothers regarding nursing, and the ruling on the father regarding the provision and clothing that belong to the mothers.

The fourth clause is like the third, because it is in the context of negation, so it is also general. It is like an explanation of the clause before it, because when a soul is not burdened beyond its capacity, no harm befalls either the mother or the father. For this reason it comes without being conjoined to the clause before it, since conjunction is not appropriate. This differs from the first two clauses, for each of them is distinct from the other and specified with a ruling not found in the other. Since burdening a soul beyond its capacity and the harming of one spouse by the other are things that recur at every moment, the two clauses come as verbal sentences, into which the negative particle "lā" is introduced, which is generally used for the future. In the reading of the one who apocopated, "﴿lā tuḍārra﴾," the prohibitive particle is introduced, which makes the imperfect verb refer to the future. The verse draws attention to the locus of compassion by saying "bi-waladihā" (because of her child), attributing the child to her, and "bi-waladihi" (because of his child), attributing the child to him. This is to solicit tenderness and compassion.

It mentions first the non-harming of the mother before the non-harming of the father, in consideration of the first two clauses, in which the ruling on the mothers was begun. Its repetition of the ruling on the father in "﴿lā tuḍārr﴾" indicates that when a feminine and a masculine noun are conjoined, the verb preceding them agrees with the one that comes first. You say: "Zayd and Hind stood up," and "Hind and Zayd stood up" (with feminine verb), and "Zayd and Hind stand up," and "Hind and Zayd stand up." This is unless the feminine noun is metaphorical and has no feminine marker, in which case it is good not to add the marker, as in His saying, exalted is He: "﴿and the sun and the moon are joined together﴾" [al-Qiyama 75:9].

"And upon the heir is the like of that." This is coordinated with His saying, "and upon the one to whom the child belongs." The two sentences before this are like an explanation of His saying "in a fair manner," and they are placed as a parenthetical clause between the two coordinated items. Yahya ibn Ya'mur read, "wa-'ala al-warathati mithlu dhalika" with the plural. The apparent meaning of "al-warith" is the heir of the one to whom the child belongs, because it is coordinated with it; and also because the one to whom the child belongs, who is the father, is the one spoken of in the whole of the preceding clause. The meaning is: when the one to whom the child belongs dies, there becomes obligatory upon his heir what was obligatory upon him of providing sustenance for the mothers and clothing them in a fair manner, and avoiding harm. This was related from 'Umar, al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Suddi. Some restricted it to those men among the heirs who are obliged to suckle, as it would have been obligatory upon the father of the infant had he been alive; this was said by Mujahid and 'Ata'. Sufyan said: the heir is the surviving one of the child's two parents after the death of the other of them; and he holds, in addition, that if the surviving one is the mother, the agnate (al-'asib) shares with her in suckling the child in proportion to his share of the inheritance, as he said: "and make him the heir among us." Qabisah ibn Dhu'ayb, al-Dahhak, and Bashir ibn Nasr, the judge of 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, said: the heir is the infant himself, meaning: upon him, from his property, when he inherits from his father, is the suckling of himself. Some said: the heir is the child; the maintenance of his two needy parents is obligatory upon him; al-Sajawandi related this from Qabisah ibn Dhu'ayb. Upon these sayings, the alif and lam in His saying "and upon the heir" stand as though they replace the pronoun referring to "the one to whom the child belongs," as if it were said: "and upon the heir of the one to whom the child belongs." 'Ata' also said, and Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, al-Suddi, Muqatil, Ibn Abi Layla, and al-Hasan ibn Salih, among others: the heir is the heir of the child. They differed: it was said the child's heir is men and women, said by Zayd ibn Thabit, Qatadah and others, and it is obligatory upon them to suckle him in proportion to their inheritances from him. It was said: his heir is from his agnates, whoever they may be, such as the grandfather, the brother, the son of the brother, the paternal uncle, and the son of the paternal uncle; this is related from 'Umar, 'Ata', al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ishaq, Ahmad, and Ibn Abi Layla. It was said: whoever is a mahram blood-relative; if he is not a mahram blood-relative, nothing is obligatory upon him; this was the view of Abu Hanifah, Abu Yusuf, and Muhammad. And al-Shafi'i said: the paternal grandfathers, then the mothers, are "like that," that is: the wage, the maintenance, and the avoidance of harm. Upon these sayings, the alif and lam stand as though they replace a pronoun referring to the child, as if it were said: "and upon his heir," meaning the heir of the child. It was said: the heir here is the one who inherits the guardianship over the suckling infant, spending from the infant's property on him, in the same way as his father used to spend. Thus there are six sayings regarding the heir, and some of them contain a detailed distinction as we have mentioned, so with the distinction there come to be ten sayings. The indication in His saying "dhalika" in "mithlu dhalika" refers to what was obligatory upon the father of providing for them and clothing them in a fair manner, as explained in the sayings on His saying "and upon the heir." This was also said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibrahim, 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Utbah ibn Mas'ud, al-Sha'bi, and al-Hasan. Some expressed this view by saying that "the like of that" is the wage of the equivalent and the maintenance. He said: this is related from 'Umar, Zayd, al-Hasan, 'Ata', Mujahid, Ibrahim, Qatadah, Qabisah, al-Suddi, and Ibn Qutaybah chose it. Al-Sha'bi also said, and al-Zuhri, al-Dahhak, Malik and his companions, and others: what is meant by His saying "the like of that" is that one should not cause harm; as for provision and clothing, nothing of them is [obligatory]. Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik that the verse included that provision and clothing are upon the heir, then that was abrogated by the consensus of the Ummah that the heir should not be harmed. End of quotation. And how could there be consensus when I have seen the views of the scholars on the obligation of that? It was said: "the like of that" is the wage of the equivalent, the maintenance, and the avoidance of harm; this is related from Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Muqatil, Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi, and al-Qadi Abu Ya'la chose it. They said: what supports this view is that it is coordinated with what precedes it, and it has been established that upon the one to whom the child belongs is the maintenance and clothing, and that he should not cause harm; so "the like of that" points to all that is upon the one to whom the child belongs.

"And if they both desire weaning by mutual consent and consultation, there is no blame upon them both." The pronoun in "aradā" refers to the mother and the one to whom the child belongs. "Al-fisal" is weaning before the completion of the two years, once the child shows independence from milk. There must be mutual consent between them; so if one of them agrees and the other refuses, he is not compelled; this was said by Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Zuhri, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, Sufyan, and others. It was said: weaning, whether it is within the two years or after the two years; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The explanation of this view is that before the two years it is only with the mutual consent of both of them, and that the infant is not harmed; but after their completion, whoever calls for weaning has that right, unless harm would befall the infant thereby. On these two views, that is a leniency after the limitation. Ibn Bahr said: al-fisal is that each of them concludes the discussion with the other by handing the child over to one of them; and that is after mutual consent and consultation, lest one of the parents undertake what would harm the child. So He, exalted, drew attention to the fact that what has a doubtful outcome is not undertaken except after the agreement of opinions. It was read: "fa-in arada", and "'an taradin" is connected to an omitted element, because it is in the position of a qualifier to "fisalan," meaning: a weaning that is occurring; al-Zamakhshari estimated it as "sadiran" (proceeding). "'An" is used for the sense of "going beyond" figuratively, because that is a meaning among the meanings. "Taradin" is of the pattern "tafa'ul," and what happened in it is what happened in "azb," the plural of "zaby," since its origin is "azbiyun" on the pattern "af'ul," so the ya' becomes waw because of the damma before it. Then, the Arabic language has no noun ending in a waw preceded by a damma other than a plural; and whenever this morphology leads to that, the waw is changed to ya' and the damma to kasra. Likewise was done in "taradin." The "tafa'ul" here, in "taradin" and "tashawurin," is according to the most common of its meanings, that it is performed by two. He placed "tashawur" last because by it the goodness and corruption of affairs and opinions becomes evident. "Minhuma" is in the position of a qualifier to "tarad," so it is connected to an omitted element, which is intended after "tashawurin," meaning: "from them both." It is possible in "tashawur" that one of them consulted the other, or that one consulted someone other than the other, so that opinions may converge on what is beneficial in that matter. "Fa-la junaha 'alayhima" is the answer to the condition. Before this answer there is an omitted clause by which the meaning is made sound; the estimate is: "then they both weaned him," or "then they both did that"; and the meaning is: there is no blame upon them both in the weaning.

* *

"And if you desire to have your children nursed by wet-nurses, there is no blame upon you when you hand over what you gave in a fair manner." The address is to the fathers and mothers, and in it there is an iltifat, for it is a shift from the third person (absence) to the second person (address), and a variation in the pronoun; because before it is "fa-in aradā fisālan," with the dual pronoun, and it is as though it returns to His saying "and the mothers" and "and upon the one to whom the child belongs." "Istarda'a" in it has a difference of opinion: whether it takes two objects directly, or whether the second object takes a preposition; there are two views. The first is the view of al-Zamakhshari, who said: istarda'a is a transitivized form from ardha'a; one says: the woman nursed the child (arda'at al-mar'atu al-sabiyya), and the child asked her to nurse (istarda'aha al-sabiyyu), so it takes two objects, just as you say: anjaha al-hajata, and the need made him succeed (istanjahathu al-hajatu); the meaning is: that you ask the wet-nurses to nurse your children, so one of the two objects is omitted for want of it, just as you say: "istanjahat al-hajatu" and do not mention whom it made succeed; and likewise is the rule for every two objects of which neither is a restatement of the first. End of his words. This is a transitivization of a transitivization: the original is "rada'a al-walad," then you say "ardha'at al-mar'atu al-walad," then you say "istarda'at al-mar'atu al-walad." The form "istaf'ala" here is for requesting: I asked the woman to nurse the child, just as you say "istasqaytu Zaydan al-ma'" and "istat'amtu 'Amran al-khubz," meaning: I asked him to give me drink and to feed me; so just as "al-khubz" and "al-ma'" are in the accusative and are not by omission of a preposition, likewise "awladakum" is in the accusative and not by omission of a preposition. The second is the view of the majority, that it takes two objects, the second with a preposition, and the preposition is omitted from "awladakum"; the estimate being: "li-awladikum" (for your children). The form "istaf'ala" has also come for requesting, transitive to the second object by a preposition, although in "af'ala" it is transitive to two objects; you say: "afhamanii Zaydun al-mas'ala" (Zayd made me understand the matter), and "istafhamtu Zaydan 'an al-mas'ala" (I asked Zayd to explain the matter to me); it did not come as "istat'amtu" would; and it becomes like "istaghfartu Allaha min al-dhanb" (I asked God's forgiveness for the sin), and it is permissible to omit "min," so you say "al-dhanb." There is no evidence in their saying "kana fulanun mustar'adan fi Bani Fulanin" (so-and-so was put out to nurse among the family of so-and-so) that it is a direct object or a prepositional object. "Fa-la junaha 'alaykum" is the answer to the condition, and before it is a clause omitted because the meaning is understood; the estimate is: "then you asked for nursing, or did that; then there is no blame upon you in the nursing." "Idha sallamtum" (when you hand over): this is an address to men specifically, and it is an iltifat in the address; and it was said it is an address to men and women, which becomes clear in the explanation of His saying "ma ataytum." "Idha sallamtum" is a condition; they said: its answer is what the first condition and its answer indicate, and that meaning is what governs "idha," and it is connected to what "'alaykum" is connected to. End of his words.
