The apparent meaning of this statement is an error; for he made the governing element of "idha" the meaning indicated by the first condition and its answer, and then he said secondly that "idha" is connected to what "'alaykum" is connected to, and this contradicts what came before it; and perhaps his saying "wa-huwa muta'allaq" (and it is connected) lost an alif from it, and it was "aw huwa muta'allaq" (or it is connected), in which case the meaning is sound; and then it would not be a condition, but purely adverbial of time.

Ibn Kathir read "ma ataytum" without the madda (short vowel form), and the rest of the seven read it with the madda. The justification of Ibn Kathir's reading is that "ataytum" means "jiktumuhu" (you brought it) and "fa'altumuhu" (you did it); one says "ata jamilan" (he did a beautiful deed), meaning: he did it, and "ata ilayhi ihsanan" (he did a kindness to him): he did it; and He said: "Verily His promise was ever come to pass" (inna wa'dahu kana ma'tiyyan), meaning: done; and Zuhayr said:

"If there is any good they have done, it is only that
the fathers of their fathers inherited it before them."

The justification for the long-vowel reading (al-madd) is that the meaning is "what you gave" (مَا أَعْطَيْتُمْ). In both readings, "مَا" is a relative pronoun (mawṣūla) meaning "that which," and its returning pronoun is omitted. When the verb means "to give" (أعطى), a second omitted element must be assumed, because it takes two objects: one is the pronoun for "مَا," and the other is the one who is, in meaning, the subject. The meaning of "مَا آتَيْتُمْ" is "what you intended to bring about or to give." The meaning of the verse, and God knows best, is the permissibility of a child being breastfed by someone other than its mother, if the parents wish this and agree on it, and they hand over the wages of the wet-nurses in a fair manner. What you hand over is then the payment for the nursing, as al-Suddi and Sufyan said. Handing over the payment is not a condition for the permissibility or validity of the nursing; rather, it is a recommended matter (al-nadb), because giving the wage to her promptly and pleasantly settles her mind and wins her affection for the child, so that she will persevere in caring for his welfare. It has also been said that "you handed over the children to whomever the two parents were content with." This was said by Qatada and al-Zuhri, but it is far-fetched, because "مَا," which is designated for what does not reason, is applied to a rational being. It has also been said that "you handed over to the mothers their wages according to what they nursed up to the time of the intention to seek nursing," said by Mujahid. It has also been said that "you handed over what you gave of the intention to seek nursing," meaning that each of the two parents handed over and was content, and this was by mutual agreement, with the intent of goodness and the desire for what is fair, said by Qatada.

Abu Ali (al-Farisi) also permitted, in "مَا آتَيْتُمْ," that "مَا" be a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyya), meaning: when you hand over the bringing (al-itā’), and the meaning is then restricted (ma'a al-qaṣr). That "مَا" be relative, meaning "that which," means that "the thing which you gave" is its payment and its giving; the modifier was omitted and the pronoun was put in its place, so the assumed meaning is "what you gave it," and then the pronoun was omitted from the relative clause. When it is a verbal-noun particle, the sentence does not need this assumption. Shayban, from Asim, related the reading "أُوتِيتُمْ" in the passive voice, meaning: what God gave you and enabled you to have of the wage and the like. God, exalted is He, says: ﴿And spend of that in which He has made you successors﴾ [al-Hadid: 7]. "بِالمَعْرُوفِ" is connected to "سَلَّمْتُمْ," meaning with the good word that brings the soul contentment, and which helps to improve the upbringing of the child. It has been said that it is connected to "آتَيْتُمْ." They said: this verse is evidence that fathers may hire wet-nurses for their children if they agree with the mothers on that. This was a pre-Islamic custom: they used to take wet-nurses for their children and free the mothers for enjoyment of them, for maintaining their bodies, and to hasten the child's arrival by the conception of a pregnancy. The Law approved this for the benefit it contains and the removal of hardship from them by cutting off what they had grown accustomed to. He placed the wage on the father by His saying: ﴿when you hand over﴾.

﴿وَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ وَاعْلَمُوا أَنَّ اللَّهَ بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ بَصِيرٌ﴾ [Fear God and know that God sees what you do.] When a command and a prohibition have preceded, it comes as an exhortation to the fear of God, exalted is He. Since many of the rulings of this verse concern the affairs of children who have no power and no protection against what is done to them, He warned and threatened with His saying: "وَاعْلَمُوا" [and know]. He used the attribute "بَصِيرٌ" [All-Seeing] as an emphasis on the comprehensive knowledge of what they do with them and the awareness of it, just as God, exalted is He, said concerning Moses, upon our Prophet and upon him be the best of prayers and peace, when he was a child: ﴿and that you may be raised under My eye﴾ [Ta-Ha: 39]. They said: the verse contains kinds of eloquence and rhetorical ornament, among them: the shifting of address (talwīn al-khiṭāb); and its opposite in ﴿وَالْوَالِدَاتُ يُرْضِعْنَ﴾ [And mothers breastfeed], for it is a report whose meaning is a command according to the majority; the emphasis with "كَامِلَيْنِ" [two complete years]; the turning away from the provision of the children to the provision of their mothers, because they are the means by which that is reached; the brevity in ﴿وَعَلَى الْوَارِثِ مِثْلُ ذَلِكَ﴾ [And upon the heir is the like of that]; the shifting of address in ﴿وَإِنْ أَرَدْتُمْ أَنْ تَسْتَرْضِعُوا أَوْلَادَكُمْ﴾ [And if you wish to have your children nursed], for it is an address to fathers and mothers, then He said ﴿إِذَا سَلَّمْتُمْ﴾ [when you hand over], which is an address to fathers specifically; and the omission in ﴿أَنْ تَسْتَرْضِعُوا﴾, whose assumed meaning is "wet-nurses for the children"; and in His saying: ﴿إِذَا سَلَّمْتُمْ مَا آتَيْتُمْ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ﴾ [when you hand over what you gave in a fair manner]. End of quotation.

These noble verses also include God's command to husbands, when they divorce their wives, to approach the end of the waiting period (al-‘idda) by keeping them, which is taking them back in a fair manner, or by releasing their way by the completion of the waiting period. He then emphasized the command to keep them in a fair manner, by explicitly forbidding keeping them to harm them. The prohibition came according to what used to happen among them in the pre-Islamic period: taking back, then divorce, then taking back, then divorce, as a means of harming the women. So they were forbidden from this ugly act, magnifying this evil deed, which is the greatest harm to women. Then God, exalted is He, mentioned that whoever commits what God forbade in this matter has wronged himself. That is, keeping women in order to harm them, and prolonging their waiting period, its real burden falls only on his own self, since he committed what God forbade. Then He forbade (p. 220) taking the signs of God in mockery, because He, exalted is He, had sent down verses concerning marriage, menstruation, oath of abstinence (īlā’), divorce, the waiting period, taking back, khul‘ (divorce at the wife's request), and abstaining from harming; and they included rulings between men and women, and the imposition of rights for them and upon them. It was the custom of the Arabs to disregard matters concerning women, to the point that they did not give inheritance to daughters, out of contempt for them. He had mentioned before this that whoever transgresses the limits of God is a wrongdoer; He reinforced this by forbidding taking the signs of God in mockery, but rather they should be received with seriousness and acceptance, even if they conflict with their customs. Then He commanded them to remember His blessing, as a reminder that whoever has been favored by someone must accept what God sends of the signs with acceptance, so that this would be thanks for His earlier blessing. Then God, exalted is He, alerted that what He sent down of the Book and wisdom is an admonition to you; it is fitting to accept it and to desist at its limits. Then He commanded the fear of God, exalted is He, and that they should know that God is Knowing of everything; nothing of your actions is hidden from Him, and He will requite you for them.

Then God, exalted is He, mentioned that when husbands divorce their wives and their waiting period has ended, do not prevent them from marrying whom they wish, if there is mutual consent between the divorced woman and her suitor. It was the custom of the Arabs that whoever among them divorced a woman irrevocably would prevent her from marrying anyone else. Then He pointed with His saying "ذَلِكَ" [that] to the prevention, and mentioned that the one who is admonished by it is the believer in God, exalted is He, and in the Last Day, because whoever is not a believer does not refrain from what God has forbidden. He alerted to belief in the Last Day because the fruit of disobeying the prohibition appears only in the Hereafter. Then He pointed with His saying: ﴿that is more purifying for you﴾ [al-Baqara: 232] to enabling marriage and not preventing it, because of the reward in it through obeying God's command, and He made clear what is feared from the gathering of the suitor and the woman in suspicion if they are prevented from marrying. Then He attributed knowledge to Himself and negated it from those addressed, since He is the Knower of hidden matters and their inner depths.

Then God, exalted is He, began to mention some of the results of marriage: the breastfeeding of children by mothers, the mention of the limit of that for one who wishes to complete it, what is due to the woman from the husband, and from his heir if the husband dies, of maintenance and clothing, and that this is in a fair manner without excess, neither upon the husband nor upon the wife. He mentioned the permissibility of weaning and separating the child, if that is by the consent of its father and mother before the two years. He also mentioned the permissibility of seeking nursing for children if the man and the wife agree on that. He pointed to giving the wage to the wet-nurses to sweeten their souls and to help them to love the little one and to embrace him until he grows up, as if his own mother had nursed him, for kindness brings about love. Then He concluded this verse with the command to the fear of God, exalted is He, and that they should know that God is All-Seeing of everything, just as He concluded the first verse with the command to fear Him, with the knowledge that God is Knowing of everything. This is an indication of requital, and a threat and warning to whoever opposes His command, exalted is He.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 234 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind, let the wives wait by themselves for four months and ten days. Then when they have reached their term, there is no blame on you for what they do with themselves in an honourable manner. And Allah is Aware of what you do.﴾ ﴿There is no blame on you for what you imply by way of proposal to women, or what you conceal within yourselves. Allah knows that you will remember them. But do not make a secret promise with them, except that you speak a fitting word. And do not resolve on the tie of marriage until the prescribed term reaches its end. And know that Allah knows what is in your hearts, so beware of Him. And know that Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 235] ﴿There is no blame on you if you divorce women before you have touched them or settled a dower for them. But provide for them, the wealthy according to his means and the poor according to his means, a provision in a fitting manner, a duty upon the good-doers.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 236] ﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them, and you have already settled a dower for them, then half of what you settled, unless they forgo it or the one in whose hand is the tie of marriage forgoes it. And that you forgo is nearer to piety. And do not forget graciousness among yourselves. Indeed Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237] ﴿Guard the prayers and the middle prayer, and stand before Allah in devotion.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238] ﴿So if you fear, then on foot or riding; and when you are safe, remember Allah as He taught you what you did not know.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 239]

Yadharu (يَذَرُ): its meaning is "yatruku" (he leaves). The imperative is used from it, but the active participle and passive participle are not used from it, and its past tense came in an irregular manner.

Khabir (خَبِيرٌ): an intensive form, from khabirtu al-shay' (I knew the thing), meaning "I knew it." From this it is said: qatala ardan khabaraha (he cultivated the land, i.e., he tested it). And khabartu Zaydan (I tested Zayd). From this root comes khabar (news), because it is the thing that one is informed of. And al-khabar (the soft land) means soft ground.

Ta'ridh (التَّعْرِيضُ): indicating a thing without explicit declaration.

Al-khitbah, with a kasrah on the kha' (الخِطْبَةُ): seeking a marriage. It is said: khataba fulanun fulanatan, meaning he asked her for the khitbah, i.e., his need. So it derives from their saying: "ma khatbuka?" meaning "what is your need and your matter?" Al-Farra' said: al-khitbah is a verbal noun with the meaning of al-khatb, and it is from your saying: "innahu yuhsinu al-qi'dah wa al-jilsah" (he is good at sitting and sitting-posture), meaning al-qu'ud and al-julus. And al-khutbah, with a dammah on the kha' (الخُطْبَةُ), is speech comprising admonition, exhortation and remembrance. Both return to al-khitab, which is speech.

Sajah used to say to her, the man would say: "khitb," and she would say: "nikh."

Akanna al-shay' (أكَنَّ الشَّيْءَ): he concealed it within himself. Kannahu: he covered it. The hamzah in akanna serves to distinguish between the two meanings, as in ashraqat al-'uqdah (the knot became tight in the rope or in the branch). The knot is well known. It is said: 'aqadtu al-hablah wa al-'ahd (I tied the rope and the covenant), and it is said: a'qadtu al-'asal (I thickened the honey). This returns to the meaning of firmness. And ta'aqqada al-amr 'alayya (the matter became difficult for me), meaning it became harsh. From this come al-'uqud (contracts).

Al-muqtir (المُقَتِّرُ): the one of limited means. Aqtara al-rajul and qattara yuqtiru and yuqattiru (the man became poor), and al-qillah (scarcity) is a meaning that encompasses all the derivations of its root. From it comes al-qatir, which is the nail of the armour, and al-qatrah, which is the lowest dust and small gnats, and al-qutar, which is the smell of the cooking-pot. Tarafah said:

"When people said in their gathering: 'Is that the smell of cooking, or the scent of perfume?'"

And al-qutur are the dwellings of hunters over water. The poet said:

"How many an archer from the Banu Tha'al, whose hands are numb in his hide-blind."

Al-nisf (النِّصْفُ): it is the part of two that is equal. It is said with a kasrah or dammah on the nun, and nassif. From it comes: "(He did not reach the mudd of one of them nor its half)," meaning its half. As one says thumn and thumayn, 'ushr and 'ushayr, sudus and sudays. From this it was said that al-nasaf is the veil placed on a woman's head, and it is called nassif. Everything that reaches half of something else is nisf. It is said: nassafa al-nahar yansifu (midday arrived), nassafa al-ma' al-qadah (the water reached half the cup), and al-izar al-sakk (the garment reached the shin), and al-ghulam al-Qur'an (the boy reached half the Qur'an). Al-Farra' related about all of this: ansafa.

Al-muhafazah 'ala al-shay' (المُحافَظَةُ عَلى الشَّيْءِ): persistence in it. It derives from al-hifz (preservation). Hafiza al-makan: he guarded it. Hafiza al-Qur'an: he remembered it in absence. It returns to the meaning of guarding. Hafiza fulan: he became angry, and ahfazahu: he made him angry. The verbal noun of hafiza in the sense of "became angry" is al-hafizah and al-hifz.

Al-rukub (الرُّكُوبُ): riding, which is well known. Rukban is the plural of rakib, which is an adjective used as a noun, so it was permissible to make it plural in the manner of nouns. Yet in the case of nouns, this is rare. They said: hajir and hujran, and like rukban: suhban and ru'yan, plurals of sahib and ra'in. If the adjective is not used as a noun, the pattern fi'lan does not come in it. The forms like diburan and qitlan are not attested in the plurals of darib and qatil.

"Those of you who die and leave wives behind, let the wives wait by themselves for four months and ten days." The connection of this verse to what came before is that when the mention of the 'iddah of divorce during menstruation had passed, and the rulings continued until the mention of breastfeeding, and within it was His saying: "And upon the heir is the like of that" [al-Baqarah: 233], meaning the heir of the child's father, the mention of the 'iddah of death came, since it differs from the 'iddah of divorce during menstruation.

Al-Jumhur read yutawaffawna (يُتَوَفَّوْنَ) with a dammah on the ya' in the passive form. 'Ali, and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim, read it with a fathah on the ya' in the active form. The meaning of this reading is that they complete their terms (yastawfuna ajalahum).

The i'rab of alladhina (الَّذِينَ): it is a mubtada' (subject), and it is disputed whether it has a khabar (predicate). Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' held that it has no khabar; rather, the statement is about the wives whose mention is connected with alladhina, since the discussion with them concerns the waiting period in months. So the khabar came about what is intended. The meaning is: whoever's husband dies, she must wait. Al-Farra, may Allah have mercy on him, recited:

"Perhaps, if the wind inclines me in an inclination, toward the son of Abi Dhayyan, he would be moistened."

He said: "la'alli," then he said: "an yatanadama," because the meaning is: "perhaps the son of Abi Dhayyan, if the wind inclines me in an inclination, that he would be moistened." And the poet said:

"Banu Asad, indeed the son of Qays and his killing, without blood-price, the abode of humiliation has become binding."

He cancelled the son of Qays, though he began with mentioning him, and reported about his killing that it was humiliation. The clarification of al-Farra's position is that when the Arabs mention nouns that are attached to them, and there is in them the meaning of the khabar, they leave out reporting about the first noun, and the khabar is about the attached noun. Its example: inna Zaydan wa ukhtahu muntaliqah (indeed Zayd and his sister are leaving), because the meaning is: indeed the sister of Zayd is leaving. The first line of poetry is not of this type; rather they cited, as something resembling this type, the poet's saying:

"So whoever asks about me, indeed I and Jirwah do not wander nor are we lent out."

The rebuttal of al-Farra, and the interpretation of the verses and the verse, is mentioned in grammar. But al-Jumhur held that it has a khabar, and they differed. It was said: it is expressed explicitly, and it is yatarabbasna (they wait), and there is no omission that corrects the meaning of the khabar, because it is connected in terms of meaning, since the nun in "yatarabbasna" refers back. It was said: to "the husbands who die," so if he had stated this explicitly and said: "yatarabbasna azwajahum" (they wait for their husbands), there would be no need for an omission, and it would be a correct statement, and so is what has the same meaning, and this is the saying of al-Zajjaj. It was said: there is an omission that corrects the meaning of the khabar-ness, and they differed about the place of the omission. It was said: it is from the mubtada', and the estimate is: "wa azwaj alladhina" (and the wives of those who), and what indicates the omitted part is His saying: "and leave wives behind" [al-Baqarah: 240]. It was said: it is from the khabar, and its estimate is: "yatarabbasna ba'dahum" (they wait after them) or "ba'da mawtihim" (after their death), as said by al-Akhfash. It was said: it is from the khabar, which is that the khabar is a sentence of a subject that is omitted and its predicate "yatarabbasna," its estimate: "their wives wait," and what is manifest indicates it, as said by al-Mubarrad. It was said: the khabar in its entirety is omitted and estimated before the mubtada', its estimate: "in what is recited to you is the ruling of those who die among you and leave wives behind." His saying: "yatarabbasna bi-anfusihinna" (they wait by themselves) is an explanation of the ruling recited, and it is a sentence with no place in i'rab. They said: this is the saying of Sibawayh. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: that is only correct if there follows in the speech a word of command, like His saying: "As for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands" [al-Ma'idah: 38]. But this verse has the meaning of a command, not its wording, so this estimate requires another estimate, which is dispensed with when the word of command is present. And the way the verse has come is fitting, that it is a preparation for His saying: "then there is no blame upon you," since the address from the beginning of the verse to its end is intended for the men among whom are the judges and the overseers. The expression of al-Akhfash and al-Mubarrad is what we have mentioned. End of his speech.

The apparent meaning of His saying "yatarabbasna" is generality for every woman whose husband has died, so it includes the slave woman, the scriptural woman, and the young girl. It is narrated from Abu Hanifah that the 'iddah of a scriptural woman is three menstrual cycles if her husband dies, and it is narrated from him that she has an 'iddah; if she was not consummated, then there is no 'iddah, unanimously. The ihdad (mourning) is derived from these two statements. The specification of the pregnant woman was said to be by His saying: "And the pregnant women, their term is that they lay down their burdens" [al-Talaq: 4], and so on. Al-Shafi'i did not specify the generality here regarding the pregnant woman except by the Sunnah, not by this verse, because it came after the mention of divorced women, so it is possible to say: it is about the divorced woman, not the woman whose husband has died. And because each of the two verses is more general than the other from one aspect and more specific from another aspect: a pregnant woman may be widowed and may not be, and the widowed woman may be pregnant and may not be. So specification was prevented.

It was said: the verse at first includes the pregnant women, then it was abrogated (nusikha) by His saying: "And the pregnant women" [al-Talaq: 4]. The 'iddah of the pregnant woman is the laying down of her burden, according to the majority. It is narrated from 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas and others that the full completion of her 'iddah is the later of the two terms, and this was chosen by Sahnun. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he retracted that.

The meaning of "yatarabbasna bi-anfusihinna" is: they wait. It was said: and tarabbus here is patience from marriage, said by al-Hasan. He said: the ihdad is nothing, and she may adorn herself and perfume herself. His statement was deemed weak. It was said: abstaining from remarriage, remaining in the house, and ihdad, which is that she refrains from adornment, from wearing dyed fine clothing such as red, yellow and green, and from perfume, and what goes in the same direction. This is the saying of the majority.

There is no explicit text in the verse about ihdad; rather tarabbus is general, clarified by the Sunnah. It is established in the hadith of al-Furay'ah that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Remain in your house until the prescribed term reaches its end," and she was a widow; she said: "So I observed 'iddah for four months and ten days." And it is authentically reported that he said: "It is not lawful for a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day to mourn over a dead person for more than three days, except over a husband; for she mourns for four months and ten days, and must remain in her house at night." This is the saying of the majority. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hanifah and others said: she may spend the night wherever she wishes. This was narrated from 'Ali, Jabir, and 'A'ishah, and 'Ata', Jabir ibn Zayd, al-Hasan and Dawud also said it. Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah said: "yatarabbasna bi-anfusihinna" and did not say: "ya'taddidna fi buyutihinna" (observe 'iddah in their houses). Let her observe 'iddah wherever she wishes for four months and ten days. They said: its meaning is "ten nights." Therefore He dropped the taa' (in 'ashran). This is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas. The intended meaning is ten nights with their days, so the tenth day is included. It was said: the ruling of the nights predominated, since nights precede days, and the days are included within them, and 'ashr is lighter in pronunciation. Her 'iddah does not end except with the completion of the tenth day. This is the saying of the majority. Al-Awza'i and Abu Bakr al-Ahamm said: the tenth day is not part of the 'iddah; rather it ends upon the completion of ten nights. Al-Mubarrad said: its meaning is "and ten periods," each period of which is a day and a night. The Arabs say: "We travelled five," meaning between a day and a night. The poet said:

"So she circled three times between day and night, and the rejection was that she should be assured and cry out."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It was also said that *ashr* (ten) refers to the nights, since the days are included with them. You never find them using the masculine form with it when they mean the days. You say *sumtu ʿashran* (I fasted ten), and if the noun were mentioned, it would fall outside their speech. A clear example of this is ﴿if you tarried not but ten [nights]﴾ [Ta-Ha: 103] and ﴿if you tarried not but a day﴾ [Ta-Ha: 104]." End of his words.

It does not need the interpretation that *ʿashr* means nights because the *tāʾ* is dropped, nor the interpretation that it means periods of time, as al-Mubarrad held. Rather, what our companions transmitted is this: when the counted noun is masculine and you omit it, you have two options. The first, which is the original form, is that the number remains as it would be if the counted noun were not omitted. So you say *ṣumtu khamsatan* (I fasted five), meaning five days. They said this is the eloquent (*fasīḥ*) usage. They said it is also permissible to drop the feminine *tāʾ* from the number altogether. Al-Kisāʾī reported from Abu al-Jarrāḥ: *ṣumnā min al-shahr khamsan* (we fasted five [days] of the month). It is well known that what is fasted of the month is only days, and *yawm* (day) is masculine. Likewise is his (the poet's) saying:

*"Otherwise, then go on as the rider went, / who completes five [days], in whose journey there is no peril."*

He means five days. What is also found in the hadith is based on this, when he (ﷺ) followed it with six of Shawwal. Once this is established, the phrase *ʿashran* comes in one of the two permissible forms. Its beauty here is that it is the end of a clause, so it resembles the verse-endings (*fawāṣil*), just as the fact that it is a verse-ending made ﴿if you tarried not but ten [nights]﴾ acceptable. Therefore this form was chosen as one of the two permissible forms. So his saying "and if it were mentioned, it would fall outside their speech" is not as he stated. Rather, if it were mentioned, it would have been in the abundant and eloquent usage that they themselves specified, since its status among them when omitted is like its status when stated in the eloquent usage. They permitted what al-Zamakhshari mentioned, though the other form is more frequent. His saying "you never find them using the masculine form with it" is not as stated; rather, using the masculine form is the abundant and eloquent usage, as we have mentioned.

His saying "a clear example of this is ﴿if you tarried not but ten﴾" we have already explained that this is in the permissible form, and that what makes it good is that it is a verse-ending. His saying "﴿if you tarried not but a day﴾" is beneficial: al-Zamakhshari mentioned that, in his view, he meant the nights, with the days included in them; so he used "but a day" to indicate that. In our view, this indicates that the phrase "ten" is meant to refer to days, because they differed about the length of the tarrying: some said ten, and the one most correct in method said a day. So "but a day" is set against their saying "but ten," and this shows that by "ten" the days are meant, since it is not a true contrast for one speaker to say "ten nights" and another to say "a day."

The apparent meaning of "four months" is what the term *shahr* (month) applies to. If the waiting period were obligated by seeing the new moon, she would count by the crescents, whether the month were full or deficient. If it became obligatory in part of a month, it is said: she completes one hundred and thirty days. It is also said: she counts the crescents that pass over her as months, and then completes the first days. Both opinions are reported from Abu Hanifa.

Since most women whose husbands die would know of it and begin the waiting period (*ʿidda*) immediately upon the death, the verb was attributed to them and emphasized with his saying "by themselves." If the period of the waiting period passed from the time of death, and evidence was established for that, and she did not know of his death until the waiting period ended, then the majority position is that her waiting period begins from the day of death. This was said by Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn ʿUmar, Jābir, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Aswad ibn Yazīd, and the jurists of the cities. Ali, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Khallās ibn ʿAmr, and Rabīʿa said: from the day the news reaches her. It seems they treated the attribution of the waiting to them as having an effect on the waiting period. It is narrated from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab and al-Shāfiʿī that they said: if evidence is established, the waiting period is from the day of death; and if no evidence is established, then from the day the news reaches her. It is also narrated from al-Shāfiʿī the same as the view of the majority. They agreed that if a pregnant woman who does not know of her husband's death until she gives birth, her waiting period is over. The verse concerning a widow only addressed her need to wait that period; therefore she has no maintenance (*nafaqa*) from the estate during the waiting period, even if she is pregnant. This was said by Jābir, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn al-Musayyab, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ḥasan, ʿIkrima, ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Yaʿlā, Yaḥyā al-Anṣārī, Rabīʿa, Mālik, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, and Ibn al-Mundhir, and it is narrated from Abu Hanifa. It was also said: she has maintenance from the whole estate. This is narrated from Ali, ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar, Shurayḥ, Ibn Sīrīn, al-Shaʿbī, Abu al-ʿĀliya, al-Nakhaʿī, Khallās ibn ʿAmr, Ḥammād ibn Abī Sulaymān, Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī, al-Thawrī, and Abu ʿUbayd.

The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿who wait by themselves for four months and ten [days]﴾ is that if she waits this period, she owes nothing more than that, even if she is among those who menstruate and did not menstruate during it. It was said: she is not cleared except by a menstrual cycle that she has within the period; otherwise she is in doubt (*mustaribah*), so she remains until her doubt is removed. The jurists agreed that this verse abrogates (*naskh*, the cancellation of a ruling by a later revelation) what follows it concerning the waiting period of a year. This is one of the strange cases of abrogation, since the second ruling abrogates the first. It was also said: the year was not abrogated, but it is not obligatory; rather it is recommended. So four months and ten days is the least a widow may observe, and the full year is the most complete and most excellent.

Some people said: there is no abrogation in this; rather it is a reduction from the year, like the prayer of the traveler, which was reduced from four to two; that was not abrogation but lightening. They said: this number was singled out for the waiting period of a widow as a means of ensuring the womb is clear (*istibrāʾ li-l-ḥaml*). Ibn Masʿūd narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "The creation of one of you is a drop for forty days, then a clot for forty days, then a lump for forty days, then the spirit is breathed into it at four months." And God added the ten because it is the time when the movement of the fetus is expected to appear, or out of consideration for the deficiency and completeness of months, or as a precaution regarding how quickly the movement appears or how slowly it appears in the fetus.

Abu al-ʿĀliya and others said: the ten were added because the breathing of the spirit occurs during them, and the appearance of the pregnancy usually occurs then. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: the child of every pregnant woman kicks in the middle of her pregnancy. Al-Rāghib said: the physicians mentioned that in most cases, if the child is male, it moves after three months, and if it is female, after four months; and ten was added to that as a precaution. He said: ten was singled out for the addition because it is the most complete and noblest of numbers, as was previously stated in ﴿those are ten complete﴾ [al-Baqara: 196]. Al-Qushayrī said: since the right of the deceased is greater, because separation from him was not by choice, the period of his death was longer. In the beginning of Islam the waiting period for death was a year, then it was reduced to four months and ten days, to lighten the clearing of the womb from the husband's water. Then, once the waiting period ended, she was permitted to marry another husband, since death does not endure as a state for anyone's entire life, as it has been said:

*"As faces decay in the dust, / so too grief decays over them."*

﴿Then when they have reached their term, there is no blame upon you for what they do with themselves in a reasonable manner﴾. "Reaching their term" means the end of the period set for the waiting. The addressees of "upon you" are the guardians, or the rulers, judges, and scholars, since they are the ones to whom matters are referred, or all believers. These are the opinions. The lifting of blame from men regarding women reaching their term is because they are the ones who object to them and enforce the rules of the waiting period, or because at that point it becomes lawful for them to marry them, since that would be forbidden during the waiting period, so the blame is removed after the waiting period ends. What they do with themselves is lawful marriage. This was said by Mujāhid and Ibn Shihāb. Or it is adornment, perfume, and moving from one dwelling to another, as said by Abu Jaʿfar al-Ṭabarī. The meaning of "in a reasonable manner" is: with witnesses. It was also said: what the Law permits of what marriage depends upon.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿in what they do with themselves﴾ refers to making a proposal in a manner that the Law does not reject, and the meaning is: if they did what is objectionable, the rulers would have had to restrain them, and if they neglected it, the blame would be upon them. End of his words. And it is good.

﴿And God is Aware of what you do﴾: this is a warning that includes admonition. *Khabīr* (Aware) is an intensive form, meaning knowledge of what is subtle and the thorough pursuit of it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 235 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you hint at in proposing to women, or what you conceal within yourselves.﴾ God removed the sin of allusion (ta'ridh) in proposing marriage, which is such as saying: "Indeed you are beautiful," "Indeed you are righteous," "Indeed I have a mind to marry," "Indeed I am desirous of you," and what is similar to that. Or: "I wish to marry, and I love such-and-such a woman," enumerating her qualities; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Or: "Indeed you are a woman of good sense, and whatever is decreed will come to pass," this was said by al-Sha'bi. Or: he describes to her himself, his pride, his noble lineage and his ancestry, as al-Baqir did with Sakina bint Handhala. Or he says to her guardian: "Do not outpace me with her," as the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Fatima bint Qays: "Stay at the house of Umm Sharik, and do not outpace me with yourself." This has been interpreted as meaning that the Prophet (ﷺ) was giving Fatima his opinion concerning whom she should marry, not that he wanted her for himself. For this reason Mujahid disliked saying "Do not outpace me with yourself," and considered it a secret promise (muwa'adah sirran). Or he says: "There is nothing wrong with you being a widow, and perhaps God will bring you good; or many a man desires you," or he sends her gifts and takes care of her affairs if he has a desire to marry her. Ibrahim said: or he says anything other than explicit declaration; this was said by Ibn Zayd. There is consensus that explicit mention of marriage is not permitted, nor is hinting at it (al-tanbih 'alayhi), nor sexual talk (al-rafath), nor mention of intercourse, nor incitement to it. The Shafi'is have used the removal of blame in allusive proposal as evidence that allusive reference to a slander-like accusation does not require the hadd penalty: just as the prohibition distinguishes the rulings of allusion and explicit statement in proposing, so too in slander.

﴿or what you conceal within yourselves﴾, that is: what you hide within yourselves of the matter of marriage, so that you neither allude to it nor mention it explicitly. The meaning is the lifting of blame from one who expresses it by allusion or who keeps it hidden in himself. If blame is lifted from one who alludes in speech, it is all the more so from one who conceals. However, these are two states of disclosure and concealment, and both are pardoned. It was also said: the meaning is that he resolves in his heart that he will explicitly declare this in the future, after the 'idda has ended; so God permitted allusion, forbade explicit declaration in the present, and permitted resolving in the heart to declare explicitly in the future. It is not permissible that concealing within oneself means inclination toward the woman, because that would be stating the obvious, since allusion to proposal is a greater matter than inclination of the heart.

﴿God knows that you will remember them﴾. This is an excuse for allusion, because when inclination arises in the heart it is difficult to repel; so God removed the blame for that. There is in it an element of reproach, like His saying: ﴿God knows that you were betraying yourselves﴾ [al-Baqara: 187]. The verb came with sin (sa), which indicates that the future time is near, not distant, because they are remembered when the bonds of their marriages have been severed by death, and souls yearn for them and desire to marry them. Al-Hasan said: the meaning of "you will remember them" is "you will propose to them," as if He said: if you are not forbidden. End. His saying "you will remember them" includes both remembrance by the tongue and remembrance of the heart; so He removed blame from allusion, which is the tongue's hinting, and from concealment within oneself, which is the remembrance of the heart.

﴿But do not make a promise to them in secret﴾. This exception (istidrak) is from the sentence before it, namely His saying "you will remember them." Remembrance occurs in various modes and aspects, so He made an exception for one aspect in which He forbade a particular kind of remembrance. Had He not made the exception, it would have been permitted, being included under the general remembrance which God informed would occur. This is like your saying: "Zayd will meet Khalid, but he should not confront him with evil." He made an exception for this state from what meeting may involve, and among its states is confrontation with evil. "Lakin" does not require an omitted sentence before it; rather, what follows "lakin" requires that what precedes it occur in meaning, not in wording, because negating confrontation with evil implies that the meeting takes place. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, where is the excepted matter in His saying "But do not make a promise to them"? I say: it is omitted, indicated by "you will remember them": "God knows that you will remember them, so remember them, but do not make a promise to them in secret." End of his words. We have mentioned that no omitted element before "lakin" is needed; rather the exception comes from His saying "you will remember them," and God did not command remembering women, neither obligatorily nor recommendedly; so there is no need to assume "so remember them," as we established before your saying: "I will meet you, but do not fear me," since meeting includes among its states being feared by the one met, so he made the exception and said: "but do not fear me."

Al-sirr (the secret) is the opposite of open (al-jahr), and it is used as a euphemism for intercourse, lawful and unlawful, since it is done in secret; it may also be used for the contract, because it is its cause. Here al-sirr has been interpreted as fornication (zina) by al-Hasan, Jabir ibn Zayd, Abu Mijlaz, al-Dahhak and al-Nakha'i. Among the instances where al-sirr is used for unlawful intercourse is the verse of al-Hutay'a:

"The secret of their neighbour is forbidden to them, while their neighbour eats the noses of the dishes."

And al-A'sha said:

"Do not approach a neighbour woman, for her secret is forbidden to you; so marry, or remain celibate forever."

Ibn Jubayr said: al-sirr here means marriage. Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is: do not marry them while concealing that, and when the 'idda ends you reveal it and consummate with them; so he called the contract with them a promise, but this wording rejects this view. Some said: it means intercourse, namely that he says to her: "If I marry you, such and such will happen," meaning what passes between them under the blanket. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr also, al-Sha'bi, Mujahid, 'Ikrima, al-Suddi, Malik and his companions, and the majority said: the meaning is: do not agree with them on a promise, a binding commitment, or a taking of covenants in secrecy and hiddenness from you. According to this view, and the view before it, "sirran" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), i.e., "secretly." According to the first two views it is in the accusative as an object. If it is a circumstantial state, the object of "tuwa'idu hunna" is omitted, its estimate being "the marriage contract." It was also said: it is accusative as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, its estimate being "a promise in secret." It was also said the estimate is "in secret," so "fi" was omitted and it is accusative in the manner of an adverb of place (zarf), with the promise in secret being an expression for a promise in terms that are disgraceful, since private conversation with them is generally about what one is shy to declare openly. What the verse indicates is that they were forbidden to make a promise to a woman during her 'idda to have intercourse with her after the 'idda by way of marriage. As for interpreting al-sirr here as fornication, it is far-fetched, because it is forbidden for a Muslim with a woman in 'idda and with others. As for the use of "promise in secret" for the contract, it is also far-fetched. As for the view of the majority, it is also far-fetched, because they were forbidden from promising marriage both secretly and openly, so there is no benefit in restricting the promise to secrecy.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 235 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Except that you say a customary word.﴾ This exception is disjunctive (munqati'), because it does not fall under "secretly" (sirran) in His words: ﴿but do not promise them secretly﴾, whatever interpretation you adopt. The "customary word" (al-qawl al-ma'ruf) is what is permitted of allusion (ta'rid). Al-Dahhak said: Among the customary word is that you say to the woman in 'idda: "Keep yourself for me, for I have a desire for you," and she says: "And I am the same." Ibn 'Atiyya said: This, in my view, is a promise (mu'adaha). Allusion is only in a man's saying: "Surely you are noble women," and "What is decreed will be," and "Surely you are admirable," and the like. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Except that you say a customary word﴾ means that you allude and do not state explicitly. If you ask: To what does the particle of exception relate? I say: to ﴿do not promise them﴾, that is, do not promise them any promise at all, except a customary promise that is not objectionable; or: do not promise them except by saying [allusively], that is, do not promise them except through (p-228) allusion. It is not permissible that it be a disjunctive exception from "secretly," because that would lead to your saying: "Do not promise them except allusion." End of al-Zamakhshari's words. This needs clarification. He made it a connected exception on the basis that it is a truncated (mufarragh) exception, and he made this in two ways. One: that it is an exception from a deleted verbal noun (masdar), which is the first aspect he mentioned, and he estimated it as: "Do not promise them a promise at all except a customary, unobjectionable promise," so the meaning is: "Do not say to them a word by which you promise them, except a customary word." This is like: "Do not strike Zayd a severe strike." The second: that it is a truncated exception from a deleted genitive-governed noun, which is the second aspect he mentioned, and he estimated it as: "except by your saying," then clarified it by his words "except by allusion." So the meaning is: "Do not promise them secretly, that is, in marriage, by any kind of speech, except by a customary speech, which is allusion." The preposition from "an" is deleted, so it remains in the accusative or genitive according to the disagreement mentioned in similar cases. The difference between this aspect and the previous one is that the previous one is in the accusative as a verbal noun, while this one is in the accusative through dropping the preposition, which is the ba' of causality.

As for his words: "It is not permissible that it be a disjunctive exception from 'secretly,' because that leads to his words: 'Do not promise them except allusion,' and allusion is not a promise," so the governing verb cannot, in his view, apply to it. In his view this is disjunctive like: "I saw no one except a donkey." But this is valid in: "I saw nothing except (p-229) a donkey," whereas it is not valid in: "Do not promise them except allusion," because allusion is not a promise; rather, what is promised is marriage. The accusative of "secretly" is as an object, so "an taqulu" ought likewise to be an object, and that is not valid there. Therefore it cannot be a disjunctive exception. This is the reasoning by which al-Zamakhshari prevented it from being disjunctive. What he went to is not correct, because the disjunctive exception is not confined to what he mentioned, namely that the preceding governing verb applies to it. The disjunctive exception is of two kinds. One: that the governing verb extends to what follows "illa," as we illustrated in your saying: "I saw no one except a donkey," and "There is no one in the house except a donkey." This type has a difference among the Arabs: the Hijazis' position is to put this kind of exception in the accusative, while the Banu Tamim's position is to make it follow what precedes it in case. In this type it is permissible to delete the first and make the preceding verb govern what follows "illa," so you say: "I saw nothing except a donkey," and "There is nothing in the house except a donkey"; and it is valid in speech: "They have no knowledge of it except following conjecture." The second kind of disjunctive exception is that the governing verb cannot extend to what follows "illa." Its ruling is accusative among all the Arabs, such as: "Increase has only what diminished," and "Benefit has only what harmed." What follows "illa" cannot be governed by "increased" or "diminished"; rather the meaning is estimated as: "It increased, but loss befell it," and "It benefited, but harm occurred." This kind shares with the first the estimation of "illa" as "lakin" ("but"), but the first allows the preceding element to govern what follows, and this does not. Given this, His words "Except that you say" are a disjunctive exception from this second kind, namely what the governing verb cannot be directed at, and the estimate is: "But allusion is permitted to you." It seems al-Zamakhshari did not know that the disjunctive exception comes in this type where the governing verb cannot be directed at what follows "illa"; therefore he prevented it. And God knows best.

The apparent sense of the prohibition in His words "do not promise them secretly" is prohibition (tahrim). Malik, in Ibn Wahb's narration from him, said concerning one who promised a woman during her 'idda and then married her after the 'idda: separation is dearer to me, whether he consummated or not, and it is one single divorce; when she is free, he proposes like other suitors. Ashhab narrated from Malik the obligation of separating the two. Ibn al-Qasim said: Ibn Harith related a similar view from Ibn al-Majishun, adding something that implies the permanence of the prohibition. Al-Shafi'i said: If he openly proposed and she openly accepted but he did not contract with her until after the 'idda ended, the marriage is valid, and openly stating both is disliked. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The community has agreed on the disliking of promising a woman during her 'idda.

﴿And do not resolve upon the tie of marriage until the prescribed term reaches its end.﴾ They were forbidden to resolve upon the tie of marriage, and if resolving is forbidden, then the contract is more fittingly forbidden. "'Uqdata" is in the accusative as an object, because "ta'zimu" is taken to include the sense of a verb that takes its object directly, so it is taken to mean: "intend," or "resolve," or "make obligatory," or "undertake," or "cut off," that is, "decide." It has been said that "'uqdata" is in the accusative as a verbal noun, and the meaning of "ta'zimu" is "ta'qidu" (contract). It has also been said that it is in the accusative through dropping the preposition, and on this estimate the sense is: "Do not resolve upon the tie of marriage." Sibawayh related that the Arabs say: "Zayd was struck on the back and the belly," meaning "on the back and the belly." The poet said:

"And indeed I spend the night hungry upon it, and I shade it, until I obtain by it the noble food."

The original is: "and I shade upon it," so "'ala" was deleted, and the verb reached the pronoun and governed it in the accusative, since the basic usage of this verb takes "'ala." Another poet said:

"I resolved upon establishing one of the morning, for a matter for which whoever leads is made to lead."

The discussion of a parallel to this was given earlier in His words: ﴿And if they resolve upon divorce﴾ [al-Baqara: 227]. The "tie of marriage" is what the validity of the marriage depends upon, according to the disagreement of the scholars on that; therefore Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The resolving of the tie is its conclusion through witnesses and the guardian." The "term of the writing reaching its end" is the completion of the 'idda, as related by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, Qatada and al-Suddi, and no one is reported to have differed from this; rather it is among the clear rulings whose interpretation is agreed upon as the completion of the 'idda. "Al-kitab" here means what is written, that is: until what was written and obligated of the 'idda reaches its term, that is, the time of its completion. Al-Zajjaj said: "Al-kitab" is the Qur'an, and it is by deletion of a qualifier: the meaning is "until the obligation of the Book reaches its term," which is what was obligated by the Book of the 'idda; when the 'idda ends, it is permissible to proceed to marry. This prohibition means prohibition. If he contracted with her during the 'idda, the judge annuls the marriage. If that was before consummation, 'Umar and the majority said the prohibition is not permanent. Malik and Ibn al-Qasim said in the Mudawwana: he shall be one of the suitors. Ibn al-Jallab related from Malik that it is permanent. If he contracted with her during the 'idda and consummated after it ended, there are two opinions among the scholars: some say it is permanent, some say it is not permanent, and these are two views from Malik. If he contracted with her during the 'idda and consummated during the 'idda, 'Umar, Malik and his companions, al-Awza'i, al-Layth, Ahmad and others said the prohibition is permanent. Malik and al-Layth said: she is not lawful to him even by right of ownership. 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibrahim, Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i, 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Abi Salama and a group said: it is not permanent; rather the two are separated, then she observes 'idda from him, and he becomes one of the suitors. Al-Hasan, Abu Hanifa, al-Layth, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq and the Medinese other than Malik said: she observes the first 'idda, and once it ends there is no harm in the second man marrying her. Malik, the people of opinion, al-Awza'i and al-Thawri said: one 'idda suffices for both of them together, whether it is by pregnancy, by menstrual periods, or by months.

﴿And know that God knows what is in your souls, so beware of Him.﴾ It has been said: the meaning is what is in your souls of desire for them, and it has been said: of fidelity or breaking of promise, as related by Ibn 'Abbas. "So beware of Him": the pronoun refers to God Most High, that is, beware His punishment. Al-Zamakhshari said: He knows what is in your souls of resolve upon what is not permitted, so beware of it and do not resolve upon it. End of quote. It is possible that in al-Zamakhshari's words the pronoun returns to what is not permitted of resolve, that is, beware what is not permitted and do not resolve upon it; so the pronoun in "beware of it" and "resolve upon it" refers to one thing. It is also possible in his words that it refers to God, and the pronoun in "upon it" refers to what is not permitted, so the two pronouns refer to different things. When He threatened them that He is aware of what is in their souls and warned them of it, He followed that with two sublime attributes to remove from them some of the fright of threat and warning and the caution of His punishment, so that the believer's heart may be balanced between hope and fear. He concluded with these two attributes, which imply exaggeration in forgiveness and forbearance, to strengthen the believer's hope in God's goodness and his longing for His forgiveness and forbearance should he slip and err. He set each meaning of warning and encouragement in a separate independent clause, and repeated the name of God for magnification and exaltation, by the one to whom the judgment is ascribed. The predicate of the first "inna" came in the present tense, because what occurs in souls recurs, so knowledge attaches to it, as if knowledge recurs with the recurrence of its object. The predicate of the second "inna" came as a noun to indicate the establishment of the attribute, and that it has become as if among the attributes of essence, even though it is among the attributes of act. It has been said that these verses contain kinds of rhetorical ornament. Among them: turning away from the address (ma'dul al-khitab), namely that the address in His words "And those who are taken in death" [al-Baqara: 234] is general while the meaning is particular. Among them: abrogation, for it abrogates the year according to most scholars. Among them: specification (ikhtisas), namely that a number is specified without this being for a reason, as in "four months and ten" [al-Baqara: 234]. Among them: metonymy (kinaya), in His words "but do not promise them secretly," where "secretly" is a metonymy for marriage, and this is among the most eloquent metonymies. Among them: allusion (ta'rid), in His words "He knows what is in your souls." Among them: threat, in His words "so beware of Him." Among them: the addition of attributes (p-231) in His words "Forgiving, Forbearing."

Revelation context: it was revealed concerning an Ansari man who married a Hanifiyya woman and did not specify a dowry. He then divorced her before he had consummated the marriage. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: (Provide for her, even if it is with your cap). This is the meaning of His words: ﴿There is no blame upon you﴾, and so on.

Its connection to what precedes it: when Allah, exalted is He, explained the ruling on women who had been consummated with and divorced, and on women whose husbands had died, He then explained the ruling on a divorced woman who had not been consummated with, and for whom no dowry had been specified, or other circumstances. The divorced women are of four kinds: one who has been consummated with and for whom a dowry was specified; its opposite; one for whom a dowry was specified but who has not been consummated with; and its opposite.

The address in His words ﴿There is no blame upon you﴾ is to the husbands. The meaning of the negation of blame here is this: when He forbade marriage with the sense of tasting pleasure and satisfying desire, and commanded marriage in pursuit of chastity, reward, and lasting companionship, it occurred to some believers that whoever divorces before consummation would have committed a part of this disliked act. So Allah lifted the blame in this matter, provided that the basis of the marriage was a good intention.

﴿As long as you have not touched them﴾: Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿tumāssūhunna﴾ (تُماسُّوهُنَّ), the imperfect of māssa (the form of fā'ala). The rest of the seven readers read it as the imperfect of massa (مَسِسْتُ). The form fā'ala implies that both spouses share in the touching. Abu Ali preferred the reading ﴿tamassūhunna﴾ on the grounds that the verbs of this category come in the triliteral form, such as nakaha (to marry), safada (to mate with), fazi'a (to be frightened), daqata (to be struck), and daraba al-fahl (the stallion mounted). Both readings are good. The touching (al-mass) and the being touched (al-mumassa) here mean sexual intercourse, as in His words: ﴿No human has touched me﴾ [Maryam: 20].

The ﴿mā﴾ in ﴿mā lam tamassūhunna﴾ is apparently a temporal verbal (maṣdariyya) particle, meaning: "for the time of not touching." Compare the poet's words:

"Indeed, I join my rope to your rope,
and I fletch my arrow with the feathers of your arrow,
as long as I do not find you on a path of guidance,
whose traces your cut-off forelock has been tracing before me, I being the tracker."

This temporal maṣdariyya ﴿mā﴾ resembles a conditional, and it implies generality, as in: "I will accompany you as long as you remain good to me," meaning: "every time the goodness continues." Some said: ﴿mā﴾ is conditional, and then they paraphrased it as ﴿an﴾ (أنْ). Allah knows best; by this they intended to explain the meaning. When ﴿mā﴾ is conditional it is a noun other than a temporal or locational noun, and it cannot here be conditional in this sense. Ibn Malik claimed that ﴿mā﴾ can be a conditional of temporal meaning. His son Badr al-Din Muhammad refuted this in some of his glosses, and interpreted what his father cited as evidence differently. We too have interpreted some of it differently from his son. All of this we have mentioned in our book al-Takmil (التكميل) among our works. Furthermore, Ibn Malik stated that what he held is not said by the grammarians, and that he himself derived it from the speech of the eloquent, in his own view. Some claimed that ﴿mā﴾ in ﴿mā lam tamassūhunna﴾ is a relative pronoun, and the meaning is: "if you divorce the women who have not been touched by you." Then the word ﴿mā﴾ would not be a conditional. This is weak, because in that case ﴿mā﴾ would function as a qualifier of the women, since he interpreted it with the meaning of "those who" (allatī), and ﴿mā﴾ is among the relative nouns that are not qualified, unlike alladhī and allatī. He used the word "touching" as a euphemism for intercourse, to teach His servants to choose the best expressions in what they say to one another.

﴿Or you specify for them a dowry﴾: here "farīḍa" (الفريضة) means the bridal gift (ṣadāq), and specifying it means naming it. The "aw" (أو) here keeps its usual sense of offering one of two things or several things. The verb after it is conjoined to ﴿tamassūhunna﴾, so it is jussive (majzūm). Or it is conjoined to a supposed underlying verbal noun, so it is in the subjunctive (manṣūb) by the hidden ﴿an﴾ after ﴿aw﴾, with the meaning of ﴿illā﴾ (except). The meaning would be: "as long as you have not touched them, except that you specify for them a dowry." Or it is conjoined to an omitted clause, the meaning being: "you have specified, or you have not specified." Or it has the meaning of waw (and), and the verb is jussive, conjoined to ﴿tamassūhunna﴾. There are four opinions: the first is that of Ibn Atiyya and others; the second is that of al-Zamakhshari; the third belongs to some scholars, whose names were not given; and the fourth is that of al-Sajawandi and others.

According to the first opinion, blame is removed from the divorcing husband when one of two conditions is absent: either intercourse or naming the dowry. As for the absence of intercourse, this is correct. As for the absence of naming the dowry, the ruling is not like this, because a woman who has been consummated with but for whom no dowry was named, the mufawwida (المفوضة, a woman whose dowry was left unspecified), if her husband divorces her, the blame is not removed from him.

According to the second opinion, blame is removed when intercourse is absent, unless a dowry was specified for her. In that case blame is not removed, even if intercourse is absent, because (p-232) the exception was made from the situations in which blame is removed, namely the situation of specifying the dowry, so blame remains in that case.

According to the third opinion, blame is removed only by the absence of intercourse, whether or not a dowry was specified. They said: the meaning of "blame" here is the obligation of the dowry, so it is removed by divorce before intercourse, whether a dowry was specified or not. If one was specified, the obligation shifts to half of it. If none was specified, there is disagreement on this. Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman said: if he divorces her without having consummated the marriage, and had not specified a dowry for her, he is compelled to pay half of the dowry of her equivalent (mahr al-mithl). Others said: she is not entitled to half of the dowry of her equivalent, but only to the mut'ah (متعة, a provision of maintenance given to a divorced woman). In this third opinion there is an omission of a clause, namely the words "you have specified," and the omission of "lam" (لم) after "aw," which is not permitted except when it is conjoined to a jussive verb, as in: "I did not stand and ride," according to the view of those who regard the governing particle of the conjoined word as implied after the conjunction particle.

According to the fourth opinion, blame is removed when intercourse and the naming of the dowry are both absent. If intercourse occurred and naming was absent, she is entitled to the dowry of her equivalent. If intercourse was absent and naming was present, then half of the named amount is due. In these two cases blame is established, and it is removed when both are absent. In this sense "blame" is applied to what is incumbent upon the divorcing husband in light of these two situations.

This verse indicates the permissibility of divorce before consummation, and they agreed on the permissibility of this. Apparently, divorcing a menstruating woman who has not been consummated with is also permissible, because the verse indicates the removal of constraint in divorcing them generally, whether they are menstruating or not. This is the view of most scholars and the well-known position of Malik's school. Malik had an opinion that prohibits divorcing a menstruating woman, whether consummated with or not. The husband's death before consummation and before specifying the dowry is treated as equivalent to divorce before consummation and before specifying the dowry, so she has neither dowry nor inheritance. This was said by Masruq, and it contradicts the principles. Ali, Zayd, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, al-Zuhri, al-Awza'i, Malik, and al-Shafi'i said: she is entitled to inheritance, and has no dowry, but she must observe the waiting period ('idda). Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, a group of the Companions, Abu Hanifa, al-Thawri, Ahmad, and Ishaq said: she is entitled to the dowry of women like her, must observe the waiting period, and is entitled to inheritance.

The apparent meaning of the verse indicates the validity of a marriage of delegation (nikah al-tafwid, a marriage in which the dowry is left unspecified), which is permissible according to the jurists of the major cities, because He, exalted is He, divided the situation of the divorced woman into two categories: a divorced woman for whom nothing was specified, and a divorced woman for whom something was specified. If he did not specify for her, and the divorce occurred before consummation, then by consensus no dowry is due to her. This was said by the judge Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi. The disagreement of Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman on this has already been mentioned, and that she is entitled to half of the dowry of her equivalent. If a dowry less than the dowry of her equivalent is specified after the contract, she is not obliged to surrender herself; if it is the dowry of her equivalent, she is obliged to surrender, and she may withhold herself until she receives her dowry.

Abu Bakr al-Asamm and Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: this verse indicates that a marriage contract without a dowry is permissible. The judge said: it does not indicate permissibility, but it indicates validity. As for its indication of validity: if it were not valid, divorce would not be legislated and maintenance would not be obligatory. As for its not indicating permissibility: validity does not necessarily entail permissibility, as evidenced by the fact that divorce during menstruation is forbidden, yet it takes effect as valid.

(And provide for them), that is: give them possession of what they may enjoy, and that thing is called mut'ah. The apparent meaning of this command is obligation. This was reported from Ali, Ibn Umar, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, Abu Qilaba, Qatada, al-Zuhri, and al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim. Shurayh, al-Hakam, Ibn Abi Layla, Malik, al-Layth, and Abu Ubayd took it to mean recommendation. The subject pronoun in "(and provide for them)" refers to the divorcing husbands, and the object pronoun refers to the women divorced before consummation and before the dowry was specified; for them the mut'ah is obligatory. This was the view of Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Jabir ibn Zayd, al-Hasan, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, and the proponents of personal opinion (ashab al-ra'y). For other divorced women it is recommended. It was reported from Ali, al-Hasan, Abu al-Aliya, and al-Zuhri that every divorced woman is entitled to mut'ah. If a dowry had been specified for her and she was divorced before consummation, Ibn Umar, Shurayh, Ibrahim, and Muhammad ibn Ali said: she has no mut'ah; rather, half of what was specified for her suffices her. Abu Thawr said: she is entitled to mut'ah, and so is every divorced woman.

The jurists of the major cities differed. Abu Hanifa, Abu Yusuf, Zufar, and Muhammad said: mut'ah is obligatory for a woman who was not consummated with and for whom no dowry was specified; if he consummated with her, he provides mut'ah for her, but he is not compelled to it. This is also the view of al-Thawri, al-Hasan ibn Salih, and al-Awza'i, except that al-Awza'i claimed that if one of the spouses is a slave, mut'ah is not obligatory, even if he divorces her before consummation. Ibn Abi Layla and Abu al-Zinad said: mut'ah is not obligatory, and they did not distinguish between a woman who was consummated with, one for whom a dowry was specified, and one for whom none was specified. Malik said: mut'ah is due to every divorced woman, whether consummated with or not, except a woman subjected to li'an (the oath of mutual imprecation), a woman who obtained khul' (divorce at her request by paying compensation), and a woman divorced before consummation for whom a dowry was specified. Al-Shafi'i said: mut'ah is due to every divorced woman if the separation came from him, except the one for whom he specified a dowry and then divorced before consummation. Ahmad said: mut'ah is obligatory for a woman divorced before consummation if no dowry was specified for her; but if he consummated with her, there is no mut'ah, and she is entitled to the dowry of her equivalent. It was reported from al-Awza'i, al-Thawri, and Abu Hanifa, and Ata', al-Nakha'i, and al-Tirmidhi also said: a woman who obtained khul' is entitled to mut'ah. The proponents of personal opinion said: a woman subjected to li'an is entitled to mut'ah. Ibn al-Qasim said: there is no mut'ah in a marriage that has been annulled (nikah mansukh, a marriage that has been dissolved or annulled). Ibn al-Mawwaz said: nor in any case where the marriage is dissolved after the contract is valid, such as one spouse coming into possession of the other. Ibn Wahb reported from Malik that a woman given the choice (al-mukhayyara) is entitled to mut'ah, unlike a slave woman freed while married to a slave husband, who then chooses; for her there is no mut'ah.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that mut'ah is due only to one of two kinds of divorced women: a woman divorced before consummation, whether or not a dowry was specified for her; and a woman divorced before the dowry was specified, whether or not she was consummated with. The discussion of His words: ﴿For divorced women is a provision in kindness﴾ [al-Baqara: 241] will come, if Allah, exalted is He, wills.

﴿Upon the affluent according to his means, and upon the straitened according to his means﴾. This confirms that the provision (mut'ah) is obligatory, since it comes after the command, which apparently indicates obligation, and it uses the particle ﴿upon﴾ (ʿalā), which is used to express obligation, as in His words: ﴿And upon the father of the child is their provision﴾ [al-Baqarah: 233], and ﴿upon them is half of what is upon the chaste women of punishment﴾ [an-Nisa': 25].

The ﴿muwsi'﴾ (al-mūsiʿ) is the wealthy one (al-mūsir), and the ﴿muqtir﴾ (al-muqtir) is the one whose circumstances are constricted. Its apparent meaning is that the husband's circumstances are considered. Whoever considers the wife's circumstances alone, or the circumstances of both the husband and the wife, contradicts the apparent meaning. This measure has come unspecified, so its method is ijtihad (independent legal reasoning, juristic effort) and the predominance of probable opinion (ghalabat al-ẓann), since nothing fixed has been stated concerning it.

The meaning of ﴿qadaruhu﴾ is the amount the husband is able to bear. Ibn ʿUmar said: its least is thirty dirhams or its equivalent. Ibn ʿAbbas said: its highest is a servant, then clothing, then maintenance. ʿAṭāʾ said: from the middle of that is a long shirt (dirʿ), a head-covering (khimār), and a wrap (milḥafah). Al-Ḥasan said: each one provides according to his capacity; this one with a servant, this one with garments, this one with a garment, this one with maintenance. This is also the view of Mālik. Al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī provided twenty thousand and jars of honey; he provided ʿĀʾishah al-Khathʿamiyyah with ten thousand, and she said: "A little provision from a beloved who is parting." Sharīḥ provided five hundred dirhams. Ibn Mujīz said: upon the holder of the register (ṣāḥib al-dīwān) is three dinars. Ibn al-Musayyab said: the best provision is a head-covering, and the least of it is a garment. Ḥammād said: he provides her with half the dowry of her equivalent (mahr mithlihā).

It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he "said to a man from the Anṣār who had married a woman without naming a dowry for her, then divorced her before touching her: ('Did you provide for her?') He said: 'I had nothing.' He said: ('Provide for her with your cap.')."

According to Abū Ḥanīfah, it must not be less than five dirhams, because the least dowry in his view is ten dirhams, so the provision must not fall below half of it. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf provided his wife, the mother of his son Abū Salamah, with a black servant. All these measures issued from their individual ijtihad, and some of them did not object to what others had reached. This indicates that these amounts are, in their view, set according to what ijtihad leads to. They are like the valuation of destroyed property and the compensation (urush) for injuries that have no fixed known measures; rather, that is according to what ijtihad leads to, and this is from the issue of valuing destroyed property.

Al-Jumhūr read ﴿ʿalā al-mūsiʿ﴾ as an active participle (ism fāʿil) from awsaʿa. Abū Ḥaywah read ﴿al-mūwassaʿ﴾ with a fatḥah on the wāw and the sīn and with shaddah, as a passive participle (ism mafʿūl) from wassaʿa. Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, and Abū Bakr read ﴿qadruhu﴾ with sukūn on the dāl in both places. Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥafṣ, Yazīd, and Rawḥ read it with fatḥah on the dāl in both places. Both are two eloquent dialects with the same meaning, as related by Abū Zayd, al-Akhfash, and others. Its meaning is what the husband is able to bear. Most of the imams of Arabic grammar hold that the two have one meaning. It has been said that the unvocalised form (with sukūn) is a maṣdar (verbal noun), and the vocalised form (with fatḥah) is an ism (noun), like ʿadd and ʿadad, and madd and madad. The qadr with sukūn was used to mean capacity (wus'): one says, "He spends according to his qadr," meaning according to his capacity. Abū Jaʿfar said: it is most often used with fatḥah when it is equal to something; one says, "This is according to the qadar of that."

It was also read ﴿qadara hu﴾ with fatḥah on the rāʾ, and they permitted two possibilities for its accusative: first, that it is in the accusative according to the meaning, because the meaning of ("And provide for them") is that each of you should give according to the measure of his capacity. Second, by supposing a verb, the estimate being: "And make obligatory upon the wealthy one his qadar." In al-Sajāwandī: Ibn Abī ʿAbalah read ﴿qadara hu﴾, meaning qaddarahu Allāh (God determined it). End of quotation. This shows that he read with fatḥah on the dāl and the rāʾ, so it is then a past-tense verb, and he made within it a concealed pronoun referring to God, and made the attached pronoun refer to the provision indicated by His words ("And provide for them"). The meaning: God determined and prescribed the provision upon the wealthy and upon the straitened. In the sentence there is an omitted pronoun whose estimate is: "upon the wealthy among you." It may be said that the definite article (al-) has taken the place of the pronoun, meaning: "upon your wealthy and upon your straitened." This sentence may be a new independent clause clarifying the state of the one who divorces in respect of provision, relative to his affluence and his straitness. It may also be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), the entity of the circumstance being the pronoun raised in His words ("And provide for them"), and the connecting element being that omitted pronoun we estimated as "among you."

﴿Provision in kindness﴾. They said: ﴿matāʿan﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar). Its clarification: the mataʿ is that by which one is provided, so it is a noun for it; then it was applied to the verbal noun by way of metaphor (majāz). The governing element for it is ("And provide for them"). Had it come according to the original verbal noun of ("And provide for them"), it would be tamtīʿan. Al-Zamakhsharī also estimated it so. They permitted that it be in the accusative as a circumstantial clause, the governing element of which is what the prepositional phrase depends on, and the owner of the circumstance is the concealed pronoun in that governing element. The estimate: the qadar of the wealthy one is settled upon him in the state of being provision. ﴿bil-maʿrūf﴾ depends on His words ("And provide for them"), or on an omitted element; then it is an attribute of ﴿matāʿan﴾, meaning: connected with what is known. The maʿrūf is what is familiar by sharia and by decency, and it is what carries no burden of excess or undue strain.

﴿A duty upon the doers of good﴾. This also confirms the obligation of provision. What is meant is the goodness of faith and Islam. It has been said: what is meant is goodness in companionship (iḥsān al-ʿishrah). Then God named them "doers of good" before the act, on account of what they will come to of goodness, like the saying: "Whoever kills a slain man, for him is his spoils." The accusative of ﴿ḥaqqan﴾ is as an attribute of ﴿matāʿan﴾, meaning: a provision in kindness, obligatory upon the doers of good; or by supposing a verb whose estimate is: "That is due, as a due"; or as a circumstantial clause of what was a circumstantial clause from it, ﴿matāʿan﴾, or from His words ﴿bil-maʿrūf﴾, meaning: by what is known, in the state of being upon the doers of good.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 237 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them, and you have already set a bridal gift for them, then half of what you have set.﴾ When he had explained the case of the divorced woman before consummation and before the setting of a bridal gift, he explained the case of the divorced woman before consummation and after the setting of the gift. The intended meaning of "touching" (al-masis) is intercourse (al-jima'), and of "obligation" (al-fari'a) is the dower (al-sadaq). The clause "and you have already set" (wa-qad faradtum) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). It covers both the obligation set at the time of the contract and the obligation set after the contract but before the divorce. So if he set a dower for her after the contract and then divorced her after setting it, the dower is halved by the divorce, because of the generality of the verse. This differs from Abu Hanifa, for in his view it is not halved, since it was not due by the contract; so she has the mahr al-mithl (the customary dower), as with the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i. He then returned to the view of his two companions. The answer to the conditional is "then half of what you have set" (fa-nisfu ma faradtum). The nominative "half" (nisfu) is the subject of a nominal sentence, and the predicate is understood as "then upon you is half of what you have set" or "then for them is half of what you have set." It is permissible to understand it as delayed, and it is permissible for it to be the predicate, meaning: "so what is obligatory is half of what you have set."
