A group read fa-nisfa with a fatha on the fa', meaning: "then pay half of what you have set." The apparent meaning of "what you have set" is that if he gave her a dower in goods ('aradh), and it remained until the time of divorce and increased or decreased, then its increase and decrease belong to both of them, and it is halved. If it was a specific thing, gold or silver, and she bought goods with it, and it increased or decreased, then he is entitled only to half of what he gave of the specific thing, not of the goods, because the goods are not what was set. Malik said: these goods are like the specific thing; the principal of their price is halved. This is a derivation based on whether it becomes clear that his ownership of half remains, or whether it returns to him after she has come to own it. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that only what was set is halved. So if he gave her something as a gift in the contract, or before it for the sake of it, it is not halved. It was said: it is in the sense of the dower. The apparent meaning of the verse is that divorce before intercourse and after the setting of the dower (p. 235) requires halving of the dower, whether he was alone with her, or kissed her, or embraced her, or the stay with her was prolonged. This is the view of al-Shafi'i and al-Hasan ibn Salih, and she has no waiting period ('idda). It is narrated from Ali, Amr ibn Umar, Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn Abbas, Ali ibn al-Hasan, and Ibrahim that she has the full dower by seclusion alone (al-khalwa). Malik said: if he was alone with her and kissed her or uncovered her, and that was recent, she has half the dower; if it was prolonged, she has the full dower, unless she waives part of it. Al-Thawri said: if he was alone with her and did not go in to her, and that was from his side, she has the full dower; if she was barren (ratqa'), she has half the dower. Abu Hanifa, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad, and Zufar said: valid seclusion (al-khalwa al-sahiha) prevents the falling away of any part of the dower after divorce, whether he had intercourse or not. Seclusion is valid when neither of them is in ihram, or sick, or menstruating, or fasting in Ramadan, or barren. When it is so, and then he divorces her, she is due half the dower if he did not have intercourse with her. The waiting period is obligatory in all these cases; if he divorces her, she observes the waiting period. Al-Awza'i said: if he went in to her at her family's house, kissed her or touched her, then divorced her without having intercourse, and he had drawn a curtain over her or closed a door, then the dower is complete. Al-Layth said: if he drew a curtain over her, the dower is due. The majority read fa-nisfu with a kasra on the nun and a damma on the fa'. Al-Sulami read it with a damma on the nun, and this is the reading of Ali and al-Asma'i from Abu Amr, and across the whole Qur'an. It has been mentioned that this is a dialect (lugha). Restricting the statement to ﴿then half of what you have set﴾ indicates that a woman divorced before touching, for whom a dower was set, is entitled to nothing but half. Malik and others said likewise that this verse excludes the woman divorced after the setting of the dower and before touching from the ruling of provision (al-tamti'), since the phrase ﴿and provide for them﴾ had already included her. Ibn al-Musayyab said: this verse abrogated (naskh) the verse of al-Ahzab. Qatada said: it abrogated the verse before it. Zayd ibn Aslam claimed that it is abrogated. A group of scholars, among them Abu Thawr, said: this verse makes clear that the woman for whom a dower was set takes half of what was set, and the verse does not address the cancellation of her provision; rather she has the provision and half of what was set. The discussion of some of this has already preceded.

﴿except that they forgo﴾ Ibn Attiyya and others stated that this is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), as Ibn Attiyya said; because their forgoing half is not of the same kind as their taking it, and the meaning is: except that they leave the half which became due to them from the husband. End. It was said: this is not as they proposed; rather it is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), but it is one of circumstances (min al-ahwal), because his statement ﴿then half of what you have set﴾ means: upon you is half of what you have set in every case, except in the case of their forgoing it from you; then it is not due. Even if the estimate is "then for them is half," the obligation is what you have set. Likewise, that it is an exception of circumstances is clear. An example of it is ﴿you will bring it to me unless you are encircled﴾ (Yusuf 12:66). However, Sibawayh prohibited that "an" and its clause occur as a circumstance, so according to Sibawayh's view, ﴿except that they forgo﴾ is a disjunctive exception. Al-Hasan read: ﴿except that they forgo it﴾, with the ha' referring to the half, and the original is "they forgo from it," meaning from the half, so they do not take it. Some said: the ha' is for pausal pronunciation (li-l-istirahah), as some interpreted that in the line of the poet:

"They are the doers of good and those who command it, through the lengths of the days, as long as righteousness is practiced."

It was given movement by analogy with the pronominal ha', and this is a weak justification. Ibn Abi Ishaq read: ﴿except that you (fem.) forgo﴾ with the ta' and two dots from above, by way of iltifat (shift of address), since their pronoun in "for them" and what precedes it is third person, so he turned to them and addressed them directly. In his address to them and making this forgoing, there is an indication of recommending and encouraging it. Al-Zamakhshari distinguished between your saying "the men forgo" (al-rijal ya'funa) and "the women forgo" (al-nisa' ya'fina): in the first the waw is a pronoun and the nun is the sign of the nominative, while in the second the waw is the verb's radical and the nun is their pronoun, and the verb is built (mabni) so that the governing word has no effect on its form. End of his distinction. This is from clear grammar, which is grasped with minimal study of this science; but he omitted to state that the radical of the verb in "the men forgo" was dropped because it met the following waw of the pronoun in a sukun. He also omitted to mention a dispute about "the women forgo." Ibn Darastawayh among the earlier scholars and al-Suhayli among the later ones held that a verb to which the feminine plural nun is attached is inflected (mu'rab) and not built (mabni), and this is attributed to the words of Sibawayh. The discussion of this question is explained in the science of grammar.

The apparent meaning of ﴿except that they forgo﴾ is generality for every woman divorced before touching for whom a dower was set; she may forgo it. They said: generality is intended here as specificity (khusus). Every woman who controls her own affair may forgo. As for one who is under guardianship (hijab) or a guardian (wasi), it is not permissible for her to forgo. As for the virgin who has no guardian (wali), Ibn Abbas and a group of the Successors and jurists said that it is permissible for her. Sahnun transmitted from Ibn al-Qasim that it is not permissible for her.

﴿or the one in whose hand is the tie of marriage forgoes﴾. This is the husband. So said Ali, Ibn Abbas, Jubayr ibn Mut'im, Shurayh (who returned to it), Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Jabir ibn Zayd, al-Dahhak, Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Ibn Shubrumah, and Abu Hanifa, and this is mentioned from al-Shafi'i. His forgoing is that he gives her the full dower. It is narrated that Jubayr ibn Mut'im married and divorced before consummation, and he completed the dower and said: "I have more right to forgiveness." This was called forgoing either by way of mushakala (correspondence of wording), because before it is ﴿except that they forgo﴾, or because it was their custom that they would hand over the dower at the time of marriage. Do you not see the Prophet's (ﷺ) words to Ali (may God ennoble his face): "Where is your Hutamiyya coat of mail?" meaning that he should give it as dower to Fatima (may God's blessings be upon the Messenger of God and upon her). Thus he called the abandonment of their taking half of what they had given "forgoing" from it. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Alqama, Tawus, al-Sha'bi, Ibrahim, Mujahid, Shurayh, Abu Salih, Ikrima, al-Zuhri, Malik, al-Shafi'i, and others that it is the guardian in whose charge the woman is: so he is the father regarding his daughter who does not control her affair, and the master regarding his slave-woman. Shurayh permitted a brother's forgoing of half the dower, and said: "I forgo the dowers of the Banu Murra, even if they dislike it." Ikrima said: it is permissible that he forgo, whether paternal uncle, brother, or father, even if she dislikes it; and the particle "or" (aw) here is for the distinction of the forgoing. ﴿Except that they forgo﴾ applies if they are among those whose forgoing is valid, or their guardian forgoes if their forgoing is not valid. The "or" here is for choice (li-l-takhyir), meaning: they have the choice between forgoing themselves or their guardian forgoing.

He preferred that it is the guardian, because it is remote that the divorcing husband should be described as one "in whose hand is the tie of marriage," or that his completing the dower should be called forgoing, or that his affair should be left obscure as if ambiguous, when he has been made clear by direct address in ﴿then half of what you have set﴾. If it had come in the same clarifying form, it would be: "except that they forgo, or you forgo, and do not forget graciousness among yourselves." This indicates that it is a third level, since he mentioned the husbands, then the wives, then the guardians. It is answered regarding the first point: ﴿in whose hand is the tie of marriage﴾ refers to him in respect of having contracted it previously, so he expressed the previous state by this, in accordance with the text that preceded in ﴿and do not resolve upon the tie of marriage﴾ (2:235), and the intended meaning of it is address to husbands. Regarding the second: it is by way of mushakala, or because he had handed the dower to her, which has already been mentioned. Regarding the third: there is no ambiguity in it, and it is a case of iltifat, since there is a shift from address to third-person reference. We said there is no ambiguity, and that it must be the husband, because the scholars agree that a father may not give away any of his daughter's property, neither to a husband nor to anyone else; so likewise the dower, since there is no difference. It is possible that his statement ﴿in whose hand is the tie of marriage﴾ is by omission of a modifier (hadhf mudaf), meaning: in whose hand is the untying of the tie of marriage, as they said regarding ﴿do not resolve upon the tie of marriage﴾ (2:235), meaning: upon the tie of marriage. If we suppose that his statement ﴿or the one in whose hand is the tie of marriage forgoes﴾ belongs to the ambiguous (mutashabih) verses, it would be obligatory to refer it back to the clear (muhkam). God the Exalted said: ﴿And give the women their bridal gifts as a free gift; but if they are pleased to give you of it willingly, then consume it with ease and wholesomeness﴾ (4:4). He said: ﴿and you have given one of them a heap of gold, take nothing from it﴾ (4:20). He said: ﴿and it is not lawful for you to take back anything of what you have given them, unless both fear that they will not keep within the bounds of God﴾ (2:229), to the end of the verse. This verse is clear (muhkam), indicating that the guardian has no entitlement in any taking of the wife's property. It was also preferred that it is the husband, because the tie of marriage was in the hand of the guardian and it passed into the hand of the husband; and because forgoing is only used of a person's ownership, and the guardian's forgoing is forgoing of what he does not own; and because his statement ﴿and do not forget graciousness among yourselves﴾ indicates that the graciousness is in a person's giving of his own property, not of another's property.

Al-Hasan read: ﴿or yafu﴾ with the waw made quiescent (sukun), so it drops in connected speech because it meets the quiescent letter after it; then when he pauses he restores it. He did this out of distaste for the fatha on the weak letter (harf al-'illa), so the fatha on it is estimated, as it is estimated on the alif in the example "lan yakhsha." Most Arabs lighten the fatha on the waw and the ya' in examples such as "lan yarmiya" and "lan yaghzuwa," so much so that our companions (the grammarians) stated that making it quiescent is a necessity of poetry. The poet said:

"Amir did not make me chief through inheritance; God refused that I should rise through a mother or a father."

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: What appears to me is that he (the reader) found a fatḥa (short vowel "a") burdensome on a waw that is final and preceded by a vowelled letter, because such a form is rare in the speech of the Arabs. Al-Khalīl (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "There does not occur in speech a final waw with fatḥa preceded by fatḥa except in their saying ʿafawa, which is the plural of ʿafw, the young of a donkey. Likewise, any vowel that precedes a waw with fatḥa is heavy." End of his words. His saying "because of its rarity in the speech of the Arabs, meaning with fatḥa and a fatḥa before it" concerns this point, which has detail. The vowel before it is either a ḍamma, a fatḥa or a kasra. If it is a ḍamma, then it is either in a verb or in a noun. If it is in a verb, it is not rare; rather, every imperfect verb, when a nāṣib (accusative-governing particle) enters on it or the emphatic nūn (nūn al-tawkīd) attaches to it, as is established in its chapter, takes fatḥa, as in lan yaghzuwa (he will not invade), hal yaghzūna (do they invade?), and the imperative ughzuna (invade!). Likewise the past tense on the pattern faʿula, as in saruwa al-rajul (the man became noble), and even what is formed from the defective (ṭ-ya) roots on faʿula, where you say laqaḍuwa al-rajul (the man was capable) and laramuwat al-yad (the hand was paralysed). This is a regular analogy as established in its chapter. If it is in a noun, then either it is formed with the feminine tāʾ (ha of feminine), or not. If it is formed with the feminine ha, it occurs frequently, as in ʿarquwa, tarquwa, qamaḥduwa and ʿanṣuwa, and issues of morphology (ʿilm al-taṣrīf) are built upon it. If the vowel is a fatḥa, then it is rare, as al-Khalīl mentioned. If the vowel is a kasra, the waw is changed to yāʾ in it, as in al-ghāzī and al-ghāziya, and al-ʿarīqiyya. Exceptional from this are: aqruwa, plural of qarw, which is the dog's licking-vessel; sawāsiwa, meaning those who are equal in evil; and maqātiwa, plural of muqtaw, which is the groom, the servant. The alif and lām in al-nikāḥ (the marriage) are for prior reference (ʿahd), meaning "the knot belonging to it." Al-Maghribī said: This is according to the method of the Basrans. Others said: the alif and lām replace a possessive (idāfa), meaning "his marriage," and a poet said:

"They have a disposition that Allah has not given to others, among people, and their dreams are not unsound."

That is: "and their dreams," and this is according to the method of the Kufans.

﴿And that you pardon is nearer to piety﴾: this is addressed to the husband and the wife, with the masculine dominating. So said Ibn ʿAbbas. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: Allah addressed everyone out of courtesy by His saying "and that you pardon is nearer to piety," meaning: O all of mankind. End of his words. What appears is that it is addressed to the husbands only, and this is also said by al-Shaʿbī, since they are the ones addressed at the beginning of the verse. This would be an iltifāt (shift), since it moved from the third-person pronoun, referring to the one in whose hand is the knot of marriage, as we chose in its interpretation, to the second-person address with which the beginning of the verse opened. That the husband's pardon is nearer to piety is because he has broken the heart of his divorcée; so he consoles her by paying her the full dowry, since she has lost his companionship, so she does not lose his gift. For there is nothing harder for women than divorce. When he gives her the full dower, she does not despair of his returning to her, and she feels that she is desired by him, and so she is consoled by that.

Al-Shaʿbī and Abu Nahīk read "wa-an yaʿfuwa" with the yāʾ and two dots below, making it third person, and it is pluralised according to the sense of "the one in whose hand is the knot of marriage," since it is generic and is not meant as one individual. It was said: this reading supports that the pardon is attributed to the husbands. It was said: pardon is nearer for each of them to avoid wronging the other. It was also said: for avoiding the disobedience of Allah.

"Aqrab" takes the preposition lām in this usage, and takes ilā as in His saying: ﴿And We are nearer to him﴾ [al-Waqiʿa: 85]. It is not said that lām means ilā, nor that lām is for causation; rather it is by way of transitivity, in the sense of the object reached by means of the prepositional particle. So the meaning of lām and the meaning of ilā are close in terms of transitivity. It has been said that lām means ilā, which would be a case of the substitution of particles (tadmīn al-ḥurūf), but the Basrans do not hold this. It was also said that lām is for causation, indicating the reason why pardon becomes nearer to piety by leaving it, and the comparative's point of reference is omitted; what made this acceptable is that the elative (ʾafʿal al-tafḍīl) occurs as the predicate of the subject. The sense is: "and pardon from you is nearer to piety than the abandonment of pardon."

﴿And do not forget graciousness among yourselves﴾: the address here has the same disagreement as in "and that you pardon." Forgetting here means abandoning, as in ﴿They forgot Allah, so He forgot them﴾ [al-Tawba: 67]. Graciousness (faḍl) is doing what is not obligatory of goodness. So from the husband it is completing the dowry, and from the wife it is leaving her half that is due to her. This was said by Mujahid. If the intended one is the husband, then it is completing the dowry. Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim entered upon Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, and he offered him his daughter, and he married her. When he left he divorced her and sent her the full dowry. He was asked: Why did you marry her? He said: She was offered to me and I disliked to refuse her. It was said: Why did you send the full dowry? He said: Then where is the graciousness?

ʿAlī, Mujahid, Abu Ḥaywa and Ibn Abi ʿAbla read "wa-lā tanāsawu al-faḍl" (do not be forgetful of... with mutual forgetting). Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: This is a reading whose meaning is well-established, since it is a place of mutual forgetting, not forgetting, except by way of likeness. End of his words. Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar read "wa-lā tansawi al-faḍl" with a kasra on the waw, according to the original principle of meeting two unvowelled letters, likening the waw that is a pronoun to the waw of law in His saying: (la-wi-staṭaʿnā). Just as they likened the waw of law to the waw of the pronoun, so they gave it a ḍamma.

He read "la-wi-staṭaʿnā" with a ḍamma on the waw, and "baynakum" governed by the verb prohibited. The word "bayna" indicates intervening and mutual relations, as in His saying: ﴿And do not eat your properties among yourselves in falsehood﴾ [al-Baqara: 188]. So this is more eloquent than a prohibition concerning something that would not occur among them, because the prohibited act, if it occurred, would be well known among them, something they had agreed upon and known about, since what passes between people is known to them.

﴿Indeed Allah is seeing of what you do﴾: He concluded this verse with this attribute indicating things that are seen, because what preceded it of pardon from the divorced women and the divorcing men, namely that he pays half of what they received or completes the dowry for them, is something witnessed and visible, so it fitted to bring the attribute related to visible things. Since the end of His saying: ﴿And those who are taken in death from among you﴾ [al-Baqara: 234] and His saying ﴿There is no blame on you concerning what they do with themselves﴾ [al-Baqara: 234] concerns matters perceived with subtlety and obscurity, He concluded that with ﴿And Allah is Aware of what you do﴾ [al-Baqara: 234]. In concluding this verse with ﴿Indeed Allah is seeing of what you do﴾ there is a beautiful promise for the doer of good and a deprivation for the one who is not a doer of good.

This noble verse and the one before it contain kinds of eloquence and branches of the science of rhetoric and eloquence: kināya (metonymy) in "an tamassūhunna"; tajnīs mughāyir (non-identical paronomasia) in "faraḍtum lahunna farīḍa"; ṭibāq (antithesis) in "al-mūsiʿ wa-al-muqtir"; emphasis by two verbal nouns in "matāʿan" and "ḥaqqan"; restriction (ikhtiṣāṣ) in "ḥaqqan ʿalā al-muḥsinīn." It may also be tatmīm (completion): when He said "ḥaqqan," it conveyed obligation; when He said "ʿalā al-muḥsinīn" it completed the meaning and showed that it is a matter of grace and goodness, not of obligation; and it generalised the sense and showed that it is a matter of grace and goodness, not of obligation. Also iltifāt (shift of address) in "wa-an taʿfū" and "wa-lā tansaw," and the departure from literal to figurative in "alladhī biyadihi ʿuqdatu al-nikāḥ," where the offer and acceptance are expressed by "the knot," which is literally tied, because of the binding of each of the spouses to the other in that contract.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 238 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Guard strictly the prayers﴾. They said: This verse is interposed between the verses concerning the widow and the divorced women, and it precedes them in revelation but comes after them in recitation and in the written arrangement of the Mushaf. They compared it to His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾ [al-Baqarah: 67], and to His words: ﴿And when you killed a soul﴾ [al-Baqarah: 72]. They said: It is possible that it is placed in sequence after the verses in which fighting is mentioned, because it explains the rules of prayer in a state of fear. They said: There has come what is connected to something even more remote than this. They claimed that His words, exalted is He: ﴿It is not by your wishful thinking, nor by the wishful thinking of the People of the Book﴾ [an-Nisa': 123], are a response to His words: ﴿And they say, None will enter Paradise unless he is a Jew or a Christian﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111]. They said: And more remote than that: ﴿A questioner asked about a punishment that will surely occur﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 1] refers back to His words: ﴿And when they said, O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], and so on. They said: It is possible that a state of fear occurred before the revelation of the completion of the rulings concerning divorced women, so Allah, exalted is He, explained the rulings of the prayer of fear when the need to explain it was pressing, then He revealed the completion of the rulings concerning divorced women. They said: It is possible that it is earlier in recitation and in the written arrangement of the Mushaf, but later in revelation, before these verses, according to His words after this verse: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 244]. All of these are sayings, as you see. What appears regarding the connection (munasabah) is that when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned a great number of the matters of husbands and wives and their rulings regarding marriage, intercourse, oaths of abstention (iyla'), divorce, reconciliation (raj'ah), breastfeeding, maintenance, clothing, the waiting period ('iddah), betrothal, provision (mut'ah), dowry (sadaq), the division of property (tashattur), and other things, these were great obligations that occupy whoever is charged with them with the greatest occupation, such that hardly anything of other deeds can fit alongside them. Each of the two spouses had made obligatory upon the other what consumes their time and reaches their utmost effort, and He commanded each of them to be good to the other, even in the state of separation. These matters could be an incitement to laziness in occupying oneself with worship, except for whomever Allah, exalted is He, grants success. So He commanded the guarding of the prayers, which are the means between Allah and His servant. And if He commanded the guarding of the rights of the children of Adam, then commanding the fulfilment of the rights of Allah is more fitting and more deserving; for this reason came: (The debt owed to Allah is more deserving of being paid). It is as if it were said: Let not your attachment to women and their affairs preoccupy you from fulfilling what Allah has enjoined upon you. Despite those great preoccupations, the guarding of the prayer is indispensable, even in a state of fear, so it must be performed on foot or while riding. And if the state of fear is more severe than the state of being preoccupied with women, then when this extremely arduous state still requires the prayer, what is less than it of the preoccupations connected with women is all the more so. It has been said: The connection of the command to guard the prayers immediately after the preceding commands is that prayer forbids indecency and wrongdoing, so that becomes a help to them in carrying out those commands and a safeguard for them against violating them. It has been said: The way it is connected to what precedes and what follows is that when Allah, exalted is He, commanded the guarding of the rights of creatures with His words: ﴿And do not forget graciousness among yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237], it was fitting that He command the guarding of the rights of the Truth. Then, since the rights of the children of Adam include what relates to life, which He has mentioned, and what relates to death, He mentioned it after that in His words: ﴿And those of you who die and leave wives, a bequest﴾ [al-Baqarah: 240], and so on. The address with (guard) is to all believers, and whether it includes the disbelievers is a matter of disagreement. (Guard) is of the pattern of: tarraqtu an-na'l (I repaired the sandal). When the meaning of repetition and persistence was implied, it was made transitive with 'ala. Some have sought to keep the verb on its more common meaning of mutual participation between two parties, so they made the guarding a matter between the servant and the Lord, as if it were said: Guard this prayer and Allah, who commanded it, will guard you. The meaning of guarding here is: constancy in its performance, or persistence in performing it at the beginning of its times, or completing its obligations and sunnas, or all of what has preceded: four sayings. The definite article in it is for the known (al-'ahd), and it refers to: the five prayers. They said: Every prayer in the Qur'an that is linked with guarding refers to the five prayers.
﴿And the middle prayer﴾. Al-Wusta: the feminine form of al-awsat (the middlemost), as a Bedouin said praising the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ):
"O most central of people in all their glories, and most noble of people in mother and in father, a dutiful one."

This is the Qur'anic term for the best or most excellent of a thing, and the most just of it, as one says: "So-and-so is from the *wasatah* (the middle, best) of his people," meaning from their notables. Is *al-Wusta* ("the middle") so named because it lies between two things, from *wasata* (to be in the middle), as when someone is "in the middle between two things"? Or is it from *wasata qawmahu* (he surpassed his people), meaning he excelled them? There are two opinions on this. What Arabic grammar requires is that *al-Wusta* be the feminine of *al-awsat* (the middle, in the sense of the superlative), with the meaning of *al-fudla*, the feminine of *al-afdal* (the best). This is like the line of verse that we have quoted: "O best (awsat) of people." That is because the elative form (*af'al al-tafdil*, the comparative/superlative pattern) is formed only from things that admit of increase and decrease. The same applies to the form of exclamation (*fi'l al-ta'ajjub*, the exclamatory construction). Anything that does not admit of increase or decrease cannot be formed into either of them. Do you not see that you do not say "Zayd is the deadest (*amwat*) of people," nor "How dead Zayd is!" (*ma amwata Zaydan*), because death is something that admits of neither increase nor decrease? Given this, the state of a thing being in the middle between two things does not admit of increase or decrease, so the elative cannot be formed from it, because there is no excelling in it. It is therefore settled that *al-Wusta* means "the most excellent and the most just," because that meaning admits of gradation. The prayer *al-Wusta* was singled out for mention, although it was already included in the general category of the prayers before it, to draw attention to its excellence over the other prayers. This is like the way He drew attention to the excellence of Gabriel and Michael by singling them out for mention in His saying: ﴿And His angels and His messengers, and Gabriel and Michael﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:98). It also draws attention to the excellence of those prophets who were singled out and mentioned separately after His saying: ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah﴾ (al-Ahzab 33:7), and to the excellence of the date palm and the pomegranate in His saying: ﴿In them are fruit, and date palms, and pomegranates﴾ (al-Rahman 55:68). We have already discussed this type of singling out in His saying: ﴿And His angels and His messengers, and Gabriel and Michael﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:98).

The scholars differed greatly, among the Companions, the Successors and the jurists after them, about what is meant by the middle prayer. For this reason Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: "The Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) were in the middle prayer like this," and he interlaced his fingers. What has been collected from the opinions is as follows.

The first: it is the 'Asr (afternoon) prayer. This was said by Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Ayyub, Ibn Umar in one narration, Samurah ibn Jundub, Abu Hurayrah, Ibn Abbas in a narration of Atiyyah, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, A'ishah in one narration, Hafsah, al-Hasan ibn al-Musayyab, Ibn Jubayr, Ata' in one narration, Tawus, al-Dahhak, al-Nakha'i, Ubayd ibn Umayr, Dhirr ibn Hubaysh, Qatadah, Abu Hanifah, Ahmad, al-Shafi'i in one opinion, and Abd al-Malik ibn Habib from the companions of Malik. It is also the view chosen by the Hafiz Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi in his book called *al-Qabas fi Sharh Muwatta' Malik ibn Anas* (The Torch on the Explanation of Malik ibn Anas's Muwatta'), and the view chosen by Abu Muhammad ibn Atiyyah in his tafsir (exegesis). Moreover, it has been widely transmitted in authentic hadith from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said on the day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab): "They have kept us busy from the middle prayer, the prayer of 'Asr. May God fill their hearts and their houses with fire." Ali said: "We used to consider it to be the dawn prayer until the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said that, and then we knew that it was 'Asr." Abu Malik al-Ash'ari and Samurah ibn Jundub related that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The middle prayer is the prayer of 'Asr." In the codex of A'ishah and the dictation of Hafsah, it reads: "and the middle prayer, which is 'Asr." Whoever narrates it as "and the prayer of 'Asr" interprets it as a conjunction joining one descriptive phrase to the other. Ubayy, Ibn Abbas and Ubayd ibn Umayr read: "and the middle prayer, the prayer of 'Asr," in apposition.

The second: it is the Fajr (dawn) prayer. This is related from Umar, Ali in one narration, Abu Musa, Mu'adh, Jabir, Abu Umamah, Ibn Umar in a narration of Mujahid, Anas, Jabir ibn Zayd, Ata', Ikrimah, Tawus in a narration of his son, Mujahid, Abd Allah ibn Shaddad, Malik, and al-Shafi'i in one opinion. Abu al-Aliyah said: "I prayed the morning prayer (al-ghadah) with the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and I asked them: 'Which is the middle prayer?' They said: 'The one you have just prayed.'" (p-241) They also related from Abu Raja' al-Utaridi who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) led us in the morning prayer, and he performed the qunut (supplication) in it before bowing, and he raised his hands. When he finished, he said: 'This is the middle prayer, which we were commanded to perform standing devoutly (qanitin).'"

The third: it is the Zuhr (noon) prayer. This is related from Ibn Umar, Zayd, Usamah, Abu Sa'id and A'ishah. In one narration they said: Zayd ibn Thabit related that "the Prophet (ﷺ) used to pray the midday prayer (al-hajirah) when people were resting in their midday heat, and no one would gather to him, so he spoke about that, and God Most High revealed: ﴿And the middle prayer﴾, meaning the Zuhr." It has also been related that behind him there would be only one or two rows, so the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I have indeed resolved to burn the houses of people who do not attend the prayer." Then this verse was revealed: ﴿Maintain the prayers, and the middle prayer﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:238).

The fourth: it is the Maghrib (sunset) prayer. This is related from Ibn Abbas and Qabisah ibn Dhu'ayb.

The fifth: it is the 'Isha' (night) prayer, the late one. Ali ibn Ahmad al-Nisaburi mentioned it in his tafsir, and Abu Umar ibn Abd al-Barr related it from a group.

The sixth: the middle prayers are the five prayers. This was said by Mu'adh ibn Jabal.

The seventh: it is one of the five prayers, but not specified. This was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, and Abu Bakr al-Warraq, and God concealed it so that all the prayers would be guarded, just as He concealed the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr) in the nights of Ramadan, the Greatest Name of God among the other names, and the moment of answered prayer on Friday. Nafi' related it from Ibn Umar, and al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham said it. It has also been related that there was a revelation: "and the middle prayer, the prayer of 'Asr," and then it was abrogated (*nusikhat*, naskh meaning the cancellation of a ruling by a later revelation) and the revelation became: ﴿Maintain the prayers, and the middle prayer﴾. From this it follows that the abrogation of its specification has occurred, and it was left indefinite after it had been specified. The commentator al-Qurtubi said: "This is the correct view, God willing, because the evidences conflict and there is no preponderance, so nothing remains except to maintain all of them and perform them."

The eighth: it is the Friday prayer, and on other days it is the Zuhr. This is related from Ali, and it was mentioned by Ibn Habib.

The ninth: it is the 'Atamah (late night, i.e. 'Isha') and the dawn prayer. This was said by Umar and Uthman.

The tenth: it is the dawn and 'Asr prayers together. This was said by Abu Bakr al-Abhari of the Maliki jurists.

Each scholar who specified a particular prayer as the middle one supported his view with hadiths that were transmitted about the excellence of that prayer, and some of them were supported by the argument that it lies between such-and-such and such-and-such. But there is no proof in any of this. The mention of the excellence of a particular prayer does not indicate that it is the one God meant by His saying: ﴿And the middle prayer﴾. Also, the fact that it lies between such-and-such and such-and-such cannot be the basis for forming the elative (*af'al al-tafdil*) from it, as we have explained above.

Our shaykh, the imam, the hadith scholar, the unique of his age and the hafiz of his time, Sharaf al-Din Abu Muhammad Abd al-Mu'min ibn Khalaf ibn Abi al-Hasan ibn al-Afif Sharaf ibn al-Khidr ibn Musa al-Dimyati, wrote a book on this subject called *Kitab Kashf al-Mughatta fi Tabyin al-Salat al-Wusta* (The Book of Uncovering the Veiled in Clarifying the Middle Prayer). We read it under his guidance, and in it he preferred that it is the 'Asr prayer, and that this is related explicitly from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Ali ibn Abi Talib related this from him, and it is widely transmitted from him, as are Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, Abd Allah ibn Abbas, Samurah ibn Jundub, Abd Allah ibn Umar, Abu Hurayrah, and Abu Hashim ibn Utbah ibn Rabi'ah. He mentioned in it the remaining of the ten opinions that we have listed, and added seven more opinions:

The first: it is only the Friday prayer. The second: it is congregational prayer in all the prayers. The third: it is the prayer of fear (salat al-khawf). The fourth: it is the witr (odd-numbered) prayer, and this was chosen by Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Muhammad al-Sakhawi, the grammarian and reciter. The fifth: it is the prayer of the 'Id al-Adha (Festival of Sacrifice). The sixth: it is the prayer of the 'Id on the day of al-Fitr (Festival of Breaking the Fast). The seventh: it is the Duha (forenoon) prayer, which was related by some and about which he was uncertain.

If this last opinion is established, the total will be seventeen opinions.

What we should rely on among them is the saying of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), which is that it is the 'Asr prayer. Our shaykh, the hafiz Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him), held this view. He informed us: the transmitter Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Abi al-Tahir Isma'il ibn Abd al-Muhsin al-Dimashqi, through my reading to him in Cairo in the lands of Egypt (may God protect it), from Abu al-Hasan al-Mu'ayyad ibn Muhammad ibn Ali al-Tusi al-Muqri', who said: The jurist of the Haram, Abu Abd Allah Muhammad ibn al-Fadl ibn Ahmad al-Sa'idi, informed us, who said: Abu al-Hasan Abd al-Ghaffar ibn Muhammad ibn Abd al-Ghaffar al-Farisi informed us (ḥ). And our teacher, the scholar Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn Ibrahim ibn al-Zubayr al-Thaqafi informed us, through my reading to him in Granada, from the island of al-Andalus, who said: Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Faraqi informed us, who said: Abu Muhammad Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Ubayd Allah al-Hajari informed us, who said: Abu Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Abd al-Aziz ibn Zughaybah al-Mushawir informed us, who said: Abu al-Abbas Ahmad ibn Umar ibn Anas ibn Dilhath informed us (ḥ). And the judge Abu Ali al-Husayn ibn Abd al-Aziz ibn Abi al-Ahwas informed us, by munawalah (handing over of a text) from Abu al-Qasim Ahmad ibn Umar ibn Ahmad al-Khazraji, who was the last one from whom he transmitted, and none of our shaykhs narrated to us from him except him, from Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Abd Allah ibn Mawhab al-Judhami, who was the last one from whom he transmitted, from Abu al-Abbas ibn Dilhath, who said: Abu al-Abbas Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Mindar informed us in Mecca. Both of them (I mean Abd al-Ghaffar and Ibn Mindar) said: Abu Ahmad Muhammad ibn Isa ibn Amrawayh al-Juludi informed us, who said: Abu Ishaq Ibrahim ibn Muhammad ibn Sufyan the jurist informed us, who said: The hafiz Abu al-Husayn Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj al-Nisaburi informed us, who said: And Awn ibn Salam al-Kufi narrated to us, who said: Muhammad ibn Talhah al-Yami narrated to us, from Zubayd, from Murrah, from Abd Allah, who said: The polytheists kept the Messenger of God (ﷺ) from the 'Asr prayer until the sun turned red or yellow. Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "They have kept us busy from the middle prayer, the prayer of 'Asr. May God fill their bellies and their graves with fire," or: "May God fill their bellies and their graves with fire." Abd Allah read: "and upon the middle prayer," repeating the preposition for emphasis. A'ishah read: "wa-al-salata" (and the prayer) in the accusative, and al-Zamakhshari explained that it is in the accusative by way of praise and specification. It is also possible that it takes account of the position of "upon the prayer," since that is in the accusative, just as you say: "I passed by Zayd and 'Amran" (in the accusative). It is related from Qalun that he read "al-Wusta" with a *sad* (al-Wusta with ṣād, i.e. al-Wuṣṭā), the sin having been changed to a *sad* because of its proximity to the *ta'* (ṭ). The discussion of this has already preceded in His saying: (al-sirat, "the path").

And stand before God in devout obedience (﴿وقُومُوا لِلَّهِ قانِتِينَ﴾). That is, submitting (muti'in), as said by al-Sha'bi, Jabir ibn Zayd, 'Ata', Ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak and al-Hasan. Or humbly attentive (khashi'in), as said by Mujahid. Or prolonging the standing (mutilin al-qiyam), as said by Ibn 'Umar and al-Rabi'. Or supplicating (da'in), as said by Ibn 'Abbas. Or silent (sakitin), as said by al-Suddi. Or worshipping (abidin). Or praying (musallin). Or reciting (qari'in); this was related from Ibn 'Umar. Or remembering God while standing (dhakirin Allah fi al-qiyam), as said by al-Zamakhshari. Or still, restraining the hands and the eyes (rakidin kaffi al-aydi wa al-absar), as said by Mujahid, and this is what he expressed earlier by "humble attentiveness" (al-khushu'). The most apparent reading is to take it as silence, since it is sound that they used to speak during prayer until this verse was revealed, whereupon they were commanded to be silent. The meaning is: stand in prayer.

It is related that when one of them stood to pray, he would be in awe of the Merciful, so that he would not let his gaze wander, nor turn his head, nor shift the pebbles, nor let his mind dwell on any worldly affair.

If qunut in the verse is silence, as the hadith indicates, then they agreed that if one speaks deliberately while knowing he is in prayer, and it is not for the correction of his prayer, his prayer is invalidated. The exception is what is related from al-Awza'i: that speech to save a life, or something of similar gravity, does not invalidate the prayer. [If one speaks] forgetfully, Malik and al-Shafi'i said it does not invalidate the prayer. From Malik there is a difference of opinion in some forms of speech between him and his companions. Abu Hanifa and al-Thawri said it invalidates the prayer, like deliberate speech, whether for the correction of the prayer or for other reasons. This is also the view of al-Nakha'i, 'Ata', al-Hasan, Qatada and Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman. The position of Ahmad varied: al-Khiraqi transmitted it as the view of Abu Hanifa, while al-Athram transmitted from him that if one speaks to correct the prayer it is not invalidated, but if for other reasons it is invalidated; and this is the view of Malik.

In God's words, ﴿وقُومُوا لِلَّهِ قانِتِينَ﴾, there is evidence that standing is required. They agreed that standing in an obligatory prayer is obligatory for every healthy person able to do it, whether he prays alone or as an imam. They differed regarding a healthy follower who prays behind an imam who is sick and sitting, unable to stand. The majority of scholars permitted this: Jabir ibn Zayd, al-Awza'i, Malik, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Ayyub, Sulayman ibn Dawud al-Hashimi, Abu Khaythama, Ibn Abi Shayba, Muhammad ibn Isma'il, and those who followed them among the people of hadith, such as Muhammad ibn Nasr and Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Khuzayma. So he prays behind him sitting, according to their school [p. 243]. Among the Companions, the following issued this ruling: Jabir, Abu Hurayra, Usayd ibn Hudayr and Qays ibn Fihr. Those who related this from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) were: Anas, A'isha, Abu Hurayra, Jabir, Ibn 'Umar and Abu Umama al-Bahili. A group permitted the prayer of one standing behind an imam who is sick and sitting. To this view went al-Shafi'i, Dawud, Zufar, and a group in Medina. It is also the transmission of al-Walid ibn Muslim from Malik, but it is a rare transmission from him. The well-known view of Malik is that no one may lead while seated; if someone does so, his prayer is invalid and theirs too, except that if he is ill, his prayer is valid and theirs is invalid. To this went Muhammad ibn al-Hasan.

Abu Hatim Muhammad ibn Hibban al-Busti said: The first to invalidate the prayer of a follower who stands when his imam prays seated was al-Mughira ibn Miqsam, the companion of al-Nakha'i. Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman took from him, and Abu Hanifa took from Hammad, and those after him among his companions followed him in this.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 239:

﴿فَإنْ خِفْتُمْ فَرِجالًا أوْ رُكْبانًا﴾ — ﴿But if you fear, then on foot or riding.﴾ When He mentioned guarding the prayers and commanded that one stand in them devoutly obedient (qanitin), there could arise for those praying a state in which they fear; so He granted them leave to pray while walking on foot, or riding. Fear includes fear of an enemy, of a wild beast, of a flood, and other things; so every matter from which one fears is permitted what this verse includes. Malik said: outside of fear of the enemy, it is recommended to repeat the prayer within its time if safety is restored. Most of the jurists hold that fear is of equal standing. "Rijalan" (رِجالًا) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), and the governing verb is omitted. They said its estimate is: "fa-ṣallū rijālan" (then pray on foot). It is good that it be estimated from the first word, i.e.: "fa-ḥāfiẓū 'alayhā rijālan" (then guard them on foot). Rijal is the plural of rājil, like qā'im and qiyām. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وأذِّنْ في النّاسِ بِالحَجِّ يَأْتُوكَ رِجالًا﴾ [al-Hajj: 27] ﴿And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage; they will come to you on foot﴾. The poet said:

؎وبَنُو غُدانَةَ شاخِصٌ أبْصارُهم يَمْشُونَ تَحْتَ بُطُونِهِنَّ رِجالا

The meaning: walking on foot. It is said of it: rajila yarjulu rajlan, when one lacks a mount and walks on his feet; so he is rājil, rajil and rajul, on the pattern of rajul as opposed to imra'a (woman), and this is the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz. They say: "So-and-so walked to the House of God barefoot and on foot" (rajulan). And it is said: rajlān, rajīl and rajl. The poet said:

؎عَلَيَّ إذا لاقَيْتُ لَيْلى بِخَلْوَةٍ ∗∗∗ أنَ ازْدارَ بَيْتَ اللَّهِ رَجْلانَ حافِيا

They said: it is also pluralized as: rijāl, rajīl, rujālā, rajālā, rajjāla, rajālā, rujlān, rajla, rajala (with the jīm vowelled with a fatḥa), ar'ila, arājil, and arājīl. ʿIkrima and Abū Mijlaz read: "fa-rujjālan" with a ḍamma on the rāʾ and a shadda on the jīm. It is narrated from ʿIkrima a light reading with a ḍamma on the rāʾ. It was also read: "fa-rujjalan" with a ḍamma on the rāʾ and a fatḥa on the jīm, shadded without an alif. It was read: "fa-rajlan" with a fatḥa on the rāʾ and sukūn on the jīm. Badīl ibn Maysara read: "fa-rijālan fa-rukbānan" with the fāʾ, and it is the plural of rākib. Al-Faḍl said: rākib is only said of the owner of a camel; for the owner of a horse it is said fāris, for the rider of a donkey ḥammār, and for the rider of a mule baghghāl. It was also said: the more eloquent is to say "ṣāḥib baghl" and "ṣāḥib ḥimār".

The apparent sense of His words ﴿فَإنْ خِفْتُمْ﴾ is the occurrence of fear in general, and that by fear in general prayer is permitted in these two states. They said: it is the dawn prayer for the one whom fear of his own life has constrained in a state of close combat, or what resembles it. As for the prayer of fear led by the imam with the people divided, its ruling is not in this verse. It was said: "fa-rijālan" means: on foot in congregation, because they walk toward the enemy in the prayer of fear; "aw rukbānan", i.e.: riding, by gesture (bi'l-īmā'). The apparent sense of His words "(fa-rijālan)" is that they perform the prayer while walking, so they pray in every state; and the rider gestures, and the obligation of facing the qibla falls from him; this is the view of al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifa said: they do not pray while walking or in close combat, so long as it is not possible to stand. The verse does not address the number of rak'as in this fear; and the majority hold that the prayer is not shortened below the number of the traveller's prayer if they are on a journey in which shortening is permitted. Al-Ḥasan, Qatada, and others said: it is prayed one rak'a by gesture. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Muzāḥim said: it is prayed one rak'a in close combat and otherwise; if one is unable, he should say the takbīr twice. Ishaq said: if he is able only to say one takbīr, it suffices for him. And if they saw a dark shape and thought it was an enemy, (p-244) then it became clear it was not an enemy, Abu Hanifa said: they repeat the prayer. The apparent sense of the verse is that whenever fear befalls him, he may pray in these two states; so if he prays one rak'a in safety and then fear arises, he mounts and completes (on the basis of what he has prayed); or the reverse: he completes and builds upon it, according to Malik, and this is one of al-Shafi'i's two opinions, and al-Muzani said so too. Abu Hanifa said: if he begins in safety and then fears, he starts afresh and does not build; if he prays in fear and then becomes safe, he builds. Abu Yusuf said: he does not build in any of this.

This verse indicates the great status of the prayer and the emphasis on seeking it, since it does not fall away even in fear; so it does not fall away for other reasons such as illness, preoccupation and the like. Even the sick person who is unable to perform it is obligated to indicate with the eye according to most scholars; and by this it is distinguished from all other acts of worship, for all of them fall away due to excuses and are relaxed concerning them.

﴿فَإذا أمِنتُمْ﴾ — ﴿But when you are secure﴾. Mujahid said: that is, you have come out of travel to the abode of residence; Al-Ṭabarī rejected this. It was said: his rejection should not be made, because he explained safety by the place of safety; for when a person returns from his journey and arrives at his abode of residence, he is safe, so travel is the locus of fear just as the abode of residence is the locus of safety. It was also said: the meaning of "fa-idhā amintum" is: your fear that compelled you to this prayer has ceased. It was said: "fa-idhā kuntum āminīn", i.e.: whenever you are in safety before or after.

﴿فاذْكُرُوا اللَّهَ﴾ — ﴿then remember God﴾ with gratitude and worship ﴿كَما عَلَّمَكُمْ﴾ — ﴿as He has taught you﴾, i.e.: He has been good to you by teaching you what you were ignorant of concerning the laws, and how you pray in a state of fear and in a state of safety. The "mā" is verbal-masdarial (maṣdariyya), and the "kāf" is for comparison. He commanded that they remember God with a remembrance that equals and matches the blessing of what He taught them; such that the one who remembers strives to make his remembrance resemble the blessing in measure and adequacy, even if he is unable to reach that. The meaning of "as He taught you" is: as He bestowed favour upon you and so taught you; so He expressed the effect by the cause, because teaching arises from God's bounty to the servant and His kindness to him. The "kāf" may also be causal, i.e.: remember God because of His teaching you, meaning that what moves you to His remembrance, gratitude and worship is His teaching you; for there is no gift greater than the gift of knowledge.

﴿ما لَمْ تَكُونُوا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ — ﴿what you did not know﴾. "Mā" is the second object of "ʿallamakum", and in it is the expression of favour through teaching upon the servant. In His words "what you did not know" is the implication that you were taught a thing which you would not have been able to reach by your intellects had He not taught it to you; i.e., had you been left without teaching you would never have known it. Al-Naqqash and others related that the meaning of "fa-dhkurū Allāh" is: pray the prayer which you have been taught, i.e., a prayer complete with all its conditions and pillars. In this case "mā" in "kamā ʿallamakum" is relative (mawṣūla), i.e.: pray the prayer as the prayer which He taught you, and by "remembrance" he expressed the prayer, and the "kāf" then is for comparison between the form of the two prayers: the prayer that was before the fear, and the prayer that was after the fear in a state of safety. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: according to this interpretation, "mā lam takūnū" is a substitute (badal) for the "mā" in His words "kamā", otherwise the wording of the verse would not be coherent. End. This is a possible derivation, and better than it is that it be a substitute for the omitted pronoun in "ʿallamakum", which refers back to "mā"; since the estimate is "ʿallamakumūhu", i.e., "He taught you what you did not know." The grammarians have permitted: "jāʾanī alladhī ḍarabtu akhāka", i.e., "I struck him, your brother", as a substitute for the omitted pronoun.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 240:

﴿And those of you who die and leave wives behind—let them bequeath for their wives a provision for a year without eviction. But if they leave, then there is no blame upon you for what they do with themselves of what is reasonable. And Allah is Mighty and Wise.﴾ ﴿For divorced women is a provision according to what is reasonable—a duty upon the righteous.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 241] ﴿Thus does Allah make clear to you His verses that you may use reason.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 242]

﴿And those of you who die and leave wives behind—let them bequeath for their wives a provision for a year without eviction﴾: The majority hold that it has been abrogated (mansukh) by the preceding verse, in which the waiting period for death is explicitly stated to be four months and ten days. Mujahid said: it is muhkam (not abrogated), and the waiting period had been established as four months and ten days, then Allah made for them a bequest from Him of residence for seven months and twenty nights; if they wished they could remain in their bequest, and if they wished they could leave. al-Tabari related this from him, and this is his statement: ﴿without eviction; but if they leave, then there is no blame upon you﴾. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the expressions that al-Tabari related from Mujahid do not indicate that the verse is muhkam, and Mujahid did not state that. al-Suddi said: that was the case, then it was abrogated by the revelation of the obligatory shares; so she took her quarter or her eighth, and she had no residence or maintenance, and bequests became for those who do not inherit. al-Qadi Abu al-Fadl 'Iyad ibn Musa al-Yahsubi and Abu Muhammad ibn 'Atiyya transmitted the consensus on the abrogation of the year by the verse before this one. al-Bukhari related from Ibn al-Zubayr who said: I said to 'Uthman: this verse in al-Baqarah, ﴿And those of you who die and leave wives behind﴾ up to His saying ﴿without eviction﴾, has been abrogated by the other, so why do you write it? He said: we leave it, my nephew; I do not change anything from its place. End of quote. 'Uthman meant: from its place where the Messenger of Allah ﷺ placed it, because the arrangement of the verses is from his action ﷺ, not from the ijtihad of the Companions.

They differed over whether the bequest was obligatory from Allah after the death of the husband. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', Qatadah, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said: she had residence and maintenance for a year after his death from his property, as long as she did not leave by her own choice; then the maintenance was abrogated by the quarter or the eighth, and the year's residence by the four months and ten days. Or was it by way of recommendation (nadb)? They recommended that they bequeath to the wives accordingly, so the phrase "those who die" would be approximate on this view. Qatadah also said this, as did al-Suddi, and al-Farisi interpreted the verse in this way in his argument.

al-Haramayn, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr read ﴿wasiyyatun﴾ with nominative (raf'), and the rest of the seven read it with accusative (nasb), with ﴿alladhina﴾ in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'). Wasiyyatun in the nominative is a subject, and it is an indefinite noun described in meaning; the estimate is: a bequest from them or from Allah, depending on the two positions regarding the bequest—whether it is obligatory from Allah, or recommended for the husbands? The predicate of this subject is his saying ﴿li-azwajihim﴾, and the clause "wasiyyatun li-azwajihim" is in the position of the predicate about ﴿alladhina﴾. They permitted that wasiyyatun be the subject, with li-azwajihim as a qualifier, and the predicate omitted, its estimate being: so upon them is a bequest for their wives. It is related from some grammarians that wasiyyatun is nominative by an omitted verb, its estimate: a bequest was prescribed upon them. It was said: likewise it is in the reading of 'Abdullah; and this should be taken as an explanation of meaning, not an explanation of i'rab, since this is not one of the places where the verb is elided. al-Zamakhshari permitted that the estimate be: and the bequest of those who die, or: and the ruling for those who die is a bequest for their wives; thus that would be a subject by omission of a modifier (mudaf). He also permitted that the estimate be: and those who die are people of a bequest, so he made the omitted element part of the predicate; and there is no necessity compelling us to claim this omission. The accusative of wasiyyatan is by an implied verb, its estimate: and those who die [should bequeath]; so ﴿alladhina﴾ is the subject, and the omitted ﴿yusuna﴾ ("they bequeath") is the predicate; Ibn 'Atiyya estimated it: li-yuwsu (let them bequeath). al-Zamakhshari permitted that ﴿alladhina﴾ be nominative as an object not named its agent (maf'ul lam yusamma fa'iluh) by an implied verb, and that wasiyyatan be accusative as a second object, its estimate: and let there be imposed upon those of you who die a bequest. This is weak, since it is not one of the places where the verb is elided. Equally weak is the one who read ﴿alladhina﴾ as nominative by an implied: "let those who die bequeath", and read wasiyyatan with nasb as an absolute object (masdar).

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "al-wasiyyatu li-azwajihim" with raf', the subject, and "li-azwajihimu" the predicate, or the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., upon them is the bequest. The accusative of mata'an is either by an implied verb from its own root, i.e., "provide for them a provision," or from a root other than its own, i.e., "Allah made for them a provision," or by his saying "wasiyyatan." Is it a masdar with tanwin that governs? Like his saying:

"Had it not been for the hope of victory from you and fear of your punishment, they would have been to us like watering-places."

The original would be: "bi-mata'in," then the preposition was dropped. If you put wasiyyatan in the accusative, then mata'an may be accusative by the verb governing wasiyyatan, and its accusative is as an absolute object, because the meaning is: he bequeaths it with a provision for such and such. They permitted that mata'an be an attribute of wasiyyatan, and a substitute and a circumstantial (hal) of the testators, i.e., providing, or possessors of provision. It may also be accusative as a circumstantial of azwajihim, i.e., provided for, or possessors of provision; and it is a hal muqaddarah (anticipated circumstance) if the bequest is from the wives. Ubayy read: "mata'un li-azwajihim mata'an ila al-hawl," and it is related from him: "fa-mata'un." The entry of the fa' into the predicate of ﴿alladhina﴾ is because it is a relative pronoun that has been given the meaning of a condition, as if it were said: whoever dies. ﴿Mata'an ila al-hawl﴾ is accusative by this masdar, since its meaning is providing, as in your saying: "I was pleased by the striking of you to Zayd, a severe striking." ﴿Ghayra ikhraj﴾ is accusative as an attribute of ﴿mata'an﴾, or as a substitute for ﴿mata'an﴾, or as a circumstantial of the wives, i.e., not expelled, or of the testators, i.e., not expelling; or as an emphatic masdar, i.e., no expulsion; said by al-Akhfash.

﴿But if they leave, then there is no blame upon you for what they do with themselves of what is reasonable﴾: The one who holds guardianship over them prevents their leaving; but if they leave by their own choice, the burden is lifted from the one who oversees their affair, since their leaving of their own choice is permissible for them, and it is made clear that their connection to the state of the deceased has ended; so he has no right to prevent them from what they do with themselves, such as remarriage, abandoning mourning, adorning themselves, going out, and presenting themselves to suitors, provided that this is reasonable according to the Sharia. "Fi ma fa'alna" is connected to what "alaykum" is connected to, i.e., there is no blame settling upon you for what they did. "Ma" is a relative pronoun, and the returning pronoun is omitted, i.e., what they did; and "min ma'ruf" is in the position of a circumstantial of the omitted pronoun in "fa'alna"; so it is connected to an omitted element, i.e., what they did being of what is reasonable. Here "min ma'ruf" comes indefinite and genitive with "min"; while in the abrogating verse, according to the majority, it comes definite and genitive with "bi", "bi-al-ma'ruf". The alif-lam in it is like its counterpart in your saying: "I met a man," then you say: "the man—his description is such and such." Likewise the preceding verse is earlier in recitation but later in revelation, and this is the reverse; and a parallel to that is ﴿The foolish among the people will say: what has turned them from their qibla﴾ [al-Baqarah: 142] according to the apparent reported sense, along with His saying ﴿We see the turning of your face towards the heaven﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144].

﴿And Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾: He concluded the verse with these two attributes. His saying "Mighty" is a manifestation of dominance and subjugation toward whoever prevents the execution of the bequest with the provision mentioned, or expels them while they do not choose to leave, and it implies a warning upon that. His saying "Wise" is a manifestation that what has been legislated of that is in accordance with wisdom, precision, and placing things in their proper places. Ibn 'Atiyya said: all of this has had its ruling removed by the agreed-upon abrogation, except what al-Tabari related from Mujahid, and there is a question about al-Tabari's view in that. End of his words. And what was related at the beginning of the verse from Mujahid, that it is muhkam, is the statement of Ibn 'Atiyya on that.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 241–242:

﴿And for divorced women there is a provision according to what is reasonable﴾. Its apparent meaning is generality, as taken by Abu Thawr. The scholars' disagreement about what may specify a general ruling (al-takhsis, specification of general terms) has already been mentioned under His words: (and provide for them), so there is no need to repeat it. "Bi al-ma'ruf" (according to what is reasonable) may be connected to what "li al-mutallaqat" (for divorced women) is connected to. It is also said it is connected to His words "mata'an" (a provision). It is also said that what is meant by "mata'" (provision) here is the maintenance of the waiting period ('iddah).

﴿A duty upon the mindful﴾. Ibn Zayd said: this verse was revealed to emphasise the matter of the mut'ah (customary gift). This is because earlier it was revealed: ﴿A duty upon the good-doers﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:236]. A man said: "If I do not wish to be good, I will not give the mut'ah," so ﴿A duty upon the mindful﴾ was revealed. The grammatical case of "haqqan" (as a duty) here is like its grammatical case in "haqqan 'ala al-muhsinin" (a duty upon the good-doers). The apparent meaning of "al-muttaqin" (the mindful) is those who are characterised by taqwa (God-consciousness), which is more specific than avoiding shirk (associating partners with God). They were singled out for mention to honour them, or because they are the most numerous to stand (in worship), and God is the swiftest of them in complying with God's command. It is also said that "'ala al-muttaqin" means those who guard against shirk.

﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you His signs﴾: that is, like this clarification that preceded of the rulings, He will make clear to you in the future what remains of the rulings with which the servants are charged.

﴿So that you may understand﴾: what is wanted from you of adhering to the laws and standing by them, because clarifying things is something that becomes clear to the intellect at the first perception, unlike unseen and ambiguous matters, in which the intellect becomes confused and hardly gains any benefit from them. It has been said: in these verses there are among the marvels of rhetorical embellishment (al-badi') and kinds of eloquence (al-fasahah): the shift from the form "if'alu" (do) to "fa'ilu" (be diligent) for intensification, which occurs in "hafizu" (guard [them]); the singling out by mention in "wa al-salat al-wusta" (and the middle prayer); the semantic antithesis (tibaq ma'nawi) in "fa-in khiftum" (if you fear), because the implied sense in "hafizu" is observing their times, and their conditions are when you are secure; and the ellipsis in "fa-in khiftum" is the enemy or what is similar to it. In "fa-rijalan" (then on foot), that is, pray on foot as men; in "wasiyyatan li-azwajihim" (a bequest for their wives) whether it is in the nominative or accusative; in "ghayra ikhraj" (without expulsion), that is, from their dwelling in which they observe the waiting period; in "fa-in kharajna min buyutihinna min ghayri ridan minhunna" (if they leave their houses without their consent); in "fima fa'alna fi anfusihinna" (regarding what they do with themselves), that is, from their inclination to marriage or adornment after the period has ended; in "bi al-ma'ruf" (in a reasonable manner), that is, by custom or by law; in "'aziz" (Mighty), that is, His retribution; in "hakim" (Wise), that is, in His rulings. In His words "haqqan" (as a duty), that is, the right of that is a duty; in "'ala al-muttaqin" (upon the mindful), that is, God's punishment; the simile in "kama 'allamakum" (as He taught you); the paronomasia of similarity (al-tajnis al-mumathil), which is when it occurs with two verbs or two nouns, and that is in "'allamakum ma lam takunu ta'lamun" (taught you what you did not know); the paronomasia of difference (al-tajnis al-mughayir) in "ghayra ikhraj fa-in kharajna"; the metaphor in "yutawaffawna" (those who die), that is, they approach death; and the repetition in "mata'an ila al-hawl" (a provision until the year's end). Then He said: "And for divorced women there is a provision," so this is for emphasis if it is the same, and for difference of meaning if it is other.

These noble verses have included the ruling on the woman whose husband has died, that her waiting period is four months and ten days, and that once their waiting period has ended there is no blame upon whoever is in charge of their affairs, whether a guardian or a judge, regarding what they do of making themselves open to proposals, adorning themselves, abandoning mourning, and marrying, and that this is in a reasonable manner in law. God, exalted is He, informed that He is aware of what proceeds from us, and that there is no blame upon whoever makes an allusion to a proposal or conceals the intention to marry within himself; and this implies that explicit declaration in it incurs blame. Then God, exalted is He, excused allusion on the grounds that souls yearn for marriage and for mention of women. God, exalted is He, forbade making a secret promise, which is marriage, and permitted a reasonable word, by which it is indicated that the woman is desired, for in that there is consolation for her and some comforting of her by it. Then He forbade concluding the marriage contract before the end of the waiting period, and informed that what is in a person's soul God knows, and commanded that one be wary. Since the command to be wary demands something to fear, He informed that He is Forgiving, who covers sins, and Forbearing, who pardons the wrongdoer, so that the fear and hope of the believer may be balanced. Then He mentioned the lifting of blame from whoever divorced a woman before consummation or before fixing a dowry for her, since it might be supposed that divorce before consummation is not permitted. Then He commanded the giving of a provision, so that this would be compensation to the woman not consummated for what she had missed from the husband, and for half the dowry that is halved by divorce, and as consolation to her, and to the one for whom no dowry was fixed; and that this provision is according to the husband's means and straitness, and He did not specify the amount, but said that it is according to what is reasonable, which is what is customary and lawful. And that this is a duty upon the good-doer. Then He mentioned that if he divorces before consummation and after fixing, then the stipulated amount is halved, so half the dowry is due to her, unless the woman pardons and takes nothing from it, or the husband pardons and pays her the full dowry if the divorce came from his side. Then He mentioned that pardon from either side is nearer to attaining taqwa for the one who pardons, since it is either one leaving his right or one giving beyond what is due. Then He forbade forgetting bounty, so in this prohibition is the command to bounty. Then He concluded this by saying He is Seeing of all their deeds, so He will reward the good-doer for his good and the wrongdoer for his wrong. When God, exalted is He, had mentioned the rulings of marriage, and they nearly covered the responsible person, He drew attention to the most noble of the acts of worship by which the responsible person draws near to God, exalted is He, and commanded that they be guarded, namely the prayers, and singled out the middle one among them by mention, as an alert to its excellence; and from its being named "the middle" its distinction over others becomes clear, and it is undoubtedly the 'Asr prayer. Then He commanded standing before God, exalted is He, while engaged in His obedience. Then, for the sake of intensifying the emphasis on the obligation of the prayers, He did not permit leaving them even in a state of fear, but commanded that they be performed in that state, whether the one in fear is walking or riding, even if that involves some deficiency in its conditions. Then He commanded that they be performed in their original state, with the completion of their conditions and forms, when the one in fear is secure, and that he perform them in the manner God taught him before the fear. And He mentioned that the women whose husbands have died have a bequest of provision until the end of a year from the husbands' death, and that they do not leave their houses during that year; but if they choose to leave and do leave, there is no blame upon the one in charge of their affairs regarding what they do with themselves. Then He informed that He is Mighty, who is not overcome or subdued, Wise, placing things in their proper places. Then God, exalted is He, mentioned that divorced women have a provision in accordance with what is known by law and custom, and this requires the generality of every divorced woman, and that this provision is a duty upon the mindful. Since God, exalted is He, had explained a number of rulings in the preceding verses, He referred to that clarification, and likened the clarification that comes for the rest of the verses to the clarification that preceded it, and that the clarification is for your hope that you understand from God His rulings (p-248), so that you avoid what God, exalted is He, has forbidden, and comply with what God, exalted is He, has commanded.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 241–242:

﴿And for divorced women there is a provision according to what is reasonable﴾. Its apparent meaning is generality, as taken by Abu Thawr. The scholars' disagreement about what may specify a general ruling (al-takhsis, specification of general terms) has already been mentioned under His words: (and provide for them), so there is no need to repeat it. "Bi al-ma'ruf" (according to what is reasonable) may be connected to what "li al-mutallaqat" (for divorced women) is connected to. ﴿A duty upon the mindful﴾. Ibn Zayd said: this verse was revealed to emphasise the matter of the mut'ah (customary gift). The apparent meaning of "al-muttaqin" (the mindful) is those who are characterised by taqwa (God-consciousness), which is more specific than avoiding shirk (associating partners with God). ﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you His signs﴾: that is, like this clarification that preceded of the rulings, He will make clear to you in the future what remains of the rulings with which the servants are charged.

﴿So that you may understand﴾: what is wanted from you of adhering to the laws and standing by them, because clarifying things is something that becomes clear to the intellect at the first perception, unlike unseen and ambiguous matters, in which the intellect becomes confused and hardly gains any benefit from them. It has been said: in these verses there are among the marvels of rhetorical embellishment (al-badi') and kinds of eloquence (al-fasahah): the shift from the form "if'alu" (do) to "fa'ilu" (be diligent) for intensification, which occurs in "hafizu" (guard [them]); the singling out by mention in "wa al-salat al-wusta" (and the middle prayer); the semantic antithesis (tibaq ma'nawi) in "fa-in khiftum" (if you fear), because the implied sense in "hafizu" is observing their times, and their conditions are when you are secure; and the ellipsis in "fa-in khiftum" is the enemy or what is similar to it. In "fa-rijalan" (then on foot), that is, pray on foot as men; in "wasiyyatan li-azwajihim" (a bequest for their wives) whether it is in the nominative or accusative; in "ghayra ikhraj" (without expulsion), that is, from their dwelling in which they observe the waiting period; in "fa-in kharajna min buyutihinna min ghayri ridan minhunna" (if they leave their houses without their consent); in "fima fa'alna fi anfusihinna" (regarding what they do with themselves), that is, from their inclination to marriage or adornment after the period has ended; in "bi al-ma'ruf" (in a reasonable manner), that is, by custom or by law; in "'aziz" (Mighty), that is, His retribution; in "hakim" (Wise), that is, in His rulings. In His words "haqqan" (as a duty), that is, the right of that is a duty; in "'ala al-muttaqin" (upon the mindful), that is, God's punishment; the simile in "kama 'allamakum" (as He taught you); the paronomasia of similarity (al-tajnis al-mumathil), which is when it occurs with two verbs or two nouns, and that is in "'allamakum ma lam takunu ta'lamun" (taught you what you did not know); the paronomasia of difference (al-tajnis al-mughayir) in "ghayra ikhraj fa-in kharajna"; the metaphor in "yutawaffawna" (those who die), that is, they approach death; and the repetition in "mata'an ila al-hawl" (a provision until the year's end). Then He said: "And for divorced women there is a provision," so this is for emphasis if it is the same, and for difference of meaning if it is other.

These noble verses have included the ruling on the woman whose husband has died, that her waiting period is four months and ten days, and that once their waiting period has ended there is no blame upon whoever is in charge of their affairs, whether a guardian or a judge, regarding what they do of making themselves open to proposals, adorning themselves, abandoning mourning, and marrying, and that this is in a reasonable manner in law. God, exalted is He, informed that He is aware of what proceeds from us, and that there is no blame upon whoever makes an allusion to a proposal or conceals the intention to marry within himself; and this implies that explicit declaration in it incurs blame. Then God, exalted is He, excused allusion on the grounds that souls yearn for marriage and for mention of women. God, exalted is He, forbade making a secret promise, which is marriage, and permitted a reasonable word, by which it is indicated that the woman is desired, for in that there is consolation for her and some comforting of her by it. Then He forbade concluding the marriage contract before the end of the waiting period, and informed that what is in a person's soul God knows, and commanded that one be wary. Since the command to be wary demands something to fear, He informed that He is Forgiving, who covers sins, and Forbearing, who pardons the wrongdoer, so that the fear and hope of the believer may be balanced. Then He mentioned the lifting of blame from whoever divorced a woman before consummation or before fixing a dowry for her, since it might be supposed that divorce before consummation is not permitted. Then He commanded the giving of a provision, so that this would be compensation to the woman not consummated for what she had missed from the husband, and for half the dowry that is halved by divorce, and as consolation to her, and to the one for whom no dowry was fixed; and that this provision is according to the husband's means and straitness, and He did not specify the amount, but said that it is according to what is reasonable, which is what is customary and lawful. And that this is a duty upon the good-doer. Then He mentioned that if he divorces before consummation and after fixing, then the stipulated amount is halved, so half the dowry is due to her, unless the woman pardons and takes nothing from it, or the husband pardons and pays her the full dowry if the divorce came from his side. Then He mentioned that pardon from either side is nearer to attaining taqwa for the one who pardons, since it is either one leaving his right or one giving beyond what is due. Then He forbade forgetting bounty, so in this prohibition is the command to bounty. Then He concluded this by saying He is Seeing of all their deeds, so He will reward the good-doer for his good and the wrongdoer for his wrong. When God, exalted is He, had mentioned the rulings of marriage, and they nearly covered the responsible person, He drew attention to the most noble of the acts of worship by which the responsible person draws near to God, exalted is He, and commanded that they be guarded, namely the prayers, and singled out the middle one among them by mention, as an alert to its excellence; and from its being named "the middle" its distinction over others becomes clear, and it is undoubtedly the 'Asr prayer. Then He commanded standing before God, exalted is He, while engaged in His obedience. Then, for the sake of intensifying the emphasis on the obligation of the prayers, He did not permit leaving them even in a state of fear, but commanded that they be performed in that state, whether the one in fear is walking or riding, even if that involves some deficiency in its conditions. Then He commanded that they be performed in their original state, with the completion of their conditions and forms, when the one in fear is secure, and that he perform them in the manner God taught him before the fear. And He mentioned that the women whose husbands have died have a bequest of provision until the end of a year from the husbands' death, and that they do not leave their houses during that year; but if they choose to leave and do leave, there is no blame upon the one in charge of their affairs regarding what they do with themselves. Then He informed that He is Mighty, who is not overcome or subdued, Wise, placing things in their proper places.
