Then God, exalted is He, mentioned that divorced women have a provision in accordance with what is known by law and custom, and this requires the generality of every divorced woman, and that this provision is a duty upon the mindful. Since God, exalted is He, had explained a number of rulings in the preceding verses, He referred to that clarification, and likened the clarification that comes for the rest of the verses to the clarification that preceded it, and that the clarification is for your hope that you understand from God His rulings (p-248), so that you avoid what God, exalted is He, has forbidden, and comply with what God, exalted is He, has commanded.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 243 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Have you not considered those who left their homes, and they were thousands, fearing death? So Allah said to them, "Die," then He brought them back to life. Indeed, Allah is ever Bounteous to the people, but most of the people do not give thanks.﴾ ﴿And fight in the way of Allah, and know that Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 244] ﴿Who is it that will lend to Allah a goodly loan, so that He may multiply it for him many times over? And Allah withholds and extends, and to Him you will be returned.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 245] ﴿Have you not considered the chiefs of the Children of Israel after Musa, when they said to a prophet of theirs, "Appoint for us a king, and we will fight in the way of Allah"? He said, "Would you perhaps, if fighting is prescribed for you, not fight?" They said, "And what is wrong with us that we should not fight in the way of Allah, when we have been driven out of our homes and our children?" But when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away, except for a few of them. And Allah is All-Knowing of the wrongdoers.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 246] ﴿And their prophet said to them, "Indeed, Allah has sent Talut as king for you." They said, "How can he have kingship over us when we are more entitled to kingship than he, and he has not been given abundant wealth?" He said, "Indeed, Allah has chosen him over you and increased him in knowledge and physical stature. And Allah gives His kingship to whom He wills. And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 247]

*Al-alf* (الألْفُ): a known number (one thousand). Its plural for paucity is *alaf* (آلافٌ), and for abundance *ulūf* (أُلُوفٌ). It is said: *ālaftu al-darāhim* (I made the dirhams into thousands) and *ālafat hiya* (they became thousands). It was also said that *ulūf* is the plural of *alf* in the pattern of *shāhid* / *shuhūd* (witness / witnesses).

*Al-qaraḍ* (القَرْضُ): cutting with the teeth. From it comes *al-miqrāḍ* (scissors), because it is used for cutting. It is said *inqaraḍa al-qawm* (the people perished), meaning they died and their news was cut off. From the same root: *aqraḍtu fulānan*, meaning I cut for so-and-so a portion of wealth. Al-Akhfash said: the Arabs say, "You have from me *qarḍ ṣidq* (a loan of truth) and *qarḍ sū'* (a loan of evil)," for a matter whose joy or harm comes to one. Al-Zajjaj said: *al-qarḍ* is good trial and evil trial. Al-Layth said: *al-qarḍ* is the name for everything for which a recompense is sought. It is said *aqraḍa fulānun fulānan*, meaning he gave him what he would be repaid with, and the noun from it is *al-qarḍ*, which is what you give so that you are rewarded for it. Ibn Kaysan said: *al-qarḍ* is that you give something so that its like returns to you. It is said *taqāraḍā al-thanā'* (they exchanged praise), meaning each of the two praised the other, and it is said *qāraḍahu al-wudda wa-al-thanā'* (he exchanged affection and praise with him). Al-Kisa'i reported *al-qirḍ* with a kasra, but the more well-known is with a fatḥa on the *qāf*.

*Al-ḍi'f* (الضِّعْفُ): the like of two equal quantities. It is also said to be the like of a thing in measure. The *ḍi'f* of a thing is three times its like. However, when it is said *ḍi'fān* (two multiples), it may be applied to two equal in measure, in the sense that each doubles the other, just as it is said *al-zawjān* (the spouses), each of whom is a spouse to the other. Some differentiated between *yuḍā'if* and *yuḍa''if*, saying: *al-taḍ'īf* is for what has been made into two like parts, and *al-muḍā'afa* is for what has been increased beyond that, more than that.

*Al-qabḍ* (القَبْضُ): gathering a thing and holding it together, and *al-basṭ* (القَبْضُ's opposite) is its opposite. From it is the verse of Abu Tammam:
*He has accustomed his palm to outstretching, so that if he were to call it to grasp, his fingertips would not respond to him.*

*Al-mala'* (المَلَأُ): the nobles among the people. It is a collective noun and is also pluralised as *amlā'*. The poet said:
*And the nobles from every group said to her, and the best of the words of men is their most correct.*
They were so named because they fill the eyes with awe, or fill the place when they are present, or because they are wealthy in what people need. Al-Farra' said: *al-mala'* means men, and throughout the Qur'an it never includes women. The same applies to *al-qawm* (people), *al-nafar* (group), and *al-rahṭ* (band). Al-Zajjaj said: *al-mala'* are the notables and the people of judgement.

*Ṭālūt* (طالُوتُ): his name in Syriac was *Sāyil*, and in Hebrew *Sā'ūl ibn Qays*, from the descendants of Binyamin ibn Ya'qub. He was named *Ṭālūt*, they say, because of his height, for he was taller than everyone by his head and shoulders. According to this, his form would be *fa'lūt*, like *raḥamūt* and *malakūt*, and so his *alif* would be converted from a *wāw*. However, what poses a difficulty for this derivation is that he is not declined (i.e., he takes no nunation), unless it is said that this structure is absent from the Arabic language and occurs only in foreign languages. Both languages agree on the root of the word, just as they claimed concerning *Ya'qūb*, that it is derived from *al-'aqib* (heel), but this structure with this meaning is absent in the Arabic language.

*Al-jism* (الجِسْمُ): known, and in the plural for abundance it is *jusūm*, when the body is large.

﴿Have you not considered those who left their homes, and they were thousands﴾: The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that whenever He, exalted is He, mentions some of the legal obligations, He follows it with some narratives (p-249) as a lesson for the listener, so that this moves him to submission and to abandoning obstinacy. He, exalted is He, had mentioned matters concerning the dead and those they left behind, so He followed this with mention of this wondrous story: how Allah caused those who left their homes to die, then brought them back to life in this world. Just as He was capable of bringing them back to life in this world, He is capable of bringing back to life those who have died in the Hereafter, and He will recompense each of them for what they did. Therefore, this story contains a reminder of the Return, and that it is certainly going to happen. It befits every intelligent person to act for his return by safeguarding the worship of his Lord and by fulfilling the rights of His servants.

It was also said: when He, exalted is He, explained the ruling on marriage, He explained the ruling on fighting, because marriage is a protection of religion, and fighting is a protection of religion, wealth and life.

It was also said: the connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when He mentioned: ﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you His signs, so that you may reason﴾ [al-Baqarah: 242], He mentioned this story because it is among His greatest signs and marvels of His power.

This interrogative hamza (هَمْزَةُ الِاسْتِفْهامِ, the hamza of interrogation) has entered upon a negative particle, so the sentence becomes an affirmation. It is possible that the addressee knew of this characteristic before the revelation of this verse, and it is also possible that he did not know it except from this verse. Its meaning is alerting and expressing wonder at the condition of these people. The seeing here is cognitive, and it has been made to imply the meaning of what is transitive with *ilā* (إلى), therefore it does not take two objects. It is as if it were said: "Has your knowledge not reached such-and-such?" Al-Raghib said: *ra'aytu* is transitive by itself without a preposition, but when the expression *alam tara* was borrowed for the meaning of *alam tanẓur* (have you not looked), it was given the same transitivity, and this is rarely used except in affirmation, as one would say *ra'aytu ilā kadhā* (I saw toward such-and-such). End.

*Alam tara* (ألَمْ تَرَ) has taken the course of an expression of wonder in their language, as came in the hadith: "*Alam tara ilā Mujazziz*" (Did you not see Mujazziz?). That was when he saw the feet of Zayd and his son Usama, and Usama was black, and he said, "These feet are part of one another." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered upon one of his wives and said, expressing wonder: "Did you not see Mujazziz?" ... the hadith. This expression has also come in the Qur'an: ﴿Have you not considered those who hypocritically said﴾ [al-Hashr: 11]; ﴿Have you not considered those who befriended a people with whom Allah is angry﴾ [al-Mujadila: 14]; ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord extended the shade﴾ [al-Furqan: 45]. The poet said:
*Did you not see me, whenever I came as a night visitor, finding in her a fragrance even when she was not perfumed?*

The address may be to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it may be to every listener. al-Sulami read *tar* (تَرْ) with a sukun on the *rā'*. They said this was on the assumption that the *rā'* was the final letter of the word, as the rajaz poet said:
*Sulaymā said, "Buy for us some sawiq (roasted grain), and buy and hasten a clever servant."*
It may also be from treating the pausal form as the continuous form, and it has come in the Qur'an with the *alif* of *al-ẓunūnā*, *al-sabīlā* and *al-rasūlā* in continuous recitation.

Those who left were a group of the Children of Israel who were commanded to strive, so they feared being killed and left their homes fleeing from that. Allah caused them to die in order to show them that nothing can save them from death. Then He brought them back to life and commanded them to fight, by His saying: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 244], and so on.

It was also said: they were a group of the Children of Israel among whom a plague had broken out, so they left fleeing from it, and Allah caused them to die. Then the rest of the Children of Israel built a wall around them, until when their bones decayed, Allah sent Hizqil, who supplicated to Allah, and He brought them back to life for him. This was related by a group of Jews to Umar ibn al-Khattab.

Al-Suddi said: they were a nation who lived before Wasit, in a village called Dawardan, where the plague struck, so they fled from it. Allah caused them to die, then brought them back to life so that they might take heed and know that there is no escape from the decree of Allah.

It was also said: Hizqil passed by them after a long time, when their bones were bare and their joints had come apart. He twisted his cheek and his fingers in wonder at what he saw. It was then revealed to him: "Call out to them to rise by the permission of Allah." So he called out, and he looked at them standing and saying: "Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You; there is no god but You."

Among those who said they fled from the plague were al-Hasan and Ammar ibn Dinar. It was also said they fled from fever, related by al-Naqqash.

The disagreement, additions and omissions in these narratives are numerous, and Allah knows best their soundness. There is no contradiction between these narratives, unless it is specified that ﴿those who left their homes﴾ are only those mentioned in that particular narrative. Otherwise, it is possible for each narrative to be mentioned as an example, since there is nothing preventing some people fleeing from jihad, (p-250) and some people fleeing from the plague, and some people fleeing from fever, and Allah causing them all to die and then bringing them back to life, so that they may take heed, and so that whoever comes after them may take heed, and so that they all may know that causing death and bringing to life are in the hand of Allah. Therefore one should not fear anything that has been decreed, nor should a clever person be deceived by a stratagem into thinking that it will save him from what Allah has willed.

﴿And they were thousands﴾: In this there is a reminder that numbers and mutual support, although they are beneficial in repelling worldly harms, are not sufficient in matters that belong to God. This is a circumstantial clause (*jumla ḥāliyya*). *Ulūf* is the plural of *alf*, and it is the plural of abundance, so it is appropriate to interpret it as more than ten thousand. It was said: six hundred thousand. Ata' said: ninety. It was said: eighty. Ata' also said: seventy. Ibn 'Abbas said: forty. He also said: a few over thirty. Abu Malik said: thirty, meaning thousands.

It has also been interpreted as the lowest number, using the plural of abundance for the plural of paucity. Abu Rawq said: ten thousand. Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: eight. Abu Salih said: seven. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said: four. 'Ata' al-Khurasani said: three thousand. Al-Baghawi said: the better view is that of the one who said they were more than ten thousand, because *ulūf* is the plural of abundance, and *ulūf* is not said for fewer than ten thousand. End.

This is not as he has stated, for one of the two plurals may be used for the other, although the original usage is that each is used for its own proper meaning. All these estimates have no proof for any of them. The wording of the Qur'an, ﴿and they were thousands﴾, does not specify a definite number. It is possible that the intended meaning of the plural *alf* is not literal, but that the purpose is multiplication, as if it were said: they left their homes while they were a numerous world, whom no counter could enumerate. He expressed this meaning by His saying: "and they were thousands," just as you may say: "I came to you a thousand times," not meaning the literal number, but meaning "I came to you many times, too numerous to count." A similar example is the poet's saying:
*He is the one who settled thousands in the atmosphere of Na'ith, the Banu Asad, the roughest of the land and most rugged.*

Perhaps those who were with him were not thousands, let alone actual thousands, but he intended multiplication, because the Arabs multiply with *alf* (thousand) and use its plural form.

The majority hold that His saying "and they were thousands" is the plural of *alf*, the known number which is ten repeated ten times. Ibn Zayd said: *ulūf* is the plural of *alf*, like *qā'id* and *qu'ūd* (sitter / sitters). That is, they left while they were united; their people's division did not drive them out, nor any strife among them, but they were in agreement. Then this group differed, and went out fleeing from death and seeking life; so Allah caused them to die in their place of refuge, according to their claim. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is one of the strange interpretations, and it is as he said. Al-Qadi said: that it is the plural of *alf* from the numeral is preferable, because the arrival of death upon them while they were a great multitude conveys greater cause for reflection. As for the arrival of death upon a people among whom there is harmony, it is like its arrival upon a people among whom there is discord, in that the aspect of reflection does not change.

﴿Fear of death﴾: this is the cause (ʿillah) of their departure, because death had overcome their assumption, whether from the plague or from jihad, and that drove them to leave. It is a maf'ul lahu (object of purpose), and the conditions for the maf'ul lahu are met in it, since it is a verbal noun whose agent and time are one.

﴿Then God said to them: "Die"﴾. Its apparent meaning is that there was a speech from God. It is said that He said this through the tongue of the Messenger who was permitted to say it to them on God's behalf. It is also said that it was through the tongue of an angel. It is related that two angels shouted at them, "Die!", and they died. It is also said that the angels heard that and took their souls. It is also said that there was no speech there at all, and that this is a kinayah (figurative expression) for their readiness to die in a single hour, and that their death was like the death of one man. The meaning is: "Then He caused them to die," but it was expressed in the manner of a person commanded to do something who hastens to comply without hesitation or refusal, like His saying: ﴿Be, and it is﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 117]. There is an ellipsis in the sentence; the estimated wording is: "So they died." The apparent meaning of this death is the separation of the souls from the bodies. It is said that they died for eight days, and then He revived them after the supplication of Hizqil (Ezekiel). It is also said seven days. It has already been mentioned in some narratives that their bones became bare and their joints came apart, and this does not happen ordinarily within eight days. This death was not the death of the appointed term; rather God made it for these people like an illness or an accident of the kind that befalls human beings, like the state of ﴿the one who passed by a town﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 259] mentioned after this.

﴿Then He revived them﴾. The conjunction with "then" (thumma) indicates the delay of the revival after the causing of death. Qatadah said: "He revived them so that they might complete their appointed terms." Its apparent meaning is that God Himself revived them without any intermediary. Muqatil said: They were the people of Hizqil; he went out and found them dead. God revealed to him: "I have made their life to be in your hands." So he said to them: "Live!" Ibn Abbas said: The prophet was Shumʿun, and the smell of the dead is found among their descendants. It is also said: The prophet was Yushaʿ ibn Nun (Joshua). Wahb said: His name was Shamwil, and he is Dhu al-Kifl. Mujahid said: When they were revived they returned to their people sweating, but the pallor of death was on their faces, and none of them would wear a garment without it becoming a greasy shroud, until they died at their appointed terms that had been written for them. It is also said that the meaning of their causing to die was their humiliation, a humiliation that goes in the manner of death; their great number and their mutual support did not avail them anything from God, then He helped them and delivered them, so that they might know God's power, that He humbles whom He wills and exalts whom He wills. It is also said: By death is meant ignorance, and by life is meant knowledge, as the body lives by the spirit. This story came before the command to fight, as an encouragement to the believers and an urging to jihad, an allusion (taʿrid) to martyrdom, and an informing that there is no escape from what God has decreed: ﴿Say: Nothing will befall us except what God has written for us﴾ [At-Tawbah: 51]. It is also a proof against the Jews and the Christians through his ﷺ (ﷺ) informing them of what they cannot deny the truth of, despite his being unlettered who did not read a book and did not study with anyone, and against the idolaters of the Arabs, since whoever has read the books would confirm him in what he reports of what he brought that is in their books.

﴿Indeed God is full of bounty toward mankind﴾. He emphasized this sentence with "inna" and the lam, and the predicate came as "la-dhu" (indeed possessor of), which indicates nobility, unlike "ṣāḥib" (companion). "Mankind" here is general, because every person has a bounty from God of every kind, and especially here, since He alerted them to what they might use to gain insight and take warning regarding the afterlife, and that it is possible by reason and certain by His information, since He returned the spirits that had departed to the decayed bodies that are visible to the eye, and kept them in them for long periods until He took them back a second time. And what bounty is greater than this bounty, since it contains all the universal principles of the saving creeds and their particulars? It is also possible that "mankind" here refers specifically to those upon whom He bestowed blessings and commanded them to fight, but they fled from it out of fear of death; so He caused them to die, then He favored them with revival and extended their life for them, so that they would be certain that there is no escape from destiny, and would make up what they had missed of acts of obedience. God related this to us as a warning that we should not follow their path, but rather that we should comply with what He commands.

﴿But most people are not thankful﴾. The bounty of God upon all people has been mentioned, through their creation, provision, and other things, so it was fitting for them to thank God for that. This exception with "but" (lākinna) is implied in His saying: ﴿Indeed God is full of bounty toward mankind﴾, and the estimated meaning is: "Therefore it is incumbent upon them to thank God for His bounty;" so He made an exception by stating that most of them are not thankful, and this indicates that the thankful are few, like His saying: ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾ [Saba': 13]. The second "mankind" is restricted to those who are obligated (mukallafin).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 244:

﴿And fight in the way of Allah﴾. This is an address to this community concerning jihad in the way of Allah. That story preceded, as we have said, as an admonition to this community not to flee from death as those (people) fled, and as encouragement and reinforcement for it. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak that it is a command to those whom Allah revived after their death to engage in jihad, i.e., He said to them, "Fight in the way of Allah." Al-Tabari said: "There is no basis for this view." End of quote. What appears to be correct is the first view, and that this verse is closely connected to His words: ﴿Guard the prayers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238], and to His words: ﴿But if you fear, then (pray) on foot or riding﴾ [al-Baqarah: 239]; because in this there is an indication of meeting the enemy. Then what came between these two verses came as an interjection (i'tiradh). His words: ﴿And for divorced women is a provision according to what is reasonable﴾ [al-Baqarah: 241] are a completion or emphasis of some rulings concerning divorced women. And His words: ﴿Have you not considered those who went forth from their homes...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 243] are a lesson from those who came before, of those who fled from death and then died, (so that) we should not turn back or shrink from fighting. The explanation of the fighter in it, and that it is "the way of Allah," contains a great incitement to fighting, since a person may fight out of zeal or to gain some worldly advantage. Fighting in the way of Allah brings about everlasting honour and eternal success.

﴿And know that Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾: He hears what those who stay behind from fighting say and what those who hasten to it say, and He knows what intentions harbour; so He will recompense for that.

(p-252) "Who is it that will lend to God a goodly loan, so that He multiplies it for him manifold?" This is given by way of establishing (*ta'sis*) and bringing close to people through what they can understand. "And God is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy." He, exalted, likened the giving of the believer in this world to what he hopes for in reward in the Hereafter as a loan, just as He likened the expending of souls and wealth for Paradise to buying and selling.

The connection of this verse to what precedes it: when He, exalted, commanded fighting in the way of God, and that leads to expending souls and wealth in exalting the religion of God, He praised the one who spends some of his wealth in obedience to God. This was less burdensome for the believers, since it involves only spending wealth and not life. So He brought this interrogative clause, which carries the sense of a request.

Ibn al-Maghribi said: When people heard this verse, they divided into three groups. The first: the Jews, who said, "The Lord of Muhammad needs us, while we are rich." This is a great ignorance, and He refuted them with His words: ﴿Indeed God has heard the saying of those who said, "Indeed God is poor and we are rich."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 181]. The second: they preferred stinginess and miserliness, and gave priority to the desire for wealth. The third: they hastened to comply, like the deed of Abu al-Dahdah and others. End of quotation.

"Man" (مَن) is an interrogative in the nominative position as the inchoative (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is "dha" (ذا). "Alladhi" (الَّذِي) is an epithet (*na't*) of "dha", or a substitute (*badal*) for it. Abu al-Baqa' prevented "man" and "dha" from being treated as a single noun, as "ma" with "dha" was, saying: "Because 'ma' is more indefinite than 'man' when 'man' refers to one who reasons." Our companions permit combining "man" with "dha" in the interrogative and making them into a single noun, just as they permit that with "ma" and "dha." So they permit, in *man dha 'indaka* (مَن ذا عِنْدَكَ), that "man" and "dha" function as a single interrogative noun.

The word of majesty (لفظ الجلالة), *Allah*, is in the accusative, governed by "yuqridu" (يُقْرِضُ), and this involves an elided genitive construction (*mudaf mahdhuf*), meaning "the servants of God who are in need." He attributed borrowing to God, who is exempt from needs, to encourage charity, just as He attributed kindness shown to the sick, the hungry and the thirsty to Himself, exalted, in His words: "O son of Adam, I was ill and you did not visit Me... I asked you for food and you did not feed Me... I asked you for drink and you did not give Me drink." This hadith is narrated by Muslim and al-Bukhari.

"Qardan" (قَرْضًا) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*masdar*) that comes in a form other than the root of the verb, as though it said *iqradan* (إقْراضًا). Or it is the direct object (*maf'ul bihi*), meaning "that which is lent" (*maqrud*), i.e. a portion of wealth, like *khalq* (خَلْق) in the sense of *makhluq* (مَخْلُوق). "Hasanan" (حَسَنًا) is in the accusative as an attribute of "qardan", which is the apparent reading. Or it is an epithet of an elided verbal noun if we parse "qardan" as the direct object, meaning *iqradan hasanan* (إقْراضًا حَسَنًا). Describing it as goodly is because it has a good intention, sincere for God; this was said by Ibn al-Mubarak. Or because the giver seeks its reward from God; or because it is good and abundant; or because it is without reminder and without harm, as said by Amr ibn Uthman; or because he seeks no return for it, as said by Sahl ibn Abdullah al-Qushayri al-Tustari.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read "fayudha''ifahu" (فَيُضَعِّفُهُ) with doubling, from *da''afa*. The rest read "fayudha'ifahu" (فَيُضاعِفُهُ), from *da'afa*. It has been mentioned that both mean the same. It was said that their meanings differ, and we mentioned this when discussing the individual words.

Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read "fayudha'ifahu" with a fatha (نَصْبِ الفاءِ), i.e. in the accusative after the *fa'*. The rest read it with a damma (بِالرَّفْعِ) as a conjunction on the relative clause (*silat al-alladhi*), which is "yuqridu" (يُقْرِضُ), or as a new sentence (*isti'naf*), meaning "so He multiplies it." The first is better, because it involves no elision. The accusative is possible as an answer to the interrogative in meaning. Although the question concerns the lender, in meaning it concerns the act of lending, so it is as if it said: "Does anyone lend to God so that He multiplies it?"

Abu 'Ali said: the nominative is better. Some grammarians held that when the interrogative is about the subject to which the judgment is attributed, and not about the judgment itself, then it is not permitted to use the accusative with an implied *an* (أنْ) after the *fa'* in the answer. But this is refuted by this continuously transmitted (*mutawatir*) reading, and by the hadith: "Whoever calls upon Me, I will respond to him; whoever seeks forgiveness from Me, I will forgive him." The same applies to all other interrogative particles, nominal and particle-based.

"Adafan" (أضْعافًا) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*) from the *ha'* (هاء) in "yudha'ifahu". It was said that it may be in the accusative as a direct object, implying the sense of "fayudha'ifahu," meaning "fayusayyiruhu" (فَيُصَيِّرُهُ), "so He makes it." It may also be in the accusative as a verbal noun, considering that the "ḍi'f" (الضِّعْف) is released into the sense of the multiplier or the multiplied, meaning multiplication or doubling, just as "al-'ata'" (العَطاء), the name of the thing given, is used in the sense of giving. It is in the plural because of the differing aspects of multiplication, considering sincerity. This multiplication is not limited, but it is great. Al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: none knows the true extent of the multiplication except God, exalted. This is also the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

Some measures of multiplication have been narrated, and in the Qur'an: ﴿like a grain that grows seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 261], and then He said: ﴿And God multiplies for whom He wills﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 261].

It was said: the verse is general, covering all forms of righteousness, such as charity, jihad and others. It was said: it is specific to spending in jihad. It was said: it is specific to charity and spending wealth on the poor and needy.

﴿And God withholds and extends﴾: that is, He deprives some people and gives to others. Or He restricts and widens; this was said by al-Hasan. Or He receives the charities and replaces what is spent with expansion. Or "qabḍ" (يَقْبِضُ) means causing death, since whoever causes someone to die has taken him, and "basṭ" (يَبْسُطُ) means giving life, since whoever extends someone's lifespan has extended him. Or He withholds some hearts so they do not open, and extends others so they send forward good for themselves. Or He withholds by hastening the term and extends by long hope. Or He withholds by danger and extends by permissibility. Or He withholds the breast and widens it. Or He withholds the hand of whomever He wills from spending in His way, and extends the hand of whomever He wills to spend; this was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi and others. Or He withholds the charity and extends the reward; this was said by al-Zajjaj. The Sufis have many sayings about *qabḍ* and *basṭ* beyond these.

Hamzah, with a variant reading from Khallad, Hafs, Hisham, Qunbul, al-Naqqash from al-Akhfash here, and Abu Qurrah from Nafi', read "yabsutu" (يَبْسُطُ) with the letter sin (س). Khabar al-Hulwani reported from Qalun from Nafi' likewise. The rest read it with the letter sad (ص).

﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾: this is a statement whose meaning is a warning, that is, He will repay you for your deeds.

It was said that this noble verse includes kinds of rhetorical devices and figures of eloquence:
- The interrogative that is treated as an expression of wonder in "Have you not seen those who..." [Al-Baqarah: 243].
- The elision between "die, then He revived them," meaning they died and then He revived them; in "God said to them," meaning the king by God's permission; in "do not give thanks," meaning do not thank Him; in "hearing" your words and "knowing" your deeds; and in "you will be returned," so that He repays each one for what he did.
- Antithesis (*tibaq*) in "die, then He revived them," and in "withholds and extends."
- Repetition in "over the people, but most of the people."
- Shift of address (*iltifat*) in "fight in the way of God."
- Simile without its particle in "a goodly loan": He likened His acceptance of the servant's spending in His way and His recompense for it to a true loan, so He applied the name of a loan to it. Also specification through the attribute "goodly."
- Paronomasia of differing kinds (*tajnis mughayir*) in "fayudha'ifahu lahu adafan."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 246 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Have you not considered the chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses, when they said to a prophet of theirs, "Appoint for us a king, that we may fight in the way of Allah"?﴾ The connection of this verse to what precedes it is clear. When He commanded the believers to fight in the way of Allah, and He had already mentioned before that the story of those who left their homes fearing death, whether by fighting or by plague, this was done to encourage and strengthen the believers and to inform them that caution does not save one from decree. He followed that with the fact that fighting was prescribed and required in the earlier nations too. So it is not one of the rulings specific to you, because what is shared is more readily accepted by the soul than an obligation by which one stands alone. The discussion of His words "Have you not considered" has already preceded, so there is no need to repeat it. As for "al-mala'" (the chiefs) here, Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "All of the people. He said: because the meaning requires it, and this is the original usage of the word. The nobles are also called al-mala' by way of figurative comparison." End of quote. He means, and Allah knows best, a figurative comparison to the whole people. The explanation of al-mala' has already been given in the discussion of the vocabulary.

﴿From the Children of Israel﴾: it is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal), so it is related to an omitted element, meaning: "being from the Children of Israel." According to the view of the Kufans, it is a relative complement to al-mala', because the definite noun with the article al- may, in their view, be a relative pronoun, as they claimed in the verse:

"By my life, you are indeed the house, most noble of its people,"

where "most noble" is, in their view, a complement to "the house," having no place in the i'rab (grammatical case analysis). Likewise, "from the Children of Israel": the governing element for it has no place in the i'rab.

﴿After Moses﴾ is related to what "from the Children of Israel" is related to, (p-254) namely "being." Two prepositions are governed by one verb because the meanings differ: the first "min" (from) is partitive, and the second "min" is for the beginning of the end point. The governing element of this adverbial phrase is "tara" (you have seen). Some said it is a substitute for "ba'd" (after), since both are times for the Children of Israel. Both views are invalid. As for the first: "Have you not considered" is an affirmation, and the meaning is: your knowledge has reached the chiefs of the Children of Israel, and you have looked at the Children of Israel when they said. But the reaching of his knowledge to them, and his looking at them, did not happen at the time of their saying to a prophet of theirs: "Appoint for us a king." If it was not an adverbial of reaching nor of looking, how can it be governed by either of them, or by one of them? This is not valid. As for the second: it is very far-fetched, because if it were a substitute for "ba'd," it would have to take the governing element, and it is not valid for it to be entered upon it: I mean, "min" that enters on "ba'd" does not enter on "idh" (when). You do not say "min idh." Even if it were one of the adverbs that "min" can enter on, like "waqt" (time) and "hin" (time), the meaning would still not be valid, because "from after Moses" is a circumstantial phrase as we established, since its governing element is "being." If you said "being from the time they said to a prophet of theirs: appoint for us a king," this meaning would not be valid. Since these two views are invalid, one looks at what governs it in a way that makes the meaning valid, and we found it: that there is an omitted element through which the meaning is valid, and this is the governing element. The estimate of that omitted element is: "Have you not considered the story of the chiefs, or the account of the chiefs, and what is in their meaning," because the persons themselves are not wondered at; rather, what happened to them is wondered at. So the meaning becomes: "Have you not considered what happened to the chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses, when they said?" The governing element of "idh" is that omitted element, and the meaning is according to its estimate. "To a prophet of theirs" is related to "they said," and the lam in it, as previously mentioned, is for communication. The name of this prophet: Shmuwil ibn Bali, said by Ibn 'Abbas and Wahb ibn Munabbih; or Shm'un, said by al-Suddi; or Yusha' ibn Nun. Al-Muhasibi said his name was 'Isa, and he weakened the view of those who said it was Yusha', on the grounds that Yusha' was the servant of Moses, peace be upon him, and between him and David were many generations. The commentators have elaborated on this, and we summarize it, saying: When Moses, peace be upon him, died, there succeeded him among the Children of Israel Yusha', who maintained the Torah among them. Then he died and Hizqil succeeded him. Then he died, and wrongdoings spread among them until they worshipped idols, so He sent to them Ilyas, then after him al-Yasa', then he died, and wrongdoings grew greatly among them. Their enemy appeared to them: the Amalekites, the people of Goliath, who were inhabitants of the coast of the Roman Sea, between Egypt and Palestine. They prevailed over them, overcame much of their lands, took many of the sons of their kings captive, imposed the jizya (poll tax) upon them, and took their Torah. They had no one to manage their affairs, and they asked Allah to send them a prophet with whom they could fight. The tribe of prophethood had been destroyed except for a pregnant woman who asked Allah to grant her a boy; so He gave her Shmuwil. He learned the Torah in the Bayt al-Maqdis (Temple), and a shaykh from among their scholars sponsored him and adopted him. When he reached prophethood, Jibril came to him while he was sleeping beside the shaykh, and the shaykh did not feel safe about him. So he called him in the shaykh's voice: "O Shmuwil!" He rose in alarm and said: "O father, you called me." He disliked to tell him "No," lest he be frightened, so he said: "O my son, sleep." This happened to him twice. Then he said to him: "If I call you a third time, do not answer me." Then Jibril appeared to him and said: "Go and convey to your people the message of your Lord; He has sent you as a prophet." So he came to them, and they denied him, and said: "If you are truthful, appoint for us a king, that we may fight in the way of Allah, as a sign of your prophethood." The stability of the Children of Israel was in gathering around kings; the king would lead the armies, and the prophet would guide and direct him. Wahb said: Shmuwil was sent as a prophet, and they remained for forty years in the best condition. Allah had dropped the obligation of jihad from them except for those who fought against them. When fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away, and then what happened with Goliath and the Amalekites took place. The meaning of "appoint for us a king" is: raise up for us someone from whom we may take orders in managing the war and to whose command we may submit. "Nuqatil" (we fight) is jussive as an answer to the imperative. The majority read it with the nun and jussive. Al-Dahhak and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read it with the ya' and the raised lam, as an attribute of "king." It was also read with the nun and the raised lam as a circumstantial phrase from the genitive noun. It was also read with the ya' and the jussive as an answer to the imperative.

﴿He said: "Would you perhaps, if fighting is prescribed for you, refrain from fighting?"﴾ When they asked their prophet to raise up a king for them, and they linked fighting to his sending, and they had been humiliated and their kings had been taken captive, pride seized them and they longed for jihad, he wanted to confirm what they asked for regarding jihad and to know what their inner selves concealed. So he asked about their likelihood of abandoning fighting if it was prescribed for them. They denied that there could be any reason for them to abandon fighting, and said: ﴿And what is wrong with us that we should not fight in the way of Allah, when we have been driven out of our homes and our children?﴾ That is, this is the condition of one who hastens to fighting, because he seeks vengeance and hopes that victory from Allah, may He be exalted, will be his. They knew that what had befallen them was only because of their sins; when they desisted and repented and returned to obedience to the prophets, their hopes of help and victory grew strong. It was said: the prophet had suspected them of cowardice and weakness in fighting, and therefore he asked, and to make clear that what he suspected and expected of them would occur from them, and it did as he expected. Nafi' read "'asitum" with a kasra on the sin here and in Surat Muhammad. The rest read it with a fatha. The discussion of "'asa" has already preceded. Abu 'Ali said: the more common is the fatha on the sin, and it is the well-known form. The basis for the kasra is the Arab saying: "he is 'as with that," like "har" and "shaj." If the verb is attached to a noun, the analogy for "'asitum" would be "'asi Zayd," like "radiya." If it is said that this is the analogy, and it is not said, it is permissible to take up both dialects and use one in place of the other, as was done with other words. End of quote. What is transmitted from the Arabs is that the sin is not kasra except with the tā' of the speaker and the addressee and the nun of the feminine plural, such as "'asitu," "'asita," and "'asin," and that is permissible, not obligatory. Elsewhere it is fatha, obligatorily. The kasra is not allowed in forms such as "'asa Zayd," "al-Zaydan 'asaya," "al-Zaydun 'asaw," "al-Hindan 'asaya," "'asaka," "'asani," and "'asahu." Abu Bakr al-Adfawi and others said that the people of the Hijaz kasra the sin of 'asa only with the pronoun specifically, and when one says "'asa Zayd," only the fatha is used. The pronoun should be restricted to what we have mentioned. Abu 'Ubayd said: if "'asaytum" were with a kasra on the sin, it would be read "'asiya Rabbukum." This is ignorance on Abu 'Ubayd's part of this dialect. The entry of "hal" upon "'asaytum" is evidence that "'asa" is a declarative verb and not an performative one. The well-known view is that "'asa" is performative, because it expresses hope, so it is similar to "la'alla." For this reason it cannot occur as a relative clause: you cannot say "the one who 'asa an yuhsina ilayya came to me." Hisham disagreed in this question and permitted connecting a relative clause to it and its occurring as a predicate, because it is evidence that it is a declarative verb, and this is permissible. The rajaz poet said:

"Do not blame me; indeed I have become fasting,"

unless it is said that this is by way of an implied verb of saying, as is said in his words:

"Indeed those whom you killed yesterday, their chief, do not suppose that their night is unlike your night, that they slept."

The first part of this passage, which is cut off, concerns the rule that *inna* and her sisters (*inna wa akhawatuha*, the particles that govern a subject and predicate) may take as their predicate only a declarative sentence, meaning one that can be true or false. This is the sound view, though there is a weak dissenting opinion on the matter. The apodosis of the conditional clause, *in kutiba 'alaykumu al-qital* (﴿If fighting is prescribed for you﴾), is omitted because it is understood from context. The conditional particle occurs in the middle of the parts of the proof for its omission, just as it occurs in His words: ﴿And indeed we, if Allah wills, will be guided﴾ [al-Baqarah: 70]. The predicate of *'asaytum* (you are likely) is *an la tuqatilu* (﴿that you will not fight﴾). This is the well-known view, on which the particle *'asa* (likely) enters upon a subject and predicate, so that *an* is an added particle in the predicate, since *'asa* indicates a delayed outcome. Whoever holds that *'asa* takes an object (maf'ul) makes *an la tuqatilu* the object, with *an* being a verbal-source particle (masdariyyah). The *wa* in *wa ma lana* (﴿And what is [the matter] with us﴾) connects this statement to what precedes it. Had it been omitted, the statement could have been taken as detached from what came before it. It is interrogative in form but a denial in meaning. As for *an la nuqatila* (that we should not fight), it means "in abandoning fighting." The preposition governing *lana* (to us), which functions as the predicate of the interrogative *ma* (which is the subject), has been omitted. *An la nuqatila* is in the accusative position, or in the genitive position according to the disagreement between Sibawayh and al-Khalil. Abu al-Hasan (al-Akhfash) held that *an* is superfluous and operates in the accusative just as the superfluous *ba'* (in) operates in the genitive. The clause is then a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning "And what is [the matter] with us that we are not fighting?" This resembles His words: ﴿What is [the matter] with you that you do not entrust us with Joseph?﴾ [Yusuf: 11]; ﴿What is [the matter] with you that you do not expect dignity from Allah?﴾ [Nuh: 13]; ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not believe in Allah?﴾ [al-Hadid: 8]; and the Arabic saying: *ma laka qa'iman?* (What is [the matter] with you, standing?). He also said: ﴿Then what is [the matter] with them that they turn away from the reminder?﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 49]. Some scholars, including Ibn Jarir, held that the *wa* in *wa an la nuqatila* is omitted, the full phrase being *wa ma lana wa li-an la nuqatila?* (And what is [the matter] with us, and [why] that we should not fight?). He said: just as you say *iyyaka an tatakallama* (beware that you speak), meaning *iyyaka wa-an tatakallama* (beware and that you speak). Neither this view nor the view of Abu al-Hasan is correct, because addition and omission deviate from the original form, and we resort to them only out of necessity. No necessity calls for them here, since the meaning is sound without addition or omission. As for *iyyaka an tatakallama*, it does not involve omitting a conjunction. Rather, *iyyaka* is taken to include the meaning of *uhdhar* (beware), so *an tatakallama* is in the accusative position, as if it were said: "Beware of speaking."

﴿And we have been driven out of our homes﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal). They denied abandoning fighting, while being in this condition of having been expelled from their homes and their children. The one who said this had not himself been expelled, but someone like him had been, and so that was an expulsion of him too. It is also possible to take it literally, since many of them had their lands seized and their children taken captive, so they fled to lands other than the ones where they had grown up, as mentioned in their story.

Ubayd ibn Umayr read *wa qad akhraja-na* (and He has expelled us), meaning the enemy. The sense of *wa abna'-ina* (and our children) is "among our children." It was also said that this is an inversion (qalb), meaning "and our children were expelled from among us." It is possible that the subject of *akhraja-na* in Ubayd's reading is a pronoun referring to Allah, meaning: "And Allah has expelled us because of our disobedience and sins. So we repent and fight in His way, so that He may return us to our homelands and reunite us with our children," just as you say: "What is [the matter] with me that I do not obey Allah, when He has punished me for disobeying Him? I should obey Him so that He does not punish me."

Al-Qushayri said: they showed boldness and firmness in fighting, defending their wealth and dwellings, when they said: ﴿And what is [the matter] with us that we should not fight in the way of Allah, when we have been expelled from our homes and our children?﴾ That is why their intention was not fulfilled, because their resolve was not sincerely devoted to the right of Allah. Had they said: "And what is [the matter] with us that we should not fight in the way of Allah, since He has commanded us and made it obligatory upon us," perhaps they would have been granted success in fulfilling what they intended.

﴿But when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away, except a few of them.﴾ This is the way of the affluent and pampered. Whenever a person is immersed in comfort, his resolve grows strong and he becomes proud, but when he is tested by some calamity, he falters. The turning away that is literally "retreat" occurs at the actual engagement in battle. Here, its meaning is that their resolve was turned away from what they had asked for, namely fighting. *Qalilan* (a few) is in the accusative as a connected exception (istithna' muttasil, where the excepted item is of the same kind as what precedes). The excepted item cannot be taken as an exception from *tawallaw* (they turned away) in the sense of the subject. If you said "I struck the people except men," it would not be correct. Yet it is correct here because the excepted term is in itself an attribute of a described noun, and because it is restricted by the phrase *minhum* (from among them). The number of this few is not specified here, but the Sunnah specifies it: it is authentically reported that when the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the number of those who were with him on the day of Badr, he said: "Three hundred and thirteen, according to the number of the people of Talut." These few remained firm in their earlier intentions, and their resolve continued to fight their enemies.

Ubayy read: *tawalla-w illa an yakuna qalilun minhum* (they turned away, except that there be a few of them). This is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati', where the excepted item is not of the same kind as what precedes), because "being" (kawn) is one of the meanings, while those excepted from them are persons. The Arabs say: *qama al-qawmu illa an yakuna Zaydun* and *Zaydan* (the people stood up, except that Zayd be [among them] / except Zayd), with the nominative and accusative. The nominative is taken with *yakuna* as a complete verb (tammah, meaning "to exist"), while the accusative is taken with it as a defective verb (naqisah, which requires a predicate in the accusative). Their subject is a concealed pronoun (mustakinn) referring to the part understood from what precedes it. The estimate is: "except that he be," meaning that some of them be Zayd. The meaning is: "The people stood up, except that Zayd be among those standing." It follows from Zayd's not being among those standing that he did not stand, so there is no difference in meaning between "The people stood up except Zayd" and "The people stood up except that Zayd be" or "Zayd."

﴿And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers.﴾ This contains a threat and warning to those who held back from fighting after it had been made obligatory upon them, by their own request and desire. It also means that turning away from what Allah has made obligatory upon the servant is wrongdoing, since wrongdoing is placing a thing in other than its proper place.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 247 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And their prophet said to them: "Indeed, Allah has sent Ṭālūt (Saul) to you as king."﴾ The Prophet's saying to them, "Indeed Allah has sent," can only be based on revelation, because they had asked him to send them a king who would fight in the way of Allah. So the Prophet informed them that Allah had sent him. It is possible that this was in response to a request from the Prophet to Allah that He send him, and it is possible that it was without his request, rather when He knew their need for him, He sent him. The exegetes (al-mufassirūn) said: he asked Allah to send them a king, so there came a staff and a horn containing holy oil (duhn al-qudus). It was said: the one who will be king will be as tall as this staff. It was said to the Prophet: "Look at the horn; when a man enters and the oil in it bubbles up, he is the king of the Children of Israel." They measured themselves against the staff, but they were not like it. Ṭālūt was a water-carrier (saqqāʾ) over water, as al-Suddī said, or a tanner (dabbāgh), as Wahb said, or a muleteer (mukāriyy). A donkey of his went missing, or donkeys of his family did. So he came to the Prophet to ask him about what had been lost to him and to ask Allah on his behalf. While he was with him, the Prophet bubbled the horn and measured him with the staff, and he was its length. So he said to him: "Bring your head close," and he brought it close, and he anointed him with the holy oil and said: "Allah has commanded me to make you king over the Children of Israel." Ṭālūt said: "Me?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Did you not know that my tribe is the lowest of the tribes of the Children of Israel?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Did you not know that my house is the lowest of the houses of the Children of Israel?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then the sign is that you will return and your father will have found his donkeys." And so it was.

The word "malikan" (مَلِكًا) is in the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative: "king" describing the state of the one sent). The apparent meaning is that Allah made him king over them. Mujāhid said its meaning is "commander (amīr) over the army."

﴿They said: "How can he have sovereignty over us, when we are more entitled to sovereignty than he, and he has not been given abundance of wealth?"﴾ This is the speech of one who is contentious and deviates from the command of Allah, and this is the habit of the Children of Israel. It would have been proper for them, when their Prophet told them on behalf of Allah, "Indeed Allah has sent Ṭālūt to you as king," to submit the matter to Allah, and that their hearts should not deny it, nor should they be amazed at it. For in what is decreed there are secrets that cannot be grasped. So they said: "How is one made king over us who is beneath us and is not from the house of kingship, which is the tribe of Judah, from which came Dāwūd (David) and Sulaymān (Solomon)? And he is not from the house of prophethood, which is the tribe of Levi, from which came Mūsā (Moses) and Hārūn (Aaron)?" Ibn al-Sā'ib said: the tribe of Ṭālūt had committed a great sin: they had lain with women openly on the roadside by day, so Allah became angry with them, and He removed prophethood and kingship from them. They were called "the tribe of sin."

In their saying, "How can he have sovereignty over us," and what follows, there is an indication that it is ingrained in human nature that the lesser should not be preferred over the superior, and that one who is not well-off is held in contempt. They found it improbable that one should rule over them who was more entitled to rule than they were, and who was poor, while sovereignty requires nobility in it, since it is then greater in souls, and requires wealth by which one can subjugate men and help him achieve the aims of kingship. They did not consider the strongest cause, which is the decree and destiny of Allah: ﴿Say: "O Allah, Owner of sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will"﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 26]. They considered the weakest cause, which is lineage and wealth: ﴿O mankind, indeed We created you from male and female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another. Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾ [al-Ḥujurāt: 13]. (There is no superiority of an Arab over a non-Arab, nor of a non-Arab over an Arab, except by piety.) (﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾ [al-Ḥujurāt: 13].) Allah the Exalted also said: ﴿And a believing slave is better than a polytheist, even though he may please you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 221]. The poet said:

The most wondrous thing to a wise man is a youth who holds back from glory,
When they are asked what high standing they have, they point to a decayed, crumbling bone.

Here "annā" (أنّى) means "how," and it is in the accusative as a ḥāl. "Yakūnu" (يَكُونُ), the apparent reading is that it is a defective (nāqiṣa) verb, and "lahu" (لَهُ) is in the position of the predicate, so it is attached to a deleted element, which is the operator of "annā." "ʿAlaynā" (عَلَيْنا) is attached to "al-mulk" (the sovereignty) in the sense of dominance: you say "so-and-so is king over the sons of so-and-so." It was also said that "ʿalaynā" is a ḥāl of "al-mulk." It is also permissible that it be a complete verb (tāmma), with "lahu" attached to "yakūnu," meaning: how does sovereignty come to be for him over us, or occur for him over us?

"Wa-naḥnu aḥaqqu" (وَنَحْنُ أحَقُّ): a nominal circumstantial clause (ḥāliyya ismiyya), to which a verbal clause is conjoined, which is: ﴿and he has not been given abundance of wealth﴾. What is conjoined to a ḥāl is also a ḥāl. The meaning is: whoever has these two attributes together, namely that there exists one more entitled than he, and his poverty, is not fit for sovereignty. "Bi-l-mulk" is attached to "aḥaqqu," "minhu" is attached to "aḥaqqu," and "min al-māl" is attached to "yu'ta." The sīn of "saʿa" (سَعَة) is vowelled with a fatḥa because it is vowelled with a fatḥa in the imperfect, since it is modelled upon it, although its analogical vowel is kasra, because its original form was "yūsiʿu," like "wathiqa yathiqu." The ʿayn of the imperfect was vowelled with a fatḥa because its final radical is a guttural letter. So this fatḥa is originally a kasra; for this reason the wāw was deleted, since it occurred in "yasiʿu" between a yāʾ and a kasra, but it was vowelled with a fatḥa for what we have mentioned. Had its original vowel been a fatḥa, the deletion of the wāw would not have been permissible. Do you not see its retention in "yawjalu"? Because it did not occur between a kasra and a yāʾ. So the verbal noun (maṣdar) and the imperative in the deletion are modelled upon the imperfect, just as they modelled "ʿiddatan" and "waʿada" upon "yaʿidu."

﴿He said: "Indeed Allah has chosen him over you"﴾, that is: He selected him as the choicest, since He, the Exalted, knows best the interests; so do not object against Allah.

﴿And He increased him broadly in knowledge and physique﴾. It was said: in knowledge of warfare. The apparent meaning is knowledge of religion and the laws. It was also said: he had been inspired and made a prophet. As for the breadth in physique, it was said: by this is meant the meanings of goodness, courage, and conquering enemies. The apparent meaning is extension and breadth in the body. Ibn ʿAbbās said: Ṭālūt was at that time the most knowledgeable man among the Children of Israel, and the most handsome and the most complete. The exegetes' statement about his height has already been mentioned. He drew attention to Ṭālūt's worthiness for sovereignty by Allah's choosing him over the Children of Israel: ﴿And your Lord creates what He wills and chooses. They do not have the choice﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 68], and by what He gave him of breadth in knowledge, which is the attribute above which nothing is more noble: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ [Fāṭir: 28]. "I am more knowledgeable than you about Allah." And [he drew attention to] breadth of body, for indeed that brings greatness in souls, awe, and strength. The Arabs often praised themselves with this. The poet said:

She brought him forth, broad of bones, as if
his turban between men were a banner.

He also said:

A champion, as if his garments were on a tree
that is stripped to make sandals of tanned hide, not a twin (of a small man).

And he said:

It became clear to me that smallness is humiliation,
and that the honoured of men are the tall ones.

They also said in praise: "long of sword-belt, high of pillar." When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) walked with tall men, he would rise above them.

Ibn Zayd said: this increase was after kingship. Wahb and al-Suddī said: before kingship. So the meaning is: He increased him above other people in breadth. [The reading is] "basṭatan" with sīn: Abū ʿAmr and Ibn Kathīr. With ṣād: Nāfiʿ, and Ibn Kathīr in the transmission of al-Naqqāsh, Zarʿān, and al-Shaymūnī, who added: "la-in baṣṭa" (لَئِنْ بَصَطْتَ), and "bi-bāṣiṭin" (بِباصِطٍ), and "ka-bāṣiṭin" (كَباصِطٍ), and "mabṣūṭatān" (مَبْصُوطَتانِ), and "wa-lā tabṣuṭhā kulla al-baṣṭ" (وَلا تَبْصُطْها كُلَّ البَصْطِ), and "awṣaṭ" (أوْصَطِ), and "fa-mā iṣṭāʿū" (فَما اصْطاعُوا), and "yaṣṭūna" (يَصْطُونَ), and "al-qiṣṭās" (القِصْطاسِ). Abū Nashīṭ also related something similar from Qālūn.

﴿And Allah gives His sovereignty to whom He wills, and Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾. Its apparent meaning is that it is part of the speech of the Prophet to them. When he knew their aim in their questions and their disputation with the proofs they presented, he completed his speech with a decisive matter, which is that Allah is the Doer who chooses, doing what He wills. When they said: ﴿and we are more entitled to sovereignty than he﴾, since in their saying there was a claim of entitlement to sovereignty, as if sovereignty were in their possession, He attributed sovereignty to Allah in His saying "king" (malikan). So the king's sovereignty is His, He disposes of it as He wills. Therefore you are not more entitled to it, for it is the sovereignty of Allah, who gives it to whom He wills. It was also said: these two sentences are not included in the Prophet's speech, rather they are information from Allah, the Exalted, to His Prophet Muḥammad (ﷺ), so they are a parenthetical insertion in this story, coming for emphasis and strengthening for whomever Allah gives sovereignty. That is: since Allah, the Exalted, is the one who disposes of His sovereignty, there is no objection to Him: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 23]. He concluded with these two attributes, since their claim had preceded, that they were the people of sovereignty, that they were the wealthy, and that Ṭālūt was not from the house of sovereignty and was poor. So He said, the Exalted: indeed He is All-Encompassing; He extends His bounty to the poor; All-Knowing of who is most entitled to sovereignty, so He places it in him and chooses him for it.

In the story of Ṭālūt there is evidence that imamate is not hereditary, because Allah denied them what they denied concerning appointing over them one who is not from the people of prophethood and kingship, and He made clear that this is merited by knowledge and strength, not by lineage. It also indicates that lineage has no share alongside knowledge and excellences of the soul, and that these take precedence over it, due to Allah's choosing Ṭālūt over them for His knowledge and power, even if they were more noble than him in lineage.

These noble verses have included the report of the story of those who left their homes, who were a countless multitude, fleeing from death, either by killing, since fighting had been enjoined upon them, or by plague; so Allah caused them to die, then brought them back to life, so that they would know that there is no escape from what Allah, the Exalted, has decreed. This is so that we do not follow what they followed, and so that we do not shrink back from fighting. So this verse came affirming for whoever strives in His way. The Exalted mentioned that He is Possessor of bounty over people, through giving them life and kindness to them, yet most of them do not render the thanks due to Allah. Then He commanded fighting in the way of Allah, and that we should know that He is All-Hearing of our words and All-Knowing of our intentions. Then He mentioned that whoever lends to Allah, Allah multiplies it for him where He sees fit. Then He mentioned that in His hand is the withholding and the extending, and that the return of all is to Him. Then the Exalted informed of the story of the chiefs (al-malaʾ) of the Children of Israel, so that we might take a lesson from it and emulate what was good in their conditions and avoid what was ugly. This is the wisdom in the stories of the earlier ones related to us, that we might take a lesson from them. When the enemy overpowered them, seizing their lands and taking their sons captive, and they had no king to govern them in matters of war, since war requires someone whose command is obeyed and around whom people unite, they asked their Prophet to raise up for them a king to lead them in jihad in the way of Allah. The Prophet anticipated from them that if fighting were enjoined upon them, they would back away from it. They answered him: "We have been wronged and expelled from our homes and our sons," and this is the hardest thing for souls: to be driven from a dwelling one has grown accustomed to, and to be separated from one's children. For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed: "O Allah, make Medina beloved to us as Mecca is beloved to us, or more." Poets often wept over dwellings and familiar places. Do you not see the saying of Bilāl:

Would that I knew whether I shall spend a night
in a valley, with idhkhir and jalīl grass around me?

(p. 258)

Qutayba ibn Sa'id, the traditionist, had been granted a share of worldly success and eminence, and people took knowledge from him. He was in Baghdad when he once passed by the place of his birth and upbringing as a child, in Baghlan. It is said that Baghlan is one of the smallest of villages. He wished that he could remain living there and give up the leadership of Baghdad, the seat of the caliphate, and that was a yearning for homeland.

[God] the Exalted mentioned that when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away from accepting it, except for a few, for he took God's command with acceptance. Then God the Exalted alluded to the wrongdoers, who are those who did not accept God's command after they had asked for it, so He will recompense them for their wrongdoing.

Then God the Exalted informed of their prophet that he said to them on behalf of God: "Indeed, God has sent Talut as king over you." He was neither of their own lineage nor of their nobility of rank, since he was not of the tribe of prophethood nor of the tribe of kingship. So they did not accept what he informed them of from God, and they began to raise objections, in keeping with their custom with their prophets. They regarded his appointment as king over them as improbable, because among them there was one who, in their view, had a better claim to kingship than he did, since no king had preceded him among his forefathers, so that he would be held in esteem by the common people; and because he was poor. These two traits weaken kingship, for precedence in leadership, rank, and wealth in property are what draw men along and subjugate free people. They did not know that the workings of destiny make the less excellent excellent.

So their prophet informed them that God the Exalted had chosen him over them and had honored him with two qualities that are intrinsic to his essence: the first, great character; and the second, knowledge, which is the mighty bounty. He was content with these two essential attributes in place of the two external attributes that lie outside the essence: boasting of a decayed bone and vaunting of wealth whose pasture is unwholesome. Then He informed that God the Exalted gives His kingship to whomever He wills, and that He is the All-Encompassing in bounty, the All-Knowing of the welfare of His servants; so there is no objection to Him.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 248 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And their prophet said to them, "Indeed, the sign of his kingdom is that the chest (tabut) will come to you, in it is tranquility (sakinah) from your Lord and a remnant of what the family of Musa and the family of Harun left behind, carried by the angels. Indeed, in that is a sign for you, if you are believers."﴾ ﴿So when Talut set out with the troops, he said, "Indeed, Allah will test you with a river. Whoever drinks from it is not of me, and whoever does not taste it is indeed of me, except for one who scoops with his hand a handful." But they drank from it, except a few of them. And when he crossed it, he and those who believed with him, they said, "We have no power today against Jalut and his troops." Those who were certain that they would meet Allah said, "How many a small company has overcome a large company by the permission of Allah! And Allah is with the patient."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 249] ﴿And when they went out to Jalut and his troops, they said, "Our Lord, pour upon us patience, make firm our feet, and help us against the disbelieving people."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 250] ﴿So they defeated them by the permission of Allah, and Dawud killed Jalut, and Allah gave him the kingdom and wisdom and taught him from what He willed. And were it not for Allah's repelling people, some by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted. But Allah is full of bounty to the worlds.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 251] ﴿These are the verses of Allah; We recite them to you in truth, and indeed you are among the messengers.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 252]

Al-tabut (the chest): well known, and it is the box (al-sunduq). Regarding tabut there are two opinions. The first: its pattern is "fa'ul," and no derivation for it is known. There is also a dialectal form with a final haa', al-tabuh, and it is possible that the haa' is a substitution for the taa' as they substituted it in pausal forms in words like "Talhah," so they said "Talhah." It is not permissible that it be "fa'alut" like "malakut," from taba yatubu, because the sense of derivation is absent from it. The other opinion: it is "fa'ul" from al-tawb, which is return, because it is a container in which things are placed and stored, so what comes out of it keeps returning to it, and its owner returns to it for what he needs of his deposits. This is what al-Zamakhshari said, and he said: it cannot be "fa'ul" because of the scarcity of such patterns, like salisa and qalaqa, and because it is an unknown combination, so it is not permissible to abandon the known for it. As for with the haa', it is "fa'ul," except for those who make its haa' a substitution for the taa', because they share the quality of hams (unvoiced breathiness) and both are among the letters of augmentation; for this reason it was substituted for the feminine taa'.

Al-sakinah: "fa'ilah" from al-sukun, which is dignity; one says, "In so-and-so there is sakinah," meaning dignity and steadfastness.

Harun: a non-Arabic name, prevented from declension for being a proper noun and non-Arabic.

Al-junud: plural of jund, which is well known, and its derivation is from al-jand, which is the hard ground, since some of them shelter behind others.

Al-ghurfah: with a dammah on the ghayn, it is the name for the amount scooped of water, like al-ukhlah for the amount eaten; with a fathah on the ghayn it is a verbal noun for a single time, like "darabtu darbah." Al-ightiraf and al-gharf are well known. Al-ghurfah also means the high raised building.

Jaawaza and jaaza al-makan: he crossed it.

Jalut: a non-Arabic name, prevented from declension for being non-Arabic and a proper noun; he was the king of the Amalekites, and it is said that the Berbers are of his lineage.

Al-fi'ah: a portion of people. It is said that it is derived from fa'a yafi'u, meaning to return, in which case the omitted letter is the middle radical; or from fa'tu ra'suhu, I broke his head, in which case the omitted letter is the final radical, as an opinion.

Ghalaba ghalban and ghalabah: he overcame. Al-aghlab: the strong, the coarse; the feminine is ghalba.

Baraza yabruzu burudan: he appeared. Imra'ah barazah: a woman whose age has made her not cover her face; from this comes al-biraz and al-mutabarraz.

Afrigh: pour out. Faraga min kadha: he became empty of it.

Thabata: he became settled and firm. Thabbatahu: he established him and made him firm so that he does not move.

Al-qadam: the foot, and it is feminine; in its diminutive one says qudayma. The derivation of this word goes back to the sense of advancing.

Hazama: he broke a thing and returned part of it upon part. The Arabs say, "hazamtu 'ala Zayd": I inclined toward him. The poet said:
"I have inclined toward you today, O daughter of Malik, so be generous to us with gifts and bestow favor."

Dawud: a non-Arabic name, prevented from declension for being a proper noun and non-Arabic, and he here is Abu Sulayman, upon our prophet and upon them both be peace, and he is Dawud ibn Iya, with a kasrah on the hamzah. It is said Dawud ibn Zakariyya ibn Yanwa, of the tribe of Yahudha ibn Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, upon our prophet and upon them all be peace.

Al-daf': turning away; dafa'a yadfa'u daf'an, and dafa'a mudafa'atan wa difa'an.

﴿And their prophet said to them, "Indeed, the sign of his kingdom is that the chest will come to you,"﴾ The apparent meaning of this verse and what precedes it indicates that they were affirming the prophethood of this prophet who was among them. Do you not see their saying: ﴿Send us a king that we may fight in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 246]? But when Allah informed them (p-261) that Allah had sent Talut to them as king, He wanted to inform them with a sign showing his kingship, by way of enhancing and drawing attention to this blessing which Allah joined to Talut's kingship and made a sign for him. Al-Tabari, relating its meaning from Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd, said: The Children of Israel were obstinate and said to their prophet: "And what is the sign of Talut's kingship?" This was by way of asking for evidence of the truthfulness of their prophet in his saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah has sent to you Talut as king﴾ [al-Baqarah: 247]. This opinion is more fitting than the first with the character of the Children of Israel, their denial and their obstinacy toward their prophets. It was also said: the prophet gave them a choice of a sign, and they chose the chest. The coming of the chest would not be a sign except if it happened in a way that breaks the custom, so that would be a sign of the truthfulness of the claim. It is possible that its coming itself is the miracle, and it is possible that what is in it is the miracle, and it is a cause of the settling of their hearts and the tranquility of their souls. Attributing the coming to the chest is a metaphor, because the chest does not come; rather it is brought, as in His saying: ﴿But when the matter is resolved upon﴾ [Muhammad: 21], ﴿so their commerce did not profit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16].

The majority read "al-tabut" with a taa'; Ubayy and Zayd read it with a haa', which is the dialect of the Ansar. The discussion of this haa' has already preceded: whether it is a substitution for the taa' or original. Ibn Abbas and Ibn al-Sa'ib said: the chest was made of shamshar wood, which is a wood from which combs are made, and upon it were plates of gold. It was also said that the plates were gilded with gold. Its length was three cubits by two cubits. Many stories have been told about this chest and differences concerning its matter. What appears is that it was a well-known chest in the knowledge of the Children of Israel; they had lost it, and it contained what Allah the Exalted mentioned, which He left vague in its state, not specifying what was in it, and that the angels carry it. We will touch briefly on some of what the exegetes and historians have said: they mentioned that Allah the Exalted sent down a chest to Adam in which were the images of the prophets and houses according to their number, and its last was the house of Muhammad ﷺ. His children passed it on after him, Shith and those after him down to Ibrahim; then it was with Isma'il, then with his son Qaydhar. His paternal cousins, the children of Ishaq, disputed it with him and said to him: "Prophethood has been removed from you except for this one light," so he refused them. One day he came to open it and it was difficult for him, so a caller from the sky called out to him: "None opens it except a prophet; so hand it over to your cousin Ya'qub." So he carried it on his back to Kan'an and handed it to Ya'qub. It remained among the Children of Israel until it reached Musa, peace be upon him, who placed in it the Torah and some of his belongings. Then the prophets of the Children of Israel inherited it until it reached Shamwil, and in it was what Allah mentioned in His Book. It was also said: Musa made the chest to gather in it the fragments of the tablets.

Al-sakinah is tranquility. Since it was obtained by the coming of the chest, the chest was made a container for it, and this is a fine metaphor, namely likening meanings to physical bodies. It came in the hadith of Imran ibn Husayn that he was reciting Surat al-Kahf while a horse was tethered beside him, and a cloud covered him, and it began to circle and draw near, and his horse began to shy away from it. When morning came he came to the Prophet ﷺ and mentioned that to him, and he said: "That was tranquility descending for the Qur'an."

In the hadith of Usayd ibn Hudayr: "While he was one night reciting in his threshing-yard..." the hadith, and in it: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Those were angels who were listening to that; and if you had continued reciting, the people would have seen them, they would not have hidden from them." So he ﷺ informed about the descent of tranquility once, and once about the descent of angels. The hadith of Usayd shows that the descent of tranquility in the hadith of Imran is by omission of a modifier, meaning: those are the companions of tranquility, and they are the angels mentioned in the hadith of Usayd; and they were described as possessors of tranquility because their faith is in utmost calm, and their obedience is constant, they do not disobey Allah in what He commands them. It has come in the (Sahih): "No people gather in one of the houses of Allah, reciting the Book of Allah and studying it among themselves, except that tranquility descends upon them, the angels surround them, mercy covers them, and Allah mentions them among those who are with Him."

So the descent of tranquility upon them is a metonymy for their being endowed with the calm of faith and the settling of that in their hearts; because whoever recites the Book of Allah and studies it obtains, by reflecting on its meanings and pondering its styles, what his heart is at rest with and his soul is settled by. It is as if he had been empty of that before reciting and studying it, so when he recited, that descended upon him. Some exegetes have said this meaning. Qatadah said: sakinah here is dignity. 'Ata' said: what they recognize of the signs, so they are at rest with them. Al-Zajjaj said something similar.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the chest is the box of the Torah; when Musa, peace be upon him, fought, he would send it ahead, and the souls of the Children of Israel would be calmed and they would not flee. Sakinah means quiet and tranquility. It is related from Ali that sakinah has a face like a human face, and it is a light wind.
