It was also said: sakinah is a figure of emerald or ruby, having a head like a cat's head, a tail like its tail, and two wings; it chirps, and the chest advances toward the enemy while they march with it; when it settles, they are steadied and calmed, and victory descends. It was also said: sakinah is good tidings from the Books of Allah sent down to Musa, Harun and those after them of the prophets, for Allah will give victory to Talut and his troops. It is also said: Allah placed the sakinah of the Children of Israel in the chest in which were the fragments of the tablets, and the staff, and the relics of the people of their prophethood; and He placed the sakinah of this nation in their hearts, distinguishing between a resting place passed around by hands, which has fled once and been overcome once, and a resting place between two fingers of the fingers of the Merciful.

Abu al-Sammak read "sakkinah," with the kaf shaddah, and "sakinah" is raised by his saying "fihi," and it is in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning: being in it is tranquility. And "min" is for the beginning of the limit, meaning: coming from your Lord, so it is in the position of a qualifier, or attached to what "fihi" is attached to. It is possible that it is for partitive meaning, on the assumption of an omitted modifier, meaning: some of the tranquilities of your Lord.

The remainder (al-baqiyya): it was said that it refers to the fragments of the tablets that broke when Musa (Moses) threw them down, upon our Prophet and upon him be blessings and peace; this is related from Ikrimah. It was said that it refers to the staff of Musa; this is related from Wahb. It was said that it refers to the staff of Musa and Harun (Aaron) and their garments, and two tablets from the Torah, and the manna; this is related from Abu Salih. It was said that it refers to knowledge and the Torah; this is related from Mujahid and Ata'. It was said that it refers to the fragments of the tablets, a basin of gold, the staff of Musa and his turban; this is related from Muqatil. It was said that it refers to a qafiz (a measure) of manna and the fragments of the tablets; this is related by Sufyan al-Thawri. It was said that it refers to the staff and the two sandals; this is also related by al-Thawri. It was said that it refers to striving in the way of Allah, and they were commanded with this; this is related from al-Dahhak. It was said that it refers to the Torah and the fragments of the tablets; this is related from al-Suddi. It was said that it refers to two tablets from the Torah, the garments of Musa and Harun and their staffs, and the word of Allah: "There is no god but Allah, the Wise, the Generous," and "Glory be to Allah, Lord of the seven heavens and Lord of the Mighty Throne," and "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds." It was said that it refers to the staff of Musa and matters from the Torah; this is related from al-Rabi'. It is possible that it is the totality of what was mentioned, contained in the Tabut (the Ark of the Covenant), so each speaker reported about some of what was in it; and by these sayings the contents of the Ark as "remainder" are confined.

"Mimma taraka" (﴿مِمّا تَرَكَ﴾, "of what he left behind") is in the position of a qualifier (sifah) of "baqiyya" (بَقِيَّةٌ), and "min" (مِن) is partitive (lil-tab'id). "Al Musa wa Al Harun" (﴿آلُ مُوسى وآلُ هارُونَ﴾, "the family of Musa and the family of Harun") are among the prophets, who are related to them by kinship or by shari'ah (religious law). What appears to be the case is that the family of Musa and the family of Harun are the prophets who came after them, for they inherited that from one another until it was lost. We will mention how it was lost, if Allah wills.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also permissible that it means 'what Musa and Harun left behind,' and 'al' (the family) is inserted (muqhamah) to magnify their status." End of quote. Another said: "'Al' here is superfluous (za'idah), and the implied meaning is: 'what Musa and Harun left behind.' From this is the saying: 'O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad and upon the family of Muhammad, and upon the family of Abi Awfa,' meaning himself; and 'He has been given this as a mizmar (a flute) from the mazamir (flutes) of the family of Dawud (David),' i.e., of Dawud; and from this is the verse of Jamil:"

*Buthayna is of the family of women, and they are only for the near; there is no union for the absent one.*

"That is, of the women." End of quote. The claim of insertion and superfluity in nouns is not held by any careful grammarian. As for al-Zamakhshari's saying, "'al' is inserted to magnify their status," if by "insertion" he means what his earlier statement indicates, when he said: "It is permissible that it means 'what Musa and Harun left behind'", then I do not know how the addition of "al" would serve to magnify the status of Musa and Harun. If by "al" he means the person itself, then "al" is used for the person of a man, so that it is as if it were said: "what Musa and Harun themselves left behind." Thus those great things contained in the Ark are attributed to being remnants of Musa and Harun themselves, not of anyone else; and "al" here functions as an emphasis, meaning that what was left of that good belongs to the very persons of Musa and Harun. Specifying them by their own persons magnifies their status; and this is "inserted" because if it were said "what Musa and Harun left behind," it would suffice, and the apparent meaning of that would be that they themselves left it, and it was inherited from them. [p. 263]

"Tahmiluhu al-malaikah" (﴿تَحْمِلُهُ المَلائِكَةُ﴾, "the angels carry it"). Mujahid read "yahmiluhu" with the ya' from below (third person masculine), and the pronoun refers to the Ark. This clause is a circumstantial (hal) clause for the Ark, meaning: the angels carrying it. It may also be an independent sentence (isti'naf), as if it were said: "Who will bring it when it has been lost?" So it is said: "The angels carry it," magnifying the greatness of this sign, namely that the one who directly brings it to you is the angels, who are prepared for great matters, and who have power, authority, and knowledge by Allah's empowerment of them in that. Do you not see their receiving the divine books and their delivering them to those to whom revelation was sent, their overturning of the cities of the disobedient, the seizing of souls, the driving of clouds, the bearing of the Throne, and other extraordinary matters? The meaning is: "the angels carry it to you."

Ibn Abbas said: "The angels brought the Ark carrying it between heaven and earth while they watched it, until they placed it before Talut (Saul)." Wahb said: "They said to their prophet: 'Specify a time when you will bring it to us.' He said: 'The morning.' So they did not sleep that night until they heard the rustling of the angels between heaven and earth."

Qatada said: "The Ark was in the wilderness (al-tih); Musa left it with Yusha' (Joshua), and it remained there, and the Children of Israel did not know of it. Then the angels carried it until they placed it in the house of Talut, and they acknowledged his kingship." Ibn Zayd said: "Unwillingly." It was also said: "The people of al-Urdunn (Jordan), a village from the villages of Filastin (Palestine), captured the Ark and placed it in the house of an idol of theirs beneath the idol. In the morning the idol was beneath the Ark, so they fixed the feet of the idol to the Ark; in the morning its hands and feet were severed, lying beneath the Ark, and their idols were overturned. So they placed it in a side of their city, and a sickness seized the necks of its people, and most of them died. So they buried it in the open ground in a place of their excretion, and whoever relieved himself there was afflicted with the fistula (nasur) and colic (qulanj), and they were perplexed. A woman from the descendants of the prophets among the Children of Israel said: 'You will not cease to see what you dislike as long as this Ark is among you; so remove it from you.' They loaded the Ark onto a cart and attached to it two bulls or two cows, and struck their flanks. So Allah appointed four angels to drive them. The Ark did not pass over any land except that it became sanctified up to the land of the Children of Israel. The Ark was placed in a land where the harvest of the Children of Israel was, and the two cows returned to their land. The Children of Israel saw nothing but the Ark, so they exclaimed "Allahu akbar" and praised Allah for making Talut king. That is His saying: ﴿تَحْمِلُهُ المَلائِكَةُ﴾ ("the angels carry it")."

Ibn Abbas also said: "The Ark and the staff are in the lake of Tiberias (Buhayrat Tabariyya); they will emerge before the Day of Resurrection." It was said: "at the descent of Isa (Jesus), upon our Prophet and upon him be peace."

* *

﴿إنَّ في ذَلِكَ لَآيَةً لَكم إنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("Indeed in that is a sign for you, if you are believers"). It was said: the reference (al-ishara) is to the Ark. The better view is that it returns to the coming (al-itya'), i.e., the coming of the Ark in the described manner, so that the end of the verse corresponds to its beginning, since its beginning is ﴿إنَّ آيَةَ مُلْكِهِ أنْ يَأْتِيَكُمُ التّابُوتُ﴾ ("Indeed the sign of his kingship is that the Ark will come to you"). The meaning is: a sign for you of his kingship and of his being chosen for you. It was also said: a sign for you of your victory over your enemy, because they used to seek victory through the Ark wherever they turned, and they were given victory.

If "in" (إنْ) is taken in its original function as a conditional particle, the meaning is: "that is a sign for you on condition of your belief," because it was said that they became unbelievers by denying their prophet. It was also said: "if it is among your concerns and aspirations to believe in what the proof establishes against you." It was also said: "if you are affirming that Allah has made Talut king for you." It was also said: "affirming that Allah's promise is true." It was also said: "(إنَّ) here means (إذْ) ('when')," and they did not ask in denial of their prophet; they asked only to know the wisdom behind it, and a question about the manner (how) is not a total denial.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 249–250 (part 1 of 2):

﴿So when Talut set out with the troops﴾. Between this clause and the one before it, something is omitted. Its implied meaning is: "Then the Ark came to them, they acknowledged his kingship, and they prepared to march out." ﴿So when Talut set out﴾, meaning he departed from his place of residence. One says "fasala 'an al-mawdi'" (he departed from the place) and "infasala" (he separated himself from it) and "jawazahu" (he passed beyond it). It is said that the original form was "fasala nafsahu" (he separated himself), and then this became common, so the object was dropped until it took the status of an intransitive verb, like "infasala." The preposition "bi" in ﴿bil-junud﴾ (with the troops) indicates circumstance, meaning that the troops were accompanying him. Their number was seventy thousand, as said by Ibn 'Abbas; or eighty thousand, as said by 'Ikrima; or one hundred thousand, as said by Muqatil; or thirty thousand.

'Ikrima said: When the Children of Israel saw the Ark, they hastened to obey it and to march out with him. Talut said to them: "Whoever has built a building and not finished it shall not march out with me, nor whoever has married a woman and not consummated the marriage with her, nor the owner of a crop he has not harvested, nor the owner of merchandise he has not sent off, nor one who has a debt owed to him or owed by him, nor the elderly, nor the sick." So there marched out with him those whose number is disputed, according to his condition. He led them, and they complained of the scarcity of water and the fear of thirst, and it was the season of intense summer heat. They took a desert route, so they asked God to cause a river to flow for them.

﴿He said: Indeed God will test you with a river﴾. Wahb said: It was the one they had proposed. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada said: It is a river between the Jordan and Palestine. It is said: It is the river of Palestine, as said by al-Suddi and Ibn 'Abbas also. The majority read "bi-nahar" with a fatha on the ha'. Mujahid, Humayd al-A'raj, Abu al-Sammak and others read it with a sukun on the ha' throughout the Qur'an.

The apparent meaning of Talut's words, "Indeed God will test you," is an inspiration, according to the view of those who say he was a prophet, or that God revealed it to their prophet, and the prophet informed Talut of that. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is possible that this was something God inspired in Talut, so his troops acted upon it, and the inspiration was made a trial from God for them. The meaning of this trial is examination. Whoever's obedience is shown by abstaining from the water is known to be obedient in other matters, and whoever is overcome by his desire for the water and disobeys the command is, in hardships, more likely to disobey. End of his words. After Talut reports what occurred to his mind as a command of God, and he states it definitively on God's behalf: ﴿Whoever drinks from it is not of me﴾, meaning: is not of my followers in this battle, nor of my partisans. This does not take them out of faith, like the saying: "Whoever cheats us is not of us," and "He is not of us who tears the collars and slaps the cheeks." Or it means: he is not connected to me and not united with me, from the saying of people: "So-and-so is of me," as if I were a part of him, because of their intermingling and their unity. Al-Nabigha said:

"When you try to commit wickedness against the lion, then I am not of you, and you are not of me."

﴿But whoever does not taste it is of me﴾, meaning: whoever does not taste it. The taste of everything is its tasting, and from it comes "tatha''um" (tasting). One says: "Tata''amtu minhu," meaning "I tasted it." The Arabs say of one whose soul does not incline toward food that one is fed from: "Its eating is easy." Ibn al-Anbari said: The Arabs say: "I fed you water," meaning "I made you taste it." And "ta'imtu al-ma'" I taste the water, meaning "dhuqtu" (I tasted it). The poet said:

"If you wish, I will forbid women to you, and if you wish, I will not let you taste sweet water or cold sleep."

Al-nuqakh means sweet water, and al-bard means sleep. One says: "I did not taste a wink of sleep." In the hadith of Abu Dharr: "In the water of Zamzam is food for food." And in the hadith: "We have no food except the two blacks, the dates and the water." The word "ta'm" applies to food and drink. This word was chosen because it is more emphatic: negating eating entails negating drinking, but negating drinking does not entail negating eating, since "ta'm" applies to tasting. Restricting eating is more burdensome in obligation than restricting drinking, since it can be achieved by placing it in the mouth, even if one does not drink, and that gives some kind of relief.

In His words ﴿but whoever does not taste it﴾ there is an indication that water is food, and this was also indicated earlier. There is disagreement over whether riba (usury) applies to it. Al-Shafi'i said: It is not permissible to sell water for water in unequal amounts, nor is deferred payment permissible for it. Malik, Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf said: That is permissible. Ibn al-'Arabi reported that the sound view within the school of Malik is that riba applies to it. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: It is among what is measured by volume or weight, so according to this, unequal exchange is not permissible in his view.

It seems that His words ﴿Whoever drinks from it﴾ by their apparent meaning indicate direct drinking from the river, so that if one takes it with a cup, drinking from that would not fall under "whoever drinks from it," if he did not drink directly from the river. In the school of Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, if one says: "If I drink from the waterskin, my slave is free," it is understood as drinking directly (by lowering the mouth), and if he scoops from it or drinks with a vessel, he does not break the oath. They said: Because God forbade drinking from the river, and forbade tasting it, and excepted from the tasting the scooping, so the prohibition on drinking remains, and this shows that scooping is not drinking. He used the phrase "whoever does not" with reference to the pronoun of the water, not to the river, to remove that ambiguity, and to make known that the aim is the prohibition of their reaching the water from the river, by drinking from it directly or indirectly. Ibn 'Atiyya said: In His words ﴿but whoever does not taste it, then he is of me﴾ there is blocking of means (sadd al-dhara'i'), because the least amount of tasting falls under the word "ta'm." So when the prohibition on tasting occurs, there is no way for drinking to occur from one who avoids tasting. Because of this emphasis, the speech did not say: "whoever does not drink from it." End of his words.

﴿Except one who scoops a scoopful with his hand﴾. This is an exception from the first clause, which is His words ﴿whoever drinks from it is not of me﴾. The meaning is: whoever scoops a scoopful with his hand, not by lowering his mouth to the water, is of me. When an exception follows two or more clauses, it may be attributed to each of them, but it primarily relates to the last one. There is a difference of opinion on this matter, which is mentioned in the science of the principles of jurisprudence. If evidence indicates that it relates to some of the clauses, the exception is from that clause. Here, evidence indicates that it relates to the first clause. The second clause was placed before the exception from the first because the second clause is indicated by the first through implication: when He mentioned that God will test them with a river, and that whoever drinks from it is not of him, it was understood from that that whoever does not drink from it is of him. So the second clause functioned as a separation between the first and the exception from it, when the first indicates it. Indeed, if it were not stated explicitly, it would be understood from the first clause. In some writings there occurs the following text: "Except one who scoops" is an exception from the first clause, and if you wish, you may make it an exception from the second clause. End of quote. It does not appear to be an exception from the second clause, because he ruled that whoever does not taste it is of him, so the exception from this would imply that whoever scoops a scoopful from it with his hand is not of him. But the matter is not like that, because it is permitted for them to scoop a scoopful with the hand, and not by lowering the mouth to it. This is the apparent meaning of the exception from the first clause, because he ruled in it that whoever drinks from it is not of him, so the exception implies that whoever scoops a scoopful from it with his hand is of him, since it is permitted for him in that. This is how exception works: it reverses from negation to affirmation, and from affirmation to negation, according to the sound view among the schools in this matter. In the exception there is something omitted, the implied meaning being: "Except one who scoops a scoopful with his hand and drinks it," or "for drinking."

The two Haramis (Meccan and Medinan readers) and Abu 'Amr read "ghurfatan" with a fatha on the ghayn. The rest read it with a damma. It is said: both are in the sense of the verbal noun. It is said: both are in the sense of the object scooped. It is said: "ghurfah" with a fatha means one time, and with a damma means what the hand holds. If it is a verbal noun, it is not of the regular pattern, since if it were of the regular pattern, one would say "ightirafah." The object of "ightaraf" would then be omitted, meaning "water." If it is in the sense of the object scooped, it is the direct object. Ibn 'Atiyya said: Abu 'Ali preferred the damma on the ghayn, and al-Tabari also preferred it, because "ghurfatan" with a fatha is a verbal noun that is not from "ightiraf." End of his words.

This preference that the exegetes and grammarians mention between the two readings is not appropriate, because all these readings are sound, transmitted, and established from the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and each has an apparent and good basis in Arabic. So it is not possible to prefer one reading over another. "Bi-yadihi" (with his hand) is connected to "ightaraf" (scooped). It is said: It is also permissible that it be a qualifier for "ghurfah," so it would be connected to the omitted element. The apparent meaning of "ghurfatan bi-yadihi" (a scoopful with his hand) is restriction to one scoop, and that it is done with the hand. Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil said: The scoop was one from which he would drink, he and his animals and his servants, and he would carry some of it. Muqatil said: He would fill his waterskin from it. It is said: God would place blessing in it, so that it would suffice for all of them, and this was a miracle for the prophet of that time. Some exegetes said: He did not mean the scoop of a palm, but meant one time with a waterskin, or a jar, or something similar. This trial with which God tested the troops of Talut was a great trial, since they were forbidden the water although it was present and abundant, in the intense heat of summer, and whoever was allowed some of it was allowed only the amount he could scoop with his hand. How much of it could reach him from that? This is more burdensome in obligation than what the people of Aylah were tested with, namely abstaining from hunting on Saturday, although it was possible for them to do so, and fish came to them in abundance on that day.

﴿So they drank from it, except a few﴾. That is, they plunged their faces into it. Its apparent meaning is that most of them drank, and that the few did not drink. The drinking that most of them did may be understood as the drinking that was not permitted and in which they transgressed. The exception would mean that those few did not drink that drinking which was not permitted. Under the "few" there would be two categories: one who did not taste it at all, and the other who scooped with their hands. This division was reported in meaning from Ibn 'Abbas: most of them drank in proportion to their certainty. The disbelievers drank like thirsty camels, and the disobedient drank less than that. Six-and-seventy thousand of the people turned back, and some of the believers remained who did not drink anything, and some of them took the scoop. As for those who drank, they were not satisfied; rather, thirst afflicted them. As for those who left the water, their condition was good, and they were more deserving than those who took the scoop. It has been said that those who drank and opposed God's command had their faces and lips blackened, so they were not satisfied, and they remained on the bank of the river, and they were cowardly about meeting the enemy, so they did not cross over and did not witness the conquest. It was also said: Rather, all of them crossed over, but only the few who did not drink attended the fighting. The exception is four thousand, as said by 'Ikrima and al-Suddi. It is also said: three hundred and thirteen.

'Abd Allah, Ubayy and al-A'mash read "illa qalilun" with a raf' (nominative). Al-Zamakhshari said: This is from their inclining toward the meaning and turning away from the wording, and it is a great principle in the science of Arabic. Since the meaning of "fashariba minhu" (so they drank from it) is the same as "falam yuti'uhu" (so they did not obey him), it was treated accordingly, as if it were said: "Only a few of them did not obey him." A similar example is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"And the bite of time, O son of Marwan, has left of the wealth only what is depleted or what is plundered."

As if he said: "There remains of the wealth only what is depleted or what is plundered." End of his words.

The meaning is that this affirmative construction, namely "so they drank from it," has the sense of a negated clause, as if it were said: "so they did not obey him." On this reading "qalilun" (قَلِيلٌ) is in the nominative. If no sense of negation were intended, the word after *illa* (إلا, "except") could not be in the nominative. It is therefore clear that its nominative case is a substitution (badal) in terms of meaning: the affirmative clause functions like a negative one. As for al-Zamakhshari's view that the word after *illa* is nominative here by way of interpretation (ta'wil), that shows he did not maintain the continuity of the construction after an affirmative clause, which is why he interpreted it that way. We say: when an affirmative clause (mujab, a positive clause) precedes, the word after *illa* may take two forms. The first is the accusative as an exception (istithna'), which is the more eloquent. The second is that the word after *illa* follows the case of the word it excludes (mustathna minhu): if that is nominative, it is nominative; if accusative, accusative; if genitive, genitive. So you say: "The people stood up, except Zayd" (qama al-qawmu illa Zaydun); "I saw the people, except Zayd" (ra'aytu al-qawma illa Zaydan); "I passed by the people, except Zayd" (marartu bi-al-qawmi illa Zaydin). This holds whether the word before *illa* is a noun or a pronoun. The grammarians differ on its i'rab (grammatical case analysis). Some said it follows the preceding word as a qualifier (na't, adjective), and some of them took this on its apparent wording, saying: the noun and the pronoun may both be qualified by what follows *illa*. Others said: a qualifier is only used with an indefinite noun or a definite noun defined by the generic article (lam al-jins). If the noun is definite by annexation, as in "your brothers stood up" (qama ikhwatuka), or by the definite article for a specific referent (al-'ahd), or by other kinds of definiteness other than the generic article, then following is not permitted and the accusative as exception is required. Others said: the grammarians here mean by qualifier (na't) the apposition ('atf al-bayan, explicative apposition). Among the following after an affirmative clause is the poet's verse:

"And every brother is parted from by his brother / By the life of your father, except the two Farqadan (stars)."

This question is fully treated in the science of grammar (ilm al-nahw). What we intended was to point out that al-Zamakhshari's interpretation of this affirmative clause as having the sense of a negation is not necessary, and that he was not mindful of what the grammarians established about the affirmative clause.

* *

﴿So when he crossed it, he and those who believed with him﴾. The apparent meaning is that none crossed the river except him and the believers. This is also related from Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi: that those who drank and disobeyed turned aside and did not cross. It was also said: rather, all of them crossed, but only a few attended the fighting. "Jawaza" (جاوَزَ) is an intransitive verb used here in the sense of "fa'ala," meaning "crossed." "Those who believed with him" refers to the number of the people of Badr. Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi said: four thousand crossed with him. Ibn Abbas said: among them were those who had drunk. They both said: when they saw Jalut and his troops, they said: "We have no strength today." Three thousand, six hundred and some eighty-odd turned back. Most of the exegetes hold that only those who did not drink, except for a handful of water, and those who did not drink at all crossed. Then the insight of these people varied: some were cowardly and a few were resolute. "Huwa" (هو) is an emphatic pronoun for the hidden pronoun in "jawazahu" (جاوَزَهُ). "Wa-alladhina" (والَّذِينَ) may be in apposition to the hidden pronoun, or the waw may be circumstantial (waw al-hal), which entails that they crossed with him. The more apparent reading is that the waw is coordinating (lil-'atf). The merging of "jawazahu" (جاوَزَهُ) into "huwa" (هو) is weak and not commended, except if the vowel of the hā' is shortened so that there is no imala (vowel inclination) in it.

﴿They said: "We have no strength today against Jalut and his troops."﴾ The speakers of this are the disbelievers who withdrew, and they are the subject of "shariba" (شَرِبُوا, "they drank"); this is the view of Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi. It was also said: it is those among the believers whose insight was weak, and they are the ones who crossed the river and were the few; this is the view of al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Zajjaj. "Taqah" (طاقَةَ) is from "tawq," meaning strength, and is from "atâqa" (أطاقَ), like "ata'a" (أطاعَ, obeyed) with the verbal noun "ta'ah," "ajaba" (أجابَ) with "jabah," and "aghara" (أغارَ) with "ghārah." "Lana" (لَنا) is related to an omitted element, since it is in the position of the predicate; it cannot be related to "taqah," for then it would be "taqatan" (tanween) with nunation, which would be required. "Al-yawma" (اليَوْمَ) is in the accusative by what is related to "lana," and "bi-Jalut" (بِجالُوتَ) is related to it. Some permitted that "bi-Jalut" be in the position of the predicate, but the meaning does not support that.

﴿Those who were certain that they would meet God said﴾. The "zann" (ظن, supposition) may be on its original basis, and the meaning of "mula qu Allah" (مُلاقُو اللَّهِ, "meeting God") is that they would be martyred on that day, because of their resolve for true fighting and their determination to meet their enemies, as happened to Abdullah ibn Hizam at Uhud and elsewhere; this is what al-Zajjaj said along with others. It was also said: they will meet God's reward because of obedience, for every person does not know the outcome of his affair, so he must be in a state of supposition. It was also said: they will meet God's obedience, for one cannot be certain that this deed of his is an act of obedience, since it may be mixed with some showing off or reputation-seeking. It was also said: they will meet God's promise to them of victory, for although it is certain, it is supposed in the first instance. It is also possible that "zann" means certainty (iqan): that is, they are certain of resurrection and return to God; this is what al-Suddi said along with others.

* *

﴿How many a small company has overcome a large company by God's leave﴾. This statement is an exhortation by those determined on fighting, and an urging to it, and a summoning of patience, and an imitation of those who were true to God. The meaning is: we do not care about Jalut and his troops, even if they are many, for numbers are not a cause of victory. The few have often prevailed over the many. Since this had occurred in past times and they knew it, they were informed with the expression "kam" (كَمْ, "how many"), which implies multiplicity. Ubayy read "wa-ka'ayyin" (وكَأيِّنْ), which is synonymous with "kam" in expressing multiplicity. Its specification (tamyiz) in the Qur'an is only found accompanied by "min" (مِن, "from"). If "min" were omitted, the specification of the declarative "kam" would be in the genitive by annexation. It was said: by implying "min," and it is permissible to put it in the accusative by analogy with the interrogative "kam." The specification of "ka'ayyin" is in the accusative, so you say: "ka'ayyin rajulan jā'aka" (how many a man has come to you). The poet said:

"I drive away despair with hope, for how many a hope has had its ease decreed after hardship."

"Kam" (كَمْ) is in the nominative position as the subject of a nominal sentence. "Min" in "min fi'atin" (مِن فِئَةٍ) is said to be superfluous, though it is not one of the places where it is superfluous. It was said: it is in the position of a qualifier for "kam." "Fi'ah" (فِئَةٍ) here is singular in meaning plural, as if it were said: many companies that were small have overcome. Al-A'sha read it with the hamzah changed into a yā', like "mīrah" for "mi'rah" (a well-rope), and this is an elegant substitution. The predicate of "kam" is the verb "ghalabat" (غَلَبَتْ, "overcame"). The meaning of "bi-idhni Allah" (بِإذْنِ اللَّهِ) is by His enabling and His granting of victory to them. In this verse is evidence for the permissibility of a small group fighting a large group, even if the latter are many times their number, when they know that it will bring harm to the enemy. As for the permissibility of fleeing from a large group when they exceed twice their number, its explanation will come in Surat al-Anfal, God willing.

﴿And God is with the patient﴾. This is an exhortation to patience in fighting, for God is with whoever is patient in support of His religion; He helps, aids and strengthens him. It is possible that this is part of their speech, and it is possible that it is a new statement from God; this is what al-Qaffal said.

﴿And when they went forth against Jalut and his troops﴾. They came out into the open (al-baraz) of the land, which is that which is apparent and level. Dueling in war means that each champion appears before his opponent so that his opponent can see him. The troops of Talut were three hundred thousand horsemen; it was said one hundred thousand; and Ikrimah said ninety thousand.

﴿They said: "Our Lord, pour upon us patience"﴾. Patience here means restraining the soul for fighting. They turned to supplication to God, Most High, calling upon Him with the word "Lord" (Rabb), which indicates reform and dominion, and in this is an indication of servanthood. Their words "pour upon us patience" are a request that He pour patience over them until it is elevated above them, so that it is for them like a vessel and they are like things contained within it.

﴿And make firm our feet﴾, so that they do not slip from the slippery places of fighting. This is a metaphor for strengthening and reinforcing their hearts. Since they asked for patience to be above them, they asked for their feet to be made firm and fixed.

﴿And help us against the disbelieving people﴾. That is: assist us against them. They used the attribute that requires the abandonment of their enemies, which is disbelief, for they used to worship idols. In their saying "Our Lord" (Rabbana) is an acknowledgment of God, Most High, of His oneness, and an acknowledgment of His lordship and servanthood.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 249–250 (part 1 of 2):

﴿So when Talut set out with the troops﴾. Between this clause and the one before it, something is omitted. Its implied meaning is: "Then the Ark came to them, they acknowledged his kingship, and they prepared to march out." ﴿So when Talut set out﴾, meaning he departed from his place of residence. One says "fasala 'an al-mawdi'" (he departed from the place) and "infasala" (he separated himself from it) and "jawazahu" (he passed beyond it). It is said that the original form was "fasala nafsahu" (he separated himself), and then this became common, so the object was dropped until it took the status of an intransitive verb, like "infasala." The preposition "bi" in ﴿bil-junud﴾ (with the troops) indicates circumstance, meaning that the troops were accompanying him. Their number was seventy thousand, as said by Ibn 'Abbas; or eighty thousand, as said by 'Ikrima; or one hundred thousand, as said by Muqatil; or thirty thousand.

'Ikrima said: When the Children of Israel saw the Ark, they hastened to obey it and to march out with him. Talut said to them: "Whoever has built a building and not finished it shall not march out with me, nor whoever has married a woman and not consummated the marriage with her, nor the owner of a crop he has not harvested, nor the owner of merchandise he has not sent off, nor one who has a debt owed to him or owed by him, nor the elderly, nor the sick." So there marched out with him those whose number is disputed, according to his condition. He led them, and they complained of the scarcity of water and the fear of thirst, and it was the season of intense summer heat. They took a desert route, so they asked God to cause a river to flow for them.

﴿He said: Indeed God will test you with a river﴾. Wahb said: It was the one they had proposed. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada said: It is a river between the Jordan and Palestine. It is said: It is the river of Palestine, as said by al-Suddi and Ibn 'Abbas also. The majority read "bi-nahar" with a fatha on the ha'. Mujahid, Humayd al-A'raj, Abu al-Sammak and others read it with a sukun on the ha' throughout the Qur'an.

The apparent meaning of Talut's words, "Indeed God will test you," is an inspiration, according to the view of those who say he was a prophet, or that God revealed it to their prophet, and the prophet informed Talut of that. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is possible that this was something God inspired in Talut, so his troops acted upon it, and the inspiration was made a trial from God for them. The meaning of this trial is examination. Whoever's obedience is shown by abstaining from the water is known to be obedient in other matters, and whoever is overcome by his desire for the water and disobeys the command is, in hardships, more likely to disobey. End of his words. After Talut reports what occurred to his mind as a command of God, and he states it definitively on God's behalf: ﴿Whoever drinks from it is not of me﴾, meaning: is not of my followers in this battle, nor of my partisans. This does not take them out of faith, like the saying: "Whoever cheats us is not of us," and "He is not of us who tears the collars and slaps the cheeks." Or it means: he is not connected to me and not united with me, from the saying of people: "So-and-so is of me," as if I were a part of him, because of their intermingling and their unity. Al-Nabigha said:

"When you try to commit wickedness against the lion, then I am not of you, and you are not of me."

﴿But whoever does not taste it is of me﴾, meaning: whoever does not taste it. The taste of everything is its tasting, and from it comes "tatha''um" (tasting). One says: "Tata''amtu minhu," meaning "I tasted it." The Arabs say of one whose soul does not incline toward food that one is fed from: "Its eating is easy." Ibn al-Anbari said: The Arabs say: "I fed you water," meaning "I made you taste it." And "ta'imtu al-ma'" I taste the water, meaning "dhuqtu" (I tasted it). The poet said:

"If you wish, I will forbid women to you, and if you wish, I will not let you taste sweet water or cold sleep."

Al-nuqakh means sweet water, and al-bard means sleep. One says: "I did not taste a wink of sleep." In the hadith of Abu Dharr: "In the water of Zamzam is food for food." And in the hadith: "We have no food except the two blacks, the dates and the water." The word "ta'm" applies to food and drink. This word was chosen because it is more emphatic: negating eating entails negating drinking, but negating drinking does not entail negating eating, since "ta'm" applies to tasting. Restricting eating is more burdensome in obligation than restricting drinking, since it can be achieved by placing it in the mouth, even if one does not drink, and that gives some kind of relief.

In His words ﴿but whoever does not taste it﴾ there is an indication that water is food, and this was also indicated earlier. There is disagreement over whether riba (usury) applies to it. Al-Shafi'i said: It is not permissible to sell water for water in unequal amounts, nor is deferred payment permissible for it. Malik, Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf said: That is permissible. Ibn al-'Arabi reported that the sound view within the school of Malik is that riba applies to it. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: It is among what is measured by volume or weight, so according to this, unequal exchange is not permissible in his view.

It seems that His words ﴿Whoever drinks from it﴾ by their apparent meaning indicate direct drinking from the river, so that if one takes it with a cup, drinking from that would not fall under "whoever drinks from it," if he did not drink directly from the river. In the school of Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, if one says: "If I drink from the waterskin, my slave is free," it is understood as drinking directly (by lowering the mouth), and if he scoops from it or drinks with a vessel, he does not break the oath. They said: Because God forbade drinking from the river, and forbade tasting it, and excepted from the tasting the scooping, so the prohibition on drinking remains, and this shows that scooping is not drinking. He used the phrase "whoever does not" with reference to the pronoun of the water, not to the river, to remove that ambiguity, and to make known that the aim is the prohibition of their reaching the water from the river, by drinking from it directly or indirectly. Ibn 'Atiyya said: In His words ﴿but whoever does not taste it, then he is of me﴾ there is blocking of means (sadd al-dhara'i'), because the least amount of tasting falls under the word "ta'm." So when the prohibition on tasting occurs, there is no way for drinking to occur from one who avoids tasting. Because of this emphasis, the speech did not say: "whoever does not drink from it." End of his words.

﴿Except one who scoops a scoopful with his hand﴾. This is an exception from the first clause, which is His words ﴿whoever drinks from it is not of me﴾. The meaning is: whoever scoops a scoopful with his hand, not by lowering his mouth to the water, is of me. When an exception follows two or more clauses, it may be attributed to each of them, but it primarily relates to the last one. There is a difference of opinion on this matter, which is mentioned in the science of the principles of jurisprudence. If evidence indicates that it relates to some of the clauses, the exception is from that clause. Here, evidence indicates that it relates to the first clause. The second clause was placed before the exception from the first because the second clause is indicated by the first through implication: when He mentioned that God will test them with a river, and that whoever drinks from it is not of him, it was understood from that that whoever does not drink from it is of him. So the second clause functioned as a separation between the first and the exception from it, when the first indicates it. Indeed, if it were not stated explicitly, it would be understood from the first clause. In some writings there occurs the following text: "Except one who scoops" is an exception from the first clause, and if you wish, you may make it an exception from the second clause. End of quote. It does not appear to be an exception from the second clause, because he ruled that whoever does not taste it is of him, so the exception from this would imply that whoever scoops a scoopful from it with his hand is not of him. But the matter is not like that, because it is permitted for them to scoop a scoopful with the hand, and not by lowering the mouth to it. This is the apparent meaning of the exception from the first clause, because he ruled in it that whoever drinks from it is not of him, so the exception implies that whoever scoops a scoopful from it with his hand is of him, since it is permitted for him in that. This is how exception works: it reverses from negation to affirmation, and from affirmation to negation, according to the sound view among the schools in this matter. In the exception there is something omitted, the implied meaning being: "Except one who scoops a scoopful with his hand and drinks it," or "for drinking."

The two Haramis (Meccan and Medinan readers) and Abu 'Amr read "ghurfatan" with a fatha on the ghayn. The rest read it with a damma. It is said: both are in the sense of the verbal noun. It is said: both are in the sense of the object scooped. It is said: "ghurfah" with a fatha means one time, and with a damma means what the hand holds. If it is a verbal noun, it is not of the regular pattern, since if it were of the regular pattern, one would say "ightirafah." The object of "ightaraf" would then be omitted, meaning "water." If it is in the sense of the object scooped, it is the direct object. Ibn 'Atiyya said: Abu 'Ali preferred the damma on the ghayn, and al-Tabari also preferred it, because "ghurfatan" with a fatha is a verbal noun that is not from "ightiraf." End of his words.

This preference that the exegetes and grammarians mention between the two readings is not appropriate, because all these readings are sound, transmitted, and established from the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and each has an apparent and good basis in Arabic. So it is not possible to prefer one reading over another. "Bi-yadihi" (with his hand) is connected to "ightaraf" (scooped). It is said: It is also permissible that it be a qualifier for "ghurfah," so it would be connected to the omitted element. The apparent meaning of "ghurfatan bi-yadihi" (a scoopful with his hand) is restriction to one scoop, and that it is done with the hand. Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil said: The scoop was one from which he would drink, he and his animals and his servants, and he would carry some of it. Muqatil said: He would fill his waterskin from it. It is said: God would place blessing in it, so that it would suffice for all of them, and this was a miracle for the prophet of that time. Some exegetes said: He did not mean the scoop of a palm, but meant one time with a waterskin, or a jar, or something similar. This trial with which God tested the troops of Talut was a great trial, since they were forbidden the water although it was present and abundant, in the intense heat of summer, and whoever was allowed some of it was allowed only the amount he could scoop with his hand. How much of it could reach him from that? This is more burdensome in obligation than what the people of Aylah were tested with, namely abstaining from hunting on Saturday, although it was possible for them to do so, and fish came to them in abundance on that day.

﴿So they drank from it, except a few﴾. That is, they plunged their faces into it. Its apparent meaning is that most of them drank, and that the few did not drink. The drinking that most of them did may be understood as the drinking that was not permitted and in which they transgressed. The exception would mean that those few did not drink that drinking which was not permitted. Under the "few" there would be two categories: one who did not taste it at all, and the other who scooped with their hands. This division was reported in meaning from Ibn 'Abbas: most of them drank in proportion to their certainty. The disbelievers drank like thirsty camels, and the disobedient drank less than that. Six-and-seventy thousand of the people turned back, and some of the believers remained who did not drink anything, and some of them took the scoop. As for those who drank, they were not satisfied; rather, thirst afflicted them. As for those who left the water, their condition was good, and they were more deserving than those who took the scoop. It has been said that those who drank and opposed God's command had their faces and lips blackened, so they were not satisfied, and they remained on the bank of the river, and they were cowardly about meeting the enemy, so they did not cross over and did not witness the conquest. It was also said: Rather, all of them crossed over, but only the few who did not drink attended the fighting. The exception is four thousand, as said by 'Ikrima and al-Suddi. It is also said: three hundred and thirteen.

'Abd Allah, Ubayy and al-A'mash read "illa qalilun" with a raf' (nominative). Al-Zamakhshari said: This is from their inclining toward the meaning and turning away from the wording, and it is a great principle in the science of Arabic. Since the meaning of "fashariba minhu" (so they drank from it) is the same as "falam yuti'uhu" (so they did not obey him), it was treated accordingly, as if it were said: "Only a few of them did not obey him." A similar example is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"And the bite of time, O son of Marwan, has left of the wealth only what is depleted or what is plundered."

As if he said: "There remains of the wealth only what is depleted or what is plundered." End of his words.

The meaning is that this affirmative construction, namely "so they drank from it," has the sense of a negated clause, as if it were said: "so they did not obey him." On this reading "qalilun" (قَلِيلٌ) is in the nominative. If no sense of negation were intended, the word after *illa* (إلا, "except") could not be in the nominative. It is therefore clear that its nominative case is a substitution (badal) in terms of meaning: the affirmative clause functions like a negative one. As for al-Zamakhshari's view that the word after *illa* is nominative here by way of interpretation (ta'wil), that shows he did not maintain the continuity of the construction after an affirmative clause, which is why he interpreted it that way. We say: when an affirmative clause (mujab, a positive clause) precedes, the word after *illa* may take two forms. The first is the accusative as an exception (istithna'), which is the more eloquent. The second is that the word after *illa* follows the case of the word it excludes (mustathna minhu): if that is nominative, it is nominative; if accusative, accusative; if genitive, genitive. So you say: "The people stood up, except Zayd" (qama al-qawmu illa Zaydun); "I saw the people, except Zayd" (ra'aytu al-qawma illa Zaydan); "I passed by the people, except Zayd" (marartu bi-al-qawmi illa Zaydin). This holds whether the word before *illa* is a noun or a pronoun. The grammarians differ on its i'rab (grammatical case analysis). Some said it follows the preceding word as a qualifier (na't, adjective), and some of them took this on its apparent wording, saying: the noun and the pronoun may both be qualified by what follows *illa*. Others said: a qualifier is only used with an indefinite noun or a definite noun defined by the generic article (lam al-jins). If the noun is definite by annexation, as in "your brothers stood up" (qama ikhwatuka), or by the definite article for a specific referent (al-'ahd), or by other kinds of definiteness other than the generic article, then following is not permitted and the accusative as exception is required. Others said: the grammarians here mean by qualifier (na't) the apposition ('atf al-bayan, explicative apposition). Among the following after an affirmative clause is the poet's verse:

"And every brother is parted from by his brother / By the life of your father, except the two Farqadan (stars)."

This question is fully treated in the science of grammar (ilm al-nahw). What we intended was to point out that al-Zamakhshari's interpretation of this affirmative clause as having the sense of a negation is not necessary, and that he was not mindful of what the grammarians established about the affirmative clause.

* *

﴿So when he crossed it, he and those who believed with him﴾. The apparent meaning is that none crossed the river except him and the believers. This is also related from Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi: that those who drank and disobeyed turned aside and did not cross. It was also said: rather, all of them crossed, but only a few attended the fighting. "Jawaza" (جاوَزَ) is an intransitive verb used here in the sense of "fa'ala," meaning "crossed." "Those who believed with him" refers to the number of the people of Badr. Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi said: four thousand crossed with him. Ibn Abbas said: among them were those who had drunk. They both said: when they saw Jalut and his troops, they said: "We have no strength today." Three thousand, six hundred and some eighty-odd turned back. Most of the exegetes hold that only those who did not drink, except for a handful of water, and those who did not drink at all crossed. Then the insight of these people varied: some were cowardly and a few were resolute. "Huwa" (هو) is an emphatic pronoun for the hidden pronoun in "jawazahu" (جاوَزَهُ). "Wa-alladhina" (والَّذِينَ) may be in apposition to the hidden pronoun, or the waw may be circumstantial (waw al-hal), which entails that they crossed with him. The more apparent reading is that the waw is coordinating (lil-'atf). The merging of "jawazahu" (جاوَزَهُ) into "huwa" (هو) is weak and not commended, except if the vowel of the hā' is shortened so that there is no imala (vowel inclination) in it.

﴿They said: "We have no strength today against Jalut and his troops."﴾ The speakers of this are the disbelievers who withdrew, and they are the subject of "shariba" (شَرِبُوا, "they drank"); this is the view of Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi. It was also said: it is those among the believers whose insight was weak, and they are the ones who crossed the river and were the few; this is the view of al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Zajjaj. "Taqah" (طاقَةَ) is from "tawq," meaning strength, and is from "atâqa" (أطاقَ), like "ata'a" (أطاعَ, obeyed) with the verbal noun "ta'ah," "ajaba" (أجابَ) with "jabah," and "aghara" (أغارَ) with "ghārah." "Lana" (لَنا) is related to an omitted element, since it is in the position of the predicate; it cannot be related to "taqah," for then it would be "taqatan" (tanween) with nunation, which would be required. "Al-yawma" (اليَوْمَ) is in the accusative by what is related to "lana," and "bi-Jalut" (بِجالُوتَ) is related to it. Some permitted that "bi-Jalut" be in the position of the predicate, but the meaning does not support that.

﴿Those who were certain that they would meet God said﴾. The "zann" (ظن, supposition) may be on its original basis, and the meaning of "mula qu Allah" (مُلاقُو اللَّهِ, "meeting God") is that they would be martyred on that day, because of their resolve for true fighting and their determination to meet their enemies, as happened to Abdullah ibn Hizam at Uhud and elsewhere; this is what al-Zajjaj said along with others. It was also said: they will meet God's reward because of obedience, for every person does not know the outcome of his affair, so he must be in a state of supposition. It was also said: they will meet God's obedience, for one cannot be certain that this deed of his is an act of obedience, since it may be mixed with some showing off or reputation-seeking. It was also said: they will meet God's promise to them of victory, for although it is certain, it is supposed in the first instance. It is also possible that "zann" means certainty (iqan): that is, they are certain of resurrection and return to God; this is what al-Suddi said along with others.

* *

﴿How many a small company has overcome a large company by God's leave﴾. This statement is an exhortation by those determined on fighting, and an urging to it, and a summoning of patience, and an imitation of those who were true to God. The meaning is: we do not care about Jalut and his troops, even if they are many, for numbers are not a cause of victory. The few have often prevailed over the many. Since this had occurred in past times and they knew it, they were informed with the expression "kam" (كَمْ, "how many"), which implies multiplicity. Ubayy read "wa-ka'ayyin" (وكَأيِّنْ), which is synonymous with "kam" in expressing multiplicity. Its specification (tamyiz) in the Qur'an is only found accompanied by "min" (مِن, "from"). If "min" were omitted, the specification of the declarative "kam" would be in the genitive by annexation. It was said: by implying "min," and it is permissible to put it in the accusative by analogy with the interrogative "kam." The specification of "ka'ayyin" is in the accusative, so you say: "ka'ayyin rajulan jā'aka" (how many a man has come to you). The poet said:

"I drive away despair with hope, for how many a hope has had its ease decreed after hardship."

"Kam" (كَمْ) is in the nominative position as the subject of a nominal sentence. "Min" in "min fi'atin" (مِن فِئَةٍ) is said to be superfluous, though it is not one of the places where it is superfluous. It was said: it is in the position of a qualifier for "kam." "Fi'ah" (فِئَةٍ) here is singular in meaning plural, as if it were said: many companies that were small have overcome. Al-A'sha read it with the hamzah changed into a yā', like "mīrah" for "mi'rah" (a well-rope), and this is an elegant substitution. The predicate of "kam" is the verb "ghalabat" (غَلَبَتْ, "overcame"). The meaning of "bi-idhni Allah" (بِإذْنِ اللَّهِ) is by His enabling and His granting of victory to them. In this verse is evidence for the permissibility of a small group fighting a large group, even if the latter are many times their number, when they know that it will bring harm to the enemy. As for the permissibility of fleeing from a large group when they exceed twice their number, its explanation will come in Surat al-Anfal, God willing.

﴿And God is with the patient﴾. This is an exhortation to patience in fighting, for God is with whoever is patient in support of His religion; He helps, aids and strengthens him. It is possible that this is part of their speech, and it is possible that it is a new statement from God; this is what al-Qaffal said.

﴿And when they went forth against Jalut and his troops﴾. They came out into the open (al-baraz) of the land, which is that which is apparent and level. Dueling in war means that each champion appears before his opponent so that his opponent can see him. The troops of Talut were three hundred thousand horsemen; it was said one hundred thousand; and Ikrimah said ninety thousand.

﴿They said: "Our Lord, pour upon us patience"﴾. Patience here means restraining the soul for fighting. They turned to supplication to God, Most High, calling upon Him with the word "Lord" (Rabb), which indicates reform and dominion, and in this is an indication of servanthood. Their words "pour upon us patience" are a request that He pour patience over them until it is elevated above them, so that it is for them like a vessel and they are like things contained within it.

﴿And make firm our feet﴾, so that they do not slip from the slippery places of fighting. This is a metaphor for strengthening and reinforcing their hearts. Since they asked for patience to be above them, they asked for their feet to be made firm and fixed.

﴿And help us against the disbelieving people﴾. That is: assist us against them. They used the attribute that requires the abandonment of their enemies, which is disbelief, for they used to worship idols. In their saying "Our Lord" (Rabbana) is an acknowledgment of God, Most High, of His oneness, and an acknowledgment of His lordship and servanthood.

﴿So they routed them by Allah's permission﴾, that is: they overcame them by Allah's empowering.

﴿And Dawud killed Jalut﴾. The commentators elaborated at length on the manner in which Dawud (David) killed Jalut (Goliath), but Allah does not specify any detail of the manner. Al-Sajawandi summarized this in a way that conveys the intended meaning. He said: He was the youngest of his brothers, meaning the thirteen sons of Iysha, father of Dawud. He had been left behind with the sheep. It was revealed to their prophet that the slayer of Jalut would be the son of Iysha on whom Talut's armor would fit. It fit no one but Dawud. It was also said: When Jalut came forward, Talut called out: "Whoever kills Jalut, I will share my kingdom with him and marry him to my daughter." Dawud came forward and struck him with a stone from a sling, and it passed through from between his eyes to the back of his neck and struck his army. A group was killed and they were routed. Then Talut regretted his condition after fulfilling it and intended to kill Dawud, and he died repentant, as al-Dahhak reported. Wahb said: He regretted before fulfilling it and died disobedient. It was also said: Dawud struck the place of Jalut's nose. It was also said: The stone shattered until some of it struck everyone in the army, like the handful that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) threw on the day of Hunayn. Al-Zamakhshari said: Dawud's father was in Talut's army with six of his sons, and Dawud was the seventh, and he was young, tending the sheep. It was revealed to Shamwil that Dawud son of Iysha would kill Jalut, so he asked for him from his father. He came, and on his way he passed three stones, each of which asked him to carry it, saying: "You will kill Jalut with us." So he put them in his pouch, threw them at Jalut and killed him. Talut married him to his daughter. It is also narrated that he envied him and wanted to kill him, then he repented. End of quotation. It is also narrated that Dawud was among the best of people at the sling. And it is narrated that the stones joined together in the pouch and became a single stone.

﴿And Allah gave him the kingdom and wisdom and taught him of what He willed﴾. It is narrated that Talut relinquished the kingdom to Dawud, so he became king. It is also narrated that the Children of Israel preferred Talut's rule because of Dawud's killing of Jalut. It is also narrated that Talut feared Dawud, so Dawud fled from him and stayed in a mountain until Talut died, and then the Children of Israel made him king. Al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi said: Dawud was made king seven years after the killing of Jalut, and the Children of Israel did not unite under one king except Dawud. There is disagreement over whether Dawud was a prophet at the time of the killing of Jalut. It was said: He was a prophet, because extraordinary events occur only through prophets. Al-Hasan said: He was not a prophet, because it is not permissible for one who is not a prophet to be placed over a prophet. Wisdom is placing matters in their right places correctly, and the perfection of that is attained only through prophethood, and it had not been given to anyone before him. Kingship was in one tribe and prophethood in another tribe. When Shamwil and Talut died, kingship and prophethood were combined for Dawud.

Muqatil said: "wisdom" is the Zabur (Psalms). It was also said: it is justice in conduct. It was also said: wisdom is knowledge and acting upon it. Al-Dahhak said: It is a chain that hung down from heaven; no one with an ailment could hold it without being healed, and disputes were judged by it. Whoever was in the right could grasp it, so that a man who had a pearl belonging to another man put it in his walking stick and handed it to him saying: "Keep it for me." Then he came to touch the chain and grasped it, because he had returned it. But it was lifted up because of the wickedness of his deception. When wisdom is mentioned, mentioning kingship before it and prophethood after it is by way of ascending order.

﴿And taught him of what He willed﴾. It was said: the craft of making armor. It was said: the speech of birds and their language, for the bees and the ants. It was said: the Zabur. It was said: a beautiful voice and melodies. It was also said: Allah did not give any of His creatures a voice like his. When he recited the Zabur, wild animals would draw near until he could take them by the neck, birds would shade him, listening attentively to him, flowing water would become still, and the wind would be calm. Drums and cymbals were made only in imitation of his voice. It was also said: "of what He willed" refers to performing acts of obedience and commanding them, and avoiding sins. The subject pronoun in (yashaʾu, "He wills") refers back to Dawud, meaning: of what Dawud wills.

* *

﴿And were it not for Allah's repelling people, some by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted﴾. Nafi', Ya'qub and Sahl read (wa-lawla difaʿ, "and were it not for the defense of"), which is the verbal noun of dafaʿa, like kataba kitaban, or the verbal noun of dafaʿa in the sense of daffaʿa. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

"I was keen to defend them, but when death comes, it cannot be repelled."

The others read (daf'u), the verbal noun of daʿa, like daraba darban. The ones repelled are the soldiers of the Muslims, and the ones repelling are the polytheists. "The earth would have been corrupted" through the killing of believers and the ruin of lands and mosques. Ibn Abbas and a group of commentators said this, and it was also said: or the Abdal (the substitutes), who are forty; whenever one dies, Allah raises another in his place. On the Day of Resurrection they will all die: twenty-two in Syria and eighteen in Iraq.

The hadith about the Abdal is narrated from Ali and Abu al-Darda', who both traced it back to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Or those mentioned in the hadith: "Were it not for worshippers bowing, infants nursing and animals grazing, the punishment would have been poured upon you in a torrent." Or: whoever prays, gives zakat and fasts is a means by which others who do not do so are repelled. Or: the believer is a means by which the disbeliever is repelled, just as the believer is tested by the disbeliever; this was said by Qatada. Or: a righteous man is a means by which the calamity is repelled from his household and neighbors. Or: the witnesses through whom rights are established; this was said by al-Thawri. Or: the ruler, or the oppressor repels the hand of the oppressor. Or: Dawud was a means by which Talut was defended, and were it not for that, the Amalekites would have overcome the Children of Israel. In that case "people" is general but the intended meaning is specific. What appears correct is that those repelled are the believers, and were it not for that, the earth would have been corrupted, because disbelief would have engulfed it and spread through all its regions. But Allah, exalted is He, does not leave any age without someone standing for the truth and calling to Allah, exalted is He, until He placed this in the community of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Al-Zamakhshari said: Were it not that Allah repels some people by means of others and restrains their corruption through them, the corrupters would have prevailed, the earth would have been corrupted, its benefits would have been lost, and its interests, such as tillage, reproduction and all that which makes the earth flourish, would have ceased. End of quotation. This is a fine statement, and the one before it is the statement of Ibn Atiyya. The verbal noun (daf' or difaʿ) is a construct with the agent as its genitive, and (baʿdahum, "some of them") is an apposition to "the people," an apposition of part from whole. The preposition (bi-baʿḍin, "by means of some") is connected to the verbal noun, and the (bi-) in it is for transitivity, so it is the second object of the verbal noun, because (daf') is transitive to one object and then extended to a second by the preposition bi-. The basic use of bi- for transitivity applies to intransitive verbs, as in ﴿He would have taken away their hearing﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:20]. When a verb is already transitive, its regular form is to transitivize it with the hamza, as you say: Zayd ate the meat (ṭaʿima Zaydun al-laḥm), then you say: I fed Zayd the meat (aṭʿamtu Zaydan al-laḥm), and you may not say: ṭaʿʿamtu Zaydan bi-al-laḥm. This occurs only rarely and is not a regular pattern. Among these are daf'a (to push) and ṣakka (to strike). You say: The stone struck the stone (ṣakka al-ḥajaru al-ḥajar), and you say: I struck the stone with the stone (ṣakkaktu al-ḥajara bi-al-ḥajar), meaning: I made it strike it. Similarly they said: I struck the two stones, one against the other (ṣakkaktu al-ḥajarayni aḥadahumā bi-al-ākhar), which is parallel to ﴿Allah's repelling of people, some by means of others﴾. So the (bi-) serves for transitivity like the hamza.

Sibawayh said, when he mentioned transitivity by the hamza and by doubling, the following text: "On this basis, I repelled people, some by means of others, on the pattern of your saying alzamtu (I obligated), as if you had said in the example: adfaʿtu, just as you say adhhabtu bihi and adhhabtuhu min ʿindinā, and akhrajtuhu, and kharajtu bihi maʿaka." Then Sibawayh said: "I struck the two stones, one against the other, on the basis that it is the object from your saying: the two stones struck, one against the other. Similarly: ﴿Were it not for Allah's defense of people, some by means of others﴾." End of Sibawayh's statement. It is not far-fetched, in your saying "I repelled some people by means of others," that the (bi-) is instrumental, so that the noun in the genitive after it is not the object in meaning; rather the one in the accusative is the object. According to Sibawayh's view, the accusative noun is the object in form and the agent in meaning. If the (bi-) is instrumental, it is correct to attribute the verb to it metaphorically, just as you say in "I wrote with the pen": "I wrote the pen" (kataba al-qalam).

The corruption is attributed to the earth literally, through ruin and the loss of benefits, or metaphorically, meaning its inhabitants.

* *

﴿But Allah is full of bounty toward the worlds﴾. The point of the corrective transition here is that when He divided people into those by means of whom others are repelled and those who are repelled, and when by repelling some by means of others the corruption of the earth was prevented, a thought might arise in the mind of one who prevailed and dominated, concerning what he wants of corruption in the earth, that Allah is not bountiful toward him, since his purposes and aims were not fulfilled. So it was corrected: even if this seeker of corruption does not reach his goals, Allah is indeed full of bounty toward him, and He does good to him, and he is included in the generality of "the worlds." Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed Allah is full of bounty toward the people﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:243]. There is no one but that Allah has a bounty upon him, even if it were only the bounty of creation (fadl al-ikhtiraʿ).

This benefit of the corrective transition that we have stated is in accordance with what the scholars of the language established: that (lakinna, "but") is used between two things that are opposed in some respect. The phrase (ʿalā al-ʿālamīn, "toward the worlds") is connected to (faḍl, "bounty"), because its verb is transitive with (ʿalā, "over/toward"), and so is the verbal noun. Sometimes (ʿalā) is omitted with the verb; you say: faḍḍaltu fulānan, meaning: over so-and-so. Both omission and presence were combined in the poet's words:

"We found Nahshal to have excelled Fuqaym, as the excellence of the son of the she-camel over the weaned calf."

When it is transitive to a direct object by doubling, the preposition remains, as in His saying: ﴿Allah has preferred those who strive with their wealth and lives over those who sit at home﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:95].

﴿تِلْكَ آياتُ اللَّهِ نَتْلُوها عَلَيْكَ بِالحَقِّ وإنَّكَ لَمِنَ المُرْسَلِينَ﴾ ("Those are the signs of God, which We recite to you in truth, and you are indeed among the messengers.") (تِلْكَ) is a demonstrative for what is distant. As for (آياتُ اللَّهِ), it has been said that they are the Qur'an. The more apparent view is that they are the signs mentioned in the earlier narrative: the departure of those who fled from death, God's causing them to die all at once and then bringing them back to life in one act, the appointment of Talut (Saul) over the Children of Israel although he was not from the sons of their kings, the bringing of the Ark (al-tabut) after it had been lost, containing remnants of the inheritance of the family of Musa (Moses) and the family of Harun (Aaron), the angels carrying it in plain view, as reported from the interpreter of the Qur'an, Ibn Abbas, the great trial at the river in the heat of summer and during a journey, the answering of the prayer of one who trusted in God for victory, the killing of Jalut (Goliath) by Dawud (David), and God's giving him kingship and wisdom. All of these are great signs, extraordinary events. God recited them to His Prophet "in truth," meaning accompanied by truth, with no falsehood or fabrication in them, and not by the words of soothsayers, but in conformity with what is in the books of the Children of Israel. The Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ has the greatest share of such narratives in seeking help from God and in preparing against the disbelievers, and in the fact that a small number may overcome a large one, and that reliance upon God and turning to Him is what one depends upon in grave matters. When He, exalted, mentioned that He had recited these signs to His Prophet, He informed him that he was among the messengers, and He confirmed this with (إنَّ) and the lam, since he reported this verse without having read any book, without studying with rabbis, and without hearing reports.

The noble verses also contain the reports of the Children of Israel, when they demanded from their prophet a sign confirming that Talut had been made their king: that the Ark which they had lost would come to them containing what it had held of tranquility (al-sakinah) and of the remnant left by the family of Musa and the family of Harun, and that the angels would be carrying it. "Indeed in that is a sign" means a sign for one who is a believer, because this is a great extraordinary event. Talut's departure with the troops and his going forth with them from their homes to meet the enemy shows that they had made him king and submitted to him. He informed them on God's behalf that He would test them with a river. It is possible that God informed him directly, or that this was through their prophet's informing him from God. Whoever drinks from it by lapping it with the mouth is not of him, but only whoever scoops a handful with his hand; and whoever does not taste it is of him. God informed that most of them disobeyed and drank from it. When they crossed the river and saw the numbers and equipment of Jalut's army, they said that they had no strength for that. But one who was certain of meeting God answered them that multitude does not indicate victory, for the few have often overcome the many by God's enabling and empowering, and that if God is with the patient, they are the victorious. So they were urged to be steadfast when meeting the enemy. When they came forth against their enemies and the eye met the eye, they turned to God, exalted, with supplication and calling for help, and asked Him for patience in fighting, for firmness of their feet at slippery places, and for victory over those who disbelieved. The outcome of this utterance and of sincere fighting was that He empowered them over their enemies, they defeated them, and their king was killed; and when the head is gone, the body goes too. God gave Dawud the kingship of the Children of Israel and prophethood, which is wisdom, and taught him what He willed, including from the Zabur (Psalms), the craft of making armor (al-labus), and other things He taught him. Then He, exalted, mentioned that the setting right of the earth is by some people repelling others. Had God not repelled from the Children of Israel through the defeat of Jalut's people and the killing of Jalut by Dawud, their enemies would have overcome them and they would have been uprooted by killing, plunder and captivity; likewise those who are in their situation. But God's bounty is the one that precedes, for He did not give their enemies power over them, and He empowered them over those enemies. Then He, exalted, informed that these verses, which contain these lessons and these extraordinary events, were recited by God to His Prophet in the truth about which there is no doubt. Then He informed him that he is a messenger among the messengers who came before him in time. Messengership is above prophethood. The evidence of his messengership is his reporting this narrative containing the striking signs that testify to the truthfulness of the one who reported them, without anyone having informed him of them except God.

* *

﴿تِلْكَ آياتُ اللَّهِ نَتْلُوها عَلَيْكَ بِالحَقِّ وإنَّكَ لَمِنَ المُرْسَلِينَ﴾ ﴿تِلْكَ الرُّسُلُ فَضَّلْنا بَعْضَهم عَلى بَعْضٍ مِنهم مَن كَلَّمَ اللَّهُ ورَفَعَ بَعْضَهم دَرَجاتٍ وآتَيْنا عِيسى ابْنَ مَرْيَمَ البَيِّناتِ وأيَّدْناهُ بِرُوحِ القُدُسِ ولَوْ شاءَ اللَّهُ ما اقْتَتَلَ الَّذِينَ مِن بَعْدِهِمْ مِن بَعْدِ ما جاءَتْهُمُ البَيِّناتُ ولَكِنِ اخْتَلَفُوا فَمِنهم مَن آمَنَ ومِنهم مَن كَفَرَ ولَوْ شاءَ اللَّهُ ما اقْتَتَلُوا ولَكِنَّ اللَّهَ يَفْعَلُ ما يُرِيدُ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 253] ("Those messengers, We preferred some of them over others. Among them are those to whom God spoke, and He raised some of them in rank. And We gave Isa (Jesus), son of Maryam, clear proofs and strengthened him with the Holy Spirit. Had God willed, those who came after them would not have fought one another after clear proofs had come to them, but they differed: some of them believed and some of them disbelieved. Had God willed, they would not have fought one another, but God does what He wills.") ﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا أنْفِقُوا مِمّا رَزَقْناكم مِن قَبْلِ أنْ يَأْتِيَ يَوْمٌ لا بَيْعٌ فِيهِ ولا خُلَّةٌ ولا شَفاعَةٌ والكافِرُونَ هُمُ الظّالِمُونَ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 254] ("O you who believe, spend from what We have provided you before there comes a Day in which there is no trading, no friendship, and no intercession. And the disbelievers are the wrongdoers.") ﴿اللَّهُ لا إلَهَ إلّا هو الحَيُّ القَيُّومُ لا تَأْخُذُهُ سِنَةٌ ولا نَوْمٌ لَهُ ما في السَّماواتِ وما في الأرْضِ مَن ذا الَّذِي يَشْفَعُ عِنْدَهُ إلّا بِإذْنِهِ يَعْلَمُ ما بَيْنَ أيْدِيهِمْ وما خَلْفَهم ولا يُحِيطُونَ بِشَيْءٍ مِن عِلْمِهِ إلّا بِما شاءَ وسِعَ كُرْسِيُّهُ السَّماواتِ والأرْضَ ولا يَؤدُهُ حِفْظُهُما وهو العَلِيُّ العَظِيمُ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255] ("God—there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting. Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission? He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills. His Throne extends over the heavens and the earth, and their preservation does not burden Him. And He is the Most High, the Most Great.") ﴿لا إكْراهَ في الدِّينِ قَدْ تَبَيَّنَ الرُّشْدُ مِنَ الغَيِّ فَمَن يَكْفُرْ بِالطّاغُوتِ ويُؤْمِن بِاللَّهِ فَقَدِ اسْتَمْسَكَ بِالعُرْوَةِ الوُثْقى لا انْفِصامَ لَها واللَّهُ سَمِيعٌ عَلِيمٌ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 256] ("There is no compulsion in religion. The right course has become distinct from error. So whoever disbelieves in the Taghut and believes in God has grasped the most trustworthy handhold, with no breaking of it. And God is Hearing and Knowing.") The word (البَيْعُ) is well known, and its verb is باعَ يَبِيعُ (ba'a, yabi'u). Whoever says أباعَ with the meaning of باعَ has erred.

Khullah (الخُلَّةُ) means friendship, as if it penetrates (تَتَخَلَّلُ) the limbs, meaning it enters among them. Khullah also means a friend. The poet said:

"Once, in the days of old, she had a friend who would steal glances at the curtained tent."

Al-sinah (السِّنَةُ) and al-wasan (الوَسَنُ): it has been said that they mean drowsiness, which is the slight languor that precedes sleep. The poet said:

"A drowsy man, whom slumber overtook, so a haze settled over his eye, yet he is not asleep."

With drowsiness some awareness remains, whereas sleep is the deep state in which awareness departs. This line shows the distinction between sinah and sleep. Ibn Zayd said: "The wasan is one who rises from sleep without understanding, to the point that he may draw a sword against his own family." But what Ibn Zayd said is not understood from the speech of the Arabs. Al-Mufaddal said: "Sinah is heaviness in the head, nu'as (drowsiness) is in the eye, and nawm (sleep) is in the heart."
