Al-kursi (الكُرْسِيُّ) is a known object made of wood or other material, on which one sits. Its yāʾ is like the yāʾ in qariyy; it is not the yāʾ of relative nisba. Its plural is karasiyy. Its interpretation as applied to God, exalted, will come later. (آدَهُ الشَّيْءُ يَؤُدُهُ) means it burdened him and he bore hardship from it. The poet said:

"Has Salma's newness been cut off today, and was she stingy, though giving never burdened her?"

Al-ghayy (الغَيُّ) is the opposite of rushd (right guidance). One says غوى الرَّجُلُ يَغْوِي, meaning he went astray in belief or opinion. It is also said أغْوى الفَصِيلُ when the young camel was overfed, and when it was hungry, it is the opposite.

Al-taghut (الطّاغُوتُ) is an intensive form from طغى يَطْغى. Al-Tabari reported يَطْغُو when one exceeds the limit with an addition to it. Its original pattern is فَعْلُوتُ; it was transposed, since its root was طَغْوُوتُ, so the lam was placed where the ʿayn was and the ʿayn where the lam was, becoming طَوْغُوتُ. Then the waw moved and the letter before it was open, so it was changed to an alif, becoming طاغُوتُ. Abu ʿAli's view is that it is a verbal noun like rahabut and jabarut, and it is applied to the singular and the plural. Sibawayh's view is that it is a singular noun, like a generic noun that applies to many and few. Abu al-Abbas (al-Mubarrad) claimed that it is a plural. Some claimed that the taʾ in طاغُوتَ replaces a radical letter of the word, and that its pattern is فاعُولٌ.

Al-ʿurwah (العُرْوَةُ) is the place of grasping, of gripping with the hands, and of holding on. Al-ʿurwah is also a tree that stays green in drought, because camels cling to it in fertile times. From ʿarawtuhu, meaning I came to him clinging to him; and iʿtarahu alam means pain attached itself to him.

Al-infisam (الِانْفِصامُ) is severance. It has been said it is breaking without separation, while al-qasm with the letter qaf is breaking with complete separation. The word al-fasm with fa' may also come with the meaning of complete separation.

﴿تِلْكَ الرُّسُلُ فَضَّلْنا بَعْضَهم عَلى بَعْضٍ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 253]. The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when He mentioned the choosing of Talut over the Children of Israel, and the favor of Dawud over them by giving him kingship and wisdom and teaching him, then addressed His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ as being among the messengers, and the apparent wording suggested equality among the messengers, He clarified that the messengers also differ in excellence, just as there was difference among non-messengers, such as Talut and the Children of Israel. (تِلْكَ) is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is (الرُّسُلُ). (فَضَّلْنا) is a circumstantial clause (jumlah ḥāliyyah), and its circumstantial referent (dhu al-ḥāl) is (الرُّسُلُ), while the governing element is the demonstrative. It is also permissible for (الرُّسُلُ) to be an adjective of the demonstrative, or an apposition (ʿaṭf bayān). The demonstrative used is تِلْكَ, which is for what is distant, because of the distance in time between them and the Prophet ﷺ. It has been said that the reference is to the messengers mentioned in this surah, or to the messengers whose knowledge was established for the Messenger of God ﷺ. The better view is that it refers to the messengers in His saying: "and you are indeed among the messengers." This does not require that he ﷺ knew their identities individually; rather he was informed that he is among the messengers, and that God preferred some of the messengers over others. He used تِلْكَ, which is for a singular feminine, although the referent is plural, because it is a broken plural (jamʿ taksīr), and a broken plural is treated like a singular feminine in description, in agreement of pronouns, and in other respects. The broken plural was used here to shorten the wording and to remove the awkwardness of repetition, for had it come as أُولَئِكَ المُرْسَلُونَ فَضَّلْنا, the wording would have been lengthy, and there would have been repetition and a shift (iltifāt) in (نَتْلُوها) and in (فَضَّلْنا), since it moves from a third-person reference to a first-person speaker, while before it the word Allah had been mentioned, which is a third-person term. The doubling in (فَضَّلْنا) is for transitivity (al-taʿdiyah), and (عَلى بَعْضٍ) is connected to (فَضَّلْنا). It has been said: the preference is by virtues beyond the obligations or the laws, over those who have no law, or by distinguishing qualities such as speech. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Since that necessitated their differing in good deeds..." and in it there is a hidden Muʿtazili implication. In this verse, God explicitly mentioned the preference of some prophets over others in general, without specifying which one is preferred. (p-273) Likewise it came in the hadith: "I am the master of the descendants of Adam." He also said: "Do not prefer me over Musa." And he said: "No one should say: I am better than Yunus ibn Matta."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 252 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Among them are those to whom Allah spoke﴾ [al-Baqarah: 253] The majority (al-Jumhur) read it with the doubling of the letter (al-tashdid) and with the word Allah in the nominative (raf'), and the returning pronoun referring to "man" (who) is omitted, its estimated form being "man kallamahu" (whom He spoke to). It was also read with Allah in the accusative (nasb), with the subject being a concealed pronoun (fa'il mustatir) in "kallama" referring back to "man." The nominative for Allah is more complete in expressing distinction than the accusative, since the nominative indicates presence and direct address from Him, may He be exalted, to the speaker, while the accusative indicates presence without direct address from Him.

Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu Nahshal and Ibn al-Sumayqa read it as "kalama Allaha" with an alif and the word Allah in the accusative, from al-mukalamah (conversation), which is the issuing of speech from two parties. From this comes the saying "Kalim Allah," meaning "the one who speaks with Allah" (mukalimuhu), an intensive form (fa'il) in the sense of the participle of the form mufa'il, like jalis (companion) and khalit (associate).

He mentioned the distinction through speech, and it is among the noblest distinctions, in that He made him (the one addressed) a place for His address and intimate discourse without any intermediary. The reports of the exegetes here are unanimous that the one spoken to here is Musa, upon our Prophet and upon him be prayers and peace. "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about Adam: 'Was he a messenger prophet?' He said: 'Yes, a prophet to whom Allah spoke (nabiyyun mukallam).'"

It is established in the hadith of the Isra' (Night Journey), where the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ascended to a station from which Jibril (Gabriel) fell behind, that there took place between him and his Lord, may He be exalted, direct addresses and exchanges. Therefore it is not far-fetched that the words "Among them are those to whom Allah spoke" [al-Baqarah: 253] include Musa, Adam and Muhammad (ﷺ), since the speaking of Allah to them is established.

In His saying "Allah spoke" [al-Baqarah: 253] there is an iltifat (shift of grammatical person), as it is a move from the first-person pronoun to an explicit third-person noun, owing to the grandeur and magnification in mentioning this glorious name, and to avoid the awkwardness of repeating the first-person pronoun, since it would have been: "We favored," "We spoke," "We raised," and "We gave."

**[Commentary of Abu Hayyan, al-Bahr al-Muhit, on Surah al-Baqarah 2:253]**

﴿And He raised some of them in rank﴾: this is Muhammad ﷺ, or Ibrahim, or Idris, peace and blessings of Allah be upon them. There are three opinions. They said: the first is the most apparent, and it is the view of Mujahid. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The wording may mean Muhammad and others whose signs were great, and the statement would then be an emphasis of the first. End of quotation. He means that it is an emphasis of His saying ﴿We preferred some of them over others﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿And He raised some of them in rank﴾ means: among them is one whom He elevated above the rest of the prophets, so that, despite their differences in merit, he was more excellent than them by many degrees. The apparent meaning is that he intended Muhammad ﷺ, because he is the one preferred over them, since he was given signs that no one else was given, numerous and reaching a thousand signs or more. Even if he had been given only the Qur'an alone, it would have been sufficient as a lofty virtue above all that the prophets were given, because it is the lasting miracle until the end of time, unlike all other miracles. In this vagueness there is an exaltation of his virtue and an elevation of his rank that is not hidden, for it bears witness that he is the knowledge that is not confused and the distinguished one that is not ambiguous. A man is asked, "Who did this?" and he replies, "One of you," or "Some of you," meaning the one known and famous for such deeds. This is more majestic than explicitly naming him and more honouring to his companion. Al-Hutay'a was asked about the best of poets. He mentioned Zuhayr and al-Nabigha, then said: "If I wished, I would mention the third." He meant himself. Had he said, "If I wished, I would mention myself," the matter would not have been exalted.

It is also permissible that he intended Ibrahim, Muhammad, and others of the prophets of firm resolve (ulu al-'azm). End of al-Zamakhshari's words. This is a good statement.

Others said: It is Muhammad ﷺ, because he was sent to all people, was given the five things that no one else was given, is the greatest of nations in number, and with him the line of prophethood was sealed, along with other great creation that was granted to him, his miracles, and his brilliant signs. Some scholars said: He ﷺ was given three thousand miracles and distinctions, and no prophet was given a miracle except that Muhammad ﷺ was given its like, and he was given additional signs beyond them.

The accusative of (darajat, "degrees") has been said to be: as an absolute object (masdar), since (daraja) means elevation; or as a masdar in the position of a circumstantial state (hal); or as a circumstantial state with an elided genitive, i.e., "possessors of degrees"; or as the second object of (rafa'a, "raised") by way of tadmin (implicit meaning), in the sense of (balagha, "reached"); or by dropping the preposition, so that the verb reaches the object directly, the preposition being either (ʿalā), (fī), or (ilā). It is also possible that it is an ibdal ishtimal (inclusive apposition), i.e., "and He raised the degrees of some of them," and the meaning is "over the degrees of some."

* *

﴿And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, the clear proofs and strengthened him with the Holy Spirit﴾: The discussion of the interpretation of this sentence has already preceded, after His saying: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book and followed up after him with messengers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 87], so repeating it here is unnecessary. He singled out those whom Allah spoke to, and Jesus, from among the prophets, because of the great signs and brilliant miracles they were given, and because their signs are present (still existing). Specifying them by mention is a censure of their followers, who did not submit to these two great messengers, and disputes and disagreement arose among them. Here, Jesus is specifically mentioned with the clear signs to condemn the deeds of the Jews, who denied his prophethood despite the manifest signs that appeared at his hands. And since our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is the one given what no one else was given in the abundance and greatness of miracles, and he is the one acknowledged as having won the prize of precedence, his mention is surrounded by the mention of these two great messengers, so that each of them may gain honour by the proximity of his mention. He is between them like the central pearl of a necklace, which adorns the pearls adjacent to it. This division varies and does not follow one style. The first clause comes as a subject and predicate, introduced by (min, "some of") which indicates division, while the second clause is verbal, its subject being the pronoun referring to the name of Allah rather than the noun itself, because of its proximity. If it had been attributed to the explicit noun, it would have been: "Among them is one whom Allah spoke to, and Allah raised..." and repetition would have been near, so the pronoun is better.

In both clauses, the one preferred among them is not named explicitly, but the first is identified by the relative clause, since it is known to the listener, and the second is identified by what is stated about him, namely that he was elevated above other messengers by degrees, and this rank belongs to no one but Muhammad ﷺ. The second clause is verbal, with a verb attributed to the pronoun of the first person (the speaker), by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), since before it there was a third-person pronoun. All of this indicates the breadth of the eloquence's varieties and the methods of the rhetoric's excellence.

* *

﴿Had Allah willed, those who came after them would not have fought one another after the clear proofs had come to them﴾: It has been said that there is an elision in the speech; the estimated meaning is: "Their communities differed and fought." (Had Allah willed) and the object of (willed) is elided, its estimate being: "that they not fight." It has been said: "that He not command fighting," said by al-Zajjaj. Mujahid said: "that they not differ with the difference that causes fighting." It has also been said: "Had Allah willed that He compel them to belief, they would not have fought." Abu 'Ali said: "by depriving them of the powers and intellects by which obligation exists, but He imposed obligation on them, so they differed with unbelief and belief." 'Ali ibn 'Isa said: "This is the will of power (mashi'at al-qudra), like: ﴿Had your Lord willed, all those on earth would have believed, all of them together﴾ [Yunus: 99], and He did not will that, but He willed to impose obligation on them, so they differed." Al-Zamakhshari said: "Had Allah willed with the will of compulsion and coercion." The answer of (law, "had") is (ma iqtatala, "they would not have fought"), a negated verb with (ma). The eloquent usage is that the lam is not added to it, as in this verse. In poor usage it is permissible for the lam to enter it, as in: "Had Zayd stood, 'Amr would not have stood."

(min ba'dihim, "after them") is a complement of (alladhina, "those who"), so it is attached to an elided verb: "those who were after them." The pronoun refers to the messengers. It has been said that it refers to Moses, Jesus, and their followers. The apparent meaning of the speech is that they are the people who came after all the messengers, but that is not so. Rather, the intended meaning is: "People did not fight after every prophet." The speech is wrapped up in a manner the listener does not fully grasp. This is like saying: "I bought horses, then I sold them," though you may have bought them horse by horse and sold them horse by horse. Likewise here: it was only differing after each prophet. (min ba'di, "after") has been said to be a substitute (badal) for (ba'dihim, "after them"). The apparent reading is that it is attached to the verb (ma iqtatala, "did not fight"), since within the clear proofs (al-bayyinat), which are the manifest evidences, there is what leads to agreement and the absence of fighting, and it is sufficient without the difference that necessitates fighting.

﴿But they differed﴾: This exception (istidrak) is clear, because what comes before it is the opposite of what comes after it, since the meaning is: "Had He willed agreement, they would have agreed, but He willed difference, so they differed."

﴿Among them were those who believed and among them were those who disbelieved﴾: One who believed does so by committing himself to the religion of the messengers and following them, and one who disbelieved does so by turning away from following the messengers out of envy, transgression, and exclusive greed for the worldly goods.

﴿Had Allah willed, they would not have fought﴾: It has been said that the sentence is repeated as an emphasis of the first, as al-Zamakhshari said. It has also been said that there is no emphasis, because the two wills differ. The first: "Had Allah willed to prevent them from fighting by depriving them of powers and intellects." The second: "Had Allah willed to command the believers to fight, but He commanded and willed that they fight." Those who affirm and those who deny divine decree (al-qadar) have clung to this verse, and this matter remained disputed until al-A'sha, in the pre-Islamic era, denied it when he said:

*"Allah has monopolized fidelity and justice, and has turned away blame from the man."*

And Labid affirmed it when he said:

*"Whom He guides to the paths of goodness is guided, well at ease; and whom He wills, He leads astray."*

﴿But Allah does what He wills﴾: This indicates that what Allah wills to do will certainly occur, and that the will of others has no effect. He, exalted is He, alone possesses the secret of wisdom in what He decrees and decides, of good and evil, and this is His act, exalted is He. Al-Zamakhshari said: "But Allah does what He wills of abandonment and protection," and this is in the manner of the Mu'tazila. It has been said: This noble verse includes types of eloquence: the division in His saying ﴿Among them is one whom Allah spoke to﴾, without intermediary, and among them one whom He spoke to through an intermediary; this division is required by the meaning. And in His saying ﴿Among them were those who believed and among them were those who disbelieved﴾, this division is explicitly stated. The specification is both indicated and explicitly stated. The repetition occurs in the word "clear proofs" and in ﴿Had Allah willed, they would not have fought﴾, according to one of the two interpretations. The elision occurs in His saying ﴿Among them is one whom Allah spoke to﴾, meaning "face to face" (kifahan), and in His saying ﴿does what He wills﴾, meaning guiding whom He wills and misguiding whom He wills.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 254:**

﴿O you who have believed, spend from what We have provided for you﴾. The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned that He willed the disagreement between believer and disbeliever and willed the fighting, and commanded the believers to it, and since jihad requires help from the one who undertakes it, He commanded spending from some of what has been provided. This includes spending in jihad. Although it is not stated explicitly, it is included in His saying "spend" (anfiqu) and enters into it with priority, since the command to spend came right after the mention of the believer and the disbeliever and their fighting. Ibn Jurayj and most scholars said: the verse is general concerning every obligatory or voluntary charity. Al-Hasan said: it concerns zakat, and zakat includes a share for the mujahidun. This was also the view of al-Zamakhshari, who said: it means obligatory spending, because the threat is connected to it: ﴿before there comes a Day in which there is no trade, nor friendship, nor intercession﴾. On that Day you will not be able to make up what you missed of spending, because there is no trade in it so that you could buy what you spend, nor friendship so that your friends would be lenient with you regarding it. If you wish that what is owed upon you of obligations be remitted, you will not find an intercessor who will intercede for you to remit obligations, because intercession there is only for an increase in grace and nothing else.

﴿And the disbelievers are the wrongdoers﴾. He meant: those who abandon zakat are the wrongdoers. He said "the disbelievers" for emphasis, as He said at the end of the verse about Hajj: "and whoever disbelieves" in place of "and whoever does not perform Hajj." Also, He made abandoning zakat one of the attributes of the disbelievers, in His saying: ﴿And woe to the polytheists who do not give zakat﴾ [Fussilat: 6]. End of his words.

His statement was refuted on the grounds that there is no threat in the verse. It is as if it were said: acquire the benefits of the Hereafter while you are in this world, for when you leave this world you cannot acquire them or earn them in the Hereafter. Al-Zamakhshari's statement that intercession there is only for an increase in grace is the view of the Mu'tazilah (a theological school), because they hold that intercession does not occur for the disobedient, so they do not enter the Fire, and it does not occur for the disobedient who have entered the Fire, so they do not leave it by intercession.

It has also been said that what is meant is spending in jihad. This is indicated by the fact that it is mentioned after the command to fight. So it is as if what is meant is spending in jihad, and this is the view of al-Asamm. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the apparent meaning of this verse is that it intends all forms of righteousness, such as spending in the good way and maintaining the ties of kinship. But the verses mentioned earlier about fighting, and that Allah repels through the believers [the harm] in the breasts of the disbelievers, make it more likely that this exhortation is specifically in the way of Allah. This is strengthened by His saying at the end of the verse, ﴿and the disbelievers are the wrongdoers﴾, meaning: so confront them with fighting, with your lives and by spending your wealth. End of his words.

Allah exhorted the servant to spend from what He has provided him. Although provision (rizq) may include what is not lawful, what is meant here is what is lawful. The phrase "from what We have provided you" is connected to the word "spend." The word "ma" (what) is a relative pronoun meaning "that which," and the returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: "We have provided you with it." It has also been said that "ma" is a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah), meaning: from Our provision to you. The phrase "before" (min qabli) is also connected to "spend." Scholars differed about the meaning of "min" (from): the first is for partitive sense (tab'id), and the second is for the starting point of the limit (ibtida' al-ghayah). Some claimed that it is connected to "We have provided you."

﴿before there comes a Day﴾. Allah, exalted is He, warned against withholding before this Day comes, which is the Day of Resurrection.

﴿There is no trade in it﴾, meaning: there is no ransom in it for your souls from the punishment of Allah. The word "trade" (bay') was mentioned because it involves exchange and taking a substitute. It has also been said: it means ransom for what you withheld of zakat, which you would buy by offering it in advance of zakat on that day. It has also been said: there is no trade in it for deeds so that they may be earned.

﴿nor friendship﴾, meaning: no friendship that requires sharing, as was the case in this world. The righteous will have friendship among themselves on that Day, but they will not need it. The friendship of others will not avail them anything against Allah.

﴿nor intercession﴾. The wording is general, but what is meant is specific, meaning: there is no intercession for the disbelievers. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So we have no intercessors, nor a close friend﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 100]. Or it means: there is no intercession except by the permission of Allah. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿and intercession does not benefit with Him except for one whom He permits﴾ [Saba: 23], and He said: ﴿and they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya: 28]. So, according to the specific reading, there is no intercession for the disbelievers, nor from them. According to the interpretation of permission, there is no intercession for the believers except by His permission. It has also been said that what is meant is the general sense, and the meaning is that the taking up of an intercessor and his dominating the one interceded for against his will does not happen at all on the Day of Resurrection. As for the intercession that occurs by the permission of Allah, exalted is He, its reality is the mercy of Allah, but Allah honors the one whom He permits to intercede. The deniers of intercession have clung to His saying "nor intercession," and believed that this is a negation of the very principle of intercession. But intercession in the Hereafter has been affirmed, conditioned upon the permission and pleasure of Allah, and the hadith of intercession, which the Ummah has received with acceptance, is authentic. So no attention is paid to whoever denies it.

Ibn Kathir, Ya'qub and Abu 'Amr read the three words with a fatha, without tanwin. Likewise: ﴿There is no trade in it nor friendship﴾ [Ibrahim: 31] in Surat Ibrahim, and ﴿There is no idle talk in it nor sinfulness﴾ [al-Tur: 23] in Surat al-Tur. The rest of the readers read all of these with a damma and tanwin. The discussion of the i'rab (grammatical case and inflection) of the noun following "la" (no), being built on fatha or being raised with tanwin, has already been covered earlier, so it suffices and there is no need to repeat it. The clause "there is no trade" is in the position of a qualifier (sifah), and it requires an implied element. The estimate is: "nor intercession in it," and it was omitted because the first "fihi" (in it) indicates it.

﴿And the disbelievers are the wrongdoers﴾, meaning: those who exceed the limits. The word "hum" (they) may be a substitute for "the disbelievers," or it may be a subject (mubtada'), or it may be a separating pronoun (fasl). 'Ata' ibn Dinar said: Praise be to Allah who said "and the disbelievers," and did not say "and the wrongdoers are the disbelievers." Had it been revealed in that form, it would have passed judgment of disbelief upon every wrongdoer, meaning one who places a thing in other than its proper place. Then no disobedient person would be free from disbelief, except one whom Allah protects from disobedience.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 255 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Allah! There is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting.﴾ This verse is called Ayat al-Kursi (the Verse of the Throne) because of the mention of the Throne (al-kursi) in it. It is established in Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Ubayy, that it is the greatest verse. In Sahih al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, it is reported that whoever recites it when he goes to his bed, there will not cease to be a guardian from Allah over him, and no devil will come near him until morning. It is also reported that it is equal to a third of the Qur'an; and it is reported that when it is recited in a house, the devils will shun that house for thirty days, and no sorcerer or sorceress will enter it for forty days. It is reported that whoever recites it when he takes his resting place, Allah will grant him security for himself, his neighbour, his neighbour's neighbour, and the households around him. It is reported: "The lord of speech is the Qur'an, the lord of the Qur'an is al-Baqarah, and the lord of al-Baqarah is the Verse of the Throne." It has been given this preeminence because of what it contains of the affirmation of Allah's oneness (tawhid), the glorification of Him, and the mention of His exalted attributes; and there is no one mentioned greater than Allah, so remembrance of Him is better than every other remembrance.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "From this it is known that the most noble of the sciences and the highest in rank with Allah is the science of justice (al-adl) and oneness (al-tawhid). Let not the great number of its opponents deter you from it, for noble men are always envied." End of his words. The people of justice and oneness whom he referred to are the Mu'tazilah; they named themselves thus. One of their poets said in some verses:

"That I support tawhid and justice in every place, exerting my utmost effort."

Al-Zamakhshari, because of his excessive love for his school of thought, nearly brings it into everything he says, even where it has no place. The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned that He preferred some prophets over others, and that among them was one whom He spoke to (interpreted as Musa, peace be upon him), and that He raised some of them in rank (interpreted as Muhammad ﷺ), and specified Isa, peace be upon him, the preference of the one followed implies the preference of the follower. The Jews and Christians had introduced innovations (bida') into their religions and creeds after their prophets, and attributed to Allah, exalted is He, what is not permissible for Him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sent to all people, among them the Arabs, who had taken deities besides Allah and associated partners with Him. So all the people to whom he ﷺ was sent were not upright in their laws and creeds. Allah, exalted is He, stated that the disbelievers are the wrongdoers (zalimun), those who place a thing in other than its place. So He brought this great verse, which indicates the singling out of Allah with oneness, and which contains His exalted attributes: life, sole dominion over the kingdom, the impossibility of His being a locus of temporal events, His ownership of what is in the heavens and the earth, the impossibility of intercession with Him except by His permission, the vastness of His knowledge, the fact that no one encompasses anything of His knowledge except by His will, the wondrous Throne which He created, vast in extent, and its description with the utmost in loftiness and greatness, and the rest of the beautiful names and exalted attributes it contains. Through them He alerted them to the correct creed, which is pure tawhid, and to discarding anything else. The discussion of the word "Allah" and of the phrase "There is no god but He" has already preceded, so there is no need to repeat it.

Al-Hayy (the Living) is a descriptive form whose verb is hayiya. It is said that its root is hayiwa, and the waw was changed to ya' because of the kasrah before it and was assimilated into the ya'. It is also said that its root is fay'al, which was lightened like mayyit becoming mayt and layyin becoming layn. It is a description of one in whom life subsists. With respect to Allah, exalted is He, it is among the attributes of His essence: He is Living with a life that has never ceased and will never cease. Here it is interpreted as "the Everlasting," as in the verse of Labid:

"If you see me today having become safe, then I am not more enduring than Kilab and Ja'far."

That is, "then you are not more enduring." Al-Tabari reported from some people that it is said: "Living" as He described Himself, and they accept that without examining it. It is also reported from some people that He is Living not by a life, and this is the view of the Mu'tazilah. For this reason al-Zamakhshari said: "Al-Hayy is the Everlasting, for whom there is no way to perish," and he is according to the terminology of the theologians (mutakallimun) who are such that they can know and have power, end of his words. By "the theologians" he meant the theologians of his own school. The discussion of describing Allah with life is mentioned in the books of the principles of religion (usul al-din).

The majority read al-Qayyum on the pattern fayyu'ul; its origin is qaywum, the ya' and waw came together, and one of them was preceded by a sukun, so the waw was changed to ya' and the ya' was assimilated into it. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Umar, Alqamah, al-Nakha'i, and al-A'mash read al-Qayyam. Alqamah also read al-Qayyim, as one says Dayyur and Dayyar. Umayyah said:

"The heaven and the stars were not created, nor the sun with the moon swimming alongside it,
He who is the Guardian, the Self-Subsisting, decreed them, and the Gathering and the Garden and the bliss,
Except for a matter whose affair is great."

Its meaning is that He is standing over every thing with what is due to it. This is how Mujahid, al-Rabi' and al-Dahhak interpreted it. Ibn Jubayr said: "The one whose existence is everlasting." Ibn Abbas said: "The one who does not cease and is not changed." Qatadah said: "The one who stands in managing His creation." Al-Hasan said: "The one who stands over every soul for what it has earned." It has been said: "The one who knows affairs," from their saying: "So-and-so stands with this book," meaning he knows what is in it. It has been said: it is derived from istiqamah (uprightness). Abu Rawq said: "The one who does not decay." Al-Zamakhshari said: "The one who is everlastingly standing in managing and preserving creation." These sayings are close to one another. They said: fayyu'ul is among the forms of intensification (mubalaghah). They permitted the raising of al-Hayy as an attribute of the subject, which is "Allah," or as a predicate after a predicate, or as a substitute (badal) for "He" or for "Allah," exalted is He, or as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "He is," or as a subject whose predicate is "la ta'khudhuhu" (slumber does not seize Him). The best of these is that it is an attribute, and what supports this is the reading of those who read al-Hayya al-Qayyuma in the accusative, which cuts it off by implying "I praise." Had it not been an attribute, cutting it off would not have been permitted. And one should not say that in this reading there is a separation between the attribute and the described by a predicate, because that is permissible and good; you say: "Zayd is standing, the intelligent one."

﴿Slumber does not seize Him, nor sleep.﴾ It is said: wasina sinatan and wasanan. The meaning is that He, exalted is He, is not heedless of the minute or the great. He expressed this by heedlessness, because it is its cause, so the name of the cause was applied to the effect. Ibn Jarir said: its meaning is that calamities and defects which distract from guarding the creatures do not befall Him. This mentioned calamity was placed in the position of all of them, and this is the understanding of the discourse, as He, exalted is He, said: "Do not say to them, 'Uff'" (17:23). It has also been said: He declared Himself free of slumber and sleep because of the rest in them, and He, exalted is He, cannot be subject to fatigue and rest. It has also been said: the meaning is that nothing overpowers or defeats Him. In the proverb: "Sleep is a sultan." Al-Zamakhshari said: this is an emphasis on al-Qayyum, because whoever is subject to this cannot be a Qayyum. From this is the hadith of Musa: that he asked the angels, and this was from his people, like the request to see Allah: "Does our Lord sleep?" So Allah revealed to them that they should wake Him three times and not leave Him to sleep. Then He said: "Take two vessels filled with water in your hands." So he took them, and Allah cast sleep upon him, so he struck one against the other and they broke. Then He revealed to him: "Say to these people: I hold the heavens and the earth by My power; if slumber or drowsiness seized Me, they would cease," end of quote. Thus al-Zamakhshari reported this report, and in it he asked the angels, and that was from his people, like the request to see (Allah), meaning that the request to see Him is for him among matters that are impossible, just as sleep is impossible for Allah, exalted is He. This is among his habits in supporting his school, mentioning it where the verse does not address that question.

Others reported this report from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ relate from Musa, peace be upon him, on the pulpit, he said: 'It occurred to Musa: Does Allah sleep?'" and he related the report close in meaning to what al-Zamakhshari mentioned. One of our contemporaries said: "This is a hadith fabricated by the Hashawiyyah, and it is impossible that Musa asked that about himself or about his people, because a believer does not doubt whether Allah sleeps or does not sleep, so how could the messengers?" End of his words.

The benefit of repeating "la" in His saying "nor sleep" is the negation of both in every state, for if "la" were dropped it would allow the negation of both together, as in your saying: "Zayd and Amr did not stand, rather one of them," and one does not say: "Zayd did not stand nor Amr, rather one of them." The view of one who made this sentence a predicate of "al-Hayy" has already been mentioned, on the basis that "al-Hayy" is the subject and it may be a predicate about Allah, so that He informs about Himself after it, according to the view of those who permit that. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that the sentence be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun concealed in al-Qayyum, meaning: "Standing over the affairs of creation, not heedless."

* *

﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth.﴾ It may be a predicate after a predicate, and it may be a resumed predicate, just as that is permissible in the sentence before it. "Ma" is for generality, encompassing everything existent, and "al-lam" is for ownership. He, exalted is He, informed that what the heavens and the earth contain belongs to Him, exalted is He. He repeated "ma" for emphasis. The mention here of what is contained rather than the container is because the intent is to negate divinity from other than Allah, exalted is He, and that it is not fitting that anything other than Him be worshipped. For what is worshipped besides Allah, whether the luminous bodies in the heavens such as the sun, the moon, and Sirius, or earthly persons such as idols and some of the children of Adam, each of them is a possession of Allah, exalted is He, a nurtured and created being. It was previously stated that He, exalted is He, is the Creator of the heavens and the earth, so He did not mention here that He is their owner, being sufficient with what preceded.

* *

﴿Who is it that intercedes with Him except by His permission?﴾ The polytheists used to claim that the idols would intercede for them with Allah, and they used to say: "We only worship them so that they bring us near to Allah in nearness." In this verse is the greatest proof of Allah's sovereignty and the magnitude of His majesty, such that no one can dare to intercede with Him except by permission from Him, exalted is He, as He said: "None shall speak except one whom the Most Merciful has permitted" (78:38). The verse indicates the existence of intercession by His permission, exalted is He. Permission here means command, as in the report: "Intercede and you will be interceded for." Or it means knowledge, or enablement, if anyone interceded without command. "Man" is in the nominative as the subject, and it is an interrogative with the meaning of negation, and for this reason "illa" entered in His saying "except by His permission." The predicate of the subject, they said, is "dha," and "alladhi" is an epithet of "dha" or a substitute for it. On this view, they said, "dha" is a demonstrative, and there is remoteness in that, because "dha," when it is a demonstrative and is the predicate of "man," the sentence would be complete with the two of them, and you see its need for the relative clause after it. What appears is that the interrogative "man" was compounded with "dha," which is what some grammarians express by saying that "dha" is superfluous, so "man dha" as a whole is in the nominative position as subject, and the relative clause after them is the predicate, since by it the meaning of the nominal sentence is completed. "Indahu" (with Him) is governed by "yashfa'u" (intercedes). It was said that it may be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "yashfa'u," so the sense would be: "intercedes while being established with Him." This was judged weak, on the grounds that the meaning is "intercedes to Him." It was said that the circumstantial sense is stronger, because if the one who is with Him and near Him does not intercede, then the intercession of another is further away. "Bi-idhnihi" (by His permission) is connected to "yashfa'u," and the "ba'" is for accompaniment, which is what is expressed as the circumstantial sense: meaning, no one intercedes with Him except one who has been given permission.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 255 (part 2 of 2):

﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them.﴾ The pronoun refers to (ma), meaning the creatures, and the masculine rational form is used by preference (ghallaba man ya'qilu). It was also said that the two pronouns in (aydihim) and (khalfahum) refer to every rational being included in His saying: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.﴾ This was said by Ibn 'Atiyya. Ibn 'Atiyya also allowed that they refer to what is indicated by (man dha), namely the angels and the prophets. It was also said that they refer to the angels. This was said by Muqatil. According to this view, (what is before them) is the matter of the Hereafter and (what is behind them) is the matter of this world. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada. Or the reverse is meant. This was said by Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj, al-Hakam ibn 'Utba, al-Suddi and his teachers. (What is before them) is what came before their creation, and (what is behind them) is what came after their creation. Or (what is before them) is what they displayed, and (what is behind them) is what they concealed. This was said by al-Mawardi. Or (what is before them) is what lies between the sky and the earth, and (what is behind them) is what is in the heavens. Or (what is before them) is their present deeds and conditions, and (what is behind them) is what will be. Or it is the reverse. Taj al-Qurra' mentioned these two views in his tafsir. Or (what is before them) is what concerns the angels regarding intercession, and (what is behind them) is what concerns this world, or the reverse. This was said by Mujahid. Or (what is before them) is what they have done, and (what is behind them) is what they are going to do. This was said by Muqatil. What appears to be correct is that this is a metaphor (kinaya) for the comprehensiveness of God's knowledge of all creatures from every direction. He mentioned these two directions to express all the directions of the one whose knowledge encompasses them, just as you say: "Zayd struck the back and the belly," meaning his whole body. The directions are borrowed to express the conditions of the things known. The meaning, then, is that He, exalted is He, knows all the conditions of the creatures, and nothing escapes Him. Therefore, neither (what is before them) nor (what is behind them) is meant to refer to any specific thing, as they claimed.
* *
﴿And they do not encompass anything of His knowledge.﴾ Ihata (encompassing) requires surrounding a thing from all its sides and enclosing it. Here (ilm) means the object of knowledge (ma'lum), because God's knowledge, which is an attribute of His essence, is not divisible. This is as in the hadith about Musa and al-Khadir: "My knowledge and your knowledge have not diminished His knowledge except as much as this sparrow has diminished this sea." The exception indicates that (ilm) here means the things known. They also say: "O Allah, forgive us Your 'ilm concerning us," meaning Your ma'lum. The meaning is: they know nothing of the unseen, which is God's ma'lum, except what He wills to make them know. This was said by al-Kalbi. Al-Zajjaj said: "Except what He informs the prophets of, confirming their prophethood." (Bi-shay'in) and (bi-ma sha'a) are both connected to (yuhituna). The connection of two prepositions of the same kind to one governing verb occurs here by way of substitution (badal), as in your saying: "I do not pass by anyone except Zayd." It is preferable to take the object of (sha'a) as (yuhitu bihi), because His saying (wa-la yuhituna) indicates it.
* *
﴿His Kursi has encompassed the heavens and the earth.﴾ Al-Jumhur read (wasi'a) with a kasra on the sin. It was also read irregularly (shadhdhan) with a sukun, and also irregularly (wis') with a sukun and a damma on the 'ayn. (The heavens and the earth) are in the nominative as the subject and predicate. The Kursi (footstool) is a great body that encompasses the heavens and the earth. It was said that it is the very Throne ('arsh). This was said by al-Hasan. Others said that it is below the Throne and above the seventh heaven. It was also said that it is beneath the earth, as the Throne is above the heaven. This was reported from al-Suddi. It was also said that the Kursi is the place of the feet of the Greatest Spirit, or another great angel. It was said that it means authority and power. The Arabs call the origin of everything the Kursi, and they call sovereignty "kursi," because the sovereign, in the state of his rule, command and prohibition, sits upon it. So it is named after its place by way of metaphor. The poet said:
"The Holy One, Lord of the Sanctuary, knows that Abu al-'Abbas is more deserving of his soul,
In the ancient mine of sovereignty, the Kursi."
It was also said that the Kursi is knowledge, because the place of the scholar is the Kursi. The attribute of a thing is named after its place by way of metaphor. From this, scholars are called "karasi," because they are relied upon, just as the stakes of the earth (awtad al-ard) are called so. From this also comes "al-karrasa" (notebook). The poet said:
"Surrounding them are white faces and a band of
Karasi (pillars) in the calamities when they befall."
That is, they return (to them). It was also said that the Kursi is the secret. The poet said:
"I have no secret regarding your affair that I conceal,
Nor a secret (kursi) of the knowledge of Allah that is created."
It was also said that the Kursi is an angel among the angels who fills the heavens and the earth. It was said that it is the power of Allah, and that it is the management of Allah. Al-Mawardi reported these two views and said: "It is the principal view relied upon." Al-Maghribi said: from "takarrasa al-shay'," meaning a thing's parts piled upon one another, and "akrastuhu" (I piled it). Al-'Ajjaj said:
"O companion, do you know a piled-up trace?
He said: Yes, I know it and I pile it up."
Another said:
"We are the karasi, Hawazin is not counted,
Like us in calamities, nor are the strongest."
Al-Zamakhshari said: In His saying "His Kursi" there are four aspects. The first: His Kursi has not been too narrow for the heavens and the earth, because of its expansiveness and vastness. This is only an image of His greatness and an imagined depiction, and there is no actual Kursi there, nor any sitting, nor any one sitting, due to His saying: ﴿They did not measure Allah with His true measure, while the earth entirely will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded in His right hand﴾ [al-Zumar: 67], without imagining an actual handful, folding or right hand. It is only an imagining of the greatness of His affair and a sensory representation. Do you not see His saying: ﴿They did not measure Allah with His true measure﴾ [al-Zumar: 67]? End of what he mentioned on this aspect. Al-Qaffal chose this meaning and said: The purpose of this speech is to depict the greatness, majesty and might of Allah, the Exalted. He addressed creation in describing His essence using what they are accustomed to with their kings and great ones. It was also said: The Kursi is of pearl, its legs are seven hundred years long, and the length of the Kursi is where those who know do not know. Ibn 'Asakir mentioned this in his History, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said it. Ibn 'Atiyya said: What the hadiths indicate is that the Kursi is a great created thing before the Throne, and the Throne is greater than it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The seven heavens in relation to the Kursi are like seven dirhams thrown into a shield." Abu Dharr said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "The Kursi in relation to the Throne is like a ring of iron thrown into a desert of the earth." This verse informs of the greatness of Allah's creatures. End of his speech.
* *
﴿And their preservation does not weigh Him down.﴾ Al-Jumhur read (ya'uduhu) with a hamza. It was read irregularly by deletion, as the hamza of (unas) was deleted. It was also read (yawuduhu) with a damma on the waw, as a substitution for the hamza, meaning: it does not burden Him and is not heavy upon Him. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada and others. Aban ibn Taghlib said: their preservation is not too great for Him. It was also said: the preservation of the heavens does not occupy Him from the preservation of the earths, nor the preservation of the earths from the preservation of the heavens. The pronoun (-hu) refers to Allah, the Exalted. It was also said that it refers to the Kursi. The apparent view is the first, so that the pronouns are consistent with one referent and do not differ, and because the attribution of preservation to the Kursi is remote.
﴿And He is the Most High, the Most Great.﴾ Al-'Aliyy is high in His majesty, and al-'Azim is great in His authority. Ibn 'Abbas said: the One who is perfect in His greatness. It was also said: al-'Azim is the one who is magnified (al-mu'azzam), as one says "al-'atiq" for "al-mu'attaq" (the aged one). Al-A'sha said:
"As if the old wine of the fanat,
Mixed with clear water."
This was denied because this attribute did not exist before creation and after their annihilation, since there would be no one to magnify Him at that time, so this saying is not permissible. It was said in reply that it is an attribute of act, like creating and providing, so what they said does not necessarily follow. It was also said: al-'Aliyy is the Exalted above His creation, the Transcendent above likeness and equals. It was also said: al-'Ali is from "'ala ya'lu," meaning he rose, that is, the High over His creation by His power. Al-'Azim is the One possessing greatness, to whom everything is inferior, so nothing is greater than Him. Al-Mawardi said: Regarding the distinction between al-'Aliyy and al-'Ali there are two views. The first: al-'Ali is the one existing in a place of height, while al-'Aliyy is the one deserving of height. The second: al-'Ali is the one who may be shared, while al-'Aliyy is the one who may not be shared. According to this second view, Allah may be described as al-'Aliyy but not al-'Ali. According to the first, He may be described as both. It was also said: al-'Aliyy is the Subduer, the Dominant over things. The Arabs say: "Fulan 'ala Fulan," meaning he overcame him and subdued him. The poet said:
"When we rose above them and prevailed over them,
We left them felled for the eagle and the hawk."
From this comes His saying: ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 4]. Al-Zamakhshari said: al-'Aliyy is the one of great rank, great sovereignty and power. End of his speech. Some people said: al-'Aliyy is exalted above His creation by the elevation of His place above the places of His creation. Ibn 'Atiyya said: This is the saying of ignorant anthropomorphists, and the proper course was not to report it. He also said: al-'Aliyy means the height of rank and station, not the height of place, because Allah is exempt from being confined in a place.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask how the sentences in the verse of the Kursi are arranged without a conjunction, I say: none of them is a sentence except that it comes as an explanation (bayan) of what precedes it, and the explanation is united with what it explains. So if a conjunction were placed between them, it would be like what the Arabs say: "between the staff and its bark." The first sentence is an explanation of His standing in managing creation and His being the Guardian over it, not heedless of it. The second is an explanation of His being the owner of what He manages. The third is an explanation of the greatness of His affair. The fourth is an explanation of His encompassing the conditions of creation, His knowledge of those He approves of, who deserve intercession, and those He does not approve of. The fifth is an explanation of the vastness of His knowledge and its connection to all the things known, or of His majesty and the greatness of His station. End of his speech.
* *
This noble verse includes the attributes of the Essence. Among them: Oneness, by His saying: ("There is no god but He"). Life, which indicates permanence, by His saying: ("the Living"). Power, by His saying: ("the Self-Subsisting"). He moved from self-subsistence to the negation of what would lead to incapacity, which is what befalls other than God, the Exalted, of heedlessness and calamities. The attribute of power is then negated from that other. He also moved from self-subsistence, which indicates power, to His sovereignty, dominance and supremacy over what is in the heavens and the earth, since sovereignty is the effect of power, for the owner has disposal over what he owns. Then will, by His saying: ﴿Who is it that intercedes with Him except by His permission?﴾ This indicates choice and will. Knowledge, by His saying: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them.﴾ Then He negated knowledge from them, except what He Himself, the Exalted, makes them know. When the attributes of the Essence, the sublime ones, were completed, and some attributes of act were included with them, and it was negated of Him, the Exalted, that He be a locus for temporal events, He concluded this with His being the Most High in rank and the Most Great in station.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 256:

﴿There is no compulsion in religion.﴾ Several reports have been mentioned concerning the occasion of its revelation, most of which convey the same meaning: that some of the sons of the Ansar had become Christians and others had become Jews, and their fathers wanted to compel them to embrace Islam, so this was revealed. Anas said: It was revealed concerning a man to whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Embrace Islam," and he said, "I find myself unwilling."

The scholars differed concerning this verse: Is it abrogated (mansukh) or not? It was said: It is abrogated, and it is one of the verses of conciliation (al-muwada'ah) which the verse of the sword (ayat al-saif) abrogated. Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: It is muhkam (not abrogated), specific to the People of the Book who pay the jizyah (poll tax). They both said: He was commanded to fight the idolaters, accepting from them nothing but Islam or the sword; then he was commanded that, concerning others than them, he should accept the jizyah. The position of Malik is that the jizyah is accepted from every disbeliever except the Quraysh, so the verse is specific to those who give the jizyah from all people, and it is not restricted to the People of the Book. Al-Kalbi said: There is no compulsion after the Arabs have embraced Islam, and the jizyah is accepted. Al-Zajjaj said: Do not attribute to disliking (karahah) one who embraced Islam under compulsion. It is said: akfarahu means he attributed to him kufr (disbelief), as the poet said:

*Wa-ta'ifatun qad akfarunI bi-hubbihim / wa-ta'ifatun qalu musi'un wa-mudhnibu*
(A group has declared me a disbeliever for my love of them, and a group has said: "He is a wrongdoer and a sinner.")

It was said: No one is compelled to embrace Islam who leaves for someone else. Abu Muslim and al-Qaffal said: Its meaning is that Allah Most High did not base the matter of faith on compulsion and coercion, but based it on capacity (al-tamakkun) and choice (al-ikhtiyar). This meaning is confirmed by the fact that when He clarified the proofs of Tawhid with a sufficient clarification, He said after that: there remains no excuse for disbelief except that one be forced to faith and compelled to it, and this is not permissible in the abode of this world, which is the abode of trial, for in compulsion and coercion in religion the meaning of trial is nullified. This is affirmed by His saying after it: ﴿The right course has become distinct from error.﴾ That is: the proofs have appeared and the clear signs have become evident, and nothing remains after them except the path of force and compulsion, which is not permissible, since it negates the obligation (taklif). What Abu Muslim and al-Qaffal said is consistent with the principles of the Mu'tazilah, and for this reason al-Zamakhshari said: Allah did not base the matter of faith on compulsion and coercion, but on capacity and choice. A similar statement is His saying: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, those on earth would have believed, all of them entirely. Then, would you compel the people until they are believers?﴾ [Yunus: 99], meaning: had He willed, He would have forced them to faith, but He did not do so, and He based the matter on choice.

The word "din" here means the community (millah) of Islam and its belief, and the definite article (al-) is for prior reference (al-'ahd). It was said: it is a substitute for the genitive construction, meaning: in the religion of Allah.

﴿The right course has become distinct from error.﴾ That is: faith has become distinguished from disbelief. This shows that "din" is the belief of Islam. The majority read "al-rushdu" on the pattern of "al-qufl"; al-Hasan read "al-rushdu" on the pattern of "al-unuq"; and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read "al-rushdu" on the pattern of "al-jubul." These readings are also reported from al-Sha'bi, al-Hasan, and Mujahid. Ibn 'Atiyyah related from Abu 'Abd al-Rahman the reading "al-rashad" with an alif. The majority assimilate the dal of "qad" into the ta' of "tabayyana." It was read irregularly (shadhdh) with clear pronunciation ("wa-tabayyana al-rushda"), with the accusative of the clear proofs and the sending of the Messenger who calls to faith. This clause seems to be like a cause (`illah) for the negation of compulsion in religion, because the clarity of right guidance and its distinctness lead to entering the religion willingly without compulsion; it has no place in the grammatical analysis (i'rab).

﴿Whoever disbelieves in the Taghut and believes in Allah has grasped the most reliable handhold.﴾ (Al-Taghut): the Shaytan. This was said by 'Umar, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, and al-Suddi. Or the sorcerer, said by Ibn Sirin and Abu al-'Aliyah. Or the soothsayer, said by Jabir, Ibn Jubayr, Rafi', and Ibn Jurayj. Or whatever is worshipped besides Allah by one who is pleased with that, like Pharaoh and Nimrod, said by al-Tabari. Or the idols, said by some. All these statements should be taken as examples, since the taghut is not restricted to any one of them. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: He placed the mention of disbelief in the taghut before belief in Allah in order to show concern for the obligation of disbelieving in the taghut, end quote.

This also suits its connection with the word "al-ghayy," and because disbelief in the taghut precedes belief in Allah, since disbelief in it is rejecting it and renouncing its worship. He did not suffice with the first clause, because it does not necessarily entail the second: one may renounce its worship without believing in Allah, but belief necessarily entails disbelief in the taghut. Yet by mentioning disbelief in the taghut, He alerts to a complete break from what one was previously associated with before faith, since explicit mention of it adds emphasis on abandoning it. The answer of the condition is "then he has grasped" (faqad istamsaka), presented in the form of a past verb preceded by "qad," which in the past denotes certainty, even though it is future in meaning, because it is the answer of the condition; this indicates that its grasping has occurred and is established, for the sake of emphasizing the consequence following the condition, and that it is certain to occur and cannot fail to happen. "Bil-'urwati" (with the handhold) is connected to "istamsaka"; the faith by which one holds on is made a handhold, and in physical things it is the place of gripping and the clasping of hands, and faith is likened to that. Al-Zamakhshari said: This is an illustration of the known through reflection and inference from the observed and sensed, so that the hearer imagines it as though he sees it with his own eye, and thus his belief is firmly established and certain. The thing likened to the handhold is faith, said by Mujahid; or Islam, said by al-Suddi; or "There is no god but Allah," said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, and al-Dahhak; or the Qur'an, also said by al-Suddi; or the Sunnah; or divine success (tawfiq); or the firm covenant; or the means that leads to the pleasure of Allah. These statements are closely related.

﴿There is no breaking of it.﴾ That is, no fracture and no severance. Al-Farra' said: al-infisam and al-inqisam are two dialects, and with the "f" (fa') is more eloquent. Some distinguished between them, saying: al-fasm is a breaking without separation, and al-qasm is a breaking with separation. This clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "al-'urwah." It was said: it relates to the hidden pronoun in "al-wuthqa." It is also permissible that it be a new predicate from Allah concerning the handhold, and "laha" (for it) is in the position of the predicate, so it is connected to an omitted element, meaning: existing for it.

﴿And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾ He mentioned these two attributes because disbelieving in the taghut and believing in Allah are things the tongue utters and the heart believes, so mention of these two attributes is appropriate. It was said: All-Hearing of your supplication, O Muhammad, All-Knowing of your eagerness and striving.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 257:**

﴿Allah is the Protector (walī) of those who believe; He brings them out from the darknesses into the light.﴾ Here *al-walī* means the helper, the supporter, or the one who loves them, or the one who takes charge of their affairs. The meaning of (āmanū) is that they wanted to believe. (*al-Ẓulumāt*, "the darknesses") here means disbelief (kufr), and (*al-Nūr*, "the light") means faith (īmān). This is said by Qatādah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and al-Rabīʿ. It has been said: (*al-Ẓulumāt*) is in the plural because of the different misguidances, and (*al-Nūr*) is in the singular because faith is one. If "bringing out" (*al-ikhrāj*) here is literal, then it applies only to those who were disbelievers and then believed. If it is figurative (*majāz*, a metaphor), then it is a metaphor for Allah's preventing them from entering the darknesses. Al-Ḥasan said: the meaning of (yukhrijuhum) is "He prevents them," even if they had not entered. The meaning is that if they were left without Allah's guidance (tawfīq), they would fall into the darknesses, so His guidance becomes the cause of removing that darkness. They said: this kind of metaphor (*isti'ārah*) is common and permissible in their speech, as Ṭufayl al-Ghanawī said:

*"If the days have been kind to me once, their misdeeds have returned to them."*

Al-Wāqidī said: everything in the Qur'an concerning "darknesses" and "light" means disbelief and faith, except the one in al-An'ām, which is: ﴿He made the darknesses and the light﴾ (Q. 6:1), where He means night and day. Al-Wāsiṭī said: He brings them out from the darknesses of their souls to their (spiritual) disciplines, such as contentment (riḍā), truthfulness (ṣidq), reliance on Allah (tawakkul), knowledge (maʿrifah), and love (maḥabbah). Abū ʿUthmān said: He brings them out from the darknesses of estrangement and separation to the light of union and companionship. Al-Zamakhsharī said: (āmanū), they wanted to believe. He shows kindness to them until He brings them out, by His gentleness and support, from disbelief to faith. Or: Allah is the Protector of the believers; He brings them out from doubts in religion if they fall into them, by guiding them and enabling them to resolve those doubts, until they come out of them into the light of certainty, end quote. According to this view, (āmanū) is taken in its literal sense.

﴿As for those who disbelieve, their protectors are the Ṭāghūt.﴾ Mujāhid and ʿAbdah ibn Abī Lubābah said: it was revealed concerning a people who believed in ʿĪsā (peace be upon him), but when Muḥammad (peace be upon him) came, they disbelieved in him. That is their being brought out from the light into the darknesses. Al-Kalbī said: they bring them out from their faith in Mūsā (peace be upon him), and from their seeking victory through Muḥammad (ﷺ), into their disbelief in him. It was also said: they bring them out from the natural disposition (*fiṭrah*) of Islam. It was also said: from the light of acknowledging the covenant. It was also said: from acknowledging with the tongue into hypocrisy (nifāq). It was also said: from the light of reward in Paradise into the darkness of punishment in Hellfire. It was also said: from the light of truth into the darkness of desire (hawā). It was also said: from the light of intellect into the darkness of ignorance. Al-Zamakhsharī said: from the light of the clear proofs (bayyināt) that become apparent to them, into the darknesses of doubt and suspicion. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: the wording of the verse does not need specification. Rather, it applies to every disbelieving nation in which some believed, such as the Arabs. Whoever among them believed, Allah is his protector; He brought him out from the darkness of disbelief into the light of faith. And whoever disbelieved after the caller (the prophet sent) appeared, his devil and seducer are as if they brought him out of faith, since he was prepared and fit to enter it. This is like saying to someone who prevented you from entering a matter: "You have expelled me, O so-and-so, from this matter," even though you never entered it at all, end quote.

The meaning of *al-Ṭāghūt* is the idol, based on His saying: ﴿My Lord, they have led many people astray﴾ (Q. 14:36). It has also been said that the devils and the Ṭāghūt are a collective noun (*ism jins*). Al-Ḥasan recited (*al-Ṭawāghīt*) in the plural.

The statements in these two sentences differ. The verse about the believers begins with the name of Allah the Exalted and tells about Him that He is the Protector of the believers, honouring them, since it begins with His name in the context of them, and because of its closeness to His saying: ﴿Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ (Q. 2:256). (p. 284) The verse about the disbelievers begins by mentioning them, as a reproach against them and a naming of them by the ugly deeds that came from them. Then it tells that their protectors are the Ṭāghūt. The Ṭāghūt is not placed first, out of contempt for it, and because it should not be made a counterpart to Allah the Exalted. Then the order of the statement is reversed in it, beginning with His saying: "their protectors," and *al-Ṭāghūt* is made the predicate, as if the Ṭāghūt were unknown, informing the addressee that the protectors of the disbelievers are the Ṭāghūt. The best view regarding (yukhrijuhum wa-yukhrijūnahum) is that it has no place in the grammatical structure (*iʿrāb*), because it comes as an explanation of the protection. It is as if, since Allah is the Protector of the believers, He explains the nature of the protection, help, and support as bringing them out from the darknesses into the light. The same applies to the disbelievers. They permitted that (yukhrijuhum) be a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), with the governing element being (walī), and that it be a second predicate. They also permitted that (yukhrijūnahum) be a circumstantial clause, with the governing element being the meaning of *al-Ṭāghūt*. This is similar to what Abū ʿAlī said about the accusative of (nazzāʿah) being a circumstantial clause, with the governing element being (laẓā). We will mention it in its proper place, if Allah wills. And (min … ilā, "from … to") are both related to (yukhriju).

﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾ The explanation of this sentence has already been given, so there is no need to repeat it.

They mentioned in these verses types of eloquence and of the science of rhetoric (*ʿilm al-bayān*). Among them, in the Verse of the Throne: the excellence of its opening, since it opens with the most glorious of the names of Allah the Exalted; the repetition of His name in eighteen places; the repetition of attributes; and the separation of the sentences from one another, not connecting them with a conjunction. Also antithesis (*ṭibāq*) in His saying: ﴿The Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting. Neither drowsiness overtakes Him nor sleep﴾ (Q. 2:255), since sleep is a kind of death and heedlessness, and the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting contradicts it. Also in His saying: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they do not encompass﴾ (Q. 2:255). Also simile (*tashbīh*) in the reading of the one who recited ﴿His Throne extends over the heavens and the earth﴾ (Q. 2:255), meaning *ka-wasiʿa* ("like the extent of"). If the Throne is a body, it is the comparison of a perceptible thing with a perceptible thing; if it is a meaning, it is the comparison of an intelligible thing with a perceptible thing. Also the shift in address (*maʿdūl al-khiṭāb*) in ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾ (Q. 2:256), if the meaning is "do not compel anyone to the religion." Also antithesis in His saying: ﴿The right course has become clear from error﴾ (Q. 2:256), and in His saying: "believed" and "disbelieved," and in His saying: ﴿from the darknesses into the light.﴾ Also repetition of "bringing out" because of the contrast of what it is attached to. Also emphasis through the pronoun in His saying: ﴿they will abide therein forever﴾.

These noble verses also include an allusion to the messengers mentioned in His saying: "Indeed you are among the messengers" (Q. 2:252). The Exalted informed that He has preferred some of them over others. He mentioned that "among them is one to whom Allah spoke" (Q. 2:253), which was explained as referring to Mūsā (peace be upon him), and he was mentioned first because of his earlier time. He also informed that He "raised some of them in rank" (Q. 2:253), which was explained as referring to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). And He mentioned a third, ʿĪsā son of Maryam. So the mention of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) comes in the middle between these two great prophets, like the middle of a necklace. Then the Exalted mentioned that the fighting of earlier peoples after the coming of the clear proofs is issued by His will.

Then He mentioned their disagreement and their division into believer and disbeliever, and that He does what He wills. Then He commanded the believers to spend from what He has provided them, before there comes a day in which there will be no benefit from trading, nor friendship, nor intercession. Then He mentioned that the disbelievers are those who transgress the limit that Allah the Exalted has set. Then He mentioned that He is the One alone in divinity. This comes after the mention of the disbelievers and the mention of the followers of Mūsā and ʿĪsā (peace be upon them both). Then He recounted His sublime attributes, which must be believed concerning Allah the Exalted: that He is one, living, self-subsisting, managing creation, not touched by any defect, owner of the heavens and the earth, knowing the hidden matters of what is known, and that no one knows anything of His knowledge except what He wills. He mentioned the greatness of His creatures, and that one of them, the Throne, extends over the heavens and the earth, and that its preserving the heavens and the earth is not heavy or burdensome for Him.

Then He mentioned that after the clarity of His sublime attributes, "there is no compulsion in religion," since the paths of right guidance have been made clear from the paths of error. Then He mentioned that whoever disbelieves in the Ṭāghūt and believes in Allah has grasped the most reliable handhold (*al-ʿurwah al-wuthqā*), the handhold of faith. He described it as "most reliable" because it never breaks or splits. He used the metaphor of a "handhold" for faith, treating the intelligible as if it were perceptible. Then the Exalted mentioned that He is the Protector of the believers, who brought them out from the darknesses of disbelief into the light of faith, and that the disbelievers have as their protectors the idols and the devils, and they are the opposite of the believers. Then He informed about the disbelievers that they are the companions of the Fire, and that they will abide therein forever in that state. And Allah knows best what is correct.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 258 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord, because Allah had given him kingship? When Abraham said, "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death," he said, "I give life and cause death." Abraham said, "Indeed, Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west." So the one who disbelieved was overwhelmed. And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ ﴿Or [consider] like the one who passed by a town that lay in ruins upon its roofs. He said, "How will Allah bring this to life after its death?" So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years, then resurrected him. He said, "How long have you remained?" He said, "I have remained a day or part of a day." He said, "Rather, you have remained a hundred years. Look at your food and your drink; they have not spoiled. And look at your donkey. [We will do this] so that We may make you a sign for the people. And look at the bones, how We raise them and then clothe them with flesh." When it became clear to him, he said, "I know that Allah is over all things capable."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 259] ﴿And [mention] when Abraham said, "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead." He said, "Have you not believed?" He said, "Yes, but [I ask] so that my heart may be assured." He said, "Take four birds and make them incline toward you, then place a portion of them on every mountain, then call them; they will come to you in haste. And know that Allah is Mighty and Wise."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260] (buhita) means he was bewildered and astonished. It is transitive on the pattern fa'ala, as in: ﴿fa-tabhutahum﴾ [so that it overwhelms them]. It is also intransitive on the patterns fa'ula, like ẓaruf, and fa'ila, like dahisha. The more common vowel in the intransitive form is the ḍamma. It is reported from some Arabs that (bahata) with a fatḥa on the ha' is intransitive. One says: bahattuhu, bahatuhu, or bahata-hu, meaning he confronted him with a lie. In a hadith: «(Indeed the Jews are a people of slander)».

Al-khawi (empty): the one that is vacant. The house became empty (khawat al-dar yakhwi, khawā), without the mad (lengthening), and khuwiyyan. The first is more eloquent. It is said: the house collapsed (khawā al-bayt inhadam), because when it collapses it becomes empty of its people. Al-khawā is hunger, because the stomach is empty of nourishment. The woman became empty (khawwat al-mar'ah and khawiyat), meaning her belly emptied at childbirth. I prepared for her a takhwiyah, meaning I made for her a khawiyyah which she eats, and it is a food. Al-khawiyy on the pattern fa'īl is level, soft ground. Khawwā al-ba'īr means the camel held its belly away from the ground in its resting place, and likewise a man in his prostration. The rajaz poet said:
"He held his belly up on five levels, with knees and soft pads."

Al-'arsh: the roof of a house, and everything prepared to shade or to shelter, is an 'arīsh (arbor). The Most High said: ﴿wa-mimmā ya'rishūn﴾ [and of what they erect]. In a hadith: «When he ordered the building of the mosque, they said: We will build it for you as a structure. He said: "No, rather a trellis like the trellis of my brother Moses." So they placed palm trunks on the stones and covered it with palm fronds and their leaves.» It is also said that al-'arsh means a building. The poet said:
"If they kill you, you have toppled their roofs, by Utaybah ibn al-Harith ibn Shihab."

(Mi'ah): the name of a rank in the number series, well known. Its plural is mi'āt and mi'īn. It is a lightened form with a deleted lām, and its lām is a yā'. So the original is mi'yah. It is said: amā'tu al-darāhim, when I made them into a hundred. (al-'ām): a known period of time. Its alif is changed from a wāw, as shown by their saying: al-'uwaym and al-a'wām. Al-Naqqāsh said: al-'ām is a verbal noun like al-'awm, and this amount of time was named after it, because it is one swim of the sun in the orbit. Al-'awm is like al-sabḥ [swimming]. The Most High said: ﴿wa-kullun fī falakin yasbaḥūn﴾ [and each in an orbit swims]. Thus al-'ām in this sense is like al-qawl and al-qāl. (al-lubth): staying and residing. (yatasannah): if the ha' is original, then it is from al-sanah [year], according to one who takes its deleted lām to be ha'. In diminutive they say: sunayhah, and in plural sanahāt. They say: sānahtu and asnahtu among Banī Fulān, and this is the dialect of the Ḥijāz. The poet said:
"She is not one of barren years, nor of the Rajabiyyah, but of the open-handed in the years of calamity."

If the ha' is for pausing, which is the preference of al-Mubarrad, then the final letter of the word is deleted for the jussive, and it is an alif changed from a wāw, according to one who takes the deleted lām of sanah to be a wāw. As evidence: sunayyah and sanawāt. From it the verb is derived, so it is said: sānaytu, asnā, and asnat. The wāw was replaced by a tā', or the alif is changed from a yā' which replaced a nūn, so it is from al-masnūn, meaning the changed. It was replaced out of disliking the joining of like letters, as they said: taẓannā, and yatalaʻʻā, the original being taẓunnīn and yatalaʻʻaʻ. Abu 'Amr said this, but al-Zajjaj rejected it. He said: because al-masnūn means poured according to the path's custom and course. Al-Naqqāsh said: it is from His saying ﴿min mā'in ghayri āsin﴾ [of water unchanged]. The grammarians rejected this view, because if it were from asina the water (became foul), the form would be lam yata'assan, since if you formed (taf'al) from eating, you would say: ta'kul. What al-Naqqāsh said may be supported by the supposition of metathesis, placing the first radical of the word in the position of the last and the middle in the position of the first, so it becomes: tasna', and its origin is ta'assan. Then the hamzah was replaced, as they said of hada', qara', and istaqra': hada, qara, and istaqra.

(al-ḥimār): the known animal. In the paucity plural it is afʻila: ahmira. In the abundance plural it is fu'ul: ḥumur, and fa'īl: ḥamīr. Anshara Allah al-mawtā and nashara-hum: God revived the dead. Nashara al-mayyit: he came back to life. The poet said:
"Until people say, when they see what they see: How strange, the dead one who rose!"

As for anshuz with a zāy, it is from al-nashz, which is what is raised from the ground. The meaning of anshaza al-shay' is to make it nāshiz, that is, raised. From it: "Rise, so rise" [infushū fa-nfushū], and a woman who is nāshiz means raised above the state she was in with her husband. (al-ṭumaʼnīnah): a verbal noun of iṭma'anna, not on the regular analogy; the analogical form would be iṭmi'nān, meaning calm. Ṭāmanatuhu means I made him calm, and ṭāmanatuhu fa-taṭāmana means I lowered it and it lowered.
