Sībawayh's view on iṭma'anna is that it is among those in which the mīm is placed before the hamzah, so it belongs to the category of metathesis (al-maqlūb). Al-Jarmi's view is that the original of iṭma'anna is like uṭāminu, and it is not from metathesis. The preference between the two views is mentioned in the science of morphology (al-taṣrīf). (al-ṭayr): a collective noun, like rakb and safar, and it is not a plural, contrary to Abu al-Hasan. Ṣāra yaṣūru: he cut. Infaʻala: it was cut off. Ṣurtuhu aṣūruhu: I inclined it. It is also said for cutting and inclining: ṣārahu yuṣayyiruhu, said Abu 'Ali. Al-Farra' said: the ḍamma in the ṣād admits both inclining and cutting, while the kasra in it admits only cutting. He also said: ṣārahu is the inverted form of ṣarrāhu 'an kadhā, meaning he cut him from such and such. Others said: the kasra means cutting and the ḍamma means inclining. (al-jabal): well known, and in the paucity plural it is ajbāl and ajbul, and in the abundance plural jibāl. (al-juz'): a part of a thing, a piece of it. Jazza'a al-shay': he made it into pieces.

﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord, because Allah had given him kingship﴾: the connection of this story is the dispute that took place between Abraham and the one who argued with him, and that he debated with that disbeliever and overpowered him and cut him off, since Allah was his protector. That disbeliever was cut off and overwhelmed, since his protector was the tyrant (al-ṭāghūt). ﴿Surely the party of Allah are the victorious﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 22]. ﴿Surely the party of Allah are the successful﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 22]. So this story became an example for the believer and the disbeliever mentioned earlier. The discussion of His saying ﴿Have you not considered those who﴾ [al-Baqarah: 243] has already passed, so there is no need to repeat it. Ali ibn Abi Talib read (alam tar) with a sukun on the rā', and this is from applying the pause form to continuous speech.

The one who argued with Abraham: he is Nimrod ibn Kan'an ibn Kush ibn Sam ibn Nuh, king of his time and owner of the fire and the gnat. This was said by Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Rabi', al-Suddi, Ibn Ishaq, Zayd ibn Aslam, and others. Ibn Jurayj said: he was the first king on earth, and Ibn 'Atiyyah rejected this. Qatadah said: he was the first to become a tyrant, and he is the owner of the tower in Babylon. It is said: he ruled the whole world and his influence penetrated it. Mujahid said: two believers ruled the earth: Sulayman and Dhu al-Qarnayn, and two disbelievers: Nimrod and Bukht Nasr. It is said: he is Nimrod ibn Yajarib ibn Kush ibn Kan'an ibn Sam ibn Nuh. It is said: Nimrod ibn Fayakh ibn 'Abir ibn Sayakh ibn Arfakhshadh ibn Sam ibn Nuh. Al-Suhayli reported that he is Nimrod ibn Kush ibn Kan'an ibn Ham ibn Nuh, and he was a king over the Sudan. His king was al-Dahhak, known as al-Izdihaq, whose name was Andarawast ibn Andarasht, and he was king of all the regions. He was the one killed by Afridun ibn Ahban. Abu Tammam Habib said in a qasidah praising al-Afshin, mentioning his seizing of Babak al-Khurrami:
"Rather, he was like al-Dahhak in his slaughter of the worlds, and you are Afridun."

He was the first to crucify and to cut off hands and feet. Nimrod is said to have ruled for four hundred years, and he had a son called Nimrod the Younger, who ruled for one year. The meaning of ﴿argued with Abraham about his Lord﴾ is: he countered his argument with a similar one, or he came with an argument that would nullify it, or he displayed contention in argument. Three opinions. They differed about the time of the dispute. It is said: they went out to a festival of theirs, and Abraham entered upon their idols and smashed them. When they returned, he said: "Do you worship what you carve?" He said to him: "Then whom do you worship?" He said: "I worship ﴿my Lord, who gives life and causes death﴾." It is also said: Nimrod used to hoard grain, and when they were in need they bought food from him. When they entered upon him, they prostrated to him. When Abraham entered, he did not prostrate to him. He said: "What is wrong with you, that you did not prostrate to me?" He said: "I do not prostrate except to my Lord." Nimrod said to him: "Who is your Lord?" He said: "﴿My Lord, who gives life and causes death﴾." In another account: whenever a people came, he asked: "Who is your Lord and your god?" They said: "You." He would say: "Provide for them." Abraham came seeking provisions, and he said to him: "Who is your Lord and your god?" He said: "﴿My Lord, who gives life and causes death﴾." It is also said: the dispute was after Abraham came out of the fire into which Nimrod had thrown him. They mention that when Nimrod did not give him provisions, he passed by a reddish sand, took some of it, went to his family and slept. They found it to be the finest food. She prepared some of it and brought it to him. He said: "Where is this from?" She said: "From the food you brought." He knew that Allah had provided for him, so he praised Allah. It is also said: he passed a red mound, took some from it, and they found it to be red wheat. Whenever he sowed it, its ear grew from its root to its branch, with grains piled up. ﴿In His Lord﴾: the pronoun may refer to Abraham, or to Nimrod, and the first is more apparent.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 258 (part 2 of 3):

﴿That Allah had given him the kingdom﴾. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (ātāhu, "had given him") refers to the one who argued (alladhī ḥājja), and this is the view of the majority. The phrase (an ātāhu, "that He had given him") is an object of purpose (mafʿūl li-ajlihi, an accusative noun stating the reason for the action), with two possible meanings. The first is that what moved him to dispute was that Allah had given him the kingdom, which made him insolent and gave him arrogance and tyranny, so he argued on that account. The second is that he put the disputation in the place of the thanks that was due to Allah, exalted is He, for giving him the kingdom, just as you say: "So-and-so opposed me because I had done him a kindness," meaning that he reversed what he owed of loyalty in return for the kindness. From this is His saying: ﴿And you make your provision that you deny?﴾ [al-Waqiʿa: 82].

Al-Zamakhshari allowed that the sense could be: he argued at the time when Allah gave him the kingdom. If he means that this involves an omitted noun (muḍāf), it is possible, though it is remote, since the argument did not take place at the time Allah gave him the kingdom. Unless "time" is taken to mean the beginning of the giving, which is not what the apparent sense requires, since the giving of the kingdom by Allah preceded the argument. And if he means that an-and-the-verb (an + verb) occupies the position of a verbal noun that stands in the position of an adverb of time, as in your saying: "I came at the setting of the star, at the arrival of the pilgrims, at the crowing of the rooster," then this is not permitted. This is because the grammarians held that only a verbal noun explicitly stated in its own form can stand in the place of an adverb of time. So it is not permitted to say: "I will come that the rooster crows," nor "I came that the rooster crowed."

Al-Mahdawi said: it is possible that the pronoun refers to Abraham, that is, that He gave him the kingship of prophethood. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: this is a strained interpretation. What al-Mahdawi mentioned as a possibility is the view of the Muʿtazila (a rationalist theological school). They said: the pronoun refers to Abraham, not to the unbeliever who argued with him, because Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqara: 124], and kingship is a covenant from Him. He also said: ﴿Or do they envy people for what Allah has given them of His bounty? We had already given the family of Abraham the Book and wisdom, and We gave them a great kingdom﴾ [al-Nisa: 54]. The view of the Muʿtazila is refuted on the grounds that Abraham was not known as a king, and by the unbeliever's saying: "I give life and cause death." Had Abraham been the king, he would not have been able to argue with him in such a situation. It is also refuted by the fact that when he said, "I give life and cause death," he brought two men, killed one and left the other alive. If he had not been a king, he would not have killed in front of Abraham without his permission, since Abraham was the king. But these points do not refute the Muʿtazila, because affirming the kingship of prophethood for Abraham does not contradict the kingship of the unbeliever, since there are two kinds of kingship: one by the excellence of rank in religion, such as prophethood and leadership; and the other by the excellence of wealth, strength, courage, domination, conquest, and having followers. The unbeliever's attainment of kingship in this second sense is possible, indeed it is an observed reality.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, how could Allah give the kingdom to an unbeliever? I say: there are two views on this. He gave him what enabled him to prevail and to dominate, namely wealth, servants, and followers, but as for domination and control in the sense of imposing will by Allah's decree, He did not. It was also said: He gave him kingship as a test for His servants. This is the end of his words. In it there is a Muʿtazili tendency, namely his saying "but as for domination and control, no," because for them it is the unbeliever who dominated and controlled, so domination and control are his own act and not the act of Allah according to them.

﴿When Abraham said: "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death"﴾. This is from Abraham in response to a question that had been put by the unbeliever, namely that he said: "Who is your Lord?" Something of this has already been mentioned in his story; otherwise a speech would not begin with this. Abraham singled out, among the signs of Allah, giving life and causing death, because they are the most wondrous and most famous of Allah's signs, and the most indicative of the perfect power (of Allah).

The governing element (al-ʿāmil) of (idh ḥājja, "when he argued") is... Al-Zamakhshari allowed that it could be a substitute (badal) for (an ātāhu, "that He had given him") if it is taken in the sense of a time. We have already mentioned the weakness of this. Also, the two adverbial phrases differ, since the time of the giving of the kingdom is not the time of his saying: ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death﴾. In Abraham's saying: ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death﴾ there is a strengthening of the view of the one who said that the pronoun in His saying "in his Lord" refers to Abraham. "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death" is a subject and predicate, and in it there is an indication that He is the one who brought the unbeliever into existence, and gives him life and causes him to die, as if he had said: "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death; He disposes of you and those like you by means that you and those like you cannot do, through these two great attributes which are observed in the world, and in which the stratagems of the wise and the medicine of physicians are of no avail." There is also in it an indication of the origin and the return (al-mabdaʾ wal-maʿād, the beginning and the end of creation). In His saying: ﴿who gives life and causes death﴾ there is evidence of exclusivity (ikhtiṣāṣ), because they have mentioned that a predicate of this form indicates exclusivity. So you say: "Zayd is the one who makes such-and-such," meaning: the one specially devoted to making it.

﴿He said: "I give life and cause death"﴾. When Abraham mentioned that his Lord is the One who gives life and causes death, the unbeliever opposed him by claiming that he gives life and causes death. He did not say: "I am the one who gives life and causes death," because that would indicate exclusivity, and his senses would refute it, since people had been given life before his existence and had died. What he meant was that this attribute which you claim is exclusive to your Lord is not so; rather, I share in it. It was said: he brought two men, killed one and released the other. It was also said: he put four men in a house until they became hungry, then he fed two of them, and they lived, and he left two without food, and they died. It was also said: he gives life by intercourse and the release of semen, and causes death by killing.

Nafiʿ recited with the affirmation of the alif in (anā, "I") when a hamza followed it, whether the hamza was open (fatḥa) or closed (ḍamma). Abu Nashit related its affirmation with a hamza that was kasra. The rest recited with the omission of the alif. They agreed on its affirmation in pause. The affirmation of the alif both in connection and in pause is the dialect of the Banu Tamim (a tribe); the dialect of others is to omit it in connection, and it is not affirmed in connection by those other than the Banu Tamim except in poetic necessity, such as his saying:

"How can I be, when I take up poetry, after grey hair, that is shame enough?"

The better view is that Nafiʿ's recitation is according to the dialect of the Banu Tamim, because it is from treating connection as if it were pause, according to the interpretation given by some of them. He said: this is very weak, and it is not something that is good to adopt in the Qur'an. This is the end of his words. So if we take this as the dialect of Tamim, it is eloquent (faṣīḥ).

﴿Abraham said: "Indeed Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west"﴾. When the unbeliever imagined that he shared with the Lord of Abraham the attribute that Abraham had mentioned, and Abraham saw from his opposition what indicated weakness of understanding or deceit, for he opposed the wording with its like and did not reflect on the difference between the two attributes, he mentioned to him something that he could not claim and could not deceive about. The commentators differed as to whether this was a transition from one proof to another, or whether it was one proof with the transition within it from one example to a clearer example. To the first view al-Zamakhshari went. He said: The objection was ready at hand, but when Abraham heard his foolish answer he did not argue against it; rather he moved on to something in which the other could not give a similar answer, in order to silence him at the outset. This is evidence for the permissibility of moving from one argument to another. This is the end of his words.

The meaning of al-Zamakhshari's words "the objection was ready at hand" is that it was there for Abraham to use: had he wished to object to him by saying, "Bring back to life whom you have caused to die," this would have supported the first argument. It has been said that he did say this to him, and he was silenced by it; and Abraham followed it with a second argument and argued against him from two angles. This was intended to end the argument, not out of inability to support the first argument. It was also said: Nimrod claimed lordship, so when he said to him, "Abraham said: My Lord is He who gives life and causes death," he said: "I give life and cause death," meaning: the one who does that is I, not the one you attribute it to. When Abraham heard his great lie and his false claim, a deceit and a disguise, he proposed to him, saying: ﴿Indeed Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west﴾. So he was silenced, his incapacity became clear, and his falsehood was shown. It was also said: when he said, "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death," Nimrod said to him: "Have you seen this?" Since he had not seen it, though he knew that Allah is able to do it, he moved to what was clear to him and to others. It was also said: he moved on because they used to revere the sun, so he indicated that it is subjected to Allah, mighty and majestic.

As for the second view, which holds that it is not a transition from one proof to another, but that the proof is one in both places, this is the view of the Muḥaqqiqūn (the verifying scholars). They said: it is that we observe things coming into being which no one can bring into being, so there must be a capable one who undertakes bringing them into being, and that is Allah, exalted is He. These have examples: among them life and death; among them clouds, thunder and lightning; among them the movements of the celestial spheres and the stars. The one who argues by proof is not permitted to move from one proof to another. Therefore what Abraham, peace be upon him, did belongs to the category in which the proof is one, not to the category in which there is a transition from one proof to another when it is clarified, from one example to another. When Abraham, in the first position, when the unbeliever asked him about his Lord, and the unbeliever claimed lordship, said: ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death﴾, then when he moved to a proof or example that was clearer and more decisive against the opponent, he turned to the name that is common among all the world, and said: ﴿Indeed Allah brings the sun from the east﴾. By this he established that his Lord, who gives life and causes death, is the One who brought you into existence, O unbeliever, and others. He did not say, "Indeed my Lord brings the sun," so as to make clear that the God of all the world is his Lord whom they worship; and because all the world admits that none brings it from the east except their God.

The coming of the (fa-, "so/then") in (fa-inna, "indeed") indicates an omitted clause before it, since if it were only the quoted speech, the fa- would not enter. It is as if the construction were: Abraham said: "Indeed Allah brings the sun," and the implied sentence, and Allah knows best, is: Abraham said: "If you claim that, or confuse matters with that, then indeed Allah brings the sun from the east." The (bāʾ, "with") in bi-l-shamsi ("the sun") is for transitivity: you say, "The sun came," and "Allah brought it," meaning He gave it life. And (min, "from") is for the starting point (ibtidāʾ al-ghāya).

﴿So the one who disbelieved was confounded﴾. The reading of the majority is in the passive form (mabniyyan li-mā lam yusamma fāʿiluhu, passive voice with the agent unnamed), and the omitted agent is Abraham, since he is the one who debated with him. When he brought the decisive argument, he confounded him with it, bewildered him, and overcame him. It is possible that the omitted agent is the verbal noun understood from "he said," meaning: the speech of Abraham bewildered him and confounded him. Ibn al-Sumayqaʿ recited (fa-bahata), with a fatḥa on the bāʾ and the hāʾ, and the apparent reading is that it is transitive, like the reading of the majority (fa-buhita) in the passive, meaning: Abraham confounded the one who disbelieved. It was also said: the meaning is: the unbeliever was confounded by Abraham, that is, he reviled Abraham when he was cut off and had no stratagem. It is possible that it is intransitive, and (alladhī kafara, "the one who disbelieved") is the subject, meaning: he was confounded, or he produced confusion. Abu Haywa recited (fa-bahuta) with a fatḥa on the bāʾ and a ḍamma on the hāʾ, and it was recited, as transmitted by al-Akhfash: (fa-bahita) with a kasra on the hāʾ.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 258 (part 3 of 3):

﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ This is a report from Allah, exalted is He, that the wrongdoer is not guided by Him. Its apparent meaning is generality, but what is meant is a specific guidance, or the wrongdoers are a specific group. Regarding the specific guidance, it was said that He does not guide them in their argument. It was also said: He does not guide them to reward in the Hereafter, nor to Paradise. It was said: He does not show them kindness, nor inspire them, nor grant them success. The wrongdoers are restricted to those who die while still wrongdoers, that is, disbelievers. What appears to be the case is that this is a report from Allah that whoever He has decreed and judged to be a wrongdoer, that is, a disbeliever, and whom He has predestined not to submit, guidance from Allah cannot reach him. ﴿Is one against whom the word of punishment has become due [equal to one who is saved]? Can you, [O Muhammad], save those who are in the Fire?﴾ [Az-Zumar: 19]. The connection of this verse with this report is clear, because it mentioned the condition of one who claimed a partnership with Allah in giving life and causing death, disguising what he did as giving life and causing death; and no one is more wrongdoing than one who claims that. So Allah, exalted is He, reported that whoever is of this description of wrongdoing, Allah does not guide him to follow the truth. Such a person is destined to lack guidance and is sealed with disbelief, because a claim like this is not something that could be confused for its claimant. Rather, it belongs to the category of heresy, philosophy and sophistry, so its claimant is only a defiant one who opposes reason. Allah prevented this disbeliever from claiming that he was the one who brings the sun from the east (p-290), for whoever is defiant in claiming to give life and cause death may be defiant in that too and claim it. Are the two matters not equal in claiming what is impossible for a human? But Allah, exalted is He, made him stunned, bewildered, perplexed and cut off, as an honour to His Prophet Abraham and a manifestation of His religion. It was also said: he did not claim that he was the one who brings it from the east because his lie would be evident to the people of his kingdom, who know that he is created, and the sun used to rise from the east before his coming into being. He did not say, "I bring it from the west," because of his knowledge of his own incapacity. So when he saw that there was no escape for him, he fell silent and was cut off.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 259 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Or like him who passed by a town﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read "aw" with a sukun on the waw. It was said that its meaning is distinction (al-tafsil), and it was said that it is choice (al-takhyir) in expressing wonder at the state of one who arises from both of them. Abu Sufyan ibn Husayn read "awa kalladhi" with a fatha on the waw, and it is a conjunctive particle (harf 'atf) to which the alif of affirmation (alif al-taqrir) has been attached; the implied sense is: "Have you not seen the like of him who...?" As for those who read "aw" as the conjunction, the majority of the exegetes hold that it is conjoined to His saying: ﴿Have you not seen him who argued﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258], on the basis of meaning (al-'atf 'ala al-ma'na), since the meaning of "Have you not seen him who..." is "Have you not seen the like of him who argued?" So His saying "or like him who passed by" is conjoined to this meaning. Conjoining on the basis of meaning is found in the speech of the Arabs; the poet said:

"A pious, pure man who did not amass spoils, neither by the oppression of a near kinsman nor by [...] wrongfully."

The meaning of his saying "did not amass" is "he was not one who amasses," and therefore he observed this meaning and conjoined to it his saying "nor by [...]." Another said:

"Did you, by your life, not see at Tha'aylabat, nor at Baydan, a swift, fast she-camel [...]
nor one who overtakes, while the night is young, with burdens [...] in some of the wadi's thickets."

The meaning: "By your life, are you not a stranger?" And since he observed this meaning, he conjoined to it his saying "nor one who overtakes." They have stated explicitly that conjoining on the basis of meaning is not systematic (la yanqas). Al-Zamakhshari said: "Or like him who..." means "Or have you seen the like of him who...?" and the verb was omitted because "Have you not seen" indicates it, since both are expressions of wonder. This is a good explanation, because the implied verb indicated by the meaning is easier than conjoining on the basis of meaning. Al-Zamakhshari himself permitted the first possibility.

It was also said that the kaf is extra (za'ida), so that "alladhi" is conjoined to "alladhi": the sense being, "Have you not seen him who argued with Ibrahim, or him who passed by a town?" It was said: just as it was added in His saying, ﴿There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ [al-Shura: 11], and in the verse of the rajaz poet:

"So they were made like stalks eaten [...]"

It is possible that this is neither by omitting a verb, nor by conjoining on the basis of meaning, nor by the extra kaf; rather the kaf is a noun, according to what Abu al-Hasan (al-Akhfash) holds, so the kaf is in the position of a genitive, conjoined to "alladhi," the sense being: "﴿Have you not seen him who argued with Ibrahim﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258], or [have you not seen] the like of 'him who passed by a town'?" The coming of the kaf as a noun, functioning as subject, as an inchoative, and as a genitive governed by a preposition, is established in the speech of the Arabs, though its interpretation is remote. So the preferable view is this last one. The problem arose for them only from the belief that the kaf is a particle, following the well-known doctrine of the Basrans. The correct view is that of Abu al-Hasan. Do you not see the subjectivity of "mithl" in the poet's words:

"Indeed, no boastful one who is weak has boasted over you, nor has the like of one who overcomes overcome you."

The discussion of the kaf is mentioned in the science of grammar (ilm al-nahw).

The one who passed by a town was 'Uzayr (Ezra), as said by 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, Abu al-'Aliyah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, al-Rabi', al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, Muqatil, Sulayman ibn Buraydah, Najiyah ibn Ka'b, and Salim al-Khawwas. It was also said: he was Irmiya' (Jeremiah), as said by Wahb, Mujahid, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, and Bakr ibn Mudar. Ibn Ishaq said: he was Irmiya', and he is al-Khidr (the Green One), and al-Naqqash related this from Wahb.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This is as we see it, unless it is a name that coincided with another name; for al-Khidr was a contemporary of Musa, whereas this one who passed by the town was, according to what Wahb related, after him by a time, from the lineage of Harun." Some of our shaykhs said: "It is possible that al-Khidr himself is meant and that he was among the long-lived, so he would have witnessed the time of the town's ruin, and he is still living according to the view of most scholars." [End of his words, p. 291.] It was also said: he was an unbeliever who passed by a town, riding a donkey, with a basket of figs, as said by al-Hasan. It was said: a man from the Children of Israel, unnamed, as said by Mujahid as related by Makki. It was said: the servant of Lut, peace be upon him. It was said: Ashi'ya'. The one who revived it after its ruin was Lausak al-Farisi, as related by al-Suhayli from al-Qutaybi.

The town (al-qaryah) was Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), as said by Wahb, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, 'Ikrimah, and al-Rabi'. Or it was the town of grapes (qaryat al-'inab), which is two farsakhs from Bayt al-Maqdis. Or it was the Holy Land, as said by al-Dahhak. Or it was the overturned town (al-mu'tafikah), as said by a group. Or it was the town from which thousands went out fearing death, as said by Ibn Zayd. Or it was the monastery of Heraclius (dayr Hiraql), as said by Ibn 'Abbas. Or it was Shabur-abad, as said by al-Kalbi. Or it was Salmayadh, as said by al-Suddi.

﴿And it was fallen upon its roofs﴾. It was said: the meaning is "empty of its people, yet standing upon its roofs," so the houses were standing. Al-Suddi said: "Fallen, its walls collapsed upon its roofs after the roofs had fallen." It was also said: "'ala" here means "with" (ma'a), i.e., with its buildings, and the roofs ('urush) are upon these buildings. This clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the agent in "passed by" or from "a town." A circumstantial phrase from an indefinite noun when it is placed after it is rare. It was also said: the clause is in the position of an attribute of "town." The word "wa" (and) weakens this view. "'Ala" is connected to an omitted element if the meaning is "empty of its people," i.e., "settled upon its roofs," or to "khawiyah" if the meaning is "fallen." It was also said: "'ala 'urushiha" is a substitute (badal) for "qaryah," i.e., he passed by its roofs. It was also said: it is in the position of an attribute of "qaryah," i.e., he passed by a town existing upon its roofs, while it was empty.

﴿He said: How will Allah bring this to life after its death?﴾ It was said: when Bukht Nassar (Nebuchadnezzar) the Babylonian ruined Bayt al-Maqdis, after the Children of Israel had committed their misdeeds, Irmiya' or 'Uzayr stood upon the town, which was like a great mound in the midst of Bayt al-Maqdis, because Bukht Nassar had ordered his troops to carry the dust to it until he made it like a mountain; so he said these words. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The passer-by was an unbeliever in resurrection, and this is the apparent meaning, because he is placed alongside Nimrod in one line, and because of the expression of disbelief, ﴿How will He bring it to life?﴾." It was also said: he was 'Uzayr or al-Khidr, and he wished to witness the revival of the dead so that his insight might increase, as Ibrahim requested. [End of his words.] Abu 'Ali said: he cannot be a prophet, because such doubt does not occur to prophets. The revival (al-ihya') and causing death (al-imatah) here are figurative (majazan): he expressed revival by re-building, and death by ruin. It was also said they are literal, in which case there is an omitted genitive construction, its sense being: "How will He bring to life the people of this town?" Or "this" (hadhihi) is a reference to what the meaning indicates, namely the decayed bones of its people, their torn corpses, and their scattered joints. On the figurative view, His saying "How will He bring it to life?" is an expression of anguish from one standing over his city, in which he had known its people and his beloved, and he set for himself an example in himself of something greater than what he asked about. On the second view, His saying "How will He bring it to life?" is an admission of inability to know the manner of revival and an exalting of the power of the One who gives life, and it is not by way of doubt. Al-Tabari related from some of them that he said: this statement was a doubt about Allah's power to revive, and therefore He set an example for him in himself.

﴿So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him﴾. That is, He revived him and gave him movement and the ability to move. It was said: when seventy years had passed since his death, during which He had protected him from beasts and birds and prevented eyes from seeing him, Allah sent an angel to a great king of the Persian kings called Lausak, and said to him: "Allah commands you to dispatch a people to rebuild Bayt al-Maqdis, Iliya' (Aelia), and its land until it returns to its best condition." The king undertook it. It was said: three thousand overseers, with each overseer a thousand workers, and they began to rebuild it. Allah destroyed Bukht Nassar with a gnat that entered his brain, and Allah saved those of the Children of Israel who remained and returned them to Bayt al-Maqdis and its surroundings, and they rebuilt it for thirty years, and they multiplied until they were as they had been in their best condition.

﴿He said: How long have you remained?﴾ The apparent view is that the speaker is Allah, the Exalted, because of His saying ﴿How We raise them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 259]. It was said: a voice from heaven; it was said: Jibril (Gabriel); it was said: a prophet; it was said: a believing man who witnessed him when he died and lived until the time of his revival. According to the view of al-Zamakhshari, he was not an unbeliever after the resurrection, which is why it was permissible for Allah to speak to him. [End of his words.] There is no explicit text in the verse that Allah spoke to him directly. "Kam" (how many) is an adverb of time, meaning: how long a period have you remained? I.e., you remained [dead], and this is a question in the form of affirmation (taqrir).

﴿He said: I have remained a day, or part of a day﴾. Ibn Jurayj, Qatadah, and al-Rabi' said: Allah caused him to die at the morning of a day, then raised him before sunset after a hundred years; so he said: "A day," before looking at the sun. Then he turned and saw a remnant of the sun, so he said: "Or part of a day." So his saying "a day" was by way of supposition (al-zann), and then when he was certain that he had not completed the day, he said: "Or part of a day." It is preferable that "aw" here is not for alternation (al-taraddud) but for retraction (al-idrab), as if he said: "Rather, part of a day." When the sun appeared to him, he retracted from the first report, which had been by way of supposition, and then reported the second by way of certainty. In His saying "or part of a day" is evidence that the word "ba'd" may be applied to the greater part of a thing.

﴿He said: Rather, you have remained a hundred years﴾. "Bal" (rather) is for conjoining this sentence to an omitted sentence, the sense being: "You did not remain this period; rather you remained a hundred years." Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and 'Asim read "labithta" with the ta' pronounced distinctly, while the rest read with assimilation (idgham), and this applies throughout the Qur'an. The specifying of the period is mentioned here in His saying "Rather, you have remained a hundred years," and it is not specified in His saying ﴿He said: You remained only a little﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 114], although they share in the answer to ﴿We remained a day or part of a day﴾ [al-Kahf: 19]. This is because the one raised in al-Baqarah is one person, so the period of Allah's causing him to die is determined, whereas those others varied in their time beneath the earth, like one who died at the beginning of the world and one who died at its end, so they were not restricted to a specific number. Therefore they were included under His saying "only a little," because the duration of the worldly life compared with the life of the Hereafter is little. And Allah, the Exalted, has knowledge encompassing the length of each one's stay; had He mentioned the duration of each one individually, it would have required many volumes to enumerate.

﴿Look at your food and your drink; they have not changed﴾. In the story of 'Uzayr, when he was delivered from Babylon he rode his donkey until he descended at the monastery of Heraclius on the bank of the Tigris. He walked around the town and saw no one in it, and most of its trees were bearing fruit. So he ate of the fruit and pressed grapes and drank from them, and he placed the surplus fruit in a basket and the surplus grapes in a skin. When he saw the ruin of the town and the destruction of its people, he said: ﴿How will He bring it to life?﴾ in wonder, not as doubt about resurrection. It was also said his drink was milk. It was said: he found the figs and grapes as he had left them, freshly picked, and the drink in its original state.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read with the deletion of the ha' in pause (al-wasl) on the basis that it is the ha' of pause (ha' al-sakt), while the rest of the Seven read with the ha' affirmed both in continuation and in pause. The more apparent view is that the ha' is original (asliyyah), though it is possible that this is from treating continuation like pause. The discussion of this word has already been mentioned in the discussion of the individual vocabulary. Ubayy read "lam yassannah" with the ta' assimilated into the sin, as "la yasma'un" was read, the original being "la yatasamma'un." Talhah ibn Musarrif and others read "li-mi'ati sanatin" in place of "lam yatassanah." 'Abd Allah read "wa-hadha sharabuka lam yatassanah." The pronoun in "yatassanah" is singular, so it may be that it refers to the drink alone, and the circumstantial clause concerning the food has been omitted, because what follows indicates it. It is also possible that the food and drink are treated with a singular pronoun because they are inseparable, so they are treated as a single item, or because they share the sense of nourishment, as if it were said: "Look at your nourishment; it has not changed." The poet said concerning two inseparable things:

"As if in the two eyes were clove grains, or ears of grain, painted with kohl, and they flowed with tears."

The clause "لَمْ يَتَسَنَّهْ" (lam yatasannah, "had not changed") is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause), and it is negated with lam. Some of our companions claimed that including the wāw (وَ) in a clause negated with lam is the preferred usage, as the poet said:

"By the hands of men who did not sharpen their swords, / and the slain did not multiply by them when they were drawn."

Some of them claimed that when the clause is negated, it is better to negate it with lammā, as in *jā'a Zaydun wa-lammā yaḍḥak* ("Zayd came, and he had not yet laughed"). He said: it may also be negated with lam and mā, as in *qāma Zaydun wa-lam yaḍḥak* or *mā yaḍḥak*, but that is very rare. End of his words. The inclusion of the wāw with lam is not better than its omission; rather, both are permissible and eloquent. This occurs in the Qur'an in several places. God the Exalted says: ﴿So they returned with a blessing from God and bounty, no harm touched them﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 174]. And God the Exalted says: ﴿Or [he who] says, "It has been revealed to me," while nothing has been revealed to him﴾ [al-Anʿām: 93]. Whoever says that negation with lam is very rare is mistaken. We have examined this question thoroughly in the chapter on the ḥāl in our book *Manhaj al-Sālik ʿalā Sharḥ Alfiyyat Ibn Mālik* (The Path of the Wayfarer on the Commentary of Ibn Mālik's Alfiyya).

﴿And look at your donkey﴾. It was said: when the hundred years had passed, God restored life to his eyes while the rest of his body was dead. Then He restored life to his body, and he was watching. Then he looked at his donkey, and its bones were scattered, white and gleaming. He heard a voice from heaven: "O decayed bones, God commands you to come together." So some of them came together upon others and joined. Then it was called out: "God commands you to clothe yourselves with flesh and skin," and it was so. It is also narrated that when God restored it to life, it brayed. It was also said: God returned life to his eyes and kept his body dead. So he looked at Īlīyāʾ (Jerusalem) and what was around it, and it was being rebuilt and renewed. Then he looked at his food and drink, and they had not changed. He looked at his donkey standing as it was on the day he tied it; it had not eaten or drunk. God restored it to life before his eyes. He looked at the mountain, and it had not changed, though the wind, rain, sun and cold of a hundred years had passed over it. Wahb and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: "And look at your donkey standing in its stall, untouched by anything for a hundred years." Al-Zamakhsharī said: this is among the greatest signs, that it lived for a hundred years without fodder or water, just as He preserved his food and drink from change.

﴿And that We may make you a sign for the people﴾. It was said: the wāw is redundant (muqḥama), meaning: "that We may make you a sign." It was also said: the lām is connected to a verb that is omitted and implied, its estimate being: "We showed you that so that you may know Our power, and so that We may make you a sign for the people." It was also said: it is connected to a verb that is omitted and whose position is delayed, meaning: "And that We may make you a sign for the people, We did that," wanting his revival after death and the preservation of what was with him. Al-Aʿmash said: his being a sign is that he came as a young man in his condition on the day he died, and found his grandchildren and sons to be old men. ʿIkrima said: he came when he was forty years old, as he was on the day he died, and he found his sons had died at the age of a hundred. It was also said: his being a sign is that he came when everyone who knew him had perished, and he was a sign for those among his people who were still alive, since they were certain of his condition through report. It was also said: a man came to his people riding his donkey and said, "I am ʿUzayr." They denied him, so he said, "Bring the Torah." He began to recite it from memory while they looked into the book, and he did not miss a single letter. So they said, "He is the son of God." No one had recited the Torah openly before ʿUzayr, so that is his being a sign. In his being made to die for this period and then revived is the greatest sign. His whole affair is a sign for people for all time, and it does not need to be restricted to some and not others. The *alif* and *lām* in *lil-nās* ("for the people") is for specificity (ʿahd) if it refers to those of his people who remained, or to those who were in his time; or for the genus (jins), since he is a sign for those who were contemporary with him and for those who come after them until the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And look at the bones, how We raise them﴾. By "bones" it is meant the bones of his own body, as said by Qatāda, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Rabīʿ and Ibn Zayd; or the bones of his donkey; or the bones of both. Al-Zamakhsharī added: or the bones of the dead whose revival he marvelled at. This is far-fetched, because they were not revived for him in this world, and it is not possible that it be said to him in the Hereafter: "And look at the bones, how We raise them." Rather, this was said to him in this world, so it cannot be interpreted except as referring to his own bones, or the bones of his donkey, or the bones of both. The most apparent is that the bones of the donkey are meant, and the estimate is: "to the bones of it." Or, according to the view of the Kufans, the *alif* and *lām* are a substitute for the pronoun, meaning: "to its bones." This is because He had already informed us that He resurrected him; then He informed us of God's dialogue with him in the question about how long he had remained dead; then He followed the command to look with the particle *fa* (then), which indicates that his revival preceded the dialogue and the command to look.

The two Ḥaramī reciters (the reciters of Mecca and Medina) and Abū ʿAmr read *nunshiruhā* with a ḍamma on the nūn and an unpointed rāʾ. Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Abū Ḥaywa and Aban from ʿĀṣim read it with a fatḥa on the nūn and an unpointed rāʾ. Both are from *anshara* and *nashara* with the meaning "to revive." *Nashara* may also mean the opposite of folding (ṭayy), as though death is the folding of the bones and limbs, and joining some of them to others is an unfolding (nashr). The rest of the seven read *nunshizuhā* with a ḍamma on the nūn and a pointed zāy. Al-Nakhaʿī read it with a fatḥa on the nūn and a ḍamma on the shīn and zāy, and this is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda, as stated by Ibn ʿAṭiyya. Al-Sakhāwandī reported from al-Nakhaʿī that he read with a fatḥa and ḍamma on the yāʾ together with the rāʾ and the zāy.

The meaning of *nunshizuhā* with a zāy is: we move them, or we raise some of them to others for assembly for revival. It is said: *nashaza* and *anshaztuhu*. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: what appears to me is that the meaning of *nushūz* (rising) is raising the bones, some to others, and *nushūz* is only a slight elevation. It is as though he stood upon the growth of the bones from the dust, and what is found of them at creation emerged. Al-Naqqāshī said: *nunshizuhā* means *nunbituhā* ("we make them grow"). Look at the usage of the Arabs and you will find it as I have mentioned. Among that: the tooth of a camel *nashaza* (protruded), and a high place of land (*nashiz*) by analogy with it, and a woman *nashazat* (became disobedient), as though she departed from the state in which she should be. And *unshuzū fa-unshuzū* ("rise, then rise"), i.e. rise little by little like the protruding of a tooth. Thus the expansion (of meaning) is by this, so *nushūz* is a kind of elevation. But in usage it is far-fetched to say of someone who rises on a wall or upper room that he *nashaza*. End of his words.

Ubayy read *kayfa nunshīhā* with a yāʾ, meaning: "we create them." Some of them said: bones do not come to life individually until some of them join with others. So the zāy is more appropriate for this meaning, as it signifies joining rather than reviving; what is described as living is the man, not the bones, and one does not say "this is a living bone." So the meaning is: "look at the bones, how We lift them from their places in the earth to the body of their owner for revival." End of his words. The reading with the rāʾ is mutawātir (transmitted through multiple uninterrupted chains), so the reading with the zāy cannot be preferred.

*Kayfa* (how) is in the accusative by *nunshizuhā*, in the manner of circumstantial accusatives (ḥāl), and the object of *nunshizuhā* is the thing qualified (dhū al-ḥāl). *Unẓur* cannot govern it, because an interrogative cannot be governed by what precedes it. They parsed *kayfa nunshizuhā* as a ḥāl of "the bones," with the estimate: "and look at the bones made alive." This is not correct, because an interrogative clause does not occur as a ḥāl. Rather, *kayfa* occurs as a ḥāl in a sentence such as *kayfa ḍarabta Zaydan?* ("how did you strike Zayd?"), and for this reason you say *qā'iman am qā'idan?* ("standing or sitting?") and the ḥāl is substituted from it. What the analysis requires is that this clause is in the position of a substitute (badal) for "the bones." This is because the visual *unẓur* is transitive with *ilā* and admits suspension (taʿlīq), so you say: *unẓur kayfa yaṣnaʿu Zayd* ("look at how Zayd acts"). God the Exalted says: ﴿Look how We have preferred some of them over others﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 21]. Then this clause is in the position of an accusative as object of *unẓur*, because what is transitive by a preposition, when suspended, becomes transitive to an object. You say: *fakkartu fī amr Zayd* ("I considered the matter of Zayd"), then you say: *fakkartu hal yajī'u Zayd?* ("I considered whether Zayd will come?"), so *hal yajī'u Zayd* is in the position of an accusative as object of *fakkartu*. Thus *fa-kayfa nunshizuhā* is a substitute for "the bones" according to its position, since its position is accusative, and this is with an omitted modifier, i.e. "look at the state of the bones, how We raise them." An analogous example is the Arabs' saying: *ʿaraftu Zaydan abū man huwa* ("I knew Zayd, whose father is who he is"), according to one of the possibilities. The clause *abū man huwa* is in the position of a substitute for *Zaydan*, the object of *ʿaraftu*, and it is with an omitted modifier, the estimate being: "I knew the story of Zayd: whose father is he?" The interrogative in the matter of suspension is not meant with its literal meaning; rather, this is among the places where the rules of the wording have prevailed over the meaning in Arabic speech. A similar case is *allāhumma ighfir lanā ayyatuhā al-ʿiṣābah* ("O God, forgive us, O you group"), in the matter of specification (ikhtiṣāṣ), where most of the rules of the vocative have prevailed, though the meaning is not the vocative. It has already been stated by us that Arabic speech has three kinds: a kind in which the wording corresponds to the meaning, and this is the majority of Arabic speech; a kind in which the rules of the wording prevail, such as this interrogative occurring in suspension and in equalization (taswiya); and a kind in which the rules of the meaning prevail, such as *aqāʾimun al-Zaydān?* ("are the two Zayds standing?"). We have examined at length the question of the interrogative occurring in suspension in our great book entitled *al-Tadhkira* ("The Reminder"), which is one of the questions that Chief Judge Taqī al-Dīn Abū al-Fatḥ Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī al-Qushayrī, known as Ibn Daqīq al-ʿId, asked me about, and he asked me to write about it for him. His question concerned the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "For indeed one of you does not know where his hand spent the night."

﴿Then We clothe them with flesh﴾. Clothing (*kuswa*) in its literal sense is what covers the body of garments. It is used here metaphorically for the flesh that He produced to cover the bone, as in His saying: ﴿Then We clothed the bones with flesh﴾ [al-Muʾminūn: 14]. This metaphor is of the utmost beauty, since it is a metaphor of an entity for an entity. The metaphor has also come in meaning for the body, as al-Nābigha said:

"Praise be to God, that my term did not come upon me until I was clothed in Islam with a garment."

It is narrated that he would witness the flesh, the sinews and the veins, how they knit together and join. What the apparent wording indicates is that God's saying to him came after the completion of his resurrection, not that the saying occurred after the revival of some of him.

The sequence introduced by "fa-" (then) in His saying "fa-unzur" (look) and what follows indicates that the bones are not meant to be the bones of the man himself. A mention of something of this was made earlier, unless "nanshuruha" was put in place of "anshartuha" and "naksuha" in place of "kasawtuha," in which case it is possible.

The command to look at the food and drink was repeated across the three miraculous signs, and it was not joined in the manner of a list of single items, because each of them is a great miracle and an extraordinary sign in its own right. He began first with looking at the bones and the drink, since they had not changed over the length of that period, and this is more eloquent, for they are among the things that decay quickly. What bears life, namely the donkey, can survive for a long time, and it can forage for itself, eat, and go to water. This is like what the Prophet (ﷺ) said about a stray camel: "It has its water-skin and its sandal; it comes to water and eats from the trees until its owner comes to it."

When he was commanded to look at the food and drink, and at the donkey, these were the things that had been with him. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and that We may make you a sign for the people﴾, meaning: We did that. And since His saying ﴿and look at your donkey﴾ was like something general, He explained to him the aspect of looking at the donkey. So the third look came as a clarification of the second look, specifying in what respect he should look at the donkey, namely the respect of its being brought back to life, and the gradual rising of its bones when they were assembled and clothed with flesh. Therefore it is not an independent act of looking, but rather a completion of the second look. For this reason the separation between the two looks by His saying ﴿and that We may make you a sign for the people﴾ is fitting. There is no inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech, as some have claimed; rather the looks are arranged one after another, and His saying ﴿and that We may make you a sign for the people﴾, and what follows it, is placed first in wording but later in rank. In this verse is the strongest proof of resurrection, since death and life occurred in the worldly abode in plain view.

﴿So when it became clear to him, he said: "I know that Allah is over all things competent."﴾ The majority (al-Jumhur) read "tabayyana" in the active voice. Ibn 'Abbas read "tubayyina lahu" in the passive voice, with an unnamed agent. Ibn al-Sumayqa' read "bayyana lahu," without the taa', in the passive voice with an unnamed agent.

On the reading of the majority, the apparent meaning is that "tabayyana" is an intransitive verb, and its subject is an implied pronoun that the meaning indicates. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "So when it became clear to him what had been unclear to him," meaning the matter of bringing the dead back to life. This should be taken as an explanation of meaning (tafsir ma'na). The explanation of the grammar (tafsir i'rab) is that one should posit an implied pronoun referring to the manner of the revival, which he found strange after death. Al-Tabari said: "When it became manifest to him by sight what had been objectionable to him regarding the power of Allah before its restoration." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is an error, because it imposes what it does not require, and it interprets according to an anomalous opinion." The weak possibility that al-Tabari reported from some of them is that they said: "This statement was a doubt about the power of Allah to revive, and for this reason he struck the example in himself," end of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari, and he began with it, said, and this is his text: "The subject of 'tabayyana' is an implied pronoun whose estimate is: 'So when it became clear to him that Allah is over all things competent, he said: I know that Allah is over all things competent.' The first was omitted because the second indicates it, as in their saying: 'He struck me and I struck Zayd.'" End of his words. Thus he made this a case of i'mal (the principle of one of two verbs governing a shared noun). This is not a case of i'mal, because the grammarians have stated explicitly that the two governing elements in this construction must share (the same element), and this is expressed by a conjunctive particle, so that the separation is not considered, and the second governing element is governed by the first. An example of this is your saying: "There came to me Zayd laughing," so that either a pronoun is placed in "jaa'ani" or in "yadhhaku," so that this verb is not an interruption. It is not an objection to this that they made, "Bring me, I will pour over it molten copper" [al-Kahf: 96], nor "Here, read my record" [al-Haqqah: 19], nor "Come, the Messenger of Allah will ask forgiveness for you" [al-Munafiqun: 5], nor "They ask you for a ruling. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning kalalah" [al-Nisa': 176], as being cases of i'mal, because these governing elements share in some respect of sharing, but no sharing has occurred either in the conjunction or in the governance. Establishing this is a discussion mentioned in grammar. So if the matter is as they stated, the second governing element is not shared between itself and "tabayyana," which is the first governing element, by a conjunctive particle or by anything else, nor is it governed by "tabayyana." Rather it is governed by "qala" (he said), and "qala" is the answer to "lamma" if we say it is a particle, and it governs "lamma" if we say it is an adverb. "Tabayyana," on this view, is in a position of genitive by the adverb. The grammarians did not mention, in a construction of this kind: "If he came, you killed Zayd," nor "When he came, you killed Zayd," nor "When he came, you struck Khalid." For this reason the grammarians transmitted that the Arabs do not say: "You honored, you humiliated Zayd."

Al-Zamakhshari has contradicted himself in his statement, for he said: "The subject of 'tabayyana' is an implied pronoun," then he estimated it: "So when it became clear to him that Allah is over all things competent, he said: 'I know,'" to the end. He said: "The first was omitted because the second indicates it, as in their saying: 'He struck me and I struck Zayd.'" Omission contradicts the implication of a pronoun for the subject. This, according to the Basrans, is an implied pronoun explained by what follows it, and the Basrans do not permit, in this type of construction, the omission of the subject at all. If he meant by "implication" omission, then he has gone over to the view of al-Kisa'i, that the subject in this construction is not implied, because that leads to a pronoun referring to what has not yet been mentioned. Rather, according to him, the subject is omitted. Textual evidence refutes him, and the poet said:

"They made me love, and I loved the modest, sweet-speaking maidens, in the days when I was bound to love and youthful passion."

As for the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, the prepositional phrase with its object is the passive subject. As for the reading of Ibn al-Sumayqa', it is an implied pronoun: that is, "He made it clear to him," meaning the manner of revival.

The majority read "qala" in the active voice, on the reading of the seven readers of the majority, and "a'lamu" as an imperfect whose pronoun refers to the passer-by. He said this as a matter of reflection, just as when a person sees something strange he says: "There is no god but Allah." Abu 'Ali said: its meaning is: "I know this kind of knowledge that I had not known," meaning: "I know by sight what I was knowing by the unseen."

As for the reading of Abu Raja', Hamza, and al-Kisa'i, "a'lam" is an imperative verb from "'alima," and the subject is a pronoun referring to Allah, exalted is He, or to the angel who said it to him on behalf of Allah. This aspect fits the preceding commands in His saying: "and look," then He said to him: "know." It is supported by the reading of 'Abd Allah and al-A'mash: "It was said: know," where "qila" is in the passive voice with an unnamed agent, and the object that is unnamed is the pronoun of the saying, not the sentence. The discussion of this was presented at the beginning of this surah at length, so there is no need to repeat it here.

They also allowed that the subject may be the pronoun of the passer-by, and that he treated himself as the addressed stranger, as if he said to himself: "Know." From this is the line:

"Bid farewell to Hurayrah . . . ."
"Did your eyes not close . . . ."
"And your night grew long . . . ."

He is only addressing himself, treating it as a stranger.

Al-Ja'bari transmitted from Abu Bakr, who said: "A'lim amran" (inform of a matter), from "a'lama." The subject of "qala" appears to be a pronoun referring to Allah, who commanded him to inform others of what he had witnessed of the power of Allah. On what they permitted for "i'lam" as a command from "'alima," the subject may be the pronoun of the passer-by.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 260 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And when Abraham said, "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead."﴾ The connection of this verse with what precedes it is quite evident, since both bring it as evidence of the resurrection attributed to God Almighty, in Abraham's words to Nimrod: ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:258]. However, the one who passed by the town was shown this in himself and in his donkey, whereas Abraham was shown it in something other than himself. The verse of the passer-by is placed before the verse of Abraham, although Abraham comes earlier in time than the passer-by, because he marvelled at the giving of life after death. Even if it was a marvel of reflection, it resembled denial; and even if it was not denial, it was closer to the story of Nimrod and Abraham. As for the case where the passer-by was an unbeliever, the connection appears in its strongest form. As for the story of Abraham, it is a request for the manner in which the giving of life is shown, so that he might witness with his own eyes what he knew in his heart, and had informed Nimrod of.

The governing element of (إذ, "when") is, as they have said, omitted, its estimate being: "And recall when he said." It has also been said that the governing element is expressed, namely (ألم تر, "have you not seen"), the meaning being: "Have you not seen when he said," and it is the object of (تر, "see"). What appears to be the case is that the governing element of (إذ) is his saying (قال أولم تؤمن, "He said: Do you not believe?"), as we established in his saying (وإذ قال ربك للملائكة, "And when your Lord said to the angels"). In opening the question with (رب, "My Lord") there is a fine courtesy of appeal and entreaty in the request, and it accords with his saying to Nimrod (ربي الذي يحيي ويميت, "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death"), because the Lord is the one who watches over his state and sets right his affairs. The ya of the possessive has been dropped, the kasra standing in for it, and this is the eloquent dialect for addressing a noun joined to the first-person ya. The particle of address has been dropped to indicate it. (أرني, "show me") is a request of desire, and it is an object of (قال, "said"). Sight here is visual; the transitivizing hamza of causation entered upon (رأى, "saw"), so it takes two objects: the first is the first-person ya, and the second is the interrogative clause. Thus (كيف تحيي الموتى, "how You give life to the dead") is in a position of accusative. The Arabs attach visual (رأى) to interrogatives in their speech, as in "Do you not see what lightning there is here," just as they attach visual seeing (نظر) to it; and this has been established.

It is known that the prophets, peace be upon them, are protected from major and minor sins that involve baseness, by consensus; so said Ibn 'Atiyyah. What we have chosen is that they are protected from major and minor sins absolutely. Given that, some exegetes have spoken here concerning the one who asked for the vision in words we set aside entirely. We say: the words of the verse do not indicate the occurrence of anything that would stain the belief, because that was a request that God show him with his own eyes the manner of giving life to the dead. For when he knew this in his heart and was certain of it, and used it as evidence against Nimrod in his saying, "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death," he sought from God Most High the sight of that, because in witnessing it there is seeing the scattered parts brought together, the dispersed limbs, and the vanished forms, and the magnifying of the dazzling power of God Most High. A question about the manner presupposes certainty about what is asked about: namely the giving of life and its establishment, and belief in it, and that it is something the heart has harboured belief in. As for what al-Mawardi reported from some people of meanings, that Abraham asked his Lord how He gives life to hearts, that is an interpretation that is worth nothing. They have stated several views on the cause of his question. One: he saw a beast that had been torn apart by beasts of prey and fish, since it was on the shore of the sea; this was said by Ibn Zayd. Or: reflection on reality and metaphor in what Nimrod said, "I give life and cause death"; this was said by Ibn Ishaq. Or: a test of the intimacy (khullah) from God, since He had given him good news of it, because the beloved (khalil) is indicated by what does not indicate others; this was said by Ibn Jubayr.

(He said: "Do you not believe?") The pronoun in (قال, "said") refers back to the Lord. The hamza is for confirmation, like his saying:
"Are you not the best of those who have ridden mounts?"
And his saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Did We not expand your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh 94:1]. The meaning is: You are the best, and We have expanded your breast. Likewise here, its meaning is: "You have already believed in the giving of life." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: a general belief which includes the act of giving life to the dead. The waw is the waw of the circumstantial clause, into which the alif of confirmation has entered (p-٢٩٨) — end of his words. That the waw here is circumstantial is not clear, because if it were circumstantial it would have to be in the accusative position, and then it would need a governing element; so the hamza of confirmation would not have entered upon this circumstantial clause. It entered only upon the clause which contains the governing element and the one who has the circumstance. The estimate would be: "Did you ask while you did not believe?" That is: did you ask in this state?

What appears to be the case is that the confirmation extends over the negated clause, and that the waw is for conjunction, as in His saying: ﴿Have they not seen that We made a secure sanctuary?﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:67] and similar. The hamza of interrogation is given priority and placed first. Our discussion of this has already preceded. For this reason the answer was (بلى, "Yes indeed") in his saying: (He said: "Yes indeed, but that my heart may be at rest"). It has been established in grammar that the answer to a confirmatory positive question, even if it has the form of a negation, the Arabs treat as the answer to a pure negation, so they answer in the form of the negation, and no attention is paid to the sense of affirmation. This is among what we have established: that in Arabic speech there is what is observed in the wording without regard to the meaning, and for this there is a reason mentioned in the science of grammar. According to what Ibn 'Atiyyah said, that the waw is for circumstance, it is not possible for the governing element of the circumstance to be answered with (بلى); because that verb is affirmative and the subject of a question, so the answer is only in affirmation with (نعم, "yes") and in denial with (لا, "no"); but answering with (بلى) is not permissible. This is according to what has been established in the science of grammar.

(He said: "Yes indeed, but that my heart may be at rest.") Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, how did He say "Do you not believe?" when He knew that he was the most firmly believing of people? I say: so that he might answer with what he answered, because of the great benefit in it for the listeners. (بلى, "Yes indeed") is an affirmation of what follows the negation; its meaning is: "Yes, I believed, (but that my heart may be at rest)," so that it may increase in tranquillity and calm by the combination of necessary knowledge with inferential knowledge, and the concurrence of proofs is more soothing to hearts and greater in insight and certainty; and because inferential knowledge admits of doubt, unlike necessary knowledge. So by the tranquillity of the heart he meant the knowledge in which there is no room for doubt. End of his words.

Inferential knowledge does not admit of doubt as he said; rather, some of it admits of doubt. As for when it is from correct premises, it does not admit of doubt, like our knowledge of the createdness of the world and of the oneness of the Creator; such a thing does not admit of doubt.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: (لِيَطْمَئِنَّ, "that it may be at rest") means: that it may be still from its reflection on the object believed in. Reflection on the form of giving life is not forbidden, just as it is for us today to reflect upon it; rather, it is reflection in which there are lessons, since it moved him to that, either the matter of the eaten bird or the saying of Nimrod, "I give life and cause death." End of his words. This is good.

The lam in his saying (لِيَطْمَئِنَّ) is connected to an omitted element after (لكن, "but"). The estimate: "But I sought the witnessing of the manner of giving life to the dead, that my heart may be at rest." The estimate of this omitted element requires the estimate of another omitted element before (لكن), so that the adversative makes sense. The estimate: "He said: Yes indeed," i.e., I believed, and I asked about nothing other than belief, but I asked that my heart may be at rest.

It was reported from Ibn Jubayr, Ibrahim, and Qatadah: "that it may increase in certainty." And from some of them: "that I may increase in belief along with my belief." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: no increase in this meaning is possible except stillness from reflection; otherwise certainty does not admit of division. End of his words.

Al-Nasrabadhi said: The Friend longed for the work of his Friend and did not accuse Him in the matter; so it was as if longing made him speak (أرني, "show me"), as Moses, peace be upon him, said; then he sought a pretext in seeing the Maker's work out of courtesy. Al-Qushayri related that it was said: he drew forth an address by this speech, until the Truth said to him: "Do you not believe?" He said: "Yes indeed," I believed, but I longed for Your saying "Do you not believe?", for by Your saying "Do you not believe?" my heart is at rest. The lover always strives to find the address of his beloved in whatever way he can.

(He said: "Take four birds.") When he asked to see the manner of giving life to the dead, God Most High answered him in that, and taught him how to proceed first. He commanded him to take four birds. God Most High did not specify of what kind the four birds were, so it is possible that the one commanded was specific, and what is said to be specific was not specified; and it is possible that he was commanded to take four, that is, four of no specified kind, since there is no great knowledge in mentioning specification. They differed about what he took. Ibn 'Abbas said: he took a peacock, an eagle, a rooster, and a crow. Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, 'Ata', Ibn Jurayj, and Ibn Zayd said likewise, except that they made a dove in place of the eagle. Ibn 'Abbas also said, as reported by 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Hubayrah from him: he took a dove, a crane, a rooster, and a peacock. In the report of al-Dahhak he said: he took a peacock, a rooster, a Sindi hen, and a goose. In another report from al-Dahhak: in place of the Sindi hen it was the ra'l, the chick of the ostrich. Mujahid, as reported by Layth, said: a rooster, a dove, a duck, and a peacock; and he said: a rooster, a dove, a duck, and a crow. 'Ata' al-Khurasani added a description to these four: a red rooster, a white dove, a green duck, and a black crow. Abu 'Abd Allah said: a peacock, a dove, a rooster, and a hoopoe.

Since he asked his Lord to show him the manner of giving life to the dead, and the word "the dead" was plural, he was answered by taking what denotes a plurality, not taking one. It has been said that this specific number was singled out as an indication of the four elements which make up the bodies of animals and plants, and these were from among the birds. It has been said: because the bird's aspiration is flight in the sky and ascent; and the Friend, peace be upon him, had as his aspiration exaltedness and reaching the dominion, so his miracle was made to match his aspiration. On the first view of specifying the four by what was specified, it has been said: the peacock was singled out as an indication of what is in man of love of adornment, rank and haughtiness; the eagle as an indication of intense craving for food and long hope; the rooster as an indication of intense craving for fulfilling the desire of sex; and the crow as an indication of intense greed and seeking. The wisdom of what they have mentioned regarding the choice of the four and their specification scarcely appears in what they have stated. The extraordinary events God Most High has brought about for His prophets differ, and the wisdom behind the particular extraordinary event God has given to each prophet is hidden from us. Do you not see the breaking of custom for Moses in some matters, and for Jesus in other matters, and for our Messenger Muhammad ﷺ and them in matters whose secret wisdom does not appear to us? Likewise, that these four should be birds: the secret of its wisdom does not appear to us. He commanded him to take the birds, that is, to hold them in his hand, so that his knowledge of the manner of giving life might be more firmly established, since sight and touch are both brought together in it.

"Ṭayr" (bird) is a collective noun for what lacks reason; it may be treated as masculine or feminine. Here it came masculine, in accordance with the saying of God Most High: (وخذ أربعة من الطير, "and take four of the birds"). It came in the most eloquent form for collective nouns in counting, where it is separated by min; so it is said: "four birds of" (أربعة من الطير) it is permissible to use the genitive construction, as God Most High says: (تسعة رهط, "nine persons"). Some of our companions stated that the genitive construction with a collective noun in counting is rare and not to be used as a model; and some stated that the collective noun for what lacks reason (p-٣٠٠) is feminine. Both of these views are incorrect.

* *

(فصرهن إليك, "Then bring them near to you") That is: cut them up; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Ishaq. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is in the Nabataean language. Abu al-Aswad said: it is in Syriac. Abu 'Ubaydah said: cut them up, and he recited for al-Khansa':
"Were he to meet what I have met, a stronghold (ḥiḍn) would have had its lofty peaks cut down by him, and they would have been split apart."

Abu Hayyan, al-Bahr al-Muhit

"Fa-surhunna" (فَصُرْهُنَّ): i.e., cut them up (تَتَقَطَّعُ). Qatadah said: "fa-silhunna" (فَصِلْهُنَّ), i.e., separate them. And from him (Qatadah): "mazziqhunna" (مَزِّقْهُنَّ) and "farriqhunna" (فَرِّقْهُنَّ), i.e., tear them and scatter them. ʿAtaʾ ibn Abi Rabah said: "idmumhunna ilayka" (اضْمُمْهُنَّ إلَيْكَ), i.e., gather them to yourself. Ibn Zayd said: "ijmaʿhunna" (اجْمَعْهُنَّ), i.e., gather them. Ibn ʿAbbas also said: "awthiqhunna" (أوْثِقْهُنَّ), i.e., bind them. Al-Dahhak said: "shaqqiqhunna" (شَقِّقْهُنَّ), in Nabataean (بِالنَّبَطِيَّةِ), i.e., cut them into pieces. Al-Kisa'i said: "amilhunna" (أمِلْهُنَّ), i.e., incline them. If "fa-surhunna" carries the meaning of inclining, then "ilayka" (إلَيْكَ) is connected to it; and if it carries the meaning of cutting, then it is connected to "khudh" (خُذْ).

Hamzah, Yazid, Khalaf, and Ruways read it with a kasra on the sad (بِكَسْرِ الصّادِ), and the rest of the seven read it with a damma (بِالضَّمِّ). Both are dialects (لُغَتانِ), as was mentioned earlier in: "sara yusawwiru" and "yasiru" (صارَ يُصَوِّرُ ويَصِيرُ), with the meaning of "amala" (أمالَ). Ibn ʿAbbas and a group read: "fa-surrhunna" (فَصُرُّهُنَّ) with a shadda on the ra and a damma or kasra on the sad, from "sarrahu yasurruhu and yasirruhu" (صَرَّهُ يَصُرُّهُ ويَصِرُّهُ), meaning he gathered it, similar to "darrahu yadurruhu and yadirruhu" (ضَرَّهُ يَضُرُّهُ ويَضِرُّهُ). That it is doubled, transitive, and comes in the pattern "yaf'ilu" with a kasra on the ʿayn is rare. And from him: "fa-sarrihunna" (فَصَرِّهُنَّ) with a fatha on the sad, a shadda on the ra, and a kasra on it, from "al-tasriya" (التَّصْرِيَةِ). This reading is narrated from ʿIkrimah. And also from him: "fa-surrhunna ilayka" (فَصُرِّهُنَّ إلَيْكَ) with a damma on the sad and a shadda on the ra. If "fa-surhunna" is interpreted with the meaning of cutting, there is no omission; if with the meaning of inclining, then there is an omission, and its estimate is: "wa-qattiʿhunna waj'alhunna ajzaʾan" (وقَطِّعْهُنَّ واجْعَلْهُنَّ أجْزاءً), "and cut them up and make them parts." And according to the interpretation of "fa-surhunna" as "amilhunna and dummuhunna ila nafsika" (أمِلْهُنَّ وضُمَّهُنَّ إلى نَفْسِكَ), that was only so that he would contemplate their forms, shapes, and adornments, so that it would not be confused for him after the revival, and he would not imagine that they were other than those.

"Then place upon every mountain of them a portion" (﴿ثُمَّ اجْعَلْ عَلى كُلِّ جَبَلٍ مِنهُنَّ جُزْءًا﴾). The generality in "every mountain" is restricted by an omitted qualifier, i.e., near you, or in your presence, without regard to a number; this was said by Mujahid. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he was commanded to place it on every quarter of the quarters of the world, but this is far-fetched. The mountains were specified by the number of the portions: it was said four, said by Qatadah and al-Rabiʿ; it was said seven, said by al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj; and it was said ten, said by Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Wazir al-Maghribi. He said about a man who bequeathed a portion of his wealth: it means a tenth, since the remains of birds were ten.

The apparent meaning is that he was commanded to place on every mountain three of them, from what his sight witnesses, such that he sees the portions and how they come together when he calls the birds. The majority read: "juz'an" (جُزْءًا) with a sukun on the zay and with a hamza; Abu Bakr read the zay with a damma. Abu Jaʿfar read: "juzzan" (جُزًّا) with the hamza omitted and a shadda on the zay; its reasoning is that when he omitted it, he doubled the zay, as he does in pausal form, as in your saying "hadha farjun" (هَذا فَرْجٌ), then he treated it as pausal. And "ijʿal" (اجْعَلْ) here may be understood to mean "alqi" (ألْقِ), in which case it is transitive to one object, and "ʿala kulli jabal" (عَلى كُلِّ جَبَلٍ) is connected to "ijʿal"; or it may mean "sayyara" (صَيَّرَ), in which case it is transitive to two objects, and the second is "ʿala kulli jabal," connected to an omitted element.

"Then call them, they will come to you running" (﴿ثُمَّ ادْعُهُنَّ يَأْتِينَكَ سَعْيًا﴾). He commanded him to call them while they were dead, so that it would be greater for him as a sign, and so that their life would be caused by his calling; for this reason he placed on his calling them their coming to him. "Sa'y" (السَّعْيُ) is hastening in a matter.

Al-Khalil said: one does not say "sa'a al-ta'ir" (سَعى الطّائِرُ), meaning in the figurative sense. Its figurative character (تَرْشِيحُهُ) here is that when he called them and they came to him, they were placed in the position of the rational being who is described as running. Their coming hastening in walking is more eloquent in the verse, since their coming to him from the mountains walking swiftly is contrary to what is known of them, which is flying; and so to make evident the greatness of the sign, since he informed him that they would come contrary to their habit of flying, and so it was. Their movement toward him was made "sa'y," since it is the walk of one diligent and eager for what he walks toward, to show their earnestness in heading to Abraham and answering his call.

The accusative of "sa'yan" (سَعْيًا) is as a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial state from the pronoun of the birds, i.e., running. It is narrated from al-Khalil that the meaning is "yatinannaka wa-anta tasʿa sa'yan" (يَأْتِينَكَ وأنْتَ تَسْعى سَعْيًا), "they come to you while you run running," so in this case the verbal noun of the verb is omitted, and it is in the position of a state from the kaf, and the meaning would be: "they come to you while you are running toward them," i.e., there is coming from them to you, and from you running to them, so that you meet them. The first aspect is more apparent. It was also said: "sa'yan" is accusative as an emphatic verbal noun, since running and coming are close in meaning.

It is narrated in the stories of the verse that Abraham took these birds, slaughtered them, cut them into small pieces, and mixed that with the blood and feathers, and placed from that mixed mass a portion on every mountain, and he stood where he could see the portions, and held the heads of the birds in his hand, then said: "Come by Allah's permission." The portions flew, the blood returned to the blood and the feathers to the feathers, until they were joined as they were at first; they remained without heads. Then he repeated the call and they came to him running, until their bodies were placed on their heads, and they flew by Allah's permission.

Al-Nahhas added: when Abraham pointed to one of them without its head, the bird moved away; and when he pointed to it with its head, it came close to him, until each bird met its head.
