Abu ʿAbd Allah said: he slaughtered them and pounded their parts in the mortar (فِي المِنحازِ), meaning the mortar (الهاوُنَ), except their heads, and made that mixture into ten parts on ten mountains; then he placed their beaks between his fingers, then called them, and they came running, the meat flying to the meat, the feathers to the feathers, and the skin to the skin, by the power of Allah the Exalted.

The exegetes unanimously agreed that Abraham cut their limbs and flesh and feathers, and mixed some of them with others along with their blood. Abu Muslim denied this and said: when Abraham requested from Allah the reviving of the dead, He showed him an example to bring the matter near to him. The intended meaning of "fa-surhunna ilayka" (﴿فَصُرْهُنَّ إلَيْكَ﴾) is: incline them, and direct them to respond, such that when you call them they will answer you. When they are like that, place on every mountain of them one of them, in its living state; then call them, they will come to you running. The purpose of this is to mention a tangible example of the return of souls to bodies in an easy manner. He rejected the view of cutting, saying: because the well-known meaning in the language of "fa-surhunna" is "amilhunna," and as for cutting and slaughtering, there is nothing in the wording that indicates it; and if the meaning were "qattiʿhunna," he would not have said "ilayka"; and its connection to "khudh" is contrary to the apparent meaning; and the pronoun in "thumma ud'uhunna" and in "ya'tinanaka" refers to them (the birds), not to the parts, and returning it to the scattered parts is contrary to the apparent meaning. Nothing in what he mentioned is conclusive.

The first view argued by the consensus of the exegetes who preceded Abu Muslim on the cutting; and that what he mentioned is not specific to Abraham, so there is no distinction for him in it; and that he asked Him to show him how He revives the dead, and there is no showing in what Abu Muslim mentioned. The apparent answer to the first view is that the apparent meaning of "thumma ij'al ʿala kulli jabalin minhunna juz'an" (﴿ثُمَّ اجْعَلْ عَلى كُلِّ جَبَلٍ مِنهُنَّ جُزْءًا﴾) indicates that those birds were made into parts, part by part, since each one of them was called a part, and each was placed on a mountain.

"And know that Allah is Almighty, All-Wise" (﴿واعْلَمْ أنَّ اللَّهَ عَزِيزٌ حَكِيمٌ﴾). "ʿAziz" (عَزِيزٌ): nothing He wills is withheld from Him; "hakim" (حَكِيمٌ): in what He wills and what He makes as a parable. Might (العِزَّةُ) includes power, since overcoming results from might. It was also said: "ʿaziz" means one who takes vengeance on those who deny the resurrection of the dead; "hakim" in raising the crumbling bones.

These three stories have included, in eloquent discourse, the mention of "qala" (قالَ) as question and answer and other than that, without conjunction; for conjunction by a particle is not needed except when the speech is such that without it, it would not stand on its own, so a conjunctive particle is used to indicate its meaning. As for when the meaning itself indicates that, then omitting the particle is better, when one part is tied to the neck of another and some parts are ordered in meaning after others. We have pointed to something of this in His saying: "And when your Lord said to the angels, 'Indeed I am placing a khalifah on the earth'" (﴿وإذْ قالَ رَبُّكَ لِلْمَلائِكَةِ إنِّي جاعِلٌ في الأرْضِ خَلِيفَةً﴾) [al-Baqarah: 30]. Among what contains this abundantly is the dialogue of Moses and Pharaoh in Surat al-Shu'ara', and the exegesis of that will come, Allah willing.

﴿The parable of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is that of a grain that sprouts seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains. Allah multiplies for whom He wills, and Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿Those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah and do not follow what they have spent with reminders of their generosity or with injury, their reward is with their Lord, and no fear shall befall them, nor shall they grieve.﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:262] ﴿A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury. And Allah is Free of need, Forbearing.﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:263] ﴿O you who believe, do not nullify your charities with reminders of generosity and injury, like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day. His parable is that of a smooth rock covered with soil; a heavy rain strikes it and leaves it bare. They have no power over anything of what they have earned. And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:264] ﴿And the parable of those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of Allah and for the firm stability of their own souls is that of a garden on a height: a heavy rain strikes it and it yields its produce twofold. And if heavy rain does not strike it, then light rain suffices. And Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:265] ﴿Would any of you wish to have a garden of date palms and grapevines, with rivers flowing beneath it, having in it every kind of fruit, while old age has overtaken him and he has weak offspring, and then a whirlwind with fire strikes it and it is burned? Thus Allah makes clear to you the signs, that you may reflect.﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:266] (p. 302) Al-habbah (the grain): a generic noun for everything that the son of Adam plants and eats for sustenance. The most well-known of these is wheat. The word "habb" is often used to mean it, and from this is the saying of al-Mutalammis:

"I have sworn never to feed the grain of Iraq for as long as time lasts, while the weevil eats the grain in the village."

The "habbat al-qalb" is its heart's core (sweydā'uhu), and al-hibbah, with a kasra on the ha', is the seeds of herbs which are not food staples, while al-hubbah with a damma is love, and al-hubb is the beloved. Al-inbat: bringing forth by way of generation. Al-sunbulah: well known, and its form is fun'ulah, so the nun is an added letter, on the basis of the saying "asbala al-zar'" (the crop released what was in it), as a garment hangs down (yansabilu). Some lexicographers have also cited "sanbala al-zar'". Some of our companions said: the nun is original, and its form is fa'lala, because fan'al is not attested, so it is like sibt and sibaṭar alongside asbala.

Al-mann: that by which something is weighed; al-mann is the measure and weight of a thing. Al-mann and al-minnah are a favour; "mann 'alayhi" means he bestowed a favour upon him. Among the names of Allah, the Exalted, is al-Mannan. Al-mann also means diminishing what is due and withholding it from its rightful owner, and from this comes the blameworthy mann, which is mentioning the favour to the one who received it in a manner of boasting over him and reckoning one's kindness against him. The root sense of mann is cutting, because the benefactor cuts off a piece of his wealth for the one he benefits.

Al-Ghaniyy: on the pattern fa'il, for intensification, from ghina, meaning one who has no need of anyone, as the poet said:

"Each of us is independent of his brother in life."

It is also said: "ghaniya bi-al-makan" meaning he settled in the place. Al-ghaniyah is the woman who is independent of adornment through her beauty.

Al-ri'a' (showing off): on the pattern fi'al, a verbal noun from ra'a, from ru'yah (seeing). Its hamza may be replaced by a ya' because of the kasra before it. It means that one shows people the righteous deed he performs so that they will praise and magnify him for it, having no intention other than that.

Al-safwan: a large smooth stone. Vocalizing its fa' with a fatha is a dialect form. It is said that it is a collective noun whose singular is safwanah. Al-Kisa'i said: the plural of safwan is safiyy, which al-Mubarrad rejected, saying: safiyy is the plural of safa, like 'asa and 'usiyy, and qafa and qufiyy. Al-Kisa'i also said: safwan is singular, and its plural is sifwan with a kasra on the sad. Al-Nahhas said: it is possible that the one with the kasra on the sad is singular. What al-Kisa'i said is not correct; rather, safwan is a plural of safa, like warl and wirlan, akh and ikhwan, and kara and karawan.

Al-turab: well known, and it is also said tawrab. "Taraba al-rajul" means he became poor, and "itraba" means he became rich, the hamza in it indicating removal, i.e., the soil (turb), which is poverty, was removed from him, and when it is removed from him he becomes rich.

Al-wabil: heavy rain. "Balat al-sama' tabill" means the sky rained, and the land is "mawbulah." Al-Nadr said: the first stage of rain is "rash," then "tass," then "tall," then "radhadh," then "nadh'," which is drops by two drops, then "hatl" and "tahtan," then finally "wabil" and "judud."

Al-wabil also means: the unwholesome; and al-wabil: a thick stick; al-wabilah: a bundle of firewood.

Al-saldu: the bare and smooth, clean of the soil that was on it. From this comes "salada jabin al-aslah" meaning the forehead of the bald man shone. It is said: "salada yasludu saladan" with a fatha on the lam, so it is "saldun" with sukun. Al-Naqqash said: al-saldu means the bare, in the dialect of Hudhayl. Aban ibn Taghlib transmitted that al-saldu is the soft among stones. Ali ibn Isa said: al-saldu is that which is devoid of good among stones, lands and others, and from it: "qadrun saloud," meaning a slow-boiling pot.

Al-rabwah: al-Khalil said: a high, good land. It is also said: "al-ribawah," and the ra' may be vocalized three ways in both forms. It is also said "rabiyah." The poet said:

"And a rain of the early spring, whose hills are green, whose slopes and heavy downpours have answered its rains."

Al-Akhfash said: the damma is preferred in rabwah, because in the plural only "ribā" is heard, and its root is from "raba al-shay'" meaning it increased and rose. As for al-Suddi's interpretation that it is what is low of the land, it is nothing.

Al-tall: the fine thin drop of rain. This is the well-known meaning in the language. Some people, including Mujahid, said al-tall is dew, but this is a figurative usage. In al-Sihah: al-tall is the weakest of rain, its plural is tilal. It is said: "tallat al-ardu" and it is "matlul" (the land has been wetted with light rain). The poet said:

"When we stopped at a place which the dew had wetted."

It is also said: "atallaha al-nada" (the dew wetted it), and "al-tallah" is the wife.

Al-nakhil: a collective noun or a broken plural, like nakhl as a generic noun, just as they said kalb and kulayb. Al-Raghib said: it was named so because it is the sifted and choice of trees, since it is the most noble of what grows, being likened to animals in that the female needs the male for fertilization, i.e., pollination, and that if its head is cut it does not bear fruit.

Al-'inab: the fruit of the vine, and it is a generic noun whose singular is 'inabah, and its plural is a'nab. It is also said: "i'nba'" with a long vowel, diptote, on the pattern of siyara' with the meaning of grape.

Al-i'sar: a violent wind that lifts dust up into the sky, which common people call the zawba'ah, as al-Zajjaj said. It is said: it is the samum wind that kills, named so because it squeezes the clouds. Its plural is a'asir.

Al-ihtiraq (burning): well known, and its verb is intransitive, while its transitive form is quadriliteral. You say: "ahraqat al-nar al-hatab wa-al-khubz" (the fire burned the firewood and the bread), and "haraqa nab al-rajul" is a triliteral intransitive when a man's tooth rubs against another out of rage, and transitive when you say: "haraqa al-rajul nabahu" meaning he rubbed his tooth against another from anger. The poet said:

"He refused oppression, while al-Nu'man grinds his tooth against it, and swords are its fortresses."

We read "al-nab" with a damma and with a fatha.

﴿The parable of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is that of a grain that sprouts seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains.﴾ The connection of this verse to what came before is that when He mentioned the story of the one who passed by a town and the story of Ibrahim, and both were among the clearest proofs of the Resurrection, He mentioned what benefits a person on the Day of Resurrection and what will bring him its benefit there, which is spending in the way of Allah. Similarly, He followed the story of those who left their homes in their thousands fearing death with His saying: ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah a good loan?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:245], and similarly after the killing of Goliath by David and His saying: ﴿And if Allah had willed, they would not have fought one another﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:253], He followed it with: ﴿O you who believe, spend from what We have provided you before there comes a Day﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:254]. Thus here He follows the mention of giving life and causing death with the mention of spending in the way of Allah, because the fruit of spending in the way of Allah truly appears on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿On the Day every soul will find what it has done of good present﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:30]. The call to spend in the way of Allah is a reminder of the Resurrection, and it is based on belief in it, for if one did not believe in its existence, he would not spend in the way of Allah. In the parable of the spending by the grain mentioned, there is also an indication of the Resurrection and of the great power, since from a single grain Allah brings forth seven hundred grains. Whoever is capable of such a wondrous matter is capable of reviving the dead, and by the common element they share: nourishment and growth.

It is said: when He mentioned the origin and the return, and the proofs of their validity, He followed that with the explanation of the laws, rulings and obligations. He began with spending wealth in the way of Allah and dwelt at length on it, then moved on to how wealth is acquired in a manner permitted by the Law. When He was general in mentioning the multiplication in His saying: ﴿many times over﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:245], and unrestricted in His saying: ﴿spend from what We have provided you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:254], He gave details in this verse and specified by mentioning the thing compared. Between these verses is an indication of His power over giving life and causing death, for without that the obligation would not be fitting, as we have mentioned. These are aspects of the connection. Here "mathal" means attribute, and therefore He said: ﴿like the parable of a grain﴾, meaning like the attribute of a grain. The supposition that the kaf is extra, or that the word "mathal" is extra, is a distant view. This verse is similar in its assumed ellipsis to His saying: ﴿And the parable of those who disbelieve is like that of one who shouts to what hears nothing but calls and cries﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:171]. So the ellipsis may be in the first part, meaning: the parable of those who spend, or in the second part, meaning: like the parable of a sower, so that the comparison is valid, or in both parts with different estimates, meaning: the parable of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah and their spender is like the parable of a grain and its sower. The discussion of this aspect has already been presented in the story of the disbeliever and the one who shouts, so let it be consulted there. (p. 304) This parable includes encouragement to spend in the way of Allah in everything that is obedience, and whose benefit returns to the Muslims. The greatest and most valuable of these is jihad to raise the word of Allah. It is said: the intended meaning of "the way of Allah" here is jihad specifically. The apparent meaning of spending in the way of Allah includes both obligatory and voluntary spending, and it requires spending on oneself in jihad and otherwise, and spending on others so that they may be strengthened by it for obedience, whether jihad or other.

Spending is likened to sowing, because a crop does not cease. The two Harami readers (Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr) and 'Asim and Ibn Dhakwan made the ta' of the feminine marker clear before the sin (in the form "al-nata" and "al-akyat"), and the rest assimilated it. Because the sin and the ta' are close in articulation, the ta' was replaced by the sin, as in "al-nas" and "al-akyas."

The bringing forth is attributed to the grain figuratively, since it was the cause of the growth, just as that is attributed to water and the earth, while the true producer is Allah. The meaning is: from the grain came forth a stalk which branched out into seven branches, in each branch an ear, and in each ear a hundred grains. This illustration depicts the multiplication as though it were standing before the eyes of the beholder. They said: the thing compared is found, and it was observed in the ear of the millet. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is found in the sorghum, the maize and others, and perhaps the stalk of wheat in fertile, productive land has many branches, so its grain reaches this extent. Even if it were not found, it would be valid as a supposition and estimate. End of his words.

Ibn Isa said: this is verified in the sorghum, and the parable is valid with what can be imagined even if it is not witnessed, as the poet said:

"You do not remain faithful to a covenant you have made, just as the ghoul changes colour in its garments."

End of his words. And as Imru' al-Qays said:

"Will he kill me while the sharp sword is my bedfellow, and blue, sharpened blades, like the fangs of ghouls?"

He specified seven from among the numbers, because, as he mentioned, it is the most a single grain can produce in stalks (ṣuʾūq). Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "A single ear of wheat may contain a hundred grains, and in the other grains there may be more. But the example was given with a hundred. The Qur'an has stated that a good deed in all acts of righteousness is multiplied tenfold, and this verse implies that the expenditure for jihad is multiplied seven hundredfold, and from that is the sound hadith." This is the end of what he mentioned.

It has been said: this number was singled out because seven is the largest of the units within ten, seventy is the largest of the units within a hundred, and seven hundred is the largest of the units within a thousand. The Arabs often observe these numbers. God, exalted, says: ﴿seven ears﴾ and ﴿seven nights﴾ [al-Ḥāqqa 69:7], "seven ears" (sabʿ sunbulāt), ﴿seven cows﴾ [Yūsuf 12:43], ﴿seven heavens﴾ [al-Baqara 2:29], ﴿seven years﴾ [Yūsuf 12:47], ﴿if you ask forgiveness for them seventy times﴾ [al-Tawba 9:80], ﴿its measure is seventy cubits﴾ [al-Ḥāqqa 69:32]. In the hadith: "to seven hundredfold," "to seven thousand," and "to that which none but God can count."

Here the specification (tamyīz, the noun clarifying the number) comes in a plural form that has no singular counterpart in the units. In Sūrat Yūsuf it comes with the sound plural ending in alif and tāʾ in His saying: ﴿and seven green ears﴾ [Yūsuf 12:43]. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you ask: why was it not said 'sabʿa sunbulāt' in its proper form of specification for the paucal plural (jamʿ al-qilla), as He said: ﴿and seven green ears﴾?" I say: this is because, when the forms of the plural were mentioned at His saying: ﴿three periods﴾ [al-Baqara 2:228], their places were interchangeable. This is the end of his words.

So this is treated as a matter of extension (ittisāʿ), with one of the two plurals placed in the position of the other by way of metaphor, since its proper form was to be specified by the paucal plural, because seven is among the smallest numbers. But what al-Zamakhsharī said is not absolute. We say: the sound plural with wāw and nūn, or with alif and tāʾ, is not used to specify numbers from three to ten unless that singular has no plural other than this one, or unless it is adjacent to something for which this plural was not used. An example of the first is His saying: ﴿seven heavens﴾ [al-Baqara 2:29], for the canopy of this heaven has no plural other than this one. As for the poet's words:

"Above seven skies (samāʾiyyā)"

they have stated that this is anomalous. And His saying: ﴿seven cows﴾ [Yūsuf 12:43], ﴿nine signs﴾ [al-Isrāʾ 17:101], and "five prayers" (khams ṣalawāt), because cow, sign and prayer have no plural other than this one, and they are not pluralized in any other form.

An example of the second is His saying: ﴿and seven green ears﴾ [Yūsuf 12:43], when it was joined by conjunction to ﴿seven cows﴾ [Yūsuf 12:43] and was adjacent to it, so its sound plural with alif and tāʾ was good. Had it not been conjoined and not adjacent, it would have been "sabʿa sanābil," as in this verse. For this reason, when it is free of an adjacent word, it comes in the form mafāʿil for the most part and preferably, although it may be pluralized with alif and tāʾ. An example of that is His saying: ﴿seven paths﴾ [al-Muʾminūn 23:17] and ﴿seven nights﴾ [al-Ḥāqqa 69:7], and He did not say "ṭarīqāt" or "laylāt," although it is permissible in the plural of ṭarīqa and layla. And His saying: ﴿ten needy persons﴾ [al-Māʾida 5:89], although it is permissible for its plural to be a sound plural, so you say "miskīnūn" and "miskīnīn." They have preferred, over the sound plural, a form of the plurals of multitude that does not resemble mafāʿil. And if there is no adjacent word whose similarity is intended, as in His saying: ﴿eight years﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ 28:27], although it is permissible for it to be pluralized with alif and tāʾ, because its singular is ḥijja, so you say ḥajjāt.

Based on what has been established: when a noun has two plurals, a sound plural (jamʿ taṣḥīḥ) and a broken plural (jamʿ taksīr), the broken plural is either a plural of multitude (kathra) or of paucity (qilla). If it is of multitude, it is either of the mafāʿil pattern or not. If it is of the mafāʿil pattern, it is preferred over the sound plural, so you say: "Three ḥamāmid came to me" (ahāmid) and "three Zaynabs" (zaynab). Use of the sound plural for paucity is permissible, so you say: "Three aḥāmid came to me" and "three Zaynabāt." If it is not of the mafāʿil pattern, then either the sound plural and the plural of multitude are both frequent for it or not. If not, the sound plural is not permitted, nor the plural of multitude except rarely. An example: "Three zuyūd came to me," "three hunūd," "I have three afluss," and it is not permitted to say "three Zaydīn," nor "three Hindāt," nor "three fulūs," except rarely.

And if the sound plural and the plural of multitude are both rare for it, the sound plural and the broken plural of paucity are preferred. An example: "three suʿādāt," "three shusūʿ," and it is permitted for paucity: "three saʿāʾid," and "three ashsuʿ."

From what we have established it is clear that His saying: ﴿seven ears﴾ (sabʿa sanābil) came according to what is established in Arabic grammar as a finite plural (jamʿ mutanāhī), and that His saying: "seven green ears" (sabʿ sunbulāt) was permitted only for the sake of harmony with ﴿seven cows﴾ and its adjacency. Therefore al-Zamakhsharī's excuse is not valid.

﴿in every ear﴾ (fī kulli sunbula) is in the position of a qualifier to (sanābil), so it is in the genitive position, or to (sabʿa), so it is in the accusative position. In both cases ﴿a hundred﴾ (miʾatu) is nominative as the subject (fāʿil), because the preposition-phrase has relied on being its qualifier, and this is better than its being nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtadaʾ), with (fī kulli) as its predicate (khabar), and the clause being a qualifier. This is because qualifying with a single word is preferable to qualifying with a clause. But an omitted element must be assumed: i.e., "in every ear of them," meaning of the ears.

It is read irregularly (shādhdhan): "miʾata ḥabba" in the accusative, with the verb assumed as (akhrajat) "produced." Ibn ʿAṭiyya assumed (anbatat) "caused to grow," and the pronoun refers to the grain (ḥabba). It was also permitted that it be accusative as an apposition (badal) of ﴿seven ears﴾. But there is a problem with this: it cannot be a total apposition of a total, because ﴿a hundred grains﴾ is not the same as ﴿seven ears﴾. Nor can it be a partial apposition of a whole, because there is no pronoun in the apposition referring back to the element it replaces. And ﴿a hundred grains﴾ is not a part of ﴿seven ears﴾, because what is contained is not a part of the container, and the ear is the container of the grain. Do you not see His saying: ﴿in every ear a hundred grains﴾? Nor can it be an apposition of inclusion (badal ishtimāl), because a pronoun does not return from the apposition to the element it replaces, and because what contains a hundred grains is one ear of the seven ears. Unless it is said that what contains the thing that contains something is itself containing that thing, and the ear contains the seven ears; so the seven contain the grain of the ear. If you assume in the sentence an omitted element, namely "it produced the grain of seven ears," then ﴿a hundred grains﴾ may be a partial apposition of a whole, with (ḥabb) omitted and (sabʿ) put in its place. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿a hundred grains﴾ is the known numeral, but it may be intended as a figure of abundance, as if it were said: "in every ear there is much grain," because the Arabs use "a hundred" for abundance. A similar usage has been mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿and they were thousands, fleeing from death﴾ [al-Baqara 2:243].

It has been said: in this verse there is evidence that cultivating crops is among the best of the livelihoods people pursue, and for this reason God struck the parable with it in His saying: ﴿the parable of those who spend their wealth﴾ [al-Baqara 2:261], and so on.

In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim: "No Muslim plants a tree or sows a crop, and a bird or a person or an animal eats from it, but it is for him a charity" (ṣadaqa). In another narration: "And whatever is taken from it is a charity." In al-Tirmidhī: "Seek provision in the hidden places of the earth," meaning crops. Some of them said, when a man said to him: "Direct me to a work I can practise":

"Seek the hidden places of the earth, and call upon its Master, perhaps one day you will be answered and provided for."

Farming is among the communal obligations (furūḍ al-kifāya), so some people are compelled to it if they agree to abandon it.

﴿And God multiplies for whom He wills﴾: i.e., this multiplication; since there is no multiplication beyond seven hundred. It has been said: He multiplies more than this number. It was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that the multiplication reaches for whomever God wills to two thousand thousand. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "This is not a sound chain of narration from him." This is the end of his words. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: He multiplies up to thousands of thousands. Abū Ḥātim, in his Ṣaḥīḥ called (al-Taqāsīm wa al-Anwāʿ), related from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: "When the verse ﴿the parable of those who spend their wealth in the way of God﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'My Lord, increase my ummah!' Then there was revealed: ﴿Only those who are patient will be given their reward without reckoning﴾ [al-Zumar 39:10]." In Sunan al-Nasāʾī there is something close to this, except that it mentions between the two verses the revelation of ﴿Who is it that will lend God a goodly loan, so He may multiply it for him many times over﴾ [al-Baqara 2:245].

His saying ﴿for whom He wills﴾ means: for whom He wills the multiplication. In it there is evidence that this is subject to God's will and His desire. al-Zamakhsharī said: "That is, He multiplies that multiplication, not for every spender, because of the differences in the states of the spenders; or He multiplies the seven hundred and increases upon it many times over for whoever deserves that." This is the end of his words. His saying "for whoever deserves that" contains a trace of the Muʿtazila (dasīsat al-iʿtizāl).

﴿And God is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾: i.e., All-Encompassing in giving, All-Knowing of the intention. It has been said: All-Encompassing in power to reward, All-Knowing of the measures of what is spent and of the reward that results from it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 262:

﴿Those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah, then do not follow what they have spent with reminders of their generosity or with injury,﴾. It was said: it was revealed concerning Uthman. It was said: concerning Ali. It was said: concerning Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf and Uthman. Ibn Awf came during the expedition of Tabuk with four thousand dirhams and left the same amount with [the Prophet]. Uthman came with a thousand camels, with their saddles and their horse-cloths, and he gave in charity the well of Rumah, which had belonged to him, for the benefit of the Muslims. It was also said: Uthman came with a thousand dinars and poured them into the lap of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When the Exalted compared the attribute of the one who spends in the way of Allah to the sower of a grain that brings forth, [so that] the multiplication of his good deeds is like the abundance of what the grain produces, and this was in general terms, He clarified in this verse that this [reward] applies only to the one who does not follow his spending with reminders of generosity or with injury, because these two nullify charity, as the Exalted informed in the verse after this. Rather, the aspect of entitlement is observed, with no recompense from the giver to the recipient and no thanks owed to him, so that his intention is purely for the Face of Allah, the Exalted. If he seeks by his spending thanks and praise, he is one who seeks reputation and show (riya'). If he seeks a return, he is a profit-seeking merchant who deserves neither praise nor thanks. Reminding of generosity (al-mann) is among the major sins. It is established in (Sahih Muslim) and elsewhere that it is one of: "the three whom Allah will not look at, nor purify, and for whom there is a painful punishment." In al-Nasa'i: "Three will not enter Paradise: the one who disobeys his parents, the habitual drinker of wine, and the one who reminds of what he has given."

In His saying ﴿then do not follow﴾, after His saying ﴿in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 261], there is an indication that the expenditure proceeds in the way of Allah, and then something follows it that nullifies it, namely reminding of generosity and injury. This has been made clear in the verse after it. So [the acceptance of the charity] is conditional, meaning its acceptance depends on a condition, which is that one does not follow it with reminders or injury. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that reminding and injury come from the giver to the recipient, whether that spending is in jihad, by way of equipping or assisting in it, or outside jihad, and whether the giver is a fighter or not. Ibn Zayd said: it concerns those who do not go out to jihad but spend while sitting at home, whereas the verse before it concerns those who go out with their selves and their wealth. For this reason the condition was placed on these and not on the former. "Injury" includes reminding and other things. Reminding was specifically mentioned and placed first because it occurs most often from the one who gives. Among reminding is that he says: "I have been good to you and supported you," or similar. Or he speaks of what he gave, so that it reaches the recipient and injures him. Among injury is that he curses the recipient, or complains about him, or says: "How persistent you are! Allah has delivered us from you, and you always come to me." Or he imposes on him the obligation to acknowledge what he conferred upon him. It was also said: injury is that he mentions his giving in the presence of someone who does not like that person to know of it. Zayd ibn Aslam said: if you think that your greeting is burdensome to the one you spent upon, while you seek the Face of Allah, then do not greet him. A woman said to him: "O Abu Usamah, direct me to a man who gives a right portion in the way of Allah, for they give only fruits. I have some hungry and ailing family members." He said to her: "May Allah not bless your family members, your hunger and your illness, for you have injured them before you give to them." (p-307)

﴿For them is their reward with their Lord, and no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve.﴾ The explanation of this clause has already been given, so it is not repeated. ﴿Those who spend﴾ is a mubtada' (subject), and the clause ﴿for them is their reward﴾ is the khabar (predicate). The subject was not made to carry the meaning of a conditional noun (ism al-shart), so the fa' (the particle of consequence) did not enter the predicate. The absence of this embedding here is because this clause explains the clause before it, and the clause before it was presented as a fixed, established matter already settled, namely the attribution of their spending to the grain described, which is a metaphor for the attainment of a great reward. So this clause came likewise. The subject and predicate in both were presented as a firm and established matter, not one whose predicate needs to attach entitlement to the occurrence of what precedes it. This differs from when the fa' enters, since it indicates that the predicate follows from the subject and that the subject is entitled to it by reason of that.

It was said: ﴿those who spend﴾ is the khabar of a deleted mubtada', its estimate being: "they are the ones who spend," and ﴿for them is their reward﴾ is in the position of a hal (circumstantial clause). This is weak, I mean making ﴿for them is their reward﴾ a hal. Rather, when ﴿those who spend﴾ is parsed as the khabar of a deleted mubtada', it is better for ﴿for them is their reward﴾ to be a fresh, independent clause, as if it were an answer to one who asks: "Do they have a reward? And with whom is their reward?" So it is said: ﴿for them is their reward with their Lord﴾. He joined it with thumma (then), which implies a interval, because one who spends in the way of Allah, in an apparent manner, does not generally reach reminding and injury immediately. Rather, if his intention was other than the Face of Allah, he would not remind or injure at once. So thumma entered for the sake of what is usual. The rule for reminding and injury, which follow the spending and accompany it, is the rule of what comes later.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning of thumma is to show the difference between the spending and the abandonment of reminding and injury, and that abandoning them is better than the spending itself, just as he made steadfastness in faith better than entering into it, by His saying: ﴿then they remained steadfast﴾ [Fussilat: 30]. End of his words. This claim of the meaning of thumma by al-Zamakhshari has been repeated, and I know of no predecessor for him in it. We have already discussed this meaning with him before this. The ma in ﴿what they have spent﴾ is a relative pronoun (mawsul) whose returning pronoun is deleted, meaning: "what they have spent." It may also be a verbal-noun (masdariyyah) particle, meaning: "their spending." And a thumma is deleted, meaning: "reminding toward the recipient, nor injury to him." As for what some of them said, that ﴿and no injury﴾ is an attribute of the giver and is a fresh clause, as if he said: "those who spend and do not remind and are not hurt by the spending," this is remote. Likewise remote is what some of them said, that His saying ﴿no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾ does not refer to the Hereafter, and that the meaning is: the right of the one who spends in the way of Allah is that he should make his soul content with it, not let reminding follow it, not fear poverty that may reach him afterwards, but rather trust in the sufficiency of Allah and not grieve if poverty befalls him.

﴿Kind speech and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury﴾. That is: a graceful response from the one asked, and pardon from the petitioner when he finds in the one asked something that burdens him, such as insistence, abuse, or insinuated abuse, as is found in many beggars. It was also said: "forgiveness" means obtaining forgiveness from God through a graceful response. It was said: "forgiveness" means pardon from the side of the petitioner, because if he is answered graciously, he excuses him. It was said: "kind speech" is supplication, consolation, and encouraging trust in what is with God. It was said: it is supplicating for one's brother in his absence. It was said: enjoining what is right is better in reward with God than charity followed by injury. It was said: it is glorifications, supplication, praise, and saying "al-hamdu lillah." "Forgiveness" means concealing one's own state and refraining from displaying the sins one has committed. "Better" means lighter on the body than charity followed by injury. It was said: "forgiveness" is limiting oneself to good speech. It was said: "forgiveness" is that one asks God for forgiveness for a shortfall in giving and for failing to fill a need. It was said: "forgiveness" here is concealing the needy person's poverty and bad condition, as Ibn Jarir said. It was said: an Arab bedouin was asked, in eloquent speech, "Who is this man?" He said: "O God, forgiveness! Bad earnings prevent one from claiming lineage." It was said: it is concealing the petitioner's request, giving him one's face (i.e., attention and dignity), and not disgracing him. It was said: its meaning is safety from disobedience. It was said: "kind speech" is that you urge others to give to him. All of this is on the basis that the address is to the one asked, because the address in the verse before this, and in the verse after this, is to the giver. It was said: the address is to the petitioner, and it is an exhortation to him to be moderate in his request, i.e., he should speak a good word, by allusion to the request or by displaying wealth where there is no necessity, and thereby gain good better than a charity followed by injury. "Kind speech" and "forgiveness" share with charity followed by injury the general quality of being good, which is benefit, even though the direction of benefit differs. The benefit of kind speech and forgiveness remains, while the benefit of that charity passes away. It is possible that the goodness here is in the sense of the saying "something is better than nothing." A poet said:

"Your refusal of generosity with a beautiful word
is dearer to me than giving with reproach."

Another said, and excelled:

"If there is no wealth one day that I can bestow
on those who ask, then I am a pliant staff (i.e., humble and gentle).

The petitioners never lack goodness from my character:
either my gift, or else a good refusal."

"Kind speech" (qawlun) is raised as the mubtada' (subject of the nominal sentence). The subject being indefinite was permitted by its description. "Forgiveness" (maghfiratun) is conjoined to the subject, so it is also a mubtada', and what permits beginning with it is an omitted description, meaning: "and forgiveness from the one asked, or from the petitioner, or from God, according to the differing opinions." "Better" (khayrun) is the khabar (predicate) for both. Al-Mahdawi and others said: they are two separate sentences, and the khabar of "kind speech" is omitted, the estimate being: "kind speech is preferable, and forgiveness is better." Ibn 'Atiyya said: in this there is a loss of the beauty of meaning, since what is implied should be like what is stated. What he said is good. It is also permitted that "kind speech" is the khabar of an omitted mubtada', its estimate being: "What is commanded is kind speech." The mention of the reminder (al-mann) in His saying "followed by" (yatba'uhā) was not needed, because injury includes reminding and other things, as we have said.

﴿And God is Rich, Forbearing﴾. That is: He is rich, not in need of charity, and forbearing, delaying punishment. It was said: He is rich, having no need of a giver who reminds and injures, and forbearing, not hastening punishment. This is a display of His displeasure and a warning.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 264–265 (part 1 of 3):

﴿O you who believe, do not nullify your charities with reminders of your generosity or with injury, like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day.﴾ When He stipulated in spending that it not be followed by reminder (mann) or injury (adha), He did not suffice with that, but made reminder and injury nullifiers of the charity, and forbade nullifying it through them, in order to strengthen the believer's avoidance of them. For this reason He addressed them with the description of faith. When reminder and injury had been mentioned twice, He repeated them here with the definite article (al-). The verse indicates that reminder and injury nullify charity. The meaning of their nullifying it is that there is no reward for it with Allah. As-Suddi holds that bad deeds do not nullify good deeds. The majority of scholars said: the charity which Allah knows its giver reminds and injures with is not accepted. It was said: Allah has set for the angel over it a sign, so he does not record it, since his intention was not for the sake of Allah's countenance. The meaning of His words ﴿do not nullify your charities﴾ is: do not bring this deed as something void, because if it is intended for other than Allah's countenance, it has been brought in the manner of nullity. Qadi Abd al-Jabbar said: it is known that the charity has already occurred and passed, so it cannot be nullified; therefore what is meant is the nullifying of its reward, since the reward has not yet been obtained and is future, so its nullification becomes through what comes to it of reminder and injury. End of his words.

Both meanings are borne by the verse. To magnify the ugliness of reminder, Allah repeated it in various parts of the discourse: He first praised the one who abstains from it, then preferred withholding over a gift followed by reminder, second, and third explicitly forbade it, and He singled out charity for the prohibition, since reminder in it is greater and more heinous. The apparent meaning of His words "with reminder" (bil-mann) is reminding the poor person, which is the view of the majority. Ibn Abbas said: reminding Allah Most High because of one's charity, and injuring the beggar. The kaf (like) is said to be in the position of an adjective to a deleted verbal noun, its estimate being "nullification (ibtalan) like the nullification of the charity of one who spends." It was also said: the kaf is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: do not nullify while resembling one who spends his wealth by show-off.

Regarding this spender there are two views. The first: he is the hypocrite. Az-Zamakhshari mentioned no other: one who spends for reputation and so that it may be said he is generous and noble; this is his intention, he does not spend seeking the pleasure of Allah and the reward of the Hereafter, because inwardly he does not believe in Allah and the Last Day. It was also said: what is meant is the open disbeliever, whose spending is to hear people say "how generous and excellent he is," and he intends by his spending only praise of himself. Makki preferred the first view, on the grounds that He attributed show-off to him, and that is the act of the hypocrite who conceals his disbelief; as for the disbeliever, he has no show-off, since he is openly hostile to the religion and open about his disbelief. The accusative of (riy'a'a) is either as an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi) or a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause. Talha ibn Musarrif read (riyaa'a) by replacing the first hamza with a ya' because of the kasra before it, and it is related from Asim.

﴿So his likeness is like a smooth rock with dust on it; then a heavy rain strikes it and leaves it bare.﴾ This is a second simile. There is disagreement about the pronoun in His words "so his likeness" (famathaluhu). The apparent view is that it refers to ﴿like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people﴾, because of its proximity and because it is singular. Allah struck for this hypocrite who shows off, or the disbeliever who boasts, the likeness of a smooth rock with dust upon it, which the observer thinks is good, fertile soil. When a heavy rain strikes it, it removes the dust from it, leaving it bare and exposed, contrary to what the observer supposed. Likewise this hypocrite: people see that he has deeds, as dust is seen upon this rock; but when the Day of Resurrection comes, they dissolve and become void, just as the rain removed what was on the rock of dust. It was also said: the pronoun in "so his likeness" refers to the one who reminds and injures, and that he is compared to two things: first, to one who spends his wealth to be seen by people; second, to a smooth rock with dust on it. In this case there is a shift from address to third person and from plural to singular.

Qadi Abd al-Jabbar said: Allah Most High mentioned two likenesses for the manner in which charity is nullified by reminder and injury. He first likened it to one who spends his wealth to be seen by people, who is also a disbeliever who does not believe in Allah and the Last Day, because the nullification of the spending of this disbelieving show-off is more evident than the nullification of the reward of the charity of one who follows it with reminder and injury. Then He likened it secondly to the rock on which dust and dirt has settled; then when a strong rain strikes it, it removes that dust from it until it is as though there were no dust or dirt on it at all. He said: just as the rain removed the dust that had settled on the rock, so reminder and injury must nullify the reward of spending after it has occurred. This is the plain statement regarding nullifying and expiating. End of his words. This rests on what we previously cited from him concerning the discussion of nullification and expiation in His words ﴿do not nullify your charities﴾, namely that the charity occurred validly and then was nullified by reminder and injury. The statement was also made that the meaning is: do not bring them about as void. This meaning is indicated by the simile in His words ﴿like one who spends﴾, for his spending occurred void because disbelief accompanied it, so it is impossible for it to exist validly. As for the second simile, according to Abd al-Jabbar and his companions, He made the rain removing that dust after it had settled on it, so likewise reminder and injury remove the reward after its entitlement has come about. According to others, the thing likened to the dust settled on the rock is the charity accompanied by corrupt intention, which, were it not for that, the charity would have had as its consequence the attainment of reward and recompense. It was said: this meaning is preferable, because when dust settles on a rock it is not stuck to it nor sunk into it; it appears connected to the eye, but in reality it is separate. Likewise spending accompanied by reminder and injury appears outwardly as an act of righteousness, but in reality it is not so. On these two views the estimate is: do not nullify the rewards of your charities, or do not nullify the root of your charities.

Ibn al-Musayyab and az-Zuhri read (safwan) with a fatha on the fa'. It was said: this is anomalous in nouns; its pattern is verbal nouns like (ghalayan) and (nazawan), and in adjectives such as "a man ṣayḥan" and "a goat 'udwan." (Turab) is nominative as the subject: dust settled upon it. "Then a heavy rain struck it" (fa-asabahu wabil) is conjoined to that verb which raised the dust. The pronoun in "fa-asabahu" refers to the rock, and it may refer to the dust. In "fa-tarakahu" it refers to the rock. In this sentence the apparent act is made like the dust, the reminding injurer or the hypocrite is like the rock, and the Day of Resurrection is like the heavy rain. According to the Mu'tazila: reminder and injury are like the heavy rain.

Al-Qaffal said: there is another possibility, namely that the deeds of servants are stored treasures for them on the Day of Resurrection. Whoever acts with sincerity is like one who casts a seed into good soil, so it multiplies for him and grows. Do you not see that He struck the likeness of this with a garden on a height? He finds it at the time he needs it. As for the reminder, the injurer and the hypocrite, they are like one who sows seed on rock which accepts no seed and in which nothing grows; upon it is a little dust which a downpour struck, so it remained an empty receptacle for seed, and when there is need for planting he finds nothing in it. End of the summary of his words. Its essence is that the simile implicitly contains seed and crop in meaning.

﴿They have no power over anything of what they have earned.﴾ There is disagreement about the pronoun in (yaqdiruna). It was said: it refers to the addressees in ﴿do not nullify your charities﴾, and it is an iltifat (shift), since it moves from address to third person. The meaning would be: if you do that, you will not be able to benefit from anything you have earned. This is far-fetched. It was said: it refers to the one who spends, since (ka-alladhi) is a genus, so you may observe its wording as in His words ﴿spends his wealth to be seen by people and does not believe﴾, where the pronoun is singular, and you may observe its meaning, since its meaning is plural. This is like ﴿like the likeness of one who kindled a fire, and when it lit up what was around him﴾ [al-Baqarah 17], then He said ﴿Allah took away their light﴾ [al-Baqarah 17]. Ibn Atiyya said: the discourse was previously carried by the wording of alladhi, and this is the usual course of Arabic speech; if it had been first carried by meaning, it would have been ugly afterward to carry it by wording. End of his words. We have previously discussed this with him in part of this, and on carrying by wording or by meaning there is detail found only in the extended books of grammar.

It was said: it refers to a known thing not mentioned in meaning: no one of creation has power to benefit from that seed cast in that dust upon the rock, because that dust has gone and what was in it has gone; likewise the reminder, the injurer and the hypocrite: none of them benefits from his deed on the Day of Resurrection. It was said: it refers to the show-off disbeliever or the hypocrite, or to the one who reminds; that is, they have no power to benefit from the reward of any of their spending, which is their earnings at the time of their need for it. They expressed spending by earning because they intended by it gain. This is like His words Exalted be He: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan 23], and His words ﴿Their deeds are like ashes which the wind blew hard upon on a stormy day﴾ [Ibrahim 18], and His words ﴿Their deeds are like a mirage in a level plain﴾ [al-Nur 39]. The hadith of the three who will be first judged on the Day of Resurrection suffices as mention of deeds done for other than Allah's countenance: the martyr, the scholar, and the generous giver.

﴿And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.﴾ That is, those who persist in disbelief; He does not guide them in their disbelief, rather it is pure misguidance; or He does not guide them in their deeds while they remain in disbelief. In this there is a preference for the one who said that the striking of the likeness refers to the disbeliever.

﴿And the likeness of those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of Allah and firming up from their own souls is like a garden on a height.﴾ When He struck the likeness of one who spent his wealth to be seen by people while not believing, He mentioned its opposite through a sensible image for the mind, so that the hearer may imagine the difference between the two opposites. This is among the wondrous methods of the eloquence of the Qur'an. When He described the one who spends with two attributes, He matched that here with two attributes: His words ﴿seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾ correspond to His words ﴿to be seen by people﴾, and His words ﴿and firming up from their own souls﴾ correspond to His words ﴿and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾, because firming (tathbit) means settling the soul upon preserving it and abandoning what corrupts it, and this arises only from certainty about the Hereafter. The three estimates found in His words ﴿the likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a grain﴾ [al-Baqarah 261] apply here too, namely: the likeness of the hypocrites is like the likeness of one who plants a grain; or the likeness of their spending is like a grain; or the likeness of the spenders and their spending is like the likeness of a grain and its planter. They permitted, regarding (ibtighaa'), that it be a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning "seeking," and that it be an object of purpose; likewise (wa-tathbitan).

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is not correct for (ibtighā'a) to be a maf'ul li-ajlihi (object of purpose), because it is coordinated with (wa-tathbītan) [and to make certain]. Nor is it correct for (wa-tathbītan) to be a maf'ul li-ajlihi, because spending is not for the sake of making certain. Makki said in (al-Mushkil): "Both are objects of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi)," but this is refuted by what we have explained. End of his words.

Tathbīt is a verbal noun (maṣdar) of thabata, and it is transitive. It is possible that the object is omitted, its implied sense being "the reward from God," meaning: "and making certain and securing for themselves the reward for that expenditure." In that case, making certain the reward and securing it from God becomes a motive for spending in the way of God. Whoever estimates the object to be other than this, i.e. "and making certain from their own selves their deeds through sincerity of intention," and takes "from themselves" to mean "min" in the sense of "lam" (for), i.e. "for their own selves," as one says: "I did that as a breaking of my desire," meaning "for my desire," then it is not clear that it is in the accusative as an object of purpose.

Ash-Sha'bi, Qatada, as-Suddi, Abu Salih and Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is "and certainty" (tayaqqun), i.e. their souls have firmly established insights, so they make them steadfast in spending. This is reinforced by the reading of one who recited (wa-tabyīnan min anfusihim) ["and clarification from their souls"]. Qatada also said: "and seeking reward (ihtisab) from their souls." Ash-Sha'bi, ad-Dahhak and al-Kalbi also said: "and affirmation (taṣdīq)," i.e. they pay zakat good-heartedly. Ibn Jubayr and Abu Malik said: "verification (taḥqīq) in their religion." Ibn Kaysan said: "sincerity and firmly establishing their souls in obedience to God in their expenditures." Az-Zajjaj said: "and being convinced when they spend that it is something for which God rewards." Ash-Sha'bi also said: "resolve (azm)." Yaman said: "insight (basīrah)." Mujahid and al-Hasan said: its meaning is that they "make firm" (yuthbitūn), i.e. they place their charities. Al-Hasan said: "A man, when he intended to give charity, would deliberate; if it was for God he would carry it out, and if doubt mixed with it, he would withhold."

Some Egyptian grammarians permitted that his words "wa-tathbītan" mean "tathabbutan" (deliberation), so it would be intransitive. He said: maṣdars may differ and some may take the place of others, and from this is His saying: ﴿And devote yourself to Him with devotion﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 8], i.e. "tabattul" (devotion). This view was rejected on the ground that this is not the case with a preceding verb in the manner of the verse. As for the verbal noun coming without being formed from a mentioned verb, it is not interpreted as other than its own verb which it has originally. You say: if the intransitive verb thabata means "to be established, to take firm root, to be confirmed and to remain," its causative form by doubling (taḍ'īf) means "to establish and to confirm."

Ibn Rawaha addressed the Messenger of God ﷺ:
"God has established what He gave you of goodness, the establishing of Jesus, and a victory like that with which they were victorious."

So the meaning, and God knows best, is that they establish themselves, from their own selves, in faith through this deed, which is the giving out of wealth, which is the counterpart of the soul, in the way of God seeking His pleasure; for such a deed is hard upon the soul, so they act to make the soul firm in faith, and what you hope from God through this difficult deed; for when it stands firm in a difficult matter, it submits and becomes humbled to it. If the establishing is attributed to them, then (min) is in the accusative position, connected to the verbal noun itself, and it is partitive, like its use in: "he shook from his flank" and "he stirred from his vigour." If the establishing is attributed in meaning to their souls, then (min) is also in the accusative position as a qualifier of the verbal noun, its implied sense being: "existing from their own selves."

Az-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: what is the meaning of the partitive? I say: its meaning is that whoever spends his wealth for the sake of God has established part of his self, and whoever spends his wealth and his soul together is the one who has established all of it: ﴿and strive in the way of God with your wealth and your selves﴾ [as-Saff: 11]. End of his words.

Apparently, his self is what establishes him and carries him to spend in the way of God; there is no motivator for him but it, because of what it has believed of faith and abundant reward. It is what prompts him to that, and what makes him firm through the goodness of its faith and the sublimity of its conviction.

Asim al-Jahdari read (ka-mathali ḥabbatin) with a ḥā'. The bā' in (bi-rabwatin) is locative (ẓarfiyyah), and it is in the position of a qualifier, so it is linked to an omitted element. He specified the rabwah for the goodness of its trees and the purity of its fruit, as the poet said, and he is al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, may God have mercy on him:
"It rose above the dew of the depths and sank low, out of reach of the thirsty, and it was content with its own watering.
So the peach and pomegranate inclined beneath it, and the date palm and olive enveloped its upper parts."

The tafsir of Ibn 'Abbas: the rabwah is an elevated place where rivers do not flow; he means the one mentioned in His saying: ﴿a heavy rain struck it﴾, which indicates that there is no running water in it. He did not mean that the species of rabwah has no running water, do you not see His saying: ﴿to a height with a place of settlement and a spring﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 50]. It was singled out because its watering is by heavy rain and not by running water, according to the custom of Arab lands, by what they perceive as abundant.

Abu 'Abdullah Muhammad ibn 'Umar al-Razi said: The exegetes said: a garden on a rabwah is better and yields more produce. About this I have a difficulty, for it is above the water, the rivers do not rise to it, and the winds strike it frequently, so its produce is not good; and if it is in a depression, waters pour into it and the traces of the winds do not reach it, so its produce is also not good; its produce is good only in level land. So the intended sense of rabwah is not what they mentioned, but rather that the land is good, such that when rain falls upon it, it swells and grows, so its produce increases and its trees become complete in it. This is supported by His saying: ﴿and you see the earth lifeless﴾ [al-Hajj: 5], and by the fact that it is in contrast to the first parable, the first (the smooth rock) not being affected by rain. End of his words. There is some abridgement in it, and what he said was said before him by al-Hasan. The rabwah is level land that does not rise above water. The poet said about the gardens of al-Hazn:
"No garden of the gardens of al-Hazn is green with plants, a green meadow upon which a heavy rain has poured."
What is not meant by the gardens of al-Hazn is the gardens of the elevated ground, as at-Tabari claimed; rather, the gardens of al-Hazn are those ascribed to Najd, and Najd is also called al-Hazn. The garden was ascribed to al-Hazn, which is Najd, because its vegetation is more fragrant, its breeze cooler and finer, so it is better than the gardens of Tihama.

Ibn 'Amir and Asim read (rabwatin) with a fatha on the rā', and the rest of the seven with a ḍamma. Their disagreement is similar in (qad aflaḥa) [al-Mu'minun: 1]. Ibn 'Abbas read with a kasra on the rā'. Abu Ja'far and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read (birabāwatin) on the pattern of kara-hah. Abu al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli read (ribāwatin) on the pattern of risalah.

﴿A heavy rain struck it﴾ is a clause in the position of a qualifier of "garden." The qualifier by the prepositional phrase was mentioned first, then the qualifier by clause; this is the more common usage in the language of the Arabs. The stable qualifier, that it is "on a rabwah," was mentioned first, then the accidental qualifier, ﴿a heavy rain struck it﴾. In describing the smooth rock, His saying ﴿upon it is dust﴾ came, then it was coordinated to it with "fa," but here it was not coordinated; rather it was brought out as a qualifier. One should consider what the difference is between the two places. It is also permissible that ﴿a heavy rain struck it﴾ be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of "garden," since it is indefinite, and it has been qualified as a circumstance of the pronoun in the prepositional phrase.

﴿So it brought forth its produce twofold﴾: "brought forth" (ātat) means "gave," and the first object is omitted; the estimate is: "so it gave its owner, or its people, its produce," just as it is omitted in His saying ﴿like the likeness of a garden﴾, i.e. the owner or planter of a garden, and because the intention is the mention of what bears fruit, not of whom it bears fruit, since that is known. The accusative of (ḍi'fayn) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). Whoever claims that (ḍi'fayn) is a second object of (ātat) has erred, and the meaning is not that. Likewise the claim of one who says that (ātat) means "brought out," and that it takes only one object, since that is not known in the language of the Arabs. Attributing the giving to it is a metaphor. (Al-'Ukul), with a ḍamma on the hamza, is the thing eaten, and here is meant the fruit. Its annexation to "the garden" is an annexation of specification, like the saddle of the beast, since fruit is not something the garden owns. The two Harams (Ibn Kathir and Nafi') and Abu 'Amr read it with a ḍamma on the hamza and a sukun on the kaf, and likewise every noun annexed to a feminine noun; Abu 'Amr transmitted this for what is annexed to a non-pronominal noun or to a masculine pronoun. The rest read it with tashdid.

The meaning of (ḍi'fayn) is twice what it used to produce because of the heavy rain and because it is on a rabwah, since the produce of elevated ground is greater and further from flood and hail. It was said: twice that of other lands; it was said: four times their amount. This is based on the view that the double of a thing is its two equals. Abu Muslim said: three times their amount. Taj al-Qurra' said: there is no basis for this in Arabic, and the giving of double is within one load. Ikrimah and 'Ata' said: the meaning of "twofold" is that it bore fruit twice in the year. In my view, it is possible that His saying (ḍi'fayn) is of that kind which is not increased by doubling a single unit, but is a comparison intended for multiplication, as if it were said: "it brought forth its produce twofold," meaning twofold after twofold, i.e. many multiples. This is more eloquent in comparing the expenditure to the garden, because the good deed does not receive the reward of two good deeds, but is multiplied many times, ten times its like, and seven hundred times and more.

﴿But if a heavy rain does not strike it, then a light rain﴾: Ibn 'Isa said: there is an ellipsis here; the estimate is: "if a heavy rain does not come upon it," as the poet said:
"When we are traced in lineage, a base woman did not bear me."
That is, she did not bear me. The meaning: the light rain suffices for it and takes the place of the heavy rain in bringing forth its fruit twofold, and that is the most noble and best of land, so its fruit does not diminish with the lack of rain. It was also said: the meaning is that if a heavy rain does not strike it, its fruit is doubled, and if a light rain strikes it, it brings forth less than it brings with the heavy rain; in every state it is not without bearing fruit. Al-Mawardi said: the crop of light rain is weaker than the crop of rain and less in produce, but in it, though little, there is steadiness and benefit. End of his words.

The claim of inversion (taqdim and ta'khir) in the verse, as some have said, that the meaning is: "a heavy rain struck it, and if a heavy rain did not strike it, then a light rain; so it brought forth its produce twofold," so that its bringing forth of the produce twofold is made to apply to both states, of the heavy rain and the light rain, is unnecessary; and inversion is among the necessities of poetry, so the Qur'an is to be exonerated from that.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: the land struck by the parable is the land of Egypt: if no rain reaches it, it is fertile, and if rain reaches it, it doubles. Az-Zamakhshari said: He likened their state before God to the garden on the rabwah, and their expenditure, much or little, to the heavy rain and the light rain. Just as each of the two rains doubles the produce of the garden, so their expenditure, whether much or little, after it is sought for the face of God and effort is exerted in it, is pure before God, increasing their nearness and the goodness of their state with Him. End of his words. Al-Mawardi said, close to the words of az-Zamakhshari: He intended by this parable that abundant righteousness is like the crop of the heavy rain, abundant in benefit, and little righteousness is like the crop of light rain, little in benefit; so one should not abandon little righteousness if one does not do much of it, just as one does not abandon the crop of light rain when one is not able to have the crop of heavy rain. End of his words.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: He likened the growth of the expenditures of these sincere people, whose charities Allah causes to flourish, to the rearing of the young camel (faṣīl) and the foal (falw), to the growth of the plants of this garden on the elevated ground described, unlike the smooth rock (ṣafwān) from which its soil has been stripped away, so that it remains bare and barren.

Ibn al-Jawzī said: The meaning of the verse is that the owner of this garden does not suffer loss, for if light rain (ṭall) reaches it, it thrives, and if heavy rain (wābil) reaches it, it doubles its yield. Likewise is the expenditure of the sincere believer. End of quotation. His statement "fa-ṭallun" (then light rain) is the response (jawāb) to the conditional, so it requires an estimated element that turns it into a complete sentence. Al-Mubarrad estimated it as a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, because the meaning indicates it, that is: then light rain is what reaches it. He began with the indefinite noun because it came in the response to the condition. Some scholars mentioned that this is among the things that permit beginning with an indefinite noun, and similar to it is what occurs in the proverb: "If a caravan (ʿīr) goes, another caravan is in the tether."

Others than al-Mubarrad estimated it as the predicate of an omitted subject, that is: so what reaches it is light rain, or so its reacher is light rain. Some estimated it as the agent (fāʿil), that is: so light rain reaches it. All these estimations are permissible. The last one, however, requires omitting the whole clause that serves as the response and retaining a complement for part of it, because whenever the fāʾ (fa) enters upon a present-tense verb, it is with an omitted subject, as in the saying of God Most High: ﴿And whoever returns, Allah will take retribution from him﴾ [al-Māʾida: 95], meaning: so He takes retribution. Likewise, this estimation is needed here, meaning: so it (i.e., the garden) is reached by light rain. As for the two previous estimations, only the omission of one of the two parts of the sentence is needed.

A parallel to what occurs in the verse is the saying of the poet:
"Unless there are camels, then goats, whose horns of their heads are like sticks."

﴿And Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾. Al-Zuhrī read it with the yāʾ (ya-taʿmalūn, "they do"), so its apparent meaning is that the pronoun refers to the hypocrites, but it may be general, not restricted to the hypocrites, referring to all people. The majority read it with the tāʾ (ta-taʿmalūn, "you do"), in address, and in it there is an iltifāt (shift of grammatical person). The meaning: nothing of the deeds and intentions, whether of showing off or of sincerity, is hidden from Him, and in it is both a promise and a warning.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 264–265 (part 1 of 3):

﴿O you who believe, do not nullify your charities with reminders of your generosity or with injury, like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day.﴾ When He stipulated in spending that it not be followed by reminder (mann) or injury (adha), He did not suffice with that, but made reminder and injury nullifiers of the charity, and forbade nullifying it through them, in order to strengthen the believer's avoidance of them. For this reason He addressed them with the description of faith. When reminder and injury had been mentioned twice, He repeated them here with the definite article (al-). The verse indicates that reminder and injury nullify charity. The meaning of their nullifying it is that there is no reward for it with Allah. As-Suddi holds that bad deeds do not nullify good deeds. The majority of scholars said: the charity which Allah knows its giver reminds and injures with is not accepted. It was said: Allah has set for the angel over it a sign, so he does not record it, since his intention was not for the sake of Allah's countenance. The meaning of His words ﴿do not nullify your charities﴾ is: do not bring this deed as something void, because if it is intended for other than Allah's countenance, it has been brought in the manner of nullity. Qadi Abd al-Jabbar said: it is known that the charity has already occurred and passed, so it cannot be nullified; therefore what is meant is the nullifying of its reward, since the reward has not yet been obtained and is future, so its nullification becomes through what comes to it of reminder and injury. End of his words.

Both meanings are borne by the verse. To magnify the ugliness of reminder, Allah repeated it in various parts of the discourse: He first praised the one who abstains from it, then preferred withholding over a gift followed by reminder, second, and third explicitly forbade it, and He singled out charity for the prohibition, since reminder in it is greater and more heinous. The apparent meaning of His words "with reminder" (bil-mann) is reminding the poor person, which is the view of the majority. Ibn Abbas said: reminding Allah Most High because of one's charity, and injuring the beggar. The kaf (like) is said to be in the position of an adjective to a deleted verbal noun, its estimate being "nullification (ibtalan) like the nullification of the charity of one who spends." It was also said: the kaf is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: do not nullify while resembling one who spends his wealth by show-off.

Regarding this spender there are two views. The first: he is the hypocrite. Az-Zamakhshari mentioned no other: one who spends for reputation and so that it may be said he is generous and noble; this is his intention, he does not spend seeking the pleasure of Allah and the reward of the Hereafter, because inwardly he does not believe in Allah and the Last Day. It was also said: what is meant is the open disbeliever, whose spending is to hear people say "how generous and excellent he is," and he intends by his spending only praise of himself. Makki preferred the first view, on the grounds that He attributed show-off to him, and that is the act of the hypocrite who conceals his disbelief; as for the disbeliever, he has no show-off, since he is openly hostile to the religion and open about his disbelief. The accusative of (riy'a'a) is either as an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi) or a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause. Talha ibn Musarrif read (riyaa'a) by replacing the first hamza with a ya' because of the kasra before it, and it is related from Asim.

﴿So his likeness is like a smooth rock with dust on it; then a heavy rain strikes it and leaves it bare.﴾ This is a second simile. There is disagreement about the pronoun in His words "so his likeness" (famathaluhu). The apparent view is that it refers to ﴿like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people﴾, because of its proximity and because it is singular. Allah struck for this hypocrite who shows off, or the disbeliever who boasts, the likeness of a smooth rock with dust upon it, which the observer thinks is good, fertile soil. When a heavy rain strikes it, it removes the dust from it, leaving it bare and exposed, contrary to what the observer supposed. Likewise this hypocrite: people see that he has deeds, as dust is seen upon this rock; but when the Day of Resurrection comes, they dissolve and become void, just as the rain removed what was on the rock of dust. It was also said: the pronoun in "so his likeness" refers to the one who reminds and injures, and that he is compared to two things: first, to one who spends his wealth to be seen by people; second, to a smooth rock with dust on it. In this case there is a shift from address to third person and from plural to singular.

Qadi Abd al-Jabbar said: Allah Most High mentioned two likenesses for the manner in which charity is nullified by reminder and injury. He first likened it to one who spends his wealth to be seen by people, who is also a disbeliever who does not believe in Allah and the Last Day, because the nullification of the spending of this disbelieving show-off is more evident than the nullification of the reward of the charity of one who follows it with reminder and injury. Then He likened it secondly to the rock on which dust and dirt has settled; then when a strong rain strikes it, it removes that dust from it until it is as though there were no dust or dirt on it at all. He said: just as the rain removed the dust that had settled on the rock, so reminder and injury must nullify the reward of spending after it has occurred. This is the plain statement regarding nullifying and expiating. End of his words. This rests on what we previously cited from him concerning the discussion of nullification and expiation in His words ﴿do not nullify your charities﴾, namely that the charity occurred validly and then was nullified by reminder and injury. The statement was also made that the meaning is: do not bring them about as void. This meaning is indicated by the simile in His words ﴿like one who spends﴾, for his spending occurred void because disbelief accompanied it, so it is impossible for it to exist validly. As for the second simile, according to Abd al-Jabbar and his companions, He made the rain removing that dust after it had settled on it, so likewise reminder and injury remove the reward after its entitlement has come about. According to others, the thing likened to the dust settled on the rock is the charity accompanied by corrupt intention, which, were it not for that, the charity would have had as its consequence the attainment of reward and recompense. It was said: this meaning is preferable, because when dust settles on a rock it is not stuck to it nor sunk into it; it appears connected to the eye, but in reality it is separate. Likewise spending accompanied by reminder and injury appears outwardly as an act of righteousness, but in reality it is not so. On these two views the estimate is: do not nullify the rewards of your charities, or do not nullify the root of your charities.

Ibn al-Musayyab and az-Zuhri read (safwan) with a fatha on the fa'. It was said: this is anomalous in nouns; its pattern is verbal nouns like (ghalayan) and (nazawan), and in adjectives such as "a man ṣayḥan" and "a goat 'udwan." (Turab) is nominative as the subject: dust settled upon it. "Then a heavy rain struck it" (fa-asabahu wabil) is conjoined to that verb which raised the dust. The pronoun in "fa-asabahu" refers to the rock, and it may refer to the dust. In "fa-tarakahu" it refers to the rock. In this sentence the apparent act is made like the dust, the reminding injurer or the hypocrite is like the rock, and the Day of Resurrection is like the heavy rain. According to the Mu'tazila: reminder and injury are like the heavy rain.

Al-Qaffal said: there is another possibility, namely that the deeds of servants are stored treasures for them on the Day of Resurrection. Whoever acts with sincerity is like one who casts a seed into good soil, so it multiplies for him and grows. Do you not see that He struck the likeness of this with a garden on a height? He finds it at the time he needs it. As for the reminder, the injurer and the hypocrite, they are like one who sows seed on rock which accepts no seed and in which nothing grows; upon it is a little dust which a downpour struck, so it remained an empty receptacle for seed, and when there is need for planting he finds nothing in it. End of the summary of his words. Its essence is that the simile implicitly contains seed and crop in meaning.

﴿They have no power over anything of what they have earned.﴾ There is disagreement about the pronoun in (yaqdiruna). It was said: it refers to the addressees in ﴿do not nullify your charities﴾, and it is an iltifat (shift), since it moves from address to third person. The meaning would be: if you do that, you will not be able to benefit from anything you have earned. This is far-fetched. It was said: it refers to the one who spends, since (ka-alladhi) is a genus, so you may observe its wording as in His words ﴿spends his wealth to be seen by people and does not believe﴾, where the pronoun is singular, and you may observe its meaning, since its meaning is plural. This is like ﴿like the likeness of one who kindled a fire, and when it lit up what was around him﴾ [al-Baqarah 17], then He said ﴿Allah took away their light﴾ [al-Baqarah 17]. Ibn Atiyya said: the discourse was previously carried by the wording of alladhi, and this is the usual course of Arabic speech; if it had been first carried by meaning, it would have been ugly afterward to carry it by wording. End of his words. We have previously discussed this with him in part of this, and on carrying by wording or by meaning there is detail found only in the extended books of grammar.

It was said: it refers to a known thing not mentioned in meaning: no one of creation has power to benefit from that seed cast in that dust upon the rock, because that dust has gone and what was in it has gone; likewise the reminder, the injurer and the hypocrite: none of them benefits from his deed on the Day of Resurrection.
