It was said: it refers to the show-off disbeliever or the hypocrite, or to the one who reminds; that is, they have no power to benefit from the reward of any of their spending, which is their earnings at the time of their need for it. They expressed spending by earning because they intended by it gain. This is like His words Exalted be He: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan 23], and His words ﴿Their deeds are like ashes which the wind blew hard upon on a stormy day﴾ [Ibrahim 18], and His words ﴿Their deeds are like a mirage in a level plain﴾ [al-Nur 39]. The hadith of the three who will be first judged on the Day of Resurrection suffices as mention of deeds done for other than Allah's countenance: the martyr, the scholar, and the generous giver.

﴿And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.﴾ That is, those who persist in disbelief; He does not guide them in their disbelief, rather it is pure misguidance; or He does not guide them in their deeds while they remain in disbelief. In this there is a preference for the one who said that the striking of the likeness refers to the disbeliever.

﴿And the likeness of those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of Allah and firming up from their own souls is like a garden on a height.﴾ When He struck the likeness of one who spent his wealth to be seen by people while not believing, He mentioned its opposite through a sensible image for the mind, so that the hearer may imagine the difference between the two opposites. This is among the wondrous methods of the eloquence of the Qur'an. When He described the one who spends with two attributes, He matched that here with two attributes: His words ﴿seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾ correspond to His words ﴿to be seen by people﴾, and His words ﴿and firming up from their own souls﴾ correspond to His words ﴿and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾, because firming (tathbit) means settling the soul upon preserving it and abandoning what corrupts it, and this arises only from certainty about the Hereafter. The three estimates found in His words ﴿the likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a grain﴾ [al-Baqarah 261] apply here too, namely: the likeness of the hypocrites is like the likeness of one who plants a grain; or the likeness of their spending is like a grain; or the likeness of the spenders and their spending is like the likeness of a grain and its planter. They permitted, regarding (ibtighaa'), that it be a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning "seeking," and that it be an object of purpose; likewise (wa-tathbitan).

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is not correct for (ibtighā'a) to be a maf'ul li-ajlihi (object of purpose), because it is coordinated with (wa-tathbītan) [and to make certain]. Nor is it correct for (wa-tathbītan) to be a maf'ul li-ajlihi, because spending is not for the sake of making certain. Makki said in (al-Mushkil): "Both are objects of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi)," but this is refuted by what we have explained. End of his words.

Tathbīt is a verbal noun (maṣdar) of thabata, and it is transitive. It is possible that the object is omitted, its implied sense being "the reward from God," meaning: "and making certain and securing for themselves the reward for that expenditure." In that case, making certain the reward and securing it from God becomes a motive for spending in the way of God. Whoever estimates the object to be other than this, i.e. "and making certain from their own selves their deeds through sincerity of intention," and takes "from themselves" to mean "min" in the sense of "lam" (for), i.e. "for their own selves," as one says: "I did that as a breaking of my desire," meaning "for my desire," then it is not clear that it is in the accusative as an object of purpose.

Ash-Sha'bi, Qatada, as-Suddi, Abu Salih and Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is "and certainty" (tayaqqun), i.e. their souls have firmly established insights, so they make them steadfast in spending. This is reinforced by the reading of one who recited (wa-tabyīnan min anfusihim) ["and clarification from their souls"]. Qatada also said: "and seeking reward (ihtisab) from their souls." Ash-Sha'bi, ad-Dahhak and al-Kalbi also said: "and affirmation (taṣdīq)," i.e. they pay zakat good-heartedly. Ibn Jubayr and Abu Malik said: "verification (taḥqīq) in their religion." Ibn Kaysan said: "sincerity and firmly establishing their souls in obedience to God in their expenditures." Az-Zajjaj said: "and being convinced when they spend that it is something for which God rewards." Ash-Sha'bi also said: "resolve (azm)." Yaman said: "insight (basīrah)." Mujahid and al-Hasan said: its meaning is that they "make firm" (yuthbitūn), i.e. they place their charities. Al-Hasan said: "A man, when he intended to give charity, would deliberate; if it was for God he would carry it out, and if doubt mixed with it, he would withhold."

Some Egyptian grammarians permitted that his words "wa-tathbītan" mean "tathabbutan" (deliberation), so it would be intransitive. He said: maṣdars may differ and some may take the place of others, and from this is His saying: ﴿And devote yourself to Him with devotion﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 8], i.e. "tabattul" (devotion). This view was rejected on the ground that this is not the case with a preceding verb in the manner of the verse. As for the verbal noun coming without being formed from a mentioned verb, it is not interpreted as other than its own verb which it has originally. You say: if the intransitive verb thabata means "to be established, to take firm root, to be confirmed and to remain," its causative form by doubling (taḍ'īf) means "to establish and to confirm."

Ibn Rawaha addressed the Messenger of God ﷺ:
"God has established what He gave you of goodness, the establishing of Jesus, and a victory like that with which they were victorious."

So the meaning, and God knows best, is that they establish themselves, from their own selves, in faith through this deed, which is the giving out of wealth, which is the counterpart of the soul, in the way of God seeking His pleasure; for such a deed is hard upon the soul, so they act to make the soul firm in faith, and what you hope from God through this difficult deed; for when it stands firm in a difficult matter, it submits and becomes humbled to it. If the establishing is attributed to them, then (min) is in the accusative position, connected to the verbal noun itself, and it is partitive, like its use in: "he shook from his flank" and "he stirred from his vigour." If the establishing is attributed in meaning to their souls, then (min) is also in the accusative position as a qualifier of the verbal noun, its implied sense being: "existing from their own selves."

Az-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: what is the meaning of the partitive? I say: its meaning is that whoever spends his wealth for the sake of God has established part of his self, and whoever spends his wealth and his soul together is the one who has established all of it: ﴿and strive in the way of God with your wealth and your selves﴾ [as-Saff: 11]. End of his words.

Apparently, his self is what establishes him and carries him to spend in the way of God; there is no motivator for him but it, because of what it has believed of faith and abundant reward. It is what prompts him to that, and what makes him firm through the goodness of its faith and the sublimity of its conviction.

Asim al-Jahdari read (ka-mathali ḥabbatin) with a ḥā'. The bā' in (bi-rabwatin) is locative (ẓarfiyyah), and it is in the position of a qualifier, so it is linked to an omitted element. He specified the rabwah for the goodness of its trees and the purity of its fruit, as the poet said, and he is al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, may God have mercy on him:
"It rose above the dew of the depths and sank low, out of reach of the thirsty, and it was content with its own watering.
So the peach and pomegranate inclined beneath it, and the date palm and olive enveloped its upper parts."

The tafsir of Ibn 'Abbas: the rabwah is an elevated place where rivers do not flow; he means the one mentioned in His saying: ﴿a heavy rain struck it﴾, which indicates that there is no running water in it. He did not mean that the species of rabwah has no running water, do you not see His saying: ﴿to a height with a place of settlement and a spring﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 50]. It was singled out because its watering is by heavy rain and not by running water, according to the custom of Arab lands, by what they perceive as abundant.

Abu 'Abdullah Muhammad ibn 'Umar al-Razi said: The exegetes said: a garden on a rabwah is better and yields more produce. About this I have a difficulty, for it is above the water, the rivers do not rise to it, and the winds strike it frequently, so its produce is not good; and if it is in a depression, waters pour into it and the traces of the winds do not reach it, so its produce is also not good; its produce is good only in level land. So the intended sense of rabwah is not what they mentioned, but rather that the land is good, such that when rain falls upon it, it swells and grows, so its produce increases and its trees become complete in it. This is supported by His saying: ﴿and you see the earth lifeless﴾ [al-Hajj: 5], and by the fact that it is in contrast to the first parable, the first (the smooth rock) not being affected by rain. End of his words. There is some abridgement in it, and what he said was said before him by al-Hasan. The rabwah is level land that does not rise above water. The poet said about the gardens of al-Hazn:
"No garden of the gardens of al-Hazn is green with plants, a green meadow upon which a heavy rain has poured."
What is not meant by the gardens of al-Hazn is the gardens of the elevated ground, as at-Tabari claimed; rather, the gardens of al-Hazn are those ascribed to Najd, and Najd is also called al-Hazn. The garden was ascribed to al-Hazn, which is Najd, because its vegetation is more fragrant, its breeze cooler and finer, so it is better than the gardens of Tihama.

Ibn 'Amir and Asim read (rabwatin) with a fatha on the rā', and the rest of the seven with a ḍamma. Their disagreement is similar in (qad aflaḥa) [al-Mu'minun: 1]. Ibn 'Abbas read with a kasra on the rā'. Abu Ja'far and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read (birabāwatin) on the pattern of kara-hah. Abu al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli read (ribāwatin) on the pattern of risalah.

﴿A heavy rain struck it﴾ is a clause in the position of a qualifier of "garden." The qualifier by the prepositional phrase was mentioned first, then the qualifier by clause; this is the more common usage in the language of the Arabs. The stable qualifier, that it is "on a rabwah," was mentioned first, then the accidental qualifier, ﴿a heavy rain struck it﴾. In describing the smooth rock, His saying ﴿upon it is dust﴾ came, then it was coordinated to it with "fa," but here it was not coordinated; rather it was brought out as a qualifier. One should consider what the difference is between the two places. It is also permissible that ﴿a heavy rain struck it﴾ be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of "garden," since it is indefinite, and it has been qualified as a circumstance of the pronoun in the prepositional phrase.

﴿So it brought forth its produce twofold﴾: "brought forth" (ātat) means "gave," and the first object is omitted; the estimate is: "so it gave its owner, or its people, its produce," just as it is omitted in His saying ﴿like the likeness of a garden﴾, i.e. the owner or planter of a garden, and because the intention is the mention of what bears fruit, not of whom it bears fruit, since that is known. The accusative of (ḍi'fayn) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). Whoever claims that (ḍi'fayn) is a second object of (ātat) has erred, and the meaning is not that. Likewise the claim of one who says that (ātat) means "brought out," and that it takes only one object, since that is not known in the language of the Arabs. Attributing the giving to it is a metaphor. (Al-'Ukul), with a ḍamma on the hamza, is the thing eaten, and here is meant the fruit. Its annexation to "the garden" is an annexation of specification, like the saddle of the beast, since fruit is not something the garden owns. The two Harams (Ibn Kathir and Nafi') and Abu 'Amr read it with a ḍamma on the hamza and a sukun on the kaf, and likewise every noun annexed to a feminine noun; Abu 'Amr transmitted this for what is annexed to a non-pronominal noun or to a masculine pronoun. The rest read it with tashdid.

The meaning of (ḍi'fayn) is twice what it used to produce because of the heavy rain and because it is on a rabwah, since the produce of elevated ground is greater and further from flood and hail. It was said: twice that of other lands; it was said: four times their amount. This is based on the view that the double of a thing is its two equals. Abu Muslim said: three times their amount. Taj al-Qurra' said: there is no basis for this in Arabic, and the giving of double is within one load. Ikrimah and 'Ata' said: the meaning of "twofold" is that it bore fruit twice in the year. In my view, it is possible that His saying (ḍi'fayn) is of that kind which is not increased by doubling a single unit, but is a comparison intended for multiplication, as if it were said: "it brought forth its produce twofold," meaning twofold after twofold, i.e. many multiples. This is more eloquent in comparing the expenditure to the garden, because the good deed does not receive the reward of two good deeds, but is multiplied many times, ten times its like, and seven hundred times and more.

﴿But if a heavy rain does not strike it, then a light rain﴾: Ibn 'Isa said: there is an ellipsis here; the estimate is: "if a heavy rain does not come upon it," as the poet said:
"When we are traced in lineage, a base woman did not bear me."
That is, she did not bear me. The meaning: the light rain suffices for it and takes the place of the heavy rain in bringing forth its fruit twofold, and that is the most noble and best of land, so its fruit does not diminish with the lack of rain. It was also said: the meaning is that if a heavy rain does not strike it, its fruit is doubled, and if a light rain strikes it, it brings forth less than it brings with the heavy rain; in every state it is not without bearing fruit. Al-Mawardi said: the crop of light rain is weaker than the crop of rain and less in produce, but in it, though little, there is steadiness and benefit. End of his words.

The claim of inversion (taqdim and ta'khir) in the verse, as some have said, that the meaning is: "a heavy rain struck it, and if a heavy rain did not strike it, then a light rain; so it brought forth its produce twofold," so that its bringing forth of the produce twofold is made to apply to both states, of the heavy rain and the light rain, is unnecessary; and inversion is among the necessities of poetry, so the Qur'an is to be exonerated from that.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: the land struck by the parable is the land of Egypt: if no rain reaches it, it is fertile, and if rain reaches it, it doubles. Az-Zamakhshari said: He likened their state before God to the garden on the rabwah, and their expenditure, much or little, to the heavy rain and the light rain. Just as each of the two rains doubles the produce of the garden, so their expenditure, whether much or little, after it is sought for the face of God and effort is exerted in it, is pure before God, increasing their nearness and the goodness of their state with Him. End of his words. Al-Mawardi said, close to the words of az-Zamakhshari: He intended by this parable that abundant righteousness is like the crop of the heavy rain, abundant in benefit, and little righteousness is like the crop of light rain, little in benefit; so one should not abandon little righteousness if one does not do much of it, just as one does not abandon the crop of light rain when one is not able to have the crop of heavy rain. End of his words.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: He likened the growth of the expenditures of these sincere people, whose charities Allah causes to flourish, to the rearing of the young camel (faṣīl) and the foal (falw), to the growth of the plants of this garden on the elevated ground described, unlike the smooth rock (ṣafwān) from which its soil has been stripped away, so that it remains bare and barren.

Ibn al-Jawzī said: The meaning of the verse is that the owner of this garden does not suffer loss, for if light rain (ṭall) reaches it, it thrives, and if heavy rain (wābil) reaches it, it doubles its yield. Likewise is the expenditure of the sincere believer. End of quotation. His statement "fa-ṭallun" (then light rain) is the response (jawāb) to the conditional, so it requires an estimated element that turns it into a complete sentence. Al-Mubarrad estimated it as a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, because the meaning indicates it, that is: then light rain is what reaches it. He began with the indefinite noun because it came in the response to the condition. Some scholars mentioned that this is among the things that permit beginning with an indefinite noun, and similar to it is what occurs in the proverb: "If a caravan (ʿīr) goes, another caravan is in the tether."

Others than al-Mubarrad estimated it as the predicate of an omitted subject, that is: so what reaches it is light rain, or so its reacher is light rain. Some estimated it as the agent (fāʿil), that is: so light rain reaches it. All these estimations are permissible. The last one, however, requires omitting the whole clause that serves as the response and retaining a complement for part of it, because whenever the fāʾ (fa) enters upon a present-tense verb, it is with an omitted subject, as in the saying of God Most High: ﴿And whoever returns, Allah will take retribution from him﴾ [al-Māʾida: 95], meaning: so He takes retribution. Likewise, this estimation is needed here, meaning: so it (i.e., the garden) is reached by light rain. As for the two previous estimations, only the omission of one of the two parts of the sentence is needed.

A parallel to what occurs in the verse is the saying of the poet:
"Unless there are camels, then goats, whose horns of their heads are like sticks."

﴿And Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾. Al-Zuhrī read it with the yāʾ (ya-taʿmalūn, "they do"), so its apparent meaning is that the pronoun refers to the hypocrites, but it may be general, not restricted to the hypocrites, referring to all people. The majority read it with the tāʾ (ta-taʿmalūn, "you do"), in address, and in it there is an iltifāt (shift of grammatical person). The meaning: nothing of the deeds and intentions, whether of showing off or of sincerity, is hidden from Him, and in it is both a promise and a warning.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 266:

﴿Would any of you wish to have a garden﴾ When the prohibition against nullifying charity through reminders and harm had preceded, and he had likened the one who does this to the one who spends to be seen by people, and had illustrated his state with the smooth rock mentioned earlier, and then illustrated the state of the one who spends seeking the Face of God, he followed all of that with this verse. Al-Suddi said: "This is another parable for the one who does good to be seen by people." Ibn Zayd said: "It is a parable for the one who reminds others of his charity." Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Rabi' and others said: "It is for the one who is negligent in obedience." Ibn Jurayj said: "It is for the one who was given youth and wealth, but did not act until both were taken from him." Ibn Abbas said: "It is for the one who performed various kinds of obedience, like a garden containing every kind of fruit, but then ended it with an evil deed, like a whirlwind. So it likens his regret, when there is no return, to the regret of an elderly man whose garden was destroyed when he was most in need of it and least able to rebuild it." A similar report is related from Umar. Al-Hasan said: "This is a parable, by God, that few understand: an old man whose body has grown weak and whose children are many, who is most in need of his garden. By God, one of you is most in need of his deeds when the world has been cut off from him."

The hamza is the interrogative particle (istifham), and the meaning is one of distancing and negation, i.e., "No one would wish that?" The word aḥad (anyone) here is not restricted to negation and the like; rather the meaning is: "Would one of you wish...?" by way of badal (substitution, i.e., the question addresses each one of you individually). Al-Hasan read jannatun (a garden) in the plural, jannāt.

﴿of palm trees and grapevines﴾ Since the palm tree and the grapevine are the noblest of trees and the most beneficial, these two were singled out for mention, and the garden was described as made of them, even though other things are in a garden. Wherever this is mentioned in the Qur'an, it specifies the palm tree rather than its fruit, and the fruit of the vine rather than the vine itself. This is because the greatest benefit of the vine is its fruit rather than its root, whereas every part of the palm tree has great benefits, equal to the benefit of its fruit: its wood, its fronds, its fibre, its leaf-sheaths, and everything else it contains. Therefore, God knows best, the mention was restricted to the palm tree and the fruit of the vine.

﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾ The explanation of this has already preceded at the beginning of this surah.

﴿For him therein is of every kind of fruit﴾ This indicates that there are in it trees other than the palm and the vine, as we mentioned before this apparent meaning. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that by "fruits" one may mean the benefits that he would obtain from them. This clause is composed of a subject (mubtada') and a predicate (khabar). According to the view of al-Akhfash, min is redundant (za'idah), and the estimated meaning is: "For him therein is every fruit," intending abundance, using the wording of generality, not that generality is actually intended. It is not permissible for it to be redundant according to the view of the Kufans, because they stipulated for its redundancy that what follows it must be indefinite (nakirah), as in "There has come from rain..." As for the view of the majority of the Basrans, its redundancy is not permissible, because they stipulated that what precedes it must be non-affirmative and what follows it must be indefinite. This requires qualification, which we have mentioned in our book Manhaj al-Salik (The Method of the Wayfarer), of our authorship. The view of the majority of the Basrans can be derived by eliding the subject, its estimated form being: "For him therein is provision," or "fruits of every kind of fruit." A similar elision is in the verse of the poet:

*As if you were one of the camels of the Banu Uqaysh,*
*Rattling behind its hind legs with a water-skin.*

The estimated meaning is: "As if you were a camel of the camels of the Banu Uqaysh," with "camel" elided, the phrase "of the camels" indicating it. Just as "fruits" was elided, indicated by ﴿of every kind of fruit﴾. Likewise is His, exalted is He, ﴿There is none of us but has a known station﴾ [al-Saffat: 164], meaning: "There is none of us..." so aḥad (none) is an elided subject (mubtada'), minnā is a qualifier (ṣifah), and what follows illa (except) is a predicate clause for the subject.

﴿and old age has struck him﴾ The apparent meaning is that the waw is for circumstance (ḥāl), with qad (indeed) estimated: "and indeed old age has struck him," like His saying: ﴿And you were dead, and He gave you life﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28], and ﴿They sat [at home] and said, "If they had obeyed us..."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 168], meaning: "And indeed you were..." and "And indeed they sat..." It has also been said that its meaning is: "and it strikes him," so the past tense is conjoined to the present tense, placing it in its position. Al-Farra' said: this is permissible with yawaddu (would wish), because it is followed sometimes by an (that) and sometimes by aw (or), so one of them may be estimated in the place of the other. Al-Zamakhshari said: It has been said that one says: "I wished that such-and-such were the case," so the conjunction is treated according to meaning, as if it were said: "Would any of you wish that he had a garden, and old age had struck him?" End of quotation.

The apparent sense of his words is that "and old age struck him" is conjoined to the complement of "would wish" (anna takūna, "that there be"), because it has the meaning of law kānat ("if it were"), since one says: "Would any of you wish that, if it were...?" This is not correct, because it is impossible for it to be conjoined to "kānat" which is preceded by law (if), since it is the object of the wish. As for ﴿and old age struck him﴾, it cannot be the object of the wish, because no one wishes for old age to strike him or desires it. But al-Zamakhshari's statement may be understood as follows: since "would any of you wish" is an interrogative whose meaning is denial, the object of the wishing is made the combination of the two things, namely having a garden and old age striking him, not that each one of them is wished for on its own. He denied the wish for their combination. The word iṣābah (striking) carries the sense of effect, which is more eloquent than "and he grew old" (wa kabira). Likewise: "a hill that a heavy rain struck (aṣābahā wābil)," and "upon it was dust, so a heavy rain struck it," and one does not say wabalat or tūbilu. Al-Kibar means advanced age and the height of years.

﴿and he has offspring who are weak﴾ It is also read ḍiṣāf (weak), and both are plurals of ḍaʿīf (weak), like ẓarīf, ẓurafā', and ẓirāf (witty). The meaning is: offspring who are young and small, and it is possible that by ḍu'afā' is meant those in need.

﴿so a whirlwind with fire in it struck it and it was burned﴾ He said: "fīhi" (in it) with a masculine pronoun, because i'ṣār (whirlwind) is masculine among the names of winds. The nominative of nār (fire) is due to its being the agent of the preceding preposition, or it is "existing therein is fire." In the conjunction with fa' (so) in His saying ﴿so a whirlwind struck it﴾ is evidence that when it had flourished and become good for benefit, the whirlwind followed it.

﴿and it was burned﴾ This is a verb of intransitive response (muṭāwa'ah) to aḥraqa (to burn), as if it were said: "there is fire in it which burned it, and it was burned," like His saying: "I made him just and he became just (anṣaftuhu fa-nṣafa)," and "I kindled it and it blazed (awqadtuhu fa-ttaqada)." This responsiveness is an undergoing of effect in the object, which has the capacity to be affected by the agent, so it is affected by it. The fire that is in the whirlwind is the scorching wind (samūm) that is in it. Ibn Mas'ud said: the samūm from which God created the jinn is one part of seventy parts of fire, meaning the fire of the Hereafter. It has been explained that it was destroyed by a thunderbolt. Al-Hasan and al-Dahhak said: "a whirlwind with fire in it" means a wind in which there is biting cold (ṣirr bard).

﴿Thus God makes clear to you the signs﴾ That is: like this clarification, parables are presented that bring things near to the mind, and He makes clear to you the indicators by which one is led to follow the truth.

﴿that perhaps you will reflect﴾ That is: that you may know your thoughts concerning what passes away and perishes of the world, and concerning what remains for you in the Hereafter, so that you may renounce the world and desire the Hereafter.

These noble verses have included, among the kinds of eloquence and forms of rhetoric, several types: the transition from the particular to the general, allusion (ishārah), simile (tashbīh), ellipsis (ḥadhf), restriction (ikhtiṣāṣ), parables (amthāl), and metaphor (majāz). All of these have been pointed out in the course of the explanation of these verses.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 267 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿O you who have believed, spend from the good things you have earned and from what We have produced for you from the earth. And do not aim at the defective therefrom to spend, while you would not accept it yourselves unless you overlook it. And know that Allah is Free of need and Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿The Shaytan threatens you with poverty and orders you to immorality, but Allah promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty. And Allah is All-Encompassing and Knowing.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 268] ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills, and whoever is given wisdom has been given much good. And none will be reminded except the people of understanding.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269] ﴿And whatever you spend or whatever vow you vow, indeed Allah knows it. And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 270] ﴿If you disclose your charities, they are good; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you, and He will remove from you some of your misdeeds. And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 271] ﴿Their guidance is not your responsibility, but Allah guides whom He wills. And whatever good you spend is for yourselves, and you spend only seeking the Face of Allah. And whatever good you spend will be repaid to you in full, and you will not be wronged.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 272] ﴿For the poor who are confined in the way of Allah and cannot move about in the land. The ignorant one thinks them wealthy because of their modesty; you know them by their mark. They do not beg people persistently. And whatever good you spend, indeed Allah is Knowing of it.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 273]

*Al-tayammum* (التَّيَمُّمُ): intending, aiming at. It is said: *amma* like *radda*, and *umam* like *ukhar*; and *tayyama* with *ta'* and *ya'*, and *ta'ammama* with *ta'* and *hamza*, all with the same meaning. Al-Khalil said: "I *amamtuhu*: I aimed in front of him; and I *yammamtuhu*: I aimed at him from whatever direction."

*(Al-khabith)* (الخَبِيثَ): the bad, the inferior; it is the opposite of *al-tayyib*, and is an active participle from *khabutha*.

*Al-ighmad* (الإغْماضُ): leniency, tolerance. It is said: *aghmada fi haqqihi*, meaning he was lenient regarding his right, accepted it and was content with it. *Al-ighmad* is also closing the eye, and it is like *al-ighda'*. *Aghmada al-rajulu* means he came to a difficult matter, as it is said *a'man*, *a'raqa* and *anjada*, meaning he went to Oman, Iraq and Najd. The root of this word is from *al-ghumudh*, which is concealment: *ghamada al-shay'* *yaghmudu ghumudan*, it became hidden. Closing the eyelid is a concealment of the eye. *Al-ghamd* is the low, hidden part of the ground.

*Al-Hamid* (الحَمِيدُ): the Praised; it is *fa'il* in the sense of *maf'ul*, and it is not systematic. The categories of *fa'il* were discussed at the beginning of this surah, and the explanation of *al-hamd* at the beginning of its surah.

*Al-nadhr* (النَّذْرُ): its root has already been discussed in His words ﴿Whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6]. It is a person binding his heart upon doing something and committing himself to it, and its origin is from fear. Its verb is *nadhara yandhiru* and *yandhuru*, with the *dhal* vowelled with *damma* or *kasra*. The Arabs used to make many vows concerning what they hoped would occur, and they also used to vow to kill their enemies, as the poet said:

*Those who revile my honour, though I have not reviled them, and those who vow my blood when I meet them.*

As for its meaning in the sacred law, its explanation will come, Allah willing.

*(Ni'imma)* (نِعِمَّ): its origin is *ni'ma*, and it is the opposite of *bi'sa*. Its rules are mentioned in grammar. The discussion of *bi'sa* was mentioned at His words ﴿Wretched is what they sold themselves for﴾ [al-Baqarah: 90].

*Al-ta'affuf* (التَّعَفُّفُ): a *tafa''ul* form from *al-'iffa*. *'Affa 'an al-shay'* means he refrained from it and abstained from seeking it. "Whoever loves and remains chaste, then dies, dies a martyr," meaning he restrained himself from the prohibitions of Allah, the Exalted. Ru'ba ibn al-'Ajjaj said:

*He abstained from its secrets after the darkness, and did not leave them after lust and passion.*

*Al-sima* (السِّيما): the mark. It may be pronounced with a long vowel, and it is said *bi-l-simiya'*, like *al-kimiya'*. The poet said:

*A boy whom Allah struck with beauty in his youth, having a mark that does not trouble the sight.*

It is from *al-wasm*, and *al-simma* is the mark. Its first letter has been placed where its middle letter is, and its middle letter where its first letter is. When lengthened as *simiya'*, the *hamza* in it is for augmentation, not for feminine marking.

*Al-ilhaf* (الإلْحافُ): persistence and insistence in asking. It is said *alhafa* and *ahfa*. The derivation of *al-ilhaf* is from *al-lihaf* (blanket), because it covers all forms of request in every situation. It was also said that it is from *alhafa al-shay'*, when he covered it and enveloped it entirely with covering, and from it comes *al-lihaf*. From it is the saying of Ibn Ahmar:

*It keeps protecting them with its two wings, and covers them with a thick, soft wing.*

He describes the male ostrich sheltering its eggs with its wings, making its wing like a blanket. The poet said:

*Then they went, musk-perfumed, covering the earth with the fringes of their waist-wrappers.*

That is, they make it like a blanket for the earth, meaning they clothe it with it. It was also said that its derivation is from *lahafa al-jabal*, because of the roughness in it. It was also said that it is from the saying: "He gave me from the surplus of his blanket," meaning he gave me from the surplus of what he had.

﴿O you who have believed, spend from the good things you have earned﴾. The texts in the hadith are consistent that the reason for the revelation of this verse was that when they were commanded to give charity, they would bring clusters of dates and hang them in the mosque so that the needy could eat from them. Some of the Companions brought *hashaf* (dry, worthless dates), and in some narrations *shis* (poor dates), and in others inferior dates, believing that this was permissible. So it was revealed. This address, the command to spend, is general for all of this community. 'Ali, 'Ubayda al-Salmani and Ibn Sirin said: it refers to the obligatory zakat. Just as it is permissible to give a small amount voluntarily, one may also give voluntarily something smaller in quantity, and a counterfeit dirham is better than a date. Based on this, the command is for obligation. The apparent meaning of the statements of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, al-Hasan and Qatada is that it refers to voluntary spending, and this is what the reason for revelation indicates: they were encouraged not to give voluntarily except the best and most selected.

The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when He mentioned the virtue of spending in the way of Allah and encouraged it, and condemned reminding and forbade it, then He mentioned the intention behind it, from showing off and seeking the pleasure of Allah, He here mentioned the description of the spender who chooses the best. Whether the command is for obligation or recommendation, most scholars hold that ﴿the good things you have earned﴾ means the best and most selected, and that *al-khabith* means the inferior. Ibn Zayd said: ﴿from the good things﴾ means the lawful, and *al-khabith* means the unlawful. 'Ali said: it is gold and silver. Mujahid said: it is trade goods.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: His words ﴿from the good things﴾ may be understood as intending neither lawfulness nor excellence. Rather the meaning is as if He said: "Spend from what you have earned," so it is only an exhortation to spend. Then the mention of *al-tayyib* was added to clarify the description of its goodness in what is earned, generally, and to affirm the blessing, just as you say: "I fed so-and-so from the most satisfying bread, and gave him to drink from the most quenching water." In this sense, *al-tayyib* includes both excellence and lawfulness. This possibility is supported by the statement of 'Abd Allah ibn Mughaffal: "There is nothing bad in the wealth of the believer." This is the end of his words. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿what you have earned﴾ is the general sense of everything acquired by the spender through effort, endeavour and toil, whether by body or by contract in trade. It was said: it is what ownership has settled upon, whether recent or old, so that inherited wealth is included, because it was earned by the one from whom it was inherited. The pronoun in *kasabtum* refers to humankind or to the believers, and this is the apparent meaning.

Al-Raghib said: the specification of what is acquired, excluding what is inherited, is because a person is more stingy with what he earns than with what he inherits, so the permission regarding the inherited is understood from its implication. This is the end of his words, and it is fine.

*Min* (مِن) is partitive, and it is in the position of the object. *Ma* (ما) in *ma kasabtum* is a relative pronoun with an omitted returning pronoun. It is also permitted that it be a verbal noun, in which case the verbal noun must be interpreted as a passive participle. Its estimate is: "from the good things of your earning," that is, of what you have earned. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that the command to spend is general over all kinds of good wealth, but it is general regarding the required amount, and requires clarification by mentioning the quantities. So it is valid to argue for the obligation of right in matters where there is disagreement, such as trade goods, charity on horses, zakat on the wealth of a child, permissible ornaments not prepared for trade, goods for sale, sheep, grazing cattle, debts, and other matters on which opinions differ.

Khuwayz Mindad said: in the verse there is evidence for the permissibility of a father eating from the property of his child, because the Prophet ﷺ said: "Your children are from the best of your earnings, so eat from the property of your children with pleasure." This is the end of his words. 'A'isha narrated from him ﷺ: "The best that a man eats is from his earnings, and his child is from his earnings."

﴿And from what We have produced for you from the earth﴾: meaning from kinds of grains, fruits, minerals and buried treasure (*rikaz*). In His words ﴿We have produced for you﴾ there is a reminder of blessing and an alert to complete favour, like His words ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29]. The meaning is "from the good things of what We have produced," and it was omitted because what precedes and follows indicates it. The preposition was repeated for emphasis, or to indicate another implied verb, so that the command is twofold. In His words ﴿and from what We have produced for you from the earth﴾ there is an indication of the obligation of zakat on what the earth produces, whether little or much, of all the other kinds, due to the generality of the verse, provided we hold that the command is for obligation. Among the scholars there is disagreement on many issues concerning what the earth produces, which are mentioned in the books of jurisprudence.

﴿And do not aim at the defective therefrom to spend﴾: this emphasizes the command, since it is understood from His words ﴿Spend from the good things you have earned﴾. In this there is an antithesis by mentioning the good things and the defective. Al-Bazzi read ﴿And do not aim﴾ with a doubled *ta'*, its original form being *tatayammamu*, so the first *ta'* was assimilated into the second. This occurs in several places in the Qur'an, and I have enumerated them in my poem on the readings called *'Iqd al-La'ali*, in verses which are:

*They turned away with the spoils (al-Anfal) and Hud, both together, and Nur, and in the trial they have reached them.*

*Tatanazzalu in Hijr and in al-Shu'ara' together, and in al-Qadr, and in al-Ahzab, not to change.*

*Tabarrajna with Tanasharuna, and Tanazza'u, Tukallamu with Tayammamu, before them, no.*

*Talqafu, anna kana, with li-ta'arafu, and its companions, fa-tafarraqa, achieve.*

*In Imran, la tafarraqu, with the women, came. Tawaffahum, takhayyaruna, for him, become clear.*

*Talahha, talaqqunahu, talazza, tarabbasu, zid la, ta'arafu, tamayyaza, tukmula.*

*Thalathin with ihda, and in al-Lat, behind him, tamannawna with ma ba'da, zaltum, tanazzala.*

*And in its beginning lighten, if before it was, at the joining, the letter of extension, extend and lengthen.*

It is narrated from Abu Rabi'a from al-Bazzi: lightening the *ta'*, like the rest of the readers. These *ta'* letters include some where the preceding letter is moving, as in ﴿So it scatters you﴾ [al-An'am: 153] and ﴿Then behold, it swallows﴾ [al-A'raf: 117]. Some are preceded by a quiescent letter of extension and softness, as in ﴿And do not aim﴾. And some are preceded by a quiescent letter that is not a letter of extension and softness, as in ﴿But if they turn away﴾ [Al 'Imran: 32], ﴿a Fire blazing﴾ [al-Layl: 14], ﴿when you received it﴾ [al-Nur: 15], ﴿Do they await?﴾ [al-Tawba: 52]. The author of *al-Mumti'* said: Sibawayh does not permit the sukun of this *ta'* in *yatakallamun* and similar forms, because when it is quiescent it requires a *alif al-wasl*, and the *alif al-wasl* does not attach to the imperfect verb. When it is joined to what precedes it, it is permitted, because it does not need a *hamzat al-wasl*. However, forms such as ﴿in tawallaw﴾ and ﴿when you received it﴾ [al-Nur: 15] are not permitted according to the Basrans in any case, because this involves the juncture of two quiescent letters, and the first quiescent is not a letter of extension and softness. This is the end of his words.

The reading of al-Bazzi is established; the community has received it with acceptance. Knowledge is not confined or restricted to what the Basrans transmitted and said, so do not look at their statement that this is not permitted.

Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) read (wa-la ta'ammamu) from amamtu, meaning "I intended," and Ibn Abbas, al-Zuhri and Muslim ibn Jundub read (tayammamu). al-Tabari related that in the reading of Abdullah it was (wa-la ta'ummu), from amamtu, meaning "I intended." Al-Khabith and al-Tayyib are two qualities that are predominantly used without the qualified noun being mentioned with them, except rarely. For this reason there came: ﴿And the good women are for good men, and the evil women are for evil men﴾ [al-Nur: 26], and: ﴿And the evil [men] are for evil [women]﴾ [al-Nur: 26]. And the Most High said: ﴿and he makes unlawful for them the evil things﴾ [al-A'raf: 157]. And the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I seek refuge in Allah from the impurity and the evil things." And "minhu" is connected to His saying (tunfiquna), and the pronoun in "minhu" refers to al-khabith. (Tunfiquna) is a circumstantial clause (hal) of the subject in (tayammamu). It has been said: it is a prospective circumstantial clause (hal muqaddara), because spending from it occurs after intending it. It is also permissible that it be a circumstantial clause of the object, because in the sentence there is a pronoun referring back to it. A group permitted that the statement at His saying (al-khabith) be a complete sentence, and then he began another statement describing the khabith, so he said: "You spend from it while you would not take it except if you close your eyes," i.e., you are lenient. It is as if this meaning is a reproach and a rebuke to people, and in it there is an alert that what is forbidden is intending the inferior part of what is in one's possession, so that one specifically spends it in the way of Allah. As for spending the inferior for one who has no other, or for one one does not intend, it is not forbidden.

﴿And you would not take it [yourselves]﴾. It has been said: this clause is resumptive, having no place in grammar. It has also been said: the waw is for the circumstantial, so the clause is in the position of an accusative. al-Bara', Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and others said: its meaning is: "And you would not take it in your debts and your rights with people, except by being lenient in that, and leaving some of your rights, while you dislike it and do not accept it." That is: do not do with Allah what you would not accept for yourselves. al-Hasan said: the meaning is: "And you would not take it if you found it being sold in the market, unless its price were reduced for you." Something similar was narrated from Ali. al-Bara' also said: its meaning is: "And you would not take it if it were given to you as a gift, unless you close your eyes," i.e., you feel shy before the giver to accept from him what you have no need for and which has no value in itself. Ibn Zayd said: "And you would not take the unlawful unless you overlook its disliked aspect." The apparent meaning is the generality of the negation of taking, by whatever way the khabith is taken, whether by taking a right or by gift.

The ha' in (bi-akhidhihi) refers back to al-khabith, and it is in the genitive by annexation, even though in meaning it is an object. Some grammarians said: the ha' is in the position of an accusative with (akhidhin), and the ha' and the nun do not combine, because the nun is extra, and the pronominal ha' is extra and attached like the attachment of the nun, so it does not combine with an attached pronoun; end of his statement. This is the view of al-Akhfash: that the tanwin and the nun may both drop for the lightness of the pronoun, not for the annexation, as in: "daribuka" (your hitter), where the kaf is an accusative pronoun. The view of the majority is that nothing of them drops for the lightness of the pronoun, and this is mentioned in grammar. Hisham permitted: "daraba-nka" (with tanwin and an accusative pronoun), and by analogy it is permissible to affirm the nun with the pronoun, and it may be supported by his saying:

"They are the doers of good and those who command it,"

and his saying:

"And he did not benefit, while people were present to him [i.e., attacking him]."

(Illa an tughmidu fihi) The position of (an) is accusative or genitive according to the one who estimated: "illa bi-an tughmidu," the particle being deleted, since its deletion is permissible and regular. It has been said: it is accusative by (tughmidu), and this is the position of the circumstantial. We have previously mentioned that Sibawayh does not permit the accusative of an and the verb, estimated as a verbal noun, in the position of a circumstantial. al-Farra' said: the meaning is that of the conditional and the consequent, because its meaning is: "If you close your eyes, you take." But "illa" fell upon "an," so it opened it. Similar to it: ﴿unless they both fear﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229] and ﴿unless they forgo﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237]. All of this is a conditional. Abu al-Abbas and others denied al-Farra's statement, and said: this "an" was never pronounced with a kasra; it is the one which, together with what follows, is estimated as a verbal noun, and it is always fathah in every case. The meaning is: "except by your closing your eyes."

al-Jumhur read (tughmidu) from aghmada, and they took it as one whose object was deleted, i.e., tughammidu, with a damma on the ta', fathah on the ghayn, and kasra on the mim, shaddah. Its meaning is the meaning of the reading of the majority. It was narrated from him: taghmidu, with fathah on the ta', sukun on the ghayn, and kasra on the mim, the present tense of ghamida, which is a dialect of aghmada. It was narrated from al-Yazidi (taghmudu) with fathah and damma on the mim, and its meaning is: "except that your opinion about it be hidden from you." It was narrated from al-Hasan (tughammadu), with shaddah on the mim and fathah. Qatadah read (tughmadu) with damma on the ta', sukun on the ghayn, and fathah on the mim, unshaddah, and its meaning is: "except that it be overlooked for you."

Abu al-Fath said: its meaning is: "except that you be found to have overlooked the matter, by your interpretation or by your leniency," as you say: "ahmada al-rajul usiba mahmudan" (the man was praised, having been found praiseworthy). It was said: the meaning of Qatadah's reading is: "except that you enter into it and are drawn to it."

﴿And know that Allah is Rich, Praiseworthy﴾. That is: He is Rich above your charities, and they are only your deeds returned to you. Praiseworthy means: praised in every state, since He is deserving of praise. al-Hasan said: "He seeks praise from His creation," i.e., He gives them blessings by which He invites their praise. It was said: He is deserving of praise for what He has obligated you to worship Him with.

﴿The Shaytan threatens you with poverty﴾, i.e., he frightens you with poverty. He says to the man: hold back, for if you give charity you will become poor. Abu Hayyan narrated from Abu Haywa, from a man of the people of al-Ribat, that he recited (al-Fuqr) with a dammah on the fa', which is a dialect form, and it was also read (al-Faqar) with two fathahs.

﴿and commands you to indecency﴾, i.e., he incites you to it as one who commands. Al-fahsha' (indecency) is said to be stinginess and withholding charity, or sins in general, or fornication; these are the views. It is also possible that al-fahsha' means foul speech, as the poet said:

"And none among them speaks indecency when they sit with us or with others."

It seems that the Shaytan threatens poverty to the one who wishes to give charity, and when he refuses, he commands him to respond to the beggar with an ugly reply, to rebuke him and humiliate him with harsh words. Ibn Mas'ud narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed, the Shaytan has a whisper (lamma) into the son of Adam, and the angel has a whisper. As for the whisper of the Shaytan, it is a threat of evil and a denial of the truth; whoever experiences that should seek refuge (in Allah). As for the whisper of the angel, it is a promise of truth and confirmation of good; whoever experiences that should praise Allah." Then he (peace be upon him) recited: ﴿The Shaytan threatens you with poverty and commands you to indecency﴾, the verse.

The Shaytan's threat is mentioned before his command, because through the threat one comes to trust him, and when a person trusts him and fears poverty, he gains power over him through the command, since command is a form of superiority over the one commanded.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "The fahish (indecent/miser) in the view of the Arabs is the stingy person." He also said: "He commands you to indecency, and incites you to stinginess and withholding charities," end of quote. Thus the second clause would be a reinforcement of the first. We have considered what the commentators explained about al-fahish in verses such as the poet's words:

"Until he takes refuge with one who is not indecent, sour, nor miserly when his companions have gained."

Another said:

"I see death snatching the noble and choosing the best property of the indecent, the harsh one."

They said: al-fahish is the one of bad character. If al-fahish meant the miser, then his saying "nor miserly" would be a reinforcement. Regarding the words of Imru' al-Qays:

"And a neck like the neck of a gazelle, not indecent."

He said its meaning is "not ugly." Al-Zamakhshari agreed with Abu Muslim in interpreting al-fahish as stingy and al-fahsha' as stinginess, as some said. Abu Muslim recited the words of Tarafa:

"The best property of the indecent, the harsh one."

He said: "The more common usage in Arabic, and in the explanation of the line he recited, is that al-fahish is one who is bad in rejecting his guests and beggars." He said: "We have found after this poetry that supports Abu Muslim's interpretation that al-fahsha' is stinginess," and a rajiz (rajaz poet) of Tayy said:

"The striver has taken what he intended; he is not a fahhash who insists on keeping the provisions."

End of quote. There is no proof in this line that he meant by al-fahhash the miser; rather it is to be understood as bad of character or bad in rejection, and the miser is understood from his saying "yusirru al-zad" (who insists on keeping the provisions).

﴿And Allah promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty﴾, i.e., a covering over your sins as a recompense for giving, and (bounty) is an increase beyond the due reward of giving. It is said: "and bounty" means that He will replace for you something better than what you spent, or a reward for it in the Hereafter (p-320). When His saying ﴿And do not aim at the bad of it to spend﴾ [al-Baqarah: 267] came before, and what drove them to that was only the stinginess and miserliness with the good, which the Shaytan incites, this sentence began with ﴿The Shaytan threatens you with poverty﴾, and that what you give of the bad is only from the prickings of the Shaytan, in order to make ugly to them what they committed by attributing it to the Shaytan, so that it is farthest from him. Then Allah the Exalted mentioned, in contrast to the Shaytan's promise, Allah's promise with two things: first, the covering of the sins they committed; second, the bounty, which is the increase of provision and expansion in this world and the Hereafter. It is narrated that in the Tawrah (Torah) there is: "My servant, spend from My provision, and I will extend My bounty upon you, for My hand is outstretched over every outstretched hand." And in the Book of Allah is its confirmation: ﴿And whatever you spend, He will replace it﴾ [Saba': 39].

﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾, i.e., All-Encompassing in generosity and bounty toward the one who spends, All-Knowing of the intentions of the one who spends. It is said: All-Knowing of where He places His bounty. Hadiths have come concerning the excellence of spending, generosity, and the blame of stinginess, among them the hadith of al-Bara', who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah loves spending and hates withholding. So eat and feed (others), and do not hoard, for then the seeking will become difficult for you." And his (ﷺ) saying: "And what disease is worse than stinginess?"

﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills﴾. Al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham read (tu'ti) with the letter ta' and (tasha'u) with the letter ta', in the second person, which is an iltifat (shift); for it is a shift from the third person absence to direct address. Al-hikmah (wisdom) is the Qur'an; this was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Muqatil and others. Ibn 'Abbas said, as narrated from him by 'Ali ibn Talhah: knowledge of the nasikh (abrogating) and mansukh (abrogated) of the Qur'an, its muhkam (clear) and mutashabih (ambiguous), its earlier and later parts. He also said, as narrated from him by Abu Salih: prophethood. This was said by al-Suddi. Ibrahim, Abu al-'Aliyah, and Qatadah said: understanding of the Qur'an. Mujahid and al-Hasan said: scrupulousness (wara') in the religion of Allah. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: fear (of Allah). Ibn Zayd, and his father Zayd ibn Aslam, said: reason in the matter of Allah. Shurayk said: understanding. Ibn Qutaybah said: knowledge and action; one is not called wise until he combines them. Mujahid also said: writing. Ibn al-Muqaffa' said: what reason testifies to its soundness. Al-Qushayri said, in what Ibn al-Qasim narrated from him: contemplation of the matter of Allah and following Him. He also said: obedience to Allah, jurisprudence, religion, and acting upon it. 'Ata' said: forgiveness. Abu 'Uthman said: a light by which one distinguishes between the whisper (waswas) and the station (maqam). In one copy it was found: "and inspiration" instead of "station." Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad said: that the thought of truth rules over you, not your desire. Bundar ibn al-Husayn said: quickness of reply together with hitting the right answer. Al-Mufaddal said: returning to what is right. Al-Kattani said: that in which the spirits find rest. It was said: a sign without a cause. It was said: making truth a witness in all states. It was said: the soundness of the religion and the reform of the world. It was said: divine knowledge (ilm laduni). It was said: stripping the secret for the arrival of inspiration. It was said: contemplation of Allah the Exalted and following Him. It was said: the sum of what was mentioned before. These are twenty-nine statements of the scholars in the interpretation of wisdom.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said, after mentioning a number of sayings on the interpretation of wisdom, the text of which is: "All these sayings, except the saying of al-Suddi, are close to one another, because wisdom is a verbal noun from ihkam (perfecting), which is perfection in deed or speech, and the Book of Allah is wisdom, and the Sunnah of His Prophet is wisdom, and everything mentioned is a part of the wisdom which is the genus," end of his words.

The interpretation of wisdom has already been given in His saying: ﴿and teaches them the Book and wisdom and purifies them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 129], so it would suffice from repeating its interpretation here; but since sayings are mentioned here that the exegetes did not mention there, it has been explained here.

﴿And whoever is given wisdom﴾. The majority read it in the passive voice, with the unnamed agent, and the pronoun of (man) is the first object of (yu'ta). Ya'qub read (wa-man yu'ti) with a kasrah on the ta', in the active voice. Al-Zamakhshari said: meaning "and whoever Allah gives it to."

If he intended the explanation of meaning, it is correct; but if he intended the explanation of i'rab (grammatical analysis), it is not so: there is no pronoun of the accusative deleted in (yu'ta); rather its object is fronted with the conditional verb, as you say: "Whichever you give a dirham, I will give him a dirham." Al-A'mash read (wa-man yu'tihi al-hikmah) with the affirmation of the pronoun which is the first object of (yu'ta), and the subject in this reading is a hidden pronoun in (yu'ta) referring to Allah the Exalted. The mention of wisdom was repeated and not replaced by a pronoun because it is in another clause, and for emphasis, and to draw attention to its nobility, its excellence, and its qualities.

﴿then he has certainly been given much good﴾. This is the answer of the conditional. The past verb accompanied by qad, which falls as an answer to the condition, may be past in form while future in meaning, as here; this is the true answer. It may also be past in both form and meaning, as in His saying: ﴿And if they deny you, messengers before you have been denied﴾ [Fatir: 4]. The denial of the messengers happened in past time; and if so, it cannot be the answer of the condition, since the condition is future, and what follows a future is future. So the answer in reality is omitted, and this indicates it; the estimation: "And if they deny you, then be consoled; for messengers before you were denied; so your situation with your people is like theirs with their people."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿much good﴾ is an indefinite of magnification, as if he said: then he has been given what much good of any kind," end of his words. What he mentioned requires that in the language of the Arabs there is an indefinite of magnification, and its proof needs to be established. Its estimation as "any much good" is only on the basis that "good" is an adjective of an omitted noun: "then he has been given good, any much good." This requires establishing such a structure from the language of the Arabs. The known rule is that when it is described by ay (which), it is only added to a word like the described noun: you say "I passed by a man, what a man," as the poet said:

"I called a man, what a man, and he answered me, and I and he were refuge and shelter."

If this is established, is it permissible to describe what is added to it? That is: if it is an adjective, you say "I passed by a man, what a noble man," or is it not permissible? The answer requires an auditory proof. Also, in its estimation "ay much good," there is the omission of the described noun and the placement of "ay" in its place as an adjective, and that is not permissible except rarely. You do not say "I saw ay man," meaning "a man, what a man," except in a rare case, like the poet's words:

"When al-Hajjaj fights ay hypocrite, he overcomes him with a sword that cuts whenever it is swung."

He means "a hypocrite, what a hypocrite." Also, in its estimation "much good, what much good," there is the omission of the adjective "ay" and the placement of the added-to word in its place, and the omission of the described noun too, so that both the described noun and the adjective are omitted together; all of this requires a proof for its establishment.

﴿And none remember except people of understanding﴾. Its origin is yatadhakkaru, so the ta' was assimilated into the dhal. "People of understanding" (ulu al-albab) are those with sound minds. In this is an incitement to act by obeying Allah, and to comply with what He commanded regarding spending, and to refrain from what He forbade regarding charity from the bad; a warning against the promise and command of the Shaytan; trust in the promise of Allah; and an alert that wisdom is the reason by which one distinguishes between truth and falsehood. He mentioned remembrance because a sensible person may be struck by heedlessness at times, then he remembers what is the good of his religion and his worldly life, and so he acts upon it.

﴿The Shaytan threatens you with poverty﴾, i.e., he frightens you with poverty. He says to the man: hold back, for if you give charity you will become poor. Abu Hayyan narrated from Abu Haywa, from a man of the people of al-Ribat, that he recited (al-Fuqr) with a dammah on the fa', which is a dialect form, and it was also read (al-Faqar) with two fathahs.

﴿and commands you to indecency﴾, i.e., he incites you to it as one who commands. Al-fahsha' (indecency) is said to be stinginess and withholding charity, or sins in general, or fornication; these are the views. It is also possible that al-fahsha' means foul speech, as the poet said:

"And none among them speaks indecency when they sit with us or with others."

It seems that the Shaytan threatens poverty to the one who wishes to give charity, and when he refuses, he commands him to respond to the beggar with an ugly reply, to rebuke him and humiliate him with harsh words. Ibn Mas'ud narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed, the Shaytan has a whisper (lamma) into the son of Adam, and the angel has a whisper. As for the whisper of the Shaytan, it is a threat of evil and a denial of the truth; whoever experiences that should seek refuge (in Allah). As for the whisper of the angel, it is a promise of truth and confirmation of good; whoever experiences that should praise Allah." Then he (peace be upon him) recited: ﴿The Shaytan threatens you with poverty and commands you to indecency﴾, the verse.

The Shaytan's threat is mentioned before his command, because through the threat one comes to trust him, and when a person trusts him and fears poverty, he gains power over him through the command, since command is a form of superiority over the one commanded.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "The fahish (indecent/miser) in the view of the Arabs is the stingy person." He also said: "He commands you to indecency, and incites you to stinginess and withholding charities," end of quote. Thus the second clause would be a reinforcement of the first. We have considered what the commentators explained about al-fahish in verses such as the poet's words:

"Until he takes refuge with one who is not indecent, sour, nor miserly when his companions have gained."

Another said:

"I see death snatching the noble and choosing the best property of the indecent, the harsh one."

They said: al-fahish is the one of bad character. If al-fahish meant the miser, then his saying "nor miserly" would be a reinforcement. Regarding the words of Imru' al-Qays:

"And a neck like the neck of a gazelle, not indecent."

He said its meaning is "not ugly." Al-Zamakhshari agreed with Abu Muslim in interpreting al-fahish as stingy and al-fahsha' as stinginess, as some said. Abu Muslim recited the words of Tarafa:

"The best property of the indecent, the harsh one."

He said: "The more common usage in Arabic, and in the explanation of the line he recited, is that al-fahish is one who is bad in rejecting his guests and beggars." He said: "We have found after this poetry that supports Abu Muslim's interpretation that al-fahsha' is stinginess," and a rajiz (rajaz poet) of Tayy said:

"The striver has taken what he intended; he is not a fahhash who insists on keeping the provisions."

End of quote. There is no proof in this line that he meant by al-fahhash the miser; rather it is to be understood as bad of character or bad in rejection, and the miser is understood from his saying "yusirru al-zad" (who insists on keeping the provisions).

﴿And Allah promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty﴾, i.e., a covering over your sins as a recompense for giving, and (bounty) is an increase beyond the due reward of giving. It is said: "and bounty" means that He will replace for you something better than what you spent, or a reward for it in the Hereafter (p-320). When His saying ﴿And do not aim at the bad of it to spend﴾ [al-Baqarah: 267] came before, and what drove them to that was only the stinginess and miserliness with the good, which the Shaytan incites, this sentence began with ﴿The Shaytan threatens you with poverty﴾, and that what you give of the bad is only from the prickings of the Shaytan, in order to make ugly to them what they committed by attributing it to the Shaytan, so that it is farthest from him. Then Allah the Exalted mentioned, in contrast to the Shaytan's promise, Allah's promise with two things: first, the covering of the sins they committed; second, the bounty, which is the increase of provision and expansion in this world and the Hereafter. It is narrated that in the Tawrah (Torah) there is: "My servant, spend from My provision, and I will extend My bounty upon you, for My hand is outstretched over every outstretched hand." And in the Book of Allah is its confirmation: ﴿And whatever you spend, He will replace it﴾ [Saba': 39].

﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾, i.e., All-Encompassing in generosity and bounty toward the one who spends, All-Knowing of the intentions of the one who spends. It is said: All-Knowing of where He places His bounty. Hadiths have come concerning the excellence of spending, generosity, and the blame of stinginess, among them the hadith of al-Bara', who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah loves spending and hates withholding. So eat and feed (others), and do not hoard, for then the seeking will become difficult for you." And his (ﷺ) saying: "And what disease is worse than stinginess?"

﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills﴾. Al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham read (tu'ti) with the letter ta' and (tasha'u) with the letter ta', in the second person, which is an iltifat (shift); for it is a shift from the third person absence to direct address. Al-hikmah (wisdom) is the Qur'an; this was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Muqatil and others. Ibn 'Abbas said, as narrated from him by 'Ali ibn Talhah: knowledge of the nasikh (abrogating) and mansukh (abrogated) of the Qur'an, its muhkam (clear) and mutashabih (ambiguous), its earlier and later parts. He also said, as narrated from him by Abu Salih: prophethood. This was said by al-Suddi. Ibrahim, Abu al-'Aliyah, and Qatadah said: understanding of the Qur'an. Mujahid and al-Hasan said: scrupulousness (wara') in the religion of Allah. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: fear (of Allah). Ibn Zayd, and his father Zayd ibn Aslam, said: reason in the matter of Allah. Shurayk said: understanding. Ibn Qutaybah said: knowledge and action; one is not called wise until he combines them. Mujahid also said: writing. Ibn al-Muqaffa' said: what reason testifies to its soundness. Al-Qushayri said, in what Ibn al-Qasim narrated from him: contemplation of the matter of Allah and following Him. He also said: obedience to Allah, jurisprudence, religion, and acting upon it. 'Ata' said: forgiveness. Abu 'Uthman said: a light by which one distinguishes between the whisper (waswas) and the station (maqam). In one copy it was found: "and inspiration" instead of "station." Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad said: that the thought of truth rules over you, not your desire. Bundar ibn al-Husayn said: quickness of reply together with hitting the right answer. Al-Mufaddal said: returning to what is right. Al-Kattani said: that in which the spirits find rest. It was said: a sign without a cause. It was said: making truth a witness in all states. It was said: the soundness of the religion and the reform of the world. It was said: divine knowledge (ilm laduni). It was said: stripping the secret for the arrival of inspiration. It was said: contemplation of Allah the Exalted and following Him. It was said: the sum of what was mentioned before. These are twenty-nine statements of the scholars in the interpretation of wisdom.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said, after mentioning a number of sayings on the interpretation of wisdom, the text of which is: "All these sayings, except the saying of al-Suddi, are close to one another, because wisdom is a verbal noun from ihkam (perfecting), which is perfection in deed or speech, and the Book of Allah is wisdom, and the Sunnah of His Prophet is wisdom, and everything mentioned is a part of the wisdom which is the genus," end of his words.

The interpretation of wisdom has already been given in His saying: ﴿and teaches them the Book and wisdom and purifies them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 129], so it would suffice from repeating its interpretation here; but since sayings are mentioned here that the exegetes did not mention there, it has been explained here.

﴿And whoever is given wisdom﴾. The majority read it in the passive voice, with the unnamed agent, and the pronoun of (man) is the first object of (yu'ta). Ya'qub read (wa-man yu'ti) with a kasrah on the ta', in the active voice. Al-Zamakhshari said: meaning "and whoever Allah gives it to."

If he intended the explanation of meaning, it is correct; but if he intended the explanation of i'rab (grammatical analysis), it is not so: there is no pronoun of the accusative deleted in (yu'ta); rather its object is fronted with the conditional verb, as you say: "Whichever you give a dirham, I will give him a dirham." Al-A'mash read (wa-man yu'tihi al-hikmah) with the affirmation of the pronoun which is the first object of (yu'ta), and the subject in this reading is a hidden pronoun in (yu'ta) referring to Allah the Exalted. The mention of wisdom was repeated and not replaced by a pronoun because it is in another clause, and for emphasis, and to draw attention to its nobility, its excellence, and its qualities.

﴿then he has certainly been given much good﴾. This is the answer of the conditional. The past verb accompanied by qad, which falls as an answer to the condition, may be past in form while future in meaning, as here; this is the true answer. It may also be past in both form and meaning, as in His saying: ﴿And if they deny you, messengers before you have been denied﴾ [Fatir: 4]. The denial of the messengers happened in past time; and if so, it cannot be the answer of the condition, since the condition is future, and what follows a future is future. So the answer in reality is omitted, and this indicates it; the estimation: "And if they deny you, then be consoled; for messengers before you were denied; so your situation with your people is like theirs with their people."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿much good﴾ is an indefinite of magnification, as if he said: then he has been given what much good of any kind," end of his words. What he mentioned requires that in the language of the Arabs there is an indefinite of magnification, and its proof needs to be established. Its estimation as "any much good" is only on the basis that "good" is an adjective of an omitted noun: "then he has been given good, any much good." This requires establishing such a structure from the language of the Arabs. The known rule is that when it is described by ay (which), it is only added to a word like the described noun: you say "I passed by a man, what a man," as the poet said:

"I called a man, what a man, and he answered me, and I and he were refuge and shelter."

If this is established, is it permissible to describe what is added to it? That is: if it is an adjective, you say "I passed by a man, what a noble man," or is it not permissible? The answer requires an auditory proof. Also, in its estimation "ay much good," there is the omission of the described noun and the placement of "ay" in its place as an adjective, and that is not permissible except rarely. You do not say "I saw ay man," meaning "a man, what a man," except in a rare case, like the poet's words:

"When al-Hajjaj fights ay hypocrite, he overcomes him with a sword that cuts whenever it is swung."

He means "a hypocrite, what a hypocrite." Also, in its estimation "much good, what much good," there is the omission of the adjective "ay" and the placement of the added-to word in its place, and the omission of the described noun too, so that both the described noun and the adjective are omitted together; all of this requires a proof for its establishment.

﴿And none remember except people of understanding﴾. Its origin is yatadhakkaru, so the ta' was assimilated into the dhal. "People of understanding" (ulu al-albab) are those with sound minds. In this is an incitement to act by obeying Allah, and to comply with what He commanded regarding spending, and to refrain from what He forbade regarding charity from the bad; a warning against the promise and command of the Shaytan; trust in the promise of Allah; and an alert that wisdom is the reason by which one distinguishes between truth and falsehood. He mentioned remembrance because a sensible person may be struck by heedlessness at times, then he remembers what is the good of his religion and his worldly life, and so he acts upon it.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 270–271 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿Whatever expenditure you spend or whatever vow you vow, indeed Allah knows it﴾ (p-322). Its apparent meaning is generality, covering every charity given in the way of Allah or in the way of Satan. Likewise, the vow is general, whether it is a vow of obedience to Allah or of disobedience to Him. He used the specifier (tamyiz) in His saying ﴿of expenditure﴾ and ﴿of vow﴾, although it is understood from His saying ﴿whatever you spend﴾ and from His saying ﴿or whatever vow you vow﴾, in order to emphasise that both the little and the much are included. And they do not spend any expenditure, small or large. It has been said that "expenditure" is restricted to zakat, because the obligatory act is joined to it, and that is the vow. The vow is of two kinds: forbidden, which is every vow made in other than obedience to Allah, and most of the vows of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic period) were of this kind; and permissible, which is either conditional or unconditional, and both are explicit, such as: "If I am cured of such-and-such illness, then upon me is a charity of a dinar," and such as: "For Allah upon me is the freeing of a slave." And it is non-explicit, such as: "If I am cured, then upon me is a charity or a vow." The rulings on vows are mentioned in the books of jurisprudence (fiqh). Mujahid said: the meaning of ﴿knows it﴾ is "counts it." Al-Zajjaj said: "He will reward for it." It has been said: "He will preserve it." These sayings are close in meaning.

This verse includes a promise and a warning, by making Allah's knowledge follow what they spent or vowed. ﴿Of expenditure﴾ and ﴿of vow﴾ have had their parallels discussed in the section on i'rab (grammatical analysis), so they are not repeated here. In His saying ﴿of vow﴾ there is an indication of the omission of a relative pronoun before ﴿you vowed﴾, its estimated form being: "or what you vowed of a vow." This is because ﴿of vow﴾ is an explanation and clarification of that omitted element, and it was omitted because it is known, and because of the indication of what is in His saying ﴿whatever you spent﴾ upon it, just as it was omitted in the poet's saying:

"Is it one of you who satirises the Messenger of Allah, while praising him and supporting him is equal?"

The estimate is: "and who praises him." Its omission is due to the indication of "who" (man) preceding it. Based on this established omission of the relative pronoun, the pronoun came singular in His saying ﴿indeed Allah knows it﴾, because the conjunction is ﴿aw﴾ (or). When the conjunction is ﴿aw﴾, the pronoun is singular, because the thing judged is one of them. Sometimes the first mentioned is taken into account, as in: "Zayd or Hind is departing (masc.)." Sometimes the second is taken into account, as in: "Zayd or Hind is departing (fem.)." As for it agreeing with what precedes it in dual or plural, this is not the case. For this reason the grammarians interpreted His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If he is rich or poor, then Allah is more entitled to both of them﴾ [al-Nisa: 135], by the interpretation mentioned in the science of grammar (nahw). And according to the path we have described, there came His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when they see a trade or a diversion, they rush to it﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 11], and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever earns a sin or a wrong, then throws it upon an innocent person﴾ [al-Nisa: 112], just as there came in this verse: ﴿indeed Allah knows it﴾. When knowledge of these rulings was absent from a group of those who spoke on the interpretation (tafsir) of this verse, they made the singular pronoun among what needs interpretation. It is related from al-Nahhas that he said: the estimate is: "Whatever expenditure you spend, indeed Allah knows it, or whatever vow you vow, indeed Allah knows it," then it was omitted. He said: this is like His saying: ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it﴾ [al-Tawbah: 34], and His saying: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer, and indeed it is difficult﴾ [al-Baqarah: 45], and the saying of the poet:

"We are with what we have, and you are with what you have, content, though opinions differ."

And the saying of another:

"He threw me with a matter from which I and my father were innocent, and for the sake of the well he threw me."

The estimate is: "We are content with what we have, and I was innocent of it, and my father was innocent," end of quote. Thus he treated ﴿aw﴾ in that as if it were ﴿waw﴾ (and). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: he made the pronoun singular in ﴿knows it﴾ although he mentioned two things, because he intended what was mentioned or explicitly stated, end of quote.

Al-Qurtubi said: this is good, for the pronoun may refer to all that was mentioned, even if it is many, end of quote. The ruling on ﴿aw﴾ has already been mentioned earlier, and it differs from ﴿waw﴾ in this respect. There is no need for Ibn 'Atiyyah's interpretation, because the verse came in accordance with the established rule in the language of the Arabs concerning ﴿aw﴾.

﴿And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾. Its apparent meaning is generality, so every wrongdoer finds no one to help him and prevent him from Allah. Muqatil said: they are the polytheists. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: they are those who spend with reminders (of their favour), with harm, and with show, and those who squander in disobedience.
