It has been said: those who spend what is unlawful.

Al-ansar (the helpers) means the assistants, plural of nasir, like habib and ahbab, and sharif and ashraf, or plural of nasir (helper, active participle), like shahid and ashhad. It came in plural form because what precedes it is plural, as in His saying: ﴿And they have no helpers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 22]. The singular corresponds to the singular, as in: ﴿You have no protector from Allah, nor helper﴾ [al-Baqarah: 120]. It cannot be said that the absence of the plural does not indicate the absence of the singular, because this is in the context of negating benefit and sufficiency and the attainment of assistance. If the plural does not find help and is not sufficient, then the singular is more fitting not to be useful or sufficient.

When Allah, may He be exalted, explained the virtue of spending in His way and urged it, and warned us against leaning towards the incitements of Satan, and reminded us of the promise of Allah which combines the happiness of the Hereafter and this world, of forgiveness and bounty, and explained that this matter and the difference between the two promises is not grasped except by one who has been specialised in wisdom, which Allah gives to whom He wills of His servants, He returned to the mention of expenditure and urging towards it, and that it is recorded with One who does not forget and does not err. The mention of wisdom, although connected to what preceded, became like a digression (istitrad), and an alerting to its mention and urging to know it.

﴿If you disclose the charities﴾, that is: if you make manifest the giving of charities. Al-Kalbi said: "When the verse ﴿Whatever expenditure you spend﴾ was revealed, they said: O Messenger of Allah, is secret charity better or open charity? So He revealed: ﴿If you disclose the charities﴾." Yazid ibn Abi Habib said: it was revealed concerning charity to the Jews and Christians, and he used to command the distribution of zakat in secret. The word ﴿the charities﴾ has apparent generality, so it includes obligatory and voluntary charity.

It has been said that the alif and lam are for definiteness (al-'ahd), so they are directed to obligatory charity, for zakat abrogated (naskh) all charities. This was said by al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Yazid ibn Abi Habib. It has also been said: the intended meaning here is voluntary charity, not the obligatory, and this is the view of the majority of the exegetes, and it was said by Sufyan al-Thawri.

They differed over whether it is better to make obligatory charity manifest or to hide it. Ibn 'Abbas and others held that making it manifest is better than hiding it, and al-Tabari related a consensus on it, and al-Qadi Abu Ya'la adopted it. Ibn 'Abbas also said: hiding voluntary charity is better than making it manifest. It is related from him: secret voluntary charities are seventy times better than public ones, and public obligatory charity is twenty-five times better than its secret form.

Al-Qurtubi said: such a matter is not said by opinion (ra'y); it is only by revelation (tawqif). Qatadah said: hiding both is better. Al-Zajjaj said: during the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, hiding zakat was better, but today people think ill, so making it manifest is better. Ibn al-'Arabi said: there is no sound hadith on the preference of secret charity over public charity, nor of public charity over secret charity.

﴿So how excellent it is﴾. The fa' is the response to the condition. Ni'ma is a verb that does not inflect, so the response needed the fa'. The agent (fa'il) of ni'ma is a hidden pronoun explained by an indefinite noun which is not singular in existence, such as "shams and qamar" (sun and moon), nor highly vague, such as ghayr, nor a superlative (af'al al-tafdil), such as "afdal minka" (better than you). The example is: "ni'ma rajulan ka-Zayd" (what an excellent man, like Zayd). The hidden pronoun is singular even if its specifier is dual or plural. They have analysed ma here as a specifier of that hidden pronoun in ni'ma, estimating it as "shay'an" (a thing). So ma is an indefinite complete (tamma) noun, neither a qualifier nor a relative. The discussion of the ma attached to these two verbs, namely ni'ma and bi'sa, has already been made at His saying: ﴿How wretched is what they sold themselves for, that they disbelieve﴾ [al-Baqarah: 90], and we mentioned the views of people concerning it, so that suffices and it is not repeated here. The pronoun ha' in "fa-ni'ma hiya" refers to the charities. It is either by omitting a modifier, meaning "so excellent is their disclosure," or it may not involve omission, but refers to the charities with the qualification of disclosure, the estimate being: "so excellent are the disclosed charities," and they are the subject (mubtada'), the predicate being the praise clause, and the connecting element is the generality in the pronoun hidden in ni'ma.

Ibn Kathir, Warsh, and Hafs read ﴿fa-ni'immā﴾ with kasra on the nun and the 'ayn, here and in al-Nisa. The reading's basis is that it follows the dialect of those who vocalise the 'ayn, saying ni'im, and they make the vowel of the nun follow the vowel of the 'ayn. Vocalising the 'ayn is the original form, and it is the dialect of Hudhayl. It cannot be on the dialect of those who make the 'ayn quiescent, because it would become like "jism malik," and that cannot be assimilated (idgham) according to what they mentioned.

Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read ﴿fa-na'immā﴾ in both places, with fatha on the nun and kasra on the 'ayn, which is the original form, because its pattern is fa'ila. Some said: the reading with kasra on the 'ayn may be on the dialect of those who make it quiescent, so when ma entered and was assimilated, the 'ayn was vocalised to avoid meeting two quiescent letters. Abu 'Amr, Qalun, and Abu Bakr read with kasra on the nun and with the vowel of the 'ayn hidden (ikhfa'), and it is related from them that it is quiescent. The first is more analogical and more well known. The basis of the hidden vowel is seeking lightness. As for quiescence, Abu 'Ubayd chose it and said: quiescence, as is related, is the dialect of the Prophet ﷺ in this word. He said to 'Amr ibn al-'As: "What an excellent wealth is the righteous wealth for the righteous man." Abu al-'Abbas, Abu Ishaq, and Abu 'Ali rejected quiescence, because it involves joining two quiescent letters in a way not according to its rule. Abu al-'Abbas said: no one can pronounce it; one only intends to join two quiescent letters, and it is vocalised and does not come out. Abu Ishaq said: the narrators did not precisely record the wording in the hadith. Abu 'Ali said: perhaps Abu 'Amr hid the vowel, so the listener thought it was quiescence. Much of what the readers have reported has been rejected, so among that is the quiescence in this place, in some of al-Bazzi's variants, in ﴿istata'u﴾ and in ﴿yakhissimun﴾. End of what was summarised from their speech.

The rejection by these people is open to question, because the imams of the readings read only by transmission from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and if error is admitted in what they transmitted of a case like this, it is admitted regarding anything else. What we choose and say is that the transmission of the seven readings is mutawatir (successively transmitted), and error in it is not possible.

﴿And if you conceal them﴾. The pronoun in the accusative in ﴿you conceal them﴾ refers to the charities, both in wording and in meaning, whatever way the charities are interpreted. It has been said: the disclosed charities are the obligatory, and the concealed are the voluntary, so the pronoun has returned to the charities in wording only, not in meaning. This is like the phrase: "'indi dirham wa nisfuhu" (I have a dirham and its half), meaning half of another dirham. Similarly, "wa in tukhfuha" means: "and if you conceal the charities other than the first," which is voluntary charity. This is contrary to the apparent meaning and to the more common usage of the Arabic language. In the case of "'indi dirham wa nisfuhu," we only needed to say that the pronoun refers to the dirham in wording and not in meaning, because the meaning compels this, since the speaker does not mean that he has a dirham and half of this dirham which he has. Likewise the poet's saying:

"As if the garments of its rider, by a wind that tears them, while it is calm in its blowing."

He means: a different wind, calm in its blowing.

﴿And give them to the poor﴾. In it there is an alert to seeking out their recipients and ensuring this, and they are the poor.

Translation of the passage (part 2 of 2):

﴿فَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ﴾ The fa' is the response of the conditional, and the pronoun (huwa) refers back to the verbal noun implied by His words ﴿وإنْ تُخْفُوها﴾. The estimated sense is: "then concealing is better for you." It is also possible that (khayrun) here is meant as "a good among goods," and (lakum) is in the position of a qualifier, so it is attached to an omitted element. The apparent reading is that it is the comparative form (af'al al-tafdil), and the thing compared to, which is omitted because the meaning points to it, is (al-ibda') [showing/disclosing], so the estimate is: "it is better for you than showing them." The apparent sense of the verse is that concealing acts of charity in general is superior, whether they are obligatory or voluntary. This is superior because the giver who conceals them is further removed from ostentation (riya'), reminding of favour (mann), and harm (adha). Even if he does not inform the poor person of himself, and conceals the charity from him so that he does not know, it is better and more beautiful, because of the purity of intention in that.

Some of the wise said: "When you do a good deed, conceal it, and when a good deed is done to you, make it known." Al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib said: "A good deed is not complete except with three qualities: hastening it, belittling it in your own eyes, and concealing it. When you hasten it, you make it pleasant; when you belittle it, you magnify it; and when you conceal it, you perfect it." Sahl ibn Harun said:

"He hides his good deeds, and God displays them;
indeed, a beauty, when you hide it, shows itself."

In "al-ibda' wa al-ikhfa'" there is a verbal antithesis (tibaq lafzi). In His words ﴿وتُؤْتُوها الفُقَراءَ﴾ there is a semantic antithesis (tibaq ma'nawi), because only the wealthy give charities, so it is as if it was said: "If the wealthy show the charities..." In this verse there is evidence that charity is a right of the poor, and there is evidence that it is permissible for the owner of property to distribute the charity himself.

﴿ويُكَفِّرُ عَنْكم مِن سَيِّئاتِكُمْ﴾ The majority read (wayukaffiru) with the waw, and it is read without the waw, and with the ya' and the ta' and the nun, with kasr and fath of the fa', and with raf', jazm and nasb of the ra'. Dropping the waw was transmitted by Abu Hatim from al-A'mash, and he reported from him that he read with ya' and jazm of the ra'; its basis is that it is a substitute (badal) for the position of His words ﴿فَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ﴾, since it is in the jussive position, and the meaning is as if: "concealing would be better for you than showing," or it is by the implied particle of conjunction, i.e., "and He will expiate."

Ibn Amir read with ya' and raf' of the ra'. Al-Hasan read with ya' and jazm of the ra', and it is reported from al-A'mash with ya' and nasb of the ra'. Ibn Abbas read with ta' and jazm of the ra', and likewise Ikrimah, except that he made the fa' fath and made the verb passive, whose subject is not named. Ibn Hurmuz, as transmitted from him by al-Mahdawi, read with ta' and raf' of the ra', and it is reported from Ikrimah and Shahr ibn Hawshab: with ta' and nasb of the ra'. Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr and Abu Bakr read with nun and raf' of the ra'. Nafi', Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read with nun and jazm.

It is reported that khafd [i.e., the genitive reading] of the ra' is from al-A'mash with nun and nasb of the ra' for the one who read with ya'.

The more evident view is that the verb is attributed to God Most High, like the reading of the one who read "wa-nukaffiru" with nun, since its pronoun is for God Most High without doubt. It was also said: it refers to al-sarf, i.e., the diverting of the charities. It is possible that it relies on concealment, i.e., "and He expiates the concealing of charities." He attributed the expiation to Him by way of metaphor, because He is the cause of expiation. As for the one who read with ta', the pronoun in the verb is for the charities. As for the one who read the ra' with raf', it is possible that the verb is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "and We expiate," or "and He expiates," i.e., God; or the concealing, i.e., "and it expiates," i.e., the charity.

It is possible that it is a resumed statement (mustanaf) with no place in i'rab, and the waw has conjoined one sentence to another. It is possible that it is conjoined to the position of what follows the fa', since if a present verb occurred after it, it would be raf'; like His words ﴿ومَن عادَ فَيَنْتَقِمُ اللَّهُ مِنهُ﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95]. As for the one who read the ra' with jazm, it is by observing the clause that came as the response (jaza'), since it is in a jussive position, like His words ﴿مَن يُضْلِلِ اللَّهُ فَلا هادِيَ لَهُ﴾ [al-A'raf: 186].

As for "nadharhum" in the reading of the one who read with jazm, and "nadharahum" for the one who read with nasb of the ra', it is by implying (an) [the particle "that"], and it is conjunction to an assumed verbal noun (masdar mutawahham). Its parallel is the reading of the one who read ﴿يُحاسِبْكم بِهِ اللَّهُ فَيَغْفِرُ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 284] with nasb of the ra'. However, here it is difficult to estimate that assumed verbal noun from His words "fa-huwa khayrun lakum," so it requires some strained analysis, unlike His words "yuhasibkum": for it one estimates "there occurs a reckoning, then forgiveness."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Its meaning is: and if you conceal them, it would be better for you, and that We expiate for you," end of quote.

The apparent sense of his statement is that his estimate "and that We expiate" is governed by a verbal noun, and is conjoined to "khayran," the predicate of the "yakun" he estimated, as if he said: "concealing would be good for you and an expiation," so "an yukaffira" is in the position of nasb.

What is established among the Basrans is that this verbal noun formed from the implied "an" with the verb following it in the nasb is raf', conjoined to an assumed raf' verbal noun, whose estimate is drawn from the meaning. So when you say: "You do not come to us so that you speak to us," the estimate is: "there is not from you a coming and then a speaking." Likewise, "If you come and do good to me, I will do good to you," the estimate is: "if there is from you a coming and a good deed, I will do good to you." Likewise, what follows the response of the conditional, like the estimate we gave for "yuhasibkum bihi Allah" [al-Baqarah: 284] in the reading of the one who made "fayaghfir" nasb. On this basis the estimate is: "and if you conceal them and give them to the poor, there will be an increase of good for concealing over good for showing, and an expiation."

Al-Mahdawi said: as for nasb of the ra': it is made similar to nasb in the response of a question, since the reward is what makes the thing necessary through the necessity of something else, like the question. Ibn Atiyyah said: jazm of the ra' is the most eloquent of these readings, because it indicates the inclusion of the expiation in the condition, and its being conditioned on concealment occurring. As for raf' of the ra', there is no such meaning in it, end of quote.

We say: raf' is more emphatic and more general, because jazm is taken as conjoined to the second conditional response, while raf' is a substitute, on the basis that the expiation is necessarily consequent on the giving of charities, whether you show them or conceal them. For we know that this expiation is connected to what precedes it, and the expiation would be restricted to concealment alone if jazm were read, since jazm restricts it to that. It cannot be said that one who shows charities does not have his evil deeds expiated, for then the expiation would encompass both kinds, showing and concealing charities, even if concealing is better than showing.

The "min" in His words "min sayyi'atikum" is for partition (tab'id), because charity does not expiate all evil deeds. Al-Tabari transmitted from a group who said that "min" is superfluous in this place. Ibn Atiyyah said: that is an error from them, and the statement of one who made it causal and estimated "min ajli dhunubikum" [because of your sins] is weak.

﴿واللَّهُ بِما تَعْمَلُونَ خَبِيرٌ﴾ God concluded with this attribute, because it indicates knowledge of what is subtle among things and hidden. Concealment is suitably concluded with the attribute connected to what is hidden. And God knows best.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 270–271 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿Whatever expenditure you spend or whatever vow you vow, indeed Allah knows it﴾ (p-322). Its apparent meaning is generality, covering every charity given in the way of Allah or in the way of Satan. Likewise, the vow is general, whether it is a vow of obedience to Allah or of disobedience to Him. He used the specifier (tamyiz) in His saying ﴿of expenditure﴾ and ﴿of vow﴾, although it is understood from His saying ﴿whatever you spend﴾ and from His saying ﴿or whatever vow you vow﴾, in order to emphasise that both the little and the much are included. And they do not spend any expenditure, small or large. It has been said that "expenditure" is restricted to zakat, because the obligatory act is joined to it, and that is the vow. The vow is of two kinds: forbidden, which is every vow made in other than obedience to Allah, and most of the vows of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic period) were of this kind; and permissible, which is either conditional or unconditional, and both are explicit, such as: "If I am cured of such-and-such illness, then upon me is a charity of a dinar," and such as: "For Allah upon me is the freeing of a slave." And it is non-explicit, such as: "If I am cured, then upon me is a charity or a vow." The rulings on vows are mentioned in the books of jurisprudence (fiqh). Mujahid said: the meaning of ﴿knows it﴾ is "counts it." Al-Zajjaj said: "He will reward for it." It has been said: "He will preserve it." These sayings are close in meaning.

This verse includes a promise and a warning, by making Allah's knowledge follow what they spent or vowed. ﴿Of expenditure﴾ and ﴿of vow﴾ have had their parallels discussed in the section on i'rab (grammatical analysis), so they are not repeated here. In His saying ﴿of vow﴾ there is an indication of the omission of a relative pronoun before ﴿you vowed﴾, its estimated form being: "or what you vowed of a vow." This is because ﴿of vow﴾ is an explanation and clarification of that omitted element, and it was omitted because it is known, and because of the indication of what is in His saying ﴿whatever you spent﴾ upon it, just as it was omitted in the poet's saying:

"Is it one of you who satirises the Messenger of Allah, while praising him and supporting him is equal?"

The estimate is: "and who praises him." Its omission is due to the indication of "who" (man) preceding it. Based on this established omission of the relative pronoun, the pronoun came singular in His saying ﴿indeed Allah knows it﴾, because the conjunction is ﴿aw﴾ (or). When the conjunction is ﴿aw﴾, the pronoun is singular, because the thing judged is one of them. Sometimes the first mentioned is taken into account, as in: "Zayd or Hind is departing (masc.)." Sometimes the second is taken into account, as in: "Zayd or Hind is departing (fem.)." As for it agreeing with what precedes it in dual or plural, this is not the case. For this reason the grammarians interpreted His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If he is rich or poor, then Allah is more entitled to both of them﴾ [al-Nisa: 135], by the interpretation mentioned in the science of grammar (nahw). And according to the path we have described, there came His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when they see a trade or a diversion, they rush to it﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 11], and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever earns a sin or a wrong, then throws it upon an innocent person﴾ [al-Nisa: 112], just as there came in this verse: ﴿indeed Allah knows it﴾. When knowledge of these rulings was absent from a group of those who spoke on the interpretation (tafsir) of this verse, they made the singular pronoun among what needs interpretation. It is related from al-Nahhas that he said: the estimate is: "Whatever expenditure you spend, indeed Allah knows it, or whatever vow you vow, indeed Allah knows it," then it was omitted. He said: this is like His saying: ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it﴾ [al-Tawbah: 34], and His saying: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer, and indeed it is difficult﴾ [al-Baqarah: 45], and the saying of the poet:

"We are with what we have, and you are with what you have, content, though opinions differ."

And the saying of another:

"He threw me with a matter from which I and my father were innocent, and for the sake of the well he threw me."

The estimate is: "We are content with what we have, and I was innocent of it, and my father was innocent," end of quote. Thus he treated ﴿aw﴾ in that as if it were ﴿waw﴾ (and). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: he made the pronoun singular in ﴿knows it﴾ although he mentioned two things, because he intended what was mentioned or explicitly stated, end of quote.

Al-Qurtubi said: this is good, for the pronoun may refer to all that was mentioned, even if it is many, end of quote. The ruling on ﴿aw﴾ has already been mentioned earlier, and it differs from ﴿waw﴾ in this respect. There is no need for Ibn 'Atiyyah's interpretation, because the verse came in accordance with the established rule in the language of the Arabs concerning ﴿aw﴾.

﴿And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾. Its apparent meaning is generality, so every wrongdoer finds no one to help him and prevent him from Allah. Muqatil said: they are the polytheists. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: they are those who spend with reminders (of their favour), with harm, and with show, and those who squander in disobedience. It has been said: those who spend what is unlawful.

Al-ansar (the helpers) means the assistants, plural of nasir, like habib and ahbab, and sharif and ashraf, or plural of nasir (helper, active participle), like shahid and ashhad. It came in plural form because what precedes it is plural, as in His saying: ﴿And they have no helpers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 22]. The singular corresponds to the singular, as in: ﴿You have no protector from Allah, nor helper﴾ [al-Baqarah: 120]. It cannot be said that the absence of the plural does not indicate the absence of the singular, because this is in the context of negating benefit and sufficiency and the attainment of assistance. If the plural does not find help and is not sufficient, then the singular is more fitting not to be useful or sufficient.

When Allah, may He be exalted, explained the virtue of spending in His way and urged it, and warned us against leaning towards the incitements of Satan, and reminded us of the promise of Allah which combines the happiness of the Hereafter and this world, of forgiveness and bounty, and explained that this matter and the difference between the two promises is not grasped except by one who has been specialised in wisdom, which Allah gives to whom He wills of His servants, He returned to the mention of expenditure and urging towards it, and that it is recorded with One who does not forget and does not err. The mention of wisdom, although connected to what preceded, became like a digression (istitrad), and an alerting to its mention and urging to know it.

﴿If you disclose the charities﴾, that is: if you make manifest the giving of charities. Al-Kalbi said: "When the verse ﴿Whatever expenditure you spend﴾ was revealed, they said: O Messenger of Allah, is secret charity better or open charity? So He revealed: ﴿If you disclose the charities﴾." Yazid ibn Abi Habib said: it was revealed concerning charity to the Jews and Christians, and he used to command the distribution of zakat in secret. The word ﴿the charities﴾ has apparent generality, so it includes obligatory and voluntary charity.

It has been said that the alif and lam are for definiteness (al-'ahd), so they are directed to obligatory charity, for zakat abrogated (naskh) all charities. This was said by al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Yazid ibn Abi Habib. It has also been said: the intended meaning here is voluntary charity, not the obligatory, and this is the view of the majority of the exegetes, and it was said by Sufyan al-Thawri.

They differed over whether it is better to make obligatory charity manifest or to hide it. Ibn 'Abbas and others held that making it manifest is better than hiding it, and al-Tabari related a consensus on it, and al-Qadi Abu Ya'la adopted it. Ibn 'Abbas also said: hiding voluntary charity is better than making it manifest. It is related from him: secret voluntary charities are seventy times better than public ones, and public obligatory charity is twenty-five times better than its secret form.

Al-Qurtubi said: such a matter is not said by opinion (ra'y); it is only by revelation (tawqif). Qatadah said: hiding both is better. Al-Zajjaj said: during the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, hiding zakat was better, but today people think ill, so making it manifest is better. Ibn al-'Arabi said: there is no sound hadith on the preference of secret charity over public charity, nor of public charity over secret charity.

﴿So how excellent it is﴾. The fa' is the response to the condition. Ni'ma is a verb that does not inflect, so the response needed the fa'. The agent (fa'il) of ni'ma is a hidden pronoun explained by an indefinite noun which is not singular in existence, such as "shams and qamar" (sun and moon), nor highly vague, such as ghayr, nor a superlative (af'al al-tafdil), such as "afdal minka" (better than you). The example is: "ni'ma rajulan ka-Zayd" (what an excellent man, like Zayd). The hidden pronoun is singular even if its specifier is dual or plural. They have analysed ma here as a specifier of that hidden pronoun in ni'ma, estimating it as "shay'an" (a thing). So ma is an indefinite complete (tamma) noun, neither a qualifier nor a relative. The discussion of the ma attached to these two verbs, namely ni'ma and bi'sa, has already been made at His saying: ﴿How wretched is what they sold themselves for, that they disbelieve﴾ [al-Baqarah: 90], and we mentioned the views of people concerning it, so that suffices and it is not repeated here. The pronoun ha' in "fa-ni'ma hiya" refers to the charities. It is either by omitting a modifier, meaning "so excellent is their disclosure," or it may not involve omission, but refers to the charities with the qualification of disclosure, the estimate being: "so excellent are the disclosed charities," and they are the subject (mubtada'), the predicate being the praise clause, and the connecting element is the generality in the pronoun hidden in ni'ma.

Ibn Kathir, Warsh, and Hafs read ﴿fa-ni'immā﴾ with kasra on the nun and the 'ayn, here and in al-Nisa. The reading's basis is that it follows the dialect of those who vocalise the 'ayn, saying ni'im, and they make the vowel of the nun follow the vowel of the 'ayn. Vocalising the 'ayn is the original form, and it is the dialect of Hudhayl. It cannot be on the dialect of those who make the 'ayn quiescent, because it would become like "jism malik," and that cannot be assimilated (idgham) according to what they mentioned.

Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read ﴿fa-na'immā﴾ in both places, with fatha on the nun and kasra on the 'ayn, which is the original form, because its pattern is fa'ila. Some said: the reading with kasra on the 'ayn may be on the dialect of those who make it quiescent, so when ma entered and was assimilated, the 'ayn was vocalised to avoid meeting two quiescent letters. Abu 'Amr, Qalun, and Abu Bakr read with kasra on the nun and with the vowel of the 'ayn hidden (ikhfa'), and it is related from them that it is quiescent. The first is more analogical and more well known. The basis of the hidden vowel is seeking lightness. As for quiescence, Abu 'Ubayd chose it and said: quiescence, as is related, is the dialect of the Prophet ﷺ in this word. He said to 'Amr ibn al-'As: "What an excellent wealth is the righteous wealth for the righteous man." Abu al-'Abbas, Abu Ishaq, and Abu 'Ali rejected quiescence, because it involves joining two quiescent letters in a way not according to its rule. Abu al-'Abbas said: no one can pronounce it; one only intends to join two quiescent letters, and it is vocalised and does not come out. Abu Ishaq said: the narrators did not precisely record the wording in the hadith. Abu 'Ali said: perhaps Abu 'Amr hid the vowel, so the listener thought it was quiescence. Much of what the readers have reported has been rejected, so among that is the quiescence in this place, in some of al-Bazzi's variants, in ﴿istata'u﴾ and in ﴿yakhissimun﴾. End of what was summarised from their speech.

What we choose and say is that the transmission of the seven readings is mutawatir (successively transmitted), and error in it is not possible.

Likewise the poet's saying:

"As if the garments of its rider, by a wind that tears them, while it is calm in its blowing."

He means: a different wind, calm in its blowing.

Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr and Abu Bakr read with nun and raf' of the ra'. Nafi', Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read with nun and jazm.

It is reported that khafd [i.e., the genitive reading] of the ra' is from al-A'mash with nun and nasb of the ra' for the one who read with ya'.

The more evident view is that the verb is attributed to God Most High, like the reading of the one who read "wa-nukaffiru" with nun, since its pronoun is for God Most High without doubt. It was also said: it refers to al-sarf, i.e., the diverting of the charities. It is possible that it relies on concealment, i.e., "and He expiates the concealing of charities." He attributed the expiation to Him by way of metaphor, because He is the cause of expiation. As for the one who read with ta', the pronoun in the verb is for the charities. As for the one who read the ra' with raf', it is possible that the verb is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "and We expiate," or "and He expiates," i.e., God; or the concealing, i.e., "and it expiates," i.e., the charity.

It is possible that it is a resumed statement (mustanaf) with no place in i'rab, and the waw has conjoined one sentence to another. It is possible that it is conjoined to the position of what follows the fa', since if a present verb occurred after it, it would be raf'; like His words ﴿ومَن عادَ فَيَنْتَقِمُ اللَّهُ مِنهُ﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95]. As for the one who read the ra' with jazm, it is by observing the clause that came as the response (jaza'), since it is in a jussive position, like His words ﴿مَن يُضْلِلِ اللَّهُ فَلا هادِيَ لَهُ﴾ [al-A'raf: 186].

As for "nadharhum" in the reading of the one who read with jazm, and "nadharahum" for the one who read with nasb of the ra', it is by implying (an) [the particle "that"], and it is conjunction to an assumed verbal noun (masdar mutawahham). Its parallel is the reading of the one who read ﴿يُحاسِبْكم بِهِ اللَّهُ فَيَغْفِرُ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 284] with nasb of the ra'. However, here it is difficult to estimate that assumed verbal noun from His words "fa-huwa khayrun lakum," so it requires some strained analysis, unlike His words "yuhasibkum": for it one estimates "there occurs a reckoning, then forgiveness."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Its meaning is: and if you conceal them, it would be better for you, and that We expiate for you," end of quote.

The apparent sense of his statement is that his estimate "and that We expiate" is governed by a verbal noun, and is conjoined to "khayran," the predicate of the "yakun" he estimated, as if he said: "concealing would be good for you and an expiation," so "an yukaffira" is in the position of nasb.

What is established among the Basrans is that this verbal noun formed from the implied "an" with the verb following it in the nasb is raf', conjoined to an assumed raf' verbal noun, whose estimate is drawn from the meaning. So when you say: "You do not come to us so that you speak to us," the estimate is: "there is not from you a coming and then a speaking." Likewise, "If you come and do good to me, I will do good to you," the estimate is: "if there is from you a coming and a good deed, I will do good to you." Likewise, what follows the response of the conditional, like the estimate we gave for "yuhasibkum bihi Allah" [al-Baqarah: 284] in the reading of the one who made "fayaghfir" nasb. On this basis the estimate is: "and if you conceal them and give them to the poor, there will be an increase of good for concealing over good for showing, and an expiation."

Al-Mahdawi said: as for nasb of the ra': it is made similar to nasb in the response of a question, since the reward is what makes the thing necessary through the necessity of something else, like the question. Ibn Atiyyah said: jazm of the ra' is the most eloquent of these readings, because it indicates the inclusion of the expiation in the condition, and its being conditioned on concealment occurring. As for raf' of the ra', there is no such meaning in it, end of quote.

We say: raf' is more emphatic and more general, because jazm is taken as conjoined to the second conditional response, while raf' is a substitute, on the basis that the expiation is necessarily consequent on the giving of charities, whether you show them or conceal them. For we know that this expiation is connected to what precedes it, and the expiation would be restricted to concealment alone if jazm were read, since jazm restricts it to that. It cannot be said that one who shows charities does not have his evil deeds expiated, for then the expiation would encompass both kinds, showing and concealing charities, even if concealing is better than showing.

The "min" in His words "min sayyi'atikum" is for partition (tab'id), because charity does not expiate all evil deeds. Al-Tabari transmitted from a group who said that "min" is superfluous in this place. Ibn Atiyyah said: that is an error from them, and the statement of one who made it causal and estimated "min ajli dhunubikum" [because of your sins] is weak.

﴿واللَّهُ بِما تَعْمَلُونَ خَبِيرٌ﴾ God concluded with this attribute, because it indicates knowledge of what is subtle among things and hidden. Concealment is suitably concluded with the attribute connected to what is hidden. And God knows best.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 272:

﴿It is not upon you to guide them, but Allah guides whom He wills.﴾ The transmitted reports differ regarding the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of this verse. Its meaning is that one who had embraced Islam disliked giving charity to his relative who was a polytheist, or to polytheists in general. Or the Prophet ﷺ forbade them from giving charity to them, or he himself refrained from doing so. A Jew had asked him, and this verse was revealed.

The apparent meaning of guidance (al-huda) is that it is the opposite of misguidance (al-dalal). It is a verbal noun (masdar) in the genitive construction with its object, meaning: it is not upon you to guide them, that is, to create guidance in their hearts. As for guidance in the sense of invitation (al-du'a'), that is upon the Prophet, but it is not intended here. In this there is consolation for the Prophet ﷺ, and it is similar to ﴿Your duty is only to convey (the message)﴾ [al-Shura: 48]. The meaning, then, is: it is not upon you to guide those who oppose you, so that you withhold charity from them in order that they enter Islam. Give to them for the sake of Allah. (Their guidance) is not in your hands.

Al-Zamakhshari (d. 538 AH) here makes guidance not the opposite of misguidance, which he understood as disbelief. He said: It is not obligatory upon you to make them guided to abstaining from what they have been forbidden: favour-reminding, harm, spending from what is bad, and other things. Your only duty is to convey the prohibitions to them, nothing more. What al-Zamakhshari said is weakened by His words: ﴿but Allah guides whom He wills﴾, for its apparent meaning is that the guidance of faith is intended. Al-Zamakhshari also said: His words ﴿but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ are a gentle appeal to one whom He knows that gentleness will benefit, so that he desists from what he has been forbidden. End of quotation. He therefore did not carry guidance in the two places upon faith as the opposite of misguidance; rather he took it as a specific kind of guidance, which is contrary to the apparent meaning, as we have stated.

It has been said: guidance here means wealth. That is, it is not upon you to make them wealthy; rather, it is upon you to console them, for Allah makes whom He wills rich. Calling wealth "guidance" follows the custom of the Arabs, as in their saying: "I was guided (rashadtu) and I was guided (ihtadaytu)" for one who prospered, and "I went astray (ghawaytu)" for one who failed and lost. On this basis is the saying of the poet:

Whoever meets good, people will praise his affair, and whoever goes astray will not lack a blamer for his error.

Explaining guidance as wealth is further from the meaning intended than al-Zamakhshari's explanation. In His words ﴿guidance (hudahum)﴾ there is an implicit antithesis (tibaq ma'nawi), since the meaning is: it is not upon you the guidance of those who have gone astray. The apparent address in ﴿it is not upon you﴾ is to the Messenger of Allah, and in this there is consolation for him ﷺ.

The connection of this sentence to what precedes it is that when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned His words ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269] and so on, it implied that not everyone whom Allah has given wisdom. Thus people, according to this implication, are divided into two categories: one to whom Allah has given wisdom, who acts by it; and one to whom He has not given it, who gropes blindly in misguidance. So this verse alerts that this category, it is not upon you to guide them. Rather, guidance and the granting of wisdom belong to Allah, exalted is He. This is to console him concerning this category, since eternal felicity has not been granted to them. It also alerts that, even if they are not guided, charity may be given to them. It has been said that the meaning of ﴿It is not upon you their guidance﴾ is: it is not upon you to compel them to guidance by making your charity conditional upon their faith, for such faith does not benefit them. Rather, what is required of them is faith by way of voluntary choice. In His words ﴿but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ there is a refutation of the Qadariyyah (a theological group who denied divine predestination), and a paronomasia (tajnis mughayir), since huda-hum is a noun and yahdi is a verb.

﴿And whatever good you spend, it is for yourselves﴾. That is: it belongs to yourselves. Its benefit and its reward return to none but you. So do not remind people of it, do not harm the poor, and do not concern yourselves with whether you encounter a Muslim or a disbeliever, for its reward is for you. Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said: The meaning of "for yourselves" is "for the people of your religion," as in His words ﴿then greet one another﴾ [al-Nur: 61] and ﴿do not kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 29], that is, the people of your religion. He alerted that the ruling of obligatory charity (fard) differs from the ruling of voluntary charity (tatawwu'), for obligatory charity is for the people of your religion only, not for disbelievers. It is related from some scholars that he used to do much good, then swear that he had never done good to anyone at all. When he was asked about this, he said: I only did it for myself, and he recites this verse.

It is related from 'Ali, may Allah honour his face, that he used to say: I have never done good to anyone, nor have I done harm to anyone. Then he recites: ﴿If you do good, you do good for yourselves; and if you do evil, it is for them﴾ [al-Isra': 7].

﴿And you spend only seeking the face of Allah﴾. That is: the expenditure that is accounted acceptable for you is only that whose giving was for seeking the face of Allah. If it is stripped of this intention, it is not counted. This is a conditional statement whose condition is elided, meaning: and whatever you spend that is counted acceptable. Thus this address is to the community (ummah). It has also been said that it is a statement from Allah that the expenditure of them, that is, the expenditure of the Companions (Sahabah), may Allah be pleased with them, occurred only in the required manner of seeking the face of Allah. This is then a testimony from Allah in their favour, and a glad tiding of its acceptance, since they intended by it the face of Allah, exalted is He. The statement thus takes the form of praise and commendation, and this address is specific to the Companions.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Your expenditure is only for seeking the face of Allah and for seeking what is with Him. So why do you remind people of it, and spend what is bad, which one would not direct to Allah? This contains an allusion to the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah, that charity was valid at first and then nullification befell it, unlike the view of others who say that favour-reminding and harm accompanied it. It has also been said that this is a negation whose meaning is a prohibition, that is: do not spend except seeking the face of Allah. Its figurative sense is that when He forbade that expenditure should occur except for the face of Allah, compliance was achieved; and when compliance is achieved, expenditure does not occur except for seeking the face of Allah. Thus the prohibition is expressed by negation for this meaning. The accusative of "seeking" (ibtigha') is a direct object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi). It has also been said that it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), its estimated form being: seeking. He expressed "face" as a reference to good pleasure, as in His words: seeking the good pleasure of Allah, and this is according to the custom of the Arabs. And Allah is exempt from being a face in the sense of a bodily part. The discussion of the attribution of "face" to Allah has already been treated fully in His words ﴿then wherever you turn, there is the face of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 115], so there is no need to repeat it.

﴿And whatever good you spend, it will be repaid to you﴾. That is: its reward will be given to you in full and multiplied. In this, and in what precedes it, there is the cutting off of their excuse for not spending, since what they spend belongs to them, where they are in need of it, and it will be repaid to them completely and in full. Therefore their expenditure should be in the best and most excellent manner. His words, exalted is He, have come: ﴿and He makes charity grow﴾ [al-Baqarah: 276]. And His saying, ﷺ, in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah: "When a servant gives charity, it falls into the hand of Allah before it falls into the hand of the beggar. Then He nurtures it for one of you just as one of you nurtures his foal or his young camel, until a morsel becomes like Mount Uhud." The pronoun in (yuwaffa) refers to "what" (ma). The meaning of its being repaid in full is the abundance of its reward.

﴿And you will not be wronged﴾. This is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah), whose governing element is ﴿yuwaffa﴾. The meaning is: you will not lose any of the reward of your expenditure.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 273 (part 1 of 2):

﴿For the poor who have been restricted in the way of Allah﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas and Muqatil said: They are the People of the Bench (ahl al-Suffa), who confined themselves to obedience to Allah, having nothing, and they numbered about four hundred. Mujahid said: They are the poor among the Emigrants (muhajirun) from Quraysh, and then it extends to whoever has the attribute of poverty. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: They are a people who were wounded in battle alongside the Prophet (ﷺ) and became disabled. Al-Kisa'i chose this view and said: "They were restricted by illness; had he meant restriction by the enemy, he would have said ḥaṣarū." The discussion of ihsar (ʾiḥṣār) and ḥaṣr has already passed in His words: ﴿And if you are prevented, then [send] what is easy of offering﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196], and it is established from the lexicon there that each of the two is said as uḥṣira and ḥuṣira, and Ibn Sidah related it.
Al-Suddi said: They were restricted by fear of the disbelievers, when they surrounded them. Qatadah said: They confined themselves to fighting, and poverty prevented them from fighting. Muhammad ibn al-Fadl said: The loftiness of their aspiration prevented them from raising their needs to anyone but Allah. Al-Zamakhshari said: Jihad restricted them, so that they cannot, because of their occupation with it, strike through the land for earning (ḍarban fi al-ard li-al-kasb), end of quote.
And ﴿lil-fuqara'﴾ is in the position of the predicate of an omitted subject, as if it were an answer to an imagined question, as if it were said: "For whom are these charities that are urged to be given?" So it was said: "For the poor," meaning: they are for the poor, thereby specifying the destination of the expenditure. It has also been said that the lam is connected to an omitted verb, its estimate being: "Be amazed at the poor," or "Make your intention toward the poor," or "Make what you spend for the poor." Al-Qaffal went too far in the estimate: "If you show the charities for the poor," and likewise whoever connected it to His words: ﴿and whatever good you spend﴾; and likewise whoever made (lil-fuqara') a substitute for His words: (fa-li-anfusikum), because of the many intervening elements that prevent that.
﴿They cannot strike through the land﴾, meaning, they cannot dispose of themselves in it, either because of their illness or because of their fear of the enemy due to their small number. Their fewness prevents them from earning through jihad, and the disbelievers' denial of their Islam prevents them from engaging in trade, so they remained poor. This negated sentence is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥal), meaning: they were restricted, unable to dispose of themselves. It is also permissible that it be a new sentence (mustaʾnafah), with no place in terms of grammatical case (iʿrab).
﴿The ignorant one thinks them wealthy because of their abstention﴾. Ibn ʿAmir, ʿAsim and Hamzah read with a fatha on the sin (al-sin) wherever it occurs, and this is the analogical reading, since its past form is on faʿila with a kasra on the ʿayn. The rest of the seven read with a kasra, and it is attested in words including: ʿamada yaʿmudu and yaʿmidu, which the grammarians have mentioned. The fatha on the sin is the dialect of Tamim, and the kasra is the dialect of the Hijaz. The meaning: because of their extreme withdrawal, their leaving off of asking, and their reliance on trust in Allah the Exalted, whoever is ignorant of their circumstances thinks them wealthy. "Min" is causal, meaning: what prompts their being thought wealthy is their abstention, because the custom of one who is wealthy in property is to abstain and not ask. "Yahsabuhum" is connected, and the object of purpose (al-maf'ul lahu) is governed there by a particle of cause, because one of the conditions of the object of purpose, namely the unity of the agent, is violated: the agent of "yahsabu" is the ignorant one, and the agent of abstention is the poor, and this condition is the more correct view. Had this condition not been violated, the governing by a particle of cause would have been better for this object of purpose, since it is defined by al-, and when it is so, the more common usage in the Arabic language is that the particle of cause enters upon it, though it is permissible to put it in the accusative, but that is rare, as they have recited:
"I will not sit out of cowardice from the battle" (lā aqʿudu al-judbān ʿan al-hayjāʾ)
meaning: for cowardice. The object of purpose is definite here because abstention had previously been practiced by them repeatedly, so it became known from them. It has been said: "min" denotes the starting point of the limit, meaning: from their abstention began the thinking of them; for the ignorant one regarding them does not think them wealthy with the wealth of abstention, rather he thinks them wealthy in property, so his thinking comes from their abstention. This is on the basis that they are abstinent with complete abstention from asking, and this is what the majority of the exegetes hold. That it is causal is more evident. It is not permissible for "min" to be connected to "aghniya'" (wealthy), because the meaning would turn to the opposite of the intended, namely: their condition is hidden from the ignorant one regarding them, so he supposes they are wealthy; but if "min" is connected to "aghniya'", the meaning becomes: the ignorant one supposes them wealthy, but by abstention, and one who is wealthy by abstention is poor in property. Ibn ʿAtiyyah permitted that "min" be a particle of specification (bayan al-jins). He said: abstention falls within the thinking (al-mahsabah), meaning that no asking appears from them; rather, it is rare. In summary, the ignorant one regarding them, while knowing their poverty, thinks them wealthy in abstention; so "min," on this interpretation, is for specification. End of quote. What he said, that this "min" in this meaning is a particle of specification in the sense used in the discussion of specification, is not correct, because it has a consideration for those who hold this meaning, in that it is estimated as a relative clause, and what it enters upon becomes the predicate of an omitted subject, as in: ﴿So avoid the abomination of the idols﴾ [al-Hajj: 30], the estimate being: "avoid the abomination which is the idols." If you said here: ﴿The ignorant one thinks them wealthy﴾ "which is abstention," this estimate would not be valid. It seems that he named the aspect by which they are wealthy a particle of specification, meaning: it specifies by what kind their wealth through abstention occurred, not wealth by property; so "min" entering upon what specifies the aspect of wealth is called a particle of specification, though it is not the term as we have previously stated. This meaning comes back to the position that "min" is causal, but it is connected to "aghniya'" and not to "yahsabuhum." It is possible that "yahsabuhum" is a circumstantial clause, and it is possible that it is a new sentence.
﴿You recognize them by their mark﴾. The address may be to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the meaning: you recognize their persons by the mark that indicates them. It may also mean: you recognize their poverty by the marks that indicate poverty, such as: the shabbiness of garments and the paleness of complexions due to poverty. Mujahid said: the mark is humility and lowliness. Al-Suddi said: destitution and hunger in their faces, and scarcity of blessing. Ibn Zayd said: the shabbiness of their clothes and the yellowness of their faces. It has been said: the trace of prostration, and Ibn ʿAtiyyah found this preferable, saying: because they were devoted to worship, so prayer predominated over them.
Al-Qurtubi said: this is shared among all the Companions, due to His words concerning them: ﴿Their mark is on their faces, from the trace of prostration﴾ [al-Fath: 29], unless the trace of prostration is greater in these. As for whoever explained the mark as humility, humility has its place in the heart, and both the wealthy and the poor share it; what distinguishes the wealthy from the poor outwardly is only the shabbiness of condition and the paleness of complexions. The Sufis have various statements on the interpretation of the mark. Al-Murtaʿish said: their dignity despite poverty. Al-Thawri said: their joy in poverty. Abu ʿUthman said: preferring what they have while in need of it. It has been said: their pride over the wealthy; it has been said: goodness of heart and brightness of face.
The "bi" is connected to "taʿrifuhum" (you recognize them), and it is causal. They permitted in this clause what they permitted in the clauses before it, of the circumstantial sense and of the new sentence. In this verse there is antithesis (ṭibaq) in two places: the first in His words "uḥṣirū" and "ḍarban fi al-ard"; the second in His words "lil-fuqara'" and "aghniya'".
﴿They do not ask people persistently﴾. When a ruling is negated of a subject qualified by a condition, the more common usage in the Arabic language is that the negation turns toward that condition, so the meaning on this reading is the affirmation of their asking, with the negation of persistence: that is, if any asking occurs from them, it is only with gentleness and concealment, not with insistence. It is also permissible that the negation falls on the ruling itself, so the condition is negated too, and on this reading the negation is of both asking and persistence, so the negation here is not directed at the condition alone. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they do not ask persistently, nor do they ask at all. A parallel to this is: "You do not come to us and speak to us." On the first reading, the meaning is: you come to us without speaking; you only come and do not speak. On the second reading: no coming from you occurs, so no speech occurs. Likewise here: no asking occurs from them at all, so no persistence occurs. He drew attention to the negation of persistence rather than of other things because of the ugliness of this attribute. The negation of this attribute is not meant alone with the existence of another; for then the first meaning would result. Rather, by negating a like attribute the intent is to negate what follows from the first negated item, because he negated the first in a general way, so its consequences are negated as well, just as when you negate coming and speaking is thereby negated, all the consequences of coming are negated: sitting together, being seen, and being in the same place. But he drew attention by mentioning one consequence for some purpose regarding the rest. Al-Zajjaj's comparison of this meaning in the verse to the poet's words:
"Upon a faint track, one is not guided by its landmark" (ʿalā lāḥibin lā yahtadī bi-manārihi)
is only a general negation of both things: no asking and no persistence; likewise: "this has neither a landmark nor guidance," not that it is like it in the particularity of negation, for then the meaning would have to be: "no persistence, so no asking," and the structure of the verse does not follow this meaning, and "no persistence, so no asking" is not valid, because from the negation of the particular one does not necessarily follow the negation of the general, as from the negation of the landmark follows the negation of guidance, which is one of its necessary consequences. The meaning of negation in the manner of the negation in the verse would only be expressed if the structure were: "they do not persist in asking people"; for from the negation of asking follows the negation of persistence, since the negation of the general indicates the negation of the particular. From all this it is concluded that the negation of two things sometimes places the negative particle on a thing, so all its accidents are negated, and some of them are mentioned for some purpose; and sometimes you place the negative particle on an accident of it, which is the intended negation, so the thing is negated by negating its accidents. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: the comparison by al-Zajjaj (meaning he) of the verse with the verse of Imru' al-Qays is not correct. Then he explained that the impossibility of the correctness of the comparison is because it is not like it in the particularity of negation: the negation of the landmark in the verse indicates the negation of guidance, whereas the negation of persistence does not indicate the negation of asking. Ibn ʿAtiyyah elaborated on this at length. We have already shown that al-Zajjaj's comparison is only in the general negation of the two things, and we have established that.
It has also been said: the meaning of "ilḥāfan" is that it is asking by which wealth is extracted because of the great gentleness of it, meaning: they do not ask people with gentleness and courtesy; and if this is not found, then it is even less likely to be found through violence. It has been said: the meaning of "ilḥāfan" is that they insist against themselves in abandoning asking, meaning: they do not ask because of their insistence on themselves in abandoning asking, and their restraint of themselves by severe imposition. It has been said: whoever asks must persist, so the negation of persistence from them absolutely necessitates the negation of asking absolutely. It has been said: it is a metaphor for the absence of displaying the traces of poverty, and the meaning: they do not add to silence the shabbiness of condition and brokenness, and what takes the place of urgent asking. This clause may be a circumstantial clause, and it may be a new sentence. Whoever permitted the circumstantial clause in these clauses while the subject is one, does so only according to the view of one who permits multiple circumstantial clauses for one subject, and it is a matter of disagreement and detail mentioned in the science of grammar.
They permitted in the parsing of "ilḥāfan" that it be an object of purpose, that it be a verbal noun (maṣdar) for an omitted verb indicated by "yasalūna," so that it is as if he said: "they do not persist," and that it be a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause, its estimate being: "they do not ask while persisting."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 273 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And whatever good you spend, indeed Allah is Knowing of it.﴾ It has preceded: ﴿And whatever good you spend, it is for yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 272] and ﴿And whatever good you spend, it will be repaid to you in full﴾ [al-Baqarah: 272]. This is not for the sake of repetition and emphasis; rather, each of them is restricted by a condition other than the condition of the other. The first: it mentions that the good a person does with others is only for himself, and that its reward returns to him. The second: it mentions that this reward, arising from the good, is paid to him in full, without any deficiency or diminution. The third: it mentions that He, exalted is He, is Knowing of what a person spends of good, and of its quantity, and of the manner of its aspects that affect the arrangement of the reward. So He brought the attribute that is aware of all that, which is: knowledge (al-'ilm).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 274:

﴿Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly﴾. Abu Dharr, Abu al-Darda', Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Umama, 'Abd Allah ibn Bishr al-Ghafiqi, Makhul, Rabah ibn Buraid and al-Awza'i said: it refers to the fodder of horses that are tethered in the way of Allah, and to their tethering. Abu Hurayra, whenever he passed by a fat horse, would recite this verse. Ibn 'Abbas also said, as did al-Kalbi: it was revealed concerning Ali. He had four dirhams (p. 331). Al-Kalbi said: he did not possess anything other than them, so he gave one dirham in charity at night, one dirham by day, one dirham secretly and one dirham openly.

Ibn 'Abbas also said: it was revealed concerning Ali, who sent a wasq of dates to the People of the Suffa at night, and concerning 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, who sent them many dirhams by day. Qatada said: it was revealed concerning those who spend without extravagance and without stinginess, end quote. It is also said: it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, who gave in charity forty thousand dinars: ten at night, ten by day, ten secretly and ten openly.

Although the verse was revealed on a specific occasion, its wording is general in all that it indicates. The meaning, as al-Zamakhshari said, is that they encompass all times and states with charity, out of their eagerness for good. Whenever the need of someone in want arose, they hastened to meet it and did not delay it, nor did they plead any excuse of time or state, end quote.

The verse does not specify the superiority of giving charity in one of the two times, nor in one of the two states, relying on the verse before it, which is: ﴿If you disclose your charities, it is good﴾ [al-Baqara: 271]. Or it came as a detailed explanation according to what actually happened in the charity of Abu Bakr and the charity of Ali. It may be said that the mention of the night before the day, and the secret before the open, indicates that superiority, since the night is the most likely time for secret charity. So it mentioned first the time in which charity is most excellent, and the state in which it is most excellent.

The ba' in (bi-al-layl) is adverbial of time (zarfiyya). The accusative of ﴿secretly and openly﴾ is because both are verbal nouns (masdar) in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: keeping it secret and making it public. Or they are two circumstantial clauses referring to the pronoun of spending, according to the view of Sibawayh. Or they are two adjectives of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: spending secretly, according to the well-known grammatical analysis (i'rab) in: qumtu tawilan, meaning: I stood for a long time (qiyaman tawilan).

﴿So they will have their reward with their Lord, and no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve﴾. The explanation of this has already passed, so we will not repeat it. The fa' entered upon (fa-lahum) because the relative pronoun includes the meaning of the conditional particle (ism al-shart) in its generality.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: the resemblance (between the relative pronoun and the conditional particle) is only found when (alladhi) is followed by a verb, and when no governing word that changes its meaning enters upon (alladhi). End quote. He thus restricted the resemblance to the case where (alladhi) is followed by a verb. This is an unrefined statement, since what he mentioned has conditions.

The first of these: this does not apply only to (alladhi). Rather, every relative pronoun other than the definite article (al-) has the same ruling as (alladhi) without disagreement. As for the definite article (al-), there is disagreement, and the view of Sibawayh is that the fa' may not enter. The second: his saying "followed by a verb" is unrestricted and restricted to the verb, which is not the case. Rather, the condition of the verb is that it be capable of receiving the conditional particle. If you say: alladhi ya'tini (the one who comes to me), or lamma ya'tini, or ma ya'tini, or laysa ya'tini, then for him is a dirham, it is not permitted, because the conditional particle cannot enter upon any of those. As for restricting it to the verb, this is not the case; rather, the adverbial phrase and the prepositional phrase are like the verb in this. So whenever the relative clause is one of these two, it is permitted for the fa' to enter. His saying: "and when no governing word enters upon (alladhi) that changes..." is an imprecise expression, because any governing word that enters upon it, whatever it is, does not change the meaning of the relative pronoun. He should have said: the meaning of the nominal sentence within the relative clause and its predicate, so that it would exclude a governing word that changes the initial meaning from wish, comparison, supposition or other than these. If you say: alladhi yazuruna fa-yuhsinu ilayna (the one who visits us and then treats us well), it is not permitted. Ibn 'Atiyya should also have mentioned that the condition for the fa' to enter the predicate is that it be deserved by the relative clause, as in what came in the verse, because the reward is only given for the spending. The question of the fa' entering the predicate of the subject requires a lengthy discussion, and some of its issues contain disagreement and detail. We have mentioned that in our book (al-Tadhkira), which we composed.

* *

﴿Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly, so they will have their reward with their Lord, and no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve﴾. ﴿Those who consume usury will not rise except as one rises whom Satan has overcome by touch. That is because they said: trade is only like usury, but Allah has permitted trade and forbidden usury. So whoever has received an admonition from his Lord and desists, for him is what has passed, and his affair is up to Allah. But whoever returns, those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally﴾. ﴿Allah destroys usury and makes charities grow. And Allah does not love every ungrateful sinner﴾ [al-Baqara: 276].

Al-riba: increase. It is said: rabā yarbū, and his other (form) is arbāhu. Arba al-rajul means he dealt in usury. From it come al-rabwa and al-rabiya (a hillock). Hatim said:

A dark spear-shaft whose joints, as if they were date-pits, have exceeded a span beyond ten.

It is written in the Qur'an with a waw and an alif after it. It may also be written with a ya' because of the kasra, and with an alif. The ba' is changed to a mim; they said al-rima, just as they changed it in kataba; they said katama. Its dual is ribawan with a waw according to the Basran grammarians, because its alif is converted from it. The Kufan grammarians said: it is written with a ya', and likewise the triliteral with a first letter that is damma, such as duha; so you say ribayan and duhayan. If it is with a fatha, such as safa, they agreed on the waw. As for legal usury (al-riba al-shar'i), it is defined in the books of jurists according to the differences of their schools.

Takhabbata: taf'ala from al-khabt, which is striking without evenness. Khabata al-ba'ir al-ard bi-akhfafihi (the camel struck the ground with its hooves). It is said of one who acts without guidance: khabta 'ashwa' (blind striking), and tawarrata fi 'amya' (he plunged into blindness). The saying of 'Alqama:

And in every tribe you have struck with a favour.

That is: you gave to whomever you wished without discernment, as generosity.

Salafa: passed and ended. From it: salif al-dahr, meaning its past. 'Ada 'awdan: returned. Some mentioned that it may mean "became", and he recited:

Our spears count the slaughtering of camels among you, and they return with broken swords.

Al-mahq: the diminution of a thing state after state. From it: al-mahaq in the crescent moon. It is said: Allah mahaqahu, so it was diminished and dwindled (fa-nmahaqa wa-amtahaqa). Al-Layth recited:

It keeps increasing until when it is complete, the return of the two newnesses (day and night) makes it decrease, then it dwindles.

**Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on 2:275–276 (Part 1 of 2)**

﴿Those who consume interest will not stand except as one stands whom Satan has driven to madness by his touch.﴾ The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that the preceding verses deal with preferring spending and charity in the way of God, and that this should come from good earnings and not from what is impure. Then he mentions a type of earning that was prevalent among them in the Jahiliyya and is impure, which is interest (riba), so that one would refrain from giving charity from what came from interest. There is also another connection: charity involves a loss of wealth, while interest involves an increase of wealth. So he digressed from the commanded to the forbidden because of the contrast between them. He presented the consumption of interest in a form that the Arabs find repulsive, following their custom of mentioning what they find strange and frightful, as in His saying: ﴿Its shoots are like the heads of devils﴾ [al-Saffat: 65], and the poet's saying:

*"And sharpened blue (spears), like the fangs of ghouls."*

And the saying of another:

*"Horses like the likenesses of the sa'ali, drinking (sharab)."*

And the saying of another:

*"A miser over them, possessed by a jinn of 'Abqar."*

Here, "consumption" (al-akl) has been said to be literal, specifically eating, and that the report about them concerns only those who consume interest. It has also been said that consumption is used to express dealing in interest and taking it, because eating is the most common way of benefiting from it, as He, exalted, said: ﴿and their taking of interest﴾ [al-Nisa': 161]. It has also been said that "interest" here is a metaphor (kinaya) for what is unlawful, and does not specifically refer to the interest of the Jahiliyya or to legal interest in the sense of the Sharia.

Al-'Adawi recited (al-Rabw) with a waw, and it has been said that this is the dialect of al-Hira, and for this reason the people of the Hijaz wrote it with a waw, because they learned writing from the people of al-Hira. This reading follows the dialect of one who pauses on *af'a* (serpent) with a waw, saying *hadhihi af'u*, so this reciter treated continuous speech as if it were pause.

Abu Zayd related that some people read it with a kasra on the ra', a damma on the ba', and a silent waw. This is a remote reading, because in the language of the Arabs there is no noun ending in a waw preceded by a damma. Rather, whenever inflection leads to that, the waw is changed to ya' and the damma to kasra. This reading has been interpreted as following the dialect of one who says *af'u* for *af'a* in pause, or that the reciter either did not properly vocalize the ba', or he called its closeness to the damma a damma.

*La yaqumuna* (they do not stand) is the predicate of *alladhina* (those who). It is mentioned in some works that it is a circumstantial clause (hal), but this is very remote, since it requires assuming a predicate without any evidence for it. The apparent meaning of this report is that it concerns those who consume interest. It has also been said that it is a report and a threat concerning those who consume interest while considering it lawful, as evidenced by their saying: ﴿Trade is only like interest﴾, and His saying: ﴿God does not love every ungrateful sinner﴾, and His saying: ﴿then be informed of war from God and His Messenger﴾ [al-Baqara: 279]. Whoever chooses war against God and His Messenger is a disbeliever. As for the standing mentioned in the verse, it has been said that it refers to the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Jubayr, al-Dahhak, al-Rabi', al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is that they will not stand up from their graves at the resurrection on the Day of Resurrection except like madmen, as a punishment for them and a disgrace before the assembled gathering, and this will be a mark by which they are recognized. This interpretation is strengthened by the reading of Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud): *la yaqumuna yawm al-qiyama* (they will not stand on the Day of Resurrection). Some said: a devil will be made to accompany him, choking him, as if he were staggering in transactions in the world, so he is recompensed in the Hereafter with the same kind of act.

It has been reported in the hadith of the Night Journey (Isra') that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) saw the consumers of interest, each man with a belly like a huge house. He described their condition: when they stood up, their bellies would tilt them over and they would fall down. In another narration, he saw their bellies like houses in which there were snakes visible from outside their bellies.

Ibn Atiyya said: As for the wording of the verse, it may be understood as comparing the state of one who stands, driven by greed and eagerness toward the trade of interest, to the standing of a madman, because desire and longing agitate him until his limbs tremble, just as one who walks quickly mixes up the form of his movements, whether out of fright or otherwise, as if he had gone mad. Al-A'sha likened his she-camel in her vigor to madness in his saying:

*"And she rises after the fatigue of travel, as if seized by a madness from the phantoms of the jinn."*

But what has been transmitted in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, and what the statements of the exegetes agree upon, weakens this interpretation. End of his words.

(This is good, except that the *kaf* in *kama* occupies the position of a circumstantial clause, or is an adjective (na't) for an omitted verbal noun (masdar), according to the disagreement mentioned earlier between Sibawayh and others, which was mentioned in several places.)

The *ma* in *kama* is apparently verbal (masdariyya), meaning: like the standing of the one. Some permitted it to mean *alladhi* (the one who), with an omitted returning pronoun, the estimated sense being: "as one stands whom Satan has driven to madness." It has been said that its meaning is like the drunkard whom Satan drags, so that he falls on his belly. Its attribution to Satan is because he obeys him in his drunkenness.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that Satan touches the human being. It has been said this is literal, an act of Satan by God's permission giving him power to do so to some people, and there is nothing in reason that prevents this. It has also been said that this is an act of God, in that He produces in him a predominance of evil or an imbalance of temperaments and their intensity, so that he is struck down. This is attributed to Satan metaphorically, by analogy with what his helpers do to those they strike down. It has also been said that it is attributed to Satan according to the belief of the Arabs that Satan touches a person and strikes him down, so the verse came in accordance with what they believed; they say: "a man is possessed" (mamsus), and "the man has gone mad." Al-Zamakhshari said: I have seen among them stories, reports, and wonders about the jinn, and denying that is, to him, like denying what is directly observed. End of his words.

*Takhabbata* here is *tafa''ala*, which agrees with the basic form *khabata*, and *tafa''ala* is one of the meanings of the form: like *ta'adda al-shay'* and *'addahu* when he passed beyond it. *Min al-mass* (from the touch): *al-mass* is madness. It is said: "he was touched (massa), so he is mamsus, and he has a touch (mass)." Ibn al-Anbari recited, may God have mercy on him:

*"I console myself with what cannot be, like one touched by madness who has not been strangled."*

Its origin is from touching with the hand, as if Satan touches a person and thereby drives him mad. Madness has been called "touch" just as Satan strikes him and treads on him with his foot, causing him to imagine things, so madness has been called a "striking" (khabta). Thus *takhabbut* is with the foot, and *mass* is with the hand. *Min al-mass* is connected to *yatakhabbatuhu* (strikes him), and it serves as an emphasis and removes the possible figurative sense of *yatakhabbatuhu*, since the latter could be understood to be not necessarily from touch. It may be intended that *takhabbut* means seduction and adorning sins, so the phrase *min al-mass* removes this possibility.

It has also been said that *min al-mass* is connected to *yaqumu* (stands), meaning: as one who is struck down stands up from his madness. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "To what is *min al-mass* connected?" I say: to *la yaqumuna*, meaning, they do not stand up from the touch that is upon them except as the one struck down stands up. End of his words.

He had earlier explained *mass* as madness. His view that *min al-mass* is connected to *la yaqumuna* is weak for two reasons. First, he explained *mass* as madness, and he had also explained that their standing will only happen in the Hereafter, and there they will have no madness or touch. It is far-fetched to use *al-mass*, which is madness, as an allusion to consuming interest in this world, so the meaning would be: "they will not stand on the Day of Resurrection, or from their graves on account of consuming interest, except as one stands whom Satan has driven to madness." If this meaning were intended, stating it plainly would be better than using the allusion of the word *mass*, since plain statement is more eloquent in deterrence and restraint.

The second reason: what follows *illa* (except) is not connected to what precedes it, unless it is within the scope of an exception. This is not within the scope of an exception. For this reason they prohibited connecting ﴿with the clear proofs and the scriptures﴾ [al-Nahl: 44] to His saying: ﴿We did not send before you except men﴾ [al-Nahl: 43], and the estimated sense is: "We did not send with the clear proofs and scriptures except men."

﴿That is because they said: trade is only like interest.﴾ The demonstrative *dhalika* refers to that particular standing of theirs in the Hereafter, and it is the subject (mubtada'), with the prepositional phrase *bi-anna-hum* as the predicate, meaning: that standing exists because of the fact that they... It has also been said that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being: "their standing is that," but in this view there is a separation between the verbal noun and its complement, which is *bi-anna-hum*, though it is not far-fetched that this is permitted because the verbal noun is omitted, so the separation by the predicate does not appear ugly. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "that punishment is because of the fact that they..." and the punishment is that standing. It is also possible that *dhalika* refers to their consumption of interest, meaning: that consumption which they made lawful, because of their saying and their belief that trade is like interest. Their basis for this is the equation they made between interest and trade. They compared trade, which is agreed to be permissible, to interest, which is forbidden, and they did not reverse the comparison, treating this interest they practiced as the original standard to which trade is compared. This is from (p-335) the reversal of comparison, which occurs in Arabic speech. Dhu al-Rumma said:

*"And sand like the hips of virgins, I crossed it."*

It is abundant in the poetry of later poets, as Abu al-Qasim ibn Hani' said:

*"As if the light of the sun is the blaze of Ja'far, when he saw the opponent, his brightness increased twofold."*

The people of the Jahiliyya, when a debt became due from a debtor, would demand payment, and the debtor would say: "Give me more time and I will add to the amount." They would do this and say: "It is the same to us whether the increase is at the beginning of the sale for profit, or at the due date in exchange for delay." So God rejected them. It has also been said that Thaqif was the most usurious of the Arabs, and when they were forbidden from it, they said: "It is only like trade."

﴿God has made trade lawful and forbidden interest.﴾ Its apparent meaning is that it is the speech of God, exalted, not theirs. In this there is a refutation of them, since they equated the two, and judgment regarding things belongs only to God, exalted; His ruling cannot be opposed or His command contravened.
