In this verse there is evidence that analogy (qiyas) cannot stand against a clear text (nass), since God, exalted, made the proof for refuting their claim to be: "God has made trade lawful and forbidden interest." Some scholars said: their analogy is corrupt, because trade is an exchange of a thing and its counter-value with no inequity in it, whereas interest involves mutual cheating (taghabun) and the consumption of wealth in falsehood, since the excess has no counterpart of its own kind, unlike trade, where the price is matched against the goods.

Ja'far al-Sadiq said: God forbade interest so that people would lend to one another. It has also been said: He forbade it because it destroys wealth and ruins people. Some said: it is possible that ﴿God has made trade lawful and forbidden interest﴾ is part of their own speech, so they knew that God had forbidden interest but opposed it with their own opinions, and that would be disbelief on their part. The apparent meaning is the generality of trade and interest in every trade and in every instance of interest, except what the proof has specified, such as the prohibition of some kinds of sales and the permission of some kinds of interest. It has also been said that both terms are ambiguous (mujmal), so one may not proceed to permit a sale or prohibit interest except with an explanation. This is the difference between a general term (amm) and an ambiguous term (mujmal). It has also been said that it is a general term to which specification has applied, and an ambiguous term to which explanation has applied. The divisions and details of trade and interest are mentioned in the books of jurisprudence (fiqh).

The apparent meaning is that the verse, as they said, concerns disbelievers, because of His saying: ﴿then what has passed is his﴾, since a believer who disobeys by dealing in interest does not keep what has passed; rather, he must retract and reverse the act, even if he was ignorant of the prohibition. But he takes on a portion of the threat of this verse.

﴿Whoever receives an admonition from his Lord and desists, for him is what has already passed.﴾ The feminine ta' is dropped from *jā'ahu* (came to him) because the verb is separated from its subject, and because the feminine marker of *maw'iẓa* (admonition) is metaphorical. Ubayy and al-Hasan read *fa-man jā'athu* with the ta', in accordance with the original form. ʿĀʾisha recited this verse when al-ʿĀliya bint Abqaʾ, the wife of Abu Ishaq al-Sabiʿi, asked her about buying a slave girl for six hundred dirhams in cash from Zayd ibn Arqam, having sold him the girl for eight hundred dirhams on credit until his stipend was paid. ʿĀʾisha said: "Wretched is what you bought and what you sold. Inform Zayd that he has nullified his jihad with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ unless he repents." Al-ʿĀliya said: "What if I take only my principal?" So ʿĀʾisha recited the verse.

The *maw'iẓa* (admonition) has been interpreted as the prohibition, or the threat of punishment, or the Qur'an; these are different opinions. The phrase *min rabbihi* (from his Lord) may be connected to *jā'athu* or to an implied verb, in which case it is an attribute of *maw'iẓa*. In the latter reading, the statement magnifies the admonition, since it came to him from his Lord, the One who oversees his welfare. Mentioning "the Lord" also serves to make the admonition acceptable, as the word "Lord" implies the reform of His servant. *Fa-intaha* (desisted) means he followed the prohibition and gave up dealing in *ribā* (usury), or gave up every forbidden form of earning. ﴿for him is what has already passed﴾ means: what he had already taken of *ribā* before the prohibition is his, and he will not be held to account for it in this world or the Hereafter. This is a ruling from Allah for those among the disbelievers of Quraysh and Thaqif who embraced Islam, and for those who used to trade there. This is according to the view that the verse is specific to the disbelievers. According to the one who says the verse is general, its meaning is: what passed before the prohibition is his.

﴿And his affair is with Allah.﴾ Apparently the pronoun in *amruhu* (his affair) refers to the one who desisted, since the context concerns him. The meaning is to reassure him and extend his hope for good, as you would say: "his affair is toward obedience, goodness and a place of hope." The word *amr* here is not restricted to *ribā* but covers all his affairs. It has also been said that it refers to the reward and the reckoning, or to pardon and punishment. It has been said that it means Allah will judge his case on the Day of Resurrection, not left to those with whom he dealt, so they will not demand anything from him. It has been said that the meaning is: his reward is with Allah for accepting the admonition, reported from al-Hasan. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to *mā salaf* (what has passed), meaning in pardoning it and dropping any liability for it. It has been said that it refers to the one who dealt in *ribā*, meaning in Allah making him firm in desisting, or returning him to sin, reported from Ibn Jubayr and Muqatil. It has been said that it refers to *ribā*, meaning in the continuation of its prohibition, or otherwise. It has been said that it means in Allah's pardon of whomever He wills, reported from Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

﴿And whoever returns﴾ to the practice of *ribā*, and to the claim that trade is like *ribā*. Sufyan said: whoever returns to the practice of *ribā* until he dies, for him is eternity. ﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾ The explanation of this sentence, which is the predicate of *man* (whoever), has been given before. The word *fīhā* (therein) is treated by meaning after being treated by form. If it refers to the disbelievers, then *khulūd* (eternity) is eternal abiding. If it refers to a sinful Muslim, then his abiding is a long stay, not eternal. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is a clear proof that sinners will be eternal in the Fire. He ended. This follows from his Mu'tazili doctrine (*al-madhhab al-iʿtizāli*) that the grave sinner is eternal in the Fire and does not leave it. It is reported from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and authenticated, that "consuming *ribā* is among the seven destructive sins." Also reported from ʿAwn ibn Abi Juhayfa, from his father, that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ cursed the consumer of *ribā*, its payer, and its scribe (its agent)." A man who saw a drunkard staggering, trying to grab the moon, asked Malik, may Allah have mercy on him: "His wife is divorced if anything enters the son of Adam's stomach that is worse than wine." Does his wife get divorced? Malik said to him, after he repeated it twice: "Your wife is divorced. I have searched the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Prophet and I have not found anything worse than *ribā*, because Allah the Exalted has declared war upon it."

﴿Allah destroys ribā﴾ meaning: He takes away its blessing, and the wealth into which it enters goes away. This was reported by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Ibn Jubayr said the same. From Ibn Masʿud: even if *ribā* increases, its end is to decline. Al-Dahhak reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that its destruction (*mihāq*) is nullifying whatever charity, kinship ties, jihad, and the like come from it.

﴿and makes charities grow﴾. It has been said that *al-irbāʾ* (growth) is literal, meaning He increases and develops them in this world by blessing and by abundant profits in the wealth from which the charity came out. It has also been said the increase is figurative, meaning the multiplication of good deeds and rewards gained by charity, as found in many verses and hadiths. Ibn al-Zubayr read, and it was reported from the Prophet ﷺ, *yumahhiqu wa-yuraббi* (*yumahhiqu* and *yurabbī*), from *maḥaqa* and *rabbā* with the doubled letter. The mention of destruction and growth contains the figure of antithesis (*al-ṭibāq*, the use of opposites). The mention of *ribā* and *yurabbī* contains the figure of paronomasia (*al-tajnīs*, similar-sounding words with different meanings).

﴿Allah does not love every ungrateful sinner.﴾ This emphasizes the severity of the matter of *ribā* and indicates that it is an act of disbelievers, not of the people of Islam. The intensive form is used for the disbeliever and the sinner, even though Allah the Exalted does not love the disbeliever in any case, as a warning about the greatness of *ribā* and of opposing Allah. It also refers to their saying ﴿trade is only like ribā﴾, and that He does not say so. Whoever equates trade with *ribā* in order to use it as evidence for eating *ribā* is only one who exaggerates in disbelief and exaggerates in sin. He mentioned *al-athīm* (the sinner) as emphasis and reinforcement, since the two words differ. Ibn Furak said: he mentioned *al-athīm* so that the shared ambiguity in *kaffār* would be removed, since it applies to the farmer who covers the seed in the earth. He ended. This is far-fetched, because the Qur'an's usage of *al-kāfir*, *al-kāfirūn* and *al-kuffār* refers only to those who disbelieve in Allah. Its application to the farmer is by a verbal indicator, as in His saying: ﴿like a rain whose vegetation pleases the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ḥadīd 57:20].

Ibn Furak also said: the meaning of the verse ﴿Allah does not love every ungrateful sinner﴾ is that He does not love one who is good and righteous, but rather wills him to be evil and wicked. It may also mean: Allah does not love the success (*tawfīq*) of the sinful disbeliever. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: these interpretations are strained. As for the first, it overreaches in extending the verb and imposes on it a meaning its wording does not bear. As for the second, its meaning is incorrect, since Allah the Exalted loves success in general and makes it beloved. The one who loves in the visible world inclines toward the beloved, shows kindness to him, is eager to preserve him, and these signs appear. Allah the Exalted wills that the disbeliever manifest what he is, and He does not have for him the distinction of love through deeds that appear on him, like what we mentioned in the visible world. That distinction exists for the believer. He ended. Love in its literal sense is natural inclination, and it is negated of Allah the Exalted. Ibn Furak took it to mean will, so it is an attribute of essence (*ṣifat dhāt*). Ibn ʿAṭiyya took it to mean kindness and showing signs, so it is an attribute of action (*ṣifat fiʿl*). The discussion of this has already been given.

**Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on 2:275–276 (Part 1 of 2)**

﴿Those who consume interest will not stand except as one stands whom Satan has driven to madness by his touch.﴾ The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that the preceding verses deal with preferring spending and charity in the way of God, and that this should come from good earnings and not from what is impure. Then he mentions a type of earning that was prevalent among them in the Jahiliyya and is impure, which is interest (riba), so that one would refrain from giving charity from what came from interest. There is also another connection: charity involves a loss of wealth, while interest involves an increase of wealth. So he digressed from the commanded to the forbidden because of the contrast between them. He presented the consumption of interest in a form that the Arabs find repulsive, following their custom of mentioning what they find strange and frightful, as in His saying: ﴿Its shoots are like the heads of devils﴾ [al-Saffat: 65], and the poet's saying:

*"And sharpened blue (spears), like the fangs of ghouls."*

And the saying of another:

*"Horses like the likenesses of the sa'ali, drinking (sharab)."*

And the saying of another:

*"A miser over them, possessed by a jinn of 'Abqar."*

Here, "consumption" (al-akl) has been said to be literal, specifically eating, and that the report about them concerns only those who consume interest. It has also been said that consumption is used to express dealing in interest and taking it, because eating is the most common way of benefiting from it, as He, exalted, said: ﴿and their taking of interest﴾ [al-Nisa': 161]. It has also been said that "interest" here is a metaphor (kinaya) for what is unlawful, and does not specifically refer to the interest of the Jahiliyya or to legal interest in the sense of the Sharia.

Al-'Adawi recited (al-Rabw) with a waw, and it has been said that this is the dialect of al-Hira, and for this reason the people of the Hijaz wrote it with a waw, because they learned writing from the people of al-Hira. This reading follows the dialect of one who pauses on *af'a* (serpent) with a waw, saying *hadhihi af'u*, so this reciter treated continuous speech as if it were pause.

Abu Zayd related that some people read it with a kasra on the ra', a damma on the ba', and a silent waw. This is a remote reading, because in the language of the Arabs there is no noun ending in a waw preceded by a damma. Rather, whenever inflection leads to that, the waw is changed to ya' and the damma to kasra. This reading has been interpreted as following the dialect of one who says *af'u* for *af'a* in pause, or that the reciter either did not properly vocalize the ba', or he called its closeness to the damma a damma.

*La yaqumuna* (they do not stand) is the predicate of *alladhina* (those who). It is mentioned in some works that it is a circumstantial clause (hal), but this is very remote, since it requires assuming a predicate without any evidence for it. The apparent meaning of this report is that it concerns those who consume interest. It has also been said that it is a report and a threat concerning those who consume interest while considering it lawful, as evidenced by their saying: ﴿Trade is only like interest﴾, and His saying: ﴿God does not love every ungrateful sinner﴾, and His saying: ﴿then be informed of war from God and His Messenger﴾ [al-Baqara: 279]. Whoever chooses war against God and His Messenger is a disbeliever. As for the standing mentioned in the verse, it has been said that it refers to the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Jubayr, al-Dahhak, al-Rabi', al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is that they will not stand up from their graves at the resurrection on the Day of Resurrection except like madmen, as a punishment for them and a disgrace before the assembled gathering, and this will be a mark by which they are recognized. This interpretation is strengthened by the reading of Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud): *la yaqumuna yawm al-qiyama* (they will not stand on the Day of Resurrection). Some said: a devil will be made to accompany him, choking him, as if he were staggering in transactions in the world, so he is recompensed in the Hereafter with the same kind of act.

It has been reported in the hadith of the Night Journey (Isra') that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) saw the consumers of interest, each man with a belly like a huge house. He described their condition: when they stood up, their bellies would tilt them over and they would fall down. In another narration, he saw their bellies like houses in which there were snakes visible from outside their bellies.

Ibn Atiyya said: As for the wording of the verse, it may be understood as comparing the state of one who stands, driven by greed and eagerness toward the trade of interest, to the standing of a madman, because desire and longing agitate him until his limbs tremble, just as one who walks quickly mixes up the form of his movements, whether out of fright or otherwise, as if he had gone mad. Al-A'sha likened his she-camel in her vigor to madness in his saying:

*"And she rises after the fatigue of travel, as if seized by a madness from the phantoms of the jinn."*

But what has been transmitted in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, and what the statements of the exegetes agree upon, weakens this interpretation. End of his words.

(This is good, except that the *kaf* in *kama* occupies the position of a circumstantial clause, or is an adjective (na't) for an omitted verbal noun (masdar), according to the disagreement mentioned earlier between Sibawayh and others, which was mentioned in several places.)

The *ma* in *kama* is apparently verbal (masdariyya), meaning: like the standing of the one. Some permitted it to mean *alladhi* (the one who), with an omitted returning pronoun, the estimated sense being: "as one stands whom Satan has driven to madness." It has been said that its meaning is like the drunkard whom Satan drags, so that he falls on his belly. Its attribution to Satan is because he obeys him in his drunkenness.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that Satan touches the human being. It has been said this is literal, an act of Satan by God's permission giving him power to do so to some people, and there is nothing in reason that prevents this. It has also been said that this is an act of God, in that He produces in him a predominance of evil or an imbalance of temperaments and their intensity, so that he is struck down. This is attributed to Satan metaphorically, by analogy with what his helpers do to those they strike down. It has also been said that it is attributed to Satan according to the belief of the Arabs that Satan touches a person and strikes him down, so the verse came in accordance with what they believed; they say: "a man is possessed" (mamsus), and "the man has gone mad." Al-Zamakhshari said: I have seen among them stories, reports, and wonders about the jinn, and denying that is, to him, like denying what is directly observed. End of his words.

*Takhabbata* here is *tafa''ala*, which agrees with the basic form *khabata*, and *tafa''ala* is one of the meanings of the form: like *ta'adda al-shay'* and *'addahu* when he passed beyond it. *Min al-mass* (from the touch): *al-mass* is madness. It is said: "he was touched (massa), so he is mamsus, and he has a touch (mass)." Ibn al-Anbari recited, may God have mercy on him:

*"I console myself with what cannot be, like one touched by madness who has not been strangled."*

Its origin is from touching with the hand, as if Satan touches a person and thereby drives him mad. Madness has been called "touch" just as Satan strikes him and treads on him with his foot, causing him to imagine things, so madness has been called a "striking" (khabta). Thus *takhabbut* is with the foot, and *mass* is with the hand. *Min al-mass* is connected to *yatakhabbatuhu* (strikes him), and it serves as an emphasis and removes the possible figurative sense of *yatakhabbatuhu*, since the latter could be understood to be not necessarily from touch. It may be intended that *takhabbut* means seduction and adorning sins, so the phrase *min al-mass* removes this possibility.

It has also been said that *min al-mass* is connected to *yaqumu* (stands), meaning: as one who is struck down stands up from his madness. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "To what is *min al-mass* connected?" I say: to *la yaqumuna*, meaning, they do not stand up from the touch that is upon them except as the one struck down stands up. End of his words.

He had earlier explained *mass* as madness. His view that *min al-mass* is connected to *la yaqumuna* is weak for two reasons. First, he explained *mass* as madness, and he had also explained that their standing will only happen in the Hereafter, and there they will have no madness or touch. It is far-fetched to use *al-mass*, which is madness, as an allusion to consuming interest in this world, so the meaning would be: "they will not stand on the Day of Resurrection, or from their graves on account of consuming interest, except as one stands whom Satan has driven to madness." If this meaning were intended, stating it plainly would be better than using the allusion of the word *mass*, since plain statement is more eloquent in deterrence and restraint.

The second reason: what follows *illa* (except) is not connected to what precedes it, unless it is within the scope of an exception. This is not within the scope of an exception. For this reason they prohibited connecting ﴿with the clear proofs and the scriptures﴾ [al-Nahl: 44] to His saying: ﴿We did not send before you except men﴾ [al-Nahl: 43], and the estimated sense is: "We did not send with the clear proofs and scriptures except men."

﴿That is because they said: trade is only like interest.﴾ The demonstrative *dhalika* refers to that particular standing of theirs in the Hereafter, and it is the subject (mubtada'), with the prepositional phrase *bi-anna-hum* as the predicate, meaning: that standing exists because of the fact that they... It has also been said that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being: "their standing is that," but in this view there is a separation between the verbal noun and its complement, which is *bi-anna-hum*, though it is not far-fetched that this is permitted because the verbal noun is omitted, so the separation by the predicate does not appear ugly. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "that punishment is because of the fact that they..." and the punishment is that standing. It is also possible that *dhalika* refers to their consumption of interest, meaning: that consumption which they made lawful, because of their saying and their belief that trade is like interest. Their basis for this is the equation they made between interest and trade. They compared trade, which is agreed to be permissible, to interest, which is forbidden, and they did not reverse the comparison, treating this interest they practiced as the original standard to which trade is compared. This is from (p-335) the reversal of comparison, which occurs in Arabic speech. Dhu al-Rumma said:

*"And sand like the hips of virgins, I crossed it."*

It is abundant in the poetry of later poets, as Abu al-Qasim ibn Hani' said:

*"As if the light of the sun is the blaze of Ja'far, when he saw the opponent, his brightness increased twofold."*

The people of the Jahiliyya, when a debt became due from a debtor, would demand payment, and the debtor would say: "Give me more time and I will add to the amount." They would do this and say: "It is the same to us whether the increase is at the beginning of the sale for profit, or at the due date in exchange for delay." So God rejected them. It has also been said that Thaqif was the most usurious of the Arabs, and when they were forbidden from it, they said: "It is only like trade."

﴿God has made trade lawful and forbidden interest.﴾ Its apparent meaning is that it is the speech of God, exalted, not theirs. In this there is a refutation of them, since they equated the two, and judgment regarding things belongs only to God, exalted; His ruling cannot be opposed or His command contravened. In this verse there is evidence that analogy (qiyas) cannot stand against a clear text (nass), since God, exalted, made the proof for refuting their claim to be: "God has made trade lawful and forbidden interest." Some scholars said: their analogy is corrupt, because trade is an exchange of a thing and its counter-value with no inequity in it, whereas interest involves mutual cheating (taghabun) and the consumption of wealth in falsehood, since the excess has no counterpart of its own kind, unlike trade, where the price is matched against the goods.

Ja'far al-Sadiq said: God forbade interest so that people would lend to one another. It has also been said: He forbade it because it destroys wealth and ruins people. Some said: it is possible that ﴿God has made trade lawful and forbidden interest﴾ is part of their own speech, so they knew that God had forbidden interest but opposed it with their own opinions, and that would be disbelief on their part. The apparent meaning is the generality of trade and interest in every trade and in every instance of interest, except what the proof has specified, such as the prohibition of some kinds of sales and the permission of some kinds of interest. It has also been said that both terms are ambiguous (mujmal), so one may not proceed to permit a sale or prohibit interest except with an explanation. This is the difference between a general term (amm) and an ambiguous term (mujmal). It has also been said that it is a general term to which specification has applied, and an ambiguous term to which explanation has applied. The divisions and details of trade and interest are mentioned in the books of jurisprudence (fiqh).

The apparent meaning is that the verse, as they said, concerns disbelievers, because of His saying: ﴿then what has passed is his﴾, since a believer who disobeys by dealing in interest does not keep what has passed; rather, he must retract and reverse the act, even if he was ignorant of the prohibition. But he takes on a portion of the threat of this verse.

﴿Whoever receives an admonition from his Lord and desists, for him is what has already passed.﴾ The feminine ta' is dropped from *jā'ahu* (came to him) because the verb is separated from its subject, and because the feminine marker of *maw'iẓa* (admonition) is metaphorical. Ubayy and al-Hasan read *fa-man jā'athu* with the ta', in accordance with the original form. ʿĀʾisha recited this verse when al-ʿĀliya bint Abqaʾ, the wife of Abu Ishaq al-Sabiʿi, asked her about buying a slave girl for six hundred dirhams in cash from Zayd ibn Arqam, having sold him the girl for eight hundred dirhams on credit until his stipend was paid. ʿĀʾisha said: "Wretched is what you bought and what you sold. Inform Zayd that he has nullified his jihad with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ unless he repents." Al-ʿĀliya said: "What if I take only my principal?" So ʿĀʾisha recited the verse.

The *maw'iẓa* (admonition) has been interpreted as the prohibition, or the threat of punishment, or the Qur'an; these are different opinions. The phrase *min rabbihi* (from his Lord) may be connected to *jā'athu* or to an implied verb, in which case it is an attribute of *maw'iẓa*. In the latter reading, the statement magnifies the admonition, since it came to him from his Lord, the One who oversees his welfare. Mentioning "the Lord" also serves to make the admonition acceptable, as the word "Lord" implies the reform of His servant. *Fa-intaha* (desisted) means he followed the prohibition and gave up dealing in *ribā* (usury), or gave up every forbidden form of earning. ﴿for him is what has already passed﴾ means: what he had already taken of *ribā* before the prohibition is his, and he will not be held to account for it in this world or the Hereafter. This is a ruling from Allah for those among the disbelievers of Quraysh and Thaqif who embraced Islam, and for those who used to trade there. This is according to the view that the verse is specific to the disbelievers. According to the one who says the verse is general, its meaning is: what passed before the prohibition is his.

﴿And his affair is with Allah.﴾ Apparently the pronoun in *amruhu* (his affair) refers to the one who desisted, since the context concerns him. The meaning is to reassure him and extend his hope for good, as you would say: "his affair is toward obedience, goodness and a place of hope." The word *amr* here is not restricted to *ribā* but covers all his affairs. It has also been said that it refers to the reward and the reckoning, or to pardon and punishment. It has been said that it means Allah will judge his case on the Day of Resurrection, not left to those with whom he dealt, so they will not demand anything from him. It has been said that the meaning is: his reward is with Allah for accepting the admonition, reported from al-Hasan. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to *mā salaf* (what has passed), meaning in pardoning it and dropping any liability for it. It has been said that it refers to the one who dealt in *ribā*, meaning in Allah making him firm in desisting, or returning him to sin, reported from Ibn Jubayr and Muqatil. It has been said that it refers to *ribā*, meaning in the continuation of its prohibition, or otherwise. It has been said that it means in Allah's pardon of whomever He wills, reported from Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

﴿And whoever returns﴾ to the practice of *ribā*, and to the claim that trade is like *ribā*. Sufyan said: whoever returns to the practice of *ribā* until he dies, for him is eternity. ﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾ The explanation of this sentence, which is the predicate of *man* (whoever), has been given before. The word *fīhā* (therein) is treated by meaning after being treated by form. If it refers to the disbelievers, then *khulūd* (eternity) is eternal abiding. If it refers to a sinful Muslim, then his abiding is a long stay, not eternal. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is a clear proof that sinners will be eternal in the Fire. He ended. This follows from his Mu'tazili doctrine (*al-madhhab al-iʿtizāli*) that the grave sinner is eternal in the Fire and does not leave it. It is reported from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and authenticated, that "consuming *ribā* is among the seven destructive sins." Also reported from ʿAwn ibn Abi Juhayfa, from his father, that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ cursed the consumer of *ribā*, its payer, and its scribe (its agent)." A man who saw a drunkard staggering, trying to grab the moon, asked Malik, may Allah have mercy on him: "His wife is divorced if anything enters the son of Adam's stomach that is worse than wine." Does his wife get divorced? Malik said to him, after he repeated it twice: "Your wife is divorced. I have searched the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Prophet and I have not found anything worse than *ribā*, because Allah the Exalted has declared war upon it."

﴿Allah destroys ribā﴾ meaning: He takes away its blessing, and the wealth into which it enters goes away. This was reported by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Ibn Jubayr said the same. From Ibn Masʿud: even if *ribā* increases, its end is to decline. Al-Dahhak reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that its destruction (*mihāq*) is nullifying whatever charity, kinship ties, jihad, and the like come from it.

﴿and makes charities grow﴾. It has been said that *al-irbāʾ* (growth) is literal, meaning He increases and develops them in this world by blessing and by abundant profits in the wealth from which the charity came out. It has also been said the increase is figurative, meaning the multiplication of good deeds and rewards gained by charity, as found in many verses and hadiths. Ibn al-Zubayr read, and it was reported from the Prophet ﷺ, *yumahhiqu wa-yuraббi* (*yumahhiqu* and *yurabbī*), from *maḥaqa* and *rabbā* with the doubled letter. The mention of destruction and growth contains the figure of antithesis (*al-ṭibāq*, the use of opposites). The mention of *ribā* and *yurabbī* contains the figure of paronomasia (*al-tajnīs*, similar-sounding words with different meanings).

﴿Allah does not love every ungrateful sinner.﴾ This emphasizes the severity of the matter of *ribā* and indicates that it is an act of disbelievers, not of the people of Islam. The intensive form is used for the disbeliever and the sinner, even though Allah the Exalted does not love the disbeliever in any case, as a warning about the greatness of *ribā* and of opposing Allah. It also refers to their saying ﴿trade is only like ribā﴾, and that He does not say so. Whoever equates trade with *ribā* in order to use it as evidence for eating *ribā* is only one who exaggerates in disbelief and exaggerates in sin. He mentioned *al-athīm* (the sinner) as emphasis and reinforcement, since the two words differ. Ibn Furak said: he mentioned *al-athīm* so that the shared ambiguity in *kaffār* would be removed, since it applies to the farmer who covers the seed in the earth. He ended. This is far-fetched, because the Qur'an's usage of *al-kāfir*, *al-kāfirūn* and *al-kuffār* refers only to those who disbelieve in Allah. Its application to the farmer is by a verbal indicator, as in His saying: ﴿like a rain whose vegetation pleases the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ḥadīd 57:20].

Ibn Furak also said: the meaning of the verse ﴿Allah does not love every ungrateful sinner﴾ is that He does not love one who is good and righteous, but rather wills him to be evil and wicked. It may also mean: Allah does not love the success (*tawfīq*) of the sinful disbeliever. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: these interpretations are strained. As for the first, it overreaches in extending the verb and imposes on it a meaning its wording does not bear. As for the second, its meaning is incorrect, since Allah the Exalted loves success in general and makes it beloved. The one who loves in the visible world inclines toward the beloved, shows kindness to him, is eager to preserve him, and these signs appear. Allah the Exalted wills that the disbeliever manifest what he is, and He does not have for him the distinction of love through deeds that appear on him, like what we mentioned in the visible world. That distinction exists for the believer. He ended. Love in its literal sense is natural inclination, and it is negated of Allah the Exalted. Ibn Furak took it to mean will, so it is an attribute of essence (*ṣifat dhāt*). Ibn ʿAṭiyya took it to mean kindness and showing signs, so it is an attribute of action (*ṣifat fiʿl*). The discussion of this has already been given.

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, establish the prayer, and give zakat, their reward is with their Lord, and there shall be no fear upon them, nor shall they grieve.﴾ The connection of this verse to what precedes it is clear. When He mentioned the state of the one who consumes riba (usury) and the one who returns to it after the admonition had come, and that he is a disbeliever and a sinner, He mentioned the opposite of those people in order to show the difference between the two states. The apparent meaning of the verse is general. Makki said: its meaning is that those who repented from consuming riba, believed in what was revealed to them, desisted from what they were forbidden, and did righteous deeds. End of quote. He specified the establishment of the prayer and the giving of zakat, although both are included in the general category of physical and financial deeds. The words of the verse have already been explained.

﴿O you who believe, fear Allah and give up what remains of riba, if you are believers.﴾ It is said: it was revealed concerning the Banu Amr ibn Umayr of Thaqif, who had riba debts owed to them by the Banu al-Mughirah of the Banu Makhzum. It is also said: it was revealed concerning Abbas, and it is said: concerning Uthman. Al-Suddi said: it was revealed concerning Abbas and Khalid ibn al-Walid, who were partners in the pre-Islamic period and who lent on riba. The summary is that they wanted to collect their riba, so it was revealed. Since His statement ﴿and his affair is for Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 275] had preceded, and the meaning was: whatever has passed (salaf) before the prohibition is his, that is, there is no liability upon him for what he took before the prohibition. It is possible that His statement "what has passed" means: what the contract was made on before, so there is no difference between what has been received and what remains as a debt. What prevents is the initiation of a new riba contract after the prohibition. God, exalted is He, removed this possibility by commanding the abandonment of what remains of riba in the earlier contracts, made before the prohibition, and that what remains as a debt of riba is like what is initiated after the prohibition. He addressed them by the name of faith to encourage them to accept the command to abandon what remains of riba. He began first with the command to fear Allah, since it is the root of everything, then He commanded a second time to abandon what remains of riba.

The ʿayn of wa-dharū was given a fatḥah by analogy with daʿaw, and the ʿayn of daʿaw was given a fatḥah by analogy with yadaʿu. The fatḥah was applied to yadaʿu, although its analogical vowel would be kasrah, since its lām is a guttural letter. Al-Hasan recited mā baqā, changing the yā into an alif, which is a dialect of Tayy and of some Arabs. ʿAlqamah ibn ʿAbdah al-Tamimi said:

"Longing has so stirred him that the pupil of his eye overflows with a copious, brimming water."

It is also narrated from him that he recited mā baqī with a sukūn on the yā. A poet said:

"By your life, I do not fear poverty so long as there remains on earth a Qaysi who drives camels."

And Jarir said:

"He is the caliph, so be content with what he has chosen for you, a man of resolute purpose in whose rule there is no injustice."

﴿if you are believers﴾. It has been stated that they are believers by the address of Allah, exalted is He, to them: ﴿O you who believe﴾. He combined the two because it is a figurative condition, for the sake of emphasis, as you say to someone whose self you wish to correct: "If you are a man, then do such-and-such." Ibn ʿAtiyyah said this. Or the meaning is: if your faith is sound, meaning that the proof of the soundness and firmness of faith is obedience to what you have been commanded in this matter. Al-Zamakhshari said this, and in it there is a subtle hint of Muʿtazilism (the rationalist school), because if the soundness of faith depends on abandoning this sin, then soundness does not coexist with committing it, and if his faith is not sound he is not a believer, which is the claim of the Muʿtazilah. It is also said that "in" (in) means "since" (idh), that is: since you are believers. Muqatil ibn Sulayman said this. It is the view of some grammarians that "in" can mean "idh," but it is weak, rejected, and not established in the language. It is also said: it is a condition meant to indicate continuity. It is said: it is meant to indicate completeness, as if faith is not complete when a person persists in a major sin, and he becomes a believer without qualification only when he avoids the major sins. Although the evidences have established that the reality of faith does not include deeds in its definition, it is said: faith varies according to its object. So the meaning of the first (O you who believe, [al-Baqarah: 282]) is with their tongues, and the meaning of the second (if you are believers) is with your hearts. It is also said: it is possible that He means: O you who believed in the prophets before Muhammad (ﷺ), give up what remains of riba, if you believe in Muhammad, since the first (faith) does not benefit except with this. This is said by Ibn Furak.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: this is rejected by what has been narrated about the occasion of revelation, meaning that it was revealed concerning Abbas and Uthman, or Abbas and Khalid, or concerning those of Thaqif who embraced Islam, and these people had not believed in prophets before accepting Islam. It is also said: it is a pure conditional in the case of Thaqif, on its own basis, because it was at the beginning of their entry into Islam. End of quote. According to this, it is not a sound condition except under the interpretation of the continuation of faith.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah mentioned that Abu al-Simak, who is al-ʿAdawi, recited here (min al-Ribu) with a kasrah on the doubled rāʾ, a ḍammah on the bāʾ, and a sukūn on the wāw. We have already mentioned his recitation in this way in His statement ﴿Those who consume riba﴾ [al-Baqarah: 275] and some discussion of it.

Abu al-Fath said: this word is anomalous in two respects. The first: moving from kasrah to ḍammah as a necessary fixed vowel. The second: a wāw coming after a ḍammah at the end of a noun, and this has not occurred except in verbs, such as yaghzu and yadʿu.

As for dhū in the Ṭāʾiyyah dialect, meaning "the one who," it is extremely anomalous. Some of them change its wāw when it is not in the nominative case. You say raʾaytu dhā qāma. The basis of the recitation is that he emphasized the alif, drawing toward it the wāw of which the alif is a replacement, on the pattern of their saying al-ṣalāh wa-l-zakāh. In general this is an anomalous recitation. End of Abu al-Fath's words.

By his saying "fixed vowel" he means that it may be incidental, as in al-ḥibk, where the kasrah of the ḥāʾ is not necessary, and as in their saying al-ridʾ in pause, where the ḍammah of the dāl is not necessary. For this reason no verbal pattern has been found in their word-forms, neither in nouns nor in verbs. As for his saying that it has not occurred except in verbs, such as yaghzu, this is as he mentioned, except that it occurs in the Six Nouns in the nominative case. So he may say: since this is not necessary in the accusative and genitive, it does not refute what they stated. We say: the ḍammah that is before the last letter is either for assimilation, so it is not a ḍammah that belongs to the original structure of the word, like the ḍammah of yaghzu.

We have already mentioned his recitation in this way in His statement ﴿Those who consume riba﴾ [al-Baqarah: 275] and some discussion of it.

Abu al-Fath said: this word is anomalous in two respects. The first: moving from kasrah to ḍammah as a necessary fixed vowel. The second: a wāw coming after a ḍammah at the end of a noun, and this has not occurred except in verbs, such as yaghzu and yadʿu.

As for dhū in the Ṭāʾiyyah dialect, meaning "the one who," it is extremely anomalous. Some of them change its wāw when it is not in the nominative case. You say raʾaytu dhā qāma. The basis of the recitation is that he emphasized the alif, drawing toward it the wāw of which the alif is a replacement, on the pattern of their saying al-ṣalāh wa-l-zakāh. In general this is an anomalous recitation. End of Abu al-Fath's words.

By his saying "fixed vowel" he means that it may be incidental, as in al-ḥibk, where the kasrah of the ḥāʾ is not necessary, and as in their saying al-ridʾ in pause, where the ḍammah of the dāl is not necessary. For this reason no verbal pattern has been found in their word-forms, neither in nouns nor in verbs. As for his saying that it has not occurred except in verbs, such as yaghzu, this is as he mentioned, except that it occurs in the Six Nouns in the nominative case. So he may say: since this is not necessary in the accusative and genitive, it does not refute what they stated. We say: the ḍammah that is before the last letter is either for assimilation, so it is not a ḍammah that belongs to the original structure of the word, like the ḍammah of yaghzu.

﴿So if you do not, then be informed of a war from Allah and His Messenger.﴾ Its apparent meaning: if you do not abandon what remains of riba. Abandonment was called an act. When they are commanded to abandon what remains of riba, that command includes the command to abandon initiating riba, by way of greater priority. Al-Razi said: if you are not acknowledging its prohibition, then be informed of a war from Allah and His Messenger. Those who held this view said: there is evidence in it that whoever disbelieves in one of the legal rulings of Islam leaves the religion, just as if he disbelieved in all of them.

Hamzah, and Abu Bakr in a transmission other than that of al-Burjumi and Ibn Ghalib from him, read fa-ādhanū, an imperative of ādhana (the fourth form), meaning "inform," like His statement ﴿Then say: I have informed you on equal terms﴾ [al-Anbiya: 109]. The remaining seven read fa-idhanū, an imperative of idhina (the triliteral form), like His statement ﴿None shall speak except one whom the Most Merciful permits﴾ [al-Naba: 38]. Al-Hasan read fa-aya-qinū bi-ḥarb ("then be certain of a war"). The apparent meaning is that the address in His statement ﴿So if you do not﴾ is to those to whom the verse was addressed, namely believers. It is said that the address is to the disbelievers who consider riba lawful. On this view, the fighting is clear. On the first view, the informing or the knowledge of the war comes by way of exaggeration in threat, not the literal war, as in the ḥadīth: "Whoever shows enmity to a friend of Mine has declared war upon Me." It is said: the intended meaning is the war itself.

We say: persistence in riba, if the one doing it is within the reach of the imam, the imam seizes him, disciplines him (taʿzīr), and imprisons him until repentance appears from him. If he is beyond reach, he is fought as a rebellious group is fought. Ibn ʿAbbas said: whoever deals in riba is asked to repent. If he repents, well and good; otherwise his neck is struck.

This statement of his should be understood as applying to one who regards riba as lawful and persists in it. The meaning of the verse is: if you do not desist, the Prophet (ﷺ) will wage war against you. It is also said: the meaning is: you are the enemies of Allah and His Messenger, meaning enemies. War calls for killing. They said: the war of Allah is the Fire, and the war of His Messenger is the sword.

It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that on the Day of Resurrection it is said to the one who consumed riba: "Take your weapon for war." The bāʾ in bi-ḥarb, on the reading with the short vowel (qaṣr), is for attachment, as you say adhina bi-kadhā, meaning "he knew of such-and-such." Ibn ʿAbbas and others said likewise: the meaning is "then be certain of a war from Allah." Al-Zamakhshari said: it is from the ear (udhun), which is listening, because it is by way of knowledge. End of quote.

The recitation of al-Hasan strengthens the recitation of the majority with the short vowel. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: in my view it is from idhn (permission). When a person permits something, he has settled it and built upon it with himself. So it is as if it was said to them: settle the war between you and Allah and His Messenger.

From the wording of the verse it follows that they are the ones who call for war and who pursue it, since they are the ones who permit it and enter into it. Included in this is their knowledge that it is the war of Allah and their certainty of it. End of his words. From this it appears that the bāʾ in bi-ḥarb is for location, meaning: then permit war, as you say udhina fī kadhā, meaning that he allowed it and empowered it.

Abu ʿAli said: whoever reads fa-ādhanū with the long vowel, its implied sense is: then inform those who do not desist from that with war, and the object is omitted. This object is established in His statement ﴿Say: I have informed you on equal terms﴾ [al-Anbiya: 109]. When they are commanded to inform others, they inevitably know themselves. He said: in informing them, He informs them of their own knowledge, but in their knowledge there is no informing of others. So the reading with the long vowel is preferable, because it is more forceful and emphatic.

Al-Tabari said: the reading with the short vowel is preferable, because it is specific to them, and the command under the long-vowel reading is to inform others. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: the two readings are equal in my view, because the addressed group is restricted, since it refers to everyone who does not abandon what remains of riba. If it is said fa-ādhanū, the command includes them all. If it is said fa-ādhinū with the long vowel, the meaning is: inform yourselves, or some of you inform others. It seems this reading allows them room for deliberation and reflection. So inform your souls of this, then consider which is better for you: abandoning riba or war. End of quote. It is related that when this was revealed, the Thaqif said: "We have no power for war against Allah and His Messenger."

The min in ﴿from Allah﴾ indicates the starting point, and in it there is great terror, for war from Allah and from His Prophet (ﷺ) cannot be borne by anyone. It is possible that it is partitive, with an elided noun, meaning: from the wars of Allah. Al-Zamakhshari said: if you say, why was it not said bi-ḥarbi Allāh wa-rasūlih? I say: this is more emphatic, because the meaning is: then permit a kind of war, great, from Allah and His Messenger. End of quote. It is more emphatic because it contains an explicit statement that the war is from Allah against them. Allah Himself is the one who wages war against them. Had it said bi-ḥarb Allāh, it could have meant the war is attributed to the agent, so Allah is the one who fights them, or attributed to the object, so they would be those who fight Allah. Thus Allah being the one who wages war against them is more forceful and more effective as an admonition than their being those who wage war against Allah.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 277–279 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And if you repent, then for you is your principal (ru'us amwalikum)﴾. That is: if you repent from riba (usury). Ru'us al-amwal (the principals) are their origins; as for the profits, they are additions and accretions upon them. Some said: if they do not repent, they become disbelievers by rejecting the ruling of Allah and deeming lawful what Allah has forbidden, so their wealth becomes fay' (spoils, property taken without battle) for the Muslims. In the restriction to the principals, together with what precedes it, there is clear evidence that they have nothing except that. The implication (mafhum) of the condition is that if they do not repent, they have no principal of their wealth. Calling the origin of wealth a "ra's" (head) is a metaphor (majaz).

﴿You do not wrong, nor are you wronged﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read the first as active (tazlimun) and the second as passive (tuzlamun). That is: you do not wrong the debtor by demanding an increase over the principal, nor are you wronged by a reduction of the principal. It was said: by delay (al-matl). Aban and al-Mufaddal, from Asim, read the first as passive and the second as active. Abu Ali (al-Farisi) preferred the reading of the majority, because it accords with His saying "and if you repent", in attributing both verbs to the subject. Reading tazlimun with an open ta' (tazlamun) would be inconsistent with what precedes it. The clause appears to be a new sentence (mustaʼnafah), and an announcement from Him, exalted is He, that when they restrict themselves to the principals, that is justice (nasafah). It was also said: the clause is a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the genitive in "lakum", and the operative element in the circumstantial phrase is the trace of verbal meaning in the preposition, as stated by al-Akhfash.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verses 280–281:**

﴿And if the debtor is in hardship, then [let there be] a respite until a time of ease.﴾ The Banu al-Mughira complained of hardship and said: "Defer us until the harvests come in." But they refused to be deferred, and so this was revealed. It was said: this verse abrogates (*naskh*) what was practised in the Jahiliyya (the pre-Islamic period) of selling a person who was unable to pay his debt. It was also said: it was enjoined at the beginning of Islam. If this is established, then it is abrogation; otherwise, it is not abrogation. *Al-'usrah* is straitened circumstances due to lack of wealth, and from it comes *jaysh al-'usrah* (the army of hardship). *Al-nazirah* is deferral, and *al-maysarah* is ease.

The majority read *dhu 'usrah* (ذُو عُسْرَةٍ), taking *kana* (كانَ) as a complete verb (*tammah*), according to the view of Sibawayh and Abu 'Ali: "And if there occurs a creditor of yours who is in hardship." Some of the Kufans permitted *kana* to be a incomplete (*naqisah*) verb here, and the predicate was estimated as: "And if there is, from among your debtors, one in hardship," so the prepositional phrase which is the predicate was omitted. It was also estimated as: "And if there is one in hardship to whom you have a right." But omitting the predicate of *kana* is not permitted according to our companions (the Basran grammarians), neither as a restriction nor as an abbreviation, for a reason they mentioned in grammar.

Ubayy, Ibn Mas'ud, 'Uthman and Ibn 'Abbas read *dha 'usrah* (ذا عُسْرَةٍ). Al-A'mash read *mu'siran* (مُعْسِرًا). Al-Dani related from Ahmad ibn Musa that it is so in the codex of Abu 'Ali. If the name of *kana* is a pronoun, its estimate is *huwa* (he), i.e., the debtor, which is indicated by what preceded in the discourse, because the one who charges interest necessarily has someone on whom he charges it.

It was also read *wa-man kana dha 'usrah* (وَمَن كانَ ذا عُسْرَةٍ), which is the reading of Aban ibn 'Uthman. Al-Mahdawi related that in the codex of 'Uthman it is *fa-in kana* (فَإنْ كانَ) with *fa*. Whoever puts *dha 'usrah* in the accusative, or reads *mu'siran*, after *wa-in kana*, it is said that it is specific to the people of usury. Whoever puts it in the nominative, it is general to all who are owed a debt. This is not binding, because the verse was brought in regard to the people of usury, and it was revealed concerning them. It was also said: the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that the original state is ease, and that poverty is an incidental, attracted condition that needs to be established.

﴿So [let there be] a respite until a time of ease.﴾ The majority read *fa-nazirah* (فَنَظِرَةٌ) on the pattern of *nabiqah*. Abu Raja', Mujahid, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Qatadah read it with a sukun on the *zay*, which is a Tamimi dialect, as they say *kabad* for *kabid*. 'Ata' read *fa-nazirah* (فَناظِرَةٌ) on the pattern of *fa'ilah*, and al-Zajjaj construed it as a verbal noun, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There will be no denying its occurrence﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 2], and like His saying: ﴿expecting that a calamity of back-breaking nature will be done to them﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 25], and like His saying: ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes﴾ [Ghafir: 19]. He said: 'Ata' read *fa-nazirah* meaning: the owner of the right is its watcher, i.e., its awaiter, or the owner of its deferral, following the manner of the relative noun, as in their saying: *makan 'ashib* and *baqil*, meaning: possessing grass and possessing herbs. And from him (Ata'): *fa-nazirah-hu* (فَناظِرَهُ) in the imperative, meaning: "so grant him respite and deal with him by it," and it ended. Ibn 'Atiyyah transmitted it. From Mujahid: they made it an imperative, and the *ha'* is the pronoun of the debtor. 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) read *fa-nazirulu-hu* (فَناظِرُوهُ), meaning: "so you are the ones who grant him respite," i.e., you are the ones who await him. So these are six readings. Whoever makes it a verbal noun or a noun of verbal action, it is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being: "So the matter and the obligation upon the creditor is a respite from him in demanding the debt from the debtor until a time of ease for him."

Nafi' alone read *maysurah* (مَيْسُرَةٍ) with a *damma* on the *sin*. The *damma* is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and it is rare, like *maqburah*, *mashrufah*, and *masrubah*, while the common form is *maf'alah* with a *fath* on the 'ayn. The majority read it with a *fath* on the *sin*, according to the common dialect, which is the dialect of the people of Najd. 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) read *ila maysurihi* (إلى مَيْسُورِهِ) on the pattern of *maf'ul*, added to the pronoun of the debtor. According to al-Akhfash it is a verbal noun, like *al-ma'qul* and *al-majlud* in their saying: "His wealth is *ma'qul* and not *majlud*," meaning: *'aql* (intellect/ wit) and *jald* (hardiness). Sibawayh did not establish *maf'ul* as a verbal noun. 'Ata' and Mujahid read *ila maysirihi* (إلى مَيْسُرِهِ) with a *damma* on the *sin* and a *kasra* on the *ra'* after it, with the pronoun of the debtor. It was also read thus with a *fath* on the *sin*, and this is explained by the omission of the *ta'* for the sake of the annexation (*idafah*), as in the poet's line:

*"And they broke with you, [like] the promise (ʿidda) of the matter which they made."*

I.e., *'iddah* (a promise). This, I mean the omission of the *ta'*, for the sake of the annexation, is the view of al-Farra' and some later grammarians. What led them to this interpretation is that *maf'al* is not among the singular nouns. As for the plural, they mentioned this in the verse of 'Adi ibn Zayd:

*"Convey to al-Nu'man from me, [the place of] refuge (ma'luk), that my imprisonment and my waiting have lasted long."*

And in the verse of Jamil:

*"Buthayna, keep to it; if you keep to 'no, no' (la la), then the many slanderers will not [stop]; what is the help (ma'un)?"*

So *ma'luk* and *ma'un* are plurals of *ma'lukah* and *ma'unah*. Likewise is his saying:

*"For a day of terror or the deeds of the noble (fi'al makram)."*

This is the interpretation of Abu 'Ali. Abu al-Fath interpreted it as singular with the *ta'* omitted from it. Sibawayh said: there is no *maf'il* in speech, meaning among the singular forms, so said Abu 'Ali. It is related from Sibawayh: *mahlak*, with the *lam* having three vowels. Al-Kisa'i permitted that *maf'il* be singular, and this does not contradict Sibawayh's view, since one says: "There is no such-and-such in speech," even if one or two letters have come from it, as if the rare is not counted nor given a ruling.

A point of the disagreement was mentioned earlier: is this respite specific to the debt of usury? This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Shurayh. Or is it general to every debtor in insolvency, whether usury or otherwise? This is the view of Abu Hurayrah, al-Hasan, 'Ata', al-Dahhak, al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham, and the majority of jurists.

Many hadiths have come concerning the virtue of granting respite to the insolvent, among them: "Whoever grants respite to one in hardship, or remits [the debt] for him, Allah will shade him in His shade on a day when there is no shade but His shade." And among them: "A servant will be brought on the Day of Resurrection and he will say: 'O Lord, I did no good deed for You ever, seeking You by it, except that You gave me wealth, and I would extend to the one in need, and grant respite to the one in hardship.' Then Allah, mighty and majestic, will say: 'I am more deserving of that than you; so overlook My servant.'"

﴿And that you give charity is better for you.﴾ That is: giving charity to the debtor of the principal or part of it is better than granting respite. This was said by al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, and the majority. It was said: "And that you give charity" (means) respite is better for you than demanding payment. This is weak, because respite for the insolvent is obligatory upon the creditor, so interpreting it as a new benefit is preferable. Also, the superlative *af'al al-tafdil* (أفْعَلَ التَّفْضِيلِ) remains upon the original sense of its description. The meaning of "good" is the attainment of a beautiful reputation in this world and a great reward in the Hereafter. Qatadah said: they were encouraged to give charity of their principal to the rich and the poor.

The majority read ﴿and that you give charity﴾ (وأنْ تَصَدَّقُوا) with the *ta'* assimilated into the *sad*. 'Asim read *tasaddaqu* (تَصَدَّقُوا) with the *ta'* deleted. In the codex of 'Abd Allah it is *tatasaddaqu* (تَتَصَدَّقُوا) with two *ta's*, which is the original form. Assimilation is a lightening, and deletion is a greater lightening.

﴿if you know﴾: he means practice; he made it among the necessary consequences of knowledge. It was said: "if you know" the excellence of charity over respite and collection. It was said: "if you know" that what your Lord has commanded you is more beneficial for you.

It was said: the last verse revealed was the verse of usury. This was said by 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas, and it is to be understood as among the last of what was revealed, because the majority said: the last verse revealed was ﴿And fear a day when you will be returned to Allah﴾. It was said: nine nights before his death; it was also related: three hours. It was said: he lived after it eighty-one days; it was said: twenty-one days; it was said: seven days. It is related that he said: "Place it between the verse of usury and the verse of debt." It is also related that he, peace be upon him, said: "Gabriel came to me and said: 'Place it at the head of two hundred and eighty verses of al-Baqarah.'" The discussion of ﴿And fear a day﴾ has preceded in His saying: ﴿And fear a day in which no soul will avail another﴾ [al-Baqarah: 123].

Ya'qub and Abu 'Amr read *turja'un* (تُرْجَعُونَ) in the active voice, and Ibn 'Abbas related from Abu 'Amr. The rest of the seven read it in the passive voice. Al-Hasan read *yurja'un* (يُرْجَعُونَ), meaning all people will return; this is from the phenomenon of *iltifat* (shift of person). Ibn Jinni said: Allah, exalted is He, was gentle with the believers, so as not to confront them with mention of the return, since it is something which makes hearts tremble. So He said to them: ﴿And fear﴾, then He shifted in the mention of the return to the third person, out of gentleness toward them, and it ended. Ubayy read *turaddun* (تُرَدُّونَ) with a *damma* on the *ta'*; Ibn 'Atiyyah related it from him. Al-Zamakhshari said: 'Abd Allah read *yaruddun* (يَرُدُّونَ), and Ubayy read *tasirun* (تَصِيرُونَ), and it ended.

The majority said: by this day is meant the Day of Resurrection. Some people said: it is the day of death. The first is more apparent, because of His saying: ﴿then every soul will be paid in full what it earned﴾. The meaning is: to the judgment of Allah and the decision of His ruling.

﴿Then every soul will be paid in full﴾: that is, it will be given its full recompense (*jaza'*) ﴿for what it earned﴾ of good and evil. In this there is a clear text linking recompense to earning, and in it is a refutation of the Jabriyya (determinists).

﴿and they will not be wronged﴾: that is, they will not be diminished from what would be the reward of righteous deeds of reward, nor will they be increased beyond the punishment for evil deeds. The pronoun in *kasabat* (كَسَبَتْ) first was returned to the wording *al-nafs* (the soul), and in His saying ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ it was returned to the meaning, for the sake of the closing rhyme (*fasilat al-ayy*), for if it had come as "and it will not be wronged," there would be no rhyme. Whoever reads *yurja'un* with the *ya'*, then *wa-hum* (وهم) in it is a third-person plural pronoun referring back to a plural third-person antecedent.

The *damma* is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and it is rare, like *maqburah*, *mashrufah*, and *masrubah*, while the common form is *maf'alah* with a *fath* on the 'ayn. The majority read it with a *fath* on the *sin*, according to the common dialect, which is the dialect of the people of Najd. 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) read *ila maysurihi* (إلى مَيْسُورِهِ) on the pattern of *maf'ul*, added to the pronoun of the debtor. According to al-Akhfash it is a verbal noun, like *al-ma'qul* and *al-majlud* in their saying: "His wealth is *ma'qul* and not *majlud*," meaning: *'aql* (intellect/ wit) and *jald* (hardiness). Sibawayh did not establish *maf'ul* as a verbal noun. 'Ata' and Mujahid read *ila maysirihi* (إلى مَيْسُرِهِ) with a *damma* on the *sin* and a *kasra* on the *ra'* after it, with the pronoun of the debtor. It was also read thus with a *fath* on the *sin*, and this is explained by the omission of the *ta'* for the sake of the annexation (*idafah*), as in the poet's line:

*"And they broke with you, [like] the promise (ʿidda) of the matter which they made."*

I.e., *'iddah* (a promise). This, I mean the omission of the *ta'*, for the sake of the annexation, is the view of al-Farra' and some later grammarians. What led them to this interpretation is that *maf'al* is not among the singular nouns. As for the plural, they mentioned this in the verse of 'Adi ibn Zayd:

*"Convey to al-Nu'man from me, [the place of] refuge (ma'luk), that my imprisonment and my waiting have lasted long."*

And in the verse of Jamil:

*"Buthayna, keep to it; if you keep to 'no, no' (la la), then the many slanderers will not [stop]; what is the help (ma'un)?"*

So *ma'luk* and *ma'un* are plurals of *ma'lukah* and *ma'unah*. Likewise is his saying:

*"For a day of terror or the deeds of the noble (fi'al makram)."*

This is the interpretation of Abu 'Ali. Abu al-Fath interpreted it as singular with the *ta'* omitted from it. Sibawayh said: there is no *maf'il* in speech, meaning among the singular forms, so said Abu 'Ali. It is related from Sibawayh: *mahlak*, with the *lam* having three vowels. Al-Kisa'i permitted that *maf'il* be singular, and this does not contradict Sibawayh's view, since one says: "There is no such-and-such in speech," even if one or two letters have come from it, as if the rare is not counted nor given a ruling.

A point of the disagreement was mentioned earlier: is this respite specific to the debt of usury? This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Shurayh. Or is it general to every debtor in insolvency, whether usury or otherwise? This is the view of Abu Hurayrah, al-Hasan, 'Ata', al-Dahhak, al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham, and the majority of jurists.

Many hadiths have come concerning the virtue of granting respite to the insolvent, among them: "Whoever grants respite to one in hardship, or remits [the debt] for him, Allah will shade him in His shade on a day when there is no shade but His shade." And among them: "A servant will be brought on the Day of Resurrection and he will say: 'O Lord, I did no good deed for You ever, seeking You by it, except that You gave me wealth, and I would extend to the one in need, and grant respite to the one in hardship.' Then Allah, mighty and majestic, will say: 'I am more deserving of that than you; so overlook My servant.'"

﴿And that you give charity is better for you.﴾ That is: giving charity to the debtor of the principal or part of it is better than granting respite. This was said by al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, and the majority. It was said: "And that you give charity" (means) respite is better for you than demanding payment. This is weak, because respite for the insolvent is obligatory upon the creditor, so interpreting it as a new benefit is preferable. Also, the superlative *af'al al-tafdil* (أفْعَلَ التَّفْضِيلِ) remains upon the original sense of its description. The meaning of "good" is the attainment of a beautiful reputation in this world and a great reward in the Hereafter. Qatadah said: they were encouraged to give charity of their principal to the rich and the poor.

The majority read ﴿and that you give charity﴾ (وأنْ تَصَدَّقُوا) with the *ta'* assimilated into the *sad*. 'Asim read *tasaddaqu* (تَصَدَّقُوا) with the *ta'* deleted. In the codex of 'Abd Allah it is *tatasaddaqu* (تَتَصَدَّقُوا) with two *ta's*, which is the original form. Assimilation is a lightening, and deletion is a greater lightening.

﴿if you know﴾: he means practice; he made it among the necessary consequences of knowledge. It was said: "if you know" the excellence of charity over respite and collection. It was said: "if you know" that what your Lord has commanded you is more beneficial for you.

It was said: the last verse revealed was the verse of usury. This was said by 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas, and it is to be understood as among the last of what was revealed, because the majority said: the last verse revealed was ﴿And fear a day when you will be returned to Allah﴾. It was said: nine nights before his death; it was also related: three hours. It was said: he lived after it eighty-one days; it was said: twenty-one days; it was said: seven days. It is related that he said: "Place it between the verse of usury and the verse of debt." It is also related that he, peace be upon him, said: "Gabriel came to me and said: 'Place it at the head of two hundred and eighty verses of al-Baqarah.'" The discussion of ﴿And fear a day﴾ has preceded in His saying: ﴿And fear a day in which no soul will avail another﴾ [al-Baqarah: 123].

Ya'qub and Abu 'Amr read *turja'un* (تُرْجَعُونَ) in the active voice, and Ibn 'Abbas related from Abu 'Amr. The rest of the seven read it in the passive voice. Al-Hasan read *yurja'un* (يُرْجَعُونَ), meaning all people will return; this is from the phenomenon of *iltifat* (shift of person). Ibn Jinni said: Allah, exalted is He, was gentle with the believers, so as not to confront them with mention of the return, since it is something which makes hearts tremble. So He said to them: ﴿And fear﴾, then He shifted in the mention of the return to the third person, out of gentleness toward them, and it ended. Ubayy read *turaddun* (تُرَدُّونَ) with a *damma* on the *ta'*; Ibn 'Atiyyah related it from him. Al-Zamakhshari said: 'Abd Allah read *yaruddun* (يَرُدُّونَ), and Ubayy read *tasirun* (تَصِيرُونَ), and it ended.

The majority said: by this day is meant the Day of Resurrection. Some people said: it is the day of death. The first is more apparent, because of His saying: ﴿then every soul will be paid in full what it earned﴾. The meaning is: to the judgment of Allah and the decision of His ruling.

﴿Then every soul will be paid in full﴾: that is, it will be given its full recompense (*jaza'*) ﴿for what it earned﴾ of good and evil. In this there is a clear text linking recompense to earning, and in it is a refutation of the Jabriyya (determinists).

﴿and they will not be wronged﴾: that is, they will not be diminished from what would be the reward of righteous deeds of reward, nor will they be increased beyond the punishment for evil deeds. The pronoun in *kasabat* (كَسَبَتْ) first was returned to the wording *al-nafs* (the soul), and in His saying ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ it was returned to the meaning, for the sake of the closing rhyme (*fasilat al-ayy*), for if it had come as "and it will not be wronged," there would be no rhyme. Whoever reads *yurja'un* with the *ya'*, then *wa-hum* (وهم) in it is a third-person plural pronoun referring back to a plural third-person antecedent.

(p. 342) ﴿O you who have believed, when you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down. Let a scribe write it between you with justice. No scribe should refuse to write as Allah has taught him. So let him write, and let the one who owes the debt dictate, and let him fear Allah, his Lord, and not diminish anything of it. But if the one who owes the debt is foolish or weak, or unable to dictate himself, let his guardian dictate with justice. And call upon two witnesses from among your men. But if there are not two men, then a man and two women from those whom you accept as witnesses, so that if one of them errs, the other can remind her. And the witnesses should not refuse when they are called. And do not be weary of writing it, whether small or large, for its term. That is more just in the sight of Allah, more upright for testimony, and closer to preventing doubt, except when it is a present trade that you conduct among yourselves; then there is no blame on you if you do not write it. And take witness when you trade with one another. Let no scribe or witness be harmed. If you do that, it is indeed sinful conduct on your part. And fear Allah; Allah teaches you, and Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾ ﴿And if you are on a journey and do not find a scribe, then a pledge taken into possession. And if one of you trusts another, let the one entrusted fulfill his trust and let him fear Allah, his Lord. And do not conceal testimony, for whoever conceals it, his heart is sinful. And Allah is Knowing of what you do.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 283] ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on earth. Whether you show what is within yourselves or conceal it, Allah will hold you accountable for it. He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills, and Allah is over all things Competent.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 284] ﴿The Messenger has believed in what was revealed to him from his Lord, and so have the believers. Each one believed in Allah, His angels, His books, and His messengers. We make no distinction between any of His messengers. And they say: We hear and we obey; Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the final return.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 285] ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity. It has what it earned, and it bears what it has earned. Our Lord, do not impose blame on us if we forget or make mistake. Our Lord, do not lay on us a burden like that which You laid on those before us. Our Lord, do not burden us with what we have no ability to bear. And pardon us, forgive us, and have mercy on us. You are our Protector, so give us victory over the disbelieving people.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286]

Tadayyana (تَدايَنَ) is a reciprocal form (tafa'ala) from dayn (debt). It is said: "I dealt with the man in debt, giving or taking," just as you say "I traded with him" (baya'tuhu) when you sell to him or he sells to you. Ru'bah said:
"I took on debt from Aruwa, and debts are paid: some were delayed, and some were paid."
It is also said: "danttu al-rajul" means I sold him on credit, and "idtanantu" means I took on debt.

Amlaa and amlaa (أمْلَ وأمْلى) are two dialectal forms: the first belongs to the people of the Hijaz and Banu Asad, and the second to Tamim. It is said: "amlaytu and amlaltu 'ala al-rajul," meaning I dictated to him what he should write. Its original linguistic sense is repetition, one time after another. The poet said:
"Oh, the abodes of the tribe at al-Sab'an, over which the two nights of wear have passed."
It is also said that the original form is amlaltu, and the lam was changed to a ya' because it is lighter.

Bakhs (البَخْسُ) means deficiency. It is said: "bakhasa yabkhasu," and it is also said with the sad (bis-sad). Bakhs also means striking the eye. From this, "bakhs of his right" is used figuratively, as in their saying "he blinded his right" (awwara haqqahu). "Tabakhasu fi al-bay'" means they cheated one another in trade, each one diminishing what the other wanted from him through trickery.

As-sa'm and as-sa'ama mean weariness with a thing and boredom with it. It is said: "sa'ima yas'amu."

As-saghir (الصَّغِيرُ) is an active participle from saghura yasghuru, and its meaning is smallness of body, and it is also used for abstract meanings. Al-qist (القِسْطُ) with a kasra on the qaf means justice, and it is said: "aqsata al-rajul," meaning he was just. With a fatha on the qaf it means injustice, and it is said: "qasata al-rajul," meaning he was unjust. Al-qist with a kasra also means a share.

Ar-rahn (الرَّهْنُ) is what is handed to the creditor as security for his debt. It is said: "rahana yarhanu rahnan." Then the verbal noun was used for the thing pledged. It is also said: "rahana al-shay'" means it lasted. The poet said:
"Meat and bread are for them, a lasting provision, and wine whose strainer pours continuously."
"Arhana lahum al-sharab" means it lasted for them. Ibn Sidah said: "rahanahu" means he made it last. It is also said: "arhana fi al-silab" when he overpriced a commodity until he took it for a large price. The poet said:
"Ibn Salma travels with it over a stretch of road, a camel of the 'Idiyyah breed, for which the dinars were pledged."
Al-'Id is a clan of Mahr. A camel of Mahr is described as noble. It is also said, regarding the pledge that is a form of securing, "arhana irhanan." Hammam ibn Murrah said:
"When I feared their claws, I escaped and gave Malik as a pledge."
(p. 343) Ibn al-A'rabi and al-Zajjaj said: it is said regarding the pledge "rahanta" and "arhanta." al-A'sha said:
"Until a hostage from his sons, Na'sh, benefits you, and al-Simak al-Farqad pledges you."
You say "rahantu lisani bi-kadha" (I pledged my tongue for such-and-such). It is not said "arhantu" in this case. When the term "rahn" was applied to the pledged item, it became a noun. It was then broken into plural forms like nouns and was put in the accusative by its verb, like objects. So you say "rahantu rahnan," like "rahantu thawban" (I pledged a garment).

Al-isr (الإصْرُ) means a heavy and difficult matter. Al-aasirah in language means a binding matter, whether of obligation, kinship, a covenant, or the like. Al-isar is the rope with which loads and the like are tied. It is said: "asara ya'siru asran." Al-isr, with a kasra on the hamza, is the noun from that. It is also reported as al-usr with a damma, and it has been read that way. The poet said:
"O preventer of injustice from overtaking their nobles, and the bearer of the burden from them after they had sweated."

﴿O you who have believed, when you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed specifically concerning the salam (advance sale) contract. That is, the salam practice of the people of Madinah was the cause of revelation. But then it encompasses all debts by consensus (ijma').

The connection of this verse with what came before is that when He commanded spending in the way of Allah and abandoning riba, and both of these involve diminishing wealth, He drew attention to a lawful way of growing and increasing wealth. He emphasized how to preserve it, and He expanded on this in this verse, commanding in it several orders, as will be explained.

He mentioned "bi-dayn" (with debt) so that the pronoun would refer to it in His saying "fa-ktubuhu" (write it down), even though it is understood from "tadayantum." Or to remove the ambiguity of tadayyana, for it may be said "tudayinu" meaning some of them repaid one another. So when He said "bi-dayn," it indicated a meaning other than this. Or it is for emphasis, or to indicate that whatever debt it is, whether small or large, and in whatever manner, whether from salam or sale.

"Ila ajalin musamman" (for a specified term): this description is not meant to exclude debts without a specified term. Rather, a debt cannot occur except for a specified term. As for unknown terms, these are not permitted. What is meant by "musamma" is a fixed and known time, such as fixing it by year, months, or days. If he said "until the harvest," or "until threshing," or "until the return of the pilgrims," it would not be permitted because it is not a specified term. "Ila ajalin" is connected either to "tadayantum," or it is in the position of a qualifier to "bi-dayn," so it is connected to an omitted element.

﴿Fa-ktubuhu﴾ (write it down): He commanded writing it, because that is more secure and safer against forgetting, and further from denial. The apparent meaning of a command is obligation. Some scholars, including al-Tabari and the Zahiris, held this. But the majority said it is a command of recommendation (nadb), by which wealth is preserved and doubt is removed. In this there is encouragement to acknowledge it and preserve it, for writing is the substitute for speech, and speech is the substitute for the heart.

It is reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Ibn Zayd, al-Sha'bi, and Ibn Juraij that they held that His saying "fa-in amina ba'dukum ba'dan" (but if one of you trusts another) [al-Baqarah: 283] is abrogating (naskh) His saying "fa-ktubuhu." al-Rabi' said: it became obligatory by His saying "fa-ktubuhu," then it was lightened by His saying "fa-in amina" [al-Baqarah: 283].

﴿And let a scribe write it between you with justice.﴾ This command is said to be obligatory as a communal duty (fard kifayah), like jihad. 'Ata' and others said: it is obligatory on the scribe to write under all circumstances. al-Sha'bi also said: if no other scribe is found, it is obligatory on him to write. al-Suddi said: it is obligatory when he is free. al-Raghib chose that the correct view is that writing is an obligation of communal duty. He said: writing between two contracting parties, even if it is not obligatory, may become obligatory on the scribe when they come to him, just as a voluntary prayer, though not obligatory for the one performing it, may become obligatory on a scholar to clarify it when a questioner comes to him.

The meaning of "baynakum" (between you) is between the creditor and the debtor, the seller and the buyer, the lender and the borrower.
