The dual form implies that neither of the parties to the transaction should be alone, because one would be suspected in the writing. When it occurs between the two of them, each one has oversight over what the scribe has written.

* *

The meaning of "bi-l-'adl" (with justice) is with truth and fairness, such that there is no inclination in his heart or in his pen toward one of them over the other.

There has been disagreement about what "bi-l-'adl" is connected to. al-Zamakhshari said: "bi-l-'adl" is connected to "katib" (scribe) as a qualifier to it, meaning a scribe trusted in what he writes, who writes with equality and caution, neither adding to what must be written nor reducing it. It also implies that the scribe should be a jurist knowledgeable of the conditions, so that his document comes out legally sound. It is a command to the two contracting parties to choose the scribe carefully, and that they should only hire a jurist who is pious.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "bi-l-'adl" is connected to His saying "wa-l-yaktub" (let him write), not to "katib," because it would follow that only a just person in himself could write a document. But a child, a slave, or a cautious person may write a document if they have the knowledge of it. As for those chosen for writing, the rulers may not leave them except as just and acceptable persons. It was also said that the "ba'" is extra, meaning "fa-l-yaktub baynakum katibu al-'adl" (let a scribe of justice write between you).

al-Qaffal said regarding the meaning of "bi-l-'adl": that what he writes should be agreed upon among the scholars, not something that is taken before a judge who finds a way to annul it with wording that does not allow interpretation, so the judge needs to pause.

al-Hasan read "wa-l-yaktub" with a kasra on the lam of the imperative, and the kasra is the original form.

﴿And no scribe should refuse to write as Allah has taught him.﴾ He forbade the scribe from refusing to write. "Katib" is indefinite in the context of a prohibition, so it is general. "An yaktuba" is the object of "wa-la ya'ba" (should not refuse). The meaning of "kama 'allamahu Allah" (as Allah has taught him) is like what Allah taught him about writing documents, without altering or changing. In this there is encouragement to exert effort in observing its conditions, which the one requesting writing may not know, and in it there is a reminder of the favour of Allah's teaching him. It was said: the meaning is as Allah commanded him with truth, so "'allama" means "a'lama" (informed). It was said: the meaning is as Allah favoured him with the book, so the kaf is causal, meaning because of what Allah favoured him with. This is like His saying "wa-ahsin kama ahsana Allah ilayk" (and do good as Allah has done good to you) [al-Qasas: 77], meaning because of Allah's goodness to you. The apparent connection of the kaf is to "an yaktuba." It was said that the sentence is complete at "an yaktuba," and the kaf is connected to "fa-l-yaktub," but this is awkward because of the fa', and because if it were connected to "fa-l-yaktub," the wording would be "fa-l-yaktub kama 'allamahu Allah," and there would be no need to front what is later in meaning.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it may be that "kama" is connected to what is in "wa-la ya'ba," meaning just as Allah has blessed him with knowledge of writing, let him not refuse, and let him be generous as he was favoured. He said (ended). This is contrary to the apparent meaning, and in this view the kaf is causal. If it is connected to "an yaktuba," then "wa-la ya'ba" is a prohibition against refusing to write in a restricted way, and then He commanded that restricted writing, as an emphatic command not to deviate from it. If it is connected to "fa-l-yaktub," then it is a prohibition against refusing to write in general, and then He commanded restricted writing.

al-Rabi' and al-Dahhak said: "wa-la ya'ba" is abrogated by His saying "la yudarra katibun wa-la shahid" (let no scribe or witness be harmed) [al-Baqarah: 282].

﴿So let him write, and let the one who owes the debt dictate.﴾ That is: let the scribe write, and let the one on whom the debt is obligated dictate, because he is the one against whom the debt is witnessed, that the debt is in his responsibility, and the one from whom security is taken by writing.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 282 (part 2 of 5):

﴿And let him fear God, his Lord﴾, in what he dictates and in what brings him closer. The Name of the Essence, which is Allah, is combined with this attribute, which is Lord (rabb). Although the Name of the Essence (ism al-dhat) is applicable to all the attributes, God mentions His being the one who nurtures him, sets his affairs right, and bestows His blessings upon him. The word ﴿Allah﴾ is placed first because watchfulness of Him, in terms of servitude and divinity (ʿubudiyya and ulUhiyya), precedes it in terms of blessings.

﴿and let him not diminish anything of it﴾, that is, let him not reduce it through deception or evasion. The one commanded to dictate is the owner of the right himself. The disassembly of the doubled letters (fakk al-mudaʿaf, i.e., undoing idgham) in ﴿let him dictate (fal-yumlil)﴾ is the dialect of the Hijaz, and this applies when the final letter is vowelled by jazm (apocope), as in this form, or in pause, as in amlil. It is not undone in the nominative or accusative. It was also read as shayyan with doubling (tashdid).

﴿If the one upon whom the right lies is a fool (safih)﴾. Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr said: he is the one ignorant of affairs and of dictation. Al-Hasan said: the child and the woman. al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: the young child. This view is considered weak, because the word safih may apply to an adult. The Qadi Abu Yaʿla mentioned that it means the squanderer (al-mubadhdhir). al-Shafiʿi said: the one who squanders his wealth and corrupts his religion. It is reported from al-Suddi that he is the fool (al-ahmaq). It was also said: the one who does not know the value of wealth, so he does not refrain from squandering it, nor does he desire to increase it. Ibn Abbas said: the one ignorant of Islam.

﴿or weak (daʿif)﴾. Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said: he is the incapable, the mute, and the one who has imbecility. Mujahid and al-Suddi said: the fool. The Qadi Abu Yaʿla and others mentioned that he is the child. It was also said: the one whose mind is defective and whose natural disposition is deficient. al-Sheikh said: the elderly. al-Tabari said: the one unable to dictate due to a speech impediment or muteness.

[p. 345] ﴿or he is unable to dictate himself (aw la yastatiʿu an yumilla huwa)﴾. Ibn Abbas said: due to a speech impediment, muteness, or absence. It was said: due to madness. It was said: due to ignorance of what is his or what is upon him. It was said: due to childhood. What appears to be correct is that these three categories are distinct. Whoever claims that ﴿aw (or)﴾ is superfluous in ﴿or weak﴾ or in this phrase, and in ﴿or he is unable﴾, his statement is invalid, since ﴿aw﴾ is not superfluous. Foolishness (safah) is the squandering of wealth and ignorance of disposing of it. Weakness (daʿf) is in the body, due to childhood or to the extreme age of an elder whose capacity to act diminishes with him. Inability to dictate is due to a speech impediment or muteness, because istitaʿa means the capacity to dictate. Most of this explanation is from al-Zamakhshari.

Ibn Atiyya said: God mentioned three types whose circumstances occur in every age, and whose right is established for them in all matters other than transactions, such as inheritances when they are divided, and other matters. The safih is the one of weak judgement regarding wealth, who does not know how to take and give well. This condition necessarily involves the restriction (hajr) of a guardian (wali) or an executor (wasi), and that is his guardian. The daʿif is the one whose mind is defective and whose natural disposition is deficient, and his guardian is an executor or a father. The one who is unable to dictate is the absent person, away from the place of witnessing, whether due to illness or otherwise, and his guardian is his agent (wakil). The mute is among the weak, and it is preferable that he is among those who are unable. Sometimes two or three of these conditions combine in one person. End of quote. There is some abridgement in it. It is the emphatic pronoun (tawkid al-damir al-mustakinn) in ﴿an yumilla﴾, and in it is a eloquence that is not hidden, because by emphasising with it the ambiguity (majaz) that the attribution of the verb to the pronoun could admit is removed, and it specifies that he is unable by himself.

It was read anomalously (shadhdh) with the ha of ﴿huwa﴾ made quiescent, even though a separated element preceded it, treating the separated pronoun as if it were attached, as with the waw, fa and lam: wa-huwa, fa-huwa, la-huwa. This is more anomalous than the reading of the one who read ﴿thumma huwa yawm al-qiyama﴾ (then he, on the Day of Resurrection), because thumma shares in being a conjunction, and it cannot be stopped upon so that the meaning is complete.

﴿then let his guardian dictate with justice (fal-yumlil waliyyuhu bil-adl)﴾. The pronoun in ﴿waliyyuhu﴾ refers to one of these three, namely the one upon whom the right lies. Ibn Atiyya's explanation of the wali has already been given. al-Zamakhshari said: the one who handles his affairs, whether an executor if he is a fool or a child, or an agent if he is unable, or an interpreter who dictates on his behalf, and he (the interpreter) confirms it. al-Tabari held that the pronoun in waliyyihi refers to the right, so the wali is the one to whom the right belongs. This was narrated from Ibn Abbas and al-Rabi.

Ibn Atiyya said: this is not authentic from Ibn Abbas. How can testimony be given concerning something while a sum is introduced into the liability of the fool, through the dictation of the one to whom the debt is owed? This is something not in the Shariʿa. al-Raghib said: it is not permissible that he be the wali of the right, as some have said, because his statement does not carry weight, since he is a claimant.

The phrase ﴿bil-adl (with justice)﴾ is connected to ﴿fal-yumlil﴾. The bāʾ may be for the state (li-l-hal). In the phrase ﴿with justice﴾ there is an exhortation to seek it for the owner of the right and for the one under guardianship. This verse has been cited as evidence for the permissibility of restricting a child, and also as evidence for the permissibility of the disposition (tasarruf) of the fool, and for the establishment of the authority of disposition for him over his own person and his wealth.

* *

﴿And call upon two witnesses from among your men (wastashhidu shahidayni min rijalikum)﴾. That is: seek two witnesses for testimony. Thus istafʿala is for seeking (talab). It is also possible that it corresponds to afʿala, that is: and make them witness (wa-ashhidu), as in istayqana being equivalent to ayqana, and istaʿjalahu meaning aʿjalahu. The word shahid is intensive (lil-mubalagha). It seems that they were commanded to seek from among those who frequently bear witness, for such a person knows the places of testimony and what he testifies to, because of the repetition of that from him. So they were commanded to seek the most perfect. In this there is an indication of uprightness (ʿadala), because such a person is not repeatedly taken as a witness by judges unless he is acceptable to them.

﴿from among your men﴾. The address is to the believers, and they are the ones with whom the verse begins. In the phrase ﴿from among your men﴾ there is an indication that a disbeliever is not to be taken as a witness. The verse does not address the testimony of disbelievers against one another. Abu Hanifa permitted that, even if their religions differ. In this there is an indication of the requirement of puberty and of the requirement of maleness for the two witnesses. The apparent meaning of the verse is that the testimony of a slave is permitted. This is the view of Shurayh, Ibn Sirin, Ibn Shubrumah, and Uthman al-Batti. It is said of him that his testimony is permitted for other than his master. It is narrated from Ali that he used to say: the testimony of a slave against a slave is valid and permitted. al-Mughira narrated from Ibrahim that he used to permit the testimony of a slave in trivial matters. It is narrated from Anas that he said: I do not know that anyone rejected the testimony of a slave. The majority, Abu Hanifa, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad, Zufar, Ibn Shubrumah in one of the two reports, Malik, Ibn Salih, Ibn Abi Layla, and al-Shafiʿi, said: the testimony of a slave is not accepted in anything. This was narrated from Ali, Ibn Abbas, and al-Hasan.

The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that the testimony of children is not considered. This was the view of al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa and his three companions, Ibn Shubrumah, and al-Shafiʿi. It was narrated from Uthman, Ibn Abbas, and Ibn al-Zubayr. Ibn Abi Layla said: the testimony of some of them against others is permitted, and this was narrated from Ali. Malik said: their testimony is permitted in wounds alone, under conditions mentioned from him in the books of jurisprudence.

The apparent meaning of the verse is the requirement of maleness alone for the two witnesses. So if the witness is blind, there is disagreement regarding the permissibility of his testimony. Abu Hanifa and Muhammad held that it is not permitted in any circumstance. This was narrated from Ali, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, and Iyas ibn Muʿawiya. Ibn Abi Layla, Abu Yusuf, and al-Shafiʿi said: if he knew (the matter) before becoming blind, it is permitted; if after, then not. Zufar said: it is not permitted except in lineage, where he testifies that so-and-so is the son of so-and-so. Shurayh and al-Shaʿbi said: his testimony is permitted. Malik said: it is permitted even if he knew the matter while blind, provided he recognised the voice, in divorce, acknowledgement, and the like. If he testifies to fornication or to a slander penalty (hadd qadhf), his testimony is not accepted.

If the witness is mute, it was said: his testimony is accepted by gesture, whether the condition arose later or was original. It was also said: it is not accepted. If he is deaf, his testimony is not accepted regarding statements, but is accepted in other matters of the senses.

If a Bedouin (badawi) testifies against a townsman (qarawi), Ibn Wahb narrated from Malik that it is not permitted except in wounds. Ibn al-Qasim narrated from him: it is not permitted in a settled place except regarding the bequest of a townsman while travelling, and in sale.

﴿And if they are not two men (fa-in lam yakunaa rajulayn)﴾. The pronoun refers to the two witnesses, that is: if the two witnesses are not two men. The meaning is that if the owner of the right neglects this, or intends that two men not be called as witnesses for some purpose of his, then on this assumption the verb kana is defective (naqisa). Others said: rather, the meaning is: if two men are not found. The testimony of two women is not permitted except when men are absent. This holds only on the belief that the pronoun in ﴿yakuna﴾ refers to two witnesses qualified as men, and kana is then complete (tamma), and rajulayn is in the accusative as an emphatic circumstantial (hal al-muʾakkada), like God's saying ﴿if they are two (fa-in kanataa ithnatayn)﴾ [an-Nisa: 176], according to the better of the two views.

﴿then a man and two women (fa-rajulun wa-imraatan)﴾. Rajul is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, that is: then the witness is a man and two women. Or it is the subject with an omitted predicate, that is: then a man and two women testify. Or it is the agent (fail), that is: then a man shall testify. Or it is a passive verb's subject, that is: then let there be called. It was said that the omitted word is falyakun (let there be). It was permitted that kana be complete, so rajul is the agent, and that it be defective, with its predicate omitted. We have already mentioned that our companions do not permit omitting the predicate of kana, neither by limitation nor by abbreviation.

It was read anomalously as ﴿wa-imraatan﴾ with a quiescent hamza. This is against analogy, and it is possible that it was made quiescent for lightness, due to the frequent succession of vowels. A parallel to this lightening of the hamza occurs in the verse of the poet:

They say in ignorance: the old man has no dependants (ʿayyil). By my life, I have become dependent, and I am childless (raqub).

He means: and I am childless (raqub). It was said he lightened the hamza by changing it to an alif, then to a hamza again after that. They say al-khaʾatam and al-ʿaʾam.

The apparent meaning of the verse requires the permissibility of the testimony of two women with a man in all contracts of debts (mudayanat), which are every contract concerning a debt, whether it is a replacement, a marriage (budʿ), usufructs, or deliberate bloodwite (dam ʿamd). Whoever claims that some contracts are excluded from the apparent meaning is not granted that unless there is evidence.

Al-Shafiʿi said: the testimony of women with men is not permitted in matters other than wealth. In a bequest, only a man is permitted, but in a bequest of wealth it is permitted. al-Layth said: the testimony of women is permitted in bequests and manumission, but not in marriage, divorce, or deliberate killing for which retaliation is taken. al-Awzaʿi said: the testimony of a man and two women is not permitted in marriage. al-Hasan ibn Hayy said: their testimony is not permitted in the hudud. al-Thawri said: it is permitted in everything except the hudud. Malik said: it is not permitted in the hudud or retaliation, nor in divorce or marriage, nor in lineages, nor in patronage (wala') or in ihsan (marital chastity for the penalty), and it is permitted in agency (wikala) and bequests if there is no manumission in them. al-Hasan and al-Dahhak said: their testimony is not permitted except in debt. Umar, Ata', and al-Shaʿbi said: it is permitted in divorce. Shurayh said: it is permitted in manumission. Umar and his son Abdullah said: the testimony of a man and two women is permitted in marriage. Ali said: it is permitted in the contract. Abu Hanifa, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad, Zufar, and Uthman al-Batti said: the testimony of women with men is not accepted in the hudud and retaliation, and it is accepted in all other rights. The evidences for these views are mentioned in the books of jurisprudence.

As for the acceptance of their testimony alone (mufradat), there is no disagreement regarding its acceptance in: childbirth, virginity, the crying out of a newborn (istihlal), and defects of women, slave women, and what runs in the same way, which is specific to women. Abu Hanifa permitted the testimony of a single upright woman regarding the sighting of the crescent moon, since it is, in his view, from the category of reporting (ikhbar). Likewise the testimony of a midwife (qabila) alone.

This is the commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 282 (part 3 of 5):

﴿of those whom you approve as witnesses﴾. It has been said that this is in the position of the description (sifa) of the clause ﴿then a man and two women﴾. It has also been said that it is a substitute (badal) for the word (rijalikum, "your men") by repetition of the governing verb, but both views are weak. The reason is that a descriptive phrase indicates that the ruling is restricted to the described party, so this description would be negated of the two male witnesses. Also, a substitute indicates restriction to the two male witnesses, so the clause ﴿a man and two women﴾ would be left without this restriction. What appears to be the case is that it is connected to the verb (wa-istashhidu, "and call to witness"), meaning: "and call to witness from among those whom you approve as witnesses," so that it is a condition on the whole. For this reason it came after mention of the whole. The address in ﴿you approve﴾ apparently is to the believers, and this indicates that among the witnesses there are some whom one would not approve. Thus this shows that they are not presumed to be of upright character (ʿadāla) simply because witnessing is established for them. Ibn Bukayr and others said: the address is to the judges. The first view is preferable, because it is the apparent meaning, even though those who are actually engaged in these cases are the judges. Rather, the address comes in general terms and some people are involved in it. It has also been said: the address is to the creditors.

They differed over the interpretation of the phrase ﴿of those whom you approve﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: from among people of merit, religion and suitability (kafāʾa). Al-Shaʿbi said: from among those who have not been accused regarding chastity or the belly. He explained it as meaning one who has not slandered a woman or a man, and has not been accused regarding lineage. It was also narrated: one against whom there is no accusation regarding chastity or the belly, meaning that he is not attributed with doubtful conduct, and it is not said of him that he is the son of fornication. Al-Hasan said: one whose lapse is not known. Al-Nakhaʿi said: one about whom there is no doubt. Al-Khassaf said: one whose good deeds outweigh his bad deeds, while avoiding major sins.

It has been said: an acceptable witness is one in whom ten qualities are combined: that he is free, mature (baligh), Muslim, upright (ʿadl), knowledgeable about what he testifies to, does not draw any benefit to himself through his testimony, does not use it to repel harm from himself, is not known for frequent error, is not known for abandoning manliness (murūwa, good conduct and dignity), and has no enmity between himself and the one against whom he testifies.

Bishr ibn al-Walid narrated from Abu Yusuf that whoever is free from the indecencies for which the hadd punishments are due, and from the grave sins for which they are required, and who performs the obligatory duties, and whose good character outweighs his minor sins, his testimony is accepted, because no servant is free from sin. But the testimony of one whose sins outweigh his good character is not accepted; nor that of one who plays chess for stakes, nor one who keeps pigeons and makes them fly, nor one who abandons the five daily prayers in congregation out of contempt, levity or wickedness (not one who abandons them out of a valid interpretation, provided he is upright), nor one who frequently swears falsely, nor one who persistently neglects the two rakʿas of the dawn prayer, nor one known for gross lying, nor one who openly reviles the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), nor one who abuses people and neighbours, nor one whom people accuse of wickedness and debauchery, nor one accused of cursing the Companions, unless people say: "We heard him reviling."

Ibn Abi Layla, Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf said: the testimony of upright people of heterodox views (ahl al-ahwāʾ) is accepted, except a group of the Rafiḍa, namely the Khaṭṭābiyya. Muhammad said: I do not accept the testimony of the Khawarij, but I accept the testimony of the Haruriyya, because they do not regard our property as lawful, whereas when they rebel they regard it as lawful. It is narrated from Abu Hanifa that the testimony of a miser is not permissible. It is narrated from Iyas ibn Muʿawiya that he did not permit the testimony of the notables of Iraq, nor of misers, nor of merchants who travel by sea. It is narrated from Bilal ibn Abi Burda, who was governor of Basra, that he did not permit the testimony of one who eats clay and plucks his beard. ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz rejected the testimony of one who plucks his lower lip hair and conceals his beard. Shurayh rejected the testimony of a man named Rabiʿa, who was called al-Kuwayfir. He was called, "O Rabiʿa!" and did not respond. He was called, "O Rabiʿa al-Kuwayfir!" and he responded. Shurayh said to him: "You were called by your name and did not answer, but when you were called by unbelief (kufr) you answered." He said: "May God set you right, it is only a nickname." Shurayh said to him: "Stand up," and said to his companion: "Bring another." It is narrated from Abu Hurayra: the testimony of the owners of donkeys is not permissible, meaning the slave-dealers (al-nakhkhāsīn). It is narrated from Shurayh that he did not permit the testimony of a bathhouse owner, nor a porter, nor one with a narrow sleeve of a cloak, nor one who says: "I testify by the testimony of God, mighty and majestic." It is narrated from Muhammad: the testimony of one who is known for frivolity (majāna) is not accepted, nor that of an effeminate man (mukhannath), nor of one who plays with pigeons and makes them fly. Ibn Abi Layla rejected the testimony of a poor man and said: one cannot be sure that his poverty will not drive him to desire wealth.

Malik said: the testimony of a beggar is not permissible regarding a large matter, but is permissible regarding a trivial matter. It is narrated from al-Shafiʿi: if the predominant state of a person is disobedience and lack of manliness, his testimony is rejected. It is also narrated from him: if the greater part of his affairs is obedience, and he has not committed a major sin, then he is upright. Manliness (murūwa) should be interpreted as self-restraint, good bearing, preservation of dignity, and avoidance of levity and frivolity. It should not be interpreted as cleanliness of clothing, fine mounts, good equipment, or a handsome appearance, because these are not conditions of testimony according to anyone among the Muslims.

They differed over the ruling regarding one in whom no doubt has appeared: must the judge inquire about him when he testifies? In the letter of ʿUmar to Abu Musa it is written: "Muslims are upright (ʿudūl) with respect to one another, except one who has been flogged for a hadd punishment, or one known for giving false testimony, or one suspected, or one who is a relative." When al-Hasan assumed the judgeship, he would accept the testimony of Muslims unless the opponent discredited the witness. Ibn Shubruma said: if the defendant challenges them, I inquire about them both in private and in public. Muhammad and Abu Yusuf said: one inquires about them even if they are not challenged, either privately or publicly. Malik said: judgment is not given on the testimony of witnesses until one has inquired about them privately. Al-Layth said: the governor used to say to the opponent: "If you have someone who can bring out their testimony, bring him; otherwise we accept their testimony against you." Al-Shafiʿi said: one inquires about him privately, and when he is found upright, one inquires about his reputation publicly.

As for what has been mentioned regarding the requirement of removing suspicion from the witness when he is upright, the jurists of the major cities agreed on the invalidity of a witness's testimony for his child or his parent, except what has been related from al-Battti, who said: the testimony of a child for his parents is permissible, and of a father for his son or his wife. It is narrated from Iyas ibn Muʿawiya that he permitted a man's testimony for his son. Abu Hanifa, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad, Zufar, Malik, al-Awzaʿi and al-Layth held that the testimony of one spouse for the other is not permissible. It is narrated from Abu Hanifa: the testimony of a dedicated employee (ajīr khāṣṣ) for his employer is not permissible, but the testimony of a shared employee (ajīr mushtarak) for him is permissible. Malik said: the testimony of an employee for the one who employs him is not permissible unless he is outstanding in uprightness. Al-Awzaʿi said: it is not permissible in any case. Al-Thawri said: it is permissible if it does not draw a benefit to himself.

As for one whose testimony was rejected for a reason, and then that reason ceased, is that testimony accepted for that matter? Abu Hanifa and his companions said: it is not accepted if it was rejected for wickedness or for marital relationship, but it is accepted if it was rejected for slavery, unbelief or childhood. Malik said: it is not accepted if it was rejected for slavery or childhood. It is narrated from ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan something similar to this.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that the witnesses in debts are two men, or one man and two women, from among those whom you approve. Therefore judgment is not given on one witness with an oath. This is the view of Abu Hanifa and his companions, Ibn Shubruma, al-Thawri, al-Hakam and al-Awzaʿi. ʿAṭāʾ also said this, and said: the first to rule by it was ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwan. al-Hakam said: the first to rule by it was Muʿawiya.

It differed from al-Zuhri. It is said that he said: "This is something people have introduced; there must be two witnesses." He also said: "I do not know it, and it is an innovation (bidʿa). The first to rule by it was Muʿawiya." It is also narrated from him that when he first assumed judgeship he ruled by one witness and an oath. Malik, al-Shafiʿi and their followers, Ahmad, Ishaq and Abu ʿUbayd said: it is ruled by this in property matters only. The Four Caliphs acted upon it, and it is the practice of the people of Medina. It is also the view of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Muʿawiya, Abu Salama, Abu al-Zinad and Rabiʿa.

* *

﴿that if one of them errs, the other may remind her﴾. Al-Aʿmash and Hamza read (in taḍilla, "if she errs") with a kasra on the hamza, making it a conditional particle, and read (fa-tudhakkira) with shadda and a damma on the rāʾ, making it the answer of the condition. The rest read (an tadilla) with a fatḥa on the hamza of (an), which is the subjunctive particle, and a fatḥa on the rāʾ of (fa-tudhakkira), as a conjunction following (an tadilla). Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read the dhāl with a sukūn and lightened the kāf, while the rest of the Seven read the dhāl with a fatḥa and shadda on the kāf.

Al-Juhdari and ʿĪsā ibn ʿImran read (tuḍalla) with a damma on the tāʾ and a fatḥa on the ḍād, in the passive voice, meaning: "forgets." This is what al-Dani reported from them. Al-Naqqash reported from al-Juhdari (an tadilla) with a damma on the tāʾ and a kasra on the ḍād, meaning: "that the testimony may go astray," as one says: "The mare and the camel went astray (aḍallat)," when they went off and one could not find them.

Ḥumayd ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and Mujahid read (fa-tudhakkira) with the kāf lightened and kasra, and a damma on the rāʾ, meaning: "so she reminds." Zayd ibn Aslam read (fa-tudhākira), from the root dh-k-r in the form of mutual remembrance.

As for the conditional clause in ﴿that if one of them errs, the other reminds﴾, on the reading of al-Aʿmash and Hamza, Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: it is in the position of a nominative, as a description of (al-mudhakkir, "the reminder"), which refers to the two women. End of quotation. It has already been noted that the phrase ﴿of those whom you approve as witnesses﴾ is in the position of a description of ﴿then a man and two women﴾, so this becomes like the sentence: "There came to me a man and two women, sensible, pregnant." Whether this structure is permissible is open to question. Rather, the sound analogical rules require placing (ḥublayān, "pregnant") before (ʿuqalāʾ, "sensible"). As for the view of those who parsed ﴿of those whom you approve﴾ as a substitute for (rijālikum, "your men"), and on the view we have preferred that it is connected to ﴿and call to witness﴾, the conditional clause cannot be a description of ﴿and two women﴾, because of the separation between the described and the description by a foreign element. As for (an tadilla) with a fatḥa on the hamza, it is in the position of the object of purpose (mafʿūl min ajlihi), meaning: "in order that she may err," with the cause, which is the misleading, treated as the effect, which is the reminding, just as the effect is sometimes treated as the cause, because they are associated and connected. So this is a statement understood in terms of its meaning, meaning: "in order that one reminds the other if she errs." A parallel is: "I prepared the timber in case the wall leans and I shore it up," and "I prepared the weapon in case the enemy attacks and I repel him." The preparation of the timber is not for the sake of the leaning; it is for shoring the wall if it leans. It is not permissible to take the sense as "lest she err," because then (fa-tudhakkira) could not be coordinated with it.

Al-Nahhas said: I heard ʿAlī ibn Sulayman relate from Abu al-ʿAbbas that the implied phrase is: "for fear that she errs." Abu Jaʿfar said: this is an error, because the meaning would then become "for fear that she is reminded," and the meaning of error here is failure to recall the testimony due to forgetfulness or heedlessness. For this reason it is contrasted with (fa-tudhakkira), which is from the root of remembering. As for what has been narrated from Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ and Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna, that the lightened reading (fa-tudhakira) means: "she makes her a male in the testimony," because the testimony of one woman is half a testimony, so when two of them testify their combined testimony becomes like the testimony of one man, al-Zamakhshari said: this is among the strange interpretations. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: this is a distant and unsound interpretation, and in contrast with error nothing suitable except remembering, end of quotation.

What they both said is correct. The wording also rejects it, both linguistically and in meaning. Linguistically, what is established is that this verb is not transitive. One says: "The woman became a mother of males (adhkarat)" when she bears males. As for "adhkarat al-mar'a" meaning "she made her like a male," this is not established. As for meaning, even if one granted that (uʾadhdhiru) means "she makes her a male," it would still be invalid, because making her male would apply to both women, since abandoning their testimony would be like the testimony of a male. So one of them would not have made the other male under this interpretation, since their testimony together would not be like the testimony of a male.

[p. 350] When the subject in ﴿that one of them errs﴾ was left unspecified by the phrase "one of them" (*iḥdāhumā*), the subject in ﴿then one of them reminds﴾ was also left unspecified by the phrase "one of them," since either of the two women may err or remind. So "one of them" does not refer to a particular woman. The meaning is: if this one errs, that one reminds her, and if that one errs, this one reminds her. The statement therefore carries a sense of generality, as though it were said: whichever of the two errs, the other reminds her.

If the explicit subject had not been mentioned after ﴿then one of them reminds﴾, it would have been necessary for the object to be implied so that it refers back to "one of them" (*iḥdāhumā*), the subject of "errs" (*taḍilla*), and then "the other" (*al-ukhrā*) would necessarily be the subject. The construction would then be: "then the other reminds her." In the Qur'anic construction, however, the more immediate understanding is that "one of them" (*iḥdāhumā*) is the subject of "reminds" (*tudhakkira*), and "the other" (*al-ukhrā*) is the object, meaning the one who has erred. This is because each of the two words is in the restricted (*maqṣūr*) form, so the one mentioned first is the subject. It is also permissible for "one of them" (*iḥdāhumā*) to be the object, with "the other" (*al-ukhrā*) as the subject, since this removes ambiguity: it is known that the one who reminds is not the one who forgets. Thus it is permissible for the object to precede and the subject to follow, as in the example "Moses broke the staff," where the subject follows the verb. On this reading, a noun is placed in the position of an object pronoun, and it is then necessary that "the other" be the subject.

As for the one who reads *an* with a fatḥa on the hamza, and *fa-tudhakkira* with a ḍamma (*al-raf'*) as a new sentence (*isti'nāf*), it is said that God said: ﴿that one of them errs﴾. The meaning is that forgetfulness predominates in the natures of women because of their coldness and moistness. For two women to both be forgetful is less likely, in reason, than for forgetfulness to come from a single woman. Therefore the two women are placed in the position of a man, so that if one of them forgets, the other reminds her. This implies the superiority of men over women.

"To remind" (*tudhakkira*) is transitive to two objects, and the second is omitted, meaning: "then one of them reminds the other of the testimony." In the statement ﴿then one of them reminds the other﴾ there is evidence that one of the conditions for the validity of giving testimony is that the witness remembers it, and that it is not permissible to rely on writing alone. Writing is commanded so that the testimony may be remembered, and this is supported by the words: ﴿except for those who testify to the truth while they know﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 86]. If he does not remember it, then he does not know it.

Abu Hanifa, Abu Yusuf and al-Shafi'i said: if he writes his own handwriting of the testimony, he does not testify until he remembers it. Muhammad ibn Abi Layla said: if he recognizes his handwriting, it is sufficient for him to testify to it. Al-Thawri said: if he remembers that he witnessed it, but does not remember the number of dirhams, he does not testify.

﴿And the witnesses must not refuse when they are called﴾. Qatada said: the occasion of its revelation was that a man used to go around in the great Hira, and people would not follow him, so God revealed this. The apparent meaning of the verse is: the witnesses must not refuse to bear testimony when they are called to it. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Rabi' and others. This prohibition is not a prohibition of unlawfulness (*taḥrīm*): he may testify, and he may not testify. This was said by Ata' and al-Hasan. Al-Sha'bi said: if no one else is available, it becomes obligatory for him to testify; if others are available, he has a choice. It was also said: the meaning is that the witnesses must not refuse, when they are called to deliver the testimony, if they had witnessed it previously. This was said by Mujahid, Ata', Ikrima, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, Ibrahim, Lahiq ibn Humayd and Ibn Zayd. Al-Naqqash narrated: the Messenger of God ﷺ explained it in this way. If this is authentic from him, peace be upon him, he would not have deviated from it, and so the prohibition would be one of unlawfulness.

Ibn Abbas also said, as did al-Hasan and al-Suddi: the verse concerns both bearing the testimony and giving it, when one is free to do so. Ibn Atiyya said: the verse, as al-Hasan said, combines both matters. Muslims are encouraged to help their brothers. When there is ample room, with many witnesses and no fear that the right will be neglected, the one who is called is encouraged to respond, and he may stay away for a slight excuse or for no excuse, with no sin upon him. When there is necessity and there is fear that the right will be neglected even slightly, the encouragement becomes stronger and approaches obligation. If it is known that the right will be lost or destroyed by the witness's delay in testifying, it is obligatory for him to stand and testify, especially if the testimony has been secured and he is being called to deliver it, for this is more emphatic, since it is a necklace around the neck and a trust that demands fulfilment. End of quotation.

* *

﴿And do not be weary of writing it, whether small or large, until its term﴾. When God forbade the witnesses from refusing when they are called to testify, He also forbade weariness in writing down the debt. All of this serves to safeguard people's property and to encourage that no dispute should arise, for when it is recorded in writing and witnessed, there is little chance of confusion, denial, or disputing the amount, the term, or the description. The "small" is mentioned first out of concern for it, and as a movement from the lower to the higher. The term is specified to show that it must be mentioned. Thus it is written as the principal debt is written, together with its due date if the due date needs to be mentioned. By mentioning the term, He indicates the description and amount of the debt, since the term is part of its attributes. Here "term" (*ajal*) means the time that the two parties to the debt agreed to name.

Al-Maturidi said: this indicates the permissibility of advance sale (*salam*) in garments, because what is eaten or weighed is not described as "small" or "large." Such descriptions apply only to things counted or measured by length. End of quotation.

This does not seem correct. "Small" and "large" here do not refer to physical bulk; they express the little and the much. Whoever contracts for a small quantity of wheat (*wayba*) or for twenty ardabs, it is correct to say of the first that it is a small right and a small debt, and of the second that it is a large debt and a large right.

It was said: the meaning of "do not be weary" is "do not be lazy." He expressed laziness by weariness (*sa'am*), because laziness is a characteristic of the hypocrite. There is a hadith: "A believer should not say: I am lazy (*kasiltu*)." This is perhaps one of the attributes God ascribed to them in His words: ﴿And when they stand up to prayer, they stand lazily﴾ [al-Nisa': 142]. It was also said: the meaning is "do not be bored."

"To write" (*an taktubū*) is in the accusative position as the direct object, since *sa'ima* is transitive without a preposition, as the poet said:

*I have grown weary of the burdens of life, and whoever lives eighty years, by your father, will grow weary.*

It was also said: *sa'ima* is transitive through a preposition (*ḥarf al-jarr*), so that "to write" (*an taktubū*) is in the accusative position by dropping the preposition, or in the genitive position according to the disagreement that preceded between Sibawayh and al-Khalil. What indicates that *sa'ima* is transitive through a preposition is the poet's words:

*I have grown weary of life and its length, and of asking these people how Labid is.*

The pronoun of the accusative in ﴿write it﴾ refers to the debt, because it was mentioned earlier, or to the right because it is nearer. The debt is the right in meaning. Whoever had many debts became bored with writing, so they were forbidden from that.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to the document (*al-kitāb*), and ﴿to write it﴾ may be abridged or fully spelled out, without harming the writing of it. End of quotation. What he said here is far-fetched.

Al-Salami read *wa-lā yasʾamū* with the letter *yā'* (third person), and likewise *an yaktubūhu*. In this reading, the apparent meaning is that the subject pronoun refers back to the witnesses. It may also be an instance of *iltifāt* (a shift from one grammatical person to another), so that it refers to the transactors or to the document. The accusative of ﴿small or large﴾ is a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*) from the *hā'* in ﴿to write it﴾. Al-Sijawandi permitted the accusative of "small" as the predicate of an implied *kāna* (was), meaning: "it was small." But there is no place for the implied *kāna* here. ﴿until its term﴾ is connected to an implied verb: "do not write it," because writing does not continue until the term of the debt, which ends in a short time. It is therefore not like the example "I traveled to Kufa." The estimate is: "to write it, remaining in the liability until the time of its falling due."

﴿That is more equitable in the sight of God﴾. The demonstrative refers to the nearest thing mentioned, which is writing. It was also said: it refers to writing, bearing witness, and everything mentioned before, by which control is achieved. "More equitable" (*aqsaṭu*) means more just. It was said: there is an irregularity in this, since it is from the quadriliteral form on the pattern *af'ala*, as one says *aqsaṭa al-rajul*, meaning he was just. From this comes ﴿and act justly﴾. They have sought to free it from the irregularity they mentioned, by making *aqsaṭu* derive from *qāsiṭ* by the way of the relative form (*nisba*), meaning "one who possesses justice." This was said by al-Zamakhshari.

Ibn Atiyya said: consider whether it is from *qasuṭa* with a ḍamma on the sīn, as one says *akrama min karuma* (more generous than he was generous). End of quotation. It was also said: it is from *al-qisṭ* with a kasra, meaning justice, which is a verbal noun from which no verb has been derived. It is not from *al-iqsāṭ* (the causative form), because the pattern *af'ala* is not formed from the causative verb form.

Al-Zamakhshari said: if you ask, from what are the comparatives *aqsaṭu* and *aqwamu* formed? I say: according to Sibawayh's view, they may be formed from *aqsaṭa* and *aqāma*. End of quotation.

Sibawayh did not state explicitly that the comparative form *af'ala* is formed from *af'ala*. This is rather derived by inference, because at the beginning of his book he stated that the form of the exclamatory (*ta'ajjub*) *af'ala* is formed from *fa'ala*, *fa'ila*, *fa'ula*, and *af'ala*. The apparent meaning is that the exclamatory *af'ala* is formed from *af'ala*. The grammarians stated that whatever the exclamatory *af'ala* is formed from, the comparative *af'ala* is also formed from. Whatever is regular in exclamation is regular in comparison, and whatever is irregular in it is irregular in comparison.

The grammarians differed about the formation of *af'ala* in exclamation in three positions: permission, prohibition, and distinction. The distinction is between whether the hamza is causative, in which case the exclamatory *af'ala* is not formed from it, or whether it is not causative, in which case it is formed from it. It is claimed that this is Sibawayh's view, and his statement "wa-af'ala" has been interpreted as referring to the *af'ala* whose hamza is not causative. Those who prohibited this entirely understood Sibawayh's words "wa-af'ala" as being in the imperative form, meaning that the exclamatory verb takes the form *af'ala*, and its formation from *fa'ala*, *fa'ila*, *fa'ula*, and *af'ala*. The arguments for these positions are fully developed in the books of grammar. What should be understood about *aqsaṭa* is that it is formed from the triliteral *qasaṭa*, meaning "to be just." Ibn al-Sayyid said in *al-Iqtiḍāb*, in his words: Ibn al-Sikkit related in *Kitāb al-Aḍdād* from Abu Ubayda: *qasaṭa* means "to act unjustly," and *qasaṭa* means "to be just," and *aqsaṭa*, with an alif, means "to be just," and only that. Ibn al-Qattaa said: *qasaṭa qusūṭan* and *qisṭan* means "to act unjustly" and "to be just," as opposites. On this basis it is not irregular. The meaning of ﴿more equitable in the sight of God﴾ is more just in God's judgment, so that no injustice occurs.

﴿and more upright for testimony﴾. If it is from *aqāma*, there is an irregularity according to some. Whoever considers it formed from *qāma* meaning "to be upright" finds no irregularity in it. Al-Zamakhshari's statement has already been cited, that it is permissible according to Sibawayh's view to derive it from *aqāma*. He also said: it is permissible for it to carry the sense of the relative form from *qawīm*. End of quotation.

Some grammarians counted *mā aqwamahu* among the irregular exclamatory forms, and considered it formed from *istaqāma* (to be straight). "For testimony" (*li-al-shahāda*) is connected to *aqwamu*, and in meaning it is an object, as when one says: "Zayd is more beating for 'Amr than Khalid." Deleting this *lām* and using the accusative is not permitted except in poetry, as the poet said:

*And more beating of us with swords are the crowns of heads.*

It may be interpreted as an implied verb: "he strikes the crowns of heads." The meaning of ﴿and more upright for testimony﴾ is more firm and more correct.

﴿and nearer to avoiding doubt﴾: that is, closer to the absence of suspicion. Al-Salami read *an lā yartābū* with the letter *yā'*. The thing being compared to, which is omitted, is justified by the fact that the comparative form *af'ala* here is the predicate of an inchoative (*mubtada'*) subject. The estimate is: "writing is more equitable, more upright, and nearer to such and such than not writing," and it was estimated as "nearer for ...," "nearer to ...," and "nearer from ...," then the preposition was dropped, leaving it in the accusative or genitive, according to the disagreement that preceded.

[p. 352]

The arrangement of these statements is extremely fine. It begins with the most noble matter, which is His saying ﴿more just in the sight of God﴾, meaning in the judgment of God. So one should follow what one has been commanded, since following it is the core of the Islamic religion. It is then followed by His saying ﴿and more upright for testimony﴾, because what comes after complying with God's command is the testimony after the writing. He says ﴿and nearer to preventing doubt﴾ in the form of the comparative (*wa-adnā*), because the absence of doubt follows from obedience to God in writing and in calling witnesses. From these two arises the greater nearness to the absence of doubt, since that is the furthest extent of ensuring that no doubt occurs. This is attained only through writing and calling witnesses, generally, so that the heart is set at ease by what has been written and witnessed.

*Tartābū* (﴿you should doubt﴾) is of the form *iftaʿala* (*ifta'ala*, the reflexive-augmented verbal pattern) from *al-rayba* (doubt), whose explanation was given earlier in His saying ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2]. It has been said that the meaning is: do not doubt the one upon whom the right lies, that he will deny it. It has been said: do not doubt the witness that he will err. It has been said: concerning the testimony, the amount of the right, and the term. It has been said: the meaning is closer to negating suspicion for the witness, the judge, and the contracting parties, and what is secured by writing and witnessing is hardly liable to suspicion, ambiguity, or dispute.

* *

﴿Except that it be a present trade which you conduct among yourselves; then there is no blame upon you that you do not write it.﴾ Regarding "present trade" (*tijāra ḥāḍira*) there are two views. One: what is immediate and does not involve a term, such as a sale and a price. Two: what the buyer takes of movable goods (*ʿurūḍ*), and this is generally only in small quantities, such as foodstuffs, unlike real estate. For this reason al-Suddī and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: this applies when it is hand to hand, you take and give. As for the sense of *idāra* (conducting, circulating), there are two views: one, that they pass it from hand to hand; two, that they trade it at every time. *Idāra* implies exchange and taking away what is received. Since real property, land, and many animals do not create a separation, and there is no fault in writing and witnessing concerning them, they are attached to the sale of debts. And since writing in a present trade circulating among them is burdensome, the blame was lifted from them in leaving it. Also, what is sold for cash, hand to hand, hardly needs writing, for the legislation of writing is only to secure debts, since by deferring them confusion arises regarding their amount, their description, and their term, and this is absent in a merchant's hand-to-hand dealing. This exception in His saying ﴿except that﴾ is *munqaṭiʿ* (disjunctive, i.e., not part of the preceding category), since what is sold without deferment does not fall under deferred debts. It has also been said that it is *muttaṣil* (continuous, i.e., part of the preceding category), referring back to His saying ﴿when you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down﴾, except that the term be short, and this is what is meant by present trade. It has been said that it is continuous and refers back to His saying ﴿and do not be weary of writing it, whether small or large, up to its term﴾.

ʿĀṣim read ﴿present trade﴾ with the accusative on both words, taking *kāna* (to be) as a defective verb (*nāqiṣa*, requiring a predicate), with the sense: "except that it be" — i.e., "that trade," meaning the trade. The rest read both in the nominative, taking *takūna* as a complete verb (*tāmma*, not requiring a predicate), with *tijāratun* as its subject. Some have permitted that *takūna* is defective, with its predicate being the clause ﴿you conduct among yourselves﴾. The negation of blame here means: there is no harm upon you in leaving writing. This is according to the view of most exegetes, since writing in their view is not obligatory; and whoever holds it to be obligatory takes *lā junāḥa* (no blame) to mean *lā ithm* (no sin).

﴿And call witnesses when you make a contract﴾. This is a command to call witnesses over any sale, whether immediate or deferred, because it is more cautious and further from any disagreement that may arise. It has been said that it refers back to the present trade: when the leaving of writing was permitted, they were commanded to call witnesses.

It has been said: this verse is abrogated by His saying ﴿but if some of you trust others﴾ [al-Baqarah 283]. This is related from al-Juḥdarī, al-Ḥasan, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yazīd, and al-Ḥakam. It has been said: it is *muḥkama* (not abrogated), and the command in this regard is obligatory. This was said by Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī, Ibn ʿUmar, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibn al-Musayyab, Jābir ibn Zayd, Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, Ibrāhīm, al-Shaʿbī, al-Nakhaʿī, Dāwūd ibn ʿAlī, his son Abū Bakr, and al-Ṭabarī.

al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it is a binding ordinance (*ʿazīma*) from God, even if it be over a bunch of herbs. ʿAṭāʾ said: call witnesses whenever you sell or buy, even for a dirham, or half a dirham, or three dirhams, or less than that. al-Ṭabarī said: it is not lawful for a Muslim, when he sells or buys, except that he call witnesses, and otherwise he would be opposing the Book of God, Mighty and Majestic. al-Ḥasan and a group went to the view that this command is for recommendation and guidance, not for a binding requirement. Ibn al-ʿArabī said: this is the view of the whole body of scholars.

﴿Let no scribe be harmed, nor any witness﴾. This is a prohibition, and that is why the *rāʾ* is vowelled with a fatḥa: because it is in the jussive (*majzūm*), and a doubled (*mushaddad*) verb in the jussive like this takes a fatḥa on its vowel for lightness, since, once assimilated (*udghima*), its vowelling is necessary; if it were unassimilated, the jussive would appear in it. This verb may be in the active voice, so the scribe and the witness are forbidden from harming anyone: by the scribe adding to the writing or altering it, and by the witness concealing the testimony, or changing it, or refusing to give it. This is the view of al-Ḥasan, Ṭāʾūs, Qatādah, and Ibn Zayd, and al-Zajjāj chose it, because of His later saying ﴿and if you do it, it is an act of defiance (*fusūq*) in you﴾, since the name of defiance applies to one who alters the writing or refuses testimony, until he wholly voids the right, and it is more appropriate than the one who harms the scribe and the witness. Also He, Exalted, said concerning one who refuses to give testimony: ﴿and whoever conceals it, his heart is sinful﴾ [al-Baqarah 283], and sinful (*āthim*) and defiant (*fāsiq*) are close in meaning. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and ʿAṭāʾ said: this is by their saying: "we are busy and have need."

It is also possible that the verb is in the passive voice, so the prohibition is that anyone harm them by causing them hardship and difficulty in leaving their work, and by demanding of them what is unbecoming in writing and testimony. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Ṭāʾūs, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and al-Suddī also said this meaning, and the reading of ʿUmar supports this possibility: ﴿let him not be harmed﴾ (*wa-lā yuḍārar*), with unassimilated form and a fatḥa on the first *rāʾ*, narrated by al-Ḍaḥḥāk from Ibn Masʿūd, and by Ibn Kathīr from Mujāhid. al-Ṭabarī chose it, because the address from the beginning of the verses is to the one for whom the writing is made and to the one for whom the testimony is given; there is no prior address to the witness or the scribe. Rather, the verse returns to the people of writing and testimony, so the prohibition to them is clearer: that the scribe and the witness not be harmed by their being distracted from their business while others are available. This view was strengthened by the argument that if the address were to the scribe and the witness, it would have said: "and if you two do it, it is an act of defiance in you two." And if the address is to the contracting parties, then those forbidden from harming are them.

Abū ʿAmr al-Dhānnī related from ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and Ibn Abī Isḥāq that the first *rāʾ* is kasra-vowelled, and related from them also the fatḥa, and the unassimilated form of the verb. The unassimilated form is the Ḥijāzī dialect, and the assimilated form is the dialect of Tamīm.

Ibn al-Qaʿqāʿ and ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd read ﴿wa-lā yuḍār﴾ with a jazm on the *rāʾ*, and this is weak, because in principle it combines three consonant clusters (sukūn), but the *alif* of lengthening functions as a vowel, so it is as if two quiescent letters remain; and pausing on it is possible, and then they applied the pausal form to continuous reading.

ʿIkrimah read ﴿wa-lā yuḍārir﴾ with a kasra on the first *rāʾ* and unassimilated, and ﴿kātiban wa-lā shahīdan﴾ with the accusative, meaning: the claimant should not begin harming them. The forms of harm are not limited. Muqsim narrated from ʿIkrimah that he read ﴿wa-lā yuḍārr﴾ with assimilation and a kasra on the *rāʾ* because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. Ibn Muḥayṣin read ﴿wa-lā yuḍārru﴾ with a ḍamma on the doubled *rāʾ*, and this is a negation whose sense is prohibition. We have already noted the elegance of the prohibition coming in the form of a negation, because a prohibition is only about what can occur; when it appears in the form of a negation, it is more emphatic, since it becomes something that should not occur and should not be expected to occur.

﴿And if you do it, it is an act of defiance in you﴾. Its apparent meaning is that the omitted object of *tafʿalū* (you do) refers back to the verbal noun implied in His saying ﴿let him not be harmed﴾: "and if you do harm (*ḍirār*), it — that is, the harm — is defiance in you," i.e., it is attached to you. Or the *bāʾ* is locative (*ẓarfiyya*), meaning "in you," and this is more emphatic, since they are made the locus of defiance.

The address in ﴿you do﴾ returns to the scribe and the witness, since His saying ﴿let him not be harmed﴾ has been assessed as active. But if it is assessed as passive, the address is to the ones for whom testimony is given. It has also been said that it refers to what the prohibition was about, and the meaning is: if you do something of what I have forbidden you, or leave something of what I have commanded you, then it is defiance in you, i.e., departure from God's command and obedience to Him. This covers all obligations.

﴿And fear God﴾, i.e., in leaving the harm, or in all His commands and prohibitions. Since His saying ﴿and if you do it, it is an act of defiance in you﴾ was a warning, He commanded the fear of God so that one does not fall into defiance.

﴿And God teaches you﴾. This is a sentence of reminder of the blessings of God, the noblest of which is teaching the sciences. It is an independent clause (*mustaʾnafa*) with no place in the grammatical structure (*iʿrāb*). It has also been said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the subject of *wa-ttaqū* (fear), its sense being: "fear God, with the teaching and guidance guaranteed to you." Abū al-Baqāʾ said: it may be a supposed circumstantial clause (*ḥāl muqaddara*). This view — I mean the circumstantial — is very weak, because the present-tense verb occurring as a circumstantial clause does not take the circumstantial *wāw* except in rare cases such as "I came and I strike his eye," and the Qur'an should not be interpreted by rare usages.

﴿And God is Knower of all things﴾. This indicates His comprehensive knowledge of all knowable things, so nothing of them escapes Him. It also implies recompense for the defiant and for the God-fearing. The name God is repeated in these three sentences to magnify the matter. Each sentence is self-standing and does not need a connection by a pronoun; rather it is sufficient to link them with a conjunction. They do not have the same meaning: the first is an exhortation to fear God; the second is a reminder of blessings; the third contains promise and threat. It has also been said that the meaning of the verse is a promise: whoever fears God, God will teach him. Some of the voluntary Sufis often cite this verse, those who shun occupation with the sciences of the Sharia, such as jurisprudence and others, when knowledge and its pursuit are mentioned to them. They say: God said, ﴿fear God, and God will teach you﴾. And from where is fear of God known? Is it known except through knowledge?

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 283 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And if you are on a journey and do not find a scribe, then [let there be] a pledge taken in hand﴾. The implication of the conditional (mafhum al-shart) requires that securing a debt by a pledge (rahn), and taking it, be ruled out when at home (fi'l-hadar) and when a scribe is available. This is because God, exalted is He, made the permissibility of that dependent on the existence of a journey (al-safar) and the absence of a scribe. Mujahid and al-Dahhak held that pledging and entrusting are only in the case of a journey; as for at home, nothing of that should be done. It is also reported from them both that they did not permit taking a pledge except in the state of travel. The majority of scholars (jumhur al-ulama') hold that a pledge is permissible at home and when a scribe is present, and that God mentioned the journey as an example of an excuse, because it is the usual context in which a scribe cannot be found and witnesses are lacking; so the securing of the debt by a pledge takes the place of writing and testimony, and by mentioning the journey He drew attention to every excuse. A scribe may also be unavailable at home, such as at times of occupation and at night. It is authentically reported that "the Messenger of God (ﷺ) pledged his coat of mail at home," and this shows that the condition is not intended to imply its opposite.

The majority read "kaatiban" (a scribe) in the singular. Ubayy, Mujahid and Abu al-Aliyah read "katban" (writing), as a verbal noun, or as a plural of katib, like sahib and sihab. The negation of the scribe implies the negation of writing, and the negation of writing also implies the negation of books (kutub).

Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak read "kuttaban" (scribes) in the plural, considering that every incident has a scribe. It is reported from Abu al-Aliyah that he read "kutuban" (books), the plural of kitab, and it was pluralised in consideration of incidents as well.

The majority read "fa-rihanun" (pledges), the plural of rahn, like ka'b and ki'ab. Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read "furuhun" with a damma on the ra' and the ha', and it is reported from them that the ha' was sukun-ed; others also read each of these forms. It is said that it is the plural of rihan, and rihan is the plural of rahan, as al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said; but the plural of a plural is not regular according to Sibawayh. It is also said that it is the plural of rahn, like saqf; and whoever reads with a sukun on the ha' has lightened furuhun, and this is a dialect in this pattern, like kutb for kutub. This was preferred by Abu Amr ibn al-Ala' and others. Abu Amr ibn al-Ala' said: "I do not know rihan except in the case of horses, and nothing else." Yunus said: "Ruhn and rihan are both Arabic; ruhn is more common for ruhun, and rihan is more common for horses." Plural of fu'ul on fu'l is rare, and among what came with ruhn is the verse of al-A'sha:

"I swore that he would not give from our sons a pledge, so that he corrupts them, like a pledge that corrupted."

And he said with a kasra on rihn for the smallest number, which I do not know to have come; its analogical form would be af'ul, so it seems they dispensed with the rare by the common.

The apparent sense of His words "maqbudatun" (taken in hand) is the requirement of possession (qabd). The people are agreed on the validity of possession by the pledgee and by his agent. As for possession by a trustee on whose hands the pledge is placed, the majority affirmed it. Ata', Qatadah, al-Hakam and Ibn Abi Layla said it is not possession. If the pledge is concluded by offer and acceptance but possession does not take place, the apparent sense of the verse is that it is not valid except by possession, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifah. The Malikis said: the pledge is binding by the contract, and the pledger is compelled to hand over the pledge so that the pledgee may take it into his possession. So possession, according to Malik, is a condition for its full benefit, and according to Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i it is a condition for its validity. They are agreed that it is not complete except by possession.

They differed about its continuation. Malik said: if he returns it by loan or otherwise, it becomes void. Abu Hanifah said: if he returns it by loan or deposit, it does not become void. Al-Shafi'i said: it becomes void by its return to the hand of the pledger in any case.

The apparent sense of the requirement of possession is that the pledged item be a valuable thing (dhat mutaqawwimah) whose sale and purchase are valid, and in which possession or handing over is feasible. The majority said: it is not permitted to pledge what is in liability (dhimmah). The Malikis said it is permitted. The majority said: the pledge of gharar is not valid, such as a runaway slave, a stray camel, foetuses in their mothers' wombs, fish in water, and fruit before it has ripened. Malik said: there is no harm in that.

They differed about the pledge of an undivided share (mushai'). Malik and al-Shafi'i said it is valid in what is divisible and what is not divisible. Abu Hanifah said it is not valid in any case. Al-Hasan ibn Salih said it is permitted in what is not divisible, and not permitted in what is divisible.

The meaning of "ala safar" is "musafirin" (being travellers). The discussion of a similar expression has already passed in the verse of fasting. His words "wa lam tajidu" (and you do not find) may be coordinated with the conditional verb, so the clause is in the place of jazm (apocopate); it may be that the waw is for the circumstance (hal), so the clause is in the place of nasb; and it may be coordinated with the predicate of kana, so the clause is in the place of nasb, because what is coordinated with the predicate is a predicate. The nominative of "fa-rihanun" is because it is the predicate of an omitted subject, the estimate being: (p-356) "then the document is pledges taken in hand."

"Fa-in amina ba'dukum ba'dan falyu'addi alladhi'tuumina amanatahu" — that is: if the creditor trusts the honesty of the debtor, and hands over his property to him without writing, witness or pledge, then the debtor shall discharge his trust, that is, what the owner of the property entrusted to him. Ubayy read "fa-in umina" in the quadriliteral passive, meaning: the people trusted him. Thus this reading was transmitted from Ubayy by al-Zamakhshari, and al-Sajawandi said. Ubayy also read "fa-in ai'tamana," from the eighth form of amn, meaning: he trusted without a document of writing or a pledge. The pronoun in "amanatahu" may return to the creditor, or it may return to the one who was trusted; and "amanah" is a verbal noun applied to the thing that is in liability, and it may be intended as the verbal noun itself, with an omitted modifier, meaning: then let him discharge the debt of his trust. The lam in "falyu'addi" is the imperative, and it is for obligation; and they agreed on the obligation of discharging debts, and the established ruling of the judge concerning it, and his compelling the debtors to it. The hamza of "falyu'addi" may be replaced by waw, as in yuwajalu, yuwakhkharu and yuwakhadhu, because of the damma before it.

Abu Bakr reported from Asim "alladhi-ttumina" with the alif raised, and he indicates the hamza by the damma; Ibn Mujahid said: this rendering is an error. Sulaym reported from Hamzah the isharat (indicating) and ishmam (rounding) of the hamza toward damma; and there is a question about the two indications mentioned.

Ibn Muhaysin and Warsh read with the replacement of the hamza by ya', as it was replaced in bi'r and dhi'b. The original of this verb is "u'tumina," with two hamzas: the first is the hamzat al-wasl, and it is damma; the second is the fa' of the word, and it is sakin, so this is replaced by waw because of the damma before it, and because of the disliked conjunction of the two hamzas. When the word is joined to what precedes it, the waw returns to its original hamza, since the cause that required its replacement, namely the hamzat al-wasl, has disappeared; and if a kasra precedes it, it may be replaced by ya' for that reason.

Asim in his irregular reading (shadhdh) read "alladhi-ttamina" by assimilating the ta' replacing the hamza, by analogy with "ittasara" in the ifti'al of yusr. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is not correct, because the ta' that changed from a hamza has the ruling of a hamza; and "ittazara" is colloquial, and likewise "ruyya" for "ru'ya." End of his words.

What al-Zamakhshari mentioned, that it is not correct and that "ittazara" is colloquial, meaning that it is a novelty of the common people with no basis in the language, has been mentioned by others, that some changed and assimilated, saying "ittaman" and "ittazara," and mentioned that this is a poor dialect. As for his words "and likewise ruyya for ru'ya," this comparison either returns to his words "ittaza'ra 'ammiyyun," so that the assimilation of ruyya is colloquial; or it returns to his words "fa-laysa bi-sahih," meaning: likewise the assimilation of ruyya is not correct. The assimilation in ruyya has been reported by al-Kisa'i.

﴿And let him fear God, his Lord﴾: that is, the punishment of God in discharging what the owner of the property entrusted to him. He combined "God" and "his Lord" in emphasis of the command of piety in discharging the debt, just as He combined them in His words: ﴿And let the one upon whom the truth is due dictate﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282]. So He commanded piety at the time of acknowledging the truth and at the time of discharging the debt that was incumbent on him; thus the command to piety encompassed him at the time of taking and at the time of fulfilment.

﴿And do not conceal testimony﴾: this is a prohibition of prohibition (nahy tahrim); do you not see the threat against the one who conceals it? The place of the prohibition is where the witness fears the loss of the right. Ibn Abbas said: the witness must testify wherever he is called to testify, and inform wherever he is asked to inform, and do not say: "Inform about it to the amir"; rather inform him of it, perhaps he will return and be restrained.

Al-Sulami read "wa-la yaktumu" with ya', in the third person (ghaybah).

﴿And whoever conceals it, his heart is sinful﴾: concealing testimony is hiding it by refraining from discharging it, and concealment is among the sins of the heart, because testimony is knowledge established in the heart; therefore He attached the sin to it. This is from expressing the part for the whole ("Indeed in the body there is a morsel: if it is sound, the whole body is sound; and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt; indeed it is the heart"). The attribution of the act to the limb by which one acts is more eloquent and emphatic; do you not see that you say: "my eye saw it," "my ear heard it," "my heart retained it"? So the sin was attributed to the heart, since it is the locus of the sin and the place where it is committed, and from it the tongue translates; and lest it be thought that concealment is among sins connected with the tongue alone; and the deeds of the hearts are greater than the deeds of all the other limbs, and they are for them like the roots from which they branch out; if the heart is humbled, the limbs are humbled.

The reading of the majority, "athimun," is an active participle from athima qalbuhu, and "qalbuhu" is raised by it as the subject; and "athimun" is the predicate of inna. Al-Zamakhshari allowed that "athimun" be a preposed predicate and "qalbuhu" a subject, and the clause would be in the place of the predicate of inna; but the Kufans do not permit this view.

Ibn Atiyyah said: it is permissible that it (i.e., athimun) be the beginning, and "qalbuhu" a subject which fills the place of the predicate, and the clause is the predicate of inna. This is not correct according to the school of Sibawayh and the majority of the Basrans; because the active participle has not depended on a particle of negation or interrogation, as in: a-qa'imun al-zaydani? and a-qa'imun al-zaydunu? and ma qa'imun al-zaydani? But it is permissible according to the school of Abu al-Hasan, for he permits: qa'imun al-zaydani? so that he raises al-zaydani by the active participle without dependence on a particle of negation or interrogation. Ibn Atiyyah said: it is permissible that "qalbuhu" be a substitute, a substitute of part from the whole, meaning: that it be a substitute for the raised pronoun hidden in "athimun"; but the first parsing is the preferred view.

Some read "qalbahu" in the accusative, and Ibn Atiyyah attributed it to Ibn Abi Ablah, and said: Makki said: it is for explanation (tafsir), meaning the specification (tamyiz); then it was weakened because it is definite; and the Kufans permit the specification to come definite. Some of them have derived it as accusative by analogy to the object, as in the saying: "I passed by a man beautiful of face" and "of countenance"; and what al-Kisa'i recited, may God have mercy on him:

"I describe her, for I am among her describers, / her hooves worn and her hindquarters scorched.
She is overcome in the shrill, and her sides' ... / a hump at the summit and thin at her flanks."

This derivation is permitted according to the school of the Kufans, prohibited according to al-Mubarrad, and permitted in poetry but not in speech according to Sibawayh. It may also be accusative as a substitute, from the subject of inna, a substitute of part from the whole, and there is no concern about separating the substitute and what it substitutes by the predicate, because that is permitted; and they have separated by the predicate between the adjective and the noun qualified, as in: "Zayd is departing, the intelligent," which Sibawayh stated, even though the governing word for the adjective and what it qualifies is one; so how much more so for the substitute, because the more correct view is that the governing word for it is other than the governing word for what it substitutes.

Al-Zamakhshari and others report that Ibn Abi Ablah read "athama qalbahu" with a fatha on the hamza, the tha' and the mim, and the tashdid on the tha', making it a past verb; and "qalbahu" with a fatha on the ba' in the accusative as object of "athama," meaning: he made it sinful.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 283 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of what you do.﴾ "What you do" is general, covering all deeds, and so it includes concealing testimony and failing to render it as it should be. In general, this is a severe warning to the one who conceals testimony, because his being known to Allah in this regard entails recompense. Although the word "knowledge" encompasses both promise and threat. Al-Sulami read (بِما يَعْمَلُونَ) with the ya' (yaʿmaluna, "they do"), in line with his reading of (وَلا يَكْتُمُوا, wa-la yaktumu, "let them not conceal") with the ya' in the third person (ghayba).

This verse includes, among the varieties of eloquence (fasahah), the paronomasia that is different in kind (al-tajnis al-mughayir) in His words: ﴿when you contract a debt with one another (idha tadayantum bi-dayn)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], and in His words: ﴿let a scribe write it down between you (wa-l-yaktub baynakum katib)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], and in His words: ﴿let not a scribe refuse to write (wa-la ya'ba katibun an yaktub)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], and in His words: ﴿and Allah teaches you, and Allah is All-Knowing of everything (wa-yu'allimukumu Allah wa-Allahu bi-kulli shay'in 'alim)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], and in His words: ﴿call upon two witnesses from among your men (wa-istashhidu shahidayni min rijalikum)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], and in His words: ﴿has been entrusted with his trust (uw'tumina amanatahu)﴾. It also includes the paronomasia that is similar in kind (al-tajnis al-mumathil) in His words: ﴿and do not conceal testimony, for whoever conceals it (wa-la taktumu al-shahadata wa-man yaktumha)﴾; and emphasis (al-ta'kid) in His words: ﴿when you contract a debt with one another (idha tadayantum bi-dayn)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], and in His words: ﴿let a scribe write it down between you justly (wa-l-yaktub baynakum katibun bi-l-'adl)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], since from His words ﴿you contract (tadayantum)﴾ is understood His words ﴿a debt (bi-dayn)﴾, and from His words ﴿let him write (fa-l-yaktub)﴾ is understood His words ﴿a scribe (katib)﴾; and antithesis (al-tibaq) in His words: ﴿lest one of them err and the other remind her (an tadilla ihdahuma fa-tudhakkira)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], because "erring" here means "forgetting"; and in His words: ﴿small or large (saghiran aw kabiran)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282]; and simile (al-tashbih) in His words: ﴿let him write as Allah has taught him (an yaktuba kama 'allamahu Allah)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282].

It includes restriction (al-ikhtisas) in His words: ﴿a scribe justly (katibun bi-l-'adl)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], in His words: ﴿let his guardian dictate justly (fa-l-yumlil waliyyuhu bi-l-'adl)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], in His words: ﴿it is more just in the sight of Allah and more upright for testimony (aqsatu 'inda Allah wa-aqwamu li-l-shahadah)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], and in His words: ﴿a present trade which you conduct among yourselves (tijaratan hadirah tudirunaha baynakum)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282].

It includes repetition (al-takrar) in His words: "so write it (fa-ktubuhu), let him write (wa-l-yaktub), and let him write as Allah has taught him (an yaktuba kama 'allamahu Allah), so let him write (fa-l-yaktub), let not a scribe refuse (wa-la ya'ba katib)"; and in His words: ﴿let the one upon whom the truth is due dictate (wa-l-yumlil alladhi 'alayhi al-haqq)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], ﴿if the one upon whom the truth is due is (fa-in kana alladhi 'alayhi al-haqq)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282]. He repeated "the truth (al-haqq)" to call to following it, and used the word "upon (ʿala)" to inform that the owner of the right has a voice and elevated standing. And in His words: ﴿lest one of them err and the other remind her (an tadilla ihdahuma fa-tudhakkira ihdahuma al-ukhra)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282]; and in His words: ﴿and fear Allah; Allah teaches you, and Allah (wa-ttaqu Allah wa-yu'allimukumu Allah wa-Allah)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282].
