It includes ellipsis (al-hadhf) in His words: ﴿O you who have believed (ya ayyuha alladhina amanu)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], where the object of faith is omitted; and in His words: ﴿specified term (musamman)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], meaning: between you. So let the scribe write, let him write the document as Allah has taught him writing and script; let him write the document of the one upon whom the truth is due, what is owed to him of the debt; let him fear Allah, his Lord, in his dictation, and not be a fool in judgment or weak in the evidence, or unable to dictate himself because of muteness or dumbness; then let his guardian dictate the debt on the scribe's behalf. And call upon your men who are designated for testimony and acceptable, so that if there is one acceptable man and two acceptable women from among the acceptable witnesses, "one of them may remind the other of the testimony," and let not the witnesses refuse to bear testimony or to render it before the judge when they are called, that is, when the owner of the right calls them to bear witness or to render it up to its appointed term set between you. That document is more just and more upright for acceptable testimony, that you not doubt the testimony, which you conduct among yourselves, and you will not need to write it down or call witnesses to it. And call witnesses when you conduct a sale, two witnesses or a man and two women. Let no scribe or witness be harmed, that is, the owner of the right, or let the owner of the right not harm a scribe or a witness; then it was elided and put into the passive. And that you do harm. Fear the punishment of Allah, and Allah teaches you what is right. If you are on a journey and do not find a scribe whose writing can be relied upon, then the pledge is a security, if some of you trust one another, and one gives another money without witnesses or pledge, his trust is to be fulfilled without injustice or procrastination; and let him fear the punishment of Allah. And do not conceal testimony from those who seek it.

The shifting of address (talwin al-khitab), which is moving from the second person (huduar) to the third person (ghayba), occurs in His words: "write it (fa-ktubuhu) and let him write (wa-l-yaktub)"; and from the third person to the second in His words: "let not a scribe refuse, and call witnesses (wa-la ya'ba katib, wa-ashhidu)"; then he moved to the third person with His words: ﴿and let him not harm (wa-la yudarra)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282]; then to the second person with His words: ﴿and do not conceal testimony (wa-la taktumu al-shahadah)﴾; then to the third person with His words: ﴿and whoever conceals it (wa-man yaktumha)﴾; then to the second person with His words: ﴿what you do (bi-ma ta'malun)﴾.

The shift from the form fa'il to the form fa'il (fa'il to fa'il), in His words: ﴿two witnesses (shahidayn)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], ﴿let not a scribe or a witness be harmed (wa-la yudarra katibun wa-la shahid)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282].

Advancing and delaying (al-taqdim wa-l-ta'khir) occurs in His words: ﴿let him write (fa-l-yaktub)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], ﴿let him dictate (wa-l-yumlil)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], or "the dictation," by advancing the writing before it. And of this is: ﴿from among the witnesses whom you accept (mimman tardawna min al-shuhada')﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], the implied meaning being: call upon those whom you accept; and of it: "and call witnesses when you conduct a sale."

End of what we have summarized from what was mentioned concerning this verse of the types of eloquence. In it, among the emphasis on preserving wealth in transactions, is what is not hidden: the command to the debtors to write; the command to the scribe to write justly; the prohibition against refusing to write; his being commanded a second time to write; the command to the one upon whom the truth is due to dictate if possible, or to his guardian if he cannot; the command (p-359) to call witnesses; the caution regarding who bears witness and how he is described; the prohibition to witnesses against refusing testimony when they are called to it; the prohibition against reluctance in writing down a debt even if it is small; the praise of precision through writing; the command to call witnesses at the time of sale; the prohibition to the scribe and witness against harming the one for whom they testify and write; the notice that harm of this kind is a transgression (fusuq); the command to piety; the reminder of the blessing of being taught; the threat after that; the guarantee during travel when there is no scribe, by a pledge taken in hand; the command to one who has been trusted to fulfill the trust of one who did not secure it with a scribe, witness, or pledge; the command to one who was trusted to be mindful of Allah, which prevents breaching the trust; the prohibition against concealing testimony; the notice that whoever conceals it has committed sin; and the threat at its end in His words: ﴿and Allah is All-Knowing of what you do.﴾ So look at this exaggeration and emphasis on preserving wealth and guarding it from loss. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) linked it with lives and blood, saying: "Whoever is killed defending his property is a martyr," and he said: "Indeed your blood, your property, and your honor are forbidden to you." And for its preservation and the prevention of its waste, and of extravagance in it, there was the restriction of bankruptcy (hajr al-iflas), the restriction of insanity (hajr al-junun), the restriction of minority (hajr al-sighar), the restriction of slavery (hajr al-riqq), the restriction of illness (hajr al-marad), and the restriction of apostasy (hajr al-irtidad).

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 284]. Al-Sha'bi and 'Ikrimah said: it was revealed concerning the concealing and the upholding of testimony; Mujahid and Muqsim reported it from Ibn 'Abbas. Muqatil and al-Waqidi said: it was revealed concerning those among the believers who take the disbelievers as allies.

Its connection (munasabah) is evident, because when He mentioned that whoever conceals testimony, his heart is sinful, He mentioned what the inner self harbors, whether he conceals it or reveals it, for Allah will call him to account for it. In this there is a warning and threat for whoever conceals testimony. And since He attached sin to the heart, He mentioned here the selves (anfus), saying: ﴿Whether you reveal what is in your selves or conceal it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 284]. The mention of this verse as the conclusion of this surah is fitting, because He, exalted is He, included in it most of the knowledge of the fundamentals and the derivative rulings: the proofs of monotheism (tawhid), prophethood (nubuwwah), the return (ma'ad), prayer, zakat, retaliation (qisas), fasting, pilgrimage, jihad, menstruation, divorce, the waiting period ('iddah), khul', ila', nursing, usury (riba), sale, and the manner of contracting debts. So it is fitting that His imposing these laws upon us should be followed by mention that He, exalted is He, owns whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, so He binds whom He wills among His creatures with whatever worship and obligations He wills.

Since these obligations have their locus of belief only in the selves and what they harbor of intentions, and the reward of one who fulfills them and the punishment of one who abandons them become manifest only in the Hereafter, He drew attention to the attribute of knowledge by which accountability occurs in the Hereafter, saying: ﴿Whether you reveal what is in your selves or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 284]. The attribute of sovereignty indicates overwhelming power, and the mention of accountability indicates all-encompassing knowledge of the great and the small. Thus through these two attributes is achieved the utmost promise to the obedient and the utmost threat to the disobedient.

The apparent sense of the lam in (lillah) is that it denotes ownership (al-milk), and He is the owner of it, because He, exalted is He, is the one who originated it and created it. It was also said: the meaning is that to Allah belongs the management (tadbir) of whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. He specified the heavens and the earth because they are the greatest of created things that can be seen, and He put the heavens first because of their greatness. He used the word "ma" (what), giving precedence to what does not reason over what reasons, because what the heavens and earth contain is mostly inanimate matter and animals, which do not reason, and their kinds are many; whereas the rational beings have few kinds, for they are three: humankind, jinn, and angels.

[p-360] **﴿Whether you show what is in your selves or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it.﴾** Apparently this is general. The meaning is that the two states, concealing and disclosing, are equal with respect to Him, the Exalted. Disclosure and concealment apply only in relation to created beings, not to Him, the Exalted, because His knowledge does not arise from the existence of things. Rather, He knows things before their creation, after their creation, and after their annihilation. The knowledge of a created being is different: it knows a thing only after it has come into existence, so its knowledge is originated (muhdath). This generality has been specified. Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah and al-Sha'bi said, and Ibn Jarir preferred this view, that it has the sense of testimony. In this verse He informs us that the one who conceals what is in his heart is held to account. It was said that it refers to devising stratagems to commit usury (riba). Mujahid said it refers to doubt and certainty. What indicates that Allah, the Exalted, holds people accountable for what the hearts harbour is His saying: ﴿And know that Allah knows what is in your selves, so beware of Him﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 235).

After this: love, will, knowledge and ignorance are actions of the heart, and they are among the greatest actions of the servants. Qadi Abd al-Jabbar said: He has made clear that actions of the heart are like actions of the limbs in that the threat of punishment covers them. He means what must be made known if it is hidden, and what must be concealed if it is revealed, of matters connected with rights. He did not intend by this what passes through the heart of which sin has been lifted. The end of his words. To what occurs in the self, Allah knows best, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) pointed by his saying: "Verily Allah, the Exalted, has overlooked for my community what it has whispered to itself, so long as it does not act upon it or speak of it." He also said: "Whether you show the deed or conceal it."

Abu Ali said: He calls His servants to account for what they conceal of their deeds and for what they display. So He forgives the one who deserves forgiveness and punishes the one who deserves punishment. It indicates that reward and punishment are merited by resolve and by all the other actions of the heart when they are obedience or disobedience.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "From the evil." This is good, because after it came the mention of forgiveness and punishment. But al-Zamakhshari appended to this his saying: ﴿So He forgives whom He wills﴾, for the one who has earned forgiveness through repentance from what was manifested or harboured, ﴿and punishes whom He wills﴾, the one who has earned punishment through persistence. The end of his words. This is a Mu'tazilite (Mu'tazili) tendency. The people of the Sunnah say that forgiveness may come from Allah, the Exalted, to one who died persisting in disobedience without repenting. Such a person is under His will: if He wills, He forgives him, and if He wills, He punishes him. ﴿Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ (An-Nisa: 48).

Then al-Zamakhshari said: The whisperings and the passing thoughts of the self are not included in what a person conceals, because these are things he has no power to be free of. Rather, it is what he believes and resolves upon. From Abdullah ibn Umar that he recited it and said: "If Allah takes us to account for this, we shall perish." Then he wept until his sobbing was heard. This was mentioned to Ibn Abbas, who said: "May Allah forgive Abu Abd al-Rahman. The Muslims have experienced what he experienced from it." Then this was revealed: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 286). The end of his words.

Ibn Atiyya said: "In your selves" implies, by the strength of the expression, that what is settled in the self, believed, and kept in thought is what is meant. As for the passing thoughts that cannot be repelled, they are not in the self except in a figurative sense. The end of his words.

Some said that this verse has been abrogated (naskh, cancellation of a ruling by a later one) by His saying: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 286). It is proper to treat this as a specification (takhsis) if we hold that the whisperings and the thoughts are included under His saying: ﴿what is in your selves﴾. The more correct view is that it is muhkam (clear, not abrogated). He calls them to account for what they did and what they did not do, of what was established in their souls, what they intended, and what they willed. So He forgives the believers, and He seizes the people of disbelief and hypocrisy with it. It was said: the punishment that is the recompense for passing thoughts is the calamities of this world, its pains, and all its distresses. This meaning is narrated from Aisha. Since the wording could include passing thoughts, the Companions were fearful, so Allah made clear what He intended by it and specified it, and stated His ruling that He does not burden a soul beyond its capacity. Passing thoughts are not within the capacity to repel. In this was their relief and the removal of their distress.

The verse is a report (khabar), and abrogation does not apply to reports. The verb (yuhasibkum, "will call you to account") is in the jussive because it is the answer to the conditional. It was said: He expressed knowledge by calling to account, since one of the explanations (tafsir, interpretations) of "the Reckoner" (al-Hasib) is "the Knower." So the meaning is that He knows what is in the secrets and the inner thoughts. It was said: the answer is conditioned on His will or on the absence of His leniency, and the sense is: He calls you to account if He wills, or He calls you to account if He does not show mercy.

Ibn Amir, Asim, Yazid, Ya'qub and Sahl read ﴿so He forgives whom He wills and punishes﴾ with nominative (raf') on both verbs, as a separate clause. This is permissible in two ways. One is that the verb is the predicate of an omitted subject. The other is that a clause of verb and subject is coordinated with what precedes it. The remaining seven readers read with the jussive, coordinating with the answer. Ibn Abbas, al-A'raj and Abu Haywa read with the accusative (nasb) on both, by supposing an implied "an" (in). With it and what follows it, a nominal verbal noun is formed in the nominative, coordinated with a verbal noun implied from the reckoning. Its sense is: "let there be a reckoning, then forgiveness and punishment."

These aspects have also come in the words of the poet:

*"If Abu Qabus perishes, the spring of the people and the sacred month will perish,*
*And we will take after him the tail of a life, back-wounded, with no hump."*

It is narrated with the jussive of "and we will take," with its nominative, and with its accusative.

Al-Ja'fi, Khallad and Talha ibn Musarrif read (yughfaru li-man yashaa'), "is forgiven to whom He wills." It is narrated that it is so in the codex (mushaf) of Abdullah. Ibn Jinni said: it is in apposition (badal) to (yuhasibkum), so it is an explanation of the reckoning. The end of his words. This is not an explanation. Rather, the two are consequences of the reckoning. An example of the jussive as apposition to the answer is His saying: ﴿Whoever does that will meet a penalty﴾ (Al-Furqan: 68), ﴿his punishment will be doubled﴾ (Al-Furqan: 69).

Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning of this apposition is the detailing of the whole reckoning, because detail is clearer than what is detailed. So it operates as the apposition of part from whole, or apposition of inclusion (ishtimal), like your saying: "I struck Zayd, his head," and "I love Zayd, his intellect." This apposition occurs in verbs just as it occurs in nouns, because both categories need clarification. The end of his words. In this there is some objection. First, his saying that the meaning of this apposition is the detailing of the whole reckoning is not correct. Forgiveness and punishment are not a detailing of the reckoning, because reckoning is only the counting and enumeration of a person's good and bad deeds, such that nothing is left out. Forgiveness and punishment are consequences of the reckoning, so reckoning does not detail forgiveness and punishment.

Second, his saying, after mentioning apposition of part from whole and of whole and apposition of inclusion, "this apposition occurs in nouns because both categories need clarification," is also problematic. Apposition of inclusion is possible and has occurred, because the verb, by what it indicates, signifies a genus under which there are kinds it includes. That is why when negation falls upon it, all kinds of that genus are negated. Apposition of part from whole, however, is not possible in verbs, since a verb does not accept division. One does not say of a verb that it has a whole and a part, except by a far-fetched figurative usage. It is not like the noun in this respect. For this reason, apposition of part from whole is impossible with respect to Allah, the Exalted, since the Creator, the Exalted, is one and is not divided nor subdivided.

Al-Zamakhshari said, when he mentioned the reading with the jussive: If you ask, how does the reader with the jussive recite? I say: he manifests the (r) and assimilates the (b). And one who assimilates the (r) into the (l) is a lahin (one who makes a grave error), committing a gross mistake. Whoever transmits this from Abu Amr is wrong twice, because he commits a grave error and attributes to the most knowledgeable of people in Arabic what indicates great ignorance. The cause of such transmissions is the weak precision of the transmitters, and the cause of weak precision is little understanding. Only the grammarians can preserve such things. The end of his words. This is in keeping with his habit of finding fault with the readers.

As for his statement that the one who assimilates the (r) into the (l) is a lahin who commits a gross mistake, and so on: this is a matter on which the grammarians have differed. Al-Khalil, Sibawayh and their followers held that it is not permissible to assimilate (r) into (l) because of the repetition (takrir) in the (r), nor into (n). Abu Sa'id said: We know of no one who disagreed with him except Ya'qub al-Hadrami, and what is narrated from Abu Amr: that he assimilated (r) into (l) when the (r) is moving and the letter before it is also moving, as in ﴿yaghfiru li-man﴾ (Al-Imran: 129), ﴿al-umuri li-kay la﴾ (An-Nahl: 70), ﴿wa-istaghfara lahumu al-Rasulu﴾ (An-Nisa: 64). If the letter before the (r) is quiescent, he assimilated it into the (l) in places of damma and kasra, as in ﴿al-anharu lahum﴾ (An-Nahl: 31), and al-naru li-yajziya. If it has fatha and the letter before it is a long vowel or other, he did not assimilate, as in ﴿min Misra li-imra'atihi﴾ (Yusuf: 21), ﴿al-abrara la-fi na'im﴾ (Al-Infitar: 13), ﴿lan tabura li-yuwaffiyahum﴾ (Fatir: 29), ﴿al-hamira li-tarkabuha﴾ (An-Nahl: 8). If the (r) is quiescent, he assimilated it into the (l) with no disagreement from him, except what Ahmad ibn Jubayr narrated without disagreement from him, from al-Yazidi, from him, that he manifested it. That is when he recites by manifesting the identical and similar letters that are both moving, and nothing else. However, the practice in his school with both modes is assimilation, as in (wa-yaghfir lakum). The end of his words.

Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' permitted it and related it as heard (sama'). Abu Ja'far al-Ru'asi agreed with them about its being heard, in transmission and permission. He is one of the imams of language and Arabic among the Kufans. Abu Amr agreed with them about assimilation, in transmission and permission, as we have mentioned. Ya'qub followed him as we have mentioned, and this is from the transmission of al-Walid ibn Hassan. Assimilation is a valid analogical position, which we have mentioned in our book (al-Takmil li-Sharh al-Tashil), by our composition. Some of our companions relied on the view that what is narrated from the readers as assimilation, which the Basrans forbade, is actually concealment (ikhfa', partial obscuring) and not assimilation. It is not permissible to believe that the readers erred, were not precise, and did not distinguish between concealment and assimilation. This man set up a chapter saying: "This is a chapter in which I mention what the readers assimilated of what he has said it is not permissible to assimilate." This is not proper, for the language of the Arabs is not confined to what the Basrans transmitted alone. The readings do not come in accordance with what the Basrans knew and transmitted. Rather, the Kufan readers nearly resemble the readers of Basra. The major Basran authority and their chief, Abu Amr ibn al-Ala', and Ya'qub al-Hadrami, and the great authorities of Kufa: al-Ru'asi, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra', all agreed on transmitting the assimilation of (r) into (l), permitted it, and related it from the Arabs. So it is obligatory to accept it and to refer to their knowledge and transmission, since one who knows is a proof against one who does not know.

As for al-Zamakhshari's statement that the transmitter of this from Abu Amr is wrong twice, it has become clear that this is correct. Those who transmitted it from him include Abu Muhammad al-Yazidi, who is an imam in grammar, an imam in readings, and an imam in languages.

Al-Naqqash said: "He forgives whom He wills" means He removes it from the one who desists, and "punishes whom He wills" means if he persists in it. Al-Thawri said: "He forgives whom He wills" refers to the great sin, and "punishes whom He wills" refers to the small.

Some people have relied on this verse to permit assigning what cannot be borne (taklif ma la yutaq). They said: they were charged with the matter of passing thoughts, and that is something that cannot be borne. Ibn Atiyya said: This is not clear. It was only an interpretation (ta'wil) that the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) gave to it, and it did not establish a charge.

﴿And Allah is over all things Powerful.﴾ When He mentioned forgiveness and punishment for whom He wills, He followed this with mention of power, because what was mentioned is a part of the objects of power.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 285 (part 1 of 2):

﴿The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord, and so do the believers.﴾ The occasion of its revelation: when the verse ﴿If you show what is in yourselves or conceal it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 284] was revealed, they were apprehensive about it. Then the matter was settled such that they said ﴿We hear and we obey﴾ [al-Nisa': 46], and they returned to humility and submission. So Allah praised them and commended them, and He placed that before His kindness to them and His removal of that distress which their misgivings had caused. Thus, exalted is He, He combined for them the honour of praise and commendation with the removal of hardship in the matter of their inner thoughts. This is the fruit of obedience and of devotion to Allah, exalted is He, just as what befell the Children of Israel was the opposite of that, through their censure and their being burdened with hardships of humiliation, wretchedness and exile, when they said ﴿We hear and we disobey﴾ [al-Baqarah: 93]. This is the fruit of disobedience and rebellion against Allah. May Allah, exalted is He, protect us from His vengeance. End of this; and it is the words of Ibn 'Atiyyah.

It has become clear, through the occasion of revelation, how this verse relates to what precedes it. Since the opening of this surah mentions the Book that was sent down, and that it is a guidance for the God-fearing (muttaqun), who are described by what they were described with: faith in the unseen, and in what was sent down to the Messenger and to those before him, its conclusion too agrees with its opening.

I have examined the beginnings of the long surahs and found that their endings correspond to them, such that scarcely anything of them is out of place. I will show this, God willing, at the end of each surah. This is among the most wondrous eloquence, where the end of a very long speech meets its beginning. It is a habit of the Arabs in many of their compositions: one of them takes up a matter, then digresses from it to another matter, then to another, and so on at length, then returns to what he had originally taken up. Whoever reflects deeply will find it easy to see the connection in what at first sight appears to have no connection. Thus Allah, exalted is He, in the end of this surah, makes clear that those believers are the community of Muhammad ﷺ.

al-Marwazi said: ﴿The Messenger believes﴾. al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ibn Sirin, and Ibn 'Abbas in one narration said: these two verses were not brought down by Jibril; he heard them (ﷺ) directly on the night of the Mi'raj without an intermediary, and al-Baqarah is Medinan except these two verses. Ibn 'Abbas in another narration, and Ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, and 'Ata' said: Jibril descended with them to him in Medina. And this is a refutation of those who say "if Allah wills" regarding their faith, because Allah, exalted is He, has testified to the faith of the believers, so doubt about it is doubt about the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He. End of his words.

The alif and lam in (al-Rasul) denote a known referent, and it is our Messenger Muhammad ﷺ. The name has frequently been used for him by Allah with this noble title. What has been sent down to him from his Lord includes all that was sent down to him from Allah, exalted is He: of creeds, of kinds of laws, and of categories of rulings, in the Qur'an and in other than it. He believes that this is revelation from Allah which reached him. He placed the Messenger first because his faith is the one that precedes, and the faith of the believers comes after his faith, since he is the one followed and they are the followers in this.

It is related that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had these verses revealed to him, he said: "He is entitled to believe." The apparent meaning is that his saying (and the believers) is conjoined to his saying (the Messenger). This is supported by the reading of 'Ali and 'Abd Allah (wa-amana al-mu'minun), where the verb is made explicit which others read as implicit. On this basis (kullun) covers both the Messenger and the believers. They also allowed that the pause may be complete at his saying (from his Lord), with (al-mu'minun) as the subject, and (kullun) as a second subject, covering the believers only, and (amana billah) is a clause in the place of the predicate of (kullun); the clause of (kullun) and its predicate is in the place of the predicate of (al-mu'minun). The connecting pronoun linking this clause to the first subject is omitted; it is a genitive pronoun whose estimated form is: each of them believed, like their saying: "Ghee is a manan for a dirham," meaning: from it for a dirham. Faith in Allah is: affirming Him and His attributes, and rejecting idols and every deity other than Him. Faith in His angels is: believing in their existence, that they are servants of Allah, and rejecting the beliefs of the Jahiliyyah concerning them. Faith in His books is: affirming everything that was sent down to the prophets whom the Book of Allah includes, and what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ reported of that. Faith in His messengers is: affirming that Allah sent them to His servants.

This order is at the height of eloquence, because faith in Allah is the first rank, which reason alone establishes, since every rational person acknowledges the existence of the Creator. Faith in His angels is the second rank, since they are like intermediaries between Allah and His servants. Faith in the books is the third rank, being the revelation which the angel receives from Allah and conveys to humans. Faith in the messengers, who draw light from the revelation, is the fourth rank, since they are later in standing than the books. Something of this order has already been discussed in His saying: ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Allah and His angels and His messengers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98]. It has also been said: the discourse concerns recognising the Truth in itself, and recognising the good for acting upon it, and perfecting the theoretical faculty through knowledge and the practical faculty through performing good deeds. The first is more noble, so it was begun with, and it is the faith mentioned. The second is what is indicated by His saying: ﴿We hear and we obey﴾. It has also been said: for the human being there is a beginning, a present state, and a return. Faith indicates the beginning, ﴿We hear and we obey﴾ indicates the present state, and ﴿Forgiveness, our Lord﴾ and what follows it indicates the return.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (wa-kitabihi) in the singular, and the rest of the Seven read (wa-kutubihi) in the plural. Whoever reads the singular intends every written thing; the object is named by the verbal noun, as in their saying: "Nasj al-Yaman," meaning its woven product. Abu 'Ali said: its meaning is that this singular is not like the singular of verbal nouns even if a multitude is meant by it, as in His saying: ﴿And call out for one destruction [thubur] and call for many destructions﴾ [al-Furqan: 14]. Rather, just as names are used in the singular when multiplicity is intended, such as "the dinar and the dirham were abundant," and their coming with the alif and lam is more common than their coming in construct, and among the construct is His saying: ﴿If you tried to count Allah's favour, you could not number it﴾ [Ibrahim: 34]. In a hadith: "Iraq withheld its dirham and its qafiz," meaning the multitude, just as what has the definite article is meant. End of the summary; its meaning is that the singular noun with alif and lam encompasses more than the construct plural.

al-Zamakhshari said: Ibn 'Abbas read (wa-kitabihi), intending the Qur'an, or the genus. And from him: "al-kitab is more than the kutub." If you ask: how can the singular be more than the plural? I say: because when the singular is intended as a genus, and the genus-quality subsists in all the individuals of the genus, nothing is left out of it; whereas the plural does not include under it except those among the plurals in which the genus-quality is present. End of his words. But it is not as he stated; because when the plural is put in construct or takes the generic alif and lam, it becomes general, and the force of a general term is a reference to each and every individual. If one says: "I freed my slaves," it covers every single slave. The indication of the plural is clearer in generality than the singular, whether it has alif and lam or is in construct. Rather, generality is not taken for the singular except by a verbal indicator, such as its being excepted from, or being qualified by a plural, as in: ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [al-'Asr: 2], ﴿except those who believed﴾ [al-'Asr: 3]; or "the yellow dinar and the white dirham ruined people"; or a semantic indicator, as in "the intention of the believer is more effective than his deed." The most that can be said is that it is like the general plural when generality is intended, and it is treated according to the wording in His saying (amana), so it is singular, as in His saying: ﴿Say: each acts according to his manner﴾ [al-Isra': 84].

Yahya ibn Ya'mar read (wa-kutbihi wa-rusline), with the taʾ and the sin silent; this is related from Nafi'. al-Hasan read (wa-rusline) with the sin silent, and this is a narration from Abu 'Amr. 'Abd Allah read (wa-kitabihi wa-liqa'ihi wa-rusulihi).

﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾. The majority read it with nun, and estimated: they say, we make no distinction. It is also possible that the estimate is: he says, we make no distinction, since he informs about himself and about others; so it is "he says" according to the wording, and "they say" according to the meaning after treating it according to the wording. On both estimates the place of this estimated item is accusative as a circumstantial state. al-Hawfi and others allowed that it is a predicate after a predicate of (kullun).

Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Ya'mar, Abu Zur'ah ibn 'Amr ibn Jarir, and Ya'qub, and the text of the narration of Abu 'Amr, read (wa-la yufarriqu) with ya', according to the wording of (kullun). Harun said: it is so in the codex of Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud: (la yufarriqun), treated according to the meaning of (kullun) after treating it according to the wording. The meaning: they are not like the Jews and Christians who believe in some and disbelieve in others. The purpose of this statement is to establish prophethood, which is the manifestation of a miracle in accordance with the claim; so singling out some over others is contradictory, not as some claimed, that the purpose is non-preference among them. (Ahad) here is the one specific to negation and the like, so it is for generality, which is why (min) entered upon it, as in His saying: ﴿Then not one of you could withhold from Him﴾ [al-Haqqah: 47]; the meaning is among their individuals. The poet said:

When the affairs of people are stirred into a commotion, they fear no one who sees them.

Some said: (ahad) is said to mean "all," and the estimate is: among all His messengers. This estimate is far-fetched in my view, because it does not conflict with their being those who distinguish between some messengers, and the purpose of the negation is this: since the Jews and Christians did not distinguish between all the messengers, but only some, namely Muhammad. So it is established that the interpretation he mentioned is false. Rather the meaning of the verse is: he does not distinguish between any of His messengers and others in prophethood. End of his words, with some abridgement. Whoever explained it as "all," or said it has the meaning of "all," does not mean anything other than generality, like: no one stood, meaning no single individual of the men, for example, nor any single individual of the women, not that he negated standing from the whole group so that it would be established for some. It is possible in my view that this is among what has the coordinated element omitted because the meaning indicates it, and the estimate is: he does not distinguish between any of His messengers and between any [other] one, so (ahad) here means (wahid), not that it is the word laid down for generality in negation. And among the omission of the coordinated element: "garments that protect you from heat" [al-Nahl: 81], meaning and cold. And the poet's saying:

There was nothing between the good, had Abu Hujr come back safe, except a few short nights.

(p-366) meaning: between the good and between me, and he omitted it, since the meaning indicates it.

﴿And they say: We hear and we obey﴾. That is: we hear your speech and obey your command. Mere hearing is not intended, but acceptance and response. He placed (we hear) before (we obey) because obligation's path is hearing, and obedience comes after it. It is fitting for the believer to be saying this throughout his life.

﴿Forgiveness, our Lord﴾: that is, for shortcoming in Your right; or because our worship, though it reaches the utmost perfection, is in comparison to Your majesty a shortcoming.

﴿And to You is the final return﴾: an affirmation of the return, that is, to Your recompense is the destination. The accusative of ﴿Forgiveness﴾ is as a verbal noun, which is among the verbal nouns whose verb acts in them while implicit. Its estimate according to Sibawayh is: "forgive us a forgiveness of Yours." al-Sajawandi said: Ibn 'Atiyyah attributed it to al-Zajjaj. al-Zamakhshari said: (ghufranaka) is accusative by an implicit verb of its own; it is said: "Forgiveness of You, not disbelief in You," meaning: we seek Your forgiveness and do not disbelieve in You. On the first estimate the clause is imperative; on the second it is declarative.

Ibn 'Usfur's statement about it is inconsistent: at one point he said it is accusative by a verb that may be made explicit, and at another point he said it is accusative whose implicit form is obligatory, and he counted it with "Subhan Allah" and its like. Some allowed its accusative as an object, meaning: we seek or ask Your forgiveness. Some allowed its nominative as a subject, meaning: Your forgiveness is our aim.

**The Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 2, Verse 285 (Part 2 of 2)**

The word ﴿al-maṣīr﴾ (المَصِيرُ) is an ism maṣdar (a verbal noun, the noun of the verb's action) from ṣāra yaṣīru, and it is patterned on maf'il, with a kasra on the ʿayn. The grammarians (al-naḥwiyyūn) differed over the pattern of the maf'il form when its ʿayn is a yāʾ, as in: yabītu, yaʿīshu, yaḥīḍu, yaqīlu, yaṣīru. Some held that it is like the sound form, as in yaḍribu, so that it is used for the masdar with a fatḥa, and for the place and time, as in ﴿wa-jaʿalnā al-nahāra maʿāshan﴾ [al-Naba': 11], meaning ʿaysh (livelihood). On this view, al-maḥīḍ means al-ḥayḍ (menstruation) and al-maṣīr means al-ṣayrūra (the state of becoming), but this is an anomaly (shādhdh).

Others held that the masdar may be patterned either on maf'il with a kasra on the ʿayn or on maf'al with a fatḥa on it, and that the place and time nouns take the kasra. This was the view of al-Zajjāj, and Abū ʿAlī (al-Fārisī) refuted him on it. Others restricted the matter to what is heard from the Arabs (al-iqtiṣār ʿalā al-samāʿ), so that wherever the Arabs formed the masdar on maf'il or maf'al we follow them. This is the more cautious position.

﴿Lā yukallifu Allāhu nafsan illā wus'ahā﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286]. Its apparent sense is that it is a new independent sentence (istiʾnāf), a report from God, the Exalted, in which He informs that He does not burden the servants, in their actions of the heart and the limbs, with anything except what is within the capacity of the one charged, and within his power of comprehension and intention. With this the matter of the passing thoughts (al-khawāṭir) is made clear, the matter which the Muslims interpreted in the verse ﴿in tubdū...﴾ (the verse), and the interpretation of those who say that it is not valid to impose what cannot be borne (taklīf mā lā yuṭāq) becomes evident. This verse is similar to ﴿Allāhu yurīdu bikumu al-yusra wa-lā yurīdu bikumu al-ʿusr﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], and ﴿wa-mā jaʿala ʿalaykum fī al-dīni min ḥaraj﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 78], and ﴿fa-ttaqū Allāha mā istaṭaʿtum﴾ [al-Taghābun: 16].

Al-Zamakhsharī said: That is, He does not burden her except with what is within her capacity and what is easy for her, short of the limit of endurance and exertion. This is a report of His justice and mercy, in accordance with ﴿Allāhu yurīdu bikumu al-yusra wa-lā yurīdu bikumu al-ʿusr﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. For it was within a person's power and capacity to pray more than the five prayers, to fast more than the month, and to perform the Hajj more than once. It has also been said that this is part of the speech of the Messenger and the believers, meaning that they said: ﴿Lā yukallifu Allāhu nafsan illā wus'ahā﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286]. The meaning is that when they said ﴿sami'nā wa-aṭa'nā﴾ (we hear and we obey), they then said: How could we not hear that and not obey? And He, the Exalted, does not burden us except with what is within our capacity? The wus' (capacity) is less than the maximum exertion in hardship, and it is what a person's power can accommodate.

Its place in the sentence (inṣiba) is as a second object (maf'ūl thānin) of ﴿yukallifu﴾. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: ﴿yukallifu﴾ transitively takes two objects, one of which is omitted, its estimated form being ʿibādatan (an act of worship) or shayʾan (something). End of quotation. If he means that its original form is like this, then it is correct, because ﴿illā wus'ahā﴾ is an exceptive construction lacking a complement (istithnāʾ mufraghun, where the exception is from an unstated object), and it is taken from the second object. But if he means that it is omitted in the grammatical analysis (al-ṣināʿa), then this is not so. Rather, the second object is ﴿wus'ahā﴾, as in: "I gave Zayd only a dirham," and "I struck only Zayd." In grammatical analysis this is the object, even if its original form was: "I did not give Zayd anything except a dirham," and "I did not strike anyone except Zayd."

Ibn Abī ʿAbla read ﴿illā wasaʿahā﴾, making it a past-tense verb, and they interpreted it as having an implied relative pronoun mā (what). On this reading, the relative clause is the second object of ﴿yukallifu﴾, just as ﴿wus'ahā﴾ is the second object in the reading of the majority. There is weakness in this, in that the relative pronoun is omitted without another relative pronoun indicating it, as in the verse of Ḥassān:

*So whoever among you satirizes the Messenger of God,
and praises him and supports him, is the same.*

That is: and whoever supports him, so the word *min* (from) was omitted because of the earlier *min* (among you). The omission of the relative pronoun should not be treated as a general rule, because the relative pronoun and its clause are like a single unit. It is also permissible that the second object of ﴿yukallifu﴾ is omitted, the meaning being understood, and that ﴿wus'ahā﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumla fī mawḍiʿ al-ḥāl). The estimate would be: God does not burden a soul with anything, except that it has its capacity, meaning: while He has granted it capacity. This estimate is preferable to omitting the relative pronoun.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: This points to the reading of Ibn Abī ʿAbla, in which there is a figure of speech (tajawwuz), because it is inverted (maqlūb). The usual wording would have been: illā wasiʿat-hu, as he said: ﴿wasiʿa kursiyyuhu al-samāwāti wa-al-arḍ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255], and ﴿wasiʿa kulla shay'in ʿilman﴾ [Ṭā Hā: 98]. But this comes under the pattern of: "I put the cap on my head," and "my mouth in the stone." End of quotation.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya discussed here the matter of imposing what cannot be borne (taklīf mā lā yuṭāq), and this is a question investigated in the foundations of religion (uṣūl al-dīn). What the apparent meaning of the verse indicates is that it does not occur.

﴿Lahā mā kasabat wa-ʿalayhā mā iktasabat﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286]. That is: what it earned of good deeds and what it acquired of evil deeds. This was said by al-Suddī and the majority of the exegetes, and there is no disagreement about it. Passing thoughts are not part of a person's earning. The sound view among the people of language is that kasb (earning) and iktisāb (acquiring) are one and the same, and the Qur'an speaks to this. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Kullu nafsin bimā kasabat rahīnatun﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 38], and He said: ﴿wa-lā taksibu kullu nafsin illā ʿalayhā﴾ [al-Anʿām: 164], and He said: ﴿Balā man kasaba sayyiʾatan wa-aḥāṭat bihi khaṭīʾatuhu﴾ [al-Baqarah: 81], and He said: ﴿bi-ghayri mā iktasabū﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 58].

Some made a distinction, saying: iktisāb is more specific than kasb, because kasb is divided into earning for oneself and earning for others, whereas iktisāb is only for oneself. It is said: *kāsib ahlihi* (the earner for his family), but one does not say: *muktasib ahlihi*. A poet said:

*You cast his earner into a dark pit.*

Al-Zamakhsharī said: What it earned of good is of benefit to it, and what it acquired of evil harms it. No one is held to account for another's sin, and no one is rewarded for another's obedience. If you ask: Why did He specify good with kasb and evil with iktisāb? I say: In iktisāb there is effort (iʿtimāl). Since evil is something the soul desires, being drawn toward it and commanding it, the soul is more active and diligent in obtaining it, so it was described as acquired (muktasaba) in that respect. Since the soul is not like that in the matter of good, good was described with a form that carries no indication of effort. End of his words.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: He repeated the verb of earning, varying the morphology (taṣrīf), for the beauty of the style of speech, as he said: ﴿fa-mahhili al-kāfirīna amhilhum ruwaydan﴾ [al-Ṭāriq: 17]. This is one view. What appears to me in this matter is that good deeds are things acquired without strain, since the one who earns them is on the highway of God's command and the path of His law. Evil deeds are acquired with exaggeration (bināʾ al-mubālagha), since the one who earns them strains in the matter, breaking through the barrier of God's prohibition and going beyond it to them. So it is fitting in the verse that the two morphological patterns are used, to guard against this meaning. End of his words.

What results from the words of al-Zamakhsharī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya is that evil and bad deeds involve effort (iʿtimāl). But al-Zamakhsharī said that the cause of the effort is the soul's appetite and its being drawn to what it wants, while Ibn ʿAṭiyya said that its cause is that the person is one who strains, breaking through the barrier of God's prohibition, so he does not commit disobedience except with strain. Al-Sajāwandī took a course close to that of Ibn ʿAṭiyya, and said: al-iftiʿāl (the iftiʿāl form) means commitment (iltizām). Its evil falls upon him, while good is shared with others through guidance and intercession.

Al-iftiʿāl means contraction (inkimāsh), and the soul contracts in evil. End of his words. And ﴿lahā﴾ came with the preposition *lām* (for), because good is something that is rejoiced in and gladdens, so it is attributed to its possession. And ﴿ʿalayhā﴾ came with *ʿalā* (upon), because evil is burdens and loads, so it is as if it has risen above it and is beneath it, carrying it. This is like when you say: "I have wealth, and upon me is a debt."

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 2, verse 286 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Our Lord, do not impose blame on us if we forget or make mistakes.﴾ This is in the grammatical construction of an implied verb of speech (*idmar al-qawl*, the omission of a verb of saying), meaning: say in your supplication, "Our Lord, do not impose blame on us." Supplication is the marrow of worship (*mukhkh al-ʿibada*), for the one who supplicates sees himself in a state of need, humility and dependence, and sees his Lord with the eye of self-sufficiency and bounty. For this reason this passage ends with supplication and humble entreaty, and each sentence of it begins with their saying "Our Lord" (*Rabbana*), signifying that they are seeking from their Lord, who is their Cherisher (*murabbi*) and the Reformer of their affairs. And because they acknowledge that they are those who are cherished, who are under the bondage of servitude and dependence. The word "Our Lord" does not appear in the final imperative sentences, because they are the consequences of the preceding sentences in which they called upon "our Lord." Each of the three preceding sentences is matched by a sentence: "do not impose blame on us" is matched by "and pardon us" (*wa-ʿfu ʿanna*); "and do not place upon us a burden" (*wa-la tahmil ʿalayna isran*) is matched by "and forgive us" (*wa-ghfir lana*); and "and do not burden us with what we have no strength to bear" is matched by "and have mercy on us" (*wa-rhamna*). This is because among the effects of not being held to account for forgetfulness and error is pardon; among the effects of not having a burden placed upon them is forgiveness; and among the effects of not being charged with what cannot be borne is mercy.

The meaning of *al-muʾakhadha* (being held to account) is punishment (*al-ʿaqiba*). The form *faʿala* here is used in the sense of the simple verb, such as *akhadha*, as in His saying: ﴿So each We seized for his sin﴾ (Surah al-ʿAnkabut, 29:40). This is one of the meanings for which the form *faʿala* is used. It was also said that it came in the form of *mufaʿala*, while it is a single act, because the wrongdoer has enabled himself and paved the way to it by his deed, so that the one who punishes his wrongdoing becomes like one who assists him in harming himself. It was also said that God, exalted is He, seizes the sinner with punishment, and the sinner, as it were, seizes his Lord by demanding pardon and generosity, since he finds no one to deliver him from the punishment of God except Him, exalted is He. For this reason the servant, when he fears Him, holds fast to Him. Each of them is expressed by the word *al-muʾakhadha* (being held to account), and *al-nisyan* (forgetting), which is the absence of remembrance, and *al-khata'* (error), are both lifted from the one charged, who is not held to account for them. ʿAta' said: "*Nasina*" means "we were ignorant," and "*akhtana*" means "we intended deliberately." Qutrub and al-Tabari said: "*Nasina*" means "we abandoned," and "*akhtana*" — al-Tabari said: "we intended"; Qutrub said: "we erred in interpretation." Al-Asmaʿi said: it is said *akhta'a* meaning "he was inattentive," and *khati'a* meaning "he did deliberately." The poet said:

*The people blame the commander when they err in what is right, and the guide is not blamed.*

Among the exegetes there are those who took *al-nisyan* and *al-akhta'* here in their apparent sense, namely those for which the one charged is not held to account, and he is excused for them if they proceed from him. This is what al-Zamakhshari permitted at the end of his discussion of this verse, and Ibn ʿAtiyya preferred it. Al-Zamakhshari said: He mentioned forgetting and error, and what is meant by them is what they are forgetful of, namely negligence and oversight. Do you not see His saying: ﴿And none made me forget it except Satan﴾ (Surah al-Kahf, 18:63)? Satan has no power to cause forgetting; he only whispers, so his whisper becomes a cause of the negligence from which forgetting results. Moreover, they were those who feared God with the fear due to Him, so no lapse proceeded from them except in the manner of forgetfulness and error. Thus their description of supplicating with this was an announcement of their innocence from what they could be held to account for, as if it were said: if forgetting and error are things for which one is held to account, then there is no cause of being held to account in them except error and forgetting. It is also permissible that a person supplicates for something he knows is already granted to him by the grace of God, seeking its continuance and acknowledging the blessing in it. End of his words.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: Many scholars held that the supplication in this verse is only for the common forgetting and error from the intended goal, and this is the correct view.

Qatada said in explaining the verse: "It reached me that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'God has overlooked for my community their forgetting and their errors.'" Al-Suddi said: "When this verse was revealed, they were overwhelmed (by fear). Gabriel said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'God has done that, O Muhammad.'" The apparent meaning of their two statements, that is Qatada and al-Suddi, is what it confirms. That is because when the believers were relieved of what they feared in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿God will call you to account for it﴾ (Surah al-Baqara, 2:284), they were commanded to supplicate for averting that kind of thing which is not within human capacity to avert, namely forgetting and error. End of his words.

It was also said: forgetting in it, and some of it, is not excused. The first is like forgetting an impurity on a garment after knowing of it. Such is what is desired, that one not be held to account for it, and it is when one abandons caution and turns away from the causes of remembrance. It was also said: this is a supplication on the basis of supposition, as if they said: if forgetting is something for which one may be held to account, then do not hold us to account for it. It was also said: being held to account for it is not impossible by reason, because when a person knows that he will be held to account for it, he continues to remember, and then nothing proceeds from him except the continuous act of remembrance, which is an arduous act for the soul, so it is good to supplicate for not being held to account for it.

This verse has been cited as evidence for the permissibility of charging with what cannot be borne. It was also said: in the verse there is evidence for the granting of pardon to those who commit major sins, because it would be an ugly request, and an ugly supplication, to read forgetting and error as things for which one is not held to account. So it is necessary that it be read as referring to what involved intentional disobedience. Forgetting would then be the omission of an action, and error the commission of an action. God, exalted is He, has commanded the believers to seek that they not be held to account for these two. This is a command from Him to them to ask Him not to punish them for their sins, and this is evidence of His granting them this request.

﴿Our Lord, and do not place upon us a burden (*isran*) as You placed it upon those before us.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Suddi, Ibn Juraij, al-Rabiʿ and Ibn Zayd said: *al-isr* is the covenant and the strict pact. Ibn Zayd also said: *al-isr* is a sin for which there is no expiation and from which there is no repentance. Malik said: *al-isr* is a severe and difficult matter. ʿAta' said: *al-isr* is transformation into apes and swine. It was said: it is sin, related by Thaʿlab. It was said: it is an obligation whose performance is difficult. It was said: it is the hastening of punishment, narrated from Qatada. al-Zajjaj said: it is a trial that tests us, like killing and wounding among the Children of Israel, and the appointment for whoever disbelieves of a roof of silver. al-Zamakhshari said: *al-ʿibʾ* is the load that *ya'sir* its bearer, that is, it holds him in place so that he cannot rise under it. The word is borrowed for arduous obligation, such as killing oneself, cutting off the place of impurity from the skin and the garment, and other things. End of his words.

al-Qaffal said: whoever looks into the fifth book of the Torah, which these Jews claim, will find what strict covenants and pacts were taken from them, and will see many marvels.

Ubayy recited *wa-la tuhammil* with the intensive form, and *aṣaran* in the plural. It is narrated from ʿAsim that he recited *uṣran* with the *hamza* vowelled with a *damma*. The phrase *alladhina min qablina* (those before us) refers to the Jews, but al-Dahhak said: and the Christians.

﴿Our Lord, and do not burden us with what we have no strength to bear.﴾ Qatada said: do not make it severe upon us as You made it severe upon those before us. al-Dahhak said: do not burden us with deeds we cannot endure. Ibn Zayd said similarly. Ibn Juraij said: do not transform us into apes and swine. Makhul and Sallam ibn Sabur said: "what we have no strength to bear" is *al-ghulma* (sexual desire). This was related by al-Naqqash from Mujahid, ʿAta' and Makhul. It is narrated that Abu al-Darda' used to say in his supplication: "And I seek refuge with You from a *ghulma* for which there is no restraint." al-Nakhaʿi said: it is love. Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhab said: it is passionate love (*ʿishq*). It was also said: it is severance (of kinship). It was said: it is the gloating of enemies. Wahb narrated that Ayyub, upon our Prophet and upon him be peace, was asked: "What was hardest for you in your trial?" He said: "The gloating of enemies." The poet said:

*You made my enemies gloat over me when you forsook me, and death is preferable to the gloating of enemies.*

al-Suddi said: the severity and the shackles that were upon the Children of Israel because of the prohibitions. It was said: it is the punishment of the Fire. It was said: it is the whisperings of the soul. These interpretations ought to be understood as illustrative examples, not as restricting the general meaning to specific cases.

The word *ma* in His saying ﴿what we have no strength to bear﴾ is general, and this is more general than the preceding one in the verse. For in that one He said ﴿and do not place upon us a burden as You placed it upon those before us,﴾ so He compared the burden (*isr*) to the burden that He placed upon those before them. Here they asked that He not burden them with what they have no strength to bear. This is more general than the earlier burden, since that was restricted by the comparison, while this is general. The intensive form in *wa-la tuhammilna* (the doubled consonant) indicates transitivity, and in Ubayy's reading of His saying *wa-la tahmil ʿalayna isran* it indicates intensity in *hammala*, like *jaraḥtu Zaydan* and *jarraḥtuhu* (I wounded Zayd, I wounded him repeatedly). It was said: "what we have no strength to bear" refers to the punishments that descended upon those before us. They first asked that He relieve them of the arduous obligations with His saying ﴿and do not place upon us a burden﴾; then secondly they asked that He relieve them of what descended upon those others of punishments because of their negligence in preserving them. End of his words.

*Al-taqa* (strength) is the capacity to do something. It is a verbal noun that came in a form contrary to the regular patterns of verbal nouns. The regular form would be *taqa*, as in *jaba* from *ajaba*, and *gharah* from *aghara*, among words that were heard and cannot be used as a basis for analogy. So one does not say *aṭala ṭalah* (from *aṭala*). This phrase admits of two meanings. One is that by "what we have no strength to bear" they mean what they have no capacity for at all, and it is beyond their power; this is the meaning on which the disagreement falls. The second is that by *al-taqa* they mean what involves severe hardship, even if it is possible to bear it.

According to the first meaning it refers to punishments and the like. According to the second meaning it refers to obligations. Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning is: do not burden us with a burden whose performance is heavy upon us, even if we are able to bear it with exertion and endurance of what is disagreeable. He addressed the Arabs according to what is understood by them. A man among them says to a man he hates: "I cannot bear to look at him," while he is able to look at him, but it is burdensome to him. Similar to it is His saying ﴿They were not able to hear﴾ (Surah Hud, 11:20).

﴿And pardon us, and forgive us, and have mercy on us.﴾ The explanation of pardon (*al-ʿafw*), forgiveness (*al-ghufran*) and mercy (*al-rahma*) has already been given. They asked for pardon, which is the overlooking of a sin and the removal of punishment; then for His covering it over them, as a protection for them from the torment of shame, because pardoning something does not necessarily imply covering it. It is said: *ʿafa ʿanhu* when one has made him stand before the sin and then removed the punishment for that sin from him. They asked first for the removal of punishment, because it is the most important, since in it lies bodily torment and spiritual bliss through the manifestation of the Originator, exalted is He, to them. Al-Raghib said: pardon (*al-ʿafw*) is the removal of sin by abandoning its punishment; forgiveness (*al-ghufran*) is the covering of sin and the manifestation of goodness in its place, so that it combines the covering of the sin with the disclosure of the goodness with which it is covered; mercy (*al-rahma*) is the outpouring of goodness upon him. The second is more eloquent than the first, and the third more eloquent than the second. End of his words.

It was also said: "pardon us" from transformation (into animals); "forgive us" from being swallowed up by the earth; and from the slander. It was also said: "pardon us" for actions, "forgive us" for words, and "have mercy on us" by the heaviness of the scales. It was also said: "pardon us" in the agonies of death, "forgive us" in the darkness of the grave, and "have mercy on us" in the terrors of the Day of Resurrection. All of these sayings are specifications without any proof for them.

﴿You are our Protector (*mawlana*).﴾ *Al-mawla* is of the pattern *mafʿal*, from *waliya yali*. It may be used as a verbal noun, a noun of time, or a noun of place. As for when it is intended to mean the possessor of the management and disposal of the aspects of harm and benefit, or the master, or the helper, or the paternal cousin, or other of its meanings, then its origin is the verbal noun. It was named by it, and the nominal character came to prevail over it, and governing particles (*al-ʿawamil*) act upon it.

﴿So help us against the disbelieving people.﴾ He introduced the *fa'* (so) to indicate causation, because His being their Protector, and the possessor of the management and direction of their affairs, results in His support for them against their enemies. As you say: "You are the brave one, so fight," and "You are the generous one, so be generous to me." That is: make us victorious over them by what You produce in our hearts of boldness and strength, and in their hearts of weakness and cowardice.

And this verse contains, among the kinds of eloquence and forms of rhetorical excellence, several features. Among them: the antithesis (tibaq) in ﴿Whether you show what is in your selves or conceal it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 284], and the semantic antithesis (tibaq ma'nawi) in ﴿For it is what it has earned, and against it is what it has earned﴾, because (laha, "for it") indicates that by which benefit is obtained, and (alayha, "against it") indicates that by which harm is obtained. Also the repetition in His saying "and whatever is on the earth," where (ma) is repeated for emphasis and attention (tanbih wa tawkid); in His saying ﴿between any of His messengers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 285]; and in His saying "what it has earned" and "what it has acquired," if we say that both have one meaning, since it means ﴿for it is what it has earned﴾. Also the distinct paronomasia (tajnis mughayir) in "amana" (believed) and "al-mu'minun" (the believers), and ellipsis (hadhf) in several places. And Allah knows best.
